To ~adōrāre~ was thus literally “to speak toward,” to direct ritual words at a god. ~Ōrāre~ is traditionally tied to ~ōs~, ~ōris~ (“mouth”), from a Proto-Indo-European root for the mouth, the speaking aperture. Cognate, through ~ōrāre~, with English ~oration~ and ~orator~.

The original gesture was sacred and verbal: one ~adored~ a deity by uttering a formula toward it, the spoken prayer at the core of the act. Roman worship even kept a bodily echo — bringing the hand to the mouth in reverence. The religious sense survives intact (one ~adore~ God), but French wore the word down to everyday hyperbole, so that one may now ~adorer~ chocolate or a film with no thought of altars. From the same ~ōrāre~ French inherits ~oraison~, ~orateur~, ~oral~, and ~adoration~, while the ~ad-~ of approach recurs across countless verbs of turning-toward.
en.adosser: Formed in French from ~a-~, ~dos~ and the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense “to set the back against.” The prefix ~a-~ comes from Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”) and here marks placing something onto a surface, so ~adosser~ is to put a back to a wall, and ~s'adosser~ is to lean one's back against something. The base ~dos~ comes from Old French, from Latin ~dorsum~ through a popular form ~dossum~; Italian ~dosso~ preserves the same Vulgar Latin shape. A building is likewise said to be ~adossé~ to a hillside or to a neighboring wall.
en.adouber:
From Old French ~adouber~ (earlier ~adober~, ~aduber~), itself from ~douber~ (“to strike”, “to dub”), and ultimately from Old Frankish *~dubban~ (“to strike”). The Old French verb was a prefixed form with ~a-~. French Wiktionary gives that Frankish source, and English Wiktionary connects the verb to the same Germanic root as English ~dub~. So ~adouber~ and ~dub~ are distant cousins: both reach back to a Germanic word for striking, and both come to mean conferring knighthood.

~Adouber~ is the ceremonial verb of medieval chivalry: to ~adouber~ a squire was to make him a knight, traditionally by a blow with the flat of a sword or a hand on the shoulder or neck, and by presenting him with his arms. Modern French uses the verb mostly in historical contexts, but it has acquired a figurative sense: to ~adouber~ someone is to endorse them, to give them one's blessing, as a leader does with a chosen successor or a party with a candidate. English ~dub~ shares the same Germanic root and kept the knightly meaning.
en.adoucir: Inherited from Old French ~adoucir~ (also ~adolcir~), which was built from ~dolz~ and ~douz~ (“sweet”), from Latin ~dulcis~ (“sweet”). By surface analysis, the verb is the prefix ~a-~ (“toward”), the adjective ~doux~ and the second-conjugation ending ~-ir~, with the sense “to make sweet, to make gentler.” It is used both literally (to sweeten a drink) and figuratively (to soften a manner, a climate or a pain). Compare ~adoucir~ with ~attendrir~ and ~assouplir~, which are built the same way.
en.adresser:
From Old French ~adrecier~ (twelfth century), composed of the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, toward”) and ~dresser~ (“to straighten, to set up, to direct”). ~dresser~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~directiare~ (“to make straight”), built on Latin ~directus~ (“straight, direct”), the past participle of ~dirigere~ (~dis-~ + ~regere~, “to guide straight”). ~regere~ rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~reg-~ (“to move in a straight line, to direct”). Through this root ~adresser~ is cognate with English ~address~, ~direct~, and ~dress~, all sharing the Vulgar Latin *~directiare~.

In Old French through the seventeenth century, ~adresser~ meant “to straighten, to set upright, to direct.” The modern senses unfold naturally from that core: to direct a letter toward someone is to ~adresser~ it; to direct words at a person is to ~adresser la parole~ to them. The English noun ~address~ — first the act of directing, later the destination written on an envelope — followed the same path. From the root *~reg-~ French drew a broad family: ~droit~ (“straight, right,” from ~directus~), ~diriger~ (“to direct”), ~dresser~ itself, ~redresser~ (“to set straight again”), and ~adresse~ in both its senses, the postal address and the “skill” of one who does things rightly.
en.adsorber:
~Adsorber~ is derived from Latin ~sorbēre~ (“to swallow, to gulp down”). The spelling shows the Latin prefix ~ad-~ (“toward, onto”) kept intact, so the verb reads as a learned, scientific formation on a Latin verb, not as a word inherited from Latin. The same Latin verb underlies ~absorber~, and the two French verbs are deliberately set against each other.

The prefix sets ~adsorber~ against ~absorber~, built on the same Latin verb with ~ab-~ (“away from”). In the language of physics and chemistry, a substance that is absorbed is taken into the bulk of another, while one that is adsorbed stays clinging to its surface. ~Résorber~ (~re-~ + ~sorbēre~) belongs to the same family, as do the English twins ~absorb~ and ~adsorb~, which are paired in the same way.
en.aduler: A learned borrowing from Latin ~adulārī~ (“to fawn on, to flatter”). The French verb ~aduler~ keeps the Latin idea of flattery and now means to praise someone to excess. The same Latin verb underlies the French nouns ~adulation~ and ~adulateur~ and English ~adulate~. Neither Wiktionary gives an intermediate stage or a further breakdown of the Latin word, so the verb's history is a direct one: it was taken over from Latin as it stood.
en.adultérer:
French ~adultérer~ is derived from Latin ~adulterare~ (“to commit adultery”). The same Latin verb gave English ~adulterate~ and Spanish ~adulterar~, and the French noun ~adultère~ belongs to the same family. For several centuries the verb kept its Latin meaning: from the fourteenth to the seventeenth century, its dominant sense was “to commit adultery.”

The modern sense of falsifying came later. Littré explains that the verb was then used in the sense of the neighboring Latin word ~adulteratio~, which concerned debasing a coin, the ~adulterator~ being the counterfeiter. By extension, the verb came to cover the falsification of many other things, medicines among them. The old meaning thus faded, and ~adultérer~ now belongs to the vocabulary of fraud and tampering rather than of marriage, while the idea of infidelity lives on in the noun ~adultère~.
en.advenir:
Modern French ~advenir~ goes back to Latin ~advenīre~ (“to arrive, to come to”), formed from ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~venīre~ (“to come”). Its exact route is not entirely settled. French Wiktionary describes it as a reworking of Old French ~avenir~, while English Wiktionary says it is inherited from Middle French ~advenir~ and may be a re-Latinization of that Old French form, with the ~d~ restored from the Latin spelling. English Wiktionary also links it to the archaic ~aveindre~ (“to take something from where it lies”), a doublet which it derives from a Vulgar Latin *~advenĭre~ or explains as influenced by ~atteindre~. Either way, the verb continues the Latin ~advenīre~ rather than being built in French from a prefix and a base.

Two outcomes of the same Latin verb therefore sit side by side in French. The Old French form ~avenir~ survives as a noun meaning “future”, while the learned spelling ~advenir~ remained as a verb meaning “to happen, to occur”. The restored ~d~ is the visible trace of the Latin spelling ~advenīre~. The sources do not agree on whether the verb is a reworking of the Old French form or an inheritance through Middle French, and the paragraph above therefore leaves that question open. What the two Wiktionaries share is the Latin starting point, ~advenīre~, and the fact that the learned spelling with ~d~ is a later feature rather than the original Old French shape. English Wiktionary adds the doublet ~aveindre~, a reminder that the older family of this verb had more than one outcome.
en.affabuler: A neologism formed from ~affabulation~; English Wiktionary instead parses it as ~a-~ plus ~fabuler~. French Wiktionary adds that the second sense, to make up stories, may have been influenced by ~fabuler~, which means to bend reality to one's own taste. The base ~fabuler~ is borrowed from Latin ~fābulārī~ (“to talk, to chat”), built on ~fābula~ (“talk, story”), from ~fārī~ (“to speak”). The verb thus draws on the Latin family of speech and story that also gave ~fable~ and ~fabuleux~.
en.affadir: ~Affadir~ is derived from the adjective ~fade~ (“bland, tasteless”) and is attested from 1226, so it is one of the older verbs of its kind. It forms a verb meaning “to make A”, here to make something tasteless, insipid or bland. The verb ending ~-ir~ is the one French uses for adjectives of this sort, as in ~grandir~ and ~grossir~, and it often goes with a prefix, as here.
en.affaiblir:
Recorded from the early twelfth century, ~affaiblir~ is built on ~faiblir~ (“to grow weak”) with the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, toward”), giving a causative sense: to render weak. The heart of the word is the adjective ~faible~ (“weak”), Old French ~foible~ / ~feble~, which descends — surprisingly — from Latin ~flēbilis~ (“lamentable, worthy of being wept over”), itself from ~flēre~ (“to weep”). The same ~flēbilis~ gives English the learned ~feeble~, borrowed through Old French.

The semantic journey is striking and well attested: a thing ~flēbilis~ was something to cry about, pitiable; from “pitiable” the sense drifted to “lacking strength, frail,” and the original tears dropped away entirely. So a French speaker who calls a signal, an argument, or an old man ~faible~ is using, at the root, a word that once meant “tear-jerking” — weakness named for the weeping it provokes. To ~affaiblir~ is then to push something toward that pitiable state. The family includes ~faible~, ~faiblir~, ~faiblesse~ (“weakness”), and ~affaiblissement~ (“weakening, decline”) — all carrying, far below the surface, the memory of ~flēre~, “to weep.”
en.affairer: The sources are tentative. French Wiktionary only refers the reader to the pronominal verb ~s'affairer~. English Wiktionary offers two possibilities: that it comes from the noun ~affaire~ (“matter, business”), or that it is a back-formation from the adjective ~affairé~ (“busy”). The noun ~affaire~ is generally explained as the phrase ~à faire~ (“to do”), so the whole family is about having something to do.
en.affaisser: ~Affaisser~ is built from ~faix~ (“load, burden”) with the prefix ~a-~ and the verb ending ~-er~. English Wiktionary explains the sense: under the weight of a load, something may bend and collapse. The noun ~faix~ is inherited from Old French ~fais~, from Latin ~fascis~ (“bundle, burden”). So the verb means to cause something to sink or give way, as if under a heavy load.
en.affaler: Borrowed from Dutch. English Wiktionary offers two possible sources and does not choose between them: ~afhalen~ (“to pick up”) or ~afvallen~ (“to fall off”). Either way, the verb reached French as a loan rather than as a formation from French parts, and its senses in modern French are “to lower, to let down” and, reflexively, “to slump down”.
en.affamer: The two sources analyze ~affamer~ differently. French Wiktionary posits a Latin verb *~affamāre~, reconstructed from Italian ~affamare~ and Occitan ~afamar~. English Wiktionary parses it as ~a-~ + ~faim~ + ~-er~, noting that ~faim~ itself reverts to the Latin noun ~fames~ (“hunger”). Either way the root is ~fames~, and the verb means to starve someone or make them hungry. ~Famine~ and ~famélique~ come from the same Latin noun.
en.affecter:
From Latin ~affectare~ (“to strive after, to aim at, to pursue eagerly”), a frequentative of ~afficere~ (“to act upon, to influence, to affect”), itself from the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward,” assimilated to ~af-~) and ~facere~ (“to do, to make”). ~Facere~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to set, to put, to make”). Cognate, through ~facere~, with Italian ~affettare~ and Spanish ~afectar~, and — through the root *~dʰeh₁-~ — with English ~do~ and ~deed~ and with Greek ~títhēmi~ (“I place”).

The Latin frequentative ~affectare~ meant “to keep doing toward,” hence “to strive after” and, with a darkening twist, “to pursue with a show one does not feel.” That second branch gave French ~affecter~ its sense “to feign,” as in affecting a calm one lacks. The other branch, from ~afficere~, gave “to affect, to move” and “to assign, to allocate.” The root *~dʰeh₁-~ is colossal: through ~facere~ it underlies ~faire~, ~défaire~, ~affaire~, ~facile~, ~fait~, and the suffix ~-fier~; through related forms it yields English ~fact~, ~factory~, and ~fashion~. To affecter a feeling is, at bottom, to ~make~ a face that does the feeling for you.
en.affectionner: ~Affectionner~ is formed from the noun ~affection~ and the verb-forming ending ~-er~, giving the sense of feeling affection for someone or something. The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin ~affectiō~ (“action of affecting”), which belongs to the Latin verb ~afficere~ (“to affect, to influence”). The ending ~-er~ goes back to Latin ~-are~, the infinitive ending of first-conjugation verbs, and it is the usual way French turns a noun into a verb.
en.affermer: ~Affermer~ is formed from the prefix ~a-~, the noun ~ferme~ and the verb ending ~-er~. It means to lease out or to take on lease, because ~ferme~ here has its old sense of a fixed lease or rent, from which the modern sense of “farm” grew. French Wiktionary also presents this ~ferme~ as a back-formation from ~fermer~ in its old sense “to fix firmly.” Behind it stands Medieval Latin ~firma~ (“lease”), whose own source is debated: it is traced either to Latin ~firmus~ (“solid”), the lease being a firmly settled agreement, or to Old English ~feorm~ (“rent, provision”).
en.affermir: Formed from ~à~ (from Old French ~a~, a merger of Latin ~ad~ and ~ab~), the adjective ~ferme~ (“firm”) and the verb ending ~-ir~, which here means making something become what the adjective says. So ~affermir~ is “to make firm”. The adjective ~ferme~ comes from Latin ~firmus~. The verb has a prefixed sibling in ~raffermir~, which adds ~r-~ for a stronger or renewed effect.
en.afficher:
From Old French ~aficher~, from Vulgar Latin *~affigicare~, a frequentative reshaping of Latin ~affigere~ (“to fasten to, to fix upon”), itself ~ad-~ (“to, onto”) plus ~figere~ (“to fix, to drive in, to plant”). ~figere~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeygʷ-~ (“to stick, to set up”). Cognate with Italian ~affiggere~ and Spanish ~afijar~, and — through ~figere~ — with English ~affix~ and ~fix~.

The sense is concrete and physical: to ~afficher~ was first to pin or nail something up against a wall, and only by extension to post a notice, then to display or flaunt anything at all — one can now ~afficher~ a price, an opinion, or a smug confidence. The doublet ~ficher~ shares the same source and the same idea of driving in (a stake, a card into a file), giving the noun ~fiche~, a slip or filing card, and the curt ~fichu~. From ~affigere~ directly come the nouns ~affiche~ (a poster) and ~affichage~ (posting or, today, a screen display). The PIE root *~dʰeygʷ-~, “to stick,” also surfaces far afield in the Germanic words for an earthwork — English ~dike~ and ~ditch~ — a heap of fixed, planted earth.
en.affiler: ~Affiler~ is explained in two ways. French Wiktionary derives it from ~filer~ with the prefix ~a-~, while English Wiktionary gives either ~fil~ (“thread, edge”) or a Vulgar Latin *~affilāre~, from Latin ~fīlum~ (“thread”). The sense is to sharpen a blade, to give it a fine edge. Italian ~affilare~, Spanish ~afilar~ and Portuguese ~afiar~ are cognates. The Latin ~fīlum~ also gave French ~fil~, and goes back to a Proto-Indo-European root *~gʷʰislo-~ (“sinew, thread”).
en.affilier: Borrowed from Latin ~affiliāre~ (also written ~adfiliāre~), “to adopt as a son,” formed from ~ad~ (“to”) and ~filius~ (“son”). The verb began as the act of taking a stranger into a family. French kept that image and moved it to institutions: to affiliate someone is to attach them to a society, a party or an organization as though they belonged to its household. The same Latin ~filius~ gave French ~fils~, its feminine ~filia~ gave ~fille~, and English ~affiliate~ is the sibling of the French verb.
en.affiner: Formed in French from ~a-~ + ~fin~ + ~-er~, a verb built in one step by adding a prefix and an ending at once, meaning “to make fine or pure.” The doubled f in the spelling is a trace of Latin ~ad-~, whose d assimilated to the next consonant. The adjective ~fin~ is traced to Latin ~fīnis~ (“boundary, limit, end”): from the idea of the utmost point it came to mean “perfect, pure, delicate,” a sense attested in Old French around 1100. The verb ~finir~ comes from the same Latin noun.
en.affirmer:
From Latin ~affirmare~ (“to make firm, to assert”), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~firmare~ (“to strengthen, to make firm”), itself from ~firmus~ (“strong, steadfast, stable”). ~firmus~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~fermos~ and ultimately to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰer-~ (“to hold, to support”). Through that root it is cognate with Sanskrit ~dhárati~ (“he holds”) and, through ~firmus~ directly, with English ~firm~ and ~farm~ and with Italian ~fermare~ and Spanish ~afirmar~.

The metaphor inside the word is concrete: to ~affirmer~ something is to make it ~firm~, to stand it up so it will not topple. Latin ~affirmare~ already carried this sense in legal and philosophical contexts — to assert as solid truth — and the verb entered French in the thirteenth century with that meaning intact. From the same root *~dʰer-~ and its Latin offshoot ~firmus~ French inherited a large family: ~ferme~ (“firm”), ~fermer~ (“to close,” by way of making fast), ~affermir~ (“to strengthen”), ~firmament~ (the “fixed” vault of heaven), and the noun ~affirmation~. The doublet ~fermer~ and ~affirmer~ is striking — one shut a door, the other shored up a claim, yet both rest on the idea of making something hold fast.
en.affleurer:
The verb goes back to Middle French ~affleurer~, built on ~fleur~ in an older sense of “surface,” with the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, toward”) and the verb ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary parses it as ~ad-~ plus ~fleur~, in the sense “ground, surface”; English Wiktionary gives the same Middle French source. The ordinary noun ~fleur~ (“flower”) comes through Old French ~flor~ from Latin ~flōrem~ (“flower; the finest part of something”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰleh₃-~ (“to bloom”).

English Wiktionary adds a twist: in some of its senses the Middle French word ~fleur~ is ultimately Germanic, from Proto-Germanic *~flōraz~, the ancestor of English ~floor~. By that account, the “surface” ~fleur~ and the “flower” ~fleur~ are two words with different histories that happen to look alike. The older sense survives in the phrase ~à fleur de~ (“level with, at the surface of”), as in ~à fleur de peau~ (“highly sensitive”). The verb covers “to surface” and “to be level with,” and the related noun ~affleurement~ names rock or ground showing at the surface. From the flower strand, which comes from Latin ~flōs~, French has ~fleurir~, ~floral~ and ~floraison~.
en.affliger:
French ~affliger~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~afflīgere~. The Latin verb is a compound of ~ad-~ (“toward, against”) and ~fligere~ (“to strike”), so it meant “to strike down, to dash against,” a physical blow. French reserves it for distress of the mind or the heart. Related forms in the other Romance languages include Italian ~affliggere~ and Spanish ~afligir~.

The Latin past participle ~afflictus~ lies behind French ~affliction~ and English ~afflict~, which reached English from the same source. The second half of the Latin compound, ~fligere~, turns up in other learned verbs that share the “strike” image, such as ~infliger~ (“to inflict”), from ~īnflīgere~, and the noun ~conflit~, from ~cōnflīgere~ (“to strike together”). In each of these, the Latin blow has become a moral or social one. The modern verb is rather formal and literary, and it is often met in the passive, as in ~être affligé de~ (“to be afflicted with”).
en.afflouer: Formed from the preposition ~à~ and the noun ~flot~ (“wave, flood”), the verb means to bring a stranded or sunken vessel back onto the water. The ~à~ gives the sense of movement toward, and the whole expresses putting a ship back afloat, which also yields the wider sense of raising or refloating something.
en.affluer:
~Affluer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~affluere~ (“to flow toward, to flow in”). The Latin verb is analyzed as ~ad-~ (“toward,” assimilated to ~af-~ before f) + ~fluere~ (“to flow”). Its basic sense is thus physical: a liquid moving toward a point. Italian ~affluire~, Spanish ~afluir~ and English ~affluent~ and ~fluent~ show the same Latin stock.

The literal sense of flowing toward something is still alive in French, but the verb is used just as often of things that behave like a liquid: blood rushing to the face, or crowds and money pouring into a place. The noun ~affluent~ names a river that flows into a larger one, and ~affluence~ names a crowd that gathers. The root ~fluere~ also underlies ~fluide~, ~flux~, ~influence~ and ~confluent~.
en.affoler: Formed from the old adjective ~fol~ (“mad”), the earlier form of modern ~fou~, with the prefix ~a-~ and the verb ending ~-er~. No verb *~foler~ stands behind it, so prefix and suffix came on together, and the ~f~ was doubled in spelling, a trace of the Latin ~ad-~ behind ~a-~. ~Affoler~ means to make someone mad, and so to throw them into a panic. Today the past participle ~affolé~ (“panicked”) is much more common than the infinitive.
en.affouiller: Derived from ~fouiller~, the verb for digging and rummaging, with the prefix ~a-~ added to give it the sense of digging at something. French Wiktionary says only that it is derived from ~fouiller~. The prefix ~a-~ comes from Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”). The verb means “to dig” in a general way, and a hydraulic sense, which is the undermining of a bank or a foundation by flowing water, is its best-known technical use.
en.affourager: ~Affourager~ is derived from the noun ~fourrage~ (“fodder”), with the verbal ending ~-er~. ~Fourrage~ is built on Old French ~feurre~ with the suffix ~-age~ and is attested in Middle French as ~fourage~. French Wiktionary also lists a rival link to ~fourrer~. The verb means to feed livestock with fodder, so it is a plain denominal verb whose sense stays close to its base.
en.affourcher: Formed from ~fourcher~ with the prefix ~a-~, from Latin ~ad-~ (“to, toward”). The base ~fourcher~ comes from the noun ~fourche~ (“fork”), inherited from Old French ~furche~ and ~forche~, from Latin ~furca~ (“pitchfork”): to ~fourcher~ is to divide in branches like a fork. The verb ~affourcher~ means “to anchor” and “to straddle”, both senses of something forked.
en.affourrager: Formed from the noun ~fourrage~ (“fodder”) with the verb ending ~-er~ and a prefix ~a-~, assimilated to ~af-~ before the ~f~, so “to feed fodder to livestock.” The noun comes from Old French ~fourage~, built on ~feurre~ (“straw, fodder”) with the suffix ~-age~. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is French’s default way of making a verb from a noun.
en.affranchir: Formed in Old French on the model of ~franchir~: the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~) added to ~franc~ (“free”) and the ending ~-ir~. The adjective ~franc~ comes from Late Latin ~Francus~ (“a Frank”), the Germanic people's name having come to mean “free”, and is cognate with English ~frank~. Where ~franchir~ drifted toward “to clear an obstacle”, ~affranchir~ kept the literal sense of “to set free”: a master ~affranchit~ a slave, and a state ~affranchit~ a colony. Its other familiar sense, to pay the postage on a letter, treats the stamp as a release from the charge.
en.affriander: ~Affriander~ is formed from ~friand~ with the ending ~-er~, and means to tempt or to make delicious. The adjective ~friand~ is an old present participle of ~frire~ (“to fry”) turned into an adjective, and it first meant “that sizzles, quivers with impatience.” The sense of a ~friand~ person, fond of dainty food, grew out of that early use, and ~affriander~ makes someone, or something, ~friand~ in that sense.
en.affrioler: The verb ~affrioler~ (“to tempt, to entice”) is derived from ~frioler~, with the prefix ~a-~ marking movement toward. The sources give nothing further on ~frioler~, so the older history of the word cannot be traced here. What is clear is the relation: ~affrioler~ is a French formation on a base that is itself rare, and in use it means to attract someone with the prospect of a pleasure or a gain.
en.affronter:
From Old French ~afronter~ (“to strike on the forehead, to face, to defy”), formed with the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, against”) on ~front~, from Latin ~frōns~, accusative ~frontem~ (“forehead, brow, front”). The underlying notion is ~ad frontem~, “to the forehead, face to face.” Cognate, through the same Latin noun, with Italian ~affrontare~, Spanish ~afrontar~, and English ~affront~ and ~front~.

The original sense was startlingly physical: to ~afronter~ someone was to strike them on the brow — to slap the face, the seat of one's dignity. From that blow grew two branches. One led to the noun ~affront~, an insult delivered “to the face,” preserving the sense of injured honor. The other softened the violence into mere confrontation: ~affronter~ now means to face, to brave, to stand up to a danger or an opponent. The forehead, in Latin thought, was where feelings showed and pride resided, which is why an attack ~ad frontem~ struck at honor itself. The same ~frōns~ gave French ~front~ (“forehead, front,” military and meteorological alike), ~frontière~ (“border,” the “front” edge of a land), ~affronter~, ~confronter~ (“to confront,” literally to set brow against brow), and ~effronté~ (“brazen,” one who has rubbed the shame off their forehead).
en.affréter: Formed in French from ~fréter~ with the prefix ~a-~. The base ~fréter~ comes from Old French ~freter~, itself built on the noun ~fret~ (“freight, the hire of a ship”). The prefix ~a-~ descends from Latin ~ad-~ (“to, toward”), and here it adds a sense of directing the action toward something. The result, ~affréter~, means “to charter,” that is, to hire a ship or aircraft for transport. The doubled ~f~ is the usual trace of Latin ~ad-~ assimilating to the consonant that follows it.
en.affubler:
The two Wiktionaries give different routes for ~affubler~, so the origin is best stated with both. French Wiktionary derives it from Old French ~afubler~, itself formed from ~fubler~ with the prefix ~a-~. English Wiktionary instead traces it to a Vulgar Latin form *~affībulāre~, built on Latin ~fībula~ (“clasp, brooch”). The sources checked here do not reconcile the two routes.

The Latin ~fībula~ was a pin or clasp for fastening a garment, and it survives in English as ~fibula~, an anatomical term for a bone. If the English Wiktionary route is right, the French verb began in the world of dress and fastening. Modern ~affubler~ means to dress someone, or oneself, in a ridiculous, ill-fitting or showy way, usually in the passive or the pronominal form (~être affublé de~, ~s'affubler de~). It is also used figuratively, of a nickname or a title pinned on a person.
en.affûter: ~Affûter~ comes from Old French ~afuster~, and it is analyzed as the prefix ~a-~ plus the noun ~fût~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~fût~ reaches French through Middle and Old French ~fust~ from Latin ~fūstis~ (“stick, club”). The sources give the formation but do not explain how a word built on a stick came to mean sharpening a blade, so that link is best left as an open question.
en.africaniser: Formed from ~africain~ with the suffix ~-iser~, in its sense “to make A”: ~africaniser~ is to give something an African character. The adjective comes from Latin ~Africanus~, derived from ~Africa~, itself from ~Afer~ (“African”). In Roman usage the name applied essentially to North Africa.
en.agacer:
The favored account, found in both Wiktionaries, runs from Old French ~aacier~ back to a Vulgar Latin verb *~adacidāre~, formed on Latin ~acidāre~ (“to make sour”), from ~acidus~ (“sour, sharp”). The image is of sourness setting one on edge. Latin ~acidus~ belongs to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂ek-~ (“sharp”), which also yielded Latin ~acer~ and ~acūtus~. The form ~agacer~ arose through a dissimilation of the two ~d~ sounds, and the Old French adjective ~agu~ (“sharp”, modern ~aigu~) is thought to have influenced its meaning. English ~acid~ and ~acute~ are cousins of the same stock.

The origin is not settled, however. The nineteenth-century scholar Diez linked ~agacer~ to Old High German ~hazjan~ (“to chase, to harass”), whence German ~hetzen~, with a Romance ~a-~ that would have turned the initial ~h~ into a ~g~. French Wiktionary mentions this alternative without adopting it. It also separates out a different Old French ~agacier~ (“to cry like a magpie”), which belongs to ~agace~ (“magpie”) and is unrelated. The meaning moved from physical sharpness toward irritation: to ~agacer~ is to annoy, to needle, or, in a lighter register, to tease. The Latin family also gave ~acide~, ~aigre~ and ~aigu~.
en.agencer: From Old French ~agencier~, built on the adjective ~gent~, ~gente~ (“noble, fair, graceful”), which is generally traced to Latin ~genitus~ (“born”), in the sense of well-born. The root idea is making something fair and elegant, and from there the verb settled on its modern sense of arranging parts into a harmonious whole. It has nothing to do with ~agence~ (“agency”), a different word that French borrowed from Italian.
en.agenouiller: ~Agenouiller~ is inherited from Old French ~agenoillier~, formed from ~genoil~ (“knee”); French Wiktionary describes it as derived from ~genoillier~ with the prefix ~a-~. Reflexively, ~s'agenouiller~ means “to kneel down.” Relatives in other Romance languages include Catalan ~agenollar~, Portuguese ~ajoelhar~, Italian ~inginocchiare~ and Romanian ~îngenunchea~.
en.agglomérer: Borrowed from Latin ~agglomerāre~. The Latin verb is generally analyzed as ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~glomerāre~ (“to gather into a ball”), from ~glomus~ (“ball, mass”). To ~agglomérer~ is to pile or press things together into a mass. English ~agglomerate~ and the French noun ~agglomération~ (“built-up urban area”) are relatives.
en.agglutiner:
Borrowed from Latin ~agglūtināre~ (“to glue, to paste or cement to something”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~glūtināre~ (“to glue”). The Latin verb itself comes from the noun ~glūten~ (“glue”). The prefix ~ad-~ assimilated to ~ag-~ before the ~g~, which is why the word has a double ~g~. Italian ~agglutinare~ and English ~agglutinate~ are close counterparts.

The noun ~glūten~ is also behind English ~gluten~. In French, ~agglutiner~ means to stick things together into a mass, and it has a technical life in biology, where cells or particles clump, and in linguistics, where an ~agglutinante~ language strings its endings together like beads. The family includes ~agglutination~, ~agglutinant~ and ~glutineux~.
en.aggraver:
French ~aggraver~ continues Latin ~aggravāre~ (“to make heavier”), from ~ad-~ plus ~gravāre~ (“to weigh down”), built on ~gravis~ (“heavy”). The adjective is ancient: it reaches back to Proto-Indo-European *~gʷréh₂us~ (“heavy”), whose offspring make a striking set — Sanskrit ~gurú~ (“heavy,” hence “weighty with authority”: the source of the modern word guru), Ancient Greek ~barús~ (“heavy,” hiding in ~baromètre~ and ~baryton~, the “deep-weighted” voice), and Gothic ~kaurus~. English ~aggravate~ is the same Latin verb in learned dress. The French word is old as well: a form ~agravet~ already appears in the eleventh-century Vie de saint Alexis, of a man borne down by illness.

Medieval French actually preferred ~agrever~, an altered form showing Vulgar Latin *~grevis~, whose vowel is usually explained by the pull of its opposite ~levis~ (“light”) — heavy and light leaning on each other; only in the fourteenth century was the verb straightened back toward Latin as ~aggraver~. The older line never died: it survives in ~grever~ (“to burden,” as taxes do), in the noun ~grief~, and in ~grièvement~, the adverb French still requires for serious wounds — ~grièvement blessé~ — while ~gravement~ serves everywhere else: two adverbs, one root, parted by a medieval vowel. Beside them stand ~grave~ and ~gravité~, where physics meets seriousness. The semantic core never moved: to aggravate a penalty, a wound or a quarrel is to add weight to it — a circonstance aggravante is, literally, a circumstance thrown onto the scale.
en.agioter: ~Agioter~ is derived from the noun ~agio~ with a verbal ending, which French Wiktionary writes ~-ter~ and English Wiktionary ~-er~. The noun ~agio~ was borrowed from Italian ~aggio~. In finance an ~agio~ is a premium, or the difference between exchange rates, and ~agioter~ came to mean “to speculate on the market,” profiting from such price differences. The verb often carries a pejorative note, since ~agiotage~ implies speculation of dubious honesty.
en.agir:
French ~agir~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~agere~ (“to drive, to set in motion, to do, to act”), adopted directly into the language in the fifteenth century rather than inherited through the slow erosion of Vulgar Latin. The Latin verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive, to lead”). Its cognates are spectacularly far-flung: Greek ~ágein~ (“to lead, to drive”), Sanskrit ~ájati~ (“he drives”), and, through the same root, English ~act~ and ~agent~. Because it entered French as a bookish import, ~agir~ kept the clean, unworn shape of its Latin model, unlike the battered everyday verbs that descend by oral tradition.

The Latin sense was concrete and forceful — to drive cattle, to push something forward — and from that physical pushing came the abstract idea of doing and behaving. French ~agir~ carries both the general sense (“to act”) and, reflexively in ~il s'agit de~, the impersonal “it is a question of.” The same root *~h₂eǵ-~ seeds a huge family in French: ~agile~ (“nimble,” literally easily driven), ~agent~, ~action~, ~agiter~, ~ambigu~ (from “driving both ways”), and even ~examen~, originally the tongue of a balance that drives toward the true weight. A single image of setting things in motion thus underlies words for nimbleness, lawsuits, anxiety, and judgment alike.
en.agiter:
~Agiter~ was borrowed in the thirteenth century from Latin ~agitāre~, “to set in vigorous motion, to drive about,” the frequentative of ~agere~, “to drive (a herd), to do”: where ~agere~ drives once, ~agitāre~ drives again and again — harried cattle, tossed seas, hounded men. ~Agere~ rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂eǵ-~, “to drive,” with cognates in Greek ~ágō~ (“I lead”) and Sanskrit ~ájati~ (“drives”). Italian ~agitare~, Spanish ~agitar~ and English ~agitate~ are all takings from the same Latin verb. French has scarcely moved the meaning: ~Agiter avant emploi~, says the medicine bottle — shake before use — and the harried herd is still faintly there.

Latin already used ~agitāre~ for minds and assemblies as well as herds — to turn a matter over, to debate it — and French inherited the full span: attested from the thirteenth century in the sense “to shake about,” the verb served, by the late sixteenth century, to ~agiter une question~ — to toss a question about — troubled minds from 1580 on, then turned political under the Revolution, breeding the ~agitateur~. The family of ~agere~ is among the largest in French — ~agir~, ~acte~, ~action~, ~agent~, ~agile~, ~agenda~ (“things to be done”) — but its best secret is ~cogiter~: Latin ~cōgitāre~, “to think,” is ~con-~ + ~agitāre~, to shake together. When Descartes wrote cogito, he was — etymologically — declaring his mind a shaken bottle; every deep thought is, by this old verb’s lights, an inner agitation.
en.agneler:
From Middle French ~agneler~, from Old French ~aigneler~ or ~agneler~, a verb formed on ~agnel~ with the ending ~-er~. ~Agnel~ was the old oblique-case form of ~agneau~ (“lamb”), and it comes from Latin ~agnellus~, a diminutive of ~agnus~ (“lamb”). The Latin diminutive lives on across the Romance languages, for example in Italian ~agnello~. In French the ending ~-el~ was later reshaped into ~-eau~, which is why the noun is ~agneau~ today while the verb kept the older stem.

To ~agneler~ is to give birth to lambs, said of a ewe, and the verb is known mostly to farmers and dictionary readers. The noun ~agneau~ (“lamb”) is the best-known descendant of the Latin word, and ~agnelet~ (“little lamb”) adds yet another diminutive. The Latin root ~agnus~ also survives in the Church's ~Agnus Dei~ (“Lamb of God”), taken straight from Latin. So the French verb for a ewe giving birth to lambs rests on the Latin diminutive ~agnellus~, itself built on ~agnus~.
en.agonir:
The origin is uncertain. French Wiktionary says it is probably a blend with the sense of Old French ~ahonnir~ or ~ahonir~ (“to cover with shame”), which the Littré records as still used in Normandy. The TLFi proposes something narrower: the form spelled ~agonie~ would have taken over its sense from ~ahonnir~.

Either way, ~ahonnir~ and its sense of shaming stand behind the modern use, as in ~agonir~ someone with insults, that is, to heap abuse on them. Both accounts therefore point to ~ahonnir~ for the meaning, while the shape of the modern verb resembles ~agonie~ (“agony, death throes”). The origin is best treated as a probable convergence of forms, not a settled descent.
en.agoniser:
~Agoniser~ is a learned verb. French Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~agonizare~ (“to fight”), while English Wiktionary traces it directly to Ancient Greek ~ἀγωνίζομαι~ (~agōnízomai~, “to contend, to struggle”). The two accounts fit together, since the Latin verb is the Greek one taken over. The Greek verb belongs to the noun ~agōn~ (“contest, struggle”) and means to take part in such a contest. English ~agonize~ and ~agony~ come from the same Greek family, which French ~agonie~ also continues.

The ancestral sense is therefore a fight, and the modern French verb narrowed it to the final struggle: ~agoniser~ means “to be dying, to be in the throes of death.” The verb can also be used figuratively of something in decline. The Greek ~agōn~ lies behind a family of learned French words: ~agonie~, ~antagoniste~ (the one who contends against), and ~protagoniste~ (the first contender, hence the leading role). So a person at death's door and the hero of a play share an ancestor in the arena of a Greek contest.
en.agrafer: ~Agrafer~ is formed with the prefix ~a-~ on an older verb ~grafer~, and it is closely tied to the noun ~agrafe~ (“clasp, hook, staple”). The prefix ~a-~ comes from Latin ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and here has the sense of putting something onto or fastening it. The modern verb means to fasten with a clasp or staple, and in informal French, to catch or nab someone.
en.agrandir:
Attested around 1280, formed from the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, toward”) and the verb ~grandir~ (“to grow”), itself built on ~grand~ (“large, great”), from Latin ~grandis~ (“large, full-grown”). The origin of ~grandis~ is genuinely uncertain: it goes back to Proto-Italic *~grandis~ of unclear source, and the older guesses linking it to a PIE root for “to swell” were rejected by De Vaan on phonetic grounds — so we leave the deeper ancestor open. Italian and Spanish ~grande~ share the same Latin word.

Where ~grandir~ describes growing of itself, the prefix ~a-~ makes ~agrandir~ transitive and causal: to make larger, to enlarge — a house, a photograph, an empire. English borrowed the parallel ~aggrandize~ through French. The native French family is compact and transparent: ~agrandissement~ (“enlargement”), ~agrandisseur~ (the photographic “enlarger”), ~grandeur~ (“greatness, size”), and ~grandir~ itself. The whole group turns on a single idea, bigness, with the prefix supplying only the push from within outward — the move from a thing growing to a hand that makes it grow.
en.agresser:
From Latin ~aggressus~, the past participle of ~aggredī~ (“to approach, to attack”), built from ~ad-~ (“toward”) and ~gradī~ (“to step”). The Latin root ~gradī~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʰredʰ-~ (“to step”), and is also the source of English ~grade~, ~progress~ and ~ingredient~. A first French verb ~agresser~ existed from the Latin form but fell out of use in the sixteenth century, so the modern verb is in effect a second coinage on the same Latin source.

The modern verb was probably remade on ~agressif~ and ~agression~, on the pattern of pairs like ~collectif~ and ~collecter~, ~exécutif~ and ~exécuter~, or ~régressif~ and ~régresser~. Dictionaries did not welcome it: Trévise in 1771 called it old-fashioned, and Quillet in 1965 dismissed it as a “barbarous neologism.” Despite the purists it settled into everyday French as the natural verb for assault, as in ~se faire agresser~ (“to be attacked”). The notion of “stepping toward” is still visible in ~agression~ and ~agressif~, and the same Latin ~gradī~ gave ~grade~ and ~gradation~ as well.
en.agripper:
Inherited from Middle French, from Old French ~agriper~ (“to snatch”), from Frankish *~angrīpan~ (“to seize”). The Frankish verb joined Proto-Germanic *~ana-~ (“on”) and *~grīpaną~ (“to take, seize”), which goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʰrebʰ-~ (“to take, seize, rake”). Cognates include Middle Dutch ~aengrīpen~ (“to grasp, seize”), Old High German ~anagrīfan~ (“to touch, grasp”) and Old English ~grīpan~ (“to seize”), related to English ~grip~.

The verb is therefore Germanic in origin, and its shape still shows the two parts: a prefix meaning “on” and a verb meaning “seize.” French Wiktionary glosses the Old French verb as “to snatch from.” French ~gripper~ (“to jam, to seize up”), a simpler verb, is a relative from the same Germanic root.
en.agréer:
Formed from the noun ~gré~ (“liking, will, pleasure”) with the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to”) and the ending ~-er~ — built on the phrase ~à gré~, “to one's liking.” The noun ~gré~ comes from Latin ~grātum~, the neuter of ~grātus~ (“pleasing, welcome, thankful”), from Proto-Italic *~gʷrātos~, from PIE *~gʷerH-~ (“to welcome, to praise”). Through that root it is cognate with Sanskrit ~gṛṇā́ti~ (“he praises”) and the Latin family of ~grātia~ and ~grātus~.

To ~agréer~ is therefore to take to one's liking — to accept favorably, to approve. The older intransitive use, “to please” (as in a thing that ~agrée~ to someone), preserves the original flavor of ~à gré~ most clearly. The same ~gré~ runs through a wide family: ~agréable~ (“pleasant”), ~agrément~ (“consent; charm”), ~gré~ itself in ~bon gré, mal gré~, ~malgré~ (“despite,” literally “ill-will”), and ~maugréer~ (“to grumble”). Latin ~grātus~ further yields ~grâce~, ~gratitude~, ~gratuit~, and agréger is unrelated — but ~ingrat~ (“ungrateful”) shares the root.
en.agréger:
Borrowed from Latin ~aggregāre~ (also spelled ~adgregāre~), formed from the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~grex~, ~gregis~ (“flock, herd”). The Latin verb meant “to bring into a flock,” and English ~aggregate~ borrowed it directly from the same Latin source. French Wiktionary records an isolated appearance in the 13th century, and the word entered common use only in the late 15th, when it was written ~aggréger~ with a doubled ~g~. The double letter was dropped in the 18th century.

The literal image of animals gathered into a flock became a figure for joining things or people into a single body: ~agréger~ means to unite parts into a whole, or to admit someone into a group. The family of ~grex~ is large. It includes ~grégaire~ (“gregarious, herd-like”), ~congrégation~ (“a gathering”), ~ségrégation~ (separation “away from the flock”) and ~agrégat~ (“aggregate”). French also uses the participle ~agrégé~ for someone who passed the ~agrégation~, the competitive examination for teaching posts.
en.agrémenter: Formed on ~agrément~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~agrément~ comes from ~agréer~ (“to accept, to approve”) plus the noun-forming suffix ~-ment~, and it was already used in Old French. It means pleasure, charm or approval. To ~agrémenter~ something is therefore to give it ~agrément~, that is, to brighten it with a pleasing touch: a dish with herbs, a story with anecdotes, a room with flowers.
en.aguerrir: ~Aguerrir~ is formed from ~guerre~ (“war”) with the prefix ~a-~ and the ending ~-ir~, added together, since no simple verb sits behind it. The prefix comes from Latin ~ad-~ and here means making something into a state; the result is “to harden”. The noun ~guerre~ is first attested in the Chanson de Roland. It comes from Frankish *~werra~ (“confusion, quarrel”) through Early Medieval Latin ~werra~, and it displaced Latin ~bellum~. English ~war~ is a cognate.
en.aguicher:
Inherited from Old French ~aguichier~, which meant “to fit a shield with its ~guiche~”. The ~guiche~ was the strap by which a shield was hung from the elbow, and the word goes back to Germanic, to a form given as *~withthja~ (“wicker band”). The verb thus began in the vocabulary of arms, and only later took on its modern, figurative sense.

By one account, the shift to the modern sense of “to entice” or “to arouse”, first in slang and then in ordinary speech, is easy to follow: the notion of provocation and of a bond between two people stayed constant. Today the verb describes teasing or tempting behavior, and it gave the adjective ~aguichant~ and the noun ~aguicheur~ (“teaser”).
en.ahaner: From Old French ~ahaner~ (“to toil”), traced by one source to Vulgar Latin *~afannare~ (“to take pains, to exert oneself”), a form related to Spanish ~afanar~ (“to strive”). The other source instead derives the verb from the Old French noun ~ahan~ (“effort, toil”) plus the ending ~-er~. The Latin step is only reconstructed. Italian ~affannare~ and ~affanno~ (“distress, breathlessness”) belong to the same family. In modern French the verb means to puff and pant from exertion, as when climbing a slope or carrying a load.
en.ahurir:
~Ahurir~ is built on Old French ~hure~, with the prefix ~a-~ and the verb ending ~-ir~. English Wiktionary traces ~hure~ to a probably Germanic source. The verb is attested first indirectly, through the old participle ~ahuri~, which meant “with bristling or disordered hair,” and only later as an infinitive: from the fifteenth century it meant “to throw into stupefaction.”

The earliest recorded sense is thus physical, an unkempt head, and the later one mental, a mind left stunned. ~Hure~ itself survives in modern French for the head of a boar and, familiarly, of a person. The participle ~ahuri~ remains in daily use as an adjective meaning “dumbfounded,” and the derived adjective ~ahurissant~ means “staggering, stunning.”
en.aicher: A fishing verb, given as a variant of ~escher~, which means to fix an ~esche~ (bait) on a hook. ~Aicher~ is thus the same word in another form, and it means “to bait a hook.” The noun ~esche~ is the angler's name for the bait itself, and it goes back to Latin ~ēsca~ (“food, bait”). A bait is, etymologically, simply something to eat, offered to the fish.
en.aider:
From Old French ~aidier~, from Latin ~adiūtāre~ (“to help, to assist”), a frequentative of ~adiuvāre~ (“to help”), itself the prefix ~ad-~ (“toward”) joined to ~iuvāre~ (“to help, to please, to delight”). The frequentative form, suggesting help given again and again, is the one that won out across the Romance languages: ~adiūtāre~ yielded Italian ~aiutare~, Spanish ~ayudar~, Portuguese ~ajudar~, and French ~aider~, and, through Old French, English ~aid~.

Latin offered two verbs of helping, and French chose the more emphatic. ~Iuvāre~ alone could mean simply “to help” but also “to delight,” a shade preserved in the impersonal ~iuvat~ (“it is pleasing”); the prefixed, intensified ~adiūtāre~ pushed the meaning firmly toward active assistance. From the same Latin family French draws ~aide~ (both the action and the helper), ~aidant~, ~entraide~ (“mutual aid”), and the learned doublet ~adjuvant~ — a substance that “helps along” a medicine or vaccine — together with ~adjudant~, a military rank, both pointing straight back to ~adiuvāre~ and ~iuvāre~.
en.aigrir: ~Aigrir~ is formed from the adjective ~aigre~ with the suffix ~-ir~, in the sense “to make sour”, and, figuratively, to embitter. The adjective ~aigre~ is inherited from Old French ~aigre~, from Vulgar Latin ~ācrus~, from Latin ~ācer~ (“sharp”). It is a doublet of the learned ~âcre~, which French took directly from Latin. The sense of sharp taste is attested in the twelfth century. ~Aigrir~ applies both to milk or wine that turn sour and to a person whom hardship leaves resentful.
en.aiguiller: Formed from ~aiguille~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Old French ~aguille~ (attested in the twelfth century according to French Wiktionary), from Late Latin ~acūcula~, a diminutive of Latin ~acus~ (“needle”). English Wiktionary adds that it may have been influenced in sound by ~aiguiser~, and compares Occitan ~agulha~. English Wiktionary glosses the noun as a needle, as in a compass; the verb means “to direct towards”.
en.aiguilleter: ~Aiguilleter~ is a denominal verb: it takes the noun ~aiguillette~ and adds the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is itself a small derivative, made from ~aiguille~ (“needle”) with the diminutive suffix ~-ette~, so the verb sits two steps away from the needle. Because ~-er~ turns a noun into a verb meaning “to provide with” or “to work with” that noun, ~aiguilleter~ means to fasten or fit with ~aiguillettes~, that is, to lace up.
en.aiguillonner: Formed from ~aiguillon~ with the verb-forming ending ~-er~, meaning “to use an aiguillon,” that is, to prod with a goad. The noun ~aiguillon~ goes back to Old French ~aguillon~ and to Early Medieval Latin ~acūleōnem~, from the Latin ~aculeus~ (“sting, prickle”), and its spelling was reshaped on ~aiguille~ (“needle”). The verb first fits its literal sense of prodding, and by extension it means to spur someone on.
en.aiguiser:
Inherited from Old French ~aguisier~, from Vulgar Latin *~acutiāre~, from Latin ~acūtus~ (“sharp”), the past participle of ~acuō~ (“to sharpen”). The other Romance languages have the same verb: Catalan ~agusar~, Italian ~aguzzare~, Occitan ~agusar~, Portuguese ~aguçar~ and Spanish ~aguzar~. To sharpen a blade, in this lineage, is literally to make it acute.

The modern spelling with ~ai-~ is puzzling, since the Old French form was ~aguisier~. English Wiktionary offers only a hypothesis: a hypothetical proto-French or late Vulgar Latin intermediate form *~ayguydzar(e)~ would explain the ~ai-~, and the Old French ~aguisier~ may then owe its shape to the influence of ~agu~ (the older form of ~aigu~). Whatever the route, the verb is cousin to ~aigu~ (“sharp”) in French and to English ~acute~, all from Latin ~acūtus~.
en.ailler: Formed from the noun ~ail~ (“garlic”) with the verb ending ~-er~, meaning “to flavour with garlic,” as in ~ailler un gigot~. The noun comes from Old French, inherited from Latin ~allium~ (“garlic”). It is a cooking verb of the same shape as ~poivrer~ or ~saler~: a seasoning noun turned into the act of adding it.
en.aimanter: ~Aimanter~ is formed from the noun ~aimant~ (“magnet”) with the verb ending ~-er~, and means to magnetize. The noun ~aimant~ descends from Vulgar Latin ~adimantem~, a form of Latin ~adamās~ (“hard iron”), itself from Ancient Greek ~ἀδάμας~ (“unconquerable”). It is the same root that gave ~diamant~, so a magnet and a diamond are etymological cousins, both named for their hardness.
en.aimer:
From Middle French ~aimer~, refashioned by analogy with the stressed conjugated forms ~(j')aime~, ~(tu) aimes~, from Old French ~amer~, from Latin ~amāre~ (“to love”), from Proto-Italic *~amā-~. The deeper root is debated, but it is often linked to PIE *~am-~, a nursery word seen in *~amma~ (“mother”), a child's term of affection. Cognate with Italian ~amare~, Spanish/Portuguese ~amar~, and Catalan ~amar~; from the same Latin stock English borrowed ~amateur~ (“lover” of an art) and ~amorous~.

The split between Old French ~amer~ and modern ~aimer~ is a tidy lesson in sound change: a stressed Latin ~a~ diphthongized while an unstressed ~a~ did not, so the conjugation once alternated between ~aime~ (stressed) and ~amons~ (unstressed). Middle French leveled the paradigm in favor of the ~aim-~ stem, leaving ~aimer~. The root ~amāre~ blossomed into one of French's richest emotional families: ~amour~, ~amant~ (“lover”), ~amoureux~, ~amitié~ (“friendship,” via ~amīcus~, “friend”), ~aimable~ (the source of English ~amiable~), and ~amateur~. Even the verb's range — from mild liking to passionate love — mirrors that of its Latin parent, which covered every shade of affection.
en.airer: Formed from the noun ~aire~ and the verb ending ~-er~. In this sense ~aire~ is the nest of a large bird of prey, and the verb means to nest or to make a nest. French Wiktionary traces ~aire~ to Latin ~ārea~ (“open space”), which also lies behind the doublets ~are~ and ~area~. English Wiktionary adds that the nest sense is probably from Latin ~ager~ instead, or is related to it, and compares Old Occitan ~agre~ (“bird's nest”). The sources therefore differ on the exact origin of the noun.
en.ajointer: Formed from ~jointer~ with the prefix ~a-~, giving “to butt, to join at the ends.” The base ~jointer~ is a verb made from the noun ~joint~, itself from ~joindre~. The prefix ~a-~ comes from Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”) and here marks bringing one piece up to another.
en.ajourer: Formed from the noun ~ajour~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to pierce with openings.” The noun ~ajour~ is itself a compound of the preposition ~à~ and the noun ~jour~ (“day”). The ending ~-er~ is the Latin ~-are~ of first-conjugation verbs, and the verb means to perforate a surface, as in openwork.
en.ajourner:
French ~ajourner~ comes from Old French ~ajorner~, which meant “to dawn, to grow light.” The Old French verb was itself built on the phrase ~a jorn~ (“to a day”), that is, to an appointed day. The noun ~jorn~ is the Old French ancestor of modern ~jour~, which descends from Late Latin ~diurnum~. In this first life the verb had nothing to do with delay: it described day breaking.

The verb then fell out of use in the seventeenth century and is missing from the first three editions of the Académie's dictionary. The nineteenth-century lexicographer Littré regretted the loss, writing that it was a pity, since French was reduced to a periphrase such as ~il fait jour~. The modern sense of putting something off to another day is a borrowing from English ~adjourn~, a word of English political language that was itself taken from Old French. The verb thus left French and came back from English with a new meaning. It appears in the fourth edition of the Académie's dictionary. Family members include ~jour~, ~journée~ and ~ajournement~.
en.ajouter:
French ~ajouter~ comes from Old French ~ajoster~ (“to bring together, to put side by side”), built ultimately on the Latin preposition and adverb ~juxtā~ (“near, beside”). The Old French verb reflects a Vulgar Latin *~adjuxtāre~, formed with the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) on ~juxtā~ — literally “to set next to.” The base ~juxtā~ itself derives from the Proto-Indo-European root *~yewg-~ (“to join, to yoke”), the same root behind Latin ~iungere~ (“to join”) and ~iugum~ (“yoke”), and behind English ~yoke~ and ~join~.

The meaning slid naturally from physical placement to arithmetic and rhetorical addition: to put one thing beside another is, in the end, to add it. Along the way Old French ~ajoster~ also meant “to bring into agreement, to fit together,” a sense that survives in its doublet ~ajuster~ (“to adjust, to fit”), relatinized straight from ~juxtā~ and kept distinct from ~ajouter~ in modern usage — one adds, the other fits. From the same ~juxtā~ French has the learned adjective ~juxtaposé~ and the noun ~juxtaposition~, while the deeper *~yewg-~ root surfaces in ~joindre~, ~jonction~, and ~conjuguer~ — fittingly, the very act of joining a verb to its endings.
en.ajuster:
Derived from French ~juste~ (“just, exact, fitting”) with the prefix ~a-~ and the verbal suffix ~-er~. ~juste~ descends from Latin ~iūstus~ (“lawful, right”), from ~iūs~ (“law, right”), and ultimately from Old Latin ~iovestos~, from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂yew-~, a root tied to sacred law and binding formulas. Through the same Latin ~iūstus~, French is cousin to English ~just~ and ~justice~.

The verb began life meaning “to make exact, to bring to a right measure,” and the modern senses — to adjust, fit, tune, tweak — all keep that idea of bringing something into proper alignment. Speakers sometimes feel ~ajuster~ as if it meant “to bring close together,” associating it with ~joindre~, but the sources derive it cleanly from ~juste~, not from ~iungere~. The same ~iūstus~ family yields French ~justesse~, ~justice~, ~ajustement~, and the English borrowing ~adjust~ — which reached English through this very Old French verb, so the two languages share the word almost intact.
en.alanguir: A derivative of ~languir~ (“to languish, to grow faint”), with the initial ~a-~ that French often uses to turn a verb or adjective into one that puts someone in a state. ~Alanguir~ is therefore transitive: it means “to make languid,” to sap someone's energy or spirit, where ~languir~ describes the state itself. ~Languir~ goes back to Latin ~languēre~ (“to be weak, to be faint”). Its relatives in modern French include ~langueur~ (“languor”) and ~languissant~ (“languishing”), and English ~languish~ and ~languor~ come from the same source.
en.alarmer: Formed from the noun ~alarme~ and the verb-forming ending ~-er~. The noun was borrowed from Italian ~all'arme~ (“to arms”), a battle cry that soldiers shouted to call the camp to defend itself or to attack, and which fused into a single word. French ~alerte~ comes from a similar Italian phrase, ~all'erta~ (“on the lookout”). The noun first meant the call to arms or a signal of danger, and the verb followed: ~alarmer~ is to sound the alarm, and then to fill someone with sudden fear or anxiety, as in ~s'alarmer~ (“to become worried”). The ending ~-er~ turns the noun into a first-conjugation verb.
en.alcaliniser: Formed from the adjective ~alcalin~ (“alkaline”) with the suffix ~-iser~, so “to make alkaline.” The adjective is itself derived from the noun ~alcali~ with the suffix ~-in~. ~Alcali~ was borrowed from Arabic, a word that English also took as ~alkali~. The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~ and here means to make or convert into.
en.alcooliser: Formed in French from ~alcool~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which means “to treat with, to turn into” the base. The noun ~alcool~ comes from Medieval Latin ~alcohol~, which borrowed it through Spanish from Arabic ~al-kuḥl~ (“kohl,” a very fine powder). The sense then moved from “fine powder” to “essence obtained by distillation, spirit of wine,” a shift that tradition credits to Paracelsus. ~Alcooliser~ therefore means to add alcohol to something or to make it alcoholic.
en.alerter: Formed from the noun ~alerte~ (“alarm, warning”) with the verbal suffix ~-er~, in the sense “to carry out” what the noun names: to sound an alert. The origin of ~alerte~ is debated. One account derives it from Old French ~a l'herte~ (“on guard”). Another treats it as borrowed from Italian ~all'erta~ (“on the lookout”), from ~erta~ (“lookout, height”), a word tied to Latin ~ērigere~ (“to raise up”), so that the phrase first meant standing on a height to watch. Either way, the noun began as a call to stay on guard, and the verb ~alerter~ turned that call into an action.
en.aleviner: ~Aleviner~ is derived from the noun ~alevin~ (“young fish”) with the verbal ending ~-er~: to stock a river or pond with young fish. The noun comes from the Old French verb ~alever~ (“to raise”), which descends from Latin ~allevare~ (“to lift up”). In Vulgar Latin that verb took on the sense “to rear young,” under the influence of ~ēlevāre~, and the ~-i-~ of ~alevin~ is attributed to the influence of ~nutrimen~.
en.aligner:
From Old French ~alignier~ (12th century), formed from ~à~ (“to”) + ~ligne~ (“line”) — literally to bring things ~to a line~. ~Ligne~ comes from Latin ~linea~ (“linen thread, line”), the feminine of ~lineus~ (“flaxen”), from ~linum~ (“flax”). The link is concrete: a builder's straight line was a stretched flax thread. ~Linum~ is matched across Indo-European by Ancient Greek ~linon~ and shows up, through Latin, in English ~line~, ~linen~, and ~lining~.

The core meaning has stayed put for nine centuries: to set things on the same straight line. From troops dressed in a row the verb spread to figures lined up in a column, words set in order, and — in the reflexive ~s'aligner sur~ — to falling into step with a policy or a standard. French slang gave it a sharper edge too: to ~aligner~ someone can mean to tell them off or to make them pay up. Modern relatives include the nouns ~alignement~ and ~ligne~ itself, the compounds ~réaligner~ and ~désaligner~, and — from the same Latin ~linum~ — ~lin~ (“flax, linen”), ~linge~, and ~lignée~.
en.alimenter:
Attested from the 14th century, ~alimenter~ is a French formation built on the noun ~aliment~ (“food, nourishment”) plus the verbal suffix ~-er~. ~Aliment~ comes from Latin ~alimentum~ (“nourishment”), a derivative of ~alere~ (“to nourish, to feed, to rear”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂el-~ (“to nourish, to grow”). Through that root it is cousin to a surprising crowd: Latin ~altus~ (“high,” literally “grown tall”), English ~old~ (originally “grown up”) and ~adult~, and even — via a Germanic branch of the same root — English ~ale~.

The metaphor inside ~alimenter~ is feeding, and it has spread well beyond the table. One still ~alimente~ a person or an animal, but one also ~alimente~ a fire with wood, a town with water, a bank account with deposits, and — figuratively — a quarrel, a rumor, or a debate, keeping it fed and alive. The Latin ~alere~ left a rich table of French words: ~aliment~, ~alimentaire~, ~alimentation~, the adjective ~adulte~ (“one who has finished growing”), and ~coalition~ (literally “a growing together”). The very word ~élément~, through Latin ~elementum~, has sometimes been traced to the same nourishing root — a fittingly elemental kinship.
en.aliter: Formed in French from the prefix ~a-~ (the Latin ~ad-~, “toward”), the noun ~lit~ (“bed”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so that ~aliter~ means to confine to bed. It is used almost only in the reflexive and in the participle: ~s'aliter~ is to take to one's bed through illness, and a person who is ~alité~ is bedridden. The noun ~lit~ descends from Latin ~lectus~ (“bed”). Prefix and suffix together frame the noun, so the verb is a French coinage on a Latin-born word, and not a verb inherited from Latin.
en.aliéner:
French ~aliéner~ is borrowed from Latin ~aliēnāre~, a verb derived from the adjective ~aliēnus~ (“foreign, belonging to another”), itself from ~alius~ (“other”). The verb therefore means, at root, “to make something another's” or “to make foreign.” The same Latin source gave Spanish ~enajenar~, and English took ~alienate~ and ~alien~ from the Latin family.

French keeps both halves of the idea. In law, ~aliéner~ means to transfer a property or a right to someone else, and the adjective ~inaliénable~ describes what cannot be given up. In the general sense, it means to turn someone away from others, or to estrange. French also used ~aliéné~ as a noun for a person considered mentally ill, which gave ~aliéniste~ for the physician. The family also includes ~aliénation~ and ~aliénable~, and the root ~alius~ lies behind ~altérer~ by way of ~alter~.
en.allaiter:
From Old French ~alaitier~, from Late Latin ~allactāre~ (“to suckle, to feed with one's milk”), a verb made from ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~lactāre~ (“to give milk, to suck”), itself built on Latin ~lac~ (“milk”). The ~d~ of ~ad-~ merged with the following ~l~, giving the double ~l~ of ~allactāre~. Modern French speakers can also read the verb as ~a-~ + ~lait~ + ~-er~, a surface analysis that matches the sense: to give the child ~lait~. English Wiktionary notes that analysis, though the Late Latin source comes first.

The Latin noun ~lac~ gave French ~lait~ by regular change, and Greek ~gála~ (“milk”) is a probable relative, a link visible in English ~galaxy~, the “milky” band of the Milky Way. In French the family is large: ~laitier~, ~laitage~, ~laiteux~, ~lactation~ and ~lactose~ all trace to ~lac~. The verb ~allaiter~ stayed narrowly attached to nursing a baby, and it now covers feeding a newborn at the breast and, by extension, animals feeding their young.
en.aller:
~Aller~ is one of the most famous suppletive verbs in French, stitched together from three unrelated Latin sources. The present forms in ~v-~ (~vais~, ~vas~, ~va~, ~vont~) come from Latin ~vādere~ (“to go, to advance”), from Proto-Indo-European *~weh₂dʰ-~ (“to go forward, to wade”), the same root that gives English ~wade~. The future and conditional in ~ir-~ (~irai~, ~irais~) descend from Latin ~īre~ (“to go”), from PIE *~h₁ey-~. The infinitive ~aller~ itself, with its ~all-~ forms, has a debated origin.

For the third stem, scholars hesitate. The traditional guess derives it from Latin ~ambulāre~ (“to walk”), but the sound changes are hard to defend. A phonetically cleaner hypothesis traces it to a Vulgar Latin *~allāre~, drawn from ~allātum~, the orphaned supine of ~afferō~ (“to bring”). French Wiktionary calls the matter genuinely uncertain, so its ancestry is best left open. The result is a single everyday verb whose “I go,” “I will go,” and “to go” each look toward a different Latin word — a living museum of how Romance speakers rebuilt the idea of motion from spare parts, the future tense reaching back to one verb while the present strode off from another.
en.allier:
French ~allier~ descends from Latin ~alligare~ (“to bind to, tie to”), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward,” assimilated to ~al-~) and the verb ~ligare~ (“to bind, tie”). ~Ligare~ traces back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~leyǵ-~ (“to bind”). The same ~alligare~ surfaces elsewhere in Romance — Italian ~allegare~, Spanish ~aliar~ — and, by way of Anglo-Norman, gave English its own ~ally~ and even ~alloy~, a true semantic twin of the metallurgical sense.

The binding image splits neatly in two. When people or states are “tied together,” ~allier~ means to ally; the noun ~alliance~ covers political pacts and the wedding ring alike. When metals are “bound together,” ~allier~ means to alloy, giving the noun ~alliage~. French even reborrowed the same Latin verb in learned form as ~alléguer~ (“to allege,” to bind in a citation), so that ~allier~ and ~alléguer~ are doublets from one source. The wider *~leyǵ-~ family is vast: through ~ligare~ come ~lier~ (“to tie”), ~lien~ (“bond, link”), ~ligament~, ~liasse~ (“bundle of papers”), and ~liage~; through the prefixed ~ob-~ form come ~obliger~ and ~obligation~ — every one of them, at root, a knot.
en.allonger:
Formed in French from the adjective ~long~ with the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, toward”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, replacing Old French ~alongier~. ~Long~ comes from Latin ~longus~ (“long”), from Proto-Italic *~dlongos~, from PIE *~dlongʰos~. Through that root it is cognate with Proto-Germanic *~langaz~, the source of English ~long~ and German ~lang~.

The verb means literally “to make long(er)” — to stretch a hem, to extend a deadline. From there French drew two vivid uses: to ~allonger~ the legs is to stretch out and lie down, and ~allonger~ a sauce is to thin it by adding liquid, making it go further. The ~longus~ family fills the language: ~long~, ~longueur~, ~longer~ (“to run alongside”), ~rallonger~, ~allongement~, and ~prolonger~. English shares the inheritance directly through ~long~ and ~length~.
en.allouer: From Latin ~allocāre~, made of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~locāre~ (“to place, to put”), itself from ~locus~ (“place”). To allot something is thus to put it in a place, to assign it to someone. English ~allow~ is generally thought to come from the same Old French verb, which is usually held to have merged two Latin sources, ~allocāre~ and ~allaudāre~ (“to praise”). The doubled l in French is the usual trace of ~ad-~ assimilating to the next consonant. The learned English cousin ~allocate~ comes straight from medieval Latin.
en.allumer:
Inherited from Old French ~alumer~ (around 1100), from Vulgar Latin *~alluminare~, an assimilated form of *~adluminare~, from ~ad-~ (“to”) + a base tied to ~lumen~ (“light”) and ~luminare~ (“to light”). Cognate with Italian ~alluminare~ and the Spanish ~alumbrar~; through ~lumen~ it is kin to English ~illuminate~ and ~luminous~. The exact internal shape of the Latin form — built on the noun ~lumen~ or on a verb ~luminare~ — is reconstructed rather than directly attested, so it carries the usual asterisk of a Vulgar-Latin form.

The sense ran from “to give light to” to “to kindle, to set alight” — to light a lamp, a fire, a candle. Modern French extended it naturally to switching on electric light and devices (« allumer la lumière », « allumer la télé »), and figuratively to kindling a passion or, in slang, to provoke or seduce someone. From the same ~lumen~ French keeps a bright family: ~lumière~ (“light”), ~lumineux~, ~illuminer~, ~allumage~ (“ignition”), and the little ~allumette~ (“match”), the small stick made for the very act of kindling. The opposite ~éteindre~ took over “to put out,” but ~allumer~ kept the whole field of bringing light into being.
en.allécher:
From Old French ~alechier~, inherited from Latin, though the sources differ on the last link. English Wiktionary says it probably comes from a Vulgar Latin *~allecticāre~, which goes back to Latin ~allectāre~. French Wiktionary gives ~allectāre~ directly, as a frequentative of ~allicere~ (“to attract”). A frequentative expresses repeated or insistent action, so the Latin verb meant “to keep drawing someone on.” Italian ~allettare~ (“to entice”) is a related descendant of the same Latin verb.

The Latin ~allicere~ is generally analyzed as ~ad-~ (“toward”) + ~lacere~ (“to lure”), which makes the French verb a cousin of other words of drawing and pleasing. Whichever intermediate form is right, the sense held steady: ~allécher~ means “to attract by the promise of something pleasant,” as a smell attracts the hungry. The same stem gave the adjective ~alléchant~ (“tempting, mouth-watering”), used of food, offers and prospects, and the noun ~allèchement~. The modern verb remains a lively one, often figurative, as when a bargain ~allèche~ a customer.
en.alléger:
From Old French ~aleger~ (“to lighten, to relieve”), from Late Latin ~alleviāre~ (“to lighten a load”), a compound of ~ad-~ and ~leviāre~, itself built on the adjective ~levis~ (“light, not heavy”). ~levis~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~leɣʷis~ and to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ (“light in weight”), which also yields Sanskrit ~laghú~, Ancient Greek ~elaphrós~ and, by way of Germanic, English ~light~ and German ~leicht~ — so the French verb and the English adjective rest, at a great remove, on one and the same ancient word for weightlessness. The classical verb ~levāre~ (“to lift, to relieve”), also formed on ~levis~, is the source of French ~lever~, so lightening and lifting are the same gesture at the root. Spanish ~aliviar~ continues the same Late Latin verb, and English took it up in learned dress as ~alleviate~.

The earliest French uses are at once very concrete and very legal: in early twelfth-century Anglo-Norman the verb meant to clear someone of an accusation, while a twelfth-century maritime sense was to lighten a ship by taking off cargo; by 1165 the pronominal form meant to grow less heavy, and by 1177 the verb could ease bodily pain. Modern French keeps the whole range — ~alléger un fardeau~, ~alléger un texte~, ~alléger une peine~ — and the food industry annexed it in ~allégé~, said of yogurt or butter. The same family gave French ~léger~, ~allégement~ and ~soulager~, whose Late Latin source *~subleviāre~ differs only in its prefix. A curiosity: the noun ~allégeance~ has two lives, the old one, “relief”, derived from ~alléger~ and archaic since the end of the eighteenth century, and the modern political one, “loyalty”, which the CNRTL treats as a separate entry borrowed from English and unrelated to lightness. The verb also carries a live spelling hesitation: the future is traditionally written ~allégera~, but the 1990 rectifications recommend ~allègera~, and both forms are current.
en.alléguer:
French ~alléguer~ is a borrowing from Latin ~allēgāre~ (“to dispatch, to send for, to cite”), built on ~ad-~ (“toward,” assimilated to ~al-~) and ~lēgāre~ (“to send as a deputy, to appoint, to bequeath”). The Latin verb ~lēgāre~ is itself a derivative of ~lēx~ (“law”), since sending someone with a commission or leaving a legacy were legal acts. Spanish ~alegar~ and Italian ~allegare~ are close counterparts.

The sense path runs from “send” to “bring forward as a plea”: ~alléguer~ is to cite a fact or an excuse, often as a pretext. Many French words come from the same ~lēgāre~ and ~lēx~ roots: ~léguer~ (“to bequeath”), ~légal~, ~délégué~, ~légat~, ~collègue~ and ~loi~. A near-twin to avoid is ~alléger~ (“to lighten”), which comes from Latin ~alleviare~ and has no relation despite the similar look.
en.alourdir: Built in French from the adjective ~lourd~ with the prefix ~a-~ and the verb ending ~-ir~, meaning “to make or become heavy.” The prefix ~a-~ comes from Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”). The origin of ~lourd~ itself is debated: French Wiktionary gives Latin ~lūridus~ (“pale yellow, livid”), while English Wiktionary favors Late Latin ~lurdus~, probably from ~lūridus~ and possibly influenced by a Frankish word for “clumsy.” French Wiktionary notes that ~alourdir~ was rare until the seventeenth century, when ~grever~ was the usual verb for weighing something down.
en.alpaguer: Formed from ~alpague~ with the first-group ending ~-er~. The noun ~alpague~ is a variant of ~alpaga~ (“alpaca”) and in the nineteenth century named a garment of alpaca hair. By metonymy it came to mean the back, as in ~tomber sur l'alpague~ (“to attack”), and finally the verb took its current sense of seizing or arresting someone. French Wiktionary compares the shift to ~colleter~.
en.alphabétiser: Formed from ~alphabet~ and the suffix ~-iser~, the verb means to teach someone the alphabet, hence to teach them to read and write. The base comes from Late Latin ~alphabētum~, borrowed from the Greek ~ἀλφάβητος~, which joins the names of the first two Greek letters, ~ἄλφα~ and ~βῆτα~. Those letter names themselves come from Phoenician ~aleph~ (“ox”) and ~beth~ (“house”). The suffix ~-iser~ is the productive French ending meaning “make, bring to a state”, so an ~alphabétisé~ person is one brought to literacy.
en.alterner: From Latin ~alternāre~, “to do by turns,” a verb built on ~alternus~ (“one after the other, in turn”), which comes from ~alter~ (“the other of two”). That small word also gave French ~autre~, so ~alterner~ and ~autre~ are distant cousins, one learned and the other inherited. Italian ~alternare~ and English ~alternate~ come from the same Latin verb. The idea at the core is strict: each of two things yields to the other in turn, and not merely a vague variety.
en.altérer:
From Latin ~alterāre~ (“to change, to make different”), a verb formed on ~alter~ (“the other, a second one”). That adjective is traced to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂el-~ (“beyond, other”), the same root as Latin ~alius~ (“other”) and English ~else~. The Latin verb gave Italian and Spanish ~alterare~ and ~alterar~, and English ~alter~ reached English through French. Inside French, the inherited descendant of ~alter~ is ~autre~, so ~altérer~ and ~autre~ are learned and popular offspring of one word.

In modern French, ~altérer~ most often means to change something for the worse: to impair, to distort, to spoil. One speaks of a document or a truth that is altered, a food that is spoiled, a color that fades. A distinct sense is “to make thirsty,” as in a throat that is ~altéré~. The family includes ~altération~, ~inaltérable~ (“unalterable”), ~altérité~ (“otherness”) and, through the same Latin ~alter~, ~alterner~ and ~alternatif~.
en.aluminer: ~Aluminer~ is formed from the noun ~alumine~ (“alumina”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, which here makes a verb meaning “to provide with N,” that is, to treat or coat something with alumina. The noun ~alumine~ comes from Latin ~alūmen~, genitive ~alūminis~ (“alum”), the mineral salt from which this oxide was first known. The ending ~-er~ itself descends from the Latin first-conjugation infinitive ending ~-are~, and it is the default way French turns a noun into a verb.
en.aluner:
Two different origins are given for ~aluner~. The first, dating from the sixteenth century, builds it on ~alun~ (“alum”) plus the verb ending ~-er~, so that it means “to treat with alum.” ~Alun~ comes from Old French ~alum~, from Latin ~alūmen~, itself formed with the Latin noun suffix ~-men~, from the Proto-Indo-European suffix *~-mn̥~. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-āre~, through Old French ~-ier~.

The second origin is a different word that happens to look the same: ~a-~ + ~lune~ + ~-er~, a verb about the Moon, related to ~alunir~, “to land on the Moon.” The prefix ~a-~ comes from Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”). ~Lune~ comes through Old French from Latin ~lūna~, from Proto-Italic *~louksnā~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~lewk-~ (“light, to shine”) with a suffix. Two unrelated roots, alum and moonlight, thus meet in one spelling.
en.alunir: ~Alunir~ is built on ~lune~ with the prefix ~a-~ and the ending ~-ir~, on the model of ~atterrir~ (“to land”) and ~amerrir~ (“to land on water”). ~Lune~ comes from Latin ~lūna~ (“moon”). The verb means to land on the Moon, and it has parallels in Italian ~allunare~, Portuguese ~alunar~ and Spanish ~alunizar~.
en.aléser:
From Old French ~alaisier~ (“to enlarge, to widen”). French Wiktionary traces it to a Vulgar Latin verb *~adlatiare~ (“to widen”) and parses it as ~a-~ + ~laize~ + ~-er~, where ~laize~ is the width of a piece of cloth. English Wiktionary gives a slightly different Vulgar Latin form, *~allātiō~, but the same ultimate source in Classical Latin ~lātus~ (“wide, broad”). The two accounts differ on the intermediate form, not on the root: the verb originally meant to make wider.

In modern French ~aléser~ is a technical term for enlarging a hole or a bore to an exact diameter, with a reamer, and its noun ~alésage~ names the bore itself. French Wiktionary notes that Littré connected the verb to ~lisse~ (“smooth”) and read it as “to make a hollow object even”, but that the real sense is to increase the caliber. Latin ~lātus~ also lies behind ~latitude~ and ~dilater~, both learned words, and behind the ~laize~ of cloth.
en.amadouer:
The origin is debated. One account has the verb inherited from Middle French ~amadouer~ (“to coax, to lure”), formed from ~a-~ and a form *~madouer~ (“to lure, to give food to”), from Old Norse ~mata~ (“to lure, to feed”), from Proto-Germanic *~matōną~ and *~matjaną~ (“to feed, to eat”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~meh₂d-~ (“wet”). On that account the word is a cognate of Icelandic ~mata~ (“to bait, to allure”), Danish ~made~ (“to feed”), Gothic ~matjan~ (“to eat”) and Old English ~mete~ (“food”), the ancestor of English ~meat~.
