Beyond “to arm,” ~armer~ acquired the feudal sense “to dub a knight” — to ceremonially fit a man out with his weapons and so make him a ~chevalier~. It later spread to any kind of equipping: one ~arme~ a ship (fitting it out for sea), ~arme~ a camera or a trap (setting its mechanism), and ~arme~ concrete with steel rods (~béton armé~, “reinforced concrete”). From the same Latin source come ~arme~ and ~armée~ (“army”), ~armure~ (“armour”), ~armurier~, ~armistice~, and, by a curious route through ~armarium~ (“a cupboard for tools”), the French ~armoire~ (“wardrobe, cabinet”).
en.armorier: A denominal verb formed from ~armoiries~ (“coat of arms, heraldic bearings”) with ~-er~, meaning “to emblazon with arms.” The noun ~armoiries~ comes from Old French ~armoierie~, built on the verb ~armoier~ or ~armoyer~. That verb meant “to fight” around 1180, then took on a new sense in 1381: “to decorate a shield with the figures of heraldry.” The new sense drew on a figurative use of ~arme~ (“weapon”). ~Armorier~ thus preserves the heraldic sense and belongs to the family of ~arme~, the word for weapons.
en.arnaquer:
The origin of ~arnaquer~ is uncertain, and the sources give two accounts. The first, which French Wiktionary finds fairly plausible in meaning and English Wiktionary reports as the common belief, is that it is a Picard form of ~harnacher~, in the slang sense of “to dress up” or “to disguise” (English Wiktionary adds “ridiculously”). The ordinary ~harnacher~ is tied to ~harnais~ (“harness”), a family that also gave English ~harness~.

The second account, offered only by French Wiktionary, is that ~arnaquer~ is an alteration of ~renaquer~ (“to show anger”), itself from ~naquer~ (“to sniff”) with the prefix ~re-~. Neither account is settled, and the sources do not describe the steps by which “dress up” or “sniff” would have become “to swindle.” What is certain is the slang register of the verb, which gave ~arnaque~ (“a scam”) and ~arnaqueur~ (“a swindler”).
en.aromatiser: ~Aromatiser~ comes from Latin ~aromatizāre~, a verb in ~-izāre~, the ending that French inherited as ~-iser~. It is built on the Latin noun ~arōma~ (“spice, aromatic plant”), itself from Greek ~ἄρωμα~. In French its sense is to give something an aroma or a flavor, and it belongs to the family of ~arôme~, ~aromate~ and ~aromatique~.
en.arpenter: Formed from the noun ~arpent~ and the verb ending ~-er~. An ~arpent~ was an old French land measure, and ~arpenter~ first meant to measure land with it, to survey. The noun comes from Late Latin ~arepennis~ (“surface of a field”), itself from Gaulish *~are-penno-~ (“end, extremity of a field”). The meaning “to stride up and down” is a figurative extension: one walks a space as a surveyor would, covering every length of it with long steps.
en.arpéger: Formed in French from the noun ~arpège~ (“arpeggio”) and the ending ~-er~, “to play a chord as an arpeggio,” with its notes in succession. The noun was borrowed from Italian ~arpeggio~, which comes from the verb ~arpeggiare~, built on ~arpa~ (“harp”). The idea behind the word is playing a chord as a harpist does.
en.arquer:
The French text derives ~arquer~ from Latin ~arcuāre~, a verb built on ~arcus~ (“bow, arch”). English Wiktionary analyzes it differently, as ~arc~ + ~-er~, with the spelling changed to keep the /k/ sound before the ending. The two accounts therefore disagree on whether the verb is inherited from Latin or coined in French, but both lead to the same root, ~arcus~, which is also the source of English ~arc~ and ~arch~.

The verb means “to bend into a curve,” and it is most familiar in its participle, as in a bowed leg or an arched back. Its French relatives are ~arc~, ~arche~ and ~arcade~, all from the Latin word for a bent shape. The root idea survives intact: to ~arquer~ something is to give it the curve of a bow.
en.arracher:
From Old French ~arrachier~, an alteration of ~esrachier~, from Latin ~exradicare~ (« to uproot »), a variant of ~eradicare~, both built on ~radix, radicis~ (« root »). The prefix shift reflects an Old French habit of swapping ~a-~ and ~es-~. ~radix~ descends from Proto-Italic *~wrādīks~ and Proto-Indo-European *~wréh₂ds~ (« root »), cognate with English ~root~, ~wort~, and ~radish~.

So ~arracher~ is etymologically « to pull out by the roots », and the modern verb keeps all the violence of that image: one « tears out » a tooth, « rips up » a plant, « wrenches » a confession from someone, or « snatches » a victory at the last moment. The buried root ~radix~ is everywhere in French once you look — ~racine~ (« root » itself), ~déraciner~ (« to uproot »), ~radical~, ~radis~ (« radish »), and ~éradiquer~ (« to eradicate ») — every one of them turning on the idea of the root that ~arracher~ so forcefully pulls free.
en.arraisonner: ~Arraisonner~ is explained as ~a-~ + ~raison~ + ~-er~, a formation in which the prefix and the verb ending are added to the noun at once. The base ~raison~ comes from Latin ~ratiō~, accusative ~ratiōnem~ (“reckoning, calculation, reasoning”), by way of Old French ~raisne~; ~ration~ is its learned doublet. The prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~) gives a sense of direction toward. A second account traces the verb instead to Old French ~araisnier~. Today it means to stop and inspect a ship, and familiarly to hail a taxi.
en.arranger:
Attested around 1160 as Old French ~arengier~, formed from ~a-~ and ~rengier~ (modern ~ranger~, “to set in rows”), itself from the noun ~renc~ or ~ranc~ (“row, line, rank” — modern ~rang~), borrowed from Frankish *~hring~ (“ring, circle”), from Proto-Germanic *~hringaz~ (“ring”), generally traced to PIE *~(s)ker-~ (“to turn, to bend”). The Germanic word is the very one that survives as English ~ring~ and German ~Ring~. English ~arrange~, ~rank~ and ~range~ were all drawn from this Old French family — and ~derange~ from its negative, ~déranger~.

Inside every tidy arrangement hides a circle of Frankish warriors. Frankish *~hring~ meant “ring,” and in Old French the circle straightened into a line: ~renc~ was a row — above all a row of fighters — and ~arengier~ meant to marshal them; the verb's earliest reflexive use was precisely “to take one's place in battle formation.” Peace then did its slow work. From “put in order,” the verb softened toward accommodation: in the eighteenth century ~s'arranger~ came to mean “to make one's arrangements” (1740), then “to suit” (1747) — whence today's ~ça m'arrange~ — and ~arranger~ even took on “to mend, to patch up” (1768). Modern French lets it stretch from the musician's ~arrangement~ of a song to the soothing ~tout s'arrange~ (“everything works out in the end”) — a long road for a word that began by drawing warriors up in a ring. Its closest French kin are ~rang~, ~rangée~, ~ranger~ and ~déranger~ — etymologically, to disturb is to break ranks.
en.arrenter: Formed from ~rente~ (“annuity, rent”) with the prefix ~a-~, which comes from the preposition ~à~, and the verbal ending ~-er~. It is a historical term meaning to lease out for a rent, that is, to put land under a ~rente~. The noun ~rente~ itself comes from the same family as ~rendre~ (“to give back, to yield”). The English word ~rent~ belongs to that family too.
en.arrimer:
French ~arrimer~ comes from Middle French ~arrimer~, itself from Old French ~arimer~ (“to dispose of goods in the appropriate manner, to store goods in the hold of a ship”). English Wiktionary traces the Old French verb to Middle English ~rimen~ (“to make room for, to clear away”), which continues Old English ~rȳman~ (“to make roomy, to widen, to clear a way”), from Proto-Germanic *~rūmijaną~ (“to make roomy, to give room”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~rewh₁-~ (“free space”). Old Norse ~rýma~ is a cognate, and so are English ~room~ and German ~Raum~.

French Wiktionary gives the same Middle English source, with the prefix ~a-~ added in French, and notes that ~rimen~ is also the ancestor of English ~ream~. The Old French verb has a sailor's sense: to arrange goods properly, above all to stow cargo in a ship's hold. That is still the core of modern ~arrimer~ (“to stow”), and the noun ~arrimage~ names the stowing. The origin carries a caveat. Old French also had ~arrumer~, which has a Portuguese counterpart ~arrumar~, but French Wiktionary judges the two words probably unrelated, so a resemblance between them should not be read as a family tie.
en.arriser: This nautical verb, “to reef a sail”, is formed from ~ris~, the term for a reef, with the prefix ~a-~ and the verb ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary adds an intermediate verb ~riser~, itself a denominal verb from ~ris~. The prefix ~a-~ comes from Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”) and here gives the idea of bringing a sail to its reefed state. Verbs of this kind usually take the prefix and the ending together, so there is no need for an earlier verb to explain the formation.
en.arriver:
From Old French ~ariver~ (“to come to shore, land”), from Vulgar Latin *~arripāre~ (“to touch the shore, come to land”), from the phrase ~ad rīpam~ (“to the shore”), built on ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) + ~rīpa~ (“riverbank, shore”). Cognate with Italian ~arrivare~ and Catalan/Occitan ~arribar~; through the root noun ~rīpa~ it is kin to English ~river~ (via Old French ~rivière~) and to the geological term ~riparian~.

The original notion was wholly nautical: after a long voyage, a ship ~arriva~ when it finally touched the bank. From this image of coming ashore the verb generalized to reaching any destination by any means, then bleached further into the impersonal sense “to happen” — what ~arrive~ is what comes to pass, as in ~il arrive que~ (“it happens that”). The same ~rīpa~ gave French ~rive~ (“bank”), ~rivière~ (“river”), ~riverain~ (“riverside resident”), and the borrowed ~arriviste~ — one who has “arrived” socially by any means, a striver. So a word that once meant simply reaching the riverbank now spans both triumphant arrival and the sheer contingency of events.
en.arriérer: A denominal verb built on ~arrière~ (“behind, back”), the French word for the back that also serves as an adverb. The sense “to put off a payment, to leave a debt behind” fits the idea of pushing something back, and the verb also meant “to fall behind” (dated). The evidence gives only this derivation from ~arrière~, with no older source language, and the verb is rare today. Its past participle ~arriéré~ lives on as a noun for overdue payments (“arrears”) and as an adjective.
en.arroger:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~arrogāre~ (“to ask for, to claim for oneself”), which is built from ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~rogāre~ (“to ask”). In Latin the verb was used of adding a person to a family by adoption or of attributing something to someone, and the sense of claiming something for oneself grew from it. French took it as a scholarly word, directly from Latin and not through Old French.

In French ~arroger~ is used almost only in the reflexive, ~s'arroger~, as in ~s'arroger un droit~: to claim a right or a privilege without having the title to it. Its relatives show how productive the root ~rogāre~ was. English has the cognate ~arrogate~ and the related ~arrogant~, whose French counterpart is ~arrogant~, while ~interroger~, ~prérogative~ and ~dérogation~ all contain the same Latin verb ~rogāre~ in other prefixed forms.
en.arrondir: Formed from the prefix ~a-~ and ~rondir~, a verb itself built from ~rond~ (“round”) and the ending ~-ir~. The prefix ~a-~ comes from Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”), and in verbs like this it carries the idea of passing into a state: ~arrondir~ is “to make round.” ~Rond~ goes back to Latin ~rotundus~, a word built on ~rota~ (“wheel”). English Wiktionary analyzes the verb in one step as ~a-~ + ~rond~ + ~-ir~, which amounts to the same thing. The sense later extended from shapes to numbers, so that one ~arrondit~ a sum to the nearest unit.
en.arroser:
From Middle French ~arrouser~, inherited from a Vulgar Latin verb *~arrōsāre~, built on the prefix ~ad-~ (“to”) and Latin ~rōs~ (“dew”). The verb literally meant to bring dew to something. Latin ~rōs~ also lies behind French ~rosée~ (“dew”) and Spanish ~rocío~ (“dew”). A famous disguise of the same word is ~romarin~ (“rosemary”), from Latin ~ros marinus~, “sea dew”; it has nothing to do with roses.

The sense moved from the gentle fall of dew to deliberately watering plants, then to wetting anything with a spray, as in the garden tool ~arrosoir~ (“watering can”) and the noun ~arrosage~. Figurative uses then multiplied. To ~arroser~ a meal or a success is to wash it down with wine, and the same verb can describe sweeping an area with gunfire, or, colloquially, bribing someone with a shower of money.
en.arrérager: Formed from the noun ~arrérages~ (“overdue payments”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so “to fall into arrears.” The noun is built on Old French ~arrere~ (modern ~arrière~, “behind”) with the suffix ~-age~; it was written ~arriérages~ in the thirteenth century and took its present form in the sixteenth. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~. The idea is of payments left behind.
en.arrêter:
From Middle French ~arrester~, from Old French ~arrester~, ~arester~ (“to stop, to halt, to fix”), from Vulgar Latin *~arrestare~, that is ~ad-~ (“to”) + ~restare~ (“to remain, to stay behind”). ~Restare~ is ~re-~ + ~stare~ (“to stand”), from PIE *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). The literal force was thus “to make remain, to bring to a standstill.” Cognate with Italian ~arrestare~ and Spanish ~arrestar~; through Old French it gave English ~arrest~.

A persistent folk etymology tried to link the word to Germanic ~Rast~ or ~Rest~ (“rest, repose”), but the true ancestor is the Latin “standing” family, not the Germanic “resting” one. From the idea of bringing motion to a halt grew the noun ~arrêt~ — both a “stop” (un arrêt de bus) and, in law, a fixed and binding “decree” or court judgment, something settled and immovable. The verb also means to decide firmly (« arrêter une date ») and to detain a suspect. The same PIE root *~steh₂-~ underlies ~rester~, ~stable~, ~station~, ~constant~, and ~stature~ — a whole vocabulary of standing and staying put.
en.articuler:
From Latin ~articulare~ (“to give joints to, to divide, to pronounce distinctly”), from ~articulus~ (“a little joint, a knuckle”), the diminutive of ~artus~ (“joint, limb”). ~Artus~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂er-~ (“to fit, to join together”), the root of an idea of fitting parts into order — cognate with Latin ~ars~ (“art, skill”) and ~arma~ (“arms, gear”), Ancient Greek ~ἄρθρον~ (“joint”), and Sanskrit ~ṛtú~ (“fixed order, season”). To articulate is, etymologically, to set in joints.

The word carries two living senses from that one image. Physically, bones ~articulate~ where they are jointed; mechanically, two parts that pivot are ~articulated~ (an ~articulated~ lorry bends at its joint). Figuratively, to ~articulate~ speech is to break the stream of sound into distinct, well-jointed syllables — and so, to express clearly. From ~articulus~ also come ~article~ (a small jointed part, then a clause, then a piece of writing) and ~articulation~; and from the same root *~h₂er-~ French keeps ~art~, ~arme~, and ~ordre~.
en.ascensionner: ~Ascensionner~ is formed from the noun ~ascension~ with the verb ending ~-er~. ~Ascension~ reached French through Old French, borrowed from Latin ~ascensiō~ (“ascent”), the noun of ~ascendere~ (“to climb up”). The verb means to climb, as a mountain, or to ascend.
en.aseptiser: Formed in French from the adjective ~aseptique~ and the verb-forming suffix ~-iser~, with the stem reshaped (~aseptique~ becomes ~asept-~). To ~aseptiser~ is to make something aseptic, free of germs, hence “to sterilize, to disinfect.” The adjective ~aseptique~ is itself built from the privative ~a-~ and ~septique~, which come from Greek. The suffix ~-iser~ was borrowed into Old French from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and it is fully productive today in technical vocabulary.
en.asperger: A learned borrowing from Latin ~aspergere~ (“to sprinkle, to scatter on”), a verb formed from ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~spargere~ (“to scatter”). The same Latin family gave French ~aspersion~ and ~disperser~. Because ~asperger~ was taken over from Latin by scholars rather than inherited, it keeps the Latin shape closely.
en.asphalter: ~Asphalter~ is formed from ~asphalte~ (“asphalt”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, in the common sense of providing something with a noun: to cover a surface with asphalt. The noun is a learned borrowing from Late Latin ~asphaltum~, itself from Ancient Greek ~ásphaltos~ (“asphalt, bitumen”). The French verb is thus a modern formation on a word that reached French from Greek by way of Latin.
en.asphyxier: French Wiktionary traces ~asphyxier~ to Ancient Greek ~σφυγμός~ (~sphygmos~, “pulse”), preceded by the privative alpha, the prefix meaning “without”: literally an “absence of pulse.” The word thus began as a statement about the heartbeat, and its modern sense of “to suffocate, to deprive of air” is a later development of that idea. The same Greek root survives in the medical term ~sphygmomanomètre~, the blood-pressure gauge.
en.aspirer:
~aspirer~ reached Old French by about 1165, from Latin ~aspīrāre~ — ~ad-~ (“toward”) plus ~spīrāre~ (“to breathe, to blow”) — literally “to breathe toward.” In Latin the verb could mean to blow favorably upon — of winds and gods — and hence to strive toward something: aspiration as a wind at your back. The deeper origin of ~spīrāre~ is uncertain; etymologists suspect an imitative formation — the word as a puff of air — and the sometimes-proposed root *~(s)peys-~ (“to blow”) is not asserted with confidence. The Romance siblings are Italian ~aspirare~ and Spanish ~aspirar~; English ~aspire~ arrived through French. From the Latin verb's noun ~spīritus~ (“breath”) French inherited ~esprit~ — mind and wit, in French, are etymologically breath.

French kept the verb's whole respiratory range. It meant “to breathe” by the thirteenth century, “to draw in by breathing” by 1393 — whence, in the age of machines, the ~aspirateur~, a vacuum cleaner that literally inhales the house — and “to long for” (~aspirer à~) from the fourteenth century. In 1529 grammarians added the phonetic sense, and left modern French a small joke: the ~h aspiré~, the “aspirated h” that blocks liaison in “les héros,” has not been aspirated for centuries — no breath survives in it; the name is the fossil of a vanished pronunciation. The family of ~spīrāre~ breathes through the whole language: ~respirer~, ~inspirer~, ~expirer~, ~transpirer~, ~conspirer~ (“to breathe together,” as plotters huddled close), and ~soupirer~, from Latin ~suspīrāre~, the breath drawn from below — a sigh. To aspire, in French as in English, is still to set your breath toward something.
en.assagir: A parasynthetic verb: the prefix ~a-~ and the ending ~-ir~ were added together to the adjective ~sage~, giving the sense “to become wise” or “to settle down.” This pattern is common for verbs that mean becoming like the base, as in ~arrondir~ and ~adoucir~. The adjective ~sage~ has two accounts. French Wiktionary derives it from Vulgar Latin *~sabius~, from Latin ~sapiēns~ (“having taste, wise”). English Wiktionary instead derives it, by way of Old and Middle French, from Latin ~sagāx~ (“keen”).
en.assaillir:
From Middle French ~assaillir~, itself from Old French ~assaillir~ (attested in the tenth century), inherited from Late Latin ~assalīre~ (“to jump on, to attack”). That form reshapes classical Latin ~assilīre~, built from the prefix ~ad-~ and ~salīre~ (“to jump”), the ~ad-~ assimilating to ~as-~ before ~s~. English took ~assail~ from the same French verb.

The leap is still visible in French. The matching noun is ~assaut~, which shows the same root as ~saut~ (“jump”), and the idioms ~sauter à la gorge~ and ~sauter sur quelqu'un~ express the same image of attacking by jumping. Other French words from Latin ~salīre~ include ~saillir~ (“to jut out”), ~saillant~ and ~tressaillir~ (“to start, to shudder”).
en.assainir: ~Assainir~ is a parasynthetic verb: the prefix ~a-~ and the ending ~-ir~ were added around the adjective ~sain~ at once, since there is no verb *~sainir~. It means to make healthy, from cleaning up a marsh or a building to putting public finances in order. The spelling ~as-~ is the usual doubling that the prefix ~a-~, from Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”), shows before an ~s~. The base ~sain~ was inherited from Old French ~sain~, from Latin ~sānus~ (“healthy”), whose Proto-Indo-European root, per English Wiktionary, is *~swā-n-~.
en.assaisonner: Formed in French from the prefix ~a-~, the noun ~saison~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, through an older verb ~saisonner~. The prefix ~a-~ comes from Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”). The first sense was “to arrange according to the season”, in particular for the care of crops (attested in 1371), and some explain it as “to ripen in due time”. Once the verb entered the kitchen, it came to mean “to bring a dish to the right point of taste with ingredients”. The noun ~saison~ comes from Latin ~satiō~ (“sowing”), so seasoning starts in a field.
en.assassiner:
French ~assassiner~ is derived from the noun ~assassin~ with the suffix ~-er~. ~assassin~ was borrowed from Italian ~assassino~, from Medieval Latin ~assassinus~, and ultimately from Arabic ~حشّاشين~ (~ḥaššāšīn~), applied to the Nizari Ismaili sect of the Alamut period. The famous gloss explains the name as “hashish-eaters,” but the sources treat that as a popular, folkloric reading rather than settled fact — the term is also linked to roots meaning “followers of the foundation [of the faith]” — so the “hashish” story should be carried as a colorful hypothesis, not asserted as the established truth.

Whatever the name's real motive, in Italian ~assassino~ came to mean a hired killer, and the verb followed: to ~assassiner~ is to murder, especially by treachery or for a cause. The Romance languages share the word — Italian ~assassino~, Spanish ~asesino~, and the English ~assassin~ borrowed through French and Italian alike — making this one of the rare everyday verbs whose root reaches back to a medieval Near-Eastern sect. French keeps the related ~assassinat~ (“assassination, murder”) and ~assassinable~ in the same grim family.
en.assembler:
From Vulgar Latin *~assimulāre~ (“to bring together, to make alike”), from ~ad-~ (“to, together”) and ~simul~ (“together, at the same time”), beside ~similis~ (“like, similar”). These trace to Proto-Italic *~semalis~ and to PIE *~sem-~ (“one, together”) — the root of oneness. The learned French doublet of this same Latin verb is ~assimiler~, while ~sembler~ (“to seem”) is its inherited, popular form. Cognate, through *~sem-~, with English ~assemble~, ~similar~, ~simultaneous~, and ~same~, and with Greek ~homós~ (“same”).

The core idea is to make things go ~together~ as one. Old French ~assembler~ meant both “to gather, to bring together” and, of armies, “to join battle” — two hosts coming together. The reflexive ~s'assembler~ (“to convene”) gave the noun ~assemblée~, the gathering itself: a French ~Assemblée nationale~ is, etymologically, a putting-of-people-into-one. From the same *~sem-~ root spread French ~sembler~, ~ensemble~ (“together,” literally ~in-simul~), ~assemblage~, ~similaire~, and ~rassembler~. That tiny root for “one” quietly underlies both the act of assembling a machine and the sense that two things merely ~seem~ alike.
en.assener:
The verb goes back to Middle French ~assener~, from Old French ~asener~, which was built on ~sen~ (“direction”). That Old French noun was Germanic: English Wiktionary gives Frankish *~sinn~ (“sense, mental faculty, way, direction”), and French Wiktionary compares Germanic ~sinno~, “direction, sense, intelligence.” The modern analysis reads the verb as ~a-~ + ~sens~ + ~-er~, with the current spelling ~sens~ standing in for the old ~sen~. French Wiktionary adds that the Germanic word is in any case related to the Indo-European root *~sent-~ (“to take a direction, to feel”).

That root links the verb to a famous family. Latin ~sentīre~ (“to feel, to perceive”), which gave French ~sentir~ and ~ressentir~, belongs to it as well, and English ~sense~ and German ~Sinn~ are members of the same family. The sources give “direction” as the base meaning, and the modern sense of dealing a blow is an outcome they do not explain further. Today the verb is used chiefly in ~assener un coup~ (“to deal a blow”).
en.asseoir:
From Latin ~assidēre~ (also ~adsidēre~), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~sedēre~ (“to sit”), meaning “to sit beside, to settle.” ~Sedēre~ comes from Proto-Indo-European *~sed-~ (“to sit”), one of the most widespread of all roots, cognate with Sanskrit ~sī́dati~, Old Church Slavonic ~sěděti~, and English ~sit~, ~seat~, and ~settle~. The French verb is attested from the tenth century, and its tangled conjugation (~assieds~, ~assoit~, ~asseyait~) preserves traces of the Latin stems in fossilized form.

From the literal sense of placing someone in a seated position, ~asseoir~ developed a rich figurative life centered on the idea of settling something firmly in place. One ~assoit~ a reputation, an argument, or a tax — establishing it on a solid base. The same image runs through architecture and warfare, where a building or a camp is ~assis~ on firm ground. The English noun ~siege~, by way of Old French ~sege~ (“seat”), comes from this same family — a besieging army “sits down” before a city. From the root *~sed-~ descend French ~asseoir~, ~siège~, ~séance~ (“a sitting, a session”), ~résider~, and ~sédentaire~ (“given to sitting”).
en.asservir:
The sources differ on the first step. French Wiktionary derives ~asservir~ from Latin ~adservire~, while English Wiktionary treats it as a French formation, ~a-~ + ~serf~ + ~-ir~, literally “to enserf,” and says it is not directly related to ~servir~ or to the Latin verb ~asservīre~. The two accounts therefore disagree about more than a detail: one makes the verb an inheritance from Latin, the other a native coinage built on the noun ~serf~, the word for a person bound to the land. On the second account, ~a-~ turns that noun into a verb, so that to be ~asservi~ is to be brought into the condition of a ~serf~, and the ending ~-ir~ marks the second conjugation. Since the evidence does not settle the matter, the origin of the verb should be called disputed.

In French, ~asservir~ means “to reduce to servitude,” and it is used of persons and peoples and, figuratively, of anyone made to obey: one can be ~asservi~ to a tyrant, to a habit or to a passion. The related noun ~asservissement~ keeps the same range. Words such as ~serviteur~, ~service~ and ~servitude~ are near in meaning, but English Wiktionary denies a direct link between ~asservir~ and ~servir~, so the resemblance should not be pressed. Whichever account is right, the meaning is clear: the one who is ~asservi~ loses freedom of action, whether to a master or to a compulsion.
en.assigner:
French ~assigner~ goes back, through Old French ~asigner~ (attested by 1160), to Latin ~assignāre~ (“to mark out, allot, assign”), formed from ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~signāre~ (“to mark, to seal”), itself built on ~signum~ (“mark, token, sign”), from Proto-Italic *~seknom~. Latin used the verb above all of land — marking out plots and allotting them to colonists, the surveyor's word before it was the bureaucrat's. Beyond Latin the trail forks, and etymologists keep both paths open: ~signum~ is traced either to PIE *~sek-~ (“to cut”), a sign as a notch cut into wood or stone, or to *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”), a sign as the thing one follows; neither account is settled. Cognates include Italian ~assegnare~, Spanish ~asignar~ and English ~assign~, which English took from the Old French verb.

Its French history is a slow march from land to law. In its earliest attestations it meant to allot someone property as a share; by 1282 it covered earmarking funds for a payment; and in the mid-fourteenth century appeared the judicial sense that dominates today — to summon someone before a court, as in ~assigner en justice~. The family of ~signum~ stocked French with relatives: ~signe~, ~signer~, ~signal~, ~désigner~ and — most charming of all — ~enseigner~ (“to teach”), from Vulgar Latin *~insignāre~, literally to press a mark into someone, as though teaching were the act of stamping signs upon a mind. Etymologically, to assign is simply to set one's mark on something — a parcel of land, a sum of money, or a defendant's court date.
en.assimiler:
French ~assimiler~ was borrowed from Latin ~assimilare~ (also ~adsimilare~), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“toward”) and ~similis~ (“like, similar”) — literally “to render alike.” ~similis~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~sem-~ (“one, together”), the root of sameness and unity. Through it ~similis~ is cognate with English ~same~ and ~similar~, with Greek ~ὁμαλός~ (“even, level”), and with the family that gave English ~assemble~, where the “together” sense shows plainly.

The semantic core never wandered far from “making alike”: whether the body assimilates food into its own substance, the mind assimilates knowledge, or a people assimilates into a society, each sense is one of incorporation into a likeness. Interestingly, the same Latin ~similis~ took a second, popular path into French as ~assembler~ (“to gather together”), so ~assimiler~ and ~assembler~ are etymological doublets of a sort — one learned, one inherited. From the same root French also holds ~semblable~ (“similar”), ~ressembler~ (“to resemble”), ~sembler~ (“to seem”), ~similaire~, ~simuler~, and ~assimilation~.
en.assister:
From Latin ~assistere~ (“to stand by, to take one's place near”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~sistere~ (“to cause to stand, to place oneself”). ~sistere~ is a reduplicated formation on ~stare~ (“to stand”), from PIE *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”) — the very root behind the worked example ~ester~. Cognate with Italian ~assistere~ and Spanish ~asistir~, and, through ~assistere~, with English ~assist~.

The literal sense is bodily and spatial: to ~assister~ was to stand beside someone. From that single posture two modern meanings unfolded in opposite directions. Stand beside an event as a bystander and you are merely present — hence ~assister à~ a concert or a meeting, “to attend.” Stand beside a person to lend a hand and you are a helper — hence ~assister~ someone in need, “to aid.” French keeps both senses live, a rare case where one verb means both “to watch” and “to help.” The reduplicated ~sistere~ seeds a whole cohort of French verbs — ~résister~, ~insister~, ~persister~, ~consister~, ~subsister~ — while the parent ~stare~ gives ~stable~, ~station~, ~stade~, and ~rester~. Behind them all stands the same upright PIE *~steh₂-~, and behind ~assister~ in particular, the ~assistant~ who simply stands close by.
en.assiéger: The sources disagree about how ~assiéger~ arose. French Wiktionary proposes a probable borrowing from Latin *~assedicāre~, formed from ~a-~ and the root of ~siéger~, and adds that Latin ~obsidēre~ (“to besiege”) may have influenced it. English Wiktionary instead treats it as a French formation from ~a-~ + ~siège~ + ~-er~. Both accounts agree on the ingredients: the prefix ~a-~ and the idea of a seat, ~siège~. The Old French form was ~assegier~. French Wiktionary notes that it meant not only “to besiege” but also “to seat, to establish,” two ideas that are very close, and it compares Latin ~adsideō~, which meant both “to sit beside” and “to camp beside, to besiege.”
en.associer:
From Late Latin ~associāre~ (“to join to, to unite, to take as a companion”), from Latin ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus ~sociāre~ (“to join, to ally”), itself derived from ~socius~ (“companion, ally, partner”). The noun ~socius~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~sokjos~ to the Proto-Indo-European root *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”): a ~socius~ was originally “a follower,” one who goes along with another. From that same root flow Latin ~sequī~ (“to follow”) and a great train of its cousins, while ~socius~ itself underlies English ~social~ and ~society~, Italian ~socio~, and Spanish ~socio~.

That the word for “partner” should spring from “follower” is a quiet lesson in how alliances were imagined: to associate with someone was, at root, to fall in behind them. In 13th-century French ~associer~ named the act of allying among companions, and the sense has stayed close to that ever since — to bring people or things into partnership, to link them in the mind. The reflexive ~s'associer~ means to join forces or go into business together. From ~socius~ and its kin French also drew ~société~, ~social~, ~associé~, ~association~, and ~sociable~.
en.assoiffer: Formed from the prefix ~a-~ and the verb ~soiffer~, itself a verb made from the noun ~soif~ (“thirst”). The prefix ~a-~ comes from Latin ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and here has the attributive sense “to give N to,” as in ~affamer~ (“to starve, to make hungry”). To ~assoiffer~ someone is therefore to give them a thirst, to make them thirsty. The spelling ~as-~ with a doubled ~s~ is a trace of Latin ~ad-~ assimilating to the consonant that follows it.
en.assombrir: ~Assombrir~ is formed on the adjective ~sombre~ (“dark, gloomy”) with the ending ~-ir~, which in verbs from adjectives means “make or become A” (compare ~grandir~, ~grossir~). The initial ~a-~ is the prefix that often accompanies such verbs, as in ~adoucir~. The verb means to make dark or gloomy.
en.assommer: ~Assommer~ is formed from the prefix ~a-~, the noun ~somme~ and the ending ~-er~. The ~somme~ meant here is the one for “sleep”, from Latin ~somnus~, which also gave ~somnambule~ and ~somnifère~; it is unrelated to the ~somme~ of Latin ~summa~ (“sum”) or the ~somme~ of Latin ~sagma~ (“packsaddle”). The prefix ~a-~, from Latin ~ad-~, expresses passage into a state or a bringing toward, and there is no simple verb underneath: the prefix and the ending were added together. Today the verb means “to stun”, “to knock out” and “to slaughter an animal”.
en.assortir:
From Old French, ~assortir~ is a derivative of ~sortir~ in its old sense of “to choose, to allot,” built with the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, toward”). The base belongs to the family of ~sorte~ and ~sort~, from Latin ~sortem~, accusative of ~sors~ (“drawing of lots, fate, share”). ~Sors~ derives from Proto-Italic *~sortis~ (“a joining, a row”), from PIE *~ser-~ (“to bind, to put together”), the same root that gave Latin ~serere~ (“to link, to arrange in a row”) and ~seriēs~. Through Old French ~sorte~, this family also yielded English ~sort~ and ~assortment~.

The semantic thread runs from “lot” to “kind” to “a matching set.” A ~sorte~ was originally a portion fallen to someone by lot, then a category of like things; to ~assortir~ was thus to gather things ~of the same sort~, to arrange them so they agree. Hence the modern senses: to match colors or fabrics, to stock a shop with a fitting range of goods (~un magasin bien assorti~), and reflexively ~s'assortir~, for one thing to harmonize with another. The binding sense of PIE *~ser-~ surfaces across French in ~série~, ~insérer~, ~assertion~, and ~dissertation~, while the “lot, fate” branch lives on in ~sort~, ~sortilège~, and ~consorts~ — etymological kin, all, of the well-matched tie and scarf.
en.assoupir:
A learned form, remade on Latin ~sopīre~ (“to put to sleep”) and carrying the ~a-~ prefix of its older twin ~assouvir~. The two verbs are doublets, which is to say the same word reaching French by two routes. ~Assouvir~ is the older and more worn one, and ~assoupir~ is the version brought back closer to the Latin model. Latin ~sopīre~ belongs with the noun ~sopor~ (“deep sleep”), the source of ~soporifique~.

The split between the doublets is now a split in meaning. ~Assouvir~ means “to satisfy” a hunger or desire, while ~assoupir~ keeps the sense of sleep: to make drowsy, to lull, and figuratively to dull a pain or quiet a quarrel. The participle ~assoupi~ describes someone half-asleep, and ~s'assoupir~ means to doze off. The learned remaking thus preserved in ~assoupir~ the sleepy sense of the Latin verb, while its twin took another path.
en.assouplir: Built in French from the adjective ~souple~ with the prefix ~a-~ and the verb ending ~-ir~, a typical pattern for “make or become A” (compare ~adoucir~, ~alourdir~). The prefix ~a-~ descends from Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”), and here it marks the passage into a state. The adjective ~souple~ comes from Old French ~sople~, which English Wiktionary traces to Latin ~supplex~ (“suppliant”), someone bending the knee. So ~assouplir~ is to make flexible, whether a muscle, a rule or a policy. There is no verb *~souplir~ behind it: the prefix and the ending arrive together.
en.assourdir: ~Assourdir~ is formed from ~sourd~ (“deaf”), the prefix ~a-~ and the ending ~-ir~, a pattern that means “to make into” the quality of the adjective: to make someone deaf, or nearly so. The base ~sourd~ comes from Old French ~sourt~, from Latin ~surdus~, which one source traces to a Proto-Indo-European root *~swer-~ (“ringing, whistling”). Italian ~assordire~ is a close parallel. The prefix ~a-~ comes from Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”), and it marks the passage into a state.
en.assouvir:
~Assouvir~ descends from Vulgar Latin *~assōpīre~, a verb built on Latin ~sōpīre~ (“to put to sleep”). That same Latin verb also produced French ~assoupir~, so ~assouvir~ and ~assoupir~ are doublets: two words from one source that took different paths. Sources differ on the gloss of the Vulgar Latin verb, “to make fall asleep, to calm” in one and “to satisfy” in the other. Either way, sleep is the starting point.

Old French also had a separate verb, ~assovir~ (variants ~assevir~, ~assuir~), meaning “to finish, to accomplish,” from Latin ~assequor~ (“to follow up to, to achieve”). The two verbs became homonyms, and ~assouvir~ took on the sense of carrying something through to its end, as with a vengeance or a passion. The verb is also said to have been influenced by ~assevir~ (“to attain”). Its twin ~assoupir~, by contrast, stayed closer to the idea of drowsiness.
en.assujettir:
From Middle French ~assubiectir~. Only English Wiktionary gives an analysis, and it is a surface one: ~a-~ + ~sujet~ + ~-ir~, with the ~a-~ pointing toward something and the ending turning the noun or adjective into a verb. The base ~sujet~ comes from Latin ~subiectus~ (“placed under, subjected”), the past participle of ~subicere~, built from ~sub-~ (“under”) and ~iacere~ (“to throw”). The verb is thus, at bottom, a word for “throwing under,” that is, putting someone beneath an authority. The Middle French spelling with ~-bi-~ still shows the Latin ~b~ that later French dropped in ~sujet~.

The central sense is political and legal: to subject a people to a ruler, or a person to a duty or a tax, as in ~assujetti à l'impôt~. A second, physical sense, “to fasten firmly, to secure,” also exists, as when one secures a plank or a cable. The family also includes ~assujettissement~, ~sujet~ and ~sujétion~. The Latin root ~iacere~ gave ~jeter~ (“to throw”), ~jet~, ~projet~, ~objet~ and ~adjectif~, which makes ~assujettir~ a distant cousin of every French word that “throws” something somewhere.
en.assumer:
Borrowed from Latin ~assumere~ (“to take to oneself, take up”), formed from the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~sumere~ (“to take”). ~Sumere~ itself is a contraction of *~subemere~, that is ~sub-~ (“up from under”) plus ~emere~ (“to take, later to buy”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁em-~ (“to take, distribute”). The root is cognate with Lithuanian ~imti~ (“to take”) and, through Latin borrowings, with English ~example~ and ~redeem~ (Latin ~redimere~, literally “to take back”).

In classical Latin ~assumere~ meant to take something up for oneself — to adopt, to claim, to take on. French preserved this in the sense of taking on a role or burden: ~assumer ses responsabilités~ (“to shoulder one's responsibilities”). A modern nuance, “to come to terms with, to own,” has grown common — to ~assumer~ one's choices is to accept them without apology. Note that French ~assumer~ has nothing to do with the English false friend “to assume” in the sense of supposing; that meaning split off in English. The ~emere~ root seeds a wide French family: ~exemple~, ~rédemption~, ~prime~ (via ~praemium~), ~prompt~, and the legal ~péremption~ — a scattered descent from a verb that first meant simply “to take.”
en.assurer:
French ~assurer~ comes from Old French ~asseürer~ (“to make safe, to give confidence to”), from Late Latin ~assecūrāre~ (“to render secure”), formed with the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) on Latin ~sēcūrus~ (“safe, free from care”). The adjective ~sēcūrus~ is itself transparent: ~sē-~ (“without, apart from”) plus ~cūra~ (“care, worry”) — so to be secure is, literally, to be “care-free.” Through the Romance line ~assurer~ is cognate with Italian ~assicurare~ and Spanish ~asegurar~; the bare ~sēcūrus~ gave both English ~secure~ and, by a worn-down French route, English ~sure~.

Latin ~sēcūrus~ left two parallel descendants in French: the inherited, phonetically eroded ~sûr~ (“sure, safe” — once spelled ~seür~) and the learned borrowing ~sécurité~ (“security”), a doublet pair from one source. The verb ~assurer~ accordingly fans out across many senses — to make sure, to assert confidently, to provide insurance, to belay a climber on a rope — all turning on the idea of removing care or danger. From the same ~cūra~ root French keeps ~assurance~ (“insurance, confidence”), ~rassurer~ (“to reassure”), ~sûreté~ (“safety”), and ~curer~ — the carefree and the careful alike springing from one Latin worry.
en.assécher: ~Assécher~ comes from Latin ~adsiccāre~ (also spelled ~assiccāre~), “to dry.” The Latin verb joins the prefix ~ad-~ (“to”) to ~siccāre~ (“to make dry”), the verb that also gave French ~sécher~ and that rests on the adjective ~siccus~ (“dry”), ancestor of ~sec~. The prefix was therefore already attached when the verb reached French; it was not added to ~sécher~ inside French. Catalan and Occitan ~assecar~ are cognates.
en.asséner: ~Asséner~ comes from Middle French ~asener~ (“to strike someone”). English Wiktionary analyses it as Old French ~a-~ plus Middle French ~sens~ (“reason, sense”) and the verb ending ~-er~. It is therefore related to English ~sense~ and to Old French ~forsener~ (“to go mad”). The source at hand does not explain how a word built on ~sens~ came to mean “to strike”, so that step is left open, and French Wiktionary gives no etymology for the verb.
en.asticoter:
~Asticoter~ is an altered form of Middle French ~dasticoter~ (“to speak German”). That verb came from ~dasticot~, a curse word brought by German mercenaries, the lansquenets, and modeled on the German oath beginning ~daß dich Gott~ (“may God...”). German ~Gott~ is the same word as English ~God~. English Wiktionary agrees on the German source and says that the curse was probably introduced by German mercenaries.

The change from ~dasticoter~ to ~asticoter~ is explained by a reanalysis. The initial ~d~ was heard as a separate particle, and the verb was perceived as a derivative of ~astiquer~, with the suffix ~-oter~, which explains why the consonant dropped away. The sources do not say how a verb of speaking German became one of needling and pestering, so that step should be left open. The modern verb is informal, and it means to annoy someone with small, repeated irritations.
en.astiquer: Formed as a denominal from ~astic~, a polishing tool, with the verb ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary derives ~astic~ from a dialect verb of Hainaut, built with a change of prefix on Old French ~estichier~ (“to fix, to pierce”). The word probably passed into the common language through the trade jargon of army cobblers, and as the shape of the polisher changed, the notion of a “point” dropped away. English Wiktionary points instead to Picard ~estiquier~, from Old French ~estiquer~, and ultimately to Frankish *~stekan~ (“to stick, pierce, sting”), the same root as ~étiquette~. In both accounts the polishing verb began with a piercing one.
en.astreindre:
~Astreindre~ is inherited from Old French ~astreindre~, from Latin ~astringere~ (“to bind, to tighten”). The Latin verb joins ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~stringere~ (“to draw tight”), a standard analysis. The same root gave the Latin participle ~strictus~, behind English ~strict~, and the learned word ~astringent~, which names something that tightens. French also kept the root in several cousins of ~astreindre~: ~étreindre~, ~restreindre~ and ~contraindre~.

The Latin sense of tying tight became, in French, a figurative one: to bind a person to a rule, a duty or a way of life. That is the modern use, always followed by ~à~, as in ~astreindre quelqu'un à un régime~ or ~s'astreindre à~ do something regularly. The noun ~astreinte~ and the adjective ~astreignant~ (“demanding”) come from it. The physical sense of squeezing is now mostly left to ~étreindre~, which gives an unusually clear case of one Latin verb splitting into neighbours of different weight.
en.atermoyer:
From Old French ~termoyer~ (also written ~termiier~), recorded in the early thirteenth century, with the prefix ~a-~. The Old French verb was built on ~terme~, which comes from Latin ~terminus~ (“boundary, limit”). The word is thinly documented at first: it is attested once around 1200-25 and then not again until 1604.

The verb now means to procrastinate, to stall, and the noun ~atermoiement~ names such a delay. Its suffix is the ~-oyer~ of ~tournoyer~ and ~larmoyer~, which often marks an action that goes on or recurs. The same Latin ~terminus~ lies behind ~terminer~ (“to finish”) and ~terminal~, and English borrowed it whole as ~terminus~.
en.atomiser: From ~atome~ plus the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to reduce to” or “to treat with.” To ~atomiser~ is to break something into tiny particles, hence to spray a liquid as a fine mist, or to destroy completely. The base ~atome~ passed through Middle French ~athome~ from Latin ~atomus~, borrowed from Ancient Greek ~átomos~ (“uncuttable”), formed from the negative ~a-~ and the root of ~tomē~ (“a cutting”). Philosophers such as Democritus used the Greek word for matter's ultimate indivisible particle, and ~-iser~ carries that idea into the verb.
en.atrophier: Formed from the noun ~atrophie~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so ~atrophier~ means to cause atrophy or to waste away. The noun ~atrophie~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~atrophia~, taken from Ancient Greek ~atrophía~ (“lack of nourishment, a wasting away”). The Greek word joins the privative prefix ~a-~ to ~trophḗ~ (“nourishment”), so atrophy is, etymologically, a failure to be fed.
en.attabler: English Wiktionary analyzes this verb as ~a-~ + ~table~ + ~-er~, a parasynthetic formation in which the prefix and the ending are added to the noun at once. The prefix ~a-~ comes from Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”), so the sense is to bring someone to the table. The noun ~table~ is inherited from Old French ~table~ and Latin ~tabula~ (“tablet”), and is a doublet of ~tôle~ and ~taule~. The verb is most often used reflexively, as in ~s'attabler~.
en.attacher:
From Old French ~estachier~ (“to fasten, fix, stake up”), a verb built on ~estache~ (“stake, post”), itself from Frankish *~stakka~ (“stake, post”), from Proto-Germanic *~stakô~, from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)teg-~ (“pole, stick, stake”). The initial vowel later shifted under the influence of the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to”). Cognate with Italian ~staccare~, Spanish ~estaca~ (“stake”), and — through the same Germanic root — with English ~stake~ and ~attach~ itself, which English borrowed back from French.

The earthy origin is a post driven into the ground: to ~attacher~ was first to tether a thing to a stake, and only later to bind, affix, or fasten in general, then figuratively to “attach” someone to a cause or person. The same base gives the perfect antonym ~détacher~ (Old French ~destachier~, “to un-stake, unfasten”), and from that pair English drew both ~attach~ and ~detach~. A surprising relative is ~tâche~ (“task”): many etymologists tie it to the same family, a “task” being originally something one is bound or pledged to do — a duty staked to a person, like an animal tethered to its post.
en.attaquer:
Attested in French from 1549, ~attaquer~ was borrowed from Italian ~attaccare~ (“to attach; to join; to assail”). The Italian verb arose by swapping the prefix of ~staccare~ (“to detach”) for ~a-~, and its tac- element is generally referred to a Germanic source — Frankish *~stakka~ (“stake, post”), the same root that gives English ~stake~. Crucially, ~attaccare~ first meant “to fasten, to attach,” and the military sense grew out of the phrase ~attaccare battaglia~, “to join battle,” literally “to fasten a fight onto” the enemy.

This makes ~attaquer~ an etymological doublet of native French ~attacher~ (“to attach”): the two are the same word, one inherited and one re-imported from Italy, which is why ~s'attaquer à~ and ~s'attacher à~ shadow each other so closely. The combative branch — to fall upon, to assail — eventually overshadowed the “fastening” sense in the borrowed form, leaving ~attacher~ to keep the literal meaning. From the same Germanic stock French also holds ~attache~, ~détacher~, and ~tache~ in some analyses, a small cluster all turning on the idea of pinning one thing fast to another.
en.attarder: Formed from ~tarder~ (“to delay, to be late”) with the prefix ~a-~, which descends from Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”). ~Tarder~ itself comes from Latin ~tardāre~ (“to slow down, to hinder”). The d of the prefix merged into the following t, giving the double tt, and the two consonants are both dentals. French Wiktionary draws a neat contrast: ~tarder~ describes a state, being late, whereas ~attarder~ describes an action, moving toward lateness, which is why the verb is most often reflexive, as in ~s'attarder~, “to linger.” English Wiktionary adds that it replaced an Old French ~atargier~ from the same source.
en.atteindre:
From Old French ~ataindre~, ~ateindre~ (“to reach, to touch”), from Latin ~attingere~ (“to touch, to reach, to border on”), itself ~ad-~ (“toward”) + ~tangere~ (“to touch”), from Proto-Italic *~tangō~, from PIE *~teh₂g-~ (“to touch”). Cognate with Italian ~attingere~ (“to draw, to obtain”) and, through the same Latin root, with English ~tangent~, ~contact~, and ~intact~.

The core sense was always physical contact, and Latin ~tangere~ already stretched from “to touch” to “to reach” and “to affect.” French inherited and developed this range: one can ~atteindre~ a summit, a target, an age, or — figuratively — be touched by an illness, ~atteint~ d'une maladie. The notion of striking a mark gave the noun ~atteinte~ (“an attack, an impairment, a blow to”), as in « porter atteinte à » (“to undermine, to infringe upon”). The same PIE root *~teh₂g-~ seeded a wide family in French through learned Latin borrowings: ~tangente~, ~contact~, ~contagion~, ~intact~, ~tactile~, and ~contigu~ all preserve, under their abstract meanings, the ancient idea of one thing touching another.
en.atteler:
French ~atteler~ most likely continues a Vulgar Latin verb *~attelare~. French Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~protelare~ (“to drive on, to carry through”), which probably took the meaning “to harness” under the influence of ~protelum~ (the trace or fastening of a team), and then had its prefix swapped to give *~attelare~. English Wiktionary gives the same chain in brief. The prefix swap is the key point: the ~pro-~ of the Latin verb gave way to ~at-~, the assimilated form of ~ad-~ (“to, toward”).

There is also a rival account. Littré treated ~atteler~ as a verb drawn from the noun ~attelle~, a part of a draft horse's collar to which the traces are fastened, which would reverse the direction of derivation. The Latin explanation is the one the two Wiktionaries favor, though the question is not fully settled. Whatever its path, the verb is about joining animals to a vehicle, and it extends to people: ~s'atteler à une tâche~ is to yoke oneself to a job. Its opposite is ~dételer~, and the harnessed team is the ~attelage~.
en.attendre:
From Old French ~atendre~ (late eleventh century), from Latin ~attendere~ (“to stretch toward, to pay attention”), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“toward”) and ~tendere~ (“to stretch”). ~tendere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch, to extend”), through which ~attendre~ is cognate with Ancient Greek ~teínō~ (“to stretch”), with Sanskrit ~tan-~ (“to stretch”), and with English ~thin~ and ~tend~. The underlying image is concrete: to attend is to stretch one's mind toward something.

In Latin, ~attendere~ literally meant to stretch (one's attention) in a direction — to heed. French inherited that sense, still visible in the old reflexive ~s'attendre à~ (“to expect”), but the everyday meaning drifted: someone whose attention is fixed on an awaited thing is, in effect, waiting for it, and so ~attendre~ became the ordinary verb “to wait.” English ~attend~ kept the original “pay attention” sense, making the two a neat false-friend pair. The root ~tendere~ produced a large French family: ~tendre~, ~étendre~, ~entendre~, ~prétendre~, ~tension~, ~intention~, ~tente~, and ~attention~ itself — all turning, one way or another, on the idea of stretching.
en.attendrir: Formed from ~a-~ + the adjective ~tendre~ (“soft, tender”) + ~-ir~, “to make tender.” Take care: this ~tendre~ is not the verb ~tendre~ (“to stretch”), from Latin ~tendere~. The adjective comes instead from Latin ~tener~, a separate word that fell together with the verb in French spelling. The prefix ~a-~ goes back to Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”), here marking a passage into a state. The verb first describes making something physically soft and then, figuratively, moving someone to compassion.
en.attenter:
~Attenter~ is borrowed from Latin ~attentāre~ (first-person form ~attento~), a learned borrowing rather than an inherited word. As standard background, the Latin verb is formed from ~ad-~ (“toward”) and ~tentāre~ (“to try, to test, to touch”). The same Latin family gave English ~attempt~ and the French words ~tenter~ (“to try, to tempt”), ~tentative~ and ~tentation~.

French uses ~attenter~ as a legal and moral term of aggression: ~attenter à la vie de quelqu'un~ is to make an attempt on someone's life, and ~attenter à~ also applies to freedoms and rights. The derived noun ~attentat~ (“attack, outrage”) is the common word for such an assault. ~Attenter~ should not be confused with ~attendre~ or ~attention~, which come from a different Latin verb, ~tendere~ (“to stretch”).
en.atterrer: Formed from ~terre~ with the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “toward”, whose final consonant assimilated to the ~t~ of the base, hence the double ~t~ in the spelling) and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~terre~ comes from Latin ~terra~ (“earth”), itself from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ters-~ (“dry”). The verb means “to fell”, bringing someone down to the ground, and so “to appall” or “to overwhelm”. It is a different verb from ~atterrir~ (“to land”).
en.atterrir: A parasynthetic formation: ~a-~ + ~terre~ + ~-ir~, with the prefix and the ending added around the noun at once, since there is no verb of the form ~terrir~ underneath. The ~a-~ is Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”), here with a doubled consonant as in many such verbs, and ~terre~ comes from Latin ~terra~, from a Proto-Indo-European root *~ters-~ (“dry”). The verb first belonged to sailing, “to make landfall, to reach the shore,” and was later applied to aircraft. It has a neighbor in ~atterrer~ (“to knock to the ground,” and so “to dismay”), a different verb of similar shape.
en.attester:
Borrowed from Latin ~attestari~ (“to bear witness to”), from ~ad-~ (“toward”) + ~testari~ (“to testify”), the verb of ~testis~ (“witness”). By the accepted account ~testis~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~tri-st-i-~, literally a “third party standing by” — from *~tréyes~ (“three”) + *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”) — the impartial third person who stands beside two disputants and observes. Cognate with Italian ~attestare~ and Spanish ~atestar~, and — through the same ~testis~ — with English ~attest~, ~testify~, and ~testament~.

So at the root of ~attester~ stands a vivid courtroom image: the neutral bystander, the third one present, whose standing-there makes a fact official. The verb means to certify that something is true, to vouch for it, and by extension to provide evidence of it — « les fouilles attestent une occupation ancienne ». Around it cluster ~attestation~ (a written certificate) and ~attestataire~. The same ~testis~ gave French a broad family: ~témoin~ (“witness,” by a worn-down path) and ~témoigner~, plus the learned ~testament~, ~protester~ (“to declare publicly”), ~contester~, and ~détester~ — all turning on the act of calling something to witness.
en.attifer: Inherited from Old French ~atifer~. The sources consulted trace it no further back than that, so its deeper origin is best left unsaid. The verb means to dress someone up, and it has long carried a mocking or critical tone. A dictionary of the seventeenth century already noted that the word was growing old-fashioned and was used almost only in a teasing manner. Even in sentences that look neutral, that mild disapproval may therefore be present.
en.attiger: The origin of this slang verb is unsettled. French Wiktionary does not derive it but calls it related to Spanish ~aquejar~ (“to torment”), and notes a variant form ~aquéjer~ in slang. It adds that Occitan ~atissar~, pronounced like ~attiger~ in Limousin and Auvergnat, has the same meaning. These resemblances are suggestive, but they are not a proven line of descent.
en.attirer:
Attested from the thirteenth century, ~attirer~ is formed from the verb ~tirer~ (“to pull, to draw”) with the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, toward”), so the word means to draw something toward oneself. ~Tirer~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~tīrāre~, whose ultimate origin is genuinely uncertain — one much-cited hypothesis derives it from a shortening of Old French ~martirer~ (“to make a martyr of, to torture”), from ~martyrium~, on the idea of drawing out and tormenting, but this remains disputed. Cognate with Italian ~tirare~ and Spanish ~tirar~.

In Old French ~atirer~ first meant “to arrange, to put in order, to adorn,” a sense English borrowed and still keeps in ~attire~ (“to dress, clothing”) — a surprising sibling of the everyday French verb. Only later did the pull of ~tirer~ reassert itself, giving the dominant modern meaning of attracting, whether a magnet drawing iron or a spectacle drawing a crowd. From ~tirer~ French keeps a busy family — ~tirage~, ~tiroir~ (“drawer,” a thing that is pulled), ~retirer~, ~soutirer~, ~étirer~, and the marksman's ~tireur~ — every one of them a kind of pulling.
en.attiser:
From Old French ~atisier~, from Vulgar Latin *~attītiāre~, a verb derived from Latin ~tītiō~ (“firebrand, burning log”). The initial ~at-~ of the Vulgar Latin form reflects the prefix ~ad-~ assimilated to the consonant that follows. Cognates survive in Italian ~attizzare~ and Spanish ~atizar~, both “to poke a fire.” The Latin noun itself also lives on in French as ~tison~ (“ember, half-burnt log”), and from it come ~tisonner~ (“to poke the fire”) and ~tisonnier~ (“poker”).

The original action was concrete: to stir the embers so the fire burns brighter. In French, ~attiser le feu~ remains an everyday phrase. The verb is also used figuratively, since a feeling can be fanned like a fire, and French speaks of ~attiser la haine~, ~attiser les tensions~ or ~attiser la curiosité~. The word thus keeps a small domestic scene, a hearth and a stick, behind its modern political and emotional uses.
en.attiédir: ~Attiédir~ is formed from the adjective ~tiède~ with the prefix ~a-~ and the ending ~-ir~, and means to make lukewarm or to cool. ~Tiède~ goes back to Latin ~tepidus~, which became ~tieve~ in Old French, in an eastern form without syncope, before ~tiède~ appeared in Middle French. The learned borrowing ~tépide~ is its doublet. The prefix ~a-~ comes from Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”) and marks passage into a state.
en.attraper:
From Old French ~atraper~, a derivative of ~trappe~ (“trap, snare”) with the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “to, toward”): literally “to catch in a trap.” ~Trappe~ comes from Old Low Frankish *~trappa~ (“snare, step”), a Germanic word also at the root of Medieval Latin ~trappa~. Its Germanic relatives include Dutch ~trap~ (“step, staircase”), German ~Treppe~ (“staircase”), and — keeping the “snare” sense — English ~trap~, which makes the English and French words cognate at the source.

The sense began at the snare and spread outward by metaphor. To ~attraper~ is to catch what flees or eludes: an animal, a thief, a passing bus, a few words overheard. From the idea of catching by surprise grew “to deceive, to take in” (one is ~attrapé~ by a ruse), preserved in ~attrape~ (“a trick, a hoax”) and the shop-window ~attrape-nigaud~ (“a booby trap for fools”). It even catches the involuntary — ~attraper un rhume~, to “catch” a cold. The Germanic ~trappa~ seeded a wide French field: ~trappe~ (a trapdoor), ~trappeur~ (the fur-trapper, re-borrowed from English ~trapper~), ~chausse-trappe~ (a caltrop or pitfall), and ~attrape-tout~ — all descendants of a Frankish word for a snare underfoot.
en.attribuer:
From Latin ~attribuere~ (“to assign, to allot, to add to”), a compound of the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward,” assimilated to ~at-~) and the verb ~tribuere~ (“to grant, to allot, to divide”). ~tribuere~ is a denominative of ~tribus~ (“a tribe,” one of the divisions of the Roman people), so that to allot something was, originally, to distribute it among the tribes. Through this root ~attribuer~ is cognate with English ~attribute~, ~tribute~, ~contribute~, ~distribute~, and ~tribe~ itself.

The political-administrative origin still shows: ~attribuer~ is to apportion a share, a credit, a role, a cause — to assign a prize, attribute a painting to a master, ascribe a motive. The reflexive ~s'attribuer~ means to claim something for oneself. French carries the whole Latin family forward: ~attribut~ (“an attribute, a grammatical predicate”), ~attribution~ (“an allocation, a remit”), ~contribuer~ and ~contribution~, ~distribuer~ and ~distribution~, ~rétribuer~ (“to pay, to remunerate”), and ~tribu~ (“a tribe”). The notion of a ~tribut~ (“tribute”) — a payment apportioned to a ruler — and that of a ~tribunal~ (the platform of the ~tribus~) sit in the same etymological neighborhood, all turning on the idea of dividing and assigning shares.
en.attrister: A parasynthetic formation: ~triste~ (“sad”) took the prefix ~a-~ and the verb ending ~-er~ at the same time, and there is no verb *~tristrer~ behind it. The prefix ~a-~ comes from Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”) and here means “to bring into a state”: ~attrister~ is to make someone sad. The adjective ~triste~ comes from Latin ~tristis~, with the doubled ~tt~ in the spelling as a trace of the assimilated ~ad-~. English ~sad~ is unrelated.
en.attrouper: ~Attrouper~ (“to gather into a crowd”) is formed from ~troupe~ and the verb ending ~-er~, with a prefix that makes the first sound double: ~a-~ (Latin ~ad-~, “toward”), the usual source of such a doubled consonant. French Wiktionary labels the prefix ~ab-~, but nothing in the sense shows Latin ~ab-~ (“away from”), so this is better read as ~a-~. The base ~troupe~ is itself a back-formation from ~troupeau~ (“herd, flock”). To gather people this way is therefore to bring them together like a herd.
en.atténuer:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~attenuāre~ (“to make thin, to weaken”), formed from ~ad-~ (“to”) and the verb ~tenuāre~, itself built on the adjective ~tenuis~ (“thin, slender”). The adjective goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ten-~ (“to stretch”): something stretched becomes thin. The same root gave Latin ~tendere~ (“to stretch”) and the Germanic words for thinness, English ~thin~ and German ~dünn~. English ~attenuate~ is a direct borrowing from the same Latin verb.

In French, ~atténuer~ has the general sense of lessening the force of something: to soften a pain, to tone down a color, to mitigate a fault or a blow. The legal phrase ~circonstances atténuantes~ (“mitigating circumstances”) rests on this sense, as does the rhetorical ~atténuation~, which softens a statement. Learned relatives from the same Latin family include ~ténu~ (“very thin, slight”) and ~extenuer~. The verb also has a technical life in optics, acoustics and electronics, where a signal is weakened as it travels.
en.auditer: Formed from the noun ~audit~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun was borrowed from English ~audit~, a word for the checking of accounts. On the French side, ~audit~ is a doublet of ~ouï~, the past participle of ~ouïr~ (“to hear”). The verb simply means to carry out such an examination, whether financial or technical.
en.auditionner: ~Auditionner~ is built on the noun ~audition~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin ~audītiō~, a noun derived from ~audīre~ (“to hear”). The verb therefore keeps the old idea of hearing: to audition is to give someone a hearing, whether a performer trying out for a part or a witness being questioned.
en.augmenter:
From Latin ~augmentāre~ (“to increase”), a late verb built on ~augmentum~ (“an increase, growth”), itself from ~augēre~ (“to increase, to enlarge”). ~Augēre~ comes from Proto-Italic *~augeō~ and from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂ewg-~ (“to grow, to increase”). The root spread widely: English ~eke~ (“to eke out”), Ancient Greek ~αὐξάνω~ (auxánō, “to grow”), Lithuanian ~áugti~ (“to grow”), and, through Latin, English ~augment~, ~author~, and ~auction~ — the last literally a sale by increasing bids.

The Latin ~augēre~ already carried the idea of making something greater, and ~augmentāre~ simply intensified it; French kept the plain sense “to make or become larger.” The same fertile root yields a surprising spread in French: ~augmenter~ and ~augmentation~, of course, but also ~auteur~ and ~autoriser~ (an ~auctor~ being one who makes a thing grow), ~auguste~ and the name ~Auguste~ (“the venerable, the one who increases”), and even ~auxiliaire~ — an auxiliary being help that augments one's own forces. What began as the simple notion of growth thus branched into authority, majesty, and aid.
en.augurer: ~Augurer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~augurāre~ (“to foretell, to act as an augur”). The Latin verb belongs to ~augur~, the Roman official who read signs to judge whether the gods approved an undertaking. French ~augure~ (“omen”) and ~inaugurer~, both also from Latin, belong to the same family, and English ~augur~ is the same word again.
en.auner: ~Auner~ is derived from the noun ~aune~ (“ell,” an old unit of cloth length) with the verbal ending ~-er~: to measure in ells. The noun comes from Old French ~alne~, from Vulgar Latin *~alina~, taken from Frankish *~alina~ (“forearm”). It is cognate with Old High German ~elina~, English ~ell~, Gothic ~aleina~ and Latin ~ulna~ (“forearm”). The measure was thus named for the length of an arm.
en.aurifier: Derived from Latin ~aurum~ (“gold”) with the suffix ~-ifier~, so the verb means to fill a tooth cavity with gold. The suffix ~-ifier~ goes back to Latin ~-ficāre~, itself from ~facere~ (“to make”), and forms verbs meaning to make or turn into the thing named. The learned pairing of a Latin noun with a French verb suffix is typical of technical vocabulary, here that of dentistry.
en.auréoler: Formed in French from ~auréole~ (“halo”) and the verb ending ~-er~, which descends from the Latin infinitive ending ~-are~ and is the default way French builds a verb on a noun, here in the sense “provide with N”: to ~auréoler~ is to surround with a halo. The noun ~auréole~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~aureola~, which French Wiktionary glosses as a “[crown] of gold”.
en.ausculter:
Borrowed from Latin ~auscultāre~ (“to listen attentively”). It is a learned doublet of ~écouter~, which descends from the very same Latin verb by the ordinary path of inheritance. Cousins of the inherited line are found across the Romance languages, among them Italian ~ascoltare~ and Spanish ~escuchar~ (“to listen”), while English took the learned form as ~auscultate~.

The pair shows how one Latin source can enter French twice. The inherited ~écouter~ was shaped by centuries of everyday speech and became the ordinary verb for listening. ~Ausculter~ was instead taken directly from Latin, with its shape almost intact, and kept the sense of careful, attentive listening. In modern French it is the medical gesture of listening to the sounds of the body's organs, with a stethoscope. The learned noun ~auscultation~ belongs to the same family.
en.authentifier: Formed in French from ~authentique~ + ~-ifier~, with the ending of the adjective dropped. ~Authentique~ comes from Latin ~authenticus~, itself from Ancient Greek ~authentikós~ (“genuine, original”). The suffix ~-ifier~ goes back to Latin ~-(i)ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”), and builds verbs meaning “to make or render so”. ~Authentifier~ therefore means “to make authentic”, that is, to certify that a document, a signature or a user is genuine. Coinages in ~-ifier~ are still productive in learned and technical French, and this is one of them.
en.authentiquer: ~Authentiquer~ (“to authenticate”) is described by French Wiktionary as built on ~authentique~ with the ending ~-er~, while English Wiktionary derives it from Medieval Latin ~authenticō~, so it is either a French formation or a loan. The adjective ~authentique~ comes from Latin ~authenticus~, which borrowed Ancient Greek ~αὐθεντικός~ (~authentikós~). The verb means to certify that something is genuine, often in a legal sense, and it sits beside the more common learned verb ~authentifier~.
en.autocensurer: Formed from ~censurer~ with the prefix ~auto-~, which gives a reflexive sense: to censor oneself. The prefix comes from Ancient Greek ~αὐτός~ (“self”). The base verb is built on the noun ~censure~ with ~-er~, and the noun was borrowed from Latin ~cēnsūra~, the office of the Roman censor, the magistrate who took the census and judged public morals.
en.autodétruire: A modern French compound of the prefix ~auto-~ and the verb ~détruire~. The prefix is taken from Greek ~autos~ (“self”) and attaches to many French words to mean “by or of oneself.” The verb ~détruire~ goes back to Latin ~dēstruere~ (“to tear down,” the opposite of ~struere~, “to build”). ~Autodétruire~, usually reflexive as ~s'autodétruire~, means “to destroy itself,” as a device programmed to self-destruct.
en.autofinancer: A compound from ~financer~ and the prefix ~auto-~, recorded in 1952; ~auto-~ is the Greek-derived element meaning “self,” so the verb means “to fund oneself.” The base ~financer~ comes from ~finance~, which arose in Old French around 1280 from ~finer~ (“to settle, pay”), an altered form of ~finir~, itself resting on Latin ~fīnis~ (“end, limit”). Paying a debt meant putting an end to it, and that is how a word for “ending” came to mean “money.”
en.autographier: Formed from ~autographie~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, the usual ending for coining French verbs, from Latin ~-are~. The noun ~autographie~ is itself built from ~auto-~ (“self”) and ~-graphie~ (“writing”). The verb means “to autograph,” that is, to treat or produce something by means of ~autographie~.
en.automatiser: Formed from the noun ~automate~ with the suffix ~-iser~, in the sense “to turn into an automaton” or “to equip with one”: to make a process run by itself. The base ~automate~ comes from Latin ~automatus~ (“self-moving”) and, through the neuter noun ~automatum~, from Ancient Greek ~αὐτόματος~ (“self-moving, self-willed”). The stem loses its final ~-e~ before the suffix. A Greek word for a thing that moves of its own accord thus ended up, after a long trip through Latin, as a verb for a modern industrial and computing task.
en.autoproclamer: Formed from the prefix ~auto-~ (“self”) and the verb ~proclamer~. The prefix comes from Ancient Greek ~αὐτός~ (“self”) and here has the reflexive sense, so to ~autoproclamer~ is to proclaim oneself something. The base comes from Latin ~proclamare~ (“to cry out”), made of ~pro-~ (“forth”) and ~clamare~ (“to shout”). Note that this verb is a modern coinage, not a Latin inheritance.
en.autopsier: ~Autopsier~ is a French formation of 1866, made from the noun ~autopsie~ with the verbal ending ~-er~: to perform an autopsy on. The noun ~autopsie~ is learned, from Greek ~autopsia~ (“seeing for oneself”), built from ~autos~ (“self”) and ~opsis~ (“sight”). In medicine it names the examination of a body to establish the cause of death. The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, is the usual way French turns a noun into a verb.
en.autoriser:
From Medieval Latin ~auctorizare~ (“to give authority to, to confirm”), from Latin ~auctor~ (“originator, author, guarantor”), itself from ~augere~ (“to increase, to make grow”) + the agent suffix ~-tor~. ~augere~ rests on Proto-Indo-European *~h₂ewg-~ (“to increase”), the source also of English ~author~, ~augment~, and ~auction~. The Old French intermediary was ~actoriser~, and ~autoriser~ stands as a doublet of ~octroyer~ (“to grant”), the popular outcome of the same Latin verb.

An ~auctor~ was originally one who “causes to grow” — who augments, vouches for, sets a thing on foot: a founder, a backer, a source of trust. To ~autoriser~ was thus to lend something the weight of such a guarantor, to make it valid and warranted; from this came both “to authorize, to permit” and the sense of conferring ~autorité~. The thread back to “growth” is invisible in modern usage yet binds a surprising kin: ~auteur~, ~autorité~, ~augmenter~, ~auguste~, ~enchère~ (“auction,” via ~auctio~), and even ~août~ (“August,” the month of ~Augustus~, “the increased, the venerable”).
en.autorépliquer: ~Autorépliquer~ (“to self-replicate”) is formed from ~répliquer~ with the prefix ~auto-~, from Greek ~αὐτός~ (“self”), here in its reflexive and automatic sense. The base ~répliquer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~replicāre~ (“to fold back”), whose family also gave English ~replicate~. The compound is a technical coinage, and the same prefix appears in ~autofinancer~.
en.avachir:
Inherited from Middle French ~avachir~ (“to lose one's energy or force”), from Old French ~avachir~ (“to sag”). The Old French verb is probably a borrowing from Old Frankish *~waikijan~ (“to soften”), from Proto-Germanic *~waikwijaną~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~weyg-~ or *~weyk-~ (“soft, pliable; to bend”). French Wiktionary calls the origin uncertain, though probably Germanic. The Frankish verb is cognate with Old High German ~weihjan~ (“to soften”), Old English ~wǣcan~ (“to weaken”) and Old Norse ~veikja~ (“to make feeble”), and through the same family with German ~weich~ (“soft”) and English ~weak~.

A tempting link with ~vache~ (“cow”) is judged very unlikely by French Wiktionary. Yet the resemblance certainly reinforced the verb, since the cow suggested slowness and softness. Gilles Ménage defined ~avachir~ as “to become slack like a cow.” So a Germanic word for softening was, in popular feeling, colored by a French animal image. The modern verb, especially in its reflexive and participial forms, describes a body or a will that sags: slumping on a sofa, a figure that loses its tone, or character that goes slack.
en.avaler: Formed from the adverb ~aval~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The adverb ~aval~ means “downward, downstream” and is explained as ~à val~, from ~à~ (Latin ~ad~, “to”) + ~val~ (from Latin ~vallis~, “valley”), the opposite of ~amont~. Another account, in English Wiktionary, sees it as a shortening of ~à valoir~. The verb first meant to send or go down, and from that came the sense of letting food slide down the throat. Figuratively, one ~avale~ an insult or a story, meaning one accepts it. The financial noun ~aval~ (“a guarantee”) is a different word, which French Wiktionary derives from Italian ~avallo~.
en.avaliser: Formed from ~aval~ (a financial guarantee) and the suffix ~-iser~, which makes a verb meaning “treat as, turn into N”: to ~avaliser~ is to back something with a guarantee. The origin of the noun is not settled. French Wiktionary gives Italian ~avallo~, itself from Arabic ~hawâla~ (“mandate”), while English Wiktionary proposes that it is probably an abbreviation of ~à valoir~. The suffix goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs.
en.avancer:
From Old French ~avancier~ (also ~avancir~), from Vulgar Latin *~abantiare~, a verb built on Late Latin ~abante~ (“before, in front”), itself a fusion of ~ab~ (“from”) and ~ante~ (“before”). ~Ante~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂énti~ (“in front, before”), which also gives Greek ~antí~ (“opposite, against”) and is cognate with English ~answer~ (originally a “swearing against”). The whole formation means, roughly, “to put forward, to move to the front.”

A charming etymological mishap haunts this word. Speakers came to feel that the ~a-~ of ~avancer~ was the ordinary prefix ~a-~, and that the rest was a stem ~vant~ — so when they wanted a noun for what lies ahead, they coined ~avant~ by clipping off that imagined prefix, even though the ~a~ was part of the root all along. The same false cut produced ~avantage~. Meanwhile ~avancer~ kept widening: from spatial movement forward it reached time (to advance a date), money (to advance a sum), and argument (to advance a claim). Kin in French include ~avant~, ~avance~, ~avantage~, ~avancement~, and ~devancer~.
en.avantager: Formed from the noun ~avantage~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, so “to give someone an advantage.” The noun comes from Old French ~avantage~ and can itself be analyzed as ~avant~ (“before, ahead”) + the noun suffix ~-age~. The ending ~-er~ goes back to the Latin infinitive ending ~-are~ and is the default for turning a noun into a verb in French.
en.avarier: A denominal verb formed from ~avarie~ (“damage, spoilage”) with the ending ~-er~, so “to damage” or, of food, “to spoil.” The noun ~avarie~ passed through Old French from medieval Mediterranean Latin ~avaria~, probably by way of Genoa, where it is attested from the 12th century in the setting of sea trade. French Wiktionary traces it probably to Arabic ~ʿawāriyya~ (“damaged goods”), from ~ʿawār~ (“fault, defect”), and English Wiktionary likewise routes it through Old Italian ~avaria~ to Arabic. The word thus belongs to the Mediterranean trading vocabulary.
en.aventurer: Formed from ~aventure~ + the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to put to the hazard of adventure”. ~Aventure~ comes from Vulgar Latin ~adventūra~, literally “things about to happen”, a neuter plural of the future participle of Latin ~advenīre~ (“to arrive, to happen”) that was reinterpreted as a feminine singular. In Old French the noun meant “fate, chance”, and that fatalistic sense survives only in ~bonne aventure~. The verb therefore means to risk, to hazard, to launch into an uncertain undertaking, and its pronominal form means “to venture” somewhere.
en.avertir:
From Old French ~avertir~, from a Vulgar Latin *~advertire~ reshaping Latin ~advertere~ (« to turn toward, to direct toward »), from ~ad-~ (« toward ») and ~vertere~ (« to turn »). ~vertere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~wertō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~wert-~ (« to turn »), cognate with English ~worth~ (via Proto-Germanic *~werþaną~, « to become »), Sanskrit ~vartate~ (« it turns »), and Russian ~vertétʹ~ (« to rotate »).

The sense « to warn » grew naturally out of « to turn toward ».
