By the late twelfth century the verb meant « to turn, to divert »; by around 1250 it had become « to turn someone's attention toward something », that is « to inform, to warn ». English ~avert~ keeps the older, literal sense — to turn danger aside — beside French's warning sense. The same root *~wert-~ is enormously productive in French: ~vers~, ~verser~, ~divertir~, ~convertir~, ~inverser~, and ~adversaire~ all turn on the idea of turning.
en.aveugler: Formed from the adjective ~aveugle~ (“blind”) and the verb ending ~-er~: to make someone blind. ~Aveugle~ comes from Old French ~avogle~, from Late Latin ~ab oculīs~ (“without eyes,” literally “away from the eyes”). It is probably a calque of a Gaulish word, ~exops~, according to the sources. The adjective drove out the older Old French words for “blind,” ~cieu~ and ~orb~, which went back to Latin ~caecus~ and ~orbus~.
en.aveulir: Formed from the adjective ~veule~ (“limp, spineless”) with the prefix ~a-~ and the ending ~-ir~. French Wiktionary describes the ~a-~ as inchoative, from Latin ~ad-~ (“to”), marking a change of state or the start of an action. The verb therefore means to make someone limp or weak. This is the typical pattern for an ~-ir~ verb from an adjective: prefix plus adjective plus ending gives “to make or become A.”
en.avilir: ~Avilir~ is built from the prefix ~a-~, the adjective ~vil~ and the second-group ending ~-ir~, which together mark a transformation. The adjective ~vil~ comes from Latin ~vīlis~ (“cheap, of little value”). The prefix ~a-~ expresses movement toward a state, so ~avilir~ means to make something vile, to cheapen it. It first described lowering the value of something, and it came to mean demeaning or debasing a person or a dignity.
en.aviser: The sources describe it in two ways. One derives Old French ~aviser~ from the noun ~avis~ (“opinion, advice”); the other analyzes it as ~a-~ + ~viser~. The second analysis rests on ~viser~, from Latin ~vīsāre~ (“to look at attentively”), a frequentative built on ~vīsere~, itself from ~vidēre~ (“to see”), from Proto-Indo-European *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”), the root also behind English ~wit~ and ~wise~. The prefix ~a-~ is Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”) by way of Old French. Either way, the sense moved from looking at something to noticing it, and then to warning or informing someone.
en.avitailler:
Formed from the prefix ~a-~, the Old French noun ~vitaille~ (“provisions”) and the verb ending ~-er~, the verb meaning “to supply with provisions.” French Wiktionary traces ~vitaille~ to Late Latin ~victualia~, the neuter plural of an adjective meaning “relating to food.” English ~victuals~, pronounced “vittles,” comes from the same source through French.

By extension the verb now covers refueling or restocking a ship or vehicle. The Latin root is ~victus~ (“food, way of living”), from ~vīvere~ (“to live”), so provisions are, etymologically, what one lives on. From the same stock come ~ravitailler~ (“to resupply”), which adds ~re-~ to this very verb, and ~victuailles~ (“provisions”), a learned borrowing from the same Latin word. The pair ~vitaille~ and ~victuailles~ shows an inherited and a learned form of one Latin word.
en.aviver: Formed from the adjective ~vif~ with the prefix ~a-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, so ~aviver~ means to make more lively or bright. ~Vif~ comes through Middle French and Old French ~vif~ from Latin ~vīvus~ (“alive, living”), from Proto-Italic *~gʷīwos~ and ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷih₃wós~ (“alive”). The sense of ~vif~ as “alive” explains the verb: to ~aviver~ something is to give it more life.
en.avoir:
From Old French ~avoir~ (also ~aveir~), from Latin ~habēre~ (“to have, hold, possess”), from Proto-Italic *~habēō~, generally traced to Proto-Indo-European *~gʰh₁bʰ-~ (“to grab, to take, to hold”). Its Romance siblings are everywhere everyday verbs: Italian ~avere~, Spanish ~haber~, Portuguese ~haver~, Romanian ~avea~. Tempting as it looks, English ~have~ is not in fact a cognate — the resemblance is a coincidence, that verb belonging to a separate Germanic family.

Latin ~habēre~ began with the concrete sense “to hold,” then widened to “to possess.” In Romance, ~avoir~ went a step further and became an auxiliary, the engine of the compound past: ~j'ai mangé~ is literally “I have eaten,” a possession of the completed act. From the impersonal ~il y a~ (“there is, there are”) French even built an existential out of mere having. The same root threads through a rich family of borrowed and inherited words: ~habit~ (a way of “holding” oneself, hence both costume and custom), ~habitude~, ~habiter~ (“to dwell”), ~exhiber~, ~prohiber~, and, through the compound ~dēbēre~ (~dē-~ + ~habēre~, “to hold away from”), the verb ~devoir~ itself. To have, to owe, to dwell — all are ways of holding.

The same auxiliary turn happened on the far side of the linguistic frontier. German ~haben~ likewise became the engine of a compound past: ~ich habe gesungen~ (“I have sung”) mirrors ~j'ai chanté~ exactly. Yet here lies a fine irony — ~haben~ and ~avoir~ are not cognates at all. Despite their near-identical look and identical meaning, German ~haben~ descends from a different Proto-Indo-European root (*~keh₂p-~, “to grasp,” the source also of Latin ~capiō~ and so of French ~capter~, ~captif~, and ~accepter~), while ~avoir~ comes from *~gʰh₁bʰ-~. Two unrelated “have” verbs were independently pressed into the very same grammatical service. That convergence is a hallmark of the Western European ~Sprachbund~ — a zone where neighboring but unrelated languages, through centuries of contact, grow shared structures: the definite article, the relative pronoun, and precisely this split between ~être~ and ~avoir~ (German ~sein~ and ~haben~) as the two auxiliaries of the past (~je suis allé~ / ~j'ai mangé~ beside ~ich bin gegangen~ / ~ich habe gegessen~). These traits feel inevitable to a European but are unusual among the world's languages. That grammar, no less than vocabulary, can be borrowed across a frontier is the quiet lesson of ~avoir~.
en.avoisiner: ~Avoisiner~ is a parasynthetic formation: the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “toward”) and the ending ~-er~ were added together to the noun ~voisin~ (“neighbor”), giving the sense of being next to, bordering on. The noun is inherited from Old French ~voisin~ (also ~veisin~), from Late Latin ~vēcīnus~, from Latin ~vīcīnus~. Spanish ~vecino~ is a cognate.
en.avorter:
From Latin ~abortāre~ (“to bring forth prematurely”), which French Wiktionary derives from ~aborior~ (“to vanish, to die before coming into the world, to miscarry”), itself from ~orior~ (“to be born, to rise”). The prefix is ~ab-~ (“away from”). English ~abort~ and Spanish ~abortar~ are borrowings of the same Latin verb.

The Latin verb ~orior~ is the source of a large family in French: ~orient~ (the land where the sun rises), ~origine~ and ~originaire~ all come from it. ~Avorter~ is the dark side of that root: an ~ab-~ of birth, a coming-forth that does not happen. In modern French the verb also applies to plans and undertakings that fail before they come to fruition, and the noun ~avorton~ (“runt, stunted creature”) is derived from it.
en.avouer:
From Old French ~avoer~ (“to acknowledge, recognize, accept as one's own — especially to recognize as a protector or lord”), from Latin ~advocare~ (“to call to oneself, summon”), built from the prefix ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and ~vocare~ (“to call”). Some authorities note an alternate influence from ~advotare~ (related to ~votum~, “a vow”), paralleling ~dévouer~ from ~devotare~. The verb is kin to Italian ~avvocare~ and to the English borrowing ~avow~.

The medieval sense was feudal and legal: to ~avouer~ a lord was publicly to acknowledge him as one's protector, and to ~avouer~ a deed was to claim and own it. From “acknowledging as one's own,” the meaning slid toward acknowledging a fact about oneself — and so to the modern sense “to confess, admit,” often something one would rather not (~avouer un crime~, ~avouer sa défaite~). The same ~vocare~ runs through a large French family: ~avocat~ (“lawyer,” the advocate “called to” a case), ~vouer~ and ~dévouer~, ~évoquer~, ~invoquer~, ~provoquer~, ~convoquer~, and ~vocation~. A confession, in this old light, is the act of calling a truth toward yourself and owning it before others.
en.avoyer: ~Avoyer~ is derived from ~voie~ (“way, path”), which comes from Latin ~via~. The French Wiktionary entry gives only this one-line derivation. The verb belongs to the vocabulary of sawing: to ~avoyer~ a saw is to set its teeth, bending them alternately to each side. The width this gives the cut is called the ~voie~ of the saw, so the verb simply means to give a saw its ~voie~.
en.avérer:
From Medieval Latin or a Vulgar Latin *~adverare~, built on ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) plus the adjective ~verus~ (“true”). ~Verus~ is inherited through Proto-Italic *~wēros~ from Proto-Indo-European *~weh₁ros~ (“true, trustworthy”) — the same root that, through Germanic, gives German ~wahr~ (“true”) and, through Old French ~verai~, the English adverb ~very~, which once meant “truly.”

The original sense was juridical: to ~avérer~ a fact was to establish it as true, to prove or verify it, and Old and Middle French used it transitively in just that way. Modern French has largely shifted to the reflexive ~s'avérer~ (“to prove to be, to turn out”) — a thing ~s'avère~ exact, or false, or impossible. This produces a famous purist's quibble: since the verb already contains “true,” the common phrase ~s'avérer faux~ (“to prove false”) is, taken literally, a small contradiction (“to prove-true to be false”), though usage has long since accepted it. From the same ~verus~ French keeps ~vrai~ (its popular descendant), ~vérité~ (“truth”), ~vérifier~ (“to verify”), and ~véridique~ (“truthful”).
en.axer:
Denominal verb from the noun ~axe~ (“axis, axle”) + ~-er~. ~Axe~ descends from Latin ~axis~ (“axle, pivot, axis”), from Proto-Italic *~aksis~, from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂eḱs-~ (“axis, axle”). The root is widely attested: it gives Ancient Greek ~áxōn~, Sanskrit ~ákṣa~ (“axle”), Lithuanian ~ašis~, and — through the inherited Germanic line — English ~axle~, while English ~axis~ is a later direct loan from Latin.

The noun ~axe~ first named the physical axle of a wheel and the geometric or astronomical axis around which things turn. From this pivot-line the verb ~axer~ developed its modern abstract meaning: “to align on an axis,” hence figuratively “to center, to focus on.” One says ~axer un débat sur~ (“to center a debate on”) a question — orienting it along a single line. Words from the same ~axis~ root include ~axe~, ~axial~, axiome (in fact unrelated, from Greek), and the technical ~désaxer~ (“to throw off axis, to unbalance”). The image stays remarkably constant: everything in this family turns on, or is arranged along, a single defining line.
en.axiomatiser: Formed with the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make, to render”) from ~axiome~; English Wiktionary instead sees the base as the adjective ~axiomatique~. Either way the root is ~axiome~, borrowed from Latin ~axioma~ (“self-evident proposition”), itself from Greek ~ἀξίωμα~. The suffix is fully productive in technical vocabulary.
en.azurer: Formed from the noun ~azur~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so ~azurer~ means to tint with blue, as in the bluing used to brighten laundry. ~Azur~ is attested in Old French, in the ~Chanson de Roland~, and is usually traced to Medieval Latin ~azurium~, from Arabic ~lāzaward~ (“lapis lazuli”), itself from Persian ~lājward~ (“lapis lazuli”). The initial ~l~ was lost because it was taken for the definite article. A rival derivation from Arabic ~azraq~ (“blue”) has been proposed.
en.aérer: Formed in French from Latin ~āēr~ (“air”) and the verbal ending ~-er~. The Latin noun is itself the Greek word for air taken over, and it is also the source of French ~air~. To ~aérer~ is to let air into a room, a garment or a text, and the figurative sense of loosening up a dense page or schedule follows naturally from it.
en.babiller:
From Middle French ~babiller~, from Old French ~babillier~ (“to stutter”), built on a root *~bab-~ that is also seen in Middle French ~baboyer~ (“to mumble”). The origin is not settled. French Wiktionary treats it as an imitation of the lip movements of babbling. English Wiktionary says it is probably Germanic, from Old Dutch *~babōn~ or *~babelōn~ (“to mumble, chatter”), from Proto-Germanic *~babalōną~ (“to chatter”), from a Proto-Indo-European sound-imitating root *~bʰa-bʰa-~ (“to talk vaguely, to mumble”). Dutch ~babbelen~, German ~pappeln~ and English ~babble~ are cognates.

The two accounts agree that the word began as a sound, the babbling of an infant or a muddled speaker, rather than as a word with a concrete meaning. In modern French, ~babiller~ means “to chat, to prattle,” often of children and sometimes of birds, with a light or mildly mocking tone. It has produced ~babil~ (“chatter”), ~babillage~ (“prattle”) and ~babillard~ (“talkative”). Whether the sound was inherited from the Germanic languages or coined independently in French, the word sits naturally beside English ~babble~, which has the same nursery-like repeated ~b~.
en.bachoter: Formed from the noun ~bachot~ and the verb ending ~-er~. ~Bachot~ is a colloquial word for the ~bac~, the French baccalauréat exam. The two sources explain it differently: as ~bac~ plus the diminutive ~-ot~, or as ~bachelier~ plus ~-ot~. The verb means to cram for an exam, preparing for it by rote.
en.badigeonner: ~Badigeonner~ is the noun ~badigeon~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to coat with badigeon,” the wash used on walls, and by extension “to smear or slather.” French Wiktionary gives the origin of ~badigeon~ itself as unknown, so the chain stops there. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is the default way French turns a noun into a verb.
en.badiner: Formed from the adjective ~badin~ (“playful, light-hearted”) with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, so the verb means to jest, to speak or act in a playful, teasing way. The adjective gives the verb its tone: someone who ~badine~ is not being serious. French also keeps the related noun ~badinage~ for light banter. The sources give no further origin for ~badin~ itself.
en.bafouer:
The origin of ~bafouer~ is uncertain, and the sources offer several rival accounts. French Wiktionary lists four. In the first, it takes its shape from Old French ~baffe~, ~beffe~ or ~buffe~ (words of mockery) with the phonetic influence of ~fou~ (“mad”). Old Occitan ~bafar~ and Italian ~beffare~, both “to mock,” come from kindred nouns ~bafa~ and ~beffa~. In the second, it is an alteration, after ~battre~ and ~fou~, of Middle French ~beffer~ (“to trick, to fool”). In the third, it was built like ~bavoler~ from ~bas~ and ~fouer~ (“to tread”), meaning to trample down. In the fourth, it is a separate word: Middle French ~bafouer~ meant to tie up with a rope, from ~baffe~ (“bundle”). English Wiktionary gives yet another account, an expressive formation on an interjection of disdain made by blowing air through pouted lips, comparable to Catalan ~baf~ (“puff”).

The sense “to treat with derision, to outrage” is cited from Montaigne's Essais, while the rope sense is cited earlier, from Rabelais's Gargantua in 1534. From scorn came the modern sense of flouting, usually of something that deserves respect, as in ~bafouer la loi~ or ~bafouer les droits de l'homme~. The adjective ~bafoué~ describes one whose dignity has been ignored. Whichever theory is right, the word keeps a hint of the mocking gesture. The Italian noun ~beffa~, a practical joke, shows the same family of mockery on the other side of the Alps.
en.bafouiller:
The origin is uncertain. The verb is attested before 1870, with the meaning “to get an answer wrong,” in the slang of the École polytechnique. The favored account is that it was borrowed from the Lyonnais (Franco-Provençal) verb ~barfouiller~, recorded in the early nineteenth century with the sense “to splash about,” and altered under the influence of ~bafouer~. Lyonnais ~barfouiller~ is itself explained as a blend of ~barbouiller~ and ~fouiller~.

If that account is right, the sense “to splash about while speaking,” hence “to stumble over one's words,” is the key to the modern meaning. ~Bafouiller~ now describes someone who speaks in a muddled, spluttering way, whether from nerves, emotion or confusion. The two verbs said to have crossed in Lyonnais are both still alive in French: ~barbouiller~ (“to smear, to daub”) and ~fouiller~ (“to rummage, to dig”). The pull of ~bafouer~ (“to scoff at, to treat with contempt”) is a proposed influence, not a settled fact, and the whole chain remains a probable reconstruction rather than a proven one.
en.bagarrer: Formed from the noun ~bagarre~ (“brawl, fight”) and the verbal ending ~-er~. The origin of the noun is uncertain. A probable account is a borrowing from Occitan ~bagarro~ (“brawl”), itself perhaps from Basque ~batzarre~ (“assembly”). Another explanation links it to a Gaulish *~baga~ (“quarrel”), and a third has it come from Italian ~sciarra~. The verb ~bagarrer~ means to scrap or scuffle, and ~se bagarrer~ is the common form in everyday speech.
en.baguenauder: ~Baguenauder~ (“to stroll, to amble”) is formed from ~baguenaude~ with the ending ~-er~. The noun is itself mysterious: Littré admitted that its origin was unknown, and he did not know whether the fruit gave its name to the idea of trifling or the reverse. The TLFi traces it to Occitan ~baganauda~ (“fruit of the bladder-senna, idleness”), from ~baganaud~ (“frivolous, rascal”) and ~baganar~ (“to be hollow”). The verb thus carries a hint of idle trifling.
en.baguer: Formed from ~bague~ (“ring”) with the verb ending ~-er~: to fit with a ring or band. The origin of ~bague~ is not fully settled. Both sources first give a Germanic one, through Middle Dutch ~bagge~ from *~baugaz~ (“ring, circlet”), a word related to German ~biegen~ (“to bend”). A rival theory derives it from Latin ~baca~ (“berry”), which is plausible in meaning but harder to square with the earliest attestations, found only in the north of France.
en.baigner:
From Old French ~baignier~, earlier ~bagner~, inherited from Vulgar Latin *~baneare~, a reshaped form of Late Latin ~balneāre~ (“to bathe”), from Latin ~balneum~ (“a bath”). The popular Latin form lost its ~l~, which explains why the Romance verbs look alike: Occitan ~banhar~, Catalan ~banyar~, Italian ~bagnare~, Spanish ~bañar~ and Portuguese ~banhar~ are all cognates. The French spelling ~baigner~ is probably a later remodeling after ~bain~ (“a bath”), the noun that comes from the same Latin ~balneum~. By this account, the ~i~ was added to the verb to match its noun, since the older ~bagner~ lacked it.

The verb began as “to give a bath to” and “to take a bath,” and it kept that concrete meaning. It then widened to anything immersed or washed by water: a river or sea ~baigne~ (“washes”) a shore, a face is ~baigné de larmes~ (“bathed in tears”), and a room can be ~baignée de lumière~ (“bathed in light”). The reflexive ~se baigner~ is the usual verb for going for a swim. Derivatives include ~baignoire~ (“bathtub”), ~baigneur~ (“bather”, also a baby doll) and ~baignade~ (“a swim, a bathing place”).
en.bailler:
~Bailler~ is inherited from Old French ~bailler~ or ~baillier~, by way of Middle French, from Latin ~bajulāre~ (“to carry”). In the late Latin period the sense of carrying shifted to that of being entrusted with a charge, and thence to handing something over. The Latin verb was built on the noun ~bajulus~ (“porter, carrier”). In Old and Middle French ~bailler~ thus meant to give, to hand over, to entrust, which explains its modern archaic senses of lending or renting.

Though the verb itself is now archaic or restricted to set phrases, its family is still alive in French. The noun ~bail~ (“lease”) and the agent noun ~bailleur~ (“lessor”) come from it, as do ~bailli~ (a royal officer, literally someone given charge of a district) and ~bailliage~ (the district under his charge). English borrowed the same family as ~bail~ and ~bailiff~. To say that something is given ~à bail~ is therefore to say that it is handed over for a term, in the old sense of the verb.
en.baiser:
Inherited from Old French ~baisier~ and Middle French ~baiser~, from Latin ~bāsiāre~ (“to kiss”), a verb made on the noun ~bāsium~ (“a kiss”). French Wiktionary says ~bāsiāre~ first named the kiss given to respected people, such as one's father, and that it gradually pushed out two older Latin words, ~suāvium~ (“a lover's kiss”) and ~osculum~ (literally a “little mouth”). Italian ~baciare~, Spanish ~besar~ and Portuguese ~beijar~ are its sisters.

The sense shift is the striking part. The sexual meaning, now dominant and vulgar, is attested from the twelfth century, and English Wiktionary describes it as arising by euphemism before becoming the main sense of the verb. The noun ~baiser~ (“a kiss”) was then derived from the verb, and it stayed innocent. As a result, speakers today say ~embrasser~ for kissing in everyday speech, and the verb ~baiser~ in its original sense survives mainly in literary or fixed uses, such as the noun ~baisemain~ (“a kiss on the hand”). Few French words have changed register so far from their Latin starting point.
en.baisser:
From Middle French, from Old French ~baissier~ (eleventh century, “to lower”), from Vulgar Latin *~bassiāre~ (“to make low”), a verb derived from Late Latin ~bassus~ (“low, base, short”). The same ~bassus~ gave French the adjective ~bas~, Italian ~basso~ and Spanish ~bajo~, and, through musical Italian, English ~bass~ — the lowest voice. *~Bassiāre~ thus means, transparently, “to bring low.”

The verb has stayed close to its literal sense throughout: to lower a thing physically — to ~baisser~ the eyes, the head, a curtain, a window — and from there to turn down (a volume, a price) and to decline (the sun lowers, prices fall, strength wanes). The reflexive ~se baisser~ means to stoop or bend down. From the same ~bas~ family come ~abaisser~ (“to lower, to humble”), ~rabaisser~ (“to belittle”), ~baisse~ (“a fall, a drop”), ~soubassement~ (“a base, a footing”), and the bas-relief of sculpture, ~bas-relief~, a carving that stands only slightly proud of its background. The whole cluster turns on a single idea: lowness, and the act of bringing down toward it.
en.balader: Formed from the noun ~ballade~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. English Wiktionary explains the leap from poem to walk by the constant wandering of troubadours, jugglers and other travelling performers, an account that is plausible but not documented in detail. ~Ballade~ comes from Old Occitan ~ballada~ (“dance song”), the text being inseparable from the music, from ~balar~ (“to dance”), itself from Late Latin ~ballare~, which may be connected to Greek ~ballízō~. So ~balader~ first meant to carry about or lead around, and then to stroll, mostly in the reflexive ~se balader~ (“to go for a walk”).
en.baladodiffuser: A compound of ~balado~ and ~diffuser~, so “to broadcast a podcast.” The first element is a clipping of ~baladodiffusion~, the term proposed by the Office québécois de la langue française in May 2005 to translate the English ~podcast~. The second is ~diffuser~ (“to broadcast”), which comes from Latin ~diffundere~ (“to pour out, to spread”). The verb is a Quebec French equivalent of “to podcast.”
en.balafrer: ~Balafrer~ is formed from the noun ~balafre~ (“gash, scar”) and the ending ~-er~, so it means to mark with a scar. The noun is a blend of ~balèvre~, itself tied to the lips of a wound through a comparison with the lips of the face, and the Old French ~laffru~ or ~lavru~ (“thick-lipped”). English Wiktionary gives the second part as Old French ~leffre~ (“lip”).
en.balancer: Formed on ~balance~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~balance~ is inherited through Old French from Vulgar Latin ~bilancia~ and Latin ~bilanx~, a compound of ~bi-~ (“twice”) and ~lanx~ (“plate, pan”): a balance with two pans. The same Latin word gave French ~bilan~ (“balance sheet”). To ~balancer~ is to move like the pans of a scale, rocking back and forth, and so to swing, sway, or weigh one thing against another. In informal French the verb also means “to throw” or “to toss out.”
en.balayer: Formed from ~balai~ (“broom”), a verb meaning “to use a broom.” The sources differ slightly on the ending: one simply adds ~-er~ to the noun, while fr.Wiktionary notes that some senses may instead come from the verb ~baler~ with the ending ~-ayer~, or at least that ~baler~ and ~balancer~ influenced how the meaning developed. The ~y~ of ~balayer~ is a feature of the ending and not a sign of an older Latin root. The core sense is the physical one, to sweep, and French extends it to anything cleared away in a broad stroke, such as doubts or opponents.
en.balbutier:
~Balbutier~ was borrowed from Latin ~balbūtīre~ (“to stammer”). English.Wiktionary adds a detail about the shape of the French verb: it is formed as if from a Latin *~balbutiāre~, a form remade from the first-person singular present ~balbūtiō~. That is why French has the ending ~-ier~ rather than a plain ~-ir~. The Latin verb is itself based on ~balbus~, the adjective for a person who stammers.

The literal sense, to speak with hesitation and halting repetition, stayed central, as with a child's first words or a speaker overcome by emotion. By extension, ~balbutier~ also means to say something in a stumbling, uncertain way. A field or an art that is just starting out is also said to ~balbutier~, as if still learning to speak. The noun ~balbutiement~ is the usual companion of the verb, and it carries the same two senses.
en.baliser: Formed from the noun ~balise~ (“beacon, marker”) and the verb ending ~-er~. The navigational noun was borrowed from Portuguese ~baliza~, and the French entry also lists a separate homonym ~balise~ tied to ~balisier~, a plant, which is not the source of this verb. To ~baliser~ is to mark a channel, a path or a runway with beacons or markers, and the sense can be extended to marking out a course of action.
en.balkaniser: Formed from ~Balkans~ with the suffix ~-iser~, in reference to the fragmentation of that region during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. The verb thus means to break a territory up into small, often hostile states. The place name itself comes from Turkish ~balkan~ (“wooded mountain range”).
en.ballaster: Formed in French from the noun ~ballast~ and the verb ending ~-er~: to lay ballast, as on a railway bed. The noun is attested in 1375 but was uncommon before the 18th century, and came by the Hanseatic sea routes from Norwegian or Danish ~ballast~ or ~barlast~, in which it first meant a “useless load.” It is composed of Old Norse ~berr~ (“bare, plain”), cognate with English ~bare~, and ~last~ (“load”), which is the same word as French ~lest~.
en.baller:
French ~baller~ is inherited from Middle French ~baller~, from Old French ~baller~ or ~baler~, from Late Latin ~ballāre~ (“to dance”). English Wiktionary adds that the Late Latin verb was itself either borrowed from, or related to, Ancient Greek ~bállō~ (“to throw”), so the dancing sense may rest on an older idea of throwing. This link is proposed rather than settled. Close cognates exist throughout Romance: Catalan ~ballar~, Italian ~ballare~, and Spanish and Portuguese ~bailar~.

In modern French, ~baller~ survives mostly in the sense “to swing, to sway,” as in ~les bras ballants~ (“dangling arms”). The sources do not trace how “dance” turned into “sway.” The Latin verb also fathered a family of dance words: ~bal~ (“ball, dance”), ~ballet~ and ~ballade~, and English borrowed ~ballet~ and ~ballad~ from the same stock.
en.ballonner: Formed from the noun ~ballon~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, so the verb means to puff out or swell like a balloon. The noun was borrowed from Italian ~pallone~ (“big ball”), in the sense of a large bomb used in fireworks. Italian ~pallone~ is itself ~palla~ (“ball”) plus the augmentative suffix ~-one~, so the ~ballon~ was, literally, a big ball.
en.ballotter: Two accounts appear in the sources. One derives this verb from ~baller~ with the suffix ~-oter~; the other treats it as a verb made on the noun ~ballotte~ (“small ball, voting ball”) with plain ~-er~, which fits the usual pattern for nouns in ~-otte~. ~Baller~ comes from Late Latin ~ballāre~ (“to dance”), and still means “to swing” in the participle ~ballant~. The meaning of the verb is to toss around or to jolt.
en.bambocher: ~Bambocher~ goes back to Italian ~bamboccio~ (“doll”), itself derived from ~bambo~ (“child”). The French verb, meaning “to feast, to carouse,” keeps a trace of that childish, doll-like root, though the sources do not say how the sense moved from “doll” to merry-making. It is a loan reshaped into the ordinary first-conjugation pattern in ~-er~.
en.banaliser: ~Banaliser~ is formed from the adjective ~banal~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which turns a base into a verb meaning “to make A” (here, to make something commonplace or ordinary). The adjective itself is derived from ~ban~ with the suffix ~-al~, and an Old French form ~bannel~ is dated to 1269. English Wiktionary relates it to Medieval Latin ~bannālis~, from ~bannus~. So the verb stands on an old medieval word that French reshaped with a modern suffix.
en.bancher: ~Bancher~ is formed from the noun ~banche~ with the verb ending ~-er~; French Wiktionary also mentions ~banc~ as a possible base. French Wiktionary describes ~banche~ as a variant form of ~banc~ (“bench”), akin to ~banque~, which French borrowed from Italian ~banca~. The sense is a builder's one: ~bancher~ is to set up formwork, or to pour concrete into it.
en.bander:
The origin of ~bander~ is not settled in the sources. English Wiktionary gives a Germanic descent: Middle French ~bander~, from Old French ~bander~ (also spelled ~bender~), from Frankish *~bandijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bandijaną~. English ~bend~ is a cognate, and the whole Germanic family revolves around a band or bond that is tied and drawn tight. French Wiktionary lists two accounts side by side. One goes back to Old High German ~binda~ (“to bind”), which is again Germanic. The other, introduced with “probably,” goes back to Occitan ~bandar~ (“to make tipsy, to exasperate”). The sources do not say which account covers which sense of the modern verb, so the Germanic descent is the better documented, and the Occitan one remains a proposal.

The modern verb has two main groups of senses. One is “to bind with a band,” as in ~bander une plaie~ (“to bandage a wound”) or ~bander les yeux~ (“to blindfold”). The other is “to stretch tight,” as in ~bander un arc~ (“to draw a bow”) or ~bander ses muscles~ (“to tense one's muscles”). The step from tying to tightening is a natural one, since a band that is tied is drawn taut. These senses sit beside the related words ~bande~ (“strip, band”), ~bandeau~ (“headband”) and ~bandage~, though this entry does not claim that every sense of ~bander~ comes from a single source. Where the origin is debated, the safest summary is that a Germanic word for binding is the best-attested ancestor.
en.bannir:
French ~bannir~ is first attested around 1100. It comes from Old French ~bannir~ (also ~banir~), borrowed from Frankish *~bannijan~, a West Germanic verb. Behind it lies Proto-Germanic *~bannijaną~ (“to banish, to forbid”), formed on the noun *~bannaz~ or *~banną~ (“prohibition, curse, order, banishment”), which French Wiktionary traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰeh₂-~ (“to speak, to say”). So the verb began as a Germanic word of proclamation, passed to the Gallo-Romans through the Franks. The cognates are Germanic: German ~Bann~ and English ~ban~ belong to the same family.

The Germanic word meant an official proclamation, a command backed by authority, and it is not far from there to “banishment,” a sentence pronounced aloud. French kept both ends. In feudal law, the lord's ~ban~ was his right to command and to compel, which is why ~banal~ first described what was subject to that ban, such as the communal oven, before it came to mean “commonplace.” The Italian verb ~bandire~ gave ~bandito~, hence French ~bandit~, an outlaw originally one who had been proclaimed outside the law. And ~abandonner~ comes from the expression ~à bandon~, “at someone's disposal,” built on the same ~ban~.
en.banquer: One account treats ~banquer~ as a compound of ~banc~ (“bench”) and ~banque~ (“bank”); another derives it from ~banque~ plus ~-er~. ~Banc~ is of Germanic origin (from Proto-Germanic *~bankiz~, “bench”), and ~banque~ is its doublet. The verb means to fork out or pay the bill.
en.banqueter: ~Banqueter~ (“to feast”) is formed from ~banquet~ and the verb ending ~-er~. ~Banquet~ came into French from Italian ~banchetto~ (“feast”), a diminutive of ~banco~ (“bench”), itself from Lombardic and Proto-Germanic *~bankiz~. The root is shared with French ~banc~ and English ~bench~. The Italian word seems to have meant a light meal taken on a small bench, and Old French ~banquet~ meant only “small bench.”
en.baptiser:
From Latin ~baptizo~ (“to wash, baptize”), itself from Ancient Greek ~baptízō~ (“to plunge, dip, immerse”), a frequentative of ~báptō~ (“to dip, dye”). The image at the root is wholly physical: total immersion in water. Christian Latin took this Greek verb and narrowed it to the rite of baptism, and French inherited the religious sense.

The original “dipping” survives in a surprising cousin: the dyeing sense of Greek ~báptō~ gives English ~baptistery~ and, distantly, the deep-blue pigment-trade word behind ~baptism~ imagery. In French the family is liturgical and rich: ~baptême~, ~baptistère~, ~baptismal~, ~anabaptiste~, ~rebaptiser~, ~débaptiser~. The verb also drifted playfully into everyday French — to ~baptiser~ a ship is to name it, and slang once used ~baptiser le vin~ for watering it down, a wink at the immersion buried in the word. From a Greek term for plunging into water came a vocabulary of naming, blessing, and christening.
en.baragouiner: Formed from the noun ~baragouin~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, with the sense of speaking in a jumbled, unintelligible way. The verb is recorded in 1578 as ~barragoiner~ and in 1580 as ~barragouiner~. The noun is a contemptuous word that dates from the late fourteenth century. Its origin is debated: it is often derived from Breton ~bara~ (“bread”) and ~gwin~ (“wine”), an account judged doubtful as early as 1935, though others still consider it probable.
en.baraquer: Formed in French from ~baraque~ (“hut, shack”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so to house troops in huts or barracks. The noun reached French through Occitan ~barraca~ from Catalan ~barraca~. English Wiktionary calls the Valencian form ~barraca~ the source and says it probably comes from a pre-Roman language of Spain, so its deeper origin is unknown.
en.baratiner: ~Baratiner~ is formed from the noun ~baratin~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The origin of ~baratin~ is told two ways. French Wiktionary derives it from Occitan ~baratin~ (“deceiver”), from Gaulish *~barato~ (“deceiver, cheat”). English Wiktionary instead builds it from Old French ~barater~ and the suffix ~-in~. Either way the idea is smooth, misleading talk, and ~baratiner~ means to chat someone up or sweet-talk them.
en.baratter:
~Baratter~ comes from Old French ~barater~ (“to shake, to stir”), attested in spellings such as ~barattrer~ and, in 1611, ~baretter~. Beyond Old French the origin is unclear. English Wiktionary suggests it may come from a Vulgar Latin *~būrattāre~, itself of obscure origin and perhaps ultimately Celtic. This is a proposal, not an established chain.

The Old French verb also gave English ~barter~, and Spanish and Portuguese ~baratar~ are listed as comparable forms. In modern French, ~baratter~ is the dairy term for agitating cream in a ~baratte~ (a churn) to make butter, which matches the Old French sense of shaking and stirring. The noun ~baratte~ is the tool, and the verb the act.
en.barber: ~Barber~ is formed from ~barbe~ (“beard”) and the verbal ending ~-er~. Its base comes from Latin ~barba~, from an earlier *~farba~ and Proto-Italic *~farðā~, from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰardʰeh₂~ (“beard”). The slang sense “to bore someone” is borrowed from ~raser~, which means both “to shave” and, in the familiar register, “to bore”: both verbs move from the face to boredom. French Wiktionary says this sense was taken over from ~raser~, and English Wiktionary compares the same pair.
en.barbifier: Formed from ~barbe~ (“beard”) with the suffix ~-ifier~, which goes back to Latin ~-ficāre~ and ultimately to ~facere~ (“to make”). The noun ~barbe~ was inherited from Old French, from Latin ~barba~, from earlier *~farba~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰardʰeh₂~ (“beard”). The verb means to shave someone's beard.
en.barboter:
The origin of ~barboter~ is uncertain. English Wiktionary traces it to an earlier ~barbetter~ (“to dig about”), from Middle French ~borbeter~ (“to shake in the mud”), and French Wiktionary gives two Old French sources that were very probably confused with one another early on: ~bourbeter~ or ~bourbouter~ (“to wade in mud”) and ~barbeter~ (“to mutter in one's beard, to grumble”). It adds that the first of these goes back to Gaulish *~borua~ (“mud”), though this is a proposal and not a settled fact.

The competing explanations show how disputed the verb is. One is ~bourbe~ (“mud, mire”) through ~bourbouter~. Another is ~barbe~ (“beard”) plus a verbal ending. A third treats it as an onomatopoeic formation, and a last, judged less likely, links it to the fish name ~barbote~. Whatever the true path, the meaning that won out is that of paddling or splashing in water or mud, the sense of the modern verb. The two ancient words probably influenced each other in both sound and sense, so the quieter, muttering sense of ~barbeter~ and the muddy sense of ~bourbeter~ may both have left a mark. Related French words include ~bourbe~, ~bourbier~ (“quagmire”) and ~barbe~.
en.barbouiller:
The origin of ~barbouiller~ is unsettled, and the sources offer three accounts. French Wiktionary says it probably comes from ~barboter~, with the ending reshaped on the model of verbs such as ~souiller~, ~brouiller~, ~touiller~ and ~patrouiller~. Littré instead derived it from ~bouille~ (“mire, bog”), with the prefix ~bar-~ and the ending ~-er~. English Wiktionary gives a third account: the original meaning would have been “to dirty one's beard,” from ~barbe~. None of these is certain.

Whatever its source, ~barbouiller~ has long meant to smear or daub, whether with dirt, paint or ink. French Wiktionary also points out that Old French had ~barbouil~ as a variant of ~garbouil~ (“uproar”), a word that leads on to ~gribouiller~ (“to scribble”). The verb sits in a cluster of messy, splashing verbs: ~barboter~ (“to splash about”), ~brouiller~, ~souiller~.
en.barder: The origin of ~barder~ is debated. French Wiktionary gives two accounts. By one, the verb is derived from ~bard~ (“handbarrow, stretcher”) plus the first-group ending ~-er~. By the other, it comes from the Arabic ~barda~ (“packsaddle”). English Wiktionary offers a simpler derivation, from ~barde~ + ~-er~. French Wiktionary also points to the related words ~bardot~, ~barde~ and ~barda~. None of the sources explains how the modern sense, “to get rough,” developed, so this entry proposes no story for it.
en.barguigner: From Old French ~bargaignier~, whose own origin is disputed. French Wiktionary reports that some trace it to Medieval Latin ~barcaniare~ (“to trade”), while others derive it from Frankish *~borganjan~ (“to borrow, to hire”), crossed with *~waidanjan~ (“to gain”). English Wiktionary gives only the Frankish source. The Frankish word is linked to Old English ~borgian~ and German ~borgen~, and all of these are traced to the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰergʰ-~. In modern French, ~barguigner~ means “to hesitate,” and it survives mostly in the negative phrase ~sans barguigner~ (“without hesitating”). English Wiktionary invites a comparison with English ~bargain~ and Portuguese ~barganhar~.
en.barioler: Probably a cross in Old French between ~barré~ and ~riolé~, two near-synonyms that both meant “striped, motley.” French Wiktionary states the blend outright, while English Wiktionary says “probably,” so it is safest to treat it as likely but not certain. The verb means to paint or dress in garish, clashing colors, and its past participle ~bariolé~ is the more common form today.
en.barrer: Formed in French from ~barre~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~, “to close or block with a bar.” The noun ~barre~ comes from Old French ~barre~ (“beam, bar, barrier”), from Vulgar Latin *~barra~, whose origin is uncertain. French Wiktionary derives it from Gaulish *~barros~. English Wiktionary offers two rival accounts: a Frankish or Germanic source, or a Celtic one related to Breton ~barri~ (“branch”). The ending ~-er~ is the usual way of turning a noun into a verb.
en.barricader: ~Barricader~ is formed from ~barricade~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~: to block or fortify with a barricade. The noun is derived from ~barrique~ (“cask”) with the suffix ~-ade~, and means literally a barrier made of casks. French sources trace it to the 1570s, in the memoirs of the military commander Blaise de Monluc, and the TLFi points to a possible influence from ~barrer~ and from Middle French ~barriquer~ (“to close with casks”). The first street barricades in Paris were indeed built partly of casks filled with earth and paving stones.
en.barrir: From Old French ~barrire~, inherited from Late Latin ~barrīre~ (“to make the sound of an elephant”), itself a verb built on Latin ~barrus~ (“elephant”). The verb names the trumpeting cry of the elephant. The ending of the infinitive is the second-conjugation ~-ir~, which in this verb continues the Latin ending ~-īre~. The Latin noun ~barrus~ did not survive in French: the animal is called ~éléphant~, a different word. The cry has its own noun in ~barrissement~, formed from ~barrir~.
en.basaner: Formed in French from ~basane~ + the verb-forming suffix ~-er~. The noun names a soft leather made from tanned sheepskin, and it reached French from Occitan ~besana~ or ~basana~, from Old Spanish ~vatanna~ (modern ~badana~), from Arabic ~biṭāna~ (“lining, liner”) by way of Andalusian Arabic. French Wiktionary notes that the shift from ~batana~ to ~basane~ passed through a Provençal intermediary. To ~basaner~ is to give skin the dark, leathery look of ~basane~, that is, to tan it.
en.basculer: From Old French ~baculer~ (“to strike the backside against the ground”), built from ~bas~ (“low”), ~cul~ (“backside”) and the verb ending ~-er~; the sense is said to be to bump someone's bottom down. Both parts are old: ~bas~ from Late Latin ~bassus~, ~cul~ from Latin ~cūlus~. The modern spelling with a pronounced ~s~ shows the influence of the noun ~bascule~ (“seesaw”), which steered the verb toward tipping or swinging over like a balance, and then to figurative shifts from one state to another.
en.baser:
From the noun ~base~ with the suffix ~-er~ (15th century). The noun ~base~ comes, through Old French, from Latin ~basis~ (“pedestal, foundation”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~βάσις~ (“a step, that on which one stands”). The Greek noun belongs to the verb ~βαίνω~ (“to go, to walk, to step”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʷem-~ (“to go, to come”). Through that same root, ~base~ is distantly cognate with English ~come~ and Latin ~venire~ (“to come”).

The path of meaning is wonderfully concrete: a ~βάσις~ was first the act of stepping, then the thing one steps onto — a pedestal — and finally any foundation or supporting surface. From that physical sense the verb ~baser~ generalized to the abstract “to found, to ground,” as in an argument ~basé sur~ the evidence. The same Greek-Latin family yields a rich harvest in modern French: ~base~ in all its senses, ~basique~, ~baside~, and ~soubassement~ (“understructure”). English ~basis~, ~base~, and ~basement~ descend along the same line, making the French verb a near twin of an everyday English word.
en.bassiner: Formed from the noun ~bassin~ (“basin”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, in the sense of bathing something with a warm liquid. The noun comes from Old French ~bacin~, from Vulgar Latin ~baccinus~ or ~baccinum~, probably of Gaulish origin; French Wiktionary links it to a Gaulish *~bacca~ (“load, burden”) via Latin ~baccus~. French Wiktionary also records an older verb, Old French ~baciner~ (“to make a racket by banging on basins”), as a source for the modern word. The ~-er~ ending is the default way French turns a noun into a first-conjugation verb.
en.baster: Borrowed from Italian ~bastare~ (“to suffice”), attested in French from the 13th century. The Italian verb meant “to be enough,” and French ~baster~ kept that idea in an old sense, “to suffice” or “to give satisfaction.” Today it survives chiefly in Swiss French with the meaning “to give in, to yield,” as one does when one has had enough. Its form is close to the Italian interjection ~basta~ (“enough!”), which comes from the same verb.
en.batailler: ~Batailler~ is formed from the noun ~bataille~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Late Latin ~battālia~ (“combat, drill of soldiers or gladiators”), an altered form of ~battuālia~. According to English Wiktionary, that word goes back to Latin ~battuō~ (“to beat”), a word of Gaulish origin. The verb means to fight, to wage battle.
en.bateler: From Old French ~basteler~, itself derived from ~bastel~. The verb meant to juggle or conjure, to perform tricks like a street entertainer. The ~s~ of the Old French form fell silent and then dropped out of the spelling. The noun ~bateleur~, a street performer or mountebank, belongs to the same family. ~Bateler~ is now rare and old-fashioned.
en.batifoler:
Following Littré, ~batifoler~ comes from Italian ~battifolle~, which meant “rampart, bulwark,” a place where, as the dictionary puts it, young people went to amuse themselves. The Italian word in turn goes back to Late Latin ~batifollum~. The sources are unsure what that word denoted: in texts of Italian origin it seems to mean “bastion,” “war machine” or “belfry,” while in texts of French origin it appears to name a kind of mill.

The verb thus took a path from military architecture to play. The route is given by Littré only as the account of the word's origin, and the exact bridge from a fortification to idle fun is not documented in the sources, so it should be read as the traditional explanation, not as a settled fact. In modern French ~batifoler~ means to frolic, to fool around in a light-hearted way. The Late Latin ~batifollum~ is the oldest form the sources can reach.
en.battre:
From Latin ~battuere~ (“to beat, to strike, to thrash”), a verb almost certainly borrowed from Gaulish: native Latin words rarely begin with ~b-~, and the Celtic cousins are clear — Welsh ~bathu~ (“to coin money, to strike”), Old Breton ~bat~, and Irish ~bath~. The ultimate source is often traced to the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰewh₂-~ (“to strike”). Rare in classical literature but vigorous in spoken Latin, ~battuere~ flourished in the Romance languages: Italian ~battere~ and Spanish ~batir~ are its direct heirs, and English ~batter~, ~battle~, and ~battalion~ all reach back to it through French.

The word's most charming offshoot is Late Latin ~battuālia~ (“the beatings”), the name for the practice combats of gladiators and soldiers; this became Old French ~bataille~ and English ~battle~ — so every battle is, etymologically, a drill in striking. ~Battre~ stayed earthily concrete in French: to beat eggs, beat a drum, beat a rival, beat a path. From it spread a wide family — ~battement~, ~bataille~, ~batterie~ (whether of guns, of a kitchen, or of a drum kit), ~combattre~, ~débattre~, ~abattre~, and ~rabattre~. Even a heated ~débat~ is, at root, two sides beating at each other. A modest verb for hitting things turns out to underlie much of the vocabulary of conflict.
en.bavarder: ~Bavarder~ is derived from ~bavard~ (“talkative”) with the verb ending ~-er~. ~Bavard~ is built from Old French ~baver~, which already had the sense “to chatter,” plus the pejorative suffix ~-ard~. English Wiktionary relates ~baver~ to ~bave~ (“spittle”). The picture is of someone who drools words, and the verb means “to chat” or “to prattle.”
en.bavasser:
French Wiktionary gives two linked accounts. The verb is formed from ~baver~ (“to drool”), used figuratively for “to talk,” with the pejorative suffix ~-asse~ and the verb ending ~-er~. It is, however, probably borrowed directly from Occitan ~bavassar~, which meant “to spill a great deal of drool” and, by extension, “to talk at random.” The sources do not settle which route is right, and the two readings agree on the stem ~bav-~.

In either case the image is the same: chatter as drivel. The suffix ~-asse~ adds a note of contempt, so ~bavasser~ is not neutral speech but idle, rambling talk. The family is the French stock of words built on ~bave~ (“drool”), among them ~baver~ and ~baveux~. The linking of speech to drool is also found in ~bavard~ and ~bavarder~, which are generally taken to belong to the same family.
en.baver: ~Baver~ is formed from the noun ~bave~ (“drool, saliva”) with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is probably imitative, from a Vulgar Latin *~baba~ built on the baby-babble sound ~bab~, a root also seen in Spanish and Portuguese ~baba~. French Wiktionary mentions an alternative, a Gaulish word *~baua~ (“mud”). The verb means “to drool,” and it gave idioms such as ~en baver~, “to have a hard time,” and ~baver sur~, “to slander.”
en.bayer:
French ~bayer~ (“to gape”) is the surviving spelling of Old French ~beer~, which English Wiktionary derives from Early Medieval Latin ~batāre~ (“to gape”). French Wiktionary treats ~bayer~ more simply as a variant of ~bâiller~ (“to yawn”), which belongs to the same family of words about open mouths. The two verbs thus tell one story from two angles: a mouth that falls open, whether from sleepiness or wonder.

The old verb ~beer~ gave modern French several words that sound nothing like ~bayer~. Its participle survives in ~béant~ (“gaping, wide open”) and in the fixed phrase ~bouche bée~ (“open-mouthed, astonished”). The Occitan cousin of the same Latin root, ~badar~, produced ~badaud~ (“gawker, idle onlooker”), a person who stands gaping at whatever passes. As for ~bayer~ itself, it is nearly restricted today to a single idiom, ~bayer aux corneilles~ (“to stare vacantly into the air, literally to gape at crows”), and to its older sense in ~bayer à~ (“to long for”). The verb has largely given way to ~bâiller~, a fossil in a phrase about daydreaming.
en.bazarder: Formed from ~bazar~ with the verb ending ~-er~, plus an unetymological ~d~ inserted on the model of verbs built on nouns in ~-ard~, such as ~cafarder~ and ~hasarder~. To ~bazarder~ is to sell off, or to get rid of things cheaply, as if turning a home into a bazaar. ~Bazar~ is first attested around 1432 in Middle French, from Ottoman Turkish ~bazar~, from Persian ~bâzâr~ (“market”); French Wiktionary instead offers Persian or Arabic directly.
en.becqueter: Formed from ~bec~ (“beak”) with the suffix ~-eter~, or, by another reading, from ~becquer~ with the same suffix. The suffix ~-eter~ (~-et~ + ~-er~) often gives a diminutive or repeated action, so ~becqueter~ is to peck again and again, or to kiss in little pecks. The noun ~bec~ comes from Old French ~bec~, from Latin ~beccus~ (“beak,” first cited of a cock, in Suetonius), itself from Gaulish *~beccos~, from Proto-Celtic *~bekkos~. A Celtic word for the beak thus survived in French through Latin.
en.becter: ~Becter~ is an informal verb derived from ~bec~ (“beak”) with the verb ending ~-er~, and means to eat. It is related to ~becqueter~, which comes from the same noun. The noun ~bec~ is inherited from Old French and goes back to Latin ~beccus~ (“beak”), recorded for the beak of a cock. Latin took the word from Gaulish ~beccos~, from Proto-Celtic *~bekkos~, so a Celtic word for the beak ended up behind a French slang word for eating.
en.bedonner: ~Bedonner~ is formed from the noun ~bedon~ (“belly, paunch”) with the verbal ending ~-er~: to grow a belly. The origin of ~bedon~ is a variant of ~bedaine~ or else of Old French ~boudine~ (“navel”), a word in the family of an imitative stem *~bod-~, which also gave ~boudin~.
en.bercer:
The origin is debated. French Wiktionary treats ~bercer~ as a verb formed on Old French ~bers~ (“cradle”). English Wiktionary gives a different chain: Middle French, then Old French ~bercier~ (“to rock”), then a Vulgar Latin form *~bertiāre~, reaching Latin through Gaulish, from a Proto-Celtic root *~berta-~ (“to shake”) related to *~bereti~ (“to carry”). The two accounts agree that the word belongs to Old French and that its core idea is a rocking motion.

Whatever its source, ~bercer~ means to rock a child in a cradle, and from there it extends to soothe and lull. The figurative sense is the most familiar: ~bercer quelqu'un d'illusions~ is to lull someone with false hopes, and ~se bercer d'illusions~ is to feed oneself on them. Related words include ~berceau~ (“cradle”), ~berceuse~ (“lullaby”) and ~bercement~ (“rocking”).
en.berner: From Old French ~bren~ (“bran, excrement”), with the letters swapped around (metathesis) around the 1480s. The verb first meant to winnow grain, or, in a coarser sense found in Rabelais, to soil with excrement. The modern sense of making a fool of someone came later, and the sources sketch no path between the two, so none is claimed here. The coarse first sense is, however, the earliest one the evidence documents.
en.besogner: ~Besogner~ is the verb made from ~besogne~ (“work, task”) with the ending ~-er~, so it means to toil or drudge. ~Besogne~ is a variant of ~besoin~, which comes through Middle and Old French ~besoing~ from Vulgar Latin *~bisonium~, itself borrowed from Frankish *~bisunnija~. A word of Germanic origin thus lies under this very French verb of labor.
en.beugler:
From Old French ~bugle~ (with the verb form ~bugler~), itself borrowed from Latin ~buculus~ (“young bull”). In Latin ~buculus~ is a diminutive of ~bōs~ (“ox, cow”), so the verb began as the noise of cattle, and the modern meaning “to moo” or “to bellow” stays close to that source. The spelling ~beugler~ is the later form of ~bugler~.

From the cattle sound the verb widened to people and machines: a crowd, a singer or a loudspeaker can all ~beugler~, usually with a hint of scorn at a loud, coarse noise. The Old French word ~bugle~ also entered English, where ~bugle~ became the name of a brass horn. The ancestor ~bōs~ gave French ~bœuf~ (from its accusative ~bovem~), together with ~bovin~ and ~bouvier~, and English has a cousin in ~cow~. Thus ~beugler~ and ~bœuf~ are relatives that grew up on opposite sides of the same animal.
en.beurrer: ~Beurrer~ is a denominal verb: ~beurre~ (“butter”) plus the ending ~-er~, “to spread with butter.” The noun comes from Old French ~burre~, from Latin ~būtȳrum~, which borrowed Greek βούτυρον, literally “cow-cheese.” The modern form ~beurre~ is a regional variant, from the east or the west of the langue d'oïl, that replaced ~burre~ by the sixteenth century. English ~butter~ is a cousin loan from the same Latin and Greek word, so the two languages share one Mediterranean ancestor for the spread.
en.biaiser: ~Biaiser~ is a denominal verb formed from ~biais~ with the suffix ~-er~: to go at a slant, and then, figuratively, to skew or to hedge. The noun ~biais~ comes from Old Occitan ~biais~ (“oblique direction, detour”), whose own origin is uncertain. Several proposals exist. One, favored by the TLFi according to English Wiktionary, is a Vulgar Latin *~biaxius~ (“with two axes”). Another, from the scholar Diez via Littré, is Late Latin ~bifax~ (“having a double look, squinting”). A third is a Greek origin through Vulgar Latin. None is settled.
en.biberonner: Formed from the noun ~biberon~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. It means “to feed from a baby bottle” and, colloquially, “to drink heavily,” as if one were always at the bottle. French Wiktionary also points to ~bibine~ for the drinking sense. The base ~biberon~ is built on Latin ~bibere~ (“to drink”) plus the suffix ~-on~, so the whole family descends from the Latin verb for drinking.
en.bicher: ~Bicher~ is inherited from Old French ~bécher~ (“to bite”), said of a fish taking the bait, itself from Latin ~beccus~ (“beak, bill”). The same Latin noun lies behind French ~bec~. Both Wiktionaries give this chain, though French Wiktionary flags the claim as needing a better reference. The sources do not say how a biting fish became the modern, informal sense of things going well, so no story is offered here.
en.bichonner: Formed from ~bichon~ (“lap dog”) with the verb ending ~-er~. The base has two proposed origins. By one account, ~bichon~ comes from Middle French and ultimately from Old French ~biche~ (“bitch”), of Germanic origin. By the other, French Wiktionary's, it is a clipping of ~barbichon~, a small shaggy dog. The English account judges the second unlikely on chronology, since ~bichon~ is attested before ~barbichon~. The verb ~bichonner~ means “to groom, to spruce up,” and its link to the dog is the one named by the base.
en.bidonner: ~Bidonner~ is a denominal from ~bidon~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~bidon~ has two senses behind two verbs: a jug or, in slang, a belly, and deception; the sense “to fabricate, make up” goes with the second. ~Bidon~ itself probably comes from Old Norse ~bida~ (“container, vessel”) by way of Norman. It is traced further to Proto-Germanic *~bidōn~ (“tub, vessel”), with Icelandic ~biða~ (“milk bucket”) as a cognate.
en.bidouiller: ~Bidouiller~ is formed from the noun ~bidouille~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, the standard way of coining a first-conjugation verb from a noun. English Wiktionary glosses ~bidouille~ as a dialectal word meaning “idiot”; the sources say nothing more about its origin. The verb itself means to fiddle or tinker with something.
en.bienvenir: French Wiktionary treats ~bienvenir~ as a compound of ~bien~ and ~venir~, where ~bien~ comes from Latin ~bene~ (“well”). English Wiktionary offers a different account: a back-formation from ~bienvenu~, which was itself a calque of a Frankish term, from Proto-Germanic *~wiljakumô~ (“welcome guest”). Either way, the verb means to welcome, literally to make someone's coming a good one.
en.biffer:
The origin of ~biffer~ is debated, and the sources give two accounts. French Wiktionary says it probably comes from Latin ~findere~ (“to split, to cleave”), in the sense of scoring a line through something. It also offers a second possibility, that the verb comes from Old French ~biffe~. English Wiktionary favors this second route and analyzes ~biffer~ as ~biffe~ (“stripe”) plus the verbal ending ~-er~.

If the Latin account is right, ~biffer~ is a distant relative of the inherited French verb ~fendre~ and of the learned ~fissure~, both from ~findere~. If the Old French account is right, it is a French verb built on a stripe or a mark, and the sense follows directly: to draw a line through a word is to put a stripe across it. Modern French uses ~biffer~ for crossing out, striking from a list or cancelling an entry. Since neither account is settled, the verb is best treated as having a probable but unproven source.
en.bifurquer: ~Bifurquer~ is a verb built on Latin ~bifurcus~ (“two-pronged”), itself made of ~bis~ (“twice”) and ~furca~ (“fork”). The Latin ~furca~ is also the source of French ~fourche~. The verb describes a road or a river dividing into two branches, like the two tines of a fork.
en.bigarrer: The origin of ~bigarrer~ is uncertain. French Wiktionary says it is probably made of ~bi-~ and Old French ~garre~, while English Wiktionary reads it as ~bis~ (“twice”) plus a form *~garrer~, from Middle French ~garre~ (“of two colors”). The deeper origin of ~garre~ is itself unclear, and one suggestion is a borrowing from Occitan or Provençal, ultimately of Germanic origin. It is rare as a verb, and survives chiefly in its participle ~bigarré~ (“motley, multicolored”) and the noun ~bigarrure~. English owes ~bigarade~, the name of the bitter orange, to the same French family.
en.bigler: ~Bigler~ is derived from ~bigle~ (“squinting”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, and means to squint or to glance sideways. The origin of ~bigle~ is uncertain. One account traces it to Latin *~bisoculāre~, from ~bis~ (“twice”) and ~oculus~ (“eye”), through Middle French ~biscler~; Littré called this etymology doubtful, and another source gives Old French ~bigre~ (“cross-eyed”) of unknown origin.
en.bigophoner: Formed in 1965 from ~bigophone~. The ~bigophone~ is a novelty instrument, a kind of kazoo, named in 1881 after its inventor Romain Bigot and the element ~-phone~. The verb first meant “to play the bigophone,” a rare use. As French slang it came to mean “to telephone,” a pun on ~-phone~, which also ends ~téléphone~.
en.bigorner: ~Bigorner~ is formed from the noun ~bigorne~ and the verb ending ~-er~. ~Bigorne~ is the name of a two-beaked anvil. It came through Old Occitan ~bigorna~ from Latin ~bicornis~ (“two-horned”), which makes it a doublet of ~bicorne~. The verb's senses, “to forge” and “to hit,” both fit the work done on an anvil.
en.biler: ~Biler~ is the verb that grew out of the expression ~se faire de la bile~ (“to worry”), and it shortens it to a single word: to fret. The noun ~bile~ is the digestive fluid, from Latin ~bilis~. The verb is chiefly used in the reflexive and in negative commands, such as telling someone not to worry.
en.biner:
~Biner~ comes from Vulgar Latin ~bīnāre~ (“to do something twice; to work the land twice”). Latin ~bīnāre~ is a derivative of ~bīnī~ (“two each, two at a time”), which belongs to ~bis~ (“twice”). French Wiktionary adds a second sense of the Latin verb, “to say two masses.” Spanish ~binar~ (“to plow over”) is a cognate, so the Latin idea of repeating a job a second time lives on across the Romance languages.

In French, ~biner~ means to hoe, that is, to loosen the topsoil with a hoe between rows of crops, a task that gardeners call a second working of the ground. The noun ~binage~ names the job and ~binette~ the tool. The word also keeps its religious sense: a priest who ~bine~ says two masses on the same day. Its Latin root ~bis~ survives in French ~bis~ (“encore”, “twice”), and the learned adjective ~binaire~ and English ~binary~ and ~binate~ come from the related Latin ~bīnī~ family.
en.biologiser: ~Biologiser~ is formed from ~biologie~ with the suffix ~-iser~, and means “to analyze from a strictly biological point of view.” The base ~biologie~ was coined in French by Jean-Baptiste Lamarck in 1802, perhaps modeled on German ~Biologie~; either way it is built from Greek ~bíos~ (“life”) and ~-logía~ (“study”). The suffix ~-iser~ gives the verb its “treat everything as N” sense.
en.biper: Formed from ~bip~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to beep.” French ~bip~ was borrowed from English ~beep~, a short sound, and is of onomatopoeic origin. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is the default way French turns a noun into a verb.
en.biscuiter: Built from ~biscuit~ with the verb ending ~-er~. ~Biscuit~ is a learned reshaping of Old French ~bescuit~, from Early Medieval Latin ~biscoctus~ (“twice-baked”), made of ~bis-~ (“twice”) and ~cuit~. In pottery the verb means to fire clay a first time without glaze, the earthenware being baked “twice-cooked” fashion.
en.biseauter: Formed in French from ~biseau~ (“bevel”) and the ending ~-er~, with a ~-t-~ inserted between the vowel-final base and the ending to avoid a hiatus. The verb means “to cut at a bevel.” The origin of ~biseau~ itself is uncertain. French Wiktionary suggests a diminutive of ~biais~ (“slant”), while English Wiktionary proposes Old French *~besel~, perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *~bisalus~ (“stone with two sides”).
en.biser: ~Biser~ is a western dialectal variant of ~baiser~ (“to kiss”). The standard verb ~baiser~ comes from Latin ~basiāre~, itself from ~basium~ (“kiss”), so ~biser~ is the same word in a regional vowel, preserved in the speech of western France. The change from ~a~ to ~i~ is a dialect trait that the sources do not describe further.
en.bisquer:
The origin of ~bisquer~ is not settled. French Wiktionary derives it from Occitan ~biscar~ (“to pester”) and refers to the related expression ~bisque, bisque, rage~. The Trésor de la langue française, by contrast, suggests a different path, from the bad reputation of the people of Biscay, though English Wiktionary labels the origin as unclear.

Whichever account is right, the verb is informal. It means to be peeved or to sulk at a setback, often in the phrase ~faire bisquer~ (“to vex someone”). The expression ~bisque, bisque, rage~ is a taunt in the same family, the sort of thing one says to tease someone who is annoyed. Because the two accounts give different families for the word, an Occitan verb of pestering on one side and an ethnic nickname on the other, the safest statement is that its origin remains open.
en.bisser: Formed from ~bis~ (“twice”) with the verb ending ~-er~, it means to repeat, above all to call for an encore or to perform one. French ~bis~ in this sense is a learned borrowing from Latin ~bis~ (“twice”). It is unrelated to the adjective ~bis~ (“greyish”), a different word of uncertain origin, which French Wiktionary connects with Italian ~bigio~. So when an audience cried ~bis~, it asked in Latin for the piece to be played twice, and French then turned the cry into a verb.
en.bistourner: French Wiktionary derives ~bistourner~ from ~tourner~ with the prefix ~bis-~, noting an Old French form ~bestorner~. The base ~tourner~ comes from Latin ~tornāre~ (“to turn on a lathe”), from ~tornus~, a borrowing from Greek ~tórnos~ (“lathe”). The usual French prefix ~bis-~ is Latin ~bis~ (“twice”), but the sources do not say that the ~bis-~ of ~bistourner~ has that sense, and the Old French form suggests it may be another element. So the verb, “to twist,” is best read as a turning in a wrong or bent direction, with the prefix of uncertain value.
en.bistrer: ~Bistrer~ is derived from ~bistre~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun names a brown pigment, and the verb means to color or darken something as if with it, hence to tan or blacken. The origin of ~bistre~ itself is unknown: it is attested since the sixteenth century, and the tempting link with ~bis~ (“grayish brown”) is considered problematic. The verb therefore rests on a word whose own history is a mystery.
en.biter: In France the verb comes from the slang of the École Polytechnique and is built on the noun ~bite~, a coarse slang word. Its meanings include “to understand” and “to humiliate”. In Quebec French, a separate account derives it from the English verb ~beat~ (“to beat”), so two origins stand side by side for the same spelling, one by derivation from a French noun and the other by borrowing from English.
en.bitter: The origin of ~bitter~, a slang verb meaning “to understand,” is uncertain, and French Wiktionary gives two competing accounts. By one, it is the Old French ~bitter~ (“to take”), probably a variant of ~butter~. By the other, it comes from the slang of the École polytechnique, where it meant “to punish,” and is derived from ~bitte~ with the ending ~-er~, following the same course as ~baiser~. The sources offered do not decide between the two, and neither tells how the modern sense “to understand” arose from it.
en.bitturer: A verb formed from the noun ~bitture~ with the ending ~-er~, in the pattern “to do or undergo what the noun names.” Here it means to get drunk, or to go on a drinking bout. The sources give no further origin for ~bitture~, so the history of the word stops at this French derivation.
en.bitumer: ~Bitumer~ is formed from the noun ~bitume~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, and means “to coat with bitumen, to asphalt.” ~Bitume~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~bitūmen~ (“bitumen”), which replaced the Old French ~betun~. That older form followed the regular path of sound change and became ~béton~ (“concrete”), so ~bitume~ and ~béton~ are doublets: one word, borrowed twice at different times.
en.biturer: ~Biturer~ (usually pronominal, ~se biturer~, “to get drunk”) is a variant of ~bitturer~. That verb is a denominal from ~bitture~, a noun recorded in 1515 and built on ~bitter~ with the suffix ~-ure~. ~Bitter~ is the nautical verb meaning to wind a cable round the bitts, the strong posts on a ship's deck. So the drinking verb comes out of the vocabulary of sailors' rope-work, though the sources do not explain how the sense moved from cable to drunkenness.
en.bivouaquer: Formed from the noun ~bivouac~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, so “to bivouac” is literally to make a bivouac. The noun reached French through Swiss mercenaries from Alemannic German ~Biiwacht~ (“a patrol of citizens added to the regular town watch in time of alarm”), made of ~bii-~ (“by-”) and ~Wacht~ (“watch, guard”). French Wiktionary links it to German ~biwacht~ (“guard”), from ~bewachen~ (“to guard”). Other European languages adopted the word mainly during the Napoleonic wars, from the form ~bivac~, which was the usual spelling before the mid-nineteenth century.
en.bizuter: From ~bizut~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, in the sense of subjecting a ~bizut~ to hazing. The noun ~bizut~ is school slang for a newcomer, and its own origin is uncertain. One possibility is a derivation from ~bisogne~ (“recruit, new soldier”), a word borrowed from Spanish and used from the mid-16th to the early 17th century, though that raises phonetic and chronological difficulties. Another is a loan from Franco-Provençal ~bésu~ (“inexperienced”) or ~bésule~ (“new student”), which also seems unlikely. The verb is thus a plain French derivation resting on a base of unknown origin.
en.blablater: ~Blablater~ is formed from the noun ~blabla~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~, in the sense of “to produce ~blabla~”: to chatter on with little to say. The writer Louis-Ferdinand Céline was one of the first to use the verb in a novel, according to French Wiktionary.
en.blackbouler:
~Blackbouler~ is a partial calque of English ~blackball~: the first half is the English ~black~ (“black”), the second the French ~boule~ (“ball”). It is not an inherited French word but a hybrid, half borrowed and half translated, and it means to vote against someone, to reject a candidate for a club or an office.

The image behind it is probably Masonic, though the sources say only “probably.” According to this account, when a candidate is proposed for initiation, the brethren vote with white balls (for) and black balls (against). A single black ball often counts for several white ones, so a candidate who draws more black than white is turned down. To be ~blackboulé~ is therefore to be refused entry. The same ~boule~ is the everyday French word for a ball or a round object, and the voting practice explains why a mere ball could decide a person's fate.
en.blaguer: ~Blaguer~ is a denominal verb: ~blague~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~blague~ was borrowed in the 18th century from Dutch ~balg~ (“envelope”) and first meant a tobacco pouch; it is recorded in a chemistry dictionary by Cadet de Gassicourt. In 1809 the sense “joke” was added, from the idea of something puffed up or swollen. The verb ~blaguer~ thus means to joke, with an etymological image of inflated talk.
en.blairer: Formed from ~blair~ and the ending ~-er~. The noun ~blair~ is slang for “nose,” a shortening of ~blaireau~, an old slang word for a nose. The verb is used almost only in the negative, ~ne pas pouvoir blairer~, “not to be able to stand someone,” and draws on the slang noun for nose.
en.blanchir:
From Old French ~blanchir~, from Vulgar Latin *~blancīre~, a verb built on Frankish *~blank~ (“shining, white”). French Wiktionary simply treats it as formed from ~blanc~; the two accounts agree, since ~blanc~ itself comes from the same Frankish word. The Franks' *~blank~ pushed aside Latin ~albus~ in Gaul, which survives only in a few remnants such as ~aube~ (“dawn”) and ~albâtre~. Italian ~bianco~ and Spanish ~blanco~ are siblings of ~blanc~, and English ~blank~ was borrowed from French ~blanc~.

The meaning of ~blanchir~ spread outward from “to make white.” One can ~blanchir~ linen, walls with lime, or vegetables by plunging them briefly into boiling water, and English ~blanch~ was borrowed from this French verb. Hair turns white with age, hence the idiom ~blanchi sous le harnais~, “grown grey under the harness,” of someone who has aged in a long career. A defendant is ~blanchi~ when cleared of suspicion, and money is ~blanchi~ when its criminal origin is hidden. The family includes ~blanchisserie~, ~blanchiment~ and ~blanchâtre~.
en.blaser: Borrowed from Dutch ~blazen~, which French Wiktionary glosses “to swell” and English Wiktionary traces back to Middle Dutch ~blâsen~ (“to blow, sound, brag”), from Old Dutch *~blāsan~ and Proto-West Germanic *~blāsan~ (“to blow”). German ~blasen~ (“to blow”) and English ~blast~ are cognates. The sources do not explain how a verb of blowing or swelling came to mean “to blunt, to dull,” so no story is offered here. The participle ~blasé~, said of someone dulled by excess, is the form most people know, and English borrowed it too.
en.blasonner: ~Blasonner~ is formed from the noun ~blason~ and the ending ~-er~, with the sense “to describe or depict a coat of arms in the technical language of heraldry.” The noun comes from Middle French ~blason~, which inherited the Old French word ~blason~ meaning “shield, escutcheon.” The shield, the thing that bore the arms, thus gave its name to the arms themselves and then to the art of describing them. From that sense, ~blasonner~ is used for any careful description of arms.
en.blasphémer:
From Old French ~blasfemer~, borrowed from Late Latin ~blasphēmāre~. The Latin verb itself comes from Ancient Greek ~blasphēmeîn~ (“to speak ill, to slander”), a word that, in Christian Latin, came to mean speaking impiously about God or sacred things. Related forms are found across Romance languages and in English: Italian ~bestemmiare~, Spanish ~blasfemar~ and English ~blaspheme~.

The verb has a surprising double in French. ~Blâmer~ (“to blame”) is a doublet of ~blasphémer~: both go back to the same Late Latin word, but ~blâmer~ was inherited and worn down over centuries of popular speech, while ~blasphémer~ was borrowed in a learned form and kept most of its Latin and Greek shape. The meanings also drifted apart. ~Blâmer~ now means to disapprove of someone for any fault, while ~blasphémer~ keeps a strictly religious force: to insult God or what a faith holds sacred. From ~blasphémer~ come ~blasphème~ and ~blasphémateur~, and English ~blame~ is itself borrowed from the same source as ~blâmer~.
en.blatérer: From Latin ~blaterāre~, which French Wiktionary explains as an imitation of sound (an onomatopoeia). The Latin verb meant to babble or prattle, and Italian has the same verb, ~blaterare~, with a similar sense of chattering on. In modern French, ~blatérer~ describes the cry of certain animals, the bleating of sheep or the braying of a camel, and it also applies to people who talk loudly and foolishly.
en.blesser:
From Old French ~blecier~ (“to bruise, to injure”), from Gallo-Romance *~blettiare~ (“to make bruised, to make soft like overripe fruit”). The ultimate source is Germanic: Frankish, from Proto-West Germanic *~blaitijan~ (“to bruise, to make discoloured”), a factitive verb formed on *~blait~ (“pale, livid, discoloured”) with the causative suffix *~-jan~. The same Germanic root surfaces in Old English ~blātian~ (“to grow pale”).

The original image was vivid and physical: to ~blesser~ was to mark flesh with the dull, discoloured patch of a bruise — the very softness an apple shows when it turns ~blet~ (“overripe, bruised”), a French word from the same Germanic family. Over time the verb shifted from this narrow sense of bruising toward the general meanings “to wound” and “to injure,” whether by blade, bullet, or accident. By extension it also came to mean “to hurt” emotionally: harsh words can ~blesser~ as surely as a weapon, and one speaks of ~amour-propre blessé~ (“wounded pride”). Related French words include the noun ~blessure~ (“wound, injury”) and the participle ~blessé~ used as a noun for a casualty or injured person.
en.blettir: The verb ~blettir~ (“to overripen”) comes from the adjective ~blet~, feminine ~blette~, which describes fruit that has gone soft and overripe. It follows the usual pattern of the ~-ir~ verbs built on adjectives, which mean “to become” what the adjective says, as with ~grandir~ (“to grow”) and ~blêmir~ (“to turn pale”). The sources trace it no further back than ~blet~, so the verb is best seen as a French formation: a fruit that is ~blet~ is one that ~blettit~.
en.bleuir: Formed from the adjective ~bleu~ (“blue”) with the verb ending ~-ir~, in the usual sense “to make or become A”: ~bleuir~ means to turn something blue or to go blue. The adjective is Germanic in origin. It descends from Old French ~bleu~ and Late Latin ~blāvus~, borrowed from Frankish *~blāu~, from Proto-Germanic *~blēwaz~. Its cognates include German ~blau~ and Dutch ~blauw~, and English ~blue~ is a loan from Anglo-Norman. French also uses ~bleu~ in oaths such as ~corbleu~ as a euphemism for ~Dieu~ (“God”).
en.blinder: Formed from ~blinde~ with the verbal suffix ~-er~. A ~blinde~ was a timber piece used to cover a trench, and the word is a borrowing from German ~Blende~, itself from ~blenden~ (“to dazzle, to blind”). The verb is built on this protective sense of ~blinde~.
en.blistériser: ~Blistériser~ means to put tablets or small goods in a blister pack. It is formed on the noun ~blister~ with the verbal suffix ~-iser~, which turns a noun into a verb of treating or putting into something. No dictionary consulted has an entry for the verb itself. French ~blister~ is borrowed from English ~blister~, which French Wiktionary traces to Old French ~blestre~. In packaging the noun names a card or plastic sheet, often printed, fitted with a transparent plastic shell. The verb belongs to the vocabulary of the packaging trade.
en.bloguer:
~bloguer~ offers one of the shortest etymological chains in French. It is formed on the noun ~blog~ with the verbal suffix ~-er~, and ~blog~ was borrowed from English at the turn of the millennium — French dictionaries date the noun to 1999 and the verb to the years just after. English ~blog~ is itself a clipping of ~weblog~, a compound of ~web~ and ~log~; that ~log~ is the sailor’s word, the ship’s record named for the piece of wood once trailed overboard to gauge a vessel’s speed. ~weblog~ was coined in 1997 by Jorn Barger; ~blog~ was cut out of it on 23 May 1999 by Peter Merholz, who divided ~weblog~ in the wrong place — as though it read ~we blog~ — and so made a verb visible inside a noun. The joke stuck, and the derivative ~blog~ all but buried ~weblog~.

The verb’s real story is orthographic. French had to decide how to write an English monosyllable in a language where ~g~ before ~e~ or ~i~ is soft: ~bloger~ would rhyme with ~loger~. The solution is the digraph ~gu-~, already used by ~blaguer~ and ~naviguer~, which keeps the hard sound through the whole paradigm — ~nous bloguons~, ~en bloguant~.
