In 2006 the Office québécois de la langue française said so explicitly, recommending ~bloguer~ and judging ~blogger~, ~bloger~ and ~blogguer~ poorly adapted to French morphology; Quebec also prefers the noun ~blogue~ to ~blog~. France largely kept ~blog~ for the noun while adopting the same ~-guer~ verb, so a French sentence can now pair ~blog~ with ~bloguer~ — a visible seam left by two different answers to the same question. The family that grew up around it is wholly French in shape: ~blogueur~, ~blogosphère~, ~blogage~ and the playful ~blogouiller~.
en.blondir: Formed from the adjective ~blond~ with the verb ending ~-ir~, the ending that turns an adjective into a verb of becoming, so “to turn blond.” In cooking it means “to brown lightly,” and the verb can also mean “to dye blond.” English Wiktionary traces ~blond~ through Medieval Latin ~blondus~ to a probable Frankish *~blund~, and French Wiktionary also says “perhaps” Old Frankish *~blŭnd~, so the Germanic origin is likely but not certain. Italian ~biondo~ and Occitan ~blon~ are relatives.
en.bloquer:
French ~bloquer~ is a denominal verb, coined in the fifteenth century from the noun ~bloc~ (“block, log”) — or its military relative ~blocus~. The noun ~bloc~ is not Latin at all: Old French ~bloc~ was taken from Middle Dutch ~blok~ (“tree-trunk”), from Proto-Germanic *~blukką~ (“beam, log”), traced by many to the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰelǵ-~ (“plank, beam”). The same Germanic word gave English ~block~ and German ~Block~, so ~bloquer~ and to ~block~ are, satisfyingly, the very same word doing the same job in two languages.

The semantics follow the wood. To set a ~bloc~ in a doorway is to jam it shut, and from that ~bloquer~ generalized to stopping, jamming, or barricading anything — a road, a door, an account, a salary, a negotiation, or, in football, an opponent. French also distinguishes the borrowed Dutch ~blokken~ (“to cram, to swot”) in some dialects, but the mainstream verb is wholly about obstruction. From the same block of wood come ~blocage~ (“blocking, a mental block”), ~débloquer~ (“to unblock, to release funds”), ~blocus~ (“blockade”), and the borrowed-back ~blockhaus~ — a whole family piled up, log upon log, from one Germanic ~bloc~.
en.blottir: The origin of ~blottir~ is unknown, and the sources offer two proposals, each given only as probable. One is German ~blotten~ or ~blotzen~ (“to crush”), a verb poorly attested in German; English Wiktionary similarly suggests, with a “perhaps,” Middle Low German ~blotten~. The other is Old French ~bloste~ (“clod of earth”), supported by a comparison with hunting language: a partridge is said to ~se blottir~, and in some provinces to be ~mottée~. Neither account is established, so the safest summary is that the word is of uncertain origin. Today ~se blottir~ means to snuggle up or huddle against something.
en.blouser: ~Blouser~ is a derivative of ~blouse~ with the ending ~-er~. In billiards, ~blouse~ is the pocket, and the reflexive ~se belouzer~ is recorded in 1654 for putting a ball in a pocket, then as ~blouser~ in 1680. That same year the popular reflexive ~se blouser~ already means “to be mistaken,” and a transitive use is recorded since the 1798 Académie. A second, separate ~blouser~ is recorded in 1935 and means “to puff out like a blouse.”
en.bluffer: ~Bluffer~ is borrowed from the English verb ~bluff~, adapted to French by the usual first-conjugation ending ~-er~. It entered French as a modern loan, first for the card-player's trick of feigning strength. In French it also took the extended sense “to astonish, to take by surprise,” as when a result bluffs someone.
en.bluter:
~Bluter~ is a Germanic loan. Old French had ~beluter~, attested down to the seventeenth century, alongside a syncopated ~bluter~ that appeared in the fourteenth. English Wiktionary gives Middle French ~buleter~ and ~beluter~, from Middle High German ~biuteln~, itself from ~biūtel~ (“sifting device”). That word goes back to Old High German ~butil~ (“pouch, bag”), from Proto-Germanic *~buzdô~ (“beetle, grub, swelling”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰūs-~ (“to move quickly”).

German has the verb ~beuteln~ and the noun ~Beutel~ (“bag, pouch”), and Dutch ~buidel~ is a cognate. English Wiktionary also compares Galician ~barutar~ and Italian ~burattare~. In French, ~bluter~ means to sift flour, and the tool for it is the ~blutoir~ (“sifting machine”). The verb also gave the nouns ~blutage~ (“sifting”) and ~bluterie~, the part of a mill where the flour is sifted.
en.blâmer:
~Blâmer~ comes from Old French ~blasmer~, which French Wiktionary traces to a Popular Latin form *~blastemare~, an alteration of Latin ~blasphemare~. English Wiktionary agrees, giving Late Latin ~blastēmāre~ as a variant of ~blasphēmāre~. The Latin verb ~blasphēmāre~ itself comes from Greek. The altered form also left cousins in other Romance languages, such as Italian ~bestemmiare~ and Romanian ~blestema~.

The circumflex on ~blâmer~ is a trace of a lost letter: the ~s~ of Old French ~blasmer~ stopped being pronounced and was replaced by the accent. French thus holds a pair of doublets from one source, ~blâmer~, the word handed down by speech, and ~blasphémer~, the learned word borrowed directly from Latin. The two diverged in meaning. ~Blasphémer~ kept the religious sense of speaking impiously, while ~blâmer~ moved to the general sense of criticizing or finding fault with. English ~blame~ came from Old French ~blasmer~, another general-knowledge point, and ~blaspheme~ is the learned cousin.
en.bléser: ~Bléser~, “to lisp,” goes back to Latin ~blaesus~ (“stammering, lisping”) through the Old French adjective ~blez~ or ~blois~. The verb was once ~bloisir~, and it was remade with the first-conjugation ending ~-er~ to give the modern form. The Latin adjective described a person who could not pronounce certain sounds clearly. French Wiktionary glosses it as “stammerer,” whereas the modern verb names the specific speech fault of lisping.
en.blêmir:
From Old French ~blesmir~, a Germanic loan. The sources differ on the exact donor. English Wiktionary gives Frankish *~blesmijan~ or *~blasmijan~ (“to grow pale; make pale”), from Proto-Germanic *~blasaz~ (“shining, white, pale”) and the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰel-~ (“to shine, be white”). French Wiktionary instead proposes Old Low Frankish *~blasmi~ or Old Norse *~blami~. Either way the word is related to German ~blass~ (“pale”), English ~blaze~ and ~bleach~, and Dutch ~bles~ (“white mark”).

The Old French ~blesmir~ became ~blêmir~ when the ~s~ fell silent and left a circumflex behind. The verb means to turn pale, from fear, illness or emotion, and it is also used of a light that fades to a wan glow. It is one of the verbs in ~-ir~ that mean “become” plus a color or quality, though here the Germanic base is no longer a separate French word. The adjective ~blême~ (“pale, wan”) and the noun ~blêmissement~ belong to the same family. English ~blaze~, in its older sense of a white mark on an animal's face, shares the root, as does Dutch ~bles~, so a pale face and a horse's white star are cousins.
en.bobiner: Formed from ~bobine~ (“bobbin, spool”) plus the verbal suffix ~-er~, with the sense “to wind thread onto a spool.” The origin of ~bobine~ is debated. The Trésor de la Langue Française considers it more likely to come from an imitative root ~bob~, evoking the movement of the lips and hence something swollen or cylindrical. Older scholars proposed Latin ~bombyx~ (“silkworm”) or ~bombus~ (“buzzing”), and English Wiktionary suggests Latin ~balbus~.
en.bocarder: Formed from ~bocard~ with the verb ending ~-er~: to ~bocarder~ is to crush ore in a stamp mill, a ~bocard~. The noun was borrowed from German ~Pochwerk~ (“stamp mill”), itself from ~pochen~ (“to crush, to pound”). The verb is a technical term of mining.
en.boire:
From Old French ~boivre~ (also ~beivre~, ~bevvre~), from Latin ~bibere~ (“to drink”). The Latin verb goes back to Proto-Italic *~pibō~, a reduplicated form whose initial ~p~ voiced to ~b~, and ultimately to the Proto-Indo-European root *~peh₃-~ (“to drink”). The kinship is spectacular: Sanskrit ~píbati~, Ancient Greek ~πῑ́νω~ (~pī́nō~), and Proto-Slavic *~piti~ all descend from the same root, as does — through a sister formation — Latin ~pōtiō~, source of English ~potion~.

The phonetic history is a small drama. The Old French stem ~bev-~ underwent labialization, passing through ~beuv-~ to ~buv-~, which is why the modern verb shifts shape across its conjugation: ~je bois~ but ~nous buvons~, ~ils boivent~ but ~je buvais~. The older ~beuv-~ form fossilized in ~beuverie~ (“drinking bout”). The same root waters a whole field of French words: ~boisson~, ~breuvage~, ~buvable~, ~buvette~, ~buveur~, and ~pourboire~ (literally “for drinking,” a tip). The everyday act named here is, etymologically, one of humanity's oldest spoken words.
en.boiser: ~Boiser~ is formed from ~bois~ (“wood”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, in the sense “to provide with wood”, which covers lining a room with panels and planting an area with trees. The noun ~bois~ comes through Middle and Old French from Early Medieval Latin ~boscus~ (“grove”), borrowed from Frankish *~busk~, from Proto-Germanic *~buskaz~. Its cognates include Italian ~bosco~, Spanish ~bosque~, Dutch ~bos~, German ~Busch~ (“bush”) and English ~bush~.
en.boiter:
From the root of Old French ~boiteux~ (“lame, limping”), ultimately tied to ~boîte~ in its old anatomical sense of the socket or cavity of a joint. The TLFi traces a derivational chain through the attested ~boistoier~ (1358) and ~boister~ (1539), the latter form supplanting the older one before settling into the modern ~boiter~. Old French and Walloon used ~boîte~ for the hollow of an articulation, so to deboiter a limb was to knock it out of its socket and to ~boiter~ was to walk on a joint that no longer sat right.

The deeper origin of ~boîte~ itself is debated, so etymologists hedge the ultimate source; what is well documented is the joint-socket image at the heart of the word. The picture is vivid: a limp framed not as weakness but as a bone riding loose in its housing. The same family gives modern French ~déboîter~, said both of a dislocated shoulder and of a car pulling out of its lane, and ~emboîter~, to fit one thing snugly into another — every one of them turning on the idea of a part seated, or unseated, in its socket.
en.boitiller: ~Boitiller~ is formed from ~boiter~ (“to limp”) with the diminutive suffix ~-iller~. The suffix softens the meaning of the base, so the verb means to limp slightly, to walk with a faint hitch. French and English Wiktionary both describe it as a diminutive of ~boiter~. The same suffix appears in other verbs of small or repeated action, such as ~sautiller~ and ~mordiller~.
en.bombarder: Formed from the noun ~bombarde~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Middle French ~bombarde~, which named an early cannon or mortar, a catapult, and also a bassoon-like wind instrument. It goes back to Latin ~bombus~ (“buzzing, booming”), a word imitating a deep sound. To ~bombarder~ was first to fire a bombard at a target, then to shell with any projectile, and figuratively to bombard someone with questions.
en.bomber: The sources give two accounts of ~bomber~. French Wiktionary lists it first as formed from ~bombe~ + ~-er~, and English Wiktionary gives only that account. ~Bombe~ was borrowed from Italian ~bomba~, from Latin ~bombus~ (“a boom”). French Wiktionary also offers a second origin for the verb, from Occitan ~bombar~ (“to leap, to rebound, to strike”). The two accounts are not settled against each other. The modern noun ~bomber~, from English, is a separate word.
en.bondir:
From Old French ~bondir~, earlier ~bundir~ (“to resound, to echo”), from Vulgar Latin *~bombitīre~, a variant of *~bombitāre~, a frequentative of Latin ~bombīre~ (“to buzz, to hum”). Behind it stands ~bombus~ (“the buzzing of bees, a booming noise”), a sound-imitating word that Latin borrowed from Greek ~bómbos~. The same Latin noun came through Italian ~bomba~ into French ~bombe~ and English ~bomb~, so a leaping verb and an explosive share an ancestor that began as a deep hum.

The odd part is the meaning. In the thirteenth century ~bondir~ shifted from “to resound” to “to jump, to spring.” French Wiktionary explains the change as a shift of register: the auditory impression of sounds rising and falling gave way to a visual impression of the same rhythm, as with a ball that bounces and rebounds. Modern French uses ~bondir~ for a leap, for a start of surprise, and figuratively for anger or joy, as when someone leaps in indignation. Its family includes the noun ~bond~ (“leap”), ~rebondir~ (“to bounce back, to take a new turn”), ~rebond~ and ~bondissant~.
en.bonifier: ~Bonifier~ is formed from the adjective ~bon~ with the suffix ~-ifier~, which makes verbs meaning “to make A.” English Wiktionary also allows that it may come directly from Latin ~bonificare~, a hedge worth keeping, since many verbs in ~-ifier~ are Latin inheritances. The base ~bon~ comes through Old French from Latin ~bonus~ (“good”), which goes back to Old Latin ~duenos~. The suffix itself goes back to Latin ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”). So ~bonifier~ means, literally, “to make good,” that is, to improve.
en.bonimenter: Formed from the noun ~boniment~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning to deliver a sales pitch or patter. The noun comes from the verb ~bonir~ (“to say, to tell”) plus the suffix ~-ment~, so ~boniment~ was at first simply a telling or a speech, before it took on its modern sense of a showman's or huckster's patter.
en.border:
Denominal verb from the noun ~bord~ (“edge, ship's side”), attested by 1170, formed with ~-er~. The noun is a borrowing from Frankish *~bord~ (“plank, side of a ship”), from Proto-Germanic *~burdą~ (“board, plank, edge”). It is therefore cognate with English ~board~, German ~Bord~, and Dutch ~boord~ — all reflexes of the same Germanic word. The deeper Indo-European source of *~burdą~ is uncertain, sometimes tied to a root *~bʰers-~ (“tip, edge”).

The noun ~bord~ first meant the side of a ship — the planking that rose along the hull — before broadening to any edge, brink, or rim. The verb ~border~ thus means “to run along the edge of,” whether a road borders a forest, a lace borders a sleeve, or a sailor handles the lines along the ship's side. From the same maritime ancestor French keeps ~aborder~ (“to come alongside, to approach”), ~déborder~ (“to overflow, to go over the edge”), ~rebord~ (“rim, ledge”), and ~bordure~ (“border, trim”). The everyday English ~aboard~ likewise harks back to being “on the ~bord~.”
en.bordurer: Formed from ~bordure~ (“border, edging”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so it means to provide something with an edging. ~Bordure~ was itself derived from ~border~ with the suffix ~-ure~, and ~border~ comes from ~bord~, a word of Germanic origin, from Frankish *~bord~. The verb is thus a French formation on a French noun, whose own roots lie in a Germanic word.
en.borner: Formed in French from the noun ~borne~ (a boundary marker, a limit) with the verb ending ~-er~. The verb first means to mark the limits of something, to fix its boundaries: one ~borne~ a field with boundary stones. From there it took the figurative sense “to confine within limits”, as in ~se borner à~ (“to limit oneself to”). The adjective ~borné~ turned that image on the mind itself, describing someone whose outlook is narrow, as if hemmed in by markers.
en.bornoyer: French Wiktionary derives ~bornoyer~ from ~borgne~ (“one-eyed”) and the suffix ~-oyer~, giving an earlier form ~borgnoyer~, which was later softened to ~bornoyer~ by dropping the ~g~. The suffix ~-oyer~ commonly means to behave like, or act as, N, which suits the verb's modern sense of sighting along an edge or a line to judge whether it is straight.
en.bosseler: Formed from the noun ~bosse~ (“bump, lump”) with the ending ~-eler~, to raise bumps on a surface, to emboss. French Wiktionary treats ~-eler~ as a diminutive suffix, while English Wiktionary simply derives the verb from ~bosse~. The noun comes from Old French ~boce~, which English Wiktionary traces to Frankish *~bottja~; French Wiktionary compares Occitan ~bossa~ and Italian ~bozza~.
en.bosser: ~Bosser~ is a slang verb first attested in 1878, probably formed from ~bosse~ (“bump, hump”) plus ~-er~, though the path from “bump” to “work” is uncertain. Sources offer three guesses: that workers bent their backs, forming a hump; that raising an anchor on a ship was the typical hard labor; or that it began as artisans' cant from the sense “to emboss.” French Wiktionary also suggests the English ~boss~ as a base. ~Bosse~ itself comes from Old French ~boce~, which English Wiktionary traces to Frankish *~bottja~.
en.bossuer: Formed from the French noun ~bosse~ (“bump, lump”), with the verb ending ~-er~ (or ~-uer~ from the noun's stem), and attested in the sixteenth century. To ~bossuer~ is to cover something with bumps or dents, as a metal pot gets when it is knocked about. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~, the usual source of French verbs coined from a noun. The sources give nothing further on where ~bosse~ itself comes from.
en.bostonner: The verb is formed from the noun ~boston~ with the ending ~-er~, which turns a noun into a verb meaning “to carry out N”: here, to dance the boston. The name itself is the city of Boston. A French account of the card game of the same name says it was reportedly invented by the besieged inhabitants of Boston during the American War of Independence, and that the French allies of the insurgents brought it home. The sources give no separate origin for the dance, so only the name's link to the city is stated here.
en.botteler: Formed from the noun ~botte~ (“bundle”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to tie into bundles,” as one does with hay or straw. The ending comes from Latin ~-are~. The origin of ~botte~ is debated. One account borrows it from Middle Dutch ~bote~ (“bundle of flax”), itself tied to a verb meaning “to strike.” Another derives it from Latin ~botulus~, a word for an assemblage of diverse things. French Wiktionary hedges and says only that it comes “no doubt” from ~bot~.
en.botter: ~Botter~ is formed from ~botte~ and the ending ~-er~; French Wiktionary also offers ~bot~ as a base. The word ~botte~ has several unrelated origins in the sources, among them Old French ~bote~ (“boot”), probably from Frankish, and Middle Dutch ~bote~ (“bundle of flax”). The sources do not settle which one lies behind the verb, so its path to the slang sense “to please”, as in ~ça me botte~, remains unclear.
en.boubouler: ~Boubouler~ is onomatopoeic, formed by imitation of the call it names. The repeated syllable ~bou-~ mimics the low, hollow hooting of an owl, which is the sense the verb carries. Words made this way have no older ancestor: the sound itself is the origin, and the verbal ending ~-er~ simply fits the imitation into the first conjugation.
en.boucaner: Formed from ~boucan~ + the verb ending ~-er~: to smoke meat or fish on a ~boucan~. The noun is most often traced to Old Tupi ~mboka'ẽ~ (“wooden grill”), the frame on which meat and fish were smoked; by metonymy the word then named the hut where the smoking was done (1666). A second account links the sense “racket” of ~boucan~ to an obsolete verb ~boucaner~ (“to imitate the cry of a goat”), from ~bouc~ (“goat”), but that story does not concern the smoking sense.
en.boucharder: French Wiktionary derives this verb from the noun ~boucharde~, and lists a second verb of the same spelling from ~bouchard~, without tracing either further. ~Boucharde~ names a hammer with a toothed face, used to roughen stone or concrete, which fits the verb's sense “to roughen a surface.”
en.boucher:
From Old French ~bousche~ (“a bundle, a handful of straw, a faggot”), itself from Vulgar Latin *~bosca~ (“brushwood, a bundle of twigs”). The noun is attested in 1461 in the sense “a bundle of hemp,” and by the fourteenth century through its derivative ~bouchon~. The same Vulgar Latin word underlies French ~bois~ and ~bosquet~, and Italian ~bosco~ and Spanish ~bosque~ (“woods”) are its cognates. Despite appearances, the verb has nothing to do with ~bouche~ (“mouth”).

The link between a wisp of straw and plugging a hole is easy to picture: the verb seems to have meant “to stop up with a wisp of straw,” and then simply “to stop up.” From the same noun, ~bouchon~ became the word for a cork or stopper, and ~boucher~ now covers corks, pipes, noses (~se boucher le nez~), views and arteries. The figurative adjective ~bouché~ means “blocked,” and in everyday speech “dim-witted.” ~Déboucher~ is the opposite: to uncork or to emerge into the open. Note that ~boucher~ the noun (“butcher”) is another word entirely, from Old French ~bouchier~, a derivative of ~bouc~ (“he-goat”).
en.bouchonner: Formed from the noun ~bouchon~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun has two proposed origins. English Wiktionary traces it through Middle French ~bouchon~ (“bundle of hemp or foliage”) and Old French ~bousche~ (“handful of straw, bundle of twigs”) to Vulgar Latin ~bosca~ and Frankish *~bosc~ (“bush”), the root of English ~bush~. French Wiktionary gives two accounts: Old French ~bousche~ (“tuft of grass”), or Occitan ~bochon~ (“small ball”). The verb’s senses, to rub down and to form a traffic jam, are both derived from the noun.
en.boucler: A denominal verb from the fourteenth century, formed from ~boucle~ plus ~-er~: first “to fasten with a buckle,” then “to curl hair into loops,” and in many figurative senses “to close, to wrap up” (finishing a file, shutting a door, locking someone up). The noun is inherited from Latin ~buccula~, the cheek strap of a helmet, a diminutive of ~bucca~ (“cheek, mouth”). The Old French noun also gave English ~buckle~, so the two words are cousins.
en.bouder:
From Old French ~bouder~ (“to sulk,” literally “to swell or push out the lip”), through Middle French. The older source is thought to be an expressive syllable, an onomatopoeic ~bod~ for something swollen, a root English Wiktionary compares with Walloon ~boder~ (“to swell”). Beyond that the picture is uncertain: English Wiktionary says it is probably from a Proto-Germanic base such as *~būd-~ (“to swell”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰew-~ (“to blow, to swell”). Proposed cognates include Old Norse ~budda~ (“purse, bag”), Old High German ~būtil~ (“purse,” modern German ~Beutel~) and English ~bud~.

The proposed origin is therefore a swelling: a sulking person pushes out a puffed lip, and that expression gave the verb. French Wiktionary ties the sound ~bod~ to ~boudin~ and ~boursoufler~, other words for swollen things, and links the sulker's lip to the phrase ~faire la lippe~. Because the root is called onomatopoeic and the Germanic link only “probable,” none of this is settled. In modern French, ~bouder~ means “to sulk” and, of a person or thing, “to shun”: one ~boude~ a restaurant, a vote, or even one's pleasure.
en.boudiner: Formed in French from ~boudin~ (“blood sausage”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so to make something take the shape of a sausage, or to squeeze it tightly, as a garment does. The origin of ~boudin~ is uncertain. It may come from an imitative root *~bod-~ (“swollen”). The alternative derivation from Latin ~botulus~ (“intestine”), through a Vulgar Latin *~botellinus~, is disputed on phonetic grounds.
en.bouffer: Inherited from Old French ~bouffer~ (“to puff up”), which comes from a Medieval Latin ~buffa~ that seems to imitate the sound and look of puffed-out cheeks. The original idea was inflation: swelling the cheeks or something else with air. The familiar informal sense “to eat” came later, plausibly from the image of cheeks stuffed with food, although the evidence gives only the “puff up” origin and not that step. The noun ~bouffe~ means “food” in the same register, and ~bouffant~ still describes a sleeve or a hairstyle that puffs out.
en.bouffir: The origin of ~bouffir~ is not settled. It is attested first only indirectly, through the old participle used as an adjective, ~boffi~ (1150-1200). French Wiktionary says the verb is either a variant of ~bouffer~ or a parallel formation on the same root. The verb means to make something swell or puff up, and the adjective ~bouffi~ (“puffy”) still carries the old participle.
en.bouffonner: Formed from the noun ~bouffon~ (“buffoon, jester”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning “to play the buffoon.” The noun was borrowed, through Middle French ~boufon~, from Italian ~buffone~, which comes from ~buffa~ (“joke”). French Wiktionary traces ~buffa~ to a root *~buff-~ imitating the puffing out of the cheeks.
en.bouger:
From Old French ~bougier~, from Vulgar Latin *~bullicāre~ (“to bubble, seethe, stir”), a frequentative of Latin ~bullīre~ (“to boil, bubble up”). The semantic path is wonderfully concrete: water that boils churns and stirs, and from that ceaseless agitation the sense slid from “to bubble” to “to stir” to simply “to move.” The same root surfaces in Catalan ~bellugar~ and, through Latin ~bullīre~, in French ~bouillir~ (“to boil”) and ~bouillon~ (“broth”).

English, fittingly, borrowed the French verb back as ~budge~ — which, like the negative French idiom, lives chiefly in the negative: nothing will budge, ça ne bouge pas. That narrowing to stubbornness is a quiet comedy of the word: a verb born from the violent churn of a boiling pot now most often denotes the refusal to move at all. From a single image of bubbling water, French drew both the rolling boil of the kitchen and the smallest twitch of a body that will not stay still.
en.bougonner: Formed from ~bougon~ (“grumbler”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to grumble.” French Wiktionary traces ~bougon~ to Old French ~boujon~, a plumber's tool. English Wiktionary describes the relationship the other way round, calling ~bougon~ a deverbal from ~bougonner~, so the sources disagree on which word came first. Either way, the verb and the noun are the same family, and the sense is the sulky, muttering manner of a grumpy person.
en.bouillir:
From Middle French ~bouillir~, from Old French ~boillir~ (“to boil, to burst”), inherited from Latin ~bullīre~ (“to bubble”), itself derived from ~bulla~ (“bubble, knob, stud”). In Italy and Gaul, ~bullīre~ displaced the older Latin verb ~fervēre~ (“to boil”), which survived on the Iberian Peninsula and in Romania: Spanish ~hervir~, Portuguese ~ferver~ and Romanian ~a fierbe~ are its descendants, while Italian has ~bollire~. English ~boil~ is a French loan from the same Old French verb.

The verb is named after what one sees in a boiling pot: ~bulla~ is a bubble, and ~bullīre~ is to produce bubbles. French drew many words from that picture. ~Bulle~ (“bubble”) is the noun itself, ~bouillon~ is the liquid in which things bubble, ~bouillie~ is a thick cooked mash, and the learned ~ébullition~ comes from the Latin compound ~ēbullīre~. The figurative uses followed naturally, as in ~bouillir de colère~ (“to seethe with anger”) and ~bouillant~ (“fiery, hot-headed”).
en.bouillonner: ~Bouillonner~ is a denominal verb: the noun ~bouillon~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is itself built on the stem of ~bouillir~ (“to boil”) with the suffix ~-on~, so a ~bouillon~ is literally something that boils. The ending ~-er~ goes back to the Latin infinitive ending ~-are~, and here it turns that noun into an action: to bubble, to froth, to seethe, as a liquid does when it boils.
en.bouillotter: French Wiktionary derives ~bouillotter~ from ~bouillotte~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, while English Wiktionary reads it as ~bouillir~ plus the suffix ~-oter~; either way the root is ~bouillir~ (“to boil”). The suffix ~-oter~ adds the idea of a small, repeated motion, so the verb means to simmer, to bubble gently. The noun ~bouillotte~ is itself built on ~bouillir~ with ~-otte~, and it names a card game, so called by analogy between the heat of a boiler and the speed of play.
en.boulanger:
The verb is built on the noun ~boulanger~ (“baker”) and is recorded from the fifteenth century. The noun comes from Picard ~boulenc~ (“maker of round loaves”), recorded in Medieval Latin about 1100 as ~bolengarius~ and as ~bolengier~ in Old French around 1170. Picard ~boulenc~ was formed from Low Frankish *~bolla~ (“round loaf, bun”) plus the Frankish suffix ~-enc~, from *~-ing~. A baker was thus, at the root, a maker of round loaves.

The Frankish word has relatives in Middle Dutch ~bolle~ (“round loaf”), which became ~bol~. Some scholars link this word to Latin ~pollen~ (“fine flour”), a proposal that remains uncertain. The noun is thus of Germanic origin. The verb ~boulanger~ means “to prepare and bake bread,” while the noun ~boulangerie~ names the shop where the work is done.
en.bouler: ~Bouler~ is a verb formed on the noun ~boule~ (“ball”) plus the ending ~-er~, with the sense of swelling or puffing up into a round shape. The origin of ~boule~ is itself debated: it comes from Old French ~bole~ (“knob”), which is traced either to Latin ~bulla~ (“bubble”), making it a doublet of ~bulle~, or to Frankish *~bollā~ (“ball, bun”), making it a doublet of ~bol~.
en.bouleverser:
~bouleverser~ is not inherited Latin but homemade Renaissance French: first recorded in 1557 as ~boulverser~ in the poet Belleau, it welds together ~bouler~ (“to send rolling like a ball,” from ~boule~, from Latin ~bulla~, “bubble, round boss”) and ~verser~ (“to tip over, to overturn,” from Latin ~versāre~, frequentative of ~vertere~, “to turn”). Philologists call it a tautological compound: both halves mean “to knock over,” so the verb says it twice. The halves carry deep roots. ~vertere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~wert-~ (“to turn”), the root of German ~werden~ (“to become” — a turning-into) and of the English suffix ~-ward~ (“turned toward”); Latin ~bulla~ named anything round and swollen, from a water bubble to the boss on a door.

For its first decades the verb stayed purely physical — walls, fortifications, furniture turned upside down. In 1622 it reached politics — to throw a kingdom into disorder — and with Pascal's Provinciales in the 1650s it crossed into the soul: to trouble someone profoundly. That inner sense conquered the language: today a piece of news bouleverse you long before any furniture falls, and ~bouleversant~ and ~bouleversement~ belong above all to emotion. The parent families thrived on their own. From ~bulla~ French gets ~bulle~ — the soap bubble, but also the papal bull, sealed with a round leaden boss — and ~bulletin~, originally a little sealed note, today the ballot in the box. From ~vertere~ come ~version~, ~vertige~, ~renverser~ and ~univers~ — the universe being, literally, everything “turned into one.” To be bouleversé is, etymologically, to be sent rolling and tipped over — an image French speakers can still feel.
en.boulocher: Formed from ~boule~ (“ball”) with the suffix ~-ocher~, a popular, mildly pejorative ending that suggests doing something in a small or petty way, as in ~flânocher~. English Wiktionary splits it as ~boule~ + ~-oche~ + ~-er~. To ~boulocher~ is to form little balls, as wool does when it pills. The noun ~boule~ comes from Old French ~bole~ (“knob”). Its source is disputed: either Latin ~bulla~ (“bubble”), or Frankish *~bollā~ (“ball, bun, bowl”).
en.boulonner: ~Boulonner~ is formed from the noun ~boulon~ (“bolt”) and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~boulon~ is in turn built on ~boule~ (“ball”) with the suffix ~-on~, so a bolt is, etymologically, a small round thing. The verb first means to fasten with bolts. Its slang sense of working hard is a later figurative use of the same verb.
en.boulotter: The origin of ~boulotter~ (“to eat”) is uncertain. French Wiktionary proposes only that it may come from ~boulot~ in the sense of “bread,” with the verbal ending, so that the verb would mean something like “to have one's bread.” That older sense of ~boulot~ has faded, since the noun now usually means “work” in everyday French, and the link between the two meanings remains a hypothesis rather than an established fact. As a verb, ~boulotter~ belongs to casual, familiar speech.
en.boumer: ~Boumer~ comes from English ~boom~ (“to rumble”) plus the French ending ~-er~. It first appeared around 1905 as ~boomer~, meaning to make a noise or to hype something. Its spelling was later reworked on the French interjection ~boum~, and the two spellings competed in the 1950s. Today it survives in the colloquial sense “to go well”, as in ~ça boume~.
en.bouquiner: Formed from ~bouquin~ and the verbal suffix ~-er~, so “to read ~bouquins~,” that is, to read for pleasure. The base ~bouquin~ is Middle French ~boucquain~ (“old book of little esteem”). It most likely comes from a Middle Dutch diminutive of ~boec~ (“book”), a cousin of English ~book~, though en.Wiktionary also allows a French derivation from the simple Dutch word.
en.bourdonner: ~Bourdonner~ comes from Old French ~bordoner~ and is linked to the noun ~bourdon~ (“bumblebee”), the insect whose low humming gives the verb its meaning. English Wiktionary parses it as ~bourdon~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, while French Wiktionary stops at the Old French verb. The verb means to buzz, hum or drone, of insects but also of voices, engines and ears. A person whose ears ~bourdonnent~ hears a ringing hum, and a ~bourdonnement~ is the sound itself.
en.bourgeonner: ~Bourgeonner~ is formed from the noun ~bourgeon~ (“bud”) with the verb ending ~-er~: to put out buds. French Wiktionary gives the Old French form ~burjuner~. Both Wiktionaries treat it as a plain denominal derivation. The sources consulted do not explain where ~bourgeon~ itself comes from.
en.bourlinguer: The origin of ~bourlinguer~ is uncertain. French Wiktionary suggests a link to ~boulingue~, a sail set above the top, and mentions Old French ~bourle~ (“ball”), which would make the verb the equivalent of “to roll one's bones,” along with ~bourler~ (“to border”). English Wiktionary offers either ~boulingue~ plus ~-er~ or a relation to ~bouléguer~ (“to move”). The verb means “to roam, to get about,” and in sailing “to tack against the wind.”
en.bourreler: ~Bourreler~ comes from the Old French form ~bourrel~, itself derived from ~bourrer~ (“to stuff”). French Wiktionary refers to ~bourreau~ (“executioner”) for the wider family. The sources give no account of how the sense developed. The modern verb is figurative: to torment, as in ~être bourrelé de remords~ (“to be tormented by remorse”).
en.bourrer: Both Wiktionaries derive ~bourrer~ from the noun ~bourre~ (“stuffing, padding, wadding”): to stuff a cushion or a pipe is to fill it with stuffing, and the verb then stretched to cramming anything full, up to force-feeding someone. French Wiktionary adds that the verb first appears in the sense of mistreating or roughing someone up, which it links to Old French ~burir~ (“to rush, to charge”, also written ~bourrir~). The sources do not connect these two lines, so the origin of that violent sense should be treated as uncertain. The stuffing image survives in idioms such as ~bourrer le crâne~ (“to fill someone's head with nonsense”).
en.boursicoter: ~Boursicoter~ comes from ~boursicot~, a word built on ~bourse~ (“purse”), and it first meant to put small sums of money aside. That sense goes back at least to the sixteenth century. The second sense, “to dabble on the stock market,” came later and was shaped by the development of ~bourse~ to mean “stock exchange”: the verb thus moved from a little purse of savings to small-scale speculation.
en.boursoufler: ~Boursoufler~ is recorded in the fifteenth century and is derived from the Old French ~bousoufle~. That is the whole documented descent. The sources give no earlier Latin or Germanic link, and French Wiktionary draws no connection to ~bourse~ (“purse”) or ~souffler~ (“to blow”), although the word's sound recalls both. The verb means to swell or puff up, and it is mostly used of skin, paint or a face that bloats.
en.bousculer:
French Wiktionary favors a blend: ~bousculer~ is said to cross Middle French ~bousser~ (“to strike, knock”) with ~culer~ (“to walk backwards”). It rejects the older explanation, an Old French ~bouteculer~ (“to search by turning things over”) built from ~bouter~, ~cul~ and ~-er~. Middle French ~bousser~ was widespread in Lorraine and Franco-Provençal territory, and is said to be borrowed from Middle High German ~bōzen~ (“to strike”), to which regional German ~boßen~ (“to beat”) is related. It corresponds to the French verb ~bouter~ (“to push”). ~Culer~ comes from ~cul~, the French word for the backside.

The account is therefore of a word half Germanic and half French, though the choice between the two origins is a matter of competing proposals, and the blend is the one the source prefers. The sense is compatible with such a blend, striking joined to backing away. The meaning spread from physical jostling to disturbing an order, a schedule or an assumption, as in ~bousculer les habitudes~. Related words include ~bousculade~ (“a crush, a jostling crowd”) and, on the ~cul~ side, ~reculer~ and ~acculer~ (“to back up, to corner”), whose stems ~-culer~ and ~cul~ are the same one that appears here.
en.bousiller: The origin of ~bousiller~ is disputed. English Wiktionary derives it from ~bouse~ (“cow dung”) plus the suffix ~-iller~, which can carry a pejorative or imprecise sense. French Wiktionary instead offers the Occitan verb ~bosilhar~ (“to destroy” or “to tattoo”), and also mentions a Celtic root *~bawa~ (“mud”). The noun ~bouse~ itself is traced to Gaulish or Ancient Ligurian, with cognates such as Occitan ~bosa~. Whichever account holds, ~bousiller~ means to wreck or botch something carelessly.
en.bouter:
From Old French ~bouter~ (“to strike, to push”) by way of Middle French, of Germanic origin: it comes from Frankish *~bautan~ or *~bōtan~ (“to push, strike, beat”), from Proto-Germanic *~bautaną~ (“to beat”). Its Germanic cousins include Old High German ~bōzzan~, Dutch ~boten~, Old English ~bēatan~ and Old Norse ~bauta~, and English ~beat~ belongs to the same family. English Wiktionary also compares Spanish ~botar~ and Italian ~buttare~. French Wiktionary traces the word further back to a Proto-Indo-European root *~bhā̆u-~ (“to strike”), which it also gives as the source of Latin ~refūtāre~ and ~fustigāre~.

In Old French the verb meant “to push” and also “to put”, and it had a further sense, “to bud, to break out in buds”. Some have proposed two separate verbs, one for “putting” and one for “budding”. French Wiktionary rejects the split as unjustified, since it sees an obvious link between pushing, or pressing, and budding. Today ~bouter~ is archaic in its general senses and survives in technical uses, such as removing flesh from the skin of an animal. The root lives on in many French words, among them ~bouton~, ~aboutir~, ~débouter~ and ~rebuter~.
en.boutonner: Formed from the noun ~bouton~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so “to fasten with buttons” (the Old French verb was ~boutoner~). The noun first meant a “bud” and is built on ~bouter~ (“to push”) plus ~-on~, and it goes back through Vulgar Latin to Frankish *~bautō~ (“that which pushes up, a bump or knob”). A bud and a button are both small knobs, which is how one word came to cover them.
en.bouturer: Both Wiktionaries give only one fact: ~bouturer~ comes from the noun ~bouture~, a cutting taken from a plant so that it will root and grow into a new one. The verb is formed with the usual ending ~-er~, which turns a noun into a verb of doing: to ~bouturer~ is to propagate a plant by cuttings, or, of a plant, to put out new shoots in that way. It is a gardener's word, and the ~bouture~ is what the gardener plants.
en.boxer: The verb meaning “to fight with fists” is formed from the noun ~boxe~ plus the ending ~-er~. ~Boxe~ is a French pseudo-anglicism built on English ~boxing~, from English ~box~ (“a blow, to strike”). French Wiktionary notes that the noun ~boxer~ belongs to unrelated stories: the dog breed comes from German, the Chinese insurgents of 1900 from English ~Boxer~ rendering a Chinese name meaning “Fists of Justice and Harmony”, and the underwear from English ~boxer shorts~.
en.boyauter: A French verb formed from the noun ~boyau~ (“gut, bowel”) with the ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~. French Wiktionary explains it with a bodily image, to twist one's guts with laughter, hence “to be doubled up with a fit of laughter.” The source gives no further history, and it does not trace ~boyau~ itself.
en.boycotter: From the English verb ~boycott~, with the French ending ~-er~ added to the borrowed word. English took it from the surname of Captain Charles ~Boycott~, an Irish land agent whom tenants and neighbors shunned in 1880 during a rent dispute. He was cut off from labor, trade and even the post, and his name became a verb for any such organized refusal to deal with someone. French borrowed it soon afterward, first as the noun ~boycott~ and then as the verb ~boycotter~. It is one of the few French verbs named for a single person's misfortune. It now covers politics, trade and elections.
en.braconner:
~Braconner~ comes from Occitan ~bracon~ with the verb ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary traces the Occitan noun to a Germanic accusative form *~brakkon~, meaning “hunting dog,” and refers readers to ~braque~, the French word for a breed of pointer. The verb therefore rests on a Germanic word for a hound that reached French by way of Occitan.

The modern verb means “to poach,” to hunt or fish illegally. Its family includes ~braque~, ~braconnier~ (the person who practices the activity) and ~braconnage~ (the activity itself). Beyond French, the Germanic hound word has well-known relatives: German ~Bracke~ and English ~brach~ both name a hunting dog. So the same Germanic word survives in several languages.
en.brader:
~Brader~ reached French through Walloon or Picard, the dialects of northern Belgium and northern France, from Middle Dutch ~braden~ (“to roast”). The Dutch verb has a cousin in German ~braten~ (“to roast, to fry”), a standard cognate from the same Germanic stock. Modern Dutch ~braden~ still means “to roast,” so the kitchen sense survives in the language from which the French verb ultimately came.

The French meaning drifted a long way from the kitchen. From “to roast” the verb passed to “to squander,” in the same figurative vein as ~flamber son argent~ (“to burn through one's money”), and from there to “to sell off at a low price,” its usual sense now. The noun ~braderie~ names a sale of this kind, and in the north of France and in Belgium it also names a large open-air sale where whole streets turn into markets.
en.brailler: From Vulgar Latin *~bragulare~, formed on Latin ~bragere~ (“to bray, to cry out”), the source of French ~braire~. French Wiktionary adds that ~bragere~ itself is of Gaulish origin and compares Gaelic ~braigh~ (“to crack, to crackle”), while English Wiktionary simply gives it as a Latin word. The two accounts differ here, so the deeper source is uncertain. English ~bray~ is a cognate. A verb that began as the braying of a donkey thus came to mean to shout, bawl or holler.
en.braire:
From Vulgar Latin *~bragire~ (or *~bragiō~), which French Wiktionary traces to a Gaulish form *~braci-~ or *~bragere~, and English Wiktionary to Gaulish *~bragu~ and Proto-Celtic *~bragyeti~. The Celtic relatives are cited with different glosses. Old Irish ~braigim~ is given as “to crackle” in one source, and ~braigid~ as “to flatulate” in the other. French Wiktionary also compares Gaelic ~braigh~ and Breton ~breugiñ~, the latter meaning “to bray.” English ~bray~ is a relative of the French verb.

The verb is thus one of the Celtic traces in French, and the exact sound it first named is left open by the sources. In modern French it is best known as the cry of the donkey, and it extends to loud, unrestrained crying or shouting. One of its senses is probably borrowed from Picard ~braire~ (“to weep, to moan”), according to French Wiktionary, which marks that sense as lacking a firm reference.
en.braiser: ~Braiser~ is a denominal verb, formed from ~braise~ (“live coals”) with the ending ~-er~: to cook over embers. The noun ~braise~ comes from Old French ~brese~, which English Wiktionary relates, with some doubt (“perhaps”), to a Gothic word *~brasa~ and Proto-Germanic *~brasō~ (“glowing coal”). French Wiktionary says only that it came through Old French from Old Dutch. Swedish ~brasa~ (“to roast”) is a cognate.
en.bramer:
From Middle French ~bramer~, itself from Old Occitan ~bramar~ (“to sing; to long for ardently”), which goes back to a Gothic form reconstructed as *~brammōn~ (or *~bramjan~). That in turn comes from Proto-Germanic *~bramjaną~ (“to bellow, roar”) and from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰrem-~. Its Germanic relatives include Middle Low German ~brammen~ (“to roar”) and Dutch ~brommen~ (“to bellow”). The verb therefore reached French by way of Occitan, not directly from a Germanic language.

The Occitan sense of ardent longing survives in Italian ~bramare~ (“to crave”), while Spanish ~bramar~ (“to bellow, roar”) kept the other side of the word, the loud cry. French follows the second path. ~Bramer~ is used above all of a stag, which ~brame~ in the rutting season, and by extension it describes a loud, prolonged cry. The noun ~brame~ (the stag's call) is the corresponding verbal noun. So a word that began as a Germanic roar passed through Gothic and Occitan song and came to rest in the forest.
en.brancarder: Formed from the noun ~brancard~ (“stretcher”) with the verbal ending ~-er~: to carry someone on a stretcher. The origin of the noun is probably tied to ~branche~. French Wiktionary derives it from the Norman-Picard form ~branque~ with the suffix ~-ard~, which names objects, as in ~billard~ and ~placard~. English Wiktionary similarly gives ~branc~, a masculine form of ~branche~, plus ~-ard~. The sources say only “probably,” so the link to ~branche~ is a likely account, not a certain one.
en.brancher:
Modern French ~brancher~ is a denominal verb built directly on the noun ~branche~ (“branch”) with the verbal suffix ~-er~. ~branche~ descends from Late Latin ~branca~ (“paw, claw”), a word the dictionaries flag as of uncertain origin: by one account it goes back to a hypothetical Gaulish *~vranca~, and through it to a Proto-Indo-European *~wronk-~ related to Proto-Balto-Slavic *~ranka~ (“hand, arm”), though the Latin form may also have been colored by ~bracchium~ (“arm”). Cognates of ~branca~ survive across Romance — Italian ~branca~, Occitan and Catalan forms — and German ~Pranke~ (“paw”) was borrowed from the same family.

The path from “paw” to “branch” runs through the image of a limb spreading out from a trunk, and ~brancher~ inherited that branching idea. Its modern senses fan out accordingly: to “branch,” to “connect” one thing to another (as a wire is plugged into a circuit), and colloquially to “turn (someone) on” to a topic. From the same noun French built ~branchage~ (“boughs”), ~embrancher~ and ~embranchement~ (“to join, junction”), ~débrancher~ (“to unplug”), and ~brindille~ stands nearby in the same arboreal field. The English ~branch~ comes, through Old French, from the very same ~branca~.
en.brandir:
French ~brandir~ comes from Old French ~brandir~, formed on ~brand~ (“sword”), which French Wiktionary derives from Germanic ~brand~ (“firebrand, burning log”). English Wiktionary only records the verb as inherited from Middle and Old French. The Germanic word has close cousins: English ~brand~ (originally a burning piece of wood, hence the later sense of a mark burned into skin) and German ~Brand~ (“fire”). Italian ~brando~ (“sword”) is a related word.

The sources do not say how “burning log” came to mean “sword,” and this entry does not guess. French Wiktionary points the reader to ~branler~ (“to shake, to wobble”) and ~brandon~ (“torch, firebrand”) as relatives of the same word. The modern verb ~brandir~ means to wave a weapon, a flag or a document, in a threatening or triumphant way. English borrowed it as ~brandish~, from the stem ~brandiss-~ of the French verb.
en.branler:
French ~branler~ is an old contraction. Middle French ~bransler~ came from Old French ~bransler~ (“to shake, to move”), itself a shortened form of ~brandeler~ (“to wobble”). That verb is built on Old French ~brant~ (“sword blade, big sword”), which French Wiktionary traces to a Germanic ~brand~ (“firebrand”). English Wiktionary gives the route through Vulgar Latin *~brandus~ (“firebrand, flaming sword, sword”), ultimately from Frankish *~brand~ (“sword”), from Proto-Germanic *~brandaz~ (“burning, flash, firebrand, flaming sword”). A Late Latin step *~brandulare~ has sometimes been proposed as the go-between, but English Wiktionary finds it unlikely, since the suffix ~-ulāre~ was no longer productive when the word was borrowed.

The chain of forms points to a weapon: a sword, ~brant~, lies behind ~brandeler~ (“to wobble”) and ~bransler~ (“to shake (a sword at), move”), and the modern verb means “to shake.” The step from ~brandeler~ to ~bransler~ contracts the word, and the spelling later lost its s, giving ~branler~. Related words keep the full root: ~brandir~ (“to brandish”), which English Wiktionary tells us to compare with English ~brandish~, and ~brandon~ (“firebrand”). In very vulgar slang ~branler~ also has a well-known sexual sense, which learners should be wary of.
en.braquer:
The origin of ~braquer~ is uncertain, and the sources do not agree on how firmly to speak. fr.Wiktionary offers, with the hedge “probably,” a Vulgar Latin verb *~brachitāre~ (“to set in motion with the arms”), derived from Latin ~bracchium~ (“arm”), which was itself borrowed from Greek ~brakhíōn~. en.Wiktionary simply says the origin is uncertain, so the Latin link should be read as a proposal and not as settled fact. The Vulgar Latin verb is a reconstruction, never attested in writing. If the proposal is right, the idea behind ~braquer~ is of turning or aiming something by means of the arm.

The meanings fit that picture. ~Braquer~ was first to aim, to point something in a given direction, as one does with a telescope, a camera or a firearm. The motorist’s sense, to turn the steering wheel sharply, comes from the same idea of swinging round, and a ~braquage~ is the turning circle. In slang, to ~braquer~ a bank is to hold it up at gunpoint, and the figurative reflexive ~se braquer~ is to dig in one’s heels, so that a ~braqué~ person has turned all their defenses against you. If the Latin source holds, French ~bras~ (“arm”), ~brasse~, ~embrasser~ (“to embrace”) and ~brassard~ (“armband”) are its relatives.
en.braser: From Middle French ~braser~, from Old French ~braser~ (“to burn”). The deeper origin is debated. One account derives it from a variant of Old French ~brese~ (“live coals”), a word of Germanic origin. The account judged more likely links it to Old Norse ~brasa~ (“to braze, to harden with fire”), from the same Proto-Germanic source. French Wiktionary glosses the Old French verb with ~embraser~ (“to set ablaze”) and ties it to ~braise~ (“embers”). ~Braise~, ~embraser~ and ~brasier~ belong to the same family.
en.brasiller:
French ~brasiller~ continues Old French ~bresillier~ (“to grill over embers”), attested in Gautier de Coinci's Miracles of the Virgin. French Wiktionary derives it from ~braise~ (“embers”), with a vowel alternation, plus the suffix ~-iller~, a verbal ending that often gives a frequentative or diminutive sense, as in ~scintiller~. The base ~braise~ is shared by Italian ~brace~ and Spanish ~brasa~.

The verb first described food cooking on embers. By extension it came to mean “to shine with a flickering glow”: the sources cite the adjectival present participle ~brasillant~ in 1613, applied to flashes of lightning in Chassignet, and in 1872 Zola's feminine ~brasillante~ in the sense of sparkling. A nautical sense is also recorded in the Encyclopédie of 1751. The family of ~braise~ includes ~braiser~, ~brasier~ and ~embraser~, which all keep the image of burning embers.
en.brasser:
From Old French ~bracier~, from ~brace~ (“malt”), which comes from Gaulish ~bracis~, Latinized as ~bracem~ by Pliny. French Wiktionary gives the Vulgar Latin intermediate as *~braciare~. The Gaulish word goes back to Proto-Celtic *~mrakis~ and, by the Wiktionary account, to the Proto-Indo-European root *~merk-~ (“to be soaked”). Celtic cousins are Scottish Gaelic ~braich~ and Welsh ~brag~, and outside Celtic the same root is compared with Latin ~marcēre~ (“to wither, droop”) and Lithuanian ~mer̃kti~ (“to soak”). The original sense is thus close to “to ferment” or “to steep.”

The spelling is a trap. Because the word does not come from ~bras~ (“arm”), the true spelling would be ~bracer~, as it was once written, though ~bras~ influenced the verb in some of its senses. A second account treats ~brasser~ instead as a denominal of ~bras~ or ~brasse~, so the origin is not beyond dispute, although the Gaulish derivation is the one French Wiktionary gives first. French Wiktionary links the root to ~braise~ in the sense of “spent grain” and to ~brai~.
en.brasseyer: An old variant of ~brasser~, which Littré and the Académie send readers to for this word. In its nautical sense it meant to trim a ship's yards by hauling on the ropes called ~bras~ that swing them, which apparently ties the word to ~bras~ (“arm”). A Normandy usage means to walk swinging one's arms. It should not be confused with the other ~brasser~, “to brew,” which comes from Old French ~bracier~ and Gaulish ~bracis~ (“malt”) and has nothing to do with the arm.
en.braver: Formed from the adjective ~brave~ (“courageous”) with the verb-forming ending ~-er~: “to treat as brave,” hence to challenge or defy, to face a danger boldly. French ~brave~ was probably borrowed from Italian ~bravo~ rather than from Spanish ~bravo~ (“wild”), and the Italian word is itself taken to be a loan from Occitan ~brau~. English ~brave~ and its doublet ~bravo~ come from the same Romance source.
en.bredouiller: ~Bredouiller~ is a reworking of Old French ~bredeler~ with the suffix ~-ouiller~, which forms verbs of sounds such as ~gazouiller~, ~cafouiller~ and ~bafouiller~. The origin of ~bredeler~ is less clear. English Wiktionary says possibly a variant of ~bretter~ or ~bretonner~ (“to talk like a Breton”). That link is only proposed, not established.
en.bretteler: The TLFi dates ~bretteler~ to 1690 (Furetière) and derives it from ~bretter~ in the sense “to cut teeth into,” with the suffix ~-eler~. It is a craft verb. It means to score or notch a surface with a toothed tool, as when a wall is scraped before renovation, or to cut teeth into stone or wood, and the Académie lists a toothed trowel as ~truelle brettelée~. Sculptors also use it for roughing out clay with a toothed tool.
en.bretter: Formed from ~brette~ with the suffix ~-er~. A ~brette~ was a long sword with a toothed blade, from the Old French phrase ~espee brette~, in which ~bret~ meant “Breton”: a “Breton sword.” The verb branched into several senses: to dress stone with a toothed chisel, a use tied to ~bretteler~ (said by some to cross ~bretèche~ with ~créneler~); to pick a quarrel, now obsolete; and, in Canada, to dawdle or wander about poking into things, from the sense of “playing with the sword.”
en.breveter: Formed from the noun ~brevet~ and the verbal ending ~-er~: to grant, or to take out, a patent. The noun is usually explained as ~brève~ (a short official letter, from Latin ~brevis~, “short”) plus the diminutive suffix ~-et~, a letter short enough to carry a royal grant or privilege, and the word later came to mean any official certificate. The lexicographer Pihan proposed instead an Arabic origin, from a word for a diploma conferring a right, but the Latin account is the standard one.
en.bricoler: ~Bricoler~ is formed from the noun ~bricole~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun appeared as ~brigole~ and then ~bricole~, borrowed from Italian ~briccola~, a kind of catapult launched by the swing of a beam. By the end of the Middle Ages, the phrase ~mettre en la bricole~ meant “to deceive.” Later, once the catapult had become obsolete as a weapon, ~bricole~ took the sense of an indirect, clever means, and the verb ~bricoler~ grew from that idea: to manage by roundabout, ingenious methods, and so to tinker. The ending ~-er~ goes back to Latin ~-are~.
en.brider: ~Brider~ is formed from the noun ~bride~ (“bridle, rein”) and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun came from Old French, which took it from Middle High German ~brīdel~, from Old High German ~brīdil~. A related Old High German form, ~brittil~, gave French ~bretelle~, and the word is cognate with English ~bridle~. The verb first meant “to put a bridle on,” as with a horse, and then “to hold back,” as in ~brider ses émotions~. It is also used in cooking, where a bird is ~bridée~, trussed, before roasting, and in ~yeux bridés~, narrow, tight-drawn eyes.
en.bridger: ~Bridger~ is a verb in ~-er~ formed on the noun ~bridge~, the card game, which French took from English ~bridge~. French Wiktionary treats the verb as a denominal and English Wiktionary as a borrowing of the English word; either way its sense is simply to play bridge. Adding ~-er~ to a borrowed noun is the usual way French fits a foreign word into the first conjugation.
en.briefer: Borrowed from English, where the noun ~brief~ means “instructions.” English had itself taken that word from French ~bref~ (“short”), so the verb is the end of a round trip: a French adjective crossed the Channel, acquired the sense of a set of concise instructions, and came back as a verb meaning to give someone those instructions. It is a modern, informal borrowing, typical of business and military vocabulary.
en.briffer: The origin of ~briffer~ is uncertain. It is linked to a dialectal form of ~bribe~ (“a large chunk of bread”) and to ~briber~ (“to gather crumbs”), found in Rabelais. The form ~brifer~ or ~briffer~ meant to eat like a glutton. It may also be compared with Occitan ~brifar~ (“to eat greedily”), a close parallel.
en.briguer: ~Briguer~ is formed from the noun ~brigue~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Italian ~briga~ (“quarrel, bother”), whose own origin is obscure; French Wiktionary also proposes Occitan ~briga~ or ~brega~ as a source. English Wiktionary treats the verb as borrowed directly from the Italian, with the original sense “to look for a fight”. The modern sense, to strive eagerly for something, is therefore a long way from its quarrelsome beginnings.
en.brillanter: Formed from ~brillant~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so that the verb means “to make shiny, to give brilliance to.” The base ~brillant~ is the present participle of ~briller~ (“to shine”), used as an adjective and as a noun. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~, the infinitive ending of the first conjugation, and is the default way French coins a verb from a noun or an adjective. The verb is thus a small French derivation, built on a participle that had already become a word of its own.
en.brillantiner: Formed from ~brillantine~ with the verb ending ~-er~: to put brilliantine on hair. ~Brillantine~ is itself built from ~brillant~ (“shiny”) and the suffix ~-ine~, so the verb means, in effect, to make the hair shine. The ~brillant~ in question is the adjective of the verb ~briller~ (“to shine”), and the ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~.
en.briller:
From Italian ~brillare~ (“to shine; also to beat the wings, to quiver”), borrowed into French around 1559. The Italian word's own origin is genuinely disputed, and the sources hedge: by one account it is a variant of Italian ~prillare~ (“to spin, to whirl”); by another it descends from Latin ~beryllus~ (“beryl,” the gemstone), in the sense “to shine like a beryl.” Littré favored the gemstone, but conceded it fails to explain the older “quiver, dart about” meaning — so the question stays open.

The semantic history is the surprising part. In its earliest French life ~briller~ did not mean “to shine” at all: it meant to be restless, to dart and quiver — a sense now obsolete except in old hunting language for an agitated dog. The luminous meaning, today the only one, seems to have grown out of that trembling motion, the way a flickering, jittering light scintillates (compare the link between English ~flick~ and ~flicker~). From the bright sense comes the whole modern family — ~brillant~ (“brilliant, shiny”), ~brillance~, ~briller de mille feux~ — and the wry idiom ~briller par son absence~ (“to be conspicuous by one's absence”).
en.brimbaler: The French Wiktionary treats ~brimbaler~ as a variant of ~bringuebaler~, which is the more common form today. Its earliest evidence is the spelling ~brinbaler~, found in the middle of the fifteenth century in Martin Le Franc's ~Le Champion des Dames~ and also used by Rabelais, in both cases in a crude sense, “to have one's pleasure of a woman.” The modern meaning, to sway, swing or rattle, is thus a later development of a word that began in a very different register. No older source language is established for it.
en.brimer: Formed with ~-er~ from the dialectal noun ~brime~, probably a blend of ~brume~ (“mist”) and ~frimas~ (“hoarfrost”). ~Brime~ meant a blast of frost or cold wind that withers fruit, and the participle ~brimé~ described grapes marked by such damage. The modern senses of ~brimer~, to bully or haze a newcomer, are a long way from this agricultural origin. The blend itself is only proposed, not proven.
en.bringuebaler:
The verb is a blend of several elements. Its core is ~baller~ (“to dance”), from Latin ~ballāre~, preceded by an element ~brimb-~ that in Middle French expressed the idea of moving about. That element also gave ~brimber~ (“to beg”), still visible in the noun ~bribe~. The older form ~brimbaler~ is an obsolete variant.

The final shape ~bringuebaler~, with its extra syllable, is attributed to the influence of Middle French ~trinqueballer~ (“to chime a bell”), itself from ~triballer~ (“to wander”), the ancestor of modern ~trimbaler~. In modern French ~bringuebaler~ (also spelled ~brinquebaler~) describes something swinging and rattling as it moves, and it is colloquial. Its kin are ~baller~, the root of ~bal~ and ~ballet~ and of English ~ball~ in the sense of a dance, and ~trimbaler~ (“to lug around”).
en.brinquebaler:
~Brinquebaler~ is an expressive formation, meaning that it was shaped by sound and feeling rather than built from clear parts. According to the TLFi, it arose from a crossing between Latin ~ballare~ (“to dance”), the source of French ~baller~, and words of the ~brimb-~ family, notably Middle French ~brimber~ (“to beg”), from which ~bribe~ comes, hence the idea of wandering or being shaken about. The forms in ~bringue-~ and ~brinque-~ probably took on the influence of ~trinqueballer~ (“to swing bells,” 1534, Rabelais), an alteration of ~triballer~ (“to go to and fro,” 1532).

The oldest attestation is ~brinbaler~, around 1440-42, in a crude sense, “to enjoy a woman.” By the 1540s it meant “to shake about,” and from the 1570s it was said of bells, a use that survives in the transitive ~brimbaler~ of the seventeenth century. The modern sense, “to sway, to oscillate,” is recorded in 1835. The verb is spelled ~bringuebaler~ or ~brinquebaler~, and the Académie also gives ~brimbaler~. It is said of a vehicle that jolts noisily along or of empty barrels that knock about.
en.briquer: A denominal verb from ~brique~ (“brick”) with ~-er~, meaning “to scrub, to polish.” The noun ~brique~ was borrowed from Middle Dutch ~bricke~ or ~brike~, itself tied to the verb ~brecken~ (“to break”), so a brick is etymologically a broken piece. French Wiktionary dates Old French ~brike~ to 1204, when it meant “puck, disc,” and gives the modern sense from the end of the thirteenth century. It also records the meaning “piece, crumb.” The Germanic family is the same one that gives English ~brick~ and ~break~.
en.briqueter: Formed from ~brique~ (“brick”) with the ending ~-er~, meaning to pave or line with brick. The noun ~brique~ was borrowed from Middle Dutch ~bricke~ or ~brike~, related to the verb ~brecken~ (“to break”), a loan that fits the brick-making tradition of Flanders. It is attested in Old French as ~brike~ in 1204, in the sense of a flat disc, and from the end of the thirteenth century with its modern sense.
en.briser:
From Old French ~brisier~, from Late Latin ~brisāre~ (“to crush, press”), widely held to be of Gaulish origin, from a Celtic *~brissu~ (“to shatter, break”). The Celtic connection is supported by cognates such as Irish ~bris~ (“to break”) and Breton ~bresk~ (“fragile”), ~brien~ (“crumbs”) and ~bruzun~ (“fragments”). The verb is thus one of the Gaulish substrate words that survived the Roman conquest beneath the Latin of Gaul.

Notably, ~briser~ displaced the older Old French ~fraindre~ (from Latin ~frangere~, “to break”), which has otherwise left only learned derivatives like ~fraction~ and ~fragment~. From the concrete sense of smashing, ~briser~ grew a rich figurative life: ~briser la glace~ (“to break the ice”), ~briser le cœur~ (“to break someone's heart”), and the cry of a wrecked spirit. Its descendants name the things that break or break things — ~brisure~, ~débris~, ~brisant~ (a breaker, a reef), and the compounds ~brise-glace~ (“icebreaker”) and ~brise-lame~ (“breakwater”).
en.brocanter:
~Brocanter~ has an uncertain origin, and French Wiktionary offers a cautious account. It links the verb to English ~broker~ (“agent, dealer”) and to Late Latin ~abrocamentum~, “the act of buying wholesale and reselling retail”. A Picard form ~broqueter~ is attested, which Godefroy defines as selling wine by the ~broc~ (a pitcher), and a Norman form ~abrokeur~.

The same source says the verb is probably related to Dutch ~brok~ (“fragment”) and German ~Brocken~ (“piece”), and ties it to the French phrase ~de bric et de broc~ through a shift in sense: to break up, to detail, to sell by the piece. The ending ~-anter~, rather than the ~-eter~ of ~broqueter~, is obscure, and is probably influenced by ~marchand~ and ~marchander~. Today ~brocanter~ means to buy, sell or barter merchandise, in the dealer's trade of second-hand goods. Because these links are only proposed, the verb is best seen as a word whose family is clear, trade by small pieces, but whose precise descent is not.
en.brocarder: ~Brocarder~ is formed from ~brocard~ (“a gibe, a jeer”) plus the verbal ending ~-er~: to mock or ridicule. The origin of the noun is uncertain, and French Wiktionary gives several accounts. One derives it from Old French ~broquer~ (“to prick”), attested in 1440. Another, introduced with “probably,” sees ~Brocardus~, the Latin name of Burchard, bishop of Worms, who around the start of the eleventh century published a book of legal sentences. A third traces it to Picard ~broque~ (“spit, skewer”).
en.brocher: Formed from the noun ~broche~ and the verb ending ~-er~, by way of Old and Middle French ~brochier~ and ~brocher~. According to French Wiktionary, it first meant to spur a horse, to prick with the spur, and so to urge on. The noun ~broche~ comes from Vulgar Latin ~brocca~ (“spike”), the feminine of Latin ~broccus~ (“with prominent teeth”), ultimately of Gaulish origin; Old Irish ~brog~ (“awl”) is a comparison. The verb is therefore built on the idea of a pointed tool piercing something, the thread behind the later senses of stitching.
en.broder:
From Old French ~brosder~ (later ~broder~), a word of Germanic origin. French Wiktionary derives it from Old Low Franconian *~brosdôn~, which it analyzes as ~borst~ (“bristle”) combined with *~brordôn~ (“to embroider”). It points to German ~Borste~ (“bristle”) and to Old Saxon ~brordôn~ (“to embroider, decorate”) and ~brord~ (“needle”). English Wiktionary gives a simpler line, a Proto-Germanic verb *~bruzdōną~ passing into Old French, without the compound. The two accounts agree on a Germanic source but differ on how it was built. Either way, ~broder~ is a Germanic loan hiding behind a French shape, with no Latin ancestor.

In French the verb meant to decorate cloth with needle and thread, and ~broder~ still does. From that came a figure: ~broder une histoire~ means to embellish a tale with invented detail, as thread embellishes plain fabric. The family includes ~broderie~ (“embroidery”), ~brodeur~ and ~brodeuse~ (“embroiderer”). The Old Saxon word for “needle” suits the craft well, but the sources do not say how the Frankish word came to mean needlework.
en.broncher: The origin is uncertain. French Wiktionary traces ~broncher~ to Old French ~bronchier~ (“to lean forward”), whose own source it calls unknown. English Wiktionary offers a proposal: Vulgar Latin *~bruncāre~, from *~bruncus~, itself a cross of Latin ~broccus~ (“projecting, pointed”) and ~truncus~ (“maimed, docked, truncated”). That blend is a hypothesis, not an established chain. The modern senses, to stumble, to flinch or to budge, are best known in the phrase ~sans broncher~, “without flinching”.
en.bronzer: ~Bronzer~ is formed from ~bronze~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun was borrowed from Italian ~bronzo~, the alloy of copper and tin. The verb first meant “to give the colour or finish of bronze,” as when a statue or an object is coated or tinted to look like it. From there came the sense of turning the skin the same warm brown, so that ~bronzer~ today usually means “to tan,” as one does in the sun.
en.brosser: Formed from the noun ~brosse~ (“brush”) and the verb ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary adds that in Old French ~brosse~ also meant “brushwood, undergrowth,” and it uses this to explain an older sense of ~brosser~, “to dash through thick woods,” and the colloquial ~tu peux te brosser~, “you can go without” (literally, “you can brush yourself”). The everyday sense of brushing clothes, hair or teeth is the one that now dominates. The two senses of the noun, the tool and the thicket, are not shown to be connected here, so the ordinary reading remains simply “to work on something with a ~brosse~.”
en.brouetter: Formed from ~brouette~ (“wheelbarrow”) with the verbal ending ~-er~: to carry something in a wheelbarrow. The noun is attested in Old French as ~brouete~ (“small cart”), and in 1690 as a kind of sedan chair. Its origin is explained two ways. Most often it is taken as a diminutive in ~-ette~ of Old French *~beroue~, from Latin ~birota~ (“two-wheeled vehicle”). English Wiktionary instead derives it from Old French ~baroueste~, a diminutive of ~barot~, from Frankish *~barwā~, a cognate of English ~barrow~, and allows that the two sources were conflated.
en.brouillasser: Recorded from 1834, ~brouillasser~ is formed from ~brouillas~, an old form of ~brouillard~ (“fog”), and the verb ending ~-er~. It is an impersonal verb for fine, misty rain: “il brouillasse” means “it is drizzling.” The TLFi also notes an earlier Middle French ~brouillasser~ meaning “to mix up, to muddle,” built on ~brouillas~ in its thirteenth-century sense of “trouble, confusion.” Both uses rest on the same noun, ~brouillas~.
en.brouiller:
From Old French ~brouiller~, from Vulgar Latin *~brodiculāre~ (French Wiktionary says Gallo-Romance), itself built on *~brodicāre~, from Late Latin ~brodium~ (“broth, stew, mixture”), which was borrowed from Proto-Germanic *~bruþą~ (“stock, broth”). Lombard ~brodigar~ (“to soil, to pollute”) is a comparison offered for the intermediate verb. The Germanic word is also the source of English ~broth~. French Wiktionary places the verb beside ~bruir~ (“to steam”), Old French ~bruller~ (“to burn”) and English ~broil~ and ~brew~, and explains the noun ~brouillard~ (“fog,” properly “vapor”) in the same way. These are comparisons to note, not steps in the chain, which is why the entry does not claim the verb comes from any of them.

A rival explanation, mentioned by Littré, connects the verb with Old Occitan ~bruelhar~ (“to sprout”) and Catalan ~brollar~ (“to gush”). French Wiktionary rejects it, since it cannot account for the three-syllable forms of the word in Old French. The word also left France and came back: Italian borrowed it as ~brogliare~, ~imbrogliare~ and ~sbrogliare~, and French took it back in the form ~imbroglio~. The safest reading is that ~brouiller~ descends from ~brodium~, with ~bruir~, ~broil~ and ~brew~ left as possible relatives.
en.brouter: A verb made from the noun ~brout~ (“young shoot of a tree”) and the ending ~-er~, written ~broster~ in Old French. To ~brouter~ is thus to feed on shoots and young growth, as goats and deer do. The noun ~brout~ comes from Frankish ~brust~ (“bud, shoot”), which French Wiktionary links to Slovene ~brst~ (“bud”) and to Latin ~frutex~ (“bush”). The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and here means “to feed on N, to work with N.”
en.broyer:
French ~broyer~ is a Germanic word in Romance clothing. English Wiktionary traces it through Middle French ~broier~ and Old French ~breier~ (“to break”) to Frankish *~brekan~ (“to break”), from Proto-Germanic *~brekaną~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰreg-~ (“to break”). French Wiktionary adds an intermediate step, a Vulgar Latin *~brecāre~ that Romance speakers fashioned from the Frankish verb. The cognates are plentiful: English ~break~, German ~brechen~, Old English ~brecan~, Spanish ~bregar~ (“to toil, to deal with”) and Italian ~sbrigare~ (“to sort out”).

The Old French verb meant simply “to break,” and French later narrowed it to breaking something into very small pieces, which is to say crushing or grinding. ~Broyer~ now covers the mortar and pestle, the mill and the industrial crusher, with the nouns ~broyeur~ (“grinder”) and ~broyage~ (“grinding”). The figurative idiom ~broyer du noir~ (“to brood”) literally grinds black, an image of the mind working over dark thoughts. The English cousin ~break~, from the same Germanic root, keeps the broad original sense.
en.bruiner: Derived from the noun ~bruine~ (“drizzle”). French Wiktionary gives that noun two entries. In the first, dated to the 12th century, it comes from Latin ~pruīna~ (“hoarfrost”), influenced by ~brume~ (“mist”); the same Latin word gave ~pruine~, the waxy bloom on a fruit's skin. For the second entry the origin is unknown. The verb, “to drizzle,” is the weather itself turned into an action.
en.bruire: From Old French ~bruire~, from Vulgar Latin *~brūgere~ (attested in the form ~brugit~), a crossing of Latin ~rugīre~ (“to roar”, whence French ~rugir~) and *~bragere~ (whence French ~braire~). English ~burr~ is a point of comparison. The present participle is traditionally ~bruyant~, which became an adjective meaning “noisy”. A rival form, ~bruissant~, was modeled on the verbs of the second group in ~-ir~, which also gave the noun ~bruissement~. This rests on a confusion, since ~bruire~ belongs to the third group in ~-ire~, and ~bruyant~ and ~bruissant~ now live side by side.
en.bruisser: Formed from ~bruit~ (“noise”) with the ending ~-er~, so “to make a noise, to rustle.” ~Bruit~ is a deverbal of ~bruire~ (“to roar”). English Wiktionary says it began as the noun use of that verb's past participle, and that ~bruire~ is an alteration, influenced by ~braire~ (“to bray”), of Latin ~rugītus~ (“roaring”). Spanish ~ruido~ is a cognate.
en.bruiter: ~Bruiter~ is formed from the noun ~bruit~ (“noise”) + ~-er~, so “to make a noise” and, in the theater and cinema, “to add the sound effects.” The noun ~bruit~ is a back-formation from the verb ~bruire~ (“to roar, to rustle”): in Old French it was the past participle of ~bruire~ used as a noun. English Wiktionary traces ~bruire~ to Latin ~rugītus~ (“roaring”), altered by association with ~braire~ (“to bray”). So the verb loops back to the noun's own source.
en.bruler:
~Bruler~ is the spelling of ~brûler~ (“to burn”) under the 1990 reform. The verb comes from Middle French ~brusler~ and Old French ~brusler~ or ~bruller~, but its deeper origin is disputed. French Wiktionary proposes a Latin chain: ~urere~ (“to burn”) with ~per-~ gave ~perurere~, then ~perustare~, shortened to ~prustare~, the direct source of Italian ~bruciare~; a diminutive ~prustolare~ would have given Old French ~brustlar~ and then ~brusler~. English Wiktionary instead starts from Latin ~ustulāre~ (“to scorch”) and calls the initial ~br-~ unexplained.

English Wiktionary lists possible outside influences without choosing among them: Old French ~bruir~ from Frankish *~brōjan~ (“to scald”), Latin ~ambūrere~ and ~combūrere~ (“to burn”), and a Gaulish cousin of Old Irish ~bruth~ (“boiling heat”). The family around the verb is clearer. French Wiktionary ties the learned words ~ustion~ and ~ustulation~ to the Latin verbs above, and ~brûlure~, ~brûlant~ and ~brûleur~ are derived from the French verb itself.
en.brunir: The verb already existed in Old French, where ~brunir~ meant “to polish, make brown”, and it descends from Middle French. It is a derivative of the adjective ~brun~ with the verb ending ~-ir~. The adjective comes from Late Latin ~brūnus~, borrowed from Frankish *~brūn~ (“brown, shiny”), from Proto-Germanic *~brūnaz~, which is cognate with English ~brown~ and German ~braun~. That old double sense, brown and gleaming, explains why ~brunir~ means both “to tan” and “to burnish metal”. English ~burnish~ comes from a variant of the same Old French verb.
en.brusquer: ~Brusquer~ is formed from the adjective ~brusque~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. The adjective was borrowed from Italian ~brusco~ (“sharp, sour”) and gradually took on the sense “lively, bold”, and it is a doublet of ~brusc~. The verb therefore means to treat someone in an abrupt, rough way, to browbeat, and by extension to hurry something along, as when one ~brusque~ an operation, forcing the pace.
en.brutaliser: Formed from the adjective ~brutal~ with the suffix ~-iser~, which turns a base into a verb of making or treating: to treat in a brutal way. The adjective ~brutal~ comes from Latin ~brutalis~ (“beastlike”), and English Wiktionary traces it to Medieval Latin ~brūtālis~ (“savage, stupid”), from ~brūtus~ (“dull, stupid”). ~Brutaliser~ means to ill-treat, to handle roughly or violently.
en.brésiller: The verb means to tint or dye with brazilwood. French Wiktionary says only that it comes from Provençal and flags that information as still to be checked, so the exact source form is left open here. The dyewood itself is the key to the sense: the verb names the act of coloring something with it.
en.brêler: Derived from Old French ~brael~ or ~braiel~ (“belt, bond”), itself taken from ~braie~. The noun named a girdle or tie, so ~brêler~ is to bind something with a rope or cord. ~Braie~ is the old word for breeches, from Latin ~brāca~, a garment the Romans associated with the Gauls. The verb is thus a small relic of a word family that began with a piece of clothing.
en.brûler:
Attested as Old French ~bruller~ (around 1120), later ~brusler~, then modern ~brûler~ — the circumflex marking the lost ~s~. The deeper origin is genuinely debated. The favoured account makes it an intensified form of Old French ~usler~ (“to scorch”), from Latin ~ustulāre~ (“to singe, scorch slightly”), a diminutive of ~ūrere~ (“to burn”). But several sources may have contributed and the matter is unsettled: a Frankish element *~brōjan~ (“to scald, sear”, source of Old French ~bruir~), the Latin participles ~ambustus~ and ~combustus~, and a Gaulish cognate of Old Irish ~bruth~ (“burning heat”) have each been proposed as shaping the ~br-~. Italian ~bruciare~ is comparably murky.

Whatever its tangle of roots, ~brûler~ settled as the ordinary French word for burning, literal and figurative.
