It heats idiom richly: ~brûler les étapes~ (“to skip the stages,” rush ahead), ~brûler la politesse~ (to leave abruptly), ~brûler ses vaisseaux~ (to burn one's boats). From it French built ~brûlure~ (“a burn”), ~brûlant~ (“burning, scalding”), ~brûleur~, and the blunt phrase ~à brûle-pourpoint~ (“point-blank”). The competing etymologies make the verb itself a small monument to how messily a common word can be assembled.
en.bucher: The TLFi derives ~bucher~ from ~bûche~ (“log”) with the ending ~-er~. The first sense is of working wood with an axe, found about 1360-70, and it later extended to stone, with the sense of knocking off projections. The informal “to work hard, to cram” is attested in Flaubert's correspondence in 1856. An older ~buskier~ (“to knock at a door”) dates from about 1200. Littré notes that Italian ~buscare~ and Spanish ~buscar~ (“to search”) resemble the French in form and, like it, go back to a word for “wood.”
en.budgéter: ~Budgéter~ is formed from ~budget~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~: to enter in a budget or plan spending. The noun was borrowed from English ~budget~, which came from Old French ~bougette~ (“bag serving as a purse”), so the word returned to French by way of English. French used it from the eighteenth century, but only for the finances of England; it took its current sense in the early nineteenth century.
en.budgétiser: Formed from ~budget~ plus the suffix ~-iser~, with the stem lengthened to ~budgét-~: to ~budgétiser~ is to enter an item in a budget. The noun came into French from English ~budget~, which goes back to Old French ~bougette~ (“bag serving as a purse”), so the two are doublets. In France the word was used from the eighteenth century, but only for the finances of England; it took its current sense in the early nineteenth. The suffix ~-iser~ means “provide with N” or “convert into N,” here “to turn into a budget line.”
en.buller: A verb made from the noun ~bulle~ (“bubble”) and the ending ~-er~, so ~buller~ is “to form bubbles.” The noun ~bulle~ was borrowed from Latin ~bulla~ (“bubble”), by way of Old and Middle French. Latin ~bulla~ was originally a small gold sphere that sons of patricians wore around the neck until the age of seventeen. ~Bulle~ is a doublet of ~boule~, the same Latin word reached by the inherited route. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and here means “to produce N.”
en.bureaucratiser: Formed from the adjective ~bureaucratique~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which marks a transformation: to make bureaucratic. The adjective derives from ~bureaucrate~ (“bureaucrat”) or ~bureaucratie~ with the suffix ~-ique~, and the ending ~-ique~ drops before ~-iser~. The verb describes the process by which an organization comes to be governed by offices, rules and paperwork.
en.buriner: Formed in French from ~burin~ + the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, meaning “to engrave or cut with a ~burin~.” The noun is borrowed from Italian ~burino~, which French Wiktionary traces to a Lombard form *~boro~ (“drill”), to be compared with Dutch ~boor~ and Old High German ~bora~, both meaning “drill.” A ~burin~ is the steel tool of engravers, and ~buriner~ thus names the work done with it, to chisel or engrave a surface.
en.buter: From Old French ~buter~ (“to push, to strike”), a variant of ~bouter~ (“to push”). The sense “to bump into, to come up against” (~buter contre~) continues that old idea of pushing. The slang sense “to kill” is tied by French Wiktionary to the noun ~but~ (“goal, target”), though the sources do not detail the steps. The verb is related to ~bouter~ and to words such as ~butée~ (“abutment, stop”), ~rebuter~ and ~débouter~.
en.butiner: Formed in French from ~butin~ (“loot, plunder”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so first “to take booty.” The other senses grew from that one, including the bee's gathering of pollen and nectar. The noun ~butin~ comes from Middle High German ~bute~, the ancestor of German ~Beute~ (“booty, prey”). French Wiktionary adds that, given Swedish ~byte~, the word may have entered French by sea routes through trade with the Hanseatic League. The German word is itself probably from Gaulish ~boudi~ (“victory, profit”) or a related Celtic term, a possibility that remains uncertain.
en.butter: ~Butter~ is formed from ~butte~ (“mound”) with the verb ending ~-er~. ~Butte~ is itself recorded as a variant, the feminine form, of ~but~ (“aim, target”). The verb is used in gardening: to ~butter~ potatoes or leeks is to heap earth up around the base of the plants in a little mound. The ending ~-er~ is the usual first-conjugation ending, the descendant of Latin ~-are~, here turning a noun into a verb meaning “to provide with” or “to work with” that noun.
en.bâcher: ~Bâcher~ is formed from the noun ~bâche~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~: to cover with a tarpaulin. The origin of ~bâche~ is uncertain; it may be a shortened form of Old French ~baschoe~, a woven basket or hamper, from Latin ~bascauda~, a word of Celtic origin. The verb has slang senses of its own. ~Se bâcher~ in the sense of going to bed is attested from 1872 and is tied to ~bâche~ as a sheet or bed. For abandoning a race in cycling, two explanations are offered: sheltering from rain, or a spread of a Swiss use meaning “to stop”.
en.bâcler:
The origin of ~bâcler~ is uncertain. The verb is thinly attested early: an isolated occurrence, a 1596 line, “ils baclent et estoupent sa bouche”, and an indirect trace in ~desbacler~ (1416). One proposal derives it from a Vulgar Latin *~bacculare~ (“to fasten with a wooden bar,” per French Wiktionary), from Latin ~baculum~ (“rod, staff”), which English Wiktionary traces to a Proto-Indo-European *~bak-~. Two rivals exist. Middle Dutch ~bakkelen~ suits the sense but not the chronology, and English Wiktionary calls that derivation discredited. The other is an exceptional vowel variant of ~boucler~ (“to fasten, to finish a job”).

The early traces concern closing and clearing rather than haste. ~Desbacler~, whose modern form is ~débâcler~, meant “to clear a harbor”: ships already unloaded left so that loaded ships arriving could take their places. That verb gave ~débâcle~. How ~bâcler~ itself reached its modern senses, “to bang out” and “to botch,” the sources do not say. If the Latin ~baculum~ is indeed the root, the verb is a distant relative of ~bacille~ (“bacillus”), which rests on a diminutive of ~baculum~. Because the Latin origin is only proposed, the safest summary is that the history is partial, and the modern sense of hasty work rests on no stated path.
en.bâfrer: The origin of ~bâfrer~, “to guzzle, to gobble,” is uncertain. French Wiktionary offers two proposals: that it may come from Middle French ~bauffrer~, itself derived from the imitative syllable ~baf~ suggesting something thick, swollen or greedy, or that it may come from a Germanic word ~baf~ (“lip”). English Wiktionary says only that the word was originally onomatopoeic. The sources therefore agree on little beyond a sound-imitating origin, and none of these accounts is settled. The verb is familiar in register and describes eating greedily and noisily.
en.bâiller:
~Bâiller~ comes from Middle French ~baailler~, from Old French ~baaillier~, inherited from a late Latin verb. The French text gives it as popular Latin ~bataclare~, from a verb *~batare~ (“to gape”), while English Wiktionary gives Early Medieval Latin ~bataculāre~ (“to yawn”); the two forms are close variants of one verb. The French text links the word to Occitan ~badalhar~, Catalan ~badallar~ and Italian ~sbadigliare~, so the verb is shared by the Romance languages.

The circumflex of ~bâiller~ marks the vanished ~a~ of Old French ~baailler~, where two vowels met. The French text glosses *~batare~ with ~bayer~ and ~béer~, “to stand open,” verbs that survive in ~bayer aux corneilles~ (“to gape at the sky”) and in ~bouche bée~ (“open-mouthed”). Besides “to yawn,” ~bâiller~ can mean “to be ajar,” of a door or a collar. The verb thus names an open mouth, whether wide with boredom or merely left open.
en.bâillonner: The verb is formed from ~bâillon~ (“gag”) and the ending ~-er~, so it means to put a gag on someone. The noun is itself derived from ~bâiller~ (“to yawn”) with the suffix ~-on~. French Wiktionary explains the choice: a gag holds the mouth open, as in a yawn. The same image underlies the figurative use, to silence someone or something by force.
en.bâter: A denominal verb: ~bât~ (“packsaddle”) plus the verb ending ~-er~, so “to fit with a packsaddle.” English Wiktionary instead presents it as inherited from Old and Middle French ~baster~, which hints at an older verb. The noun ~bât~ comes from Old French ~bast~, from Vulgar Latin *~bastum~, a noun derived from a verb *~bastāre~ (“to carry”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~βαστάζειν~ (~bastázein~, “to lift, bear”). The ending ~-er~ is the Latin ~-are~ of first-conjugation verbs. A packsaddle is thus, etymologically, “that which carries,” and ~bât~ displaced the older ~somme~ in that role.
en.bâtir:
From Old French ~bastir~ (“to baste, to interweave”), from Old Low Frankish *~bastjan~ (“to assemble, to interlace fibers”), from a Proto-Germanic root meaning bast, the fibrous inner bark used for tying and weaving. The word is cognate with German ~Bast~ and Dutch ~bast~ (“bast, inner bark”). The circumflex of ~bâtir~ marks a lost ~s~ that the older spelling ~bastir~ still showed.

The development is a small lesson in how houses were once made. From the sense “to weave, to lash together with bast,” the word moved to “to make a fence of stakes interwoven with branches,” the wattle of early construction, and from there simply to “to build, to erect.” French thus reached its grand modern verb — ~bâtir~ une maison, une cathédrale, une fortune — from a humble word for tying plant fibers together. (The competing guess that linked it to ~bât~, “packsaddle,” or ~bâton~, “stick,” is rejected by the TLFi.) The Frankish origin left a compact French family: ~bâtiment~ (“building”), ~bâtisse~ (“edifice”), ~bâtisseur~ (“builder”), and ~rebâtir~ (“to rebuild”) — all standing on a foundation of woven bast. The older sewing sense survives separately in ~bâtir~ meaning “to tack, to baste” cloth.
en.bâtonner: ~Bâtonner~ is formed from ~bâton~ with the verb ending ~-er~, and means to strike with a stick. ~Bâton~ comes from Old French ~baston~, probably from Vulgar Latin ~bastōnem~, a form of Late Latin ~bastum~ (“stick”), attested in the fourth century. ~Bastum~ may itself come from a verb ~bastāre~ (“to carry”), which would link it to Ancient Greek ~bastázein~; this is only a probable link.
en.béatifier:
Borrowed from Latin ~beātificāre~ (“to make happy, to bless”). The Latin verb joins ~beātus~ (“happy, blessed”), the past participle of ~beāre~ (“to make happy”), to the verb-forming element ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”), so it means literally “to make blessed.” Italian ~beatificare~, Spanish ~beatificar~ and English ~beatify~ are its learned relatives.

In French the verb belongs to the language of the Church: ~béatifier~ is to declare a deceased person blessed, the step that precedes canonization. Its family includes ~béat~ (“blissful”, today often tinged with naive contentment), ~béatitude~ (“bliss”) and ~béatification~. The element ~-ficāre~ is also at work in many French verbs in ~-fier~, such as ~glorifier~, ~purifier~ and ~sanctifier~, which likewise come from Latin verbs in ~-ficāre~.
en.bécoter: A denominal verb on ~bécot~ (“a little kiss, a peck”), meaning to kiss, to smooch. The sources disagree on which way the derivation runs: ~bécot~ is either a diminutive of ~bec~ (“beak”) in the sense of a kiss with the suffix ~-ot~, so that a kiss is a little peck with the beak, or a noun backformed from ~bécoter~ itself. The verb carries the usual ending ~-er~, which descends from Latin ~-are~.
en.béer: ~Béer~ is the modern spelling of Old French ~baer~ (“to open wide”), which French Wiktionary derives from a Vulgar Latin verb reconstructed as *~batare~. English Wiktionary treats ~béer~ as a variant of ~bayer~ (“to gape”), and French Wiktionary adds that ~béer~, ~bâiller~ and ~bayer~ share one origin. The verb is now rare and lives on mostly in the participle ~béant~ (“gaping”) and in the expression ~bouche bée~ (“open-mouthed”), while its sibling survives in ~bayer aux corneilles~ (“to stand gaping, daydreaming”).
en.bégayer: Formed from ~bègue~ (“stammerer”) with the suffix ~-ayer~, and found in Old French as ~beguer~ or ~besguer~. The base ~bègue~ in turn comes from the Old French verb ~beguer~, so the noun and the verb grew from one stem. The deeper origin is obscure. English Wiktionary most likely traces it to Middle Dutch ~beggen~ (“to chat”), but that word is itself of uncertain origin, and several other proposed sources are rejected.
en.bégueter: From the imitative syllable ~bé~, the cry of a goat; French Wiktionary sends the reader to ~bêler~. ~Bégueter~ is thus a verb of the same sound as ~bêler~ (“to bleat”), which itself goes back to Latin ~bālāre~. In both words the sound of the animal does the work of the root, and no older source word is needed.
en.bémoliser: Formed from the musical term ~bémol~ (“flat”) with the suffix ~-iser~, so “to flatten a note,” and by extension to soften. The noun comes from Medieval Latin ~b molle~ (“soft B”). The flat sign looks like a small ~b~, which distinguished it from the letter. The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~ and here means to treat with or provide with the base.
en.bénir:
From Old French ~beneïr~, inherited from Latin ~benedīcere~, a compound of ~bene~ (“well”) and ~dīcere~ (“to say”), so literally “to speak well of.” Latin ~dīcere~ is the everyday verb of speaking that gave French ~dire~. Its sister ~maledīcere~ (“to speak ill of”) gave ~maudire~, which makes ~bénir~ and ~maudire~ a matched pair of blessing and cursing. The Latin verb lived on across the Romance languages: Italian ~benedire~ and Spanish ~bendecir~ are its cognates, and English ~benediction~ is a learned borrowing from the related Latin noun ~benedictio~.

The meaning stayed close to the Latin, in a religious setting: a priest or a parent calls down divine favor on someone or something. Figuratively, one ~bénit~ a person or a day for which one is grateful, as in the phrase “je bénis le jour où…”. French keeps two participles. ~Béni~ is the ordinary one, while ~bénit~ survives only for things consecrated by a priest, as in ~eau bénite~ (“holy water”) and ~pain bénit~ (“consecrated bread”). The family is still large: ~bénédiction~ and ~bénédicité~ (the prayer before a meal, from Latin ~benedicite~, “bless ye”) come straight from the Latin, and the given name ~Benoît~ descends from Latin ~Benedictus~ (“blessed”).
en.bénéficier:
From the noun ~bénéfice~, itself from Latin ~beneficium~ (“a kindness, favor, service”); the verb mirrors Medieval Latin ~beneficiāre~ (“to grant a benefice to”). ~Beneficium~ is built from ~bene~ (“well”) and a combining form of ~facere~ (“to do, to make”), so it means literally “a thing well done.” ~Facere~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to set, put, place”), shared with English ~do~ and ~deed~ and with Greek ~títhēmi~ (“I place”). Romance kin include Italian ~beneficiare~ and Spanish ~beneficiar~.

The Latin word named an act of generosity, a good turn done for another. In the Middle Ages the Church narrowed ~beneficium~ to a very specific gift: a ~bénéfice~ became an endowed ecclesiastical post and the income that came with it — a clergyman’s living. From that benefit-as-income the word broadened back out to commercial profit and, in the verb ~bénéficier~, to the general sense “to enjoy, to profit from” an advantage. The ~bene-~ element survives in ~bénir~ (“to bless”), ~bénévole~ (“volunteer,” literally “well-wishing”), and ~bienfait~ (“good deed”); the ~facere~ element seeds a teeming family — ~faire~, ~défaire~, ~parfait~, ~bienfaiteur~, and the everyday ~bénéfice~ itself.
en.béqueter: Formed from the noun ~bec~ (“beak”) with a verb ending, so it means to peck at something. ~Bec~ comes from Old French ~bec~, from Latin ~beccus~ (“beak”), which Suetonius records for a rooster's beak. Latin took it from Gaulish *~beccos~, from Proto-Celtic *~bekkos~.
en.béquiller: Formed from ~béquille~ (“crutch”) with the ending ~-er~, so “to walk on crutches.” The noun is a diminutive of ~bec~ (“beak”), named for the shape of the crosspiece that tops the cane. The verb also applies to a motorcycle, where it means to lower the kickstand, which is likewise called a crutch in French.
en.bétonner: Formed from the noun ~béton~ plus ~-er~, “to build or cover with concrete.” The noun ~béton~ is attested in Old French around 1165 as ~betun~ (“mortar”), from Vulgar Latin *~bittūmen~, from Latin ~bitūmen~ (“bitumen”). It is a doublet of ~bitume~, which was borrowed later straight from Latin.
en.bêcher: Formed from ~bêche~ (“spade”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so “to work with a spade,” hence “to dig.” English Wiktionary traces ~bêche~ through Old French ~besche~ and Late Latin ~besca~ to Frankish *~bikkju~ (“pickaxe, spade”). French Wiktionary instead proposes a Celtic source, close to Breton ~bac'h~, so the deep origin of the noun is debated. In familiar French the verb also means “to badmouth,” a figurative extension of the digging sense.
en.bêcheveter: Formed from the noun ~bêchevet~ (“double bedhead”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so the verb means to place things head to tail, or to turn them upside down. The noun comes from Old French ~bechevet~, which goes back to Latin ~biceps~ (“two-headed”). The circumflex of the modern spelling is a hypercorrection: speakers took the word for a compound of ~bis~ and ~chevet~ and added an accent as if an ~s~ had fallen silent. The same word, altered, gave ~tête-bêche~.
en.bêler:
Inherited from Late Latin ~bēlāre~, a variant of Latin ~bālō~, a verb that imitates the cry of a sheep or goat. The Latin verb is described as formed on the onomatopoeia for that cry, and the imitation is still easy to hear in the French syllable “bê” and in English “baa.” Its relatives elsewhere in Romance include Spanish ~balar~ and Italian ~belare~.

Because the word is imitative, its sound still resembles the animal it names. The sense stayed remarkably stable from Latin to today: ~bêler~ is first of all what sheep, goats and lambs do. By extension, it describes a person who speaks or sings in a thin, quavering, complaining voice, with a faint mockery. The noun ~bêlement~ names the cry itself. English ~bleat~ imitates the same sound, but it is a native Germanic formation and a separate word rather than a descendant of ~bālō~.
en.bêtifier: Formed from ~bête~ with the suffix ~-ifier~, which makes verbs meaning “to make A” or “to turn into N”: to make someone a mindless ~bête~, to dull or brutalize, and, used intransitively, to act childishly. The noun ~bête~ comes from Old French ~beste~, which goes back to Latin ~bestia~ (“beast”). The suffix ~-ifier~ descends from Latin ~-(i)ficāre~, itself from ~facere~ (“to make”).
en.bûcher: Formed from ~bûche~ (“log”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, so ~bûcher~ means to hew and, in familiar speech, to study hard. ~Bûche~ comes from Old French ~busche~ (“piece of wood to be burned”), from Vulgar Latin *~busca~, attested in the eleventh century with the sense of firewood, from Frankish *~busk~, from Proto-Germanic *~buskaz~. English ~bush~ is a cognate, and the word is linked to ~bois~.
en.cabaler: Formed from ~cabale~ and the verb ending ~-er~. ~Cabale~ comes from Hebrew ~qabbālāh~ (“received tradition”), derived from ~qibbel~ (“to receive by tradition”), through Medieval Latin ~cabbala~. The noun later came to mean a faction or plot, and ~cabaler~ means “to scheme as part of a cabal” or “to make one.”
en.cabaner: Formed on the noun ~cabane~ with the verb ending ~-er~. In the sense recorded here, ~cabane~ was a shelter made from an overturned canoe, and the verb means to turn a boat over, to capsize. The dwellings of Native American peoples also came to be called ~cabanes~, which links the word to the idea of living in a hut or cabin. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is French's default way of turning a noun into a verb.
en.cabosser: ~Cabosser~ is formed from ~bosse~ (“bump, lump”), the ending ~-er~ and the prefix ~ca-~, with the English-language source adding an influence from ~caboche~. The prefix is a popular element of obscure origin that carries no clear meaning of its own, and it appears in few verbs. The base ~bosse~ comes from Old French ~boce~, which one source traces to Frankish *~bottja~; Italian ~bozza~ is a comparable word. To ~cabosser~ is to dent or batter an object by raising bumps on it.
en.caboter: The origin is uncertain. French Wiktionary derives it from ~cap~ with the suffix ~-oter~, with influence or borrowing from Spanish ~cabo~ (“cape”); the idea is of sailing from cape to cape. ~Cap~ comes from Occitan ~cap~, from Latin ~caput~ (“head”), and is a doublet of ~chef~. A popular story ties the verb to the explorers Sebastian or John Cabot, but the CNRTL rejects it because the chronology does not support it.
en.cabotiner: Formed from ~cabotin~ with the verb ending ~-er~, it means to ham it up or show off. For ~cabotin~ as an actor, French Wiktionary cites a nineteenth-century account that rejects the derivation from ~caboter~. By that account, the word began as the surname of a Mr. Cabotin, a travelling charlatan and showman who sold drugs and played farces, and the proper name then became a common noun for a poor actor. A distinct ~cabotin~ for a fish is a different word, from ~cabot~ plus ~-in~.
en.cabrer: Probably a verb formed on ~cabre~, a word meaning “goat,” with the suffix ~-er~, used of a horse rearing up. Occitan ~cabrar~ and Spanish ~cabrear~ are attested later, which counts against them as the source. The origin remains presumed rather than proven.
en.cabrioler: Formed from the noun ~cabriole~ (“caper, leap”) plus the verbal ending ~-er~, so the verb means to make such leaps. The noun was borrowed from Italian ~capriola~, first as ~capriole~ with a final ~-e~ fitted to French habits. The Italian word means a “kid's jump” and derives from ~capra~ (“goat”), which comes from Latin. The image is of a young goat bounding about, which is exactly what the verb describes.
en.cacaber:
~Cacaber~ is taken from Latin ~cacabare~, a verb that imitates a sound: the repeated syllables of its stem echo the call of a bird. Latin already used it of the partridge. French applies it to the cry of the partridge and also of the quail and the guinea fowl. The verb thus comes straight from Latin, with no later French formation added to it.

The French cross-reference points to ~caqueter~ (“to cackle”), the verb for the cry of a hen, which belongs to the same sound-imitating family. Both are verbs of bird calls, shaped by imitation rather than built from a word with an earlier meaning. ~Cacaber~ itself remains a rare word, confined to the vocabulary of hunting and of birds.
en.cacarder: ~Cacarder~ is an onomatopoeic verb: its sound imitates the harsh cry it names, that of a goose or a jay. Its repeated syllable ~ca-ca~ mimics the cackle itself. The sources give no older source language and no date, which is typical of words that were simply made by ear, and the sense is purely descriptive.
en.cacher:
From Old French ~cachier~ (also ~quachier~), from Vulgar Latin *~coacticare~ (“to compress, to press together”), a frequentative formed on Latin ~coactare~ (“to constrain, to force”), itself from ~cogere~ (“to drive together, to compel,” from ~co-~ + ~agere~, “to drive”). Through ~cogere~ the verb is cognate with Italian ~quattare~ and with the French doublet ~cacher~ beside the learned ~coaguler~.

The original idea was purely physical: to press or squeeze something down. The path to “to hide” runs through that pressing — what is pressed flat or tucked away is concealed — and the sense “to hide” stayed comparatively rare until the 16th century, when ~cacher~ rose to displace older rivals for concealment such as ~musser~, ~esconser~, and ~repondre~. The pressing sense survives in the cousin ~écacher~ (“to crush, to flatten”). From the same Latin ~cogere~ family French keeps ~cachette~ (“hiding place”), ~cache~, ~cache-cache~ (the game “hide-and-seek”), ~cachot~ (“dungeon”), and ~cachotterie~ (“a small secret”) — a whole nest of words for hiding spun out of an ancient verb meaning, of all things, “to squeeze.”
en.cacheter: ~Cacheter~ (“to seal”) is formed from the noun ~cachet~ (“seal”) and the verb ending ~-er~, and means to close or stamp something with a seal. The noun ~cachet~ is in turn built from ~cacher~, taken in the sense of “to press,” and the suffix ~-et~. This ~cacher~ is distinct from the ordinary ~cacher~ (“to hide”), so a seal is, etymologically, something pressed. The ending ~-er~ comes from the Latin first-conjugation ending ~-are~, as in ~chanter~.
en.cachetonner: Formed from ~cacheton~, a variant of ~cachet~, and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~cachet~ is itself ~cacher~ in the old sense of “to press” plus the suffix ~-et~, so the root idea is a pressed mark or seal. The verb is colloquial and means to seek payment for one's services.
en.cadastrer: Formed from ~cadastre~ (“land register”) and the verb ending ~-er~: to survey land or enter it in the register. The noun was borrowed from Occitan ~cathastre~, which came from Italian ~catastro~ (modern ~catasto~) and ultimately from Venetan ~catastico~, recorded in 1185 as a list of citizens holding taxable property, according to French Wiktionary. Behind it lies Byzantine Greek ~κατάστιχον~ (~katástikhon~, “line by line”), built on Ancient Greek ~στίχος~ (“line, row”). The register's name is thus, at bottom, a list written line by line.
en.cadenasser: ~Cadenasser~ is formed from ~cadenas~ (“padlock”) plus the verbal ending ~-er~: to fasten with a padlock. The noun was borrowed from Old Occitan ~cadenat~, from Late Latin ~catēnātum~, which derives from Latin ~catēna~ (“chain”), so a padlock is etymologically a “chained” thing. The noun was also spelled ~cadenat~, and shorter-lived relatives existed: ~cadenaté~ is found in 1606 and ~cadenater~ in 1834.
en.cadencer: ~Cadencer~ is derived from ~cadence~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to give a regular rhythm to.” ~Cadence~ was borrowed from Italian ~cadenza~, first in the sense of a conclusion and then, in the sixteenth century, of a rhythm. The Italian word is traced to a Vulgar Latin ~cadentia~, from the verb ~cadere~ (“to fall, to end”). That makes ~cadence~ a doublet of ~chance~.
en.cadrer:
French ~cadrer~ goes back to Latin ~quadrāre~ (“to make square, to fit, to agree”), from ~quadrus~ (“square”), a relative of ~quattuor~ (“four”), from the Proto-Indo-European word *~kʷetwóres~ (“four”). The sources describe it in two ways: one calls it a borrowing from Latin, the other a verb built on ~cadre~ (“frame”). The two views are compatible, since ~cadre~ itself reached French from Italian ~quadro~, from Latin ~quadrum~ (“square”). Italian ~quadrare~ and Spanish ~cuadrar~ are parallel descendants of ~quadrāre~, and ~carrer~ is a doublet of ~cadrer~: the same Latin verb arriving by another route.

The earliest idea is geometric: to ~cadrer~ is to square one thing to another so that the two line up. From there French drew the figurative sense “to agree with, to be consistent”, as in cela cadre avec ce que je sais (“that fits what I know”). The sense “to frame” a photograph or a shot is a second development, probably drawn from the noun ~cadre~, and it likely explains why speakers now feel the verb as derived from ~cadre~. The family also includes ~carré~ (“square”), ~carreau~, ~équarrir~ and ~quadrature~.
en.cafarder: Formally a derivative of ~cafard~ with the verb ending ~-er~. In 1584 it meant to practice ~cafardie~, that is, to be a hypocrite by feigning a religion. The noun is usually traced to Arabic ~kāfir~ (“unbeliever”), its ending Frenchified to ~-ard~. The order of attestation raises a doubt, though: the verb is recorded in 1508, before the noun (“bigot,” 1512). One alternative account therefore builds the verb on ~farder~ (“to disguise”) with a prefix ~ca-~, “to hide well,” making the noun a back-formation. The origin is debated. The modern sense, “to tattle,” belongs to the same world of hypocrisy and informing.
en.cafeter: French Wiktionary lists two verbs ~cafeter~. The first, used in the Ardennes, is plainly ~café~ plus the ending ~-er~ and means “to drink coffee.” The second is a spelling of ~cafter~ (“to inform on, to rat”), which is formed from ~cafard~ and ~-er~. The noun ~cafard~ is traced to Arabic ~kāfir~ (“unbeliever”), reshaped with the French ending ~-ard~. It first meant a hypocrite or bigot before it named the cockroach. The origin of ~cafard~ is debated, and one rival account builds it on ~farder~ (“to disguise”). The sense of one who reports on others links ~cafard~ to ~mouchard~.
en.cafouiller: ~Cafouiller~ comes from Picard, the northern dialect of the Oïl languages, where it is built from the prefix ~ca-~ and the verb ~fouiller~ (“to dig, to rummage”). The sense is thus one of rummaging about in a disorderly way, which fits its modern meanings of floundering, muddling and, of a machine or a plan, working badly or falling apart.
en.cafter: ~Cafter~ is formed from ~cafard~ and the ending ~-er~, with the sense “to inform on, to rat.” The noun is traced to Arabic ~kāfir~ (“unbeliever”), reshaped with the French ending ~-ard~, and it first meant a hypocrite or bigot before it named the cockroach. French Wiktionary also notes that the origin of ~cafard~ is debated: one rival explanation builds it on ~farder~ (“to disguise”), as a hypocrite who hides his game well. The sense of one who reports on others links ~cafard~ to ~mouchard~.
en.cahoter:
The origin of ~cahoter~ is uncertain. The Trésor de la langue française favors a derivation from Middle Dutch ~hotten~ (“to shake”), the verb behind French ~hocher~. French Wiktionary calls that the more likely account and judges a composition of a prefix ~ca-~ and a Frankish *~hottôn~ (“to shake”) improbable. Other proposals exist. Some derive the word from Latin ~quatere~ (“to shake”) through a frequentative *~quatottare~, an idea that does not convince etymologists, while English Wiktionary mentions Latin ~quatiō~ by way of Frankish *~hottôn~ (compare German ~hotzen~). An imitative origin is also possible.

Whatever its source, the verb means “to jolt, to bump,” typically of a vehicle on a rough road, and in the passive of someone tossed about. Its noun ~cahot~ (“a jolt, a bump in the road”) and the adjective ~cahoteux~ (“bumpy”) belong to the same family. French Wiktionary points to ~cohue~ and ~chahuter~ as words to compare. Since only competing hypotheses exist, the safest summary is a verb of shaking whose origin remains uncertain, with Middle Dutch as the favored source.
en.cailler:
~Cailler~ is inherited from Old French ~quailler~ or ~coaillier~, which came from a Vulgar Latin verb *~coaglāre~ or *~quaglāre~. That form is a syncopated shortening of Latin ~coāgulāre~ (“to coagulate”), with the middle vowel dropped in everyday speech. French also took over the full Latin verb as ~coaguler~, so ~cailler~ and ~coaguler~ are doublets: one worn down by popular use, the other borrowed straight from Latin.

The same Latin verb lives on elsewhere in Romance: Spanish ~cuajar~, Portuguese ~coalhar~ and Italian ~cagliare~ are its relatives, and French ~caillot~ (“clot”) and ~caillé~ (“curdled”) belong to the same family. The two French verbs show how a word can split. ~Coaguler~ kept the full Latin shape and a learned tone. ~Cailler~ took the popular route and still covers milk that curdles and blood that clots. French Wiktionary also records a separate regional ~cailler~, from the Angevin word ~cail~ (“sleep”), a homonym with a different origin.
en.caillouter: The verb is a denominal of ~caillou~ (“pebble, stone”) with the ending ~-er~, first attested in 1769 and meaning to make a road with crushed stone. The origin of ~caillou~ is debated. French Wiktionary derives it, through Norman or Picard forms, from Gaulish *~caliauo-~ (“stony”). English Wiktionary calls the origin uncertain, perhaps Gaulish too and less likely tied to a Germanic word for stone. Whatever the answer, the verb is a French coinage on the noun: to lay ~caillou~ down.
en.cajoler: The origin is uncertain, and the two Wiktionaries give different accounts. French Wiktionary says only that it may come from Middle French ~gayoler~ (“to chatter”). English Wiktionary proposes a blend of two verbs. One is Middle French ~cageoler~ (“to chatter like a jay”), from the dialect diminutive ~gajole~ of ~geai~ (“jay”). The other is Old French ~gaioler~ (“to entice into a cage”), from ~gaiole~, which goes back to Late Latin ~caveola~, a diminutive of Latin ~cavea~ (“cage, coop”). Latin ~cavea~ is also the well-known source of French ~cage~, and ~geôle~ (“jail”) descends from the same ~gaiole~. Today ~cajoler~ means both to coax with affection and, of a child, to cuddle.
en.calaminer: Formed from the noun ~calamine~ plus the verb ending ~-er~: said of an engine whose parts become clogged with carbon deposits. The noun ~calamine~ names a zinc ore. It comes from Late Latin ~calamina~, a variant of Latin ~cadmea~, which traces back to Greek ~Κάδμος~ (~Kádmos~, “Cadmus”). The engine sense is a figurative extension: the crust that forms in a cylinder was likened to the mineral. The sources do not state this link, so it is offered as the likely reading.
en.calamistrer: From Latin ~calamistrum~, “curling iron,” a heated tool for curling hair. French Wiktionary derives the Latin word from Ancient Greek ~κάλαμος~ (“reed”), because the tool resembled a reed stalk. The verb thus means “to curl with the iron,” that is, to curl hair with such a tool, and it is built directly on the Latin word. The same Greek word also gave Latin ~calamus~ (“reed, pen”), from which a diminutive ~calamellus~ (“small reed”) lies behind French ~chalumeau~ and English ~shawm~. The family is thus that of the humble reed, which supplied pipes, writing pens and, here, a hair-curling tool.
en.calancher: A slang verb meaning to die. French Wiktionary derives it from ~caler~ (“to stop, to weaken”), whose sense is traced to a sailing term meaning to lower a boat's sail. The source gives no further detail, so the extra ending ~-ancher~ is left unexplained here.
en.calandrer: Formed from ~calandre~ with the verb ending ~-er~. A ~calandre~ is a machine with heated rollers through which cloth, paper or other sheet material is passed to press and gloss it, so the verb means to put material through such a machine.
en.calciner:
French ~calciner~ goes back to Latin ~calx~, accusative ~calcem~, which meant “lime” and also “limestone.” French Wiktionary adds that ~calx~ is a word related to the adjective ~calcarius~ (“of lime”). Calcining is, in the strict sense, the heating of a mineral such as limestone to a high temperature, and the everyday verb extends to charring or burning something to a crisp.

The Latin noun left many traces. French ~chaux~ (“lime”) comes from it, along with ~calcaire~ (“limestone”) and the chemical name ~calcium~, which is also built on ~calx~. Latin ~calculus~, a diminutive meaning “small pebble,” gave French ~calcul~, because pebbles were once used for counting. Beyond French, English ~chalk~ and German ~Kalk~ are old borrowings from the same Latin word.
en.calculer:
From Latin ~calculāre~ (“to reckon, compute”), from ~calculus~, the diminutive of ~calx~ (“limestone, pebble”). A ~calculus~ was a small stone — and specifically the little counters that Romans pushed along the grooves of an ~abacus~ to do sums. To calculate was, literally, to move pebbles. ~Calx~ is perhaps borrowed from Greek ~khálix~ (“gravel, small stone”), though the connection is uncertain. Italian ~calcolare~ and Spanish ~calcular~ share the root.

The charm of this etymology is how it fossilizes an ancient counting board inside a word for abstract arithmetic: every calculation still carries, etymologically, a handful of pebbles. The same ~calculus~ gives medicine its sense of a “stone” formed in the body — a kidney ~calculus~ — and gives mathematics the ~calculus~ of Newton and Leibniz, the supreme reckoning. French keeps ~calcul~ (both “calculation” and the medical “stone”), ~calculer~, ~calculateur~, and ~calculatrice~. From the parent ~calx~ in its limestone sense also descend ~chaux~ (“lime”) and ~calcaire~ (“limestone, calcareous”), so the humble pebble underlies both arithmetic and the white cliffs of chalk.
en.caler:
French has more than one verb ~caler~, of two different origins, and the senses asked about belong to the second. The older ~caler~ (attested around 1165, “to lower a sail”) comes from Old Occitan ~calar~ (“to lower”), traced to Ancient Greek ~khaláō~ (“to slacken, lower the mast”); the TLFi notes this sense is unattested in Latin and survives directly from the Greek in the Mediterranean nautical world. From “lower the sails” it drifted figuratively to “to yield, back down,” and to an engine that ~cale~ — stalls and dies.

The ~caler~ of “to wedge, to jam, to immobilize” is a separate, denominal verb built on the noun ~cale~ (“wedge, chock”). The deeper origin of that ~cale~ is uncertain: en.Wiktionary derives the wedge-sense ~cale~ — by one account — from German ~Keil~ (“wedge”), a hypothesis worth flagging rather than asserting. From wedging an object steady the verb took its everyday meanings: to chock a wheel, to prop something firm, to ~se caler~ comfortably in an armchair, and colloquially to be ~calé~ — well-fixed, hence “clued-up, expert.” Relatives include ~décaler~, ~recaler~, and the noun ~calage~.
en.caleter: ~Caleter~ (“to leave quickly, to flee”) is probably derived from ~caler~ in the sense of “to give way, to flee.” The origin is not certain. French Wiktionary cites the Grand Larousse de la langue française (1971), which considers it “no doubt” an iterative form of ~caler~. An iterative form of a verb expresses a repeated or drawn-out action, which suits the picture of someone backing off again and again. The verb is colloquial, and it is mostly met in the pronominal form ~se caleter~.
en.calfater:
French Wiktionary derives ~calfater~ from Italian ~calafatare~ or Occitan ~calafatar~, which come from the Arabic verb ~qalafa~. Medieval Greek ~kalafatēs~ (“caulker”) is attested in 1057, but it is judged unlikely to have been the go-between into the Romance languages. The Arabic word is itself said to descend from a Late Latin form *~calefare~, from Classical Latin ~calefacere~ and ~calefactāre~ (“to heat”), because pitch is heated to caulk a ship.

The path is therefore a Mediterranean round trip, in which a Latin word went east into Arabic and came back west with a changed shape and a technical meaning. French Wiktionary compares it to the similar journey of ~abricot~. Latin ~calefacere~, from ~calēre~ (“to be hot”) and ~facere~ (“to make”), is also the source of French ~chauffer~ by another road. In modern French ~calfater~ means to make a hull watertight by packing its seams with tarred oakum, and it gave ~calfat~ and ~calfatage~.
en.calfeutrer:
French Wiktionary traces ~calfeutrer~ to Old French ~calefaterie~ (“caulking”), properly a derivative of ~calfater~ with the suffix ~-erie~, itself from Arabic ~qalafa~. Out of this came ~calfeutrer~, reshaped under the influence of ~feutre~ (“felt”), since felt served as stuffing for the gaps. English Wiktionary describes the verb more simply as a blend of ~calfater~ and ~feutre~. Either way, the verb unites a seafaring word of Arabic origin, the sealing of a ship's seams, with the cloth that came to plug the cracks.

The modern meaning is to stop up the gaps of a door, window or room against drafts, as with weatherstripping. The reflexive ~se calfeutrer~ is also used, figuratively, for shutting oneself away snugly indoors. The family is small and transparent: ~calfater~ is the older verb for caulking a vessel, ~calfeutrage~ is the noun for the sealing itself, and ~feutre~ is the fabric whose name altered the shape of the verb.
en.calibrer: French Wiktionary calls ~calibrer~ a denominal verb built on ~calibre~ (“bore, size, standard”), while English Wiktionary gives a borrowing from Italian ~calibrare~. The sources do not settle which route is right, and neither gives a date. A calibre is a measure of size, such as the bore of a gun, so ~calibrer~ is to measure or adjust something against a given size.
en.calligraphier: Formed in French from the noun ~calligraphie~ and the verb ending ~-er~, meaning “to write in fine, decorative handwriting.” The noun is borrowed from Ancient Greek ~kalligraphía~, a compound of ~kállos~ (“beauty”) and ~graphía~ (“writing”). Calligraphy is thus, literally, “beautiful writing.” The second element is the same Greek ~graphía~ found in ~orthographe~ and ~géographie~, among many other French words.
en.calmer: Formed from the noun ~calme~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, although English Wiktionary also allows that the verb may be borrowed directly from Italian ~calmare~. The noun comes, by one account, from Occitan ~cauma~ (“heat, calm”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~kaûma~ (“heat”). English Wiktionary instead prefers a path through Italian ~calma~, or possibly an Iberian language, from the same Greek word. Either way, the root meant scorching heat before it meant stillness. The older Occitan verb ~caumar~ gave French ~chômer~ (“to stop working”) as a doublet of ~calmer~, and ~chômer~ is the earlier of the two in French.
en.calmir: ~Calmir~ is built from the noun ~calme~ and the verbal ending ~-ir~, as French Wiktionary indicates, and its entry refers readers to ~calmer~. The ending ~-ir~ often makes verbs meaning “become” something, which fits the sense: it describes the wind or the sea becoming calm. ~Calmir~ is a specialized, maritime-flavored cousin of the common ~calmer~, which says that someone or something is soothed or made calm.
en.calomnier:
~Calomnier~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~calumniārī~ (“to accuse falsely, to slander”). It is not the only French descendant of that Latin verb. Old French had the inherited form ~chalengier~, which meant roughly “to dispute, to claim,” and it crossed the Channel into English as ~challenge~. French later took the word back from English as ~challenge~ and ~challenger~. So the same Latin verb reached French twice, once by learned borrowing as ~calomnier~, and once by a round trip through English.

The Latin verb is generally derived from the noun ~calumnia~ (“false accusation”), from which French drew the noun ~calomnie~, along with ~calomnieux~ and ~calomniateur~. The learned spelling kept the Latin ~-mn-~, where the inherited ~chalengier~ had worn the word down beyond easy recognition. In modern French, ~calomnier~ is a firm word for damaging someone's reputation with false statements. The English ~calumniate~ and ~calumny~ are learned relatives of the same Latin source.
en.calorifuger: ~Calorifuger~ (“to insulate”) is formed from the adjective and noun ~calorifuge~ with the verb ending ~-er~. ~Calorifuge~ itself combines Latin ~caloris~, the genitive of ~calor~ (“heat”), with the suffix ~-fuge~, which comes from Latin ~fugere~ (“to flee”). The verb simply turns the technical word for a heat-retaining material into an action: to cover a pipe, a boiler or a wall with such a material. It is a modern, technical coinage built from learned Latin parts, and ~-er~, the default ending for new French verbs, makes it conjugate like ~chanter~.
en.calquer: A borrowing from Italian ~calcare~ (“to press, to tread”), from Latin ~calcāre~ (“to tread”). The sense developed from pressing on a drawing to transfer it onto another sheet, which is “tracing,” and then to any close copying: one ~calque~ a model, an attitude, a plan. The noun ~calque~ is linked to the verb, but the sources disagree about which came first: French sources derive the noun from Italian ~calco~, while English Wiktionary derives it from ~calquer~. Either way, both lead to the same Latin ~calcāre~. The same Latin verb also gave French ~inculquer~, “to stamp in.”
en.calter: ~Calter~ has no history of its own in French Wiktionary, which simply sends the reader to ~caleter~. The two are variants of one slang verb, both meaning to leave quickly or flee, so whatever origin ~caleter~ has is that of ~calter~ too. The sources at hand give no source language or earlier form for either, and nothing more can be said safely beyond that shared identity.
en.cambrer:
The origin of ~cambrer~ is uncertain. It is probably a derivative of the word ~cambre~ (“curved”), a form from Picard or Norman, that is, Old Northern French, which goes back to Latin ~camur~ (“curved, bent”). A less likely account derives the verb from Latin ~camerāre~ (“to vault”). The verb first appears with the sense “to make a detour”.

Today ~cambrer~ means to arch, above all the back or the foot. The reflexive ~se cambrer~ means to arch oneself, and the related ~cambrure~ names the curve itself, ~cambré~ the arched shape. The origin is thus a choice between a Picard or Norman word for “curved” and a Latin verb for “vaulting”, and both lead to the same image of a bent line.
en.cambrioler: ~Cambrioler~ is formed from the noun ~cambriole~ (“room”) with the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Occitan ~cambra~ (“room”), with the suffix ~-ole~, and ultimately from Latin ~camera~ (“vault, curved roof”). To ~cambrioler~ is thus, literally, to work a ~cambriole~, that is, to break into someone's room and rob it. The Latin ~camera~ also gave French ~chambre~ and, through a different route, English ~chamber~ and ~camera~.
en.camer: Formed from the noun ~came~ and the ending ~-er~, so “to dope oneself,” most often in the pronominal form ~se camer~. The noun ~came~ is a clipping of ~camelote~ (“junk, shoddy goods”) according to both Wiktionaries, which then took the slang sense of “drug.” It is unrelated to the homonym ~came~ (“cam of a wheel”), borrowed from Germanic. The underlying idea is that of cheap stuff, which is exactly what the slang word first suggested.
en.camionner: Formed from ~camion~ (“truck”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to transport by truck.” The origin of ~camion~ is unknown. French Wiktionary mentions two hypotheses, a Picard origin related to ~chemin~ (“way”) or a link with Latin ~chamulcus~ (“low cart”), and notes that the word was rare and absent from the Académie's dictionary until its 1835 edition. English Wiktionary gives the same two ideas, and traces the Latin word to Greek.
en.camoufler:
The origin of ~camoufler~ is debated. French Wiktionary considers it more probably a derivative of ~camouflet~ (~camouflet~ + ~-er~) than a direct borrowing from Italian ~camuffare~ (“to hide, to disguise”). English Wiktionary also says the verb most likely comes from ~camouflet~, but it presents ~camouflet~ itself as a borrowing from Italian ~camuffare~. So the two sources agree on the immediate base and differ on where that base came from.

For ~camouflet~, French Wiktionary offers a different account: Old French ~chault mouflet~, in which the pejorative prefix ~ca-~ replaced ~chaud~ (“hot”) and ~moufle~ meant “chubby face”. The same source explains the sense “to conceal” as issuing from an earlier sense “smoke”, but it gives no intermediate steps, so that link is best treated as a hypothesis. Both routes remain proposals rather than settled facts. The family is better known today through ~camouflage~, the noun built on ~camoufler~, which English later borrowed under the same spelling. Italian ~camuffare~ is the word to compare if the borrowing account is right.
en.camper: The origin is uncertain, and the one source available gives two accounts. By one, ~camper~ is simply a verb formed on the noun ~camp~. By the other, it is a Latinising reworking, based on Latin ~campus~ (“field”), of Old French ~champier~ (“to range over the fields, to camp”), a verb that also produced ~champer~; in that case ~camper~ may be the Picard form of that older word. Either way the root is ~campus~, the Latin “field,” and the sense is that of settling on open ground. French also uses ~camper~ figuratively, as in ~camper sur ses positions~ (“to stand one's ground”).
en.canaliser: Formed from the noun ~canal~ and the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make, to provide with”). The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin ~canālis~ (“pipe, channel”), and it is a doublet of ~chenal~, the form of the same Latin word that was inherited and worn down in speech. To ~canaliser~ is first to provide a river with canals or to put it into a channel, then, figuratively, to direct energy, anger or a crowd along a single path.
en.canarder: Formed from ~canard~ and the verb ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary says the verb was inspired by duck-hunting methods, which fits its meaning of firing at someone from cover. The noun is of uncertain origin. French Wiktionary links it to the imitative root of Old French ~caner~ (“to cackle”) plus the suffix ~-art~. English Wiktionary offers that route or another, from Old French ~cane~, which also meant “boat”, from Frankish *~kanō~ (“boat, vessel”). The origin of ~canard~ itself is thus open, and ~canarder~ inherits that doubt.
en.cancaner: A verb formed on the noun ~cancan~. French has two unrelated words of that shape, and the sources do not say which lies behind the verb. One comes from Latin ~quamquam~ (“although”), which gave a word for a university harangue, then for noise and tittle-tattle, and perhaps relates to Old French ~caquehan~ (“tumultuous assembly”). The other is a child's name for the duck, imitating its cry and evoking its waddle. The two senses of ~cancaner~, to gossip and to quack, fit the two sources neatly, though that match is an inference.
en.cancériser: ~Cancériser~ is formed from ~cancer~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which forms verbs of conversion: to turn into cancer, or to make cancerous. The noun ~cancer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~cancer~ (“crab, canker, cancer”). It is a doublet of the inherited ~chancre~, which descends from the same Latin word by the ordinary route of sound change.
en.candir: Formed from ~candi~ (as in ~sucre candi~, crystallized sugar) with the verb ending ~-ir~, so “to become crystallized,” said of sugar. ~Candi~ comes from Arabic ~qandī~, from ~qand~ (“cane sugar”), and, according to English Wiktionary, entered French in the sixteenth century through Italian ~candi~. The ending ~-ir~ is the second-conjugation ending, from Latin ~-ire~, here in its usual role of making a verb of the type “to become A.”
en.caner: ~Caner~ is formed from ~cane~ with the ending ~-er~, from the expression ~faire la cane~, literally “to act like a duck,” which was used of someone who ducks out or backs down. The sense “to die” is slang that grew from the same verb. The origin of ~cane~ itself is explained in two ways. French Wiktionary treats it as a back-formation from ~canard~ with the suffix dropped, while English Wiktionary traces it through Middle French and Old French to a Germanic word for “boat,” Middle Low German ~kane~, whose cognates include German ~Kahn~. The sources disagree here.
en.canneler: ~Canneler~ means to cut grooves or flutes in a surface, as on a column. The source derives it from ~canne~ (“cane, reed”) and ~canal~ (“channel”), glossing it as digging little channels. The idea is of a surface carved with long, narrow furrows that recall hollow reed stems. The noun ~cannelure~ names the groove itself, and the adjective ~cannelé~ describes the fluted result.
en.canner: French has two homographic verbs ~canner~. One is formed from the noun ~canne~ (“cane”) and the ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Latin ~canna~ (“reed”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~κάννα~ (~kánna~, “reed”), itself from Akkadian ~qanû~. The other is a recent borrowing built on English ~can~ (“tin”) with the French ending ~-er~, in the sense of preserving food in cans.
en.cannibaliser: ~Cannibaliser~ is formed from ~cannibale~ with the suffix ~-iser~, which here means to treat as or turn into: the figurative use of the idea of eating one's own kind. The noun ~cannibale~ was borrowed from Spanish ~caníbal~, from ~caniba~ or ~cariba~, words used by the Taínos whom Columbus met on Hispaniola. According to Columbus, they named the feared peoples of the east of the island, who fought other indigenous groups and ate their victims.
en.canoniser: ~Canoniser~ comes from Late Latin ~canonizare~, a verb built on ~canon~ (“rule, standard”), itself from Greek ~kanōn~, with the ending ~-izāre~ that Latin used for Greek-style verbs. French ~canon~ and ~canonique~ belong to the same family. The verb means to declare someone a saint officially.
en.canonner: ~Canonner~ is formed from ~canon~ with the verb ending ~-er~: to fire a cannon at, to bombard. The artillery noun ~canon~ is derived from ~canne~ (“cane, reed”) with the suffix ~-on~, and matches Italian ~cannone~, from which English Wiktionary says most weapon senses of the French word were borrowed. The verb thus belongs to the family of ~canne~.
en.canoter: Formed from the noun ~canot~ (“small boat”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to go boating” or canoeing. The noun has a double ancestry. It continues in part the Old French ~cane~ (“boat”), from Middle Low German ~kane~ and ultimately Proto-Germanic, and in part an alteration of Middle French ~canoe~, from Spanish ~canoa~, a word that Spanish took from an Arawakan language of the Bahamas. The same Spanish word returned to French much later, through English, as ~canoë~.
en.cantonner: Formed in French from the noun ~canton~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, in the sense “to station troops in a district”, then “to confine to a limited area”. The noun ~canton~ comes from Old Occitan ~canton~ (“corner, canton”), which was adopted from a northern Italian form ~cantone~ (“edge, corner”), ultimately built on a Latin ~cant-~ (“rim”) with an augmentative ending. By one proposal that French Wiktionary mentions, the Italian word may have a Gaulish source meaning “circle”. A soldier ~cantonné~ is posted to his corner of the map.
en.canuler: Formed from ~canule~ with the verb ending ~-er~. A ~canule~ is the small tube of a syringe, and the verb alludes to the unpleasantness of enemas given with one, hence “to bore, to annoy.” The noun comes from Latin ~cannula~ (“little reed”), a diminutive of ~canna~, which also gave ~canne~. The figurative use appears in 1907, when a bore could be called as tiresome as a clyster.
en.caoutchouter: Formed from ~caoutchouc~ (“rubber”) with the first-group ending ~-er~, so it means to coat something with rubber. The noun was borrowed from Spanish ~caucho~, or its early variant ~cauchuc~, which comes from Quechua ~kawchu~. French Wiktionary records its first attestation in a letter by Charles Marie de La Condamine to the Académie des Sciences.
en.caparaçonner: Formed from the noun ~caparaçon~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning “to cover a horse with a caparison, an ornamental cloth.” The noun was borrowed from Spanish ~caparazón~. English Wiktionary suggests it may be related to ~carapace~, with the sounds swapped, plus the suffix ~-on~; this is only a possibility.
en.capeler: A nautical term meaning to pass the eye of a hawser over a bollard. The French source ties it to the Latin word for “head,” ~caput~, which also gave Old French ~capel~ (“hat”) and so the family of ~chapeau~. The sources give no intermediate steps or date for the verb itself, so its exact route from the Latin word is not documented here. The verb remains a specialist word of seamanship and is rarely met outside it.
en.capeyer: Derived from ~cape~ with the verb suffix ~-eyer~, a variant of ~-oyer~. In nautical language the verb means to heave to, to ride out weather under reduced sail. The noun ~cape~ is explained as Renaissance French ~cappe~, from Latin ~cappa~ (“hood”) through Occitan ~capa~ (“cloak”); English Wiktionary calls it a borrowing from Old Occitan, a doublet of the inherited ~chape~. The suffix ~-eyer~ gives the idea of an extended action, here a way of holding the ship's position.
en.capitaliser: Formed in French from ~capital~ and the suffix ~-iser~, with the sense “to turn into capital, to accumulate.” The base ~capital~ comes from Latin ~capitālis~ (“of the head”), from ~caput~ (“head”). In the financial sense, French Wiktionary suggests it is either the adjective used as a noun or a borrowing, by way of Lombard bankers, from Italian ~capitale~ (thirteenth century), the “main sum” on which interest accrues. The word ~capital~ is also the learned doublet of Old French ~chatel~, which survives in ~cheptel~ (“livestock”): the “head” of wealth became both money and cattle.
en.capitonner: Formed from the noun ~capiton~ and the verbal suffix ~-er~, so “to provide with ~capiton~,” the padding or quilting used to upholster seats and walls. The sources do not trace ~capiton~ itself any further, so this is as far back as the story can safely be told.
en.capituler:
~Capituler~ is a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ~capitulāre~, a verb built on Latin ~capitulum~ (“chapter, small head”), the diminutive of ~caput~ (“head”). It is a close relative of ~chapitre~, which is the same Latin word reached by the inherited, popular route. Italian ~capitolare~ and Spanish ~capitular~ are parallel descendants. The same ~caput~ lies behind ~chef~, ~capitale~, ~capitaine~, ~capitaliser~ and ~capitulation~. The chapters of a treaty and the head of a body thus share one Latin ancestor.

French Wiktionary explains the sense by a chain of narrowing. By one account, the verb first meant “to negotiate each chapter of an agreement.” It then specialized to negotiating the chapters of a surrender, and finally became a synonym of “to give in, to give up the fight.” The modern figurative use, as in capitulating to a demand, is the last stage.
en.capoter: ~Capoter~ is formed from the noun ~capot~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~: to overturn, and by extension to fail. The noun ~capot~ is derived from ~cape~ with the suffix ~-ot~, and ~cape~ goes back to Late Latin ~cappa~ (“cloak, hood”). The nautical phrase ~faire capot~ (“to capsize”) dates from the seventeenth century and probably has the same origin. By contrast, ~capoter~ itself is not attested before the arrival of cars, with their ~capots~ (“bonnets”) and ~capotes~ (“hoods”), so its modern sense of flipping over came with the motor age.
en.capsuler: Formed from ~capsule~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to provide with a capsule.” The noun ~capsule~ comes, by standard etymology, from Latin ~capsula~, a diminutive of ~capsa~ (“box, case”). The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, is the usual way to coin a verb from a noun. The verb means to fit a capsule on something, typically a bottle, so as to seal it.
en.capter:
Borrowed in the 15th century from Latin ~captāre~ (“to try to seize, to grasp at, to angle for”), the frequentative of ~capere~ (“to take, seize”), from Proto-Italic *~kapjō~, from PIE *~kh₂pyéti~, root *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp”) — the root that also gave English ~heave~ and German ~heben~. Latin capere spread through Romance: Italian ~capire~ came to mean “to understand” (to grasp!), Spanish ~caber~ “to fit.” French, meanwhile, had already inherited the family twice in popular form before borrowing capter from the books: Vulgar Latin *~captiāre~ became ~chasser~ (“to hunt”) — and, through Norman ~cachier~ and Old French ~chacier~, the English doublets ~catch~ and ~chase~ — while *~accaptare~ became ~acheter~ (“to buy”): hunting, catching, chasing and shopping, all one verb of seizing.

In Latin, ~captāre~ was the verb of hunters, anglers — and flatterers. Orators practiced the ~captātiō benevolentiae~, the ritual “capture of the audience's goodwill”; Horace mocked Rome's legacy-hunters, whose art was ~captāre testāmenta~, “to angle for wills” — and French law still calls inheritance-grabbing by undue influence ~captation~. Hence the verb's first French sense, to win by insinuation (15th century): for centuries capter kept a faintly sinister air. Engineering redeemed it: from 1863 one collects the waters of a spring (~capter une source~); the 20th century added radio — ~capter une station~, ~capter des ondes~ — then attention itself, ~capter l'attention~. Familiar French has even rejoined Italian capire: ~tu captes ?~ — “you get it?” The wider family: ~captif~, ~captiver~, ~capture~, ~capable~, plus the great verbs in ~-cevoir~ — ~recevoir~, ~percevoir~, ~concevoir~, ~décevoir~ — from Latin compounds of capere in ~-cipere~.
en.captiver: ~Captiver~ comes, according to French Wiktionary, from Latin ~captīvāre~. That verb is derived from the adjective and noun ~captīvus~ (“taken prisoner, captive”), which itself belongs to ~capere~ (“to take, to seize”). English has the same family in ~captive~ and ~captivate~. The same Latin root ~capere~ runs through a large family of French words, among them ~capter~, ~capture~, ~captif~, ~captivité~ and ~captivant~. The word ~chétif~ (“puny, sickly”) also descends from ~captīvus~ by a different path.
en.capturer:
A relatively recent and learned formation: ~capturer~ is derived inside French from the noun ~capture~ plus the verbal suffix ~-er~. ~Capture~ in turn comes from Latin ~captūra~ (“a catching, a taking”), a noun built on ~captus~, the past participle of ~capere~ (“to seize, take”). That verb descends from Proto-Italic *~kapjō~ and from PIE *~keh₂p-~ (“to seize, grasp”). Through this root Latin ~capere~ is cognate with English ~have~ and ~heave~ (both from Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~) and with Ancient Greek ~κάπτω~ (~káptō~, “to gulp down”).

French long expressed “to catch” with native verbs like ~prendre~ and ~saisir~; ~capturer~ entered later as a more technical, deliberate word — to capture a fugitive, a fortress, an animal, an image. Because it was built on the noun rather than inherited directly, it carries the clean Latin stem ~capt-~ rather than a worn-down popular form. The same ~capere~ seeds a vast family in French: ~captif~, ~captiver~, ~captivité~, ~capable~, ~recevoir~, ~concevoir~, ~capacité~, and ~occuper~. English drew from the same well with ~captive~, ~capture~, and ~capable~.
en.caqueter: First attested in ~Les Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles~ (1462). Its origin is probably the sound ~kak~, imitating the noises of a farmyard, and English Wiktionary simply calls it onomatopoeic. It is the cry of a hen turned into a verb, which then extended to human chatter, to cackle and to prattle.
en.caracoler: A denominal verb formed from ~caracole~ with the ending ~-er~. The noun was borrowed from Spanish ~caracol~ (“snail, zigzag”), a word English Wiktionary calls of unclear origin. The verb therefore ties its sense to winding, zigzag movement and not to any Latin verb of its own. Its modern senses include prancing about and, figuratively, leading the pack.
en.caractériser:
From the noun ~caractère~ plus the suffix ~-iser~. ~Caractère~ comes from Latin ~character~, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~χαρακτήρ~ (~kharaktḗr~), an “engraved mark, stamp, distinctive impression,” derived from ~χαράσσω~ (~kharássō~, “to engrave, scratch, sharpen”). Originally the word named both the engraver's tool and the mark it cut — a stamped sign that set one thing apart from another. The suffix ~-iser~ descends from Latin ~-izāre~, from Greek ~-ίζειν~ (~-ízein~), the ending behind English ~-ize~.

The semantic arc is elegant: a physical ~mark~ engraved on metal or wax became the figurative “stamp” of a personality, then the sum of traits defining a person, and finally any distinguishing feature at all. To ~caractériser~ is thus to identify the mark that sets something apart — to pin down its defining trait. The Greek root left French a sizeable family: ~caractère~, ~caractéristique~, ~caractérisation~, and ~caractériel~. English ~character~, ~characteristic~, and ~characterize~ are the exact cousins, and even the typographic ~character~ on a screen preserves the original sense of an engraved, distinctive sign.
en.caramboler: ~Caramboler~ is derived from ~carambole~, the name of a ball in billiards, and is itself recorded in the older form ~caramboller~. The verb first belonged to the game, then broadened to mean “to bump into, to collide with,” which is the sense of the modern verb. The same base gave ~carambolage~, a collision of several vehicles in a row, as of billiard balls knocking one another.
en.caraméliser: ~Caraméliser~ is formed from the noun ~caramel~ and the suffix ~-iser~, here in the sense “to turn into, to treat with.” The noun is borrowed from Spanish ~caramelo~, itself from Portuguese ~caramelo~. Its deeper origin is debated. English Wiktionary says it probably comes from Late Latin ~calamellus~ (“little reed”), which makes it a doublet of ~chalumeau~. French Wiktionary prefers this account, comparing the shape of hardened sugar to a reed, over a derivation from Latin ~cannamella~ (“sugar cane”), and also mentions an Arabic proposal.
en.carapater: ~Carapater~ is presented as a portmanteau of ~se carrer~, in the sense of “to flee,” and ~patte~ (“paw, leg”). The verb means “to run away,” and it is used reflexively as ~se carapater~. Read this way, it pictures someone taking to their legs. It is a colloquial word, the kind of playful blend that slang produces easily.
en.carbonater: This verb is formed from the noun ~carbonate~ with the verb ending ~-er~, and means to carbonate. The noun is a chemical term built from ~carbone~ and the suffix ~-ate~, and ~carbone~ goes back to Latin ~carbōnem~ (“charcoal”), the accusative of ~carbō~. Inherited French ~charbon~ (“coal”) comes from the same Latin word.
en.carboniser: ~Carboniser~ is formed from the noun ~carbone~ with the suffix ~-iser~, and means “to reduce to carbon, to char.” The base ~carbone~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~carbō~, ~carbōnis~ (“charcoal”), coined in 1789 by the chemist Lavoisier, with Guyton de Morveau according to the French text. They chose it to distinguish the element from the older French word ~charbon~, which comes from the same Latin word, so the two are doublets.
en.carburer: Formed from the noun ~carbure~ (“carbide”) and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is itself built on ~carbone~ with the suffix ~-ure~. The verb first meant to combine with carbon, and by extension to mix air with fuel in an engine. In everyday French it also means, figuratively, to run well or to work hard.
en.carcailler: An imitative verb, built from the sound itself. ~Carcailler~ renders the harsh, repeated call of the quail, and the French verb is used for that cry. French Wiktionary gives only “onomatopoeia” as its origin, so there is no older word behind it to trace. Names of animal calls often arise this way, by echoing the noise rather than by descending from an earlier word.
en.carder: Formed from ~carde~ (“carding comb, teasel head”) with the verbal ending ~-er~: ~carder~ means “to card,” to comb out tangled wool, cotton or flax with a toothed tool so that the fibres lie in one direction. The noun ~carde~ was borrowed from Medieval Latin ~cardō~ (“carding tool”), from Latin ~carduus~ (“thistle”). The spiky heads of the plant gave the tool its name. ~Carde~ is a doublet of ~cardon~ and ~chardon~, the latter being the ordinary French word for the thistle itself.
en.carencer: ~Carencer~ is formed from the noun ~carence~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, so it means to cause a deficiency in someone, from ~carence~ (“lack, deficiency”). The noun was borrowed from Late Latin ~carentia~ (“want, privation”), from Latin ~careō~ (“to lack”). The ending ~-er~ is the default way to turn a noun into a verb, which explains why this medical-sounding verb was coined from the noun.
en.caresser: Borrowed from Italian ~carezzare~ (“to cherish”), and also analyzable in French as the noun ~caresse~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~caresse~ was itself borrowed from Italian ~carezza~, which belongs to the family of ~caro~ (“dear”). The sense is thus “to treat as dear”: from cherishing, the verb came to mean touching or stroking tenderly, and by extension “to toy with” an idea or a hope. The ending ~-er~ is the usual first-conjugation ending, from Latin ~-are~.
en.carguer:
~Carguer~ is borrowed from Occitan ~cargar~ (“to load”), or alternatively from Spanish ~cargar~ (“to load”), both sources being offered by French Wiktionary. Both go back to a Latin root reconstructed as *~carricāre~, a verb built on Latin ~carrus~ (“cart”), so “to load a cart.” Italian ~caricare~ and Portuguese ~carregar~ are cousins of the same Latin verb. English owes ~cargo~ and ~charge~ to the family as well.

In French the verb became a sailor's term. To ~carguer~ a sail is to furl or gather it up with the lines called ~cargues~ so that it hangs bunched against the yard. The sense that is current today is attested in the seventeenth century, in 1690. The same Latin verb also reached French by the inherited route, as ~charger~, so ~carguer~ and ~charger~ are doublets. Their relatives include ~charge~, ~cargaison~, ~cargo~ and ~chariot~, all of them recalling the cart at the bottom of the family.
en.caricaturer: ~Caricaturer~ is formed from the noun ~caricature~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun was originally borrowed from Italian, where ~caricatura~ is built on the verb ~caricare~ (“to load, to exaggerate”). The verb means to draw or portray someone in an exaggerated way, which fits that Italian origin.
en.carier: A denominal verb: ~carie~ plus the ending ~-er~, “to rot, to decay”, said first of teeth and bones. The noun ~carie~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~caries~ (“rot”), so the verb adds the common French verbal ending to a word that came whole from Latin. The ending ~-er~ descends from the Latin first-conjugation ending ~-are~ and is the default for new French verbs. The past participle ~carié~ is the form most often met, as in a decayed tooth.
en.carillonner: Formed from ~carillon~ with the verb ending ~-er~, it means to ring or peal bells. The noun comes from Old French forms such as ~careignon~ or ~quarrillon~, from Late Latin ~quaterniō~ (“group of four things”). According to French Wiktionary, the earliest carillons were sets of four bells, which explains the choice of a word for four. A musical instrument of many bells thus keeps in its name the memory of a modest quartet.
en.carotter: French Wiktionary explains ~carotter~, in the sense of extorting something from someone, as coming from the expression ~tirer une carotte~. The verb thus reflects a figurative phrase built on the noun ~carotte~ and not a straightforward derivation. Its modern sense is “to swindle” or “to wangle,” getting something out of someone by trickery. No source gives an older history or an explanation of the image behind the phrase.
en.carreler: Formed from ~carrel~, an older variant of ~carreau~ (“square, tile”), plus the verb ending ~-er~, and attested already in Middle French as ~carreler~. The noun ~carreau~ descends from Old French ~quarel~, from Vulgar Latin *~quadrellus~, a diminutive of Latin ~quadrus~ (“square”). It first meant a crossbow bolt around 1080, and by about 1160 it named a small hard tile for floors and walls. To ~carreler~ is therefore to cover a surface with square tiles, and ~carrelage~ is the result.
en.carrer:
From Latin ~quadrāre~ (“to make square, to fit”), attested in French from the twelfth century. The Latin verb comes from ~quadrus~ (“square”), itself from ~quattuor~ (“four”), and so from the PIE numeral *~kʷetwóres~ (“four”). Through that root ~carrer~ is a distant cognate of English ~four~, Ancient Greek ~téssares~ and Sanskrit ~catur~ — and a near relative of every learned ~quadr-~ word in French. A separate, regional ~carrer~ meaning “to put, to place” is, by one account, borrowed from Occitan ~carrar~.

The literal sense is geometric — to ~carrer~ a stone or a number is to square it — but the verb's liveliest life is reflexive. ~Se carrer~ once meant to walk squarely, with a broad and self-important bearing, and came to mean to settle oneself comfortably and squarely into a chair. From the same Latin root descend ~carré~ (“square”), ~carreau~ (“tile, pane”), ~carrefour~ (“crossroads,” a place where four ways meet), ~équarrir~ and the borrowed ~quadrant~.
en.carrosser: Formed from the noun ~carrosse~ with the verb ending ~-er~. Because a ~carrosse~ was a coach, the verb came to mean to fit a vehicle with its body, the part that the noun ~carrosserie~ names. The noun comes from Middle French ~carroche~, borrowed from Italian ~carrozza~, a Tuscan form of older ~carroccia~, which was derived from ~carro~ (“cart, chariot”) with the suffix ~-occia~. The vehicle word thus reached French from Italy, and the verb turned it into an action.
en.carroyer: Formed from ~carré~ (“square”) plus the suffix ~-oyer~: to divide into squares, as when a map or drawing is covered with a grid. The adjective ~carré~ is inherited from Old French ~quarré~, from Latin ~quadrātus~, from ~quadrāre~, itself from ~quadrus~ and ultimately from ~quattuor~ (“four”). ~Carré~ has a learned doublet in ~cadrat~. The suffix ~-oyer~ is not productive today, so ~carroyer~ is an older formation.
en.carter: ~Carter~ is a noun-based verb: ~carte~ plus the ending ~-er~, in the sense “to check someone's age by looking at an identity card.” The noun ~carte~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~charta~ (“paper, document, book”), itself from Ancient Greek ~χάρτης~ (~khártēs~, “sheet of papyrus or paper”). It is a cousin of French ~charte~, which comes from the same Latin word. The verb is a recent, colloquial formation: the card has become the thing one is asked to show.
en.cartographier:
~cartographier~ is a young verb built on an old word: it derives from ~cartographie~ (~carte~ plus the suffix ~-graphie~, from Greek ~gráphein~, “to write”), and is first recorded in 1906. ~carte~ itself was borrowed from Latin ~charta~ (“a sheet of papyrus prepared for writing,” hence “a written document”), which Latin had taken from Ancient Greek ~χάρτης~ (~khártēs~). The same Latin word reached French twice: through its diminutive ~chartula~ came ~charte~, attested in the eleventh century, so ~carte~ and ~charte~ are doublets. Italian ~carta~ and Spanish ~carta~ continue the same noun, and Old French ~carte~ gave English both ~chart~ and ~card~.

The Greek source is a dead end for etymologists: ~khártēs~ was long derived from ~kharássō~ (“to scratch, to inscribe”), but Beekes and Chantraine both reject that link and treat the word’s origin as unknown — one proposal makes it a Phoenician borrowing, but the question is unsettled. The French coinage is better documented: ~cartographie~ first appears in 1832 in the hellenizing spelling ~chartographie~, closer to Greek ~khártēs~ than to French ~carte~, and the modern spelling follows in 1838, though the ~ch-~ form was still being recorded in the 1860s. The verb waited nearly seventy years more and arrived only in 1906 — mapping was a discipline long before it was something one simply did. Today ~cartographier~ has slipped its geographic moorings: one maps a genome, a network, a supply chain. From the same Latin ~charta~ modern French keeps ~carte~, ~charte~, ~carton~ and ~cartouche~.
en.cartonner: Formed from ~carton~ (“cardboard”) with the verb-forming ending ~-er~, in the sense “to provide with N”: to cover or bind something with cardboard. ~Carton~ itself was borrowed from Italian ~cartone~, which goes back to Latin ~charta~ (“paper”), the same word that gave English ~chart~ and ~card~ their start. The slang sense “to be a huge hit” is a later figurative extension, and the sources do not spell out its path.
en.caréner: ~Caréner~ is formed from the noun ~carène~ (“hull, keel”) with the ending ~-er~, meaning to clean and repair a ship's hull, and later to give a vehicle a streamlined shell. The noun was borrowed from Italian ~carena~, which comes from Latin ~carīna~, a word meaning “nutshell” and by extension the keel or hull of a ship.
en.cascader: Formed from the noun ~cascade~ plus the verbal suffix ~-er~. The noun itself was borrowed from Italian ~cascata~, the feminine past participle of ~cascare~ (“to fall”), so a ~cascade~ is literally something that has fallen. The verb turns that noun back into an action: ~cascader~ means to tumble down in the manner of a waterfall, and the sense “to cascade” is the one it carries today.
en.caser: Formed in French from ~case~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning “to put in a compartment, to find a place for.” The sources do not agree about the noun. English Wiktionary says it was borrowed from Latin ~casa~ (“hut, cabin”), with the other senses, including the square of a chessboard or compartment, a semantic loan from Spanish ~casa~, and calls it a doublet of ~chez~. French Wiktionary instead cites English ~case~, which probably concerns another sense of the word. Either way the verb means to slot something into its place, and by extension to find a job or a spouse for someone.
en.caserner: ~Caserner~ is formed from ~caserne~ and the ending ~-er~: “to lodge troops in barracks.” The noun was borrowed from Old Occitan ~cazerna~, a variant of ~quazerna~, from Latin ~quaterna~, the neuter plural of ~quaternus~ (“four each”). It is thus a doublet of ~cahier~, which French inherited from the same Latin word, and of the later borrowing ~quaterne~. The military sense of “quarters” is the one that survived in ~caserne~, and the verb applies it to soldiers being housed in them.
en.casquer: The origin of ~casquer~ is uncertain, and the two Wiktionaries pair its senses with the origins differently. One account derives it from ~casque~ (“helmet”), borrowed from Spanish ~casco~ (“skull, helmet”), which replaced the older ~heaume~; English Wiktionary adds that ~casqué~, older than the verb, may have been taken as a past participle. The other account borrows it from Italian ~cascare~ (“to fall”), the source of ~cascade~, and gives the sense “to fall into a trap”; English Wiktionary treats “to pay up” as a development of that sense. The modern meanings are to pay up and to fall into a trap.
en.casse-croûter: Formed on the noun ~casse-croûte~ with the verb ending ~-er~, in the sense “to have a snack.” The noun is a compound of ~casser~ (“to break”) and ~croûte~ (“crust”), and its snack sense comes from the expression ~casser la croûte~. ~Casser~ goes back to Latin ~quassāre~ (“to shatter”), blended in French with Late Latin ~cassāre~ (“to annul”). ~Croûte~ comes from Latin ~crūsta~ (“crust”). The image is of breaking into a crust of bread.
en.casser:
French ~casser~ first appears around 1100 as ~quasser~ “to break into pieces,” taking its modern shape by about 1160. It descends from Latin ~quassāre~ “to shake violently, to shatter,” itself a frequentative — an intensive, repetitive form — of ~quatere~ “to shake.” That verb goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~kʷet-~ “to shake.” The same Latin source, by way of Old French, gave English ~quash~ “to crush, to annul.” But a second, homophonous Latin verb left its mark too: Late Latin ~cassāre~ “to annul, to make void,” derived from the adjective ~cassus~ “empty, vain.” The two converged so completely in French that one verb came to carry both meanings.

This fusion explains a remarkable split in sense. The ~quassāre~ side gives the physical meanings — to break a glass, and figuratively to wear out or exhaust. The ~cassāre~ side gives the legal one: “to annul, to overturn,” enshrined in the Cour de cassation, France's supreme court, which can quash a lower judgment. So when a verdict is set aside, it is, etymologically, declared empty rather than broken.
