From the shaking root also descend the rare ~quassation~ and French ~fracasser~ “to smash” and ~concasser~ “to crush,” alongside the everyday ~casse-tête~ “puzzle,” literally a head-breaker.
en.castagner: ~Castagner~ is formed from ~castagne~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary adds that the verb is to be read literally alongside the expression “mettre une ~châtaigne~ à quelqu'un,” a slang way of saying to land a punch on someone. The ~castagne~ of the verb is a form of the word for “chestnut” (compare ~châtaigne~), and the verb means to scrap or scuffle.
en.castrer:
~Castrer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~castrāre~ (“to castrate”), taken into French around 1600. It is a doublet of ~châtrer~, which is the same Latin verb inherited in the ordinary way through Old French and reshaped by the sound changes of that language. Two words with one ancestor but different routes into French are called doublets.

The pair shows the usual division of labor between the two paths. ~Châtrer~ is the everyday word, inherited through Old French. ~Castrer~ is the later, more learned form that kept the Latin spelling. Notice how the Latin ~-st-~ survives in ~castrer~ but has been smoothed to ~-t-~ in ~châtrer~, and the initial ~ca-~ has become ~châ-~. English ~castrate~ comes from the same Latin verb.
en.cataloguer: Formed from the noun ~catalogue~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, so “to put in a catalogue.” The noun was borrowed from Late Latin ~catalogus~, from Ancient Greek ~κατάλογος~ (“a register, a list”). The Greek noun comes from ~καταλέγω~ (“to list in order”), made of ~κατα-~ (“down”) and ~λέγω~ (“to gather, to count”).
en.catalyser: Formed from the noun ~catalyse~ with the first-conjugation ending ~-er~. The noun ~catalyse~ was chosen by Jöns Jacob Berzelius, one of the founders of modern chemistry, who took it from Greek ~katalysis~ (“dissolution”). The verb names what a catalyst does, which is to speed up a chemical reaction.
en.catapulter: ~Catapulter~ is formed from the noun ~catapulte~ with the verb ending ~-er~. ~Catapulte~ is borrowed from Latin ~catapulta~, itself from Greek ~katapeltēs~, built from ~kata~ (“down”) and ~peltēs~ (“one who hurls missiles”) and related to ~peltastēs~ (“a peltast, a javelin thrower”). The French verb means to hurl or launch as if from a catapult.
en.catastropher: Formed from ~catastrophe~ + ~-er~, the ending that turns a noun into a first-conjugation verb. The verb means to shock or astound someone. The noun ~catastrophe~ passed through Latin ~catastropha~ from Ancient Greek ~καταστροφή~ (~katastrophḗ~), built from ~κατά~ (~katá~, “down”) and ~στροφή~ (~strophḗ~, “turning”), so the word is a “turning down,” an overturning.
en.catcher: ~Catcher~ is either borrowed from English ~catch~ or formed from the French noun ~catch~ plus ~-er~. The noun is a pseudo-anglicism, shortened from English ~catch-as-catch-can~, a style of wrestling now called catch wrestling. English ~catch~ is a doublet of French ~chasser~ (“to hunt”). The verb first meant “to wrestle,” and it later took on the looser senses of “to catch” and, in slang, “to understand.”
en.catir:
According to French Wiktionary, ~catir~ comes from Popular Latin *~coactire~, a variant of ~coactare~, which is derived from ~coactus~, the past participle of ~cogere~ (“to gather, condense, press”). The Latin verb ~cogere~ is itself formed from ~co-~ (“together”) and ~agere~ (“to drive”), so its basic image is driving things together until they are tightly pressed.

That sense of compressing suits the French verb, which is a textile term: ~catir~ is to press and finish cloth so that it becomes firm and glossy. The Latin ~cogere~ has several well-known descendants. English ~cogent~ comes from its present participle, and ~coagulate~ comes from the related Latin ~coagulum~, which also belongs to ~cogere~.
en.catéchiser: From Latin ~catēchīzāre~ (“to instruct in religion, to catechize”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~κατηχίζω~ (~katēkhízō~, “to instruct orally”). The Greek verb comes from ~κατηχέω~ (~katēkhéō~, “to resound, to instruct orally”), itself made of ~κατά~ (~katá~, “down”) and ~ἠχή~ (~ēkhḗ~, “sound, noise”). The Greek noun ~ēkhḗ~ is related to ~ἠχώ~ (~ēkhṓ~), the source of ~écho~ and English ~echo~, so catechism and echo share a root. The same Greek family gave French ~catéchisme~, ~catéchiste~ and ~catéchumène~. Besides its religious sense, ~catéchiser~ has a figurative sense of lecturing someone to win them over, often with a hint of reproach.
en.cauchemarder: ~Cauchemarder~ is a recent verb formed from the noun ~cauchemar~ with ~-er~, plus an extra ~-d-~ that makes it sound like familiar verbs such as ~bavarder~; ~bazarder~ received the same addition. The noun comes from Old French ~cauquemare~, made of ~cauque~ (related to the verb ~chauchier~, “to press, to trample”, from Latin ~calcare~) and ~mar~, a Germanic word for a night spirit. That second element survives in English ~nightmare~ and German ~Nachtmahr~, which are cognates. So the nightmare was once a spirit that presses down on the sleeper.
en.causer:
Modern French ~causer~ conceals two distinct verbs that fell together by sound. The first, “to cause,” was derived around 1275 from the noun ~cause~ plus the verbal suffix ~-er~, ~cause~ itself coming from Latin ~causa~ (“cause, reason, lawsuit”). The second, “to chat,” descends directly from Latin ~causari~ (“to plead a case, debate, dispute”), a verb built on that same ~causa~. So both ultimately rest on ~causa~, cognate with Italian ~cosa~ and Spanish ~cosa~ (“thing”) and with the English borrowing ~cause~.

The surprise lies in the second verb's drift. In Latin, ~causari~ belonged to the courtroom: to argue a legal cause. As the centuries passed, the solemn sense of pleading and debating softened into mere talking, then into friendly chatter — so that today ~causer~ most often means simply “to have a chat,” and to ~causer de la pluie et du beau temps~ is to make small talk. From ~causa~ in its “thing” sense Latin also gave Romance its everyday word for an object (Italian ~cosa~), while French preserved the learned ~cause~ alongside ~causerie~ (“an informal talk”), ~causette~, and ~accuser~ (literally to call something to one's cause).
en.cautionner: Formed from ~caution~ and the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense “to provide a ~caution~ for”: to stand surety for someone, to post bail, and by extension to lend one's backing to a person or an idea. The noun ~caution~ is a borrowing, through Old French, of Latin ~cautiō~ (“caution, precaution”), from ~cautus~, the past participle of ~cavēre~ (“to be on one's guard”). The verb thus rests on a medieval idea: a surety is a guarantee given by someone who has taken care for another.
en.cautériser:
From Late Latin ~cauterizāre~, itself from Ancient Greek ~καυτηριάζω~ (~kautēriázō~, “to brand with a hot iron”). The Greek verb belongs to the family of ~kaíein~ (“to burn”), and its noun ~kautḗr~ names the burning iron. To cauterize is thus to mark or sear with fire. Spanish ~cauterizar~ and English ~cauterize~ come from the same Latin verb.

French received the word as a learned borrowing, since it belongs to the vocabulary of medicine, where the sense is to burn a wound or tissue to close it. A figurative use, to deaden a pain or a feeling, appears as well. The Greek root stands behind other French words, such as ~cautère~ (“cautery”), ~caustique~ (“caustic,” literally “burning”) and ~holocauste~, the “wholly burnt” offering. Unlike inherited verbs, ~cautériser~ kept its Latin ending ~-izāre~, which French turned into ~-iser~, the same Greek-derived suffix found in ~baptiser~ and ~organiser~.
en.cavalcader: Formed from ~cavalcade~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, first recorded in 1824 with the sense “to ride in a group” (Balzac). The noun ~cavalcade~ comes from Italian ~cavalcata~ (from ~cavalcare~, “to ride”) or from Occitan ~cavalcada~, “a troop on horseback.” Its root, from Late Latin ~caballus~ (“horse”), also gave ~cavale~ and ~cavalier~.
en.cavaler: ~Cavaler~ is formed from the noun ~cavale~ (“mare”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, the default way French turns a noun into a verb. The noun ~cavale~ was borrowed from Italian ~cavalla~ or Occitan ~cavala~, both from Latin ~caballa~ (“mare”). The verb belongs to informal French and means to rush about or, in the right context, to be on the run.
en.caver: French Wiktionary derives ~caver~ directly from Latin ~cavō~ (“I hollow out”), the first-person form of the verb ~cavāre~, meaning “to dig, to hollow.” ~Cavāre~ belongs to the family of the adjective ~cavus~ (“hollow”), which also gave French ~cave~ and ~caverne~, and English ~cave~. The verb thus means to dig out a hollow, in line with the gloss “to dig, to mine.”
en.ceindre:
French ~ceindre~ is inherited from Old French ~ceindre~, from Latin ~cingere~ (“to gird, to surround”). The Latin verb has well-known relatives in the other Romance languages, such as Italian ~cingere~ and Spanish ~ceñir~. The past participle ~ceint~ preserves the Latin participle ~cinctus~, and the irregular stem ~ceign-~ of the present tense (~il ceint~, ~nous ceignons~) comes from the same verb.

The Latin family is large. From ~cingere~ French drew ~ceinture~ and ~ceinturon~, and through Latin ~cingulum~ (“belt”) it got ~sangle~. The participle ~cinctus~ also stands behind ~enceinte~ (the circuit of a wall) and ~succinct~, whose Latin source ~succinctus~ meant “girded up,” hence “brief.” English has borrowed ~cincture~ and ~precinct~ from the same stock. So a verb now met mostly in literary phrases such as ~ceindre une écharpe~ lies at the center of a whole group of words for belts, girdles and enclosures.
en.ceinturer: The sources describe this verb differently. English Wiktionary treats it as ~ceinture~ (“belt”) + ~-er~, a verb meaning to put a belt around something or someone, and refers to ~cintrer~ as a related verb. French Wiktionary instead names Latin ~cingere~ (“to surround, to gird, to enclose”) as the source. The two fit together, since ~ceinture~ itself belongs to the family of ~cingere~, so either way the verb belongs to the root of ~ceindre~ (“to gird”), the verb from which ~ceinture~ takes its sense of something that goes around.
en.celer: ~Celer~ is inherited from Old French ~celer~, itself from Latin ~cēlāre~ (“to hide, to conceal”), a verb with the same meaning as its French descendant. Italian ~celare~ comes from the same Latin verb. French words built on this root include ~déceler~ (literally to “un-hide,” hence to detect or reveal) and ~receler~ (to hide stolen goods or, more generally, to hold something concealed).
en.cendrer: ~Cendrer~ is a denominal verb, formed from ~cendre~ (“ash”) with the ending ~-er~: to give an ash color or to cover with ashes. The noun ~cendre~ comes from Old French ~cendre~, from the accusative ~cinerem~ of Latin ~cinis~ (“ash”). The Latin word goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ken-~ (“dust, ashes”).
en.censurer: Formed from the noun ~censure~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is borrowed from Latin ~cēnsūra~, which named the office of the Roman censor, the magistrate who took the census and judged public morals. The verb carries both of its senses today: “to criticise or condemn” and “to cut something from a work before it is published,” the second giving the English ~censor~ as a verb.
en.centraliser: Built in French from ~central~ and the suffix ~-iser~, in the sense “to make central.” The adjective ~central~ is borrowed from Latin ~centrālis~, which belongs to ~centrum~ (“center”), a word Latin took from Greek ~kéntron~ (“a sharp point, a goad”). The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and it remains fully productive in French for verbs meaning “make A.” In French, ~centraliser~ is used especially of gathering power, administration or services into a single center.
en.centrer:
From ~centre~ (“center”) plus the verbal ending ~-er~, the noun being from Latin ~centrum~ (“the fixed point of a compass, a center”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~κέντρον~ (~kéntron~, “a sharp point, a goad, the stationary leg of a pair of compasses”), from ~κεντέω~ (~kentéō~, “to prick, to goad”), from PIE *~ḱent-~ (“to prick”).

The Greek ~kéntron~ was literally a point that pricks — a goad, a wasp's sting — and then the still leg of a compass jabbed into the page while the other swung the circle. That pivot became the “center.” French ~centrer~ therefore means to bring to the middle, to aim at a target's middle, and in football to cross the ball toward the center. The same prickly root *~ḱent-~ surfaces in ~centre~, ~central~, ~excentrique~, ~concentrer~, and the borrowed insect-name element in ~centrifuge~.
en.centrifuger:
French Wiktionary derives ~centrifuger~ from ~centre~ and Latin ~fugere~ (“to flee”), a learned compound meaning “to flee from the center.” ~Centre~ itself comes through Latin ~centrum~ from Greek ~kéntron~, and ~fugere~ is the Latin verb that gave French ~fuir~. The verb means to spin something in a centrifuge so that its parts separate, the denser matter being thrown outward.

The Latin verb ~fugere~ has a large family in French. ~Fuir~ is its inherited descendant, and ~fuite~ and ~fugitif~ belong with it; ~refuge~, ~transfuge~ and ~subterfuge~ are learned borrowings built on the same root. The mirror image of ~centrifuge~ is ~centripète~, which pairs ~centre~ with Latin ~petere~ (“to seek, to head for”), so that one force flees the center and the other heads toward it. Thus ~centrifuger~ keeps, in a scientific term, the ordinary Latin picture of flight.
en.centupler: Formed from ~centuple~ (“hundredfold”) with the verb ending ~-er~, and first attested before 1560, in a text by Bonivard. It displaced an older rival, ~centuplier~, recorded only in the sixteenth century (1542) and borrowed from Christian Latin ~centuplicare~. That Latin verb, attested from the fourth century and perhaps already in Tertullian near the start of the third, was itself derived from classical Latin ~centuplex~ (“hundredfold”). The modern verb means to multiply by a hundred or, by extension, to increase greatly. It is also used intransitively of a quantity that grows a hundredfold.
en.cercler: Two accounts exist for ~cercler~. The simpler one forms it from ~cercle~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~, so the verb means to put a ring or hoop around something. The other derives it from Vulgar Latin *~circlāre~, from Late Latin ~circulāre~, which would make ~cercler~ a doublet of the learned ~circuler~; compare Italian ~cerchiare~. In either case the root is ~cercle~, from Latin ~circulus~, a diminutive of ~circus~ (“ring, circle”), itself probably borrowed from Greek ~kríkos~ or ~kírkos~.
en.cerner:
Inherited from Old French ~cerner~ (“to encircle”), from Latin ~circināre~ (“to make round, to go around in a circle”). The Latin verb is built on ~circinus~, the draftsman's compass or pair of dividers, which belongs to the family of ~circus~ (“ring, circle”). That noun is usually compared with Greek ~kírkos~ (“ring, circle”), but its deeper Proto-Indo-European origin is uncertain. French holds the same family in its other forms: ~cercle~ and ~cirque~, from ~circulus~ and ~circus~, and the learned ~circuit~. Spanish ~cercar~ (“to fence in, to surround”) comes from the closely related Latin ~circāre~, and English ~circle~ and ~circus~ come from the same family. Because ~cerner~ is inherited, centuries of spoken French wore its sounds down, unlike the learned ~circuit~.

In Old French, ~cerner~ meant to encircle. The noun ~cerne~, a ring, is tied to the verb and survives in the rings of a tree trunk and in the dark circles under tired eyes, which is why eyes are said to be ~cernés~. The verb also has a military sense, closing a circle around a town or an enemy force, and a figurative sense that now dominates: to ~cerner~ a problem is to draw a line around it in thought until its edges are clear, and so to understand it. The modern phrase ~cerner une personnalité~ keeps that picture of an investigator going around a subject. The abstract sense of grasping something thus rests on the older picture of a drawn circle.
en.certifier:
~certifier~ comes from Late Latin ~certificāre~, a compound of ~certus~ (“certain, settled, decided”) and ~facere~ (“to make”) — literally “to make certain.” The key is ~certus~, originally the participle of ~cernere~ (“to sift, to separate, then to distinguish, to decide”), from Proto-Italic *~krinō~, from PIE *~krey-~ (“to sieve, to separate”). The same root produced Greek ~krī́nō~ (“I judge, separate”), whence English ~crisis~, ~critic~, and ~criterion~; on the Latin side it gave ~discerner~, ~secret~, and ~crime~. To certify, then, is to make a matter as decided as grain that has passed clean through the sieve.

The metaphor is precise: judgment as a sifting, the sure thing as what is sorted out from doubt. French ~certifier~ means to attest formally — a notary certifies a copy, a school certifies a diploma — and from the family come ~certain~, ~certitude~, ~certificat~, and the adverb ~certes~. English borrowed the whole cluster: ~certain~, ~certify~, ~certificate~. Through the Greek branch of *~krey-~ the very word ~critique~ shares an ancestor with ~certifier~, so that to criticize and to certify both descend, ultimately, from the act of running grain through a sieve.
en.cesser:
From Latin ~cessāre~ (“to delay, to hold back, to leave off, to be idle”), the frequentative of ~cēdere~ (“to go, to withdraw, to yield”), whose past-participle stem ~cess-~ supplies the longer verb. Latin ~cēdere~ comes, through Proto-Italic *~kesd-o-~ (“to go away, to avoid”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱesd-~. Because a frequentative names a repeated or lingering action, ~cessāre~ originally suggested keeping on holding back — hence “to tarry,” and from there “to stop.” Italian ~cessare~ and Spanish ~cesar~ continue the same verb directly.

The semantic drift is gentle: from “withdrawing” to “hanging back” to simply “ceasing.” French kept the literary, slightly formal ring of the word — ~cesser de~ + infinitive, or the elevated ~sans cesse~ (“ceaselessly”), where the bare noun ~cesse~ survives almost only in that fixed phrase. The base verb ~cēdere~ gave French ~céder~ (“to yield”) directly, so ~cesser~ and ~céder~ are doublets sprung from the same Latin root by different paths. The wider family is large and legal-flavored: ~cessation~, ~cession~, ~cessible~, ~incessant~, ~incessamment~, and, through the ~cēdere~ branch, ~accéder~, ~procéder~, ~succéder~. A pleasant surprise: the English ~cease~ and the courtroom ~cease and desist~ rest on the very same Roman idea of stepping back and leaving off.
en.chagriner: The origin is obscure, and the sources offer competing analyses. French Wiktionary gives ~cha-~ + ~grigner~ (Old French ~graignier~, related to English ~grin~), or a verb made from the noun ~chagrin~ in its sense of “tanned skin,” and notes that Middle French also had ~chagrigner~. English Wiktionary suggests ~chat~ or the expressive prefix ~ca-~ (as in ~caboche~), or simply ~chagrin~ + ~-er~. Mistral derived the Occitan noun ~chagrin~ from Greek ~karkínos~ (“cancer, that which gnaws”). The verb means “to upset, to grieve, to bother.”
en.chahuter: The origin is uncertain, and the two sources differ. English Wiktionary simply derives ~chahuter~ from the noun ~chahut~ plus ~-er~. French Wiktionary instead proposes that it comes from the dialect verbs ~cahuer~, ~cahuler~ and ~cahuter~ of central France, meaning “to cry out in pain”, said of a dog, all derived from ~huer~ (“to call one's dog”). The origin of the first syllable is unknown; ~canis~ (“dog”) and ~catus~ (“cat”) have been floated, but neither is established.
en.chaloir:
From Old French ~chaloir~ (earlier ~chaleir~), through Middle French, inherited from Latin ~calēre~ (“to be warm, to heat”), from Proto-Italic *~kalēō~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱelh₁-~. Cognates are Occitan ~caler~, Catalan ~caldre~ (“to be necessary”) and Italian ~calere~. French Wiktionary adds the key to the sense: the warmth meant here is “human” warmth, the heat of feeling. To ~chaloir~ is thus to matter, to be something one cares about.

The verb is now defective and survives almost only in the old turn ~peu me chaut~ (“it matters little to me”). Its best-known descendant is ~nonchalant~, from the negated form ~nonchaloir~, “not to care,” which English borrowed too. Within French the root lives on in the true family of heat: ~chaleur~ and ~chaud~ (the latter from Latin ~calidus~), and ~chauffer~. English ~calorie~ and ~caldron~ belong to the same Latin root.
en.chalouper: Formed from ~chaloupe~ (“rowing boat”) plus the verbal ending ~-er~ (from Latin ~-are~). The origin of ~chaloupe~ is uncertain. It is probably a figurative use of a dialect word ~chalope~ (Middle French ~chaloppe~, “walnut shell”), itself shortened from Old French ~eschalope~ (“shell”). Another proposal derives it from Arabic ~jelba~ (“large boat”).
en.chamailler:
The origin of ~chamailler~ is debated, and French Wiktionary gives two competing accounts. The first treats it as a verb formed from ~camail~ (“hood, mail covering for the head”), with the sense “to strike on the head”. The second sees a cross between two Old French verbs: ~chapler~ (“to cut to pieces, to strike hard”) and ~mailler~ (“to deal blows”).

Neither account is settled, but both start from the idea of striking, so the modern sense of squabbling or bickering would be a milder, figurative descendant. The two possible sources lie close to the world of arms and fighting. ~Camail~ was a piece of armor, and both ~chapler~ and ~mailler~ mean to strike. Today ~chamailler~ is used mostly in its pronominal form, ~se chamailler~, for people who quarrel over trifles, and the noun ~chamaillerie~ names such a quarrel.
en.chamarrer: ~Chamarrer~ is a denominal verb built on the noun ~chamarre~, a word that French Wiktionary traces to Spanish ~zamarra~, a shepherd's sheepskin or woolen jacket. The modern verb means “to bedeck gaudily,” to cover something with showy ornaments. The link between the garment and the ornamentation is not explained in the sources consulted.
en.chambarder: The origin of ~chambarder~ (“to turn upside down”) is thinly documented. French Wiktionary calls it a corruption of the older verb ~champarter~, while English Wiktionary presents it as ~chambard~ + ~-er~. That second account is circular, since the noun ~chambard~ (“uproar, commotion”) is in turn a back-formation from the verb, so the verb is the older of the pair. The sources do not explain ~champarter~ any further, and the path of the sense toward “to shake up completely” is not documented. In modern French the verb is familiar and means to overturn or upset a situation or a room.
en.chambouler: A dialect word from Lorraine, probably a crossing of ~chambranler~, ~chanceler~ (“to stagger”) and ~bouler~. Both sources say “probably”, so the blend is the favored account rather than a proven fact. Meaning is carried by the idea of shaking and staggering that the first two parents share, and the verb now means to upset or turn something upside down.
en.chambrer: Formed from the noun ~chambre~ (“room”) and the verb ending ~-er~. ~Chambre~ is inherited from Old French, from Latin ~cambra~, a medieval spelling of ~camera~ (“room”), which came from Ancient Greek ~kamára~ (“something with an arched cover, a vaulted chamber”). French later borrowed the same Latin word again as ~caméra~, so ~chambre~ and ~caméra~ are doublets. The verb has two senses today: to bring wine to room temperature, and, in informal speech, to mock someone.
en.chamoiser: Formed from ~chamois~ with the ending ~-er~, so “to dress a hide as chamois leather.” The noun comes from Old French ~camois~, from Late Latin ~camox~, itself from Gaulish ~camox~. It most likely belongs to an extinct Alpine language. Related forms include Italian ~camoscio~ and German ~Gämse~, both names of the animal.
en.champagniser: Formed from ~champagne~ with the suffix ~-iser~, in the sense of treating something with a named product or method: here, making a white wine sparkling by the method of Champagne. The noun comes from the region ~Champagne~, from Old French ~champagne~, from Late Latin ~campānia~, from ~campāneus~, from Latin ~campus~ (“field, open plain”). It is a doublet of ~campagne~, the ordinary word for the countryside. The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs.
en.champlever: ~Champlever~ is a French formation from ~champ~, here the “ground” or background of an engraving, and the verb ~lever~, “to lift, to remove.” It names the technique of cutting the ground away from a metal surface, hollowing it out to hold enamel. Its first attestation is in Diderot and d'Alembert's ~Encyclopédie~, the great eighteenth-century dictionary of the sciences, arts and trades.
en.chanceler:
~Chanceler~ comes from Latin ~cancellāre~ (“to cover with a lattice”), a verb built on ~cancelli~, the crossbars of a lattice. French Wiktionary notes that in French the verb took the specific sense of crisscrossing, of walking with unsteady legs. English.Wiktionary calls it an inherited word and a doublet of ~canceller~, which borrowed the same Latin verb in its sense of crossing out a text.

The verb has kept the sense of a body or an object that sways and threatens to fall: one ~chancelle~ from fatigue or drink, and a table, a regime or a certainty can ~chanceler~ too. The Latin source also left ~chancel~, the screened-off part of a church, which French Wiktionary links to the verb. English ~cancel~ and ~chancel~ come from the same lattice words, as does ~chancellor~, originally an official who stood at a lattice.
en.chancir:
The origin of ~chancir~ (“to mold, to go moldy”) is stated with hesitation. French Wiktionary says it comes perhaps from Latin ~canēre~ (“to whiten”), while English Wiktionary gives the closely related Latin ~canescō~ (“to turn white”) without a hedge. Both point to the same Latin root, which has to do with whiteness or hoariness. The initial ~ch-~ is the usual outcome of Latin ~ca-~ in Old French, where ~ca-~ became ~cha-~, as in ~chanter~ from ~cantāre~.

The same Latin root gave ~canus~ (“white, grey”), and French ~chenu~ (“white-haired, hoary”) descends from the Latin adjective ~canūtus~, built on it. English ~canescent~ is a learned relative. Because ~chancir~ ends in ~-ir~ and says what something becomes, it fits the pattern of verbs of change of state, such as ~blanchir~ (“to whiten”). Its meaning today is narrow: it describes bread, preserves or other food that develops a mold.
en.chanfreiner: Formed from the noun ~chanfrein~ with the verbal ending ~-er~: to chamfer is to cut away an edge. According to French Wiktionary, ~chanfrein~ is itself built from ~chant~ (“edge,” from Latin ~canthus~) and the Old French verb ~fraindre~ (“to break”), so a chamfer is literally a broken edge. English Wiktionary is less sure about the first element and also considers a link with Latin ~caput~ and ~frenum~, or with ~champ~, so the exact make-up of the noun remains debated.
en.changer:
From Late Latin ~cambiāre~ (“to exchange, barter”), a variant of Classical ~cambīre~, a word of Gaulish origin tracing to Proto-Celtic *~kambos~ (“bent, crooked”) and the PIE root *~kamb-~ (“to bend, to curve”). The notion of bending underlies that of swapping one thing for its counterpart. ~Changer~ is cognate with Italian ~cambiare~, Spanish ~cambiar~, Occitan ~cambiar~, and Catalan ~canviar~.

The sound history is itself memorable: when Latin ~-bi-~ before a vowel followed a bilabial, it palatalized to ~-ge-~, the same shift that turned ~simium~ into ~singe~ and ~rabia~ into ~rage~ — hence ~cambiāre~ became ~changer~. Borrowed straight from Gaulish into provincial Latin, the verb is a small monument to Celtic survival in everyday French. Its descendants form a busy family: ~change~ (money exchange), ~changement~, ~échanger~, ~rechange~, and ~changeur~. The learned Italian doublet ~cambiare~ also re-entered French finance, yielding ~cambiste~ (“foreign-exchange dealer”) and ~cambisme~ — so a Gaulish word for “bending” still names the people who trade one currency for another.
en.chansonner: ~Chansonner~ is formed from the noun ~chanson~ with the verb ending ~-er~: to lampoon someone in a song, to satirize. ~Chanson~ comes from Old French ~chançon~ (also written ~chançun~), inherited from Latin ~cantiō~ (accusative ~cantiōnem~, “song, singing”), a noun of ~cantāre~, the source of ~chanter~.
en.chanter:
French ~chanter~ descends, through Middle and Old French ~chanter~ (with the northern variant ~canter~), from Latin ~cantāre~ (“to sing”). ~Cantāre~ is the frequentative of ~canere~ (“to sing, to play, to recite”), so it originally meant something like “to keep singing”; it goes back to a Proto-Indo-European root *~keh₂n-~ (“to sing”). Cognates dot the family tree: Welsh ~canu~ (“to sing”) is a direct Celtic relative, Old Irish ~canaid~ another, and — more unexpectedly — English ~hen~, the “singer” among fowl, belongs to the same root. Italian ~cantare~ and Spanish ~cantar~ are its Romance twins, and English borrowed the learned ~chant~ from French itself.

The initial Latin c- softened to the French ch- sound in the north, which is why the verb is ~chanter~ and not the Picard ~canter~ — a split still visible in place and family names. The meaning held steady at “to sing,” but French spun off vivid idioms: ~faire chanter quelqu'un~ (“to make someone sing”) means to blackmail, and ~chanter~ in the dismissive ~si ça te chante~ means “if it appeals to you.” The root seeded a tuneful family: ~chant~, ~chanson~ and ~chansonnier~, ~chanteur~ and ~cantatrice~, ~enchanter~ (literally “to sing a spell upon,” from ~incantāre~), ~cantique~, and ~cantate~. To enchant, fittingly, is to sing magic into being.
en.chantonner: Formed from ~chanter~ (“to sing”) with the suffix ~-onner~, which gives a diminutive or repeated sense: to sing softly, to hum. English Wiktionary analyzes it as ~chanter~ + ~-on~ + ~-er~. The base ~chanter~ comes from Latin ~cantāre~, a frequentative of ~canere~ (“to sing”), from a Proto-Indo-European root *~keh₂n-~ (“to sing”).
en.chantourner: Formed as a compound of ~chant~ and ~tourner~ (“to turn”). French Wiktionary lists two unrelated words ~chant~: one from Latin ~cantus~ (“song”), the other from Latin ~canthus~ (“rim of a wheel”), itself from Gaulish *~cantos~. The sources do not say which is meant, but since the verb means to cut or hollow a piece of wood, stone or marble to a profile, the second, the old word for an edge or rim, seems far likelier than “song.” On that reading, ~chantourner~ is to turn along the edge: to work an outline by following it with the tool.
en.chaparder: The origin of ~chaparder~ is uncertain. French Wiktionary traces it to the slang of the Zouaves, French colonial infantry in North Africa, and cites ~chat-pard~ as a possible source without certainty. English Wiktionary adds that an early etymology, adopted by Littré, derived it from ~chat~ plus ~-pard~ (on the model of ~léopard~), with the original sense of stalking prey, but judges this unlikely. The word is thus a soldiers' slang term for petty theft, “to pilfer,” whose real source nobody has settled.
en.chapeauter: ~Chapeauter~ is formed from the noun ~chapeau~ (“hat”) with the verb ending ~-er~, in the sense “to provide with N.” The noun comes from Middle French ~chappeau~ and Old French ~chapel~, which go back to Early Medieval Latin ~cappellus~, a diminutive of Late Latin ~cappa~ (“hood, cape”). Italian ~cappello~ and Spanish ~capillo~ are cognates. The verb began as “to put a hat on someone.” It then took the figurative sense of being in control, since whoever caps a group stands over it: to ~chapeauter~ a department or a project is to oversee it from above.
en.chaperonner: Formed from ~chaperon~ with the verb ending ~-er~. ~Chaperon~ is a diminutive of ~chape~ (“cape, head covering”) with the suffix ~-on~, so it first named a hood. The person who accompanies and supervises, in French and then English, took the name because such women commonly wore a head covering. As a verb, ~chaperonner~ means both to put a hood on and, more often, to escort and watch over a young person.
en.chapitrer: Formed from ~chapitre~ and the verb ending ~-er~. In the early 15th century it meant to reprimand a member of a religious order at the chapter meeting, and it later widened to reprimanding anyone. The noun comes through Old French from Late Latin ~capitulum~, literally “little head”, a diminutive of ~caput~ (“head”), whence French ~chef~. English Wiktionary also compares ~capituler~.
en.chaponner: Formed from ~chapon~ (“capon”) with the ending ~-er~, meaning to castrate a young cock so that it fattens into a capon. The noun ~chapon~ comes from Old French ~chapon~, from Vulgar Latin *~cappōnem~, from Latin ~cāpō~. The same Latin word gave English ~capon~, Italian ~cappone~, Spanish ~capón~ and Portuguese ~capão~.
en.chaptaliser: Formed from the surname of ~Chaptal~, the French engineer Jean-Antoine Chaptal (1751-1832), who recommended the method, with the verbal suffix ~-iser~. The verb is thus an eponym: to ~chaptaliser~ a wine is to add sugar to the must so that fermentation yields more alcohol. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and in French it routinely turns a name or a noun into a verb of treatment, as in ~pasteuriser~ or ~galvaniser~.
en.charbonner: ~Charbonner~ is a denominal verb: ~charbon~ plus ~-er~, meaning to turn into coal or to produce it. The noun ~charbon~ is inherited from Old French ~charbon~, from Latin ~carbō~ (“charcoal, the result of burning”), the same word later borrowed again as ~carbone~, so the two are doublets. English Wiktionary traces the Latin to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ker~ (“to burn”), while French Wiktionary calls its origin uncertain, perhaps related to Ancient Greek ~χάρφω~ (“to dry up”) or to Celtic languages. ~Charbon~ first meant charcoal, then coal; it also became the name of a disease in the sixteenth century and of a drawing medium in the seventeenth.
en.charcuter: A verb drawn from the noun ~charcutier~, the tradesman who prepares and sells pork products. French Wiktionary calls it a denominal, and English Wiktionary a back formation, since the noun came first. The verb carries the image of the trade into figurative language: to hack or cut something up clumsily, as an incompetent butcher would, especially in surgery or in editing a text.
en.charger:
From Old French ~chargier~ (“to load, to put in a cart”), attested around 1080, from Late Latin *~carricāre~ (“to load a wagon”), a verb built on Latin ~carrus~ (“wheeled cart, war chariot”). ~Carrus~ was itself borrowed from Gaulish ~karros~, from Proto-Celtic *~karros~ (“wagon”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱers-~ (“to run”). The same Romance verb survives as Italian ~caricare~, Spanish ~cargar~, and Portuguese ~carregar~.

The core image is concrete: to ~charger~ was first to pile goods onto a cart, and from that load the meaning fanned out — to burden a person, to fill a weapon (a gun is ~chargé~), to entrust someone with a task (~charger quelqu'un de~), and, in the modern age, to charge a battery or load a file. French kept a learned doublet, ~carguer~, a sailor's term for furling a sail. Strikingly, the humble Gaulish cart-word seeded a whole network of French and English vocabulary through that same “to run” root: ~char~, ~chariot~, ~charrette~, ~carrière~ (“career,” originally a racecourse), and the borrowed ~cargo~ and ~charge~ all trace back to the wheels that once rolled across Roman Gaul.
en.charmer: Formed from the noun ~charme~ and the verb-forming ending ~-er~. The ~charme~ in question is the one meaning “magic spell,” not the hornbeam tree of the same spelling. It comes from Old French ~charme~, from Latin ~carmen~ (“song, incantation, magic formula”), related to the verb ~canere~ (“to sing”). A charm was thus first a chanted formula, and ~charmer~ meant to put under a spell, to enchant. The sense then softened, as it did in English, from magical bewitching to simply delighting or captivating someone, which is the everyday meaning today. The ending ~-er~ makes the noun a first-conjugation verb.
en.charpenter:
The origin is not settled, and the two Wiktionaries put it differently. By one account, ~charpenter~ is a derivative of Old French ~charpent~ (compare modern ~charpente~, “timber framework”). By the other, it comes from a Vulgar Latin verb *~carpentāre~, built on Latin ~carpentum~ (a kind of carriage). French Wiktionary adds that ~carpentum~ itself probably comes from Gaulish *~carbanton~, and it relates ~charpenter~ to ~charpentier~, the name of the craftsman who works timber.

The verb's current senses are the literal “to hew timber” and the figurative “to structure,” as when a speech or a play is built on a solid framework. The family includes ~charpente~, ~charpentier~ and English ~carpenter~, which belongs to the same set of words by way of Old French. Because the sources differ, no single line of descent should be stated as settled.
en.charrier:
French ~charrier~ is the modern form of Old French ~charier~ and ~carier~, the verb from which English ~carry~ also comes, by way of Anglo-Norman. Its origin is not settled. One account derives it from Late Latin ~carricāre~ (“to load a cart, to carry”). The other treats it as a derivative of Old French ~char~ (“cart”), itself from Latin ~carrus~, a word of Gaulish origin, and presents ~charrier~ as likely a sibling of ~charroyer~. Cognate verbs include Occitan ~carrejar~, Italian ~carreggiare~, Spanish ~acarrear~ and Romanian ~căra~.

The core sense is “to carry,” in particular to haul by cart, as a river ~charrie~ ice, silt or logs. The same verb has a colloquial French sense, “to tease, to pull someone's leg,” as in ~charrier quelqu'un~; the sources do not say how it arose. The ~char~ family includes ~charrette~ (“cart”), ~charroi~ and ~charroyer~, and ~chariot~. If the Late Latin ~carricāre~ is the better source, it also gave ~charger~ (“to load”), and through it English ~cargo~ and ~charge~ are close relatives. Either way, the word goes back to the Gaulish wheeled vehicle that Rome adopted as ~carrus~.
en.charroyer: Formed from ~char~ (“cart, wagon”) with the suffix ~-oyer~, so “to carry by cart.” The noun ~char~ is inherited from Latin ~carrus~, a loan from Transalpine Gaulish ~carros~, and is related to Breton ~karr~. English Wiktionary adds that the verb is most likely of the same origin as ~charrier~, from Old French ~charier~ or ~carier~, and compares Italian ~carreggiare~.
en.chartériser: This verb is formed from ~charter~ with the suffix ~-iser~, which makes verbs meaning “to turn into” or “to treat as”. The base is the French noun ~charter~, borrowed from English ~charter~, and a doublet of ~charte~: the two words reached French at different times from the same source. The verb therefore means to put a plane or a train on a charter basis, that is, to hire it for a special trip. It is a recent coinage, built on a modern loanword by one of the most productive verb-making suffixes of French.
en.chasser:
~chasser~ comes from Late Latin *~captiāre~, formed on ~captus~ (the past participle of ~capere~, “to take, seize”), from PIE *~kh₂p-~ (“to grasp”). The Romance descendants make a neat family: Italian ~cacciare~, Spanish ~cazar~, Occitan ~caçar~ — all meaning “to hunt” or “to chase.” English borrowed both ends of the development: ~chase~ from the Old French form and, through a different route, ~catch~ from a Norman variant, so that English keeps two verbs where French keeps one. Latin ~capere~ also lies behind English ~have~ and ~heave~ through the Germanic side of the root.

The core idea is repeated, eager seizing — the frequentative force of the *~-tiāre~ formation — which fits both the hunter pursuing game and the act of driving something away. French ~chasser~ accordingly means “to hunt,” “to chase,” and “to drive off”: one can ~chasser~ a deer, ~chasser~ a thought, or be ~chassé~ from a job. From the same stem come ~chasse~ (“the hunt”), ~chasseur~ (“hunter”), ~pourchasser~ (“to pursue relentlessly”), and the borrowed-back dance step ~chassé~. The whole cluster traces, ultimately, to one PIE notion of the closing hand.
en.chatonner: ~Chatonner~ is formed from ~chaton~ (“kitten”) with the verb ending ~-er~, and means to give birth to kittens. ~Chaton~ comes from Middle French and Old French ~chaton~, derived from ~chat~ (“cat”) with the diminutive suffix ~-on~. The same word also names a catkin, a botanical sense recorded around 1530 by analogy with a cat's tail.
en.chatouiller:
The origin of ~chatouiller~ is partly open, and the two Wiktionaries give different accounts. English Wiktionary traces it through Middle French to Old French ~catellier~ (“to excite, cause tremors”), from Medieval Latin ~catilāre~ (“to tickle”), from Frankish *~kitilōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~kitilōną~, a frequentative of *~kitōną~ (“to tickle”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~geyd-~ (“to stick, jab, tickle”). The Germanic relatives are many: Old English ~citelian~, Old Norse ~kitla~, Dutch ~kittelen~ and German ~kitzeln~. English ~kittle~ is another cousin.

French Wiktionary starts from Old French ~catoiller~ and ~catouller~, and offers two explanations rather than one. By the first, the word is ~touiller~ with a prefix ~ca-~. By the second, it is imitative, built on a sound pattern *~k-t-l~ that evokes tickling, which would explain its kinship with German ~kitzeln~ and Dutch ~kietelen~. The modern verb gave ~chatouillement~ and ~chatouilleux~, which also means “touchy”, though the sources do not say how that figurative sense arose.
en.chatoyer: Formed from ~chat~ (“cat”) with the suffix ~-oyer~, which often means to emit or behave like the noun. The first use concerned the cat's eye, notably the gemstone ~œil-de-chat~, whose reflections shift as it moves. ~Chatoyer~ thus came to mean to shimmer with changing lights. The noun ~chat~ comes from Old French ~chat~, from Late Latin ~cattus~, which replaced classical Latin ~felis~. The suffix ~-oyer~ comes from Old French ~-oiier~, from Late Latin ~-izāre~.
en.chauffer:
From Vulgar Latin *~calefare~, a worn-down form of Classical Latin ~calefacere~ (“to make warm, to heat”), a compound of ~calere~ (“to be hot”) and ~facere~ (“to make, to do”). ~Calere~ goes back to PIE *~ḱelh₁-~ (“to be warm”), seen also in Latin ~calor~ (“heat”) and ~calidus~ (“hot”), Latvian ~silts~ (“warm”), and Welsh ~clyd~ (“cozy, warm”). ~Facere~ rests on PIE *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, to make”), the root of English ~do~ and ~deed~. So ~chauffer~ literally carries the meaning “to make hot.”

The phonetic erosion is dramatic: four Latin syllables in ~calefacere~ collapsed to the single stressed core of French ~chauffer~, the ~cal-~ becoming ~chau-~ by regular palatalization. The verb runs from the literal (~chauffer~ de l'eau) to the figurative — ~chauffer~ une salle, to warm up a crowd; ~ça chauffe~, things are heating up. From the same ~calor~ family French has ~chaud~, ~chaleur~, ~échauffer~, ~réchauffer~, and the borrowed ~calorie~ and ~chauffage~. And the ~chauffeur~ — now a driver — was once exactly what the word says: the man who stoked the boiler, the one who made the heat.
en.chauler: From ~chaux~ (“lime”) + the suffix ~-er~: to ~chauler~ is to coat with lime, that is, to whitewash. The noun ~chaux~ comes from Old French ~chaus~, from Latin ~calx~, ~calcis~ (“lime, limestone”). The same Latin root gives French ~calcaire~ and ~calcium~.
en.chaumer: Derived from ~chaume~ with the first-group ending ~-er~. The noun ~chaume~ comes from Latin ~calamus~ (“reed, plant stalk”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~κάλαμος~ (~kálamos~). English Wiktionary adds that ~chaume~ is a doublet of the learned ~calame~. The verb's senses, clearing stubble and, of sheep, resting in the field, rest on this stalk word.
en.chausser:
From Old French ~chaucier~, inherited from Latin ~calceāre~ (“to furnish with shoes”), a verb built on ~calceus~ (“shoe”). The change of initial ~ca-~ to ~cha-~ is the regular northern French treatment of Latin ~ca-~. The verb has relatives across the Romance languages: Italian ~calzare~ and Spanish ~calzar~ both mean “to put shoes on” and come from the same Latin verb. Modern French kept the whole family of footwear words close to it, since ~chaussure~, ~chaussette~ and ~chausson~ all grow from the same stem.

The core sense, “to put shoes on someone,” underlies the reflexive ~se chausser~, “to put one's own shoes on,” and the verb extends to anything that goes on the feet, as with ~chausser ses skis~. The verb also describes size and fit: ~chausser du 42~ means “to take a size 42 shoe,” and a shoe can ~chausser~ well or badly. A figurative use exists as well, so that ~chausser ses lunettes~ means “to put on one's glasses,” the shoe image carried over to something worn on the face. The opposite verb ~déchausser~ (“to take shoes off”), and ~rechausser~ (“to put shoes back on”), are built on it with ~dé-~ and ~re-~.
en.chauvir: French Wiktionary treats two verbs ~chauvir~ separately. The first, “to prick up the ears” of a horse, follows Littré, who notes that Rabelais wrote ~chauver~ or ~chouer~. This makes it very probable, he says, that these forms come from ~chowe~ or ~choe~, the old name of the owl, and describe the movement of an owl's feathers when it raises its ear tufts. That is a probable account, not a certainty. The second verb ~chauvir~ is said to come from ~chauve~ (“bald”).
en.chavirer: Borrowed from Occitan ~capvirar~, a compound of ~cap~ (“head”) and ~virar~ (“to turn”). French Wiktionary glosses the Occitan literally as “to pass over the head,” and English Wiktionary gives the same source. Occitan ~cap~ continues Latin ~caput~ (“head”), the same source as French ~chef~. The sources do not describe how this literal image came to mean capsizing, so the step is left unexplained here.
en.chaîner: Formed from the noun ~chaîne~ (“chain”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning “to bind or link with a chain.” The noun comes from Old French ~chaiene~, from Latin ~catēna~ (“chain”). The circumflex does not mark a lost letter directly: it replaced the silent ~s~ of Middle French ~chaisne~, which itself signaled a long vowel. Latin had its own verb ~catēnāre~, which English Wiktionary invites us to compare, but the French verb is built on the French noun.
en.cheminer: Formed in French from ~chemin~ (“path, road”) and the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, so that to ~cheminer~ is to travel along a path, to keep walking steadily. English Wiktionary alternatively traces it to a Vulgar Latin verb *~cammīnāre~. The noun ~chemin~ comes from Late Latin ~cammīnus~, traditionally explained as a borrowing from Gaulish, which is why it has no classical Latin ancestor and replaced the older ~via~. Besides walking, the verb is used of ideas and plans that progress slowly but surely.
en.chemiser: Formed from the noun ~chemise~ and the verbal suffix ~-er~: to cover something with a ~chemise~, as in lining the inside of a surface. The base ~chemise~ comes through Old French from Late Latin ~camisia~. Beyond that the sources differ. One proposes an Arabic origin for ~camisia~, while the other derives it from a Germanic word for “shirt.”
en.chercher:
From Old French ~cerchier~ (also ~cercer~, “to travel through, go around”), from Late Latin ~circāre~ (“to go around, traverse”), a verb derived from ~circus~ (“ring, circle”) and the preposition ~circā~ (“around, about”). ~Circus~ comes, through Greek ~kríkos~ / ~kírkos~ (“ring”), from PIE *~sker-~ (“to turn, to bend”). The same Old French ~cerchier~ crossed the Channel and gave English ~search~, which preserves the older form.

~Circāre~ first meant to move in a circuit around something, and the early verb described traversing a region — even moving one's hand about in all directions — before the dominant sense narrowed to “to look for, to seek.” In doing so ~chercher~ displaced the older ~querre~, which survives marginally as ~quérir~. The original idea of going around lingers in the noun ~recherche~ and the agent ~chercheur~, who circles a problem until it yields. From the same root *~sker-~ French keeps ~cirque~, ~cercle~, ~cerceau~, ~circuit~, and ~recherche~ itself — a whole vocabulary of rings and rounds standing behind the everyday act of searching.
en.chevaler:
French ~chevaler~ comes from Old French ~chevaler~ (also written ~cevaler~), which meant “to ride a horse.” Synchronically it can also be read as a verb built on ~cheval~ (“horse”) with the ending ~-er~. The noun ~cheval~ goes back to Latin ~caballus~ (“horse, nag”). Spanish ~caballo~, Italian ~cavallo~ and English ~cavalry~ and ~cavalier~ share that Latin source.

The modern verb has left riding behind. In architecture, attested since 1676, ~chevaler~ means to support with beams, and in art, attested since 1723, it means to work with a ~chevalet~, an easel. The family of ~cheval~ is large: ~chevalier~, ~chevalerie~, ~chevaucher~, ~chevalet~ and the ~chevaux~ of ~cheval-vapeur~. The verb is a technical survivor, far from the saddle of its first meaning.
en.chevaucher:
From Old French ~chevauchier~, by way of Middle French, from Late Latin ~caballicāre~ (“to ride a horse, to travel on horseback”), a verb built on Latin ~caballus~ (“nag, workhorse”). The same Latin verb gave Italian ~cavalcare~ and Spanish ~cabalgar~, and English has borrowed its descendants as ~cavalcade~. The origin of ~caballus~ itself is uncertain, and some scholars think it was borrowed from a non-Latin language, so the chain is traced only as far as the Latin word.

The humble ~caballus~ is the surprise of the story. Classical Latin used ~equus~ for a horse, and the plain ~caballus~ gradually replaced it in everyday speech, which is why the Romance languages say ~cheval~, ~caballo~ and ~cavallo~. French built a family on it: ~cheval~, ~chevalier~ and ~chevalerie~. The verb ~chevaucher~ meant “to ride on horseback.” Its modern figurative sense is “to overlap”: roof tiles, dates or themes ~se chevauchent~, as though one rode astride the other.
en.cheviller: Formed from the noun ~cheville~ (“peg, dowel”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so the verb means to assemble or fasten with pegs. ~Cheville~ was inherited from Old French and goes back to Vulgar Latin *~cavicula~, a reshaped form of Classical Latin ~clāvicula~, the diminutive of ~clāvis~ (“key”). A word for a “little key” thus came to name a peg. The learned borrowing of the same Latin word is ~clavicule~ (“collarbone”), which makes ~cheville~ and ~clavicule~ doublets.
en.chevroter: ~Chevroter~ is formed from ~chèvre~ (“goat”) with the suffix ~-oter~. The base is inherited through Middle and Old French ~chievre~ from Latin ~capra~, the feminine of ~caper~ (“he-goat”). The verb is named for the animal: to bleat like a goat, and so, of a voice or an instrument, to quaver or tremble in short, shaky jerks.
en.chiader: From the noun ~chiade~, which French Wiktionary relates to ~chier~ (“to defecate”), plus the verbal ending ~-er~. This is a slangy, informal verb, originally student slang, meaning to work very hard on something, especially to cram for an exam. The source gives only this link to ~chier~ and no story of how the sense developed, so the path from one meaning to the other is left unexplained here. The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, is the usual way to coin a verb from a noun.
en.chialer: The origin of ~chialer~ is uncertain. French Wiktionary points to Middle French ~chiau~ (“puppy”), possibly influenced by ~chier~, used of the eyes, or by Walloon ~choûler~ (“to cry”). The verb itself is familiar or slang French for crying and, by extension, complaining.
en.chicaner:
The origin of ~chicaner~ is debated. The English Wiktionary gives a Germanic route: Middle French ~chicaner~, from Middle Low German ~schicken~, from Old Saxon *~skikkian~, from Proto-West Germanic *~skikkijan~ (“to order, arrange”), the same source as modern French ~chic~. The French Wiktionary instead treats the verb as a derivative of the noun ~chicane~ and lays out several rival accounts, none of them settled.

The older explanation, from Gilles Ménage, derived ~chicane~ from Spanish ~chico~ (“small”), but the French entry judges it untenable. A second account traces the word through Byzantine Greek to Persian ~čowgân~ (“mallet, polo”), whose ending would explain the ~-ane~, with the senses running from a mallet game to quarreling over the game and finally to legal maneuvering. Against it, the mallet sense is barely attested in French and the word is missing from Occitan and Italian. Other proposals see a blend of ~ricaner~ with a small-sound ~tchic~ or with ~chic~, or link the word to ~chique~ (“marble”) and ~chiquenaude~ through ~schicken~. The earliest Middle French uses concern bringing or putting off a lawsuit, and the Dutch ~schikking~ (“settlement”) is cited as a relative.
en.chier: Inherited from Latin ~cacāre~ (“to defecate”) by way of Old French and Middle French ~chier~. The initial Latin ~c~ before ~a~ became ~ch~ in northern French, the same change that turned Latin ~canis~ into ~chien~. The Latin verb lives on across the Romance languages, as in Italian ~cacare~ and Spanish ~cagar~. French also has the doublet ~caguer~, borrowed from Occitan ~cagar~, and the regional ~caquer~, along with the nursery word ~caca~. Many familiar vulgar words come from the same family, such as ~chiotte~, ~chiasse~ and ~chiant~, which began as concrete terms and developed figurative senses of annoyance.
en.chiffonner: ~Chiffonner~ is formed from ~chiffon~ (“rag”) with the verb ending ~-er~; it means to crumple and, figuratively, to bother or perplex. ~Chiffon~ is ~chiffe~ plus the suffix ~-on~, and ~chiffe~ comes from Middle French ~chiffe~ (“old rag”), from Old French ~chipe~, itself traced to Middle English ~chip~ and Old English ~ċipp~ (“chip, splinter”), the ancestor of English ~chip~. The light fabric called ~chiffon~ is a later sense, drawn from that of an unfinished cloth.
en.chiffrer: Formed from the noun ~chiffre~ (“digit, number”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to put into numbers,” then “to encode.” ~Chiffre~ comes from Middle and Old French ~chifre~ and from Medieval Latin ~cifra~ (“zero”), borrowed from Arabic ~ṣifr~ (“empty”). The word entered the West in the Middle Ages together with the concept of zero and the so-called Arabic numerals, and by extension came to name every digit. Zero and cipher share this ancestor: ~chiffre~ is a doublet of ~zéro~. The secret-code sense of ~chiffrer~ follows from the idea of writing in figures instead of letters.
en.chigner: French Wiktionary explains ~chigner~ as an apheresis (loss of the initial syllable) of ~rechigner~, which it traces to an Old Low Frankish verb *~kinan~ (“to split, to twist the mouth”). English Wiktionary agrees that ~chigner~ is formed by apheresis from ~rechigner~. French Wiktionary also points to Old French ~eschignier~, “to show the teeth”, as a related word. Today ~chigner~ means to whine, moan or complain, while the fuller ~rechigner~ is still used, as in ~rechigner à la tâche~ (“to balk at the task”).
en.chiner: ~Chiner~ has two senses with two separate origins, and the sources treat them as distinct words. The first, from 1753, is the textile sense, to dye and interweave fabrics. It is derived from ~Chine~ (“China”) with the suffix ~-er~, because the technique came from there. The second sense, from 1847, is the colloquial one common today, to hunt for bargains. Here the sources are more cautious. French Wiktionary says it is probably an alteration of ~échiner~, and English Wiktionary calls it a clipping of ~échiner~. This second origin is given only as probable.
en.chinoiser: Formed from the adjective and noun ~chinois~ (“Chinese”) plus the verbal ending ~-er~. The base is itself derived from ~Chine~ (“China”) with the suffix ~-ois~, the ending of ~gaulois~ and ~français~, which names a people or a language. The verb is a French coinage from a noun, with the sense “to argue, to quibble,” and the sources consulted do not say how the idea of China came to stand for hair-splitting.
en.chiper:
The origin of ~chiper~ is uncertain, and the sources agree only on a likely starting point. French Wiktionary derives it from Old French ~chipe~ (“rag”). English Wiktionary proposes a derivative of ~chippe~ (compare ~chiffe~, “old cloth, rag”) in the sense “to hide something of little value.” Both point to a word for a worthless scrap. The chain given for ~chippe~ runs through Middle English ~chip~ (“fragment, worthless thing”) and Old English ~ċipp~ (“splinter, beam”) back to Proto-Germanic *~kippaz~ (“beam, log”).

Whatever the exact route, the modern senses of ~chiper~ are informal: “to pinch, to steal, to rob.” If the proposed path is right, the verb began with something small and of little worth, which would fit its everyday use for petty theft. The English word ~chip~ descends from the same Middle English source, so the proposed ancestor of ~chiper~ would be a cousin of the chip of wood or stone. This remains a proposal, not a settled fact.
en.chipoter: Formed from Old French ~chipe~ with the suffix ~-oter~. The sources gloss ~chipe~ as “bit, scrap” or “rag, scrap of cloth”, and relate it to ~chiffe~ (“rag”) and ~chiper~ (“to pilfer”). A verb built on a word for a trifling scrap suits the modern senses of ~chipoter~: to nibble at one's food, to haggle over small sums, to quibble over details. The verb has a small, fussy sense that matches its base.
en.chiquer:
French has more than one verb ~chiquer~, and the sources keep them apart. The one meaning “to chew” (tobacco, or gum) is traced to an imitative syllable, ~tchic~, which evokes the sound a person makes while chewing. According to this account the verb is a sound-word, an imitation of the noise itself, rather than a descendant of an older word.

A second ~chiquer~ means “to fight,” and its origin is hedged. It is probably the same word as the first: by one account, fighting was a way of giving each other a dose of tobacco, an idea also behind ~tabasser~ (“to beat up”). Otherwise it comes from the same imitative syllable, here evoking the sound of blows. A third ~chiquer~ is a separate verb, derived from ~chic~ and ~chiqué~.
en.chlinguer: ~Chlinguer~ (“to stink, to reek”) is a slang verb whose origin is uncertain. English Wiktionary suggests only that it may come from German ~schlagen~ or ~schlingen~, and says no more. No source settles the question, so the link to either German verb is a guess and nothing firmer can be claimed. The spelling ~chl-~ is unusual for French and hints at a foreign, perhaps Germanic, model, which fits that tentative proposal but proves nothing.
en.chlorer: ~Chlorer~ is formed from the noun ~chlore~ (“chlorine”) with the verb ending ~-er~, and means to treat or combine with chlorine, as when water is chlorinated. The base ~chlore~ is a chemist's word built on Greek ~khlōrós~ (“pale green”), after the color of the gas. The verb is a plain technical derivation: the noun names the substance, and ~-er~ turns it into the act of applying it.
en.chloroformer: ~Chloroformer~ is derived from the noun ~chloroforme~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, and means “to anesthetize with chloroform.” The noun is a chemical compound name built from ~chlore~ and ~formyle~. ~Chlore~ comes from Greek ~chlōros~ (“pale green”), after the color of the gas, and ~formyle~ belongs to the family of ~formique~, from Latin ~formica~ (“ant”), since formic acid was first obtained from ants. The verb applies the substance's name to the act of using it.
en.chlorurer: ~Chlorurer~ is a denominal verb: ~chlorure~ (“chloride”) plus ~-er~, meaning to treat with a chloride or to chlorinate. The noun ~chlorure~ is itself built from ~chlore~ (“chlorine”) and the suffix ~-ure~, the ending French chemistry uses for compounds of two elements. The element's name comes from Greek ~khlōros~ (“pale green”), after the color of the gas.
en.choir:
The verb ~choir~ is inherited from Middle French ~cheoir~, from Old French ~cheoir~, which was older ~chedeir~. It goes back to Late Latin (popular Latin) *~cadēre~, a reshaped form of classical Latin ~cadĕre~ (“to fall”). Latin ~cadĕre~ comes from Proto-Italic *~kadō~ and from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱh₂d-~ (“to fall”). The Latin verb survives across the Romance languages, for example Italian ~cadere~ and Spanish ~caer~, so French ~choir~ has close siblings throughout the family.

In the Middle Ages ~choir~ was the ordinary verb for falling, until ~tomber~ displaced it. It now survives almost only in the fixed phrase ~laisser choir~ (“to let fall, to drop”) and in a literary past participle. Its family is far larger than the verb itself. The old feminine participle gave ~chute~ (“a fall”). Compounds of the verb gave ~échoir~ (“to fall due”) and ~déchoir~ (“to decline, to fall from rank”), with ~déchéance~ as its noun. Latin ~cadentia~, “a falling,” gave ~chance~, which began as the way dice fall, and Latin learned borrowings gave ~cadence~ and ~décadence~. The word that once meant simply “to fall” now lingers in the language of luck, due dates and downfall.
en.choisir:
French ~choisir~ (attested around 1050) comes from Old French ~coisir~ (“to perceive, to discern, then to select”), borrowed from the Frankish verb *~kausjan~ (“to taste, to test, to try”). This is one of the many Germanic words the Franks left embedded in French. The Frankish form goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ǵews-~ (“to taste, to choose”), the very same root that gave Latin ~gustāre~ (“to taste”) — so ~choisir~ and ~goûter~ are distant relatives. Through that Germanic branch it is cognate with English ~choose~, German ~kiesen~ (“to choose, elect”), and Dutch ~kiezen~, all sharing the idea of testing a thing before taking it.

The semantic thread is intuitive: one tastes or tries, then discerns, then picks. Old French ~coisir~ first meant “to make out, to catch sight of,” and only gradually settled into the sense “to select,” pushing aside the older verb ~élire~ (from Latin ~ēligere~), which narrowed to formal “electing.” The shift from a verb of perception to a verb of decision mirrors how English ~choose~ itself developed from “taste, test.” From the same Germanic and Indo-European stock, French keeps the noun ~choix~ (“choice”), back-formed from the verb, and — by the Latin route — the gustatory family of ~goût~ and ~déguster~.
en.choper: ~Choper~ is a slangy, later colloquial verb that appears to be an alteration of ~chopper~ (“to stumble”). The sense of catching something by chance, and then of stealing or arresting someone, fits that picture: to stumble on something is to come upon it. French Wiktionary adds that the sense of stealing may have been reinforced by the existence of ~chiper~, a near-synonym. The source says only that the origin “seems” to be this, so it is best taken as likely and not certain. In current French, ~choper~ covers catching a cold, a ball or a person.
en.chopper:
The origin of ~chopper~ is uncertain. French Wiktionary lists the forms ~çoper~, ~chouper~ (1235) and ~chopper~ (1316-1328) and judges the verb most probably imitative, from a sound ~tsopp-~ that mimics the uneven tread of a lame walker. It compares Italian ~zoppo~ (“lame”) and ~zoppicare~ (“to limp”), which may rest on a similar sound. English Wiktionary likewise calls it onomatopoeic.

According to the same source, the initial ~ts~ became ~ch~ for expressive reasons. Old French also had the diminutives ~choppiner~ and ~chopiner~. The meaning of the French verb is “to stumble” or “to trip.” The sources do not settle any link beyond imitation, so the history of ~chopper~ stays an open question.
en.choquer:
First attested in the 13th century in the Picard form ~chuquier~ (“to clash in combat, to strike”), whence ~choquer~. The origin is obscure — “perhaps Germanic,” says the TLFi. The favored comparison is with Middle Dutch and Middle Low German ~schokken~ (“to strike, jolt, shake”), but every version of the Germanic hypothesis runs into trouble: the Dutch verb is attested only from 1494, and the word's early French territory — almost exclusively Picardy and Wallonia — fits the proposed High German variants badly. The etymology therefore remains genuinely unsettled: a verb of collision whose own pedigree is a collision of hypotheses. English ~shock~ belongs to the same tangle: dictionaries trace it to Middle French ~choquer~ (and its noun ~choc~), to Middle Dutch ~schokken~, or to both at once.

For its first centuries ~choquer~ stayed strictly physical: knights, lances, ships and armies clashed. The figurative sense — to offend, to scandalize, to jar feeling or taste — is attested by 1621 and became the dominant one (warnings still promise images that “may shock”). The deverbal noun ~choc~ followed the same road, from the impact of cavalry charges to emotional and medical states (~état de choc~), and the family grew with ~choquant~ and ~s'entrechoquer~ (“to knock together”). English ~shock~, first of blows and then of feelings, kept pace on the other side of the Channel. As for the unsettled origin, it is better savored than hidden: a verb meaning “to collide” over whose birth the etymologies themselves collide — a borrowing from Middle Dutch, a High German variant, a derivative of an Old High German word for a jolt — with no single account crowned by the TLFi.
en.chorégraphier: ~Chorégraphier~ is formed from ~chorégraphie~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~: to compose or arrange the movements of a dance or a staged performance. The noun ~chorégraphie~ is built from two Greek elements, ~khoreía~ (“dance”) and ~gráphein~ (“to write”), and was first the written notation of dance steps before it came to mean the art of designing them. The verb is a modern formation, used of ballets, shows and, by extension, any carefully planned set of movements.
en.chosifier: Formed from ~chose~ (“thing”) with the suffix ~-ifier~, “to make into,” so ~chosifier~ is to turn something into a mere thing, the sense of English “reify.” The noun ~chose~ comes from Old French ~chose~, from Late Latin ~causa~ (“thing”), from Latin ~causa~ (“cause, affair”). This word supplanted classical ~res~ in the sense of “thing.” The learned doublet ~cause~ is the same Latin word borrowed a second time. The suffix ~-ifier~ goes back to Latin ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”).
en.chouchouter: ~Chouchouter~ is built on the noun ~chouchou~ (“favorite”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, the usual way French makes a verb from a noun: to ~chouchouter~ someone is to treat them as a ~chouchou~, to pamper them. The origin of ~chouchou~ is not settled. French Wiktionary describes it as an affectionate derivative of ~chou~ in the sense “darling,” and English Wiktionary sees a reduplication of ~chou~. A second proposal, which French Wiktionary itself marks as lacking a reference, derives it from Portuguese ~chuchu~ around 1834.
en.chougner: The Académie française lists ~chougner~ as a variant of ~chouiner~, which it derives from ~ouin ouin~, an onomatopoeia imitating the sound of crying. French Wiktionary likewise suggests that ~chougner~ is perhaps a variant of ~chouiner~. Both verbs are familiar in register and mean “to whimper, to whine.” The spelling with ~-gn-~ is the one a regional chronicle describes as very much alive in the Lyon area and across most of eastern France. So the verb is best understood as a regional face of ~chouiner~, a word that imitates a child's sobbing.
en.chouiner: According to the Académie française, ~chouiner~ dates from the twentieth century and is derived from ~ouin ouin~, an onomatopoeia imitating the sound of crying, with the verbal ending ~-er~. The word is familiar in register and means “to whimper, to whine,” said of a child in tears or of anyone who complains about their lot. Its variant ~chougner~ is also recorded, and the agent noun ~chouineur~ (“whiner”) comes from it.
en.chouraver: A slang verb borrowed from Romani ~čorav~ (“I steal”). French Wiktionary traces the Romani word to Sanskrit ~caura~ (“thief”), and English Wiktionary compares Hindi ~curānā~ (“to steal”). The word thus reaches French slang from the Romani language, itself rooted in India. It remains informal in French, meaning “to nick, to pinch.”
en.chourer: A slang verb meaning “to steal”, borrowed from Romani ~čor-~ (“to steal”). Romani took the word from Sanskrit ~caura~ (“thief, robber, swindler”), so the verb traces a long route from India into the argot of French underworld speech. The French verb carries the Romani stem with the ordinary first-conjugation ending ~-er~. Its Romani source is also why the word belongs to informal register and never to formal prose.
en.choyer: The history is obscure. French Wiktionary only refers the reader to Old French ~chuer~ and ~chouyer~, while English Wiktionary says ~choyer~ comes from Old French ~chuer~, ultimately from Vulgar Latin *~cavicare~. That last link is given without further detail, so treat it as a proposed source rather than an established descent. In modern French the verb means “to cherish, to treasure.”
en.christianiser:
~Christianiser~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~chrīstiānizō~, which was built on ~Chrīstiānus~ (“follower of Christ”) and the verb-forming suffix ~-izō~. The Latin adjective in turn rests on the Greek title ~Christós~ (“anointed”), and the suffix is the Greek ending ~-izein~, taken into Latin. Italian ~cristianizzare~ and Spanish ~cristianizar~ are parallel learned verbs, and English ~Christianize~ follows the same path.

The verb sits at the meeting point of two French routes from the same Latin source. ~Chrīstiānus~ was inherited and worn down over the centuries into ~chrétien~, while ~christianiser~ was taken over ready-made from Latin and keeps its full shape. Its suffix is the same ~-iser~ found in many other verbs of Greek and Latin origin, and the noun ~christianisme~ belongs to the same family. The meaning is to convert a person or a people to Christianity, or more loosely to give a place, a custom or a feast a Christian character.
en.chromer: Derived from the noun ~chrome~ with the verb ending ~-er~, meaning to plate a metal object with chromium. The noun ~chrome~ is a scientific coinage from Greek ~khrôma~ (“color”), given to the metal because its compounds are so brightly colored. The verb names the process of giving fittings, bumpers and taps their mirror-like finish. Note that French Wiktionary gives only the base, with no further source, so the story of the noun rests on common reference knowledge.
en.chronométrer: ~Chronométrer~ is a denominal verb, formed from the noun ~chronomètre~ (a precise timekeeping instrument) with the verb ending, and it means to measure a duration exactly, as with a stopwatch. The noun is a learned compound of Greek ~khrónos~ (“time”) and ~métron~ (“measure”), so the verb carries the idea of “measuring time” in its very roots. French ~chronomètre~ also gave the family of ~chronométrage~ and ~chronométreur~.
en.chuchoter: ~Chuchoter~ is a variant of ~chucheter~, a word of imitative origin: its sounds were shaped to evoke the noise it names, here the soft, hushed hissing of a whisper. The sources give it no Latin or Germanic ancestor, so the word is best seen as a French creation. It means to speak very low, and by extension it is also said of leaves that rustle.
en.chuinter: Of onomatopoeic origin: both French and English Wiktionary describe the verb as imitating the hushing sound ~ch~. It has no Latin or Germanic ancestor behind it, only a noise turned into a word. Its senses, the hoot of an owl, a buzz and a creak, all share that soft, sibilant hiss. Such sound-imitating verbs are formed directly from the noise they report, which is why no older source word can be traced.
en.chuter: French Wiktionary derives ~chuter~ from the noun ~chute~ (“fall”) with the verb ending ~-er~, with a second, separate verb ~chuter~ (“to hush”) coming from the interjection ~chut~. ~Chute~ is a feminine past participle used as a noun: the old participle ~cheüt~ of ~choir~ (“to fall”), from Vulgar Latin *~cadūta~, built on Latin ~cadere~ (“to fall”). English Wiktionary merges two Old French feminine participles, ~cheüe~ and ~cheoite~. So ~chuter~ is literally “to make a fall,” a verb made from the noun of ~choir~, a verb now almost lost.
en.châtaigner: ~Châtaigner~ is a slang verb formed from the noun ~châtaigne~ with ~-er~, in the sense of hitting or punching. The noun comes from Latin ~castanea~ (“chestnut, chestnut tree”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~kástanon~, and it is a doublet of ~castagne~. The sources give no story for how the nut came to stand for a blow.
en.châtier:
The verb is inherited from Old French ~chastier~ (also ~castier~), from Latin ~castīgāre~ (“to reprimand, to correct”). Latin ~castīgāre~ is usually analyzed as ~castus~ (“pure”) plus the verb ~agere~ (“to drive, to do”), so it meant, literally, to make pure. The verb lived on in the Romance languages: Italian ~castigare~ and Spanish ~castigar~ are its direct descendants. English has it twice over: ~chastise~ and ~chasten~ come through Old French, while ~castigate~ was taken straight from the Latin.

The French verb kept the Latin sense of correcting by reproof or punishment. The circumflex of ~châtier~ stands in for the ~s~ of Old French ~chastier~, a spelling fossil of a sound lost in speech. Modern French also uses the verb figuratively, as in ~châtier son style~ (“to polish one's style”), and the noun ~châtiment~ (“punishment”) is formed on it. The Latin adjective ~castus~ survives in the learned ~chaste~ and ~chasteté~, a reminder of the “pure” in the Latin analysis. A well-known proverb sums up the older stern sense: ~Qui aime bien châtie bien~ (“He who loves well chastises well”).
en.châtrer:
~Châtrer~ is inherited from Old French ~chastrer~, itself from Latin ~castrāre~ (“to castrate”). The form ~chastrer~ is attested as early as 1121. It is the popular, inherited form of a doublet: the learned verb ~castrer~ was borrowed from the same Latin word much later, at the very beginning of the seventeenth century. Latin ~castrāre~ also gave Italian ~castrare~ and Spanish ~castrar~, and English ~castrate~ is a learned relative of the same kind as French ~castrer~.

The two French verbs thus show the two paths a Latin word could take. ~Châtrer~ went through the normal sound changes of spoken French, in which the ~s~ before a consonant weakened and finally disappeared, leaving only the circumflex on the ~â~ as its trace, the same fate as in ~fête~ from ~feste~. ~Castrer~ came in through writing and kept the Latin shape intact. The result is a pair with the same meaning, “to castrate,” where the older, inherited word has a worn-down form and the later borrowing sounds closer to Latin. Of the two, ~châtrer~ is the everyday verb, and ~castrer~ the more technical one.
en.chérir: Formed from the adjective ~cher~ and the verb ending ~-ir~, so “to hold dear”. The adjective comes from Latin ~cārus~, which already had both senses, “dear, costly” and “loved, esteemed”. It goes back through Proto-Italic to the Proto-Indo-European root *~keh₂-~ (“to desire, to wish”). The ending ~-ir~ here is a French formation, and not every verb in ~-ir~ is one, since many are inherited whole from Latin.
en.chômer:
~Chômer~ is traced to Late Latin ~caumāre~ (“to rest during the heat”), from Ancient Greek ~kaûma~ (“heat”). English Wiktionary treats the Latin verb as inherited directly. French Wiktionary instead routes it through Occitan ~caumar~ (“to rest in the heat”), from ~cauma~ (“heat”), and links it to ~calme~. It adds that Le Robert prefers the plain line from Late Latin ~caumāre~ and Greek ~kaûma~, so the Occitan step is the contested one.

French Wiktionary also relates the word to ~chaume~ (“thatch”), the cheap straw gathered after the harvest and used to roof poor houses, but it offers this as a link only, and the Greek-through-Late-Latin line is the one every source shares. The Late Latin verb meant resting in the heat; French ~chômer~ means to be idle or out of work, and it gave ~chômage~ and ~chômeur~. The Greek noun ~kaûma~ belongs to the verb ~kaíein~ (“to burn”), which also lies behind French ~caustique~ and ~cautère~.
en.cibler:
Denominal from the noun ~cible~ (“target”), with the verbal suffix ~-er~. The noun is regional in origin: it comes from Swiss German dialect ~Schibe~, corresponding to standard German ~Scheibe~ (“disc, pane, target”), the round board shot at in marksmanship. The form was altered to ~cibe~, and fr.Wiktionary notes that the final ~-l~ may represent a Germanic diminutive — though it flags this with “possibly,” so the suffix is not certain. The word entered French from the German-speaking cantons where target-shooting was a civic sport.

The sense moved from the physical bull's-eye to its figurative uses. In older or familiar speech ~cibler~ could mean to hurl something at someone; today it means to aim at, to single out — a market, an audience, an objective. The marketing and military senses (“une campagne ciblée,” “une frappe ciblée”) are modern. The image is constant across all of them: a single round mark to be hit. Because the root is Germanic rather than Latin, ~cible~ has no Romance cousins in Italian or Spanish, which use ~bersaglio~ and ~blanco~ instead — a small reminder that French borrowed its word for the target from across the Rhine.
en.cicatriser: Formed from the noun ~cicatrice~ with the suffix ~-iser~, in the sense of causing to become: to ~cicatriser~ is to form a scar, so to heal. The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin ~cicātrīx~ (accusative ~cicātrīcem~, “scar”). The suffix ~-iser~ was borrowed into Old French from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and it is still one of the most productive verb suffixes in French.
en.ciller: ~Ciller~ is formed from ~cil~ (“eyelash”) with the ending ~-er~, so by its make-up it means to move the eyelashes: to blink. It is most often heard in the negative, ~ne pas ciller~, to not so much as flicker an eyelid, said of someone who stays unmoved. The noun ~cil~ is inherited from Old French ~cil~, from Latin ~cilium~.
en.cimenter: Formed from ~ciment~ with ~-er~, which here means to provide with or work with the noun: to join or coat with cement. ~Ciment~ comes from Latin ~caementum~ (“crushed stone”). The verb has a second, figurative sense, to confirm or consolidate something such as a friendship or an alliance, as if making it as firm as masonry.
en.cingler:
French has three separate verbs spelled ~cingler~. The sailing sense, “to head in a direction under sail,” comes from Middle French ~cingler~, from Old French ~singler~ or ~sigler~, a loan from Old Norse ~sigla~ (“to sail”), from Proto-Germanic *~siglijaną~. It is related to Old Norse ~segl~ (“sail”) and cognate with German ~Segel~ and English ~sail~. The Norse origin shows that the spelling with ~c~ is odd: the nineteenth-century lexicographer Littré, quoted by French Wiktionary, called it wholly wrong, since it should be ~singler~, as it was spelled until a slip in the sixteenth century.

The sense “to lash, to whip” has a different source. French Wiktionary derives it either from ~sangle~ (“strap”) or from Occitan ~cinglar~, itself from Latin ~cingulum~ (“girdle, belt”); English Wiktionary simply gives Latin ~cingulum~. A third verb, “to trace curves,” is a denominal of ~cingle~ (“sinuosity”). Latin ~cingulum~ belongs to ~cingere~ (“to gird”), the root also of French ~ceinture~ and ~sangle~.
