So ~cingler~ unites a Norse sailing word and a Latin belt word in one spelling.
en.cintrer: The sources trace ~cintrer~ to Latin by two routes. French Wiktionary derives it from ~cingere~ (“to gird, to surround”), a verb equivalent to ~ceindre~. English Wiktionary instead gives Vulgar Latin *~cinctūrāre~, from ~cinctūra~, the source of ~ceinture~, and compares the French coinage ~ceinturer~. Both lead to the idea of a band around something. The modern senses, to bend, to vault, or to take in a garment at the waist, are those of the gloss.
en.cinématographier: Formed from the noun ~cinématographe~ with the verb ending ~-er~: to film. The noun was coined in the 1890s from Greek ~κίνημα~ (kínēma, “movement”) and ~-graphe~, from Greek ~γράφω~ (gráphō, “to write”), so the machine was named for “writing movement.” The verb applies the name of the apparatus to its use.
en.circoncire:
From Latin ~circumcīdere~ (“to cut around”), a compound of ~circum~ (“around”) and ~caedere~ (“to cut”). French borrowed the verb whole, which is why it cannot be split into a French prefix and base. The Latin verb gave Italian ~circoncidere~ and Spanish ~circuncidar~, and English took ~circumcise~ from the same source.

The first element ~circum~ is the source of French ~circonférence~ and ~circonstance~, while ~caedere~ is a prolific root in the Romance languages. Its compounds gave ~décider~ (literally “to cut off,” hence to settle), ~inciser~, ~concis~ and ~précis~. The noun ~circoncision~ is learned too, from the Latin noun derived from the verb. In modern French ~circoncire~ is a technical and religious verb, and it is used mostly in the infinitive, the past participle ~circoncis~ and the noun.
en.circonscrire:
French ~circonscrire~ was borrowed from Latin ~circumscrībere~ (“to draw a line around, to limit”), made of ~circum~ (“around”) and ~scrībere~ (“to write, to scratch, to draw”). The Latin verb ~scrībere~ first meant to scratch lines on a surface, long before it meant to write in the modern sense. English ~circumscribe~ is a parallel borrowing of the same Latin verb, and the Romance languages have Italian ~circoscrivere~ and Spanish ~circunscribir~. Its second half is the root of a very large family of words about writing, including English ~scribe~ and ~describe~.

The Latin sense is a geometric one: to trace a circle or outline around something. Figurative use followed, as in English: to confine a thing within bounds, whether a fire, an epidemic or a subject of discussion. In French, ~circonscrire un incendie~ is to keep a fire from spreading, and ~circonscrire un sujet~ is to define its limits. Geometers still speak of a circle ~circonscrit~ to a triangle, one that passes through all its corners. Its conjugation follows ~écrire~ (past participle ~circonscrit~), because the two verbs share the Latin ~scrībere~. The family reaches ~circonscription~ (“district, constituency”), the word for a territory drawn on a map with a boundary line, as well as ~écrire~, ~décrire~ and ~inscrire~.
en.circonvenir:
~Circonvenir~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~circumvenīre~, which is formed from ~circum~ (“around”) and ~venīre~ (“to come”). The Latin verb meant literally “to come around,” hence to surround or encircle, and also, figuratively, to get around someone by trickery. Italian ~circonvenire~ and English ~circumvent~ are the same Latin verb in other languages, so French shares the word in its learned form with its neighbors.

It is the second, figurative sense that survived in French, where ~circonvenir~ means to outmaneuver, manipulate or win someone over by cunning. The verb is a learned relative of the inherited ~venir~, which descends from the same Latin ~venīre~, and of ~convenir~, ~prévenir~ and ~parvenir~, all built on that verb. The first element ~circum~ also appears in ~circonférence~, ~circuit~ and ~circonscrire~.
en.circuler:
From Latin ~circulāri~ (“to form a circle, move in a circle”), from ~circulus~ (“little ring, circle”), the diminutive of ~circus~ (“ring, circle”). ~Circus~ was borrowed from Ancient Greek ~κρίκος~ / ~κίρκος~ (~kríkos~ / ~kírkos~, “ring”), tracing to PIE *~(s)ker-~ (“to turn, bend”); through the Germanic side of that turning root stands English ~ring~.

The diminutive matters: a ~circulus~ is a small circle, a hoop, a ring — and to ~circuler~ is to travel that closed loop and return, motion that comes back on itself. From the literal ring the verb opened onto every kind of going-round: blood ~circule~ through the body, money and rumours ~circulent~ through society, and a policeman's ~Circulez!~ orders a crowd to keep moving along. The same ~circulus~ gives ~circulaire~ (both the shape and the letter sent round to many readers) and ~circulation~ (of traffic, blood, currency); the parent ~circus~ survives in ~cirque~, the ring where performers turn. What unites them all is the closed curve of *~(s)ker-~ — the path that bends back to where it began.
en.cirer: ~Cirer~ is formed from the noun ~cire~ (“wax”) and the verb ending ~-er~; it therefore means to treat with wax. The noun is inherited, through Middle and Old French ~cire~, from Latin ~cēra~, which meant wax, but also sealing wax, a writing tablet and a wax figure.
en.cisailler: ~Cisailler~ is formed from the noun ~cisaille~ (“shears”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so “to cut with shears.” The noun comes from Latin *~caesaculum~, built with the suffix ~-culum~ on ~caedere~ (“to cut”). The word belongs to the same family as ~ciseau~.
en.ciseler: From Old French ~ciseler~, built on ~cisel~, a cutting tool, with the verb ending ~-er~. English Wiktionary glosses ~cisel~ as a pair of scissors or blade, and the word survives in modern French in the plural ~ciseaux~ (“scissors”) and in ~ciseau~ (“chisel”). To ~ciseler~ is to work metal, stone or wood with a chisel, hence to carve or engrave finely; in cooking it means to chop herbs or spices very small, as with a blade. English ~chisel~ is a cognate, borrowed from the Anglo-Norman form of the same Old French word. The sources consulted do not trace ~cisel~ further back, so no Latin source is claimed here.
en.citer:
From Latin ~citare~ (“to set in motion, rouse, summon, call forth”), the frequentative of ~ciēre~ (“to move, stir, call”). The verb was borrowed into French as a learned word. ~ciēre~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~keih₁-~ (“to set in motion, to move”), making it cognate with Greek ~kīneîn~ (“to move, set in motion” — the source of ~cinéma~ and ~kinetic~) and with Sanskrit ~cyávate~ (“he stirs himself, sets out”). To cite is, etymologically, to put something or someone into motion.

That original kinetic sense explains the verb’s spread of meanings. To ~citer~ first meant to “summon” — to call a person before a court or to muster troops — and from “calling someone forth” came “calling forth someone’s words,” that is, to quote, and “calling out a name,” to mention. The motion sense stays vivid in the Latin-built relatives French inherited: ~exciter~ (“to excite, stir up,” from ~ex-~ + ~citare~), ~inciter~ (“to incite, urge on”), ~susciter~ (“to arouse, give rise to”), and ~solliciter~. The noun ~citation~ keeps both the courtroom summons and the quoted passage under one roof — two faces of a single act of “calling forth.”
en.civiliser: Both Wiktionaries analyze the verb as ~civil~ + ~-iser~, a suffix that builds verbs meaning “to make A.” The adjective ~civil~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~cīvīlis~ (“of citizens”), reaching French by way of Old French ~civil~. To ~civiliser~ is therefore to make someone civil, in the sense of belonging to an ordered society of citizens. Latin ~cīvīlis~ is built on ~cīvis~ (“citizen”), the same root that gives French ~cité~ and ~citoyen~.
en.clabauder: Formed from the noun ~clabaud~ with the verbal ending ~-er~: to bark noisily and for no reason, as a ~clabaud~ does. A ~clabaud~ was a hunting dog with drooping ears that barks without cause, and the word was soon applied to people who yap or gossip. Its own origin is uncertain. Littré compared Walloon ~clabot~ (“small bell hung on an animal's neck”) and Germanic verbs such as Dutch ~klappen~ and German ~klaffen~ (“to yap, to chatter”). French Wiktionary also proposes an ~-aud~ derivative of a verb *~claber~, a variant of ~clapper~.
en.claironner: ~Claironner~ is a denominal verb: the noun ~clairon~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~clairon~ is itself a derivative of ~clair~ (“clear”) with the suffix ~-on~, naming an instrument that gives a clear sound. So ~claironner~ first meant to sound the bugle, and by extension to announce something loudly and widely, to trumpet it from the rooftops, which is the sense of “yell” in its gloss.
en.clamecer: ~Clamecer~ (“to die,” in slang) is an orthographic variant of ~clamser~, and its origin is uncertain. French Wiktionary gives it no derivation and sends readers to ~clamser~, a verb of the nineteenth century. There three hypotheses are offered: ~crampe~ (“cramp”), supported by an earlier variant ~crampser~; ~clamps~, a surgical instrument whose misuse could kill; or a phonetic deformation of ~collapser~. None is settled.
en.clamer:
Inherited from Old French ~clamer~, from Latin ~clāmāre~ (“to cry out, to shout”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~kelh₁-~ (“to shout”). The Latin verb gave Italian ~chiamare~ and Spanish ~llamar~, both meaning “to call,” which shows how far its sense shifted in the south. English took it through Old French as ~claim~, and learned borrowings from Latin gave ~proclaim~, ~exclaim~ and ~acclaim~.

In French, ~clamer~ kept the loud, public sense of the Latin: to cry something out, and by extension to proclaim it, as in ~clamer son innocence~. The verb is now literary and fairly rare, which is why most speakers meet it only through its prefixed relatives: ~proclamer~, ~réclamer~, ~acclamer~, ~exclamer~ and ~déclamer~. The noun ~clameur~, a loud outcry, belongs to the same family, as does the learned ~clamant~ in the phrase ~injustice clamante~. The simple verb thus survives as the root of a family it has outlived.
en.clamper: Formed from ~clamp~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~clamp~ is borrowed from English ~clamp~, so the verb is a French coinage built on an English loan, meaning “to clamp,” that is, to fasten with a clamp. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~, the infinitive ending of the first conjugation, and is the default way French coins verbs from nouns.
en.clamser: The origin of this slang verb for dying is uncertain, and the sources offer several guesses. It is first attested as ~crapser~ and ~crampser~, which has suggested a link with ~crampe~ (“cramp”), or else an imitative origin. Other proposals tie it to ~clamps~, a surgical instrument whose misuse could kill, or to ~collapser~ (“to collapse”) by distortion. None of these is settled, and the verb is simply colloquial French for dying.
en.clapir: The origin of ~clapir~ is not certain. French Wiktionary treats it as a variant of ~glapir~ (the yelp of a fox or a small dog), probably under the influence of ~clapier~. That word, a rabbit hutch or warren, shares an origin with another ~clapir~ meaning “to hide in the stones.” Both rest on Old Occitan ~clap~ (“stony ground, heap of stones”). The verb may thus have two layers: the cry, from ~glapir~, and the animal's home, the heap of stones in which rabbits shelter, which would have colored the verb through ~clapier~.
en.clapoter: A frequentative-style formation on ~claper~ (“to clap”) with the suffix ~-oter~; French Wiktionary instead parses the first attestation, ~clappetter~, as built from ~clapper~, ~-eter~ and ~-oter~, and links it to ~clapet~. The base ~claper~ comes from an imitative root *~klapp-~, perhaps with some influence from Dutch ~klappen~ (“to clap”). The verb names the small slapping sound of water against a hull or a shore, and its sound is the whole etymology.
en.clapper: From Old French ~claper~, which French Wiktionary links to the noun ~clap~ (“a sharp, dry sound”) and notes in the sixteenth century. The verb names the act of producing that sound, and in modern French it is used mainly in the phrase ~clapper de la langue~, to click one's tongue against the palate. The sources give no deeper origin for ~clap~, so the line stops there.
en.claquemurer: A compound of ~claquer~ and ~mur~ (“wall”), so literally “to throw into walls.” The first element is the sound-word ~claquer~ (“to clap, to slap”), which French and English Wiktionary trace differently, as an imitation of the noise ~clac~ or as a borrowing from Dutch. In the seventeenth century Antoine Oudin recorded in his dictionary (1640) a noun ~claquemur~, a kind of game, which he translated by Italian ~abattimuro~. The verb now means to shut someone up within four walls, to confine them.
en.claquer:
French ~claquer~ is a sound word. English Wiktionary traces it through Middle French and Old French ~claquer~ (“to clack, clap, clatter”) to Middle Dutch ~klacken~ (“to clack, crack, whack”), then Old Dutch *~klakon~ and Proto-Germanic *~klakōną~ (“to clap, chirp”). French Wiktionary presents it instead as built on the imitative ~clac~, the noise of a sharp, short slap, and notes the kinship with Dutch ~klakken~ and German ~klacken~. The two accounts differ on whether the verb was imitated afresh in French or came in from Dutch, and the evidence does not settle the matter. Either way the meaning stays close to a sharp, dry noise. French Wiktionary adds ~cliquer~ as a close relative.

From the clap, the senses spread. A door, a whip or a set of teeth ~claque~ in the sense of making a sharp noise, and slang stretched the verb to squandering money. The noun ~claque~ means a slap, and also the group of people paid to applaud, a sense English Wiktionary ties to the practice of hiring audience members at the Paris Opera. French Wiktionary links another slang noun to the verb in its sense of spending lavishly. Tap dancing is ~claquettes~, named for the clatter of the shoes. English Wiktionary also lists a separate, homonymous verb built on ~claque~ (“vamp”), a shoe part, which is a different word.
en.claqueter: An onomatopoeia: the verb imitates a sharp, repeated clapping sound. It is used of the stork, whose cry is a rapid clatter of the bill. French Wiktionary gives no source word, so the verb is best seen as a sound-imitating coinage, in the same imitative family as ~claquer~.
en.clarifier: Borrowed from Latin ~clārificāre~, a compound of ~clārus~ (“clear, bright”) and ~facere~ (“to make”), so “to make clear.” French Wiktionary offers a second reading, that the verb was built in French from ~clair~ plus the suffix ~-ifier~, which comes to the same meaning. ~Clārus~ is also the source of French ~clair~, and English ~clarify~ is the matching verb. The word still serves two worlds: literally, to ~clarifier~ a liquid such as butter or a broth is to make it clear, and figuratively it means to make a situation or an idea easy to understand.
en.classer:
From the noun ~classe~ (“class, category”), with the suffix ~-er~. The noun was borrowed from Latin ~classis~, a word that originally meant a “summons” or “call to arms” and then the categories of citizens that could be called up — the political-military divisions into which the Roman census sorted the population by wealth. Cognates of the verb include Italian ~classificare~ and Spanish ~clasificar~, and through the noun, English ~class~ and ~classify~.

The semantic journey runs from the muster-roll to the filing cabinet. From the Roman census-classes, ~classe~ generalized into any rank or category, then into the schoolroom ~classe~ and, by extension, the verb ~classer~: to sort, to file, to rank. The military memory lingers in French phrases — a ~classe d'âge~ is a cohort of conscripts, and ~classer une affaire~ is to file a case away, to close it. The noun also spawned ~classique~ (“classical,” first the literature of the top “class” of writers), and the verb gave ~classement~ (a ranking or league table), ~classeur~ (a binder or filing folder), and ~classification~. The prefixed forms ~reclasser~ (to reclassify, or to redeploy a worker) and ~déclasser~ (to downgrade) round out a family all descended from a Roman call to arms.
en.classifier: ~Classifier~ is formed from ~classe~ with the suffix ~-ifier~, which here means to organize according to a class. French Wiktionary adds that the suffix was borrowed on the model of a Latin type ~classificare~, built from ~classis~ and ~facere~ (“to make”). The noun ~classe~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~classis~, which originally meant a summons, and so the different categories of citizens who could be called up for military service. The suffix ~-ifier~ itself goes back to Latin ~-(i)ficāre~, from ~facere~.
en.claudiquer:
From Latin ~claudicāre~ (“to limp”), a verb built on the adjective ~claudus~ (“lame”). French Wiktionary gives the Latin verb as the source. English Wiktionary offers two routes, a learned borrowing from ~claudicāre~ or a back-formation from the participle ~claudicant~. The two accounts differ, and the sources do not settle the point. The verb means to limp, and it is rare and literary.

Its family is small and bookish. ~Claudicant~ (“limping”) and ~claudication~ (“a limp”), the latter used chiefly in medicine, belong to the same learned layer, and English has ~claudication~ too. ~Claudiquer~ is rarely heard in everyday talk, where ~boiter~ is the ordinary verb. When it appears, it is often figurative, applied to an argument, a rhythm or a policy that goes unevenly.
en.claustrer:
A learned verb built on Latin ~claustrum~ (plural ~claustra~), the word for an enclosure or a bolt that shuts something in. French Wiktionary calls it the learned counterpart of ~cloîtrer~, and English Wiktionary likewise forms it from the root of ~claustrum~. The Latin noun is the standard derivative of ~claudere~ (“to close, to shut”), so ~claustrer~ means to shut someone away, to confine them as in a cloister.

The two verbs show a familiar French pattern. ~Cloîtrer~ descends from the Latin noun by the popular route, through ~cloître~, and ~claustrer~ was reshaped on the Latin form itself, which is why it keeps the ~-au-~ of ~claustrum~. The root is productive in French: ~clore~, ~clôture~, ~conclure~, ~exclure~ and ~enclos~ all go back to ~claudere~ or its compounds. English has taken the Latin noun twice: ~cloister~ came through Old French, and ~claustrophobia~ was built on ~claustrum~ directly. Today ~claustrer~ is a rare, literary word, mostly in the reflexive, ~se claustrer~ (“to shut oneself away”).
en.claveter: Formed from ~clavette~ and the verb ending ~-er~. A ~clavette~ is a small key or pin, a diminutive of the word that gives ~clef~, so ~claveter~ means “to secure with a pin or key.” The root is the same Latin ~clāvis~ (“key”) that underlies ~clef~.
en.clayonner: Formed from the noun ~clayon~ and the ending ~-er~. The noun is itself a derivative of ~claie~ (a hurdle, a wattle panel) with the suffix ~-on~, which matches Occitan ~cledon~. To ~clayonner~ is therefore to shore up the bank of a ditch or road with ~clayons~, that is, with wattle. The ending ~-er~ goes back to the Latin infinitive ending ~-are~.
en.clicher: Both Wiktionaries call ~clicher~ imitative: it echoes the sound of the typographic mold striking molten metal, a sound close to ~clic~ in French and ~click~ in English. The verb belongs to the printing trade, where it means to make a stereotype plate, and it also covers taking a photograph. The noun ~cliché~, which English borrowed from French, comes from the past participle of the same verb.
en.cligner:
The origin of ~cligner~ is uncertain, and the explanations differ. By one account it comes from Old French ~cliner~ (“to bow, to greet with a bow”), of unknown origin, whose sense shifted to “lowering the eyelid”; it may be related to ~clore~. By another, Old French ~clignier~ probably comes from a Vulgar Latin *~clūdiniare~, from *~clūdināre~, a derivative of ~clūdō~, a variant of Latin ~claudō~ (“to close, to shut”), the source of ~clore~. The shape of the word may then have been influenced by ~cliner~, a descendant of Latin ~clināre~ (“to lean”), or more probably by ~guigner~ (“to peek”).

Whichever account is right, the sense is settled: ~cligner~ means to half-close the eyes, and above all to blink or wink, as in ~cligner des yeux~ (“to blink”). Its family includes ~clignoter~ (“to flicker”), ~clignotant~ (“turn signal”) and ~clin d'œil~ (“wink”). Each rival root also has French descendants: ~clore~ (“to close”) gives ~clos~ and ~clôture~, and ~clināre~ gives ~incliner~ (“to tilt”).
en.clignoter: Formed from ~cligner~ (“to blink, to half-close the eyes”) and the suffix ~-oter~, which here gives a diminutive or frequentative sense, “a little, repeatedly.” The origin of ~cligner~ is debated: by one account it comes from Old French ~cliner~ (“to bow”), by another from a Vulgar Latin *~clūdiniare~, linked to Latin ~claudō~ (“to close”). ~Clignoter~ means to blink rapidly, or to flicker, as a light does, and gave ~clignotant~ (“turn signal”).
en.climatiser: Formed in French from ~climat~ and the verb-forming suffix ~-iser~, so to ~climatiser~ is to give a space a controlled climate, in other words to air-condition it. The base ~climat~ came into French from Latin ~clima~ (genitive ~climatis~), borrowed from Greek ~klíma~. That Greek word meant the slope of the earth toward the poles, then a zone or region, then its weather. It comes from the verb ~klinein~ (“to lean, to incline”). A climate is thus, at the root, a slant. The shortened colloquial form is ~clim~, and the noun ~climatiseur~ names the machine.
en.cliquer:
Formed in French from the onomatopoeia ~clic~, an imitation of a short, dry sound — the snap of a latch or the tap of a key — to which the verbal ending ~-er~ was added. It belongs to a small family of sound-words that includes ~claquer~ (“to slam, to clack”) and ~clicher~ (which gave ~cliché~, originally a printer's stereotype plate, named for the clicking noise the casting tool made). The pair ~clic~ and ~clac~ even survive together in the expression ~clic-clac~.

For most of its life ~cliquer~ named a faint mechanical noise and was rare. Its fortune was made by the computer mouse: the modern sense “to click” is a calque on English ~click~, itself an independent onomatopoeia of the same kind, so the two languages arrived at nearly identical words by imitating the same sound. From the family come ~cliquet~ (“a pawl, a ratchet”), ~cliqueter~ and ~cliquetis~ (“to jingle / a jingling”), and the borrowed ~cliché~. Few verbs show so clearly how a noise, frozen into a syllable, can be conjugated.
en.cliqueter: Formed from ~cliquer~ with the suffix ~-eter~, a frequentative: to click again and again, hence to jingle, rattle or clink. English Wiktionary traces it through Middle French ~cliqueter~ to Old French ~cliketer~. The base ~cliquer~ is built on the onomatopoeia ~clic~, imitating a short, dry sound, and the noun ~cliquetis~ names the sound the verb describes.
en.clisser: Formed from the noun ~clisse~ (a wicker cover) with the verb ending ~-er~: ~clisser~ is “to cover a bottle with wickerwork.” According to French Wiktionary, ~clisse~ came from ~clice~ (a piece of split wood), which gave ~cliche~ (“plaited wicker”) and then ~clisse~. It is also explained as a clipped form of ~éclisse~, the initial ~es-~ having been mistaken for a prefix and dropped.
en.cliver:
~Cliver~ is a borrowing from Dutch ~klieven~ (“to split, to cleave”), a word of Germanic origin, and it dates from the sixteenth century. Dutch ~klieven~ belongs to the Germanic verbs for splitting, and it is a relative of English ~cleave~ and German ~klieben~. The word is a loan from a neighboring Germanic language, which makes it unusual among French verbs for splitting, since most of those come from Latin.

Its English cousin ~cleave~ has the odd property of meaning both “to split” and “to cling,” because two different old verbs merged, but French ~cliver~ keeps only the first sense. ~Cliver~ means to split something along its natural lines, and it is used chiefly of crystals and rocks. The noun ~clivage~ (“cleavage”) belongs to the same family, and in modern French it is also used figuratively for a split dividing a group.
en.clochardiser: ~Clochardiser~ is formed from ~clochard~ (“tramp”) with the suffix ~-iser~, “to turn into, to make like N”: to reduce someone to the life of a tramp, or to let a place or person become run-down. The origin of ~clochard~ itself is disputed. One account derives it from ~clocher~ (“to limp”) + ~-ard~, another from ~cloche~ (“clumsy person, oaf”) + ~-ard~, and French Wiktionary combines the two as a compound of ~clocher~, ~cloche~ and ~-ard~. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~.
en.clocher: Sources give two accounts of ~clocher~. One treats it as a verb formed on ~cloche~ (“bell”) with ~-er~. The other makes it inherited from a Vulgar Latin *~cloppicāre~, from ~cloppus~ (“lame”), which displaced classical ~claudicāre~ and is linked to French ~clop~ and ~clopin-clopant~. French Wiktionary does not rule the bell out: a bell is an object that swings, and Old French ~clocheter~ meant both “to tinkle like a little bell” and “to sway”. The noun ~cloche~ itself comes from Late Latin ~clocca~, attested in the seventh century; the sources trace it to Gaulish or Proto-Celtic.
en.cloisonner: Formed from ~cloison~ (“partition”) plus the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~cloison~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~clausiōnem~ (“a closing”), built on Latin ~clausum~, the past participle of ~claudere~ (“to close”), the verb that French inherited as ~clore~. So ~cloisonner~ means to divide a space with partitions. By extension it describes separating things into watertight compartments, as in the figurative sense of “to compartmentalize”.
en.cloner: ~Cloner~ is a denominal verb: it is formed from the noun ~clone~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, so it means to produce a clone. French Wiktionary treats ~clone~ as very probably borrowed from English ~clone~, first attested in the horticultural sense in 1903. The English word itself comes from Ancient Greek ~κλών~ (“twig, young shoot”), a plant cutting that grows into a copy of its parent, possibly from an Indo-European root meaning “to cut.” The suffix ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, is the default ending for new verbs, which is why ~cloner~ conjugates like ~chanter~.
en.clopiner: From Old French ~clopin~ (“lame, hobbling”), with an Old French verb ~cloper~, “to limp,” derived from Late Latin *~cloppus~. English Wiktionary gives the base as ~clop~ (“hobbling”) and likewise traces it to Late Latin *~cloppus~, a form known only by reconstruction. The modern verb ~clopiner~ means “to limp, to hobble along.” It is best known in the adverbial phrase ~clopin-clopant~, “limping along,” and it shares the root of ~éclopé~ (“footsore, lame”).
en.cloquer: Formed from ~cloque~ (“blister”) with ~-er~, the verb means to blister or to form blisters. The noun ~cloque~ is a Norman and Picard form of ~cloche~ (“bell”), dialects in which the Latin hard consonant did not turn into the French ~ch~ sound.
en.clore:
From Old French ~clore~ (early 12th century), from Latin ~claudere~ (“to shut, close, lock”), from Proto-Italic *~klaudō~, from PIE *~kleh₂u-~ (“hook, peg, key”). The same root gave Ancient Greek ~κλείς~ (~kleís~, “key, bolt”) and, through Germanic, Old High German ~sliozan~ (“to lock, conclude”); it is also the source, through Latin, of English ~close~, ~clause~, and ~cloister~.

The noun behind it all was essentially a key or bolt — to ~claudere~ was to set the bar across the door. French inherited the verb directly, but ~clore~ led a troubled life: several of its conjugated forms collided with those of ~clouer~ (“to nail”), and it steadily ceded ground to ~fermer~, surviving now mainly in fixed and elevated uses (~clore~ un débat, un compte). Yet the root is everywhere in its descendants: the participle gave ~clos~ and ~clôture~, the prefixed compounds ~enclore~, ~exclure~, ~inclure~, ~conclure~, and ~reclus~, and the learned ~clé~ / ~clef~ preserves the original “key.” A verb in retreat, anchoring a vast and thriving family.
en.clouer: ~Clouer~ is formed from ~clou~ (“nail”) with the verb ending ~-er~, “to fasten with nails.” English Wiktionary adds an alternative: it may instead descend from Late Latin ~clāvāre~, itself from Latin ~clāvus~, compare Italian ~chiavare~ and Catalan ~clavar~. Either way the root is the same, since ~clou~ comes from Latin ~clāvus~ and, through Proto-Italic *~klāwos~, from Proto-Indo-European *~kleh₂u-~. The older spelling ~cloer~ is attested in the Life of Saint Giles.
en.clouter: Formed from ~clou~ (“nail”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, with a ~-t-~ between them. This ~-t-~ is euphonic: it keeps the vowel of ~clou~ from meeting that of ~-er~ and distinguishes ~clouter~ (“to stud with nails”) from ~clouer~ (“to nail”). ~Clou~ is inherited from Old French ~clou~, from Latin ~clāvus~, from Proto-Italic *~klāwos~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~kleh₂u-~.
en.cloîtrer: ~Cloîtrer~ is built on the noun ~cloître~ (“cloister”) and the ending ~-er~, and it is first attested in 1623. The noun comes from Latin ~claustrum~ (“enclosure, bolt”). The verb means “to shut up in a cloister,” and so, more broadly, to confine someone in a closed place.
en.clôturer: From the noun ~clôture~ + the verb ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Old French ~closture~, from Late Latin ~clausūra~ (“a closing”), built on ~clausus~, the past participle of ~claudere~ (“to close”). The circumflex of ~clôture~ may come from a crossing with Latin ~claustra~ (“barrier, enclosure”), though that is only a suggestion. The verb first meant to surround with a fence, and then, figuratively, to bring something to a close, as when one ~clôture~ a meeting, a debate or an account. English ~closure~ comes from the same Old French word.
en.coacher: Borrowed from English ~coach~ and given the French verb ending ~-er~, which is the default for new verbs. The result means to coach someone, that is, to train or guide them. The evidence traces the verb no further back than the English noun, and a second line in French Wiktionary about the origin of the noun itself is left aside here because it is unclear which word it describes.
en.coaguler:
~Coaguler~ is a learned verb, borrowed from Latin ~coāgulāre~ (“to curdle, to make clot”). It is a doublet of ~cailler~, which descends from the same Latin verb by the ordinary phonetic changes of spoken French. Latin ~coāgulāre~ was built on the noun ~coāgulum~ (“rennet, a curdling agent”), itself related to ~cōgere~ (“to drive together”).

The two French verbs share a source but live in different registers. ~Cailler~ is the everyday word, used of milk and blood, while ~coaguler~ is technical and scientific, used of blood, proteins and sauces. Related words follow the same split: ~caillé~, ~caillot~ and ~caillebotte~ on the inherited side, ~coagulation~, ~coagulant~ and ~anticoagulant~ on the learned side. Italian ~cagliare~ and Spanish ~cuajar~ are inherited descendants of the same Latin verb, and English ~coagulate~ was borrowed from it.
en.coaliser: ~Coaliser~ is derived from ~coalition~ with the suffix ~-iser~, by a substitution of suffix: the ending ~-ition~ of the noun gives way to ~-iser~. French Wiktionary refers the reader to ~coalescer~, the related verb. The noun ~coalition~ comes from Latin ~coalitio~, borrowed through Medieval Latin ~coalitiōnem~ from Latin ~coalitus~ (“fellowship, communion”). The verb means “to unite in a coalition.”
en.coasser:
Borrowed from Latin ~coaxāre~, which came from Greek ~koáx~, an imitation of the cry of a frog. Like many verbs for animal sounds, it is an onomatopoeia: the word was built to sound like what it names, so it has no deeper root to trace. The sound itself passed from Greek into Latin and from Latin into French, and the French rendering of the cry is ~couac~.

The verb is used of frogs, and by extension of any harsh, croaking voice. French has the noun ~couac~, which the sources describe as an imitation of the cry, and which also names a sour note or a squawk in speech or music. Because the base is an imitation, the Greek, Latin and French forms all echo one another.
en.cocher: Formed from the noun ~coche~ (“notch”) and the verb ending ~-er~. The ~coche~ in question was originally a stick that people cut notches into to keep a tally, and then the notch itself, so ~cocher~ first meant to notch and then to mark with a stroke, hence to tick a box. The origin of that noun is uncertain. One proposal is Italian ~cocca~ (“notch on an arrow”), a sense also found in the Occitan verb ~encocar~ (“to nock an arrow”). The word is not the same as ~coche~ (“coach”), from Hungarian ~kocsi~, nor as ~coche~ (“sow”), related to ~cochon~. French ~encoche~ (“notch”) belongs to the same family.
en.cochonner: Derived from French ~cochon~ (“pig”) with the verb ending ~-er~. The sources say nothing more about the noun. The sense “to mess up” is the familiar one: to do a job as carelessly as a pig might, which is how the metaphor is usually read.
en.cocoter: ~Cocoter~ is formed from ~cocotte~ with the ending ~-er~, and means to stink, in slang, and also to yap or blather. The noun ~cocotte~ is imitative of a hen's clucking and was applied in many senses connected more or less directly to the hen. A second account, found on French Wiktionary, derives it by a change of suffix from ~cocasse~ or ~coquasse~, old words for various vessels, themselves altered from ~coquemar~ (“kettle”). The verb is a close twin of ~cocotter~, which has a double ~t~ and the same senses.
en.cocotter: ~Cocotter~ is formed from ~cocotte~ with the ending ~-er~. The noun ~cocotte~ is imitative of a hen's clucking, and French Wiktionary adds that it may instead come by a change of suffix from ~cocasse~, an old name for a vessel. For the slang sense “to stink,” French Wiktionary proposes that the verb probably derives from the phrase ~sentir la cocotte~ (“to smell of the cocotte”), alluding to the perfumes worn by women of easy virtue. The related senses of yapping and blathering are listed beside it, with no explanation given.
en.cocufier: Formed from ~cocu~ (“cuckold”) and the suffix ~-ifier~, so “to make someone a cuckold.” By French Wiktionary's account, ~cocu~ comes from the cuckoo, whose female lays eggs in other birds' nests; the usage is attested from the fifteenth century. The sources add that ~coucou~ itself derives from Old French ~cocu~, and one alternative etymology draws on a Latin form ~cucutus~. The suffix ~-ifier~ comes from Latin ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”), and here yields the verb for being unfaithful to a spouse.
en.coder: Either a denominal verb built on ~code~ and the ending ~-er~, or a borrowing of English ~to code~, recorded as a verb from 1815; fr.Wiktionary offers both. French ~code~ comes from Latin ~codex~, a variant of ~caudex~ (“tree trunk”), which came to name books, then books of laws, and finally the body of written laws itself. The sense “secret code” arrived later from English ~code~ (attested in 1808), where French had used ~chiffre~. The computing sense, “to write the code of a program,” dates from 1947.
en.codifier: ~Codifier~ is formed from ~code~ and the suffix ~-ifier~, meaning “to put into a code.” French Wiktionary also allows that it may instead come from English ~codify~, attested in 1800, while English Wiktionary gives Latin ~cōdex~ plus ~-ifier~. ~Code~ comes from Latin ~cōdex~, a variant of ~caudex~ (“tree trunk”), the wooden block from which writing tablets and then books were made. The word named books, then law books in particular, and finally the body of laws they contained. The suffix ~-ifier~ goes back to Latin ~-ficāre~ (“to make”), so ~codifier~ is literally to make into a code.
en.coexister:
Both Wiktionaries agree on the formation: ~co-~ (“together”) + ~exister~, though French Wiktionary adds a Latin model, ~coexsistere~, which French speakers felt as a compound of those two parts. The core is Latin ~exsistere~ (“to step forth, to emerge, to be”), made of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~sistere~ (“to set, to stand”). That last verb is a reduplicated formation on ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~steh₂-~, the same root as in English ~stand~.

The sense has therefore moved from “stand forth” to “be there” to “be there together.” Latin ~exsistere~ gave French ~exister~, and the ~co-~ prefix added the idea of sharing the same time or space: nations, species or ideas that ~coexist~, without one replacing the other. A whole family shares the ~sistere~ element: ~persister~, ~résister~, ~subsister~, ~consister~, ~assister~ and ~insister~, as well as ~coexistence~ and ~coexistant~. Seen this way, ~coexister~ is a verb about “standing out” together.
en.coffrer: ~Coffrer~ is a denominal verb: the noun ~coffre~ (“chest, trunk”) plus the ending ~-er~. The noun came from Old French ~cofre~, from Latin ~cophinus~ (“basket”), which in turn borrowed Ancient Greek ~kóphinos~ (“basket”). French also kept a doublet of the same word, ~couffin~. The verb has two senses built on the noun: to lock someone or something up, and, in building, to make formwork, the wooden mold into which concrete is poured.
en.cofinancer: ~Cofinancer~ is a modern French formation: ~financer~ plus the prefix ~co-~, the productive form of Latin ~con-~ (“with”), which expresses joint action, so “to fund together.” The base ~financer~ is a verb made from the noun ~finance~, which arose in Old French around 1280 from ~finer~ (“to settle, to pay”), an altered form of ~finir~. All of this rests on Latin ~fīnis~ (“end, limit”): paying a debt was a way of making an end of it.
en.cogiter:
Borrowed from Latin ~cōgitāre~ (“to think, to ponder”). Latin ~cōgitāre~ is generally analyzed as ~co-~ (“together”) plus ~agitāre~ (“to set in motion, to turn over”), so “to turn things over together in the mind.” English ~cogitate~ is a direct borrowing of the same Latin verb, and Latin ~cōgitō~ is the verb of Descartes's famous ~cogito, ergo sum~.

French ~cogiter~ is a learned reborrowing, and it is a doublet of ~cuider~, the form that Latin ~cōgitāre~ gave by ordinary inheritance. ~Cuider~ (“to think, to believe”) was a common verb in Old French but is now obsolete. The inherited verb faded, while the learned one lives on with a faintly ironic tone: ~cogiter~ today means to think hard, often with a humorous suggestion of heavy mental labor, as in ~il cogite à son prochain roman~. Related French words include ~cogitation~ and ~agiter~.
en.cogner: From Old French ~coignier~, inherited from Latin ~cuneāre~ (“to wedge”), a verb built on ~cuneus~ (“wedge”). The same Latin noun gave French ~coin~, which still means “wedge” in some uses and also “corner,” an object that is wedge-shaped. The sense of ~cogner~ moved from driving in a wedge to striking hard, so that one now ~cogne~ a door, a head or a nail. The shift is the obvious one, from the tool to the blow that drives it, though the sources do not narrate it. The verb is familiar and a little colloquial, and it also means “to fight” in slang.
en.cogérer: Formed from ~gérer~ with the prefix ~co-~, the modern form of Latin ~con-~ (“with, together”), used for joint action. It means to run something jointly with others. The base ~gérer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~gerere~ (“to carry, to conduct, to manage”), the same root as ~gestion~ and ~geste~. Since ~co-~ is productive today, ~cogérer~ is a recent coinage that sits alongside ~copiloter~ and ~cofinancer~.
en.cohabiter: Borrowed from Latin ~cohabitāre~ (“to live together”), built from ~co-~ (“with”) and ~habitāre~ (“to dwell”). The Latin verb ~habitāre~ is itself a frequentative of ~habēre~ (“to have, to hold”), so to dwell somewhere was, etymologically, to keep holding it. The same ~habitāre~ gave French ~habiter~, which makes ~cohabiter~ a learned relative of an everyday verb: the word was taken whole from Latin, not assembled in French from ~co-~ and ~habiter~.
en.coiffer: Formed from the noun ~coiffe~ (“headdress, cap”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so the verb first meant “to put a cap on.” The noun comes from Late Latin ~cofia~, whose origin is obscure but probably Germanic: English Wiktionary traces it to an Old High German diminutive of ~kuffa~ (“hood, cap”), a relative of English ~cop~ (“top, crest”). The sense then widened from covering the head to dressing the hair, hence the modern meaning “to do someone's hair.” The old spelling ~coeffe~ survived in dictionaries until the eighteenth century.
en.coincer: Formed in French from the noun ~coin~ (“wedge, corner”) with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is inherited from Old French ~coin~, from Latin ~cuneus~ (“wedge”), which also gave French the learned ~cunéiforme~ (“wedge-shaped”). To ~coincer~ is therefore to fix something with a wedge, so that it jams and cannot move, and by extension to trap a person in a corner or in a tight spot: ~se faire coincer~ is to get caught.
en.cokéfier: Formed from the noun ~coke~ with the verb ending ~-fier~ (“to make”), so “to turn into coke,” as when coal is heated until only the carbon residue remains. The noun is borrowed from English ~coke~, the residue left by roasting coal in an oven; a separate borrowing gave French the ~coke~ of cocaine. The ending ~-fier~ comes from Latin ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to do, to make”).
en.collaborer:
Borrowed from Latin ~collaborare~ (“to work together”), from ~com-~ (“with”) + ~laborare~ (“to labor”), the verb of the noun ~labor~ (“toil, work”). The origin of ~labor~ itself is uncertain: one account links it to the verb ~labare~ (“to totter”), imagining a worker swaying under a heavy load, but the linguist De Vaan rejects this without offering a replacement, and other roots have been proposed. So the appealing image of toil as a “tottering under burden” should be flagged as disputed, not assumed. Cognate with Italian ~collaborare~ and Spanish ~colaborar~, and, through the same ~labor~, with English ~labor~ and ~elaborate~.

~Collaborer~ entered French only in the 19th century, a learned re-borrowing rather than an inherited form, which is why it kept its Latin shape so cleanly. Its everyday sense is positive — to work jointly on a shared task — but the 20th century gave it a dark second life: under the Occupation, ~collaborer~ came to mean cooperating with the enemy, spawning the noun ~collaborateur~ and its scornful clipped form ~collabo~. From the same ~labor~ French also keeps ~labeur~ (“hard toil”), ~laborieux~, ~laboratoire~, ~élaborer~, and the older ~labourer~ (“to plough”), the field-work sense of working the land.
en.collapser: A modern borrowing of the English ~collapse~ with the French verb-forming ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary gives this simple account: the English word was taken over and made to conjugate like any first-group verb. The English verb itself comes from Latin ~collapsus~, the past participle of ~collābī~ (“to fall together”). It is a casual, often humorous word, used of a person or a structure that gives way.
en.collationner: Formed from ~collation~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, to collate, that is to compare a text with another in order to check it. ~Collation~ is borrowed from Latin ~collātiō~ (“gathering”). The noun's sense of a light meal comes from the gathering of monks for a meal.
en.collecter:
A denominal verb built on the noun ~collecte~ (« a collection, a gathering »), from Latin ~collecta~ (« contribution, levy »), the feminine of the participle ~collectus~. That participle belongs to ~colligere~ (« to gather together »), itself ~com-~ (« together ») + ~legere~ (« to pick, choose, read »), from Proto-Indo-European *~leǵ-~ (« to collect, gather »). Cognates of the base abound: Italian ~cogliere~, Spanish ~coger~, and — through the same root — English ~collect~, ~legend~, and ~lecture~.

Latin ~legere~ first meant the physical act of « picking up » and only later « reading, » as one gathers letters with the eye; that semantic leap echoes through the whole family. French inherited the popular line in ~cueillir~ (« to pick ») and the learned line in ~collecter~, ~collection~, ~collectif~, ~recueillir~, and ~récolte~ (« harvest »). The same *~leǵ-~ underlies ~lire~ (« to read »), ~légion~, ~élire~ (« to elect »), and ~négliger~ (« to neglect »), literally « not to gather up. »
en.collectionner: ~Collectionner~ is formed from the noun ~collection~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~: to gather things of one kind for pleasure or study. ~Collection~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~collēctiō~ (“a gathering”), from ~colligere~ (“to gather together”), made of ~com-~ and ~legere~ (“to pick, to gather”). The same Latin verb reached French by the popular route as ~cueillir~, so ~collectionner~ and ~cueillir~ are distant cousins.
en.collectiviser: Formed from ~collectif~ with the suffix ~-iser~, which makes a verb meaning “to make or turn into”: to collectivize is to place property or production under collective ownership. ~Collectif~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~collectivus~, a word that Latin built on ~colligere~ (“to gather”). The same suffix gives ~nationaliser~ and ~privatiser~, which also turn an adjective or noun into a change of status.
en.coller:
A denominal verb, formed in French directly from the noun ~colle~ (“glue, paste”). That noun comes from Vulgar Latin *~colla~, borrowed from Ancient Greek ~κόλλα~ (~kólla~, “glue”). The Greek word is the same one hidden inside English ~collagen~ (literally “glue-producer”) and ~protocol~, and it gives French ~collage~, ~colloïde~, and ~collagène~.

To ~coller~ is first of all to stick or glue one thing to another, but French has let the verb wander into a wealth of figurative and slang senses. Something that fits or works can ~coller~ (~ça colle~, “that works, that’s fine”); a person who clings to you ~colle~; and in everyday speech to ~coller~ someone is to stump them with a hard question — which is exactly why ~une colle~ became student slang for a tough quiz or oral exam, and why a school detention is also ~une colle~ (originally being “stuck” at school). A demanding examiner is even called a ~colleur~. From the same Greek-derived root come ~décoller~ (“to unstick,” and so “to take off” in an aeroplane), ~encoller~, and the noun ~colle~ in all its glue-bound and exam-bound meanings.
en.colleter: Formed from ~collet~ (“collar”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, the ordinary ending that turns a noun into a first-conjugation verb. ~Collet~ is inherited from Middle French and is itself analysed as ~col~ (“neck, collar”) + the suffix ~-et~. The verb means to seize someone by the collar, or to wrap something around it.
en.colliger:
Borrowed from Latin ~colligere~ (“to gather, to collect”). The Latin verb is built from ~com-~ (“together,” assimilated to ~col-~ before ~l~) and ~legere~ (“to gather, to pick, to read”). English ~collect~ and Italian ~cogliere~ come from the same Latin verb, as does Spanish ~coger~. The simple verb ~legere~ kept both of its senses in Latin, which is why its French descendant ~lire~ means “to read” while the gathering sense lives on in the compound.

French has this Latin verb twice. The inherited form is ~cueillir~, which descended through Old French and became an everyday verb, while ~colliger~ was a later learned loan taken directly from Latin, so the two are doublets. ~Colliger~ stayed a formal word for gathering passages, facts or data in order to compile them. The root ~legere~ also gave ~élire~ and ~collection~, and the noun ~collecte~ comes from the Latin participle of ~colligere~. Compared with ~cueillir~, which picks flowers and fruit, ~colliger~ picks only texts and information.
en.colloquer:
There are two French verbs ~colloquer~, both learned borrowings from Latin. The first, the one that means “to place, to lodge someone,” comes from Latin ~collocāre~ (“to set in place”), built from ~con-~ and ~locāre~ (“to place”), itself from ~locus~ (“place”). It is a doublet of ~coucher~: the Latin verb was inherited into Old French and worn down into ~coucher~, then borrowed a second time in its learned, unaltered shape. Spanish ~colocar~ and Italian ~collocare~ descend from the same Latin verb, as does English ~collocate~.

The second ~colloquer~ comes from Latin ~colloquī~ (“to speak with, to converse”), a deponent verb formed from ~con-~ and ~loquī~ (“to speak”). The two verbs are accidental homonyms, one about placing and the other about talking, and they met only because Latin ~col-~ was the assimilated form of ~con-~ in both. The speaking verb belongs to a large family: ~loquī~ underlies French ~colloque~ (“conference, symposium”), ~locuteur~, ~élocution~, ~éloquent~ and ~loquace~, and English ~colloquy~. The placing verb shares its root with ~lieu~ and ~local~, which also go back to ~locus~.
en.colmater: ~Colmater~ is a denominal verb: French ~colmate~ (“land used for filling”) plus the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~colmate~ was borrowed from Italian ~colmata~ (“filled”), from the verb ~colmare~ (“to fill up”). English Wiktionary traces ~colmare~ to Latin ~cumulāre~ (“to heap up, fill”), related to ~cumulus~ (“a heap”). Italian ~colmare~ and Spanish and Portuguese ~colmar~ are cognates. The modern verb thus means to fill in a gap or plug a leak.
en.coloniser: Formed in French from ~colonie~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which makes verbs meaning “to turn into, to treat with, to provide with.” French Wiktionary adds that the verb may instead be borrowed from English ~colonize~, attested in 1622, so the exact path is uncertain. The base ~colonie~ goes back to Latin ~colōnia~, a settlement of ~colōnī~, and was used in Middle French from the fourteenth century. English Wiktionary notes that ~colonie~ is a doublet of ~Cologne~, the German city founded as a Roman colony.
en.colorer:
From Latin ~colorare~ (“to color, to give color to”), the verb formed on ~color~ (“color, hue, outward appearance”). The noun descends from Old Latin ~colōs~, from Proto-Italic *~kelōs~, from PIE *~ḱel-~ (“to cover, to conceal”) with the suffix *~-ōs~. Color, then, was first what covers a thing — its surface, its outward show. From that same root *~ḱel-~ come, through Latin, ~conceal~ and ~cell~ (a hidden chamber), and through Germanic, English ~hall~, ~hell~ (the covered-over place), ~hull~, and ~helmet~ — all things that cover or hide.

The link between “color” and “concealment” is the skin of appearances: the hue is the cover laid over the substance. French keeps ~colorer~ for giving or taking on color, often figuratively (a story ~coloré~ by emotion), and distinguishes it from ~colorier~, the later verb for filling in a drawing with crayons. Both descend from ~color~, alongside ~coloris~, ~coloration~, ~décolorer~, and ~incolore~. The borrowed cognate ~couleur~ travelled the popular route from the same ~color~. The étymon's quiet lesson is that color was understood as a veil — the visible covering through which we read what lies beneath.
en.colorier: ~Colorier~ is formed from the noun ~coloris~ and the verb ending ~-er~, meaning to apply color. The origin of ~coloris~ is explained in two ways. French Wiktionary sees either a derivative of ~colorer~ with the suffix ~-is~, or a noun taken from Italian ~colorito~ (“colored”) with the ending swapped. English Wiktionary prefers the Italian borrowing and gives the other as a surface analysis; it also relates the word to ~couleur~.
en.coloriser: ~Coloriser~ is a Frenchification of the English verb ~colorize~, which is used in the same sense: to add color to something originally in black and white, such as a film or a photograph. The ending ~-iser~ is the French counterpart of English ~-ize~, which share a Late Latin and Greek source. The French verb was therefore adapted from English rather than inherited or built on an older French base.
en.colporter:
From Latin ~comportāre~ (“to carry together, to bring to one place”), formed from ~com-~ (“with, together”) and ~portāre~ (“to carry”). That Latin verb gave French ~comporter~, whose meanings today differ from the one at hand, and ~colporter~ is a second, reshaped descendant of it. Other Romance verbs from ~portāre~ include Italian ~portare~ and Spanish ~portar~, so the Latin verb for carrying is alive across the family.

In Middle French the verb appears as ~colporter~, explained by French Wiktionary as ~porter à col~ (“to carry on the shoulders or around the neck”), a compound of ~col~ (“neck”) and ~porter~. According to French Wiktionary, the change of ~com-~ to ~col-~ served to keep ~comporter~ and ~colporter~ apart, and English Wiktionary likewise gives differentiation from ~comporter~ as the reason. The sources do not say whether the neck was in mind from the start or was a later reinterpretation. The French word ~col~ comes from Latin ~collum~, and ~portāre~ underlies many more verbs, among them ~porter~, ~apporter~, ~transporter~, ~importer~ and ~exporter~.
en.coltiner: The two Wiktionaries give related but different accounts of ~coltiner~. French Wiktionary derives it from ~coltin~, itself from ~col~ (“neck”). English Wiktionary derives it from ~colletin~ + ~-er~, where ~colletin~ is ~collet~ (“collar”) + ~-in~. Both routes lead to the family of ~col~, the neck. The suffix ~-er~ is the ordinary French ending that makes a verb from a noun, from Latin ~-are~.
en.combattre:
A French compound of the prefix ~com-~ (a form of ~con-~, here “with, against”) and the verb ~battre~ (“to beat, to strike”) — literally, to beat against one another. French ~battre~ descends from Latin ~battuere~ (“to beat, to strike”), a word the Romans seem to have borrowed from Gaulish; its further origin is debated, perhaps a Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰat-~ (“to strike”), with a possible Celtic cognate in Welsh ~bathu~ (“to beat, to coin”).

The compound was already in Old French (~combatre~), and its sense has scarcely budged: to fight, to do battle, and figuratively to oppose or strive against (one ~combats~ an idea, a disease, an injustice). The whole ~battuere~ family is a battlefield in itself: from it French draws ~combat~, ~combattant~, ~bataille~ (“battle,” via Late Latin ~battālia~), ~bataillon~, ~débattre~ (“to debate,” to beat back and forth), ~abattre~ (“to fell, to slaughter,” whence ~abattoir~), ~rabattre~, and the simple ~battre~ of beating eggs or hearts. English borrowed much of the same cluster — ~combat~, ~battle~, ~battalion~, ~debate~, ~abattoir~ — all of it ringing with the old sound of blows struck.
en.combiner:
From Late Latin ~combīnāre~ (“to join two by two, to pair”), formed from ~com-~ (“together”) and the distributive numeral ~bīnī~ (“two each, in pairs”). ~Bīnī~ comes from Proto-Italic *~dwiznos~, built on ~bis~ (“twice”) — both ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root for “two,” *~dwóh₁~. Cognate, through that root, with English ~binary~ and ~twin~, with Latin ~duo~, and with the Italian and Spanish doublets ~combinare~ and ~combinar~.

The verb's literal sense — “to set things two by two” — is still visible: to ~combiner~ is to bring elements together so they pair up and work as one. From the same ~bis~ / ~bīnī~ stock French inherited a whole numerical family: ~binaire~, ~combinaison~, ~combinatoire~, and the everyday ~combine~ (a scheme or trick) and ~combinard~ (a schemer). The English ~combine~ is the same Latin verb, borrowed; in farming, a “combine harvester” is so named because it combines several operations. What began as a precise Roman way of counting in twos thus widened into the general idea of joining, arranging, and contriving — and, less flatteringly, of cooking up a clever ~combine~.
en.combler:
From Latin ~cumulāre~ (“to heap up, pile, accumulate”), a denominative verb from ~cumulus~ (“a heap, mound”). The connection of ~cumulus~ to a PIE source (~perhaps~ *~ḱuh₁mós~) is marked as uncertain in the sources, so the deep root is best left open. The Latin noun ~cumulus~ survives untouched as the meteorologists' name for the heaped, piled-up cloud, and the learned family ~cumuler~ and ~accumuler~ comes straight from the Latin verb.

While those learned doublets kept the literal “heaping,” the inherited popular form ~combler~ traveled further. To heap something to the brim is to fill it completely, so ~combler~ came to mean “to fill up” — a ditch, a gap, a hole (one ~comble une lacune~). From filling to the brim it rose to the figurative sense of satisfying utterly: to ~combler~ someone is to fulfil their every wish, to shower them so fully that nothing is left wanting — ~comblé de bonheur~, “overflowing with happiness.” The noun ~comble~ (“the height, the summit, the very top”) preserves the original image of the heap piled as high as it will go.
en.commander:
From Old French ~comander~ (eleventh century), from Vulgar Latin *~commandare~, an alteration of Latin ~commendare~ (“to entrust, to commit to one's care”), formed from ~com-~ (intensive) + ~mandare~ (“to hand over, to charge with a task”). ~Mandare~ itself is usually traced to ~manus~ (“hand”) + ~dare~ (“to give”) — to “give into the hand.” The Romance cousins are everywhere: Italian ~comandare~, Spanish ~comandar~ and ~mandar~, and, by Norman transmission, English ~command~.

The semantic slide is striking. In classical Latin ~commendare~ leaned toward “to entrust, to recommend,” but in Late Latin and Old French it hardened into “to order, to have authority over”: what you place in someone's hand as a charge becomes what you impose on them as a command. French preserves both faces of the word — ~commander~ a soldier is to give an order, while ~commander~ a meal is to place one's request, the older sense of “committing a task” still visible at the table. Kin from the same root crowd the language: ~commande~, ~commandement~, ~commandant~, ~recommander~, and, directly from ~mandare~, ~mander~, ~mandat~, and ~demander~.
en.commanditer: Formed from the noun ~commandite~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~: to finance or sponsor a venture, or to commission it. The noun ~commandite~ comes from Italian ~accomandita~, itself from ~accomandare~ (“to entrust”). French Wiktionary notes a misdivision: the article attached itself to the Italian word and was then cut in the wrong place, which is how the initial ~a-~ was lost. So a word for entrusting money to someone passed through Italian commerce before settling into French.
en.commencer:
From Old French ~comencier~ (“to begin”), from Vulgar Latin *~cominitiāre~, from ~com-~ (an intensive of ~cum~, “with, together”) + ~initiāre~ (“to initiate, begin”), from ~initium~ (“a beginning, entrance”), itself from ~inīre~ (“to go in,” ~in-~ + ~īre~, “to go”). Cognate with Italian ~cominciare~, Spanish ~comenzar~, and Portuguese ~começar~; English ~commence~ was borrowed from the Old French verb.

The sense traces back to a literal act of entering: ~initium~ is the going-in, the threshold of a thing, and to ~initiāre~ was to set someone or something on its way — in religion, to admit to the rites (hence English ~initiation~). Vulgar Latin reinforced it with ~com-~ and reshaped it as *~cominitiāre~, simply “to begin.” From the same ~īre~ (“to go,” PIE *~ey-~) French draws a surprising scatter of words once you trace the path — ~initial~, ~initier~, ~initiative~ — and ~īre~ itself underlies ~issue~ (“a going out”) and the future stems of ~aller~. ~Recommencer~ (“to begin again”) layers ~re-~ on top, while the noun ~commencement~ names the start that ~commencer~ performs.
en.commenter:
From Latin ~commentari~ (“to consider thoroughly, to discuss, to interpret”), a deponent verb tied to ~commentus~, past participle of ~comminisci~ (“to contrive, to devise”), formed from ~com-~ (intensive) and a verb on the root of ~mens~ (“mind”). The ultimate source is Proto-Indo-European *~men-~ (“to think”) — one of the most prolific of all roots. Through it ~commenter~ is kin to English ~mind~, ~mental~, and ~mention~, to Latin ~memini~ (“I remember”), and, more remotely, to a vast family of words about thought and memory.

Latin ~commentari~ meant to think a thing over fully and then to expound it, and that double motion — to ponder, then to explain — survives in French: to ~commenter~ a text is to annotate and interpret it, while to ~commenter~ a match is to provide a running spoken account. The internet sense, leaving a ~commentaire~ under a post, is only the newest layer over this very old idea of remarking upon. From the same ~men-~ root French gathers ~commentaire~, ~mental~, ~mention~, ~réminiscence~, and ~mémoire~ — a whole vocabulary of the thinking mind grown from one syllable.
en.commercer: Formed in French from the noun ~commerce~ and the verb-forming ending ~-er~, and attested in Middle French. The noun was borrowed from Latin ~commercium~ (“trade, dealings”), itself built from ~com-~ (“together”) and ~merx~ (“goods, wares”). The verb therefore means, at heart, to deal in wares with others. It is intransitive and now somewhat literary: one ~commerce~ with someone, in the old sense of keeping company or doing business with them, whereas modern speech prefers ~faire du commerce~. The ending ~-er~ is the ordinary one for turning a noun into a first-conjugation verb.
en.commercialiser:
Derived from the adjective ~commercial~ plus the suffix ~-iser~, which forms verbs of “making into” something. ~Commercial~ rests on ~commerce~, borrowed from Latin ~commercium~ (“trade, traffic in goods”), from ~com-~ (“together”) + ~merx~ (“merchandise, wares”). The ultimate origin of ~merx~ is uncertain: De Vaan suspects an Etruscan source, linking it to the god-name ~Mercurius~, while more recent proposals reconstruct an Indo-European root — none of these accounts is settled. The same ~merx~ family gave English ~merchant~, ~commerce~, and ~market~.

~Commercialiser~ is a 19th- and 20th-century coinage, born when economies needed a word for turning a thing into an object of trade — bringing a product to market, putting it on sale. It can carry a faint pejorative edge, the sense of cheapening something by making it for profit, as when one speaks of having « commercialisé » a holiday or a tradition. Around it cluster ~commercialisation~, ~commercialisable~, and the negatives ~incommercialisable~ and ~précommercialiser~. Through the disputed but vivid ~Mercurius~ connection, the patron of merchants and messengers hovers — by one account — behind every act of bringing wares to the marketplace.
en.commettre:
From Latin ~committere~ (“to bring together, to join, to entrust, to perpetrate”), compounded from ~com-~ (“together, with”) and ~mittere~ (“to send, to let go, to throw”). Latin ~mittere~ goes back to a Proto-Indo-European root reconstructed as *~meit-~ (“to exchange, to remove”), whose sense shifted from “exchange, give” to “let go, send.” The Old French ~commetre~ inherited both branches of meaning. English ~commit~ is the learned borrowing of the same ~committere~, and Italian ~commettere~ and Spanish ~cometer~ are direct cognates.

The two faces of ~commettre~ trace back to ~com-~ + ~mittere~: from “to send together, to entrust” come the senses of appointing or charging someone with a task, while from a darker sense of “to bring about” comes the modern, dominant meaning — to ~commettre~ a crime, an error, a sin. The shared root ~mittere~ seeds an enormous French vocabulary: ~mettre~ itself, plus ~admettre~, ~permettre~, ~promettre~, ~soumettre~, ~transmettre~, ~mission~, ~message~, and ~messe~ (the Mass, from the dismissal ~ite, missa est~). The administrative offspring of ~committere~ proper — ~commis~, ~commissaire~, ~commission~, ~commissure~ — preserve the older idea of someone or something entrusted and brought together.
en.commissionner: Formed from the noun ~commission~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to give a commission to, to appoint or entrust with a task.” The noun was borrowed from Latin ~commissiō~, and the ~-er~ ending turns it into a first-conjugation verb in the usual way for a noun of this kind. It is used in commercial and administrative contexts, for instance of an agent paid by commission.
en.commotionner: Formed from the noun ~commotion~ with the verbal ending ~-er~: “to give a shock, to concuss.” French Wiktionary gives no more than that, and the noun ~commotion~ comes from Latin ~commotio~ (“agitation”), related to ~commovere~ (“to shake up”). The verb is most at home in the participle, ~commotionné~, said of someone shaken by a blow or by bad news.
en.commuer:
From Middle French ~commuer~, itself from Latin ~commūtāre~ (“to change, to alter”), a compound of ~com-~ (“thoroughly”) and ~mūtāre~ (“to change”). The French form was shaped under the influence of ~muer~, the inherited verb from ~mūtāre~, which explains the ending ~-uer~. So ~commuer~ is a learned verb whose final shape was pulled toward a native one, and it sits beside ~muer~ as a close relative rather than a plain descendant of the Latin verb alone.

In modern French it is a legal word, used mainly of a sentence: ~commuer une peine~ means to replace a penalty with a lighter one. English ~commute~ comes from the same Latin source and has the same legal use in “to commute a sentence.” The Latin root ~mūtāre~ also underlies ~muer~ (“to molt, to change”), ~mutation~, ~commutation~, ~commutateur~, ~permuter~ and ~transmuer~, a family of verbs and nouns all built around the idea of change.
en.communaliser: ~Communaliser~ is formed from the adjective ~communal~ with the suffix ~-iser~, “to make A”: to make communal, or to place under a commune. ~Communal~ is itself derived from ~commun~ with the suffix ~-al~, and by another account is a learned borrowing from Late Latin ~commūnālis~, from Latin ~commūnis~ (“common”), the source of ~commun~. The suffix ~-iser~ descends from Late Latin ~-izāre~.
en.communier:
Borrowed, according to the TLFi, from Ecclesiastical Latin ~commūnicāre~. It is therefore a learned word taken from the language of the Church, not one inherited through Old French. The Latin verb meant “to share, to make common” and is built on the adjective ~commūnis~ (“common”). English ~communicate~ comes from the same Latin verb, so the idea of making something common runs through all three languages.

French borrowed the same Latin verb a second time, later, as ~communiquer~, so ~communier~ and ~communiquer~ are doublets. In modern French, ~communier~ is tied to the Church and to receiving the Eucharist, while ~communiquer~ means passing on news or information. Both keep the idea of something held in common, as do ~commun~, ~communion~ and ~communauté~, all of which go back to ~commūnis~.
en.communiquer:
From Latin ~communicare~ (“to share, to make common, to impart”), the verb of ~communis~ (“common, shared by all”). ~communis~ is usually analysed as a Proto-Italic compound *~kom-moin-i-~, from *~kom-~ (“together”) plus a form of the Proto-Indo-European root *~mey-~ (“to change, to exchange”), the same root behind Latin ~munus~ (“duty, gift, public office”) and ~mutuus~ (“reciprocal”). It is a learned doublet of French ~communier~ (“to take communion”), which descends from the same Latin verb by the ordinary popular route. Cognate in sense with English ~common~ and ~mutual~, and with Gothic ~gamains~ (“common”).

In Latin, to ~communicare~ was to put something into the common stock — to share a meal, a duty, or a piece of news. French inherited both the sacred branch, where what is shared is the Eucharist (~communier~), and the secular branch, where what is shared is information (~communiquer~). The modern explosion of senses — to transmit, to connect, to get a message across — grew naturally from that core idea of holding something in common. The same root *~mey-~ feeds a large French family: ~commun~, ~communauté~, ~communisme~, ~communication~, ~municipal~, and ~immunité~, this last literally an exemption from the shared ~munus~, the public duty owed to the city.
en.commuter: A learned borrowing from Latin ~commūtāre~ (“to exchange, to change completely”), which is built on ~mutāre~ (“to change”) with an intensive ~com-~. French holds two forms of this one verb, ~commuter~ and its doublet ~commuer~. English ~commute~ comes from the same Latin verb, and so is a cognate. The Latin sense of exchange explains the two uses glossed here: to switch one thing for another, and to commute a sentence, that is, to replace a penalty by a lighter one. The root ~mutāre~ is behind many French words, among them ~muer~, ~mutation~, ~permuter~, ~transmuer~ and the noun ~commutation~. The doublet ~commuer~ is a small reminder that the same Latin word can reach French in two forms.
en.commémorer:
French ~commémorer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~commemorāre~ (“to recall, to remember”), formed from ~com-~ (an intensifying prefix, “thoroughly, together”) and ~memorāre~ (“to bring to mind, to mention”). That verb comes from the adjective ~memor~ (“mindful, remembering”), which belongs to a large Indo-European family of words about remembering, generally traced to a root *~(s)mer-~. English has taken the same Latin verb directly as ~commemorate~, and also the noun ~memory~ through Old French. The Romance languages kept the learned verb in parallel forms, such as Italian ~commemorare~ and Spanish ~conmemorar~.

In Latin, ~commemorāre~ meant both to call something back to one's own mind and to remind others of it, and the second sense is the one that matters in French: to recall a person or an event publicly, by a ceremony or a monument. A ~commémoration~ is therefore a shared act of memory, as when a country marks an anniversary or a church marks a saint's day. The verb belongs to a lively family of French words built on the same Latin base, among them ~mémoire~, ~mémorable~, ~mémorial~ and ~remémorer~ (“to call to mind again”). The cluster shows how the idea of remembering was reshaped by the learned vocabulary of Latin: the everyday French ~se souvenir~ comes from another route, while the formal words for memory, from ~mémorial~ to ~commémorer~, all keep the Latin ~mem-~ intact.
en.compacter: ~Compacter~ is a plain formation on the adjective ~compact~ (“dense, closely packed”) with the verbal suffix ~-er~: to compact something is to make it compact. The adjective ~compact~ is itself a learned word, generally traced to the Latin ~compactus~, a participle of the verb ~compingere~ (“to join together”). The verb is thus a French coinage built on a Latin-derived adjective, not an inherited Latin verb.
en.comparaître: ~Comparaître~ is a remaking, on the model of ~paraître~, of the older verb ~comparoir~, which came from Latin ~comparēre~ (“to appear, to be visible”), built on ~pārēre~ with the prefix ~con-~ (“with, together”). Its base ~paraître~ goes back to Vulgar Latin *~parēscere~, an inchoative (“begin to…”) verb formed on ~pārēre~. So the prefix was already in the Latin verb rather than freshly added in French. The sense narrowed to the legal one, “to appear in person before a judge,” as in ~comparaître devant le tribunal~.
en.comparer:
From Latin ~comparāre~ (“to pair, to match, to set side by side”), a compound of ~com-~ (“together, with”) and ~parāre~ (“to make ready, to furnish”), and closely tied to ~pār~ (“equal, a pair”). ~Parāre~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“to produce, to procure, to bring forth”). Cognate through ~parāre~ with Italian ~comparare~ and Spanish ~comparar~, and through ~pār~ with English ~pair~ and ~peer~.

The original image is one of pairing: to ~comparāre~ was to bring two things together as a matched set, and from that act of setting equals beside each other grew the modern sense of weighing one against another. The kinship with ~pār~ keeps that idea of equality alive — a comparison still implies things placed on a level. From ~parāre~ French draws a remarkably broad family: ~préparer~ (“to make ready beforehand”), ~réparer~ (“to set right again”), ~séparer~ (“to make ready apart”), and ~parer~ itself, while ~pār~ yields ~pair~, ~paire~, ~pareil~, and ~comparaison~. Behind all of them lies the same quiet idea of furnishing, matching, and bringing things into order.
en.comparoir:
From Latin ~comparere~ (“to appear, to present oneself”), a compound of ~com-~ (“with, fully”) and ~parēre~ (“to appear, to be visible”). French ~comparoir~ is a doublet of ~comparaître~: both go back to the same Latin verb. In French it is a term of law, meaning “to appear before a judge.” It must not be confused with ~comparer~ (“to compare”), which comes from a different Latin verb, ~comparāre~.

The root of ~parēre~ stands behind many French words: ~paraître~, ~apparaître~ and ~disparaître~, along with ~apparition~ and ~transparent~. Spanish ~comparecer~ and Italian ~comparire~ are close cousins of the verb, and English ~appear~ comes from the same Latin family by way of Old French. The everyday verb for showing up in court today is ~comparaître~, while ~comparoir~ survives as a legal archaism, a fossil of an older form of the same word.
en.compartimenter: Formed from ~compartiment~ (“compartment”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so ~compartimenter~ is “to divide into compartments,” literally or figuratively, as when work or ideas are kept apart. The base ~compartiment~ was borrowed from Italian ~compartimento~, which derives from the verb ~compartire~ (“to divide, to share out”). English ~compartment~ comes from the same Italian word, by way of French.
en.compasser: Formed from ~passer~ with the prefix ~con-~, after Medieval Latin ~compassāre~ (“to measure with steps”). The base ~passer~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~passāre~ (“to step”), from Latin ~passus~ (“step, pace”). The prefix ~con-~ is Latin for “with, together”. ~Compasser~ originally meant to measure by pacing, and later by the compass that took the same name, hence the sense of planning and regulating something carefully. The noun ~compas~ belongs to the same family.
en.compatir:
Borrowed from Latin ~compati~ (“to suffer with”), formed from ~con-~ (“with”) and ~patior~ (“to suffer”). French adapted it as a fourth-conjugation verb in ~-ir~, as it did with the related ~pâtir~. French Wiktionary points to ~sympathiser~ as a sister word, built on a Greek model with the same meaning of “feeling with.”

The sense stayed close to its source. To ~compatir~ is to share in someone's pain, usually followed by ~à~, as in ~compatir à la douleur de quelqu'un~. The Latin ~patior~ is the root of a large family: ~patient~, ~passion~, ~pâtir~ and ~compassion~, which is the noun that most directly mirrors ~compatir~. English ~compassion~ and ~passive~ come from the same source. The word is a small lesson in how Latin ~con-~ (“with”) turns an experience into a shared one.
en.compenser:
From Latin ~compēnsāre~ (“to weigh together, to counterbalance”), formed from ~com-~ (“together”) and ~pēnsāre~, the frequentative of ~pendere~ (“to weigh, to pay”). ~Pendere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~pendō~ and PIE *~(s)pend-~ (“to pull, to stretch, to spin”). Through that root it is cognate with English ~spin~ and ~span~, the thread first being stretched, then weighed.

The metaphor is a balance scale: to ~compenser~ is to set one weight against another until the pans level out — hence “to offset, to make up for” a loss. The ~pendere~ family is unusually rich because weighing and paying were the same act when coins were weighed out: from it French drew ~peser~ (“to weigh”), ~penser~ (“to think,” to weigh things in the mind), ~dépenser~, ~dispenser~, ~pension~, and ~poids~ (“weight”). ~Compensation~ and ~compensatoire~ round out the immediate family.
en.compiler: Borrowed from Latin ~compīlāre~. In classical Latin the verb meant to plunder or to snatch up and carry off, and only later, in Late and Medieval Latin, did it come to mean gathering written material from various sources into a single work, which is the sense French has had since the Middle Ages. Its deeper origin is uncertain. The twentieth century gave it a new life in computing, where English ~compile~ and the noun ~compiler~ named the program that translates source code, and French took that sense back. Spanish ~compilar~, Italian ~compilare~ and English ~compile~ share the Latin source.
en.compisser: Formed from ~pisser~ with the prefix ~com-~, giving “to urinate on.” The prefix comes from Latin ~com-~ (“with, together”) and here reads as an intensive, “all over.” The base ~pisser~ comes from Middle French and Old French ~pissier~, from a Vulgar Latin form *~pīssiāre~. Its origin is uncertain, and French Wiktionary calls it an onomatopoeia. Related forms include Italian ~pisciare~, English ~piss~ and German ~pissen~.
en.complaire: Borrowed into Middle French from Latin ~complacēre~, which by surface analysis is ~com-~ (an intensive prefix) + ~plaire~, the Latin ancestor of which is ~placēre~ (“to please”). Today the verb survives mostly in the reflexive ~se complaire dans~ (“to take pleasure in, to wallow in”), where one pleases oneself. The same root gives French ~plaire~, ~complaisant~ and ~complaisance~.
en.complexer: Formed from the noun ~complexe~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, so ~complexer~ means to give someone a complex, to make them feel insecure. ~Complexe~ comes from Latin ~complexus~, the past participle of ~complecti~ (“to embrace, to encompass”), whose sense developed toward “made of different, interlocking elements”. The psychological sense of the noun, as in an inferiority complex, was borrowed from German ~Komplex~.
en.complexifier: Formed from ~complexe~ + ~-ifier~, “to make complex.” The adjective is a learned borrowing from Latin ~complexus~, the past participle of ~complecti~ (“to embrace”), whose sense moved toward “made of different interlocked elements.” The suffix ~-ifier~ goes back to Latin ~-ificāre~, itself built on ~facere~ (“to make”), and it still forms learned and technical verbs from adjectives, as in ~intensifier~ and ~densifier~. The word thus means, almost literally, “to make intertwined.”
en.complimenter: ~Complimenter~ is formed from ~compliment~ and the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense of paying someone a compliment. Its first attestation is from 1634, in a work by Marie de Gournay, where it is presented as a neologism, so her readers were meant to take it for a fresh coinage. The verb is thus a young word beside its noun. Today it is an ordinary verb, used to praise or congratulate someone, as in complimenter quelqu'un sur sa réussite, and it has long since lost its air of novelty.
en.compliquer:
From Latin ~complicāre~ (“to fold together, to roll up”), formed from the prefix ~com-~ (“together”) and ~plicāre~ (“to fold”). ~plicāre~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~plek-~ (“to plait, to fold”), shared with Greek ~plékein~ (“to braid”) and, by way of Germanic, with English ~fold~ and ~ply~. French took ~compliquer~ as a learned borrowing, which kept it close to its Latin shape.

The original picture is physical: things folded over one another until they tangle. From that, ~compliquer~ moved naturally to the abstract sense of entangling a matter, multiplying its parts and difficulties — the literal “folded-together” becoming the figurative “involved, intricate.” English preserves the same image in ~complicate~ and in the doublet ~complice~/~accomplice~, a partner “folded in” to a plot. ~complicāre~ belongs to the broad *~plek-~ family that runs through French on the stem ~plicāre~: alongside ~compliqué~ (“complicated”) and ~complication~ stand ~appliquer~, ~impliquer~, ~expliquer~ (to “unfold,” hence to make clear), ~répliquer~, ~plier~, ~pli~, and ~ployer~. So to ~compliquer~ something and to ~expliquer~ it are exact opposites in their root image — folding together versus folding open.
en.comploter: ~Comploter~ is formed from the noun ~complot~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~: to hatch a plot.
