From Middle French ~contaminer~, from Old French ~contaminer~, borrowed from Latin ~contāmināre~ (“to bring into contact, to defile”). The Latin word's own origin is obscure. By one account it is ~cum~ (“with”) plus a form tied to ~tangere~ (“to touch”), through a hypothetical *~taminare~ and an equally hypothetical noun *~tamen~ (“impure contact”), perhaps once a religious term. Ancient writers already disagreed, and some took it as ~cum~ plus a verb ~taminare~ (“to soil”). Another dispute concerns ~contamen~: Ernout and Meillet judge it probably a late back-formation from ~contaminare~, not its source. French ~entamer~ is often set beside it. The verb ~tangere~ itself also gave ~tangible~ and ~tangente~, while the common verb for touching, ~toucher~, comes instead from an imitative *~toccare~.

In French the verb is attested from the 12th century, cited in ~Li Fet des Romains~ (dated 1213 or 1215), in the sense “to defile by impure contact.” It fell out of use in the 17th century, and Furetière already called it old. In 1863 medicine took it up again, and it entered everyday language, displacing ~contagionner~ (from ~contagion~). The Latin verb could also mean, in a literary sense, “to make unrecognizable by mixing,” a use that still echoes in the figurative ~contaminer~. Related French words include ~contamination~, ~décontaminer~ and ~contact~.
en.contempler: ~Contempler~ is borrowed from Latin ~contemplārī~ (“to observe, to look at attentively”). The Latin verb is traditionally explained as ~con-~ plus ~templum~, the space of sky or ground that an augur marked out to watch for omens, so that to contemplate meant first to observe within that consecrated space. The sense then widened to any steady, reverent gaze, and in religious and philosophical French to silent meditation on the divine. The same ~templum~ gave French ~temple~, and English ~contemplate~ is a direct borrowing of the Latin verb.
en.conteneuriser: Formed from ~conteneur~ and the suffix ~-iser~, so “to convert to containers.” The noun ~conteneur~ was built from ~contenir~ (“to contain”) plus ~-eur~, as a way of gallicizing the English ~container~, which at first meant simply a thing that contains before taking its specific shipping sense. The suffix ~-iser~, from Late Latin ~-izāre~, makes verbs meaning “to make A” or “to convert into N.” The verb ~conteneuriser~ thus means to organize freight transport around standardized containers.
en.contenir:
From Latin ~continēre~ (“to hold together, to keep within, to contain”), ~com-~ (“together”) + ~tenēre~ (“to hold”). ~Tenēre~ is a stative verb from PIE *~ten-~ (“to stretch, to draw taut”) — to hold being conceived as keeping something under tension. The root reaches across Indo-European to Greek ~teínō~ (“I stretch”), Sanskrit ~tanóti~ (“he stretches”), and English ~thin~ (stretched out). Through Old French, ~continēre~ gave the modern ~contenir~; Italian ~contenere~ and Spanish ~contener~ are cognates.

The image of “holding together” unfolds in every modern sense. A vessel ~contient~ a liquid (holds it within); a hall ~contient~ a thousand people (takes them in); and figuratively one ~contient~ one's anger or a crowd (holds it back, restrains it) — hence the noun ~contenance~ (“composure,” the holding-together of one's bearing). What is held inside is the ~contenu~ (“contents”), and the thing that holds it is the ~contenant~ (“container”). The vast *~ten-~ family runs through French ~tenir~, ~contenir~, ~retenir~ (“to hold back”), ~maintenir~ (“to hold in the hand, to maintain”), ~soutenir~ (“to hold up, to support”), ~obtenir~, ~continu~ (“continuous”), and ~teneur~ — and, more distantly, ~tendre~ (“to stretch”) and ~tension~.
en.contenter:
From the French adjective ~content~ (“satisfied, pleased”), with the verbal suffix ~-er~. ~Content~ comes from Latin ~contentus~ (“contained, satisfied”), the past participle of ~continēre~ (“to hold together, to contain”), from ~con-~ (“together”) and ~tenēre~ (“to hold”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). Cognate, through *~ten-~, with English ~thin~ and ~tend~.

The metaphor is quietly beautiful: to be ~content~ is to be “contained,” held within bounds — desire kept from stretching past what one has. To ~contenter~ someone is therefore to hold their wishes inside a satisfying limit. The same ~tenēre~ gave French a great clan of holding-verbs and nouns: ~tenir~, ~contenir~, ~retenir~, ~maintenir~, ~obtenir~, ~contenu~, ~teneur~, and ~contenance~. The deeper PIE sense of “stretching” surfaces elsewhere too, in ~tendre~, ~tension~, and ~tente~ (a “stretched” canvas). So a contented person is, etymologically, one whose wants stay neatly held together rather than stretched thin.
en.conter:
Inherited from Old French ~conter~, from Latin ~computāre~ (“to calculate, to reckon, to count up”), built from ~com-~ (“together”) and ~putāre~ (“to reckon, to think”). It is the same word as French ~compter~, which is a learned respelling that appeared in the thirteenth century and took over the sense of “to calculate.” The two words are therefore doublets, and English ~count~, ~compute~ and ~account~ belong to the same family.

The shift from “to count” to “to tell” happened through the idea of enumerating: to go through the facts one by one, a story being a list of events set in order. English shows the same shift, since ~tell~ once meant “to count,” which survives in ~bank teller~ and in ~to tell the beads~, and German ~erzählen~ (“to tell”) is built on ~zählen~ (“to count”). In French the verb ~conter~ settled in the sense of “to relate a story,” with ~raconter~ as its prefixed, everyday form. Related words include ~conte~ (“tale”), ~conteur~, ~raconter~, ~compte~, ~décompte~ and ~comptable~. The old phrase ~en conter à quelqu'un~ is a trace of the meaning “to tell tall tales.”
en.contester:
From Latin ~contestārī~ (“to call to witness, to begin a lawsuit by calling witnesses”), from ~con-~ (“together”) and ~testārī~ (“to bear witness”), itself from ~testis~ (“witness”). Latin ~testis~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~tristos~ and ultimately to a PIE compound *~tristh₂s~, literally “a third party standing by” — from *~tréyes~ (“three”) and *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”), the disinterested third person who stands present at a dispute. Cognate descendants include Spanish ~contestar~, Italian ~contestare~ and English ~contest~; the same ~testis~ gave English ~testify~ and ~testament~.

The original legal scene is precise: to ~contester~ a suit was to open it formally before witnesses, both sides calling on others to attest the facts. From that courtroom setting the word drifted toward the adversarial heart of the proceeding — the clash of claims — and so came to mean “to dispute, to challenge, to call into question.” Modern French keeps the contentious sense in ~contestation~, ~contestable~ and ~contestataire~ (“protester”). It is a neat etymological irony that a verb now meaning “to challenge” began with the calm, sworn presence of a neutral onlooker.
en.contingenter: Formed from the noun ~contingent~ with the verb ending ~-er~. In the sense of a share or quota, ~contingent~ gave a verb meaning “to assign a quota to,” hence “to restrict by quota.” The base was borrowed from Latin ~contingentem~, the present participle of ~contingere~ (“to touch”), literally “touching,” which in Latin could also mean “to fall to one's lot.”
en.continuer:
From Latin ~continuāre~ (“to join together, to make continuous, to prolong”), derived from ~continuus~ (“uninterrupted, connected”), itself from ~continēre~ (“to hold together”). ~Continēre~ is ~con-~ (“together”) plus ~tenēre~ (“to hold”), which descends from PIE *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). Through that root ~continuer~ is cognate with English ~thin~, ~tend~, and ~tenant~, and with Greek ~teínein~ (“to stretch”).

The link between “stretch” and “hold” lies in the idea of keeping something taut and unbroken: a continuous thing is one stretched out without a gap. From ~tenēre~ French inherited ~tenir~ and a great clan of relatives — ~contenir~, ~maintenir~, ~retenir~, ~soutenir~, ~obtenir~ — while ~continuus~ yields ~continu~, ~continuel~, ~continuité~, and the adverb ~continûment~. The same PIE root, by way of the “stretching” sense, also gives ~tension~, ~tendre~, and ~tendon~. So when one ~continue~ a task, one is, in the deep logic of the word, holding its thread stretched taut so that it does not snap — keeping the line unbroken from one moment to the next.
en.contorsionner: Formed from ~contorsion~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~ (from Latin ~-are~). The noun ~contorsion~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~contortio~, so the verb is a French coinage on a Latin-derived noun. It means to twist something, or oneself, into a strained shape.
en.contourner:
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *~contornāre~, formed from ~cum~ (“with, around”) and ~tornāre~ (“to turn, to round off on a lathe”). The Latin verb ~tornāre~ comes from the noun ~tornus~ (“lathe”), borrowed from Greek ~τόρνος~ (~tórnos~, “a tool for drawing a circle”), so the verb comes from the craftsman's lathe. French also reads the verb as a prefixed formation, ~con-~ plus ~tourner~. Italian has ~contornare~ and the noun ~contorno~, and English ~contour~ came from the Italian noun through French.

In modern French, ~contourner~ is very common in the sense of going around something instead of through it, and it has figurative senses: to bypass an obstacle, to sidestep a difficulty or evade a rule, as in ~contourner la loi~ (“to circumvent the law”). The family also includes ~tourner~ itself, ~tour~, ~détour~ and ~détourner~, all descended from the lathe's turn.
en.contracter:
A learned word built on the stem of Latin ~contractus~, the past participle of ~contrahere~ (“to draw together”), itself made of ~con-~ (“with, together”) and ~trahere~ (“to pull, to drag, to draw toward oneself”). The Latin verb ~trahere~ is reconstructed from Proto-Indo-European *~tragʰ-~ (“to draw”) and left many French offspring: the inherited ~traire~ (“to milk”), ~train~, ~trait~ and ~traîner~, and learned relatives such as ~tracter~ and ~attraction~. Italian ~contrarre~ and Spanish ~contraer~ are inherited from ~contrahere~, whereas French ~contracter~ is a later learned coinage. English ~contract~ and ~tract~ come from the same Latin family.

The interest of the verb lies in how many things one can “draw together”. ~Contrahere~ passed from “to gather, to bind” to “to ally, to form an alliance,” then to “to make a transaction, to conclude a contract”, which is why the noun ~contrat~, from ~contractus~, sits so close to it. French ~contracter~ keeps all these threads: a muscle is drawn together, a debt or an obligation is taken on by binding oneself, and an illness is caught. The sense of shrinking explains the noun ~contraction~ of childbirth and of grammar, where two words are drawn into one. Behind these uses lies a single gesture, that of pulling something closer.
en.contractualiser: ~Contractualiser~ is the adjective ~contractuel~ + the suffix ~-iser~, “to make contractual, to put under contract.” The base ~contractuel~ is explained in one source as Latin ~contractus~ (“contract”) + ~-el~ and in the other as ~contrat~ + ~-el~. The suffix ~-iser~ makes a verb meaning “to render A.” It is a modern administrative and legal coinage.
en.contraindre:
From Old French ~constreindre~, from Latin ~constringere~ (“to bind together, to fetter, to compress”), formed from ~com-~ (“together”) and ~stringere~ (“to draw tight, to bind”). ~stringere~ traces to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “to stroke, to press, to draw tight,” and gives English ~strain~, ~strict~, ~stress~, and even ~strangle~, plus Italian ~costringere~ and English ~constrain~ directly from the same Latin verb.

The physical image is one of tying tightly: to constrain someone was to bind them so they could not move freely. From that the verb passed to the figurative — to compel, to force a hand, to leave no choice. French keeps the family of ~-stringere~ verbs unusually intact, each with its own prefix and its own narrowed sense: ~étreindre~ (to embrace, to clutch), ~astreindre~ (to subject to an obligation), ~restreindre~ (to restrict), and ~contraindre~ (to compel) — a neat set of bindings loosened and tightened by their prefixes. The learned doublets ~constriction~ and ~constricteur~ (as in the snake) come from the same root by the bookish route. So when something is ~contraignant~, the word still whispers its origin: it is, quite literally, something that binds you tight.
en.contrarier: ~Contrarier~ comes from Old French ~contrarier~, itself from Latin ~contrāriāre~ (“to oppose”), a verb formed on the adjective ~contrārius~ (“opposite, contrary”), from the preposition ~contrā~ (“against”). It is not a verb built on ~contrariété~: the noun ~contrariété~ comes from Latin ~contrārietās~ (“opposition”), so the noun and the verb are cousins rather than parent and child. The original sense was “to oppose, to thwart,” as in ~contrarier un projet~ (“to hinder a plan”). In everyday French, the verb weakened to “to annoy, to upset” (~ça me contrarie~), often of a mild frustration.
en.contraster: The sources disagree slightly. French Wiktionary derives the verb from the noun ~contraste~, which was borrowed from Italian ~contrasto~, itself drawn from ~contrastare~ and ultimately Latin ~contrā~ + ~stāre~ (“to stand against”). English Wiktionary instead derives the verb directly from Latin ~contrāstāre~ (“to resist, to withstand”). Both routes end at the same Latin pair: ~contrā~ (“against”) and ~stāre~ (“to stand”). To ~contraster~ is thus to stand opposite something, and so to differ sharply from it. The noun ~contraste~ is the more familiar half of the pair.
en.contre-attaquer: Formed from ~attaquer~ with the prefix ~contre-~ (“against, counter-”), from Latin ~contra~. The base was borrowed into French in 1549 from Italian ~attaccare~ (“to attach, to join, to assail”), which first meant “to fasten” and gained its military sense from the phrase ~attaccare battaglia~ (“to join battle”). The prefix is the same one in ~contre-indiquer~ and ~contresigner~, and English ~counter-~ is its cousin through Old French.
en.contre-indiquer: Formed from the verb ~indiquer~ with the prefix ~contre-~, which expresses opposition: to ~contre-indiquer~ is to indicate that something should not be done, typically a treatment. The prefix comes from Latin ~contra~ (“against”). The base ~indiquer~ is from Latin ~indicāre~ (“to point out, to make known”), formed on ~index~ (“pointer”), from the root of ~dīcere~ (“to say”). The verb is the counterpart of ~indiquer~, and the noun ~contre-indication~ is built the same way.
en.contre-manifester: Formed from ~contre-~ (“against”) and ~manifester~ (“to demonstrate”), or possibly as a back-formation from ~contre-manifestation~, ~contre-manifester~ means to take part in a counter-demonstration. No dictionary gives a dated etymology. The Académie records it as intransitive, and an example is found in Henri Jeanson's memoir of 1971, where he writes that he and a few friends were counter-demonstrating. The 1990 reform spelling is ~contremanifester~.
en.contre-passer: ~Contre-passer~ is formed from the prefix ~contre-~ and the verb ~passer~. The prefix comes from Latin ~contra~ (“facing, against”), attested in Old French as ~cuntre~ around 1100. The verb has an accounting sense, to cancel an entry by one of the same amount and opposite direction, and an older sense of transferring a sum from one merchant's books to another's. French Wiktionary treats it as a variant spelling of ~contrepasser~, the form of the 1990 spelling reform.
en.contre-tirer: Formed from ~contre-~ (“against, counter-”) and ~tirer~. The TLFi dates the verb to 1576 in the sense “to represent, to reproduce.” In 1690 it appears as a printing term: to pull a counterproof by taking a second impression from a freshly printed proof. The TLFi explains ~tirer~ here as “to trace, to reproduce,” whence “to print, to make a proof.” The hyphenated spelling is the variant of ~contretirer~ that follows the 1990 spelling reform.
en.contrebalancer: Formed from ~balancer~ and the prefix ~contre-~ (“against,” from Latin ~contra~), here in its sense of counterweight or compensation: to set one weight against another. ~Balancer~ derives from the noun ~balance~, inherited through Old French from Vulgar Latin ~bilancia~ and Latin ~bilanx~, a compound of ~bi-~ (“twice”) and ~lanx~ (“plate, pan”): a scale with two pans. The same Latin word gave French ~bilan~.
en.contrebattre: ~Contrebattre~ is formed from ~battre~ and the prefix ~contre-~, which expresses opposition: to beat back, to counter. The prefix comes from Latin ~contra~ (“against”). The base ~battre~ descends from Latin ~battuere~ (“to beat, to strike”), a verb probably borrowed from Gaulish, which also gave Italian ~battere~ and, through French, English ~battle~. The same base underlies ~combattre~, ~débattre~ and ~abattre~.
en.contrebraquer: ~Contrebraquer~ is formed from ~braquer~ with the prefix ~contre-~ (from Latin ~contra~, “against”): to turn the steering wheel against the direction of a skid or turn, in other words to countersteer. The base ~braquer~ has an uncertain origin. fr.Wiktionary proposes, with a hedge, a Vulgar Latin *~brachitāre~ derived from Latin ~bracchium~ (“arm”), but en.Wiktionary calls the origin uncertain, so this link is only a proposal. Its sense “to aim, to turn” later extended to steering a vehicle.
en.contrebuter: ~Contrebuter~ is formed from the verb ~bouter~ or ~buter~ with the prefix ~contre-~ (“against”). The sources name both base verbs, which were close in form and sense, and do not choose between them. The result means to prop something up by pushing against it from the other side, as a buttress holds up a wall.
en.contrecarrer: The sources disagree on how ~contrecarrer~ was formed. French Wiktionary derives it from the noun ~contre-carre~, while English Wiktionary analyzes it as ~contre-~ (“against,” from Latin ~contra~) + ~carrer~. Either way the verb means to oppose or thwart. The base ~carrer~ (“to square”) comes from Latin ~quadrāre~ (“to make square”), from ~quadrus~ and ultimately from ~quattuor~ (“four”), which ties the verb to the family of ~carré~, ~carreau~ and ~carrefour~.
en.contredire:
~Contredire~ was inherited from Old French ~contredire~, which was itself borrowed from Latin ~contrādīcere~ (“to speak against”), built from ~contrā~ (“against”) and ~dīcere~ (“to say”). French today analyzes it as ~contre-~ + ~dire~. The Latin verb ~dīcere~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, to point out”): to say is, at root, to point something out. The same root gave Greek ~deíknymi~ (“I show”), German ~zeigen~ (“to show”) and English ~teach~, as well as French ~dicter~ and ~dictionnaire~.

One feature of ~contredire~ is the second-person plural of the present indicative. The simple verb ~dire~ has ~vous dites~, but ~contredire~ follows ~dédire~, ~interdire~, ~médire~ and ~prédire~ and keeps the regular ending: ~vous contredisez~. The meaning has barely moved since Latin: to say the opposite of what another person says, then to be at odds with a fact, and, reflexively, with oneself. The old noun ~contredit~ survives in the fixed phrase ~sans contredit~ (“beyond dispute”), while ~contradiction~ and ~contradictoire~ are the later learned forms, and English ~contradict~ was borrowed directly from the Latin verb.
en.contrefaire: ~Contrefaire~ is inherited from Old French ~contrefaire~, from Late Latin *~contrāfaciō~, made of ~contrā~ (“against”) and ~faciō~ (“to make”). By surface analysis it is ~contre-~ + ~faire~, so it means to make something in opposition to, or in imitation of, an original: to forge, to mimic, to disguise. ~Faire~ comes from Latin ~facere~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, place”). English ~counterfeit~ was borrowed from the Old French past participle of this verb.
en.contreficher: Formed from ~ficher~ with the prefix ~contre-~, and attested from 1990. It is the polite, euphemistic form of the cruder expression with ~foutre~, as ~ficher~ itself is: “not to give a darn.” The base ~ficher~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~fīg(i)cāre~, a frequentative of Latin ~fīgere~ (“to fasten, to drive in”). The prefix ~contre-~ comes from Latin ~contra~ (“against”) and here adds an emphatic touch of opposition to the dismissal.
en.contrefoutre: Formed in French from ~contre-~ + ~foutre~, in the vulgar expression ~s'en contrefoutre~, an emphatic variant of ~s'en foutre~ (“not to care”). The prefix ~contre-~ comes from Latin ~contra~ (“against”). The base ~foutre~ descends from Vulgar Latin *~fŭttĕre~, from Latin ~futuō~ (“to copulate with”), and its sexual sense has faded into a general vulgar verb of doing and of not caring. The compound therefore keeps the register of its base, firmly vulgar.
en.contremanifester: Formed from ~manifester~ with the prefix ~contre-~, which comes from Latin ~contra~ (“against”) and expresses opposition. The verb means to take part in a counterdemonstration, that is, to demonstrate in the street against another demonstration. It is a transparent French coinage, and its two spellings, ~contremanifester~ and ~contre-manifester~, are the same verb.
en.contrepasser: Formed from ~passer~ with the prefix ~contre-~, which here marks a second action in the opposite direction: ~contrepasser~ is “to cancel, to annul” something previously passed. The prefix comes from Latin ~contra~ (“against”). The base ~passer~ is attested around 1050 and descends from Vulgar Latin *~passāre~, built on Latin ~passus~ (“step”), whence also French ~pas~. It shares its Italian and Spanish cousins ~passare~ and ~pasar~.
en.contrer: A nineteenth-century coinage, formed from the preposition ~contre~ (“against”) plus the verb ending ~-er~: to oppose, to block, to counter. The preposition is inherited from Latin ~contra~ (“opposite, against”), and its first written appearance with a final ~e~, as ~cuntre~, dates from about 1100. The verb is thus a young word built on a very old one, a pattern that French uses freely whenever a preposition needs to become an action.
en.contresigner: Formed from ~signer~ with the prefix ~contre-~ (“against”). To countersign is to add a second signature that verifies or confirms the first, so ~contre-~ marks a second action in the same direction rather than opposition. The base ~signer~ comes from Latin ~signare~ (“to mark with a sign”), from ~signum~ (“sign, mark”), and the prefix from Latin ~contra~ (“against”).
en.contretirer: Formed from ~tirer~ with the prefix ~contre-~, from Latin ~contra~ (“against”). In printing and engraving it means to make a counterproof, pulling a reversed impression from a fresh print or drawing. The base ~tirer~ has a debated origin. The leading hypothesis derives it from Gothic *~tairan~ (“to tear”), while a rival account sees a shortening of Old French ~martirier~ (“to torture”). Its printing sense is visible in ~tirage~, a press-run.
en.contrevenir: A learned borrowing from Latin ~contrāvenīre~ (“to oppose, to act against”), a term of legal Latin. By surface analysis it looks like ~contre-~ (“against”) + ~venir~ (“to come”), and a French speaker can read it that way, but the verb came ready-made from Latin. It is used of breaking a law or a rule, “to contravene.”
en.contribuer:
From Latin ~contribuere~ (“to bring together, contribute, give as a share”), from ~con-~ (“together”) and ~tribuere~ (“to allot, assign, grant”). The verb ~tribuere~ derives from ~tribus~, the “tribe,” so its core sense was to “distribute among the tribes”; ~tribus~ is often connected to the Proto-Indo-European numeral root *~trey-~ (“three”), pointing to an archaic threefold division of the Roman people. Cognate with Italian ~contribuire~ and Spanish ~contribuir~, and — through ~tribuere~ — with English ~contribute~, ~distribute~, and ~tribute~.

The political origin is the memorable detail: long before it meant “to help,” ~contribuere~ described carving a populace up by tribe and assigning each its share of duties and taxes. From that fiscal sense — paying one's portion into a common pot — grew the modern meaning of voluntarily giving toward a shared end, whether money, effort, or an article. The same ~tribus~ underlies a wide French family: ~tribu~ itself, ~tribut~ (“tribute, levy”), ~attribuer~, ~distribuer~, ~rétribuer~, and ~tribun~, the Roman magistrate who was originally the head of a tribe. The noun ~contribution~ preserves the old tax sense in expressions referring to public levies.
en.contrister:
Borrowed from Latin ~contristāre~ (“to sadden, to distress”), a verb that keeps the Latin shape almost untouched. It is built on ~tristāre~ (“to make sad”) with the prefix ~con-~, which here strengthens the sense, and ~tristāre~ itself comes from the adjective ~tristis~ (“sad”). The French verb is therefore a learned borrowing, taken directly from Latin rather than inherited through spoken use.

The Latin adjective ~tristis~ gave French ~triste~ and ~tristesse~, and the common verb ~attrister~ (“to sadden”) belongs to the same family. Italian and Spanish ~triste~ are cognates. Next to the everyday ~attrister~, ~contrister~ is a learned word with the same meaning, “to sadden, to distress,” and it stands as a reminder of how French often kept a Latin verb alongside a native formation on the same root.
en.controverser: Formed in French from ~controverse~ and the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense “to debate, to dispute.” The noun ~controverse~ was borrowed from Latin ~controversia~, from ~controversus~ (“turned the other way”), itself built from ~contrā~ (“against”) and ~versus~ (“turned”), the participle of ~vertere~. A controversy is thus, literally, a matter on which people face opposite directions. The English evidence adds that the noun passed through Old French ~controversie~ and Middle French ~controverse~. The verb is much rarer than the noun.
en.contrôler:
From Old French ~contrerole~ / ~contre-rolle~, a clerk's “counter-roll”: a duplicate register kept alongside the original to verify it. The word joins ~contre-~ (“against, counter,” from Latin ~contra~) and ~rôle~ (“roll, scroll of parchment,” from Latin ~rotulus~, “little wheel,” diminutive of ~rota~, “wheel”). To ~contrôler~ an account was thus to check it against its mirror-copy. In the nineteenth century the sense of “mastery, command” was reinforced by English ~control~ — itself borrowed from this very French word centuries earlier and sent home with a new meaning.

The semantic arc runs from bookkeeping to power. The original act — comparing one register against another — generalized into “to verify, to inspect,” which is still the dominant French sense: a ticket ~contrôleur~ checks, a ~contrôle~ is an inspection or a roadside check, false. From the English re-import came the further idea of holding something in one's grip, of steering it. The ~rotulus~ branch flourished elsewhere too: French ~rôle~ kept its theatrical and administrative life (an actor's part was once literally the scroll bearing the lines), and ~rouleau~, ~enrôler~, and ~contrôle~ all descend from the humble Latin ~rota~, the turning wheel.
en.contusionner: Formed from the noun ~contusion~ (“bruise”) with the verb ending ~-er~; the TLFi calls it a denominative. The participle comes first: ~contusionné~ is found in 1672, when Madame de Sévigné wrote of bruised arms, and the infinitive ~contusionner~ is recorded in 1819 in Boiste's dictionary. The verb means to injure by contusion, that is, to bruise. Littré likewise names only ~contusion~ as its source.
en.convaincre:
From Latin ~convincere~ (“to refute, to prove conclusively, to convict”), formed from the prefix ~con-~ (an intensive use of ~cum~, “with, completely”) and ~vincere~ (“to conquer, to defeat”). ~Vincere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~winkō~ and to the Proto-Indo-European root *~weik-~ (“to overcome, to fight”), reached through a nasal-infixed form *~wi-n-k-~. Cognate, through ~vincere~, with Italian ~vincere~ and Spanish ~vencer~ (“to win”), and with the borrowed English doublet ~convince~.

The Latin sense was forensic: to ~convincere~ someone was to defeat them decisively in argument, and so to prove them guilty or in error. French kept the verb close to this combative origin — to ~convaincre~ is, etymologically, to vanquish another's resistance with reasons until they yield. The same root *~weik-~ runs through a large family of French and English words built on ~vincere~: ~vaincre~ (“to defeat”), ~invincible~, ~victoire~, convaincre's near-twin ~convaincu~, and the legal ~conviction~. The Latin past participle ~convictus~ even gave English ~convict~, preserving the courtroom flavor that French ~convaincre~ has largely traded for the gentler work of persuasion.
en.convenir:
From Latin ~convenire~ (“to come together, to assemble, to agree”), a compound of ~con-~ (“with, together”) and ~venire~ (“to come”). ~venire~ descends from Proto-Italic *~gʷeniō~ and ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷem-~ (“to come, to go”). Cognate with Italian ~convenire~ and Spanish ~convenir~, and — through the same PIE root — with English ~come~ and Latin-derived ~convene~.

The literal sense, “to come together,” fans out beautifully in modern French. When people come together they reach accord, hence ~convenir~ “to agree, to admit”; when a thing comes together well with a situation it fits, hence “to suit, to be convenient.” The same gathering image gives ~couvent~ (a convent, those who have come together) and ~convention~ (an agreement reached in common). The PIE root *~gʷem-~ is among the most fertile in the language, underlying through ~venire~ a whole battery of French verbs — ~venir~, ~devenir~, ~revenir~, ~prévenir~, ~parvenir~, ~survenir~ — and, via the supine ~ventum~, the nouns ~avenue~ and ~événement~. The everyday ~ça me convient~ thus carries, fossilized within it, the ancient picture of two paths meeting.
en.converger: ~Converger~ is borrowed from Latin ~convergere~, formed from ~con-~ (“together”) and ~vergere~ (“to bend, to incline”). The picture is of lines or paths that lean toward one another until they meet at a point. French first used it for geometry and optics, where rays and lines converge, and then figuratively for opinions, efforts or interests that draw together. Its mirror image is ~diverger~, which bends apart instead. English ~converge~ comes from the same Latin verb.
en.converser: Borrowed from Latin ~conversārī~ (“to keep company with, to associate with”), a deponent verb built from ~con-~ (“with”) and ~versārī~, a frequentative of ~vertere~ (“to turn”). French now uses it for exchanging words with someone. English ~converse~ and French ~conversation~ come from the same Latin verb.
en.convertir:
From Latin ~convertere~ (“to turn around, transform”), a compound of the prefix ~con-~ (“together, completely”) and ~vertere~ (“to turn”). ~Vertere~ descends from Proto-Italic *~wertō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~wert-~ (“to turn”). The root is widespread: it gives Sanskrit ~vártate~ (“turns”), and through Proto-Germanic *~werþaną~ (“to become”) the English ~-ward~ and ~worth~ and German ~werden~ — the link between turning and coming-to-be.

The Latin verb of physical turning broadened into many figurative directions, all kept in French. ~Convertir~ can mean to transform one substance into another, to exchange currency or property, to turn someone toward a new faith — the religious sense that made the ~converti~ — or to change an opinion. The same root *~wert-~ underlies a vast French family: ~conversion~, ~convertisseur~, ~divertir~, ~inverser~, ~pervertir~, ~revers~, and ~verser~. Across all of them runs the single image at the heart of ~vertere~: a turning, whether of an object, a currency, a soul, or a mind.
en.convier:
From Old French ~cunveer~ and ~cunvier~, inherited from Vulgar Latin *~convitāre~ (“to invite”), attested in Medieval Latin as ~convitare~. The shape of this verb is probably explained as a cross between Latin ~invītāre~ (“to invite”) and ~convivium~ (“a banquet, a feast together”), a noun built from ~con-~ (“together”) and the root of ~vīvere~ (“to live”). The origin is thus a blend rather than a plain derivation, and it stays a hypothesis. The verb has relatives elsewhere in Romance: Italian ~convitare~ and Portuguese ~convidar~ (and Spanish ~convidar~) follow the same Vulgar Latin form.

If the blend is right, ~convier~ carried from the start the idea of an invitation to share a table. In modern French it keeps a formal, slightly literary tone: one ~convie~ guests to a ceremony or ~convie~ someone to reflect (~convier à la réflexion~), where ordinary speech would say ~inviter~. The two words are rivals from the same Latin source ~invītāre~, if the blend is right, but ~inviter~ is the plain everyday verb. The family also includes ~convive~ (“a guest at table”), from Latin ~convīva~, and ~convivial~ and ~convivialité~, which preserve the shared-meal image.
en.convivialiser: Formed from the adjective ~convivial~ with the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to make convivial.” ~Convivial~ is borrowed from Latin ~convivālis~ (“relating to a communal meal”). The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and it forms verbs meaning to make or render something so.
en.convoiter:
From Old French ~convoitier~, an altered form of the older ~coveitier~ and ~covoitier~; the ~con-~ spelling arose by analogy with the prefix ~con-~. The sources differ on the step before that. English Wiktionary posits a Vulgar Latin verb *~cupidietāre~, built on *~cupidietās~, a reshaping of Classical Latin ~cupiditās~ (“desire, greed”) on the model of words like ~medietās~. French Wiktionary instead starts from Latin ~cupiō~ (“to desire”), whose frequentative *~cupitāre~ in Late Latin would have given the Old French verb, and it adds that a passage through the noun ~cupiditās~ is conceivable. Both accounts meet at the same Latin root, ~cupere~. English ~covet~ is the same word borrowed from Old French, and ~cupidity~ and ~Cupid~ belong to the same Latin family.

The French account leans on a general habit of the spoken language: Latin verbs were often replaced by their frequentatives, built on the supine, as with ~habiter~, ~bouger~ and ~exploiter~. The consonants tell their own story. The Latin ~p~ between vowels became ~v~ in French, the same change that turned Latin ~cūpa~ into ~cuve~. The meaning, by contrast, stayed remarkably steady: ~convoiter~ is to desire what belongs to someone else or lies out of reach, with an edge of greed. Its family includes ~convoitise~ (“covetousness”) and the learned ~cupidité~, a reminder that two words from one root can arrive by different roads, one worn down by the people and one lifted straight from Latin.
en.convoler:
From Latin ~convolāre~ (“to fly together, to rush together”), a verb made of ~con-~ (“with, together”) and ~volāre~ (“to fly”). French Wiktionary points to these two parts, ~con-~ and ~voler~, as the key to the word. The Latin verb ~volāre~ lived on as French ~voler~, which today means both “to fly” and, by a separate development, “to steal.”

In modern French ~convoler~ almost never appears alone. It lives in the fixed, mock-solemn phrase ~convoler en justes noces~ (“to marry”), and the plain verb is jocular, ironic or deliberately formal. The Latin root ~volāre~ belongs to a wide family. It gave ~volée~, ~volière~ and ~volatil~, and through learned borrowings English ~volatile~. In this case French took the Latin verb whole and kept only a narrow, ceremonious use of it.
en.convoquer:
From Latin ~convocāre~ (“to call together, assemble”), from ~con-~ (“together”) plus ~vocāre~ (“to call”). ~vocāre~ rests on ~vōx~ (“voice”), from Proto-Indo-European *~wekʷ-~ (“to speak, utter”). Cognate, through that root, with English ~voice~ and ~vocal~ and with Sanskrit ~वाच्~ (~vāc~, “speech”).

The image is exact: to ~convoquer~ is to use the voice to gather people in one place. French keeps this in its formal registers — a court ~convoquer~ a witness, a director ~convoquer~ the staff, an assembly is ~convoquée~ into session. From the same ~vocāre~ / ~vōx~ stem French drew a large family: appeler's learned twin ~invoquer~, plus ~évoquer~, ~provoquer~, ~révoquer~, ~vocation~, ~vocal~, and ~voix~ itself. Every ~convocation~ is, at heart, a calling-together by voice.
en.convoyer:
From Old French ~conveier~, from Late or Vulgar Latin *~conviāre~ (“to travel together with”), a verb built from ~con-~ (“with”) and ~via~ (“road, way”). The same Old French verb gave English ~convey~, which entered English as a loan. ~Convoyer~ thus means, at root, to go along the road with someone, an idea that explains its modern sense of escorting a person or a cargo.

French ~convoyer~ is used for escorting ships, vehicles or goods, and sometimes people, so that they arrive safely. Its noun ~convoi~ is a convoy, and ~convoyeur~ is the person or the vessel that escorts, as in ~convoyeur de fonds~ (“cash-in-transit guard”). The English ~convoy~ is a borrowing of the French noun. The Latin ~via~ is the root of a large family: ~voie~, ~voyage~, ~voyager~, ~dévier~ and ~envoyer~, and the Italian and Spanish ~via~ and ~vía~.
en.convulser:
From Latin ~convellere~ (“to tear away, to pull violently”), a verb formed from ~con-~ (“together, thoroughly”) and ~vellere~ (“to pluck, to pull”). The French verb is a learned borrowing, and it kept the violent core of the Latin: to ~convulser~ is to shake or twist something in a spasm, whether a body or a face. French Wiktionary names ~convellere~ itself as the source.

Related learned words in French include ~convulsion~, ~convulsif~ and ~convulsionner~, all tied to the Latin participle ~convulsus~. The root ~vellere~ lives on in ~révulsion~ (“a pulling back”), ~évulsion~ (“tearing out”) and ~avulsion~, and in English ~convulse~ and ~revulsion~. The verb is often met as a past participle, as in a face ~convulsé~ by rage or fear.
en.convulsionner: Derived from the noun ~convulsion~ with the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense of causing convulsions or throwing someone into them. ~Convulsion~ was borrowed from Latin ~convulsiō~ (accusative ~convulsiōnem~), the noun of the verb ~convellere~ (“to pull violently, to tear away”). The Latin verb joins ~con-~ and ~vellere~ (“to pluck”).
en.coopter:
Borrowed from Latin ~cooptāre~ (“to choose, to associate”), a compound of ~co-~ (“together”) and ~optāre~ (“to choose, to wish for”). The verb thus means to choose someone to join you. French ~coopter~ keeps that sense: to admit a new member to a body by the decision of its existing members, without an outside election.

The Latin verb ~optāre~ is the base of several French words. ~Opter~ (“to choose between alternatives”) and ~option~ are learned borrowings from it, and ~adopter~ descends from Latin ~adoptāre~ (~ad-~ + ~optāre~), literally “to choose for oneself.” The prefix ~co-~ is Latin ~con-~ (“with, together”), from the preposition ~cum~. English took the verb as ~coopt~ and ~co-opt~, with the same sense of absorbing someone into a group, and sometimes a hint of neutralizing a critic by giving them a place inside.
en.coopérer:
From Latin ~cooperari~ (“to work together”), formed from ~co-~, the form of ~cum-~ (“with”) before a vowel, and ~operari~ (“to work, to labor”). The Latin verb ~operari~ is built on ~opus~ (“work, task”), the same root as French ~œuvre~, and English ~cooperate~ and Italian ~cooperare~ descend from the same Latin verb. French ~coopérer~ keeps the learned stem ~opér-~, unlike the popular verb ~ouvrer~, which also comes from ~operari~ but followed the ordinary sound changes of inherited words.

The idea of joint labor has hardly moved since Latin: to ~coopérer~ is still to work with others toward a shared end. The family around it is large. ~Opérer~ and ~opération~ come from ~operari~ and ~opus~ by learned routes, and ~coopération~ and ~coopératif~ share the prefix. The Latin plural of ~opus~, ~opera~ (“works”), came through Italian as ~opéra~, so an opera is, etymologically, a collection of works.
en.coordonner:
~Coordonner~ is ~ordonner~ (“to order, arrange”) prefixed with ~co-~ (Latin ~cum~, “with, together”), the whole meaning “to arrange things together.” ~Ordonner~ descends from Latin ~ordinare~, from ~ōrdō~ (“row, rank, order”), from Proto-Italic *~ordō~, from PIE *~h₂er-~ (“to fit together”) — the same root that gave Latin ~artus~ (“joint”) and, through it, English ~art~ and ~article~.

The oldest image under ~ōrdō~ is weaving: a row of threads fitted side by side on the loom, things set in their proper place. ~Coordonner~ adds the togetherness of ~cum~, so that to coordinate is to fit several ordered series into one working whole — exactly what the grammatical sense preserves, where ~coordonner~ links clauses of equal rank by a conjonction de ~coordination~. The verb is learned and relatively late, and French smoothed its vowels to align it with ~ordonner~ rather than keep a stiffer *coordiner. Around it cluster ~coordination~, ~coordinateur~, and ~coordonnée~ (the mathematician's “coordinate,” a number that fixes a point's place in an ordered grid). To coordinate is, etymologically, to fit ranks together.
en.copermuter: Formed from ~permuter~ with the prefix ~co-~, the modern form of Latin ~con-~ (“with, together”), which marks a joint or reciprocal action. The base ~permuter~ is a learned verb from Latin ~permūtāre~, built from ~per-~ (“thoroughly”) and ~mūtāre~ (“to change”). The compound means to exchange one benefice for another with a partner who exchanges in return, each party giving up a position to take the other's.
en.copier:
From Medieval Latin ~copiare~ (“to copy out, transcribe”), derived from Classical Latin ~copia~ (“abundance, plenty”), which also gave French ~copie~. ~copia~ is itself a compound of ~co-~ (“with, together”) and ~ops~ (“wealth, resources”), the latter from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₃ep-~ (“to work, produce”). Through that root ~copia~ is cognate with English ~copious~ and ~cornucopia~ — the “horn of plenty.”

The semantic leap from “abundance” to “copy” happened in the medieval scriptorium: to copy a text by hand was, literally, to make it abundant, to multiply the available exemplars. From ~copia~'s sense of plenty, ~copiare~ took on the new meaning of reproducing, and modern French ~copier~ runs from faithful transcription to imitation and, in the classroom, to cheating off a neighbor. English borrowed the word through Old French as ~copy~, shifting it firmly toward “duplicate.” The same ~copia~ underlies French ~copie~, ~copieux~ (“copious, ample”), and ~photocopie~.
en.copiloter: ~Copiloter~ is formed from ~piloter~ with the prefix ~co-~, the modern form of Latin ~con-~ (“with, together”), used for joint action: to share the piloting of a vehicle or the steering of a project. ~Piloter~ comes from the noun ~pilote~, which French borrowed from Italian ~pilota~ in the sixteenth century. Its deeper source is probably Byzantine Greek, though that is a reconstruction.
en.copiner: From ~copine~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. ~Copine~ is the feminine of ~copain~ (“pal”), formed by analogy with words in ~-in~ and ~-ine~. ~Copain~ is a colloquial alteration of Old French ~compain~, the subject-case form of ~compagnon~, from Late Latin ~compāniō~, built from ~com-~ (“with”) and ~pānis~ (“bread”): a companion is someone who shares your bread. English Wiktionary adds that this was probably a loan translation of a Frankish word meaning “messmate.” So ~copiner~, “to be pals,” is a bread-sharing word at heart.
en.coposséder: Formed from ~posséder~ with the prefix ~co-~, from Latin ~con-~ (“with, together”), for joint action: to co-own. The base ~posséder~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~possidēre~, a compound of ~potis~ (“master, able”) and ~sedēre~ (“to sit”), so to possess was to “sit as master.” It replaced the inherited Old French verb ~posseoir~. The same Latin root ~sedēre~ gave ~asseoir~ and ~siège~, while ~potis~ lies behind ~pouvoir~ and ~puissant~.
en.coproduire: Formed from the verb ~produire~ with the prefix ~co-~, which marks joint action: to ~coproduire~ is to produce together with others. The prefix comes from Latin ~con-~ (“with, together”), from ~cum~ (“with”), and in modern coinages it takes the short form ~co-~. The base ~produire~ comes from Latin ~producere~ (“to lead forward”), built from ~pro-~ (“forward”) and ~ducere~ (“to lead”), the same root as ~conduire~ and ~traduire~.
en.copuler:
French ~copuler~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~cōpulāre~ (“to bind, to join”). It is a doublet of the inherited verb ~coupler~, which came down from the same Latin word through Old French and wore down in sound. The Latin verb is built on the noun ~cōpula~ (“bond, tie”), which also lies behind French ~copule~ and ~couple~.

The family is rich in French. ~Coupler~ is the everyday form and ~couple~ its noun, while ~copule~ is the learned noun, used in grammar for the verb that links subject and predicate. English has drawn on the same Latin root for ~couple~ and ~copulate~. The learned verb ~copuler~ took the narrow sense of sexual union, whereas the inherited ~coupler~ kept the broad sense of joining two things together, so the two doublets have drifted far apart in register.
en.coqueter: Formed from the adjective ~coquet~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The adjective is derived from ~coq~ (“rooster”) with the diminutive suffix ~-et~, and is attested from 1611 in the sense of a little rooster. The verb means to flirt, to behave in a coquettish manner. The sources give no story linking the bird to the later sense, so none is offered here.
en.cordeler: ~Cordeler~ is formed from the noun ~corde~ (“rope”) and the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense of fashioning something into a rope. The noun ~corde~ is a French form of Latin ~corda~, itself borrowed from Latin ~chorda~ (“gut, string”), which comes from Ancient Greek ~khordḗ~ (“string of gut, cord”). The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, is the usual means of making a verb from a noun.
en.corder: ~Corder~ is formed from ~corde~ (“rope”) plus the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is a Frenchified form of Latin ~corda~ (attested around 980), itself borrowed from Latin ~chorda~ (“gut, cord”), from Ancient Greek ~khordḗ~ (“string of gut”). The verb first meant to twist or braid into a rope. Around 1200 it is attested with the sense of binding with cords, and in 1265 with that of measuring cloth with a cord.
en.cordonner: Formed from the noun ~cordon~ with the verb ending ~-er~. ~Cordon~ is itself built on ~corde~ (“rope”) with the diminutive suffix ~-on~, an Old French formation, so it is literally a small rope. In French it names a thin cord made of a material other than hemp and, from 1671, a broad ribbon worn as an honorific badge, as in ~cordon bleu~. The verb ~cordonner~ means to twist something into the form of a rope.
en.cornaquer: ~Cornaquer~ (“to guide, to lead around”) is formed from ~cornac~ (“elephant driver, guide”) with the ending ~-er~. The noun came into French from Portuguese ~cornaca~, which comes from Sinhalese ~kūruwa-nāyaka~ (“elephant trainer”), made of ~kūruwa~ (“elephant department”) and Sanskrit ~nāyaka~ (“guide, leader”). The verb is playful: to ~cornaquer~ someone is to shepherd a visitor or newcomer as a mahout steers his elephant.
en.corner: Formed from the noun ~corne~ (“horn”) and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun comes through Old French ~corne~ from Vulgar Latin *~corna~, which was the Latin neuter plural ~cornua~ taken for a feminine singular, the plural of ~cornū~ (“horn”). The verb covers several senses, among them to sound a horn, to blare and to dog-ear a page.
en.correctionnaliser: ~Correctionnaliser~ is formed from the adjective ~correctionnel~ with the suffix ~-iser~, in the legal sense of reducing a serious offense to a lesser one, tried in a tribunal correctionnel instead of the assizes. The adjective ~correctionnel~ is itself derived from ~correction~ with the suffix ~-el~. The ending of the base is reshaped before ~-iser~, as often happens with this suffix, which here means “to make (something) correctionnel”.
en.correspondre:
French ~correspondre~ comes from Medieval Latin ~correspondēre~, formed from ~respondēre~ (“to answer, to respond”) with the prefix ~con-~ / ~cor-~ (“with, together”). ~Respondēre~ is itself ~re-~ (“back”) plus ~spondēre~ (“to pledge, to promise solemnly”), from Proto-Italic *~spondeō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~spend-~ (“to perform a rite, to make an offering”). The Greek cognates ~spéndō~ (“to pour a libation”) and ~spondḗ~ (“libation, solemn truce”) preserve the religious flavour; through the same Latin verb English gained ~respond~, ~sponsor~, and ~spouse~.

The literal idea is mutual pledging: to ~correspondre~ is etymologically “to pledge back together,” one party answering another in kind. From this came two great branches. The first is the abstract sense “to match, to agree, to be in harmony” — colours that ~correspondent~ to one another. The second is the sense “to exchange letters,” reciprocal answering carried on at a distance, which gave the noun ~correspondance~ and, by a charming extension, the ~correspondance~ one makes between two metro lines. The buried root surfaces across French in ~répondre~, ~époux~ and ~épouse~ (a spouse is one solemnly pledged), ~répons~, and ~spontané~. A solemn libation poured to seal an oath has become, in the end, a postcard.
en.corriger:
From Latin ~corrigere~ (“to set straight, reform, amend”), a compound of ~cum~ (“with, together”) — reduced to ~cor-~ before ~r~ — and ~regere~ (“to direct, guide, rule”). ~Regere~ descends from PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten, direct, make right”), one of the most productive roots in the language, source also of Latin ~rēx~ (“king”) and ~rēctus~ (“straight, right”). Through that root ~corriger~ is cognate with English ~right~ and German ~recht~, and with Italian ~correggere~ and Spanish ~corregir~. The literal Latin image is concrete: to “straighten thoroughly,” to bring a crooked thing back into line.

That spatial metaphor — making the bent straight — underlies every modern sense. To correct an error is to straighten what has gone awry; to correct a pupil or a fault is to guide conduct back onto the right path. French preserved the schoolroom sense of marking and grading work, ~corriger une copie~, alongside the moral one of ~se corriger~ (“to mend one's ways”). From the same root *~h₃reǵ-~ French draws a wide family: ~diriger~, ~régir~, ~règle~, ~droit~ (from ~dīrēctus~), ~roi~, and ~correct~ itself, the learned doublet of the past participle. The crooked line made straight runs quietly through them all.
en.corroborer:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~corrōborāre~ (“to strengthen; to corroborate”), taken from the written language rather than inherited through Old French. French Wiktionary traces the Latin verb to ~rōbur~ (“strength”). The Latin verb is analyzed as ~com-~ (here an intensifier) + ~rōbur~ + the verb ending ~-āre~, so it literally means “to make very strong”. English ~corroborate~ is another descendant of the same Latin verb.

The Latin verb already carried both the physical sense of strengthening and the figurative one of confirming, and French took over the second sense as its main one: to ~corroborer~ a statement is to lend it strength by backing it with further evidence. The same Latin noun ~rōbur~ (also “oak”) lies behind ~robuste~, from ~rōbustus~. English has both sides of the family, ~corroborate~ and ~robust~.
en.corroder:
~Corroder~ reaches French through Old and Middle French from Latin ~corrōdere~ (“to gnaw away”). The Latin verb joins ~com-~, here an intensifier that becomes ~cor-~ before ~r~, to ~rōdere~ (“to gnaw”). The verb is also found in Portuguese ~corroer~. Italian ~corrodere~ and Spanish ~corroer~ are its relatives, and English ~corrode~ was borrowed from the same Latin verb.

The simple verb ~rōdere~ is also the source of English ~rodent~ and, with a prefix, of French ~éroder~ and ~érosion~ (through ~ērōdere~, “to gnaw off”), while ~corrodere~ gave ~corrosion~ and ~corrosif~. Where the Latin verb meant gnawing, French ~corroder~ is used of rust or an acid eating into metal, and figuratively of anything that wears something away slowly.
en.corrompre:
Taken into Old French from Latin ~corrumpere~ (“to break totally, to destroy, to spoil”), formed from the intensive prefix ~com-~ (“thoroughly”) and ~rumpere~ (“to break”). English Wiktionary notes that the French verb was reshaped on ~rompre~, the inherited descendant of ~rumpere~, so ~corrompre~ looks and conjugates like its simple verb. English ~corrupt~ was borrowed from the Latin past participle ~corruptus~, and ~rupture~, ~erupt~ and ~interrupt~ come from the same ~rumpere~.

Latin already used ~corrumpere~ for more than physical breaking. It meant to spoil, to taint, to seduce, and to bribe a witness or a judge, and French kept the whole range. In modern French the verb covers moral depravity (~corrompre la jeunesse~), bribery (~corrompre un fonctionnaire~), and, more rarely, physical decay. The idea is always one of something whole being broken. The noun ~corruption~ gives the political scandal its name, ~corrupteur~ is the briber, and the adjective ~incorruptible~ was famously used of Robespierre. The family also includes ~rompre~, ~rupture~, ~interrompre~ and ~irruption~.
en.corroyer: ~Corroyer~ is a leatherworking term meaning to dress tanned leather so that it becomes supple. Its origin is not certain. It is possibly from Late Latin ~conredare~ (“to prepare”), which would itself be an adaptation of Gothic ~garēdan~ (“to arrange”). The trade gave French ~corroyeur~, the craftsman who finishes leather after the tanner. If the Late Latin derivation holds, English has a descendant of the same Old French verb: ~curry~, as in “to curry leather” (and “to curry a horse”), with ~currier~ for the leather dresser. The verb is now chiefly technical.
en.corréler: ~Corréler~ is a back-formation from ~corrélation~, which French borrowed from Late Latin ~correlātiō~, built on ~con-~ (“together”) and ~relātiō~ (“a bringing back, a relation”). The verb was made by stripping the noun's ending and adding the infinitive ending ~-er~, the reverse of the usual order in which a verb gives a noun. It means “to put two things in relation, to establish a statistical link between them,” and it is used above all in science and statistics, where one variable is ~corrélée~ with another.
en.corser: Both Wiktionaries derive ~corser~ from ~corps~ (“body”) plus ~-er~, with fr.Wiktionary specifying the old spelling ~cors~. The idea is to give something body: to make a drink, a sauce or a dish stronger, fuller, more highly flavored, and by extension to make a story or a situation more intense. ~Corps~ itself comes from Latin ~corpus~. The reflexive ~se corser~ is the common modern use: when a plot or a problem ~se corse~, it thickens and gets harder. The suffix ~-er~ is the usual one for building a verb from a noun.
en.corseter: Formed from the noun ~corset~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so ~corseter~ means to put a corset on someone. ~Corset~ is built on Old French ~cors~ (“body”) with the diminutive ~-et~, and the same ~cors~ gave ~corser~ (“to give body to”). Its first written trace is Medieval Latin ~corsetus~ (late twelfth century), a kind of man's surcoat. The modern sense of a boned, laced undergarment dates only from the nineteenth century.
en.cosigner: Formed from ~signer~ and the prefix ~co-~, which marks joint action: to sign together with another party. The prefix comes from Latin ~con-~ (“with, together”), from ~cum~, and it is the only form still used to coin new verbs. The base ~signer~ comes from Latin ~signare~ (“to mark with a sign, to seal”), derived from ~signum~ (“sign, mark”). Italian ~segnare~ and English ~sign~ share this source.
en.cosmétiquer: Derived from the noun ~cosmétique~ with the verb ending ~-er~, meaning to apply cosmetics. ~Cosmétique~ goes back to Ancient Greek ~kosmētikós~ (“decorative, well-ordered”), from ~kosmētḗs~ (“orderer, arranger”), from ~kosméō~ (“to arrange, to adorn”), which comes from ~kósmos~ (“order, world”). In Latin ~cosmetes~ came to mean a slave in charge of the mistress's adornment and makeup, which is how an idea of cosmic order ended up at the dressing table.
en.costumer: Formed from ~costume~ and the verb ending ~-er~, in the sense of putting someone in a costume or dressing in one. The noun ~costume~ was borrowed from Italian ~costume~ (“custom”), from Latin ~cōnsuētūdinem~ (“custom, habit”), so it is a doublet of ~consuétude~ and ~coutume~. French first took it in its general sense of custom, which narrowed to dress prescribed by custom, then to dress in general, and finally to a man's clothing.
en.coter:
Modern French ~coter~ is a denominal verb, drawn from the noun ~cote~. That noun was borrowed from Medieval Latin ~quota~ (clipped from ~quota pars~, “the share due from each person”), the feminine of Latin ~quotus~ (“which in order? what number?”), itself built on ~quot~ (“how many”). The chain reaches back to the Proto-Indo-European interrogative stem *~kʷo-~, the same pronominal root behind Latin ~quis~ and ~quod~. Through ~quota~, the noun ~cote~ is an etymological doublet of the international word ~quota~ and a cousin of English ~quote~, which passed through Medieval Latin ~quotare~ (“to mark off by numbers”).

From the bookkeeper's ~quota pars~ — each person's numbered share on a tax roll — ~cote~ branched into a surprising spread of senses: a figure marked on a plan (a dimension), a price quoted on the exchange, a horse's odds, a library shelfmark, and a grade given to a pupil's work. The verb ~coter~ inherited this whole range, so that today one may ~coter~ a security, a drawing, or an essay. The same numbering instinct lives on in ~quote-part~ (“share, portion”), ~quotient~, ~quotidien~ (literally “however many days there are,” hence “daily”), and ~quorum~ — all heirs of that small Latin question ~quot~, “how many?”
en.cotiser: Formed from the noun ~cote~ with the suffix ~-iser~. ~Cote~ is from Old French ~quote~, itself from Medieval Latin ~quota~, built on Latin ~quotus~ (“how many?”), the same source as ~quota~ and the French ~quote-part~ (“share”). The verb first meant to fix each person's share of a sum, then to pay one's share, which is how ~cotiser~ now means “to pay dues or contributions,” as in ~cotiser à la Sécurité sociale~. In the reflexive, ~se cotiser~ is to chip in together.
en.cotonner: ~Cotonner~ is a denominal verb formed from ~coton~ with the ending ~-er~. It means “to become covered in fuzz,” and so to take on the look of cotton. The base ~coton~ is Old French, ultimately from Arabic ~quṭun~ (“cotton”). It is cognate with Spanish ~algodón~, which keeps the Arabic article, and with English ~cotton~, German ~Kattun~ and Dutch ~katoen~.
en.couchailler: Formed from ~coucher~ with the pejorative suffix ~-ailler~, giving the sense of sleeping around. The base ~coucher~ comes from Old French ~couchier~, from Latin ~collocare~ (“to place, lay in position”), built on ~con-~ and ~locare~. From laying down a body, it came to mean “to put to bed” and “to go to bed.” The suffix ~-ailler~ adds a note of petty or disreputable repetition, as in ~criailler~ or ~discutailler~.
en.coucher:
From Old French ~couchier~ (also ~colchier~), from Latin ~collocare~ (“to place, lay in position”), formed from the prefix ~con-~ (“together, thoroughly”) and ~locare~ (“to place”), itself derived from ~locus~ (“place”). Old Latin had ~stlocus~, traditionally traced to Proto-Indo-European *~stel-~ (“to put, place”), though that derivation is now treated cautiously. Latin ~collocare~ also gave Spanish ~colgar~ and Italian ~coricare~, and, through learned borrowing, English ~collocate~.

In Latin ~collocare~ meant to set something carefully in its place — to arrange, to position, even to invest money or marry off a daughter (placing her well). French ~coucher~ specialized toward one kind of placing: laying a body down, hence “to put to bed,” “to lie down,” and reflexively ~se coucher~ (“to go to bed”). From the horizontal it spread to the sun that ~se couche~ (“sets”), to writing something down (~coucher par écrit~, “to put in writing”), and to the noun ~couche~ (“a layer”). Beside it stands the learned doublet ~colloquer~ and the broad ~locus~ family — ~lieu~, ~local~, ~localiser~, ~louer~ (“to rent,” from ~locare~) — all built on the idea of a place.
en.couder:
The verb ~couder~ is built on the noun ~coude~ (“elbow”), which comes from Latin ~cubitus~, the Latin word for the elbow. The verb means to bend or fold something into the shape of an elbow. Latin ~cubitus~ has relatives elsewhere: Spanish ~codo~ (“elbow”) descends from it, and English ~cubit~, the ancient unit of length measured from the elbow, was borrowed from it.

The noun ~coude~ also names any sharp change of direction, such as the bend of a river or a road, and it sits at the center of a small family of French words. ~Coudée~ is the old unit of length, the French counterpart of the ancient cubit. ~Accouder~ means “to lean on the elbow” and ~coudoyer~ means “to brush against with the elbow”. The adjective ~coudé~ (“bent at an angle”) describes things shaped in that way. All of them share the Latin source ~cubitus~.
en.coudoyer: ~Coudoyer~ is formed from ~coude~ (“elbow”) with the suffix ~-oyer~, which can mean applying N or acting repeatedly: to jostle with the elbow, and so to rub shoulders with, to meet regularly. The noun ~coude~ comes through Middle French from Old French ~cute~ (first attested 1121-35) and ~cote~, inherited from Latin ~cubitus~ (“elbow, cubit”). English ~cubitus~ is a doublet, borrowed directly from Latin, and the unit ~cubit~ comes from the same Latin word. The ending ~-oyer~ itself is a form of Late Latin ~-izāre~, which also gave the learned ~-iser~.
en.coudre:
From Middle French ~coudre~, from Old French ~coudre~ or ~cosdre~, from Vulgar Latin *~cōsere~, an altered form of Classical Latin ~cōnsuere~ (“to sew together”), itself built on ~suere~ (“to sew”). The original Old French infinitive was *~cosre~, and a ~d~ slipped in as a gliding sound between the ~s~ and the ~r~. The ~s~ then went silent, and dropped from the spelling early on. The ~d~ of present forms such as ~je couds~ is analogical, since the expected form would have been ~je cous~. English ~sew~ is a distant cousin of Latin ~suere~, and the same family gave ~suture~.

Latin ~cōnsuere~ meant to sew pieces together, so the verb has meant “to join with a thread” from the start. The past participle ~cousu~ comes from Latin ~cōnsūtus~, and several words kept the Latin stem: ~couture~ (“sewing, a seam”), ~couturier~, ~couturière~ and ~recoudre~ (“to sew back”). French also uses ~coudre~ figuratively, in ~cousu de fil blanc~ (“sewn with white thread”), said of a ruse that is too obvious to fool anyone. The noun ~coudre~ (“hazel”) is a separate word, an altered form of Latin ~corylus~.
en.couillonner: A denominal verb: ~couillon~ plus the ending ~-er~, meaning to fool or trick someone, as one treats a ~couillon~ (a fool). The noun comes from Old French ~coillon~ (“testicle”), from Late Latin ~cōleōnem~, derived from Latin ~cōleus~ (“sack, bag; scrotum”), and by surface analysis it is ~couille~ + ~-on~. Occitan has the parallel verb ~colhonar~. The ending ~-er~ descends from the Latin first-conjugation ending ~-are~ and is the default way French makes verbs from nouns.
en.couiner: Formed from the imitative syllable ~coin~, a sound-word that also lies behind ~coincoin~ (a duck's quack), ~couic~ and ~cuicui~, with the verb ending ~-er~. The verb means to make a thin, high sound, to creak, squeak or squeal. Like its relatives it has no older source: it imitates the noise it names. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is French's usual way of making a verb from a noun or a sound.
en.couler:
From Latin ~cōlāre~ (“to strain, filter, purify”), derived from the noun ~cōlum~ (“a strainer, sieve”). The filtering sense is the original one, still faintly audible in the old phrase ~couler le lait~ (“to strain the milk”). The Romance descendants keep close: Italian ~colare~, Spanish ~colar~, Portuguese ~coar~ — all about passing a liquid through a cloth or sieve. This ~cōlō~ is etymologically distinct from the Latin ~colō~ meaning “to cultivate.”

From straining, the meaning slid naturally to the liquid's own movement — to flow, to trickle, to run — and then, of a boat letting water through, to sink. So the same verb that strains milk also sends a ship to the bottom: ~couler~ un navire. The figurative reach is wide, from ~couler des jours heureux~ (“to spend happy days,” days that flow by) to a reputation one ~coule~. Its family is large: ~coulée~, ~coulis~, ~coulant~, ~couloir~ (a corridor, a channel for passage), ~découler~ (“to follow, ensue”) and ~écouler~.
en.coulisser: Formed from the noun ~coulisse~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, “to slide,” in the manner of something running in a ~coulisse~ (a groove or slot). English Wiktionary derives ~coulisse~ from ~coulis~, and French Wiktionary calls it the feminine noun use of ~coulis~ and sends readers to ~couloir~, so it belongs to the family of ~couler~ (“to flow, to run”).
en.coupailler: Formed from ~couper~ (“to cut”) with the pejorative suffix ~-ailler~, which turns the action into a clumsy or repeated one: to cut, but not well. The TLFi gives 1870 as the first attestation, in Goncourt. Léon Bloy used it in 1893 in a grim image of prisoners ~coupaillés~ into small pieces. The suffix ~-ailler~ works the same way in ~criailler~ and ~tirailler~.
en.coupasser: Formed from ~couper~ (“to cut”) with the suffix ~-asser~, which gives a pejorative or depreciative sense: to cut badly or without result. The base comes from Old French ~colper~, built on the noun ~colp~ (modern ~coup~, “blow”), which goes back through Vulgar Latin to Late Latin ~colaphus~ and Greek ~kólaphos~ (“a slap”). The suffix, formed in the fifteenth century, is still productive in familiar speech, as in ~rêvasser~ and ~traînasser~.
en.couper:
From Old French ~colper~, ~couper~ (eleventh century), derived from the noun ~colp~ (modern ~coup~, “a blow”) with the verbal suffix ~-er~: to ~couper~ is literally to “separate with a blow.” The noun goes back through Vulgar Latin ~colpus~ to Late Latin ~colaphus~, itself borrowed from Greek ~kólaphos~ (“a blow on the cheek, a slap”). Cognates of the noun include Italian ~colpo~ and Spanish ~golpe~, both meaning “blow, strike.”

The striking thing — fitting for a word born of a slap — is how far the meaning travelled from violence. In Old French the sense had already moved from “to strike” to “to cut,” cutting being the result of a blow with a blade, and the original Greek “box on the ear” faded entirely. From there ~couper~ spread into a huge range of idioms: ~couper l'eau~ (to cut off the water), ~couper la parole~ (to interrupt), ~couper les ponts~ (to break off relations), and from 1610 the wine-merchant's ~couper~, to dilute or blend a wine with water or another vintage. Modern French keeps a rich family around the noun ~coup~ — ~coupe~ (a cut, and a cup or trophy), ~coupon~, ~découper~ (to cut out), ~couperet~ (the cleaver, and the guillotine's blade) — all ultimately a single Greek slap.
en.coupler:
French ~coupler~ comes from Latin ~cōpulāre~ (“to join together, to bind”), a verb built on ~cōpula~ (“bond, tie, link”). Latin ~cōpula~ is generally explained as ~co-~ (“together”) plus a root meaning “to fasten.” The Latin verb reached French twice. The popular, inherited form gave ~coupler~, while a later learned borrowing gave the doublet ~copuler~, whose sense of sexual union is now the only one it keeps. The noun ~couple~ and the grammatical term ~copule~ come from the same source, and English ~couple~ and ~copula~ are cousins, ~couple~ having come through Old French.

The verb’s meaning has always centered on joining two things so that they work together. In French it covers coupling railway carriages, linking devices or circuits, pairing animals, and, figuratively, combining two elements. The two doublets show how a single Latin word can split by register: ~coupler~ stayed technical and everyday, while ~copuler~ was borrowed later for the biological sense and remains learned. The family also includes ~couple~, ~accoupler~, ~découpler~, ~copule~ and ~copulation~, all built on the image of a tie between two partners.
en.courbaturer: Formed from ~courbature~ (“bodily ache”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to afflict with aches.” The noun ~courbature~ has an uncertain origin. The likeliest account derives it from the adjective ~courbatu~ plus the suffix ~-ure~. The verb is an ordinary denominal in ~-er~, where the ending turns a noun into an action that applies or inflicts what the noun names.
en.courber:
From Latin ~curvāre~ (“to bend, to make crooked”), from the adjective ~curvus~ (“bent”). French Wiktionary notes that in Vulgar Latin the verb became *~curbare~, with the ~v~ hardening to ~b~, a shift that is frequent in Romance speech. That is the form French inherited, and it explains the ~b~ in ~courber~ against the ~v~ of the learned relatives. English ~curve~ belongs to the same Latin family.

The literal sense is to bend something straight into an arc: a branch under fruit, a back under a load. The figurative uses followed naturally, as in ~courber l'échine~ (“to bow one's back, to submit”) and ~se courber~ (“to stoop, to bow down”), and in the old idea of ~courber la tête~ (“to bow the head”). The family includes ~courbe~ (“curve”), ~courbure~ (“curvature”), ~recourber~ (“to bend back”) and ~incurver~ (“to curve inward”), the last borrowed back from the Latin ~curvus~ family in learned form.
en.courir:
From Old French ~courre~, ~corre~ (“to run”), from Latin ~currere~ (“to run, to hasten”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱers-~ (“to run”). The infinitive ~courir~ is an analogical reshaping that, from the fourteenth century onward, displaced the older ~courre~ on the model of other verbs. Cognate, through ~currere~, with Italian ~correre~ and Spanish ~correr~, and — through the same PIE root *~ḱers-~ — with English ~horse~ and ~hurry~ and with the Latin-borrowed ~current~ and ~career~.

The old form ~courre~ has not vanished entirely: it survives, fossilized, in the hunting term ~chasse à courre~ (“hunting with hounds on horseback”), a phrase that still uses the medieval infinitive. ~Currere~ is one of Latin's most mobile roots, and French is full of its offspring: ~course~, ~coureur~, ~courrier~ (originally a “runner” who carried messages), ~courant~, ~concourir~, ~parcourir~, ~secourir~, and ~recourir~. The English ~courier~, ~course~, ~current~, ~occur~, and ~excursion~ all descend from the same running root, as does ~corridor~ — etymologically a “running-place.” Few Latin verbs have sprinted so far through the vocabulary of its daughter languages.
en.couronner: From Old French ~coroner~, inherited from Latin ~corōnāre~ (“to crown”), the verb built on Latin ~corōna~ (“crown, wreath”). By surface analysis, the modern spelling can also be read as ~couronne~ + ~-er~, a verb formed on the French noun. The Latin noun gave French ~couronne~. Italian ~coronare~ and Spanish ~coronar~ continue the Latin verb, and English ~crown~, ~coronation~ and ~corona~ belong to the same family.
en.courre:
~Courre~ is the old infinitive of ~courir~. It comes from Old French ~courre~, inherited from Latin ~currere~ (“to run”). Italian ~correre~ and Spanish ~correr~ are its sisters, and English has the Latin verb's descendants in ~current~ and ~course~, both borrowed through French. In Old French ~courre~ was the normal infinitive, and ~courir~ later replaced it in everyday speech.

Modern French keeps ~courre~ only as a fossil in hunting language, where it survives in the fixed expression ~chasse à courre~ (“hunting with hounds and horses”) and in phrases such as ~courre le cerf~ (“to hunt the stag”). That is why the verb is rarely conjugated today. The Latin source has left many learned and inherited relatives in French: ~concourir~, ~discourir~, ~parcourir~, ~secourir~, ~cours~, ~courant~ and ~courrier~ all rest on ~currere~. The old infinitive also explains the future and conditional of ~courir~, ~courrai~ and ~courrais~, which are built on ~courre~ and not on ~courir~.
en.courroucer:
From Old French ~corocier~ or ~correcier~, attested in 1170, inherited from Vulgar Latin *~corruptiāre~. That form was remade from ~corruptus~, the past participle of Latin ~corrumpere~ (“to corrupt, spoil”). The Latin verb is standardly analyzed as ~com-~ (an intensifier) plus ~rumpere~ (“to break”), so “to break thoroughly.” It also gave French ~corrompre~, which is therefore a cousin of ~courroucer~ even though the two meanings have drifted far apart.

In modern French, ~courroucer~ is literary and means “to enrage, to infuriate,” and it is mostly met as a past participle or a reflexive verb: ~être courroucé~ or ~se courroucer~. The noun ~courroux~ (“wrath”), a literary word of the same family, is its counterpart. The family around ~corrumpere~ is large: ~corrompre~, ~corruption~, ~corrupteur~ and the English ~corrupt~ all descend from the Latin verb, while ~rompre~ and ~rupture~ come from the simple ~rumpere~. The pair ~courroucer~ and ~corrompre~ shows one Latin verb reaching French in two shapes, one remade from its past participle, the other taken from the verb itself.
en.courser: Formed in French from ~course~ and the first-group ending ~-er~. The noun ~course~ is itself derived from ~cours~, with influence from Italian ~corsa~, and ~cours~ goes back to Latin ~cursus~ (“a running, course”), from ~currō~ (“to run”). So the verb belongs to the large family of Latin ~currere~, which also gave ~courir~, ~concours~ and ~recours~. ~Courser~ is a familiar word meaning “to chase after someone,” as in ~courser quelqu'un~: it turns the run of the noun back into an action, a pursuit at full speed.
en.court-circuiter: ~Court-circuiter~ is the noun ~court-circuit~ + the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun is a calque of English ~short circuit~, a compound of ~court~ and ~circuit~; the French explanation is that in an accidental fault the circuit becomes too short to offer enough resistance. The verb began with the electrical sense and then took the figurative sense “to bypass,” as when one skips an intermediate step or authority.
en.courtauder: Formed from ~courtaud~ and the ending ~-er~, a verb meaning to dock the tail of an animal. The base ~courtaud~ is built on ~court~ (“short”) with the suffix ~-aud~, and comes through Middle French ~courtault~; Italian ~cortaldo~ is a cognate. The idea is to make the animal ~courtaud~, that is, short, cut short.
en.courtiser: ~Courtiser~ was borrowed from Italian ~corteggiare~, a verb built on ~corte~ (“court”), the Italian counterpart of French ~cour~. Both nouns go back to Latin ~cohors~ (“enclosure, retinue”). It is thus a loan rather than an inherited word. Its meanings are “to court” and “to woo”: to pay attention to someone in order to win their favor.
en.cousiner: ~Cousiner~ is formed from the noun ~cousin~ with ~-er~, in the sense of behaving as cousins do, hence of getting along. The origin of ~cousin~ is uncertain. One account derives it from Latin ~consobrinus~ (“cousin on the mother's side”) through a shortened form *~consinus~. Another proposes a descent from a Latin form built on ~culex~ (“gnat”). The noun is attested from the sixteenth century.
en.couter:
From Latin ~constāre~ (“to stand firm, to be fixed”, and also “to stand at a price, to cost”), formed from ~con-~ and ~stāre~ (“to stand”). In the Romance-speaking lands the verb became ~costāre~, whence Italian ~costare~, Catalan, Spanish and Occitan ~costar~, and Portuguese ~custar~. In French ~costar~ lengthened to ~couster~ before the ~s~ stopped being pronounced, which gave modern ~coûter~. English ~cost~ is a cousin by borrowing from French.

In Old French the verb was already used impersonally for price, as in Chrétien de Troyes: ~Et dient que trop chier li coste~, “and they say it costs him too dear”. The modern spelling ~couter~ is the 1990 rectified one for ~coûter~. The Latin meaning “to stand” explains the sense: a thing that stands at a price is one that costs it. French has ~ester~ and ~constant~ from the same family of ~stāre~, and ~coût~ and ~coûteux~ as relatives of the verb.
en.couver:
Inherited from Latin ~cubāre~ (“to lie down, to recline”). fr.Wiktionary adds that the Latin verb was used in the sense of ~incubāre~ (“to lie upon”), the source of English ~incubate~ and French ~incuber~, and that the figurative sense of a fire smoldering under the ashes comes from the same ~cubāre~ taken as “to lie.” Hatching is the image: a hen lies on her eggs. Italian ~covare~ also comes from ~cubāre~, and the Latin family includes ~cubiculum~ (“bedroom”, the source of English ~cubicle~) and ~concumbere~, from which French ~concubine~ ultimately derives, as does ~succomber~ through ~succumbere~ (“to lie down under”).

In French, ~couver~ first meant what a hen does, that is, to sit on eggs to hatch them, with the noun ~couvée~ (“brood”) and ~couveuse~ (“incubator”) as its products. The idea of tender, patient sitting then spread to people: one ~couve~ a child, meaning one over-protects it, or ~couve~ someone with the eyes, meaning gazes at them with longing. It also took a darker turn. An illness, a plot or a resentment can ~couver~, that is, develop in silence before breaking out, in the same way as a fire that smolders under cold ash. Do not confuse it with ~couvrir~ (“to cover”) and ~couvercle~ (“lid”), which come from Latin ~cooperīre~ and merely look alike.
en.couvrir:
From Old French ~covrir~, from Latin ~cooperire~ (“to cover wholly, to cover over”), a compound of ~co-~ (an intensive form of ~cum~, “with, together”) and ~operire~ (“to close, to cover”). ~operire~ comes from a Proto-Indo-European compound *~op-wer-yo-~, joining *~op-~ (“over”) with the root *~wer-~ (“to cover, to shut”). ~couvrir~ is cognate with Italian ~coprire~ and Spanish ~cubrir~, and — through Old French ~covert~ — with English ~cover~ and ~covert~.

A neat irony hides in the family. The same root *~wer-~ produced a near-mirror verb, ~aperire~ (“to open, to uncover”), from *~ap-wer-yo-~: change the prefix from “over” to “off, away” and covering becomes uncovering. That ~aperire~ gave French ~ouvrir~ (“to open”) and English ~overt~ and ~aperture~ — so ~couvrir~ and ~ouvrir~, perfect opposites in meaning, are siblings built on one root. From ~cooperire~ French drew a rich harvest: ~couvert~ (“covered,” also a table setting and shelter), ~couverture~ (“blanket, cover”), ~couvercle~ (“lid”), ~découvrir~ (“to uncover, to discover”), and the vivid compounds ~couvre-chef~ (“headgear”) and ~couvre-feu~ (literally “cover-fire,” the medieval ~curfew~).
en.coéditer: Formed from ~éditer~ with the prefix ~co-~, which marks joint action: to ~coéditer~ is to edit or publish together with someone else. The base ~éditer~ goes back to Latin ~ēdere~ (“to give out, publish”), from ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~dare~ (“to give”), and was built in French around 1784, partly from the nouns ~édition~ and ~éditeur~. The prefix ~co-~ comes from Latin ~con-~ (“with, together”), from the preposition ~cum~. It is the form still used to coin new verbs of shared activity, such as ~cogérer~ and ~copiloter~.
en.coïncider: Borrowed from Medieval Latin ~coincidere~ (“to fall together”), formed on Latin ~incidere~ (“to fall upon, to fall into”).
