English Wiktionary gives the source simply as Latin ~coincidō~. By standard analysis, ~incidere~ is ~in-~ + ~cadere~ (“to fall”), and ~coincidere~ adds ~co-~ (“together”). The literal picture of two things falling together gives French ~coïncider~ its modern sense of events, positions or opinions that match. The same Latin verb gave English ~coincide~, Italian ~coincidere~ and Spanish ~coincidir~, and ~incidere~ also gave French ~incident~.
en.coïter: ~Coïter~ is formed from the noun ~coït~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~coït~ is a learned borrowing, through Middle French ~coit~, from Latin ~coitus~ (“union, joining”), from ~coīre~ (“to go together”). That Latin verb is ~co-~ (“together”) plus ~īre~ (“to go”). The French verb is thus a clinical, late formation, built on a Latin word that itself meant only a coming together.
en.coûter:
From Middle French ~couster~, from Old French ~couster~, from Latin ~constāre~ (“to stand firm, to stand together,” and so “to be fixed at a price, to cost”), the infinitive of ~cōnstō~. The verb is built from the intensive prefix ~com-~ and ~stāre~ (“to stand”), the same root that gives English ~stand~ and ~stay~. Italian ~costare~ and Spanish ~costar~ are its everyday cousins, and English ~cost~ is borrowed, through Old French, from the very same source.

The semantic leap from “to stand” to “to cost” runs through the idea of a price at which something is fixed or settled: what a thing ~constat~ is what it firmly “stands at.” Old French ~couster~ kept this commercial sense, and modern French extended it figuratively — an effort, a sacrifice, or a mistake can ~coûter~ dearly without any money changing hands, as in the proverb ~coûte que coûte~ (“cost what it may, at all costs”). From the same Latin ~stāre~ descend a broad family of French words, including ~constant~, ~coût~ (the noun “cost”), ~constance~, and — through ~constāre~ itself — ~contraster~ and ~contraste~, where things are made to “stand against” one another.
en.cracher:
The origin is debated. French Wiktionary derives it from an imitative syllable ~crac~, present in both the Romance and the Germanic worlds. English Wiktionary gives Old French ~crachier~ (“to eject from the mouth”), from Vulgar Latin *~craccare~, also imitative, and says it may have come by way of Frankish *~hrākijan~ or *~hrakkjan~. Cognates support the Germanic route: Old High German ~hrahhan~ (“to spew, spit”), Old English ~hrǣċan~ (“to retch, cough up, spit”) and Old Norse ~hrǽkja~ (“to hawk, spit”). They descend from Proto-Germanic *~hrēkijaną~ (“to spit, retch”), itself perhaps related to a sound-word *~krakōn~ (“to make a cracking sound”). So the verb may be pure sound-imitation or a loan from the Franks, or a blend of the two.

Whatever its source, the verb has stayed close to the physical act. Its family includes ~crachat~ (“spit, spittle”) and ~crachoir~ (“spittoon”). French Wiktionary also offers a hedged explanation for the expression ~tout craché~, said of a striking likeness: it may come from a comparison between a ~crachat~ and a drop of water, in the manner of the phrase for two people alike as two drops of water. The sources only offer this as a possibility, so it is best held lightly. Figuratively, ~cracher~ can also mean to hand something out with disdain or to pay up reluctantly.
en.crachiner:
The origin of ~crachiner~ (“to drizzle”) is reported in two ways. French Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~crassus~ (“thick”), a word said sometimes of rain or fog, while English Wiktionary simply treats it as a derivative of ~cracher~ (“to spit”). The two accounts differ, so the origin should be regarded as uncertain rather than settled. Either way, the verb today names a fine, light rain.

If the first account is right, ~crachiner~ belongs to a large family. Latin ~crassus~ gave French both ~gras~, by the inherited route, and ~crasse~, a learned form, while Italian ~grasso~ is a cognate and English ~crass~ a borrowing. If the second account holds, the verb is instead a French derivative of ~cracher~, and the Latin word has no part in it. The question remains open.
en.crachoter: ~Crachoter~ is formed from ~cracher~ (“to spit”) with the suffix ~-oter~, which gives a verb a sense of small, repeated or weak action: to spit a little, again and again, or to sputter and crackle, as a radio or an old engine does. The base ~cracher~ has a debated origin. It may be pure sound-imitation, or it may come from Old French ~crachier~, possibly through Frankish *~hrākijan~ or *~hrakkjan~, with Old English ~hrǣċan~ (“to retch, spit”) as a cognate. The related nouns ~crachat~ and ~crachoir~ complete the family.
en.crachouiller: Formed from ~cracher~ (“to spit”) with the ending ~-ouiller~. Both Wiktionaries give only this derivation. The ending gives a lighter, repeated or ragged sense, so the verb describes spitting a little at a time, and by extension a sputtering sound. The sources say nothing more about its date or its history.
en.crailler: Of imitative origin: the TLFi derives it from a sound-imitating stem of the type ~krakk-~, the same family as ~crac~ and ~cracher~. It adds, as a possibility, that the word may have passed through the verb ~grailler~ (“to cry out”), which would link it to Latin ~gracula~ (“female jackdaw”). Littré says simply that it is an onomatopoeia. The TLFi dates it to the middle of the sixteenth century, in Amyot. It first described the cry of the crow and, by extension, of some other birds.
en.craindre:
From Old French ~criembre~, ~creindre~ (attested as early as the ninth-century ~Cantilène de sainte Eulalie~), later reshaped to ~craindre~ on the model of other ~-aindre~ verbs like ~plaindre~ and ~fraindre~. The source is Gallo-Roman *~cremere~, an alteration of Latin *~tremere~ (“to tremble, to quake”) under the influence of a Gaulish form related to ~critos~ (“trembling, shudder”). The Latin verb descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~trem-~ (“to tremble”), cognate with Greek ~trémō~ (“I tremble”) and Italian ~tremare~. English ~tremble~ and ~tremor~ belong to the same family.

The shift from “to tremble” to “to fear” is intuitive: dread makes the body shake, so the physical tremor lent its name to the emotion. The Celtic colouring of the initial ~cr-~ is a rare visible trace of Gaulish on a Latin verb, a substrate fingerprint left as Latin settled over Gaul. From the same ~trem-~ root, but borrowed by the learned route, French also possesses ~trembler~ (through Late Latin ~tremulāre~), ~trémousser~ (“to wriggle”), ~tremblement~ (“trembling, earthquake”), and ~trémolo~. So the homely ~craindre~ and the literary ~trembler~ are, beneath their very different shapes, two reflexes of a single ancient shudder.
en.cramer:
~Cramer~ was borrowed from Occitan ~cramar~ (“to burn”), a form recorded in Gascony, the Limousin and the Auvergne. Occitan ~cramar~ is a variant of ~cremar~, which descends from Latin ~cremāre~ (“to burn”). The verb therefore shares its Latin source with Italian ~cremare~ and Spanish ~cremar~ (“to cremate”) and with English ~cremate~, and it reached standard French from the south rather than by the inherited route.

~Cramer~ has a twin in French. The verb ~crémer~ comes from the same Latin ~cremāre~, and the two are doublets: words from one source that entered the language separately. ~Crémer~ keeps the narrow sense of cremating, the sense also found in ~crémation~ and ~crématoire~. ~Cramer~ went its own way and covers burning in general, including the sense of smoking.
en.cramponner: ~Cramponner~ is formed from ~crampon~ with the verb ending ~-er~, and means to fasten with a hook or spike, or, as a reflexive, to cling on. French Wiktionary traces ~crampon~ to Old Low Frankish *~krampo~ (“hook”), the masculine counterpart of *~krampa~, which is also the source of ~crampe~. English Wiktionary describes it instead as a diminutive of Old French ~crampe~. Either way, the noun is tied to ~crampe~.
en.cranter: Formed from ~cran~ (“notch”) with the verb ending ~-er~, with an intervening ~-t-~ that is only a linking consonant: ~cranter~ means “to cut notches in.” The origin of ~cran~ is debated. French Wiktionary offers a few possibilities: a verbal noun of Old French ~crener~ or ~cren~ (“notch”), a verbal noun of ~craner~, or, in von Wartburg's view, a pre-Roman root ~kranno-~ (“stone, rock”). English Wiktionary favors a deverbal of ~créner~, probably of Gaulish origin.
en.crapahuter: ~Crapahuter~ is a verb made from the noun ~crapahut~ with the ending ~-er~. ~Crapahut~ began in the slang of the Saint-Cyr military academy, where cadets jokingly pronounced the name of a gymnastics apparatus, the ~crapaud~ (“toad”), as ~crapaü~. The word was later applied to gruelling marches and manoeuvres, and the verb, attested since the 1960s, means to trudge or slog across rough ground, especially on military exercises.
en.crapoter: Formed from ~crapaud~ (“toad”) plus the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense “to smoke without inhaling, to puff.” The noun ~crapaud~ is attested as ~crapot~ or ~crapaut~ in Old French and is built with the suffix ~-aud~ on a Frankish word *~krappa~ (“hook”), a reference to the toad's hooked feet. The sources do not explain how a toad led to puffing on a cigarette, so the link is left open.
en.craqueler: Formed from ~craquer~ (“to crack, to snap”) with the suffix ~-eler~, which has a diminutive or repeated sense, so ~craqueler~ is “to crack in many small fissures,” as old paint or glaze does. The base ~craquer~ imitates a sharp snapping sound. Its deeper origin is debated: it may be a native echoic coinage or a borrowing from a Germanic verb such as Middle Dutch ~kraken~. English ~crackle~ is an exact parallel, built the same way from ~crack~.
en.craquer:
Modern French ~craquer~ (1544) is built on the onomatopoeia ~crac~, an imitation of a sharp snapping sound. The deeper origin is genuinely debated: French sources such as the TLFi treat the word as a native echoic formation, while other accounts derive it instead from a Germanic verb — Middle Dutch ~kraken~ (“to crack, crackle”), traced back to Frankish *~krakōn~ and ultimately to an imitative Proto-Indo-European *~gerg-~ (“to caw, shout”). The two stories are hard to separate precisely because the sound itself is so naturally imitative that several languages coined near-identical words independently. By either account, English ~crack~ (from Old English ~cracian~) belongs to the same echoic family.

From the literal noise of something snapping, ~craquer~ branched widely. The figurative sense “to threaten ruin, to give way” is attested from 1718 — a structure, a nerve, or a resolve that ~craque~ is one about to break. Slang lent it “to die” and, later, “to crack under pressure” or even “to fall for” someone. The petroleum and computing senses (1967 onward) were re-modeled on English ~crack~. The same root cluster gives French ~craquement~ (“a cracking sound”), craquer’s noun ~craque~ (“a tall tale”), and ~craquelure~, the fine web of cracks prized on old varnished paintings.
en.craqueter: Formed from ~craquer~ as a diminutive, with the suffix ~-eter~: where ~craquer~ names a single sharp crack, ~craqueter~ names a series of small, repeated ones, as in a fire, dry wood or an old floor. Verbs in ~-eter~ often carry this sense of smallness or repetition, as in ~voleter~ beside ~voler~. The base ~craquer~ is an imitation of the sound itself, and the English ~crack~ and ~crackle~ and the German ~knacken~ imitate the same noise independently.
en.crasher: ~Crasher~ is a recent borrowing from English ~crash~, which French took as a noun and then turned into a verb by adding the ending ~-er~, the usual way of fitting an English verb into the first conjugation. It means to smash a vehicle, especially an aircraft or a car, or to land one badly, and the reflexive ~se crasher~ is common in speech. Unlike most verbs on this site, it has no Latin ancestry. It simply reflects the English crash of vehicles and machines.
en.cravacher: Formed from ~cravache~ (“riding crop, quirt”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning “to whip” and, figuratively, “to work flat out.” The noun is a long-distance traveler. French borrowed ~cravache~ from German ~Karbatsche~, which came from Polish ~karbacz~, and the Polish word came from Ottoman Turkish ~kırbaç~ (“whip”). French Wiktionary describes the route as Turkish by way of the Slavic languages. A word for a rider's whip thus moved from Turkish across Poland and Germany into French.
en.cravater: Formed from the noun ~cravate~ (“necktie”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to put a tie on someone.” The noun is a borrowing of the word for a Croat, Croatian ~Hrvat~, possibly through German ~Kroate~. It came to name the band of cloth worn around the neck like that of Croatian horsemen. So every ~cravate~ is, etymologically, a “Croat,” and ~cravater~ means to dress someone in one.
en.crawler: A denominal verb built on ~crawl~, the swimming stroke, with the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to swim the crawl.” The noun ~crawl~ was itself borrowed into French from English. The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, is the default way French makes a verb from a noun, here in the sense “to practice or carry out” that noun. French also has a separate, more recent ~crawler~ (a web-indexing robot), borrowed directly from the English noun ~crawler~, so the two words are homographs of different formation.
en.crayonner: Formed from ~crayon~ and the verb ending ~-er~: to work with a pencil, to sketch or scribble. The noun ~crayon~ is itself derived from ~craie~ (“chalk”) with the diminutive suffix ~-on~, and ~craie~ comes from Latin ~crēta~ (“chalk, clay”). A pencil is therefore, etymologically, a little chalk.
en.creuser:
A denominal verb from the noun and adjective ~creux~ (« hollow »), attested as a noun (« cavity ») around 1121 and as an adjective around 1180. The origin of ~creux~ is of disputed origin: the dictionaries reconstruct a Late Latin *~crosus~ (« hollow »), which they call « probably » the source, while noting it « perhaps » rests on a Celtic, that is Gaulish, base. The Latin etymon is itself unattested, and the sources frankly label the whole « of uncertain origin. »

From « to make hollow, » ~creuser~ broadened to « to dig » in the ordinary sense — a well, a ditch, a tunnel — and then to the figurative « to dig into, » as one ~creuse~ a question to its depths, or « creuser l'écart » to widen a gap in a race or a score. The hollow also gnaws: « ça me ~creuse~ » means hunger is digging at the stomach. Modern kin of the base include the noun ~creux~ itself, ~creuset~ (« crucible, » a hollow vessel), and the past participle ~creusé~ used as a noun for a dug-out hollow. Cognates appear in Old Occitan ~cros~ and northern Italian dialects, confirming the Gallo-Romance spread even as the deepest source stays unproven.
en.crevasser: Formed from the noun ~crevasse~ with the verbal ending ~-er~: to cover with cracks, as cold does to hands or lips. The noun ~crevasse~ was ~crevace~ in Old French and is derived from ~crever~ (“to burst”) with the suffix ~-asse~, by way of popular Latin ~crepacia~, from ~crepāre~. The Latin verb ~crepāre~ meant “to crack, to burst”, and it is the ancestor of ~crever~ itself. The ending ~-er~ comes from the Latin first-conjugation ending ~-are~.
en.crever:
From Old French ~crever~, inherited from Latin ~crepāre~ (“to rattle, to creak, to crack”). The Latin verb imitates a sharp noise, and its first sense was about sound. Italian ~crepare~ and Romanian ~crăpa~ come from the same Latin verb, and, like French, both reached the informal sense of “to die.” The learned side of the family gives French ~crépiter~, “to crackle,” borrowed from a Latin verb built on ~crepāre~. In French, the original idea of something bursting with a crack was extended from the noise to the break itself.

French Wiktionary traces the development as a slide from “to burst,” in the sense of a loud crack, to “to split” (compare the noun ~crevée~, a slash in a garment), and finally to “to die.” It notes that figurative speech shows the same drift in laughter, where ~éclater de rire~, ~se fendre la gueule~ and ~mourir de rire~ all point to something bursting open. Today ~crever~ covers a tire that bursts (~crevaison~), a balloon that pops, hunger or work that wears one out, and, in blunt registers, dying. From the verb come ~crevasse~ (a split in ice or earth) and ~crevé~ (“exhausted”).
en.criailler: ~Criailler~ is formed from ~crier~ and the suffix ~-ailler~, which makes verbs of repeated or petty action: to cry out again and again, to squawk or whine. The base ~crier~ comes from Old French ~crier~, attested about 980, from Vulgar Latin *~critare~, a reduction of Latin ~quiritare~ (“to cry out”). The origin of ~quiritare~ is disputed: one old account links it to calling on the Roman citizens, the ~Quirites~, for help, while others see it as imitative.
en.cribler: ~Cribler~ is inherited from Middle French ~cribler~ and Old French ~cribler~ or ~crieuler~. French Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~cribellāre~. English Wiktionary gives Late Latin ~crīblāre~, a dissimilated form of Classical ~crībrāre~, and notes the surface analysis ~crible~ plus ~-er~. The shared Latin source is the sieve (~crībrum~), so the verb literally means to pass something through a sieve, and then, figuratively, to riddle with holes.
en.crier:
From Old French ~crier~ (also ~crider~), attested by about 980, from Vulgar Latin *~critare~, a reduction of Latin ~quiritare~ (“to cry out, wail, shriek”); compare Old Occitan ~cridar~. The origin of ~quiritare~ is disputed: De Vaan accepts the ancient idea that it meant to call upon the ~Quirites~, the Roman citizens, for help; others derive it from ~queror~ (“to complain”), though the phonetics are hard to trace, or treat it as onomatopoeic. A comparison with Frankish *~krītan~ (“to cry out”) has also been noted. The sources leave the matter open.

Whatever its source, the verb has always named the raising of the voice — in alarm, in pain, in protest, in proclamation. French keeps the full range, from a child's cry to a vendor crying his wares. From the same stem come ~cri~ (“cry, shout”), ~criard~ (“shrill, garish”), ~crieur~ (“crier, hawker”), ~criailler~ (“to squawk”), and the prefixed ~s'écrier~ (“to exclaim”). If the disputed Quirites story is right, then every French ~cri~ faintly echoes an ancient Roman shouting for his fellow citizens.
en.criminaliser: Formed from the adjective ~criminel~ and the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to make criminal,” that is, to treat an act or a person as a crime or as criminal. The adjective comes from Old French ~criminal~, itself borrowed from Late Latin or legal Latin ~criminālis~, from Latin ~crīmen~ (“accusation, charge, crime”). The suffix ~-iser~ is productive in administrative, legal and journalistic French for verbs meaning “make A” or “convert into N,” as in ~dépénaliser~ for its opposite.
en.criser: Formed from ~crise~ with the verb ending ~-er~, in the colloquial sense of throwing a fit or freaking out. The base ~crise~ was borrowed from Medieval Latin ~crisis~ (“severe manifestation of a disease”), which came from Greek ~κρίσις~ (“judgment”). So the verb rests on a medical word for the decisive turn of an illness, which French later stretched to any outburst or emergency. The formation is a recent, transparent derivation in French.
en.crisper: ~Crisper~ is borrowed from Latin ~crispāre~ (“to curl, to wrinkle”), a verb tied to the adjective ~crispus~ (“curly”). English Wiktionary notes that ~crêper~ (“to crimp, to frizz”) may be an inherited doublet, that is, the same Latin word coming down by the ordinary route of sound change while ~crisper~ was taken over later in its Latin form. The English adjective ~crisp~ is a distant relative that traces to the same Latin source. The French adjective ~crispé~ and the noun ~crispation~ belong to the same family.
en.crisser: The French verb ~crisser~ comes from Old French ~crisner~, which is to be linked to Frankish *~kriskjan~ (“to squeal or creak”). The link is proposed rather than proven. French Wiktionary points to ~grincer~ and ~grincher~ as related verbs. A squeaking wheel, a tire on gravel, boots on dry snow and chalk on a board all ~crissent~. Quebec French has a second, unrelated ~crisser~, built on the swear word ~crisse~ plus ~-er~. ~Crisse~ is a Quebec respelling of ~Christ~, so that verb is an oath turned into a verb and has nothing to do with noise. The two verbs share a spelling by coincidence.
en.cristalliser: Formed from ~cristal~ and the suffix ~-iser~, “to make into”, so ~cristalliser~ means to turn into crystals. ~Cristal~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~crystallus~ (“ice”, then “rock crystal”), which comes from Greek ~krústallos~ (“ice”), a derivative of ~krúos~ (“frost”). The name reflects an ancient notion that clear quartz was ice frozen hard. The verb passed from chemistry and mineralogy to figures of speech: an opinion, a plan or a feeling ~cristallise~ when it hardens into a definite form.
en.criticailler: Formed from ~critiquer~ with the pejorative suffix ~-ailler~, which gives verbs of petty or ill-humored repeated action: to find fault for the sake of it. ~Critiquer~ was built on ~critique~, from Latin ~criticus~ and Ancient Greek ~kritikós~ (“able to judge”), from ~krínō~ (“to separate, to judge”). The suffix is also found in ~discutailler~ and ~criailler~.
en.critiquer:
A denominal verb, recorded in 1546, built on the noun and adjective ~critique~, borrowed from Latin ~criticus~, itself from Ancient Greek ~κριτικός~ (~kritikós~, “able to discern or judge”), from ~κριτής~ (~kritḗs~, “a judge”), from the verb ~κρίνω~ (~krínō~, “to separate, sift, decide, judge”). That verb goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~krey-~ (“to sieve, separate, distinguish”). Through Latin ~cernere~ and ~crīmen~ the same root reaches English ~certain~, ~crime~, ~discern~, and ~crisis~.

The buried image is a sieve: to judge is to sift, separating the sound from the unsound. A ~critique~ in Greek and early French was first one who discerns and evaluates — a literary or medical judge — and ~critiquer~ began neutrally as “to examine and appraise.” Only later did the pejorative tilt set in, so that today ~critiquer~ leans toward finding fault. French keeps the whole spread from this root: ~critique~ (both “a critic” and “a review”), ~critère~ (“criterion,” a means of sifting), ~crise~ (“crisis,” a decisive turning point), and ~hypocrite~ — etymologically one who answers from under a mask, judging in disguise.
en.croasser: Formed from the onomatopoeia ~croa~, which imitates the cry of a crow, and the suffix ~-asser~. The suffix is the same one that appears in ~rêvasser~ and often adds a shade of repetition or contempt, so the verb suggests a cry repeated over and over. It means “to caw” and, of a person, “to croak.”
en.crocher: Formed from ~croc~ (“hook”) plus the verbal ending ~-er~ (from Latin ~-are~), meaning to catch with a hook. French Wiktionary traces ~croc~ to Old Frankish *~krok~, while English Wiktionary allows either Frankish or Old Norse ~krókr~, both from Proto-Germanic *~krōkaz~ (“hook”). English ~crook~ is a cognate.
en.crocheter: Formed from the noun ~crochet~ (“small hook”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so “to work with a hook,” hence “to pick a lock.” The base ~crochet~ is itself built from ~croc~ (“hook”) and the diminutive suffix ~-et~, with a sound change in the spelling. A figurative sense, “to sidestep,” also exists. The verb thus carries two derivations in a row: a hook, a small hook, then the act of using one.
en.croire:
From Middle French ~croire~, from Old French ~creire~, ~croire~, from Latin ~crēdere~ (“to entrust as a loan; to trust, to have confidence in”). The Latin verb continues a Proto-Indo-European compound *~ḱred-dʰeh₁-~, literally “to place one's heart,” fusing *~ḱred-~ (the oblique stem of “heart”) with *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, set, place”). The same archaic compound surfaces far afield: Sanskrit ~śrad-dhā~ (“faith, trust”) and Old Irish ~creitid~ (“believes”) preserve the identical heart-placing image.

The earliest Latin sense was concrete and commercial — to ~crēdere~ was to entrust money to someone, to extend credit, trusting they would repay. From this lending of trust grew the sense “to have confidence,” and during the Christian era the strong religious meaning “to believe, to hold as an article of faith” developed and came to dominate. The metaphor at the bottom — belief as setting one's heart on something — is one of the oldest in Indo-European. From ~crēdere~ French inherited or borrowed a rich set: ~croyance~, ~croyant~, ~crédit~, ~crédible~, ~créance~, ~crédule~, and the liturgical ~credo~ (Latin for “I believe”).
en.croiser:
A denominal verb, derived from the noun ~croix~ (“cross”) with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~. ~Croix~ descends from Latin ~crux~ (genitive ~crucis~, “stake, cross”), the instrument on which the condemned were impaled or crucified. The same ~crux~ gave Italian ~croce~, Spanish ~cruz~, and — by way of Old Norse and Old Irish ~cros~ — English ~cross~ itself.

The ultimate origin of Latin ~crux~ is uncertain and best left open. The French verb means, fundamentally, “to put in the form of a cross”: one ~croise~ one's arms, two roads ~se croisent~ (intersect), and two travellers ~se croisent~ when their paths cross going opposite ways. From ~croix~ the language built a rich field: ~croisement~ (“crossing, intersection,” and in biology “crossbreeding”), ~croisière~ (“cruise,” a ship originally “crossing” to and fro on patrol), ~croisé~ (“crusader,” one who took the cross), and ~croisade~ (“crusade”). Through Latin ~crux~ the same root reaches English ~crucial~, ~crucify~, ~crusade~, and ~cruise~ — every one of them shaped, literally or figuratively, like a cross.
en.croquer:
The origin of ~croquer~ is not settled, and the sources offer two accounts. French Wiktionary treats it as imitative, from the onomatopoeia ~croc~, the dry sound of something hard breaking under the teeth, related to ~cric~ and ~crac~. English Wiktionary instead derives it from Middle French ~croquer~ and Old French ~crokier~ (“to slap, to hit”), and says it is probably a variant of the verb that became modern ~craquer~ (“to crack, to crunch”). The two accounts are compatible in spirit, since both link the verb to a family of sound-imitating words, but they disagree on whether the starting point is the sound itself or an older verb of striking.

Whatever its source, the verb's meanings are easy to follow. ~Croquer~ can describe the crunch of something hard under the teeth, hence ~croquer~ (“to eat with a crunch”) and the adjective ~croquant~ (“crunchy”). It also reaches consuming money, ~croquer sa fortune~ (“to squander one's wealth”), and drawing a quick outline, whence ~croquis~ (“sketch”). The sources do not trace how these senses grew from one another. Related words include ~croquette~, ~croque-monsieur~ and ~croque-mort~, and the sound-word family also contains ~craquer~.
en.crosser: ~Crosser~ is formed from ~crosse~ with the verb ending ~-er~: to hit with a ~crosse~, whether hockey stick, lacrosse stick or golf club. The noun ~crosse~ comes from Old French ~croce~ (“shepherd's staff”), borrowed from a Germanic language, probably Frankish *~krukkja~ (“crutch”). It is a cognate of Dutch ~kruk~, German ~Krücke~ and English ~crutch~, and French Wiktionary links it to ~croc~ (“hook”).
en.crotter: Formed from the noun ~crotte~ (“dropping”) plus the verb ending ~-er~: to ~crotter~ is to soil with droppings or mud. The noun comes from Old French ~crote~. English Wiktionary records it from the late twelfth century in ~crotes de chievres~ (“goat droppings”) and derives it, probably, from Old Dutch *~krotta~, a form deduced from Rhine Franconian ~krotz~, with an original sense of “ball-shaped excrement.” The suffix ~-er~ is the usual means of turning a noun into a verb meaning “provide with N” or “apply N.”
en.crouler:
The origin of ~crouler~ is uncertain, and the sources offer rival accounts. French Wiktionary lists Old French ~croller~ (“to shake, to tremble”) and the sense “to fall into ruins” from the twelfth century. One proposal is a Vulgar Latin verb *~crotalāre~ (“to shake”), from Latin ~crotalum~ (“rattle”). Another is Vulgar Latin *~corrotulāre~, built from ~co-~ and the root of ~rouler~ (“to roll”). English Wiktionary favors, with a hedge, a Vulgar Latin frequentative *~corrutulāre~ of Latin ~corruere~ (“to collapse”), and if so, Italian ~crollare~ is a cognate.

The recorded senses run from shaking to falling into ruins, and French Wiktionary lists later specialized uses, one dated 1721 meaning to launch a ship. It also floats a third account, in which the verb is imitative, grouped with ~courlis~ and ~croûter~. None of these proposals is settled, so the safest statement is that the verb is of uncertain origin. The meaning that survives is collapse, and the family includes ~écrouler~, formed with a prefix, and the participle ~croulant~ (“crumbling”).
en.croupir: Formed from the noun ~croupe~ (“rump”) with the ending ~-ir~ rather than the usual ~-er~, so ~croupir~ is a second-conjugation verb built on a noun. ~Croupe~ comes from Old French ~crope~, of Germanic origin, traced more precisely to Old Frankish *~kruppa~. Today ~croupir~ means to stagnate, to wallow or to rot.
en.croustiller:
French Wiktionary derives ~croustiller~ from Old Occitan ~croustilha~ (“to crunch”), itself built on ~crousta~ (“crust”) with the verb ending ~-iller~. English Wiktionary gives a plainer account, simply from ~croûte~ (“crust”), the French form of the same word. The two views agree on the root. In Latin that root is ~crusta~ (“rind, shell, crust”), the source of ~croûte~ and of Occitan ~crousta~.

The verb means to crunch or munch, and to become crisper. Its best-known relative is the adjective ~croustillant~ (“crusty, crunchy”), from the present participle, which also gives the figurative sense “racy” of a story. Other relatives of ~crusta~ in French include ~croûte~, ~croûton~ and ~crustacé~, and the English ~crust~ comes from the same Latin word. ~Croustiller~ itself is now rarer than its participle.
en.crouter: Derived from ~croûte~ (“crust”) with the verb ending ~-er~, according to the TLFi. The oldest sense is physical: in the eleventh century ~croster~ was said of bread forming a crust, and before 1593 Amyot used the verb for “to cover with a crust.” The slang sense “to eat” is attested in 1879, in Huysmans, and the word is now informal.
en.croître:
From Middle French ~croistre~, from Old French ~creistre~ (“to grow, prosper”), from Latin ~crescere~ (“to grow”), an inchoative verb (“to begin to grow”) built on the Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱer-~ (“to grow, become bigger”) — the same root that gave Latin ~creare~ (“to create”) and the grain-goddess ~Ceres~. It is the everyday cousin of Italian ~crescere~ and Spanish ~crecer~.

Through Latin ~crescere~ and Old French ~creistre~, an astonishing crowd of English words shares this ancestry: ~crescent~ (“the growing moon”), ~increase~, ~accrue~, ~recruit~ (a fresh “growth” of soldiers), ~crew~, and — via ~concrescere~ “to grow together” — ~concrete~. In French the family is just as wide: ~croissance~ (“growth”), ~croissant~ (“growing,” hence the crescent-shaped pastry), ~accroître~ and ~décroître~, and ~crû~ (a wine's “growth,” its vineyard of origin). The inchoative ~-sc-~ that marks ~crescere~ as “entering into growth” is the very element that, worn down, gives French verbs like ~croître~ their distinctive look.
en.croûter:
From Old French ~croster~ (“to form a crust, to cover with a crust”), itself from Latin ~crusta~ (“crust, hard shell”). The Latin noun named any hard outer layer, and the verb simply turned that layer into an action: to become covered with a crust, or to cover something with one. The same Latin word reached English as ~crust~, by way of Old French.

Modern French ~croûter~ keeps the literal sense of forming a crust, and it also has a familiar-register sense, “to eat.” The noun ~croûte~ is the center of the family, which includes ~croûton~, ~encroûter~ (“to coat with a crust”) and ~écroûter~ (“to strip off the crust”). Latin ~crusta~ also gave the learned verb ~incruster~ (“to inlay, to encrust”), a distant relative of the homely ~croûter~. The circumflex in ~croûte~ and ~croûter~ marks the lost ~s~ of Old French ~croste~.
en.crucifier:
From Latin ~crucifigere~ (“to fasten to a cross”), a compound of ~crux~ (“cross”) and ~figere~ (“to fix, to fasten, to nail”). The Latin noun ~crux~ is the source of French ~croix~, and the same pair of elements gave Italian ~crocifiggere~ and English ~crucify~. The Latin imperative ~crucifige~ (“crucify!”) is the form recorded in the French Wiktionary entry.

The ending of ~crucifier~ looks like the productive suffix ~-ifier~, but that is a surface resemblance: the ~-fi-~ comes from ~figere~, not from ~facere~ (“to make”). The related noun shows the real stem. French ~crucifixion~ is explained by ~figere~ and is not *~crucifiction~, as an ~-fier~ verb would lead one to expect. The same ~figere~ gave French ~fixe~ and ~fixer~, and the compound ~crucifix~ keeps the Latin participle ~crucifixus~ (“fastened to a cross”) intact.
en.crypter: A back-formation: French Wiktionary says ~crypter~ arose from ~encrypter~ by dropping the prefix ~en-~. The longer verb rests on the root ~crypt-~, which French took from Greek ~kruptós~ (“hidden”), the same root as in ~crypte~, ~cryptographie~ and ~cryptogramme~. To ~crypter~ a message is therefore, at root, to hide it. Many language authorities prefer ~chiffrer~ for this sense, but ~crypter~ is common in everyday French about files, messages and television signals.
en.cryptographier: Formed from ~cryptographie~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to encrypt.” The noun is analysed in two ways: as ~cryptographe~ plus ~-ie~ (French Wiktionary), or as ~crypto-~ plus ~-graphie~ (English Wiktionary). Both rest on Greek elements meaning “hidden” and “writing.”
en.crâner: Formed from ~crâne~ with the verbal ending ~-er~: to show off. The adjective ~crâne~ meant a reckless, bold person, and is the same word as ~crâne~ (“skull”). English Wiktionary suggests, with a “probably,” that the image is of a reckless person charging head first, much like Spanish ~calavera~ (“reckless person, libertine”). The noun for “skull” was borrowed into Middle French from Medieval Latin ~crānium~, itself from Greek ~kraníon~ (“skull, head”).
en.crécher: ~Crécher~ is formed from the noun ~crèche~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The sources give no route for the informal sense “to live, to crash.” ~Crèche~ itself is Germanic in origin: it comes from Old French ~creche~ (“manger, feeding trough”), by way of Late Latin ~cripia~ from a Frankish word reconstructed as *~krippija~. It is cognate with German ~Krippe~ and English ~crib~.
en.crédibiliser: Formed from the adjective ~crédible~ with the suffix ~-iser~, which makes verbs meaning “to make A”: ~crédibiliser~ means to make credible. ~Crédible~ was borrowed from Latin ~crēdibilis~ (“believable”), from ~crēdō~ (“to believe”), and it is related to ~croyable~. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs.
en.créditer: Formed from the noun ~crédit~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun was borrowed from Italian ~credito~, from Latin ~crēditum~, the supine of ~crēdere~ (“to believe, to trust”). Credit is thus literally the belief that a borrower will repay. To ~créditer~ an account is to enter a sum in it, extending that trust or the amount owed to it.
en.créer:
From Old French ~creer~, from Latin ~creāre~ (“to bring forth, to produce, to beget”). The verb belongs to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱer-~ (“to grow, to nourish”), and its oldest Latin sense was close to “to make grow.” That same root stands behind ~crēscere~ (“to grow, to arise”) and behind ~Cerēs~, the Roman goddess of grain and agriculture — so to “create” is etymologically to cause to flourish. Cognate verbs survive as Italian ~creare~ and Spanish ~crear~, and the family entered English as ~create~ and ~creature~.

In classical Latin ~creāre~ already covered both the divine act of bringing the world into being and the civic act of electing or appointing a magistrate, who was “created” by the people's vote. French ~créer~ inherited chiefly the productive, originating sense — to bring something new into existence — while keeping a foothold in officialdom, as when a post or a title is “created.” From the same Latin verb and the broader root come a rich family of French words, among them ~création~, ~créature~, ~créateur~, ~créatif~, and, through ~crēscere~, ~croître~ (“to grow”) and ~croissant~ (“growing; crescent; croissant”). The English ~recruit~, a fresh “growth” of new soldiers, springs from the same image of growing.
en.crémer: Two unrelated verbs share this spelling. The one glossed “to add cream” is formed from ~crème~ and the ending ~-er~. The other is a learned borrowing from Latin ~cremāre~ (“to burn”), and it is a doublet of ~cramer~: the same Latin verb reached French both by the learned road, as ~crémer~, and by the popular road, as ~cramer~ (compare slang ~cramé~, “burnt”). This second verb is the root of ~crémation~ and ~crématoire~, and of English ~cremate~. The cream sense is French-internal, while the burning sense goes back to Latin.
en.créneler: Formed from ~crenel~, the old form of ~créneau~ (“battlement, crenel”), with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~. The verb means to provide with ~créneaux~, that is, to cut regular notches into the top of a wall or into the edge of an object. The ~-er~ ending descends from Latin ~-are~ and is the ordinary way French builds verbs on nouns. The base ~crenel~ is no longer the usual spelling: the modern noun ~créneau~ replaced it, while the verb kept the older stem and so preserves a trace of the earlier word.
en.créner: The only source gives a cross-reference to Old French ~crener~ (“to notch”), so ~créner~ is inherited from that verb, without a further origin stated. The sense “to notch” explains the modern technical use: in typography ~créner~ means to kern a letter, that is, to cut away part of its body so that a neighboring letter can tuck in.
en.créoliser: Formed from ~créole~ with the suffix ~-iser~: to make creole, or to give a language or culture a creole character. The noun is borrowed from Spanish ~criollo~, from Portuguese ~crioulo~, which meant a servant raised in the household. It derives from ~criar~ (“to raise”), itself from Latin ~creō~ (“to create”). French Wiktionary also mentions a folk etymology from a Spanish “create it,” but it has no historical basis.
en.crépir: The French text calls ~crépir~ a doublet of ~crêper~ with the ending ~-ir~. It first meant “to shrivel, to become grainy,” and in masonry it means “to give a wall its grain,” that is, to roughcast or render it. ~Crêper~ is ~crêpe~ + ~-er~, from Old French ~crespe~, from Latin ~crispus~ (“curly, crinkled”). The idea of something wrinkled or tightly curled thus underlies both verbs. The same root gave ~crépu~ (“frizzy”) and the learned ~crisper~.
en.crépiter:
Borrowed from Latin ~crepitāre~ (“to make a sharp, repeated sound”), a frequentative of ~crepāre~ (“to crack, to rattle”). A frequentative is a verb that repeats the action of its base, so ~crepitāre~ is literally “to crack again and again.” That fits the French verb well: it describes a fire, hail or gunfire, a rapid series of small dry noises rather than one crack.

The base verb ~crepāre~ lived on in French as ~crever~ (“to burst”), which shows how one Latin root can split into a learned and an inherited branch. The learned side gave ~crépiter~ and the noun ~crépitement~ in French, and English borrowed the same Latin verb as ~crepitate~. Today ~crépiter~ is used of fire, rain on a roof, applause or frying oil, and figuratively of a burst of words or sparks of wit. The sense has stayed close to its Latin source: a sound made of many tiny, quick snaps.
en.crétiniser: ~Crétiniser~ is formed from the noun ~crétin~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which makes verbs meaning “to make A” or “to turn into N”: to make someone a cretin. The origin of ~crétin~ is debated. The accounts include a Franco-Provençal form of ~chrétien~ (“Christian”), used as a word of pity for afflicted people and later turned pejorative; a German ~Kreidling~, from ~Kreide~ (“chalk”), for the pale skin; and a derivation from ~crêt~ (“ridge”), the cretin being a mountain dweller.
en.crêper: ~Crêper~ is formed from ~crêpe~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~: to give a crinkled, frizzy texture, above all to backcomb hair. The noun ~crêpe~ is the modern form of Old French ~crespe~, from Latin ~crispus~ (“curly, crinkled”). The verb carries that original idea of something wrinkled or tightly curled, and it is most often heard in ~se crêper les cheveux~, to tease one's hair into volume, and in the participle ~crêpé~. The same root also gave ~crépu~ (“frizzy”) and the learned ~crisper~.
en.cuber: Formed from ~cube~ plus the verbal suffix ~-er~, with the sense “to raise a number to the third power.” The noun was borrowed from Latin ~cubus~ (“die”), which in turn came from Ancient Greek ~kúbos~ (“die”). A cube was thus named after the gaming die, a solid with six equal square faces.
en.cueillir:
From Old French ~coillir~, inherited from Latin ~colligere~ (“to gather, to collect”), itself ~con-~ (“together”) + ~legere~ (“to gather, to pick”). The modern spelling needs explaining. In Old French the stressed forms of the verb, such as ~cueil~, had a diphthong from an open Latin vowel, as in Old French ~cuer~, which became ~cœur~. The infinitive took its stem from those stressed forms, and its ending ~-ir~ was a later analogical reshaping, partly on the past form ~coilli~. The original infinitives, ~cueudre~, ~cueildre~ and ~cueldre~, fell out of use. ~Cueillir~ is a doublet of the learned ~colliger~, which took the same Latin verb straight from the book. English ~collect~ comes from the same Latin source, and the root of ~legere~ also lies behind ~lire~, ~élire~ and ~lecture~.

The Latin verb meant to gather things together, and French narrowed it to picking flowers and fruit, though the broader sense survives in ~accueillir~ (“to welcome”, literally to gather someone to oneself) and ~recueillir~ (“to collect”, also “to gather in thought”). The noun ~cueillette~ names the harvest of wild or garden produce. The verb has a famous conjugation, with its ~-e~ endings in the present (~je cueille~) and the future ~cueillerai~. Behind the whole family stands a Proto-Indo-European sense of gathering, preserved as well in Greek ~légein~ and in English ~legend~, literally “what is to be read”.
en.cuirasser: ~Cuirasser~ is formed from the noun ~cuirasse~ (“cuirass, breastplate”) with the ending ~-er~, and means to armor, most often in the reflexive ~se cuirasser~, “to steel oneself.” The noun comes from Old French ~cuirace~, probably borrowed from Old Occitan ~coirassa~, Italian ~corazza~ or Old Aragonese ~cuyraça~, from Late Latin ~coriacea~ (“leather garment”), ultimately from Latin ~corium~ (“hide”). It was probably influenced by French ~cuir~, and it is a doublet of ~coriace~.
en.cuire:
From Gallo-Romance *~cocere~, a reshaping of Late Latin ~cocere~, itself an alteration of Classical Latin ~coquere~ (“to cook”). The earlier Latin form was *~quoquō~, dissimilated from Proto-Italic *~kʷekʷō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~pekʷ-~ (“to cook, to ripen”). The root is widespread: it gives Ancient Greek ~πέσσω~ (~péssō~, “to cook, to digest”), Sanskrit ~pácati~ (“he cooks”), and survives faintly in English ~cook~ (a Latin borrowing).

The verb has always covered both the cook’s fire and nature’s slow heat: one can ~cuire~ a meal, but fruit and grain also ~cuire~ as they ripen under the sun, faithful to the root’s double sense of “cook” and “ripen.” French extends ~cuire~ to the sting of pain — a wound or sunburned skin can ~cuire~ (“to smart, to burn”) — and to bitter experience, as in the warning ~il vous en cuira~ (“you’ll regret it, you’ll pay for it”). The same Latin ~coquere~ left a trail of French words: ~cuisine~ and ~cuisinier~, ~cuit~ and ~biscuit~ (“twice-cooked”), ~cuisson~, the archaic ~queux~ (“cook”), and ~cocotte~ (“a small cooking pot”).
en.cuisiner:
~cuisiner~ is simply ~cuisine~ plus the verb ending ~-er~ — and it is attested as far back as the thirteenth-century Chanson d'Antioche. ~cuisine~ descends from Late Latin ~coquīna~ (“kitchen”), from classical ~coquere~ (“to cook; to ripen”). That verb's history holds a small phonetic marvel: Proto-Indo-European *~pekʷ-~ (“to cook, to ripen”) should have given Latin a p-initial verb, but the first consonant assimilated to the second, *~kʷekʷō~, yielding ~coquō~ — in Latin, even the word bubbles. The root's relatives span the family: Sanskrit ~pácati~ and Greek ~péssō~ (“cooks, ripens”), Italian ~cucina~, Spanish ~cocina~ — and English ~kitchen~ with German ~Küche~, both from a very early Germanic borrowing of ~coquīna~: the Anglo-Saxon kitchen is a Latin room.

In French the root cooked up a whole pantry: ~cuire~ and ~cuisson~, ~biscuit~ (literally “twice-cooked,” the hard bread of soldiers and sailors), ~charcuterie~ (from ~chair cuite~, “cooked flesh”), and ~précoce~, from Latin ~praecox~ — “early-ripening,” that is, “cooked ahead of time.” The most surprising descendant took the long way home: Latin ~praecoqua~, “early-ripening peaches,” passed into Greek, then into Arabic as ~al-barqūq~, then through Iberia into French as ~abricot~ — the apricot is etymologically the “precocious” fruit, a Latin word that toured the Mediterranean for a millennium. As for ~cuisiner~ itself, it long meant simply “to do the cooking”; in the nineteenth century it turned figurative, and by 1881 ~cuisiner quelqu'un~ meant to interrogate someone relentlessly — the very metaphor English found in “to grill.”
en.cuiter: A colloquial verb formed from ~cuite~ with the ending ~-er~, used as ~se cuiter~, “to get drunk.” The noun ~cuite~ is the feminine past participle of ~cuire~ (“to cook”) turned into a noun, and in slang it means a drinking bout, as in ~prendre une cuite~. The verb is informal and belongs to speech rather than formal writing.
en.cuivrer: ~Cuivrer~ is formed from the noun ~cuivre~ (“copper”) with the verb ending ~-er~, in the sense “to provide with N”: to coat something with copper. The noun is inherited from Old French ~cuivre~, from Latin ~cuprum~ and ~cupreum~ (~aes~), which are popular variants of ~Cyprium~ (“of Cyprus”). Latin took the word from Ancient Greek ~Kúpros~ (“Cyprus”), the island from which the Romans very probably imported their copper. They did not adopt the Greek word ~khalkós~ for the metal, and named it after its place of origin by metonymy. The same Latin word gave Spanish ~cobre~ and Romanian ~cupru~.
en.culbuter: ~Culbuter~ is a compound of Middle French ~culer~ (“to strike on the backside”) and ~buter~, a variant of ~bouter~ (“to push”). The verb is also attested in the spelling ~cullebuter~. The first element is built on ~cul~ (“backside”), which comes from Latin ~cūlus~. The modern verb means “to take a tumble,” to fall over.
en.culer: Two accounts appear. One derives ~culer~ from the noun ~cul~ (“the back part of an object”) plus the verb ending ~-er~. The other sees it as ~enculer~ with its first syllable dropped. Either way the base is ~cul~, from Latin ~culus~ (“buttocks”). The verb is used in nautical French for going astern, which fits the idea of moving rear end first.
en.culminer: Borrowed from Medieval Latin ~culmināre~ (“to crown, to bring to a peak”), a verb formed on Latin ~culmen~ (“top, summit, ridge”). The French verb keeps the image of a summit: a career, a crisis or a story ~culmine~ when it reaches its highest point, and the expression ~point culminant~ names that peak. English ~culminate~ is a parallel borrowing from the same Latin verb, so the two languages share both the word and the picture of reaching the top.
en.culotter: Formed on the noun ~culotte~ (“breeches”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so one sense of the verb is to clothe someone in breeches and another is to season a pipe or a pan through use. The noun ~culotte~ is built from ~cul~ and the suffix ~-otte~, like a feminine of ~culot~. The double ~t~ of the verb follows the noun. ~Cul~ comes from Latin ~cūlus~ (“backside”) by way of Old French. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is French's default way of making a verb from a noun.
en.culpabiliser: ~Culpabiliser~ is formed from Late Latin ~culpabilis~ (“blameworthy”), the source of French ~coupable~, with the verb-forming suffix ~-iser~. The Latin adjective is built on ~culpa~ (“fault, blame”). The verb therefore means, literally, to make someone ~coupable~, and by extension to make them feel guilty. So French holds two descendants of one Latin adjective: the inherited ~coupable~ and this derived verb.
en.cultiver:
Attested 1119 as a learned reshaping of Old French ~coutiver~, refashioned on Latin ~cultus~ (“tillage, cultivation, worship”) and more precisely on a reconstructed *~cultivus~ derived from ~cultiō~ (“cultivation”). The whole family rests on Latin ~colere~ (“to till, to tend, to inhabit, to worship”), from Proto-Italic *~kʷelō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~kʷelh₁-~ (“to turn, to move around, and so to dwell”). Cognate, through that root, with English ~wheel~ and with Ancient Greek ~télos~ (“end, purpose”).

The semantic arc is remarkable: a root meaning “to turn / revolve” drifted to “to dwell where one turns about,” then to “to till the ground one dwells on,” and finally to “to tend and revere” — which is why ~colere~ fathered at once ~cultiver~ (the field), ~culture~ (the mind), ~colon~ and ~colonie~ (settlers who inhabit), and ~culte~ (worship). To ~cultiver~ a garden, a talent, or a friendship is the same gesture under three guises: patient tending. French even keeps coining on this stem — playful forms like ~culturer~ show the suffixation is still alive.
en.cumuler:
Borrowed in 1354, in Bersuire's translation of Livy, from Latin ~cumulāre~ (“to heap up, to pile high”), from ~cumulus~ (“heap, pile”), a noun sometimes traced — the evidence is admittedly thin — to PIE *~ḱewh₁-~ (“to swell”), which would make it distant kin to Greek ~κῦμα~ (“swell, wave”). The Latin verb had in fact already entered French once before, by inheritance rather than borrowing: worn down by a millennium of speech, ~cumulāre~ had become ~combler~ (“to fill to the brim, to fulfill”) and ~cumulus~ had become ~comble~ — so ~cumuler~ and ~combler~ are doublets, the learned and the popular face of a single verb. Spanish shows the same split between popular ~colmar~ and learned ~acumular~; English ~accumulate~ and ~cumulative~ complete the family portrait.

The borrowed twin took the paperwork. Where ~combler~ stayed warm and concrete — one fills a gap, showers someone with joy — ~cumuler~ specialized in administration: by 1690 it meant joining several legal claims together, and by 1784 holding several positions at once, the sense behind the very French debate over the ~cumul des mandats~, a politician's stacking of elected offices. The parent noun meanwhile had a second, airier career: in 1803 the Englishman Luke Howard, father of cloud classification, chose ~cumulus~ to name the puffy heaped cloud of fair weather, and French adopted it in turn — every summer sky is, etymologically, piled high. As for ~comble~, it gave French the attic (~les combles~, the space heaped under the roof), the phrase ~de fond en comble~ (“from top to bottom”) and the cry ~c'est un comble !~ — “that's the last straw,” literally the point where the measure overflows.
en.curer:
~Curer~ goes back to Latin ~cūrāre~ (“to take care of, to treat”). French Wiktionary gives the Latin verb directly. English Wiktionary adds that the verb was inherited by way of Old French ~curer~, itself borrowed from Latin. The Latin verb derives from the noun ~cūra~ (“care”), a standard analysis. The cognate English verb ~cure~ comes from the same Latin source.

In French the verb means to clean out or scrape, as in ~curer un fossé~ (“to clear a ditch”) or ~se curer les dents~. The sources consulted do not say how the sense moved from “to care for” to this one. The Latin noun ~cūra~ is behind many other French words. ~Cure~ (“treatment”), ~curé~ (the priest charged with the “care” of souls), ~curieux~ (originally “careful”), ~sécurité~ (“freedom from care”) and ~récurer~ (“to scour”, with ~re-~) all belong to this family, as do English ~curious~ and ~accurate~.
en.cureter: Formed from ~curette~ (“scraper, curette”) with the verbal ending ~-er~: to scrape a cavity with that instrument, as in the surgical operation of curettage. The noun is itself built from the verb ~curer~ (“to clean out”) and the diminutive suffix ~-ette~, so a ~curette~ is literally a small cleaning tool. The verb ~curer~ comes from Latin ~cūrāre~ (“to take care of”).
en.customiser: ~Customiser~ was borrowed from English ~customise~ (or ~customize~), meaning to adapt something to a buyer's wishes or make it to order. French Wiktionary links the English verb to ~customer~, in the sense of a merchant adapting goods to the client and producing made-to-measure items. The French verb takes the regular ending of the verbs in ~-iser~.
en.cuveler: Derived from the noun ~cuve~ (“vat, tub”) with the suffix ~-eler~, which here means “to provide with”: to line a mine shaft with planking. ~Cuve~ was inherited from Old French ~cuve~, from Latin ~cūpa~. It is a doublet of ~coupe~ (“cup”), which came from a Late Latin variant, ~cuppa~. The suffix is little used today, and ~cuveler~ is one of the old verbs the TLFi cites for it.
en.cuver: The sense “to ferment” is formed from ~cuve~ (“vat”) with ~-er~ and is first attested in 1433. ~Cuve~ is inherited from Latin ~cūpa~, which also gave ~coupe~ through a Late Latin variant; the two are doublets. The other senses, such as sleeping off wine (~cuver son vin~), are explained in two ways: either they come from the same noun, the drinker being likened to a vat, or they come from Latin ~cubāre~ (“to lie down, to sleep”), a variant of ~couver~. The sources do not settle between the two.
en.cyanoser: Formed from ~cyanose~ and the suffix ~-iser~. ~Cyanose~ was coined by François Sulpice Beudant from Ancient Greek ~κυάνεος~ (~kuáneos~, “dark blue”) and the suffix ~-ose~. The suffix ~-iser~ builds verbs meaning to make or cause, so the verb means “to cause cyanosis,” a bluish discoloration of the skin or tissue.
en.cylindrer: Formed from the noun ~cylindre~ (“cylinder”), and recorded from 1765. The verb means “to roll” or “to shape into a cylinder,” as when a road surface is rolled flat or a sheet of metal is passed between rollers. The noun comes from Latin ~cylindrus~, borrowed from Greek ~κύλινδρος~ (“roller”).
en.câbler: ~Câbler~ is a denominal verb: the noun ~câble~ plus the ending ~-er~, so to fit with a cable or to cable. The noun comes from Late Latin ~capulum~, which gave Old French ~chable~ and ~cheable~. The Norman and Picard form ~cable~, strong in the vocabulary of ships, ousted the Francien ~chable~ for good in the eighteenth century. English Wiktionary adds that Vulgar Latin *~caplum~, a contracted form of ~capulum~, lay between, and relates the Latin to ~capiō~ (“to take”).
en.câliner:
French Wiktionary says the verb is probably a borrowing from Norman ~caliner~ (“to rest in the shade”), itself derived from ~caline~ (“heavy, stifling heat”). Both Wiktionaries trace ~caline~ to Vulgar Latin *~calina~. French Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~calēre~ (“to be hot”), and English Wiktionary from ~calidus~ (“warm”), which belong to the same family. The suffix ~-er~ turns the noun into a verb.

The sense moved from oppressive heat to the slackness it brings. French Wiktionary points to ~chômer~ for the same shift from “heat” to “laziness, indolence,” and the sources do not describe the later step to “cuddle.” Because the Norman source is only probable, the origin is best held loosely. The same Latin family gave the French adjective ~chaud~ and the noun ~chaleur~, so ~câliner~ is a distant cousin of both. The noun ~câlin~ (“cuddle”) belongs to the same family.
en.céder:
Borrowed from Latin ~cedere~ (“to go, walk, withdraw, yield”). The traditional analysis, going back to Pokorny, reconstructs ~cedere~ from an element *~ce-~ plus the root of ~sedere~ (“to sit”), giving a sense like “to go away by stepping aside.” The verb is cognate with the family seen in Ancient Greek ~ὁδός~ (“road, way”) and shares the broad Indo-European notion of going. From the idea of giving up one's place came the sense of conceding.

In Latin ~cedere~ first meant simply to move or walk, then to withdraw and so to give way; affairs were said to ~cedere~ well or badly, to “go” well or badly. French ~céder~ kept the yielding sense: to cede territory, to give up, to give in (~céder à la tentation~, “to yield to temptation”), and also to break or collapse under strain — a rope or a dam that ~cède~. Latin contrasted yielding with standing firm (~obstare~, ~resistere~). The same root threads through a large legal and motional French vocabulary: ~cession~, ~accéder~, ~procéder~, ~succéder~, ~précéder~, ~recéder~, and ~incessible~ — each preserving the original image of going, stepping, and giving way.
en.célébrer:
From Latin ~celebrāre~ (“to frequent, to throng, to solemnize, to praise”), derived from the adjective ~celeber~ (“crowded, populous, much-frequented”). The further origin of ~celeber~ is uncertain and best left unguessed, but the Latin verb is the clear and well-attested source of French ~célébrer~, English ~celebrate~, Italian ~celebrare~, and Spanish ~celebrar~.

The surprise is in that root adjective: ~celeber~ first meant simply “crowded” — a place thick with people. A spot that drew throngs was busy, then renowned, then famous, and a ceremony that drew throngs was a grand public occasion. So ~celebrāre~ slid from “to attend in great numbers” to “to mark with solemn pomp” and finally “to honor, to extol.” Both modern strands survive in French: one ~célèbre~ a mass or a marriage (the solemn, ritual sense) and one ~célèbre~ a victory or a hero (the festive, praising sense). From the same ~celeber~ come ~célèbre~ (“famous”) and ~célébrité~ (“fame, a celebrity”) — and the thread back to the beginning is plain, for to be a celebrity is, etymologically, to be surrounded by a crowd.
en.cémenter: Formed from the noun ~cément~ with the verb ending ~-er~, the technical word for case-hardening steel by heating it in contact with carbon. The noun ~cément~ is borrowed from Latin ~caementum~ and is a doublet of ~ciment~. The two French words thus share one Latin source, and ~cémenter~ belongs to the metalworking branch of the family.
en.césariser: ~Césariser~ (“to give the César Award to”) is formed with the suffix ~-iser~, “to make, to treat with,” on ~César~, the name of the French film prize. French Wiktionary also offers a second account, deriving the verb from ~césarienne~ + ~-iser~. That noun is the feminine of ~césarien~. By the traditional explanation, Latin ~Caesar~ or ~Caeso~ was a surname given to children delivered by an incision, from ~caedere~ (“to cut”), whence the later ~césarienne~. Which derivation suits which sense is left open.
en.côcher:
From Old French ~cauchier~ (also ~chauchier~), inherited from Latin ~calcāre~ (“to tread, to trample”). ~Calcāre~ is itself derived from ~calx~ (“heel”), so the verb is literally one that uses the heel, and hence one that treads or tramples. In the vocabulary of birds, ~côcher~ means “to mate,” said of a male covering a female.

The Latin verb gave French several words by different routes. Through Old French came ~cauchemar~, the nightmare that “presses” on the sleeper, and English ~caulk~ (to pack seams so that they are watertight) comes from the Norman form of the same verb. French borrowed the verb a second time from Italian, giving ~calquer~ (“to trace a copy”), and learned compounds such as ~inculquer~ (“to instill”) rest on the same Latin stem.
en.côtoyer: Derived from the noun ~côte~ with the verb suffix ~-oyer~, and inherited from Old French ~costoier~. The noun ~côte~ comes from Latin ~costa~ (“rib, side”) and had the senses of “rib,” “slope” and “coast.” The suffix ~-oyer~ often gives the sense of continued action or of acting along or by means of something, as in ~tutoyer~. So ~côtoyer~ meant literally “to go along the side (or the coast),” as when a ship hugs the shore. The figurative sense “to rub shoulders with, to associate with” grew from that image of moving alongside.
en.dactylographier: ~Dactylographier~ is formed from the noun ~dactylographie~ (“typewriting”) and the verb ending ~-er~, meaning “to type”. French Wiktionary analyzes ~dactylographie~ as ~dactylo-~ (“finger”) + ~-graphie~ (“writing”), a pair of Greek-derived elements, while English Wiktionary derives it from ~dactylographe~ (“typist”) + ~-ie~. Either way, the picture is of writing with the fingers. The Greek source of ~dactylo-~ is the word for “finger”, a general-knowledge detail that also gives ~dactylo~, the everyday French word for a typist.
en.daigner:
From Old French ~deignier~, inherited from Latin ~dignārī~ (“to deem worthy”), a verb built on the adjective ~dignus~ (“worthy”). Italian ~degnare~ is its cognate and descends from the same Latin verb. The Latin adjective is also the source of French ~digne~ (“worthy”) and ~dignité~, as well as English ~dignity~ and ~deign~, the latter borrowed from the French verb.

The Latin sense was to consider someone or something worthy, and French ~daigner~ turned this into the act of granting a favor from above: to see fit to do something, often with a hint of condescension. Today it is used almost only before an infinitive, and very often in the negative, as when someone ~ne daigne pas répondre~. The verb has an opposite in ~dédaigner~ (“to disdain”), which Old French formed by adding a negative prefix to ~deignier~, and English ~disdain~ comes from it. The family also includes ~indigne~ (“unworthy”).
en.daller: ~Daller~ is derived from the noun ~dalle~ (“paving slab”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, and means to pave with slabs. The TLFi finds it first in 1319, an isolated attestation, and again in 1800. The noun is itself a Norman word, probably borrowed, perhaps as a nautical term, from Old Norse ~dæla~, a channel for draining water on a ship. The slab sense of ~dalle~ is attested later, in 1676.
en.damasquiner: Formed from ~damasquin~ (“of Damascus”) with the verb suffix ~-er~. The adjective ~damasquin~ was borrowed from Italian ~damaschino~ and served in Old French as a name for damask. The verb ~damasquiner~ means to damascene, that is, to treat metal in the manner named after the city, and so it carries the name of Damascus into a craft term.
en.damasser: ~Damasser~ is formed from the noun ~damas~ with the verb ending ~-er~, and means to work a fabric into damask. ~Damas~ is the name of the Syrian city of Damascus, after which the fabric was named. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~, the infinitive ending of the first conjugation, and is the usual way French coins verbs from nouns.
en.damer: French has two verbs ~damer~, from two different words ~dame~. In chess, ~damer~ means to turn a piece into a queen, from ~dame~ (“queen”), which is Old French ~dame~, from Late Latin ~domna~, a shortened form of Latin ~domina~ (“mistress of the house”). The other, “to groom snow,” comes from a separate ~dame~ (“beetle, rammer”), a tool for packing material down. Both verbs add the suffix ~-er~ to a noun.
en.damner: From Latin ~damnāre~ (“to condemn”), a verb built on ~damnum~ (“loss, damage”). The French verb is a learned borrowing, and Latin ~damnāre~ also gave Italian ~dannare~. English took the word from Old French as ~damn~, and the prefixed Latin form ~condemnāre~ gave French ~condamner~ and English ~condemn~. In Latin the verb belonged to the language of courts: to ~damnāre~ someone was to pronounce a sentence against them. ~Damnum~ itself reached French by the popular road as ~dommage~, so ~dommage~ (“damage, pity”) and ~damner~ are distant relatives. Also from this family are ~damnation~ and ~condamner~.
en.dandiner: ~Dandiner~ is usually explained as ~dandin~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~; English Wiktionary also offers a Middle Dutch source, ~dantinnen~ (“to trifle”), so the origin is not fully settled. ~Dandin~ itself comes from an expressive stem ~dand-~ that evokes a back-and-forth motion and hesitation; compare ~dadais~. The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, turns the noun into a verb, and ~dandiner~ means to sway from one foot to the other, to waddle along with a heavy side-to-side motion.
en.danser:
From Old French ~dancier~ (twelfth century), a verb of the langue d'oïl whose ultimate origin is genuinely uncertain. The leading account makes it Frankish, but the sources offer two competing Germanic etymons and flag a difficulty with each. By one hypothesis it descends from Frankish *~dintjan~ (compare Dutch ~deinzen~, « to move about, draw back »), though the expected vowel would be /i/, not the /a/ of ~danser~; by another it goes back to Frankish *~dansōn~ (« to draw, drag »), picturing the dance as a stately, gliding step. Neither is settled.

French ~danser~ was a triumphant export: it spread far beyond its home, giving English ~dance~, and standing beside Spanish ~danzar~ and Italian ~danzare~ (which borrowed it alongside their native ~bailar~ and ~ballare~, from a different root *~ball-~). Modern kin of the verb include ~danse~, ~danseur~, ~danseuse~, and ~dancing~. A vivid old idiom, « faire ~danser~ les écus, » meant to make coins « dance » out of a purse — a turn of phrase sometimes cited in support of the « drag, pull » hypothesis, though that origin remains unproven.
en.dansoter: The verb is derived from ~danser~ (“to dance”) with the ending ~-oter~. This suffix usually softens or belittles the action of the base verb, so the result means to dance a little, or to dance badly, as the gloss “dance poorly” has it. It works like ~vivoter~ (“to get by barely”), formed from ~vivre~ (“to live”). The sources give only ~danser~ as the origin, and the verb belongs to the group of light, slightly mocking formations in ~-oter~.
en.dansotter: Formed from ~danser~ (“to dance”) with the suffix ~-oter~, which gives a verb a diminutive, slightly belittling sense: to dance a little, or badly. The TLFi dates it to 1648, in Scarron's burlesque ~Virgile travesti~. Wiktionary treats it as a spelling variant of ~dansoter~. The verb belongs to the same small family as ~chantonner~ and ~vivoter~, where a modest ending turns a vigorous action into a halting one.
en.darder: Formed from the noun ~dard~ (“dart, javelin”) with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, so the verb means to hurl or shoot something like a dart. The noun came into French through Old French ~dart~ from Frankish *~daroth~ (“throwing weapon”), a word with cousins in Old High German ~tart~ and Old Norse ~darraðr~. French Wiktionary also offers a Gaulish alternative, ~darso~, with the same sense. The two accounts are not reconciled in the sources, so the Germanic origin is the better documented one.
en.dater:
A fourteenth-century formation from the noun ~date~, with the suffix ~-er~. ~date~ comes from Latin ~data~, the feminine past participle of ~dare~ (“to give”), lifted from the formula ~data littera~ (“letter given”) — the phrase Roman and medieval scribes wrote before the place and day a document was issued, as in ~data Romae~ (“given at Rome”). ~dare~ descends from PIE *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). Cognate with Italian ~datare~ and Spanish ~datar~, and, through ~data~, with English ~date~.

So the very notion of a calendar “date” is fossilized inside a giving: a letter was “given” on such a day, and the participle naming the act of giving slid over to name the day itself. To ~dater~ a document is to record that moment of issue; from there the verb grew the intransitive sense “to be old-fashioned,” as in ~ça date~ — a thing so plainly of its time that it betrays its age. The same ~dare~ root runs deep in French through ~donner~, ~don~, ~dose~, and learned ~data~; and ~dater~ itself anchors a tidy family — ~datation~, ~datable~, ~antidater~, and ~postdater~ — every one of them still quietly turning on the idea of something “given” at a fixed point in time.
en.dauber:
French Wiktionary distinguishes two verbs ~dauber~ and records a third proposal. The first verb is of Germanic origin, from ~dubban~ (“to strike”), the source of ~adouber~ (“to dub a knight”) by prefixation. This fits the sense “to hit,” and the figurative “to run down, to mock someone,” as in ~dauber sur quelqu'un~.

The second verb is tied to ~daube~, a cooking term, which comes from Italian ~dobba~ (“marinade”). Some etymologists link it to the first verb, on the idea that meat cooked in a ~daube~ must be beaten to make it tender. According to Alain Rey, the verb would instead come probably from Latin ~dealbāre~ (“to whiten”). These accounts compete, and the sources do not settle which one explains each sense. The origin of ~dauber~ is therefore best treated as disputed.
en.dealer: Formed from ~deal~, a noun borrowed from English ~deal~ (“bargain, business”), with the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to deal drugs.” The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is the default way French turns a noun, borrowed ones included, into a verb.
en.demander:
From Old French ~demander~ (attested around 980), from Latin ~dēmandāre~ (“to entrust, to commit; to charge with”), built from ~dē-~ (“fully, away”) and ~mandāre~ (“to commit to one's charge, to order”). ~mandāre~ itself is transparently ~manus~ (“hand”) plus a verb of giving, so its literal sense is “to put into someone's hand” — to entrust. ~manus~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~man-~ / *~meh₂-~ (“hand”). Cognate verbs survive as Italian ~domandare~ and Spanish ~demandar~, and the ~mandāre~ family entered English as ~mandate~, ~command~, ~commend~, and the legal ~demand~.

The semantic shift from “to entrust, to commit” toward “to ask, to request” happened within Latin and Romance: charging someone with a task slid into requesting something of them. French ~demander~ therefore lost the heavy sense of “entrust” and became the everyday verb for “to ask” — a question, a favour, a price. English ~demand~ kept a more forceful, insistent tone, which is why the French ~demander~ is a notorious false friend: ~je vous demande~ is a polite “I ask you,” not “I demand of you.” From ~manus~ and ~mandāre~ come a broad French family, including ~commander~ (“to order”), ~recommander~ (“to recommend”), ~mandat~ (“mandate; warrant”), and ~mander~ (“to summon”).
en.demeurer:
From Old French ~demorer~, ~demourer~ (“to delay, to remain, to dwell”), from Latin ~demorari~ (“to linger, to tarry, to stay”), a compound of the prefix ~de-~ and the deponent verb ~morari~ (“to delay, to tarry”), itself from the noun ~mora~ (“a delay, a pause”). Cognate with Italian ~dimorare~ (“to dwell, to reside”), Spanish ~morar~ (“to dwell”) and Portuguese ~morar~ (“to live, to reside”), all reflexes of the same family.

The Latin sense was strictly temporal — to be held up, to be delayed — and that meaning survived early on: the medieval expression ~sans demeurer~ meant “without delay.” But a thing that lingers in a place comes to belong there, and so ~demeurer~ drifted from “to tarry” toward “to remain” and finally “to dwell, to reside,” the meaning the verb still carries when one asks where someone ~demeure~. French preserves both threads: the residential one in the noun ~demeure~ (“a dwelling”), and the old temporal one in the legal locution ~mettre en demeure~ (“to serve formal notice,” literally to put someone in a state of delay or default) and in the adverb ~désormais~, whose buried ~-mais~ goes back to the same ~mora~. The participle ~demeurant~ even works as a connective, ~au demeurant~ meaning “for the rest, moreover.”
en.densifier: ~Densifier~ is formed from the adjective ~dense~ with the suffix ~-ifier~, which goes back to Latin ~-ficāre~ (“to make”). It means to make something denser or to become denser. The base ~dense~ is borrowed from Latin ~densus~ (“thick, packed, bushy”).
en.denteler: ~Denteler~ is built on the verb ~denter~ (“to furnish with teeth”), itself formed from the noun ~dent~ (“tooth”), with the suffix ~-eler~. That suffix is rare today. It forms verbs of small or repeated action, and here it gives a sense of cutting many little teeth, hence “to indent, to notch” an edge.
en.desceller: Formed from ~sceller~ with the prefix ~dé-~, in its ~des-~ form before ~s~, so that the sound stays [s]. The prefix reverses the base: to ~sceller~ is to close or fix with a seal, and to ~desceller~ is to break that seal, or to pull loose something fixed in place with cement or plaster. The base comes from Old French ~seeler~, from Latin ~sigillāre~ and its noun ~sigillum~, a “little sign,” the seal pressed into wax.
en.descendre:
From Latin ~dēscendere~ (“to climb down, to go down”), a compound of the prefix ~dē-~ (“down from”) and ~scandere~ (“to climb, to mount”). ~Scandere~ derives from Proto-Indo-European *~skend-~ (“to leap up, to climb”), so the Latin verb is, literally, a “climbing-down” — a downward motion expressed, paradoxically, by a verb of ascent. The root shows up across Latin in ~ascendere~ (“to climb up”) and ~trānscendere~ (“to climb across”), and survives in English borrowings such as ~ascend~, ~descend~, and ~transcend~.

Attested in French from the eleventh century, ~descendre~ kept its plain sense of moving from a higher point to a lower one. By the eighteenth century it had acquired a figurative use — “to derive one's origin from,” as one ~descends~ from an ancestor — turning a movement through space into a movement through generations, down the branches of a family tree. The same root *~skend-~ underlies the noun ~descendant~ (“offspring”) and ~descente~ (“a going down, a raid”). The wider Latin family of ~scandere~ also reached French in the learned word ~scander~ (“to scan verse”), where the climbing sense survives in the metrical “stepping” through a line of poetry.
en.desquamer: Borrowed from Latin ~dēsquāmāre~ (“to scale a fish, to remove the scales”), formed from the prefix ~dē-~ (“off, away”) and the noun ~squāma~ (“scale”). The verb is a learned word, and its base is the same Latin ~squāma~ that gave French the noun ~squame~ (“a flake of skin”). ~Desquamer~ means to shed scales or to flake off in thin layers, and it is chiefly a medical word, applied to skin that peels after a burn, an illness or sunburn. The family of ~squāma~ in learned French includes ~squame~, ~squameux~ (“scaly”) and ~desquamation~, and English shares the Latin root in ~squamous~ and ~desquamate~. The ordinary French word for the scale of a fish, ~écaille~, belongs to a different, Germanic family, so ~desquamer~ is the technical cousin of the everyday ~écailler~.
en.dessabler: ~Dessabler~ is built on ~sabler~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the action: to take sand out of something. The base ~sabler~ comes from the noun ~sable~ (“sand”), from Old French ~sable~ and Vulgar Latin ~sablum~, a contracted form of Latin ~sabulum~ (“sand, gravel”). It has nothing to do with the other French ~sable~, the fur and heraldic color. Before an s, the prefix is written ~des-~ with a doubled s, so that it stays pronounced [s].
en.dessaisir: Formed in French from the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ~saisir~. The prefix, spelled ~dess-~ before the ~s~ so that it stays unvoiced, comes from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”) and here reverses the base. The base ~saisir~ comes from Old French, from Medieval Latin ~sacire~, a word of Germanic origin that first meant “to put someone legally in possession.” ~Dessaisir~ undoes that act: it means “to take possession away from someone,” as when a court is relieved of a case, and in the reflexive “to give up, to part with.”
en.dessaler: Formed from ~saler~ (“to salt”) with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the action: the verb means to remove the salt from something. The base ~saler~ is built on Latin ~sal~ (“salt”), which also gave French ~sel~ and ~salaire~ and is cognate with English ~salt~ and German ~Salz~. ~Saler~ kept its concrete sense of seasoning or preserving with salt almost unchanged, and the figurative ~salé~ is used of a price or a joke that “stings”. The prefix ~dés-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.dessangler: Formed from the noun ~sangle~ (“girth, strap”) with the prefix ~dés-~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so it means to undo a girth. ~Sangle~ was inherited from Old French ~cengle~, from Vulgar Latin *~cingla~, from Late Latin ~cingula~, from Latin ~cingulum~ (“belt”). The prefix ~dés-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and the ending ~-er~ from Latin ~-are~.
en.dessaouler: The TLFi dates ~dessaouler~ to 1557 and derives it from ~soûler~ (“to make drunk”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which goes back to Latin ~dis-~. Before a base beginning with s, the prefix is written ~des-~ with a doubled s so that the s stays voiceless, hence the spelling. The prefix undoes the state: ~dessaouler~ means to rid someone of the effects of drunkenness, or, intransitively, to stop being drunk. It is a variant spelling of ~dessouler~, which the Académie labels popular.
en.dessaper: This verb is formed from ~saper~ with the prefix ~dés-~, spelled ~dess-~ before an s so that it stays voiceless. The prefix reverses the base: if ~saper~ means “to dress”, in its slang sense, then ~dessaper~ means “to undress”. The base is itself obscure. French has several verbs ~saper~, one from Italian ~zappare~ (“to dig”), and the sources do not agree on the origin of the one meaning “to dress”: one suggests, with a maybe, a link to cutting a garment, while the other calls it unknown.
en.desseller: Formed from ~seller~ (“to saddle”) with the prefix ~dé-~, spelled ~des-~ before an s, which reverses the action: to take the saddle off. ~Seller~ is built on ~selle~ (“saddle”), from Latin ~sella~ (“seat”) and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~sed-~ (“to sit”), which English ~sit~ shares.
en.desserrer: Formed in French from ~serrer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, here in its spelling ~des-~, written with a double s so that it stays pronounced [s]. The prefix reverses the base: to ~desserrer~ is to undo a tightening, as with a knot or a belt. ~Serrer~ comes from Old French ~serrer~ (“to close, lock fast”), from Late Latin ~serāre~ (“to close with a bar”), from Latin ~sera~ (“a bar or bolt for a door”). The same ~sera~ underlies French ~serrure~ (“lock”).
en.dessertir: ~Dessertir~ is formed from ~sertir~ with the prefix ~dé-~, here in its ~des-~ spelling before an initial ~s~, written with a doubled ~s~ so that it stays sounded as ~s~. The prefix reverses the base, which comes from Old French ~sartir~. ~Sertir~ means to set a gem in its mount, or more broadly to crimp by folding metal around a piece. To ~dessertir~ is therefore to remove a stone from its setting. The sources give nothing older for ~sertir~, so its deeper origin is left aside.
en.desservir:
From ~des-~ (a privative prefix, from Latin ~dis-~) + ~servir~ (« to serve »), the latter from Latin ~servire~ (« to serve »), a verb derived from ~servus~ (« slave, servant ») whose own deeper origin the dictionaries call uncertain, perhaps from Proto-Italic *~serwos~. The prefix points two ways at once, which is why ~desservir~ carries strikingly different meanings under one spelling.
