In its plain sense the ~des-~ « undoes » the serving: to ~desservir~ a table is to clear away the dishes, the reverse of « servir. » Figuratively it sours into « to do a disservice, » to harm someone's cause — « cette remarque l'a ~desservi~ » (« that remark worked against him »). Yet a third, positive sense developed in the language of duty and route: a priest ~dessert~ a parish (« serves » a village church), and a bus or train line ~dessert~ a town (« provides service to » it). The shared family runs through ~service~, ~serviteur~, ~serveur~, ~servile~, and ~asservir~ (« to enslave »); ~desservir~ alone manages to mean both « to serve a place » and « to do a bad turn. »
en.dessiller: ~Dessiller~ is a variant spelling of ~déciller~, built from ~cil~ (“eyelash”) with the prefix ~dé-~ (Old French ~des-~ and ~de-~ were both used, so the two spellings share one prefix) and the suffix ~-er~; English Wiktionary treats it as inherited from Old French ~descillier~. ~Cil~ comes from Latin ~cilium~. Littré complained that ~dessiller~ is a bad spelling, since the word comes from ~cil~, but the Académie kept it. According to French Wiktionary, the word comes from falconry: ~ciller~ meant to sew a bird of prey's eyelids shut to tame it, so the lids then had to be unstitched, and its eyes ~dessillés~. The figurative sense, to open someone's eyes, followed.
en.dessiner:
From Latin ~designare~ (“to mark out, to designate, to trace”), a compound of the prefix ~de-~ and the verb ~signare~ (“to mark with a sign”), itself from ~signum~ (“a sign, a mark”). The route into French was indirect: the Italian ~disegnare~ — which had specialized toward the sense “to draw” — reshaped the older French word, giving the modern ~dessiner~. The very same Latin ~designare~ also descends straight into French as ~désigner~ (“to designate, to point out”), so ~dessiner~ and ~désigner~ are a doublet. English ~design~ and ~designate~, Spanish ~diseñar~, and Portuguese ~desenhar~ belong to the same family.

The split is telling. Latin ~designare~ meant to mark something out — and that single act forks two ways: you can mark a thing in order to point to it (whence ~désigner~) or mark lines on a surface to depict it (whence ~dessiner~). The noun ~dessin~ (“a drawing”) and ~dessein~ (“a design, an intention”) were long spelled alike and only later prised apart, preserving in French the old kinship between drawing a figure and forming a plan. Through ~signum~, ~dessiner~ is also cousin to ~signe~, ~signal~, ~signer~, ~signature~, ~enseigne~ (“a shop sign”), and ~enseigner~ (“to teach,” literally to mark out for someone).
en.dessoler: Formed from ~sole~ (“sole”) with the prefix ~dé-~, spelled ~des-~ before an s, which here marks removal: to take off the sole. ~Sole~ is inherited from Vulgar Latin *~sola~, from Latin ~solea~ (“sandal, sole”). French Wiktionary records a second, homograph verb, built with the same prefix on ~assoler~, so two different verbs share this spelling.
en.dessouder: ~Dessouder~ is ~souder~ with the prefix ~des-~, which here reverses the action: to undo a soldered joint. The prefix is written ~des-~ with a doubled s before a base that begins with s, so that the s stays voiceless. ~Souder~ comes from Old French ~solder~, inherited from Latin ~solidāre~ (“to make solid”), built on ~solidus~ (“solid”), and English ~solder~ was borrowed from the same Old French verb. The prefix goes back, through Old French, to Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.dessoûler: Formed from ~soûler~ with the reversing prefix ~dé-~: to sober up, or to make someone sober. The base ~soûler~ has two sources according to French Wiktionary. One verb comes from Old French ~sauler~, from Latin ~satullare~ (“to sate, to fill up”), and it is related to ~saturer~. A second verb, listed separately, is built from the adjective ~soul~. The meaning moved from satisfying hunger to the modern “to get drunk,” and ~dessoûler~ reverses that.
en.dessuinter: ~Dessuinter~ is formed from the noun ~suint~ with the prefix ~des-~, which marks removal. The noun ~suint~ names the natural grease in sheep's wool, and it is related to ~suer~ (“to sweat”), from which it derives. The prefix ~des-~ is the form of ~dé-~ used before an initial ~s~, written with a doubled ~s~ to keep the sound. The verb thus means to remove the grease from wool, in effect to take away its “sweat.”
en.dessécher: ~Dessécher~ has two accounts that fit together. English Wiktionary calls it inherited from Old French, from Latin ~dēsiccāre~. French Wiktionary instead derives it from ~sécher~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which takes the form ~des-~ before an initial s. Both readings reach the same pieces, a prefix and the verb ~sécher~, which comes from Latin ~siccāre~ (“to make dry”), built on the adjective ~siccus~ (“dry”).
en.destiner:
From Latin ~destinare~ (“to make fast, fix, establish, resolve upon”), formed from the prefix ~de-~ and an element ~-stinare~ connected to ~stare~ (“to stand”). It thus belongs to the great family of the Proto-Indo-European root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”), through a nasal-infixed derivative meaning roughly “to make stand firm.” The same root and the same ~-stinare~ element appear in Latin ~obstinare~ (“to stand firm against”), which gives French ~obstiner~, and at a deeper level it links ~destiner~ to Greek ~histēmi~ (“I cause to stand”) and to English ~stand~.

The metaphor is striking: to destine something is to make it ~stand fixed~, to settle it firmly in place for a purpose — fate as a thing nailed down in advance. Latin ~destinare~ ran from the concrete (“to fasten, to fix a target”) to the abstract (“to resolve, to set apart for”), and French kept the “set apart for a purpose” sense in ~destiner quelqu'un à une carrière~. The past-participle noun ~destinata~ underlies the idea of a fixed endpoint, surfacing in ~destination~ and ~destinée~, while the abstract noun gives ~destin~ (“fate, that which is fixed”). The same *~steh₂-~ root, so prolific in French, also yields ~stable~, ~constant~, ~obstiner~, and a host of words built on standing firm.
en.destituer: From Latin ~dēstituere~, a verb of the standard type built from the prefix ~dē-~ and the verb ~statuere~ (“to set, to place”), the same verb that gave French ~statuer~ and ~instituer~. Its sense in Latin was “to set aside, to abandon”, and French ~destituer~ is a learned borrowing that means to dismiss someone from a post, to strip an official of office. Italian ~destituire~, Spanish ~destituir~ and English ~destitute~ (via Latin ~dēstitūtus~) are cousins from the same source.
en.devancer: Derived from ~devant~ (“in front”), on the pattern of ~avancer~, whose own ancestry is Latin ~ab ante~ (“from before”). The verb means “to get in front of”: to outstrip someone, and by extension to anticipate a move or a wish before it is expressed. The idea of being in front is present in the base, so the sense has stayed close to its literal image.
en.devenir:
From Latin ~dēvenīre~ (“to come down to, to arrive at, to fall into a state”), formed from the prefix ~dē-~ (“down, from”) and ~venīre~ (“to come”), the source of French ~venir~. Latin ~venīre~ descends from Proto-Italic *~gʷenjō~ and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʷem-~ (“to come, to step”), one of the most productive verbal roots in the family. Through that root ~devenir~ is cognate with Italian ~divenire~ and Spanish ~devenir~, and, more distantly, with English ~come~ and German ~kommen~, which spring from the same PIE source.

The metaphor at the heart of the word is motion turned into transformation: to ~devenir~ something is, etymologically, to ~come~ to it, to arrive at a new state as one arrives at a place. Latin already used ~dēvenīre~ for falling into a condition, and French generalized it into the ordinary verb of becoming. The root *~gʷem-~ seeded a remarkable crowd of French words through ~venīre~ and its Latin relatives: ~venir~, ~avenir~ (“future,” literally what is “to come”), ~revenir~, ~convenir~, ~prévenir~, ~aventure~, ~revenu~, and ~souvenir~ — the last a memory that, etymologically, “comes up from below” into the mind.
en.deviner:
From Latin ~divinare~ (“to foresee, to prophesy, to be inspired by a god”), from ~divinus~ (“of a god, divine”), from ~divus~ (“god, deity”), from Proto-Italic *~deiwos~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~deywós~ (“god, celestial being”), itself a derivative of *~dyew-~ (“the bright sky, daylight”). This is one of the great roots: it also gives Latin ~deus~ and ~Jupiter~, Greek ~Zeus~, Sanskrit ~deva~, and the divinity in French ~dieu~. The same family fed Italian ~indovinare~ and Spanish ~adivinar~.

The semantic shift is striking. ~divinare~ first meant to know things by divine inspiration — the prophet's gift of seeing the hidden. As that solemn sense secularized, ~deviner~ slid all the way down to the everyday “to guess,” the small daily act of foreseeing without proof. A pleasing detail lurks in the root: *~dyew-~ originally pointed at the shining daytime sky, so the “god” of ~divinare~ was, at the very bottom, a luminous one — and the diviner's insight is, etymologically, a kind of light. The family persists in ~devin~ (“soothsayer”), ~devinette~ (“riddle”), and the learned ~divination~ and ~divin~.
en.deviser:
Inherited from Old French ~deviser~, from Vulgar Latin *~devisāre~, a dissimilated form of *~divisāre~: the two ~i~ sounds were made unlike, one becoming ~e~. French Wiktionary calls *~divisāre~ a frequentative of ~dīvidere~ (“to divide”), built on its supine ~dīvīsum~. French Wiktionary also offers a second reading, in which the verb is made on the noun ~devis~.

The step from dividing to chatting is not spelled out in the sources. French Wiktionary points instead to idioms such as ~tailler une bavette~ and ~tailler le bout de gras~, in which cutting also stands for chatting, as parallels for the link. The learned verb ~diviser~ comes from the same Latin source, so ~deviser~ and ~diviser~ are cousins. ~Devis~ (“estimate”) and ~devise~ (“motto, currency”) belong to the same family.
en.devoir:
From Old French ~devoir~ (also ~deveir~), from Latin ~dēbēre~ (“to owe, to be bound to”). The Latin verb is a contraction of *~dēhibēre~, from ~dē-~ (“from, away”) plus ~habēre~ (“to have, hold”) — literally “to hold away from someone,” that is, to keep what is theirs and so to owe it. Through ~habēre~ it shares the root of ~avoir~. Romance cousins include Spanish ~deber~ and Italian ~dovere~, both meaning “to owe” and “must.”

The meaning traveled a clean path: from “to hold something belonging to another” (to owe), to the felt pressure of that obligation (“to be bound to”), to a pure modal of necessity (“must, ought”). French ~devoir~ carries all three at once — ~je te dois cent euros~ (I owe you), ~je dois partir~ (I must leave) — and, like ~pouvoir~, it froze into a noun: ~le devoir~ (“duty”), and in the plural ~les devoirs~ (“homework”). From the same Latin ~dēbēre~ and its noun ~dēbitum~ come ~dette~ (“debt”), the learned doublet ~débit~, and ~débiteur~; and English borrowed ~debt~, ~debit~, and — by way of the Old French phrase “to put in devoir” — ~endeavour~.
en.diaboliser: ~Diaboliser~ means “to demonize,” to portray someone or something as devilish. French Wiktionary derives it from ~diabolique~ with the suffix ~-iser~, while English Wiktionary starts from Latin ~diabolus~ (“devil”) plus ~-iser~; the two agree on the root and differ on whether the adjective was the intermediate step. Taken from the adjective, ~diabolique~ loses its ending before ~-iser~. That adjective comes from Late Latin ~diabolicus~, from Greek ~diábolos~ (“the Devil”).
en.diagnostiquer:
French ~diagnostiquer~ is a denominal verb, built on the noun ~diagnostic~ with the verb ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary adds that the family goes back to Ancient Greek ~diagignṓskein~ (“to examine thoroughly”), a verb that joins ~dia-~ (“through, apart”) to ~gignṓskein~ (“to know”). English Wiktionary gives only the French step, ~diagnostic~ plus ~-er~, so the two accounts fit together: the Greek verb stands behind the noun, and the French verb is a derivation from it. The ending ~-er~ is the ordinary first-conjugation ending, from Latin ~-are~, which French uses to turn a noun into a verb of doing or applying what the noun names.

The Greek sense was that of examining something thoroughly, and the French noun ~diagnostic~ keeps that idea: it names the identification of an illness from its signs. The verb ~diagnostiquer~ is the act itself, so a physician ~diagnostique~ a disease from its symptoms. Because the verb is built on the noun and not borrowed whole from Greek, it belongs to French derivation, like ~torturer~ or ~alerter~, and its ending is that of any regular verb in ~-er~. The long Greek history sits behind the noun, while the verb itself is a plain French formation.
en.dialectiser: Formed from ~dialectique~ with the suffix ~-iser~, meaning to treat or render according to the noun: to treat a question dialectically, or to give it a dialectical form. The base ~dialectique~ comes from Latin ~dialectica~ and ~dialecticus~, themselves from Greek ~dialektikḗ~ and ~dialektikós~, the art of discourse and argument. The suffix ~-iser~ was borrowed from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and is fully productive in learned French.
en.dialoguer: A denominal verb formed from ~dialogue~ plus ~-er~, meaning “to hold a dialogue,” and by extension “to negotiate, to talk things through.” The noun came through Latin ~dialogus~ from Ancient Greek ~διάλογος~ (“conversation, discourse”), itself built on ~διά~ (“through, between”) and ~λόγος~ (“speech”). French did not follow the Greek pattern of derivatives in ~-logie~ or ~-logique~ here. It applied its own Latin-style suffixes to the borrowed noun instead, which is how ~dialoguer~ and ~dialogal~ came about.
en.dialyser:
Dialyser is a French verb made on the noun ~dialyse~, which French Wiktionary traces to Ancient Greek ~διαλύω~ (~dialúō~, “to separate”). The Greek verb is built from ~dia-~ (“apart, through”) and ~lúein~ (“to loosen, to release”), and its noun ~dialusis~ meant a loosening or dissolving. French took the noun as a learned scientific word and formed the verb from it with ~-er~. The same verb ~lúein~ lies behind other French terms of science, such as ~analyse~ and ~paralysie~.

In chemistry, ~dialyser~ means to separate substances in a solution by passing them through a membrane. In medicine, it means to treat a patient whose kidneys cannot clean the blood by filtering it through such a membrane, and ~dialyse~, ~dialyseur~ and ~dialysé~ belong to the same family. The idea of separating is the one the Greek verb carried: a dissolving or releasing apart of things that were mixed together. English ~dialyze~ and ~dialysis~ come from the same Greek source.
en.diamanter: Formed from ~diamant~ with the verb ending ~-er~, it means to adorn with diamonds. French ~diamant~ comes from Old French ~diamant~ and Late Latin ~diamas~, probably a metathesis of ~adimas~, which also gave ~aimant~ (“magnet”). Behind both stands Latin ~adamās~, from Greek ~ἀδάμας~ (“hard”). Diamond and magnet are thus doublets in French, two outcomes of one Greek word for something unbreakable.
en.diaphragmer: Formed from the noun ~diaphragme~ and the verb ending ~-er~, in the sense “to fit with a diaphragm,” notably to adjust the opening of a lens. ~Diaphragme~ comes from Latin ~diaphragma~, borrowed from Greek ~diáphragma~ (“partition, separation”), the word used for the muscle that divides the chest from the abdomen. The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, is the ordinary way French makes a verb out of a noun.
en.diaprer:
From Old French ~diaspre~ (“silk cloth with floral patterns or arabesques”), plus the verb ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary links ~diaspre~ to ~jaspe~ and says that ~diaprer~ properly means “to jasper,” that is, to mottle a surface the way the stone ~jaspe~ is mottled. The stone's name, ~jaspe~ in French, goes back through Latin ~iaspis~ to Greek.

Modern French uses ~diaprer~ chiefly in literary prose, for light or color that variegates something, as when dawn ~diapre~ the sky or a meadow is dappled with flowers. The past participle ~diapré~ is the commonest form, and the noun ~diaprure~ names the effect. English has a distant relative in ~jasper~, from the same Latin and Greek stone name.
en.dicter:
French ~dicter~ is borrowed from Latin ~dictāre~ (“to say, to repeat”), an iterative of ~dīcere~ (“to say”). An iterative verb expresses a repeated or insistent action, so the Latin word already carried the idea of saying something again and again. Old French had its own related verb, ~ditier~, which English Wiktionary invites us to compare. The Latin verb also lives on in Italian ~dettare~, Spanish ~dictar~ and English ~dictate~.

The base ~dīcere~ is the ancestor of French ~dire~, and it also stands behind ~prédire~, ~contredire~ and ~édit~. Words built on the same Latin family include ~dictée~ (“dictation”), ~dictateur~, ~dictature~ and ~dictionnaire~. In modern French, ~dicter~ means to say something aloud for someone else to write down, and figuratively to impose a decision or a course of action, as in ~dicter sa loi~ (“to lay down the law”).
en.diffamer:
Borrowed from Latin ~diffamare~ (“to defame, disparage, decry”), a verb built on ~fama~ (“rumor, reputation”). The Latin verb is analyzed as ~fama~ with the prefix ~dis-~ (“apart”), so the idea is of damaging a reputation. Both French and English Wiktionary give this straightforward learned borrowing. Italian ~diffamare~ and Spanish ~difamar~ are its sister forms in the other Romance languages, and English ~defame~ draws on the same Latin source.

The root ~fama~ gave French a small family. ~Fameux~ (“famous”) and ~famé~, found in the phrase ~mal famé~ (“of ill repute”), carry the word for reputation, and ~infâme~ comes from Latin ~infamis~ (“of ill repute”). From ~diffamer~ French drew ~diffamation~ and ~diffamatoire~, and ~diffamation~ is also the name of a legal offence, where the verb keeps its Latin sense of attacking someone's good name. English ~fame~ belongs to this same Latin family. The prefix has no work left to do in French, because ~famer~ does not exist: the verb came whole from Latin and was never built in French.
en.diffracter: ~Diffracter~ is formed from the noun ~diffraction~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, a back-formation in the language of physics. English.Wiktionary instead derives it from Latin ~diffractus~ (“shattered”) plus ~-er~. The noun ~diffraction~ itself comes from ~diffractus~ with the suffix ~-ion~. The Latin participle belongs to a verb meaning to break apart, which fits the sense: to ~diffracter~ a wave or a beam of light is to make it spread and bend as it passes an obstacle or an opening.
en.diffuser:
A 15th-century formation, built on the adjective ~diffus~ (“diffuse, spread out”) plus the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, created to render the Latin verb ~diffundere~ (“to pour out, to spread”). That verb is ~dis-~ (“apart, in different directions”) plus ~fundere~ (“to pour”), whose past participle ~diffusus~ gave ~diffus~. ~Fundere~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~ǵʰewd-~, an extension of *~ǵʰew-~ (“to pour”), cognate with Ancient Greek ~χέω~ (~kheō~, “I pour”) and Gothic ~giutan~ (“to pour”).

The image is liquid: ~diffundere~ meant to pour a fluid so that it spreads in every direction, and ~diffuser~ kept that sense of even, outward spreading — of light, heat, or a scent through a room. From there it took on “to circulate, to disseminate,” and in the twentieth century became the standard word for broadcasting by radio and television. French built a whole series of verbs on ~fundere~ for pouring in different directions: ~infuser~ (to pour in), ~perfuser~ (to pour through), ~transfuser~ (to pour across), and ~confus~ — literally “poured together,” hence muddled. The noun ~diffusion~ shares the same source.
en.différencier:
A variant of older ~différentier~, from Late Latin ~differentiare~, from ~differentia~ (“difference, distinction”). ~Differentia~ is built on ~differre~ (“to carry apart, to differ”), itself ~dis-~ (“apart”) + ~ferre~ (“to carry, to bear”). The verb ~ferre~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰer-~ (“to carry, to bear”), one of the most widely attested of all roots — cognate with English ~bear~, Ancient Greek ~φέρω~ (“I carry”), and Sanskrit ~भरति~ (~bharati~, “he carries”). To differentiate is, at root, to carry two things apart from each other.

The Romance languages keep the verb almost unchanged: Spanish and Portuguese ~diferenciar~, Catalan ~diferenciar~. From the general sense of telling things apart, mathematics borrowed a precise one — to ~differentiate~ a function, computing how it changes over an infinitesimal increment. French relatives include ~différence~, ~différent~, ~différer~ (which forks into “to differ” and “to defer”), ~différenciation~, and ~indifférent~. The root *~bʰer-~ alone fans out across ~conférer~, ~préférer~, ~transférer~, ~offrir~, and ~souffrir~ — each a different way of carrying or bearing.
en.différentier: ~Différentier~ is borrowed from scholastic Latin ~differentiare~ (“to differentiate”), attested around 1360. In French it appears in the 14th century, in Christine de Pisan, and in 1690 Furetière defines it as “to distinguish by the difference.” A second, mathematical sense dates from 1754, when the Encyclopédie uses it for taking the differential of a quantity in calculus; the TLFi treats this second use as a spelling variant of ~différencier~. English ~differentiate~ and the French noun ~différence~ belong to the same Latin family.
en.différer:
From Latin ~differre~ (« to carry apart, to scatter, to postpone, to be unlike »), a compound of ~dis-~ (« apart ») and ~ferre~ (« to carry, to bear »). ~ferre~ comes from Proto-Italic *~ferō~ and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰer-~ (« to bear, to carry »), one of the most widely attested roots of the family. Through that root it is cognate with English ~bear~, Ancient Greek ~φέρω~ (« I carry »), and Sanskrit ~bʰarati~ (« he carries »).

The two modern French senses both fall straight out of « to carry apart ». Things carried apart in time are put off — hence « to defer, to postpone »; things carried apart in nature are unalike — hence « to differ ». English inherited the very same split in the doublet ~defer~ and ~differ~. The prolific root *~bʰer-~ surfaces across French in ~conférer~, ~préférer~, ~offrir~, ~souffrir~, and the noun ~différence~, all carrying, in their Latin bones, the idea of bearing something from one place to another.
en.digitaliser: Formed from the adjective and noun ~digitale~ with the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to make or convert into.” French Wiktionary also gives a second account, that the verb comes from English ~digitalize~, and English Wiktionary says only that, so the French verb may well be a calque of the English one. The base ~digitale~ comes from Latin ~digitālis~, from ~digitus~ (“finger”). The sense is to turn information into digits, that is, into a numerical form that a computer can store, a sense close to ~numériser~, the rival French verb.
en.digresser: Formed from the stem of ~digression~ with the verb ending ~-er~, on the pattern of ~progresser~ and ~régresser~: to ~digresser~ is to stray from the main subject. ~Digression~ is from Latin ~dīgressiōnem~, from ~digredi~ (“to go away, to depart”), a verb made of ~dis-~ (“apart”) and ~gradī~ (“to step”). The verb is thus a back-formation, built by cutting off the noun's ending and adding ~-er~, not inherited from the Latin verb itself.
en.digérer:
Learned borrowing from Latin ~digerere~ (“to carry apart, to scatter, to dissolve, to digest”), built from ~dis-~ (“apart”) and ~gerere~ (“to carry, to bear”). Because French took it directly from written Latin, it kept a Latin look and never went through the everyday sound changes of Old French. English ~digest~ comes from the participle of the same Latin verb, and Italian ~digerire~ and Spanish ~digerir~ are its Romance counterparts.

The Latin verb first meant to carry things off in different directions, hence to spread out, arrange or separate. Physicians and writers then applied it to what the body does with food, dividing and dissolving it into parts that can be absorbed, and that sense became the dominant one. French also stretched it figuratively: it can mean to absorb a piece of information, or to swallow an insult or a defeat. The same family includes ~digestion~ and ~indigeste~, and the simple verb ~gerere~ lies behind ~gérer~ and ~suggérer~, while its participle ~gestus~ gave ~geste~.
en.dilacérer:
Borrowed from Latin ~dilacerāre~ (“to tear apart”); French Wiktionary sends the reader on to ~lacérer~ for the root. The Latin verb is analysed as ~dī-~ (“apart”) plus ~lacerāre~ (“to tear, to mangle”), which is itself built on the adjective ~lacer~ (“torn”). The sense is therefore to rip something into pieces, not just to rip it.

French has two learned verbs from this Latin family. ~Lacérer~ comes from ~lacerāre~, and ~dilacérer~ from its prefixed form. Both are scholarly borrowings, taken from Latin by writers and not worn down by centuries of speech. The noun ~dilacération~ stands beside the verb, and English has ~lacerate~ from the same Latin source. ~Dilacérer~ is a rare, strong word for tearing something to shreds, found mostly in written French.
en.dilapider: ~Dilapider~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~dilapidāre~. The Latin verb is formed from ~dis-~ (“apart”) and ~lapidāre~, from ~lapis~ (“stone”). It means to squander, to waste a fortune or an inheritance piece by piece. French took the verb directly from Latin as a scholarly word, which is why it keeps a form close to its source.
en.dilater: ~Dilater~ comes from Latin ~dilātāre~ (“to widen, to spread out”), built on the adjective ~lātus~ (“wide”) with the prefix ~dī-~, which carries a sense of spreading apart. The Latin adjective also lies behind French ~latitude~, and English borrowed ~dilate~ from the same source. The sense stayed close to its Latin root: to make something wider, whether a pupil, a blood vessel or a gas, and by extension to expand.
en.diligenter: ~Diligenter~ is formed from the adjective ~diligent~ and the verb ending ~-er~, which turns a noun or adjective into a first-conjugation verb. The adjective is a learned word taken from Latin ~diligēns~ (“careful, attentive”). The verb means to expedite, that is, to carry something out promptly and with care. Both French and English Wiktionary agree on this simple formation, and neither gives a date. Today the verb is rare and belongs mostly to administrative or formal French.
en.diluer: Borrowed from Latin ~dīluō~, “to wash away, to dissolve, to dilute,” built from ~dis-~ (“apart”) and ~luō~ (“to wash, to bathe”). To ~diluer~ a liquid is therefore to wash its strength away by adding water. The same Latin pair gave ~dīluvium~ (“flood”), source of French ~déluge~, and Latin ~abluere~ gave French ~ablution~. The figurative sense, to weaken an idea, an argument or a shareholding by spreading it thinner, is a later extension of the physical meaning.
en.dimensionner: ~Dimensionner~ is built on the noun ~dimension~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to give a dimension to” and so “to size.” The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin ~dīmensiō~, which French Wiktionary links to ~dīmetīrī~ (“to measure in every direction”). The second sense of the verb, “to size up,” rests on the modern figurative sense of ~dimension~, “aspect, character,” so one may ~dimensionner~ a problem as well as a pipe or a beam.
en.diminuer:
French ~diminuer~ comes from Latin ~dēminuere~ (“to make smaller, to lessen”), formed from ~dē-~ (“down, from”) plus ~minuere~ (“to make small, to reduce”). The simple verb ~minuere~ rests on the adjective stem of ~minor~ / ~minus~ (“less”), and the whole family traces to a Proto-Indo-European root *~mey-~ (“small, to lessen”). That root is widespread: Gothic ~mins~ (“less”), Ancient Greek ~minúthō~ (“to diminish”), and Sanskrit ~minā́ti~ (“to lessen, to damage”) are all cousins, as is English ~minor~, borrowed from Latin. Italian ~diminuire~ and Spanish ~disminuir~ are its Romance siblings.

The classical sense, “to break into smaller pieces, to reduce,” narrowed cleanly into the modern “to decrease.” A delightful surprise lies in the relatives: the past participle ~minūtus~ (“made small”) gave French ~menu~ — both the adjective (“slender, fine,” as in ~menu peuple~, “the small folk”) and the noun ~menu~, originally a “detailed,” i.e. finely itemized, list, which English then borrowed back for restaurant cards. The same ~minūtus~ also produced ~minute~ (the time unit, a “small” division of the hour). Around this root cluster French ~diminution~, ~diminutif~, ~moindre~ (the irregular comparative, straight from ~minor~), ~mince~ (“thin”), and the learned ~minimum~ and ~minuscule~. To diminish, etymologically, is simply to make ever more ~menu~.
en.dinguer: From the sound-word ~ding~, which imitates the swinging of bells, according to French Wiktionary and English Wiktionary alike. It is an imitative verb with no older ancestor. Its colloquial senses, to fall heavily or to go flying, as in ~envoyer dinguer~ (“to send flying”), are the modern ones.
en.diphtonguer: Formed from the noun ~diphtongue~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, which turns a noun into a verb: to make into a diphthong, or to pronounce as one. The noun was borrowed from Latin ~diphthongus~, itself from Ancient Greek ~δίφθογγος~ (~díphthongos~, “having two sounds”). It was spelled ~diphthongue~ until 1878. The Greek word joins “two” and “sound,” which is exactly what a diphthong is: two vowel sounds sliding together within a single syllable.
en.diplômer:
A denominal verb coined in 1841 from the noun ~diplôme~. That noun comes from Latin ~diploma~ (“an official document, license”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~díplōma~, literally “a thing folded in two,” from ~diplóos~ (“double, twofold”) via the verb ~diplóō~ (“to double, fold over”). The Greek word itself joins ~dís~ (“twice”) to the root ~-plóos~ (“-fold”).

The image at the bottom of the word is wonderfully concrete: a ~diplôme~ was a sheet of paper folded once over, the form Roman authorities used for a permit or a grant of privilege. From “folded document” the sense narrowed to the certificate awarded for completed study, and ~diplômer~ means to confer such a certificate — hence ~diplômé~, “holding a degree, qualified.” The ~-plóos~ root that gives “fold” runs through a learned family in French: ~diplôme~, ~diplomate~ (one entrusted with folded credentials), and the mathematical ~triple~ and ~multiple~ share the same fold-counting idea.
en.dire:
From Old and Middle French ~dire~, from Vulgar Latin *~dīgere~, a reshaping of Classical Latin ~dīcere~ (“to say, to pronounce, to express in words”). The popular form *~dīgere~ arose by analogy with verbs in ~-gere~ whose past participles ended in ~-ctum~, a pattern ~dīcere~ shared (its participle ~dictum~). The verb goes back to Proto-Italic *~deikō~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, to point out”). Through that root ~dire~ is cognate with English ~token~ and ~teach~, and with German ~zeigen~ (“to show”).

The leap from “to show” to “to say” is the heart of the story: to speak was first to point something out, to indicate it in words. That older sense of pointing survives all around the Latin family — in ~doigt~ (“finger,” from ~digitus~), in ~indiquer~, and in ~index~. From ~dīcere~ itself French inherited a crowd of words: ~dit~ (“said, saying”), the prefixed ~prédire~ (“to foretell”), ~contredire~ (“to contradict”), ~interdire~ (“to forbid,” literally “to say between”), and ~maudire~ (“to curse,” from ~maledīcere~, “to speak ill”). The learned ~diction~, ~dictée~, and ~verdict~ (“a true saying”) carry the original Latin ~dict-~ stem unworn.
en.diriger:
A learned fourteenth-century borrowing from Latin ~dirigere~ (“to set straight, align, guide”), formed from the prefix ~dis-~ (“apart, in different directions”) and ~regere~ (“to guide, rule, keep straight”). ~Regere~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₃reg-~ (“to move in a straight line, to direct”), one of the great roots of kingship and rightness. Through it ~diriger~ is cognate with English ~right~ and German ~recht~, and with Latin ~rex~ (“king,” the one who keeps the realm straight).

The governing image is the straight line. To direct is to set something on a straight course, whether a road, a gaze, an enterprise, or an orchestra; the reflexive ~se diriger vers~ (“to head toward”) keeps the literal sense of taking a straight bearing. The past participle of ~regere~ was ~rectus~ (“straight, right”), which gave French ~droit~ — so ~diriger~ and ~droit~ are cousins under the skin. Because French borrowed ~dirigere~ directly from Latin rather than inheriting it through the spoken chain, it kept its bookish shape. From the same *~h₃reg-~ root come a broad family: ~direct~, ~direction~, ~directeur~, ~dresser~, ~adresse~, ~régir~, ~règle~, and ~roi~.
en.discerner:
French ~discerner~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~discernere~ (“to separate, to set apart”), formed from ~dis-~ (“apart”) and ~cernere~ (“to sift, to separate, to decide”). Like many learned verbs, it was fitted into the regular first conjugation in ~-er~. The Latin verb ~cernere~ is related to Ancient Greek ~krínein~ (“to separate, to judge”), which gave ~crise~ and ~critique~ by way of Greek and Latin.

The Latin image is of a sieve: to ~discernere~ was to sift grain from chaff, then to tell one thing from another, and finally to see clearly. French kept the mental sense almost exclusively. To ~discerner~ is to make out a shape in the fog or a motive behind a gesture, and the noun ~discernement~ names good judgment itself. The root ~cernere~ left many descendants in French through its relatives: ~certain~ (originally “decided, settled”), ~décret~ and ~décréter~, ~secret~ (“set apart”) and ~concerner~ (“to sift together,” hence “to relate to”).
en.discipliner: ~Discipliner~ is a denominal verb formed on ~discipline~ with the ending ~-er~, meaning “to subject to discipline.” The noun comes from Latin ~disciplina~ (“instruction, teaching”), derived from ~discipulus~ (“pupil, disciple”), itself from ~discere~ (“to learn”). The verb therefore carries the idea of training that is learned, then enforced; the gloss “punish” shows how far the sense of schooling stretched toward correction.
en.discontinuer: Formed from ~continuer~ with the prefix ~dis-~, which marks negation or reversal, so ~discontinuer~ means to stop what was continuous. The prefix is a learned borrowing from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart, in different directions”), unlike the inherited ~dé-~. The base ~continuer~ comes from Latin ~continuāre~ (“to join together, to make continuous”), from ~continuus~ (“uninterrupted”), from ~continēre~ (“to hold together”), itself ~con-~ plus ~tenēre~ (“to hold”).
en.disconvenir:
~Disconvenir~ is explained in two ways. French Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~disconvenire~, while English Wiktionary treats it as ~dis-~ plus ~convenir~ and compares Italian ~disconvenire~. Either way, the pieces are clear. Latin ~convenīre~ is ~con-~ (“together”) plus ~venīre~ (“to come”), literally “to come together”, and ~dis-~ (“apart”) reverses it: not to come together, hence to disagree or to be unsuitable.

The verb thus sits inside a large family. Its positive twin ~convenir~ means both “to suit” and “to agree”, and it gave ~convenable~, ~convenance~ and, through the Latin noun, ~convention~, a coming together of parties on shared terms. The second half, ~venir~, is one of the most common verbs of French and descends from Latin ~venīre~, as do Italian ~venire~ and Spanish ~venir~. Where ~convenir~ is the verb of fitting and harmony, ~disconvenir~ is its mirror, the verb of mismatch, and it is far rarer today, a literary relic beside the everyday ~convenir~.
en.discorder:
~Discorder~ comes from Latin ~discordāre~ (“to be at odds, to differ”), which gave Old French ~descorder~ (“to divide, to set at odds”). The Latin verb is built on the adjective ~discors~ (“at variance”), itself formed from ~dis-~ (“apart”) and ~cor~ (“heart”): to be in discord is, etymologically, to have hearts that pull apart.

The word has a large family around it. The noun ~discorde~ and the adjective ~discordant~ are the best-known French relatives. Its opposite, built on the same ~cor~, is ~concorder~ (“to agree”), and ~accorder~ belongs to the same circle of “heart” words. Italian ~discordare~, Spanish ~discordar~ and English ~discord~ come from the same Latin verb.
en.discounter: Formed from the noun ~discount~ plus the verb ending ~-er~: to sell at a discount, to reduce a price. French took ~discount~ from English ~discount~ (“rebate”), itself from Old French ~desconter~, so the word went to English and came back. The French verb is a modern formation, a small piece of commercial vocabulary shaped on the English loan.
en.discourir: A learned borrowing from Latin ~discurrere~, which is built on ~dis-~ (“in different directions”) and ~currere~ (“to run”), so literally “to run about”. The sense moved from running to talking at length, as in ~discourir~ on a subject. The sources do not explain that shift. The same Latin verb gave French the noun ~discours~ and English ~discourse~, and ~courir~ descends from ~currere~.
en.discriminer: ~Discriminer~ is borrowed from Latin ~discrimināre~ (“to separate, to distinguish, to differentiate”), a verb built on ~discrimen~ (“separation, distinction”). French Wiktionary routes it through the adjective ~discriminant~, itself from the Latin participle ~discrimināns~. It has the relatives ~discrimination~ and ~discriminatoire~ in French and ~discriminate~ in English.
en.discréditer: Formed from the prefix ~dis-~ and ~créditer~, which is built on the noun ~crédit~, with ~dis-~ marking reversal: to take away someone's credit. English Wiktionary adds that it may perhaps come through an earlier ~désaccréditer~. The noun ~crédit~ was borrowed from Italian ~credito~, from Latin ~crēditum~, from ~crēdere~ (“to believe, to trust”), so credit is literally trust, and to discredit is to destroy it. The prefix ~dis-~ is a learned borrowing from Latin, a doublet of the inherited ~dé-~.
en.discrétiser: Formed from ~discret~ with the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to make discrete”: to turn something continuous into separate, distinct values. The adjective ~discret~ was inherited from Old French and borrowed from Latin ~discrētus~ (“separate, divided”), the past participle of ~discernere~ (“to separate, distinguish”). The sense of “discreet, reserved” and the sense of “separate, distinct” both come from that same Latin word. This verb takes the second, technical meaning.
en.disculper:
~Disculper~ is built on Latin ~culpa~ (“fault, blame”), and the sources give two routes. English Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~disculpāre~, itself ~dis-~ (“apart, away”) + ~culpa~. French Wiktionary instead starts from Old French ~descouper~, formed on ~coulpe~ (“fault”), whose stem was then remodeled on the Latin ~culpa~. Both agree that the verb means to clear someone of blame. Spanish and Catalan ~disculpar~ are the same word.

The root ~culpa~ is a large family in French. ~Coulpe~, the inherited Old French form, survives only in the set phrase ~battre sa coulpe~ (“to beat one's breast in repentance”), while French also has ~coupable~, ~culpabilité~, ~inculper~ (“to charge with a fault”) and ~disculper~ itself. ~Inculper~ and ~disculper~ are neat opposites: one places the blame on a person, the other takes it away. English has ~culpable~ from the same Latin source.
en.discutailler: Formed from ~discuter~ (“to discuss”) with the pejorative suffix ~-ailler~, so “to discuss badly, to quibble at length.” The base comes from Latin ~discutere~, “to strike apart, to shatter,” made of ~dis-~ and ~quatere~ (“to shake”): a debate was first a matter broken into pieces for examination. The suffix ~-ailler~ turns this into a petty, repeated, half-hearted argument, as in ~criailler~ or ~tirailler~.
en.discuter:
From Latin ~discutere~ (“to strike apart, to shatter, to break up by shaking”), compounded from ~dis-~ (“apart, asunder”) and ~quatere~ (“to shake, to strike”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~kʷēt-~ (“to shake”). That root also yielded the frequentative ~quassāre~ (“to shatter”), source of English ~quash~, and is cognate with German ~schütteln~ (“to shake”). Italian preserves the verb almost unchanged as ~discutere~.

The original sense was strikingly physical — to dash to pieces, to make something fly apart by shaking it. Late Latin already shifted ~discutere~ toward the figurative: to “shake apart” a question meant to examine it, to break a matter down into its elements. From there the modern senses follow naturally — to debate, to thrash out, and in everyday French simply to chat (« discuter avec un ami »). The image is a good one to remember: a discussion is, etymologically, a controlled shattering of a topic into examinable fragments. The same root underlies a cluster of French words sharing the idea of striking or shaking — ~discussion~, ~indiscutable~, ~percuter~ (“to strike, to collide”), ~percussion~, and ~secouer~ (“to shake”), the last descending from Latin ~succutere~.
en.disgracier: ~Disgracier~ is formed from the noun ~disgrâce~ and the ending ~-er~, meaning “to put out of favor.” The noun was borrowed from Italian ~disgrazia~, although Old French already had its own ~desgrace~. The verb sits beside ~gracier~ (“to pardon”) and the adjective ~disgracieux~, all drawing on the family of ~grâce~. Its sense of withdrawing a ruler's favor suits the court setting in which the Italian word was taken up.
en.disjoindre:
From Latin ~disjungere~ (“to separate, to unyoke”), formed from ~dis-~ (“apart”) and ~jungere~ (“to join”). French Wiktionary traces the verb straight to the Latin compound, while English Wiktionary describes it as ~dis-~ plus ~joindre~; either way the result is the same, a verb that undoes the action of ~joindre~. ~Joindre~ itself descends from ~jungere~, so the pair preserves the Latin opposition of ~jungere~ and ~disjungere~ almost unchanged. English ~disjoin~ was built on the same model.

~Disjoindre~ is a formal and often legal or technical word: one disjoins two cases, two questions or two parts of a whole. It is conjugated like ~joindre~. The family of ~jungere~ is large in French: ~joindre~, ~conjoindre~, ~adjoindre~, ~rejoindre~, ~jonction~ and ~conjonction~ all share it. The electrical term ~disjoncteur~ (a circuit breaker) and the verb ~disjoncter~ belong to the same Latin source: a circuit breaker literally breaks the join.
en.disjoncter:
A modern coinage, formed from the stem of Latin ~disjunctus~, the past participle of ~disjungere~ (“to disjoin, to separate”). That Latin verb combines ~dis-~ (“apart”) and ~jungere~ (“to join”). The French verb thus means, at root, to separate what was joined, and in practice it names the cutting of an electrical circuit, as when a breaker trips.

Because ~disjoncter~ is a neologism, it was built straight from the Latin participle and not inherited from Old French. It sits beside older learned words from the same Latin verb, such as ~disjoindre~ and ~disjonction~, and shares its root ~jungere~ with the inherited ~joindre~ and with ~conjoindre~ and ~jonction~. The related noun ~disjoncteur~ (“circuit breaker”) is the device whose action the verb describes.
en.disloquer:
~Disloquer~ has two accounts in the sources. French Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~dislocare~ (“to displace”), made of ~dis-~ (“apart”) and ~locare~ (“to place”). English Wiktionary instead calls it a back-formation from the noun ~dislocation~. Both accounts use the same Latin elements and differ on whether the verb was borrowed from a Latin verb or cut back from the noun. The Latin ~locare~ belongs to ~locus~ (“place”), the source of French ~lieu~ and ~local~.

French Wiktionary illustrates the verb with a medical use. A French translation of the Latin version of Dioscorides, the ancient author on medicinal substances, renders passages as “les jointures disloquées” and “la matrice disloquée,” joints and a womb that are out of place. Modern French extends the verb well beyond the body: the glosses “break up,” “split up” and “smash up” show that a group, an assembly or a whole structure can be ~disloqué~ in the same way. The Latin ~locus~ lies behind a whole family of French words, among them ~lieu~, ~local~, ~location~, ~allouer~ and ~dislocation~.
en.disparaître:
First attested in 1509, ~disparaître~ was formed in French from the verb ~paraître~ (“to appear, seem”) with the prefix ~dis-~ (expressing reversal or removal), modeled on the Latin ~dispārēre~ (“to vanish”). That Latin verb had already produced an Old French ~disparoir~ (“to disappear”), but the older form was ousted by the new compound built on ~paraître~. The base ~paraître~ itself comes, through Old French ~paroistre~, from Vulgar Latin *~pārēscere~, an inchoative of Latin ~pārēre~ (“to come into view, to appear, to obey”). Spanish ~desaparecer~ and Italian ~disparire~ / ~sparire~ are its Romance counterparts; English ~disappear~ is a parallel ~dis-~ formation on ~appear~.

The key word is the prefix. Where ~paraître~ presents something to view and ~apparaître~ brings it forth, ~dis-~ undoes the showing: ~disparaître~ is, etymologically, “to un-appear.” Latin ~pārēre~ also carried the sense “to obey” — a servant who “appears” at command — which is why the same root gives French ~apparaître~, ~apparition~, ~apparent~, and the noun ~apparence~, alongside the more surprising ~parer~ in some of its uses. The whole family circles the act of becoming, or ceasing to be, visible. A neat detail: French rebuilt this verb from native parts in the Renaissance rather than simply inheriting the worn-down ~disparoir~, choosing transparency of form over the older sound-changed shape.
en.dispatcher:
A borrowing from English ~dispatch~ (“to send off”). English took that verb from Spanish and Portuguese ~despachar~ or from Italian ~dispacciare~, which go back to Occitan ~despachar~ (“to get rid of”), from Middle French ~despeechier~ (“to free”), itself from Old French. The word thus travelled through Occitan, the Iberian languages or Italian, and English before coming home in English dress.

Its sense in French, to send out or allocate, is that of the English verb. French already had a native descendant of the same Middle French ~despeechier~: ~dépêcher~ (“to hurry, to send quickly”), so ~dispatcher~ is a distant doublet that returned by way of English. On the usual analysis, ~despeechier~ was the opposite of Old French ~empeechier~, which gave ~empêcher~ (“to hinder”): to free from an obstacle, against to put one in the way.
en.dispenser:
From Latin ~dispensare~, a frequentative of ~dispendere~ (“to weigh out, pay out”), itself ~dis-~ (“apart”) + ~pendere~ (“to weigh, to pay”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)pend-~ (“to stretch, to weigh”). Because the Romans weighed out coin and goods, ~pendere~ meant both “to weigh” and “to pay” — a sense preserved in English ~pension~ and, through related ~pendere~ “to hang,” in ~pendant~ and ~ponder~.

The original picture is a steward literally weighing out portions to distribute them; from “to weigh out, to deal out in measure” came “to dispense, to administer,” and then the legal sense “to release someone from an obligation” — to ~dispenser~ a person from a duty is to measure out an exemption. French kept the family ~dispense~ (“exemption”), ~dispensaire~ (“dispensary”), and ~indispensable~, literally “that cannot be dispensed with.” The same root *~(s)pend-~ underlies ~dépenser~, ~suspendre~, ~peser~, and ~pensée~ — for to think was, figuratively, to weigh.
en.disperser:
From Latin ~dispersus~, the past participle of ~dispergere~ (“to scatter, spread abroad”), itself ~dis-~ (“apart, in different directions”) + ~spargere~ (“to scatter, strew, sprinkle”). The base verb ~spargere~ gives Italian ~spargere~ and underlies English ~sparse~ and ~aspersion~; the prefix ~dis-~ survives across the Romance languages. The deep root of ~spargere~ is debated: it is often traced to a Proto-Indo-European *~sperh₂g-~ linked to words for crackling and roaring, but de Vaan and Schrijver prefer a g-extension of *~sper-~ (“to scatter, strew”), tied to Ancient Greek ~speírō~ (“to sow”).

The Latin sense — flinging things in every direction — passed almost unchanged into French: to ~disperser~ a crowd, a fortune, or a fog is to send its parts flying apart. The same Latin family seeds a cluster of French words: ~dispersion~, éparpiller being a separate formation, but ~asperger~ (“to sprinkle”) and the liturgical ~aspersion~ both rest on ~spargere~, as does ~épars~ (“scattered, sparse”). What unites them is the image of a hand casting seed or water broadcast over a field — the literal gesture of sowing, generalized to anything strewn too thin to gather back.
en.disposer:
From Latin ~dispōnere~ (“to set out, to arrange in different places”), from the prefix ~dis-~ (“apart, in different directions”) and ~pōnere~ (“to put, to place”). ~Pōnere~ is itself widely analyzed as an old compound of *~po-~ (“off, away”) and ~sinere~ (“to leave, to let”), with the past participle ~positus~. In its French form, ~disposer~ joined the great ~-poser~ family, where the descendants of ~pōnere~ blended with those of Late Latin *~pausāre~ (“to cease, to set down”).

The sense is one of placing things apart in good order: to ~disposer~ is to arrange, to lay out, to organize, and reflexively ~se disposer à~ is to get ready to act. From “having things arranged to one's liking” came the idiom ~disposer de~ (“to have at one's disposal”). The ~pōnere~ family blossomed into a regiment of French verbs — ~poser~, ~composer~, ~proposer~, ~exposer~, ~imposer~, ~déposer~ — plus nouns like ~position~, ~disposition~, and ~dépôt~. Curiously, ~disponible~ (“available”) preserves the original Latin ~n~ that ~disposer~ itself has lost, a small fossil of ~dispōnere~ hiding inside the modern word.
en.disputailler: Formed from ~disputer~ with the pejorative suffix ~-ailler~, attested from 1596. The suffix gives a slightly scornful, frequentative sense, so ~disputailler~ means to dispute needlessly and at length, to quarrel over trifles. The base ~disputer~ comes from Latin ~disputāre~ (“to discuss, to examine in detail”), formed from ~dis-~ and ~putāre~.
en.disputer:
From Latin ~disputāre~, from ~dis-~ (“apart, asunder”) plus ~putāre~ (“to reckon, consider, think — originally to clean, prune”). The literal image is striking: ~putāre~ first meant to lop and clean a tree of its excess branches, and ~disputāre~ to prune an argument apart, clearing away the dead wood to reckon up what is sound. The deeper Proto-Indo-European root of ~putāre~ is uncertain, so its first sense is reconstructed cautiously, but the pruning-then-reckoning development is well attested in Latin.

The French verb appears in the 12th century meaning to debate or discuss; only from the 17th century does it drift toward today's dominant sense of quarreling or vying for something — a familiar slide from reasoned argument to plain argument. The same ~putāre~ underlies a remarkable spread of French words: ~computer~ ideas became to ~compter~ and ~conter~, and the root yields ~réputer~ (and ~réputation~), ~amputer~, ~imputer~, and ~député~ (one reckoned off, delegated). A single verb for cleaning a tree thus branched into counting, calculating, reputation, and the noisy art of the dispute.
en.disqualifier: ~Disqualifier~ was borrowed from English ~disqualify~, which is built from the prefix ~dis-~ and ~qualify~ (the English counterpart of French ~qualifier~). French Wiktionary describes it as a straight loan, while English Wiktionary presents it as English ~disqualify~ with the French infinitive ending ~-er~ in place of the English ending. The two descriptions agree on the essentials: the verb came into French from English, and the French ending ~-er~ is the one that welcomes new verbs. The sense is to declare someone unfit or ineligible, most often an athlete or a competitor who has broken the rules.
en.disserter: ~Disserter~ was borrowed from Latin ~dissertāre~ (“to set out, to discuss”). French Wiktionary derives that verb from ~disserere~, glossed as stringing reasonings together in a line. Italian ~dissertare~ is a cognate. English ~dissertation~ comes from the same Latin family. The verb thus keeps the idea of presenting an argument step by step, as in a lecture or an essay.
en.dissimuler:
French ~dissimuler~ was borrowed around 1355 from Latin ~dissimulāre~ (“to conceal, to pretend that something is not”), formed from ~dis-~ (apart, negation) and ~simulāre~ (“to feign, to make like”), itself from ~similis~ (“similar, alike”). Behind ~similis~ lie Proto-Italic *~semalis~ and ultimately the Proto-Indo-European root *~sem-~ (“one, together”), which also yields English ~same~: to simulate is to make one thing pass for “the same” as another. The Romance family kept the verb — Italian ~dissimulare~, Spanish ~disimular~ — and English took ~dissemble~ as well as the more learned ~dissimulate~ from the same Latin source.

Classical rhetoric drew a neat line between the twins: ~simulāre~ is to pretend that something is — to display what does not exist — while ~dissimulāre~ is to pretend that something is not — to hide what does. French preserved the pair as ~simuler~ and ~dissimuler~: the con artist simulates riches and dissimulates debts. The verb's most famous hour is the Latin maxim “Qui nescit dissimulare, nescit regnare” (“he who cannot dissemble cannot reign”), traditionally said to have been the device of Louis XI, the arch-schemer among French kings — though historians note that the attribution itself is uncertain, the maxim having also been credited to medieval emperors. The root *~sem-~ spread far beyond deception: ~sembler~, ~ressembler~, ~assembler~, ~ensemble~, ~similaire~ and ~simultané~ all descend from it — a whole vocabulary of likeness and togetherness, within which dissimuler is the art of using resemblance to hide.
en.dissiper:
Borrowed from Latin ~dissipāre~ (“to scatter, to disperse, to squander”). The Latin verb is usually analysed as ~dis-~ (“apart”) plus an archaic verb ~supāre~ (“to throw”), so that to ~dissiper~ is, at bottom, to throw things in all directions. Both Wiktionaries trace it directly to Latin. English ~dissipate~ and Italian ~dissipare~ are borrowings of the same Latin verb, and Spanish ~disipar~ is the same word again in a Spanish dress.

The sense moved from the physical to the abstract. The Latin verb covered scattering a crowd or an army, and also wasting money by throwing it away. French kept both strands: ~dissiper~ means to make clouds, fog, fears or doubts vanish, and in an older use, to squander a fortune. The reflexive form adds a schoolroom sense, since a ~dissipé~ pupil is one whose attention has scattered and who cannot stay quiet. The family includes ~dissipation~, ~dissipateur~ (“spendthrift”), and ~dissipé~. The scattering image is the thread through all of them.
en.dissocier: Borrowed from Latin ~dissociāre~ (“to separate, to disunite”), built from the prefix ~dis-~ (“apart”) and ~sociāre~ (“to join, to ally”), itself from ~socius~ (“companion, ally”). The verb is thus the exact opposite of ~associer~, which pairs ~ad-~ with the same ~sociāre~. In French the sense is to pull apart things that had been joined, such as ideas, people or chemical compounds. The family includes ~société~, ~social~ and ~sociable~.
en.dissoner:
From Latin ~dissonāre~ (“to sound discordant, to be out of harmony”), a verb built from the prefix ~dis-~ (“apart, in different directions”) and ~sonāre~ (“to sound, to make a noise”). The French verb is a learned borrowing that keeps the Latin shape almost untouched. Italian ~dissonare~ and Spanish ~disonar~ continue the same Latin verb, and English ~dissonant~ comes from its present participle.

The simple verb ~sonāre~ is the source of French ~sonner~ and, with other prefixes, of ~résonner~ and ~consonne~, literally a letter that “sounds with” a vowel. ~Dissoner~ stands opposite to that idea of sounding together: it describes notes or voices that clash. Its family includes the noun ~dissonance~ and the adjective ~dissonant~. As a verb it is now rare and belongs to literary or musical writing, while the family nouns are far more common, including in the figurative sense of a jarring contrast between ideas or tones.
en.dissoudre:
From Old French — the Sermons of Saint Bernard (late 12th century) already use the participle ~dissoluz~ — with medieval forms like ~dessoudre~ later reshaped on the model of ~absoudre~; from Latin ~dissolvere~ (“to loosen apart, undo, break up”), from ~dis-~ (“apart”) + ~solvere~ (“to loosen, untie, release — and to pay”). ~solvere~ goes back to ~se-~ (“away”) + ~luere~, from PIE *~lewh₁-~ (“to loosen”), the root of Greek ~lúō~ (“I loosen, I undo”) and — through Old Norse — of English ~loose~. Cognate with Italian ~dissolvere~, Spanish ~disolver~ and English ~dissolve~.

Latin ~solvere~ led a double life: to untie, and to pay — paying being how one unties oneself from a debt, a sense French keeps in ~solvable~ and ~insolvable~ (able, or unable, to pay). The whole French family is about undoing bonds: ~absoudre~ unties the sinner, ~résoudre~ untangles the problem, a ~solution~ is at once what dissolves and what unknots a difficulty, with ~soluble~, ~solvant~ and ~dissolution~ alongside. A ~dissolu~ person is literally someone come untied — morals loosened. The Greek twin ~lúō~ produced ~analyse~ (etymologically a loosening up into parts) and ~paralysie~ (a loosening of the limbs at one side). And French presidents wield the same chemistry as sugar cubes: dissolving the Assemblée nationale and dissolving sugar are one gesture — undoing what held together. The participle offers a last curiosity: masculine ~dissous~ against feminine ~dissoute~, with the spelling ~dissout~ admitted by the 1990 rectifications.
en.dissuader:
French ~dissuader~ was borrowed from Latin ~dissuādēre~ (“to advise against”), made of ~dis-~ (“apart, away”) and ~suādēre~ (“to advise, to urge”). The Latin verb ~suādēre~ is related to the adjective ~suāvis~ (“sweet, pleasant”), and both go back to a Proto-Indo-European root *~swād-~ (“sweet, pleasant”). Its cognate in English is ~sweet~, inherited through Germanic, while ~suave~ and ~persuade~ are borrowings from the Latin family. English ~dissuade~ was taken from the same Latin verb, as were Italian ~dissuadere~ and Spanish ~disuadir~.

The original idea behind ~suādēre~ is a pleasant one: to advise someone is to make a course of action seem sweet to them. Persuasion, in this picture, is a sweetening of the will. The prefix ~dis-~ turns that around, so that ~dissuader~ means to talk someone out of something, to turn them away from a plan. Its mirror verb is ~persuader~ (“to convince”), built with the prefix ~per-~ (“thoroughly”), and the pair ~persuader~ and ~dissuader~ is a neat illustration of how the same root can push in opposite directions. Other French words from the same Latin root include ~suave~ (“smooth, gentle”), ~persuasion~, ~dissuasion~ and ~dissuasif~ (“deterrent”), the last of which became common in the vocabulary of strategy, in the phrase ~force de dissuasion~ (“deterrent force”).
en.disséminer: From Latin ~dissēmināre~ (“to scatter seed”), formed from ~dis-~ (“apart”) and ~sēmināre~ (“to sow”), itself from ~sēmen~ (“seed”). French took the verb over directly from Latin as a learned borrowing. The same Latin verb was borrowed into English as ~disseminate~, and it gave Italian ~disseminare~ and Spanish ~diseminar~ as well. The root ~sēmen~ lies behind several other French words: ~semer~ (“to sow”), ~semence~ (“seed”), ~inséminer~ and ~séminaire~.
en.disséquer:
French ~disséquer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~dissecāre~ (“to cut up”). The Latin verb joins ~dis-~ (“apart”) to ~secāre~ (“to cut”), so it means to cut in pieces. English ~dissect~ is a close twin, taken from the same Latin source, and the match between the two verbs shows how directly French reused the Latin word rather than reshaping it over the centuries.

Because it was borrowed whole from Latin, ~disséquer~ keeps both Latin parts in plain sight. The root ~secāre~ is a productive one, and it gave French ~section~, ~secteur~, ~segment~, ~sécante~ and ~insecte~. English cousins include ~section~, ~sector~ and ~segment~ too. The verb stayed literal, “to cut apart,” and is used chiefly for the cutting up of a body or a specimen for study, with a figurative use for breaking a text or an argument into parts.
en.distancer: ~Distancer~ has two competing accounts. French Wiktionary traces it to a Middle French verb, from Old French ~distancer~, and adds that it can be analyzed as ~distance~ plus ~-er~. English Wiktionary instead calls it a borrowing from English ~distance~ plus ~-er~. Both rest on the noun ~distance~, which comes from Latin ~distantia~, formed on ~distāre~ (“to stand apart”). The sources disagree on whether the verb was coined in French or came back from English, so the safe summary is that it means to leave a rival far behind, with a noun of space at its core.
en.distancier: ~Distancier~ is built on the noun ~distance~ with a verbal ending, ~-ier~ in English Wiktionary's analysis, giving a verb for putting at a distance. The noun reached French from Latin ~distantia~ (“distance, remoteness”), through Old French ~destance~ and Middle French ~distance~; in Old French it also covered senses such as “difference” and “quarrel.” The verb is best known in the reflexive ~se distancier~, “to detach oneself.”
en.distendre: ~Distendre~ is borrowed from Latin ~distendere~, a compound generally analyzed as ~dis-~ (“apart”) and ~tendere~ (“to stretch”): to stretch in different directions. The word entered French by the learned route and kept the Latin shape. It means to stretch something until it is slack or swollen, and the same Latin verb gave English ~distend~. French ~tendre~, ~tension~ and ~distension~ belong to the same family.
en.distiller: A learned borrowing from Latin ~dēstillāre~ (“to trickle down, to distil”), built from the prefix ~dē-~ (“down”) and the verb ~stillāre~, which comes from ~stilla~ (“drop”). The word therefore pictures liquid falling drop by drop, which is exactly what happens at the end of a still. The same ~stilla~ lies behind ~instiller~ (“to put in drop by drop”). English ~distil~ and Spanish ~destilar~ have parallel histories. The verb later specialised in the technique of vaporising a liquid and condensing it again, giving ~distillation~, ~distillateur~ and ~distillerie~.
en.distinguer:
From Latin ~distinguere~ (“to separate, to mark off, to distinguish”), from ~dis-~ (“apart”) + ~stinguere~ (“to prick, to mark with points”). ~Stinguere~ rests on a Proto-Italic *~stengʷō~, from a Proto-Indo-European root *~steygʷ-~ broadly associated with sharp points and pricking. Through that family the word is connected to English ~stick~, ~sting~, and ~stigma~, and to Greek ~stízō~ (“to tattoo, to prick”). The image at the bottom is concrete: to distinguish was to set things apart by pricking marks between them.

From that literal marking-off the verb climbed to the mental act of telling one thing from another, and then to the social sense in ~distingué~, “distinguished, set apart by excellence” — the same gesture of marking out, now applied to merit. A neat in-house relative is ~éteindre~ (“to extinguish”), from Latin ~exstinguere~: the prick-and-mark root, with a different prefix, came to mean snuffing a flame, perhaps via the idea of pricking it out. French keeps the learned line in ~distinct~, ~distinction~, ~distinctement~, and ~indistinct~, all sharpened, etymologically, to a point.
en.distordre: The sources give two accounts. French Wiktionary treats ~distordre~ as ~tordre~ with the prefix ~dis-~. English Wiktionary instead calls it a borrowing from Latin ~distorquēre~ (“to twist apart, to contort”), conjugated like ~tordre~. The two are not far apart, since the Latin verb is itself ~dis-~ (“apart”) plus ~torquēre~ (“to twist”), and ~tordre~ descends from ~torquēre~. Its everyday relatives are better known: ~tordre~ itself and ~torsion~, borrowed from Latin. English ~distort~ is the same Latin word, reaching English through the participle. The much more frequent noun ~distorsion~ is its closest kin.
en.distraire:
Borrowed from Latin ~distrahere~ (“to pull apart, to pull in different directions”), formed from ~dis-~ (“apart”) and ~trahere~ (“to pull, to drag”). The verb was fitted into the pattern of the native French verb ~traire~ (“to milk”), and so it conjugates like it (~je distrais~, ~nous distrayons~). ~Traire~ itself continues a Vulgar Latin variant of ~trahere~, so the two verbs are cousins brought together again. Italian ~distrarre~, Spanish ~distraer~ and English ~distract~ are relatives of the same Latin verb.

The Latin picture of something torn in two directions survives in the legal and financial sense of ~distraire~, to take a part away from a whole or divert funds. The mental sense followed: to pull attention away, hence ~distrait~ (“absent-minded”), and then, more pleasantly, to take someone's mind off worries, hence “to amuse.” That is the sense of ~se distraire~ (“to amuse oneself”) and of ~distraction~. The root ~trahere~ also gave ~traction~, ~attraction~, ~extraire~, ~soustraire~, ~abstraire~, ~trait~ and ~portrait~.
en.distribuer:
From Latin ~distribuere~ (“to deal out, divide, apportion”), a compound of the prefix ~dis-~ (“apart, individually”) and the verb ~tribuere~ (“to assign, grant, allot”). That verb is itself drawn from ~tribus~, a “tribe” or division of the Roman people: to ~tribuere~ was originally to allot something among the tribes. French borrowed ~distribuer~ as a learned word directly from Latin, which is why it shows none of the wear of a verb passed down through Old French speech. Through ~tribuere~ it is cognate with English ~distribute~, ~tribute~, ~attribute~, and ~contribute~.

The semantic core is division followed by sharing out. From the civic act of apportioning duties among the Roman ~tribus~, ~distribuere~ generalized to any dividing-and-dealing-out: of goods, of letters, of roles in a play. Modern French ~distribuer~ covers handing out cards, delivering mail, and casting actors (~la distribution~ d'un film is its cast). The root ~tribus~ proved remarkably fertile: French inherited ~tribu~ (“tribe”) itself, ~tribut~ (“tribute”), ~attribuer~ (“to attribute”), ~contribuer~ (“to contribute”), ~rétribuer~ (“to remunerate”), and ~tributaire~ (“tributary”). It even survives in the unexpected ~tribunal~ and ~tribun~, since a ~tribunus~ was originally the head of a tribe — so the courtroom and the postal carrier share, distantly, the same ancestral division of Rome's people.
en.divaguer:
Borrowed from Latin ~dīvagārī~ (“to wander here and there”), made of ~dī-~ (“apart”) and ~vagārī~ (“to wander”). The simple verb ~vaguer~ comes from the same ~vagārī~, so French holds both the plain and the prefixed form of the Latin verb. Spanish ~divagar~ and Italian ~divagare~ are its counterparts, and English borrowed the same Latin verb as ~divagate~.

Modern French uses this verb mostly for speech and thought that stray: to ramble, to talk at random, to lose the thread. Its Latin root ~vagārī~ belongs to the family of ~vagus~ (“wandering”), which gave French ~vague~, and of ~vagabond~. ~Extravagant~, built on ~extrā~ (“outside”) and ~vagārī~, shares the same root: one who wanders beyond the bounds.
en.diverger: Borrowed from Latin, with the sources giving slightly different forms: French Wiktionary cites ~devergere~ (“to incline, to lean”) and English Wiktionary ~dīvergō~. French Wiktionary adds that the verb was taken to serve as the opposite of ~converger~. The Latin verb is generally analyzed as ~dis-~ (“apart”) plus ~vergere~ (“to turn, to incline”), so to diverge is to lean away in different directions, the mirror image of ~converger~, which leans together. Italian ~divergere~, Spanish ~divergir~ and English ~diverge~ are relatives, and French also has ~divergent~ and ~divergence~.
en.diversifier:
From Medieval Latin ~diversificare~, attested in the 13th century, a compound of Latin ~diversus~ (“diverse, turned different ways”) and ~facere~ (“to make, to do”). ~diversus~ is the past participle of ~divertere~ (~dis-~ + ~vertere~, “to turn aside”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~wert-~ (“to turn”). Through ~vertere~ it is kin to the English words ~divert~, ~version~, and ~verse~, all of which preserve the idea of a turning.

The literal force of ~diversificare~ was “to make turned-apart,” that is, to make things branch off in different directions — exactly the modern senses “to diversify” and “to broaden.” The image is concrete: things diverge by being turned away from one another. From the same ancestor ~vertere~ French inherited a sprawling family — ~divers~, ~diversité~, ~divertir~ (“to divert, amuse”), ~convertir~, ~inverser~, and ~version~ — while ~facere~ supplies the “-fier” of countless verbs like ~simplifier~ and ~modifier~.
en.divertir:
From Latin ~dīvertere~ (“to turn aside, to turn away”), built from ~dis-~ (“apart”) and ~vertere~ (“to turn”). Latin ~vertere~ goes back to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “to turn,” which also underlies German ~werden~ (“to become,” originally “to turn into”). Italian ~divertire~ and Spanish ~divertir~ continue the same Latin verb, and English ~divert~ was borrowed from it, so the four languages share both the form and the original image of turning something off its course.

The original meaning of French ~divertir~ was exactly that, and it survives in the legal and financial sense: to ~divertir~ funds is to turn them away from their proper use, that is, to misappropriate them. The now dominant meaning came by a short step. To turn someone’s attention away from their cares is to amuse them, and the reflexive ~se divertir~ came to mean “to enjoy oneself.” From it come ~divertissement~ (“entertainment,” and in music a light interlude) and the adjective ~divertissant~. The Latin family around ~vertere~ is large in French, with ~vers~, ~version~, ~convertir~, ~pervertir~ and ~avertir~, and even ~divorce~, which comes from the Latin ~dīvortium~, a variant of ~dīvertium~, the “turning away” of one spouse from the other.
en.diviniser: Formed in French from the adjective ~divin~ and the verbal suffix ~-iser~, which means “to make A.” So ~diviniser~ is “to make divine,” that is, to deify. The base ~divin~ comes from Latin ~dīvīnus~, itself derived from ~dīvus~ (“divine”) with the adjective suffix ~-inus~. English Wiktionary adds that ~divin~ is a doublet of ~devin~ (“soothsayer”).
en.diviser:
From Latin ~dīvidere~ (“to force apart, to separate, to distribute, to share out”). The verb is an assimilated ~dis-~ (“apart”) prefixed to a root *~videre~ meaning “to separate,” which de Vaan traces to a Proto-Indo-European *~(d)widʰ-~ (“to separate, to divide in two”). This root is unrelated to ~vidēre~ “to see”; it is, however, the same one behind Latin ~viduus~ (“bereft, void”) and so behind ~vidua~ (“widow”) — division and widowhood share an idea of being set apart. Italian ~dividere~ and Spanish ~dividir~ are cognates, as is English ~divide~.

French actually inherited this verb twice. The popular, orally transmitted form became ~deviser~ (originally “to divide up,” later “to chat, to converse” — talk that goes back and forth, portioned out between speakers), while the learned, book-borrowed form gave ~diviser~, keeping the plain mathematical and physical sense of separating into parts. From the same source come ~division~, ~diviseur~, ~divisible~, ~divisibilité~, and ~divisionnaire~, plus, through ~vidua~, the surprising relatives ~veuf~ and ~veuve~ (“widower, widow”) and ~divorce~ — all turning on the ancient image of two things pulled asunder.
en.divorcer: Formed from the noun ~divorce~ with the first-group ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Latin ~dīvortium~ (“separation, divorce”), from the verb ~dīvortere~, a variant of ~dīvertere~ (“to turn aside, to separate from”). The Latin picture is of two paths turning away from each other, which fits the idea of a marriage coming apart. English ~divorce~ comes from the same Latin word through French. The verb ~divorcer~ is therefore a French creation on a Latin noun, not a verb inherited from Latin.
en.divulguer: A learned borrowing from Latin ~dīvulgāre~ (“to spread among the people, to make public”), built from ~dī-~, a form of ~dis-~ (“in all directions”), and ~vulgāre~ (“to make common, to publish”). ~Vulgāre~ comes from ~vulgus~ (“the common people, the crowd”), which also gave French ~vulgaire~ and the ~Vulgate~, the “common” Latin Bible. Italian ~divulgare~, Spanish ~divulgar~ and English ~divulge~ are learned borrowings of the same Latin verb. In Latin the sense was neutral, simply broadcasting; in modern French ~divulguer~ is used above all for revealing what was meant to stay hidden, such as a secret or a name.
en.diéser: Formed as a verb from the noun ~dièse~ (“sharp”) with the ending ~-er~, so that it means “to mark a note with a sharp.” The noun is borrowed from Latin ~diesis~ (“quarter-tone”), which in Late Latin came to mean “semitone,” and ultimately from Ancient Greek ~δίεσις~ (~díesis~). The musical term thus kept its Greek roots, while the verb is a purely French derivation on top of it.
en.documenter: Formed in French from the noun ~document~ and the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense “to support with documents, to supply with evidence.” The noun ~document~ is a borrowing from Latin ~documentum~ (“lesson, example, proof”), derived from the verb ~docēre~ (“to teach, to show”). The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is the usual way French turns a noun into a first-group verb. The reflexive ~se documenter~ (“to research a subject, to gather information”) is common, while ~documenter~ itself also covers recording a process in writing.
en.dodeliner: ~Dodeliner~ is closely tied to ~dodo~, the nursery word for sleep, and to the gesture of rocking a child. English Wiktionary derives it from ~dodiner~. Very similar words exist in other European languages: English ~dandle~, Italian ~dondolare~ and German ~dändeln~. French ~dada~ and ~dandiner~ share a comparable formation.
en.dogmatiser:
French ~dogmatiser~ comes by way of Latin ~dogmatizō~, from Ancient Greek ~dogmatízō~ (“to decree”). The Greek verb is built on ~dógma~ (“opinion, decree”), a noun that belongs to ~dokeîn~ (“to seem, to think”), with the verb-forming ending ~-ízō~. That ending passed into Latin as ~-izāre~ and into French as ~-iser~, the same suffix that gave ~baptiser~ and ~organiser~. English has the same chain in ~dogmatize~, and the Greek noun is the source of ~dogma~ in both languages.

The verb keeps its Greek sense of laying down a rule: in theology, to set forth a point of doctrine as a dogma, and in everyday speech, to pronounce opinions in an authoritative, peremptory tone. It belongs to a family of learned words built on the same Greek noun: ~dogme~, ~dogmatique~, ~dogmatisme~ and ~dogmatiste~. Unlike many verbs in ~-iser~, it is not a French formation on a base but a verb received whole from Latin and Greek.
en.doigter: Formed from ~doigt~ with the verb ending ~-er~, it means to finger a piece of music or to mark the fingering. French ~doigt~ comes from Old French ~doi~ or ~dei~, from Vulgar Latin *~dĭtus~, an alteration of Latin ~digitus~ (“finger”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~deyǵ-~ (“to show, to point out”). The root also gave ~index~ and ~juge~, according to French Wiktionary. The ~g~ in the modern spelling was added in Middle French in imitation of the Latin form, and it also keeps the noun apart from the verb form ~doit~.
en.doler: Borrowed from Latin ~dolāre~ (“to hew, to shape with an axe”). The verb is attested in French in 1384, in a text that lists it among the tasks of splitting, thinning and laying wooden roof tiles. In modern French it means to plane or to dress a surface smooth. The tool noun ~doloire~, a broad-bladed axe used by coopers and carpenters, belongs to the same Latin family.
en.domestiquer: Formed from the adjective ~domestique~ (“of the household”) and the verb ending ~-er~: to make an animal domestic, that is, to tame it. The adjective comes from Latin ~domesticus~, which French Wiktionary ties to ~domus~ (“house”). Latin ~domesticus~ is a regular derivative of ~domus~ with the suffix ~-ticus~. English ~domestic~ is a close relative, and so is French ~domicile~.
en.domicilier: Formed from the noun ~domicile~ with the ordinary verb ending ~-er~ (English Wiktionary writes the ending as ~-ier~, but it is the same verbal ending). The verb means “to give a legal residence to someone or something,” and ~être domicilié~ is “to reside, to be registered at an address.” The noun ~domicile~ is a borrowing of Latin ~domicilium~ (“dwelling”), itself derived from ~domus~ (“house”), the root behind ~domestique~ and ~dôme~.
en.dominer:
From Latin ~dominārī~ (“to be master, to rule, to reign”), a verb derived from ~dominus~ (“master, lord of the household”), which in turn comes from ~domus~ (“house, home”). The chain reaches back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dem-~ (“house, household; to build”). The same ~dominus~ underlies Italian ~dominare~ and Spanish ~dominar~, while ~domus~ shows up across the family in Greek ~domos~ (“house”) and, by a Germanic detour, in English ~timber~ (originally “building material”).

The striking thing is how authority grew out of the home: the ~dominus~ was first simply the head of a ~domus~, the master of a household, and his domestic command broadened into mastery, rule, and at last sheer ascendancy. To ~dominer~ now ranges from a sovereign ruling a realm to a peak ~dominating~ a valley below — physical and figurative supremacy alike. The same root flowered into a large French family: ~maison~ (from ~mansiō~), ~domestique~, ~domicile~, ~domaine~, ~dame~ (from ~domina~), ~madame~, ~dominical~, and the borrowed ~dôme~, all gathered, ultimately, around the idea of the house and its lord.
en.dompter:
French ~dompter~ comes from Old French ~donter~ (with a variant ~danter~), from Latin ~domitāre~ (“to tame, to subdue”), a frequentative of ~domāre~ (“to tame, to break in”). A frequentative is a verb built to express repeated or intensified action. The Latin verb has relatives in other Romance languages, among them Spanish ~domar~ and Italian ~domare~. English also owes it a word: ~daunt~ comes from the Old French variant ~danter~, so to daunt someone is, etymologically, a cousin of taming them.

The ~p~ of ~dompter~ is not inherited. In Latin ~domitāre~, the unstressed ~i~ in an open syllable dropped out in the first or second century AD, bringing ~m~ and ~t~ together, and speakers eased the clash by slipping in a ~p~ around the fourth century. That ~p~ stopped being pronounced by the ninth century, which is why Old French wrote ~donter~. The Dictionnaire de l'Académie française spelled it ~domter~ in 1694 and 1718, restored the ~p~ in 1740 and has kept it since, except that the 1798 edition gave both forms. English Wiktionary compares Old French ~dampner~ (Latin ~damnō~, Modern French ~damner~), another word with an unetymological ~p~. Modern relatives include ~dompteur~, ~domptable~ and ~indomptable~.
en.donner:
