From Old French ~doner~, from Latin ~dōnāre~ (“to give as a gift, to bestow”), itself built on the noun ~dōnum~ (“gift”). Both go back to Proto-Indo-European *~deh₃-~ (“to give”), by way of *~deh₃nom~ (“gift”). Through that root ~donner~ is cognate with Spanish ~donar~ and Italian ~donare~, with Sanskrit ~dā~ (“to give”), and with Greek ~dōron~ (“gift,” as in the name Theodore, “gift of god”).

A quiet upset lies behind the everyday verb. Classical Latin had two words here: plain ~dăre~ (“to give”) and ~dōnāre~ (“to make a gift of”). In Gaul, ~dăre~ was driven out early and almost completely, so French took its ordinary “give” from the more ceremonious ~dōnāre~ — where Spanish and Italian kept ~dăre~ alive in ~dar~ and ~dare~. From the same root French keeps ~don~ (“gift”), ~donateur~ (“donor”), ~donation~, and ~pardonner~ (“to forgive,” literally “to give thoroughly”), while the learned ~dose~ and ~anecdote~ reach back through Greek to the very same *~deh₃-~. The gift, in French, swallowed the verb of plain giving whole.
en.doper: Borrowed from English ~to dope~ (“to drug”). English ~dope~ is itself usually traced to Dutch ~doop~ (“dipping sauce”), and its senses moved from a thick liquid to a narcotic and then to the act of drugging, notably racehorses and later athletes. French took the verb up in that sporting sense, and it then spread to ~se doper~ (“to take performance-enhancing drugs”) and to the figurative “to boost, to stimulate,” as in ~doper les ventes~ (“to boost sales”).
en.dorer:
From Latin ~deaurāre~ (“to gild, cover with gold”), from ~de-~ (here intensive) plus ~aurum~ (“gold”), from Proto-Italic *~auzom~, from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂ews-~ (“to shine, glow; dawn”) — the same root that gave Latin ~aurōra~ (“dawn”). Cognate Romance reflexes include Italian ~dorare~ and Spanish ~dorar~; the noun ~aurum~ itself survives in French ~or~ (“gold”) and in English borrowings like ~auriferous~.

The metaphor is bright and old: gold was the metal of the glowing dawn. From “to cover with gold” French ~dorer~ broadened to any warm golden colouring — sunlight that ~dore~ the wheat, an egg-wash that gilds a pastry crust. The figurative idiom ~dorer la pilule~ (“to gild the pill”) means to sweeten unwelcome news, the way an apothecary once coated a bitter pill in gold leaf. From the same ~aurum~ root French keeps ~doré~, ~dorure~, ~orfèvre~ (“goldsmith”), and ~oriflamme~; ~aurore~ (“dawn”) preserves, intact, the original Indo-European image of shining light.
en.dorloter: ~Dorloter~ is formed from Old French ~dorelot~ + ~-er~. The noun meant “lock of hair, curl” and also “ribbon, fringe,” and then “one who curls and primps himself,” whence “darling, favorite.” The verb is first attested in the fourteenth century in the sense “to curl” (~friser~), and only later took its modern meaning “to pamper, to cosset.” The suffix ~-er~ is the ordinary French ending that turns a noun into a verb, from Latin ~-are~.
en.dormir:
From Middle French ~dormir~, from Old French ~dormir~ (attested around 1100), from Latin ~dormīre~ (“to sleep”), from Proto-Italic *~dormiō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~drem-~ (“to sleep”). Cognate, through the Latin verb, with Italian ~dormire~, Spanish and Portuguese ~dormir~, and Catalan ~dormir~; through the PIE root, with Old Church Slavonic ~drěmati~ (“to doze”) and Sanskrit ~drāti~ (“sleeps”).

Unusually for a common verb, the meaning never wandered: ~dormir~ has meant simply “to sleep” for two thousand years, with idiomatic extensions like ~dormir comme une souche~ (“to sleep like a log”) and ~qui dort dîne~ (“he who sleeps, dines”). The Latin root proved richly generative. From ~dormīre~ and its relatives French drew ~dormeur~ (“sleeper”), ~dormant~ (“sleeping, dormant,” as in ~eau dormante~, “still water”), ~endormir~ (“to put to sleep”), ~rendormir~ (“to send back to sleep”), and ~dortoir~ (“dormitory”). English borrowed many of the same: ~dormant~, ~dormitory~, and even ~dormouse~, the “sleeping mouse.” The architectural ~dormer~ window, too, descends from this root — once a window for a sleeping-room.
en.doser: Formed from the noun ~dose~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so ~doser~ means “to measure out a dose.” The noun ~dose~ is a learned borrowing of Latin ~dosis~, which Latin took from Ancient Greek ~dósis~ (“a giving, a gift”). Related to it through the same family of “giving” is ~dot~ (“dowry”). From medicine the verb spread to cooking and chemistry, and then to the figurative use of weighing one's words or efforts.
en.doter:
From Latin ~dotare~ (“to endow, to provide with a dowry”), a denominative verb built on the noun ~dos~, stem ~dot-~ (“dowry, marriage portion”). That noun goes back to Proto-Italic *~dōtis~ and to the Proto-Indo-European root *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). Through that root ~doter~ is cognate with a remarkable spread of words: Ancient Greek ~dōron~ (“gift”) and ~dosis~ (“a giving, a dose”), Latin ~donare~ (“to give”), and the English borrowings ~donate~, ~dose~, and even ~date~ (from the Roman dating formula “given on such a day”).

The verb began in the law of marriage: to ~doter~ a daughter was to settle a dowry on her, the property she brought to the household. From that contractual core the sense widened generously. To ~doter~ came to mean to furnish or equip with any advantage — funds, talents, qualities — so that today a region may be ~doté~ with resources, a person ~doté~ with charm, a school ~doté~ of a new library. French keeps the original noun ~dot~ (“dowry”) alongside the derived ~dotation~ (“endowment, allocation”). The same *~deh₃-~ root, entering French through learned Latin, also yields ~donner~, ~don~, ~donation~, ~dose~, and ~anecdote~ (Greek for something “not given out,” i.e. unpublished).
en.double-cliquer: ~Double-cliquer~ is formed from the noun ~double-clic~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is itself a compound of ~double~ and ~clic~. The verb thus means to perform a double click, a computer gesture of the modern age, and it follows the usual pattern of turning a noun into a first-conjugation verb.
en.doubler:
French ~doubler~ comes from the adjective ~double~, from Latin ~duplus~ (“twofold”), with the verb continuing Late Latin ~duplāre~ (“to double”). ~Duplus~ is ~duo~ (“two”) plus ~-plus~ (“-fold”): the first from Proto-Indo-European *~dwóh₁~ (“two”), the second from the root *~pleḱ-~ (“to fold, weave”). It is cognate with English ~double~ and ~duo~, with Ancient Greek ~diplóos~ (“twofold”), and, through the same fold-element, with English ~ply~ and ~-fold~.

The core sense is “to make twofold,” but ~doubler~ has fanned out remarkably. To line a coat is to ~doubler~ it — to give it a second, inner layer (hence ~doublure~, “lining,” and also a stand-in or understudy). On the road, to ~doubler~ a car is to overtake it, briefly running two abreast. In cinema, to ~doubler~ a film is to dub it, laying a second voice over the first. Each sense is a literal doubling. The family also gives ~redoubler~ (“to redouble; to repeat a school year”) and ~dédoubler~ (“to split in two”).
en.doublonner: ~Doublonner~ is formed from the noun ~doublon~ and ~-er~, with the sense “to overlap, to be redundant.” ~Doublon~ has two origins. In printing, it comes from ~double~ plus the suffix ~-on~, and names a word or line set twice by mistake. In another sense, it was borrowed from Spanish ~doblón~, a gold coin worth two others. The verb's meaning of redundancy fits the first, typographic ~doublon~, an element that appears twice where once was enough.
en.doucher: ~Doucher~ is a denominal verb: the noun ~douche~ plus the verb-forming ending ~-er~, with the sense “to give or take a shower.” The noun was borrowed from Italian ~doccia~ (“jet of water, conduit, pipe”). French Wiktionary traces the Italian word further to Latin ~ductiō~ (“conduit”), the same family as French ~conduire~ and ~conduit~. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-āre~ and is the default way to coin a verb from a noun in French.
en.doucir: Formed from the adjective ~doux~ (“soft, sweet”) with the verb ending ~-ir~, so it means to make soft or smooth, whence the technical sense “to polish, to smooth”. ~Doux~ comes from Old French ~dous~ (also spelled ~dulz~), from Latin ~dulcis~ (“sweet”). The same adjective gave ~douceur~ and ~adoucir~, which is the commoner verb for making something gentler.
en.douer:
From Old French ~doer~ (twelfth century), from Latin ~dōtāre~ (“to provide with a dowry, to endow”), a derivative of ~dōs~, genitive ~dōtis~ (“dowry”), from Proto-Italic *~dōtis~, from PIE *~déh₃tis~ (“gift, act of giving”), built on the root *~deh₃-~ (“to give”) — the root of Latin ~dare~ (“to give”) and ~dōnum~ (“gift”). Cognate with Italian ~dotare~ and Spanish ~dotar~; English ~endow~ comes straight from Anglo-Norman ~endouer~, built on this very French verb.

At first ~douer~ meant exactly what its Latin parent meant: to settle a dowry on a bride (late twelfth century). By about 1210 it had taken the figurative leap that defines it today: nature, heaven or fortune endows someone with a quality. Modern French has all but retired the active verb, which lives on chiefly in the participle ~doué~ — to be gifted at mathematics is, etymologically, to have received one's talent as a dowry from nature. French in fact owns the Latin verb twice: ~douer~ is the form worn smooth by a millennium of speech, while ~doter~ was borrowed back from books — a classic popular/learned doublet, the two now divided by use, one endowing institutions with funds, the other persons with gifts. The noun behind them was given to French twice as well: Latin ~dōs~ produced ~dot~ (“dowry”), while the same PIE *~déh₃tis~, travelling through Greek ~δόσις~ (“a giving”), produced ~dose~ — a dowry and a dose are, etymologically, one and the same “gift.” The wider family of *~deh₃-~ includes ~donner~, ~don~, ~donation~ and ~pardonner~.
en.douiller:
The origin of ~douiller~ is uncertain, and the two Wiktionaries offer different accounts. French Wiktionary proposes that it may derive from ~douillet~ (itself from Old French ~douille~, “soft,” plus ~-et~), or may be a new first-conjugation formation on the Old French verb ~douloir~ (“to suffer”), which survived in dialects, where a form ~deuillant~ (“suffering”) is attested. English Wiktionary gives two separate verbs: one inherited from Old French ~dueillier~, from ~duel~ (“pain”), and one from ~douille~ (“money”) plus ~-er~.

The verb carries two senses, “to hurt” and, in slang, “to pay up.” French Wiktionary finds the passage from one to the other easy to explain and points to ~douloureuse~ in the sense of “bill.” Whether the two senses spring from one source or from two separate words is exactly what the sources leave open.
en.douter:
Attested in Old French from around 980, from Latin ~dubitāre~ (“to waver, hesitate, doubt”), a frequentative connected to ~dubius~ (“doubtful, uncertain”) and ultimately to ~duo~ (“two”). The image at the heart of doubt is being pulled between two ways: to doubt is to hover between two possibilities, unable to commit. Italian ~dubitare~ and Spanish ~dudar~ carry the same Latin root, and English ~doubt~ borrowed it through French.

The earliest French sense was not intellectual uncertainty but fear: in Old French ~douter~ meant “to dread, to fear” — to be of two minds before a danger. This sense survives intact in the compound ~redouter~ (“to dread”). Over time the verb shifted from fearing to questioning, from apprehension to mere uncertainty. The reflexive ~se douter de~ then swung almost to the opposite — “to suspect, to surmise,” to be fairly sure of something. The silent ~b~ in English ~doubt~ was reinserted by scholars to mirror Latin ~dubitāre~; French spelling never restored it. From the same root come ~doute~, ~douteux~, ~indubitable~, and ~dubitatif~.
en.dracher: A Belgian regionalism for pouring rain. It comes from Walloon ~drachî~ (same meaning), itself borrowed from West Flemish ~draschen~ (“to rain heavily”). The verb is thus a loan across the language border between Dutch-speaking and French-speaking Belgium, passing from a Flemish dialect into Walloon and then into Belgian French.
en.drageonner: Formed from ~drageon~ (“shoot, sucker”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to put forth shoots.” ~Drageon~ comes from Old Frankish *~draiƀjō~ (“shoot”), from the verb *~draiƀjan~ (“to push”), related to German ~treiben~ and English ~drive~. A shoot, in this account, is something pushed out of the plant. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~.
en.draguer: Formed from the noun ~drague~ with ~-er~; English Wiktionary adds that Middle French had ~dragger~ (“to dredge”). For the noun, French Wiktionary gives English ~drag~ (“hook, net”), while English Wiktionary traces Middle English ~dragge~ to Old Norse ~draga~ (“something dragged”), cognate with English ~dray~. Both route the word through English. The verb first meant to dredge or trawl. The slang sense “to flirt” is probably metaphorical, according to French Wiktionary: the charmer draws in victims as a net draws in fish.
en.dragéifier: Formed from the noun ~dragée~ (“sugared almond, sugar-coated sweet”) with the verbal suffix ~-ifier~, meaning to give something a sugar-shell coating, as with a pill or a candy. The suffix ~-ifier~ derives from Latin ~-ficāre~, itself from ~facere~ (“to make”), and it builds verbs meaning “to make into” (~clarifier~, ~simplifier~). ~Dragéifier~ is a technical term of confectionery and pharmacy.
en.drainer: The sources differ slightly on the route. French Wiktionary sees a derivative of the noun ~drain~ plus the suffix ~-er~, which turns a noun into a verb, while English Wiktionary calls it a straight borrowing from the English verb ~drain~. Either way the root is English: French ~drain~ (“channel for carrying off water”) was itself borrowed from English ~drain~. The English word thus crossed the Channel, and the French verb ~drainer~ means to drain off a liquid, whether water from soil or, figuratively, money, talent or traffic. The suffix ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is the default for new verbs.
en.dramatiser: Formed from the noun ~drame~ with the suffix ~-iser~, which makes verbs meaning “to make, to treat as, to turn into.” English Wiktionary dates the verb to the 19th century. The base ~drame~ is borrowed from Latin ~drāma~, which comes from Ancient Greek ~δρᾶμα~ (~drâma~, “play, action performed on stage”). To ~dramatiser~ something is therefore to turn it into a drama, or to treat it as one, by making it more theatrical than it was.
en.draper: ~Draper~ is built on ~drap~ (“cloth”) with the verb ending ~-er~, and it already existed in Old French, where it meant both “to drape” and “to full cloth” (to beat woollen cloth until it thickens). ~Drap~ goes back to Late Latin ~drappus~ (“cloth”), first recorded in the Capitularies of Charlemagne. Its deeper origin is not settled. English Wiktionary calls Old Low Frankish *~drap~ probable, a word tied to a Germanic root meaning “to beat”, while French Wiktionary says Gaulish.
en.draver: A Canadian French verb borrowed from English ~drive~ and altered in pronunciation by French Canadians. The source says the word came from those who went to the United States to do this work, which was driving logs down rivers by floating them. The sense “to transport timber by floating it” is thus a specialized use of the English verb, reshaped by French speakers in the logging trade.
en.drayer: The origin of ~drayer~ (“to flesh hides”) is unsettled, and three accounts compete. According to the FEW, it comes from Dutch ~draaien~ (“to turn, to twist”), because the tool used for the job, the ~drayoire~, has two cutting edges and can therefore be turned during use. Jules Ronjat proposed instead a borrowing from Provençal ~draia~ (“to sift, to winnow”). Littré, for his part, “conjectured” an alteration of ~draguer~, in the sense “to pull, to clean.” None of these is established.
en.dresser:
From Late Latin *~directiāre~ (“to straighten, to set upright”), a verb built on Latin ~directus~ (“straight, direct”), the past participle of ~dīrigere~ (“to lay straight, to direct”). That verb combines ~dis-~ with ~regere~ (“to rule, to keep straight”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten, to make right”) — the root behind English ~right~ and ~royal~. French ~direct~, ~droit~, ~adresse~, and ~dresser~ are all doublets descending from this single Latin family.

The core idea is “to make straight, to set up vertically,” and French ~dresser~ fans out from it impressively. One ~dresse~ a tent, a ladder, or a statue (raises it upright), ~dresse~ a table (sets it), ~dresse~ a list or a report (draws it up), and ~dresse~ the dishes on a plate (arranges them) — the source of culinary ~dressage~ (“plating”). Applied to animals and people, ~dresser~ means “to train, to break in, to tame,” straightening behaviour into obedience; a trained horse undergoes ~dressage~, the term now used in English for the equestrian discipline. Related French words include ~dressage~, ~redresser~ (“to straighten again, to set right”), ~adresse~ (both “address” and “skill”), and ~dresseur~ (“animal trainer”).
en.dribbler: Borrowed from English ~dribble~ (“to drip, to trickle”), whose figurative sporting sense, moving a ball along in small controlled touches, French took over with the verb. In French, ~dribbler~ means “to dribble a ball” in football, basketball or handball, and figuratively “to get around an opponent” or to outwit someone. The English verb is a loan in the strict sense: French did not form it from native material, and it carries its English spelling, with the ~bb~, intact.
en.dribler: ~Dribler~ is a variant spelling of ~dribbler~, the French verb borrowed from English ~dribble~. It is a sports verb: it means to dribble a ball, that is, to move it forward by repeated short touches while keeping it away from opponents. As a modern borrowing, its story belongs to the English word, and French simply gave it a first-conjugation ending.
en.driver: The sources give two accounts. French Wiktionary lists one as a dialectal variant of ~dériver~ (“to drift off course”), which fits the sense “to roam.” It lists the other as coming from English ~drive~, perhaps also as a verb built on the noun ~drive~ with ~-er~. English Wiktionary treats it as an adapted borrowing of English ~drive~ plus ~-er~, which fits the golfing sense “to drive a ball.”
en.droguer: Formed from the noun ~drogue~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The origin of ~drogue~ itself is uncertain. English Wiktionary has it first attested in Middle French around 1462, probably from Middle Dutch ~droge~ (modern Dutch ~droog~, “dry”). French Wiktionary mentions that same Dutch word and also an Italian ~droga~ (“sugared almond”) as possible sources, and in the end calls the origin unknown. The verb followed the noun and means “to dose with drugs” or, reflexively, “to take drugs.”
en.droper: In the golf sense, ~droper~ is a borrowing of English ~drop~ with the French verb ending ~-er~: to drop the ball in a new position after it has landed somewhere it cannot be played. French Wiktionary also records a separate, older slang verb, an aphaeresis of ~adroper~, soldiers' argot said to come from a pidgin ~adrop~, itself derived from Arabic ~azreb~ (“hurry up”). The two are distinct words that happen to share a spelling.
en.dropper: Two accounts appear in the sources. The first treats ~dropper~ as a borrowing of English ~drop~ with the French infinitive ending ~-er~, matching the sense “to drop”. French Wiktionary also gives a second, separate origin for a slang verb of the same shape: an aphaeresis of ~adroper~, soldiers' slang from the sabir word ~adrop~, itself derived from Arabic ~azreb~ (“hurry up”). The two accounts are independent.
en.drosser: French Wiktionary traces the verb to Dutch ~drossen~ rather than treating it as derived from ~drosse~ (a nautical term for a steering rope). English Wiktionary agrees on Dutch but notes it could be a reverse borrowing, and says both are probably ultimately from Italian ~trozza~ (“gooseneck”). The origin of ~drosse~ is itself debated: a cross of ~drisse~ and ~trosse~, or Italian ~trozza~. The verb means “to put a ship off course.”
en.duper: ~Duper~ is the verb built on ~dupe~ with the ending ~-er~, meaning “to trick” or “to fool”. The noun ~dupe~ is traced to Middle French ~duppe~. The older stages of its history are left aside here because the sources consulted do not document them firmly enough to state.
en.duplexer: Formed from the noun ~duplex~ with the verb ending ~-er~: to connect two places by a duplex link. The noun ~duplex~ was borrowed from Latin ~duplex~ (“double”), a word built from ~duo~ (“two”) and the root of ~plicāre~ (“to fold”), so literally “two-fold.” The ending ~-er~ is the usual way French makes a verb from a noun and goes back to Latin ~-are~.
en.dupliquer:
~Dupliquer~ is borrowed from Latin ~duplicāre~ (“to double”), which comes from ~duplex~ (“double”), literally “folded in two,” as French Wiktionary puts it. In the usual analysis, ~duplex~ joins ~duo~ (“two”) to a root meaning “fold,” the same one found in ~plicāre~ (“to fold”), the verb to which French Wiktionary sends the reader. English ~duplicate~ is the same Latin verb, borrowed separately.

The key to the word is therefore that Latin fold. ~Plicāre~ is behind a large French family, some of it inherited and some learned: ~plier~, ~pli~, ~replier~, ~déployer~, ~employer~, ~impliquer~, ~expliquer~, ~compliquer~ and ~multiplier~. In ~dupliquer~ the image is of a single thing folded back on itself to make two, and the verb now covers any act of making an exact second copy, from a file to a key.
en.durcir: ~Durcir~ means “to become hard” or “to make hard,” and its source is the Latin inchoative verb ~dūrēscere~ (“to harden”), formed on the adjective ~dūrus~ (“hard”). The sources differ on the route. French Wiktionary derives ~durcir~ directly from Latin ~dūrēscere~, while English Wiktionary treats it as a back-formation from ~endurcir~, itself based on the Latin verb. Either way Latin ~dūrēscere~ stands behind it. The adjective ~dūrus~ lives on in French ~dur~, and the verb in the figurative uses of ~durcir~: an argument, a tone or a conflict can harden, not only a material.
en.durer:
From Latin ~durare~ (“to harden, to endure, to last”), attested in French from the 11th century. ~Durare~ derives from the adjective ~durus~ (“hard”), whose deeper Indo-European origin is debated — one account ties it to a root meaning “long” (compare Ancient Greek ~dērós~, “long-lasting,” and Sanskrit ~dūrá~, “far”), another to *~deru-~ (“hard, firm,” as of wood). Whichever holds, the link between hardness and persistence is plain: what is hard endures. Romance kept the verb in Italian ~durare~ and Spanish ~durar~.

Latin ~durare~ already spanned the physical and the temporal — to make hard, but also to hold out and to last — and French settled firmly on the temporal: to ~durer~ is to go on in time, to last. A storm, a friendship, or a battery can ~durer~. The hardness sense lives on in the sibling adjective ~dur~ (“hard, tough”) and its kin ~durcir~ (“to harden”), ~dureté~ (“hardness”), and ~endurer~ (“to endure”). The time sense surfaces in ~durée~ (“duration”) and the preposition ~durant~ (“during”), which began life as a present participle of ~durer~ — “while X is lasting.”
en.duveter: Formed from ~duvet~ (“down”) with the verb suffix ~-er~: to become downy. The noun ~duvet~ is an unexplained alteration of Old French ~dumet~, a diminutive of ~dum~ or ~dun~, which was borrowed from Old Norse ~dúnn~ (“down”). French Wiktionary suggests the forms in ~m~ probably arose from ~dun~ under the influence of ~plume~. The Norse word, from Proto-Germanic *~dūnaz~, also gave Danish ~dun~, German ~Daune~ and English ~down~.
en.dynamiser: Formed in French from the adjective ~dynamique~ with the verb suffix ~-iser~, which replaces the ending ~-ique~ ; the suffix means “to make A”, so ~dynamiser~ is to make something dynamic, to energize it. The adjective ~dynamique~ is a learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ~dynamikós~ (“powerful, effective”), derived from ~dýnamis~ (“power”). The suffix ~-iser~ itself comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and is fully productive in modern French in technical and journalistic registers, as in ~moderniser~ and ~automatiser~. The same Greek ~dýnamis~ is behind ~dynamite~ and ~dynamo~.
en.dynamiter: Formed from ~dynamite~ and the verb ending ~-er~: to blow something up with dynamite. The noun was coined as ~dynamit~ in Swedish by the explosive's inventor, Alfred Nobel, from Ancient Greek ~dýnamis~ (“power”), and it is related to ~dynamique~. The French verb took the explosive as its instrument, and it is also used figuratively for shaking something up or demolishing it.
en.déambuler: Borrowed from Latin ~deambulāre~; compare Italian ~deambulare~ and Spanish ~deambular~. The Latin verb is formed from ~dē-~ and ~ambulāre~ (“to walk”), which also lies behind ~ambulant~ and ~ambulance~ and, through Old French, English ~amble~. French ~déambuler~ means to stroll or walk about, and the related noun ~déambulateur~ names a walking frame.
en.débagouler: The verb is formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and the older verb ~bagouler~. ~Bagouler~ itself comes from Old French ~bagouler~ and is tied to ~bagou~ (“glib talk”); English Wiktionary analyzes it on the surface as ~bagou~ + ~-er~. The prefix ~dé-~ is one of the most productive in French, and its senses of removal, separation or release fit a verb used for spewing out, whether food or a flood of abuse. The two senses given for the modern verb, to vomit and to hurl insults, both involve something forced out.
en.déballer: ~Déballer~ is formed in one step from ~dé-~, ~balle~ and the verb ending ~-er~: to unpack is to take something out of its bale or bundle. The prefix ~dé-~ marks removal here. The ~balle~ in question is the “large bundle, package”, from Old French ~bale~ (“rolled-up bundle”) and Medieval Latin ~bala~, of Germanic origin, which French Wiktionary specifies as Old Low Frankish *~bala~. It is a cognate of English ~ball~. French has other, unrelated words ~balle~, such as the ball borrowed from Italian.
en.déballonner: Formed from ~ballonner~ (“to swell like a balloon”) and the prefix ~dé-~, which generally reverses the action of its base. ~Ballonner~ comes from the noun ~ballon~, borrowed from Italian ~pallone~ (“big ball”), at first a large firework bomb; ~pallone~ is itself ~palla~ (“ball”) plus the augmentative suffix ~-one~. The slang sense, “to back down, to chicken out,” is recorded in 1894 in Charles Virmaitre's Dictionnaire d'Argot fin-de-siècle.
en.débanaliser: ~Débanaliser~ is formed from ~banaliser~ and the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to make something less commonplace again. The base is built on the adjective ~banal~ with the suffix ~-iser~. ~Banal~ itself derives from ~ban~, and an Old French form ~bannel~ is dated to 1269. It is also related to Medieval Latin ~bannālis~, from ~bannus~. The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.débander: From ~bander~ with the reversing prefix ~dé-~: to ~débander~ is to undo what ~bander~ did, that is, to take off a bandage or blindfold (~débander les yeux~), or to release a stretched thing such as a bow. The base ~bander~ has an unsettled origin. The better-documented account is Germanic, through Frankish *~bandijan~, and French Wiktionary adds a proposed alternative from Occitan ~bandar~. Its senses cluster around the idea of binding with a band and of drawing something taut, and ~dé-~ simply reverses either one.
en.débaptiser: Formed in French from ~baptiser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the base: to strip someone of the name given at baptism, and so, more broadly, to rename. ~Baptiser~ itself comes from Latin ~baptizo~ (“to wash, baptize”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~baptízō~ (“to plunge, immerse”). Christian Latin narrowed that Greek verb of immersion to the rite of baptism, and French inherited the religious sense. The result is a verb that undoes a christening and replaces the name it conferred.
en.débarbouiller: Formed from ~barbouiller~ and the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to undo the smearing by washing, as in washing someone's face. The origin of ~barbouiller~ is unsettled. One account derives it from ~barboter~, Littré preferred ~bouille~ (“mire”), and a third reads it as “to dirty one's beard,” from ~barbe~. The prefix goes back to Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.débarder: Formed from ~barder~ with the prefix ~dé-~. The origin of ~barder~ is debated: by one account it derives from ~bard~ (“handbarrow, stretcher”), by another from Arabic ~barda~ (“packsaddle”). The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). None of the sources explains how the sense “to transport logs” developed, so no story is offered for it.
en.débarquer:
Formed from the noun ~barque~ (« small boat »), with the prefix ~dé-~ (« off, from ») and the suffix ~-er~, by parasynthetic derivation — that is, prefix and suffix were added at once to the noun. ~barque~ comes from Late Latin ~barca~, traced through Latin ~bāris~ to Ancient Greek ~βᾶρις~ (« Egyptian river-boat »), which is itself, by most accounts, of Egyptian origin — a faint memory of Nile barges riding in the word.

Built on « boat », ~débarquer~ means literally « to take off the boat » and so « to unload » cargo, then « to disembark », to get off the ship. From there it lightened into everyday and slang uses: to « turn up » unexpectedly (« il a débarqué chez moi »), or, of a person abruptly dismissed, to be « kicked out » of a job. Its mirror-twin ~embarquer~ (« to embark, to load aboard ») is built the same way on ~barque~, and the pair frames the whole voyage — going aboard and stepping back ashore.
en.débarrasser:
French ~débarrasser~ pairs the privative prefix ~dé-~ (“un-, away”) with ~barrasser~, the family of ~embarrasser~ (“to hinder, encumber”) and ~embarras~ (“obstruction”). These rest on the noun ~barre~ (“bar”), itself from Vulgar Latin *~barra~, a word of disputed origin: by one account it goes back to Old Frankish *~bara~ (“bar, beam, barrier”), and ultimately to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰerH-~ (“to strike, pierce”); an alternative ties it instead to a Celtic source related to Breton ~barri~ (“branch, twig”). The Iberian languages developed the verb in parallel — Spanish ~embarazar~, Portuguese ~embaraçar~ — and French ~débarrasser~ appears to echo a Spanish ~desembarazar~.

The underlying picture is concrete: a ~barre~ is a bar laid across a way, and to ~embarrasser~ is to clutter that way with obstacles, while to ~débarrasser~ is to clear the bars away. The reflexive ~se débarrasser de~ (“to rid oneself of”) keeps that sense of shedding an encumbrance. From *~barra~ French also drew ~barre~, ~barrière~ (“barrier”), ~barreau~, ~barrage~, ~débarras~ (“lumber-room, riddance”), and the borrowed English ~bar~, ~barrier~, and ~embarrass~ — the last carrying the same Romance figure of a path obstructed.
en.débarrer: ~Débarrer~ is formed from ~barrer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base verb, so it means “to unbar”. The base ~barrer~ comes from the noun ~barre~, whose origin is uncertain: French Wiktionary derives it from Gaulish *~barros~, while English Wiktionary offers a Germanic source or a Celtic one. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), through Old French ~des-~.
en.débattre:
From Old French ~debatre~ (“to fight, struggle, quarrel, discuss,” attested around 1050), from ~de-~ + ~batre~ (“to beat”), which gave modern ~battre~. ~Battre~ descends through Middle French from Latin ~battere~, a Vulgar form of Classical ~battuere~ (“to beat, strike”). That Latin verb is itself a puzzle: it was rare in literary Latin, and sources flag its origin as uncertain — ~perhaps~ borrowed from Gaulish or Germanic, and ultimately onomatopoeic. The Romance cousins line up neatly: Italian ~dibattere~, Spanish ~debatir~, Catalan ~debatre~.

The development is vivid. The ~de-~ here is intensive, and ~débattre~ began as a thoroughly physical word — to thrash about, to fight, to wrangle. From the body the sense rose to the voice: a ~débat~ (first attested as a verbal form ~debat~ around 1050) became a verbal struggle, an argument made with words rather than blows. The reflexive ~se débattre~ kept the old muscular meaning, “to thrash about, to struggle.” From the same ~battre~ come ~bataille~, ~combat~, ~abattre~, ~rabattre~, and the borrowed-back English doublets ~battle~, ~batter~, and ~debate~.
en.débaucher: ~Débaucher~ is inherited from Old French ~desbaucher~, which begins with ~des-~, the Old French form of the prefix that became ~dé-~. French Wiktionary links the verb to the Old French noun ~bauc~ (“beam”) and compares French ~ébauche~ and ~ébaucher~, as well as English ~balk~. The sources do not explain how a word tied to beams came to mean “to lay off”, so that step is best left open. What the evidence supports is the chain itself: ~bauc~, then ~desbaucher~, then ~débaucher~.
en.débecter: Formed from ~becqueter~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action of the base. English Wiktionary glosses the base as “to eat,” so the verb is literally “to uneat.” That fits the senses of disgust and vomiting, which are the reverse of taking food in. The base ~becqueter~ comes from ~bec~ (“beak”) plus the frequentative suffix ~-eter~, so it first meant to peck, and ~bec~ itself reaches French from Latin ~beccus~, a word of Gaulish origin. A word for a bird's beak thus ended up, by way of slang for eating, in a verb for turning the stomach.
en.débenzoler: Formed from ~benzol~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to remove the benzol” from a mixture, such as a gas or an oil. ~Benzol~ is the industrial name for the benzene obtained from coal tar. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and marks removal. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~, French’s default way of making a verb from a noun.
en.débiliter:
Borrowed from Latin ~dēbilitāre~ (“to cripple, to make infirm, to weaken”), a verb built on ~dēbilis~ (“weak”). The sources quote early French uses: a physician's treatise attributed to Arnaud de Villeneuve says that vomiting “débilite l'estomac,” a text by the humanist Guillaume Budé speaks of men already old or “débilités,” and a psalter has a virtue “débilitée” by poverty. In each, the verb keeps the Latin sense of weakening a body or a strength.

French ~débile~ and ~débilité~ come from the same Latin family, and the verb now belongs to formal and medical writing, where it describes anything that saps strength or resistance. The Latin verb passed into other languages as well: Spanish ~debilitar~, Italian ~debilitare~, and English ~debilitate~ all descend from or borrow ~dēbilitāre~.
en.débillarder: ~Débillarder~ is formed, according to French Wiktionary, from ~billard~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ending ~-er~. ~Billard~ derives from ~bille~ (“piece of wood”) with the suffix ~-ard~, and first meant a curved stick for playing ball games; the modern sense of a table with raised edges dates from 1680. The verb means “to cut diagonally”.
en.débiner:
The origin of ~débiner~ is obscure, and French Wiktionary offers only tentative readings. One looks to Old French, which had ~rebinee~ (“resumption”), ~rebineur~ (“someone who retracts”) and ~rebis~ (“again”), the last from Latin ~bini~ (“twice”); see ~biner~. The sources do not explain how this family would have led to ~débiner~.

The other reading is a popular formation, perhaps like ~rambiner~, in which a prefix was swapped: ~dé-~ in place of ~com-~ in ~combiner~, with the sense of undoing, taking apart or smashing. On that view ~débiner~ is related to the nouns ~débine~ and ~combine~. Both readings are proposals, so the word's true source stays open.
en.débiter: The sources give two origins for two senses. The older sense “to cut up” (timber, meat) is explained as ~dé-~ + ~bitte~ + ~-er~, literally “to make into pieces”. ~Bitte~ is a nautical term borrowed from Old Norse ~biti~ (“beam”), from a root meaning “to split”, *~bʰeyd-~. The commercial sense “to sell steadily, to turn out in quantity”, and its figurative use for reciting at length, is explained as ~débit~ + ~-er~. ~Débit~ comes from Latin ~debitum~ (“debt”), the neuter participle of ~dēbēre~ (“to owe”), which is why ~débit~ also names the debit side of an account.
en.déblatérer:
French ~déblatérer~ is borrowed from Latin ~deblaterāre~ (“to say wildly, to babble on”). The Latin verb is built on ~blaterāre~ (“to babble”), which was formed as an imitation of the sound of idle talk, and on the prefix ~dē-~, which here is intensive. So the word is imitative at its root.

The simpler Latin verb ~blaterāre~ survives in French as ~blatérer~, used of the cry of the camel and the ram, and French also has the learned ~déblatérer~, which is used of people who talk at length and spitefully, usually against someone: ~déblatérer contre quelqu'un~. The two verbs show how an imitation of noise became both an animal term and a term of reproach for human speech.
en.déblayer: From Old French ~desbleer~ or ~deblaver~, “to clear the land of its grain.” English Wiktionary analyzes it as ~dé-~ + ~blé~ (“grain, wheat”) + the verb ending ~-er~, with ~dé-~ marking removal. The verb originally concerned ground cleared of its crop, and it later widened to mean clearing away rubble, snow or any obstacle. French Wiktionary links it to ~remblayer~, which shares the same origin.
en.débloquer: ~Débloquer~ is ~dé-~ + ~bloquer~, with ~dé-~ reversing the action of the base: to undo a blockage, to free what was jammed, and by extension to release funds or lift a freeze. The base ~bloquer~ comes from the noun ~bloc~ (“log, block”), an Old French loan from Middle Dutch ~blok~ (“tree trunk”), so the family is Germanic despite its French look, and English ~block~ is the same word. The prefix ~dé-~ descends from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and is one of the most productive prefixes of French, as in ~défaire~ and ~déplier~.
en.débobiner: Formed from ~bobiner~ (“to wind thread onto a spool”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to unwind or unspool. The base verb comes from ~bobine~ (“bobbin, spool”) plus ~-er~. The origin of ~bobine~ is debated. The Trésor de la Langue Française prefers an imitative root ~bob~, evoking something swollen or cylindrical, while older scholars proposed Latin ~bombyx~ (“silkworm”) or ~bombus~ (“buzzing”).
en.déboguer: ~Déboguer~ is a French adaptation of English ~debug~. The French form keeps the meaning of the English verb, “to find and remove errors from a program,” and dresses it in the ordinary first-conjugation ending ~-er~. The spelling with ~gu~ keeps the hard [g] sound before the endings in ~-e~ and ~-é~, as in ~fatiguer~. Like many computing terms, it entered French by calquing English rather than through any older word of its own.
en.déboiser: Formed from ~boiser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here marks removal: ~déboiser~ is “to strip of trees,” to clear a hillside of its forest. ~Boiser~ itself is built on ~bois~ (“wood”) and means “to provide with wood,” whether a room with paneling or a slope with trees. The noun ~bois~ comes through Old French from Early Medieval Latin ~boscus~ (“grove”), borrowed from Frankish *~busk~. It has cognates in Italian ~bosco~, Spanish ~bosque~, German ~Busch~ and English ~bush~. The word ~déboisement~ names the resulting deforestation.
en.débonder: Formed from ~bonde~ (“bung,” the plug that closes the hole of a barrel or the outlet of a pond) with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The prefix marks removal: ~débonder~ is to take out the bung and so let the contents flow. Figuratively, the verb can mean to pour out one's feelings. The prefix ~dé-~ descends from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.déborder: Formed from ~dé-~, the noun ~bord~ (“edge”) and the ending ~-er~; French Wiktionary parses it instead as ~dé-~ on the verb ~border~, which comes to the same thing. Here ~dé-~ expresses going beyond or away from: to ~déborder~ is to pass over the edge, hence to overflow, and in the military sense to outflank. The noun ~bord~ is a Frankish borrowing and is cognate with English ~board~. Hence ~débordé~, “swamped” with work. Spanish and Catalan ~desbordar~ are cognate, built the same way.
en.débosseler: Formed from ~bosseler~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to take the bumps out of an object. The base comes from the noun ~bosse~ (“bump”) with the ending ~-eler~, and means to raise bumps on a surface or to emboss. The noun ~bosse~ comes from Old French ~boce~, which English Wiktionary traces to Frankish *~bottja~.
en.débotter: Formed from ~botter~ and the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to take someone's boots off. English Wiktionary reads it as ~dé-~ plus ~botte~ plus ~-er~, which gives the same result. The noun ~botte~ has several unrelated origins in the sources, among them Old French ~bote~ (“boot”), probably from Frankish. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”) by way of Old French ~des-~. ~Débotter~ is the literal opposite of putting boots on.
en.déboucher:
~Déboucher~ is ~dé-~ + ~boucher~ (“to stop up”), attested as ~debochier~ in the thirteenth century — and, against all appearances, the family has nothing to do with ~bouche~, “mouth.” The verb ~boucher~ was drawn from Old French ~bousche~, “wisp of straw, bundle of brushwood”: to stop a hole was, concretely, to stuff it with straw. ~Bousche~ continues a Vulgar Latin *~bosca~, “brushwood,” of the same family as ~bois~ (“wood”), with kin in Italian ~bosco~ and Spanish ~bosque~ (“forest”). So the corkscrew’s verb descends from underbrush: what you remove when you unblock is, etymologically, a fistful of twigs. The same ~bousche~ produced ~bouchon~ — first a twist of straw, then the cork it became, and in today’s French also a traffic jam: cars stoppered in the road like wine in the neck of a bottle.

Then comes the twist. Alongside “unblock, uncork,” French uses the same verb for “to emerge, to open onto”: a street, a river, a line of reasoning débouche somewhere. Lexicographers split here: the TLFi files this intransitive use (attested in the seventeenth century) as a second verb, built this time on ~bouche~ — the mouth of a street, of a river — while other dictionaries fold every sense into one formation on ~boucher~. Either way the irony stands: a family that owes nothing to the mouth ended up borrowing it, or at least leaning on it. The offspring map both senses: ~débouché~, “outlet, opening, career prospect,” belongs to the mouth side; ~reboucher~ (“to stop up again”) to the straw side; and ~embouchure~ — the river’s mouth, the trumpet’s mouthpiece — though built directly on ~bouche~, shows how readily French lets openings speak.
en.déboucler: Formed from ~boucler~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to undo what ~boucler~ did. English Wiktionary reads it as ~dé-~ + ~boucle~ + ~-er~. ~Boucler~ is a fourteenth-century verb meaning “to fasten with a buckle,” then “to curl hair into loops.” The noun ~boucle~ comes from Latin ~buccula~, the cheek strap of a helmet, a diminutive of ~bucca~ (“cheek”), and it also gave English ~buckle~. So ~déboucler~ means “to unbuckle,” and, of hair, “to undo curls.”
en.débouler: ~Débouler~ is formed in French from ~bouler~ with the prefix ~dé-~. The base ~bouler~ is a verb built on the noun ~boule~ (“ball”), whose own origin is debated: it comes from Old French ~bole~ (“knob”), traced either to Latin ~bulla~ (“bubble”) or to Frankish *~bollā~ (“ball, bun”). The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and in verbs like this it can express setting in motion or going away rather than a plain reversal. The sources do not spell out which sense it carries here.
en.débouquer: Formed from ~bouque~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ending ~-er~, in the same way as ~déboucher~: to come out of a narrow channel, as if leaving the “mouth” of it behind. The noun ~bouque~ comes from Latin ~bucca~; English Wiktionary adds that it was borrowed from Old Occitan ~boca~, making it a doublet of ~bouche~. The prefix ~dé-~ has the sense of removal or exit, and the whole word is a nautical term.
en.débourber: Formed from ~bourbe~ (“mud”) with the prefix ~dé-~ and the ending ~-er~: to get something out of the mud, or to clear mud away. The noun ~bourbe~ is traced to a Gaulish *~borua~ (“hot spring, muddy water”), related to a Gaulish word meaning “to boil,” and to the name of the hot-spring god ~Borvo~. English Wiktionary gives this Gaulish origin only as proposed (*~borwa~).
en.débourrer: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and ~bourrer~, a verb built on ~bourre~ (“stuffing, padding”). The prefix ~dé-~, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), reverses the base: where ~bourrer~ is to stuff, ~débourrer~ is to remove the stuffing, as when emptying a pipe. The verb has other, specialized senses, to break in a young horse and, of a plant, to burst into bud. French Wiktionary gives no more than the derivation from ~bourrer~, so the way those uses developed is not documented there.
en.débourser: ~Débourser~ is formed from ~bourse~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and the suffix ~-er~, so it names money taken out of the purse. The prefix ~dé-~ here marks removal, and the base is a noun, not a verb. ~Bourse~ comes from Old French ~borse~, from Latin ~bursa~, which came from Greek ~βύρσα~ (“hide, skin”). The word for a pouch is thus named for the leather it was made of. The stock-market sense of ~bourse~ is a separate borrowing from Dutch ~beurs~.
en.déboussoler: ~Déboussoler~ (“to disorient”) is a back-formation: both Wiktionaries derive it from the adjective ~déboussolé~ rather than the other way round, so the participial adjective came first and the verb was extracted from it. The adjective is transparently modeled on ~boussole~ (“compass”), with the prefix ~dé-~ marking removal, so to be ~déboussolé~ is to have lost one's bearings. The verb is used figuratively of people who are confused or thrown off course.
en.débouter: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and ~bouter~, and already present in Old and Middle French as ~debouter~. The base ~bouter~ (“to push, to strike”) is of Germanic origin, from Frankish *~bautan~ or *~bōtan~, from Proto-Germanic *~bautaną~ (“to beat”), a family that includes English ~beat~. The prefix here marks driving away, and the verb means to dismiss, notably in law, to reject someone's claim. The same root also gave ~bouton~, ~aboutir~ and ~rebuter~.
en.déboutonner: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and ~boutonner~, so “to undo the buttons.” The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~, and reverses the base. ~Boutonner~ is the noun ~bouton~ + ~-er~, “to fasten with buttons.” ~Bouton~ first meant “bud” and is built on ~bouter~ (“to push”) + ~-on~, going back through Vulgar Latin to Frankish *~bautō~ (“that which pushes up, a bump or knob”). A bud and a button are both small knobs, which is how one word came to cover both. ~Déboutonner~ means “to unbutton.”
en.déboîter: Formed from ~boîte~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, so literally “to take out of the box.” The prefix ~dé-~ marks removal. The noun ~boîte~ comes from Old French ~boiste~, from Late Latin ~buxida~, which blended Latin ~pyxis~ (“small box,” from Greek) with ~buxus~ (“box tree”). English ~box~ is a doublet.
en.débraguetter: This verb is a parasynthetic formation: the noun ~braguette~ (the fly of trousers) took the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ending ~-er~ at the same time, since there is no verb *braguetter to which the prefix was added. The prefix ~dé-~ expresses reversal or removal, so the verb means to undo what the ~braguette~ closes, that is, to unfasten one's fly. The result is a playful, everyday verb with a plain French pedigree.
en.débrailler:
~Débrailler~ is a parasynthetic verb, built at once with the prefix ~dé-~ and the suffix ~-er~ on ~braie~ (“breeches”). French Wiktionary traces ~braie~ to Latin ~braca~, probably of Celtic origin, and says the verb is not related to ~brailler~ (“to bawl”). English Wiktionary reaches the same place through Old French ~braiel~ (“belt”), the strap that held the ~braies~ up. The prefix ~dé-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), here has its undoing sense.

So, etymologically, ~se débrailler~ is “to loosen one's belt”, with the indecency that can follow when the breeches slip, and the modern verb still describes someone letting clothing hang open. French Wiktionary notes that the old ~braiel~ named the belt itself, so the verb is a close relative of ~braie~ rather than of any noise. Latin ~braca~ also lives on in Spanish ~bragas~ and Italian ~brache~, both garments of the lower body.
en.débrancher: ~Débrancher~ is formed from ~brancher~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which marks separation, so it means “to disconnect, to unplug.” ~Brancher~ is built on the noun ~branche~ (“branch”), which comes from Late Latin ~branca~ (“paw, claw”), a word of uncertain origin. The image is of a limb spreading from a trunk, and ~brancher~ came to mean “to connect” one thing to another, as a wire to a circuit. ~Débrancher~ reverses that connection. English ~branch~ comes from the same Latin word.
en.débrayer: Both Wiktionaries treat ~débrayer~ as formed from ~braie~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and the ending ~-er~, a parasynthetic verb. ~Braie~ is an old word with several senses, among them breeches, a wooden crosspiece on a windmill and an iron band round a forge hammer's handle. The sources do not say which sense gave the verb. The word comes from Latin ~braca~ (“breeches”), traced to Gaulish. The verb now means to declutch, and, in the labor sense, to stop work and go on strike.
en.débrider: Formed from ~brider~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses it: to ~débrider~ is to take the bridle off a horse. The base ~brider~ is made from the noun ~bride~ and ~-er~. The noun came into Old French from Middle High German ~brīdel~, from Old High German ~brīdil~, and it is cognate with English ~bridle~. From the horse, ~brider~ widened to “hold back,” so ~débrider~ can also mean to release what was held back.
en.débriefer: An anglicism, built on English ~brief~ (“quick instructions”) with the prefix ~dé-~. The English noun and verb ~brief~ were themselves taken from French ~bref~ (“short”), so the word is in part a return of a French word after a round trip through English. To ~débriefer~ is to question or hold a meeting with someone after a mission or an event, the reverse of giving instructions beforehand. It belongs to a modern, business and military register.
en.débrocher: ~Débrocher~ (“to take off the spit”) is a compound of ~dé-~ and ~broche~ (“spit, skewer”), with the verb ending ~-er~. The prefix ~dé-~, from Latin ~dis-~, marks reversal: ~débrocher~ undoes what ~embrocher~ (“to skewer”) did. In the kitchen, it means to remove roasted meat from the spit. The prefix is not the noun ~dé~ (“die, thimble”).
en.débrouiller: From ~brouiller~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to untangle what has been muddled. The base comes from Old French ~brouiller~, built on Vulgar Latin *~brodiculāre~ and, behind it, Late Latin ~brodium~ (“broth, stew, mixture”), itself borrowed from Proto-Germanic *~bruþą~ (“stock, broth”), the source of English ~broth~. French Wiktionary rejects a rival route through Old Occitan ~bruelhar~. The verb is a clean case of ~dé-~ plus a French verb, and the gloss “to manage, to figure something out” grew from the idea of sorting out a tangle.
en.débroussailler: A parasynthetic verb: the prefix ~dé-~ (“removal”) and the ending ~-er~ were added together to the noun ~broussaille~ (“brushwood, undergrowth”). It therefore means “to remove the undergrowth.” The base ~broussaille~ comes from ~brosse~, with an older sense of brush or scrub, by way of the Middle French form ~brossaille~ and the suffix ~-aille~. There is no verb ~broussailler~ behind it, which is why the prefix and the ending count as one move. The figurative sense, to clear the ground of a problem, grew from the literal act of clearing a field.
en.débucher: Formed in French from the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ~bucher~, with French Wiktionary pointing to the related ~débusquer~ and ~déboquer~. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and in French verbs it often marks reversal or removal. The TLFi derives ~bucher~ from ~bûche~ (“log”) plus ~-er~; its first sense, around 1360-70, was working wood with an axe, and Littré links Italian ~buscare~ and Spanish ~buscar~ (“to search”) to the same word for “wood.” The sources do not spell out how these combine into the sense “to break cover.”
en.débudgétiser: ~Débudgétiser~ is formed from ~budgétiser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to remove an item from the budget. ~Budgétiser~ comes from ~budget~ plus ~-iser~, with the stem lengthened to ~budgét-~. The noun ~budget~ entered French from English ~budget~, which goes back to Old French ~bougette~ (“small bag, purse”), so the two are doublets.
en.débureaucratiser: Formed from ~bureaucratiser~ with the reversing prefix ~dé-~: to strip something of its bureaucratic character. The base is built from the adjective ~bureaucratique~ and the suffix ~-iser~, so ~bureaucratiser~ means to make bureaucratic. That adjective derives from ~bureaucrate~ or ~bureaucratie~ with the suffix ~-ique~, which drops before ~-iser~. The verb describes an organization coming to be run by offices, rules and paperwork, and ~débureaucratiser~ undoes that process, simplifying the system.
en.débusquer: Two accounts exist. French Wiktionary derives it from ~bosquet~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here marks removal: to dislodge from a thicket. English Wiktionary instead traces it to ~débucher~, itself from ~bûche~ (“log”). The sources at hand do not decide between them. The noun ~bosquet~ (“grove”) was probably borrowed from Occitan ~bosquet~ (“small wood”), a diminutive of ~bòsc~ with the suffix ~-et~. English Wiktionary traces the Occitan word to Frankish *~busk~ and compares Italian ~boschetto~.
en.débuter:
A French formation (16th century) from the noun ~but~ (“a goal, a target, an aim”) with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~but~ is of debated origin: it may be a variant of ~bout~ (“an end, a tip”), or come from Old Norse ~butr~ (“a log, a block”), perhaps as the wooden mark one aimed at. Either way, ~débuter~ literally means to move away from the ~but~ — the term comes from games of bowls and target sports, where to ~débuter~ was to make the opening throw that knocks a ball off its mark.

From that opening cast the verb generalized to “to make a first move, to begin,” and especially to begin a public career: an actor, a singer, or a politician ~débute~ when first appearing before the public. French borrowed this sense out again as the noun ~début~ (“a beginning, a first appearance”), which English then took as ~debut~ along with ~debutante~ (a young woman making her ~début~ in society). The opposite end of the same game survives in ~buter~ (“to strike against, to stumble”) and the related ~butoir~ (“a buffer, a stop”), all circling the original notion of the mark struck at the start of play.
en.débâcler: Formed from ~bâcler~ with the prefix ~dé-~. The base is of uncertain origin: one proposal derives it from a Vulgar Latin verb meaning “to fasten with a wooden bar,” built on Latin ~baculum~ (“staff”), while two rivals are a Middle Dutch source and a variant of ~boucler~. The older form ~desbacler~ is attested in 1416 and meant “to clear a harbor”: ships already unloaded left so that loaded ones could take their places. That verb also gave the noun ~débâcle~. The sources do not say how the sense of ice breaking up arose.
en.débâillonner: Formed from ~bâillonner~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to remove a gag. The base comes from ~bâillon~ (“gag”) and the ending ~-er~, and the noun itself derives from ~bâiller~ (“to yawn”) with the suffix ~-on~, because a gag holds the mouth open. By extension, the verb also means to free someone or something from enforced silence, to lift censorship.
en.débâter: ~Débâter~ is formed from ~bâter~ (“to fit with a packsaddle”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: “to take the packsaddle off,” hence “to unsaddle” a pack animal. The base is built on the noun ~bât~ (“packsaddle”) with the verb ending ~-er~, though one analysis sees ~bâter~ as inherited from Old French ~baster~. The noun ~bât~ comes from Old French ~bast~, from Vulgar Latin *~bastum~, linked to a verb *~bastāre~ (“to carry”) borrowed from Ancient Greek ~βαστάζειν~ (~bastázein~, “to lift, bear”).
en.débâtir: Formed from ~bâti~, the past participle of ~bâtir~ (“to build”), with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action. The gloss is “to unbaste” (to remove the temporary stitches of a garment), with a rare sense of “to demolish” as the opposite of building. Because the base is a participle, the verb is a French formation rather than an inherited one.
en.décacheter: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and ~cacheter~ (“to seal”), meaning to undo a seal and so to open a letter or package. The prefix here has its commonest force, reversal. The base ~cacheter~ is built on the noun ~cachet~ (“seal”), which in turn comes from ~cacher~ in the sense “to press”, a verb distinct from ordinary ~cacher~ (“to hide”), so a seal is, etymologically, something pressed. ~Décacheter~ is thus to undo what was pressed shut.
en.décadrer: Formed from ~cadrer~ and the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the action: to take something out of its frame, or to frame it badly. ~Cadrer~ goes back to Latin ~quadrāre~ (“to make square, to fit”), from ~quadrus~ (“square”), and was reached either as a borrowing from Latin or as a verb built on ~cadre~ (“frame”). The sense of ~décadrer~ follows from the sense “to frame” a picture or shot, with ~dé-~ undoing it.
en.décaisser: Formed from ~caisse~ (“cash box, till”) with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, so that the verb means to take money out of the till, hence to pay out. ~Caisse~ comes from Middle French, which took it from Occitan ~caissa~, from Latin ~capsa~ (“box”). It is a doublet of ~châsse~ (“reliquary”) and ~casse~.
en.décalaminer: ~Décalaminer~ is formed from the noun ~calamine~, the prefix ~dé-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~: to remove the carbon deposit from an engine. The prefix ~dé-~ marks removal, from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The noun ~calamine~ comes from Medieval Latin ~calamīna~, a variant of Latin ~cadmīa~, ultimately from Greek ~Kadmeía~, from ~Kádmos~ (“Cadmus”). It named a zinc ore, and the engine sense extends the word to the hard deposit scraped off.
en.décalcifier: ~Décalcifier~ is formed from ~calcifier~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to remove calcium, to strip a tissue or a substance of its calcium. ~Calcifier~ is itself built from ~calcium~ and the suffix ~-ifier~ (“to make”). The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.décaler: Formed in French from the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ~caler~, in its sense of wedging or immobilizing. That ~caler~ is built on the noun ~cale~ (“wedge”), whose deeper origin is uncertain; by one account it comes from German ~Keil~ (“wedge”). The prefix ~dé-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), usually reverses the action of its base, so to ~décaler~ is to take away the wedge and knock something out of its fixed position. The sense then widened to moving anything by one notch, whether an object, a schedule or a date.
en.décalquer: ~Décalquer~ is formed from ~calquer~ with the prefix ~dé-~. Here the prefix does not simply undo the base: the two verbs are close in sense, ~décalquer~ meaning to trace or transfer a design from a model. The base ~calquer~ was borrowed from Italian ~calcare~ (“to press, to tread”), from Latin ~calcāre~ (“to tread”). The idea is of pressing on a drawing to transfer it onto another sheet. The same Latin verb gave French ~inculquer~, “to stamp in.”
en.décamper: ~Décamper~ is formed from ~camper~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to leave a camp, hence to clear off in a hurry. The older spelling was ~descamper~. The base ~camper~ has an uncertain origin. It is either a verb formed on ~camp~ or a Latinising reworking of Old French ~champier~, and in both cases the root is Latin ~campus~ (“field”). The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.décaniller: French Wiktionary traces ~décaniller~ (“to decamp, to go away”) to Lyonnais ~canille~ (“leg”), which gave the dialect verb ~se decanilli~ (“to run away”). The sources go no further: no older chain of descent is given, and the role of the prefix ~dé-~ is not analysed. The sense of fleeing fits the “leg” of the source word, a familiar way of saying that someone takes to their heels.
en.décanter:
A learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ~dēcanthāre~, which French Wiktionary derives from Latin ~canthus~ and relates to Spanish ~decantar~ and Italian ~decantare~. French Wiktionary writes the Latin verb with an asterisk, as a reconstructed form, and the two Wiktionaries give only a brief outline, so the finer steps of its formation are not firmly documented here. English ~decant~ belongs to the same family.

In modern French, ~décanter~ is a term from chemistry and the kitchen: to let a liquid settle so that the sediment falls to the bottom, then to pour off the clear part. Figuratively, one says that a situation or an idea ~se décante~ when time lets the essential separate from the confused. The noun ~décantation~ names the process.
en.décaper: Formed from ~cape~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and the ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary explains the image as grime treated like a cape, a covering that has to be taken off, so stripping or scouring a surface is taking that cover off. The base ~cape~ reached French in the Renaissance, through Occitan ~capa~ (“cloak”), from Late Latin ~cappa~ (“head covering”), and it is a doublet of ~chape~, the form that came down by regular sound change.
en.décapitaliser: ~Décapitaliser~ is built on ~capitaliser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base, so it means to strip a city of its status as capital. ~Capitaliser~ is a French formation from ~capital~ and the suffix ~-iser~, in the financial sense “to turn into capital.” ~Capital~ goes back to Latin ~capitālis~ (“of the head”), from ~caput~ (“head”). The base's financial sense and the verb's sense of a capital city are not the same, but both rest on ~capital~.
en.décapiter:
~Décapiter~ is borrowed from Late Latin ~dēcapitāre~, literally “to de-head,” built on ~dē-~ (“off, away”) and ~caput~ (“head”). English Wiktionary glosses the Latin verb that way, and French Wiktionary agrees on the ~caput~ root. The same Latin noun lies behind a large French family, among them ~chef~, ~cap~, ~chapitre~ and ~capital~, and English ~decapitate~ is a parallel borrowing from the same Late Latin verb.

The verb has meant to cut off the head, and French has used the figurative sense, too, of removing the leader of a group, as when a movement or a company is decapitated. The Latin pattern is the same as in many verbs that remove a part of the body or a thing: a prefix of removal on the noun for what is taken away.
en.décapoter: Formed from ~capote~ (here, the folding hood of a car) with the prefix ~dé-~, which marks removal, and the verbal ending ~-er~: to lower or take off a convertible's top. The noun ~capote~ is derived from ~capot~ with the diminutive suffix ~-ote~, and both ultimately go back to Latin ~caput~ (“head”), the idea being a covering for the head. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.décapsuler: ~Décapsuler~ is formed from ~capsule~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and the ending ~-er~: “to remove the cap from a bottle.” ~Capsule~ was borrowed from Latin ~capsula~, a diminutive of ~capsa~ (“box, case”), which also gave ~caisse~ through inheritance. The prefix ~dé-~ marks removal from a noun base, as in ~déplumer~. The tool that does the job is the ~décapsuleur~.
en.décapuchonner: Formed from ~capuchonner~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to take a hood or cap off. The base ~capuchonner~ is itself a verb derived from the noun ~capuchon~ (“hood”), so the word is a derivation stacked in two steps: ~capuchon~, then ~capuchonner~ (to cover with a hood), then ~décapuchonner~. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and is still fully productive.
en.décarbonater: Formed from ~carbonate~ with the reversing prefix ~dé-~: to remove the carbonate from something. The base is built from ~carbone~ with the chemical suffix ~-ate~, from Latin ~-ātus~. ~Carbone~ itself comes from Latin ~carbō~, ~carbōnem~ (“coal”). The prefix ~dé-~, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), marks the removal of the substance named. The verb is a modern chemical term.
en.décarburer: Formed from ~carburer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to remove the carbon from a metal, especially steel or cast iron. English Wiktionary instead analyses it as ~dé-~ + ~carbure~ + ~-er~. Both routes lead to ~carbure~ (“carbide”), a noun built on ~carbone~ with the suffix ~-ure~. The base ~carburer~ first meant to combine with carbon, then to mix air with fuel in an engine.
en.décarcasser: ~Décarcasser~ is formed from the noun ~carcasse~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, so literally it means to take apart a carcass. Used reflexively, it came to mean to bend over backwards. The origin of ~carcasse~ itself is obscure; it may be related to Old French ~charcois~ (“carcass, body”), whose own origin is unknown. The prefix ~dé-~ here carries the sense of removal.
en.décarreler: Formed from ~carreler~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to ~décarreler~ is to take up the tiles that were laid. The base ~carreler~ means to cover a surface with square tiles, and comes from ~carreau~, descended from Old French ~quarel~ and Vulgar Latin *~quadrellus~, a diminutive of Latin ~quadrus~ (“square”). A tiled floor is thus, etymologically, a floor of little squares.
en.décatir: Formed from ~catir~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to remove the pressed, glossy finish from a woollen fabric. The base ~catir~ comes, according to French Wiktionary, from Popular Latin *~coactire~, a variant of ~coactare~, derived from ~coactus~, the past participle of ~cogere~ (“to gather, press”). That Latin verb is ~co-~ (“together”) plus ~agere~ (“to drive”), so it pictures things driven together until they are pressed tight. ~Catir~ is a textile term for firming and glossing cloth, and ~décatir~ undoes the process.
en.décauser: Formed from ~causer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The verb is a regionalism of French Wallonia, where it means to denigrate. Modern ~causer~ covers two verbs that merged by sound, “to cause” and “to chat.” Both rest on Latin ~causa~ (“cause, reason, lawsuit”), and the second comes from Latin ~causari~ (“to plead a case”), a courtroom verb that softened into everyday talk.
en.décavaillonner: Formed from ~cavaillon~ with the prefix ~dé-~. The verb belongs to vine-growing and means to till the soil close to the vines, working the strip that a plough leaves untouched. The French Wiktionary entry gives only this formation and no older source.
en.décaver: Formed from ~caver~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which marks removal or deprivation: the verb means to wipe out one of the players. The base ~caver~ comes straight from Latin ~cavō~, the first-person form of ~cavāre~ (“to hollow out, to dig”), from the family of the adjective ~cavus~ (“hollow”), which also gave French ~cave~ and English ~cave~.
en.déceler: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ (reversal) and ~celer~ (“to hide”), so literally “to un-hide.” The base ~celer~ is inherited from Old French ~celer~, from Latin ~cēlāre~ (“to conceal”), which Italian ~celare~ also continues. The result is a verb of discovery: to detect something that was hidden, or to reveal it, as when a test ~décèle~ a trace of something. Its sibling ~receler~ comes from the same base.
en.décentraliser: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and ~centraliser~, not from ~central~ directly. The prefix, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), here reverses the base verb. ~Centraliser~ is itself ~central~ plus the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make A”), and ~central~ comes from Latin ~centrālis~, the adjective of ~centrum~ (“center”). To ~décentraliser~ is therefore to undo a centralization, that is, to shift powers away from the center.
en.décentrer: Formed from ~centrer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the base: ~décentrer~ means to move something away from the center. ~Centrer~ is ~centre~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~, and ~centre~ comes through Latin ~centrum~ from Ancient Greek ~κέντρον~ (~kéntron~), a sharp point or goad and also the fixed leg of a pair of compasses. The prefix ~dé-~ descends from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.décercler: Formed from ~cercler~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to take off the hoops or circles that had been put around something, such as a barrel. The base ~cercler~ is either built on ~cercle~ with the verbal ending, or descends from Late Latin ~circulāre~, in which case it is a doublet of ~circuler~. Either way the root is ~cercle~, from Latin ~circulus~, a diminutive of ~circus~ (“ring”). The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.décerner:
~Décerner~ was borrowed around 1247 from Latin ~dēcernere~, “to decide, to decree”: ~dē-~ + ~cernere~, “to sift, to separate, to distinguish — and hence to decide.” ~Cernere~ rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~krey-~, “to sieve,” one of the great mental metaphors of the family: its Greek cognate ~krínō~, “to separate, to judge,” underlies ~crise~, ~critique~ and ~critère~, while English ~riddle~ — the coarse sieve, not the puzzle — sifts on the Germanic side. Within Latin the same root yielded ~crībrum~, “sieve” (French ~crible~), ~certus~, “settled, certain” (French ~certain~), and ~crīmen~, originally the charge brought to judgment (French ~crime~). To decide, in this family, is always to shake the grain until one thing alone is left in the mesh.

In Rome, ~dēcernere~ was the Senate’s verb: it decreed wars, honors, triumphs. French first used ~décerner~ for solemn pronouncements — around 1247 “to declare,” by 1548 “to confer by decree” — and the judicial thread survives intact in ~décerner un mandat d'arrêt~, “to issue an arrest warrant.” But everyday modern French reserves the verb almost entirely for glory: one décerne prizes, medals, diplomas, palms. A jury awarding the Prix Goncourt performs, verb and gesture, the old senatorial decree of a triumph. From the participle of the same Latin verb, ~dēcrētum~, come French ~décret~ and English ~decree~; ~discerner~ and ~concerner~ keep other compounds of ~cernere~ alive. The semantic chain is tidy: sift, then decide, then decree, then bestow — every prize ceremony is the last pass of a very old sieve.
en.décerveler: ~Décerveler~ (“to remove the brain, to brainwash”) is formed from ~cervelle~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here expresses removal. ~Cervelle~ comes by way of Old French ~cervele~ from Latin ~cerebella~, the plural of ~cerebellum~ (“brain”), which popular Latin took for a feminine singular. The same ~cerebellum~ gave French ~cerveau~. The Chroniques de Saint-Denis already use ~décerveler~ in the sense of blowing out someone's brains.
en.décevoir:
From Old French ~decevoir~ (also ~deceveir~), from Latin ~dēcipere~, compounded from ~de-~ plus ~capere~ (“to take, seize, catch”). The root verb ~capere~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂p-~ (also reconstructed *~kap-~, “to grasp, seize”), the same root behind English ~have~ and ~heave~ and German ~haben~. The literal Latin sense is vivid: ~dēcipere~ meant “to catch out, ensnare, take in” — and so, to deceive. Spanish ~decebir~ is largely archaic, but English ~deceive~ comes by the very same path.

Here the French semantic history is the surprise. Old French ~decevoir~ meant exactly “to deceive, beguile,” matching the Latin and matching its English twin. Over centuries French softened the word: from actively tricking someone to merely failing their hopes, so that modern ~décevoir~ means “to disappoint.” The old harsh sense has migrated entirely to ~tromper~. The buried “catching” survives in the noun family — ~déception~ (now “disappointment,” once “deception”), ~déçu~ (“disappointed”), ~décevant~ (“disappointing”) — and the same ~capere~ root feeds ~recevoir~, ~concevoir~, and ~percevoir~, a whole network of French verbs built on the idea of taking in.
en.déchanter: ~Déchanter~ is a French derivation from ~chanter~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which usually reverses the base verb, so it is literally “to un-sing.” English Wiktionary also cites Old French ~deschanter~ and Vulgar Latin ~discantāre~, so the verb may be older than a simple French formation. The base ~chanter~ descends from Latin ~cantāre~ (“to sing”), and ~dé-~ comes from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), through Old French ~des-~. The modern sense is figurative: to become disillusioned.
en.déchaperonner: Formed from ~chaperonner~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which expresses removal: to ~déchaperonner~ is to take off a hood. The base ~chaperonner~ comes from ~chaperon~, a diminutive of ~chape~ (“cape, head covering”), which first named a hood. The sense of a person who escorts and supervises a young woman was drawn from it later, but the verb ~déchaperonner~ keeps to the literal hood.
en.décharger: Formed from ~charger~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action of the base. English Wiktionary adds that the pair already existed in Old French as ~deschargier~, from Late Latin ~discarricāre~, so the prefixed verb is older than French itself. The base ~charger~ goes back to Late Latin ~carricāre~ (“to load a wagon”), from Latin ~carrus~ (“wheeled wagon”), a word of Gaulish origin. To ~décharger~ is therefore, first, to unload a cart, and from there to relieve someone of a burden, to fire off a weapon, or to clear a defendant.
en.décharner:
~Décharner~ is borrowed from Latin ~decarnare~ (“to remove the flesh”), a verb built from the prefix ~dē-~ (“off, away”) and ~carō~ (genitive ~carnis~, “flesh”). The Latin verb is the exact ancestor of the French one, which keeps the sense of stripping flesh away and so, by extension, of making a body gaunt.

In modern French the verb is rarely used as a finite verb; it lives mostly in its participle ~décharné~, which describes a face, a body or a landscape stripped to the bone. The root ~carō~ gave French its inherited word ~chair~ (“flesh”) and the learned family ~charnel~, ~charnu~ (“fleshy”), ~carnage~, ~carnivore~ and ~carnation~. Cognates abound elsewhere: Italian and Spanish ~carne~, English ~carnal~ and ~carnivore~.
en.déchaumer: Formed from ~chaume~ (“stubble”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which here means removal: to clear a field of the stubble left after harvest. The noun comes from Latin ~calamus~ (“reed, stalk”), and the same word gives the French ~chaume~ of thatched roofs, since the straw that covers a cottage is the same stalk as the stubble in a field. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.déchausser: Inherited from Old French ~deschaucier~. It can be analyzed on the surface as ~dé-~ + ~chausser~, with the prefix reversing the base, or as coming from Late Latin ~discalceāre~, built on Latin ~calceāre~. Either way it means “to take off one's shoes.” The base ~chausser~ comes from Latin ~calceāre~ (“to furnish with shoes”), from ~calceus~ (“shoe”), which also gave Italian ~calzare~ and Spanish ~calzar~.
en.déchaîner: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and ~chaîner~ (“to bind with a chain”), so literally “to take the chains off.” The base is built on the noun ~chaîne~, which comes from Old French ~chaiene~ and Latin ~catēna~ (“chain”). The prefix ~dé-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”) by way of Old French ~des-~, reverses the action of the base verb. The sense then moves from freeing what is chained to letting a force loose.
en.déchiffonner: Formed from ~chiffonner~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to smooth out what has been crumpled, as in ironing wrinkled clothes. ~Chiffonner~ comes from ~chiffon~ (“rag”), which is ~chiffe~ plus the suffix ~-on~; ~chiffe~ is traced through Old French ~chipe~ to Middle English ~chip~ and Old English ~ċipp~ (“chip, splinter”), the ancestor of English ~chip~. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.déchiffrer: Formed from ~chiffrer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to undo what ~chiffrer~ (“to put into code”) did. The base comes from the noun ~chiffre~, from Old French ~chifre~ and Medieval Latin ~cifra~ (“zero”), borrowed from Arabic ~ṣifr~ (“empty”). The word reached the West with the concept of zero and the so-called Arabic numerals, and ~chiffre~ is a doublet of ~zéro~. A secret message written in figures instead of letters is thus a ~chiffre~, and to ~déchiffrer~ it is to read it, a sense widened to anything hard to read, such as bad handwriting or a musical score.
en.déchiqueter: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and ~échiqueter~, a verb that the sources link, with some hesitation, to ~échiquier~ (“chessboard”). French Wiktionary marks that link with a question mark, so it is better taken as likely than certain. The prefix ~dé-~ is the productive French one, which can mark reversal, removal or an intensive sense with no clear opposite. The sources do not explain how a verb tied to the chessboard came to mean cutting into small pieces, so that step is left unexplained here.
en.déchirer:
From Old French ~escirer~, which became ~descirer~ and then Middle French ~deschirer~ as the prefix ~es-~ was replaced by ~dé-~. The verb itself is Germanic: it comes from Frankish *~skeran~ (“to shear, cut”), from Proto-Germanic *~skeraną~ (“to shear, shave, cut”). Cognates are easy to find in the Germanic languages: Old English ~scieran~, whence English ~shear~, and German ~scheren~. Dutch ~scheuren~ (“to tear”) is a near relative.

The French verb moved from cutting to tearing: where the Germanic root describes a clean cut of wool or hair, ~déchirer~ is to rip cloth, paper or flesh apart. The figurative uses came easily, since a heart, a country or a silence can all be torn: hence ~déchirant~ (“heartbreaking”) and ~déchirure~ (“a tear, a rip”). Modern slang turned it around again, so that something that ~déchire~ is spectacular. The verb is a reminder of how many everyday French words came from the speech of the Franks, who ruled Gaul after the Romans.
en.déchlorurer: Formed from ~chlorure~ (“chloride”) with the prefix ~dé-~, here meaning removal, and the ending ~-er~: to eliminate chlorides. ~Chlorure~ is itself built from ~chlore~ and the suffix ~-ure~, which in chemistry names compounds of an element. ~Chlore~ is a learned name taken from Greek ~khlōros~ (“pale green”), the color of the gas.
en.déchoir:
French ~déchoir~ comes from Old French ~decheoir~. Both Wiktionaries trace it to a form of the Latin verb ~cadere~ (“to fall”) with the prefix ~dē-~ (“down, away”), but they differ on the middle step. French Wiktionary gives Medieval Latin ~decadere~, while English Wiktionary gives Vulgar Latin *~dēcadere~, from Latin ~dēcidere~. English ~decay~ is related to it.
