The simple verb survives in French as ~choir~, an old and now literary word for “to fall,” and French Wiktionary notes that ~déchoir~ is another descendant of it.

The sense is a fall in rank, wealth or standing, and the verb has kept to that figurative use: one ~déchoit~ of one's position, not of a ladder. Like ~choir~, it is a defective verb, with a restricted set of forms. The same Latin ~cadere~ has given a large family: ~échoir~ (“to fall due”), ~échéance~ (“deadline, due date”), ~déchéance~ (“downfall, forfeiture”), ~chance~, which began as the “falling” of the dice, and ~cadence~, the “falling” of the voice.
en.déchristianiser: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and ~christianiser~, “to undo conversion to Christianity.” The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~, and reverses the base. ~Christianiser~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~chrīstiānizō~, built on ~Chrīstiānus~ (“follower of Christ”), which rests on Greek ~Christós~ (“anointed”). Inherited ~chrétien~ comes from the same Latin word, worn down over the centuries, while ~christianiser~ was taken ready-made. ~Déchristianiser~ means “to strip a person, a people or a place of its Christian character.”
en.décider:
From Latin ~dēcīdere~ (“to cut off, settle, decide a question”), formed from the prefix ~dē-~ (“off, away”) and ~caedere~ (“to cut, to strike, to fell”). ~Caedere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~kaidō~, from PIE *~kh₂eyd-~ (“to cut, to hew”). The image is concrete and decisive: to decide is to cut a difficulty off at a stroke. Through the same root ~décider~ is related to English ~caesura~ and to the whole ~-cide~ family of words.

Where our deliberations feel like weighing, the Roman metaphor was a blade severing the tangle of a dispute — a resolution reached by cutting rather than by pondering. From the root ~caedere~ French inherited a sharp-edged vocabulary: ~concis~ (literally “cut short”), ~précis~ (“cut off in front,” hence “exact”), ~incisif~, ~circoncision~, and the murderous ~-cide~ suffix in ~homicide~, ~suicide~, and ~insecticide~ (an ~insecte~ being itself “cut into” segments, though from a different root). ~Décider~ thus shares its ancestry with both the surgeon's precision and the killer's blow — every decision a small, clean cut through uncertainty.
en.décimaliser: Formed from the adjective ~décimal~ with the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make A”), so “to make decimal,” as when a currency or measure system is converted to base ten. The adjective ~décimal~ was taken from Late Latin ~decimālis~, from Latin ~decimus~ (“tenth”). The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which itself transcribed a Greek verb ending, and it is fully productive in technical and administrative French.
en.décimer:
French ~décimer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~decimāre~, a verb built on ~decem~ (“ten”). The Latin verb meant “to take a tenth,” so the fraction is written into the word. ~Decem~ is the ancestor of French ~dix~ and Spanish ~diez~, and it is a cognate of English ~ten~ and German ~zehn~.

The Latin sense is far narrower than the modern one. Today ~décimer~ describes any heavy toll taken on a population, an army or a herd, whatever the actual fraction, and English ~decimate~ followed the same path. The Latin root also lies behind several everyday French words: ~décimal~, ~décime~ (a tenth part), ~dizaine~ and ~décembre~, the month that was the tenth of the early Roman calendar.
en.décintrer: Formed from ~cintrer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, so it reverses the vaulting: to remove the temporary supports under a finished arch. The base traces to Latin by two routes, either ~cingere~ (“to gird”), or Vulgar Latin *~cinctūrāre~ from ~cinctūra~, the source of ~ceinture~. Both lead to the idea of a band around something.
en.déclamer: Borrowed from Latin ~dēclāmāre~, which is formed from ~dē-~ and ~clāmāre~ (“to cry out, to shout”). In Latin it described speaking aloud in the manner of a rhetorical exercise, the practice speeches of students of oratory. The root ~clāmāre~ is one of the most productive in French, giving ~clameur~ and the verbs ~proclamer~, ~acclamer~, ~exclamer~ and ~réclamer~. English took the family twice, as ~declaim~ from the Latin source and ~claim~ from the Old French descendant of ~clāmāre~. In modern French ~déclamer~ means to recite in a solemn tone, and also to speak out against something.
en.déclarer:
From Latin ~declarare~ (“to make clear, to announce, to reveal”), a compound of the prefix ~de-~ (here intensive, “thoroughly”) and ~clarare~ (“to make bright or clear”), a verb formed on the adjective ~clarus~ (“clear, bright, distinct”). ~Clarus~ descends from Proto-Italic and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~kelh₁-~ (“to call, to cry out”) — the same root behind Latin ~calare~ (“to proclaim”) and ~clamare~ (“to shout”). Italian ~dichiarare~ and Spanish ~declarar~ are the Romance siblings, and English ~declare~ is a borrowing from the same French stem.

The metaphor is light: to ~déclarer~ is to bring something out of obscurity into the open, to make it bright and plain to all. From this came the formal senses of announcing officially — declaring war, declaring one's love, declaring goods at customs, declaring income to the tax office. French ~déclaration~ carries the same weight, as in the ~Déclaration des droits de l'homme~. The underlying ~clarus~ seeds a luminous family in French: ~clair~, ~clarté~, ~clairière~ (a clearing where light enters the forest), ~clairvoyant~, ~éclairer~, and ~clarifier~ — all turning on the idea of brightness made manifest.
en.déclasser: Formed in French from ~classer~ (“to sort, to rank”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which most often reverses or removes: to ~déclasser~ is to take something out of its class, hence to demote, relegate or strike from a list. ~Classer~ is built on the noun ~classe~, borrowed from Latin ~classis~, a word that first meant a “summons” and then the divisions into which the Roman census sorted citizens by wealth. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.déclassifier: Formed from ~classifier~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the base: to remove the classification that made something secret. The base ~classifier~ is built from ~classe~ and ~-ifier~, a suffix going back to Latin ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”). The noun ~classe~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~classis~, which first meant a summons and so the categories of citizens who could be called up for military service.
en.déclaveter: Formed from ~claveter~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the base verb. To ~claveter~ is to secure a part with a ~clavette~, a small key or pin, so to ~déclaveter~ is to take that pin out. The ~clavette~ is a diminutive of the word that gives ~clef~, and the root is Latin ~clāvis~ (“key”). The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, itself from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.déclencher:
~Déclencher~ is built on ~clenche~ (“latch, door-lever”) with the prefix ~dé-~, the literal sense being to lift the latch off its catch. ~Clenche~ comes from Old Frankish *~klinka~ (“latch”), a Germanic word; it belongs with German ~Klinke~ (“handle, latch”) and Swedish ~klinka~, the family resting on a Germanic base imitating the click of the mechanism.

The picture is mechanical and precise: a ~clenche~ is the pivoting bar that holds a door shut, and to ~déclencher~ it is to disengage that bar so the door — or any restrained thing — springs free. From a smith's term for a latch, French abstracted one of its most useful modern verbs: one now triggers an alarm, an offensive, a chemical reaction, a crisis. The opposite move kept its own prefix in ~enclencher~ (“to engage, set in motion”), where the latch is pushed home rather than released. Around the same root cluster ~déclenchement~ (“triggering”), ~déclencheur~ (“the trigger, the shutter-release of a camera”), and ~redéclencher~. The everyday abstraction “to set off” still hides a small medieval door-catch clicking open.
en.décliner:
From Latin ~dēclīnāre~ (“to bend aside, to turn away, to inflect”), from ~dē-~ (“away, down”) and ~clīnāre~ (“to lean, to bend”). The verb ~clīnāre~ rests on PIE *~ḱley-~ (“to lean, to incline”), one of the most widely reflected roots in the family: it gives Greek ~klínein~ (“to lean”), English ~lean~, German ~lehnen~, and, through Latin, English ~incline~ and ~decline~. Romance descendants run parallel in Italian ~declinare~, Spanish ~declinar~ and Portuguese ~declinar~.

The core image is of bending or sloping away from an upright, central position. From that single picture Latin already drew several branches: the grammarian’s “to decline” a noun (to bend its endings through the cases), the astronomer’s declination, and the everyday “to turn aside” or “to slope downward.” French inherited the whole spread, so that ~décliner~ can mean to refuse (“to turn away” an offer), to weaken or wane (the sun, one’s health, a day declining toward evening), and to set out in series — to ~décliner~ one’s identity, or a brand to ~décliner~ a product in several versions. The shared thread is departure from a high or central state. French keeps ~déclin~ (“decline”), ~déclinaison~ (“declension”) and ~déclinable~.
en.décliqueter: Formed from ~cliquet~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and a verbal ending, hence “to release the catch of.” ~Cliquet~ (a catch that clicks) derives from ~cliquer~, which names the sound the device makes. The prefix ~dé-~, from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), marks the undoing of the action here.
en.décloisonner: Formed in French from ~cloisonner~ with the reversing prefix ~dé-~. The base ~cloisonner~ is ~cloison~ (“partition”) plus the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~cloison~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~clausiōnem~ (“a closing”), built on ~clausum~, the participle of Latin ~claudere~ (“to close”), which French inherited as ~clore~. The prefix ~dé-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), undoes the walling-off. ~Décloisonner~ thus means to remove partitions, and by extension to open up separate departments, fields or services to one another.
en.déclore: English Wiktionary treats this verb as inherited from Old French ~desclore~, noting that by surface analysis it reads as ~dé-~ + ~clore~ (“to close”). It may also correspond to Latin ~discludere~, through a Vulgar Latin form *~disclaudō~; Occitan ~desclaure~, Catalan ~descloure~, Italian ~dischiudere~ and Romanian ~deschide~ are compared. The meaning is the opposite of ~clore~, “to open, to uncover.” The base ~clore~ comes from Latin ~claudere~ (“to shut”), and the prefix ~dé-~ marks reversal: to undo a closing.
en.déclouer: Formed from ~clouer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to ~déclouer~ is to pull out the nails, to unnail. It is attested in Old French in the thirteenth century as ~descloer~ and ~desclauer~. The base ~clouer~ comes from ~clou~ (“nail”), from Latin ~clāvus~, with a possible alternative in Late Latin ~clāvāre~. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The opposite verb pair ~clouer~ and ~déclouer~ goes back to the age of the Old French verbs.
en.décléricaliser: ~Décléricaliser~ is built on the adjective ~clérical~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and the suffix ~-iser~. The adjective was taken from Latin ~clēricālis~, which belongs to the family of ~clerc~ (“cleric”). The prefix ~dé-~ reverses, so the verb means to remove the influence of the clergy from something, such as an institution or a school system. The suffix ~-iser~ makes verbs meaning “make” or “convert.” The verb is a recent learned formation of political and administrative vocabulary.
en.décocher: ~Décocher~ is a parasynthetic verb: the prefix ~dé-~ and the ending ~-er~ around the noun ~coche~, a notch. French Wiktionary derives this ~coche~ from Italian ~cocca~ (“notch on an arrow”), the same sense found in Occitan ~encocar~ (“to nock”). The verb first means to shoot an arrow, and it was extended to throwing or launching something, a blow or a remark. Here ~dé-~ marks removal or release. English Wiktionary instead parses the verb as ~dé-~ plus the verb ~cocher~, so the exact base is not settled in the sources.
en.décoder: Formed from ~coder~ (“to encode”) and the reversing prefix ~dé-~, so that ~décoder~ means to undo a coding and read the original message. The base verb is either built on ~code~ or borrowed from English ~to code~, and the noun ~code~ comes from Latin ~codex~, a variant of ~caudex~ (“tree trunk”), which came to name wooden-tablet books, then law books, then the body of laws itself. The sense “secret code” reached French later from English. ~Décoder~ then applies to ciphers, television signals, and by extension to interpreting any hard-to-read message or behavior.
en.décoffrer: Formed from ~coffrer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to ~décoffrer~ is to remove the formwork after concrete has set. ~Coffrer~ comes from ~coffre~ (“chest”), from Old French ~cofre~, from Latin ~cophinus~ (“basket”), borrowed from Greek ~kóphinos~. French kept a doublet of the same word in ~couffin~. In building, ~coffrer~ means to make the wooden mould into which concrete is poured.
en.décoiffer: ~Décoiffer~ goes back to Middle French ~descoifer~, and synchronically it is formed from ~coiffer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the base: to undo what ~coiffer~ does to the head. Its two senses follow from that, since the verb can mean to ruin someone's hairstyle or to knock off a hat. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, itself from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.décoincer: Formed from ~coincer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to ~décoincer~ is to free something that was jammed. The base ~coincer~ comes from the noun ~coin~ (“wedge, corner”), inherited from Old French ~coin~, from Latin ~cuneus~ (“wedge”). To wedge something is to make it stick fast, so to unwedge it is to loosen it. The figurative sense “loosen up,” for a stiff or inhibited person, follows naturally.
en.décoller: Two verbs share this spelling. The commoner one is formed from ~dé-~ (reversal) and ~coller~ (“to stick,” from ~colle~, “glue”), so it means to unstick. An aircraft that “comes unstuck” from the ground ~décolle~, which is the sense of “taking off.” The second verb is a learned borrowing from Latin ~dēcollāre~ (“to behead”), built on ~collum~ (“neck”), the same word that gave French ~cou~. This older verb survives mostly in the literary ~décollation~ (“beheading”) and the noun ~décolleté~ (“low-cut neckline”).
en.décolleter: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and ~colleter~, itself the noun ~collet~ (“collar”) plus ~-er~; French Wiktionary gives ~colleter~ as the base, English Wiktionary ~collet~ + ~-er~, and the two agree in substance. The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~, and here it marks removal. ~Collet~ is inherited from Middle French and analyzed as ~col~ (“neck, collar”) + the suffix ~-et~. ~Décolleter~ means “to bare the neck,” and so “to cut a garment low at the neck.”
en.décoloniser: From ~dé-~ + ~coloniser~, itself ~colon~ + ~-iser~. The base ~colon~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~colōnus~ (“cultivator, settler”), derived from ~colere~ (“to cultivate”). The prefix ~dé-~, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), reverses the verb, and ~-iser~, from Late Latin ~-izāre~, forms verbs meaning “to cause to become” or “to treat as.” So ~décoloniser~ means to undo colonization: to end a colonial relationship.
en.décolorer:
~Décolorer~ is recorded in French from 1694, built from the prefix ~dé-~ (reversal, loss) and ~colorer~. French Wiktionary adds that it was apparently remade on the model of the Latin verb ~dēcolōrāre~ (“to lose color, to grow dull”), and English Wiktionary likewise compares Latin ~dēcolōrō~. So the word has a double face: a French formation in appearance, with a Latin ancestor standing behind it. Latin ~dēcolōrāre~ itself joins ~dē-~ (“away from”) to ~color~ (“color”).

The verb ~colorer~ comes from Latin ~colōrāre~, from ~color~, the same source as French ~couleur~. Around ~décolorer~ gathers a small family: ~décoloration~ (“fading, bleaching”), ~décolorant~ (“bleaching agent”), ~incolore~ (“colorless”), and ~colorier~ and ~coloriser~. The modern verb means to remove or lose color, whether by sun, washing or bleach; hair is the classic case of the transitive verb, and a faded fabric the classic case of the pronominal ~se décolorer~. The verb and its Latin model are close enough that French simply reclaimed what Latin had already said.
en.décolérer: Formed with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action, on ~colérer~ (“to be angry”), itself a verb built from ~colère~ (“anger”); English Wiktionary analyzes it directly as ~dé-~ + ~colère~ + ~-er~. To ~décolérer~ is to stop being angry, to calm down. In practice it appears almost only in the negative, as in ~ne pas décolérer~, said of someone who stays angry.
en.décommander: ~Décommander~ is formed from ~commander~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the base: to ~décommander~ is to undo an order, an appointment or an invitation, in other words to cancel it. The base ~commander~ comes from Old French ~comander~, from Vulgar Latin *~commandare~, an alteration of Latin ~commendare~ (“to entrust”), itself built on ~com-~ and ~mandare~ (“to hand over, to charge with a task”). The same chain gave English ~command~. Because ~commander~ also means to place an order for a meal or goods, ~décommander~ applies just as well to a booking or a purchase as to a guest: you call off what you had set in motion.
en.décommettre: Formed from ~commettre~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: where ~commettre~ joins strands together, ~décommettre~ unravels or untwists them. The base comes from Latin ~committere~ (“to bring together, to entrust”), from ~com-~ (“together”) and ~mittere~ (“to send”). The prefix ~dé-~ descends from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). English ~commit~ is the learned borrowing of the same Latin verb.
en.décommuniser: Formed from ~communiser~ with the prefix ~dé-~. The base ~communiser~ is built on the stem of ~communiste~ plus the suffix ~-iser~, so it means to make communist in character. The prefix ~dé-~, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), reverses that action, so ~décommuniser~ means to undo communist influence or character. It is a typical pairing in political vocabulary, where ~dé-~ is attached to a verb in ~-iser~, as in ~déstaliniser~.
en.décompacter: ~Décompacter~ is formed from ~compacter~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to undo compacting, as when a compressed file is unpacked. The base ~compacter~ is a French formation on the adjective ~compact~, from Latin ~compactus~, the participle of ~compingere~ (“to join together”). So the verb is a modern French coinage resting on a Latin-derived adjective, not an inherited Latin verb.
en.décompenser: ~Décompenser~ is formed from ~compenser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here marks the end or reversal of a state: to stop being compensated. The base ~compenser~ comes from Latin ~compēnsāre~ (“to weigh together, to counterbalance”), from ~com-~ (“together”) and ~pēnsāre~, a frequentative of ~pendere~ (“to weigh, to pay”). Through that root it shares a family with ~peser~, ~penser~ and ~dépenser~. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.décomplexer: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ (removal) and ~complexer~, “to give someone a complex,” which is the noun ~complexe~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Latin ~complexus~, the past participle of ~complecti~ (“to embrace, to encompass”), and its psychological sense, as in an inferiority complex, was borrowed from German ~Komplex~. ~Décomplexer~ is thus to remove someone's inhibitions and make them feel at ease, and in the reflexive, to shed one's own.
en.décomposer: Formed in French from the prefix ~dé-~ (reversal, “undoing”) and ~composer~, so “to undo a composition, to break something into its parts.” The base ~composer~ comes from Latin ~componere~ (“to put together”, from ~com-~ + ~ponere~) but was reshaped in Old French on ~poser~, which explains its odd form. ~Décomposer~ has a literal sense, such as splitting a compound or a number into its elements, and a physical one: matter that rots is said to ~se décomposer~. By extension, a face ~décomposé~ is one drawn with shock or grief, as though its features had fallen apart.
en.décompresser: Borrowed from English ~to decompress~, which French Wiktionary breaks down with the prefixes ~dé-~ and ~con-~ and the verb ~presser~ (“to press”): in other words, “to undo the pressing together.” The first sense was technical, to release pressure on a gas, a diver or a computer file. French then took up the figurative, informal sense “to relax, to unwind,” treating stress as a pressure that can be released. The verb is therefore a recent import dressed in entirely Latin parts, which French speakers can read at once.
en.décomprimer: ~Décomprimer~ is formed from ~comprimer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action of the base: to ~décomprimer~ is to release what was squeezed together. ~Comprimer~ is a borrowing of Latin ~comprimere~ (“to press together”), from ~com-~ and ~premere~ (“to press”), a verb that gave French a whole series in ~-primer~. The verb is used for gas, for diver's air pressure, for files that were compressed, and figuratively for a person who lets tension go.
en.décompter: ~Décompter~ is formed from ~compter~ and the prefix ~dé-~, which here marks taking away: to count off, to deduct. The prefix descends from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The base ~compter~ is a learned respelling of Old French ~conter~, from Latin ~computare~ (“to reckon”), made of ~com-~ and ~putare~. The silent ~p~ in ~compter~ restores the Latin spelling, and ~décompter~ inherits it.
en.déconcentrer: Formed in French from ~concentrer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which undoes the base: to ~déconcentrer~ is to scatter what had been gathered. The sense “to distract” applies to attention (a noise ~déconcentre~ a student), while the administrative sense “to devolve” applies to power, handed from a central authority to local offices. The base ~concentrer~ was coined in 17th-century French from ~centrer~ with ~con-~ (“together”), on ~centre~, from Latin ~centrum~, borrowed from Greek ~kéntron~ (“sharp point, compass pivot”).
en.déconcerter: French inherited the verb from Middle French ~desconcerter~, which both Wiktionaries record. English Wiktionary analyzes it as ~des-~ (“dis-”) + ~concerter~ (“to bring into agreement, to organize”). The prefix undoes the base, so the verb originally speaks of upsetting an agreement or arrangement. Modern ~déconcerter~ means to throw someone off balance, to baffle. The prefix ~des-~ later became ~dé-~, as in many other French verbs.
en.déconditionner: ~Déconditionner~ is built from ~conditionner~ with the reversing prefix ~dé-~. The base appeared in the late thirteenth century as a verb on the noun ~condition~, borrowed from Latin ~condicio~ (“agreement, stipulation”). Among its later senses were “to condition a product for sale” and, from 1928, the psychological sense of ~réflexe conditionné~, a calque of the English phrase made famous by Pavlov. ~Déconditionner~ undoes either kind: it unpacks a product, or frees a person from an acquired conditioning.
en.décongeler: ~Décongeler~ is formed from ~congeler~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to ~décongeler~ is to undo freezing, to thaw. The base ~congeler~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~congelāre~ (“to freeze solid”), made of ~con-~ and ~gelāre~ (“to freeze”), from the noun ~gelu~ (“frost, ice”). English ~congeal~ is a relative that came in through French. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). In everyday use the verb belongs to the kitchen, where it names what one does to food taken out of the ~congélateur~.
en.décongestionner: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and ~congestionner~, so “to undo congestion.” The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~, and here it reverses the base. ~Congestionner~ is built on ~congestion~, from Latin ~congestiō~ (“a heap”), from ~congerere~ (“to heap up”), itself ~con-~ (“together”) + ~gerere~ (“to carry”). The idea is accumulation, of blood in an organ or of traffic on a road. ~Décongestionner~ means “to relieve congestion” in either sense.
en.déconnecter: Formed in French from the prefix ~dé-~ and ~connecter~. The prefix, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), here reverses the base verb: to undo a connection. The base ~connecter~ is attested from around 1780 and comes from Latin ~conectere~ (“to bind together”), built from ~con-~ (“together”) and ~nectere~ (“to bind, to tie”). So ~déconnecter~ literally means to untie what was tied together, first said of wires and circuits and later of anyone logging off a network. The reflexive ~se déconnecter~ now means “to log out,” and, by extension, “to switch off mentally.”
en.déconner: Formed in French from the prefix ~dé-~, the noun ~con~ and the ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary notes that only the first sense follows this formation. The figurative senses (to talk nonsense, to joke around, to mess up) were modeled on ~délirer~ and have no direct etymological link to it. The noun ~con~ comes from Latin ~cunnus~ (“sheath, by analogy the vulva”), which is why the word was long vulgar. English Wiktionary glosses the verb literally as “to pull out of the ~con~.”
en.déconseiller: Formed from ~conseiller~ (“to advise”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the base: to advise against rather than to advise. ~Conseiller~ is inherited from Old French ~conseilier~, from Latin ~cōnsiliārī~ (“to take counsel”), built on ~cōnsilium~ (“counsel, deliberation”), a word that probably began as a “calling together” (~con-~ plus a root related to ~calāre~, “to call”). The same Latin noun gave Italian ~consiglio~, Spanish ~consejo~ and, through Old French, English ~counsel~. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and is one of the most productive prefixes in French.
en.déconsidérer: ~Déconsidérer~ is formed from ~considérer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here marks the reversal of a state: to ~déconsidérer~ someone is to undo the regard in which they were held, to discredit them. The base ~considérer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~considerare~ (“to examine attentively, to contemplate”), built on ~con-~ (“together, thoroughly”) and a stem linked to ~sidus~ (“star”), a connection traditionally explained through the stargazing of augurs. The prefix ~dé-~ itself comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). So the verb takes “careful regard” and removes it.
en.déconsigner: Formed from ~consigner~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to release from confinement, to return a deposit, to reimburse. The base ~consigner~ comes from Latin ~cōnsignāre~, made of ~con-~ (“together, thoroughly”) and ~signāre~ (“to mark, to seal”), from ~signum~ (“mark, sign, seal”). French ~consigner~ means to set down in writing, to deposit, and to confine, as soldiers are kept to barracks, so ~déconsigner~ undoes the last two. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.déconstruire: Formed in French from ~construire~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the action of the base. ~Construire~ comes from Latin ~construere~ (“to pile up, to build”), made of ~con-~ (“together”) and ~struere~ (“to heap up, to arrange in layers”). That verb goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~strew-~ (“to strew, to spread out”), which also gave English ~strew~. So the verb means, etymologically, to take apart what was piled up in ordered layers. The ~struere~ family also gave French ~structure~, ~instruire~ and ~détruire~.
en.décontaminer: Formed from ~contaminer~ with the reversing prefix ~dé-~, so “to undo contamination.” The base is a learned verb: ~contaminer~ was borrowed from Latin ~contāmināre~ (“to defile by contact”), a word whose own origin is obscure. French attests it from the 12th century, but it fell out of use in the 17th and was revived by medicine in 1863. The prefix ~dé-~, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), is one of the most productive in French, and here it names the removal of the pollutant, whether chemical, radioactive or biological.
en.décontenancer: ~Décontenancer~ is built on ~contenance~ (“bearing, composure”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which undoes the base, and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to make someone lose their composure.” Another analysis sees it as a back-formation from the participle ~décontenancé~. The base ~contenance~ comes from Old French ~countenance~, formed from ~contenir~ with the suffix ~-ance~ (compare Late Latin ~continentia~).
en.décontracter: ~Décontracter~ is formed from ~contracter~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to undo a contraction, and so to relax. The base ~contracter~ is a learned word built on Latin ~contractus~, the past participle of ~contrahere~ (“to draw together”), made of ~con-~ (“together”) and ~trahere~ (“to pull”). The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). Relaxing a muscle or a person is, then, literally undoing the drawing together.
en.décorder: Formed from ~corde~ (“rope, cord”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which marks removal, and the verbal ending ~-er~: to take the rope off or undo a cord. The noun was borrowed from Latin ~corda~, itself from Latin ~chorda~ (“gut, string”), which Latin took from Greek ~χορδή~ (“string of gut”). The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.décorer:
From Latin ~decorāre~ (“to adorn, beautify”), from ~decus~ / ~decor~ (“grace, ornament, seemliness”), from Proto-Italic *~dekos~, from PIE *~deḱ-~ (“to take, to accept, to be fitting”). The same root reaches widely: through Latin ~decēre~ (“to be becoming”) come ~décent~ and ~dignité~, and the root is cognate with Ancient Greek ~δοκεῖν~ (~dokeîn~, “to seem, think fit”).

The key is that ~decus~ did not mean ornament for its own sake but what is fitting — beauty as propriety. To ~decorate~ was to give a thing the adornment proper to it, which is why the very same notion sits inside ~décent~ (“suitable”) and inside ~décorer~ in its honorific sense: to ~décorer~ a soldier is to confer the distinction his conduct merits, not to prettify him. From this root spread ~décor~, ~décoration~, ~décoratif~, ~décorateur~, and, by the ~decēre~ branch, the whole family of fitness and worth. Decoration, in the word's bones, is less about glitter than about giving each thing its due grace.
en.décorner: ~Décorner~ is formed from ~corner~ with the prefix ~dé-~, in its sense of removal or reversal. ~Corner~ itself is built on the noun ~corne~ (“horn”), which comes through Old French from Vulgar Latin *~corna~, the Latin neuter plural ~cornua~ taken for a feminine singular. The verb thus means “to take off the horns,” as with cattle, and it can also mean to undo a page that has been dog-eared with ~corner~.
en.décortiquer:
From Latin ~dēcorticāre~ (“to strip off bark”), formed from ~dē-~ (“off, away”) and ~cortex~ (“bark, rind”), whose stem ~cortic-~ shows in the verb. French took it in as a learned word, while its relative ~écorcher~ (“to skin, to flay”), from a Latin verb ~excorticāre~ built in the same way, came down by the popular route. English ~decorticate~ and ~cortex~ come from the same Latin words.

The literal sense is to remove bark or husk: ~décortiquer~ is what one does to shrimp, nuts, rice or grain, and the verb also serves for stripping a tree. By a short step it became figurative: to ~décortiquer~ a text, a speech or a problem is to peel back its outer layer and examine what lies underneath. In anatomy the same Latin ~cortex~ survives in ~cortex~ and ~cortical~, so the brain's outer layer is named for bark.
en.découcher: Formed in French from ~coucher~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here expresses the reverse or absence of the base action: to sleep away from one's own bed, to stay out all night. The base ~coucher~ comes from Old French ~couchier~, from Latin ~collocāre~ (“to place, to lay in position”), itself built from ~con-~ (“together, thoroughly”) and ~locāre~ (“to place”), from ~locus~ (“place”). The prefix ~dé-~ goes back to Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.découdre: ~Découdre~ is the prefix ~dé-~ added to ~coudre~ (“to sew”), so it means literally “to unsew,” to take out stitches. The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and here has its commonest sense, the reversal of the base verb. ~Coudre~ itself descends from Latin ~cōnsuere~ (“to sew together”).
en.découler:
From the prefix ~dé-~ (here marking downward motion or origin) and ~couler~ (“to flow, to run”). ~Couler~ comes from Latin ~colare~ (“to filter, to strain”), from the noun ~colum~ (“sieve, strainer”). The Romance descendants of ~colare~ keep the watery sense throughout: Italian ~colare~, Spanish ~colar~, Portuguese ~coar~. The original picture is liquid passing through a filter — and from straining, the French verb shifted to the broader idea of flowing freely.

~Découler~ is literally water trickling down a slope, drop running after drop. From that physical image French built an abstract one: a conclusion ~follows from~ a premise the way a stream descends from its source — naturally, by gravity, without a break in the chain. The flowing sense is also why ~couler~ can mean a boat sinking (going under the water) and time passing. Relatives include ~écouler~ (“to flow out; to sell off”), ~couloir~ (“corridor,” a channel things run along), ~coulis~ and ~coulée~, and ~colander~ in English, borrowed from the same Latin ~colum~.
en.découper:
Formed from ~couper~ (“to cut”) with the prefix ~dé-~ (here marking division into pieces). ~Couper~ derives from the noun ~coup~ (“a blow”): to cut was “to separate with a blow.” ~Coup~ runs back through Old French ~colp~ and Late Latin *~colpus~ to Latin ~colaphus~ (“a blow with the fist, a box on the ear”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~κόλαφος~ (~kólaphos~, “a cuff, a slap”).

The striking image survives the etymology: the oldest cutting was done by chopping, a blow that parts the thing struck. ~Découper~ specializes this into “to cut up” — to carve a roast, to chop vegetables, to cut shapes out of paper. The ~coup~ family is one of the most productive in French: ~coup~, ~couper~, ~coupure~, ~coupon~, ~découpage~, ~entrecouper~, and ~recouper~. The English ~coup~, ~coupon~, and ~coupé~ are all later borrowings from this same French stock.
en.découpler: ~Découpler~ is formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ~coupler~, and it reverses its base: to uncouple what was coupled, to separate two linked devices, circuits or carriages. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”) by way of Old French ~des-~. The base ~coupler~ comes from Latin ~cōpulāre~ (“to join, to bind”), built on ~cōpula~ (“bond, link”). French also borrowed a later learned doublet of the same Latin verb, ~copuler~.
en.décourager: From Old French ~descouragier~, built from the prefix ~des-~ (the ancestor of ~dé-~) and ~corage~, the ancestor of modern ~courage~. In Old French ~corage~ meant the heart, in the sense of spirit and feeling, from Latin ~cor~ (“heart”). To ~décourager~ is therefore, quite literally, to take the heart out of someone. The prefix ~dé-~ marks that removal. Middle French ~descourager~ was also borrowed by English as ~discourage~. The opposite verb, ~encourager~, puts the heart back in.
en.découronner: Formed from ~couronner~ (“to crown”) with the reversing prefix ~dé-~, so “to uncrown.” The base comes from Old French ~coroner~, inherited from Latin ~corōnāre~, a verb built on ~corōna~ (“crown, wreath”). ~Dé-~ goes back to Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”) and undoes the action of the base: to take the crown away from someone, and so, by extension, to strip a person of sovereign status.
en.découvrir:
French ~découvrir~ is a transparent compound: the prefix ~dé-~ (“un-, reversal”) joined to ~couvrir~ (“to cover”), descending through Old French ~descovrir~ from Late Latin ~discooperīre~. The base ~couvrir~ comes from Latin ~cooperīre~ (“to cover over”), an intensive ~co(m)-~ plus ~operīre~ (“to close, to cover”), which rests on a Proto-Indo-European compound of *~op-~ (“over”) and the root *~wer-~ (“to cover, to enclose”). Curiously, the very same *~wer-~ root, with a different prefix, gives Latin ~aperīre~ (“to open, to uncover”) — so covering and uncovering are etymological twins.

The word's literal sense is simply “to uncover”: to remove the ~couverture~ from something. From taking the lid off came the figurative leap to “to find out, to reveal, to discover” — to uncover a truth, a land, a secret. English ~discover~ took exactly the same path from the same Late Latin source. The family is broad in French: ~couvrir~, ~couverture~ (“cover, blanket”), ~couvert~ (a place setting, what is “covered”), ~recouvrir~, and the nouns of finding, ~découverte~ (“a discovery”) and ~découvreur~. The age of exploration is, etymologically, an age of lifting lids — every ~découverte~ a veil pulled back.
en.décrasser: ~Décrasser~ is formed from ~crasse~ (“grime”) with the prefix ~dé-~ and the ending ~-er~: to remove the dirt, hence to clean up or scrub. The prefix expresses removal here, taken from a noun, so the verb has no plain opposite ~crasser~. The noun ~crasse~ is the feminine of the Old French adjective ~cras~, from Latin ~crassus~ (“thick, fat, coarse”), and it is a doublet of ~gras~.
en.décreuser: A variant of ~décruser~, a silk-working term meaning to scald cocoons so that the thread unwinds easily, or to treat raw silk in a bath that strips off its gum. The TLFi dates the verb to 1669 and explains it as a borrowing from the Occitan of Dauphiné and Languedoc, ~descrusa~ or ~decrusa~, with ~décreuser~ itself taken from a Middle Dauphiné form, ~deskroesa~. Littré proposed a different reading: ~dé-~ plus the adjective ~cru~ (“raw”), the workers' speech having altered the verb. The origin of the form is therefore not settled.
en.décrier: French Wiktionary derives ~décrier~ from ~crier~ with the prefix ~dé-~, and English Wiktionary gives it as Middle and Old French ~descrier~; the two agree that it reverses the base: where ~crier~ proclaims, ~décrier~ speaks against publicly. The base ~crier~ is attested by about 980 and comes from Vulgar Latin *~critare~, a reduction of Latin ~quiritare~ (“to cry out”). The origin of ~quiritare~ is disputed, and the sources leave it open. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~.
en.décrire:
From Latin ~describere~ (“to copy off, to sketch, to describe”), a compound of the prefix ~de-~ (“down, off”) and ~scribere~ (“to write”). French refashioned the verb on the model of ~écrire~, giving ~décrire~. ~scribere~ originally meant “to scratch or carve marks,” from the Proto-Indo-European root *~skribʰ-~, an extended form of *~sker-~ (“to cut”). Through this root ~décrire~ is cognate with English ~scribe~ and ~script~, and — by an early Latin loan into Germanic — with English ~shrive~ and German ~schreiben~ (“to write”).

The buried image is one of cutting: the earliest writing was incised into wood, clay, or stone, and ~scribere~ named that scratching. In ~describere~ the prefix ~de-~ adds the idea of tracing something off or sketching it out, point by point — which is just what a description does, drawing a verbal outline of its subject. The same root left French a dense cluster of ~-crire~ verbs, each with its prefix: ~écrire~ (“to write”), ~inscrire~ (“to inscribe”), ~prescrire~ (“to prescribe”), ~souscrire~ (“to subscribe”), and ~transcrire~ (“to transcribe”), alongside the nouns ~description~, ~écriture~, and ~scribe~ itself.
en.décrisper: ~Décrisper~ (“to unclench, to ease”) is formed from ~crisper~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action of the base. ~Crisper~ is borrowed from Latin ~crispāre~ (“to curl, to wrinkle”), a verb tied to the adjective ~crispus~ (“curly”). French ~crispé~ and ~crispation~ belong to the same family. So ~décrisper~ means to undo a tightening, whether of a hand, a face or, figuratively, a tense situation.
en.décrocher:
From the prefix ~dé-~ (“un-, away”) and the now-archaic verb ~crocher~ (“to hook”), derived from the noun ~croc~ (“hook”). ~Croc~ came through Old French from Frankish *~krōk~ (“hook”) — or, by an alternative account the sources allow, from Old Norse ~krókr~ (“hook, bend”) — both leading back to Proto-Germanic *~krōkaz~. The word is therefore a Germanic import into a Romance language, and it is cognate with English ~crook~ and ~crooked~, which carry the same notion of something bent.

Literally ~décrocher~ means to lift a thing off its hook: a coat, a painting, a telephone receiver — French still says ~décrocher~ for picking up a ringing phone. From there the senses fan out figuratively: to ~land~ a prize or a job (to unhook it from where it hung, just out of reach), and, in aviation, for a wing to ~stall~ — to lose its grip on the air. Relatives include ~accrocher~ (“to hang up, to snag”), ~raccrocher~ (“to hang up the phone”), ~décrochage~ (“stalling; dropping out”), ~décrochement~, and the ~crochet~ (“little hook”) used for needlework.
en.décroiser: Formed from ~croiser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which undoes the base: to uncross, as one uncrosses one's arms. ~Croiser~ is itself built on ~croix~ (“cross”), from Latin ~crux~ (“stake, cross”), whose ultimate origin is uncertain. Latin ~crux~ also gave Italian ~croce~ and Spanish ~cruz~, and English ~cross~ came by way of Old Irish and Old Norse.
en.décrotter: Formed from ~crotter~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: where ~crotter~ is to soil with droppings or mud, ~décrotter~ is to clean that mud off. The base rests on the noun ~crotte~, from Old French ~crote~, attested in the late twelfth century and probably from an Old Dutch form *~krotta~ whose original sense was ball-shaped dung. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.décroître:
The origin is debated. French Wiktionary derives ~décroître~ from Latin ~decrēscere~ (“to grow less”), while English Wiktionary says it comes either from ~dé-~ + ~croître~ or from Old French ~descreistre~, and that it perhaps corresponds to the Latin verb but is more likely an internal French formation. Either way the Latin model is ~dē-~ (“down, away”) + ~crēscere~ (“to grow”), an inchoative verb from the root of ~creāre~, itself from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱerh₃-~ (“to grow”). Italian ~decrescere~ and Spanish ~decrecer~ are the Latin verb inherited, and English ~decrease~ came from the Old French form.

The meaning is the mirror of ~croître~: where a thing grew, it now shrinks, as with daylight after midsummer or a river after a flood. The noun ~décrue~ names exactly that fall of floodwater. In recent decades ~décroissance~ has also become the name of an economic movement that argues for “degrowth.” The family of the root is rich: ~croissant~ (the pastry takes its name from the crescent moon, literally “the growing one”), ~accroître~, ~croissance~, and ~créer~.
en.décruer: Formed from the adjective ~cru~ (“raw”) with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to strip of rawness,” which gives the sense “to scour.” The adjective comes from Latin ~crūdus~ (“raw”), which English borrowed as ~crude~. The prefix ~dé-~ descends from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and marks removal. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~.
en.décruser: Formed from the adjective ~cru~ (“raw”) with the verb ending ~-er~ and an “euphonic” ~s~ that joins the two, the removal prefix ~dé-~ being visible in the form. The raw state in question is that of silk: before it is boiled, the silk cocoon is said to be ~cru~. To ~décruser~ is therefore to degum the silk, stripping off the natural gum that coats the raw thread.
en.décrypter: From ~crypter~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the action of the base. French Wiktionary says ~crypter~ is itself a back-formation from ~encrypter~, with the prefix ~en-~ dropped. The root ~crypt-~ is Greek ~kruptós~ (“hidden”), also found in ~crypte~, ~cryptographie~ and ~cryptogramme~. To ~décrypter~ a message is therefore to take it from hidden to readable. ~Dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), the same prefix as in ~défaire~ and ~débloquer~.
en.décrédibiliser: Formed in French from ~crédibiliser~ with the reversing prefix ~dé-~. The base ~crédibiliser~ is built on the adjective ~crédible~ and the suffix ~-iser~, and means to make credible. ~Crédible~ was borrowed from Latin ~crēdibilis~ (“believable”), from ~crēdō~ (“to believe”). The prefix ~dé-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), undoes the credibility. ~Décrédibiliser~ means to discredit, to strip a person or an idea of the trust it enjoyed.
en.décréditer: Formed from ~crédit~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to take away someone's credit”: to discredit or disgrace. The noun ~crédit~ was borrowed from Italian ~credito~, from Latin ~crēditum~, the supine of ~crēdere~ (“to believe, to entrust”). Credit was thus literally the trust that a borrower will repay, and ~décréditer~ destroys that trust.
en.décrépir: Formed from ~crépir~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to strip the rough coat of plaster from a wall. The base ~crépir~ is a doublet of ~crêper~ with the ending ~-ir~. It first meant “to shrivel, to become grainy,” and in masonry it came to mean “to give a wall its grain,” that is, to roughcast it. Behind both verbs stands Old French ~crespe~, from Latin ~crispus~ (“curly, crinkled”). The same root gave ~crépu~ (“frizzy”) and the learned ~crisper~. So ~décrépir~ undoes what ~crépir~ did to the wall.
en.décréter: Formed from the noun ~décret~ and the ending ~-er~. ~Décret~ comes from Old French ~decré~ and ~decret~, borrowed from Latin ~dēcrētum~ (“decision, ordinance”), the past participle of ~dēcernere~ (“to decide”). That Latin verb joined ~dē-~ and ~cernere~ (“to sift, to separate, to judge”), the same ~cernere~ behind ~discerner~ and ~certain~. To ~décréter~ is therefore to issue a decree, and by extension to declare something with the weight of an order.
en.décrêper: Formed from ~crêper~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which undoes the action of the base: to take the frizz or crimp out of hair. ~Dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The base ~crêper~ is built on the noun ~crêpe~, the modern form of Old French ~crespe~, from Latin ~crispus~ (“curly, crinkled”), and it means to give a frizzy texture, above all by backcombing. The same Latin root also gave ~crépu~ and the learned ~crisper~.
en.décuivrer: Formed from the noun ~cuivre~ (“copper”) with the prefix ~dé-~ (“removal”) and the verb ending ~-er~: to strip copper from something. The noun comes from Latin ~cuprum~ and its variant ~cuprēum~, popular forms of ~Cyprium~ (“of Cyprus”), from the Greek name of the island, ~Kúpros~. The Romans most likely imported their copper from Cyprus, and named the metal after the island by metonymy, rather than adopting the Greek ~khalkós~. Learned chemical words such as ~cuprique~ keep the Latin form.
en.déculasser: Formed from ~culasse~ (“breech”) with the prefix ~dé-~, so it means to remove the breech of a firearm. The noun ~culasse~ is itself a French derivation from ~cul~ with the suffix ~-asse~, the rear end of the barrel being named for its position. The prefix ~dé-~ here marks removal of a part, the commonest sense of the prefix on a noun base.
en.déculotter: A parasynthetic verb: ~dé-~ + ~culotte~ + ~-er~, “to take off someone's breeches or underpants.” The prefix ~dé-~ marks removal, as in ~déboiser~ or ~dévoiler~. The base ~culotte~ is itself a derivative of ~cul~ (“backside”) with the suffix ~-otte~, and ~cul~ comes from Latin ~cūlus~. The related ~culot~ is built the same way. The verb is used of removing trousers, often as a prank or a punishment, and in the pronominal form ~se déculotter~, it has the figurative sense of backing down in a cowardly way.
en.déculpabiliser: Formed from ~culpabiliser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here marks the cessation of a state: to relieve someone of guilt. The base is built on Late Latin ~culpabilis~ (“blameworthy”), the source of French ~coupable~, with the verb-forming suffix ~-iser~. The Latin adjective rests on ~culpa~ (“fault, blame”). The verb is a modern, mostly psychological coinage that undoes the earlier ~culpabiliser~, “to make someone feel guilty”.
en.décupler: Formed from the adjective and noun ~décuple~ (“tenfold”) and the verb suffix ~-er~, with the sense “to multiply by ten.” French Wiktionary traces ~décuple~ to Latin ~decuplus~, a word that combines ~decem~ (“ten”) with a multiplying element. The suffix ~-er~ comes from the Latin infinitive ending ~-āre~ and is the default way to make a verb from a noun or adjective. By extension, the verb now often means to increase greatly, with no exact factor of ten in mind.
en.décuver: Built on the noun ~cuve~ (“vat”) with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. Here ~dé-~ marks removal: to ~décuver~ is to take wine or grapes out of the vat. ~Cuve~ is inherited from Old French ~cuve~, from Latin ~cūpa~, and is a doublet of ~coupe~, which came through a Late Latin variant of the same word. So the “cup” on a table and the “vat” in a cellar share one ancestor.
en.décéder:
From Latin ~dēcēdere~ (“to go away, to withdraw, to depart”), formed from the prefix ~dē-~ (“away, from”) and ~cēdere~ (“to go, to yield, to withdraw”). ~Cēdere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~kezdō~ and, by one reconstruction, to a Proto-Indo-European *~ḱesd-~ (“to go away, to drive off”); the deeper history is disputed. Through ~cēdere~ it is cognate with Italian ~cedere~, Spanish ~ceder~, and English ~cede~, ~concede~, and ~cease~.

The Latin ~dēcēdere~ was at first wholly neutral — “to withdraw, to step aside, to depart” — and only by gentle euphemism came to mean “to depart this life,” to die. French kept exactly this softened sense: ~décéder~ is the formal, administrative, and respectful word for dying, the verb of death certificates and obituaries, where the blunt ~mourir~ would jar. Its companion noun is ~décès~, from Latin ~dēcessus~ (“a departure”), and one who has died is ~décédé~. From the same ~cēdere~ French gathered a large family of measured movements: ~céder~, ~accéder~, ~procéder~, ~succéder~, ~précéder~, ~excéder~, and the nouns ~accès~, ~succès~, and ~procès~ — each a kind of going, yielding, or coming-to.
en.décélérer: Formed in French from ~dé-~ and the stem of ~accélérer~, on the model of that verb: to slow down, the reverse of accelerating. The base ~accélérer~ is borrowed from Latin ~accelerāre~, built from ~ad-~ (“toward”) and ~celer~ (“fast”). So ~décélérer~ is a modern coinage, not a Latin inheritance. It reuses the Latin root ~celer~ with the opposite prefix.
en.décérébrer:
~Décérébrer~ is formed from the prefix ~dé-~, Latin ~cerebrum~ (“brain”) and the verbal ending ~-er~. The Latin noun ~cerebrum~ is the source of the learned French adjective ~cérébral~ and of Spanish ~cerebro~, while French ~cerveau~ and Italian ~cervello~ come from its diminutive ~cerebellum~. English ~cerebral~ and ~cerebrum~ come from the same Latin source, so the French verb sits in a large family built on one Latin word for the brain.

The prefix ~dé-~ marks removal or deprivation, so the verb means to take away the brain, or in practice its higher functions. It is a technical term of physiology and medicine: a decerebrate animal is one whose cerebrum has been removed or cut off from the rest of the nervous system. Outside the laboratory the participle ~décérébré~ is also used figuratively of someone seen as brainless.
en.dédaigner: French Wiktionary analyzes it as ~dé-~ plus ~daigner~, while English Wiktionary gives Old French ~desdeignier~, from ~deignier~ (modern ~daigner~), perhaps matching a Vulgar Latin *~disdignāre~ or Latin ~dēdignārī~. The base ~daigner~ comes from Latin ~dignārī~ (“to deem worthy”), from ~dignus~ (“worthy”). Cognates include Italian ~disdegnare~, Spanish ~desdeñar~ and Portuguese ~desdenhar~, and English ~disdain~ was borrowed from French. ~Dédaigner~ is the opposite of ~daigner~: to treat as unworthy, to scorn.
en.dédicacer: ~Dédicacer~ is derived from the noun ~dédicace~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~. ~Dédicace~ comes from Latin ~dēdicātiō~ (“consecration, inauguration”). The verb appears once in the 15th century in its religious sense, to consecrate a place, and only becomes common in the 19th century with its present meaning: to inscribe a book or a photograph to someone, hence to autograph it.
en.dédier:
Borrowed from Latin ~dedicare~ (“to proclaim, to consecrate, to dedicate”), a compound of ~de-~ (“completely, solemnly”) and ~dicare~ (“to proclaim, to set apart”), a durative variant of ~dicere~ (“to say,” the ancestor of French ~dire~). The chain reaches back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~deyḱ-~ (“to point out, to show”). It is cognate with English ~dedicate~, with Greek ~deíknumi~ (“to show”), and with Latin ~digitus~ (“finger,” the pointing thing) and ~index~.

The earliest sense was religious: to ~dedicate~ a temple was to point it out solemnly to a god, to declare it his. From that consecration the verb softened into the familiar “to dedicate a book to someone,” the modern offering of a work in another's honor. French keeps both the learned and the popular line: ~dédier~ for the solemn dedication, the noun ~dédicace~, and the back-formed ~dédicacer~ (“to autograph,” to sign a copy). Through the same root *~deyḱ-~ run a surprising company of words — ~dire~ and ~diction~, ~index~ and ~indiquer~ — all turning, at bottom, on the simple act of pointing and saying so.
en.dédifférencier: ~Dédifférencier~ is formed from ~différencier~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here marks the reversal of a process: to undo a differentiation. ~Différencier~ comes from Late Latin ~differentiare~, from ~differentia~ (“difference”), built on ~differre~, that is ~dis-~ (“apart”) + ~ferre~ (“to carry”). To differentiate is, at root, to carry two things apart. The prefix ~dé-~ descends from Latin ~dis-~ through Old French ~des-~. The verb is a technical one, used for cells or tissues that lose their specialized character and return to a less specialized state.
en.dédire: ~Dédire~ is formed from ~dire~ (“to say”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: literally “to unsay.” It is used mostly in the reflexive, ~se dédire~, “to go back on one's word,” and as a transitive verb it means “to retract.” The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The base ~dire~ descends from Vulgar Latin *~dīgere~, a reshaping of Latin ~dīcere~ (“to say”).
en.dédommager: Formed from ~dommage~ (“harm, loss”) with the prefix ~dé-~ and the ending ~-er~ together; no verb ~dommager~ stands behind it. The prefix expresses removal, so the verb means “to take away the harm,” hence to compensate. ~Dommage~ evolved from Old French ~damage~, which goes back to Latin ~damnum~ (“loss, harm”). English Wiktionary adds that the vowel may have shifted under the influence of Old French ~dongier~ (“danger”). The English word ~damage~ is a relative, borrowed from the Old French form.
en.dédorer: ~Dédorer~ is formed from ~dorer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to strip off gilding, and so to tarnish or dull a surface that had been gilded. The base ~dorer~ comes from Latin ~deaurāre~ (“to gild”), built on ~aurum~ (“gold”), the source of French ~or~. The same prefix and base thus produce an exact opposite, as in other pairs where ~dé-~ undoes what the simple verb did.
en.dédouaner: Formed in French from the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ~douaner~, itself from the noun ~douane~ (“customs”), so ~dédouaner~ is “to clear goods through customs,” literally to take them out of the customs system. The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”) and here marks removal, as in ~dépanner~ or ~déplumer~. English Wiktionary analyzes the verb as ~dé-~ + ~douane~ + ~-er~ in one step, while French Wiktionary goes through ~douaner~. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~.
en.dédoubler: ~Dédoubler~ is formed from the verb ~doubler~ and the prefix ~dé-~, which usually reverses or undoes its base. French ~doubler~ comes from the adjective ~double~, from Latin ~duplus~ (“twofold”), made of ~duo~ (“two”) and a “-fold” element, and it continues Late Latin ~duplāre~. So the new verb is the undoing of a doubling: to divide into two something that was one, or to separate what had been merged. French Wiktionary notes that it stayed rare until the nineteenth century. English ~double~ is a close cousin.
en.dédramatiser: ~Dédramatiser~ is formed from ~dramatiser~ and the prefix ~dé-~, which here marks the end of a state: to make something less dramatic. ~Dramatiser~ itself is built from ~drame~ and the suffix ~-iser~. English Wiktionary gives ~drame~ as borrowed from Latin ~drāma~, from Ancient Greek ~drâma~ (“play, drama”), and French Wiktionary glosses the Greek as an action performed on stage. French Wiktionary instead analyses the verb as ~drame~ with both ~dé-~ and ~-iser~ at once.
en.déduire:
From Latin ~deducere~ (“to lead down, to draw away, to derive”), the prefix ~de-~ (“down, away from”) joined to ~ducere~ (“to lead, to draw”). ~Ducere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~doukō~ and PIE *~dewk-~ (“to draw, to pull”). The same root, through Proto-Germanic, gives English ~tow~ (“to pull”) and German ~ziehen~ (“to pull”) and ~Herzog~ (“duke,” literally an “army-leader”).

The two English glosses sit side by side in the Latin: ~deducere~ meant both to lead something physically away (whence “to deduct,” to take an amount off) and to draw a conclusion out of premises (whence “to deduce,” to derive logically). French keeps the whole leading family from ~ducere~: ~conduire~ (“to drive, to lead”), ~produire~ (“to bring forth”), ~réduire~ (“to lead back, to reduce”), ~traduire~ (“to lead across,” hence to translate), and the learned ~duc~ (“duke”) and ~conduit~. To deduce, in this old image, is to lead a thought downward and outward to its necessary end.
en.défaillir: Formed from ~faillir~ with the prefix ~dé-~. The base is Old French ~faillir~ (“to be lacking, to fail”), from Vulgar Latin *~fallīre~, a remodeling of Latin ~fallere~ (“to deceive”). The same Latin verb lies behind Italian ~fallire~ and Spanish ~fallar~, and, through Old French, English ~fail~. ~Défaillir~ keeps the idea of strength or courage giving out, hence “to faint.” Its family includes ~faute~, ~faillite~ and ~infaillible~.
en.défaire:
Formed from ~faire~ (“to do, to make”) with the prefix ~dé-~ (from Latin ~dis-~, denoting reversal or separation), so literally “to un-make.” The base ~faire~ descends from Latin ~facere~ (“to do, to make”), from PIE *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to set, to put, to make”) — the same vast root behind English ~do~ and ~deed~ and German ~tun~. ~Dé-~ + ~faire~ thus negates the act: it returns a thing to the state it was in before the making.

From that single idea the senses fan out: to empty a container, to unfasten clothing, to untie a knot, to cancel an arrangement, to dissolve a bond. The military sense “to defeat, to rout” is the same gesture writ large — to undo an enemy's array, to break their order. English ~defeat~ travelled the very same path, from Old French ~desfait~. The proverb ~faire et défaire, c'est toujours travailler~ (“to make and unmake is still to work”) catches the verb's spirit. Kindred forms include ~défait~ (“undone; defeated”), ~défaite~ (“defeat”), and the reflexive ~se défaire de~ (“to get rid of”).
en.défalquer:
~Défalquer~ comes from Medieval Latin ~dēfalcāre~ (“to cut off, to lop”), attested from 1288. The Latin verb is formed from ~dē-~ (“off”) and ~falcāre~ (“to mow”), a derivative of ~falx~ (“sickle, scythe, pruning hook”). The image behind the verb is therefore a blade at work: to cut something away from a whole.

The same Latin ~falx~ gave French ~faux~ (“scythe”), and ~falcāre~ gave ~faucher~ (“to mow”), so ~défalquer~ is a learned cousin of everyday words from the field. English borrowed the same source as ~defalcate~. In modern French ~défalquer~ has left the meadow for the account book: it means to deduct a sum from a total, and the noun ~défalcation~ names such a deduction. The sources give no story for the move from cutting to deducting, so it can only be described, not explained.
en.défatiguer: Formed from ~fatiguer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to relieve fatigue, to refresh. The base comes from Latin ~fatigāre~ (“to weary, to harass”). Within Latin the verb seems built on an unattested *~fatis~ (“weariness”), and its ultimate origin is unknown. The Latin sense of wearing someone down is the same as the modern French one, which makes ~défatiguer~ a neat mirror image of ~fatiguer~.
en.défaufiler: Formed from ~faufiler~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses an action. ~Faufiler~ means to baste, that is, to hold a seam together with long temporary stitches. French Wiktionary explains it as an old compound of Old French ~fors~ (“outside”) and ~filer~ (“to spin, to draw out a thread”), with the influence of ~faux~ (“false”). ~Défaufiler~ therefore means to take out that provisional stitching once it has done its job.
en.défausser: ~Défausser~ is formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ~fausser~, and it reverses its base: where ~fausser~ means to make false, to warp or to bend, ~défausser~ means to straighten what has been bent. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and here marks the undoing of an action. The base ~fausser~ descends from Old French ~falser~, which came from Late Latin ~falsāre~ (“to falsify”), from Latin ~falsus~ (“false”). Italian ~falsare~ and English ~false~ are relatives.
en.défavoriser: Formed from ~favoriser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, ~défavoriser~ means “to put at a disadvantage, to treat less favorably,” the reversal of ~favoriser~. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and here marks the opposite of the base verb. The base ~favoriser~ comes from ~faveur~, from Latin ~favor~, a noun built on the verb ~favēre~ (“to be favorable to”). Latin ~favēre~ began as a religious word, used in the formula ~favēre linguīs~, a call to hold one's tongue during a rite. The disadvantaged, in a sense, are those from whom favor has been withheld.
en.défendre:
From Latin ~defendere~ (“to ward off, to repel, to defend”), attested in French around 1100. The verb is ~de-~ (“away”) plus *~fendere~ (“to strike, to thrust”), a root preserved only in compounds and traced to Proto-Indo-European *~gʷʰen-~ (“to strike, to kill”). Its twin compound is ~offendere~ (“to strike against, to offend”), and the pair survive together in English ~defend~ and ~offend~. The same PIE root lies, far back, behind a wide scatter of striking-words across the family.

The original idea was martial: to ~defendere~ was to strike a blow away from someone, to fend off an attacker — English keeps the bare core in ~fend~ and ~fender~. From “to keep harm away” the French verb branched in two directions. One is the familiar “to protect, to defend.” The other, surprising to learners, is “to forbid”: ~défendre~ à quelqu'un de faire quelque chose means to bar them from it — to ward off an action rather than a foe. So the same verb both shields and prohibits. Related French words include ~défense~ (which means both “defence” and “prohibition,” and also an elephant's tusk) and ~offenser~.
en.défenestrer: Formed in French from the prefix ~dé-~, the Old French noun ~fenestre~ (“window”, today fenêtre) and the verb ending ~-er~. English Wiktionary traces the noun to Latin ~fenestra~ (“window”). The prefix expresses removal, as in many verbs built on a noun: to throw someone out of a window, and in practice to throw them out of it. The old spelling ~fenestre~ survives inside the verb, which keeps the ~-s-~ that ~fenêtre~ later replaced with a circumflex.
en.déferler: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and ~ferler~ (“to furl” a sail), so literally “to unfurl.” The origin of ~ferler~ is uncertain: French Wiktionary proposes, with a hedge, that it comes from Latin ~ferula~ (source of ~férule~), and English Wiktionary offers the same Latin word only as a possibility. The modern verb is used of waves that break and rush forward, and figuratively of crowds, emotions or trends that surge in a mass.
en.déferrer: ~Déferrer~ is built from the prefix ~dé-~, the noun ~fer~ (“iron”) and the verb ending ~-er~: “to remove the iron” from something. The prefix ~dé-~ here marks removal, as in verbs formed on a noun. The noun ~fer~ descends from Latin ~ferrum~, which also gave Italian ~ferro~ and Spanish ~hierro~.
en.défeuiller: Formed from ~feuille~ with the prefix ~dé-~ (removal) and the verbal ending ~-er~: to ~défeuiller~ is to strip the leaves from a plant. The noun ~feuille~ comes through Old French ~fueille~ and Late Latin ~folia~ from Latin ~folium~ (“leaf”). It is a doublet of ~folio~, which was borrowed directly from Latin. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~.
en.défeutrer: Formed from ~feutrer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses an action: the verb means to undo the felting of wool. ~Feutrer~ is built on the noun ~feutre~ (“felt”), from Old French ~feltre~, from Frankish *~filtir~ (“coarse cloth”). The noun is cognate with English ~felt~ and German ~Filz~. Felt is made by pounding wool fibers until they mat together, so ~défeutrer~ names the opposite process, loosening the matted fibers.
en.défibrer: Formed from ~fibre~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so that it means “to remove the fibers.” ~Fibre~ is a learned word taken from Latin ~fibra~, itself linked to ~fiber~ (“at the extremity”). The prefix ~dé-~ marks removal, and ~-er~ turns the noun into a verb.
en.déficeler: Formed from ~ficeler~ (“to tie up with string”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which marks reversal, so “to undo the string, to unwrap.” The base verb is built on ~ficelle~ (“string, twine”) plus the ending ~-er~. ~Ficelle~ probably comes from a Vulgar Latin *~filicella~, derived from Latin ~fīlum~ (“thread”). The prefix ~dé-~ goes back to Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.défier:
~Défier~ is explained as ~dé-~ + ~fier~ (“to trust, to entrust”), with the influence of Latin ~diffīdere~ (“to distrust”), itself made of ~dis-~ and ~fīdere~ (“to trust”). The French base ~fier~ continues Vulgar Latin *~fīdāre~, a verb drawn from ~fidus~ (“faithful”) and related to ~fidēs~ (“trust, faith”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰeydʰ-~ (“to trust, to persuade”). English ~defy~ borrowed the French verb, while English ~faith~ comes from Latin ~fidēs~ by way of Old French. So the verb contains the idea of trust twice over, once in its base and once in the Latin verb that colored it.

The sense “to challenge” is the surprising part. In medieval usage the verb first meant to withdraw one's pledged faith, as when a vassal formally broke his bond with his lord or an enemy declared war. A formal challenge to combat followed, and from there came the modern senses “to challenge, to dare, to defy”. The reflexive ~se défier de~ keeps the older meaning of mistrust, so the verb holds two opposite attitudes, boldness toward someone and distrust of them, both springing from a trust that has been broken. Its relatives include ~confier~, ~méfier~, ~défiance~, ~confiance~, ~fidèle~ and ~foi~.
en.défigurer: ~Défigurer~ is formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ~figurer~, according to French Wiktionary. English Wiktionary instead builds it from ~dé-~, the noun ~figure~ and ~-er~. In both accounts the prefix takes away or spoils, so to ~défigurer~ is to ruin a face's shape. The base ~figurer~ comes from Latin ~figurāre~ (“to shape”), from ~figura~ (“shape, form”), itself built on ~fingere~ (“to mould”). Its relatives in French include ~figure~, ~configurer~ and ~feindre~.
en.défiler:
~défiler~ is built from the prefix ~dé-~ and ~filer~ (“to spin thread, to run in a line”), with the related noun ~file~ (“a rank, a single line of people”); both ~filer~ and ~file~ rest on Latin ~filum~ (“thread”). The word thus straddles two images. On one reading ~dé-~ + ~filer~ means literally “to unthread,” to pull the thread out of something — the sense alive in ~se défiler~ (“to slip away, to wriggle out”), as a thread slides free of the needle.

On the other reading, the one behind “to parade,” the unit is ~file~: to ~défiler~ is to move past in a single column, the way troops march one rank behind another, each soldier a bead on a thread. From this come the military ~défilé~ (a narrow pass through which a column must thread itself in file) and the civilian ~défilé~ — a procession, and by extension a fashion show, where models walk the runway in succession. The shared Latin ~filum~ unites a wide French family: ~fil~, ~file~, ~filer~, ~filet~, ~enfiler~ (“to thread, to string together”), and ~profil~ — all turning on the single idea of a thread, literal or marched.
en.définir:
From Old French ~diffinir~, ~definir~, a learned borrowing from Latin ~dēfīnīre~ (“to bound, to limit, to determine precisely”), built from the prefix ~dē-~ and the verb ~fīnīre~ (“to finish, to set bounds”), itself from ~fīnis~ (“a boundary, a limit, an end”). The Old French scribes favored the spelling ~diffinir~, with ~dis-~ becoming ~dif-~ before the ~f~, partly to keep the word distinct from the classical sense of ~dēfīnīre~. Through ~fīnis~ the verb is kin to Italian ~definire~, Spanish ~definir~, and English ~define~ and ~finish~. The deeper origin of ~fīnis~ is uncertain, though it is often tentatively linked to ~fīgere~ (“to fix, to fasten”), as if a limit were a stake driven into the ground.

The Latin ~dēfīnīre~ meant literally “to mark off within boundaries,” and that spatial image still lives inside the abstract modern sense: to ~définir~ a word is to fence in its meaning, to say where it ends and where it does not. The verb entered French in the 13th century as a scholarly term and kept its precise, intellectual flavor. From the same ~fīnis~ family French inherited a wide harvest of words, among them ~fin~, ~finir~, ~final~, ~définition~, ~définitif~, ~indéfini~, and ~confiner~ — all turning, in one way or another, on the idea of a border or an end.
en.défiscaliser: Formed in French from ~fiscaliser~ with the reversing prefix ~dé-~. The base ~fiscaliser~ is built on the adjective ~fiscal~ and the suffix ~-iser~, and it means to subject to taxation. ~Fiscal~ was borrowed from Latin ~fiscālis~ (“relating to the fisc”). The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and here it undoes the base. So ~défiscaliser~ means to reduce or remove the taxation on something, typically an investment or an income.
en.déflagrer:
From Latin ~deflagrare~ (“to burn down, to be consumed by fire”), which French Wiktionary gives as the source. The Latin verb is formed from ~dē-~ (“down, completely”) and ~flagrare~ (“to blaze, to burn”). English took the same Latin word as ~deflagrate~, so the two languages share both the verb and its learned shape.

In modern French, ~déflagrer~ is a technical verb for a substance that burns very fast with a flame, without the supersonic shock of a true detonation. The noun ~déflagration~ is much commoner and has spread to mean any violent explosion. The root ~flagrare~ lies behind other French words. ~Flagrant~ comes from the Latin participle ~flagrans~ (“blazing”), and its old sense survives in ~flagrant délit~, a crime caught in the act, as if still burning. The learned ~conflagration~ comes from the same family.
en.défleurir: Formed from ~fleurir~ (“to bloom”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which marks reversal: to lose or shed blossoms. The base verb comes from Latin ~florire~, a Vulgar Latin reshaping of ~florere~ (“to bloom”), from ~flos~ (“flower”), itself from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰleh₃-~ (“to bloom”). The same root gives English ~bloom~ and ~blossom~ on the Germanic side. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.déflorer:
~Déflorer~ comes from Latin, though the sources frame it in two ways. French Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~dēflōrāre~, while English Wiktionary reads it as French ~dé-~ + ~fleur~ (“flower”) + ~-er~, reinforced by the Late Latin verb. The Latin verb is built from ~dē-~ (“off, away”) and ~flōs~ (“flower”), so it means literally to strip something of its flowers. The French form shows the same parts, which is why the two accounts agree on the result.

Modern ~déflorer~ has two main uses: the literal and formal one, to deprive a girl or woman of her virginity, and the figurative one, to spoil something by robbing it of its freshness. Its relatives are the words built on ~flōs~, which French inherited as ~fleur~ and borrowed in learned form as ~flore~ and ~floral~, with ~fleurir~ coming from the related Latin verb ~flōrēre~. English ~deflower~ carries both senses too.
en.défléchir: Formed from ~fléchir~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which adds the idea of bending away: ~défléchir~ is to deflect, to bend aside. The base is inherited from Old French ~flechir~, from Vulgar Latin *~flecticāre~, a frequentative of Latin ~flectere~ (“to bend”). The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). Learned relatives of the same Latin root include ~flexion~ and ~flexible~.
en.défolier:
Borrowed from Latin ~dēfoliāre~ (“to strip of leaves”), a verb formed from the prefix ~dē-~ (“off, away”), the noun ~folium~ (“leaf”) and the verbal ending ~-āre~. English Wiktionary gives this as the whole account, and French Wiktionary cites the same Latin verb. French took it as a learned verb, as did English ~defoliate~, so the two languages share a word that neither inherited.

The Latin noun ~folium~ is the source of a whole family of French words. ~Feuille~ is its inherited form, ~feuillage~ is a derivative of ~feuille~, and the learned words include ~folio~, ~foliole~ and ~exfolier~ (“to peel off in thin layers”). English draws ~foil~ and ~folio~ from the same source. ~Défolier~ is also close to the French verb ~défeuiller~ (“to strip of leaves”), which is built on ~feuille~ rather than on the Latin noun. In modern French ~défolier~ is a technical verb, used of removing the foliage of plants or trees, and ~défoliation~ is the noun.
en.défoncer: ~Défoncer~ is built on ~foncer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, according to English Wiktionary. French Wiktionary parses it a little differently, as ~dé-~ + ~fond~ + the verb ending ~-er~. Either way the root is ~fond~ (“bottom”), from Latin ~fundus~ (“bottom, foundation, estate”), which goes back to a Proto-Indo-European form *~bʰudʰmḗn~ and is cognate with English ~bottom~ and German ~Boden~. The prefix ~dé-~ commonly marks removal or reversal, which suits a verb about breaking or digging through the bottom of something. The family also includes ~enfoncer~ and ~foncer~ itself.
en.déforcer: Formed from ~force~ with the prefix ~dé-~, so the verb means to take away someone's strength or power. The noun ~force~ comes from Late Latin ~fortia~, a noun made from the neuter plural of Latin ~fortis~ (“strong”). The prefix ~dé-~ here marks removal or deprivation, undoing what the base provides.
en.déforester: Formed from ~forêt~, in its older form ~forest~, with the prefix ~dé-~ and the ending ~-er~: to strip an area of its forest. The verb thus reverses the idea of planting or covering with woods. French Wiktionary traces the base through Old and Middle French ~forest~, and the verb belongs to the family of ~forêt~, ~forestier~ and ~reforester~. It is a transparent French formation, closely parallel to English ~deforest~.
en.déformer: A learned borrowing from Latin ~dēformāre~ (“to disfigure, to misshape”), built from ~dē-~ (“away, down”) and ~formāre~ (“to shape”), which comes from ~forma~ (“shape”). Because French already had ~former~, the verb can also be read on the surface as ~dé-~ + ~former~, a literal “un-shaping.” That reading suits the meaning well: to ~déformer~ something is to pull it out of its proper shape, whether a piece of metal, a face, or, figuratively, a fact or a quotation. The same Latin noun gives ~forme~, ~formation~ and ~difforme~.
en.défouler: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ (reversal) and ~fouler~. The base descends from Old French ~foler~, from Vulgar Latin *~fullāre~ (“to trample, to full cloth”), from Latin ~fullō~ (“fuller”), the cloth-worker who cleaned and thickened cloth by pressing it. English ~fuller~ comes from the same Latin word. ~Fouler~ broadened to “to press down, to crush,” and ~défouler~ reverses that pressure: in the reflexive ~se défouler~ one lets off steam, releasing tension, and the transitive verb can mean to relieve someone of it.
en.défourailler: ~Défourailler~ is a slang verb made of the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ~fourailler~, and the French source glosses it as “to draw from the sheath”. The prefix reverses the base, so the idea is to take a weapon out of its holder, and in the same slang register the verb came to mean to pull out a gun. The base ~fourailler~ is not explained by the sources, so nothing more can be said of its history.
en.défourner: Formed from the noun ~four~ (“oven”) with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to take out of the oven.” It is the opposite of ~enfourner~, which puts something in. The noun ~four~ descends from Latin ~furnus~, and the same root survives in ~fourneau~, ~fournil~ and ~fournier~. English Wiktionary traces ~furnus~ further, to a Proto-Indo-European root for “warm, hot.”
en.défrayer: ~Défrayer~ is ~frayer~ with the prefix ~dé-~. French Wiktionary gives Old French ~frayer~ as “to pay the costs of,” and English Wiktionary calls ~frayer~ a rare verb derived from ~frais~ (“expenses”). The prefix marks removal, so ~défrayer~ means “to relieve someone of the expenses,” by paying them. English ~defray~ is a related form. The verb survives in the phrase ~défrayer la chronique~.
en.défraîchir: Formed in French from ~dé-~, ~fraîche~ (“fresh,” the feminine of ~frais~) and the second-conjugation ending ~-ir~, so “to take the freshness from.” The prefix ~dé-~ goes back through Old French ~des-~ to Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”) and here expresses removal. The ending ~-ir~, from Latin ~-ire~, typically builds verbs meaning “make or become” from adjectives, as in ~grandir~ from ~grand~. Only English Wiktionary gives an analysis of this verb.
en.défricher: ~Défricher~ is formed from ~friche~ (“fallow land, wasteland”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which expresses removal, and the ending ~-er~. To ~défricher~ is thus to take away a land's fallow state, to clear it for cultivation, and by extension to lay the groundwork of a subject. The origin of ~friche~ itself is uncertain. One proposal links it to Middle Dutch ~versch~ or ~virsch~ (“fresh, new”), related to ~frais~, for newly won land; another, attributed to Grimm, derives it from Latin ~frango~ (“to break”), as in breaking clods.
en.défriper: Formed in French from ~friper~ (“to crumple”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action of the base: ~défriper~ is “to uncrumple,” to smooth out what has been rumpled. The base ~friper~ goes back to Old French ~freper~, tied to the noun ~frepe~ (“rag, old clothes”), whose own origin is uncertain; a link to Late Latin ~falappa~ has been proposed but is not settled. The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
