The family of the base is better known than the verb: ~friperie~ (secondhand clothes), ~fripier~ and the participle ~fripé~ (“rumpled”).
en.défriser: Formed from ~friser~ (“to curl”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to take the curl out of hair. The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The origin of ~friser~ is uncertain. French Wiktionary proposes, with a “perhaps,” a link to ~frire~ (“to fry”), curled edges being the common image. English Wiktionary instead suggests a Germanic source, a form like Old Frisian ~frisle~ (“curly hair”), related to English ~frizz~. Either route fits the sense of curling hair.
en.défroisser: Formed from ~froisser~ (“to crumple”) and the prefix ~dé-~, which undoes the action: to smooth out creases, hence to iron. The base ~froisser~ reworks Old French ~fruisser~, from a Vulgar Latin verb reconstructed as *~frustiāre~ (“to break into pieces”), from Latin ~frustum~ (“piece, fragment”). The verb thus began as a word for smashing and softened into the gentler “to crease” of modern French, though the sources do not date the shift.
en.défroncer: Formed from ~froncer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to undo gathers, folds or pleats. The base comes from the noun ~fronce~, from Old French ~fronces~, and behind it from Frankish *~hrunkja~ (“wrinkle”). The Germanic family includes German ~Runzel~ and English ~ruck~. The prefix ~dé-~ descends from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). A frown and a gathered skirt are the same wrinkle, so ~défroncer~ smooths both.
en.défroquer: From ~froc~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which marks removal: literally, to strip someone of the ~froc~, the monk's habit. Today it is used only figuratively. The noun ~froc~ comes from Old French ~froc~ and Frankish *~hrokk~ (“robe, tunic”), from Proto-Germanic *~hrukkaz~. It is cognate with German ~Rock~ and Old English ~rocc~, and English ~frock~ belongs to the same family.
en.défruiter: Formed from ~fruit~ with the prefix ~dé-~, meaning to strip of fruit. ~Fruit~ comes from Latin ~frūctus~, a derivative of ~fruor~ (“to enjoy, to have the benefit of”), a noun that already covered the senses we know, including proceeds and produce. Middle French spelled it ~fruict~ in a Latinizing style. The prefix ~dé-~, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), expresses removal when attached to a noun.
en.déféquer:
Borrowed as a learned word from Latin ~dēfaecāre~ (“to purge of dregs, to clarify”), a verb made of ~dē-~ (“away from”) and ~faex~ (“dregs, lees”). The Latin noun ~faex~ has left descendants in French, notably ~fèces~, and in English, where ~feces~ and ~defecate~ are borrowed from the same Latin family.

In Latin, the verb applied to clearing a liquid, such as wine, of its sediment. French ~déféquer~ keeps that learned stamp and is now mostly a medical or formal term for emptying the bowels. Its relatives in French are ~fèces~ and ~défécation~. A modern speaker rarely senses the “dregs” inside the word, since the Latin noun ~faex~ never became an everyday French word.
en.déférer:
French ~déférer~ comes from Latin ~dēferre~, a compound of ~dē-~ (“down, away”) and ~ferre~ (“to carry, to bear”). The simple verb ~ferre~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰer-~ (“to carry”), the same root behind English ~bear~, German ~gebären~ and Greek ~phérein~. French borrowed ~dēferre~ as a learned verb rather than inheriting it through speech. English has taken the same Latin verb as ~defer~ in the sense of yielding to someone's wishes.

The Latin verb meant literally to carry down or carry away, and from there to bring something before someone: to report a matter, to hand over an honor, to lay a case before an authority. French kept two main uses. The legal one is to refer a person or a case to a court, as in ~déférer un accusé à la justice~. The courteous one is to yield to another's opinion or authority, ~déférer à l'avis de quelqu'un~, which gave the noun ~déférence~ (“deference, respect”) and the adjective ~déférent~. The root ~ferre~ is among the most productive in French vocabulary. It also gave ~référer~, ~conférer~, ~transférer~, ~préférer~, ~différer~ and ~offrir~, all rooted in the idea of carrying.
en.dégager:
Modern French ~dégager~ is built from the verb ~gager~ (“to pledge, to pawn”) with the privative prefix ~dé-~, which reverses an action. Its earliest attested form, ~desguagier~ (1174–76), meant quite literally “to redeem something pledged” — to recover from a pawnbroker the ~gage~ one had deposited as security. That noun ~gage~ was no Latin inheritance but a Frankish loan, *~waddi~ “pledge, deposit,” from Proto-Germanic *~wadi~ and ultimately the Proto-Indo-European root *~wedʰ-~ “to pledge, to redeem a pledge.” The same Germanic root surfaces in Dutch ~wedde~ “salary” and German ~Wette~ “a bet,” and, by a parallel borrowing into English through Norman French, in ~wage~. English ~wed~ descends from the same source: to marry was once to pledge oneself, the bridal vow being literally a pledge.

From the concrete medieval sense of buying back a pledge, ~dégager~ drifted toward abstraction. By around 1180 it could mean “to set free, to release,” and by the mid-thirteenth century “to clear away, to strip of a covering.” A pledge, once recovered, leaves one unencumbered — hence the modern senses of freeing, clearing, and emitting (a gas, a scent). The same Frankish family enriched French with ~gageure~ “a wager” and ~engager~ “to commit, to involve,” while ~dégagement~ names the very act of disengaging — the precise reversal of putting something in pledge.
en.dégainer: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ (removal) and ~gainer~, from the noun ~gaine~ (“sheath”) with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun comes through Middle French ~guaine~ and Old French ~guaïne~ from Latin ~vāgīna~ (“sheath, scabbard”), and is a doublet of the learned ~vagin~. Italian ~guaina~ and Spanish ~vaina~ are cognates. The initial ~g~ in place of Latin ~v~ is attributed to Germanic influence. ~Dégainer~ is to draw a weapon from its sheath, and by extension to pull out a tool or a phone quickly.
en.déganter: ~Déganter~ is formed from the noun ~gant~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ending ~-er~: to take the gloves off a hand. ~Gant~ comes from Old French ~guant~, attested in the ~Chanson de Roland~, from Frankish *~want~ (“mitten”), from Proto-Germanic *~wantuz~. Its cognates include Middle Dutch ~want~ and Italian ~guanto~ and Spanish ~guante~. The word first belonged to military vocabulary.
en.dégarnir: Formed from ~garnir~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base verb: to ~dégarnir~ is to strip away what ~garnir~ supplies. ~Garnir~ itself comes from Old French ~guarnir~ (“to protect oneself, arm up”), which English Wiktionary traces to Frankish *~warnijan~ (“to ward, take care of something”). That Germanic origin explains the initial ~g-~, since ~w-~ regularly became ~gu-~ and then ~g-~ in French, as in ~guerre~. The oldest senses of ~garnir~ were protecting, fortifying and equipping, which later softened into furnishing and adorning. So ~dégarnir~ describes emptying, stripping or thinning out something that had been fitted or furnished.
en.dégasoliner: A spelling variant of ~dégazoliner~, to which French Wiktionary sends the reader. Like it, the verb means to treat natural gas so as to remove its liquid part. It is formed with the prefix ~dé-~ (“removal”) on the same word family as ~gazole~, French for diesel oil, a respelling of English ~gas oil~ modeled on ~pétrole~. See ~dégazoliner~ for the details.
en.dégauchir: Formed from ~gauchir~ with the reversing prefix ~dé-~. In craft vocabulary it means to true up a surface, to plane out a warp, “to take the twist out of” a board. The base ~gauchir~ comes from Old French ~gauchir~ (also ~gauchier~). English Wiktionary traces it to Frankish and offers *~wenkijan~ and *~walkijan~ as proposed sources, so the exact Germanic form is uncertain. The change of an initial ~w~ to ~gu-~ or ~g-~ is the usual French treatment of Frankish words. The prefix ~dé-~ undoes the bending: what ~gauchir~ warps, ~dégauchir~ straightens.
en.dégazer: Formed from ~gaz~ (“gas”) with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~: to remove gas, as when a tanker vents its tanks. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and here marks removal. The noun ~gaz~ was coined in the seventeenth century by the Flemish chemist Van Helmont, from Greek ~khaos~. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~. French has a second, unrelated verb ~gazer~ built on ~gaze~ (“gauze”), but the sense here belongs to ~gaz~.
en.dégazoliner: Formed with the prefix ~dé-~ (“removal”) on the family of ~gazole~, which is a French respelling of English ~gas oil~ modeled on ~pétrole~. The verb is a technical term meaning to treat natural gas to remove its liquid part, the heavier hydrocarbons that condense out of it. The spelling ~dégasoliner~ is a variant.
en.dégazonner: Formed from the noun ~gazon~ (“turf, lawn”) with the prefix ~dé-~ (“removal”) and the ending ~-er~: to strip away the sod. The noun comes from Old French ~gason~ and ~wason~ (a form attested in 1213), from Frankish *~wasō~ (“turf, clod covered with grass”). German ~Wasen~ (“lawn”) is a cognate, and the Frankish word is also related to French ~vase~ (“mud”) and English ~ooze~.
en.dégeler: ~Dégeler~ is formed from ~geler~ with the prefix ~dé-~, here in its commonest function, reversing the action of the base verb: freezing becomes thawing. The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The base ~geler~ descends from Latin ~gelāre~ (“to freeze”), from ~gelu~ (“frost”). ~Dégeler~ is used for ice and soil, for defrosting food, and figuratively for easing a frozen situation or relationship.
en.dégermer: Formed from ~germer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here marks removal: to take the germ off or out. The base ~germer~ comes from Latin ~germināre~ (“to sprout, to bud”), the verb of ~germen~ (“sprout, seed”), and the same Latin noun gave ~germe~, which names an embryo or sprout and, by extension, a microbe. ~Dégermer~ therefore undoes what ~germer~ and ~germe~ describe, by stripping away the germ.
en.dégivrer: ~Dégivrer~ is formed from ~givrer~ (“to cover with frost”) and the reversing prefix ~dé-~, so it means to remove frost or ice. ~Givrer~ is built on ~givre~ (“frost, rime”), which appears in Old French as ~joivre~ in the fourteenth century. By one account, only proposed as possible, ~givre~ was borrowed through Franco-Provençal ~gevro~ from a Frankish word *~gibara~ (“drool”), related to German ~Geifer~.
en.déglacer: ~Déglacer~ is made from ~glacer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base verb: to remove ice from something. Its base ~glacer~ comes from Latin ~glaciāre~ (“to freeze”), formed on ~glaciēs~ (“ice”). In the kitchen ~déglacer~ has a specialized meaning, to deglaze a pan. The prefix ~dé-~ itself comes from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.déglinguer: The origin of ~déglinguer~ is uncertain. The usual proposal is that it is an alteration of the nautical term ~déclinquer~, meaning to take apart or dislocate a boat built with overlapping planks called ~clin~ (formerly ~clinc~). If that is right, the verb began as a shipwright's word for dismantling a hull and then widened to mean wrecking or knocking anything to pieces, which fits the modern slang sense of “to knacker” a machine.
en.dégluer: Formed from ~glu~ (“birdlime”) with the prefix ~dé-~ and the ending ~-er~: to free from birdlime, or to unstick. The noun ~glu~ comes from Old French and Late Latin ~glūtem~, from Latin ~glūten~ (“glue”). The prefix ~dé-~ goes back to Latin ~dis-~ and reverses the action.
en.déglutir:
French ~déglutir~ is borrowed from Latin ~degluttīre~ (“to swallow down”). By the standard analysis the Latin verb joins the prefix ~dē-~ (“down”) to ~gluttīre~ (“to swallow”). The French verb keeps both the form and the sense of its source: to swallow, to get food or drink down the throat. Italian ~deglutire~ is a parallel descendant of the same Latin verb.

The Latin root has a lively French family. ~Glouton~ descends from the related Latin noun ~gluttō~ (“glutton”), and ~engloutir~ (“to gobble up”) belongs to the same verb family. English has ~glutton~, borrowed through Old French from the same Latin noun. Closest to home is ~déglutition~, the noun for the act of swallowing, which keeps the Latin shape intact.
en.dégober: No dictionary states the formation of ~dégober~, but its form matches the prefix ~dé-~ added to ~gober~ (“to swallow”), the reverse of swallowing, just as ~dégorger~ is ~dé-~ plus ~gorger~. It is a term of oyster farming. Oysters ~dégobent~ when they disgorge, and oyster-growers make them do so by placing them in parks flushed by the tide. An 1849 text gives ~dégober~ as the way Norman fishermen say ~dégorger~, and an 1852 report to the Académie des sciences calls it the technical term. The base ~gober~ is borrowed from Gaulish *~gobbos~ (“beak, snout”), so the verb would carry a Celtic root.
en.dégobiller: ~Dégobiller~ is formed from ~gober~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and the suffix ~-iller~: to bring up again what was swallowed, to vomit. The base ~gober~ is a verb of swallowing whole, and it descends from Gaulish *~gobbos~ (“beak, snout”), so this slangy verb rests on one of the few words French kept from Gaulish. The Irish and Scottish Gaelic ~gob~ (“beak”) are related Celtic words.
en.dégoiser: Built on the stem of ~gosier~ (“throat”) with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. It was first used of birds, in the sense “to sing,” and French Wiktionary points to ~égosiller~ for comparison. That noun descends from Old French ~geuse~ and ~josier~, themselves from Late Latin ~geusiae~ (“sides of the throat”), attested in Marcellus in the fifth century and borrowed from Gaulish. Welsh ~gewai~ (“glutton”) is a possible cognate. Today the verb means to rattle off words, to speak volubly.
en.dégommer: ~Dégommer~ is built on ~gomme~ (“gum”) with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ending ~-er~. Another analysis reads it as ~dé-~ + ~gommer~. The prefix expresses removal, so the literal idea is “to take off the gum.” The noun ~gomme~ comes from Late Latin ~gumma~, from Latin ~gummi~, from Ancient Greek ~κόμμι~ (~kómmi~), which is in turn traced to Egyptian ~qmyt~ (“gum, resin”). French also uses the verb in the figurative senses “to unseat” or “to zap.”
en.dégonfler: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ~gonfler~, in the reversing sense “to undo swelling.” The base is inherited from Latin ~cōnflāre~ (~com-~ “together” + ~flāre~ “to blow”), with the initial ~c-~ becoming ~g-~ in French. The related Latin compounds ~sufflāre~ and ~inflāre~ gave ~souffler~ and ~enfler~. To ~dégonfler~ is to let the air out, and figuratively to lose one's nerve.
en.dégorger: Formed from ~gorger~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base; Middle French already had ~desgorger~. ~Gorger~ means “to fill the throat, to stuff”, from the noun ~gorge~ (“throat”), inherited from Old French and traced back to Late Latin ~gurga~. So ~dégorger~ means “to empty out the throat”, hence “to disgorge” and, of a stream or a pipe, “to spill into” or “to flow into” something else.
en.dégoter: The origin of ~dégoter~ is uncertain. French Wiktionary offers, with a hedge, a derivation from Angevin ~got~ (“hole”), the place for the ball in a game. If that is right, the verb belongs to a regional word rather than to Latin or Frankish. The modern verb means “to dig up” in the figurative sense of finding or turning up something.
en.dégotter: The origin is obscure. The TLFi first records the verb in 1694 as a game term, “to push one's ball toward the goal,” and cites an Anjou cry used before a shot. By 1740 it meant “to displace,” by 1757 “to dislodge from a post,” and in 1846 “to discover, to find,” in a slang glossary. The TLFi suggests a possible link with Angevin ~got~ (“hole for the ball in a game”). An older link to ~gal~ or ~gau~ (“pebble,” see ~galet~) is phonetically difficult. The spelling ~dégoter~ is a variant.
en.dégouliner: ~Dégouliner~ comes from Old French ~dégouler~ (“to pour out, to spill over”), of which it is an extended form. The Old French verb described liquid escaping freely from its container, whereas the modern verb has narrowed that idea to liquid running down in slow trickles or drips. It is a familiar, expressive word of everyday French.
en.dégoupiller: ~Dégoupiller~ (“to unpin”) is formed from ~goupille~ (“pin, peg”) with the prefix ~dé-~ and the ending ~-er~, so it means to remove the pin. Here ~dé-~ marks removal, as in ~dépanner~ or ~déplumer~, where the base is a noun. The noun ~goupille~ was originally the name of a female fox, from Old French ~golpille~, the feminine of ~golpil~. The technical sense may come from a resemblance to a fox's tail or from the cleverness of the device, but the sources only offer this as a possibility.
en.dégourdir: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~, the adjective ~gourd~ (“numb, stiff with cold”) and the verbal ending ~-ir~. The adjective comes from Latin ~gurdus~ by way of Old French. The prefix ~dé-~ here reverses a state, so ~dégourdir~ means “to take away the numbness”: to warm up stiff fingers or to stretch one's legs. By extension the verb is used of a person who is made less awkward and more lively, as in ~se dégourdir~. It belongs to the family of verbs in which ~dé-~ undoes a state expressed by an adjective.
en.dégoutter: Formed in French from ~goutter~ (“to drip”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which comes from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). Here the prefix does not undo the base: the verb simply means “to fall drop by drop, to drip.” The base ~goutter~ is itself made from the noun ~goutte~ plus the ending ~-er~. The noun came through Old French ~gote~ from Latin ~gutta~ (“drop”), and Middle French restored the second t to mirror the Latin spelling.
en.dégoûter: The sources disagree about the direction of derivation. English Wiktionary gives an Old French verb ~desgouster~ (“to put off one's appetite”), made of ~des-~ (“dis-,” undoing) and ~gouster~ (“to taste”), from Latin ~gustāre~ (“to taste”). It adds that ~dégoûter~ may rather be derived from the noun ~dégoût~, itself from ~goût~, and French Wiktionary takes that view. Each of the two words is in turn described as a deverbal of the other, so the order of birth stays uncertain. The older meaning, “to put off one's appetite,” still shows through in the modern sense “to disgust.”
en.dégrader:
From Late Latin ~degradāre~ (“to demote, strip of rank”), attested in French from 1174, built from ~de-~ (“down from”) + ~gradus~ (“step, rank, degree”). ~Gradus~ comes from ~gradī~ / ~gradior~ (“to step, walk”), from Proto-Italic *~graðus~, from Proto-Indo-European *~gʰredʰ-~ (“to walk, stride”). The root is cognate with English ~grade~, ~gradual~, and ~degree~ (itself ~de-~ + ~gradus~ via French ~degré~).

The literal sense is to make someone “step down” a rank — a ceremonial demotion, as a knight or officer was formally stripped of insignia. From this social ~dégrader~ the verb extended along a second axis to physical deterioration: a façade, a colour, an environment can ~se dégrader~, sliding step by step down toward ruin. Both senses share the picture of descending a graded scale. The same ~gradus~ root gives French ~grade~, ~degré~, ~graduel~, ~gradation~, ~progrès~ (“a stepping forward”), ~régresser~, and ~dégradé~ — the last a painter's and hairdresser's term for a smooth gradient, the very deterioration of one tone into the next made beautiful.
en.dégrafer: English Wiktionary analyzes this verb as ~dé-~ + ~grafer~. The prefix ~dé-~ reverses the action of the base, so ~dégrafer~ is “to unclasp, to unhook,” the undoing of fastening a clasp. The base ~grafer~ is an older verb for fastening with a clasp, and the sources give nothing further about its own origin.
en.dégraisser: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ (removal) and ~graisser~, which is the noun ~graisse~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is attested in Old French as ~craisse~, from Vulgar Latin *~crassia~, built on Latin ~crassus~ (“thick, fat”), which also gave French ~gras~. ~Dégraisser~ means to remove the fat or grease from something: to skim a broth, to clean a stained garment, or to trim a workforce, in the figurative sense of cutting excess.
en.dégravoyer: French Wiktionary derives it from ~dégrever~ with the suffix ~-oyer~, and refers the reader to ~grève~, ~gravats~ and ~gravois~, the family of gravel and rubble. The base ~dégrever~ is ~dé-~ + ~grever~, from Latin ~gravāre~ (“to load”), so it means to unburden. The sense here, to lay bare, is a technical one that the sources do not trace further. The ending ~-oyer~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~ and often marks a repeated or continuing action.
en.dégrever: Formed from ~grever~ and the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to unburden. The base comes from Old French ~grever~, which English Wiktionary calls a borrowing from Latin ~gravāre~ (“to load”), with some influence from a Vulgar Latin adjective *~grevis~, from Latin ~gravis~ (“heavy”). French Wiktionary instead gives popular Latin ~gravare~ or ~grevare~. Either way the family is that of “heavy,” and ~aggraver~ belongs to it. By the seventeenth century ~grever~ survived mainly for taxes weighing on a country, so ~dégrever~ means to relieve of a tax burden.
en.dégringoler:
From Middle French ~desgringueler~ (“to throw into confusion”, attested in 1595), itself built from the prefix ~dé-~ and Old French ~gringoller~ (“to tumble down”). Both Wiktionaries agree that ~gringoller~ is of Germanic origin, borrowed from Middle Dutch ~cringelen~ (“to turn in circles”). That verb is a frequentative of ~kringen~ (“to roll”) and rests on ~kring~ (“circle”), from Old Dutch *~kring~ and Proto-Germanic *~kringaz~.

The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The Middle French verb meant “to throw into confusion”, whereas modern ~dégringoler~ means “to fall down”. English Wiktionary explains the image as that of someone tumbling in successive circles, which fits a Dutch root meaning “circle”; this is an explanation of the sense, not a documented sequence of uses. French Wiktionary also lists the Picard verbs ~déringoler~ and ~dégribouler~ as related forms.
en.dégripper: Formed from ~gripper~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to free what has jammed. The base comes, by English Wiktionary's account, from Frankish *~grīpan~ through Old French, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʰreyb-~ (“to grab”), and is a doublet of ~griffer~. French Wiktionary agrees on a Germanic source and compares English ~grip~. The original sense of ~gripper~ was to seize; the modern one is of a mechanism that seizes up, so ~dégripper~ means to unblock it.
en.dégriser: Formed from ~griser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to undo what ~griser~ did, so to sober up, or to bring someone back down from elation. ~Griser~ comes from the adjective ~gris~ with the verb ending ~-er~, first meaning “to make grey” and later “to intoxicate, to elate.” ~Gris~ is from Frankish *~grīs~ and Proto-Germanic *~grīsaz~ (“grey”), related to Dutch ~grijs~ and German ~greis~ (“hoary”). The prefix ~dé-~ descends from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.dégrosser: A variant of ~dégrossir~, the usual verb. French Wiktionary gives no other history for ~dégrosser~, which shows the same prefix ~dé-~ (“removal”) and the same base meaning “coarse, thick.” The gloss “to reduce, to draw smaller” fits the idea of taking away bulk, as in rough-hewing a piece of work before the finer stage.
en.dégrossir: ~Dégrossir~ is formed from ~grossir~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses or removes. The base ~grossir~ is made from the adjective ~gros~ (“big, thick”), from Late Latin ~grossus~ (“thick”), plus the ending ~-ir~, meaning “to become big.” The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). ~Dégrossir~ is used for working a rough block or draft into a first shape, and figuratively for smoothing a person's manners.
en.dégrouiller: This verb is formed from ~grouiller~ with the prefix ~dé-~. Its base has a tangled history: it may come from Middle Dutch ~grollen~ (“to rumble, grumble”) through Old French, or, by another account, be a merger of two Old French verbs. Middle French ~grouiller~ already covered “to stir, to hasten”, and the sense of hurrying survives in this verb, mostly in the reflexive form ~se dégrouiller~, “to get a move on”. Here the prefix does not simply reverse the base: it gives the sense of getting going, as in ~se démener~.
en.dégrouper: ~Dégrouper~ is formed from ~grouper~ with the reversing prefix ~dé-~, so it means to undo a grouping, to separate. ~Grouper~ comes from the noun ~groupe~, borrowed in the seventeenth century from Italian ~gruppo~ (“knot, cluster”), which came from a Germanic source reconstructed as *~kruppaz~ (“rounded mass”). That Germanic word also lies behind English ~crop~ and German ~Kropf~.
en.dégréer: ~Dégréer~ is formed from ~gréer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to strip a ship of its rigging. The base ~gréer~ comes from Old French ~agreier~ (“to equip”), borrowed from Old Norse ~greiða~ (“to make ready, to equip”), a word related to English ~ready~. The French verb stayed tied to the sea: ~gréer~ means to fit a vessel with masts, yards, sails and ropes, and ~dégréer~ takes all of this away again.
en.déguerpir:
~Déguerpir~ comes through Middle French ~déguerpir~ and ~deswerpir~ (“to leave”) from Old French ~deguerpir~ (“to abandon”), which joins ~de-~ to ~guerpir~ (“to give up, abandon”). ~Guerpir~ is of Germanic origin, from Frankish *~wurpijan~ (“to throw, cast off”), from Proto-Germanic *~werpaną~ (“to throw”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~werb-~ (“to turn, twist”). Occitan ~degurpir~ is a close parallel.

The Germanic kin of the Frankish verb include Old High German ~werfan~ and Old English ~weorpan~ (“to throw, cast, cast away”), as well as German ~werfen~ and English ~warp~. The original idea was therefore to throw away what one held, and ~guerpir~ meant to give up or abandon. Germanic w- regularly became gu- in Old French, as in ~guerre~ (“war”) and ~garder~. ~Déguerpir~ moved from “abandon” to leaving a place, usually in haste: modern ~déguerpir~ means to clear out, to skedaddle.
en.dégueulasser: ~Dégueulasser~ is formed from the adjective ~dégueulasse~ (“disgusting”) and the verbal ending ~-er~: to make something dirty or disgusting. The adjective is itself built from the verb ~dégueuler~ (“to vomit”) with the suffix ~-asse~, a slangy, pejorative ending. The verb is therefore a layered coinage, from a verb to an adjective and back to a verb, and belongs to very informal French.
en.dégueuler: ~Dégueuler~ is a parasynthetic verb: the prefix ~dé-~ and the ending ~-er~ were added together to the noun ~gueule~ (“mouth, maw”). The prefix marks removal, so the verb means to send something out through the mouth, as in ~dégorger~ (“to disgorge”). ~Gueule~ comes from Old French ~gole~, from Latin ~gula~ (“gullet”), and is a doublet of ~goulet~. The verb is an informal word for vomiting.
en.déguiser: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~, the noun ~guise~ (“manner, way”) and the verb ending ~-er~, via Old French ~desguiser~. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~, and here it points toward changing one's usual manner. ~Guise~ comes from Old French ~guise~ and Frankish *~wīsa~, from Proto-Germanic *~wīsǭ~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~weyd-~ (“to see”). English ~wise~ (as in ~likewise~) and German ~Weise~ are cognates. Hence ~déguiser~ originally means “to alter one's way of appearing,” and later “to disguise.”
en.dégurgiter: ~Dégurgiter~ is formed from ~ingurgiter~ (“to swallow”) by swapping the prefix ~in-~, which means “into,” for ~dé-~, which expresses the opposite. Where ~ingurgiter~ sends something down the throat, ~dégurgiter~ brings it back up, hence “to regurgitate.” The base ~ingurgiter~ comes from Latin ~ingurgitāre~, built on ~gurges~ (“whirlpool, gullet”), which is standard background. The coinage is thus a playful mirror of its base, and it is far rarer than the learned ~régurgiter~, which covers the same ground.
en.déguster:
French ~déguster~ comes from Latin ~degustare~ (“to taste, to sample”), formed from the prefix ~de-~ and ~gustare~ (“to taste”), itself from ~gustus~ (“a tasting, a taste”). That noun descends from Proto-Italic *~gustus~ and Proto-Indo-European *~ǵéwstus~ (“taste”), from the root *~ǵews-~ (“to taste, to choose”). The same root produced English ~choose~ and ~gusto~, German ~kiesen~ (“to choose”), and, through Latin, Spanish ~gustar~ and Italian ~gustare~. The everyday French noun ~goût~ (“taste”) is the worn-down heir of ~gustus~.

The Indo-European root joined tasting and choosing, as if to taste were already to judge — the same instinct preserved in English ~gusto~, “hearty enjoyment.” French ~déguster~ kept the careful, appreciative side of that idea: not merely to eat but to savor attentively, to assess a wine or a dish. From the family come ~goût~, ~goûter~, ~dégustation~, ~ragoût~ (“stew,” literally something that restores the appetite), and ~dégoût~ (“disgust”), where the prefix flips savor into its opposite. A ~dégustateur~ is a professional taster whose whole craft is built on this Latin verb.
en.dégénérer:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~dēgenerāre~ (“to depart from one's kind, to fall below one's ancestors”), formed from ~dē-~ (“away from”) and ~genus~ (“birth, race, kind”). Latin ~genus~ comes from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ǵenh₁-~ (“to beget”), the same root that gave English ~kin~. English ~degenerate~ is borrowed from the Latin verb, and the Latin noun ~genus~ is the source of French ~genre~ and of the English word ~genus~ in biology.

The Latin idea was literally one of lineage: a person or animal who ~degenerates~ no longer matches the quality of the ancestors. French kept this moral and biological sense, as when a breed or a family ~dégénère~, and then extended it to decline in general. In medicine, a tissue or a disease ~dégénère~ when it worsens, and the adjective ~dégénératif~ describes such conditions. In everyday speech, a situation or a discussion ~dégénère~ when it turns bad, often with ~en~, as in ~dégénérer en bagarre~ (“to degenerate into a brawl”). The same Latin root appears in ~génération~ and ~général~, a reminder that “kind” and “begetting” share a source.
en.déhaler: Formed from ~haler~ with the prefix ~dé-~, a nautical verb meaning to tow a ship out of a berth or to warp it along with ropes. The base ~haler~ comes from Old French ~haler~ (“to pull”), borrowed from Frankish *~halōn~ (“to haul, drag, fetch”). English ~haul~ and German ~holen~ are cognates. French Wiktionary also records a separate line, a Germanic cry *~hara~ that gave Old French ~haro~ and later ~haler~ in the sense of urging on with shouts. The sources do not say whether the two strands merged.
en.déhancher: Formed from ~hanche~ (“hip”) with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, the verb means to sway the hips. ~Hanche~ is not Latin: it comes from Old French, from Proto-Germanic *~hanka~, and gave Italian and Spanish ~anca~ as well as English ~haunch~. It replaced Latin ~coxa~, which survives in French as ~cuisse~ (“thigh”). ~Dé-~ goes back to Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and ~-er~ to the Latin first-conjugation ending ~-are~.
en.déharnacher: Formed from ~harnacher~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to take the harness off. ~Dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The base ~harnacher~ derives from ~harnais~, the gear of a horse. An older verb, ~harnescier~ (“to put the harness on a horse”), is attested in the thirteenth century, so the base is old in French rather than a recent coinage.
en.déhotter: The Dictionnaire des régionalismes de France derives ~déhotter~ from Old French ~hot~ (“obstacle”), with the prefix ~dé-~, which undoes the base. The first sense is to get out of a place where one is bogged down, and figuratively to get oneself out of a fix. The word arose in the north-east (Champagne, the Ardennes, the Meuse) and is attested in 1611 in Cotgrave's dictionary. Its antonym ~enhotter~ is attested in the same source, and the adjective ~enhoté~ (“hampered in one's movements”) appears in 1807. Slang then took the verb up in the early twentieth century in the senses “to leave quickly” and “to chase off.”
en.déhouiller: Formed from ~houille~ (“coal”) with the prefix ~dé-~ and a verbal ending, hence “to remove coal from.” ~Houille~ is probably borrowed from Old Walloon (Liégeois) ~hulhes~, itself probably from Frankish *~hukila~ (“pile, mound”). The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and marks removal here.
en.déifier:
From Latin ~deificāre~ (“to make a god”), from ~deus~ (“god”) and the verbal element ~-ficāre~, a combining form of ~facere~ (“to make”). French Wiktionary notes that the related Latin adjective ~deificus~ could also mean “made by God.” The ~dé-~ at the start is therefore not the French prefix of reversal but the stem of ~deus~, so ~déifier~ is not “un-” anything. It means to raise someone or something to the rank of a god.

The Latin noun ~deus~ gave French ~dieu~ by the inherited route, and its adjective ~dīvīnus~ gave ~divin~. The learned vocabulary closest to ~déifier~ includes ~déité~ and ~déification~, and English ~deify~ comes from the same Latin verb. The ending ~-ficāre~ turned up in many French verbs in ~-fier~, such as ~sanctifier~ and ~glorifier~, which likewise mean “to make holy” or “to make glorious.” In ~déifier~ the model is the same: to deify is to make divine, and so the verb is used both of pagan apotheosis and, figuratively, of excessive admiration.
en.déjanter: Formed from ~dé-~, the noun ~jante~ (“wheel rim”) and the verb ending ~-er~. The original transitive sense was technical: to remove the rims, the wooden circles forming the edge of a wheel. That sense fell out of use, and the verb was formed afresh in 1945 in cycling for a tyre that comes off its rim. The informal sense “to go crazy” is a figurative extension of “to come off the rim.” The noun ~jante~ is inherited from Old French, from a Vulgar Latin *~gambita~ or *~cambita~, borrowed from Gaulish *~cambitā~, a derivative of Proto-Celtic *~kambos~ (“curved”).
en.déjauger: Formed from ~jauge~ and the prefix ~dé-~, with the verb ending. ~Jauge~ is a noun, not a verb: it comes from Old French ~jauge~ (“gauging rod”), from Frankish *~galgā~ (“measuring rod, pole”), related to Old English ~ġealga~ (“gallows”). A boat's draft was measured by its ~jauge~, its depth in the water, so ~déjauger~ describes a hull that lifts out of the water and planes, ceasing to sink to its gauged depth.
en.déjeter: Formed from ~jeter~ with the prefix ~dé-~, in the sense of throwing out of true: to warp or twist. French Wiktionary points to the Latin verbs ~dejectare~ and ~dejicere~ as parallels. The base ~jeter~ comes from Old French ~jeter~, from Vulgar Latin *~jectāre~, from Latin ~jactāre~ (“to fling repeatedly”), the frequentative of ~jacere~ (“to throw”). Italian ~gettare~ is a cognate.
en.déjeuner: The origin is explained in two ways. One account derives it from Old French ~desjeüner~, formed from ~jeûner~ (“to fast”) with the prefix ~des-~, literally “to stop fasting.” The other starts from Late Latin ~ieiūnāre~ and a Vulgar Latin *~disieiūnāre~. French Wiktionary gives the sequence ~disjejunare~, then *~disjunare~, then ~desjuner~ (attested 1606), ~desjeuner~ (1694) and, from 1798, ~déjeuner~. The root is Latin ~ieiūnus~ (“fasting, hungry”). ~Déjeuner~ was originally the first meal of the day, the one that breaks the fast, as in Spanish ~desayunar~ and English ~breakfast~. The same Latin verb is also the ancestor of ~dîner~, so the two are doublets.
en.déjouer: Formed in French from ~dé-~ and ~jouer~ (“to play”). The prefix marks reversal or negation: to ~déjouer~ a plan is to counter what another has played, whence “to foil, to thwart.” The base ~jouer~ comes from Old French ~joer~, from Latin ~iocāre~ (“to joke”), from ~iocus~ (“joke, game”), which also gave English ~joke~. Latin ~iocāre~ broadened from jesting to all play and displaced the classical verb ~lūdere~ as the everyday word for playing.
en.déjucher: Formed from ~jucher~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to leave the perch. The base ~jucher~ (“to perch”) comes from Old French ~juchier~ or ~joquier~, probably formed on the noun ~juc~ or ~joc~, a roost for hens. So ~déjucher~ means to come down from the roost, said of birds and, jokingly, of people who had been sitting high up.
en.déjuger: Formed in French from ~juger~ (“to judge”) and the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action of its base. ~Déjuger~ is to undo a judgment already given. The base ~juger~ comes from Latin ~jūdicāre~ (“to judge, to pass sentence”), a compound of ~jūs~ (“law, right”) and ~dīcere~ (“to say”), so to judge was, etymologically, to “speak the law.” Italian ~giudicare~ and Spanish ~juzgar~ are its sister forms, and English ~judge~ reached us through Old French.
en.délabialiser: Formed from ~labialiser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the base: to ~délabialiser~ a sound is to strip it of its lip articulation, such as rounding. The base ~labialiser~ was built on the adjective ~labiale~ and the suffix ~-iser~ (from Late Latin ~-izāre~), and ~labiale~ comes from Latin ~labium~ (“lip”). The prefix ~dé-~ itself descends from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and it is still fully productive for coining verbs of undoing in technical vocabularies like this one.
en.délabrer:
~Délabrer~ (“to ruin, to leave in a state of decay”) is inherited from Middle French ~délabrer~ and its variant ~deslabrer~, and its origin is not fully settled. French Wiktionary explains it as a reshaping of *~délabeler~ (“to fall to rags”), the two ~l~ sounds having been dissimilated, from ~label~. English Wiktionary agrees on ~dé-~ plus a derivative of ~label~ or ~lambel~ (“strip”), but adds that it may come instead from Frankish *~lappiʀu~.

On either route the root is a Frankish word, *~lappā~ (“cloth, rag, lobe”), which English Wiktionary traces to a Proto-Indo-European root *~leb-~ (“blade”). Its Germanic cousins are Old High German ~lappa~ (“corner of clothing, flap”) and Old English ~læppa~ (“skirt of a garment, piece, lobe”), the source of English ~lap~ and ~lappet~. The image behind ~délabrer~ is thus of something torn into hanging strips. The modern verb applies it to buildings, health and fortunes, and it is most often met as the participle ~délabré~.
en.délabyrinther: Formed from ~labyrinthe~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here expresses removal: to ~délabyrinther~ is to take the maze out of something, that is, to clarify or simplify it. The base noun ~labyrinthe~ comes from Latin ~labyrinthus~ (“a building from which it is hard to find the way out”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~labúrinthos~ (“labyrinth,” also “fisherman's trap”). The prefix is attached to a noun, not to a verb, so there is no simple verb ~labyrinther~ for it to undo.
en.délacer:
From Old French ~deslacer~ or ~deslacier~, which corresponds to modern French ~dé-~ + ~lacer~, the prefix marking the reversal of an action: to undo what ~lacer~ did. The prefix ~dé-~ goes back to Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The base verb ~lacer~ (“to fasten with a cord”) comes from ~lacs~ (“cord, noose”), which derives from Latin ~laqueus~ (“noose, snare”). English took the same Old French word as ~lace~, and Spanish ~lazo~, the source of English ~lasso~, comes from the same Latin noun.

The Old French spelling shows how the prefix evolved: the ~s~ of ~des-~ fell silent in the Middle Ages, and modern spelling replaced it with the acute accent of ~dé-~, as in ~déchirer~ or ~défaire~. The verb is used for loosening a shoe, a corset or a bodice, and it sits in a family of cord words: ~lacet~ (“shoelace”), ~enlacer~ (“to entwine”), ~entrelacer~ (“to interlace”) and ~lacis~ (“network”). Its mirror image ~lacer~ and its opposite ~délacer~ thus pair like ~nouer~ and ~dénouer~: a tied cord and the gesture that frees it.
en.délainer: Formed from ~laine~ (“wool”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which here expresses removal: to strip the wool from a sheepskin. ~Laine~ comes from Latin ~lana~, itself from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂wl̥h₁neh₂~, which also gave English ~wool~, German ~Wolle~ and Ancient Greek ~lênos~.
en.délaisser: Formed in French from ~laisser~ with the prefix ~dé-~. The base descends from Latin ~laxāre~ (“to loosen, to let go”), built on ~laxus~ (“slack”), the root that also gave English ~lax~ and ~slack~; Old French ~laissier~ already meant “to leave, to allow, to abandon.” Here ~dé-~ does not simply undo ~laisser~. It adds the idea of leaving away from oneself, so that ~délaisser~ means “to forsake, to abandon, to neglect,” a heavier act than merely leaving something behind.
en.délaiter: Formed from the noun ~lait~ (“milk”) with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ending ~-er~; Littré analyzes it simply as ~dé-~ plus ~lait~. The prefix marks removal. Two trades use the verb: in butter-making, it means to remove the buttermilk from the churn once the butter has formed, and in oyster farming it is said of an oyster that loses its milk.
en.délarder: Formed from ~larder~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which marks removal. The base ~larder~ means to stud meat with strips of fat, and comes from ~lard~, inherited from Old French and ultimately from Latin ~lārdum~ (“bacon fat”). ~Délarder~ takes the idea of cutting away and applies it to trades such as masonry and carpentry, where it means to splay, that is, to cut an edge at a slant.
en.délasser: Formed from ~lasser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the base: to take away weariness. The base ~lasser~ is inherited from Latin ~lassāre~ (“to tire”), built on the adjective ~lassus~ (“tired”). So ~délasser~ means to relieve someone of fatigue, to refresh or relax, and its pronominal form ~se délasser~ is to unwind. It is a close relative of ~lassitude~ and ~inlassable~, and its adjective ancestor also appears in ~hélas~.
en.délaver: Formed from ~laver~ (“to wash”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which here adds the idea of washing something out or away: to soak, to dilute, to fade a color by washing. The base ~laver~ comes from Latin ~lavāre~ (“to wash, to bathe”), preserved in Italian ~lavare~ and Spanish and Portuguese ~lavar~. The past participle ~délavé~ is the common form today, as in faded jeans or a pale, watery sky.
en.délayer:
The origin of ~délayer~ is uncertain. The account that both Wiktionaries offer, with a “perhaps,” starts from Latin ~dēliquāre~ (“to decant, to pour from one vessel to another, to clarify”). English Wiktionary adds an intermediate Vulgar Latin form, *~delicāre~. Both add the influence of the Old French verb ~delaier~ (see ~délai~), which English Wiktionary presents as a different, unrelated word acting only phonetically.

Littré, quoted by French Wiktionary, was more categorical and proposed a rival origin. For him ~délayer~ comes from Latin ~dilatare~ (“to spread out, lengthen”), like ~délai~, because to dilute a mixture you stretch it with a liquid. Old French ~delaier~ meant “to cause a delay” and, in his view, came from the same ~dilatare~; he noted that the Berry dialect keeps ~dilayer~ for “to delay.” He added that the usual Old French word for diluting was ~allaier~, built the same way with the preposition ~à~. Both accounts are proposals, and neither is settled.
en.délecter: ~Délecter~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~dēlectāre~ (“to attract, to lure, to delight”). The Latin verb is usually analyzed as an intensive form of ~dēlicere~, built on ~dē-~ and ~lacere~ (“to lure”), which makes it a relative of French ~allécher~. Spanish ~deleitar~ and English ~delectable~ and ~delight~ come from the same Latin source. In modern French the verb is used mostly in the reflexive, ~se délecter~, “to take great pleasure” in something. The derived nouns and adjectives keep the Latin shape: ~délectation~ and ~délectable~. A close but separate relative is ~délice~, which comes from the Latin noun ~dēlicium~.
en.délester: Formed in French from ~lester~ with the reversing prefix ~dé-~. The base ~lester~ is ~lest~ (“ballast”) plus the verb ending ~-er~, “to load with ballast.” The noun ~lest~ is Germanic, traced to Dutch or Old Dutch ~last~ (“weight”). The prefix ~dé-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), undoes the loading. ~Délester~ means to jettison ballast, as from a ship or balloon, and by extension to relieve something of a burden, as when traffic is rerouted.
en.délibérer:
Borrowed from Latin ~dēlīberāre~ (“to weigh, to ponder”), which is generally analyzed as ~dē-~ plus ~lībrāre~ (“to weigh”), from ~lībra~ (“scale, balance”). Deliberating was thus, in the image, weighing a question on a pair of scales. Italian ~deliberare~, Spanish ~deliberar~ and English ~deliberate~ are cognates, all learned descendants of the same Latin verb. The Latin noun ~lībra~ also gave French ~livre~ (the unit of weight, not the book) and, with ~aequus~ (“equal”), ~équilibre~. The Latin source also gave the English zodiac sign ~Libra~.

The French verb kept the idea of careful weighing, first in the mind of one person, then in councils, juries and assemblies, where ~délibérer~ means to discuss before deciding. In law, the court ~délibère~ out of the public eye before giving its judgment, and a case held back for decision is said to be ~en délibéré~. Related words are ~délibération~, ~délibéré~ (“deliberate, considered”) and ~délibérément~. One trap deserves a warning: ~délibérer~ is unrelated to ~libérer~ (“to free”), which comes from Latin ~līberāre~ and ~līber~ (“free”), so the two share spelling but not ancestry.
en.délier: ~Délier~ is ~lier~ (“to bind”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to untie. Historically it is inherited from Old French ~deslier~, from Vulgar Latin ~disligāre~ (attested in the Reichenau Glossary), itself ~dis-~ (“apart”) + ~ligāre~ (“to tie”). Related verbs include Spanish ~desliar~, Portuguese ~desligar~ and Italian ~slegare~. The sense extended from untying a rope to releasing someone from an obligation or a promise.
en.délignifier: Formed from ~lignifier~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to remove the lignin, the woody substance, from plant matter. ~Lignifier~ is from Latin ~lignum~ (“wood”) and the suffix ~-fier~, from Latin ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”), so “to make into wood”. ~Dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.délimiter:
French took ~délimiter~ from Latin ~dēlīmitāre~ (“to mark out the boundaries of”). The Latin verb joined the prefix ~dē-~ (“completely, off”) to ~līmitāre~ (“to bound, to set limits to”), itself a verb built on the noun ~līmes~, genitive ~līmitis~ (“boundary, path between fields, frontier”). Modern French can still analyze it as ~dé-~ + ~limiter~, but the verb arrived already formed from Latin. Italian ~delimitare~ and Spanish ~delimitar~ have the same shape, and English ~delimit~ came the same learned route.

In Roman usage ~līmes~ was first the strip of ground left between two fields, then the boundary line of a property, and finally the fortified frontier of the empire. ~Délimiter~ keeps that concrete picture: to trace the border of a territory, a field or a zone. French then stretched it to abstract borders, such as delimiting a subject, a role or a responsibility. The family is large: ~limite~ (borrowed from ~līmes~), ~limiter~, ~illimité~ and ~limitrophe~ (“bordering”) all belong to it.
en.délinéamenter: Formed from the noun ~délinéament~ and the ending ~-er~, meaning to outline or delineate. The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin ~delineamentum~, itself from ~delineare~ (“to sketch out”), the verb that also lies behind ~délinéation~. The ending ~-er~ comes from the Latin infinitive ending ~-are~.
en.délinéer: Borrowed from Latin ~dēlīneāre~ (“to sketch, to outline”). The Latin verb is a compound of ~dē-~ (“down, completely”) and ~līneāre~ (“to draw a line”), built on ~līnea~ (“line”). In French it is a learned, rare word meaning to trace the outline of something. The Latin noun ~līnea~ itself began as “linen thread,” a derivative of ~līnum~ (“flax”), since a taut cord was the ancient tool for drawing a straight line. The word ~līnea~ gave French ~ligne~, by inheritance. Learned borrowings from the same Latin family include ~linéaire~ and ~linéament~ (“feature, outline”). French also formed ~aligner~ and ~lignée~ on ~ligne~. English ~delineate~ is the same Latin verb borrowed independently, and it is far more common than its French cousin.
en.délirer:
~Délirer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~dēlīrāre~ (“to be crazy, to rave”). French Wiktionary derives the Latin verb from ~līra~ (“furrow”), with the prefix ~dē-~ (“away from”). The verb is therefore built on a picture from the plough: to ~dēlīrāre~ was, literally, to step out of the furrow, to wander off the straight line.

French Wiktionary invites a comparison with ~dérailler~ for both sense and construction. That verb, built on ~rail~, uses the same figure of leaving the track, and also means “to talk nonsense”. In modern French ~délirer~ covers the medical sense of being in a state of delirium, from fever or mental illness, and the looser sense of talking wildly or getting carried away. The noun ~délire~ and the adjective ~délirant~ belong to the same family, and English ~delirium~ and ~delirious~ come from the same Latin source. The learned borrowing kept the Latin image intact, even though few speakers see a field in it today.
en.déliter: Formed from ~liter~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the base: to undo what was laid in layers, so a stone or a slate splits and crumbles along its beds. The base ~liter~ has two accounts in French Wiktionary and the sources do not choose between them. One derives it from ~lit~ (“bed,” from Latin ~lectus~), which would suit laying things in layers. The other derives it from ~liste~ and recalls Old French ~lister~ (“to make the selvage of a cloth”).
en.délivrer:
Attested from the 11th century, from Late Latin ~dēlīberāre~ (“to set free”), built on ~līberāre~ (“to set at liberty”), itself from the adjective ~līber~ (“free”). ~Līber~ descends from Proto-Italic *~louðeros~ and Proto-Indo-European *~h₁lewdʰeros~ (“free,” originally “belonging to the people”), making it a distant cognate of Greek ~eleútheros~ (“free”) and German ~Leute~ (“people”).

Note that this Late Latin ~dēlīberāre~ (“to free”) is a different word from Classical Latin ~dēlīberāre~ (“to weigh, deliberate”), which gave French ~délibérer~ — the two are etymological twins that diverged. ~Délivrer~ kept the sense of releasing: freeing a captive, relieving someone of a burden, and, in the obstetric sense, delivering a mother of her child. The “handing over” sense of English ~deliver~ developed in the parallel Old French chain and survives in French ~livrer~ (“to hand over, deliver goods”) and the noun ~livraison~. From the root ~līber~ French draws ~liberté~, ~libérer~, ~libéral~, and ~délivrance~ — the whole vocabulary of freedom radiating from a single Latin adjective meaning simply “free.”
en.délocaliser: Built on ~localiser~ (“to fix in a place”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the idea. French Wiktionary instead parses it as ~dé-~ + ~local~ + ~-iser~, the same pieces in a different order. The adjective ~local~ is a learned borrowing from Late Latin ~locālis~, from Latin ~locus~ (“place”), and ~-iser~ is the suffix that makes verbs meaning “to render” or “to turn into”. So ~délocaliser~ means literally to take something out of its place. In modern French it usually describes a company moving production or services abroad to cut costs, and more loosely detaching anything from its original location.
en.déloger: ~Déloger~ is formed from ~loger~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here expresses removal: to make someone leave the place where they are lodged. The base ~loger~ is a verb built on the noun ~loge~, from Old French ~loge~ (“hut, arbor, shelter”), borrowed from Frankish *~laubja~ (“shelter of foliage”). The same Frankish word, passed through Old French, gave English ~lodge~. The prefix ~dé-~ itself comes from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.délurer: ~Délurer~ is the modern form of ~déleurrer~ (“to undeceive”), made from the prefix ~dé-~, the noun ~leurre~ (“lure, decoy”) and the verb ending ~-er~. The prefix ~dé-~ removes what the base names, so the original sense was to free someone from a deception. Today the verb has shifted to mean making someone streetwise, sharpening their wits.
en.délustrer: Formed from ~lustre~ with the prefix ~dé-~, meaning to take away the shine. French has two nouns ~lustre~: one from Latin ~lustrum~ (a purifying sacrifice held every five years), the other, the one meaning “sheen,” borrowed from Italian ~lustro~ (“brilliance”), a noun built on the verb ~lustrare~. The second is the base here, since ~délustrer~ removes the gloss from a fabric or a surface.
en.déluter: Formed from ~luter~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to ~déluter~ is to remove the ~lut~ that sealed something. To ~luter~ is to coat or close a joint with ~lut~, a clay-like paste. The noun ~lut~ was borrowed from Latin ~lutum~ (“mud, clay”), so the verb carries a little Latin mud into the workshop and the laboratory.
en.déléaturer: Formed from the noun ~déléatur~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is a borrowing of Latin ~deleātur~ (“let it be deleted”), the word a proofreader writes in the margin to order a passage struck out. The verb thus means to demand the suppression of something, as if marking it with a ~déléatur~. It follows the pattern of other Latin formulas turned into French nouns, such as ~imprimatur~ and ~exequatur~.
en.délégitimer: Formed from ~légitimer~ (“to legitimize”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to strip something of legitimacy. French Wiktionary instead analyses it as ~dés-~ + ~légitime~; either way the root is ~légitime~, which entered Old French in the thirteenth century from Latin ~lēgitimus~ (“lawful, in accordance with the law”). The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.déléguer:
~Déléguer~ comes from Latin ~delegare~ (« to send away on a commission, to assign, to entrust »), made of ~de-~ and the first-conjugation verb ~legare~ (« to depute, to commission, to bequeath »). This ~legare~ is a denominal from ~lex~, ~legis~ (« law, formal motion »): to ~legare~ was to bind someone or something by a formal legal act. It must be kept apart from the third-conjugation ~legere~ (« to gather, to read »), a different verb despite the shared spelling. Italian ~delegare~, Spanish ~delegar~, and English ~delegate~ all descend from the same Latin source.

The legal core still shows: to ~déléguer~ is to hand over authority or a task by formal commission — a power, a vote, a representative sent in one's stead. From ~legare~ French also keeps ~léguer~ (« to bequeath ») and ~legs~ (« a legacy »), and from the noun ~lex~ a broad family of law-words: ~légal~, ~législation~, ~loyal~, and the ~délégué~ who carries another's mandate. English ~legacy~, ~legate~, and ~delegate~ belong to the same lineage.
en.démagnétiser: Formed from ~magnétiser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to remove magnetism. The base is built with the suffix ~-iser~ from ~magnétique~, borrowed from Latin ~magnēticus~, from the Greek adjective for “of Magnesia,” the region that gave magnets their name. A related use, for erasing a magnetic card or tape, extends the same idea.
en.démaigrir: Formed from ~maigrir~ (“to grow thin”) with the prefix ~dé-~. The TLFi gives two separate lines. For the ordinary sense, dated 1798 in the Académie, ~dé-~ comes from Latin ~dis-~ and marks the opposite. For the craftsman's sense, dated 1676, when Félibien says masons call stone joints too “fat” and say the joints must be reduced, using ~démaigrir~, it takes ~dé-~ from Latin ~de-~ in an intensive sense. The verb now means, in dated familiar use, to lose weight, and in masonry and carpentry to reduce the thickness of a piece.
en.démailler:
~Démailler~ (“to unravel, to undo the stitches”) comes from Old French ~desmailler~, formed from the prefix ~des-~ (modern ~dé-~), the noun ~maille~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The prefix reverses, so the verb means “to take the ~mailles~ apart”. The noun ~maille~ is the loop of a knitted fabric or the mesh of a net, and goes back to Latin ~macula~ (“spot, mesh of a net”).

The same noun lies behind a small French family: ~maillon~ (“a link of a chain”) and ~maillot~, and the English ~mail~ of “chain mail” is a distant relative through Old French. The verb is used of a stocking or sweater that ~se démaille~ when a thread breaks and a run opens, and of a net whose mesh has parted. The prefix ~dé-~ is the same one that reverses ~défaire~ or ~déplier~, here applied to a noun, so the verb means something like “to un-mesh”.
en.démailloter: Formed in French from the prefix ~dé-~, the noun ~maillot~ (swaddling clothes) and the verbal ending ~-er~, probably by analogy with ~emmaillotter~, “to swaddle.” Where ~emmaillotter~ wraps a baby in ~maillot~, ~démailloter~ undoes the wrapping. The noun ~maillot~ comes from Old French ~mailloel~, itself from ~maille~. The prefix ~dé-~ expresses reversal, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and the ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~.
en.démancher: Formed with the prefix ~dé-~ as the opposite of ~emmancher~ (“to fit with a handle”), so “to take off the handle.” Here ~dé-~ marks reversal, the commonest use of the prefix: the verb undoes what ~emmancher~ does. It also has the figurative sense “to go wrong.”
en.démanger: ~Démanger~ is ~manger~ (“to eat”) with the prefix ~dé-~, as in ~ça me démange~ (“it itches”). The base ~manger~ comes from Old French ~mangier~, from Late Latin ~manducare~ (“to chew, to eat”). The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The sources do not say how the itching sense developed.
en.démanteler: ~Démanteler~ is built on ~mantel~, the Old French form (10th century) of ~manteau~ (“cloak”), with the prefix ~dé-~, which here means removal. It appeared in the 16th century in the sense of tearing down a fortress's walls, as if stripping the cloak from it. The French source gives a second account: the verb may have been formed from ~emmanteler~ by swapping ~em-~ for ~dé-~. By the 19th century it had broadened to mean pulling down or breaking up in general.
en.démantibuler: The older form was ~desmandibuler~, “to break someone's jaw”, built from the prefix ~dé-~, the noun ~mandibule~ (“jaw”) and the verbal ending ~-er~. The prefix here is not a plain reversal but one of removal or destruction, and the verb widened from the jaw to anything smashed or taken apart, hence “to smash to smithereens”. The noun ~mandibule~ is a learned borrowing from Late Latin ~mandibula~, from Latin ~mandō~ (“to chew”).
en.démaquiller: ~Démaquiller~ is formed from ~maquiller~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action of its base: to remove makeup. The base ~maquiller~ is of Germanic ancestry, traced to a Picard verb related to Middle Dutch ~maken~ (“to make”). It meant simply “to do, to make” before slipping into slang, then into theatre slang in 1840 with the sense “to make up an actor's face.” ~Démaquiller~ simply undoes that late sense.
en.démarcher: The sources analyze it differently. French Wiktionary derives it from ~marcher~ with the prefix ~dé-~, while English Wiktionary derives it from the noun ~démarche~ (“step taken, approach”) plus ~-er~; since ~démarche~ itself comes from the same verb, both lead back to ~marcher~. The sense is “to canvass,” meaning to go from door to door or client to client. As for ~marcher~, it comes from Old French ~marchier~ (“to trample”), probably from Frankish *~markôn~ (“to mark, to press with the foot”), though a rival theory from Latin ~marcus~ (“hammer”) has never been ruled out.
en.démarier: Composed of ~marier~ and the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action, so the verb means to unmarry or to undo a marriage. The base ~marier~ is attested from 1145 and comes from Latin ~maritare~ (“to marry”), derived from ~maritus~ (“husband”). The same Latin word survives in Italian ~maritare~ and Spanish ~maridar~, and English borrowed French ~marier~ as ~marry~. A verb for tying a couple together is thus matched by one for loosening that tie.
en.démarquer: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ~marquer~ (“to mark”), so it means “to remove a mark.” The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Latin ~dis-~ and reverses the action of its base. ~Marquer~ goes back to a Germanic noun *~marka~ (“boundary, sign set at a limit”) of Frankish origin, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~merǵ-~ (“boundary, edge”); English ~mark~ and German ~Mark~ are cognates. A label or a brand is a mark, and ~démarquer~ takes it away, which is why the verb is used for taking a mark off merchandise or for copying a work while hiding its source.
en.démarrer:
From a syncope of older French ~désamarrer~ (“to cast off moorings”), formed from the prefix ~dé-~ (reversal) and ~amarrer~ (“to moor, to make fast”), a nautical term borrowed from Dutch ~aanmarren~ (“to tie, to fasten”). ~démarrer~ thus began life on the water, with ~amarre~ (“a mooring rope”) and ~amarrer~ as its close relatives in French.

The original picture is purely maritime: to ~démarrer~ was to untie a ship from the quay so it could leave port. Once the lines were loosed, the vessel got under way — and it is that moment of getting under way, of breaking from rest into motion, that the verb kept as its core when it drifted ashore. By extension ~démarrer~ came to mean starting a car or an engine, launching a business, or kicking off any undertaking, and in cycling slang a rider who ~démarre~ suddenly accelerates away from the pack. The same idea of casting off survives in the everyday opposite ~amarrer~ and in the noun ~démarrage~ (“startup, getaway”). It is a quietly vivid metaphor: every time a French driver starts the engine, the language remembers a sailor slipping the ropes and pulling away from the dock.
en.démascler:
This verb comes from Occitan ~demasclar~ (“to emasculate”), whose root is Latin ~masculus~ (“male”). The French verb is therefore a borrowing from Occitan, and a technical term meaning “to strip the bark from a cork oak”. The sources give the Occitan origin only; they do not explain how a verb of castration came to describe bark-stripping.

Latin ~masculus~ is a diminutive of ~mās~ (“male”). It produced French ~mâle~ through Old French ~masle~, as well as the learned words ~masculin~ and ~émasculer~, the last of which keeps the Latin sense of “to emasculate”. Italian ~maschio~ and Spanish ~macho~ are other descendants. ~Démascler~ is thus a regional cousin of ~émasculer~, from the same Latin root.
en.démasquer: Formed from ~masquer~ (“to mask”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses it: to ~démasquer~ is to take off someone's mask. The French Wiktionary entry derives it from the noun ~masque~ with the same prefix. The verb is used literally for removing a mask and figuratively for exposing a hidden identity or intention. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.démastiquer: The verb is formed from ~mastic~ (“putty, mastic”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which expresses removal: to take the putty off, as from a window pane. ~Mastic~ comes from Latin ~masticum~ or ~mastichē~ (“gum, mastic resin”), which in turn comes from Ancient Greek ~μαστίχη~, a word tied to a verb meaning “to chew.” The resin of the mastic tree gave its name to the sealing paste, and the verb undoes the work of applying it.
en.dématérialiser: ~Dématérialiser~ is best read as the prefix ~dé-~, here meaning removal, added to ~matérialiser~, itself formed from ~matériel~ plus ~-iser~. French Wiktionary parses it in one go from ~matériel~ with both affixes, which comes to the same thing. ~Matériel~ comes from Late Latin ~māteriālis~, from ~māteria~ (“wood, substance”), which in turn derives from ~māter~ (“mother”). The verb means to strip something of its physical form, as with paperless documents.
en.démembrer:
~Démembrer~ is inherited from Old French ~desmembrer~. Morphologically it is the prefix ~dé-~ (the Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~, “apart”), the noun ~membre~ (“limb”) and the verbal ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary refers it to ~dé-~ and an old verb ~membrer~. The noun ~membre~ is from Latin ~membrum~ (“limb, part of the body”), so ~démembrer~ literally means to take a body apart limb from limb.

The literal sense, cutting up a body, gave rise to many figurative ones. One ~démembre~ an empire, a company, an estate or a criminal network when one breaks it into separate parts, and ~démembrement~ is the noun for this. ~Membre~ itself has spread from the body to groups, so a ~membre~ of a club is a limb of the group, and the verb ~remembrer~ and the noun ~remembrement~ are used for regrouping scattered farm plots. English ~dismember~ comes from the same Old French verb.
en.démener: ~Démener~ is formed from ~mener~ (“to lead”) with the prefix ~dé-~. Here the prefix does not reverse the base; French Wiktionary treats it as intensive, so the verb is not an “un-leading.” Hence ~se démener~, to struggle and thrash about. The base ~mener~ comes from Old French ~mener~, from Late Latin ~minare~ (“to drive animals”), itself from Latin ~minari~ (“to threaten”), a verb built on ~minae~ (“threats”). The same Latin source gave French ~menacer~ and ~menace~.
en.démentir: Formed in French from ~mentir~ (“to lie”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which here cancels what the base does: to ~démentir~ a claim is to give it the lie, to deny or disprove it, and by extension to be at odds with something, as when the facts contradict a rumor. The base ~mentir~ comes from Old French and from Vulgar Latin *~mentīre~, a regularized form of Latin ~mentīrī~ (“to lie”), built on ~mēns~ (“mind”), so that lying is, etymologically, an invention of the mind. The English cognate of that root is ~mind~.
en.démerder: ~Démerder~ is formed from the prefix ~dé-~, the noun ~merde~ and the verb ending ~-er~, literally “to remove oneself from the shit.” The prefix ~dé-~ here expresses removal, as in ~dépanner~, and the verb is used mostly in the reflexive, ~se démerder~, with the figurative sense “to manage, to get by on one's own.” It is a vulgar word, and the picture it paints is of getting oneself out of a mess.
en.démettre: ~Démettre~ is formed from ~mettre~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which gives a sense of removal: to take someone out of a post, hence “to dismiss.” The base ~mettre~ comes from Old French ~metre~, from Latin ~mittere~ (“to send, to let go”). Classical ~mittere~ meant “to send,” and the modern sense “to put” developed later in the Romance languages. Italian ~mettere~ and Spanish ~meter~ are its cognates, and English ~mission~ and ~transmit~ are learned relatives.
en.démeubler: ~Démeubler~ is formed from ~meubler~ (“to furnish”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to strip a room of its furniture. The base comes from the noun ~meuble~ plus the ending ~-er~, and ~meuble~ descends from Latin ~mōbilis~ (“movable”). In Latin law, ~mōbilis~ named movable property, as opposed to ~immōbilis~, which gave ~immeuble~ (“building”). Furniture was thus first what you could carry away, and ~démeubler~ simply carries it away again.
en.démieller: Formed from ~mieller~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action. The base ~mieller~ is itself built on ~miel~ (“honey”) with ~-er~; ~miel~ comes from Latin ~mel~. To ~démieller~ is thus to take the honey out of a hive, the opposite of providing or filling with honey.
en.démilitariser: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and ~militariser~, so “to undo militarization.” The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~, and reverses the base. ~Militariser~ is ~militaire~ + ~-iser~, a suffix that makes verbs meaning “to make A.” The adjective ~militaire~ was borrowed through Middle French from Latin ~mīlitāris~ (“relating to war”), related to ~mīles~ (“soldier”). ~Démilitariser~ means “to remove military forces or character from,” as in a demilitarized zone.
en.déminer: ~Déminer~ is formed from ~miner~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to clear a place of mines. The base ~miner~ comes from the noun ~mine~, which descends from Vulgar Latin *~mina~ and ultimately from Gaulish *~meina~ (“ore, metal”), a word cognate with Welsh ~mwyn~. ~Miner~ meant to work a mine and to dig tunnels, which also gave the figurative sense of undermining.
en.déminéraliser: ~Déminéraliser~ combines the prefix ~dé-~, the adjective ~minéral~ and the suffix ~-iser~: “to remove the minerals” from something. The prefix ~dé-~ marks removal or cessation, and ~-iser~ makes the verb. The base ~minéral~ is a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ~minerālis~, which is tied to the Latin word for a mine, ~minera~ (the origin of the noun ~mine~ is the subject of another entry).
en.démissionner: Formed in French from ~démission~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~démission~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~dimissio~ (“release, dismissal”), taken in to serve as the abstract noun for the verb ~démettre~. The ending ~-er~ turns the noun into a verb meaning “to give one's démission,” that is, to resign from a post.
en.démobiliser: ~Démobiliser~ is ~mobiliser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the base verb: to undo a mobilization. The base ~mobiliser~ is a young verb, formed in 1765 from ~mobile~ and the suffix ~-iser~. ~Mobile~ continues Latin ~mobilis~ (“movable”), from ~movēre~ (“to move”). The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.démocratiser:
Formed in French from ~démocratie~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-iser~. The base word goes back to Greek ~dēmokratía~, a compound of ~dêmos~ (“the people”) and ~krátos~ (“power, rule”), so “rule by the people.” The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Greek ~-ízein~ through Late Latin ~-izare~, and it is the standard French tool for turning a noun or adjective into “to make X” or “to behave like X.” English has the exact parallel ~democratize~, built the same way.

The verb first appeared in Middle French with the intransitive sense “to live under a democracy.” The modern political sense, “to make something democratic” or “to open it to everyone,” developed later, and it now applies to anything from institutions to luxury goods or technology. Because the base is Greek, the family is rich in learned words: ~démocrate~, ~démocratique~, ~démocratie~, and, from the same ~-cratie~ element, ~aristocratie~ and ~autocratie~, plus ~démagogue~ and ~démographie~ from the ~dêmos~ element.
en.démoder: ~Démoder~ is formed from the noun ~mode~ (“fashion”) with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ending ~-er~. Here ~dé-~ expresses removal or the end of a state: to ~démoder~ is to take away the quality of being in fashion, and the verb is mostly met in the participle ~démodé~. The base ~mode~ comes from Latin ~modus~ (“measure, manner”), through Old French.
en.démoduler: ~Démoduler~ is built from ~moduler~ with the reversing prefix ~dé-~, which undoes the action of the base. ~Moduler~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~modulārī~ (“to measure, to regulate”), from ~modulus~, a diminutive of ~modus~ (“measure”). Where ~moduler~ in radio and electronics means to vary a carrier wave according to a signal, ~démoduler~ recovers that original signal from the wave. The verb therefore belongs to the technical vocabulary of telecommunications.
en.démolir:
Borrowed from Latin ~dēmōlīrī~ (“to demolish, to pull down”), a deponent verb made of ~dē-~ (“down, undo”) and ~mōlīrī~ (“to set in motion, to build, to heave”). Latin ~mōlīrī~ comes from the noun ~mōlēs~ (“a massive structure, a heavy mass”). The Latin infinitive in ~-īrī~ was reshaped in French as a regular ~-ir~ verb of the second group, hence ~nous démolissons~. English ~demolish~ was borrowed from the French verb.

The prefix ~dē-~ makes the meaning an exact reversal: since ~mōlīrī~ could mean to erect a great structure, ~démolir~ is to un-build it. French kept the literal sense of tearing down a building, and then extended it to wrecking a theory, a reputation or an opponent, and in familiar speech to hurting someone badly. The root ~mōlēs~ left several other French words: ~môle~ (“a breakwater, a jetty”), and ~molécule~, coined in modern Latin as a diminutive of ~mōlēs~, a “little mass.”
en.démonter: From the prefix ~dé-~ + ~monter~. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and reverses the action of the base. The verb ~monter~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~montāre~ (“to go up”), built on Latin ~mons~ (“mountain”). Since ~monter~ also means “to assemble” (one ~monte~ a machine, a tent or a shelf), ~démonter~ undoes that assembly: it means to take apart or dismantle. It also keeps the older sense of ~monter~ as “to ride,” which gives the sense of unseating a rider, and, figuratively, of throwing someone off balance, as in the common ~ne pas se démonter~, “to keep one's composure.”
en.démontrer:
From Latin ~dēmonstrāre~ (“to point out, show clearly, prove”), a compound of the prefix ~dē-~ (here intensive, “fully”) and ~mōnstrāre~ (“to show”). ~Mōnstrāre~ derives from ~mōnstrum~ (“a portent, a sign from the gods”), itself from ~monēre~ (“to warn, remind”), tracing back to the PIE root *~men-~ (“to think”). So at bottom “to demonstrate” means to make the mind take notice. Cognate with Italian ~dimostrare~ and Spanish ~demostrar~, and — borrowed — with English ~demonstrate~; the plainer French ~montrer~ shares the same ~mōnstrāre~ ancestor.

The Latin verb already split between simply showing and rigorously proving, and French kept ~démontrer~ on the side of proof: where ~montrer~ merely displays, ~démontrer~ establishes by argument. Mathematics adopted it wholesale, and the classroom flourish ~ce qu'il fallait démontrer~ (“which was to be proved”) still closes a proof, abbreviated ~CQFD~. The frightening cousin ~mōnstrum~ — a divine warning made flesh — gave French ~monstre~, so the family yokes the rational demonstration to the prodigy. From the same root *~men-~ come ~mention~, ~admonester~, and ~mémoire~ all keep the ancient sense of the mind remembering and being warned.
en.démonétiser: Formed from ~monétiser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the verb: to strip something of its status as money. The base ~monétiser~ was built in French from Latin ~monēta~ (“mint, coin”) and the suffix ~-iser~. The same Latin word came down by inheritance as ~monnaie~, so ~démonétiser~ is a learned relative of ~monnayer~. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.démoraliser: ~Démoraliser~ is analyzed in two ways: French Wiktionary derives it from ~moral~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and the suffix ~-iser~, while English Wiktionary derives it from ~dé-~ plus ~moraliser~. The word ~moral~ is a learned borrowing, through Old and Middle French ~moral~, from Latin ~morālis~ (“relating to customs and manners”). The prefix ~dé-~ marks removal, so the verb means to strip of morals or morale, and its senses range from “corrupt the morals of” to “sap the morale of.”
en.démordre: Formed from ~mordre~ and the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the base: to ~démordre~ is to let go of what one has bitten. The base ~mordre~ comes from Old French, from Vulgar Latin *~mordĕre~, from Latin ~mordēre~ (“to bite”). The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The verb is now almost always figurative and negative: someone who ne ~démord~ pas de an opinion refuses to release it, like a dog that will not open its jaws.
en.démotiver: ~Démotiver~ is formed from ~motiver~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here expresses the undoing of a state: to take away someone's motivation. The base ~motiver~ comes from the noun ~motif~, a learned borrowing from Late Latin ~mōtīvus~ (“that sets in motion”), itself from Latin ~movēre~ (“to move”). So the verb carries, underneath, the old idea of what moves a person to act, and ~démotiver~ is to remove that push. It is a modern formation, built on the model of many ~dé-~ verbs that cancel a condition.
en.démoucheter: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ~moucheter~. In fencing, to ~démoucheter~ a foil is to take off its safety tip, the reverse of fitting it. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and expresses reversal or removal.
en.démouler: ~Démouler~ is formed from ~mouler~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action of the base: to take something out of the mold it was shaped in. ~Mouler~ itself comes from the noun ~moule~, inherited from Old French ~modle~, an early borrowing from Latin ~modulus~ (“measure”). This ~moule~ is a doublet of ~module~ and is unrelated to the ~moule~ of mussels, which comes from Latin ~mūsculus~.
en.démoustiquer: Formed from ~moustique~ with the prefix ~dé-~ (removal) and the verbal ending ~-er~: to ~démoustiquer~ a place is to rid it of mosquitoes. The noun was borrowed from Spanish ~mosquito~, a diminutive of ~mosca~ (“fly”), from Latin ~musca~, which also gave French ~mouche~. The spelling ~mousquite~ became ~moustique~ through a swap of sounds, possibly helped by the influence of ~tique~ (“tick”).
en.démultiplier: Formed from ~multiplier~ with the prefix ~dé-~. French Wiktionary traces ~dé-~ to Latin ~de-~ or ~dis-~ and notes that it usually gives a word its opposite sense. ~Multiplier~ is a learned verb from Latin ~multiplicare~, built on ~multus~ (“many”) and ~plicare~ (“to fold”). In mechanics ~démultiplier~ means to reduce the speed of a movement through gearing, trading speed for force, which fits the reversing sense of the prefix.
en.démunir: Derived from ~munir~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to ~démunir~ someone is to take away what they were equipped with. The base ~munir~ comes from Latin ~mūnīre~ (“to fortify, to defend”), built on ~moenia~ (“city walls”). It first meant to fortify a place, and from the late sixteenth century it broadened to “to supply, to provide with what is needed.” The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”) and here marks removal, so the verb means “to deprive of means or resources.” It appears above all in the participle ~démuni~ (“destitute, at a loss”) and in the reflexive ~se démunir de~ (“to part with”).
en.démuseler: ~Démuseler~ is formed from ~museler~ (“to muzzle”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to take a muzzle off. ~Museler~ itself is built on ~musel~, the Old and Middle French form of ~museau~ (“snout”), and English ~muzzle~ comes from the same Old French ~musel~. The prefix ~dé-~ descends from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). Since ~museler~ also means “to silence someone”, ~démuseler~ can likewise be heard in a figurative sense, as freeing someone to speak.
en.démutiser: Built on Latin ~mūtus~ (“mute, dumb”) with the verb suffix ~-iser~ and the prefix ~dé-~ (“removal”), so it means to undo muteness: to restore speech or to teach someone to speak. The Latin adjective is the source of French ~muet~ and of the learned ~mutisme~, and of Italian and Spanish ~muto~ and ~mudo~. The verb is a modern French coinage that works on the pattern of ~dé-~ + base + ~-iser~, as in ~déculpabiliser~.
en.démystifier: Formed in French from ~mystifier~ with the negative prefix ~dé-~.
