The base ~mystifier~ is built from Ancient Greek ~μύστης~ (“one initiated into the mysteries”), by way of Latin ~mysta~, plus the verb suffix ~-ifier~, from Latin ~-ficāre~ (“to make”). The prefix ~dé-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), reverses it. ~Démystifier~ means to strip away an illusion or a false aura, “to demystify.” The Greek root also lies behind ~mystère~ and ~mystique~, and English ~mystic~ and ~mystery~.
en.démythifier: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and ~mythifier~, so “to undo the making of a myth.” The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~, and reverses the base. ~Mythifier~ is ~mythe~ + ~-ifier~, “to make into.” The noun ~mythe~ came through Latin ~mythos~ from Ancient Greek ~mûthos~ (“tale, fable”). ~Mythifier~ turns a person, event or idea into a myth, often by idealizing it, and ~démythifier~ strips that away: “to debunk, to demythologize.”
en.démyéliniser: Formed from ~myéline~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to strip of myelin.” The noun ~myéline~ combines Greek ~μυελός~ (~muelós~, “marrow”) with the suffix ~-ine~. Myelin is the fatty sheath that surrounds nerve fibers, and the verb is a medical term for destroying it. The prefix ~dé-~ marks the removal, and ~-iser~ turns the noun into a verb of treatment or change.
en.démâter: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and ~mâter~, so “to remove the mast.” The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~, and reverses the base. ~Mâter~ is ~mât~ + ~-er~, “to fit a ship with a mast.” ~Mât~ comes from Middle and Old French ~mast~, from Early Medieval Latin ~mastus~, from Frankish *~mast~, from Proto-Germanic *~mastaz~. The circumflex stands for a lost ~s~. ~Démâter~ means “to dismast,” of a ship that loses its mast, for example in a storm.
en.démédicaliser: Formed from ~médicaliser~ with the reversing prefix ~dé-~: to remove the medical character from something. The base is built from the adjective ~médical~ and the suffix ~-iser~ (“to treat as”), so ~médicaliser~ means to bring under medical care and authority. ~Médical~ is borrowed from Latin ~medicālis~ (“of a physician”), from ~medicus~ and the verb ~medērī~ (“to heal”). The verb is modern and often applied to life events, such as childbirth or old age, that had come to be treated as medical matters.
en.déménager: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ (reversal, removal) and ~ménager~, which is itself the noun ~ménage~ (“household”) plus the verb ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary notes that ~ménager~ already existed in Old French with the sense “to dwell, to live in a place.” So ~déménager~ undoes the settling of a household: to take one's belongings out of a dwelling and leave it, or more loosely to move furniture and objects from one place to another. The verb is a near mirror of ~emménager~, built on the same base.
en.démériter: ~Démériter~ is formed from the noun ~démérite~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~démérite~ comes from Latin ~dēmeritum~, which fr.Wiktionary gives as its source. The verb means to act in a way that makes one unworthy, to lose the esteem or favor one had, and it is the opposite of ~mériter~, which shares the same Latin family. The prefix in the Latin source is a different matter from the French ~dé-~, so the verb is not analyzed here as ~dé-~ plus ~mériter~; the sources take the noun as the base.
en.démêler: Formed from ~mêler~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action, so that ~démêler~ means “to undo a mixing, to untangle”. French Wiktionary dates the Old French form ~desmedler~ to about 1155, and English Wiktionary adds that it is inherited from Middle French. The base ~mêler~ comes from Old French ~mesler~, from Vulgar Latin *~misculare~, from Latin ~miscere~ (“to mix”). The circumflex marks the lost ~s~. Besides the physical sense of combing out tangles, the verb is used figuratively, for sorting out a confused matter.
en.dénasaliser: Formed from ~nasaliser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to take away the nasal quality of a sound. ~Nasaliser~ is built on ~nasal~, a learned word borrowed from Medieval Latin ~nāsālis~, from Latin ~nāsus~ (“nose”). French ~nez~ descends from the same ~nāsus~ by inheritance. To ~dénasaliser~ is thus to stop pronouncing a sound through the nose.
en.dénationaliser: Formed from ~nationaliser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to undo nationalization. The base ~nationaliser~ is built from the adjective ~national~ and the suffix ~-iser~ (“make A”). ~National~ itself comes from ~nation~ and ~-al~, and French Wiktionary records it in 1534 as ~nacional~, at first a term of religious organization. ~Nation~ comes through Old French ~nacion~ from Latin ~nātiō~. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.dénatter: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ~natter~ (“to braid”), hence “to undo braided hair.” The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and marks the reverse of the action expressed by the base. The verb is thus the exact opposite of ~natter~: the braid is not made but taken apart, strand by strand.
en.dénaturaliser: Formed from ~naturaliser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to strip someone of a nationality acquired by naturalization. The base ~naturaliser~ is built with the suffix ~-iser~ on ~naturel~, from Latin ~naturalis~ (“natural”), and means to admit a foreigner as a citizen, and also to stuff a dead animal. ~Dénaturaliser~ keeps the first sense and undoes it.
en.dénaturer: Inherited from Old French ~desnaturer~, which can be analysed as ~dé-~ + ~nature~ + ~-er~. The noun ~nature~ comes from Latin ~nātūra~ (“birth, natural character, the course of things”), itself from ~nascor~ (“to be born”). The prefix ~dé-~ (from Latin ~dis-~, “apart”) expresses removal, so ~dénaturer~ is to strip something of its natural character. From there the verb took two paths: the physical one, to alter a substance so that it can no longer be used as it was (denatured alcohol), and the figurative one, to distort or misrepresent a fact, a text or someone's words.
en.dénazifier: ~Dénazifier~ is formed from ~nazifier~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to remove Nazi influence. ~Nazifier~ is built on ~nazi~ with the suffix ~-fier~, as in English “-ify,” so “to make Nazi.” The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The verb belongs to the post-war vocabulary, from the effort to purge German institutions and public life of Nazi influence.
en.déneiger: Formed in French with the prefix ~dé-~ and ~neiger~ (“to snow”), or, as French Wiktionary words it, from ~dé-~, the noun ~neige~ and the verb ending: to remove snow from a place. The base ~neiger~ comes through Old French ~negier~ from Vulgar Latin *~nivicāre~, built on Latin ~nivem~ (“snow”). Italian ~nevicare~ is its parallel.
en.déniaiser: ~Déniaiser~ is built on the adjective ~niais~ (“naive, simple”) with the prefix ~dé-~, in its sense of removal, and the verb ending ~-er~: to take away someone's naivety, to make them worldly-wise, and often to initiate them in love. ~Niais~ comes from Old French ~niais~, from Vulgar Latin *~nīdāx~, derived from Latin ~nīdus~ (“nest”).
en.dénicher: Formed from ~nicher~ (“to nest”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses or removes: to take out of the nest. The base comes from Old French ~nigier~ and Vulgar Latin *~nīdicāre~, a verb built on Latin ~nīdus~ (“nest”), the same word that gave French ~nid~. The literal sense is to drive a bird or its young from its nest, and the figurative one, to find something hidden or rare, followed: to unearth a bargain, a talent or a culprit. The verb is therefore a neat reversal of ~se nicher~ (“to nestle”).
en.dénicotiniser: Formed from ~nicotine~ with the prefix ~dé-~, meaning to remove nicotine from something. The base ~nicotine~ came into French from English ~nicotin~, itself derived from ~nicotiane~ with the suffix ~-ine~. It is named after the French diplomat Jean Nicot (1530–1604). The prefix ~dé-~, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), here expresses removal, the sense it takes when attached to a noun.
en.dénier: ~Dénier~ is formed in French from ~dé-~ + ~nier~ (“to deny”), modeled on Latin ~dēnegāre~, itself ~dē-~ + ~negāre~. In this verb the prefix ~dé-~ does not reverse the base but strengthens it, as the French source notes. ~Nier~ comes from Latin ~negāre~, so the pair ~nier~ and ~dénier~ echoes ~negāre~ and ~dēnegāre~ in Latin. Today ~dénier~ means to deny or to refuse to grant, as in ~dénier un droit~ (“to deny someone a right”).
en.dénigrer: A learned borrowing from Latin ~dēnigrāre~ (“to blacken”), made of ~dē-~ and ~niger~ (“black”). The verb was taken whole from Latin, not inherited through Old French. ~Niger~ is also the ancestor of French ~noir~, and English ~denigrate~ is a borrowing of the same Latin verb. To run someone down is, etymologically, to blacken them.
en.dénitrifier: Formed from ~nitrifier~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here marks reversal. ~Nitrifier~ is built from ~nitrate~ and the suffix ~-ifier~, from Latin ~-ficāre~ (from ~facere~, “to make”), and means “to turn into nitrate.” ~Nitrate~ itself derives from ~nitre~. The verb therefore names the opposite process, the undoing of nitrification, a term of chemistry and soil science.
en.déniveler: Formed from ~niveler~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action of its base. Where ~niveler~ means “to make level,” ~déniveler~ means “to make uneven.” The base ~niveler~ comes from the noun ~niveau~, which goes back through Old French ~nivel~ and ~livel~ to Latin ~lībella~ (“a small level, a plumb instrument”).
en.dénombrer:
From Latin ~dīnumerāre~ (“to count, to enumerate”), built from ~dī-~, a form of ~dis-~ (“apart”), and ~numerāre~ (“to count”), which comes from ~numerus~ (“number”). The simple verb ~nombrer~ comes from the same ~numerāre~. In the noun, the Latin ~numerum~ was reduced in Old French to ~nomre~, and a ~b~ appeared between the ~m~ and the ~r~ to ease the pronunciation, which gave ~nombre~. English ~number~ was borrowed from the French form.

The noun ~dénombrement~ was used for a census, a head count of a population or an army. The Latin family has other branches in French: ~numéro~ and ~numéral~ are learned borrowings, ~énumérer~ is another verb built on ~numerāre~, and ~innombrable~ (“countless”) is the adjective that denies it. The English ~enumerate~ and ~numeral~ belong to this same family.
en.dénommer:
First attested around 1170 as ~denonmer~, borrowed from Latin ~dēnōmināre~ (“to name, to designate”), from ~dē-~ (here an intensifier) and ~nōmināre~ (“to name”), the verb of ~nōmen~ (“name”). ~nōmen~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~nōmn̥~ and to PIE *~h₁nómn̥~ (“name”) — one of the most widely preserved roots in the family. Its cognates are everywhere: English ~name~ and ~noun~ (both doublets), Greek ~ónoma~, German ~Name~, Sanskrit ~nā́man~. The sense “to assign a name to” settled in by about 1250.

The ~dē-~ here does not subtract, as it does in ~défaire~; it reinforces, giving ~dénommer~ the flavor of naming explicitly or designating by name. That precise nuance survives in administrative and grammatical French — a ~dénomination~ is an official designation, and the ~dénominateur~ of a fraction is, literally, the number that “names” the parts. From the same ~nōmen~ descend French ~nom~, ~nommer~, ~renommée~ (“fame,” the “re-naming” people give you), ~pronom~, and the learned ~nominal~ and ~nominer~. The PIE root threads through English ~nominate~, ~ignominy~, and ~misnomer~ — a sprawling clan all turning on the simple act of giving a thing its name.
en.dénoncer:
From Old French ~denoncier~ (also ~denuntier~), from Latin ~dēnūntiāre~ (“to announce, to proclaim, to give formal notice”), a compound of ~dē-~ (here intensive) and ~nūntiāre~ (“to report, to bring news”), itself from ~nūntius~ (“messenger, message”). The origin of ~nūntius~ is uncertain; De Vaan tentatively traces it to a Proto-Indo-European root *~newH-~ (“to shout, to cry out”), fitting the herald who proclaims aloud. The Latin verb is cognate with Italian ~denunziare~ and Spanish ~denunciar~, and shares its second element with English ~announce~ and ~pronounce~.

In Latin and Old French the verb was neutral: simply “to make something known officially,” especially a treaty, a declaration of war, or a legal notice. Over time the sense darkened. To “give formal notice” against a person slid toward “to accuse, to inform on,” and modern French ~dénoncer~ now carries a strongly negative charge — to betray a wrongdoer to the authorities, or to publicly condemn an injustice. The older neutral meaning lingers only in formal registers, as when a state ~dénonce~ a treaty (declares it void). From the same ~nūntius~ stem come French ~annoncer~, ~prononcer~, ~énoncer~, and the noun ~nonce~ (a papal envoy — a messenger still).
en.dénoter: ~Dénoter~ is formed from ~noter~ (“to mark, to note”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which here is not a simple reversal. ~Noter~ comes from Latin ~notāre~ (“to mark, to write down”), itself built on ~nota~ (“a mark, a sign”). The verb means “to indicate, to point to,” and in older use it could also mean “to stick out, to clash.” That second sense arose, doubtless, by confusion with ~détonner~ (“to be out of tune, to clash”). The same ~nota~ underlies ~note~, ~notable~ and ~notice~.
en.dénouer: Formed from ~nouer~ with the reversing prefix ~dé-~ (Old French ~desnouer~), so literally “to undo a knot.” The base ~nouer~ comes through Old French ~noer~ from Latin ~nōdāre~, built on ~nōdus~ (“knot”), the source of French ~nœud~. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The figurative sense, “to resolve,” follows the figurative ~nouer~: if a plot is tied, the ~dénouement~ is where it is untied.
en.dénoyauter: ~Dénoyauter~ is built on ~noyau~ (“stone, pit”) with the prefix ~dé-~, meaning removal, and the ending ~-er~, with a euphonic ~t~ between the vowel-final noun and the ending. It means to remove the stones from fruit. The noun ~noyau~ is traced by French Wiktionary to Late Latin ~nucālis~ (“nut-like”), from ~nux~ (“nut”). English Wiktionary gives that or, alternatively, a diminutive of ~nōdus~ (“knot”) as the source.
en.dénoyer: Formed from ~noyer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to drain the water from something that was flooded, as a mine or a field. The base ~noyer~ is inherited from Old French ~neier~, from Latin ~necāre~ (“to kill”), a verb that narrowed in Romance to “kill by immersion,” that is, to drown. The sense “to cover with water, to flood” is recorded from 1500, and ~dénoyer~ undoes exactly that sense.
en.dénucléariser: ~Dénucléariser~ combines the prefix ~dé-~, the adjective ~nucléaire~ and the suffix ~-iser~, and means “to rid of nuclear weapons or installations.” It was coined on the model of ~militaire~ and ~démilitariser~. The adjective ~nucléaire~ is a derivative of ~nucléus~ (“nucleus”) with the suffix ~-aire~. Here ~-iser~ means “to make or convert,” and ~dé-~ reverses it: to undo the nuclear status of a zone or a state.
en.dénuder: ~Dénuder~ is borrowed from Latin ~dēnūdāre~ (“to strip bare, to uncover, to reveal”), as both Wiktionaries agree. The Latin verb joins the prefix ~dē-~ to the adjective ~nūdus~ (“naked”), the source of French ~nu~. English Wiktionary notes an inherited doublet, ~dénuer~, which came down through Old French instead of being borrowed.
en.dénuer:
French ~dénuer~ is inherited from Latin ~dēnūdāre~ (“to strip bare”), which was built on ~nūdus~ (“naked”). It reached French through an altered Latin form ~disnūdāre~, which gave Old French ~desnuer~, whose ~s~ later vanished. Spanish ~desnudar~ is its direct cousin, and French also later borrowed the Latin verb a second time as the learned doublet ~dénuder~.

The verb began as a physical act, to strip someone or something bare. In modern French that concrete sense has largely passed to ~dénuder~, while ~dénuer~ survives mostly in the figurative sense of depriving, leaving someone without something. Its past participle is far commoner than the verb itself, in phrases like ~dénué de sens~ (“devoid of meaning”) or ~dénué de scrupules~ (“unscrupulous”). The underlying Latin adjective ~nūdus~ also gave French ~nu~ (“naked”) and, through learned borrowing, English ~nude~. Behind the abstract complaint that an argument is ~dénué de fondement~ lies, then, an image of something stripped to nothing.
en.dénébuler: Built on Latin ~nebula~ (“cloud, mist”) with the prefix ~dé-~ (“removal”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so it means to clear away mist or fog. The Latin noun also gave French the learned words ~nébuleux~ and ~nébuleuse~, and English ~nebula~. The verb is a technical, learned coinage in which the mist is something to be removed.
en.dénébuliser: Formed from ~nébuliser~ with the prefix ~dé-~ (“removal”). The base is built on Latin ~nebula~ (“cloud, vapor”) with the verb suffix ~-iser~, so ~nébuliser~ means to turn into a fine mist, and ~dénébuliser~ means to demist or defog, to remove that mist. It is a close doublet in sense of ~dénébuler~, which is built straight on the Latin noun with ~-er~.
en.dépailler: Formed from ~paille~ with the prefix ~dé-~ (removal) and the verbal ending ~-er~: to ~dépailler~ is to strip the straw from something. The noun ~paille~ comes from Latin ~palea~ (“straw, chaff”) by way of Old French. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.dépalisser: Formed from ~palisser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to take away the supports that hold the branches of a fruit tree to a trellis. The base ~palisser~ comes from ~palis~ (“fence of stakes, trellis”) and the ending ~-er~. The noun ~palis~ derives from Old French ~pel~ (“stake”), which gave modern ~pal~.
en.dépanner: ~Dépanner~ is formed from ~panne~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and the ending ~-er~, in the sense “to remove the breakdown.” The ~panne~ meant here began as a nautical term, a variant of ~penne~, the tip of a ship's yard, which recalls the point of a feather. French ~mettre en panne~ (1611) meant to set the yards so as to stop the ship, ~en panne~ came to mean “held up, unable to act” in the eighteenth century, and by 1879 it described a mechanism that had stopped working.
en.dépaqueter: The verb is built from ~paqueter~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action of the base verb, as in ~défaire~ (“to undo”). ~Paqueter~ is in turn derived from the noun ~paquet~ (“package, bundle”) with the ending ~-er~, and means to make something into a package. So ~dépaqueter~ is the opposite action: to take things out of their package, hence “to unpack.” It is a two-step French formation, with a noun at its base.
en.déparasiter: Formed from ~parasite~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which expresses removal, and the verb ending ~-er~: to rid something of parasites. ~Parasite~ is borrowed from Latin ~parasītus~, itself from Ancient Greek ~parásitos~, built from ~para-~ (“beside”) and ~sîtos~ (“food”), so that the original parasite was literally one who takes his food beside another.
en.dépareiller:
~Dépareiller~ is formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ending ~-er~ on the adjective ~pareil~ (“alike”), so it means “to undo a match.” The adjective ~pareil~ goes back to Latin ~parilis~ (“similar, equal”), a derivative of ~pār~ (“equal”). To ~dépareiller~ is to separate the members of a matching set, such as a pair of gloves or a service of plates, leaving them odd.

The family of Latin ~pār~ is large in French. It gives ~pair~, ~paire~, ~pareil~, ~parité~ and, with the prefix ~com-~, ~comparer~. English cognates include ~peer~, ~pair~ and ~par~. The participle ~dépareillé~ is the most common form and means “odd, mismatched,” as in ~des chaussettes dépareillées~. The verb itself is rarer and usually means to break up a complete set.
en.déparer:
From Old French ~desparer~ (“to strip, to undo, to part”), which French Wiktionary analyzes as ~parer~ with the prefix ~dé-~ (from Old French ~des-~). English Wiktionary agrees, calling the modern verb inherited from Old French and describing the ~dé-~ + ~parer~ analysis as a surface one. The base ~parer~ (“to adorn”) goes back to Latin ~parāre~ (“to prepare, to make ready”).

The modern verb is used figuratively: something that ~dépare~ a place or a person spoils its appearance, and the verb is nearly always met in the negative, as in a thing that “ne déparerait pas” a room. Latin ~parāre~ is a prolific root. It gave French ~parer~ and ~parure~, and through prefixed forms ~préparer~, ~réparer~ and ~séparer~, as well as English ~prepare~ and ~repair~.
en.déparier: The verb is built from the noun ~paire~ (“pair”) with the privative prefix ~dé-~, which expresses removal or undoing, and the verb ending ~-er~. It means literally “to undo a pair”: to split up two things that belonged together, such as a mated couple of birds. The sources give no older source language for it, so it is best read as a plain French formation, coined by adding ~dé-~ to a noun and turning the result into a first-conjugation verb.
en.déparler: Formed from ~parler~ and the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses or undoes the base: to un-speak, to speak wrongly or against someone. The sense “to speak ill of, to blame” is attested around 1160, early in the history of French. The base ~parler~ comes from Old French, from Late Latin ~parabolāre~, built on Latin ~parabola~ (“comparison, parable”), itself from Greek ~παραβολή~. Today ~déparler~ survives mostly in regional use, for talking nonsense or speaking ill, and in a dated sense of ceasing to talk.
en.départager: ~Départager~ is formed from ~partager~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which marks reversal here: undoing the even balance between two parties. The base ~partager~ is a fairly young verb, coined around 1553 from the noun ~partage~ (“division, sharing”) and from ~part~, which comes from Latin ~pars~ (“part, share”). It came to replace the older ~partir~ (“to divide”), which had drifted to mean only “to leave.”
en.départementaliser: Formed from ~départemental~ with the suffix ~-iser~, “to give a departmental organization to.” The adjective ~départemental~ is built from ~département~ with the suffix ~-al~. The suffix ~-iser~, from Late Latin ~-izāre~, makes verbs meaning “to make” or “to turn into,” and is productive in administrative French.
en.départir:
From Middle French ~departir~, from Old French ~departir~, from Late Latin ~departīre~, built from Latin ~de-~ and ~partiō~ (“to divide, to share”), a verb based on ~pars~ (“part”). Both Wiktionaries also allow a simpler analysis as ~dé-~ plus ~partir~, so the two accounts coexist. English ~depart~ was borrowed from the same Old French verb. The Latin ~partiō~ also gave ~partir~ itself, whose modern sense “to leave” grew out of the older sense “to divide, to separate.”

The old meaning of ~départir~ was “to divide up, to distribute,” and from there “to separate, to leave.” Once ~partir~ had taken over the sense of leaving, ~départir~ was left with a narrow literary role. It survives mainly in the reflexive ~se départir de~ (“to give up, to depart from”), nearly always in the negative, as in ~ne pas se départir de son calme~ (“not to lose one's composure”), and in the formal sense “to allot,” as in a power or a task allotted to someone. The noun ~départ~ (“departure”) and the verb ~répartir~ (“to distribute”) belong to the same family as ~part~, ~partie~ and ~partition~.
en.dépasser:
A French compound of the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ~passer~ (“to pass”), the ~dé-~ here marking the idea of going beyond or past a limit. ~Passer~ descends from Vulgar Latin *~passare~, a verb derived from the Latin noun ~passus~ (“a step, a pace”). That noun is itself the past participle of ~pandere~ (“to spread, to stretch out”), from Proto-Indo-European *~peth₂-~ (“to spread”). Cognates of ~passer~ are everywhere in Romance — Spanish ~pasar~, Italian ~passare~ — and English borrowed both ~pass~ and ~pace~ from the same source.

The underlying image is the stride: a ~passus~ was the distance covered by a step, so ~passer~ first meant to move step by step from one place to another, to go past. ~Dépasser~ sharpens this into “to go beyond” — to overtake a car, to exceed a limit, to surpass a rival, or even, figuratively, for a problem to be beyond someone (cela me ~dépasse~). The prefix ~dé-~ adds the sense of moving clear past a mark. From the same ~passer~ French built ~passage~, ~passant~, ~passerelle~, ~surpasser~, ~trépasser~ (“to pass away, to die”), and ~repasser~ (“to pass again,” hence “to iron”).
en.dépassionner: Formed from ~passionner~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which marks the cessation of a state: to take the heat out of a debate or a conflict. The base ~passionner~ is built on the noun ~passion~, from Latin ~passionem~ (“suffering, enduring”), the action noun of ~patior~ (“to suffer”). The first sense of ~passion~ was thus “being acted upon”, which later widened to strong feeling. To ~dépassionner~ a subject is to calm that feeling and bring it back to a level discussion.
en.dépatouiller: The sources disagree on the formation. English Wiktionary analyzes ~dépatouiller~ as ~dé-~ + ~patouille~ + ~-er~, with ~patouille~ inherited from Middle French ~patoueil~. French Wiktionary instead composes it from ~dépatter~ and ~-ouiller~. On the first analysis, the prefix ~dé-~ (from Latin ~dis-~, “apart”) reverses the entanglement, so the verb means “to get out of a mess”; ~se dépatouiller~ is “to extricate oneself,” with the muddy tone of ~patouiller~ (“to flounder in the mud”).
en.dépatrier: The verb is formed from the noun ~patrie~ (“homeland”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which expresses removal or deprivation. ~Patrie~ is borrowed from Latin ~patria~ (“land of one's forefathers”), itself derived from ~pater~ (“father”), the source of French ~père~. So ~dépatrier~ means to deprive someone of their homeland, which is why the gloss reads “take away someone's home country.” The sources describe it as a plain French formation, with a noun as its base.
en.dépaver: Formed from ~paver~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to remove the cobblestones from a road. ~Paver~ is inherited from Old French, from Vulgar Latin *~pavāre~ (“to beat down”), from Latin ~pavīre~ (“to beat, tread down”). The image behind paving is a surface beaten flat, and the same Latin family gave ~pavement~ and ~pavé~.
en.dépayser: ~Dépayser~ is a parasynthetic verb, built on the noun ~pays~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and the ending ~-er~ added together. The prefix expresses removal, so the verb means to take someone out of their usual country or surroundings, hence to disorient them or to give a change of scenery. The noun ~pays~ comes through Old French ~pais~ from Late Latin ~pāgēnsis~ (“inhabitant of a district”), derived from Latin ~pāgus~ (“countryside, district”). Italian ~paese~ is a cognate, and Spanish ~país~ was borrowed from French.
en.dépecer: ~Dépecer~ is built from the prefix ~dé-~, the noun ~pièce~ and the ending ~-er~, so its base is a noun, not a verb. The prefix expresses removal: to ~dépecer~ is to take something apart into pieces, to cut it up. The noun ~pièce~ comes from Gaulish *~pettia~ by way of Medieval Latin ~petia~, a Gaulish form reconstructed with the help of Breton ~pezh~ and Welsh ~peth~. The word spread through the Romance languages as Spanish ~pieza~, Italian ~pezza~ and Portuguese ~peça~, and reached English as ~piece~.
en.dépeigner: ~Dépeigner~ is formed from ~peigner~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to undo the combing, and so to mess up someone's hair. ~Peigner~ is inherited from Old French ~paigner~, from Latin ~pectināre~ (“to comb”), formed on ~pecten~ (“comb”). Italian ~pettinare~ and Spanish ~peinar~ come from the same Latin verb. The prefix ~dé-~ descends from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”) through Old French ~des-~. The noun ~peigne~ and words such as ~peignoir~ and ~peignée~ belong to the same family.
en.dépeindre:
~Dépeindre~ is explained in two compatible ways. French Wiktionary treats it as borrowed from Latin ~dēpingere~ (“to paint, to depict, to describe”), reshaped on the model of ~peindre~, while English Wiktionary simply analyses it as ~dé-~ + ~peindre~. Either way, the Latin ancestor ~pingere~ (“to paint”) lies behind the base. It descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~peyḱ-~ (“to mark, to colour”). In Latin, ~dēpingere~ meant both to paint something and to describe it.

That double meaning is what French kept. Modern ~dépeindre~ usually means to describe vividly, as though painting with words (~dépeindre la situation~). The family of ~pingere~ gave French ~peinture~ and ~peintre~ (through Latin ~pictūra~ and ~pictor~), as well as ~pigment~. The verb is irregular like ~peindre~ (~il dépeint~). A rarer sense, “to strip off paint,” reads ~dé-~ as the French prefix of removal, which is how the English analysis ~dé-~ + ~peindre~ would naturally be taken.
en.dépendre:
From Latin ~dependere~ (“to hang down, to hang from”), formed from the prefix ~de-~ (“down, from”) and the verb ~pendere~ (“to hang”), from Proto-Italic *~pendēō~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)pend-~ (“to stretch, to pull, to draw”). Cognate forms include English ~pendant~, ~suspend~, and ~pendulum~, all sharing the image of something stretched and hanging.

French ~dépendre~ carries two senses that are really one. The concrete meaning — to ~dépendre~ a picture is to take it down off its hook — preserves the literal Latin “to hang from.” The abstract meaning grew by metaphor: that which hangs from something else relies on it, is suspended from it, and so to ~dépendre de~ someone is to “depend on” them, to hang from their support. The same root *~(s)pend-~ spread through a remarkable family, because in Latin ~pendere~ also meant “to weigh” and “to pay” — money was once weighed out. From it French inherited ~suspendre~, ~pendre~, ~pension~, ~dépense~, ~pendule~, and ~appendice~, while the “weighing” branch gave ~peser~ and, through Spanish, the ~peso~. The English ~pound~ and even ~spider~ (the “spinner,” a stretcher of thread) belong to the same ancient web.
en.dépenser:
Attested from the 12th century, derived from the noun ~dépense~ (“expenditure”) with the verbal ending ~-er~. ~dépense~ comes from Latin ~dispensa~, the substantivized neuter past participle of ~dispendere~ (“to weigh out in distributing, hence to pay out”), ~dis-~ + ~pendere~ (“to weigh, to pay”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)pend-~ (“to stretch, to weigh”). The Latin noun ~dispendium~ already meant “cost, expense.”

The metaphor at the root is unmistakably mercantile: to spend was to weigh out portions of one's wealth, coin by coin, just as a steward weighed out rations. From money the verb spread to spending time, effort, or energy — one ~dépense~ one's strength as one ~dépense~ one's savings. Sharing the same ancestor ~pendere~ and the root *~(s)pend-~ are ~dispenser~, ~peser~ (“to weigh”), ~suspendre~, ~pension~, and ~pensée~ — a whole family in which weighing, paying, and pondering are one act.
en.dépersonnaliser: From ~dé-~ + ~personnaliser~. The base is itself a modern coinage: ~personnel~ plus the suffix ~-iser~. ~Personnel~ comes through Old French from Latin ~persōnālis~, from ~persōna~, a word that first named the mask worn by an actor. The prefix ~dé-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), here reverses the base: to ~dépersonnaliser~ is to strip something of its personal character, making it impersonal or anonymous.
en.dépeupler: ~Dépeupler~ is formed from ~peupler~ (“to populate”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base verb: to remove the inhabitants from a place. ~Peupler~ itself is built on ~peuple~, from Latin ~populus~. French Wiktionary adds that Latin had a parallel verb, ~depopulare~, so the French verb has a classical counterpart even though it was formed on ~peupler~. English borrowed the Latin verb as “depopulate,” while French built its own.
en.déphaser: ~Déphaser~ is formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ~phaser~, itself made from ~phase~, and means to put out of phase. The prefix ~dé-~, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), here reverses the base, as in ~défaire~.
en.déphosphorer: Formed from ~phosphore~ with the prefix ~dé-~ (“removal”) and the verb ending ~-er~: to remove phosphorus, for instance from iron. The noun comes from Latin ~phosphorus~, itself from Greek ~phōsphóros~ (“bringer of light”), a compound of ~phôs~ (“light”) and ~phérō~ (“to carry”). It was first the name of the morning star, and the element was named for the white glow it gives off in the dark when exposed to the oxygen in the air.
en.dépiauter: A rustic variant of ~dépeauter~, built from the prefix ~dé-~ (“off, away”), ~piau~ (a Picard form of ~peau~, “skin”), an epenthetic ~-t-~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The ~-t-~ is not a suffix of its own, only a consonant inserted between the vowel-final base and the ending. The literal sense is to remove the skin, as of a rabbit, and the verb extends to stripping off clothes or, figuratively, to taking something apart piece by piece.
en.dépiler:
~Dépiler~ (“to remove hair”) is traced by French Wiktionary to Latin ~dēpilāre~, and English Wiktionary calls it borrowed from that verb. The Latin was formed from the prefix ~dē-~ (“off, away”) and ~pilus~ (“hair”), so it meant “to pluck out the hair.” French Wiktionary also gives a second analysis, in which the verb is derived from a noun ~pile~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and the ending ~-er~, so the origin is not told by a single account.

The Latin root ~pilus~ is the source of the inherited French ~poil~ (“hair”) and of the learned ~pilosité~. The verb ~dépiler~ and its adjective ~dépilatoire~ are the bookish side of the family, used for hair removal in medicine and cosmetics. English took the same Latin verb as ~depilate~ and ~depilatory~. If the Latin account is right, ~dépiler~ is not really ~dé-~ plus a French base: the prefix and the root were fused before French existed.
en.dépiquer: Formed from ~piquer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which usually reverses the action of the base (from Latin ~dis-~, “apart”). The base ~piquer~ appears in the second half of the thirteenth century and its origin is debated. The TLFi favors a Vulgar Latin *~pīkkāre~ built on an expressive root imitating a sharp tap, and the verb has relatives in Italian ~piccare~ and Spanish ~picar~. French Wiktionary instead derives it from ~pic~, whose name goes back to Latin ~pīcus~ (“woodpecker”). The verb ~dépiquer~ is a French formation on that base.
en.dépister: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and ~pister~ (“to follow a trail”), literally “to look for the trail of.” The base verb comes from the noun ~piste~ (“track”), borrowed from Italian ~pista~. French Wiktionary traces that Italian word to the verb ~pistare~ (“to trample, to crush”), from Latin ~pistare~ (“to pound”), while English Wiktionary treats it as a variant of ~pesta~ (“footprint”). Both accounts agree on the picture of a track as what feet leave behind. The verb covers tracking an animal and, today, screening for a disease.
en.dépiter: ~Dépiter~ is formed from the noun ~dépit~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, and it means to vex or annoy someone, to cause them ~dépit~. The noun comes from Old French ~despit~ (“contempt”), attested from the twelfth to the seventeenth century, from Latin ~dēspectus~, a noun from ~dēspicere~ (“to look down on, to despise”). The same Latin verb is behind ~respect~ and ~répit~, according to fr.Wiktionary's cross-references, but the verb ~dépiter~ is now mostly found in the reflexive form ~se dépiter~, meaning to be vexed.
en.déplacer:
A French formation, ~déplacer~ is built from the verb ~placer~ (“to place”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses or undoes an action — to ~déplacer~ is literally to un-place, to take a thing from where it was set. ~Placer~ derives from ~place~, from Old French ~place~, from Latin ~platea~ (“broad street, open square, courtyard”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~πλατεῖα~ (~plateîa~, “broad way”), the feminine of “broad,” from the Proto-Indo-European root *~pleth₂-~ (“to spread out, to be flat”). Cognate with Italian ~piazza~, Spanish ~plaza~, and German ~Platz~.

The surprise is that the everyday French ~place~ began as a width: a ~platea~ was a wide thoroughfare, named for its flatness and breadth, and only later did the word narrow to a “spot” where a thing or person belongs. ~Placer~ assigns that spot; ~dé-~ revokes it. The same flat-and-broad root spread across French into ~place~, ~plat~, ~plateau~, ~plaine~, ~plan~, ~esplanade~, and ~remplacer~ (“to re-place, to replace”). Thus to ~déplacer~ furniture, a meeting, or oneself is, at root, to lift it off its flat appointed ground and set it elsewhere.
en.déplafonner: Formed in French from ~plafonner~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses its base: to remove a ceiling or upper limit. The verb ~plafonner~ comes from the noun ~plafond~, itself a compound of ~plat~ (“flat”) and ~fond~ (“bottom”), at first a flat surface seen as the bottom of a structure, then a ceiling. ~Plafonner~ took on the figurative sense of reaching a limit and capping something at a fixed maximum, and ~déplafonner~ lifts that cap.
en.déplaire: Built on ~plaire~ with the prefix ~dé-~ as a reversal: what ~plaire~ does, ~déplaire~ undoes, “to displease.” The French verb follows Latin ~displicēre~ (“to displease”), which was ~dis-~ plus ~placēre~ (“to please”), and ~dé-~ is the French outcome of ~dis-~ by way of Old French ~des-~. The Latin ~placēre~ is also behind Italian ~piacere~, Spanish ~placer~ and English ~please~, so the verb is a clear mirror image of a very old and widespread one.
en.déplanter: ~Déplanter~ is formed from ~planter~ and the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to pull a plant out of the ground, or to transplant it. The base descends from Latin ~plantare~, built on ~planta~. The noun first meant “sole of the foot,” though the link to the botanical sense (“shoot, cutting”) is only partly documented. The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.déplier: ~Déplier~ is ~dé-~ + ~plier~, the prefix reversing the action of the base: to unfold what had been folded. The base ~plier~ continues Latin ~plicāre~ (“to fold”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, to weave”), the same root as Greek ~plékō~ (“I weave”). The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The verb ~déployer~, from the same Latin root, is a near relative, so a map unfolded and an army deployed share one ancestor.
en.déplisser: Formed from ~plisser~ with the reversing prefix ~dé-~: to undo pleats or creases, “to unwrinkle.” The base is built on the noun ~pli~ (“fold”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, so ~plisser~ is “to make folds in.” French Wiktionary derives ~pli~ from Old French ~ploi~, taken from ~ploier~, while English Wiktionary calls it a back-formation from ~plier~ (“to fold”). The prefix ~dé-~, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), reverses this action and smooths out what was folded.
en.déplomber: Formed from ~plomber~ and the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to remove the lead. ~Plomber~ is built on ~plomb~ (“lead”), from Latin ~plumbum~, and meant to fit or seal with lead, as in sealing a package with a lead seal or filling a tooth. ~Déplomber~ undoes this: to break or remove such a seal, or to take out a filling. The same Latin metal gave Italian ~piombo~, Spanish ~plomo~, and English ~plumb~ and ~plumber~.
en.déplorer:
French ~déplorer~ (attested in the 12th century) is borrowed from Latin ~deplorare~ (“to weep over, to lament aloud”), formed from the intensifying prefix ~de-~ and the verb ~plorare~ (“to wail, to cry out, to weep aloud”). ~Plorare~ originally denoted not silent tears but loud, voiced weeping — a cry. Its deeper origin is uncertain; one proposal links it to a PIE *~pleh₃(w)-~ (“to flow”), but the connection is tentative and is best left flagged as such rather than asserted. Latin built a whole family of prefixed ~plorare~ verbs: ~deplorare~, ~implorare~ (“to beg, to cry to”), and ~explorare~ — which began as “to cry out” (perhaps a hunter's shout) before drifting to “to search out, explore.”

The sense traveled from full-throated mourning to the cooler modern range of ~déplorer~: to lament a loss, but also simply to regret or disapprove of something — ~déplorer~ une décision is to deplore it, not to weep over it. The vivid origin survives in the related ~éploré~ (“in tears, tearful”), still close to the literal wailing. From the same ~plorare~ stem French keeps ~implorer~ (“to implore, to beg”) and ~explorer~ (“to explore”), whose tie to weeping is now wholly invisible — a hunter's cry frozen, etymologically, inside every act of exploration.
en.déployer:
From Old French ~desploier~ (“to unfold”), formed from the prefix ~dé-~ (“un-, reversal”) and ~ployer~ (“to bend, to fold”). ~ployer~ — a doublet of modern ~plier~ — descends from Latin ~plicāre~ (“to fold, to roll up”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~plek-~ (“to plait, to fold”). The same root gives English ~ply~, ~pleat~, and ~fold~, Greek ~plekein~ (“to plait”), and a whole French cluster including ~plier~, ~pli~, and ~déplier~.

The literal sense is the heart of the word: to deploy is to un-fold. A folded banner, a folded sail, a folded map — ~déployer~ spreads it out flat and open. From this concrete gesture the verb stretched into military language, where troops once tightly packed are unfolded across a field of battle, and then into everyday figurative use: one deploys energy, charm, or arguments, spreading them out for full effect. English ~deploy~ and ~display~ are in fact the same word arriving twice, both from this ~desploier~. The shared root *~plek-~ runs through a remarkably wide family of French words — ~simple~, ~double~, ~complexe~, ~exploit~, ~employer~, and ~appliquer~ among them — all turning, in one way or another, on the idea of folds laid one against another.
en.déplumer: Formed from ~plumer~ with the prefix ~dé-~. The base verb is built on ~plume~ with ~-er~ and already means “to pluck”, so ~dé-~ adds no new idea beyond insisting on the stripping of feathers. The noun ~plume~ comes from Old French ~plume~, from Latin ~plūma~ (“feather, down”). The base ~plumer~ also has a figurative sense, “to swindle”.
en.déplâtrer: Formed from ~plâtrer~ and the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to remove the plaster. The base ~plâtrer~ comes from the noun ~plâtre~, inherited from Old French ~plastre~ (about 1165), from Vulgar Latin *~plastrum~, from Latin ~emplastrum~, from Greek ~émplastron~ (“daub, salve”). The noun is a form of ~emplâtre~ with its first syllable dropped. ~Déplâtrer~ therefore covers both senses of its base, taking plaster off a wall and taking a cast off a limb.
en.dépointer: Formed from ~pointer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action of the base (from Latin ~dis-~, “apart”), so “to un-point.” The base ~pointer~ was built within French on the noun ~point~, from Latin ~punctum~ (“a prick, a dot”), the past participle of ~pungere~ (“to prick”). Since ~pointer~ can mean “to clock in” or “to aim,” ~dépointer~ gives the opposites, “to clock out” and “to stop aiming a weapon.”
en.dépoitrailler: Formed from ~poitrail~ with the prefix ~dé-~, so the verb means to bare one's chest. The noun ~poitrail~ comes from Latin ~pectoralis~ through Old French ~poitral~, reshaped with the suffix ~-ail~; it is a doublet of ~pectoral~. The prefix ~dé-~ marks uncovering, the opposite of having the chest covered.
en.dépolariser: Formed from ~polariser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action of the base: to undo polarization. The base ~polariser~ is built from Latin ~polaris~ (“polar, of the pole”) and the verbal suffix ~-iser~, and ~polaris~ in turn rests on ~polus~, the pole of the sky or of an axis, a word Latin took from Greek. The verb belongs to the vocabulary of physics, where ~polariser~ means giving light or a magnet a direction. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.dépolir: ~Dépolir~ is built on ~polir~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to take the polish off a surface, as with glass or metal, leaving it dull. The base ~polir~ was borrowed from Latin ~polīre~ (“to smooth, to polish”) through Old French, and it is the source of Italian ~pulire~, Spanish ~pulir~ and English ~polish~. Latin ~polītus~, the participle, gave the adjective ~polite~ in English, a sign of how smoothness became a matter of manners.
en.dépolitiser: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and ~politiser~, itself ~politique~ plus the suffix ~-iser~. The adjective ~politique~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~politicus~, which came from Ancient Greek ~politikós~, built on ~polítēs~ (“citizen”) with the suffix ~-ikós~. The suffix ~-iser~ means “make A,” so ~politiser~ is to give something a political character, and ~dé-~ reverses that: ~dépolitiser~ is to strip the political dimension from a subject, a debate or a person.
en.dépolluer: Formed from ~polluer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action of the base: to ~dépolluer~ is to clean up what has been polluted. The base ~polluer~ is borrowed from Latin ~polluere~ (“to defile, contaminate”), once used of ritual or moral impurity and later narrowed in French to physical contamination of air, water and soil. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and it is among the most productive prefixes in French for undoing a state.
en.dépolymériser: Formed from ~polymériser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which marks reversal: to ~dépolymériser~ is to break a polymer back down into smaller units. ~Polymériser~ is itself made from ~polymère~ and the suffix ~-iser~. The noun ~polymère~ comes from Greek ~polumerês~ (“composed of many parts”), analyzed as ~poly-~ and ~-mère~. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~.
en.déporter:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~dēportāre~ (“to carry away, to convey”), formed from ~dē-~ (“away from”) and ~portāre~ (“to carry”). French speakers can still parse it as ~dé-~ plus ~porter~, and English Wiktionary describes that as a surface analysis rather than the real history, since the verb arrived from Latin already formed. ~Portāre~ gave French ~porter~ and, among others, English ~port~ in ~portable~ and ~transport~, which come from related Latin forms.

In Roman law, ~dēportāre~ also meant to banish someone, notably to an island, and the Latin noun ~dēportātiō~ named that punishment. French kept this sense of removal by authority: ~déporter~ is to send a person away from a country or into forced exile or confinement. The word took a grim weight in the twentieth century with mass deportations, and the nouns ~déportation~ and ~déporté~ are now bound to that history. In a milder, physical sense, ~déporter~ also describes a vehicle or a current pushing something off course.
en.déposer:
Formed in French from the prefix ~dé-~ (“down, away,” from Latin ~de-~) and the verb ~poser~ (“to place, to set”). ~Poser~ has a famously tangled history: in form it continues Late Latin ~pausāre~ (“to halt, to cease,” borrowed from Greek ~pausis~, “a stopping”), seen in early Christian epitaphs such as ~hic pausat in pace~. But in meaning it merged with Latin ~ponere~ (“to put,” past participle ~positus~), so completely that all the French “-poser” verbs took over the senses of ~ponere~ — hence the nouns in ~-position~ rather than ~-pausation~.

With ~dé-~ added, the verb first meant “to set down what one was carrying,” then spread to “to lay aside,” “to entrust” (to ~déposer~ money at a bank), and figuratively “to depose,” to set a ruler down from the throne. The double parentage still shows in the family: from the ~pausāre~ side come ~pause~ and ~repos~ (“rest”), while the ~ponere~ side surfaces in ~déposition~, ~dépôt~, and the cousins ~exposer~, ~imposer~, and ~proposer~ — a whole conjugation built on a verb that, etymologically, means both “to rest” and “to put.”
en.déposséder: ~Déposséder~ is formed from ~posséder~ with the prefix ~dé-~, here meaning removal: “to take away what someone holds.” ~Posséder~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~possidēre~ (“to own, to hold”), which replaced the inherited Old French ~posseoir~. The Latin verb joins ~potis~ (“master, able”) and ~sedēre~ (“to sit”), so it pictured an owner “seated as master.” The French family also includes ~possession~, ~possesseur~ and ~possessif~.
en.dépoter: ~Dépoter~ is formed from the noun ~pot~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here expresses removal: to take a plant out of its pot. The base ~pot~ is inherited from Old French ~pot~, from Vulgar Latin ~pottus~ (“pot, jar”), from Frankish *~pott~, from Proto-Germanic *~puttaz~ (“pot, jar, tub”), a word that also gave English ~pot~. The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and builds verbs from nouns by taking away what the noun names.
en.dépouiller:
French ~dépouiller~ is inherited from Middle French ~despouiller~, from Old French ~despoillier~ (attested in the twelfth century), from Latin ~dēspoliāre~, itself built from ~dē-~ (“off”) and ~spoliāre~ (“to strip, to plunder”). The verb ~spoliāre~ comes from the noun ~spolium~, which meant the hide stripped from an animal and, by extension, booty taken from an enemy. Catalan ~despullar~ and Romanian ~despuia~ are close relatives, and English ~spoil~ and ~despoil~ share the same Latin ancestry.

The literal first sense is to skin an animal, to take off its hide. From there the verb widened to stripping a person of clothing or of possessions, and then to any removal of a covering. A later set of senses is more surprising: ~dépouiller~ also means to go through documents. French Wiktionary dates the sense of examining an account to 1690, and ~dépouiller le scrutin~ is to count the ballots. One way to see the link is that the contents of the ballot box or the file are stripped out and laid bare, though the sources do not spell this out. Related words include ~dépouille~ (“hide, remains”), ~dépouillement~, ~spolier~ and ~spoliation~.
en.dépourvoir:
~Dépourvoir~ is built from the privative prefix ~dé-~ (Latin ~dis-~, “apart, away”) on ~pourvoir~ (“to provide, to supply”), which descends from Latin ~prōvidēre~ (“to foresee, to look ahead for, to provide for”). That verb is itself transparent: ~prō-~ (“ahead, in front”) joined to ~vidēre~ (“to see”), from Proto-Italic *~widēō~ and ultimately from PIE *~weyd-~ (“to see”), one of the most productive roots in the family. Latin ~prōvidēre~ passed into Old French as ~porveoir~, and the earliest French trace of the negative form is the participle ~desporveu~, attested in 1190. The same Latin verb produced Italian ~provvedere~, Spanish ~proveer~, Portuguese ~prover~ and Catalan ~proveir~; crossing the Channel with the Normans, it gave English three words at once — ~provide~, taken from the Latin, alongside ~purvey~ and ~purview~, which came by the softer Anglo-Norman route.

~Dépourvoir~ is the rare negative twin of ~pourvoir~: where one supplies, the other strips bare. It is a defective verb, and spectacularly so. The TLFi records it only in the infinitive and the compound tenses, and adds the deflating remark that its dictionary examples answer to no attested usage at all, more recent dictionaries having dropped the entry altogether. What survives is the participle: ~dépourvu~ (“devoid of, destitute of”), and above all the phrase ~prendre au dépourvu~ (“to catch off guard”) — literally, to catch someone who has not provided ahead. The same root *~weyd-~ runs through the whole French vocabulary of seeing and foreseeing: ~voir~, ~prévoir~, ~évident~, ~providence~. Its best-disguised descendant is ~prudent~, from Latin ~prūdēns~, a worn-down contraction of ~prōvidēns~ (“seeing ahead”): a prudent person is, etymologically, one who saw it coming.
en.dépoussiérer: ~Dépoussiérer~ is built from the noun ~poussière~ (“dust”) with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The prefix expresses removal, as in other verbs made from a noun: to take the dust off. The noun ~poussière~ comes from Old French ~pousiere~, derived from ~pous~, which goes back to Latin ~pulvis~ (“dust”) through a Vulgar Latin neuter form *~pulvus~. Beyond wiping dust from objects, the verb is used figuratively, for freshening up something old or dated.
en.dépoétiser: ~Dépoétiser~ is formed from ~poétiser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to strip something of its poetry. ~Poétiser~ is built on ~poète~ with ~-iser~, and ~poète~ was borrowed from Latin ~poēta~, from Ancient Greek ~ποιητής~ (“maker, poet”), from ~ποιέω~ (“to make, to compose”). A poet is thus etymologically a “maker”, and to ~dépoétiser~ is to un-make that quality.
en.dépraver:
~Dépraver~ was taken from Latin ~dēprāvāre~ (“to corrupt”), which is ~dē-~ plus ~prāvus~ (“crooked, perverse”). The Latin verb meant to make crooked, hence to twist from what is right, and French kept the figurative sense. Because it came from Latin already formed, ~dépraver~ is not the French prefix ~dé-~ added to a verb *~praver~, a form that does not exist. Related Romance verbs include Italian ~depravare~ and Spanish ~depravar~, and English took ~deprave~ from the same Latin source.

In French, ~dépraver~ means to corrupt morally, to pervert taste, habits or character, and it is used more often in the past participle ~dépravé~, a person whose morals have been twisted. The family includes ~dépravation~, the state or act of being corrupted. The root ~prāvus~ itself gave little else to French, so ~dépraver~ and its relatives are somewhat isolated learned words.
en.déprendre: Formed from ~prendre~ with the prefix ~dé-~. The base ~prendre~ comes from Latin ~prēndere~, a contracted form of ~prehendere~ (“to seize”). The prefix ~dé-~ undoes the taking, so the verb means “to detach, to let go” and, said of a person, “to abandon.” The same base produced a whole prefixed family: ~apprendre~, ~comprendre~, ~reprendre~, ~surprendre~.
en.dépressuriser: Formed from ~pressuriser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to release the pressure of a sealed space, such as an aircraft cabin. The base was borrowed from English ~pressurize~, itself built on ~pressure~ and ~-ize~. English Wiktionary instead analyzes the French verb as ~pressure~ plus ~-iser~, and French Wiktionary notes that a verb based on ~pression~ would have been possible too. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.déprimer:
~Déprimer~ comes from Latin ~dēprimere~, a compound of ~dē-~ (“down”) and ~premere~ (“to press”), meaning “to press down, to push under.” English has the same verb as ~depress~, and the same Latin ~premere~ stands behind ~press~, ~express~, ~oppress~ and ~repress~. The sense of lowering by pressure is easy to see in the parts: ~dē-~ gives the direction and ~premere~ the force.

In modern French ~déprimer~ is both transitive (“to discourage, to weaken”) and intransitive (“to feel depressed”), and the adjective ~déprimé~ and noun ~dépression~ cover the mood, the weather system and the economic slump alike. The step from a pressed-down surface to a pressed-down spirit is the same picture in French and English: something that weighs on a person's morale. The Latin ~premere~ also gave ~presser~, ~pression~, ~exprimer~, ~opprimer~, ~réprimer~, ~imprimer~ and ~comprimer~, a family built on the gesture of pushing.
en.dépriser:
From Old French ~depreiser~ or ~desprisier~ (twelfth century, “to show contempt for”), inherited from Late Latin ~dēpretiāre~ (“to lower the price of, to undervalue”). That verb is built from ~dē-~ (“down, away”) and ~pretium~ (“worth, price”), the noun that also gave French ~prix~. French Wiktionary presents the verb as a derivative of ~priser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, and the two accounts fit together, since ~priser~ goes back to the Latin verb ~pretiāre~ (“to value”). ~Dépriser~ is a doublet of ~déprécier~, which comes from the same Late Latin verb by a learned route.

The Late Latin source meant “to lower the price of,” and the recorded Old French sense is already the contemptuous one. The verb is uncommon today, and its many relatives are more familiar. The root ~pretium~ gives French ~prix~, ~priser~, ~mépriser~ (“to despise”), ~apprécier~, ~précieux~ and ~dépréciation~. It also lies behind Italian ~prezzo~ and Spanish ~precio~. English has it twice over through Old French, as ~price~ and ~praise~.
en.déprogrammer: Formed from ~programmer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to ~déprogrammer~ is to take something off a schedule, such as a show, a screening or a meeting, or to pull it from the air. The base ~programmer~ comes from the noun ~programme~, which French took from Greek ~prógramma~ (“public written notice”), from ~prográphein~ (“to write beforehand, to write publicly”). The sense of coding a computer was added to ~programmer~ in the twentieth century, but ~déprogrammer~ is used chiefly for cancelling a scheduled event.
en.déprolétariser: ~Déprolétariser~ is formed from ~prolétariser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the base: to undo the reduction of a person or class to the condition of proletarians. The base is built on ~prolétaire~ with the suffix ~-iser~. ~Prolétaire~ is borrowed from Latin ~prolētārius~, a poor Roman citizen who served the state mainly through his children, from ~prōlēs~ (“offspring”). The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.déprotéger: Formed from ~protéger~ with the reversing prefix ~dé-~: to remove protection from something. The base comes from Latin ~protegere~ (“to cover in front, to shelter”), a compound of ~pro-~ (“in front”) and ~tegere~ (“to cover”). The root of ~tegere~ is the Proto-Indo-European *~(s)teg-~ (“to cover, to roof”), shared with Greek ~stégein~ and English ~thatch~. Italian ~proteggere~ and Spanish ~proteger~ are the Romance parallels, and English ~protect~ comes from the same Latin verb.
en.déprécier:
French ~déprécier~ was borrowed from Late Latin ~dēpretiāre~, a verb built on Latin ~pretium~ (“price, value”) with the prefix ~dē-~ (“down”). It is a doublet of ~dépriser~: the two verbs share the same Latin source but reached French in different forms, so they stand side by side as separate words. The Latin noun ~pretium~ is the root of many familiar French words, such as ~prix~ and ~précieux~.

The sense of the verb is to lower the value of something, whether in money or in esteem. English ~depreciate~ comes from the same Late Latin verb. The family around ~pretium~ is large: ~priser~ (“to value”), ~apprécier~ and ~mépriser~ all belong to it, and English ~price~, ~praise~ and ~appreciate~ come from the same Latin stock. The pair ~déprécier~ and ~dépriser~ thus shows how French can take one Latin verb twice and give each version its own career.
en.dépuceler: ~Dépuceler~ is built from ~pucelle~ (“maiden, virgin”) with the prefix ~dé-~, in its sense of removal, and the verb ending ~-er~: to take away a girl's virginity, hence to deflower. ~Pucelle~ itself goes back to Old French ~pucele~, first attested in the 10th century as ~pulcella~, from Vulgar Latin *~pūllicella~. Its origin is debated. It may be a diminutive of Latin ~pullus~ (“young animal, chick”), or ~pullus~ may be a contraction of *~purulus~, from ~purus~ (“pure”). A third account derives it from Latin ~puella~ (“girl”).
en.dépulper: Formed from ~pulpe~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ending ~-er~, an analysis that French and English Wiktionary share. ~Pulpe~ is borrowed from Latin ~pulpa~ (“flesh”). With ~dé-~ marking removal, the verb describes taking the pulp from a fruit; it can also mean to mash something to a pulp.
en.dépurer: French Wiktionary derives ~dépurer~ from ~épurer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, while English Wiktionary treats it as borrowed from Medieval Latin ~dēpūrāre~, from ~pūrus~ (“pure”); the two accounts agree on the idea of purifying. The base ~épurer~ continues Old French ~espurer~, attested about 1220 with the senses “to purify” and “to purge.” It is built on ~é-~ (“out”) and ~pur~, going back to Latin ~pūrus~.
en.députer:
From Latin ~deputare~, formed from ~de-~ and ~putare~ (“to reckon, estimate, consider”). ~putare~ began as “to clean, to prune,” a denominative of ~putus~ (“clean”); the shift from trimming to reckoning runs through the idea of cutting away to get a clear account — the same metaphor seen in deciding (Latin ~decidere~, literally “to cut off”). The deeper Proto-Indo-European root of ~putus~ is uncertain and is best left unstated. In Latin ~deputare~ meant “to count off, to assign,” and from that French drew ~députer~: to assign someone, to send them off charged with a duty.

The semantic heart is delegation — to ~députer~ is to appoint a person to act on others' behalf. That sense crystallized in the great nouns of representative government: a ~député~ is one sent to deliberate for those who chose him, and a ~députation~ is a delegation dispatched on a mission. From the same ~putare~ French gathers a wide harvest — ~compter~ and ~conter~ (both from ~computare~), ~réputation~, ~dispute~, and ~amputer~ — a family in which the old senses of pruning and of reckoning still quietly coexist.
en.dépénaliser: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ (“undoing”) and ~pénal~ (“penal”), or from the verb ~pénaliser~, as the two Wiktionaries phrase it. The adjective ~pénal~ was borrowed from Latin ~poenālis~, itself related to ~peine~ (“penalty”). The verb means to remove the criminal status from an act, so that it is no longer punished by criminal law.
en.dépérir: A learned borrowing from Latin ~dēpereō~, which French Wiktionary traces back to ~périr~. Latin ~perīre~ (“to perish, to be lost”) is ~per-~ (“through, away”) plus ~īre~ (“to go”), and the prefix ~dē-~ strengthens it, so the Latin verb means roughly “to be utterly lost.” In French, ~dépérir~ settled on the slower sense of wasting away: a plant, a business or a person that declines and fades. It stays close to ~périr~ and ~périssable~.
en.dépêcher:
From Old French ~despeechier~ (also ~despescher~), built from the prefix ~dés-~ (“undo, remove”) and the stem of ~empeschier~ (“to hinder”), the ancestor of modern ~empêcher~. That Old French verb comes from Late Latin ~impedicāre~ (“to shackle, to entangle”), from ~pedica~ (“a fetter”), from ~pēs~ (“foot”). So ~dépêcher~ literally unshackles: it removes the fetter from the feet.

Etymologically, ~dépêcher~ means to remove obstacles and entanglements in order to get a task done promptly. The noun ~dépêche~ (“a message sent urgently,” then “a telegram”) belongs to the same family, and the reflexive ~se dépêcher~ (“to hurry”) is the commonest use today. The picture is of a traveler or a task freed from its shackles, and ~empêcher~ is the shackle itself.
en.dépêtrer: The verb is the opposite of ~empêtrer~ (“to entangle”). French Wiktionary explains it as a contraction of ~désempêtrer~, while English Wiktionary sees a formation on the model of ~empêtrer~, with the prefix ~dé-~ replacing ~em-~. In both accounts the reversing prefix ~dé-~, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), undoes the entangling, so the verb means to free from a tangle.
en.déqualifier: Formed in French from ~qualifier~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base verb, so “to strip of qualification” and thus to deskill. The base comes from Medieval Latin ~qualificare~, built from Latin ~qualis~ (“of what kind”) and ~facere~ (“to make”). The prefix ~dé-~ goes back through Old French ~des-~ to Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The family of ~qualis~ includes ~qualité~ and ~quel~, and the ending ~-ficare~ recurs in ~modifier~ and ~vérifier~.
en.déraciner: The verb is formed from ~raciner~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses it. The base ~raciner~ is itself ~racine~ (“root”) + ~-er~, “to take root,” and is rare today. So ~déraciner~ means to undo the rooting, to pull out by the roots, and by extension to uproot a person from their home. The noun ~racine~ is inherited from Late Latin ~radīcīna~, built on Latin ~rādīx~ (“root”).
en.dérader: Formed from ~rade~ (“roadstead,” a sheltered anchorage) with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. It means, of a ship, to be driven from its anchorage out to sea. The noun ~rade~ entered Middle French in the fifteenth century from Middle English ~rade~, an early form of ~rode~, from Old English ~rād~ (“a ride, riding”). It is therefore a doublet of ~raid~, and it is related to English ~road~. The prefix ~dé-~ marks the removal, here from the anchorage.
en.dérager: Formed from ~rager~ (“to rage”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which marks cessation: to stop being angry. ~Rager~ is built on the noun ~rage~, from Vulgar Latin *~rabia~, an altered form of Latin ~rabiēs~ (“rage”). The ~-bi-~ became ~-ge~ in French, as in ~singe~ from Latin ~simium~. Spanish ~rabia~ is a cognate.
en.déraidir: Formed from ~raidir~ (“to make stiff”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: “to make less stiff.” ~Raidir~ is built on the adjective ~raide~ with the ending ~-ir~; ~raide~ is the modern spelling of ~roide~, from Old French ~roit~, from Latin ~rigidus~, of which the learned ~rigide~ is a doublet.
en.dérailler: Formed from ~rail~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ending ~-er~: “to leave the rails”. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and here it expresses removal from the base. The base ~rail~ was borrowed from English ~rail~, as both Wiktionaries record, and English Wiktionary adds that it is a doublet of ~règle~, ~reille~, ~rigole~ and ~rille~, words that share a common ancestor but reached French by different routes.
en.déraisonner: Formed from ~raisonner~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to reason badly, to talk without reason. English Wiktionary instead derives it from the noun ~déraison~ (“unreason”) plus ~-er~, and notes an Old French ~deraisnier~; either way the result is the opposite of ~raisonner~. That base verb comes from the noun ~raison~, from Latin ~ratio~ (“reckoning, reasoning”), and in Old French ~raisnier~ meant “to speak”. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.déramer: Formed from ~ramer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base. ~Ramer~ is built on ~rame~ (“oar”), from Latin ~rēmus~, and means to row. ~Dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The verb is used for fanning paper.
en.déranger:
From Old French ~ranger~ (earlier ~rengier~, “to arrange in a row”), a denominal verb from ~rang~ (“rank, row”), prefixed with ~dé-~ (Latin ~dis-~, marking reversal). The noun ~rang~ is not Latin at all: it comes from Old French ~renc~, borrowed from Frankish *~hring~ (“ring, circle”), from Proto-Germanic *~hringaz~ (“ring, circle”). It is thus a cognate of English ~ring~ and German ~Ring~ — and, by a curious loop, of English ~rank~, which English borrowed back from French ~rang~.

The semantics are wonderfully concrete. To ~ranger~ is to set things in their proper row; ~déranger~ is to break that order — to pull a thing out of its rank. From this literal “disarrangement” the verb broadened to the figurative “to disturb, to bother,” the sense that now dominates: ~déranger quelqu'un~ is to intrude on someone's peace, not to muddle their furniture. The Germanic “circle” at the root surfaces across the modern family: ~ranger~ (“to tidy”), ~rangée~ (“a row”), and ~rang~ (“rank”) itself. So the everyday apology ~je ne veux pas vous déranger~ rests, etymologically, on the image of not knocking someone out of their ring.
en.déraper:
~Déraper~ is descended from a dialectal Middle French ~déraper~ (“to tear at”), taken from Occitan ~derapar~ or ~derrabar~ (“to tear, to uproot”); French Wiktionary gives the Occitan form ~desrapar~. The Occitan verb is analyzed as ~de-~ + ~rapar~ (“to seize, to remove”), and ~rapar~ is traced to a Gothic verb *~rapōn~ (“to snatch, to steal”), from Proto-Germanic *~hrapōną~ (“to scratch, touch, pluck out, snatch”).

Behind the Germanic verb, English Wiktionary places the Proto-Indo-European roots *~(s)kreb(h)-~ and *~(s)kerb(h)-~ (“to turn, bend, shrink”), themselves from *~(s)ker-~ (“to turn, bend”). Old English ~hreppan~ (“to touch, treat”) and Old Norse ~hreppa~ (“to touch, grasp, receive”) are cognates, and English Wiktionary points to ~raffle~ for the wider family. By the Occitan stage the sense had reached “to tear away, to uproot,” but the sources do not trace how the verb arrived at its modern senses of “to skid, to slide” and “to get out of hand.”
en.déraser: Formed from ~raser~ with the prefix ~dé-~: to level a wall or a piece of ground down to a lower height. The base ~raser~ is inherited from Old French, from Vulgar Latin *~rāsāre~, a frequentative built on ~rāsus~, the past participle of Latin ~rādō~ (“to shave, to scratch”). Modern ~raser~ covers “to shave,” “to raze” and “to bore.” Here the prefix does not undo ~raser~ but intensifies it, lowering something that is already flush.
en.dératiser: Formed from ~rat~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and the suffix ~-iser~: to ~dératiser~ is to rid a place, such as a ship, a cellar or a warehouse, of its rats. The prefix ~dé-~ marks removal, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~. The noun ~rat~ is of Germanic origin, from Old High German ~rato~ or a Frankish *~rato~, though the TLFi alternatively proposes an imitation of the sound of gnawing, and other accounts suggest a Celtic source. Its English counterpart ~rat~ is a cognate, and so are German ~Ratte~ and Dutch ~rat~.
en.dérayer: French Wiktionary gives more than one account. The main one derives it from ~rayer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, in the sense “to stop furrowing,” so “to finish plowing”; it is traced to Old French ~desreer~ and ~desroyer~ and related to Occitan ~desreiar~. A second account sees an alteration of ~drayer~ that speakers reinterpreted as ~dé-~ + ~rayer~. A third, for a different sense, reads it as “to remove stripes.” The base ~rayer~ is formed on ~raie~ (“line, furrow”).
en.déresponsabiliser: Formed from ~responsabiliser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the base: to ~déresponsabiliser~ someone is to take away their sense of responsibility. The base ~responsabiliser~ was built in French on the adjective ~responsable~ plus ~-iser~ (“to make responsible”). That adjective rests on ~réponse~ (“answer”) with ~-able~, so a responsible person is one who can be called to answer. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and is often paired with ~-iser~ verbs to mark the end of a state.
en.dérider: Formed from ~rider~ (“to wrinkle”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which here marks removal. ~Dérider~ therefore means to smooth the wrinkles from something and, by extension, to cheer someone up, since a furrowed brow relaxes into a smile. The base ~rider~ is probably descended from Old High German ~rīdan~ (“to turn, twist”) through Old French, and is the verb behind the noun ~ride~ (“wrinkle”). Neither Wiktionary explains how “twist” became “wrinkle.”
en.dériver:
In the sense “to derive, to originate from,” ~dériver~ comes from Latin ~dērīvāre~, literally “to draw off a watercourse,” from ~dē-~ (“away from”) and ~rīvus~ (“stream, brook”). French sources are emphatic on one point that catches everyone out: despite appearances, the verb descends from ~rīvus~ (the water), not from ~rive~ (“bank, shore,” Latin ~rīpa~). To derive a result is thus to channel it off from its source as one would divert a stream. Italian ~derivare~ and Spanish ~derivar~ carry the same image.

From “draw off water” the verb broadened to “flow from, proceed from,” giving the grammarian's ~dérivé~ (“derivative”) and ~dérivation~. There is, however, a homonym to flag: the nautical ~dériver~, “to drift off course,” which the TLFi traces not to ~rīvus~ at all but to a borrowing influenced by English ~to drive~ (“to push, to drive along”), recorded from the early 16th century — and explicitly not, despite the tempting picture, to ~rive~. The two strands are best kept apart. From ~rīvus~ French also has ~rivière~ (“river”) and ~ru~, and the English doublets ~derive~ and ~rivulet~.
en.dérober:
From Old French ~desrober~ (“to steal, to strip”), formed from ~des-~ and ~rober~ (“to steal”). ~Rober~ itself comes from Late Latin ~raubāre~, borrowed from Frankish *~raubōn~ (“to plunder”), from Proto-Germanic *~raubōną~ (“to rob”). The Germanic verb has cousins elsewhere: English ~rob~ (borrowed through Old French), German ~rauben~, Italian ~rubare~ and Spanish ~robar~. French Wiktionary also gives a second analysis of ~dérober~, as derived from ~robe~, so the sources offer two routes.

The Germanic word for plunder reached French along with the Franks. To ~dérober~ something from sight is to hide it, and ~à la dérobée~ means “furtively”. The reflexive ~se dérober~ means “to slip away, to avoid a duty or a question”, and is also what a horse does when it balks at a jump, giving the noun ~dérobade~.
en.dérocher: Formed from ~rocher~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here marks removal: to clear rocks away. ~Rocher~ is built on ~roche~ (from an earlier ~rochier~), and ~roche~ comes from Late Latin ~rocca~, of uncertain and probably pre-Latin origin. Compare Italian ~rocca~, Spanish ~roca~ and English ~rock~. The prefix ~dé-~ descends from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and in verbs built on a noun it often means “take away what the noun names.”
en.déroder: Formed from ~roder~ with the prefix ~dé-~. The base comes from Latin ~rōdere~ (“to gnaw, to wear away”), which also gave Italian ~rodere~, French ~éroder~ and ~corroder~, and English ~rodent~, ~erode~ and ~corrode~. In modern French ~roder~ means to run in an engine or, figuratively, to smooth out a method through use. ~Déroder~ carries the prefix's sense of removal, and the verb is glossed as thinning a forest by clearing dead wood.
en.déroger:
From Latin ~dērogāre~, formed from ~dē-~ (“away, down”) and ~rogāre~ (“to ask”). In Roman public law ~rogāre~ meant to put a proposal to the people for a vote, and so ~dērogāre~ meant to repeal part of a law or to take something away from it. The same ~rogāre~ is in several other French verbs: ~interroger~ (“to question”), ~proroger~ (“to extend a term”), ~abroger~ (“to repeal”), and ~arroger~ (“to claim wrongly”). English ~derogate~ and ~derogatory~ come from the Latin as well.

The French verb began as a legal term for partially suspending an existing rule, and from there it grew to mean to depart from a rule or an obligation: ~déroger à la règle~ is to make an exception to it. A curious older use belongs to the social history of France. A nobleman who took up a trade or any occupation judged unworthy of his rank was said to ~déroger~, and risked losing his noble status. The sense of lowering oneself lingers in phrases such as ~déroger à son rang~. The family also has ~dérogation~ (“exemption”) and ~dérogatoire~.
en.dérougir: The verb is formed from ~rougir~ (“to turn red”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action of the base: to cause something to stop being red. ~Rougir~ is built on the adjective ~rouge~ with the ending ~-ir~, which makes verbs of becoming, and is attested in Old French as ~rogir~. ~Rouge~ itself comes through Old French ~roge~ from Latin ~rubeus~ (“reddish”). It is a French formation, undoing the change that ~rougir~ describes.
en.dérouiller: ~Dérouiller~ is formed from ~rouiller~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the base: to remove the rust. ~Rouiller~ is a denominal on ~rouille~ (“rust”), already found in Old French. The noun comes from Old French ~reoïlle~, from Late or Vulgar Latin *~robicula~, a diminutive of Latin ~rōbīgō~ (“rust”), which English Wiktionary links to ~rūfus~ (“red”), so rust was named for its color. The prefix ~dé-~ descends from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”) and is one of the most productive prefixes in French.
en.dérouler:
From the verb ~rouler~ (“to roll”) with the privative, reversing prefix ~dé-~ (Latin ~dis-~), so literally “to un-roll.” ~Rouler~ comes from Old French ~roeler~, a derivative of ~roele~ (“little wheel”), from Latin ~rotella~, a diminutive of ~rota~ (“wheel”). ~Rota~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~Hrot-eh₂-~, from the root *~Hret-~ (“to run, to roll”), which also gave German ~Rad~ (“wheel”), Sanskrit ~ratha~ (“chariot”), and Lithuanian ~ratas~ (“wheel”).

The whole word is a small machine of meaning: a wheel (~rota~) turns, so a scroll or carpet ~se déroule~ when its rolled-up length is let out flat. From the literal “unroll” grew the figurative senses “to unfold, to take place over time” — events that ~se déroulent~ like a banner being released. The opposite ~enrouler~ rolls something back up. From the same ~rota~ come a rich family: ~roue~ (“wheel”), ~rouleau~, ~roulette~, ~rotule~ (“kneecap,” the little wheel of the knee), ~rotation~, ~ronde~, and even ~rôle~ — originally a ~rotulus~, a rolled-up sheet of parchment on which an actor's lines were written.
en.dérouter: ~Dérouter~ is formed from ~dé-~ (reversal, removal), the noun ~route~ and the verb ending ~-er~. It is a close parallel of ~dévoyer~, according to English Wiktionary. Its first sense is “to send off course,” and the figurative “to disconcert” follows from it. The noun ~route~ comes from Old French ~rote~, from Latin ~rupta~, the “broken” way (~via rupta~), from the verb ~rumpere~ (“to break”). French Wiktionary notes that some scholars prefer a pre-Roman Celtic origin instead. The noun ~déroute~, “rout, defeat,” comes from an older sense of ~route~ and not from the verb.
en.déréaliser: ~Déréaliser~ is built on ~réaliser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the base: to strip something of its link with reality. The root is ~réel~, from Late Latin ~reālis~ (“relating to material things”), a derivative of Latin ~rēs~ (“thing”). The verb ~réaliser~ is itself a French formation, ~réel~ plus ~-iser~. The sense “to make unreal” is mostly psychological or philosophical, and the same family gives ~irréel~ and ~réalité~.
en.déréglementer: Formed from ~réglementer~ (“to regulate”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the base: to remove rules rather than impose them. This is the “cessation of a state” use of ~dé-~, common in political and technical vocabulary. ~Réglementer~ itself rests on the noun ~règlement~ (“regulation”), which is built from ~régler~ (“to regulate, to settle”) and the suffix ~-ment~. The verb is therefore a layered French formation: ~régler~, then ~règlement~, then ~réglementer~, then its undoing.
en.dérégler: ~Dérégler~ is formed from ~régler~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to upset what had been set in order, hence “to disturb, to disrupt.” The base ~régler~ is a denominal verb from the noun ~règle~ (“rule, ruler”), itself from Latin ~rēgula~ (“straight stick, rule”), a derivative of ~regere~ (“to keep straight, to direct”). The same Latin family gave French ~régulier~ and ~réguler~.
en.désabonner: ~Désabonner~ is ~abonner~ with the reversing prefix ~dés-~, the form of ~dé-~ used before a vowel, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). To ~désabonner~ is therefore to undo a subscription. The base ~abonner~ comes from Old French ~aboner~ (“to set boundaries”), itself from ~bone~ (“boundary marker, limit”), a noun of unknown ultimate origin. The modern sense of subscribing is a later development from the idea of fixing a limit, and the sources do not document that step.
en.désabuser: ~Désabuser~ is formed from ~abuser~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to undo a deception, hence “to set someone straight.” The base ~abuser~ comes from the noun ~abus~ plus ~-er~, and ~abus~ from Latin ~abūsus~ (“misuse”), from the verb ~abūtī~ (“to use up, to use wrongly”).
