Among its senses, ~abuser~ meant “to mislead,” and ~désabuser~ is its exact opposite.
en.désaccentuer: Formed from ~accentuer~ with the prefix ~dés-~, so it means to strip the accents or diacritics from a text. ~Accentuer~ is attested from the 12th century, from Medieval Latin ~accentuāre~, from Latin ~accentus~, built from ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~cantus~ (“song”), a calque of Greek ~prosōidía~. An accent was thus a “song” added to a syllable. ~Dés-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.désacclimater: Formed from ~acclimater~ with the prefix ~dés-~, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), which reverses the base: to de-acclimatize. The base was formed on ~climat~ with ~a-~, from Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”), and the ending ~-er~, so “to bring to a climate.” ~Climat~ came through Latin ~clima~ from Greek ~klíma~, the “inclination” of the earth toward the pole, and so a zone. The Greek word belongs to the verb ~klínein~ (“to incline”).
en.désaccorder: Formed from ~accorder~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base verb. ~Dés-~ is the form of ~dé-~ used before a vowel, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The base ~accorder~ comes from Late Latin ~accordare~ (“to bring into agreement”), built on ~ad-~ (“toward”) and ~cor~ (“heart”). To ~désaccorder~ is thus to undo that agreement: to put an instrument out of tune, or, in the reflexive and figurative uses, to bring discord where there had been harmony.
en.désaccoupler: Formed from ~accoupler~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the action: to undo a coupling. The base ~accoupler~ is itself ~coupler~ with ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~), and ~coupler~ comes from Latin ~cōpulāre~ (“to join together”), built on ~cōpula~ (“bond, tie”). The prefix ~dés-~ goes back through Old French ~des-~ to Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). So ~désaccoupler~ means to take apart what was paired: to uncouple machines, to separate animals that were mated, to release things that were joined.
en.désaccoutumer: Formed from ~accoutumer~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: ~désaccoutumer~ is “to wean off a habit.” The base goes back to Old French ~acostumer~, attested at the end of the twelfth century, built on ~coutume~ from Latin ~cōnsuētūdinem~ (“habit”). The prefix ~dés-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and appears as ~dés-~ here because the base begins with a vowel.
en.désacidifier: ~Désacidifier~ is formed from ~acidifier~ and the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the action: to remove or neutralize acidity. The base ~acidifier~ is built on the adjective ~acide~ and the suffix ~-ifier~ (“to make acid”). ~Acide~ was borrowed from Latin ~acidus~ (“sour”), from the verb ~aceō~ (“to be sour”). The prefix ~dés-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and takes its ~s~ before a vowel.
en.désaciérer: Formed from ~aciérer~ (“to turn iron into steel”) with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the process: to ~désaciérer~ is to take steel back toward iron, that is, to decarburize it. The form ~dés-~ is the one used before a vowel. The base ~aciérer~ comes from ~acier~ (“steel”), from Late Latin ~acciarium~, itself from Latin ~acies~ (“point, sharp edge”). Italian ~acciaio~ and Spanish ~acero~ come from the same Late Latin word. The prefix goes back through Old French ~des-~ to Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.désacraliser: ~Désacraliser~ is formed from ~sacraliser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the base: to strip something of its sacred character. The base ~sacraliser~ (“to make sacred”) is built from the adjective ~sacral~ and the suffix ~-iser~, and ~sacral~ is a learned creation on Latin ~sacer~ (“sacred”). So ~désacraliser~ undoes the setting-apart that ~sacraliser~ performs, and it is used both of places or objects and, figuratively, of ideas or institutions that people stop treating as untouchable.
en.désactiver:
French ~désactiver~ is a transparent modern formation: the privative prefix ~dés-~ (Latin ~dis-~, marking removal or reversal) added to ~activer~ (“to activate”). ~Activer~ derives from the adjective ~actif~, from Latin ~activus~, built on ~actus~, the past participle of ~agere~ (“to drive, to do, to act”). ~Agere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~agō~ and to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive”), one of the great verbs of the family: it surfaces in Ancient Greek ~ágō~ (“I lead”), in Sanskrit ~ájati~ (“drives”), and, through Latin, in a flood of English words from ~act~ and ~agent~ to ~agile~.

Semantically ~désactiver~ simply reverses ~activer~: to switch off, disable, or render inert a mechanism, an account, a defense system. It is overwhelmingly a word of the technical and digital age — one ~désactive~ an alarm, a button, an option, a virus — and its very modernity shows how a Latin root for “driving cattle” has been press-ganged into the vocabulary of software. The same *~h₂eǵ-~ root, through ~agere~ and its participle ~actus~, underlies a huge French family: ~agir~, ~acte~, ~action~, ~acteur~, ~agent~, ~agile~, ~exiger~, and ~rédiger~ — all, at bottom, about setting something in motion.
en.désadapter: Formed from ~adapter~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to ~désadapter~ is to make something or someone unsuited to what it was fitted for. The prefix is spelled ~dés-~ before a vowel, so the ~s~ is pronounced [z]. It comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The base ~adapter~ comes from Latin ~adaptāre~ (“to fit to”), made of ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~aptāre~ (“to fit”), from the adjective ~aptus~, which also gave French ~apte~. The verb is mostly met in its participle ~désadapté~ and in the noun ~désadaptation~, in psychology and education.
en.désaffecter: Formed in French from the prefix ~dés-~ and the verb ~affecter~, so ~désaffecter~ is “to take out of its assigned use,” as when a building or a church stops serving its purpose. The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”) and here reverses the base. The base ~affecter~ has a sense “to assign, to allocate,” which comes from Latin ~afficere~, built from ~ad-~ and ~facere~ (“to do, to make”); its other branch, “to feign,” comes from Latin ~affectare~. Only the assigning sense is reversed here.
en.désaffectionner: ~Désaffectionner~ is formed from ~affectionner~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to cease to feel affection for someone or something. The prefix takes the form ~dés-~ before a vowel. The base ~affectionner~ is built on the noun ~affection~ and the verb ending ~-er~, and ~affection~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~affectiō~ (“action of affecting”), from the verb ~afficere~.
en.désaffilier: Formed from ~affilier~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which marks reversal: to undo an affiliation. The base was borrowed from Latin ~affiliāre~, made of ~ad~ (“to”) and ~filius~ (“son”), and first meant “to adopt as a son.” French moved that image to institutions, attaching someone to a society or party as though to a household. The same ~filius~ gave French ~fils~.
en.désagrafer: Formed from ~agrafer~ with the prefix ~dés-~ (“undoing”), so it means to unfasten what a clasp or staple holds. The base ~agrafer~ was built with ~a-~, from Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”), on an older verb ~grafer~, and is closely tied to the noun ~agrafe~ (“clasp, hook, staple”). The prefix ~dés-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.désagréger: Formed in French from ~agréger~ with the reversing prefix ~dés-~. The base ~agréger~ was borrowed from Latin ~aggregāre~, from ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~grex~ (“flock”), so “to bring into a flock.” It became a figure for joining parts into one body. The prefix ~dés-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), reverses this. ~Désagréger~ means to break up a whole into its parts, “to disintegrate,” of rock, a group or a coalition. The ~grex~ family also gave ~grégaire~, ~congrégation~, ~ségrégation~ and ~agrégat~.
en.désaimanter: ~Désaimanter~ is formed from ~aimanter~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to remove magnetism. ~Aimanter~ itself comes from the noun ~aimant~ (“magnet”) plus ~-er~. ~Aimant~ descends from Vulgar Latin ~adimantem~, a form of Latin ~adamās~, from Ancient Greek ~ἀδάμας~ (“unconquerable”). The same root gave ~diamant~, so a magnet and a diamond are cousins, both named for their hardness. The prefix ~dés-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), takes the ~s~ form before the vowel of ~aimanter~.
en.désaisonnaliser: Formed from ~saison~ with the prefix ~dé-~ (removal) and the suffix ~-iser~: to ~désaisonnaliser~ data is to remove the seasonal variations from it. The noun ~saison~ comes from Old French ~saison~, from Latin ~satiō~ (“act of sowing”), built on ~serere~ (“to sow”), so the season was first the time for planting. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, and the prefix ~dé-~ from Latin ~dis-~.
en.désajuster: ~Désajuster~ is formed from ~ajuster~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which undoes the base: to put out of adjustment, to disarrange. The base ~ajuster~ comes from ~juste~ (“exact, fitting”) with ~a-~ and ~-er~, and ~juste~ descends from Latin ~iūstus~ (“lawful, right”). English ~adjust~ reached English through this same Old French verb, so ~désajuster~ is, in a sense, the opposite of a word English also uses.
en.désaligner: Formed from ~aligner~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the action: to break up a line, as of ranks of soldiers. ~Aligner~ comes from Old French ~alignier~ (twelfth century), built on ~à~ and ~ligne~. ~Ligne~ descends from Latin ~linea~ (“linen thread, line”), from ~linum~ (“flax”), since a builder's straight line was originally a stretched thread. The prefix ~dés-~ comes from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”) through Old French ~des-~.
en.désaliéner: Formed from ~aliéner~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which marks reversal: to undo alienation. The base was borrowed from Latin ~aliēnāre~, from ~aliēnus~ (“belonging to another”), itself from ~alius~ (“other”). It first meant “to make something another's” or “to make foreign.” French uses it in law for transferring a right, and generally for estranging someone.
en.désalper: Formed from ~alpe~ (a high mountain pasture) with the prefix ~dés-~ (“removal”): to leave the alp, as Swiss cows do when they come down from the high pastures in autumn. The noun is attested from 1405 and comes from Latin ~alpes~ (“the Alps”), itself supposed to rest on a pre-Indo-European root *~alp-~ (“mountain, height”). The ceremonial descent of the herds gave the verb its best-known use.
en.désaltérer: ~Désaltérer~ is formed from ~altérer~ with the prefix ~dés-~ (the form of ~dé-~ before a vowel, from Latin ~dis-~, “apart”), which reverses the base. Here the base is the sense of ~altérer~ meaning “to make thirsty,” so ~désaltérer~ means to undo the thirst, that is, to quench it. That sense is distinct from the more common “to change for the worse.” The base itself comes from Latin ~alterāre~ (“to change”), formed on ~alter~ (“the other”).
en.désambiguïser: Formed from the adjective ~ambigu~ with the suffix ~-iser~ and the prefix ~dés-~: to remove an ambiguity, “to make unambiguous.” The adjective is borrowed from Latin ~ambiguus~, from ~ambigere~ (“to doubt”), which French Wiktionary analyzes as ~amb-~ (“around”) and ~agere~ (“to drive”), literally “driving two ways.” The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~ and forms verbs meaning “to make A,” and ~dés-~ reverses the result. The two affixes together give a technical verb.
en.désamianter: Formed from the prefix ~dés-~, the noun ~amiante~ and the ending ~-er~, “to remove asbestos from” a building. The prefix ~dés-~ expresses removal, here of the material named by the noun. The noun ~amiante~ came through Latin ~amiantus~ from Ancient Greek ~amíantos~, built on the privative ~a-~ (“not”) and ~miaínō~ (“to stain, contaminate”), because the mineral was thought to stay unsoiled by fire. The word thus meant “undefiled” before it named a hazard.
en.désamidonner: Formed from ~amidonner~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to ~désamidonner~ is to remove the starch. The base ~amidonner~ means to stiffen with ~amidon~ (“starch”), a noun borrowed from Medieval Latin ~amidum~, an altered form of Latin ~amylum~, itself from Ancient Greek ~ámulon~ (“unmilled”), a name for the finest flour. The form ~dés-~ is used because the base begins with a vowel.
en.désaminer: Formed from ~aminé~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which marks removal. The base ~aminé~ is itself built on ~amine~, the name of a class of nitrogen compounds, with the suffix ~-é~. In biochemistry the verb means to strip an amine group from a molecule. The prefix ~dés-~ is the form of ~dé-~ used before a vowel, and it comes from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.désamorcer: Formed from ~amorcer~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which builds a verb of opposite meaning. So ~désamorcer~ undoes what ~amorcer~ does. The sources go no deeper for this verb. Its senses today include defusing a device and, figuratively, forestalling a crisis.
en.désaper: A slang verb formed from ~sape~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ending, meaning “to undress.” Here ~sape~ is the colloquial word for clothing, a back-formation from the verb ~saper~ (“to dress”), so ~désaper~ reverses it: to take the clothes off. Do not confuse this ~sape~ with the homonym from Latin ~sappa~ (“hoe”), which is a different word.
en.désapparier: Formed from ~apparier~ with the prefix ~dés-~ (“undoing”), so it means to separate what had been paired, such as birds. The base ~apparier~ comes from Old French ~aparier~, built on ~pair~ with the prefix ~ad-~ and the ending ~-er~. The noun ~pair~ goes back to Latin ~pār~ (“equal, matching”), which also gave French ~paire~, ~pareil~ and ~impair~. The doubled ~p~ of the modern spelling reflects the ~ad-~ prefix.
en.désappointer: Formed from the prefix ~dés-~ and ~appointer~. The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~, and reverses the base. ~Appointer~ is from Old French ~apointier~, on its face ~a-~ + ~point~ + ~-er~, perhaps matching Late Latin ~appunctāre~. Its oldest sense was “to cut to a point,” and it later meant “to settle,” then “to pay,” as in ~appointements~ (“salary”). In Louisiana French, ~désappointer~ means “to dismiss” and also “to disappoint,” the latter a semantic loan from English ~disappoint~.
en.désapprendre: ~Désapprendre~ is ~apprendre~ with the prefix ~dés-~ (the form of ~dé-~ before a vowel), which reverses the base: to unlearn, to put aside what one has learned. ~Apprendre~ comes from Latin ~apprehendere~ (“to seize, to grasp”), from ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~prehendere~ (“to grasp”), reduced in Old French to ~aprendre~. The prefix ~dés-~ descends from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”) by way of Old French ~des-~.
en.désapprouver: ~Désapprouver~ is formed from the verb ~approuver~ and the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses its base and takes the form ~dés-~ before a vowel. The base ~approuver~ goes back to Latin ~approbāre~ (“to approve, to assent to”), made of ~ad-~ (“toward”) and ~probāre~ (“to test, to deem good”), from ~probus~ (“good, upright”). To ~désapprouver~ is therefore to withhold the judgment of “good” that ~approuver~ gives. French Wiktionary and English Wiktionary agree on this prefixed formation.
en.désapprovisionner: Formed in French from ~approvisionner~ and the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to stop supplying or stocking. The base ~approvisionner~ is built on the noun ~provision~, a learned borrowing from Latin ~prōvīsiō~ (“foresight, preparation”), from ~prōvidēre~, “to see ahead.” The prefix ~dés-~ is the form taken by ~dé-~ before a vowel, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The verb thus undoes what ~approvisionner~ does, whether in stocking a shop or funding an account.
en.désargenter: Formed from ~argenter~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which removes what the base verb applies: to strip off a coat of silver. The base is built on ~argent~ with ~-er~, with the sense “to provide with silver”, and ~argent~ comes from Latin ~argentum~ (“silver”), a word related to Ancient Greek ~argós~ (“white, shining”). The participle ~désargenté~ is also used in everyday French, figuratively, of someone short of money.
en.désarmer: Inherited from Old French ~desarmer~, which can be analyzed as ~dés-~ + ~armer~. The prefix ~dés-~ descends from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and here marks reversal: to undo the act of arming. The base ~armer~ comes from Latin ~armāre~, built on ~arma~ (“weapons, tools”), from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “to fit together.” The verb means to take weapons from someone, then, by extension, to reduce a country's forces, to defuse a bomb or an alarm, to retire a ship from service, or even to soften an opponent's anger.
en.désarrimer: ~Désarrimer~ is formed from ~arrimer~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to undo what was stowed. ~Arrimer~ is a sailor's verb meaning “to stow cargo securely,” traced through Old French ~arimer~ to Middle English ~rimen~ (“to make room”), a relative of English ~room~ and German ~Raum~. The prefix ~dés-~ comes from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”) and appears before a vowel, hence the ~s~ sounded as a ~z~. To ~désarrimer~ is to let a load come loose or shift, as when cargo breaks free of its lashings.
en.désarticuler: Formed from ~articuler~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base verb: to ~désarticuler~ is to undo a joint, as in dislocating a limb. ~Dés-~ is the form of the prefix ~dé-~ used before a vowel. ~Articuler~ comes from Latin ~articulare~ (“to give joints to, to divide, to pronounce distinctly”), from ~articulus~ (“a little joint, a knuckle”), the diminutive of ~artus~ (“joint, limb”). The verb therefore keeps the physical image of a joint at its core, now applied by reversal to what has been jointed.
en.désarçonner: Formed from the prefix ~dés-~, ~arçon~ (the “tree” or frame of a saddle) and the verb ending ~-er~. The French text analyzes it as ~dés-~ added to ~arçonner~, itself a verb made on ~arçon~, while English Wiktionary reads it as ~dés-~ + ~arçon~ + ~-er~ in one step. The prefix ~dés-~ marks removal, so the verb means to dislodge a rider from the saddle, to unhorse. The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.désassembler: Formed in French from ~assembler~ with the prefix ~dés-~, the form of ~dé-~ before a vowel. ~Désassembler~ undoes what ~assembler~ does: it means to take something to pieces. The base ~assembler~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~assimulāre~ (“to bring together”), built from ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~simul~ (“together”). Its learned doublet is ~assimiler~, and ~sembler~ is the inherited form of the same Latin verb.
en.désassimiler: Formed from ~assimiler~ with the prefix ~dés-~ (“undoing”), so it means to reverse assimilation. The base was borrowed from Latin ~assimilare~, built from ~ad-~ (“toward”) and ~similis~ (“like, similar”), literally “to make alike.” The Latin adjective ~similis~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~sem-~ (“one, together”), which also underlies French ~semblable~ and ~ressembler~. The prefix ~dés-~ comes from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.désassortir: ~Désassortir~ is formed from ~assortir~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to spoil the match of things that were suited to each other. The base ~assortir~ is built on the old sense of ~sortir~ (“to choose, to allot”) with ~a-~, and it belongs to the family of ~sorte~, from Latin ~sors~ (“lot, fate, share”). To ~assortir~ was to bring together things of the same sort, so ~désassortir~ is to break up such a set. English ~sort~ and ~assortment~ come from the same source.
en.désatomiser: Formed from ~atome~ with the prefix ~dés-~ and the suffix ~-iser~, to mean “to strip of atomic weapons.” The noun ~atome~ was taken from Latin ~atomus~, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~ἄτομος~ (“uncuttable”), built from ~a-~ (“not”) and a root meaning “cut.” For the ancient atomists, such as Democritus and Epicurus, it was the smallest possible particle of matter. The meaning shifted to the nuclear sense in the twentieth century, and after 1945 ~atome~ came to evoke the bomb, which gives this verb its modern sense.
en.désavantager: Formed from ~avantager~ (“to give an advantage to”) with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: ~désavantager~ is “to put at a disadvantage.” The prefix takes the form ~dés-~, with a pronounced s, because ~avantager~ begins with a vowel. The base is itself a French verb built on the noun ~avantage~, which comes from Old French and can be analyzed as ~avant~ (“ahead”) plus the noun suffix ~-age~. The verb ending ~-er~ goes back to the Latin infinitive ending ~-are~, so the whole word is a stack of three French-made layers on a single adverb.
en.désavouer: Formed from ~avouer~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to ~désavouer~ is to refuse to acknowledge as one's own what one had owned or might have owned, such as a statement or a person. The base ~avouer~ comes from Old French ~avoer~ (“to acknowledge, to accept as one's own”), from Latin ~advocare~ (“to call to oneself”), made of ~ad-~ and ~vocare~ (“to call”). The form ~dés-~ is the usual one before a vowel, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.désaxer: Formed in French from ~axe~ with the prefix ~dés-~ (the form ~dé-~ takes before a vowel), literally “to remove from its axis.” The noun ~axe~ is borrowed from Latin ~axis~ and has an inherited doublet, ~ais~. The literal sense is to knock something off its axis, and the verb is used figuratively for unbalancing or derailing a person or a plan.
en.désaérer: Formed from ~aérer~ with the prefix ~dés-~, so it means to remove the air from something, as in deaerating a liquid. ~Aérer~ is formed in French from Latin ~āēr~ (“air”) and the verb ending ~-er~, and the Latin noun is the Greek word for air taken over. ~Dés-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.désectoriser: Formed from ~sectoriser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses it: to end the division of something into sectors. The base is ~secteur~ plus the suffix ~-iser~, and ~secteur~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~sector~ (“one who cuts”). The coinage belongs to administrative French, where ~dé-~ is productive and undoes such divisions.
en.désembobiner: Formed from ~embobiner~ with the prefix ~dés-~ (“undoing”): to unwind. In its literal sense the base is built on ~bobine~ (“reel, spool”), with ~em-~ (“onto”) and ~-er~, so ~embobiner~ is to wind thread onto a spool, and ~désembobiner~ is to wind it off. The figurative sense of ~embobiner~, “to hoodwink,” is traced to a different source, ~embabouiner~. The origin of ~bobine~ is debated; the TLFi favors an imitative root ~bob~, evoking something swollen and round.
en.désembourber: Formed from ~embourber~ with the reversing prefix ~dés-~: to draw out of the mire. The base is itself built from ~en-~, the noun ~bourbe~ (“mire”) and the ending ~-er~, so ~embourber~ means to put into the mud and hence to get stuck, in mud or in a difficulty. The noun ~bourbe~ is traced to a proposed Gaulish word *~borua~, for a bubbling hot spring, related to the Gaulish god of hot springs attested in inscriptions at Bourbon-Lancy and Bourbonne-les-Bains.
en.désembourgeoiser: Formed from ~embourgeoiser~ with the prefix ~dés-~ (undoing), so “to stop being bourgeois.” ~Embourgeoiser~ is built on ~bourgeois~ with ~em-~ (a spelling of ~en-~) and ~-er~. ~Bourgeois~ comes from Late Latin ~burgensis~, formed on Latin ~burgus~ (“fortified place”), of uncertain origin; a Germanic and a Greek source have both been proposed.
en.désembouteiller: Formed from ~embouteiller~ with the prefix ~dés-~ (undoing), so “to undo a bottleneck.” ~Embouteiller~ is built on ~bouteille~ with ~em-~ (a spelling of ~en-~) and ~-er~: first “to bottle,” then “to clog a road with traffic.” ~Bouteille~ comes from Old French ~botele~, from Late Latin ~butticula~, a diminutive of ~buttis~ (“a kind of vessel”).
en.désembuer: Formed from ~embuer~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to remove the mist from something, as from a car windshield. ~Embuer~ itself comes from the noun ~buée~ (“mist, condensation”). ~Buée~ came from Old French ~buee~ (“laundry”), from Vulgar Latin *~būcāta~, ultimately from a Frankish verb meaning “to soak, to wash.” The prefix ~dés-~ comes from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”) and takes its ~s~ before a vowel. The verb thus undoes what ~embuer~ did, and its distant root lies in medieval laundry steam.
en.désemparer: ~Désemparer~ is formed from the verb ~emparer~ (“to fortify”) and the prefix ~dés-~, which undoes its base. ~Emparer~ comes from Occitan ~emparar~ (“to protect, defend, lay claim to”), from a Vulgar Latin form *~imparare~ that is tied to ~parare~ (“to prepare, to ward off”). In the defensive sense of its base, ~désemparer~ means to strip something of its defenses, a picture that fits the gloss “to disable a ship.” Both Wiktionaries agree on the prefixed formation.
en.désemplir: ~Désemplir~ is formed from ~emplir~ (“to fill”) with the prefix ~dés-~, the form of ~dé-~ used before a vowel, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), which normally reverses the base verb. In practice the verb is used almost only in the negative, ~ne pas désemplir~, to say that a place is always full. The base ~emplir~ comes from Latin ~implēre~ (~in-~ + ~plēre~, “to fill”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~pleh₁-~, which also gave Latin ~plēnus~ (“full”) and English ~full~.
en.désencadrer: Formed from ~encadrer~ (“to frame”) with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the action: to take something out of its frame. ~Encadrer~ is itself built on ~cadre~, borrowed in the sixteenth century from Italian ~quadro~ (“square”), from Latin ~quadrum~, a word ultimately tied to ~quattuor~ (“four”). A frame is therefore, etymologically, a four-cornered thing. The prefix ~dés-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and is fully productive for undoing a verb's action.
en.désenchanter: Formed from ~enchanter~ and the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to undo a spell, and so to strip away illusion. The base comes from Old French ~enchanter~, probably borrowed from Latin ~incantāre~ (“to chant, to bewitch”), built on ~in-~ and ~cantāre~, a frequentative of ~canere~ (“to sing”). Singing over someone thus became casting a spell, and the prefix takes that spell away again. The participle ~désenchanté~ (“disillusioned”) is common in modern French.
en.désenchaîner: ~Désenchaîner~ is formed from ~enchaîner~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to free from chains, literally or figuratively. The base ~enchaîner~ is built on the noun ~chaîne~ with ~en-~ and ~-er~, and ~chaîne~ comes from Old French ~chaeine~, from Latin ~catena~ (“chain”). The deeper origin of ~catena~ is disputed. The same Latin word gave Italian ~catena~, Spanish ~cadena~ and, through Old French, English ~chain~.
en.désenclaver: Formed in French from ~enclaver~ with the reversing prefix ~dés-~. The base ~enclaver~ goes back to Late Latin ~inclavare~ (“to shut in with a key”), from ~in-~ (“in”) and ~clāvis~ (“key”). Latin ~clāvis~ is also the source of French ~clé~. The prefix ~dés-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), reverses the enclosing, so ~désenclaver~ means to open up an isolated place, typically by building roads or rail links. The noun ~enclave~, a territory surrounded by another, belongs to the same family, as do ~clavicule~ and ~conclave~.
en.désencombrer: Formed from the prefix ~dés-~ and ~encombrer~, so “to undo the clutter.” The prefix ~dés-~, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), reverses the base verb, and takes this form before a vowel. The base ~encombrer~ has a debated origin: French Wiktionary says the TLFi derives it from ~combre~ (“barrier”), despite a chronological gap, while English Wiktionary traces it through Medieval Latin ~incombrāre~ (“to hinder, to burden”). ~Désencombrer~ means to clear away what obstructs a space or a mind, to declutter.
en.désencrasser: ~Désencrasser~ is built on ~encrasser~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base, so it means to clean off the grime. The base ~encrasser~ is formed from the prefix ~en-~, the noun ~crasse~ (“grime, filth”) and the ending ~-er~, so it means “to cover with filth” and then “to clog.” ~Crasse~ goes back to Latin ~crassus~ (“thick, coarse”). The verb thus undoes a coating that had built up until it was thick with dirt.
en.désendetter: Formed in French from ~endetter~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base verb, so “to get out of debt” and so to deleverage. Old French had ~desdeter~. The base ~endetter~ is built on ~dette~, from Old French ~dete~, from Late Latin ~debita~, from Latin ~debēre~ (“to owe”). The prefix ~dés-~ is the form of ~dé-~ before a vowel; it comes from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.désenfler: Formed from ~enfler~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the action: to go down, to deflate. The base ~enfler~ is inherited from Old French ~enfler~, from Latin ~īnflāre~, made of ~in-~ (“in”) and ~flāre~ (“to blow”), so literally to blow into and hence to swell. The prefix ~dés-~, used before a vowel, goes back through Old French ~des-~ to Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.désenfumer: Formed from ~enfumer~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to clear smoke from a smoke-filled space. ~Enfumer~ is itself ~fumer~ (“to smoke, to give off smoke”) with the prefix ~en-~, so the verb stacks two prefixes on one root, the second undoing the work of the first.
en.désengager: ~Désengager~ is formed from ~engager~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the action of the base verb: to disengage is to undo an engagement. The spelling ~dés-~ is the one used before a vowel, and the prefix descends from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The base ~engager~ comes from Old French ~engagier~, itself built on ~gagier~ (“to pledge”) and ultimately on ~gage~, a word French took from Frankish *~wadi~ (“pledge”). To withdraw from a commitment is thus, etymologically, to take back a pledge.
en.désengluer: Formed from ~engluer~ and the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to free from something sticky. The base ~engluer~ is ~en-~ plus ~glu~ (“birdlime”) plus the verb ending: to coat with sticky glue, and so to trap, as birds are caught on limed branches. The prefix ~dés-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). ~Désengluer~ thus means to pull a trapped creature, or by extension a person, out of the sticky mess.
en.désengorger: Formed from the prefix ~dés-~ and ~engorger~. The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and here it reverses the base. ~Engorger~ is built on ~gorge~ (“throat”) with ~en-~ and ~-er~, so its picture is of something stuffed into the throat, hence blocked. ~Gorge~ comes from Old French ~gorge~, from Late Latin ~gurga~, related to Latin ~gurges~ (“whirlpool, gulf”). ~Désengorger~ therefore means “to unclog, to clear a blockage,” of a pipe, a road or a service.
en.désengourdir: Formed from ~engourdir~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the action: to restore feeling to a numbed limb or body. The base ~engourdir~ is a parasynthetic verb, built around the adjective ~gourd~ (“numb”) with ~en-~ and ~-ir~, and ~gourd~ itself comes from Latin ~gurdus~. The prefix ~dés-~ is the vowel-initial form of ~dé-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.désengrener: Formed from ~engrener~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the action of the base. The base ~engrener~ is built on ~grain~, from Latin ~granum~ (“grain”), and meant “to fill with grain” and, by another route, “to set in motion.” Prefixed with ~dés-~ (from Old French ~des-~, Latin ~dis-~, “apart”), it undoes the engagement: ~désengrener~ is to throw a mechanism out of gear.
en.désenivrer: The verb is formed from ~enivrer~ (“to make drunk”) with the prefix ~dés-~, the form that ~dé-~ takes before a vowel and that reverses the action of the base. ~Enivrer~ goes back to Latin ~inebriāre~, built on ~ēbrius~ (“drunk”), the source of ~ivre~. Sources also read it as ~en-~ + ~ivre~ + ~-er~, and the two readings agree. The result means to undo drunkenness, hence “to sober up.”
en.désennuyer: Formed from ~ennuyer~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: ~désennuyer~ is to relieve someone of boredom. The base is inherited from Old French ~enoiier~, from Late Latin ~inodiāre~, which French Wiktionary explains as built on the phrase ~in odio esse~ (“to be an object of hatred”). The verb once had a far stronger sense, to torment or to make hateful, and weakened over the centuries to “to bore, to bother.” The prefix is ~dés-~ rather than ~dé-~ because the base begins with a vowel.
en.désenrayer: Formed from ~enrayer~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the action (the ~s~ is kept before a vowel). The base ~enrayer~ comes from ~en-~ + ~rai~ (“spoke of a wheel”) + ~-er~, and ~rai~ descends from Latin ~radius~ (“staff, spoke, ray”). Where ~enrayer~ is to jam a wheel or check a movement, ~désenrayer~ is to free what was jammed, as a mechanism that had seized up.
en.désensabler: Formed from ~ensabler~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to free from sand, as one frees a stranded boat or a silted channel. The base is built from ~en-~ (“into, onto”), ~sable~ (“sand”) and the ending ~-er~. The noun ~sable~ comes from Latin ~sabulum~ (“sand, gravel”) through Old French, and is a different word from ~sable~ in fur and heraldry.
en.désensibiliser: Formed from ~sensibiliser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the base: to make less sensitive. The base is a modern derivative of ~sensible~ with the suffix ~-iser~, and ~sensible~ comes from Latin ~sēnsibilis~, from ~sēnsus~, the past participle of ~sentīre~ (“to feel”). ~Sensibiliser~ began in photography, spread to medicine and now mostly means “to raise awareness”; its opposite undoes the heightened sensitivity.
en.désensorceler: Formed from ~ensorceler~ (“to bewitch”) with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the action: to lift a spell. ~Ensorceler~ comes from Old French ~ensorcerer~, built on ~sorcier~ (“sorcerer”) with ~en-~, so “to put under a sorcerer's power.” The modern form arose by dissimilation, when the first of two r sounds became an l. The prefix takes the form ~dés-~ before a vowel.
en.désentoiler: Formed from ~entoiler~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the action. ~Entoiler~ is itself ~toiler~ with the prefix ~en-~, meaning to mount on canvas. ~Désentoiler~ thus names the restorer's operation of removing a painting from its old canvas in order to transfer it onto a new one. The prefix ~dés-~ is the form ~dé-~ takes before a vowel, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.désentortiller: Formed from ~entortiller~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the action: to untangle. The origin of ~entortiller~ is disputed. By one account it comes from a Vulgar Latin verb *~intortiliāre~, from Latin ~tortilis~ (“twisted”). By another it derives from ~entort~, the past participle of the old verb ~entordre~, from Latin ~intorquēre~, which also gave ~entorse~. Either way the idea is twisting, and the family includes ~tortiller~.
en.désentraver: ~Désentraver~ is built from ~entraver~ with the reversing prefix ~dés-~, which takes the form ~dés-~ before a vowel. It means to take off hobbles or fetters, and so, figuratively, to free someone or something from what holds it back. The origin of the base is hedged: ~entraver~ may be borrowed from Old Occitan ~entravar~ or formed in French, and in both accounts it goes back to Latin ~trabs~ (“beam”), a beam being what restrains an animal's legs.
en.désenvaser: Formed from ~envaser~ (“to silt up”) with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the action: to clear silt from a harbor, a channel or a pond. ~Envaser~ itself is ~en-~ + ~vase~ (“mud, silt”) + ~-er~, and this ~vase~ is a Germanic word that reached French through Middle Dutch ~wase~ (“mud, silt”). It has nothing to do with the ~vase~ that means a vessel, which comes from Latin ~vās~. The form ~dés-~ is the one used before a vowel, so that the s is pronounced like z.
en.désenvenimer: Formed from ~envenimer~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base verb: where ~envenimer~ puts venom in, this verb takes it out. The base is built on ~venin~, which comes from Old French ~venim~ and ultimately from Latin ~venēnum~ (“poison”), the source also of Italian ~veleno~ and Spanish ~veneno~. The prefix ~dés-~ is the form of ~dé-~ used before a vowel; it comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.désenverguer: Formed from ~enverguer~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the action: to unbend a sail from its yard. ~Enverguer~ is borrowed from Occitan ~envergar~, a sailor's word, and its stem is that of ~vergue~, the yard itself, which goes back to Latin ~virga~ (“rod, switch”). The prefix ~dés-~ is the form of ~dé-~ used before a vowel, from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The noun ~envergure~ belongs to the same family of rigging vocabulary.
en.désenvoûter: Formed from ~envoûter~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to lift a spell. The base is built from the prefix ~en-~, Old French ~volt~ (“face”) and the ending ~-er~. Old French ~volt~ comes from Latin ~vultus~ (“face”). English Wiktionary suggests that the sense comes from folk magic worked on wax images of a victim's face. That is one source's account, offered as plausible and not as established.
en.déserter:
Borrowed from Late Latin ~dēsertāre~ (“to abandon”), from Latin ~dēsertus~ (“abandoned”), the past participle of ~dēserere~ (“to forsake”). That verb is made of ~dē-~ (a prefix of undoing) and ~serere~ (“to join, to link up”), so to forsake is, literally, to undo a bond. Spanish ~desertar~ is a cognate, and English has taken the verb as ~desert~ through French.

The participle ~dēsertus~ also gave French the noun ~désert~ (“abandoned, empty place”) by an older route, so the soldier who flees and the Sahara share an ancestor: a desert is a place left behind. ~Déserter~ first applied to leaving a place, and the military sense of abandoning one's post or army came to dominate, giving ~déserteur~ and ~désertion~. The figurative uses remain alive: ~déserter~ is said of the countryside, a cause or a meeting. The other half of the Latin compound, ~serere~, lives on in ~série~ and ~insérer~.
en.désertifier: Formed in French from the noun ~désert~ with the verbal suffix ~-ifier~, which builds verbs meaning “to make” or “to turn into.” The noun ~désert~ comes from Latin ~dēsertum~ (“desert, wilderness, solitude”). The verb means “to turn into a desert,” and its commonest use today is in the reflexive, for a region that loses its vegetation and its people. Its derived noun ~désertification~ is a standard term in discussions of climate and land use.
en.désespérer: ~Désespérer~ is formed from ~espérer~ (“to hope”) and the privative prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the verb: to lose hope. English Wiktionary also notes the Old French form ~desperer~, which shows the word is old. ~Espérer~ goes back to Latin ~spērāre~ (“to hope”), from ~spēs~ (“hope”), and Latin already had ~dēspērāre~, built the same way. English ~despair~ came from the Old French verb. The French verb can be intransitive (“to despair”) or take ~de~ (“to give up hope of something”).
en.désexciter: Formed from ~exciter~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to bring an excited system back from its excited state. ~Exciter~ comes from Latin ~excitāre~ (“to rouse”), in French use by about 1180, and science later adopted it for the excited states of atoms and neurons. The prefix ~dés-~ is the form of ~dé-~ before a vowel, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.désexualiser: ~Désexualiser~ is formed from ~sexualiser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the base: to remove the sexual character from something. ~Sexualiser~ is itself built on the adjective ~sexuel~ with the suffix ~-iser~. ~Sexuel~ is a learned borrowing from Late Latin ~sexualis~, and ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs. The prefix goes back to Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). Before a vowel it takes the form ~dés-~.
en.déshabiller:
~Déshabiller~ comes from Middle French ~desabiller~, the prefix ~des-~ (from Latin ~dis-~, “apart”) on ~abiller~, the earlier form of ~habiller~. On the surface it reads as ~dés-~ + ~habiller~, “to undo the dressing.” The base has a stranger past than its everyday meaning suggests: ~habiller~ goes back to Old French ~abillier~, “to prepare a log of wood,” formed on ~bille~ (“log”).

The base shifted meaning in stages. In the 13th century Middle French ~abiller~ had broadened to “to make ready,” and in the 15th century the spelling ~habiller~ and the sense “to clothe” took hold, under the influence of the unrelated noun ~habit~ (“garment”), which comes from Latin ~habitus~, from ~habēre~ (“to have, to hold”). The notion of clothing thus entered the verb by contact with a lookalike. From ~habiller~ French also built ~rhabiller~ (“to dress again”) and ~habillement~ (“clothing”).
en.déshabituer: Formed from ~habituer~ and the prefix ~dés-~ (the form of ~dé-~ used before a vowel or silent h), which reverses the base: to rid someone of a habit. The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The base is from Old French ~abituer~ (“to clothe”), from Medieval Latin ~habituare~, built on Latin ~habitus~ (“bearing, dress, habit”), a noun from ~habēre~ (“to have”).
en.désherber: Formed from the noun ~herbe~ with the prefix ~dés-~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so the verb means to remove the weeds. The prefix takes the form ~dés-~ because the h is silent, and it expresses removal. ~Herbe~ is inherited from Old French, from Latin ~herba~, which goes back ultimately to the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʰreH₁-~ (“to grow, become green”).
en.déshonorer: Formed from ~honorer~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which marks the opposite: “to bring dishonor on.” The prefix takes its ~s~ before the silent ~h~, and it descends from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The base ~honorer~ comes from Latin ~honorāre~, a verb built on ~honor~ (older ~honos~, “honor, esteem, public office”). English ~dishonor~ belongs to the same family.
en.déshuiler: Formed from ~huiler~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which expresses removal: to take the oil out of something. ~Huiler~ is built on ~huile~, from Old French ~oile~, from Latin ~oleum~, itself from ~olea~ (“olive”), a borrowing of Greek ~elaía~. The initial ~h~ of ~huile~ is not etymological; Middle French scribes added it to show that the ~u~ was a vowel.
en.déshumaniser: Formed from ~humaniser~ with the prefix ~dés-~, the form of ~dé-~ before a vowel or a mute h, here with the sense of undoing the base: to dehumanize. The prefix ~dé-~ goes back to Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). ~Humaniser~ is built on ~humain~ and the verb ending ~-iser~, from Latin ~humānus~, itself based on ~homō~ (“human being”). To dehumanize is thus to strip away what makes someone ~humain~.
en.déshydrater: Formed from the prefix ~dés-~ (removal) and ~hydrater~, which is the noun ~hydrate~ with the verb ending ~-er~, “to combine with water.” The noun is a learned coinage built on the Greek root of ~hýdōr~ (“water”), as ~hydr-~, plus the chemical suffix ~-ate~. ~Déshydrater~ is to remove the water from something: to dry a food, or to leave a body short of fluid. The same Greek ~hýdōr~ lies behind many scientific words.
en.déshydrogéner: Formed from the prefix ~dés-~ (the form of ~dé-~ before a vowel or mute h, here marking removal) and the noun ~hydrogène~, plus the verb ending ~-er~, so “to remove hydrogen.” ~Hydrogène~ was proposed by Lavoisier and his colleagues in 1783 from ~hydro-~ (Ancient Greek ~hýdōr~, “water”) and ~-gène~ (from Greek ~gennân~, “to generate”). It literally means “water-former,” because hydrogen proved to be, with oxygen, a constituent of water.
en.déshypothéquer: Formed from ~hypothéquer~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to ~déshypothéquer~ is to lift the mortgage from a property. The base ~hypothéquer~ comes from the noun ~hypothèque~, borrowed from Latin ~hypothēca~ (“pledge given as security for a loan”) and from Ancient Greek ~hupothḗkē~ (“pledge, deposit”). The Greek word is built on ~hypo-~ (“under”), so a pledge is, etymologically, something placed beneath.
en.déshériter: Formed from ~hériter~ (“to inherit”) with the prefix ~dés-~, the form of ~dé-~ used before a mute h. The prefix reverses the base, so ~déshériter~ means “to cut someone out of an inheritance.” The base comes from Late Latin ~hērēditāre~, built on ~hērēditās~ (“inheritance”) and ~hērēs~ (“heir”). The same family gave ~héritier~, ~héritage~ and ~hérédité~.
en.désigner:
From Latin ~designare~ (“to mark out, to point out, to designate”), a compound of the prefix ~de-~ (“out, off”) and a verb built on ~signum~ (“mark, sign, token, military standard”). The deeper origin of ~signum~ is genuinely disputed: some derive it from the Proto-Indo-European root *~sek-~ (“to cut”), as “something cut or carved out,” while others connect it to *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”), as the standard one follows. ~désigner~ is cognate with English ~design~ and ~designate~ and with Italian ~designare~, all resting on ~signum~.

The core image in ~designare~ is of marking something out so that it stands apart — pointing to it, singling it out. From this came both the act of indicating (to ~désigner~ a culprit, a successor, a meeting place) and, by a separate route through Italian ~disegno~, the artistic sense of “design” and “drawing.” French actually carries a doublet here: the learned ~désigner~ and the popular ~dessiner~ (“to draw”) both descend from ~designare~, the one keeping the sense of pointing out, the other the sense of tracing a figure. From the same ~signum~ French inherited ~signe~ (“sign”), ~signal~, ~signer~ (“to sign”), ~enseigne~ (“ensign, shop-sign”), and ~insigne~ (“insignia”) — a whole vocabulary of marks and tokens.
en.désillusionner: Formed from the prefix ~dés-~ and ~illusionner~, so “to remove someone's illusion.” The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~, and reverses the base. ~Illusionner~ is the noun ~illusion~ + ~-er~, “to give someone an illusion, to delude.” ~Illusion~ comes from Latin ~illusio~ (“irony, illusion, deception”), from ~illudere~ (“to play with, to mock”), so mockery is the older sense. ~Désillusionner~ means “to disillusion, to burst someone's bubble.”
en.désincarner: ~Désincarner~ is formed from ~incarner~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base verb, so it means “to disembody”. The base ~incarner~ was borrowed in 1372 from Ecclesiastical Latin ~incarnāre~ (“to make flesh”), from ~in-~ and ~carō~ (“flesh”). The prefix ~dés-~ comes from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and appears as ~dés-~ before a vowel. The verb thus undoes the theological idea of becoming flesh.
en.désincruster: Formed from ~incruster~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to remove a crust or deposit. The base ~incruster~ comes from Old French, itself a learned borrowing from Latin ~incrustāre~ (“to cover with a crust”), made of ~in-~ (“on, into”) and ~crusta~ (“crust, rind, shell”). The same ~crusta~ gives French ~croûte~. ~Incruster~ names a hard layer forming, as limescale in a kettle, so ~désincruster~ names the cleaning that takes it off. The prefix ~dés-~ is the form of ~dé-~ used before a vowel.
en.désindexer: Formed from ~indexer~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base verb: to detach wages or prices from the reference figure they were pegged to, or to remove an entry from an index. The base ~indexer~ is a twentieth-century coinage from the noun ~index~ with ~-er~. ~Index~ comes from Latin ~index~ (“one who points out; forefinger; a list”), built on ~indicāre~ (“to point out”), and shares a root with Latin ~digitus~ (“finger”). The prefix has the form ~dés-~ because the base begins with a vowel.
en.désindustrialiser: Formed from ~industrialiser~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to reduce or dismantle industry in a region or country. The base is built with the suffix ~-iser~ on ~industriel~, which comes from ~industrie~ and goes back to Latin ~industria~ (“diligence, activity”). Like its base, the verb is a modern learned coinage.
en.désinfecter: ~Désinfecter~ is built from the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the action of a verb, and ~infecter~. The base, ~infecter~, comes from Latin ~infectāre~ (“to stain, to taint”), which belongs to ~inficere~, “to dip in, to dye.” The earliest sense was thus about steeping cloth in dye, and from staining it drifted to contaminating with poison or disease. ~Désinfecter~ undoes that last step: it means to rid a wound, a surface or a room of the germs that infect. The form ~dés-~ appears before a vowel, so that the ~s~ is pronounced as a ~z~ sound.
en.désinformer: ~Désinformer~ is formed from ~informer~ and the prefix ~dés-~, which negates or reverses the base: to give false or distorted information on purpose. The base ~informer~ comes from Latin ~informare~ (“to give shape to”), made of ~in-~ and ~formare~ (“to shape”), from ~forma~ (“form”). The prefix descends from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). Unlike a plain ~mal informer~, the verb suggests deliberate deception, and it belongs to the vocabulary of propaganda and the press.
en.désinhiber: Formed from ~inhiber~ (“to inhibit”) with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: ~désinhiber~ is “to free from inhibitions.” The prefix takes the form ~dés-~ rather than ~dé-~ because the base begins with a vowel. The base ~inhiber~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~inhibēre~ (“to hold back”), built from ~in-~ and ~habēre~ (“to have, to hold”). English ~inhibit~ comes from the same Latin verb. The root ~habēre~ also gave French ~avoir~ and the learned ~habit~ and ~prohiber~.
en.désinsectiser: Formed from ~insecte~ with the prefix ~dés-~ (“removal”) and the suffix ~-iser~: to rid a place of insects. The base ~insecte~ is borrowed from Latin ~insectum~ (~insecta~ in the plural), literally “cut,” a name that points to the segments into which an insect's body appears divided. The form ~dés-~ appears before a vowel, and ~-iser~ builds verbs meaning “to treat with” or “to make.”
en.désinstaller: Formed from the prefix ~dés-~ and the verb ~installer~, in the reversing sense “to undo.” The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and takes the form ~dés-~ before a vowel. The base ~installer~ comes from Medieval Latin ~installāre~ (“to put into a stall, to establish in office”), built on ~in-~ and ~stallum~, a word borrowed from Frankish *~stall~. To ~désinstaller~ a program is therefore to undo its installation.
en.désintoxiquer: Formed from ~intoxiquer~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to rid a person of a poison or of an addiction. The prefix ~dés-~ is the form of ~dé-~ before a vowel, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The base ~intoxiquer~ is a learned re-formation on Latin *~intoxicāre~, from ~in-~ and ~toxicum~ (“poison”). The same Latin verb had earlier come down by the popular route as Old French ~entoschier~, which is now lost. English ~intoxicate~ is a separate borrowing.
en.désintégrer: Formed from the verb ~intégrer~ with the prefix ~dés-~, the form ~dé-~ takes before a vowel. The prefix reverses the base: to ~désintégrer~ is to undo integration. ~Intégrer~ comes from Latin ~integrāre~ (“to make whole”), built on the adjective ~integer~ (“whole, untouched”), itself ~in-~ (“not”) plus a root linked to ~tangere~ (“to touch”). A thing disintegrated is therefore one whose wholeness has been taken apart. The prefix itself descends from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.désintéresser: Formed from ~intéresser~ with the prefix ~dés-~, the form ~dé-~ takes before a vowel so that the s is pronounced. The prefix undoes or removes what the base does: to ~désintéresser~ someone is to take away their stake in the matter, which fits the sense “to pay off, to compensate.” The sense “to lose interest” appears with the reflexive ~se désintéresser~. The base ~intéresser~ comes from Latin ~interesse~ (“to be between, to take part in”), from ~inter~ (“between”) and ~esse~ (“to be”), and the verb entered French in the fourteenth century.
en.désinvestir: Formed from ~investir~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base verb: to withdraw what one had invested. The base comes from Latin ~investīre~ (“to clothe, surround”), built on ~in-~ (“in”) and ~vestīre~ (“to dress”), from ~vestis~ (“garment”). ~Investir~ first meant to robe someone in the insignia of an office, then to besiege a town, and from the early seventeenth century to put money into a venture. ~Désinvestir~ undoes the financial sense above all, and also the broader one of ceasing to commit effort or interest.
en.désirer:
From Latin ~desiderare~ (“to long for, to feel the want of”), which most analyses break down as ~de-~ plus the noun ~sidus~ (genitive ~sideris~, “star, constellation, heavenly body”). The verb passed through Old French ~desirer~ into the modern form. It is the close sibling of ~considerare~ (“to examine attentively”), built on the same stellar noun, and survives in Italian ~desiderare~ and Spanish ~desear~.

The stellar imagery is the memorable part, though its exact logic is debated. One traditional reading places the word in the mouths of augurs or sailors: to scan the night sky for an awaited star and not find it — to note its absence — was to feel ~desiderare~, the ache of something missing, while ~considerare~ was to study the stars present overhead. From “to miss what is absent,” the sense broadened to the general longing of modern ~désirer~. The Latin participle ~desideratum~ survives untranslated in English and French as a thing wished for, and the same ~sidus~ underlies the French family ~sidéral~ (“of the stars”) and ~sidérer~ (“to stun, to dumbfound”), once “to be struck by a baleful star.”
en.désister: From Latin ~desistere~, itself formed from ~sistere~ (“to set, to stand”) and the prefix ~dē-~ (“away from”), so that the Latin verb means “to stand away, to leave off.” French took it up chiefly as the reflexive ~se désister~, “to withdraw” from a claim, a candidacy or a lawsuit. The same Latin ~sistere~ lies behind ~exister~, ~résister~, ~persister~, ~consister~ and ~subsister~.
en.désobliger: Formed from ~obliger~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: where ~obliger~ is to put someone under an obligation or to do them a kindness, ~désobliger~ is to displease or offend them. The base comes from Old French ~obligier~, from Latin ~obligāre~ (“to bind”), made of ~ob-~ (“to, toward, against”) and ~ligāre~ (“to bind”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~leyǵ-~ (“to bind”). The same ~ligāre~ gave ~lier~ and ~allier~.
en.désobstruer: Formed from ~obstruer~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to clear what is blocked. The base was borrowed from Latin ~obstruere~ (“to block up”), which joins ~ob-~ (“in the way of”) to ~struere~ (“to pile up, to build”), so to obstruct is to build something in the way. The same root gave ~construire~, ~détruire~, ~instruire~ and ~structure~, and English ~obstruct~ comes from the same Latin verb.
en.désobéir: Formed in French from ~obéir~ with the prefix ~dé-~, here in its form ~dés-~, used before a vowel so that the s is pronounced [z]. The prefix reverses the base: ~désobéir~ is to refuse the obedience that the base expresses. ~Obéir~ comes from Old French ~obeir~ (early 12th century), from Latin ~oboedīre~ (“to give ear to, hence to submit to”), formed from ~ob-~ (“toward”) and ~audīre~ (“to hear”). English ~obey~ was lifted from the same Old French verb. Obedience is, etymologically, a way of listening.
en.désocialiser: Formed in French on ~social~, with the prefix ~dé-~ and the suffix ~-iser~, or, on the other reading the sources allow, from ~socialiser~ with ~dé-~. Either way the verb reverses socializing: it means to strip someone of social ties or integration. The base ~social~ comes from Latin ~sociālis~ (“of companionship or association”), from ~socius~ (“companion, ally”). The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and it makes verbs meaning “to make A.”
en.désodoriser: Formed from ~odoriser~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which here reverses the base: to ~désodoriser~ is to remove odor. The base ~odoriser~ is itself built on ~odeur~ with the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to give an odor to.” The form ~dés-~ is the spelling of ~dé-~ before a vowel, so that the ~s~ is pronounced. English Wiktionary parses it instead as ~dés-~ + ~odor~ + ~-iser~ in a single step.
en.désoler:
From Latin ~dēsōlāre~ (“to leave alone, to lay waste, to abandon”), from ~dē-~ (intensive) and ~sōlus~ (“alone, single”). The deeper origin of ~sōlus~ is genuinely unsettled — it is said to have baffled etymologists for generations. One traditional account traces it through Proto-Italic to the reflexive PIE *~swé~ (“oneself”), giving the sense “by oneself”; De Vaan instead proposes a link to *~solh₂-~ (“whole, healthy”), kin to ~salvus~. The sources present these as competing hypotheses, not settled fact. Whatever its root, ~sōlus~ gave Spanish ~solo~, Italian ~solo~ and French ~seul~, and lies behind English ~sole~ and ~solo~.

The earliest French sense was the strong Latin one: to ~désoler~ a country was to devastate and depopulate it, to leave it desolate and alone. From that ruin the meaning softened over time toward the emotional — to lay waste to someone’s spirits, hence “to distress, to grieve.” Today the polite ~désolé~ (“sorry”) is a faded ember of that old devastation; the speaker claims, etymologically, to be laid waste. French keeps the family in ~désolation~ and ~désolant~ (“distressing”), both still tinged with the original sense of emptiness left behind.
en.désolidariser: Formed in French from ~solidariser~ with the reversing prefix ~dé-~. The base ~solidariser~ is built on the adjective ~solidaire~ and the suffix ~-iser~, and means to bind people or things together. ~Solidaire~ comes from ~solide~ and is tied to the Latin legal phrase ~in solidum~ (“for the whole”), the idea of being jointly bound for the entirety. The prefix ~dé-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), undoes the bond. ~Désolidariser~ means to break up a group or detach someone from it, and ~se désolidariser~ means to publicly distance oneself.
en.désoperculer: ~Désoperculer~ is formed from ~operculer~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to remove a cover. ~Operculer~ is a verb made from the noun ~opercule~ (“lid, cover”). The prefix ~dés-~ comes from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”) and takes its ~s~ form before a vowel. The verb is used by beekeepers for uncapping honeycomb, the wax caps that seal the cells before the honey is extracted.
en.désopiler: ~Désopiler~ is formed from the prefix ~dés-~ and ~opiler~ (“to block”), and meant to clear an obstruction. The base ~opiler~ comes from Latin ~oppilare~ (“to obstruct”). The sense comes from the expression ~désopiler la rate~, “to unblock the spleen,” since a blocked spleen was once thought to cause irritability and gloom. Clearing it made a person cheerful, and so ~désopiler~ came to mean “to make laugh.”
en.désorbiter: Formed from ~orbite~ (“orbit”) with the prefix ~dés-~, giving “to remove from orbit,” as when a satellite is brought down. The noun ~orbite~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~orbita~ (“rut, track,” and later “course of the stars”), related to ~orbe~. The prefix ~dés-~ is the form of ~dé-~ used before a vowel, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.désorganiser: Formed from the prefix ~dés-~ (“un-”) and the verb ~organiser~, in the reversing sense of undoing an arrangement. The base ~organiser~ was built from the noun ~organe~, which goes back to Latin ~organum~ and Ancient Greek ~ὄργανον~ (“tool, instrument”), derived from ~ἔργον~ (“work”). To ~désorganiser~ is to upset the working order of something.
en.désorienter: ~Désorienter~ is formed from ~orienter~ and the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to take away someone's bearings. The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and takes the form ~dés-~ before a vowel. The base ~orienter~ was built, around 1485, on the noun ~orient~ (“the East”), from Latin ~oriens~, the present participle of ~orīrī~ (“to rise”), literally “the rising” sun. Orienting something first meant aligning it toward the east, so to ~désorienter~ is, at root, to lose that alignment.
en.désosser: Formed at once with a prefix and a suffix on the noun ~os~ (“bone”): ~dés-~, which marks removal, and ~-er~. The prefix takes the form ~dés-~ rather than ~dé-~ because the base begins with a vowel. So ~désosser~ is to take the bones out, and by extension to take something apart. ~Os~ comes from Latin ~os~, ~ossis~ (“bone”), through the popular variant ~ossum~, and ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃ésth₁~.
en.désoxygéner: Formed from ~oxygéner~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the action: to remove the oxygen from something. The base is a denominal built on ~oxygène~, the name Lavoisier coined in 1778 from Greek ~ὀξύς~ (“sharp, acid”) and ~γένος~ (“birth, origin”). He wrongly thought the gas was a constituent of every acid, so the name means “acid-producer.” The prefix ~dés-~, used before a vowel, goes back through Old French ~des-~ to Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.déstabiliser: Formed in French from the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ~stabiliser~, meaning “to make unstable”. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and here reverses the base. The base ~stabiliser~ is built on ~stable~, from Latin ~stabilis~ (“standing firm”), which comes from ~stāre~ (“to stand”), with the suffix ~-iser~. English ~stand~ shares the same Proto-Indo-European root *~steh₂-~. The verb literally undoes a standing.
en.déstaliniser: ~Déstaliniser~ combines the prefix ~dé-~ (here “to undo, to bring to an end”) with the name ~Staline~ and the verb suffix ~-iser~, giving “to destalinize,” to dismantle the Stalinist system. The name ~Staline~ is the French form of Russian ~Сталин~, which is tied to ~сталь~ (“steel”). The prefix and suffix work together in the pattern seen in ~dédramatiser~: ~-iser~ builds a verb from the name, and ~dé-~ reverses it.
en.déstocker: ~Déstocker~ is formed from ~stocker~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to run down a stock, to sell off or release what had been held in reserve. The base ~stocker~ was built in French on the noun ~stock~, borrowed from English ~stock~ in its commercial sense. English ~stock~ goes back to Old English ~stocc~ (“tree-trunk, post”), so the verb carries a distant image of a wooden post. The related noun ~déstockage~ names the clearance itself.
en.déstructurer: ~Déstructurer~ is formed from ~structurer~ and the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the base verb: to undo a structure. ~Structurer~ is itself a denominal verb built on ~structure~, from Latin ~strūctūra~, the action noun of ~struere~ (“to pile up, to build”). That Latin verb goes back to a Proto-Indo-European root *~strew-~ (“to strew, to spread out”), which also gave English ~strew~. The family reaches French through compounds of ~struere~ such as ~construire~ and ~détruire~.
en.désulfiter: Formed from the chemical noun ~sulfite~ with the prefix ~dé-~, and so meaning to remove the sulfites from something. The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). Here it works as it often does before a noun: it expresses removal of what the noun names, and the verb ending ~-er~ completes the verb, much as in other ~dé-~ + noun + ~-er~ verbs.
en.désulfurer: ~Désulfurer~ is formed from ~sulfurer~ (“to treat with sulfur”) and the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to remove the sulfur from something. The base is built on the chemical noun ~sulfure~, a learned word resting on Latin ~sulfur~ (“sulfur”), with the verb ending ~-er~. The prefix descends from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.désunir: ~Désunir~ is built from ~unir~ and the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the action of the base verb: to ~désunir~ is to undo a union, to separate what had been joined. The base ~unir~ comes from Latin ~unire~ (“to make one”), from ~unus~ (“one”), the source of French ~un~, ~union~ and ~unité~. The prefix descends from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The verb is thus the exact opposite of ~unir~ and a counterpart of ~réunir~ (“to bring together again”). It is used of couples, parties, families and groups that fall apart.
en.désynchroniser: Formed from ~synchroniser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which undoes the action of the base verb: to put things out of sync. The base was built in French on the adjective ~synchrone~ with ~-iser~, and ~synchrone~ comes through Latin ~synchronus~ from Ancient Greek ~sýnkhronos~, made of ~sýn~ (“with”) and ~khrónos~ (“time”). The prefix ~dé-~ goes back through Old French ~des-~ to Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.déséchouer: A French formation from ~échouer~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to get a stranded ship afloat again. The base ~échouer~ has a famously obscure origin, and the TLFi leaves it open. It appears around 1559 of galleys run aground, means “to touch bottom and stop” by 1573, and takes the figurative sense “to fail” by 1660. The prefix ~dés-~ is the form of ~dé-~ used before a vowel, and it comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.désénerver: Formed from ~énerver~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the action: to calm someone down. The base comes from Latin ~ēnervāre~ (“to cut the sinews of, to weaken”), from ~ex-~ and ~nervus~ (“sinew”). Its meaning moved from weakening to irritating, so ~désénerver~ undoes the modern sense, not the Latin one.
en.désépaissir: Formed from ~épaissir~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to make something less thick. ~Épaissir~ is itself built on the adjective ~épais~ (“thick”), which French Wiktionary traces to Latin ~spissus~ (“thick, dense”), with the verb ending ~-ir~. The prefix ~dés-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and takes this spelling before a vowel. So ~désépaissir~ stacks two French layers on a Latin adjective: thick, then thicken, then undo the thickening.
en.déséquilibrer: ~Déséquilibrer~ is ~équilibrer~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base: to unbalance is to undo a balance. The form ~dés-~ is the one used before a vowel, and it descends from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The base verb comes from the noun ~équilibre~, borrowed from Latin ~aequilibrium~, a compound of ~aequus~ (“equal, level”) and ~libra~ (“balance, scales”): the state in which the two pans of a scale hang level.
en.déséquiper: ~Déséquiper~ is formed from ~équiper~ with the prefix ~dés-~, a form of ~dé-~ that reverses the verb: to strip of equipment. The base ~équiper~ comes from Old French ~esquiper~, borrowed from Old Norse ~skipa~ (“to fit out a vessel”), from ~skip~ (“ship”). A word that began by rigging a ship is thus undone here, so ~déséquiper~ means to take away what had been supplied.
en.désétatiser: Formed from ~étatiser~ with the prefix ~dés-~, which reverses the base verb: to take something back out of State control. The base ~étatiser~ is built on ~État~ (the capitalized form of ~état~) with the suffix ~-iser~, and means to bring an industry or service under the State, hence “to nationalize.” The noun ~état~ comes from Latin ~status~ (“standing”). The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and it remains productive in administrative and journalistic French. The prefix takes the form ~dés-~ because the base begins with a vowel.
en.détacher:
Two French verbs spelled ~détacher~ have run together. The sense here — “to remove spots and stains” — is formed straightforwardly from ~tache~ (“stain, spot”) with the prefix ~dé-~ (marking removal), so that to ~détacher~ a garment is to take the stains out of it. The homonym meaning “to untie, to separate” comes instead from Old French ~destachier~, the ~dé-~ counterpart of ~attacher~ (“to attach”); that family is usually traced to a Frankish or Germanic root for a stake or fastening, the same one behind English ~attach~ and ~detach~ (borrowed from French).

The stain-removing verb keeps to its narrow, useful trade: it belongs to laundering and cleaning, and its derivatives are concrete and modern — ~détachant~ (“stain remover”) and ~détachage~ (“stain removal”), beside the base ~tache~ itself. Its quiet usefulness is a reminder that not every French verb climbs back to Rome; this one is built, late and locally, from a humble native noun. The untying ~détacher~, by contrast, carries the abstract senses of separation, secondment and emotional detachment — a good example of how French spelling can fuse two unrelated histories into a single shape.
en.détailler:
Derived from ~tailler~ (“to cut, carve”) with the prefix ~dé-~. ~tailler~ comes from Old French ~taillier~, from Late Latin ~taliāre~ (“to cut”), from Latin ~talea~ (“a cutting, twig, slip for planting”). Through ~taliāre~, ~tailler~ is cousin to Italian ~tagliare~ and Spanish ~tajar~, and the noun ~taille~ ultimately gave English ~tally~ and ~tailor~ (the cutter of cloth). The prefix ~dé-~ here carries the sense of separation, breaking apart.

To ~détailler~ was first to “cut into pieces” — to divide a whole into its small parts. From dividing physical things grew two important commercial and intellectual senses. Cutting goods into small lots to sell piecemeal gave ~détail~ the meaning “retail” (selling in small quantities, opposed to ~en gros~, “wholesale”); ~vendre au détail~ is to retail. And describing a thing part by part — examining its every small piece — gave the everyday sense “to detail, to recount minutely.” The noun ~détail~ thus carries both ideas at once: a “detail” is a small part cut from the whole, whether of merchandise or of a description. Relatives in modern French include ~tailler~, ~taille~, ~tailleur~, ~détaillant~ (“retailer”), and ~entailler~ (“to notch”).
en.détaler: Formed from ~étaler~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which usually reverses the base verb. It is attested in Old French as ~destaler~. The base ~étaler~ goes back to the Old French noun ~estal~ (“stand, stall”), itself from Frankish *~stal~. Modern ~détaler~, “to scamper off,” is far from a plain reversal of ~étaler~ (“to spread out, display”).
en.détartrer: Formed from the noun ~tartre~ (“tartar, scale”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which here marks removal, and the ending ~-er~, so “to remove the scale from,” whether from teeth, a kettle or a boiler. French Wiktionary traces ~tartre~ to Late Latin *~tartarum~, known through its derivative ~tartaralis~ (“tartared”), and from there to Persian ~dard~ (“sediment, deposit”). English Wiktionary gives the verb as ~dé-~ + ~tartre~ + ~-er~, the same pattern.
en.détaxer: Formed in French from ~taxer~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the base: ~détaxer~ means “to remove a tax from, to lower or lift a tax on” goods or a person. The base ~taxer~ comes from Latin ~taxāre~ (“to estimate, to rate”) through Old French, and gave English ~tax~. The same pair of prefix and verb appears in ~surtaxer~, the opposite of ~détaxer~, which means “to tax too heavily.”
en.détecter:
~Détecter~ is a 20th-century word (first attested 1929), and its immediate origin is debated. The CNRTL gives two accounts side by side: either it was derived within French from ~détecteur~ with the verbal suffix ~-er~, or it was borrowed from English ~to detect~. Both lead back to the same Latin source: ~dētegere~ (“to uncover, expose”), from ~de-~ (“off, away”) and ~tegere~ (“to cover”), from PIE *~(s)teg-~ (“to cover, roof”), which also gave English ~thatch~ and ~deck~.

The literal Latin image is undressing — pulling the cover off something hidden — and the modern technical sense kept exactly that: a detector strips away concealment to reveal a signal, a flaw, a presence. The English route is plausible because the word arrived precisely with radio and physics vocabulary, where English led; but since French already had ~détecteur~, native back-formation cannot be ruled out, and the sources do not settle it. From the same ~tegere~ come ~protéger~, ~tégument~, and ~toit~ / ~toiture~ (the “cover” overhead), and from the prefixed verb, ~détection~ and ~détective~.
en.déteindre: ~Déteindre~ is formed from ~teindre~ and the prefix ~dé-~, and it already existed in Old French as ~desteindre~. The prefix reverses the base: where ~teindre~ means to put colour into cloth, ~déteindre~ means to lose colour or to let it run onto other fabric. The base descends from Latin ~tingere~ (“to dip, to dye”), which also gave Italian ~tingere~ and Spanish ~teñir~, and is the ancestor of ~teinte~, ~teinture~ and English ~tint~. The prefix comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.dételer: Formed from ~atteler~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to unharness a horse or unyoke a bull. French Wiktionary adds that Littré derived the base from the noun ~attelle~. The verb ~atteler~ itself most likely continues a Vulgar Latin *~attelare~, which French Wiktionary derives from Latin ~protelare~ (“to drive on”) with a swap of prefix, though Littré's rival view makes it a verb drawn from ~attelle~, the part of a draft horse's collar to which the traces are fastened. The question is not fully settled.
en.détendre:
From Latin ~detendere~ (“to unstretch, slacken, take down”), from ~dē-~ (here reversive, “un-”) plus ~tendere~ (“to stretch, draw tight”). ~tendere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). Cognate, through that root, with Ancient Greek ~τείνω~ (“to stretch”), English ~thin~, and German ~dehnen~ (“to stretch”).

If ~tendre~ is to pull taut, ~détendre~ is to let off the tension: one ~détendre~ a bow, a spring, a rope — and then, figuratively, one's nerves, one's mood, the atmosphere of a room. The reflexive ~se détendre~ is the everyday French for “to relax, unwind.” From the same *~ten-~ root French keeps a broad family: ~tendre~, ~étendre~ (“to spread”), ~tension~, ~tendon~, ~attendre~, ~entendre~, and the noun ~détente~ — which travelled into diplomacy as the very word for an easing of strained relations. To ~détendre~ is, at root, to let what was pulled tight go slack.
en.détenir:
From Latin ~detinēre~ (“to hold back, keep occupied, retain”), a compound of ~de-~ (here intensive or “away”) and ~tenēre~ (“to hold”), reshaped in French on the model of the inherited verb ~tenir~. ~Tenēre~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~tenēō~ to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ten-~ (“to stretch, draw taut”). The same root surfaces in Greek ~teínō~ (“I stretch”) and Sanskrit ~tanóti~, and ~tenēre~ itself lives on in Italian ~tenere~ and Spanish ~tener~.

French attests ~détenir~ early — around 1160 in the sense “to seize,” then “to hold someone back, restrain” by 1176, and by 1306 the now-dominant “to hold prisoner.” The trajectory runs from simply holding to holding against someone's will: to detain is to keep a grip on a person or thing that would otherwise slip free, which is why the same verb covers both holding a record and holding an inmate. The link between holding and stretching is the taut rope or sinew one keeps tight; from *~ten-~ French inherits a dense web of words, among them ~tenir~, ~tendre~ (“to stretch”), ~tension~, ~tenace~, ~contenir~, ~maintenir~, and the noun ~détenu~ (“detainee”), the one held fast.
en.déterger:
~Déterger~ comes from Latin ~detergere~ (“to remove by wiping or rubbing”), reached through Middle French ~deterger~. The Latin verb is made of ~dē-~ (“off, away”) and ~tergere~ (“to wipe”). French thus took the verb over as a learned word, which explains its technical, medical register: the sense stayed close to the Latin one of wiping something away so that the surface beneath is clean.

In modern French, ~déterger~ is used for cleaning a surface or a wound, removing dirt or secretions. Its family is learned as well. ~Détergent~ (“cleaning agent”) comes from the present participle of the Latin verb, and ~détersif~ is a related adjective and noun for the same idea. English ~deterge~ and ~detergent~ were borrowed along the same learned path. As with most such Latin loans, the verb has stayed rare in everyday speech while its derivatives became common household words.
en.déterminer:
From Latin ~determinare~ (“to bound, fix limits to”), from ~de-~ (here intensive) and ~terminare~ (“to limit”), itself from ~terminus~ (“boundary, boundary-stone”). The noun ~terminus~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ter-~ (“peg, post, boundary-marker”), which also gave Greek ~terma~ (“end-point, goal”). Cognate with Italian ~determinare~ and Spanish ~determinar~, and — through ~terminus~ — with English ~determine~, ~term~, and ~terminal~.

The surprise is the boundary-stone at the root: to ~déterminer~ is etymologically to “mark the limits” of a thing, to drive its boundary-posts so that it is fixed and unambiguous. The Romans even worshipped a god ~Terminus~, guardian of boundary-stones, honored at the festival of the ~Terminalia~. From the spatial act of bordering grew the abstract senses of settling a question, fixing a value, and resolving someone to act. The same ~terminus~ underlies a generous French family — ~terme~, ~terminer~, ~terminus~, ~terminal~, ~exterminer~, and ~indéterminé~ — all of them, in the end, about reaching or fixing a limit.
en.déterrer: ~Déterrer~ is formed from ~enterrer~ (“to bury”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to dig up what was buried. Old French already had the form ~desterer~. The base ~enterrer~ is ~en-~ plus a verb on ~terre~, from Latin ~terra~ (“earth”), which goes back to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “dry.” That makes ~terre~ a distant cousin of English ~thirst~.
en.détester:
French ~détester~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~detestari~ (“to curse, to denounce, to call down evil upon”), formed from ~de-~ (here “away, down”) and ~testari~ (“to bear witness”), a verb derived from ~testis~ (“a witness”). And ~testis~ hides a small drama: it goes back, by the standard account, to Proto-Italic *~tristos~ and PIE *~tristh₂s~ — literally a “third party standing by,” from *~tréyes~ (“three”) plus *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). A witness was the impartial third person who stood beside the two parties to a dispute. So ~detestari~ first meant to invoke the gods as witnesses against someone — to curse them under solemn testimony.

The heat of that curse cooled, over centuries, into the modern ~détester~: no longer to call down divine judgment, merely to hate or strongly dislike. The original courtroom image is still legible in the verb's cousins, all sharing ~testis~: ~témoin~ (“witness,” via Old French) and ~témoigner~, ~attester~, ~contester~, ~protester~, and ~testament~ — the document by which one “testifies” one's will. To ~détester~ a dish, then, is the faded echo of once standing up, a third party, to swear before the gods against it.
en.détirer: This verb is formed from ~tirer~ (“to pull”) with the prefix ~dé-~. The French source refers readers to ~étirer~, built on the same verb with ~é-~, so the two are close variants meaning “to stretch by pulling”. The prefix here does not reverse the base: it adds the idea of pulling out and apart. The origin of ~tirer~ itself is debated. The leading hypothesis derives it from a Germanic (Gothic) word for tearing, while a rival account sees a shortening of Old French ~martirier~ (“to torture”).
en.détoner:
