Learned borrowing from Latin ~detonāre~ (“to thunder down, to thunder forth”), itself formed from ~dē-~ (“down”) and ~tonāre~ (“to thunder”). The verb reached French already complete, so it is not a French prefix-plus-base formation. Latin ~tonāre~ lives on in the inherited French verb ~tonner~ (“to thunder”), and its relatives include English ~thunder~ and German ~Donner~, which belong to the same Indo-European family.

In French the verb means “to explode with a loud report,” and it gave ~détonation~ and ~détonateur~. It must not be confused with ~détonner~ (“to be out of tune”), a homophone built on ~ton~ with ~dé-~ and unrelated to thunder. Another member of the family is ~étonner~ (“to astonish”), which also goes back to ~tonāre~ through a Vulgar Latin compound, and from whose Old French form English took ~astonish~.
en.détonner: ~Détonner~ is built on the noun ~ton~ (“tone, pitch”) with the prefix ~dé-~ and the ending ~-er~, and it means to sing or play out of tune, or, figuratively, to clash with its surroundings. The noun ~ton~ was borrowed from Latin ~tonus~, itself from Ancient Greek ~tonos~ (“cord, tension of a lyre string, musical mode, accent”). Beware of the spelling: ~détoner~ with one ~n~ (“to explode”) is a different verb, linked to ~tonner~ (from Latin ~tonāre~, “to thunder”). Fr.Wiktionary notes that writers do not always keep the two apart.
en.détordre: Formed from ~tordre~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to untwist what has been twisted. The base ~tordre~ is inherited from Old French ~tordre~, itself from Vulgar Latin *~torcĕre~, reshaping Latin ~torquēre~ (“to twist”). The same Latin verb gave English ~torture~, ~torque~ and ~contort~, and French ~tort~, ~tordu~ and ~torsion~.
en.détortiller: Formed from ~tortiller~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: to untwist or unravel what has been twisted. French Wiktionary notes an older spelling ~destortoiller~. The base is of unsettled origin: it is either inherited from Vulgar Latin *~tortiliāre~, built on Latin ~tortilis~ (“twisted”), or a regressive form of ~entortiller~. Behind it lies Latin ~torquēre~ (“to twist”), which also gave ~tordre~ and ~torsion~.
en.détourer: Formed from the noun ~tour~ with the prefix ~dé-~, the pattern ~dé-~ + noun + ~-er~ that usually expresses removal or deprivation; the verb means “to silhouette.” The noun ~tour~ covers several different words, one from Latin ~turris~ (“tower”) and one from Latin ~tornus~ (“lathe, potter's wheel”), and the evidence does not say which lies behind this verb.
en.détourner:
From Old French ~torner~ (“to turn”), the modern verb being ~tourner~ with the prefix ~dé-~ (Latin ~dis-~, “apart, away”), from Latin ~tornāre~ (“to turn on a lathe, to round off”), from ~tornus~ (“a lathe, a turner's tool”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~τόρνος~ (~tórnos~, “tool for drawing a circle”), from PIE *~terh₁-~ (“to rub, to turn by twisting”). Cognate, through ~tourner~, with Italian ~tornare~ and Spanish ~tornar~.

The lathe sense is the heart of the family: to turn wood on a spinning tool. From “turn” French built a crowd of words on ~tour~ (“a turn, a lathe”): ~détour~, ~contour~, ~retour~, and the verb ~tourner~ itself. ~Détourner~ adds ~dé-~ to mean “to turn aside,” hence “to divert” a river or a plane, and figuratively “to distract” someone or to embezzle (~détourner des fonds~). The same root *~terh₁-~ surfaces in ~tour~, ~tournoi~, ~tournevis~, and the borrowed ~tornade~.
en.détoxiquer: ~Détoxiquer~ is formed from ~toxique~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which marks removal, and the verbal ending, so it means “to rid of poison.” The base comes from Latin ~toxicus~ (“poisoned”) and ~toxicum~ (“poison”), which were borrowed from Greek ~toxikón~, short for “poison for arrows,” a word built on ~tóxon~ (“bow”). The poison thus took its name from the weapon it was smeared on.
en.détracter: French ~détracter~ comes from Latin ~detractāre~ (“to disparage, to belittle”), also spelled ~detrectāre~. This is a frequentative of ~detrahere~ (“to draw off, to take away”), built from ~dē-~ (“away”) and ~trahere~ (“to pull, to drag”). English ~detract~ is a parallel borrowing from the same Latin family. In French the verb is a learned, somewhat literary word, meaning to speak ill of someone or to run down their merit. It sits beside the more familiar noun ~détracteur~ (“one who disparages”), which is far more common than the verb. The root ~trahere~ has a huge family in French: ~traire~ (“to milk”), ~trait~, ~traiter~, ~tracteur~, ~attraction~, ~distraire~ and ~extraire~.
en.détraquer: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~, the Middle French noun ~trac~ (“trace, track”) and the verb ending ~-er~. The first sense was built on the idea of removing something from its track. The current sense, to put something out of order or unsettle it, appeared only about a century later. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and ~-er~ from Latin ~-are~. The sources trace ~trac~ no further. The word is a French coinage on a Middle French noun, so it is not a loan from an older language.
en.détremper: ~Détremper~ is formed from ~tremper~ with the prefix ~dé-~, giving a verb for soaking something thoroughly or thinning it with liquid, as in watering down mortar or colour. The base ~tremper~ is inherited from Middle French, where it was a metathesis of Old French ~temprer~, from Latin ~temperāre~ (“to mix in due proportion”). That Latin verb also gave the learned doublet ~tempérer~. The older idea of mixing a liquid in measure thus lives on in ~détremper~, which has kept the sense of a substance made soft by water.
en.détromper: ~Détromper~ is built from the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ~tromper~ (“to deceive”), so it means to undo a deception, to free someone from an error or an illusion. ~Tromper~ is itself derived from the noun ~trompe~ (“horn”) and is attested from the late 12th century. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), and here marks reversal. The verb is most often reflexive: ~se détromper~ means “to see one's mistake,” and the common imperative ~détrompez-vous~ is an invitation to drop a false belief.
en.détroquer: French Wiktionary derives ~détroquer~ from the Old French noun ~troche~, also spelled ~troque~, which meant “bundle” or “cluster.” The verb has the sense “to detach,” as if separating one item from a bunch. The prefix ~dé-~ commonly expresses removal or reversal, and it fits that reading, although the source states the derivation only from the noun. No date or further history is given for the verb.
en.détrousser: Formed from ~trousser~ with the prefix ~dé-~ (Old French ~destrusser~, with ~des-~). French Wiktionary treats it as a derivation, while English Wiktionary calls it only a surface analysis. The prefix ~dé-~ comes from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The base ~trousser~ comes from Old French ~trusser~, from a Vulgar Latin *~torsāre~ built on the participle of ~torqueō~ (“to twist”), the root of ~tordre~ and ~torsion~. Today ~détrousser~ means to rob someone of what they wear or carry.
en.détruire:
From Old French ~destruire~, from Vulgar Latin *~destrugere~, a remodeling of Classical Latin ~destruere~ (“to tear down, to demolish”). The verb joins the prefix ~de-~ (here “un-, reversal”) and ~struere~ (“to pile up, to build”), from Proto-Italic *~strowō~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~strew-~ (“to strew, to spread out”). Through that root it is cognate with English ~strew~ and, via the Latin compounds, with ~structure~ and ~construct~.

The etymology is beautifully exact: if ~struere~ is to build by piling up, then ~de-struere~ is to take the pile apart — to un-build. ~Détruire~ is thus the precise opposite of ~construire~ (~con-~ + ~struere~, “to pile together”), its twin and antonym in a single root. The family is tightly knit in French: ~construire~, ~instruire~ (literally “to build into,” hence “to teach”), ~structure~, ~industrie~, and the noun ~destruction~ all rest on the same ~struere~. There is a quiet irony in the shared root: to instruct, to construct, and to destroy are, etymologically, three ways of handling the same heap — building it up into the mind, into a wall, or pulling it back down.
en.détrôner: Formed from ~trône~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ending ~-er~; English Wiktionary equivalently reads it as ~dé-~ + ~trôner~. The prefix ~dé-~ conveys removal, here “to take off the throne”. The noun ~trône~ comes from Middle French ~throne~ and Old French ~trone~, from Latin ~thronus~, borrowed in turn from Ancient Greek ~θρόνος~ (~thrónos~, “seat, chair”). Italian ~trono~ is a cognate. The verb applies literally to deposing a monarch and figuratively to ousting a champion or a leader.
en.détériorer: Borrowed from Late Latin ~deteriorāre~ (“to make worse”), a verb built on the Latin comparative adjective ~deterior~ (“worse, lower in quality”). French took it as a learned word, and it can be transitive, to damage something, or pronominal, as in ~se détériorer~, to decline in condition. English ~deteriorate~ is a borrowing of the same Latin verb.
en.dévaler: ~Dévaler~ is built around the noun ~val~ (“valley”), with the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ending ~-er~ added together. ~Val~ is inherited from Old French ~val~, from Latin ~vallis~ (“valley”). English Wiktionary adds that the verb itself is inherited from Middle French ~dévaler~, from Old French ~devaler~, and that the ~dé- + val + -er~ analysis is only a surface one. The formation suggests the idea of going down toward the valley, which fits the modern meaning “to rush down a slope.” Here ~dé-~ does not reverse a base verb, since there is none.
en.dévaliser: ~Dévaliser~ is built on ~valise~ (“suitcase”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which here undoes or removes, and the verb ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary traces it to Middle French ~devalizer~. The literal idea is to strip someone of their ~valise~, that is, of their baggage, and from there to rob them of everything they carry. Modern French uses ~dévaliser~ for robbing a person, burgling a house or emptying a shop, and playfully for buying out a store's stock or raiding a fridge.
en.dévaloriser: ~Dévaloriser~ is formed from ~valoriser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the base verb: to ~valoriser~ is to enhance the worth of something, and to ~dévaloriser~ is to lower it. ~Valoriser~ is a French coinage of around 1925, built from ~valeur~ and the suffix ~-iser~. ~Valeur~ comes from Latin ~valor~, from ~valēre~ (“to be strong, to be worth”), whose root also gives English ~value~ and ~valid~. The family includes ~dévalorisation~, ~revaloriser~, ~valoir~ and ~vaillant~. The verb is used for currencies and goods and, in the psychological sense, for belittling a person or oneself.
en.dévaluer: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ~évaluer~ (“to assess”). English Wiktionary adds that it is a calque of English ~devalue~, which is a possible influence rather than a settled fact. The base ~évaluer~ comes from Old French ~esvaluer~, built on the noun ~value~ (“worth”), itself from ~valoir~ and ultimately Latin ~valere~ (“to be worth”). To ~dévaluer~ is thus to take away part of an assessed worth, as when a currency is lowered in value.
en.dévaster: ~Dévaster~ is a borrowing from Latin ~dēvastāre~ (“to lay waste completely”), built from ~dē-~, here an intensifier, and ~vastāre~ (“to ravage”). That verb comes from the adjective ~vastus~ (“empty, desolate”), which also gave French ~vaste~ and English ~vast~. English ~devastate~ is a parallel borrowing of the same Latin verb. The idea is of a land stripped until it lies empty.
en.développer:
From Old French ~desveloper~ (attested around 1170 as ~desvoleper~, “to bring out of what envelops it”), formed as the antonym of ~enveloper~ (“to wrap up”) with the separative prefix ~des-~. The shared core ~-veloper~ has an obscure origin that etymologists have never settled: it is also the root of Italian ~viluppo~ (“tangle, bundle”) and its derivative ~sviluppo~ (“development”), but no convincing Latin or Germanic source for the bare stem has won acceptance, so honest dictionaries leave it unexplained. English ~develop~ was borrowed from the French verb.

The image behind ~développer~ is concrete and tactile: to ~unwrap~ a parcel, to peel away a covering and let what was hidden come into the open. From that literal unwrapping the verb extended to “to expand, unfold, set out at length,” then to the modern senses of growing, elaborating an argument, processing photographic film, and — most recently — writing software. The opposite gesture survives intact in ~enveloper~ and in the noun ~enveloppe~. From the same family come ~développement~, ~développeur~, and the adjective ~développable~. The contrast between wrapping and unwrapping still animates the pair: where ~enveloper~ conceals, ~développer~ reveals.
en.dévergonder:
From ~dé-~ (“un-”) + Middle French ~vergonde~ + ~-er~, so literally “to shed one's shame”. ~Vergonde~ is a variant of ~vergogne~, the old word for shame, which French inherited from Latin ~verecundia~ (“modesty, shame”), a noun built on ~verēri~ (“to revere, to fear”). The Latin word lived on across the Romance languages: Italian ~vergogna~ and Spanish ~vergüenza~ are its cousins.

The prefix ~dé-~, from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), reverses a state here: a person who is ~dévergondé~ has put off modesty and restraint. Hence the verb's sense of losing one's shame and being led astray, and the participle ~dévergondé~ now also works as an adjective for the shameless or dissolute. ~Vergogne~ itself has almost vanished from everyday French outside the fixed phrase ~sans vergogne~ (“shamelessly”), so this verb is one of the places where the old word still shows through.
en.déverguer: Formed from the prefix ~dé-~ (undoing) and the nautical noun ~vergue~ (“yard,” the spar that holds a sail), plus the verb ending ~-er~. To ~déverguer~ is to unbend the sails from the yards. ~Vergue~ is a variant of ~verge~, and English Wiktionary traces it to Norman ~vèrgue~, from Latin ~virga~ (“rod”).
en.dévernir: Formed from ~vernir~ (“to varnish”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action of the base (from Latin ~dis-~, “apart”), so “to strip varnish.” The base ~vernir~ is built on the noun ~vernis~, which appears in Old French as ~verniz~ and comes from Medieval Latin ~veronīx~. Behind it stands Byzantine Greek ~βερενίκη~ (“resin, amber”). French Wiktionary links these Greek names to the city of Berenice, while English Wiktionary calls that only possible and warns that it may be a false etymology.
en.déverrouiller: ~Déverrouiller~ combines the prefix ~dé-~ with ~verrouiller~ (“to bolt”) and means to undo the bolt, hence to unlock or unfasten. The French Wiktionary adds that it continues Old French ~desverroillier~. The base comes from ~verrou~ (“bolt”), from Old French ~veroil~, which goes back to a Latin form of ~veruculum~, a diminutive of ~verū~ (“spit, skewer”). The prefix ~dé-~ descends from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”) and marks reversal. The verb serves for physical locks and, figuratively, for a blocked situation.
en.déverser: Formed in French from the prefix ~dé-~ and the verb ~verser~ (“to pour”). Here ~dé-~ does not simply undo the base: it adds the idea of pouring something away or out, in quantity. ~Verser~ comes from Late Latin *~versāre~, a repeated-action form of Latin ~vertere~ (“to turn”), because pouring means turning a container over. So ~déverser~ can describe a river emptying into the sea, a truck unloading its cargo, or, figuratively, a stream of insults. The same family gives ~déversoir~, a spillway.
en.dévider: Both Wiktionaries give ~dévider~ as ~vider~ with the prefix ~dé-~. The base ~vider~ comes from Old French ~vuidier~, from the adjective ~vuit~ (“empty”), itself descending from the Latin family of ~vacuus~ (“empty”) and ~vacāre~ (“to be empty”). The prefix ~dé-~ goes back to Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”). The verb means “to unwind thread from a reel or skein,” and by extension “to reel off” a long speech or a string of details. Its link to emptying is plain on the surface, though the sources say nothing about how the sense developed.
en.dévier:
Borrowed from Latin ~dēviāre~ (“to turn aside from the road”), built from the prefix ~dē-~ (“away from”) and ~via~ (“road, way”). French already had a cousin of its own, Old French ~desvoier~, formed with a different prefix, which survives as ~dévoyer~. Italian ~deviare~ and English ~deviate~ also come from the Latin verb.

The image is literal: to ~dévier~ is to leave the track. French applies it to a vehicle or a river pushed off course, then figuratively to an idea, a policy or a conversation, and in physics and sport to a ray or a ball that is deflected and a blow that is parried. Learned ~dévier~ and inherited ~dévoyer~ show French keeping two versions of one idea: the first is neutral, while the second often carries a moral tinge, as when a young person is led astray. The root ~via~ survives in ~voie~ and in ~envoyer~, literally “to put on the way”.
en.dévirer: Formed from ~virer~ (“to turn”) with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action of the base (from Latin ~dis-~, “apart”), so “to turn back.” In the nautical sense, this means turning a capstan the other way to slacken a line. The origin of ~virer~ is debated. The favored account is a Vulgar Latin *~virāre~ (“to turn”), probably an alteration of ~vibrāre~ (“to shake”), which would make ~virer~ a doublet of ~vibrer~. French Wiktionary also attributes a second sense of ~dévirer~ to the writer Jean Giono, though it words this cautiously.
en.dévirginiser: The verb ~dévirginiser~ comes from Latin ~devirginare~ (“to deflower”), built on ~virgo~ (“maiden, virgin”), with the French ending ~-iser~. The Latin verb joins the prefix ~dē-~ (“off, away”) to ~virgo~ and the verbal ending ~-āre~, so the idea is to take away someone's virginity. The ending ~-iser~, ultimately from Late Latin ~-izāre~, is the usual way French dresses such verbs. The Latin noun ~virgo~ gave French ~vierge~ by inheritance, and the learned words ~virginal~ and ~virginité~ by borrowing. English ~virgin~ comes from the same Latin word through Old French.
en.déviriliser: Formed from ~viriliser~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which here marks the reversal of the base verb: to remove virility, the opposite of making virile. The base is built on the adjective ~viril~, which comes from Latin ~virīlis~, itself derived from ~vir~ (“man”), with the verbal suffix ~-iser~. That suffix goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs. French Wiktionary gives ~déviriliser~ as a plain derivative of ~viriliser~.
en.dévisager: A parasynthetic formation: the prefix ~dé-~ and the ending ~-er~ were added to the noun ~visage~ at once, since no verb *~visager~ lies behind it. ~Visage~ comes from Old French ~visage~, built from ~vis~ (“face”) plus ~-age~; ~vis~ goes back to Latin ~visus~ and still lives in ~vis-à-vis~. The Académie française recorded ~dévisager~ in the first edition of its dictionary, in 1694. The sense is “to stare hard at someone's face,” and the prefix here has no obvious “undo” meaning.
en.dévisser: Formed from ~visser~ (“to screw”) and the prefix ~dé-~, which here reverses the action: to unscrew. The base verb comes from the noun ~vis~ (“screw”), which descends from Latin ~vītis~ (“vine, tendril”); French Wiktionary links that word to ~viēre~ (“to twist”), so the screw was named for the spiral of a tendril. The prefix ~dé-~, from Old French ~des-~ and Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”), supplies the opposite action: it undoes what the base verb does.
en.dévitaliser: ~Dévitaliser~ is built on the adjective ~vital~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and the suffix ~-iser~: “to deprive of vitality.” The adjective ~vital~ comes from Latin ~vītālis~ (“of life, life-giving”) through Old French. The prefix ~dé-~ marks the cessation of a state, and ~-iser~ turns the adjective into a verb meaning “to make.” The verb is also the usual French term for devitalizing a tooth, that is, for a root canal.
en.dévitrifier: This verb is formed from ~vitrifier~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the base: to devitrify is to undo vitrification, so that glass loses its glassy state. The base ~vitrifier~ is built on ~vitre~ (“windowpane”) with the suffix ~-ifier~ (“to make”, from Latin ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~). ~Vitre~ was borrowed from Latin ~vitrum~ (“glass”), which makes it a doublet of ~verre~. Spanish ~vidrio~ and Catalan ~vidre~ are cousins from the same Latin word.
en.dévoiler:
A French formation of the seventeenth century, built from the prefix ~dé-~ (a privative, “un-, removal of”) plus the verb ~voiler~ (“to veil, to cover with a veil”). ~Voiler~ is itself denominal, from the noun ~voile~, which descends from Latin ~vela~, the plural of ~velum~ (“sail, cloth, covering, curtain”). Through ~velum~ it is kin to English ~veil~ and ~reveal~ and to Spanish ~velo~.

The morphology is wonderfully transparent: where ~voiler~ puts a veil on, ~dé-~ takes it off, so ~dévoiler~ is literally “to un-veil.” The verb runs in step with the concrete and the figurative at once — to ~dévoiler~ a statue at its inauguration, and to ~dévoiler~ a secret, a plot, one's true intentions. Latin ~velum~ is the common ancestor of a small French cluster: the noun ~voile~ (notice that it is masculine, “the veil,” but feminine, “the sail,” the two meanings split by gender), the verbs ~voiler~ and ~révéler~ (from Latin ~revelare~, “to draw back the veil”), and ~vélum~ itself, the awning of an arena. To reveal and to unveil are, at root, the very same gesture.
en.dévolter: Formed from ~volt~ with the prefix ~dé-~ and the ending ~-er~, meaning to reduce the voltage. The unit ~volt~ was named for the Italian physicist Alessandro Volta, and French took the word through English. Here ~dé-~ marks a lowering or removal, as in ~dégeler~ or ~déconnecter~.
en.dévorer:
From Latin ~dēvorāre~ (“to swallow down, to devour, to engulf”), a learned borrowing built from ~dē-~ (“down, completely”) and ~vorāre~ (“to swallow, to gulp”). The simple verb ~vorāre~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʷerh₃-~ (“to swallow”), which also lies behind Greek ~bora~ (“food, meat”) and Sanskrit words for swallowing. Latin ~dēvorāre~ lived on in the Romance languages: Italian has ~divorare~ and Spanish ~devorar~. English ~devour~ came in through French, not from the Latin directly.

The prefix ~dē-~ here is intensive, so the verb means not merely to swallow but to swallow up entirely, and French quickly let that appetite spill over into figurative uses. Flames ~dévorent~ a building, a reader ~dévore~ a novel, a lover ~dévore~ someone with his eyes, and remorse or jealousy ~dévore~ a person from within. The bare Latin verb ~vorāre~ did not survive in French, but it left its mark in learned vocabulary: ~vorace~, ~voracité~, and the family of diet words built on the Latin ending ~-vorus~, among them ~carnivore~, ~herbivore~ and ~omnivore~. So the monster of an appetite and the vegetarian's label share one ancestor.
en.dévouer: Formed in French from the prefix ~dé-~ and ~vouer~, and based on Latin ~dēvovēre~ (“to consecrate by a vow”), through Old French ~devoer~. The Latin verb could mean dedicating something to a god and even doomed someone to the gods below. ~Vouer~ itself goes back to the idea of a solemn promise, linked to Latin ~vōtum~ (“vow”). The French verb lost the darker side. ~Dévouer~ now means to give up, to consecrate, and its reflexive form ~se dévouer~ means to sacrifice oneself for a cause or for others. Related words are ~dévot~, ~dévotion~ and ~vœu~.
en.dévoyer: ~Dévoyer~ is formed from the prefix ~dé-~, the noun ~voie~ (“way, road”) and the verb ending ~-er~. The prefix marks removal, so the verb literally means “to take off the road” and, figuratively, “to lead astray.” ~Voie~ is inherited from Old French ~voie~, from Latin ~via~ (“road”), of which it is a doublet. English Wiktionary notes that it is unrelated to ~voir~, despite the resemblance.
en.dévêtir: Formed from ~vêtir~ with the prefix ~dé-~, which reverses the action: the verb means to take someone's clothes off. English Wiktionary gives Old French ~desvestir~ as the immediate source, which shows the verb is older than modern French. The base ~vêtir~ comes from Latin ~vestīre~ (“to clothe”), built on ~vestis~ (“garment”). The old ~s~ before the ~t~ fell silent and survives only as the circumflex of ~vêtir~. The prefix comes from Latin ~dis-~ (“apart”).
en.dîner:
From Old French ~disner~, inherited from Vulgar Latin *~disiūnāre~, itself from ~disieiūnāre~ or ~disjejūnāre~ (“to break the fast”). That Latin verb joined ~dis-~ (“undoing”) to Late Latin ~iēiūnāre~ (“to fast”), from Latin ~ieiūnus~ (“fasting”). French ~dîner~ is thus a doublet of ~déjeuner~, which comes from the very same source by a different phonetic route. English borrowed the family from Old French as ~dine~ and ~dinner~.

The circumflex of ~dîner~ is a scar: it stands in for the ~s~ of Old French ~disner~, which fell silent in the Middle Ages. The meaning tells a small story about eating habits. Originally the verb named the first meal of the day, the one that ended the overnight fast. As the main meal drifted later, ~déjeuner~ took over the morning meal, and ~dîner~ followed the main meal toward the evening. The older timetable survives in Belgium, Switzerland and Quebec, where ~dîner~ still means to eat at midday and ~souper~ names the evening meal. French thus keeps, inside one verb, a memory of breaking a fast.
en.effacer:
Attested in the twelfth century, ~effacer~ is a French parasynthetic formation: the noun ~face~ (“face, surface”), from Latin ~facies~ (“appearance, face, surface”), framed by the prefix ~é-~ (from Latin ~ex-~, “out, away”) and the verbal ending ~-er~. It has an Occitan counterpart, ~esfassar~. The literal sense built into the word is striking: to ~effacer~ is, etymologically, to take the face off something — to remove its surface, its outward showing.

From that vivid image — stripping the visible skin from a thing — the verb generalized to making any mark disappear: erasing writing, rubbing out a stain, fading a color. It then climbed into the figurative, where it means to cancel or wipe away (effacer une dette, une faute), to outshine or eclipse (son talent ~efface~ celui des autres), and, reflexively, to withdraw discreetly (s’~effacer~ pour laisser passer quelqu’un). The same ~facies~ root spreads through French in ~face~, ~surface~, ~façade~, and ~facette~, so that every time one ~efface~ a word, one is, by the word’s own logic, peeling away a little face.
en.effarer: French Wiktionary describes ~effarer~ (“to scare, to frighten”) as derived from the adjective ~effaré~ (“frightened”). The sources consulted trace it no further, so its deeper ancestry is deliberately left open here rather than guessed. The verb ending ~-er~ comes from the Latin first-conjugation ending ~-are~, the ending that turned ~cantare~ into ~chanter~. On the evidence available, then, this is a modest entry: a verb whose recorded origin stops at an adjective, with nothing firmer to add.
en.effaroucher: Formed from ~farouche~ with the prefix ~é-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, so that the verb means to make an animal shy or drive it off. ~Farouche~ comes from Old French ~faroche~, an alteration of ~forasche~, itself from Late Latin ~forāsticus~ (“belonging outside”), from Latin ~forās~ (“out of doors”). The adjective thus began as “from outside, foreign” and came to mean “badly tamed, wild”. A dialectal form ~fourâche~, from which ~farouche~ arose by metathesis, survives in many regions.
en.effectuer:
From Latin ~effectuāre~, a verb built on ~effectus~ (“an accomplishment, a result, an effect”), itself the past participle of ~efficere~ (“to bring about, accomplish”). ~Efficere~ is ~ex-~ (“out”) plus a combining form of ~facere~ (“to make, to do”), from Proto-Italic *~fakiō~, from PIE *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, to set, to place”). Through that same root ~effectuer~ is cognate with English ~do~ and ~deed~ and with German ~tun~.

The Latin ~efficere~ described carrying a thing all the way through to its finished result, and the derived noun ~effectus~ named that result — the modern ~effet~. From this came the learned verb ~effectuer~, which keeps the precise, almost technical flavor of its origin: one ~effectue~ a calculation, a payment, or an experiment, bringing a defined procedure to completion. The PIE root *~dʰeh₁-~ is extraordinarily prolific: ~faire~ itself descends from ~facere~, and the family includes ~effet~, ~affecter~, ~parfait~ (“thoroughly done”), and ~fait~. A surprising relative is ~thème~, which reaches French through Greek from the same root meaning “something set down.”
en.effeuiller: ~Effeuiller~ is a parasynthetic verb, built on the noun ~feuille~ (“leaf”) with the prefix ~é-~ and the ending ~-er~. The prefix has its sense of removal, so the verb means to strip the leaves or petals from something. English Wiktionary compares ~exfolier~, a learned verb of the same shape. The noun ~feuille~ comes through Old French ~fueille~ from Late Latin ~folia~, an old plural of Latin ~folium~ (“leaf”). It is a doublet of ~folio~, which was borrowed straight from Latin, and its cognates include Italian ~foglia~ and Spanish ~hoja~.
en.effiler: Formed from ~filer~ with the prefix ~ex-~, which becomes ~ef-~ before an f, and which here suggests drawing something out. ~Filer~ comes from Late Latin ~filare~ (“to spin into thread”), from ~filum~ (“thread”), so ~effiler~ is to reduce something to threads or to a fine edge. That gives the senses “to thin” and “to taper”, and, for fabric, “to fray”.
en.effilocher: Formed from ~filoche~ with the prefix ~é-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, the verb means to fray fabric into loose threads. ~Filoche~ is itself a derivative of ~fil~ (“thread”) with the suffix ~-oche~. The prefix ~é-~ comes from Latin ~ex-~ (“out of, away from”) through Old French ~es-~, and here it suggests threads pulled out of the weave. ~-er~ comes from the Latin ending ~-are~.
en.effiloquer: Now old-fashioned, ~effiloquer~ is a variant of ~effilocher~, which the TLFi derives from ~filoche~ with the prefix ~é-~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The idea is to pull cloth apart thread by thread. ~Effilocher~ is recorded in 1657 for wool recovered from rags and in 1761 for unpicking fabric. Today it also means to fray, and figuratively to wear away, as in Flaubert's flesh that ~s'effiloquait~ in red shreds (1857).
en.effleurer: French Wiktionary derives ~effleurer~ from ~fleurer~ with the prefix ~ex-~, which assimilates to ~ef-~ before the f. It first meant “to strip of flowers,” and by the sixteenth century “to touch lightly.” English Wiktionary gives Old French ~esflourer~ for the same pieces and adds that, in some senses, the verb comes instead from Middle French ~fleur~ (“surface, top layer”), ultimately Germanic and related to English ~floor~. On that second account, touching lightly is skimming a surface.
en.effleurir: This verb is formed from ~fleurir~ with the prefix ~é-~, which is the Latin ~ex-~ in a learned form, assimilated to ~ef-~ before the ~f~. The base ~fleurir~ comes from Vulgar Latin ~florire~, a reshaping of Latin ~florere~ (“to bloom”), from ~flos~ (“flower”), and from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰleh₃-~ (“to bloom”). The verb means “to effloresce”, and it belongs to the same family as ~fleur~, ~floraison~ and ~flore~.
en.effondrer: Inherited from Old French ~esfondrer~, itself from Vulgar Latin *~exfunderāre~, a verb built on ~fundus~ (“bottom”). The prefix ~ex-~ means “out”, so the picture is of something whose bottom gives way, which is how a floor, a roof or a wall collapses. Catalan ~esfondrar~ is a parallel. The base ~fundus~ also stands behind French ~fond~, ~fonder~ and ~profond~, which shows how many meanings grew from one Latin word for the lowest part of a thing.
en.efforcer:
From Old French ~esforcier~, an intensive formation on ~forcier~ (“to force”) with the prefix ~es-~ (from Latin ~ex-~), matching a Vulgar Latin *~exfortiāre~ (“to put forth one's strength”). Beneath both lies Late Latin ~fortia~ (“strength”) — originally the neuter plural of the adjective ~fortis~ (“strong”), reinterpreted as a feminine noun — the source of French ~force~. ~Fortis~ itself goes back through Old Latin ~forctis~ to Proto-Italic *~forktis~; beyond that the trail forks, scholars hesitating between the PIE roots *~bʰerǵʰ-~ (“to rise, be high”) and *~dʰerǵʰ-~ (“to hold fast, be firm”). Cognate with Italian ~sforzare~ — whose musical imperative ~sforzando~, “forcing” the note, decorates scores the world over — and Spanish ~esforzarse~.

The verb stands at the very dawn of French literature: around 1050, the Vie de saint Alexis, one of the oldest French poems, already uses ~esforcer~ for striving in the service of God. From the beginning it leaned toward the reflexive — force applied to oneself — and modern French confines it there entirely: ~s'efforcer~ exists only with its pronoun, strength turned inward against one's own limits. Its Old French deverbal noun survives as ~effort~, which English borrowed whole. English in fact adopted much of the family: ~force~, ~fort~, ~fortress~, ~effort~ and ~comfort~ — this last from Old French ~conforter~, Late Latin ~confortāre~, literally “to make thoroughly strong”: to comfort someone is, etymologically, to give them back their strength. On the French side stand ~forcer~, ~renforcer~, ~forteresse~, ~fortifier~ and ~réconforter~.
en.effranger: Derived from the noun ~frange~ (“fringe”) with the prefix ~é-~ and the verb ending ~-er~, according to the TLFi, which dates it to 1863 in Goncourt. The transitive verb means to unravel the edge of a fabric so that the threads hang like a fringe. Used reflexively, it means to fray through wear, as a skirt or a sleeve does.
en.effrayer:
French ~effrayer~ comes from Old French ~esfreer~ (also ~esfraer~, ~esfreder~), through Middle French ~effreer~. It is a Germanic word in Latin dress. English Wiktionary derives it from a Vulgar Latin verb *~exfridāre~, built by adding the Latin prefix ~ex-~ to a Frankish *~friþu~ (“security, peace”), from Proto-Germanic *~friþuz~ (“peace”). That noun belongs to the family of *~frijōną~ (“to free; to love”), from Proto-Indo-European *~prāy-~ (“to like, to love”), alongside the variant *~prēy-~. English borrowed the Old French verb as ~affray~. So the chain runs from a Proto-Indo-European root for liking and loving, through Germanic words for peace and security, into Vulgar Latin and Old French.

The Germanic origin deserves a careful reading. Of the two Wiktionaries, only the English one gives the Frankish chain, and it presents the path through *~exfridāre~ as a reconstruction, which is what the asterisk means: the Vulgar Latin verb is not attested but inferred from its descendants. French Wiktionary cites only the Old French forms ~esfreer~, ~esfraer~ and ~esfreder~ and sends the reader to ~effarer~. The variation among those Old French forms is itself worth noticing, since the same verb appeared with several endings before the modern spelling ~effrayer~ settled. Neither source offers a date, so none is given here. The modern verb means “to frighten, to scare.”
en.effriter: Formed from ~fruiter~ with the prefix ~ex-~, and ~fruiter~ is itself a verb built on the noun ~fruit~. In Old French, ~effriter~ was a variant of ~effruiter~, which meant “to exhaust a soil”, that is, to strip it of its fruit. The modern sense “to crumble” was influenced by the adjective ~friable~. French Wiktionary is the only source here, and it gives no date.
en.efféminer:
Borrowed from classical Latin ~effēminare~ (“to make feminine”). The Latin verb is built from ~ex-~ and ~fēmina~ (“woman”), with the ~x~ of the prefix assimilating to the following ~f~, which explains the double ~f~ of the French spelling. The Latin participle ~effēminātus~ gave English ~effeminate~, a close parallel to the French participle ~efféminé~.

The family of ~fēmina~ is large in French. Inherited ~femme~ descends from it, and learned words such as ~féminin~ and ~féminité~ were later drawn from Latin. Within that family, ~efféminer~ is a literary verb, one that describes making a man or a people soft, weak or womanlike, which is why the gloss runs from “make effeminate” to “weaken.” Like its English cousin, it carries an old and now often dated view of what counts as manly, so modern French usually meets it in the adjective ~efféminé~ rather than in the infinitive.
en.emballer: Formed in French from the prefix ~en-~, the noun ~balle~ (“bundle, packet”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to put into a bundle, to pack up.” The prefix ~en-~ is from Latin ~in~ (“in, into”) and here carries its locative sense, with a noun base. As the spelling of the French form shows, ~emballer~ takes ~em-~ before the ~b~, which is only a spelling variant of ~en-~.
en.embarbouiller: Formed from ~barbouiller~ with the prefix ~en-~, which here adds the sense of putting something into the state described, so the verb means to smear or to confuse. The base has an unsettled origin: it may come from ~barboter~, from ~bouille~ (“mire”), or from ~barbe~, and none of these accounts is certain. The family is one of messy, splashing verbs, including ~brouiller~ and ~souiller~.
en.embarquer:
~Embarquer~ is a parasynthetic derivative of ~barque~ (“boat”), formed at once with the prefix ~en-~ (Latin ~in-~, “into”) and the verbal suffix ~-er~ — literally “to put into a boat.” ~Barque~ comes from Latin ~barca~ (“ship's boat”), and the Romance cousins are everywhere: Italian ~imbarcare~, Spanish and Portuguese ~embarcar~ all match it step for step.

The original act was concrete — loading goods or people aboard a ~barque~ — and from there the verb cast off in every direction. One ~embarque~ passengers, but one also ~s'embarque~ in a marriage, a lawsuit, or a doubtful scheme, the boat becoming a metaphor for any committing venture one can no longer easily leave. French preserves the seafaring caution in the idiom ~s'embarquer~ sans biscuit (“to set out without provisions,” i.e. unprepared), a reminder of voyages where forgetting the ship's biscuit could be fatal. The same ~barque~ underlies ~embarquement~, ~débarquer~ (“to land, disembark”) and ~rembarquer~. Modern slang even lets the police ~embarquer~ a suspect — bundling him aboard the van as one would aboard a hull.
en.embarrasser: Borrowed from Spanish ~embarazar~ (“to hinder, to encumber”). The word entered French as a verb of physical obstruction: to ~embarrasser~ a passage is to clutter or block it, and a person weighed down with luggage is ~embarrassé~. From that concrete sense the meaning moved to the social one: to put someone in an awkward position, to make them uneasy. English ~embarrass~ is a related loan from the same family of words and shows the same movement from “hinder” to “disconcert.”
en.embarrer: Formed from ~barrer~ with the prefix ~en-~, which gives the sense of putting in or providing with. ~Embarrer~ is to bar or to block something by means of a bar, and, by extension, to chock it. The base ~barrer~ is itself ~barre~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~, and the noun ~barre~ comes from Old French ~barre~ (“beam, bar, barrier”), from Vulgar Latin *~barra~, whose origin is uncertain. The sources offer a Gaulish, a Germanic or a Celtic source, without settling it.
en.embastiller: ~Embastiller~ (“to imprison, traditionally in the Bastille”) is a parasynthetic verb: it is built from the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”), the name ~Bastille~ and the verb ending ~-er~, with the prefix and the ending added together. ~Bastille~ is itself from the common noun ~bastille~ (“fortress”), which became the name of the famous Paris prison. The verb therefore means “to put in the Bastille,” and by extension “to imprison.”
en.embattre: Formed from ~battre~ with the prefix ~em-~, a spelling of ~en-~ before ~b~. The TLFi cites an early use in the Chanson de Roland, around 1100, in the sense “to drive in,” and the wheelwright's sense is recorded in 1369-70. Today ~embattre~ means to fit a metal tire on a wheel, as on a cart, and to retouch a metal tool with a hammer. The Académie also allows the spelling ~embatre~, though it calls it less good.
en.embaucher: The two Wiktionaries explain ~embaucher~ differently. French Wiktionary derives it from ~débaucher~ by swapping the prefix ~dé-~ for ~en-~. English Wiktionary analyzes it as ~en-~ plus ~bauche~ plus the ending ~-er~, a parasynthetic formation; French Wiktionary refers ~bauche~ to ~bauge~. The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”) and gives the sense “to bring into”: to embauche someone is to take them on, in contrast with ~débaucher~, to lay them off or lure them away.
en.embaumer: The verb is formed from ~baume~ (“balm”) with the prefix ~en-~ and the ending ~-er~, which together mean “to put balm into.” The noun ~baume~ comes from Old French ~basme~, from Latin ~balsamum~, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ~βάλσαμον~ (bálsamon). The same verb covers two senses, to embalm a body with balm and to fill the air with a sweet fragrance.
en.embellir: Formed in French from the prefix ~en-~ (spelled ~em-~ before ~b~), the adjective ~bel~ and the ending ~-ir~. The base is the old form of ~beau~, which survives before a vowel (~bel homme~) and which is not the unit of sound named for Bell. The sense is “to make beautiful,” a typical case where ~en-~ turns an adjective into a verb of change, built together with the second-conjugation ending ~-ir~. Compare ~enrichir~, “to make rich.”
en.emberlificoter: The origin is uncertain. The sources suggest that ~emberlificoter~ is a distortion of ~emberlucoquer~ or ~embrelicoquer~, older verbs of the same meaning. One can imagine that the word was deliberately tangled to match its sense, though that is only a supposition. It means “to entangle, to muddle,” and, by extension, to confuse someone with convoluted talk.
en.emblaver:
~Emblaver~ (“to sow a field with wheat”) is built from the prefix ~en-~ and Old French ~blaver~, a verb of the same meaning, itself from the noun ~blave~. That noun was medieval Latin ~blava~ (“grain, wheat”), which in turn goes back to Frankish ~blâd~ (“produce of a field”). English Wiktionary adds that the verb is first attested in Old French as a variant of ~emblaier~ and ~emblayer~.

The Frankish word that sits at the bottom of this chain also gave French ~blé~ (“wheat”), so ~emblaver~ is, at heart, a verb meaning “to put into wheat.” It has a doublet in the popular form ~bléer~, which developed along the ordinary route of sound change. Today ~emblaver~ is a technical term of farming, used of a field sown with grain, and it belongs to the same family as ~blé~.
en.embobeliner: French Wiktionary derives this colloquial verb from Old French ~bobelin~ (“coarse shoe”). The verb means to hoodwink someone or wrap them around one's finger. The sources at hand do not explain how a word for a rough shoe came to mean this, so that link is left open rather than guessed.
en.embobiner: In its literal sense, ~embobiner~ is built on ~bobine~ (“reel, spool”), with the prefix ~em-~ (the spelling of ~en-~ before b, here meaning “put in or onto”) and the ending ~-er~: to wind thread onto a spool. The figurative sense, “to hoodwink,” is traced by French Wiktionary to a different source, ~embabouiner~. The origin of ~bobine~ itself is debated. Older scholars proposed Latin ~bombyx~ (“silkworm”) or ~bombus~ (“buzzing”), but the TLFi judges it more likely to come from an imitative root ~bob~, evoking something swollen and rounded.
en.embosser: Formed from ~bosser~ with the prefix ~en-~ (from Latin ~in-~), used in the nautical sense: a ship is moored fore and aft by means of a rope called a ~bosse~. The base is thus a sailor's verb tied to ~bosse~ in the sense of “rope,” and not the slang ~bosser~ (“to work”).
en.emboucher: Formed from ~bouche~ (“mouth”) with the prefix ~en-~ and the verb ending ~-er~: to put something in the mouth, whether a wind instrument to the lips or a bit in a horse's mouth. English Wiktionary adds that it may correspond to a Vulgar Latin ~imbuccāre~, from Latin ~bucca~ (“cheek”), and compares Spanish and Portuguese ~embocar~ and Italian ~imboccare~. The noun ~bouche~ comes from Old French ~boche~, from Latin ~bucca~, which replaced classical Latin ~os~ in all the Romance languages.
en.embouquer: Formed from the noun ~bouque~ with the prefix ~em-~ (the form of ~en-~ before ~b~), in its sense “into”: to enter the mouth of a strait or channel, “to put oneself into the opening.” The sources differ on the noun. French Wiktionary takes ~bouque~ from Latin ~bucca~, while English Wiktionary says it was borrowed from Old Occitan ~boca~ and calls it a doublet of ~bouche~. Either way, it belongs with ~bouche~ (“mouth”), which explains why an opening in the coast could be called a mouth.
en.embourber: Formed from ~en-~, the noun ~bourbe~ (“mire”) and the ending ~-er~: to ~embourber~ is to put into the mire, and so to get stuck in mud or in a difficulty. The noun ~bourbe~ is traced to a proposed Gaulish word, *~borua~, for a bubbling hot spring, related to the Gaulish god of hot springs, who is attested in inscriptions at Bourbon-Lancy and Bourbonne-les-Bains.
en.embourgeoiser:
~Embourgeoiser~ is built from ~bourgeois~ with the prefix ~em-~ (the spelling of ~en-~ before b, from Latin ~in-~) and the ending ~-er~. The noun ~bourgeois~ passed through Middle French ~bourgois~ and Old French ~borgeis~ from Late Latin ~burgensis~, formed on Latin ~burgus~ (“fortified place”) with the suffix ~-ēnsis~, which marks origin or belonging. Where ~burgus~ itself comes from is uncertain: a Germanic source, Proto-Germanic *~burgz~, and a Greek one, ~púrgos~ (“tower”), have both been proposed.

French ~bourg~ (“market town, large village”), ~bourgade~ and ~bourgeoisie~ belong to the same family, and English ~borough~ and ~burgher~ and German ~Burg~ (“castle”) are relatives of the Germanic word. ~Embourgeoiser~ means to make bourgeois, or to become bourgeois: to take on the habits, comforts and outlook of the middle class. It is used of a person, a movement or a neighbourhood that settles into respectability, and in the sense “to gentrify” it describes a district taken over by more affluent residents.
en.embouteiller: Formed from ~bouteille~ with the prefix ~em-~, a spelling of ~en-~ before ~b~, and the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to put into a bottle.” ~Bouteille~ comes from Old French ~botele~ or ~boteille~, from Late Latin ~butticula~, a diminutive of ~buttis~ (“a kind of vessel”), which medieval Latin used for a cask or wineskin. The verb means to bottle a liquid and, by extension, to clog a road with traffic.
en.embouter: ~Embouter~ is a verb made from the noun ~embout~ (“nozzle, tip”) with the ending ~-er~, and it means to fit something with a tip or a nozzle. The noun ~embout~ is itself a compound of the preposition ~en~ (“in, on”) and the noun ~bout~ (“end”), so the idea is literally to put something “on the end.” The pattern is the ordinary one in which an ~-er~ verb is coined to mean “provide with” the thing the noun names.
en.emboutir: ~Emboutir~ comes from Middle French ~emboutir~ and is analyzed as ~en-~ + ~bout~ + ~-ir~. The noun ~bout~ was an Old French word for “a blow,” derived from ~bouter~ (“to strike, to push”), of Germanic origin. The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”). French uses the verb to mean to emboss and to crash into.
en.emboîter: ~Emboîter~ is a parasynthetic verb: the prefix ~em-~, a spelling of ~en-~ (from Latin ~in-~, “in, into”) before b, joined to ~boîte~ (“box”) and the ending ~-er~, in the sense of putting something into a box or fitting it in. The noun ~boîte~ comes from Old French ~boiste~, from Late Latin ~buxida~ or ~buxita~, from Latin ~pyxis~ and Greek ~puxís~ (“small boxwood box”), which are related to Latin ~buxus~ (“box tree”). English ~box~ is a doublet.
en.embrancher: Formed from ~brancher~ with the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”): to join or link up, as one line or pipe connects onto another. The base ~brancher~ is a verb built on the noun ~branche~, which descends from Late Latin ~branca~ (“paw, claw”). The origin of ~branca~ is uncertain; by one account it goes back to a hypothetical Gaulish *~vranca~, though the Latin form may also have been influenced by ~bracchium~ (“arm”). English ~branch~ comes from the same ~branca~ through Old French. The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~.
en.embraquer: Formed from ~braquer~ with the prefix ~en-~, which here adds a sense of putting something into or onto the action; the verb means to haul in. The origin of the base is uncertain. French Wiktionary proposes, with a hedge, a Vulgar Latin *~brachitāre~ built on Latin ~bracchium~ (“arm”), while English Wiktionary only says the origin is unknown, so the Latin link is a proposal and not settled fact.
en.embraser: French Wiktionary analyzes it as the prefix ~en-~ plus ~braser~, though it notes that the TLFi prefers ~en-~ + ~braise~ + ~-er~. The base ~braser~ comes from Middle French and Old French ~braser~ (“to burn”), whose deeper origin is debated. One account derives it from a variant of Old French ~brese~ (“live coals”), of Germanic origin. The one judged more likely links it to Old Norse ~brasa~ (“to braze, to harden with fire”). Either way the word belongs with ~braise~ (“embers”) and ~brasier~. ~Embraser~ means to set ablaze, and figuratively to fire up the passions.
en.embrasser:
From Old French ~embracier~ (attested around 1080), formed from ~en-~ (“in”) + ~brace~/~bras~ (“arm, the two arms”), from Latin ~bracchium~ (“arm, forearm”). ~Bracchium~ was borrowed into Latin from Ancient Greek ~βραχίων~ (~brakhíōn~, “upper arm”). The Romance descendants of the noun are everywhere: Italian ~braccio~, Spanish ~brazo~, French ~bras~. Through Latin ~bracchium~, ~embrasser~ is cognate with English ~brace~ and ~embrace~ and, more distantly, ~bracelet~.

The literal sense is built into the word: ~embrasser~ meant “to take into one's arms,” to enfold. Only later did French let the gesture stand for the lips, so that today ~embrasser~ ordinarily means “to kiss” — a semantic drift from the encircling arms to the meeting of mouths. The older bodily meaning survives in ~s'embrasser~ and in figurative uses: one can ~embrasser~ a cause, a career, or a whole subject “at a glance” (~embrasser du regard~), holding it as if within the arms. From the same ~bras~ come ~brassée~ (“an armful”), ~embrassade~, ~brasser~, and ~bracelet~.
en.embrayer: ~Embrayer~ is a parasynthetic verb, formed with the prefix ~en-~, the noun ~braie~ and the ending ~-er~. ~Braie~ comes from Latin ~brāca~ (“breeches”), itself borrowed from Gaulish. Besides “breeches,” ~braie~ had technical senses in French, among them a wooden crosspiece in a windmill and an iron band around a forge hammer's handle. The modern verb is a mechanical term: to engage a clutch, and by extension to set something in motion.
en.embrever: The origin of ~embrever~ is uncertain. The TLFi records Old French ~enbevrer~ (“to soak”) around 1190, then ~embevrer~ as a technical term in 1223 and in the sense “to drive in” around 1225, before the word reappears in 1701. Because of this late appearance, the TLFi prefers a change of prefix from ~abevrer~ (the source of ~abreuver~) over a Vulgar Latin *~imbiberare~ built on Latin ~imbibere~ (“to drink in”). Littré guessed that a piece of wood might “water” another by engaging in it. The modern verb means to join two beams with a notched joint.
en.embrigader: Formed from the prefix ~en-~, the noun ~brigade~ and the verbal suffix ~-er~, a parasynthetic verb meaning “to put into a brigade.” The noun came through Middle French from Italian ~brigata~. The verb now means to recruit or enlist people into a group, often against their will.
en.embringuer: The origin of ~embringuer~ is uncertain. It may come from the Germanic verb *~bringan~, the source of Gothic ~briggan~, English ~bring~ and German ~bringen~, all meaning “to bring, to carry.” The Germanic verb itself is tied to the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰrenk-~ in Pokorny's dictionary, but that is a further proposal on top of the French one. Whatever its source, the modern French verb means “to drag someone into an affair,” usually a troublesome one, and its reflexive form ~s'embringuer~ means “to get oneself mixed up in” something. It is a familiar, colloquial word.
en.embrocher: Formed from ~broche~ (“spit, skewer”) with the prefix ~en-~ (from Latin ~in-~) and the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to put on a spit.” The noun ~broche~ comes from Old French, from Latin ~brocca~ (“pointed thing”), the feminine of ~broccus~ (“prominent-toothed”). English Wiktionary adds that this Latin word is probably of Gaulish origin.
en.embroncher: From Old French ~embronchier~ (“to cover”), formed with the prefix ~en-~ and the verb ~broncher~. The prefix ~en-~ often adds the idea of putting something into or onto a state or place, and the Old French verb carried the sense of covering. Modern French keeps the verb as a technical word with the sense of laying or setting something in position, as in the gloss.
en.embrouiller: Formed from ~brouiller~ with the prefix ~en-~, which here marks bringing something into the state the base names. The base is traced to Old French ~brouiller~, from a Vulgar Latin form built on Late Latin ~brodium~ (“broth, stew, mixture”), itself taken from Proto-Germanic *~bruþą~ (“stock, broth”), the source of English ~broth~. A rival account linking the verb to Old Occitan ~bruelhar~ (“to sprout”) is rejected by French Wiktionary. The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”), so the verb means to put into a muddle, to entangle.
en.embroussailler: Formed from ~broussaille~ (“brushwood, undergrowth”) with the prefix ~en-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, so literally “to cover with brush.” The TLFi dates it to the nineteenth century. Its first example is from the Goncourts' journal in 1854, in the participle, of undergrowth. In 1874 Alphonse Daudet used it figuratively, of interminable incidents that tangle women's speech, and in 1876 he used the participle in the sense of “covered like a thicket.” Today the verb covers a plot of land with brambles, and by analogy it can describe windblown hair. In literary French it also means to make something confused or tangled, as digressions can do to a talk.
en.embrumer: ~Embrumer~ is formed from ~brume~ (“mist”) with the prefix ~en-~, which becomes ~em-~ before ~b~, and the verb ending ~-er~. It means to fill or cover with mist. The noun ~brume~ is inherited from Old French ~brume~, itself borrowed from Latin ~brūma~ (“winter, winter solstice, cold weather”), possibly through Old Occitan ~bruma~. A word for mist thus descends from a Latin word for the cold season.
en.embuer: Formed in French from the noun ~buée~ with the prefix ~en-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, so that ~embuer~ means “to cover with condensation,” as a cold windowpane is misted over. The noun ~buée~ comes from Old French ~buee~ (“laundry, wash”), from Vulgar Latin *~būcāta~ (“soaked”), ultimately from a Frankish verb *~būkōn~ (“to soak, wash”). The steam of the wash is what gave ~buée~ its modern sense of “mist, condensation.”
en.embusquer: ~Embusquer~ (“to put in ambush, to station in hiding”) is, according to French Wiktionary, a remaking of Old French ~embuschier~ on the model of Italian ~imboscare~ (“to hide, to lay an ambush”), which is derived from ~bosco~ (“wood”). The Old French verb is itself linked by that source to ~embûche~ (“snare, ambush”), to the prefix ~em-~ and to ~busquer~. The French verb thus blends a native line with an Italian influence, and both lead to the same idea of concealment. From the verb come ~s'embusquer~, “to lie in wait,” and the noun ~embuscade~ (“ambush”). English ~ambush~ is a cousin by way of Old French.
en.embêter: A parasynthetic formation: the prefix ~en-~ and the suffix ~-er~ were added at the same time around the adjective and noun ~bête~, since no *~bêter~ or *~embête~ stands in between. The base ~bête~ comes from Old French ~beste~, probably borrowed in part from Latin ~bēstia~ (“beast”), and the circumflex marks the lost ~s~ of the old spelling. The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~, and the suffix ~-er~ from Latin ~-are~. The verb means to bother, annoy or pester someone, and its base shows what the speaker thinks of the person being annoyed.
en.emmagasiner: ~Emmagasiner~ is a parasynthetic verb: the prefix ~en-~ (spelled ~em-~ before a following m) and the ending ~-er~ were added together to ~magasin~, giving “to put into storage.” ~Magasin~ is first attested in 1389 and descends from Old French ~maguesin~ (“storeroom”). Its source is Arabic ~maḵāzin~, plural of ~maḵzan~ (“storehouse”), from ~ḵazana~ (“to store”). English Wiktionary says it came either from a regional Romance language, where Medieval Latin ~magazenum~ appears in a contract about storehouses in Maghreb ports, or from Italian ~magazzino~. It is a doublet of English ~magazine~.
en.emmailloter: Formed from ~maillot~ with the prefix ~en-~ (spelled ~em-~ before m) and the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to put into a ~maillot~,” that is, to wrap in swaddling clothes. The base ~maillot~ comes from Old French ~mailloel~, itself derived from ~maille~. By extension the verb means to wrap or bind something tightly in bands or cloth.
en.emmancher: Formed in French from ~manche~ with the prefix ~en-~ (written ~em-~ before ~m~) and the verb ending ~-er~. The French noun ~manche~ has two sources, both from Latin ~manus~ (“hand”). One is ~manica~ (“sleeve”), the other ~manicus~ (“handle”). The verb's senses of fitting a handle onto a tool and of helping someone into the sleeves of a garment match those two nouns.
en.emmener:
Compound of the prefix ~en-~ (from Latin ~inde~/~in-~, conveying motion away) and ~mener~ (“to lead, conduct”). ~Mener~ descends from Latin ~minare~ (“to drive animals by shouting and threatening”), a Late Latin development of ~minari~ (“to threaten”), which is built on ~minae~ (“threats”). So leading was first a matter of driving livestock forward with menacing cries.

The semantic journey is vivid: from threatening (~minari~), to herding beasts along by threats (~minare~), to simply leading or conducting anyone or anything (~mener~). Adding ~en-~ gives ~emmener~, to lead away, to take someone off with you — distinguished in careful French from ~amener~ (“to bring toward”) and ~ramener~ (“to bring back”): one ~emmène~ a person away to the cinema but ~amène~ them here. The ~minare~/~minari~ family is surprisingly large in French: ~menacer~ (“to threaten”), ~menace~, ~promener~ (“to take for a walk”), ~amener~, ~ramener~, and ~meneur~ (“leader, ringleader”) — a cluster of words whose shared ancestor was the herdsman's threatening shout.
en.emmerder: Formed in French from the prefix ~en-~ (spelled ~em-~ before ~m~), the noun ~merde~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~merde~ is inherited from Old French through Latin ~merda~ (“excrement”). The prefix gives the sense “to cover, to supply with,” so the verb means literally “to smother in filth,” and it quickly became the vulgar everyday word for annoying or bothering someone. The pronominal ~s'emmerder~ means “to be bored stiff.”
en.emmieller: Formed from ~mieller~ with the prefix ~en-~, spelled ~em-~ before ~m~. The base ~mieller~ is itself derived from ~miel~ (“honey”) with the verb ending ~-er~. The verb means “to coat with honey” or “to sweeten with honey.” The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”) and here has a locative sense: to put honey on or into something. ~Miel~ goes back to Latin ~mel~, the source of the French word for honey.
en.emmitoufler: ~Emmitoufler~ is formed from the prefix ~en-~ (here ~em-~ before ~m~), a base ~mitoufle~ and the ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary explains ~mitoufle~ as an obsolete synonym of ~mitaine~ (“mitten”), while English Wiktionary starts from the Middle French adjective ~mitouflé~ (“wearing mittens”). Either way the verb began with the idea of covering the hands and grew into wrapping the whole person warmly. It is used of bundling up against the cold, as in ~s'emmitoufler dans une écharpe~.
en.emmouscailler: Formed from ~mouscaille~ with the prefix ~en-~ (the n became m before m) and the verb ending ~-er~, so it means to bother someone, as if burying them in muck. ~Mouscaille~ derives from the slang word ~mousse~ (“excrement”), from Gaulish *~mudia~ (“excrement, filth”), found in the Celtic languages (Old Breton ~mous~, Breton ~mouez~ “stench”), plus an expressive second element.
en.emmurer: ~Emmurer~ is formed from the prefix ~en-~ (spelled ~em-~ before m), the noun ~mur~ and the verbal ending ~-er~; equivalently, it is ~en-~ added to ~murer~ (“to wall up”). The noun ~mur~ goes back through Old French to Latin ~mūrus~ (“city wall, rampart”), and ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”). The result means to shut someone inside walls, to wall in or wall up.
en.emménager: Formed from the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”) and ~ménager~, which is itself the noun ~ménage~ (“household”) plus the verb ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary notes that ~ménager~ already appeared in Old French with the sense “to dwell, to live in a place.” ~Emménager~ is thus “to get into a household”: it first described installing furniture in a dwelling (a transitive use) and now chiefly means to move into a new home. Its mirror image is ~déménager~, built on the same base.
en.emmétrer: This verb is formed from ~métrer~ with the prefix ~en-~, spelled ~em-~ before a ~m~. The base ~métrer~ is itself built on the noun ~mètre~ with the ending ~-er~, so it means “to measure in metres”. French Wiktionary notes that the vowel changes from ~è~ to ~é~ because the ending opens the syllable. ~Mètre~ goes back to Ancient Greek ~μέτρον~ (“measure”), directly or through Latin ~metrum~, the measure of a verse. The prefix here is ~en-~ in its sense of putting something into an arrangement.
en.emmêler: ~Emmêler~ is ~mêler~ (“to mix”) with the prefix ~en-~, which is spelled ~em-~ before a following m. The prefix comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”) through Old French, and the verb means “to tangle.” The base ~mêler~ comes from Old French ~mesler~, from Vulgar Latin *~misculare~, a derivative of Latin ~miscere~ (“to mix”). The circumflex of ~mêler~ stands for the ~s~ of that older spelling, and ~emmêler~ keeps the same mark.
en.empailler: A parasynthetic verb, built at once with the prefix ~en-~ and the ending ~-er~ on the noun ~paille~ (“straw”), so “to put straw in.” It is best known for stuffing dead animals, as in taxidermy, and it also covers filling a chair seat with straw. ~Paille~ is inherited from Old French and Latin ~palea~ (“straw, chaff”), which English Wiktionary traces to a Proto-Indo-European root *~pel-~ (“flour, dust”). The prefix ~en-~, from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”), has the locative sense “put into,” and ~-er~ makes the verb. There is no French verb *~empaille~ underneath.
en.empaler:
From Old French ~empaler~, inherited from Late Latin ~impālāre~, itself from Latin ~pālus~ (“stake, pole”). French Wiktionary instead describes it as a French formation, from the prefix ~en-~ (spelled ~em-~ before ~p~), the noun ~pal~ and the ending ~-er~; en.Wiktionary notes that this is the surface analysis. The Latin source and the French parts match, so the two views are two readings of the same word: to put on a stake.

The noun ~pal~ is attested in Old French in the twelfth century as a variant of ~pel~, from Latin ~pālus~, and it is a doublet of ~pieu~, which took the popular route from the same Latin word. The TLFi, however, treats Old French ~pal~ as a learned borrowing, though en.Wiktionary notes it may be only a dialectal variant. The verb ~empaler~ names the punishment of driving a stake through a body, and the same Latin root is behind ~palissade~.
en.empanner: Composed of ~en~ and ~panne~, it is a sailing term meaning to gybe, that is, to swing the sails across from one side to the other when the wind is behind. The prefix ~en~ comes from Latin ~in~ (“in, on”). For ~panne~, French Wiktionary gives the sailing sense as a variant of ~penne~, the end of a yard, a word that recalls a feather's tip. The verb is thus the sailor's phrase for putting the sails into the wind, compressed into one word.
en.empaqueter: ~Empaqueter~ is formed from the verb ~paqueter~ with the prefix ~en-~, which here carries the locative sense “put in or into”, so the verb means to put something into a package. The base ~paqueter~ is itself derived from the noun ~paquet~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. The prefix ~en-~ descends from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”) by way of Old French ~en-~, and still helps coin verbs of enclosing.
en.emparer:
From Occitan ~emparar~ (“to protect, defend, lay claim to, seize”), from a Vulgar Latin *~imparare~, which the sources explain as a reshaping of *~imperare~ (“to command, master”) under the influence of ~parare~ (“to prepare, ward off”). It is cognate with Catalan ~emparar~ and connects to the ~parare~ family that also gives ~rempart~ and ~remparer~. In French the verb is attested in a defensive sense in the 14th century and in the possessive sense — “to seize” — by the first half of the 16th.

The two senses sit on a hinge between defense and aggression: to ward off and to take hold are two sides of laying claim to something. Modern French keeps only the reflexive ~s'emparer de~ (“to seize, take possession of”), the defensive meaning having faded. The ~parare~ root is prolific in French — ~parer~, ~séparer~, ~préparer~, ~réparer~, ~apparat~ — and the kindred ~rempart~ still names the very wall behind which one once took shelter.
en.empatter: ~Empatter~ is formed from ~patter~ and the prefix ~en-~. ~Patter~ itself derives from ~patte~, in two lines of meaning: the paw of an animal, and a tab of cloth. The prefix ~en-~, from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”), gives the sense of providing with something, here a ~patte~.
en.empaumer: Formed from ~paumer~ with the prefix ~em-~, a spelling of ~en-~ before ~p~. The base ~paumer~ is built on ~paume~ (“palm of the hand”), which comes from Latin ~palma~, with the verb ending ~-er~. The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ and has a locative sense, so that ~empaumer~ means to take into the palm, hence “to grasp.” ~Paume~ is a doublet of ~palme~, and English ~palm~ is a cognate. The verb thus keeps the older sense of seizing in the hand, unlike its slang relative ~se paumer~.
en.empenner: Formed from ~penne~ with the prefix ~en-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to fit with feathers,” the work of fletching an arrow. ~Penne~ comes from Latin ~pinna~ or ~penna~ (“feather, wing”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~péth₂r̥~ (“feather, wing”). The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”) and the ending ~-er~ from Latin ~-are~.
en.emperler: Formed from the noun ~perle~ (“pearl”) with the prefix ~en-~, here spelled ~em-~ before ~p~, and the verbal suffix ~-er~, in the sense “to provide with pearls”: to ~emperler~ is to adorn or cover something with pearls. The noun ~perle~ comes through Old French and Medieval Latin ~perla~, probably from Latin ~perula~ (“little pear”); the alternative account derives it from ~perna~ (“haunch,” also a leg-shaped shellfish) through a diminutive *~pernula~. The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”), so the verb literally means to set something in pearls. The result is a poetic word, often used for dew drops or sweat beading on skin.
en.empeser: The sources give two accounts of ~empeser~ (“to starch”). French Wiktionary derives it from ~empois~ (earlier ~empoix~), itself from ~poix~ (“pitch”, from Latin ~pix~), the starch paste being likened to that sticky substance. It lists a separate Old French verb ~empeser~ (“to make heavy”), and notes that the TLFi does not distinguish the two. English Wiktionary instead derives the starch word from Old French ~empoise~ (“weight”), from Latin ~impēnsa~. Which account is right is unsettled, so the verb's history is best taken as two possible paths.
en.empester: Formed from the noun ~peste~ (“plague”) with the prefix ~en-~ (spelled ~em-~ before p) and the verb ending ~-er~: “to infect with plague,” then “to make stink.” The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin ~pestis~ (“scourge”). French Wiktionary instead presents ~pester~ as the base, but that verb is itself built on ~peste~.
en.empierrer: Formed from the prefix ~en-~ (spelled ~em-~ before ~p~) and the verb ~pierrer~, with that verb itself a denominal built on ~pierre~ (“stone”); the corresponding Old French verb was ~perrer~. English Wiktionary gives the same parts as ~em-~ + ~pierre~ + ~-er~. The prefix, from Latin ~in-~, here has a locative sense, “to put into or onto.” The verb therefore means to cover or fill with stone, and it is used above all for road-building: to lay a surface of crushed stone or broken rock on a road or a track.
en.empiffrer: ~Empiffrer~ is formed on a base ~piffre~ with the prefix ~en-~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to stuff oneself.” French Wiktionary derives it from Old French ~pifre~ (“big eater”), probably from an expressive stem ~piff-~ evoking bulk. The suggestion of an expressive stem is a probability, not a certainty.
en.empiler: ~Empiler~ is built from ~pile~ (“a heap of objects laid one on another”) with the prefix ~en-~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The prefix is spelled ~em-~ before p, but it is the same prefix, here with its locative sense of “putting into”: to empiler is to put things into a pile. The noun ~pile~ comes from Latin ~pila~ (“pillar, column”). The verb is attested in the first quarter of the 13th century, in the Miserere of Renclus de Molliens. French later derived the nouns ~empilage~ and ~empilement~ from it.
en.empirer:
French ~empirer~ goes back to Old French ~empirier~ and ~empoirier~, with an early spelling ~ampairer~ recorded in a manuscript of the Vie de saint Alexis in the St Albans Psalter. Its make-up is explained in two ways. French Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~pējorāre~ (“to make worse”), which would have gained a prefix in Late Latin to give *~impējorāre~. English Wiktionary instead analyses the Old French verb as ~en-~ + ~pire~ (“worse”) + ~-er~. Both accounts rest on the same base, Latin ~pējor~ (“worse”), the comparative that French kept as ~pire~. Spanish ~empeorar~ is built in the same way.

Because its base is a comparative, ~empirer~ is a verb built on “worse” itself rather than on a plain adjective. The prefix ~en-~ works here as it does in ~enrichir~ and ~embellir~, turning a quality into a change of state. The Latin verb has other descendants. English ~impair~ comes, by general etymological tradition, from the Old French relative ~empeirer~, and English ~pejorative~ reached English through French ~péjoratif~. In French the same root also survives in ~pire~, ~pis~ and ~péjoratif~, so ~empirer~ sits in a small family that all says, in one way or another, that things are getting worse.
en.empiéter: Built on ~pied~ (“foot”) with both a prefix and a suffix at once, ~en-~ + ~pied~ + ~-er~. The noun ~pied~ comes from Latin ~pēs~ (“foot”). The Old French verb ~empieter~ had the sense “to trample underfoot, to vanquish,” and also “to give a foot to something,” as in ~empiéter~ a column, that is, to provide it with a base. Both senses are literal, built on the image of the foot. The evidence supplied does not trace how these older senses led to the modern “to encroach,” so that step is left open.
en.emplafonner: Formed from ~plafonner~ with the prefix ~em-~, a spelling of ~en-~ used before p. The base comes from ~plafond~, itself a compound of ~plat~ (“flat”) and ~fond~ (“bottom”), and first meant to fit a ceiling. The sense of the derived verb, to slam or crash into something, is familiar and figurative, and the sources do not explain how it arose.
en.emplir:
From Old French ~emplir~, inherited from Latin ~implēre~ (“to fill up”), a compound of ~in-~ (“in”) and ~plēre~ (“to fill”). Late Latin reshaped the verb as *~implīre~, which explains the French ending in ~-ir~. The root is generally traced to Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₁-~ (“to fill”), the source of Latin ~plēnus~ (“full”), of English ~full~, and of German ~voll~. Spanish ~henchir~ is another descendant of ~implēre~, a reminder of how far the same Latin verb could travel.

~Emplir~ is the older verb, and ~remplir~ (~r-~ + ~emplir~, the vowel of ~re-~ dropping before the vowel of the base) took over everyday speech, so that ~emplir~ now sounds literary or elevated, as in a heart filled with joy. The sense of ~remplir~ is “to fill up,” not “to fill again.” The same Latin family gave a whole cluster of French words: ~plein~ (“full”), ~plénitude~, ~complet~ (from ~complētus~, “filled up, finished”), and ~accomplir~, whose “accomplishing” is, at bottom, a filling to the brim.
en.employer:
From Old French ~emploier~, from Latin ~implicare~ (“to fold in, to enfold, to involve”), a compound of ~in-~ (“in”) and ~plicare~ (“to fold”). ~plicare~ descends from PIE *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, to fold”). The verb is a doublet of the learned ~impliquer~, borrowed straight from Latin much later, while ~employer~ took the slow popular road through Old French. Cognate with Spanish ~emplear~ and Italian ~impiegare~, and, through ~implicare~, with English ~employ~ and ~imply~.

The semantic journey is a quiet marvel: from “to fold something in” grew the idea of “folding a thing into a task,” hence putting it to use, hence — of a person — giving them work. The same Latin ~implicare~ thus gave French both ~employer~ (to use, to hire) and ~impliquer~ (to involve, to entangle), two faces of one act of folding-in. ~plicare~ seeds a broad family: ~ployer~ and ~plier~ (its native French descendants), ~appliquer~, ~déployer~, ~replier~, and the noun ~pli~ (“a fold, a crease”) all share that root, as do English ~ply~ and ~plait~. From ~employer~ itself come ~emploi~, ~employé~, and ~employeur~ — the worker, after all, being someone “folded into” the work.
en.empocher: Formed from the prefix ~en-~ and ~pocher~, which is built on the noun ~poche~ (“pocket, bag”), by way of Old French ~pochier~ (“to enclose in a bag”). The noun comes from Frankish *~pokkō~ and is a cognate of English ~pouch~ and ~pocket~. ~Empocher~ means to put in one's pocket, and so to take or receive, especially money or a gain, as in ~empocher une somme~ (“to pocket a sum”).
en.empoigner:
The verb comes from Old French ~enpuignier~ (attested in 1174), from Latin ~impugnare~, which French Wiktionary glosses as “to attack with the fists.” The Latin verb is ~in-~ plus ~pugnare~ (“to fight”), itself built on ~pugnus~ (“fist”). Modern French ~empoigner~ has lost that violence and means “to grasp firmly.” English Wiktionary nonetheless analyzes it as ~en-~ + ~poing~ + ~-er~, and French Wiktionary adds that, from a present-day point of view, it can be read as ~poigne~ with ~en-~ and ~-er~.

Two readings therefore coexist: a descent from Latin through Old French, and an analysis in which speakers feel ~empoigner~ as a verb built on the closed fist. The family stays close. ~Poing~ (“fist”) comes from ~pugnus~, and ~poignée~ (“handful, handle”) and ~poignet~ (“wrist”) are built on it. Learned French kept the fighting side: ~impugner~ (“to challenge, to attack”) and ~pugnace~ (“combative”) belong to the same Latin family. The words for the hand and the words for the fight are thus one family.
en.empoisonner: Built from ~poison~ with the prefix ~en-~ (spelled ~em-~ before ~p~) and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to put poison into”, then “to poison”. The noun ~poison~ is inherited through Old French ~poison~ from Latin ~pōtiōnem~ (“a drink”). It is a doublet of ~potion~, which French borrowed later, straight from Latin. A single Latin word for a drink therefore gave a deadly sense by the popular route and a medicinal or magical one by the learned route. English has the same pair, ~poison~ and ~potion~.
en.empoissonner: French Wiktionary traces ~empoissonner~ to Middle French ~empoissonner~, from Old French ~enpuissonner~. Looking at it from the modern language, it is formed from ~poissonner~ with the prefix ~em-~, and English Wiktionary parses it as ~en-~ plus ~poisson~ (“fish”) plus the verb ending ~-er~. The sense is “to stock a pond or river with fish.” Despite the resemblance, it has no connection with ~empoisonner~, “to poison.”
en.emporter:
A French compound: the prefix ~en-~ (from Latin ~inde~, “from there, away”) joined to the verb ~porter~ (“to carry”), attested already around the year 980 as ~enportet~. The base ~porter~ descends from Latin ~portāre~ (“to carry, to bear”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“to lead through, to pass over”), the same root behind Latin ~porta~ (“gate”) and ~portus~ (“harbor”). Italian ~portare~ and Spanish ~portar~ are its siblings, and through the root English gained ~port~ and the kindred ~ford~.

The prefix ~en-~ carries the idea of taking something away with oneself, so ~emporter~ is to carry off — food “to go” is ~à emporter~. From physical carrying the verb won vivid figurative force: a storm or a fever may ~emporter~ a life, and to win a contest is to ~l'emporter~ (literally “to carry it off”). The reflexive ~s'emporter~ means to be carried away by anger, to lose one's temper. From the same ~portāre~ French drew a broad family — ~porter~, ~apporter~, ~rapporter~, ~transporter~, ~importer~, ~exporter~, ~supporter~, and the noun ~portée~ — all pivoting on the act of carrying.
en.empoter: Formed from ~pot~ with the prefix ~en-~, spelled ~em-~ before ~p~, and the verbal ending ~-er~. The prefix gives the sense of putting into, so ~empoter~ is to put a plant in a pot, or, in the technical sense, to load a liquid into a container. The noun ~pot~ comes from Old French ~pot~, from Vulgar Latin ~pottum~, from Frankish *~pott~, from Proto-Germanic *~puttaz~ (“pot, jar, tub”). English ~pot~ belongs to the same family.
en.empourprer: Formed from the verb ~pourprer~ with the prefix ~en-~, which here means to bring about a state: to make something purple. English Wiktionary parses it as ~en-~ + ~pourpre~ + ~-er~, while French Wiktionary gives ~pourprer~ as the intermediate step, itself from ~pourpre~ (“purple”). The verb is used of the sky at sunset and, in the reflexive ~s'empourprer~, of a face that flushes with embarrassment or anger. The sense moves from a color given to a thing to the color that rises in someone's cheeks.
en.empoussiérer: A parasynthetic formation: ~en-~ + ~poussière~ + ~-er~, with the prefix and the verb ending added around the noun at the same time, so there is no verb ~poussiérer~ underneath. The prefix ~en-~ gives the sense “to cover with” or “to provide with,” so the verb means to make something dusty. The noun ~poussière~ comes from Old French ~pousiere~, derived from ~pous~ (“dust”), which goes back through Vulgar Latin to Latin ~pulvis~ (“dust, powder”).
en.empreindre:
French ~empreindre~ comes from Latin ~imprimere~ (“to press into, to imprint”), built from ~in-~ (“in, onto”) and ~premere~ (“to press”). The two Wiktionaries differ slightly in confidence: one gives the Latin verb as the direct source, the other calls the verb inherited, possibly by way of a Vulgar Latin form *~impremere~ that keeps the vowel of ~premere~. Either way, ~empreindre~ is the popular, inherited word, and it has a learned twin. ~Imprimer~ was borrowed from the same Latin verb at a later stage, so the two are doublets. Italian ~imprimere~ and Spanish ~imprimir~ continue the same Latin verb.

The original image is physical: pressing a seal or a die into wax or metal so that it leaves a mark.
