French kept that picture alive in figurative uses, where a face is ~empreint~ de tristesse (“marked with sadness”) or a style bears the stamp of its author. The noun ~empreinte~, built on the past participle, names the mark itself, from the footprint to the fingerprint and, in our own time, the carbon footprint. Meanwhile ~imprimer~ took over the technical sense of printing on paper. The root ~premere~ also gives ~presser~ (through Latin ~pressāre~), ~pression~ and ~impression~. The verb is conjugated like ~peindre~, hence the odd ~gn~ in ~empreignons~.
en.empresser: ~Empresser~ is formed from the prefix ~en-~ and the verb ~presser~. ~Presser~ comes from Old French ~presser~ (“to oppress, torment”), from Latin ~pressāre~ (“to press hard”), an intensive of ~premere~ (“to press, squeeze”). The prefix ~en-~, from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”), puts the pressing inside a situation: to be caught up in the crowd, and so to bustle. Today the verb lives almost only in its reflexive form, with the sense of hurrying eagerly or attending zealously to someone, and the participle ~empressé~ describes an attentive, eager person.
en.emprisonner: ~Emprisonner~ is formed from ~en-~ (“in”), ~prison~ and the verbal ending ~-er~: literally, to put into prison. The noun ~prison~ is inherited from Old French ~prison~, which continues Latin ~prēnsiō~, a contracted form of ~prehēnsiō~ (“a seizing, an arrest”), from ~prehendere~ (“to seize, to grasp”). A ~prison~ was therefore first the act of seizing someone, and only later the place where the seized person was kept. The same Latin verb gave French ~prendre~, and English borrowed the French verb as ~imprison~.
en.emprunter:
From Vulgar Latin *~impromutuāre~, reshaped from Classical Latin ~promutuārī~ (“to borrow in advance”), built on ~mutuus~ (“lent, borrowed, reciprocal”). ~mutuus~ derives from the Proto-Indo-European root *~mei-~ (“to change, to exchange”), the same root behind English ~mutual~, French ~muer~ and ~mutuel~, and Latin ~mūtāre~ (“to change”), source of ~muter~ and ~commun~.

The etymology fits the idea perfectly: borrowing is an exchange you promise to reverse, a thing given on the understanding it will change hands back again. From the financial sense of taking a loan, ~emprunter~ broadened to borrowing of every kind — borrowing a book, borrowing words from another language, borrowing a friend's umbrella. Most evocatively, French uses it for roads and paths: one ~emprunte~ a route, a corridor, a staircase — literally “borrowing” the way one travels, as if the road were lent for the duration of the journey. The related noun ~emprunt~ names both a loan and a linguistic loanword. The deep root *~mei-~ thus links the humble act of borrowing to the grand idea of change and exchange that also gives ~mutuel~, ~commun~, and ~migrer~.
en.emprésurer: Formed from ~présure~ with the prefix ~em-~, the form of ~en-~ before ~p~, and a verbal ending: to ~emprésurer~ milk is to add rennet so that it curdles. French Wiktionary derives ~présure~ from ~prise~ with the suffix ~-ure~, in the sense of “coagulation”. English Wiktionary traces it through Old French ~prisure~ to a Vulgar Latin *~prēnsūra~, from Latin ~prehēnsum~. The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in”).
en.empuantir: ~Empuantir~ (“to stink out, to fill with a stench”) is built on ~puant~, the present participle of the verb ~puer~ (“to stink”). It follows the familiar French pattern of verbs in ~em-~ and ~-ir~, such as ~embellir~, which turn a quality into a process: to ~empuantir~ a room is to make it stink. The participle ~puant~ is itself a good example of a verb form that settled into use as an ordinary adjective.
en.empâter: Formed from ~pâte~ with the prefix ~em-~, the spelling of ~en-~ (from Latin ~in-~, “in, into”) before ~p~, and the verbal ending ~-er~: to coat or thicken something into a pasty mass. The noun ~pâte~ comes through Middle and Old French ~paste~ from Late Latin ~pasta~ (“paste”), which came from Ancient Greek ~παστά~ (“barley porridge”). Italian ~pasta~ and English ~paste~ come from the same Late Latin word.
en.empêcher:
From Old French ~empeechier~, from Late Latin ~impedicare~ (“to fetter, to entangle, to catch by the feet”), a compound of ~in-~ (“in, into”) and ~pedica~ (“a shackle, a foot-fetter”), itself from ~pes~ (genitive ~pedis~, “foot”). ~pes~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ped-~ (“foot”), making ~empêcher~ a distant cousin of English ~foot~, ~pedal~, and ~pedestrian~, and a closer relative of English ~impeach~, which entered through the same Old French verb.

The original picture is vividly physical: to ~empêcher~ someone was to shackle their feet so they could not move — to entangle and hold them fast. From that literal fettering the meaning lifted into the abstract “to prevent, to hinder,” which is all that survives in modern French. Its etymological twin tells a charming story: ~dépêcher~ began as the opposite gesture, “to un-fetter,” to free the feet and so to hurry — whence the reflexive ~se dépêcher~ (“to hurry up”) and the noun ~dépêche~ (a message “sent in haste”). English ~impeach~, by contrast, drifted from “to impede” toward “to accuse,” crossing paths along the way with unrelated Latin ~impetere~. The root *~ped-~ thus underlies an unexpected pair: to be ~empêché~ is to have one's feet tied, while to ~dépêcher~ is to set them free.
en.empêtrer:
From Old French ~empasturer~ (also spelled ~empaistrer~, “to hobble”), which comes from Vulgar Latin *~impastoriāre~, a verb built on Latin ~pāstōrius~ (“of a shepherd”). According to fr.Wiktionary, the underlying image is the shepherd's rope, Latin ~chorda pāstōria~, used to tie an animal's legs. Old French also had the nouns ~empasture~ and ~empasturon~ (“hobble”), the latter related to modern ~paturon~ (“pastern”), the part of the leg where the hobble is fastened.

The verb began, then, as a term of animal husbandry: to hobble a beast so that it cannot wander. In the Old French spelling ~empaistrer~ the ~s~ later fell silent, and the circumflex of ~empêtrer~ stands in for it, a standard pattern in French spelling. French kept the notion of restraint and widened it to ensnaring or entangling, and ~s'empêtrer~ now describes anyone caught up in something, whether a tangle of cords or a mess of difficulties. The root of the Latin source word is the same as that of French ~pasteur~ and ~pâtre~, the shepherd himself.
en.enamourer: ~Enamourer~ is made of the prefix ~en-~, the noun ~amour~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The prefix gives the sense “to put into” a state, so the verb means to inspire love, and its reflexive form ~s'enamourer de~ means to fall in love with someone. The noun ~amour~ comes from Latin ~amor~ by way of Old French. Its form is slightly odd: regular sound change would have produced ~ameur~, which does exist in Old French, and the usual explanation is an influence from Old Occitan.
en.encabaner: Formed from ~cabane~ with the prefix ~en-~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so the verb means to put into a hut. Its senses, putting silkworms on racks, shutting someone up and keeping them indoors, all grow from that idea of enclosure. The noun ~cabane~ came from Occitan ~cabana~ and Late Latin ~capanna~; French Wiktionary adds a Gaulish origin, while English Wiktionary lists it as a doublet of ~cabine~.
en.encadrer:
Formed from the noun ~cadre~ (“frame”) with the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”), so literally “to put into a frame.” ~Cadre~ was borrowed in the 16th century from Italian ~quadro~ (“square, painting”), from Latin ~quadrum~ (“a square”), from ~quadrus~, ultimately from ~quattuor~ (“four”). That numeral goes back to PIE *~kʷetwóres~ (“four”), the same root that yields English ~four~ and ~quarter~, Latin ~quartus~, and Greek ~téssares~. A frame, then, is etymologically a four-cornered thing.

The meaning fanned out from the literal picture-frame to anything that encloses or bounds: to ~encadrer~ a photo, but also to ~encadrer~ troops or staff — to supervise and hold them within structure. From this military and managerial sense French draws ~cadre~ for an executive or officer and ~encadrement~ for supervision. The same ~quadrum~ family gave French ~carré~, ~quadrille~, ~escadre~ and ~escadron~ (a squadron being, originally, a body of soldiers drawn up in a square), and ~cadran~ (a dial, once four-cornered). The whole cluster is built on the number four.
en.encager: Formed from ~cage~ with the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, which turns a noun into a verb: the sense is “to put into a cage.” ~Cage~ itself is inherited from Old French ~cage~, from Latin ~cavea~ (“hollow, beehive”). The Latin word belongs with ~cavus~ (“hollow”), which also gave French ~cave~ and ~caverne~, so a cage is, at root, a hollow space. The ending ~-er~ comes from the Latin first-conjugation ending ~-are~.
en.encaisser:
Formed within French from ~en-~ + ~caisse~ + ~-er~, literally “to put into a box”. ~caisse~ is not an inherited word: the CNRTL takes it from Old Occitan ~caissa~, attested in the thirteenth century and carried north by trade, itself from Latin ~capsa~ (“box, book-case”), a noun usually connected with ~capere~ (“to take”). French had already inherited ~capsa~ by the regular sound changes as ~châsse~, the chest holding a saint’s relics, so ~caisse~ and ~châsse~ are in effect doublets: the same Latin box, one arriving by evolution and one by import. In Cicero the Latin word named the cylindrical case that held book rolls, and in Pliny a container for fruit, so the sense of a purpose-built receptacle was there from the start. The same etymon gave Italian ~cassa~, Spanish ~caja~ and, through Norman French ~casse~, English ~case~; English ~cash~, originally a money-box, and ~capsule~ belong to the family too.

The sense history is a tidy chain of containers. In 1510 ~encaisser~ meant to pack goods into a crate, and gardeners still ~encaissent~ trees by potting them in wooden boxes. In 1690 the box became specifically the cash box, and to ~encaisser~ was to put money into it; by 1832 the verb had shed the box and simply meant to receive or collect a sum, which is its central modern sense — ~encaisser un chèque~, ~encaisser les recettes~. A third, geographical use appeared in 1791: a river ~encaissée~ between steep slopes is boxed in, and the participle survives in ~une vallée encaissée~. The colloquial sense dates from 1867, with ~encaisser un soufflet~, to take a slap, and it broadened to enduring punishment of any kind and then to ~ne pas pouvoir encaisser quelqu’un~, to be unable to stand someone. The dictionaries record the usage without settling the image behind it: the body imagined as a strongbox absorbing blows, or the blow simply received the way money is. The family includes ~caissier~, ~caisson~, ~encaissement~ and ~tiroir-caisse~.
en.encapsuler: Built from the noun ~capsule~ with the prefix ~en-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, so ~encapsuler~ means to enclose in a capsule, and by extension to encapsulate. ~Capsule~ was borrowed from Latin ~capsula~, a diminutive of ~capsa~ (“box, case”), the same word that gave French ~caisse~. The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”) and builds verbs of putting something inside. Because ~capsule~ is a noun, the verb is a parasynthetic formation: prefix and suffix were attached at the same time.
en.encapuchonner: ~Encapuchonner~ is formed from ~capuchonner~ with the prefix ~en-~, and ~capuchonner~ is in turn made from ~capuchon~ (“hood”). The verb means to cover with a hood and, in a sense recorded for it, to lead a monastic life. The prefix ~en-~ gives the idea of putting something in or on.
en.encaquer: Built in French from ~caque~, the barrel in which salted herrings were packed, with the prefix ~en-~ (“into”) and the verb ending ~-er~: ~encaquer~ is “to pack into a ~caque~.” The noun is attested in 1337 in ~caqueharenc~ (“herring ~caque~”). It was probably borrowed from Old Norse ~kaggi~ (“keg, barrel”), which makes it a cousin of English ~keg~. French Wiktionary rejects a derivation from Dutch ~kaak~ (“gill”) because that word is later than ~caque~.
en.encarter: ~Encarter~ is formed from the noun ~carte~ (“card”), the prefix ~en-~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The prefix has the sense “put into,” so the verb means “to slip a card or flyer into” something. ~Carte~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~charta~ (“paper, document, book”), itself from Ancient Greek ~khártēs~ (“sheet of papyrus or paper”). French ~charte~ is a cognate.
en.encartonner: Formed from ~cartonner~ with the prefix ~en-~, in its sense of putting something into: to pack goods into cartons, or to insert a loose sheet in a publication. The base ~cartonner~ is built on ~carton~ (“cardboard”) with the ending ~-er~, meaning to cover or bind with cardboard. ~Carton~ was itself borrowed from Italian ~cartone~, which goes back to Latin ~charta~ (“paper”), the source also of English ~chart~ and ~card~.
en.encaserner: Formed from the noun ~caserne~ (“barracks”) with the prefix ~en-~ and the ending ~-er~: to put soldiers into barracks. The noun is borrowed from Old Occitan ~cazerna~, from Latin ~quaterna~, the neuter plural of ~quaternus~. English Wiktionary calls ~caserne~ a doublet of ~cahier~, which was inherited from the same Latin source, and of ~quaterne~, a later borrowing. French Wiktionary links the sense to the military “quarters.” The prefix ~en-~, from Latin ~in-~ (“in”), has its locative sense of putting into.
en.encastrer:
French ~encastrer~ is a Renaissance borrowing from Italian ~incastrare~ (“to set in, to fit into a notch”), and the French verb was first written ~incastrer~. French Wiktionary traces the Italian to a Late Latin *~incastrare~ (“to set”), earlier derived from the noun ~incastratura~ (“tenon”), which is itself probably built on Latin ~castrum~ (“fortress”). English Wiktionary gives the shorter chain from Late Latin ~incastrāre~ to ~castrum~, and stresses that the verb is unrelated to French ~castrer~ (“to castrate”).

The link to a fortress is the surprising part, and it is only “probable” in French Wiktionary. The sources do not say how a word for a stronghold came to mean a joint that fits into a cut, so that stage should be taken as unexplained. The Latin ~castrum~ has a plural ~castra~ (“camp”) that survives in English place names ending in ~-chester~ and ~-caster~. French also derived the noun ~encastrement~ from the verb. As for ~castrer~, it descends from another Latin verb entirely, and the resemblance of the two spellings is a coincidence.
en.encaustiquer: Formed from ~encaustique~ (“wax polish”) with the verb suffix ~-er~: to polish or wax with it. The noun ~encaustique~ comes from Latin ~encaustica~ (“the art of painting with encaustic”), which goes back further to Ancient Greek ~ἔγκαυστος~ (“burnt”). French Wiktionary links the word to ~en-~ and ~caustique~, a relative of the Greek stem for burning.
en.encaver: Formed from ~caver~ with the prefix ~en-~ (“into”): to ~encaver~ is to put something, typically wine, into a cellar. English Wiktionary instead analyzes it as ~en-~ plus the noun ~cave~ plus ~-er~. Either way the root is Latin ~cavus~ (“hollow”), which gave ~cave~ and ~caverne~, and the verb ~caver~ comes from Latin ~cavāre~ (“to hollow out”). The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in”).
en.enceindre:
~Enceindre~ matches Latin ~incingere~, “to gird about, to wrap round”: ~in-~ + ~cingere~, “to gird.” The French history has a wrinkle the dictionaries note: the thirteenth century said ~aceindre~ — for the TLFi rather a native compound of ~a-~ and ~ceindre~ — and the form ~enceindre~ (early fourteenth century, first as ~ençaint~) looks like a remodeling of it, the prefix swapped to echo the Latin verb. ~Ceindre~ itself continues ~cingere~, whose deeper ancestry is uncertain: a root *~kenk-~, “to gird, to bind,” has been proposed, but the comparisons remain debated. The kin are clear nearer home: Italian ~cingere~, Spanish ~ceñir~, and a string of English borrowings — ~succinct~, from ~succinctus~, “girded up,” the orator with robes tucked for action; ~precinct~, the space “girded about”; even ~shingles~, the disease, from ~cingulum~, “belt,” for the rash that belts the torso.

~Enceindre~ is the verb of city walls — one girds a town with ramparts — and its participle made the noun ~enceinte~: the ring of fortifications, then any enclosed space, and in today’s French also a loudspeaker, the ~enceinte acoustique~ that boxes sound in. Then there is the adjective ~enceinte~, “pregnant,” from Late Latin ~incincta~ — and here the dictionaries genuinely disagree. Read as the participle of ~incingere~, it means “girded about”: the woman wrapped, encircled. But a tradition as old as Isidore of Seville glosses it the other way — ~incincta, id est sine cinctu~, “that is, without a girdle”: the woman who has loosened her belt. And modern etymologists often suspect the word is really a folk-etymological reshaping of classical ~inciēns~, “pregnant,” an old term tied to the idea of swelling. Girded, ungirded, or neither: the question is still open, and best enjoyed that way. The home family runs from ~ceinture~ and ~ceinturon~ to the fortress and the hi-fi — and to that one adjective French students learn to reserve for expectancy alone.
en.encenser: ~Encenser~ is formed from the noun ~encens~ (“incense”) with the verb ending ~-er~. English Wiktionary adds that it may instead be inherited from Old French, itself a borrowing from Latin ~incēnsāre~, and that the surface analysis ~encens~ plus ~-er~ gives the same result. The noun ~encens~ comes from Late Latin ~incēnsum~, a thing burned as an offering, from Latin ~incendō~ (“to set on fire”), the verb that also gave French ~incendie~. The verb means to cense with incense and, figuratively, to flatter.
en.encercler: Formed from the prefix ~en-~ and ~cercler~, itself from ~cercle~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so “to put a ring around.” A rival account takes ~cercler~ from Vulgar Latin *~circlāre~, from Late Latin ~circulāre~. Either way the root is ~cercle~, from Latin ~circulus~, a diminutive of ~circus~ (“ring, circle”), probably borrowed from Greek ~kríkos~ or ~kírkos~. ~Encercler~ means to surround with a ring, or to draw a circle around something, literally or in military and police use.
en.enchanter:
From Old French ~enchanter~, which English Wiktionary says was “probably borrowed” from Latin ~incantāre~ (“to chant, to enchant, to bewitch”). That Latin verb was built from ~in-~ (“in, upon”) and ~cantāre~, a frequentative of ~canere~ (“to sing”), which goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~keh₂n-~ (“to sing”). Because the verb is likely a borrowing and not a direct inheritance, French also has the learned doublet ~incanter~. The Latin verb also gave Italian ~incantare~ and Spanish ~encantar~, and English ~enchant~ is a loan from French.

The development is a simple and striking one: singing over someone became casting a spell on them. French Wiktionary notes how close the link between song and magic is, which is also why ~incantation~ and ~chant~ belong to one family. From “to put under a spell,” ~enchanter~ weakened to “to delight, to charm,” and in modern French it is used both of fairy-tale magic and of ordinary delight, as in ~Enchanté~ (“Pleased to meet you”). The family includes ~enchanteur~ (“sorcerer, charmer”), ~enchantement~, ~désenchanté~ (“disillusioned”), ~chanter~ and ~chant~.
en.enchatonner: Formed from ~chaton~ with the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”) and the verb ending ~-er~: to ~enchatonner~ is to set a stone in the bezel of a ring. This ~chaton~ is the part of a ring that holds a stone, from Old French ~chastun~, from Frankish *~kastō~ (“box, case”), a word related to German ~Kasten~ and Dutch ~kast~. It is a different word from ~chaton~ meaning “kitten” (and “catkin”), which is a diminutive of ~chat~.
en.enchausser: Formed from ~chausser~ with the prefix ~en-~, which here adds the sense of putting something in or on. The base ~chausser~ comes from Old French ~chaucier~, inherited from Latin ~calceāre~ (“to furnish with shoes”), built on ~calceus~ (“shoe”). Italian ~calzare~ and Spanish ~calzar~ come from the same Latin verb. ~Enchausser~ shares its senses of putting footwear on someone, shoeing a horse and mulching, all of them kinds of covering.
en.enchaîner:
A verb built from the noun ~chaîne~ (“chain”) with the prefix ~en-~ and the ending ~-er~. ~chaîne~ comes from Old French ~chaeine~, from Latin ~catena~ (“chain”). The origin of ~catena~ itself is disputed: it is reconstructed from a Proto-Italic *~katesnā~ and sometimes tied to ~cassis~ (“hunting-net”) and a root meaning “to plait,” but several scholars — Martirosyan among them — judge it a borrowing from a Mediterranean substrate rather than an inherited Indo-European word. The deeper source is best left open. The same ~catena~ gives Italian ~catena~, Spanish ~cadena~, and, through Old French, English ~chain~.

Literally ~enchaîner~ means “to put in chains,” and from binding a captive came the figurative senses “to shackle, to subjugate, to enslave.” A further metaphor — links following link — yielded “to link up, to concatenate,” as one ~enchaîne~ ideas or scenes. The French family includes ~chaîne~, ~chaînon~ (“link”), ~déchaîner~ (“to unchain, to unleash”), and the learned ~concaténer~, drawn straight from Latin ~catenare~.
en.enchemiser: Formed from the noun ~chemise~ with the prefix ~en-~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to put into a ~chemise~,” which also means a folder or file cover. The noun comes from Old French ~chemise~ and Late Latin ~camisia~, whose own origin is uncertain: French Wiktionary suggests it may be Arabic, while English Wiktionary traces it to a Germanic word for “shirt.” The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”) and marks putting something inside.
en.enchevaucher: Formed from ~chevaucher~ with the prefix ~en-~. The base comes from Old French ~chevauchier~, from Late Latin ~caballicāre~ (“to ride a horse”), built on Latin ~caballus~ (“nag, workhorse”), a word of uncertain origin. The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”). The verb has the figurative sense “to overlap,” the way roof tiles lie one partly over another, as if one were riding astride the other.
en.enchevêtrer:
French ~enchevêtrer~ comes from Middle French and Old French ~enchevestrer~, but the sources give two accounts of how that verb arose. By surface analysis it is ~en-~ + ~chevêtre~ + the verb ending. According to the TLFi, it is instead inherited from a Vulgar Latin *~incapistrāre~ or *~encapistrāre~, itself formed on Latin ~capistrāre~, and French Wiktionary likewise links it to ~chevêtre~. The related forms in other Romance languages favor the Latin line: Catalan, Occitan and Spanish ~encabestrar~, Portuguese ~encabrestar~, Italian ~incapestrare~, Romanian ~încăpăstra~ and Sardinian ~incrabistare~ are all built the same way.

So the verb belongs to a family that spans the Romance world, and its French form is the product of the usual sound changes: the ~capis-~ of the Latin source became ~chevest-~ in Old French, and the lost s survives as the circumflex of ~chevêtre~ and ~enchevêtrer~. The modern sense is “to tangle up, to entangle,” and figuratively “to involve.” The noun ~enchevêtrement~ (“tangle”) belongs to the same family. The sources do not explain how the sense of tangling developed from the older forms, so that step is best left open.
en.enchâsser: ~Enchâsser~ is a parasynthetic verb, built at once from the prefix ~en-~, the noun ~châsse~ and the ending ~-er~. The prefix has its locative sense, “put into,” so the verb means to set something inside a ~châsse~, an enclosing case. The noun comes from Latin ~capsa~ (“box, chest,” later “coffin”), which also gave French the doublets ~caisse~, ~casse~ and ~case~. A similarly built verb is ~encaisser~, which puts something into a ~caisse~.
en.enchérir: Formed from the prefix ~en-~ and ~chérir~ (itself ~cher~ + ~-ir~), so “to make or become dear.” French Wiktionary gives ~chérir~ as the base, English Wiktionary analyzes ~en-~ + ~cher~ + ~-ir~, and the two amount to the same thing. The adjective ~cher~ comes from Latin ~cārus~ (“dear, costly”). The verb has two senses, “to become more expensive” and “to bid higher at an auction.”
en.enclaver:
French ~enclaver~ goes back to Late Latin ~inclavare~ (“to shut in with a key”), which English Wiktionary writes as Vulgar Latin *~inclāvāre~. The Latin verb is analyzed as ~in-~ (“in”) plus ~clāvis~ (“key”) plus the verb ending ~-āre~. Latin ~clāvis~ is the ancestor of French ~clé~, Italian ~chiave~ and Spanish ~llave~, so an ~enclaver~ is, at bottom, to lock something in.

The modern verb covers more than locks: it is used of places hemmed in by surrounding land, and the noun ~enclave~, a piece of territory surrounded by another, belongs to the same family. English borrowed ~enclave~ from French. The key word has other French relatives, among them ~clavicule~ (“collarbone”, from a Latin diminutive meaning a little key) and ~conclave~, from Latin ~cum clāve~ (“with a key”), the locked room in which cardinals elect a pope.
en.enclencher: Built from the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”) and ~clencher~, itself a verb formed from ~clenche~, the latch of a door. French Wiktionary glosses it literally as “to put into the latch.” English Wiktionary parses it slightly differently, as ~en-~ plus ~clenche~ plus ~-er~. Either way, to ~enclencher~ is to engage a latch or a gear, and by extension to set a mechanism, a process or a reform in motion.
en.encliqueter: Formed from ~cliquet~ (“pawl, ratchet catch”) with the prefix ~en-~, so “to lock in with a pawl.” The noun ~cliquet~ is explained as coming from ~cliquer~, the clicking noise the pawl makes. The verb carries the senses “to engage” and “to clip into.”
en.enclore:
~Enclore~ looks like ~en-~ + ~clore~, and French Wiktionary reads it that way. English Wiktionary instead treats it as inherited from Old French ~enclore~, from Vulgar Latin *~inclaudere~, itself a remodeling of Latin ~inclūdere~ (“to shut in”). That Latin verb was built from ~in-~ (“in”) and ~claudere~ (“to shut, close”), the source of French ~clore~. Either way the meaning is “to shut in,” and the verb long covered both enclosing a piece of land and fortifying a town.

The learned borrowing ~inclure~ comes from the same Latin ~inclūdere~, so ~enclore~ and ~inclure~ are doublets, one inherited and one taken later from Latin. The family of ~claudere~ in French is large: ~clos~, ~clôture~, ~exclure~, ~conclure~, ~reclus~ and ~clé~ all belong to it. The past participle gave the noun ~enclos~ (“enclosure, paddock”), and English ~enclose~ and ~include~ are relatives from French and Latin. Like ~clore~ itself, ~enclore~ is now literary and rare, mostly met in the participle ~enclos~.
en.enclouer: Formed from ~clouer~ and the prefix ~en-~: to drive a nail into something. English Wiktionary adds that the verb comes from Old French ~encloer~, and that it may alternatively descend from Vulgar Latin *~inclāvāre~, from Late Latin ~clāvāre~, from Latin ~clāvus~. Either way the root is the same: ~clouer~ is built on ~clou~ (“nail”), from Latin ~clāvus~. The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in”) and adds the idea of putting something in.
en.encocher: Formed from the prefix ~en-~ (“in, onto”) and the verb ~cocher~, so “to put a notch on” something. The base comes from the noun ~coche~, a notch cut into a stick to keep a tally; its own origin is uncertain, with Italian ~cocca~ (“notch on an arrow”) proposed as a source. That arrow sense survives in the Occitan verb ~encocar~, and it is the main sense of ~encocher~ today: to fit an arrow's notch onto the bowstring. The noun ~encoche~ (“notch”) belongs to the same family.
en.encoder: ~Encoder~ is a modern borrowing from the English verb ~encode~. According to the TLFi, it has been attested in French since 1964, which fits its technical, twentieth-century use. As general background, the English verb is built from the prefix ~en-~ and the noun ~code~. In French the English form was simply given the ordinary ~-er~ ending of the first conjugation, so ~encoder~ conjugates like ~chanter~ and slots into the language without any other change.
en.encoller: ~Encoller~ is formed from ~coller~ (“to glue, to stick”) with the prefix ~en-~, here in its sense of putting something onto or into: “to coat with glue.” The base ~coller~ is built on the noun ~colle~ (“glue”), which comes from Vulgar Latin *~colla~, borrowed from Ancient Greek ~κόλλα~ (~kólla~, “glue”). The same Greek word hides in English ~collagen~ and ~protocol~, and in French ~collage~ and ~colloïde~.
en.encombrer:
The origin is debated. French Wiktionary gives Old French ~encombrer~ (“to seize, to hinder”) and says the TLFi derives it from ~combre~ (“barrier”), despite a chronological gap, since ~combre~ is attested only in the fifteenth century. That word would come from a Gaulish word that French Wiktionary writes *~comberos~ (“barrage on a river”). English Wiktionary gives a similar chain through Early Medieval Latin ~incombrāre~ (“to hinder, to burden”) from ~combrus~ (“barricade of felled trees”), possibly from Gaulish *~komberū~, and compares Breton ~kember~, Irish ~comar~ and Welsh ~cymmer~. It traces the Celtic word to *~kombereti~ (“to bring together”), from *~kom-~ (“with”) and the Proto-Indo-European verb *~bʰéreti~ (“to carry”). It also records an alternative: Latin ~cumulus~ (“heap, pile”).

If the Celtic account is right, the picture is vivid: a pile of tree trunks across a river that blocks the way. The sense would then have broadened to any obstruction, then to a burden or a hindrance, and finally to something merely too bulky or too crowded. English ~encumber~ was borrowed from the French verb. The family includes ~encombrement~, ~encombrant~ (“bulky”) and ~désencombrer~ (“to clear”), while the Indo-European root *~bʰéreti~ is the same one that gave Latin ~ferre~ and English ~bear~.
en.encorder: ~Encorder~ is formed from the prefix ~en-~ and the verb ~corder~, itself built on ~corde~ (“rope”) with the ending ~-er~. The noun ~corde~ is a French form of Latin ~corda~ (attested around 980), borrowed from Latin ~chorda~ (“gut, cord”), from Ancient Greek ~khordḗ~ (“string of gut”). The prefix ~en-~, from Latin ~in-~, has its usual sense of putting something into or onto another: to ~encorder~ is to put a rope on someone or something, hence to rope up or to connect with a rope. The base ~corder~ already meant to bind with cords around 1200.
en.encorner: ~Encorner~ (“to gore, to horn, to cuckold”) is formed with ~en-~ on the noun ~corne~ (“horn”) and the verb ending ~-er~, though one account starts from the verb ~corner~ instead. The noun ~corne~ is the Latin neuter plural ~cornua~ taken for a feminine singular, from ~cornū~. The verb means to strike with the horns, as a bull does, or to provide with horns. It also carries the figurative sense of making a husband a cuckold, since horns are the traditional mark of the deceived husband.
en.encourager:
Formed in Old French from the noun ~courage~ with the prefix ~en-~ (“to put into, to make”) and the verbal suffix ~-er~ — literally “to put courage into.” ~Courage~ derives from ~cœur~ (“heart”), from Latin ~cor~ (“heart”), via a Vulgar Latin ~coraticum~. ~Cor~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱerd-~ (“heart”), source of Ancient Greek ~kardía~, Sanskrit ~hṛ́daya~, German ~Herz~, and English ~heart~ itself. For the medieval French, the heart was the seat of courage, so to embolden someone was, quite literally, to put heart into them.

The metaphor is the same one English keeps in “to hearten” and “take heart,” and it shows how concrete the abstraction once was. To ~encourager~ runs from rousing a wavering soldier to gently spurring a child or backing a worthy cause. Its opposite, ~décourager~, takes the heart back out. From the same root come a cluster of heart-words in French: ~cœur~, ~courage~, ~cordial~, ~accord~, ~courroux~, and ~écœurer~ (“to sicken, to disgust” — literally to turn the stomach, or heart). The medical prefix ~cardio-~, borrowed from Greek, descends from the very same Indo-European root.
en.encourir: Built from the prefix ~en-~ and ~courir~, as a calque of Latin ~incurrere~ (“to run against, run into”), whose ~in-~ the French prefix ~en-~ translates. ~Courir~ itself comes from Latin ~currere~ (“to run”). To ~encourir~ is thus to run into something, usually something unwelcome: ~encourir une peine~, ~un blâme~, ~la colère de quelqu'un~. English ~incur~ comes from the same Latin verb, so the two words are close relatives. The sense is of a risk or penalty one runs into, rather than one imposed from outside.
en.encrasser: Formed with the prefix ~en-~ on ~crasse~ (“grime, filth”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to cover with filth,” hence “to foul, to clog.” French Wiktionary instead builds it on the verb ~crasser~, which it derives either from ~crasse~ or from Latin ~crassāre~. The noun ~crasse~ goes back to Latin ~crassus~ (“thick, coarse”). The two accounts agree on the sense: something gets coated until it is thick with dirt.
en.encrer: ~Encrer~ is formed from ~encre~ (“ink”) plus the verb-forming ending ~-er~, meaning to apply ink to something. The noun comes from Old French ~enque~, from Late Latin ~encaustum~, from Ancient Greek ~ἔγκαυστον~. French Wiktionary links the Greek word to the idea of burning, as in French ~encaustique~, and notes that it named the red ink the Greek emperors signed with. Italian ~inchiostro~ is a cognate descendant of the same source.
en.encroûter: The two Wiktionaries read this verb differently. French Wiktionary traces it to Latin ~incrustare~ (“to cover with a crust”), while English Wiktionary analyzes it as ~en-~ + ~croûte~ + ~-er~ and compares ~incruster~. The two accounts are not necessarily opposed: the Latin verb is formed from ~in-~ and ~crusta~ (“crust, rind”), and ~croûte~ itself descends from ~crusta~, so both lead back to the same Latin noun. The meaning is “to cover with a crust,” literally and figuratively. The learned form ~incruster~ is a close relative, borrowed from the same Latin verb. ~Croûte~ gave the whole family of the crust, among them ~croûton~ and ~croûter~, and the Latin ~crusta~ lies behind English ~crust~ and ~crustacean~.
en.enculer: Formed in French from ~culer~ with the prefix ~en-~, in the sense “to place at the back.” The sexual sense appears in the 19th century. The base ~culer~ is explained as ~cul~ plus ~-er~, and ~cul~ comes from Latin ~culus~ (“buttocks”). The prefix ~en-~ descends from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”). French Wiktionary notes that Italian has a parallel vulgar verb, which makes a Vulgar Latin *~inculare~ conceivable, though not certain. The writer Louis-Ferdinand Céline used the word and its derivatives often in the 20th century, notably in ~Mort à crédit~ (1936). It is a vulgar word, with figurative uses such as “to defraud.”
en.encuver: Formed from ~cuve~ (“vat”) with the prefix ~en-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to put into a vat or tank,” as in winemaking. The noun ~cuve~ is inherited from Old French ~cuve~, from Latin ~cūpa~ (“cask, tub”). It is a doublet of ~coupe~ (“cup”), which came from a Late Latin variant. The prefix ~en-~, from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”), expresses the putting in.
en.endenter: ~Endenter~ is formed with the prefix ~en-~ on ~denter~, itself a verb made from the noun ~dent~ (“tooth”). English Wiktionary gives the same parts in one step, ~en-~ + ~dent~ + ~-er~. The sense is “to provide with teeth,” the prefix ~en-~ meaning “put in” or “provide with.” ~Dent~ comes from Latin ~dens~ (“tooth”). French Wiktionary cites the Old French line ~escu endenté~, a shield with toothed edges, in a text by Huon de Méry, an early use of the participle.
en.endetter: Formed in French from ~en-~, ~dette~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so the verb means to put into debt. The noun ~dette~ comes from Old French ~dete~, from Late Latin ~debita~, the neuter plural of ~debitum~ (“what is owed”), from Latin ~debēre~ (“to owe”). English ~debt~ is borrowed from the same French word, and ~débit~ is a doublet of ~dette~. The same pattern gave Occitan and Catalan ~endeutar~, Spanish ~endeudar~ and Portuguese ~endividar~. The reflexive ~s'endetter~, “to get into debt,” is the form used most.
en.endeuiller: Formed in French from the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into,” from Latin ~in-~), the noun ~deuil~ (“mourning, grief”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so ~endeuiller~ is “to plunge into mourning.” The noun ~deuil~ is an alteration of Old French ~duel~ (plural ~dueus~), whose modern spelling was possibly reshaped on the model of ~œil~ and ~yeux~. Its source is probably Late Latin ~dolus~, derived from Latin ~dolor~ (“pain”), or else a Vulgar Latin *~dolium~. The French and English Wiktionaries differ slightly on this last step.
en.endiabler: ~Endiabler~ is a parasynthetic verb: the noun ~diable~ (“devil”) received the prefix ~en-~ and the ending ~-er~ at once. Reading ~en-~ as “provide with,” the verb amounts to “to put the devil into,” and it is used for frenzied, wild behavior. The noun ~diable~ comes from Old French ~diable~ or ~deable~, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin ~diabolus~, from Greek ~diábolos~.
en.endiguer: ~Endiguer~ is formed with the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into,” from Latin ~in-~) on the verb ~diguer~, “to dike”; English Wiktionary instead parses it as ~en-~ + ~digue~ + ~-er~. It means to hold back with a dike, and so, figuratively, to curb or contain. The base ~diguer~ goes back through Middle French and Old French ~dikier~ to Middle Dutch ~diken~ (“to dig, ditch, dam”), a Germanic word related to English ~dig~.
en.endimancher: ~Endimancher~ is built on ~dimanche~ (“Sunday”) with the prefix ~en-~ and the ending ~-er~, so it means to dress someone in Sunday best. ~Dimanche~ is inherited from Old French ~diemenche~, from Late Latin ~diēs Dominicus~ (“day of the Lord”). The verb therefore hides a Christian day name, and ~en-~ here has the sense of providing with the noun.
en.endoctriner: Built in French on ~doctrine~ with both the prefix ~en-~ and the ending ~-er~, a parasynthetic formation: neither ~endoctrine~ nor ~doctriner~ is needed as a base. The noun ~doctrine~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~doctrīna~ (“teaching, instruction”), from ~docēre~ (“to teach”). The prefix ~en-~ gives the sense of putting something into someone, so ~endoctriner~ is to instill a doctrine, and hence to teach or indoctrinate.
en.endommager:
~Endommager~ appeared around 1165 as ~endamagier~: ~en-~ + ~dommage~, the noun of harm, with the verb ending. ~Dommage~ is Old French ~damage~, from ~dam~ (“loss, hurt”) — Latin ~damnum~, “loss, expense, fine, penalty” — plus the suffix ~-age~. ~Damnum~ continues Proto-Italic *~dapnom~ and is generally linked to the root *~deh₂p-~ of ~daps~, “sacrificial feast,” and Greek ~dapánē~, “expenditure”: at bottom, a loss is what the feast costs. The Romance cousins are Italian ~danno~ and Spanish ~daño~; English, meanwhile, simply took the Old French words whole — ~damage~ is the Old French noun unchanged, and Spenser could still write ~endamage~, borrowed from ~endamagier~, in The Faerie Queene.

~Damnum~ was as much a lawyer’s word as a mourner’s: it covered the fine a court imposed as well as the loss a storm inflicted, and both strands reached French. On the judicial side, ~damnāre~ (“to sentence, to inflict a damnum”) and its compound ~condemnāre~ gave ~damner~ and ~condamner~ — and, through Old French, English ~damn~: the curse is a court sentence in miniature. On the civil side stand ~dommage~, the polite ~C'est dommage~ (“what a pity” — literally “it’s a loss”), ~dédommager~ (“to compensate”), and the legal phrase ~dommages et intérêts~, “damages.” ~Endommager~ itself stayed concrete and material — one endommage a roof, a cable, a painting, not a person. French thus spreads across a whole family what English does with the single word damage: the etymology’s old accounting — feast, expense, loss — still keeps the books underneath.
en.endormir:
~Endormir~ is in the Chanson de Roland (around 1100, as the participle ~endormi~, “asleep”) and continues classical Latin ~indormīre~: ~in-~ + ~dormīre~, “to sleep.” In Latin the compound took the dative and meant “to sleep on or over something” — and so, pointedly, “to be slack, to neglect”: a magistrate could fall asleep over a case the way one nods over a book; Late Latin added “to grow numb,” said of a limb. ~Dormīre~ rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~drem-~, “to sleep,” with cognates in Greek ~darthánō~, Sanskrit ~drāti~ and Old Church Slavonic ~drěmati~ (“to doze”); Italian ~dormire~ and Spanish ~dormir~ keep the simple verb, where French raised the compound to head of household alongside ~dormir~.

French sharpened a useful division: ~endormir~ puts to sleep, ~s'endormir~ falls asleep. Around the causative, the figurative senses bloomed early and never faded. By about 1175 the verb meant “to lull, to deceive” — to endormir someone’s vigilance is still to talk it to sleep — and Boileau, in 1660, used it for the bore’s special power over an audience. Medicine made it gentle: ~on va vous endormir~ is what French anesthetists still say — “we are going to put you to sleep.” The family includes ~dormeur~, ~dortoir~ (“dormitory”), ~rendormir~, ~endormissement~, and the loveliest title in the language, ~la Belle au bois dormant~ — Sleeping Beauty. English drew on the same Latin stock for ~dormant~ and ~dormitory~: a dormant volcano is simply one that sleeps. Etymologically, then, the verb never strays: whether it numbs a leg, bores a theater, lulls suspicion or soothes a child, ~endormir~ keeps doing the one thing its root has done since *~drem-~ — it makes something sleep.
en.endosser: Formed on the noun ~dos~ (“back”) with the prefix ~en-~ (“on, onto”) and the verb ending ~-er~. No verb *~dosser~ stands behind it, so the prefix and suffix were added together. The noun ~dos~ is inherited from Old French ~dos~, from Latin ~dorsum~ through a Vulgar Latin form ~dossum~, with cousins in Italian ~dosso~ and Catalan ~dors~. To ~endosser~ is literally to put something on one's back, as with a coat or a pack. The sense then shifted to taking on a burden, a task or a responsibility, and to signing the back of a cheque to transfer it, which is the sense behind English “endorse.”
en.enduire:
Inherited from Old French ~enduire~, from Latin ~indūcere~ (“to lead in, to bring in”), formed from ~in-~ (“in, on”) and ~dūcere~ (“to lead”). The Latin verb ~dūcere~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dewk-~ (“to lead, to pull”), which also lies behind English ~tow~ and ~tug~ through Germanic, and behind German ~ziehen~. Italian ~indurre~ and Spanish ~inducir~ continue ~indūcere~ in their own way. ~Enduire~ is a doublet of ~induire~, which was borrowed from the same Latin verb later and in a more learned form.

The two French verbs divided the work. The learned ~induire~ kept the abstract senses of the Latin, to lead into, to induce, to infer, as in ~induire en erreur~. The inherited ~enduire~ developed the physical sense of spreading a layer over a surface: plaster on a wall, varnish on wood, grease on a mould. The noun ~enduit~ (“coating, plaster”), built on its participle, is the commonest everyday survivor. ~Enduire~ conjugates like ~conduire~, one of many French verbs built on ~dūcere~, together with ~produire~, ~réduire~, ~séduire~ and ~déduire~.
en.endurcir: This verb is formed from ~durcir~ with the prefix ~en-~, which here means “to become” or “to make”: to harden, to toughen. The sources disagree on the route. French Wiktionary derives it from ~durcir~, while English Wiktionary analyzes it as ~en-~ + ~dur~ + ~-ir~, based on the Latin verbs ~indūrēscere~ and ~dūrēscere~. Either way the root is the Latin adjective ~dūrus~ (“hard”), which lives on in French ~dur~.
en.endurer:
French ~endurer~ comes from Latin ~indūrāre~ (“to harden”), made of ~in-~ and ~dūrus~ (“hard”). English Wiktionary treats it as inherited through Old French ~endurer~, which was already attested around 1050, while the TLFi calls it a semi-learned borrowing. Either way it is an old word, and a later learned borrowing of the same Latin verb gave ~indurer~, so ~endurer~ is its doublet. The adjective ~dūrus~ survives as French ~dur~, Italian and Spanish ~duro~, and the same root stands behind ~durer~ (“to last”), ~durable~ and ~endurcir~. English ~endure~ was borrowed from the French verb.

The meaning moved from the physical to the moral. Latin ~indūrāre~ meant “to make hard,” and to harden oneself against pain is to hold out against it, so French ~endurer~ came to mean “to bear, to suffer patiently.” The step is natural, though the sources do not document it in detail. The modern verb keeps a literary flavor and often governs a hardship: one ~endure~ cold, insults or years of difficulty. The original sense of hardening survives in the relatives ~endurcir~ and ~endurci~, which still describe a hardened heart.
en.endêver: ~Endêver~ is built from the prefix ~en-~ and the Old French verb ~desver~ (“to rave, to be mad”). ~Desver~ is inherited from Vulgar Latin *~deexvagāre~, which goes back to Latin ~vagus~ (“wandering”). The Latin source is made of ~dē-~, ~ex-~ and ~vagāre~ (“to wander”), and the verb ~rêver~ is a relative of ~desver~. The sense of ~endêver~ runs parallel to that of ~enrager~: to be driven half out of one's wits by vexation. The Latin root ~vagus~ also gave French ~vague~ and ~vagabond~.
en.enfanter: Formed from the noun ~enfant~ (“child”) with the verbalizing ending ~-er~, in the sense “produce N”: to bring a child into the world. The noun comes, through Old French, from Latin ~īnfantem~, accusative of ~īnfāns~ (“not speaking”). French Wiktionary dates its first uses, in the sense of a small boy or girl, to the late tenth century, and its sense of “adolescent” to about 1100. A verb of birth thus rests on a word whose Latin ancestor described a child too young to talk.
en.enfariner: ~Enfariner~ means to coat with flour. The sources analyze it either as ~en-~ + ~fariner~ or as ~en-~ + ~farine~ + ~-er~, which amounts to the same thing. ~Fariner~ is a verb made from ~farine~ (“flour”), which is inherited from Old French and goes back to Latin ~farīna~, a derivative of ~far~, a word for wheat or spelt. Similar verbs exist elsewhere: Spanish ~enharinar~ and Italian ~infarinare~ are close parallels.
en.enfaîter: ~Enfaîter~ is a parasynthetic verb: ~en-~ and the ending ~-er~ added together to the noun ~faîte~ (“ridge, top of a roof”), so “to provide with a ridge,” hence “to cover the ridge of a roof with tiles.” The noun was ~festre~ in Old French and comes from a Germanic root, *~first~ (“roof ridge”), which survives in German ~First~. The spelling ~faîte~ was reshaped in the Renaissance by association with Latin ~fastīgium~, which is not its source.
en.enfermer:
From Old French (12th century), formed from ~en-~ (“in”) + ~fermer~ (“to close, shut”). ~Fermer~ comes from Latin ~firmāre~ (“to make firm, fasten, secure”), from ~firmus~ (“firm, steadfast, strong”). ~Firmus~ descends from Proto-Italic *~fermos~ and from PIE *~dʰer-mo-s~ (“holding”), built on the root *~dʰer-~ (“to hold, support”). Through that root it is cognate with Sanskrit ~धर्म~ (~dharma~, “that which holds, law”) and, in the Romance family, with Italian ~fermo~ and Spanish ~firme~; English borrowed ~firm~ from the same Latin word.

The semantic logic is one of fastening: to “make firm” a door is to shut it fast, and so Latin ~firmāre~ gave French ~fermer~, “to close.” Prefix it with ~en-~ and you close someone or something ~inside~ — to ~enfermer~ is to shut in, to lock up, to confine. The word ranges from the literal (a prisoner, an animal, a treasure) to the figurative (to ~s'enfermer~ in silence or in one's certainties). From the same Latin firmness come ~ferme~ (“firm,” and also the farm, once a fixed lease), ~fermeture~, ~affermir~, ~confirmer~, and ~firme~.
en.enferrer: Formed from the prefix ~en-~ and ~ferrer~, so it means “to put onto iron.” The base ~ferrer~ goes back to Latin ~ferrum~ (“iron”), possibly through Late Latin *~ferrāre~ and Old French ~ferrer~, and it first meant to fit with iron, as when a horse is shod. ~Enferrer~ shifted the picture to the iron blade: to run an opponent through with a sword or a bayonet. The family of ~fer~ also gives ~ferraille~ and ~ferronnerie~.
en.enficher: Formed from the prefix ~en-~ (from Latin ~in-~, “in, into”) and ~fiche~, a form tied to the verb ~ficher~. The base entry notes that ~ficher~ became the polite stand-in for vulgar ~foutre~, which comes from Latin ~futuere~, so ~je m'en fiche~ stands beside ~je m'en fous~. ~Enficher~ is the technical verb: “to plug in,” to push a connector or pin into its socket, with ~en-~ giving the sense of putting something in.
en.enfieller: This verb is formed from ~fiel~ (“bile, gall”) with the prefix ~en-~ and the ending ~-er~, and literally means “to fill with bile”. Bile was long held to be the seat of anger and bitterness, which is why the verb means “to fill with rage”. The noun ~fiel~ is inherited from Vulgar Latin ~felem~, from Latin ~fel~ (“bile”). The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ and here has its sense of putting something inside.
en.enfiler: Formed from the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into,” from Latin ~in-~) and the verb ~filer~, which derives from ~fil~ (“thread”). The verb ~filer~ goes back to Late Latin ~filāre~ (“to spin into thread”), from Latin ~filum~ (“thread”). The sense is concrete: to put something onto a thread, as one threads a needle or strings beads on a cord. By extension the verb came to cover slipping on a garment, and entering a street or passage in a line. Both sources point to ~fil~ and ~filer~, so the formation is plainly French.
en.enfiévrer: Formed from the prefix ~en-~, the noun ~fièvre~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so that it means “to put a fever into.” The noun ~fièvre~ is inherited from Old and Middle French ~fievre~, from Latin ~febris~ (“fever”). The literal sense, to make feverish, gave way to a figurative one: to ~enfiévrer~ a crowd or a debate is to stir it up or rouse it, as if heat had spread through it.
en.enflammer:
French ~enflammer~ comes from Old French ~enflamer~, itself from Latin ~inflammāre~ (“to set alight”), a verb built from ~in-~ (“in, upon”) and ~flamma~ (“flame”). The doubled ~m~ of the modern spelling is a Latinizing respelling that brought the word closer to its Latin model. The sources also allow a second reading: seen from inside French, the verb looks like a parasynthetic formation from ~en-~, ~flamme~ and ~-er~. The two accounts give the same verb in practice, and the evidence does not rule either out, so the safest statement is that the word is Latin in origin and French in its present shape and spelling, with the prefix ~en-~ doing the work that Latin ~in-~ once did.

The family around ~flamma~ is large in French and includes ~flamme~, ~flambeau~, ~flamber~, ~inflammable~ and ~inflammation~, the last two being learned borrowings from Latin rather than inherited words. Beside them stands ~enflammer~, which keeps the popular French prefix ~en-~ where the learned words keep the Latin ~in-~. The modern verb thus has two layers in its history: a popular French form that took on the Latin shape in its spelling, and a learned vocabulary of fire that sits close by. Which of the two readings of its formation is the truer one is a question the sources leave open, and either way the word is a descendant of Latin ~flamma~.
en.enfler:
French ~enfler~ is inherited from Old French ~enfler~, which comes from Latin ~īnflāre~, “to blow into, to swell.” This is the inherited line of the word, the one that passed from Latin to French through speech. The Latin verb joins ~in-~ (“in”) to ~flāre~ (“to blow”). Spanish ~hinchar~ also descends from ~īnflāre~ by regular sound change.

French has learned relatives of ~enfler~ that stay close to the Latin shape, such as ~inflation~ and English ~inflate~. The inherited line gave ~enfler~ and ~enflure~ (“swelling”). French ~souffler~ (“to blow”) belongs to the same family through Latin ~sufflāre~, built on the same ~flāre~. The sense development is easy to follow: to blow air into something is to make it swell, and French ~enfler~ can speak of a limb, a river, a sail or a price.
en.enfleurer: Formed from ~fleur~ (“flower”) with the prefix ~en-~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so the verb means to impregnate with flowers, hence to give a perfume the scent of flowers. The noun ~fleur~ comes from Old French ~flor~, from Latin ~flōrem~ (“flower; the finest part of something”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰleh₃-~ (“to bloom”). The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”) and here carries a sense of putting something into or providing with.
en.enfoncer:
French ~enfoncer~ is built from the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”) and the verb ~foncer~, which derives from the noun ~fond~ / ~fonds~ (“bottom, depth”). ~fond~ comes from Latin ~fundus~ (“bottom, base, ground”), which goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰudʰmḗn~ (“bottom”). That root is cognate with English ~bottom~, German ~Boden~ (“ground”), Ancient Greek ~πυθμήν~ (“bottom, base”), and Sanskrit ~बुध्न~ (~budhna~).

The literal sense is to drive something “to the bottom,” to push it deep in — a nail, a stake, a hand into a pocket. From there the meaning fans out vividly: to ~enfoncer~ a door is to break it in by force; to ~enfoncer~ an enemy line is to pierce and rout it, hence “to defeat”; and intransitively or reflexively, ~s'enfoncer~ is to sink down, to founder, to plunge into water, debt, or darkness. From the same ~fundus~ French keeps ~fond~, ~fonder~ (“to found”), ~fondation~ (“foundation”), ~foncier~ (“pertaining to land”), ~défoncer~ (“to smash in”), and ~profond~ (“deep”) — the whole family circling the idea of a base and what lies at it.
en.enfouir:
From Vulgar Latin *~infodīre~, a reshaping of Latin ~infodere~ (“to bury, to dig in”), formed from ~in-~ (“in”) and ~fodere~ (“to dig”). The simple verb survives in French as ~fouir~ (“to dig”), and the Latin ~fodere~ is generally traced to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “to dig.” The Latin verb moved into the ~-ire~ conjugation in popular speech, which is why French ended up with ~enfouir~ and ~fouir~, both in ~-ir~, rather than in ~-re~.

The meaning has stayed close to the Latin: to put something into the ground and cover it, as in ~enfouir un trésor~. It then widened to hiding something deep, as in ~enfouir un secret~ or ~enfouir sa tête dans l'oreiller~. The family of ~fodere~ is rich: French ~fouiller~ (“to search, to dig through”) and ~fouille~ (“excavation”) come from it, as do ~fossé~ (“ditch”) from Latin ~fossa~, a dug trench, and the learned ~fossile~, from Latin ~fossilis~ (“dug up”), which first meant anything unearthed before it was limited to ancient remains.
en.enfourcher: Formed from the prefix ~en-~ (from Latin ~in-~, “in, into”) and ~fourche~, the noun behind the verb ~fourcher~; French Wiktionary gives ~fourcher~ as the base, English Wiktionary the noun, and the two amount to the same thing. ~Fourche~ was inherited from Old French ~furche~ and ~forche~, from Latin ~furca~ (“pitchfork”). The verb ~enfourcher~ means “to get on, to mount,” as one mounts a horse or a bicycle. Its base ~fourcher~ survives mainly in ~la langue m'a fourché~, said of a slip of the tongue.
en.enfourner: Formed in French from the prefix ~en-~, the noun ~four~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to put in the oven.” The noun ~four~ goes back to Latin ~furnus~ (“oven”). The verb has relatives across the Romance languages, which built it the same way: Catalan, Occitan and Portuguese ~enfornar~, Italian ~infornare~ and Spanish ~enhornar~. Besides baking, French uses it in familiar speech for swallowing food in great haste, and for shoving something into a place.
en.enfreindre:
From Old French ~enfraindre~, inherited through Vulgar Latin *~īnfrangere~ from Latin ~īnfringere~ (“to break, to damage”), which combines the prefix ~in-~ with ~frangere~ (“to break”). In classical Latin the vowel of ~frangere~ normally weakened to ~i~ inside a compound, giving ~īnfringere~, but the Vulgar Latin form restored the ~a~ of the simple verb, and that is the shape French inherited. English ~infringe~ was borrowed from the same Latin ~īnfringere~.

The verb began as a physical image, to break something, and it now applies almost only to rules: one ~enfreint~ a law, a ban or a treaty, which makes it a close relative of the English “infringe.” Its conjugation follows the pattern of ~craindre~ and ~peindre~, with a ~-gn-~ in many forms. The root ~frangere~ lives on in a large French family, including ~fraction~, ~fracture~, ~fragile~ and ~infraction~, which was borrowed later from Latin and is the noun that most clearly shows the kinship with ~enfreindre~.
en.enfuir: Formed in French from ~fuir~ with the prefix ~en-~, today used almost only in the reflexive ~s'enfuir~, “to run away.” Here ~en-~ carries the sense of “away,” which French Wiktionary ties to Latin ~inde~ (“from there”) and which also lies behind ~s'en aller~. The base ~fuir~ descends from Old French ~fuir~, from Vulgar Latin *~fūgīre~, a reshaping of Latin ~fugere~ (“to flee”), whose root goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰewg-~ and is shared with Ancient Greek ~pheúgō~.
en.enfutailler: Formed from ~futaille~ with the prefix ~en-~ and the verb ending ~-er~, meaning to put into casks. The noun ~futaille~ was ~fustaille~ in Old French and is itself built on ~fût~ (“cask”) with the suffix ~-aille~, which gives a collective sense, casks in general. The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”) and here has its locative sense: to put something inside.
en.enfûter: Formed in French from the prefix ~en-~, the noun ~fût~ (“keg, cask”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, so the verb means “to put into a cask.” The noun ~fût~ comes through Old French ~fust~ from Latin ~fūstis~ (“stick, club”), so the cask is named from a piece of wood. The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”) and here has its locative sense of putting something inside, as in ~enterrer~ or ~encadrer~.
en.engager:
From Old French ~engagier~, derived from ~gagier~ (“to pledge”) with the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”). The base noun is ~gage~ (“pledge, security”), which French took from Frankish *~wadi~, from Proto-Germanic *~wadją~ (“pledge”), in turn from the Proto-Indo-European root *~wedʰ-~ (“to pledge, bind”). The Frankish word also passed into Medieval Latin as ~vadium~. Through this Germanic source, ~gage~ is a doublet of the borrowed English ~wage~, and a cousin of English ~wed~ and German ~Wette~ (“bet, wager”).

To ~engager~ was first to put something “into pledge” — to pawn it, to bind it as security. From this concrete sense of staking a guarantee grew the whole modern fan of meanings: to bind oneself by a promise (to commit), to bind another to oneself by hiring, and to draw a person or thing into an action (to involve, to engage in battle). The reflexive ~s'engager~ kept the strongest flavor of the original pledge — “to commit oneself.” The same family yields ~gage~, ~gager~ (“to wager”), ~dégager~ (“to release, free up”), and the borrowed-back ~engagement~. That a word for emotional and professional commitment began as a banker's word for a pawned object is a fitting reminder that to promise is, etymologically, to put something on the line.
en.engainer: Built from ~gaine~ (“sheath”) with the prefix ~en-~ and the ending ~-er~, so “to put into a sheath.” Here ~en-~ has its locative sense, “in, into.” The noun ~gaine~ comes from Latin ~vāgīna~ (“sheath, scabbard”) by way of Old French ~guaïne~. The initial g- reflects Germanic influence, which one theory ties to a Frankish word *~wāgi~ (“cup”), while another credits the speech of Frankish warriors, who used the word most. It is a doublet of ~vagin~ and a cognate of Italian ~guaina~ and Spanish ~vaina~.
en.engazonner: Formed from the prefix ~en-~ (from Latin ~in-~, “in, into”) and ~gazonner~, itself the noun ~gazon~ plus ~-er~: to cover ground with turf. ~Gazon~ comes from Old French ~gason~ or ~wason~, borrowed from Old Frankish *~waso~, a clod of earth covered with grass. The German word ~Wasen~ (“lawn”) is a cognate. The Germanic initial ~w-~ became ~g-~ in central French, as in ~guerre~ and ~garder~. ~Engazonner~ means “to turf, to lay grass over.”
en.engendrer:
From Middle French ~engendrer~, from Old French ~engendrer~ (also ~engenrer~, with an intrusive ~d~ between ~n~ and ~r~, exactly as in ~gendre~ “son-in-law”), from Latin ~ingenerāre~ (“to implant, beget, produce”), itself ~in-~ (“in, into”) plus ~generāre~ (“to beget, bring forth”), from ~genus~ (“birth, race, kind”). The chain reaches back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~genh₁-~ (“to give birth, beget”). The same root surfaces in English ~generate~, ~genus~, and ~kin~, and in Spanish ~engendrar~.

Latin ~ingenerāre~ already carried the sense of bringing a living thing into being, and Old French ~engendrer~ kept that biological core: to father, to procreate. From there the verb spread figuratively to whatever one thing causes another to produce — a fault that ~engendre~ a quarrel, a policy that begets unrest. French still says ~engendrer~ for both senses, biological and causal. The prolific *~genh₁-~ family fills the modern language: ~gendre~, ~genre~, ~génération~, ~gène~, ~génie~, and ~ingénieur~ all descend from the same idea of birth, kind, and inborn capacity.
en.englober: Formed on ~globe~ with the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”) and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~globe~ was borrowed from Latin ~globus~ (“ball, sphere”), which French Wiktionary links to Latin ~gleba~ (“clod”) and ~glomerāre~ (“to roll into a ball”). To ~englober~ something is thus to put it inside a sphere, and so to treat it as part of a larger whole: a plan that ~englobe~s several measures includes them all in one round shape.
en.engloutir:
French ~engloutir~ is usually traced to Old French ~englotir~, from Late Latin ~ingluttīre~, built with ~in-~ (“in”) on Latin ~gluttiō~ (“to swallow”). French Wiktionary gives only the Latin ~inglutire~ as the source. English Wiktionary adds an alternative: that the verb was formed within Old French from ~en-~ plus ~glotir~, a verb of the same Latin family. Both accounts end at the same Latin ~gluttiō~, so the dispute concerns where the prefix was added, not the root. English ~glutton~, which came through Old French ~gloton~, belongs to the same Latin family.

The literal sense is to swallow greedily, to gulp something down in one go. From there the image widened: the sea can ~engloutir~ a ship, a flood a village, and a spender can ~engloutir~ a whole fortune in a few months. In each case something vanishes whole into a larger appetite. The same root lives on in French ~glouton~ (“glutton”) and ~gloutonnerie~, which share the Latin ~glutt-~ stem, and in ~engloutissement~, the noun for being swallowed up.
en.engluer: ~Engluer~ is formed from the prefix ~en-~ and ~glu~ (“birdlime”) with the verb ending ~-er~, as English Wiktionary analyzes it. French Wiktionary reads the same word as ~en-~ plus the verb ~gluer~, itself from ~glu~, so both accounts end up in the same place. The prefix ~en-~, from Latin ~in-~ (“in”), adds the sense of covering or putting into, so ~engluer~ is to coat with sticky glue, and so to trap, as birds are caught on limed branches.
en.engober: Formed from ~gober~ with the prefix ~en-~, the verb means to cover with ~engobe~, a thin coating of clay on pottery. ~Gober~ is one of the few French words inherited from Gaulish, from *~gobbos~ (“beak, snout”), which has relatives in Irish and Scottish Gaelic ~gob~. The sources do not explain how the sense of swallowing in ~gober~ led to that of coating.
en.engommer: Formed from the noun ~gomme~ with the verb ending ~-er~, meaning to coat with gum or rubber. The noun was borrowed from Late Latin ~gumma~, from Latin ~gummi~, from Greek ~kómmi~. The sources trace the Greek word back further, to an Egyptian word for a resin. The Latin and Greek word named the sticky sap of certain trees, and the French noun kept that sense before ~gomme~ also came to mean a rubber eraser.
en.engoncer: Formed in French from ~gond~ (“hinge”), taken from its Old French plural form ~gons~, with the prefix ~en-~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The surface analysis is a parasynthetic one: the prefix and the suffix are added together to the noun, as in many verbs of the type ~en-~ + noun + ~-er~. Today ~engoncer~ is said of a garment, such as a tight collar or a heavy coat, that makes a person look as if they had no neck, with the head sunk between the shoulders.
en.engorger: ~Engorger~ is built on ~gorge~ (“throat”) with the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”, from Latin ~in-~) and the verbal ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary derives it from the verb ~gorger~, while English Wiktionary prefers en- + noun + -er, as in ~engouer~; either way the picture is of something stuffed into the throat. The noun ~gorge~ comes from Old French ~gorge~, from Late Latin ~gurga~, related to Latin ~gurges~ (“whirlpool, gulf”). From the idea of blocking a passage, the modern verb means to clog, clog up or congest.
en.engouer:
From Middle French ~angouer~ (“to choke by force-feeding”), built on ~goue~ (“cheek, throat”). That ~goue~ comes from an unidentified dialect form, which French Wiktionary ties, like ~joue~, ~jabot~, ~gave~ and ~gaver~, to a Gaulish *~gaba~. English Wiktionary likewise links the verb to ~joue~ (“cheek”), so both sources place the origin in the mouth and throat, with Gaulish as the deepest layer.

The Middle French sense, to choke someone by cramming, is far from the modern one, “to become passionate or infatuated (with),” and the sources do not detail the steps between them. The family is a rich one: ~joue~, ~jabot~ and ~gaver~, all tied to the same Gaulish source by French Wiktionary, and ~gober~, to which it refers. Within the verb's own family, ~engouement~ (“infatuation, craze”) is the related noun.
en.engouffrer: Built in French on ~gouffre~ (“abyss, chasm”) with the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”) and the verb ending ~-er~: to swallow up in a chasm, hence “to engulf” or “to gobble up.” ~Gouffre~ comes from Old French ~gofre~ or ~goufre~, from Late Latin ~colfus~ or ~culfus~, a variant of ~colpus~, itself borrowed from Greek ~kólpos~ (“bend, hollow fold”), with letters swapped along the way. The sense “gulf, bend of the coast” lives on in the close relative ~golfe~.
en.engourdir: A parasynthetic verb: the prefix ~en-~ and the ending ~-ir~ were added around the adjective ~gourd~ (“numb”), giving a verb that means “to make numb.” ~Gourd~ comes from Latin ~gurdus~. The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ and here marks becoming or making; the ending ~-ir~ is the second-conjugation ending used for verbs built on adjectives.
en.engraisser: The two sources differ. French Wiktionary analyzes it as the prefix ~en-~ plus ~graisser~, which is the noun ~graisse~ plus ~-er~. English Wiktionary instead calls it inherited from Vulgar Latin *~ingrassiare~, from *~incrassiare~, from Latin ~crassus~ (“thick, fat”), comparing Italian ~ingrassare~, Spanish ~engrasar~ and Romanian ~îngrășa~. Both routes lead to the same Latin ~crassus~, which also gave French ~gras~. ~Engraisser~ means to make fat or to grow fat, of animals as of people, and by extension to enrich.
en.engranger: Built from the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”), the noun ~grange~ (“barn”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so literally “to put into the barn.” The noun ~grange~ comes from Old French ~grange~, from Vulgar Latin *~grānica~, a derivative of Latin ~grānum~ (“grain”): a ~grange~ was a place for storing grain. The verb first described bringing in the harvest, and it extends easily to any gathering and storing: one ~engrange~ crops, but also profits, memories or points. The word keeps a rural picture behind a very general figurative sense.
en.engraver: The sources give two readings. One sees the verb as a substitution of prefix on Old French ~agraver~, itself built on ~grave~ (“shore, gravel”) with ~a-~ and ~-er~. The other analyzes it as ~en-~ + ~graver~, and English Wiktionary adds that it is inherited from Middle French ~engraver~. Either way, the meaning rests on ~grave~ in its old sense of gravel or shingle: to ~engraver~ is to cover with gravel or, of a boat, to run aground on it.
en.engrener: Formed from the prefix ~en-~ (from Latin ~in-~, “in, into”) and ~grener~, the verb from ~grain~ or ~graine~ with ~-er~; English Wiktionary gives ~en-~ + ~grain~ + ~-er~, and the two agree. ~Grain~ comes from Latin ~granum~ (“grain”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵr̥h₂nóm~. The same Latin word underlies ~graine~ and ~grenier~, and English ~grain~ and ~garner~ come from it too. ~Engrener~ means “to fill with grain” and, by another route, “to set in motion.”
en.engrosser: From Middle French ~engrosser~, itself an alteration, influenced by the adjective ~gros~ (“big, thick”), of Old French ~engroissier~. That verb was formed from the prefix ~en-~ and Old French ~groisse~ (“bigness, thickness”), with the verb ending ~-er~. The root is therefore ~gros~, a word that French inherited from Late Latin ~grossus~ (“thick”). The meaning in modern French is a familiar and rather crude way to say that a man has made a woman pregnant. The same family is large. ~Gros~ gave ~grossir~ (“to grow bigger”), ~grosseur~ (“size, swelling”), ~grossesse~ (“pregnancy”) and ~grossier~ (“coarse”). English borrowed it as ~gross~, and the Italian cousin is ~grosso~. In French, ~engrosser~ stays strongly colloquial, and it is far from the neutral ~féconder~ or the medical ~rendre enceinte~.
en.engueuler: Built around the noun ~gueule~ with the prefix ~en-~ and the suffix ~-er~ added at once, a parasynthetic formation. The noun comes from Old French ~gole~ or ~goule~, from Latin ~gula~ (“gullet, throat”). The prefix ~en-~ goes back to Latin ~in-~, and the ending ~-er~ to Latin ~-are~. The result is a slangy verb meaning “to tell someone off.”
en.enguirlander: ~Enguirlander~ is formed from ~en-~ + ~guirlande~ + ~-er~, literally “to deck with garlands.” ~Guirlande~ comes from Old French ~garlande~, probably derived from Frankish *~weron~ (“to bedeck, adorn”), itself from or related to Proto-Germanic *~wīraz~; compare Old High German ~wieren~ and English ~wire~. The figurative sense “to tell off” is very common today, and it serves as a milder substitute for the cruder ~engueuler~.
en.enhardir: ~Enhardir~ means “to embolden.” English Wiktionary analyzes it as ~en-~ + ~hardi~ (“bold”) + ~-ir~, while French Wiktionary derives it from the verb ~hardir~ with the prefix ~en-~; either way the formation is French. The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”) and is factitive here, “to make.” The ending ~-ir~ is the second-conjugation ending that turns an adjective into a verb meaning “to make or become,” as in ~enrichir~ and ~embellir~. So ~enhardir~ is, literally, “to make bold.”
en.enharnacher: Formed from ~harnacher~ with the prefix ~en-~ (to equip with), a variant of the older verb that already meant to put a harness on a horse. ~Harnacher~ comes from ~harnais~, the gear of a horse, and an earlier verb ~harnescier~ is attested in the thirteenth century. The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”).
en.enherber: Formed from ~herber~ with the prefix ~en-~. The base ~herber~ is itself a verb built on ~herbe~ (“grass, herb”), from Latin ~herba~. The prefix ~en-~ carries its usual sense of “providing with,” the thing provided being grass. ~Enherber~ has two recorded senses, “to cover with grass” and “to poison.”
en.enivrer:
The two Wiktionaries frame ~enivrer~ differently. French Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~inebriāre~ (“to make drunk”), while English Wiktionary treats it as a French formation, ~en-~ + ~ivre~ + ~-er~. The two accounts fit together, because ~ivre~ (“drunk”) itself continues Latin ~ēbrius~, and ~inebriāre~ is built on that same adjective with the prefix ~in-~.

The Latin verb also reached French a second time as a learned word, ~inébrier~, a rare form that sits beside the everyday ~enivrer~. The pair is a small case of the usual French doublet pattern: one word handed down by speech, another taken directly from Latin by writers. English took the learned route and has ~inebriate~, built on the same Latin verb. In modern French, ~enivrer~ is used both literally, of alcohol, and figuratively, of anything that goes to the head, such as success or perfume. Related French words include ~ivre~, ~ivresse~, ~ivrogne~ and the learned ~ébriété~.
en.enjamber: ~Enjamber~ is attested in Middle French with the same meaning, and it is a formation in which the prefix ~en-~, the noun ~jambe~ (“leg”) and the verb ending ~-er~ were combined: to straddle or stride over something is to put one's legs across it. As standard background, ~jambe~ comes from Late Latin ~gamba~. The poetic term ~enjambement~, a verse that runs over into the next line, is a later derivative of the verb.
en.enjoindre: ~Enjoindre~ goes back to Latin ~iniungere~ (~in-~ + ~iungere~, “to join”), which in Latin could mean to attach something to someone, hence to impose a task on them. It is first recorded around 1191 in Old French as ~anjoindre~, a form later reshaped after ~joindre~, so that the verb now looks like a prefixed ~joindre~. In modern French it means to order or to command formally. The noun ~injonction~ is a direct learned descendant, and ~joindre~ and ~jonction~ share the same Latin root ~iungere~.
en.enjoliver:
~Enjoliver~ is built with ~en-~, which here means “to make, to put into a state,” on Old French ~jolif~ (“pretty”), whose feminine was ~jolive~. French sources trace it to Old French ~ajoliver~, a verb already formed from the same adjective. The adjective later lost its ending, giving Modern French ~joli~. The prefix ~en-~ is the Old French descendant of Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”), and in verbs like ~embellir~ it carries the sense “to make or become.”

The root of the family is ~jolif~, which English borrowed from Old French as ~jolly~. In French the adjective became ~joli~, and from it come ~joliesse~ and ~enjoliver~, with the nouns ~enjolivement~ and ~enjoliveur~, the latter now best known as the name of a car's wheel cover. The verb means “to embellish, to make prettier,” literally with ornaments and figuratively with details added to a story. It is a good example of how French builds a verb on an adjective with ~en-~, as in ~embellir~ and ~enrichir~, where the same prefix means “to make X.”
en.enjuiver: ~Enjuiver~ is a pejorative, antisemitic coinage formed from the prefix ~en-~, the noun and adjective ~juif~ and the ending ~-er~. The base ~juif~ is inherited from Middle French and Old French ~juiu~, from Latin ~Iūdaeus~, borrowed from Greek ~Ioudaîos~, which goes back to the name of Judah. The word is recorded here for completeness and not as a recommendation: its sense depends entirely on a hostile stereotype, and it is not a neutral term.
en.enjôler: Composed of ~en~, ~geôle~ (“jail”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, and so a variant of ~engeôler~, with the same parts. The modern sense, “to bewitch, to win over by flattery,” is figurative, and the sources give no further account of how it developed from the idea of the jail.
en.enkyster: Formed from ~kyste~ (“cyst”) with the prefix ~en-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, so it means to enclose in a cyst or to become enclosed in one. The noun ~kyste~ is borrowed from Ancient Greek ~κύστις~ (“pouch, bladder”). The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”) by way of Old French.
en.enlacer: Formed from the prefix ~en-~ and ~lacer~. The base comes from Old French ~lacier~, from Latin ~laqueāre~ (“to bind, to entwine”), built on ~laqueus~ (“noose, snare”), and the same Latin source gave English ~lace~. ~Enlacer~ is to wrap around: to entwine threads or branches around something, or to hold someone in an embrace. The family includes ~lacs~ (“snare”), ~lacet~ (“small cord”), ~entrelacer~ and ~délacer~.
en.enlaidir: ~Enlaidir~ is built from the prefix ~en-~ and ~laidir~ (“to become ugly”), a verb formed on the adjective ~laid~ (“ugly”) with the ending ~-ir~. The prefix goes back to Latin ~in-~ through Old French ~en-~. Prefix and second-conjugation ending work together here, as in ~enrichir~ and ~embellir~: the verb means to make ugly or to become ugly.
en.enlever:
Formed within French from the prefix ~en-~ and the verb ~lever~ (“to lift, raise”). ~Lever~ comes from Latin ~levāre~ (“to lift, lighten, relieve”), a verb built on the adjective ~levis~ (“light, not heavy”), from the PIE root *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ (“light, nimble”). Through that root ~enlever~ is distantly cognate with English ~light~ (in weight) and, via Latin borrowings, with ~levity~ and ~elevate~; Italian and Spanish keep the parent in ~levare~ and ~llevar~. The prefix ~en-~, from Latin ~inde~ or ~in~, adds a sense of motion away — so the compound means roughly “to lift up and off.”

The core idea is a lifting that becomes a taking-away. To lift a thing off a surface is to remove it, and French let the sense fan out: one can ~enlever~ a stain, a coat, a difficulty, or — more darkly — a person, giving the noun ~enlèvement~ its double life as both “removal” and “abduction.” The same lightening root colors a surprising spread of vocabulary: ~léger~, ~alléger~, ~soulever~, ~élever~, ~prélever~, and ~levée~ all carry the memory of ~levāre~. Even ~levain~ (“leaven”), the agent that lifts dough, belongs to the family — a reminder that to raise and to make light were once one and the same act.
en.enliasser: Formed from ~liasse~ (“bundle”) with the prefix ~en-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to bundle together,” usually of papers. The noun ~liasse~ is itself derived from ~lier~ (“to tie”) with the suffix ~-asse~. The prefix ~en-~, from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”), expresses the putting into a bundle, in the same way as in ~enrouler~.
en.enlier: Formed from ~lier~ (“to link, to bind”) with the prefix ~en-~, which here means “in, into.” ~Lier~ comes from Latin ~ligāre~ (“to bind”), and the prefix ~en-~ from Latin ~in-~. The verb is a masonry term: to lay stones so that they bind into one another, each course tied into the next, rather than simply stacked.
en.enliser: ~Enliser~ is built from the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”), ~lise~ (“quicksand”), a word from the Norman dialect, and the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to get stuck in quicksand.” French Wiktionary adds that ~lise~ goes back to Gaulish *~ligisja~, from *~liga~ (“silt”). The verb thus pairs a Latin prefix with a Celtic word for mud.
en.enluminer:
Borrowed from Latin ~illūmināre~ (“to light up”), with the prefix changed from ~il-~ (a form of ~in-~) to ~en-~, as English Wiktionary notes. The Latin verb is built on ~in-~ and the noun ~lūmen~ (“light”). Because French also borrowed the same Latin verb unchanged as ~illuminer~, the two are doublets: one reshaped by the common ~en-~ prefix, the other kept close to Latin spelling.

The doublets drifted apart in use. ~Illuminer~ is the general verb for lighting up or enlightening, while ~enluminer~ came to be the technical word for decorating manuscripts with colors and gold, as in medieval books, and it can also mean to brighten a face or sky. The noun ~enluminure~ names such a painted page. All of these share the Latin root of ~lumière~ (“light”), ~luminaire~ and ~lumineux~, along with English ~illuminate~.
en.ennoblir:
From Old French ~ennoblir~, built from the prefix ~en-~, the adjective ~noble~ and the verb ending ~-ir~, so that the verb means “to make noble.” The adjective ~noble~ reached French through Old and Middle French as a learned borrowing from Latin ~nōbilis~.
