Latin ~nōbilis~ is usually analyzed as a formation on the verb ~nōscere~ (“to get to know”), with the suffix ~-bilis~. English ~noble~ and ~ennoble~, Italian ~nobile~ and Spanish ~noble~ all come from the same Latin word.

The pattern ~en-~ + adjective + ~-ir~ is the classic way French coins verbs meaning “become” or “make A,” as in ~enrichir~ and ~embellir~. ~Ennoblir~ is mostly figurative: a deed, a feeling or a cause can be said to ennoble someone. The related verb ~anoblir~ is the one that means “to confer a title of nobility.” Around ~noble~ French has ~noblesse~, ~nobiliaire~ and the Latin-shaped negative ~ignoble~, which comes from Latin ~ignōbilis~ (“of low birth, obscure”).
en.ennuager: Formed from ~nuager~ with the prefix ~en-~. The base ~nuager~ is itself ~nuage~ (“cloud”) plus the verb suffix ~-er~, so ~ennuager~ means to cloud over. The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”), through Old French ~en-~, and with a noun base it carries the sense of providing with it: to fill with clouds, or to become clouded.
en.ennuyer:
~Ennuyer~ is inherited from Old French ~enoiier~ (also spelled ~enuier~ and ~anoier~), from Late Latin ~inodiāre~. French Wiktionary explains the Latin verb as formed on the phrase ~in odio esse~ (“to be an object of hatred”), from ~odium~ (“hatred”). The sense was therefore “to be hateful to someone.” Related languages took the same verb: Spanish ~enojar~ (“to anger”) and Italian ~annoiare~ (“to bore, to annoy”) descend from it, and English ~annoy~ was borrowed from Old French ~anoier~.

The history of ~ennuyer~ is a long weakening. In Old French it was strong: to make odious, to torment, to cause grief or hatred. By the classical age the noun ~ennui~ could still mean deep distress, as in the tragedies of Racine, and only later faded into the modern sense of boredom. The verb followed, and today ~ennuyer~ means to bore or to bother. Its relatives include ~ennui~, ~ennuyeux~, ~désennuyer~ and, from the Latin noun ~odium~ itself, ~odieux~. English ~annoy~ shows the same path of softening, from “hatred” to mere irritation.
en.enorgueillir: Formed from the prefix ~en-~, the noun ~orgueil~ (“pride”) and the ending ~-ir~, in the pattern of making or becoming: to fill someone with pride. The noun is Germanic in origin. French Wiktionary derives ~orgueil~ from Old Frankish *~urgôli~ (“pride”), compared with Old High German ~urguol~ (“outstanding”), and records it as ~orgolz~ around 980, then ~orgoill~ in 1080 and ~orgueil~ in 1130. It replaced Latin ~superbia~, and Italian ~orgoglio~ and Spanish ~orgullo~ show the same replacement.
en.enquiquiner:
The origin of ~enquiquiner~ is uncertain. French Wiktionary proposes that it is probably derived from ~kiki~ with the prefix ~en-~ and the suffix ~-iner~. English Wiktionary similarly suggests ~en-~ plus an imitative element ~-kik-~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. Either way, the verb reads as an expressive, colloquial coinage meaning “to annoy.”

The base ~kiki~ is itself obscure. French Wiktionary offers two explanations. By one, ~kiki~ is a clipped form of ~kikiriki~, a rendering of the cock's crow, with early senses such as “small animal, chick” and “throat.” By the other, it is a shortening of ~riquiqui~. The suffix ~-iner~ is not productive today and appears only in a handful of colloquial verbs, such as ~jaspiner~. Since the sources hedge at every step, the safest summary is that ~enquiquiner~ is an informal, probably imitative creation, and that its exact path to the sense “annoy” is not documented.
en.enquérir:
French ~enquérir~ is inherited from Old French ~enquerre~, from Latin ~inquīrere~ (“to search into, to inquire”). English Wiktionary adds that the verb changed conjugation on the way, as ~quérir~ did, ending in ~-ir~ instead of ~-re~. ~Inquīrere~ is ~in-~ (“into”) plus ~quaerere~ (“to seek, to ask”). English ~inquire~ and ~enquire~ descend from the same Latin verb through Old French, and so are cognates.

The root ~quaerere~ is one of the most productive in French: ~quérir~, ~acquérir~, ~conquérir~, ~requérir~, ~enquête~ (“investigation”) and ~question~ all come from it, as do English ~query~ and ~quest~. Today ~enquérir~ is nearly always used in the pronominal form ~s'enquérir de~ (“to ask about, to inquire into”), a formal expression, while the noun ~enquête~ carries the everyday load.
en.enquêter: Formed from the noun ~enquête~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Latin ~inquīsīta~ (the feminine past participle of ~inquīrere~, “to look into”), used as a noun in Medieval Latin as ~inquesta~ and giving Old French ~enqueste~. ~Inquīrere~ is itself from ~in-~ + ~quaerere~ (“to seek”), the source of English ~inquire~. French already had an irregular verb for this, ~enquérir~, so speakers made a regular first-group verb from the noun, a pattern fr.Wiktionary compares to ~solutionner~. The result, ~enquêter~, means to carry out an investigation or a survey.
en.enraciner: Formed from the prefix ~en-~ and the verb ~raciner~ (“to take root”), itself made from the noun ~racine~ (“root”) with the ending ~-er~. The noun is inherited from Late Latin ~radīcīna~, built on Latin ~rādīx~ (“root”). The prefix ~en-~, from Latin ~in-~, here means “provide with” its noun, so ~enraciner~ is “to put down roots” or “to cause to take root,” literally of a plant and figuratively of an idea, a habit or a person. Its opposite ~déraciner~ is built on the same noun, and both are far commoner today than the rare ~raciner~.
en.enrager: Formed from the prefix ~en-~ and ~rager~, itself from the noun ~rage~; the verb is attested already in Old French and corresponds to ~en-~ + ~rage~ + ~-er~. The noun comes from Late Latin *~rabia~, an altered form of Latin ~rabiēs~ (“rage, madness”), and Spanish ~rabia~ is a cognate. ~Enrager~ means to be in a rage or to be furious, as in ~faire enrager~ (“to drive someone mad”). An archaic sense, “to have rabies,” stays close to the Latin source.
en.enrayer: Formed from the prefix ~en-~, the noun ~rai~ (“spoke of a wheel”) and the verb ending ~-er~. The word ~rai~ descends from Latin ~radius~ (“staff, spoke, ray”), which is also the ultimate source of ~rayon~. The picture behind ~enrayer~ is a cart wheel, presumably stopped by jamming something among its spokes. From braking a wheel the verb widened to checking anything in motion, as in halting an epidemic or inflation, and to a firearm that jams.
en.enregistrer:
From the noun ~registre~ (“register, record book”) with the prefix ~en-~ (“to put into”) and the first-conjugation verb suffix ~-er~. The noun ~registre~ comes from Old French ~registre~, from Medieval Latin ~registrum~, an altered form of Late Latin ~regesta~ (“things recorded, a list”), the neuter plural of the past participle of Latin ~regerere~ (“to carry back, record”), from ~re-~ (“back”) and ~gerere~ (“to carry, bear”). Cognate with English ~register~ and ~registry~, and — through ~gerere~ — with English ~gesture~ and ~digest~.

So to ~enregistrer~ is literally to “put into the record book,” and the surprise lies in that book: the original meaning of ~regerere~ was “to carry back,” a clerk physically carrying entries back to be filed. The doubled ~-r-~ of ~registrum~ is unetymological, picked up in Medieval Latin by analogy with other nouns in ~-istrum~. The verb broadened from formal registration of acts and births to the modern senses of recording sound, capturing data, and saving a file on a computer. From the same ~gerere~ family French inherited ~geste~, ~gérer~, ~digérer~, and ~suggérer~, while ~registre~ itself spread into Dutch, German, and the Scandinavian languages.
en.enrhumer: ~Enrhumer~ is built on the noun ~rhume~ (“cold”) with both the prefix ~en-~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to give someone a cold,” and ~s'enrhumer~ is “to catch one.” The prefix ~en-~, from Latin ~in-~, here carries the sense of providing with the noun. The base ~rhume~ is a learned word: it comes from Late Latin ~rheuma~, borrowed from Ancient Greek ~ῥεῦμα~ (“flow”), since a cold was once thought of as a flow of humors.
en.enrichir:
French ~enrichir~ is a parasynthetic verb — formed in a single stroke from the adjective ~riche~ (“rich”) with the prefix ~en-~ (“to make, to put into”) and the verbal suffix ~-ir~, literally “to make rich.” The adjective ~riche~ is itself a Germanic loan: Old French took it from the Frankish *~rīki~ (“powerful, mighty”), from Proto-Germanic *~rīkijaz~. Through that Germanic family ~riche~ is cognate with German ~reich~, Dutch ~rijk~, and English ~rich~, and with Gothic ~reiks~ (“ruler, mighty one”). The Germanic word was itself borrowed early from Celtic, akin to Gaulish *~rīx~ and Old Irish ~rí~ (“king”), all from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to rule, to direct in a straight line”) — the same root as Latin ~rēx~ (“king”).

The original force of the word was “powerful,” not “wealthy”: in early Old French a ~riche~ man was a mighty one, and only in the thirteenth century did the sense of material prosperity prevail. ~Enrichir~ thus once leaned toward “to make mighty” before settling on “to make wealthy” and, by extension, “to enhance” — one enriches a soil, a language, or a uranium sample. From the same stock French keeps ~riche~, ~richesse~ (“wealth”), and the borrowed ~Reich~, while the deeper root surfaces in ~roi~, ~régir~, and ~royal~.
en.enrober: ~Enrober~ is built on the noun ~robe~ with the prefix ~en-~ and the verb ending ~-er~. It first meant “to dress in a robe”, around 1220 in the work of Gautier de Coincy, and the sense of wrapping something in a covering is recorded in 1858. The noun ~robe~ is of Germanic origin, from a word *~rauba~ (“booty”), which is also behind ~dérober~. Old French ~robe~ itself meant “booty, spoils of war” (first recorded in 1155) before it came to mean clothing, the garment taken from someone who had been plundered.
en.enrocher: Formed from ~rocher~ (“rock”) with the prefix ~en-~, which here means to put in or to provide with: to protect a bank or foundation with a riprap of rocks. ~Rocher~ is derived from ~roche~, which comes from Late Latin ~rocca~, of uncertain and probably pre-Latin origin. Compare Italian ~rocca~, Spanish ~roca~ and English ~rock~.
en.enrouer:
~Enrouer~ comes from Old French ~enrouir~, which later passed into the first conjugation. English Wiktionary analyzes it as ~en-~ plus Old French ~ro~ (“hoarse”), from Latin ~raucus~ (“hoarse”). The same Latin adjective was borrowed a second time as the learned ~rauque~, so ~rauque~ and the ~-rou-~ of ~enrouer~ are two routes from one source. English ~raucous~ belongs to the same Latin family.

Do not confuse it with another Old French ~enrouer~, which meant “to put on the wheel, to subject to the torture of the wheel.” That verb belongs with ~rouer~ and the noun ~roue~, not with ~raucus~. In modern French only the “make hoarse” sense survives, and the verb is met mostly through its participle ~enroué~, describing a voice or a person who has lost clarity of voice. The Latin source is also behind the descriptive adjective ~rauque~, used of harsh, low voices.
en.enrouler: Formed from the verb ~rouler~ with the prefix ~en-~, which here has its locative sense of putting something in or around. To ~enrouler~ is to wind something into a roll or around an object. The base ~rouler~ goes back to Old French ~roeler~, built on ~roele~ (“little wheel”), from Late Latin ~rotella~, a diminutive of Latin ~rota~ (“wheel”). Cognates of ~rota~ include German ~Rad~ and Lithuanian ~ratas~. The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”) by way of Old French.
en.enrubanner: ~Enrubanner~ is a parasynthetic formation: the prefix ~en-~ (“in, onto”), the noun ~ruban~ (“ribbon”) and the verbal ending ~-er~. It means to adorn or tie with ribbons. The noun ~ruban~ comes from Old French ~riban~, whose ~i~ was rounded before the ~b~, and further back from a Middle Dutch form ~ringhband~, a compound of two Germanic words meaning “ring” and “band”. ~Hauban~ and ~raban~ are related words that likewise lost their final ~d~.
en.enrégimenter: Formed from ~régiment~ with the prefix ~en-~ and the verb ending ~-er~: to put someone into a regiment, hence “to enlist.” The noun ~régiment~ comes from Late Latin ~regimentum~ (“direction for government”), from Latin ~regere~ (“to rule”). The prefix ~en-~, from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”), carries the sense of putting into. It can also be used figuratively, for bringing people under a party or a cause.
en.enrésiner: Formed from ~résine~ (“resin”) with the prefix ~en-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun was borrowed from Latin ~resīna~. The prefix ~en-~, from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”), here makes a verb of providing: ~enrésiner~ is to plant with resinous trees, that is, with conifers. It belongs to the same pattern as ~enraciner~ (“to root”).
en.enrôler: ~Enrôler~ comes from Old French ~enroller~, formed from ~en-~ (“in, into”), ~rolle~ (“registration”) and ~-er~, and means to put a name down on a roll. The noun ~rolle~ was a rolled-up parchment, from Latin ~rotulus~, a diminutive of ~rota~ (“wheel”). Modern ~rôle~ is the same word, which once also named the text of a play.
en.ensabler: Formed from ~sabler~ with the prefix ~en-~, which gives the sense “into, onto”: to cover or fill with sand. The English Wiktionary parses it as ~en-~ + ~sable~ (“sand”) + ~-er~. Both analyses give the same result. The noun ~sable~ comes from Latin ~sabulum~ (“sand, gravel”) by way of Old French, and is a different word from the ~sable~ of fur and heraldry. The verb is used of a channel that silts up and of a boat that runs aground on sand.
en.ensacher: Formed from the noun ~sac~ with the prefix ~en-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning “to put into a sack.” The ~h~ is added only for the pronunciation. ~Sac~ comes from Latin ~saccus~, which was borrowed from Greek ~sákkos~ (“sack, sackcloth”), a word of Semitic origin. The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”), here with its sense of placing something inside.
en.ensanglanter: ~Ensanglanter~ is built from the adjective ~sanglant~ (“bloody”), the prefix ~en-~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The prefix has the sense “cover with, put into,” so the verb means “to cover with shed blood.” ~Sanglant~ is inherited from Late Latin ~sanguilentus~, a variant of ~sanguinolentus~, the source of the learned French ~sanguinolent~. Behind both lies Latin ~sanguis~ (“blood”).
en.ensauvager: ~Ensauvager~ is formed from ~sauvage~ with the prefix ~en-~ and the ending ~-er~: to make wild, or to become wild. The base is inherited through Old French ~salvage~ from Latin ~silvāticus~ (“of the forest”), from ~silva~ (“forest”). The word thus keeps a trace of the woods: to turn something toward the wild, away from the tamed.
en.enseigner:
From Old French ~enseignier~ (attested around 1050), from Vulgar Latin *~insignare~, an alteration of Latin ~insignire~ (“to mark, to distinguish, to make conspicuous”), compounded from the prefix ~in-~ and ~signum~ (“mark, sign”). ~Signum~ is, by one influential account, traced to the Proto-Indo-European root *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”) — the standard one follows — though some scholars favor a root meaning “to cut.” Cognate with Italian ~insegnare~ and Spanish ~enseñar~ (“to teach”).

The path from “marking” to “teaching” is the heart of the story: to *~insignare~ was to set a sign upon something, to point it out — and to point something out to a learner is to teach it. French preserves both ends. The original “marking” sense survives in ~enseigne~ (a shop's “sign,” and once a military “ensign” or standard-bearer), while the verb ~enseigner~ moved wholly into instruction. From the same ~signum~ spring ~signe~, ~signal~, ~signaler~, ~désigner~, and ~insigne~, and English ~ensign~, ~sign~, and ~insignia~. A teacher, etymologically, is one who sets up signposts — marking the road so the pupil may follow it.
en.ensemencer: Formed from ~en-~, the noun ~semence~ (“seed”) and the ending ~-er~, in the sense “to provide with”: to ~ensemencer~ a field is to supply it with seed, that is, to sow it. The noun ~semence~ came through Old French from Late Latin ~sementia~, itself derived from Latin ~sēmen~ (“seed”).
en.enserrer: Formed from ~serrer~ (“to press, to clasp”) with the prefix ~en-~, here in its sense of enclosing: to clasp all around. French Wiktionary gives a second analysis, ~en-~ plus the noun ~serre~, without choosing between them. ~Serrer~ comes from Old French ~serrer~ (“to close, to lock fast”), from Late Latin ~serāre~ (“to close with a bar”), from Latin ~sera~ (“a bar, a bolt”).
en.ensevelir: French ~ensevelir~ is formed from the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”) and the Old French verb ~sevelir~, which comes from Latin ~sepelīre~ (“to bury”). English Wiktionary adds that the Latin verb presumably reached French through a Vulgar Latin form ~sepellīre~. The base ~sevelir~ no longer exists on its own in French, so ~ensevelir~ is the form that survived. The Latin verb also lies behind learned French words such as ~sépulture~ and ~sépulcre~, and Italian ~seppellire~ is its direct descendant.
en.ensiler: Formed from ~silo~ with the prefix ~en-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning “to put into a silo,” which French Wiktionary glosses as ~mettre en silo~. The prefix ~en-~ has the locative sense “in, into,” as in ~enrouler~. The noun ~silo~ was borrowed from Spanish, which in turn took it via Basque ~zilo~ (“granary”) from Latin ~sirus~ (“a vessel for storing grain”), from Greek ~sirós~ (“silo”), possibly of Hebrew or Phoenician origin.
en.ensoleiller: Formed from ~en-~ and ~soleiller~, which is itself ~soleil~ + ~-er~; English Wiktionary analyzes it directly as ~en-~ + ~soleil~ + ~-er~. The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”) and here has its sense of providing with something, so the verb means to fill with sunlight. The noun ~soleil~ descends from Latin ~sōl~ (“sun”), through a Vulgar Latin diminutive form. Today the verb is used literally, for a room bathed in sun, and figuratively, for a face, a day or a mood that is brightened.
en.ensorceler: ~Ensorceler~ comes from Old French ~ensorcerer~, formed from ~sorcier~ (“sorcerer”) with the prefix ~en-~, which gives the sense “to put under the power of a sorcerer”. The modern form arose by dissimilation, when the first of the two ~r~ sounds became an ~l~. The prefix and the base are clear, and the sources trace ~sorcier~ no further.
en.ensuivre:
From Latin ~īnsequī~ (“to follow closely, to come right after”), in the Vulgar Latin form *~insequere~, which, as the deponent verbs of Classical Latin did, took an ordinary active shape. The verb is ~in-~ + ~sequī~ (“to follow”), and its development in French ran parallel to that of ~sequī~, which became ~suivre~. Words of the same Latin family include ~séquence~, ~suite~ and ~poursuivre~, and English ~sequel~ and ~sue~ are relatives that came through French.

In use, ~ensuivre~ means to follow as a consequence, and it appears mostly in the third person (~il s'ensuit que~, “it follows that”). French Wiktionary notes an interesting wobble. Speakers tend to reanalyse the verb as ~en~ + ~suivre~, so one commonly hears ~il s'en est suivi~ in compound tenses where the older rule would have said ~il s'est ensuivi~. For the same reason ~s'ensuivre de quelque chose~ is rare, because a complement introduced by ~de~ feels redundant next to ~en~. The verb thus shows a fossilised prefix, ~en-~ from Latin ~in-~, being pulled apart again by the speakers' own sense of the language.
en.entabler: Formed from ~table~ with the prefix ~en-~, from Latin ~in-~. ~Table~ was inherited from Old French ~table~, from Latin ~tabula~ (“plank, tablet”), the source of every later sense of the word. In horsemanship, ~entabler~ describes a horse whose hips move before its shoulders.
en.entacher: Formed from the prefix ~en-~ and ~tacher~ (“to stain”), a verb tied to the noun ~tache~ (“stain”), so literally “to put a stain on.” The prefix ~en-~, from Latin ~in-~, marks here the placing of the stain on something, and the verb extends to anything marred or tainted. The origin of ~tache~ is debated: one hypothesis derives it from Gothic ~taikns~ (“sign”), another treats it as a back-formation from the verb. The sources do not settle the matter.
en.entailler: ~Entailler~ is formed from the verb ~tailler~ and the prefix ~en-~, which here has its locative sense of “in, into”, so the verb means to cut into something, to make a notch or gash. ~Tailler~ comes from Old French ~talier~, from Late Latin ~taliare~ (“to cut, to split”), from Latin ~talea~ (“a cutting, slip, rod”). The noun ~entaille~ (“notch”) belongs to the same family, as do ~taille~ and ~détail~.
en.entamer:
From Late Latin ~intamināre~ (“to soil, to profane”), attested in French from about 1120, with the sense “to begin, to undertake” following by around 1245. The origin is debated. The TLFi connects ~intamināre~ only “probably” to ~tangere~ (“to touch”) — the same touch-root behind ~contaminer~ — so the descent is offered with an explicit hedge rather than as fact. A separate hypothesis sets Latin aside altogether and proposes a Gaulish source, comparing Breton ~tamm~ (“piece”) and ~tennañ~ (“to withdraw, to extract”). The sources present these as competing accounts.

Whatever the root, the development is vivid: from a word meaning “to soil or violate the wholeness of” a thing grew the idea of breaching an intact surface — making the first cut into a loaf, a cask, or a reserve. From that first incision came the abstract “to begin” (to ~entamer~ a conversation or negotiations) and “to eat into, to diminish” (to ~entamer~ one’s savings or someone’s resolve). The French family stays close to the cutting image: ~entame~ (“the first slice”), ~entamure~ (“an incision”) and ~entamable~.
en.entarter: ~Entarter~ combines the prefix ~en-~, the noun ~tarte~ and the ending ~-er~: “to hit someone in the face with a pie.” ~Tarte~ is a variant of ~tourte~, from Late Latin ~torta~, itself short for Latin ~torta panis~ (“round loaf”). The prefix ~en-~ means “to put into or onto,” and the verb applies it to a pie thrown at a public figure. Only the pie survives in the sense of the verb, not the bread.
en.entartrer: Formed from ~tartre~ with the prefix ~en-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~: “to coat with tartar, to scale up.” The prefix ~en-~ has the sense “put in or onto,” as in ~entourer~. The base ~tartre~ comes, according to French Wiktionary, from Late Latin ~tartarum~, known through its derived form ~tartaralis~, which is itself traced to Persian ~dard~ (“sediment, deposit”). The verb thus names the chalky deposit that builds up in kettles, pipes and teeth.
en.entasser: Formed from the prefix ~en-~ (“into”), the noun ~tas~ (“heap, pile”) and the verbal ending ~-er~: to put into a heap. The noun's origin is not fully settled. English Wiktionary derives Old French ~tas~ from a Frankish *~tas~ (“mass”), comparing Dutch ~tas~ (“heap”), while French Wiktionary calls the origin obscure and mentions both a Frankish source and, more doubtfully, a link with Latin ~stāre~ (“to stand”). The Germanic account is the one that finds cognates elsewhere. The verb moved from piling up objects to crowding people together and, figuratively, to hoarding money.
en.entendre:
From Old French ~entendre~ (« to pay attention, to understand, to hear »), from Latin ~intendere~ (« to stretch toward, to direct one's attention »), formed from ~in-~ (« toward ») and ~tendere~ (« to stretch »). ~tendere~ rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~ten-~ (“to stretch”), the same root behind English ~tend~, ~tension~, and ~thin~, and behind French ~tendre~ and ~tension~. Italian ~intendere~ and Spanish ~entender~ are its close Romance kin.

The original metaphor is bodily: to ~intendere~ was to stretch the mind toward something, as a bow is drawn toward its mark. From « directing attention » the verb split two ways. In medieval usage it came to mean « to understand » — a sense French still keeps in ~entendement~ and the phrase ~bien entendu~ — and then, by a further drift, « to hear », the everyday meaning today. Its noun ~entente~ (« understanding, agreement ») gave English the diplomatic ~entente~. From the same root *~ten-~ spring ~tendre~, ~tendance~, ~attendre~ (« to await »), ~prétendre~, and ~étendre~ (« to spread out »).
en.enter:
French ~enter~ (“to graft”) comes from a Late Latin verb *~imputāre~ (“to graft”), which looks identical to classical ~imputāre~ (“to reckon, to attribute”) but is a different word. It was built on ~inpotus~ (“graft”), a word recorded in the Salic Law, and that word in turn comes from Ancient Greek ~ἔμφυτος~ (“implanted”). One source gives the Late Latin verb in a contracted form, *~imptāre~. Related forms elsewhere in the south include Old Occitan ~empeut~ (“graft”), Provençal ~enpeutar~ and Catalan ~empeltar~.

The Greek ~φ~ was rendered as ~p~ and not as ~f~ in this word, which is why the older forms carry a ~p~, as ~empeut~ shows. The Greek word probably travelled together with the practice of grafting itself, by way of the Greek colonies and traders on the Mediterranean coast of Gaul, before the Roman conquest. This route is the likely account rather than a documented one. The same Greek source also gave French the legal terms ~emphytéose~, ~emphytéote~ and ~emphytéotique~, which concern a long lease on land.
en.enterrer:
From the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”) and a verb on ~terre~ (“earth, ground”), from Latin ~terra~ (“land, earth, soil”). ~Terra~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~terzā~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~ters-~ (“dry”) — so the earth was named, originally, as the ~dry~ land set against the sea. By the same root English has ~thirst~ (the state of being dry), making ~terre~ and ~thirst~ distant cousins. The literal force of ~enterrer~ is exact: to put something into the earth.

The core sense is to bury — a body, a treasure, a bone the dog hides. From there French extends it figuratively: to ~enterrer~ a plan or a project is to lay it in the ground for good, to abandon it; and to ~enterrer~ a rival is to outlive them. From ~terra~ flow a great many words: ~terrain~, ~territoire~, ~terrestre~, ~terrasse~, ~atterrir~ (“to land,” to come to earth), ~déterrer~ (“to dig up”), ~souterrain~ (“underground”), and even ~terrier~ — both the burrow and the dog bred to go down it.
en.enthousiasmer: A verb made from the noun ~enthousiasme~ with the verbalizing ending ~-er~, meaning “to fill with enthusiasm.” The noun is attested in French since at least 1546, in Rabelais, and came through Latin ~enthusiasmus~ from Greek ~enthousiasmós~ (“inspiration, divine possession”). The Greek word rests on ~éntheos~ (“inspired by a god”), formed of ~en~ (“in”) and ~theós~ (“god”). To be enthusiastic was thus, literally, to have a god within.
en.enticher:
~Enticher~ goes back to Old French ~entechier~ (“to endow with a quality or a defect”), built on ~teche~ (“quality, good or bad”), a variant of ~tache~ (“mark, stain”). English Wiktionary presents the modern verb as a back-formation from the participle ~entiché~, from Old French ~entechié~, whereas French Wiktionary derives it from the verb ~entechier~ itself. Its cousin is ~entacher~ (“to sully”), which belongs to the same family as ~teche~.

The stem vowel changed from e to i under the influence of the Old French verb ~enticier~ (“to incite”). In the Renaissance, ~entiché~ described a fruit beginning to spoil and, more broadly, a person corrupted by a vice: one could be ~entiché~ of that vice. Today the word is used mostly as the participle ~entiché de~ (“infatuated with”) and in the reflexive ~s'enticher de~.
en.entonner: ~Entonner~ has two separate sources, each a parasynthetic formation with the prefix ~en-~ and the suffix ~-er~. In the sense of striking up a song, it is built on ~ton~ (“tone, pitch”), which comes from Latin ~tonus~, itself from Greek ~tónos~ (“string, tension, musical mode”). In the sense of putting liquid into a cask, it is built on ~tonne~ (“barrel”). The prefix ~en-~ gives the sense “put into” or “provide with,” so the two verbs mean, respectively, to put into pitch and to put into a barrel.
en.entortiller:
The origin of ~entortiller~ (Old French ~entorteiller~) is disputed. By the first account, it comes from a Vulgar Latin verb *~intortiliāre~, derived from the Latin adjective ~tortilis~ (“twisted, coiled”). This rests on the age of the word and on matching verbs in neighboring languages: Spanish ~entortijar~, Catalan ~entortellar~, Italian ~intortigliare~ and Romanian ~întortochea~. If it is right, the simpler French verb ~tortiller~ is itself derived from ~entortiller~, not the reverse.

By a second account, ~entortiller~ derives from ~entort~, the past participle of the old verb ~entordre~, from Latin ~intorquēre~, the source of ~entorse~ (“sprain”). In that case ~tortiller~ and ~entortiller~ formed independently. The modern verb keeps the physical sense of winding something around another thing, and also means “to win over.” The two accounts share the idea of twisting, and the family includes ~tortiller~ and ~entorse~.
en.entourer:
A denominal verb formed from ~entour~ (“surroundings, what is round about”), which is ~en~ (“in”) + ~tour~ (“a turn, a going-around”). ~Tour~ comes from Latin ~tornus~ (“a lathe, a turner's tool for tracing circles”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~τόρνος~, from Proto-Indo-European *~terh₁-~ (“to rub, bore, turn by twisting”). Cognate, through ~tornus~ and the verb ~tornāre~, with Italian ~tornare~, Spanish ~tornar~, and English ~turn~ and ~tour~.

The image is geometric: to ~entourer~ is to set things all around, as a circle is traced by a turning point. An older form ~entourner~ survived into the 16th century before being smoothed to ~entourer~. From it French draws ~entourage~ (the people round about a person) and ~entour~ in the literary ~à l'entour~ (“round about”). The deeper ~tour~/~tornus~ family is vast: ~tourner~, ~tour~ (both the masculine “turn/circuit” and the feminine “tower” by a different route), ~détour~, ~contour~, ~tournoi~, ~tornade~ (via Spanish), and ~tour~ in ~faire le tour~. All circle back to the carpenter's lathe — a tool that makes roundness by turning, the very gesture of surrounding.
en.entraccuser: Formed from the prefix ~entre-~, which expresses reciprocal action as in ~s'entraider~, on ~accuser~: to accuse one another. The prefix goes back to Latin ~inter~ (“between”). The base ~accuser~ comes from Latin ~accūsāre~ (“to call to account, to bring a charge against”), built on ~ad-~ (“toward”) and ~causa~ (“cause, lawsuit”), so to accuse was to bring a case against someone. Italian ~accusare~ and Spanish ~acusar~ are direct cognates. The same ~causa~ gives ~cause~ and ~excuser~.
en.entradmirer: Formed from ~admirer~ with the prefix ~entr-~ (the form of ~entre-~ before a vowel), which marks reciprocal action: people who ~s'entradmirent~ admire one another. The base ~admirer~, attested from 1360, comes from Latin ~admirārī~, built from ~ad-~ (“toward”) and ~mirārī~ (“to wonder at”). Italian ~ammirare~ and Spanish ~admirar~ are its relatives.
en.entraider: Formed in the Middle Ages from ~aider~ (“to help”) and the prefix ~entre-~ (“between”), which marks reciprocal action: helping one another. The verb is used mostly in its pronominal form, and the noun ~entraide~ follows the same pattern. ~Entre-~ comes from Latin ~inter~; ~aider~ comes from Old French ~aidier~, from Latin ~adiūtāre~ (“to help”), a frequentative of ~adiuvāre~. Italian ~aiutare~ and Spanish ~ayudar~ descend from the same Latin verb.
en.entrapercevoir: Formed in French from ~apercevoir~ with the prefix ~entr-~, an elided form of ~entre-~ (written ~entr'apercevoir~ in older French). The prefix goes back to Latin ~inter~ (“between”) and often marks a partial or half-completed action, so “to glimpse” is to perceive only in part. The base ~apercevoir~ comes from ~percevoir~, which continues Latin ~percipere~ (~per-~ + ~capere~, “to seize”). English ~perceive~ shares that source.
en.entraver:
French has two verbs spelled ~entraver~, and the sources hedge on the first. The common one, “to hobble, to hinder,” is explained in two ways. It may be borrowed from Old Occitan ~entravar~ (“to put a beam on”), from ~trau~ (“beam”), itself from Latin ~trabs~, accusative ~trabem~ (“beam”). Or it may have been built in French from ~en-~ and Old French ~tref~ (“beam”), which has the same Latin source. The two accounts agree that a beam lies at the root of the word. They differ only on whether French took the verb ready-made from Occitan or assembled it from its own parts, and the evidence does not choose between them. That is why the origin of this first ~entraver~ is best told as a possibility rather than a certainty.

The second ~entraver~ is a different word. It descends from Old French ~enterver~ (“to understand”), which goes back to Latin ~interrogāre~ (“to ask, to question”). It is therefore a doublet of ~interroger~, since both go back to the same Latin verb by different routes. English Wiktionary adds that the form of ~enterver~ was influenced by the first ~entraver~, which is why the two verbs now look identical. A verb for blocking movement and a verb for understanding a question thus share one spelling, partly as a result of that influence. Its Old French ancestor already meant “to understand,” a sense that comes from the Latin question and not from beams. For this second verb the hedge falls away, because the evidence traces it plainly to Latin.
en.entraîner:
From Old French ~traîner~ (~traïner~, “to drag, to trail”), prefixed with ~en-~ (from Latin ~in-~). The base verb descends from Vulgar Latin *~traginare~, a derivative of *~tragere~, itself reshaped from Classical Latin ~trahere~ (“to pull, to draw, to drag”). The deeper origin of ~trahere~ is uncertain — perhaps a Proto-Indo-European *~dʰregʰ-~ — but its past participle ~tractus~ seeded an enormous Latin and English family. Cognate descendants of the same base appear in Italian ~trainare~ and Spanish ~entrenar~ (“to train”).

The literal sense was physical: to drag something along behind oneself, as a current ~entraîne~ a swimmer or a horse drags a cart. From “to pull along” grew the figurative “to lead, to carry away, to bring about as a consequence,” and then the modern athletic sense “to train, to coach” — to repeatedly put someone through their paces, drawing them toward fitness. English borrowed this last sense as ~train~. The shared root ~trahere~ / ~tractus~ underlies a wealth of French words, among them ~traire~ (“to milk”), ~trait~, ~tracter~, ~traction~, ~abstrait~, ~extraire~, and ~portrait~ — all turning on the idea of drawing or pulling.
en.entre-déchirer: Formed from ~déchirer~ (“to tear”) with the prefix ~entre-~, which marks reciprocal action: usually as a pronominal verb, to tear one another apart, in a fight or figuratively. This hyphenated type is a literary or rhetorical formation. The base ~déchirer~ is a Germanic loan: Old French ~escirer~ came from Frankish *~skeran~ (“to shear, cut”), a cousin of English ~shear~ and German ~scheren~, and the prefix ~es-~ was later replaced by ~dé-~.
en.entre-détruire: Formed from ~détruire~ with the prefix ~entre-~, which here marks a reciprocal action: “to destroy each other.” The prefix comes from Latin ~inter~ (“between”), and hyphenated coinages like this one are literary. The base ~détruire~ comes from Old French ~destruire~, from Latin ~destruere~, built on ~de-~ and ~struere~ (“to pile up, to build”). So ~entre-détruire~ literally describes people, or forces, tearing down one another's work.
en.entre-dévorer: Formed from the prefix ~entre-~ and the verb ~dévorer~ (“to devour”), in the reciprocal sense: to devour one another. The prefix goes back to Old French ~entre-~, from Latin ~inter~ (“between”), and in verbs it often marks an action shared between two parties, as in ~s'entre-tuer~. The base ~dévorer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~dēvorāre~, built from ~dē-~ (“down, completely”) and ~vorāre~ (“to swallow”). The hyphenated verb is a literary and rhetorical coinage, used almost always in its pronominal form for rivals, factions or creatures that destroy each other.
en.entre-manger: Formed from ~manger~ (“to eat”) with the prefix ~entre-~, in its reciprocal sense: ~s'entre-manger~ means “to eat one another,” each devouring the other. The prefix comes from Latin ~inter~ (“between”). The base ~manger~ descends from Old French ~mangier~ and Late Latin ~manducāre~ (“to chew, to eat”), a verb built on ~manducus~ (“glutton”), itself from ~mandere~ (“to chew”). The same Latin verb gave Italian ~mangiare~. The compound is a literary coinage, rare outside figurative use, such as peoples or factions who devour each other.
en.entre-nuire: Formed from ~nuire~ with the prefix ~entre-~, which gives a reciprocal sense: “to harm each other.” ~Nuire~ comes from Old French ~nuisir~ (about 1119), reshaped by about 1160, from Vulgar Latin *~nocĕre~, an altered form of Latin ~nocēre~ (“to harm”). The prefix ~entre-~ comes from Old French ~entre-~, from Latin ~inter~ (“between”), and the hyphen is the traditional spelling.
en.entre-regarder: Formed from the prefix ~entre-~ and ~regarder~ (“to look at”), in the reciprocal sense: two people looking at each other, as in ~s'entre-regarder~. The prefix comes from Old French ~entre-~, from Latin ~inter~ (“between”). The base ~regarder~ comes from Old French ~regarder~, formed from ~garder~ (“to guard, to watch over”) with ~re-~. ~Garder~ in turn comes from Late Latin *~wardāre~, borrowed from Frankish *~wardōn~ (“to keep watch”), so the verb for looking has a Germanic ancestor. English ~ward~ and ~guard~ are related words.
en.entre-tuer: ~Entre-tuer~ is the verb ~tuer~ with the prefix ~entre-~, joined by a hyphen in the traditional spelling before 1990. The prefix comes from Old French ~entre-~, from Latin ~inter~ (“between”), and gives a reciprocal sense, so the verb, usually pronominal as in ~s'entre-tuer~, means “to kill one another.” As for the base, the app's entry for ~tuer~ traces it to Old French ~tuer~ and Late Latin ~tūtāre~ (“to put out a fire”), a sense that slid from extinguishing to killing.
en.entre-égorger: A French formation: the reciprocal prefix ~entre-~ (“one another”), as in ~s'entre-tuer~ and ~s'entre-déchirer~, added to ~égorger~ and used pronominally, so ~s'entre-égorger~ means “to cut one another's throats.” The base ~égorger~ is attested around 1450 and is built from ~é-~ (from Latin ~ex-~, “out”) and ~gorge~ (“throat”). ~Gorge~ comes from popular Latin ~gurga~, a variant of ~gurges~ (“whirlpool, gulf”), the throat being named for the gaping hole it resembles. The verb began literal, to slit a throat, and widened to slaughter and massacre.
en.entrebâiller: Formed from the prefix ~entre-~ (from Latin ~inter~, “between”) and ~bâiller~, with ~entre-~ giving the sense of partial action, so “to open halfway.” ~Bâiller~ comes from Old French ~baaillier~, inherited from a late Latin verb; French Wiktionary gives popular Latin ~bataclare~, English Wiktionary Early Medieval Latin ~bataculāre~ (“to yawn”). Besides “to yawn,” ~bâiller~ can mean “to be ajar,” of a door or a collar, and ~entrebâiller~ means “to half-open, to leave ajar.” The circumflex marks the vanished ~a~ of ~baaillier~.
en.entrechoquer: Formed from ~choquer~ with the prefix ~entre-~ (“between”), from Latin ~inter~, giving the sense of two things striking each other: “to knock together, to clink.” The fused spelling is the one of the 1990 spelling rectifications, but French Wiktionary notes it was in use long before and appears in earlier Académie dictionaries. The base ~choquer~ is attested from the 13th century in Picard ~chuquier~, and its origin is obscure, perhaps Germanic according to the TLFi.
en.entrecouper: ~Entrecouper~ is formed from ~couper~ and the prefix ~entre-~, in its “in between” sense, hence “to interrupt, to intersperse.” ~Entre-~ comes from Old French ~entre-~, from Latin ~inter~ (“between”). ~Couper~ comes from Old French ~colper~, from the noun ~colp~ (“blow”), which goes back through Vulgar Latin ~colpus~ and Late Latin ~colaphus~ to Greek ~kólaphos~ (“a blow on the cheek”).
en.entrecroiser: ~Entrecroiser~ is ~croiser~ with the prefix ~entre-~, which comes from Old French ~entre-~ and Latin ~inter~ (“between”). It gives the sense “to cross one another,” as lines, threads or paths do. The base ~croiser~ is itself a verb built on ~croix~, which descends from Latin ~crux~ (“stake, cross”). English ~cross~ is a distant relative of that Latin word, by way of Old Norse and Old Irish.
en.entredéchirer: ~Entredéchirer~ is formed from ~déchirer~ (“to tear”) and the prefix ~entre-~, which here marks reciprocal action: to tear one another to pieces, usually in the pronominal form. The prefix comes from Old French ~entre-~, from Latin ~inter~ (“between”), and hyphenated reciprocal verbs of this type are literary or rhetorical coinages. The base ~déchirer~ is Germanic. It comes from Old French ~escirer~, itself from Frankish *~skeran~ (“to shear, cut”), cognate with English ~shear~ and German ~scheren~. A word for shearing wool thus ended up describing people ripping each other apart.
en.entredétruire: ~Entredétruire~ is formed from ~détruire~ with the prefix ~entre-~, which here marks reciprocity: “to destroy one another.” It is used mostly as the reflexive ~s'entredétruire~. The form is written as one word, with the prefix attached, under the French spelling reform of 1990, which fused many such compounds that were previously hyphenated.
en.entredévorer: Formed from ~dévorer~ with the prefix ~entre-~, which here carries the sense “between, one another,” so that the verb is used of beings that devour each other. French Wiktionary dates the formation to 1990. The base ~dévorer~ goes back to Latin ~dēvorāre~, built from ~dē-~ and ~vorāre~ (“to swallow”), an analysis that is standard background. The prefix ~entre-~ comes from Latin ~inter~ (“between”). The pronominal form ~s'entredévorer~ is the natural one, as in ~s'entre-tuer~, to kill each other.
en.entrelacer: Formed from the prefix ~entre-~ (“between,” from Latin ~inter~) and ~lacer~. The base comes from Old French ~lacier~, from Latin ~laqueāre~ (“to bind, to entwine”), built on ~laqueus~ (“noose, snare”), and the same Latin source gave English ~lace~. ~Entrelacer~ means to interlace: to weave or twist things together so that they pass over and under one another, whether threads, branches or, figuratively, lives. Its relatives include ~enlacer~, ~lacet~ and ~délacer~.
en.entrelarder: ~Entrelarder~ is formed from ~larder~ with the prefix ~entre-~ (“between”), from Latin ~inter~. English Wiktionary gives it as inherited from Middle French and Old French ~entrelarder~ (“to thrust into the flesh,” 1176-1181), but the formation is transparent: to lard between, that is, to stud meat with strips of fat. ~Larder~ comes from ~lard~, inherited from Old French and Latin ~lārdum~ (“bacon fat”). The figurative sense, “to intersperse,” as in a text studded with quotations or insults, follows from the image of fat slipped between the fibers of the meat.
en.entremanger: Formed from ~manger~ with the prefix ~entre-~, which expresses reciprocal action: “to eat one another.” The base ~manger~ comes from Old French ~mangier~, from Late Latin ~manducare~ (“to chew, to eat”), a derivative of Latin ~mandere~ (“to chew”). The prefix ~entre-~ comes from Old French ~entre-~, from Latin ~inter~ (“between”), and appears in verbs such as ~s’entraider~ and ~s’entretuer~. The verb is almost always pronominal, as in ~s’entremanger~.
en.entremettre: ~Entremettre~ is analysed as the prefix ~entre-~ plus the verb ~mettre~, and French Wiktionary points to Latin ~intromittere~ (“to send in”) as a model. The prefix ~entre-~ comes from Latin ~inter~ (“between”), here in its sense of mediation, so the verb means to put or insert between. It survives mostly in the reflexive ~s'entremettre~, “to intervene, to mediate.” The base ~mettre~ comes from Latin ~mittere~ (“to send”), whose meaning drifted to “put” in Vulgar Latin.
en.entremêler: ~Entremêler~ is formed from the prefix ~entre-~ and the verb ~mêler~. The prefix comes from Old French ~entre-~, from Latin ~inter~ (“between”), and here has the sense of “in between, among.” The base ~mêler~ comes from Old French ~mesler~, from Vulgar Latin *~misculare~, a derivative of Latin ~miscere~ (“to mix”); the circumflex stands for the lost s. The verb means to mix things so that they stay intertwined, to interweave.
en.entrenuire: Formed from ~nuire~ (“to harm”) with the prefix ~entre-~, which gives a reciprocal sense, as in ~s'entre-tuer~ or ~s'entraider~: in its pronominal use, to ~entrenuire~ is to harm one another. Wiktionnaire treats it as a spelling of ~s'entre-nuire~. The base ~nuire~ comes from Old French ~nuisir~, from Vulgar Latin *~nocĕre~, an altered form of Latin ~nocēre~ (“to harm”). That Latin verb is kin to ~nex~ (“violent death”), so harming is, at the root, setting someone on the way to perishing.
en.entreposer: Formed from ~poser~ and the prefix ~entre-~, from Old French ~entre-~ and Latin ~inter~ (“between”). It means to put goods into a depot or warehouse, and it is the source of the noun ~entrepôt~ (“warehouse, storage depot”), which English also borrowed. The prefix has no clearly compositional force here, as in many old words with ~entre-~, so the verb is best read as a lexicalized unit. The base ~poser~ goes back to Late Latin ~pausare~ (“to halt, to rest”), which in speech took over the sense “to put, to set down” from Latin ~ponere~.
en.entreprendre:
Formed in Old French from the prefix ~entre-~ (“between, among”), from Latin ~inter~, and the verb ~prendre~ (“to take”). ~Prendre~ descends from Latin ~prehendere~ (“to grasp, seize”), itself ~prae-~ (“before”) plus a root ~-hendere~ from PIE *~gʰed-~ (“to seize, take”). Through that root it is cognate with English ~get~ and ~forget~ and with Greek ~khandánō~ (“to hold, contain”). The compound is often read as a calque of the Frankish *~underneman~ (literally “to take among / take under”), the same notion that English keeps in ~undertake~ — to take a task upon oneself.

The image is of reaching in among possibilities and seizing one — taking something on. French let ~entreprendre~ mean to begin a venture, a project, even an effort against someone (~entreprendre quelqu'un~). From it grew the powerhouse noun ~entreprise~ (“undertaking, business firm”) and the agent ~entrepreneur~, which English then borrowed back wholesale for the figure who launches ventures. From the ~prehendere~ root French also keeps ~prendre~, ~apprendre~ (“to take to oneself,” hence “to learn”), ~comprendre~ (“to take together,” hence “to understand”), ~surprendre~, and ~prison~ — a whole web of taking, learning, and grasping.
en.entrer:
From Old French ~entrer~, from Latin ~intrāre~ (“to enter, to go inside”), a denominal verb from ~intrā~ (“within, inside”). ~intrā~ goes back through *~interus~ (“inner,” the source also of ~interior~) to the Proto-Indo-European *~h₁énteros~ (“inner, what is inside”), itself from *~h₁én~ (“in”) — the same little particle behind English ~in~ and Latin ~in~. The Romance cousins all line up: Italian ~entrare~, Spanish ~entrar~, Portuguese ~entrar~.

The verb has stayed close to its plain spatial sense — “to go in” — for two thousand years, which is part of why it remains one of the most common verbs in French. Its figurative reach grew, though: one can ~entrer~ a profession, ~entrer~ data into a machine, or ~entrer~ into a discussion. The ~intrā-~ / ~inter-~ pair seeded a large family in French: the literal ~entrée~ (“entrance,” and the dish that “enters” a meal), ~rentrer~ (“to re-enter, to go back home”), ~entrer~'s causative ~introduire~ (“to lead in”), and the cluster ~intérieur~, ~interne~, ~intime~ — every one of them, at bottom, about being or going “inside.”
en.entreregarder: Formed from ~regarder~ with the prefix ~entre-~, which comes from Old French ~entre-~, from Latin ~inter~ (“between”). The result means “to look at each other”. The base ~regarder~ is from Old French ~regarder~, itself ~re-~ + ~garder~. ~Garder~ goes back through Late Latin *~wardāre~ to Frankish *~wardōn~ (“to keep watch”), a Germanic root shared with English ~ward~ and ~guard~. The sense moved from “to keep, watch over” toward “to look at”.
en.entretailler: Formed from ~tailler~ with the prefix ~entre-~, which marks an action done to each other. In veterinary use it describes a horse that knocks its legs together as it walks, so that they cut into one another. No dictionary gives a formal etymology, so this reading comes from the parts. ~Tailler~ comes from Old French ~talier~, from Late Latin ~taliare~ (“to cut”), derived from Latin ~talea~ (“a cutting, slip”).
en.entretenir:
A compound coined in Old French (12th century) from ~entre~ (“between, mutually”) and ~tenir~ (“to hold”), literally “to hold between” or “to hold together.” ~Entre~ comes from Latin ~inter~ (“between”), and ~tenir~ from Latin ~tenere~ (“to hold, to keep”), which goes back through Proto-Italic to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). That root also yielded Ancient Greek ~teínō~ (“I stretch”), Sanskrit ~tanóti~, and English ~thin~ — holding conceived as keeping something taut.

The earliest sense was reciprocal: parties who ~entretenir~ one another held together, supported each other. From “holding together” the verb branched in two directions. One leads to material upkeep — to ~entretenir~ a house, a garden, or a car is to keep it in good condition by sustained care; ~entretien~ is its noun, “maintenance.” The other leads to the social and conversational: to ~entretenir~ someone is to keep them in talk, hence ~s'entretenir avec~ (“to converse with”) and ~entretien~ in the sense of “interview.” The same root *~ten-~ underlies a sprawling French family — ~tenir~, ~retenir~, ~contenir~, ~maintenir~, ~tendre~, ~tension~ — all turning on holding, stretching, and keeping.
en.entretoiser: Formed from ~entretoise~ with the verb ending ~-er~, an analysis that French and English Wiktionary share. The noun ~entretoise~ (“brace, crosspiece”) is a compound of ~entre~ (“between”) and ~toise~. The verb means to fix an ~entretoise~ between two beams, so as to hold them apart or steady.
en.entretuer: ~Entretuer~ is formed from the verb ~tuer~ (“to kill”) and the prefix ~entre-~ (“between”, from Latin ~inter~), in the reciprocal sense: in the pronominal form ~s'entretuer~, people kill each other. It was traditionally written with a hyphen, and the 1990 spelling reform fused the prefix to the verb. The base ~tuer~ comes from Old French ~tuer~ (“to strike, stun, extinguish”), from Late Latin ~tūtāre~ (“to put out a fire”), an altered form of ~tūtāri~, a frequentative of ~tuērī~ (“to protect”). A verb of protection thus became the common French word for killing.
en.entrevoir: French Wiktionary derives ~entrevoir~ from ~voir~ with the prefix ~entre-~, in the sense of seeing something only partly or briefly, a “glimpse”. English Wiktionary instead treats it as inherited from Vulgar Latin *~intervidēre~, built on ~inter~ (“between”) and ~vidēre~ (“to see”). Either way, the base verb is ~voir~, from Latin ~vidēre~, and the idea is the same: seeing between things or at a half-distance. The sense then extended to foresee dimly, as one glimpses a possibility.
en.entrevoûter: Formed from the noun ~entrevous~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The origin of ~entrevous~ is uncertain, and the sources offer two accounts. Littré thought it was formed from ~entre~ and ~voussoir~ or ~voûte~, despite its irregular shape. The Quillet dictionary suggested that it might instead be a variant of ~entrevaus~, the plural of ~entreval~, which would be a rendering of Latin ~intervallum~ (“interval”). In either case the verb is a trade term for filling the spaces of a structure, here with plaster.
en.entrouvrir: ~Entrouvrir~ is built on ~ouvrir~ (“to open”) with the prefix ~entr-~, the form that ~entre-~ takes before a vowel; the prefix comes from Old French ~entre-~ and Latin ~inter~ (“between”). Here it marks a partial action, so the verb means “to half-open” or “to leave ajar”. The base ~ouvrir~ goes back to Latin ~aperīre~ through a Vulgar Latin *~operīre~, reshaped on its opposite ~cooperīre~ (“to cover”). Italian ~aprire~ and Spanish ~abrir~ are its cousins.
en.entrégorger: Formed from ~égorger~ with the prefix ~entre-~, which marks reciprocal action: people who ~s'entrégorgent~ cut one another's throats. The base ~égorger~ is a French formation attested around 1450, from the prefix ~é-~ (“out”) and the noun ~gorge~ (“throat”), which goes back to popular Latin ~gurga~. Like other verbs in ~entre-~ of this kind, it is a literary coinage, used for violent mutual action.
en.entuber: Formed in French from the noun ~tube~ with the prefix ~en-~ and the ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Latin ~tubus~ (“tube, pipe”). The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”) and ~-er~ from Latin ~-are~. The verb is slang and means “to dupe, to swindle,” a figurative use of a word whose basic sense is to put something into a tube.
en.enténébrer: ~Enténébrer~ (“to plunge into darkness”) is formed from ~ténèbres~ (“darkness”) with the prefix ~en-~, which here means “to put into” or “to provide with”. The noun ~ténèbres~ is a borrowing of Latin ~tenebrae~, which had the same meaning and was plural in form. The verb is literary: it is used for shadows that gather over a place, and figuratively for a mind or a mood that darkens.
en.entériner:
From Old French ~enterin~ (“entire, whole”), which French Wiktionary derives from a Latin form *~integrīnus~, built on ~integer~ (“whole”). The same Latin word reached French by the inherited route as ~entier~, so ~entériner~ and ~entier~ are close relatives. Latin ~integer~ is ~in-~ (“not”) plus the root of ~tangere~ (“to touch”), meaning literally “untouched”, hence intact and complete. English holds the same word twice: ~entire~ came through Old French ~entier~, and ~integer~ was taken straight from the Latin.

So ~entériner~ means, properly, “to make whole”. The sense is legal: to give an act or decision its full and definitive validity, hence to ratify or confirm. Today it often describes accepting a done deal, as in ~entériner une décision~. The Latin root is behind a learned family in French: ~intègre~ (“upright, of unbroken integrity”), ~intégral~, and ~intégrer~, which adds a piece to a whole. Its popular cousin ~entier~ kept the old everyday form.
en.entêter: ~Entêter~ is a parasynthetic verb: the prefix ~en-~ (“in, into”), the noun ~tête~ (“head”) and the verb ending ~-er~ were added together. Literally it is something like “to put into the head,” and the sense developed toward being stubborn or obstinate. The noun ~tête~ comes from Old French ~teste~, from Latin ~testa~ (“pot, jug, brick”), with a stage as “skull” in popular speech. It displaced the older French ~chef~, from Latin ~caput~, whose original sense survives mostly in set expressions.
en.envahir:
From Latin ~invadere~ (“to go into, attack, invade”), which compounds the prefix ~in-~ (“into”) with the verb ~vadere~ (“to go, advance, rush”). ~vadere~ descends from Proto-Italic *~wāðō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~weh₂dʰ-~ (“to advance, go”). Through that root the Latin verb is cognate with English ~wade~ (from Old English ~wadan~), which kept the older sense of forging ahead on foot, especially through water.

The core image is aggressive forward motion — to ~vadere~ is to stride or rush, and to ~invadere~ is to rush in upon. French inherited it as a verb of overrunning: an army ~envahit~ a country, but so do weeds, water, doubt, or a smell that fills a room. From ~vadere~ and its compounds French also draws ~évader~ (“to escape,” to rush out) and ~s'évanouir~, while the noun side gives ~invasion~ and ~envahisseur~ (“invader”). The same restless “going” sits beneath them all.
en.envaser: ~Envaser~ (“to silt up”) is a parasynthetic verb, formed from the prefix ~en-~, the noun ~vase~ (“mud, silt”) and the verb ending ~-er~. This ~vase~ is a Germanic word. It came through Middle French from Middle Dutch ~wase~ (“mud, silt”), from Proto-Germanic *~wasô~ (“moisture, ground”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~wes-~ (“moist, wet”). It is unrelated to the ~vase~ that means a vessel, from Latin ~vās~. The verb means “to put or get into the mud,” hence to clog with silt.
en.envelopper:
From Old French ~envoloper~ (also ~anveloper~), by way of Middle French ~enveloper~. French Wiktionary takes it as probably formed from ~veloper~ with the prefix ~en-~, while noting that ~envoloper~ is attested before ~veloper~. English Wiktionary instead derives it from ~en-~ plus Old French ~voluper~ (“to wrap up”), compare Italian ~-viluppare~, from a Vulgar Latin *~vlopp-~. That in turn is traced to Proto-Germanic *~wrappaną~ or *~wlappaną~ (“to wrap, to roll up”), and ultimately to a Proto-Indo-European root *~werb-~ (“to turn, to bend”). The deeper chain is thus a proposal, not a certainty. English ~wrap~ and ~lap~ (“to fold”) are kin to this Germanic stock.

The core sense is to wrap something so that it is entirely covered. The same root gave ~développer~ (originally to unwrap), ~enveloppe~ and, in English, ~envelop~ and ~envelope~. Montaigne uses the verb in the sixteenth century, writing of a man “wrapped and bundled up” whose worth is that of the sheath and not of the sword.
en.envenimer: Formed from ~venin~ with the prefix ~en-~ and the ending ~-er~, and inherited from Old French ~envenimer~. To envenom is to put venom into something, and the verb is also used figuratively for making a quarrel or a wound worse. The base ~venin~ comes from Old French ~venim~, from Vulgar Latin *~venīmen~, from early medieval Latin ~venīnum~, from Classical Latin ~venēnum~ (“poison”), which also gave Italian ~veleno~ and Spanish ~veneno~.
en.enverguer:
~Enverguer~ (“to bend a sail to its yard”) is borrowed from Occitan ~envergar~, which has the same meaning. It is therefore not an heir of Latin through Old French but a sailor's word taken from the southern Romance language. Its stem is the one found in French ~vergue~, the yard itself, a word that goes back to Latin ~virga~ (“rod, switch”).

The ~vergue~ is the horizontal spar from which a sail hangs, and ~enverguer~ belongs to this vocabulary of rigging. The noun ~envergure~ comes from the same family. It denotes the breadth of a sail along its yard, the wingspan of a bird or an aircraft, and, figuratively, the scope or stature of a person or a project, as in ~un esprit de grande envergure~. Latin ~virga~ also lies behind ~verge~ and, through its diminutive ~virgula~, behind ~virgule~ (“comma”). Today the verb is a technical sailing term, while the noun is far more common in everyday French.
en.envider: Formed from the prefix ~en-~ and the stem of ~dévider~, by antonymy. Where ~dévider~ unwinds thread from a reel, ~envider~ winds it on, here onto a spindle or bobbin. The prefix ~en-~ is the locative one, “in, onto,” from Latin ~in-~, and it stands in opposition to the ~dé-~ of ~dévider~, which reverses the action. The verb belongs to the vocabulary of spinning and weaving.
en.envier: Formed in French from ~envie~ + ~-er~, “to feel envy toward.” The noun ~envie~ comes from Latin ~invidia~ (“envy, ill will”), itself from ~invidēre~, “to look at with hostility”, literally to look upon someone (~in-~ + ~vidēre~, “to see”). French Wiktionary also gives a separate account that ties an ~envier~ to Latin ~invitāre~ (“to invite”), which looks like a different, homonymous verb and not the one meaning “to envy.” English ~envy~ comes from the same Latin noun, by way of Old French.
en.environner: ~Environner~ is formed from ~environ~ with the ending ~-er~, and means “to surround”. ~Environ~ comes from Old French ~environ~ (“around”), made of ~en~ (“in”) and ~viron~ (“circle, turn”). ~Viron~ belongs to ~virer~ (“to turn, to veer”), a verb still used in modern French.
en.envisager:
From ~en-~ + ~visage~ (“face”) + ~-er~, attested from the sixteenth century. The noun ~visage~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~visaticum~, a derivative of Latin ~visus~ (“sight, appearance”), the past participle of ~vidēre~ (“to see”), from Proto-Indo-European *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”). The verb thus literally meant “to bring before one's face,” “to look someone in the face.” Through the same root *~weyd-~ it is cognate with English ~vision~ and ~view~, and, more distantly, with English ~wit~ and ~wise~ and Greek ~idéā~.

The development is a tidy metaphor. To ~envisager~ someone was first to gaze at their ~visage~; from “having a face before one's eyes” the verb drifted to the mental sense of “having something in view,” then to “to contemplate, to consider” a possibility — to picture it inwardly as one would a face. English borrowed the word as ~envisage~ with this same abstract meaning. The root *~weyd-~ seeded a large French family, including ~vision~, ~visible~, ~viser~, ~aviser~, ~prévoir~, and ~évident~, all of which turn, one way or another, on the act of seeing.
en.envoiler: Formed from the prefix ~en-~ and the word ~voile~ (the French source cites the noun, the English one the verb ~voiler~), with the sense of warping or bending. ~Voile~ comes from Latin ~vēlum~ (“sail, cloth”) through Old French; in Vulgar Latin the plural ~vēla~ was reanalyzed as a feminine singular, which explains the feminine ~voile~ for a sail. The prefix ~en-~ comes from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”), here building a verb meaning to put into a state.
en.envoler: A compound of the adverb ~en~ (“away, from there”) and ~voler~ (“to fly”), used reflexively: ~s'envoler~ is literally “to fly away.” The adverb ~en~ goes back to Latin ~inde~ (“from there”), and ~voler~ comes from Latin ~volāre~ (“to fly”). The verb is not related to Latin ~involāre~, despite the similar look. From the flight of a bird or a plane, the sense widened to whatever vanishes as if on wings: hopes, time, a stolen purse.
en.envoyer:
From Latin ~inviāre~ (“to send on a journey, to travel over”), ~in-~ (“in, onto”) + ~via~ (“road, way”). ~Via~ comes from Proto-Italic *~wijā~; the PIE source is debated, but it is plausibly a doublet of English ~way~, both descending from a root for travelling or pursuing. To send someone was, literally, to “put them on the road.” Italian ~inviare~ and Spanish ~enviar~ are direct cognates, and ~via~ itself survives unchanged as the English and international preposition ~via~ (“by way of”).

The Latin sense “to set on the way” narrowed in French to “to dispatch, to send” — a letter, a messenger, a signal. A curious wrinkle lies in the conjugation: the future and conditional stems (~enverrai~, ~enverrais~) do not follow the verb's own pattern but were reshaped in the 18th century by analogy with ~voir~ (“to see”), an unrelated verb that merely sounded similar — so ~envoyer~ borrows the future of a stranger. The everyday ~envoyer chercher~ means “to send for,” and the noun ~envoi~ is the act or the parcel sent; the past participle gives the ~envoyé~ (“envoy, dispatched agent”), borrowed into English as ~envoy~. The ~via~ root also yields French ~voie~ (“way, lane”), ~voyage~, ~dévoyer~ (“to lead astray”), ~convoyer~ (“to convey, to escort”), and ~renvoyer~ (“to send back”).
en.envoûter:
French ~envoûter~ is formed from the prefix ~en-~, Old French ~volt~ (also spelled ~vout~, “face, features”) and the verb ending ~-er~. Old French ~volt~ comes from Latin ~vultus~ (“face”), which also lies behind Italian ~volto~ (“face”). French Wiktionary gives the shorter account, a derivative of ~volt~, while English Wiktionary spells out the prefix and the suffix.

English Wiktionary offers an explanation of the sense: some forms of folk magic were practiced with wax or other effigies of the victim's face, so that to bewitch someone was, literally, to work on their face. This is that source's account only, and French Wiktionary does not repeat it, so it should be read as a plausible explanation and not as an established fact.
en.ergoter: The sources offer two accounts. One makes ~ergoter~ a verb built on ~ergot~, the sharp spur on a cock's leg that serves in fighting, with the ending ~-er~. ~Ergot~ is ~argot~ in Old French, perhaps from a root *~arg-~ for pointed things, or from Latin ~argūtus~ (“sharp”). The other account traces the verb to the Latin particle ~ergo~ (“therefore”), which scholastic doctors used constantly, often with little substance. Both fit the modern sense: ~ergoter~ is “to quibble, to cavil,” and in gardening “to prune.”
en.errer:
From Old French ~errer~, from Latin ~errāre~ (“to wander, to stray”). The Latin verb lived on in Italian ~errare~ and Spanish ~errar~, and English ~err~ is a learned borrowing of the same word. Latin ~errāre~ already carried two ideas at once: to roam physically and to stray from the truth. The second idea fed the noun ~erreur~ and learned adjectives such as ~erroné~, while ~aberrant~ comes from Latin ~aberrāre~ (“to stray away”).

The history is tangled, because Old French also had an ~errer~ meaning “to travel, to ride,” as in the ~chevalier errant~, the knight-errant who rode from adventure to adventure. According to Wartburg, that sense of going to and fro comes from Latin ~iterāre~, while the sense of making a mistake comes from ~errāre~. The two verbs would then have merged into a single French form. In modern French ~errer~ means only to wander, to drift without a goal, of a person, a gaze or a ghost. The idea of a mistake has passed to ~se tromper~ and survives in ~erreur~ and its learned family. The image of aimless roaming, though, is the one the knight-errant left behind.
en.esbigner:
The origin of ~esbigner~ is uncertain, and French Wiktionary gives two competing accounts. One derives it from Italian slang ~svignare~ (“to decamp”, literally “to leave the vine”), from ~vigna~ (“vineyard”), though the shift from ~v~ to ~b~ is acknowledged to be a difficulty. The other derives it from Occitan ~s'esbinhar~ (“to slip away, to make oneself scarce”), formed from ~binhar~ (“to look”) with the prefix ~es-~, the equivalent of ~ex-~.

Both proposals agree on the sense: to leave quickly and discreetly, to slip away. The verb belongs to the familiar register, and the Italian account places it in slang. Which route is right is not settled. The Italian source word ~vigna~ goes back to Latin ~vīnea~, which also gives French ~vigne~, so if that account holds, the verb would be a distant relative of ~vigne~ and ~vin~. The Occitan account links it instead to the French verb ~bigner~ (“to look”).
en.esbroufer: A verb made from the noun ~esbroufe~ (“swagger, bluster”) with the ending ~-er~, meaning to show off or to bluff. The noun comes from Occitan ~esbroufo~ or ~esbrofa~ (“to snort, to shake oneself”), itself from Italian ~sbruffare~ (“to spray, to splash”). The image is of a noisy burst of spray, which became a figure for loud, impressive behavior.
en.escalader: ~Escalader~ is a verb made from the noun ~escalade~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, in the sense “to carry out an escalade.” The noun is traced by French Wiktionary to Occitan ~escalada~, the feminine past participle of ~escalar~ (“to climb”), literally “to go up by a ladder.” English Wiktionary instead derives ~escalade~ from Italian ~scalata~, so the route of the noun is not settled between the two sources. Both point to the idea of a ladder, which is how a wall was once scaled. The sources supplied for the verb itself give no date of first use.
en.escamoter: The origin of ~escamoter~ is uncertain, and the two Wiktionaries give two accounts. The first, preferred as “probably,” derives it from an old Occitan ~escamotar~ or ~escambotar~, from ~escamar~ (“to unravel, to scale”), from Latin ~squāma~ (“fish scale”); Italian ~squamare~ (“to scale”) is compared. The alternative derives it from Spanish ~escamotar~, perhaps from Latin ~excommutare~, formed from ~ex~ (“out”) and ~commutare~ (“to exchange”). The sources do not settle the matter.
en.escher: Formed from the noun ~esche~ (“bait”) plus the verb ending ~-er~: to ~escher~ is to put bait on a hook. The noun comes from Latin ~esca~ (“food,” then “bait”). French Wiktionary adds that ~esche~ first named the small wood used to start a fire and recovered its Latin sense of bait around the thirteenth century. The suffix ~-er~ makes a verb meaning “provide with N,” so a hook ~eschée~ is simply one fitted with its bait.
en.esclaffer: French ~esclaffer~ is a borrowing from Occitan ~esclafar~. French Wiktionary notes that its first user in French was Rabelais, which places the word in the sixteenth century. It reached the language, then, not through the long inheritance from Latin that shaped most French verbs but as a loan from the south of France, where Occitan was spoken. In modern French the verb is nearly always pronominal: ~s'esclaffer~ means to burst out laughing, loudly and suddenly.
en.esclavager: Formed in French from the noun ~esclavage~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, so the verb means “to enslave.” The noun ~esclavage~ is a derivative of ~esclave~ with the suffix ~-age~. The word ~esclave~ comes from Latin ~sclavus~ (“Slav”), because in the early Middle Ages many slaves were Slavs, and they left their name to slaves and to slavery. The ending ~-er~ is the ordinary first-conjugation ending, from Latin ~-are~.
en.escompter: The evidence available ties ~escompter~ to ~compter~ (“to count”) and to the noun ~escompte~ (“discount”), without spelling out the intermediate steps, so only the outline can be given with confidence. ~Compter~ comes from Latin ~computāre~ (“to calculate”). The verb first belongs to banking: to ~escompter~ a bill is to pay its holder now, less a deduction for the time still to run. From that financial sense it passed into everyday French, where ~escompter~ means to count on something in advance, to expect it, as in ~escompter un succès~.
en.escorter: From ~escorte~ (“escort”) plus the verb ending ~-er~, which turns a noun into a verb. The noun was borrowed from Italian ~scorta~, and both Wiktionaries also point the verb itself to Italian ~scortare~, so French may have drawn on the Italian verb and noun together. The ending ~-er~ goes back to Latin ~-are~, the first-conjugation ending that French uses for almost every new verb. The sense is “to accompany for protection”.
en.escrimer:
French Wiktionary derives ~escrimer~ from ~escrime~, while English Wiktionary gives a direct descent from Middle French ~escremir~ and Old French ~escremir~, ~escermir~ or ~eschirmir~, from Frankish *~skirmijan~, from a Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)ker-~. The two accounts fit together, because ~escrime~ is itself a reshaping of Old French ~escremie~ (“combat”), a noun built on ~escremir~ (“to fight”). That verb comes from Old Low Frankish *~skirmjan~ (“to defend, protect”), cognate with German ~schirmen~.

The modern spelling owes something to Italy. ~Escrime~ was remade on the model of Italian ~scrima~ (“the art of handling the sword”), an art that came to France from Italy, as Montaigne attests: “Nous allons apprendre en Italie à escrimer.” Today the verb is used chiefly in the sense “to struggle, to exert oneself,” as in ~s'escrimer à faire quelque chose~, while the sporting sense is carried by the noun ~escrime~ and the phrase ~faire de l'escrime~. English ~skirmish~ is, by standard etymology, a relative through the same Old French verb. French ~escrimeur~ (“fencer”) belongs to the family.
en.escroquer:
~Escroquer~ was borrowed from Italian ~scroccare~ (“to steal”). French Wiktionary derives that verb from Italian ~crocco~ (“to unhook, to scrounge”), and English Wiktionary agrees that ~crocco~ is of Germanic origin and sets it beside English ~crook~. English Wiktionary adds that, on a surface analysis, the French verb can also be read as ~escroc~ + ~-er~. Either way, the road leads back through Italy.

The noun ~escroc~ (“swindler”) was itself borrowed from Italian ~scrocco~ (“sponger”). English Wiktionary traces ~scrocco~ to an Old High German form *~scurgo~, known from ~fiurscurgo~ (“fire-maker, stoker”) and related to the verb ~scurgen~. German ~Schurke~ (“scoundrel”) and ~schüren~ (“to stoke”) are the modern reflexes it cites. The two accounts of the Germanic root, ~crocco~ on one side and ~scurgo~ on the other, are therefore not the same, and the sources do not settle between them. What is clear is the Italian intermediary and the French sense: to obtain something by trickery, to swindle.
en.espacer: Formed in French from the noun ~espace~ and the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense “to put space between things.” The noun ~espace~ comes from Old French ~espace~, borrowed from Latin ~spatium~, a word that covered a stadium, a racecourse, an extent of ground and a stretch of time. The modern verb keeps both the spatial idea, as in spacing out the letters of a word or the trees in a row, and the temporal one, as in spacing out visits or payments. The same Latin word gave English ~space~, also through French.
en.espionner: Formed from the noun ~espion~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is from Middle French *~espion~, found only in the verb ~espionner~, from Old French ~espion~ (“one assigned to observe”). It may alternatively come from Old French ~espie~ under the influence of Italian ~spione~, or be borrowed outright from ~spione~. The pronunciation of the ~s~, silent since the 13th century, was restored under the Italian influence.
en.espérer:
From Latin ~sperare~ (“to hope, to look forward to”), formed from the noun ~spes~ (“hope”). Through Proto-Italic *~spēs~, the word traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~speh₁-~ (“to prosper, to turn out well”), the same root that lies behind Latin ~prosperus~ (“favorable, thriving”), source of French ~prospérer~. Its Romance siblings are everywhere: Spanish ~esperar~, Italian ~sperare~, Portuguese ~esperar~ — though in Spanish the verb has split its labor, also meaning “to wait,” since waiting and hoping are close kin.

The core sense — to look forward to a good outcome — has held remarkably steady from Latin into French. Old French had the form ~esperer~ with an initial vowel that French later dropped in the noun, giving ~espoir~ (the everyday word) beside ~espérance~ (a loftier, more sustained hope, drawn from the present participle). The negative prefix ~dé-~ yields the dark twins ~désespérer~ and ~désespoir~, the loss of all hope. Theological French ranks ~l'espérance~ among the three theological virtues, alongside faith and charity. From the same Indo-European root of thriving come ~prospère~, ~prospérité~, and ~prospérer~ — so that to ~espérer~ and to prosper are, far back, the same impulse toward things turning out well.
en.esquicher: From Occitan ~esquichar~ (“to squeeze, to press”), according to both French and English Wiktionary. French Wiktionary refers readers to ~écacher~ for the same word. For the use in card games, Littré proposes a different origin, from Old French ~eschisser~ (“to slip, to glide”). The two accounts are therefore not settled: the Occitan origin is the one given for the general sense, and the Old French verb is offered as an alternative for the card-game term.
en.esquinter:
A borrowing from Occitan ~esquintar~, which goes back to Old Occitan ~esquintar~. The origin is not certain, but the favored account is that it comes from a Vulgar Latin verb *~exquintāre~ (“to divide into five”), built from Latin ~ex-~ (“out, apart”) and ~quintus~ (“fifth”). French Wiktionary gives the same Latin source, glossed “to cut into five”. The chain is therefore Latin to Old Occitan to Occitan to French, with the French verb arriving as a regional word from the south.

The Latin ordinal ~quintus~ belongs to the family of ~quīnque~ (“five”), which became French ~cinq~; the same ~quintus~ underlies ~quinte~ (a fifth, in music) and ~quintette~ through Italian. In French ~esquinter~ is a familiar verb meaning to damage, wreck or wear out, said of objects and of people, especially in the reflexive: ~s'esquinter~ is to wear oneself out. The sources do not say how “cutting into five” became “wrecking”, so that step stays unexplained.
en.esquisser: Borrowed from Italian ~schizzare~ (“to squirt, to splash,” and so “to sketch quickly”), the verb is attested in French in 1651, after an earlier Middle French form ~esquicher~. The noun ~esquisse~ belongs to the same family. English ~sketch~ is a relative by a parallel route: it came in through Dutch ~schets~ from the Italian noun ~schizzo~. The idea is that of a rapid, rough drawing made in a few strokes, and French extended it to any first outline, as in ~esquisser un sourire~ (“to give a faint smile”).
en.esquiver:
~Esquiver~ has a layered history. Old French had a verb ~eschiver~ (related to ~échif~ and ~échiffe~, according to French Wiktionary), which English Wiktionary traces to Proto-West Germanic *~skiuhan~. The modern French form, however, is a later borrowing: Middle French ~esquiver~ (“to escape”) came from Spanish ~esquivar~ (“to avoid, reject, elude”) or, in French Wiktionary's alternative, from Italian ~schivare~ (“to avoid, flee”). English Wiktionary says the Spanish verb itself came from Old French, and French Wiktionary says the same of the Italian one, so the word left French and returned in a new spelling.

The Germanic root is the same one that, by general account, gave English ~eschew~, which also came from Old French ~eschiver~. Related words include German ~scheuen~ and English ~shy~. In French the verb means to dodge a blow, to duck, or to evade or elude, and it gave the noun ~esquive~ (“dodge”). The origin is not fully settled, however: English Wiktionary adds that Spanish ~esquivar~ may instead be formed from ~esquivo~, which would be a different route from the Germanic one.
en.essaimer: Formed from ~essaim~ (“swarm”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so “to swarm.” ~Essaim~ is inherited from Latin ~exāmen~ (“swarm of bees”), a doublet of the learned ~examen~. It first appears as ~essain~ in the chronicle of the dukes of Normandy by the poet Benoît de Sainte-Maure. English Wiktionary treats a direct descent from a Vulgar Latin verb ~exāmināre~ as less likely. Compare Italian ~sciamare~, Spanish ~enjambrar~ and Catalan ~eixamar~.
en.essanger:
French Wiktionary derives ~essanger~ probably from Latin ~exaniare~, a verb glossed as “to squeeze the ~sanie~ out of something.” The Latin word is built on the prefix ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~sanies~, the thin, bloody matter that seeps from a wound or sore. The word “probably” matters here: the descent from this Latin verb is a proposal, not an established fact.

If the proposal is right, the verb widened its sense from wringing out discharge to getting dirt out of something in general, which is how the modern verb is glossed: to get dirt off, to clean. French kept the Latin noun as a learned word, ~sanie~ (“bloody pus”), along with the adjective ~sanieux~ (“full of such discharge”).
en.essarter: Formed from the noun ~essart~ (“clearing”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to clear land of trees.” ~Essart~ comes from Late Latin *~exsartum~, attested only as ~exartum~, from a verb *~exsarire~ made of ~ex-~ (“out”) and Latin ~sarrire~ (“to weed”). The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~.
en.essayer:
A denominal verb from the noun ~essai~ (“a trial, an attempt, an assay”), with Old French forms ~essaiier~ and ~assaier~. The noun ~essai~ comes from Late Latin ~exagium~ (“a weighing”), built on the verb ~exigō~ / ~exigere~ (“to weigh, to measure, to drive out”), which is ~ex-~ (“out”) + ~agere~ (“to drive, to do”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive”).
