That root also gave Greek ~ágō~ (“to lead”) and Sanskrit ~ájati~. From the same ~exagium~ come Italian ~saggio~, Spanish ~ensayo~, and, through Anglo-Norman ~assai~, the English ~assay~ and ~essay~.

The key image is the scale. To weigh a coin or an ore was to ~exigō~ it — to “drive it out” to its exact measure — so ~exagium~ named the test of a metal's purity, and ~essayer~ first meant “to assay, to test.” From testing a thing it broadened to “trying” anything: trying on clothes (~essayer une robe~), trying out a car, or simply attempting a deed. The same family yields French ~essai~ (a trial, and the literary “essay”), ~essayage~ (“fitting,” of garments), ~essayiste~ (“essayist”), and ~essayeur~ (“assayer”) — and, through ~agere~, the immense crop of ~agir~, ~acte~, and ~agent~.
en.essorer: ~Essorer~ is inherited from Old French ~essorer~, from Vulgar Latin *~exaurare~ (“to rise into the air; to expose to air”), made of Latin ~ex~ (“out”) and ~aura~ (“air, breeze”). English ~soar~ comes from the same Old French verb. The Latin sense “to expose to the air” fits the modern idea of drying something by airing it. The noun ~essor~ (“flight, upswing”) belongs to the same family.
en.essoriller: Formed from ~oreille~ (“ear”) with the privative prefix ~es-~, from Latin ~ex-~, and the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to take the ears off.” The TLFi attests ~essoreiller~ in 1303 in a charter. Littré, by contrast, proposes Latin ~ex~ plus ~auricula~ (“ear”), without going through French ~oreille~. In older use the verb meant to mutilate a person by cutting off the ears. Today it means to crop the ears of an animal, such as a boxer dog.
en.essoucher: Formed from the noun ~souche~ (“stump”) with the prefix ~é-~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to uproot stumps.” The noun comes from Old French ~çoche~ and Gaulish *~tsukka~ (“piece”), which English Wiktionary traces in turn to a Proto-Germanic word for “stock, stump”; English ~stock~ is its cousin. The prefix ~é-~ descends from Old French ~es-~, from Latin ~ex-~ (“out of”), and marks removal. The verb ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~.
en.essouffler: ~Essouffler~ is formed from ~souffler~ with the prefix ~es-~, the Old French ancestor of modern ~é-~, which comes from Latin ~ex-~ (“out”). Here the prefix adds no real notion of removal. It marks a result, “to put out of breath.” English Wiktionary simply says it derives from ~souffler~. ~Souffler~ comes from Old French ~sofler~, from Latin ~sufflāre~ (“to blow on, to inflate”), made of ~sub-~ and ~flāre~ (“to blow”).
en.essuyer: Inherited from Old French ~essuier~, from Latin ~exsūcāre~ (“to extract the juice from, to dry out”), formed from ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~sūcus~ (“juice, sap”). The original idea was thus to draw the moisture out of something, and the verb narrowed from drying to wiping a wet surface. French later extended it to enduring, as in ~essuyer un refus~ (“to suffer a refusal”), and the sources I used do not explain that shift. The Latin ~sūcus~ also gave French ~suc~ (“juice”) and ~succulent~.
en.estamper:
~Estamper~ is inherited from Middle French ~estamper~ (also ~stamper~ and ~étamper~), from Old French ~estamper~ (“to crush”). English Wiktionary traces that verb to Frankish *~stampôn~ (“to crush”) or to Old High German ~stampfōn~ (modern German ~stampfen~), from Proto-West Germanic *~stampōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~stampōną~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~stembʰ-~ (“to trample down”).

French Wiktionary explains the spelling. Compared with the variant ~étamper~, the ~s~ was kept in writing and in pronunciation under the influence of ~estampe~ and of Italian ~stampare~. The modern senses, “to emboss” and “to stamp,” are far from “to crush,” and the sources do not narrate the shift. The Germanic root survives in English ~stamp~, a cognate of the German verb, and in the French noun ~estampe~.
en.estampiller: Formed from the noun ~estampille~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, so “to mark with a stamp.” The noun was borrowed from Spanish ~estampilla~, and the verb simply put the usual French ~-er~ ending on it. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is the standard way to make a verb from a noun.
en.ester:
From Old French ~ester~ (“to stand, to remain”), inherited from Latin ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from Proto-Italic *~stāō~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). Latin ~stāre~ lived on as an everyday verb in the Romance languages. Italian ~stare~ (“to stay, to be”) and Spanish and Portuguese ~estar~ (“to be,” of a state or a place) are its direct descendants, and in Spanish ~estar~ shares the work of “to be” with ~ser~. English has the root twice over. Its native cousin is ~stand~, inherited through Proto-Germanic from the same PIE root, like German ~stehen~. Its loan is ~stay~, which entered Middle English from an Anglo-Norman form of ~ester~ itself. French thus lent English a verb that it would all but lose at home.

In Old French, ~ester~ was a full verb meaning “to stand” or “to remain,” and stronger neighbors gradually divided its territory. ~Rester~, which comes from Latin ~restāre~ (~re-~ + ~stāre~, “to stand back, to remain”) and not from ~ester~, took over the sense “to stay.” More surprisingly, ~être~ absorbed part of the conjugation of ~ester~. The past participle ~été~, the present participle ~étant~ and the imperfect ~étais~ descend not from Latin ~esse~ (“to be”) but from forms of ~stāre~, so ~être~ is a suppletive verb, and its “having been” is, etymologically, a “having stood.” Stripped of these roles, ~ester~ survives in modern French only as a defective legal term, in the fixed expression ~ester en justice~ (“to take legal action, to appear in court”), and is used almost only in the infinitive: a fossil of a once-central verb. The same PIE root *~steh₂-~ underlies a vast family of French words, among them ~stable~, ~station~, ~statue~, ~constant~, and ~rester~ itself.
en.esthétiser: Formed from ~esthétique~ with the suffix ~-iser~, so the verb means to give something an aesthetic character or to treat it from the point of view of beauty. The base is a borrowing of Ancient Greek ~aisthētikós~ (“able to perceive, perceptible”), which English Wiktionary says reached the modern languages through New Latin ~aesthēticus~. The word thus began as a term about perception by the senses before it came to mean the study of beauty.
en.estimer:
French ~estimer~ comes from Latin ~aestimāre~ (older ~aestumāre~), “to value, to appraise, to reckon the worth of.” Its origin is debated. The traditional analysis splits it into ~aes~ (“bronze, copper, money”) plus an element meaning “to cut,” glossing it as “one who cuts the bronze” — that is, a minter weighing out coin; the linguist de Vaan instead links it to Proto-Indo-European *~h₂eys-~ (“to seek”). Through Old French the word fanned out into doublets: learned ~estimer~ kept the Latin sense, while a popular line gave Old French ~aesmer~, source of English ~aim~ (originally “to estimate, to calculate a target”); English also borrowed ~esteem~ and ~estimate~, and Italian ~stimare~ and Spanish ~estimar~ are cognate.

The semantic arc runs from the marketplace to the heart. At first ~estimer~ meant to set a monetary value — to appraise — and that commercial sense lives on in ~estimer~ un bien (“to value a property”) and in ~estimation~. From “to reckon worth” grew the gentler “to judge, to reckon” (~j'estime que~, “I reckon that”) and finally the warm “to hold in high regard, to esteem” a person. The same root yields ~estime~, ~inestimable~, ~surestimer~, and ~sous-estimer~. If the old etymology is right, a feeling as lofty as esteem began at the mint, with someone literally cutting and weighing metal to fix a price.
en.estiver: French Wiktionary treats ~estiver~ as two separate verbs. The first comes from Old Occitan ~estivar~, which continues Latin ~aestīvāre~ (“to spend the summer”), from ~aestās~ (“summer”); English ~estivate~ comes from the same Latin verb. The second is a different word. French Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~stīpāre~ (“to compress, to cram”) through Italian ~stipare~. The two verbs happen to share a spelling, one from the season of summer and the other from packing things tight. The second is related to English ~stevedore~, which came by way of Spanish ~estibar~ from the same Latin verb.
en.estomaquer:
The sources differ on how ~estomaquer~ arose. French Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~stomachārī~ (“to be irritated”). English Wiktionary treats it as French ~estomac~ plus the verb ending ~-er~ and compares Latin ~stomachor~, the same verb in its first-person form. Either way, the Latin verb is built on ~stomachus~, itself borrowed from Greek ~stómakhos~, and the French noun ~estomac~ goes back to the same word.

In modern French, ~estomaquer~ means “to flabbergast, to stupefy”: to leave someone so astonished that they can hardly react. The verb belongs to a family built on Latin ~stomachus~, which includes the noun ~estomac~, the learned adjective ~stomacal~ and ~stomachique~, which describes a remedy for the stomach. English ~stomach~ is a relative: it reached English through Old French ~estomac~, from the same Latin and Greek source.
en.estomper: Formed from ~estompe~ + the verbal ending ~-er~. ~Estompe~ is a borrowing from Dutch ~stomp~ (“stump, blunt end”), cognate with English ~stump~. In French the ~estompe~ is the stub of rolled paper or leather that artists use to smudge and soften pencil or charcoal lines, and ~estomper~ first meant to shade a drawing with it. The sense then widened, so that ~estomper~ now means to blur outlines, to dim a color or to soften a memory, and its pronominal form says that a shape or a feeling fades away.
en.estoquer:
From Old French ~estoquier~ or ~estochier~ (“to thrust, to stab”); compare the noun ~estoc~ (“a rapier, a thrusting point”). English Wiktionary gives the deeper origin as probable, not certain: Middle Dutch ~stoken~ (“to jab, to poke”) or Middle High German ~stoken~ (“to pierce”), both from Proto-Germanic *~stukōną~ (“to push, to thrust”), from a Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)teug-~ (“to beat, to push”). English ~stoke~ belongs to the same family.

The sense stayed close to the sword: ~estoquer~ meant to strike with the point rather than the edge, and modern French glosses it as “to run through, to impale.” The noun ~estoc~ lives on in the fixed phrase ~frapper d'estoc et de taille~, “to strike with the point and with the edge.” The Germanic donor remains debated, since the sources name two candidates and do not choose.
en.estourbir: The origin is disputed. By one account, ~estourbir~ comes from ~stourbe~ or ~chtourbe~, derived from Alsatian ~storb~ (“dead”), related to the past participle of German ~sterben~ (“to die”). By another, it comes from Occitan ~estorbir~ (or ~estorbar~), “to knock out,” itself from Latin ~exturbare~. French Wiktionary lays out both without choosing. The verb means “to stun, to knock out.”
en.estrapader: Formed from the noun ~estrapade~ with the verb ending ~-er~: to ~estrapader~ is to subject someone to the ~estrapade~, a torture in which the victim is hoisted by the bound wrists. The noun comes from Italian ~strappata~, from ~strappare~ (“to pull, to tear away”), and the earlier French form ~estrepement~ is also recorded. The torture is named after the violent jerk of the pull.
en.estrapasser:
Borrowed from Italian ~strapazzare~ (“to mistreat, to overwork”), with an initial ~e-~ added in French. French Wiktionary adds that the Italian verb perhaps comes from a form ~strappare~, which it labels Latin, as it does for the French noun ~estrapade~. That last link is a hedge, not a settled chain. The Italian ~strappare~ means “to tear, to pull violently.”

In French, ~estrapasser~ is a horsemanship term meaning to tire a horse out by overworking it, which keeps the Italian sense of rough treatment. The Italian parent lives on in everyday speech: ~uova strapazzate~ are scrambled eggs, eggs that have been roughly handled. If the proposed link holds, ~estrapasser~ and ~estrapade~ are relatives, since ~estrapade~ names a violent jerk, or a punishment in which a person is hoisted and dropped.
en.estropier: ~Estropier~ is a borrowing from Italian ~stroppiare~, which has the same meaning, “to cripple, to maim.” In modern French the verb covers physical maiming and, by extension, spoiling something such as a word or a text. Its past participle ~estropié~ (“crippled”) is also used as a noun for a person left lame or maimed, which is probably how most French speakers meet the word today.
en.estérifier: Formed from ~ester~ and the suffix ~-ifier~, so “to turn into an ester.” Here ~ester~ is the chemical term for a compound formed from an acid and an alcohol, not the Old French verb ~ester~ (“to stand”), which is only a homograph. The suffix ~-ifier~ comes from Latin ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”), and in learned and technical French it builds verbs meaning “to make A” or “to convert into N.” The verb ~estérifier~ names the chemical reaction that produces an ester.
en.ethniciser: Formed from ~ethnique~ with the verbal suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to make ethnic” or “to frame in ethnic terms.” The base ~ethnique~ comes from Latin ~ethnicus~, itself from Ancient Greek ~ethnikós~, derived from ~éthnos~ (“people, nation”). In Latin the word came to mean “pagan, heathen,” a sense that English ~ethnic~ preserved for a while before taking on the modern one.
en.euphoriser: Formed from ~euphorie~ with the suffix ~-iser~: to induce a state of euphoria. The noun is a learned borrowing from Greek ~εὐφορία~ (“the state of being well, healthy”), from ~εὔφορος~ (“well-borne, healthy”). It was first attested in French in the writing of the physician Philippe Hecquet, and English ~euphoria~ is attested in 1727. The verb is a modern coinage in the medical register.
en.européaniser: Formed from the adjective ~européen~ and the suffix ~-iser~, so it means to make something European in character. The adjective is first recorded in the form ~europien~, with the noun ~Européen~ dated to 1721. English Wiktionary derives it from New Latin ~Eurōpaeānus~, built on Classical Latin ~Eurōpaeus~, which itself came from the Greek adjective ~Εὐρωπαῖος~ (“European”), from ~Εὐρώπη~ (“Europe”). The suffix ~-iser~ is the usual French ending for verbs meaning “make or render”.
en.euthanasier: Formed from ~euthanasie~ with the verb-forming ending ~-er~, in the sense “to put to death painlessly.” The noun ~euthanasie~ came into French from English ~euthanasia~, attested from 1606, which itself was borrowed from Ancient Greek ~euthanasía~ (“good death, dying well”), from ~eu-~ (“well”) and ~thánatos~ (“death”). The verb is a modern coinage on top of an older learned noun, and ~-er~ gives it the usual meaning “to carry out N.”
en.exacerber: From Latin ~exacerbāre~, which French Wiktionary glosses first as “to aggravate” and later as “to affect deeply.” The Latin verb is built on ~ex-~ and the adjective ~acerbus~ (“harsh, bitter”), so to exacerbate is, at root, to make something harsher. English ~exacerbate~ is the same Latin verb taken over directly. The Latin adjective ~acerbus~ survives in French ~acerbe~ (“sharp, biting,” of a remark) and in English ~acerbic~. The matching French noun is ~exacerbation~.
en.exagérer:
Learned borrowing from Latin ~exaggerāre~ (“to heap up, to amplify”), which French Wiktionary explains as coming from ~agger~ (“mound, embankment”). French Wiktionary glosses the Latin verb as “to bank up, to increase”, so the physical image comes first: ~ex-~ plus ~aggerāre~ meant to pile up earth into a bank, and ~agger~ named the heap or embankment so built. ~Agger~ is generally linked to ~aggerere~ (“to carry toward”), a compound of ~gerere~ (“to carry”). Italian ~esagerare~, Spanish ~exagerar~ and English ~exaggerate~ are its relatives, all borrowed from the Latin verb. The French verb, like the Latin one, thus rests on a concrete picture of heaping material up before it was used of words and claims. To exaggerate, in this light, is to heap something higher than it stands.

The meaning later became figurative: to heap up came to mean to increase or amplify, and ~exagérer~ now means to represent something as greater than it is, so the old picture of earthworks has faded from view. The Latin root ~gerere~ (“to carry, to bear”) reaches French through ~gérer~ (“to manage”), ~digérer~ and ~suggérer~, so the same carrying verb that sits behind the mound also provides these familiar verbs. French also writes the verb ~exagérer~ with a single g where the Latin spelling had a double one, a simplification that the English ~exaggerate~ did not make. To go from heaping up earth to heaping up words is a short step.
en.exalter:
Borrowed from Latin ~exaltāre~ (“to raise up, to elevate”), a verb formed from ~ex-~ (“out, up”) and ~altus~ (“high”). English Wiktionary traces ~altus~ to a Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂el-~ (“to grow”) with the suffix *~-tós~, so “high” is, at the deepest level, “grown up.” The Latin verb has descendants in several languages: Italian ~esaltare~, Spanish and Portuguese ~exaltar~, and English ~exalt~, which is the same Latin verb borrowed separately.

In French the verb keeps the idea of lifting, but turns it figurative. ~Exalter~ means to raise someone or something in praise, and so to excite or to fill with enthusiasm, which is where the sense “thrill” or “elate” belongs, and the reflexive ~s'exalter~ describes someone working themselves into a fervor. The root ~altus~ also lives in French ~haut~ (“high”), as well as in ~hauteur~ and ~altitude~. A cousin built on the same Latin word is ~exhausser~ (“to raise”), which French Wiktionary uses to gloss the Latin verb.
en.examiner:
From Latin ~exāmināre~ (“to weigh carefully”), from the noun ~exāmen~. ~Exāmen~ is a contraction of *~exagmen~, from ~ex-~ (“out”) plus the root of ~agere~ (“to drive, set in motion”) and the instrumental suffix ~-men~ — literally “that which drives out” or “the means of driving.” ~Agere~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive, lead”), the root behind English ~act~ and ~agent~.

The surprise lies in what ~exāmen~ first named: the tongue or needle of a balance, the slender pointer driven by the weights that shows when the scale is true. To examine, then, was to read the balance-needle — to weigh a thing precisely and judge its worth. From the scales the sense generalized to any careful scrutiny, the testing of a candidate, the inspection of evidence. Curiously, ~exāmen~ also meant a “swarm of bees,” another mass set in motion by the same root. The PIE *~h₂eǵ-~ gives French an enormous family through ~agere~ and its compounds: ~agir~, ~agent~, ~action~, ~exiger~, ~exact~ (a doublet relative of ~examen~), ~rédiger~, and ~naviguer~.
en.exaspérer: ~Exaspérer~ is borrowed from Latin ~exasperāre~ (“to make rough, harsh,” and figuratively “to irritate, to exasperate”). French Wiktionary links it to ~âpre~ and ~aspérité~, which share the Latin root ~asper~ (“rough”). English ~exasperate~ comes from the same Latin verb. The French verb thus keeps the figure of a surface roughened until it rubs raw.
en.exaucer:
~Exaucer~ began as a spelling variant of ~exhausser~ (“to raise”), which comes from Old French ~exalcier~. That verb was built from Latin ~ex-~ (“out, up”) and a Vulgar Latin verb *~altiāre~, modeled on Classical Latin ~exaltāre~ (“to raise, extol”). Behind all of these stands Latin ~altus~ (“high”), which also gave French ~haut~, while ~exaltāre~ passed into English as ~exalt~.

The sense “to grant a prayer” is the interesting part. French Wiktionary explains it directly: to ~exaucer~ a prayer is to carry it upward, toward God. English Wiktionary is more cautious and says the sense may have been influenced by Latin ~exaudīre~ (“to hear, to heed”), a verb made of ~ex-~ and ~audīre~ (“to hear”). The two proposals differ, and the sources do not say which one prevailed. Other French words from ~altus~ include ~hauteur~ and ~exalter~.
en.excaver:
Borrowed from Latin ~excavāre~ (“to hollow out, to dig out”), a verb made of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~cavāre~ (“to hollow”). The base ~cavāre~ comes from the adjective ~cavus~ (“hollow”). Italian ~scavare~, from the same Latin verb, means “to dig”, and Spanish ~excavar~ and English ~excavate~ are parallel borrowings from the Latin. French ~excaver~ is a learned verb, so it keeps the Latin shape.

The Latin adjective ~cavus~ gave French a whole family of words about hollows: ~cave~, ~caverne~, ~cavité~ and ~concave~, the last built with ~con-~. Words built on ~excavāre~ itself include ~excavation~ and ~excavateur~ (the digging machine). ~Excaver~ is a learned verb with a technical feel, used for digging out earth, as an archaeologist or a builder does, and it stands next to the more ordinary ~creuser~.
en.exceller: ~Exceller~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~excellere~ (“to be superior”). In the usual analysis of the Latin word it combines ~ex-~ (“out, up”) with a rare simple verb ~-cellere~ (“to rise, to tower”), so excelling is rising above the rest. French took it straight from Latin instead of inheriting it, which is why its shape stays so close to the original. The same Latin verb gave the English cognate ~excel~, and French has the related ~excellent~ and ~excellence~, which come from the Latin present participle.
en.excentrer: Built on the verb ~centrer~ (“to center”) with the prefix ~ex-~, which carries the idea of “outside.” To ~excentrer~ something is therefore to move it out of the center, to offset it. Only French Wiktionary gives an origin for this verb, and it states a plain prefixed formation. The prefix ~ex-~ comes from Latin and is the same learned element found in ~excentrique~ (“off-center, eccentric”).
en.excepter:
French ~excepter~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~exceptāre~, which French Wiktionary derives from ~excipere~ (“to take out, to pick out”). That verb combines ~ex-~ (“out”) with ~capere~ (“to take, to seize”). The Latin idea is thus one of taking something out of a larger whole, and French kept it as a learned word rather than one passed down through the spoken language.

The image is literal: to ~excepter~ something is to take it out of a group so that a general rule no longer covers it. In modern French the verb is rather formal and survives mostly through its participle ~excepté~, which has hardened into a preposition meaning “except.” The noun ~exception~ and the adjective ~exceptionnel~ belong to the same family, as do many French words built on ~capere~, among them ~accepter~, ~concevoir~, ~recevoir~, ~percevoir~ and ~capable~.
en.exciper:
Borrowed from Latin ~excipere~ (“to take out, to receive, to except”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~capere~ (“to take”), which rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~kap-~ (“to grasp”). English Wiktionary lists the Latin form as ~excipāre~, with ~excipere~ as the infinitive. French took the verb in its legal sense of invoking an exception, and it has stayed mostly in that register.

In law ~exciper de~ means to rely on something as a defense or objection: one ~excipe de sa bonne foi~ (“pleads one's good faith”). The sense follows that of the Latin verb, “to take out” and so “to set aside, to make an exception,” which also gave the Latin noun ~exceptio~. French has the learned family ~exception~, ~excepter~ and ~exceptionnel~, and English ~except~ and ~exception~ come from the same source. The root ~capere~ also lies behind ~accepter~, ~recevoir~, ~concevoir~ and ~capter~, though not by way of ~exciper~.
en.exciser:
~Exciser~ is formed in French from the supine ~excīsum~ of the Latin verb ~excīdere~ (“to cut out, to remove by cutting”) plus the verb ending ~-er~. It is therefore a learned verb, built on a Latin form rather than inherited from Latin through the spoken language. Latin ~excīdere~ is made of ~ex-~ (“out of”) and ~caedere~ (“to cut, to strike”). English ~excise~ and ~excision~ come from the same Latin source.

The verb ~exciser~ is used in medicine for cutting out a part, such as a tissue or a growth. The root ~caedere~ is a rich family in French, appearing in ~incision~, ~concis~, ~précis~, ~décision~ and ~homicide~, all of which involve a cut. The same root also gives the suffix ~-cide~ in words such as ~suicide~.
en.exciter:
From Latin ~excitāre~ (“to rouse, to call forth, to wake”), in French use by about 1180. The Latin verb is the frequentative of ~exciēre~ (“to call out, to summon”), from ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~ciēre~ (“to set in motion”), from Proto-Italic *~kieō~, from PIE *~keyh₂-~ (“to set in motion”). Through that root it is cousin to Greek ~κινέω~ (“to move”) — the ancestor of French ~cinéma~ and English ~kinetic~: the cinema and excitement are, at bottom, one and the same idea of setting things moving. Italian ~eccitare~, Spanish ~excitar~ and English ~excite~ all carry the same Latin verb, the English one having passed through French on its way.

The verb began gently: its first French sense, around 1180, was simply “to wake someone up.” From rousing sleepers it moved to rousing feelings — “to spur, to stimulate” (about 1223), “to stir indignation” (1587) — then to bodily reactions (1613), and modern science adopted it wholesale: neurons fire and atoms enter excited states under its name. The richest surprise is the verb's hidden kin: ~ciēre~ bred a clutch of French verbs through its own frequentative ~citāre~ (“to make come, to summon”) — ~citer~ (first to summon before a court, only later to quote), ~réciter~, ~inciter~, ~susciter~ — and above all ~ressusciter~, exciter's solemn near-twin: where ~exciter~ rouses you from sleep, ~ressusciter~ (from ~re-~ and ~suscitāre~, “to raise up again”) rouses you from death. Resurrection and excitement differ, in Latin's bookkeeping, by little more than a prefix.
en.exclamer: ~Exclamer~ is borrowed from Latin ~exclāmāre~ (“to cry out”), built from ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~clāmāre~ (“to shout, to call”). The verb is now used almost only in its reflexive form ~s'exclamer~, “to cry out in surprise or admiration.” The Latin ~clāmāre~ also gave many French relatives, including ~réclamer~, ~proclamer~, ~acclamer~, ~déclamer~ and the noun ~clameur~.
en.exclure:
From Latin ~exclūdere~ (“to shut out, to exclude”), which passed through Old French ~excluder~ and Middle French ~exclure~ to reach its modern form. The Latin verb is a compound of the prefix ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~claudere~ (“to close, to shut”). ~claudere~ descends from Proto-Italic *~klaudō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~kleh₂u-~ (“hook, peg, bolt” — the things that lock a door). Cognate, through ~claudere~, with Italian ~escludere~ and Spanish ~excluir~; through the root, with Ancient Greek ~kleís~ (“key, bolt”).

The image is concrete: to ~exclure~ is to shut someone or something out the door, ~ex~ + ~claudere~, and the figurative “to exclude, to leave out, to rule out” grew naturally from that. The Latin ~claudere~ is one of the great hinges of French vocabulary, surviving in a swarm of related verbs: ~clore~ and ~clôturer~ (“to close, to enclose”), ~conclure~ (“to conclude,” to close together), ~inclure~ (“to include,” to shut in), ~reclure~ (whence ~reclus~, “recluse”), and the noun family ~clôture~, ~clé~/~clef~ (“key”), and ~clavier~ (“keyboard”). So an exclusion is, etymologically, a locking-out, and a conclusion a locking-together.
en.excommunier:
Borrowed from Late Latin ~excommunicāre~ (“to put out of the community”), with the form influenced by French ~communier~. The Latin verb is built from ~ex-~ (“out of”) and ~commūnicāre~ (“to share, to join”), from ~commūnis~ (“common”). It displaced the inherited Old French verb ~escomengier~, which had developed naturally from the same Latin word. The learned form thus replaced the popular one, and French was left with a verb that sounds closer to Latin than to the speech of the early Middle Ages.

The verb has always carried its Church meaning: to cut someone off from the sacraments and from the community of believers. Its family is large, and it is mostly learned: ~commun~, ~communion~, ~communier~, ~communiquer~ and ~communauté~ all share the Latin root ~commūnis~. The ~communier~ that influenced it is the verb for receiving the Eucharist, which makes ~excommunier~ its exact opposite. Other languages made the same learned borrowing: Spanish ~excomulgar~, Italian ~scomunicare~ and English ~excommunicate~. In modern French the verb is also used figuratively, for banishing someone from a group or a party.
en.excorier:
~Excorier~ is borrowed from Late Latin ~excoriāre~, which was built on Latin ~ex-~ (“out of, off”) and ~corium~ (“skin, hide, leather”). The Latin verb meant “to strip the skin off,” and French took it over in the same sense: to graze or flay the skin. English ~excoriate~ is a loan from the same Latin verb.

French keeps ~excorier~ as a learned word, used in medicine and in literary registers for skin that has been rubbed raw, and it is rare in everyday speech. The noun ~excoriation~ belongs with it. Latin ~corium~ is also the source of the French ~cuir~ (“leather”) and of ~cuirasse~ (“body armor,” first made of leather). So an ~excorier~ is, etymologically, a taking-off of the leather.
en.excréter:
From Latin ~excernere~ (“to sift out, to separate”), through its past participle ~excretus~. French Wiktionary gives the Latin verb as the source, while English Wiktionary describes ~excréter~ as a learned formation from the root of ~excrétion~ or from ~excretus~. Latin ~excernere~ is made of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~cernere~ (“to sift, to distinguish”). The verb means to expel waste matter from the body.

The sieving image is the old one: ~excernere~ literally means to sift something out. The same ~cernere~ underlies a family of French words, among them ~discerner~, ~sécréter~, ~excrément~ and ~excrétion~, as well as ~concerner~. The pair ~excréter~ and ~sécréter~ is instructive: both are learned verbs for what the body gives off, one for waste and the other for useful substances. English ~excrete~ has the same Latin source.
en.excursionner: ~Excursionner~ is formed from the noun ~excursion~ with the verb ending ~-er~: to go on an excursion, to take a trip. ~Excursion~ was borrowed from Latin ~excursiō~, a noun of the Latin verb ~excurrere~ (~ex-~ + ~currere~, “to run out”), so the family begins with the idea of running or sallying out.
en.excuser:
From Old French ~escuser~, from Latin ~excūsāre~ (“to free from a charge, to excuse”), the exact antonym of ~accūsāre~ (“to accuse”). Both are built on ~causa~ (“cause, legal case, lawsuit”): to ~accuse~ is to put someone ~into~ a case (~ac-~, from ~ad-~), to ~excuse~ is to take them ~out~ of it (~ex-~, “out of”). The deeper origin of ~causa~ is uncertain — en.Wiktionary notes a proposed tie to ~cūdere~ (“to strike”) but adds that some doubt any Indo-European source — so the chain is best traced no further than the Latin noun. Cognate with Italian ~scusare~ and Spanish ~excusar~.

The legal metaphor is the whole story: French ~excuser~ still means to lift the blame off someone, to release them from the “case” pending against them. The same ~causa~ took a startling semantic turn in Late Latin, drifting from “lawsuit” to “matter” to plain “thing” — which is why Italian ~cosa~ and Spanish ~cosa~ both mean “thing,” and why French ~chose~ does too. So ~excuser~ and ~chose~ are quiet cousins. From the same family come ~accuser~, ~causer~ (“to chat,” itself once “to plead a cause”), ~causal~, and the noun ~cause~. The pronominal ~s'excuser~ (“to apologize”) literally has one declare oneself out of the case.
en.excéder: From Latin ~excēdere~ (“to go out, to go beyond”), formed from ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~cēdere~ (“to go, to yield”). The verb first meant to go past a limit, as when a sum or a speed ~excède~ a threshold. By extension it came to mean pushing a person past the limit of their patience, hence “to exasperate, to wear out.” The same Latin pair of elements underlies ~excès~ and ~excessif~, and the root ~cēdere~ lives on in ~céder~ (“to yield”), ~procéder~ and ~succéder~.
en.exemplifier: Formed from ~exemple~ with the suffix ~-ifier~, so the verb means to illustrate by an example, or literally to “make an example”. The noun was borrowed from Latin ~exemplum~ and displaced the Old French ~essainple~. The suffix ~-ifier~ comes from Latin ~-(i)ficāre~, which goes back to ~facere~ (“to make”), and is still used to coin learned and technical verbs.
en.exempter: Formed from the adjective ~exempt~ and the verb ending ~-er~; Italian ~esentare~ is a parallel. The adjective is borrowed from Latin ~exemptus~, the past participle of ~eximere~ (“to take out, to remove”), built on ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~emere~ (“to take, to buy”). To ~exempter~ someone is thus, literally, to take them out of an obligation such as a tax or a duty. The adjective also gave a French noun, ~exempt~, for a kind of police officer, often picked from soldiers who had themselves been exempted from ordinary service.
en.exercer:
From Old French ~essercer~ (attested 1121–34), from Latin ~exercēre~ (“to keep busy, train, practice, work”), a compound of the prefix ~ex-~ (“out, away”) and ~arcēre~ (“to enclose, hold in, keep off”). Latin ~arcēre~ goes back, through Proto-Italic ~arkeō~, to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂erk-~ (“to hold, contain, protect”), the same root behind ~arx~ (“citadel”) and ~arca~ (“chest, box”). Italian ~esercitare~ and Spanish ~ejercer~ are its Romance cousins, and English ~exercise~ enters through the same Latin verb.

The inner logic is vivid: if ~arcēre~ means “to hold in,” then ~exercēre~ is literally “to hold out of an enclosure” — to let loose, to put to work — which is exactly what one does when driving penned animals to labor or marching soldiers from camp onto the drill field. From that image of setting energy in motion grew the senses of training, practicing a skill, and wielding a power, all of which ~exercer~ keeps: one exercises a profession, exercises authority, or exercises the body. The same root family yields French ~exercice~, ~exorciser~ (a different ~ex-~ compound, but the Latinate feel is kin), and the more distant ~arche~ and ~coffre~ of the storage sense. The surprising kinship is that a verb of vigorous activity hides, at its heart, a word for shutting things in.
en.exfiltrer: Formed from ~filtrer~ with the prefix ~ex-~ (“out”), so it means to get something or someone out through a barrier. The base ~filtrer~ comes from the noun ~filtre~, a learned borrowing from Latin ~filtrum~, attested in the eighth century and taken, according to French Wiktionary, from Frankish. It is a doublet of ~feutre~ (“felt”): to filter was first to pass a liquid through felt.
en.exfolier:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~exfoliāre~ (“to strip of leaves”), built, by the standard analysis, from ~ex-~ (“out, off”) and ~folium~ (“leaf”). English Wiktionary invites comparison with ~effeuiller~, the everyday French verb for stripping leaves, which is formed in French from the same two ideas and works as the popular counterpart of this learned verb. The borrowed form keeps the Latin shape almost intact.

The Latin ~folium~ is also behind ~feuille~, through Old French, and so behind ~feuillage~ and ~effeuiller~. Learned borrowings such as ~folio~ keep the Latin form. English took the same verb as ~exfoliate~. The botanical sense of stripping leaves remains in French, together with the broader sense of shedding or removing thin layers.
en.exhaler:
French ~exhaler~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~exhālāre~, a compound of the prefix ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~hālāre~ (“to breathe, to blow”), the verb French Wiktionary names as its base. The Latin form also underlies Spanish ~exhalar~ and English ~exhale~, and Italian ~esalare~. French took the word in directly rather than inheriting it, which is why it keeps the learned ~h~ in the middle.

In modern French, ~exhaler~ covers more than breathing out. It means to give off an odor or vapor, and, figuratively, to let out something held back, such as a secret or a sigh. The sources do not say in what order these senses arose. The sense of breathing and the sense of emitting sit close together, since both describe something escaping from within. Related words in French include ~exhalaison~ (“a vapor given off”) and ~inhaler~ (“to breathe in”), which pairs the same Latin verb with the opposite prefix, ~in-~. In the family also stand ~exhalation~ and the Latin noun ~halitus~ (“breath”), source of English ~halitosis~.
en.exhausser: Formed from ~hausser~ with the prefix ~ex-~, and attested as Old French ~exalcier~ by the early twelfth century. The base ~hausser~ comes from Old French ~haucier~, from Vulgar Latin *~altiāre~, from Latin ~altus~ (“high”). ~Exhausser~ means to raise something higher, especially a building, and it is now rather formal.
en.exhiber:
From Latin ~exhibēre~, borrowed into French as a learned word. The Latin verb is analyzed as ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~habēre~ (“to hold, to have”), so it meant “to hold out,” that is, to present or produce something for others to see. English ~exhibit~ is the same Latin verb taken over, and the weakening of ~habēre~ to ~-hibēre~ inside compounds is a regular Latin vowel change that also gave ~prohibēre~ and ~inhibēre~.

The simple verb ~habēre~ is the ancestor of French ~avoir~ (“to have”), but ~exhibēre~ stayed close to its Latin form because it entered French by learned borrowing, not by inheritance. Related French words are ~inhiber~, ~prohiber~ and ~exhibition~. In modern French ~exhiber~ means to show something openly, sometimes with a hint of display, as in showing off.
en.exhorter:
~Exhorter~ was borrowed into French from Latin ~exhortārī~ (“to encourage, to urge on”), a deponent verb made of ~ex-~ (“out,” here intensifying) and ~hortārī~ (“to urge, to cheer on”). Latin ~hortārī~ is usually analysed as a frequentative of the older verb ~horīrī~, also “to urge.” The Latin family of encouragement then passed into the Romance languages by learned routes. Italian ~esortare~ and Spanish ~exhortar~ are parallel borrowings of the same Latin verb, not inherited descendants, and English ~exhort~ was taken in the same bookish way.

Because it was a borrowing, ~exhorter~ kept its Latin shape rather than wearing down through sound change, which is why it still carries the silent ~h~ that the Latin spelling preserved. The sense has stayed close to the Latin: to urge someone by speech toward a course of action or a virtue, in a register that is solemn, religious or oratorical (~exhorter à la patience~). The noun ~exhortation~ and the rare adjective ~hortatif~ come from the same Latin family, and all of them keep the idea of spurring someone on with words rather than with force.
en.exhumer: A learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ~exhumāre~, which English Wiktionary analyzes as ~ex-~ (“out of”) + ~humō~ (“to bury”); French Wiktionary writes the source as Latin ~ex humare~. The Latin verb ~humāre~ belongs to ~humus~ (“earth, ground”), so to ~exhumer~ is literally to take out of the ground. The mirror-image verb is ~inhumer~ (“to bury”), built on the same ~humāre~, and the pair belong to funeral and legal vocabulary: one ~inhume~ a body, and a court may order it exhumed. The word ~humus~ itself passed into French and English as the name of the soil layer, and it is also behind ~humble~, through ~humilis~, “close to the ground”. English ~exhume~ is a direct cognate of the French verb.
en.exhéréder:
Borrowed from Latin ~exhērēdāre~ (“to disinherit”). The Latin verb is formed from ~ex-~ (“out, away from”) and ~hērēs~ (“heir”), so it means literally to remove someone from the line of heirs. It is a learned borrowing, taken whole from legal Latin rather than inherited through the spoken language, which is why it keeps the Latin ~ex-~ and the written ~h~.

The verb belongs to the vocabulary of inheritance law, where it describes a testator cutting a would-be heir out of a will. It is related to ~héritier~ (“heir”), ~hériter~ (“to inherit”) and ~héritage~ (“inheritance”), all of which come from the Latin ~hērēs~ and its derivatives. Its meaning is thus the exact opposite of ~hériter~, and it is the learned relative of the plainer ~déshériter~. The word is rare outside legal and historical writing, and the related noun ~exhérédation~ names the act of disinheriting.
en.exiger:
From Latin ~exigere~ (“to drive out, to demand, to exact, to weigh precisely”), compounded from ~ex-~ (“out, thoroughly”) and ~agere~ (“to drive, to lead, to do”). ~Agere~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive, to set in motion”). Cognate, through ~agere~, with Italian ~esigere~ and Spanish ~exigir~, and — through the root *~h₂eǵ-~ — with Greek ~ágō~ (“I lead”), Sanskrit ~ájati~ (“drives”), and English ~act~ and ~agent~.

The Latin verb carried a striking double sense: literally “to drive out,” but also “to weigh exactly,” from the image of driving a scale's beam level — whence the adjective ~exact~ (“driven to precision”). French ~exiger~ kept the forceful side, “to demand as one's due,” the creditor driving out what is owed. The root *~h₂eǵ-~, through ~agere~ and its participle ~actus~, is among Latin's most productive: French owes it ~agir~, ~agent~, ~acte~, ~action~, ~exact~, ~rédiger~, and ~naviguer~, while English gathers ~act~, ~agent~, ~agile~, ~exact~, ~exigent~, and ~ambiguous~ from the same driving root. To exiger a thing is to drive it out of someone, forcefully and to the last measure.
en.exiler: Formed from the noun ~exil~ with the first-group ending ~-er~, though the two Wiktionaries tell it slightly differently. French Wiktionary treats it as a plain derivative of ~exil~, while English Wiktionary describes a semi-learned reshaping of Old French ~essillier~, from Late Latin ~exiliāre~. The noun ~exil~ comes from Latin ~exilium~ (also spelled ~exsilium~), which was linked either to ~exsul~ (“banished, living abroad”) or to ~exsilīre~ (“to leap out”); the choice between them is open. The first French attestation of the noun dates from 1080.
en.exister:
From Latin ~existere~, also written ~exsistere~ (“to step forth, to come into being, to appear”), a compound of the prefix ~ex-~ (“out, forth”) and ~sistere~ (“to cause to stand, to set down”). ~sistere~ is a reduplicated form of ~stare~ (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”), one of the great roots of the family. Through it ~exister~ is cognate with Ancient Greek ~hístēmi~ (“to make stand”), with English ~stand~ and ~stay~, and with the whole Romance family of standing verbs.

The literal Latin sense was vivid: to ~exsistere~ was to stand out, to step into view, to emerge — existence imagined as a coming-forth from hidden ground into the visible. French borrowed the verb in learned form, keeping the philosophical sense “to be, to have being” while letting the original spatial image fade. The same root *~steh₂-~ gives French an enormous progeny: ~être~ (whose past participle ~été~ comes from ~status~, not from ~esse~), ~rester~, ~stable~, ~station~, ~statue~, ~constant~, ~instant~, ~assister~, ~résister~, and ~consister~ — a vast family in which everything ultimately stands.
en.exonder: Formed in French from ~onde~ with the prefix ~ex-~ (“out of”) and the verb ending ~-er~, a parasynthetic verb meaning “to emerge from the water.” English Wiktionary instead derives it from the adjective ~exondé~, attested in 1839, which suggests the participle came first. The base ~onde~ comes through Old French from Latin ~unda~ (“wave, water, agitation”), so the verb says, literally, to come out of the waves. The prefix is the learned form of the Latin ~ex-~ rather than the everyday French ~é-~.
en.exonérer: A learned borrowing from Latin ~exonerāre~ (“to unload, to relieve of a burden”), formed from ~ex-~ (“off, out of”) and ~onerāre~ (“to load”), itself from ~onus~ (“burden”). French kept the figurative sense: to release someone from a charge, tax or obligation. English ~exonerate~ was borrowed from the same Latin verb, and the burden root also gives French ~onéreux~ (“costly”) and English ~onerous~.
en.exorciser:
French ~exorciser~ comes from Latin ~exorcizāre~. That verb is a Late Latin loan from Greek ~exorkízein~ (“to bind by oath, to adjure”), built from ~ex-~ and ~horkos~ (“oath”). The ending ~-izāre~ is the one that Late Latin used to take over Greek verbs, and it is the ancestor of French ~-iser~.

In French the verb belongs to the language of the Church, where it means to drive out an evil spirit by solemn formulas. The same Greek source gave French ~exorcisme~ (“the rite”) and ~exorciste~ (“the one who performs it”), and the verb lives on in English as ~exorcize~. The idea of an oath or an adjuration stays visible in the Greek parts, though the sources at hand do not trace how the Christian sense arose.
en.expatrier: ~Expatrier~ is formed in French from the noun ~patrie~, the prefix ~ex-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, “to send out of one's homeland.” The prefix is the learned form of Latin ~ex-~ (“out of”), and ~patrie~ comes from Latin ~patria~ (“land of the fathers”), from ~pater~ (“father”). The verb is the counterpart of ~rapatrier~, which uses the same noun. Most often today it appears in the pronominal form ~s'expatrier~, “to leave one's country to live abroad.”
en.expectorer:
From Latin ~expectorāre~ (“to drive out of the heart”), formed from ~ex-~ (“out of”) and ~pectus~ (“chest, breast, heart”). The Latin noun ~pectus~ named the breast both as a part of the body and as the seat of the feelings, so the Latin verb literally meant to chase something out of the heart or chest. The verb was thus formed in Latin and borrowed whole into French, not assembled from French parts. English ~expectorate~ and Italian ~espettorare~ come from the same Latin verb.

In French the verb is now chiefly medical, “to bring up phlegm from the chest by coughing,” and it can also be used, humorously or disapprovingly, for spitting. The root ~pectus~ gave a family of learned French words: ~pectoral~ (“of the chest”), ~expectorant~ (“a medicine that helps clear the lungs”) and ~expectoration~. The prefix ~ex-~ is the same one found in ~expulser~ and ~exclure~, and the muscle called ~pectoral~ takes its name from the chest it covers. Both Latin parts are transparent, which makes the French verb easy to analyse even though it was never built in French.
en.expertiser: ~Expertiser~ is the noun ~expertise~ + the verbal ending ~-er~, “to carry out an expertise on something,” that is, to appraise or assess it. The noun is itself built from ~expert~ + the suffix ~-ise~. Behind ~expert~ stands Latin ~expertus~ (“tried, proven”), the participle of ~experīrī~ (“to try”). The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is the default way to turn a noun into a first-conjugation verb.
en.expier:
Borrowed from Latin ~expiāre~ (“to atone for, to purify by a rite”), formed from ~ex-~ (“out, thoroughly”) and ~piāre~ (“to appease with a rite or sacrifice”). The verb ~piāre~ belongs to the family of the adjective ~pius~ (“dutiful, devout”). Italian ~espiare~ and Spanish ~expiar~ are its counterparts, and English borrowed the same Latin verb as ~expiate~.

French ~expier~ keeps the religious and moral flavor of the Latin: to pay for a fault or a crime by suffering a penalty, as in ~expier ses péchés~. The noun ~expiation~ and the adjective ~expiatoire~ belong to its family. Through ~pius~, the root also reaches ~pieux~ (“devout”), ~impie~ (“impious”), and the pair ~piété~ and ~pitié~, two French forms of Latin ~pietātem~, one learned and one inherited.
en.expirer:
Learned borrowing from Latin ~exspīrāre~ (“to breathe out”), formed from ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~spīrāre~ (“to breathe”). Because it was taken straight from Latin and not inherited, the French form is close to the Latin one. Its cousins in the family include ~respirer~ (“to breathe again”), ~inspirer~ (“to breathe in”), ~conspirer~ (“to breathe together”) and ~transpirer~. The noun ~esprit~ is a distant relative as well, from Latin ~spīritus~, “breath”. English ~expire~ and Italian ~espirare~ share the same Latin source.

The verb has had a double life ever since. Its physical sense is to breathe out, as opposed to ~inspirer~, and it still has this meaning in medicine. A figurative sense arose early: to breathe one's last, hence to die, which is the sense of the English verb in the phrase “he expired”. From dying it was an easy step to the ending of things that have a lifespan, so a passport, a contract or a deadline ~expire~. The Latin habit of treating life as a breath, the soul leaving the body in the final exhalation, explains why “to breathe out” could come to mean both dying and running out.
en.expliciter: Formed from the adjective ~explicite~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to make explicit”. The adjective comes from Latin ~explicitus~ (“unfolded, clear”), the past participle of ~explicāre~ (“to unfold, to unroll”), itself ~ex-~ plus ~plicāre~ (“to fold”). The image is of something unrolled so that nothing stays hidden in the folds, which is why ~expliciter~ means to state a thing openly instead of leaving it implied. English ~explicit~ comes from the same Latin participle.
en.expliquer:
From Latin ~explicare~ (« to unfold, to unroll »), formed from ~ex-~ (« out ») and ~plicare~ (« to fold »). ~plicare~ rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~pleḱ-~ (“to fold, to plait”). Through this root ~expliquer~ is kin to French ~plier~ (“to fold”) and ~ployer~, and to a crowd of English borrowings — ~ply~, ~apply~, ~deploy~, ~employ~, ~explicit~ — all carrying the buried metaphor of folding and unfolding.

The Latin picture is concrete: a papyrus scroll rolled up, then ~explicare~ — unrolled — so its text lies open to be read. From « unrolling a scroll » the verb moved to « laying a matter open », and so to the modern sense « to make clear, to account for ». A fellow word travelled the opposite way: ~compliquer~ (« to fold together ») describes what is tangled, while ~expliquer~ undoes the tangle. The same root *~pleḱ-~ branches widely in French: ~pli~ (« a fold »), ~plier~, ~appliquer~, ~impliquer~, ~déployer~, ~exploiter~, and ~simple~ itself (« once-folded »).
en.exploiter:
From Vulgar Latin *~explicitāre~, a frequentative of Latin ~explicare~ (“to unfold, unravel, explain”), itself ~ex-~ (“out”) plus ~plicare~ (“to fold”), from Proto-Indo-European *~plek-~ (“to plait, fold”). It surfaces in Old French as ~espleitier~ / ~esploitier~ (“to accomplish, carry out”) and shares its root with English ~exploit~ and, through the same Latin ~plicare~, with Spanish ~explotar~.

The path runs from the literal to the figurative: from “unfolding” a thing, to “carrying it out,” to “making it yield a profit.” Early Old French ~espleitier~ meant “to accomplish,” and the related noun gave English its ~exploit~, a notable feat or achievement. By 1560 the modern ~exploiter~ had settled into “to make productive, to turn to account” — a farm, a mine, a resource — and only later acquired the darker, pejorative sense of using a person unfairly. The same ancestral *~plek-~ branches widely in French through ~plicare~ and its kin: ~plier~ (“to fold”), ~ployer~, ~appliquer~, ~compliquer~, and ~expliquer~, that last one the learned doublet of ~exploiter~ — both descend from ~explicare~, one borrowed straight from Latin, the other worn down through popular speech.
en.explorer:
French ~explorer~ comes straight from Latin ~explorare~ (“to observe, examine, scout out, explore”). The verb is transparently ~ex-~ (“out”) plus ~plorare~ (“to cry out, weep, wail”). The deepest origin of ~plorare~ is uncertain — etymologists do not assign it a secure Proto-Indo-European root — so we stop, honestly, at the Latin. Through ~explorare~ the word spread across Europe: Italian ~esplorare~, Spanish ~explorar~, and, via French, English ~explore~ and ~exploration~.

The surprising part is buried in ~plorare~, “to cry out.” The ancient — and quite plausible — explanation makes ~explorare~ a hunters' term: to ~explorer~ a region was first to scout it by sending up a shout, the cry that flushed or signalled game. From that very physical sense of beating the bush, the verb climbed to the cool, deliberate “investigate, examine” of the scholar, the surgeon (who ~explore~ a wound), and the geographer. The same tearful root ~plorare~ is hiding in plain sight in two other French verbs: ~déplorer~ (“to deplore, lament,” to weep ~de-~ thoroughly) and ~implorer~ (“to implore,” to weep ~in-~ toward someone in entreaty) — so that ~explorer~, ~déplorer~, and ~implorer~ form a small trio all founded on a cry.
en.exploser:
A back-formation dated to 1801: ~exploser~ was coined in French from the stem of ~explosion~ plus the suffix ~-er~. ~Explosion~ rests on Latin ~explōdere~, from ~ex-~ (“out”) + ~plaudere~ (“to clap, to applaud”). The deep root is given cautiously: ~plaudere~ is tentatively traced to PIE *~pleh₂-~ (“flat, to spread”), but the connection is marked uncertain. Through ~plaudere~, ~exploser~ is cognate with ~applaudir~ and ~plausible~.

The memorable detail lives in the Latin theater. ~Explōdere~ originally meant to drive a performer off the stage by clapping and hooting — to “clap him out.” From this noisy expulsion the word drifted toward the idea of a sudden, forceful bursting-out, and by the time French built ~explosion~ and then ~exploser~, the sense had become the violent release we know: a bomb, a boiler, a temper. The verb arrived only at the turn of the nineteenth century, when chemistry and artillery needed a precise word for it. Modern French relatives include ~explosion~, ~explosif~, and the contrasting ~imploser~ (a twentieth-century coinage on the same pattern).
en.exporter:
~Exporter~ was borrowed from classical Latin ~exportare~ (“to carry out, to carry away”), from ~ex-~ (“out of”) and ~portare~ (“to carry”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“to pass through, to go across”) — the root behind Latin ~porta~ (“gate”) and ~portus~ (“harbour”) and, on the Germanic side, English ~fare~ and ~ferry~. An isolated medieval form, ~soi esporter~, of obscure sense, appears around 1245; the verb proper, meaning “to carry outside,” surfaces in the early sixteenth century, and the commercial sense in 1756. For that last step the TLFi keeps a prudent hedge: the trade meaning arose perhaps under the influence of English ~to export~ (attested in 1665) — a word England had itself taken from the very same Latin ~exportare~.

If the English influence is real — it is proposed, not proven — then ~exporter~ made a tidy round trip: out of Latin into English commerce, then back across the Channel just in time for the free-trade debates of the eighteenth century, where d'Argenson's journal (1756) shows it at work. Etymologically, every export simply passes through the ~porta~, the gate, on its way to the ~portus~, the port. The carrying family is enormous: ~porter~, ~transporter~, ~importer~, ~déporter~, ~reporter~, ~porte~, ~port~, ~portefeuille~, ~portemanteau~ — and ~opportun~, by the classical account from ~ob portum~, said of the wind that blows a ship toward harbour: the opportune is what carries you safely to port. ~Exporter~ is the same gesture turned seaward: goods, words and ideas carried out through the gate.
en.exposer:
A French compound of the prefix ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~poser~ (“to place, to put”), formed to render the Latin verb ~exponere~ (“to set out, to expose”), which had evolved regularly into Old French ~espondre~. The ~poser~ element comes from Late Latin ~pausare~ (“to pause, to set down”), whose Romance descendants absorbed the senses of Latin ~ponere~ (“to place”), past participle ~positus~. Through ~positus~ the family is cognate with English ~pose~, ~position~, and ~compose~, and Latin ~ponere~ also gave Spanish ~poner~ and Italian ~porre~.

The literal meaning is to “set out,” to place something where it can be seen — and from this grew several modern senses at once: to ~exposer~ a painting is to display it (whence an ~exposition~), to ~exposer~ an idea is to set it forth, and to ~exposer~ someone to danger is to put them out where the danger can reach them. The construction with ~poser~ rather than the inherited ~espondre~ shows French rebuilding a Latin verb from transparent native parts. The same ~poser~ generated a large family: ~déposer~, ~composer~, ~disposer~, ~proposer~, ~imposer~, and the noun ~position~.
en.exprimer:
French ~exprimer~ comes from Latin ~exprimere~ (“to press out, to squeeze out, to portray vividly”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~premere~ (“to press”). ~Premere~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~per-~ (“to strike, to press”), the same root that, through Latin, gives English ~press~ and ~print~. Italian keeps ~esprimere~ and Spanish ~exprimir~ (“to squeeze”), preserving the very physical core sense.

The metaphor at the heart of the word is wonderfully concrete: to ~exprimer~ is to press something out, the way one squeezes juice from a fruit — and indeed ~exprimer le jus d'un citron~ is still good French. From this literal squeezing the Romans drew the figurative “to press a meaning out into words, to portray,” and that abstract sense, “to express, to convey,” is what dominates modern French. The buried ~premere~ runs through a large family: ~comprimer~, ~imprimer~ (“to print,” literally to press onto), ~opprimer~, ~supprimer~, ~déprimer~, and the nouns ~pression~ and ~expression~. So when one ~exprime~ a feeling, one is, etymologically, wringing it out under pressure until it spills into speech.
en.exproprier: Formed, according to English Wiktionary, from the prefix ~ex-~ (“out of”) and ~approprier~, with the ~ap-~ dropped. ~Approprier~ comes from Latin ~appropriāre~, a verb built on ~proprius~ (“one's own”). The sense is the legal one: to take a property out of its owner's hands, by authority of the state. English ~expropriate~ is a close counterpart.
en.expulser:
From Latin ~expulsāre~ (“to drive out, to thrust away”), a frequentative of ~expellere~ (“to drive out”), which is ~ex-~ (“out”) + ~pellere~ (“to push, to drive”). The Latin verb goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~pel-~ (“to thrust, to strike”). Frequentatives such as ~expulsāre~ express a repeated or forceful action, so the word carries the idea of driving something out with some insistence. French did not inherit it: ~expulser~ is a learned borrowing, taken directly from Latin, and that is what sets it apart from its cousin ~pousser~.

The two French verbs show how the same Latin family can enter a language by two doors. The plain verb ~pulsāre~ (“to push, to beat”) was inherited and worn down over the centuries into ~pousser~, and the learned ~expulser~ keeps the Latin shape almost intact. English shows the same pattern with ~expel~, from the simple ~expellere~, and ~push~, which is borrowed from French ~pousser~. In use, ~expulser~ is the verb of authority: one expels a pupil from school, a tenant from a flat, a foreigner from a country, or a gas from the lungs. The root also gives ~pouls~, ~impulsion~, ~répulsion~, ~repousser~ and ~propulser~.
en.expurger:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~expurgāre~ (“to cleanse out”), built from ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~purgāre~ (“to cleanse”). It is the learned counterpart of the Old French verb ~espurgier~, which came from the same Latin source. English ~expurgate~ comes from the same Latin verb, and Italian ~espurgare~ and Spanish ~expurgar~ follow it.

The verb is used chiefly of texts, from which offending passages are cut. Its root ~purgāre~ gives French a large family, including the inherited verb ~purger~ and the learned ~purgatoire~ and ~purgation~. The Old French ~espurgier~ and the learned ~expurger~ make a pair of an older inherited form and a later learned one, a pattern common in French vocabulary.
en.expédier:
French Wiktionary traces ~expédier~ through Old French ~expedier~ from Latin ~expedīre~, while English Wiktionary instead analyses it as ~expédient~ plus ~-er~; the two accounts disagree. The Latin verb is usually read as a compound of ~ex-~ (“out of”) and the root of ~pēs~, genitive ~pedis~ (“foot”), its literal sense being to free the feet from a snare or from mud, hence to extricate and to make ready. The Indo-European root *~ped-~ (“foot”) is shared with English ~foot~ and Greek ~poús~. The opposite verb was ~impedīre~ (“to entangle the feet”), which gave English ~impede~, and French ~empêcher~ comes from the related ~impedicāre~. English ~expedite~ comes from ~expedīre~ too.

From freeing the feet, the sense moved to clearing an obstacle and getting something out of the way. ~Expédier~ thus came to mean to dispatch: to send off goods or letters, and also to dispatch business quickly, as when one ~expédie~ a task or a visitor. In slang, to ~expédier~ someone can mean to send him packing, or worse. The family includes ~expédition~ (a shipment, or a voyage with a goal), ~expéditeur~ (“sender”), ~expéditif~ (“quick”) and ~expédient~ (“a way out of a difficulty”). More distant cousins from the same root *~ped-~ are ~pied~ and ~pédale~.
en.expérimenter:
From Latin ~experimentare~, a late verb built on ~experimentum~ (“a trial, a proof”), itself from the verb ~experiri~ (“to try, to put to the test”). That verb is ~ex-~ (“out, thoroughly”) joined to a lost simple verb *~periri~ (“to try, to risk”), whose root survives in ~periculum~ (“trial, danger”). The deeper Proto-Indo-European source is debated: it is often traced to *~per-~ (“to go through, to cross”), though some, like De Vaan, prefer *~perh₃-~ tied to ~pario~ (“to bring forth”). Cognate Latin verbs from the same family include ~comperire~ and ~reperire~ (“to find out”). Through the “going through” sense, English ~peril~ and ~experience~ belong to the same web.

The Latin verb meant to know a thing by living through it, so to experiment and to experience were one idea. French long kept both senses in ~expérimenter~, and the noun ~expérience~ still serves for both a scientific trial and lived experience. From the same root grew ~péril~, ~périlleux~, and ~expert~ (one who has been tested). The doubling of meaning is no accident: to the Romans, true knowledge was what you had risked something to learn.
en.exsuder:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~exsūdāre~ (“to sweat out, to exude”), made of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~sūdāre~ (“to sweat”), so that the verb is literally “to sweat out.” Compare the inherited ~suer~: the same Latin verb ~sūdāre~ came into French twice over, once by ordinary sound change and once, with its prefix, by the learned route.

~Exsuder~ is technical. It is used of resin, moisture or fluids that seep out through a surface, in botany, medicine and geology. The family is large: ~suer~, ~sueur~ and ~sudation~ come from the simple verb, and ~exsudation~ and ~exsudat~ from the prefixed one. English ~exude~ is borrowed from the same Latin ~exsūdāre~.
en.extasier: Built on ~extase~ with the verbal ending ~-ier~, in the sense of being in ecstasy or raving about something. French Wiktionary instead points to the Ancient Greek word behind ~extase~, ~ἔκστασις~ (~ékstasis~, “transport”). The two accounts fit together: the noun comes from the Greek word, and the verb was formed on the noun.
en.exterminer:
From Latin ~extermināre~ (“to drive out, banish, cast out”). The Latin verb is generally analyzed as ~ex-~ (“out of”) plus ~terminus~ (“boundary, limit”), so to ~exterminer~ was originally to push someone beyond the borders. The same Latin ~terminus~ gave French ~terme~, ~terminer~ and ~terminal~, and English borrowed the verb as ~exterminate~.

The modern sense is far harsher than the Latin one. Where ~extermināre~ meant to expel, French ~exterminer~ means to destroy completely, to wipe out, whether people, animals or pests. The step from “driving beyond the limit” to “leaving nothing behind” is a natural one, but the sources consulted do not describe how it came about, so it is best taken as a sense shift rather than a documented story. The related noun ~extermination~ comes from the same Latin family.
en.externaliser: ~Externaliser~ is borrowed from English ~externalize~, itself built from ~external~ plus ~-ize~, which French spells ~-iser~. The ~-al-~ betrays the English origin, since the French adjective is ~externe~ with no ~-al~. The meaning has also shifted: English ~externalize~ does not mean “to outsource,” whereas French ~externaliser~ does, in the business sense of handing a task to an outside firm. It is a modern word, formed in English and adapted into French.
en.extirper:
Borrowed from Latin ~exstirpāre~ (“to uproot”), formed from ~ex-~ (“out of”) and ~stirps~ (“stump, root”). In Old French the verb appears as ~estreper~, according to French Wiktionary, and English Wiktionary lists ~étréper~ as a doublet of ~extirper~, so the same Latin verb reached French in more than one form. Related descendants elsewhere include Italian ~estirpare~, Spanish ~extirpar~ and English ~extirpate~, all learned forms close to the Latin.

In French the verb means to pull something out with effort, and it also serves for figurative uprooting, as of a vice or an error. The learned spelling with ~x~ and ~p~ keeps the shape of the Latin ~ex-~ + ~stirps~ visible, while ~estreper~ is the Old French form of the same verb.
en.extorquer:
Borrowed from Latin ~extorquēre~ (“to wrench out, to obtain by force”), a learned verb. Old French had its own inherited descendant of the same Latin verb, ~estordre~, which came from a Vulgar Latin form *~extorcere~. The Latin verb is built from ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~torquēre~ (“to twist”), so the underlying image is of twisting something out of someone's grasp.

The root ~torquēre~ is a productive family in French. Its inherited branch gives ~tordre~ (“to twist”), and its learned branch gives ~torsion~ and ~extorsion~ (“the act of extorting”), the noun that belongs directly to ~extorquer~. English borrowed the verb as ~extort~ and the noun as ~extortion~. In modern French, ~extorquer~ is a formal word, used of money, a signature, a confession or a promise obtained by threat, violence or deceit.
en.extrader:
Built from the prefix ~ex-~ (“out of”) and the Latin verb ~tradere~ (“to hand over, deliver”), according to French Wiktionary. Latin ~tradere~ is generally analyzed as ~trans-~ (“across”) plus ~dare~ (“to give”), so the verb is, etymologically, to give across and out. The compound is a learned formation, built from Latin pieces rather than inherited, and it belongs to the language of law: to ~extrader~ is to hand a person accused or convicted of a crime over to the authorities of another state that claims them.

The Latin verb ~tradere~ has a rich family in French. Inherited through Old French, it became ~trahir~ (“to betray”), with ~trahison~ and ~traître~ following. Learned borrowings include ~tradition~ (“a handing down”) and ~extradition~, the noun that names the legal act. ~Dare~ itself, the second element, underlies ~rendre~ (from Latin ~reddere~, ~re-~ + ~dare~) as well as other compounds. So ~extrader~ and ~trahir~ are two verbs from one Latin parent: one is used of handing a person over to justice, the other of betraying.
en.extraire:
From Latin ~extrahere~ (“to draw out, to drag forth”), compounded of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~trahere~ (“to pull, to draw”). The form ~extraire~ shows the regular Old French reshaping of ~-trahere~ on the model of ~traire~ (“to draw, to milk”). The verb ~trahere~ is traced to the Proto-Indo-European root *~tragʰ-~ (“to draw, to drag”); it left Italian ~trarre~ and the learned ~estrarre~, Spanish ~traer~, and is held — though the correspondence is debated — to be akin to English ~draw~ and ~drag~.

The sense is wonderfully concrete: ~extrahere~ meant to haul something physically out — a tooth, a thorn, an army from a trap. French kept that literal pull (to ~extraire~ a tooth, ore from a mine, juice from a fruit) and added abstract ones, from extracting a passage out of a book to taking a square root in mathematics. The participle stem ~tract-~ of ~trahere~ seeded a huge family in French: ~trait~, ~traiter~, ~traîner~, ~attirer~, ~abstraire~, ~soustraire~, ~distraire~, and the bookish ~extraction~ and ~extrait~ — all turning on the idea of drawing or pulling.
en.extrapoler: ~Extrapoler~ was formed in French on ~interpoler~ by swapping its first element, ~inter-~, for ~extra-~ (“outside”). French Wiktionary says it properly meant “to strike out interpolations”. The modern sense, “to extend beyond the known data”, is the one in current use, but the sources at hand do not trace how the verb moved from the one meaning to the other.
en.extravaguer: Formed from the adjective ~extravagant~, reinterpreted as a present participle, so that a verb ~extravaguer~ (“to talk nonsense, to rave”) was drawn out of it. The adjective ~extravagant~ itself rests on Latin ~extra~ (“outside”) and ~vagari~ (“to wander”). The verb is a learned, rare word, and ~extravagant~ remains the common French relative.
en.extravaser:
Formed in French from Latin ~extrā~ (“outside”) and ~vās~ (“vessel, container”), on the model of ~transvaser~, with the prefix swapped. Where ~transvaser~ means to pour a liquid from one container into another, ~extravaser~ means to escape or be driven out of the container altogether. The Latin noun ~vās~ (plural ~vāsa~) denoted a vessel of any kind. The prefix ~extrā~ is the adverb and preposition “outside,” a form of ~ex~ (“out of”).

The verb is a learned, mostly medical word: blood, lymph or another fluid ~s'extravase~ when it leaks out of the vessels that contain it into the surrounding tissue. The noun ~extravasation~ is the corresponding term. The family of ~vās~ in French is wide. It includes ~vase~, ~vaisselle~, ~vaisseau~, which means both a ship and a blood vessel, and ~transvaser~, the verb on which ~extravaser~ was modeled. English ~extravasate~ is a close parallel.
en.exténuer:
Taken from Latin ~extenuāre~ (“to make thin, to diminish, to weaken”). The Latin verb is built on ~ex-~ (“out, thoroughly”) and the adjective ~tenuis~ (“thin”), so ~extenuāre~ meant to thin something out until almost nothing was left. English borrowed the same verb as ~extenuate~, and the adjective ~tenuis~ also stands behind English ~tenuous~ and ~attenuate~.

The French verb keeps the Latin senses of thinning and weakening, but its common modern sense is stronger: to exhaust, to wear someone out completely. It is met most often as the participle ~exténué~ (“worn out”). Two French words come from the same Latin adjective ~tenuis~: ~ténu~ (“fine, slender”) and ~atténuer~ (“to lessen, to soften”). English ~extenuate~ has stayed closer to the Latin meaning, as in “extenuating circumstances,” where a fault is made to look lighter. One Latin verb has thus produced a French verb of fatigue and an English verb of excuse.
en.extérioriser: Formed from ~extérieur~ and the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to make outward,” hence to show or express what was inward. English Wiktionary treats the base as Latin ~exterior~ (“more outside”) and compares French ~intérioriser~, its opposite. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which first transcribed Greek verbs, and it now forms verbs meaning “make or turn into.”
en.exulcérer: ~Exulcérer~ is traced in two ways. English Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~exulcerāre~, while French Wiktionary treats it as ~ulcérer~ with the prefix ~ex-~. The two views are compatible, since the Latin verb is itself ~ex-~ + ~ulcerāre~. The base ~ulcérer~ is a learned borrowing from ~ulcerāre~ (“to cause an ulcer”), from ~ulcus~ (“sore, ulcer”), which is generally linked to Greek ~hélkos~ (“wound”). ~Exulcérer~ means to make sore, to irritate a wound, and it is a medical and literary word that is much rarer than its base ~ulcérer~.
en.exulter:
From Middle French ~exulter~, borrowed from Latin ~exsultāre~ (“to leap”), a frequentative of ~exsiliō~ (“to jump up”). The Latin verb is built from ~ex-~ (“out, up”) and ~salīre~ (“to leap”). The simple verb ~exsiliō~ named a single jump upward, while the frequentative form evokes repeated, vigorous leaping. English ~exult~ is a borrowing of the same Latin verb, so the two languages took the learned word rather than letting it evolve in speech.

The Latin base ~salīre~ is the root of a lively French family. ~Saillir~ (“to jut out”) and ~saillant~ come directly from it; ~assaillir~ (“to assault”) and ~tressaillir~ (“to start, to shudder”) are formed on it; and ~sauter~ comes from ~saltāre~, the frequentative of ~salīre~ and a parallel to ~exsultāre~. French ~exulter~ lost the physical leap and kept only the leap of the heart: to rejoice openly, to be overjoyed. It is a literary word, used of triumph or intense joy, and it sits at the formal end of the register, far from the everyday ~sauter~ that shares its ancestry.
en.exécrer:
Borrowed from Latin ~exsecrārī~ (“to detest, to curse”), which French Wiktionary derives from ~ex-~ and ~sacer~ (“sacred”). The vowel of ~sacer~ changed from ~a~ to ~e~ inside the compound, the same alternation seen in ~consacrer~ and ~consécration~. The learned form keeps the Latin shape almost intact, and the verb means to loathe, to hold in horror.

The Latin family goes back to ~sacer~, and the French descendants include ~sacré~, ~sacrer~, ~consacrer~, ~sacrifice~ and ~sacerdoce~, with ~exécration~ for the abhorrence itself and ~exécrable~ for what deserves it. English has ~execrate~ and ~execrable~ from the same verb. In modern French ~exécrer~ is a strong, rather literary word, a step beyond ~détester~.
en.exécuter:
From Latin ~exsecūtus~, the past participle of ~exsequī~ (“to follow out, to pursue to the end, to carry through”), compounded from ~ex-~ (“out, thoroughly”) and ~sequī~ (“to follow”). Latin ~sequī~ rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”), one of the most fertile roots in the European languages. Italian ~eseguire~ and Spanish ~ejecutar~ are cognates; through the same ~sequī~, French is kin with English ~execute~, ~sequence~, ~pursue~, and ~suite~.

The core image is following a thing all the way through to its end — and from “to follow through” came “to carry out, to accomplish.” The grim sense of “to put to death” is a specialization: to ~exécuter~ a sentence was to carry it out, and the phrase contracted onto the prisoner. The reflexive ~s'exécuter~ keeps the gentler meaning, “to comply, to do what is required.” The root ~sequī~ scatters across French: ~suivre~ (“to follow”), ~suite~, ~conséquence~, ~poursuivre~, ~persécuter~, ~obséquieux~, and ~second~ (“following, the one that follows first”). Modern relatives of ~exécuter~ itself include ~exécution~, ~exécutif~, ~exécutant~, ~exécutable~, and ~inexécutable~.
en.fabriquer:
Attested from the twelfth century, ~fabriquer~ is a learned reshaping of Latin ~fabricāre~ (“to build, to construct, to fashion”), itself derived from ~fabrica~ (“workshop, craft, skilled production”) and ultimately from ~faber~ (“artisan, smith, worker in hard materials”). ~Faber~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~fafro-~ and probably to a Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰabʰ-~ (“to fit together, to be skilful”). Cognate with English ~forge~ and ~fabric~, and — through that same root — with Armenian ~darbin~ (“smith”).

The popular, inherited descendant of ~fabricāre~ in French is in fact ~forger~ (by way of ~fabrica~ → ~faverge~ → ~forge~): ~fabriquer~ and ~forger~ are doublets, one borrowed from the books, the other worn smooth by centuries of speech. The learned form kept the broad Latin sense of skilled making, which is why ~fabriquer~ today covers honest manufacture as readily as the dishonest kind — one can ~fabriquer~ a chair or ~fabriquer~ a false alibi. The shared workshop root survives across French in ~fabrique~, ~fabrication~, ~fabricant~, ~préfabriqué~, and ~forgeron~, every one of them, at bottom, a thing made by a skilled hand.
en.fabuler:
Borrowed from Latin ~fābulārī~ (“to talk, to chat”), a deponent verb built on ~fābula~ (“talk, story”), itself from ~fārī~ (“to speak”). The word fell out of use in French and is absent from the dictionaries of the Académie française and from Littré. It returned in the twentieth century, tied to the noun ~fabulation~. It has a doublet in ~hâbler~ (“to brag, to talk big”), which came by a longer route, through Spanish ~hablar~, from the same Latin verb.

Because its revival is recent, ~fabuler~ sounds modern. It means to invent stories, often to bend reality, and psychology uses it for confabulation. The French family around ~fābula~ is rich: ~fable~, ~fabuleux~, ~fabuliste~, ~affabulation~ and ~fabulation~. English has ~fable~ and ~fabulous~, and Spanish ~hablar~ (“to speak”) shows how far the Latin verb traveled in meaning, from telling tales to ordinary speech.
en.facetter: A denominal verb: ~facette~ plus the ending ~-er~, “to cut facets on”, as a jeweler does to a gemstone. The noun ~facette~ is itself a French formation, ~face~ plus the diminutive suffix ~-ette~, so a facet is literally a little face. The verb therefore rests on two layers of ordinary French suffixation, and its ultimate source is the Latin ~facies~ behind ~face~.
en.faciliter:
From Italian ~facilitare~ (“to make easy”), borrowed in the sixteenth century, from Italian ~facile~ (“easy”), from Latin ~facilis~ (“easy, feasible”). The adjective ~facilis~ was built from the verb ~facere~ (“to do, to make”) plus the suffix ~-ilis~ — literally “do-able” — and traces, through Proto-Italic *~fakiō~, to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, to place, to do”). The same root gives Greek ~tithēmi~ (“I place”) and English ~do~ and ~deed~.

The core idea has always been ease: to ~faciliter~ something is to render it ~facile~, to smooth its path. French already had the learned adjective ~facile~ when it reached across the Alps for the Italian verb, Italy being the prestige source of so much Renaissance vocabulary. The fertile root *~dʰeh₁-~ — “to do, to make” — seeded a vast French family far beyond ease: ~faire~ itself, ~facteur~, ~facture~, ~faculté~, ~difficile~ (literally “not easy”), and ~fait~, the bare past participle “done” that became the noun “fact.” Even ~affaire~ (à + ~faire~, “to do”) and the suffix ~-fier~ in countless verbs descend from this same Latin ~facere~. To facilitate, then, is etymologically to make the making easy.
en.facturer: Formed in French from the noun ~facture~ and the ending ~-er~, in the sense “to provide with an invoice, to bill.” The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin ~factūra~ (“a making, a manufacture”), from ~facere~ (“to make, to do”). It is a doublet of the Old French ~faiture~, the form that developed naturally from the same Latin word. In French, ~facture~ came to name the itemized bill for goods supplied, and ~facturer~ is the act of drawing it up or charging an amount on it.
en.fagoter: ~Fagoter~ is formed from the noun ~fagot~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~fagot~ comes from Old French ~fagot~, inherited through Middle French; it names a bundle of sticks. The verb has the matching sense of binding into a bundle, and a figurative one, to dress up. The sources give no further account of how the second sense arose.
en.faiblir: ~Faiblir~ is formed from the adjective ~faible~ and the verb ending ~-ir~, in the familiar sense “to become weak”. The adjective comes through Old French ~feble~ and ~foible~ from Vulgar Latin *~febilis~, a dissimilated form of Latin ~flēbilis~ (“worthy of tears, lamentable”). The learned doublet ~flébile~ was borrowed later, and English ~feeble~ is a relative.
en.failler: Formed from the noun ~faille~ (“crack, fault”). Sources differ on that noun. One account makes it a verbal noun of ~faillir~.
