Another derives it from Old French ~faille~, of obscure origin, perhaps borrowed from Old Frankish. Middle Dutch ~falie~ is probably a loan from French. So the verb means to crack or fissure, and its deepest origin is uncertain.
en.faillir:
From Old French ~faillir~ (“to be lacking, to fail, to err”), from Vulgar Latin *~fallīre~, a remodelling of Classical Latin ~fallere~ (“to deceive, to trick, to escape notice”). The Latin verb is often traced to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “to stumble, to deceive,” and it is plausibly cognate with Ancient Greek ~σφάλλω~ (~sphállō~, “to make stumble, to trip up”), though the precise reconstruction is disputed. Through Latin ~fallere~, ~faillir~ is kin to Italian ~fallire~ (“to fail, to go bankrupt”) and Spanish ~fallar~, and, by way of Old French, to English ~fail~ and ~fault~.

The sense shifted from deceiving someone to letting them down, then to falling short oneself. French kept a vivid trace of the older meaning: ~il s'en faut~ (“it is lacking”) and the impersonal ~falloir~ (“to be necessary”) spring from the very same Latin ~fallere~, the idea of something missing hardening into the idea of something required. Modern ~faillir~ is now used above all with an infinitive to mean “to nearly do” — ~j'ai failli tomber~, “I almost fell” — a ghost of failure that never quite happened. The same family yields ~faute~, ~faillite~ (“bankruptcy”), ~défaillir~, ~infaillible~, and the borrowed ~fallacieux~.
en.fainéanter: Formed from ~fainéant~ and the infinitive ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary analyzes ~fainéant~ as ~fait~ (“does”) + ~néant~ (“nothing”), while English Wiktionary says it comes from ~feignant~, the present participle of ~feindre~ (“to feign”), remotivated by folk etymology. Scheler distinguishes the two words, though the similarity of sound and sense made ~feignant~ a popular synonym of ~fainéant~. The verb means “to idle about.”
en.faire:
From Old French ~faire~, from Latin ~facere~ (“to make, to do”), from Proto-Italic *~fakiō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, place, set”). Romance cousins include Italian ~fare~ and Spanish ~hacer~. Through the same root come Greek ~títhēmi~ (“I place,” source of ~thesis~ and ~theme~), German ~tun~, and English ~do~ and ~deed~ — so the French “to make” and the English “to do” are, deep down, the same word.

The shift from “to put, set” to “to make, do” is natural enough: to make a thing is to set it in place. French ~faire~ swallowed an enormous range of senses, from manufacturing to weather (~il fait beau~) to causation (~faire faire~, “to have done”). A phonetic curiosity hides in its conjugation: the past historic ~fis~, ~fit~ comes not from the infinitive stem but from the Latin perfect ~fēcī~, whose long vowel left the telltale ~-i-~. From ~facere~ and its participle ~factum~ flow a vast progeny: ~fait~, ~façon~, ~facile~, ~facteur~, ~facture~, ~affaire~, ~défaire~, ~satisfaire~, and the learned ~-fier~ verbs (~modifier~, ~simplifier~) — every one a way of making.
en.faisander: Formed from ~faisan~ (“pheasant”) with ~-er~, plus a ~-d-~ added by analogy with words in ~-and~. The bird's name comes from Old French ~feisan~, from Latin ~phāsiānus~, which English Wiktionary traces to Ancient Greek ~φασιανός~ (~phasianós~). French Wiktionary says the Latin name means “from the Phasis,” a river of Colchis, whence the bird was supposedly brought back by Jason's companions in search of the Golden Fleece. To ~faisander~ is to hang game meat until it ripens.
en.falloir:
From Old French ~faloir~, an offshoot of ~faillir~ (“to fail, to be lacking”), from Vulgar Latin *~fallīre~, a reshaping of Classical Latin ~fallere~ (“to trip up, to deceive, to be wanting”). ~Fallere~ goes back to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “to stumble,” the same source as Greek ~sphallein~ (“to throw down, to make fall”) and Sanskrit ~skhalate~ (“he stumbles”). The impersonal ~falloir~ split off from ~faillir~ under the pull of its third-person form ~faut~ (Latin ~fallit~), remodeled on the pattern of ~valoir~.

The semantic journey is remarkable: from “to be lacking” the impersonal “it lacks” drifted into “it is needed,” and so a verb of deficiency became French's chief verb of necessity, ~il faut~ (“one must”). The notion of falling short survives across its relatives: ~défaillir~ (“to faint, to give way”), ~faillite~ (“bankruptcy,” a merchant who has failed), and ~faute~ and ~défaut~ (“fault, flaw, lack”). English borrowed the same family in ~fail~, ~fault~, ~false~, and ~fallacy~. So the polite ~il faut~ that opens a thousand French sentences is, etymologically, a quiet confession that something is missing.
en.falsifier:
French Wiktionary derives ~falsifier~ from Latin ~falsificare~, while English Wiktionary says it was formed from Latin ~falsus~ plus the learned ending ~-ifier~; the two accounts agree that it is a learned verb built on ~falsus~. ~Falsificare~ combines ~falsus~ (“false”) with ~-ficare~, a verb ending related to ~facere~ (“to make”), so the verb means “to make false”. In French, ~falsus~ also gave the everyday adjective ~faux~, and ~-ficare~ gave the suffix ~-fier~.

The verb means to alter something so as to deceive: to forge a signature, doctor accounts, adulterate a product. The family is a good example of learned and popular French side by side. The learned ~falsifier~ kept the Latin ~-s-~ and the Latin shape, while ~faux~ is the worn-down inherited form. Cognates are easy to spot in other languages, such as English ~falsify~ and Spanish ~falsificar~.
en.faluner: A denominal verb built on ~falun~, a shelly sand used as a soil dressing, with the verb ending ~-er~: to fertilize land with it. The origin of ~falun~ is uncertain. French Wiktionary suggests either “tawny silt” or a derivation from Occitan ~palun~ (as Frédéric Mistral held), while English Wiktionary gives Occitan ~falun~ as the likely source.
en.familiariser: ~Familiariser~ is built on ~familier~ with the verbal suffix ~-iser~, which makes verbs meaning “to make, to render.” French Wiktionary cites the Latin ~familiāris~ (“of the household”) as the source of ~familier~, from ~familia~ (“household”), so the verb says literally “to make someone feel at home with something.” The suffix ~-iser~ itself comes from Greek through Late Latin and is one of the most productive verb-forming endings in French. Used first of making people at ease, ~familiariser~ now mostly means to get someone used to an idea or a skill, as in ~se familiariser avec~ (“to become familiar with”).
en.fanatiser: Formed from ~fanatique~ with the verbal suffix ~-iser~: to make someone fanatical. The adjective ~fanatique~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~fānāticus~ (“inspired, in a frenzy”), said of the priests of Bellona, and derived from ~fānum~ (“temple”). The word was applied to a person who believed himself carried away by a divine fury and imagined he received revelations. The suffix ~-iser~ makes verbs meaning “to make, to render”.
en.faner:
French ~faner~ comes from Old French ~fener~ (“to make hay”), which descends from a Vulgar Latin verb *~fenāre~ built on Latin ~fenum~ (“hay”). Middle French shows the verb as ~fanir~. Occitan ~fenar~ is a parallel descendant. The root noun ~fenum~ also gave French ~foin~ (“hay”), as well as Italian ~fieno~ and Spanish ~heno~.

Today ~faner~ covers two meanings that sit close together: to turn and dry cut grass in the field, which is the old sense of “making hay,” and, of a flower or a face, to wither and lose its freshness. The old farming sense lives on in ~fenaison~ (“haymaking, hay harvest”) and in ~faneur~ (“hay-maker”), while the participle ~fané~ is the everyday word for a faded flower or a worn colour. The verb thus moved from the work of the meadow to a figure for decay, and it is a good example of an agricultural word that spread to general speech. The path between the two senses is not described in the sources, so it is best read as a plausible link, not a documented one.
en.fanfaronner: ~Fanfaronner~ is formed from the noun ~fanfaron~ (“braggart”) with the verbal ending ~-er~: to act the braggart, to swagger. The noun was borrowed from Spanish ~fanfarrón~, which is perhaps related to Arabic ~farfār~ (“chatterer”); French Wiktionary states the Arabic origin more firmly, English Wiktionary only as a possibility. The noun ~fanfare~ is a relative, so the family that includes the brass flourish also includes the swaggerer.
en.fantasmer: ~Fantasmer~ is a denominal verb formed from ~fantasme~ and the ending ~-er~, with the sense “to indulge in fantasies”. The noun ~fantasme~ was borrowed from Latin ~phantasma~ (“apparition, specter”), which in turn comes from Greek ~phántasma~ (“apparition”). It is a doublet of ~fantôme~, the older popular form of the same word. French Wiktionary notes that the noun spread widely in the twentieth century through psychoanalysis, which is the register in which the verb is most at home today.
en.farcir:
From Latin ~farcīre~ (“to cram, to stuff”), inherited through Old French. Its compound ~infarcire~ (“to stuff into”) has a past participle ~infarctus~, which lies behind the medical term ~infarctus~ (“infarct,” a region of tissue clogged and cut off from its blood supply). English took the same medical word as ~infarct~. The sources give no firmly established deeper root, so the chain stops at Latin.

The French noun ~farce~ (“stuffing”) comes from the same Latin verb, and it gave English ~farce~. The theatrical sense is usually explained as follows: in the Middle Ages, short comic scenes were “stuffed” into the solemn performances of religious plays, and the name of the filling came to name the genre. A farce is thus, etymologically, a stuffing. Other French words from the same source include ~farci~, ~farcissure~ and ~infarctus~. The verb is also used figuratively, as in ~farcir un texte de citations~, to cram a text with quotations.
en.farder:
Probably from Old French ~farder~ (“to apply make-up”), via Middle French ~farder~, itself borrowed from Frankish *~farwidōn~ (“to dye, to colour”). English Wiktionary traces the Frankish verb to Proto-Germanic *~farwiþōną~ and *~farwō~ (“colour”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~perḱ-~ (“motley, coloured”). Germanic relatives include Old High German ~farwjan~, German ~färben~ (“to dye”) and ~Farbe~ (“colour”), and Dutch ~verven~, along with Gothic ~farwa~ (“colour”).

The French verb narrowed that sense of colouring to the face: ~farder~ means to put on make-up, and ~se farder~ to make oneself up. By extension it also means to disguise or dress up the truth. The noun ~fard~ names make-up, and the expression ~sans fard~ means plainly, without disguise. The Frankish origin is given with a hedge in French Wiktionary, which also offers a plain derivation from the noun ~fard~ plus ~-er~.
en.farfouiller: Formed from ~fouiller~ (“to dig into, search”) with a prefix ~far-~ of uncertain origin; no source gives it a sense or an ancestor. The base descends from Old French ~fooiller~, probably from a reconstructed Vulgar Latin *~fodiculāre~, a diminutive of Latin ~fodicāre~ (“to pierce”), which is a frequentative of ~fodere~ (“to dig”). The same ~fodere~ gave ~fouir~. The familiar verb ~farfouiller~ means “to rummage around.”
en.fariner: ~Fariner~ is a denominal verb formed from the noun ~farine~ (“flour”) and the ending ~-er~, in the sense “to coat with flour”. The noun ~farine~ is inherited from Old French and goes back to Latin ~farīna~, itself derived from ~far~, a word for wheat, spelt or coarse grain. Behind a modern kitchen verb, then, stands an ancient word for the grain that was ground. French cooks still ~fariner~ a work surface or a piece of fish before cooking, and a floured face is called ~enfariné~.
en.farter: Formed from the noun ~fart~ (“ski wax”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, so ~farter~ means “to wax skis.” French Wiktionary says the noun ~fart~ itself comes from Norwegian. The verb is thus a French formation built on a borrowed word, in the vocabulary of skiing, a sport whose terms often came from Scandinavia.
en.fasciner:
~Fasciner~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~fascināre~ (“to bewitch, to cast the evil eye on”), which displaced the inherited Old French form ~fesnier~, the verb that would have developed naturally from the same Latin word. The Latin verb comes from the noun ~fascinum~ (“spell, evil eye”), whose own origin is uncertain. Italian ~affascinare~ and English ~fascinate~ are its relatives. French Wiktionary also gives a second account, a verb formed on ~fascine~ (“bundle, small faggot”); the sources do not reconcile the two, so the origin through ~fascināre~ is the better documented one but not the only one proposed.

The first sense was dark and magical: to fascinate was to harm or paralyze someone with a look, as the evil eye was supposed to do. The harm gradually dropped away, and what stayed was the idea of being held motionless by a gaze, which is how the modern sense, to captivate, was born. The image of a snake that fascinates its prey keeps the old meaning alive. The learned form won out over ~fesnier~, which left no descendant in modern French, and the family continues in ~fascination~ and ~fascinant~.
en.fasciser: Formed on the stem of ~fascisme~ with the suffix ~-iser~, a suffix that turns a noun into a verb meaning to convert to or impose something. ~Fasciser~ means to impose fascism on a country or a people. The noun ~fascisme~ comes from Italian ~fascismo~, itself from ~fascio~ (“bundle”), the word behind the Italian movement's name. The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs.
en.faseyer: Borrowed from Dutch ~faselen~ (“to shake, to agitate”). The French verb keeps the idea of agitation but applies it to cloth moving in the wind: it describes a sail or a flag that flaps. Both Wiktionaries give the Dutch verb as the source and trace nothing earlier, so the story begins with that borrowing.
en.fatiguer:
From Latin ~fatigāre~ (“to weary, to tire, to harass”). Within Latin the verb seems built on an unattested *~fatis~ (“weariness, exhaustion”) plus a suffixal form of ~agere~ (“to drive, to do”) — to “drive someone to exhaustion” — and it keeps company with ~affatim~ (“to satiety, enough”) and ~fessus~ (“tired”). Beyond Latin, however, the trail goes cold: the ultimate origin is classed as unknown. De Vaan rejects an older attempt to attach *~fatis~ to a PIE root *~dʰeh₁-~ “to vanish,” faulting it for vague semantics and phonology — so the deep root is genuinely uncertain, not settled.

The sense has held remarkably steady: Latin ~fatigāre~ already meant to wear down, exhaust, or pester, exactly as French ~fatiguer~ does. The figurative reaches are old too — one can ~fatiguer~ the soil by overworking it, or even (in cookery) ~fatiguer~ a salad by tossing it until the leaves go limp. From the same stem French keeps the adjective and noun ~fatigue~, ~fatigant~ (“tiring”), ~infatigable~ (“tireless”), ~défatiguer~ (“to rest, to refresh”), and the medical asthénie is unrelated, but ~fatigabilité~ is kin.
en.faucarder: Formed from the noun ~faucard~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. The verb means to cut aquatic plants, such as the weeds that choke a stream or pond. The base ~faucard~ is built on the Picard verb ~fauquer~ (“to mow”) with the suffix ~-ard~, so the word is a regional cousin of ~faucher~.
en.faucher:
French ~faucher~ is the inherited descendant of Vulgar Latin ~falcāre~ (English Wiktionary also proposes ~falciāre~, compare Italian ~falciare~), a verb built on Latin ~falx~, accusative ~falcem~ (“sickle, scythe”). The usual French sound changes explain the shape: ~al~ before a consonant became ~au~, as in ~faux~, and ~ca~ became ~cha~. English Wiktionary traces ~falx~ back to the Proto-Indo-European forms *~dhalk-~ or *~dhalg-~ (“a cutting tool”).

The verb's first sense is concrete: to cut grass or grain with a scythe, to mow. From mowing it came to cover knocking things down in one sweep, so that ~faucher~ can also mean “to mow down,” “to run over” or “to knock down.” The same Latin noun gave ~faux~ (“scythe”) and ~faucille~ (“sickle”), and the verb gave ~faucheur~ and ~faucheuse~ (“mower”). Italian ~falciare~ is a close cousin of the verb.
en.faufiler: According to French Wiktionary, ~faufiler~ is an old compound of ~fors~ (an Old French word meaning “outside,” modern ~hors~) and ~filer~ (“to spin, to draw out a thread”), with the influence of ~faux~ (“false”). The word names the sewing technique of basting, that is, stitching loosely with a temporary thread, and also means, figuratively, to slip or thread one's way through a crowd or a place. Only French Wiktionary offers an origin, and it gives no further detail.
en.fausser:
Inherited from Old French ~falser~, from Late Latin ~falsāre~ (“to falsify”), itself from Latin ~falsus~ (“false, deceptive”). Latin ~falsus~ is the participle of ~fallere~ (“to deceive”). The sound change is regular: an ~l~ before a consonant became a vowel in Old French, so ~falser~ became ~fauser~ and then ~fausser~, the same change that turned ~falsus~ into the adjective ~faux~. Italian ~falsare~, Spanish ~falsear~ and English ~false~ are relatives.

French ~fausser~ means “to make false, to distort”. It applies to a ruling or a result that is skewed, to a key or a lock that is bent, and to a sound that is off pitch, so a ~fausse note~ is a wrong note. In the fixed expression to ~fausser compagnie~ to someone is to slip away, leaving them behind. The learned verb ~falsifier~ (“to falsify”) belongs to the same Latin family.
en.fauter: Formed from the noun ~faute~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to commit a fault, to make a mistake.” The noun comes from Old French ~faute~, from Vulgar Latin *~fallita~, which stands in for Latin ~falsus~, a participle of ~fallere~ (“to deceive, to fail”). Spanish and Portuguese ~falta~ (“lack”) are cousins, and ~faute~ is a doublet of ~faillite~ (“bankruptcy”). English ~fault~ is a relative from the same French source.
en.favoriser:
From the noun ~faveur~ (“favor, goodwill”), itself from Latin ~favor~ (“favor, support, applause”), a noun built on the verb ~favēre~ (“to be favorable, to be well-disposed toward”). The verb was coined in French by attaching the productive verbal suffix ~-iser~ to the stem of ~faveur~, on the model of Latin ~favor~. Related Romance forms include Italian ~favorire~ and Spanish ~favorecer~, both expressing the same idea of granting one's favor.

Latin ~favēre~ originally belonged to the language of religion, where it meant to look kindly upon a rite, and the formula ~favēre linguīs~ (“to favor with the tongues”) actually commanded onlookers to keep a reverent silence so as not to spoil a ceremony with ill-omened words. From this notion of benevolent regard the family broadened to mean showing preference, supporting, or advantaging — the senses ~favoriser~ carries today, including a faintly negative one of unfair preferment. The same root nourishes a tight cluster of French words: ~faveur~, ~favorable~, ~favori~ (borrowed back from Italian ~favorito~), ~favoritisme~, and the everyday ~favori~ of a web browser. Even English ~favor~ and ~favorite~ are, through Old French, members of this household descended from a Roman idea of divine and social goodwill.
en.faxer: ~Faxer~ is formed from the noun ~fax~ with the verb ending ~-er~, and means to send by fax. The noun was borrowed from English ~fax~, itself a clipped form of ~facsimile~. The verb is a modern, fully regular first-conjugation coinage, built the way French routinely turns a technical noun into an action.
en.fayoter: Formed from the noun ~fayot~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Occitan ~faiòu~ or ~faviòu~, from Latin ~phaseolus~ (“bean”). It passed from the kitchen to the barracks: ~fayot~ came to mean a re-enlisted soldier, which the Académie explains by the idea that such a man returned to the army as beans return to the menu. The verb, built on that slang noun, is the colloquial one meaning to fawn over superiors.
en.façonner: Formed in French from ~façon~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning “to give a shape, to work on.” The noun ~façon~ (“way, shape, manner”) comes through Old French and Middle French from Latin ~factiōnem~, the accusative of ~factiō~ (“a making, power of doing”), from ~facere~ (“to make”). French ~faction~ is a learned doublet of the same Latin word. So ~façonner~ is, at heart, “to put into a manner of making.”
en.feindre:
~Feindre~ is inherited from Old French ~feindre~, also spelled ~faindre~, from Latin ~fingere~ (“to shape, to form”). Being inherited, the word was reshaped by centuries of sound change, while its learned relatives kept a form closer to the Latin. Italian ~fingere~ and Spanish ~fingir~ come from the same Latin verb. English ~feign~ was taken from the Old French stem, and English ~fiction~ comes from the Latin family of ~fingere~.

French Wiktionary notes that the shift from “shaping” to “pretending” is the same one seen in ~fiction~, from Latin ~fictio~ (“a shaping”). To feign is therefore, at root, to fashion something. The noun ~feinte~ (“feint”), the adjective ~feint~, ~figure~, ~figurer~, ~effigie~ and ~fictif~ all belong to the same family, as does the learned ~fiction~ itself.
en.feinter: ~Feinter~ is formed from the noun ~feinte~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~feinte~ is the feminine past participle of ~feindre~ used as a noun. French Wiktionary notes that ~feinter~ is not an exact synonym of ~feindre~, and sees in it a general tendency of speakers to prefer regular first-group verbs to third-group ones, much as ~solutionner~ has gained ground against ~résoudre~.
en.fendiller: Formed from ~fendre~ (“to split”) with the suffix ~-iller~, which gives a small, repeated action: to crack in many fine lines, as with old paint or dry earth. English Wiktionary also floats a less likely route from a Vulgar Latin *~findiclāre~, from Latin ~findō~, and compares Old Occitan ~fendilhar~. Either way the root is the Latin verb ~findere~ (“to split”), which also gave Italian ~fendere~ and Spanish ~hender~. The suffix works the same way in ~sautiller~ (from ~sauter~) and ~mordiller~ (from ~mordre~).
en.fendre:
From Old French ~fendre~, inherited from Latin ~findere~ (“to split, to open, to burst”), from Proto-Italic *~findō~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰeyd-~ (“to split”). Latin ~findere~ survives in other Romance languages: Italian ~fendere~ and Spanish ~hender~ are its descendants. English has the same root in its native verb ~bite~, a Germanic cousin from the same Indo-European root. Italian and Spanish thus keep the Latin verb as an everyday word, while English reached the same ancestor by a native route.

French ~fendre~ kept the core sense of cutting something open along a line, as in chopping wood or cracking a surface. The family is large. The inherited line gave ~fente~ (“slit, crack”), ~fendu~, ~fendiller~ (“to crack finely”) and ~refendre~. The Latin participle ~fissus~ fed the learned words ~fissure~, ~fission~ and ~fissile~, which French and English share.
en.fenêtrer: ~Fenêtrer~ is a denominal verb: French Wiktionary says it is formed on the noun ~fenêtre~ (“window”), with the usual verbal ending ~-er~. It means “to make openings for windows” or “to fit with windows.” The noun comes from Latin ~fenestra~ (“window”), which also gave Italian ~finestra~. English kept the Latin root in the learned word ~defenestrate~, literally “to throw out of a window.”
en.ferler: The origin of ~ferler~ is uncertain. French Wiktionary proposes, with a hedge, that it comes from Latin ~ferula~, source of ~férule~, and refers the reader to ~ferlet~. English Wiktionary likewise links it to Old French ~ferlier~ and offers Latin ~ferula~ only as a possibility. The modern verb means “to furl” or “to roll up” a sail. No more than this can be said with confidence.
en.fermenter: Both French and English Wiktionary describe ~fermenter~ as a borrowing from Latin ~fermentāre~ (“to ferment, to leaven”), not as a verb formed inside French. The Latin verb is built on the noun ~fermentum~ (“leaven, yeast”). That same noun gave French ~ferment~ and ~fermentation~. The verb has close relatives in Spanish ~fermentar~, Italian ~fermentare~ and English ~ferment~, all descended from the same Latin family.
en.fermer:
From Old French ~fermer~ (“to close, to fasten, to make firm, to build”), from Latin ~firmare~ (“to strengthen, to make firm, to secure”), a verb built on the adjective ~firmus~ (“firm, steadfast, solid”). ~firmus~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰer-~ (“to hold, to support”), the same root that gives Sanskrit ~dharma~ (“that which upholds, law, order”). Through Latin ~firmus~, the French verb is cognate with Italian ~fermare~ and Spanish ~firmar~ (“to sign”), and with English ~firm~ and ~confirm~.

The semantic leap is the surprise here: ~firmare~ meant “to make firm, to secure,” and a door was secured by being fastened shut — so “to make fast” slid into “to close.” In Late Latin the closing sense took hold, and Old French ~fermer~ went on to displace the older ~clore~ (from Latin ~claudere~), which became homonymically tangled with ~clouer~ (“to nail”) and retreated into technical use. A folk etymology once linked ~fermer~ to ~fer~ (“iron”), imagining iron bars, but scholars reject it. The same root *~dʰer-~ underlies ~ferme~ (“firm,” and the noun “farm”), ~fermeté~, ~affermir~, ~confirmer~, and ~fermeture~ — and even the agricultural ~ferme~ traces back through the idea of a fixed, secured holding of land.
en.ferrailler: ~Ferrailler~ is formed from ~ferraille~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~ferraille~ (“scrap iron”) is itself made of ~fer~ (“iron”) and the suffix ~-aille~, and ~fer~ descends from Latin ~ferrum~. The verb has senses on both sides of the trade: to deal in or recycle scrap metal, and to cross swords with someone.
en.ferrer:
From Old French ~ferrer~, which goes back to Late Latin *~ferrāre~, known from the participle ~ferrātus~ (“fitted with iron”), itself from Latin ~ferrum~ (“iron”). The sources differ slightly on the route: one has the French verb inherited from the Late Latin form, the other allows that it was formed afresh in Old French from ~fer~ (“iron”). Either way the chain is short. Italian ~ferrare~, Catalan and Portuguese ~ferrar~ and Spanish ~herrar~ (where Latin f- became h-) are its sisters, and English ~farrier~ comes from Old French ~ferrier~, from Latin ~ferrārius~ (“blacksmith”).

The core sense is to fit with iron: to ~ferrer~ a horse is to shoe it, and anglers use the verb for setting the hook in a fish's mouth. Old French already had the ~chemin ferré~, found in Chrétien de Troyes, a road laid with stones on a firm bed so that one did not sink into it. The participle also took a figurative turn: someone ~ferré~ on a subject is solidly armed with knowledge, as in être ferré en histoire. ~Fer~ itself gives ~ferraille~, ~ferronnerie~ and ~maréchal-ferrant~, the farrier.
en.ferrouter: A modern blend of ~chemin de fer~ (“railway”) and ~route~ (“road”). To ~ferrouter~ is to carry road vehicles, such as trucks, on trains, so that the load travels partly by rail and partly by road. The word is a technical term of freight transport.
en.fertiliser: From ~fertile~ plus the suffix ~-iser~, which means “to make A”: to ~fertiliser~ is to make land fertile. The adjective ~fertile~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~fertilis~ (“fruitful”). The suffix ~-iser~ is Late Latin ~-izāre~ in origin, a Greek-derived ending that French has used productively for centuries to build verbs from adjectives and nouns. The result is the usual word for enriching soil, and it also applies figuratively to anything made more productive, such as the mind.
en.fesser:
~Fesser~ is inherited from Middle French ~fesser~, a derivative of Old French ~faisse~ (“band, tie”), which comes from Latin ~fascia~ (“band, bandage”). The Late Latin verb ~fasciāre~ (“to wrap with bands”) is a close relative, and Old French also had a verb ~faissier~. English borrowed ~fascia~ directly from Latin, so the word reached English by a learned route, while ~fesser~ came down the inherited one.

The sources do not agree on the sense. By one account, the verb first meant “to beat with a rod”, and only later, by association with ~fesse~ (“buttock”), came to mean “to strike on the buttocks.” English Wiktionary agrees that the spelling and the sense were influenced by ~fesse~, which is unrelated to ~fascia~. Other sources reject this and derive ~fesser~ simply from ~fesse~. They point out that Old French ~faissier~ meant “to wrap in bands” or “to stripe a cloth,” and that the sense “to beat with a rod” does not appear there. Today the verb means “to spank.”
en.festonner: ~Festonner~ is formed from the noun ~feston~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, which turns a noun into a verb meaning to provide with, or work into, that noun. The noun ~feston~ was borrowed from Italian ~festone~ (“festive ornament”), a garland-like decoration. To ~festonner~ something is therefore to trim or edge it with festoons, or with scalloped, garland-like curves.
en.festoyer:
From Old French ~festeer~, later ~festeier~ and ~festoyer~, which English Wiktionary traces to a Vulgar Latin *~festizāre~; French Wiktionary instead treats it as derived from the Old French noun ~feste~ with the suffix ~-oier~. The two accounts agree on the base, the noun ~feste~ (“feast, festival”), which is the ancestor of modern ~fête~ and comes from Latin ~fēsta~. The verb thus means “to make a feast” or “to celebrate with a banquet.”

A small spelling detail records the verb's history. According to French Wiktionary, ~festoyer~ had dropped out of use and was revived around the eighteenth century, which is why it kept its ~s~ while ~fête~ lost it and took a circumflex. The same family includes ~fête~, ~festin~, ~festival~ and ~festif~, and English took the noun as ~feast~ from Old French ~feste~, and later ~fete~ from modern French. Today ~festoyer~ is a literary verb for feasting and merrymaking, and it also appears in the sense of welcoming guests with a banquet.
en.feuiller: Formed from the noun ~feuille~ (“leaf”) plus the verbal ending ~-er~, so ~feuiller~ means to put out leaves, to come into leaf. ~Feuille~ is inherited from Middle French ~feuille~ and Old French ~fueille~, which come from Late Latin ~folia~, originally the plural of Latin ~folium~ (“leaf”). The Latin word is itself probably traced back to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “to blossom”. ~Folium~ also survives as the learned doublet ~folio~, and cognates include Spanish ~hoja~, Italian ~foglia~ and Portuguese ~folha~.
en.feuilleter: Formed from the noun ~feuillet~ (“leaf of a book, thin sheet”) with the verb ending ~-er~, although English Wiktionary derives it straight from ~feuille~. ~Feuillet~ is a diminutive of ~feuille~ (“leaf”), from Old French ~feuil~, from Latin ~folia~, the plural of ~folium~ (“leaf”). The verb is attested as early as the thirteenth century in a different sense, and it developed two uses from the image of a thin leaf: to turn the pages of a book quickly, and to roll out dough into thin layers, as in ~pâte feuilletée~ (“puff pastry”). English ~folio~ and ~foil~ are cousins from the same Latin word.
en.feuler:
The origin of ~feuler~ is obscure. French Wiktionary says it is probably an onomatopoeia, like most animal cries. Littré recorded the verb in the form ~félir~ and derived it from Latin ~felis~ (“cat”). That derivation is only an old proposal, and the more cautious view is to treat the word as imitative.

Either way, the verb belongs to the cat world: it is the specialized word for the cry of a cat or a tiger. If the Latin connection were right, ~feuler~ would be a distant relative of ~félin~ (“feline”), which comes from the Latin adjective of ~felis~. If the word is imitative, no ancestor needs to be sought, since the sound itself would have given the word its shape.
en.feutrer: Formed from ~feutre~ (“felt”) plus the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense “to make into felt” and, by extension, “to muffle.” The noun comes from Old French ~feltre~, from Frankish *~filtir~ (“coarse cloth”), from Proto-Germanic *~filtizō~. It is cognate with English ~felt~ and German ~Filz~. French Wiktionary links the root more distantly to Latin ~pellō~ (“to beat, to drive”), since wool fibers must be pounded to make them mat together.
en.fiabiliser: ~Fiabiliser~ is formed from ~fiable~ with the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to make A,” so it means to make more reliable. The adjective ~fiable~ is a reworking of Old French ~feavle~ (around 1190), derived from ~se fier~ (“to trust”); Old French also had ~feable~ (“sure, faithful”), from ~fei~ (“faith”). Rare after the 17th century, ~fiable~ was revived around 1968 for a mechanism unlikely to fail, then used more broadly to mean “credible.”
en.fiancer: ~Fiancer~ comes from Old French ~fiancer~ or ~fiancier~, a derivative of the noun ~fiance~ (“trust, faith, fidelity, assurance”) with the verb ending ~-er~. English Wiktionary adds that it passed through Middle French and compares Italian ~fidanzare~. The verb therefore began as “to pledge one's trust”, and French later narrowed it to the promise of marriage. The noun ~fiance~ belongs to the family of ~foi~ and ~confier~, descended from Latin ~fidere~ (“to trust”).
en.ficeler: Formed from ~ficelle~ (“string, twine”) plus the verb ending ~-er~, so “to tie up with string.” ~Ficelle~ probably comes from a Vulgar Latin *~filicella~, derived from Latin ~fīlum~ (“thread”). French Wiktionary also mentions a possible *~funicella~, from Latin ~funicula~ (“small rope”), but phonetic reasons argue against it, as does the fact that forms like ~aficelés~ already appear in the twelfth century.
en.fiche: A variant of ~ficher~, which became, out of social propriety, the acceptable synonym of the vulgar ~foutre~. Speakers then gave ~fiche~ an infinitive that does not match the forms of that verb, and a past participle ~fichu~, modeled on ~foutu~. This is why ~je m'en fiche~ stands beside ~je m'en fous~ with the same meaning but a gentler tone. ~Foutre~ itself comes from Latin ~futuere~.
en.ficher:
From Middle French ~ficher~ and Old French ~fichier~, itself from Vulgar Latin *~fīg(i)cāre~, a frequentative built on Latin ~fīgere~ (“to fasten, to drive in, to pierce, to nail up”). French Wiktionary lists the Latin verb's senses as running from “to plant” and “to nail” to “to post up” and “to hang”, and adds that the participle of the Latin verb also gave French ~fixer~, ~fixe~ and ~affixe~. Those words are relatives of ~ficher~, not its descendants. French Wiktionary also derives the verb from the noun ~fiche~, whereas English Wiktionary derives all of it from Old French, so the two accounts differ on how much of ~ficher~ comes from ~fiche~.

The most familiar development is the colloquial one. French Wiktionary presents ~ficher~ as a euphemism for ~foutre~, as the reshaping of the participle ~fichu~ on ~foutu~ shows. English Wiktionary likewise calls the “give a damn” sense a minced oath of ~foutre~ (“to fuck”). In phrases meaning “to give a damn” or “to do”, ~ficher~ stands in for the cruder verb. A verb whose Latin source meant to drive things in and fix them in place thus ended up as the polite stand-in for a vulgar one.
en.fidéliser: Formed from ~fidèle~ (“faithful, loyal”) + ~-iser~ (“to make, to turn into”), so “to make loyal,” especially of customers or members. The adjective ~fidèle~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~fidēlis~ (“loyal, trustworthy”), from ~fidēs~ (“faith, trust”). It replaced the inherited Old French form ~feoil~, which survives as ~féal~, and it became common only from the sixteenth century. The suffix ~-iser~ reaches French from Late Latin ~-izāre~, itself taken from Greek, and is still very productive for coining verbs from adjectives and nouns.
en.fienter: Formed from the noun ~fiente~ (“droppings, dung”) with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Vulgar Latin *~femita~, built on ~femus~, an altered form of Latin ~fimus~ (“dung, manure”). That same Latin ~fimus~ also lies behind ~fumier~, so ~fiente~ and ~fumier~ are doublets: two forms of one Latin word.
en.fier:
Inherited from Old French ~fier~, from Vulgar Latin *~fīdāre~, a reshaping of Latin ~fīdere~ (“to trust”). The Latin verb belongs to a Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰeydʰ-~ (“to trust, to persuade”), which also gave Greek ~peíthō~ (“to persuade”). The Latin word family is large: ~fīdēs~ (“trust, faith”), ~fīdus~ (“faithful”) and ~confīdere~ (“to trust fully”). English ~faith~ and ~fidelity~ are the same family, borrowed through French. Spanish ~fiar~ and Italian ~fidare~ are direct cousins of the French verb.

In French, ~fier~ meant to entrust, to hand something over in confidence, a sense kept in ~confier~ (“to entrust”). The modern verb is nearly always reflexive: ~se fier à quelqu'un~ is to trust someone, and the command ~Ne vous y fiez pas~ means “Don't trust it.” The lone ~fier~ is a trap for learners, because the adjective ~fier~ (“proud”) is an unrelated word that comes from Latin ~ferus~ (“wild, fierce”), and it shares only its spelling. The verb gives ~défier~ (“to defy”, originally to renounce trust) and ~méfier~ (“to distrust”), and the wider Latin family gives ~confiance~, ~fidèle~ and ~foi~.
en.figer:
Where ~figer~ comes from is disputed, and the two accounts run in opposite directions. By the first, which English Wiktionary adopts, the verb comes from Old French ~fegier~, itself from Vulgar Latin *~feticāre~ (“to take on the look of liver”), built on *~feticum~ (“liver”), an alteration of Latin ~ficatum~. French Wiktionary gives this as the view of some authors. By the second account, which French Wiktionary attributes to others, the order is reversed: ~foie~ comes from ~figer~, through a popular form *~figicare~ modeled on Latin ~figere~ (“to fix in the ground, to drive in, to fasten”), whose participle is ~fixus~. English Wiktionary mentions only the first account, while French Wiktionary sets the two side by side.

Because the sources disagree, the question cannot be settled here. If the first account holds, ~figer~ is a cousin of ~foie~, and the verb would originally have meant something like taking on the look of liver. If the second holds, ~figer~ belongs to the family of ~fixus~, the participle of the Latin verb ~figere~, which has to do with fastening something in place. Either way, the modern verb has the sense “to freeze” or “to set,” and in the reflexive ~se figer~ it describes something that stops moving. The sources do not allow a choice between the two origins.
en.fignoler: The origin of ~fignoler~ is uncertain, and two accounts compete. The first, going back to the dictionary of Trévoux, which wrote the verb ~fignoler~ or ~finioler~, ties it to ~fin~ (“fine”), so that it would mean to bring something to fineness. The second links it to the Savoyard Franco-Provençal ~feniola~, a diminutive of ~fèna~ (“woman”), meaning a little woman who primps, and to the verb ~feniolar~ (“to get oneself up, to preen”). Neither account is settled.
en.figurer:
From Latin ~figurare~ (“to form, to shape, to fashion”), derived from ~figura~ (“shape, form, figure”), itself built on the verb ~fingere~ (“to mould, to shape, especially in clay”). ~fingere~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeyǵʰ-~ (“to knead, to form, to build”), the same root that gives Latin ~fictus~ (“shaped, feigned”) and, in the Germanic branch, English ~dough~ and the ~-dy~ of Old English placenames. Cognate with Italian ~figurare~ and Spanish ~figurar~.

The root meaning is hands working clay, and ~figura~ kept that sculptural sense of an outline or moulded shape. From “to give shape to,” French ~figurer~ branched in several directions: to represent or depict (a drawing ~figure~ a scene), to be present in a series — to “appear in a list,” to be included among others — and, reflexively, ~se figurer~, to picture something to oneself, to imagine. The same family is rich in French: ~figure~ (face, figure), ~figuratif~, ~figurine~, ~défigurer~ (to disfigure), ~préfigurer~, and ~configurer~. Through its sibling ~fingere~ come ~feindre~ (“to feign”) and ~fiction~ — a reminder that the line between shaping something and making it up has always been thin.
en.filer:
French ~filer~ comes from Late Latin ~filare~ (“to spin into thread”), from the noun ~filum~ (“thread”); it can equally be felt as a denominal of French ~fil~ (“thread”), its inherited descendant. ~filum~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~gʷʰislo-~ (“sinew, thread”), and is cognate with Lithuanian ~gysla~ (“vein, sinew”), Proto-Slavic *~žila~ (“vein”), and Sanskrit ~jyā~ (“bowstring”) — a web of words for thin, stringy fibers.

The original sense is concrete: to spin fiber into thread, as a spider “spins” its web (~filer sa toile~) or a spinner draws out a thread. From the steady, drawn-out motion of the spindle the verb slid into senses of smooth, continuous movement — to ~filer~ is to glide along quickly, even to “slip away” — and then, by a memorable specialization, to “tail” or follow someone discreetly, paying out one's path behind them like thread. From the same ~filum~ French keeps ~fil~, ~filet~ (“net; thin stream; fillet”), ~ficelle~ (“string”), ~filature~ (“spinning mill; the act of shadowing”), ~défiler~ (“to file past”), and ~profil~ (“profile”).
en.fileter: From ~filet~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary explains ~filet~ as a diminutive of ~fil~ (“thread”) formed with the suffix ~-et~, from Latin ~filum~ (“thread”); English Wiktionary gives a different route through Old French ~filé~, the past participle of ~filer~, with a change of suffix. The verb ~fileter~ means to cut a thread on a screw or bolt, from the sense of ~filet~ as the thin ridge of a screw. The ending ~-er~ is the ordinary way of making a verb from a noun.
en.filialiser: Formed from ~filiale~ + ~-iser~, a suffix meaning “to convert into N”: ~filialiser~ is to turn a business unit into a subsidiary. The noun ~filiale~ comes from Latin ~filialis~, built on ~filius~ (“son”) with the suffix ~-alis~, which marks belonging or dependence. A subsidiary is thus, etymologically, a “filial” company that depends on its parent. The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~ and is fully productive in administrative and business French.
en.filigraner: ~Filigraner~ is formed from the noun ~filigrane~ with the ending ~-er~, which turns nouns into first-group verbs. ~Filigrane~ was borrowed from Italian ~filigrana~, a compound of ~filo~ (“thread”) and ~grana~ (“grain”), a name for delicate metalwork made of fine twisted threads dotted with tiny beads. French ~filigrane~ also names the watermark in paper, so ~filigraner~ means to decorate with filigree or to mark a sheet with a watermark.
en.filmer:
~Filmer~ is a denominal verb on the noun ~film~, which French borrowed from English ~film~ in the late 19th century as photography and cinema arrived. The English noun goes back to Middle English ~filme~ and Old English ~filmen~ (« membrane, thin skin »), from Proto-West Germanic *~filmīn~, tied to Proto-Germanic *~felma-~ (« skin, hide ») and ultimately PIE *~pel-~ (« skin, to cover »). So the word for a cinematic ~film~ began as a word for skin.

The sense « thin coating » is recorded by 1577; by 1845 it named the layer of light-sensitive gel on a photographic plate, and by 1895 the celluloid strip itself — and then, by extension, the moving picture recorded on it. French ~filmer~ inherited that final, fully cinematic sense: to ~filmer~ is to record images on film, or now digitally, to shoot a scene. From the same Germanic *~pel-~ « skin » root English keeps ~fell~ (« hide ») and ~film~ itself; French, having borrowed only the noun, built ~filmer~, ~filmage~, and ~cinéma~ around it.
en.filocher: French Wiktionary derives ~filocher~ from either ~filoche~ or ~filer~ and does not choose between them. ~Filer~ is the ordinary verb for “to spin” and, in everyday French, “to go fast” or “to follow closely,” which fits the sense of tailing someone. The ending of ~filocher~ is typical of colloquial French verbs, and the verb belongs to informal speech, where it means to follow or shadow a person.
en.filouter: Formed from ~filou~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~filou~ (“crook, swindler”) is probably a dialectal form of ~fileur~ (“spinner”), according to both French and English Wiktionary. The verb means “to swindle, to cheat,” that is, to act as a ~filou~ does.
en.filtrer: ~Filtrer~ is formed from ~filtre~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~filtre~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~filtrum~, attested in the eighth century and itself taken, according to French Wiktionary, from Frankish. It is a doublet of ~feutre~ (“felt”), the material the first filters were made of: to filter was originally to pass a liquid through a piece of felt. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and turns the noun into the verb “to pass through a filter,” a sense later extended to sounds, light, news and people.
en.finaliser: Formed from the adjective ~final~ (“last, ultimate”) with the verb suffix ~-iser~, and attested from 1936 in the sense of “to give a final form to, to bring to completion.” The adjective comes from Latin ~fīnālis~, from ~fīnis~ (“end, limit”). The suffix ~-iser~ is the learned French form of Late Latin ~-izāre~, from Greek ~-izein~. A later sense, “to complete,” is probably influenced by English ~finalize~.
en.financer:
Denominal verb from the noun ~finance~, which arose in Old French (around 1280) from the verb ~finer~ (“to bring to an end; to settle, pay”), an altered form of ~finir~ (“to finish”), with the suffix ~-ance~. All of this rests on Latin ~fīnis~ (“boundary, limit, end”). The early ~finance~ meant the ending or settling of a matter — and since settling an affair so often meant paying it off, Old French ~fin~ itself could mean “money.” Cognate with Italian ~finanza~ and Spanish ~finanza~, and — borrowed — with English ~finance~ and ~final~, all anchored in ~fīnis~.

The slide from “ending” to “money” is the heart of the story: to ~finer~ a debt was to make an end of it by payment, so the noun drifted from “settlement” to “payment,” then by the fifteenth century to “monetary resources,” as in ~trésorier des finances~ (“treasurer of finances”). Medieval Latin ~financia~ even named a tax or levy. The modern verb ~financer~ — to fund, to provide money for — is the natural offspring. From the same ~fīnis~ French keeps a broad family: ~finir~, ~fin~, ~final~, ~définir~, ~confiner~, and ~affiner~ — boundaries and endings everywhere, with money the great settler of ends.
en.financiariser: Formed from ~financier~ with the suffix ~-iser~, so the verb means to give something a financial character, to subject an activity or an economy to the logic of finance. The noun ~financier~ derives from ~finance~ with ~-ier~ and first named a person who handled public finances; the adjective appeared in 1752. The suffix ~-iser~, from Late Latin ~-izāre~, remains productive for technical and administrative verbs.
en.finasser: ~Finasser~ is formed from ~finesse~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is taken here in its sense of “cunning, trickery”, and ~finesse~ itself is built from ~fin~ (“fine, subtle”) and the suffix ~-esse~. The verb therefore means to use small tricks and shrewd manoeuvres to get one's way, with a faintly disapproving tone.
en.finir:
From Old French ~finir~ (with the variants ~fenir~ and ~finer~), from Latin ~fīnīre~ (“to limit, to bound, then to finish”), itself derived from the noun ~fīnis~ (“boundary, limit, border, end”). The deeper origin of ~fīnis~ is disputed: it is often referred — perhaps from an earlier *~fignis~ — to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeygʷ-~ (“to stick, set up”), the root behind Latin ~fīgō~ (“to fix”), a boundary being something “fixed” in the ground; an alternative links it to ~findō~ (“to split”). Cognate verbs are Italian ~finire~ and Spanish ~finir~.

The path of meaning runs from space to time: a ~fīnis~ was first a physical border between fields or peoples — hence the plural ~fīnēs~ for a country's “territory” — and from “to set a limit” the verb slid to “to bring to an end.” The same root spread widely in French: the noun ~fin~ (“end”), ~final~, ~finale~, ~finalité~, ~finir~'s cousin ~définir~ (“to define,” to set the ~fīnēs~ of a meaning) with ~définition~, ~infini~ (“endless”), ~finitude~, and the commercial ~finance~ — originally the “settling, ending” of a debt by payment.
en.fiscaliser: Formed from the adjective ~fiscal~ with the suffix ~-iser~, so ~fiscaliser~ means to subject to taxation, to make taxable. ~Fiscal~ was borrowed from Latin ~fiscālis~ (“relating to the fisc”). The verb is used mostly in administrative writing, where ~taxer~ or ~imposer~ would not be euphemistic enough, and ~fiscaliser~ is the softer choice. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~.
en.fissurer: ~Fissurer~ is formed from the noun ~fissure~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, which French inherited from Latin ~-āre~. The verb means “to crack”, that is, to open a fissure in something. The noun ~fissure~ came into Old French as a learned loan from Latin ~fissūra~ (“cleft”), a word built on the verb ~findere~ (“to split”). English ~fissure~ comes from the same Latin noun.
en.fixer:
From Latin ~fixus~, the past participle of ~figere~ (“to drive in, to plant, to fasten”). ~Figere~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeygʷ-~ (“to stick, to set up”), which also yielded, through Germanic, English ~ditch~ and ~dike~ and German ~Teich~ (“pond”) — all things dug into or stuck in the ground. The Latin participial stem ~fix-~ gave Italian ~fissare~ and Spanish ~fijar~, and the same ~figere~ produced the diminutive ~fibula~ (“clasp, brooch”), a pin that fastens.

The earliest French sense stayed close to the Latin: to ~fixer~ was to make something fast, to set it firmly in place, then to settle the eyes upon it — hence ~fixer du regard~, “to stare at.” From “to make immovable” flowed “to determine, to settle definitively,” as in ~fixer une date~ or ~fixer un prix~. In the twentieth century French re-borrowed the modern repair sense from English ~to fix~, layering a fresh meaning atop the old. From the same root come ~fixe~, ~fixation~, ~fixe~ as a noun (a regular salary), ~préfixe~, ~suffixe~, and ~crucifier~ (literally “to fasten to a cross”). To ~fixer~ something is, at bottom, to plant it where it cannot move.
en.flageller:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~flagellāre~ (“to scourge, whip”), a verb formed on ~flagellum~ (“whip, scourge”). Latin ~flagellum~ is a diminutive of ~flagrum~ (“whip”). Because the borrowing came through written Latin and not through the spoken language, the verb kept its Latin shape. The inherited route from the same Latin verb produced a different word, ~fêler~ (“to crack”), so ~flageller~ and ~fêler~ are doublets, one learned and one worn down by centuries of speech.

The Latin noun ~flagellum~ also gave French ~fléau~, which means both a flail and, figuratively, a scourge or plague. The learned side of the family includes ~flagellation~ and ~flagelle~, the whip-like tail of a microorganism. English ~flagellate~ is another borrowing of the same Latin verb, and Italian ~flagellare~ is its cousin. ~Flageller~ can describe a literal whipping, as in religious penance, or a figurative lashing, as when a critic ~flagelle~ a policy.
en.flageoler: The origin of ~flageoler~ (“to tremble on one's legs”) is uncertain. The TLFi dates the sense to the mid-eighteenth century, with Rousseau's phrase about legs that ~flageolent~ under him, and proposes that it may derive from ~flageolet~, the small flute, in the sense of a thin leg, though that sense is attested only in the nineteenth century. Older French used ~flageoler~ for playing the flageolet and, figuratively, for talking nonsense. Littré lays out the same sequence of senses, from playing the flageolet to chattering to flattering, and asks whether the modern sense of wobbling came from spindly, unsteady legs being likened to flageolets.
en.flagorner:
The origin of ~flagorner~ is uncertain. English Wiktionary lists it as a Middle French verb ~flagorner~ and calls its origin obscure, while French Wiktionary derives it from the Old French verb ~flageoler~. The two accounts do not coincide, and neither names a Latin source, so the earliest history of the word stays open.

English Wiktionary also floats a possible blend of ~flatter~ (“to flatter”) and ~corner~ (“to blow a horn”). That is only a conjecture, and the sources do not settle between it and the derivation from ~flageoler~. In modern French, ~flagorner~ means to flatter crudely or servilely, and it gives ~flagorneur~ (“sycophant”) and ~flagornerie~ (“fawning flattery”).
en.flairer:
~Flairer~ comes from Old French ~flairier~, inherited from Vulgar or Late Latin ~flāgrāre~. This was a dissimilated form of Latin ~frāgrāre~ (“to give off a strong smell, to smell sweet”): the first ~r~ of ~frāgrāre~ became ~l~ so that the two ~r~ sounds no longer repeated. English Wiktionary traces ~frāgrāre~ back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰreh₂g-~ (“to smell”) plus the suffix *~-ro-~. The classical form survives in English ~fragrant~ and ~fragrance~, while the altered Vulgar Latin form is the one that reached French.

The meaning turned around on the way. The Latin verb described a thing that gives off an odor, while the French verb describes the one who picks it up: ~flairer~ means “to smell, to sniff at,” the act of an animal or a person following a scent. From that base French drew the noun ~flair~ (“sense of smell,” then “intuition”), and ~flairer~ itself is used figuratively, as when someone ~flaire~ a trap or a bargain. English borrowed the noun as ~flair~, in the sense of a keen instinct.
en.flamber: The verb is formed from the noun ~flambe~ (“tall flame”) and the verb ending ~-er~. It is recorded only once in the twelfth century, and it replaced the older French verb ~flammer~, which came from Latin ~flammāre~ (“to set on fire”), derived from ~flamma~ (“flame”). The verb means “to burn with a bright flame” and, in cooking, “to flambé” a dish with alcohol. By a figurative extension, it also means “to squander,” as in ~flamber son argent~, money going up in smoke.
en.flamboyer: The sources give two routes. English Wiktionary has it inherited from Old French ~flambeier~, from Vulgar Latin *~flammizāre~ (with the influence of ~flambe~), from Latin ~flamma~ (“flame”). French Wiktionary treats it as derived from ~flamber~ with the suffix ~-oyer~. Both agree that the root is ~flamma~ and that ~-oyer~, which marks continuing action or emission, gives the sense “to blaze, to give off flames.” The verb replaced the older ~flammer~. The suffix ~-oyer~ and the learned ~-iser~ come from the same Late Latin ending.
en.flancher:
The origin of ~flancher~, first attested in 1835, is uncertain, and French Wiktionary offers three accounts. The first derives it from Old French ~flenchir~, a variant of ~flechir~, ~flechier~ and ~flangier~ (all “to bend, to give way”), but it admits that the long gap in time between ~flenchir~ and ~flancher~ is hard to bridge. English Wiktionary likewise says only that the word is perhaps derived from Old French ~flenchir~ (“to weaken”), perhaps with influence from ~flanc~ (“flank, side”).

The two other accounts are more modest still. One sees the verb as a collateral form of ~flanquer~ and ~flaquer~ (“to knock down, to throw to the ground”). The other proposes ~flacher~ (“to go soft, to give way”), from ~flache~. None of the three is settled, and all of them agree on the sense: the verb describes giving way under pressure, whether a person losing nerve or a thing failing, which matches the modern gloss “to drop out” or “to wimp out”. The first account links it to ~fléchir~ (“to bend”), the verb for yielding that survives in modern French.
en.flanquer: French Wiktionary lists two verbs. The first, “to flank,” was made from the noun ~flanc~ (“side”) with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Frankish *~hlanka~ (“hip”), a form that English Wiktionary gives as *~hlanku~, and is cognate with Italian ~fianco~. The second, the colloquial “to fling, to chuck” (~flanquer un coup~, to land a blow), is described only as used in place of ~flaquer~; neither Wiktionary gives the origin of that sense, so it stays unexplained here.
en.flasher: Borrowed from English ~flash~ (“to emit a flash of light”), with the French infinitive ending ~-er~ attached to fit it into the first conjugation. The English verb gave French a family of modern senses, but the core idea is still a sudden burst of light.
en.flatter:
French ~flatter~ descends from Old French ~flater~ (“to deceive by hiding the truth, to stroke with the palm”), which English Wiktionary traces to Frankish *~flat~ (“palm, flat of the hand”), from Proto-Germanic *~flatą~ (“palm, sole”) and its relative *~flataz~ (“flat”), from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “flat, broad.” Cognates include Old High German ~flazza~ (“palm of the hand”), Old Saxon ~flat~ (“flat”) and Old Norse ~flatr~ (“flat”), the source of English ~flat~. English also borrowed the verb itself, ~flatter~, from Old French. English Wiktionary points to ~flétrir~ for further reading on the family.

The oldest image is physical: to ~flatter~ was to stroke with the flat of the hand. Already in Old French the verb had slid into a moral sense, to coax or deceive with soft words, and that sense won out: today ~flatter~ means to praise someone beyond what is deserved in order to please. A second line of meaning kept the idea of gentle contact and pleasing effect, as when a dress ~flatte~ the figure or a sound ~flatte~ the ear. Related words include ~flatteur~ and ~flatterie~, and the sense of “stroking” makes the verb a close cousin of ~caresser~ in its earliest use.
en.flemmarder: ~Flemmarder~ is a denominal verb: ~flemmard~ plus the ending ~-er~. The noun ~flemmard~ (“lazybones”) is itself built on ~flemme~ (“laziness”) with the suffix ~-ard~, which often forms nouns for people with a marked trait. The verb is informal and means to laze about, to do nothing in particular, which is exactly what a ~flemmard~ does.
en.fleurer: The verb ~fleurer~ (“to give off a smell”) is labeled a derivative of ~fleur~ by French Wiktionary, but the flower may not be involved. English Wiktionary connects it with an old noun ~fleur~ meaning “odour,” now surviving only in dialects, from Old French ~flaour~ (the source of English ~flavour~), ultimately from Latin ~flātus~ (“a blowing, breath”). It also allows that ~fleurer~ may simply be a variant of ~flairer~ (“to sniff out”). The link with the flower noun, from Latin ~flōrem~, is therefore doubtful. Formally, the verb takes the ending ~-er~. The origin remains unsettled.
en.fleurir:
From Latin ~florire~, a Vulgar Latin reshaping of Classical ~florere~ (“to bloom, to flourish”), from ~flos~, stem ~flor-~ (“flower”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰleh₃-~ (“to bloom, to flourish”). The same root, on its Germanic side, gives English ~bloom~, ~blossom~, and ~blade~, and the Gothic ~blōma~ (“flower”) — so the French and English words for flowering are deep cousins.

French kept two strands of meaning side by side. The regular ~fleurir~ means “to flower, to bloom”; but in the figurative sense “to flourish, to thrive,” the older present participle survives as ~florissant~ (and the past ~florissait~), preserving the Latin ~flor-~ rather than the diphthongized ~fleur-~ — a rare doublet within one verb. From the same root grew ~fleur~ (“flower”), ~floraison~ (“blooming”), ~flore~ (“flora”), ~refleurir~, and ~défleurir~. To say a city ~florissait~ was to picture it literally in flower.
en.flexibiliser: ~Flexibiliser~ is formed from ~flexible~ with the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make A”), so it means to make supple or more flexible. ~Flexible~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~flexibilis~, from ~flectere~ (“to bend”), and was still spelled ~fléxible~ in the 1762 edition of the Académie dictionary.
en.flinguer: A slang verb made from ~flingue~ (“gun”) and the ending ~-er~, so ~flinguer~ is “to shoot, to gun down.” The origin of ~flingue~ itself is uncertain. The most likely account makes it a borrowing from ~flinke~ or ~flingge~, Bavarian forms of German ~Flinte~ (“musket, shotgun”). Another suggestion points to the Picard ~flingot~. Some sources call its origin simply unknown. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and here means “to strike with N, to use N.”
en.flipper: A borrowing from English ~flip~, in the slang sense “to freak out”. French Wiktionary explains the English verb as a shortening of the expression ~flip one's lid~ (“to make one's lid fly off”), and glosses it with the French idioms ~péter les plombs~ and ~péter un câble~. French gave the English verb its usual first-conjugation ending ~-er~, so ~flipper~ conjugates like any ordinary verb of that class. The image behind it is a container whose cover blows off under pressure.
en.fliquer: Formed from the slang noun ~flic~ (“cop”) with the ending ~-er~, so “to police, to keep under watch.” The origin of ~flic~ is itself uncertain. It probably comes from German ~Flick~, a word for a “young man” or “boy” that French Wiktionary dates to 1510. By another account, it comes from German ~Fliege~ (“fly”), because ~mouche~ (“fly”) had long been slang for a spy or informer. English Wiktionary gives the same two accounts, so the verb rests on a base whose origin is debated.
en.flirter: ~Flirter~ is borrowed from English ~flirt~ and fitted with the French infinitive ending, which makes it a fairly recent addition to the language. English Wiktionary notes that forms spelled with -eu- may have arisen through the influence of ~fleur~ (“flower”), though it presents this only as a possibility.
en.floconner: Formed from the noun ~flocon~ (“flake”) with the verbal suffix ~-er~: to ~floconner~ is to form flakes or to fall in flakes, as snow or wool does. The noun ~flocon~ is itself a derivative of ~floc~ with the suffix ~-on~, and ~floc~ comes from Latin ~floccus~ (“a tuft of wool”). The verb thus carries a small piece of Latin textile vocabulary through two French suffixes. English ~floc~ and ~flock~ (in the sense of tuft or wool) are related, though they reached English by another path, so they are left aside here.
en.floculer:
From Latin ~flocculus~ (“small flake”), a diminutive of ~floccus~ (“tuft of wool”). The French verb describes fine particles in a liquid clumping together into loose flakes, which settle out or float as a soft mass. The same Latin word gave English ~floccule~ and ~flocculate~, and the chemical sense is shared across the two languages.

The Latin root ~floccus~ is also behind the everyday French ~flocon~ (“flake”, as in ~flocon de neige~), so a snowflake and a flocculated colloid are, by origin, cousins. The verb belongs to the vocabulary of chemistry and water treatment, where flocculation is the stage in which particles gather into flakes that can be filtered or left to settle.
en.flotter:
~Flotter~ comes from Middle French ~flotter~, from Old French ~floter~ (“to float”), itself from Frankish *~flotōn~ (“to float, swim”), a Germanic verb that the Franks brought to Gaul. Frankish goes back to Proto-Germanic *~flutōną~ (“to float, swim”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~plew-~ (“to flow, swim”). Its Germanic relatives are Middle Dutch ~vlōten~, Old English ~flotian~ and Old Norse ~flota~ (“to float, to launch”), and English ~float~ is the sibling that never left Germanic ground. The same root also gave Latin ~pluere~ (“to rain”) and Greek ~plein~ (“to sail”), so the rain, the ship and the log on the river share an ancestor.

The verb was first about water: to float, to drift. It then spread to whatever moves like a floating thing. A flag flutters in the wind, a smell or a mood hangs in the air, a crowd mills about, and a hesitating person ~flotte~ between two choices. French Wiktionary links the verb to the noun ~flot~ (“wave”) and, for one of its senses, to ~flotte~, without settling the details; the Frankish descent above comes from English Wiktionary. The family is large: ~flottant~, ~flotteur~ (“float”), ~flottement~ (“wavering”) and ~flotte~ itself, which can mean a fleet or, in slang, water.
en.flouer:
The origin of ~flouer~ (“to swindle, to con”) is uncertain. French Wiktionary notes that the word enjoyed a revival from 1827, thanks to a text by Grandval, and that its origin is unsettled. It is compared with ~frouer~ (“to cheat at play”), which is said to come from Old French ~froer~ (“to break, to shatter,” used more of a weapon), itself from Latin ~fraudāre~ (“to defraud”). English Wiktionary likewise offers only a maybe: the verb may ultimately come from Latin ~fraudāre~, which would make it a doublet of ~frauder~.

If that hypothesis holds, ~flouer~ would be a distant and heavily worn cousin of ~frauder~, the learned borrowing of the same Latin verb, and the family would include ~fraude~ and ~fraudeur~. The chain is not settled, so none of the intermediate steps should be taken as established. A different ~flouer~ also exists, a separate verb built on the adjective ~flou~ (“blurred, hazy”), with the sense of making something blurry. It is a homonym, not a variant of the swindler's verb.
en.fluctuer:
~Fluctuer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~fluctuāre~ (“to be tossed on the waves, to float”). The Latin verb is generally analyzed as a derivative of ~fluctus~ (“wave”), itself related to ~fluere~ (“to flow”). English ~fluctuate~ was likewise taken from Latin, so the two verbs are parallel borrowings rather than one from the other.

The verb began as a maritime image: something that ~fluctue~ is carried up and down by the sea. French kept that picture for the figurative sense, so a price, a mood or an opinion that ~fluctue~ rises and falls like a swell. The same Latin root ~fluere~ also stands behind ~flux~, ~fluide~, ~affluent~ and ~influence~, and ~fluctuation~ and ~fluctuant~ come straight from ~fluctuāre~.
en.fluer:
From Latin ~fluere~ (“to flow”), which French reshaped into a first-conjugation verb in ~-er~. The Latin infinitive ended in ~-ere~, a different conjugation from the French one, so the change of class is a real reshaping. Italian ~fluire~ and Spanish ~fluir~ descend from the same Latin verb, and English ~fluent~ and ~fluid~ are learned words built on the same root.

In modern French ~fluer~ is rare, and its compounds are far more common than the simple verb: ~affluer~, ~refluer~, ~influer~, ~confluer~. The nouns ~flux~ and ~fluide~, and ~influence~, belong to the same Latin family. A French speaker meets the root far more often in these derived words than in ~fluer~ itself.
en.fluidifier: Formed from ~fluide~ with the suffix ~-ifier~, meaning “to make fluid.” ~Fluide~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~fluidus~, from the verb ~fluere~ (“to flow”). The suffix ~-ifier~ goes back to Latin ~-ficāre~, which comes from ~facere~ (“to make”). It is productive in learned and technical French, as in ~complexifier~ or ~intensifier~. The verb is used of liquids, and figuratively of traffic or exchanges, which are made to run more freely.
en.flâner:
~Flâner~ entered French in the 19th century (its first spelling was ~flaner~) from the Norman verb ~flan(n)er~. Both Wiktionaries trace the Norman verb to Old Norse ~flana~, glossed as “to get into something heedlessly” or “to rush about thoughtlessly.” Icelandic ~flana~ (“to rush, to act rashly”) is cited as a cognate, and Norwegian ~flane~ is given as a related verb meaning “to wander.”

The sources do not explain how a verb of rash, heedless rushing became one of unhurried strolling, so that shift is best left as an open question. What they do show is that the word is a late arrival from a regional dialect, and not a Latin inheritance like most French verbs. It has since given French ~flâneur~ and ~flânerie~, and English borrowed ~flâneur~ for a person who wanders a city to watch it.
en.flécher: ~Flécher~ is formed from the noun ~flèche~ (“arrow”) and the verb ending ~-er~, and means to mark something with arrows. ~Flèche~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~fleccia~, borrowed from a Frankish word reconstructed as *~fliukkijā~. French Wiktionary glosses that Frankish word, literally, as “the one that flies” and relates it to Dutch ~vliegen~ (“to fly”). It also notes that Old French ~fliche~, from Old Norse ~flikki~, influenced the word.
en.fléchir:
~Fléchir~ is inherited from Old French ~flechir~, which replaced an earlier ~flechier~ when the verb changed class. That came from Vulgar Latin *~flecticāre~, a frequentative built on Latin ~flectere~ (“to bend”). French Wiktionary adds that ~flectere~ is a synonym of ~flexāre~ (“to bend, to curve”). English has taken the same root in ~flex~ and ~reflect~.

The inherited ~fléchir~ has many learned siblings drawn straight from Latin: ~flexible~, ~flexion~, ~inflexible~ and ~genuflexion~. Among them is ~réfléchir~, which comes from Latin ~reflectere~ (“to bend back”) and now means “to think.” In modern French ~fléchir~ means to bend or fold, and it is also used of yielding, as when a person bends before an argument or pressure.
en.flétrir:
The evidence gives two strands that meet in one verb. The first is the Old French adjective ~flaistre~ (also ~flestre~, “limp, withered”), from Latin ~flaccidus~ (“soft, limp”), which gave Middle French ~flestrir~. The second is Old French ~flatir~, from Frankish *~flattjan~ (“to move the palm of one's hand”), itself from Proto-Germanic *~flatjaną~ (“to flatten”). From ~flatir~ came ~flastrir~, an alteration attested from the mid-thirteenth century and reshaped under the influence of the first word.

The two accounts are told separately in the sources, and neither says which weighed more in the sense of the modern verb, which is “to wither”. What is clear is that both ancestors left descendants elsewhere. Latin ~flaccidus~ survives in French ~flasque~'s learned cousin ~flaccide~ and in English ~flaccid~, and the Germanic root behind ~flatir~ is the one English knows as ~flat~ and ~flatten~. A Latin word for limpness and a Frankish word for flattening thus ended up sharing a single French verb.
en.flûter: Formed from ~flûte~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, which turns a noun into a verb: “to play the flute”. French Wiktionary traces ~flûte~ to Old French ~flaute~ and Old Occitan ~flauta~, perhaps ultimately from Latin ~flāre~ (“to blow”). English Wiktionary gives Old French ~fleüte~ from Old Occitan ~flaut~, and adds that the contraction of the Old French hiatus left a long vowel in Middle French, which the circumflex of ~flûte~ now marks.
en.focaliser: Formed from the adjective ~focal~ plus the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make, to bring to”), with the stem losing its ending: to bring to a focus, to concentrate on one point, whether light rays or attention. The adjective is a learned formation from New Latin ~focālis~, built on Latin ~focus~ (“hearth, fire”), the same word that gave the inherited French ~foyer~. The optical sense of “burning point” where rays meet explains the shift from fireplace to focal point.
en.foirer: ~Foirer~ is formed from the noun ~foire~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. English Wiktionary ties the sense “to mess up” to ~foire~ in the sense “diarrhea,” which is inherited from Latin ~foria~. French Wiktionary adds that a second, homonymous verb comes from the other ~foire~ (“fair”), from Latin ~feria~ (“feast day”); the two nouns are unrelated in origin.
en.foisonner: Formed from the noun ~foison~ (“abundance”) plus ~-er~, giving a verb that means to abound or teem. The noun comes from Latin ~fūsiō~ (“a pouring out, a spreading”), through Old and Middle French ~foison~. It is a doublet of ~fusion~, a learned borrowing from the same Latin word, so the popular and learned descendants have drifted far apart in meaning.
en.folioter: Derived from ~folio~ with the verb ending ~-er~, attested in 1832 according to the TLFi. A ~folio~ is the number given to a leaf of a book or manuscript, and ~folio~ itself is the Latin ablative of ~folium~ (“leaf”). The verb means to number the leaves of a manuscript, a register or a book, and by extension, in printing, to set the folios of a work. The Académie notes that an old edition may be ~folioté~ without being paginated, since a leaf carries two pages but only one number.
en.folkloriser: Formed from ~folklore~ with the suffix ~-iser~, here in its sense “to make into, to treat as N.” ~Folklore~ is a borrowing from English, a compound of ~folk~ (“people”) and ~lore~ (“legend, story”). ~Folkloriser~ therefore means to turn something into folklore, or to treat it as folklore.
en.folâtrer: Formed from the adjective ~folâtre~ (“playfully silly”) and the ending ~-er~, which here means “to act like N,” the verb means to frolic or play about. The adjective is itself a derivative of ~fol~, the older form of ~fou~ (“mad, foolish”), with the suffix ~-âtre~. The verb thus describes behaving in the manner of someone a little foolish, in a light-hearted way.
en.fomenter: From Latin ~fōmentāre~ (“to keep a fire going”), a verb made from ~fōmentum~, which meant both “fuel for a fire” and “poultice, soothing remedy”, and which comes from ~fovēre~ (“to warm”). French Wiktionary simply says Latin, while English Wiktionary labels the source Medieval Latin ~fomentāre~. English ~foment~ is the same borrowing.
en.foncer:
Derived from ~fons~, an older form of ~fond~ and ~fonds~ (« bottom, base, fund »), which descend from Latin ~fundus~ (« bottom, foundation, estate »). ~fundus~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰudʰmḗn~ (« bottom »), cognate with English ~bottom~ and German ~Boden~ (« ground, soil »). So ~foncer~ is, at root, « to deal with the bottom of a thing ».

From that base the verb fanned out concretely — « to fit a bottom into » a cask, then « to dig down », and so « to darken », since to deepen a color is to drive it toward its depths. The sense « to charge, to rush at » is explained differently: the sources tie it not to a literal lunge but to the figurative ~fondre sur~ (« to swoop down on ») and the idea of going ~à fond~ (« all the way, full tilt »), so the « charging » ~foncer~ is best read as a variant of that expression rather than as the same word's plain extension. The family includes ~fond~, ~fonds~, ~enfoncer~, ~défoncer~, ~foncé~ (« dark »), and ~fonceur~ (« a go-getter »).
en.fonctionnariser: Formed from ~fonctionnaire~ (“civil servant, official”) + the suffix ~-iser~, “to make into a civil servant, to give civil-service status to.” The noun ~fonctionnaire~ is itself built from ~fonction~ with the suffix ~-aire~. The suffix ~-iser~, from Late Latin ~-izāre~ and ultimately Greek, forms verbs meaning “to make” or “to convert into,” and is fully productive in administrative and journalistic French.
en.fonctionner:
Unlike most verbs in this app, ~fonctionner~ is young and home-grown: it is a denominal coinage, attested around 1787, formed directly on the French noun ~fonction~ (“function, role, duty”). That noun comes from Latin ~functio~ (“a performing, an execution”), the action-noun of the deponent verb ~fungi~ (“to perform, discharge, carry out an office”), whose past participle was ~functus~. Through Latin, ~fonction~ is the close kin of ~défunt~ (“deceased”), literally one who has ~discharged~ life — the ~de-~ marking completion of the duty of living.

The sense development is neat. ~Fonction~ first named a duty or office one performs; the verb ~fonctionner~ then meant “to perform one's function,” and from there spread to machinery and systems — a clock, an engine, an institution that ~works~ by doing what it is meant to do. The word arrives just as the mechanical age does, and it carries that flavour: when a French speaker says ~ça fonctionne~, the metaphor is of a thing duly discharging its office. From the same ~fungi~ / ~functio~ root come ~fonctionnaire~ (“civil servant,” one charged with a function), ~fonctionnel~, ~dysfonctionnement~, and the mathematical ~fonction~.
en.fonder:
From Old French ~fonder~, from Latin ~fundare~ (“to lay a foundation, to establish”), a denominal verb built on the noun ~fundus~ (“bottom, base, the ground of an estate”). ~fundus~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~funðos~ to a Proto-Indo-European *~bʰudʰmḗn~ (“bottom”), the same root that yielded English ~bottom~ and Ancient Greek ~puthmḗn~ (“bottom of a vessel”). The Romance cousins are everywhere: Italian ~fondare~ and Spanish ~fundar~, both “to found.”

To found something is literally to give it a ~fundus~ — to lay its lowest part, its base, before anything can be raised on top. From this concrete sense of laying a footing came the abstract one of establishing an institution, a city, or a doctrine, and figuratively of grounding an argument “on” solid reasons. French kept the underlying noun too, as ~fond~ (“bottom, background”) and ~fonds~ (“fund, capital, a piece of land”), and the doublet relationship there is striking: the financial ~fonds~ and the scenic ~fond~ are the same Latin ~fundus~ wearing two spellings. Other descendants include ~fondation~ (“foundation”), ~fondement~ (“basis”), ~profond~ (“deep,” literally “toward the bottom”), and ~foncier~ (“pertaining to land”). The English ~fund~, ~found~, ~foundation~, and ~profound~ all trace back to the same Latin base.
en.fondre:
~fondre~ comes from Latin ~fundere~ (“to pour, to pour out, to melt”), attested in French from around 1050. Its PIE root is *~ǵʰew-~ (“to pour”), seen in the extended form *~ǵʰew-d-~; the Greek cognate ~khéō~ (“I pour”) and Gothic ~giutan~ belong to the same family. From the molten-metal sense English borrowed ~found~ (as in casting a bell) and ~foundry~, while ~fundere~ also gave ~fuse~ and ~confound~. So the metalworker's foundry and the French verb for melting share one ancient idea of pouring.

The spread of senses is striking. From “to pour” came “to melt” (metal, snow, butter), then “to blend” — colors that ~se fondre~ into one another, giving ~fondu~ in film and ~fondue~ at the table. A separate, vivid branch is ~fondre sur~, “to swoop down on,” as a hawk drops on its prey: the image is of the bird pouring itself down out of the sky. From the same stem French built ~fonte~ (“cast iron; melting”), ~fonderie~ (“foundry”), ~fondation~ and ~fonder~ via the related ~fundus~ family, and ~fusion~. One root, *~ǵʰew-~, runs from a libation poured to the gods to chocolate melting in a pot.
en.forcer:
From Vulgar Latin *~fortiare~, built on Late Latin ~fortia~ (“strength, force”), which was the substantivized neuter plural of the classical adjective ~fortis~ (“strong, brave, firm”). Attested in French since the eleventh century, ~forcer~ is cousin to Italian ~forzare~ and Spanish ~forzar~, and the whole family is kin to the English borrowings ~force~ and ~fort~.

The verb's path follows the noun ~force~, which was carved from that neuter plural ~fortia~ — literally “strong things.” To ~forcer~ originally meant to apply strength, and from there it branched: to force a door, to force a lock, to force someone's hand, to force a plant in a hothouse, even to overstrain (~se forcer~, “to push oneself too hard”). In hunting, ~forcer~ a stag is to run it to exhaustion. The same ~fortis~ underlies a robust French lineage: ~fort~ (“strong”), ~force~, ~forcené~ (“frenzied,” originally “out of one's senses”), ~renforcer~, ~effort~, and ~confort~ (which reached English as ~comfort~ before returning). What began as a Roman soldier's praise — ~fortis~, brave and steadfast — became the verb for any exertion of power, gentle or brutal.
