en.forcir: ~Forcir~ is a French formation with the verbal ending ~-ir~, in the “become A” pattern of ~grossir~ and ~grandir~: to become stronger or stouter. The sources differ on its base. French Wiktionary derives it from the adjective ~fort~ (“strong”), shaped on the noun ~force~, while English Wiktionary derives it directly from ~force~. Either way the root is Latin. ~Force~ comes from Late Latin ~fortia~, built on the neuter plural of ~fortis~ (“strong, brave”), and its ~o~ was kept by analogy with ~fort~.
en.forclore: Formed from the dead prefix ~for-~ and ~clore~, with the sense of shutting out, a term of law meaning to debar someone from a right. French Wiktionary instead reads the first element as the old preposition ~fors~ (“outside”), and the origin of ~for-~ is itself debated, possibly from Late Latin ~forīs~ (“outside”) shaped on a Frankish prefix *~fur-~. The base ~clore~ comes from Latin ~claudere~ (“to shut, close”). The prefix is no longer productive and survives only in a few old verbs, ~forfaire~ and ~fourvoyer~ among them.
en.forer:
From Latin ~forāre~ (“to pierce, to bore through”), a learned borrowing, as en.Wiktionary calls it. The Latin verb has a noun beside it, ~forāmen~ (“hole, opening”), and the pair belongs to a Proto-Indo-European family of words for piercing and cutting. The Germanic branch of that family gave English ~bore~ and German ~bohren~, so the verb that French uses for drilling a well is a distant cousin of the verb English uses for the same job. Italian ~forare~ continues the Latin verb directly.

In French, ~forer~ is the technical verb of drilling: one drills a well, a tunnel, a hole in a wall, or an oil field. It has produced a small family of its own, with ~forage~ (“drilling”), ~foreur~ (“driller”), ~foret~ (“drill bit”) and ~foreuse~ (“drilling rig”). The compound ~perforer~, from Latin ~perforāre~ (“to pierce through”), shows the same root with a prefix. Because ~forer~ was borrowed from Latin rather than inherited, it kept the Latin shape almost untouched.
en.forfaire: ~Forfaire~ comes from Old French ~forfaire~, formed from ~faire~ with the old prefix ~for-~. The verb ~faire~ is the inherited descendant of Latin ~facere~ (“to make, to do”), the same source as Italian ~fare~ and Spanish ~hacer~. The prefix ~for-~ is dead in modern French, and its origin is debated: it is traced either to Late Latin ~forīs~ (“outside”), shaped on a Frankish prefix, or to ~fors~ (“outside”). In ~forfaire~ it carries the idea of a wrong action, so the verb means to act outside what is right, to fail in one's duty. It is one of the few old verbs, with ~fourvoyer~ and ~forclore~, that still keep this prefix.
en.forger:
Recorded from the twelfth century, ~forger~ comes from Latin ~fabricāre~ (“to fashion, build, construct”), from ~faber~ (“craftsman, smith, worker in hard materials”). The deep origin of ~faber~ is uncertain; it is often referred to a Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰabʰ-~ (“to fit together, be fitting”), with proposed cognates including Armenian ~darbin~ (“smith”) and, by some accounts, English ~deft~ and ~daft~. ~fabricāre~ also yielded, by a learned borrowing, the French doublet ~fabriquer~ (“to manufacture”), so French has two reflexes of one Latin verb.

The popular, mouth-worn line of descent narrowed ~fabricāre~ from making in general to the smith's particular making: hammering hot metal. Old French ~forgier~ already meant working iron at the anvil, and from that concrete craft the figurative senses fanned out — to ~forger~ a sword, a chain, but also to forge an alliance, a destiny, or, more darkly, a false document (whence English ~forge~ in the sense “to counterfeit”). The same Latin ~faber~ family gives French ~forge~ (the smithy itself), ~forgeron~ (“blacksmith”), and the archaic ~fèvre~ that survives in the surname ~Lefebvre~ — quite literally “the smith.”
en.forjeter: A compound of Old French ~fors~ (“outside”) and ~jeter~ (“to throw”), literally “to throw out.” The TLFi attests it in the first half of the twelfth century in the sense “to push away,” as in a Psalter. In 1543 it appears in architecture for a wall or building that juts out of plumb or out of line. That is the sense the Académie keeps today, for a structure built overhanging or leaning outward.
en.forlancer: A compound of ~fors~ and ~lancer~ (“to throw, to hurl”), literally to throw outside, hence to flush out. The first element is the old preposition ~fors~ (“outside”), from Latin ~foris~, which replaced classical Latin ~extra~ in most Romance languages: compare Spanish ~fuera~, Portuguese ~fora~, Italian ~fuori~ and Romanian ~afară~. ~Fors~ is a doublet of ~hors~, the form that survived in modern French.
en.forligner: From Old French ~forlignier~ (“to leave the ranks, to fail to honor the line one comes from”), formed from ~lignier~ with the prefix ~for-~. The base belongs to the family of ~ligne~ and ~lignée~, which come from Latin ~linea~ (“line, linen thread”). The prefix ~for-~ comes from Latin ~foris~ (“outside”), the same element as in ~fors~, the old word for “outside” that became modern ~hors~. The verb is glossed “to degenerate,” which fits the older sense of failing to honor one's lineage. The same prefix ~for-~ appears in ~forfait~ and ~forclore~, and English has it in ~forfeit~ and ~foreclose~, both borrowed from Old French.
en.forlonger: A hunting verb built in French by swapping prefixes. The TLFi explains it as ~éloigner~ (“to move away”) or ~élonger~, with ~fors-~ (“out, outside”) put in place of ~es-~. The first sense, “to move away,” appears around 1175 as ~forsloignier~. Around 1375 the verb is recorded in the language of the hunt, of game that gains a considerable lead on the hounds. The Académie still lists it as a term of venery: a stag that ~forlonge~ is pulling ever further ahead of the pack. Littré reads it as ~fors~ or ~hors~ plus ~longer~, as in ~allonger~ and ~prolonger~, all tied to ~long~ and ~loin~.
en.formaliser: Two histories share one form. The pronominal ~se formaliser~ (“to take offense”) is formed from ~formel~ and the suffix ~-iser~, while the transitive ~formaliser~ (“to make formal”) is, according to French Wiktionary, a borrowing from English ~formalize~. ~Formel~ comes from Latin ~formālis~, from ~forma~ (“form”), which also gave French ~forme~. The “offense” sense grew from the idea of being scandalized by a breach of form: someone who ~se formalise~ is shocked that the proprieties have not been observed. The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~.
en.formater: Formed in French from the noun ~format~ and the suffix ~-er~, probably under the influence of the English verb to format. The base ~format~ has two proposed origins. French Wiktionary derives it either from ~former~ with the suffix ~-at~, or, more likely, from Italian ~formato~, itself from ~formare~. English Wiktionary instead sends it through German ~Format~ from Latin ~fōrmātus~ (“formed”). All the routes lead back to Latin, but their order is unsettled. The verb meant to give a book or sheet its shape, then to prepare a disk for use, a sense that came with computing.
en.former:
From Latin ~formare~ (“to shape, to fashion, to form”), derived from ~forma~ (“shape, figure, mold, beauty”). The deeper origin of ~forma~ is uncertain; one long-standing hypothesis derives it from Ancient Greek ~morphē~ (“shape, form”), perhaps with a swapping of consonants and possibly transmitted through Etruscan, though this remains unproven. Cognate with Italian ~formare~ and Spanish ~formar~.

The verb began concretely — to give matter a shape, to mold — and then climbed into the abstract: to constitute (« former un gouvernement »), to develop a skill, and especially to train or educate a person, so that ~formation~ in modern French means “training” as much as “formation.” The same ~forma~ branched into a remarkably productive family of French words: ~forme~, ~format~, ~formule~, ~formel~, ~uniforme~, ~conforme~, ~déformer~, ~réformer~, and ~transformer~. From a single word for “shape,” French built a whole architecture of forming, reforming, and transforming.
en.formoler: Formed from ~formol~ and the verb ending ~-er~, meaning “to disinfect with formol.” The noun ~formol~ was coined by the chemist Auguste Trillat, from the adjective ~formique~ with the chemical suffix ~-ol~ replacing the earlier ending. ~Formique~ itself refers to formic acid, named after ants. The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, is the usual means of turning a noun into a verb in French, here for the act of applying the product.
en.formuler:
A denominal verb coined in French (around the late 18th century) from the noun ~formule~ (“formula, set form of words”), itself from Latin ~formula~, a diminutive of ~forma~ (“shape, form, mould”). Latin ~forma~ stands beside the verb ~formāre~, source of French ~former~ (“to form”); a ~formula~ was literally a “little form,” a small fixed pattern. Cognate descendants of ~forma~ include English ~form~ and ~formula~ and Italian ~forma~.

A ~formula~ began as a legal and ceremonial template — a precise wording you had to follow exactly — and that flavour of fixed, exact expression carried into ~formuler~: to put a thought into a defined, careful form of words. One ~formule~ une hypothèse, a request, an objection — always shaping vague intention into explicit statement. The same ~forma~ root spread widely in French: ~forme~, ~former~, ~formule~, ~formulaire~ (“form, printed template”), ~formel~ (“formal, explicit”), and ~formalité~. Across these the underlying idea is constant — giving a shapeless content a clear, repeatable shape.
en.forniquer:
From Latin ~fornicārī~ (“to fornicate”), a verb built on ~fornix~ (“arch, vault; brothel”). The French source explains the brothel sense by the vaulted rooms in which prostitutes were housed in ancient Rome, so the word passed from a piece of architecture to the people who worked beneath it. English ~fornicate~ is taken from the same Latin verb.

The story of ~forniquer~ is one of narrowing and moral coloring. ~Fornix~ began as a plain building term for an arch or vault, then came to mean the brothel, and the verb ~fornicārī~ named the activity associated with it. French ~forniquer~ keeps that sense, but today it is a learned, religious or jocular word, far from everyday speech. It belongs to a small family: ~fornication~ (the act) and ~fornicateur~ (the person), both learned formations on the Latin verb. The architectural meaning survives in the learned vocabulary of anatomy, where ~fornix~ is used for arch-shaped structures of the body. The French verb thus preserves, in its Latin ancestor, the memory of a Roman vault.
en.fortifier:
From Middle French ~fortifier~, borrowed from Late Latin ~fortificāre~ (“to strengthen, to fortify”), a compound of Latin ~fortis~ (“strong”) and a verbal element ~-ficāre~ related to ~facere~ (“to make”). The verb therefore meant, quite literally, “to make strong.” Italian ~fortificare~ and Spanish ~fortificar~ come from the same Latin verb, and English ~fortify~ was borrowed from French. Latin ~fortis~ itself is the ancestor of French ~fort~, and a whole family grew up around it.

In French, ~fortifier~ means to make a place or a person stronger. It is used of a town given walls, towers and ramparts, and equally of bodies and minds, so that one fortifies one's health, one's resolve or an argument. The family includes ~fortification~, ~fortin~ (“small fort”) and ~forteresse~, and other French words are also built on the idea of strength, among them ~réconforter~ (“to put strength back into”) and ~effort~.
en.fossiliser: ~Fossiliser~ is formed from the noun or adjective ~fossile~ with the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to turn into a fossil,” and figuratively “to become fixed and unchanging.” The base ~fossile~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~fossilis~ (“dug up”), from the verb ~fodiō~ (“to dig”), and it is related to ~fosse~ (“pit”). A fossil is thus, at root, something dug out of the earth.
en.fouailler: The origin of ~fouailler~ is explained in two ways. French Wiktionary derives it from Middle French ~foueiller~ (14th century), itself from ~fouet~ (“whip”), which comes in turn from ~fou~, an old name for the beech tree, from Latin ~fagus~ (“beech”). Latin ~fagus~ is a relative of German ~Buche~ in the same family of tree names. English Wiktionary offers a different route: Middle French ~fouaille~ (“faggot,” a bundle of sticks) plus the ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary also gives a second account, from ~fouaille~ in the sense “cooked entrails,” shaped by its resemblance to ~fouiller~ (“to rummage”). The sources therefore disagree, and the origin is debated. What is clear is the family: ~fouet~ gave ~fouetter~, and ~fouailler~ means to lash again and again.
en.foudroyer: Formed from ~foudre~ (“lightning”) plus the suffix ~-oyer~, which can mean to act like or emit the noun, so ~foudroyer~ is to strike with lightning and, by extension, to devastate. English Wiktionary traces ~foudre~ from Old French ~foudre~, from Latin ~fulgura~, the plural of ~fulgur~ (“lightning”), or alternatively from ~fulgere~ (“to flash”). The suffix ~-oyer~ comes from Old French ~-oiier~, from Late Latin ~-izāre~. Verbs of the same pattern include ~flamboyer~ and ~verdoyer~.
en.fouetter: Formed from the noun ~fouet~ (“whip”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to use a whip.” The noun is a diminutive in ~-et~ of Old French ~fou~ (“beech”), from Latin ~fagus~ (“beech”), so a ~fouet~ was originally a little beech switch; it is first found in a thirteenth-century fabliau. French Wiktionary adds that the slang sense “to stink” is a separate matter, from Latin ~foetēre~ (“to stink”), reshaped by the image of a smell that strikes the nose like a lash.
en.fouger:
French Wiktionary derives ~fouger~ (“to root,” as a boar does) from Latin ~fodicāre~, itself drawn from ~fodere~ (“to dig”). It adds, with a hedge, that the verb may also come from Middle French ~fouge~ (“fern”), a food boars are fond of. The two accounts are offered side by side, and neither is presented as settled.

The Latin verb ~fodere~ is the better-known source, and it gave French ~fouir~ (“to dig”) by regular inheritance, along with learned relatives such as ~fossile~ and ~fosse~ (“pit”). The fern account explains the same verb differently: the boar roots because it looks for ~fouge~, and the name of the food would have given the verb. ~Fouger~ is a hunting term, used of the boar as it turns up the ground with its snout, and it belongs to the vocabulary of venery.
en.fouiller:
French ~fouiller~ comes from Old French ~fooiller~, which goes back to a Vulgar Latin verb reconstructed as *~fodiculāre~ (a contracted *~fodiclāre~ is also cited). That is a diminutive of Latin ~fodicāre~ (“to pierce”), itself a frequentative of ~fodere~ (“to dig”). The same ~fodere~ gave French ~fouir~, which English Wiktionary invites us to compare with ~fouiller~. The chain therefore runs from digging, to repeated piercing, to a diminutive of that piercing, the frequentative and the diminutive each adding a sense of small, repeated action. The Vulgar Latin stage is reconstructed and not attested, so it is a scholarly inference and not a recorded word.

The modern sense is that of searching: to ~fouiller~ is to dig into something, or to rummage through it, in order to find what lies inside. The noun ~fouille~ names the act, in the ~fouilles~ (“excavations”) of archaeologists and in the search of a person or a place by the police. The verb keeps this double character, literal digging and figurative probing, which suits a word whose ancestors were all verbs of digging and piercing. Its relative ~fouir~ shares the Latin source, so the two verbs form a pair, ~fouir~ for plain digging and ~fouiller~ for the searching kind.
en.fouiner: ~Fouiner~ is formed from the noun ~fouine~ (“beech marten”) plus the verb ending ~-er~, in the sense “act like N,” so the verb means to rummage around and poke into things. The noun ~fouine~ comes from Old French ~foene~ (attested 1160), an alteration of Vulgar Latin ~fagina~ (~mustela~), literally the marten “of the beech.” The animal's name is thus the base of a verb for nosy searching.
en.fouir:
From Latin ~fodere~ (“to dig”), which became *~fodīre~ in Vulgar Latin, with the verb passing into the ~-ire~ conjugation. Old French ~fouir~, also spelled ~fuir~, is the regular outcome. The Old French form ~fuir~ was thus identical in shape to the unrelated ~fuir~ (“to flee”), yet only ~fouir~ survived in the sense of digging. Its noun ~fossa~ (“ditch”) spread widely in the Romance languages.

In modern French, ~fouir~ means to dig, grub or burrow, and it is used mainly of animals that dig the ground, such as moles, badgers and rabbits. Its agent noun ~fouisseur~ names such burrowing animals. The Latin root also supplies a learned family: ~fosse~ (“pit, ditch”), ~fossé~ (“ditch”) and ~fossile~, from Latin ~fossilis~ (“dug up”), which English borrowed as ~fossil~. ~Fouiller~ (“to search, to excavate”) and ~fouille~ belong to the same family. Digging in the earth thus gave French its word for the remains found there.
en.fouler:
From Old French ~foler~ (“to crush, to act wickedly”), whose Middle French form was ~fouller~, from Vulgar Latin *~fullāre~ (“to trample, to full cloth”), from Latin ~fullō~ (“fuller”). French Wiktionary gives the same chain through Late Latin ~fullāre~ (“to practice the fuller's trade”). A ~fullō~ was a cloth-worker who cleaned and thickened cloth, and English ~fuller~, with its verb ~to full~, comes from the same Latin word.

So ~fouler~ began as a craft verb: the fuller worked cloth by pressing and trampling it, and the French verb broadened to “to tread on, to press down, to crush.” Hence ~fouler le sol~ (“to set foot on a land”), ~fouler aux pieds~ (“to trample underfoot,” and figuratively to flout), and ~se fouler la cheville~ (“to sprain one's ankle”). Related words keep the pressing sense: ~foulée~ (“a stride, a footfall”), ~foulure~ (“a sprain”) and ~foulon~ (“a fuller”), the last still a trade name. Old French also used the verb for harsh treatment, which fits the figurative ~fouler aux pieds~.
en.fourbir:
~Fourbir~ comes from Old French ~forbir~ (Middle French ~fourbir~), a verb that French inherited from Frankish, the Germanic language of the Franks. The Frankish source is reconstructed as *~furbjan~ (“to clean”), or as *~furbēn~ in another account of the same word. Germanic cousins survive in Old High German ~furban~ (“to clean”) and Middle High German ~vürben~ (“to clean”). English ~furbish~ corresponds to it.

In French the verb meant to clean and polish, especially metal, until it shone. That sense is still alive in the figurative expression ~fourbir ses armes~, “to prepare for a fight,” and in the noun ~fourbisseur~, the craftsman who cleaned and polished weapons. Like many French verbs of cleaning and craft, it is a Germanic word that entered Gallo-Romance through the Franks.
en.fourcher: Formed from the noun ~fourche~ (“fork”) plus the verb ending ~-er~: to ~fourcher~ is to divide into branches like a fork, or to work with a pitchfork. The noun was inherited from Old French ~furche~ and ~forche~, from Latin ~furca~ (“pitchfork”). The suffix ~-er~ makes a verb of doing from a noun. The verb survives mainly in the expression ~la langue m'a fourché~, where the tongue, as if it had forked, takes the wrong path and says one word for another.
en.fourgonner: Formed from ~fourgon~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. The verb means to poke the embers of a fire, using a ~fourgon~, an oven poker. Wiktionary traces ~fourgon~ to Vulgar Latin *~furicō~, from *~furicāre~ (“to ferret about”), which goes back to Latin ~fur~ (“thief”). French Wiktionary notes an early attestation as ~forgon~ in the glosses of Rashi, and one nineteenth-century scholar treats ~fourgon~ as a doublet of ~fourchon~. The vehicle sense of ~fourgon~ (a van) probably came later.
en.fourguer:
According to French Wiktionary, ~fourguer~ comes from a reconstructed Vulgar Latin verb *~furicare~ (“to rummage, to poke about”), and is listed as related to ~fourgon~, ~furet~ and ~forger~. The word is first recorded in 1821, as slang. English Wiktionary gives no etymology for it. The verb means to sell off goods, and by extension to get rid of something.

The sources do not explain how a verb of rummaging became one of selling, so that link remains open. Its register is clear, though: ~fourguer~ began as argot and is now familiar speech for foisting something unwanted on someone, as in ~fourguer une vieille voiture~. Its listed relatives are a mixed group: ~fourgon~ (a van or poker), ~furet~ (a ferret, an animal that pokes into holes) and ~forger~. French Wiktionary gives these as related words, without detailing how the links work.
en.fourmiller: The sources frame this verb differently. French Wiktionary simply derives it from ~fourmi~ (“ant”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, while English Wiktionary treats it as inherited from Old French ~formiier~, itself from Latin ~formīcāre~, and compares Italian ~formicolare~ and Spanish ~hormiguear~. The noun ~fourmi~ came through Middle French from Old French ~formie~ (also ~furmi~), from a Vulgar Latin *~formicus~, itself from classical Latin ~formīca~ (“ant”).
en.fournir:
From Old French ~fornir~ (also ~furnir~), borrowed from Frankish *~frumjan~ (“to accomplish, carry out, provide”), from a Germanic base *~fruma~ (“first, foremost; advantage, benefit”). The verb is cousin to Italian ~fornire~ and to the borrowed English ~furnish~ (which English took straight from this Old French verb), and through its Germanic root to German ~fromm~ (“pious, devout,” earlier “useful, upright”). The unexpected nasal ~n~ of the modern stem arose under the influence of the near-synonym ~garnir~ (“to garnish, equip”).

The original idea was “to carry through, accomplish, make ready,” which slid easily into “to provide what is needed, to equip.” From “equipping” came the modern core senses: to supply, to provide, to furnish. The noun ~fourniture~ (“supply, supplies”) and the agent ~fournisseur~ (“supplier”) carry the commercial weight today, while ~fourni~ as an adjective means “well-stocked” or, of hair and beards, “thick, abundant.” It is a tidy irony that English ~furnish~ — which in English narrowed toward outfitting a room with furniture — and French ~fournir~ — which stayed broad, “to supply anything” — are the very same Frankish word, sent down two paths. Kin in French include ~fourniture~, ~fournisseur~, ~fournil~, and ~fourni~.
en.fourrager: ~Fourrager~ is formed from the noun ~fourrage~ (“fodder”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, in the sense of gathering fodder, then of rummaging about as if searching for it. The noun is itself a derivative of Old French ~feurre~ (an old word for straw or fodder) with the suffix ~-age~, and it is attested in Middle French as ~fourage~. So the verb sits at the end of a short chain: ~feurre~, ~fourrage~, ~fourrager~.
en.fourrer: ~Fourrer~ is derived from Old French ~fuerre~ (also written ~feurre~), meaning “sheath,” with the verb ending ~-er~. The same Old French noun survives in modern ~fourreau~ (“sheath, scabbard”). As general background, ~fourrure~ (“fur”) belongs to the same family, as a lining stuffed or fitted into a garment. From the idea of a covering that something slides into, the verb came to mean to push or stuff one thing into another. The sources give only the Old French noun, so its own earlier origin is left aside here.
en.fourvoyer:
~Fourvoyer~ is inherited from Old French ~forvoier~, built from the prefix ~for-~, the noun ~voie~ (“way”) and the verb ending ~-er~. The prefix is old and no longer productive, and its own origin is debated: either Late Latin ~forīs~ (“outside”) shaped on a Frankish prefix *~fur-~, or ~fors~ (“outside”). In this verb it means “wrongly, astray,” and the vowel of ~for-~ became ~ou~ in the modern spelling. The noun ~voie~ descends from Latin ~via~ (“road”) and is a doublet of the learned ~via~. It is unrelated to ~voir~.

The sources also raise a second possibility. The verb may be a calque of a Frankish verb *~farleidian~, which has relatives in Old Saxon ~farlēdian~, Dutch ~verleiden~ and German ~verleiten~. This is only a suggestion, marked as “perhaps,” and the evidence does not settle it. If it is right, French copied the structure of the Germanic verb and not its words. Only a few old verbs, such as ~forfaire~ and ~forclore~, keep the prefix ~for-~ today.
en.foutre:
From Vulgar Latin *~fŭttĕre~, with expressive doubling of the t, from Classical Latin ~futuere~ (“to copulate with”), infinitive of ~futuō~. The PIE root is uncertain: one proposal connects ~futuō~ to *~bʰew-~ (“to strike, to hit”) and to Latin ~fūstis~ (“club, staff”), but the sources flag this as no more than possible. The Latin verb is the unmistakable ancestor of a whole Romance set — Italian ~fottere~, Spanish ~joder~, Portuguese ~foder~, Romanian ~fute~ — and of French ~foutre~ itself.

Originally crude and sexual, ~foutre~ has had its literal sense largely worn away, surviving today as a vulgar, very general verb of doing, putting and caring — or pointedly not caring. One ~se fout~ of something to mean one does not give a darn about it, and the imperative sends someone away. The register is firmly vulgar and, in the old literal sense, archaic. The French family it spawned is large and idiomatic: ~foutu~ (“done for”), ~foutaise~ (“rubbish”), ~foutoir~ (“shambles”) and the set phrases ~foutre le camp~ (“to clear off”) and ~s’en foutre~ (“to not care a bit”).
en.fracasser:
French ~fracasser~ is borrowed from Italian ~fracassare~ (“to break to pieces”). The earlier history of the Italian verb is not certain. French Wiktionary says it probably comes from a combination of Latin ~frangere~ (“to break”) and Latin ~quassāre~ (“to shake, to shatter”), while English Wiktionary stops at the Italian word and offers nothing further. The blend is therefore a probable account, not a settled one.

If the blend is right, the verb pairs two Latin verbs of breaking, which would explain its violent sense of smashing something into pieces with noise. Both parent verbs left descendants in French. ~Frangere~ gave ~fracture~, ~fragile~, ~fraction~ and ~enfreindre~ (“to infringe”), and ~quassāre~ gave ~casser~ (“to break”) and ~concasser~ (“to crush”). English shares the first family through ~fracture~ and ~fragile~. The noun ~fracas~ (“din, crash”) belongs with the verb.
en.fractionner: ~Fractionner~ is a denominal verb formed from the noun ~fraction~ and the ending ~-er~; it means to divide into fractions or parts. The noun ~fraction~ comes from Old French ~fraction~, borrowed from Late Latin ~fractio~, derived from the verb ~frangere~ (“to break”), itself from the Indo-European root *~bʰreg-~. The sense “act of breaking” is attested from 1187, first in liturgical vocabulary; “portion of a whole” from 1273; the mathematical sense appeared in French in the second half of the 13th century.
en.fracturer: Formed from the noun ~fracture~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, a denominal verb meaning “to cause a fracture in”. The noun reached French as a learned borrowing from Latin ~fractūra~, a derivative of ~frangere~ (“to break”). English Wiktionary adds that the inherited Old French counterpart was ~fraiture~, a reminder that the same Latin word once entered French by the popular route too. The ending ~-er~ comes from the Latin first-conjugation ~-are~, the default way French coins new verbs from nouns.
en.fragiliser: ~Fragiliser~ is ~fragile~ + the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to make fragile, to weaken”. The base ~fragile~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~fragilis~ (“breakable, brittle, perishable”), from ~frangere~ (“to break”). The same Latin word had already reached French by popular evolution as ~frêle~, so ~fragile~ and ~frêle~ are doublets. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~ and forms verbs meaning “to make A”, as in ~fragiliser~ and ~actualiser~.
en.fragmenter: Formed from the noun ~fragment~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so “to break into fragments.” The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin ~fragmentum~ (“a piece, remnant”), derived from ~frangere~ (“to break”). French ~fragile~ and ~fraction~, like English ~fragile~ and ~fraction~, belong to the same family.
en.fraiser: ~Fraiser~ is generally explained as formed from ~fraise~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~, from the milling cutter called a ~fraise~, which was named by analogy with the ruff collar of the same name and its pleated, notched edge. That collar took its name in turn from the fruit ~fraise~ (“strawberry”), which comes from Latin ~frāga~. English.Wiktionary also allows another origin, from a Vulgar Latin *~fresāre~, based on the Latin participle ~fresum~ of ~frendō~, and compares Spanish ~fresar~. The sources do not settle the matter. To ~fraiser~ is to machine metal or wood with such a cutter, or to countersink a hole.
en.framboiser: ~Framboiser~ is derived from the noun ~framboise~ (“raspberry”) with the verbal ending ~-er~: to flavor or color with raspberry. The noun comes from Old French ~frambeise~, borrowed from Frankish *~brāmabasi~ (“blackberry”), a compound of the words for “bramble” and “berry” that also gave Dutch ~braambes~ and German ~Brombeere~. The initial ~f-~ replaced ~b-~ under the influence of ~fraise~ (“strawberry”).
en.franchir:
French ~franchir~ is formed from the adjective ~franc~ (“free”) with the ending ~-ir~. ~Franc~ comes from Late Latin ~Francus~ (“a Frank”), from the Germanic name of the ~Franks~; in Frankish Gaul only the Franks held full legal freedom, so the ethnic name came to mean “free.” It is thus cognate with English ~frank~, ~Frankish~, and the name ~France~. Old French ~franchir~ / ~franchier~ first meant “to set free,” a literal sense that the parallel ~affranchir~ (“to enfranchise, free”) still preserves.

From “to free” the verb took a striking turn: “to free oneself of a burden,” then “to clear an obstacle by leaping or climbing it,” and finally “to go beyond a limit,” displacing the older Old French ~transir~ in that role. So to ~franchir~ a river, a doorway, or a threshold is, etymologically, to win free of it. The family includes ~franchise~ (“frankness; franchise; exemption”), ~franchissement~ (“crossing”), and ~infranchissable~ (“impassable”), and idioms like ~franchir~ le pas, “to take the plunge.”
en.franchiser: ~Franchiser~ is a denominal verb, ~franchise~ + ~-er~, and English Wiktionary adds that it may be a calque of the English verb ~franchise~. The noun ~franchise~ is inherited from Old French ~franchise~ (“freedom, privileged liberty”), formed from ~franc~ (“free”) and ~-ise~, from Latin ~-itia~. French Wiktionary notes that the commercial sense of the noun was taken from English. The verb means “to franchise,” to grant a business the right to operate under another's name.
en.franciser: ~Franciser~ is formed from the stem of ~français~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which gives the sense of making something conform to a model, as in ~latiniser~ and ~angliciser~. The verb thus means to make French, to give a French form or character to something. The base ~français~ goes back to Old French ~franceis~ or ~françois~, from Latin ~Franciscus~ and ultimately ~Francus~, the Latin name for a Frank. French Wiktionary adds that, within French, the word can be read as ~France~ plus ~-ais~.
en.franger: Formed in French from the noun ~frange~ (“fringe”) with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, in the sense “to provide with a fringe.” The noun ~frange~ comes from Old French ~frenge~, from a Vulgar Latin *~frimbia~, itself a metathesis (a swap in the order of sounds) of Late Latin ~fimbria~, from Latin ~fimbriae~ (“fibers, threads, fringe”). The ~-er~ ending goes back to the Latin first-conjugation ending ~-are~ and is the default way of coining verbs from nouns. English ~fringe~ is a related word that likewise comes from the Old French noun.
en.fransquillonner: Formed from the noun ~fransquillon~ with the verb ending ~-er~. According to Jacques Mercier (2003), ~fransquillon~ dates from the eighteenth century and derives from ~francillon~. A ~fransquillon~ is a Belgian who affects a Parisian way of speaking, so the verb is a Belgian regionalism meaning to speak French in an affected manner in order to hide one's own accent.
en.frapper:
From Old French ~fraper~ (attested 1178), most likely from Frankish *~hrapōn~ (“to snatch, seize quickly”), of Germanic origin. The same Germanic stem ~hrap-~ surfaces in Dutch ~rapen~ (“to gather, seize”), German ~raffen~ (“to snatch up”), and Old Norse ~hreppa~ (“to obtain, reach”), all turning on the idea of grabbing something swiftly and forcefully. Romance absorbed the word too, giving Italian ~frappare~. The initial ~f~ is the telltale mark of a Frankish loan reshaped in Gallo-Romance mouths.

The meaning shifted from a quick snatching to a sudden, forceful blow — the gesture of striking. From there ~frapper~ spread generously: one hits a nail, a clock strikes the hour, a coin is struck (~frapper monnaie~), and, figuratively, a sight or a fact strikes you — ~ça m'a frappé~, “that struck me.” It even yields ~frappé~ for an iced, “shaken” drink. Modern relatives include ~frappe~ (a strike, or typing), ~frappant~ (“striking, remarkable”), and ~frappeur~. The Germanic input here is a reminder that beneath Latinate French runs a strong Frankish current, left by the Germanic people who gave France its very name.
en.fraterniser:
From Latin ~fraternus~ (“brotherly”) plus the verbal suffix ~-iser~. Latin ~fraternus~ is the adjective built on ~frater~ (“brother”), and the suffix gives the sense “to act as a brother.” French also has the twin verb ~fraternaliser~: the two descend from the same Latin adjective and carry the same suffix, which is why French Wiktionary calls them doublets.

The Latin noun ~frater~ is the source of French ~frère~, and it has famous Germanic cousins in English ~brother~ and German ~Bruder~. The family around ~fraternus~ in French includes ~fraternel~, ~fraternité~ and the learned ~confraternité~, and ~fraternité~ is the third term of the French motto, after liberty and equality. In modern French ~fraterniser~ means to mingle in a friendly way, especially with people one might be expected to keep apart, such as former enemies.
en.frauder:
Borrowed from Latin ~fraudāre~ (“to harm by fraud, to cheat”), a verb formed on the noun ~fraus~ (“deceit, fraud”). In Latin it meant to harm someone by fraud. French ~frauder~ keeps this core, the idea of wronging a person or an institution through deceit. English ~fraud~ and ~defraud~ go back to the same Latin family.

The family is large and mostly learned. French ~fraude~ and the adjective ~frauduleux~ (“fraudulent”) come from the Latin noun and adjective, while ~fraudeur~ names the person who commits the fraud. ~Défrauder~ (“to cheat, to swindle”) comes from Latin ~dēfraudāre~, a strengthened form of the same verb. In modern French ~frauder~ is used mostly of cheating a system rather than a person: one cheats the tax authorities, customs or an exam, and the verb can also be used without an object, meaning “to cheat.” Spanish ~defraudar~ and Italian ~frodare~ are cousins.
en.frayer:
The origin of ~frayer~ is not settled, and French Wiktionary treats it as at least two verbs. The sense “to rub, to brush against” (and, of fish, “to spawn”) comes from Old French ~froier~ (English Wiktionary gives ~freier~), inherited from Latin ~fricāre~ (“to rub”). The same Latin verb gave the learned word ~friction~, which French and English share. A separate verb, “to incur expense” (~faire des frais~), is a back-formation from the noun ~frais~ (“expense”). The TLFi does not separate the verbs at all.

The sense “to open a path” is the puzzle. Littré observes that it is not found before Froissart and offers three possibilities, none of them certain. It may be the same verb as ~froier~, though rubbing hardly explains clearing a way. It may be the old verb ~froer~ (“to break”), since a road is a broken way, Latin ~via rupta~, with its vowels pulled into line with ~frayer~. Or it may be an irregular derivative of Latin ~fractus~ (“broken”). Littré finds the meaning and the form good in the last two accounts, so the question stays open.
en.fraîchir: Formed from the adjective ~frais~ (feminine ~fraîche~, “cool, fresh”) with the ending ~-ir~, meaning “to turn cooler,” and attested in Old French as ~freschir~. It is used above all of the wind: ~le vent fraîchit~ (“the wind is freshening”). The circumflex of ~fraîche~ stands in for the ~s~ still visible in the Old French spelling. The adjective itself is of Germanic origin, a cousin of English ~fresh~ and German ~frisch~.
en.fredonner: The verb is formed from the noun ~fredon~ (“refrain”) and the ending ~-er~, so it means to sing something softly, without words or on a murmur, as one hums a tune. French Wiktionary traces the noun ~fredon~ to Latin ~fritinnīre~ (“to twitter, to chirp”), which makes the humming a distant echo of birdsong. The route from the Latin verb to the French noun is not detailed in the sources.
en.freiner:
From Latin ~frēnāre~ (“to bridle, to check”), built on ~frēnum~ (“bridle, bit”), the source of French ~frein~. An Old French verb ~frener~ already existed in the sense of bridling or restraining, and English Wiktionary notes that the modern verb can equally be read as ~frein~ plus ~-er~. The Latin verb has sister forms elsewhere: Italian ~frenare~ and Spanish ~frenar~.

The meaning shows how a technology can borrow an image from the stable. The Latin noun ~frēnum~ was the bit that checks a horse, and the verb first meant to bridle or restrain; English Wiktionary gives 1907 as a date for the modern verb, in the early age of the motor car. Figurative uses are easy to find: one ~freine~ spending, ambition or an impulse. The Latin family also gave ~refréner~ (“to hold back”), with English ~refrain~ from the same ~refrēnāre~ by way of Old French, and ~effréné~ (“unbridled”), the opposite of a bridled ardor, as well as ~frein~ itself.
en.frelater:
~Frelater~ is borrowed from Middle Dutch ~verlaten~, which meant “to decant,” that is, to pour a liquid from one container into another. The Dutch verb is made of the prefix ~ver-~ and ~laten~ (“to let, to leave”), and modern Dutch ~verlaten~ means “to leave, to abandon.” The simple verb ~laten~ is a cognate of German ~lassen~ and English ~let~, and ~ver-~ corresponds to German ~ver-~ and English ~for-~.

French kept the sense “to decant,” and from it developed the meaning “to alter the purity of a liquid.” Modern ~frelater~ therefore means to adulterate a wine or another drink, and by extension to corrupt or debase something. The past participle ~frelaté~ also serves as an adjective, “adulterated, tainted,” and the action is named by the noun ~frelatage~.
en.fretter: ~Fretter~ is a denominal from ~frette~, a band that reinforces something, hence “to reinforce with ferrules.” The basic sense of ~frette~ appears to be “reinforcement,” which ties it to Old French ~freter~ or ~ferter~ (“to consolidate, to strengthen”), described as a verb formed on ~ferté~ and turned into ~freter~ by metathesis, the swapping of two sounds. The ending ~-er~ forms verbs meaning “to provide with” the noun.
en.fricasser:
The origin of ~fricasser~ is debated. French Wiktionary derives it from ~frire~ (“to fry”) and ~casser~ (“to break”), a blend. English Wiktionary favors, as probable, a Vulgar Latin frequentative *~frīgicāre~, from Latin ~frīgō~ (“to roast, to fry”), and gives the blend of ~frire~ and ~casser~ only as a possibility. The two accounts agree that frying is at the root; they differ on whether the second half is a Latin suffix or the French verb ~casser~.

The verb ~frire~ itself comes from Latin ~frīgere~, the same verb, so both accounts lead to the idea of cooking in fat. From ~fricasser~ French formed the noun ~fricassée~ (a dish of meat cooked in a sauce), and English borrowed it as ~fricassee~. The verb means to cook food in this way, and in slang it also took the sense of engaging in debauchery.
en.fricoter: ~Fricoter~ is built on ~fricot~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, and it means to cook a stew and, colloquially, to flirt. ~Fricot~ is a popular derivative of ~fricasser~ (or of ~fricassée~), formed with the suffix ~-ot~, and is found in the eighteenth century in the sense of “feasting.” So a verb of the kitchen and of a lively table lies behind the modern word.
en.frictionner: Formed from the noun ~friction~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so it means to rub, especially the body, to warm it or to apply a lotion. The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin ~frictiō~ (“the act of rubbing”), which comes from the verb ~fricāre~ (“to rub”). Because the noun was borrowed whole from Latin, the verb is a later French coinage on top of a learned word, a pattern common for medical and technical terms. English ~friction~ was borrowed from the same Latin noun.
en.frigorifier: The two Wiktionaries agree that this verb is built on ~frigorifique~ (“refrigerating, cooling”). French Wiktionary calls it a verbal derivative of that adjective, as ~pacifier~ stands to ~pacifique~, while English Wiktionary analyzes it as the stem ~frigor-~ plus ~-ifier~. The suffix ~-ifier~ goes back to Latin ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”), so the verb means “to make cold.” The adjective itself is built on Latin ~frigus~ (“cold”).
en.frimer: Formed from the noun ~frime~ with the verb ending ~-er~, in the colloquial sense of showing off. French Wiktionary traces ~frime~ to Old French ~frume~ (“mine”, an old word for a look or expression of the face) and refers to ~frimousse~ for the same source. The sources say no more about how a facial look led to showing off, so that link is left open here.
en.fringuer:
The better-documented ~fringuer~ is the one meaning “to dress.” English Wiktionary has it inherited from Middle French ~fringuer~, a denominal of Old French ~fringue~ (“garment, clothing”). The word is not Latin and is likely Germanic, possibly from Frankish *~hringila~ (“ring, loop”), related to Old High German ~ringila~, modern German ~Ringel~. French Wiktionary likewise treats this verb as derived from ~fringues~ and from the Old French verb ~fringuer~. The Frankish link is a proposal, not a certainty.

French Wiktionary also lists a separate, homonymous verb ~fringuer~, with a different story: it may come from Ancient Greek ~afrigao~ (“I jump”) or from ~afrizo~ (“I foam”), again without certainty. The clothing verb is the one in common use today, usually as the reflexive ~se fringuer~, “to get dressed, to dress up.” Its noun ~fringues~, a colloquial word for “clothes,” belongs to the same family.
en.friper:
~Friper~ comes from Old French ~freper~ (“to crumple”), a verb that goes with the noun ~frepe~ (“frayed; rag, old clothes”). The origin of ~frepe~ is uncertain. One proposal links it to Late Latin ~falappa~ (“shaving, scrap”), a word that is itself of uncertain origin and probably not Latin at all. Both Wiktionaries give this link only as a possibility, so it should not be taken as settled.

The noun side of the family is the better known. ~Friperie~ is the trade in secondhand clothes, or the shop that sells them, and a ~fripier~ is the dealer, both tied to the old sense “rag, old clothes” of ~frepe~. ~Friper~ itself kept the sense “to crumple,” and its participle ~fripé~ describes rumpled clothes or a worn face.
en.frire:
From Old French ~frire~, inherited from Latin ~frīgere~ (“to fry, to roast”), which both Wiktionaries trace to the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰer-~. Latin ~frīgere~ also lies behind Italian ~friggere~ and Spanish ~freír~. English took its verb ~fry~ from the Old French verb, so English and French share the word even though they pronounce it very differently.

In French, ~frire~ is a defective verb: it lacks several forms, such as the plural of the present tense, and speakers fill the gaps with ~faire frire~. The family of words around it includes ~frit~ (“fried”), ~friture~ (“frying, fried food”) and ~friteuse~ (“deep fryer”). One caution: Latin ~frīgere~ is a different verb from ~frīgēre~ (“to be cold”), which gave ~frigide~ in French. The Latin forms differ only in the length of one vowel, but their stories are separate.
en.friser:
The origin is uncertain, and the two Wiktionaries offer different answers. French Wiktionary proposes, with a “perhaps,” that it comes from ~frire~ (“to fry”), the curled, crinkled edges of frying food having suggested the comparison. English Wiktionary instead derives it from a Germanic source, a form like Old Frisian ~frisle~ (“curly hair”), from Proto-Germanic *~frisaz~ (“curly, frizzy”), and links it to English ~frizz~. The hair-curling sense fits either route, so the question stays open.

The literal meaning is to curl hair, and the participle ~frisé~ describes curly hair, curly endive (~chicorée frisée~) and similar crinkly things. From there the verb developed a figurative sense, “to graze, to skim past,” as in ~friser l'accident~ (“to come within a hair of an accident”), and ~friser la quarantaine~ (“to be close to forty”). The family includes ~frisé~, ~frisure~, ~frisette~ and ~frisottis~.
en.frisotter: Formed from ~friser~ with the suffix ~-otter~, which gives a small, light or repeated action in the familiar register: ~frisotter~ is to curl lightly, in small curls. The base ~friser~ has an uncertain origin. French Wiktionary proposes, with a “perhaps,” a link to ~frire~ (“to fry”), the crinkled edges of frying food suggesting curls. English Wiktionary instead derives it from a Germanic source such as Old Frisian ~frisle~ (“curly hair”), from Proto-Germanic *~frisaz~ (“curly”), and links it to English ~frizz~. The curling sense fits either route.
en.frissonner: Formed from the noun ~frisson~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, so “to have a shiver.” The noun comes from Late Latin *~frīctiōnem~, derived from Latin ~frīgeō~ (“to be cold”). It is unrelated to Classical Latin ~frictiō~, which French borrowed separately as ~friction~. The ending ~-er~ goes back to Latin ~-are~ and is the usual way to make a verb from a noun.
en.friter: ~Friter~ is a variant spelling of ~fritter~, and it is used chiefly in the pronominal form ~se friter~. The older verb ~fritter~ is formed from the noun ~fritte~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~fritte~ was borrowed from Italian ~fritta~ (“fried matter”) and is attested as a glassmaking term from the fourteenth or fifteenth century. The verb began as a technical term of that same trade, naming the operation of fritting or sintering the raw materials. French Wiktionary gives no separate origin for ~friter~ itself.
en.fritter: ~Fritter~ is formed from ~fritte~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~fritte~ is borrowed from Italian ~fritta~ (“fried matter”), attested as a glassmaking term from the fourteenth or fifteenth century. The verb is a technical term from the same trade, naming the operation of fritting or sintering.
en.froisser:
~Froisser~ is a reworking of Old French ~fruisser~, which goes back to a Vulgar Latin verb reconstructed as *~frustiāre~ (“to break into pieces”). That verb comes from Latin ~frustum~ (“piece, fragment”). French Wiktionary traces ~frustum~ through Proto-Italic *~frustom~ to a Proto-Indo-European form *~bʰrus-to-~, derived from a root *~bʰrews-~ (“to break”). English borrowed ~frustum~ directly from Latin, using it in geometry for the slice of a cone or pyramid left when the top is cut off.

The verb thus began as a word for smashing something into bits and later softened into the gentler “to crumple, to crease” of modern French, as when one crumples paper or fabric. The sources do not date that shift, so it is best seen as a general softening from breaking to wrinkling. French also uses ~froisser~ figuratively, for offending someone, and has the related ~froissement~, ~froissé~ and ~froissable~, along with ~infroissable~ (“crease-proof”).
en.froncer:
From Middle French ~fronce~ (“frown, wrinkle”), from Old French ~fronces~ or ~fronche~, which meant “frown,” “wrinkles” and “small creases in cloth.” Behind it stands Frankish *~hrunkja~ (“wrinkle”), from Proto-Germanic *~hrunkijō~ (“fold, wrinkle”), which English Wiktionary traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~sker-~ (“to turn, bend”). Its Germanic cousins include Old High German ~runza~ (German ~Runzel~, “wrinkle”), Middle Dutch ~ronse~ (“frown”) and Old Norse ~hrukka~ (“wrinkle”), as well as English ~ruck~.

The verb was drawn from the noun and kept both of its meanings. It describes knitting the brows, as in ~froncer les sourcils~ (“to frown”), and also gathering cloth into small folds. A frown and a gathered skirt are the same wrinkle, seen on a face and on fabric. The noun survives too, as ~fronce~ (“a gather in fabric”), and ~froncement~ names the act of frowning or puckering.
en.fronder: ~Fronder~ is a verb formed from the noun ~fronde~ (“sling”) with the ending ~-er~, first meaning “to hurl with a sling”. The noun is an alteration of Old French ~flondre~, probably from Latin ~funda~ (“sling”) through a diminutive, Vulgar Latin *~fundula~. Italian ~fionda~ is a comparable form. The figurative sense “to criticize, to defy authority” came from the verb. The historical ~Fronde~, the revolt, takes its meaning from this verb, not the other way round.
en.frotter: The origin is uncertain. The verb comes from Middle French ~frotter~, from Old French ~froter~ (“to stroke, wipe, rub”). The usual assumption is that it goes back to Latin ~frictāre~, a frequentative of ~fricāre~ (“to rub, to polish, to curry”) formed from its past participle ~frictus~, but this remains an assumption. French Wiktionary adds that ~frotter~ is generally thought to share its source with ~frétiller~ and ~frictionner~, which it also traces to a Latin ~frictāre~. ~Frictionner~ is the one that kept the Latin shape most closely.
en.frouer: ~Frouer~ is most probably formed on the imitative syllable ~frou~, and it means to cry out as an owl or a pigeon does. French Wiktionary prefers this explanation to a descent from Old French ~frouer~ or ~froier~ (“to rub, to break open”). It refers the reader to ~flouer~ (“to swindle”), but it states that a path from a bird's cry to deceiving by imitating that cry is not established. The origin is therefore best treated as imitative, with the older verb as a rejected rival.
en.froufrouter: Formed from ~froufrou~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning to rustle, as silk or petticoats do. The noun ~froufrou~ is an onomatopoeia, a word that imitates the sound of rustling fabric. The verb therefore keeps the echoic quality of its base, with a doubled syllable that mimics the repeated whisper of cloth.
en.fructifier: ~Fructifier~ comes from Late Latin ~fructificāre~, itself formed from Latin ~fructus~ (“fruit”). French ~fruit~ descends from the same Latin noun. The verb means literally to bear fruit, and it is also used figuratively of money or efforts that yield a return.
en.frustrer:
Borrowed from Latin ~frūstrāre~ (“to deceive, to disappoint, to make vain”), formed on the adverb ~frūstrā~ (“in vain, to no purpose”). Latin ~frūstrā~ is usually linked to ~fraus~ (“deceit, harm”), though the exact derivation is debated. The verb passed into Italian ~frustrare~ and Spanish ~frustrar~, and English ~frustrate~ comes from the same Latin source.

The Latin verb meant to trick someone's expectations or to leave a plan empty, and French ~frustrer~ carries that idea of depriving someone of what they were counting on. The emotional meaning that dominates today is the sour feeling of being blocked from a goal. That is why ~frustré~ now describes a mood as readily as a deprivation. The same Latin root gives ~frustration~ and ~frustrant~ in French, and the sense of thwarted effort is still visible in the ancestor ~frūstrā~, which meant simply that something was done for nothing.
en.frégater: ~Frégater~ (“to build a ship frigate-style”) is formed from the noun ~frégate~ with the ending ~-er~. The noun, a naval term for a fast warship, was borrowed from Italian ~fregata~. In shipbuilding, to ~frégater~ a hull is to give it the lean, long lines of a frigate. The same noun gave its name to the seabird, the ~frégate~, by way of a comparison with the fast ship.
en.frémir:
From Old French and Middle French ~fremir~, from Vulgar Latin *~fremīre~, an altered form of Latin ~fremere~ (“to roar, to rumble, to murmur”), which shifted to the ~-ire~ conjugation in everyday speech. English Wiktionary traces Latin ~fremō~ to the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰrem-~ (“to growl, to roar”). Its cognates include Greek ~brémein~ (“to roar”), and the Greek epithet ~Brómios~ (“the roarer”), a name of Dionysus.

The fascinating shift is from sound to movement. Latin ~fremere~ named a noise, the roar of a crowd, the rumble of the sea, the rustle of a murmur. French ~frémir~ kept that sense for a time and then moved toward what the body does when moved by such sounds: to tremble, to quiver with fear, cold or emotion. A third sense belongs to cooking: water that ~frémit~ is just below the boil, still rippling and murmuring. The noun ~frémissement~ and the adjective ~frémissant~ cover both the trembling and the quiet stir.
en.fréquenter:
First attested around 1190, ~fréquenter~ comes from Latin ~frequentāre~ (“to visit often, to crowd, to celebrate”), a verb built on the adjective ~frequēns~ (“crowded, numerous, repeated”), the same adjective that gives French ~fréquent~, Spanish ~frecuente~, Italian ~frequente~, and English ~frequent~. The deeper origin of ~frequēns~ is disputed: by one account it descends from a Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰrekʷ-~ (“to cram, to stuff”), connected to Latin ~farcīre~ (“to cram”) and Greek ~phrássō~ (“to fence in”), but Beekes judged the Greek comparison quite uncertain, and other scholars propose different roots entirely. The chain back to Latin, however, is secure.

The Latin sense clustered around density and repetition — a ~frequēns~ place was a thronged one — and ~frequentāre~ meant to fill a place by going there again and again. French kept exactly this idea of habitual, repeated presence: one ~fréquente~ a café, a school, or a circle of friends, and by extension the people one keeps company with. The notion of regularity left modern French ~fréquence~ (“frequency”) and ~fréquentation~ (“association”), while the social sense survives in the slightly old-fashioned use of ~fréquenter~ for courting someone.
en.fréter: From Old French ~freter~, itself derived from the noun ~fret~ (“freight, the hire of a ship”) with the verb ending ~-er~. The modern verb ~fréter~ means “to charter a boat,” that is, to hire it for transport. French ~fret~ is also the root of ~affréter~, a close relative.
en.frétiller: From Old French ~froitier~ (“to rub”), according to both Wiktionaries. French ~frétiller~ means to wriggle, as a fish or a puppy's tail does, and the sources do not describe how the sense passed from rubbing to wriggling, so no story is offered here. The shape of the verb, with its ~-iller~ ending, is the mark of an old, lively word of the everyday vocabulary.
en.frôler: The origin of ~frôler~ is uncertain. Old French ~froller~ meant “to rub, to thrash”. French Wiktionary derives it from an imitative ~frou~, the sound of something brushing past, and adds that it may be related to ~froisser~ and ~frotter~, comparing Italian ~frullare~ (“to whisk, to beat”). English Wiktionary says only that it is probably imitative. The sense softened from rubbing hard to touching lightly, so ~frôler~ now means to brush against, to graze, or to narrowly miss, and figuratively to come close to something. The rustling ~frou-frou~ is plausibly the same imitation.
en.fuguer: Formed from ~fugue~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. ~Fugue~ comes from Latin ~fuga~ (“flight”). French Wiktionary adds that the musical sense was borrowed from Italian ~fuga~, a word that also gave ~fougue~ through the variant ~foga~. English Wiktionary agrees on Italian and notes that the sense “flight,” which is the one behind the verb, may be a fresh borrowing from Italian in the 18th century. The verb means to run away, especially to leave home on impulse.
en.fuir:
French ~fuir~ descends from Old French ~fuir~, from Vulgar Latin *~fūgīre~, a reshaping of Classical Latin ~fugere~ (“to flee”), built on the perfect stem ~fūgī~. The root traces to Proto-Italic *~fugiō~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~bʰewg-~ (“to flee, run away”). The same Latin verb gave Spanish ~huir~, Italian ~fuggire~, and Portuguese ~fugir~; through the shared root it is cognate with Ancient Greek ~pheúgō~ (“I flee”) and with Latin ~fuga~ (“flight”), source of English ~fugitive~ and ~refuge~.

The sense has stayed remarkably stable: from Latin to modern French, ~fuir~ has always meant “to flee.” French extended it to inanimate subjects, so that a pipe or a roof can ~fuir~ — “leak” — the water escaping as if running away. From the same family come ~fuite~ (“flight, leak”), ~fuyard~ (“runaway”), and the reflexive ~s'enfuir~ (“to flee away”). The learned Greco-Latin branch supplies ~fugace~ (“fleeting”) and the musical ~fugue~, a form in which the voices seem to chase and flee one another.
en.fulgurer:
From Latin ~fulgurāre~ (“to hurl lightning, to flash”), a verb built on ~fulgur~ (“lightning”). English Wiktionary adds that the French verb may instead have been drawn from the adjective ~fulgurant~, so it is either a direct borrowing or a back-formation, and the sources do not decide between the two. The Latin noun ~fulgur~ is also the ancestor of French ~foudre~ (“lightning bolt”), which took the long inherited road, while ~fulgurer~ and its relatives took the learned one. English ~fulgurate~ comes from the same Latin verb.

The modern verb is rare and literary: it means to flash like lightning, or to shine with sudden brilliance. Its family is much more common than the verb itself. ~Fulgurant~ describes anything sudden and dazzling, as in a lightning-fast rise or a blinding pain, and ~fulguration~ names a flash or a sudden discharge. ~Fulgurite~ is the glassy tube formed in sand where lightning strikes. French thus has two words from one Latin source, ~foudre~ at home in everyday speech and the ~fulgur-~ family kept for poetry, science and striking images.
en.fulminer:
Borrowed from Latin ~fulmināre~ (“to hurl lightning, to flash”), itself derived from ~fulmen~ (“lightning bolt”). The Latin noun is generally linked to ~fulgēre~ (“to flash, to shine”), the verb behind ~fulgurant~ and the learned ~fulgurer~. The Latin verb passed into other Romance languages and into English: Italian and Spanish ~fulminare~ and ~fulminar~, and English ~fulminate~ are all borrowings of the same ~fulmināre~.

The literal sense of hurling a thunderbolt lives on mostly in the figurative language of anger. To ~fulminer~ is to explode in rage, typically ~fulminer contre~ someone or something, as if one were casting lightning at them. The participle ~fulminant~ describes anything sudden and devastating, from a glance to a disease. The French word ~foudre~ descends from Latin ~fulgur~, a close relative of ~fulmen~. In chemistry, the explosive salts called ~fulminates~ take their name from the same Latin root, an echo of their thunderclap detonation.
en.fumer:
From Latin ~fūmāre~ (“to smoke, to steam, to emit vapor”), from the noun ~fūmus~ (“smoke”), from Proto-Italic *~fūmos~, from PIE *~dʰuh₂mós~ (“smoke”). Cognate with Sanskrit ~धूम~ (~dhūmá~), Ancient Greek ~θῡμός~ (~thūmós~, “spirit, breath”), and — from the same root — English ~fume~ and ~dust~.

Latin ~fūmāre~ was first about anything that smoked or steamed: a chimney, a hot dish, a misty field. French ~fumer~ kept all of this — a chimney ~fume~, soup ~fume~ — and only later took on “to smoke tobacco.” A separate homonym ~fumer~ “to manure a field” comes instead from ~fimus~ (“dung”) and should not be confused with it. From ~fūmus~ the language drew ~fumée~ (“smoke”), ~fumeur~, ~fumoir~, and ~parfum~ (literally “through-smoke,” recalling scent rising as incense burned). The deep root *~dʰuh₂mós~ also underlies the borrowed ~fumeux~.
en.fumiger:
Borrowed from Latin ~fūmigāre~ (“to smoke, to fumigate”). The Latin verb is built from ~fūmus~ (“smoke”) and the verbal element ~-igāre~, from ~agere~ (“to drive, to make”), so it literally means “to make smoke.” French borrowed it as a learned verb, which is why it keeps the Latin shape almost untouched. The sense is to expose something to smoke or vapor, typically to disinfect it or rid it of vermin.

The Latin noun ~fūmus~ lives on in the inherited French ~fumée~ (“smoke”) and ~fumer~ (“to smoke”), and in ~fumet~ and ~parfum~. Learned words in the same family include ~fumigation~ and ~fumigène~. English ~fumigate~ is borrowed from the same Latin verb, and Italian ~fumigare~ is its cousin. In French ~fumiger~ is a rare technical verb, far less common than ~fumer~.
en.fureter: Formed from ~furet~ (“ferret”) and the ending ~-er~. The verb was first used in a sense tied to the animal, and around 1547 it took the sense “to search everywhere, to rummage.” The noun ~furet~ comes from Old French, from Vulgar Latin *~fūrittus~ (literally “little thief”), a diminutive of Latin ~fūr~ (“thief”). The neighboring Old French ~fuiron~ (“weasel, ferret”) goes back to the same source.
en.fuseler: Formed from the Old French noun ~fusel~ (modern ~fuseau~, “spindle”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, and meaning “to give the shape of a spindle, to taper.” The noun ~fuseau~ is a diminutive built on Old French *~fus~ and descends from Latin ~fūsus~ (“spindle”). It is related to Italian ~fusilli~, the spiral-shaped pasta whose name also evokes a spindle.
en.fuser: ~Fuser~ is a learned verb built on Latin ~fūsus~, the past participle of ~fundere~ (“to pour, to melt”), and so it is a relative of ~fusion~. Its inherited cousin is ~fondre~, which descends from the same Latin verb through ordinary sound change. The senses “to melt,” “to spread, to gush” and, of laughter or cries, “to ring out” all spring from the idea of liquid flowing. French Wiktionary adds that some senses were influenced by ~fusée~, which probably colored the sense of something shooting off or bursting forth.
en.fusiller: Formed from ~fusil~ and the ending ~-er~, so “to use a ~fusil~ on” someone. The noun comes from Old French ~fuisil~ (also ~foisil~), from Vulgar Latin *~focīlis~ (as in a “fire stone”), from Latin ~focus~ (“hearth, fire”). Italian ~fucile~ is a relative. A ~fusil~ was first a steel for striking sparks from flint, and the name passed to the flintlock gun that used one. The verb came to mean “to shoot with a rifle,” hence “to execute by firing squad.”
en.fusionner:
A denominal verb built on the noun ~fusion~, which French took from Latin ~fusio~ (“a pouring, a melting”), itself from the verb ~fundere~ (“to pour, to melt”), past participle ~fusus~. ~Fundere~ descends from Proto-Italic *~hundō~ and from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵʰew-~ (“to pour”), the root behind Ancient Greek ~χέω~ (“I pour”) and Gothic ~giutan~. Through that same root, English ~found~ (“to cast metal”) and ~fuse~ are cognates. The verb ~fondre~ (“to melt”) is the directly inherited French outcome of ~fundere~, making ~fusionner~ and ~fondre~ relatives across the learned/popular divide.

The noun ~fusion~ first named the literal melting of metals — pouring molten substances together so they become one mass. ~Fusionner~ generalized that picture: two companies, parties, or files now merge as readily as two metals. The metallurgical sense survives in nuclear ~fusion~ and in ~fusible~ (“a fuse, what melts”). From the same Latin verb come ~fondre~, ~fonte~ (“cast iron, melting”), ~fondue~, ~confus~ (“poured together, muddled”), ~profus~, and ~diffus~ — a whole network turning on the idea of liquid spreading and mingling.
en.fustiger: A learned borrowing from Latin ~fūstīgāre~ (“to beat with a stick”), built on ~fūstis~ (“club, cudgel”). The literal sense was “to cudgel,” and the modern sense, “to criticize publicly and harshly,” is a figurative extension in which words take the place of the stick. The Latin noun ~fūstis~ is also behind French ~fût~ (“shaft, trunk, cask”), which was inherited rather than borrowed, so the two words are distant relatives despite looking unlike. English ~fustigate~ comes from the same Latin verb.
en.fâcher:
From Old French ~faschier~ (Middle French ~fascher~). The origin is probably Vulgar Latin *~fasticāre~, an altered form of Late Latin ~fastidiāre~ (“to feel disgust”), from Classical Latin ~fastīdīre~. French Wiktionary points to the Old Occitan noun ~fastic~ (“disgust”) as supporting evidence for the reconstructed Vulgar Latin form, but the intermediate form is reconstructed, not attested, so the chain is a likely one rather than a proven one.

In modern French, ~fâcher~ means “to anger, to annoy”, and the reflexive ~se fâcher~ (“to become angry”) is the main use. Now ~être fâché~ can mean “to be upset” or “to have fallen out” with someone. The Latin source ~fastīdīre~ also lies behind English ~fastidious~, and the French adjective ~fâcheux~ (“annoying”) and the noun ~fâcherie~ (“quarrel”) belong to the same family.
en.féconder: ~Féconder~ is borrowed from Latin ~fēcundāre~ (“to make fruitful”), a verb built on the adjective ~fēcundus~ (“fertile, fruitful”); on the surface it can also be read as ~fécond~ + ~-er~. It means to fertilize or impregnate. The same Latin adjective gave French ~fécond~, ~fécondité~ and ~fécondation~, and English ~fecund~ and ~fecundity~.
en.féculer: Formed from the noun ~fécule~ with the verb ending ~-er~: to ~féculer~ is to turn something into starch. The noun ~fécule~ is borrowed from Latin ~faecula~, from ~faex~ (“sediment, dregs”), and was first the sediment left by a liquid. The modern sense of a starch extracted from a plant is a later narrowing.
en.fédéraliser: Formed from the adjective ~fédéral~ with the suffix ~-iser~, which coins verbs meaning “to make A” or “to convert into”: to give a federal structure to. The adjective ~fédéral~ goes back to Latin ~foedus~ (genitive ~foederis~, “treaty of alliance”), the same word that stands behind ~fédération~. The suffix ~-iser~ was borrowed into Old French from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and it remains fully productive in administrative and political vocabulary.
en.fédérer:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~foederāre~ (“to unite by treaty, to bring together through an alliance”), a verb built on the noun ~foedus~ (genitive ~foederis~, “treaty, league”). The noun is generally linked to ~fidere~ (“to trust”) and ~fides~ (“faith, good faith”), since a treaty was at bottom a pledge of trust between parties; the shared root is reconstructed as Proto-Indo-European *~bʰeydʰ-~ (“to trust, to persuade”). French holds this family on two levels: the inherited branch gave ~foi~ (“faith”), and learned borrowings gave ~fidèle~ and ~fédéral~. Spanish ~federar~ and Italian ~federare~ are sibling borrowings, and English took ~federal~ and ~confederate~ from the same Latin source.

In French the verb is a learned borrowing, and its life is tied to the political words around it. ~Fédéral~ and ~fédération~ carried the charge of the Revolution, whose Fête de la Fédération on 14 July 1790 gathered delegates from across the country to swear union. A sports body ~fédère~ its clubs, and a ~projet fédérateur~ draws people around a shared aim. The Latin diphthong ~oe~ regularly became ~é~ in learned French words, which is why ~foedus~ left ~fédérer~ and ~fédéral~ and not something with an ~oi~. The kinship with ~foi~ is easy to miss, yet the whole family rests on it, since a treaty was a pledge of trust.
en.féliciter:
From Latin ~felicitare~ (“to make happy, to bless”), from ~felicitas~ (“happiness, good fortune”), from ~felix~ (“happy, fortunate”). What surprises here is the original sense of ~felix~: not “glad” but ~fruitful~, ~fertile~. The sources trace it to Proto-Indo-European *~dʰeh₁(y)-~ (“to suckle, to nourish”) — the same nurturing root behind Latin ~femina~ (“woman”), ~filius~ (“son”), and ~fecundus~ (“fertile”). A ~felix~ field was one that bore fruit; only later did fruitfulness become fortune, and fortune become happiness.

So to ~féliciter~ someone is, at the root, to wish them fruitful good fortune. The word keeps purely social company today — congratulations on a success, a marriage, a birth. French relatives include ~félicité~ (“bliss”), ~félicitations~, and the given name ~Félix~; through the same PIE root run ~femme~, ~fils~, and ~fécond~. The bridge from “fertile” to “happy” is the quietly memorable fact of this entry: a word of congratulation that began, far back, in the image of a nursing mother and a fruiting field.
en.féminiser: ~Féminiser~ is formed from the adjective ~féminin~ with the suffix ~-iser~, and means to make feminine or to give a feminine character to something. ~Féminin~ is a learned borrowing, attested in Old French as ~femenin~ and ~feminin~ (in the Roman de Troie), from Latin ~fēminīnus~, which derives from ~fēmina~ (“woman”). The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and today forms verbs meaning “to make A.”
en.férir: From Old French ~ferir~, which French Wiktionary derives “possibly” from Latin ~ferīre~ (“to strike”), while English Wiktionary states plainly that it was inherited through Middle French. Latin ~ferīre~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~ferjō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~bʰerH-~. Italian ~ferire~ and Spanish ~herir~ (“to wound”) are Romance relatives. Modern ~férir~ is nearly extinct. It survives in the fixed phrase ~sans coup férir~ (“without striking a blow”), and its past participle lives on in the adjective ~féru~, as in ~féru de~ (“smitten with”).
en.fétichiser: ~Fétichiser~ is formed from ~fétiche~ and the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to turn into a fetish.” The noun was borrowed from Portuguese ~feitiço~ (“artificial,” then “spell, charm”), the name given to objects of worship by African peoples during colonization. The Portuguese word derives from Latin ~factīcius~ (“artificial”), from ~facere~ (“to make”). French has the same Latin word twice: ~fétiche~ by the Portuguese route and ~factice~ directly. The verb now carries a wider, figurative sense of making something an object of excessive attachment.
en.fêler:
~Fêler~ probably comes from Vulgar Latin *~fagellare~, an altered form of Latin ~flagellare~ (“to whip, to beat”). The link is probable rather than certain, and the intermediate Vulgar Latin form is reconstructed, not attested. ~Flagellare~ is itself built on ~flagellum~ (“whip”). ~Fêler~ and ~flageller~ are therefore doublets: one Latin verb that French received twice, once heavily reshaped and once as a learned borrowing.

The path from “to beat” to “to crack” is not spelled out, so what can be said is where the word stands now. ~Fêler~ means to crack something brittle, such as glass or porcelain, without breaking it through, and its participle ~fêlé~ also means, colloquially, “crazy.” The noun ~fêlure~ names the crack itself. ~Flageller~ kept the original sense of whipping, hence ~flagellation~ and the biological term ~flagelle~.
en.fêter:
Inherited from Old French ~fester~, a denominal verb built from the noun ~fête~ (Old French ~feste~) plus the suffix ~-er~. The noun descends from Latin ~festa~, the plural of ~festum~ (“feast day, holiday”), taken as a feminine singular in Vulgar Latin. ~Festum~ goes back through Proto-Italic to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeh₁s-~ (“sacred, religious”), which also yielded Latin ~fanum~ (“temple”) and ~feriae~ (“holidays”). Cognate with Italian ~festa~ and Spanish ~fiesta~, and — through Old French — with English ~feast~ and ~festival~.

The root *~dʰeh₁s-~ belonged to the vocabulary of the sacred, so a ~fête~ was first a religious observance before the word broadened to any joyful celebration. From the same family French keeps ~férié~ (a “jour férié” is a public holiday), ~festin~ (“banquet”), ~festival~, and ~festivité~. The verb today carries the warmth of marking an occasion: one says « on a fêté son anniversaire » or « il faut fêter ça », where the act of celebrating is itself the point. The doublet ~feria~, the Spanish-style fair, re-entered French from Spanish, preserving the older sense of a holy day given over to public rejoicing.
en.gabarier: Formed from the noun ~gabarit~ with the verb ending ~-er~: the verb means to check something against a ~gabarit~, a template or gauge, hence to verify. The noun comes from Occitan ~gabarrit~, an alteration of ~garbi~, which French Wiktionary traces to Gothic *~garwi~ (“preparation, model”); English Wiktionary gives Provençal ~gabarrit~ from Proto-Germanic *~garwaz~ (“prepared, ready”).
en.gadgétiser: Formed from the noun ~gadget~ with the verb suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to turn into a gadget.” French borrowed ~gadget~ from English, which had itself taken the word from French in the first place, so the root has made a round trip across the Channel. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, itself a transcription of Greek verbal endings, and builds verbs of the type “convert into” (~numériser~, ~scolariser~).
en.gaffer: Formed from ~gaffe~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, so ~gaffer~ means to make a gaffe, to blunder. The origin of ~gaffe~ is explained in more than one way, depending on the sense. For the hook, one account gives Old Occitan ~gaf~ (“clasp, hook”), itself from Gothic ~gafah~ (“clasp”), built from ~ga-~ (an intensifier) and ~fahan~ (“to catch”); another gives English ~gaff~. The slang phrase ~faire gaffe~ (“to pay attention”) is traced to Old French ~guetter~ (“to watch”). The taping sense comes from English ~gaffer tape~.
en.gager:
The origin of ~gager~ is Germanic, but the exact path is not fully settled. One account derives it from the noun ~gage~ (“pledge”) or from Old French ~guagier~, which came from ~guage~, a descendant of Frankish *~waddi~, itself from Proto-Germanic *~wadja~ (“pledge”). French Wiktionary traces that further to the Proto-Indo-European root *~wedʰ-~. English Wiktionary says a Vulgar Latin verb *~wadiare~ (from *~wadium~) may have stood in between, but this is only a possibility.

The core idea is a pledge handed over as a guarantee, which fits both senses of ~gager~, “to guarantee” and “to bet.” Walloon ~wadjî~ is a regional relative. English borrowed the same word from Anglo-Norman or Old Northern French in a variant with an initial w, which is why ~wage~ and ~wager~ look different from ~gager~. In French the family includes ~gage~ and ~dégager~. In everyday speech ~gager que~ means “to bet that.”
en.gagner:
From Old French ~gaaignier~ (“to earn, win, cultivate, forage”), from Late Latin *~wadaniāre~, borrowed from Frankish *~waidanjan~ (“to forage, graze, pasture, hunt for food”). This rests on a Germanic base for hunting and pursuit, *~waiþō~ (“pasture, hunting ground”), and ultimately the Proto-Indo-European root *~weyh₁-~ (“to chase after, pursue, strive for”). Through the same Germanic source come German ~Weide~ (“pasture”) and Old Norse ~veiðr~ (“hunt”), while English ~gain~ was borrowed straight from the Old French verb.

The history is a journey from field to fortune. The earliest sense was agricultural and pastoral — to work the land, to graze animals, to forage — the toil by which medieval people drew sustenance from the earth. From “to get one's living from the land” the meaning broadened to “to earn,” then to “to obtain, acquire,” and finally to the triumphant modern “to win.” The compound ~gagne-pain~ (“breadwinner,” literally “earn-bread”) preserves the older laboring sense beautifully. The French family includes ~gain~, ~gagnant~ (“winner”), ~regagner~ (“to regain”), ~gagne-pain~, and the dialectal ~gagnage~ (“grazing land”) — a quiet memory of the pastures where the word was born.
en.gainer: Formed from the noun ~gaine~ (“sheath”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, so ~gainer~ means to cover or sheathe. ~Gaine~ comes through Middle French ~guaine~ and Old French ~guaïne~ from Latin ~vāgīna~ (“sheath, scabbard”), and is a doublet of the learned ~vagin~. Italian ~guaina~ and Spanish ~vaina~ are cognates. The initial g in place of Latin v is attributed to Germanic influence: one theory sees a confluence with a Germanic word *~wāgi~ (“vessel, bowl”), another notes that, as a military term, the word was used mostly among Frankish warriors.
en.galber: ~Galber~ is formed from the noun ~galbe~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, which comes from Latin ~-are~. It means “to curve,” that is, to give something a curved, shapely outline. This is a denominal verb: French took an existing noun and turned it into an action by adding the ending, as it does for ~filtrer~ from ~filtre~.
en.galipoter: Formed from the noun ~galipot~ with the verb ending ~-er~, in the sense of coating something with galipot, a pine resin. French Wiktionary explains ~galipot~ in turn as ~galipe~ (“pine shaving”) plus the suffix ~-ot~. The ending ~-er~ is the usual way French turns a noun into a verb; it goes back to Latin ~-are~, the infinitive ending of first-conjugation verbs, as in ~cantare~, which gave ~chanter~. So ~galipoter~ is a French coinage, not a Latin inheritance.
en.galonner:
~Galonner~ comes from the verb ~galoner~, which French Wiktionary calls Old French and glosses as “to adorn with ribbons”, and English Wiktionary calls Middle French. The origin beyond that is uncertain. One suggestion links it to ~galant~. English Wiktionary proposes the Old French verb ~galer~ (“to have fun, to enjoy oneself”) but notes a formal difficulty: the suffix ~-onner~ rarely appears before the nineteenth century.

The verb means to trim with braid, and the noun ~galon~ (“braid”) belongs to the same family. It is best known in the plural, ~galons~, the stripes of an officer's rank, which gives the expression ~prendre du galon~ (“to be promoted”). English ~galloon~ was borrowed from the French noun, and ~galant~, if the first suggestion holds, would share the root of ~galer~. Because the sources only propose a link to ~galant~ and ~galer~, the early history of ~galonner~ should be considered open.
en.galoper:
French ~galoper~ comes from Old French ~galoper~, also spelled ~gualoper~, by way of Middle French. Its origin is probably Frankish, the Germanic language of the early Franks: a compound *~wala hlaupan~, literally “to run well,” built from *~wala~ (“well”) and *~hlaupan~ (“to run”). The Germanic halves still have living descendants, and German ~wohl laufen~ and Dutch ~wel lopen~ match the phrase word for word. The French source hedges with “probably,” and the Romance form that bridges the gap, *~(g)wa(la)loppāre~, is itself a reconstruction.

The initial ~gu-~ of Old French ~gualoper~ reflects the usual French treatment of the Germanic initial w, as in ~guerre~ and ~garder~, which are also of Germanic origin. The verb crossed borders: English ~gallop~ was borrowed from French, and Italian ~galoppare~ and Spanish ~galopar~ are related forms. The noun ~galop~, along with ~galopade~ and ~galopin~, belongs to the same family. The “run well” explanation is attractive, but it remains a proposal: the sources say “probably,” not “certainly.”
en.galvaniser: ~Galvaniser~ comes from the name of the Italian physiologist Luigi Galvani (1737–1798), who showed the existence of an “animal electricity” using frog muscles, together with the verb suffix ~-iser~ (“to treat with”). In the sense “to protect with a layer of zinc,” the first technique used was electrolysis, which links the process to electrical work of the kind he pioneered.
en.galvauder:
