Standard accounts treat ~galvauder~ as an ironic cross between two Old French words: ~galer~ (“to enjoy oneself, to amuse someone”) and ~ravauder~ (“to mend, to patch”). French Wiktionary connects ~galer~ with ~galant~ and ~gala~, so one half of the blend is festive, the other humble and domestic. The account is generally accepted rather than documented by attestation, so it is best held loosely.

The sense of ~galvauder~ moved on from both parents. It means “to squander, to waste,” and above all “to cheapen or tarnish” something of value, such as a reputation, a talent or a word worn out by overuse. The participle ~galvaudé~ describes a hackneyed expression or a debased notion. French keeps the two halves of the blend in ~galant~, ~gala~ and ~ravauder~, so the word sits between the pleasures of the feast and the patching of old cloth.
en.galéjer: Formed from the noun ~galéjade~ (“a tall tale, a bit of banter”) with the ending ~-er~. The noun is borrowed from Occitan ~galejada~ (“banter”), a form recorded in Frédéric Mistral's Occitan dictionary ~Lou Tresor dóu Felibrige~ of 1878. The verb thus carries a bit of Provence into French, in the sense of joking or telling tall stories.
en.galérer: ~Galérer~ is formed from ~galère~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun, which French took from Catalan ~galera~, comes from Medieval Latin ~galēra~, a variant of ~galea~ and ultimately from Byzantine Greek. It named the oared warship, and by the Renaissance it also meant the sentence of rowing in one as a convict. The modern figurative sense, “an ordeal,” prepared the slang verb: to ~galérer~ is to struggle, to have a hard time, as if chained to the oar.
en.gambader: Formed from the noun ~gambade~ (“a leap, a caper”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so “to make capers.” The origin of ~gambade~ is not fully settled. French Wiktionary derives it from ~gambe~, an old variant of ~jambe~ (“leg”), plus the suffix ~-ade~, or else borrows it from Occitan ~gambada~ (“leap, stride”). Either way the word comes down to the leg.
en.gamberger: The sources trace it, apparently, to ~compter~ (“to count, to reckon”): an unattested slang form *~comperger~, made by adding an ending ~-erger~, then ~comberger~, ~gomberger~ and finally ~gamberger~. French Wiktionary adds that the sense of walking about is to be compared with ~gambader~ (“to skip about”). The modern sense is to think hard.
en.gambiller: Formed from ~gambille~ with the verb ending ~-er~. In the sense “small leg,” ~gambille~ is a diminutive of ~gambe~, a variant of ~jambe~ (“leg”), with the suffix ~-ille~. The noun sense “dance” runs the other way and derives from the verb. The verb thus means, in the first instance, to move one's little legs, and it is used for jigging about and dancing.
en.gangrener: Formed from the noun ~gangrène~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, so “to affect with gangrene,” with the figurative sense “to corrupt utterly.” English Wiktionary instead calls it a back-formation from the participle ~gangrené~, so the two accounts differ on the route but agree on the result. The noun ~gangrène~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~gangraena~, itself from Ancient Greek ~gángraina~ (γάγγραινα).
en.gangréner: A variant spelling of ~gangrener~, which French Wiktionary describes as a seventeenth-century formation from the noun ~gangrène~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~gangrène~ goes back through Latin ~gangraena~ to Greek, the same source as English ~gangrene~. The verb means to affect with gangrene and, figuratively, to corrupt thoroughly, as when a vice or a scandal spreads through an institution like a rot.
en.ganser: Formed from the noun ~ganse~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so ~ganser~ means to provide something with a ~ganse~, that is, to edge or border it. The noun ~ganse~ (also spelled ~gance~) is traced to Occitan ~gansa~ (“loop, link”), probably from Ancient Greek ~gampsós~ (“curved”). The idea of a curved loop of cord or braid thus lies behind the trimming.
en.ganter: ~Ganter~ is formed from the noun ~gant~ (“glove”) + ~-er~, “to provide with a glove.” The noun comes from Old French ~guant~, attested in the ~Chanson de Roland~, from Frankish *~want~ (“mitten”), from Proto-Germanic *~wantuz~, at first in the vocabulary of arms. Its Romance cognates are Italian ~guanto~ and Spanish ~guante~. The suffix ~-er~ is the ordinary French ending that makes a verb from a noun.
en.garancer: Formed from ~garance~ (“madder”) with the verbal ending ~-er~ (from Latin ~-are~), so “to dye with madder.” The noun comes from Old French ~garance~ (also ~warance~), from medieval Latin ~warentia~ (“scarlet dye”), from Frankish *~wrattjā~ and Proto-Germanic *~wratjō~ (“red dye”). Old English ~wrætte~ and Old High German ~rezza~ are cognates.
en.garantir:
From Old French ~garantir~, a denominal verb formed around 1100 from the noun ~garant~ (“warrantor, protector”) plus the verbal suffix ~-ir~. ~garant~ first appears as ~guarant~, of Frankish origin: from ~warand~, related to the Germanic verb ~warjan~ (“to defend, ward off, vouch for”), from Proto-Germanic *~warjaną~, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~wer-~ (“to cover, protect”). The initial Germanic ~w-~ regularly became ~gu-~ then ~g-~ in central Old French, while the northern dialects kept the ~w-~ — which is why English borrowed both ~warrant~ (from Norman ~warant~) and ~guarantee~ (from the southern ~garant~) as a doublet of the same word.

The core idea is standing surety: a ~garant~ is someone who vouches for you and shields you from loss, and to ~garantir~ is to give that protective pledge. From the legal sense of warranting title and quality, the meaning broadened to “to assure, to safeguard, to protect from” — one can ~garantir~ a result, or ~garantir~ oneself from the cold. The same Frankish stem ~warjan~ gave French ~guérir~ (“to heal,” originally “to protect, defend”), and the family includes ~garantie~ (“warranty, guarantee”) and ~garde~. German preserves a relative in ~gewähren~ (“to grant, vouchsafe”).
en.garder:
From Old French ~guarder~ (later ~garder~), from Medieval Latin *~wardare~, itself a borrowing from Frankish *~wardōn~ (“to watch, to guard”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~wer-~ (“to perceive, to watch out for”). The Frankish initial ~w-~ regularly became ~gu-~ then ~g-~ in central Old French, while the Norman dialect kept the ~w-~ that English borrowed: so French ~garder~ and English ~guard~ are doublets of one and the same Germanic word, and English ~ward~ and ~warden~ preserve the older form. German ~warten~ (“to wait on, to tend”) is a cognate.

The root idea is keeping watch, and from vigilant attention the verb spread to keeping, retaining, and looking after: to guard a fortress, to keep a secret, to look after a child. The reflexive ~se garder de~ (“to beware of”) holds the original sense of wariness. The prefixed ~regarder~ — ~re-~ + ~garder~ — drifted from “to watch over” to simply “to look at,” and gave the noun ~regard~ (“gaze”) and ~égard~ (“consideration”). The Germanic root spreads through French ~garde~, ~gardien~, ~garderie~, ~sauvegarder~, and ~avant-garde~, and feeds back into English as ~reward~ and ~regard~.
en.garer:
From Middle French ~garrer~ and Old French ~garer~, ~warer~ and ~varer~, a word of Germanic origin. It is traced either to Old Frankish *~warōn~ (“to guard, to keep watch”) or to Old Norse ~varask~ (“to be on one's guard”), or to both, and both lead back to Proto-Germanic *~warōną~ (“to watch over, to protect”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~wer-~ (“to perceive, to heed”). Cognates include Old High German ~warōn~ and Old English ~warian~ (“to guard, to be wary”), and English ~ware~, as in ~beware~. In French the verb is distantly related to ~garder~, ~garde~ and ~garnir~.

The Old French verb meant “to protect, to shelter,” and its reflexive ~se garer~ meant “to take shelter, to step aside out of harm's way,” as in the cry ~garez-vous~ (“mind out”). Pulling a boat into a basin, or a train onto a siding, was likewise a way of putting it out of the way, and the noun ~gare~ is generally linked to this sense before it came to name a railway station. Only later did ~garer~ narrow to its modern main sense, “to park” a vehicle, and ~se garer~ means “to pull over.” The interjection ~gare à toi~ (“watch out”) keeps the older warning sense.
en.gargariser:
~Gargariser~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~gargarizāre~ (“to gargle”). The Latin verb was itself taken from Greek ~gargarízein~, a word that imitates the sound of liquid bubbling in the throat. French took the verb in its medical sense: to rinse the mouth and throat with a liquid, usually without swallowing it. The Greek noun ~gargarismós~ lies behind French ~gargarisme~, the usual word for a mouthwash or gargle.

The most lively use of the verb today is figurative. In ~se gargariser de~ followed by a noun, a speaker is said to relish something with self-satisfaction, as in ~se gargariser de grands mots~ (“to revel in big words”). The verb is a learned cousin of the sound-imitating words of the gurgling family, but its shape comes directly from Latin and Greek, not from popular speech.
en.gargouiller: From Old French ~jargoillier~, a verb derived from ~gargoule~ (“throat”). ~Gargouiller~ is to make a gurgling or rumbling noise, as water in a pipe or a stomach does. The same noun ~gargoule~ stands behind the related ~gargouille~, the water spout of a cathedral, and through it English ~gargoyle~, which was borrowed from Old French. English ~gargle~ is generally explained in the same way, as a borrowing from the Old French word for the throat. The French nouns ~gargouillement~ and ~gargouillis~ name the sound itself.
en.garnir:
Inherited from Middle French ~garnir~, from Old French ~guarnir~ (“to protect oneself, arm up”), which English Wiktionary traces to Frankish *~warnijan~ (“to ward, take care of something”). That form is in turn from Proto-Germanic *~warnijaną~ (“to be careful, take heed, refuse”) and ultimately from a Proto-Indo-European root *~wer-~ (“to close, cover, protect”). The Frankish origin means that the initial ~w-~ became ~gu-~ and then ~g-~ in French, as it did in ~guerre~. Italian ~guarnire~ and Portuguese ~guarnir~ are cognates of the Romance side. On the Germanic side, the same root is found in Middle Dutch ~waernen~, Old English ~wiernan~ (“to withhold, refuse”) and Old Norse ~varna~, and English ~warn~ is related.

The oldest senses of Old French ~garnir~ are of protection: to warn, to fortify a stronghold, to equip and supply it. From there come ~garnison~, the troops that supply a fort, and English ~garrison~. Over time the idea of providing and equipping weakened into that of furnishing, then into that of adorning: you ~garnir~ a dish with parsley or a dress with lace. English ~garnish~ took the same road, borrowed from the Old French stem ~garniss-~. French ~garniture~, ~garni~ (a furnished lodging) and ~dégarnir~ belong to the same family.
en.garrotter: Formed from the noun ~garrot~ with the first-group ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary lists more than one noun ~garrot~. One is built with the suffix ~-ot~ on Old Occitan ~garra~ (“leg”), a link English Wiktionary also gives, and which relates it to ~jarret~. Another goes back to an Old French ~garrot~, from Gaulish *~garra~, and a third, the duck, is from Old French ~garre~. The sources do not say which one the verb comes from.
en.gaspiller:
The origin of ~gaspiller~ is uncertain; it is attested in Middle French with the sense “to waste.” One hypothesis sees it as a modification of Middle French ~gaspailler~ (“to throw back, to reject”), from Old French ~gaspail~ or ~vaspale~, words tied to wheat. Old Northern French ~waspail~ (“chaff”) would go back to Frankish *~wispila~ (“measure of grain”) and, beyond it, to Proto-Germanic *~wisp-~. English ~wisp~, Middle Dutch ~wispel~ and Norwegian ~visp~ are cognates.

A rival account connects the verb to Frankish *~gaspilþijan~ (“to waste”), from Proto-Germanic *~spilþijaną~ (“to destroy, waste”) and the Proto-Indo-European root *~spel-~ (“to break off, split”). That would make it a cousin of Old High German ~gaspildan~ (“to squander”), Middle Dutch ~spillen~ (“to waste”) and Old English ~ġespillan~ (“to spill, waste, spend”), and so of English ~spill~ and Dutch ~verspillen~. The sources do not decide between the two accounts. Either way, the noun ~gaspillage~ is built on the verb.
en.gauchir:
From Old French ~gauchir~ or ~gauchier~, passed on through Middle French. English Wiktionary traces it to Frankish, giving *~wenkijan~ and *~walkijan~ (or *~walkan~) as the proposed sources, so the exact Germanic form is uncertain. As often happens in words from Frankish, an initial ~w~ became ~gu-~ or ~g-~ in French. Today the verb is easy to read as ~gauche~ plus ~-ir~, and that surface analysis is natural, but it is not given as the historical one.

The sense is of swerving away from a straight line: to warp, to bend, to dodge. Hence ~gauchir~ is used of a plank or a metal sheet that goes out of true, and figuratively of someone who sidesteps a question. The adjective ~gauche~ (“left, awkward”) belongs to the same family, and English borrowed it back as ~gauche~ (“clumsy”). English ~wince~ is a relative of the same Frankish word through Old French.
en.gaufrer: ~Gaufrer~ is formed from ~gaufre~ and the verb ending ~-er~. It means to imprint patterns with irons on cloth or paper, and the noun ~gaufre~ later took the matching sense of “embossed pattern” as a back-formation from the verb, in the seventeenth century. The base ~gaufre~ (“waffle”) comes through Middle French from Old French ~walfre~ (about 1185), itself traced to Middle Dutch ~wafel~ or to a Frankish form. English ~waffle~ is a cognate, and German ~Wabe~ (“honeycomb”) is related.
en.gauler: Formed in French from ~gaule~ + the suffix ~-er~. English Wiktionary describes it as inherited from Middle French ~gauler~ (“to knock down with a pole”) and Old French ~gauler~ or ~wauller~ (“to fight with a pole”). The noun ~gaule~ (“long pole”) is traced there to Frankish *~walu~ (“stick”), cognate with Gothic ~walus~ and Old English ~walu~. French Wiktionary is more cautious: it says ~gaule~ is probably from Latin ~vallus~ (“stake”), mentions Gothic as Diez's preference and raises Celtic as another possibility. The verb means to beat down with a pole.
en.gausser: The origin of ~gausser~ is uncertain. It was perhaps borrowed from Spanish ~gozarse~ (“to rejoice”), itself derived from Latin ~gaudēre~ (“to rejoice”), but that is only a proposal. If it holds, ~gausser~ belongs to the family of Latin ~gaudēre~, which also gave Spanish ~gozar~ (“to enjoy”) and French ~joie~ and ~jouir~. In modern French, ~se gausser de~ means “to mock” or “to scoff at”, and the verb has a somewhat literary ring.
en.gaver: Derived from the Old French dialect word ~gave~ (“crop, throat”), the bird's gullet. French Wiktionary links ~gave~ with ~jabot~ (“crop”), while English Wiktionary calls it a doublet of ~joue~ (“cheek”), so the root is not agreed upon. The verb first meant to stuff the throat with food, as in force-feeding geese and ducks (~gavage~). It then widened to “to gorge,” in ~se gaver~, and in slang to “to bore or annoy.”
en.gazer: Two homonymous verbs share this form. One is a denominal of ~gaz~ (“gas”), a word coined in the seventeenth century by the Flemish chemist Van Helmont from Greek ~khaos~; it covers treating with gas, and the colloquial expression for things going well. The other is built on ~gaze~ (“gauze”), a fabric word that is probably borrowed from Arabic ~qazz~ (“silk”). The old idea that the cloth took its name from the city of Gaza is speculative; the CNRTL notes there is no proof that any such industry existed there. Both verbs add the ending ~-er~.
en.gazonner: Formed from the noun ~gazon~ (“turf, lawn”) with the verbal ending ~-er~: to ~gazonner~ is to cover ground with turf. ~Gazon~ comes from Old French ~gason~ or ~wason~, borrowed from Old Frankish *~waso~, a clod of earth covered with grass. The German word ~Wasen~ (“lawn”) is a cognate. The initial ~w-~ of the Germanic word became ~g-~ in central French, as in ~guerre~ and ~garder~, while northern forms such as the Walloon ~waezon~ kept the old sound.
en.gazouiller: ~Gazouiller~ is of onomatopoeic origin, built on the sound ~gazou~ and related to ~jaser~ (“to chatter”). It first described the chirping of birds and the babble of small children, and the sound of water. In the Internet sense, “to tweet”, it is a calque of English ~tweet~, which gave an old word of bird noise a new digital career.
en.gazéifier: Formed from ~gaz~ with the suffix ~-ifier~ (“to make”), so it means to turn into gas or to add gas. The noun ~gaz~ was borrowed from Dutch ~gas~, a word proposed by Jean-Baptiste Van Helmont (1577-1644) on the basis of Latin ~chaos~, with the spelling ~g~ following the Flemish pronunciation of ~ch-~.
en.geindre:
Inherited from Old French ~giembre~, from Latin ~gemere~ (“to groan, to lament”). In the course of its history the verb was remade as ~geindre~ on the pattern of the verbs in ~-eindre~, such as ~peindre~ and ~feindre~, which explains its odd modern shape and its stem in ~-gn-~. The Latin verb survives in Italian ~gemere~ and Spanish ~gemir~.

French has kept the Latin verb twice. ~Gémir~ is a doublet of ~geindre~, both descending from ~gemere~, but they now differ in use: ~gémir~ can express pain, grief or pleasure, while ~geindre~ suggests whining and complaining. The adjective ~geignard~ (“whiny”) is formed from it, and the noun ~gémissement~ belongs to ~gémir~.
en.geler:
~Geler~ is inherited from Old French ~geler~, itself from Latin ~gelāre~ (“to freeze, to congeal”), a verb built on the noun ~gelū~ (“frost, icy cold”). The Latin noun belongs to the Proto-Indo-European root *~gel-~ (“cold; to freeze”), which also fed the Germanic languages: English ~cold~ and ~cool~ and German ~kalt~ descend from it, with the regular Germanic shift of g to k. Italian ~gelare~ and Spanish ~helar~ are the sibling verbs, so a Romance speaker and an English speaker who complain of the cold are, without knowing it, using relatives.

In French the verb is both impersonal, as in ~il gèle~ (“it is freezing”), and transitive, as in freezing water, a bank account or prices; the figurative uses, to freeze relations or to chill someone's blood, are natural extensions. The Latin noun and verb produced a whole family: ~gel~, ~gelée~ (what has frozen or set, whence English ~jelly~), ~congeler~, ~dégeler~ and ~gélatine~. Italian added ~gelato~, which English borrowed. Even the humble jelly on the table is, etymologically, a frost that has set.
en.gemmer: ~Gemmer~ is a denominal verb: the noun ~gemme~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, whose sense here is “work on N,” so “to work on or tap with a ~gemme~.” The noun ~gemme~ comes from Latin ~gemma~, which meant both “bud” and “gem.” The Latin word also reached English as ~gem~, by a separate road. As a verb, ~gemmer~ is a technical term, used for tapping a tree.
en.gendarmer: Formed from ~gendarme~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, usually in the pronominal form ~se gendarmer~, “to protest, to bristle.” The noun ~gendarme~ is a fusion of ~gens d'armes~, “people of arms,” that is, armed men. English Wiktionary adds that the singular was extracted from the plural ~gendarmes~, which had been respelled from ~gens d'armes~. The verb thus turns a figure of armed authority into an attitude of reaction.
en.gerber: ~Gerber~ is derived from ~gerbe~ (“sheaf”) with the verb ending ~-er~, and English Wiktionary adds that it is attested in Middle French. ~Gerbe~ comes from Old French ~jarbe~ or ~garbe~, borrowed from Frankish *~garbā~ (“sheaf”). Dutch ~garf~, German ~Garbe~ and Occitan ~garba~ are relatives. The basic sense is “to bind into sheaves,” and the sources do not explain the later sense “to throw up.”
en.gercer:
From Middle French ~gerser~ (14th century), itself from Old French ~jarser~ or ~garser~ (“to wound, to gash,” 12th century). Sources hedge on what lies behind it. The usual account derives it from Late Latin ~charaxāre~ or ~caraxāre~ (“to scarify, to scratch”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~χαράσσειν~ (~kharássein~, “to cut, incise”). An alternative is a Latin form *~carptiāre~, from ~carpere~ (“to pluck”). Spanish ~sajar~ and Galician ~sarxar~, both “to cut open,” were borrowed from Old French.

Today ~gercer~ is said of skin, lips or hands that crack or chap, as cold or dryness splits them. It is common in the reflexive ~se gercer~ and in the participle ~gercé~. The noun ~gerçure~ (“a chap, a crack”) belongs to the family. If the Greek origin is right, ~gercer~ is distant kin of ~caractère~, which comes from Greek ~χαρακτήρ~, a mark engraved, from the same root. French Wiktionary also compares Walloon ~garsi~ (“to cup,” that is, to scarify the skin).
en.germaniser: Formed in French from ~germain~ and the suffix ~-iser~, on the model of ~latiniser~. The first sense was “to use Germanic words,” and the verb later came to mean to make German in culture or language. The base here is the adjective ~germain~, an adjectivation of ~Germain~, which comes from Latin ~Germānus~ (“German”). French Wiktionary notes it is probably unrelated to the ordinary adjective ~germain~ (“of the same stock,” as in ~cousin germain~), from another Latin ~germānus~. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~.
en.germer:
French ~germer~ comes from Latin ~germināre~ (“to sprout, to bud”), the verb of the noun ~germen~ (“sprout, bud, seed”). English Wiktionary describes it as a borrowing, which fits a learned word, and French Wiktionary refers readers to ~germe~ and ~germiner~ as related words. The Latin noun gave French ~germe~ and English ~germ~, and the Latin verb gave English ~germinate~. Italian ~germinare~ is a direct parallel. In Latin, the noun ~germen~ already named the part of a plant from which new growth springs, and the verb ~germināre~ named the act of putting it forth.

The sense stayed botanical for a long time: a seed puts out a first shoot when it germinates. From that picture grew the figurative uses, an idea, a plan or a feeling that begins to take form quietly before it shows. The noun traveled further than the verb. ~Germe~ names the embryo and, by extension, a microbe. The Republican calendar of 1793 named its spring month ~Germinal~ after the same Latin verb, the month when seeds sprout, and Zola took it as the title of his novel of coal miners, an image of hope pushing up through the soil.
en.gesticuler:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~gesticulārī~ (“to make mimicking gestures”). The Latin verb is built on ~gesticulus~, a diminutive of ~gestus~ (“bearing, movement”), which belongs to ~gerere~ (“to carry, to conduct oneself”). In French the verb has kept the sense of the Latin: to move the arms and hands much and excitedly, usually while speaking.

The family of ~gerere~ is large in French. ~Gestus~ gave ~geste~ (“gesture”) and its adjective ~gestuel~, while the learned ~gesticulation~ belongs to ~gesticuler~. Other relatives built on the same Latin verb include ~gérer~ (“to manage”) and ~gestion~, as well as ~digérer~, ~suggérer~ and ~congestion~. English has ~gesture~ and ~gesticulate~ from the same Latin source.
en.gicler:
The origin of ~gicler~ is debated. French Wiktionary derives it, with caution, from a form *~cisculare~ of unknown origin, perhaps imitative, reaching French through Franco-Provençal ~jicler~ or ~gigler~; the earliest attestations are from Lyon. English Wiktionary instead sees a borrowing from Franco-Provençal ~gicllar~ or Occitan ~gisclar~, from Vulgar Latin *~cistulāre~, an alteration of Latin ~fistulāre~ (“to play the flute”), from ~fistula~ (“flute”).

English Wiktionary compares Catalan ~xisclar~ and Spanish ~chillar~. Old variants of the verb turn up in several regions of France with the senses “to gush”, “to project a liquid” and “to splash”. Modern ~gicler~ means “to squirt” or “to spurt”, and it gave ~gicleur~, the calibrated jet of a carburetor.
en.gifler: ~Gifler~ is the noun ~gifle~ (“slap”) plus the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to slap.” The noun is recorded with the sense “cheek.” It comes from Middle French ~gifle~ and Old French ~giffe~, from Old Dutch *~kifel~ (“cheek, jaw”), from Frankish *~kebr~ and Proto-Germanic *~kebrą~. German ~Kiefer~ (“jaw”) is related.
en.gigoter: ~Gigoter~ is formed from ~giguer~ with the suffix ~-oter~, which gives a verb a frequentative or diminutive sense: small movements repeated. It is attested from 1694, at first in the sense of “to kick.” The base ~giguer~ is an Old French verb meaning “to frolic,” itself derived from ~gigue~ (“fiddle”). The modern sense is “to wriggle about.”
en.givrer: Formed from ~givre~ (“frost, rime”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, so ~givrer~ means to cover with frost, to ice up. ~Givre~ appears in Old French as ~joivre~ in the fourteenth century; by one account it was borrowed, through Franco-Provençal ~gevro~, from a Frankish word *~gibara~ meaning “drool”, related to German ~Geifer~ and Low German ~Gieber~. That Frankish origin is itself presented only as possible. A separate etymology traces another word ~givre~ to Latin ~vipera~ (“viper”) through Old French ~vouivre~.
en.glacer:
Inherited from Latin ~glaciāre~ (“to freeze, to turn to ice”), a verb formed on the noun ~glaciēs~ (“ice”). French also treats it today as the noun ~glace~ plus ~-er~. The Latin word is generally traced to the Proto-Indo-European root *~gel-~ (“cold, to freeze”), which also gave Latin ~gelū~ (“frost”) and so French ~geler~, a close relative of ~glacer~. The same root is the source of the Germanic family that includes English ~cold~. Italian has ~ghiaccio~ (“ice”) and the verb ~ghiacciare~.

French ~glacer~ means to freeze something solid or cover it with ice, and it is used figuratively: fear or a cold look can “freeze” a person, and a cold manner chills a conversation. In the kitchen it means to coat with a shiny, smooth layer, as in icing a cake or glazing a roast. The noun ~glace~ covers a whole range from ice to ice cream to a polished mirror, which is why the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles is the Galerie des Glaces. Descendants include ~glaçon~ (“ice cube”), ~glacier~ (a mass of ice) and the learned ~glacial~, along with ~déglacer~ (“to deglaze a pan”).
en.glairer: This verb is formed from the noun ~glaire~ (“egg white”) with the ending ~-er~, and means “to smear with egg white”. The noun descends from Old French ~glaire~ and Vulgar Latin ~clāria~, from Latin ~clārus~ (“clear”), because egg white is clear. French Wiktionary adds that the word may have been crossed with Latin ~glarea~ (“gravel”), and notes that the change of ~c~ to ~g~ has parallels, as in ~gras~ from ~crassus~ and ~église~ from ~ecclesia~. Italian ~chiara~ has the same meaning as ~glaire~.
en.glaiser: Formed from the noun ~glaise~ (“clay”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to treat with clay,” as in spreading clay on a surface. The noun comes from Old French ~gloise~ or ~glaise~, and its origin is uncertain. One theory derives it from a Gaulish *~glisa~, supposedly attested in the Late Latin ~glisomarga~ (a kind of marl). Others suggest a Germanic source, compared with Dutch ~klei~ and English ~clay~, or Latin ~glis~ (“thick clay”).
en.glander: Formed from the noun ~gland~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~gland~ (“acorn”) comes from Old French ~glant~, from Latin ~glandem~ (accusative of ~glans~). French Wiktionary says its origin is uncertain, probably a merging of Latin ~glans~, ~glandis~ and ~glandula~, the source of ~glande~. The sources at hand do not explain how a verb built on the acorn came to mean “to loaf about,” so no story is offered here.
en.glandouiller: Formed from the verb ~glander~ and the suffix ~-ouiller~. ~Glander~ itself is built on the noun ~gland~ (“acorn”), from Latin ~glandem~, though the sources do not explain how the acorn came to mean loafing about. The suffix ~-ouiller~, made of ~-ouille~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, is a familiar, colloquial ending that turns a verb into a small, weak or idle version of itself, as in ~pendouiller~ or ~mâchouiller~. So ~glandouiller~ is a more drawn-out, lazier ~glander~: the same idleness, spread out in a series of aimless little movements.
en.glaner:
From Old French ~glener~, from Late Latin ~glenāre~. French Wiktionary traces the Late Latin verb to Gaulish *~gleno~ (“I gather”) and compares Old Irish ~do-glinn~ (“he gathers”) and ~glenim~ (“I collect”), which it links to Latin ~glutinō~ (“to stick together”). English Wiktionary agrees that ~glenāre~ is a Celtic borrowing from Gaulish, but is more cautious about the root and says only that it is possibly from Proto-Celtic *~glanos~.

The Celtic origin is thus the accepted account, while the exact Gaulish form and its deeper links are not settled. The Old French verb ~glener~ also passed into English, where it became ~glean~. Modern French ~glaner~ keeps the sense “to gather,” and it is used both literally and figuratively for picking up scattered pieces, such as facts or information.
en.glapir: ~Glapir~ is an alteration of ~glatir~, which is inherited from Latin ~glattīre~ (“to yelp”). Why a ~p~ replaced the ~t~ is uncertain. Two French verbs, ~glapir~ and ~glatir~, thus differ by a single consonant while going back to the same Latin source. In modern French ~glapir~ covers the sharp, high-pitched cries of small animals such as puppies and foxes, and, of people, a shrill, piercing voice. The older form ~glatir~ survives in a narrower role, for the cry of the eagle. The noun ~glapissement~ names the sound itself.
en.glatir: ~Glatir~ comes from Latin ~glattīre~ (“to yelp”). In modern French it is a rare, literary verb used above all of the eagle, whose shrill cry is its ~glatissement~, and, in a second sense, of a dog barking again and again. It is a second-group verb, so the eagle ~glatit~. Its Latin source gives it the sense of a short, sharp animal cry, and French has kept that meaning.
en.glavioter: Derived from the noun ~glaviot~ (“spit”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, hence “to spit.” The noun is probably an alteration of ~claviot~, a disease of sheep (sheeppox), reshaped under the influence of ~glaire~ (“mucus”). Sheeppox is marked by an excess of mucus.
en.glisser:
Attested in Old French as ~glicier~, ~glisser~ arose from a blend of two verbs: ~glier~ (“to glide”), from the Frankish *~glidan~ (“to glide”), crossed with ~glacer~ (“to freeze, to make slippery”), from Latin ~glaciāre~. The Germanic *~glidan~ is a true cognate of English ~glide~ and is kin to German ~gleiten~; the icy half pulls in the family of ~glace~ (“ice”) and ~glacier~.

The two ancestors merged so neatly because they describe the same sensation — moving smoothly and uncontrollably over a slick surface, as one does on ice. From that core, ~glisser~ fanned out across French: a foot ~glisse~ on a wet floor (to slip), a sled ~glisse~ down a slope (to slide), a hand ~glisse~ into a pocket (to slip in quietly), and a remark can ~glisser~ over a subject without dwelling on it. The reflexive ~se glisser~ means to slip or sneak in. Modern descendants include ~glissade~ (“a slide, a glissade” — borrowed straight into English ballet and mountaineering vocabulary), ~glissant~ (“slippery”), and ~glissement~ (“a sliding, a shift”). It is one of those French words whose Frankish, Germanic blood still shows beneath the Romance surface.
en.glisser-déposer: ~Glisser-déposer~ is a compound of the two verbs ~glisser~ (“to slide”) and ~déposer~ (“to put down”). It names the computer gesture known in English as drag and drop: sliding an item across the screen and letting it go in a new place. ~Glisser~ is of Germanic origin, from Frankish, while ~déposer~ is built from the prefix ~dé-~ and ~poser~. The two verbs are simply set side by side, hyphenated, to describe the gesture step by step.
en.globaliser: ~Globaliser~ is formed from the adjective ~global~ and the verbal suffix ~-iser~ (“-ize”), which makes verbs meaning “to make A” or “to bring under N”. The adjective ~global~ was itself built from ~globe~ and the suffix ~-al~, and ~globe~ comes from Latin ~globus~ (“globe, sphere”). So ~globaliser~ is a modern French coinage assembled entirely from French parts, with a Latin word for a sphere at the bottom of the stack. Its English counterpart ~globalize~ ends in the same suffix.
en.glorifier:
From Latin ~glōrificāre~ (“to glorify”), a compound of ~glōria~ (“glory, fame”) and ~-ficāre~, a verb ending that comes from ~facere~ (“to make”). The same Latin verb gave Italian ~glorificare~ and Spanish ~glorificar~, and English ~glorify~ came through Old French. The origin of Latin ~glōria~ itself is unclear, and the sources consulted do not offer a settled root.

The literal meaning is “to make glorious,” and the verb is used to praise or exalt someone, with a slightly lofty tone, as in ~glorifier un héros~. The reflexive ~se glorifier de~ means “to boast of.” The same ending ~-ficāre~ underlies a large number of French verbs in ~-fier~, such as ~magnifier~, ~purifier~ and ~clarifier~, each meaning “to make” something. The noun ~gloire~ and the adjective ~glorieux~ belong to the family, as does ~glorification~.
en.gloser: ~Gloser~ is a denominal verb: the noun ~glose~ (“gloss, marginal explanation”) plus the first-conjugation ending ~-er~, which turns nouns into verbs. The noun came through Old French from Medieval Latin ~glossa~ (“explanation of a difficult word”), which goes back to Greek ~glôssa~ (“tongue”). The verb therefore means to furnish a text with glosses, that is, to annotate it or comment on it.
en.glouglouter: Formed from the onomatopoeia ~glouglou~ with the linking ~-t-~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The base imitates the gurgle of liquid, and by extension the call of a turkey, which is why the verb covers both. The word ~onomatopoeia~ itself reached French through Latin from the Greek for “making names.”
en.glousser:
~Glousser~ descends from Middle French ~glousser~, from Old French ~clocier~ (attested in 1350), from Vulgar Latin *~clociare~, itself from Latin ~glocire~ (“to cluck”). The Latin verb is imitative: a word that copies the hen's own sound. The initial consonant alternates between c and g from one form to the next.

Because the word imitates a sound, it keeps company with other French echoic words such as ~glou~ and ~glouglou~, which render a gurgling liquid. ~Glousser~ names the call of a hen, extended to the gobble of a turkey, and figuratively it describes a person who chortles or giggles, a laugh broken into short throaty notes. The noun ~gloussement~ names the sound itself.
en.glycériner: Formed in French from the noun ~glycérine~ and the verb ending ~-er~: to add or treat with glycerine. The noun was coined in 1823 by the French chemist Michel-Eugène Chevreul from Ancient Greek ~γλυκερός~ (~glykerós~, “sweet”) and the chemical suffix ~-ine~, because the substance tastes sweet. The verb is a technical derivation from that name.
en.gléner: ~Gléner~ has two histories that meet in one spelling. In sailors' French it is a nautical verb, “to coil a rope,” derived from the noun ~glène~, a coil of cordage. In Swiss French it is also a variant of ~glaner~ (“to gather leftover ears of grain”). The TLFi dates ~glaner~ to around 1223 and derives it from Late Latin ~glenare~, which it traces to a Gaulish source, with Irish parallels.
en.gober:
Borrowed from Gaulish *~gobbos~ (“beak, muzzle, snout”), which goes back to Proto-Celtic *~gobbos~ and, according to en.Wiktionary, to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ǵoph₃o-~ (“to eat, to masticate,” said of animals). French therefore owes this verb to the Celtic language spoken in Gaul before Latin. Related Celtic words still exist: Irish ~gob~ and Scottish Gaelic ~gob~ (“beak, bill”), as well as English ~gob~, which survives in British slang for the mouth. Fr.Wiktionary adds Welsh ~gwp~ as a related word for a bird's head.

The noun for a beak or mouth became in French a verb of swallowing, and ~gober~ means to swallow something whole, in one gulp: an oyster, an egg, a fly. From the literal sense came the figurative one of swallowing a story without questioning it, so that ~gober~ also means to be gullible. The verb is one of the small stock of French words that survived from Gaulish.
en.goberger: Formed in the 16th century from Old French ~goberge~ (“boasting, bluster”) with the verbal ending ~-er~. The older sense of the verb was to welcome someone with abundant food. The pronominal ~se goberger~ then came to mean, informally, “to treat oneself well,” especially by eating generously, and also “to mock someone.” The sources go back no further than the Old French noun.
en.godailler: ~Godailler~ is formed from the noun ~godaille~ with the verb ending ~-er~. English Wiktionary gives this formation and nothing more, so the earlier history of ~godaille~ is not documented here. The verb is informal and carries the senses of eating or drinking to excess and, in a distinct use, of being creased.
en.goder:
The sources give more than one account of ~goder~, depending on the sense. For the sense “to be creased,” French Wiktionary derives it from the stem of ~godron~ (a ruffle or pleat) plus the verbal ending ~-er~, and sends the reader to ~godet~. For the sense “to enjoy oneself,” it is “probably” derived from Middle French ~gauder~, from Latin ~gaudēre~ (“to rejoice”). A slang sense is a coinage built on ~gode~ plus ~-er~.

The verb is therefore best treated as a set of separate formations that merged into one spelling. The Latin ~gaudēre~ is also the source of the noun ~gaudium~ (“joy”), ancestor of French ~joie~, so the “rejoicing” strand of ~goder~ would be a cousin of ~joie~ and ~joyeux~. The “creased” sense, by contrast, belongs to the ~godron~ and ~godet~ family of folds and hollows. The entry does not claim one origin for all senses, because the sources do not.
en.godiller: Formed from ~godille~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The origin of ~godille~ itself is obscure; French Wiktionary says only that it probably comes from the north-west of France. The verb covers two activities: to scull, that is, to propel a boat with a single oar worked at the stern, and, in skiing, to ski with the quick short turns known in German as ~wedeln~.
en.godronner: Formed from the noun ~godron~ with the suffix ~-er~: to ~godronner~ is to decorate with ~godrons~, the rounded ribs or flutings used on silverware, linen collars and pleated cloth. The noun was first written ~goderon~, and French Wiktionary derives it from ~godet~, the small cup or drinking vessel, presumably because the repeated hollows of the molding recall a row of little cups. The verb is the technical word of the goldsmith and the milliner, and gave the noun ~godronnage~.
en.goinfrer: ~Goinfrer~ is formed from the noun ~goinfre~ (“glutton”) with the verb ending ~-er~. The origin of ~goinfre~ is uncertain. One hypothesis links it to ~Galafre~ or ~Golafre~, names of heroes in epic songs and chivalric romances. Another points to Old French ~goufre~ and ~golfarin~, both meaning “glutton,” which are associated with ~gouffre~ and ~golfe~. The verb, to stuff oneself, thus rests on a word whose own story remains open.
en.gominer: Formed from ~gomina~ + ~-er~: the verb means to put ~gomina~, a hair gel, on one's hair. The product gave hair a smooth, glossy, plastered-down look, and it was very popular in the 1950s, when it turns up in many films of the period. The verb is a plain denominal in ~-er~, the French ending that turns a noun into “to apply N”.
en.gommer: From ~gomme~ (“gum”) and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~gomme~ comes from Latin ~gummi~ (also spelled ~cummis~), borrowed directly from Greek ~kómmi~, which French Wiktionary says was itself taken from Egyptian, as the name of a plant exudate. The verb covers two sides: to coat with gum, and the more common modern sense of erasing, presumably through ~gomme~ meaning an eraser. The figurative sense followed, to blur or tone down something, as in ~gommer~ the differences between two things.
en.gondoler: Formed from the noun ~gondole~ plus the verb ending ~-er~; the verb means “to crinkle, to warp.” The noun is borrowed from Italian ~gondola~, which French Wiktionary traces through Venetian to Byzantine Greek ~kontoúra~ (“short tail”), from ~kontós~ (“short”) and ~ourá~ (“tail”).
en.gonfler:
Inherited from Latin ~cōnflāre~, a compound of ~com-~ (“together”) and ~flāre~ (“to blow”). It meant literally “to blow together”, in practice to fan a fire into life by blowing on it. In French the initial ~c-~ became ~g-~, and Italian ~gonfiare~ shows the same voicing. Two sister compounds of ~flāre~ also survive in French: ~sufflāre~ gave ~souffler~ (“to blow”) and ~inflāre~ gave ~enfler~ (“to swell”). English borrowed the Latin forms directly, as ~conflate~ (“to blow together”, hence to fuse) and ~inflate~.

From fanning a fire, the sense moved to filling something with air and making it swell: one ~gonfler~ a tire, a balloon or a sail, and a river ~gonfle~ when its waters rise. Figurative uses followed, such as inflating figures or puffing up with pride. Two colloquial senses are lively. The adjective ~gonflé~ means “cheeky, daring”, and the slang ~gonfler~ someone means to annoy or bore them. The family includes ~dégonfler~ (“to deflate”, and figuratively to lose one's nerve), ~regonfler~ and ~gonflement~.
en.gorger: Formed from the noun ~gorge~ (“throat”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, literally “to fill the throat,” hence “to stuff with food or drink” and, reflexively, “to gorge oneself.” The noun is inherited from Old French ~gorge~, from Late Latin ~gurga~, related to Latin ~gurges~ (“whirlpool, gulf”). French Wiktionary explains the image as a comparison of the throat to a gaping opening. Compare German ~Gurgel~ (“throat”), which belongs to the same sound-imitating family.
en.gouacher: Formed from the noun ~gouache~ with the verbal ending ~-er~: “to paint with gouache.” The noun was borrowed from Italian ~guazzo~, a painting term attested from the early sixteenth century. French Wiktionary says it meant properly “flooded ground, marsh,” from Latin ~aquatio~ (“a place where water is found”), while English Wiktionary glosses it as “water paint, splash.” Gouache is paint thinned with water, which fits both senses.
en.gouailler: French Wiktionary derives ~gouailler~ from the same stem as ~engouer~, with the suffix ~-ailler~. That suffix often adds a sense of repeated, slightly disparaging action. The sources give nothing further on the stem or its date, so the path from this stem to the modern sense, “to mock, to jeer at,” is not documented here.
en.goudronner: Formed from the noun ~goudron~ and the verb ending ~-er~, in the sense “to coat with tar.” The noun comes from Arabic ~qaṭrān~ (“tar, asphalt”), passing through Medieval Latin ~catarannus~ and Old French ~catran~ to Middle French ~goutren~. Its form was influenced by French ~goutte~ (“drop”). So ~goudronner~ is a French verb built on a word that traveled from Arabic through Latin.
en.gouger: This verb is formed from the noun ~gouge~ (“gouge”, a curved chisel) with the ending ~-er~, and means “to work a material with a gouge”. The tool's name comes from Old French and, before that, from Late Latin ~gubia~, also written ~gulbia~. French Wiktionary derives that Latin word from Gaulish ~gulbia~ (“beak”), while English Wiktionary says only that its origin is Gaulish or Basque. The Gaulish account is the more detailed one, but the origin of the tool word is not settled.
en.goujonner: A denominal verb formed on ~goujon~ with the verb ending ~-er~, in the sense of fitting with a dowel. The noun ~goujon~ covers two unrelated words. One is a “small gouge,” formed from ~gouge~ with the suffix ~-on~. The other is the fish, from Middle French ~gouvion~ and Latin ~gōbiōnem~, from ~gōbius~, which came from Ancient Greek ~kōbiós~.
en.goupiller: Formed from ~goupille~ and the ending ~-er~, the verb means to fasten with a pin. The noun ~goupille~ (“pin, cotter pin”) was originally a word for a vixen. It comes from Middle French ~goupille~ and Old French ~golpille~, the feminine of ~golpil~, and can be read as the feminine of ~goupil~ (“fox”). French Wiktionary suggests, with a hedge, that the technical sense may come from a resemblance to a fox's tail or from the cleverness of the device.
en.gourer: The origin of ~gourer~ is uncertain. The account both Wiktionaries favor runs through Arabic ~ḡarra~ (“to deceive”), with the French verb ending ~-er~ added, and French Wiktionary calls it the more probable. The old participle ~gorré~ meant “tricked, duped.” A rival explanation derives it from the root of ~goret~ (“piglet”), as if to “act like a pig,” but French Wiktionary judges that account poorly founded. In modern French the verb is colloquial, as in ~se gourer~ (“to get it wrong”).
en.gourmander: ~Gourmander~ is formed from ~gourmand~ and the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense influenced, according to one French Wiktionary entry, by ~gourmer~. Among its senses is “to scold.” The base ~gourmand~ comes from Middle French ~gourmant~ (“glutton”), of uncertain origin. One tentative proposal starts from ~groom~ (“servant”), with a sense shift comparable to that of ~goinfre~.
en.gournabler: Formed from the noun ~gournable~ with the verb ending ~-er~, meaning to fasten with a treenail. The noun comes from Dutch, from a form *~gordnagel~, made of ~gorden~ (“to gird, to buckle”) and ~nagel~ (“nail”), so literally a “fastening nail.” The shape ~gournable~ arose by dissimilation of the two ~g~ sounds and by the attraction of words ending in ~-able~.
en.goutter: Formed from the noun ~goutte~ (“drop”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning “to fall drop by drop.” The noun comes through Old French ~gote~ from Latin ~gutta~ (“drop”); the second ~t~ was added back in Middle French to mirror the Latin spelling. Do not confuse ~goutter~ with ~goûter~ (“to taste”), which comes from Latin ~gustāre~ and is a different verb altogether.
en.gouverner:
From Latin ~gubernare~ (“to steer a ship; to direct, to govern”), which Latin borrowed from Ancient Greek ~κυβερνάω~ (~kubernáō~, “to steer”). The pre-Greek origin is unsettled: Beekes assigns ~kubernáō~ to a Mediterranean (Pre-Greek) substrate, while others have tried to link it to a Proto-Indo-European root *~kʷerb-~ (“to turn”) — the safe statement is that the trail goes cold in Greek. Through Latin, the verb gave Italian ~governare~, Spanish ~gobernar~, and English ~govern~.

The original sense was nautical — to hold the tiller — and that maritime image still steers the French family: ~gouvernail~ is the “rudder,” and ~gouverner~ keeps a literal nautical use alongside its political one. The metaphor of guiding a ship became the metaphor of guiding a state, giving ~gouvernement~ (“government”) and ~gouverneur~. The most famous offshoot is indirect: from the same Greek ~κυβερνήτης~ (~kubernḗtēs~, “steersman”) Norbert Wiener coined ~cybernetics~ in 1948 — so the prefix ~cyber-~ of the digital age and the everyday verb ~gouverner~ both descend, through different doors, from a Greek pilot at the helm.
en.goûter:
From Middle French ~gouster~, from Old French ~gouster~, from Latin ~gustāre~ (“to taste, sample”), from ~gustus~ (“a tasting”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵews-~ (“to taste; to choose”). The double meaning of that root — to taste and to choose — is telling: to taste is to try, and to try is to select. Italian ~gustare~ and Spanish ~gustar~ (“to please, to like”) continue the same Latin verb.

The root *~ǵews-~ ranges widely. Through Latin it gives French ~goût~, ~dégoûter~, ~dégustation~, and English ~gusto~ (by way of Italian) and ~disgust~; through Germanic, the “choose” side of the root surfaces in English ~choose~ and ~choice~. In French, ~goûter~ also became the noun ~le goûter~, the afternoon snack — a small tasting between meals. The circle from “taste” to “judgment” closes neatly in the word ~goût~ itself, which, as in English ~taste~, names both the sensation on the tongue and the faculty of aesthetic discernment.
en.gracier: Formed from the noun ~grâce~ with the verbal ending ~-er~: to grant ~grâce~, that is, a pardon. French Wiktionary notes that the verb is written without the circumflex that ~grâce~ carries; English Wiktionary adds a Medieval Latin ~grātiō~ and calls the French-internal analysis a surface one. ~Grâce~ comes, through Old French ~grace~, from Latin ~grātia~ (“thanks, gratitude”), related to ~grātus~; the circumflex marks an irregular lengthening of the vowel.
en.graduer: Borrowed from scholastic Latin ~graduāre~, a verb built on ~gradus~ (“step”). French Wiktionary calls it a collateral form of the older ~grader~. The sense is to mark with steps or degrees, hence “to calibrate” a scale. The Latin ~gradus~ also gave French ~grade~ and ~degré~. The French noun ~gradus~, the title of a dictionary known as ~Gradus ad Parnassum~, is a separate later word and not the source of the verb.
en.graffiter: Formed from the noun ~graffiti~ plus the verb ending ~-er~: to cover with graffiti. French took ~graffiti~ from the Italian plural of ~graffito~, which goes back to Latin ~graphium~ (“stylus”), the pointed tool used for scratching letters. So the verb carries the old image of marks scratched into a surface, even when the surface is a wall and the tool a spray can.
en.grailler: ~Grailler~ is really three verbs that share a spelling. One, “to croak,” is formed from ~graille~ (“crow”). Another, “to sound a horn,” comes from Old French ~gresler~ (“to blow the trumpet”), from ~graile~ and ~graisle~ (“thin, shrill”), which derive from Latin ~gracilis~ (“slender”). The third, the slang “to eat,” comes from ~graille~ (“food”), said to be a back-formation from ~graillon~, which is related to ~griller~.
en.graillonner: ~Graillonner~ is a denominal verb built from ~graillon~ (the smell of burnt fat) with ~-er~, so it means “to smell of grease.” The noun is analyzed as ~grailler~ + ~-on~, from Old French ~graïllier~ (“to roast on a grill”), the verb behind ~griller~. The TLFi, however, takes the verb ~grailler~ to be formed from the noun rather than the reverse, so the two words are certainly related, though the direction of derivation is debated.
en.grainer: ~Grainer~ was formed in French from two closely related nouns with the verb ending ~-er~. Its first sense, giving something a grainy surface or reducing it to grains, comes from ~grain~ (“grain, granule”). Its other senses, tied to seed, come from ~graine~ (“seed”). Both nouns go back to Latin ~grānum~ (“grain, seed”).
en.graisser: Formed from the noun ~graisse~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, meaning “to provide with fat or grease”. The noun is attested in Old French as ~craisse~, from Vulgar Latin *~crassia~, built on the Latin adjective ~crassus~ (“thick, fat”), which also gave French ~gras~. According to French Wiktionary, ~graisser~ displaced the verb ~oindre~, whose conjugation is notoriously hard, so a simple first-conjugation verb replaced a difficult one.
en.grammaticaliser: Formed from the adjective ~grammatical~ with the suffix ~-iser~, so “to make grammatical,” the term of linguistics for turning a word or expression into a grammatical element. The adjective comes from Middle French ~grammatical~, from Late Latin ~grammaticālis~. The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, itself transcribing Greek verbs. The base word thus has the same learned lineage as ~grammaire~.
en.grandir:
A French formation rather than a Latin inheritance: ~grandir~ was built on the adjective ~grand~ with the second-conjugation suffix ~-ir~, the same machinery that turns ~rouge~ into ~rougir~ or ~vieux~ into ~vieillir~. The adjective ~grand~ comes from Old French ~grant~, from Latin ~grandis~ (“large, great, grown-up”), with Romance cognates in Italian ~grande~ and Spanish ~grande~; English borrowed ~grand~ from the same Latin word through Anglo-Norman.

The deeper origin of ~grandis~ is genuinely uncertain. It is sometimes connected to a PIE root for “swelling,” *~gʷʰrendʰ-~, a derivation favored by Pokorny but rejected by de Vaan on phonetic grounds; others have tried a root meaning “to grind,” which would make it a distant relative of English ~great~. Because the sources disagree, the chain beyond Latin is best left open. The meaning is transparent throughout: to ~grandir~ is to become ~grand~ — taller, older, more important. From the same adjective French draws ~grandeur~, ~agrandir~, ~grandiose~, and the kinship terms ~grand-mère~ and ~grand-père~.
en.graniter: Formed from ~granit~ (“granite”) with the verb ending ~-er~, “to paint a surface in imitation of granite.” The noun first meant a kind of oriental jasper and took its present sense in 1665. It was borrowed from Italian ~granito~ (“grained”), from ~grano~ (“grain”), because of the speckled grain of the stone.
en.granuler: A learned derivation from ~granule~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, in the sense “to make into grains.” The TLFi dates the verb to 1611, with the meaning “to reduce to seeds” (Cotgrave), and to 1675, with “to reduce to grains” (Lémery, in his chemistry course). The noun ~granulé~ (“granule, pellet”) is recorded in 1908. ~Granule~ is a small grain, from Latin ~granulum~, a diminutive of ~granum~ (“grain”), the source of French ~grain~.
en.graphiter: Formed from ~graphite~ and the verb ending ~-er~, in the sense “to coat or treat with graphite.” The noun ~graphite~ was borrowed from German ~Graphit~, attested in 1789 and coined by the mineralogist Abraham Gottlob Werner. The German word rests on Greek ~gráphō~ (“to write”), since the mineral leaves a mark on paper. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is the default way to coin a verb from a noun in French.
en.grappiller: ~Grappiller~ is a variant of the older verb ~grapper~ (“to pick grapes”), which is built on ~grappe~ (“bunch of grapes”). Its ending was reshaped under the influence of ~piller~ (“to plunder”). The verb means to pick grapes and, by extension, to scrape together small gains here and there; the ending borrowed from ~piller~ suits that figurative sense of picking up bits and pieces.
en.grasseyer: ~Grasseyer~ is formed from ~gras~ with the suffix ~-eyer~, a variant of ~-oyer~, and means to speak with a throaty r. The adjective ~gras~ is inherited from Old French ~gras~, from Late Latin ~grassus~, which came from Latin ~crassus~, originally “thick” but used expressively to mean “fat.” The change of initial ~c~ to ~g~ is probably due to the influence of ~grossus~ (“big”). French Wiktionary gives ~gras~ a doublet, ~crasse~, which kept the Latin consonant.
en.graticuler:
A verb formed from the noun ~graticule~, which comes from Latin ~craticula~ (“small grill, small grating”). The Latin word is a diminutive of ~crātis~ (“wickerwork, hurdle, lattice”), so the underlying image is a small lattice of crossing bars. The French verb applies that image to a drawing: to ~graticuler~ a design is to divide it into squares with a network of crossing lines.

The same Latin word has a better-known descent in French. ~Craticula~ and its variant ~craticulum~ are the source of ~grille~ and ~gril~, so ~graticuler~ and the kitchen ~gril~ share one ancestor, a small lattice, whether of iron bars or of ruled lines. English took over the pair ~grill~ and ~grille~ from French as well.
en.gratifier:
Borrowed from Latin ~grātificārī~, a compound of ~grātus~ (“kind, pleasing”) and ~facere~ (“to make”), so the verb meant literally “to make pleasing.” It is a learned word, taken straight from Latin rather than inherited through the spoken language. Spanish ~gratificar~ and Italian ~gratificare~ come from the same Latin source, and so does English ~gratify~.

The ending ~-fier~ in French verbs such as ~modifier~, ~qualifier~ and ~vérifier~ is the same compound element, the Latin ~-ficāre~ built on ~facere~ (a verb that survives in everyday French as ~faire~). In modern French, ~gratifier~ means to bestow something pleasing on someone, to reward or present them with it. Its other relatives come from ~grātus~: ~gré~, ~grâce~, ~gratuit~ and ~gratitude~.
en.gratiner: ~Gratiner~ is formed from the noun ~gratin~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, and means to cook a dish so that it forms a browned crust. ~Gratin~ is a deverbal noun made from ~gratter~ (“to scrape”) with the suffix ~-in~. The cooking term is thus related to the verb ~gratter~, and the verb ~gratiner~ continues that line.
en.gratouiller: A variant spelling of ~grattouiller~, which French Wiktionary derives from ~gratter~ (“to scratch”) under the influence of ~chatouiller~ (“to tickle”). The word thus blends the two verbs, and it means both “to itch” and “to scratch”. It is first attested in 1881. The spelling with a single ~t~ is the variant; the entry for ~grattouiller~ carries the etymology.
en.gratter:
From Old French ~grater~, via an attested Medieval Latin ~cratare~, borrowed from Old Low Frankish *~krattōn~ (“to scrape, to scratch”), from Proto-Germanic *~krattōną~. English Wiktionary traces the Germanic verb to the Proto-Indo-European root *~gred-~, with the Albanian noun ~gërresë~ (“rasp”) as a possible cousin. The Germanic relatives are easy to see: German ~kratzen~ (“to scratch”), Swedish ~kratta~ (“to rake”) and the regional English ~scrat~. French then passed the verb on to its neighbors, as Occitan and Catalan ~gratar~ and Italian ~grattare~ show.

The verb is one of the many words that the Franks left in Gallo-Romance. It means “to scrape” a surface with something rough, and also “to scratch” an itch, as in ~se gratter~. A family of everyday words grew from it: ~gratin~, originally the crust scraped from the bottom of a pot, ~grattoir~ (“scraper”), ~grattage~ and ~gratte-ciel~, a calque of English “skyscraper”, which literally scratches the sky.
en.grattouiller: A blend of ~gratter~ (“to scratch”) and ~chatouiller~ (“to tickle”), according to English Wiktionary. The word takes its opening from ~gratter~ and its ending from ~chatouiller~. Its meaning, “to itch, to scratch,” sits between those of its two parents: the rubbing of the one and the light irritation of the other.
en.graver:
From Old French ~graver~ (“to dig, to carve”), borrowed from Frankish *~graban~ (“to dig”), from Proto-Germanic *~grabaną~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʰrebʰ-~ (“to dig, scratch, bury”). It is therefore a Germanic word, not a Latin one — a cognate of German ~graben~ (“to dig”) and of English ~grave~, the source of ~engrave~, as well as of Old Church Slavonic ~grebǫ~ (“I dig, bury”).

The earliest French sense was the literal “to hollow out” of the Frankish verb; from cutting into the earth it narrowed to cutting into a hard surface — incising stone, metal, or wood with a tool. From that came the figurative “to imprint deeply,” as a memory ~gravée~ in the mind, and in the digital age the curious sense of “to burn” a CD or DVD, where a laser once again cuts a pattern into a hard material. The same Frankish stock yields the French family ~graveur~ (“engraver”), ~gravure~ (“engraving”), and ~regraver~ (“to re-engrave”).
en.gravillonner: Formed from ~gravillon~ and the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense “to cover with gravel,” as one does a road. The noun ~gravillon~ dates from about 1571 and is itself derived from ~grave~ (“gravel, grit”), so the verb is a small family tree of French derivations: ~grave~, then ~gravillon~, then ~gravillonner~.
en.gravir:
Inherited from Old French ~gravir~ (also ~graver~), from Frankish *~krawjan~, a verb meaning “to help oneself with claws.” French Wiktionary derives it from a Frankish noun *~krawa~ (“claw”), the source of Old French ~graue~ (“claw”). English Wiktionary adds that the Frankish word is related to Proto-Germanic *~krauwōn~ and ultimately goes back to a Proto-Indo-European root *~ger-~ (“to wind, to twist”), and compares Proto-Germanic *~krōkaz~ (“hook”), a word that English Wiktionary treats as a relative.

The picture behind the verb is of climbing with the help of claws, gripping a surface to pull oneself upward, so that ~gravir~ suggests climbing by hold and grip, and not by walking. Today one ~gravit~ a hill, a stair or a mountain, always with effort, and the verb is also used figuratively, as in ~gravir les échelons~ (“to climb the ladder”). The word keeps its Frankish heritage, one of the many everyday French verbs that the Franks left behind. The English text states the link to claws as a relationship (“related to”) and not a derivation, so the claw image is the accepted but not the only possible reading.
en.graviter: ~Graviter~ is a learned borrowing from New Latin ~grāvitāre~, which was itself made from Latin ~grāvitās~ (“weight, heaviness”). French Wiktionary simply derives it from ~gravitas~. The same Latin noun gave French ~gravité~, and the verb, which first described bodies drawn by weight, now also has the figurative sense of moving in the orbit of someone or something.
en.grecquer: ~Grecquer~ is a denominal verb, formed on the noun ~grecque~. In bookbinding and similar trades the ~grecque~ is a fine saw used to cut grooves, and ~grecquer~ means to make such incisions. The noun is the feminine form of ~grec~ (“Greek”), which goes back to Latin ~Graecus~. The reason the tool took this name is not given in the sources used here.
en.greffer:
From ~greffe~, which French Wiktionary derives from Latin ~graphium~ (“stylus”), with the diminutive ~graphiolum~ behind the botanical sense. In Middle French the verb was spelled ~graffer~. Latin ~graphium~ was itself a borrowing from Greek, from the verb ~γράφειν~ (“to scratch, to write”), the same Greek root that underlies English ~graph~ and ~graphite~. English ~graft~ was borrowed from the Old French noun.

The usual explanation is a matter of shape. A stylus was a pointed rod for writing on wax, and the slender cut shoot inserted into a tree is said to have resembled it, so the noun ~greffe~ named the shoot, and the verb ~greffer~ the act of inserting it. French then carried the gardener's term into surgery, for tissue or an organ moved from one body to another, and into figurative use, for one thing attached to another. The same stylus gave a legal sense: the ~greffe~ is a court's registry, kept by the ~greffier~, the clerk who writes. Two worlds, trees and tribunals, thus share one ancestor in the writing tool.
en.grelotter: ~Grelotter~ is formed from ~grelot~ (“small bell”) and the verb ending ~-er~, and means to shiver or tremble. An expression ~trembler le grelet~ (“to tremble with cold”) is recorded in 1547. The noun ~grelot~ goes back to a Germanic root with vowel alternation, ~grill-~, ~grell-~, ~groll-~ and ~grüll-~, tied to words for shouting and growling: Middle High German ~grillen~ (“to cry out in anger”) and Middle Dutch ~grollen~ (“to growl”).
en.grenailler: Formed from the noun ~grenaille~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is ~grain~ or ~graine~ with the suffix ~-aille~, and designates small grains or granules of metal. The verb therefore means to reduce a substance to such grains: to granulate.
en.greneler: From ~grain~ (“grain, seed, fine granule”), from Latin ~grānum~, with the diminutive suffix ~-el~ and the verbal suffix ~-er~. The verb means to give a surface a grainy texture, as when leather, paper or metal is worked to produce small bumps. The suffix ~-el~ gives the idea of many small grains, so the verb literally sets out to make a surface “little-grained”. French Wiktionary points to ~grenu~ (“grainy”), which shows the same stem spelled with an ~e~ instead of the ~ai~ of ~grain~.
en.grener: Formed from ~grain~ or ~graine~ (“seed”) with the verbal ending ~-er~: to produce seeds, or to reduce something to grains. The noun ~grain~ comes from Latin ~granum~ (“grain”), which goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~ǵr̥h₂nóm~. The same Latin word underlies ~graine~ and ~grenier~, and English ~grain~ and ~garner~ come from it too.
en.grenouiller: Formed from ~grenouille~ (“frog”) with the verbal ending ~-er~. The original sense was to splash about in water like a frog, then by extension to wallow in wine, to tipple. The modern sense of scheming or engaging in shady dealings appeared shortly before 1945. ~Grenouille~ comes from Old French ~grenoille~, an alteration of ~renoille~, from Vulgar Latin *~ranucula~, a diminutive of Latin ~rāna~ (“frog”). French Wiktionary suggests that the initial ~g-~ may owe something to words imitating birdsong, or to a Gaulish word.
en.grever:
From Old French ~grever~, which English Wiktionary describes as borrowed from Latin ~gravāre~ (“to load”), with influence from the Vulgar Latin adjective *~grevis~ (compare ~grief~), itself from Latin ~gravis~ (“heavy”). French Wiktionary instead gives popular Latin ~gravare~ or ~grevare~, glossed as loading in the concrete sense, causing harm, afflicting. Either way the verb belongs to the family of ~gravis~, “heavy”, and so to the idea of weighing something down.

French Wiktionary describes the classical sense as “to cause harm, to lay a burden on”. By the seventeenth century nobody loaded a cart or a boat with it any longer, and the word survived in figurative use, as of taxes weighing on a country or on the state. It belongs to the same family as ~aggraver~ and ~aggravation~, from popular Latin ~aggrevare~.
en.gribouiller: From Dutch ~kriebelen~, with the same meaning (“to scribble”), plus the suffix ~-ouiller~. French Wiktionary dates the word to 1611. The ending ~-ouiller~ is a French suffix that adds a frequentative or slightly pejorative nuance, as in ~fouiller~ and ~bafouiller~, so ~gribouiller~ suggests a messy, repeated scrawl. That fits its modern sense of “to scribble, to doodle,” and it is also a borrowing from the Low Countries, along with many other everyday words.
en.griffer: The origin of ~griffer~ (“to scratch”) is disputed. French Wiktionary treats it as a verb formed on the noun ~griffe~ (“claw”) with the ending ~-er~. English Wiktionary gives Old French ~grifer~ and offers two possibilities: either it is derived from ~griffe~, or it comes from Old High German ~grīfan~ (“to grasp”), from Proto-Germanic *~grīpaną~. On the second account, ~griffer~ is a doublet of ~gripper~ (“to seize, to jam”). In both versions the meaning is to rake with claws or nails.
en.griffonner: Formed from ~griffer~ (“to scratch”) with the suffix ~-onner~, which on a verb base usually gives a repeated, attenuated or careless action, as in ~chantonner~ or ~mâchonner~. So ~griffonner~ is “to scratch away” and, by extension, to write or draw hastily and badly, to scribble. The base ~griffer~ has a disputed origin: it is either a verb built on ~griffe~ (“claw”) or, on another account, a Germanic borrowing related to Old High German ~grīfan~ (“to grasp”). Either way, the notion behind the family is that of marking with a claw or nail.
en.grigner: From Old French ~graignier~, related to English ~grin~, which means a grimace that shows the teeth or a forced smile. That sense lies behind “to bare one's teeth,” and then behind the creases and wrinkles that a badly folded fabric makes. The ~gn~ sound of the French verb is explained by its closeness in meaning to ~grogner~ (“to grumble, to growl”).
en.grignoter:
Built in French from ~grigner~ and the suffix ~-oter~, which makes frequentative and diminutive verbs, as in ~clignoter~ and ~tapoter~. The base ~grigner~ comes from Frankish *~grinan~ (“to grimace”), a Germanic verb cognate with English ~grin~ and German ~greinen~ (“to whine”). ~Grigner~ is nearly gone from modern French but survives in set phrases such as ~grigner des dents~ (“to bare one's teeth”).

The sources do not explain how a verb for grimacing came to mean “to nibble,” and the link is presumably the teeth, in small, repeated bites. The verb has since spread from food to money and territory. One ~grignote~ a savings account, a lead in the polls or a rival's market share, a little at a time. Related words include ~grignotage~ (“snacking, gradual erosion”), and the modern ~grignotine~, a snack food.
en.grillager: ~Grillager~ is formed from the noun ~grillage~ (“wire netting, fencing”) with the verb ending ~-er~, and means to enclose or fit something with such netting. The noun is itself a derivative: ~grille~ (“grating, grille”) plus the suffix ~-age~, attested from the 1730s or 1740s according to English Wiktionary. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is the default way French turns a noun into a verb, as in ~téléphone~ to ~téléphoner~. So ~grillager~ is a chain of two short steps: ~grille~, then ~grillage~, then the verb.
en.griller: Formed from ~grille~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~grille~ goes back to Latin ~crāticula~ (“small grill”), a diminutive of ~crātis~ (“wickerwork, hurdle”), and appears in Old French as ~gradilie~, then ~graille~ about 1200. It first meant a lattice of crossed bars used for punishment by fire. The verb originally meant to put someone to death by fire, then to roast, and it weakened to light burning, to toast, and, informally, to smoke a cigarette. Figurative senses followed: to burn out a machine, to run a signal, or to eliminate a competitor.
en.grimacer: Formed from the noun ~grimace~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so “to make a wry face.” English Wiktionary traces ~grimace~ through Old French to ~grime~ (“mask”) plus a pejorative ending ~-ace~, from Old Frankish *~grīma~ (“mask”), whose relatives include Old English ~grīma~. French Wiktionary adds that the Frankish word fed two families: magic, with ~grimoire~, and facial expression, with ~grimer~.
en.grimer: ~Grimer~ is formed from the noun ~grime~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, which turns nouns into verbs. ~Grime~ is tied to ~grimace~, and French Wiktionary records that in 1694 ~faire la grime~ meant “to pull a face.” English Wiktionary traces ~grime~ to Middle French, where it meant “mask,” and before that to Old French ~grime~, from Frankish *~grīmo~, from Proto-Germanic *~grīmô~. The verb is thus built on a word for a mask, and its modern sense is to make up someone's face.
en.grimper:
Attested in the late 15th century, ~grimper~ is, by the favored account, a nasalized variant of Middle French ~gripper~ (“to grip, to seize, to claw”), reshaped under the pull of ~ramper~ (“to crawl, to creep”), to which it was close in meaning. The hedge is real — fr.Wiktionary marks the derivation as merely ~probable~ — but the source verb is clear: ~gripper~ comes from Frankish *~grīpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~grīpaną~, from PIE *~gʰreyb-~ (“to grab, to grasp”). It is thus cognate with English ~grip~ and ~gripe~ and German ~greifen~ — a Germanic word that slipped into Romance French.

The semantics fit the proposed origin beautifully: to climb a wall or a tree is to ~grip~ it hand over hand, hauling yourself up by what you can clutch — and the borrowed ~n~ of ~ramper~ left ~grimper~ sounding like its crawling cousin. Modern French keeps both the literal sense (to scale, to clamber) and the figurative (prices that ~grimpent~, “shoot up”). From the same ~gripper~ stem branch French ~gripper~ (now also “to seize up,” of a machine), ~grippe~ (“the flu,” once “a sudden grab” or whim), ~agripper~ (“to grab hold of”), and ~grippe-sou~ (“a skinflint,” one who claws after pennies). The climber and the influenza share, surprisingly, one grasping root.
en.grincer: ~Grincer~ has two accounts. French Wiktionary derives it from Old French ~grisser~ and calls it a doublet of ~crisser~, another verb of harsh, scraping sound. English Wiktionary instead gives earlier ~grigner~, originally from Old High German ~grînan~. The two chains differ and neither text says how they connect, so the origin is only partly settled. The verb's senses, such as squeaking, creaking and gnashing the teeth, all concern harsh sound.
en.gripper:
English Wiktionary gives a full chain: Old French *~gripper~, from Frankish *~grīpan~, from Proto-Germanic *~grīpaną~, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʰreyb-~ (“to grab, grasp”). French Wiktionary agrees on a Germanic source and compares English ~grip~ and Dutch ~grijpen~. German ~greifen~ is a further cousin from the same Germanic verb, as general background. The verb is a doublet of ~griffer~.

A doublet means that two French words came from one source by different routes, here the same Germanic verb reaching French in two forms. The original sense, now old-fashioned according to French Wiktionary, was to seize or grab, and it is still clear in ~griffer~ (“to scratch with claws”). Modern ~gripper~ is used of mechanisms that jam or seize up, as with an engine that seizes (~le moteur se grippe~). The noun ~grippe~ (“flu”) is generally derived from this verb, as is ~grippage~ (“seizing up”).
en.grisailler: Formed from the noun ~grisaille~ and the verb ending ~-er~, in the sense “to turn gray, to paint in grays.” The noun ~grisaille~ is itself built on the adjective ~gris~ (“gray”) with the suffix ~-aille~, and names a painting done in shades of gray. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is French's default way of making a verb from a noun. The verb is thus a double derivation: ~gris~, then ~grisaille~, then ~grisailler~.
en.griser: ~Griser~ is formed from the adjective ~gris~ with the verb ending ~-er~, first in the sense “to make or become grey.” It later acquired the figurative sense “to intoxicate, to elate.” ~Gris~ comes from Frankish *~grīs~ and, behind it, Proto-Germanic *~grīsaz~ (“grey”), and is related to Dutch ~grijs~ and German ~greis~ (“hoary”). Medieval Latin ~griseus~ took the word back from the Germanic, and it gave Italian ~grigio~.
en.grisoller: French Wiktionary explains ~grisoller~ simply as an onomatopoeia: a word made to imitate a sound rather than inherited from an earlier word. The sound in question is the song of the lark, and the verb means to sing as a lark does. Neither Wiktionary gives any Latin, Germanic or other ancestor for it, so the imitation of the bird's song is the whole of its etymology.
en.grisonner: Formed from ~grison~ (“graying, grey-haired”) and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is itself a derivative of ~gris~ (“grey”) with the suffix ~-on~. The verb therefore means to turn grey, most often said of hair. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~, the infinitive ending of the first conjugation, and is the usual way French coins verbs from nouns.
en.griveler: ~Griveler~ is formed from ~grive~ (“thrush”) with the suffix ~-eler~. French Wiktionary explains the choice of bird: the thrush was reputed for the greed with which it gathers its food and for the raids it makes on vineyards. The origin of ~grive~ is uncertain. It may be onomatopoeic, or, as one account has it, it may come from Old French ~griu~ (“Greek”), since the migratory thrush was thought to winter in Greece. The verb means to leave without paying or to make money on the side.
en.grognasser: ~Grognasser~ is derived from ~grogner~ with the suffix ~-asser~. The base ~grogner~ comes from Latin ~grunnīre~ (“to grunt”), the cry of a pig, by way of Old French ~gronir~. The suffix ~-asser~, a French formation of the fifteenth century, gives verbs a frequentative or depreciative nuance, as in ~rêvasser~ and ~traînasser~. ~Grognasser~ therefore means to grumble repeatedly and without conviction, a low and tired version of ~grogner~. Its gloss “to whine, to whinge” captures that grudging tone.
en.grogner:
From Latin ~grunnīre~ (“to grunt,” said of the cry of a pig), which reached French by way of Old French ~gronir~. The Old French verb is easily compared with ~groin~, the French word for a pig's snout. Latin ~grunnīre~ also lived on elsewhere in the Romance languages: Spanish ~gruñir~ and Italian ~grugnire~ are its descendants. The French verb therefore began as the name of an animal noise.

The meaning has widened well beyond the sty. The verb now covers the grunt of a pig, the growl of a dog and the grumbling of a person who protests under their breath. The family is lively: ~grognement~ names the sound itself, ~grognon~ describes a grumpy person, and ~grognard~ (“grumbler”) became the nickname of Napoleon's veteran soldiers. The link with ~groin~, suggested by the Old French form, is presented in the sources only as a natural comparison, not as a proven descent.
en.grognonner: Formed from ~grognon~ with the verb ending ~-er~, to mean “grumble” or “growl” like a grouch. The base ~grognon~ was itself built on the verb ~grogner~ (“to grunt, to growl”) with the suffix ~-on~. The word is therefore a derivation of a derivation: a verb gave an agent-like adjective, and that adjective gave back a second verb.
en.grommeler:
From Old French ~grumeler~ (“to murmur, grumble”), borrowed from Middle Dutch ~grommelen~ (“to murmur, mutter, grunt”), a frequentative of ~grommen~. French Wiktionary instead analyzes it as Old French ~grommer~ (twelfth century), itself borrowed from Middle Dutch ~grommen~, plus the frequentative suffix ~-eler~, with ~grummeler~ attested in the thirteenth century. Either way the source is Dutch. Related words include Low German ~grummeln~ and German ~grummeln~, both meaning “to grumble.”

The frequentative ending matters here: where ~grommen~ is a single growl, ~grommeler~ is a growl repeated, a low continuous muttering. Dutch thus lent French a word that imitates the sound it names. English ~grumble~ is a cousin of the Dutch verb. ~Grommeler~ is used of people who mutter their discontent, and of things that rumble softly, but it is a distinct word from ~gronder~ (“to scold, to rumble”), which comes from Latin ~grundīre~ and only resembles it in sound.
en.gronder: From Old French ~gronder~, attested around 1230 and preceded by forms such as ~grondre~ and ~grondir~, from Latin ~grundīre~, a variant of ~grunnīre~ (“to grunt”). The Latin verb is probably imitative, an attempt to put the pig's sound into a word. The sense widened from animal noises to any low, deep sound: thunder, a cannon or a crowd ~gronde~. It also took on a human use, “to scold,” when a person grumbles at a child. The related ~grogner~ comes from ~grunnīre~ as well, and the two verbs sit side by side.
en.grossir: Formed from the adjective ~gros~ (“big, thick”) and the ending ~-ir~, in the pattern of deadjectival verbs meaning “to become A,” so ~grossir~ is “to grow big.” ~Gros~ comes from Old French ~gros~ and from Late Latin ~grossus~ (“thick”). The adjective was also borrowed by English as ~gross~. The ending ~-ir~ goes back to Latin ~-ire~, and the same pattern gave ~grandir~ from ~grand~. The verb works both ways, “to become bigger” and “to make bigger,” which is why it serves for people who gain weight, for a magnifying glass, and for a rumor.
en.grossoyer: The verb is derived from the noun ~grosse~ with the suffix ~-oyer~. In the legal vocabulary the verb belongs to, a ~grosse~ is the engrossed or fair copy of a deed or judgment, and the verb means to produce such a copy, as the gloss “make a fair copy (of a legal document)” says. The suffix ~-oyer~ is a French verb-forming ending of the sense “to treat with, to apply N,” which fits a verb meaning to make a ~grosse~ of a document. The sources give no earlier origin.
en.grouiller:
The Middle French verb ~grouiller~ already covered a wide range: “to shake, stir, agitate, scold, hasten, swarm, teem, crawl”. English Wiktionary derives it from Old French ~grouiller~ (“to rumble”), an alteration of Old French ~grouller~ (“to growl”), from Middle Dutch ~grollen~ (“to rumble, growl, grumble, scold”). The chain continues through Old Dutch *~grullen~ and Proto-Germanic *~gruljaną~ (“to shout, make angry, provoke”) to the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʰer-~ (“to rattle, make a noise, grumble”). Its cognates include Middle High German ~grüllen~ (“to scorn, jeer”) and Old English ~griellan~ (“to anger, vex”).
