The origin is debated. French Wiktionary instead sees a merger of two Old French verbs, ~grouiller~ (“to rumble”) and ~crouler~ (“to stir about”). English Wiktionary also offers an alternate etymology for the sense “to crawl”: from Frankish *~grubilōn~ (“to dig, burrow, rummage, crawl”), from Proto-Germanic *~grubilōną~ and the root *~gʰrebʰ-~ (“to dig, scrape”). On that account, the cognates are German ~grübeln~ (“to brood”) and Old Norse ~grúfla~ (“to bend low, creep”). The sources do not settle whether the swarming senses grew from the noisy verb or from a separate crawling one. Modern French keeps the mix: ~grouiller~ is said of crowds and insects, and the related words include ~grouillant~ and ~grouillement~.
en.grouper:
Derived from French ~groupe~ with the suffix ~-er~. ~groupe~ was borrowed in the 17th century from Italian ~gruppo~ (also ~groppo~, “a knot, a cluster, a round mass”), which came through Vulgar Latin *~cruppus~ from a Germanic source — Frankish or Lombardic — going back to Proto-Germanic *~kruppaz~ (“a compressed round mass; lump; the crop of a bird”). So a group is, at heart, a knot or rounded clump of things bunched together.

That Germanic *~kruppaz~ is the same word that, in the native English line, became ~crop~ (originally the rounded pouch in a bird's gullet, then the rounded head of a plant, then a harvest) and German ~Kropf~ (“crop, goitre”). The deeper pre-Germanic root is, by the sources' own admission, uncertain, so the chain is best stopped at *~kruppaz~. From ~groupe~ French built ~grouper~, ~regrouper~, ~groupement~, and ~groupuscule~; English borrowed the noun and verb back as ~group~ — making the bird's crop, the harvest, and the committee all distant relations.
en.gruger:
French ~gruger~ is a borrowing, either from Dutch ~gruizen~ (“to crush, grind”) or, by French Wiktionary's alternative account, from Norman ~grujaer~ (same sense). Both belong to the Germanic family that also gave French ~gruau~ (“groats, oatmeal”), the coarsely broken grain. The source verbs mean “to crush”, a long way from the modern sense of fleecing a person.

Modern French uses ~gruger~ almost only in the figurative sense of “to dupe, to con, to rob,” as in ~se faire gruger~, to be fleeced by someone who takes advantage of you. The sense of being ground down by another person is not far from the idea of crushing, though the sources do not narrate the shift. In the family of the verb, ~gruau~ is the one everyday relative, still used for the flour of oats or wheat, and it keeps the original image of grain broken into pieces.
en.grumeler: Derived from the noun ~grumeau~ (“clot, lump”), formerly ~grumel~, with the verb ending ~-er~, so the verb means to form lumps. ~Grumeau~ descends from Old French ~grumiel~ and from Latin ~grumulus~ (“little mound”), a diminutive of ~grumus~ (“mound”). A lumpy sauce is thus, etymologically, one dotted with tiny hillocks.
en.gréciser:
The two Wiktionaries differ on ~gréciser~. French Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~graecizāre~, a verb built on ~Graecus~ (“Greek”), while English Wiktionary analyses it as French ~grec~ plus the suffix ~-iser~. Either way, the verb means to give a Greek form or character to something, in particular to render a word or name in Greek.

The suffix ~-iser~ itself comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and French Wiktionary dates its productive use to the mid-sixteenth century, with ~latiniser~ and ~gréciser~ as its first examples. The two verbs form a natural pair: ~latiniser~ puts into Latin, ~gréciser~ into Greek. The root is the Latin ~Graecus~, which gave French ~grec~, the country name ~Grèce~ and the learned family of ~gréco-romain~ and ~grécité~.
en.gréer:
From Old French ~agreier~ (“to equip”), borrowed from Old Norse ~greiða~ (“to make ready, to equip”). English Wiktionary adds a neat twist: the initial ~a-~ was attached in Old French by analogy with verbs like ~abiller~, then removed again in Middle French, which gave ~greer~ and ~grayer~, in order to avoid confusion with ~agreer~, the ancestor of ~agréer~. The Norse word has a Germanic cousin in English ~ready~, which comes from the same family of words meaning “prepared.”

The sense stayed anchored in the sea: to ~gréer~ a ship is to fit it with masts, yards, sails and ropes, and the noun ~gréement~ names this whole rigging. Modern French keeps the verb almost entirely for ships and, by extension, for boats under sail. The agent noun ~gréeur~ names the person who does it.
en.gréser: Formed from the noun ~grès~ (“sandstone”) plus the verbal ending ~-er~, with the sense of smoothing or polishing a surface with sandstone. The noun comes from Frankish *~greot~ (“gravel”), the language of the Franks, to be compared with Old High German ~griez~ and Middle Dutch ~griet~. Frankish *~greot~ goes back to Proto-Germanic *~greutą~ (“grit, sandstone”).
en.grésiller: French Wiktionary distinguishes two entries. The first comes from Old Frankish *~grisilôn~ (“to hail”) and means to fall as sleet; the noun ~grésil~ (“sleet”) belongs with it. The second is the verb of crackling and sizzling, which it explains as an alteration of the Middle French ~grediller~ under the influence of the first. The modern verb thus covers both sleet falling and the noises of crackling and sizzling. English Wiktionary gives no etymology, so the Frankish origin rests on French Wiktionary alone.
en.grêler:
~Grêler~ (“to hail”) comes from Old French ~gresler~ (“to produce hail”), from Old Frankish *~grisilōn~ (“to hail”), itself from a West Germanic form *~grisilōn~. The Germanic verb is related to the French verb ~grésiller~ (“to crackle, to sizzle”), which makes a pleasing link between the rattle of ice on a roof and the sputter of fat in a pan. Frankish, the language of the Germanic conquerors of Gaul, left French a good number of weather and field words of this kind.

In modern French ~grêler~ is mostly impersonal: ~il grêle~ means “it is hailing”. The noun ~grêle~ belongs to the same family. As in many French words, the circumflex marks a lost ~s~, the one still visible in the Old French spelling ~gresler~. The verb can also be used with a crop or an orchard as its object, for the damage that a storm of hail does, and its participle ~grêlé~ describes a face scarred as if by hail, the sense of “pockmarked”.
en.guerroyer:
From Old French ~guerroiier~ (“to make war”). English Wiktionary calls this inherited from Vulgar Latin *~werrizāre~, while French Wiktionary hedges, giving a Vulgar Latin *~werrizō~ or *~werrizare~ with a “perhaps.” The Old French verb can also be read as a simple derivative of ~guerre~ (“war”) with the verbal suffix ~-oyer~. Behind it all stands the noun ~guerre~, which is standardly derived from Frankish *~werra~, a Germanic word. Spanish ~guerrear~ (“to wage war”), which French Wiktionary cites as a parallel, and Italian ~guerreggiare~ show the same family in the sister languages.

The Germanic origin of ~guerre~ is itself a curiosity, because Latin already had perfectly good words for war, ~bellum~ above all. Yet Romance speakers adopted the Frankish word, and ~bellum~ survives in French only in learned words such as ~belliqueux~ and ~belligérant~. English ~war~ comes from the same Germanic word, by way of Norman French. In modern French, ~guerroyer~ is literary or old-fashioned for “to wage war,” and it can be used lightly or figuratively for “to bicker, to keep up a fight,” as the sense “to hassle” suggests. ~Guerrier~ (“warrior”) belongs to the same family.
en.guetter:
French ~guetter~ is inherited from Old French ~gaitier~ (also spelled ~guaitier~), a Germanic loan taken from Frankish *~wahtōn~ (“to watch, guard”), also given as *~wahtjan~. The Frankish verb was itself a derivative of the noun *~wahta~ (“guard, watch”), which goes back to Proto-Germanic *~wahtwō~ (“guard, watch”). English Wiktionary traces that Germanic noun further to the Proto-Indo-European root *~weǵ-~ (“to be fresh, cheerful, awake”), so the underlying idea is one of being alert and awake. The French verb kept that meaning close to its source: to keep watch, to observe attentively, and by extension to lie in wait for something or someone. The chain thus runs from Proto-Indo-European to Proto-Germanic, then Frankish, Old French and modern French, with the Germanic stage supplying both the sound and the sense.

The shift of Frankish ~w~ to ~gu~ in French is a change also seen in ~gagner~, from Frankish *~waidanjan~ (“to forage, graze”). In an Anglo-Norman or Old Northern French variant the initial ~w~ was kept instead, and that variant is the source of English ~wait~, which therefore descends ultimately from the same origin as the French verb. English ~watch~ is a cousin from the same Germanic family. Two words that look unrelated, ~guetter~ and ~wait~, are thus the same Germanic word that took different forms in different dialects. In ~guetter~ itself, the ~gu~ is simply the French way of writing a Germanic ~w~ sound.
en.gueuler: ~Gueuler~ is formed from the noun ~gueule~ (“mouth”) and the verb ending ~-er~, and means to yell or scream. The noun comes from Old French ~gole~ (also ~goule~), from Latin ~gula~ (“gullet, throat”). French Wiktionary adds that the heraldic term ~gueules~ (“red”) may be related to it, though this is still debated. The ending ~-er~ goes back to Latin ~-are~ and is the usual way French builds a verb from a noun.
en.gueuletonner: ~Gueuletonner~ (“to feast”) comes from ~gueuleton~ (a hearty meal), itself derived from ~gueule~, plus the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~gueule~ is inherited from Old French ~gole~, from Latin ~gula~ (“gullet, throat”), and is a doublet of ~goulet~. So the verb means, in effect, to put the gullet to work, by eating well and heartily.
en.guider:
A reshaping, under the influence of the noun ~guide~, of Old French ~guier~ (“to guide, to lead”), which goes back to the Old Frankish ~witan~ (“to show the way, to watch over”). This Germanic verb belongs to a family meaning “to know, to see, to point out”: it is cognate with Old English ~wīsian~ (“to guide, to direct”), German ~weisen~ (“to show, to point”), and, more distantly through the same Indo-European root, with Latin ~vidēre~ (“to see”). The reshaped form was reinforced by Italian ~guidare~ and Spanish ~guiar~, which English in turn borrowed as ~guide~.

The Frankish root joins seeing and showing: one who can see the path can point it out, and so ~guider~ means to lead another along a way, whether a road, a course of study, or a moral life. The initial ~gu-~ is the tell-tale Germanic ~w-~ as adapted by Old French, the same shift seen in ~guerre~ (from ~werra~) and ~garder~ (from ~wardōn~). From ~guide~ and ~guider~ French built a tidy family: ~guidage~, ~guidance~, ~guidon~ (the handlebar that steers a bicycle), and the modern ~téléguider~ (“to guide from afar, to remote-control”).
en.guigner:
From Old French ~guignier~ (“to make a sign with the eye”), inherited from Frankish *~wingjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~winkaną~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~weng-~ (“to bow, bend, arch, curve”). The same Germanic verb gave English ~wink~ and German ~winken~. The change of initial ~w~ to ~gu-~ is typical of Frankish words in French, as in ~guerre~ and ~garder~.

The original sense was to make a sign with the eye, a wink or a sidelong signal. In French today the verb means to eye something on the sly, to sneak a glance at it, and, familiarly, to eye something one covets, as in ~guigner~ a prize or a place. The verb remains informal, while ~wink~ stayed the plain English word.
en.guillemeter: Formed from the noun ~guillemet~ (“quotation mark”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, so the verb means to put in quotation marks. English Wiktionary explains ~guillemet~ as a diminutive of the given name ~Guillaume~ (“William”), after the French typecutter Guillaume Le Bé (1525 to 1598), and dates the word to 1677. This is the account on record, and the link to Le Bé is a traditional attribution rather than a certainty.
en.guillocher:
The origin of ~guillocher~ is uncertain, and the sources give three accounts. The first derives it from Italian ~ghiocciare~ (“to drip”), itself said to cross ~goccia~ (“drop”) with ~ghiotto~ (“glutton”). On this view ~ghiocciare~ is supposed to have taken the sense “to decorate with interlaced lines” from the architectural use of Latin ~gutta~, Italian ~goccia~ and French ~goutte~, all words for “drop.” This is a supposition, not an attested step.

Two rivals are on record. The Quillet encyclopedic dictionary (1934) proposed an inventor of this kind of decoration named Guilloche. Alain Rey's historical dictionary instead links the verb to ~guille~ (“stick”), a variant of ~quille~, because of the shape of the ornaments. Neither account is established, so the origin is best called debated. The craft itself is clear: ~guillocher~ means to engrave a surface with fine interlaced lines.
en.guillotiner: ~Guillotiner~ is formed from ~guillotine~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~: to execute with the guillotine. The noun comes from the name of the physician Joseph-Ignace Guillotin (1738–1814), who in 1789 put before the Constituent Assembly the proposal that every person condemned to death should have the head cut off. His surname is a diminutive of ~Guillot~. The device therefore carries its proponent's name, and the verb simply turns that name-turned-noun into an action.
en.guincher:
~Guincher~ comes from Old French ~guenchir~, a transitive verb meaning “to swerve, to turn aside,” and so “to dodge, to avoid.” According to French Wiktionary, ~guenchir~ is itself of Germanic origin, from Old Frankish *~wenkjan~ (“to waver”). German ~wanken~ (“to sway, to totter”) belongs to the same Germanic family and shows the same idea of unsteady, sideways motion.

The modern verb is a long way from its source in meaning. Where Old French spoke of swerving or evading, ~guincher~ is now a casual, slangy word for dancing, in the spirit of English “to boogie.” The sources give no intermediate steps, so the link from the sideways motion of ~guenchir~ to the dance floor is only a tempting parallel in the idea of swaying. The noun ~guinche~, a popular dance hall or dance party, belongs to the same family, and the verb is typical of familiar speech.
en.guinder:
French Wiktionary traces ~guinder~ to Old Norman ~winder~, from Old Norse ~vinda~ (“to wind, to plait; to brandish”). English Wiktionary instead offers Old High German ~windan~ or Old Norse ~vinda~, both from Proto-Germanic *~windaną~, so the two sources disagree on the exact route but agree on the Germanic root. Cognates include Dutch ~winden~, German ~winden~ and English ~wind~ in the sense “to coil.” The initial ~w~ became ~gu-~ when the word entered French, a common treatment of Germanic ~w~.

The Germanic sense of winding or coiling gained a narrower meaning in French, that of hoisting, and French Wiktionary attributes the narrowing to the word's passage into French. Modern ~guinder~ means to raise or hoist something, and by extension to set it up with effort. Its past participle ~guindé~ is the usual adjective for stiff, starchy or affected manners. The noun ~guindeau~ (“windlass”), the winch that winds up a cable, is generally given as belonging to the same family.
en.guiper: French ~guiper~ (“to wind, to twist”) comes from Old Frankish *~wīpan~ (“to wrap around, to envelop”), the language of the Franks who ruled Gaul. French Wiktionary links the Frankish verb to German ~weben~ (“to weave”), Old High German *~wīfan~ (“to twist”) and English ~wipe~, all held to be cognates. The initial ~gu-~ is a trace of the borrowing: Romance speakers rendered the Germanic w as ~gu-~ or ~g-~, which is why Frankish words in this layer start that way in French, as in ~guerre~ and ~garder~. The noun ~guipure~, a kind of lace, is built on ~guiper~.
en.guéer: ~Guéer~ is formed from the noun ~gué~ (“ford”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, and is found in Old French as ~guaër~. English Wiktionary also offers a less likely alternative: Late Latin ~vadāre~, reshaped by Germanic influence into a Vulgar Latin *~wadāre~, compare Italian ~guadare~. The noun ~gué~ most probably comes from Old Frankish *~wad~, from Proto-Germanic *~wadą~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~weh₂dʰ-~ (“to go, to wade”). Latin ~vadum~ is an Indo-European cousin and may have reinforced it; English ~wade~ is a more distant relative.
en.guérir:
First attested in the 11th century as ~guarir~, and tellingly its earliest meaning was “to protect, to safeguard,” not “to heal.” It comes from Frankish *~warjan~ (“to defend, ward off, protect”), a Germanic verb whose initial ~w~ regularly became ~gu~ in Old French (compare ~guerre~ from *~werra~, ~garder~, ~guetter~). The Germanic source is cognate with German ~wehren~ (“to fend off, defend”) and with English ~ward~ and ~warn~.

The semantic journey is the memorable part: to “protect” a sick body against its illness, to defend it, slid naturally into “to cure, to heal,” and the protective sense faded, leaving only the medical one. So a French doctor's ~guérir~ still carries, fossilized within it, the older idea of mounting a defense. The same Germanic family gave French ~garantir~ (“to guarantee, vouch for”), ~garnir~ (“to furnish, fortify”), and ~guérite~ (“sentry box, watchtower”) — a cluster all circling protection, watching, and defense, from which ~guérir~ alone slipped over into the gentler work of healing.
en.guêtrer: A denominal verb built on the noun ~guêtre~ (“gaiter,” a covering for the lower leg) with the first-conjugation ending ~-er~, which comes from Latin ~-are~. It means “to put gaiters on” someone. The French source gives only this derivation and does not trace ~guêtre~ itself any further.
en.gâcher:
French ~gâcher~ comes from Old French ~gaschier~, with variants ~guaschier~, ~waschier~ and ~gasser~, a Germanic loan whose first meaning was “to wash, to soak, to dilute with water.” French Wiktionary derives it from Frankish *~waskon~, and English Wiktionary adds an Old Dutch step before Frankish *~waskan~, from Proto-Germanic *~waskaną~ (“to wash”). English Wiktionary traces that root to the Proto-Indo-European root *~wod-~ (“wet”). The English native cousin is ~wash~, and Old English ~wasċan~ is the same word. Italian ~guazzare~ (“to splash, to wallow”) comes from the same Germanic root. The initial ~w~ became ~g~ or ~gu~ in French, as in ~guerre~ and ~garder~, both Germanic loans too.

The path from washing to wrecking is not fully documented. ~Gâcher~ kept a technical sense in building, “to mix plaster or mortar with water,” and French Wiktionary suggests, with the word probably, that the meaning “to botch” arose because plaster or mortar once mixed and left to harden cannot be reused. This is a plausible explanation rather than a settled one. Old French already had senses like “to soil, to spoil,” which English Wiktionary lists beside “to wash.” The verb gave ~gâchis~, a mess or waste, and ~gâcheur~, and in modern French one ~gâche~ a talent, an evening, or a dish.
en.gâter: From Old French ~gaster~, which meant “to lay waste, to devastate.” English Wiktionary inherits it through Middle French ~gaster~. The Old French verb is usually traced to Latin ~vastāre~ (“to lay waste”), though the sources stop at Old French. The sense softened a great deal over the centuries: a verb for ravaging a country came to mean spoiling a harvest, then spoiling food, a plan, or a child by indulgence. The circumflex of modern ~gâter~ marks the lost ~s~ of ~gaster~, a trace of the older spelling.
en.gâtifier: Formed from ~gâteux~ with the suffix ~-ifier~, meaning to become gaga, to go soft in the head. The base ~gâteux~ goes back to Old French ~gaster~ (“to spoil, to waste, to spill a liquid”), which already meant to soil oneself in the twelfth century. In 1835 it appears in hospital slang as a pejorative variant of ~gâteur~, someone who soils the sheets. The suffix ~-ifier~, from Latin ~-ficāre~ (“to make”), turns that condition into a verb of becoming.
en.gélifier: Formed from ~gel~ or, according to French Wiktionary, possibly ~gelée~, with the suffix ~-ifier~, which makes verbs meaning “to turn into.” To ~gélifier~ is to turn a liquid into a gel. ~Gel~ in the sense of frost is inherited from Latin ~gelū~, from a Proto-Indo-European root *~gel-~ (“cold”). For the chemical sense, compare English ~gel~ and French ~gélatine~. The suffix ~-ifier~ comes from Latin ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”).
en.géminer:
~Géminer~ comes from Latin ~geminare~ (“to double”), a verb formed on the adjective ~geminus~ (“twin, paired”). The French verb was taken straight from Latin rather than inherited through the spoken language, and it belongs to technical vocabulary, above all phonetics, where to geminate a consonant is to double it, as in Italian ~palla~ (“ball”) against ~pala~ (“shovel”).

The Latin root has a large family. ~Geminus~ gave the Latin name ~Gemini~ (“the Twins”), and through a diminutive form it gave the everyday Old French descendants ~jumeau~ and ~jumelle~ (“twin”), as well as ~jumeler~ (“to pair, to twin”). Learned borrowings from the same root include ~gémeaux~, ~gémination~ and ~géminé~. English kept ~geminate~ from the same Latin verb, and ~Gemini~ unchanged. So ~géminer~ and ~jumeler~ are two routes from one Latin word, one learned and one popular.
en.gémir: From Old French ~gemir~, borrowed from Latin ~gemere~ (“to groan, to moan”). It has a twin in French: ~geindre~, the properly native form of the same Latin verb. Such pairs are called doublets: one word was inherited and reshaped by centuries of sound change, the other was taken from Latin in a more learned manner and kept closer to its model. Italian ~gemere~ and Spanish ~gemir~ are cognate descendants of the same Latin verb. The infinitive can also serve as a noun, and the same Latin root lives on in ~gémissement~, a “groan,” formed in French from the verb.
en.généraliser:
French ~généraliser~ is formed from the adjective ~général~ and the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make, to render”). The adjective ~général~ comes from Latin ~generalis~ (“of or belonging to a kind or class”), built from ~genus~, genitive ~generis~ (“kind, race, stock”), plus the suffix ~-alis~. ~Genus~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ǵenh₁-~ (“to give birth, to beget”). That immensely fertile root also yields Greek ~génos~, English ~kin~ and ~kind~, and Latin ~gignere~ (“to beget”) — so to ~généraliser~ is, at root, to speak of a whole begotten family at once.

The semantic move is from “belonging to a genus” to “extend to a whole class”: to generalize is to take what is true of one and apply it to the kind. The verb is attested in the modern abstract sense from the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the age of method and classification. The same root *~ǵenh₁-~ saturates French vocabulary: ~genre~, ~général~, ~génération~, ~gène~, ~génie~, ~ingénieux~, and ~gent~ all bear its mark, a sprawling lineage from a single Indo-European word for birth.
en.générer:
From Latin ~generare~ (“to beget, to produce, to generate”), a derivative of ~genus~ (“birth, origin, kind, race”), which descends from Proto-Italic *~genos~ and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ǵenh₁-~ (“to beget, to produce”). The same root gave Ancient Greek ~génos~ (“race, stock”), Sanskrit ~jánas~, and — through Germanic — English ~kin~ and ~kind~. Romance kept the verb alive as Italian ~generare~, Spanish ~generar~, and Portuguese ~generar~.

French borrowed ~générer~ learnedly from Latin rather than inheriting it through ordinary sound change, which is why it keeps its Latin shape so transparently. Its meaning has stayed close to the source — to bring into being, to produce — though modern usage leans heavily on technical and scientific senses: a machine, a reaction, or a computer program may ~générer~ output. The Proto-Indo-European root *~ǵenh₁-~ is astonishingly fertile in French, lying behind ~genre~, ~général~, ~généreux~, ~génération~, ~génie~, ~gendre~, and even ~gens~ — a whole family clustered around the ideas of birth, kind, and lineage that the original root named.
en.gérer:
From Latin ~gerere~ (~gestum~) (“to carry, to bear, to produce, to conduct, to manage, to perform”), whose perfect and supine stem in ~gest-~ arose because an older ~s~ became ~r~ between vowels by the regular Latin sound change called rhotacism. According to de Vaan, ~gerere~ goes back through a post-PIE *~h₂ǵ-es-~ to the same Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive, to lead”) that gave Latin ~agere~ (“to drive, to do”), the ancestor of French ~agir~. The verb was a learned borrowing, taken straight from Latin rather than inherited through the slow erosion of everyday speech.

In Latin, ~gerere~ ranged from the concrete “to carry on one's person” to the figurative “to carry out, to administer,” as in ~bellum gerere~ (“to wage war”) and ~rem gerere~ (“to manage an affair”). French kept the administrative sense: to ~gérer~ is to handle, to run, to take charge of. The ~s/r~ split left a rich double family in modern French: from the ~ger-~ side come ~gérer~, ~gérant~, ~ingérer~, ~digérer~, and ~suggérer~; from the ~gest-~ side come ~gestion~, ~geste~, and ~gesticuler~. So a manager who oversees ~la gestion~ of a company and an actor who studies his ~gestes~ on stage are, etymologically, both simply carrying something.
en.gésir:
From Old French ~gesir~ (also ~jesir~), “to lie, to be lying down,” from Latin ~iacēre~ (“to lie, to be stretched out”), from Proto-Italic *~jakēō~, from PIE *~yeh₁-~. This verb of resting belongs beside its causative twin ~iacere~ (short ~e~), “to throw” — what is thrown comes to lie. Cognate with Italian ~giacere~ and Spanish ~yacer~, both still living verbs of lying, and, through the Latin family, with the ~ject~ words English borrowed (~project~, ~reject~) from the throwing branch.

In Old French ~gesir~ was fully conjugated and ordinary, but it withered into one of French's most defective verbs, surviving chiefly in the present, the imperfect, and the participle ~gisant~ — which also became the noun for the recumbent stone effigy carved atop a tomb. Above all it fossilized in the funerary formula ~ci-gît~ (“here lies”), and its plural ~ci-gisent~, still cut into gravestones. The everyday roles of lying and resting passed to other verbs, leaving ~gésir~ a word of the deathbed and the tomb. The same Latin root seeded a wide French vocabulary of lying and location: ~adjacent~ (from ~ad-~ + ~iacēre~, “to lie next to”), the geological ~gisement~ (an ore deposit, where minerals “lie”), the ~gîte~ (a resting-place or lodging), and the learned ~jacent~.
en.gêner:
Denominal verb from the noun ~gêne~, formed with ~-er~. The noun appeared in the 12th century as ~gehine~, from Old French ~gehir~ (“to confess, to avow”), itself from Frankish *~jehhjan~ (“to say, to confess”), with the suffix ~-ine~ (as in ~haine~, ~saisine~). Through Middle French the form ~gehenne~ arose by attraction to ~géhenne~ (“hell, torment”) — a word that travelled from Hebrew ~Gē-Hinnōm~ (the Valley of Hinnom near Jerusalem) through Ancient Greek ~géenna~ into Ecclesiastical Latin ~gehenna~.

The noun first named the torture used to wring out a confession, then weakened to “severe constraint,” then to the everyday “discomfort, embarrassment, awkwardness” of today. The verb ~gêner~ followed the same descent from torment to mere inconvenience: to be ~gêné~ once meant to be racked, now only to feel ill at ease. Mind the homophone: ~gène~ (“gene”) shares the pronunciation but not the history, having entered French much later from scientific English. From the same family come the adjective ~gêné~ and, by the hellish detour, ~géhenne~ itself.
en.gîter: Formed from the noun ~gîte~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Old French ~giste~, the past participle of ~gesir~ (modern ~gésir~, “to lie, to be located”). A ~gîte~ is thus literally a place where one lies, and ~gîter~ is to take up such a lodging or shelter.
en.habiliter:
French ~habiliter~ entered the language in the fourteenth century as Middle French ~(h)abiliter~, borrowed from Latin ~habilitāre~ (“to make fit, to enable”). The Latin verb rests on the adjective ~habilis~ (“easy to handle, suitable, apt”), which comes from ~habēre~ (“to hold, to have”): what is easy to hold is easy to use. Latin ~habēre~ is also the source of the Romance verbs for “to have,” such as French ~avoir~, Italian ~avere~ and Spanish ~haber~. English ~able~ and ~ability~ belong to the same family and reached English through Old French. French speakers can still see ~habile~ plus a verbal ending inside the word, but the verb was not coined in French.

The meaning moved from “to make capable” to “to give someone the legal capacity to act.” Today ~habiliter~ is chiefly a legal and administrative verb: an authority is empowered, in French ~habilité~, to sign, to inspect or to act for others. French universities even grant an ~habilitation à diriger des recherches~, the qualification that lets a researcher supervise doctoral students. Its relatives show the same root at work: ~habile~ (“skilful”), ~habileté~, ~inhabile~ and ~réhabiliter~, which restores someone's standing, literally making them fit again. The pair ~habile~ and ~habiliter~ separates a personal quality from a conferred status: one is skilled by nature, the other is made fit by a decision.
en.habiller:
French ~habiller~ has one of the most surprising etymologies in the language: it began in carpentry, not in the wardrobe. It comes from Old French ~abillier~, “to prepare a log of wood,” built on ~bille~ (“log, billet of wood”) via ~biller~. The ~h~ and the modern sense arrived later: by the 13th century Middle French ~abiller~ had generalized to “to make ready, to prepare,” and in the 15th century the spelling ~habiller~ and the meaning “to clothe” took hold under the influence of the unrelated noun ~habit~ (“garment”).

So the “dress” sense is a kind of accident: a verb for dressing timber was pulled toward dressing people because it sounded like the word for clothes. The base ~bille~ survives in French in the woodworking and billiard senses, and the false magnet ~habit~ descends instead from Latin ~habitus~, from ~habēre~ (“to have, to hold”). From ~habiller~ French built ~déshabiller~ (“to undress”), ~rhabiller~ (“to dress again, to mend”), and ~habillement~ (“clothing”). The same logic of “preparing” still flickers in technical phrases like ~habiller~ a text or a window display.
en.habiter:
From Latin ~habitāre~ (“to dwell, inhabit, occupy”), the frequentative of ~habēre~ (“to have, hold”): to ~habitāre~ is, etymologically, “to keep having,” to hold a place continually. ~Habēre~ descends from the PIE root *~gʰeh₁bʰ-~ (“to grab, take hold of”). A common but false intuition pairs Latin ~habēre~ with English ~have~; the two merely resemble each other, for English ~have~ in fact descends from a different root, the one behind Latin ~capere~ (“to seize”). The true Romance heirs of ~habēre~ are French ~avoir~, Italian ~avere~, and Spanish ~haber~; ~habitāre~ itself gave Italian ~abitare~ and Spanish ~habitar~.

The frequentative force — having again and again — is precisely what turns “to hold” into “to dwell”: a home is a place one has and has, steadily, over time. French kept the residing sense, ~habiter une ville~ (“to live in a city”), and extended it to occupation more broadly, even figuratively, as a feeling may ~habiter~ someone. From ~habitāre~ flow ~habitant~, ~habitation~, ~habitat~, and ~cohabiter~; from the parent ~habēre~ come ~habit~ (clothing, once “what one habitually wears”), ~habitude~, and ~avoir~ — the holding, the having, and the dwelling all branches of one grasping root.
en.habituer:
From Old French ~abituer~ (« to clothe, to dress »), from Medieval Latin ~habituare~ (« to accustom »), itself based on Latin ~habitus~ (« condition, bearing, dress, habit »), a noun from ~habēre~ (« to have, to hold »). The deeper origin of ~habēre~ is debated: it is often traced to a Proto-Indo-European root *~gʰeh₁bʰ-~ (« to grab, to take »), but the connection is uncertain, and the once-popular link with English ~give~ is now doubted.

The path of meaning is striking. ~habitus~ named one's outward « bearing » or « dress » — the source, too, of a monk's ~habit~ — and so Old French ~abituer~ first meant « to clothe ». Because a settled way of being shades easily into a settled way of acting, the word slid from outward garb to ingrained custom, giving the modern sense « to get used to ». The same Latin family populates French richly: ~habit~, ~habitude~, ~habituel~, and, through ~habitare~ (« to dwell »), ~habiter~ and ~habitant~.
en.hacher: French ~hacher~ is usually explained as a verb formed from ~hache~ (“axe”) plus the ending ~-er~, as in Old French ~hachier~ (“to chop up”). ~Hache~ itself is a Germanic loan, from Frankish *~happjā~, the same source as Old High German ~happia~ (“hatchet”). English Wiktionary gives a different route: a verb inherited from Old and Middle French, from Frankish *~hakkōn~ and Proto-Germanic *~hakkōną~ (“to chop”), which also gave English ~hack~. Either way the root is Germanic, and the meaning has stayed the same: to cut into small pieces.
en.hachurer: From the noun ~hachure~, formed on ~hacher~ (“to chop”), a verb of the ~hache~ (“axe”) family. English Wiktionary traces this family through Medieval Latin ~hapia~ to a Germanic source, so the family is ultimately a Germanic loan. French Wiktionary gives only the short line “from ~hachure~.” The verb ~hachurer~ means to cover a drawing, map or engraving with ~hachures~, the fine parallel lines that shade a surface or mark relief. The family is large in French: ~hache~, ~hachette~, ~hacher~, ~hachis~ (“minced meat”) and ~hachoir~ (“chopper”) all belong to it. English borrowed the idea too, since ~hatch~ in the sense of drawing shading lines comes from the same French source.
en.halener:
~Halener~ goes back to Old French ~alener~, from Early Medieval Latin ~alēnāre~, which is a metathesis of classical Latin ~anhēlāre~ (“to breathe out, to pant”). The sounds of the Latin word were shuffled on the way, so that the ~n~ and the ~l~ swapped places. Compare Catalan and Occitan ~alenar~.

The initial ~h~ of the modern spelling was never in the Old French verb. It was added later by analogy with Latin ~halāre~ (“to exhale an odor, to breathe”), a spelling reform that tied the word to a verb of similar meaning. That same Latin ~halāre~ also gave French ~exhaler~. ~Haleine~ (“breath”) is generally counted in the same family.
en.haler:
From Old French ~haler~ (“to pull, haul”), borrowed from Frankish *~halōn~ (“to haul, drag, fetch”), a form shared with Old Dutch. Frankish goes back to Proto-Germanic *~halōną~ (“to call, fetch, summon”), which English Wiktionary treats as a conflation of two Proto-Indo-European roots, *~kelə-~ (“to lift”) and *~kelh₁-~ (“to shout, call”). German ~holen~ (“to fetch”), Old High German ~halōn~ and Old English ~ġeholian~ (“to get, obtain”) are cognates, and English ~haul~ belongs to the same family.

The sources do not tell a single story for this verb. French Wiktionary records, in a second note, a separate line concerning a cry: Germanic *~hara~ (“here, this way”) gave Old French ~hare~, then ~haro~ in the twelfth century (a shout raised against a wrongdoing), ~harer~ in the fourteenth (“to urge on with shouts”) and, in the fifteenth, ~haler~ with that same sense. The sources do not say whether the two strands merged, so they are best kept apart. The main line, from Frankish, gives the sense of pulling, hauling and towing, and it left French ~halage~ (“towing”).
en.haleter: ~Haleter~ is formed from ~haler~ with the suffix ~-et-~, which often marks an action repeated or done in short bursts, as in ~cliqueter~. The base ~haler~ comes from Old French ~haler~ (“to pull, haul”), borrowed from Frankish *~halōn~ (“to haul, drag, fetch”); English ~haul~ and German ~holen~ are cognates. French Wiktionary also records a separate line for ~haler~ through a Germanic cry, *~hara~ (“here, this way”), and the sources do not say whether the two strands merged.
en.halluciner: According to French Wiktionary, ~halluciner~ is derived from ~halluciné~ (“hallucinated”) with the verbal ending ~-er~. It was first recorded in Victor Hugo, in the transitive sense, and spread in youth slang in the 1980s as an intransitive verb. English Wiktionary instead calls it a borrowing from Latin ~hālūcinārī~. ~Halluciné~ itself is a learned borrowing from Latin ~hallucinatus~, past participle of ~hallucinari~ (“to dream standing up, to ramble”), a verb that French Wiktionary links to Greek ~ἀλύειν~ (~alúein~, “to wander, to be beside oneself”).
en.halogéner: Formed from the noun ~halogène~ with the verb ending ~-er~, meaning to treat with a halogen. The noun was taken from Swedish ~halogen~, built from Greek ~hals~ (“salt”) and ~génos~ (“origin, birth”), so a halogen is literally a “salt-maker.” Table salt, sodium chloride, is a compound of an alkali metal with a halogen, chlorine, which explains the name.
en.hameçonner: ~Hameçonner~ is formed from the noun ~hameçon~ (“fish hook”) with the verb ending ~-er~. ~Hameçon~ comes from Old French ~hameçon~ or ~ameçon~, a derivative of Old French ~haim~ or ~aim~ (“hook”), which goes back to Latin ~hāmus~ (“hook”). Today the verb is used in the senses “to phish” and “to scam”.
en.hancher: ~Hancher~ (“to put one's weight on one hip”) is formed from the noun ~hanche~ (“hip”) with the verb ending ~-er~. It echoes an Old French verb ~hanchier~, which meant “to trip someone up”. The modern verb is used for a person who stands with the weight shifted onto one leg, so that one hip juts out.
en.handicaper:
Derived from the noun ~handicap~, borrowed from English, with the sporting sense attested in French in 1854 and the figurative “to put at a disadvantage” by 1889. The English word, attested from the 1650s, contracts the phrase ~hand in cap~ (also written ~hand i’ the cap~). It named a bartering and wagering game: two parties and a neutral umpire each put forfeit money into a cap, and the players plunged in their hands and withdrew them either full or empty to signal whether they accepted the umpire’s valuation of an uneven exchange. This “hand-in-cap” origin is given as the established account.

By the eighteenth century the umpire’s task of equalizing an unfair match had passed to horse racing, where a superior horse was made to carry extra weight — the ~handicap~. From the racetrack the word spread to any imposed disadvantage, and only around 1890 did it acquire the sense of an encumbrance or disability. French ~handicaper~ thus reaches all the way back to coins drawn blind from a hat. The family in French includes ~handicap~, ~handicapé~ and ~handicapeur~.
en.hannetonner: Formed from the noun ~hanneton~ with the verb ending ~-er~, meaning to exterminate cockchafers. The noun comes from Old French ~haneton~, from Frankish *~hanō~ (“rooster”), with diminutive endings, so the insect is literally a “little rooster.” Frankish *~hanō~ is related to Dutch ~haan~ and German ~Hahn~, both meaning “rooster.” English ~cockchafer~ has a similar first element, probably an allusion to the insect's clumsy flight.
en.hanter:
From Middle French ~hanter~, from Old French ~hanter~ (“to frequent, to dwell in a place”). The deeper source is Germanic, and the two Wiktionaries phrase it differently. French Wiktionary derives it from Old Norse ~heimta~ (“to lead home”), from ~heim~ (“home”). English Wiktionary allows Old English ~hāmettan~ (“to bring home, to house”), Old Norse ~heimta~, or both, all from Proto-Germanic *~haimatjaną~ (“to bring home”). Either way the root is the one behind English ~home~ and German ~Heim~, both cognates. The verb is well attested in Normandy and spread from there across the rest of the northern langue d'oïl area.

The original sense was to frequent a place, to visit it often. The ghostly sense is recent: it appears in the nineteenth century, in step with the fashion for English things and the first fantasy novels, probably through a crossing with English ~haunt~, which itself came from Old French ~hanter~. The word may thus have made a round trip through English and come back with spectres. The Norman dialect, however, already had ~hanter~ for “visited by ghosts” and ~hant~ for “ghost, revenant”, so the influence may not have been purely English. Compare also Walloon ~hanter~ (“to court, to go out with”).
en.happer: From Old French ~happer~ (“to seize, snap up”), whose origin is obscure. It may be onomatopoeic, imitating a sudden snap. Alternatively it is Germanic, either from Proto-West Germanic *~happā~ (“hook, clasp”) or related to Middle Dutch ~happen~ (“to snap, bite”), which survives as modern Dutch ~happen~, and to German ~Happen~ (“morsel, snack”). The sources do not settle the matter, so each of these routes is only a proposal. What is certain is the Old French verb itself, which French inherited and which still means to seize something suddenly.
en.haranguer: Borrowed from Italian ~arringare~, “to address a crowd, to speak solemnly before an assembly.” In French the verb carries a silent but aspirated ~h~, so there is no liaison or elision before it: ~je harangue~ keeps the words apart. It has kept the sense of the Italian: ~haranguer~ is to address a crowd or a troop in a loud, stirring speech, and in a weaker, often ironic use, to lecture someone at length or to rile them up.
en.harasser: The origin of ~harasser~ is explained in two ways. French Wiktionary treats it as a denominal verb on Old French ~harace~ or ~harache~, found mainly in expressions such as ~courre a la harache~ (“to pursue”) and ~prendre aucun par la harache~ (“to seize someone by force”), a word used only in Brittany and Normandy. English Wiktionary instead derives it from ~harer~ (“to set a dog on”), of Germanic origin, from Frankish *~hara~ (“here, hither”), from Proto-Germanic *~hē₂r~ (“here, hither”). The sources thus disagree on the immediate base. On the second account the root is the same as in English ~here~. The verb also passed into English as ~harass~, and in modern French it means “to exhaust, to wear out.”
en.harceler:
~Harceler~ comes from Middle French ~harceller~ (attested in 1478), a popular variant of ~herseler~. That form was built on ~herser~ (“to harrow”) with the diminutive ending ~-eler~, and ~herser~ in turn comes from ~herse~, the toothed frame dragged over ploughed soil to break up clods. The noun ~herse~ is generally traced to Latin ~hirpex~ (“harrow”). The verb is thus a distant relative of the farmer's harrow, however far the modern sense has traveled from the field.

How the word moved from fields to people is not spelled out in the sources. Today ~harceler~ means to harass, to hound, to hassle, to pester persistently. Modern French uses it in the expressions ~harcèlement moral~ and ~harcèlement sexuel~, which have given the word a legal edge. The related noun ~herse~ survives in French in its own senses, and ~herser~ still means “to harrow a field,” so the agricultural root is still visible beside the figurative verb.
en.harder: French Wiktionary lists two separate verbs spelled ~harder~. The first is formed on ~harde~ (a herd or pack, especially of hunting animals) with the ending ~-er~, and means “to couple or harness together”; compare ~enharder~. The noun ~harde~ comes from Middle French, Old French ~herde~ and Frankish *~herda~, cognate with English ~herd~ and German ~Herde~, and is not to be confused with ~horde~, which is Mongolian in origin. The second ~harder~ is formed on ~hardes~ (“clothes”), and means “to clothe.”
en.haricoter: The origin of ~haricoter~ is uncertain, and French Wiktionary gives two accounts. According to the scholar Génin, the verb is the old verb ~harigoter~, which meant “to cut up, to tear to pieces.” By another account, the word comes from the habit of playing a game while keeping score with beans. Neither explanation is settled, and the sources do not choose between them. The modern sense is to take small risks in gambling or business, to haggle over small gains.
en.harmoniser: Formed from ~harmonie~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which builds verbs meaning “to make or render” something. ~Harmonie~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~harmonia~, itself taken from Ancient Greek ~ἁρμονία~ (~harmonía~, “union, agreement”); it was written ~armonie~ in Old French. The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, a form that transcribed Greek verbs, and it remains productive today. So ~harmoniser~ is, literally, “to make harmonious”: to bring things into agreement.
en.harnacher: From ~harnais~ (“harness”), the gear of a horse. An older verb ~harnescier~ (“to put the harness on a horse”) is attested in the thirteenth century, so the verb is old in French rather than a recent coinage. In Quebec French, a specific and criticized use of ~harnacher~ is imitated from the English verb ~harness~.
en.harpailler: A compound of ~harper~ (“to grab, to seize”) and the suffix ~-ailler~, which gives a verb a petty, repeated, slightly pejorative action. The verb means to squabble or quarrel, with the sense of people grabbing at one another over trifles.
en.harper: The origin of ~harper~ is uncertain, and the sources disagree. French Wiktionary first calls it a verb formed from ~harpe~ (“harp”), then adds that it is probably from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ghrebh-~ (“to seize”), which it links to Latin ~harpagō~ (“grappling hook”) and English ~grab~. English Wiktionary instead gives Old High German ~harfan~ (“to seize”). The two accounts are in tension, since the noun ~harpe~ may itself be taken from the verb. The verb is used of a horse that lifts a hind leg high, and, in a dated sense, of grasping something forcefully.
en.harponner: From ~harpon~ (“harpoon”) + the suffix ~-er~: to ~harponner~ is to strike or catch with a harpoon. French Wiktionary derives the noun from ~harper~ with the suffix ~-on~, while English Wiktionary traces Old French ~harpon~ to Latin ~harpaga~, a rare variant of ~harpagō~, from Ancient Greek ~ἁρπάγη~ (“hook”), from ~ἁρπάζω~ (“to snatch, to seize”). The two accounts differ on the route, but both point to a word for gripping and seizing.
en.hasarder: Formed in French from ~hasard~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so “to expose to chance, to risk.” The noun ~hasard~ comes from Old French ~hasart~, from Spanish ~azar~, from Andalusi Arabic ~az-zahr~ (“the die, the game of dice”). The Arabic word is tied to ~zahr~ (“flower”), after the flower that marked the winning face of the die. The initial ~h-~ was originally purely graphic, and the final ~-d~ is an addition. English Wiktionary compares Italian ~azzardare~, a parallel verb. ~Hasarder~ means to venture or risk, as in ~hasarder une remarque~.
en.haubaner: Formed from ~hauban~ and the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense “to secure with a stay,” a wire or rope. The noun ~hauban~ was borrowed from Old Norse ~höfuðbenda~ (“shroud-rope, stay”), a compound of ~höfuð~ (“head”) and ~benda~ (“bond”). French Wiktionary compares German ~Haupt~ and ~Band~, relatives of these two elements.
en.hausser:
From Old French ~haucier~, from Vulgar Latin *~altiāre~ (“to raise”), a verb derived from Latin ~altus~ (“high”). French Wiktionary calls *~altiāre~ a collateral form of the Latin verb ~altāre~ (“to raise up”), itself built on the comparative ~altior~ (“higher”). Cognates elsewhere in Romance include Spanish ~alzar~, Italian ~alzare~, Catalan ~alçar~, Occitan ~auçar~ and Romanian ~înălța~. Latin ~altus~ is generally traced to ~alere~ (“to nourish”), so “high” began as “grown.”

The aspirated initial ~h~ of ~hausser~, which blocks liaison, is the same one found in ~haut~ and is usually attributed to Frankish influence on the Latin word. The meaning stayed close to the root: to make something higher, whether literally or figuratively. French speaks of ~hausser les épaules~ (“to shrug”), ~hausser le ton~ (“to raise one's voice”) and ~hausser les prix~ (“to raise prices”). The noun ~hausse~ (“rise”) is derived from the verb, and the prefixed verbs ~rehausser~ (“to heighten, to enhance”) and ~exhausser~ (“to raise up, to grant”) belong to the same family, as does ~haut~ itself.
en.haver: The verb ~haver~ is a mining term meaning to undercut a seam. It matches Old French ~hauwer~ (“to hoe”) and probably comes from Old High German ~hauen~ (“to hew, to cut down”), related to Old Low Frankish *~hauwa~ (“hoe”). German ~Hauer~ (“miner”) comes from the same verb and in turn gave Czech ~havíř~ (“miner”). The origin is given only as probable, so the link to Germanic is likely rather than proven. English ~hew~ is a cousin of German ~hauen~, as is the French ~houe~ (“hoe”) through Frankish.
en.havir: French Wiktionary derives ~havir~ (“to singe, scorch”) from ~hâve~ with the ending ~-ir~, but English Wiktionary treats the origin as open. It traces the verb to Old French ~havir~ (“to desire ardently”), which came either from Old French ~have~ (“pale, dull”) or from Frankish *~haiju~ (“heat, burning”), akin to Old High German ~heiēn~ (“to scorch”). The adjective ~hâve~ itself comes from Frankish *~haswa-~, “hare-grey,” and is related to German ~Hase~ (“hare”). The link to heat and scorching is the more natural fit for the modern sense, but the sources do not settle it.
en.haïr:
From Old French ~haïr~ (also ~hadir~, ~haier~), from Frankish/Old Low Franconian *~hatjan~, from Proto-Germanic *~hatjaną~ (“to hate”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~kad-~ (“sorrow, hatred”). It is a direct cognate of English ~hate~, German ~hassen~, and Dutch ~haten~ — a rare Germanic intruder among the overwhelmingly Latinate verbs of French, carried in by the Franks who gave their name to France itself.

The meaning has held remarkably steady — to detest — but the conjugation of ~haïr~ is one of the strangest in the language, which is precisely what makes it memorable. The diaeresis (tréma) on the ~ï~ is kept throughout, forcing the disyllabic /a.i/ of ~nous haïssons~ and ~je haïssais~ — except in the three singular persons of the présent and the singular imperative, where it vanishes: ~je hais~, ~tu hais~, ~il hait~, imperative ~hais~, all pronounced as one syllable /ɛ/. The ~h~ is aspirate, so it blocks elision and liaison: one writes ~je hais~, never j'hais, and says ~le haïr~ with an audible gap. In the passé simple and imperfect subjonctif the tréma even usurps the circumflex other verbs take, yielding ~nous haïmes~, ~vous haïtes~, ~qu'il haït~ rather than -îmes/-îtes/-ît. Finally, a living regional variation: in Canadian French the singular keeps the tréma and stays disyllabic — ~je haïs~, ~tu haïs~, ~il haït~ /a.i/ — diverging from the standard monosyllabic ~je hais~. From the same Germanic root spring ~haine~, ~haineux~, and ~haïssable~.
en.helléniser:
From Ancient Greek ~Ἑλληνίζω~ (~Hellēnízō~, “to speak Greek, to behave like a Hellene”). The Greek verb is built on ~Hellēn~ (“Hellene, Greek”) with the verbal ending ~-ízō~, the ending that Late Latin transcribed as ~-izāre~ and that French turned into ~-iser~. The French verb is therefore a learned borrowing that wears the shape of a native ~-iser~ verb, and English ~Hellenize~ was formed in the same way.

In French, ~helléniser~ means to give something a Greek character, whether a language, a name, a people or a culture, and it can also be used reflexively. It is the verbal member of a learned family: ~Hellène~ (“Greek”), ~hellénique~, ~hellénisme~ and ~hellénistique~, the last used for the period that followed Alexander the Great. The Greek ending ~-ízō~ was extremely productive and gave a long line of verbs, so that ~helléniser~ sits beside ~latiniser~, ~gréciser~ and many others. A word about speaking Greek thus became, in French, a word for spreading Greek ways.
en.hennir:
From Latin ~hinnīre~ (“to neigh”). The verb names the characteristic cry of the horse. French ~hennir~ is the inherited descendant, with the vowel of the first syllable opening from ~i~ to ~e~ before the double nasal. It belongs to the second conjugation, so it takes the ending ~-iss-~ in the plural and the imperfect, as in ~ils hennissent~.

The French noun ~hennissement~ (“neigh”) is formed on the verb in the usual way. The verb is chiefly used of horses, but it extends to people: someone who ~hennit~ is laughing in a loud, shrill, braying manner, or crying out harshly. The word is a small survivor of a Latin verb of animal sound that French kept almost unchanged in meaning.
en.herbager: ~Herbager~ is a denominal verb, formed from the noun ~herbage~ with the ending ~-er~. It means to put livestock out to graze on grass, or to graze. The noun ~herbage~ was inherited from Old French ~erbage~ and goes back to Early Medieval Latin ~herbāticum~, from Latin ~herba~ (“grass”). On the surface it is simply ~herbe~ plus the suffix ~-age~, “grass” plus a collective ending.
en.herboriser: French Wiktionary derives ~herboriser~ from ~harboriste~ with the suffix ~-iser~, which coins verbs from nouns and adjectives. The suffix was borrowed into Old French from Late Latin ~-izāre~, itself a transcription of Greek verbs. Here it turns the noun for a dealer in medicinal plants into a verb for the work itself: to go out and gather herbs for medicinal use, or, in the gloss's wording, to herborize.
en.hercher:
~Hercher~ is a Walloon word that French took up. The TLFi derives it from a Low Latin verb *~hirpicāre~ (“to harrow”), a form it reconstructs and supports with Italian forms of the type ~erpicare~ and with Occitan and Franco-Provençal dialect forms. That verb in turn comes from Latin ~hirpex~ (“harrow”), the source of French ~herse~. The earliest record is the Walloon ~heirchier~, around 1385, in the sense “to drag.”

In French the verb is first recorded as ~hiercher~ in 1769, in a technical use in the mines, then as ~herscher~ in 1873 and ~hercher~ in 1875. It names a miner's task: to push the mine cars and wagons by hand, and the Académie gives it as intransitive. The Liège Walloon forms ~hièrtchî~ and ~hèrtchî~ show the dialect source of the word. The chain from ~hirpex~ ties the verb to the family of ~herse~, the farm harrow, even though the work it now describes has nothing to do with fields.
en.herscher:
A verb of the fourteenth century, borrowed from Old Liège ~hercher~ (“to drag”), which was itself descended from Latin ~hirpex~ (“harrow”). The Latin word named the toothed farm implement that is dragged across a field. The French verb is intransitive, and it entered the language from the dialect of Liège rather than by the inherited route.

The Latin ~hirpex~ also underlies French ~herse~ (“harrow”), which is inherited, so ~herscher~ and ~herse~ are distant relatives that reached French by different roads. Italian ~erpice~ (“harrow”) descends from the same Latin source. Today ~herscher~ is a rare verb, used in the sense “to push a cart,” and a good example of a regional word borrowed into the common language.
en.herser: A verb made from the noun ~herse~ (“harrow”) and the ending ~-er~, so ~herser~ is “to work the soil with a harrow.” The noun ~herse~ comes from Old French ~herce~, from Latin ~hirpex~ (accusative ~hirpicem~), a word for a harrow. The initial ~h~ is said to be onomatopoeic, though it may also owe something to the unrelated Germanic words for the tool, Old Norse ~herfi~ and English ~harrow~. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and turns a noun into a verb meaning “to work with N.”
en.heurter:
French ~heurter~ goes back to Old French ~hurter~ (“to collide, to butt”), attested by 1119, but its deeper source is disputed. The account favored by the TLFi derives it from Frankish *~hūrt~ (“ram”), making the verb literally “to butt like a ram”; comparison is drawn with Old Norse ~hrútr~ (“ram”) and Welsh ~hwrdd~ (“ram”). A rival hypothesis posits a Vulgar Latin *~ūritāre~, “to charge like an aurochs,” from Latin ~ūrus~ (“aurochs”) — either way, a large horned beast lurks behind the word. The verb has Germanic kin in Dutch ~horten~ and Middle High German ~hurten~ (“to crash into”), and one famous offshoot in English: ~hurt~ is generally held to be borrowed from Old Northern French ~hurter~, sliding from “knock against” to “injure.”

The form ~hurter~ held the field into the sixteenth century, when the vowel opened before the r and modern ~heurter~ triumphed. The figurative reach came early: by about 1180 the verb could mean “to oppose, to offend,” and modern French still lets sensibilities, colors and interests collide — ~se heurter à~ is “to run up against.” The family is compact and concrete: a ~heurt~ is a clash or a bump, and a ~heurtoir~ is a door knocker — etymologically, if the favored origin is right, a little ram with which every visitor butts the house. English ~hurt~, meanwhile, carries this Old French collision through everyday speech: to be hurt is, historically, to have been struck.
en.hiberner:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~hībernāre~ (“to spend the winter”). The Latin verb is built on ~hībernus~ (“of winter, wintry”), a derivative of ~hiems~ (“winter”). It is the learned twin of ~hiverner~: the two are doublets, one taken directly from the written Latin, the other having come down through the spoken language. Spanish ~invernar~ is a cousin of the same Latin verb, and English ~hibernate~ was borrowed from it too.

French therefore has two verbs for the same Latin source, and they went their separate ways. ~Hiverner~ is the older, popular form, with its everyday sound, and it kept the general sense of passing the winter somewhere. ~Hiberner~ kept the Latin spelling and became the technical term of biology, for animals that pass the cold season in a state of torpor. The same Latin family gave French ~hiver~ (“winter”), the adjective ~hibernal~ (“of winter”) and the noun ~hibernation~.
en.hier: Borrowed from Middle Dutch ~heien~, which had the same meaning as the French verb: to drive something in or pound it down with a heavy tool. The French verb came directly from the Low Countries and has no Latin ancestry. Its modern use is technical, for work of this pounding kind.
en.hisser: Borrowed from Middle Low German ~hissen~ (French Wiktionary says “German”), and it is of imitative origin according to French Wiktionary. Dutch ~hijsen~, Italian ~issare~ and English ~hoist~ are related. It appears in Rabelais's ~Quart Livre~ as the hauling cry ~inse !~ (“heave!”), with the spelling ~ysser~ recorded in 1573. The reflexive ~se hisser~ (“to haul oneself up”) is recorded in the eighteenth century.
en.historier: ~Historier~ is a denominal verb built on ~histoire~, which French Wiktionary traces to Latin ~historia~. The verb thus belongs to the large French family of words descended from ~historia~. The sources consulted for this verb stop at that derivation and give no date or sense history, so nothing more is claimed here.
en.hiverner:
Inherited from Latin ~hībernāre~ (“to spend the winter”). The Latin verb belongs to the adjective ~hībernus~ (“of winter, wintry”), itself tied to the noun ~hiems~ (“winter”). French has a learned doublet, ~hiberner~, built on the same Latin verb, so the language holds two forms of one word: the everyday ~hiverner~ and the more technical ~hiberner~. English took the learned form in ~hibernate~ and the adjective in ~hibernal~.

The two French verbs divided the work. ~Hiverner~ keeps the broad, concrete sense of passing the winter somewhere, of people, flocks or ships sheltering through the cold season, and of birds or animals that spend the winter in a given region. ~Hiberner~, the learned doublet, is the biologists' verb for the deep winter dormancy of marmots or bears, and gave ~hibernation~. The same Latin root underlies the French noun ~hiver~ (“winter”), which comes from Latin ~hībernum~ (“winter season”) and shows how much the inherited word has worn down compared with its learned relatives.
en.hiérarchiser: Formed in French from ~hiérarchie~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-iser~, the verb means “to arrange in a hierarchy, to rank by importance.” The noun ~hiérarchie~ was borrowed from Latin ~hierarchia~, which came from Greek ~ἱεράρχης~ (~hierarkhēs~, “hierarch,” the holder of a sacred office). That Greek word joins ~ἱερός~ (“sacred”) and ~ἄρχειν~ (“to rule”), so a hierarchy was first a sacred order of rule, such as the ranks of the Church. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and in French it means “to make, to treat as.” To ~hiérarchiser~ is therefore to give things a rank, as one does with priorities.
en.hocher:
From Middle French ~hochier~, from Old French ~hochier~ (“to shake, jostle, swing, twitch”), from Frankish *~hotsōn~ or *~hottisōn~, itself from *~hottōn~ (“to shake, toss”). English Wiktionary traces this to Proto-Germanic *~hud-~ (“to swing, rock, shake”) and proposes a Proto-Indo-European root, either *~(s)ket-~ or *~kwēt-~, so that deeper step is uncertain. Cognates include Dutch ~hutsen~ (“to shake”), Old English ~hūdenian~ (“to rock, shake”) and English ~hustle~.

French Wiktionary gives the same Frankish source and relates it to Flemish ~hotsen~ and Walloon ~hossî~ (“to swing”). It also lists a second account, under which ~hocher~ is derived from the noun ~hoche~, so the origin is not settled in one line. The best-known use today is ~hocher la tête~ (“to nod, or shake one's head”), and the rattle ~hochet~ is a related word.
en.hogner: The origin of this verb, meaning “to growl, to grumble”, is uncertain. French Wiktionary suggests, with a maybe, that it comes from ~honnir~ (“to disgrace, to scorn”), under the phonetic and semantic influence of ~grogner~ (“to grumble”). It also lists Norman forms with the sense “to cry, to complain”, among them ~honer~, ~houiner~, ~higner~ and ~ouiner~, along with the phrase ~hanter entre ses dents~. No firmer ancestry is established.
en.hollandiser: Formed from the place name ~Hollande~, a region of the Netherlands, with the suffix ~-iser~. This suffix goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~ and means “to make A,” so the verb means to give something or someone Dutch character or manners. The name ~Hollande~ is often used loosely for the whole country.
en.holographier: Formed from the noun ~holographe~ with the verb ending ~-ier~, meaning to write a document, especially a will, entirely in one's own hand. ~Holographe~ is learned vocabulary, built on Greek ~holos~ (“whole”) and ~graphein~ (“to write”): a holograph is written wholly by the hand of the person who signs it.
en.homogénéifier: Formed from the adjective ~homogène~ with the suffix ~-ifier~, meaning to make homogeneous. The adjective comes through Latin ~homogeneus~ from Greek ~homogenēs~ (“of the same kind”), built on ~homo-~ (“same”) and ~genos~ (“birth, race, kind”). The suffix ~-ifier~ comes from Latin ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”), so the verb is literally “to make of the same kind.”
en.homogénéiser: ~Homogénéiser~ is ~homogène~ plus the suffix ~-iser~, with a small respelling of the stem. ~Homogène~ comes from Ancient Greek ~homogenḗs~ (“of the same race or kind”), through Latin ~homogeneus~. The Greek word is made of ~homo-~ (“same”) and ~génos~ (“birth, race, kind”). The verb means to make uniform.
en.homologuer:
Borrowed from Latin ~homologāre~ (“to agree, to approve”), which in turn goes back to Greek ~homologeîn~ (“to say the same thing, to agree”), built from ~homós~ (“same”) and a verb of speaking related to ~lógos~ (“word”). The original idea is therefore that of two parties saying the same thing and so being in agreement. The Greek-derived relatives ~homologie~ (“correspondence between parts”) and ~homologue~ (“corresponding, equivalent”) are cited by French Wiktionary as part of the same family.

In French, ~homologuer~ is a legal and administrative verb. A court ~homologue~ an agreement when it confirms it and gives it official force, and the modern uses extend that picture: an authority ~homologue~ a record in sport, a product that has passed a standard, or a decision. The participle ~homologué~ (“officially approved, type-approved”) is common on labels and in sports reports. English has the related ~homologous~ and ~homology~, as well as the rare legal verb ~homologate~.
en.hongrer: A denominal verb formed from ~hongre~, the word for a gelded horse. To ~hongrer~ a horse is to castrate it, turning it into a ~hongre~. The ending ~-er~ is the usual way French builds a verb on a noun, here with the sense “to make into, to turn into.”
en.hongroyer: Formed from the adjective ~hongrois~ with the verb ending ~-er~, meaning to tan leather with alum. The method was originally associated with Hungary, hence the name. The adjective ~hongrois~ is built on ~Hongrie~ with the adjective suffix ~-ois~, so the verb says, in effect, “to treat in the Hungarian way.”
en.honnir:
The verb comes from Middle French ~honnir~ and Old French ~honir~, which go back to Vulgar Latin *~haunīre~ (“to shame, to dishonor”). That Romance verb is the adaptation of a Frankish word, *~haunjan~ (“to humble, to humiliate”), romanized in northern Gaul. The Frankish word descends from Proto-Germanic *~haunijaną~ (“to make low, to humble”), which English Wiktionary traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~kaw-~ (“to be evil, to make evil”). The Germanic family is wide: German ~höhnen~, Dutch ~honen~, Old English ~hīenan~ (“to humble, to abase”) and Gothic ~haunjan~ (“to humiliate, to abase”) are cognates.

Frankish gave French other words too: English Wiktionary derives ~honte~ (“shame”) from the same source, so ~honnir~ and ~honte~ are cousins. The Latin-style ending ~-īre~ explains why ~honnir~ is a second-group verb, like ~finir~. The verb survives in the motto ~Honni soit qui mal y pense~ (“Shame on whoever thinks evil of it”).
en.honorer:
French ~honorer~ comes from Latin ~honorare~ (“to honor, to do honor to”), a denominal verb from ~honor~, older ~honos~ (“honor, esteem, public office”). The deeper origin of ~honos~ is unknown: scholars note that a Proto-Indo-European shape like *~ǵʰon-~ would be expected, but there are no clear cognates in other languages, so the root remains obscure — a striking blank for so central a Roman word. Cognate developments survive in Italian ~onorare~ and Spanish ~honrar~, and English ~honor~ / ~honour~ is borrowed from the same Latin family through Old French.

For the Romans, ~honos~ named not only esteem but public office and the dignity it conferred — the ~cursus honorum~ was the “course of honors,” the ladder of magistracies a senator climbed. French ~honorer~ kept the active sense of paying respect, and extended into commerce: to ~honorer~ a debt or a signature is to make good on it, to do it the honor of payment. From the same noun French has ~honneur~, ~honorable~, ~honoraire~ (“honorary,” and as a noun a professional's fee), and ~déshonorer~ — a whole vocabulary of esteem grown from a Latin word whose own ancestry has been lost.
en.hoqueter:
English Wiktionary gives ~hoqueter~ as inherited from Middle French ~hoqueter~, with a variant *~icqueter~, probably of Germanic origin and ultimately imitative of the sound itself. It compares Old Norse ~hixta~ (“to hiccup”), Middle High German ~heschezen~ and ~heschitzen~ (“to gulp, burp, sob”), Middle Dutch ~hicken~ (“to hiccup”) and the obsolete English ~hicket~ and ~hyckock~. The Germanic link is thus a likelihood, not a certainty.

Because the word imitates a bodily noise, its sound does the work that a root usually does, and the English ~hiccup~ is another imitative formation of the same kind. The French noun ~hoquet~ (“hiccup”) is the natural companion of the verb. Modern ~hoqueter~ means to hiccup, and also to make short, jerky, hiccup-like sounds.
en.hormoner: Formed from ~hormone~ and the ending ~-er~: to treat with hormones. The noun was proposed in English by W. M. Bayliss and E. H. Starling and built on Ancient Greek ~hormḗ~ (“impulse”), related to the participle of ~hormáō~ (“to set in motion”). A hormone is, etymologically, what sets something in motion.
en.horrifier:
~Horrifier~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~horrificāre~ (“to cause horror, to make bristle with fear”). The Latin verb is built from ~horror~ (“bristling, shuddering, dread”) and the causative element ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”). The same Latin root ~horrēre~ (“to bristle, to shudder”) gave French ~horreur~ and ~horrible~, and English ~horror~ and ~horrify~ come from the same Latin family.

The formation matters because ~-fier~ is the French descendant of ~-ficāre~: ~horrifier~ belongs with ~terrifier~, ~pacifier~, ~vérifier~ and ~clarifier~, verbs meaning “to make X.” In ~horrifier~ the meaning has not drifted from Latin, since to horrify is still to fill someone with horror. The related adjective ~horrifique~ belongs to the same family as ~horreur~ and ~horrible~.
en.horripiler: ~Horripiler~ is borrowed from Late Latin ~horripilāre~ (“to have one's hair bristle”), a compound of Latin ~horrēre~ (“to bristle, to shudder”) and ~pilus~ (“hair”). Its literal sense, to make the hair stand on end, belongs to the same learned register as the noun ~horripilation~, the medical word for goosebumps. The main modern sense of the verb is to exasperate or infuriate, as in Ça m'horripile. Both halves of the Latin compound have French descendants. ~Horrēre~ stands behind ~horreur~, ~horrible~ and ~horrifier~, while ~pilus~ gave ~poil~ by the popular path and learned words such as ~pilosité~. The verb is thus a close relative of ~horreur~.
en.hospitaliser: Formed in the 19th century from ~hôpital~ with the suffix ~-iser~ (“to provide with, to treat with”), the stem being reshaped on the Latin form that survives in ~hospitalier~. The noun ~hôpital~ comes from Old French ~hospital~, borrowed from Late Latin ~hospitāle~ (“guesthouse, hospital”), from Latin ~hospitālis~ (“hospitable”). The word began as a place of welcome for guests, the poor and the sick, and is a doublet of ~hôtel~. To ~hospitaliser~ someone is to admit them to a hospital.
en.hotter: Formed from the noun ~hotte~ (“carrying basket”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, and attested by the lexicographer Randle Cotgrave: “to carry in a basket on one's back.” The sources disagree about the noun. French Wiktionary derives it from a Swiss dialect word ~hutte~, from dialectal German ~Hotze~ (“basket”), while English Wiktionary borrows it from Frankish *~hotta~ (“basket”), comparing regional German ~Hotte~. Both lines point to a Germanic word for a basket.
en.houblonner: Formed from ~houblon~ (“hops”) with the verb suffix ~-er~, which here means “to provide with”: to add hops to, as brewers do to beer. French Wiktionary treats it simply as a noun turned into a first-conjugation verb by adding ~-er~. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~, the infinitive of the first conjugation, and it remains the default way to coin new French verbs.
en.houler: ~Houler~ is formed from the noun ~houle~ (“swell”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, so it describes the sea swelling and rolling. French Wiktionary dates ~houle~ to 1484 and derives it from Norman ~houle~ (“hollow, cavity in the rocks by the sea”), from Old Norse ~hol~ (“cavity”). English Wiktionary adds that the sense of swell probably comes from the bulges and hollows of the waves. The Old Norse word is a cousin of English ~hole~ and ~hollow~.
en.houpper: Derived from the noun ~houppe~ (“tuft”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so it means to arrange something in tufts. ~Houppe~ is a variant of ~houpe~ (1350), traced to Old Frankish *~huppo~, a form restored from Flemish ~hoppe~ (“tuft of grass or plants”) and Rhenish ~hupp~ (“heap of straw, laundry, and so on”). The same Germanic word is behind ~huppe~, the name of the hoopoe, whose crest is a tuft.
en.hourder: Formed from the noun ~hourd~ with the verb ending ~-er~. ~Hourd~ comes from Old French ~hourt~ (also ~hurt~), which French Wiktionary traces to Old Frankish *~hurd~ (“hurdle, wattle”). English ~hurdle~ is a Germanic cousin of the Frankish word. The verb, a building term, means to fill with rubble.
en.hourdir: French Wiktionary derives ~hourdir~ from the noun ~hourdis~, a term for rubble or rough masonry filling, and the verb means “to fill with rubble.” The noun ~hourdis~ is itself a derivative of the verb ~hourder~ with the suffix ~-is~, so the verb and noun are closely tied. The ending ~-ir~ is the second-conjugation ending, here used to coin a verb. The sources give no older origin for ~hourder~, so the trail stops at French.
en.houspiller:
The origin is debated. French Wiktionary traces ~houspiller~ to Old French ~houcepignier~ (“to vent anger, to mistreat”), glossed as ~pigner~ with a ~houssoir~. English Wiktionary instead gives Middle French ~houssepillier~ (“to mistreat by shaking or growling”) and Norman ~gouspiller~ (“to shake, thrash, ill-treat”), both from a root *~housp-~ or *~gousp-~ (“to scorn, scold”). That root is either from or akin to Old English ~hosp~ (“reproach, insult”), as Diez held, or from Proto-West Germanic *~husp~, from Proto-Indo-European *~kūd-~ (“to mock”).

The Germanic account has support in the relatives it cites: Old English ~husc~ (“mockery, scorn”), Old High German ~hosc~ (“invective, mockery”) and the Norwegian dialect verb ~huta~ (“to shout at, treat contemptuously”). Whichever origin is right, the French verb has kept a family of senses around rough verbal and physical treatment: ~houspiller~ is to scold, rebuke or harass someone, and in older use to torment them.
en.housser: From ~housse~ (“a protective cover”) + the suffix ~-er~: to ~housser~ is to cover with a ~housse~, and the second gloss, to dust, is also given for this verb. English Wiktionary traces the verb through Middle French and Old French ~houcier~. The noun ~housse~ comes from Frankish *~hulfti~ (“cover, blanket, saddle-cloth”), via Vulgar Latin, and is cognate with Old High German ~hulft~. French Wiktionary also lists a separate verb from ~houx~ (“holly”), which fell out of use early in the nineteenth century.
en.hucher:
From Old French ~huchier~ (“to cry out”). French Wiktionary gives two accounts of its origin. The first sees an onomatopoeia ~hu~, the same cry found in ~hue~, ~huer~, ~hululer~ and ~hurler~, and in Czech ~hučet~ and ~houkat~, which share the same ~k~ extension. The second derives it from Old Low Frankish *~hûkôn~ (“to crouch”), cognate with German ~hocken~ and Dutch ~huiken~. The sources thus leave the origin open between an imitative cry and a Germanic borrowing.

The verb means to call out or shout. On the imitative account, ~hucher~ belongs to a family of French verbs that imitate loud cries: ~huer~ (“to boo, to hoot”), ~hurler~ (“to howl”) and ~hululer~ (“to hoot, as an owl does”) all rest on the same ~hu~ sound. On the Frankish account the verb would instead be a Germanic borrowing, tied to a crouching posture; the sources do not explain how that sense gave the meaning “to cry out.”
en.huer:
Old French ~huer~ meant “to shout to frighten an animal” or “to urge dogs on in a hunt,” and passed into Middle French as ~huer~ (“to hoot”). Its origin is uncertain, and the two Wiktionaries differ. French Wiktionary derives it from the imitative cry ~hue~, a sound made rather than a word inherited. English Wiktionary proposes, as probable, a borrowing from a reconstructed Old Norse *~huta~ (“to shout, to make a noise”), and compares Norwegian ~huta~ (“to shout, to shout commands at a dog”). Neither account is established, so the origin is best left open.

The first uses belonged to the hunt, shouting at hounds and game, and the verb then widened to shouting at anyone in disapproval, which is why ~huer~ means “to boo” today. The related noun ~huée~ names the booing or hooting of a crowd, and one still boos a speaker or a referee. The cry ~hue~ also survives in the phrase tirer à hue et à dia (“to pull in opposite directions”), from the calls of carters to their horses.
en.huiler: ~Huiler~ (“to oil”) is formed from the noun ~huile~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Middle French ~huyle~, from Old French ~oile~, from Latin ~oleum~ (“olive oil”), itself from ~olea~ (“olive”), a borrowing of Greek ~elaía~. The initial ~h~ is not etymological: Middle French scribes added it to show that the ~u~ was a vowel, since ~u~ and ~v~ were written alike and ~uile~ could be misread as ~vile~. The same habit explains the ~h~ of ~huit~. The suffix ~-er~ goes back to Latin ~-are~ and here means “to coat with, to apply” the noun.
en.hululer:
~Hululer~ (“to hoot, to cry like an owl”) is a learned borrowing from Latin ~ululāre~ (“to howl”), with an expressive initial ~h~ added in French. Old French had the verb ~uller~ from the same source, without the ~h~. The Latin verb is thought of as imitating the sound it names, which would explain its repeated ~u~ syllables.

The interest of ~hululer~ is that it has a twin. French ~hurler~ (“to howl”) is its inherited doublet: it came down from the same Latin source by the ordinary route of sound change and also picked up the expressive ~h~. The learned ~hululer~ was taken later from the Latin form and specialized in the cry of the owl, as in ~hululement~. English borrowed the Latin verb too, as ~ululate~.
en.humaniser: ~Humaniser~ is formed from the Latin stem ~humanus~ (“human, humane”), the source of French ~humain~, with the verb ending ~-iser~ (“to make A”). It means to make more human or humane, or to civilize. Latin ~humanus~ is itself built on ~homō~ (“human being”). The same Latin word underlies ~humanité~ and ~humanisme~, and English ~human~.
en.humecter: ~Humecter~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~hūmectāre~ (“to moisten”), a verb built on the adjective ~hūmectus~ (“moist”), itself from the verb ~hūmēre~ (“to be wet”). It entered French whole, which is why its ~-ect-~ cluster is intact; an inherited form would have worn it down. Italian and Spanish kept the same root in ~umido~ and ~húmedo~. The Latin family is wider than this verb. Related to ~hūmēre~ are ~hūmor~ (“fluid, moisture”), which gave French ~humeur~, and ~hūmidus~, which gave ~humide~ and, with ~-ifier~, the verb ~humidifier~. English ~humid~, ~humor~ and ~humectant~ come from the same Latin family.
en.humer: ~Humer~ (“to sniff, to breathe in a smell”) is of onomatopoeic origin. French Wiktionary derives it from the sound ~hum~, an imitation of air being drawn in through the nose or mouth, and English Wiktionary agrees on the imitative origin. Words of this kind are made from the noise of the action itself rather than inherited from an older language, so there is no Latin ancestor to trace. The verb is used for savouring a smell, a drink or the air, and it has kept that sensory sense.
en.humidifier: Formed from ~humide~ (“humid”) and the suffix ~-ifier~ (“make A”): to ~humidifier~ is to make moist. The adjective is borrowed from Latin ~hūmidus~, a variant of ~ūmidus~. The suffix comes from Latin ~-ificāre~, which goes back to ~facere~ (“to make”), so the verb is, at the root, “to make damp”.
en.humilier:
From Latin ~humiliāre~, a verb meaning “to make humble.” The Latin verb is built on the adjective ~humilis~ (“low, humble”), itself from ~humus~ (“ground”), so to be humble is, literally, to be close to the ground. The same Latin adjective gave French ~humble~ and ~humilité~, and English ~humble~ and ~humility~ come from it too.

French borrowed the verb as a learned word, and its meaning has darkened. French Wiktionary notes that ~humilier~ now carries negative connotations. Where the Latin verb simply described lowering someone, French ~humilier~ means to wound a person's dignity, to make them feel shame. A related reflexive use, ~s'humilier~, keeps a more neutral note of self-abasement, as before a superior.
