en.humoter: The TLFi files ~humoter~ under ~humer~ and marks it as a hapax, a word recorded only once. Its single attestation is in Verlaine's ~Mes prisons~ (1893), where a man sucks on a cheap cigar while ~humoter~-ing a mug of beer. The sense is “to take in a liquid in small sips.” The base ~humer~ is attested before 1105 in Judeo-French with the sense “to drink by sucking in,” and the TLFi derives it from the imitative syllable ~hum-~, which suggests drawing in air.
en.hurler:
The verb ~hurler~ is inherited from Old French ~hurler~, from Vulgar (Late) Latin ~ūrulāre~. That form is a dissimilation of classical Latin ~ululāre~ (“to howl”): the two ~l~ sounds of the original were too alike, so the first one turned into an ~r~. Latin ~ululāre~ is itself an imitative word, built from a reduplicated Proto-Indo-European imitative root, which is to say that it was made to sound like the cry it names. The initial ~h~ is not Latin. French Wiktionary calls it an expressive aspirated ~h~, while English Wiktionary suggests it might owe something to Frankish *~hūilōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~hūwilōną~, the relative of English ~howl~.

The verb is used of people shouting in pain, anger or fear, and it extends to anything loud and jarring: one can ~hurler de rire~ (“to roar with laughter”), and colors or styles are said to ~hurler~ when they clash. The idiom ~hurler avec les loups~ (“to howl with the wolves”) means to follow the crowd. French also kept the learned Latin forms as doublets: ~ululer~ and ~hululer~. Related words include ~hurlement~ (“a howl”) and ~hurleur~, as in ~singe hurleur~ (“howler monkey”). Because the ~h~ is aspirated, there is no liaison before ~hurler~, and the origin of that ~h~ is exactly what the two sources disagree about.
en.hutter: Formed from the noun ~hutte~ and the verb ending ~-er~: to build a hut for shelter. The noun is Germanic. English Wiktionary traces it through Old French ~hute~ and Old High German ~hutta~ to Proto-Germanic *~hudjǭ~ (“hut, shelter”), related to Old English ~hȳdan~ (“to hide”), while French Wiktionary instead points to Gothic ~hēþjō~ (“chamber”). Its relatives include German ~Hütte~, Danish ~hytte~ and Swedish ~hydda~.
en.hybrider: Formed on the noun and adjective ~hybride~ with the verb ending ~-er~: to cross different varieties or species, to produce a hybrid. ~Hybride~ comes from Latin ~hibrida~ (“bastard, of mixed blood”), which was respelled ~hybrida~ through a false association with Greek ~ὕβρις~ (~húbris~, “excess”). The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is the usual way French makes first-group verbs from nouns and adjectives.
en.hydrater: Formed from the noun ~hydrate~ with the verb suffix ~-er~, so “to combine with water, to supply water to”. The noun is a scholarly coinage built from the Greek root of ~hýdōr~ (“water”), as ~hydr-~, plus the chemical suffix ~-ate~. French Wiktionary calls it a learned derivative of the Greek word. The verb thus rests on the same Greek ~hýdōr~ that sits behind a long list of scientific words.
en.hydrofuger: Formed from the adjective ~hydrofuge~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The adjective combines the prefix ~hydro-~ (“water”, from Greek) and the suffix ~-fuge~ (from Latin ~fugere~, “to flee”), so it describes what drives water away. The verb means to treat a surface or material to make it repel water.
en.hydrogéner: Formed from ~hydrogène~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to combine with hydrogen.” The noun was coined by the French chemist Antoine Lavoisier, whose 1783 proposal built it from ~hydro-~, from Greek ~ὕδωρ~ (“water”), and ~-gène~, from Greek ~gennan~ (“to generate”). Once water was shown to be made of hydrogen and oxygen, the name took its etymological sense of “water-former.” The verb simply turns that element into an action, applying hydrogen to a substance.
en.hydrolyser: ~Hydrolyser~ is formed from the noun ~hydrolyse~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, and means “to subject to hydrolysis.” The noun is a learned compound of the combining forms ~hydro-~ and ~-lyse~, which come from Greek ~ὕδωρ~ (“water”) and ~λύσις~ (“dissolution”): a breaking down by water. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is the usual way French makes a verb from a noun.
en.hypertrophier: Formed from the noun ~hypertrophie~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, so the verb means to cause or undergo hypertrophy, an excessive growth. The noun is built from two Greek elements: ~hyper-~, from Ancient Greek ~ὑπέρ~ (“above, beyond”), and ~-trophie~, from Ancient Greek ~τροφή~ (“nutrition”). Put together, it literally means “over-nourishment”, a growth beyond the normal.
en.hypnotiser: Formed from the adjective ~hypnotique~ by swapping its ending for the suffix ~-iser~, as French Wiktionary describes it, giving a verb meaning “to put under hypnosis”. ~Hypnotique~ comes from Late Latin ~hypnōticus~ (“narcotic”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~ὑπνωτικός~ (~hypnōtikós~, “soporific”), a derivative of ~ὕπνος~ (~hýpnos~, “sleep”). The verb thus ends up meaning, literally, “to make sleepy”, and figuratively “to fascinate completely”.
en.hypostasier: Formed from ~hypostase~ and the verb ending ~-er~, meaning “to hypostatize.” The noun was borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin ~hypostasis~, itself from Ancient Greek ~ὑπόστασις~. French Wiktionary refers back to ~hypo-~ and ~stase~, the Greek elements meaning roughly “under” and “standing.”
en.hypothéquer: Formed in French as a denominal verb from ~hypothèque~ (“mortgage”) with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun was borrowed from Latin ~hypothēca~ (“pledge given as surety for a loan”), itself from Ancient Greek ~hupothḗkē~ (“pledge, deposit”). To ~hypothéquer~ a property is therefore to put it up as security for a debt. The Greek word is built from ~hypo-~ (“under”) and a root meaning “to put”, so a pledge is, etymologically, something placed under.
en.hâbler: ~Hâbler~ was borrowed in the sixteenth century from Spanish ~hablar~ (“to speak”). It is a doublet of ~fabuler~: both go back to Latin ~fabulārī~ (“to talk, to chat”), one through Spanish and the other directly. In French the borrowed verb took a pejorative turn, “to speak boastfully, to exaggerate,” which French Wiktionary attributes to the idea sixteenth-century Frenchmen had of Spaniards. The related noun ~hâblerie~ keeps the sense of bragging.
en.hâler:
The origin of ~hâler~ is not settled. French Wiktionary gives two accounts. The first derives it from a Latin form *~assulāre~, a diminutive of ~assāre~ (“to roast”), by way of Old French ~haslé~. The second, offered with a “perhaps”, points to Old Frankish *~hallôn~ (“to dry out”) and calls that the word's etymological sense. The circumflex of the modern spelling stands for a lost s, as the old form ~haslé~ shows.

Both accounts point to the same idea, that of drying or roasting under heat, which is the picture behind the modern verb: sun and wind that darken the skin give it a tan. The verb gave the adjective ~hâlé~ (“tanned, weathered”) and the noun ~hâle~ (“tan”). The Latin source ~assāre~ is a verb built on ~assus~ (“roasted”), so on the first account ~hâler~ belongs to the Latin vocabulary of cooking.
en.hâter: Formed on the noun ~hâte~ (“haste, urgency”) and the ending ~-er~, and recorded in Old French as ~haster~. The noun comes from Old French ~haste~, from Frankish *~haist~ (“violence, vehemence”), compare Old High German ~heisti~ (“violent”), and was taken into Gallo-Romance very early. The sense thus moved from violence to urgency. The circumflex stands for the lost s of the Old French spelling. English ~haste~ was borrowed from the same French word, and German ~Hast~ likewise.
en.héberger:
From Old French ~herbergier~ (“to lodge, to shelter, to make camp”), from Frankish *~heriberga~ (“lodging, shelter”), a compound of *~heri~ (“army, host”) and *~berga~ (“shelter, protection”) — the underlying sense being a shelter for an army, a military billet. Both elements are Germanic, set down through Proto-West Germanic *~harjabergu~. The very same compound, taken into English through Old French, gave ~harbinger~ (originally one who went ahead to arrange lodgings) and is kin to ~harbor~; German keeps it as ~Herberge~ (“hostel”).

The martial origin faded as the word came to mean simply “to put someone up,” then “to house” anything — today a server hosts (~héberge~) a website. The most striking relative is ~auberge~ (“inn”): it descends from the very same Frankish *~heriberga~, taking a different phonetic path through Provençal, so ~héberger~ and ~auberge~ are doublets — two French words from one Germanic source. The agent noun ~hébergeur~ now names a web-hosting provider, and ~hébergement~ covers both lodging and digital hosting.
en.hébraïser:
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ~Ἑβραΐζω~ (~Hebraḯzō~), a verb meaning to speak Hebrew or to act in a Hebrew manner. English Wiktionary adds that, by surface analysis, French speakers can also read it as ~hébreu~ or ~hébraïque~ plus the suffix ~-iser~. The Greek verb was built on the Greek name of the Hebrews with the ending ~-ίζω~, the pattern from which Late Latin ~-izāre~ and French ~-iser~ descend.

The French verb has two senses, “to Hebraize,” meaning to give something a Hebrew character, and “to study Hebrew.” It is a learned word, used in the history of religion and scholarship. The family is the one built on ~hébreu~: ~hébraïque~ (“Hebrew,” as an adjective) and ~hébraïsant~, the name of a scholar of Hebrew, which is the present participle of this very verb. English ~Hebraize~ is a close parallel, and the same Greek verb ending lies behind a long series of French verbs in ~-iser~.
en.hébéter:
French ~hébéter~ is borrowed from Latin ~hebetāre~ (“to blunt, to weaken”). The Latin verb is built, by the standard analysis, on the adjective ~hebes~ (“blunt, dull”), so it literally describes taking the edge off something. The French verb kept the same sense in the figurative field: to dull the mind, to leave someone dazed and stupefied, with the faculties numbed.

The verb is the basis of the past participle ~hébété~ (“dazed, stupefied”), which is far more common today than the infinitive, and it belongs with the noun ~hébétude~. The idea sits close to French ~émousser~ (“to blunt”), which gives the literal sense where ~hébéter~ gives the mental one. The two are independent words, but the pair shows how a worn edge became a common way to speak of a dulled mind. Both the physical and the mental use rest on the same notion of lost sharpness.
en.héler:
~Héler~ is a nautical word of Norse origin, as French Wiktionary notes of many sea terms. English Wiktionary gives the chain: Middle French ~heiler~ (“to hail”), from Middle English ~heilen~ (“to greet, to call to”), from ~hail~ or ~heil~ (“health”), from Old Norse ~heill~ (“health”). That comes from Proto-Germanic *~hailą~ (“health”), from *~hailaz~ (“whole, hale, safe”), from Proto-Indo-European *~kéh₂ilos~ (“safe, unharmed”). Old English ~hǣl~ is a cognate.

The same root gave English ~whole~ and ~hale~, which are cognates in the Germanic family. French Wiktionary compares ~héler~ to Germanic ~haln~, from which ~hallo~ comes and from which ~allô~ derives, but this link is only a comparison. Today ~héler~ means to call out to someone at a distance, such as a taxi or a boat.
en.hélitreuiller: Formed from the prefix ~héli-~ and ~treuiller~, so “to winch up by helicopter.” The element ~héli-~ was extracted from ~hélicoptère~ by metanalysis, and that word goes back to Greek ~ἕλιξ~ (“spiral”) via Latin ~helix~. ~Treuiller~ is ~treuil~ (“winch”) + ~-er~. ~Treuil~ comes from Old French, from Vulgar Latin *~troculum~, a reshaped form of Latin ~torculum~ (“press”), so a pressing machine gave its name to a lifting device. No other French verb uses ~héli-~.
en.hérisser:
~Hérisser~ appears in Old French as ~hericer~. It goes back to Vulgar Latin *~ericiare~, a verb built on Latin ~erīcius~ (“hedgehog”), so the original idea is to make something bristle like a hedgehog. The Latin noun is also the source of Spanish ~erizo~ (“hedgehog”) and of the French noun ~hérisson~, which belongs to the same family as the verb.

The initial ~h~ is the puzzle, since the Latin word has none. French Wiktionary lists several explanations and settles on none: the ~h~ may be expressive in origin, it may come from the influence of Latin ~hirsutus~ (“hairy, bristly”), or it may reflect the ~h~ of an archaic Latin form ~herīcius~. The verb is used of hair, fur and feathers standing on end, and figuratively of someone bristling with irritation. The Latin ~hirsutus~ also gave French ~hirsute~.
en.hérissonner: ~Hérissonner~ is formed from ~hérisson~ (“hedgehog”) with the verb ending ~-er~, and it means to bristle, to stand on end like a hedgehog's spines. The noun comes from Old French ~heriçon~, a derivative of an unattested ~eriz~ with the suffix ~-on~, and that stem goes back to Latin ~ēricius~, “hedgehog.” The initial ~h~ in French is probably expressive. An alternative Vulgar Latin source, ~ēriciōnem~, has been proposed but would have given ~erçon~ instead.
en.hériter:
From Late Latin ~hērēditāre~ (“to inherit”), a verb formed on ~hērēditās~ (“inheritance”) and ~hērēs~ (“heir”). ~hērēs~ is traced to Proto-Indo-European *~ǵʰeh₁ro-~ (“bereft, derelict”), from the root *~ǵʰeh₁-~ (“to leave behind, abandon”) — an heir being, by this account, the one to whom what is “left behind” passes. Cognate, through that root, with Ancient Greek ~χήρα~ (“widow”), literally a woman left behind.

The semantic core is loss turned to gain: what one party leaves vacant, another receives. French ~hériter~ runs from the strictly legal — to ~hériter~ an estate — to the figurative, ~hériter~ a temperament, a name, a problem. From the same ~hērēs~ / ~hērēditās~ stem French built a tight family: ~héritier~ (“heir”), ~héritage~ (“inheritance”), ~hérédité~ (“heredity”), ~déshériter~ (“to disinherit”), and ~cohéritier~. Behind the cheerful idea of inheriting lies the older, bleaker image of an estate left empty by a death.
en.hésiter:
From Latin ~haesitare~ (“to be stuck, to stammer, to waver, to hesitate”), the frequentative or intensive of ~haerere~ (“to stick, to cling, to remain fixed”). ~Haerere~ is of uncertain origin; scholars have proposed a Proto-Indo-European *~gʰays-~ (“to stick, to be fixed”), though the connection is debated. Through its prefixed compounds the verb is well attested in French and English: ~adhaerere~ gave ~adhérer~ and English ~adhere~, while ~cohaerere~ gave ~cohérent~ and ~cohere~.

The physical sense came first: ~haerere~ meant to stick fast, to be caught and unable to move on. ~Haesitare~ intensified this into repeated sticking — and the metaphor for the tongue and the mind was immediate, since one who ~hésite~ is, in effect, stuck, unable to move forward, caught between choices. Latin already used it both of a stammering speaker and of a wavering mind, and French ~hésiter~ inherited the figurative core directly. The shared root gives French ~adhérer~, ~adhésif~, ~adhérence~, ~cohérent~, and ~incohérent~ — all built on the same idea of clinging or sticking together.
en.hôler: ~Hôler~ comes from an onomatopoeia: the word imitates the sound it names, the hooting of the tawny owl. Because it is built from a sound and not inherited from an older word, it has no Latin or Germanic ancestor to trace. It is a specialized verb, used for the cry of this owl.
en.identifier:
Coined in the eighteenth century from the noun ~identité~ plus the verb-forming suffix ~-ifier~ (“to make, to render”). ~Identité~ comes from Late Latin ~identitas~, built on ~idem~ (“the same”) with the abstract suffix ~-itas~ — itself a calque, a loan-translation, of Ancient Greek ~ταὐτότης~ (~tautótēs~, “sameness”). The suffix ~-ifier~ descends from Latin ~-ificare~, from ~facere~ (“to make, to do”), so to ~identifier~ is etymologically “to make the same.” Italian ~identificare~ and Spanish ~identificar~ are parallel formations.

The oldest sense is exactly that literal one: to ~identifier~ two things was to treat them as one and the same, to equate them, a usage that survives in ~s'identifier à un personnage~ (“to identify with a character”). From “to declare identical” grew the everyday sense “to recognize, to establish who or what something is,” as a witness might ~identifier~ a suspect. The computer age added a further twist: ~s'identifier~ now also means “to log in,” to prove to a machine that one is the same person as the holder of the account, by means of an ~identifiant~ (“username, login”). The same family includes ~identité~, ~identique~, ~identification~, and ~identifiant~ — all turning on the simple Latin notion of ~idem~, sameness.
en.idolâtrer: Formed from the adjective and noun ~idolâtre~ (“idolater”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to worship idols,” and by extension “to adore excessively.” ~Idolâtre~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~īdōlolatrēs~, with haplology, the loss of a repeated syllable, and the Latin word was itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~εἰδωλολάτρης~ (~eidōlolátrēs~). By general analysis the Greek compound joins ~eídōlon~ (“image, idol”) and ~latreía~-type worship. The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, makes a verb meaning “act as” the noun.
en.idéaliser: ~Idéaliser~ is formed from the adjective ~idéal~ with the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make A”): to make something ideal. The adjective ~idéal~ comes from Late Latin ~ideālis~ (“existing in idea”), from Ancient Greek ~ἰδέᾱ~ (~idéā~, “idea”). The same Greek word gave French ~idée~.
en.ignifuger: Formed from the adjective ~ignifuge~ with the verb ending ~-er~, to mean “to make fireproof.” ~Ignifuge~ is a learned compound of ~igni-~, from Latin ~ignis~ (“fire”), and ~-fuge~ (“that flees or puts to flight”), from Latin ~fugere~ (“to flee”), which goes back to the Indo-European root *~bʰeug-~ (“to flee”). Something ~ignifuge~ thus makes fire run away. The same ~-fuge~ appears in ~vermifuge~ and ~centrifuge~.
en.ignorer:
From Latin ~ignōrāre~ (“to not know, to be unacquainted with”), built on ~ignārus~ (“unaware, ignorant”), which is the negative prefix ~in-~ (“not”) attached to a root meaning “knowing,” related to ~gnārus~ (“acquainted with”) and the verb ~(g)nōscere~ (“to come to know”). That root goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~ǵneh₃-~ (“to know, to recognize”) — one of the great word-families of Indo-European, cognate with English ~know~ and ~can~, Greek ~gignṓskō~, and the whole Latin clan of ~nōscere~, ~nōtus~, and ~nōbilis~ (“knowable, hence noteworthy”).

The word's core sense is privative: ~ignorer~ means, first, “to be unaware of, to not know” — a quiet statement of a gap in knowledge, as in ~j'ignore son nom~ (“I don't know his name”). Curiously, English ~ignore~, borrowed from the same Latin verb, drifted toward a deliberate act — to know perfectly well and pay no heed — and modern French ~ignorer~ has, under English influence, picked up that second sense too: to snub, to disregard on purpose. From the root *~ǵneh₃-~ spring a vast French family, among them ~connaître~, ~reconnaître~, ~noble~, ~notice~, and the noun ~ignorance~ itself.
en.illimiter:
~Illimiter~ is a rare, literary verb, and a young one: it is first recorded in 1792-93, meaning “to make something last without end,” then shortly before 1801 in the sense “to free from all limits, to give boundless scope.” Its construction runs backwards: instead of an adjective born of a verb's participle, here the adjective ~illimité~ (~il-~, the shape ~in-~ takes before ~l~, + ~limité~) begat the verb. Behind it stands ~limiter~, borrowed from Latin ~limitare~ (“to bound, to enclose within limits”), from ~limes~ (genitive ~limitis~), “boundary path, frontier,” generally analysed as built on ~limus~ (“oblique, transverse”); a link with ~limen~ (“threshold”) is sometimes suggested but remains uncertain. English ~limit~, Italian ~limitare~ and Spanish ~limitar~ are kin.

Latin ~limes~ began humbly, as the unploughed strip between two fields — the track marking where mine ends and yours begins — and rose to name the fortified frontier of the whole Roman Empire, which historians still call the ~limes~. One descendant preserves the garrison: ~limitrophe~, today merely “bordering,” comes from late Latin ~limitrophus~, a Greco-Latin hybrid (~limes~ + Greek ~-trophos~, “nourishing”) coined for lands set aside to feed the frontier troops. Against this family of fences, ~illimiter~ is the gesture that tears them up — and its birthdate speaks: a verb meaning “to remove every limit,” coined in 1792-93, in the thick of the French Revolution. It never displaced its parent: French reaches daily for ~illimité~ — ~forfait illimité~ — while the verb survives in the margins, beside ~limite~, ~délimiter~ and ~limitation~.
en.illuminer:
Borrowed from Latin ~illūmināre~ (“to illuminate, to light up, to brighten”), a verb built on the prefix ~in-~ (“in, upon”) and ~lūmen~ (“light”). Latin ~lūmen~ belongs with ~lux~ to the Proto-Indo-European root *~lewk-~ (“to shine”), which also gave English ~light~. Italian ~illuminare~ and Spanish ~iluminar~ descend from the same Latin verb, and so does English ~illuminate~. French has two relatives built on the same ~lūmen~, ~allumer~ and ~enluminer~, and they are worth comparing with it. ~Illuminer~ is a learned borrowing that keeps its Latin outline almost untouched, whereas ~allumer~ (“to light, to switch on”) has a less Latin-looking shape. The same ~lūmen~ stands behind ~lumière~, ~luminaire~, ~lumineux~ and ~allumette~, so a single Latin noun lights a whole corner of the French vocabulary.

The Latin verb was concrete, meaning to light up or brighten, and French ~illuminer~ still carries that sense of flooding a place or an object with light. It also has a figurative sense, to enlighten, as in a face lit up by sudden understanding, and the English verb ~illuminate~ shows the same double life. ~Enluminer~ took a specialized path, since it came to describe painting manuscripts with bright colors and gold, which gives ~enluminure~ (“illumination”) and matches the English phrase “illuminated manuscript”. The family therefore splits three ways: ~allumer~ keeps the everyday act of lighting, ~illuminer~ keeps the learned sense of lighting up and enlightening, and ~enluminer~ keeps the painter's craft of making a page shine. All three begin from one Latin noun for light, and each shows a different path that a word could take into French.
en.illusionner: Formed from the noun ~illusion~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, so the verb means to give someone an illusion, to delude them. The noun comes from Latin ~illusio~ (“irony, illusion, deception”), derived from ~illudere~ (“to play with, to mock”). The Latin sense of mockery is thus the older one, and the idea of a deceptive appearance grew out of it. French ~illusionner~ keeps only the deceptive side: to lead someone into taking a false appearance for the truth.
en.illustrer:
From Latin ~illustrāre~ (“to light up, illuminate,” figuratively “to make clear, explain, render distinguished”), from ~in-~ (“in, upon”) + ~lustrāre~ (“to shed light over, brighten”), kindred with ~lūx~ (“light”) and ~lūmen~, all from Proto-Indo-European *~lewk-~ (“bright, to shine”). Cognate, through that root, with Ancient Greek ~λευκός~ (“white, bright”), English ~light~ and ~lucid~, and French ~lumière~ and ~luire~.

The whole history of the verb is a metaphor of light. To ~illustrer~ was first to shine light upon something; from there it meant to make a matter clear — to ~illustrate~ an idea with an example — and also to cast luster on a name, to make it famous, which is why an ~homme illustre~ is a distinguished, “brilliant” man and ~illustre~ means renowned. The now-dominant sense, to ~illustrer~ a book with pictures, is the most recent layer, the images “lighting up” the text. The same *~lewk-~ glows through a wide French family: ~lustre~ (both the chandelier and the sheen of polish), ~lustrer~, ~élucider~ (to “light out” a difficulty), ~lucide~, ~translucide~, and ~lumineux~ — every one of them, at bottom, a word about shining.
en.imaginer:
From Latin ~imaginari~ (“to picture to oneself, to form a mental image”), a verb derived from the noun ~imago~ (genitive ~imaginis~, “image, likeness, copy, statue”). ~imago~ belongs to the same family as ~imitari~ (“to imitate, to copy”) and ~aemulus~ (“rival, emulator”), tracing back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂eym-~ (“to copy, to imitate”). Through ~imago~ and ~imaginari~ the French verb is cognate with Italian ~immaginare~, Spanish ~imaginar~, and English ~imagine~ and ~image~.

The Latin ~imago~ was first a concrete thing — a portrait, a wax ancestral mask, a statue — and ~imaginari~ meant to carry such an image in the mind. French took the verb in the 13th century already abstract: to picture, then to suppose or invent. The kinship with ~imitari~ is telling, for to imagine was, at root, to make an inner copy of the world. From the same family French keeps ~image~, ~imaginaire~, ~imagination~, ~imaginatif~, and ~imagerie~; the surprising cousin ~émule~ (“emulator, rival”) comes from ~aemulus~ at the far end of the same root, so that one who imagines and one who emulates are, etymologically, both makers of likenesses.
en.imbiber: ~Imbiber~ is borrowed from Latin ~imbibere~ (“to drink in, to absorb”), formed from ~in-~ (written ~im-~ before ~b~) and ~bibere~ (“to drink”). English Wiktionary describes it as inherited from Old French, where it was itself a borrowing from Latin. Its doublet is ~emboire~, which comes from the same Latin verb. The simple verb lives on in ordinary French ~boire~, and the family also gives ~boisson~ and ~biberon~. English ~imbibe~ comes from the same Latin source.
en.imbriquer: ~Imbriquer~ is a back-formation from the participle ~imbriqué~, which French Wiktionary derives from Latin ~imbricāre~ and which is attested from the sixteenth century. The Latin verb is formed on ~imbrex~, a curved roof tile, and meant “to shape like or cover with tiles.” The image is of tiles overlapping on a roof, one partly covering the next. French extends it to things that fit into each other: ~des éléments imbriqués~, ~s'imbriquer~, ~des boucles imbriquées~ in programming. English ~imbricate~ comes from the same Latin.
en.imiter: ~Imiter~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~imitārī~ (“to copy, to be like, to represent, to counterfeit”). The Latin verb is generally linked to ~imāgō~ (“image, likeness”), so to imitate is, at root, to make an image of something. French later formed the nouns ~imitation~ and ~imitateur~ on the same Latin stem, and English ~imitate~ comes from the same source. The French verb kept the full range of the Latin sense, from respectful copying of a model to mockery and forgery.
en.immatriculer:
A learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ~immātrīculāre~, which joins the prefix ~in-~ (“in”) to Late Latin ~mātrīcula~, “a little register.” That noun is a diminutive of ~mātrīx~, which meant first a breeding female, then the womb, and in Late Latin a public roll or list. ~Mātrīx~ itself comes from ~māter~ (“mother”). To ~immatriculer~ is therefore to enter a name on the roll. French also has the noun ~matricule~ from the same source, and English ~matriculate~ is a close relative.

The path from “mother” to “register” is a short one: the matrix is the source from which things are born, and the register is the source record from which each person or thing is identified. In French the verb entered administrative language, where it covers many kinds of listing. A car is ~immatriculée~ when it receives its registration number, a company when it joins the trade register, a soldier or a prisoner when he gets his ~matricule~. English ~matriculate~ kept the university sense, to be enrolled as a student. The family also includes ~immatriculation~, ~matricule~ and, further back, ~matrice~ and ~maternel~.
en.immerger: Borrowed as a learned word from Latin ~immergere~ (“to plunge into”), made from ~in-~ (“in”) and ~mergere~ (“to dip, to plunge”). The same Latin verb gave English ~immerse~, by way of its participle ~immersus~. French took the word whole rather than inheriting it, which is why its shape stays close to the Latin. Its relatives are ~immersion~ and ~immergé~, and its mirror images are ~émerger~ (“to come out of the water”) and ~submerger~.
en.immigrer: Borrowed from Latin ~immigrāre~, which is analyzed as ~in-~ (“in, into”) + ~migrāre~ (“to move, to migrate”). French ~immigrer~ names the arrival side of a move: coming into a country to settle there. Its counterpart ~émigrer~ looks at the same journey from the point of departure. The same Latin root gives French ~migrer~, ~migration~ and ~migrant~.
en.immiscer: Borrowed from Latin ~immisceō~ (“to mix in”), which is analyzed as ~in-~ (“in, into”) + ~miscēre~ (“to mix”). The figurative reflexive ~s'immiscer dans~ (“to interfere in”) is easy to read from that sense: the person is mixed into other people's affairs. The same Latin root underlies French ~mixte~.
en.immobiliser: Formed in French from the adjective ~immobile~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which builds verbs meaning “to make or render A”: to ~immobiliser~ is to make something immobile. The adjective ~immobile~ goes back to Latin ~immōbilis~ (“unmovable”), itself analyzable as ~im-~ (“not”) plus ~mobile~, and it is a doublet of ~immeuble~ (“building, real estate”), the same Latin word reaching French by a different route. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which had transcribed Greek verbs, and it remains fully productive in technical and administrative French.
en.immoler: Borrowed from Latin ~immolāre~, which French Wiktionary glosses as “to sprinkle the victim of a sacrifice with sacred meal.” The Latin verb is analyzed as ~im-~ (“on”) + ~mola~, a word meaning “millstone” or “meal.” The verb is therefore built on the grain-based ritual offering, not on the act of killing. Italian ~immolare~ and English ~immolate~ are close relatives, borrowed from the same Latin verb. The Latin noun ~mola~ is also the ancestor of French ~meule~ (“millstone”), and it is related to the verb ~moudre~ (“to grind”), whose Latin source is ~molere~. The reflexive ~s'immoler~ extends the idea to sacrificing oneself. Modern French uses ~immoler~ of any sacrifice or slaughter.
en.immortaliser: ~Immortaliser~ is built from the adjective ~immortel~ plus the verb-forming suffix ~-iser~, which means “to make A”, here “to make immortal.” As often with this suffix, the stem changes shape, so ~immortel~ becomes ~immortal-~ before the ending, as ~réel~ does in ~réaliser~. The adjective itself comes from Latin ~immortālis~, which English Wiktionary also analyzes on the French surface as ~im-~ (“not”) + ~mortel~. The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, a transcription of Greek verbs, and remains fully productive in French today.
en.immuniser: Formed from the adjective ~immun~ plus ~-iser~, which here has the sense “to make A,” so ~immuniser~ is to make someone immune. The adjective comes from Latin ~immunis~ (“free of a duty,” literally “dutyless”) and existed in legal French with that sense of exempt. The medical sense of ~immun~ came under the influence of English ~immune~. The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, which carried Greek verbs into Latin.
en.impacter:
~Impacter~ is built on the noun ~impact~, which French took from Latin ~impactus~, the past participle of ~impingere~ (“to strike against, to drive into, to force upon”). ~Impingere~ is ~in-~ (“into, against”) joined to ~pangere~ (“to fasten, to drive in, to fix”), from PIE *~peh₂ǵ-~ (“to attach, to fix”). The Latin verb was inherited across Romance with the plain physical sense of shoving: Italian ~impingere~, Romanian ~împinge~, Catalan ~empènyer~ and Occitan ~empénher~ all mean, roughly, “to push.” French took no such inheritance; it borrowed the learned participle as the noun ~impact~, and English did the same twice over, borrowing both ~impact~ and, straight from the infinitive, ~impinge~. The root's basic image is a stake driven home, something fixed in place by force — and Latin ~pāx~ (“peace”), the ancestor of French ~paix~, is traditionally, though not unanimously, attached to the same root family: peace as an agreement pinned down.

The verb itself is recent and fiercely contested. French had the noun for a long time and only latterly built a verb on it, under visible pressure from English ~to impact~. It entered the Petit Robert in 2006 and the Petit Larousse in 2010, and it is still missing from the TLFi altogether: look ~impacter~ up on the CNRTL and the site replies that the form cannot be found. The Académie française is blunt about why it exists at all, holding that the verbal form was created wrongly, in imitation of English, and recommending ~affecter~ or a periphrasis such as ~avoir des conséquences sur~. Defenders answer that one word beats four, and administrative and business French has adopted it wholesale. The older physical sense survives in ballistics and in medicine, where a fracture or a tooth may be ~impacté~. Related French words are few and all learned: ~impact~ and ~impacter~ themselves, beside ~compact~, from ~compingere~, another compound of ~pangere~.
en.impartir:
Borrowed from Late Latin ~impartīre~, a variant of ~impertiō~ (“to share out, to bestow”), which was formed from ~in-~ (“to, upon”) and Latin ~partiō~ (“to divide, to share”). French Wiktionary adds that the form was refashioned: the older Latin ~impertire~ was reshaped on the model of the French verb ~partir~, so that the modern verb differs in its vowel from the Latin one. The two Wiktionaries thus agree on the Latin source and differ only in what they stress, the Latin variant in one case and the refashioning in the other.

The core idea is to give someone the share that falls to them. In French, ~impartir~ is a learned verb of law and administration, found almost only in set phrases such as ~impartir un délai~ (“to allot a deadline”) or ~les pouvoirs impartis~ (“the powers assigned”). Because ~partir~ supplied the model, ~impartir~ looks like a compound of ~in-~ and ~partir~, but it came from a Latin verb already formed and was not built in French from those pieces.
en.impatienter: Formed from the adjective ~impatient~ with the ending ~-er~, which turns it into a verb meaning “to make impatient” and, reflexively, “to lose patience.” ~Impatient~ is a borrowing from Latin ~impatiens~ and can be analyzed as ~im-~ (“not”) plus ~patient~, from ~patiens~, the participle of ~patī~ (“to suffer, to endure”).
en.impatroniser: The only account of ~impatroniser~ derives it from Latin ~patronus~ (“patron”), but that line is itself flagged as needing a reference, and the source does not spell out the formation. The verb means “to take charge, to take over.” Its relation to French ~patron~, from the same Latin word, is plain, but the exact path of the prefix and ending remains undocumented.
en.imperméabiliser: ~Imperméabiliser~ is formed from the adjective ~imperméable~ and the suffix ~-iser~, and means to make waterproof. The adjective comes from Latin ~impermeabilis~ (“that cannot be crossed”), made of ~in-~ (“not”) and ~permeabilis~ (“passable”). The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs.
en.implanter:
From Latin ~implantāre~, a compound of the prefix ~in-~ (here “in, into”) and ~plantāre~ (“to plant”), itself from the noun ~planta~. In Latin ~planta~ first meant “the sole of the foot”; the sense “shoot, cutting” is generally traced to a separate, homophonous ~planta~ back-formed to an unattested verb. The deeper root is debated, the favored account deriving it from PIE *~pleh₂-~ (“flat”). Through ~plantāre~ French shares a cognate with English ~plant~ and with Italian ~piantare~ and Spanish ~plantar~.

The metaphor is agricultural: to ~implanter~ something is to set it as firmly as a seedling pressed into soil. From the literal planting of a cutting the verb spread to settling people and institutions — une usine, une idée — and, in modern medicine, to the surgical fixing of an ~implant~. French ~implantation~, ~plante~, ~planter~ and ~plantation~ all belong to the same Latin stock, the whole family rooted in the act of pushing a shoot into the ground.
en.impliquer:
From Latin ~implicare~ (“to fold in, to entangle, to involve”), a compound of ~in-~ (“in”) and ~plicare~ (“to fold”). ~Plicare~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, to weave”), itself an extension of *~pel-~ (“to fold”), and is closely allied to ~plectere~ (“to braid”). Cognates of the family include English ~ply~, ~pleat~, and ~fold~, and the Latin verb survives directly in Spanish ~plegar~ and Italian ~piegare~ (“to fold”).

The literal picture is of folding one thing into another until the two are tangled together — and from that knot of entanglement grew the figurative senses. To ~impliquer~ someone is to fold them into an affair, hence “to implicate, to involve, to accuse”; to ~impliquer~ a consequence is to have it folded in, hence “to imply.” French inherited a rich cluster from ~plicare~: ~appliquer~ (to fold toward, to apply), ~compliquer~ (to fold together, to complicate), ~expliquer~ (to unfold, to explain), ~plier~ and ~ployer~ (to fold), and ~pli~ (“a fold, a crease”). The doublet ~employer~ also belongs here, from ~implicare~ by the popular route, while ~impliquer~ is the learned borrowing.
en.implorer:
French ~implorer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~implōrāre~, glossed in French Wiktionary as “to weep in, to implore.” The Latin verb joins ~in-~ (here in its assimilated form ~im-~) to ~plōrāre~ (“to weep, to wail”). Spanish ~implorar~ and Italian ~implorare~ are parallel learned forms, and English ~implore~ comes from the same Latin verb.

The humbler inherited cousin of ~plōrāre~ passed into Old French as ~plorer~ and became modern ~pleurer~, “to cry,” and in Spanish it gave ~llorar~. So ~implorer~ and ~pleurer~ are two descendants of one Latin verb, one learned and one inherited. The Latin ~dēplōrāre~ gave ~déplorer~ in the same way, so ~implorer~, ~déplorer~ and ~pleurer~ form a small family around weeping.
en.imploser: A calque of English ~implode~, attested as early as 1881. In French it was built on the model of ~exploser~ by replacing the first element with ~in-~ (“in, inward”), so that ~imploser~ means “to burst inward” where ~exploser~ means “to burst outward”. It is a modern coinage, with no ancestor in Old French or Latin.
en.implémenter: ~Implémenter~ is a borrowing from English ~implement~, which French adapted to its own system by giving it the ending ~-er~ of the first conjugation. The verb belongs to the vocabulary of computing and project management, where it means to put a design or a plan into effect.
en.importer:
French ~importer~ holds two verbs of separate descent. The commercial sense (“to bring in goods”) comes from Latin ~importare~ (“to bring in, carry in”), built from the prefix ~in-~ (“into”) and ~portare~ (“to carry”). ~Portare~ traces back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“to lead across, pass over”), the same root behind Latin ~portus~ (“harbour”) and ~porta~ (“gate”), and cognate with English ~ford~ and German ~Furt~ — a ford being, like a harbour, a place of crossing. The sense “to matter, to be important” was instead borrowed from Italian ~importare~ (“to be of consequence”).

The two strands meet in the underlying idea of something being ~carried in~. Goods carried into a country are ~imported~; a matter that ~carries~ weight, that bears upon us, is one that ~imports~ — hence the adjective ~important~ and the noun ~importance~, which entered French through the Italian sense. The impersonal construction ~il importe~ (“it matters”) preserves that figurative line: the thing weighs on the situation, it is borne in. From the same *~per-~ root and the ~portare~ family French draws a crowd of carrying words: ~porter~, ~exporter~, ~transporter~, ~rapporter~, and ~portable~, alongside the harbour-words ~port~ and ~porte~.
en.importuner: From ~importun~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. The adjective ~importun~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~importūnus~, formed with the negative prefix ~in-~ and meaning “unsuitable, troublesome.” An ~importun~ person turns up at the wrong moment, and ~importuner~ is the action of doing so: to pester or bother someone. The ending ~-er~ is the ordinary way of turning a noun or adjective into a first-conjugation verb. English ~importune~ is a close relative from the same Latin word.
en.imposer:
From Latin ~imponere~ (“to place upon, to set on”), a compound of the prefix ~in-~ (here assimilated to ~im-~, “on, upon”) and ~ponere~ (“to put, to place”). Old French reshaped the learned Latin verb on the model of ~poser~ — itself from Late Latin ~pausare~ (“to halt, to set down”) — so that French ~imposer~ formally belongs to the ~poser~ family rather than continuing ~ponere~ directly. Cognate formations appear in Italian ~imporre~ and Spanish ~imponer~, while English borrowed ~impose~ from the same French stem.

The literal sense of laying one thing on another lived on in religious usage — ~l'imposition des mains~, the laying on of hands — and in printing, where pages are ~imposées~, arranged on the sheet. From physical placing the verb moved to figurative burdens: to impose a duty, a silence, a will upon someone. A fiscal branch gave Latin-derived ~impôt~ (“tax”), literally something “placed upon” the taxpayer, and ~imposition~. The reflexive ~s'imposer~ shifted again, to mean “to assert oneself” or “to be unavoidable.” The same ~ponere~ underlies a great cluster of French verbs — ~poser~, ~composer~, ~disposer~, ~proposer~, ~exposer~ — and the nouns ~position~ and ~dépôt~.
en.impressionner:
Attested in 1762, ~impressionner~ is a French creation: a verb minted from the noun ~impression~, itself borrowed from Latin ~impressio~ (“a pressing into; an assault; a mark stamped on the mind”), from ~imprimere~ (“to press into”), built on ~in-~ plus ~premere~ (“to press”). The forms outside the present stem point to Proto-Italic *~pres-~, probably from *~pr-es-~, an extension of the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“to push, to strike, to press”) — the deeper chain is reconstructed with some caution. Through ~premere~ the verb is kin to Italian ~impressionare~ and Spanish ~impresionar~ — and, more unexpectedly, to English ~press~ and ~print~, the latter from Old French ~preinte~, the “pressed-in” mark, cousin of French ~empreinte~.

At first ~impressionner~ meant to strike someone with a vivid impression; nineteenth-century science then took the word literally: physiologists spoke of stimuli that ~impressionnent~ the senses, and from 1862 photographers said that light ~impressionne~ a plate — a beam physically pressing in its mark, faithful to ~premere~. The family's most famous offspring was born of a sneer: in 1874 the critic Louis Leroy, mocking Monet's canvas ~Impression, soleil levant~, branded the painters ~impressionnistes~, and the insult became the name of the movement. The same pressing root runs through ~imprimer~, ~empreinte~, ~presser~, ~pression~, ~comprimer~, ~opprimer~ and ~exprimer~ — this last meaning, etymologically, to press a thought out of the mind as juice is pressed from fruit.
en.imprimer:
From Latin ~imprimere~ (“to press into, press upon, stamp, imprint”), a compound of the prefix ~in-~ (“into, upon”) and ~premere~ (“to press”), itself from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “to press, strike.” The Latin verb is cognate with the source of Italian ~imprimere~ and Spanish ~imprimir~, and through ~premere~ it is kin to the English borrowings ~press~ and ~print~.

Long before machines, ~imprimere~ described pressing a seal into wax or stamping a mark — leaving a physical impression. When movable type arrived in the fifteenth century, French applied this verb to the new craft of pressing inked letters onto paper, and the modern sense “to print” was born; the older sense survives in figurative phrases like ~imprimer un mouvement~ (“to impart a motion”). The same Latin ~premere~ seeded a wide family in French: ~empreinte~ (“imprint, footprint”), ~épreuve~ (“proof, test”), ~exprimer~ (“to express,” literally to press out), ~comprimer~, and ~pression~. Even ~printemps~ (“spring”) belongs to a neighboring story of pressing forth. Most charmingly, the noun ~imprimante~ (“printer”), the household machine, is a direct descendant of a verb that once meant nothing more than mashing a signet ring into hot wax.
en.improviser:
French took ~improviser~ from Italian ~improvvisare~ (“to speak or act without preparation”), a verb formed on the adjective ~improvviso~ (“unforeseen”). The Italian adjective comes from Latin ~imprōvīsus~ (“unforeseen, unexpected”), made of ~in-~ (“not”) and ~prōvīsus~, the past participle of ~prōvidēre~ (“to foresee”). That verb is ~prō-~ (“ahead”) + ~vidēre~ (“to see”), and ~vidēre~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”), which is also the source of English ~wit~. So the verb literally describes what has not been seen ahead of time.

The word later broadened to any task done without preparation: one ~improvise~ a speech, a meal, a solution. The same Latin family stands behind French ~providence~, and the Italian adverbial phrase ~all'improvviso~ is the source of the French expression ~à l'improviste~, “unexpectedly.” Note that the Latin verb ~prōvidēre~ also gave ~pourvoir~ (“to provide”), through a different, inherited route.
en.imprégner:
Borrowed from Latin ~impraegnāre~ (“to make pregnant, to fertilize”), a verb built on ~in-~ (“in”) and the adjective ~praegnāns~ (“pregnant”). That adjective is usually analyzed as ~prae~ (“before”) plus a stem related to ~nāscī~ (“to be born”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ǵenh₁-~ (“to beget, to be born”), so the underlying picture is of a woman “before birth.” The same Latin source gave English ~impregnate~ and ~pregnant~, Italian ~impregnare~ and Spanish ~impregnar~. Inside French, the same root appears in the inherited ~naître~, which comes from ~nāscī~.

The Latin verb meant literally to make a woman pregnant. In French, ~imprégner~ now describes saturating a body with a substance, a cloth ~imprégné~ of oil or a room ~imprégné~ of smoke, and, figuratively, filling a mind or a culture with an idea or an influence, as in the reflexive ~s'imprégner de~ (“to soak up”). Its family includes ~imprégnation~ (“saturation”) and the learned adjective ~prégnant~, with the noun ~prégnance~, used in psychology and linguistics for an idea or form that strongly imposes itself. Note that ~imprenable~ (“impregnable”) belongs to ~prendre~ and is no relative of ~imprégner~ at all.
en.impulser: French ~impulser~ is given by French Wiktionary as a borrowing from Latin ~impulsāre~, a frequentative (a verb of repeated or intensified action) of ~impellere~ (“to push against, to drive on”), made from ~in-~ and ~pellere~ (“to push, to drive”). The Latin sense of repeated pushing explains the modern French meaning, “to give an impetus to, to drive forward,” used of projects, economies and policies. The same stem lies behind ~impulsion~, ~impulsif~ and ~pulsion~, and the related Latin verb ~pulsāre~ gave ~pousser~ (“to push”). The verb is thus a close cousin of ~pousser~, with its prefix meaning “against” in the sense of force applied.
en.imputer:
Borrowed from Latin ~imputāre~ (“to enter in an account, to charge to someone”), a compound of ~in-~ (“in, onto”) and ~putāre~ (“to reckon, to think over”). The simple verb ~putāre~ gave French no direct descendant, but it appears in ~compter~, ~disputer~, ~députer~, ~réputer~ and ~amputer~, all with their own prefixes. Spanish ~imputar~, Italian ~imputare~ and English ~impute~ are borrowings of the same Latin verb.

The Latin verb belonged first to bookkeeping: to ~imputāre~ a sum was to put it down to someone's account. The figure then carried over into law and morality, where what is entered in a person's account is a debt, a fault or a merit. French ~imputer~ keeps that double life. One imputes a crime or a mistake to someone (“to attribute it to them”), and in accounting one imputes an expense to a particular budget. The nouns ~imputation~ and ~imputabilité~ (“the fact of being attributable to someone”) belong to the same family.
en.impétrer:
From Latin ~impetrāre~ (“to obtain, to accomplish”), a learned borrowing used in French as a legal and administrative term. The Latin verb is traditionally analyzed as ~in-~ + ~patrāre~ (“to bring about, to carry out”), the notion being to get a request through to its end. The Latin noun ~impetrātiō~ (“obtaining”) lies behind the French noun ~impétration~, and ~impétrant~ comes from the present participle of the same verb.

In French ~impétrer~ means “to obtain by right or by request” something one has solicited, such as a title, a diploma, a grant or a favor from an authority. It is rare outside legal and official language. The family is small and learned: ~impétrant~ designates the person who obtains a diploma or a grant, and ~impétration~ the act of obtaining it. English has the parallel legal verb ~impetrate~, a learned borrowing from the same Latin verb, and ~perpetrate~ is a more distant relative of ~patrāre~.
en.inactiver: Two analyses are given: ~in-~ plus ~activer~, or ~inactif~ plus ~-er~. In either case the prefix is the negative ~in-~, from Latin ~in-~ (“not”), so ~inactiver~ means to make inactive. The base ~activer~ comes from ~actif~ plus ~-er~, and ~actif~ from Latin ~āctīvus~, from ~agere~ (“to drive, to do”). The verb is chiefly technical: to inactivate a substance, a gene, a virus or a function, the opposite of switching it on. Its sense is thus the near mirror of ~activer~.
en.inaugurer:
From Latin ~inaugurare~ (“to take the auguries, to consecrate by augury”), from ~in-~ plus ~augurare~, the verb of the ~augur~, the Roman priest who read omens. The origin of ~augur~ itself is disputed: De Vaan prefers a derivation from ~augere~ (“to increase”), via an Old Latin *~augos~ (“increase, reinforcement”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂ewg-~ (“to grow”) — cognate with Sanskrit ~ojas~ (“strength”); an older proposal instead joins ~avis~ (“bird”) and ~garrire~ (“to chatter”), from the watching of birds. The sources mark the matter as unsettled.

In Roman practice no public undertaking began without consulting the gods through augury; ~inaugurare~ meant to inaugurate a magistrate, temple, or rite by first taking the auspices. The religious ceremony faded, but the sense of a solemn formal opening remained, and that is the meaning French inherited: one inaugurates a building, a monument, an era. The French form is attested from the fourteenth century. From the same source come ~augurer~, ~augure~, ~inaugural~, ~inauguration~ — words that still carry, faintly, the memory of priests scanning the flight of birds.
en.incarcérer:
A learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ~incarcerare~, formed from ~in-~ (“in, into”) and ~carcer~ (“prison”), so literally “to put in prison.” Latin ~carcer~ meant a prison or, in the plural, the starting stalls of a racecourse; its origin is not clear, and the sources give no deeper root. English ~incarcerate~ is the exact counterpart, borrowed from the same Medieval Latin verb.

Latin ~carcer~ had already reached French by the inherited route, as Old French ~chartre~ (“prison”), preserved in the expression ~chartre privée~ (“illegal private imprisonment”). ~Incarcérer~ came later, as a formal, administrative word, which is why it feels heavier than the everyday ~emprisonner~ and ~mettre en prison~. Related French words include ~incarcération~, ~carcéral~, ~excarcérer~ (“to release from prison”) and ~réincarcérer~.
en.incarner:
Borrowed (1372) from Ecclesiastical Latin ~incarnāre~ (“to make flesh”), from the prefix ~in-~ (“into”) and ~carō~ (“flesh”), from Proto-Italic *~karō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)ker-~ (“to cut”). Old French had the inherited form ~encharner~ alongside this learned borrowing. The flesh-word ~carō~ keeps surprising company: through that cutting root it is cognate with English ~shear~ and Ancient Greek ~κείρω~ (“to shear, cut off”) — flesh conceived, it seems, as the portion cut from the carcass.

First a theological term — the Word made flesh, God taking on a body — ~incarner~ broadened to mean embodying any abstraction: an actor incarnates a role, a leader incarnates a cause. The same Latin ~carō~ (stem ~carn-~) seeds a whole pantry and lexicon of French words: ~carnivore~, ~charnel~, ~charcuterie~ (cooked flesh), ~carnage~, and ~carnaval~ — by one common account the farewell to meat before Lent, though that festive reading is itself disputed. From a single word for flesh, French built terms for the spiritual, the sensual, the butcher's craft, and the slaughter — the body in all its registers.
en.incendier: Formed in French from ~incendie~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, “to set on fire.” The noun is a borrowing from Latin ~incendium~ (“fire, conflagration”), from ~incendere~ (“to set alight”). English Wiktionary adds that it was perhaps influenced by Occitan ~incendi~, an older form that may be inherited or an early borrowing. The verb applies to buildings, forests or anything burned down, and in the figurative sense to inflame the passions or the spirit. A related French word is ~incendiaire~ (“arsonist; inflammatory”).
en.incidenter: Formed from the noun ~incident~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun was a learned borrowing from Latin ~incidens~ (“falling upon”), the present participle of ~incidere~. The verb means “to raise an incident” and, in the setting of a trial or a debate, “to disrupt proceedings” by interrupting them with secondary issues.
en.incinérer: ~Incinérer~ is borrowed from Latin ~incinerāre~, a verb made from the prefix ~in-~ and ~cinis~, ~cineris~ (“ash”), so it means “to turn to ash.” The Latin noun ~cinis~ is also the source of French ~cendre~, which descends from the accusative form ~cinerem~, and of the adjective ~cinéraire~, “relating to ashes.” English ~incinerate~ comes from the same Latin verb.
en.inciser:
From Middle French ~inciser~, from Old French ~enciser~, from a Late or Vulgar Latin verb *~incīsāre~, a frequentative of Latin ~incidō~, ~incidere~ (“to cut into”). The two Wiktionaries agree on ~incidere~ and on the later form *~incīsāre~. The Latin verb is made of ~in-~ (“in, into”) and ~caedere~ (“to cut”), whose vowel weakened to ~-cid-~ in compounds.

The verb keeps its literal sense of making a cut into something. Its family includes ~incision~ (“a cut”), ~incisif~ (“sharp, cutting”) and ~incisive~ (“incisor”). The Latin root ~caedere~ also lies behind several other French words: ~précis~ (from ~praecīsus~, literally “cut off”), ~concis~ (“concise”) and ~décider~ (from ~dēcīdere~, “to cut off, to settle”). English has the same family in ~incision~ and ~incisor~.
en.inciter:
From Latin ~incitāre~ (“to urge on, set in motion”), from ~in-~ (intensive here) plus ~citāre~ (“to set moving, summon”), itself a frequentative of ~ciēre~ (“to stir, set in motion”), from Proto-Indo-European *~keyh₂-~ (“to move, set in motion”). The root is one of motion-giving: to incite is to put another into movement, to be the push behind their action. It is cognate, through that root, with Ancient Greek ~κῑνέω~ (“to move,” source of kinetic), and with a whole English family — ~excite~, ~recite~, and cite itself.

First attested in French in the 14th century, ~inciter~ has always meant to spur someone to do something, now often with a faint coloring of pushing toward the unwise or the unlawful (inciter à la haine). A separate technical sense entered around 1800 from the vitalist medicine of the Scottish physician John Brown, where to incite was to stimulate a tissue. From the same motion-root French gathered ~exciter~, ~réciter~, ~susciter~, and ~solliciter~ — a cluster of verbs all turning on the act of setting something, or someone, in motion.
en.incliner:
From Latin ~inclīnāre~ (“to bend, lean, tilt”), from ~in-~ (“toward”) plus ~clīnāre~ (“to bend, lean”). ~clīnāre~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~kleināō~ and ultimately to Proto-Indo-European *~ḱley-~ (“to lean, incline”). Cognate, through that root, with Ancient Greek ~κλίνω~ (“to lean”), English ~lean~, and German ~lehnen~ — all images of a body or thing tipping out of upright.

French ~incliner~ runs from the physical to the moral: one may ~incliner~ the head, a surface may ~incliner~ toward the horizon, and figuratively a person ~incliner~ toward an opinion — a leaning of the mind. The same *~ḱley-~ root produced a rich French family: ~décliner~, ~clin~ (as in ~clin d'œil~, “wink”), ~inclination~, and, by way of the related Greek and Latin senses of a “bed” one leans back on, ~climat~ (originally the “slope” of the earth) and the borrowed ~clinique~. To ~incliner~ is to let the upright yield, gently, to a slope.
en.inclure:
From Latin ~includere~ (“to shut in, enclose, include”), from ~in-~ (“in”) and ~claudere~ (“to close, shut”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~klau-~ (“hook, peg,” used as a bar or bolt, hence “to close”). Cognate with Italian ~includere~ and Spanish ~incluir~, and — through ~claudere~ — with English ~include~, ~exclude~, and ~close~.

The literal image is concrete: to ~inclure~ is to “shut something in,” to enclose it within a boundary so that it counts as part of the whole. The Latin ~claudere~ rests on a homely Indo-European notion — the hook or peg that bars a door — which also yielded ~clavis~ (“key”) and ~clavus~ (“nail”). The modern French ~inclure~ has a famously defective conjugation, and a curious irregularity sets it apart from its sibling ~conclure~: its past participle is ~inclus~, with an ~-s~, against the ~conclu~ of ~conclure~. From the same ~claudere~ family French inherited a remarkable crowd of words — ~clé~, ~clore~, ~conclure~, ~exclure~, ~enclore~, ~clôture~, and ~cloître~ — all of them turning, etymologically, on the act of shutting.
en.incomber:
~Incomber~ comes from Latin ~incumbere~ (“to lie upon, to lean on”). English Wiktionary gives the source simply as Latin ~incumbō~. French Wiktionary adds that ~incumbere~ was itself derived from ~incubāre~ (“to lie, to be stretched out somewhere”), which in turn comes from ~cubō~ (“to lie, to be stretched out”), with the prefix ~in-~. The Latin verb thus describes someone lying or leaning on something. The two Wiktionaries agree on the Latin source, and only French Wiktionary traces its inner structure, so the sources say no more about how the verb entered French.

The Latin sense is physical, whereas the French verb keeps only a figurative one. The image is of a weight resting on a person: a task, a charge or a responsibility lies on them, and they must see to it. In modern French, ~incomber~ is used almost only in the third person and with ~à~, as in ~il incombe à quelqu'un de~, which means “it falls to someone to.” The gloss “behoove” renders this sense of a duty that rests on someone.
en.incommoder:
~Incommoder~ comes from Latin ~incommodāre~ (“to cause trouble, to be inconvenient”). The Latin verb is built on the adjective ~incommodus~ (“inconvenient”), formed from the negative prefix ~in-~ and ~commodus~ (“fitting, convenient”), itself made of ~com-~ and ~modus~ (“measure”). What is ~commodus~ thus fits the measure of its purpose. French took the verb over in its Latin form, with the ending of the first conjugation.

The meaning has kept its Latin shape: to ~incommoder~ is to bother or inconvenience someone, whether by a noise, a smell, a crowd or a draught, and the verb also covers making someone slightly unwell. It belongs to a family that includes the adjective ~incommode~, the noun ~incommodité~ and the opposite words ~commode~ and ~commodité~. The verb ~accommoder~ also comes from the same ~commodus~, and so does the English word ~commodious~.
en.incorporer:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~incorporare~ (“to form into a body, to embody”), from ~in-~ (“into”) + ~corpus~ (“body”). ~Corpus~ descends from PIE *~kʷrep-~ (“body, form, appearance”), the same root that, through Latin, gives French ~corps~, ~corset~, ~corsage~, ~corporel~, and ~corpuscule~, and that surfaces in the English borrowings ~corpse~, ~corps~, and ~corporation~. Because it was taken straight from Latin by scholars rather than worn down through Old French, ~incorporer~ keeps its Latin shape almost intact.

The literal sense is to make several things into one ~corps~ — one body. From there French branched in two directions. Materially, to ~incorporer~ is to blend one substance into another until they form a single mass, the everyday verb of the cook folding eggs into a batter. Institutionally, it is to absorb people or land into a larger body: enrolling recruits into a regiment, annexing a province to a kingdom, admitting a member to a corporation. Modern relatives built on the same stem include ~réincorporer~, ~désincorporer~, ~incorporable~, and the noun ~incorporation~, all preserving the founding image of many parts knit into one body.
en.incriminer: A learned word, rare before the French Revolution, borrowed from Medieval Latin ~incrīmināre~ and built on Latin ~crīmen~ (“charge, accusation”) and its verb ~crīminārī~ (“to accuse”). The noun ~crīmen~ is also the source of French ~crime~ and English ~crime~, and English ~incriminate~ shares the same Medieval Latin origin. In French, ~incriminer~ supplanted ~criminaliser~ in the sense “to declare criminal,” and it now means to accuse someone of a wrongdoing or to cast suspicion on a person or thing.
en.incruster:
From Old French ~incruster~, itself a learned borrowing from Latin ~incrustāre~ (“to cover with a crust”), made of ~in-~ (“on, into”) and ~crusta~ (“crust, rind, shell”). Latin ~crusta~ is the source of French ~croûte~ and of English ~crust~, which entered English by way of Old French. Italian ~incrostare~ and Spanish ~incrustar~ are parallel descendants of the same Latin verb.

The original idea is decorative: to ~incruster~ is to set a hard material into a surface, as a craftsman inlays a table with mother-of-pearl, ivory or gems, so that the ornament seems to grow into the object. The verb also names the opposite process, a mineral deposit forming a hard layer, which is why a kettle becomes ~incrusté~ with limescale. The figurative reflexive ~s'incruster~ means to settle in and refuse to leave, like a guest who will not go home. The family of ~crusta~ also gives ~croûton~, ~croûte~, ~écroûter~ and ~crustacé~, the last a name for animals with a hard shell.
en.incuber:
From Latin ~incubāre~ (“to hatch, to sit upon”), the verb of a hen on her eggs. It is a learned borrowing. Its Latin parts are ~in-~ (“on, upon”) and ~cubāre~ (“to lie down”), so the verb literally means to lie upon something. It is tied to the Latin noun ~incubo~, and the senses connected with business are more recent than the others.

The nouns ~incubation~ and ~incubateur~ belong to the same family. The business senses are newer: a startup is now said to be ~incubée~ when an organization shelters it in its early days. The simple Latin verb ~cubāre~ also gave French ~couver~, so a hen ~couve~ her eggs and a firm ~incube~ its young projects from the same Latin root. The related Latin noun ~incubo~, the spirit that lies on a sleeper, gave ~incube~ in French and ~incubus~ in English.
en.inculper:
Borrowed from Latin ~inculpāre~ (“to blame, to accuse”), which French Wiktionary derives from ~culpa~ (“fault, blame”), and which English Wiktionary labels Late Latin. It is a learned verb, taken from the written language rather than inherited. It is generally analyzed as ~in-~ + ~culpa~ + the verb ending ~-āre~, so it is a verb made on the word for fault.

The Latin noun ~culpa~ also gave French ~coulpe~ (“fault, guilt”), which survives in the phrase ~battre sa coulpe~. French Wiktionary lists ~coupable~ and ~culpabiliser~ among the related words. In modern French, ~inculper~ has the legal sense of formally charging someone with an offense, as in ~être inculpé de fraude~. Italian ~colpa~ and Spanish ~culpa~ are close cousins, and so is English ~inculpate~.
en.inculquer:
Borrowed from Latin ~inculcāre~. As standard background, the Latin verb is formed from ~in-~ (“in, upon”) and ~calcāre~ (“to tread, to press with the heel”), itself from ~calx~ (“heel”). Its Latin meaning was to stamp in or force in by pressing. The learned word reached English as ~inculcate~, and Italian and Spanish have ~inculcare~ and ~inculcar~.

French kept the figurative side of the Latin verb. To ~inculquer~ a value or a habit is to fix it in someone's mind by pressing it in, usually by repetition. The same verb ~calcāre~ left a more popular trace in French, since ~cauchemar~ contains Old French ~caucher~ (“to press, to trample”), from ~calcāre~. A learned word and a popular one thus share a root, with ~inculquer~ staying close to the Latin and ~cauchemar~ having been worn down over time.
en.incurver:
~Incurver~ was borrowed from Latin ~incurvāre~ (“to bend inwards, to bow, to curve”), itself built from ~in~ (“in, inward”) and ~curvō~ (“to bend”). The simple verb ~courber~ is the inherited, everyday counterpart. It comes from the same Latin root through the ordinary line of descent, while ~incurver~ was taken over later from written Latin, with its prefix intact.

Behind ~curvō~ lies the Latin adjective ~curvus~ (“curved, bent”), which is also the source of French ~courbe~ (“curve”) and of English ~curve~. The French family includes ~courber~, ~courbure~ and ~recourber~, with ~incurver~ standing as the learned member. Its meaning is to bend something into a curve, usually inward, and it is most often met in the participle ~incurvé~ and in the reflexive ~s'incurver~, said of a line, a blade or a back that bends. It is a technical and literary word, much rarer than ~courber~.
en.indemniser: Built on ~indemne~ (“unharmed”) with a verbal ending, which French Wiktionary reads as ~-er~ and English Wiktionary as ~-iser~. The base ~indemne~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~indemnis~, formed from ~in-~ (“not”) and ~damnum~ (“damage, loss”). To ~indemniser~ someone is therefore to make them “undamaged” again, by paying for the harm or loss they suffered. The verb belongs to the vocabulary of law and insurance, as do ~indemnité~ (“compensation”) and the English ~indemnify~.
en.indexer:
From the noun ~index~ with the verbal suffix ~-er~, a twentieth-century coinage. French ~index~ comes from Latin ~index~ (“one who points out, an informer; a forefinger; a title or list”), a deverbal noun built on ~indicāre~ (“to point out, indicate”), itself ~in-~ + ~dīcāre~ (“to proclaim”), from the PIE root *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, point out”). The very same root, in its bare finger-sense, produced Latin ~digitus~ (“finger”) — so the pointing forefinger and the pointing word-list share an ancestry. Cognate in spirit with English ~index~ and ~indicate~, borrowed from the same Latin stock.

The Latin ~index~ already wandered from the human hand to the printed page: the finger that points became the marginal mark, then the table that points a reader to a passage. French inherited this bookish sense, and the modern verb ~indexer~ — to enter something into such a list — is younger still, a workaday derivative born of catalogues and archives. The computer age stretched it further, to the indexing of databases and search engines, and economics borrowed it for pegging wages or prices to a reference figure, as in ~indexer sur l'inflation~. From the same Latin family French also keeps ~indice~, ~indication~, ~dédier~, and ~digital~ — a tidy cluster all tracing back to the gesture of pointing.
en.indifférer: This verb is a back-formation from the adjective ~indifférent~, the sources say, though French Wiktionary presents it as ~différer~ with the prefix ~in-~. The base ~différer~ comes from Latin ~differre~ (~dis-~ + ~ferre~, “to carry apart”), which gave both “to postpone” and “to be unlike.” The adjective ~indifférent~ means “not different,” hence “making no difference,” and the verb ~indifférer~ means to leave someone unmoved.
en.indigner: Borrowed from Latin ~indignārī~ (“to regard as unworthy, to be indignant”), a deponent verb built on the adjective ~indignus~ (“unworthy”). To be indignant is, literally, to find something unworthy. Old French had a form ~endaigner~, and French Wiktionary sends readers to ~daigner~ (“to deign”), which comes from the positive side of the same Latin family, ~dignus~ (“worthy”). The related French words ~digne~, ~dignité~ and ~indigne~ all point to that same Latin adjective.
en.indiquer:
From Latin ~indicāre~ (“to point out, to make known”), a denominal verb formed on ~index~ (“pointer, forefinger, informer”), which joins the prefix ~in-~ (“toward”) to the root of ~dīcere~ (“to say”). That root is Proto-Indo-European *~deyḱ-~ (“to point out, to show”), the same source as Greek ~deiknumi~ (“I show”) and, through Germanic, English ~teach~ and ~token~. The Romance heirs include Italian ~indicare~ and Spanish ~indicar~.

The original gesture is literally that of the index finger pointing something out, and from “to point at” the verb broadened to “to indicate, to show, to suggest.” The shared root *~deyḱ-~ is astonishingly fertile in French: ~dire~ itself, ~dicter~, ~indice~ (“clue”), ~indication~, and the legal ~juridiction~ (from ~iūs dīcere~, “to declare the law”) all descend from the idea of pointing or pronouncing. English doublets such as ~indicate~, ~dictate~, ~predict~, and ~verdict~ travel the same path. Each time one ~indique~ the way, one is, in effect, extending an ancient pointing finger across several thousand years of language.
en.indisposer: ~Indisposer~ is a compound of ~in-~ and ~disposer~. French Wiktionary connects it with the adjective ~indispos~, which comes from Latin ~indispositus~ (“confused”). The prefix ~in-~ here is negative, so the verb originally described putting someone out of the right state, or out of sorts. From there it developed the senses of making a person unwell or slightly ill, and of upsetting or irritating them, as in the glosses “annoy, upset”.
en.individualiser: Formed from ~individuel~ and the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to make” something what the base describes: to make individual, to tailor to a person. English Wiktionary treats ~individuel~ as a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ~indīviduālis~, while French Wiktionary derives it from ~individu~ with the suffix ~-el~. Both routes lead to Latin ~indīviduus~ (“indivisible”), the source of ~individu~: an individual is, etymologically, what cannot be divided further. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~ and is still productive.
en.induire:
From Latin ~inducere~ (“to lead in, bring on, induce”), from ~in-~ (“into”) and ~ducere~ (“to lead”). Latin ~ducere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~doukō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~dewk-~ (“to draw, pull”). That root spread widely: it is cognate with English ~tow~, ~tug~, and ~team~, with German ~ziehen~ (“to pull”) and ~Herzog~ (“duke”), and — through Latin ~dux~ — with English ~duke~.

The metaphor inside ~induire~ is one of leading someone toward a conclusion or an act. French keeps both the logical sense (in science, ~induire~ is to reason from particulars) and the cautionary one: ~induire en erreur~ means “to lead astray, mislead.” The ~-ducere~ family is enormous in French, since every prefix produced a verb: ~conduire~, ~produire~, ~réduire~, ~traduire~, ~séduire~, alongside the nouns ~induction~, ~inducteur~, and the participle ~induit~. All of them still carry the old gesture of drawing or leading.
en.indurer: Both Wiktionaries describe ~indurer~ as formed from the adjective ~dur~ (“hard”) with the prefix ~in-~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to make hard.” The adjective ~dur~ is inherited from Old French and goes back to Latin ~dūrus~ (“hard”). The ~in-~ here is the Latin locative prefix (“in, into”), used to build verbs of becoming or making, not the negative ~in-~. The verb is chiefly a learned word, and its relatives include ~durcir~ and ~endurer~.
en.industrialiser: Formed from the adjective ~industriel~ (“industrial”) and the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to make industrial.” ~Industriel~ is itself built from ~industrie~ and the adjective suffix ~-el~, and it goes back to Middle French ~industrial~. ~Industrie~ comes from Latin ~industria~ (“diligence, activity”). The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and the stem of the base loses its ending before it: ~industriel~ becomes ~industrial-~ in the verb. The result is a typical modern coinage, a long learned verb assembled from familiar parts.
en.infantiliser: ~Infantiliser~ is formed from the adjective ~infantile~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which forms verbs meaning “to make A”, so it means to treat or make someone childlike. The adjective ~infantile~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~infantilis~. The suffix ~-iser~ is fully productive in modern French, and its stem often changes before it; here the adjective keeps its shape except for the dropped final vowel.
en.infatuer:
~Infatuer~ is borrowed from Latin ~infatuāre~ (“to make foolish”), a verb formed on ~fatuus~ (“silly, foolish”). Analyzed in the usual way, ~infatuāre~ is ~in-~ plus ~fatuus~ plus the verbal ending ~-āre~. The French verb keeps the sense of the Latin: to fill someone with a foolish self-regard, to make conceited.

The verb is now found almost only as a past participle, ~infatué~, and in the reflexive: ~être infatué de soi-même~ is to be full of oneself. Its base ~fatuus~ also gave French ~fat~, an old and literary word for a smug, self-satisfied man, and the learned noun ~fatuité~ (“smug vanity”). English has taken the same Latin verb as ~infatuate~, whose usual sense, to inspire with a foolish passion, has drifted from the French one.
en.infecter:
Borrowed from Latin ~infectāre~ (“to stain, to taint”), a verb tied to ~īnfectus~, the past participle of ~inficere~ (“to dip in, to dye, to taint”). The two Wiktionaries phrase the link a little differently, one calling ~infectāre~ a frequentative of ~inficere~ and the other deriving the verb from its participle, but both root it in ~inficere~, itself ~in-~ + ~facere~ (“to do, to make”). Latin ~facere~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, to place”), which is also the source of English ~do~. French ~faire~ descends from the same ~facere~, so ~infecter~ is a distant relative of everyday ~faire~.

The earliest Latin sense was physical: to ~inficere~ cloth was to steep it in dye, and so to stain it. From coloring came tainting, and from tainting came contamination by poison or disease, the main modern sense of ~infecter~ with a wound, a body or a water supply as the object. The adjective ~infect~ (“foul, revolting”) comes from the same Latin stem, which shows how the “stained” meaning drifted toward “repellent.” The family includes ~infection~, ~infectieux~ and ~désinfecter~ (“to disinfect”).
en.infester: French Wiktionary gives ~infester~ as coming from Latin ~infestare~. ~Infestare~ means “to attack, to molest,” and is formed on the adjective ~infestus~ (“hostile, unsafe”). English ~infest~ comes from the same Latin verb. In French the verb is used of pests or dangers that overrun a place.
en.infiltrer: Formed from ~in-~ (“in, into”) + ~filtrer~, “to seep into as through a filter.” The prefix is the locative ~in-~ of Latin, not the negative one. The base ~filtrer~ comes from the noun ~filtre~, a learned borrowing from Latin ~filtrum~, which French Wiktionary traces to Frankish. It is a doublet of ~feutre~ (“felt”), the material the first filters were made of. From liquids passing through a barrier, ~infiltrer~ extended to people, ideas and spies getting past defenses unseen.
en.infirmer:
Borrowed directly from Latin ~infirmāre~ (“to weaken, to make infirm”). The Latin verb rests on the adjective ~infirmus~ (“weak”), which is ~in-~ (“not”) + ~firmus~ (“strong, firm”). The same adjective gave French ~infirme~ and ~infirmité~, and English borrowed ~infirm~ and ~infirmity~ from it, while ~firmus~ itself lies behind French ~ferme~, ~affermir~ and ~confirmer~.

The literal sense, “to make weak,” is the root of the modern uses. Today ~infirmer~ is mostly abstract: one weakens an argument, undermines a hypothesis, or invalidates a decision, as a higher court may do with a judgment. The verb is thus the exact opposite of ~confirmer~, built on the same ~firmus~. Where ~confirmer~ makes something firm, ~infirmer~ takes its firmness away.
en.infliger:
~infliger~ was borrowed in the fifteenth century from Latin ~īnflīgere~ (“to strike against, to deal a blow or a wound”), from ~in-~ (“on, against”) plus ~flīgere~ (“to strike, to strike down”), from PIE *~bʰleyǵ-~ (“to strike”) — a root whose other branches produced Greek ~θλίβω~ (~thlíbō~, “to press, to crush”) and Latvian ~bliêzt~ (“to beat”). In classical Latin the verb was concretely violent: one inflicted a blow, a wound, a collision. Medieval Latin, by about 1250, had already bent it toward the courtroom — “to punish” — and it was in that juridical dress that French adopted it: the first attestation, in 1451, concerns a penalty to be ~infligée~. English ~inflict~, Italian ~infliggere~ and Spanish ~infligir~ are parallel borrowings from the same Latin verb.

French never let the verb forget its violence: a defeat, a fine or a humiliation is still ~infligée~ — abstract blows, every one. The reflexive ~s'infliger~ appeared in 1807, first of religious self-mortification — penance struck upon oneself — long before its modern ironic shadings. The family of ~flīgere~ is a study in directed violence: ~affliger~, from ~afflīgere~ (“to knock to the ground”); ~conflit~, from ~cōnflīgere~ (“to clash together”); and English ~profligate~, from ~prōflīgāre~ (“to strike down, to ruin”) — etymologically, someone who has battered his own fortune to pieces. To inflict is, at root, simply to land the blow.
en.influencer:
~influencer~ is a denominal verb built on the noun ~influence~, which French took from Medieval Latin ~influentia~, a derivative of Latin ~influere~ (“to flow into”), itself ~in-~ (“into”) plus ~fluere~ (“to flow”), from a Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰlewH-~ (“to overflow”). The remarkable thing is the original meaning of ~influence~, attested around 1240: it named an ethereal fluid supposed to flow down from the stars and act upon human beings and their destinies — astrology’s invisible emanation.

From that cosmic outpouring the word drifted, by the late thirteenth century, to the slow continuous action one person or thing exerts upon another, and only much later to prestige and authority (l’~influence~ française). The verb ~influencer~ — to sway, to act upon — formalized that human sense, and modern French has lately borrowed back English ~influenceur~ for the social-media figure. The same ~fluere~ family floods French with ~fluide~, ~flux~, ~affluence~, ~confluent~, and ~superflu~ (“superfluous,” literally over-flowing) — a whole watercourse of words from one Latin verb of flowing, with ~influencer~ still quietly carrying its starlight at the source.
en.influer: Learned borrowing from Latin ~īnfluere~ (“to flow in”), built from ~in-~ (“into”) and ~fluere~ (“to flow”). The Latin image is a stream running into something, and French kept the picture while turning it figurative: to influence is to make one's effect flow into another thing or person. The same Latin verb ~fluere~ lies behind ~fluide~, ~flux~ and ~affluent~, so the verb sits in a large family of words about flowing.
