en.infléchir: French Wiktionary explains ~infléchir~ as ~in-~ plus ~fléchir~ (“to bend”), shaped to match the noun ~inflexion~, itself tied to ~fléchir~ and ~flexion~. ~Fléchir~ comes from Latin ~flectere~ (“to bend”), and ~flexion~ shares that Latin source. The verb therefore means “to bend, to curve.” English ~inflect~ and ~inflection~ belong to the same Latin family.
en.informatiser: Formed from ~informatique~ and the suffix ~-iser~, so “to equip with computing”; the ending ~-ique~ of the base drops away before the suffix. The suffix comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, itself a transcription of Greek verbs. The base is a coinage of the 1960s credited to Philippe Dreyfus. French Wiktionary derives it from ~information~ by swapping the suffix, while English Wiktionary calls it a blend of ~information~ and ~automatique~. It is said that Charles de Gaulle settled the name in a cabinet meeting by choosing ~informatique~ over ~ordinatique~. German ~Informatik~ dates from 1957.
en.informer:
From Latin ~informare~ (“to give shape to, to fashion, to form an idea of”), built from the prefix ~in-~ (“into”) and the verb ~formare~ (“to shape”), itself from the noun ~forma~ (“shape, form, figure”). The ultimate origin of ~forma~ is uncertain; it may be connected to Ancient Greek ~morphē~ (“shape”), perhaps through a swapping of sounds, but this is not secure, so it is best left as a Latin word of debated parentage. English borrowed the same verb as ~inform~.

The original meaning was concrete and even philosophical: to ~informer~ was to give form to matter, to impress a shape upon it — in scholastic thought the soul was said to “inform” the body. From “shaping someone's mind” grew the modern sense of furnishing the mind with knowledge: to inform is to form a person's understanding by pouring facts into it. The hugely productive ~forma~ seeded a whole French family: ~forme~, ~former~, ~format~, ~formule~, ~uniforme~ (“of one form”), ~transformer~, ~conforme~, and ~difforme~. And from ~informer~ itself, by way of the data that shapes our knowledge, came ~information~ — and, in our own century, the entire vocabulary of ~informatique~.
en.infuser: ~Infuser~ is a denominal verb, formed on the noun ~infusion~ according to French Wiktionary. It belongs to a family of French verbs built on the Latin verb ~fundere~ (“to pour”), alongside ~diffuser~, ~perfuser~ and ~transfuser~, where ~infuser~ means “to pour in.” The senses “infuse” and “inject” fit that image.
en.inféoder:
Borrowed from Medieval Latin ~infeodare~ (“to grant a fief”), formed from ~in-~ and ~feodum~ (“fief”), as French Wiktionary explains. French first records it as a past participle, ~infeode~, in 1411, taken from Medieval Latin ~infeodatus~. The verb then was rebuilt on that participle, or taken directly from Medieval Latin, and is noted by Richelet in 1680. It replaced an older ~infeuder~ (1393), itself from Medieval Latin ~infeudare~ (1097) and ~feudum~. English Wiktionary says only “from ~féodal~,” which does not fit the dates given above.

The root is the medieval ~feodum~ or ~feudum~, the word for a fief, which also gives French ~fief~ and ~féodal~. To ~inféoder~ meant to grant land as a fief, binding the vassal to a lord. In modern French the verb is used figuratively: to ~inféoder~ is to make someone or something dependent on a power, and ~s'inféoder à~ a party or an interest means to tie oneself to it.
en.inférer:
Taken from Latin ~īnferō~ (infinitive ~īnferre~), a compound of ~in-~ (“in, into”) and ~ferre~ (“to carry, to bring”), so “to carry in, to bring to bear.” French ~inférer~ keeps the Latin shape almost whole. Its relatives abroad include Italian ~inferire~ and English ~infer~, with its noun ~inference~. In French the verb now means to draw a conclusion from known facts, and it belongs to a formal, written register.

Its closest family is the one built on Latin ~ferre~: ~conférer~, ~référer~, ~préférer~, ~différer~, ~transférer~, ~offrir~ and ~souffrir~ all trace to it, and the French of ~inférer~ even conjugates like ~préférer~. Do not confuse it with the unrelated adjective ~inférieur~, from Latin ~īnferus~ (“lower”), which looks similar but comes from a different word.
en.inférioriser: Formed from the adjective ~inférieur~ with the suffix ~-iser~, in the sense “to make or treat as inferior.” The adjective comes from Latin ~inferior~ (“lower”), the comparative of ~inferus~ (“below”). The suffix, borrowed from Late Latin ~-izāre~, turns the adjective into a verb. The sense is a social and psychological one: to belittle someone, to make them feel lower than others.
en.ingurgiter: Borrowed from Latin ~ingurgitāre~ (“to pour in, to gulp down”), built on the prefix ~in-~ (“into”) and the noun ~gurges~ (“gorge”). The Latin noun ~gurges~ also meant “whirlpool.” The verb was taken into French as a learned word, directly from Latin and not through Old French. French kept the Latin sense of swallowing in large quantities, often with a hint of haste or greed: one ~ingurgite~ a meal, a drink or, figuratively, a pile of facts. English has also borrowed ~ingurgitate~.
en.ingénier:
~Ingénier~ (“to strive, to rack one's brains”) is a learned word tied to Latin ~ingenium~ (“natural talent, cleverness”). The two Wiktionaries tell it slightly differently. English Wiktionary treats it as formed directly from ~ingenium~. French Wiktionary derives it from ~engin~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, with a late learned spelling that pulled it back toward the Latin form. Either way, ~ingenium~ stands behind it, and the ~in-~ spelling is a deliberate Latinizing touch rather than the natural evolution of the sounds.

The Latin word is generally analyzed as ~in-~ (“in”) plus the root of ~gignere~ (“to beget”), so ~ingenium~ was what one is born with, one's innate disposition. That makes ~ingénier~ a cousin of ~engin~ (“device, contrivance”), of ~ingénieur~ and ~ingénieux~, and of English ~engine~, ~ingenious~ and ~ingenuity~. In modern French the verb survives almost only in the reflexive ~s'ingénier à~ followed by an infinitive, meaning to devote one's wits and effort to doing something. Its sense of cleverness applied with effort still echoes ~ingenium~.
en.ingérer:
French ~ingérer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~ingerere~. English Wiktionary writes the source as ~ingere~, which looks like a slip for the same verb. ~Ingerere~ is ~in-~ (“into”) + ~gerere~ (“to carry, to bring”), so the verb is literally “to carry in” and, in Latin, “to heap on” or “to force upon.” French kept the learned form, and English ~ingest~ is a close counterpart.

In modern French, ~ingérer~ means “to take food or drink into the body,” while the reflexive ~s'ingérer~ means “to interfere, to meddle,” a sense that fits “forcing oneself into” a matter. The Latin ~gerere~ lives on in many French words: ~gérer~ (“to manage”), ~gestion~, ~geste~, ~digérer~ (the counterpart of ~ingérer~ with ~dis-~ in place of ~in-~), ~suggérer~ and ~congestion~. English ~digest~ and ~suggest~ come from the same root.
en.inhaler: Borrowed from Latin ~inhalare~. The Latin verb is built from ~in-~ (“in”) and ~halare~ (“to breathe”), the same second element as in ~exhaler~ (“to breathe out”), so the pair ~inhaler~ and ~exhaler~ mirrors in and out. English ~inhale~ is a close cousin.
en.inhiber: ~Inhiber~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~inhibēre~ (“to hold back, to restrain”). The Latin verb is a compound of the prefix ~in-~ and ~habēre~ (“to have, to hold”), with the usual weakening of the vowel inside a compound. English ~inhibit~ comes from the same Latin verb. The root ~habēre~ is one of the most productive in Latin. In French it lives on directly as ~avoir~, and through learned borrowings in ~habit~, ~habiter~, ~prohiber~ and ~exhiber~. ~Prohiber~ and ~exhiber~ are sister compounds of ~inhiber~ and, like it, were formed with prefixes that give the sense of holding back, holding out or holding forward. ~Inhiber~ keeps the sense of restraint, in physiology, psychology and everyday speech. A person who is ~inhibé~ is held back, as the Latin “to restrain” suggests.
en.inhumer:
~Inhumer~ is a borrowing from Latin ~inhumāre~, which English Wiktionary labels Ecclesiastical Latin, with the sense “to put into the ground.” It is made of ~in-~ (“in”) and ~humus~ (“earth, soil”). French kept both sides of the pair: ~humus~ for the soil layer and ~inhumer~ for putting a person into it.

The verb is the formal word for burial, used in administrative and ceremonial French (~inhumer un défunt~, ~permis d'inhumer~), where ~enterrer~ would sound more everyday. Its opposite is ~exhumer~, “to dig up,” with the prefix ~ex-~ (“out of”), and ~exhumer~ in turn took on the figurative sense of bringing a forgotten thing back to light. A related noun is ~inhumation~.
en.initialiser: The two Wiktionaries differ slightly. French Wiktionary calls ~initialiser~ a borrowing from English ~initialize~, while English Wiktionary parses it as French ~initial~ + ~-iser~. The English verb is itself ~initial~ + ~-ize~, so the parts are the same either way. The adjective ~initial~ comes from Latin ~initiālis~, from ~initium~ (“entrance, a going in”), hence “beginning.” The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and means “to make or render” what the base names.
en.initier:
From Latin ~initiare~ (“to begin; to admit into the mysteries”), a denominal verb from ~initium~ (“a beginning, entrance”). That noun is itself built on ~inire~ (“to go in, enter”), from ~in-~ (“into”) plus ~ire~ (“to go”), the verb of motion that descends from PIE *~ey-~ (“to go”) — the same root behind English ~exit~ and ~transit~ and Latin ~iter~ (“journey”). Romance cognates of the verb include Spanish ~iniciar~ and Italian ~iniziare~.

In Latin the religious sense was central: to ~initiare~ was to lead someone across the threshold into secret rites, a sense French preserved when one is ~initié~ to the mysteries of a craft or a cult. From there it broadened to imparting any first knowledge — initiating a pupil into mathematics. The plainer sense “to begin, to start” (initier un projet) is now common, but it remains contested: the Académie française judges it not condemnable in itself yet spreading to excess, since French already has ~commencer~ and ~entamer~. From the same ~initium~ come ~initial~, ~initiation~, and ~initiative~.
en.injecter: Borrowed from Latin ~iniectāre~ (also spelled ~injectāre~), a frequentative verb built on ~iniectus~, the past participle of ~inicere~ (“to throw in”). That verb combined ~in-~ (“in”) and ~iacere~ (“to throw”), the same root behind French ~jeter~, “to throw.” So to ~injecter~ is, literally, to throw something inside. The word first served for forcing a liquid into a cavity or body, and the medical sense of a syringe injection grew from it. The related learned words ~injection~, ~éjecter~ and ~projeter~ share the Latin ~iacere~ in their make-up.
en.injurier: Borrowed from Late Latin ~iniūriāre~, itself drawn from the Latin deponent verb ~iniūriārī~ (“to cause an injustice, to wrong”). It belongs with the French noun ~injure~, and the two words are best seen as relatives rather than a verb built on a noun. In Latin the idea was one of wrongdoing in general. French narrowed it to wrongs done in words, so that ~injurier~ means “to hurl abuse at someone,” while the noun ~injure~ keeps both the “insult” sense and, in some contexts, the older “wrong.”
en.innerver:
The French text traces ~innerver~ to Latin ~nervus~ (“nerve”), and its shape, with an ~in-~ prefix, suggests a learned coinage on that word, as in English ~innervate~. The verb is a technical term of anatomy meaning “to supply with nerves.” Latin ~nervus~ also gave English ~nerve~ and German ~Nerv~, which came through French or Latin as learned borrowings.

The Latin word is the source of a whole family in French: ~nerf~, ~nerveux~, ~nervure~ and ~nervosité~. Its most surprising member is ~énerver~, which comes from Latin ~ēnervāre~, “to cut the sinews” (~ē-~ + ~nervus~). The older sense of ~énerver~ was to weaken, and the modern “to irritate” came later. ~Innerver~ turns the family in the opposite direction, toward giving an organ or a limb its nerves and so its power to feel and move.
en.innocenter: From ~innocent~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. The base ~innocent~ is borrowed from Latin ~innocentem~ (“harmless”), through Old French ~inocent~. The Latin word is built from the negative prefix ~in-~ and ~nocēns~, the present participle of ~nocēre~ (“to hurt”), so an innocent person is literally one who does no harm. The denominal verb ~innocenter~ means to declare someone innocent or to clear them of blame, the reverse of finding them guilty.
en.innover:
French borrowed ~innover~ from Latin ~innovāre~ (“to renew, to alter”), a verb built from the prefix ~in-~ (“in, upon”) and ~novāre~ (“to make new, to renew; also to invent”), itself from the adjective ~novus~ (“new”). Latin ~novus~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~néwos~ (“new”). English ~new~ and German ~neu~ are native cousins, and Greek ~néos~ is another.

The Latin verb often carried a mildly negative flavor, because ~innovāre~ could mean to disturb the established order, and the Roman phrase ~res novae~ (“new things”) was a way of saying revolution. French kept the neutral sense “to introduce something new.” Its family includes ~innovation~, ~innovateur~, ~novateur~ and ~rénover~ (“to renew”). From the same Latin ~novus~ come ~nouveau~, ~nouvelle~ and ~novice~. The month name ~novembre~ is not one of them: it comes from ~novem~ (“nine”), because November was once the ninth month.
en.inoculer:
Borrowed from Latin ~inoculāre~ (“to graft”). The Latin verb is generally analyzed as ~in-~ (“in, into”) + ~oculus~, a word that means “eye” and, in gardening, also “bud.” To graft by budding was, so to speak, to set an eye into a plant. Related forms in other languages include English ~inoculate~, Italian ~inoculare~ and Spanish ~inocular~, all learned borrowings from the same Latin verb.

In French, ~inoculer~ today is used mainly for introducing a germ, a virus or a vaccine into the body; a modern use also speaks, figuratively, of instilling an idea or a feeling in someone. The Latin ~oculus~ is also the ancestor of the ordinary French ~œil~, and of learned words such as ~oculaire~ and ~oculiste~, so a bud, an eye and an injection are distant relatives.
en.inonder:
Borrowed from Latin ~inundāre~ (“to flood, to overflow”), made of ~in-~ (“in, upon”) and a verb built on ~unda~ (“wave, water”). Italian ~inondare~ is its sister form. Latin ~unda~ is thought to be a distant relative of English ~water~ and ~wet~ through the Proto-Indo-European root for “water.” French borrowed the verb directly from Latin and kept its meaning almost unchanged: water covers land and floods it.

Besides rivers and rain, ~inonder~ has long served figuratively, for something that arrives in overwhelming quantity: a room ~inondée~ de lumière, a market ~inondé~ de produits, a speaker ~inondé~ de messages. Latin ~unda~ also gave several French words by other roads. ~Onde~ (“wave”), ~ondée~ (“a sudden shower”), ~ondoyer~ (“to ripple”) and ~ondulation~ come from it. Even ~abonder~ (“to abound”), from Latin ~abundāre~, “to overflow,” preserves the same wave, and so do its relatives ~abondance~ and ~redonder~. The learned family around ~inonder~ includes ~inondation~ and ~inondable~.
en.inquiéter:
From Latin ~inquietare~ (“to disturb, to trouble”), built from the negating prefix ~in-~ and ~quietare~ (“to quiet, to calm”), itself from ~quies~ (“rest, repose”). ~quies~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~kʷyeh₁-~ (“to rest”) — and through that root the verb keeps surprising company: the same root, by way of Proto-Germanic *~hwīlō~, yields English ~while~, so the worry in ~inquiéter~ and a quiet ~while~ spent resting are distant cousins. Latin ~quies~ also gives ~quietus~, ancestor of English ~quiet~, and ~tranquillus~ (“tranquil”).

The word is built as a privation: ~in-~ undoes the rest of ~quies~, so to ~inquiéter~ is literally to un-quiet, to rob of repose. French preserves that image exactly — to worry someone is to take away their peace of mind. The reflexive ~s'inquiéter~ (“to worry, to fret”) turns the disturbance inward, and the adjective ~inquiet~ (“anxious”) names the restless state itself. From the same ~quies~ French keeps the noun ~quiétude~ (“quietude”) and its negative twin ~inquiétude~ (“anxiety”), and the borrowed ~tranquille~ — all of them measuring distance from, or loss of, that ancient repose.
en.inscrire:
From Latin ~īnscrībere~ (“to write in, to write upon, to enroll”), a compound of the prefix ~in-~ (“in, into, upon”) and the verb ~scrībere~ (“to write”). The French form was reshaped on the model of ~écrire~, the inherited descendant of ~scrībere~. Latin ~scrībere~ originally meant “to scratch, to incise marks,” for the earliest writing was cutting signs into wood, stone, or clay; it comes from Proto-Italic *~skreiβō~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)kreybʰ-~ (“to scratch, to cut”). The same Latin verb spread far: French ~écrire~, Italian ~scrivere~, German ~schreiben~, and English ~scribe~ and ~script~ all descend from it.

The prefix ~in-~ gives the verb its particular flavor: not merely to write, but to write something into a register, a stone, a list. From that come the two faces of modern ~inscrire~ — the monumental sense of carving a name into marble, and the bureaucratic sense of entering a name on a roll, hence “to sign up, to register.” The reflexive ~s'inscrire~ means to enroll oneself, and the legal phrase ~s'inscrire en faux~ means to formally contest a claim. The ~scrībere~ family richly stocks French with ~écrire~, ~écriture~, ~inscription~, ~scribe~, ~prescrire~, ~décrire~, and ~manuscrit~.
en.insculper:
From Latin ~insculpere~ (“to carve in, to engrave”), a compound of ~in-~ (“in, into”) and ~sculpere~ (“to carve”). The Latin verb came into French whole, as a learned borrowing, rather than being built from French parts. Latin ~sculpere~ is the root of a family that spans the Romance languages: Italian ~scolpire~ and Spanish ~esculpir~ both descend from it, and English ~sculpt~ comes to English through French.

In French, ~insculper~ is a rare, learned verb whose gloss is “to stamp”: to press a mark into a material, as the Latin compound implies. Its closest French relatives are ~sculpter~ and ~sculpture~, which belong to the same root, while the prefix ~in-~ links it to verbs of impressing or engraving. It is a good example of a Latin compound that French borrowed with its prefix already attached.
en.insculpter:
From Latin ~insculpere~ (“to carve into, to engrave”), a verb built from the prefix ~in-~ (“in, on”) and ~sculpere~ (“to carve”). The French verb is a learned borrowing, taken straight from Latin rather than inherited through Old French, and it keeps the idea of cutting or pressing a mark into a surface. The ending ~-er~ fits the Latin infinitive in ~-ere~ into the first conjugation, as French does with most learned verbs.

The simple verb ~sculpere~ lies behind French ~sculpter~, ~sculpture~ and ~sculpteur~, so ~insculpter~ is a close relative of these familiar words. Where ~sculpter~ names the art of carving, ~insculpter~ is a rare, learned verb meaning to engrave or imprint something on a surface. English has a parallel learned verb, ~insculp~, from the same Latin source.
en.insensibiliser: Formed from the adjective ~insensible~ and the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make”), so it means to make insensitive: to anesthetize, or to desensitize someone to an allergen. ~Insensible~ was inherited from Old French ~insensible~, from Late Latin ~īnsēnsibilis~, built from ~in-~ (“not”) and ~sensibilis~ (“able to feel”). The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and is fully productive in technical and medical language.
en.insinuer:
~Insinuer~ is a learned borrowing. It passed through Old and Middle French from Latin ~īnsinuō~, which English Wiktionary analyzes as ~in-~ (“in”) joined to ~sinuō~ (“to bend, curve”). The verb ~sinuō~ comes from the noun ~sinus~ (“curve, fold”), itself the ancestor of the French words ~sinus~ and ~sinueux~. The same Latin verb gave English ~insinuate~.

Because the verb is built on a word for a curve, it belongs to a family of words about winding and bending. Its meaning in French is figurative: to suggest something indirectly, without stating it outright, or, in the pronominal form ~s'insinuer~, to slip into a place or a person's favor. Related French words include ~insinuation~ and ~insinuant~, and the verb shares its root with ~sinueux~ (“winding”) and ~sinuosité~.
en.insister:
From Latin ~insistere~ (“to stand on, to set foot upon, to persist”), built from the prefix ~in-~ (“on, upon”) and ~sistere~ (“to cause to stand, to set”). ~sistere~ is itself a reduplicated form of ~stāre~ (“to stand”), going back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). Through this same ~sistere~ family, French gained ~consister~, ~persister~, ~résister~, and ~subsister~; the English cognate ~insist~ comes by the same Latin road, alongside ~persist~ and ~desist~.

The image hiding inside ~insister~ is physical: to insist was once to literally plant your feet on something and stand there. Latin ~insistere~ meant to step onto a path or to take up a firm position, and from that bodily stance grew the figurative sense of dwelling on a point and refusing to budge — exactly what we mean when we say someone insists. French borrowed the verb from learned Latin rather than inheriting it through everyday speech, which is why it keeps its clean Latin shape. The far-flung relatives of the root *~steh₂-~ are everywhere in French: ~stable~, ~station~, ~statue~, ~constant~, and even the past participle ~été~ of ~être~. To insist, etymologically, is simply to keep standing your ground.
en.insoler:
Borrowed from Latin ~insolāre~ (“to expose to the sun”). Latin built the verb from the preposition ~in-~ (“in, upon”) and the noun ~sōl~ (“sun”), so it described setting something out in the sunlight. French kept the sense of exposing a thing or a person to the sun, which also covers the modern sense “to sunbathe.”

The family is the Latin ~sōl~. The learned noun ~insolation~ (“exposure to sunlight, sunstroke”) belongs to it, and ~solaire~ and ~solarium~ share the root, as does English ~solar~. The everyday word for the sun, ~soleil~, is a distant relative through a Latin diminutive. A false friend lurks nearby: ~insolent~ looks like a cousin but comes from Latin ~insolēns~ (“unusual, arrogant”), a different word.
en.insolubiliser: Formed from ~insoluble~ with the suffix ~-iser~, which here means “to make”: to make something insoluble. ~Insoluble~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~insolubilis~, built from ~in-~ (“not”) and ~soluble~. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs.
en.insonoriser: ~Insonoriser~ is formed from the adjective ~insonore~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which means to make or render something. The adjective is itself a compound of the negative prefix ~in-~ and ~sonore~, so ~insonore~ describes what does not carry sound. To ~insonoriser~ a room is therefore to make it soundproof. The final ~-e~ of the base disappears before the suffix, as it does in many ~-iser~ verbs.
en.inspecter: ~Inspecter~ comes from Latin ~inspectāre~, which French Wiktionary analyzes as ~in-~ (“in, on”) plus ~spectāre~ (“to look at”). The Latin verb ~spectāre~ is itself a frequentative of ~specere~ (“to look”), and it stands behind French ~spectacle~ and ~respecter~. The related noun ~inspection~ and the person who carries it out, the ~inspecteur~, belong to the same family, and English ~inspect~ comes from the same Latin source.
en.inspirer:
From Latin ~inspīrāre~ (“to breathe into, to blow upon”), a compound of the prefix ~in-~ (“into”) and the verb ~spīrāre~ (“to breathe”). Latin ~spīrāre~ is usually traced to a Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)peys-~ (“to blow, to breathe”), though some scholars suspect it is simply an onomatopoeia imitating the sound of breathing. Italian ~ispirare~ and Spanish ~inspirar~ continue the same Latin verb, and English ~inspire~ arrives through Old French.

The twin meanings of ~inspirer~ — “to breathe in” and “to inspire” — are not a coincidence but the original picture: a god or a Muse was imagined literally breathing an idea into a person. From that physical inhalation grew the figurative “inspiration,” the in-breathed thought, and French keeps both senses side by side: one inspires deeply at the doctor's, and a landscape inspires a poet. The same root yields a remarkably breathy family — ~expirer~ (to breathe out, hence also to die), ~respirer~, ~aspirer~, ~soupirer~, ~conspirer~ (to “breathe together,” i.e. to plot in whispered agreement), and the nouns ~esprit~ and ~spiritueux~. Most striking of all, French ~esprit~ and English ~spirit~ descend from ~spīritus~ (“breath”): the soul itself was, to the Roman mind, a kind of breathing — a thought ~inspirer~ quietly preserves.
en.installer:
From Medieval Latin ~installāre~ (“to put into a stall, to establish in office”), from the prefix ~in-~ (“in”) and ~stallum~ (“stall, seat”), itself borrowed from Frankish *~stall~ (“place, position, stable-stall”), from Proto-Germanic *~stallaz~. That Germanic word goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~stel-~ (“to place, to set, to stand firm”). Old French had the related noun ~estal~ (“position, market-stall, standing-place”).

The earliest sense was strikingly ceremonial: to ~installer~ was to seat a canon or bishop in his ~stall~ in the choir, formally placing him in his office. From that solemn enthroning the verb spread to ordinary placing — to install a person in a post, to set up furniture or a machine, and reflexively ~s'installer~, to settle in, to make oneself at home. The Germanic *~stall~ that entered French here is, distantly, kin to the native ~stalle~ (a choir-stall) and to English ~stall~ and ~install~ themselves. So the French ~installer~ is a Germanic stall dressed in Latin robes, carried into French by the ceremonies of the medieval Church.
en.instaurer:
~instaurer~ comes from Latin ~īnstaurāre~ (“to set up, establish, renew”), built from ~in-~ and a *~staurō~ element, from Proto-Italic *~stauros~, from PIE *~steh₂u-ro-~, an extension of *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”) — the same root that stands behind a vast family of “standing” words. So to instaurer something is, at root, to set it standing. The shared root links it to Greek ~stauros~ (“upright stake, pole”), a cognate rather than the ancestor; one French source names ~stauros~ as the origin, but the better-supported account makes both words parallel branches of *~steh₂-~.

The Latin verb meant both “to erect” and “to renew,” the second sense arising from re-erecting what had decayed — a development reinforced by its twin ~restaurāre~. French kept the “set up, establish” value: one can ~instaurer~ a regime, a custom, or a dialogue. The same Latin pair gave ~restaurer~ (“to restore, to refresh”) and, borrowed into English, ~restore~ and ~store~; through the wider *~steh₂-~ family come ~stable~, ~station~, ~stature~, and ~constant~. The German repair idiom ~in Stand setzen~, “to set in standing,” mirrors the very same metaphor.
en.instiguer:
Borrowed from Latin ~instigare~ (“to goad, to urge on”), a verb of the first conjugation, which is why the French infinitive ends in ~-er~, as ~cantare~ gave ~chanter~. The Latin verb carries the prefix ~in-~ (“on, against”), and its sense is that of prodding someone forward. Italian ~instigare~, Spanish ~instigar~ and English ~instigate~ are all borrowings from the same Latin verb, so the word is shared across several languages of Western Europe.

Because ~instiguer~ was taken from Latin by learned writers, it kept a shape close to its source, unlike inherited verbs of the same type, which wore down considerably. Its family is learned too: the noun ~instigation~ and the agent noun ~instigateur~ come from Latin forms of the same verb. In use, ~instiguer~ means to push someone to act, most often in a bad cause, and it is a formal word, much rarer than ~instigateur~.
en.instiller:
From Latin ~instillāre~ (“to pour in drop by drop”), a verb built from ~in-~ (“in, into”) and ~stillāre~ (“to drip”), itself from ~stilla~ (“a drop”). French Wiktionary refers the reader to ~distiller~ for the rest of the story, since the two verbs share the same Latin core and differ only in the prefix.

The French verb keeps both the literal sense, to put a liquid in drop by drop, as when medicine is instilled into the eye, and a figurative sense, to introduce something gradually, such as an idea or a feeling. Related words in French include ~distiller~ and ~instillation~. English ~instill~ comes from the same Latin verb, and so does Spanish ~instilar~.
en.instituer:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~instituere~ (“to set up, establish, train”), from ~in-~ (“in, upon”) + ~statuere~ (“to set up, place”), which is itself built on ~stare~ (“to stand”). The chain runs back through Proto-Italic to PIE *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”), one of the great Indo-European roots, source of an enormous family that includes English ~stand~, ~stay~, ~statue~, and ~status~. ~Instituere~ thus literally means to “stand something up,” to set it firmly in place.

From that founding image French drew the abstract sense of bringing an institution, a custom, or a law into being. The verb also kept a precise legal use — to ~instituer~ an heir is to name one by will — alongside the sense of appointing someone to an office. Because it was taken straight from Latin, ~instituer~ keeps a transparent kinship with its siblings ~constituer~, ~destituer~, ~restituer~, ~substituer~, and ~prostituer~, all from compounds of ~statuere~. Its own offspring are central to French life: ~institut~, ~institution~, ~instituteur~ and ~institutrice~ (the schoolteacher who “sets up” young minds), and ~réinstituer~ — all standing on the same root *~steh₂-~.
en.institutionnaliser: ~Institutionnaliser~ is formed from the adjective ~institutionnel~ with the verb suffix ~-iser~; it means to make something an institution, to give it institutional form. The adjective is in turn built on the noun ~institution~ with the adjective ending ~-el~. Before ~-iser~, the ending ~-el~ is reshaped into ~-al-~, a common change in formations in ~-iser~, as with ~réel~ giving ~réaliser~.
en.instruire:
From Middle French ~instruire~, from Old French ~enstruire~ or ~estruire~ (with the prefix later respelled in a Latin form), from Latin ~īnstruō~ (“to build, arrange, equip, teach”). The Latin verb is ~in-~ (“in, upon”) plus ~struō~ (“to pile up, to build”), which comes from the Proto-Indo-European root *~sterh₃-~ (“to spread”). English ~strew~ is a distant Germanic cousin of that root. Italian ~istruire~ and Spanish ~instruir~ continue the Latin verb, and English ~instruct~ was borrowed from its participle ~īnstructus~.

The physical sense came first: to construct, to arrange, to fit out with what is needed, as an army or a ship is equipped. From equipping a thing the verb moved to equipping a mind, hence teaching, and French kept both senses together for a long time. In law, ~instruire~ took a separate path and means to prepare a case by gathering evidence, which is why a ~juge d'instruction~ is an investigating magistrate and not a teacher. The same Latin root gave ~instruction~, ~instrument~, ~construire~, ~détruire~ and ~structure~, all of them reaching back to the image of building up.
en.instrumentaliser: ~Instrumentaliser~ is built from the adjective ~instrumental~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which makes verbs meaning “to make” or “to treat as” what the base says: to treat a person or cause as a mere tool. The adjective is older than the verb. It appeared in Middle French around 1370, in Oresme, as a learned borrowing from medieval Latin ~instrumentālis~, from Latin ~instrūmentum~ (“tool, equipment”). The suffix ~-iser~ reached French from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which had itself transcribed Greek verbs, and it remains fully productive in administrative and journalistic French.
en.instrumenter: Formed in French from ~instrument~ with the ending ~-er~, which turns a noun into a verb. The noun reached French from Latin ~īnstrūmentum~ (“tool, equipment”), by way of Old French and Middle French. The verb covers a range of senses, from drawing up a legal document to scoring music for an orchestra.
en.insuffler:
~Insuffler~ was borrowed from Late Latin ~īnsufflāre~ (“to blow into”), made of ~in-~ (“in”) and ~sufflāre~ (“to blow up, to inflate”). In turn, ~sufflāre~ combines ~sub-~ with ~flāre~ (“to blow”), which goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰleh₁-~ (“to blow”). The simple verb ~souffler~ was inherited from the very same ~sufflāre~, so French holds two forms of one Latin word: the everyday ~souffler~, worn down by centuries of sound change, and the learned ~insuffler~, which kept its Latin shape and its prefix.

French uses the verb in two ways. In the literal sense, ~insuffler~ describes blowing air or a substance into something, as in medical practice (~insuffler de l'air~). In the figurative sense, it means to instil or inspire, as breath that carries an idea or an emotion into someone (~insuffler du courage~). The picture is the same as in ~inspirer~, which also treats a feeling as something breathed in. The family around the Latin root also includes ~enfler~, from Latin ~īnflāre~ (“to inflate”), and ~soufflet~ (“bellows”), a reminder of how many French words descend from the act of blowing.
en.insulter:
French ~insulter~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~īnsultāre~ (“to leap upon, to attack, to insult”), which means it came into French already formed and was not built there. English Wiktionary adds a second reading: within French, the verb can also be seen as the noun ~insulte~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. The two accounts can be held together: the verb was borrowed from Latin, and the French noun and verb are tied closely enough that the verb can be read as the noun plus its ending. The ending ~-er~ is the first-conjugation ending, from Latin ~-are~.

The Latin gloss itself runs from “to leap upon” to “to attack” to “to insult”, so physical attack and verbal attack already sat together in one verb before French borrowed it. The meaning in modern French is the last of these, to offend someone with words. The ending of ~insulter~ is the ordinary first-conjugation ending, just as ~chanter~ came from Latin ~cantare~, and that is why the verb looks so regular. It is a learned word and not an inherited one, meaning that it reached French by way of written Latin and not through the spoken language.
en.insupporter: A back-formation from the adjective ~insupportable~ (“unbearable”): the speaker removed the ending ~-able~ and added a verb ending, working backward from the adjective to a verb. The adjective itself is the negative of ~supportable~, built on the verb ~supporter~ (“to bear, to endure”). The result is a verb meaning “to be unbearable” or “to irritate beyond endurance,” a rare, mostly colloquial coinage that makes the adjective's idea an action.
en.insurger:
Borrowed from Latin ~insurgere~ (“to rise up against, to attack”), formed from ~in-~ (“against, upon”) and ~surgere~ (“to rise”). ~Surgere~ itself is a contraction of ~surrigere~, built from ~sub-~ and ~regere~ (“to keep straight, to direct”), which descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten”). That root also gave English ~right~ and ~rule~ through other channels, and Italian has ~insorgere~ for the same verb.

The Latin sense was physical before it was political: ~insurgere~ meant to stand up on something, then to rise against someone. French took the verb as a learned borrowing and uses it almost only reflexively, ~s'insurger~, “to rise in revolt, to protest.” The family is large. ~Insurrection~ and ~insurgé~ share the prefix, and ~surgir~, a related borrowing from ~surgere~, keeps the sense of rising up suddenly. Less obviously, ~source~ comes from the participle of ~surgere~, since a spring is water that rises, and ~résurrection~ and ~ressource~ belong here too. A rebel is, etymologically, someone who gets up.
en.inséminer:
~Inséminer~ is a learned borrowing from Late Latin ~īnsēmināre~ (“to sow in”), formed from ~in-~ (“in”) and ~sēmināre~ (“to sow”), a verb built on ~sēmen~ (“seed”). The Latin image is agricultural: to scatter seed into the soil. The noun ~sēmen~ itself belongs to the family of the Latin verb ~serere~ (“to sow”), so the whole group is about planting and sowing.

The verb ~sēmināre~ also lived on by the inherited route, as French ~semer~, so ~inséminer~ and ~semer~ are two descendants of one Latin family, one learned and one popular. The noun ~sēmen~ lies behind ~semence~, ~séminal~ and ~séminaire~, and English took ~inseminate~ from the same Late Latin verb. In modern French ~inséminer~ is a technical, medical and veterinary word for introducing seed to fertilize, far from the field of its Latin ancestor.
en.insérer:
From Latin ~inserere~ (“to set in, graft, insert”), from ~in-~ (“in, into”) plus the verb ~serere~ (“to join, link, weave together”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ser-~ (“to bind, put in a row”). This ~serere~ of joining must be kept apart from its Latin twin meaning “to sow”: ~inserere~ is built on the weaving sense, so to insert is, at root, to thread one thing into the fabric of another.

That binding root is unusually productive. Through it ~insérer~ is kin to ~série~ (a row, a sequence), to ~insert~ and ~assertion~ in English, and to a whole cluster of words about putting things in order or linking them. In French ~insérer~ ranges from the physical (slip a coin into a slot, a clause into a contract) to the social (s'insérer dans la société, to find one's place). The metaphor underneath has never quite faded: every insertion is a small act of weaving, slotting a new strand into an existing row so that it holds.
en.intailler: From the noun ~intaille~, with the verb ending ~-er~; French Wiktionary dates the verb to 1860. It is a term of the art of gem engraving, meaning to engrave in hollow on a precious or hard stone. The noun ~intaille~ names such a stone, cut in hollow to serve as a seal or signet, and it was borrowed from Italian ~intaglio~ (“cut, engraving”). The verb is therefore a French coinage on an Italian loan, made to describe the work that produces an ~intaille~.
en.intellectualiser: ~Intellectualiser~ is formed from ~intellectuel~ with the suffix ~-iser~, which makes verbs meaning “to make A” or “to treat as N”: to give something an intellectual character, or to deal with an emotion or problem in abstract, rational terms. The stem is reshaped to ~intellectual-~ before the suffix. The adjective is a learned borrowing from Latin ~intellectualis~, tied to ~intellegere~ (“to discern, to understand”), itself from ~inter~ (“between”) and ~legere~ (“to gather, to choose, to read”).
en.intensifier: Formed from ~intense~ with the suffix ~-ifier~, which makes verbs meaning “to make A”, so ~intensifier~ means to make more intense. The adjective ~intense~ comes from Latin ~intēnsus~, the past participle of ~intendere~ (“to stretch, to strain”). The suffix ~-ifier~ goes back to Latin ~-(i)ficāre~, itself from ~facere~ (“to make”). Intensity is thus, etymologically, tension, and to intensify is to stretch something tighter.
en.intenter: ~Intenter~ was borrowed from Latin ~intentāre~ (“to direct toward, to aim at”), a frequentative verb tied to ~intendere~ (“to stretch toward”), itself made of ~in-~ (“toward”) and ~tendere~ (“to stretch”). The picture is of pointing something at a target. French uses it almost only in legal language, where one ~intente~ an action or a lawsuit against someone, directing proceedings at them (~intenter un procès~). That makes it a close relative of ~intention~ and ~tendre~, which share the same root.
en.interagir: Probably formed from the prefix ~inter-~ (“between,” from Latin ~inter-~) and the verb ~agir~, with the sense of reciprocal action. French Wiktionary also allows that it may be a back-formation from ~interaction~, attested in 1874. The base ~agir~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~agere~ (“to drive, to do”), which entered French in the fifteenth century and comes from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive”). So to ~interagir~ is to act on one another, each party driving the other.
en.intercaler:
Borrowed from Latin ~intercalāre~ (“to proclaim an extra day or month”), built from the prefix ~inter-~ (“between”) and the verb ~calāre~ (“to call out, to proclaim”). As background, ~calāre~ is the verb behind the Roman ~Kalendae~, the first day of the month, which was announced aloud. French ~calendes~ and ~calendrier~ and English ~calendar~ come from the same family.

In Latin, ~intercalāre~ was a calendar term: when the year drifted out of step with the seasons, an extra day or month was announced and slipped in. In French, the verb means more generally to put something between other things, such as a page in a book, a card in a file or a remark in a speech. A trace of the original calendar use survives in ~intercalaire~, as in ~jour intercalaire~ (“an added day”), alongside ~feuillet intercalaire~ (“a divider sheet”).
en.intercepter: ~Intercepter~ was formed in French from the noun ~interception~, on the model of the pairs ~accepter~ and ~acception~, ~excepter~ and ~exception~. In other words, speakers coined the verb backwards from the noun, copying a pattern already in the language. The noun ~interception~ goes back to Latin, from ~intercipere~ (“to seize on the way”), and so the verb ultimately belongs to the same family as ~capter~ and the many verbs in ~-cevoir~.
en.interclasser: Formed in French from ~classer~ (“to sort, to file”) with the prefix ~inter-~ (“between”). The base comes from the noun ~classe~, borrowed from Latin ~classis~, which first meant a “summons” and then the property-based divisions into which the Roman census sorted citizens. The prefix goes back to Latin ~inter-~, so ~interclasser~ means, literally, to sort between: to merge two sets of items (files, cards, documents) so that they fall into a single common order.
en.interconnecter: ~Interconnecter~ is built from ~connecter~ and the prefix ~inter-~ (Latin ~inter~, “between, amid”), which here gives a reciprocal sense: to join things to one another. ~Connecter~ is attested in French from around 1780 and comes from Latin ~conectere~, “to bind together,” from ~con-~ (“together”) + ~nectere~ (“to bind, to tie”). So the verb is, etymologically, a binding together of things among themselves.
en.intercéder:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~intercēdere~ (“to go between, to intervene”), a compound of ~inter-~ (“between”) and ~cēdere~ (“to go, to yield”). The Latin verb could mean to step in on behalf of someone, and also to veto, as when a Roman tribune interposed himself against a measure. French kept the sense of stepping in on another's behalf. English ~intercede~ is a parallel borrowing from the same Latin word.

In French, ~intercéder~ means to plead for someone, to speak in support of another before a person of authority, as in ~intercéder en faveur de quelqu'un~. Its register is formal, often religious: saints are asked to ~intercéder~ for the faithful. The noun ~intercession~ and the agent ~intercesseur~ belong to the same family. The second element ~cēdere~ yields a large French family of learned and inherited words: ~céder~, ~concéder~, ~précéder~, ~procéder~, ~succéder~, ~excès~ and ~procès~.
en.interdire:
From Old French ~entredire~, ~entredire~, a learned reshaping after Latin ~interdicere~ (“to forbid, to pronounce a prohibition”), itself ~inter-~ (“between, among”) + ~dicere~ (“to say, to speak”). ~dicere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, to point out”), the same root that gives Latin ~index~ and ~iudex~ (“judge,” one who points out the law) and, through Germanic, English ~teach~ and ~token~. Cognate Romance forms include Italian ~interdire~ and Spanish ~interdecir~.

In Roman usage an ~interdictum~ was a magistrate's formal order — quite literally a thing pronounced ~inter~ the parties — and the verb kept this flavour of authoritative speech that closes off an action. Old French ~entredit~ named the ecclesiastical ~interdit~, the dread papal sanction that suspended public worship over a whole realm. The modern legal and everyday senses (“forbid, ban”) grew directly from this idea of a prohibition laid down by spoken authority; a related figurative sense, “to dumbfound,” survives in ~rester interdit~ (“to be left speechless”), as if struck silent by a verdict. From the same ~dicere~ French inherited a large family: ~dire~, ~prédire~, ~contredire~, ~maudire~, ~verdict~, ~juge~, and ~indice~.
en.interfolier: ~Interfolier~ is built from two Latin words, ~inter~ (“between”) and ~folium~ (“leaf”), with the French verb ending ~-er~. It means to interleave: to put leaves between the leaves. Latin ~inter~ is the same word that gives French ~entre~ and many learned verbs in ~inter-~, such as ~intercaler~. Latin ~folium~ (“leaf”) has a large family. Its plural ~folia~ was taken for a feminine singular and became French ~feuille~, so ~interfolier~ is a learned relative of the everyday word, alongside ~feuillet~ and ~feuilleter~. The same Latin word lies behind Italian ~foglio~, Spanish ~hoja~ and English ~folio~ and ~foliage~.
en.interférer:
By the account of French Wiktionary, ~interférer~ goes back to Old French ~entreferir~ (“to strike one another, to clash”), a derivative of ~férir~ (“to strike”) with the prefix ~entre-~ (“between”), and reached modern French by way of English ~interfere~. English Wiktionary describes it more simply as borrowed from English ~interfere~, so the two accounts agree on the English link. Old French ~férir~ itself comes from Latin ~ferīre~ (“to strike”).

The Old French meaning was physical: two things ~entreferir~ when they strike each other. ~Férir~ has all but vanished from modern French; it survives in the fixed expression ~sans coup férir~ (“without striking a blow”). Modern ~interférer~ is abstract and means “to interfere,” as when one thing gets in the way of another. If the French account is right, this is a word that left French, was reshaped in English, and came home again. Its family includes the noun ~interférence~.
en.interjeter: Formed from ~jeter~ (“to throw”) with the Latin-derived prefix ~inter-~ (“between”). Old French had the inherited equivalent ~entrejeter~, which the learned form replaced. The base ~jeter~ comes through Old French and Vulgar Latin *~jectāre~ from Latin ~jactāre~, a frequentative of ~jacere~ (“to throw”). The verb survives chiefly in law, in ~interjeter appel~, “to lodge an appeal.”
en.interligner: Formed from ~interligne~ and the verb ending ~-er~: to interline, that is, to write or place something in the space between lines. The noun ~interligne~ is itself built from ~ligne~ with the prefix ~inter-~ (“between”), and ~ligne~ comes from Latin ~linea~.
en.interloquer: Borrowed from Latin ~interloquī~, a deponent verb that meant “to cut someone off in speech, to interrupt.” The Latin verb joins ~inter~ (“between”) and ~loquī~ (“to speak”), the same ~loquī~ that lies behind French ~locution~, ~éloquent~ and ~loquace~. The modern meaning has moved on from interrupting someone to leaving them speechless: ~interloquer~ means “to take aback, to disconcert,” as when a remark stops a person short.
en.internationaliser: Formed from ~international~ with the suffix ~-iser~, “to make international.” The adjective is itself built from ~inter-~ (“between”) and ~national~. According to French Wiktionary, it entered French through Dumont's translation of Jeremy Bentham's work on the principles of morals and legislation, published in 1780. The suffix ~-iser~ descends from Late Latin ~-izāre~. The verb has been used for businesses, conflicts and languages that cross borders.
en.interner: Formed in French from the adjective ~interne~ (“inner”) and the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense “to shut up inside.” The adjective is a learned borrowing from Latin ~internus~ (“inward”). To ~interner~ someone is to confine them within a place they cannot leave, whether wartime internment, political detention or, in the commonest modern use, commitment to a psychiatric hospital.
en.interpeller:
From Latin ~interpellāre~ (“to interrupt by speaking, break in on, accost”), from ~inter-~ (“between”) plus a verb on ~pellō~ (“to push, drive, strike”). ~pellō~ traces to Proto-Indo-European *~pelh₂-~. The compound is literally “to drive in between” — to thrust one's words into another's path. Related, through ~pellō~, to Latin ~appellāre~ (“to address, call”) and ~compellō~ (“to drive together, compel”); cognate in the Romance languages with Italian ~interpellare~ and Spanish ~interpelar~.

French ~interpeller~ keeps that interruptive push: to ~interpeller~ someone is to call out to, hail, or sharply question them — and in parliamentary and legal use, to demand that a minister or witness answer. The verb is notorious for its spelling: it keeps the Latin double ~-ll-~, and the 1990 orthographic reform permits the regularized ~interpeler~, though the older form persists. From the same ~pellō~ stem French also draws ~appeler~, ~rappeler~, and ~propulser~ — a family all about driving voices and bodies forward.
en.interpoler:
Borrowed from Latin ~interpolāre~. By standard analysis the Latin verb is built on ~inter~ (“between”) and the root of ~polīre~ (“to polish, smooth”), through the adjective ~interpolis~, so that its parts are “between” and “polish.” The verb passed into French as a learned borrowing, and the same Latin source gave English ~interpolate~, Italian ~interpolare~ and Spanish ~interpolar~. French ~polir~ (“to polish”), which comes from Latin ~polīre~, is a distant relative through its root.

In modern French, ~interpoler~ has two main domains. In textual scholarship it means to insert into a text words that were not in the original, as a copyist or editor might. In mathematics and computing it means to estimate values between known data points, as when software interpolates the pixels of an enlarged image. Its noun is ~interpolation~. The related French word ~interpeller~ (“to call out to”) looks similar but is a different verb, from Latin ~interpellāre~.
en.interposer: Two accounts are given for this verb, and the sources do not choose between them. By one, it is French ~inter-~ (“between”) added to ~poser~ (“to put, to place”). By the other, it is a blend of Latin ~interposuī~ (the perfect of ~interpōnere~, “to put between”) with the Latin verb ~pausāre~ (“to pause”). The second account has a good deal of background behind it: French ~poser~ itself comes from ~pausāre~, which in Late Latin came to be used for “to put down,” taking over the work of the Latin verb ~pōnere~ and its perfect ~posuī~. The meaning is the same under either route: to place between two things, and by extension to intervene, as in ~s'interposer~ (“to step in between”).
en.interpréter:
From Latin ~interpretārī~ (“to explain, expound, translate”), the verb formed on ~interpres~ (genitive ~interpretis~, “a go-between, agent, translator”). The noun splits into ~inter-~ (“between”) and a second element widely connected to ~pretium~ (“price, value”) and beyond it to the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“to traffic in, to sell”) — an ~interpres~ being one who stands between two parties and brokers meaning across them. French preserves the noun directly as ~interprète~. Italian ~interpretare~ and Spanish ~interpretar~ descend from the same Latin verb, as does English ~interpret~.

The original ~interpres~ was a middleman — a negotiator, a broker, then a translator standing between two tongues. From mediating between languages the sense broadened to mediating between a text and its reader: to ~interpréter~ is to draw out a hidden or disputed meaning, whether of a law, a dream, or a difficult passage. A further branch carries the word into performance, where to ~interpréter~ a role or a sonata is to render it, to make its meaning audible. The exact second root remains debated, which is why scholars hedge it; still, the same Latin family yields French ~interprète~, ~interprétation~, and ~interprétariat~.
en.interpénétrer: Formed from ~pénétrer~ with the prefix ~inter-~, from Latin ~inter-~ (“between, amid”), in its reciprocal sense: things that interpenetrate enter into one another. The base ~pénétrer~ was borrowed from Latin ~penetrāre~ (“to enter, to pierce”), first attested in French around 1314, and built on the family of ~penitus~ (“deeply, inwardly”). Its core image is depth, the innermost part of a thing. English ~penetrate~ comes from the same Latin verb through French. The prefix ~inter-~ is a learned one, with ~entre-~ as its native synonym.
en.interroger:
From Latin ~interrogare~ (“to ask, to question”), a compound of the preposition ~inter~ (“between, among”) and the verb ~rogare~ (“to ask, to request”). ~rogare~ is usually traced to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten, to direct in a straight line”), so that asking may have begun as a figurative “stretching out” of the hand toward someone. The same root gives Latin ~regere~ (“to rule, to keep straight”) and ~rex~ (“king”). Cognate through ~rogare~ with English ~rogation~ and, more distantly through the root, with English ~right~ and ~regent~.

The ~inter~ in ~interrogare~ carries the idea of an exchange passing back and forth between two parties — the to-and-fro of question and answer. From the neutral Latin sense “to ask,” French ~interroger~ specialized toward pointed, official, or insistent questioning: a judge, a teacher, or a police officer ~interroge~, where one merely ~demande~ a favor. The same ~rogare~ surfaces across French in a string of relatives: ~rogatoire~ (as in a ~commission rogatoire~, a judicial request), ~abroger~ (to repeal, literally to “ask away” a law), ~déroger~, ~proroger~, and ~prérogative~ — a cluster in which the original gesture of asking has hardened into the formal vocabulary of law and authority.
en.interrompre:
From Latin ~interrumpere~ (“to break apart, to interrupt”), ~inter-~ (“between”) + ~rumpere~ (“to break”), from a Proto-Indo-European root *~Hrewp-~ (“to break, tear”), with a Sanskrit cognate ~lumpáti~ (“breaks, plunders”). The earliest French forms were native re-buildings on ~entre-~ + ~rompre~ (~entrerompre~, around 1160), later re-latinized to match ~interrumpere~.

The literal sense is to “break in between” — to snap the continuity of a speech, an action, or a road. Through ~rumpere~ this verb belongs to a large and vivid family: French ~rompre~ (“to break”), ~corrompre~ (“to corrupt,” literally “to break thoroughly”), ~interruption~, and ~rupture~. English shares the harvest — ~rupture~, ~abrupt~, ~corrupt~, and even ~route~ and ~rout~, both from a Latin ~rupta~ (“a broken-through way, a broken line of soldiers”). To interrupt someone is, etymologically, to break the thread of their words.
en.intervenir:
From Latin ~intervenīre~ (“to come between, intervene, interrupt, occur”), a compound of the prefix ~inter-~ (“between, among”) and ~venīre~ (“to come”). ~venīre~ descends from Proto-Italic *~gʷenjō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~gʷem-~ (“to come, to go”), one of the most widely attested roots in the family: it is cognate with English ~come~, Greek ~baínein~ (“to go, step”), and Sanskrit ~gam-~ (“to go”). To intervene is, literally, “to come between.”

The Latin verb already carried both senses the French keeps: a physical or social one — to step in, to interpose oneself in an affair — and a temporal one, “to happen, to occur in the meantime,” as when an event ~intervient~ unexpectedly. French inherited the prefixed family richly: ~venir~ (“to come”), ~devenir~ (“to become”), ~revenir~ (“to come back”), ~prévenir~ (“to forewarn, to prevent,” literally “to come before”), ~parvenir~, ~survenir~, and ~convenir~ (“to suit, agree”). The same root surfaces in the learned ~avenir~ (“future,” what is “to come”) and in ~événement~ (“event,” something that “comes out”). Even ~aventure~ — what is “about to come” — belongs to this kin. To intervene is thus to insert a coming squarely in the middle of events.
en.intervertir: Borrowed from Latin ~intervertere~, a compound of ~inter-~ (“between”) and ~vertere~ (“to turn”). The Latin verb meant to turn something aside from its course, to divert or misappropriate it. French took it as a learned word. The simple verb ~vertere~ is the center of a large family: French ~verser~, ~version~, ~divertir~, ~convertir~, ~pervertir~ and ~inverser~ all descend from it or its relatives, and English has ~convert~, ~divert~, ~pervert~ and ~invert~, the last from a neighbouring Latin compound. In modern French ~intervertir~ is used for exchanging two things, as in ~intervertir les rôles~, or for reversing an order.
en.interviewer: A verb formed from the noun ~interview~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~, and the noun itself comes from English. The route is circular. English ~interview~ was taken from Old French ~entreveue~ (“a meeting”), a noun from ~entreveoir~, which joined ~entre-~ (“between”) to ~veoir~ (“to see”), from Latin ~videre~. French then borrowed the English word back, with its new sense of a journalist questioning a person, and gave it a regular first-group ending. So when a reporter ~interviewe~ someone, the word has crossed the Channel twice.
en.intimer: Borrowed from Latin ~intimāre~ (“to put in, to announce, to make known”), the verb of ~intimus~ (“innermost”), the same adjective that gave French ~intime~. English ~intimate~, in the sense “to hint, to announce,” comes from the same Latin verb. In French, ~intimer~ is a formal word, used for telling someone something with authority, as in ~intimer l'ordre de partir~ (“to order someone to leave”). It also has a legal sense, to summon someone to appear. The adjective ~intime~ and the noun ~intimité~ belong to the same family, but they developed along the other branch of the Latin word, that of closeness and privacy, while ~intimer~ kept the sense of forceful notification.
en.intimider: ~Intimider~ is analysed in two ways. French Wiktionary derives it from ~timide~ with the prefix ~in-~ and the suffix ~-er~, a parasynthetic formation meaning to make timid. English Wiktionary instead calls it a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ~intimidāre~ (“to make afraid”), itself built on Latin ~timidus~ (“afraid, timid”). Either way, the root is ~timidus~, which comes from the Latin verb ~timere~ (“to fear”). ~Timide~ and ~timoré~ belong to the same family. To intimidate is to cause someone to fear or to lose their nerve.
en.intituler:
From Latin ~intitulare~ (“to give a title to, to inscribe”), a derivative of ~titulus~ (“title, label, inscription, placard”). The origin of ~titulus~ is uncertain — possibly borrowed from Etruscan, the substrate that gave Latin several culture-words of obscure pedigree. From ~titulus~ the Romance languages drew their words for “title”: Spanish ~título~, Italian ~titolo~, and French ~titre~ (via Old French ~title~); English ~title~ and the tiny ~tittle~ (the dot over an i) are doublets from the very same Latin word.

In Roman use a ~titulus~ was an inscribed tablet or notice — the placard naming a thing, even the board nailed above the cross. To ~intituler~ a work is therefore literally to fix a heading on it, to give it its name, and the verb still means “to title, to entitle.” The reflexive ~s'intituler~ means “to be called, to bear the title of.” French keeps a rich family around ~titre~: ~titrer~ (“to give a title, to assay”), ~sous-titre~ (“subtitle”), ~titulaire~ (“holder, titular”), and the verb ~intituler~ itself, all turning on the idea of the name set at the head of a thing.
en.intoxiquer:
French ~intoxiquer~ is a learned re-formation on a Latin form *~intoxicāre~, which English Wiktionary gives with an asterisk. Latin ~intoxicāre~ is analyzed as ~in-~ plus ~toxicum~ (“poison”). The same Latin word had earlier come down by the popular route into Old French as ~entoschier~, so the verb exists in French twice: once in its worn-down medieval shape, which is now gone, and once in the scholarly spelling that restored the Latin form. French Wiktionary points to ~toxique~ for the root.

The learned shape is the one that survived. Modern ~intoxiquer~ means to poison, and it also has a figurative use: to saturate someone's mind with propaganda or false information. The noun ~intoxication~ and the adjective ~toxique~ belong to the family, as does ~désintoxiquer~ (“to detoxify”). English ~intoxicate~ is a separate borrowing from the Medieval Latin verb, and in English it came to describe drunkenness rather than poisoning.
en.intriguer:
French Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~intricāre~ (“to entangle, to embarrass”), while English Wiktionary says it was borrowed from Italian ~intrigare~; the two accounts differ on the route, and the sources do not settle it. Latin ~intricāre~ is built from ~in-~ (“in”) and ~trīcae~ (“hindrances, tangles, trifles”). The verb is a doublet of ~intriquer~. Spanish ~intrigar~ and English ~intrigue~ belong to the same family, the English verb being a borrowing from French.

The Latin sense is the literal one: to tangle someone in difficulties, to put them in a bind. In French the verb covers the tangles of plotting, so that to ~intriguer~ is to weave secret schemes and pull strings, and also a second, everyday sense: to puzzle or to arouse curiosity, as when an odd detail intrigues you. The two senses keep the original image of something knotted and hard to untangle. The family includes ~intrigue~, ~intrigant~ and ~intriqué~, and the learned ~inextricable~ is a distant relative through the Latin verb ~extricāre~, “to untangle.”
en.intriquer:
A learned borrowing of the twentieth century from Latin ~intrīcāre~ (“to entangle, to embroil”). The Latin verb is built on ~in-~ (“in”) and ~trīcae~ (“trifles, snarls, difficulties”). The same Latin verb reached French by another road and gave ~intriguer~, which is why the two French verbs are doublets: one came by that other road, the other is a fresh dip into the Latin source.

The Latin family is large. ~Extricāre~ (“to disentangle”) is the opposite verb, and its negative adjective lives on in French ~inextricable~ and English ~inextricable~. English ~intricate~ and French ~intrigue~ belong to the same family. ~Intriquer~ itself is a rare, learned verb, far less common than ~intriguer~, and it keeps the plain Latin meaning of getting something tangled up or becoming tangled.
en.introduire:
From Latin ~introducere~ (“to lead in, to bring inside”), a compound of the adverb ~intro~ (“inward, within”) and the verb ~ducere~ (“to lead, to conduct”). ~intro~ is itself built on ~in~ (“in”); ~ducere~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dewk-~ (“to lead, to draw”), which in the Germanic branch yields English ~tow~ and ~tug~ and German ~ziehen~ (“to pull”). Old French reshaped the inherited form as ~entreduire~ before the learned ~introduire~ prevailed. Cognate with English ~introduce~ and Italian ~introdurre~.

The literal image is of leading something or someone inward — across a threshold, into a room, into a society. French ~introduire~ keeps this concretely physical sense (to insert, to put in: ~introduire une clé dans la serrure~) alongside the social one (to introduce a person, to bring them into a circle) and the abstract (to introduce an idea, a law, a custom). The root *~dewk-~ is one of the great engines of French vocabulary through ~ducere~ and its participle ~ductus~: ~conduire~, ~produire~, ~réduire~, ~séduire~, ~traduire~, plus the nouns ~duc~ (“duke,” a leader), ~conduite~, and ~aqueduc~. To ~introduire~ is, etymologically, simply to lead in.
en.introniser:
From Late Latin ~inthronizāre~ (also spelled ~intronizāre~), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~enthronízein~ (“to place on a throne”), a verb formed from ~en~ (“in”) and ~thrónos~ (“throne”). The Late Latin ending ~-izāre~ is the usual way Latin transcribed Greek verbs in ~-ízein~, and French ~-iser~ descends from it. The Greek noun ~thrónos~ also passed into Latin as ~thronus~ and from there into French as ~trône~.

The French verb keeps the original sense of placing someone on a throne and extends it to inducting someone into an office. The same noun gave ~détrôner~ (“to dethrone”) and ~intronisation~ (“enthronement”). English ~enthrone~ is built on the same Greek noun, and the verb and its noun show the Greek prefix ~en~ rendered as ~in-~ in the Late Latin form.
en.intégrer:
From Latin ~integrāre~ (“to make whole, restore, renew”), a verb built on the adjective ~integer~ (“whole, intact, untouched”). That adjective is itself ~in-~ (“not”) plus a form related to ~tangere~ (“to touch”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~tag-~ (“to touch, handle”): the ~integer~ is literally the “untouched,” the thing left whole. The same root gives Latin ~tangere~, ~tactus~, and ~intāctus~. French ~intégrer~ entered first as a learned, rare word in the 14th century, then was effectively reborrowed in the 19th.

The arc of meaning runs from “to restore to wholeness” to “to make something part of a whole.” That second sense powers all the modern uses: to incorporate elements into a system, to admit a person into a group, to ~intégrer~ a prestigious school (a peculiarly French use meaning to gain admission), and the mathematician's “to integrate.” Because ~integer~ meant “untouched, undivided,” its descendants split between two notions — moral wholeness and numerical wholeness — so that the same root underlies both ~intégrité~ (uprightness) and the English ~integer~ (a whole number). Kin in modern French include ~intégral~, ~intégration~, ~réintégrer~, ~désintégrer~, and, through Old French, the everyday ~entier~ (“entire, whole”).
en.intéresser:
From Latin ~interesse~ (“to be among, to be between, to take part in”), a compound of the preposition ~inter~ (“between, among”) and ~esse~ (“to be”), the latter from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₁es-~ (“to be”) that also underlies English ~is~ and German ~ist~. From the impersonal Latin phrase ~interest~ (“it matters, it concerns”) French drew both the noun ~intérêt~ and, in the fourteenth century, the verb ~intéresser~. Italian preserves the parallel ~interessare~ and Spanish ~interesar~.

The semantic thread runs from physical position to mental engagement: what is literally “among” us, what lies “between” the parties, is what concerns them — and what concerns us is what holds our attention. So ~intéresser~ came to mean both “to involve someone, to give them a stake in something” and “to arouse someone's curiosity.” The financial sense survives in ~intéressement~, an employee profit-sharing scheme — a share, quite literally, in what is at stake. The same ~inter~ prefix runs through a crowd of French words such as ~international~, ~intervalle~, ~interrompre~, and ~entretenir~, while ~esse~ surfaces, much disguised, in ~essence~ and in the irregular forms of ~être~. To find something ~intéressant~ is, at root, to feel oneself caught up in the midst of it.
en.intérioriser: Formed from ~intérieur~ + ~-iser~, on the model of ~extérioriser~, with the sense “to make interior.” The adjective ~intérieur~ is borrowed from Latin ~interior~, the comparative of ~inter~ (“between, within”), so it means “more within.” The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and in French it turns adjectives and nouns into verbs meaning “to make A” or “to convert into N.” Here the thing made inward is typically a feeling, a rule or an idea.
en.invaginer: Formed with the prefix ~in-~ on Latin ~vagina~ (“sheath, scabbard”), as French Wiktionary describes it. The Latin word is also the source of French ~gaine~, which took its initial g- under Germanic influence, and of the learned ~vagin~, so ~gaine~ and ~vagin~ are doublets. Italian ~guaina~ and Spanish ~vaina~ are inherited cousins of ~gaine~. English ~invaginate~ follows the same Latin pattern, and the related ~engainer~ is built on ~gaine~ with ~en-~.
en.invalider: Formed from the adjective ~invalide~ with the verb ending ~-er~: to ~invalider~ is to make something invalid, such as an election or a ticket. The adjective comes from Latin ~invalidus~ (“weak, not strong”), made of ~in-~ (“not”) and ~validus~ (“strong”). French Wiktionary refers to ~valider~ for the positive counterpart, and the English gloss “void” captures the sense of stripping something of legal force.
en.invectiver: ~Invectiver~ is formed from the noun ~invective~ and the verbal ending ~-er~: to hurl invective at someone, to shout abuse. The noun is itself a substantivation of the adjective ~invectif~, with the word ~parole~ (“speech”) understood, so an ~invective~ was originally an abusive speech. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is the usual way French turns a noun into a verb.
en.inventer:
From Latin ~inventum~, the supine of ~invenīre~ (“to come upon, to find, to discover”), a compound of ~in-~ (“on, upon”) and ~venīre~ (“to come”). Latin ~venīre~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʷem-~ (“to come, to step”) — the very same root, remarkably, that surfaces in the Germanic branch as English ~come~ and German ~kommen~. To ~invenīre~ was literally to “come upon” something. The Spanish ~inventar~ shares the ancestry.

The semantic pivot is the difference between finding and making up: in Latin and early French the word leaned toward discovery — you ~invent~ a thing by coming upon what was already there (a sense fossilized in the legal and archaeological ~invention~, the “finding” of relics or treasure). Only by about 1450 did French ~inventer~ tip toward the modern sense of contriving something that did not exist before, and thence to the pejorative “to make up, to fabricate” (~inventer une excuse~). From the same ~venīre~ come a great crowd of French words — ~venir~, ~avenir~, ~événement~, ~convenir~, ~revenir~, ~souvenir~, ~prévenir~ — all turning on the idea of coming.
en.inventorier: ~Inventorier~ is derived from medieval Latin ~inventorium~, a variant of ~inventarium~ (“list of goods, inventory”), which gave Old French ~inventoire~. The Latin noun belongs to the family of ~invenīre~ (“to find”), since an inventory lists what has been found. The French verb means “to draw up an inventory,” and ~répertorier~ was formed in a very similar way. The related noun is ~inventaire~, and English ~inventory~ comes from the same Latin word.
en.inverser:
From Latin ~inversare~, a frequentative built on ~inversus~, the past participle of ~invertere~ (“to turn upside down”) — itself the prefix ~in-~ (“in, against”) joined to ~vertere~ (“to turn”). ~Vertere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~wertō~ and PIE *~wert-~ (“to turn”). The root is wide-flung: Sanskrit ~vártate~ (“it turns”), and, through Proto-Germanic, English ~-ward~ (as in “toward”) and ~worth~, which began as a verb meaning “to become, to turn into.”

French inherited the popular doublet ~envers~ (“wrong side, reverse”) directly, while ~inverser~ and the adjective ~inverse~ are the more learned, Latinate reborrowings of the same family. To ~inverser~ is to swap two things into each other's place, to reverse an order or a polarity. From ~vertere~ flowed an enormous progeny of French words built on its many prefixes: ~convertir~, ~divertir~, ~pervertir~, ~avertir~, ~revers~, ~version~, and ~vertige~ (the world quite literally “turning”). Few Latin verbs turned out to be so productive.
en.invertir:
~Invertir~ (“to invert”) is borrowed from Latin ~invertere~ (“to turn upside down, to turn around”), not inherited through Old French. The Latin verb was formed from ~in-~ (“in, toward”) and ~vertere~ (“to turn”). Because it entered French as a learned word, it kept the shape of its Latin model, and its sense of reversing something is the Latin one carried over almost unchanged.

The Latin verb ~vertere~ is the root of a large French family. Inherited from it is ~verser~ (“to pour, to tip over”). Learned descendants include ~version~, ~inverse~, ~inversion~ and ~invertir~ itself. English has taken the same Latin verb as ~invert~. In French ~invertir~ is a rare verb, and the more common ~inverser~ is the usual word in everyday use.
en.investir:
From Latin ~investīre~ (“to clothe, dress, surround”), from ~in-~ (“in, into”) + ~vestīre~ (“to dress, clothe”), itself from ~vestis~ (“garment, clothing”), from Proto-Indo-European *~wes-~ (“to clothe”). Cognate with Italian ~investire~ and Spanish ~investir~, and — through the same ~vestis~ — with French ~vêtir~, ~veste~, and ~vêtement~, and with English ~vest~ and ~vestment~.

The oldest sense was literal then ceremonial: to ~investir~ someone was to robe them in the insignia of an office, hence “to install in a dignity” — the source of ~investiture~, the medieval rite by which a lord clothed a vassal in his fief. From the garment that wraps came the military ~investir~ (“to besiege, to surround a place”), the army girding a town as cloth girds a body. The financial sense — to ~investir~ capital — is the most surprising turn: it arose in the early 1600s, probably through Italian ~investire~ in the East-Indies trade, on the image of giving money a new “dress,” clothing it in a fresh and profitable form. The same root yields ~travesti~ (“cross-dressed”), literally a re-clothing, and ~transvestisme~.
en.inviter:
From Latin ~invītāre~ (“to invite, to summon, to entertain”), attested in French from 1356. The deeper origin is genuinely uncertain: some scholars connect it to ~invocāre~ (“to call upon”), while others reconstruct a Proto-Indo-European base *~weyh₁-~ (“to chase, to pursue”), via a participle *~weyh₁-to-~ (“pursued, sought after”). Because the etymology is disputed, the chain beyond Latin is best left open. The Latin verb passed regularly into Italian ~invitare~, Spanish ~invitar~, and Catalan ~invitar~; English ~invite~ came in through Middle French ~inviter~.

The Latin sense already blended hospitality with enticement — to ~invītāre~ was to summon a guest but also to allure — and French preserves both shades, from ~inviter à dîner~ (“to invite to dinner”) to ~inviter à la prudence~ (“to urge caution”). A striking offshoot survives in card-playing: from the “luring” sense came Spanish and Catalan ~envidar~ (“to stake, to bet”), as a player invites the others to wager. In modern French the family stays compact — chiefly ~inviter~, ~invitation~, ~invité~, and ~invite~ (“an enticement”) — a small but sociable corner of the lexicon.
en.invoquer:
Borrowed from Latin ~invocare~ (“to call upon, to call for help”), from ~in-~ (“upon, toward”) + ~vocare~ (“to call”), the verb of ~vox~ (“voice”). ~Vox~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~wekʷ-~ (“to speak, to utter”), through the noun-form *~wṓkʷs~. Cognate with Italian ~invocare~ and Spanish ~invocar~; through the same PIE root, kin to Sanskrit ~vāc~ (“speech”) and, more distantly, to a great family of “voice” words.

The oldest sense is the sacred one: to call a god or higher power by name, to summon aid from above — one still « invoque Dieu » or « invoque les mânes » of the dead. From that solemn act the verb broadened to citing an authority or a text in argument (« invoquer la loi »), and then, more weakly still, to pleading a reason or excuse (« invoquer la fatigue »). The connecting thread is calling something up by naming it. From the same ~vox~ and ~vocare~ French keeps ~voix~ (“voice”), ~vocal~, ~évoquer~ (“to call to mind”), ~provoquer~, ~convoquer~, and ~révoquer~ — a whole family built on the act of the calling voice.
en.ioder: Formed from ~iode~ (“iodine”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so ~ioder~ means “to treat with iodine.” The element ~iode~ was named by the French chemist Gay-Lussac, in 1812 or 1813 according to the sources, from the Greek adjective ~ἰοειδής~ (~ioeidḗs~, “violet-colored”), because iodine gives off violet vapor when heated. The English word ~iodine~ comes from the same French coinage.
en.iodler: Attested in French in 1872 as ~iodler~, and in 1891 as ~jodler~. The TLFi derives it from the dialectal German ~jodeln~, recorded in 1796 and common in the Alemannic Alpine regions, where this kind of vocal music was practiced. ~Jodeln~ is an old alteration of ~joelen~ or ~jolen~, built on the imitative cry ~jo~ expressing joy, like Middle High German ~jôlen~ (“to shout for joy”) and Middle Dutch ~joelen~. From the same source French also took ~iouler~ (1840). The Académie sends ~iodler~ to ~iouler~, and French Wiktionary gives ~yodler~ as a variant.
en.ioniser: Formed from ~ion~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which here means “convert into, treat with N”: to ~ioniser~ is to turn atoms or molecules into ions. French ~ion~ is borrowed from English ~ion~, a word created by Michael Faraday from Greek ~ión~ (“going”). The suffix goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs.
en.iriser: ~Iriser~ means “to make iridescent.” English Wiktionary derives it from ~iris~ plus ~-er~, and French Wiktionary ties ~iris~ to Iris, the messenger of the gods in Greek myth, who had shining wings of every color. French Wiktionary adds, with a request for a reference, that poets called the rainbow the trace of her foot as she came down from Olympus; ~iris~ is also the Greek word for “rainbow.”
en.ironiser: Formed from the noun ~ironie~ with the verbal suffix ~-iser~: to speak or act ironically. ~Ironie~ is borrowed from Latin ~ironia~, itself from Ancient Greek ~eirōneía~, which French Wiktionary glosses as “questioning while feigning ignorance,” the Socratic manner. Classical Latin kept from the Greek only the notion of pretense: a joke or mockery hidden under a serious tone, which consists in saying the opposite of what one means.
en.irradier: ~Irradier~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~irradiāre~ (“to shine into”). The Latin verb combines ~in-~ (“in, into”) with ~radiāre~ (“to emit rays”), a verb built on ~radius~ (“ray”). In French it means to irradiate, to shed rays on or through something. Its relatives in French include ~radier~, which also comes from ~radiāre~, and ~radiation~.
en.irriguer: A learned borrowing from Latin ~irrigāre~ (“to lead water onto, to water”), made of ~in-~ (“onto”), assimilated to ~ir-~ before the following ~r~, and ~rigāre~ (“to water, to moisten”). French kept the agricultural sense of watering land by channels and added a medical one, in which blood ~irrigue~ a tissue. English ~irrigate~ and Italian ~irrigare~ are borrowings of the same Latin verb.
en.irriter: Borrowed from Latin ~irrītāre~ (“to excite, to provoke, to rouse to anger”), a verb whose own origin within Latin is obscure. The same Latin verb gave Spanish and Portuguese ~irritar~ and Italian ~irritare~, and English ~irritate~. In French it covers both the emotional sense, to annoy or anger, and the physical one, to inflame a tissue or skin, as seen in ~irritant~, ~irritation~ and ~irritable~.
en.islamiser: Formed in French from ~islam~ and the verb suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to convert to Islam” or “to make Islamic.” The noun ~islam~ is borrowed from Arabic ~ʾislām~ (“submission to God”), and names both the religion and, in the older usage, the act of surrender to the divine will. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and it is regularly used to build verbs meaning “to convert into” or “to make A.”
en.isoler:
