Borrowed in the seventeenth century from Italian ~isolare~ (“to make into an island, to set apart”), itself from ~isola~ (“island”), from Latin ~īnsula~ (“island”). The French adjective ~isolé~ was attested slightly earlier, taken from Italian ~isolato~ (Latin ~īnsulātus~, “made into an island”), and the verb was back-formed from it. Latin ~īnsula~ is also the source of Italian ~isola~, Spanish ~isla~, and — through a different route, with ~île~ — French itself; English ~isle~ and ~isolated~ belong to the same family.

The earliest French use, in 1653, was strictly geographic: a branch of the Nile was said to ~isoler~ a meadow, to cut it off like an island. From there the meaning spread to any setting-apart — a hermit who ~s'isole~, a patient in quarantine, a wire that one must ~isoler~ electrically (hence the English “insulate”). The development was reinforced by the native French ~seul~ (“alone”), which colored the verb toward solitude. The same ~īnsula~ yields a large modern family: ~isolation~, ~isolement~, ~isolant~ (“insulator, insulating”), ~isolateur~, ~isoloir~ (the voting booth), and the geographic ~presqu'île~ (“peninsula,” a calque of Latin ~paene īnsula~, “almost an island”).
en.issir:
From Old French ~issir~ (also ~eissir~, “to go out, to come forth”), from Latin ~exīre~ (“to go out, depart”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~īre~ (“to go”). ~Īre~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₁ey-~ (“to go”), one of the great verbs of motion, cognate with Greek ~eîmi~ (“I will go”) and Sanskrit ~éti~ (“he goes”). Romance kin include Italian ~uscire~ (from a related ~ūsciō~) and the Spanish noun reflexes of the same family.

In medieval French, ~issir~ was a fully living verb meaning “to exit.” Then it lost its own battle for survival: in the sixteenth century speakers increasingly preferred ~sortir~, and by the seventeenth ~issir~ had all but vanished as a conjugated verb. Yet it did not die — it fossilized into its participles. The past participle ~issu~ (“descended from, born of”) is thoroughly alive (“~issu~ d'une famille modeste”), and the noun ~issue~ (“a way out, an outcome”) is one of the most common words in French. The same ~exīre~ surfaces in the borrowed ~exit~, and the root ~īre~ underlies a scattered band of French descendants from the verb ~aller~’s suppletive forms to nouns like ~transit~ and ~initiation~ — wanderings, all, of a verb that simply meant “to go.”
en.italianiser: Formed from ~italien~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which turns a noun or adjective into a verb meaning “to make like” or “to convert to.” ~Italien~ is borrowed from Italian ~italiano~. The verb means “to make Italian,” that is, to give something an Italian character.
en.itérer: Borrowed from Latin ~iterāre~ (“to do again, to repeat”), a verb built on the adverb ~iterum~ (“again, a second time”). The same Latin verb gave Italian ~iterare~ and Spanish ~iterar~, and English has ~iterate~ from it. The learned family in French includes ~itératif~, ~itération~ and, with the prefix ~re-~, ~réitérer~, which is far commoner in everyday speech and means “to repeat, to do again.” The bare ~itérer~ is rare and technical. It is used above all in mathematics and computing, for repeating a calculation or a loop so as to approach a result by successive steps. In that sense the English ~iterate~ and its noun ~iteration~ are in everyday use among programmers.
en.ixer: ~Ixer~ is a verb built on the name of the letter X. French Wiktionary explains that the letter, pronounced “iks”, is respelled as it sounds, ~ix~ or ~ixe~, and English Wiktionary likewise calls it a phonetic transcription of the letter. The first-conjugation ending ~-er~ is then added. The result is a verb meaning “to X-rate”, that is, to make something X-rated.
en.jabler: This cooper's verb, “to cut the groove in barrel staves”, is formed from the noun ~jable~ (the groove itself) with the ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Latin ~gabalus~ (“cross, gallows”), which French Wiktionary traces to Gaulish *~gabalos~ (“fork”). Celtic cognates are Irish ~gabhal~, Welsh ~gafl~ and Breton ~gaol~, all with the sense of a fork.
en.jaboter: Built on ~jabot~ with the verb ending ~-er~, and first used by Gherardi. The noun ~jabot~ (a bird's crop) has an uncertain origin: one account traces it to Gaulish *~gaba~ (“beak, mouth”), another links it to ~gaver~ (“to force-feed”), and a third proposes a Celtic borrowing. The verb means “to jabber,” as if chattering from the throat.
en.jacasser: ~Jacasser~ is said to be an alteration of ~jacqueter~. English Wiktionary instead derives it from ~jacques~ (“magpie”), noting that male first names were often given to birds, as with ~pierrot~ (“sparrow”). The two accounts agree on the picture: the verb first described the harsh chatter of a magpie, then, figuratively, people who chatter or jabber on.
en.jacter: ~Jacter~ is a shortened form of ~jacqueter~, an older verb meaning to chatter or chat, now dated, which is attested in the sixteenth century. French Wiktionary gives as its source ~jaquette~ (“magpie”) or ~jacque~ (“jay”), and relates it to ~jacasser~ (“to chatter”). Modern ~jacter~ is an informal word for talking or chatting.
en.jaillir:
The origin of ~jaillir~ is uncertain, but the favored account is Celtic. French Wiktionary derives Old French ~galir~ and ~jalir~ from Gaulish *~gali-~ (“to boil, to gush, to well up”), related to a Gaulish noun *~galia~ (“strength”), and compares Irish ~gailim~ (“I boil”). English Wiktionary is more cautious: possibly from a Vulgar Latin verb *~galīre~, itself from Transalpine Gaulish *~gali-~. Both accounts agree on the Gaulish root, so the verb would be one of the few French words surviving from the Celtic language spoken in Gaul, though the intermediate Latin step is a conjecture.

French Wiktionary lists the Old French forms ~galir~, ~jalir~ and ~jaillir~ side by side, and the modern spelling is the last of these. The image is of liquid boiling up and bursting forth: water springs, flames, sparks and light all ~jaillissent~, and the same verb serves figuratively for ideas, cries and truths that burst out. The prefixed ~rejaillir~ (“to spurt back, to splash up”) and the words ~jaillissement~ and ~jaillissant~ continue the family. A Celtic root, if the account is right, would thus be preserved in a verb of sudden, vigorous movement.
en.jalonner: Formed in French from the noun ~jalon~ (“marker stake”) and the suffix ~-er~, so ~jalonner~ means to mark out a line or route with stakes. The base ~jalon~ is attested from 1613 in the spelling ~jallon~, and its origin is uncertain. French sources cite the German dictionary FEW, which proposes a link to ~jaillir~ (“to spurt out”), and Auguste Scheler instead linked it to ~jauger~ (“to gauge”). Both are only suggestions. The suffix ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~. The verb also works figuratively: a career or a story is ~jalonné~ by its key events.
en.jalouser: ~Jalouser~ is formed from the adjective ~jaloux~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so it means to be jealous of someone, to envy. The adjective was inherited from Old French ~jalous~, from Late Latin ~zēlōsus~ (“full of zeal”), from ~zēlus~, which comes from Ancient Greek ~zêlos~ (“zeal, jealousy”). Italian ~geloso~ and Spanish ~celoso~ are cognates. The modern ending ~-oux~ is now thought to come from Old Occitan ~gelos~ rather than being inherited straight from Latin, which would have given ~-eux~. The Greek word is also the source of ~zèle~, so ~jaloux~ and ~zèle~ share a Greek ancestor.
en.japoniser: Formed from ~Japon~ (“Japan”) with the suffix ~-iser~, in the sense “to make Japanese” or “to give a Japanese character to.” The country name came into French from Portuguese ~Japão~, which goes back through Malay and Hokkien to Chinese ~日本~, “the land of the rising sun.” Marco Polo's ~Cipango~ is an earlier form of the same name. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, itself from Greek. So the verb joins a Chinese name carried by Portuguese sailors to a Greek-Latin ending.
en.japper:
French ~japper~ (“to yap, to yelp”) comes from Middle French ~japper~, from Old French ~japer~ (“to bark, to howl, to scream”), a word related to Old Occitan ~japar~ (“to bark”). French Wiktionary gives the Occitan form as the source, while English Wiktionary treats it as a relative; the two lines of descent are close in any case. The ultimate origin is probably Germanic, perhaps through Frankish *~galpōn~ (“to boast, to brag, to bark”), from Proto-Germanic *~galpōną~ (“to sound out, to boast”).

The Germanic link rests on a set of cognates: Old Saxon ~galpōn~ (“to cry loudly, to brag”), Low German ~galpen~ (“to bark, to howl”), Middle High German ~gelpfen~ (“to scream, to bark, to boast”), Old Norse ~gjalpa~ (“to yelp”) and Swedish dialectal ~galpa~ (“to cry”). English ~yap~ is also worth comparing. The Frankish step is only suggested, so the safest summary is that ~japper~ is a verb of probable Germanic stock, now used of small dogs and of people who chatter shrilly.
en.jardiner: ~Jardiner~ is formed from ~jardin~ with the verb ending ~-er~: to garden is to work a garden. ~Jardin~ comes from Old French ~jardin~ and Medieval Latin ~jardinus~ (or ~gardinium~), from Old Frankish *~gardin~, the oblique case of *~gardō~ (“enclosure, yard”). That word descends from Proto-Germanic *~gardô~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʰordʰos~ (“hedge, enclosure”). Its native cousins are Old High German ~gart~ and English ~yard~, while English ~garden~ came through an Anglo-Norman variant.
en.jargonner: Formed from ~jargon~ + the verb ending ~-er~, “to speak jargon, to babble.” French has two words ~jargon~ in the sources. One is inherited from Old French ~jargon~ (“chirping of birds”), from a root ~garg~ imitating the sound of the throat, and so related to ~gorge~ and ~gargariser~; its initial ~j~ is a softened ~g~, as in ~jambe~. The other was borrowed from Italian ~giargone~ (“a variety of diamond”) and is a doublet of ~zircon~. From the thirteenth to the eighteenth century ~jargon~ also named the language, judged secret or hard to understand, of thieves, beggars and other outsiders, before ~argot~ replaced it.
en.jarreter: Formed from the noun ~jarret~ (“hamstring, back of the knee”) with the ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, giving the sense “to wear a garter.” The noun ~jarret~ is traced to Gaulish *~garra~ (“leg”), which English Wiktionary places behind a Vulgar Latin form. The Gaulish word is related to Welsh ~gar~ and goes back to Proto-Celtic *~garros~, whose own origin is uncertain.
en.jaser: The origin of ~jaser~ (“to chat, to gossip”) is uncertain. French Wiktionary proposes, as a probability, that it shares the stem *~gas-~ with ~gazouiller~ (“to chirp, to babble”). English Wiktionary likewise calls it probably onomatopoeic. The two views fit together: a word that imitates the sound of chatter would naturally resemble other words for small, rapid noises. No Latin or Germanic source is established, so the verb is best treated as an expressive formation.
en.jasper: Formed from the noun ~jaspe~ (“jasper”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, which turns a noun into a verb. To ~jasper~ is to mottle or vein a surface, such as the edge of a book or a piece of wood, so that it looks like the stone. The noun ~jaspe~ comes from Latin ~iaspis~. The ending ~-er~ descends from the Latin ending ~-are~ of first-conjugation infinitives, as in ~cantare~, which gave ~chanter~.
en.jaspiner: Probably a cross between ~jaser~ (“to chatter”) and an unrecorded *~japiner~, itself derived from ~japper~ (“to yap”) with the colloquial suffix ~-iner~. ~Japper~ goes back to Old French ~japer~ (“to bark, to scream”), related to Old Occitan ~japar~, and its remote origin is probably Germanic, though the Frankish step is only suggested. The result is a slang verb meaning “to speak.”
en.jauger: Formed from the noun ~jauge~ and the verb ending ~-er~, via Old French ~jaugier~ and Middle French ~jauger~, “to measure with a gauge.” The noun ~jauge~ comes from Old French, which took it from Frankish *~galga~ (“measuring rod, pole”), from Proto-Germanic *~galgô~ (“pole, stake, cross”). Its cognates include Old English ~ġealga~ and Old Norse ~galgi~ (“cross-beam, gallows”). English ~gauge~ is a relative of the same Old French word.
en.jaunir: Formed from the adjective ~jaune~ with ~-ir~, the ending used for verbs meaning “to become” or “to make” the quality: to turn yellow, or to make yellow. ~Jaune~ is attested in Old French as ~jalne~ in 1080, and comes from Latin ~galbinus~, a derivative of ~galbus~ (“pale green, yellow”). The same Latin word thus gave French its yellow, and the verb is a later formation from it.
en.javeler: ~Javeler~ is formed from ~javelle~, the bundle of cut grain stalks left to dry in the field, plus the verbal ending ~-er~. The verb means to lay cut cereal out in such bundles. The noun ~javelle~ comes from Latin ~gabella~, which was itself borrowed from Gaulish ~gabali~ (“taking, seizure”), a word related to Middle Irish ~gabáil~ (“to take”). The ending ~-er~ is the usual way French turns a noun into a verb, here in the sense of working with or applying the noun.
en.javelliser: ~Javelliser~ is formed from ~javel~ and the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to disinfect with bleach.” ~Javel~ is a shortening of ~eau de Javel~, a name that comes from the village of Javel, now a district of Paris, where the product was first made. The suffix ~-iser~ here has the sense “to treat with,” as in ~pasteuriser~. The verb thus preserves a place name inside a technical term for chlorinating water.
en.jerker: ~Jerker~ (“to dance the jerk”) is formed from the noun ~jerk~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. French ~jerk~ is a borrowing from English ~jerk~, the name of a dance of the 1960s. The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, is the default way French turns a borrowed word into a verb, as in ~filtrer~ or ~coder~. English ~jerk~ itself is the word for a sharp, sudden movement, which suits the dance's abrupt style.
en.jeter:
From Old French ~jeter~ (“to throw”), from Vulgar Latin *~jectāre~, from Latin ~jactāre~ (“to toss about, to fling repeatedly”), the frequentative of ~jacere~ (“to throw”). A frequentative names a repeated or vigorous action, so ~jactāre~ is “to keep throwing, to hurl about.” ~Jacere~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~Hyeh₁-~ (“to throw, to let fly”). Cognate with Italian ~gettare~ and Spanish ~echar~.

That buried ~jacere~ is one of the most productive roots in the learned vocabulary: its past participle ~iactus~ and its compounds gave a long file of French words in ~-jeter~ and ~-jecter~ — ~projeter~ and ~projet~ (“thrown forward”), ~rejeter~ (“thrown back”), ~injecter~ (“thrown in”), ~objet~ (“thrown before”), ~sujet~ (“thrown under”), and ~trajet~ (“a throwing across”). The plain verb keeps the simple gesture of casting away, which is why ~jeter~ ranges from hurling a stone to throwing out the rubbish to “casting” a glance (~jeter un coup d'œil~). Even ~jeton~ — a thrown-down counter — and the cast water of a ~jet~ d'eau trace back to the same Latin act of letting fly.
en.jeûner:
~Jeûner~ is inherited from Old French ~jeüner~, which comes from Latin ~iēiūnāre~ (“to fast”), a verb built on the adjective ~iēiūnus~ (“fasting, hungry”). Because it is inherited, it reached French through ordinary speech rather than as a borrowing from written Latin. The Latin verb also lives on in Spanish ~ayunar~ (“to fast”), so the Romance languages kept one common word for going without food.

French built several words on this stem. The noun ~jeûne~ names the fast itself, and ~déjeuner~ is, etymologically, the breaking of the fast, from Old French ~desjeüner~ (~des-~ + ~jeüner~). ~Dîner~ is traditionally traced to the same stem. English took the adjective straight from Latin as ~jejune~, which now means “dull, lacking substance.”
en.jobarder: Formed from the noun ~jobard~ (“simpleton, dupe”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so the verb means to treat someone as a ~jobard~, that is, to fool or trick them. The noun is itself derived from Old French ~jobe~ (“fool, simpleton”) with the suffix ~-ard~, which often marks a person with a pronounced trait. The ending ~-er~ goes back to Latin ~-are~, the ending of first-conjugation verbs.
en.jodler: Borrowed from Alpine German ~jodeln~ (recorded 1796), the vocal style of Upper Bavaria, the Tyrol, Carinthia and Switzerland. French has it as ~iodler~ in 1872 and ~jodler~ in 1891. ~Jodeln~ is itself an old alteration of ~joelen~ or ~jolen~, built on the imitative cry ~jo~, which expresses joy. Middle High German ~jôlen~ and Middle Dutch ~joelen~ (“to shout for joy”) are relatives, as is German ~johlen~ (“to yell”). From the same cry French also drew ~iouler~ (1840), to which the Académie's dictionary refers readers.
en.jogger: Borrowed from English ~jog~ and given the French verbal ending ~-er~, like many other English loans in modern French. The French verb means “to go jogging,” to run at a gentle, regular pace for exercise. English ~jog~ is the source word, and French also took the related noun ~jogging~ from English. The verb is a recent arrival, and it follows the regular first-group conjugation, which is why English verbs so easily acquire French endings.
en.joindre:
From Latin ~jungere~ (“to join, yoke, unite”), descended from the Proto-Indo-European root *~yewg-~ (“to join, yoke”). This is one of the deepest and most widespread roots in Indo-European: it gives Sanskrit ~yoga~ (“union, yoking”), Greek ~zeugnumi~ (“I yoke”), German ~Joch~, and the English ~yoke~ — itself a cognate of the very root, alongside the borrowed ~join~ and ~junction~. Italian ~giungere~ and Spanish ~juntar~ are the Romance kin.

The Latin sense of binding two things together survives intact: one can ~joindre~ two pieces of wood, ~joindre les mains~ (clasp the hands), ~joindre l'utile à l'agréable~ (combine the useful and the pleasant), or — in a thoroughly modern turn — ~joindre~ someone by telephone, that is, reach them. The past participle ~joint~ also names a seal or gasket. The root's reach in French is enormous: ~jonction~, ~adjoindre~, ~rejoindre~, ~conjoint~ (“spouse,” one yoked together with you), ~disjoindre~, ~jointure~, and the borrowed joindre-family aside, even ~joug~ (“yoke”) itself descends from ~jungere~'s noun ~jugum~. From an ox's wooden yoke to a married couple to a phone call, all are, at heart, a yoking-together.
en.jointoyer: ~Jointoyer~ is formed from ~joint~ with the suffix ~-oyer~, and means to fill or finish the joints between stones or bricks, usually with mortar. The noun ~joint~ is the past participle of ~joindre~ used as a noun, from Latin ~iūnctus~. The suffix ~-oyer~ comes from Old French ~-oiier~, from Late Latin ~-izāre~, and is no longer used to coin new verbs, which makes ~jointoyer~ an older formation.
en.joncer: Formed from the noun ~jonc~ (“rush, cane”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, which comes from Latin ~-are~ and turns a noun into a verb. The noun ~jonc~ descends from Latin ~iuncus~ (“bulrush; cane made from a bulrush”) by way of Old and Middle French. The verb names the work of covering a chair with such plant material, rattan being the cane in question.
en.joncher: Formed from ~jonc~ (“reed, rush”) plus the verb ending ~-er~. ~Jonc~ is inherited from Old French ~jonc~, by way of Middle French, from Latin ~iuncus~ (“bulrush; cane made from a bulrush”). English Wiktionary notes that stalks of cane were often used as a floor covering in the Middle Ages, a practice that may lie behind the verb's sense of covering a surface with scattered things.
en.jongler:
From Old French ~jogler~ (attested around 1160), itself from Latin ~ioculārī~ (“to joke, to jest”), a verb built on ~iocus~ (“joke”), the word that also stands behind English ~joke~ and ~jocular~. The modern form, with its nasal vowel, shows the influence of a second Old French verb, ~jangler~ (“to chatter, to joke,” twelfth century), which French Wiktionary traces to Frankish *~jangalôn~. The verb is thus a Latin word reshaped by a Germanic one.

English took the verb from Old French as well, and ~juggle~ comes from the same ~jogler~. Both Old French verbs belonged to the world of amusing an audience, and ~jongler~ kept that spirit. The sources do not trace the steps from joking to handling balls, so the link between the two senses is left open here. In modern French ~jongler~ means “to juggle,” and also, figuratively, to keep several things in the air at once, such as schedules or figures. The family also includes ~jongleur~ (“juggler, entertainer”) and ~jonglage~ (“juggling”).
en.joualiser: Formed from ~joual~ with the verb suffix ~-iser~, meaning to speak joual, the working-class sociolect of Quebec. The word ~joual~ is a spelling of the way ~cheval~ (“horse”) sounds in that speech. By the account in the sources, it was first used in this sense in 1938 by Claude-Henri Grignon, then became widely known in 1959 when André Laurendeau used it in the newspaper Le Devoir. Brother Untel, Jean-Paul Desbiens, is often wrongly credited with coining it. The suffix ~-iser~ here means to act or speak in the manner of the base.
en.jouer:
From Old French ~joer~, ~jouer~ (“to play, jest, frolic”), from Latin ~iocāre~ (“to joke, jest”), a Vulgar-Latin variant of the Classical deponent ~iocārī~, from the noun ~iocus~ (“joke, jest, game”). Cognate with Italian ~giocare~, Spanish ~jugar~, and Portuguese ~jogar~; from ~iocus~ English borrowed ~joke~ and ~jocular~.

A quiet upset hides here: Classical Latin's main verb for playing was ~lūdere~ (the source of ~ludique~ and ~illusion~), while ~iocārī~ meant narrowly to jest with words. Over Late Latin the joking verb broadened to cover all play and amusement and ousted ~lūdere~ from everyday speech, so French inherited ~jouer~ for everything from children's games to performing music and acting a role. From the related noun ~iocus~ came ~jeu~ (“game”), and from ~jeu~ the reduplicated nursery word ~joujou~ and the toy ~jouet~. The word's reach in modern French is remarkably wide — one ~joue~ a sport, an instrument, a part on stage, a card, the stock market, and even, figuratively, with someone's feelings — all descended from a Roman word that meant, at first, merely a good-natured joke.
en.jouir:
Attested at the start of the twelfth century, ~jouir~ comes through Old French ~joïr~ from Latin ~gaudēre~ (“to rejoice, to take inner delight in”), which in Vulgar Latin shifted to ~gaudīre~, joining the productive ~-īre~ conjugation. ~gaudēre~ is thought to derive, by way of an unattested *~gāvidus~, from a Proto-Indo-European root *~geh₂u-~ (“to rejoice”), with Greek cognates such as ~gánumai~ (“to be glad”). From ~gaudēre~ Latin also formed ~gaudium~ (“joy”), source of French ~joie~ and English ~joy~.

The Latin sense was broad, warm delight, and Old French ~joïr~ kept it. French then specialized the verb toward possession and benefit: to ~jouir~ de quelque chose is to enjoy the use of it, hence the legal ~jouissance~ (“usufruct, enjoyment of a right”). Alongside this practical sense the word also narrowed, from the twelfth century onward, toward intense bodily pleasure, and in modern French ~jouir~ used absolutely means to reach sexual climax — a development already plain in eighteenth-century literature. The same ~gaud-~ root surfaces in French ~jouissance~, ~joie~, ~réjouir~ (“to gladden”), and the borrowed ~gaudriole~ — a startling spread from a single Latin verb of rejoicing.
en.jouter:
~Jouter~ comes from Old French ~joster~, inherited from Vulgar Latin *~iuxtāre~, a late verb meaning “to be adjacent,” itself built on the Latin adverb and preposition ~iuxtā~ (“close to, next to”). The same Latin source gave French a second verb, ~jouxter~, the learned and more conservative form that keeps the ~x~ and means “to adjoin.” The two are cousins that split apart in form and in sense.

The pair shows how one Latin word can yield a doublet: ~jouxter~ stayed close to the written Latin and kept the meaning of neighboring, while ~jouter~ took the popular path through Old French and is the verb for medieval tilting, the sporting combat between mounted knights. Today ~jouter~ survives in this historical sense, and figuratively for a lively verbal contest. English ~joust~ was borrowed from the Old French verb. The Latin ~iuxtā~ also lies behind the learned prefix ~juxta-~, as in ~juxtaposer~ (“to place side by side”).
en.jouxter:
French ~jouxter~ (“to adjoin, to border on”) is a learned verb whose sources give two slightly different routes. French Wiktionary derives it from Late Latin ~juxtāre~ (“to be adjacent”), from Latin ~iuxtā~ (“beside, close to”). English Wiktionary derives it from an older ~jouxte~, a form respelled to match its Latin ancestor ~iūxta~, and compares ~jouter~.

That comparison hides a surprise. The ordinary French verb ~jouter~ (“to joust”) is related to the same Latin source, and English ~joust~ was borrowed from the Old French verb. Back in learned French, the Latin preposition ~iuxtā~ also produced ~juxtaposer~ (“to place side by side”), and ~jouxter~ itself is now rare and mostly found in legal and administrative language. The ~x~ in its spelling is a reminder that it was reshaped to look like its Latin source.
en.jubiler: Borrowed from Latin ~iūbilāre~ (“to shout for joy”), which gave Old French ~jubler~. The resemblance to ~jubilé~ (“jubilee”) is a trap: French Wiktionary states that the two words have no common etymology. English ~jubilant~ and French ~jubilation~ come from the same Latin verb.
en.jucher: ~Jucher~ (“to perch”) is inherited from Old French ~juchier~ or ~joquier~ (“to perch”). The French Wiktionary treats it as a verb formed on the noun ~juc~, itself from Old French ~joc~, which English Wiktionary glosses as “chicken roost.” The verb is therefore, at root, to go up to a roost. The ending ~-er~ is the Latin first-conjugation ending ~-are~ in French dress. ~Jucher~ is used of birds and, humorously or figuratively, of people sitting high up.
en.judaïser:
From Latin ~jūdaizāre~, in classical spelling ~iūdaizāre~, a verb meaning “to follow Jewish customs.” The Latin word is a borrowing of Greek ~ἰουδαΐζειν~, built from ~Ἰουδαῖος~ (“Jew, Judean”) and the Greek verbal suffix ~-ίζειν~. That suffix is the ancestor of French ~-iser~, so ~judaïser~ carries the ending of ~civiliser~ and ~organiser~ in a much older form. In French the verb means to adopt Jewish practices or to impose them on others.

The Latin noun ~Iūdaeus~ (“Jew”) is also the source of French ~juif~, which came through Old French, and of the learned ~judaïsme~, ~judaïque~ and ~judéen~. The diaeresis in ~judaïser~ shows that the ~a~ and the ~i~ are pronounced separately, as in ~naïf~ and ~haïr~. English has borrowed the same verb as ~Judaize~, so the two languages share the Greek suffix as well as the root. The verb is rare today and belongs to historical, religious and literary writing, where it describes movements or persons said to lean toward Jewish observance.
en.judiciariser: ~Judiciariser~ (“to judicialize”) is formed from the adjective ~judiciaire~ with the suffix ~-iser~, “to make, to convert into”: to bring a matter under the courts or turn a social or political question into a legal one. The adjective ~judiciaire~ is borrowed from Latin ~jūdiciārius~ (“relating to justice or to the courts”), which derives from ~jūdicāre~ (“to judge”). The ending ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and it is the usual way of making verbs from adjectives in technical and administrative French.
en.juger:
From Latin ~jūdicāre~ (“to judge, to pass sentence”), itself transparently a compound of ~jūs~ (“law, right”) and the verb ~dīcere~ (“to say, to pronounce”) — so that to judge was literally “to speak the law.” Latin ~jūs~ derives, through Proto-Italic ~jowos~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂yew-~ (“right, justice”), while ~dīcere~ goes back to *~deyḱ-~ (“to show, to point out”), the root that also gives English ~teach~ and ~token~. Italian ~giudicare~ and Spanish ~juzgar~ are the sister forms; English ~judge~ arrives through Old French ~jugier~.

The agent noun ~jūdex~ (“one who declares the law,” our ~judge~) shows the compound at work: in Roman practice what made law was not the doing of it but the solemn pronouncing of it, and from this act of speech sprang a whole vocabulary — ~iūdicium~, ~iūrisdictio~, and the rest. In French the verb spread from the courtroom into everyday assessment: to judge a distance, to deem something wise, to form an opinion. The same root family flowers richly: ~jugement~, ~juge~, ~préjuger~ and its noun ~préjugé~, ~déjuger~, ~méjuger~, and the legal ~jury~ borrowed back through English. Tucked inside this common verb is a memory of the Roman magistrate gravely speaking the right into being.
en.juguler:
~Juguler~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~iugulāre~ (“to cut the throat, to kill”). The Latin verb is built on ~iugulum~ (“throat, collarbone”), a word generally linked to ~iugum~ (“yoke”). French took the verb straight from Latin, as a scholarly word, and not through the long chain of Old French that shapes inherited verbs.

In Latin the verb described a violent act against a person; the modern French sense, “to stamp out, to do away with,” is figurative. The same Latin family gives French ~jugulaire~, which is both the adjective for the throat veins and the name of a helmet's chin strap, and English ~jugular~.
en.jumeler: ~Jumeler~ (“to twin, to pair up”) is formed from the noun ~jumeau~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~jumeau~ is a variant of an older form, Old French ~jumel~ or ~gemel~, from Latin ~gemellus~, a diminutive of ~geminus~ (“twin”). The change from ~gemel~ to ~jumel~ is attributed to labialisation, the vowel being rounded next to ~m~. The related Italian ~gemello~ and Spanish ~gemelo~ come from the same Latin word. The suffix ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, here gives the sense “to make into twins,” and by extension to join two things as a pair.
en.juponner: Formed from the noun ~jupon~ (“petticoat”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so it means roughly “to dress, to plump up” with a petticoat. ~Jupon~ was inherited from Middle French and is itself built on ~jupe~ (“skirt”) with the suffix ~-on~. The verb is therefore a French formation, two steps removed from its base: ~jupe~ gives ~jupon~, and ~jupon~ gives the verb.
en.jurer:
Inherited from Old French ~jurer~ (“to swear, to take an oath,” and also “to betroth”), from Latin ~iurare~ (also written ~jurare~), “to swear,” the verb of the noun ~ius~ (“law, right, what is binding”). Cognate with Italian ~giurare~ and Spanish ~jurar~; through the noun ~ius~ it belongs to the family that gave English ~jury~, ~just~, and ~judge~, while the act itself parallels English ~swear~.

To ~jurer~ was first to bind oneself by a solemn oath, calling law or the gods to guarantee one's word — « jurer fidélité », « jurer sur la Bible ». From that grave sense the verb developed two everyday descendants. One is to curse or swear profanely — to utter a ~juron~ (“a swear-word”) — as a charretier (carter) was proverbially said to do (« jurer comme un charretier »). The other, more surprising, is a sense of clashing: two colors that « jurent » together are ones that grate against each other, an oath turned into visual discord. From the same ~ius~ French keeps ~juré~ (“juror”), ~jury~, ~juridique~, ~justice~, and ~parjure~ (“perjury”) — the whole vocabulary of law and the sworn word.
en.justifier:
From Latin ~justificare~ (“to make just, to render righteous”), a compound of ~justus~ (“just, righteous”) + the combining form of ~facere~ (“to make, to do”). ~Justus~ derives from ~jus~ (“law, right”), from an Old Latin ~iovestos~ resting on the stem of ~jus~, and ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂yew-~, denoting binding law or sacred formula. Through ~jus~ the word is cognate with English ~just~, ~jury~, and ~judge~; through ~facere~, from PIE *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, to set”), it joins a vast Indo-European family.

First a theological and legal word — “to make righteous,” “to clear of a charge” — ~justifier~ then drifted toward the everyday “to give good reason for, to vindicate.” A delightful late detour is the typographer's sense: to ~justifier~ a line of text is to make its margins straight and “right,” spacing the words until the edge is even — the abstract idea of rectitude turned into the literal squaring of a column. The root ~jus~ runs deep in French through ~juste~, ~justice~, ~juger~, ~jury~, and ~juridique~, while ~facere~ surfaces in countless verbs in ~-fier~, among them ~vérifier~, ~modifier~, and ~simplifier~.
en.juter: ~Juter~ is formed from ~jus~ and the ending ~-er~, with an added ~t~ that is also found in ~juteux~. This ~t~ is called epenthetic: it is not part of the base, but slips in between the stem and the ending. The verb means “to give off juice,” or, transitively, “to juice.” The same intruding ~t~ gives the adjective ~juteux~ (“juicy”).
en.juxtaposer: The sources give two accounts. French Wiktionary derives ~juxtaposer~ from ~poser~ with the prefix ~juxta-~ (“beside”), itself from Latin ~iuxta~ (“near, beside”). English Wiktionary offers that same analysis or a direct borrowing from Latin ~iūxtāpōnō~. The base ~poser~ comes from Late Latin ~pausare~ (“to halt”), which came to carry the sense of placing that belonged to Latin ~ponere~. Either way the verb means to set things side by side.
en.kidnapper: Borrowed from English ~kidnap~, which French adopted as a verb ending in ~-er~. French Wiktionary analyzes the English word as a compound of ~kid~ (“child”) and ~nab~ (“to snatch”), the sense being to carry off a child; English Wiktionary simply records the borrowing and does not give that breakdown, so the compound analysis should be read as one account only. The English verb was originally about taking children, but in French ~kidnapper~ covers carrying off anyone by force.
en.kifer: A variant spelling of ~kiffer~. That verb is formed from the noun ~kif~ and the ending ~-er~, which makes a first-conjugation verb from a noun. The noun is a borrowing from Maghrebi Arabic, Moroccan or Algerian ~kīf~ (“hashish”), which goes back to Arabic ~kayf~ (“opiate”). The verb, meaning to like or to love, is thus a French coinage built on an Arabic loanword.
en.kiffer: ~Kiffer~ is formed from the noun ~kif~ and the verb ending ~-er~, which turns a noun into a first-conjugation verb. The noun ~kif~ is itself a borrowing from Maghrebi Arabic: Moroccan or Algerian Arabic ~kīf~ (“hashish”), which goes back to Arabic ~kayf~ (“opiate”). The verb, meaning “to like” or “to love,” is thus a French coinage built on an Arabic loanword.
en.kilométrer: ~Kilométrer~ is formed from the noun ~kilomètre~ with the verb ending ~-er~, and means to measure or mark out in kilometers. The noun is itself a compound of the prefix ~kilo-~, which comes from Ancient Greek ~χίλιοι~ (“a thousand”), and ~mètre~, which passed through Latin ~metrum~ from Ancient Greek ~μέτρον~ (“measure”). A kilometer is therefore, literally, a thousand measures, and the verb turns that unit into an action.
en.klaxonner: ~Klaxonner~ is formed from the noun ~klaxon~ (“horn, hooter”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so “to sound a horn.” French borrowed the noun from English ~klaxon~, a word invented by its first manufacturer, F. W. Lovell, after Greek ~κλάζω~ (~klázō~, “to shriek”). The verb now covers honking any car horn.
en.kératiniser: Formed from ~kératine~ with the suffix ~-iser~, which makes verbs meaning “to convert into” or “to treat with” the base: to turn into or become keratin. The noun ~kératine~ comes from Ancient Greek ~κεράτινος~ (“made of horn”), and English ~keratin~ is recorded from 1848.
en.labelliser: ~Labelliser~ is formed in French from ~label~ + the verbal suffix ~-iser~ (“to make, to treat as”), and means to give a product or a service an official label, hence to certify or approve it. The base made a round trip: French ~label~ was borrowed back from English ~label~ (“tag, strip attached to something”), which came from Old French ~lambel~ (“fringe, strip”). The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and it is fully productive in technical, administrative and journalistic French. Verbs such as ~moderniser~ and ~numériser~ follow the same pattern.
en.labialiser: Formed from the adjective ~labiale~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which makes verbs meaning “to render A” or “to treat with N.” To ~labialiser~ a sound is to give it a lip articulation, such as rounding. ~Labiale~ itself comes from Latin ~labium~ (“lip”), and ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~.
en.labourer:
~Labourer~ comes from Middle French ~labourer~ and Old French ~laborer~, borrowed from Latin ~labōrāre~ (“to work”), a verb related to the noun ~labor~ (“toil”). The Latin verb also lives on in Italian ~lavorare~ (“to work”) and Spanish ~labrar~ (“to work, to till”). In French, ~laboratoire~ and ~élaborer~ belong to the same family, as does English ~labor~.

The meaning narrowed gradually, from “to work” to “to work hard,” then to “to work the land.” In that last sense the verb replaced Latin ~arare~ (“to plow”) and its Old French offspring ~arer~ (compare ~arable~ and ~araire~). By a paradox French Wiktionary points out, ~arer~ has a maritime sense. The older, broader meaning lingered: in the seventeenth century Madame de Sévigné still used the verb in its classical sense of “to be in difficulty.”
en.lacer:
From Old French ~lacier~, itself from Latin ~laqueāre~ (“to bind, to ensnare, to entwine, to tie tightly”). The Latin verb is built on ~laqueus~ (“noose, snare”), so it first describes tying with a cord or loop. The same Latin source passed into English by way of Old French, where it gave ~lace~.

Modern French ~lacer~ keeps this concrete sense: to fasten or tie with a cord, as one laces shoes or a bodice. A whole family grew from the root. Among French words are ~lacs~ (“snare, noose”), ~lacet~ (“lace, small cord”), ~enlacer~ (“to entwine”), ~entrelacer~ (“to interlace”) and ~délacer~ (“to unlace”). The cord that ties and the cord that traps share one origin.
en.lacérer: From Latin ~lacerāre~ (“to tear, to mangle”), a verb derived from the adjective ~lacer~ (“torn”). French took the verb straight from Latin as a learned borrowing, and the same verb gave English ~lacerate~ and the French noun ~lacération~. Modern ~lacérer~ means “to tear to shreds”, whether papers, posters, a garment or skin, and it keeps the learned, somewhat violent tone of its Latin source.
en.lainer: Formed in French from the noun ~laine~ (“wool”) plus ~-er~, the ending that turns nouns into first-conjugation verbs; here it means to work a cloth so as to raise its nap. ~Laine~ comes from Latin ~lāna~ (“wool”), traced back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₂wĺ̥h₁neh₂~. The same root gave English ~wool~, German ~Wolle~ and Ancient Greek ~lênos~ (λῆνος), all cognates of the French word.
en.laisser:
French ~laisser~ descends through Old French ~laissier~ — already attested in the ninth-century ~Séquence de sainte Eulalie~, one of the oldest texts in the language — from Latin ~laxare~ (“to loosen, to slacken, to let go”). That verb is built on the adjective ~laxus~ (“loose, slack, wide”), which traces to Proto-Indo-European *~sleg-~ (“to be slack, to be languid”). The same root surfaces in English ~slack~, ~lax~, and ~relax~, and in Latin ~languere~ (“to be faint”), so the verb of letting-go is, at its core, a verb of going loose.

The semantic path is intuitive: to loosen one's grip is to let go, and to let go is to leave behind or to permit. Old French ~laissier~ already spanned “to let, to allow, to abandon,” and modern ~laisser~ keeps all of these — ~laisse-moi~ (“leave me alone”), ~laisser faire~ (“to let happen”). From ~laxare~ French also drew the doublet ~lâcher~ (“to release, to let go”), the noun ~laisse~ (a dog's leash, literally something slackened out), and, more distantly through ~laxus~, the learned ~laxatif~ and ~relâcher~. The economic doctrine of ~laissez-faire~ preserves, fossilized in a slogan, the verb's oldest instinct: loosen your hold and let things run.
en.laitonner: Derived from ~laiton~ (“brass”) with the verb ending ~-er~. The TLFi treats the verb under the entry for the noun. The noun is attested around 1170-80 as ~laton~ and around 1220 as ~laiton~. It was borrowed from Arabic ~lāṭūn~ (“copper”), which in turn goes back to Turkish ~altun~ (“gold”). Medieval Latin of Spain had ~allatone~ as early as 832, from the Arabic word with its article ~al-~ fused on. The verb is a technical term meaning to fit something with brass wire, as in ~laitonner~ a lampshade, or to coat it with a thin layer of brass by electrolysis.
en.lambrisser: ~Lambrisser~ is recorded in the twelfth century as ~lambruschier~, then as ~lambroissier~ and ~lambrisser~. It is generally traced to the noun ~lambruche~, which comes from Latin ~labrusca~ (“wild vine”), with the verbal ending ~-er~; English Wiktionary alternatively offers ~lambris~ or a Vulgar Latin verb ~lambruscare~. The TLFi, as reported, gives it the original sense of decorating with a vine motif, since wall coverings often drew on that plant. A later gloss of the word as “panel” is the sense the modern verb keeps.
en.lamenter: A learned borrowing: ~lamenter~ was taken directly from Latin ~lamentārī~ (“to weep, to cry”) rather than evolving through the everyday speech of Old French. The Latin verb is built on the noun ~lamentum~ (“a wail, a lament”). The same Latin family reached English as ~lament~. In modern French the verb is used above all in the pronominal form ~se lamenter~, “to moan about one's lot,” though the transitive sense “to bewail” survives in literary writing.
en.lamer: ~Lamer~ is a verb built on the noun ~lame~ (“thin plate, blade”) with the ending ~-er~, in the sense “to flatten”. ~Lame~ comes through Middle and Old French from Latin ~lāmina~, which French also borrowed a second time as the learned doublet ~lamine~.
en.laminer: ~Laminer~ is a learned derivative of Latin ~lamina~ (“thin plate, blade”), a word that also gave French ~lame~. French Wiktionary and English Wiktionary agree on this origin, and the verb was formed in French from the Latin noun rather than inherited from a Latin verb. English ~lamina~ and ~laminate~ come from the same Latin noun. The sources consulted do not explain how the sense “to crush” arose beside the sense “to laminate”.
en.lamper: ~Lamper~ is described as a nasalized form of ~laper~ (“to lap up”), that is, the same verb with an added nasal sound, an ~m~ slipped in before the ~p~. English Wiktionary simply refers the reader to ~laper~. It is a drinker's word, used for downing a drink in big gulps, to quaff or swig, which makes it a livelier cousin of the verb for lapping with the tongue.
en.lancer:
From Old French ~lancier~, from Late Latin ~lanceāre~ (“to wield or hurl a lance”), derived from ~lancea~ (“lance, light spear”), a word the Romans likely borrowed from a Celtic or Iberian source. The throwing weapon gave its name to the act of throwing. Italian ~lanciare~ and Spanish ~lanzar~ are cognate, and English ~lance~ and ~launch~ both descend, through French, from the same ~lancea~.

The verb began as something a soldier did with a spear — to cast it forward — and from that violent gesture generalized to any forceful throw, then to figurative launches: one ~lance~ a rocket, a product, a fashion, or a rumor. English ~launch~ is the same word, borrowed from Old French and specialized into the sense of setting a ship or a venture in motion. The native family is rich: the noun ~lance~, plus ~lancement~, ~lanceur~ (a “launcher,” including a rocket), ~relancer~ and ~relance~ (to throw again, to revive), and ~élancer~ / ~élan~, where the idea of hurling oneself forward yields both a sudden pain and a surge of momentum.
en.lanciner: ~Lanciner~ is borrowed from Latin ~lancināre~ (“to tear to pieces, to mangle”). French Wiktionary specifies that the French verb was taken from the present participle ~lancinans~ of that Latin verb, while English Wiktionary simply calls it a borrowing from the verb. The modern verb is about piercing rather than tearing: ~lanciner~ means to cause shooting pains and, figuratively, to torment or haunt, as a worry or an obsession does. The adjective ~lancinant~, far more common, keeps both uses: a ~douleur lancinante~ (“a shooting pain”) or a ~souvenir lancinant~ (“a haunting memory”). English took the same Latin verb as the learned ~lancinate~ (“to pierce”).
en.langer: ~Langer~ is derived from ~lange~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to wrap a baby in swaddling clothes” or, today, “to put a diaper on.” ~Lange~ comes from Latin ~laneus~ (“made of wool”) by way of Old French ~lange~ (“woollen”), and the noun sense of baby garment appeared only around the sixteenth century. The wool of ~laneus~ is the same as that of Latin ~lāna~.
en.langueyer: Formed from ~langue~ (“tongue”) with the suffix ~-oyer~, and attested in Old French as ~langoier~, “to wag the tongue.” The noun ~langue~ comes from Latin ~lingua~. The suffix ~-oyer~ is the inherited counterpart of the learned ~-iser~. In modern French the verb has a narrow, technical sense: to inspect a pig's tongue for disease.
en.languir: ~Languir~ is inherited from Old French ~languir~, from Late Latin ~languīre~, from Latin ~languēre~ (“to be faint, to be weak”). The Latin verb belonged to the second conjugation, and in Late Latin it passed to the fourth, which is why French has ~-ir~ and not ~-oir~. The same Latin root underlies the French noun ~langueur~ and the participle ~languissant~. English ~languish~ is a borrowing from the French verb, built on its stem ~languiss-~, and English ~languid~ comes from the related Latin adjective ~languidus~.
en.lanterner: Formed from the noun ~lanterne~ plus the verbal suffix ~-er~. The noun comes from Latin ~lanterna~ (“lantern”). The verb is used in the sense of dawdling, wasting time or putting something off, and sources give no further account of how that sense grew out of the lantern.
en.laper:
The sources differ. French Wiktionary derives ~laper~ from an imitative syllable, ~lap~, copying the sound of lapping, and sees no need to assume a Germanic loan. English Wiktionary instead gives a Germanic origin, through German ~lappen~, Old High German ~gilepfen~ and Proto-Germanic *~lapōną~ (“to lick, to lap”), itself from an imitative Proto-Indo-European *~leh₂b-~ (“to lap, to lick”). On both accounts the word imitates the sound of a tongue taking up liquid.

That imitative character explains how similar words appear in unrelated places. French Wiktionary lists German ~lappen~, Middle Dutch ~lapen~ (“to lick noisily”) and English ~lap~, but also Latin ~lambere~ (“to lick”), Genoese ~lappa~ (“drink”) and Andalusian ~lapo~ (“sip”). ~Laper~ means to drink by licking, as a cat or a dog does, and it is used of the animal's way of taking water or milk. Whether it was inherited from Germanic or coined afresh from the sound, the verb is a small piece of onomatopoeia.
en.lapider:
Borrowed from Latin ~lapidāre~ (“to stone, to pelt with stones”), a verb built on ~lapis~ (“stone”). In Latin the verb described a concrete act, throwing stones at someone, and French kept that literal sense for the punishment of stoning. Italian ~lapidare~ and Spanish ~lapidar~ continue the same Latin verb, and English took ~lapidate~ from it.

The noun ~lapis~ is the root of several French words. ~Lapidaire~ describes what is cut or carved in stone, and by extension a terse, inscription-like phrase, the ~formule lapidaire~. ~Dilapider~ (“to squander”) comes from Latin ~dīlapidāre~, built on ~lapis~ with ~dis-~ (“apart”), and English ~dilapidated~ is a relative. Meanwhile ~lapider~ has developed a figurative sense of its own: to assail someone with harsh words or public condemnation, a verbal stoning. The literal act and the figurative one now live side by side.
en.lapidifier:
Formed in French from Latin ~lapis~, genitive ~lapidis~ (“stone”), and the verbal suffix ~-fier~, which goes back to Latin ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”). The verb therefore means, literally, to make into stone: to turn something into stone, or to harden it. The stem ~lapid-~ is the Latin genitive stem, which is why the verb has a ~d~ where the nominative ~lapis~ has an ~s~.

French keeps a small learned family around the Latin word for stone. ~Lapidaire~ (“of stone, concise and carved like an inscription”) and ~lapider~ (“to stone”) belong to it, as does ~dilapider~ (“to squander”), from Latin ~dīlapidāre~, said first of stones scattered. English shares the family in ~lapidary~ and ~dilapidated~. ~Lapidifier~ is a rare learned word.
en.lapiner: ~Lapiner~ (“to give birth,” said of a rabbit) was first written ~lapinner~. It is formed from ~lapine~ (“doe rabbit”) with the verb ending ~-er~, in the sense of “to do what a ~lapine~ does.” The noun ~lapine~ is itself formed from ~lapin~ (“rabbit”) with the feminine suffix ~-ine~. A slang sense of the verb is attested from 1907.
en.laquer: ~Laquer~ is built on the noun ~laque~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, which here means “to coat or provide with N”: to coat something with lacquer. The noun reached French through Middle French ~lache~ (“resinous material”), a borrowing from Arabic ~lakk~. French Wiktionary traces the Arabic word further back through Persian ~lāk~ and Hindustani ~lākh~ to Sanskrit ~lākṣā~, the name of the resinous secretion produced by trees of the Far East when an insect pricks them. The noun ~laque~ is recorded in the sense of a lacquered art object in 1738.
en.larder: ~Larder~ is formed from ~lard~ (“bacon fat”) with the ending ~-er~, in the sense of providing something with a noun: to stud meat with strips of fat. The noun is inherited from Old French ~lard~, from Latin ~lārdum~ (“bacon fat”). The verb also has figurative senses, such as to pierce a body with blows, ~larder de coups de couteau~ (“to stab repeatedly”).
en.larguer: The verb ~larguer~ is formed from the noun ~largue~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~largue~ itself derives from Italian ~largo~ (“wide, broad”). French Wiktionary also allows another route, a direct borrowing from Spanish ~largar~ with the same sense, so the exact path is not settled. The word began as a sailors' term for letting a rope or sail out, giving it slack, which explains the nautical sense “to ease a line.” From there it spread to dropping something, as in ~larguer une bombe~, and finally to the slang sense “to ditch, to dump,” as when one ~largue~ a partner.
en.larmoyer: The verb is built on ~larme~ (“tear”) with the verb-forming suffix ~-oyer~. English Wiktionary adds that it comes from Old French ~larmoiier~, itself from Vulgar Latin *~lacrimizāre~. The noun ~larme~ descends from Old French ~larme~ and ~lerme~, from Latin ~lacrima~ (“tear”), which English Wiktionary traces to the Proto-Indo-European form *~dáḱru-~. The verb means to shed tears, to weep, and by extension to whine or to run, as eyes do.
en.laryngectomiser: Formed from ~laryngectomie~ with the verb suffix ~-iser~, meaning to perform a laryngectomy on someone. The noun is a medical term made of ~laryngo-~ (from ~larynx~) and ~-ectomie~, the element for surgical removal. The suffix ~-iser~ turns the noun into a verb meaning to subject to the operation, a pattern typical of technical and medical French.
en.lasser: Inherited from Latin ~lassāre~ (“to tire, to weary”), a verb built on the adjective ~lassus~ (“tired”). The adjective survived in Old French as ~las~, and it lives on in the exclamation ~hélas~, literally “oh, wretched me” (~hé~ + ~las~). The verb kept its Latin sense of making someone weary, then came to mean getting fed up with something, especially in the reflexive: ~se lasser de~ (“to grow tired of”). The same family gave ~lassitude~, ~délasser~ (“to relax”) and ~inlassable~ (“untiring”).
en.latiniser:
French Wiktionary derives ~latiniser~ from Latin ~latinizāre~ (“to translate into Latin”), described as a Hellenizing variant of ~latinare~. English Wiktionary gives Medieval Latin ~latīnizāre~, and also notes that by surface analysis the verb is ~latin~ + ~-iser~. The ending is Late Latin ~-izāre~, itself a transcription of the Greek verb ending ~-ízein~. French Wiktionary dates the productive use of ~-iser~ to the mid-sixteenth century, with ~latiniser~ and ~gréciser~ as its early examples.

The verb has several senses: to give a Latin form to a word, to translate into Latin, and to bring a people or a language under Latin or Roman influence. It rests on the adjective and noun ~latin~, from Latin ~Latīnus~, the word for the people of ~Latium~. The same family gave French ~latinisme~, ~latiniste~ and ~latinité~. English ~Latinize~, Italian ~latinizzare~ and Spanish ~latinizar~ are parallel formations, so the verb is one of the many ~-iser~ words that Europe shares across its languages.
en.latter: ~Latter~ comes from ~latte~ (“lath”) and the verb ending ~-er~, and means to fit with laths. It also has a slang sense, “to kick hard.” The noun ~latte~ is of Germanic origin: it reached French through Late Latin ~latta~, and English Wiktionary suggests Frankish *~lattu~ as the source. It is related to German ~Latte~, Dutch ~lat~ and English ~lath~, and to Italian ~latta~ and Spanish ~lata~.
en.laver:
From Latin ~lavāre~ (“to wash, bathe”), from Proto-Italic *~lawō~, from the PIE root *~lewh₃-~ (“to wash”). The root is widespread: cognate forms include Ancient Greek ~loúō~ (“I wash”) and, through Germanic, Old English ~lēaþor~, the ancestor of English ~lather~. The Romance sisters all preserve the verb plainly — Italian ~lavare~, Spanish and Portuguese ~lavar~ — making it one of the most stable everyday words inherited from Latin.

The sense has scarcely shifted in two thousand years: to cleanse with water, literally and then morally, as in ~laver son honneur~ (“to cleanse one's honor”) or ~laver un affront~. The same root flows through a surprising crowd of French words: ~lavabo~ (literally Latin “I shall wash,” from the priest's washing of hands), ~lavande~ (lavender, named for the bath water it scented), ~lavoir~ (a washhouse), ~lavage~, ~lessive~ and even ~déluge~ — and, borrowed from Italian, ~lave~, the “washing” flood of molten rock from a volcano.
en.layer: ~Layer~ covers three separate histories on French Wiktionary. The first, which seems to match “to cut a path through a forest,” comes from Middle French ~layer~ and Old French ~layer~, from Old Frankish *~lākan~ (“to provide with a mark indicating a boundary”). The second is a Middle French ~layer~ (“to cut facing stripes on a stone”), formed from ~laie~ (“stripe cut on a stone”) and ~-er~. The third is borrowed from Occitan ~laiar~ or ~laguiar~. English Wiktionary gives only the Frankish line, so that is the best-supported account of the forest sense.
en.laïciser: ~Laïciser~ is formed from ~laïc~ and the suffix ~-iser~ (French Wiktionary writes the ending as a verbalizing ~-er~), and means to secularize. The base ~laïc~ is borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin ~laicus~ (“common, ordinary”), itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ~laïkós~ (“of the people”). The same Latin word also gave the older French ~lai~.
en.laïusser: Formed from the noun ~laïus~ and the ending ~-er~, meaning to hold forth. The noun comes from Latin ~Laïus~ and Ancient Greek ~Láïos~, the mythical king of Thebes and father of Oedipus. Writing the speech of Laius to Oedipus was a composition subject in the entrance examination of the École Polytechnique, and the word entered the school's student slang before reaching everyday French as a name for a long speech.
en.lemmatiser: ~Lemmatiser~ (“to lemmatize”) is formed from ~lemme~ with the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to treat with” or “to reduce to”. In linguistics it means to group the inflected forms of a word under one headword. The noun ~lemme~ is a borrowing of Latin ~lemma~, from Ancient Greek ~lêmma~, which meant “gain, profit” and also the basis of a syllogism.
en.lessiver: Formed from the noun ~lessive~ plus ~-er~, “to wash with lye,” hence “to launder,” and figuratively “to wear out.” The noun ~lessive~ descends from Old French ~lissive~, from Latin ~lixīva~, a noun use of ~lixīvus~ (“made into lye”) in the phrase ~aqua lixīva~. Italian ~lisciva~ and Spanish ~lejía~ are cognates. The vowel of the first syllable shifted from ~i~ to ~e~ by dissimilation, according to French Wiktionary.
en.lester: ~Lester~ is derived from ~lest~ (“ballast”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to load with ballast.” The noun is Germanic. French Wiktionary derives it from Dutch ~last~ (“weight”), while English Wiktionary routes it through Old French ~last~ and ~lest~, from Old Dutch ~last~. Both accounts agree on a Low Countries source. The ship's ballast, a heavy load, thus gave a verb that also works figuratively for weighing something down.
en.leurrer: Formed in French from the noun ~leurre~ (“lure, bait”) with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Old French ~loire~, from Old Low Frankish ~lôþr~ (“bait”), and is compared with Middle High German ~luoder~ (“bait, something that attracts”). English ~lure~ is a loan from the same Old French word. To ~leurrer~ someone is to draw them in with a bait, and so to deceive them.
en.lever:
From Latin ~levare~ (“to lift, to raise, to make light”), a denominative verb from the adjective ~levis~ (“light, not heavy”). That adjective descends from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ (“light, nimble”), the root that also gives English ~light~ and ~lung~. Romance kept the verb everywhere: Italian ~levare~, Spanish ~llevar~ (“to carry”), Portuguese ~levar~, Catalan and Occitan ~levar~.

The core idea is making something rise. From it French grew an unusually large family. The everyday ~lever~ covers raising, lifting, and getting up; with prefixes it yields ~élever~ (“to raise, to bring up”), ~enlever~ (“to remove, to carry off”), ~relever~ (“to lift again, to note”), and ~soulever~ (“to heave up”). The past participle ~levé~ and the action noun ~levée~ gave English ~levee~ (a raised riverbank) and ~levy~ (a raising of troops or taxes), while the tool that raises a load came through Old French as English ~lever~. Even bread remembers the root: ~levure~ (“yeast”) and ~levain~ (“leaven, sourdough”) are what make dough ~lever~ — rise. And the curtain-raising sense survives in ~le lever du soleil~, the sunrise, and historically in ~le lever du roi~, the king's ceremonial rising.
en.levretter: ~Levretter~ is formed from the noun ~levrette~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun is a Middle French word, ~levrerete~, built on ~lévrier~ (“greyhound”) with the diminutive suffix ~-ette~, and names a female greyhound. It largely replaced the older ~levriere~. The verb has two senses: to hunt with greyhounds, and, of a hare or rabbit, to give birth, the young being called ~levrauts~ in the same family of words.
en.lexicaliser: Formed from the adjective ~lexical~ with the suffix ~-iser~, in the sense “to make lexical,” as when a phrase becomes a fixed word of the language. The adjective is derived from ~lexique~ with the suffix ~-al~. English Wiktionary traces it to Latin ~lexis~, from Ancient Greek ~λέξις~ (~léxis~, “word”). The verb thus rests on a Greek word for “word.”
en.liaisonner: Formed from the noun ~liaison~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is traced either to Late Latin ~ligātiōnem~, from Latin ~ligō~ (“to bind”), or to ~lier~ plus the suffix ~-aison~, modeled on the Latin word. The verb is a mason's term: to bond bricks or stones, or to fill their joints with mortar, which is to bind them together.
en.libeller: Formed from the noun ~libelle~ and the ending ~-er~, which turns a noun into a verb. ~Libelle~ was borrowed from Latin ~libellus~ (“little book, short writing”), a diminutive of ~liber~ (“book”). The verb first meant to draw up a text in precise, formal terms, the way a clerk words a legal document, and that sense of wording something exactly survives in the modern use for writing out a check or a form. English ~libel~ comes from the same Latin word, and French ~libelle~ also came to mean a defamatory pamphlet.
en.libéraliser: ~Libéraliser~ is formed from the adjective ~libéral~ with a verbal suffix, ~-iser~, giving the sense “to make more liberal”. The base is the adjective ~libéral~, and the suffix is the usual French one for such verbs. The adjective ~libéral~ was borrowed from Latin ~līberālis~ (“befitting a free person”), derived from ~līber~ (“free”). The root meaning of “free” therefore sits beneath modern uses such as ~libéraliser~ the economy or the rules for an activity.
en.libérer:
French ~libérer~ comes from Latin ~līberāre~ (“to set free”), a verb built on the adjective ~līber~ (“free”). That adjective traces to a Proto-Indo-European *~h₁léwdʰeros~ (“free,” literally “belonging to the people”), from the root *~h₁lewdʰ-~ (“to grow, to rise; people”). The cognates are illuminating: Ancient Greek ~eleútheros~ (“free”) shares the exact formation, while German ~Leute~ and Russian ~ljúdi~ (both “people”) preserve the “people” sense of the same root — freedom, anciently, was the condition of those who belonged to the folk. Notably, Latin ~līberāre~ also descended by the popular route into French ~livrer~ (“to deliver, to hand over”), so ~libérer~ and ~livrer~ are doublets, one learned, one inherited.

~Libérer~ is the relearned, bookish form, restored close to its Latin shape, and it kept the core sense “to set free”: to free a prisoner, to release from an obligation, and — a more mundane modern turn — to vacate, as one ~libère~ a hotel room or a parking space. The adjective ~līber~ and its verb seeded a large French family: ~liberté~, ~libéral~ and ~libéralité~, ~libération~ and ~libérateur~, ~délivrer~ (through ~livrer~), and the borrowed ~libertin~. The motto ~Liberté, égalité, fraternité~ enshrines the noun at the heart of French identity. To liberate, etymologically, is to restore someone to the free condition of the people.
en.licencier:
From Middle French ~licencier~ (also written ~licensier~ or ~licentier~), borrowed from Medieval Latin ~licentiāre~, a verb built on Latin ~licentia~ (“freedom, permission”). That noun comes from ~licēre~ (“to be allowed”), the same verb that gave French ~licite~ and ~illicite~. The family is wide: English ~license~ and ~licentious~ come from the same Latin noun, and Italian ~licenziare~ and Spanish ~licenciar~ are cognate verbs.

The Latin noun covered both freedom and permission. French reached from there the harsher sense of dismissing an employee, now its usual meaning and the source of ~licenciement~ (“layoff”). Related words show the other faces of the root. A ~licencié~ may be a laid-off worker, the holder of a university ~licence~ degree, or a licensed member of a sports federation, all of them tied to a permission granted. And ~licencieux~ (“licentious”) shows freedom pushed too far.
en.licher: The sources treat ~licher~ as a variant of ~lécher~ (“to lick”), not as an independent word, so its origin is that of ~lécher~. The two verbs differ in their stem vowel, and ~licher~ is the less usual form. Besides the sense “to lick,” ~licher~ carries the colloquial meaning “to drink.” It is a good example of a familiar-register spelling that lives beside a standard verb and keeps the same family of meaning.
en.liciter: French ~liciter~ is borrowed from Latin ~licitārī~ (“to bid at an auction”). It means “to put up for auction,” and it survives mostly in law, alongside the noun ~licitation~, the sale at auction of property held jointly. The sources at hand give no intermediate steps.
en.lier:
From Latin ~ligāre~ (“to bind, to tie”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~leyǵ-~ (“to bind”). Old French had both the popular form ~lier~ and learned spellings, and the verb passed into English as the borrowed ~liable~ and ~liaison~. Cognates from the same root include Albanian ~lidh~ (“I bind”); within Romance the verb lives on as Italian ~legare~ and Spanish ~ligar~.

The meaning stays close to its root: to ~lier~ is to bind, to fasten, to tie together — ropes, ideas, people. From physical binding grew the abstract senses: ~lier conversation~ (“to strike up a conversation”), to be ~lié~ to someone by friendship, and even a cook's sense, to ~lier~ a sauce by thickening it so the ingredients hold together. The root *~leyǵ-~ produced a dense French family: ~lien~ (“bond, link”), ~liane~ (the binding jungle vine), ~ligament~, ~ligature~, ~ligoter~ (“to tie up”), ~allier~ and ~alliance~, ~obliger~, and ~religion~ — often explained as that which binds the faithful. English ~ally~, ~oblige~, and ~rely~ share the same knot.
en.lifter: Borrowed from English ~lift~, used as a verb in French. The English word is the source of several French senses that spread in the twentieth century. ~Lifter~ means to give a facelift to someone or something, in the figurative sense of refreshing an image or a product too. In tennis and other ball sports it means to hit the ball with an upward lift, as in a lob over an opponent. The verb takes the regular ~-er~ ending of the first conjugation and conjugates like any other French verb of that group.
en.ligaturer: Formed in French from the noun ~ligature~ + the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, with the sense “to tie up with a ligature.” The noun came through Middle French from Late Latin ~ligātūra~, from ~ligātus~, the past participle of Latin ~ligō~ (“to tie, to bind”). That Latin verb also lies behind French ~lier~, which descends from the related infinitive ~ligāre~. So ~ligaturer~ means, etymologically, to bind something with a binding.
en.ligner: From Latin ~līneāre~ (“to draw a straight line”), the verb of Latin ~līnea~ (“line, string”), which gave French the noun ~ligne~. The verb thus has two ties: it descends from the Latin verb, and it is also felt as a verb built on ~ligne~ with the suffix ~-er~. Its senses follow the noun: to rule lines on a page, to mark with lines, and, in angling, to fish with a line. The same family gives ~aligner~ and ~linéaire~.
en.lignifier: From Latin ~lignum~ (“wood”) and the verbal suffix ~-fier~, which goes back to Latin ~-ficāre~ and ultimately to ~facere~ (“to make”). The verb thus means “to make into wood,” and it is used mostly in botany, of plant tissue that becomes woody as it hardens. In the pronominal form ~se lignifier~, it describes a plant stem turning into wood. The Latin noun ~lignum~ gave French a small learned family. ~Ligneux~ (“woody”) is the adjective, and ~lignite~ names a brown, woody-looking coal. The suffix is the same one found in ~planifier~. English has the matching ~ligneous~ and ~lignify~, built on the same Latin base.
en.ligoter: ~Ligoter~ is formed from the noun ~ligot~ (“bond, tie”) with the ending ~-er~, and means to bind someone hand and foot. English Wiktionary gives this analysis, and the French text sends the reader to ~ligature~, a word of the Latin family of ~ligāre~ (“to tie”). The base ~ligot~ itself is traced to Gascon ~ligo~, “bond, chain, tie,” so the verb may owe its form to the south-west of France while sharing its sense with the Latin root.
en.liguer: ~Liguer~ is formed from the noun ~ligue~ (“league”) with the verb ending ~-er~, meaning “to unite in a league,” and it is most often used reflexively, as ~se liguer~. The noun ~ligue~ came through Middle French from Italian ~liga~ or ~lega~, itself drawn from the Italian verb ~legare~ and ultimately from Latin ~ligāre~ (“to tie”). A league is thus, etymologically, a group that has been tied together.
en.limer: ~Limer~ means “to file” or smooth with a file. French Wiktionary traces it straight to Latin ~līmāre~ (“to file, to polish”), while English Wiktionary offers two options: the same Latin verb, or the French noun ~lime~ (the tool, a file) plus the verb ending ~-er~. The sources therefore leave open whether the verb was inherited from Latin or built in French on ~lime~, and either way it is tied to the idea of the file.
en.limiter:
From Latin ~līmitāre~ (“to bound, to fix a boundary”), a verb formed on the noun ~līmes~ (genitive ~līmitis~), meaning “a boundary path, a balk between fields, a frontier.” The deeper root is debated: ~līmes~ is sometimes linked to ~līmen~ (“threshold”) and to an idea of a transverse or slanting line, but the connection is uncertain and best left open. Cognate with Italian ~limitare~ and Spanish ~limitar~.

The surprising history lives in the noun. To a Roman surveyor a ~līmes~ was first a balk, the strip of unploughed earth marking off one field from the next; the same word then named the great fortified frontiers of the Empire — the ~Limes~ along the Rhine and the Danube — the very limit of the Roman world. From “the edge as a marked line” the verb ~limiter~ kept both the literal “to mark out, to bound” and the figurative “to restrict, to limit.” French preserves the whole boundary family: ~limite~ (“limit, boundary”), ~limitrophe~ (“bordering, adjacent”), ~illimité~ (“unlimited”), and ~délimiter~ (“to delimit, to mark the bounds of”).
en.limoger: ~Limoger~ is formed from the city name ~Limoges~ and the verb ending ~-er~. In 1914, at the start of the First World War, Marshal Joffre relieved a number of senior officers of their commands and sent them to Limoges, far from the front. The expression itself is attested only from 1916. The city's name comes from Latin ~Lemovices~, the name of the Gaulish people who founded it, and it replaced the older name ~Augustoritum~.
en.limousiner: Formed from ~limousin~ (“mason”) plus the verbal ending ~-er~, so it means to do a mason's work, to build with stone. The noun ~limousin~ in this sense comes from the Occitan ~lemosin~, which is the name of the Limousin region, so the trade word is literally the region's name. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is the default way French turns a noun into a verb.
en.liquider: ~Liquider~ is a borrowing from Italian ~liquidare~, itself derived from the adjective ~liquido~ (“liquid”), from Latin ~liquidus~. The Italian verb belonged to the language of commerce and meant “to turn assets into cash,” that is, to make them liquid, and by extension to settle an account. French took over that financial sense and then widened it: to ~liquider~ a stock is to sell it off, to ~liquider~ a debt is to clear it, and in slang to ~liquider~ someone is to get rid of them for good, which is to say to kill them.
en.liquéfier:
French ~liquéfier~ comes from Latin ~liquefacere~ (“to make liquid, to melt”). The Latin verb joins ~liquēre~ (“to be liquid, to be clear”) and ~facere~ (“to make”). The ending ~-fier~ is the French descendant of that ~facere~, and it appears in many verbs borrowed from Latin compounds of the same pattern, such as ~purifier~ and ~magnifier~. Italian ~liquefare~ is a parallel descendant, and English ~liquefy~ is a borrowing of the French verb.

Because ~facere~ is hidden in the ending, ~liquéfier~ is a “make-liquid” verb in the strictest sense, even though a speaker no longer hears the Latin verb in it. The first half of the Latin compound is the source of the adjective ~liquide~ and the noun ~liqueur~ in French. The noun ~liquéfaction~ is closer to the Latin, since its ~-faction~ keeps the stem of ~facere~ in a form that French did not reduce to ~-fier~. The verb is used both for melting solids and for turning a gas into a liquid.
en.lire:
From Old French ~lire~, from Latin ~legere~ (“to gather, to collect; to read”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~leǵ-~ (“to gather, to collect, to pick up”). The literal Latin meaning was “to gather,” and “to read” developed from the idea of gathering up the letters of a text with the eye, or picking out words one by one. The cognate Greek verb ~λέγω~ (légō) shows the same root branching toward “to pick out” and then “to say, to speak.” Reflexes of ~legere~ survive as Italian ~leggere~, Spanish ~leer~, and Portuguese ~ler~, and the root entered English through Latin borrowings like ~lecture~ and ~legible~.

The semantic journey from “gathering grain or wood” to “reading a page” is one of the most evocative in the Latin vocabulary: the reader is a kind of harvester, going along the line and collecting meaning. The prefixed forms of ~legere~ are everywhere in modern French — ~élire~ (“to elect,” literally “to gather out, to pick out”), ~cueillir~ (“to gather, to pick”), and the learned ~collecter~ and ~sélectionner~. From the same root come ~lecture~ (“reading”), ~lecteur~ (“reader”), ~légende~ (“legend; caption,” originally “things to be read”), ~légion~, and the family of ~-lège~ words such as ~florilège~ (“anthology,” a “gathering of flowers”), and even ~intelligent~ (“choosing between, discerning”).
en.liserer: The verb means to edge a fabric or garment with a narrow ribbon or border. French Wiktionary derives it from the noun ~liseré~ (“narrow edging”) with ~-er~. The base's own entry, however, says that ~liseré~ comes from the verb form ~lisérer~, so the two words chase each other in a circle, and the available sources give no older source for the family.
en.lisser:
The origin of ~lisser~ is debated. French Wiktionary cites the form ~lischier~, in the sense “to iron with a hot iron,” in the glosses of Rashi, and proposes that it arose from a crossing of two Latin words: ~lixāre~ (“to boil in water, to extract by leaching”) and ~allīsus~ (“worn, rubbed down”). Ironing and smoothing were done with hot water, which would explain the first. English Wiktionary prefers another route, a borrowing from Italian ~liscio~ (“smooth, polished”), and lists the crossing only among other theories. Spanish and Portuguese ~liso~ and Catalan ~llis~ show that the family was widespread, but the sources do not settle which way the word traveled.

If the ~lixāre~ account is right, ~lisser~ is a cousin of ~lessive~ (“lye, laundry”) and ~lessiver~, since all of them would rest on Latin ~lixa~ (“lye”), a washing liquid. The word seems to have spread widely only from the 17th century, long after the medieval attestation. Its sense then stayed close to its core idea, making a surface even and free of roughness. If the Italian account is right instead, ~lisser~ is a relatively late loan that joined the French vocabulary of polishing and finishing. Either way, the verb and the adjective ~lisse~ belong together, and only a fuller trail of attestations could say which came first.
en.lister:
Modern French ~lister~ is a denominal verb built directly on the noun ~liste~ (“list”). An older, unrelated-in-sense ~lister~ already existed in Old French around 1165, meaning “to make the border or selvage of cloth,” but the modern verb “to make a list” is a fresh nineteenth-to-twentieth-century coinage (attested 1962) from ~liste~. The noun itself, like Italian and Occitan ~lista~ and Catalan ~llista~, comes from a Germanic word for “strip, border, edge,” reconstructed as Proto-West Germanic *~līstā~. Cognate with German ~Leiste~ (“strip, ledge”), Dutch ~lijst~, and English ~list~, which carries both the “strip/selvage” and “enumeration” senses.

The two meanings of ~liste~ are one image seen twice: a strip of material and a strip of writing. The “enumeration” sense entered French from Italian ~lista~, attested from the fourteenth century, during the Renaissance. By one account the Germanic word goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~leys-~ (“to trace, to track”), though the sources present this only as a possibility. From the same family French has ~liste~, ~listel~ (an architectural fillet or band), ~lister~, and the calque ~liste noire~ (“blacklist”), borrowed in sense from English.
en.lisérer: ~Lisérer~ is derived from ~lisière~ (“edge, border”), and means “to edge with ribbon,” that is, to trim the border of a fabric or garment with a narrow band. The French source gives only this one-step derivation, with no older source language behind it.
en.liter: French Wiktionary gives two accounts of ~liter~, and the sources do not settle between them. One makes it a verb built on ~lit~ (“bed”) and the verb-forming ending ~-er~, which would suit the sense of laying things in layers. The noun ~lit~ is inherited from Latin ~lectus~. The other builds it on ~liste~ and ~-er~, and recalls that Old French ~lister~ meant “to make the selvage of a cloth.” The ending ~-er~ itself descends from the Latin first-conjugation ending ~-are~.
en.lithographier: Formed from the noun ~lithographie~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to print by lithography.” The noun is built from Greek ~líthos~ (“stone”) and ~gráphō~ (“to write”). In French it first meant a study of stones, and the modern printing sense came through German ~Lithographie~. Littré defines the process as one invented in 1793 by the German Senefelder, which reproduces on paper, with a press, what has been written or drawn on a stone of a particular kind. The verb simply turns that technique into an action.
en.livrer:
From Old French ~livrer~, from Latin ~liberare~ (“to set free, to release”), the verbal derivative of ~liber~ (“free”). Latin ~liber~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~louðeros~ and Proto-Indo-European *~h₁lewdʰero-~, from the root *~h₁lewdʰ-~ (“people, to grow”). The same root produced Greek ~eleutheros~ (“free”) and, through the “people” sense, German ~Leute~ (“people”). The Latin verb itself survives doubly in French: as learned ~libérer~ and as inherited, worn-down ~livrer~.

The semantic drift is remarkable. ~Liberare~ first meant “to free, to release,” then “to release something into someone's hands” — that is, to hand over. From “release into another's keeping” came the everyday sense “to deliver” a parcel or goods, whence the noun ~livraison~ (“delivery”). The darker sense “to betray, to give up to the enemy” is the same gesture turned sinister: to ~livrer~ someone is to hand them over. The reflexive ~se livrer~ means “to give oneself over” to an activity or to surrender. The compound ~délivrer~ keeps the original sense “to set free.” Other descendants of *~h₁lewdʰ-~ include ~libre~, ~liberté~, and ~libéral~.
en.lober: The main senses of ~lober~ are denominal, from ~lob~ plus ~-er~. The noun ~lob~ is borrowed from English, where it names a ball hit in a high arc, notably in tennis and football. To ~lober~ is to send a ball over an opponent's head in this way. French Wiktionary lists a third, unrelated sense of ~lober~ (“to praise”) from Frankish ~lobên~, a separate word that only happens to share the same spelling.
en.lobotomiser: Formed from ~lobotomie~ (“lobotomy”) with the verbal suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to subject to a lobotomy.” The noun is built from two Ancient Greek elements, ~λοβός~ (~lobós~, “lobe”) and ~τομή~ (~tomê~, “cut, incision”), the cutting of a brain lobe. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and in French it forms verbs meaning “treat with” or “convert into” the base. The verb is also used figuratively, for dulling someone's mind or will.
en.localiser:
Formed within French from the adjective ~local~ plus the suffix ~-iser~. ~local~ comes from Late Latin ~localis~ (“of a place”), a derivative of ~locus~ (“place”). The deeper origin of ~locus~ is uncertain: it appears in Old Latin as ~stlocus~, which would point to a Proto-Italic *~stlokos~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~stel-~ (“to set, place”), though the etymologist de Vaan is skeptical of this step and leaves the question open. Through ~locus~, French ~local~ is kin to ~lieu~ and to English ~local~ and ~locate~.

The verb's two modern senses both flow from “place.” To ~localiser~ is to determine where something is — to locate it — and also to confine something to one place, to localize it, as one localizes a fire or an infection.
