From the same ~locus~ French draws ~lieu~, ~local~ (noun and adjective), ~localité~, ~location~, and ~localisation~, the whole cluster organized around the idea of a spot on the map.
en.locher:
The origin of ~locher~ is obscure, and the sources offer several rival accounts. English Wiktionary calls the source Germanic. Diez linked it to Middle High German ~lücke~ (“slack, loose, shaky”), whose descendant is German ~locker~ (“loose”). Others prefer an Old Low Frankish *~luggi~, the source of ~lücke~, with a Latin suffix ~-icare~, but this does not explain the open vowel of the French word. Brüch proposed Old Norse ~loka~ (“to let hang”), though the change of an intervocalic ~k~ to ~ch~ makes that doubtful.

A Latin account also exists. Tilander derived Old French ~eslochier~ (modern ~élocher~) from a reconstructed *~eslocicare~, itself built on ~locus~ (“place”), and suggested that ~lochier~ arose from it by back-formation. The verb is regional: it describes a horseshoe that shakes or comes loose, particularly in Belgium, Normandy and the Vosges. Its meaning overlaps with that of ~cloche~ and ~clocher~, which the sources cite as sharing part of its semantic field.
en.lock-outer: ~Lock-outer~ is a French verb formed from the noun ~lock-out~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun was borrowed from English ~lock out~ (“to shut out, to close in order to prevent entry”), the term for an employer's closing of a workplace to keep employees out. French thus first took the English phrase as a noun and then gave it a regular first-conjugation verb, the usual treatment for a recent loan.
en.lockouter: ~Lockouter~ is a verb built on the noun ~lock-out~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is a borrowing of the English phrase ~lock out~ (“to shut out, to close in order to keep people from entering”), so the French verb ultimately rests on an English expression. The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, is the default way of turning a noun into a French verb, and here it yields a verb meaning “to lock out.”
en.lofer: Formed from ~lof~ with the verb ending ~-er~, a sailing term meaning to steer closer to the wind. The base ~lof~ was borrowed from Dutch ~loef~, according to French Wiktionary. English ~luff~ is a relative, a sailing word with the same meaning that also reaches back to Dutch. The verb is therefore a French derivation built on a Dutch loanword, one more mark of the Low Countries' influence on French maritime vocabulary.
en.loger:
Denominal verb from the noun ~loge~ + ~-er~. ~Loge~ comes from Old French ~loge~ (“hut, arbor, shelter”), borrowed from Frankish *~laubja~ (“shelter of foliage, leafy bower”), a Germanic word built on the same root as German ~Laube~ (“arbor, bower”) and ~Laub~ (“foliage”). The same Frankish source, lent into English through Old French, gave English ~lodge~ and ~lobby~.

The earliest ~loge~ was literally a leaf-roofed shelter; from “to provide shelter” the verb ~loger~ broadened to “to house, to accommodate,” then to the everyday “to stay, to be lodged.” Military French kept the older flavor in ~loger les troupes~ (“to quarter the troops”). The noun meanwhile branched into the theater ~loge~ (“box”), the concierge's ~loge~, and the Masonic ~loge~ (“lodge”), this last re-borrowed under English influence. Related French words include ~logement~ (“housing”), ~logis~ (“dwelling”), loger's compound ~déloger~ (“to dislodge, drive out”), and ~logeur~ (“landlord”). The leafy origin survives only as an etymological memory beneath all these tidy modern rooms.
en.longer: From the adjective ~long~ + the verb ending ~-er~. The adjective is inherited from Old French ~lonc~, from Latin ~longus~ (“long”), and is cognate with English ~long~. The ending ~-er~ turns a word into a first-conjugation verb, here with the sense “to go along the length of.” To ~longer~ a wall, a river or a road is to follow it, keeping it alongside, since what one follows is its length. The same adjective gave ~longueur~, ~allonger~ and ~prolonger~, and it is the word that English borrowed in ~chaise longue~, “long chair.”
en.lorgner:
French ~lorgner~ is a verb built on Old French ~lorgne~ (“squinting, cross-eyed”). English Wiktionary traces that adjective to Proto-Germanic *~lūrni-~, from a root *~lūr-~ or *~lūraną~ (“to spy, to watch”), and says this root is of uncertain origin. It may possibly go back to Proto-Indo-European *~lewk-~ (“to see”), but that link is only a suggestion. The words compared with it are Dutch ~loens~ (“cross-eyed”) and Latin ~luscus~ (“half-blind”).

So the origin is debated at its deepest level, and even the Germanic step rests on English Wiktionary alone, since French Wiktionary stops at Old French ~lorgne~. The sense of the verb fits an adjective for a crooked, sidelong gaze: to ~lorgner~ is to eye something or someone on the sly, often with desire or envy. The derived nouns ~lorgnon~ and ~lorgnette~ name eyeglasses held up to the face for looking, which is why the verb can also mean to look through such a glass.
en.lotionner: ~Lotionner~ is formed from the noun ~lotion~ with the verb ending ~-er~: to apply lotion to, to rub with lotion. ~Lotion~ was borrowed from Latin ~lōtiō~ (“washing”), the noun of the Latin verb for washing, so the family began with the idea of a liquid used to cleanse.
en.lotir: ~Lotir~ (“to divide into lots”) is formed from the noun ~lot~ with the verbal ending ~-ir~. The noun comes from Old French ~lot~ (also spelled ~loz~), from a Frankish word *~lot~, from the Germanic form *~hlutą~, which also gave English ~lot~. The sense moved from the object used to draw lots to the share each person receives, and that is the share that ~lotir~ hands out: to divide land into portions and assign them. French Wiktionary adds that an older tradition links the Germanic word to Latin ~clāvis~ (“key”); the TLFi-style sources do not rely on it. The ending ~-ir~ is used here in its less common role of forming a verb from a noun.
en.louanger: Formed from the noun ~louange~ (“praise”) with the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun is itself derived from ~louer~ with the suffix ~-ange~, so the verb is a second step built on a noun that already came from a verb. ~Louer~ (“to praise”) comes from Latin ~laudāre~. ~Louanger~ is a literary verb, more formal than ~louer~, meaning to shower with praise.
en.loucher: ~Loucher~ (“to squint”) is formed from the adjective ~louche~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The adjective is the feminine form ~losche~ of Old French ~lois~, generalized to both genders, from Latin ~luscus~ (“one-eyed”). Italian ~losco~ is a cognate, and it shares with ~louche~ the later shift to “shady, dubious.” A different noun ~louche~ (“ladle”) is unrelated: it comes from Old Frankish, through Old French ~louce~, and only coincides in form.
en.louer:
In the sense “to rent, to lease,” from Old French ~loer~, ~loier~, ~luer~, from Latin ~locāre~ (“to place, to let out, to lease”), a verb built on ~locus~ (“place, spot”). ~locus~ comes from Old Latin ~stlocus~, perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European root *~stel-~ (“to place, to set”), though de Vaan judges this derivation uncertain and leaves the origin open; the same *~stel-~ would link it, through Germanic, to English ~stall~. To ~locāre~ was literally to put something in a place — and so to place it at someone's disposal for a price.

The leasing sense flows directly from “to place”: letting a field, a house, or one's labour is placing it in another's hands for hire. Modern ~louer~ covers both renting from and renting to, and the root ~locus~ runs through a tidy French family — ~loyer~ (“rent payment”), ~location~ (“rental”), ~locataire~ (“tenant”), ~locatif~, and ~allouer~ (“to allocate”). A famous homonym shadows this verb: the other ~louer~, “to praise,” descends instead from Latin ~laudāre~ (“to praise”) by way of Old French ~loer~, and survives in ~louange~ (“praise”) and ~laudatif~. The two ~louer~s fell together in sound and spelling but were never related — one places a thing for hire, the other lifts a person with praise.
en.louper: Formed from ~loup~ used in the sense of “flaw, defect”, plus the verb ending ~-er~. The word ~loup~ is also the wolf: it comes from Latin ~lupus~ (“wolf”), with the modern spelling shaped by eastern dialects and by the feminine ~louve~, as against the regular central form ~leu~ preserved in ~à la queue leu leu~. From “flaw”, ~louper~ meant to botch a piece of work, and then, more broadly, to miss or fail at something, as in ~louper son train~.
en.lourder: Formed from the slang noun ~lourde~ (“door”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, so the verb means to show someone the door, hence to dismiss or get rid of them. The noun ~lourde~ is the adjective ~lourd~ (“heavy”) turned into a feminine noun. The verb belongs to the informal, slangy register, as in ~lourder~ an employee for “to give someone the boot.”
en.lourer: The TLFi derives ~lourer~ from ~loure~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. It is attested before 1607 in a pastoral poem by Vauquelin de La Fresnaye, and the musical sense appears in the Académie in 1798: ~lourer~ is to play notes smoothly, detached but without cutting them short. ~Loure~ names an old bagpipe and the slow dance associated with it. The TLFi does not say how the musical sense grew out of the noun, so the link is left unexplained.
en.louveter: Formed from the noun ~louve~ (“she-wolf”) with the suffix ~-eter~. The noun is inherited from Latin ~lupa~, the feminine of ~lupus~ (“wolf”). The suffix, made of ~-et~ and ~-er~, is old and no longer productive. The verb has two unrelated-looking senses, “to give birth, said of a she-wolf” (to whelp) and “to tease wool.” The sources do not explain how the second sense came from the first.
en.louvoyer: Formed from ~lof~ with the suffix ~-oyer~, which expresses a repeated or continuing action. The noun ~lof~ is the French form of Dutch ~loef~ and corresponds to English ~luff~, a sailor's word for the side facing the wind. The verb is first recorded as ~louyer~ in 1529, then as ~lovoyer~ in 1621. It first described a ship working against the wind, and it later also came to mean “to hedge,” to move evasively in speech or action.
en.lover:
The nautical French ~lover~ (“to coil a rope”) was borrowed around 1678 from Low German ~lofen~ (“to turn, to luff”), a seafarers' term that entered French through the Atlantic and North Sea sailing trade. It belongs to the same Germanic field as the maritime ~lof~ (“luff, windward side”) and English ~luff~ — the act of turning a vessel toward the wind. The Germanic and Dutch nautical vocabulary supplied French with a whole rigging of such loanwords, of which ~lover~ is one neatly coiled example.

From “to turn” the verb specialized into “to wind a rope into neat concentric rings on deck,” the coil itself recalling a turned spiral. Its most vivid modern life is reflexive and figurative: ~se lover~ means “to curl up, to nestle,” as a cat or a snake coils itself into a comfortable spiral — ~le chat se love dans un fauteuil~ (“the cat curls up in an armchair”). A nautical term for stowing rope thus became one of French's most affectionate words for snuggling, the rope's tidy spiral transferred to a sleeping body.
en.lubrifier:
~Lubrifier~ is built from Latin ~lūbricus~ (“slippery”) and the verbal suffix ~-ifier~. French Wiktionary ties the ending to Latin ~fierī~ (“to become”), so the verb means “to make slippery.” It follows the pattern of many French verbs in ~-ifier~, such as ~clarifier~, ~purifier~ and ~simplifier~, which share the sense “to make” plus an adjective. The Latin adjective ~lūbricus~ described anything that slides, smooth or greasy.

In modern French, ~lubrifier~ is a technical verb meaning to coat moving parts or surfaces with oil or grease to reduce friction. Its family comes from the same Latin root: the noun ~lubrifiant~ (“lubricant”) and the noun ~lubrification~ follow the verb, while ~lubrique~ (“lewd”) is a separate learned adjective from the same Latin ~lūbricus~. English ~lubricate~ and ~lubricant~ belong to the same Latin family, though they come from the Latin verb ~lūbricāre~ rather than from the French verb.
en.luger: Formed from ~luge~ (“sled”) with the ending ~-er~, so “to go sledding.” The noun comes from Franco-Provençal ~lujhe~, which matches Late Latin ~leudia~ (fifth century), of Gaulish origin. The sources give the Gaulish form as *~(s)leudia~ or *~stludio~. English Wiktionary traces it to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₃sleydʰ-~ (“slippery”). Irish ~slaod~ is a Celtic relative.
en.luire:
Inherited from Latin ~lūcēre~ (“to shine, to be light”), which belongs to a family built on the Proto-Indo-European root *~lewk-~ (“light, brightness”). The regular Old French outcome was ~luisir~, and ~luire~ is a variant that replaced it under the influence of its future forms, the same shift seen in ~nuire~, ~plaire~ and ~taire~ (from older ~nuisir~, ~plaisir~ and ~taisir~). The stressed Latin ~-ē-~ after a palatal sound gave the ~-ir~ ending, as in ~placēre~ becoming ~plaisir~. The root is also found in Latin ~lūx~ (“light”) and ~lūmen~, in English ~light~ and in German ~Licht~.

The old ~-is-~ stem survives in the present participle and adjective ~luisant~ (“shining”), as in ~ver luisant~, and in the form ~il luisait~. The verb is mostly literary now and appears chiefly in the third person, of stars, eyes, a wet road or a sheen. Related French words include ~reluire~, ~lueur~, ~lumière~, ~lucide~ and ~luciole~ (“firefly”), and even ~lune~, from the same family. Few verbs show the way a Latin verb can slip into a different conjugation class so clearly.
en.lustrer:
Taken from Latin ~lustrāre~, a verb of the first conjugation, which French Wiktionary gives as its source. The Latin verb was built on ~lustrum~, the Roman rite of purification performed at the end of each census period, so that it could mean “to purify by ritual” or “to go around.” French took it as ~lustrer~, which in modern use means to give a surface a shine.

The French family has several members. There are the noun ~lustre~ (“shine, gloss”), the noun ~lustrage~ (“the act of giving a shine”), the adjective-participle ~lustrant~ and the prefixed ~délustrer~ (“to remove the shine”) and ~relustrer~ (“to polish again”). English has ~lustrate~, a learned borrowing of the same Latin verb, used for the ritual sense.
en.luter: Formed on the noun ~lut~ plus the verb ending ~-er~: to ~luter~ is to coat or seal with ~lut~, the clay-like paste used to close joints. The noun is attested in Old French in the 12th century and was borrowed from Latin ~lutum~ (“mud, clay”). The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, is the usual way French builds a verb on a noun, in the sense of “apply” or “provide with.” The verb thus carries a small piece of Latin mud into modern workshop and laboratory vocabulary.
en.lutiner: Formed in French from ~lutin~ (“imp, goblin”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so to behave like a ~lutin~: to tease or pester. The noun ~lutin~ passed through Old French ~netun~, ~nuiton~ and ~luiton~, and seems to go back to Latin ~Neptūnus~, the sea god, reinterpreted as a demon in the early Middle Ages. In his ~Corps de philosophie~, the scholar Scipion Dupleix explained ~lutiner~ as frightening someone at night in the manner of a spirit.
en.lutter:
From Old French ~luitier~ (also ~loitier~, ~luiter~; “to wrestle, to struggle”), attested in the Chanson de Roland around 1080, from Latin ~luctārī~ (“to wrestle, to struggle”). The Latin verb goes back to Proto-Italic *~lukto-~ and ultimately to a Proto-Indo-European root *~lewg-~ (“to bend, to twist”) — fittingly, since wrestling is a contest of twisting bodies. Cognate with Italian ~lottare~ and Spanish ~luchar~ (in which Latin ~-ct-~ regularly became ~-ch-~), and, through the prefixed Latin ~reluctārī~ (“to struggle against”), with English ~reluctant~.

The Old French diphthong ~-ui-~ held on for centuries; the reduction to plain ~-u-~ in ~lutter~ is unusual and dates only to the early seventeenth century, paralleling the pairs ~fruit~/~fruité~ and ~nuit~/~nuitée~. The sense has stayed remarkably stable: from the literal grappling of two wrestlers it broadened to any struggle, physical, moral, or political — one may ~lutter~ against an illness, against injustice, or against sleep. Words of the same family in modern French include the noun ~lutte~ (the sport and any struggle), the agent noun ~lutteur~ (“wrestler”), and the adjective ~luttable~. The learned English borrowing ~reluctant~ preserves, etymologically, the image of someone wrestling back against what is asked of them.
en.luxer:
From Latin ~lūxāre~ (“to dislocate”), a first-conjugation verb. Its ending ~-āre~ became the French ~-er~, just as ~cantare~ became ~chanter~. The French verb keeps the sense of its source: to put a joint out of its socket. English has the same verb as ~luxate~, taken from Latin as well, so the two languages share a rare, learned word for a very ordinary injury.

In modern French ~luxer~ belongs mostly to medical vocabulary: ~se luxer l'épaule~ is to dislocate one's own shoulder. The noun ~luxation~ (“dislocation”) is part of the same family, and so is the English noun ~luxation~, which comes from the same Latin verb. The look-alikes ~luxe~ and ~luxueux~ should not be confused with this family, since they concern luxury and not joints. ~Luxer~ is a precise, clinical verb, and its past participle ~luxé~ describes a joint that is out of place.
en.lyncher: Borrowed from the English verb ~to lynch~, which comes from the phrase ~Lynch law~. French Wiktionary attests ~lyncher~ from 1857, in translation. It attributes the summary, trial-less justice that the phrase names to William Lynch (1736-1796), a Virginia slaveholder and judge. The verb entered French along with the practice of mob justice that it describes.
en.lyophiliser: ~Lyophiliser~ is built on the adjective ~lyophile~ with the verbal suffix ~-iser~, and it is the technical verb for freeze-drying. The adjective is learned and made from Greek ~λύω~ (~lúō~, “to loosen, to dissolve”) and ~-phile~, from Greek ~φίλος~ (~phílos~, “beloved, loving”). It is a cousin of English ~lyophilize~, formed the same way.
en.lyser: Formed from ~lyse~ + ~-er~, the ending that turns a noun into a first-conjugation verb: ~lyser~ is to subject something, typically a cell, to lysis, that is, to dissolve it. The noun ~lyse~ comes from Ancient Greek ~λύσις~ (~lúsis~, “dissolution”). The Greek noun is related to the verb ~λύειν~ (~lúein~, “to loosen”), which also lies behind ~analyse~ and ~paralysie~.
en.lâcher:
From Old French ~laschier~ (attested 1080, in the ~Chanson de Roland~), later ~lascher~, from Vulgar Latin *~lassicare~, a dissimilated form of *~laxicare~, itself a frequentative of Latin ~laxare~ (“to loosen, slacken, relax”). ~laxare~ derives from the adjective ~laxus~ (“loose, slack”), which goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~(s)leg-~ (“to be slack, languid”). The same ~laxare~ gave French ~laisser~ (“to let, leave”), and ~laxus~ surfaces directly in English ~lax~, Italian ~lasso~, and Spanish ~laxo~.

The core idea was always one of slackening: to ~lâcher~ a rope is to let its tension go, and from there the verb fanned out into “to release,” “to let go,” “to drop,” and “to abandon.” The familiar sense “to chicken out” (se dégonfler) is a modern figurative extension of the same loosening. From the adjective ~laxus~ French also kept ~lâche~ (“slack” and, of a person, “cowardly”) — a doublet of the verb's own meaning — alongside the learned borrowings ~laxatif~ and ~relâcher~, all turning on the notion of letting tension out.
en.lécher:
French ~lécher~ comes from Old French ~lechier~, which is probably Germanic in origin. French Wiktionary derives it from Old Frankish *~lekkōn~ (“to lick”), attested in the tenth century and continued by Flemish ~lekken~ and German ~lecken~. A variant *~likkōn~, continued by standard Dutch ~likken~, gave a second Old French form, ~lichier~. English ~lick~ belongs to the same Germanic family. English Wiktionary says the word is “probably” from Frankish *~likkōn~, routed through a Vulgar Latin *~liccāre~, ancestor of Italian ~leccare~. Both accounts therefore place a Germanic word at the start, though they differ over whether Vulgar Latin stands between it and French.

The origin is therefore not entirely settled. English Wiktionary offers an alternative: an early contraction of a Vulgar Latin *~ligicāre~, denasalized from *~lingicāre~, which rests on Classical Latin ~lingere~ (“to lick”). The argument runs by analogy with ~ficher~, generally derived from *~fīgicāre~, from ~fīgere~. French Wiktionary gives only the Frankish source and mentions no rival. Neither account is certain, and the sources do not rule one out in favor of the other. The meaning, at least, has barely moved from “to pass the tongue over.” Figurative uses grew around it: ~lécher les vitrines~ is to window-shop, and ~léché~ describes a work polished to excess. The family includes ~lèche-vitrines~ and ~lécheur~.
en.légaliser: ~Légaliser~ is formed from the adjective ~légal~ with the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to make legal”. ~Légal~ was borrowed from Latin ~lēgālis~ (“relating to the law”). English Wiktionary adds that it is a doublet of ~loyal~, a word that came down through Old French by a more popular route. The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and today it is fully productive in administrative and technical French.
en.légender: Formed from ~légende~ + ~-er~, a verb coined from a noun in the sense “to provide with a caption.” The noun ~légende~ came through Old French ~legende~ from Medieval Latin ~legenda~, the feminine of Latin ~legendus~ (“to be read”), the gerundive of ~legēre~ (“to read”). That original sense, “what must be read,” gave French two derived meanings: an explanatory inscription, such as a caption or a map key, and a tale glorifying a famous figure. The verb draws on the first one, putting the text that must be read next to an image.
en.légiférer: Drawn from Latin ~legifer~ (“lawgiver”), a compound of ~lex~, ~legis~ (“law”) and ~ferō~ (“to bring, to bear”), so that to ~légiférer~ is, etymologically, to bear the law. Both halves left many French descendants. ~Lex~ gave ~légal~ and ~législation~, while ~ferō~, which goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰer-~ (“to carry”), gave ~transférer~, ~conifère~ and ~référer~. English ~bear~ is a native cousin of that same root. The verb is a learned word of the legal and political vocabulary, used for the making of laws by a legislature, as in ~légiférer sur un sujet~.
en.légitimer: Formed from the adjective ~légitime~ (“lawful, legitimate”) with the verb ending ~-er~, or possibly borrowed directly from Medieval Latin ~legitimāre~; English Wiktionary gives both routes. The adjective entered French from Latin ~lēgitimus~ (“in accordance with the law”), in Old French as ~legitime~ by the thirteenth century. ~Lēgitimus~ is built on ~lēx~ (“law”), the root of ~loi~ and ~légal~. The verb means to make lawful or to justify, and it has long been used for formally recognizing a child born outside marriage.
en.léguer:
Borrowed from Latin ~lēgāre~, a verb formed from the noun ~lex~ (genitive ~lēgis~, “law”), which also gave French ~loi~. French Wiktionary calls it a denominative of ~lex~ and explains the verb's logic through its two uses. For persons, ~lēgāre~ meant someone “sent by a law,” and for things it described transmission by will. In early Roman law such transmissions also took place by a law, passed in a popular assembly, the ~testamentum calatis comitiis~. The verb was thus tied to law from the start, and the noun ~lex~ stands behind it.

The two uses show how a word built on law could cover both sending someone and handing something down. In modern French the verb is used well beyond wills: one ~lègue~ a house, but also a tradition, a habit or a problem to the next generation. The root idea of a transfer authorised by a rule remains in these uses, although that continuity is an observation about the meanings rather than something the sources state. French Wiktionary treats ~léguer~ as a direct borrowing from the Latin verb, not a French formation on ~loi~, though the two words share the noun ~lex~ as their source.
en.lénifier:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~lenifico~ (“to soften, to soothe”), a verb built from the adjective ~lēnis~ (“soft, gentle, mild”) and the verbal element ~-ficāre~, itself from ~facere~ (“to make”). In its parts the verb means “to make mild.” French did not inherit the word through the spoken tradition; it took it straight from Latin and kept its Latin shape, which places it among the verbs in ~-fier~.

French has several relatives of the verb. ~Lénitif~ names a soothing remedy, and ~lénifiant~, the present participle used as an adjective, describes whatever calms or softens, often figuratively, as of reassuring words. The ending ~-fier~ is the same Latin ~facere~ seen in ~clarifier~, ~simplifier~ and ~purifier~, verbs that all mean “to make” the quality named by their first element. English ~lenient~ and ~lenify~ come from the same Latin family. The verb itself belongs to a literary register.
en.léser:
French ~léser~ comes through Middle French ~leser~ from Latin ~laedere~ (“to hurt, to damage, to offend”), by way of its past participle ~laesus~. Latin ~laedere~ has no secure Proto-Indo-European root. The verb gave Latin a whole family: compounds like ~collidere~ (“to strike together”) and ~ēlidere~ (“to strike out”) lie behind English ~collide~ and French ~élider~, and the noun ~laesiō~ (“an injury”) gave French ~lésion~, English ~lesion~, a term of medicine. The vowel of ~laedere~ shifted in the compounds, which is why they no longer look like their base.

In French, ~léser~ stayed a formal word, used when a person's interests, rights or body suffer harm: ~léser les intérêts de quelqu'un~ is to wrong someone's interests, and the injured party in a lawsuit is the ~partie lésée~. In medicine it describes damage to a tissue or an organ. Its most striking relic is ~lèse-majesté~, from Latin ~laesa maiestas~ (“injured majesty”), the old crime of offending the sovereign, which survives in French as a figure of speech for any insult to a person who expects deference.
en.lésiner: ~Lésiner~ is formed from the noun ~lésine~ (“stinginess”) with the verb ending ~-er~, and means to skimp or be stingy. The noun was borrowed from Italian ~lesina~ (“awl”), which makes it a doublet of French ~alêne~. According to the traditional account reported by French Wiktionary, a group of Italians so miserly that they resoled their own shoes took the name ~Compagnia della lesina~, “company of the awl.”
en.léviger:
From Latin ~levigare~, which French Wiktionary glosses “to lighten.” Latin in fact had two near-identical verbs: ~lēvigāre~ (“to make smooth”), from ~lēvis~ (“smooth”), and ~levigāre~ (“to lighten”), from ~levis~ (“light”). The French verb is a learned borrowing, taken from Latin rather than inherited through Old French, which explains its bookish ring. Its sense, to grind a substance finely, sits closer to “making smooth” than to “making light.”

In French the verb means to grind or crush a material finely, a technical use. English has the learned cousin ~levigate~, borrowed from the same Latin verb. The Latin adjective ~levis~ (“light”) also lies behind French ~léger~ and ~alléger~ (“to lighten”) and, through ~levāre~ (“to raise”), behind ~lever~. The two Latin adjectives ~lēvis~ and ~levis~ differ only in the length of the first vowel, which is why the sources easily confuse the two verbs.
en.léviter:
~Léviter~ is a learned verb whose sources differ slightly. French Wiktionary derives it from English ~levitate~, itself built on Latin ~levitās~ (“lightness”), while English Wiktionary points directly to Latin ~levāre~ (“to lift”). Both belong to one Latin family, that of the adjective ~levis~ (“light”), so the verb describes a body that hovers in the air without support. English ~levity~ comes from ~levitās~ as well.

The Latin verb ~levāre~ is a prolific one. Its prefixed forms ~ēlevāre~, ~relevāre~ and ~sublevāre~ gave French ~élever~, ~relever~ and ~soulever~, and ~lever~ itself and ~levier~ (“lever”) belong to the family. ~Léger~ (“light”) comes from the same Latin adjective ~levis~, as does Italian ~leggero~. Beside these everyday words, ~léviter~ is a learned latecomer rather than an inherited word.
en.lézarder: ~Lézarder~ is formed with the verbal ending ~-er~ on ~lézarde~, the word for a crack in a wall. French Wiktionary derives ~lézarde~ from ~lézard~ (“lizard”) and the suffix ~-arde~, by an analogy of shape with the curved tail of the animal. A second verb ~lézarder~ is built directly on ~lézard~ and has a different, lazier sense: to bask in the sun like a lizard. Both verbs are denominal, and the two sources agree on that.
en.macadamiser: Formed from ~macadam~ with the verbal suffix ~-iser~. The noun was borrowed from English ~macadam~, named for the Scottish engineer John Loudon McAdam, who devised the road-building process called macadamization. It first described a road surfaced by that method. To ~macadamiser~ a road is to surface it that way. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs.
en.machiner:
Borrowed from Latin ~māchinārī~ (“to scheme, to plot”), a deponent verb based on ~māchina~ (“machine, contrivance, device, scheme”), which was itself an early borrowing from Ancient Greek. The Latin verb meant, in the words of fr.Wiktionary, to combine, imagine or carry out something ingenious, and it is from this that the sense of plotting comes. The French verb was taken straight from the Latin and sits beside the noun ~machine~, from the same Latin word.

In French ~machiner~ has two uses. The older one is to plot, as in ~machiner un complot~; the other, to equip with machines, belongs to the modern world of ~machine~ and ~mécanique~. The English cousin ~machinate~ follows the first sense, and the noun ~machination~ exists in both languages for a hidden plot.
en.macler:
The origin of ~macler~ is uncertain, and French Wiktionary gives two accounts side by side. One says only that the origin is unknown. The other treats the verb as a derivative of ~macle~, which it traces to Latin ~macula~ (“mesh”). The verb belongs to glassmaking, where it means to stir molten glass, and the evidence does not say how that technical sense connects to the noun it may come from.

The Latin word ~macula~ meant both “spot” and “mesh of a net,” and it gave French ~maille~ (the link of a chain or a stitch of knitting) by regular inheritance. ~Macle~ is a technical noun that shares that Latin source, if the derivation proposed above holds. Because the link between the glassmaker's verb and the senses of ~macle~ is not documented, it stays open. ~Macler~ is rare outside its trade, a word of the workshop with a hedged history.
en.maculer:
Borrowed from Latin ~maculāre~ (“to stain, to blemish”, and figuratively “to defile”), a verb made from ~macula~ (“spot, stain”). The sense was both physical and moral from the start, and French kept both: a page can be ~maculé~ with ink, and a reputation can be stained as well. The verb is a learned borrowing, not an inherited word, which is why it keeps the Latin shape so closely.

Latin ~macula~ is also behind English ~macula~ and ~immaculate~, and behind French ~immaculé~ (“without stain”), which is formed with the negative prefix ~in-~ on the participle of ~maculāre~. Modern ~maculer~ is a literary or technical verb meaning “to mark a surface with spots or smears”, and it is mostly met as the participle ~maculé~ (“stained”), as in ~maculé de sang~ (“stained with blood”).
en.macérer: ~Macérer~ was borrowed from Latin ~mācerāre~ (“to soften, to steep”), the Latin infinitive ending ~-āre~ becoming French ~-er~. It was taken directly from the Latin verb. The same Latin verb also gave English ~macerate~, and French has the related noun ~macération~. The French verb keeps the Latin sense of leaving something to soak in a liquid until it softens.
en.magasiner: Formed from ~magasin~ + ~-er~, “to go to the stores.” French Wiktionary calls it a calque of English ~shop~, and English Wiktionary says it was possibly influenced by that word. The noun ~magasin~ is attested from 1389 and comes from Old French ~maguesin~ (“storeroom”), either from a regional language or from Italian ~magazzino~, itself from Arabic ~maḵāzin~, the plural of ~maḵzan~ (“storehouse”). It is a doublet of English ~magazine~, which took the same word by another route.
en.magner: The verb is tied to ~manier~ (“to handle”), though the two Wiktionaries phrase the link differently. French Wiktionary calls it a deformation of ~manier~ in that verb's old sense of “to move” or “to bestir oneself”. English Wiktionary derives it from Old French ~manoier~ (“to move”), a variant of ~manier~. Either way ~manier~ is the root, and it comes from ~main~ (“hand”), itself from Latin ~manus~. The modern colloquial sense is “to hurry up, to get a move on”.
en.magnifier:
~Magnifier~ is borrowed from Latin ~magnificāre~ (“to extol, to glorify”). That verb is built on ~magnificus~ (“splendid, grand”), which combines ~magnus~ (“great”) with a form of ~facere~ (“to make”), so the literal idea is “to make great.” The word is a learned borrowing, taken from Latin rather than inherited through the spoken language, which is why it keeps the Latin shape so closely.

In French the verb has been used chiefly in a religious setting, to glorify God. The best-known trace of the Latin verb is the hymn ~Magnificat~, whose first word is its Latin form. Related words from the same Latin roots include ~magnifique~, ~magnificence~ and ~magnitude~, and English ~magnify~ and ~magnificent~ belong to the same family. In everyday modern French ~magnifier~ is a literary word, used to say that something is idealized or praised beyond the ordinary.
en.magnétiser: ~Magnétiser~ is formed with the suffix ~-iser~, which makes verbs meaning “to make” or “to treat with.” French Wiktionary derives it from ~magnétique~, while English Wiktionary analyzes it as ~magnet~ + ~-iser~. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs. ~Magnétique~ is borrowed from Latin ~magnēticus~, from the Greek adjective ~Μαγνητικός~ (“of Magnesia”).
en.magnétoscoper: Formed from ~magnétoscope~ with the verb ending ~-er~: to record on a videocassette recorder. The noun is itself a compound of the prefix ~magnéto-~ (“magnetic”) and the suffix ~-scope~ (“instrument for viewing”), a name that describes a machine viewing and recording pictures on magnetic tape.
en.magouiller: ~Magouiller~ is a verb formed from ~magouille~ and the ending ~-er~. The origin of ~magouille~ is obscure. One proposal is that it comes from a descendant of Gaulish ~marga~ (“mud, clay, marl”), preserved in dialect words such as ~margouiller~ (“to wade, to dirty, to fiddle with”) and ~margouille~, and influenced in meaning by ~maquignon~ and ~maquignonner~. Another is that it comes from one of the senses of Spanish ~magullar~. Neither is settled.
en.maigrir: Formed from the adjective ~maigre~ (“thin”) with the verb ending ~-ir~, in the pattern of French verbs that mean “to become” the quality of the adjective, as ~grandir~ comes from ~grand~. ~Maigre~ is inherited from Old French ~megre~, from Latin ~macer~ (accusative ~macrum~), which goes back to a Proto-Indo-European root. The ~-gr-~ spelling of the modern form was perhaps influenced by ~aigre~, or it may be semi-learned, and a dialect form ~maire~ is the regular phonetic result. So ~maigrir~ means to become thin, to lose weight.
en.mailler: Formed from ~maille~ (“mesh, stitch”) with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, so ~mailler~ means to make into or work with meshes. English Wiktionary traces ~maille~ to Old French ~maille~, from Vulgar Latin *~macla~, itself inherited from Latin ~macula~, a word that meant both “spot” and “mesh.” ~Macula~ also survives as the learned doublet ~macule~. The French noun has other, unrelated homonyms (one from Latin ~medialis~, which also gave ~médaille~), but the mesh sense is the one behind this verb.
en.maintenir:
From Old French ~maintenir~ (“to protect, to defend, to uphold”), from Medieval Latin ~manutenere~, a fusion of the Latin phrase ~manu tenere~ (“to hold in the hand”) — ~manu~, the ablative of ~manus~ (“hand”), plus ~tenere~ (“to hold”). ~manus~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~man-~ (“hand”), while ~tenere~ rests on *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). Through this compound the verb is cognate with Italian ~mantenere~, Spanish ~mantener~, and English ~maintain~.

To maintain was first, literally, to keep a thing in hand — hence to support, protect, or defend, the dominant Old French sense. From “to hold up” grew the modern senses “to keep in a given state,” “to assert (an opinion),” and “to keep up, to service.” The last sense, the upkeep of machines and roads, is reinforced in modern French as a calque on English ~maintain~. From ~manus~ French draws ~main~, ~manuel~, ~manier~, and ~manœuvre~; from ~tenere~ come ~tenir~, ~retenir~, ~contenir~, and ~maintenance~ — so that the simple act of holding something in one's hand stands, etymologically, behind a vast machinery of holding, keeping, and managing.
en.majorer: ~Majorer~ is tied to Latin ~maior~ (“greater”), the comparative of ~magnus~ (“big”). French Wiktionary treats it as a French verb formed on ~major~ with the first-group ending ~-er~, while English Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~maiōrāre~ (“to augment”), a verb that was itself built on ~maior~. The two accounts differ on whether the verb was formed in French or inherited from the Latin verb, but they agree on the base. The meaning is “to make greater,” most often a price, a rate or an estimate, and sometimes by extension to overestimate.
en.malaxer: ~Malaxer~ was borrowed from Latin ~malaxāre~ (“to soften”), which English Wiktionary traces to Ancient Greek ~μαλάσσω~ (~malássō~). The verb thus came into French through Latin from Greek, a learned route for a word that names a humble gesture: working a substance by hand until it softens, as with dough or clay. The sources give no other details about its history.
en.malléabiliser: Formed from the adjective ~malléable~ with the suffix ~-iser~, which means “to make A,” so the verb means to make something malleable. The adjective is built from Latin ~malleus~ (“hammer”) plus ~-able~: a malleable metal is one that can be shaped by hammering. The verb is a technical coinage, used of materials that are treated so as to be workable.
en.malmener: A compound of ~mal~ (“badly”) and the verb ~mener~ (“to lead, to drive”). The element ~mal~ comes from Latin ~malus~ (“bad”) and its adverb ~male~ (“badly”), a root that Italian, Spanish and Portuguese share. ~Malmener~ therefore means literally to lead or handle badly, and it came to mean to treat someone roughly, to manhandle. It is used of people who are physically or verbally mistreated and, in sport or politics, of a side that is pushed around by its opponent.
en.malter: ~Malter~ is formed from the noun ~malt~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, with the sense “to turn grain into malt”. Both Wiktionaries give ~malt~ as borrowed from English ~malt~, a Germanic word. English Wiktionary adds, for the French word, a descent through Frankish from Proto-Germanic *~maltą~, but the sources do not agree on that route, and French Wiktionary gives the English borrowing alone.
en.maltraiter: Formed in French from ~mal-~ (“badly”) and ~traiter~ (“to treat”), so it means “to treat badly.” The prefix is the adverb ~mal~ fused to the verb, from Latin ~male~ (“badly”), from ~malus~ (“bad”). The base ~traiter~ comes from Latin ~tractāre~ (“to handle, to deal with”), a frequentative of ~trahere~ (“to draw, to pull”), and is related to Italian ~trattare~ and Spanish ~tratar~. Because ~traiter~ covers every kind of handling, from treating a patient to discussing a subject, ~maltraiter~ picks out the negative case: to handle a person roughly or abusively.
en.manager: A modern borrowing from English. French took the English verb ~manage~ and gave it the regular ending ~-er~, so ~manager~ conjugates like any first-group verb and means “to manage” or “to run” a team, a project or a business. Since the word comes straight from English, it has no past in French older than the loan itself.
en.mandater: Formed in French from ~mandat~ with the verb-forming ending ~-er~, so that ~mandater~ means to give someone a mandate, to commission or appoint them to act. The noun ~mandat~ was borrowed from Latin ~mandātum~ (“commission, order”), from ~mandāre~ (“to entrust, to order”), which English Wiktionary analyzes as ~manus~ (“hand”) plus ~dare~ (“to put, to give”), literally putting something in someone's hand. The same Latin verb gave French ~commander~ and ~demander~, so a mandate shares its ancestry with orders and requests.
en.mander:
From Old French ~mander~, inherited from Latin ~mandāre~. French Wiktionary links it to its better-known relatives ~commander~, ~recommander~ and ~demander~, all built on the same Latin verb. Latin ~mandāre~ is generally analyzed as ~manus~ (“hand”) + ~dare~ (“to give”), which would make it “to put into someone's hand,” hence to entrust or order. Italian ~mandare~ (“to send”) and Spanish ~mandar~ (“to order”) descend from it too.

In French, ~mander~ kept the sense of sending word or an order to someone, and so covers “to command,” “to summon” and “to inform by message.” Today it is a literary or old-fashioned verb, long since overshadowed by its prefixed offspring ~commander~, ~demander~ and ~recommander~. The same Latin source gave ~mandat~, ~mandement~ and ~contremander~, and English borrowed it as ~mandate~, ~command~ and ~demand~.
en.manger:
From Middle French ~manger~, from Old French ~mangier~, from Late Latin ~manducare~ (“to chew, to eat”), a derivative of ~manducus~ (“glutton”), itself from ~mandere~ (“to chew”). ~mandere~ is traced to Proto-Indo-European *~mendʰ-~ (“to chew”). Cognate with Italian ~mangiare~ and Occitan ~manjar~, both Gallo-Romance reflexes, and — through ~mandere~ — with English ~mandible~ and ~mange~.

The choice of word is itself a small comedy. Where Spanish and Portuguese kept a verb for plain eating (~comer~, from ~comedere~), Gaul preferred ~manducare~, a coarse, popular term meaning roughly “to munch, to champ.” Its source noun ~manducus~ named a glutton, and in Roman farce a ~Manducus~ was a grotesque masked figure with great clacking jaws — so French speakers, etymologically, do not dine so much as chomp. The same root *~mendʰ-~, by way of ~mandibula~, gives the anatomical ~mandibule~ (the jaw), while ~manducare~ itself yielded the learned ~manducation~ and the homely ~mangeoire~, a feeding trough — the very word English borrowed as ~manger~. Modern French ~mâcher~ (“to chew”), by contrast, comes from a different Latin verb, ~masticare~.
en.manier:
The two sources give different routes to one origin. French Wiktionary derives Old French ~maneier~ from ~main~ with the suffix ~-eyer~, while English Wiktionary traces it to Vulgar Latin *~manizāre~. Both rest on Latin ~manus~ (“hand”), so the verb is at bottom “to work with the hand.” Italian ~maneggiare~ is a relative, and French in turn borrowed ~manège~ from it. English ~manage~ is also a loan from the Italian verb, which gives the English word a surprising ancestor in the hand.

The meaning stayed tied to the hand: to handle an object, wield a tool, knead dough, and then by extension to work a language, a concept or a piece of software. The noun ~maniement~ and the adjective ~maniable~ (“easy to handle”) follow the same line. ~Manège~ took a different turn, first the training of horses and then the riding school, and eventually the merry-go-round and the figurative scheme or maneuver. The same hand also lies behind ~manuel~, ~manœuvre~ (from Latin ~manū operāre~, “to work by hand”) and ~main~ itself.
en.manifester:
From Latin ~manifestāre~ (“to make plain, reveal”), from the adjective ~manifestus~ (“caught in the act, evident, palpable”). That adjective opens with ~manus~ (“hand”), but its second element ~-festus~ is genuinely disputed. One long-standing reading links it to a verb of striking, also seen in ~īnfestus~ (“hostile”) and the family of ~dēfendere~ — so ~manifestus~ would picture a wrongdoer literally ~struck~ or ~seized~ by the hand, caught red-handed. ~Manus~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~manus~ and continues in French ~main~.

The word entered French around 1100. From “caught in the act” the adjective broadened to “plainly visible,” and the verb ~manifester~ to “make evident, show openly.” Its most public modern sense — to ~demonstrate~ in the streets, to ~protest~ — is a nineteenth-century political development: a crowd makes its will manifest by becoming visible. From the same Latin stock French keeps ~manifeste~ (both adjective and the noun ~manifeste~, a public declaration), ~manifestation~, and ~manifestant~. English ~manifest~, ~manifesto~ (through Italian), and ~manifestation~ are cousins, all carrying that ancient image of something laid bare to the hand.
en.manigancer: Formed in French from the noun ~manigance~ and the ending ~-er~, “to scheme, to plot.” The origin of ~manigance~ itself is obscure. Its first element is ultimately Latin ~manus~ (“hand”), but the suffix is unexplained. Littré compared ~manigance~ with ~manège~ and with ~manigotter~ (“to play with the hands”), which suggests a sense of sleight of hand and underhand dealing.
en.manipuler:
A late verb, formed in the 18th century as a denominal of the French noun ~manipule~, originally a pharmacist's term; Medieval Latin already had ~manipulare~ (“to handle”). ~manipule~ comes from Latin ~manipulus~ (“a handful”), a compound of ~manus~ (“hand”) and the root of ~plere~ (“to fill”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~pleh₁-~ (“to fill”). So a ~manipulus~ is, etymologically, “what fills the hand.”

The word's most vivid life was military: a Roman ~manipulus~ was a tactical unit, said to have first rallied around a bundle of hay tied to a pole — a literal handful raised as a standard before the eagle was adopted. From “handful” the pharmacist's ~manipule~ became a measured handful of ingredients, and the verb meant “to handle” substances by hand; only later did ~manipuler~ acquire the figurative, often pejorative sense “to manipulate” people or facts. Kin in French include ~manipulation~, ~manipulateur~, and — from the same ~manus~ — ~manuel~, ~manœuvre~, and ~manuscrit~.
en.manquer:
Unlike most French verbs, ~manquer~ is not inherited but borrowed, from Italian ~mancare~ (“to lack, to be wanting”), itself from the Latin adjective ~mancus~ (“maimed, crippled, defective”). ~mancus~ originally described a hand maimed or missing, and is connected to ~manus~ (“hand”); both are referred to a Proto-Indo-European *~mh₂nkó-~ (“maimed in the hand”), beside ~manus~ from the root for “hand.” The same adjective survives as Italian ~manco~ and Spanish ~manco~ (“one-handed, maimed”).

From “maimed” the Italian word generalized to “to be missing, to fall short,” and French took it over in the sixteenth century, gradually pushing aside the older native ~faillir~. The most surprising development is grammatical rather than semantic: in the sense “to be missed,” ~manquer~ inverts subject and object, so that ~tu me manques~ literally says “you are lacking to me” yet means “I miss you” — the person felt as absent is the grammatical subject, and the verb agrees with them, as in ~mes amis me manquent~ (“I miss my friends”). The same root gave French the noun ~manque~ (“lack”), the verb ~manquement~ (“a failing, a breach”), and ~manchot~ (“one-armed,” also the name for a penguin), all circling the ancient idea of a defective, incomplete hand.
en.manucurer: From the noun ~manucure~, with the first-group ending ~-er~, it means to give someone a manicure. The noun, which in French names both the care of the hands and the person who provides it, is a learned formation on Latin ~manus~ (“hand”) and ~cūra~ (“care”), the same pair that English ~manicure~ rests on.
en.manufacturer: Formed in French from the noun ~manufacture~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ~manufactūra~ (“making by hand”), built from ~manū~ (“by hand”) and ~factūra~ (“act of making”). The two halves live on in French as ~main~ (“hand”) and ~facture~. Although the Latin parts literally speak of the hand, the verb simply means “to manufacture”, that is, to produce goods.
en.manutentionner: ~Manutentionner~ is formed from the noun ~manutention~ with ~-er~: to handle goods, to process them through a warehouse or workshop. The noun is a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ~manūtentiō~ (“maintenance”), from the verb ~manūtenēre~ (“to maintain”), which is built on the Latin words for “hand” and “to hold” and is also the source of French ~maintenir~. So the verb preserves, at three removes, the image of holding something in the hand.
en.manœuvrer:
From Old French ~manovrer~, from Vulgar Latin *~manuoperare~, which was built from Classical Latin ~manu~ (“with the hand”) and ~operārī~ (“to work”). The compound thus meant, literally, “to work by hand.” Its two halves are familiar Latin words: ~manus~ (“hand”) and ~operārī~, the verb that belongs to ~opus~ (“work”). English borrowed the word from French as ~maneuver~.

The Latin root ~manus~ underlies a large French family: ~main~, ~manuel~, ~manuscrit~, ~manier~. The root of ~operārī~ and ~opus~ gave ~œuvre~, ~opérer~ and ~ouvrer~. The ~œuvr~ of ~manœuvrer~ is the same ~œuvre~ that means “work” in French, which explains the unusual spelling with the ligature ~œ~. In modern French the verb covers handling a vehicle or a piece of equipment, moving troops or ships, and, figuratively, steering a person or a situation toward a goal by skillful, sometimes calculating, means.
en.mapper: Formed from ~mappe~ with the verb ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary says the sense “to map” comes from English ~map~ (“map”), while English Wiktionary traces the base to Latin ~mappa~ (“napkin, cloth”). The base is a learned borrowing rather than an inherited word, because the inherited form of ~mappa~ is ~nappe~ (“tablecloth”). So ~mapper~ is a modern verb, in computing and cartography, that sits on a very old Latin root.
en.maquer: A slang verb formed on ~mac~ (“pimp”), itself a short form of ~maquereau~ (“pimp,” also the fish). English Wiktionary gives the descent as ~mac~ and ~maquereau~, while French Wiktionary calls ~maquer~ a denominal verb of ~mac~ and links it with Old French ~mascher~ and Italian ~ammaccare~. The older sense is to live off, or to act as, a pimp. The verb now chiefly appears in ~se maquer~, an informal expression for taking up with someone as a couple.
en.maquereauter: Formed from ~maquereau~ with the verb ending ~-er~, meaning to act as a pimp. The origin of the noun is uncertain. One account derives it from Old French ~maquerel~ and links it to the family of ~maquer~ (“to strike, bruise”), with the fish named for its spotted skin. Another traces it to Middle Dutch ~makelaer~ (“broker, go-between”), from ~makelen~ (“to trade”), a relative of ~maken~ (“to make”). A third account appeals to a folk belief that the fish brought male and female herrings together. The verb adds the ending ~-er~ to the procurer sense of the noun.
en.maquetter: A denominal verb: ~maquette~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning to make or lay out a ~maquette~, a mock-up or dummy. The noun ~maquette~ comes from Italian ~macchietta~ (“speck, little spot”), a diminutive of ~macchia~ (“spot”), which goes back to Latin ~macula~ (“spot, stain”). The ending ~-er~ is the default way French turns a noun into a verb, and it descends from the Latin first-conjugation ending ~-are~.
en.maquignonner: A denominal verb on ~maquignon~ (“horse dealer”) with the verb ending ~-er~: to deal in horses and, figuratively, to use shady sales tactics. The origin of ~maquignon~ is given two ways. French Wiktionary derives it from Dutch ~makelen~ (“to trade”); English Wiktionary suggests it comes from ~maquereau~ with a change of suffix, on the model of ~barguigner~.
en.maquiller:
~Maquiller~ is a French verb of Germanic ancestry. English Wiktionary derives it from Middle French ~macquiller~ (“to work, to do”) by two routes it gives side by side. One runs through an Old French verb *~makier~ (“to build, to make”), from Frankish *~makjan~ or *~makōn~, or from Old Dutch ~macōn~, all from Proto-West Germanic *~makōn~ and, ultimately, a Proto-Indo-European root *~mag-~ (“to knead, to mix, to make”). The other runs through Picard ~maquier~, borrowed from Middle Dutch ~maken~. French Wiktionary follows the Picard route and adds the suffix ~-iller~. German ~machen~ and Old English ~macian~ are cousins, and English ~make~ descends from the latter.

The verb began as a plain “to do, to make,” and its modern sense came late. French Wiktionary says it passed into slang with the meaning “to falsify,” then into theatre slang in 1840 with the meaning “to make up an actor's face,” and finally lost the slang sense to mean “to apply cosmetics, to embellish a face.” The sources do not say why a Picard verb of making ended up in slang. The same verb gave French ~maquillage~ and ~maquilleur~. A plain verb of making, in short, that ended by meaning the art of making up a face.
en.marabouter: Formed from the noun ~marabout~ and the verb ending ~-er~, in the way that ~ensorceler~ comes from ~sorcier~: to put under a spell, as a marabout is believed to do. The noun comes through Portuguese ~maraboto~ from Arabic ~murābiṭ~, a man who lived in a ~ribāṭ~, a fortified convent on a frontier. The word later came to mean a holy man or hermit, and by extension the tomb of such a man, and then any sacred object or animal.
en.marauder: From ~maraud~ + the suffix ~-er~: to ~marauder~ is to act like a ~maraud~, a rascal or vagabond. The origin of ~maraud~ itself is debated. English Wiktionary traces it to Old French *~marault~ (“beggar, vagabond”), from ~marir~ (“to trouble, to stray”), itself from Frankish. French Wiktionary lists rival accounts: a figurative use of a dialect word for the tomcat, imitating its purring or caterwauling, or a derivative of ~marre~ (“a kind of hoe”), or Bugge's proposed *~maraldus~. None is settled.
en.marbrer: Formed from ~marbre~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~ (from Latin ~-are~), meaning to give the veined look of marble. The noun comes through Old French from Latin ~marmor~, from Greek ~μάρμαρος~ (~mármaros~). The Greek word's origin is debated. One account links it to ~μαραίνω~ (“to break”), so “cut stone”; another to ~μαρμαίρω~ (“to shine”), so “gleaming stone.”
en.marchander: ~Marchander~ is formed from ~marchand~ (“merchant”) with the verb ending ~-er~, and means to haggle over a price. It is attested in the 12th century as Old French ~markëander~, in the Renclus de Moiliens's Li romans de Carité. The noun comes from Old French ~marceant~, from Vulgar Latin *~mercatantem~, the accusative of the present participle of *~mercatare~, itself from Latin ~mercatus~ (“market”). A merchant is thus, etymologically, someone who deals in the market, and to haggle is to behave like one.
en.marcher:
From Middle French ~marcher~, from Old French ~marchier~ (“to trample, to tread underfoot”), attested around 1170. The most widely accepted source is Frankish *~markôn~ (“to mark, to press with the foot”), reaching French through Old High German ~marcôn~ — a Germanic verb of the Franks rather than a Latin inheritance. A competing hypothesis, going back to Scheler, instead derives it from Latin ~marcus~ (“a hammer”), through the image of feet hammering the ground; the question is genuinely unsettled.

The oldest sense was “to trample, to tread on,” preserved in the related ~marc~ (“the pressed residue of grapes or olives”), the pulp left underfoot. From that came the ordinary “to walk,” then a remarkable spread of figurative uses: an army on the ~marche~, a plan that ~marche~ (“works, goes well”), and the slangy ~ça marche~ (“all right, it's a deal”). One must not confuse this verb with the noun ~marché~ (“a market,” from Latin ~mercatus~), an unrelated homonym. From the verb the language draws ~marche~ (“a step, a march”), ~démarche~ (“a gait; a course of action”), and ~marcheur~ (“a walker”).
en.marcotter: Formed in French from the noun ~marcotte~ (“a layer,” a shoot rooted while still on the parent plant) and the ending ~-er~, so “to propagate by layering.” The origin of ~marcotte~ is uncertain. One account sees a Gaulish word mentioned by the Roman author Columella as ~marcus~. Another connects the dialectal variant ~margotte~ and Italian ~margotta~ to Latin ~mergere~ (“to plunge”), which suits a shoot buried in the soil.
en.margauder: French Wiktionary explains ~margauder~ as a compound of ~margot~, altered to ~margaud~, and the verb ending ~-er~. It gives no older source language and no date. The verb is a cry-verb for the mating call of certain animals, and the formation rests on a single line of evidence, so nothing more can be said with confidence.
en.marger: Formed on the noun ~marge~ (“margin”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so it is a verb coined in French for dealing with a margin. The noun is inherited from Old French and goes back to Latin ~marginem~, accusative of ~margō~ (“edge, border”), which English Wiktionary traces to Proto-Indo-European *~mórǵs~. English ~margin~ comes from the same Latin word. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~, and is the default way French turns a noun into a first-group verb.
en.marginaliser: Formed from the adjective ~marginal~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which builds verbs meaning “to make A” or “to treat as A.” The adjective ~marginal~ is a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ~marginalis~, from Latin ~margo~ (“edge, border”), the source of French ~marge~ (“margin”). To ~marginaliser~ someone or something is therefore to push it to the margin, out of the central part of society, the economy or a debate.
en.marginer: ~Marginer~ is formed from ~marge~ (“margin”) with the verb ending ~-er~, and means to write notes in the margins of a text. The noun ~marge~ comes from Old French and from Latin ~margo~, accusative ~marginem~ (“edge”), which is traced back to a Proto-Indo-European form *~mórǵs~. English ~margin~ comes from the same Latin word. The verb is a literal one: it simply acts on the edge of the page.
en.margoter: Formed from ~margot~ with the verb ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary notes that ~margot~ already existed in Old French. The verb is a specialized one that names the call of the quail. The sources do not explain how ~margot~ came to be linked with the bird's cry, so nothing more can be said with confidence about the sense.
en.margotter: Formed from ~margot~ and the verb ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary gives only that ~margot~ comes from an Old French word of the same form, and states no further origin, so nothing more can be said with confidence about the base. The verb has the narrow sense “to make a mating call,” used of certain birds. The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, is the ordinary way French builds a verb on a noun, here “to act or cry like N.”
en.marier:
Attested from 1145, from Latin ~maritare~ (“to marry, to give in marriage”), derived from ~maritus~ (“husband, married man”). ~Maritus~ is generally connected to ~mas~ (“male”) and perhaps to an Indo-European element meaning “young woman, bride,” though the deeper derivation is debated and best left open. Italian keeps the noun in ~marito~ (“husband”) and the verb ~maritare~, while Spanish has ~maridar~ beside ~marido~; English borrowed French ~marier~ as ~marry~.

In its earliest French use ~marier~ meant “to give someone in marriage,” the active role of the parent or matchmaker; the reflexive ~se marier~ (“to get married”) appears by around 1170. Beyond the wedding, the verb developed a graceful figurative life: one can ~marier~ colors, flavors, or ideas — that is, blend them harmoniously, as in ~ce vin se marie bien avec le poisson~. The same root gives French ~mari~ (“husband”), ~mariage~, ~marié~ and ~mariée~ (“groom” and “bride”), and ~remarier~. It is worth noting that ~marier~ (“to wed”) and ~Marie~ (the given name) are unrelated despite the resemblance — a coincidence that has confused many a learner, but never the etymology.
en.mariner: Borrowed from Italian ~marinare~, itself from ~marino~ (“of the sea”), which goes back to Latin ~marīnus~, from ~mare~ (“sea”). The verb originally meant to preserve fish or meat in brine, that is, in salted seawater, hence “to pickle.” The modern sense of soaking food in a seasoned liquid before cooking developed from that older preserving technique. The same sea-word underlies French ~marin~ (“sailor”), ~marine~ and ~marinade~.
en.marivauder: From the family name of Pierre Carlet de Chamblain de ~Marivaux~ (1688-1763), the French dramatist, with the verbal ending ~-er~. His comedies are known for refined, subtle talk about love, and ~marivauder~ means to flirt wittily or to speak of love in an affected, elaborate way. The noun ~marivaudage~ names the same manner. The verb is thus an eponym, built on a writer's name much as ~merceriser~ is built on an inventor's.
en.marketer:
From English ~market~, a word that English Wiktionary traces to Old Northern French ~market~ (“commerce, marketplace, trade”), from Latin ~mercātus~ (“market, trade”), the past participle of ~mercārī~ (“to deal in, to buy, to trade”). That verb derives from ~merx~ (genitive ~mercis~, “merchandise, wares”), from Proto-Italic *~merk-~, and English Wiktionary traces the root to Etruscan. French then added its own verb ending ~-er~ to the English noun, as it does with borrowings such as ~tester~ and ~scanner~.

The Latin ~mercātus~ also reached French by the inherited route as ~marché~ (“market”), so ~marketer~ and ~marché~ are cousins, separated by a trip across the Channel. The family of ~merx~ is large: ~marchand~ (“merchant”), ~marchandise~, ~commerce~, ~mercantile~ and ~marchander~ (“to haggle”). ~Marketer~ belongs to the vocabulary of business, “to promote and sell a product by marketing,” and is often felt as jargon next to the older ~commercialiser~.
en.marmiter: From ~marmite~ (“cooking pot”), used in military slang for a heavy shell. The sources differ on the link. Some read ~marmite~ as the shell itself, a “big shell”, but the more plausible account is that it names the crater a shell leaves in the ground, which looks like a cooking pot. Either way, ~marmiter~ means to pound a position with shells, the verb ending ~-er~ being added to the slang noun.
en.marmonner: ~Marmonner~ is imitative in origin: French sources see in it the sound ~marm~, evoking a confused murmur, and English sources compare ~murmurer~, which is itself imitative. It means “to murmur, to mumble,” to speak low and unclearly. The verb is therefore not built from a base word but from the sound that it describes.
en.marmoriser:
Formed from Latin ~marmor~ (“marble”) and the verb-forming suffix ~-iser~: to give something the look of marble, or to turn it into marble. The suffix comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, itself a transcription of Greek verbs. The Latin noun ~marmor~ is the same word that gave French ~marbre~ (where the first ~r~ became ~b~, a dissimilation) and Italian ~marmo~. Latin took ~marmor~ from Greek ~mármaros~, a “gleaming stone”.

The family is divided between inherited and learned words. The popular line gave ~marbre~, ~marbrer~ (to streak like marble) and ~marbrure~. The learned line stayed closer to Latin and gave ~marmoréen~ (“marble-like”) and ~marmorisation~, and ~marmoriser~ belongs to it, since it keeps the Latin stem intact. English has both lines too: ~marble~ came through Old French, while ~marmoreal~ was drawn straight from Latin. Spanish ~mármol~ and German ~Marmor~ show the same word in other languages.
en.marmotter: An alteration of ~marmonner~. Both verbs share the syllable ~marm-~, which evokes a confused murmur, and that sound explains why they mean much the same thing: to mumble or mutter. Both describe speech that is low, indistinct and half swallowed, spoken between the teeth rather than aloud, so the meaning of each verb is carried largely by the sound of its first syllable.
en.marner:
English Wiktionary derives ~marner~ from the noun ~marne~ (“marl,” a clay-rich limestone soil) plus the verb ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary adds that the verb, dated 1564, is a remaking of the older ~marler~ (1207), which meant “to improve the soil with marl.” The noun comes from Old French ~marle~ (variant ~marne~), from Late Latin ~margila~, which French Wiktionary says was influenced by ~argilla~ (“clay”), and ultimately from Gaulish ~marga~, a word Pliny recorded. English Wiktionary instead gives ~margila~ as a Gaulish diminutive of ~marga~.

The slang sense, “to slog, to work hard,” is first dated 1837 and is probably an extension of the farming verb, the labor of spreading marl being heavy. That link is only “probable” in the source, so treat it as a plausible explanation rather than a proven one. A second note in French Wiktionary, itself flagged as unsupported, says the word probably shares an origin with ~marge~. English ~marl~ is a cousin of the same French word.
en.maronner: The origin of ~maronner~ is uncertain, and the sources offer competing accounts. One dates the verb to around 1709 and derives it from ~marron~ (“fugitive slave”), by way of English ~maroon~. A second proposes a link with ~marmonner~, or with ~maraud~ in its old sense of “tomcat.” A third simply derives it from ~maraud~ in that same sense. None of these is settled, so the verb is best treated as a word whose path is debated, with the ~marron~ account carrying the earliest date.
en.maroufler: Formed from ~maroufle~ + ~-er~, the ending that turns a noun into a verb: ~maroufler~ is to glue a canvas onto a backing. The noun ~maroufle~ began as a variant of ~maraud~ (“rascal”), and its sense of “glue” is rare before the nineteenth century. Two explanations are offered for that sense: painters jokingly equating ~maraud~ with glue, or an assimilation of the gluing spatula to the ~marre~ (“curved shovel”).
en.marquer:
French ~marquer~ comes from Old French ~merchier~ (“to make a mark to distinguish something”), an Anglo-Norman and Picard form. Its ancestor is the Germanic noun *~marka~ (“boundary, border, sign set at a limit”), of Frankish origin, from Proto-Indo-European *~merǵ-~ (“boundary, edge”). The modern vowel ~a~ was pulled in by ~marcher~ and by the Italian ~marcare~ and Spanish ~marcar~, themselves from the same Germanic root. Cognate forms abound: English ~mark~, Dutch ~mark~, German ~Mark~, Swedish ~mark~, and even Latin ~margo~ (“edge,” whence French ~marge~).

The oldest sense was territorial: a *~marka~ was a frontier zone, and a ~marquis~ was originally the count of such a borderland, the ~marche~. From “a sign planted at a boundary” the noun ~marque~ generalized to any distinguishing sign, and ~marquer~ to the act of inscribing one — branding cattle, noting down a figure, scoring a goal (this last sense reinforced in the nineteenth century by English ~to mark~). The root spread widely in French: ~marche~ (a border province, as in les Marches), ~marquise~, ~démarquer~, and ~marqueterie~ all belong to it, and through English so do ~demarcation~ and ~marquee~. What began as the line dividing two lands now means simply leaving a trace.
en.marrer: The origin of ~se marrer~ is uncertain. French Wiktionary gives two proposals: the Old French verb ~se marrir~ (“to grieve”), or Spanish ~marear~ (“to bore, to make dizzy”), with ~marearse~ (“to get seasick”). English Wiktionary favors the Spanish source, with the sense shifting from “to get dizzy” to “to be bored” and then, by antiphrasis, to “to be amused.” Whatever the source, the verb first meant “to be bored” and only later came to mean laughing at something that should have been tedious. The noun ~marre~ (as in ~j'en ai marre~) is not the base: French Wiktionary treats it as a back-formation from the verb, and the TLFi rejects any link with ~marrir~.
en.marsouiner: Formed from the noun ~marsouin~ (“porpoise”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so the verb describes moving through the water the way a porpoise does. French Wiktionary traces ~marsouin~ through Norman to Old Norse ~marsvín~, literally “sea pig,” from ~mari~ (“sea”) and ~svín~ (“pig”); it is related to English ~mereswine~ and German ~Meerschwein~. English Wiktionary is more cautious about the route, listing Old English, Old Frankish, Middle Dutch and Old Norse as possible Germanic sources, all from a Proto-Germanic word for dolphin or porpoise.
en.marteler: Inherited from Middle French and Old French ~marteler~, itself formed from Old French ~martel~ (“hammer”, the older form of ~marteau~) and the verbal ending ~-er~. ~Martel~ goes back to Late Latin ~martellus~ (“hammer”). The sense is simply to hammer, to strike repeatedly, whether metal, a door or a rhythm. It then widened figuratively, so that one ~martèle~ one's words, pronouncing each syllable with force, or drives a point home by insistent repetition. Dutch ~martelen~ and the English word ~martel~ are cognates of the Old French noun.
en.martyriser: ~Martyriser~ is formed from ~martyr~ with the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make, to treat as”), and it means “to torment” and, by extension, “to bully”. The noun ~martyr~ comes from Latin ~martyr~, from Ancient Greek ~mártus~ (“witness”). It appears in Old French as ~martir~ around 1050, and a variant ~martre~ survives in place names such as ~Montmartre~, which in most cases mark former places of burial or execution.
en.masculiniser: Formed from the adjective ~masculin~ with the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to make masculine.” The adjective is borrowed from Latin ~masculinus~ (“male, of the masculine gender”), from ~masculus~ (“male, manly”), itself from ~mas~ (“male”), by way of Old French ~masculin~. The verb applies to bodies, jobs and professions alike.
en.masquer:
French ~masquer~ is a denominal verb built on the noun ~masque~ (“mask”) with the suffix ~-er~. ~masque~ was borrowed from Italian ~maschera~, and there the trail forks, for the deeper origin is genuinely disputed. By one account it comes from a pre-Romance *~maska~ meaning “black,” recalling that the earliest disguise was simply a blackened face; by another it goes back to Medieval Latin ~masca~ (“witch, specter, nightmare”), itself of uncertain origin; and by a third, much-cited account it derives from Arabic ~مسخرة~ (~masḵara~, “buffoon, mockery”), from a root meaning “to mock.” The TLFi and Littré are wary of the Arabic hypothesis rather than endorsing it, so the question stays open.

Whatever its source, the noun gave French a verb meaning to “mask,” “hide,” or “conceal,” and figuratively to disguise an intention or a flavor. Whichever etymology one favors, the family is broad and international: French ~masque~, ~mascarade~ (“masquerade”), and ~démasquer~ (“to unmask”) sit beside English ~mask~ and ~mascara~ — the cosmetic name itself reflecting that old thread of darkening the face — all converging on the single idea of a covering laid over the true face.
en.massacrer:
French ~massacrer~ is inherited from Middle French ~massacrer~, from Old French ~macecler~ or ~macecrer~. The probable source, though not a certain one, is a Vulgar Latin verb *~matteuculāre~, formed from *~matteuca~, the word that also gave French ~massue~ (“club”). English Wiktionary traces that Vulgar Latin noun further back to *~mattea~ or Late Latin ~mattia~, and ultimately to Latin ~mateola~, glossed there as “hoe.” This last stretch of the chain is a reconstruction, so the origin should be read as likely rather than proven. English ~massacre~ was borrowed from French.

If the chain is right, the verb would have meant “to strike with a club,” which would fit the sense of “to slaughter,” though the sources do not trace that development. The Old French forms ~macecler~ and ~macecrer~ are given as two variants of one word. Today the verb covers the killing of many people and also the careless destruction of things. In everyday French, one can ~massacrer~ a song, a piece of music or a foreign language, which means to perform or speak it so badly that it is ruined, a figurative use of the same violence. The word ~massue~, named above, keeps the memory of that weapon.
en.masser:
The origin of ~masser~ (“to massage”) is debated, and the dictionaries record more than one account. The one English Wiktionary calls probable is a borrowing, around the end of the eighteenth century, from Arabic ~massa~ (مَسَّ, “to touch, to feel”). The same source offers a rival: Portuguese ~amassar~. French Wiktionary lists three accounts for the French verb, among them the Arabic one, a derivation from ~masse~ in the sense of “lump, heap,” and a derivation from another ~masse~, meaning “club.”

Because the accounts conflict, nothing here can be asserted as settled, and the sense that a lump or a club might have given a verb of massage is not explained in the sources. If the Arabic or the Portuguese account is right, the verb is a late borrowing, from around the end of the eighteenth century.
en.massicoter: ~Massicoter~ (“to trim with a paper guillotine”) is formed from the noun ~massicot~ with the ending ~-er~. The machine is traced to the name of its French inventor, Guillaume Massiquot (1797-1870), and the noun was also once spelled ~massiquot~. French Wiktionary adds another account: ~massicot~ would come from Italian ~marzacotto~ (“a kind of varnish”), itself from Arabic. English Wiktionary says the word was influenced by that Italian word, which ultimately goes back to an Arabic term for lead oxide. The inventor's name remains the usual explanation of the machine's name.
en.massifier: Formed from ~masse~ and the suffix ~-ifier~, so it means to make something massive in scale, to extend it to the masses. The noun ~masse~ comes from Latin ~massa~ (“lump, heap”), which English Wiktionary traces to Greek ~μᾶζα~ (“barley bread”). The suffix ~-ifier~ goes back to Latin ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”), and is still productive in learned and journalistic French. ~Massifier~ is typically said of education or production that is opened to a large public.
en.mastiquer: ~Mastiquer~ has two stories, both told by French Wiktionary. In the sense “to chew,” it is a learned borrowing from Latin ~masticāre~ (“to chew”), and English Wiktionary notes that it is a doublet of ~mâcher~, which descends from the same Latin verb by the inherited, worn-down route. In the sense “to fill or seal with putty,” it is a denominal verb, formed from the noun ~mastic~, the resin and the sealing paste made from it. English ~masticate~ and the noun ~mastication~ are parallel learned descendants of the same Latin verb, as are Italian ~masticare~ and Spanish ~masticar~. The noun ~mastic~ gives the second branch: ~mastiquer~ in the workshop is to apply ~mastic~ and so to fill a crack or seal a pane.
en.masturber:
~Masturber~ is borrowed from Latin ~masturbārī~, a deponent verb, that is, one with passive endings and an active sense, meaning to masturbate. French took it over as a regular verb in ~-er~, replacing the Latin infinitive ending. The same Latin word gave Italian ~masturbare~, Spanish and Portuguese ~masturbar~, German ~masturbieren~ and English ~masturbate~, so the verb is one of the shared learned vocabulary of Western Europe.

French built a small family on the borrowed verb: the nouns ~masturbation~ and ~masturbateur~. The verb is used mostly in the reflexive form ~se masturber~. It also has a familiar figurative use in the idiom ~se masturber le cerveau~ (“to overthink”), applied to someone who goes round in circles over a problem without getting anywhere.
en.matelasser: ~Matelasser~ is a denominal verb: ~matelas~ (“mattress”) plus ~-er~, meaning to pad or cushion. The noun comes from Old French ~materas~, probably from Italian ~materasso~, and ultimately from Arabic ~maṭraḥ~ (“carpet, place where something is thrown”), from ~ṭaraḥa~ (“to throw”). It is a doublet of ~matras~.
en.mater: Two senses, two stories. The chess and “subdue” sense is a denominal of ~mat~ (“checkmated”) with the ending ~-er~. The chess word ~mat~ comes from ~échec et mat~, which French Wiktionary traces to Arabic ~māt~ (“dead”) and English Wiktionary to Persian ~šâh mât~ (“the king is ambushed”). The slang sense “to eye, to ogle” has an uncertain origin. It may come from the Spanish ~mata~ (“bush”), perhaps through North African French ~faire la mata~ (“to lie in wait”), which would tie it to Spanish ~mata~ as well. Only the chess origin is well established.
en.materner:
From Latin ~māternus~ (“of a mother, maternal”), itself from ~māter~ (“mother”), with the French verb ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary gives ~māter~ directly as the source, and English Wiktionary the adjective ~māternus~. Either way the root is the Latin word for “mother”, a cognate of English ~mother~ and German ~Mutter~. The verb means to mother someone, and by extension to mollycoddle them.

The same Latin family gave French ~mère~, inherited from ~māter~, and the learned ~maternel~ and ~maternité~, built on ~māternus~. The ~école maternelle~ (nursery school) carries the same adjective. Compared with those words, ~materner~ is rarer and often has a slightly critical edge, as in treating an adult like a child. The verb thus pairs the plain sense “to act as a mother to” with its figurative “to smother with care”.
en.mathématiser: ~Mathématiser~ is formed from ~mathématiques~ (“mathematics”) with the suffix ~-iser~, which makes verbs meaning to make or render, to treat with, to convert into. The verb thus means to put something into mathematical terms. The noun is the plural of ~mathématique~, a learned borrowing from Latin ~mathēmaticus~, itself from Ancient Greek ~μαθηματικός~ (~mathēmatikós~, “fond of learning”).
en.matir: Formed from ~mat~ (“dull, unpolished, matte”) and the verb ending ~-ir~, in the pattern of deadjectival verbs meaning “to make A”: to ~matir~ is to dull a surface, for instance a metal that was shiny. The origin of ~mat~ is disputed. French Wiktionary gives an Old French ~mat~, but notes that one nineteenth-century scholar derived it from Arabic ~māt~ (“dead”), the word of the chess phrase ~échec et mat~ (English Wiktionary adds Persian ~šāh māt~ for that phrase). English Wiktionary alternatively suggests Latin ~mattus~, from ~madere~ (“to be wet, soft”), with an Italian cousin ~matto~. The sources disagree, so only the formation is certain.
en.matraquer: ~Matraquer~ is formed from ~matraque~ (“club, truncheon”) plus the verbal ending ~-er~: to beat with a club. By extension it also means to hammer a message home, as in heavy advertising. The noun was borrowed from vernacular Arabic ~maṭraqa~, compare literary Arabic ~miṭraqa~ (“hammer”). Spanish ~matraca~ comes from the same Arabic word.
en.matricer: ~Matricer~ is derived from the noun ~matrice~ (“matrix, die”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, so it means to shape something with a die or to treat it as a matrix. It has a doublet in ~matrixer~, formed from the same noun in a different shape. The two verbs are variant formations on one base rather than separate inheritances.
en.matérialiser: Formed in French from ~matériel~ (“material”) and the verb suffix ~-iser~ (“to make, to turn into”). The verb means to give material form to something, and then, figuratively, to make it real or bring it about.
