The adjective ~matériel~ is inherited from Old French ~materiel~, from Late Latin ~māteriālis~ (“made of matter”), from Latin ~māteria~ (“wood, material, substance”), which one source links to ~māter~ (“mother”). The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, which carried Greek verbs into Latin and then into French, where it became one of the most productive verb-makers of technical and administrative language.
en.maudire:
French ~maudire~ comes from Old French ~maldire~ (Middle French ~maudire~, ~mauldire~), a semi-learned borrowing from Latin ~maledīcere~, “to slander, to curse.” French Wiktionary glosses the Latin verb as “to utter bad words, to insult,” and analyzes it as a compound of the adverb ~mălĕ~ (“badly”) and the verb ~dīcere~ (“to say”). English Wiktionary likewise treats the French word as equivalent to ~mal~ plus ~dire~. A semi-learned borrowing is a word taken from Latin through the written, scholarly channel, but early enough to be reshaped by ordinary French sound change, which is why it did not stay a pure Latin form. That reshaping is visible in the step from ~maldire~ to ~maudire~.

Old French had a second verb for the same idea, ~maleir~. French Wiktionary says it was formed differently from ~maledīcere~, and English Wiktionary says it may have been inherited, so the sources leave open exactly how ~maleir~ arose, and no origin is asserted for it here. What French Wiktionary does state is that ~maudire~ supplanted ~maleir~. The verb that survived was therefore the one built on the Latin compound ~maledīcere~, which is itself the sum of ~male~ and ~dīcere~, and the verb of different make dropped out of use. Both sources agree on the main line of descent, from Latin ~maledīcere~ through Old French ~maldire~ to modern ~maudire~. They differ only in the weight they give the rival ~maleir~ and in the label “semi-learned,” which only English Wiktionary uses.
en.maugréer:
From Old French ~maugré~ (“ill will”) with the verb ending ~-er~. Old French ~maugré~ was a compound of ~mau~ (“bad”) and ~gré~ (“pleasure, will”), from Latin ~malus~ (“bad”) and ~grātum~ (“pleasing”). Both parts are standard Latin vocabulary: ~malus~ also gave French ~mal~, and ~grātum~ is the source of French ~gré~, as in ~savoir gré~ (“to be grateful”).

The same Old French ~maugré~ survives in the preposition ~malgré~ (“in spite of”), literally “with bad will,” so ~maugréer~ and ~malgré~ are close relatives. The verb turns that ill will into speech: to ~maugréer~ is to grumble, to voice one's displeasure under one's breath. The other half of the compound lives on in ~gré~ itself, in ~agréer~ (“to accept, to approve”) and in the learned ~gratuit~, all from Latin ~grātum~.
en.maximaliser: ~Maximaliser~ is formed from the adjective ~maximal~ and the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to make as great as possible.” ~Maximal~ is itself built from ~maximum~ and the adjectival suffix ~-al~, and ~maximum~ is the Latin word for “greatest.” The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs. The verb overlaps with ~maximiser~ in current usage.
en.maximiser: A modern borrowing from English ~maximize~, which French then fitted with the ordinary verb ending ~-er~, hence ~maximiser~ in the first conjugation. The English verb was built on ~maximum~, a Latin neuter adjective meaning “greatest,” the superlative of ~magnus~ (“great”). French already had ~maximum~, ~maximal~ and the opposite verb ~minimiser~, so the new verb filled an obvious gap. It means to bring something, a profit or a chance, to its highest possible level.
en.mazouter: Formed from ~mazout~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to soil or pollute with fuel oil.” The noun ~mazout~ was borrowed from Russian ~mazut~ (“fuel oil”). French Wiktionary adds that the Russian word itself comes from Arabic, from a word meaning “residue.” The verb is mostly met in the passive, for something fouled by an oil spill or by heavy fuel.
en.maçonner: ~Maçonner~ is formed from ~maçon~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, so it means to do a mason's work: to face a wall, to render it, or to brick up an opening. Old French ~maçon~ goes back to Late Latin ~maciōnem~, attested in the seventh century in Isidore of Seville. French Wiktionary derives that Latin word from Frankish *~makjo~, built on *~makôn~ (“to build, to make”), which makes Dutch ~maken~, German ~machen~ and English ~make~ cognates. English Wiktionary only compares Old High German ~mahhōn~ (“to make”).
en.maîtriser:
Coined in the late fourteenth century from the noun ~maîtrise~ (“mastery”), itself derived from ~maître~ (“master”). ~maître~ comes from Old French ~maistre~, from Latin ~magister~ (“master, chief, teacher”), which is a comparative formation: ~magis~ (“more”) plus the contrastive suffix ~-ter~, literally “the one who is greater.” ~magis~ rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~meǵ-~ (“great”), the same root behind Latin ~magnus~ (“great”). From ~magister~ also descend Italian ~maestro~, Spanish ~maestro~, German ~Meister~, and, through Norman French, English ~master~ and ~mister~.

The verb means to make oneself master of something: to ~maîtriser~ a language, a fire, one's emotions, an adversary. The chain ~maître~ → ~maîtrise~ → ~maîtriser~ shows French building a verb on a noun on a noun, each step adding the idea of acquired control. The deep root *~meǵ-~ fans out into a huge French family beyond the ~maître~ line: ~majeur~ (“major”), ~maxime~, ~maximum~, ~magnitude~, ~magnat~, ~magnifique~, ~majesté~, and even ~maire~ (“mayor”) — all carrying, like ~maîtriser~ itself, the ancient sense of greatness, of being more. To master is, etymologically, to make oneself the greater party.
en.menacer:
From Vulgar Latin *~mināciāre~, a verb built on Latin ~mināciae~ (“threats”), which displaced Classical Latin ~minārī~ (“to threaten”). ~Minārī~ derives from ~minae~ (“threats”), a noun whose oldest, concrete sense referred to projecting or jutting points — the menacing overhang of a cliff or a battlement. The same Gallo-Romance form gave Italian ~minacciare~, Spanish ~amenazar~, Portuguese ~ameaçar~, and Catalan ~amenaçar~.

The striking detail is the bridge between architecture and intimidation: ~minae~ first named the things that loom and jut forward, and only then the abstract sense of a threat that looms over someone. To threaten was, etymologically, to thrust something forward menacingly. The verb settled into modern French ~menacer~ with senses ranging from open intimidation to the impersonal “to endanger” (a deadline that threatens, a wall that threatens to collapse). From the same Latin root come ~menace~ itself, the adjective ~menaçant~, and — through ~minārī~ in its sense of driving cattle forward with shouted threats — the verbs ~mener~ (“to lead”) and its compounds ~amener~, ~emmener~, and ~promener~, in which the old idea of driving forward survives stripped of any hostility.
en.mendier: ~Mendier~ is inherited from Latin ~mendīcāre~ (“to beg”), a verb formed on the Latin noun ~mendīcus~ (“beggar”). The same family gave French ~mendiant~ and ~mendicité~, and English borrowed ~mendicant~ from it. Related verbs in other Romance languages include Italian ~mendicare~ and Spanish ~mendigar~.
en.mendigoter: ~Mendigoter~ is formed from the noun ~mendigot~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~mendigot~ is a familiar word for a beggar, built from ~mendiant~ with the suffix ~-ot~, on the model of ~parigot~. The suffix ~-ot~ gives a slightly slangy, dismissive tone, and the verb means “to beg” or “to panhandle.” It is a colloquial, mildly contemptuous alternative to ~mendier~.
en.mener:
From Old French ~mener~ (“to lead, to drive”), from Late Latin ~minare~ (“to drive animals”), from Latin ~minari~ (“to threaten”), derived from ~minae~ (“threats, menaces”). ~Minae~ traces to PIE *~men-~ (“to project, to jut out”) — the same root behind Latin ~mons~ (“mountain,” something jutting up) and ~eminere~ (“to stand out”). A threat, in this image, is something that “looms” over you. Cognate with Spanish ~menear~ and Italian ~menare~.

The semantic journey is vivid: a herdsman drove his beasts forward by shouting threats at them, so ~minari~ (“to threaten”) slid in Late Latin into ~minare~ (“to drive, to lead livestock”), and finally into the neutral French ~mener~ (“to lead, to conduct, to take somewhere”). The threatening sense did not vanish — it survives in the doublet ~menacer~ (“to threaten”) and the noun ~menace~, both from the same ~minae~. From the “jutting” root also come ~mont~, ~montagne~, ~éminent~, and ~proéminent~, while ~mener~ itself heads a busy family: ~amener~, ~emmener~, ~ramener~, ~promener~, and ~démener~.
en.menotter: ~Menotter~ is formed from ~menotte~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~: to put ~menottes~ on someone. The noun ~menotte~ is itself built from ~main~ (“hand”, from Latin ~manus~) and the diminutive suffix ~-otte~, so a ~menotte~ was a “little hand”, and the word came to denote the shackle fitted around the wrists. The verb means to handcuff, and ~menotter~ is the everyday word for it, in police and legal contexts as in common speech.
en.mensualiser: ~Mensualiser~ is formed from the adjective ~mensuel~ (“monthly”) and the verb-forming suffix ~-iser~. The adjective rests on Latin ~mensualis~, built on ~mensis~ (“month”). The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Latin ~-izō~ and means “to make or turn into.” To ~mensualiser~ is therefore to make something monthly, above all to switch a payment, a salary or a tax to monthly instalments instead of a longer or shorter cycle. The verb is a modern formation, but its roots lie in the Latin word for a month.
en.mentionner:
From the noun ~mention~, from Latin ~mentio~ (“a calling to mind, a making mention”), an action noun built on the root of ~mens~, ~mentis~ (“mind”). The verb itself was reinforced by Italian ~menzionare~ before settling into French. ~mens~ descends from PIE *~men-~ (“to think”), one of the great roots of the family. Cognate, through that root, with English ~mention~ and Italian ~menzionare~.

To ~mentionner~ is, at root, to bring a thing “to mind” by naming it aloud — the act of speech and the act of memory folded together. The PIE *~men-~ behind ~mens~ is astonishingly fertile across French and beyond: it gives ~mental~, ~mémoire~, ~commentaire~, ~démence~, ~réminiscence~, and the borrowed ~mantra~, and through other branches reaches English ~mind~ and Greek ~mania~. Even the Latin ~memento~ (“remember!”) and the legal ~compos mentis~ spring from the same source. ~mentionner~ sits at the verbal edge of this vast mental family — where thinking, remembering, and saying meet — and has bred its own small offshoots, ~mentionnable~ and the rather charming negative ~immentionnable~, for the thing one had better not bring to anyone's mind at all.
en.mentir:
From Old French ~mentir~, attested from the late tenth century in the Passion poem — one of the very oldest French texts — from Vulgar Latin *~mentīre~, a regularized form of Classical Latin ~mentīrī~ (“to lie, to deceive, to feign”), built on ~mēns~, genitive ~mentis~ (“mind”), from PIE *~méntis~ (“thought”), on the root *~men-~ (“to think”) — the root that also gave English ~mind~. Cognate with Italian ~mentire~, Spanish ~mentir~, Portuguese ~mentir~ and Romanian ~minți~: all of Romance kept the liar's verb alive.

The scandal of ~mentir~ lodges in its root: lying is, etymologically, an operation of the mind. ~Mentīrī~ seems first to have meant something like “to be inventive, to conjure up” — the mind's products shading from imagination into fabrication — so that the liar is, at bottom, an inventor; Latin ~commentum~ (“invention, fabrication”), from the same root, preserves the link. Grammar added its own twist: ~mentīrī~ was a deponent verb, passive in form yet active in meaning, a refinement that the everyday Latin of Gaul flattened into the regular *~mentīre~ behind the French verb. The family gathers ~menteur~, ~menterie~, ~démentir~ and ~mensonge~, while the parent ~mēns~ stands behind ~mental~, ~mention~ and ~démence~ — to be ~dément~ is, literally, to be out of one's mind. French letters sealed the verb's celebrity: La Fontaine's Fox opens the most famous flattery in the language with ~sans mentir~ (“no lie…”), swearing his honesty in the very act of lying.
en.menuiser:
The two Wiktionaries tell different stories. French Wiktionary treats ~menuiser~ as built on the adjective ~menu~ (“small”) with the suffix ~-iser~, and also as a verb drawn from the noun ~menuiserie~. English Wiktionary instead gives an inherited descent from Old French ~menusier~, from Vulgar Latin *~minūtiāre~, from Latin ~minūtus~, the source of French ~menu~. Both accounts therefore lead back to the same Latin adjective, even if they disagree on the route.

Latin ~minūtus~ (“made small”) is the participle of ~minuere~ (“to lessen”), so the root idea of the family is smallness. The sources do not say how that idea came to name the carpenter's craft, and the verb itself is rare. Related French words include ~menuiserie~, ~menuisier~, ~diminuer~ and ~minutie~, and English ~minute~ (“tiny”) comes from the same Latin adjective.
en.mercantiliser: ~Mercantiliser~ is formed from the adjective ~mercantile~ with the suffix ~-iser~, meaning to turn something into a matter of trade and profit, to commercialize it. The base ~mercantile~ was borrowed from Italian ~mercantile~. The verb is a modern, often critical coinage: it describes bringing into the marketplace something that was not there before.
en.merceriser: Borrowed from English ~mercerize~, which takes its name from John ~Mercer~, the British inventor of the technique in 1844. The process treats cotton thread or fabric with a caustic solution to give it strength and a silky sheen. French also has the nouns ~mercerisage~ and ~mercerisation~ for it. The verb is thus an eponym: a craftsman's surname, turned into a verb by the suffix ~-ize~ in English and ~-iser~ in French.
en.merder: Formed in French from ~merde~ (“shit”) and the first-group ending ~-er~. The noun ~merde~ is inherited from Old French ~merde~, from Latin ~merda~, so the vulgar word has been in the language since Latin times. ~Merder~ is a slang verb, meaning “to mess up” or “to go wrong,” as in ~ça a merdé~. The verb thus does what many ~-er~ verbs do, turning a noun into an action, here “to produce a mess” or “to fail.” It is a coarse, colloquial word, but a very common one in everyday French.
en.merdoyer: ~Merdoyer~ is first recorded in 1884 in schoolboy slang. It is derived from ~merder~ with the verbal suffix ~-oyer~, or alternatively from ~merdoie~. Either way it rests on ~merde~, which descends from Latin ~merda~ (“excrement”), and the suffix ~-oyer~ gives the verb a drawn-out, floundering sense: to muddle along, to get confused, to make a mess of things.
en.meringuer: Formed from ~meringue~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so “to coat with meringue.” The noun first appears in Massialot's cookbook, and its origin is debated. English Wiktionary gives Dutch ~meringue~, itself of Latin or Germanic origin. French Wiktionary weighs several accounts: a Latin ~meringa~ from ~merenda~ (“evening snack”) by way of Dutch, which it treats with caution; the Swiss town of ~Meiringen~, where a pastry cook named Gasparini is said to have worked; and it rejects the Polish and German proposals.
en.messeoir: Inherited from Old French ~meseoir~, built from the prefix ~més-~ (“badly, wrongly”) and ~seoir~. The prefix goes back to Frankish *~missa-~ and Proto-Germanic *~missa-~. The base ~seoir~ comes from Latin ~sedēre~ (“to sit”) and came to mean “to suit, to be fitting”. ~Messeoir~ is its opposite: what ~sied~ is becoming, what ~messied~ is unbecoming. Like ~seoir~, it survives only as a defective verb, found almost only in the third person.
en.mesurer:
From Late Latin ~mensurare~ (“to measure, to estimate”), derived from ~mensura~ (“a measuring, a measure”), itself from ~mensus~, the past participle of the classical verb ~metiri~ (“to measure”). ~metiri~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~meh₁-~ (“to measure”). That same root, through the noun *~mḗh₁n̥s~ (“moon, month” — the moon being an early measure of time), connects ~mesurer~ to English ~moon~, ~month~, and ~Monday~, and to the Greek-derived ~meter~. Cognate with Italian ~misurare~; Spanish and Portuguese instead kept the old ~metiri~ in their ~medir~.

Late Latin ~mensurare~ gradually displaced classical ~metiri~ from the fourth century on, and it is the ancestor of the ordinary measuring verbs of Gallo-Romance. From the literal act of measuring, French ~mesurer~ extended to weighing or judging (~mesurer ses mots~, to weigh one's words) and, reflexively, ~se mesurer à quelqu'un~, to pit oneself against someone. The root family is wide in French: ~mesure~, ~démesure~ (excess, the lack of measure), ~commensurable~, and the learned ~dimension~. Through the moon branch of *~meh₁-~ come ~mois~ (“month”) and the scientific ~-mètre~ of ~kilomètre~ and ~thermomètre~ — all of them, in the end, ways of taking the measure of the world.
en.mettre:
From Old French ~metre~, from Latin ~mittere~ (“to send, to let go, to release”). The Latin verb likely goes back to Proto-Italic *~meitō~ and to a Proto-Indo-European root *~meyth₂-~ (“to exchange, to remove”), an extension of *~mey-~ (“to change”) — though the deepest reconstruction is debated, and accuracy here counsels caution. Through ~mittere~, ~mettre~ is cognate with Italian ~mettere~ and Spanish ~meter~, and with the English borrowings ~mission~ and ~transmit~.

The surprise is the meaning. Classical ~mittere~ meant “to send,” yet modern French ~mettre~ means “to put.” The shift from sending something away to setting it down took place in Vulgar Latin, where “let go” drifted toward “place,” and French carried the new sense forward completely. The original idea of sending survives instead in the prefixed forms, which French rebuilt on the learned stem ~-mettre~: ~permettre~ (“to permit,” “to let through”), ~promettre~ (“to send forth, to promise”), ~transmettre~ (“to transmit”), ~soumettre~ (“to submit”), and ~émettre~ (“to emit”). The supine stem ~miss-~ yields the noun family ~mission~, ~message~, ~messe~ (“Mass,” from the dismissal ~ite, missa est~), and ~mise~ (“a placing, a stake”) — the latter showing the “put” sense, the former the older “send.”
en.meubler: ~Meubler~ is formed from ~meuble~ (“piece of furniture”) plus the verbal ending ~-er~, with the sense “to provide with furniture.” The noun ~meuble~ comes from Latin ~mōbilis~ (“movable”), through a Vulgar Latin form altered by analogy with ~movēre~ (“to move”). Latin legal language used ~mōbilis~ for movable possessions, the opposite of ~immōbilis~, which gave French ~immeuble~ (“building”). It is a doublet of ~mobile~. Furniture was thus, at first, whatever you could carry away, and ~meubler~ later extended to filling an empty space, even a silence.
en.meugler: A semi-learned borrowing from Latin ~mūgilāre~, a rare verb. French Wiktionary notes that Suetonius used it for the cry of the wild ass. Latin ~mūgilāre~ had already given Old French ~mullier~, and that older form is still heard in Normandy as ~meullier~, with the sense of mooing. In modern French, ~meugler~ means “to moo, to low,” the cry of cattle. A better-known cousin is Latin ~mūgīre~ (“to low, to bellow”), which gave French ~mugir~, used for the same cry and also for the roar of the wind or the sea.
en.meuler: ~Meuler~ is formed from the noun ~meule~ (“grindstone”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, and means to sharpen on a grindstone. The noun is inherited from Old French ~mole~ and ~muele~, from Latin ~mola~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~melh₂-~ (“to grind, crush”). The sources give other origins for the ~meule~ of hay, which is a different word.
en.meurtrir:
From Old French ~meurtrir~ or ~murtrir~ (“to kill, to murder”), borrowed from Frankish *~murþrijan~ (“to murder”), a Germanic verb. English Wiktionary takes it back through Proto-Germanic *~murþrijaną~ to a Proto-Indo-European noun *~mrtro-~ (“murder, death”), from the root *~mer-~ (“to die”). The Germanic relatives are familiar: English ~murder~, German ~Mord~ and ~ermorden~, and Old English ~morþor~ (“death, murder”). In Middle French the verb already carried the weaker senses “to bruise” and “to hurt.”

In Old French the verb meant “to cause death, to kill,” and that sense survives in the noun ~meurtre~, a deverbal. In the Renaissance the verb weakened: ~assassiner~ took over the meaning “to kill,” while ~meurtrir~ slid toward “to bruise, to hurt.” French Wiktionary compares ~mortifier~, which followed the same path from causing death to wounding and humiliating. Today ~meurtrir~ is the verb for a bruise, and the family includes ~meurtre~, ~meurtrier~ and ~meurtrissure~.
en.miauler: Tied to the cat's cry ~miaou~, with the verbal ending ~-er~, so the verb means “to make the sound ~miaou~”. The cry itself is onomatopoeic. French Wiktionary records an earlier spelling ~miault~, attested in 1552 in Rabelais, with the noun use dated 1611 and the form ~miaou~ 1619. English Wiktionary adds that ~miauler~ is already found in Old French and Middle French.
en.michetonner: Formed from the noun ~micheton~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun comes from ~miché~ or ~michet~, popular forms of the first name ~Michel~. The verb is slang and refers to casual prostitution. The ending ~-er~ is the ordinary way French turns a noun into a verb, here meaning to act as, or deal with, a ~micheton~.
en.microcopier: A French formation: the noun ~microcopie~ (a copy made at a very reduced scale, on microfilm or microfiche) plus the verb ending ~-er~, which turns a noun into a verb meaning “to carry out N.” ~Microcopier~ therefore means “to make a microcopy of,” that is, to copy a document onto microfilm or microfiche. The ending ~-er~ goes back to the Latin first-conjugation ending ~-are~, as in ~cantare~, which became ~chanter~.
en.microfilmer: Formed from the noun ~microfilm~ plus the verbal suffix ~-er~, with the sense “to record on microfilm.” The noun is itself a compound of the prefix ~micro-~ (“very small”) and ~film~. The verb is a twentieth-century technical word for photographing documents at a greatly reduced size.
en.microniser: Formed from ~micron~ with the suffix ~-iser~, “to reduce to particles measured in microns, to micronize.” The noun ~micron~ comes from Ancient Greek ~mikrón~, the neuter of ~mikrós~ (“small”). The suffix ~-iser~, from Late Latin ~-izāre~, makes verbs meaning “to convert into” or “to treat by means of,” and is productive in technical vocabulary.
en.mignoter: A verbal derivative of ~mignot~, an old word of the ~mignon~ family, and attested around 1400 with the sense “to take on a languishing air.” The sense in the modern language, “to coddle, to cosset,” grew from this older one: to treat someone tenderly, with caresses and attentions. Writers such as Théophile Gautier used it in this familiar sense. The sources consulted do not trace ~mignot~ itself any further.
en.migrer:
Borrowed from Latin ~migrāre~ (“to travel far, to move from one place to another”). English ~migrate~ and Italian and Spanish ~migrare~ and ~migrar~ are its equivalents. Its place in the family is clearest through its prefixed neighbours, ~émigrer~ (“to leave one's country”) and ~immigrer~ (“to arrive in a country”), both also taken from Latin.

The core of the sense is a change of place with an intention to settle somewhere else or to return later. French uses ~migrer~ for birds and other animals that move with the seasons, as well as for peoples, though ~émigrer~ and ~immigrer~ are the usual verbs for people changing country. A recent use is in computing, where ~migrer~ means to transfer data or a system from one platform to another. The family also supplies ~migration~, ~migrateur~ (“migratory”), ~migrant~ and ~migratoire~.
en.mijoter:
The origin of ~mijoter~ is debated, and only the outline is safe. French Wiktionary derives it from Old French ~musgode~ (“provision of food”), of Germanic origin. English Wiktionary gives a similar but more detailed account: the verb would be borrowed from a western dialect form like ~migeotter~ (“to ripen”), which goes back to Old French ~migoe~ or ~murjoe~ (“provision of food”). That noun probably comes from a Frankish *~mūsgauda~, whose first element may have been *~mūs~ (“mouse”). The mouse is only a proposal, so treat it as such. If it holds, the word is kin to English ~mouse~ and German ~Maus~.

Whatever its exact path, the sense moved from stored food and slow ripening toward the kitchen: ~mijoter~ came to mean cooking gently over a low flame, for a long time. A ~mijotée~ is a dish left to simmer, and a ~mijoteuse~ is a slow cooker. The verb also went figurative. In everyday French, ~mijoter~ can mean to hatch something quietly, as in a plan or a scheme, as if ideas too could be left to simmer until they are ready.
en.militariser: ~Militariser~ is formed from the adjective ~militaire~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which makes verbs meaning “to make A” or “to subject to N”, so ~militariser~ is “to make military”. The adjective ~militaire~ was borrowed from Middle French and goes back to Latin ~mīlitāris~ (“relating to war”), which is related to ~mīles~ (“soldier”). The suffix ~-iser~ is fully productive in technical and journalistic French, which explains why verbs like this one are easy to coin.
en.militer: Borrowed from Latin ~mīlitāre~ (“to be a soldier, to serve in the army”), a verb from ~mīles~ (“soldier”). The French verb first kept this sense of military service, but the figurative meaning won out: to ~militer~ is to fight for a cause, a party or an idea, as if enlisted in its ranks. The same Latin family gave ~militaire~, ~militant~ and, in English, ~military~ and ~militate~.
en.mimer: ~Mimer~ is a denominal verb: ~mime~ plus the ending ~-er~, meaning to act as a mime or to imitate. ~Mime~ comes from Latin ~mimus~, itself from Ancient Greek ~mîmos~, the word for a mimic performer. The ending ~-er~ goes back to the Latin first-conjugation ending ~-are~ and is the usual way French turns a noun into a verb.
en.minauder: Built on ~mine~ (“look, expression”), which both Wiktionaries say was taken from Breton ~min~ (“beak, muzzle”). English Wiktionary adds that ~mine~ reached French through Norman. The verb ~minauder~ describes pulling affected faces: to simper, to put on coy, mincing airs. The Breton word for a snout thus lies behind the French word for a person's put-on expression, and so behind a verb of affected manners.
en.mincir: ~Mincir~ is built on the adjective ~mince~ (“thin”) with the verbal ending ~-ir~, in its sense “to become A,” hence “to become thinner.” ~Mince~ is attested in the sense “slender of build” in 1560. Its own origin is debated. French Wiktionary treats it as a back-formation from the verb ~mincer~, derived from a Latin form *~minutiare~, from ~minutus~ (“small”). English Wiktionary instead takes ~mincer~ from Old French ~mincier~, from Frankish *~minnistō~ (“smaller, finer”) or *~minnisōn~ (“to make smaller”).
en.miner: Formed from the noun ~mine~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Vulgar Latin *~mina~, from Gaulish *~meina~ (“ore, metal”), cognate with Welsh ~mwyn~. To ~miner~ is thus to work a mine, to dig tunnels, and from digging tunnels came to undermine in the figurative sense, as in wearing down morale or health. Other French words spelled ~mine~, such as the one for facial expression or the Greek weight, have unrelated origins.
en.miniaturiser: Formed from ~miniature~ with the suffix ~-iser~, so that it means “to make very small.” The base ~miniature~ was borrowed from Italian ~miniatura~, which comes from ~miniare~ (“to decorate with small figures”) and ultimately from Latin ~miniō~ (“to paint with red lead, to paint red”). The word first described red-lettered manuscript illustrations, and its modern “tiny” sense was reinforced by the unrelated ~mini~ and ~minimum~. English Wiktionary likewise notes that it has no link to ~minuscule~.
en.minimiser: ~Minimiser~ is a borrowing from English ~minimize~, which was formed on Latin ~minimus~ (“smallest”) with the suffix ~-ize~. The French form uses the equivalent ending ~-iser~, so the verb looks native, but its model is English. Its two senses are “to reduce to the smallest possible amount” and, more commonly in everyday speech, “to play down, to make something seem smaller than it is.” ~Minimus~ is the superlative of Latin ~parvus~ in sense, and the same Latin word gave French ~minimum~ and ~minime~.
en.minorer: ~Minorer~ is a borrowing from Latin ~minōrāre~ (“to make smaller”), which reached French through Middle French ~minorer~. The Latin verb is built on ~minor~ (“smaller”). The French verb means “to underrate, to lower the value of,” and it is the counterpart of ~majorer~. From the same Latin adjective French has ~mineur~, ~minorité~ and ~moindre~, and English has ~minor~ and ~minus~.
en.minuter: Formed from the noun ~minute~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is attested in 1392 and comes from Latin ~minūta~, the feminine of ~minutus~ (“small”), meaning a small part resulting from dividing the hour or the degree. It is an inherited-versus-learned pair with ~menu~, a doublet that came down the popular route. From the noun, ~minuter~ was coined as a verb of working with minutes: to time something precisely, or to set down the minutes of a meeting.
en.minéraliser: Formed from ~minéral~ with the suffix ~-iser~, the verb means to turn into or enrich with mineral matter. ~Minéral~ is a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ~minerālis~, derived from Latin ~minera~ (“mine”). The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and usually means “convert into” or “treat with”, as in ~minéraliser~ water or soil.
en.mirer: ~Mirer~ is inherited from Old French ~mirer~, which comes from Latin ~mīrārī~ (“to marvel at”). The Latin verb belongs to the family of the adjective ~mīrus~ (“wonderful”). Spanish ~mirar~ (“to look”) descends from the same verb, and Italian has ~mirare~ (“to aim, to gaze”). In Latin, ~mīrārī~ was about astonishment; in French the verb means to look at something attentively, even fixedly, hence “to stare” or “to watch intently.” It also has the sense of taking aim, and the reflexive ~se mirer~ means to look at oneself, as in water or in a mirror. The same Latin family gave French ~admirer~ (from ~admīrārī~), ~miracle~ (from ~mīrāculum~) and ~mirage~, a word drawn from ~mirer~.
en.miroiter: ~Miroiter~ is derived from the noun ~miroir~ (“mirror”), meaning to flash or sparkle like a mirror surface. The expected form would be *~miroirer~, but the two ~r~ sounds were dissimilated, and the second became ~t~, which gave ~miroiter~. The adjective ~miroité~ (“shimmering”) is attested from the sixteenth century.
en.miser:
~miser~ is a young verb with an ancient pedigree. It was coined from the noun ~mise~ (“a putting; what one puts down — a stake”), the substantivized feminine past participle of ~mettre~ (“to put”), which descends from Latin ~mittere~ (“to let go, to send”), from Proto-Italic *~meitō~, from PIE *~meyth₂-~ (“to exchange”), an outgrowth of *~mey-~ (“to change, to exchange”); the Latin verb's sense slid from exchanging to bestowing to sending. Between Latin and Romance it shifted once more, from “send” to “put” — the sense ~mettre~ has carried ever since. Italian ~mettere~ and Spanish ~meter~ are its Romance siblings, and through Latin compounds English received ~mission~, ~message~ and ~missile~ — all, at root, things sent.

First attested in 1669 in the sense “to raise the bidding at a sale,” ~miser~ stayed close to tables where money is laid down: when Balzac used it transitively around 1840, it meant squarely “to stake, to wager.” The pleasure of the word is how much French it carries inside: a ~mise~ is anything put — ~mise en scène~, ~mise en place~, ~mise à jour~ — so that the gambler's ~mise~ is simply “what has been put” on the table, frozen into a noun and then reanimated as a verb. To ~miser~, in French, is etymologically just to put. The idiom ~miser sur les deux tableaux~ — betting on both sides at once — is attested by 1935.
en.miter: ~Miter~ is formed from the noun ~mite~ (“moth, mite”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, and means to be eaten by moths or mites. The noun was borrowed from Middle Dutch ~mīte~, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *~mītǭ~, literally “cutter”, from the verb *~maitaną~ (“to cut”). The word is related to Old English ~mīte~, the source of English ~mite~.
en.mithridatiser:
The verb is an eponym, built from the name of Mithridates VI, king of Pontus, with the verbal suffix ~-iser~ (Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs). According to the legend, the king, fearing assassination by poison, accustomed himself to swallowing increasing doses of it. Defeated by Pompey, he is said to have been unable to end his life by poison and had a mercenary kill him. A rarer variant, ~mithridater~, also exists.

To ~mithridatiser~ someone is to immunize them against a poison by giving small, gradually increasing doses, and the sense extends figuratively to hardening a person against anything harmful by repeated exposure. The same king gave French the noun ~mithridatisme~ for this tolerance. Because the story of the self-poisoning king is a legend, the verb preserves the tale rather than a verified medical history.
en.mitiger: From Old French ~mitiguer~, a learned borrowing of Latin ~mītigāre~ (“to soften, to make mild”). The Latin verb is generally explained as built on ~mītis~ (“mild, soft”) with a verbal element related to ~agere~ (“to drive, to do”), so it means “to make mild”. English ~mitigate~ comes from the same Latin verb. French ~mitiger~ is used of a penalty, a measure or a feeling that is made less harsh. Its participle ~mitigé~ took a curious turn in the modern language: from “softened” it came to mean “mixed, lukewarm”, as in un avis mitigé (“a mixed opinion”).
en.mitonner: Formed from ~miton~ (“bread soup, panade”), a word of western France, with the verbal ending ~-er~. ~Miton~ is an irregular derivative of ~mie~, the soft inside of a loaf; a variant ~mietton~, meaning “crumbled”, plainly comes from ~miette~ (“crumb”) with the suffix ~-on~. The verb is thus tied to the making of bread soup, and it now describes any slow, gentle cooking: to simmer.
en.mitrailler: ~Mitrailler~ is a denominal verb: the noun ~mitraille~ plus the ending ~-er~, meaning to fire ~mitraille~ at someone and, today, to rake them with machine-gun fire. The noun comes from Old French ~mitaille~, a derivative of ~mite~ (“small Flemish coin”). It first meant small change, then scrap metal, and by 1667 the scrap with which cannons were loaded, which is grapeshot. English Wiktionary traces ~mite~ to Old Dutch ~mite~ (“something small”), from Proto-Germanic *~mītǭ~.
en.mixer: Borrowed from English ~mix~ (“to blend”), the same verb that gives French the noun ~mixeur~ (“blender”). The English verb itself arose as a back-formation from an older adjective ~mixt~ (“mixed”), which came through Old French ~mixte~ from Latin ~mixtus~, the past participle of ~miscēre~ (“to mix”). The word therefore returned to French after traveling through English, and French already had the old adjective ~mixte~ and the native verb ~mêler~, descended from the same Latin ~miscēre~. In French ~mixer~ names kitchen blending and, in audio, the combining of tracks into a final mix.
en.mixtionner: ~Mixtionner~ is a denominal verb: it adds the ending ~-er~ to the noun ~mixtion~, a learned borrowing from Latin ~mixtiō~ (“mixture”). The verb therefore means to mix, and in particular to blend ingredients into a preparation, which is why it also carries the sense of concocting. It is a rarer and more technical relative of the everyday ~mélanger~, and keeps the Latin ~-tion~ shape of its base.
en.mobiliser:
French ~mobiliser~ is a young verb, formed in 1765 from the adjective ~mobile~ plus the suffix ~-iser~ (“to render mobile”). ~Mobile~ continues Latin ~mobilis~ (“movable”), itself a worn-down form of an earlier *~movibilis~, built on the verb ~movēre~ (“to move”) with the suffix ~-bilis~. ~Movēre~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~mewh₁-~ (“to move, push away”). Through ~movēre~ and ~mobilis~, French is kin to Italian ~mobile~, Spanish ~móvil~, and English ~move~, ~mobile~, and ~motion~.

The word was born military: to ~mobiliser~ was to put an army on the move, to call reserves from civilian rest into active war — the opposite of ~démobiliser~. From the parade-ground it spread to any rousing of dormant resources: one ~mobilise~ public opinion, funds, energy, or a team. French even reborrowed ~mobile~ as the noun for a hanging sculpture and, lately, for the ~téléphone mobile~. The same restless root *~mewh₁-~ moves through a crowd of French words: ~mouvoir~ and ~mouvement~ (the inherited line), ~émouvoir~ and ~émotion~ (“to move out,” to stir feeling), ~automobile~, ~immobile~, ~meuble~ (“furniture,” the “movable” goods of a household), and ~mobilier~ — all, like ~mobiliser~, refusing to stand still.
en.modeler: Formed from the noun ~modèle~ (“model”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to shape after a model.” ~Modèle~ is borrowed from Italian ~modello~ in the sixteenth century. The Italian word comes from Vulgar Latin *~modellus~, a diminutive of Latin ~modulus~ (“measure, standard”), itself a diminutive of ~modus~ (“measure, manner”). The word first meant a small-scale representation of something to be built large. The verb ~modeler~ naturally describes the sculptor's art of giving a form to clay or wax, and has extended to anything given shape by a pattern.
en.moderniser: Formed from ~moderne~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which builds verbs meaning “to make A.” The base comes from Late Latin ~modernus~ (“recent, current”), built on the adverb ~modo~ (“just now”), itself the ablative of ~modus~ (“measure, manner”). The suffix goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and is fully productive in French: to ~moderniser~ is simply to make something modern, as ~numériser~ makes it digital. English ~modernize~ is the matching formation from the same elements.
en.modifier:
Attested in 1355, from Latin ~modificāre~ (“to set a measure to, to regulate, to limit”), a compound of ~modus~ (“measure, manner, limit”) and the verb-forming element ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make, to do”). Latin ~modus~ is generally connected to the Proto-Indo-European root *~med-~ (“to measure, to take appropriate measures”). Through ~modificāre~, French ~modifier~ is matched by Italian ~modificare~ and Spanish ~modificar~, and the underlying ~modus~ surfaces in English borrowings such as ~mode~, ~model~, and ~modify~.

The original idea was not change but limit: to ~modificāre~ was to fix the measure or bounds of something, to keep it within proper proportion. The modern sense of altering grew naturally from this — to set new measures is, in effect, to change. ~Modus~ proved astonishingly fertile in French, branching into ~mode~ (both “fashion” and “grammatical mood”), ~modèle~, ~moule~ (“mould,” the inherited popular form of ~modulus~), ~module~, ~modeste~, ~modéré~, ~commode~, and ~accommoder~ — a whole family circling the idea of fitting a thing to its proper measure.
en.moduler:
~Moduler~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~modulārī~ (“to measure, to regulate, to set to a rhythm”), a verb built on ~modulus~ (“a small measure, a rhythm, a melody”). That noun is a diminutive of ~modus~ (“measure, manner”), which comes from the Proto-Indo-European root *~med-~ (“to take appropriate measures”). The same root underlies Latin ~modestus~ and ~modērārī~, so “modest” and “moderate” are, etymologically, people who keep to the measure. Further afield, English ~mete~ (as in “to mete out”) and German ~messen~ (“to measure”) are native Germanic cousins, while Italian ~modulare~ and Spanish ~modular~ are learned relatives of the French verb.

In French the verb first belonged to music: to modulate was to vary the voice or a melody according to the measure, and above all to pass from one key to another. From there it widened to any adjustment by degrees, such as modulating a tax, a tone of voice or, in radio, the signal carried by a wave, whence ~modulation~ in the phrase “frequency modulation”. Latin ~modulus~ also gave ~module~, the standard unit of a building or a course, and, by a long popular evolution, ~moule~ (“mold”), the object that gives a shape its measure. Other descendants of ~modus~ include ~mode~, ~modeste~ and ~modérer~.
en.modéliser: Formed in French from ~modèle~ with the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make into, to treat as”): to ~modéliser~ is to build a model of a phenomenon, that is, to represent it in simplified form so as to study or predict it. The noun ~modèle~ came into French from Old Italian ~modello~, which continues Vulgar Latin *~modellus~, a diminutive of Latin ~modulus~ (“measure, standard”), itself a diminutive of ~modus~ (“measure, manner”). It first named a small-scale version of something to be built on a larger scale.
en.modérer:
Borrowed from Latin ~moderārī~ (“to keep within measure, regulate, restrain”), built on a stem *~moder-~ / ~modes-~ that also gives ~modestus~ (“modest”) and rests on ~modus~ (“measure, manner, limit”). ~modus~ descends from Proto-Italic *~medos~ and Proto-Indo-European *~med-~ (“to measure, take appropriate measures”). To moderate is therefore, at root, to hold something to its proper measure.

That root *~med-~ branches astonishingly far. Through Latin ~modus~ it gives French ~mode~, ~moderne~, ~modeste~, ~modeler~, and ~modérer~; the related verb ~medērī~ (“to heal”) gives ~médecin~ and English ~medical~ and ~remedy~; and the ~modus~ family extends to English ~mode~, ~modest~, and ~moderate~. The native Germanic reflex of *~med-~ surfaces in English ~mete~ (“to measure out”), while the “take thought, weigh” sense survives in ~meditate~. Greek ~médomai~ (“to be mindful of, plan”) belongs to the same stock — measuring, healing, and deliberating all turning out to be one ancient idea.
en.moirer: Formed from the noun ~moire~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. The verb means “to give a moiré pattern to something,” the rippled, watered look that the noun ~moire~ names. The ending ~-er~ turns the noun into an action: to treat a surface so that it takes on that look. The participle ~moiré~ doubles as an adjective for a fabric or surface with that appearance.
en.moiser: ~Moiser~ is formed from the noun ~moise~ and the ending ~-er~, with the sense of bracing a timber frame with a ~moise~, a pair of crosspieces. The noun comes from Middle and Old French ~moise~ and, on the usual account, from Latin ~mensa~ (“table”). Devic offered a different guess, an Arabic word for “parallel,” which the French entry mentions as a minority view.
en.moisir: ~Moisir~ is inherited from Latin ~mūcēre~ (“to be moldy”). The sound changes are instructive. Latin long ~ū~ normally gives French ~u~, so one would expect *~muisir~, but ~oi~ appears here as in ~foison~, ~froment~ and ~oignon~, from Latin ~fūsiōnem~, ~frūmentum~ and ~ūniōnem~. The ending ~-ir~ in place of Latin ~-ēre~ is regular: the preceding ~c~ palatalized, as in ~gésir~, ~loisir~ and ~plaisir~, from Latin ~iacēre~, ~licēre~ and ~placēre~. Beyond its concrete meaning, “to go moldy,” the verb also carries the figurative senses “to hang around” and “to gather dust.” ~Moisir~ gave ~moisi~ (“mold, moldy”) and ~moisissure~.
en.moissonner: ~Moissonner~ is a denominal verb: the noun ~moisson~ (“harvest”) plus the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to bring in the harvest, to reap.” The noun is inherited from Old French ~messon~ (also ~meissun~), from Latin ~messiōnem~, the accusative of ~messiō~ (“harvest”). The spelling with ~-oi-~ shows how French shifted an old vowel sound in the Middle Ages. The verb keeps both its literal sense of cutting grain and a figurative one, as when one ~moissonne~ medals or laurels.
en.moitir: Formed from the adjective ~moite~ (“damp”) with the verb ending ~-ir~, in the usual pattern of “to make or become A”: to dampen, to moisten. ~Moite~ comes from Old French ~moiste~. French Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~mūcidus~ (“mouldy”), while English Wiktionary describes a cross between a Vulgar Latin *~mucidus~ and forms of ~mustum~ (“new wine”).
en.molester:
Borrowed from Latin ~molestāre~ (“to trouble, to annoy”), a verb formed on the adjective ~molestus~ (“burdensome, troublesome”). That adjective in turn belongs to ~mōlēs~ (“a heavy mass, a burden”), the word that also gave French ~môle~ in the sense of a massive pier. The Latin verb survives in several languages: Spanish and Portuguese ~molestar~, Italian ~molestare~ and English ~molest~, all learned borrowings of the same word.

Where Latin ~molestāre~ meant merely to bother or to harass, French ~molester~ today means to ill-treat someone physically, as in se faire molester par une bande, to be roughed up by a gang. It is a false friend with English ~molest~, which today most often means to abuse sexually, a sense ~molester~ does not carry. The same Latin ~mōlēs~ also underlies ~démolir~.
en.moleter: Formed from ~molette~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so it means to work a surface with a ~molette~, the small toothed wheel that gives metal its knurled grip. The noun ~molette~ is a diminutive of ~meule~ (“grindstone”) with the suffix ~-ette~, so the tool is literally a little wheel. The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, is the usual French way of making a verb from a noun, here “to use N.”
en.mollarder: Formed from the noun ~mollard~ (“gob of spit”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so “to spit a gob.” The noun is built on ~mol~ (“soft”) with the suffix ~-ard~, probably because of the soft, pulpy consistency of what it names, according to French Wiktionary. English Wiktionary instead links it to ~mou~ (“soft, wet”), which is the same adjective in its modern form. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is French’s default way of making a verb from a noun.
en.mollir:
French Wiktionary derives ~mollir~ from Latin ~mollīre~ (“to soften”). English Wiktionary gives two possible routes: that same Latin verb, or a verb formed in French from the adjective ~mou~ (Old French ~mol~, feminine ~molle~). The difference is small, because the Latin verb is itself built on Latin ~mollis~ (“soft”), which is also the source of the adjective ~mou~.

In modern French ~mollir~ covers three senses: “to soften,” “to weaken,” and “to slacken.” The family is large. ~Mou~ and ~mollesse~ share its root, ~amollir~ and ~ramollir~ are prefixed relatives, and ~émollient~ is a learned word for a softening agent. English has the same Latin root in ~mollify~, from Latin ~mollificāre~ (“to make soft”), formed from ~mollis~ and ~facere~ (“to make”).
en.momifier: ~Momifier~ is formed from ~momie~ (“mummy”) with the suffix ~-ifier~, from Latin ~-ficāre~ (“to make”), so it means to turn into a mummy. ~Momie~ comes from medieval Latin ~mummia~, borrowed from Arabic ~mūmyāʾ~ (“a mixture of pitch and bitumen used to embalm the dead”), itself derived from Persian ~mūm~ (“wax”). The word named the embalming substance before it named the embalmed body, and later took figurative senses such as a dried-up or very old person.
en.monder:
From Latin ~mundāre~ (“to clean”), a verb built on the adjective ~mundus~ (“clean, neat”). In French, to ~monder~ is to clean a grain or a nut of its husk, to peel almonds by scalding them (~amandes mondées~), or to blanch vegetables. The same Latin adjective, with the negative prefix ~in-~, gives ~immundus~ (“unclean”), which French took as ~immonde~ (“foul, filthy”).

In modern French ~monder~ is a technical and somewhat old-fashioned verb, but it has a better-known relative: ~émonder~, meaning “to prune” a tree by cutting away what is useless, and by extension “to clean up” a piece of writing. Another French word, ~mondain~ (“worldly, society-minded”), comes from a different Latin word, ~mundus~ meaning “world,” a homonym of the adjective ~mundus~ (“clean”); the two are not the same word. Learning that ~monder~ means “to cleanse” also helps with ~immonde~ and ~émonder~.
en.mondialiser: Formed from the adjective ~mondial~ + the suffix ~-iser~. ~Mondial~ comes from Latin ~mundialis~, a derivative of ~mundus~ (“world”); English Wiktionary adds that it reached French through Middle French, where it first contrasted the worldly, material sphere with the spiritual. The suffix ~-iser~ is borrowed from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and in French it means “to make or render A”. ~Mondialiser~ thus means “to make worldwide”, and its pronominal form means “to become global”. The verb and its noun ~mondialisation~ are best known from debates about the global economy.
en.monnayer: ~Monnayer~ is formed from the noun ~monnaie~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, with the sense of turning something into coin or money. ~Monnaie~ is inherited from Old French ~moneie~, from Latin ~monēta~, and is cognate with English ~money~, Italian ~moneta~ and Spanish ~moneda~. Coins were struck at the temple of Juno ~Monēta~ in Rome. By the traditional account, her name was tied to Latin ~monēre~ (“to warn”) through a legend in which she warned the Romans of the Gauls' arrival. By metonymy, the mint gave its name to the die used to strike coins, and then to money itself.
en.monologuer: ~Monologuer~ is formed from the noun ~monologue~ with the verb ending ~-er~, meaning “to deliver a monologue,” to talk at length without letting anyone answer. ~Monologue~ was modeled on ~dialogue~ and came into Middle French (first attested in 1508) from Byzantine Greek ~monólogos~, built on the elements for “alone” and “speech.”
en.monopoliser: ~Monopoliser~ is formed from the noun ~monopole~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which turns a noun into a verb meaning “to make into, to treat as.” The noun comes through Latin ~monopōlium~ from Ancient Greek ~monopṓlion~ (“exclusive right of sale”), built from ~mónos~ (“alone”) and ~pōléō~ (“to sell”). To ~monopoliser~ is thus to hold the sole right to something, and the verb extends this to keeping a thing, such as a conversation, entirely for oneself.
en.monter:
From Vulgar Latin *~montāre~ (“to go up, to climb”), a verb coined from the Latin noun ~mons~ (genitive ~montis~, “mountain, mount”). ~Mons~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~men-~ (“to project, jut out”) — a mountain being, precisely, the land that sticks up. Through that root it is cognate with Latin ~ēminēre~ (“to stand out”) and ~prōminēre~ (“to project”). Romance kin include Italian ~montare~ and Spanish ~montar~, and the borrowed English ~mount~.

The coinage is delightfully literal — to “mountain” one’s way along, that is, to go up. From physical ascent the verb climbed into a remarkable range of senses: prices ~montent~ (rise), one ~monte~ a horse, a stage, or a flight of stairs, and one ~monte~ a machine, a tent, or a play by assembling its parts. The same ~mons~ underlies ~mont~, ~montagne~, ~monticule~, and ~amont~ (“upstream”), while compounds give ~remonter~, ~surmonter~ (“to overcome,” to rise above an obstacle), ~démonter~, and ~monture~ (a mount or a frame). The wider PIE root *~men-~ resurfaces in the borrowed ~éminent~ and ~proéminent~, words for things that, like mountains, stand out from their surroundings.
en.montrer:
From Middle French ~monstrer~, from Old French ~mostrer~ (an early past participle ~mostret~ is attested around 936), from Latin ~mōnstrāre~ (“to show, point out, indicate”). The verb derives from the noun ~mōnstrum~ (“a divine sign, portent, omen”), itself built on ~monēre~ (“to warn, advise, remind”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~men-~ (“to think”). Cognate with Italian ~mostrare~, Spanish ~mostrar~, and Portuguese ~mostrar~, all of which kept the plain sense “to show.” English borrowed from the same family in ~demonstrate~ and ~monster~.

The semantic thread is striking: a ~mōnstrum~ was something the gods caused to appear in order to show humans a warning — a portent. From that idea of an alarming sign came the English ~monster~, while French held instead to the neutral act of pointing something out. The link back to ~monēre~ (“to warn”) ties showing to thinking and remembering: to show is to make someone notice. From the same root *~men-~ spread a wide family of French words, among them ~montre~ (“watch,” literally a device that shows the time), ~démontrer~, ~remontrer~, ~monument~, and — through ~monēre~ — ~admonester~.
en.monétiser:
Formed in French from Latin ~monēta~ (“mint, coin”) with the suffix ~-iser~, so it is a learned word. The same Latin word reached French by inheritance as ~monnaie~, which makes ~monétiser~ a scholarly relative of ~monnayer~. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, itself from Greek; its popular doublet is ~-oyer~. English has the same Latin word twice, as ~mint~ and ~money~.

The modern meaning of ~monétiser~ is to turn something into money, whether an asset, an audience or a debt. Its family is the one that descends from ~monēta~: the inherited ~monnaie~ (“coin, change, currency”) and ~monnayer~ (“to mint, to exchange for money”), and the learned ~monétaire~ (“monetary”) and ~monétique~ (the electronic-payment sector). The choice between ~monnayer~ and ~monétiser~ is partly one of register, since ~monétiser~ sounds technical and financial, while ~monnayer~ stays closer to the concrete act of selling for money.
en.moquer:
The origin of ~moquer~ is uncertain. English Wiktionary traces it to Middle Dutch ~mocken~ (“to mumble”) or Middle Low German ~mucken~ (“to grumble”), both from an Old Saxon verb of the type *~mokkian~ (“to low, to mumble”), from Proto-Germanic *~mukkijaną~ and ultimately a Proto-Indo-European imitative root *~mūg-~ (“to low, to mumble”). On that account ~moquer~ is a doublet of ~mugir~ (“to moo”) and a cognate of German ~mucksen~. French Wiktionary calls the origin obscure instead. It compares Venetian ~mocar~ (“to mock”) and Piedmontese ~moca~ (“grimace”), perhaps linked to Latin ~maccus~ (“buffoon”) or Ancient Greek ~μῶκος~ (“mockery”). It judges the proposed link to Old Norse ~moka~ (“to shovel dung”) too weakly supported, both in meaning and in its Norman background.

Whatever its source, the verb appears in Old French as ~moquer~ (Middle French ~mocquer~) and is now mostly reflexive: ~se moquer de~ means to make fun of. If the Germanic account is right, the word began as a vocal sound, a mumble or low, that turned derisive. That remains an account, not a settled fact. The family includes ~moquerie~ (“mockery”) and ~moqueur~ (“mocker”), and English ~mock~ belongs to the same family.
en.moquetter: Formed from the noun ~moquette~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so ~moquetter~ means to cover with carpet. The origin of ~moquette~ is debated. Some link it to English ~mockado~, a cloth used for clothing in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Others point to the old forms ~mosquet~ and ~mosquete~, which recall ~mosquée~, and suggest that the first ~moquette~ was a mosque carpet. The modern sense of a fitted floor covering is the later one.
en.moraliser: ~Moraliser~ is formed from the adjective ~moral~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which gives the sense of making something take on a quality, here moral behavior, or of speaking in a moral tone. The adjective ~moral~ came into Old French as a borrowing from Latin ~morālis~ (“relating to customs”), a word built on ~mōs~, ~mōris~ (“custom, habit”). English ~moral~ and ~morale~ belong to the same family.
en.morceler: Formed from the noun ~morceau~ (“piece, bit”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, in the sense “make into N”: to cut something into pieces. The noun goes back to Latin ~mordēre~ (“to bite”). French Wiktionary derives it from Old French ~mors~ and Latin ~morsus~ (“bite”), while English Wiktionary routes it through Old French ~morsel~ and a medieval Latin diminutive, ~morsellum~ (“a little piece”), but both accounts start from the bite. The slide from “bite” to “mouthful” to “part of a whole” has a parallel in English, with bit and bite.
en.mordancer: ~Mordancer~ is formed from ~mordant~ with the ending ~-er~. The noun ~mordant~ is the present participle of ~mordre~ (“to bite”) turned into an adjective and then a noun, and it names, in dyeing and engraving, a substance that “bites.” To ~mordancer~ is to treat something with a mordant. The ~-er~ ending is the usual one for coining a verb meaning “apply” the thing the noun names.
en.mordiller: Formed from ~mordre~ (“to bite”) with the suffix ~-iller~, which marks a repeated or small action: to bite lightly and again and again, to nibble. The base ~mordre~ comes from Old French ~mordre~, from Vulgar Latin *~mordĕre~, itself from Latin ~mordēre~ (“to bite”), which lives on in Italian ~mordere~ and Spanish ~morder~.
en.mordre:
From Old French ~mordre~, from Vulgar Latin *~mordĕre~, itself from Classical Latin ~mordēre~ (“to bite”). The Vulgar Latin form is a reshaping with a short vowel: the classical second-conjugation verb was moved into the third conjugation. The Latin verb lived on in the other Romance languages, as in Italian ~mordere~ and Spanish ~morder~.

The sense has barely moved from the physical act of biting. French uses it figuratively for a sharp grip, as when a tool, a frost or a hobby ~mord~. The family is rich in learned and everyday words: ~mordant~ (“biting, incisive”), ~morsure~ (“a bite”), and ~remords~, literally a thing that bites again, a gnawing guilt. French also kept the Latin adverb ~mordicus~, “stubbornly, with one's teeth,” in the phrase ~soutenir mordicus~, a vivid fossil from the same Latin verb.
en.morfler:
~Morfler~ is a variant of ~morfiler~ (“to eat”), a slang verb. The sources do not agree on where ~morfiler~ comes from. By one account it derives from ~morfier~ (“to eat greedily”), the verb behind ~morfaler~, ~morfal~ and ~morfaloux~. By another, it was reshaped through a change of suffix from the Germanic and Dutch ~murfelen~, a diminutive of ~murfen~ (“to gnaw”).

The modern verb, in the sense of “to pay for it” or “to be in for it”, thus belongs to a family of popular French words that began around eating. Whichever origin is right, the verb sits among ~morfiler~ and ~morfaler~, forms that are all colloquial. The Dutch option would make it a distant cousin of a word for gnawing, while the first account keeps it entirely within French slang for gluttonous eating.
en.morfondre:
From Middle French ~morfondre~, a compound of two parts. The first is Franco-Provençal ~mor~ or ~more~ (“snout”), from Vulgar Latin *~murrum~ (“muzzle, snout”); English Wiktionary marks a possible Celtic origin for that Latin word with a question mark. The second is ~fondre~, from Old French ~fondre~, from Latin ~fundere~ (“to pour, to melt”). English ~morfound~ is a cognate. French Wiktionary gives only the simpler statement that it comes from Old French ~morfondre~, so the two sources differ on whether the compound was formed in Old or Middle French.

The second element ties ~morfondre~ to a large family. Latin ~fundere~ is the ancestor of ~fondre~ and, through its compounds, of ~confondre~ (“to confuse”). Learned words built on the same stem include ~fusion~, ~effusion~ and ~infusion~. French uses the verb almost only in the pronominal form ~se morfondre~, and its modern sense is to pine away, mope or wait around fretfully. The elements of the compound, a snout and a melting, no longer play any visible part in that sense.
en.morigéner:
The two Wiktionaries give different routes. French Wiktionary derives ~morigéner~ directly from Latin ~mōrigerārī~ (“to be complaisant, docile”), with a dissimilation of the two ~r~ sounds, so that the second became ~n~. English Wiktionary traces it, first attested in the 13th century, through Middle French ~moriginer~ (“to educate, to rear”) and Old French ~moriginé~ (“well-mannered”), borrowed from Medieval Latin ~mōrigenātus~ (“endowed with good character”), from ~mōrigenus~, a variant of classical ~mōrigerus~.

The Latin adjective ~mōrigerus~ is built from ~mōs~ (“custom, manner”) and the root of ~gerere~ (“to carry, to bear”), so its sense is literally “bearing oneself according to another's wishes.” The Middle French verb meant “to educate,” while the modern French sense is to scold or lecture. The same two Latin roots stand behind many French words: ~mœurs~ (“manners, morals”) is the plural of ~mōs~, and ~gérer~ and ~gestion~ come from ~gerere~.
en.mortaiser: Formed from the noun ~mortaise~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to cut a mortise.” French Wiktionary traces ~mortaise~ only to Old French ~mortaise~, while English Wiktionary derives it from Arabic ~mūrtāz~ (“fastened”). The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is the usual way to coin a verb from a noun.
en.mortifier:
From Latin ~mortificāre~, borrowed into French as a learned word. The Latin verb is built on ~mors~ (“death”), with a second element related to ~facere~ (“to make”), so it meant “to cause death, to kill.” Its ending ~-ficāre~ is the one found in Latin ~purificāre~ and ~sanctificāre~, which French turned into ~purifier~ and ~sanctifier~. Related words in other languages are Italian ~mortificare~, Spanish and Portuguese ~mortificar~ and English ~mortify~.

The literal meaning, to put to death, gave way in French to figurative ones. In religious language ~mortifier~ means to subdue the body and its desires through penance, and in everyday speech it means to humiliate someone deeply, which is the sense the learner meets most often. The root ~mors~ is the same as in ~mort~, ~mortel~ and ~mortalité~, so ~mortifier~ keeps a trace of death even when it only describes embarrassment.
en.motiver:
French ~motiver~ derives from the noun ~motif~ (“motive, ground, pattern”) with a verbal ending, ~motif~ being a learned borrowing from Late Latin ~mōtīvus~ (“moving, that sets in motion”), from Latin ~movēre~ (“to move”). ~Movēre~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~moweō~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~mewh₁-~ (“to move, push away”). Through that root and through ~movēre~ it is cognate with English ~move~ (via Anglo-Norman), ~motion~, ~motor~, and ~emotion~ — the last literally a “moving-out” of feeling.

The semantics are doubly apt: a ~motif~ is what moves you to act, so to ~motiver~ is both “to give someone a motive, to spur on” and “to state the grounds for” a decision — French administrative prose speaks of a décision ~motivée~, one whose reasons are set out. The same Latin verb seeded a vast family in French: ~mouvoir~, ~mouvement~, ~émouvoir~, ~moteur~, ~motion~, and the borrowed ~motivation~ — all turning on the ancient idea of setting something in motion.
en.motoriser: Formed from ~moteur~ (“motor, engine”) and the verb-forming suffix ~-iser~, in the sense “to provide with a motor.” ~Moteur~ is a borrowing of Latin ~motor~ (“mover”), from ~movere~ (“to move”). It displaced Old French ~mouveur~, which meant an instigator, someone who sets things in motion. The meaning “machine that sets things moving” is comparatively recent and is dated to 1744. The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and it is fully productive today for coining verbs that mean “to make or to provide with.”
en.motter: ~Motter~ is a denominal verb, formed from ~motte~ (“mound”) and the ending ~-er~, and it means “to go to ground.” The noun ~motte~ comes from Frankish, the Germanic language of the Franks, and is recorded in Medieval Latin as ~motta~ in the ninth century. The Germanic word is thought to have meant “mud, peat, turf,” and related words include Dutch ~mot~ (“sawdust, peat dust”) and Old English ~mot~ (“speck”).
en.moucharder: Formed from ~mouchard~ plus the verb ending ~-er~: to act as an informer, to tell tales. The noun ~mouchard~ is built on ~mouche~ (“fly”) with the pejorative suffix ~-ard~. French Wiktionary cites an account that links it to Antoine de Mouchy, an anti-Protestant theologian whose spies were first called ~mouches~ and then ~mouchards~; it also notes that Saint Chrysostom likened slanderers to flies, which feed on rot. Wiktionary flags the first account as needing a source, so the link to Mouchy is best treated as a tradition.
en.moucher: From Late Latin ~muccare~, a verb built on the Latin noun ~muccus~ (“mucus, snot”; the English Wiktionary gives the related spelling ~mucus~ as the source). The verb is thus literally “to clear the snot,” which is how it came to mean “to blow one's nose.” The Latin noun family also gave English ~mucus~, and French ~mouchoir~ (“handkerchief”) is built on ~moucher~. French Wiktionary adds that the figurative sense “to put someone in their place” belongs with ~moquer~ and not with this verb.
en.moucheronner: Formed from ~moucheron~ (“gnat, small fly”) with the verb ending ~-er~. It describes a fish leaping out of the water to catch flies. The noun is explained in two ways: as ~mouche~ (“fly”) with the suffix ~-eron~, or as ~moucher~ with the suffix ~-on~, via an Old French ~moucheron~. Either way, the verb turns the little insect into the action of hunting it.
en.moucheter: ~Moucheter~ is formed from ~mouche~ (“fly”) and the verb suffix ~-eter~, which can carry a diminutive sense, “to do something in small touches,” as in ~tacheter~. English Wiktionary treats the verb as inherited from Middle French ~moucheter~. ~Mouche~ comes from Latin ~musca~, probably an imitation of the insect's buzzing, from a Proto-Indo-European root *~mus-~ (“a fly”). French ~moucheter~ means to fleck or speckle a surface with small spots.
en.moudre:
From Old French ~moudre~ (earlier ~moldre~), inherited from Latin ~molere~ (“to grind”), itself from the Proto-Indo-European root *~melh₂-~ (“to grind”). The Old French infinitive was originally *~molre~, and a d slipped in between the two consonants as a transitional sound, just as in ~coudre~ (“to sew”). The root is well represented across the family. Spanish ~moler~ is the direct cognate, while English ~meal~ (“ground grain”) and German ~mahlen~ (“to grind”) come from the Germanic branch of the same root.

Grinding grain was among the oldest daily chores, and the root left many traces. Latin ~mola~ (“millstone”) gave French ~meule~, Late Latin ~molīnum~ (“mill”) gave ~moulin~, and the learned borrowing ~molaire~ names the grinding tooth. ~Moudre~ itself has shrunk. Its conjugation is awkward: ~mouds~ in the singular but ~moulons~ in the plural, with the l coming back in the imperfect, the past historic and the subjunctive. Speakers have therefore drifted toward easier verbs of the first group, and ~moudre~ survives mainly in the infinitive, the first three persons of the present, the future and the participle ~moulu~, as in moudre du café.
en.moufeter: A variant spelling of ~moufter~, a slangy verb first recorded in 1896 in an argot dictionary and used chiefly in the phrase “ne pas moufter,” to say nothing, not to protest. The TLFi explains it as a variant of ~mouveter~ (“to stir, to move”), itself derived from ~mouvoir~ (“to move”) or from ~mouver~ in Old and Middle French. ~Mouveter~ is recorded from the mid-sixteenth century and survives in regional speech. The Académie notes that the spelling ~moufeter~ also occurs.
en.moufter: ~Moufter~ is traced to Old French ~mouveter~ (“to stir, to move”), itself derived from ~mouvoir~ (“to move”), the verb that comes from Latin ~movēre~. The modern verb has narrowed and shifted: to stir, in the old sense, became to stir up a fuss, that is, to protest or to object. In practice it survives mostly in negative phrases, where someone does not so much as stir or say a word.
en.mouiller:
From Old French ~moillier~, inherited from Vulgar Latin *~molliāre~ (“to soak”), a verb built on Latin ~mollis~ (“soft”). The idea is that soaking makes a thing soft: the verb began as “to soften by steeping” and settled on simply “to wet.” French Wiktionary treats the Vulgar Latin form as a variant of Latin ~mollīre~ (“to soften”), itself from ~mollis~. The same ~mollis~ lies behind French ~mou~ (“soft”). Occitan ~molhar~ is a sister verb from the same source. The form *~molliāre~ is reconstructed, never attested, hence the asterisk.

The spelling hides a sound change: Latin ~-lli-~ became a palatal l in Old French, which is why the verb carries ~-ill-~. Grammarians later named such sounds after this very verb: a ~l mouillé~ is a “wet l.” Sailors gave it another turn, since ~mouiller l'ancre~ is to drop anchor, the anchor being put into the water. Related French words include ~mou~, ~mollesse~ (“softness”), ~amollir~ (“to soften”), ~mouillage~ (“anchorage”) and ~mouillette~, the strip of bread dipped in a soft-boiled egg.
en.mouler: ~Mouler~ is formed from the noun ~moule~ (“mold”) plus the verbal ending ~-er~: to shape something in a mold, then by extension to fit closely, as a garment clings to the body. This ~moule~ is inherited from Old French ~modle~, an early borrowing (11th century) from Latin ~modulus~ (“measure”), and so it is a doublet of ~module~. It is a different word from the ~moule~ of mussels, which comes from Latin ~mūsculus~.
en.mouliner: ~Mouliner~ is formed from ~moulin~ (“mill”) with the verb ending ~-er~, and means to mill or grind. The noun ~moulin~ goes back to Old French ~molin~, from Late Latin ~molīnum~. English Wiktionary derives that word from the adjective ~molīnus~ and the Latin verb ~molō~ (“to grind”), while French Wiktionary connects it to ~mola~ (“millstone”). The two accounts agree on the idea: a mill is the place where grain is ground.
en.moulurer: Formed in French from the noun ~moulure~ (“molding”) and the verbal ending ~-er~. The verb means “to decorate with moldings” or “to cut a molding into” a piece of wood, stone or plaster. Its pattern is the usual one for verbs of craft: the noun names the finished feature, and the verb names the act of giving it to a surface.
en.mourir:
From Old French ~mourir~, ~morir~, from Vulgar Latin *~morīre~, a reshaping of Classical Latin ~morī~ (“to die”), a deponent verb. This goes back to Proto-Italic *~morjōr~ and to the Proto-Indo-European root *~mer-~ (“to die”). The root is one of the most widespread in the family: cognates include Sanskrit ~mṛtyú~ (“death”), Lithuanian ~mirti~, Proto-Slavic *~merti~, and, through Proto-Germanic *~murþaz~, words for “murder.” The Romance sisters ~morire~ (Italian) and ~morir~ (Spanish) descend from the same Vulgar Latin verb.

The classical verb ~morī~ was deponent — passive in form, active in meaning — and Vulgar Latin regularized it into an ordinary active *~morīre~, the ancestor of every Romance form. From the same root Latin built the noun ~mors~ (“death”) and the participle ~mortuus~ (“dead”), which together seeded a large French family: ~mort~, ~mortel~, ~mortalité~, ~immortel~, ~mortuaire~, ~morgue~, and the borrowed ~moribond~ (“dying”) from ~moribundus~. A curious offshoot is ~amortir~ (“to deaden, to cushion, to amortize”), literally “to bring toward death,” whence the financial ~amortissement~ — a debt slowly “put to death” by repayment.
en.mousser: ~Mousser~ is formed from ~mousse~ (“foam, lather”) with the ending ~-er~, so “to foam.” The noun is one of several French homonyms, and the sources do not agree on its origin. The foam sense is probably a figurative use of the word for moss, ~mousse~, which comes from Old French ~mosse~ and Frankish *~mosa~. Another explanation points to a southern word of Gaulish origin. The verb gave the idiom ~se faire mousser~, “to show oneself off,” in which one froths up one's own reputation.
en.moutonner: ~Moutonner~ is formed from ~mouton~ (“sheep”) and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Old French ~moton~, from Vulgar Latin *~multōnem~, itself from Gaulish *~multon-~ and Proto-Celtic *~moltos~. The Celtic word originally named a castrated male sheep, and its relatives include Welsh ~mollt~. It displaced Latin ~vervex~ and ~ovis~ in much of Gallo-Romance. The verb is built on the animal's name, and its sense of “to foam, froth” is a figurative one.
en.mouvementer: Formed in French from the noun ~mouvement~ and the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense “to give movement to, to enliven.” The noun comes from Old French ~movement~ (attested in 1190) and Medieval Latin ~mōvimentum~, from the Latin verb ~movēre~ (“to move”); it can also be read as ~mouvoir~ + ~-ment~. The verb itself is rare today, and it is mostly met through its participle ~mouvementé~, which describes something eventful, lively or full of incident, such as a trip, a meeting or a career.
en.mouvoir:
From Old French ~movoir~ (also ~moveir~), passing through Middle French ~mouvoir~, inherited from Latin ~movēre~ (“to move”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~m(y)ewh₁-~ (“to move”). Latin ~movēre~ survives across the Romance languages: Italian ~muovere~ and Spanish ~mover~ are its direct descendants. English ~move~ is a loan that came by way of Anglo-Norman from the same Latin verb, and its relatives ~motion~, ~motor~ and ~mobile~ all come from Latin forms of ~movēre~.

The Old French form ~movoir~ became ~mouvoir~ when the vowel shifted, and the verb stayed irregular, with a stem that alternates between ~meu-~ and ~mouv-~, as in ~il meut~ and ~nous mouvons~. Its past participle ~mû~ carries a circumflex only to keep it apart from the plain syllable ~mu~. Today ~mouvoir~ sounds literary or technical, and everyday French prefers ~bouger~ or ~déplacer~, but the family remains rich: ~mouvement~, ~moteur~, ~motif~ and ~émouvoir~ (“to stir the feelings”), and also ~promouvoir~ (“to promote”) and ~meuble~, which means “movable” before it means furniture. The reflexive ~se mouvoir~ is still used for any body, living or not, that moves of its own accord.
en.moyenner: Formed from ~moyen~ and the verb ending ~-er~, though the sources hesitate over which noun or sense is behind it: either ~moyen~ (“means”), giving “to find or use a means” and so “to obtain”, or ~moyenne~ (“average”), giving “to calculate the mean”. The adjective ~moyen~ comes from Latin ~mediānus~ (“in the middle”), from ~medius~ (“middle”), and is a doublet of the learned ~médian~. The sense “to obtain” belongs to the older noun ~moyen~ in the sense of “means, way”.
en.mucher: A variant of ~musser~ (“to hide”), now found mainly as the reflexive ~se mucher~, “to hide oneself,” in literary writing. French Wiktionary derives ~musser~ from a Gaulish root *~muk-~, which gave Old French ~mucier~, though it leaves the century open. The sources do not go further, so the path from Gaulish to the modern forms is not detailed here.
en.muer:
From Old French ~muer~ (also ~muder~), by way of Middle French, inherited from Latin ~mūtāre~ (“to change”). The Latin verb also lives on in Italian ~mutare~ and Spanish ~mudar~. French took the same word twice: once by ordinary inheritance, which wore ~mūtāre~ down to ~muer~, and once as the learned loan ~muter~, so ~muer~ and ~muter~ are doublets. English borrowed the verb too, through Anglo-Norman, as ~mew~, used of a bird shedding its feathers.

In modern French, ~muer~ is mostly about change of a biological kind. Animals shed hair, feathers, skin or antlers, and a boy's voice breaks, as in ~sa voix mue~. The noun ~mue~ names the molt itself, while the older, wider sense “to change, to transform” survives in the literary ~muer en~. The lost ~t~ between two vowels is typical of Latin verbs in ~-āre~, as in ~suer~ from ~sūdāre~. The learned side of the family, closer to the Latin spelling, gives ~mutation~, ~immuable~ and ~commuer~, all built on the same verb.
en.mugir:
From Latin ~mūgīre~ (“to low, to bellow”), the word for the sound a cow or ox makes. Old French had inherited it in the normal way as ~muir~ or ~muire~, and the modern form ~mugir~ is a later alteration of that inherited verb, reshaped on the Latin original. Italian ~muggire~ and Spanish ~mugir~ are the corresponding descendants, and the Latin word itself was imitative, echoing the low call of cattle.

In French ~mugir~ names the cry of cattle, but it has long been extended to any deep, prolonged roar: the sea, the wind, a storm, a crowd or an angry man can all ~mugir~. The family is small and close to the verb. ~Mugissement~ is the noun for the cry, and ~mugissant~ is the adjective used of a roaring sea or storm. Because the verb was relatinized after Old French, it shows an odd case of a word that had already been inherited and was then pulled back toward its source.
en.multiplier:
From Old French ~multiplier~, from Latin ~multiplicāre~ (“to multiply, to increase, to repeat”), formed from ~multi-~ (“many,” from ~multus~) and ~plicāre~ (“to fold”). ~plicāre~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~plek-~ (“to plait, to fold”), which also gave Greek ~plékein~ (“to braid”) and, through Germanic, English ~fold~ and ~ply~. So to multiply is, at root, to “many-fold” — to lay something over itself again and again.

The folding image is wonderfully concrete: a cloth doubled and redoubled grows in layers exactly as a number grows under multiplication. Latin ~multiplicāre~ served both the arithmetical sense and the broader “to increase in number,” and modern ~multiplier~ keeps both, from the times table to multiplying one's efforts. The *~plek-~ root unfolds across a large French family built on ~plicāre~ and its noun ~plicātūra~: ~plier~ and ~ployer~ (“to fold, to bend”), ~pli~ (“a fold, a crease”), ~plisser~ (“to pleat”), ~appliquer~, ~compliquer~, ~impliquer~, ~expliquer~, ~répliquer~, and ~déployer~ (“to deploy,” literally to “unfold”). The learned ~-plicāre~ verbs and the popular ~plier~ are two streams from the same source, so the schoolchild's ~multiplication~ and the seamstress's ~pli~ share one ancient act of folding.
en.municipaliser: ~Municipaliser~ (“to place under municipal control”) is formed from ~municipal~ with the suffix ~-iser~, which makes verbs meaning “to make” or “to convert into”. The adjective is a borrowing of Latin ~mūnicipālis~ (“of a free town”), from ~mūniceps~ (“citizen of a free town”), itself made of ~mūnus~ (“duty”) and ~capiō~ (“to take”). A ~mūniceps~ was thus one who took on the duties of a community. The verb is administrative: a service is ~municipalisé~ when a town takes it over.
en.munir:
From Latin ~mūnīre~ (earlier ~moenīre~, “to wall in, fortify, defend”), built on ~moenia~ (“city walls, ramparts,” Old Latin ~moene~) with the verbal suffix ~-īre~. The ultimate root is cautiously traced to PIE *~mey-~ (“to fix, strengthen, build”), though the deep connection is not certain. From the related Latin material come the English cognates ~munition~, ~ammunition~, ~mural~, and ~rampart~, all keeping the old sense of walls and defense.

The French history shows a clear softening. ~Munir~ first meant “to fortify, defend” (attested 1350) — to gird a place with walls. By the late sixteenth century (1580, in Montaigne) the sense had broadened from military fortification to ordinary provisioning: to ~munir~ someone is to equip or supply them with what they need, and ~se munir de~ is to provide oneself with — an umbrella, a passport, patience. The martial origin survives chiefly in ~munition~ (“ammunition”) and in the participle ~muni de~ (“furnished with, carrying”). The root's fortifying sense also shows through learned relatives like ~rempart~ and ~mur~ (the latter from Latin ~mūrus~, of the same defensive world).
en.murer: ~Murer~ is formed from the noun ~mur~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, and means to enclose with a wall or to block an opening with masonry. The noun descends through Middle and Old French ~mur~ from Latin ~mūrus~ (“city wall, rampart”), itself from Old Latin *~moiros~, and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~mey-~ (“to strengthen”).
