The same Latin word gave Italian ~muro~ and Spanish ~muro~. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and turns the noun into an action: to provide with a wall, and so to wall up.
en.murmurer: Inherited from Old French ~murmurer~, itself borrowed from Latin ~murmurāre~ (“to murmur, to rumble”). The Latin verb comes from the noun ~murmur~, a sound-imitative word whose repeated syllable mimics a low, continuous hum. The echo in the sound survives intact, which is why the verb still suits a stream, a crowd, or a quiet complaint.
en.musarder: ~Musarder~ is built on ~musard~ (“a dawdler, an idler”) with the verbal suffix ~-er~. The noun ~musard~ is itself a derivative of the verb ~muser~ with the suffix ~-ard~, which makes nouns for people marked by a habit. So the verb makes a loop: ~muser~ gave ~musard~, and ~musard~ gave ~musarder~, a verb that means the same as ~muser~, to dawdle or idle about. The longer form is the one that suggests a slow, wandering stroll, and the pair shows French building a second verb on a noun that had itself come from the first.
en.muscler: Formed from the noun ~muscle~ with the verb ending ~-er~: to give someone muscles, or to develop them. ~Muscle~ comes, via Middle French, from Latin ~mūsculus~, literally “little mouse”, a diminutive of ~mūs~ (“mouse”). Greek had the same double meaning in ~mûs~, “mouse” and “muscle” (and also “mussel”), and the image usually given is of a small animal rippling under the skin. French ~moule~ (“mussel”) is an inherited doublet of ~muscle~. Latin ~mūs~ and English ~mouse~ go back to the Proto-Indo-European *~mūs~ (“mouse, rat”).
en.museler: ~Museler~ is formed from ~musel~, the Middle and Old French form of ~museau~ (“muzzle, snout”), with the verb ending ~-er~: to put a muzzle on. As standard background, English ~muzzle~ comes from the same Old French ~musel~. The figurative sense, “to silence someone”, builds on the literal one.
en.muser:
From Old French ~muser~ (“to loiter, dawdle, idle”), whose origin is genuinely debated. The favored account derives it from ~muse~ (“snout, muzzle”), perhaps from Medieval Latin ~musum~, itself of uncertain origin — the image being someone standing nose in the air, muzzle agape, going nowhere. The TLFi and Littré record competing hypotheses: a Germanic source (Old High German ~muezôn~, “to be idle”) and a link to ~musa~ (“muse”). No account is settled, so the snout etymology should be read as proposed, not proven.

Whatever its root, ~muser~ meant to waste time, to dawdle — and from it, by way of Old French, English borrowed both ~amuser~ (originally “to make someone stare idly, to divert”) and possibly the verb to ~muse~. The snout sense, if correct, also surfaces in ~museau~ (a beast's muzzle). In modern French ~muser~ has grown rare and faintly literary, a word for the pleasant aimless wandering of mind or feet; ~musarder~ carries the same flavor. The connection to the goddesses of art, charming as it is, rests on one of the rejected hypotheses — a coincidence of sound, not a shared root.
en.musiquer: Formed from the noun ~musique~ with the verb suffix ~-er~, giving the sense “to make music”. The noun comes from Old French ~musique~, itself borrowed from Latin ~mūsica~, which in turn goes back to Ancient Greek ~mousikḗ~ (“art of the Muses”), derived from ~Moûsa~ (“Muse”). So the verb carries a very old idea inside a recent-looking formation: to practice the art of the Muses.
en.musser:
From Old French ~muchier~ (also ~mucier~, ~mucer~, “to hide”), which gave Middle French ~musser~. The deeper source is disputed between the two Wiktionaries. English Wiktionary derives it from Frankish *~mukkjan~ or *~mukōn~ (“to hide, skulk”), from Proto-Germanic *~mukjaną~ (“to hide, waylay, steal”), from a Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)mūg-~ (“to rob, steal”), and compares Old High German ~mūhhōn~ (“to hide”). French Wiktionary instead gives a Gaulish *~muk-~ behind the Old French verb.

Modern ~musser~ is a literary or regional word, mostly found in the reflexive ~se musser~ (“to hide oneself”). On the Germanic account, the old verb covered hiding, lying in wait and stealing, which fits a word for sneaking about. English Wiktionary also links English ~mooch~ to this Old French verb, so the word reached English by way of French. Whichever source is right, ~musser~ is not a French formation on a base but a verb that already existed in Old French.
en.muter:
French ~muter~ has several uses, and the sources trace them differently. In one account it is a learned derivative of Latin ~mūtāre~ (“to change, to exchange”), the verb that had already given ~muer~ in everyday speech, so ~muter~ and ~muer~ are doublets, one scholarly and one popular. This is the account that fits the sense of transferring someone to a new post.

French Wiktionary gives two further accounts for other senses. For the winemaker's ~muter~ (“to stop the fermentation of grape juice”), it proposes Latin ~mūtus~ (“mute”), because the wine no longer expresses itself. This is an explanation offered by the dictionary, not a settled fact. For the modern sense of switching off the sound of a device, it points to the English verb ~mute~ (“to make mute”). The sources thus treat ~mūtus~ and ~mūtāre~ as separate Latin words, so a single French spelling may hide a Latin verb of change, a Latin adjective of silence and an English verb, and no one origin covers every sense.
en.mutiler: ~Mutiler~ comes from Latin ~mutilāre~ (“to cut off, to maim”). The Latin verb is built on the adjective ~mutilus~ (“maimed, cut short”), and English ~mutilate~ is borrowed from the same verb. Italian ~mutilare~ and Spanish ~mutilar~ come from it too. French ~mutilé~ and ~mutilation~ belong to the family, and the verb is used both of bodily injury and, figuratively, of cutting a text or a work so badly that it loses its shape.
en.mutiner: Formed in French from the adjective and noun ~mutin~ (“rebellious,” “a rebel”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, so that ~mutiner~ means “to revolt,” especially in the form ~se mutiner~, as a crew or garrison does against its officers. The base ~mutin~ is itself a derivative of ~meute~ with the suffix ~-in~. ~Meute~ is the word for a pack of hounds, and the family also includes ~mutinerie~ (“mutiny”), whose English counterpart is ~mutiny~.
en.mutualiser: French Wiktionary ties ~mutualiser~ to Latin ~mutuus~ (“lent, borrowed, reciprocal”), the word behind French ~mutuel~. The verb has the shape of a modern French formation with the ending ~-iser~, meaning “to make mutual, to share among several.” Its further ancestry is uncertain. By one account, ~mutuus~ was shaped by the Proto-Indo-European root *~mei-th-~ (“to exchange”), which would make it a relative of Latin ~mūtāre~ (“to change”). That link is a proposal, not a settled fact.
en.mystifier:
Formed from Ancient Greek ~μύστης~ (“one initiated into the mysteries”) plus the French verb suffix ~-ifier~. English Wiktionary gives Latin ~mysta~ as the immediate source of the first element, so the French word is built on a Latin borrowing of the Greek noun. The Greek noun could be read passively (one who is initiated into the mysteries) or actively (one who initiates others into them), and it names a person tied to secret rites.

Today ~mystifier~ means “to fool, to hoax, to dupe.” The sources do not describe how the sense passed from ritual initiation to deceiving someone, so no path is offered here. The suffix ~-ifier~ is the usual French verb-forming ending, going back to Latin ~-ficāre~ (“to make”), the same one found in ~simplifier~ and ~clarifier~. The Greek family also stands behind French ~mystère~ and ~mystique~, two words tied to secret rites and hidden meaning, and English ~mystic~ and ~mystery~ are relatives of the same family.
en.mythifier: Formed from ~mythe~ (“myth”) plus the suffix ~-ifier~, meaning “to make into.” The noun ~mythe~ came through Latin ~mythos~ from Ancient Greek ~mûthos~ (“tale, fable”). ~Mythifier~ therefore means to turn a person, event or idea into a myth, often by exaggerating or idealizing it.
en.mâcher:
From Middle French ~mascher~, from Old French ~maschier~ (also ~mascier~), inherited from Late Latin ~masticāre~ (“to chew”). The s before the ch fell silent and was later dropped from the spelling, leaving the circumflex as its trace, as in ~hôpital~ and ~forêt~. Spanish and Portuguese ~mascar~ descend from the same Latin verb, and Italian has ~masticare~. French also took ~masticāre~ a second time as the learned ~mastiquer~, so ~mâcher~ and ~mastiquer~ are doublets, and English ~masticate~ comes from the same Latin verb. The earlier history of ~masticāre~ is left aside here.

Like most verbs of bodily action, ~mâcher~ spread into figurative speech. To refuse to ~mâcher ses mots~ is to speak bluntly, without softening one's words, and to ~mâcher le travail~ to someone is to do the hard part for them, as one chews food for another. The verbs ~mâchonner~ (“to chew slowly, to mumble”) and ~mâchouiller~ (“to chew absently”) are derived from it, and ~mâchoire~ (“jaw”), the organ that does the chewing, belongs to the same family.
en.mâchonner: Formed from ~mâcher~ (“to chew”) and the suffix ~-onner~, which gives a repeated, aimless or half-hearted action, as in ~chantonner~. The base ~mâcher~ descends from Middle French ~mascher~ and Late Latin ~masticāre~, and the circumflex marks the s that once stood before the ch. French took the same Latin verb a second time as the learned ~mastiquer~, so the two are doublets. ~Mâchonner~ thus means to chew slowly and absentmindedly, or to mumble as if chewing.
en.mâchouiller: ~Mâchouiller~ is formed from the verb ~mâcher~ (“to chew”) with the popular, pejorative suffix ~-ouiller~. The suffix gives a sense of doing the action in a weak, repeated or careless way, so the verb means to chew idly or without much effect, to chomp on something without really eating it.
en.mâchurer: Attested in 1507 as ~mascurer~, from the same family as ~masque~. The verb is also described as a denominal of the noun ~mâchure~. Its sense is “to blacken, to smear with soot.” The sources give no more detail on how these words are connected.
en.mâter: Formed from ~mât~ (“mast”) with the verb ending ~-er~: to ~mâter~ a ship is to fit it with a mast, or to raise the mast. ~Mât~ comes from Middle French ~mast~ and Old French ~mast~, from Early Medieval Latin ~mastus~, from Frankish *~mast~, from Proto-Germanic *~mastaz~. The circumflex stands for a lost ~s~, which is why the old spelling ~mast~ still shows. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~.
en.mâtiner: From ~mâtin~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. A ~mâtin~ is a large, strong dog, and the word descends from Old French ~mastin~, from Vulgar Latin *~mānsuētīnus~ (“tamed”), from Classical Latin ~mānsuētus~ (“tamed”). English ~mastiff~ is a cognate. To ~mâtiner~ is to crossbreed, above all to mate a purebred animal with a mongrel, and by extension to mix or blend things of different kinds. The ~-er~ ending is the ordinary way of making a verb from a noun.
en.mécaniser: Formed in French from ~mécanique~ with the suffix ~-iser~. According to French Wiktionary, the verb first appeared in the sense of practicing a manual trade. ~Mécanique~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~mechanicus~ (“of or belonging to machines”), itself from Ancient Greek ~mēkhanikós~, from ~mēkhanḗ~ (“a machine, contrivance”), the source of ~machine~. The suffix ~-iser~ here makes a verb meaning “to convert into” or “to provide with”, which is the modern sense of ~mécaniser~: to equip with machines.
en.mécher: Formed from the noun ~mèche~ plus ~-er~, with two technical senses: to sulfur, and to pack a wound. French Wiktionary traces ~mèche~ to Old French ~meche~, meaning a strip of lint, which fits the surgical sense. English Wiktionary derives Old French ~mesche~ from Late Latin *~micca~ or Vulgar Latin *~mysca~, an alteration of Latin ~myxa~ (“sebesten tree”), though it marks that entry as incomplete. The origin of ~mèche~ is therefore not firmly settled.
en.méconduire: Formed from ~conduire~ with the prefix ~mé-~ (“wrongly, badly”), hence “to conduct oneself badly.” The prefix comes from Old French ~mes-~, from Frankish *~missa-~, and is a cognate of English ~mis-~. ~Conduire~ comes from Latin ~conducere~ (~con-~ + ~ducere~, “to lead”), whose participle gave ~conduite~, the French word for behavior. The prefix is no longer productive.
en.méconnaître: ~Méconnaître~ is formed from ~connaître~ with the prefix ~mé-~, which means “wrongly, badly.” The prefix comes from Old French ~mes-~, from Frankish *~missa-~ and Proto-Germanic *~missa-~, and is related to English ~mis-~. The base ~connaître~ descends from Latin ~cognōscere~ (“to get to know”). To ~méconnaître~ someone or something is therefore to know or judge it wrongly, whether by ignoring it, failing to recognize its worth, or being unaware of it.
en.mécontenter: ~Mécontenter~ is formed from ~contenter~ with the prefix ~mé-~, which here reverses the sense of the base. The prefix comes from Old French ~mes-~ (“badly, wrongly”), itself from Frankish *~missa-~ and related to English ~mis-~. The base ~contenter~ rests on ~content~, from Latin ~contentus~ (“contained, satisfied”), the past participle of ~continēre~. To ~mécontenter~ someone is therefore to leave them unsatisfied, whence the sense “to displease” and the adjective ~mécontent~.
en.médailler: Formed from ~médaille~ + ~-er~, “to award a medal to.” The noun ~médaille~ was borrowed from Italian ~medaglia~, which comes from a medieval Latin form of ~mediālis~ (“middle, median”). French Wiktionary adds that the early form named a coin worth half a denier, and English Wiktionary notes that ~médaille~ is a doublet of ~maille~. A medal thus began, in this account, as a “small half” coin, a long way from the honor it now signals.
en.médiatiser: Derived from ~média~ with the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make, to turn into”), with a ~t~ slipped in between the two for ease of pronunciation. ~Média~ is a French borrowing of English ~media~, short for ~mass media~, which in turn is the plural of Latin ~medium~ (“middle”), a word that reached the sense of a channel or means of communication. So ~médiatiser~ means to give something coverage in the press, radio and television, or to make it widely known through those channels. The same Latin ~medium~ gave French ~médium~, and the plural ~media~ is the source of the shortened, everyday form.
en.médicaliser: Formed from the adjective ~médical~ with the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make, to treat as”): to give something a medical character, or to bring it under medical care and authority. The adjective is borrowed from Latin ~medicālis~ (“of a physician”), from ~medicus~ (“physician”), itself from the verb ~medērī~ (“to heal”). The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed a Greek ending, and is the usual way for French to coin verbs of this kind in technical and administrative language. The verb is modern and often used for social or human conditions, such as childbirth or old age, that become treated as medical matters.
en.médire: Inherited from Old French ~mesdire~, which joined the prefix ~mes-~ (modern ~mé-~, “badly, wrongly”) to ~dire~ (“to say”): to speak ill of someone, to slander. The prefix comes from Frankish *~missa-~ and is related to English ~mis-~, while ~dire~ continues Latin ~dīcere~, as does ~maudire~ (from ~maledīcere~, “to speak ill”), which French Wiktionary cites for comparison. French thus has two verbs for speaking ill, one with a Germanic prefix and one with a Latin one.
en.méditer: A learned borrowing from Latin ~meditārī~ (“to reflect on, to contemplate”), a deponent verb, one that has passive form with active meaning. The Latin verb also covered “to practice, to rehearse,” a sense still audible in the idea of mental exercise. French took the word into the learned vocabulary, where it kept its core sense of turning something over in the mind, and it gave ~méditation~ and ~méditatif~.
en.méduser:
~Méduser~ is built directly on the proper name ~Méduse~ (“Medusa”) plus the verb ending ~-er~. The name is that of the Gorgon of Greek mythology, which French received through Latin ~Medūsa~ from Greek ~Μέδουσα~ (~Médousa~). The same name gave English ~Medusa~, and French also uses ~méduse~ as the common noun for the jellyfish, so a single mythological name lies behind a monster, a sea animal and a verb. The story behind the verb is that Medusa was the Gorgon whose gaze turned anyone who met it to stone.

The verb is a coinage from a name. Its starting point is literal: to ~méduser~ someone would be to do to them what Medusa did to her victims, to freeze them with a look. Modern French keeps only the figurative result. ~Méduser~ means “to stupefy, to leave dumbfounded,” and the person so affected is rooted to the spot by astonishment, not by magic.
en.méfier: Formed in French from the prefix ~mé-~ and the verb ~fier~. The prefix comes from Old French ~mes-~ (“badly, wrongly”), from Frankish *~missa-~, and is related to English ~mis-~. Here it reverses the base, so ~se méfier~ is to withhold trust. The base ~fier~ is inherited from Old French ~fier~, from Vulgar Latin *~fīdāre~, a reshaping of Latin ~fīdere~ (“to trust”), the source of ~foi~, ~fidèle~ and ~confiance~. Note that the adjective ~fier~ (“proud”) is an unrelated word.
en.mégir: ~Mégir~ is a denominal verb: French Wiktionary derives it from ~mégie~, the craft of tawing, that is, dressing skins with alum to make white leather. The noun ~mégie~ is in turn traced to ~mégis~. French Wiktionary also links the word to Old French ~megier~ (“to treat, to heal”). The verb takes the second-conjugation ending ~-ir~.
en.mégisser: ~Mégisser~ is formed from the noun ~mégis~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. A ~mégis~ was the bath of alum, salt and ashes in which skins were steeped to make soft, supple leather, and the verb means to treat a hide this way. The noun comes from Old French ~megeis~. The trade of the ~mégissier~ was thus named after the bath itself, and the verb after the noun.
en.mégoter: Formed in French from ~mégot~ + the verbal suffix ~-er~, meaning “to skimp, to haggle over trifles.” The noun ~mégot~ is probably, by the account of both Wiktionaries, from the regional verb ~mégauder~ (“to suckle”), from ~mégaud~, from ~mègue~ (“whey”), from Vulgar Latin *~mesga~, itself from Gaulish. Compare Old Irish ~medc~ and Welsh ~maidd~, both meaning “whey.” This chain is only probable. The verb applies the word for a cigarette end to a stingy habit.
en.méjuger: Formed from ~juger~ and the prefix ~mé-~, meaning “wrongly, badly.” The prefix comes from Old French ~mes-~, from Frankish *~missa-~, and is cognate with English ~mis-~. ~Juger~ goes back to Latin ~jūdicāre~ (“to judge”), built from ~jūs~ (“law”) and ~dīcere~ (“to say”). ~Méjuger~ therefore means “to judge wrongly, to misjudge.”
en.mélanger:
A denominal verb from the noun ~mélange~ (“mixture”), which is itself derived from ~mêler~ (“to mix, to mingle”). ~mêler~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~misculāre~, a frequentative of Classical Latin ~miscēre~ (“to mix, to mingle, to stir up”). Cognate, through *~misculāre~, with Spanish ~mezclar~, Occitan ~mesclar~, and Italian ~mescolare~; through ~miscēre~, with English ~mix~ and ~miscellaneous~.

The chain is tidy: ~miscēre~ gave the frequentative *~misculāre~, which became Old French ~mesler~ and then ~mêler~; from ~mêler~ French formed the noun ~mélange~, and from that noun, in turn, the verb ~mélanger~. So ~mélanger~ is etymologically a verb made from a noun made from a verb. French usage keeps a delicate distinction: ~mêler~ tends toward intermingling or muddling things together, while ~mélanger~ leans toward deliberately combining them into a blend. The Latin root ~miscēre~ left a wide trail, including ~mixte~ (“mixed”), ~mixture~, ~miscible~ (“mixable”), ~promiscuité~ (“promiscuity”), ~méli-mélo~ (“jumble”), and the learned ~immiscer~ (“to interfere,” literally to mix oneself in).
en.mémoriser: From the noun ~mémoire~ + the suffix ~-iser~, which forms verbs meaning “to make into, to treat as.” To ~mémoriser~ is to commit something to memory. The noun ~mémoire~ is inherited from Latin ~memoria~ (“memory”), from the adjective ~memor~ (“mindful, remembering”). The same Latin root gives ~mémorial~, ~mémorable~ and ~commémorer~, and English has ~memory~, ~memorize~ and ~remember~ from related stock.
en.ménager: A verb formed from the noun ~ménage~ with the suffix ~-er~. French Wiktionary notes that it already appears in Old French, where it meant “to dwell, to live in a place.” That early sense, tied to the household, is a long way from the modern meanings “to use sparingly” and “to treat gently,” and the sources supplied here do not say how one led to the other. The same noun ~ménage~ is the base of ~déménager~, so the two verbs are cousins within one word family.
en.méprendre: ~Méprendre~ comes from Old French ~mesprendre~ and is formed from the prefix ~mé-~ and ~prendre~ (“to take”); English Wiktionary compares ~misapprehend~. ~Prendre~ comes from Latin ~prehendere~ (“to seize”), and ~mé-~ gives the sense of taking wrongly, hence “to mistake.” Today the verb is used almost only in the pronominal ~se méprendre~ (“to be mistaken”).
en.mépriser: Formed from ~priser~ (“to value, to prize”) with the old prefix ~més-~ (later ~mé-~), which marks something done badly or wrongly. Old French ~mespriser~ meant literally “to value less”, to refuse something its worth. ~Priser~ belongs to the family of ~prix~ and goes back to Latin ~pretium~ (“price, worth”), so to despise is, etymologically, to underprice someone. The prefix is of Germanic origin and a cousin of English ~mis-~, and English has the exact parallel in the rare ~mispraise~. Other Romance languages formed the same verb: Spanish ~menospreciar~, Portuguese ~menosprezar~ and Occitan ~mespresar~.
en.mériter:
A denominal verb built on the noun ~mérite~, itself from Latin ~meritum~ (“that which is earned, reward, desert”), the past participle of the verb ~merere~ / ~mereor~ (“to earn, to deserve, to serve for pay”). That verb descends through Proto-Italic from the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)mer-~ (“to assign, to allot”), which also gave Ancient Greek ~méros~ (“share, portion”) and ~meíromai~ (“to receive as one's due”). To deserve, in this light, is to receive the portion allotted to you.

The Latin sense sat squarely in the world of wages and military service — a soldier ~merere~ his pay, literally earning it by serving. French narrowed and abstracted this into the modern moral sense: to ~mériter~ is to be worthy of a reward or, increasingly, of anything at all, good or bad — one can ~mériter~ a prize or a punishment. The root remains visible in a tight French cluster: ~mérite~, ~méritoire~, ~méritant~, ~démériter~, and ~émérite~ (“emeritus,” one whose long service has earned honorable retirement). The Latin verb's military flavor also survives, distantly, in the English borrowing ~merit~ and in ~mercenary~, a soldier who serves purely for what he earns.
en.mésallier: Formed from ~allier~ with the prefix ~més-~, which means “wrongly, badly.” The verb is used of marrying beneath one's rank, in the sense “to ally oneself badly.” The base ~allier~ comes from Latin ~alligare~ (“to bind to”). The prefix descends from Old French ~mes-~, itself from Frankish *~missa-~, and is a cousin of English ~mis-~. The form ~més-~ is used before a vowel.
en.mésestimer: Formed from the prefix ~més-~ and the verb ~estimer~ (“to value, to esteem”). The prefix is the Old French ~mes-~ (“badly, wrongly”), from Frankish *~missa-~, the same source as English ~mis-~ and German ~miss-~, and it takes the form ~més-~ before a vowel. The base ~estimer~ comes from Latin ~aestimāre~ (“to value, to appraise”), so the verb means to value wrongly, in practice to think too little of someone or something, to hold in low esteem. The prefix is no longer productive: French now prefers ~mal~ or ~sous-~, as in ~sous-estimer~, but ~mésestimer~ remains in the language, with a slightly literary tone.
en.mésuser: ~Mésuser~ is formed from ~user~ with the prefix ~més-~, from Old French ~mes-~ (“badly, wrongly”), itself from a Frankish form ~missa-~. It means to use wrongly, to misuse, and it is mostly met in the construction ~mésuser de~. The base ~user~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~ūsāre~, built on the past participle of Latin ~ūtī~ (“to use”).
en.métaboliser: Formed from the stem of ~métabolisme~ plus the verb suffix ~-iser~, so “to subject to metabolism.” The ending ~-isme~ of the base is clipped before the suffix. The noun comes from Ancient Greek ~metabolḗ~ (“change”) plus ~-isme~, and ~metabolḗ~ itself joins ~metá~ (“beyond, across”) to ~bállō~ (“to throw”). The suffix ~-iser~ is fully productive in technical vocabulary, which suits a scientific verb like this one.
en.métalliser: Formed from the noun ~métal~ with the suffix ~-iser~, in the sense “to convert into, or coat with, N”: to make something metallic. ~Métal~ comes from Latin ~metallum~, which meant “mine” (and also “metal, quarry”), borrowed in turn from Ancient Greek ~μέταλλον~ (~métallon~, “mine, quarry”). English Wiktionary calls the Greek word of unknown origin. So the word for the material began as the word for the place it was dug from.
en.métamorphiser: French Wiktionary describes ~métamorphiser~ as a back-formation from ~métamorphisme~ or ~métamorphique~, shaped with the suffix ~-iser~. That suffix makes verbs meaning “to make into” or “to subject to,” so the sense is “to transform,” in the way of a metamorphosis.
en.métamorphoser: A denominal verb built on the noun ~métamorphose~ with the verb ending ~-er~, “to transform”. The noun was borrowed from Latin ~metamorphōsis~, from Ancient Greek ~metamórphōsis~ (“transformation”), itself from the verb ~metamorphoûn~, made of ~metá~ (a prefix of change) and ~morphḗ~ (“form”). The verb thus names a change of form in the literal Greek sense, and it keeps the flavor of the ancient myths of transformation.
en.métisser: ~Métisser~ is formed from the noun ~métis~ (“of mixed origin”) with the verbal ending ~-er~. ~Métis~ comes from Middle and Old French ~mestis~, from Late Latin ~mixtīcius~ (“born of a mixed race”), from ~mixtus~, the past participle of ~miscēre~ (“to mix”). Portuguese ~mestiço~, Spanish ~mestizo~ and Italian ~meticcio~ are cognates. The pronounced final s of ~métis~ is explained by the influence of the forms ~metice~ and ~mestice~, more common in the 17th and 18th centuries.
en.métrer: ~Métrer~ is formed from the noun ~mètre~ with the verb ending ~-er~: to measure in metres. The noun goes back to Ancient Greek ~μέτρον~ (“measure”), whether directly or through Latin ~metrum~, which meant the measure of a verse. French Wiktionary also notes the change in the vowel: the è of ~mètre~, in a closed syllable, becomes é in ~métrer~, because the ending opens the syllable.
en.météoriser:
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ~μετεωρίζω~ (“to raise into the air, to swell, to inflate”). The Greek verb is built on the adjective ~μετέωρος~ (“raised up, in the air”) with the verbal ending ~-ίζω~, the same ending that Late Latin transcribed as ~-izāre~ and that French took over as ~-iser~. French Wiktionary points to ~météore~ and ~-iser~ as the two pieces.

The verb has a family of its own in French. ~Météore~ comes from the Greek word for things high above, and English ~meteor~ shares that source. In French the learned medical word ~météorisme~ names the swelling of the abdomen with gas, which is the idea behind ~météoriser~ (“to bloat”). The word thus belongs to the same family as ~météorologie~, though its meaning is closer to the Greek “swelling” than to the weather.
en.mêler:
From Old French ~mesler~ (attested around 980, also ~mescler~), from Vulgar Latin *~misculare~, a derivative of Latin ~miscere~ (“to mix, mingle”). The Latin verb goes back to PIE *~meyḱ-~ (“to mix”), a root with broad cognates: Ancient Greek ~mísgō~, Sanskrit ~miśra~ (“mixed”), and English ~mix~ and ~mash~. Romance cognates of the same Vulgar Latin form include Spanish ~mezclar~, Occitan ~mesclar~, and Italian ~mescolare~.

The circumflex of ~mêler~ marks a lost ~s~ still visible in the Old French ~mesler~ and in the English ~meddle~ and ~medley~, which French handed on through the same root. The core sense — to mix or blend — branched into the figurative: to ~mêler~ is to shuffle (cards), to mingle, and reflexively ~se mêler de~ is to meddle in, to involve oneself where one may not belong. From the same ~miscere~ French draws ~mélange~, ~mixte~, ~promiscuité~, and ~pêle-mêle~; English keeps ~miscellaneous~ from the related ~miscellaneus~.
en.mûrir:
From Old French ~meürer~, inherited from Latin ~mātūrāre~ (“to make ripe, to bring to maturity”), a verb built on the adjective ~mātūrus~ (“ripe, timely”). French ~mûr~ (“ripe”) comes from the same Latin adjective, and English Wiktionary also analyzes the verb as ~mûr~ plus ~-ir~, which fits the later form. The same Latin family gave Italian ~maturare~ and Spanish ~madurar~. English reached it through learned borrowing, with ~mature~ and ~maturity~, not through the everyday inherited route.

The verb underwent an unusual change of conjugation. In Old French it was a first-group verb in ~-er~, and regular shifts normally run toward that group, but ~meürer~ moved into the second group and became ~mûrir~. The Latin ~t~ between vowels fell away, which left a diphthong that spelled the stem ~meur-~ in Middle French. The circumflex of ~mûr~ marks that lost sound, and does not serve to tell ~mûrs~ from ~murs~; the 1990 spelling rectifications proposed dropping it. The learned doublet ~maturer~ keeps the Latin ~t~, and so do ~maturité~, ~prématuré~ and ~immature~. Figuratively, one ~mûrit~ a plan or a decision, letting it ripen.
en.nacrer: ~Nacrer~ is a denominal verb, formed from the noun ~nacre~ (“mother-of-pearl”) with the verbal ending ~-er~. It means to give something the iridescent look of mother-of-pearl. The sources give nothing further about the history of the verb itself, or about the origin of ~nacre~.
en.nager:
From Old French ~nagier~ (“to sail, to row”), inherited from a reduced form of Latin ~nāvigāre~ (“to sail”), the verb built on ~nāvis~ (“ship”). The learned French verb ~naviguer~ is a later borrowing of the same Latin word, which makes ~nager~ and ~naviguer~ doublets. Old French already had a verb for swimming, ~noer~, from Latin ~natāre~ (“to swim”), which French Wiktionary traces through a Vulgar Latin form ~notāre~. Spanish ~nadar~ is a close relative of that older verb.

The story of ~nager~ is one of replacement. A verb that once meant “to travel by water, to row” slowly took over the meaning of “to swim” and pushed out ~noer~, which disappeared. The shift is easy to follow: moving through water by one's own strokes is a kind of rowing with the body. Traces of the older sense remain in nautical talk, where ~nage~ can refer to rowing. Modern French also has the figurative ~nager dans le bonheur~ (“to be swimming in happiness”) and the idiom ~savoir nager~ (“to know how to swim”), and the family includes ~nageur~, ~nageoire~ (“fin”) and ~nage~. English ~navigate~ is the learned cousin.
en.nanifier: Formed from ~nain~ (“dwarf”) and the suffix ~-ifier~, which builds verbs meaning “to make” or “to turn into.” ~Nain~ is inherited from Old French ~nain~, from Latin ~nānus~ (“dwarf”), and is related to the learned prefix ~nano-~. ~Nanifier~ thus means “to stunt, to make dwarfish,” and the suffix itself goes back to Latin ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”).
en.nantir:
From Old French ~nantir~ (“to seize the guarantors”), a verb built on ~nant~ (“pledge, security”), which is probably from Old Norse ~nám~ (“taking, seizure”). French Wiktionary words the chain slightly differently: ~nant~ was reshaped on ~nan~, the plural of ~nam~, which was itself borrowed from the Old Norse word. The Norse noun goes back to Proto-Germanic *~nēmą~ (“taking”) and to the Proto-Indo-European root *~nem-~ (“to give or take one's due”).

The root is the same one found in Old High German ~nām~ (“robbery”) and in Old English ~niman~ (“to take, seize”), which survives in the archaic English ~nim~. The Norse origin of ~nant~ is described as probable rather than certain. In modern French, ~nantir~ means to provide someone with security or with something needed, and the reflexive ~se nantir de~ means “to provide oneself with”. The adjective ~nanti~, as in ~bien nanti~, came to mean “well-off”.
en.napper: Formed from ~nappe~ and ~-er~, a cooking term meaning to coat a dish with sauce. The noun ~nappe~ is from Latin ~mappa~ (“napkin, cloth”), with an altered initial consonant. The image is presumably that of a cloth spread over a table, here a smooth sheet of sauce laid over the food. This is the denominal sense of ~-er~, “to provide with” the base. English ~map~ and ~napkin~ also come from Latin ~mappa~ (through the cloth sense), and ~nappe~ still means a tablecloth in French.
en.narguer: The sources differ slightly. French Wiktionary derives ~narguer~ from Latin ~naricare~, itself from ~naris~ (“nostril, nose”). English Wiktionary says “probably” from Vulgar Latin *~nārificō~, a humorous formation on ~nāris~, reaching French through Occitan ~nariguar~. Both agree on the Latin word for the nose, still visible in French ~narine~, “nostril”. The intermediate steps are a proposal, not a certainty.
en.narrer: ~Narrer~ is borrowed from Latin ~narrāre~, a verb that French Wiktionary glosses as “to make known, set out, recount, tell, describe.” It is a learned verb that stayed close to its Latin source in both form and sense. Its family is easy to recognize: ~narration~, ~narrateur~ and ~narratif~ in French, ~narrate~ and ~narrative~ in English, ~narrare~ in Italian and ~narrar~ in Spanish.
en.nasaliser: Formed from ~nasal~ with the suffix ~-iser~, in its sense “to make A”: ~nasaliser~ is to give a sound a nasal quality, to pronounce it through the nose. The adjective ~nasal~ is a learned word, borrowed from Medieval Latin ~nāsālis~, from Latin ~nāsus~ (“nose”). French ~nez~ descends from the same ~nāsus~ by inheritance, while ~nasal~ and ~nasaliser~ are its learned relatives.
en.nasiller: Formed from ~nez~ (“nose”) with the suffix ~-iller~, a suffix that often gives a repeated or imprecise action: to ~nasiller~ is to speak through the nose. French Wiktionary refers to ~nasonner~ for the same formation. The noun ~nez~ comes from Old French ~nes~, from Latin ~nasus~, which has relatives in English ~nose~ and German ~Nase~.
en.nationaliser: Formed from the adjective ~national~ with the suffix ~-iser~ (“make A”): to make something national. ~National~ is itself built from ~nation~ and ~-al~, and French Wiktionary records it in 1534 as ~nacional~, at first a term of religious organization. ~Nation~ comes, through Old French ~nacion~, from Latin ~nātiō~.
en.natter: A denominal verb formed from ~natte~ (“mat, braid of straw”) with the verbal ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary dates its earliest form, ~nater~, to 1344. The noun ~natte~ goes back through Old and Middle French ~nate~ to Vulgar Latin *~natta~, a variant of Latin ~matta~ (“rush mat”). English Wiktionary adds that ~matta~ may itself come from Punic or Phoenician, a Semitic source. ~Natter~ means “to plait, to braid,” so the verb names the weaving that makes a ~natte~, whether of straw or of hair.
en.naturaliser: Formed with the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make, to treat as”) on ~naturel~, which comes from Latin ~naturalis~ (“natural”). Sources differ slightly on the immediate base: French Wiktionary links the verb directly to Latin ~naturalis~ plus ~-iser~, while English Wiktionary builds it on French ~naturel~. The verb has two quite different senses, to naturalize, meaning to admit a foreigner as a citizen, and to stuff a dead animal for display. Both rest on the same idea of making something “natural.”
en.naviguer:
Borrowed in the late 14th century (first in the poet Eustache Deschamps) from Latin ~nāvigāre~ (“to sail, to travel by water”), formed on ~nāvis~ (“ship”) with a verbal element drawn from ~agere~ (“to drive”): to navigate is, literally, to drive a ship. ~nāvis~ continues PIE *~neh₂us~ (“boat”), which also gave Greek ~naûs~. Cognate with Italian ~navigare~, Spanish ~navegar~ and English ~navigate~. But French already owned this Latin verb in inherited, sound-worn form: navigare had become Old French ~nagier~ — modern ~nager~ — making ~naviguer~ and ~nager~ a doublet: the same word taken twice, once by ear across a thousand years, once fresh from the books.

~nager~ originally meant “to sail, to row”; only in Middle French did it finish capturing the sense “to swim” from the older verb ~noer~, the inherited form of Latin ~natāre~ — whose learned line survives in ~natation~. With its inherited verb busy swimming, French simply re-borrowed ~nāvigāre~ from Latin as ~naviguer~ to do the sailing. The family is a small fleet: ~navire~ and ~nef~ (“ship”), ~naval~; and, through Greek ~naûs~, ~nautique~ and ~nausée~ — originally seasickness, the “ship-sickness,” later any queasiness at all — plus the modern crews in ~-naute~: ~astronaute~, ~internaute~. The verb keeps extending its waters: French now says ~naviguer sur Internet~, in a ~navigateur~ (browser) — so the verb of Magellan's crossings also names an evening of idle browsing.
en.navrer:
From Middle French ~navrer~ (“to wound”), from Old French ~navrer~ or ~nafrer~ (“to hurt by piercing or cutting, to pierce the heart, to break someone's heart”). It is first attested in Norman texts, and later, through chivalric literature, in texts from Central and Southern France. Its ultimate origin is uncertain.

The likelier proposal derives it from Old Norse ~nafra~ (“to pierce with an auger”), from ~nafarr~ (“auger”), and Catalan ~nafrar~ (“to wound”) is a comparable form. An alternative proposal from Latin ~naufragāre~ (“to make shipwrecked, to ruin”) has also been made, but it is considered less likely: that Latin verb would normally have given Old French *~nofraier~ or *~noufrayer~, not ~navrer~ or ~nafrer~. Whichever source is right, Old French already used the verb both for physical wounds and for heartbreak. Today it means to grieve or dismay someone, as in ~navré~ (“sorry”), and ~navrant~ describes what is distressing.
en.naître:
From Middle French ~naistre~, from Old French ~naistre~, ~nestre~, from Vulgar Latin *~nascere~ (“to be born,” and figuratively “to originate, to arise”), a remodeling of the Classical Latin deponent ~nāscī~ (first-person ~nāscor~), earlier ~gnāscī~ (~gnāscor~), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ǵenh₁-~ (“to beget, give birth, produce”). That root is one of the most fertile in Indo-European, cognate with Greek ~gígnomai~ (“to be born, become”), English ~kin~ and ~kind~, and visible in Latin ~genus~ and ~gignere~ (“to beget”).

Classical Latin had a deponent verb — passive in form but active in meaning — which Vulgar Latin reshaped into an ordinary active infinitive *~nascere~, the ancestor of the modern French verb. The figurative sense was present early: rivers, ideas, and disputes could all “be born,” and French keeps this fully, speaking of a doubt or a friendship that ~naît~. From the same root *~ǵenh₁-~ French draws a vast harvest: ~naissance~, ~né~, ~nature~, ~natif~, ~nation~, ~genre~, ~gène~, ~générer~, and ~ingénu~ (literally “native-born, freeborn”).
en.neiger: Modern French ~neiger~ comes through Middle French ~neiger~ from Old French ~negier~, which descends from Vulgar Latin *~nivicāre~. This reconstructed verb was built on Latin ~nivem~ (“snow”), the accusative form of the noun ~nix~. Italian ~nevicare~ (“to snow”) comes from the same Vulgar Latin verb, so the two languages made their weather verb in parallel from the Latin noun. The Latin root also survives in the French adjective ~nival~ (“of snow”).
en.nervurer: Formed from ~nervure~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~ (from Latin ~-are~), meaning to provide with ribs, as on a vault or a leaf. The noun ~nervure~ is itself built on ~nerf~ with the suffix ~-ure~, so the verb stacks two French formations on a single root.
en.nettoyer:
From Old French ~netoiier~ (also ~netier~, ~neteier~), reshaped on the adjective ~net~ (“clean, neat”), from Vulgar Latin *~nitidiāre~ / Late Latin ~nitidāre~ (“to make clean, brighten”), from Latin ~nitidus~ (“shining, polished”), itself from ~niteō~ (“to shine, glisten”). The thread running through the whole chain is light: to clean a thing was, etymologically, to make it shine.

Latin ~nitidus~ first meant gleaming or glossy — of a polished surface, a sleek animal, well-fed skin — and only in Late Latin slid toward “clean,” the sheen of a thing standing in for its purity. French keeps both ends of that history: the adjective ~net~ can mean spotless, but also crisp or sharp (a clear image, a net price). From the same source come ~netteté~ (clarity, sharpness), ~nettoyage~ and ~nettoiement~ (two cleanings, the second more administrative — street-sweeping and refuse), and ~nettoyeur~ (a cleaner). The everyday French verb for scrubbing a floor thus carries, far back, the idea of restoring a thing's shine.
en.neutraliser: Formed in French from ~neutral~ and the verb-forming suffix ~-iser~, so to ~neutraliser~ is to make neutral, to cancel out an effect or a danger. The base ~neutral~ comes from Latin ~neutrālis~ (“of neither kind”), which belongs to ~neuter~ (“neither of two”), made of ~ne-~ (“not”) and ~uter~ (“either”). The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, itself taken from Greek. The verb serves in chemistry (an acid and a base cancel out), in the military (a position is put out of action) and in everyday talk (a rival is blocked).
en.nicher:
From Old French ~nigier~, from Vulgar Latin *~nīdicāre~, a verb formed on ~nīdus~ (“nest”). Classical Latin had the longer verb ~nīdificāre~, and the popular form is a shorter, everyday counterpart of it. English Wiktionary and French Wiktionary give the same chain, so the line from Latin to French is not in dispute. The Vulgar Latin form is a reconstruction, which is why it carries an asterisk: it is not directly attested but is the form the later Romance words require. The same noun ~nīdus~ lies behind French ~nid~, so ~nicher~ and ~nid~ are two descendants of one Latin word, one a verb and one a noun. The verb is therefore inherited through Old French, not coined in French from the noun ~nid~.

The verb ~nicher~ originally meant to make a nest, or for a bird to settle in one. From there the sense widened to people, who ~se nicher~ (“to nestle”) in a snug spot, and the casual sense “to hang out, to live” is presumably a further extension of the same image. That development is an inference from the meanings, not something the sources narrate. Related French words include ~nichée~ (“a brood”) and ~dénicher~ (“to drive out of the nest,” and so “to unearth”). All of them lead back to the picture of a nest, and to the Latin ~nīdus~ that named it.
en.nickeler: ~Nickeler~ (“to nickel-plate”) is formed from the noun ~nickel~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to coat with nickel.” The metal's name was borrowed from German ~Nickel~ or Swedish ~nickel~. It was introduced by the Swedish chemist Axel Fredrik Cronstedt and derived from the German ~Kupfernickel~, “copper of Nickel.” German miners used that name rather scornfully for an ore that looked like copper ore but yielded none. ~Nickel~ was the name of a mountain spirit in their folklore, like the trolls and goblins of other traditions.
en.nidifier:
Borrowed from Latin ~nīdificāre~ (“to build a nest”), a compound of ~nīdus~ (“nest”) and the verb ~faciō~ (“to make”), in its combining form ~-ficāre~. The Latin noun ~nīdus~ lives on as French ~nid~, while ~faciō~ gave French ~faire~, so the learned verb is a literal “nest-making” built from two everyday ancestors.

The ending ~-ifier~ is the same as in ~clarifier~ or ~purifier~, a learned pattern that French took from Latin verbs in ~-ficāre~. The verb is technical and mostly belongs to ornithology and natural history, where its noun ~nidification~ names nest-building. English ~nest~ and German ~Nest~ are cognates of Latin ~nīdus~.
en.nieller: Formed from ~nielle~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. Forms such as ~neielez~ appear around 1100 in the Chanson de Roland. One ~nielle~ is a plant, from Old French ~neiele~ and Latin ~nigella~ (“blackish”), from ~niger~ (“black”). It is a doublet of the learned ~nigelle~. A second ~nielle~, the blight that blackens wheat, is explained either from Latin ~nebula~ (“fog”) or from ~nigella~, by comparing the black grains with the plant's black seeds. The sources do not settle which.
en.nier:
From Old French ~neier~ (attested around 980), later ~nier~, from Latin ~negare~ (“to deny, say no”). ~negare~ is built on the negative particle ~nec~ / ~ne-~ (“not”), so that to deny is, at root, simply to say “no.” That negation belongs to the Proto-Indo-European negator *~ne~, which also underlies English ~no~ and ~not~ and the ~ne-~ of French ~ne... pas~.

The sense has stayed close to its origin — to declare untrue, to refuse to admit — but Latin ~negare~ seeded a wide field. Its compound ~renegare~ gave French ~renier~ (“to disown, renounce”) and, through Spanish, the noun ~renégat~; ~denegare~ yielded the legal ~dénier~ and ~déni~. Beyond French, ~negare~ shows up in English ~negate~, ~deny~ (itself borrowed from Old French ~deneier~), and ~renegade~. All of them turn on that ancient, blunt “no.”
en.nimber: ~Nimber~ is formed from the noun ~nimbe~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~: to surround with a halo, or, figuratively, to crown with glory. The noun ~nimbe~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~nimbus~, which meant “cloud” and, figuratively, “halo”. The Latin word is also the source of English ~nimbus~. Because the Latin sense passed from a bright cloud around a divine figure to the luminous circle shown behind a saint's head, the French verb belongs mainly to literary and artistic language, and is most often met in the participle ~nimbé~.
en.nipper: ~Nipper~ is a denominal verb formed from ~nippes~ (“clothes”), a familiar plural noun, with the ending ~-er~. It means “to dress, to rig out,” and is usually met in the reflexive ~se nipper~, “to get dressed.” Like its base, the verb belongs to informal speech. The sources give no deeper origin for ~nippes~ here.
en.niquer: The origin of ~niquer~ is debated, and the sources offer three accounts. One derives it from ~nique~ in the phrase ~faire la nique~ (“to thumb one's nose”) + ~-er~; ~nique~ itself comes from Old French ~nic~, of Germanic origin by way of Frankish *~hnukēn~. A second, which English Wiktionary calls the accepted one, borrows it from North African Arabic ~nik~ (“to have sex”) through the trade pidgin called ~sabir~, from Classical Arabic ~nakaḥa~. A third sees an abbreviation of ~forniquer~ that passed into slang. The sense “to deceive, to destroy” is a later extension of the vulgar one.
en.nitrater: ~Nitrater~ is formed from the noun ~nitrate~ with ~-er~: to treat with a nitrate, to convert into a nitrate. The noun ~nitrate~ was built on ~nitre~ (saltpetre) with the chemical suffix ~-ate~, a pattern that Latin already shows in ~nitratus~ (“treated with nitre”). The verb is therefore a late, technical formation, two derivational steps from the old word ~nitre~.
en.nitrer: Formed from the noun ~nitre~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~nitre~ is the old name for saltpeter, and the verb means to treat with nitre or to turn into a nitrate. The related verb ~nitrurer~ goes with the noun ~nitrure~ (“nitride”), a different chemical term.
en.nitrifier: ~Nitrifier~ is formed from ~nitrate~ and the suffix ~-ifier~. ~Nitrate~ is itself derived from ~nitre~ with the suffix ~-ate~, and has a Latin counterpart in ~nitratus~. The suffix ~-ifier~ comes from Latin ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”), so the verb means “to turn into nitrate.”
en.nitrurer: Formed from the noun ~nitrure~, the chemical term for a compound of nitrogen with another element, with the verb ending ~-er~. ~Nitrurer~ means to nitride: to combine with nitrogen or treat with it, as is done to harden the surface of steel.
en.niveler: Formed from the noun ~niveau~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, via the Old French form ~nivel~, so “to make level.” English Wiktionary traces ~niveau~ to Old French ~nivel~ (earlier ~livel~), from Vulgar Latin *~libellus~, from Latin ~lībella~. English ~level~ and Spanish ~nivel~ are cognates. The change from ~livel~ to ~nivel~ is a swap of initial consonant that the sources do not explain.
en.noircir:
From Old French ~noircir~, inherited from Vulgar Latin *~nigricīre~, which reshaped Latin ~nigrēscere~ (“to become black”). That Latin verb is an inchoative, a verb of “starting to be,” built on the adjective ~niger~ (“black”). The same ~niger~ lies behind Italian ~nero~ and Spanish ~negro~, so the French verb has close cousins across the Romance languages.

The change from ~nigrēscere~ to *~nigricīre~ is a change of conjugation: the Latin ending in ~-ēscere~ was replaced in popular speech by one in ~-īre~, which is the road to the French ~-ir~ verbs. Modern ~noircir~ means both “to turn black” and “to make black,” and it is used literally (soot ~noircit~ a wall) and figuratively (to blacken a reputation). French has several relatives of the adjective ~noir~, which comes from ~niger~, including the noun ~noirceur~ (“blackness, wickedness”).
en.noliser: French ~noliser~ (“to charter”) comes from Old French ~noliser~, with the same meaning. According to French Wiktionary, the Old French verb comes from Medieval Latin ~naulizare~, from Latin ~naulum~ (“freight, passage money”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~naûlon~. The word thus kept its commercial sense of hiring a vessel through Greek, Latin and French. The verb has a small family. The noun ~nolis~ (a chartered freight or the price of one) is a deverbal noun formed from ~noliser~, and ~nolisement~ is the act of chartering. Although it ends in ~-iser~, the verb is not a French coinage on that suffix: it was already a verb in Old French.
en.nomadiser: Formed from ~nomade~ with the verbal suffix ~-iser~, which turns a noun or adjective into a verb meaning “to act as, to live as”: ~nomadiser~ is “to live as a nomad.” The base ~nomade~ reached French through Middle French. French Wiktionary traces it to Latin ~Nomas~, ~Nomadis~, itself from Greek ~nomás~ (“pastoral, nomadic”), the word for people who move with their herds.
en.nombrer:
From Latin ~numerāre~ (“to count, to number”), a verb built on ~numerus~ (“number”). French Wiktionary gives this single link as the origin. Classical Latin ~numerāre~ also gave Italian and Spanish ~numerar~. The French noun ~nombre~ comes from ~numerus~ as well, and its ~b~ is the regular sound change that arose in the cluster -mr- when the Latin word's middle vowel was lost. English ~number~ and ~numeral~ reached English through French and Latin.

In modern French ~nombrer~ is literary and rare, used for “to count” or “to enumerate,” and mostly in the participle ~nombré~. Its compound ~dénombrer~ (“to count up”) is far more common, as is ~innombrable~ (“countless”). The same Latin root yields ~numéro~, borrowed later from Italian, and the learned ~numéral~, ~numérique~, ~énumérer~ and ~numérotation~. Where inheritance gave ~nombre~ with its ~b~, learned borrowing kept the older ~numer-~ shape, so the family splits into two sound-forms of one Latin word.
en.nominaliser: Formed from ~nominal~ with the suffix ~-iser~, which means “to make”: to turn something into a noun, or to treat it as nominal. ~Nominal~ is borrowed from Latin ~nominālis~ (“concerning the name”), a word that medieval Latin specialized as a term of scholastic philosophy. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs.
en.nommer:
From Old French ~nomer~, ~nommer~ (attested in the 10th century), from Latin ~nōmināre~ (“to name, to call by name, to appoint”), derived from ~nōmen~ (“name”). Latin ~nōmen~ descends through Proto-Italic *~nōmn̥~ from the Proto-Indo-European *~h₁nómn̥~ (“name”), one of the most widely preserved words in the whole family. Its cognates ring out across the languages: Ancient Greek ~ὄνομα~ (~ónoma~), Sanskrit ~nā́man~, German ~Name~, and English ~name~ all reflect the same ancient root, as do Italian ~nominare~ and Spanish ~nombrar~ for the verb.

Latin ~nōmināre~ carried from the start the double duty the French verb still bears: simply “to call by a name” and, more formally, “to designate someone for an office.” That second sense gives modern ~nommer~ its use in appointments — to ~nommer~ a minister or a director is to name them to the post. English borrowed the same Latin verb twice over, as ~nominate~ and, through French, as ~name~ in spirit. From ~nōmen~ French also inherited ~nom~, ~nominer~, ~nomination~, ~nominal~, ~pronom~, ~renom~, and ~surnom~ — a whole constellation turning on the act of naming.
en.nordir: Formed from the noun ~nord~ (“north”) with the verbal ending ~-ir~: to turn toward the north. The noun came into French through Old French ~nort~ from Old English ~norþ~, rather than from Dutch or Norse. French Wiktionary adds that it was first used in Normandy, from where it spread to other regions. English Wiktionary traces the English word back to Proto-Germanic *~nurþraz~. The ending ~-ir~ here forms a verb of becoming or turning from a noun, in the same way as ~-er~ does with other nouns.
en.normaliser: Formed from ~normal~ and the verb suffix ~-iser~ (“to make, to render”), so the verb means to make something conform to a norm. ~Normal~ was borrowed from Latin ~nōrmālis~, which one source also analyzes as ~norme~ + ~-al~ by surface analysis. Behind it stands Latin ~nōrma~ (“carpenter's square, rule”), a tool for checking that an angle is right. The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, taken from Greek, and is fully productive in modern French for coining verbs of change.
en.noter:
From Latin ~notare~ (“to mark, to write down, to indicate”), a denominal verb formed on the noun ~nota~ (“a mark, sign, written note”). Tradition long linked ~nota~ to the verb ~noscere~ (“to know”), making it “a mark by which something is known” and connecting it to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ǵneh₃-~ (“to know”); modern scholars such as de Vaan judge this uncertain, and the deeper origin of ~nota~ is best treated as unresolved. Related forms include Italian ~notare~ and Spanish ~notar~, and English borrowed both ~note~ and ~notation~.

The meanings of the French verb all radiate from making a mark. To ~noter~ is to jot something down, to notice or remark a fact, to mark a musical pitch with notes — and, distinctively in French schools, to grade: a teacher ~note~ a pupil's work by assigning it a mark out of twenty. The same ~nota~ survives whole in the scholarly tag ~nota bene~ (“note well”), abbreviated ~N.B.~ The wider family in French includes ~note~ (“note, grade, bill”), ~notable~ (“noteworthy”), ~notaire~ (“notary,” one who records), ~notice~ (“an explanatory note”), and ~annoter~ (“to annotate”); through Latin, English ~notable~, ~notary~, and ~notorious~ share the root.
en.notifier:
French ~notifier~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~notificāre~ (“to make known”), a compound of ~nōtus~ (“known”) and the verbal element ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”). English Wiktionary, citing the TLFi, describes it as a loan from the Latin of the law courts, with the sense of indicating or declaring. ~Nōtus~ is the participle of ~nōscere~ (older ~gnōscere~, “to come to know”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ǵneh₃-~ (“to know”), which also gave English ~know~ and Greek ~γιγνώσκω~.

The formula “to make known” is the whole story: ~notifier~ is the verb of official announcement, whether a decision is served on a party, a change reaches an employer or a message appears on a phone. Its sibling verbs share the ending ~-ficāre~, which French usually shortened to ~-fier~, as in ~modifier~, ~rectifier~ and ~clarifier~. The root *~ǵneh₃-~ and the participle ~nōtus~ feed a large French family: ~notion~, ~notoire~, ~notice~ and ~connaître~. A ~notification~ is, etymologically, the act of making something known, which is why the word has stayed legal and formal for so long.
en.nouer: From Middle French ~nouer~, from Old French ~noer~, inherited from Latin ~nōdāre~ (“to make a knot”). The Latin verb is built on ~nōdus~ (“knot”), which gave French the noun ~nœud~. The literal sense survives in ~nouer ses lacets~ (“to tie one's laces”). It also reaches bonds that are not made of rope: one can tie a friendship or a plot (~nouer une amitié~, ~nouer une intrigue~), and the ~nœud~ of a story is the point where its threads are drawn tight.
en.nourrir:
From Latin ~nūtrīre~ (“to suckle, to nurse, to feed”), which evolved into French around the year 1000 with the assimilation of the cluster ~-tr-~ into ~-rr-~ — giving the doubled ~r~ that the modern spelling faithfully preserves. ~Nūtrīre~ is reconstructed from a Proto-Indo-European form *~(s)neu-~ (“to suckle, to flow”), possibly tied to the root *~sneh₂-~ (“to flow”), the same watery idea behind mother's milk. It is cognate with the Romance family of Italian ~nutrire~ and Spanish ~nutrir~, and, through Old French ~norrir~, with English ~nourish~, ~nurse~, and ~nutrition~.

The original sense was intimate — a mother or wet-nurse (Latin ~nūtrīx~) giving the breast. From there it widened to “to feed” in general, then to “to raise, to bring up” a child, and finally to a host of figurative uses: one ~nourrit~ a hope, a grudge, an illusion, a conversation, feeding it so it grows. The metaphor of feeding-as-sustaining runs deep in French. From the same root descend ~nourriture~ (“food”), ~nourrisson~ (“infant, suckling”), ~nourrice~ (“wet-nurse”), and, through the learned Latin doublet, ~nutrition~ and ~nutriment~.
en.novelliser: Borrowed from English ~novelize~ (“to turn into a novel”), itself formed from English ~novel~ and the suffix ~-ize~. The French verb keeps the English sense: to adapt a film or other work as a novel. The ending of ~novelliser~ matches the French suffix ~-iser~.
en.nover:
~Nover~ is a legal term attested in Middle French in 1482, taken from Latin ~novāre~ (“to change, to make new, to innovate”). That is the account of English Wiktionary, which calls it a borrowing from Latin, and of French Wiktionary, which adds that speakers can also feel it as the noun ~novation~ plus the ending ~-er~, patterned on the pair ~innovation~ and ~innover~. The Latin verb is built on the adjective ~novus~ (“new”). In law, to ~nover~ a debt or an obligation is to replace it with a new one.

The Latin adjective ~novus~ is one of the most productive roots of the language. Inherited, it gave ~nouveau~ and ~nouvelle~. Learned borrowings gave ~novateur~ and ~novation~, and the prefixed verbs ~innover~ and ~rénover~, which share the Latin verb ~novāre~ with ~nover~. English ~novel~, ~innovate~ and ~renovate~ belong to the same family. ~Nover~ is the least visible of these, a technical word confined to contract law, but its structure shows the same pattern: a Latin verb for making something new, kept in a narrow professional sense.
en.novéliser: Borrowed from English ~novelize~, a verb meaning to turn a story, a film or a real event into a novel. The English verb is built on ~novel~ with the suffix ~-ize~, which French renders as ~-iser~, so the borrowing fits an existing pattern of French verbs in ~-iser~. French thus took in a ready-made English coinage rather than building the verb from ~roman~.
en.noyauter: Formed from ~noyau~ (“kernel, stone, core”) with the verbal ending ~-er~ and an inserted ~-t-~, as in ~tuyauter~ (from ~tuyau~). The ~-t-~ is a euphonic consonant: it keeps the final vowel of ~noyau~ from running straight into the ending. The verb means to infiltrate.
en.noyer:
The verb ~noyer~ is inherited from Old French ~neier~ (also written ~noier~), from Latin ~necāre~ (“to kill”). The odd thing is how far the meaning narrowed. In Latin, ~necāre~ could mean to kill by any means, but in the Romance languages it specialized into “to kill by immersion,” that is, to drown. The same narrowing appears in other cognates: Catalan ~negar~, Italian ~annegare~, Spanish ~anegar~ and Romanian ~îneca~. French took other verbs for general killing, while the old Latin verb kept only its watery corner.

Within French, the meaning kept spreading. The sense “to cover with water, to flood” is recorded from 1500, so a field or an engine can be ~noyé~. In the seventeenth century the verb took the figurative sense of absorbing something into a vast or confusing whole, as when a detail is ~noyé~ in a mass of text or a person is ~noyé~ in a crowd. The reflexive form ~se noyer~, for a person drowning, is recorded from 1774. The idiom ~noyer le poisson~ (“to drown the fish”) means to evade an issue by muddying it. The noun ~noyade~ (“a drowning”) comes from the verb. A word that once simply meant “to kill” thus ended up, in ordinary use, as the word for drowning.
en.nuancer: ~Nuancer~ is built on the noun ~nuance~ and the verb ending ~-er~, which descends from Latin ~-are~. ~Nuance~ is itself derived from the verb ~nuer~ (“to shade colors”) with the suffix ~-ance~, and began as a word for a gradation of color. The painter's term then became a general one for any fine difference of degree or meaning, and ~nuancer~ followed: to give something shades, and so to qualify or temper a statement so that it is no longer all black or all white. The chain is entirely French, with no Latin verb behind it.
en.nucléariser: A French formation from ~nucléaire~ (“nuclear”) and the verbal suffix ~-iser~, which turns a noun or adjective into a verb meaning “to make A” or “to convert into N.” French Wiktionary dates the verb to 1915. ~Nucléaire~ itself comes from the Latin ~nucleus~ (“kernel”), a standard etymology, and in the atomic age ~nucléariser~ came to mean to equip a country or an economy with nuclear weapons or nuclear power. The suffix ~-iser~ is fully productive in technical and journalistic French, as in ~numériser~ and ~informatiser~.
en.nuire:
From Old French ~nuisir~ (circa 1119), reshaped as ~nuire~ by about 1160, from Vulgar Latin *~nocĕre~, an altered form of classical ~nocēre~ (“to harm”), from Proto-Italic *~nokeō~, an old causative built on the PIE root *~neḱ-~ (“to perish, to disappear”): to harm someone is, at the root, to set them on the way to perishing. The Latin kin make the darkness plain: ~nex~ (“violent death”), ~noxius~ (“harmful”) and ~innocēns~ — literally “one who does no harm.” Cognate with Italian ~nuocere~, Old Spanish ~nocir~, Sanskrit ~naśyati~ (“perishes”) and Greek ~nekrós~ (“corpse”), whence French ~nécropole~ and ~nécrose~.

French kept the root busy. From nuire come ~nuisible~ and ~nuisance~ — borrowed by English as ~nuisance~, surely the politest descendant “violent death” ever produced — while learned ~nocif~ and ~innocuité~ came straight from Latin; an ~innocent~ is etymologically a harmless one. The root's most startling French relative is ~noyer~ (“to drown”): Latin ~necāre~ (“to put to death”) narrowed in popular Latin to killing by water specifically. And one luminous, disputed jewel: ~nectar~, the drink that kept the gods deathless, has traditionally been read as a poetic compound *~neḱ-~ + *~-terh₂-~, “overcoming death” — a reading the dictionaries still record while flagging it as uncertain, rival accounts treating the Greek word as a borrowing. If the traditional analysis is right, ~nuire~ and ~nectar~ are distant kin: the harm that pushes toward death, and the drink that defeats it.
en.numériser: ~Numériser~ was formed in French from ~numérique~ and the verb suffix ~-iser~ (“to make, to convert into”), with the stem shortened to ~numér-~ before the suffix. The adjective ~numérique~ rests on Latin ~numerus~ (“number”), the same root that gave ~nombre~ and ~numéro~. In the electronics sense, ~numérique~ is a loan translation of English ~digital~, so ~numériser~ means “to convert into digital form”: to scan a document, to digitize a sound or an image.
en.numéroter: Formed from the noun ~numéro~ (“number”) with a verbal ending, which English Wiktionary analyzes as ~-oter~ and French Wiktionary simply as a derivation of the noun. ~Numéro~ was borrowed from Italian ~numero~, from Latin ~numerus~ (“number”), so it is a doublet of ~nombre~, the form of the same Latin word that French inherited. The verb means to assign numbers to things in order. The suffix ~-oter~ often gives verbs a diminutive or repeated flavor, as in ~clignoter~ (“to blink repeatedly”).
en.néantiser: Formed from ~néant~ (“nothingness”) with the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make, to convert into”): ~néantiser~ is to reduce to nothing, to annihilate. The noun ~néant~ comes from Old French ~nient~, attested in 1050, whose origin is unknown. It probably descends from a Vulgar Latin phrase *~ne gentem~, literally “no living being,” made of the negative ~ne~ and ~gens~, ~gentis~ (“a set of beings”), though English Wiktionary also offers ~ne entem~ (“not existing”) as an alternative. Italian ~niente~ is a comparable form.
en.nécessiter:
From Medieval Latin ~necessitare~ (“to constrain, to compel”), a verb built on Latin ~necessitas~ (“necessity, inevitability”), itself from ~necesse~ (“unavoidable, needful”). ~Necesse~ is usually analysed as ~ne-~ (“not”) + a form related to ~cedere~ / ~cessus~ (“to yield, to give way”) — literally “that from which one cannot withdraw,” that which cannot be escaped. The French verb is attested from the fourteenth century and has Romance siblings: Italian ~necessitare~, Spanish ~necesitar~, and Portuguese ~necessitar~, all expressing need or compulsion.

The meaning has stayed remarkably close to its Latin core of inescapability. To ~nécessiter~ something is to render it unavoidable — to require it as a consequence one cannot dodge. There is a faint logic embedded in the word: if ~necesse~ is what one cannot yield from, then to necessitate is to box a situation in until only one outcome remains. From the same family French keeps ~nécessité~, ~nécessaire~, and the adverb ~nécessairement~, while the underlying ~cedere~ also gave French ~céder~, ~cesser~, and ~succès~ — a reminder that the very idea of necessity is built, etymologically, on the refusal to give ground.
en.nécroser: ~Nécroser~ is formed from ~nécrose~ with the ending ~-er~: to cause necrosis in tissue, or to undergo it. The noun ~nécrose~ comes from Ancient Greek ~nékrōsis~ (“mortification”), a noun built on ~nekrós~ (“dead”). The verb is a medical term, and the participle ~nécrosé~ describes dead tissue.
en.négliger:
Borrowed from Latin ~neglegere~ (also spelled ~negligere~, “to disregard, not attend to, slight”), a compound of the negative particle ~nec~ (“not”) and ~legere~ (“to gather, pick, choose, read”). ~legere~ comes from Proto-Indo-European *~leǵ-~ (“to gather, collect”), the root behind Greek ~légein~ (“to gather, say”) and ~lógos~. To neglect is, etymologically, to not gather up — to let things lie ungathered, unchosen.

That root *~leǵ-~ is one of the most productive in the European vocabulary. From ~legere~ and its compounds come French ~lire~, ~élire~, ~collecter~, ~négligence~, and ~négligé~ (the loose garment is literally “the un-gathered, careless” one); English inherits ~lecture~, ~legend~, ~collect~, ~elect~, ~select~, ~intelligent~, and ~neglect~ itself. The Greek branch, through ~lógos~, supplies the entire ~-logy~ family. The image at the bottom of all of them — picking out and gathering together — makes neglect simply its refusal: the things one declines to pick up.
en.négocier:
Borrowed from Latin ~negōtiārī~ (“to do business, to trade”), attested in French in 1484, from ~negōtium~ (“business, occupation”). That noun is transparently ~nec~ (“not”) joined to ~ōtium~ (“leisure, ease”): business is, literally, “not-leisure.” The descent gave Spanish ~negocio~, Italian ~negozio~ and French ~négoce~; English ~negotiate~ comes from the same Latin verb. Two cautions are worth carrying. First, ~ōtium~ itself is of uncertain origin — one proposal traces it to PIE *~h₂ewtyom~ (“forlorn, deserted”), but the sources flag this as merely possible. Second, ~negōtium~ is often called a calque of Greek ~ἀσχολίᾱ~ (askholíā, “lack of leisure”); the oddity, noted by etymologists, is that a faithful calque would have produced *~inōtium~ rather than ~negōtium~, so the borrowing account is debated.

Whatever its deepest root, the meaning developed from “to conduct business” toward the modern “to bargain, to come to terms,” and figuratively “to manage” a difficulty or a bend in the road. The Latin family is rich in French: ~négoce~, ~négociant~, ~négociation~ and the borrowed ~otium~-relative ~oisif~ (“idle”), which preserves, in its very sense, the leisure that business was defined against.
en.objecter: Borrowed from Latin ~objectāre~, which analyzes as ~ob-~ (“against, in the way of”) plus ~iactāre~ (“to throw”), a frequentative of ~iacere~ (“to throw”), so literally “to throw in the way of.” English ~object~, the verb, comes from the same Latin verb, and French ~objection~ belongs to the same family.
en.objectiver: ~Objectiver~ is formed from the adjective ~objectif~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, and means “to make objective” or “to give objective form to.” French Wiktionary derives ~objectif~ from ~objet~ plus the suffix ~-if~, whereas English Wiktionary calls it a learned borrowing from Latin ~objectivus~; the two accounts differ. ~Objet~ itself comes from Latin ~objectum~ (“that which is placed before”), the neuter past participle of ~obicere~ or ~objicere~ (“to throw or place before”), built on ~jacere~ (“to throw”) with the prefix ~ob-~ (“before”).
en.obliger:
From Old French ~obligier~, from Latin ~obligāre~ (“to bind, to tie up, to bind by obligation”), a compound of the prefix ~ob-~ (“to, toward, against”) and ~ligāre~ (“to bind, to tie”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~leyǵ-~ (“to bind”). The same root, through ~ligāre~, gives a startling spread of words: Italian ~obbligare~, Spanish ~obligar~, and in English ~ligament~, ~ligature~, ~liable~, ~ally~, ~rely~, and ~league~.

The metaphor is physical: an obligation is a ~bond~ presented symmetrically — French ~lien~, English ~bond~ — a tie that binds a person to a duty, exactly as a rope binds a thing. Latin ~obligāre~ could even be used of binding a wound or of making a liquid set, but the figurative sense of binding by law, promise, or gratitude prevailed. French keeps two faces of this: ~obliger~ can compel (~la loi m'oblige~, the law requires me to) or, more gently, do a favour that places someone under a pleasant debt — hence ~obligé~ as “much obliged” and ~obligeant~ as “obliging, helpful.” The same ~ligāre~ underlies the everyday ~lier~ (“to bind, to link”), ~allier~ (“to ally”), ~relier~ (“to connect, to bind a book”), and the legal ~obligation~. Even ~religion~ may belong here, if it is, as some held, a “binding back” to the divine.
en.obliquer: From Latin ~obliquāre~ (“to slant, to turn aside”), a verb made from the adjective ~obliquus~ (“slanting, sideways”). The French verb keeps the idea of leaving a straight line and turning off to one side. The same Latin adjective gave French ~oblique~ and ~obliquité~ and English ~oblique~. The evidence documents only this one Latin step.
en.oblitérer: From Latin ~oblitterāre~ (spelled ~obliterāre~ in some texts), which French Wiktionary analyzes as ~ob-~ (“over”) + ~littera~ (“letter, written mark”). The Latin verb meant “to efface, to blot out”, which fits the verb's modern senses: to cancel a stamp or ticket with a postmark, and, in medicine, to block a vessel or passage. English ~obliterate~ is a cognate descendant of the same Latin verb, and French has the noun ~oblitération~.
en.obnubiler:
From Middle French ~obnubiler~ (also ~obnubuler~), earlier Old French ~obnubler~ and ~obnublir~, borrowed from Latin ~obnūbilāre~ (“to cover with clouds”). The Latin verb is built from ~ob-~ (“over, in front of”) and ~nūbilus~ (“cloudy”), a derivative of ~nūbēs~ (“cloud”). The word was thus a learned borrowing from the start, and its French spellings wavered through the Old and Middle French periods before the modern form settled.

The word first applied to sight, literally: to ~obnubiler~ was to cloud the vision. It then passed to thought, figuratively, and by extension to a mind darkened by a stubborn obsession. In modern French ~obnubiler~ is used mostly in that last sense, often in the passive or the participle: one is ~obnubilé~ by an idea, a fear or a goal. The Latin ~nūbēs~ also gave ~nue~ (“cloud”, now literary), with its derivatives ~nuée~ (“a mass of cloud, a swarm”) and ~nuage~ (“cloud”), the everyday word for what the verb ~obnubiler~ once evoked.
en.obombrer:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~obumbrāre~ (“to shade, to overshadow”). The Latin verb is a compound of ~ob-~ (“over, in the way of”) and ~umbrāre~ (“to cast shade”), a verb built on ~umbra~ (“shade, shadow”). French took it over whole, keeping the Latin form, which is why the ~b~ of ~ob-~ survives beside the ~b~ of ~umbra~. The verb is rare and literary, and means to shade or darken.

The Latin noun ~umbra~ is the root of a whole French family. ~Ombre~ is its inherited form, and ~ombrage~, ~ombrager~, ~pénombre~ and ~ombrelle~ (by way of Italian ~ombrella~) all belong to it. Italian ~ombra~ is its direct descendant, and Spanish ~sombra~ is a close relative. English has borrowed the Latin word itself in ~umbra~, and ~umbrella~ comes from Italian. ~Obombrer~ is the learned sibling in this family. It keeps the Latin prefix and its sense of shadow thrown across something, where ~ombrager~, the everyday verb, only says to give shade.
en.obscurcir:
French Wiktionary explains ~obscurcir~ as a derivative of the adjective ~obscur~ with the verb ending ~-ir~, while English Wiktionary says only that it was inherited from Old French ~obscurcir~. The adjective comes from Latin ~obscurus~ and reached Old French as ~oscur~. In Middle French the ~b~ was put back by learned influence from the Latin spelling, which is why the modern word is written ~obscur~. English ~obscure~ comes from the same Latin source.

The verb is attested very early, in the Cambridge Psalter or in Benoît de Sainte-Maure's ~Roman de Troie~ (around 1160 to 1170), under the forms ~oscurir~ and ~oscurcir~. The odd ~-c-~ in the longer form is explained as an addition on the model of ~noircir~ and ~éclaircir~, two verbs that also turn a colour or quality into a process (“to make black,” “to make clear”). A shorter verb, ~obscurer~, exists beside it, so French has two ways to say “to darken.” Today ~obscurcir~ covers both literal darkening and figurative blurring, as when a question or a meaning becomes less clear.
en.observer:
From Latin ~observare~ (“to watch over, attend to, guard, comply with”), a compound of the prefix ~ob-~ (“toward, before”) and ~servare~ (“to keep, guard, watch over, preserve”). The Latin verb was borrowed into French as a learned word as early as the tenth century. ~servare~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~ser-~ (“to protect, watch over”), so that to observe is, at root, to keep watch toward something. The same Latin verb gives Italian ~osservare~, Spanish ~observar~, and, through Old French, English ~observe~.

The meaning fans out neatly from “keeping one’s gaze on”: one ~observes~ the stars (watches), ~observes~ a custom (keeps, complies with), and ~observes~ that it is raining (notices and remarks). The protective sense of ~servare~ survives more plainly in its many French descendants: ~conserver~ (“to keep”), ~réserver~ (“to set aside”), ~préserver~ (“to shield”), and the noun ~observatoire~. Curiously, the same root *~ser-~ that meant “to guard” also stands behind Latin ~servus~ (“slave, servant”) — probably first a “guardian” or “herdsman” before the sense darkened — and thus, distantly, behind French ~serf~ and ~servir~. The watcher and the servant share an ancestor.
en.obstiner: From Latin ~obstināre~ (“to be determined, to persevere”). French Wiktionary explains it as formed on a verb *~stanāre~, an equivalent of ~stāre~ (“to stand”), with the prefix ~ob-~ (“against”), so the underlying picture is that of standing firm against something. The verb is now used mostly in the pronominal form ~s'obstiner~, “to persist stubbornly.” The adjective ~obstiné~ and the noun ~obstination~ belong to the same family. Italian ~ostinare~ and English ~obstinate~ come from the same Latin verb.
en.obstruer:
French ~obstruer~ is a borrowing from Latin ~obstruere~ (“to block up, to build against”). The Latin verb joins ~ob-~ (“against, in the way of”) to ~struere~ (“to pile up, to build”), so to obstruct is, literally, to build something in the way. English ~obstruct~ comes from the same Latin verb.

The verb ~struere~ is a prolific root. French ~construire~ (“to build together”), ~détruire~ (“to unbuild”), ~instruire~ (“to teach”) and ~structure~ all trace back to it, as do their English counterparts ~construct~, ~instruct~ and ~structure~. French ~obstruer~ itself belongs to the learned register: the related noun ~obstruction~ is the more familiar form, and the verb is used mainly of passages, pipes and vessels that become blocked.
en.obséder:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~obsidēre~ (“to sit opposite, to besiege, to blockade”), made of ~ob-~ (“against, before”) and ~sedēre~ (“to sit”). French Wiktionary notes that the accent in ~obséder~ seems to come from the influence of ~posséder~. Latin ~sedēre~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~sed-~ (“to sit”), whose descendants include English ~sit~, German ~sitzen~ and Greek ~hézomai~ (“I sit”). The literal picture is a military one: an army sits down before a town and holds it under siege.

From the idea of being surrounded and hounded by a force, the verb passed to a thought or a worry that will not leave: to be ~obsédé~ by an idea is to be besieged by it. The relatives are many, including ~obsession~, ~obsidional~ (“relating to a siege”), ~siège~, ~assiéger~, ~séance~ and ~présider~.
en.obtempérer:
~Obtempérer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~obtemperāre~ (“to comply with, to conform to, to obey”), built from ~ob~ (here “toward, in the face of”) and ~temperāre~ (“to show restraint, to moderate”). The French text glosses it as “to restrain oneself before” someone, which captures the idea: yielding to an authority by holding one's own will in check. The simple verb ~temperāre~ is the source of French ~tempérer~ and of English ~temper~ and ~temperate~.

In French, ~obtempérer~ is a formal word of law and administration, almost always followed by ~à~: one obeys an order or a summons. Its best-known appearance is the offense of ~refus d'obtempérer~, refusing to comply with a police order. Other members of the family are ~tempérer~, ~tempérament~ and ~température~, all resting on the notion of a right measure or mixture. ~Obtempérer~ keeps the moral side of that idea, the measured submission of one will to another.
en.obtenir:
French ~obtenir~ comes from Latin ~obtinēre~ (“to hold firmly, to possess fully, to maintain”), a compound of the prefix ~ob-~ (“against, toward”) and the verb ~tenēre~ (“to hold”). Rather than evolving by regular sound change, it was refashioned in French on the model of the inherited verb ~tenir~ (“to hold”), so that its endings march in step with its everyday relative. The root ~tenēre~ descends from Proto-Italic *~tenēō~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~ten-~ (“to stretch, draw”), the link between stretching and holding being the idea of keeping something taut.
