That root is cognate with Ancient Greek ~teínō~ (“I stretch”) and Sanskrit ~tanóti~ (“stretches”).

The sense narrowed from the Latin “hold fast, keep possession of” to the modern French “to get, to come to have,” the result of an effort that secures and keeps something. The prefix ~ob-~ adds the nuance of reaching toward a goal — one obtains by holding on against resistance. French is unusually rich in cousins built on ~tenir~: ~contenir~ (“contain,” to hold together), ~maintenir~ (“maintain,” to hold by hand), ~retenir~ (“retain”), ~soutenir~ (“sustain”), ~détenir~ (“detain”), and ~appartenir~ (“belong”). Even the adverb ~maintenant~ (“now”) hides the root, from Latin ~manū tenendō~ (“holding in the hand”).
en.obturer:
Borrowed from Latin ~obtūrāre~ (“to block up, to stop up”). The verb entered French as a learned word, not through everyday speech, and kept its Latin sense of closing an opening so that nothing can pass: to ~obturer~ a hole, a pipe, a leak or a cavity is to plug it. Its register has stayed technical, at home in plumbing, dentistry and medicine.

The verb has a small family of technical words. ~Obturation~ names the act of sealing, notably in dentistry, where it is the filling of a cavity. ~Obturateur~ names the thing that seals: a valve, a plug, and in photography the shutter that opens and closes over the lens. It is a learned verb from Latin, with no common inherited relative in everyday French.
en.obvenir:
From Latin ~obvenīre~ (“to fall to, to befall, to come to one's lot”). The Latin verb is a compound of ~ob-~ (“toward, in the way of”) and ~venīre~ (“to come”). French took it over in the sense of “to fall to someone,” of a share, an inheritance or a duty that devolves upon a person.

The second half of the compound is the root of French ~venir~, which has a whole tribe of prefixed relatives built the same way: ~advenir~, ~convenir~, ~devenir~, ~parvenir~, ~survenir~. Italian ~venire~ and Spanish ~venir~ are cousins from the same Latin verb. Unlike most of these, ~obvenir~ never became an everyday word: it is a rare, learned verb of legal and administrative language, a bookish near-synonym of ~échoir~, and it is little used in modern French.
en.obvier:
Borrowed from Latin ~obviāre~ (“to prevent, to meet in the way”). The Latin verb is built on ~obvius~ (“in the way, meeting”), itself from ~ob-~ (“toward, against”) and ~via~ (“way, road”). Italian ~ovviare~ and Spanish ~obviar~ are its relatives, and English took the same verb as ~obviate~, while the English adjective ~obvious~ comes from ~obvius~.

Latin ~via~ is one of the most fertile roots of French. Inherited ~voie~ descends from it, as do ~dévier~ (from Late Latin ~dēviāre~, “to turn aside”) and ~envoyer~ (from Late Latin ~inviāre~, “to put on the road”). ~Obvier~ remained a learned, formal verb: it is used in the construction ~obvier à~ followed by an inconvenience or danger, and means to forestall it by taking measures in advance. It has none of the everyday use of ~voie~ and ~envoyer~.
en.obéir:
From Old French ~obeir~ (early 12th century, in the Voyage de saint Brendan), from Latin ~oboedīre~ (“to give ear to, hence to submit to”), from ~ob-~ (“toward”) + ~audīre~ (“to hear”). ~audīre~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~awizdiō~, a compound of PIE *~h₂ewis~ (“clearly, manifestly” — from *~h₂ew-~, “to perceive”) and *~dʰh₁-~ (“to render”): to hear is “to render clear.” The same perceptual root underlies Greek ~aisthánomai~ (“I perceive”), source of French ~esthétique~ and ~anesthésie~. Cognates of the verb itself: Italian ~obbedire~, Spanish ~obedecer~ — and English ~obey~, lifted from the Old French verb.

Etymologically, obedience is a way of listening: ~oboedīre~ is to turn one's ear toward someone. French keeps the hearing close by. The inherited child of ~audīre~ is ~ouïr~, today almost confined to ~ouï-dire~ (“hearsay”) and to legal memory — English and American courtrooms still open with ~oyez~, “hear ye,” the Old French imperative carried to England by the Normans — while the learned line gave ~audience~, ~auditeur~, ~audition~, ~audible~. Meanwhile obéir widened its empire along dates the TLFi records: people obey wills (12th century), matter obeys forces (1377), passions get obeyed (1550), and by 1671 animals and machines “execute the commanded movement.” Grammar preserves a fossil: the verb now takes its object with à (~obéir à quelqu'un~), yet French still allows the passive ~être obéi~ — a relic of the days when one obeyed someone directly. Family: ~obéissance~, ~obéissant~, ~désobéir~.
en.obérer: ~Obérer~ is formed from the adjective ~obéré~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The adjective came first, and the verb followed, dated to 1690 by French Wiktionary. The verb means to burden someone with heavy financial charges, to the point of leading toward debt and ruin. By extension it came to mean to limit or restrict the capacity of something, in political, business or military contexts. The sources give no older source for the adjective, so the history of the word begins at the adjective itself.
en.occasionner: A denominal verb built from ~occasion~ plus the first-conjugation ending ~-er~, meaning “to give rise to, to cause.” The noun was borrowed from Latin ~occāsiō~ (“opportunity, favorable moment”). The learned verb displaced the inherited Old French ~ochoisonner~, which had come down from the same Latin word by regular sound change; the old noun ~ochoison~ (also ~achaison~, reshaped under the influence of Latin ~accūsātiō~) lived alongside it for a time, a reminder that French borrowed the same Latin word twice.
en.occidentaliser: Formed from the adjective ~occidental~ plus the verbal suffix ~-iser~, meaning to make Western in character. The adjective was borrowed from Latin ~occidentālis~ (“western”). The verb is used of cultures, customs and countries that take on the habits of the West.
en.occire:
~Occire~ comes from Middle French ~occire~, itself from Old French ~ocire~, whose spelling was later adjusted to restore the Latin consonant. The Latin source is ~occīdere~ (“to kill”), but the French verb did not descend from it unchanged. It passed through an altered Vulgar Latin form, *~auccīdō~ (also written ~aucidere~). English Wiktionary suggests the alteration may reflect the influence of another verb such as ~auferō~ (“to carry away”), but this is only a possibility.

Latin ~occīdere~ is built from ~ob-~ and ~caedere~ (“to cut, to strike down”). The same ~caedere~ lies behind ~homicide~, ~suicide~ and ~incision~ in French, and Italian ~uccidere~ (“to kill”) is a relative of ~occire~ from the same Latin verb. In modern French, ~occire~ is archaic. It survives mainly in the past participle ~occis~ (“slain”) and in deliberately old-fashioned or jocular style.
en.occlure:
Borrowed from Latin ~occlūdere~ (“to shut up, to close off”), built from the prefix ~ob-~ (“against, in the way of”) and ~claudere~ (“to close”). French Wiktionary notes that it is formed on the model of ~conclure~, which pairs a different prefix with the same verb. The verb is a learned borrowing, with no inherited ancestor in Old French, and it is defective in modern French, used chiefly in the participle and the infinitive.

The Latin verb ~claudere~ is the source of a wide French family. The inherited form is ~clore~ (“to close”), which has largely given way to ~fermer~, and the Latin prefixed verbs gave ~conclure~, ~exclure~ and ~inclure~. They are all built like ~occlure~, with one prefix and the same stem, and the participle forms (~conclu~, ~exclu~, ~inclus~) show the same pattern. English borrowed the same Latin verb as ~occlude~, and its noun ~occlusion~ has a French twin of the same form.
en.occulter: The sources give two routes. French Wiktionary derives ~occulter~ directly from Latin ~occultāre~ (“to hide”), while English Wiktionary analyzes it as the adjective ~occulte~ + the verb ending ~-er~. Both lead to the same Latin family, since ~occulte~ itself comes from Latin ~occultus~ (“hidden, secret”). The core idea is concealment. French uses the verb figuratively, as in ~occulter un problème~ (“to hide a problem, to push it out of sight”), and also in astronomy, where one body blocks another from view, the noun for which is ~occultation~. English ~occult~ comes from the same Latin adjective.
en.occuper:
From Latin ~occupāre~ (“to seize, take possession of, take before others”), an intensive compound of ~ob-~ (“toward, over”) and ~capere~ (“to grasp, seize, take”). ~Capere~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~kapjō~ to the Proto-Indo-European root *~kap-~ (“to grasp”), which — perhaps unexpectedly — also gave English ~have~ and ~heave~, and underlies Latin ~captīvus~ and ~capax~. Romance kin include Italian ~occupare~ and Spanish ~ocupar~.

The Latin verb already carried a competitive edge: to ~occupāre~ was to grab something before someone else could, to get there first. That sense of prior seizure survives in the military meaning — an army that ~occupe~ a territory has taken and now holds it. But French let the word soften and spread. Today one can ~occuper~ a seat, ~occuper~ a job, or ~occuper~ an afternoon, and the reflexive ~s'occuper de~ means simply “to busy oneself with, to take care of.” The same ~capere~ seeded an enormous family of French words through its many prefixed forms: ~capter~, ~accepter~, ~concevoir~, ~recevoir~, ~capable~, ~captif~, and the noun ~préoccupation~ — an anxiety that has, quite literally, seized the mind in advance.
en.octavier: ~Octavier~ is derived from the musical noun ~octave~ with the verbal ending ~-er~: to sound a note an octave higher, or to play in octaves. The noun comes from Latin ~octavus~ (“eighth”), the interval being counted as the eighth note of the scale.
en.octroyer:
Inherited from Middle French ~octroyer~, from Old French ~otroiier~, from Early Medieval Latin ~auctōrizāre~ (“to authorize”), a verb built on Latin ~auctor~ (“originator, authority”), itself tied to ~augēre~ (“to increase”). Old French wrote the verb without the Latin ~c~, and the modern spelling with ~c~ is a later restoration after the Latin model: first in writing, then, from Early Modern French, in pronunciation. The same Latin verb thus reached French by two routes, which makes ~octroyer~ a doublet of ~autoriser~, the form that kept closer to the Latin.

To authorize something is to grant it, and the Old French verb meant to grant or concede a request, a favor, a privilege. Modern ~octroyer~ keeps that formal, slightly lofty tone: a power decides, and ~octroie~ a loan, a delay, a right or a charter. The noun ~octroi~ named a tax levied at the gates of a town on goods entering it, and survives in ~octroi de mer~ in the French overseas territories. The pair ~octroyer~ and ~autoriser~ shows two fates of one Latin word, one worn down by speech and later patched up in spelling, the other taken straight from Latin. English ~author~ and ~authority~ come from the same Latin ~auctor~, as does French ~auteur~.
en.octupler: Formed from the adjective ~octuple~ (“eightfold”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to multiply by eight.” The adjective comes from Latin ~octuplus~, built on ~octo~ (“eight”). It belongs to the series that includes ~doubler~, ~tripler~, ~quadrupler~ and ~centupler~, in which a multiplier adjective becomes a verb meaning to multiply by that number.
en.offenser: ~Offenser~ is formed in French from ~offense~ and the ending ~-er~, rather than borrowed directly from Latin, according to French Wiktionary; English Wiktionary gives the same formation and adds Latin ~offēnsāre~ (“to strike against”) behind it. ~Offense~ comes from Latin ~offēnsa~. ~Offēnsāre~ is the frequentative of ~offendere~ (“to strike against”), which gave the older French ~offendre~ (“to transgress, to offend”); the new verb replaced it.
en.officialiser: Formed from ~officiel~ + the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to make official”. ~Officiel~ comes from Old French and Latin ~officiālis~, the adjective of ~officium~ (“duty, service, public function”), so something ~officiel~ is literally what belongs to an office. The suffix ~-iser~ is borrowed from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and in French it makes verbs of the type “render A”. ~Officialiser~ thus means to give a fact, a decision or a status an official character, for instance by announcing or recording it formally.
en.officier: The verb ~officier~ (“to officiate”) comes from Middle French ~officier~, borrowed from Medieval Latin ~officiāre~. Underneath lies the Latin noun ~officium~ (“duty, service”), the source of ~office~ and ~officiel~. French Wiktionary treats the noun ~officier~ (“officer”) separately: it derives from Medieval Latin ~officiārius~, so the two words share a spelling but not a path, and the verb was formed independently of the noun.
en.offrir:
From Old French ~ofrir~, ~offrir~ (“to offer, present”), from Late Latin ~offerīre~, a reshaping of Classical Latin ~offerre~ (“to bring before, present, offer”), itself ~ob-~ (“before, toward”) + ~ferre~ (“to carry, bear”), from Proto-Italic *~ferō~, from PIE *~bʰer-~ (“to carry, to bear”). Cognate with Italian ~offrire~, Spanish ~ofrecer~, and Catalan ~oferir~; through the same root *~bʰer-~ it is kin to English ~bear~ and ~birth~, and to German ~gebären~ (“to give birth”).

The Latin sense was concretely physical — to carry something forward and set it before another — and the verb early took on a religious coloring, the ~oblātiō~ laid before a god, so that to offer was to present a gift or sacrifice. French kept both the everyday sense of giving a present and the ceremonial one. The root *~bʰer-~ is among the most fertile in Indo-European, and through ~ferre~ it seeded a vast French family: ~offrande~ and ~offre~, but also ~conférer~, ~transférer~, ~souffrir~ (literally “to bear from below”), and the nouns in ~-fère~ such as ~mammifère~ (bearer of breasts). Even ~fertile~ — that which bears — belongs to the same stock.
en.offusquer: ~Offusquer~ is borrowed from Latin ~offuscāre~, built from the prefix ~of-~ (a form of ~ob-~) and ~fuscō~ (“to darken”), a verb from the adjective ~fuscus~ (“dark”). The two Wiktionaries gloss the Latin verb differently: French Wiktionary gives “to obscure,” English Wiktionary gives, for Ecclesiastical Latin, “to vilify, to degrade.” English ~obfuscate~ comes from the variant ~obfuscāre~ of the same Latin verb. The sources consulted do not describe how the sense moved from darkening to “offend,” so no story is offered here.
en.oindre:
Inherited from Latin ~ungere~ (“to anoint, to smear with oil”). The verb first took the shape ~oinre~, and a d then slipped in between the n and the r, an epenthetic sound that eases the cluster, as in ~gendre~, ~moindre~, ~feindre~ and ~peindre~, which gave ~oindre~. Italian ~ungere~ and Spanish ~ungir~ continue the same Latin verb.

A learned family surrounds the verb. ~Onguent~ (“ointment”) comes from Latin ~unguentum~, the same source as English ~unguent~, and English ~ointment~ is a relative by way of Old French. ~Onction~ (“anointing”) comes from Latin ~ūnctiō~, and the participle survives as ~oint~, notably in ~l'oint du Seigneur~ (“the Lord's anointed”) and in ~extrême-onction~ (“last rites”). Today ~oindre~ itself is mostly religious or literary: it is the verb of ritual consecration with oil, or of smearing with an unguent.
en.oiseler:
~Oiseler~ comes from Middle French ~oiseler~, itself from Old French ~oiseler~, a derivative of Old French ~oisel~ (“bird”) with the verbal suffix ~-er~. Old French ~oisel~ descends from a Latin diminutive form, usually given as *~avicellus~, built on ~avis~ (“bird”) with the diminutive ending ~-cellus~. Italian ~uccello~ comes from the same Latin source, and Spanish ~ave~ comes straight from ~avis~.

The verb names an activity, hunting small birds, and its sense tracks its base closely. The modern noun ~oiseau~ is the later form of ~oisel~, and the verb kept the older shape. The family includes ~oiseleur~ (“bird-catcher”) and ~oisellerie~ (“bird trade”). Learned words built on the Latin root ~avis~ include ~aviaire~ and ~aviculture~, and ~avion~, which was coined from it in French. ~Oiseler~ itself is now rare and belongs to hunting vocabulary.
en.ombrager: Formed from the noun ~ombrage~ (“shade, foliage that casts shade”) and the verbal ending ~-er~: to cover with shade. The noun is either built from ~ombre~ plus the suffix ~-age~, or inherited from Old French ~ombrage~ and ultimately from Latin ~umbrāticus~ (“of the shade”); either way it rests on Latin ~umbra~ (“shade, shadow”). English ~umbrage~ is the same word, and shares the figurative sense of the noun: to take ~ombrage~ is to feel offended, as if a shadow had fallen across one's pride. The verb itself stays largely literal, to shade, and figuratively to cast a shadow over someone.
en.ombrer:
~Ombrer~ is given as ~ombre~ (“shade, shadow”) plus the verbal ending ~-er~, and French sources add that it is probably related to the Middle French verbs ~ombroier~, ~ombriier~ and ~ombroyer~. The sources therefore do not settle whether it was coined afresh from the noun or continues one of those older verbs. The noun ~ombre~ is inherited from Latin ~umbra~ (“shade, shadow”), which also gave Italian ~ombra~.

The meaning is the plain one: to give shade to something, and above all to shade a drawing or painting. The family is large because ~umbra~ was productive. In French it gave ~ombrage~ (“shade, foliage that casts it”), ~ombrageux~, ~ombrelle~ (“parasol”) and ~pénombre~ (“partial shade”), and English borrowed ~umbrella~ from the same Latin word through Italian, along with ~penumbra~. The verb itself stayed a modest, technical one beside these.
en.omettre:
Borrowed in Middle French from Latin ~omittere~ (“to let go, to leave out”) and refashioned on the French verb ~mettre~, which is why it ends like its relatives. The Latin verb is usually analysed as ~ob-~ plus ~mittere~ (“to send, to let go”), with the ~ob-~ reduced to ~o-~. English ~omit~ was taken from the same Latin verb, and the English noun ~mission~ and French ~mettre~ both come from ~mittere~ as well.

The literal picture is “to let something go by.” In Latin, ~omittere~ covered letting go of a plan, ignoring a point, or skipping over something in a speech, and French kept the sense of leaving out. Because it was reshaped on ~mettre~, ~omettre~ is conjugated like it (~j'omets~, ~omis~). It sits in a large family of ~-mettre~ verbs borrowed from Latin compounds of ~mittere~: ~admettre~, ~commettre~, ~permettre~, ~promettre~, ~soumettre~, along with ~omission~, the noun that preserves the Latin stem unchanged.
en.ondoyer:
From Old French ~ondoiier~. The two Wiktionaries give different routes. One explains it as a frequentative of Old French ~onder~, from Latin ~undāre~ (“to surge, to move in waves”). The other sees it as inherited from Vulgar Latin *~undizāre~, and adds that it can also be read as ~onde~ + ~-oyer~. Either way the source is the Latin noun ~unda~ (“wave”), which is also the root of French ~onde~.

The family is large. French ~onde~, ~ondée~ (“downpour”), ~onduler~, ~ondulation~, ~inonder~ and ~abonder~ (from Latin ~abundāre~, “to overflow”) all descend from ~unda~, and English ~undulate~, ~inundate~ and ~abound~ come from the same Latin family. The verb ~ondoyer~ means to sway or undulate like waves, as grain does in the wind. It also has a religious sense, to baptize in an emergency with water poured over the head, without the full ceremony.
en.onduler:
French ~onduler~ is a back-formation from ~ondulation~, not an inherited verb. The pair corresponds to Medieval or later Latin ~undulare~, built on Late Latin ~undula~ (“little wave”), a diminutive of Latin ~unda~ (“wave”). French ~onde~ is the descendant of ~unda~, so ~onduler~ is, at one remove, simply the verb of the wave.

The meaning followed the image. ~Onduler~ describes anything that moves or lies in a wavy line, such as hair, a field of wheat, a flag or a snake, and the related noun ~ondulation~ gives the same idea of gentle repeated rise and fall. The same Latin ~unda~ lies behind several French words that are not obviously waves: ~inonder~ (“to flood”), from Latin ~inundare~, ~abonder~ (“to abound”), from Latin ~abundare~, and ~ondine~ (“water nymph”). English borrowed from the same family: ~undulate~, ~inundate~, ~abound~ and ~redundant~.
en.opacifier: Formed from ~opaque~ with the suffix ~-ifier~, to make opaque. The suffix comes from Latin ~-ficāre~, which goes back to ~facere~ (“to make”). ~Opaque~ is borrowed from Latin ~opācus~ (“shaded, shady, dark”), a word of unknown origin and a doublet of ~ubac~, the shady side of a mountain.
en.opaliser: Formed from ~opale~ with the verbal suffix ~-iser~: to ~opaliser~ is to give a milky, iridescent look like that of an opal. The noun comes from Latin ~opalus~, borrowed from Greek ~ὀπάλλιος~ and, according to French Wiktionary, going back further to a Sanskrit word ~úpalah~ (“precious stone”). The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs.
en.opiner:
Borrowed from Latin ~opīnārī~ (“to be of the opinion, to suppose”), a deponent verb, one that is passive in form but active in sense. The noun ~opīniō~ belongs to the same family and gave French ~opinion~. English ~opine~ and Spanish ~opinar~ also go back to this Latin verb. French ~opiner~ kept the Latin sense: to give one's view on a matter under discussion, usually in a formal setting.

In modern French ~opiner~ is a formal, slightly old-fashioned verb meaning to give one's opinion, most often to express agreement. It survives in the set phrase ~opiner du bonnet~, “to nod in agreement,” while everyday vocabulary uses ~penser~ or ~estimer~ instead. The noun ~opinion~ is far more common than the verb. The family therefore shows a familiar pattern: a Latin verb lives on mostly through its noun.
en.opiniâtrer: ~Opiniâtrer~ is formed from the adjective ~opiniâtre~ (“stubborn”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, so it means to make someone stubborn and, in the pronominal form, to dig in one's heels over an opinion. The word is old: a pamphlet of 1576 speaks of people who ~s'oppiniastrent~ in an error of which they have long been convinced, and says that for this reason one must proceed against them by the sword. The verb is now literary, and mostly appears as ~s'opiniâtrer~ (“to persist stubbornly”).
en.opposer:
From Latin ~opponere~ (“to set against, to place opposite, to oppose”), refashioned in French after the verb ~poser~. ~opponere~ is a compound of the prefix ~ob-~ (“against, toward”) and ~ponere~ (“to put, to place”), whose past participle ~positus~ supplies the form ~oppositus~. The origin of ~ponere~ is debated — traditionally read as ~po-~ + ~sinere~ (“to set down, to let lie”) — so the deep root is best left open. Through ~opponere~ the verb is cognate with Italian ~opporre~, Spanish ~oponer~, and English ~oppose~ and ~opponent~.

The image inside ~opponere~ is spatial: to set one thing facing another, hence to set them against each other. French ~opposer~ kept this — to place in contrast, to set in conflict, to raise an objection. A neat detail is that French rebuilt the inherited verb on native ~poser~ rather than carrying the Latin stem intact, a common Old French habit that also reshaped ~composer~, ~déposer~, and ~exposer~. From the ~ob-~ + ~ponere~ family French keeps ~opposé~, ~opposition~, ~opposant~, and ~opposable~ (as in the opposable thumb) — a small constellation of confrontation all built on the simple idea of “placing toward.”
en.oppresser:
Borrowed from Latin ~oppressus~ (“overwhelmed, crushed”), with the French verb ending ~-er~. The Latin word is the past participle of ~opprimere~ (“to press down on, to crush”), made of ~ob-~ (“against, upon”) and ~premere~ (“to press”). The verb is therefore built on a participle, whereas its sibling ~opprimer~ was taken from the Latin infinitive. Two French verbs thus grew out of one Latin verb by different doors, and they ended up with different jobs.

In modern French ~oppresser~ is mostly physical: to weigh on the chest, to stifle, to make someone breathless, as when heat or anxiety does. ~Opprimer~ is the verb for tyranny and persecution. ~Oppression~ and ~oppresseur~ belong to the same family. The root ~premere~ also gave ~pression~, ~exprimer~, ~réprimer~ and ~presser~, so a thread of pressing runs through all of them.
en.opprimer: Borrowed from Latin ~opprimere~ (“to press down, crush”). The Latin verb is a compound of ~ob-~ (“against, upon”) and ~premere~ (“to press”). Related words include ~oppression~, ~oppresseur~, ~pression~, ~exprimer~ and ~réprimer~, all from ~premere~ or its compounds; Italian ~opprimere~ and English ~oppress~ come from the same Latin verb.
en.opter:
Borrowed from Latin ~optare~ (“to choose, to wish for”). ~Optare~ is a frequentative built on a lost verb *~opere~, surviving chiefly in its derivatives, and is connected to ~optio~ (“choice, free choice”) and to ~opinor~ (“to weigh, to suppose”). The same circle of ideas — choosing, seeing, preferring — links it loosely to Ancient Greek ~ὄψομαι~ (“I shall see”), so that to opt was, at root, to fix one's gaze on what one wants.

Latin ~optare~ meant both to wish and to choose, and that double sense survives faintly in French ~opter~, which has narrowed to the act of choosing between alternatives: ~opter pour~ (“to opt for, to plump for”) one option over another. It is a measured, almost administrative word — one ~opte~ for a tax regime or a nationality. The prefixed Latin ~adoptare~ (“to choose to oneself”) gave French ~adopter~, to take a person or an idea as one's own. The ~optare~ family runs through modern French in ~option~, ~optionnel~, ~optant~, ~adopter~, and ~cooptation~ — every one of them turning on the act of deliberate choice.
en.optimaliser: Formed from the adjective ~optimal~ with the verbal suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to make optimal”: to bring something to its best state. The adjective is built on ~optimum~, a form of Latin ~optimus~ (“best”). It is a synonym of ~optimiser~, which builds on the same idea.
en.optimiser:
A learned modern coinage. French ~optimiser~ (attested 1906) was modeled on English ~optimize~ (1844, “to make as good as possible”), itself built on Latin ~optimum~, the neuter of ~optimus~ (“best”), the irregular superlative of ~bonus~ (“good”). Latin ~optimus~ is generally connected to ~ops~ / ~opes~ (“wealth, resources, abundance”) — the “best” being, originally, the richest or most resourceful — and so to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₃ep-~ (“to work, to produce in abundance”), which also gives ~opus~ (“work”) and ~copia~ (“plenty”).

The word’s lineage is more philosophical than most: ~optimum~ entered learned use through Leibniz, who argued that ours is the “best of all possible worlds,” le meilleur des mondes possibles — the seed of ~optimisme~ (1737) and ~optimiste~. From the bare idea of the best, the verb ~optimiser~ generalized to “to make as good as possible,” and has since bred a small family of its own — ~optimisation~, ~optimiseur~, ~suroptimiser~ (“to over-optimize”), and the parallel ~optimaliser~ formed on ~optimal~. Through ~ops~ the same root also stands behind ~copieux~, ~opulent~, and ~œuvre~.
en.opérer:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~operārī~ (“to work, to labor, to be busy”), itself from the noun ~opus~ (“work, deed, accomplishment”). Latin ~opus~ goes back to a Proto-Indo-European root *~h₃ep-~ (“to work, to produce in abundance, ability”). It is the scholarly twin of the inherited French ~ouvrer~ and ~œuvrer~, which came down by oral transmission from the same ~operārī~ — a doublet, the bookish form beside the homegrown one. Italian ~operare~ and Spanish ~obrar~ are cognates; English ~operate~ and ~opera~ share the root.

From the plain sense “to work, to act,” ~opérer~ spread to specialized fields: a surgeon ~opère~ on a patient, a process ~opère~ a transformation, a change ~s'opère~ (“takes place”). The same ~opus~ family is everywhere in French: the inherited ~œuvre~ (“work, body of work”) and ~ouvrier~ (“worker”) on the popular side, and on the learned side ~opération~, ~opérateur~, ~opératoire~, ~coopérer~, and the borrowed Italian ~opéra~ (literally “a work”). Even ~opulence~ belongs here, through Latin ~ops~ (“wealth, resources”), kin to ~opus~: at the deepest level, work, abundance, and riches spring from one Indo-European idea of productive power.
en.oraliser: Formed from the adjective ~oral~ plus the suffix ~-iser~, in the sense of “to make oral”, to express something by mouth. The adjective ~oral~ is learned: it was built on Latin ~ōs~, ~ōris~ (“mouth”) with the adjectival suffix ~-al~, taken from Latin ~-ālis~. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, itself a transcription of Greek verbs, and it is still fully productive in technical and administrative French, where it turns adjectives and nouns into verbs meaning “make A”.
en.orbiter: ~Orbiter~ is a French verb made from the noun ~orbite~ and the ending ~-er~, with the sense “to move in an orbit.” The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin ~orbita~, which meant a rut left by a wheel and also the course of the stars, and which is related to ~orbe~. The word therefore moved from the track of a cart to the path of a heavenly body. The verb applies to satellites, planets and spacecraft that circle another body.
en.orchestrer: Formed in French from ~orchestre~ and the verb ending ~-er~, which turns a noun into a verb. The noun ~orchestre~ is a borrowing of Ancient Greek ~ὀρχήστρα~ (~orkhḗstra~), the space between the spectators and the stage where the chorus performed its movements. The word was feminine, like its Greek source, until the 18th century. The name of that space was later transferred to the musicians who played in it, and ~orchestrer~ means to arrange music for such an ensemble, and by extension to organize something, such as a campaign, with a conductor's control.
en.ordonnancer: Formed from the noun ~ordonnance~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, the sense being “to authorize”. ~Ordonnance~ is itself built from ~ordonner~ with the suffix ~-ance~, and in one of its senses the noun is also an ellipsis of the phrase ~officier d'ordonnance~. The verb ~ordonner~ belongs to the family of Latin ~ordō~ (“row, order”), so ~ordonnancer~ is, at several removes, a verb of putting things in order.
en.ordonner:
From Latin ~ordināre~ (“to set in order, to arrange, to dispose in rows”), from ~ordō~ (“row, rank, order”). In Old French ~ordināre~ first gave ~ordiner~ and ~ordener~, which by around 1200 had become ~ordonner~, probably reshaped under the influence of ~donner~ (“to give”), as in “donner des ordres.” ~Ordō~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~ordō~ and is plausibly tied to the PIE root *~h₂er-~ (“to fit together”), the same family as Latin ~artus~ (“joint”).

~Ordō~ first named a row of threads on a weaver's loom, so the abstract idea of “order” is woven, literally, from textile work. This double parentage — Latin order plus French ~donner~ — gave the verb its split modern range: to arrange or sort out things, and to command or prescribe (a doctor who ~ordonne~ a remedy issues an ~ordonnance~). From ~ordō~ / ~ordināre~ French keeps a broad family: ~ordre~, ~ordinaire~, ~ordonnance~, ~ordinateur~ (the “orderer” that became the computer), ~coordonner~, ~subordonner~, and ~désordre~.
en.organiser:
A sixteenth-century verb formed from the noun ~organe~ plus the suffix ~-iser~, but resting on a much older base: Medieval Latin ~organizare~ meant “to play a musical instrument,” whence the fourteenth-century Middle French ~organiser~, “to play the organ.” The noun ~organe~ goes back to Latin ~organum~, borrowed from Ancient Greek ~ὄργανον~ (~órganon~), “tool, instrument, organ of the body,” itself derived from ~ἔργον~ (~érgon~), “work,” from the Proto-Indo-European root *~werǵ-~ (“to do, work”). Through that root it is cognate with English ~work~ and with the Greek-derived ~energy~.

The semantic journey is striking: from a bodily ~organe~ — a part that does its appointed work — to the idea of furnishing a living being with coordinated working parts, and finally to arranging any set of elements into a functioning whole. By the seventeenth century ~organiser~ had shed its musical and purely biological senses for the general meaning “to structure, set in order,” and the modern sense of planning an event followed naturally. The same root and family yield ~organisme~, ~organisation~, ~organe~ itself, and indirectly ~énergie~. To organize, etymologically, is to give something organs — to make it work like a body.
en.organsiner: Formed from ~organsin~ (“organzine,” a silk thread twisted from several strands) with the verb ending ~-er~, so the verb means to twist silk into organzine. According to French Wiktionary, ~organsin~ comes from Italian ~organzino~, which in turn would come from Urgench, the city from which this silk was reputed to come; the page flags that claim as needing a source. The ending ~-er~ goes back to Latin ~-are~.
en.orienter:
A denominal verb (around 1485) built on the noun ~orient~ (“the East”), from Latin ~oriens~, the present participle of ~orīrī~ (“to rise, to arise”) — literally “the rising,” the quarter where the sun comes up. ~Orīrī~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~orjōr~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₃er-~ (“to stir, to rise”), shared with Ancient Greek ~ὄρνυμι~ (~órnūmi~, “to rouse, set in motion”) and Sanskrit ~ऋणोति~ (~ṛṇóti~).

The word's history is literally a matter of which way you turn. To ~orienter~ first meant to set a building — above all a church — facing ~east~, toward the rising sun and Jerusalem. From that act of physical alignment grew the figurative senses: to position something by the compass, then to ~guide~ a person, to steer choices and careers (~orientation~ scolaire). To lose that alignment is to ~désorienter~, “to disorient.” The same Latin verb yielded ~origine~ (a “rising,” a beginning), ~oriental~, and ~orientation~; English ~orient~, ~origin~, ~original~, and ~abort~ (etymologically “to fail to rise”) all spring from the same idea of rising into being.
en.originer: Formed in French from ~origine~ and the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense “to originate, to have as a source.” The noun ~origine~ is borrowed from Latin ~orīgō~, ~orīginis~ (“beginning, source, birth”), and it replaced an older popular form ~orine~, inherited from the same Latin word. The Latin noun belongs to ~orīrī~ (“to rise, to arise”), so an origin is literally a rising. The verb is rare compared with ~provenir~ and ~dériver~, which cover the same ground in everyday French.
en.ornementer: A denominal verb formed from the noun ~ornement~ with the ending ~-er~, meaning “to provide with ornaments.” The noun came through Middle French and Old French ~ornement~ from Latin ~ornāmentum~ (“equipment, decoration”). English Wiktionary notes that, within French, ~ornement~ can be read as ~orner~ plus ~-ment~. The verb ~orner~ (“to adorn”) descends from Latin ~ornāre~, so ~ornementer~ ends up as a longer, more specific cousin of ~orner~, which it shares a root with.
en.orner:
French ~orner~ comes from Latin ~ornare~ (“to equip, to fit out, to adorn”), present ~orno~. The verb is generally explained as a syncopated form of *~ordnō~, from ~ordo~ (“order, row, arrangement”), making it a doublet of ~ordinare~ (“to set in order”) — to adorn being, at bottom, to set things rightly in their array. ~Ordo~ in turn probably goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂er-~ (“to fit together, to join”), the same root behind Latin ~artus~ (“joint, limb”) and, through Greek, English ~art~ and ~harmony~.

If this account is right, the link between ornament and order is etymological, not just poetic: to ~orner~ is to arrange, to fit each element into a fitting whole. The military Romans first used ~ornare~ for equipping troops and outfitting ships before it settled into “to decorate.” From the same verb French has ~ornement~, ~ornemental~, the past participle ~orné~, and ornière is unrelated despite appearances. The deeper root *~h₂er-~ also feeds ~ordre~, ~ordinaire~, ~art~, and ~harmonie~ — a family in which decoration and right arrangement were never far apart.
en.orthographier: Formed from the noun ~orthographie~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so that it means “to write a word in a given spelling.” The noun comes through Latin ~orthographia~ from Hellenistic Greek ~ὀρθογραφία~ (~orthographía~), which combines ~ὀρθός~ (~orthós~, “correct”) and ~γράφω~ (~gráphō~, “to write”). The verb thus carries the old idea of “writing correctly” inside it, even though in everyday French it simply means “to spell,” right or wrong.
en.osciller: Borrowed from Late Latin ~oscillāre~ (“to swing”), a verb formed on Latin ~oscillum~ (“swing”). English Wiktionary gives the source simply as Latin ~oscillāre~. The verb passed into French as a learned word, and the family also supplied English ~oscillate~ and ~oscillation~, along with French ~oscillation~ and ~oscillateur~. The French verb keeps the physical sense of a swinging back and forth and also extends it to hesitation between two choices, which fits the Latin picture of a swing.
en.oser:
From Late Latin ~ausāre~, a verb built on ~ausus~, the past participle of Classical Latin ~audēre~ (“to dare, to be bold”). The classical verb was itself a stative formed on the adjective ~avidus~ (“eager, greedy”), so that to dare was, at root, to be hungry for something. The reconstructed deeper source is a Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂weh₁-~ (“to be eager, to desire”). Italian ~osare~, Spanish ~osar~, and Portuguese ~ousar~ are direct Romance cognates.

Late Latin reshaped the irregular ~audēre~ into the regular ~ausāre~, and from this came Old French ~oser~, unchanged in form to this day. The meaning has held firm: ~oser~ is to venture, to have the audacity to act or speak. Because the classical adjective family survived alongside it through learned borrowing, French keeps a striking split: the everyday ~oser~ next to the bookish ~audace~ (“audacity”), ~audacieux~ (“audacious”), and ~avide~ (“eager, avid”) — all ultimately the same Latin nest. Modern French derivatives of ~oser~ include the adjective ~osé~ (“daring, risqué”), the agent noun ~oseur~, and the rare ~réoser~ (“to dare again”). English ~audacious~ reaches the same root by the learned path, through ~audāx~.
en.ossifier: Formed from ~os~ (“bone”) with the suffix ~-ifier~, on the model of verbs such as ~nidifier~. The suffix goes back to Latin ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”), so ~ossifier~ is “to make into bone,” and in its reflexive use, to turn into bone. The noun ~os~ comes from Latin ~os~, ~ossis~ (“bone”). English ~ossify~ is the same formation.
en.ouater: Formed from ~ouate~ (“cotton wadding”) plus the verbal suffix ~-er~, meaning to line or pad with wadding. The origin of ~ouate~ is obscure. Proposals include a link to Italian ~ovatta~, which is rejected because the Italian word is later, and a form of ~ouette~ (“gosling”) for goose down. Another explanation is that Old French ~l'aoite~ (“addition, lining”) was reanalyzed as ~la oite~. An Arabic source is thought difficult.
en.ouatiner: Formed from ~ouatine~ with the verb ending ~-er~. ~Ouatine~ is a quilted, wadded fabric, itself derived from ~ouate~ (“wadding”). The verb means “to quilt,” that is, to pad a garment or lining with ~ouatine~. The chain is thus ~ouate~, ~ouatine~, ~ouatiner~, each step adding a suffix.
en.oublier:
From Old French ~oblier~, ~oublier~ (attested early as ~oblider~, around 980), from Vulgar Latin *~oblītāre~, a verb built in Gaul and Iberia on ~oblītus~, the past participle of Latin ~oblīvīscī~ (“to forget”). Classical Latin had no simple successor that survived into Romance, so the Romance languages reached for the participle ~oblītus~ and forged a fresh verb upon it — a common workaround. The same *~oblītāre~ gives Italian ~obliare~ and the poetic ~oblio~, Spanish ~olvidar~, and Portuguese ~olvidar~, and the learned doublet ~oubli~ / English ~oblivion~ preserves the Latin form more visibly.

The Latin ~oblīvīscī~ is often connected to ~lēvis~ (“smooth”), as though to forget were to let a memory be rubbed smooth, wiped from the surface of the mind — a vivid image whether or not the link is certain. Old French ~oblier~ softened its first vowel under the influence of rounding to become ~oublier~, the modern shape. Alongside the everyday verb the language kept the more literary ~oubli~ (“forgetfulness, oblivion”) and the learned borrowing ~oblitérer~ (“to obliterate, to cancel”), which returns directly to the same Latin root for its sense of effacement.
en.ouiller: From Old French ~ouillier~, derived from ~œil~ (“eye”), which descends from Latin ~oculus~. The modern verb ~ouiller~ is a term of the wine trade, “to top up a barrel.” It is thus a French derivation, not a borrowing from Latin. The same Latin ~oculus~ lies behind French ~oculaire~ (“of the eye”) and English ~ocular~.
en.ourdir: ~Ourdir~ descends from Old French ~ordir~, itself from Latin ~ōrdīre~, a parallel form of the classical verb ~ōrdīrī~. The classical verb meant “to lay a warp, to weave one's web” (said of a spider) and, figuratively, “to begin, to undertake something.” In French the weaving sense lived on as a technical term. To ~ourdir~ is to prepare the warp, laying out the lengthwise threads before weaving. Its figurative sense, “to plot, to hatch a scheme,” is the other major use, in phrases like ~ourdir un complot~. The trade gave French the noun ~ourdissage~ for the warping operation. The Latin verb survives elsewhere in learned words: ~exorde~, the opening of a speech, comes from Latin ~exōrdium~ (“beginning”), from ~exōrdīrī~, which is ~ex-~ plus ~ōrdīrī~.
en.ourler: ~Ourler~ (formerly ~orler~) is usually explained as a verb made from the noun ~orle~ (“edge, border”) plus ~-er~; one source instead treats it as inherited from a Vulgar Latin verb *~orulāre~. Either way the root is the same. ~Orle~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~ōrula~, a diminutive of Latin ~ōra~ (“edge”), which also gave ~ourlet~. Italian ~orlare~ and Spanish ~orlar~ are comparable verbs. To ~ourler~ is to finish the edge of a piece of cloth by folding it over and stitching it, and the verb is the everyday word for making a hem.
en.outiller: Formed from ~outil~ (“tool”) with the verb ending ~-er~: to equip with tools. The noun comes from Middle French ~outil~, from Old French ~ustilz~ (“equipment, things taken along for a journey”), first attested in 1174 in the sense of a made object used for work. Its Latin source is ~ūtēnsilia~ (“necessary objects, utensils”), derived from ~ūtī~ (“to use”), also the source of French ~ustensile~.
en.outrager: Formed from the noun ~outrage~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so “to commit an outrage against, to offend greatly.” The noun is inherited from Old French ~oltrage~. French Wiktionary analyzes it as ~outrer~ + ~-age~, an “act of going beyond,” from Latin *~ultratĭcum~, from ~ultra~ (“beyond”), so an outrage is a going too far.
en.outrepasser: A compound of ~outre~ (“beyond”) and ~passer~, literally “to pass beyond,” hence “to exceed, to overstep.” The same pair appears in the reversed phrase ~passer outre~, and Italian has the parallels ~oltrepassare~ and ~passare oltre~. ~Outre~, an adverb and preposition, is inherited from Old French ~oltre~ and Latin ~ultra~, the source also of Italian ~oltre~ and, as a learned doublet, of the prefix ~ultra-~.
en.outrer: ~Outrer~ is built on ~outre~ with the verb ending ~-er~, and it means “to exaggerate” and “to outrage”. The adverb and preposition ~outre~ (“beyond”) descends from Latin ~ultra~ through Old French ~oltre~, and it was also an adverb in Old and Middle French. It is a doublet of the learned prefix ~ultra-~ and a cognate of Italian ~oltre~. The sources list a second French ~outre~, borrowed from Latin ~uter~, but the one from ~ultra~ is the one that fits the sense of the verb.
en.ouvrer:
From Latin ~operārī~ (“to work, labor, be busy”), a verb built on ~opus~, genitive ~operis~ (“work, deed, labor”). The Latin noun descends from Proto-Italic *~opos~ and Proto-Indo-European *~h₃ep-os~ (“work”), from the verbal root *~h₃ep-~ (“to work, produce”), cognate with Sanskrit ~ápas~ (“work”) and underlying English ~opulent~ and ~opus~. The inherited French verb ~ouvrer~ thus means simply “to work,” and it is the popular doublet of the learned borrowing ~opérer~ (“to operate”).

~ouvrer~ was once an everyday verb but has largely faded, partly because its conjugated forms collided with those of ~ouvrir~ (“to open”); to avoid the confusion it was often refashioned as ~œuvrer~ (“to work, labor at”). The root nonetheless seeded a large French family: the agent noun ~ouvrier~ (“worker”), the adjective ~ouvrable~ (as in ~jour ouvrable~, “working day”), ~œuvre~ (“work, creation”), ~chef-d'œuvre~ (“masterpiece”), and ~main-d'œuvre~ (“labor, workforce”). Through the learned branch come ~opérer~, ~opération~, and ~coopérer~. A single PIE notion of “doing work” thus spans the laborer’s working day and the artist’s finished masterpiece.
en.ouvrir:
French ~ouvrir~ (attested near 980 in the form ~obrirent~, “they opened”) comes from Latin ~aperīre~ (“to open”), by way of a Vulgar Latin *~operīre~. The vowel change from ~a-~ to ~o-~ was no accident: spoken Latin remodeled ~aperīre~ on its antonym ~cooperīre~ (“to cover up,” source of French ~couvrir~), so that the verb for opening and the verb for covering came to rhyme. Latin ~aperīre~ itself is generally traced to a prefix *~ap-~ (“off, away”) plus a root meaning “to cover,” the whole literally “to un-cover.” Through the Romance line it is cognate with Italian ~aprire~ and Spanish ~abrir~, the everyday words for “to open.”

The paired remodeling of ~ouvrir~ and ~couvrir~ is a tidy case of two opposites pulled into the same shape by their very oppositeness — to this day they conjugate alike. The basic sense “to open” has stayed remarkably stable across two millennia, branching into figurative uses (to open a debate, a heart, a road). From ~ouvrir~ French derives ~ouverture~ (“opening, overture”), ~ouvert~ (“open”), and ~ouvre-boîte~ (“can-opener”); the learned Latin stem reappears in ~apéritif~ (a drink that “opens” the appetite), while ~apertura~ lives on in the technical ~aperture~ shared with English.
en.ouïr:
From Middle French ~ouïr~, from Old French ~oïr~, “to hear,” from Latin ~audīre~ (“to hear, to listen”), the present infinitive of ~audio~, from PIE *~au-~ (“to perceive”). Cognate with Italian ~udire~ and Spanish ~oír~, both of which remain the everyday verbs for hearing in their languages — unlike their French sibling, which lost that office. In French the ground was taken over by ~entendre~ (originally “to direct one's attention toward”), which slid from “to attend to” into plain “to hear.”

As ~entendre~ expanded, ~ouïr~ contracted into a defective relic, fossilized in a handful of set phrases: ~ouï-dire~ (“hearsay,” literally “heard-say”), the herald's archaic cry ~oyez~ (“hear ye!”), still echoed in courtrooms, and the perfect ~j'ai ouï dire~ (“I have heard tell”). The adjective ~inouï~ (“unheard-of, extraordinary”) preserves the old participle, and the related noun ~ouïe~ now names the very sense of hearing. The Latin root remains hugely productive in French through later borrowings: ~audience~, ~auditeur~, and the modern ~audio~. Even ~obéir~ belongs here — from Latin ~oboedīre~ (~ob-~ + ~audīre~), literally “to lend one's ear to,” so that to obey is, at root, to listen.
en.ovationner: Formed from the noun ~ovation~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, giving the sense “to acclaim with an ovation, to cheer.” The noun ~ovation~ was borrowed from Latin ~ovātiō~, a word that the Romans used for a lesser form of triumph. The suffix ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is the ordinary way French makes verbs from nouns, here in the sense “to give N.” So ~ovationner~ means to give someone an ~ovation~: to greet a speaker, a performer or a champion with sustained, enthusiastic applause.
en.ovuler: ~Ovuler~ is a denominal verb: ~ovule~ plus ~-er~, meaning to release an egg cell from the ovary. The base ~ovule~ comes from Latin ~ovum~ (“egg”) with the diminutive suffix ~-ule~, so an ~ovule~ is literally a “little egg.” The ending ~-er~ is the default way French builds a verb on a noun. The related ~ovulation~ names the event, and the Latin ~ovum~ also gave the learned ~ovaire~ and the adjective ~ovale~, while the everyday ~œuf~ is its inherited form.
en.oxyder: Formed from ~oxyde~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, in the sense “to combine with oxygen”. The noun has two accounts. French Wiktionary derives it from Ancient Greek ~ὀξύς~ (~oxús~, “sharp, acid”) plus ~-ide~, as coined by Guyton de Morveau in the chemical nomenclature, with the spelling ~oxyde~ settled in 1801. English Wiktionary calls it a blend of ~oxygène~ and ~acide~, coined by Guyton de Morveau and Lavoisier. Both lead back to the Greek ~oxús~.
en.oxygéner: ~Oxygéner~ is a denominal formed on ~oxygène~ with the verb suffix ~-er~. The noun was built from Greek ~ὀξύς~ (“sharp, sour, acid”) and ~γένος~ (“birth, origin”). Antoine Lavoisier coined it in 1778, on the mistaken belief that this gas was a constituent of all acids, so the name means “acid-producer”. The modern ending ~-gène~ was introduced by Fourcroy in 1786, and the noun form by Guyton de Morveau in 1787. The gas itself was discovered by Joseph Priestley in 1774.
en.ozoniser: ~Ozoniser~ is formed from the noun ~ozone~ with the suffix ~-iser~, meaning to treat with ozone or convert into it. The noun ~ozone~ was borrowed from German ~Ozon~, built on the present participle of Greek ~ózō~ (“to give off a smell”), a name inspired by the gas's sharp odor. The verb is thus a scientific coinage: a Greek verb of smelling, passed through German and turned into French by a standard suffix.
en.pacager: A denominal verb formed from ~pacage~ (“pasturage”) with the suffix ~-er~: to graze. The noun ~pacage~ comes from Late Latin *~pascuaticum~, an unattested form built on Latin ~pascere~ (“to feed, to graze”). The same Latin verb gave French ~paître~, the older and more familiar verb for grazing, so ~pacager~ and ~paître~ are two descendants of one root.
en.pacifier:
French ~pacifier~ comes from Latin ~pācificāre~ (“to make peace”), itself built on ~pāx~ (“peace”). The Latin verb joins ~pāx~ to the verbal element of ~facere~ (“to make, to do”), so its literal sense is “to make peace.” The same Latin word survives in the Romance languages as Italian ~pace~ and Spanish ~paz~, and English took it twice: as ~peace~ by way of Old French, and as ~pacify~ from the Latin verb through French.

The meaning of the French verb stayed close to its source: to bring peace to a region, a conflict or a troubled person. The noun ~pāx~ has given French a whole family of words, among them ~paix~ (“peace”), ~pacifique~ (“peaceful”), ~paisible~ (“quiet, calm”) and ~apaiser~ (“to calm”). Seen this way, ~pacifier~ is the learned, Latin-shaped cousin of ~apaiser~, which took the popular route through Old French.
en.pacquer: ~Pacquer~ means to pack salted fish in layers in a barrel for transport, and the TLFi attests it in 1423 as ~packer~. It is derived from Middle French ~pacque~ (“pack, bundle”; compare ~paquet~) with the verbal ending ~-er~. Earlier Anglo-Norman ~enpaker~ (1294) and medieval Latin ~impaccare~ and ~paccare~, all in English-ruled territory, are probably derived from words borrowed from English ~pack~, which in turn the TLFi traces to the Dutch word behind ~pacque~. The verb thus belongs to the North Sea herring and cod trade, whose vocabulary travelled between Dutch, English and French.
en.pacser: Formed from ~PACS~ with the first-conjugation ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~. ~PACS~ is an acronym for ~pacte civil de solidarité~ (“civil solidarity pact”), the French civil partnership. The verb turns the name of the institution into an action, “to enter into a PACS,” and is a good example of an acronym absorbed into the regular conjugation.
en.pactiser: ~Pactiser~ is formed from ~pacte~ plus the suffix ~-iser~, which here gives the sense “to make a pact.” ~Pacte~ was borrowed in Middle French (fourteenth century) from Latin ~pactum~ (“agreement, treaty, contract”). French Wiktionary links ~pactum~ to the word for peace: it is the past participle of ~paciscor~, a verb glossed as “to make peace.” The verb has long carried a figurative sense too, to come to terms with something unpleasant, as in ~pactiser avec le diable~ or ~pactiser avec sa conscience~.
en.paganiser:
Borrowed from Late Latin ~paganizāre~, attested in the fourth century with the sense “to take part in pagan rites.” The Latin verb was formed on ~pāgānus~ with the Greek-derived verbal suffix ~-izāre~, the ancestor of French ~-iser~. In later Latin the verb broadened to mean “to profess paganism, to live as a pagan.” French Wiktionary points to ~judaïser~ as a parallel formation.

Latin ~pāgānus~ meant “of the village, rustic” and was derived from ~pāgus~ (“district, village”). It came to mean “civilian” and then, in the Christian West, “non-Christian,” which is how the same word gave French ~païen~ and, by learned borrowing, ~paganisme~. English has ~pagan~ from the same source. Unlike ~païen~, which evolved in everyday speech, ~paganiser~ was borrowed whole from Latin.
en.pagayer: Formed in French from ~pagaie~ (“paddle”) and the ending ~-er~, “to paddle.” The noun was borrowed, according to French Wiktionary, from Malay ~pengayuh~; English Wiktionary adds that it came through Dutch ~pagaai~, and that the Malay word derives from ~kayuh~. French Wiktionary cites its first attestation in Alexandre de Chaumont's account of the embassy to the court of Siam.
en.paginer: ~Paginer~ (“to paginate”) is a learned derivative of Latin ~pagina~ (“page”) with the French verb ending ~-er~, according to French Wiktionary. It means to number the pages of a book or document, and so to lay it out in pages. The same Latin word gave French ~page~ and English ~page~. The ending ~-er~ comes from the Latin first-conjugation ending ~-are~.
en.pagnoter: Formed from the noun ~pagnot~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, hence the slang sense “to go to bed.” ~Pagnot~ is itself derived from ~pagne~, a word for “bed,” with the suffix ~-ot~; a variant ~pagnote~ has the same sense. The verb thus means, in effect, to head for one's pagnot. The ending ~-er~ is the usual French way of coining a verb from a noun.
en.paillassonner: A French formation from the noun ~paillasson~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is itself derived from ~paillasse~ with the suffix ~-on~, so the verb sits at the end of a short chain. Because ~paillasson~ names a mat of straw, ~paillassonner~ means “to cover with straw mats,” the denominal sense “to provide with N.” The ending ~-er~ comes from the Latin ending ~-are~.
en.pailler: ~Pailler~ is a verb made from the noun ~paille~ (“straw”) with the verb ending ~-er~: to cover or fill with straw. The noun is inherited from Old French ~paille~, from Latin ~palea~ (“straw, chaff”), which English Wiktionary traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~pel-~ (“flour, dust”). The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-āre~, the infinitive ending of the first conjugation.
en.pailleter: ~Pailleter~ is formed from the noun ~paillette~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun is itself a derivative of ~paille~ (“straw”) with the diminutive suffix ~-ette~, so a ~paillette~ is, etymologically, a little straw, and the word came to name a spangle or small shiny flake. The verb means to decorate or strew something with such spangles, in English to bespangle.
en.palabrer: Formed from the noun ~palabre~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, “to hold a long, endless discussion.” The noun ~palabre~ was borrowed from Spanish ~palabra~ (“word”), which comes from Latin ~parabola~. English Wiktionary adds that ~palabre~ is a doublet of ~parole~ and ~parabole~, the other two French descendants of that Latin word.
en.palanquer: Formed from ~palan~ (“hoist, tackle”) with the verb ending ~-er~: ~palanquer~ is “to lift with a hoist.” The noun was borrowed from Italian ~palanco~, a variant of ~paranco~. English Wiktionary traces that Italian word to Vulgar Latin ~palanca~, an alteration of Latin ~phalanga~. English Wiktionary also points to the related French ~planche~ and ~palanque~.
en.palataliser: ~Palataliser~ is formed from the adjective ~palatal~ with the suffix ~-iser~, meaning to make a sound palatal, that is, to pronounce it with the tongue raised toward the hard palate. The base ~palatal~ comes from Latin ~palatum~ (“palate”). The suffix ~-iser~, from Late Latin and Greek roots, is the standard way French builds verbs meaning “to make A” or “to convert into N,” and it is fully productive in technical vocabulary like linguistics.
en.palettiser: Formed in French from the noun ~palette~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which builds verbs meaning “to turn into, to treat with, to equip with.” Here the noun is the loading platform, so ~palettiser~ means to stack goods on a pallet. The noun ~palette~ was itself built in French, in the late 18th century, from ~pale~ with the diminutive suffix ~-ette~. The suffix ~-iser~ reached French from Late Latin ~-izāre~, a transcription of Greek verb endings, and became productive in French in the sixteenth century.
en.palissader: Formed from ~palissade~ with the verb ending ~-er~: to fence or fortify with a palisade. ~Palissade~ is either derived from ~palis~ (“stake”) with the suffix ~-ade~, or borrowed from Old Occitan ~palissada~; both ultimately go back to a derivative of Latin ~palus~.
en.palisser: Formed from ~palis~ (“fence of stakes, trellis”) plus the verbal ending ~-er~ (from Latin ~-are~), so “to fasten onto a trellis,” as is done with fruit trees and vines. The noun ~palis~ derives from Old French ~pel~ (“stake”), the word that gave modern ~pal~.
en.palissonner: A denominal verb made from the noun ~palisson~ with the ending ~-er~. The noun ~palisson~ is itself derived from ~pal~, the old word for a stake. ~Palissonner~ is a technical verb meaning “to stake,” that is, to work something with stakes. The ending ~-er~ goes back to the Latin first-conjugation ending ~-are~.
en.pallier:
Borrowed from Late Latin ~palliāre~ (“to cover with a cloak”), a verb formed on Latin ~pallium~ (“cloak, mantle”), a rectangular Greek-style cloak. Italian ~palliare~ and Spanish ~paliar~ are relatives. The same Latin noun gave English ~pall~ (a cloth thrown over a coffin) and the ecclesiastical ~pallium~, a woolen band worn by archbishops.

The literal sense, “to cloak,” is usually thought to have moved to the figurative “to cover up, to disguise” a fault or a wrong, and from there to treating something only on the surface, hiding a problem without curing it. The step is easy to imagine, but the sources do not trace or date it. Modern French ~pallier~ means “to make up for, to compensate for, to remedy,” as in ~pallier un manque~ (“to make up for a shortage”). The medical adjective ~palliatif~ (“that eases symptoms without curing”) and the English ~palliative~ belong to the same family.
en.palper: ~Palper~ (“to palpate, to feel with the hands”) is a learned borrowing from Latin ~palpāre~ (“to touch gently, to stroke”), according to English Wiktionary. It is used literally for examining by touch, as a doctor does, and colloquially for receiving money. The same Latin verb underlies the family of ~palpable~ and ~palpation~ in French, and of ~palpable~ and ~palpate~ in English.
en.palpiter: ~Palpiter~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~palpitāre~ (“to throb, to tremble”), a verb generally analyzed as a frequentative of ~palpāre~ (“to touch gently, to stroke”). It reached French through the written, scholarly route rather than by the slow sound changes of popular speech, which is why it kept the Latin shape almost intact. In modern French it describes a heart that beats fast, and it can also mean to jump around. English ~palpitate~ is a separate borrowing of the same Latin verb, and English ~palpable~ comes from ~palpāre~.
en.panacher: ~Panacher~ is formed from the noun ~panache~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun is a loan from Italian ~pennacchio~ (“bunch of feathers on a helmet”), reached through Middle French ~pennache~, and the Italian word goes back to Late Latin ~pinnāculum~. It is a doublet of ~pinacle~, which came into French by a different route. The verb first meant to decorate with a plume, and its later senses of mixing colors and then of mixing things in general (a ~panaché~ can be a mixture of beer and lemonade) extend from the idea of variegated feathers.
en.paner: ~Paner~ is formed from ~pain~ and the verb ending ~-er~, in the sense of coating food in breadcrumbs. ~Pain~ comes through Middle and Old French from Latin ~panem~, the accusative of ~panis~ (“bread”). The ending ~-er~ goes back to the Latin first-conjugation ending ~-are~ and here turns a noun into a verb: roughly, “to provide with bread.”
en.panifier:
French ~panifier~ was borrowed from Medieval Latin ~panificāre~ (“to make bread”). English Wiktionary notes that it is not found as such in Old or Middle French, though Old French ~panegier~ is comparable. The Latin verb is built from ~pānis~ (“bread”) and the element ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”), the same pattern as ~clarifier~ or ~purifier~. Italian ~panificare~ and Spanish ~panificar~ are parallel formations.

The verb means to turn flour into bread, and it has stayed a technical word of bakers and food scientists, notably in ~panification~ (“bread-making”) and ~panifiable~ (“fit for bread”: of a cereal, one whose flour can make a loaf). Its root ~pānis~ is the ancestor of ~pain~ and of a large family: ~panier~, originally a bread basket, ~panetier~, an officer in charge of bread, ~panade~, and ~compagnon~, literally someone with whom one shares bread.
en.paniquer: ~Paniquer~ is formed from the noun ~panique~ and the verb ending ~-er~, meaning to be seized by sudden fear. The noun was first an adjective, from Middle French ~panique~, a learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ~panikós~ (“of Pan”). The god Pan was believed to be the source of mysterious sounds that caused contagious, groundless fear in herds, in crowds and in people in lonely places. French Wiktionary adds that the phrase ~peur panique~ (“panic fear”) was shortened to the noun ~panique~.
en.panneauter: Formed from ~panneau~ with the verb ending ~-er~, and also described as a respelling of ~panoter~. The noun ~panneau~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~pannellus~, from Latin ~pannus~ (“piece of cloth”), through Old French ~pannel~ and ~peniau~. It first meant a piece of cloth, including a stretched net, which explains the hunting sense of ~panneauter~, “to set nets for small game.” The same Old French word gave English ~panel~, a doublet of ~panneau~.
en.panoramiquer: ~Panoramiquer~ is a verb made from the adjective ~panoramique~ and the verb ending ~-er~, in the sense of taking a panoramic shot. French Wiktionary derives the adjective from ~panorama~ with the suffix ~-ique~, and ~panorama~ itself was assembled from Greek parts, ~pan-~ (“all”) and ~horama~ (“view”). The ending ~-er~ is the ordinary way French turns a noun or adjective into a first-conjugation verb, as in ~filtrer~ or ~téléphoner~. The result is a modern coinage, a verb named after the sweeping view it produces.
en.panosser: Formed from the noun ~panosse~ (“floor cloth”) by adding the verb ending ~-er~. ~Panosser~ means “to mop the floor,” that is, to go over it with a ~panosse~. Verbs made straight from a tool or object noun in this way name the action done with that object. The sources give no earlier origin for ~panosse~ itself, so the story stops at that noun rather than guessing at a deeper source.
en.panser: ~Panser~ is a doublet of ~penser~ (“to think”): the two were long spelled the same way, and ~panser~ is the specialized form. Its sense of “to take care of, to tend” derives from ~penser à~ and ~penser de~. The spelling ~panser~ was fixed in the seventeenth century. The verb now covers dressing a wound and grooming a horse.
en.panteler: ~Panteler~ comes from Old French ~pantoiser~, which also gave the adjective ~pantois~, but the verb was refashioned with the suffix ~-eler~, which was more common in French. That suffix, little productive today, often carried a frequentative or diminutive nuance, a small action repeated, and it has been supplanted by ~-iller~. The modern verb means “to pant”, to breathe in short, quick gasps.
en.pantoufler: ~Pantoufler~ is built on ~pantoufle~ (“slipper”) with the verb ending ~-er~, and means to leave the civil service for the private sector. The sense comes from École polytechnique slang, where the ~pantoufle~ was the sum to be repaid by a graduate who broke the ten-year commitment to public service. Quite often it was the hiring company that paid it. The noun ~pantoufle~ has an uncertain origin: it may be a formation with a suffix ~-oufle~ on ~pan~ (“piece of cloth”), or, as English Wiktionary notes, a borrowing from Italian ~pantofola~.
en.papillonner: Formed from the noun ~papillon~ (“butterfly”) plus the verb ending ~-er~, meaning to flit like a butterfly. French Wiktionary notes the image: a butterfly goes from flower to flower without attachment, and so does a person who flits from one thing or person to another. The noun comes from Latin ~papiliōnem~, the accusative of ~papiliō~. In Old French it appears as ~papeillon~, a variant of ~paveillon~, which survives as the doublet ~pavillon~ (“pavilion”), a tent being likened to a butterfly's wings.
en.papilloter: Formed on the noun ~papillote~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, in the manner of the frequentative suffix ~-oter~ (as in ~chevroter~), which suggests small, repeated movements: to blink, flutter or flicker. The noun is the feminine of Old French ~papillot~ (“spangle, little butterfly”), related to ~papillon~ (“butterfly”), the glittering spangles being compared to shimmering wings. English Wiktionary instead derives the verb directly from ~papillon~ with ~-oter~, but either way the butterfly is behind it.
en.papoter: ~Papoter~ is built with the suffix ~-oter~ on Old French ~papier~ (“to mutter”), related to ~papeter~ (“to babble”). English Wiktionary traces the root to an imitative sound ~papp-~, tied to the movement of the lips and also found in Latin ~pappare~ (“to eat”). French ~papelard~ belongs to the same family.
en.parachever: ~Parachever~ is formed from the prefix ~par-~ and ~achever~. The prefix is inherited from Latin ~per-~ (“through, thoroughly”) and adds the idea of carrying something through to its end, so the verb means to complete or bring to perfection; it is a literary word. The base ~achever~ is an Old French verb built on ~chief~ (“head, end”), from Latin ~caput~ (“head”), in the phrase ~venir a chief~, “to come to an end.” English ~achieve~ is a borrowing of the same verb.
en.parachuter: Formed from the noun ~parachute~ and the verb ending ~-er~, which turns a noun into a verb: to use a parachute, hence to drop by parachute. The noun is itself a compound of the prefix ~para-~, meaning protection against, and ~chute~ (“fall”), so a parachute is literally a device that protects against a fall. The verb simply applies the familiar pattern of ~-er~, the ending inherited from Latin ~-are~ and still the default for coining new French verbs.
en.parader: ~Parader~ is a denominal verb formed on the noun ~parade~ with the ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary relates ~parade~ to ~parer~, while English Wiktionary says ~parade~ comes from Spanish ~parada~. The verb means “to strut, to show off,” the sense of putting oneself on display as in a military or ceremonial march.
en.parafer: Formed from the noun ~parafe~ (“initials, flourish of a signature”) with the verb ending ~-er~; French Wiktionary calls it a denominal. The verb means “to initial a document” or “to sign it,” that is, to mark it with a ~parafe~. The noun has the variant spelling ~paraphe~, and the verb likewise has the longer form ~parapher~.
en.paraffiner: Formed in French from the noun ~paraffine~ and the verb ending ~-er~: to coat or impregnate with paraffin. The noun comes from German ~Paraffin~, a word coined in 1830 by the chemist Karl von Reichenbach from Latin ~parum affinis~ (“of little affinity”), because the substance reacts so little with other chemicals. The verb is thus a modern technical derivation, sitting at the end of a chain that starts with two ordinary Latin words.
en.paralyser: Formed from the noun ~paralysie~ with the suffix ~-iser~, which here means “to cause to suffer N”, with the ending of the noun reshaped. The noun ~paralysie~ was borrowed from Latin ~paralysis~ (“palsy”), from Ancient Greek ~παράλυσις~ (“loosening”). The Greek word is built on the idea of a body or limb loosened and unstrung, so to ~paralyser~ is to strike with palsy, and figuratively to bring a person, a city or a process to a standstill.
en.paramétrer: Formed from ~paramètre~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so it means to set the parameters of something, as in configuring software. The noun ~paramètre~ is itself built on the Greek elements ~παρά~ (“beside”) and ~μέτρον~ (“measure”). The verb is a modern, technical coinage, and its transparent derivation is typical of how French turns a learned noun into an action.
en.parangonner: Formed from the noun ~parangon~ (“model, comparison”) with the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun was borrowed from Spanish ~parangón~ (“comparison”), which in turn comes from Italian ~paragonare~. The verb means to compare, to hold one thing up against another as a standard. English ~paragon~ has the same Romance origin.
en.parapher: Formed from ~paraphe~ (“flourish, initials”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so “to put one's ~paraphe~ on” a page. ~Paraphe~ is a medieval corruption of ~paragraphe~, according to French Wiktionary. English Wiktionary offers two routes: either a shortening of ~paragraphe~, or a borrowing from Medieval Latin ~paraphus~, itself a shortened form of Latin ~paragraphus~. Either way, the root is the ~paragraph~ of Greek-derived Latin, once the mark that set off a passage.
en.paraphraser: Formed from ~paraphrase~ and the verb ending ~-er~: to ~paraphraser~ is to restate in other words. The noun comes from Latin ~paraphrasis~, and French Wiktionary points to the Ancient Greek verb ~paraphrázô~ (“to paraphrase, to say otherwise”). The ending ~-er~ descends from Latin ~-are~.
en.parasiter: French ~parasiter~ comes from Latin ~parasitārī~, itself from Ancient Greek ~parasitéō~ (“to eat beside, to eat at someone's place”). The Greek verb is formed on ~sîtos~ (“food”) with the prefix ~para-~ (“beside”), a standard analysis. The same Greek stem produced the noun ~parasitos~, a person who dines at another's expense, from which French ~parasite~ and English ~parasite~ descend. In French, ~parasiter~ keeps the idea of living off another: a biological parasite lives on its host and, figuratively, a person or a noise can ~parasiter~ a conversation, a signal or a process.
en.paraître:
From Middle French ~paroistre~, from Old French ~paroistre~, ~pareistre~, from Vulgar Latin *~parēscere~, an inchoative (“begin to…”) verb formed on Latin ~pārēre~ (“to appear, to show oneself, to be visible”). ~Pārēre~ traces through Proto-Italic *~pāzēō~ to PIE *~peh₂s-~ (“to watch, to look out for”), an s-extension of *~peh₂-~ (“to protect”). Cognate with Italian ~parere~ and Spanish ~parecer~, both meaning “to seem.”

The inchoative ending *~-ēscere~ is the heart of the story: it turned the plain ~pārēre~ (“to be visible”) into “to come into view, to begin to appear,” capturing the very moment a thing surfaces — which is exactly the nuance modern ~paraître~ keeps in “to appear, to seem, to come out” (a book ~paraît~ when it is published). ~Pārēre~ also combined with prefixes to give ~apparēre~, source of French ~apparaître~ (“to appear”) and the noun ~apparition~, and ~comparēre~, source of ~comparaître~ (“to appear in court”). From the same family French keeps ~apparence~ (“appearance”) and ~transparent~, all turning on the simple idea of being seen.
en.parcelliser: Formed in French from ~parcelle~ + the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to divide into small plots or pieces.” The noun comes from Old French ~parcelle~, from Late Latin ~particella~, a diminutive of Latin ~particula~, itself a diminutive of ~pars~ (“part”). It is more or less a doublet of ~particule~. The suffix ~-iser~, from Late Latin ~-izāre~, turns a noun into a verb of making or converting. To ~parcelliser~ is thus to turn a whole into parcels, whether land, work or a task.
en.parcheminer: ~Parcheminer~ (“to turn into parchment, to make look like parchment”) is formed from the noun ~parchemin~ and the verb ending ~-er~. ~Parchemin~ comes from Late Latin ~pergamēna~ (“skin of Pergamon”), because the city of Pergamon produced this material in antiquity. Its form in Old French came by way of Vulgar Latin *~pergamīnus~. In northern France the word was also influenced by ~parge~ (“sheepskin leather”), which goes back to ~parthica~, “skin from the land of the Parthians.” The verb applies the noun to a surface that becomes dry and yellowed.
en.parcourir:
From Old French, a compound of the prefix ~par-~ (from Latin ~per-~, “through, thoroughly”) and the verb ~courir~ (“to run”), modeled on Latin ~percurrere~ (“to run through, traverse”). The base ~courir~ descends from Latin ~currere~ (“to run”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ḱers-~ (“to run”). The whole family is mirrored in Italian ~percorrere~ and Spanish ~recorrer~.

The prefix ~par-~ here is intensive and exhaustive: not merely to run, but to run over the whole extent of something. So ~parcourir~ kept a literal sense — to travel across or traverse a region — while developing the figurative one English borrows in “to skim”: to run one's eyes over a page, to ~parcourir~ a book. The same ~currere~ is astonishingly fertile in French, giving ~courir~, ~courrier~ (“mail,” once carried by a running messenger), ~courant~ (“current, running”), ~concourir~, ~secourir~ (“to succour,” literally “to run to the aid of”), and the noun ~cours~. Through Latin it also seeded English ~current~, ~course~, ~corridor~, and even ~car~ — all, at root, things that run.
en.pardonner:
Attested from the end of the 10th century (in the ~Passion~), ~pardonner~ comes from Late Latin ~perdonāre~, a compound of the intensive prefix ~per-~ (“thoroughly, completely”) and ~donāre~ (“to give, to grant”). ~Donāre~ derives from ~donum~ (“gift”), from PIE *~deh₃nom~ (“gift”), from the root *~deh₃-~ (“to give”) — the same root behind ~donner~, ~donation~, and ~donateur~. The compound is mirrored across Romance: Italian ~perdonare~, Spanish and Occitan ~perdonar~; through Old French ~pardoner~ it also gave English ~pardon~.

The construction is vivid once unpacked: ~per-~ + ~donāre~ means “to give utterly, to remit a debt completely” — to make a clean gift of what one was owed. The earliest French sense was concrete mercy, “to spare, to grant someone their life,” before settling into the modern range of forgiving an offense and excusing a small lapse (~pardonnez-moi~). The shift of ~per-~ to ~par-~ is regular in French (compare ~parfaire~, ~parvenir~, ~parcourir~), where the prefix keeps its sense of completion. The whole family of *~deh₃-~ is one of generosity: ~don~, ~pardon~, ~donateur~, ~condonation~, and the learned ~dot~ (“dowry,” from ~dōs~) — so that to ~pardonner~ is, at root, to give a wrong away entirely.
en.parementer: ~Parementer~ is formed from the noun ~parement~ with the verb ending ~-er~, and means to face or adorn. ~Parement~ is derived from ~parer~ (“to adorn”) with the suffix ~-ment~, and descends from Old French ~parement~, from Medieval Latin ~parāmentum~, itself from Latin ~parō~ (“to adorn”) with ~-mentum~. A ~parement~ is a decorative facing or ornament, so the verb means to provide something with one.
en.parer:
From Latin ~parāre~ (“to make ready, to prepare, to arrange”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“to produce, to procure”). The same root yields English ~prepare~, ~apparatus~, and ~separate~, Spanish ~parar~, and Italian ~parare~. In French, ~parer~ split into senses borrowed back from those neighbors: the defensive “to parry, to ward off” owes to Italian ~parare~ (“to block”), while the equestrian “to halt a horse” echoes Spanish ~parar~ (“to stop”).

Underneath all these meanings lies a single old idea: to get something ready. From “prepare” the verb slid easily toward “arrange attractively,” and so ~parer~ came to mean to adorn or bedeck — a bride is ~parée~ for her wedding, a room ~paré~ for a feast. The fighting sense took a different path through Italy: to make yourself ready against a blow is to fend it off, hence to parry. French keeps both alive at once, and the root *~per-~ blossoms across the language in ~préparer~, ~appareil~, ~séparer~, ~rempart~, ~parade~, and ~parure~ (“finery”). One Latin verb meaning simply “to make ready” thus learned to decorate, to defend, and to bring a galloping horse to a clean stop.
en.paresser: ~Paresser~ is formed from the noun ~paresse~ (“laziness”) plus the verbal ending ~-er~, which here makes a verb meaning “to behave like” the noun, that is, to idle or loll about. ~Paresse~ comes from Old French ~peresce~, inherited from Latin ~pigritia~ (“sluggishness”). Italian ~pigrizia~, Spanish ~pereza~ and Portuguese ~preguiça~ are its cousins. English Wiktionary notes that the verb is attested in an earlier spelling, ~perecer~.
en.parfaire:
From Middle French ~parfaire~, from Old French ~parfaire~, borrowed from Latin ~perficere~ (“to carry through, to complete”) and reshaped by analogy with ~faire~. English Wiktionary instead presents it as ~par-~ + ~faire~, which is the same story seen from French: ~par-~ is the Old French form of Latin ~per-~ (“thoroughly”). Latin ~perficere~ is ~per-~ plus ~facere~ (“to do, to make”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, to set”), which also gives English ~do~ and German ~tun~.

The meaning has hardly changed: to ~parfaire~ is to bring something to full completion, to finish it off properly, as in ~parfaire son éducation~ or ~parfaire un tableau~. The verb now belongs to a careful, literary register and is mostly met in the infinitive and the participles. Its past participle ~parfait~ became an independent adjective, “perfect.” The learned ~perfectionner~ and ~perfection~ come directly from the Latin family, while ~parfaire~ shows how French reshaped the same Latin verb in popular speech. The long family of ~faire~ includes ~défaire~, ~refaire~, ~satisfaire~ and ~fait~.
en.parfiler: Formed from ~filer~ with the prefix ~par-~, from Latin ~per-~ (“through, thoroughly”), and glossed “to unthread, to unravel.” The prefix is no longer productive and survives only in a few old or literary verbs such as ~parfaire~ and ~parsemer~, where it is intensive or marks completion. ~Filer~ comes from Late Latin ~filare~ (“to spin into thread”), from ~filum~ (“thread”).
en.parfondre: ~Parfondre~ is made of the prefix ~par-~ and the verb ~fondre~ (“to melt”). The prefix ~par-~, from Latin ~per~ (“through”), gives the action a sense of completeness, as in ~parfaire~ (“to complete”), so the verb means to melt thoroughly, hence the technical sense “to fuse.” ~Fondre~ itself comes from Latin ~fundere~ (“to pour, to melt”), the same verb behind ~fusion~.
en.parfumer: The analysis is disputed. French Wiktionary derives it as ~fumer~ with the prefix ~par-~ (from Latin ~per-~, “through, thoroughly”), first with the sense of fumigating.
