English Wiktionary instead takes the Middle French verb as probably borrowed from Old Occitan or from Italian ~perfumare~, itself Latin ~per-~ plus ~fūmāre~. Either way the parts are the same: ~fūmāre~ (“to smoke, to steam”) comes from ~fūmus~ (“smoke”). The noun ~parfum~ keeps the picture of a scent that rises through smoke, as from burning incense.
en.parier: The sources agree that ~parier~ rests on the idea of a pair but differ on the exact Old French verb. French Wiktionary gives Old French ~pairier~ (“to make a pair, to put on an equal footing, to couple”), the verb that also gave ~apparier~, and traces it to Latin ~pariō~ (“to make equal”). English Wiktionary describes a blend of Old French ~perier~ (“to be part of a pair, to be equal”), from ~per~ (“pair”), and ~pairier~ (“to mate, to couple”), from ~paire~, remodelled after Latin ~pariāre~ (“to make equal”). Either way the thread is equality. French ~pair~, ~paire~ and ~pareil~ belong to the Latin family of ~pār~ (“equal”), and English ~pair~ and ~peer~ come from the same Latin source through French.
en.parjurer: From Latin ~perjurāre~ (“to swear falsely, to break an oath”), a compound of ~per-~ and ~jurāre~ (“to swear”). In Old French the Latin ~per-~ became ~par-~, which explains the shape of the modern verb. It is used in the reflexive, ~se parjurer~, “to break one's oath.” The base ~jurer~ (“to swear”) descends from Latin ~jurāre~, and French has the noun ~parjure~ (both “perjury” and “perjurer”). Spanish ~perjurar~ and English ~perjure~ come from the same Latin verb.
en.parlementer: ~Parlementer~ is a denominal verb: the noun ~parlement~ plus the ending ~-er~. The noun is itself built on ~parler~ (“to speak”) with the suffix ~-ment~, and it successively meant a conversation, the act of speaking, a remark, and then a deliberative assembly, in France and in England under the Anglo-Norman kings. Medieval Latin ~parlamentum~ was taken from the French and is attested from 1250. The verb keeps the conversational side of the noun: to talk things over, to negotiate, to parley.
en.parler:
From Old French ~parler~, from Late Latin ~parabolāre~ (“to speak, to converse”), a verb built on Latin ~parabola~ (“comparison, parable; speech”). ~parabola~ was borrowed from Ancient Greek ~παραβολή~ (parabolḗ, “a placing side by side, comparison”), from ~παρά~ (pará, “beside”) and ~βάλλειν~ (bállein, “to throw, to cast”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʷelH-~ (“to throw, to reach”). To “speak,” then, is etymologically to “throw words side by side.” Cognate verbs survive as Italian ~parlare~, while Spanish chose a different reflex of the same noun in ~palabra~ (“word”); English took ~parable~, ~parley~, and ~palaver~ from the same Greek source.

The striking detail is that the ordinary French word for talking comes not from Latin's neutral ~loquī~ (“to speak”) but from a churchy, rhetorical word for a “comparison” or “parable” — the speech of sermons and figures. In the mouths of Late Latin speakers ~parabola~ shed its lofty sense and came to mean simply “word, speech,” which is why French ~parole~ means “(the spoken) word” and ~parler~ means “to talk.” From the same root come a large family, including ~parole~, ~parleur~, ~pourparler~ (“negotiation, parley”), and the borrowed ~parabole~ (“parable; parabola”), which kept the geometric and biblical senses the everyday verb left behind.
en.parodier: Formed from ~parodie~ + ~-er~, a verb coined from a noun. The noun ~parodie~ was borrowed either from Latin ~parodia~ or directly from Greek ~παρῳδία~, a compound of ~παρά~ (“beside, alongside”) and ~ᾠδή~ (“song”), the same ~ᾠδή~ that lies behind English ~ode~. The sources consulted do not decide between the Latin and the Greek route. The ending ~-er~ is the usual first-conjugation ending that turns a noun into a verb, as in ~filtre~ and ~filtrer~.
en.parquer: Built on the noun ~parc~ (“enclosure, park”) with the verb ending ~-er~: to pen, to corral, or to park. Sources differ on where ~parc~ comes from. French Wiktionary derives it from Late Latin ~parricus~ (“enclosure”), itself from a pre-Latin word *~parra~ (“pole”), and notes that ~parricus~ passed very early into the Germanic languages, giving German ~Pferch~ and English ~parrock~. English Wiktionary instead lists ~parricus~ as Early Medieval Latin, possibly borrowed from Frankish *~parrik~.
en.parqueter: ~Parqueter~ is formed from ~parquet~ and the ending ~-er~: “to lay a wooden floor.” The noun ~parquet~ is built from ~parc~ with the diminutive ~-et~, literally a “little park,” that is, a small enclosure. That older sense is said to survive in Picard, and compare Walloon ~pårtchet~ (“small plot”). In joinery the word came to mean an assembly of panels, then any regular arrangement of wooden strips, which is the floor the verb now names.
en.parrainer: Formed from the noun ~parrain~ (“godfather”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to act as a godfather to,” hence “to sponsor.” ~Parrain~ comes from Old French ~parrain~ and from Early Medieval Latin ~patrīnus~, the man who held a child at baptism. English Wiktionary derives ~patrīnus~ from Latin ~pater~ (“father”), whereas French Wiktionary links it to Latin ~patruus~ (“paternal uncle”), so the last step is uncertain. The ecclesiastical sense of spiritual father was later widened to anyone who vouches for or backs a person, a project or an event.
en.parsemer: ~Parsemer~ is ~par-~ + ~semer~. The prefix ~par-~, a variant of Latin ~per-~ (“through, thoroughly”), only intensifies the base here: to sow or scatter all over, to strew. The verb ~semer~ comes from Latin ~sēmināre~ (“to sow”), drawn from ~sēmen~ (“seed”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~seh₁-~ (“to sow”), which is also the source of English ~sow~. From the field the verb moved to anything scattered thickly, such as a text dotted with quotations. The prefix ~par-~ no longer forms new verbs, and ~parsemer~ is one of its few survivors.
en.partager:
French ~partager~ is a relatively young verb, coined around 1553 from the noun ~partage~ (“division, sharing”) plus the verbal suffix ~-er~. Behind it stands ~part~ (“share, portion”), from Latin ~pars~, accusative ~partem~ (“a part, a share”), which traces to Proto-Indo-European *~perh₂-~ (“to grant, to allot”). The root is widely fertile, related to Latin ~portiō~ (“portion”) and surfacing in English ~part~, ~portion~, and ~parcel~. Greek ~péprōtai~ (“it has been allotted”) carries the same notion of a share handed out by fate.

The coinage answered a real gap in the language. The older inherited verb ~partir~, from Latin ~partīre~ (“to divide”), had drifted away to mean only “to depart, to leave” — a share of a journey split off, as it were, from the rest. With ~partir~ no longer usable for “to divide,” French built a fresh verb on the noun ~partage~ to recover the lost sense. The root still ramifies widely: ~part~, ~partie~, ~parti~, ~partager~, ~partenaire~ (“partner”), ~parcelle~, ~départ~ and ~répartir~. The fixed phrase ~à part~ (“apart, aside”) and the verb ~partir~ itself remind us that to depart and to share a portion spring from one and the same idea of dividing.
en.participer:
From Latin ~participāre~ (“to share, to take part in”), a compound of ~pars~ / ~partis~ (“a part, a share”) and ~capere~ (“to take, to seize”) — literally “to take a part.” ~Capere~ descends from PIE *~kh₂p-~ (“to grasp, to seize”), through which ~participer~ is cognate with English ~have~ and ~heave~ and with German ~haben~. ~Pars~ also gives French ~part~, ~partie~, and ~partir~.

The Latin verb fused the having of a portion with the act of seizing it, so that to participate is to take one's share of a common thing. From ~capere~ flows an immense French family — ~captif~, ~capter~, ~recevoir~, ~concevoir~, ~accepter~, ~capable~ — while ~pars~ supplies ~partager~, ~parti~, ~partiel~, and ~répartir~. From ~participāre~ itself come the close relatives ~participant~, ~participation~, and the grammatical ~participe~ (the participle, so called because it “takes part” in the natures of both verb and adjective). Thus the dry term of grammar and the lively act of joining in a cause are, etymologically, the very same gesture of taking a share.
en.particulariser:
~Particulariser~ is formed from the Latin adjective ~particulāris~ and the suffix ~-iser~, according to French Wiktionary. The suffix ~-iser~ itself goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs. The Latin adjective ~particulāris~ is an adjective built on ~particula~ (“small part”), a diminutive of ~pars~ (“part”). The French verb means “to make particular,” to treat something in its individual details.

The family is large. ~Pars~ lies behind ~part~, ~partie~ and ~partager~, while ~particula~ gave ~particule~. The adjective ~particulier~ is the everyday French relative of ~particulāris~, and it is the word the verb is built on in sense if not in form. English has the same family: ~particular~ and ~particularize~ both come, directly or through French, from the same Latin source.
en.partir:
From Old French ~partir~ (“to divide, to share, to separate”), from Latin ~partīre~, a variant of Classical Latin ~partīrī~ (“to divide, to share out”), a verb built on ~pars~, ~partis~ (“a part, share, portion”). The noun is generally traced to a Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ in the sense “to grant, to allot.” Through ~pars~, ~partir~ is kin to Italian ~partire~ and Spanish ~partir~, and, by way of Old French, to English ~part~, ~party~, and ~depart~.

The modern meaning hides an older one. For centuries ~partir~ meant “to divide” — a sense still alive in the saying ~avoir maille à partir~ (“to have a bone to pick,” literally a tiny coin to split). The notion of leaving grew from the reflexive ~se partir~, “to separate oneself” from a person or place; the reflexive faded but its directional sense stayed, leaving ~partir~ to mean simply “to depart.” The dividing sense lives on in ~répartir~, ~partager~, ~partage~, ~partie~ (“part, match”), ~parti~ (“party, side”), ~partition~, and ~particule~ — and, more distantly through ~pars~, in ~parcelle~ and the borrowed ~portion~.
en.partouser: Formed in French from the noun ~partouse~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, which turns the noun into a verb meaning “to take part in an orgy.” The noun ~partouse~ is itself a colloquial derivative of ~partie~ (“party, gathering”) with the suffix ~-ouse~, a familiar ending of popular speech. The ending ~-er~ is the ordinary first-conjugation ending, from Latin ~-are~, and is the default way to coin a verb from a noun.
en.partouzer: Formed from the noun ~partouze~ with the verb ending ~-er~, meaning “to take part in an orgy.” The noun first meant a card game, and was derived from ~partie~ with the suffix ~-ouze~. Its modern sexual sense came later, and French has related expressions such as ~partie carrée~, an orgy with two couples, and ~partie fine~. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~, the first-conjugation infinitive ending. The verb is thus a slang coinage resting on a word whose first sense was a harmless round of cards.
en.parvenir:
From Latin ~pervenire~ (“to arrive, to reach”), a compound of ~per-~ (“through, all the way”) and ~venire~ (“to come”). ~venire~ descends from Proto-Italic *~gʷeniō~ and from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷem-~ (“to come, to go”). Cognate with Italian ~pervenire~ and Spanish ~prevenir~ in form, and — through *~gʷem-~ — with English ~come~ and the learned ~advent~.

The prefix ~per-~ supplies the crucial nuance: not merely to come, but to come through, to come all the way to the end — hence “to reach, to attain.” French keeps both the literal and the figurative: a letter ~parvient~ to its addressee, and a person ~parvient~ to wealth or to a goal. From this last sense comes the loaded noun ~parvenu~, literally “one who has arrived,” used scornfully of the newly rich who reached high station from low birth — a social judgment hiding inside a participle. The shared root *~gʷem-~ links ~parvenir~ to the whole French ~venir~ family — ~devenir~, ~revenir~, ~convenir~, ~survenir~, ~prévenir~ — every one of them a different way of coming.
en.passementer: ~Passementer~ is a denominal verb: the noun ~passement~ with the ending ~-er~. The noun ~passement~ (“trimming, braid”) is itself formed from the verb ~passer~ with the suffix ~-ment~. The verb means to decorate a garment or piece of furniture with such trimmings. The chain is therefore ~passer~, then ~passement~, then ~passementer~, each step a regular French formation. The related ~passementerie~ names the craft.
en.passepoiler: Formed from ~passepoil~ with the verb ending ~-er~: to trim an edge with piping. The base ~passepoil~ is a compound of ~passe~ and ~poil~ (“hair”), as French Wiktionary gives it. It names the narrow cord or strip of fabric sewn into a seam or along an edge in tailoring and upholstery. The verb simply turns that noun into the action of putting it on.
en.passer:
Attested from around 1050, from Vulgar Latin *~passāre~ (“to cross, to step”), derived from Latin ~passus~ (“step, pace”), which is the past participle of ~pandere~ (“to spread, to stretch out [the legs]”), from PIE *~peth₂-~ (“to spread”). A step is, etymologically, a “spreading” of the legs. Cognate with Italian ~passare~ and Spanish ~pasar~; the noun ~passus~ also gave French ~pas~ and, by borrowing, English ~pass~ and ~pace~.

Few French verbs sprawl across so many meanings: one ~passe~ a river (to cross), ~passe~ an exam, ~passe~ the salt, ~passe~ time, and time itself ~passe~. All trace back to the simple image of stepping across a threshold. The same root *~peth₂-~ surfaces in the Latin ~pandere~ family, from which French draws ~expansion~ and ~épandre~, and the ~passus~ branch yields a crowd of everyday words: ~passage~, ~passager~, ~passeport~ (literally a document for “passing a port”), ~dépasser~, ~surpasser~, ~repasser~, and ~trépasser~ — “to pass beyond,” the old, gentle word for dying. To “pass away” is thus, in French as in English, to take a final step across.
en.passionner:
A French formation: ~passionner~ is a denominal verb from the noun ~passion~, which came through Middle French from Latin ~passionem~ (“suffering, enduring”), the action noun of the deponent verb ~patior~ (“to suffer, undergo, be acted upon”). The Latin verb is usually traced to PIE *~peh₁-~ (“to hurt”), though its morphology is irregular and the connection is not beyond debate. From ~patior~ English draws ~patient~, ~passive~, and ~compassion~ — all of them, like ~passion~, originally about being acted upon rather than acting.

The oldest French ~passion~ was Christian: the suffering of Christ, the ~Passion~. From that root sense of strong feeling endured, the word swelled to mean any overmastering emotion or love. The verb ~passionner~ followed: to ~passionner~ someone is to seize them with that intensity, and a debate that ~passionne~ a crowd inflames it. The thread from “to suffer” to “to be impassioned” is the idea of an emotion that takes you over. From the same ~patior~ French keeps ~pâtir~ (“to suffer”), ~patient~, ~passif~, and ~compassion~.
en.pasteuriser: Formed from the surname of Louis Pasteur and the suffix ~-iser~, in the sense of subjecting to the heat treatment he devised. The suffix ~-iser~ can mean “treat with, subject to” a person's or place's name, as in ~galvaniser~. The surname ~Pasteur~ is itself the common word ~pasteur~ (“shepherd”), from Latin ~pastōrem~. A verb named for a scientist thus rests on a word first used of shepherds.
en.pasticher: Formed on the noun ~pastiche~ with the verb ending ~-er~: to imitate someone's style, to produce a pastiche. ~Pastiche~ was borrowed from Italian ~pasticcio~ (“pie, muddle”), and its sense of “mixture” explains the artistic meaning of a work that blends or reworks an original. Behind the Italian, English Wiktionary traces Vulgar Latin *~pastīcius~, Late Latin ~pasta~ and Greek ~pastá~ (“barley porridge”), so the word began in the kitchen before it reached the studio.
en.patauger: Derived from ~patte~ (“paw, foot”). French Wiktionary gives the verb as ~patoier~ in the 13th century and ~patauger~ from the 17th. Today it means to splash about in water or mud and, figuratively, to flounder, getting nowhere in a task.
en.patienter: Formed in French from the adjective and noun ~patient~ and the verb ending ~-er~, and meaning “to be patient, to wait.” The base ~patient~ comes from Old French ~patient~, borrowed from Latin ~patiens~ (accusative ~patientem~), the present participle of ~patī~ (“to suffer, to endure”). The family thus rests on the Latin idea of putting up with something, which is also the root of English ~patient~ and ~passion~. In French, ~patienter~ turned that quality into an action, most often an instruction to wait one's turn or to hold on.
en.patiner: Two sources list two separate derivations with the ending ~-er~. One builds the verb on ~patin~ (“skate”), the other on ~patine~ (“patina”), and the form is the same in both. The noun ~patin~ is attested in Old French with the sense “thick-soled shoe,” and is derived from ~patte~ (“paw”) with the suffix ~-in~; Italian ~pattino~ is related. The ice-skating sense of ~patiner~ fits the first derivation, since a ~patin~ is what one skates on. The sources do not say how much weight to give each of the two origins in the other senses.
en.patoiser: Formed from ~patois~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so it means to speak in patois. The noun ~patois~ comes from Old French ~patois~ (“rude, incomprehensible speech”), an alteration of an earlier *~patoi~ drawn from the verb ~patoier~ (“to gesticulate, to handle clumsily”). That verb rests on ~pate~ (“paw”), from Vulgar Latin *~patta~, itself from Frankish *~patta~ (“paw, sole of the foot”). A dialect was thus first named for clumsy, pawing speech.
en.patouiller: ~Patouiller~ comes from Old French ~patoiller~, a derivative of ~patte~ (“paw, foot”) with the suffix ~-ouiller~. That suffix often gives a verb a sense of repeated, untidy action, as in ~barbouiller~ (“to daub”). The verb thus describes what one does with the ~patte~ again and again: to splash about in water or mud, and by extension to fumble around clumsily.
en.patronner: Formed from the noun ~patron~ and the verbal suffix ~-er~, so “to act as a ~patron~,” that is, to sponsor or support. The base ~patron~ comes from Old French ~patron~ (“patron, protector”), from Latin ~patrōnus~, derived from ~pater~ (“father”). A patron was thus first a father-like protector.
en.patrouiller: ~Patrouiller~ is described as a variant of ~patouiller~, a verb whose original sense was “to walk on wet ground.” English Wiktionary adds that the ~r~ was taken from similar-sounding verbs such as ~vadrouiller~ (“to roam about”). So the verb that now means “to go the rounds” began, on this account, as a word for floundering through mud, with an extra ~r~ borrowed from a neighbor.
en.paumer: ~Paumer~ is formed from the noun ~paume~ (“palm of the hand”) with the verb ending ~-er~, and it first meant to take in the hand. ~Paume~ comes from Latin ~palma~ (“hollow of the hand”), from Proto-Indo-European *~pl̥h₂meh₂~, and is a doublet of ~palme~; English ~palm~ is a cognate. In modern slang the sense of “taking” was reversed into “losing, mislaying,” and the verb then acquired a pronominal form, ~se paumer~ (“to get lost”).
en.paumoyer: A French formation on the noun ~paume~ (“palm of the hand”) with a verb ending, meaning “to haul in by hand.” The noun ~paume~ came through Old and Middle French from Latin ~palma~ (“hollow of the hand”). ~Palma~ also gave French ~palme~ (“palm leaf”), a doublet of ~paume~.
en.paupériser:
The sources give two accounts. French Wiktionary says ~paupériser~ was borrowed from English ~pauperize~, while English Wiktionary describes it as built from Latin ~pauper~ (“poor”) plus the suffix ~-iser~. The two are compatible if the French verb was modeled on the English one, itself made from the Latin adjective and the Greek-derived ending ~-ize~; the evidence does not settle the order. Either way, Latin ~pauper~ is the root, and the verb means to reduce a person or a social group to poverty.

Latin ~pauper~ also gave French ~pauvre~ through the ordinary inherited route, so ~pauvre~ and ~paupériser~ are doublet-like relatives, one popular and one learned. The learned side includes ~paupérisme~ (“mass poverty”) and the verb ~appauvrir~ is a separate French formation on ~pauvre~. The ~-iser~ ending is a fully productive suffix meaning “to cause to become,” and ~paupériser~ is typical of its use in economic and journalistic writing, where one speaks of the ~paupérisation~ of the middle class.
en.pauser: ~Pauser~ is formed from the noun ~pause~ and the verbal ending ~-er~; French Wiktionary adds a cross-reference to ~poser~. ~Pause~ comes from Latin ~pausa~ (“cessation, halt, truce”), itself from Greek ~paûsis~ (“cessation”). English Wiktionary notes that Middle French ~pause~ may be only a relatinized spelling of Old French ~pose~ (“moment, period of time”), also taken from the Latin noun, so ~pause~ and ~pose~ cannot be separated entirely. This is why ~pauser~ and ~poser~ are relatives.
en.pavaner: Formed from ~pavane~, a stately processional dance, plus the verbal ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary also cites the older ~se paonner~ (1544), from ~paon~ (“peacock”), as a contributor, so the modern verb probably blends the two. The dance name is borrowed from dialectal Italian ~pavana~, a contraction of ~padovana~, “of Padua,” because Padua is ~Pava~ in the local dialect. ~Se pavaner~ means to strut about showing off, as if performing a slow, proud dance.
en.paver: Inherited from Old French ~paver~ (“to pave, to cover”), from Vulgar Latin *~pavāre~ (“to beat down, to smash”), from Latin ~pavīre~ (“to beat, strike, ram, tread down”). French Wiktionary also records the French verb ~pavir~ from the same ~pavīre~, which it glosses as “to beat the earth, to level.” The image behind paving is therefore a beaten surface: ground tamped flat before anything else is laid on it. The Latin noun ~pavīmentum~ (“a beaten floor”) belongs to the same family and gave French ~pavement~. English ~pave~ and ~pavement~ are loans from French, and French also has ~pavé~ for a paving stone and for the street itself.
en.pavoiser: ~Pavoiser~ is a denominal verb: ~pavois~ plus the ending ~-er~. ~Pavois~ was borrowed from Italian ~pavese~ (“of Pavia”), as in the ~scudo pavese~, a large shield of the kind made in or named after that city. The modern naval sense of ~pavois~ comes from such shields being lashed along a ship's side to protect its marines, so ~pavoiser~ came to mean to dress a ship, or a building, with flags.
en.payer:
From Old French ~paiier~, ~payer~, from Latin ~pācāre~ (“to pacify, to appease”), a verb built on ~pāx~ (“peace”). ~Pāx~ goes back to PIE *~peh₂ḱ-~ (“to fasten, to join, to settle”), the root that also gave Latin ~pangere~ (“to fix, to drive in”) and ~pacīscī~ (“to make a pact”); through its Germanic line the same root underlies English ~fang~. Cognate with Italian ~pagare~ and Spanish ~pagar~.

The semantic leap is the memorable part. In Classical Latin ~pācāre~ meant “to make peaceful, to subdue,” but in the money-minded Latin of the Middle Ages it narrowed to a very particular kind of appeasement: to pacify a creditor by settling the debt. To pay was, literally, to make peace with the person you owed. That sense crossed into Old French and crowded out the older one entirely, so that French ~payer~ now means only “to pay.” The peaceful origin is still visible in the cousins of ~pāx~ that French preserves — ~paix~ (“peace”), ~apaiser~ (“to appease”), ~pacifier~, ~pacte~ — a quiet reminder that a settled bill and a settled quarrel were once the same act.
en.paître:
From Old French ~paistre~, a form attested around 1050, inherited from Latin ~pāscere~ (“to graze, to feed”). Latin ~pāscere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~pāskō~, which in turn goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~peh₂-~ (“to protect”). The Latin verb lives on in Italian ~pascere~ and Spanish ~pacer~, and English borrowed ~pasture~ and ~pastor~ from the same Latin family.

The circumflex of modern ~paître~ stands in for the ~s~ of ~paistre~, which fell silent and then disappeared from the spelling. The verb is used today mainly of animals feeding in a field. Many French words belong to the same Latin family: ~pâture~ (“pasture, feed”), ~pâturage~ (“grazing land”), ~pasteur~ (“shepherd, pastor”) and ~repaître~ (“to feed, to satisfy”).
en.peaufiner: French Wiktionary builds ~peaufiner~ from ~peau~, ~fin~ and the verb ending ~-er~, literally “to make the skin fine”. It was first used in the reflexive, ~se peaufiner~, to mean “to groom oneself with care”. Around 1885 it became a transitive verb meaning “to clean with a chamois skin”. English Wiktionary agrees on the French compound and dates it to the nineteenth century. The tie to ~peau~ has since faded, and the verb now means to put the finishing touches to something.
en.peigner: ~Peigner~ is inherited from Old French ~paigner~, from Latin ~pectināre~ (“to comb”), a verb formed on ~pecten~ (“comb”). Italian ~pettinare~ and Spanish ~peinar~ descend from the same Latin verb. The noun ~peigne~ and the family of derived words, such as ~peignoir~, ~dépeigner~ and ~peignée~, belong to the same line.
en.peindre:
From Middle and Old French ~peindre~, from Latin ~pingere~ (“to paint, to dye, to embroider, to tattoo, to embellish”), from a nasal-infixed Proto-Indo-European *~pi-n-ḱ-~, from the root *~peyḱ-~ (“to mark, to color; spotted”). The deep sense is marking or cutting a sign into a surface. Through this root ~peindre~ is cognate with Greek ~poikílos~ (“dappled, embroidered”), Sanskrit ~piṃśáti~ (“he cuts, adorns”), and the Old English ~fāh~ (“stained, variegated”).

That the same Latin verb meant both “to paint” and “to embroider” and “to tattoo” recalls a time when all of these were ways of marking a surface with color. French narrowed ~peindre~ to the brush, but kept the figurative reach: one can ~peindre~ a character or a scene in words, “to depict” it. The Latin participle ~pictus~ and noun ~pictūra~ entered French as the learned doublets ~pictural~ and the borrowed ~pictura~ behind ~peinture~, while ~pingere~ itself gave ~peintre~ (“painter”) and ~peinture~. From ~pigmentum~ (“coloring matter”) came both ~pigment~ and, by a worn-down popular route, ~piment~ (“chili pepper”); the same root colors Italian ~pingere~ and Spanish ~pintar~.
en.peiner: Formed on ~peine~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, continuing Old French ~pener~. The noun ~peine~ is inherited from Old French ~peine~, from Latin ~poena~ (“penalty, punishment”), which itself came from Ancient Greek ~poinḗ~ (“penalty, fine, blood-money”). The verb has two uses: intransitive, “to toil, to struggle” (the older sense of suffering effort), and transitive, “to cause pain to, to distress.” The adverb ~à peine~ (“hardly”) is a separate word, from Latin ~paene~ (“almost”).
en.peinturer:
~Peinturer~ comes from Middle French ~peinturer~, itself from Old French ~peinturer~, so it is an old verb, not a modern coinage. In present-day French it can be analyzed as built on the noun ~peinture~ (“painting, paint”) with the verb ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~. The noun ~peinture~ descends from Latin ~pictūra~ (“painting”), formed on the verb ~pingere~ (“to paint”), the same verb that gave French ~peindre~.

Latin ~pingere~ has a large family in French. The inherited line gives ~peindre~, ~peinture~ and ~peintre~, while learned borrowings keep the Latin ~ct~, as in ~pictural~. English drew on the same Latin source for ~picture~. Although ~peinturer~ and ~peindre~ both mean “to paint”, they are two separate verbs: ~peindre~ is inherited directly from Latin, while ~peinturer~ is a distinct verb tied to the noun ~peinture~.
en.peinturlurer: A blend, or portmanteau, of ~peinturer~ (“to paint”) and ~turelure~. Both Wiktionaries agree on this: the verb is an alteration of ~peinturer~ shaped by ~turelure~, whose sound gives it a playful, sing-song ring. The result keeps the idea of painting but adds a note of disdain: to ~peinturlurer~ is to daub, to slap on colour clumsily or in loud, gaudy patches.
en.peler: From Old French ~peler~, itself from Late Latin ~pilāre~ (“to remove hair, to depilate”), a verb built on Latin ~pilus~ (“hair”). The original sense was thus to strip hair, then to strip the skin or rind off something, which is how ~peler~ came to mean “to peel” a fruit or a vegetable. English Wiktionary adds that the form may have been influenced by the Old French noun ~pel~, a point French Wiktionary does not mention. The same Latin ~pilus~ gave French ~poil~ (“hair”) by regular sound change, so ~peler~ and ~poil~ are cousins.
en.peller: Formed from the noun ~pelle~ (“shovel”) plus the verb ending ~-er~: to ~peller~ is to move something with a shovel. The noun was inherited from Old French ~pele~, from Latin ~pāla~ (“shovel, spade”), which also meant the bezel of a ring and the shoulder blade. Its doublet in French is ~pale~, the blade of an oar or propeller, which has a dialectal or Occitan origin. The suffix ~-er~ makes a verb meaning “work with N” or “apply N,” the usual route for tool names.
en.pelleter: Formed in French from ~pelle~ (“shovel”) with the suffix ~-et~ and the ending ~-er~, “to shovel.” The noun ~pelle~ comes from Latin ~pāla~ (“spade, shovel”), which also gave the doublet ~pale~, the blade of a propeller or oar. The suffix ~-et~ is diminutive and ~-er~ makes the verb, so ~pelleter~ is used for shifting loose material, such as earth or snow, with a shovel.
en.peloter: Formed from ~pelote~ and the ending ~-er~. The noun ~pelote~ (“small ball”) comes from Old French ~pelute~, attested around 1119, from a Late Latin form reconstructed as *~pilotta~, a diminutive of Latin ~pila~ (“ball”). The verb has two main senses, to roll into a ball and, in slang, to feel someone up. The sources do not say how the second grew from the first.
en.pelotonner: Formed from ~peloton~ and the ending ~-er~, the verb means to wind into a ball and, in the reflexive, to curl up. The noun ~peloton~ is ~pelote~ plus the suffix ~-on~, and in 1578 it took the sense “group of soldiers.” The base ~pelote~ (“small ball”) comes from Old French ~pelute~, from Latin ~pila~ (“ball”) through a reconstructed Late Latin diminutive *~pilotta~.
en.pelucher: ~Pelucher~ is formed from the noun ~peluche~ (“plush”) with the verb ending ~-er~, and it means “to become fluffy,” as a fabric does when its fibres lift and shed. ~Peluche~ itself derives from Old French ~peluchier~ (“to pluck, to peel”), glossed in French as picking out tangled hairs.
en.pencher:
From Old French ~pengier~ (“to be out of plumb”), attested in 1256, from Vulgar Latin *~pendicare~, a derivative of Latin ~pendere~ (“to hang”). The modern form ~pencher~ appears from 1530. ~Pendere~ descends from Proto-Italic *~pendēō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~(s)pend-~ (“to stretch, pull, draw”). The root surfaces in Romance ~pendere~ verbs and, more distantly, in English ~pension~ and ~pendant~.

The semantic thread runs from hanging to leaning to inclining: a thing that hangs off true is tilted, and from physical tilt the verb passed to mental tendency — one ~penche pour~ an idea, leans toward it. The related ~pendere~ also meant “to weigh, to pay,” because coins and goods were once weighed in a hanging scale-pan; that image of suspension links the family. From the same root French keeps ~pente~ (“slope”), ~penchant~ (“inclination, leaning”), ~pendre~ (“to hang”), and ~pendule~. To lean, in French, is still quietly to hang at an angle.
en.pendiller: Formed from ~pendre~ with the suffix ~-iller~, which gives a frequentative or diminutive sense: to hang and sway in small repeated movements. The same pattern gives ~sautiller~ from ~sauter~. The base ~pendre~ descends from Late Latin ~pendĕre~, standing for Classical ~pendēre~ (“to hang, to be suspended”), which Latin built on a Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)pend-~ (“to pull; to spin”).
en.pendouiller: Formed from ~pendre~ (“to hang”) with the familiar, slightly pejorative suffix ~-ouiller~, which makes a small, weak or idle version of the base: ~pendouiller~ is to dangle. ~Pendre~ comes from Latin ~pendēre~ (“to hang, be suspended”), and Italian ~pendere~ is its direct cousin. The same pattern gives ~glandouiller~ (from ~glander~) and ~mâchouiller~ (from ~mâcher~).
en.pendre:
~Pendre~ comes from Old French ~pendre~, itself from Late Latin ~pendĕre~, with a short e, which stands in for Classical Latin ~pendēre~ (“to hang, to be suspended”). Latin had two near-twin verbs: the intransitive ~pendēre~ (“to hang”) and the transitive ~pendere~ (“to make hang, to weigh”). Their conjugations were confused in Late Latin, which is why French ~pendre~ works both ways, “to hang something” and “to hang down”. The Latin verb is traced to Proto-Italic *~pendēō~ and to the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)pend-~ (“to pull; to spin”). Italian ~pendere~ is the direct cousin of the French verb.

Since a pair of scales hangs from its beam, Latin ~pendere~ also meant “to weigh” and so “to pay out”. Its frequentative ~pensāre~ (“to weigh carefully”) gave French ~peser~ and ~penser~, so “to think” is, etymologically, “to weigh in the mind”. Modern ~pendre~ covers hanging a coat, hanging a criminal, and the intransitive droop or sag, as in cheeks that hang. The family is large: ~suspendre~, ~dépendre~ and ~pendule~ (the hanging weight of a clock). English borrowed many of these as ~suspend~, ~depend~, ~pendulum~ and ~pensive~.
en.penduler: ~Penduler~ is formed from ~pendule~ (“pendulum”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, so it means to swing like a pendulum, and by extension to shuttle back and forth, for instance between home and work. The source adds, with a hedge, that the verb is probably to be compared with German ~pendeln~, which has the same senses of swinging and commuting. The exact relation between the two words is therefore not settled: they may be parallel formations or one may have influenced the other.
en.penser:
From Middle and Old French ~penser~ (also spelled ~panser~), from Latin ~pensāre~ (“to weigh carefully, to ponder”). ~pensāre~ is the frequentative of ~pendere~ (“to weigh, to hang”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)pend-~ (“to stretch, to pull, to spin”) — the image of weights hanging from the arm of a balance. So to “think” is, at root, to “weigh” — to hold ideas in the scales of the mind. ~penser~ is a learned doublet of French ~peser~ (“to weigh”), which descends from the very same Latin verb by the ordinary popular route; the two split apart, one keeping the literal weight, the other the mental one. Cognate reflexes survive as Italian ~pensare~ and Spanish ~pensar~, and the family entered English as ~pensive~ and ~ponder~.

The metaphor of mental weighing is ancient and vivid, and French preserves it throughout the vocabulary of thought. Curiously, the alternate spelling ~panser~ peeled off into a separate verb meaning “to dress a wound, to groom (a horse)” — originally “to take thought for, to attend to” an animal or an injury, the same act of careful consideration applied to care. From ~pensāre~ and ~pendere~ come a wide French family, including ~pensée~ (“thought; pansy”), ~pensif~ (“pensive”), ~penseur~ (“thinker”), and, through the weighing sense, ~dépenser~ (“to spend, to weigh out money”) and ~récompense~ (“reward”).
en.pensionner: ~Pensionner~ is formed from the noun ~pension~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, and means to pay someone a pension, a sum of money at regular intervals. The noun ~pension~ came through Old French from Latin ~pēnsiō~ (“payment, rent”), from ~pēnsus~, the past participle of ~pendere~ (“to weigh, to pay”); the one Latin verb covered both weighing and paying. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~.
en.percer:
From Vulgar Latin *~pertusiare~ (“to pierce”), a verb derived from ~pertusum~, the supine of Latin ~pertundere~ (“to thrust through, to bore”) — the prefix ~per-~ (“through”) joined to ~tundere~ (“to strike, to beat”). The same ~pertusum~ gave Old French ~pertuis~ (“a hole, an opening”), a word still found in place-names and in old technical vocabulary, naming the very gap that piercing leaves behind.

To ~percer~ is to make a hole through something, but the verb quickly grew figurative meanings that the English glosses capture: to percer a mystery is to see through it, and a young talent who ~perce~ is one who “breaks through” to success. French keeps several relatives close to the surface: ~perçage~ and ~perceuse~ (the drilling and the drill), ~percée~ (“a breakthrough,” military or otherwise), and ~transpercer~ (“to run through”). The image is consistent across them all — a sharp passage driven clean through a barrier, whether that barrier is a plank, a secret, or an obstacle to fame.
en.percevoir:
French ~percevoir~ comes from Latin ~percipere~ (“to seize wholly, to take in, to perceive”), formed from ~per-~ (“thoroughly, completely”) plus ~capere~ (“to seize, to take”). ~Capere~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~kapjō~ to a Proto-Indo-European root *~kap-~ (“to grasp, to seize”), which also surfaces in the Germanic family — English ~have~ and ~heave~ are distant cousins through Proto-Germanic *~habjaną~. The French form was remodeled on ~recevoir~ and ~apercevoir~, all sharing the ~-cevoir~ stem from ~capere~; Italian keeps the more transparent ~percepire~.

The Latin verb already united the physical and the mental: to “take in completely,” whether grasping an object or grasping an idea. French inherited both. ~Percevoir~ still means “to take in through the senses or the mind” — to perceive a sound, to make out a meaning — but it also carries a strikingly concrete administrative sense, “to collect, to levy,” as when the state ~perçoit~ a tax: a literal seizing of money. From this comes ~percepteur~, the tax collector. Around ~capere~ and its compound French clusters ~perception~, ~perceptible~ and ~imperceptible~, ~apercevoir~ and ~apperçu~, plus the wider ~capter~, ~capable~, ~capture~, and ~recevoir~. To perceive, etymologically, is to grasp a thing whole — with the hand, the ear, or the understanding.
en.percher: Formed in French from the noun ~perche~ (“pole”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning “to set on a perch”, and so “to roost, to settle up high”. The noun ~perche~ comes from Old French ~perche~, from Latin ~pertica~ (“long pole”), probably through a contracted Vulgar Latin form. The fish also called ~perche~ is a separate word, from Latin ~perca~ and Greek ~pérkē~, which means “spotted”. The verb belongs to the pole, since a bird sits on a pole and not on a fish.
en.percuter:
From Latin ~percutere~ (“to strike through, to hit hard”). The Latin verb is traditionally analyzed as ~per-~ (“through, thoroughly”) plus ~-cutere~, a combining form of ~quatere~ (“to shake, to strike”). The same ~-cutere~ appears in ~discuter~ (from Latin ~discutere~) and ~secouer~ (from ~succutere~), and the participle stem of ~percutere~ gave ~percussion~, a word English also borrowed.

French ~percuter~ means to strike or to crash into something, usually with force, as when a vehicle hits an obstacle. Its relatives show how one Latin verb spread in several directions. ~Percussion~ names the striking of instruments, and ~concussion~ comes from the compound ~concutere~. The French verb is a learned borrowing, close to its Latin source in both form and sense.
en.perdre:
From Latin ~perdere~ (« to destroy, to ruin, to lose utterly »), formed from the prefix ~per-~ (« through, to the end, to destruction ») and the verb ~dare~ (« to give »). ~dare~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~deh₃-~ (“to give”), shared by Ancient Greek ~dídōmi~ (“I give”), Sanskrit ~dádāti~, and — through Latin — English ~donate~ and ~date~. Italian ~perdere~ and Spanish ~perder~ are its Romance siblings.

The literal sense is striking: ~per-~ + ~dare~ is to « give thoroughly away », to give until nothing is left — hence « to destroy » and then « to lose ». The intensive prefix turned the act of giving into the act of losing, a quiet reminder that loss is open-handedness pushed past return. French keeps the whole spread: to ~perdre~ a key, a battle, one's time (~perdre son temps~), or one's way (~se perdre~). From the same verb come ~perte~ (« loss »), ~perdition~, and the adjective ~perdu~, while the root ~dare~ also yields ~donner~, ~rendre~, ~vendre~, and ~pardonner~.
en.perdurer:
From Latin ~perdūrāre~ (“to last, to endure to the end”), a compound of ~per-~ (“through”) and ~dūrāre~ (“to harden, to last”). In this verb the prefix is intensive: it does not add a new direction, it adds the idea of going the whole way. The base ~dūrāre~ comes from the adjective ~dūrus~ (“hard”). Spanish ~perdurar~ and Italian ~perdurare~ are the sister forms, and English has the learned ~perdure~ (“to endure”).

In French, ~perdurer~ is a learned word and a stronger one than ~durer~: it speaks of what continues to exist in spite of time or trouble, as in ~la tradition perdure~ (“the tradition lives on”). Its relatives include ~durer~ (“to last”), ~dur~ (“hard”), ~durable~ and ~endurer~ (“to endure, to bear”), and English has ~endure~, ~duration~ and ~during~ from the same Latin root. Note that ~perdurer~ is formed in Latin, not in French: there is no French verb ~per-~ + ~durer~ in the formation.
en.perfectionner: ~Perfectionner~ is formed from the noun ~perfection~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, which turns a noun into a verb: to bring something toward perfection, to refine it. ~Perfection~ came through Middle French from Latin ~perfectiō~ (“complete achievement”), from ~perficere~ (“to finish, to carry through”), itself made of ~per-~ (“through, thoroughly”) and ~facere~ (“to do”). So the idea at the heart of the word is thoroughness: something done all the way through. The verb thus says “to make more complete,” which is why it is used for skills, techniques and tools that are improved step by step.
en.perforer: French ~perforer~ is borrowed straight from Latin ~perforāre~, “to bore or pierce through.” By textbook analysis the Latin verb joins ~per-~ (“through”) to ~forāre~ (“to bore”). That second element survives in the inherited French ~forer~ (“to drill”), so ~forer~ and ~perforer~ are related, one native and one learned. The same Latin verb gave Spanish and Italian ~perforar~ and ~perforare~, and English ~perforate~. Related French words include ~perforation~ and ~perforateur~, along with ~foret~, the drill bit.
en.perfuser:
~Perfuser~ is a back-formation from ~perfusion~: the noun came first, and the verb was made from it by dropping the ending. French Wiktionary traces ~perfusion~ to Latin ~perfundere~ (“to pour through”), a compound of ~per-~ (“through”) and ~fundere~ (“to pour”). The verb is a medical term for running a fluid through a body or an organ. As a back-formation it is a creation of French, not a word inherited from Latin.

The Latin verb ~fundere~ left many traces in French. Its past participle ~fusus~ lies behind ~fusion~ and ~diffuser~, and with other prefixes it gave ~infuser~ and ~confondre~. Its inherited, popular descendant is ~fondre~ (“to melt”), so ~perfuser~ and ~fondre~ are distant cousins. English ~perfuse~ and ~perfusion~ come from the same Latin source.
en.perler: ~Perler~ is formed from the noun ~perle~ (“pearl”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, in the sense “to form into beads.” The origin of the noun is debated. One account runs through Old French ~perle~ and Medieval Latin ~perla~ to Latin ~perula~ (“little pear”). The other, which French Wiktionary gives, goes through an unattested Medieval Latin diminutive *~pernula~ to Latin ~perna~ (“haunch,” also a marine bivalve shaped like a leg of lamb).
en.permanenter: From ~permanente~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. A ~permanente~ is the hairdressing treatment known in English as a “perm.” The noun arose by ellipsis from the phrase ~ondulation permanente~ (“permanent wave”), with the adjective ~permanent~ turned into a noun. Adding ~-er~, the usual ending for coining verbs from nouns, gave ~permanenter~, “to give someone a perm.” The word thus keeps the idea of “lasting” that ~permanent~ expresses: the wave was meant to stay in the hair, unlike a set that washes out.
en.permettre:
From Latin ~permittere~ (“to let pass, to allow, to entrust”), formed from the prefix ~per-~ (“through, thoroughly”) and the verb ~mittere~ (“to send, to let go”). French reshaped it on the native model of ~mettre~, giving ~permettre~. Since ~mittere~ rests on a Proto-Indo-European root *~meyth₂-~ (“to exchange, to remove”), ~permettre~ shares its deep ancestry with Italian ~permettere~ and Spanish ~permitir~, and with English ~permit~, borrowed straight from the Latin.

The literal force of ~per-~ + ~mittere~ is vivid: to permit is to “let through,” to send a thing all the way along its path rather than block it. From the same supine stem ~permiss-~ French draws ~permis~ (both the past participle “permitted” and the noun “permit, licence,” as in ~permis de conduire~, “driving licence”) and ~permission~. The verb keeps the company of its siblings built on ~mettre~ — ~promettre~, ~soumettre~, ~transmettre~, ~émettre~ — a tidy set in which a single prefix recolors the shared idea of sending: ~pro-~ forward, ~sub-~ under, ~trans-~ across, ~ex-~ out, and ~per-~ all the way through.
en.permuter:
From Latin ~permūtāre~ (“to transform, to exchange”), a verb built from ~per-~ (“thoroughly”) and ~mūtāre~ (“to change”). Middle French also had the variants ~permuer~ and ~parmuer~, which kept the ending of the spoken tradition, whereas the modern ~permuter~ matches the Latin infinitive more closely. English ~permute~ is a borrowing of the same Latin verb, and ~mutate~ comes from its simple base.

The Latin verb ~mūtāre~ gave French a whole family. ~Muer~ is its inherited descendant, while ~muter~, ~mutation~, ~commuter~ and ~transmuter~ are learned borrowings. In modern French, ~permuter~ means “to swap” two things or two people, as when colleagues exchange posts, and it is also the mathematician's word for rearranging the order of a set of elements.
en.peroxyder: ~Peroxyder~ is formed from the noun ~peroxyde~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, so it means to turn into a peroxide, to treat with peroxide. The noun is itself a compound of the prefix ~per-~ and ~oxyde~ (“oxide”), the chemical term for an oxide with a high proportion of oxygen. It is a technical formation from the vocabulary of chemistry.
en.perpétrer:
From Latin ~perpetrāre~ (“to carry through, to accomplish”), a learned borrowing, and not a word that passed through the popular sound changes of Old French. The Latin verb is built from ~per-~ (“through, to the end”) and ~patrāre~ (“to bring about, to bring to pass”), whose own origin is unclear. It meant simply to carry something out to completion, with no bad overtones. The same ~patrāre~ gave ~impetrāre~ (“to obtain by request”), borrowed into French as ~impétrer~, a legal term. English ~perpetrate~ was borrowed from the same Latin verb.

The path of the meaning is the interesting part. In Latin, ~perpetrāre~ was neutral, since one could accomplish a good deed as readily as a bad one. In French, as in English, the verb narrowed to the sense it has today: one ~perpètre~ a crime, an outrage, a massacre, an attack, never a good action. Do not confuse it with ~perpétuer~ (“to make perpetual”), from ~perpetuus~, which merely sounds alike. The noun ~perpétration~ and the agent noun ~perpétrateur~ follow the same pattern.
en.perpétuer:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~perpetuāre~ (“to make continuous, to cause to last without a break”), attested in French around 1370 in Jean le Fèvre. The Latin verb is built on the adjective ~perpetuus~ (“continuous, unbroken, lasting”), analyzed as ~per-~ (“through”) plus the root of ~petere~ (“to seek, to make for”): what is ~perpetuus~ goes, literally, right the way through. The same formation lies behind the rarer Latin ~perpes~. ~petere~ itself goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~peth₂-~ (“to fly, to rush”). Roman institutional language leaned on the adjective in fixed phrases such as ~in perpetuum~ (“for ever”) and ~quaestiones perpetuae~, the standing courts of the late republic, and it is that administrative flavor of permanence that the French verb inherited. Italian ~perpetuare~, Spanish ~perpetuar~ and English ~perpetuate~ are parallel borrowings of the same Latin verb.

French received the adjective long before the verb: ~perpétuel~ was already in medieval use, and the noun ~perpétuité~ supplied the legal formula ~à perpétuité~, which is why a life sentence in French is, literally, a perpetuity. The verb began as a transitive one — to perpetuate a name, a memory, an institution — and acquired its pronominal form ~se perpétuer~ by 1549, the sense in which a species, a custom or an error keeps itself going. That reflexive use carries the modern sting: what ~se perpétue~ today is usually something one would rather see stop, an inequality or a stereotype, so a verb whose Latin ancestor described unbroken duration now most often reports an unwelcome persistence. The ~petere~ family is large in French — ~appétit~, ~compétition~, ~pétition~, ~répéter~, ~impétueux~ — and the ~perpetuus~ branch adds ~perpétuation~, ~perpétuel~ and the musical ~mouvement perpétuel~.
en.perquisitionner: ~Perquisitionner~ is formed from ~perquisition~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so “to carry out a search,” the kind a police officer or magistrate conducts. The noun comes from Late Latin ~perquisitio~, from Latin ~perquirō~ (“to search thoroughly”), which joins ~per-~ (“through, thoroughly”) to ~quaerere~ (“to seek”). The same ~quaerere~ lies behind ~acquisition~ and ~réquisition~.
en.persifler: The origin is disputed. The account most often given is that ~persifler~ is ~siffler~ (“to hiss, to boo”) with the intensive prefix ~per-~. Others, such as Élisabeth Bourguinat, suppose that ~persifler~ and ~persiflage~ come from the play ~Persiflès~ by Nicolas Racot de Grandval. If the first account holds, the base ~siffler~ comes from Old French ~sifler~, itself probably from a regional variant of Latin ~sībilāre~ (“to hiss”). The verb means to mock or tease someone ironically.
en.persister: Borrowed from Latin ~persistere~ (“to continue steadfastly, to stand firm”), formed from ~per-~ (“through, thoroughly”) and ~sistere~ (“to set, to stand”). ~Sistere~ is a reduplicated present built on the root of ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *~steh₂-~, so to persist is, etymologically, to stand through to the end. French has a whole family built on ~sistere~: ~résister~, ~exister~, ~assister~, ~consister~, ~subsister~ and ~insister~. English ~persist~ was borrowed from the same Latin verb.
en.personnaliser:
From the adjective ~personnel~ (“personal”) plus the verb-forming suffix ~-iser~ — a modern, regular coinage rather than an inherited verb. ~Personnel~ itself goes back, through Old French, to Latin ~persōnālis~ (“of a person”), from ~persōna~. That noun first meant the ~mask~ worn by an actor on the Roman stage, then the dramatic ~role~ played behind it, and only later the human being who plays a role in life. Its own origin is debated: many trace ~persōna~ to Etruscan ~phersu~, itself perhaps linked to Ancient Greek ~πρόσωπον~ (~prósōpon~, “face, mask”).

The suffix ~-iser~ descends from Latin ~-izāre~, borrowed from Greek ~-ίζειν~ (~-ízein~), the same productive ending behind English ~-ize~. To ~personnaliser~ is thus, etymologically, to stamp something with the ~mask~ of an individual — to make it bear a particular face. The Latin root spread widely in French: ~personne~, ~personnage~, ~personnalité~, ~personnel~ (both the adjective and the noun “staff”), and the legal ~personnalité juridique~. English ~person~, ~personnel~, and ~persona~ share the same theatrical ancestor, a reminder that the modern idea of a unique self began as a hollow wooden face.
en.personnifier: Formed from the noun ~personne~ with the suffix ~-ifier~, in the sense “to turn into, or give the form of, N”: to ~personnifier~ is to give a person's form to an idea or object. ~Personne~ comes from Latin ~persona~, which meant a theatre mask and then a role or character. The suffix ~-ifier~ comes from Latin ~-(i)ficāre~, going back to ~facere~ (“to make”), so the verb means, in effect, “to make into a person”.
en.persuader:
Attested from 1370, borrowed from Latin ~persuādēre~ (“to convince thoroughly”), from ~per-~ (“thoroughly”) + ~suādēre~ (“to advise, urge”). ~suādēre~ comes from Proto-Italic *~swādejō~ and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~sweh₂d-~ (“to be sweet, pleasing”) — the very root behind Latin ~suāvis~ (“sweet, agreeable”). So the act of persuading is, at root, a sweetening: to make your view palatable to another.

That same *~sweh₂d-~ gives a surprisingly broad cousinage. Through Germanic it yields English ~sweet~; through Latin ~suāvis~ it yields French ~suave~ and English ~suave~ and ~persuade~; and through Greek it underlies ~hedonism~ (from ~hēdús~, “sweet, pleasant”). French descendants and relatives include ~persuasion~, ~persuasif~, ~dissuader~, and ~suave~ itself. The thread running through all of them — sweetness, pleasantness, persuasion — is one of the tidiest semantic webs in the language: to persuade someone is, etymologically, to make a thing taste good to them.
en.persécuter:
The sources differ slightly. French Wiktionary derives the verb from Latin ~persequor~ (“I pursue”), while English Wiktionary calls it a back-formation from ~persécuteur~, the agent noun, which itself comes from Latin ~persecūtor~. The two accounts agree on the root: Latin ~persequī~ (“to follow through, to pursue relentlessly”), made of ~per-~ (“through, thoroughly”) and ~sequī~ (“to follow”). Latin ~sequī~ goes back to a Proto-Indo-European root *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”), which gave English ~sequel~ and ~sequence~ through Latin, and Latin ~secundus~ (“following, second”).

The Latin verb was neutral and could mean simply to chase or to carry out a plan. Christian Latin gave the noun ~persecūtor~ its dark sense, the one applied to the Roman emperors who hunted believers, and French inherited that sense. From there the verb widened in two directions: to hound a group for its beliefs, and, more lightly, to harass or pester someone, as in ~persécuter~ quelqu'un de questions. The same ~sequī~ underlies French ~suivre~, ~suite~, ~séquence~, ~poursuivre~ and ~second~.
en.persévérer: Borrowed from Latin ~persevērāre~ (“to persist”), by way of Old French ~perseverer~ according to English Wiktionary. The Latin verb is built on ~per-~ (“through, thoroughly”) and the adjective ~sevērus~ (“serious, strict”). French ~sévère~, ~persévérant~ and ~persévérance~ are related; Italian ~perseverare~ and English ~persevere~ come from the same Latin verb.
en.perturber:
From Old French ~perturber~, a learned borrowing from Latin ~perturbāre~ (“to throw into confusion, disturb greatly”), from ~per-~ (“thoroughly”) + ~turbāre~ (“to disturb, agitate”), itself from ~turba~ (“turmoil, crowd, disorder”). ~turba~ is probably borrowed from Ancient Greek ~τύρβη~ (~túrbē~, “tumult, disorder”), and the family is often traced to a Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)twerH-~ (“to swirl, whirl”), the same root that, through Germanic, gave English ~storm~. The Latin verb is the ancestor of Italian ~perturbare~ and Spanish ~perturbar~.

The core image is of a crowd thrown into disorder: ~per-~ intensifies ~turbāre~, so to ~perturber~ is to stir something up completely. The same ~turba~ underlies a remarkable spread of French and English words: ~trouble~ (through Vulgar Latin), ~turbine~, ~turbulent~, ~perturbation~, and the murky adjective ~turbide~. Note that the Greek source of ~turba~ is flagged as merely probable in the sources, and the deeper Indo-European connection — though widely cited — is not beyond dispute; the English cognate ~storm~ rests on that proposed root rather than on a settled descent.
en.pervertir: ~Pervertir~ was borrowed from Latin ~pervertere~ (“to overturn, to turn upside down”), with a change of conjugation class: the Latin ending ~-ere~ became French ~-ir~. Latin ~pervertere~ is built from ~per-~ (“thoroughly”) and ~vertere~ (“to turn”), the verb behind ~convertir~, ~divertir~ and ~invertir~ as well. The Latin sense is physical, whereas French uses ~pervertir~ for “to corrupt” or “to worsen”.
en.pervibrer: Formed from ~vibrer~ with the prefix ~per-~, and used in building to compact concrete with a vibrating tool. The base ~vibrer~ was borrowed from Latin ~vibrāre~ (“to shake, to brandish, to quiver”). The prefix ~per-~ is the Latin word for “through,” here with the sense of thoroughness, so the verb suggests shaking a mass through and through. ~Pervibrer~ is a rare technical coinage, as ~per-~ is no longer a productive prefix on French verbs.
en.peser:
From Old French ~peser~ (“to weigh”), from Vulgar Latin *~pesare~, an alteration of Latin ~pēnsāre~ (“to weigh carefully, weigh out”), the frequentative of ~pendere~ (“to weigh, to hang”), from Proto-Italic *~pendō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)pend-~ (“to pull, to stretch, to spin”). Cognate with Italian ~pesare~ and Spanish ~pesar~, and — through the same Latin verb — with the noun ~poids~ and, more distantly, English ~pension~ and ~pendant~.

The Latin ~pēnsāre~ split into two French verbs that are, etymologically, twins: ~peser~ kept the concrete sense of placing something on a balance, while its learned doublet ~penser~ (“to think”) took up the figurative “to weigh in the mind, to ponder.” To think, in this old image, was to weigh ideas against one another. The metaphor still surfaces in ~peser ses mots~ (“to weigh one's words”) and in the impersonal ~peser~ meaning “to weigh upon, to burden.” From the same root *~(s)pend-~ French inherited a broad family: ~pendre~ (“to hang”), ~suspendre~, ~dépenser~ (literally “to weigh out, to pay out”), ~compenser~, and the noun ~poids~ itself, whose silent ~d~ was added by scribes who wrongly linked it to Latin ~pondus~ (“weight”).
en.pester: Formed from the noun ~peste~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The verb first meant to treat someone as a ~peste~, that is, to call them a plague. The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin ~pestis~ (“scourge”). The verb then softened into the modern sense of ranting or fulminating against someone or something.
en.petit-déjeuner: The verb ~petit-déjeuner~ is formed from the noun phrase ~petit déjeuner~ (“breakfast”), with the verb ending ~-er~, so the formation parse pointing to ~petit~ alone is incomplete. The adjective ~petit~ is a Gallo-Romance word, traced either to Latin ~pitinnus~ (“small”) or to ~petilus~ (“thin”), and the question is open. The noun phrase literally means “small lunch,” and the verb turns that meal into an action.
en.peupler:
Denominal verb from the noun ~peuple~ (“people”) + ~-er~. ~Peuple~ descends from Latin ~populus~ (“people, nation, the populace”). The deeper origin of ~populus~ is genuinely unsettled: by one account it goes back to a reduplicated form of the root of ~pleō~ (“to fill”), Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₁-~, making “the people” literally a fullness or a crowd; another hypothesis proposes an Etruscan source, and the standard handbooks flag the further origin as simply unknown. Honest sources keep both options open.

A pointed twist: the Latin verb ~populārī~ did not mean “to populate” but its near-opposite, “to ravage, lay waste” (as an army “peoples” a land with soldiers). French ~peupler~, rebuilt natively from ~peuple~, took the constructive sense “to fill with inhabitants, to populate,” so the French verb and its Latin near-namesake pull in contrary directions. From the same ~populus~ root French inherited ~peuple~, ~peuplade~, ~population~, ~populaire~, ~populeux~, and ~public~ (through ~pūblicus~), alongside the learned ~dépeupler~ (“to depopulate”).
en.phagocyter:
~Phagocyter~ is the verb of ~phagocyte~ (“a cell that engulfs particles”), formed with ~-er~. The noun came into French through German ~Phagocyten~ (1884), a scientific coinage from two Greek elements: ~φάγος~ (“glutton”), related to the verb ~phagein~ (“to eat”), and ~kutos~ (“cell, cavity”). A phagocyte is therefore, literally, an “eating cell.”

The verb keeps the biological sense, “to engulf and digest,” as when a white blood cell destroys a bacterium, and it has taken on a figurative one, “to swallow up, to absorb entirely.” The two Greek halves are very productive in French scientific vocabulary. ~Phago-~ appears in ~anthropophage~ (“man-eater”), and ~-cyte~ in ~leucocyte~.
en.philosopher: ~Philosopher~ is borrowed from Latin ~philosophārī~ (“to philosophize”), according to French Wiktionary. The Latin verb is built on ~philosophus~, a loan from Greek ~philósophos~ (“lover of wisdom”), made of ~phílos~ (“loving”) and ~sophía~ (“wisdom”). The French nouns ~philosophe~ and ~philosophie~ come from the same Greek source, so the verb belongs to a family whose name literally means “love of wisdom.”
en.phosphater: ~Phosphater~ is a denominal verb: the noun ~phosphate~ plus the ending ~-er~, in the usual sense of applying a noun, here to treat or provide something with phosphate. The noun is itself a French formation, from ~phosphore~ with the suffix ~-ate~, the ending used for chemical salts.
en.phosphorer: ~Phosphorer~ is a verb made from the noun ~phosphore~ with the ending ~-er~. The noun is the name of the chemical element, whose Greek source ~phōsphoros~ means “light-bringer” (from ~phōs~, “light,” and ~pherein~, “to carry”). The verb has a technical sense, to treat with phosphorus or a phosphate, and a familiar one, to think hard or rack one's brains. The sources do not explain how the second sense arose from the first.
en.photocopier: ~Photocopier~ is formed on the noun ~photocopie~ with the verb ending ~-er~, and it means “to reproduce a document by a photographic process.” ~Photocopie~ combines the prefix ~photo-~, from Greek ~phôs~ (genitive ~phōtós~, “light”), with ~copie~, from Latin ~copia~ (“abundance”). English Wiktionary instead analyses the verb as ~photo-~ plus ~copier~.
en.photographier: ~Photographier~ is formed from the noun ~photographie~ with the verbal ending ~-er~: to take a photograph. ~Photographie~ is a learned compound of two Greek elements, ~φῶς~ (~phôs~, genitive ~phōtós~, “light”) and ~γράφω~ (~gráphō~, “to write, to draw”), so a photograph is literally a “writing with light.” The noun was coined in the 19th century, when the technique itself was invented, and the verb followed from it. English ~photograph~ and German ~fotografieren~ were formed on the same Greek parts.
en.phraser: Formed from the noun ~phrase~ and the verbal suffix ~-er~, so “to phrase,” to shape something into phrases. The base ~phrase~ comes from Latin ~phrasis~ (“diction”), which borrowed Greek ~phrásis~ (“manner of expression”), from the verb ~phrázō~ (“to tell, to express”).
en.piaffer: ~Piaffer~ is of onomatopoeic origin: the word imitates the sound and the action it names, a horse stamping or pawing the ground. No older source word is recorded for it, so it does not descend from a Latin or Germanic verb. Its sound-imitating shape is the whole of its story.
en.piailler: ~Piailler~ is most likely imitative, built on the sound ~pi~, which evokes the cry of small animals, with a verb ending. It means to cheep or chirp, and by extension to make a high-pitched noise. French Wiktionary lists it beside ~piper~, ~piauler~ and ~pioupiouter~, which imitate the same cry, and English Wiktionary compares ~piaf~ (“sparrow”).
en.pianoter: Formed from the noun ~piano~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun is borrowed from Italian ~piano~, a clipping of ~pianoforte~, which joins ~piano~ (“soft”) and ~forte~ (“loud”). The instrument got that name because the older keyboard instruments, notably the harpsichord, could not vary their volume. ~Pianoter~ carries the instrument's name over to tapping the fingers as on a keyboard, and so to typing on a computer.
en.piauler: First written ~pioler~ and ~pieuler~ (1552), ~piauler~ is derived, like ~piailler~, from an imitative stem ~pi-~ that evokes a shrill sound. It belongs to the family of verbs that copy the cheeping of chicks and small birds, and it was later extended to any thin, plaintive cry, such as that of a child or a cat. Its spelling has shifted from ~pioler~ to ~piauler~ but the sound origin is unchanged.
en.picoler: Borrowed and adapted from Italian ~piccolo~, which French Wiktionary glosses as both “small wine” and “small transverse flute.” The slang verb ~picoler~ means to drink, especially to tipple alcohol regularly. French Wiktionary points to ~flûter~, another verb for drinking, as a parallel. The Italian word is the same ~piccolo~ that English uses for the small flute, and it means “little.”
en.picorer: The origin is not settled. Both Wiktionaries point to ~piquer~ (“to prick, to sting”) as the source, and English Wiktionary adds that the word began as military slang and that the link is only probable. In modern French the verb means to peck or to nibble, and how it came from the older sense is not explained by the sources, so no story is offered here.
en.picoter: Formed from ~piquer~ (“to prick, to sting”) with the suffix ~-oter~, which adds a sense of small, repeated action: ~picoter~ is “to prick again and again,” hence “to sting, to tingle, to peck,” and figuratively “to pester.” The base ~piquer~ appeared in the late thirteenth century, and its origin is debated. The TLFi favors a Vulgar Latin *~pīkkāre~ built on an expressive root imitating a sharp tap, while French Wiktionary instead derives it from ~pic~, a pickaxe or woodpecker. The related noun ~picot~ names a small point or loop.
en.pieuter: Derived from the slang noun ~pieu~, which in this register means “bed.” The ordinary meaning of ~pieu~ is a stake driven into the ground, so the slang use is a figurative one, and ~pieuter~, with the verb ending ~-er~, means to sleep, to go to bed. Both Wiktionaries give the origin as the slang sense of ~pieu~ and say no more. The verb is informal and belongs to the same set of slang words for the bed and sleeping as ~se pieuter~ and ~pioncer~.
en.pifer: The verb comes from ~pif~, a familiar French word for “nose.” The sources give nothing more: they do not say how the nose led to the sense “to put up with,” so that step is best left unexplained. As a familiar word drawn from a part of the body, it belongs to colloquial French, and the ending ~-er~ is the ordinary mark of a first-conjugation verb.
en.piffer: ~Piffer~ is formed from the slang noun ~pif~ (“nose”) with the verbal ending ~-er~. The origin of ~pif~ itself is unsettled: French Wiktionary links one sense to a ~piff-~ that suggests bulk, while English Wiktionary calls it possibly onomatopoeic. The verb is mostly heard in the negative, ~ne pas pouvoir piffer quelqu'un~, “to be unable to stand someone.”
en.pigeonner: Formed in French from the noun ~pigeon~ with the verb ending ~-er~, from the characteristics attributed to the bird, which yield the sense “to dupe, to fleece.” The noun is Old French ~pijon~, from Late Latin ~pīpiōnem~, built on Latin ~pīpiō~ (“young bird”), literally a “little bird that chirps,” from ~pīpiāre~ (“to chirp”). The family is a small one in French, but the figurative sense of ~pigeon~ as a gullible victim is the key to this verb.
en.piger:
French Wiktionary traces ~piger~ to popular Latin *~pedicus~ (“that catches in a trap”), from Latin ~pedica~ (“snare”). English Wiktionary agrees on a Late Latin *~pedicus~, an adjective meaning “caught,” and says the verb is “believed” to come from it, so the link is likely rather than certain. It adds that ~piger~ is a doublet of ~piéger~. A ~pedica~ was a snare or fetter for the feet, and the word is built on ~pes~ (“foot”).

According to French Wiktionary, the word took on a range of meanings corresponding to “to trap, to catch” during the nineteenth century. The slang sense “to understand,” to catch on, fits that line, though no source spells out the step. French Wiktionary also lists a second ~piger~, formed on ~pige~ (“measure”). French words from the same Latin family include ~piège~, ~piéger~ and ~pied~, the last from ~pes~.
en.pigmenter: ~Pigmenter~ is built on the noun ~pigment~ and the ending ~-er~, and means “to colour with pigment.” The noun is a borrowing from Latin ~pigmentum~ (“colour for painting”), formed from ~pingere~ (“to paint”) and the suffix ~-mentum~. Latin ~pigmentum~ has a doublet in French, ~piment~, which French took from Spanish by a different route.
en.pignocher: The origin of ~pignocher~ is uncertain. English Wiktionary treats it as an alteration of Middle French ~espinocher~, from ~espinoche~ (“morsel”). French Wiktionary also gives ~espinocher~ (“to busy oneself with trifles”), relates it to ~pinailler~, and cites Littré, who compares ~picocher~, ~picorer~ and ~picoter~. A second account derives it from ~peigner~ with the suffix ~-ocher~, using the quarrelsome sense “to thrash.”
en.piler: The origin of ~piler~ is given two ways. One account takes it from Latin ~pīlāre~ (“to ram down, to press”), itself from ~pīla~ (“column”); the other treats it as a French verb formed on the noun ~pile~ plus ~-er~. The sources do not settle which is right, and the two may in fact converge. The sense is “to pound or crush,” as in a mortar. Related to it is ~pilon~, the pounding tool, and a colloquial use turned the verb toward braking hard.
en.piller: The origin of ~piller~ is uncertain, and the two Wiktionaries differ. French Wiktionary proposes no Latin source and only records how the meaning developed: first “to handle roughly, to harass” (compare Old French ~espillier~ and ~despillier~), then “to strip someone of their belongings, often by trickery”, and in the fourteenth century ~peillier~, “to seize something by force”. English Wiktionary instead derives it, through Middle French ~piller~ and Old French ~pillier~, from Latin ~pilleus~ (“felt cap”), a link the French text does not endorse, so treat it as a proposal. The family includes ~pillage~ and ~pillard~, and English borrowed ~pillage~ from French.
en.pilonner: ~Pilonner~ is a French derivative of ~pilon~ (“pestle, pounder”) with the verb ending ~-er~. Its earliest attested sense, from 1723, belongs to wool-working: to stir wool in a cauldron with a wooden shovel in order to remove its grease. A glassmaking use is recorded in 1803, and in 1888 slang gave it the meaning “to beg.” The best-known modern sense dates from the First World War: in 1916 it was used for hammering a position with artillery shells, and a 1918 text uses it too. The verb thus passed from the workshop to the battlefield, and it now covers pounding, grinding and bombarding.
en.piloter:
A denominal verb from the noun ~pilote~ (« pilot, helmsman »), which French borrowed in the sixteenth century from Italian ~pilota~. The Italian form is itself an alteration of an earlier ~pedotta~ / ~pedoto~, traced — by a reconstruction the dictionaries mark as unattested — to a Byzantine Greek *~pēdōtēs~ (« steersman »), from Ancient Greek ~pēdon~ (« blade of an oar, steering oar »). The ~pil-~ form is probably owed to influence from the Italian verb ~pileggiare~ (« to navigate »), so even the modern shape rests partly on a proposed crossing rather than a clean line.

From the sea the word climbed into every vehicle: one ~pilote~ a ship, then a plane, a race car, even a company. The verb spread its senses outward — to guide, to steer, to manage, and figuratively to « pilot » a project through to completion. English took the same ~pilot~ from French. Modern relatives include ~pilotage~, ~copilote~, ~télépiloter~ (« to fly a drone »), and the noun ~pilote~ used adjectivally, as in a ~projet~ ~pilote~ (« pilot project »).
en.pimenter: ~Pimenter~ is formed from ~piment~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, and means to season with hot pepper or, figuratively, to spice something up. The noun ~piment~ is inherited from Latin ~pigmentum~ (“pigment, coloring matter”): in Old French ~piment~ (also ~pimenc~) meant “balsam, fragrant spice,” and some modern senses were later influenced by Spanish ~pimiento~. French also borrowed the Latin word directly as ~pigment~, so ~piment~ and ~pigment~ are doublets.
en.pinailler: The origin of ~pinailler~ is uncertain. French Wiktionary dates the verb to 1934 and says nothing more about where it comes from, and English Wiktionary likewise calls it uncertain. It means “to nitpick” or “to split hairs,” that is, to quibble over tiny details. Since no source traces it to a base word or an older language, the honest etymology is an open question.
en.pincer: The origin of ~pincer~ is uncertain. English Wiktionary says only that it is inherited from Old French ~pincier~ (“to pinch”). French Wiktionary proposes an expressive root ~pints~, also seen in Spanish ~pinchar~ (“to prick”) and Italian ~pinzare~ (“to sting,” of an insect). It adds that this root would come, by nasalization, from a root ~pic~ (“pointed”), which would also underlie Spanish ~pizcar~. Treat that as a proposal, not a settled account. Within French the verb has produced ~pince~, ~pincée~ and ~pincette~, all built around the gripping gesture of finger and thumb.
en.pindariser: A learned verb formed on the name of ~Pindare~ (Pindar), the Greek poet of antiquity, with the verb-forming suffix ~-iser~, “to act like N.” ~Pindariser~ means “to write like Pindar,” and by extension to write in a lofty, ornate, high-flown style, as Pindar's celebrated odes were thought to be.
en.pinter: ~Pinter~ is a slang verb formed from ~pinte~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, with the sense of drinking, even getting drunk. The noun ~pinte~, a measure for drink, comes from Vulgar Latin *~pincta~ (“a mark used to indicate the level on vessels”), from Latin ~pictus~ (“painted”), the participle of ~pingō~ (“to paint”). French Wiktionary traces the same line through a Late Latin *~pinctus~. So the drinker's word goes back to a painted mark on a cup.
en.piocher: ~Piocher~ is formed on the noun ~pioche~ (“pickaxe”): its first sense is to dig or break up ground with one. The meaning then extended figuratively to working hard at something, hence to cram or to swot. The sources I could draw on give nothing further, neither an origin for ~pioche~ itself nor a date for the figurative sense.
en.pioncer:
The origin of ~pioncer~ is uncertain. One account derives it from the slang verb ~piausser~ (“to lie down”, attested in 1628), which comes from the noun ~piausse~ (“bed”, attested in 1562) and from slang ~piau~ (“bed”), a dialect form of ~peau~ (“skin”), a bed made of skins. In this account the form was then altered after ~ronfler~ (“to snore”).

The same family shows a parallel line. Alongside ~piau~ and ~piausser~ stands the group ~peau~ and ~peausser~, with ~le peaux huré~ recorded in 1596 as a word for “the bed”, and, more recently, ~pieu~ and ~pieuter~, which are still slang for the bed and for going to bed. The modern verb is informal, a familiar word for sleeping.
en.piper: French Wiktionary gives two accounts without choosing between them. By one, ~piper~ comes from Latin ~pipāre~ (“to chirp, to peep”). By the other, it comes from English ~pipe~. The verb now means to load dice or mark playing cards for cheating. The origin is therefore uncertain, and the sources at hand do not say which account, if either, explains that sense.
en.pique-niquer: ~Pique-niquer~ is the noun ~pique-nique~ + the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun is explained as ~piquer~ (here “to pick at food”) + ~nique~ (“a small thing of no value”), a meal to which each guest brings a share. French Wiktionary also notes that English ~picnic~ was itself taken from French, so the word made a round trip. The verb turns the outing into an action, “to have a picnic.” The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is the default way to coin a new French verb.
en.piqueniquer: This verb is formed from the noun ~pique-nique~ with the ending ~-er~, and means “to have a picnic”. The noun is explained as ~piquer~ (here “to pick at food”) joined to ~nique~ (“a small thing of no value”), in the sense of a meal to which each guest brings a share. French Wiktionary also records English ~picnic~, itself taken from French, with the sense of a shared meal in the countryside.
en.piquer:
~piquer~ surfaces in the second half of the thirteenth century, and its origin is debated. The explanation favored by the TLFi posits a Vulgar Latin *~pīkkāre~, built on an expressive, onomatopoeic root *~pikk-~ imitating a sharp tap — the high vowel suggesting the point, the crisp consonants the little explosion of the blow. The verb's spread is pan-Romance — Italian ~piccare~, Spanish ~picar~ — which argues for a popular root older than any one language. A rival account, the one French Wiktionary gives, instead derives the verb from ~pic~ (“pick; woodpecker”), whose name goes back to Latin ~pīcus~ (“woodpecker”) — on that reading, nature's own striker of sharp blows would stand behind the verb. Either way, no classical Latin ancestor is attested: piquer is a child of the spoken language.

From “to prick” the verb fanned out into one of the busiest words in French: bees, needles, curiosity and wounded pride all piquent, and the slang sense “to steal” — snatching something with one quick jab — was already in use by the late Middle Ages. The family is everywhere: ~pique~ the weapon (and the card suit French calls by that name), ~piquant~, ~piqûre~, ~piquet~. The most charming member is ~pique-nique~, attested by 1694, from ~piquer~ in the sense “to pick at food” plus ~nique~ (“a little thing of no value”). English borrowed it as ~picnic~, tied the word firmly to eating outdoors, and nineteenth-century French then took that fashion back from English — a word that went on a picnic and came home changed. English ~pique~, the sting of wounded pride, is the same French prick in genteel dress.
en.piqueter: ~Piqueter~ is formed from the noun ~piquet~ (“stake, small pointed post”) with the suffix ~-eter~, a combination of ~-et~ and ~-er~. The noun is itself a derivative of ~piquer~ (“to prick”) with ~-et~. The verb first meant to attack with blows of a pick. Its modern sense, to dot or speckle a surface, is read as a frequentative of ~piquer~, as in repeated small pricks, while the sense of marking out with stakes follows ~piquet~ directly.
en.pirater: Formed from the noun ~pirate~ and the verb ending ~-er~, which turns a noun into a verb meaning “to act as N.” The noun ~pirate~ was borrowed from Latin ~pirata~, itself taken from Greek ~peiratēs~ (“brigand, sea-raider”). The verb first meant “to practice piracy,” then was applied by analogy to illegally copying software, music or films, and to breaking into computer systems. The figurative sense treats the copier as a sea-robber who takes what belongs to others.
en.pirouetter: Formed in French from the noun ~pirouette~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun first meant a “spinning top,” attested in the 15th century, and descends from an Old French ~pirouette~ (“a kind of top”). English Wiktionary analyzes it as a Gallo-Roman root *~pir-~ (“peg, plug”), which also gave Italian ~piruolo~ (“peg top”), plus the diminutive ~-ette~. The dancer's turn on one foot took its name from the toy, and the verb ~pirouetter~ means to spin in this way, literally or figuratively.
en.pisser:
From Middle French ~pisser~, from Old French ~pissier~, which goes back to a Vulgar Latin form *~pīssiāre~. The origin of that form is uncertain. French Wiktionary calls it an onomatopoeia, and English Wiktionary says it is possibly Germanic but more likely echoic.
