The verb has relatives across Europe: Italian ~pisciare~, Occitan ~pissar~, Catalan ~pixar~, Romanian ~pișa~, English ~piss~ and German ~pissen~.

French Wiktionary notes two limits on the story. The verb is absent from the Celtic languages, and it is hard to connect to Latin ~pitissare~ (“to spit”), so that link cannot be taken for granted. In French, ~pisser~ is a vulgar word, and its family includes ~pissat~, ~pissotière~ and ~pissenlit~, which is the French name of the dandelion.
en.pister: Formed from the noun ~piste~ (“track, trail”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning “to follow a trail,” and then “to tail someone.” The noun was borrowed from Italian ~pista~. French Wiktionary derives that word from the verb ~pistare~ (“to trample, to crush”), from Latin ~pistare~ (“to pound”), the sense still heard in Italian ~pistone~ (“pestle”). English Wiktionary instead treats ~pista~ as a variant of ~pesta~ (“footprint”). Both accounts agree on the picture: a track is what feet leave behind.
en.pistonner: ~Pistonner~ is formed from ~piston~ with the verbal ending ~-er~; its figurative sense is to pull strings for someone. ~Piston~ was borrowed in the sixteenth century, in the sense of “pestle,” from Italian ~pistone~, from Latin ~pistāre~ (“to pound”). It is also tied to an old French verb ~pister~ (“to pound”). The mechanical piston and the slang senses are later uses of the same word.
en.pitonner: Formed from ~piton~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to drive in a piton” in climbing. The noun ~piton~ comes from Occitan, from a stem ~pitt-~ expressing something small and therefore pointed, plus the suffix ~-on~. In Quebec French ~piton~ also names the buttons of an electrical or electronic device, and French Wiktionary records a second verb ~pitonner~ built on that sense.
en.pivoter: Formed from the noun ~pivot~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, so “to turn on a pivot.” The noun is of uncertain origin. French Wiktionary tentatively links it to a form related to Latin ~pungere~ (“to prick”), by way of words for a tooth or point such as Old Occitan ~pua~ and Catalan ~pua~, but English Wiktionary just calls the origin uncertain. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~.
en.piéger: ~Piéger~ is formed on the noun ~piège~ (“trap, snare”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, and it is already recorded in Old French as ~piegier~, so it is no recent coinage. The noun comes from Latin ~pedica~ (“fetter for the feet, snare”), derived from ~pēs~, ~pedis~ (“foot”): a trap was, at root, something that catches the foot. From “to set a trap for” the verb extended to “to catch in a trap” and, figuratively, “to trick”. Today it also means to booby-trap a car or a parcel. The ending ~-er~ is the ordinary way French turns a noun into a verb.
en.piéter: From Latin ~peditāre~ (“to go on foot”), itself drawn from ~pedes~ (“one who goes on foot”). That Latin word belongs to the same family as French ~pied~ (“foot”), which descends from Latin ~pēs~. In French the verb now has a narrow use: it mostly describes a bird walking on the ground, and it can also mean to plant one's feet firmly.
en.piétiner: Formed from ~piéter~ with the ending ~-iner~, an expressive verb suffix that is not productive and has no established origin. The base ~piéter~ comes from Latin ~peditāre~ (“to go on foot”), drawn from ~pedes~ (“one who goes on foot”), a word of the family of ~pied~, from Latin ~pēs~ (“foot”). French ~piétiner~ means to stamp one's feet or to trample, and since 1866 also, figuratively, to make no progress.
en.placarder: Formed as a verb from the noun ~placard~, taken in its old sense of a notice stuck on a wall: to ~placarder~ is to post such a notice, and by extension to plaster a surface with them. That old sense of the noun has been largely overtaken by the modern meaning of ~placard~ as a cupboard, but the verb kept the older one.
en.placardiser: A neologism built on the expression ~mettre au placard~ (“to put in the cupboard”), with the suffix ~-iser~. To put someone in the cupboard is to shelve them, and ~placardiser~ names the gradual stripping of an employee's powers and duties. English Wiktionary derives the verb straight from the noun ~placard~. The suffix ~-iser~ was borrowed from Late Latin ~-izāre~ and is fully productive in administrative and journalistic vocabulary.
en.placer:
A denominal verb of the 16th century, ~placer~ was formed from the noun ~place~ plus the verbal suffix ~-er~. The noun ~place~ comes from Old French ~place~, from Vulgar Latin *~plattĕa~, an altered form of Latin ~platēa~ (“a broad street, an open space”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~πλατεῖα~ (~plateîa~, “broad,” in ~plateîa hodós~, “a broad way”). The Greek adjective rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~pleth₂-~ (“flat, broad, to spread”). Through that root ~place~ is cousin to Italian ~piazza~ and Spanish ~plaza~, and to English ~place~ and ~flat~.

The journey of meaning runs from “a wide road” to “an open square in a town” to, more abstractly, “a spot, a position, a rank.” Once the noun could name any position whatever, French speakers naturally coined a verb for putting something into its position — and so, around 1564, ~placer~ appeared, meaning “to set in a place, to seat.” From the same broad-and-flat root *~pleth₂-~ French gathered ~plat~, ~plateau~, ~platane~ (the plane tree, named for its wide leaves), ~plaine~, and ~aplatir~, while ~place~ itself spun off ~placement~, ~remplacer~, and ~déplacer~.
en.plafonner: Formed in French from ~plafond~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~plafond~ is itself a compound of ~plat~ (“flat”) and ~fond~ (“bottom”), so it first meant a flat surface seen as the bottom of a structure, then a ceiling. The verb originally meant “to fit with a ceiling.” Later it took on a figurative sense, “to reach a ceiling”: of prices, wages or performance, to rise to a limit and go no higher, and hence to cap something at a fixed maximum.
en.plagier: ~Plagier~ is a back-formation from the noun ~plagiaire~ (“plagiarist”). A back-formation works backwards: the noun is the older word, and the verb was derived by trimming its ending and adding a verbal one. The verb thus names what a ~plagiaire~ does, which is to pass off another person's work as one's own. English ~plagiarize~ and ~plagiarism~ belong to the same family.
en.plaider: The two Wiktionaries differ slightly on the route. French Wiktionary treats ~plaider~ as a verb formed on the old noun ~plaid~ (“lawsuit, hearing”), while English Wiktionary traces Old French ~plaidier~ from ~plait~, possibly matching a Vulgar Latin verb. Both lead to Latin ~placitum~ (“what pleases”), from ~placēre~ (“to please”), the source of French ~plaire~. In medieval legal Latin that word came to mean a decision, then an appearance before a court, then a lawsuit, and medieval Latin also had a verb ~placitare~ with the sense “to plead”. Courts still say ~plaise à la cour~. English ~plead~ is cognate. The ~plaid~ of Scottish cloth is an unrelated homonym.
en.plaindre:
From Old French ~plaindre~, from Latin ~plangere~ (“to beat, to strike; to beat the breast in grief; to lament”), from Proto-Italic *~plāngō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₂g-~ (“to strike”). The root's striking sense survives in cognates: Latin ~plectere~ (“to beat, punish”), Ancient Greek ~πλήσσω~ (“I strike”), and Old Church Slavonic ~plakati~ (“to weep, beat the breast”).

The memorable detail lies in the root itself: ~plangere~ named the physical gesture of mourning — striking one's own breast — from which the sense of lamenting grew. The Romance descendants split the inheritance: Italian ~piangere~ and Spanish ~plañir~ kept the weeping sense, while French shifted the active verb toward feeling sorrow for another, “to pity,” reserving the reflexive ~se plaindre~ for “to complain.” From the same root come ~plainte~ (“complaint, lament”), ~plaintif~ (“plaintive”), and the legal ~plaignant~ (“plaintiff”). Behind the courtroom complaint and the gentle act of pity alike stands one ancient image: a hand beating against the chest.
en.plaire:
Modern French ~plaire~ comes, through Old French, from Latin ~placēre~ (“to please, to be agreeable, to satisfy”). In Old French the infinitive was long ~plaisir~ (the source of the noun ~plaisir~, “pleasure”), and ~plaire~ is most likely a later analogical reshaping modeled on verbs like ~faire~, working back from forms such as ~il plaît~. The deeper origin is debated: the Latin verb is tied to ~plācāre~ (“to soothe, to appease”), and many trace both to a Proto-Indo-European root *~pleh₂k-~ (“flat, to be calm”); De Vaan instead reconstructs *~pleHk-~ (“to please, to permit”), with secure cognates only in Tocharian ~plāk-~ (“to please, to agree”). Romance kept the verb alive everywhere: Italian ~piacere~ and Spanish ~placer~ are its siblings, and English borrowed the family as ~please~ and ~pleasure~.

From the start the sense was “to give satisfaction,” and it never strayed far. A striking trace is the fossilized impersonal ~plaît-il ?~ (“pardon?”) and the courteous ~s'il vous plaît~ (“if it pleases you,” i.e. “please”), where the verb survives in a frozen subjunctive-flavored politeness formula. The same Latin stock seeded a wide family in French: ~plaisir~, ~complaire~ and ~déplaire~, the adjective ~plaisant~, ~complaisant~, and ~placide~ (“placid, calm,” straight from ~plācidus~). Through Latin ~plācāre~ French also gained the learned apaiser's cousin ~placation~ and the verb ~placer~ in its rarer sense. Few verbs so thoroughly stayed put: ~plaire~ has meant essentially the same thing for two thousand years.
en.plaisanter: Formed from ~plaisant~ (“pleasing, amusing”) + ~-er~, “to speak or act in an amusing way.” It is first attested in Middle French, in the sense of “to jest.” The base ~plaisant~ is the present participle of ~plaire~ (“to please”), which comes from Latin ~placēre~. The verb gradually replaced Old French ~gaber~ (“to mock, to joke”), which has since vanished from the language. The sense has remained stable since, from light teasing to saying something not meant seriously.
en.plancher: Formed from the noun ~planche~ and the verb ending ~-er~; the Old French verb ~planchier~ is recorded around 1135. The noun ~planche~ comes from Vulgar Latin ~planca~, a contracted form of *~palanca~, from Greek ~phálanx~ (“log, stout stick”), the same word that gave ~phalange~. The verb first meant “to lay a floor of boards.” The modern sense, “to work hard on a subject, to be quizzed,” is a student slang development from the board of the classroom, and fits the same pattern as ~bûcher~.
en.planchéier: This verb is formed from ~planche~ (“board, plank”) with the suffix ~-oyer~, an older verb ending that no longer makes new verbs, and means “to cover with boards”. The noun ~planche~ comes from Old French and, before that, from Late Latin ~planca~, a contraction of ~palanca~. That Latin word goes back to Ancient Greek ~φάλαγξ~ (“log, stout stick”), the same Greek word that gave French ~phalange~, so a plank and a phalanx of soldiers share an ancestor.
en.planer: French Wiktionary gives two accounts that it treats as related: a verb formed on ~plain~ (“flat, level”) with ~-er~, and a descent from Late Latin ~planāre~, itself from ~planus~. English Wiktionary gives only the first, from ~plain~, which comes from Latin ~plānus~ (“flat, level”). Either way, the idea is flatness: a bird that ~plane~s glides on outspread wings, held level in the air. The sense then widened to any smooth floating motion, and figuratively to being lost in a daydream or high on something, as in ~planer~ (“to be out of touch with reality”).
en.planifier: Built from ~plan~ and the verbal suffix ~-ifier~, with the sense “to organize according to a plan.” The suffix descends from Latin ~-(i)ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”), so ~planifier~ is literally “to make into a plan.” The noun ~plan~ has a disputed history: it is either a learned re-borrowing of Latin ~planus~ (“flat, level”), a doublet of ~plain~, or a back-formation from ~planter~ (earlier ~plant~), whose sense of a layout drawn on the ground widened to “project.” Suffix and verb are at home in learned, technical and administrative French, where ~-ifier~ is still productive.
en.planquer: ~Planquer~ is an alteration of ~planter~, used in an old slang sense “to put, to hide.” French Wiktionary adds, with a “perhaps,” that ~plaquer~ in the sense “to put, to apply” may have crossed with it. English Wiktionary gives only the alteration of ~planter~. The core of the story is therefore a slang twist on a familiar verb, and the second influence is a proposal, not an established fact.
en.planter:
From Latin ~plantare~, a verb built on ~planta~. The noun ~planta~ originally meant “the sole of the foot”; from Proto-Italic *~plantā~ it traces to Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₂-~ (“flat, to spread”), the root that also gives English ~floor~ and ~field~ and Latin ~planus~ (“level”). Sister forms appear as Italian ~piantare~, Spanish ~plantar~, and — borrowed early into Germanic — English ~plant~ and German ~pflanzen~.

The link between “sole of the foot” and “to plant” is appealing but should be handled with care: lexicographers note that the botanical ~planta~ (“shoot, cutting”) may be a separate word, and the agricultural verb is often reconstructed as having meant “to press the earth (with the sole of the foot)” to set a cutting — a plausible but partly conjectural bridge rather than a documented step. From that core sense of fixing something firmly into the ground French generalized to “drive in” a nail or stake and to “pitch” a tent, and figuratively to ~planter~ someone (to leave them stranded). The modern computing sense — a program that ~plante~ (“crashes”) — extends the image of something abruptly stopping dead, stuck fast. Related French words include ~plante~, ~plantation~, and ~plant~ (“seedling”).
en.plaquer: The two Wiktionaries disagree on direction, but both lead to Dutch. French Wiktionary derives the verb ~plaquer~ directly from Dutch ~placken~ (“to stick, to patch”), making the noun ~plaque~ a back-formation from it. English Wiktionary does the reverse and reads ~plaquer~ as ~plaque~ + ~-er~, with ~plaque~ itself from Middle Dutch ~placke~ (“disk, patch”), from Proto-Germanic *~plaggą~ (“patch”). The core idea is a flat piece applied to a surface, hence “to plate, to veneer.” From that image come the figurative senses of pressing flat, as in a tackle in rugby.
en.plasmifier: A French formation from the noun ~plasma~ and the verb suffix ~-ifier~, “to make, to turn into,” which comes from Latin ~-ficāre~ and ultimately ~facere~ (“to make”). ~Plasmifier~ therefore means “to turn into plasma.” The base ~plasma~ is Latin ~plasma~ (“form, figure”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~πλάσμα~ (~plásma~, “something molded, a figure”).
en.plastifier: Formed from ~plastique~ plus the suffix ~-ifier~, which can mean “to put into the form of, to treat with” a noun; ~plastifier~ thus means to coat or cover with plastic, hence “to laminate.” The base ~plastique~ was borrowed into Middle French from Latin ~plasticus~, itself from Greek ~plastikós~ (“relating to moulding”), from the verb ~plássein~ (“to mould, to form”), which also gave ~plasma~. The suffix ~-ifier~ goes back to Latin ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”).
en.plastiquer: Formed from the noun ~plastic~ (“plastic explosive”) with the verbal suffix ~-er~: to ~plastiquer~ is to blow something up with it. ~Plastic~ was borrowed from English ~plastic explosive~. According to French Wiktionary, the explosive was introduced to the United States by the British in 1940, and the samples brought by the Tizard mission bore the French label ~explosif plastique~, because they had been packed to be parachuted to the French Resistance.
en.plastronner: Formed from ~plastron~ with the verb ending ~-er~, it means to swagger. The noun ~plastron~ was borrowed from Italian ~piastrone~, a derivative of ~piastra~ (“plate”). French Wiktionary links ~piastra~ to ~piastre~ and ~plâtre~, so this verb belongs to a family of words that began with the idea of a flat plate or sheet. The sources do not say how the sense of strutting arose from the noun, so the link between the two meanings is left open.
en.platiner: Formed in French from ~platine~ (“platinum”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so to coat or treat with platinum. The metal's name was borrowed from Spanish ~platina~, a diminutive of ~plata~ (“silver”), because of the metal's silvery look. It spread across Europe in the eighteenth century, from Spanish America.
en.pleurer:
From Middle and Old French ~plorer~ (“to weep, lament”), attested around 980, from Latin ~plorare~ (“to cry out, wail, lament”), which in popular speech displaced classical ~lacrimare~ (“to shed tears”). The modern infinitive ~pleurer~ arose by analogy with the stressed present forms ~je pleure~, ~tu pleures~. The deeper origin of ~plorare~ is uncertain: it is perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *~pleh₃(w)-~ (“to flow”), a tidy fit for tears, though the sources flag this as merely possible rather than established.

In Latin, ~plorare~ first meant to cry out in distress; the sense narrowed over time from vocal lamentation to the physical act of shedding tears, which is the dominant meaning in French today. The same stem yields a rich family of modern words: ~pleur~ (“a tear, weeping”), ~éploré~ (“tearful, grief-stricken”), and the prefixed ~déplorer~ (~dé-~ + ~plorer~, “to deplore, lament”) with its noun ~déploration~. French thus keeps both registers of the old verb — the quiet falling of tears and the loud voicing of grief.
en.pleurnicher:
~Pleurnicher~ was formerly spelled ~pleurmicher~. It is built on ~pleurer~ (“to weep”), but the rest of the word is uncertain. English Wiktionary treats it as simply derived from ~pleurer~, while French Wiktionary adds that the second element is perhaps the Old French ~michier~ (“to beat senseless”). That suggestion is only tentative, so the origin of the ending should be regarded as unsettled.

The verb ~pleurer~ is inherited from Latin ~plōrāre~, and French Wiktionary points further to the family of ~plaindre~ (Latin ~plangō~, “to strike, to lament”). ~Pleurnicher~ means to whine, to cry in a small, tearful way. Its noun ~pleurnicheur~ (“crybaby”) and ~pleurnicherie~ are common, and the verb stays in everyday, mildly scornful speech.
en.pleuvasser: Formed from ~pleuvoir~ (“to rain”) with the suffix ~-asser~, which gives a verb a dismissive, intermittent sense, as in ~rêvasser~. It means to rain a little or on and off. The Académie lists it as a familiar impersonal verb, used only with ~il~, like the verb it comes from. ~Pleuvoir~ itself goes back to Latin ~pluere~.
en.pleuviner: ~Pleuviner~ comes from Old French ~ploviner~, which English Wiktionary analyzes as ~pleuvoir~ (“to rain”) plus the suffix ~-iner~. The ending gives the verb a lighter, lesser sense than its base: to drizzle rather than to rain. The base ~pleuvoir~ itself goes back to Latin ~pluere~ (“to rain”).
en.pleuvioter: ~Pleuvioter~ is a compound formation built on ~pleuvoir~ (“to rain”) with the suffix ~-ot~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. The suffix ~-ot~ is a diminutive, and with it the verb describes weak, intermittent rain: a drizzle. It resembles ~pleuvasser~, which uses ~-asser~ for a similar light nuance. The base ~pleuvoir~ is an impersonal verb, and ~pleuvioter~ keeps that behavior, so it is used mainly in the third person singular.
en.pleuvoir:
From Old French ~plovoir~, earlier ~pluveir~, from Vulgar Latin *~plovēre~, a reshaping of Latin ~pluere~ (“to rain”). The Vulgar Latin form moved the verb from the third conjugation to the second, and the imperfect ~plovebat~, attested in Petronius, shows the change was already under way in spoken Latin. Latin ~pluere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~plowō~ and to the Proto-Indo-European root *~plew-~ (“to run, to flow”). The same root gave Ancient Greek ~plýnō~ (“to wash”) and ~pléō~ (“to sail”), the Czech verbs ~plout~ and ~plavat~, and English ~flow~ and ~flood~. Italian ~piovere~ and Spanish ~llover~ are sister descendants of the Latin verb.

So rain and flowing water are old relatives: the root describes liquid on the move, and ~pleuvoir~ is the verb that specialized in water falling from the sky. Modern French uses it almost only in the impersonal ~il pleut~, though it can take a figurative subject, as when blows or compliments ~pleuvent~. Its noun is ~pluie~, from Latin ~pluvia~, and the family includes ~pluvieux~, ~pluvial~ and ~parapluie~, literally a thing “against rain.”
en.pleuvoter:
~Pleuvoter~ is built on ~pleuvoir~ (“to rain”) with the diminutive and frequentative suffix ~-oter~, which turns a verb into a small, repeated version of itself. The verb ~pleuvoir~ goes back to a popular Latin form *~plŏvēre~, attested in Petronius as ~plovebat~, the imperfect. It stands beside Classical Latin ~pluere~ (“to rain”), the form that the learned vocabulary kept.

Where ~pleuvoir~ is rain in general, ~pleuvoter~ is its modest cousin: to drizzle, to rain a little at a time. The Latin verb has well-known relatives across the Romance languages, among them Italian ~piovere~, Spanish ~llover~ and Portuguese ~chover~. In French the family includes the noun ~pluie~, the adjective ~pluvieux~, the learned ~pluvial~, and ~Pluviôse~, the rainy month of the Revolutionary calendar. In English, ~pluvial~ is the same learned borrowing. The diminutive pattern is lively in French, where ~-oter~ also gives ~vivoter~ and ~clignoter~.
en.plier:
~Plier~ is as old as French itself: the form ~pleier~ appears in 881 in the Sequence of Saint Eulalia, one of the very first texts written in the language — nothing, says the poem, could “bend” the young martyr. It continues Latin ~plicāre~ (“to fold, to roll up”), beside ~plectere~ (“to plait”) and Greek ~plékō~ (“I weave”), all from the Proto-Indo-European root *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, to weave”). Old French ~pleier~, ~ploier~ yielded the twin modern verbs ~plier~ and ~ployer~ — one Latin verb split in two. Italian ~piegare~ (“to fold, to bend”) is the straightforward cousin; the surprising ones are Spanish ~llegar~ and Portuguese ~chegar~, “to arrive,” from the same ~plicāre~ — by the usual account from sailors’ and soldiers’ speech, where folding the sails, or folding the tents, meant journey’s end.

For centuries ~plier~ and ~ployer~ were mere variants; only in the seventeenth century did grammarians try to share out the work — folding for ~plier~, bending for ~ployer~ — a division still felt today, with ~déployer~ (“to unfold, to deploy”) on the bending side. The Latin family kept folding itself into the abstract vocabulary of French: ~expliquer~, from ~explicāre~, is literally “to unfold” what was creased; ~impliquer~ and ~employer~ both continue ~implicāre~, “to fold in”; ~compliquer~ is “to fold together”; ~répliquer~, “to fold back”; ~multiplier~, “to fold many times.” English took ~deploy~ and ~employ~ from the French verbs, and ~pliers~ and ~pliable~ from ~plier~ itself. The homely noun ~pli~ (“fold, crease, habit”) gives ~prendre le pli~, “to get into the habit”: folded paper keeps its crease — and so, French suggests, do we.
en.plisser: ~Plisser~ is formed from the noun ~pli~ (“fold”) with the ending ~-er~, so “to make folds in”, whence “to pleat” and “to crease”. The noun ~pli~ is itself a verbal noun. French Wiktionary derives it from Old French ~ploi~, taken from ~ploier~, and English Wiktionary calls it a back-formation from ~plier~ (“to fold”). English ~ply~ (“layer”) is in turn a loan from ~pli~.
en.plomber:
French ~plomber~ is built on the noun ~plomb~ (“lead”) with the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun descends from Latin ~plumbum~ (“lead”), whose own earlier origin is uncertain. French Wiktionary also points to the Latin verb ~plumbāre~ (“to seal or solder with lead”), so the French verb may owe something to a Latin ancestor as well as to the French noun. The metal left the same mark in sister languages: Italian ~piombo~ and ~piombare~, Spanish ~plomo~. English took the root from Latin and French too, in ~plumb~ (a lead weight on a line) and ~plumber~, originally a worker in lead.

The verb's senses all follow the metal's properties. ~Plomber~ first meant to fit or seal with lead, hence ~plomber une dent~ (to fill a tooth, giving ~plombage~) and to seal a package with a lead seal. Lead's weight gave the sense “to weigh down,” and then the figurative one of becoming a burden. The same noun ~plomb~ gave ~plombier~ (“plumber”), and ~aplomb~, which first described what hangs straight down along a plumb line and then a person's steady composure.
en.plonger:
From Old French ~plongier~ (twelfth century), from Vulgar Latin *~plumbicāre~, a verb derived from Latin ~plumbum~ (“lead, the metal”). The idea is vivid: to ~plonger~ is to drop like a lead weight, to sink as a plumb-line does. The same *~plumbicāre~ underlies Italian ~piombare~ (“to fall heavily, to plunge”). ~plumbum~ itself is a word of uncertain, probably non-Indo-European origin, perhaps borrowed from an extinct language of the western Mediterranean where lead was mined; scholars doubt the old guess linking it to Greek ~mólybdos~.

The metaphor of the lead sinker runs all through the word's history. A sounding-lead dropped to measure depth gave both the act of plunging into water and, figuratively, the act of immersing oneself — one is ~plongé~ in thought, in darkness, in despair. From the same ~plumbum~ French drew a tightly related cluster: ~plomb~ (“lead”), ~plomber~ (“to fill a tooth, to seal with lead”), ~plombier~ (“plumber,” once a worker in lead pipes), ~plombage~ (“filling”), and ~aplomb~ (“perpendicularity, poise” — literally “to the plumb”). English ~plumb~, ~plummet~, and ~plunge~ are cousins through the same metallic root, so the diver, the plumber, and the person of great ~aplomb~ all owe their words to a lump of lead.
en.ployer:
Inherited from Old French ~ploier~ (earlier ~pleier~ or ~pleiier~, attested around 1100), from Latin ~plicāre~ (“to fold, to coil”), whose Proto-Indo-European root is *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, to weave”). English Wiktionary calls ~ployer~ a variant of ~plier~, and French Wiktionary calls the two a doublet: the same Latin verb reached French in two successive shapes, and both survive.

Today ~ployer~ is used mostly for bending under weight or pressure, of a branch, a knee or a back, and figuratively for giving way, as in ~ployer sous le poids~. ~Plier~ took over the everyday sense of folding. Latin ~plicāre~ left many other French words: the noun ~pli~ (“fold”), and ~déployer~, ~employer~, ~expliquer~ and ~appliquer~, which come through the Latin compounds ~displicāre~, ~implicāre~, ~explicāre~ and ~applicāre~. All of them keep the image of a fold.
en.plucher: Derived from ~peluche~ (“plush”), the soft fabric with a long nap, by turning the noun into a verb with the ending ~-er~. The verb describes something that fluffs up or becomes fluffy, taking on the look of plush. This is a common pattern in French: the ending makes a verb meaning to take on, or to use, what the noun names. English Wiktionary gives only this one-line derivation.
en.plumer: ~Plumer~ is formed from ~plume~ (“feather”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, with the sense “to remove the feathers from”. The noun ~plume~ comes from Old French ~plume~, from Latin ~plūma~ (“feather, down”). Besides the literal plucking, the verb has the figurative sense “to swindle”.
en.pluviner: A variant of ~pleuviner~, “to drizzle,” itself formed from ~pleuvoir~ (“to rain”) with the diminutive suffix ~-iner~. The TLFi traces ~ploviner~ to 1216, in Guillaume le Clerc, and the spelling ~pleuviner~ to 1560. The Académie calls it familiar and gives ~bruiner~ as a synonym. Simenon wrote ~il pluvinait~ in 1958. Littré also notes the Genevan forms ~pleuvigner~ and ~plouvigner~.
en.plâtrer: ~Plâtrer~ is formed from ~plâtre~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~: to cover with plaster, and so, in medicine, to put a limb in a plaster cast. The noun is inherited from Old French ~plastre~ (first attested around 1165), from Vulgar Latin *~plastrum~, from Latin ~emplastrum~, from Ancient Greek ~émplastron~ (“daub, salve”). French Wiktionary describes ~plâtre~ as a form of ~emplâtre~ with its first syllable dropped, and English Wiktionary notes that it is a doublet of ~piastre~.
en.plébisciter: ~Plébisciter~ is formed from the noun ~plébiscite~ and the verb suffix ~-er~. ~Plébiscite~ is a borrowing from Latin ~plebiscitum~, made of ~plebs~ (“the common people”) and ~scitum~ (“decree”). In Rome a ~plebiscitum~ was a measure voted by the assembly of the plebs. French first used the noun for a direct vote of a whole people, and the verb followed: to ~plébisciter~ is to approve something by such a vote. By extension, it now often means to acclaim a person or a product by a large majority, as when the public ~plébiscite~ a candidate.
en.pocharder: Formed from ~pochard~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so it means to get drunk, to become a ~pochard~. The noun is derived from ~poche~ (“pocket, bag”) with the suffix ~-ard~, in the sense of someone filled like a bag; French Wiktionary compares the expression ~sac à vin~ (“wine sack”). The suffix ~-ard~ often marks a person with a trait, often a pejorative one, and the verb turns that trait into an action.
en.pocher: ~Pocher~ is a verb made from the noun ~poche~ (“pocket, bag”), via Old French ~pochier~ (“to enclose in a bag”). The noun comes from Frankish *~pokkō~ and is a cognate of English ~pouch~ and ~pocket~. That base explains the cooking sense, “to poach.” The black-eye sense may instead come from an old verb ~poucher~ (“to crush with the thumb”), and the artist's sense “to sketch roughly” is probably figurative, either “to do loosely, like a bag” or, by one guess, a modeler's “pressing with the thumb.” The sources hedge on both.
en.podzoliser: Formed from the noun ~podzol~ with the verb suffix ~-iser~, which turns a noun into a verb meaning “to convert into” or “to subject to.” The soil term ~podzol~ was borrowed from Russian ~podzol~, itself built from ~pod~ (“under”) and ~zola~ (“ash”), a name for the ash-gray layer found beneath the surface of such soils. The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, a transcription of Greek verbal endings, and is fully productive in technical vocabulary.
en.poignarder: Built on ~poignard~ (“dagger”) with the verbal suffix ~-er~, so “to stab with a dagger.” ~Poignard~ is an altered form of Old French ~poignal~, from Vulgar Latin *~pugnāle~, itself from Latin ~pugnus~ (“fist”), the source of French ~poing~. Italian ~pugnale~ and Spanish ~puñal~ are cognates. The dagger thus owes its name, etymologically, to the fist.
en.poiler: A variant spelling of ~poêler~ in the pronominal verb ~se poêler~, a slang expression meaning to laugh hard. The spelling ~poiler~ simply writes the same word with ~oi~ for ~oê~. The sources consulted give no deeper origin for ~poêler~ in this sense, so none is claimed here.
en.poindre:
Inherited from Old French ~poindre~ (also ~puindre~), from Latin ~pungere~ (“to prick, to sting”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~pewǵ-~ (“to prick, to punch”). The Latin supine ~punctum~ gave French ~point~, the same pattern by which ~iungere~ and its supine ~iunctum~ gave ~joindre~ and ~joint~. Italian ~pungere~ is a direct cousin, and English borrowed ~pungent~ and ~puncture~ from the same Latin verb.

Old French ~poindre~ meant to prick or pierce, and so to sting or to afflict, as with a pang of pain or remorse. From there the verb developed the sense of appearing, of beginning to show: ~le jour point~ means that day is breaking. Like many verbs of the third group in ~-re~, it lost ground to first-conjugation synonyms such as ~piquer~ and ~pousser~, and today it survives mostly in literary use. The one form still common is the present participle ~poignant~ (“moving, harrowing”), whose meaning has drifted so far that few speakers connect it with the verb. Related words are ~point~, ~pointe~, ~poinçon~, ~ponctuer~ and ~pointer~.
en.pointer:
Formed within French from the noun ~point~ plus the verbal suffix ~-er~. The noun ~point~ comes from Latin ~punctum~ (“a prick, a dot”), the past participle of ~pungere~ (“to prick, sting”), which goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~pewǵ-~ (“to prick, punch”). Through ~punctum~, French ~point~ is a doublet of ~pointe~ and is cognate with Italian ~punto~ and Spanish ~punto~, while ~pungere~ itself surfaces in English ~puncture~ and ~pungent~.

An older inherited verb, ~poindre~, carried the literal “to prick” sense directly from ~pungere~; but French speakers tend to shy away from third-group verbs, and the regular ~pointer~, rebuilt on the noun, largely displaced it. The meanings all radiate from the dot or tip: to ~pointer~ is to aim at or indicate a point, to mark with dots, and — from the dot once made beside a worker's name on a register — “to clock in.” The same root gives French ~poindre~, ~poignant~, ~ponctuel~, and ~ponctuation~.
en.pointiller: ~Pointiller~ is dated to 1608 and derived from the adjective ~pointillé~, which French Wiktionary dates to 1414. Its first sense is to make a surface of small dots, with a pen, an engraver's burin, a brush or a pencil, as in stippling. Figurative senses followed: to nitpick, to quibble over trifles, and to needle someone with disagreeable remarks. In the pronominal form, ~se pointiller~ means to bicker over insignificant things.
en.poinçonner: Formed from the noun ~poinçon~ (“punch, stamp, hallmarking tool”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so the verb means to mark or pierce with that tool. The noun comes from Old French ~poinçon~, itself probably derived from a Vulgar Latin verb *~punctiāre~ (“to prick”), built on Latin ~punctus~ (“pricked, a point”). In Old French the tool was a pointed instrument for piercing, used to stamp gold and silver work. English Wiktionary notes that ~poinçon~ is a doublet of ~ponction~, and compares Italian ~punzone~ and Spanish ~punzón~.
en.poireauter: Formed from the noun ~poireau~ (“leek”) with the verb ending ~-er~, with an epenthetic ~t~ inserted between them. ~Poireau~ comes from the older ~porreau~ and Old French ~por~, from Latin ~porrum~ (“leek”). The change from ~porreau~ to ~poireau~ began in the Paris region, probably under the influence of ~poire~ (“pear”). The informal verb ~poireauter~ means to hang around, to wait about.
en.poisser: Formed from ~poix~ (“pitch, resin”) with the verb ending ~-er~: to coat with pitch, hence to make sticky, and, colloquially, to nab. The noun ~poix~ is inherited from Old French ~peiz~, from Latin ~pix~ (accusative ~picem~), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~pī́ts~ (“pitch, resin”).
en.poivrer: Formed from the noun ~poivre~ (“pepper”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to season with pepper”. The noun descends from Latin ~piper~, borrowed from Greek and ultimately from an Indian source, Sanskrit ~pippalī~ (“long pepper”). English ~pepper~ shares the same Latin ancestor. The verb ~poivrer~ is used literally, for seasoning a dish, and figuratively through the adjective ~poivré~, applied to a spicy, risqué story or joke.
en.polariser: Formed from Latin ~polaris~ (“polar, of the pole”) with the verbal suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to make polar” or “to give poles to.” Latin ~polaris~ is itself an adjective built on ~polus~, the “pole” of the sky or of an axis, a word Latin took from Greek. The verb belongs to the vocabulary of physics, where it describes giving light or a magnet a direction, and it later broadened to the figurative sense of dividing opinion into two opposed camps.
en.policer: Formed from the noun ~police~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. The meaning “to civilize, to refine” fits the older sense of ~police~, “good order, orderly government”, which comes from Latin ~politia~ (“political organization, government of the city”), itself from Greek ~πολιτεία~ (~politeía~). To ~policer~ a people was to bring them under orderly government, and so to make them civilized. A different ~police~, the insurance policy, comes from Italian ~polizza~, but it does not fit this sense.
en.polir:
Borrowed into French from Latin ~polīre~ (“to smooth, to polish”), through Old French ~polir~. The Latin verb is the source of Italian ~pulire~ and Spanish ~pulir~, and it also lies behind English ~polish~, which was taken from the stem ~poliss-~ of the Old French verb. The past participle of the Latin verb, ~polītus~ (“smoothed, refined”), became an adjective and was borrowed by English as ~polite~.

That adjective points to the most interesting development in the family. A surface that has been rubbed smooth is also one that has lost its roughness, and the image moved easily to manners and style: French ~poli~ means both “polished” and “polite,” and ~politesse~ is the quality of a person whose manners have been smoothed. The verb itself kept both senses, “to polish a stone, a metal, a floor” and “to refine a text or a style.” Related French words include ~poli~, ~polissage~, ~polissoir~ and ~politesse~.
en.polissonner: ~Polissonner~ is derived from ~polisson~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, and means to behave like a ~polisson~, to be naughty. The noun comes from Middle French ~polisse~ (“theft”), itself derived from Middle French ~polir~ (“to wash, clean”), already used for disposing of goods after stealing them. ~Polisson~ first named a rogue, an adult with a pejorative sense (1653), then a dirty, mischievous boy (1680), then a disobedient, playful child (1762). A licentious sense, as adjective (1685) and as noun (1695), also appeared.
en.politiquer: From ~politique~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. The base ~politique~ comes from Latin ~politicus~, itself from Ancient Greek ~politikós~, formed from ~polítēs~ (“citizen”) and the adjective suffix ~-ikós~. So the word goes back to what concerns citizens and the affairs of the city. The denominal verb ~politiquer~ means to talk about politics or to engage in political discussion, often with a slightly dismissive tone, as of idle debate.
en.politiser: Formed from ~politique~ (“political”) with the verb suffix ~-iser~, which means to make or render something that quality: to give a political character to. The stem loses ~-ique~ before the ending. The adjective ~politique~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~politicus~, itself from Ancient Greek ~πολιτικός~ (~politikós~), built on ~πολίτης~ (“citizen”) with the suffix ~-ικός~. So the word is, at its root, “of the citizen.”
en.polluer: ~Polluer~ is borrowed from Latin ~polluere~ (“to defile, to soil, to contaminate”), often used of ritual or moral impurity, as when a sanctuary or a person was made unfit for sacred use. French kept the sense of defilement and later narrowed it to the physical contamination of air, water and soil, a meaning that became common only in the modern era. The same Latin verb gave the nouns ~pollution~ and ~polluant~ in French, and English ~pollute~ and ~pollution~.
en.polycopier: ~Polycopier~ is formed from ~copier~ with the prefix ~poly-~, from Ancient Greek ~πολύς~ (“many, much”), so “to make many copies.” It is tied to the noun ~polycopié~, a duplicated document. The base ~copier~ comes from Medieval Latin ~copiare~ (“to transcribe”), derived from Latin ~copia~ (“abundance”).
en.polymériser: ~Polymériser~ is formed from ~polymère~ and the suffix ~-iser~, and means to polymerize, to turn into a polymer. The noun ~polymère~ comes from Ancient Greek ~polumerês~ (“complex, made of many parts”), and English Wiktionary analyzes it as ~poly-~ plus ~-mère~. The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs.
en.polémiquer: Formed from ~polémique~ and the verb ending ~-er~: to ~polémiquer~ is to take part in a controversy. The noun is a learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ~polemikós~ (“of war, warlike”), from ~pólemos~ (“combat, war”), so a polemic is etymologically a verbal war. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is the usual way French turns a noun into a verb.
en.pommader: Formed from the noun ~pommade~ (“pomade, ointment”) and the ending ~-er~, ~pommader~ means to coat with pomade. It is first recorded in 1581, in Sébillet, with that literal sense. In 1867 Delvau lists a figurative use, “to soothe, to flatter,” as if one were smoothing someone over with ointment.
en.pommeler: Derived from ~pommer~, itself a verb from ~pomme~ (“apple”), with the ending ~-eler~, a rare suffix once frequentative or diminutive. The noun comes from Old French ~pome~, from Latin ~pōma~, the plural of ~pōmum~ (“fruit”), later felt as a feminine singular. Some analyses prefer to see ~pomme~ plus a plain ~-er~. Either way, the verb is built on the noun for an apple, and it describes a sky or a coat marked with small round patches.
en.pommer: ~Pommer~ is a denominal verb: the noun ~pomme~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~, with the sense of developing fruit. The noun is inherited from Middle French ~pomme~ and Old French ~pome~, from Latin ~pōma~, the plural of ~pōmum~ (“fruit”), reanalyzed as a feminine singular. The Latin word displaced classical ~mālum~ in the sense “apple” in Gaul and northern Italy. English Wiktionary traces ~pōmum~ to Proto-Indo-European *~h₂po-h₁ém-os~ (“taken off”). Compare English ~pome~.
en.pomper: Formed from the noun ~pompe~ (“pump”) with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun came into Middle French, probably from Middle Dutch ~pompe~, a word related to Middle Low German ~pumpe~ and apparently sound-imitative, used by North Sea sailors. This ~pompe~ has nothing to do with the homonym meaning “pageantry,” which comes from Latin ~pompa~ and Greek ~pompḗ~ (“procession”). From the sense of drawing liquid with a pump, ~pomper~ branched into figurative and slang uses, among them the sense “to copy.”
en.pomponner: Formed from ~pompon~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so “to adorn with pompons,” hence “to primp, to titivate.” French Wiktionary derives ~pompon~ from ~pompe~ (in the sense of ceremonial display) plus the suffix ~-on~. English Wiktionary dates ~pompon~ to 1556 and says it may come from a root ~pomp-~ expressing roundness, or else be related to ~pompe~. The origin of the noun is therefore not fully settled, but the verb's meaning of dressing oneself up is clear.
en.poncer: ~Poncer~ has two proposed origins on French Wiktionary. The sense “to sand, rub down” is traced to Latin ~pumicare~; English Wiktionary gives a compatible account, ~ponce~ (“pumice”) + ~-er~, a verb made from the name of the abrasive stone. French Wiktionary also lists a second, separate origin from Latin ~pungere~ (“to prick, to pierce”) but does not say which sense it covers, so the sanding sense rests on the pumice account.
en.ponctionner:
~Ponctionner~ is traced in two ways. By one account it is the noun ~ponction~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~; by the other it comes straight from Latin ~pungere~ (“to prick, to sting”). The two fit together, since the learned noun ~ponction~ rests on the same Latin verb (it descends from Latin ~punctiō~, a “pricking”), so the verb is a French formation on a Latin root. The Latin ~pungere~ is also the source of English ~pungent~ and ~puncture~, and of the French ~point~, a pricked mark.

The sense runs from the surgeon's needle to the tax collector's. In medicine, ~ponctionner~ means to puncture a cavity or an organ, to draw off fluid or take a sample. Figuratively it means to deduct a sum, to take a cut from an income or an account. The same Latin ~pungere~ underlies a lively French family: ~poindre~ (“to sting, to dawn”), ~pointe~, ~poignant~, ~ponctuer~ and ~ponctuel~, the last two via the related Latin ~punctum~ (“point, dot”).
en.ponctuer: Borrowed from Medieval Latin ~punctuāre~ (“to mark with points”), a verb formed on Latin ~punctus~. Latin ~punctus~ (“a point, a prick”) is the participle of ~pungere~ (“to prick, to pierce”). The same noun lies behind French ~point~, and English has ~punctuate~, ~puncture~ and ~point~ from the same Latin family. The verb thus began as a way of describing text marked with dots, which is the sense that French ~ponctuer~ keeps when it refers to punctuation.
en.pondre:
From Old French ~pondre~, inherited from Latin ~pōnere~ (“to put, to place”), itself from Proto-Italic *~pozinō~. The Latin verb has living relatives across the Romance languages: Italian ~porre~ and Spanish ~poner~ (“to put”). Spanish ~poner~ is a well-known false friend of ~pondre~, although the two are cognates: Spanish kept the general sense “to put,” while French narrowed it to one very particular act of putting.

The narrowing came through an ellipsis: ~ponere ova~ (“to put down eggs”) lost its object, and the verb alone came to mean “to lay eggs.” The letter d of ~pondre~ is epenthetic, a consonant that slipped in between the n and the r once the vowel between them dropped out, just as ~cinerem~ became ~cendre~. The everyday French verb ~poser~ comes from a different Latin verb, ~pausāre~ (“to pause”), yet it took over most of the territory of ~pōnere~, which is why ~pondre~ survives almost only in the egg sense. French keeps ~ponte~ (“egg-laying”) and ~pondeuse~ (“laying hen”).
en.pondérer:
French ~pondérer~ comes from Old French ~ponderer~ (“to weigh, to consider”), itself taken from Latin ~ponderāre~ (“to weigh, to judge”), a verb formed on ~pondus~ (“weight”). The Latin noun ~pondus~ is closely tied to the verb ~pendere~ (“to weigh, to hang”), the source of French ~pendre~ and ~peser~ through other routes. English kept the Latin verb as ~ponder~, which also came through Old French, and Spanish has ~ponderar~ and Italian ~ponderare~. The word thus belongs to a family built on the old image of a scale, where weighing something means letting it hang from a beam.

Already in Latin, ~ponderāre~ had a double life: to weigh an object in the hand, and to weigh a matter in the mind, that is, to consider it carefully. Old French kept both, and modern French has added technical senses. In general language, ~pondérer~ means to balance or moderate, as when one tempers a claim, and in statistics and economics it means to give each element a weight in proportion to its importance, as in a ~moyenne pondérée~ (“weighted average”). The family includes ~pondération~ (“balance, weighting”), ~impondérable~ (“something that cannot be weighed, an unforeseeable factor”), ~prépondérant~ (“carrying more weight”) and ~pondéreux~ (“heavy, bulky”, of goods). English ~ponder~ preserves only the mental meaning, while French uses its verb on the scales of both thought and calculation.
en.ponter: ~Ponter~ has two competing explanations. One reads it as a denominal verb from ~pont~ (“bridge”) plus ~-er~, with the sense of building a bridge; ~pont~ is inherited from Latin ~pons~, ~pontis~. The other, for the gaming sense, derives it from ~ponte~ in the abstract sense of a “deposit” or stake, a pattern compared by French Wiktionary with ~mise~ and ~miser~ from ~mettre~. English Wiktionary gives a related account from ~pont~, an obsolete past participle of ~pondre~ (“to lay, to put”), from Latin ~ponere~.
en.pontifier: Formed from ~pontife~ (“pontiff”) with the verb ending ~-er~, literally “to act like a pontiff.” The noun is a learned borrowing, through Middle French, from Latin ~pontifex~. In modern French the verb has the figurative sense of speaking in a solemn, self-important way, as a pontiff would.
en.populariser: ~Populariser~ is formed from the adjective ~populaire~ with the suffix ~-iser~, in the sense “to make popular, to spread among the people.” The adjective ~populaire~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~populāris~ (“of the people”), itself from ~populus~ (“people”). The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, ultimately a Greek verb ending, and is still fully productive in French. Related words from the same Latin root include ~peuple~ and ~population~.
en.poquer: From West Flemish ~pokken~ (“to strike”), according to French Wiktionary. English Wiktionary is more cautious: it calls the word Germanic, perhaps from Middle Dutch ~poken~ or Middle Low German ~poken~, both from Proto-Germanic *~puk-~, which is probably imitative. Either way, the verb is a Germanic loan with no Latin ancestor. French uses it for bumping, bruising or damaging something. English ~poke~ is likewise tied to the Middle Dutch and Low German verb, so the two languages share a word for a thrust or a blow.
en.porter:
French ~porter~ descends directly from Latin ~portāre~ (“to carry, to bring”), kept intact through Old French ~porter~. The Latin verb belongs to Proto-Indo-European *~per-~ (“to lead across, to pass over”), a root deeply concerned with passage and crossing: from it come Latin ~porta~ (“gate”) and ~portus~ (“harbor, passage”), Greek ~póros~ (“ford, passage”), and — through the Germanic branch — English ~fare~ and ~ford~ and German ~fahren~ (“to travel”). To carry, in this old view, is to make something cross a distance.

Latin ~portāre~ was so productive that its prefixed compounds flooded into French: ~apporter~, ~emporter~, ~rapporter~, ~supporter~, ~transporter~, ~comporter~, ~exporter~, and ~importer~ — the last giving us both “to import” and the impersonal ~il importe~ (“it matters”), since what is “carried in” bears weight. The plain verb meanwhile spread far beyond literal carrying into “to wear” (~porter une robe~) and “to bear” a feeling or a name. From the same family come the nouns ~port~ (a harbor, the place of passage) and ~portail~, and the French fashion phrase ~prêt-à-porter~ (“ready to wear”). A single root for crossing thus links harbors, gates, journeys, and the clothes on one's back.
en.portraiturer: ~Portraiturer~ (“to paint a portrait, to portray”) is a coinage, called a neologism by French Wiktionary. It is derived with the verb ending ~-er~ from ~portrait~, according to French Wiktionary, while English Wiktionary takes ~portraiture~ as the base instead. The two bases are close in sense, since ~portraiture~ is the art or act of making a ~portrait~, and either way the verb means to make someone's likeness.
en.poser:
From Late Latin ~pausare~ (“to halt, to cease”), from the noun ~pausa~ (“a pause, a stop”), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~παῦσις~ (~paûsis~, “a stopping”), from the verb ~παύω~ (~paúō~, “to make cease”). The original idea was rest and cessation — ~pausare~ appears on early Christian epitaphs in the phrase “here he rests in peace.” English ~pose~ and ~pause~ both trace to this family, alongside Italian ~posare~ and Spanish ~posar~.

The great surprise of ~poser~ is that its modern meaning is not really its own. The Latin verb meaning “to put, to place” was ~ponere~, with past participle ~positus~; but ~ponere~ and ~pausare~ collided in spoken Latin, and ~poser~ swallowed the sense of placing that by rights belonged to ~ponere~. The fingerprint of this merger is everywhere: every compound of ~ponere~ surfaces in French as ~-poser~ — ~déposer~, ~exposer~, ~imposer~, ~proposer~, ~composer~ — yet their nouns keep the older Latin stem and end in ~-ition~ (~position~, ~exposition~, ~proposition~), not the ~-ation~ a verb in ~poser~ would predict. So ~poser~ today means “to put down, to set, to ask a question, to pose for a portrait,” carrying a sense it borrowed wholesale from a verb it eclipsed.
en.positionner:
A recent French formation, derived from the noun ~position~ plus the verbal suffix ~-er~. ~Position~ itself comes from Latin ~positio~ (“a placing, position”), from ~positus~, the past participle of ~ponere~ (“to put, place”). ~Ponere~ is analyzed as ~po-~ (a reduced form of an old preposition meaning “away, off”) plus ~sinere~ (“to let, set down”), the latter from Proto-Indo-European *~tḱey-~ (“to settle, build”). Cognate descendants of ~ponere~ include Spanish ~poner~ and, through the participle, English ~position~, ~posit~, and ~pose~.

As a verb, ~positionner~ is young and was long viewed with suspicion: the Académie française condemned its use outside technical and military contexts, where it meant to place troops or equipment at a precise spot. It has since spread into ordinary and commercial language — one speaks of how a product ~se positionne~ on the market. From the same Latin root come ~poser~, ~position~, ~positionnement~, and the prefixed ~repositionner~ and ~prépositionner~. The family traces a long arc from a Latin verb of simple placing to a modern verb of strategic placement.
en.positiver: Formed from the adjective ~positif~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The adjective comes from Latin ~positīvus~ (“placed, established, conventional”), from the idea of something that rests on a base. The intransitive use, “to think positively,” seems to have been introduced, or at least popularized, in 1988 by the supermarket chain Carrefour with its advertising slogan “Avec Carrefour, je positive.” The origin of that use is thus a slogan, not an older tradition.
en.posséder:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~possidēre~ (“to own, to hold, to occupy”), which supplanted the inherited Old French verb ~posseoir~. Latin ~possidēre~ is a compound of ~potis~ (“able, having power, master”) and ~sedēre~ (“to sit”): to possess was literally “to sit as master,” to occupy a place with authority. The element ~potis~ comes from the Proto-Indo-European *~pótis~ (“lord, master”), and ~sedēre~ from the root *~sed-~ (“to sit”) — the very root behind English ~sit~ and German ~sitzen~. Roman jurists used ~possidēre~ first of all for landholding, and the image of an owner seated firmly on his ground sits at the bottom of the word.

That picture of sitting-in-power proved durable: to ~posséder~ is to hold a thing so firmly that one is settled upon it, and the verb stretched from land to goods to qualities and, eerily, to people “possessed” by spirits. The ~sedēre~ root seeded a large French family — ~asseoir~, ~séance~, ~sédentaire~, ~résider~, and ~siège~ — while ~potis~ surfaces in ~pouvoir~, ~puissant~, and ~possible~. From ~possidēre~ itself French keeps ~possession~, ~possesseur~, ~possessif~, and ~déposséder~.
en.postdater: ~Postdater~ is formed from ~dater~ with the prefix ~post-~, “to date a document later than the true date.” ~Dater~ comes from the noun ~date~, from Latin ~data~, the feminine past participle of ~dare~ (“to give”), taken from the formula ~data littera~ (“letter given”) that scribes wrote before the place and day of issue. ~Dare~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). The prefix ~post-~ comes from Latin ~post~ (“after”). English Wiktionary instead derives the French verb from the noun ~postdate~ plus ~-er~, which is itself ~post-~ + ~date~.
en.poster:
The verb ~poster~ (“to mail”) is denominal, formed from the noun ~poste~. That noun was borrowed in the fifteenth century from Italian ~posta~ (“relay station”), descended from Latin ~posita~, the feminine past participle of ~ponere~ (“to put, place”). A ~posta~ was a place where fresh horses were “posted” along a route — a relay station for couriers — and from this came the whole vocabulary of the mail. The chain links to Italian ~posta~ and Spanish ~posta~, and to the English ~post~.

French has, in fact, several verbs ~poster~ that look alike. One, also denominal from ~poste~ in its military sense, means “to station, to position” (~poster une sentinelle~); a more recent one borrows English ~post~ in the sense of publishing online. But the postal ~poster~ — to drop a letter into the mail — flows straight from those relay stations where messages were laid down and relayed onward. The base verb ~ponere~ is a giant of French word-formation, yielding ~poser~, ~position~, ~composer~, ~déposer~, ~exposer~, ~proposer~, and the noun ~poste~ in all its senses, from a post office to a job ~poste~ to a radio ~poste~ — every one of them, at root, something “placed.”
en.postfacer: The verb is formed from the noun ~postface~ (“afterword”) plus the verb ending ~-er~, so it means to write an afterword for a book. ~Postface~ was itself modelled on ~préface~, a blend of ~post-~ (“after”) and ~préface~, with ~post-~ standing in for the ~pré-~ (“before”) of its model. Coining a verb from a noun by adding ~-er~ is the ordinary, fully productive way French makes new first-conjugation verbs, and this one follows the familiar sense “provide something with the noun”.
en.postillonner: Formed from ~postillon~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The base ~postillon~ is a calque of Italian ~postiglione~, itself from ~posta~; French Wiktionary adds that it was drawn from ~poste~ in the sense “relay of horses,” with the suffix ~-illon~. The verb now means to splutter, spraying saliva while speaking. The sources trace the formation but give no account of how the word moved from the coach-driver sense of its base to this one, so the link is not documented here.
en.postposer: Formed in French from ~poser~ with the prefix ~post-~ (“after, behind”), so “to place after.” English Wiktionary instead sees Latin ~postponere~ reshaped on French ~poser~. Either way the base is ~poser~, from Late Latin ~pausare~ (“to halt”), which took over the sense of placing that belonged to Latin ~ponere~. The prefix ~post-~ comes from Latin ~post~ (“after, behind”).
en.postsynchroniser: Formed from ~synchroniser~ with the prefix ~post-~, from Latin ~post~ (“after”). The verb means to dub: to record the sound for a film after the images have been shot, then fit it to them. The base ~synchroniser~ is built on ~synchrone~ with ~-iser~, and the adjective comes through Latin ~synchronus~ from Greek ~sýnkhronos~, made of ~sýn~ (“with”) and ~khrónos~ (“time”).
en.postuler:
Borrowed from Latin ~postulāre~ (“to ask, to demand”). The Latin verb belongs to the family of ~poscere~ (“to ask for, to demand”), which comes from the Proto-Indo-European root *~preḱ-~ (“to ask”). Latin ~precārī~ (“to pray”), source of English ~pray~, comes from the same root, as does German ~fragen~ (“to ask”). Italian ~postulare~, Spanish ~postular~ and English ~postulate~ are cognates, the last borrowed from the Latin participle form. English Wiktionary also treats one sense of the French verb as a back-formation from the noun ~postulat~ (“postulate”).

In Latin, ~postulāre~ had a legal side: to demand something from a magistrate or to bring a case before a court. French kept the idea of a formal request. Today ~postuler~ most often means to apply for a job or a position, the person asking for something that others will grant or refuse. A second, logical sense exists as well: to lay something down as a postulate, to take a proposition as given without proof. Related words are ~postulat~, ~postulant~ (“a candidate for a religious order”) and ~postulation~.
en.postériser: ~Postériser~ is formed from ~poster~ with the suffix ~-iser~, in the sense of making something into a poster or showing it as one. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, ultimately a Greek verb ending, and here means “to turn into”. The verb is a modern coinage.
en.potabiliser: ~Potabiliser~ is formed from the adjective ~potable~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which makes verbs meaning “to make A”: to make water fit to drink. The adjective is borrowed from Latin ~potabilis~ (“that can be drunk”), from the verb ~potare~ (“to drink”). ~Potable~ already means “drinkable,” so the verb adds the idea of a treatment that brings that state about.
en.potasser: The origin of ~potasser~ is uncertain, and the sources offer three proposals. One takes ~potache~ (“boarding pupil”) as its root. Another sees a derivative of ~pot~ with the suffix ~-asser~. A third builds it on ~potasse~ (“potash”), comparing the feverish work of students to the bubbling of potash in certain chemical reactions. None is established. The verb means to cram or to review intensively.
en.potentialiser: Formed from the adjective ~potentiel~ (“potential”) and the verbal suffix ~-iser~, in the pattern “make or render A.” English Wiktionary gives the base simply as ~potential~; as in ~réel~ and ~réaliser~, the stem is reshaped before the suffix. The verb is glossed in English as “to potentiate” or “to potentialize,” a technical coinage of the kind ~-iser~ produces freely in administrative, scientific and journalistic French. The suffix ~-iser~ itself comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs.
en.potiner: ~Potiner~ (“to gossip”) is traditionally analyzed as ~potin~ (“gossip”) plus the verb ending ~-er~, but English Wiktionary notes that the verb was probably coined before the noun, which was written down earlier. French Wiktionary offers a different line: ~potine~ was a “foot warmer for the evening gathering,” and ~potiner~ would have come from it. A possible but contested thesis links the verb to the ~potine~ that Norman women brought along in winter to their gatherings for chatting, and ~potiner~ would then have drifted to “to gossip” by semantic slippage. The origin is therefore debated, and no source settles it.
en.poudrer: ~Poudrer~ is formed from the noun ~poudre~ and the verb ending ~-er~, in the sense “to provide with N”: to cover or sprinkle with powder. The noun is inherited from Old French ~poudre~ (also ~poldre~), from Late Latin ~pulvera~, a neuter plural formed on Latin ~pulvis~ (“dust, powder”). English Wiktionary traces ~pulvis~ further to Proto-Indo-European *~pel-~ (“dust, flour”). French ~pulvériser~ is a related word from the same Latin root.
en.poudroyer: ~Poudroyer~ is formed from ~poudre~ with the suffix ~-oyer~: to rise or swirl in clouds of dust, as a road does in the sun. The base ~poudre~ is inherited from Old French ~poudre~, from Late Latin ~pulvera~, based on Latin ~pulvis~ (“dust”). The same Latin word is behind ~pulvériser~, and English Wiktionary traces it to a Proto-Indo-European root *~pel-~ (“dust, flour”).
en.pouffer: ~Pouffer~ is a denominal verb: ~pouf~ plus the ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary derives ~pouf~ from an onomatopoeia and refers readers to ~pif~, ~paf~ and ~piaffer~. The sound imitated is a sudden puff of breath, and the verb describes a person who bursts out laughing with the lips tight, so that the laugh explodes in a puff, usually in the expression ~pouffer de rire~ (“to snort with laughter”). The same imitative pattern also lies behind ~bouffer~, to which French Wiktionary refers for comparison.
en.pouliner: Formed from ~poulain~ (“foal”) with the verb ending ~-er~: a mare that ~poulines~ gives birth to a foal. ~Poulain~ comes from Old French ~poulain~, from Late or Vulgar Latin ~pullāmen~, a collective built on Latin ~pullus~ (“young of an animal”). The medieval diminutive ~poulenet~ even crossed the Channel to become English ~pony~ before returning to French as ~poney~. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~, the usual ending for coining a French verb from a noun.
en.pouponner: Formed from ~poupon~ (“baby, chubby infant”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to fuss over a baby.” The noun ~poupon~ is an alteration of Old French ~poupard~, with the suffix changed to ~-on~. English Wiktionary connects it with ~poupée~ (“doll”). Its first appearance in French is in Rabelais's ~Gargantua~. The verb takes the baby as its object of care: to dote on one, or look after it with affectionate attention.
en.pourchasser:
~Pourchasser~ comes from Middle French, which took it from Old French ~porchacier~ (“to seek to obtain”), formed from ~por-~ and ~chacier~. The base ~chacier~ goes back to Late Latin ~captiāre~ (“to capture”), from Latin ~captāre~. The same ancestor lies behind the plain verb ~chasser~ (“to hunt, to chase”), so ~pourchasser~ is, in effect, ~chasser~ with a prefix attached long ago, and English ~chase~ is a loan of the same Old French ~chacier~.

In Old French the verb meant “to seek to obtain,” a purposeful sense, and the modern verb has taken the harsher meaning “to pursue without relent.” The prefix ~pour-~ is the Old French ~por-~ in modern spelling. As standard background, ~captāre~ is a frequentative of ~capere~ (“to take”), the root behind French ~capter~ and ~captif~.
en.pourfendre: Formed in French from ~fendre~ with the prefix ~pour-~. The base ~fendre~ comes from Old French ~fendre~, inherited from Latin ~findere~ (“to split”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰeyd-~ (“to split”). The same root gave English ~bite~. The sources derive the prefix ~pour-~ from Latin ~per-~ or ~pro~, not from the modern preposition, and in this old verb it suggests a thorough action. ~Pourfendre~ originally meant to cleave someone right through with a sword, and it now often means to attack or criticize fiercely, as in ~pourfendre la corruption~.
en.pourlécher: Formed from ~lécher~ (“to lick”) with the prefix ~pour-~, which here adds an idea of thoroughness, so that the verb means to lick all around or all over. It is best known in the reflexive expression se pourlécher les babines, to lick one's chops, which is used figuratively for relishing something in advance or in memory.
en.pourrir:
From Old French ~porrir~, inherited from Vulgar Latin *~putrīre~, an adjusted form of Latin ~putrēre~ (“to be rotten”). That verb belongs to ~puter~ (“rotten, stinking”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~puH-~ (“to rot, to stink”). The change of conjugation is the interesting part: classical ~putrēre~ was a verb of the ~-ēre~ class, which French did not keep, and Vulgar Latin moved it to the ~-īre~ class while borrowing endings from the related verb ~putrēscere~ (“to become rotten”). The same root gave Spanish ~pudrir~. English ~foul~ is a Germanic cousin from the same PIE root, and English ~pus~ comes from a related Latin word.

In French, the short Latin ~u~ became ~o~ in Old French, then ~ou~, which turned ~porrir~ into ~pourrir~. The verb still means to decay, whether of fruit, wood or flesh, and it also describes a situation that worsens through neglect, as in the spoiled child or a conflict that ~pourrit~. Related words include ~pourri~, ~pourriture~ and ~pourrissement~. The learned doublets ~putride~, ~putréfier~ and ~putréfaction~ came directly from Latin and keep the original ~put-~.
en.poursuivre:
From Old French ~pursivre~ (twelfth century), later ~porsuivir~, a compound of ~por-~ / ~pour-~ (“forth, forward”) and ~suivre~ (“to follow”), refashioned on the model of Latin ~prosequi~ (“to follow after, to pursue, to escort”), from ~pro-~ (“forward”) and ~sequi~ (“to follow”). ~sequi~ derives through Proto-Italic *~sekʷōr~ from a Proto-Indo-European *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”), cognate with Ancient Greek ~hépomai~ and Sanskrit ~sácate~ (both “to follow”). From the same Latin verb English has ~pursue~.

The sense fans out from the simple act of following hard after someone. To ~poursuivre~ is to chase a fleeing enemy, to carry on a task one has begun, to hound or torment someone (a memory can ~poursuivre~ you), and, in law, to prosecute — to pursue a defendant through the courts. That last sense is the living trace of the Roman ~prosequi~, the formal “following up” of a legal action. The shared root *~sekʷ-~ is astonishingly fertile in French: ~suivre~ itself, ~suite~ (“that which follows”), ~ensuite~ (“next”), ~conséquence~ (“that which follows from”), ~séquence~ (“sequence”), and ~poursuite~ (“pursuit, prosecution”) all grow from it, as do English ~sequel~, ~suite~, and ~second~.
en.pourvoir:
From Old French ~porveoir~, from Latin ~providere~ (“to foresee, to provide”), a compound of ~pro-~ (“ahead, forward”) and ~videre~ (“to see”) — literally “to see ahead.” ~Videre~ descends from Proto-Italic *~widēō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”), the prolific root behind English ~wit~ and ~wise~, German ~wissen~ (“to know”), and Sanskrit ~veda~ (“knowledge”).

The Latin sense of foreseeing slid naturally into that of making provision for what one foresees: to provide, to furnish, to supply, and in law to appoint to an office or appeal to a higher court. French kept this spread — one ~pourvoit~ a household with food, a post with a holder, a need with a remedy. Cognate Romance descendants include Spanish ~proveer~ and Italian ~provvedere~. From the same Latin verb French has ~pourvu~ (“provided”), ~pourvoyeur~ (“purveyor, supplier”), and ~pourvoirie~. To provide, etymologically, is first to look ahead.
en.pousser:
From Old French ~poulser~ (also ~polser~), from Latin ~pulsare~ (“to beat, to strike, to push repeatedly”), the frequentative of ~pellere~ (“to drive, to beat, to strike”). ~pellere~ rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~pel-~ (“to thrust, to strike, to drive”). Through this root the French verb is cognate with Italian ~pulsare~ and, more distantly, with English ~push~ (likewise from ~pulsare~ via Old French) and with English ~felt~ (the matted fabric beaten together).

The Latin ~pulsare~ was forceful and repetitive — to strike again and again — which is why its descendants spread across the senses of beating, throbbing, and driving forward. French ~pousser~ kept the “drive forward” thread: to push a cart, to urge someone on, even to sprout (a plant ~pousse~). From the same ~pellere~ family French gathers a striking crowd: ~pouls~ (“pulse,” the beating of the blood), ~pulsation~, ~pulsion~, ~repousser~ (“to push back, to repel”), ~propulser~, ~expulser~, and ~compulser~ — so that a heartbeat, a psychological drive, and a shove all answer to one ancient verb meaning “to strike.”
en.poutser: A Swiss French spelling variant of ~poutzer~, which is borrowed from German ~putzen~. The verb is used chiefly in Switzerland and means “to clean,” “to dust” or “to polish.” It also has figurative senses, such as clearing something out, eliminating it or finishing it off. The word thus came into French from its German-speaking neighbor, and the ~tz~ spelling of ~poutzer~ stays closer to the German original than ~poutser~ does.
en.pouvoir:
From Old French ~pooir~ (also ~povoir~), from Vulgar Latin *~potēre~, a regularized infinitive built to replace the irregular Classical Latin ~posse~ (“to be able”). ~Posse~ was itself a fusion of ~potis~ (“able, capable, master of”) and ~esse~ (“to be”) — literally “to be capable.” The root is Proto-Indo-European *~poti-~ (“powerful, master, lord”). Romance cousins include Spanish ~poder~, Portuguese ~poder~, and Italian ~potere~, each serving as both verb and noun.

Because ~posse~ was so irregular, late spoken Latin rebuilt a tidy ~potēre~ on the model of its present participle ~potēns~ (“being able”), and from this regularized stem French ~pouvoir~ descends; the medial ~-v-~ crept in later to break the awkward hiatus of ~pooir~. The same PIE root *~poti-~ powers a remarkable spread of words: ~puissant~ and ~puissance~ (through a parallel Vulgar Latin *~possiēns~), the borrowed doublets ~potent~ and ~potentiel~, ~potentat~, and even ~despote~ (Greek ~despótēs~, a “house-master,” from the same *~poti-~). And ~pouvoir~ shows the language’s habit of freezing an infinitive into a noun: ~le pouvoir~, “power” itself.
en.poétiser: Formed from ~poète~ with the suffix ~-iser~, so the verb means to make poetic or to put into verse. The noun ~poète~ was borrowed from Latin ~poēta~, itself from Ancient Greek ~ποιητής~ (“author, maker, poet”), derived from ~ποιέω~ (“to make, to compose”). A poet is thus etymologically a “maker”. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs.
en.poêler: Formed from ~poêle~ (“frying pan”) and the verb suffix ~-er~, with the sense “to cook in a pan.” French Wiktionary notes that the word first appears as ~poëlé(e)~, used as a noun and an adjective. French has three unrelated words spelled ~poêle~: a heating stove, from Latin ~pensilis~; a cloth, from Latin ~pallium~; and the pan. The verb fits the pan, which comes from Latin ~patella~ (“small dish”) through Old French ~paelle~. Latin ~patella~ is also the source, by way of Spanish, of ~paella~, a doublet of the French word.
en.praliner: ~Praliner~ is formed from the noun ~praline~ + ~-er~, with the sense “to coat with caramelized sugar.” The noun comes from ~prasline~, named after César de Choiseul, comte du Plessis-Praslin (1602–1675), a marshal of France, whose cook is credited with inventing the recipe. The suffix ~-er~ is the ordinary French ending for making a verb from a noun, from Latin ~-are~.
en.pratiquer:
Built in French on the noun ~pratique~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. ~Pratique~ comes from Late Latin ~practicus~ (“practical, active”), a borrowing of Greek ~praktikós~ (“fit for action, effective”), from ~praktós~, the verbal adjective of ~prássein~ (Attic ~práttein~, “to do, to act, to accomplish,” literally “to pass through, to traverse”), which goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“to cross, to pass over”). It is cognate with English ~practice~ and ~practical~, themselves drawn from the same Greek source through Medieval Latin ~practicare~.

The Greek word carried a strong philosophical charge — Aristotle opposed the ~praktikós~ life of action to the contemplative — and that sense of “doing rather than merely knowing” still colors the French verb. ~Pratiquer~ means to carry something out in deed: to practise a craft, a religion, or a sport, to do rather than to theorize. From the same root the modern language keeps ~pratique~ (both noun and adjective), ~praticien~ (“a practitioner”), the learned doublet ~praxis~, and ~pragmatique~ (“pragmatic”) — a cluster of words all insisting, against mere theory, on the act itself.
en.prendre:
From Middle and Old French ~prendre~, also ~prindre~ (attested 842), from Latin ~prēndere~, a contracted form of ~prehendere~ (“to grasp, to seize”). That verb breaks down into the prefix ~prae-~ (“before, in front of”) and a root ~-hendere~, from Proto-Indo-European *~ǵʰend-~ (“to seize, to take”). Through that root ~prendre~ is cognate with Greek ~khandánein~ (“to hold, to contain”) and — strikingly — with English ~get~ and ~forget~.

In Late Latin ~prēndere~ pushed aside the classical ~capere~ (“to take”) in Gaul, becoming the ordinary verb for taking, and its Italian sibling ~prendere~ did the same. The Latin past participle ~prēnsus~ left its own descendants, and the supine stem ~prehēns-~ resurfaces in the learned French ~préhension~ and ~appréhender~ (“to apprehend, to dread”). ~Prendre~ also anchors one of the busiest prefix families in French: ~apprendre~ (“to learn,” literally “to take to oneself”), ~comprendre~ (“to understand,” “to take together”), ~surprendre~ (“to surprise,” “to overtake”), ~entreprendre~ (“to undertake”), and ~reprendre~ (“to resume”). The shared image — a hand or a mind closing around its object — runs quietly through them all.
en.prescrire:
From Latin ~praescribere~ (“to write before, to set down in advance, to dictate”), a compound of the prefix ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) and ~scribere~ (“to write”). The verb ~scribere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~skreiβō~ and ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)kreybʰ-~ (“to scratch, to incise”) — the same root that, through Germanic, yields English ~scribe~ and ~shrive~, German ~schreiben~, and is echoed in Ancient Greek ~σκάριφος~ (“a pointed stylus”). The literal image is a mark scratched into a surface before the fact.

The prefix ~prae-~ gives the word its two living senses: to write something down beforehand. In law a right is ~prescribed~ when long usage settles it in advance; in medicine a physician writes out a remedy ahead of treatment. French keeps both, plus the negative ~proscrire~ (“to outlaw,” literally to post a name up beforehand). From the same Latin verb descend ~prescription~, ~prescripteur~, ~prescriptible~, and the participle ~prescrit~, while the bare root ~scribere~ seeds an enormous family: ~écrire~, ~décrire~, ~inscrire~, ~souscrire~, and ~manuscrit~.
en.pressentir: From Latin ~praesentīre~ (“to sense beforehand”), a compound of ~prae-~ (“before”) and ~sentīre~ (“to feel, to perceive”). French Wiktionary treats it as a borrowing of the Latin verb, while English Wiktionary reads it as ~pré-~ plus ~sentir~; the two readings describe the same parts, since ~sentir~ itself descends from ~sentīre~. The meaning has hardly moved: ~pressentir~ is to perceive something before it happens, as a hunch or foreboding rather than as knowledge. The noun ~pressentiment~ (“premonition”) comes from the same verb.
en.presser:
From Old French ~presser~ (“to oppress, torment”), attested around 1160, from Latin ~pressare~ (“to press hard”), the frequentative-intensive of ~premere~ (“to press, squeeze, harass”). The verb ~premere~ is usually traced to a PIE *~pres-~ (“to press”), perhaps an extension of *~per-~ (“to strike, push”), though the present stem is thought to be reshaped on the model of ~tremere~, so the deep reconstruction carries some uncertainty. From ~premere~ and its participle ~pressus~ English draws ~press~, ~print~, and ~pressure~; Italian has ~pressare~.

The Latin intensive already leaned toward force — not just pressing but pressing hard, oppressing. French kept the physical sense (to ~presser~ a fruit, a button) and spun out a temporal one: to ~presser~ someone is to hurry them, and reflexively ~se presser~ is to make haste. The same crowding image gives ~la presse~ for a thronging crowd and, later, the printing ~press~ that squeezes ink onto paper. From the same root French keeps ~pression~, ~pressoir~ (a wine ~press~), ~exprimer~, and ~comprimer~.
en.pressurer: French Wiktionary derives ~pressurer~ from ~pressoir~ (“press”) and the verb ending ~-er~, as shown by the Old French verb ~pressoirer~, with the influence of the suffix ~-ure~. English Wiktionary instead gives a plain formation from ~pressure~ and ~-er~. The two accounts differ, but both point to the family of ~presser~, which comes from Latin ~pressāre~, a frequentative of ~premere~ (“to press”). The same Latin root also gave ~presse~, ~pression~, ~impression~ and ~exprimer~, and English borrowed ~press~ and ~pressure~ from it. Today the verb means “to squeeze” and, figuratively, “to extort”.
en.pressuriser: ~Pressuriser~ is borrowed from English ~pressurize~, which is itself formed from ~pressure~ with the suffix ~-ize~. French Wiktionary compares the related ~pressurer~ and observes that a form based on ~pression~, such as *~pressionner~, would have been possible too. English Wiktionary instead analyzes the French verb as ~pressure~ plus the suffix ~-iser~, whose sense is to make or treat with something. The verb means to keep a space, such as an aircraft cabin, at a higher pressure than the air outside. A French speaker may also say ~mettre sous pression~.
en.prier:
From Middle French ~prier~, from Old French ~proier~ and ~preier~ (attested by 881), from Latin ~precari~ (“to ask, entreat, pray”), a deponent verb built on the noun ~prex~ (“request, prayer”). The root is Proto-Indo-European *~preḱ-~ (“to ask”), a strikingly productive root: it gives Sanskrit ~pṛcchati~ (“asks”), German ~fragen~ (“to ask”), Dutch ~vragen~, and Latin ~poscere~ (“to demand”). English ~pray~ is a sibling, borrowed through the very same Old French ~preier~.

Latin ~precari~ covered both senses French still carries: the secular “to request, to beg” and the sacred “to pray.” French keeps them side by side — one may ~prier~ a guest to be seated as readily as ~prier~ a saint — and the polite formula “je vous en prie” (“please / you're welcome”) preserves the older entreating force, now worn down to mere courtesy. From the same ~preḱ-~ root French has the noun ~prière~ (“prayer”) and the adjective ~précaire~ (“precarious”), which entered through Latin ~precarius~ — originally “obtained by begging,” hence held only at another's pleasure and therefore uncertain.
en.primer:
From the adjective ~prime~ (“first”), attested in this verbal use from the 17th century, ultimately from Latin ~primus~ (“first, foremost, chief”).
