Latin ~primus~ goes back through an earlier *~prismos~ to the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“forward, before, beyond”) — the same root family that yields ~premier~ (from Latin ~primarius~), ~prince~, and a great many “fore-” words across Indo-European. By one account Old French already had ~premir~ in a kindred sense, suggesting native continuity rather than a fresh Latin draught.

The semantic line runs straight from “first”: to ~primer~ is to come first, to take precedence, to dominate or prevail — ~la sécurité prime~ (“safety comes first / takes priority”), ~primer sur~ (“to outweigh, to override”). Beware a homonym: a separate 19th-century ~primer~, denominal from ~prime~ in its sense “bonus, prize,” means “to award a prize,” and is unrelated to the “first” sense despite sharing the spelling. The “foremost” family is everywhere in French — ~premier~, ~primaire~, ~primauté~ (“primacy”), ~primordial~ — all turning on the idea of standing before all the rest.
en.priser: This spelling covers two verbs that have separate origins, and both Wiktionaries record both. One is formed from the noun ~prise~ (“a taking, a pinch”), itself from the past participle of ~prendre~ (“to take”), descended from Latin ~prensus~ and ~prehendere~ (“to seize”); this is ~priser~ in the sense of taking snuff. The other is inherited from Late Latin ~pretiāre~ (“to appraise”), from Latin ~pretium~ (“price”), the source of French ~prix~; this is ~priser~ in the sense of valuing or prizing. English Wiktionary stresses that the second is unrelated to ~prendre~, though French speakers may link them in their minds. The ending ~-er~ is the ordinary first-conjugation verb ending.
en.privatiser: ~Privatiser~ is a modern French formation built on the adjective ~privé~ (“private”), itself from Latin ~prīvātus~ (“set apart, belonging to an individual rather than the state”), with the verb-forming suffix ~-iser~, which goes back to Greek ~-ίζειν~ through Late Latin ~-izāre~. French Wiktionary adds that the verb was coined on the model of American English ~privatize~, so it is partly a calque of an English word that itself was built from the same Latin base. Its sense is “to transfer a public enterprise to private ownership,” the mirror of ~nationaliser~, and it spread with the economic policies of the late twentieth century.
en.priver:
From Latin ~privare~ (“to deprive, to free from, to set apart”), derived from the adjective ~privus~ (“single, individual, one's own”), from Proto-Italic *~preiwos~, ultimately from PIE *~per-~ (“in front, forward”), via a sense shift from “(being) in front” to “standing apart, separate.” Cognate with Italian ~privare~ and Spanish ~privar~, and the source, through French, of English ~deprive~ and ~private~.

The key is that ~privus~ meant “set apart, belonging to one alone” — hence ~privare~ first meant “to set apart,” then “to take away from, to deprive.” The same adjective gave the idea of what is withdrawn from public view: ~privé~ (“private”) and, with a darker color, ~privation~ (“hardship, want”). Roman ~privilegium~ — a law (~lex~) made for a single (~privus~) individual — became French ~privilège~, originally a right set apart for one person. The literary ~privauté~ (“familiarity, intimacy”) preserves the sense of the private and personal. To deprive someone is, etymologically, to set what they had apart from them.
en.privilégier:
Denominal verb from the noun ~privilège~, which comes from Latin ~prīvilēgium~ (“a law affecting a single person”), a compound of ~prīvus~ (“private, belonging to one individual”) and ~lēx~, stem ~lēg-~ (“law”). ~Prīvus~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~preiwos~, the same source as ~prīvātus~; ~lēx~ derives from the root *~leǵ-~ (“to gather, collect”), the laws being what is “laid down” or “collected.” Cognate with Italian ~privilegiare~ and Spanish ~privilegiar~, and — borrowed — with English ~privilege~. Literally, then, a ~privilège~ is private legislation: a rule carved out for one.

The Roman ~prīvilēgium~ was originally a neutral, even pejorative, term — a special law against an individual — but it drifted toward favorable exception, the sense of a granted advantage that medieval charters and royal grants entrenched. From the noun French built the verb ~privilégier~, “to favor, to give precedence,” now common in the bland modern sense of choosing one option over another, as in ~privilégier une approche~ (“to favor an approach”). The two halves seeded large families: ~prīvus~ gave ~privé~, ~priver~, and ~privation~, while ~lēx~ gave ~légal~, ~loi~, ~légiférer~, and ~privilège~ itself — the personal and the legal forever fused in a single word.
en.proclamer:
From Latin ~proclamare~ (“to cry out, to call aloud”), the prefix ~pro-~ (“forth, before, in public”) joined to ~clamare~ (“to shout, to call out”). ~Clamare~ descends from Proto-Italic *~klāmā-~ and from PIE *~kelh₁-~ (“to shout, to call”). Through Old French ~clamer~, the root reached English as ~claim~, and it lives on in the Romance verbs of calling: Italian ~chiamare~, Spanish ~llamar~, Portuguese ~chamar~.

To ~proclamer~ is to make something known by calling it out before everyone — to declare a republic, an emperor, or the winner of a contest. The same ~clamare~ seeded a noisy family of French words, all ringing with the idea of shouting: ~clamer~ (“to cry out”), ~clameur~ (“clamor”), ~réclamer~ (“to call back, to demand”), ~déclamer~ (“to declaim”), and ~s'exclamer~ (“to exclaim”). Even the quiet legal word ~réclame~ (“advertisement”) once meant a public cry. The verb keeps its ancient force: a proclamation is, at root, a shout made loud enough for a whole people to hear.
en.procréer:
~Procréer~ is borrowed from Latin ~prōcreāre~ (“to beget, to bring forth”). The Latin verb joins ~prō-~ (“forth”) to ~creāre~ (“to create, to bring into being”), so procreating is, literally, bringing something forth into the world. It kept this meaning from Latin to modern French: to engender children, a formal word for what everyday language calls ~avoir un enfant~ or ~faire un enfant~.

The second half of the verb is the root of a large family. ~Créer~ comes from Latin ~creāre~, and so do ~création~, ~créateur~, ~créature~ and ~récréer~ (“to re-create”). The learned noun ~procréation~ and the agent noun ~procréateur~ belong to the same Latin source as ~procréer~. Other Romance languages kept the verb nearly unchanged: Italian ~procreare~ and Spanish ~procrear~. English took it from Latin as ~procreate~, so the French and English words are cousins that never met on the way.
en.procurer:
From Old French ~procurer~, from Latin ~procurare~ (“to manage, attend to, take care of on behalf of another”), a compound of the prefix ~pro-~ (“on behalf of, for”) and the verb ~curare~ (“to care for, attend to”), from the noun ~cura~ (“care, concern”). That noun goes back to Proto-Italic *~koizā~ and, by the usual account, to PIE *~kʷeys-~ (“to heed, observe”). The same ~cura~ seeds a wide family in English: ~cure~, ~curious~, ~secure~ (literally ~sēcūrus~, “without care”), and even ~sure~. Romance cognates of the verb include Spanish ~procurar~ and Italian ~procurare~.

The Latin sense was administrative — to look after someone else's affairs, whence the ~procurator~ who managed an estate or a province. French narrowed this to “obtaining” something for someone, and, when the subject is a thing rather than a person, “to bring about” (a pleasure, a worry). English borrowed the noun ~procurer~ along a seedier path, for one who procures clients for a prostitute. From the same ~cura~ French keeps ~cure~, ~curieux~, and ~sûr~; the underlying idea is always attentive care directed toward an end.
en.procéder:
From Latin ~procedere~ (“to go forward, to advance, to result”), compounded from ~pro-~ (“forward, before”) and ~cedere~ (“to go, to withdraw, to yield”). ~Cedere~ descends from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “to go, to yield,” and ~pro-~ from the root *~per-~ (“forward, through”). Cognate, through ~cedere~, with the whole prefixed family that gave Italian ~procedere~ and Spanish ~proceder~, and with English ~proceed~ and ~process~.

The literal Latin sense — “to step forward” — branched in French into two living strands. One keeps the spatial and temporal idea of advancing: a ceremony, an investigation, or a chemical reaction ~procède~ in orderly steps. The other, “to behave, to act,” comes from the notion of how one goes about a thing. ~Cedere~ is among Latin's most generous roots, supplying French with ~céder~, ~accéder~, ~concéder~, ~précéder~, ~succéder~, ~procès~, and ~procédure~ — the last two preserving the legal sense of a matter that goes ~forward~ through stages. The English noun ~process~ and the verb ~proceed~ are the same word twice borrowed, and a ~procession~ is, etymologically, simply a going-forward made into a ceremony.
en.prodiguer:
French ~prodiguer~ is a borrowing from Latin ~prōdigere~ (“to drive forth, to squander”), made of ~prō-~ (“forth”) and ~agere~ (“to drive, to do”), the vowel of ~agere~ weakening to ~i~ inside the compound. ~Agere~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive”), shared with Ancient Greek ~ágein~ (“to lead”). The French form has a small oddity. A regular evolution would have given *~prodiger~, on the pattern of ~rédiger~, ~exiger~ and ~transiger~, which come from Latin verbs of the same shape. The ~-guer~ ending was instead shaped by the adjective ~prodigue~, which pulled the verb toward its own spelling and sound.

The image is of wealth driven out the door. Latin ~prōdigere~ meant to waste or squander, and the adjective ~prōdigus~ described the spendthrift. French ~prodigue~ kept that sense, as in the parable of the ~fils prodigue~ (“prodigal son”). The verb, however, turned kindly: ~prodiguer~ now means to give freely and abundantly, as in ~prodiguer des soins~ or ~des conseils~, with no hint of waste. Related words include ~prodigalité~ and, from the same root ~agere~, ~agir~, ~agent~ and ~exiger~.
en.produire:
From Latin ~producere~ (“to lead forward, bring forth”), a compound of the prefix ~pro-~ (“forward, before”) and the verb ~ducere~ (“to lead, draw”). ~Ducere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~doukō~ and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~dewk-~ (“to lead, draw, pull”), which also gives English ~tow~ and German ~Zug~ (“a pull, a draught”). Within French, ~ducere~ is the engine of a whole verb family: ~conduire~, ~réduire~, ~traduire~, and ~produire~ all share the same “leading” core.

The Latin sense was literally agricultural and theatrical at once — to “lead forth” crops from the earth, or to bring a witness or an actor forward into view. French kept both strands: ~produire~ still means “to bring forth” (goods, fruit, an effect) and, in legal usage, “to produce, to bring forward” a document or witness. From the past participle ~produit~ comes the everyday noun for a “product,” and the root spreads further into ~production~, ~producteur~, ~productif~, and ~productivité~. Behind the modern factory floor lies an old image of pulling something out and leading it into the light.
en.profaner: ~Profaner~ comes directly from Latin ~profānāre~ (“to desecrate”). As standard background, the Latin verb rests on the adjective ~profānus~, which is analysed as ~pro-~ (“before, in front of”) and ~fānum~ (“temple”), that is, outside the sacred precinct. The same adjective gave French ~profane~, and ~fānum~ is also behind ~fanatique~. English ~profane~ and Italian ~profanare~ are close relatives.
en.professer:
~Professer~ comes from Latin ~profiteor~ (“to declare openly, to avow”), a verb usually analyzed as ~pro-~ (“forth”) + ~fateor~ (“to admit, to acknowledge”). English Wiktionary adds that the French form was influenced by the noun ~professeur~. The French Académie records the verb with its three main senses from 1694 onward.

The shape of ~professer~ reflects the Latin past participle ~professus~, not the present stem ~profit-~, which is why the verb has the double ~ss~ that also appears in ~profession~ and ~professeur~. To ~professer~ is to declare something publicly, whether an opinion, a faith or a doctrine, and also to teach a subject. The verb has a close cousin in ~confesser~, built from the same ~fateor~ with ~con-~. English kept the root in ~profess~, ~profession~ and ~confess~.
en.professionnaliser: Formed in French from the adjective ~professionnel~ and the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to make A”: to ~professionnaliser~ is to turn an activity into a profession, or to make someone or something more professional. French Wiktionary adds that it was modeled on the English verb to professionalize. The base ~professionnel~ is itself a derivative of ~profession~ plus the adjectival suffix ~-el~. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which had transcribed Greek verbs, and in French it remains productive in administrative and journalistic language, where long verbs like this one are common.
en.profiler: ~Profiler~ is either formed in French on the noun ~profil~ with the ending ~-er~, or borrowed directly from Italian ~profilare~; the sources leave the question open. The noun ~profil~ is itself an Italian loan, from ~profilo~, which replaced Old French ~porfil~ (“border, contour”) with a narrower sense: the outline of something seen from the side. The verb therefore means to draw or shape an outline, then, more broadly, to give something a particular shape, and, reflexively, to stand out against a background. The ending ~-er~ is the usual verb-forming suffix of French, from Latin ~-are~.
en.profiter:
A denominal verb formed from the noun ~profit~. That noun comes from Latin ~profectus~ (“progress, growth, advantage”), the past participle of ~prōficere~ (“to advance, make progress, be useful”), built from ~prō-~ (“forward”) plus ~facere~ (“to make, do”). ~facere~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, place, set”), making French ~profiter~ a distant cousin of English ~do~ and ~deed~, of Greek ~tithēnai~ (“to put, place”), and of German ~tun~.

The literal Latin sense is “to make forward” — to advance. From “advance, gain ground” grew the noun's notion of material “profit, gain,” and the verb ~profiter~ took its main modern meanings from there: to profit from, to take advantage of, to make the most of (~profiter de la vie~, “to make the most of life”). A gentler branch keeps the older flavor of growth and benefit: ~profiter à quelqu'un~ means “to be beneficial to someone,” and regionally ~profiter~ can even mean “to thrive, grow well,” as a child or a plant does. The vast ~facere~ family fills modern French — ~faire~, ~profit~, ~bénéfice~, ~parfaire~, ~défaire~, ~confiture~ — so that to profit is, at root, simply to make headway.
en.proférer: ~Proférer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~proferō~ (infinitive ~proferre~), “to bring forth.” The Latin verb joins ~pro-~ (“forward”) to ~ferre~ (“to carry”). The same ~ferre~ underlies French ~conférer~, ~référer~ and ~transférer~. The French verb is restricted to speech: bringing words out, often with force.
en.programmer:
Denominal from the noun ~programme~, which French took (17th–18th century) from Greek ~prógramma~ (πρόγραμμα, “a public written notice, an edict”), from ~prográphein~ (“to write publicly, to write beforehand”): ~pró-~ (“before, in front”) plus ~gráphein~ (“to write”). ~Gráphein~ traces to PIE *~gerbʰ-~ (“to scratch, to carve”), since the earliest writing was incised — the same root that gives, through Germanic, English ~carve~, and through Greek, ~graphic~ and ~grammar~. A program was, at root, a notice scratched up in public view.

The word's modern career is striking. From “public notice” it became the printed list of a concert or theater bill, then any planned sequence of events, then — in the 20th century — the set of coded instructions fed to a computer, whence ~programmer~ in the sense of writing software. French now uses ~programmer~ for both: to schedule (a film, a meeting) and to code. The ~gráphein~ family is vast in French: ~graphique~, ~grammaire~, ~paragraphe~, ~biographie~, ~orthographe~. All of them lead back to the carved mark — writing remembered as scratching.
en.progresser:
A late and learned formation, attested only in 1832, ~progresser~ was built within French on the stem of ~progrès~ and ~progression~ plus the verbal suffix ~-er~. The family traces to Latin ~prōgressus~, the past participle of ~prōgredī~ (“to step forward, to advance”), from the prefix ~prō-~ (“forward”) and ~gradī~ (“to step, to walk”), itself from ~gradus~ (“a step”), from Proto-Indo-European *~gʰredʰ-~ (“to walk, to stride”). Through that root it is cognate with Italian ~progredire~, Spanish ~progresar~, and English ~progress~ and ~grade~.

The image at the heart of the word is the footstep: to ~progresser~ is, etymologically, to keep putting one foot ahead of the other. The verb arrived late because French long made do with the noun ~progrès~ and the verb ~avancer~; the 19th century, with its faith in onward march, seems to have wanted a verb of its own for the idea. From the same Latin ~gradī~ and ~gradus~ French drew a stepping family: ~progrès~, ~progression~, ~grade~, ~gradin~, ~graduel~, ~dégrader~, and the cousins ~agresser~ (“to step toward, to attack”), ~régresser~, ~digresser~, and ~transgresser~ — each a different direction taken from the same Latin stride.
en.prohiber:
From Latin ~prohibēre~ (“to hold back, to keep away, to forbid”), a learned borrowing. The Latin verb joins ~pro-~ (“forth, in front”) to ~habēre~ (“to have, to hold”), so to prohibit is, at bottom, to hold something at a distance. The same ~habēre~ is the ancestor of the everyday French verb ~avoir~ and, through its frequentative ~habitāre~ (“to dwell”), of ~habiter~. Italian ~proibire~ and Spanish ~prohibir~ descend from the Latin verb, and English ~prohibit~ was borrowed from it as well.

~Prohiber~ is a formal word, at home in laws and regulations, where one forbids the import of certain goods or the sale of a product, while everyday speech prefers ~interdire~ or ~défendre~. The Latin verb belonged to the second conjugation, but French fitted it into the first group in ~-er~, as it did with many learned borrowings. The noun ~prohibition~ and the adjective ~prohibitif~ (said of prices so high that they act as a ban) come from the same Latin verb. Other French words built on ~habēre~ with a different prefix include ~exhiber~ (“to hold out to view”), ~inhiber~ (“to hold in check”) and ~habile~ (“easy to handle, skillful”).
en.projeter:
~Projeter~ appears in the 16th century, reshaping the older Old French ~pourjeter~ on the model of Latin ~projectare~, the frequentative of ~projicere~ (« to throw forward »). That verb is ~pro-~ (« forward ») + ~jacere~ (« to throw »), from PIE *~yeh₁-~ (« to throw, to send »). The simple verb ~jeter~ (from ~jactare~) is its native French sibling; Italian ~progettare~ and Spanish ~proyectar~ are Romance cousins, and English borrowed both ~project~ and ~projectile~ from the same Latin stem.

The literal sense « to throw or cast forward » is still alive — one can ~projeter~ a shadow, a beam of light, or a person across a room. From hurling something physically forward, the verb reached toward the future: to ~projeter~ a trip or a building is to throw a plan ahead of oneself, to design what does not yet exist. The noun ~projet~ captures exactly this forward-thrown intention. The same ~jacere~ underlies a wide French family — ~objet~, ~sujet~, ~trajet~, ~rejeter~, ~injecter~, and ~adjacent~ — each preserving a buried « throw ».
en.proliférer:
~Proliférer~ is built from two Latin elements, ~prōlēs~ (“offspring”) and ~ferre~ (“to bear, to carry”), so that it means, literally, to bear offspring. The Latin verb ~ferre~ comes from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bher-~ (“to carry, to bear children”). That root is also behind English ~bear~, Ancient Greek ~phérein~ and Sanskrit ~bharati~, all meaning “to carry,” and behind a great many learned French verbs in ~-férer~.

In French the verb is used of living things that multiply and, by extension, of anything that quickly increases in number. Several French words share its Latin parts. ~Transférer~, ~conférer~, ~référer~ and ~différer~ all contain ~ferre~, while ~prolétaire~ and ~prolifique~ both start from ~prōlēs~. Words in ~-fère~ follow the same pattern: they name what bears something, as in ~conifère~ (cone-bearing). English ~proliferate~ is the matching counterpart.
en.prolonger:
Attested from 1213, from Late Latin ~prōlongāre~ (“to lengthen, to extend”), a compound of the prefix ~prō-~ (“forward”) and ~longus~ (“long”). Latin ~longus~ descends from Proto-Italic *~dlongos~ and Proto-Indo-European *~dlongʰos~ (“long”), the same root that, through Germanic, yielded English ~long~ and German ~lang~. Cognate, through ~prōlongāre~, with Italian ~prolungare~ and Spanish ~prolongar~.

The image is spatial first: ~prō-~ + ~longus~ means to draw something out lengthwise, to make it longer in front. French applied that both to space — ~prolonger~ a road or a line — and, more often, to time, where to ~prolonger~ a stay, a contract, or a debate is to stretch its duration onward. A learned doublet exists: alongside ~prolonger~, French also has ~allonger~ (“to lengthen,” from ~ad~ + ~longus~), the more concrete, everyday verb for making a sleeve or a step longer. The root ~longus~ runs deep in the language: ~long~, ~longueur~ (“length”), ~longer~ (“to run alongside”), ~allonger~, ~élonger~, and the learned ~longitude~ all spring from it, as does ~lent~ in spirit through the Latin sense of drawn-out slowness.
en.prolétariser: ~Prolétariser~ is formed from ~prolétaire~ with the suffix ~-iser~, which turns a noun into a verb meaning “to convert into N” or “to make N”: to reduce a person or a social class to the condition of proletarians. The noun ~prolétaire~ is borrowed from Latin ~prolētārius~, the name of a poor Roman citizen who counted for the state only through his children. It derives from ~prōlēs~ (“offspring”), itself from ~prō-~ and ~alere~ (“to nourish”). The ending ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs.
en.promener:
From Old French ~pourmener~ (attested around 1150), “to lead about, to take from place to place,” built from ~pour-~ and ~mener~ (“to lead”); the modern ~promener~ (14th century) is a learned remodeling that traded the native prefix for a Latin-looking ~pro-~. ~mener~ descends from popular Latin ~mināre~, the drover's verb — “to drive animals onward with shouts and threats” — which in classical Latin was ~minārī~ (“to threaten”), from ~minae~ (“threats,” literally “projecting points, overhangs”), traced to the PIE root *~men-~ (“to project, stand out”). Cognate with Italian ~menare~ (“to lead”), and, within the same Latin family, with French ~menace~ — borrowed by English as ~menace~ — as well as ~mont~ and ~montagne~, from Latin ~mōns~, another thing that juts.

Latin ~mināre~ belonged to the countryside: you moved cattle by walking behind them, shouting and cracking a whip, literally “threatening” them forward. Settled into Old French as plain “to lead,” the verb softened completely, and ~promener~ specialized in leading creatures out for air. The reflexive ~se promener~ (“to go for a walk”) is attested by about 1485, soon followed by the noun ~promenade~. A leisurely Sunday stroll thus descends, step for step, from threats bellowed at oxen — and someone walking a dog re-enacts the original scene, minus the shouting. The same ~mener~ produced a whole family of French verbs: ~amener~, ~emmener~, ~ramener~, ~malmener~ (“to manhandle”) and ~surmener~ — to overdrive a horse, hence to overwork — while ~menace~ keeps the old threat undisguised.
en.promettre:
From Latin ~promittere~ (“to send forth, hold out, promise”), built on ~pro-~ (“forth, before”) plus ~mittere~ (“to release, let go, send”). The verb came down regularly through Old French ~prometre~. According to Michiel de Vaan, ~mittere~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~meyth₂-~ (“to exchange, remove”). It is matched by Italian ~promettere~ and Spanish ~prometer~, and English ~promise~ comes from the related participle ~promissum~.

The literal image is generous: to ~promittere~ is to “send forth” your word ahead of you, to put a thing forward for someone. The vast ~mittere~ family is one of Latin's most productive, and French inherits or borrows a crowd of its compounds — ~mettre~ (“to put,” the popular outcome of ~mittere~ itself), ~admettre~, ~commettre~, ~permettre~, ~soumettre~, ~transmettre~ — alongside the learned ~-mission~ words ~mission~, ~émission~, and ~promesse~ (from ~promissa~), the noun beside the verb. So a promise is, etymologically, something “sent ahead” — a word dispatched into the future to be honoured later.
en.promotionner: Formed in French from the noun ~promotion~ and the ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Latin ~promotio~, derived from ~promovere~ (“to move forward”), the source of French ~promouvoir~. French Wiktionary notes that ~promotionner~ tends to replace ~promouvoir~, a common pattern in which a first-group verb takes over from a third-group one, as ~solutionner~ did for ~résoudre~. It is mostly used in commerce, for pushing a product with special offers.
en.promouvoir:
From Latin ~prōmovēre~ (“to move forward, to advance, to push on”), a compound of the prefix ~prō-~ (“forward, forth”) and ~movēre~ (“to move”). ~Movēre~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~mewh₁-~ (“to move, to push away”), and is cognate with English ~move~ (a Norman loan from the same Latin verb) and ~motor~, and with the Romance family of Italian ~muovere~ and Spanish ~mover~. The Latin verb reached French as a learned borrowing, which is why ~promouvoir~ keeps its irregular Latinate conjugation.

The image is bodily and concrete: to ~promote~ is to “move someone forward,” to push them up a rank. From this Roman sense of military and civil advancement, the verb broadened. One can ~promouvoir~ a colleague to a higher post, ~promouvoir~ a cause or an idea (to further its progress), and, in the most modern and commercial sense, ~promouvoir~ a product — to advertise it, an echo of the English ~promotion~ that re-entered French. Even in chess, a pawn that reaches the last rank is ~promu~. From the root *~mewh₁-~ descend a great crowd of French words, among them ~mouvoir~, ~émouvoir~, ~mouvement~, ~moteur~, ~émotion~, and ~mobile~.
en.prompter: ~Prompter~ is formed from ~prompt~ with the verb ending ~-er~, in the modern sense of giving instructions to an AI system. The base ~prompt~ has two sources in the evidence: the older adjective, a learned borrowing from Latin ~promptus~ (“visible, ready, available”), and the noun, borrowed from English ~prompt~, which is itself from the same Latin word. The verb is thus a recent French coinage on an English-influenced noun whose root is Latin.
en.promulguer:
From Latin ~promulgāre~ (“to post publicly, to publish”), borrowed directly into French. English Wiktionary analyzes the Latin verb as ~prō-~ (“forth”) + ~mulgeō~ (“to milk”), but it flags the etymology as incomplete, so this analysis should be treated as a proposal rather than a settled fact. The Latin verb has descendants across the Romance languages: Italian ~promulgare~ and Spanish, Portuguese and Catalan ~promulgar~. English took the same verb as ~promulgate~, and also as the rarer ~promulge~.

The core idea is making something public: the Latin verb meant to post a notice or publish it, and the French verb keeps that sense of putting a text before everyone. In modern French it is a formal word of law and government. One ~promulgue~ a law once it has been voted, which is the act that makes it official and enforceable, and the noun ~promulgation~ names that step. The verb has also spread to wider figurative uses, such as spreading a doctrine or a rule, and it remains a learned, written-register word with no everyday cousins in the spoken language.
en.prononcer:
From Old French ~prononcier~, from Latin ~prōnūntiāre~ (“to proclaim, announce, declare, recite”), from ~prō-~ (“forth, in public”) + ~nūntiāre~ (“to report, announce”), a verb built on ~nūntius~ (“messenger, message”), traditionally traced to Proto-Indo-European *~néw-~ (“to shout”). Cognate with Italian ~pronunciare~ and Spanish ~pronunciar~, and — through the same ~nūntiāre~ — with English ~pronounce~, ~announce~, and ~denounce~.

The core image is a herald carrying words ~forth~ before the public, which explains why the verb still spans both “to declare” (a court ~prononce~ a sentence) and “to articulate” (to ~prononcer~ a word aloud). The messenger ~nūntius~ seeded a wide family: with ~ad-~, ~annoncer~ (“to announce”); with ~dē-~, ~dénoncer~ (“to denounce”); with ~re-~, ~renoncer~ (“to renounce,” literally to report back that one withdraws); plus ~énoncer~ and the nouns ~nonce~ (the papal ambassador) and ~annonce~. A curious wrinkle: the noun ~prononciation~ keeps the ~-nci-~ of its Latin parent, while the verb worn smooth in the mouth became ~prononcer~ — the very word doing, in its own history, the softening it describes.
en.pronostiquer: Formed from the noun ~pronostic~ with the verb suffix ~-er~, so “to make a forecast”. The noun comes from Latin ~prognosticus~, borrowed from Ancient Greek ~prognōstikós~ (“foreknowing”). English Wiktionary splits the Greek word into ~pro-~ (“before”) and ~gnōstikós~ (“relating to knowledge”), from the verb ~gignṓskō~ (“to know”). The verb thus literally means to know ahead of time, though in practice the knowledge is a guess.
en.propager:
From Latin ~propagāre~ (“to propagate, to extend, to layer a vine”), a verb formed on ~propāgō~ (“a shoot, a layer, offspring”). The Latin noun is usually linked to the root of ~pangere~ (“to fasten, drive in”), and so to ~pāx~ (“peace”) and ~pactum~ (“agreement”), the underlying idea being of something fixed in the ground. English ~propagate~, Italian ~propagare~ and Spanish ~propagar~ are parallel descendants.

The verb began in the vineyard. To ~propager~ a vine was to bend a branch down and bury it so that it took root and became a new plant, and the word carried the sense of “extending a line” and of lineage. Out of that gardener's trick came the broader senses of multiplying and spreading, whether a fire, a rumour, a disease or a species. The same agricultural idea lives on in French ~provigner~, which comes from a related Latin verb, ~propāgināre~. The famous modern relative is ~propagande~, which comes from the Latin phrase ~Congregatio de propaganda fide~ (“congregation for propagating the faith”), a papal body of 1622. Others include ~propagateur~, ~propagation~ and ~propagule~.
en.prophétiser:
~Prophétiser~ is inherited from Old French ~prophetisier~, which came from Latin ~prophētizāre~, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~προφητίζω~ (~prophētízō~, “to prophesy”). The Greek verb derives from the noun ~προφήτης~ (~prophḗtēs~), “one who speaks on behalf of a god”, formed from ~pro-~ (“forth, on behalf of”) and a root meaning “to speak”. French ~prophète~ and English ~prophet~ come from the same Greek noun.

Seen from modern French, the verb looks like ~prophète~ plus ~-iser~, and that reading is not wrong in spirit. The ending is the one found in ~moderniser~ or ~actualiser~: the Greek verb suffix ~-ίζω~, which Late Latin transcribed as ~-izāre~ and Old French as ~-iser~. So ~prophétiser~ did not take a French suffix; it arrived with its ending already attached. Its relatives in French include ~prophète~, ~prophétie~, ~prophétique~ and ~prophétesse~.
en.proportionner: ~Proportionner~ is built on the noun ~proportion~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, “to provide with N”: to make something proportionate, to adjust one thing to another. The noun is inherited from Old French ~proportion~, a borrowing from Latin ~prōportiō~ (accusative ~prōportiōnem~), which meant “proportion, symmetry, analogy.”
en.proposer:
From Old French ~proposer~, a French reshaping of Latin ~prōpōnere~ (“to set forth, to put before”), formed from ~prō-~ (“before, forward”) + ~pōnere~ (“to put, to place”). When the verb passed into French, its second element was remodeled on ~poser~ (“to place”) — which actually descends from Latin ~pausāre~, “to pause” — so that ~prōpōnere~ became ~proposer~ by analogy. Cognate with Italian ~proporre~ and Spanish ~proponer~, and, through ~pōnere~, with English ~propose~ and ~propound~.

The Latin ~pōnere~ has a debated deep origin — traditionally analyzed as ~po-~ + ~sinere~ (“to set aside, let”), with its participle ~positus~ giving the family its ~-pos-~ forms. The literal sense, “to place before” someone for consideration, drifted naturally into “to put forward an idea,” to suggest. French built a rich crowd of relatives on this ~poser~ pattern: ~proposition~, ~proposer~'s siblings ~composer~, ~disposer~, ~exposer~, ~imposer~, ~opposer~, ~supposer~, and the noun ~propos~ (“words, remarks, purpose”). The learned ~positus~ branch adds ~position~, ~posture~, and ~dépôt~. From “placing” one builds an entire grammar of arrangement, intention, and debate.
en.propulser: Borrowed from Latin ~propulsāre~ (“to drive away, to repel”), a frequentative of ~propellere~ (“to push forward”), built on ~pro-~ (“forward”) and ~pellere~ (“to drive, to push”). The Latin verb leaned toward warding something off, while French ~propulser~ means to drive something forward, in line with the related noun ~propulsion~. The base ~pellere~ is also behind ~impulsion~, ~expulser~ and, through ~pulsāre~, French ~pousser~.
en.proroger: ~Proroger~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~prōrogāre~. The Latin verb is generally analyzed as ~prō-~ (“forward”) plus ~rogāre~ (“to ask”), and its sense in French is to extend or to postpone, as when a deadline or a legislative session is prolonged. The same ~rogāre~ lies behind ~interroger~ (“to question”), ~déroger~ and ~arroger~, and the noun ~prorogation~ is the direct counterpart of the verb. English ~prorogue~ is a related borrowing.
en.proscrire:
From Latin ~prōscrībere~ (“to make public in writing, to post a notice; to outlaw, to banish”), formed from ~prō~ (“before, in public”) and ~scrībere~ (“to write”). French took it as a learned borrowing and conjugates it like ~écrire~. ~Scrībere~ is also the source of ~écrire~ itself, as well as ~inscrire~, ~décrire~, ~souscrire~ and ~prescrire~. English ~proscribe~, Italian ~proscrivere~ and Spanish ~proscribir~ come from the same Latin verb.

The story is a grim one from Roman history. A ~proscriptio~ was a notice posted in public naming men who had been declared outlaws: anyone could kill them, and their property was seized. Sulla issued such lists in 82 BC, and the triumvirs revived the practice in 43 BC. French ~proscrire~ is used figuratively to mean “to forbid, to condemn, to ban”, applied to words, habits or products. Beware of the lookalike ~prescrire~ (“to order, to prescribe”): ~proscrire~ forbids, ~prescrire~ commands. Related words are ~proscription~, ~proscrit~ and ~écrit~.
en.prospecter:
French ~prospecter~ comes from the English verb ~prospect~, attested from 1841 in the sense of searching for gold or mineral deposits. That sense is a specialization of an older English ~prospect~ (“to look ahead, to look into the distance, to examine head-on”), which comes from Latin ~prospectare~. The verb is thus a Latin word that French took in by way of English, as a technical term of mining.

Latin ~prospectare~ is a frequentative of ~prospicere~ (“to look out over”), built on ~pro-~ (“forward”) and the root of ~specere~ (“to look”). The same Latin family gave French ~prospection~, ~prospectus~, ~inspecter~, ~spectacle~ and ~respect~. Modern French ~prospecter~ has left the mines behind in part, since it also covers canvassing for customers, but it still keeps the old image of scanning the horizon for something worth finding.
en.prospérer:
From Old French ~prosperer~, borrowed from Latin ~prosperāre~ (“to make fortunate, to cause to succeed”), a verb built on the adjective ~prosper~ (“favorable, fortunate”). The origin of ~prosper~ is not fully settled, but the most common account links it to ~prō~ and the same root as Latin ~spēs~ (“hope”), itself from the Proto-Indo-European root *~speh₁-~ (“to thrive, to succeed”). English ~speed~ is a native cousin, since it first meant “success” before it meant “haste.” Italian ~prosperare~ and Spanish ~prosperar~ are parallel borrowings, as is English ~prosper~.

In Latin, ~prosperāre~ could be said of a god or the weather making a harvest or an enterprise succeed. In modern French the verb is used chiefly of the person or business that ~prospère~, thriving. The possible connection with hope is worth noticing. The family includes ~prospère~ and ~prospérité~, and, through the same Latin root, ~espérer~ and ~espoir~, which come from ~spēs~ and ~sperāre~.
en.prosterner:
Borrowed from Latin ~prosternere~ (“to lay low, to throw down”), which is built from ~pro~ (“forward”) and ~sternere~ (“to stretch out, to spread”). French Wiktionary gives the same parts, and English Wiktionary simply calls the verb a borrowing from Latin ~prōsternō~. The Latin participle ~prostratus~ gave English ~prostrate~ and the French adjective ~prostré~. The verb is therefore a learned import from Latin, not a word shaped by popular sound change.

Taken piece by piece, the Latin verb pictures a body stretched out forward, and French keeps this physical sense. The verb is most often reflexive: ~se prosterner~ means to bow down or to throw oneself to the ground before someone, in reverence or in submission. The noun ~prosternation~ and the more usual ~prostration~, from the Latin supine stem, belong to the same family, as does the figurative use for abject deference. The second Latin element, ~sternere~, also lies behind ~stratus~ and the French ~strate~, so the same root that flattens a person to the floor lays down layers of rock.
en.prostituer: Borrowed from Latin ~prōstituere~ (“to prostitute, corrupt”; French Wiktionary glosses it “to sell, to sell oneself”). The Latin verb is formed from ~prō-~ (“forward”) and a form of ~statuere~ (“to set up, place”). It entered French as a learned word, keeping the Latin shape almost intact, and its figurative sense, to sell one's talent or honor, sits beside the literal one in modern French.
en.protester: A learned borrowing from Latin ~prōtestārī~ (“to declare publicly, to bear witness in front of others”), formed from ~prō-~ (“forth, in public”) and ~testārī~ (“to testify”), which comes from ~testis~ (“witness”). The older French sense was to declare something solemnly, as in ~protester de son innocence~ (“to protest one's innocence”), a meaning that survives. The sense of speaking out against something developed from that public declaration. The same ~testārī~ lies behind ~attester~, ~contester~ and ~testament~.
en.protéger:
From Latin ~protegere~ (“to cover in front, to shelter, to defend”), a compound of the prefix ~pro-~ (“before, in front of”) and ~tegere~ (“to cover”). The verb ~tegere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~tegō~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)teg-~ (“to cover, to roof”), shared with Ancient Greek ~στέγειν~ (~stégein~, “to cover”), German ~Dach~ (“roof”), and English ~thatch~ and ~deck~. Italian ~proteggere~ and Spanish ~proteger~ are the Romance parallels; English ~protect~ comes from the same Latin verb.

The literal picture is a soldier holding a shield in front — covering before — and from this concrete shelter the sense rose to abstract protection, defense, and patronage. The earlier, more popular French outcome of ~tegere~ was distinct: through related forms French got ~toit~ (“roof,” from ~tectum~) and the verb couvrir comes from a different root, but ~protéger~ kept the learned Latin shape, borrowed late in the 14th century. The same *~(s)teg-~ root surfaces across French in ~tuile~ (“roof tile,” from ~tegula~), ~toge~ (the Roman ~toga~, a “covering” garment), ~protection~, ~tégument~, and ~détecter~ — the last literally an “un-covering.”
en.prouver:
From Latin ~probare~ (“to test, to examine, to approve, to demonstrate”), a verb derived from the adjective ~probus~ (“good, upright, of fine quality”). ~Probus~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~proβwos~ and to a Proto-Indo-European formation *~pro-bʰuH-~, literally “being in front, growing forward well,” from *~pro-~ (“forward”) and the root *~bʰuH-~ (“to be, to grow”). Cognate, through this root, with Sanskrit ~prabhú~ (“excellent, foremost”), and with English ~prove~ and ~probe~.

The Latin chain of meaning is elegant: what is ~probus~ is upright and sound; to ~probare~ is to test something to see whether it measures up, and then to approve or demonstrate that it does. French ~prouver~ kept the demonstrative end of that arc — to establish a truth — while the testing sense lingers in ~éprouver~ (“to test, to experience”) and ~épreuve~ (“trial, ordeal, proof-sheet”). The same root yields ~probe~ (“upright”), ~probité~, ~approuver~, ~réprouver~, and the printer's ~épreuve~. English inherited a whole cluster — ~prove~, ~proof~, ~probable~, ~probation~, ~approve~ — all turning on the old idea that to prove a thing is, at heart, to find it good.
en.provenir:
From Latin ~provenire~ (“to come forth, to arise, to grow up”), a compound of the prefix ~pro-~ (“forth, forward”) and the verb ~venire~ (“to come”). ~venire~ descends from Proto-Italic *~gʷeniō~ and from the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʷem-~ (“to come, to go”), which makes ~provenir~ a distant cousin of English ~come~, Greek ~baínō~ (“I walk”), and Sanskrit ~gácchati~ (“he goes”). Italian ~provenire~ and Spanish ~provenir~ continue the same Latin compound.

The Latin verb was vividly literal — to come forth, even to sprout or be born — and the agricultural image of a crop “coming forth” underlies the noun ~provenance~, originally the yield or produce of a place, now its source or origin. Modern ~provenir~ keeps this sense of issuing from a point of departure, whether a word ~provient~ from Latin or a sound ~provient~ from the next room. The base ~venir~ is one of the most fertile verbs in French, throwing off a whole prefixed family: ~devenir~ (“to become”), ~revenir~ (“to come back”), ~convenir~ (“to suit, to agree”), ~prévenir~ (“to warn, to forestall”), ~survenir~ (“to occur”), and ~parvenir~ (“to reach, to attain”). The root *~gʷem-~ thus quietly powers a sizeable corner of the French lexicon.
en.provigner: Formed from the noun ~provin~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. A ~provin~ is a vine shoot bent into the ground to take root, and ~provigner~ means to propagate a vine this way. The noun comes from Old French ~provain~, from Latin ~propāginem~, the accusative of ~propāgō~ (“cutting, shoot”). The same Latin family gave French the learned ~propager~, so ~provigner~ and ~propager~ are distant cousins.
en.provisionner: Formed from the noun ~provision~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning “to supply with provisions” and, in finance, “to put money into an account” or “to set funds aside.” The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin ~prōvīsiō~ (“foresight, preparation”), from ~prōvidēre~ (“to provide”), literally “to see ahead.” The idea survives in the financial sense: money set aside is money kept for a need that has been foreseen.
en.provoquer:
From Latin ~provocare~ (“to call forth, to challenge, to appeal”), from ~pro-~ (“forth, forward”) + ~vocare~ (“to call”). ~vocare~ is built on ~vox~ (“voice”), from Proto-Indo-European *~wokʷ-~, the root of ~vox~ and of English ~voice~ and ~vocal~. Old French had a popular variant ~porvochier~; the learned ~provoquer~ established itself by the mid-fourteenth century, notably in Pierre Bersuire's translation of Livy. Romance cognates include Italian ~provocare~ and Spanish ~provocar~.

In Rome, to ~provocare~ was literally to “call someone out” — to summon, to challenge to combat, and, crucially, to ~provocare ad populum~, to appeal a magistrate's sentence to the people, a cornerstone of Republican liberty. The combative edge survived: the verb came to mean “to incite, to challenge, to bring about,” keeping a sense of summoning a reaction into being, whether a quarrel, an illness, or a result. From the same ~vocare~ and ~vox~ French inherited a chorus of words: ~évoquer~, ~invoquer~, ~convoquer~, ~révoquer~, ~vocation~, ~voix~, and ~voyelle~.
en.préaviser: Formed from ~aviser~ with the prefix ~pré-~, from Latin ~prae-~ (“before”), so it means to warn or inform someone beforehand. The base ~aviser~ is explained in two ways: from the noun ~avis~, or as ~a-~ plus ~viser~, which goes back to Latin ~vīsāre~ (“to look at attentively”) and ultimately ~vidēre~ (“to see”). The verb belongs to administrative and legal language, where notice must be given in advance.
en.précariser: Formed from ~précaire~ and the suffix ~-iser~ (“make A”): to ~précariser~ is to make something precarious. The adjective is borrowed from Latin ~precārius~, “obtained by prayer”, hence not assured, and is a doublet of ~prière~ (“prayer”). English Wiktionary compares the parallel formations Spanish ~precarizar~ and Italian ~precarizzare~, which suggests a verb coined along similar lines in several Romance languages.
en.précautionner: Formed from the noun ~précaution~ with the verb ending ~-er~: ~précautionner~ is “to put on one's guard.” The noun is a learned borrowing from Late Latin ~praecautiō~, from ~praecavēre~ (“to guard against beforehand”), made of ~prae-~ (“before”) and ~cavēre~ (“to beware”). Latin ~cavēre~ is also the source of English ~caveat~.
en.préchauffer: Formed from ~chauffer~ with the prefix ~pré-~, from Latin ~prae-~ (“before”), meaning “to heat beforehand,” as in ~préchauffer le four~. The base ~chauffer~ descends from Vulgar Latin *~calefare~, a worn-down form of Latin ~calefacere~ (“to make warm”), built from ~calere~ (“to be hot”) and ~facere~ (“to make”). The prefix is productive in technical and everyday vocabulary, alongside verbs like ~prépayer~ and ~présélectionner~, and the verb is a modern coinage for a modern appliance.
en.précipiter:
French ~précipiter~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~praecipitare~ (“to throw headlong, to hurl down”), a verb built on the adjective ~praeceps~ (“headfirst, headlong, steep”). ~Praeceps~ is itself ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) + ~caput~ (“head”) — so to ~praecipitare~ was, vividly, to send something “head-first” off a height. ~Caput~ descends from Proto-Italic *~kaput~ and PIE *~káput~ (“head”), the same root that, through Proto-Germanic, yields English ~head~ and German ~Haupt~. The picture is almost cartoonish: a body pitched forward, head leading, tumbling down a cliff.

That headlong image fans out into every modern sense. To ~précipiter~ someone is to throw them down or push them off; to ~précipiter~ an event is to rush it forward too fast; reflexively, ~se précipiter~ is to dash or rush headlong. Chemistry borrowed the verb for a substance that drops out of solution as a solid — a ~précipité~ — falling to the bottom just as a body falls from a height. From the same ~caput~ root French keeps ~chef~ (originally “head,” hence “leader”), ~capitaine~, ~capital~, ~chapitre~, and even ~couvre-chef~ (“headgear”). The adjective ~précipité~ (“hasty”) and the adverb ~précipitamment~ (“hurriedly”) preserve the original rush of the fall.
en.préciser:
French ~préciser~ is a verb formed from the adjective ~précis~ (“precise, exact”) with the first-conjugation suffix ~-er~. ~Précis~ comes from Latin ~praecīsus~ (“cut off, abridged, abrupt”), the past participle of ~praecīdere~ (“to cut off in front, to cut short”), itself ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) plus ~caedere~ (“to cut, to strike, to fell”). ~Caedere~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~kaidō~ to Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂id-~ (“to strike, to hew”), with cognates such as Sanskrit ~khídati~ (“to tear”) and Old High German ~heia~ (“mallet”).

The governing metaphor is sharpness: what is ~précis~ has had every excess pared away, leaving a clean cut. To ~préciser~ is thus to trim a vague statement down to its exact edge — to specify, to make sharp. The same ~caedere~ runs through a surprisingly bloody cluster of relatives: the suffix ~-cide~ in ~homicide~ and ~suicide~ (a “cutting down”), and the doublet ~concis~ (“cut together, concise”). English drew ~precise~, ~concise~, ~decide~, and even ~scissors~ from the same Latin stem. There is a quiet paradox here — the word for verbal exactness descends from a verb for hacking and felling, as if precision were a kind of clean amputation of everything imprecise.
en.précompter: ~Précompter~ is formed from ~compter~ with the prefix ~pré-~, from Latin ~prae-~ (“before”), and means to deduct in advance, to count something out beforehand. The base ~compter~ is a learned respelling, with its ~p~ restored, of Old French ~conter~, from Latin ~computare~ (“to reckon”), made of ~com-~ and ~putare~. Old French ~conter~ meant both “to count” and “to tell”, and the two senses later split into ~compter~ and ~conter~.
en.préconiser:
From Late Latin ~praeconizare~ (“to proclaim, to publish”), attested as ~preconizer~ in 1321, derived from Latin ~praeco~, ~praeconis~ (“public crier, herald”). The origin of ~praeco~ itself is disputed: by one account it comes by syncope from *~praedicō~ (~prae-~ + ~dicere~, “to declare beforehand”), while Ernout and Meillet derive it instead from *~praevocō~ (~prae-~ + ~vocāre~, “to call out before”). Either way, a ~praeco~ was the official voice that cried public announcements aloud.

The verb long meant simply “to proclaim, to publish,” faithful to the herald who shouted the news in the square. Only around 1660 did it shift to its modern sense “to recommend, to extol,” as if the public crier now praised rather than merely announced. The same Latin ~praeco~ left little progeny in French, but the kindred root ~dicere~ (if the first hypothesis holds) seeds a vast family — ~dire~, ~prédire~, ~contredire~ — while ~vocāre~ (the rival hypothesis) underlies ~vocation~ and ~convoquer~.
en.précéder:
From Latin ~praecedere~ (“to go before, precede”), a compound of ~prae-~ (“before, in front of”) and ~cedere~ (“to go, to yield, to give way”). Latin ~cedere~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~kesdō~ to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ked-~ (“to go, to yield”). The same ~cedere~, fitted with different prefixes, produced a whole battery of French and English verbs of motion and giving-way: ~accéder~, ~concéder~, ~excéder~, ~procéder~, ~succéder~, and English ~accede~, ~concede~, ~recede~, and ~secede~.

The Latin sense was concrete and spatial — to physically walk in front of someone — and French ~précéder~ has kept that literal core while extending it to precedence in time, rank, and logic: one event precedes another, one dignitary precedes another in a procession. The supine stem ~cessum~ (rather than ~ced-~) supplies a parallel set of nouns, which is why French has ~procession~, ~succession~, and the astronomical ~précession~, the slow gyration of a spinning axis. From the same family come ~accès~, ~succès~, ~procédé~, and ~cesser~ (“to cease”), all turning on the idea of going, stepping, or giving way.
en.prédestiner: Borrowed from Latin ~praedestināre~ (“to appoint in advance”), built from ~prae-~ (“before”) and ~destināre~ (“to assign to”). In Christian Latin the verb took on the sense of preparing something in advance from all eternity, which is the theological meaning behind ~prédestiner~. French speakers can also read it as ~pré-~ plus ~destiner~, as English Wiktionary does.
en.prédiquer:
~Prédiquer~ is borrowed from Latin ~praedicāre~ (“to proclaim publicly, to declare”). The Latin verb is built from the prefix ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) and ~dicāre~ (“to make known, to proclaim”), a relative of ~dīcere~ (“to say”). The learned French verb is thus a close copy of its Latin model, and Italian ~predicare~ and Spanish ~predicar~ continue the same Latin verb.

Latin ~praedicāre~ also had an inherited, worn-down life in French: ~prêcher~, “to preach,” which comes from the same verb through Old French. ~Prédiquer~ is the learned doublet that kept the Latin shape. Its main modern use is in logic and grammar, where to ~prédiquer~ is to assert something of a subject, to attribute a property to it. The same family supplies ~prédicat~ (“predicate”), ~prédicateur~ (“preacher”) and ~prédication~ (“preaching”). English ~predicate~ and ~preach~ come from the same Latin verb, the first directly and the second through French.
en.prédire:
French ~prédire~ comes from Latin ~praedīcere~ (“to say beforehand”). English Wiktionary describes it as inherited from Middle French ~predire~, itself borrowed from the Latin verb. ~Praedīcere~ is a compound of ~prae-~ (“before”) and ~dīcere~ (“to say”). Spanish ~predecir~ and Italian ~predire~ are close cousins, and English ~predict~ comes from the same Latin verb.

The second element ~dīcere~ is the root of a large family. French ~dire~ descends from it, and so do ~dicter~, ~édit~, ~verdict~ and ~dictionnaire~, some inherited and some learned. Another compound of the same verb, ~contredire~, is built like ~prédire~. ~Prédire~ is conjugated like ~dire~ except in the second person plural of the present, ~vous prédisez~, where ~dire~ keeps ~vous dites~.
en.prédisposer: Inherited from Middle French ~prédisposer~, which by surface analysis is ~pré-~ + ~disposer~. The prefix ~pré-~ comes from Latin ~prae-~ (“before, in front of”) and here means “beforehand.” The base ~disposer~ goes back to Latin ~dispōnere~ (“to set out, to arrange in different places”), from ~dis-~ (“apart”) and ~pōnere~ (“to put, to place”). The verb therefore means to arrange or incline someone in advance, long before the matter at hand arises.
en.prédominer: Formed from ~dominer~ with the prefix ~pré-~, which here carries the sense “in front of, over”: to ~prédominer~ is to hold sway over others. The base ~dominer~ comes from Latin ~dominārī~ (“to be master, to rule”), a verb derived from ~dominus~ (“master of the house”), which in turn comes from ~domus~ (“house”). The prefix goes back to Latin ~prae-~ (“before, in front of”). The same ~dominus~ gave Italian ~dominare~ and Spanish ~dominar~.
en.prédéterminer: Formed from ~déterminer~ with the prefix ~pré-~ (“before, in advance”), so “to determine beforehand.” ~Déterminer~ comes from Latin ~determinare~ (“to bound, to fix limits to”), made of ~de-~ and ~terminare~ (“to limit”), which rests on ~terminus~ (“boundary, boundary-stone”). The prefix ~pré-~ is from Latin ~prae-~ (“before, in front of”). The verb thus means to settle the limits of something ahead of time.
en.préempter: A back-formation from ~préemption~, a learned word whose second half goes back to Latin ~emptio~ (“purchase”), from ~emere~ (“to buy”). The sources describe the route a little differently. French Wiktionary analyses it as the prefix ~pré-~ plus ~emptio~, while English Wiktionary traces ~préemption~ to Latin ~praeēmptiāre~. In both accounts the verb means to buy or claim something ahead of others, a right of purchase exercised first.
en.préexister: ~Préexister~ is formed from ~exister~ with the prefix ~pré-~ (“beforehand”), so it means to exist before something else. The base ~exister~ was borrowed from Latin ~existere~, itself ~ex-~ (“out”) + ~sistere~ (“to set, to stand”), literally “to step forth.” The prefix ~pré-~ comes from Latin ~prae-~ (“before, in front of”).
en.préfacer: Formed from the noun ~préface~ and the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, with the sense “to write a preface for” a book. The noun descends from Old French ~preface~, borrowed from Medieval Latin ~prefatia~, which comes from Classical Latin ~praefātiō~ (“preface, prologue”). That Latin noun derives from ~praefor~ (“to speak beforehand”), made of ~prae-~ (“beforehand”) and ~for~ (“to speak”). A ~préface~ is therefore, etymologically, something said in advance, and ~préfacer~ means to supply one.
en.préfigurer: The sources differ on the route. French Wiktionary derives it directly from Late Latin ~praefigurāre~, while English Wiktionary treats it as French ~pré-~ (“before”) plus ~figurer~. Either way the elements are the same: the prefix ~pré-~, from Latin ~prae-~ (“before”), and ~figurer~, from Latin ~figurāre~ (“to shape, to form”), from ~figūra~ (“shape”). To ~préfigurer~ is to foreshadow, to present in advance the shape of something to come, a sense long familiar in theology, where an Old Testament event prefigures a New Testament one.
en.préfixer: ~Préfixer~ is built on the noun ~préfixe~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, and means “to add a prefix to.” The noun was borrowed from Latin ~praefixus~ (“fixed in front”), which also gave French the adjective ~préfix~. The grammatical sense of ~préfixe~ is the one the verb relies on.
en.préformer: Formed from ~former~ with the prefix ~pré-~, which comes from Latin ~prae-~ (“before, in front of”), so “to form beforehand.” The base ~former~ comes from Latin ~formare~ (“to shape, to fashion”), derived from ~forma~ (“shape, figure, mold, beauty”). That noun also gave French ~forme~, ~format~, ~formule~ and ~transformer~. The prefix ~pré-~ is productive for the idea of “in advance,” as in ~préchauffer~.
en.préférer:
From Latin ~praeferre~ (“to carry before, set before, prefer”), formed from the prefix ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) and the verb ~ferre~ (“to carry, bear”). ~Ferre~ descends from Proto-Italic *~ferō~ and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰer-~ (“to carry, to bear”), one of the most widespread roots in the family. Through that root it is cognate with Ancient Greek ~phérein~ (“to carry”), Sanskrit ~bhárati~ (“he carries”), and the Germanic verbs of bearing — English ~bear~ and German ~gebären~ (“to give birth”).

The image behind the word is concrete: to prefer something is literally to ~carry~ it out in front, to hold it ahead of the rest. Latin already used ~praeferre~ in this figurative sense of valuing one thing above another, and French inherited the metaphor whole. The supine stem of ~ferre~ was the irregular ~lātum~, which is why the ~fer-~ family and the ~lat-~ family in French look unrelated despite sharing a verb: from ~prae-~ + ~ferre~ comes ~préférer~, and the parallel ~prae-~ formations gave ~préface~ and ~préférence~. The same root *~bʰer-~ runs through a large French vocabulary of carrying and bringing: ~offrir~, ~souffrir~, ~conférer~, ~transférer~, and ~référer~ are all, etymologically, manners of bearing a load.
en.préjudicier: ~Préjudicier~ is a denominal verb made from ~préjudice~ with the verbal ending ~-ier~, and it means to harm or be detrimental to. ~Préjudice~ was inherited from Old French and borrowed from Latin ~praeiūdicium~ (“previous judgment or damage”), itself from ~prae-~ (“before”) and ~iūdicium~ (“judgment”). The Latin word thus joins a prior judgment with the harm it can do.
en.préjuger: Two accounts sit side by side. French Wiktionary derives ~préjuger~ from Latin ~praeiudicāre~ and also reads it, as a synchronic matter, as ~pré-~ (“before”) plus ~juger~ (“to judge”); English Wiktionary calls it ~pré-~ plus ~juger~ and an adaptation of the Latin verb. The Latin source, ~praeiudicāre~, is itself ~prae-~ plus ~iudicāre~ (“to judge”), so both the Latin and the French say “to judge in advance.” The base ~juger~ descends from ~iudicāre~. Related words include ~préjugé~ and ~préjudice~, and English ~prejudge~ and ~prejudice~.
en.prélasser: French Wiktionary explains ~prélasser~ as derived from ~prélat~ plus ~-er~, by way of an older ~se prelater~ (“to behave like a prelate”), with an ironic influence from ~lasser~ (“to tire”). A ~prélat~ is a high church dignitary, and the word comes from Latin ~praelātus~ (“preferred, chosen”). The picture is of someone lounging with the self-satisfied ease of a churchman. Today ~se prélasser~ means to sprawl comfortably and laze about, and the ~-las-~ of ~lasser~ gives the verb a faint sound of weariness.
en.prélever:
~Prélever~ was borrowed from medieval Latin ~praelevare~ (“to take beforehand”), from ~prae-~ (“before”) and ~levare~ (“to lift, to lighten”), a verb built on the adjective ~levis~ (“light in weight”), from Proto-Italic *~leɣʷis~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ — the very root that, through Germanic, gives English ~light~. Latin ~levare~ had a prolific Romance career: it became Italian ~levare~, French ~lever~ and Spanish ~llevar~, where “to lift” drifted into “to carry,” the raised load ending up borne away. ~Prélever~ is thus the learned cousin of the everyday verb ~lever~, assembled not in French but already in the Latin of the Middle Ages.

The verb entered French through the tax office: it is first recorded in 1629 meaning “to levy a duty upon,” and in 1690 Furetière defines it as taking a share from a mass before any division. That administrative chill never left it: the modern State ~prélève~ taxes (the famous ~prélèvements obligatoires~), the bank performs a ~prélèvement automatique~ on an account, and the nurse takes a ~prélèvement sanguin~ — in every case a part removed from a whole before the rest is shared or spent. Around it floats an airy family: ~lever~, ~élever~, ~soulever~, ~enlever~, ~relever~, ~léger~, the ~levain~ that makes dough rise, the ~levant~ where the sun comes up. ~Prélever~ alone kept the accountant's gesture: lift a little off the top, first.
en.préluder:
From Latin ~praeludere~, formed from ~prae-~ (“before”) and ~lūdere~ (“to play”), so literally “to play beforehand”. French took the verb over from Latin, and it is closely tied to the noun ~prélude~. English ~prelude~ comes from the same Latin family, and Spanish ~preludiar~ and Italian ~preludiare~ are the matching verbs in those languages.

In French, ~préluder~ means to introduce something or to be a prelude to it, as a musician warms up before the piece, or as an event announces a larger one. The Latin root ~lūdere~ (“to play”) underlies a family of French words, among them ~ludique~, ~illusion~ (from ~illudere~, “to play with, to mock”), ~allusion~ and ~interlude~.
en.prémunir:
Borrowed from Latin ~praemūnīre~ (“to fortify in advance, to protect”), a compound of ~prae-~ (“before”) and ~mūnīre~ (“to fortify”). Unlike most French verbs of this shape, it did not pass through spoken Old French: it was taken directly from written Latin, which is why it keeps the learned prefix ~pré-~ and the ending ~-unir~. The simple verb ~mūnīre~ also reached French as ~munir~ (“to provide with”), and its noun ~mūnītiō~ gave ~munition~.

The Latin meaning was military: to strengthen a position, with walls and defenses, before an attack comes. French kept the idea of advance protection but moved it from fortresses to people. Today ~prémunir~ means “to protect against a future danger” and is used almost only with a preposition, as in ~prémunir quelqu'un contre le froid~ or ~se prémunir contre les risques~. A related sense is “to warn,” since a person who has been forewarned is armed against the harm to come. The verb is thus a small fortress built around the image of a wall put up before the enemy arrives.
en.préméditer: Borrowed from Latin ~praemeditārī~, the verb ~méditer~ with the prefix ~pré-~ attached in Latin already: ~prae-~ (“before”) plus ~meditārī~ (“to think over, to ponder”). The French verb therefore means to think something over, and so to plan it, in advance. It was not built in French from ~pré-~ and ~méditer~, although those are the matching French elements.
en.prénommer: Formed from the noun ~prénom~ (“first name”) with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~: to give a first name to someone, or to call a person by that name. The noun ~prénom~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~praenomen~, the personal name that a Roman placed before the family name. In French the noun can also be read as ~pré-~ + ~nom~, since the parts are still visible, but the Latin word shows that the whole was borrowed, not built on French soil.
en.préoccuper:
From Latin ~praeoccupāre~ (“to seize beforehand, occupy in advance”), from ~prae-~ (“before”) plus ~occupāre~ (“to seize, take possession of”). ~occupāre~ is itself ~ob-~ (“toward, against”) plus the stem of ~capiō~ (“to take, seize”), from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp, seize”). Cognate, through that root, with English ~have~, ~heave~, and ~capture~.

The literal Latin sense is military and temporal — to grab a position before the enemy does. French ~préoccuper~ moved that seizure inward: what occupies the mind ahead of everything else comes to weigh on it, so ~préoccuper~ slid from “to take up in advance” to “to absorb, to worry.” Today ~se préoccuper de~ means “to concern oneself with,” and a ~préoccupation~ is a care or anxiety. From the same ~capiō~ root French keeps a teeming family: ~occuper~, ~capter~, ~captiver~, ~recevoir~, ~concevoir~, and ~capable~ — all built on the ancient gesture of grasping.
en.préparer:
From Latin ~praeparare~ (“to make ready beforehand”), a compound of the prefix ~prae-~ (“before, in advance”) and ~parare~ (“to make ready, to prepare, to furnish”). The verb ~parare~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~perh₃-~ (“to grant, to allot, to provide”), which also yielded Latin ~parere~ (“to give birth, to produce”) and is glimpsed in Ancient Greek ~ἔπορον~ (~époron~, “I furnished”) and Sanskrit ~pṛṇāti~ (“he grants”). Italian ~preparare~ and Spanish ~preparar~ are the sister forms; English borrowed ~prepare~ from the same Latin source.

The kernel is ~parare~, “to get something ready,” and the prefix ~prae-~ simply pulls the readiness ahead in time — to arrange in advance. The bare root ~parare~ survives in French ~parer~, which split into two senses: “to adorn” (to make ready for display) and “to ward off” a blow, the source of ~parade~ and the fencing ~parer~. The same ~parare~ underlies a remarkable spread of French words: ~préparer~, ~réparer~ (“to make ready again,” hence “to repair”), ~séparer~, ~comparer~, ~emparer~, and ~appareil~ — and, through the related ~imperare~, the imperial vocabulary of ~empereur~ and ~empire~.
en.prépayer: ~Prépayer~ is formed from ~payer~ with the prefix ~pré-~, which means beforehand: to pay in advance. The prefix comes from Latin ~prae-~ (“before, in front of”). The base ~payer~ comes from Old French ~paiier~, from Latin ~pācāre~ (“to pacify, to appease”), a verb built on ~pāx~ (“peace”). The sense of paying arose from appeasing a creditor by settling a debt, so ~prépayer~ is, etymologically, to make peace with a creditor ahead of time.
en.préposer: French Wiktionary presents ~préposer~ as ~poser~ with the prefix ~pré-~, but English Wiktionary traces it to Latin ~praepositus~, the past participle of ~praepōnere~ (“to place before, to put in charge”), with the ~t~ lost under the influence of ~poser~. The Latin verb is ~prae-~ (“before”) plus ~pōnere~ (“to put”). The verb ~poser~ itself comes from Late Latin ~pausare~, which in spoken Latin took over the meaning of ~pōnere~. That is how ~préposer~, a descendant of ~praepōnere~, ended up wearing the shape of ~poser~. The learned noun ~préposition~ comes from Latin ~praepositiō~, and ~préposé~, used as a noun, is an official or an employee in charge of a task, as in ~préposé des postes~ for a mail carrier. Its relatives ~proposer~, ~déposer~ and ~composer~ show the same remodeling of ~pōnere~ on ~poser~.
en.prérégler: ~Prérégler~ is formed from ~régler~ with the prefix ~pré-~ (“beforehand”), and means to set or adjust something in advance. ~Régler~ was made in the thirteenth century from ~règle~, which comes from Latin ~rēgula~ (“ruler”), a derivative of ~regere~ (“to keep straight, to direct”). The prefix ~pré-~ comes from Latin ~prae-~ (“before”).
en.présager:
French Wiktionary derives ~présager~ from Latin ~praesagīre~, which gave ~presagir~ in the sixteenth century. English Wiktionary instead treats the verb as built on the noun ~présage~ plus the ending ~-er~, so the two accounts differ on the route. The Latin verb is generally analyzed as ~prae-~ (“before”) and ~sagīre~ (“to perceive keenly”), so to presage is to sense in advance.

Latin ~sagīre~ is related to the adjective ~sagax~ (“keen, perceptive”), which gave French ~sagace~ and English ~sagacious~ as cognates, and the Latin noun ~praesagium~ (“omen”) is the source of ~présage~. A ~présage~ is therefore a sign perceived beforehand, and ~présager~ is to read one or to be one. The two accounts are not exclusive in practice, since the noun and the verb are close kin, but the sources do not say which came first in French.
en.présenter:
From Old French ~presenter~, from Latin ~praesentāre~ (“to place before, to show”), a verb formed on the adjective ~praesēns~ (“present, at hand”). That adjective is itself the present participle of ~praeesse~ (“to be before, to be at the head of”), built from ~prae-~ (“before, in front of”) and ~esse~ (“to be”). The deep root is therefore the Proto-Indo-European verb of being, *~h₁es-~ (“to be”), the same root that gives Latin ~est~ and English ~is~. Cognate verbs survive across the Romance languages, among them Italian ~presentare~ and Spanish ~presentar~, and the family passed into English as ~present~.

The literal image behind ~praesentāre~ is spatial: to make something ~praesēns~ is to set it physically “before” someone, in front of their eyes. From “to place before” the verb naturally acquired the senses of showing, offering, and introducing, and French ~présenter~ still carries all of these — one presents a gift, a person, or an argument. The same adjective ~praesēns~ gave French the noun and adjective ~présent~, covering both “the present moment” and “a present, a gift,” the latter through the old idea of something placed before a recipient. From the prefix ~prae-~ and this same field come many related French words, including ~présence~, ~présentation~, and ~représenter~ (“to represent, to perform again”).
en.préserver:
From Latin ~praeservare~ (“to guard beforehand, keep safe in advance”), formed on ~prae-~ (“before, in advance”) plus ~servare~ (“to keep, guard, watch over, save”). Latin ~servare~ goes back through Proto-Italic to a Proto-Indo-European root *~ser-~ (“to protect, watch over”), with a likely cognate in Avestan ~haraiti~ (“heeds, protects”). The verb is matched by Italian ~preservare~ and Spanish ~preservar~, and English borrowed it as ~preserve~.

The prefix ~prae-~ carries the whole nuance: not merely to keep, but to keep something ahead of harm — to shield it in advance from a danger. Latin ~servare~ should not be confused with its near-homophone ~servire~ (“to serve,” from ~servus~, “slave”); they are distinct roots that French keeps apart. From ~servare~ French inherits and borrows a guarding family: ~conserver~ (“to keep, conserve”), ~observer~ (originally “to watch over, attend to”), ~réserver~ (“to keep back”), and ~préservatif~, which means a protective agent in general but, in everyday French, a condom — a “preserver” in the most literal sense.
en.présider:
From Latin ~praesidere~ (“to sit before, to preside over, to guard”), a compound of ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) and ~sedere~ (“to sit”). ~Sedere~ descends from Proto-Italic *~sedēō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~sed-~ (“to sit”) — one of the great Indo-European roots, cognate with English ~sit~ and ~settle~, German ~sitzen~, and Sanskrit ~sī́dati~ (“sits”).

The image is concrete: the one who presides is literally the one who sits before the assembly, at its head. From this seat of precedence grew the senses of guarding, directing, and chairing a body — to ~présider~ a meeting, a court, a republic. French built a whole institutional vocabulary on the verb: ~président~, ~présidence~, ~présidentiel~, alongside ~coprésider~ and ~vice-présider~. The same root *~sed-~ runs through ~séant~, ~siège~, ~résider~, and ~asseoir~. Beneath the dignity of high office lies a humble physical fact — to preside is to take the foremost seat.
en.présumer:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~praesūmere~, a compound of ~prae-~ (“before”) and ~sūmere~ (“to take”): literally “to take beforehand.” The same Latin verb gave English ~presume~, Italian ~presumere~ and Spanish ~presumir~, and the Spanish verb has drifted furthest, since it now usually means “to boast.” Its Latin parent ~sūmere~ also sits inside a whole family of French verbs built on prefixes, such as ~assumer~, ~résumer~ and ~consumer~.

The path from “take beforehand” to “suppose” is short: to take something before it has been proved is to take it for granted. French kept both the neutral sense of “assuming” and a more pointed one, since ~présumer de ses forces~ means to overestimate one's strength, as if one had credited oneself in advance with more than one possessed. The noun ~présomption~ shows the same split. In law, it is a conclusion the court draws from known facts, as in ~présomption d'innocence~, while in everyday speech it is overconfidence, and the adjective ~présomptueux~ describes someone who takes too much for granted about himself. The verb is a good reminder that a ~présumé~ fact is only a fact accepted ahead of its proof.
en.présupposer: Formed from ~supposer~ with the prefix ~pré-~, “beforehand”: to ~présupposer~ is to assume something in advance, as a condition for what follows. The base ~supposer~ is a French formation modelled on Latin ~supponere~ (“to put under”), reshaped on the native verb ~poser~ (“to place”). The prefix goes back to Latin ~prae-~ (“before, in front of”). English ~suppose~ and Italian ~supporre~ are its cousins.
en.présurer: ~Présurer~ is formed from ~présure~ (“rennet”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, and means to curdle milk with rennet. The two Wiktionaries give different accounts of the noun. French Wiktionary derives older ~prisure~ from ~prise~ with the suffix ~-ure~, in the sense of “coagulation.” English Wiktionary traces Old French ~prisure~ to Vulgar Latin *~prēnsūra~, from Latin ~prehēnsum~. Both accounts rest on the idea of “taking,” as milk takes or sets.
en.présélectionner: Built from ~sélectionner~ with the prefix ~pré-~ (“beforehand”); English Wiktionary also allows ~présélection~ + ~-er~ as the path. The base ~sélectionner~ is a nineteenth-century verb drawn from ~sélection~, from Latin ~selectio~ (“a choosing out”), the action noun of ~seligere~, a compound of ~se-~ (“apart”) and ~legere~ (“to pick, to gather, to read”). The prefix ~pré-~ comes from Latin ~prae-~ (“before, in front of”). The result means to choose or set something in advance, whether shortlisting candidates or presetting a function.
en.prétendre:
From Latin ~praetendere~ (“to stretch forth, hold out before, allege as a pretext”), formed from ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) and ~tendere~ (“to stretch”). ~Tendere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~tendō~ and, with a ~d~-extension, to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ten-~ (“to stretch, draw out”). The kinship reaches far: Ancient Greek ~τείνω~ (~teínō~), Sanskrit ~तनोति~ (~tanóti~), and, through Germanic, English ~thin~ — all stretchings of one ancient thread. French took the verb in the 14th century.

The metaphor at the heart of ~prétendre~ is striking: to hold something stretched out before you, like a screen or a banner. From that came “to put forward as a claim” — to claim a right, to allege a fact, to pretend to (aspire to) a throne or a hand in marriage. English ~pretend~ drifted toward “feign,” but French keeps the older sense of asserting and aspiring; a ~prétendant~ is a suitor or a claimant to power. The *~ten-~ family is vast in French: ~tendre~, ~tension~, ~tente~, ~étendre~, ~intention~, ~attendre~, and ~prétention~ — every one of them, at root, a stretching.
en.prétexter:
The two Wiktionaries describe the verb differently. French Wiktionary derives it directly from Latin ~praetexere~ (“to border, to embroider,” and also “to put forward as a pretext”), while English Wiktionary treats it as French ~prétexte~ plus ~-er~. The two accounts are compatible, since ~prétexte~ itself comes from the same Latin family. As background, ~praetexere~ is formed from ~prae-~ (“in front”) and ~texere~ (“to weave”).

The Latin verb already carried both sense groups, the physical one of bordering or embroidering and the figurative one of putting forward a pretext, and French kept the figurative one. To ~prétexter~ something is to give it as a reason that may not be the real one, as in ~prétexter une migraine~ (“to plead a headache”). The root ~texere~ is also behind many French words, among them ~texte~, ~textile~, ~tissu~ and ~tisser~.
en.prévaloir: A learned borrowing from Latin ~praevalēre~ (“to have greater strength, to be more powerful”), made of ~prae-~ (“before, beyond”) and ~valēre~ (“to be strong, to be worth”). French already had ~valoir~, the inherited descendant of that same Latin verb, so ~pré-~ + ~valoir~ is a fair surface reading, but the Latin compound came first. The verb means to hold the upper hand, as an argument or a right does over another. It conjugates like ~valoir~ with one telltale exception, the subjunctive ~prévale~ rather than ~prévaille~. English ~prevail~ comes from the same Latin verb, and ~valid~ and ~value~ come from ~valēre~.
en.prévariquer:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~praevāricor~ (infinitive ~praevāricārī~), a verb of legal and moral vocabulary. Latin speakers could analyze it as ~prae-~ (“before, beyond”) + ~vāricāre~ (“to straddle, to walk with the legs apart”), from ~vārus~ (“bent, bow-legged”). French took the verb whole from the written Latin of scholars and lawyers rather than inheriting it through speech, which is why it keeps the Latin shape so closely.

In modern French, ~prévariquer~ is a rare, formal verb meaning “to neglect one's duty,” said of someone in a position of trust who betrays it through bad faith. It is the base of ~prévarication~ and ~prévaricateur~, the forms by which most speakers meet the family, usually in news reports about officials. English ~prevaricate~ and Spanish ~prevaricar~ come from the same Latin verb. In English, though, the word drifted toward “to speak evasively,” a sense that French ~prévariquer~ never took.
en.prévenir:
From Latin ~praevenire~ (“to come before, anticipate, forestall”), a compound of the prefix ~prae-~ (“before, in front of”) and ~venire~ (“to come”). The verb ~venire~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʷem-~ (“to come, go, step”), the same root that, through Germanic, yields English ~come~, and that in Greek gives ~bainō~ (“I go”) and in Sanskrit ~gam-~. Italian ~prevenire~ and Spanish ~prevenir~ are its Romance siblings.

The literal “to come before” spread into several modern meanings that still circle anticipation. To ~prévenir~ can mean to warn or notify someone in advance (~prévenir un ami~), to prevent or forestall something (~prévenir une maladie~ — hence the proverb ~mieux vaut prévenir que guérir~, “prevention is better than cure”), or, in older usage, to favorably or unfavorably predispose someone, surviving in the adjective ~prévenu~ (“biased,” and in law “the accused”). The same ~venire~ powers a huge French family: ~venir~, ~devenir~, ~revenir~, ~convenir~, ~parvenir~, ~survenir~, ~avenir~ (“future,” what is “to come”), and ~événement~. To warn a friend, in this light, is simply to arrive ahead of the trouble.
en.prévoir:
From Latin ~praevidere~ (« to see beforehand, to foresee »), formed from ~prae-~ (« before, in front ») and ~videre~ (« to see »). ~videre~ descends through Proto-Italic *~widēō~ from the Proto-Indo-European root *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”) — a root whose sense slid from seeing to knowing. Through it ~prévoir~ is cognate with English ~wit~, ~wise~, and ~witness~, with German ~wissen~ (“to know”), and, by way of Greek, with ~idea~.

Latin already used ~praevidere~ both literally, « to catch sight of in the distance », and figuratively, « to anticipate ».
