French inherited only the figurative core: to ~prévoir~ is to see with the mind's eye what has not yet happened. The verb conjugates like ~voir~ except in the future and conditional, where it keeps a regular ~prévoirai~ rather than the irregular ~verrai~ — a small grammatical seam revealing its compound origin. The same root *~weyd-~ underlies a wide French family: ~voir~ itself, ~vision~, ~évident~ (« seen clearly »), ~prévision~, ~prévoyant~, and ~revoir~.
en.préétablir: ~Préétablir~ is formed from ~établir~ with the prefix ~pré-~ (from Latin ~prae-~, “before”), in the sense “to establish beforehand.” The base ~établir~ comes from Old French ~establir~, from Latin ~stabilīre~ (“to make firm”), built on ~stabilis~ and ultimately on ~stāre~ (“to stand”). To ~préétablir~ something is therefore to fix it in advance.
en.prêcher:
Inherited from Old French ~prëechier~, from Latin ~praedicāre~ (“to proclaim in public”), built from ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) and ~dicāre~ (“to proclaim, to declare”), a verb related to ~dīcere~ (“to say”). The ~d~ between vowels dropped out along the way, which is why Old French ~prëechier~ looks so unlike its source. Regional languages show the spread: Occitan ~predicar~ and Corsican ~predicà~ stay close to the Latin, while Norman ~prêchi~ and Picard ~prêcher~ follow the French pattern. Italian ~predicare~ and Spanish ~predicar~ keep the full Latin shape, and English ~preach~ was borrowed from the Old French verb.

In classical Latin the verb meant to announce something publicly, as a herald does, and also to praise or declare. Christian writers adopted it for proclaiming the Gospel, and that religious sense won out in the Romance languages. French then widened it to any moralizing or advocacy, usually with a faintly ironic edge when the speaker lectures others. The family includes ~prêche~, ~prêcheur~, ~prédicateur~ and ~prédication~, plus the learned ~prédicat~, the grammatical predicate, from the Latin participle for “what is declared” about the subject.
en.prêter:
French ~prêter~ comes through Old French ~prester~ from Latin ~praestare~ (“to stand before, to be at hand, to furnish, to provide”). The verb is ~prae-~ (“before, in front”) plus ~stāre~ (“to stand”), and so reaches the deep Proto-Indo-European root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”) — making ~prêter~ a distant cousin of ~résister~, ~rester~, and ~stable~. The circumflex in ~prêter~ is a tombstone for a lost ~s~: it marks where the ~s~ of ~prester~ fell silent. Italian ~prestare~ and Spanish ~prestar~ carry the same Latin verb.

The sense-shift is a small drama of generosity. Latin ~praestare~ literally meant “to stand before,” hence “to stand surety, to make good, to supply” — to have something ready ~prae manu~, “at hand.” That readiness is preserved in the adjective ~prêt~ (“ready”), an etymological sibling of the verb. From “to furnish what is ready” the Romance languages narrowed to “to lend,” and French ~prêter~ now means putting something at another's disposal on the promise of return — money, a book, even, figuratively, ~prêter l'oreille~ (“to lend an ear”) or ~prêter serment~ (“to take an oath”). The same root supplies ~prêt~ (“a loan”), ~emprunter~'s partner in finance, and the learned ~prestation~ (“a service rendered, a benefit”).
en.prôner: Formed in French from ~prône~ + ~-er~, “to give the prône,” the Sunday sermon, and from there “to preach, to extol.” The noun has an odd history. Old French ~prosne~ named the grating that separated the nave from the choir, in front of which the priest stood to speak, and the word then passed to the sermon itself. It goes back through Vulgar Latin *~protinum~ and Latin ~prothyra~ to Greek ~próthura~ (“vestibule”), from ~pro-~ (“before”) and ~thura~ (“door”), a cousin of English ~door~. A word for the porch of a house thus ended as a verb for praising something insistently.
en.psalmodier: Formed from ~psalmodie~ (“psalmody”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so “to chant psalms,” then more loosely “to intone” or “to drone.” The noun was borrowed from Latin ~psalmōdia~, which took it from Koine Greek ~ψαλμῳδία~, a word tied to ~psalmus~, the source of French ~psaume~. The verb thus stays close to its religious origin even when it describes any monotonous recitation.
en.psychanalyser: ~Psychanalyser~ is the verb of ~psychanalyse~ (“psychoanalysis”), formed with the ending ~-er~. The noun is built from the prefix ~psych-~ (“mind”) and ~analyse~ (“analysis”). A competing analysis sees the suffix ~-iser~ instead, or, on the surface, simply ~psych-~ + ~analyser~. Either way the meaning is transparent: “to submit someone to psychoanalysis.”
en.psychiatriser: Formed from ~psychiatrique~ with the suffix ~-iser~: to treat something as a psychiatric matter, or to subject someone to psychiatric care. The adjective is itself built from ~psychiatrie~ and the suffix ~-ique~. The verb therefore stacks several French formations on a learned base.
en.publier:
From Latin ~pūblicāre~ (“to make public, to bring before the people”), a verb derived from the adjective ~pūblicus~ (“public, belonging to the people”), itself ultimately from ~populus~ (“the people, the populace”). The adjective's form was likely colored by ~pūbēs~ (“adult, grown men”), but its core is the people, ~populus~. Cognate Romance descendants include Italian ~pubblicare~ and Spanish ~publicar~; English ~publish~ came through Old French ~publier~ with its characteristic ~-sh~.

To ~pūblicāre~ originally meant to make something the property of the people — including, harshly, to confiscate private goods for the state. From this “to make common/open” the dominant sense narrowed to “to announce openly, proclaim,” and then, with the printing press, to “bring out in print, issue a book.” French ~publier~ now serves both the everyday “to publish” and the formal proclaiming of banns or laws. From ~populus~ and ~pūblicus~ descend a broad family in French: ~public~, ~publication~, ~publicité~, ~république~ (~rēs pūblica~, “the public thing”), ~peuple~, ~populaire~, and ~population~.
en.puddler: ~Puddler~ is borrowed from English ~puddle~, the verb that in iron-making means to stir molten pig iron so as to refine it. The English word is the same as the one for a small pool of water, from the idea of working the metal like mud. French added its own ~-er~ ending to the borrowed verb, as it routinely does with English loans.
en.puer:
From Old French ~puir~, itself from Vulgar Latin *~putīre~, a respelled form of Classical Latin ~pūtēre~ (“to stink, to rot”), the infinitive of ~pūteō~. The shift from ~-ēre~ to ~-īre~ is a change of conjugation class, and the Old French infinitive ~puir~ eventually became modern ~puer~. Behind the Latin verb lies the Proto-Indo-European root *~puH-~ (“to rot, to stink”), which also produced Latin ~pūs~ (“pus”) and, through Proto-Germanic, English ~foul~.

French kept the blunt physical sense of the Latin verb: ~puer~ means to give off a foul smell, and the idea easily turns figurative, as in puer l'argent (“to reek of money,” meaning to flaunt one’s wealth). Its present participle became an adjective, ~puant~, which gave the noun ~puanteur~. Scholars took other words of the family straight from Latin, among them ~putride~, ~putréfier~ and ~pus~. The root *~puH-~ thus ties a bad smell, rot and pus into a single family, and English ~foul~ is its Germanic cousin.
en.puiser:
~puiser~ is a French derivative of ~puits~ (“a well”), which in Old French was written ~puis~; the verb means literally “to draw from a well.” ~puits~ itself descends from Latin ~puteus~ (“well, pit, cistern”), a word whose own origin is uncertain — de Vaan suspects it may be a loanword, while an older proposal tied it to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “to cut, strike,” imagining the well as a hole struck into the ground. The Latin ~puteus~ also gave Italian ~pozzo~ and Spanish ~pozo~, and, borrowed into Germanic, lies behind English ~pit~.

From the concrete act of lowering a bucket, ~puiser~ broadened into one of the most graceful metaphors in French: one ~puise~ water, but equally one ~puise~ strength from a friendship, inspiration in a memory, or arguments in a book — drawing up something held in a hidden reserve. The same ~puits~ family yields ~épuiser~ (“to exhaust,” literally to draw a well dry, to ~é-~ /“out” + draw until nothing rises), ~inépuisable~ (“inexhaustible”), ~puisard~ (“a soakaway, sump”), and ~puisatier~ (“a well-digger”) — a whole vocabulary organized around the bucket and the deep cool water it brings up.
en.pulluler: Borrowed directly from Latin ~pullulāre~, so it kept the shape of its source instead of being worn down by centuries of speech. The Latin verb is built on ~pullulus~, a diminutive of ~pullus~ (“young animal, chick”). The family of ~pullus~ also came down the popular road: ~poule~ (“hen”) goes back to Latin ~pulla~, the feminine of ~pullus~, and ~poulain~ (“foal”) belongs to the same family. Italian ~pullulare~ and Spanish ~pulular~ are close relatives, and English took the verb as ~pullulate~. Today ~pulluler~ describes things that multiply in great numbers, such as insects, ideas or businesses.
en.pulvériser: Learned borrowing, in the late sixteenth century, from Late Latin ~pulverizāre~ (“to reduce to powder”), a verb formed on Latin ~pulvis~, ~pulveris~ (“dust, powder”). The same Latin noun reached French by the inherited route as ~poudre~ and ~poussière~, which makes ~pulvériser~ their learned sibling. The sense was physical at first, grinding something into powder, then spray (~pulvériser un liquide~), and finally figurative: to ~pulvériser~ a record is to smash it to dust. English ~pulverize~ has the same Latin source.
en.punaiser: Formed from ~punaise~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, the verb meaning to fix something with a drawing pin. The noun ~punaise~ names both the bedbug and the pin. It is the feminine of the old adjective ~punais~ (“foul-smelling”), from Vulgar Latin *~pūtināsius~, built on Latin ~puteō~ (“to stink”) and ~nāsus~ (“nose”). The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, is the default way French turns a noun into a verb meaning “provide with” or “apply”.
en.punir:
From Old French ~punir~, from Latin ~pūnīre~ (earlier ~poenīre~), a verb built on the noun ~poena~ (“penalty, fine, punishment”) with the fourth-conjugation suffix ~-īre~. ~Poena~ was itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~ποινή~ (~poinḗ~, “blood-price, recompense, penalty”), from PIE *~kʷoynéh₂~, from the root *~kʷey-~ (“to pay, to atone”). The same root surfaces in Greek ~timḗ~ (“price, honor”) and Avestan ~kaēnā~ (“punishment”). Cognate Romance verbs include Italian ~punire~ and Spanish ~punir~; English ~punish~ came through Old French ~puniss-~, the stem of the present participle.

The core idea was never mere pain but ~payment~ — a penalty exacted to settle a wrong, a debt of vengeance discharged. That accounting sense explains the rich French family around it: ~punition~, ~punitif~, and the legal ~impuni~ / ~impunité~ (“unpunished,” literally “un-paid-for”). Most telling is the noun ~poena~ itself, which entered French twice: learnedly preserved in this verb, but inherited by ordinary speech as ~peine~ (“pain, trouble, sorrow,” and still “penalty” in ~peine de mort~). Through Old French, that same ~poena~ also gave English ~pain~, so that ~peine~ and ~pain~ are doublets — and a French speaker who takes ~la peine~ to do something is, etymologically, paying a penalty for it.
en.purger: From Old French ~purgier~, inherited from Latin ~pūrgō~ (“to clean, purify”). The Latin verb is built on the adjective ~pūrus~ (“clean, pure”) with a verb-forming element ~-igō~, which goes back to ~agere~ (“to drive, to do”), so the verb meant roughly “to make clean.” Italian ~purgare~, Spanish ~purgar~ and English ~purge~ descend from or were borrowed from the same Latin verb. Modern French ~purger~ covers literal cleansing and the legal phrase ~purger une peine~ (“to serve a sentence”); the sources do not say how that legal sense arose. Related French words include ~pur~, ~purifier~, ~épurer~ and ~purgatoire~.
en.purifier: French ~purifier~ is a borrowing from Latin ~pūrificāre~ (“to make pure, to cleanse”), itself built from ~pūrus~ (“pure, clean”) and the combining form of ~facere~ (“to make”). The same pattern, an adjective followed by ~-ficāre~, gave ~justifier~, ~clarifier~ and ~qualifier~. In Latin the verb often had a religious sense, since purification was a matter of ritual. French also has ~pur~ and ~pureté~ from ~pūrus~, and ~épurer~, a related verb that adds the prefix ~é-~.
en.putréfier: ~Putréfier~ (“to rot, to putrefy”) comes from Latin ~putrefacere~, a compound of ~putris~ (“rotten”) and ~facere~ (“to make”), so it meant “to make rotten.” The Latin adjective ~putris~ is the root of a small family in French. The inherited ~pourrir~ comes from the same stock by the ordinary route of sound change, while ~putride~ and ~putréfaction~ were taken over later from the Latin forms. English has ~putrid~ and ~putrefy~, borrowed from the same Latin words. Thus ~putréfier~ stands beside ~pourrir~ as its learned counterpart: the first is used for decay in a scientific or literary register, and the second for ordinary rotting.
en.pyramider: ~Pyramider~ (“to form a pyramid”) is formed on the noun ~pyramide~ with the verb ending ~-er~. ~Pyramide~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~pȳramis~ (also found as ~pyramida~), which itself comes from Ancient Greek ~πυραμίς~ (~puramís~). The verb is used mostly of things that rise to a point, such as a heap or a column of figures, and so makes an action out of the shape.
en.pyrograver: ~Pyrograver~ is formed from ~graver~ with the prefix ~pyro-~, from Ancient Greek ~pûr~ (“fire”): to engrave with fire, burning a design into wood or leather. The base ~graver~ is a Germanic word, from Old French and Frankish *~graban~ (“to dig”), and is cognate with German ~graben~. The verb thus joins a Greek prefix to a Frankish verb.
en.pâlir: ~Pâlir~ is a verb built on the adjective ~pâle~ with the ending ~-ir~, in the sense “to become pale”. It already existed in Old French as ~palir~, attested in the twelfth century. The adjective ~pâle~ comes from Latin ~pallidus~ (“pale, pallid”). One source notes that Old French would normally have reduced the Latin word further, so ~pâle~ may be a learned borrowing, or a regional development. It is a doublet of the learned ~pallide~, which keeps the Latin shape more closely. The ~-ir~ ending is the second-conjugation ending that French often attaches to adjectives to mean “become”, as in ~grandir~ or ~grossir~.
en.pâmer: From Old French ~pasmer~, which comes from a Latin verb *~spasmare~ built on ~spasmus~ (“spasm”). The Old French ~s~ before a consonant later fell silent, and the circumflex of ~pâmer~ marks its loss. In modern French the verb survives mostly in the reflexive ~se pâmer~ (“to swoon”). The Latin ~spasmus~, itself a loan from Greek, also gave French the learned noun ~spasme~ and the adjective ~spasmodique~, and English ~spasm~. ~Pâmoison~, the old noun for a fainting fit, belongs to the same family.
en.pâtir:
~Pâtir~ is the French form of Latin ~patī~ (“to bear, to endure”). French Wiktionary calls it a Frenchification of the Latin verb, while English Wiktionary traces it through Middle French ~patir~, borrowed from Latin. Italian ~patire~ (“to suffer”) comes from the same Latin verb. English never kept the verb itself, but it has ~patient~, ~passive~ and ~passion~, all descended from ~patī~ and its participles.

In modern French ~pâtir~ means to suffer, to be the one who bears harm, and it is used chiefly with ~de~, as in ~pâtir de la crise~. The Latin verb has left a large family in French: ~patient~ and ~patience~, ~passif~, ~passion~, and the compounds ~compatir~ (“to feel with”) and ~compassion~.
en.pâtisser:
~Pâtisser~ descends from Old French ~pasticier~ (“to make pâté, to make pastry”), which came from an unattested noun *~pastitz~ (compare Old Occitan ~pastis~ and Italian ~pasticcio~). That noun goes back to Vulgar Latin *~pastīcius~, from Late Latin ~pasta~ (“paste”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~παστά~ (~pastá~, “barley porridge”). The Greek word comes from ~παστός~ (~pastós~, “salted”), from ~πάσσω~ (~pássō~, “to sprinkle”). The circumflex in ~pâte~ and ~pâtisser~ marks the lost ~s~ of ~pasta~.

The same chain gives ~pasticher~, a doublet of ~pâtisser~: a ~pastiche~ was originally an Italian pie of mixed ingredients, and so a work imitating others. French ~pastis~ is a relative, and English ~paste~ and ~pastry~ come from the same Late Latin source. The noun ~pâtisserie~ and the trade of the ~pâtissier~ are the everyday descendants.
en.pâturer: Formed from ~pâture~ (“pasture, grazing”) with the verbal ending ~-er~. ~Pâture~ is inherited from Old French ~pasture~, from Latin ~pastūra~ (“the act of grazing”), a noun from ~pastus~ (“feeding”). The same Latin root lies behind ~paître~ (“to graze”), so ~pâturer~ is a close cousin of that verb. The circumflex marks the lost s of ~pasture~.
en.pécher:
French ~pécher~ is inherited from Old French ~pechier~, which comes from Latin ~peccāre~ (“to make a mistake, to sin”). The Latin verb was sound but not religious: it first meant to go wrong or stumble, and Christian writers made it the standard word for sin. The ending ~-ccāre~ became ~-chier~ in Old French, as in other Latin verbs of the same shape. Italian ~peccare~ and Spanish ~pecar~ are its direct cousins, and the Latin noun ~peccātum~ gave ~péché~ (“sin”).

The family is full of learned words. ~Impeccable~ comes from Latin ~impeccābilis~ (“unable to sin”) and weakened from moral perfection to mere faultlessness, as in an ~impeccable~ suit. ~Peccadille~, a small fault, was borrowed from Spanish ~pecadillo~, a diminutive of ~pecado~. A caution is in order: the verb ~pêcher~ (“to fish”) and the fruit tree ~pêcher~ have a circumflex and unrelated origins, since the fishing verb comes from Latin ~piscāri~ (“to fish”). Only the accent keeps ~pécher~ apart from them.
en.pédaler: Formed in French from ~pédale~ (“pedal”) and the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, with the sense “to work a pedal.” The noun was borrowed from Italian ~pedale~ (“organ pedal”), which comes from Latin ~pedālis~ (“of the foot”), built on ~pēs~ (“foot”). The suffix ~-er~ goes back to the Latin infinitive ending ~-āre~ and is the ordinary way French turns a noun into a verb, as in ~filtrer~ from ~filtre~. So ~pédaler~ means, literally, to operate pedals, above all those of a bicycle.
en.pénaliser: Both Wiktionaries describe ~pénaliser~ as a borrowing from English ~penalize~, though French Wiktionary adds that it matches what French could have built from ~pénal~ and the suffix ~-iser~. ~Pénal~ comes from Latin ~poenālis~, from ~poena~ (“punishment”), which also gave ~peine~. The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, and means “to make” or “to subject to.” To ~pénaliser~ is therefore to subject someone to a penalty, whether a legal sanction, a sporting foul or a disadvantage.
en.pénétrer:
From Latin ~penetrāre~ (“to enter, to pierce, to penetrate”), first attested in French around 1314. The verb was built within Latin itself from ~penitus~ (“deeply, inwardly”) and the family of ~penes~ (“within, in the house of”), shaped by analogy with ~intrō~ (“to enter”). The underlying idea is one of the innermost recess of a dwelling — the ~penus~, the household store kept deep inside. Cognate Romance forms descend in parallel: Italian ~penetrare~, Spanish ~penetrar~, Portuguese ~penetrar~. English ~penetrate~ was borrowed from the same Latin source by way of French.

The sense has stayed remarkably stable: to pass into the interior of something, whether a forest, a wall, or a mystery. From the literal “to enter” grew the figurative “to grasp,” so that one can ~pénétrer~ a secret or a person’s intentions, and a person can be pénétré (“filled, imbued”) with an emotion. Modern French keeps a small family from the root, including ~pénétration~, ~pénétrant~ and ~impénétrable~. The shared image throughout is depth — reaching the part of a thing that lies furthest within.
en.pépier:
A variant of the older verb ~piper~ (“to utter small cries”), itself imitative of the thin, repeated sound of young birds. The origin is onomatopoeic and goes back well beyond French: Latin had the verb ~pīpiō~ for the same cheeping sound, and English ~peep~ is a comparable imitative word. The doubled first syllable of ~pépier~ suits the sound it describes.

In modern French, ~pépier~ is the standard verb for the chirping of small birds, especially sparrows, and the noun ~pépiement~ names the sound. It is also used of people who chatter in thin, high voices. The older ~piper~ survives as well. In the fixed phrase ~ne pas piper mot~ (“not to say a word”), it keeps the sense of “to utter a sound,” and from it comes ~pipeau~, the little reed pipe that bird-catchers once used to lure birds. Because all of these words imitate sound rather than descend from a single ancestor, they form a family by resemblance more than by strict inheritance.
en.pérenniser:
Formed in French from the Latin adjective ~perennis~ and the verb ending ~-er~. Latin ~perennis~ is built from ~per~ (“through”) and ~annus~ (“year”), so it first meant “lasting through the years”, and from there “lasting, unceasing”. The same adjective gave English ~perennial~, and its second element ~annus~ is the source of French ~an~ and ~année~.

The verb takes the Latin idea of lasting through the years and makes it active: to ~pérenniser~ something is to make it durable, to give it a future. It sits among a family of words around ~annus~, including ~annuel~, ~anniversaire~ and ~annuaire~, while the adjective ~pérenne~ and the noun ~pérennité~ come straight from ~perennis~ and ~perennitas~. The “perennial” plant of the garden is the same word again, a plant that lasts year after year.
en.péricliter:
Learned borrowing from Latin ~perīclitārī~ (“to try, test, risk, endanger”), a deponent verb, meaning one with passive-looking forms and an active sense. It is built on ~perīculum~ (“trial, danger”), the noun that also gave French ~péril~ and English ~peril~. Taken straight from written Latin rather than inherited through speech, it is a learned word, and its shape stayed close to the Latin.

The Latin verb covered a range that runs from putting something to the test, through risking it, to exposing it to danger. In modern French, ~péricliter~ is used of a business, an institution or a fortune that is “going downhill.” The family is small and transparent: ~péril~, ~périlleux~ (“perilous”) and, in English, ~peril~ and ~perilous~ all rest on ~perīculum~, and ~péricliter~ is the one member of the group that is a verb.
en.périmer:
Borrowed from Latin ~perimere~ (“to destroy”). The Latin verb is built from the prefix ~per-~ (“through, completely”) and ~emere~, an old verb for “to take,” so it first meant something like “to take away completely.” The same ~emere~ (later “to buy”) appears in many Latin compounds that French borrowed, such as ~exempt~ and ~rédemption~.

Where Latin spoke of destruction, French ~périmer~ speaks of lapse: a thing that has run past its date is ~périmé~, whether a yogurt, a passport or an idea, and a document can ~se périmer~ (“to expire”). The English gloss runs from “become obsolete” to “expire.” The participle of the Latin verb, ~peremptus~, also gave French ~péremption~ (“lapse, expiry,” as in ~date de péremption~) and ~péremptoire~ (“final, not to be argued with”), two words that show the older sense of something cut off for good.
en.périphraser: ~Périphraser~ is formed from the noun ~périphrase~ with the verb-forming ending ~-er~, and means “to use periphrasis,” that is, to speak in a roundabout way. The noun was borrowed from Latin ~periphrasis~, itself from Ancient Greek ~períphrasis~ (“circumlocution”), a word built on the same root as ~phrase~. The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, is the default way French coins a verb from a noun, here in the sense “to carry out N.”
en.périr:
From Old French ~perir~, passed on through Middle French ~perir~, from Latin ~perīre~ (“to perish, to be lost”). Latin ~perīre~ is a compound of the preposition and prefix ~per-~ (“through”) and the verb ~īre~ (“to go”), so it literally means “to go through,” which can be read as going all the way to the end, and hence to ruin. Latin ~īre~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₁ei-~ (“to go”). Italian ~perire~ is a close cousin. English ~perish~ is itself a French loan, built on the stem ~periss-~ of the Old French verb.

The literal picture of a journey that ends in loss turned ~perīre~ into a Latin word for dying, being destroyed or going to waste, and French kept that range, from people who ~périssent~ at sea to empires and ideas that come to nothing. The same family gave ~périssable~ (“that can spoil”) and ~impérissable~ (“undying”). The simple verb ~īre~ left no infinitive in French, since ~aller~ replaced it, but its stem lives on in learned words such as ~transit~ and ~itinéraire~, and in the stem of the future ~irai~.
en.pérorer:
From Latin ~perōrāre~ (“to speak at length, to harangue; to conclude a speech”), formed from ~per-~ (“through, to the end”) and ~ōrāre~ (“to speak as an orator”). In Roman rhetoric the verb named the closing section of a speech, its ~peroratio~, and the French sense “to speak until the end” keeps that idea of going right through a discourse. The learned borrowing entered French as ~pérorer~, and English ~perorate~ comes from the same Latin verb.

Latin ~ōrāre~ is related to ~ōs~ (“mouth”), and the same root gives a large French family: ~orateur~ (“speaker”), ~oraison~ (“prayer”), ~oral~ and ~adorer~ (literally “to address”). ~Pérorer~ stayed closest to the rhetorical sense, since it is still about long speaking. Modern French nonetheless uses it with irony, for someone who holds forth at length and pompously, often with little to say. The noun ~péroraison~ is its companion, but it has kept the neutral, technical sense of a speech's conclusion.
en.pétarader: A denominal verb, formed from ~pétarade~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~pétarade~ (“a series of small explosions, backfiring”) comes from Occitan ~petarrada~ and belongs to the family of ~pet~, ~péter~ and ~pétard~. It was introduced into French by Rabelais. The verb therefore means to make that crackling, popping noise, as an engine does when it backfires. The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, is the default way of coining a verb from a noun in French.
en.péter: Formed in French from the noun ~pet~ (“fart”) with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is inherited from Old French ~pet~, from Latin ~pēditum~ (“a fart”). The verb is therefore literally “to let off a ~pet~”, and its everyday and vulgar register comes with it. By extension ~péter~ took the sense of a sudden sharp noise and then of bursting or breaking: a tire ~pète~, a cable ~pète~, and ~péter les plombs~ is to snap.
en.pétiller: Formed from ~pet~ with the suffix ~-iller~, a verb for repeated small noises and movements. French Wiktionary dates it to 1453. The word ~pet~ is French for a “fart”, so the verb began as a way to name a rapid series of small pops. Later senses are the ones in use today: to crackle, to bubble, to sparkle.
en.pétitionner: Formed from the noun ~pétition~ and the ending ~-er~, which here means “to carry out N,” the verb means to present or sign a petition. The noun comes from Old French ~peticiun~, borrowed from Latin ~petitiōnem~, from ~petitio~, itself from ~petere~ (“to seek, to ask”). The same Latin verb lies behind ~appétit~ and ~compétition~.
en.pétrarquiser: ~Pétrarquiser~ is built on the name ~Pétrarque~, the French form of ~Petrarca~, the Italian poet Francesco Petrarca (1304-1374), with the suffix ~-iser~. The suffix gives the verb the sense of imitating him, of writing or behaving as he did, and in practice it names the imitation of his poetic style. The verb is a learned coinage of the kind that turns a famous name into an action.
en.pétrifier:
~Pétrifier~ was formed in French from Latin ~petra~ (“stone, rock”) and the suffix ~-ifier~. That suffix goes back to Latin ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”), so the verb means literally “to make into stone.” Latin ~petra~ was itself taken from Greek ~pétra~ (“rock”). It lives on in French ~pierre~, Italian ~pietra~ and Spanish ~piedra~.

The literal sense, turning something into stone, gave French its geological and figurative uses. A person ~pétrifié~ is rooted to the spot, as if made of rock, which matches the gloss “to paralyze.” The same Latin ~petra~ also stands behind ~pétrole~ (“oil from rock,” with Latin ~oleum~), ~pierre~ and the name ~Pierre~. English ~petrify~ and ~petroleum~ belong to the same family.
en.pétrir:
From Old French ~pestrir~, which comes from a Late Latin form *~pistrīre~, reconstructed rather than attested. English Wiktionary calls it a derivative of Latin ~pistor~ (“baker”); French Wiktionary names instead the feminine ~pistrix~ (“woman baker”) as the base. French ~pétrin~ (“kneading trough”) comes from Latin ~pistrīnum~, so the two words belong to one family. The ~-ir~ ending of ~pétrir~ is therefore inherited from Latin, not added in French to an adjective. The verb has no earlier French base; only the Late Latin form stands behind it.

The ~s~ of ~pestrir~ later fell silent and left an accent behind, as in ~être~ from ~estre~, which gave the modern ~pétrir~. The meaning spread from dough to other soft materials that hands can shape, and then to figurative use: one speaks of someone ~pétri~ d'orgueil or ~pétri~ de talent. ~Pétrin~ gave the familiar idiom ~être dans le pétrin~ (“to be in a fix”), and the family also includes ~pétrissage~, the act of kneading.
en.pétuner: Formed from ~pétun~, an old French word for tobacco, with the verb ending ~-er~: ~pétuner~ is to smoke or take snuff. ~Pétun~ is attested from 1558. Its source is a word of the Tupi-Guarani languages of Brazil, Old Tupi ~petyma~ according to English Wiktionary, which reached French by way of Portuguese ~petum~. The verb followed a little later. Both words were then displaced by ~tabac~ and survive only in some western dialects and in Canada.
en.pêcher:
From Old French ~peschier~ (also spelled ~peskier~), inherited from Latin ~piscārī~ (“to fish”), a verb built on ~piscis~ (“fish”). French Wiktionary adds that in popular Latin the verb became an ordinary active verb, *~piscare~. Latin ~piscis~ has a Germanic cousin in English ~fish~ and German ~Fisch~, from the same Indo-European word for the animal.

The Latin verb was a deponent, one that took passive endings with an active meaning, and popular Latin regularized it into *~piscare~, which is the form French descends from. From the same family come ~pêche~ (“fishing”), ~pêcheur~, ~poisson~ and the learned words ~piscine~ and ~pisciculture~. Beware the homograph ~pêcher~ (“peach tree”), which comes from an entirely different Latin source.
en.quadriller: ~Quadriller~ is formed, according to French Wiktionary, from ~quadrillé~ (“marked with crossing lines”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, itself the descendant of the Latin first-conjugation ending ~-āre~. French Wiktionary in turn derives ~quadrillé~ from ~quadrille~. The verb means to mark out a surface with a network of crossing lines, as in a grid or a criss-cross pattern.
en.quadrupler: From Latin ~quadruplare~, itself from ~quadruplus~ (“fourfold, quadruple”). The Latin adjective joins the element for “four,” as in ~quattuor~, to ~-plus~ (“-fold”), the ending also found in ~duplus~ and ~triplus~. French ~quadrupler~ means to multiply by four or to become four times larger, and sits beside ~doubler~ and ~tripler~. The adjective and noun ~quadruple~ come from the same Latin word.
en.qualifier:
From Medieval Latin ~qualificare~, a compound of Latin ~qualis~ (“of what kind, of what sort”) and the verb ~facere~ (“to make”), via the suffix ~-ficare~ — literally “to make of a certain kind.” ~qualis~ derives from the PIE interrogative-relative stem *~kʷo-~, the same pronoun base that lies behind “who” and “which.” The abstract noun ~qualitas~ was famously coined by Cicero as a calque of Greek ~ποιότης~ (“quality”), itself minted by Plato from ~ποῖος~ (“of what nature”). Cognate with Italian ~qualificare~, Spanish ~calificar~, and English ~qualify~.

The original sense was to attribute a quality to something — to say what kind of thing it is. From there ~qualifier~ branched in two directions: grammatically, an adjective ~qualifie~ a noun by describing it; and socially and legally, to ~qualifier~ became to give a title or designation, then to deem someone fit, competent, “qualified.” The sporting sense — a team that ~se qualifie~ for the next round — is a modern extension of that “proving fit” idea. From the same ~qualis~ root spring ~qualité~, ~qualitatif~, and the interrogative ~quel~ itself; the ~-ficare~ ending, meanwhile, recurs across a whole regiment of French verbs such as ~modifier~, ~vérifier~, and ~simplifier~, each one a small act of “making.”
en.quantifier: French ~quantifier~ is a modern borrowing from English ~quantify~, which in turn was built on Latin ~quantus~ (“how much”) and the verb-forming element ~-ficare~ (from ~facere~, “to make”). To ~quantifier~ is thus “to make into a quantity,” to express something as a number or a measure. The English verb gave French a convenient word for the technical and scientific vocabulary of measurement, in which French already had the nouns ~quantité~ and ~quantification~ from the same Latin root. The verb is a reminder that English, for much of its learned vocabulary, borrowed from Latin through French and now sometimes lends it back.
en.quarderonner: A technical verb formed on the phrase ~quart de rond~, the name of a molding whose profile is a quarter of a circle, with the verb ending ~-er~. ~Quarderonner~ means “to cut into a quarter-round molding,” that is, to give an edge or piece that profile. The phrase joins ~quart~ (“a fourth part”) and ~rond~ (“round”), and the ending ~-er~ comes from the Latin first-conjugation ending ~-are~.
en.quartager: A French formation built from three parts: the noun ~quart~ (“a fourth”), the noun suffix ~-age~ and the verb ending ~-er~. It is an agricultural term meaning “to perform a fourth cultivation,” a fourth working of the soil, so the “fourth” in the word is the count of the plowings. The ending ~-er~ comes from the Latin first-conjugation ending ~-are~.
en.quereller: Formed from the noun ~querelle~ (“quarrel”) with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, giving the sense “to scold, to pick a quarrel with.” The noun comes from Old French ~querele~, from Latin ~querella~ (“complaint”), a derivative of the deponent verb ~queror~ (“to lament, to complain”). The word therefore began in the language of grievance: a ~querelle~ was first a complaint voiced, and only later a dispute between two parties. The ~-er~ ending descends from Latin ~-are~ and is the usual tool for turning French nouns into verbs. In modern French ~quereller~ is used mostly in its pronominal form, ~se quereller~, “to bicker.”
en.questionner: ~Questionner~ is formed from ~question~ with the verbal ending ~-er~: to put questions to someone. ~Question~ entered Old French in the 12th century as a learned borrowing from Latin ~quaestiō~ (“a seeking, an inquiry”), from ~quaerere~ (“to seek, to ask”). Because it was learned, it kept its ~s~ before a consonant, unlike the popular word ~quête~ from the same root. In older French, ~question~ also named judicial interrogation under torture, and ~questionner~ could mean to subject someone to it, before the verb settled on its mild modern sense.
en.queuter: Formed from ~queue~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, with a euphonic ~-t-~ inserted between the vowel-final base and the ending. The noun ~queue~ means “tail,” and also “cue,” which explains the billiards sense of ~queuter~, to foul a shot; the slang sense of botching something follows. ~Queue~ comes from Old French ~coe~ or ~cue~, from Latin ~cōda~, a variant of ~cauda~ (“tail”). Its learned doublet in English is ~coda~.
en.quintessencier: Formed from the noun ~quintessence~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is from Latin ~quinta essentia~ (“fifth essence”), itself a calque of Greek ~pemptousía~ (“fifth substance”), the fifth element beyond the four classical ones. The verb is rare and means to extract the purest essence of something, or, in a pejorative sense, to over-refine it.
en.quintupler: Formed from ~quintuple~ + ~-er~, an ending that turns a noun or adjective into a verb: ~quintupler~ is to multiply by five, or to become five times as large. The adjective ~quintuple~ reached French through Middle French from Latin ~quīntuplus~, itself built from ~quīntus~ (“fifth”) and ~-plus~ (“-fold”), the same ending as in ~double~ and ~triple~. The family of ~doubler~, ~tripler~ and ~quadrupler~ follows the same pattern.
en.quittancer: Formed from ~quittance~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to give a receipt.” The noun ~quittance~ is built from ~quitter~ (“to make quits”) with ~-ance~, and ~quitter~ itself rests on the adjective ~quitte~ (“quits”). The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is the usual way to coin a verb from a noun.
en.quitter:
Modern French ~quitter~ is a verb built from the adjective ~quitte~ (“free of an obligation, even, discharged”) with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~. ~Quitte~ descends from Latin ~quietus~ (“at rest, calm, undisturbed”), the perfect participle of ~quiēscere~ (“to repose”), from the noun ~quies~ (“rest”), all from Proto-Indo-European *~kʷyeh₁-~ (“to rest”). The very same Latin ~quietus~ gives French the doublet ~quiet~ (“calm”) and, through a popular variant ~quētus~, the archaic ~coi~ (“still, hushed”); English ~quiet~, ~quit~, and ~coy~ are cognate, the last borrowed from Old French ~coi~.

The semantic thread runs from “rest” to “release.” In medieval law a person who was ~quitte~ had been left “at peace,” freed from a debt or duty; to ~quitter~ someone was therefore to discharge them, to acquit them of what they owed — a sense still alive in “~quitter~ quelqu'un d'une dette.” From “to release” the verb slid to “to let go of, to part from,” and finally to the everyday “to leave.” The same root produced ~acquitter~, ~quittance~ (“a receipt”), and ~quiétude~, and is buried in English ~acquit~ and ~requite~. A fitting irony hides in the chain: a verb that now means restless departure, “to leave,” was born from a word meaning perfect tranquillity.
en.quémander: ~Quémander~ comes from Middle French ~caimander~ (1539), a form that persisted until the eighteenth century, itself from Middle French ~caïmand~ (“beggar”), attested in 1393. The verb thus began as one built on the word for a beggar, and it kept the sense of asking for something humbly, insistently or shamelessly. The sources do not trace ~caïmand~ any further back, so its own origin remains open.
en.quérir:
From Middle French ~querir~, which came from Old French ~querre~ (“to seek”) with a change of conjugation, from Latin ~quaerere~ (“to seek”). The Old French sense survives in some northern French dialects (the langues d'oïl), as in Walloon ~cweri~. The Latin verb also gave Spanish and Portuguese ~querer~, which drifted to “to want,” so “seeking” and “wanting” share one ancestor.

Modern French uses ~quérir~ almost only in the infinitive, after verbs of motion, as in ~aller quérir~ or ~envoyer quérir~, with the sense “to fetch,” and the word feels old-fashioned. Its family is far livelier, since the Latin compounds of ~quaerere~ gave ~acquérir~, ~conquérir~, ~requérir~ and ~enquérir~, along with learned relatives such as ~question~, ~quête~ and ~enquête~. English took ~inquire~, ~query~ and ~quest~ from the same Latin verb.
en.quêter: Formed in French from the noun ~quête~ (Old French ~queste~, “search”) and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Latin ~quaesita~, a form of the verb ~quaerere~ (“to seek”). English Wiktionary instead routes the verb itself through Latin ~quaestāre~ (“to search”), and the English ~quest~ is a cognate. The verb first meant “to look for,” and it now commonly means “to collect alms or donations,” as in a church collection.
en.rabaisser: Formed from ~abaisser~ with the prefix ~r-~, the form ~re-~ takes before a vowel. ~Abaisser~ is ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “toward”) plus ~baisser~ (“to lower”), which goes back to Vulgar Latin *~bassiāre~, built on Late Latin ~bassus~ (“low”). Like its base, rabaisser covers both the physical and the moral: to lower something, and to belittle or humble someone.
en.rabattre: Formed in French from ~battre~ and a prefix, though the sources analyse it differently. English Wiktionary sees ~re-~ added to ~abattre~, while French Wiktionary describes a compound of ~ra-~ and ~battre~; ~ra-~ is an old variant of ~re-~, so the two accounts differ more in bookkeeping than in meaning. Either way the core is ~battre~, from Latin ~battuere~ (“to beat, to strike”), probably borrowed from Gaulish. The prefix ~re-~ adds a sense of return or repetition, so the verb meant roughly “to beat down again,” and from there “to fold down, to lower, to reduce, to deduct,” the range of senses it still has.
en.rabibocher: French Wiktionary derives ~rabibocher~, probably, from a dialectal stem ~bib~ meaning “small thing,” the same one found in ~bibelot~ (“trinket”). The verb would then have meant, etymologically, “to patch up”: to mend with small pieces. English Wiktionary likewise relates it to ~bibelot~. The modern sense of reconciling people, often after a quarrel, is thus a figurative extension of repairing something, though the sources do not describe the stages in between.
en.rabioter: ~Rabioter~ is a straightforward derivation: the noun ~rabiot~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~rabiot~ names an extra or leftover portion, and the verb, glossed here as “to appropriate,” means to help oneself to such extras, in other words to pocket small gains on the side. Both words belong to familiar speech. The sources give no date for the verb, and they do not trace ~rabiot~ itself any further.
en.raboter: Formed from ~rabot~ (“plane”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to work with a plane.” The two Wiktionaries disagree about the noun. French Wiktionary derives ~rabot~ from ~rabote~ (“doe rabbit”), perhaps alluding to the blade jutting from the tool like a rabbit's tooth. English Wiktionary instead calls it a diminutive of Middle Dutch ~robbe~ (“rabbit”), of the family of German ~Robbe~ (“seal”) and English ~rabbit~. Either way the tool is connected with a rabbit, and the verb means to smooth wood with a plane.
en.rabougrir: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ and the older verb ~abougrir~, which was itself built from ~a-~, ~bougre~ and the verb ending ~-ir~. French Wiktionary notes that ~bougre~ had taken the sense “weak, puny,” so ~abougrir~ meant to make or become stunted. The prefix ~re-~ here does not clearly mean “again”; it simply reinforces the idea, as an intensive. Today ~rabougrir~ means to stunt, usually of a plant or a person whose growth is stopped, and the participle ~rabougri~ describes a shriveled, undersized thing.
en.rabouter: ~Rabouter~ is built on ~abouter~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again, back”), here in its reduced form ~r-~ before the vowel. The base ~abouter~ comes from Old French ~abouter~, which is also the source of English ~abut~. It is made of ~a-~ and ~bout~ (“end”) and means to bring ends together, joining one piece to another end to end. ~Rabouter~ keeps that sense: it means to join pieces end to end. The prefix ~re-~ itself goes back to Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”), and the sources give no more than a reinforcement or repetition of the base's action.
en.rabrouer: Formed from the prefix ~ra-~ and the Old French verb ~brouer~ (“to scold”), which disappeared around the sixteenth century. The prefix ~ra-~ is an old variant of ~re-~, found in several inherited verbs. ~Brouer~ was itself derived from ~breu~, the word that also gave modern ~brouet~ (“broth”). The sense of the verb in modern French, to snub or treat someone harshly, goes back to this lost Old French verb of scolding.
en.rabâcher: The origin of ~rabâcher~ is uncertain, and the two Wiktionaries propose different analyses. French Wiktionary derives it from Old French ~rabascher~ (“to make a racket like a goblin”), built on a radical ~rab-~ that expresses making noise (compare ~rabouin~, “devil, goblin”) plus the suffix ~-âcher~. It notes that Old French also had ~rabaster~ (“to make noise, to cause an uproar”). English Wiktionary instead derives it from a root *~rabb-~, possibly from a pre-Roman substrate, which might also lie behind ~rabaster~. The circumflex marks an s that was lost: ~rabascher~ became ~rabâcher~.
en.raccommoder: ~Raccommoder~ is formed from ~accommoder~ with the prefix ~re-~, here in its older shape ~ra-~. The base comes from Latin ~accommodāre~ (“to fit to, to adapt”), built on ~ad-~ and ~commodus~ (“fitting”), a compound of ~com-~ and ~modus~ (“measure”). The prefix adds the idea of doing again or of restoring, so ~raccommoder~ means to put right what no longer fits: to mend a garment or an object, and also to reconcile people who have quarrelled, as in ~se raccommoder~ (“to make up”).
en.raccompagner: Formed from ~accompagner~ and the prefix ~r-~, here meaning a return to the starting point: to take someone back home. The base comes from Old French ~acompaignier~, from ~compaing~ or ~compagnon~ (“companion”). That word goes back to Late Latin ~companio~, literally ~cum~ (“with”) + ~panis~ (“bread”), probably a calque of Gothic ~gahlaiba~. To ~accompagner~ is thus, at root, to share bread with someone, and ~raccompagner~ adds the way back.
en.raccorder: Formed in French from ~accorder~ with the prefix ~r-~, a variant of ~re-~ used before a vowel. The base ~accorder~ comes from Late Latin ~accordare~, built from ~ad-~ (“toward”) and ~cor~, ~cordis~ (“heart”): literally “to bring hearts together.” Here the prefix has the sense of joining again or joining up, so ~raccorder~ means to connect two parts so that they fit, whether pipes, roads or the edges of a piece of wallpaper. The image of agreement in ~accorder~ carries over: what is joined must match.
en.raccourcir: From ~accourcir~ with the prefix ~r-~, the form of ~re-~ used before a vowel. The base is an archaic verb from Old French ~acorcier~, built from ~a-~ + ~court~ + ~-ir~, “to make short.” The adjective ~court~ comes from Latin ~curtus~ (“cut short”), which English borrowed as ~curt~. Here ~re-~ descends from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”), but it adds no real idea of repetition: the verb simply means “to shorten.” Modern French has largely replaced ~accourcir~ with ~raccourcir~.
en.raccrocher: Formed from ~accrocher~ and the prefix ~re-~, which loses its vowel and appears as ~r-~ before the initial ~a~ of the base. The base verb is built on ~croc~ (“hook”), a Frankish borrowing cognate with English ~crook~, so the idea is “to put on a hook.” With the prefix, ~raccrocher~ means to hang back up or hang again, then to hang up a telephone receiver, and by extension to catch hold again. The prefix repeats or returns the action, as in many other French verbs. The figurative uses are many: ~raccrocher~ is also to give up a profession, especially in sport, as when an athlete “hangs up” the gloves or the boots.
en.racheter:
~racheter~ is transparently ~r-~ (from Latin ~re-~, “again, back”) prefixed to ~acheter~ (“to buy”), and the interest lies in ~acheter~ itself. That verb comes from Old French ~achater~, from Vulgar Latin *~accaptāre~, a reinforcement with ~ad-~ of ~captāre~ (“to try to seize, to grab at”), the frequentative of ~capere~ (“to take”), from PIE *~kh₂p-~ (“to grasp”). The Romance cognates are everyday verbs: Italian ~accattare~ and, more distantly, Spanish reflexes of the same family. So “to buy” in French is literally “to seek to seize toward oneself.”

The prefix turns acquisition into re-acquisition, and ~racheter~ spans a remarkable range: to buy back what one sold, to buy someone out, to ransom a captive, and — in the theological register — to redeem. That last sense gave ~rachat~ (“redemption, buyout”) and rédempteur's near-synonym in everyday speech. Through ~capere~ the same root reaches a huge family — ~capter~, ~captif~, ~capable~, ~recevoir~ — and even, by other routes, English ~catch~ and ~chase~. A note of caution: some hold that *~accaptāre~ was reshaped from Latin ~acceptāre~; the sources present this as a possibility, not a settled fact.
en.raciner: Formed from the noun ~racine~ (“root”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning “to take root.” The noun is inherited from Late Latin ~radīcīna~, a diminutive-like form built on Latin ~rādīx~ (“root”) with the suffix ~-īna~. Latin ~rādīx~ goes back to a Proto-Indo-European form usually reconstructed as *~wréh₂ds~. The verb is rare today, while its prefixed relatives ~enraciner~ and ~déraciner~, built on the same noun, are common.
en.racketter: Formed from ~racket~ with the verb-forming ending ~-er~, with the doubled ~t~ keeping the vowel short. The noun ~racket~ was borrowed into French from English ~racket~, and the French verb follows the usual pattern of turning a noun into a first-conjugation verb: to practice ~racket~ on someone, which is to racketeer. It is a modern borrowing, so its story belongs to the English word.
en.racler:
~Racler~ was borrowed from Occitan ~rasclar~ (“to scrape”), from Vulgar Latin *~rasclare~ or *~rasiculare~, a diminutive-like formation on a verb *~rasicare~. English Wiktionary connects it to Latin ~rasculum~, from ~rasus~, while French Wiktionary derives *~rasicare~ from Classical Latin ~radere~ (“to scrape”), of which ~rasus~ is the participle. Italian ~raschiare~ is a comparable verb.

The French verb is a doublet of ~râler~. ~Racler~ itself kept the physical meaning of scraping a surface clean, and it gave ~racloir~, ~raclée~ and ~raclette~, the dish named for the knife-scraping of melted cheese. Its Latin ancestor ~radere~ also gave ~raser~ (“to shave”), ~rasoir~ and ~rature~, and English ~raze~ and ~erase~.
en.racoler: ~Racoler~, formerly spelled ~raccoler~, is formed from ~accoler~ with the prefix ~re-~ in its old form ~ra-~. The base ~accoler~ is built on ~col~ (“neck”), from Latin ~collum~, and meant in Old French “to throw one's arms around someone's neck”, so “to embrace”. The sources give no story for how the verb came to mean soliciting or touting, so only the formation is certain, and the modern sense of soliciting has drifted far from the neck.
en.raconter:
From Old French ~raconter~ (attested c. 1130–40), formed with the prefix ~re-~ on ~aconter~, itself ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~) plus ~conter~ (“to tell, to count”). ~Conter~ descends from Latin ~computare~ (“to calculate, to reckon”), a compound of ~com-~ and ~putare~ (“to reckon, to estimate”). The very same Latin verb gave French its doublet ~compter~ (“to count”), so ~conter~ and ~compter~ are etymological twins, split apart by spelling and sense. Cognates include Spanish ~contar~ and Italian ~contare~, which likewise mean both “to count” and “to tell,” and English ~count~ and ~compute~.

The semantic thread is the link between enumerating and narrating: to “tell” a tale was once to “count off” its events one by one — English preserves the same metaphor in a bank ~teller~, who tells out money. ~Raconter~ adds an intensifying ~re-~ to ~aconter~, yielding “to recount, to relate in full.” Over time ~conter~ specialized toward fiction (a ~conte~ is a tale or fairy story), while ~raconter~ became the everyday verb for telling what happened. From the same ~computare~ flow ~compte~, ~comptable~, ~conte~, ~conteur~, and the learned ~computer~ (“to compute”).
en.racornir: Built on the noun ~corne~ (“horn”) with the prefix ~ra-~ and the verbal ending ~-ir~, so that ~racornir~ means to make or become as hard as horn. The prefix ~ra-~ is an old form of ~re-~, here not marking repetition. ~Corne~ comes through Old French from Vulgar Latin *~corna~, which arose when ~cornua~, the plural of Latin ~cornū~, was taken for a feminine singular. French Wiktionary compares it with the Biblical Hebrew and Arabic words for “horn.”
en.rader: ~Rader~ is formed from the noun ~rade~ (“roadstead”) and the verbal ending ~-er~: to lie at anchor in a sheltered spot near the shore. English Wiktionary says ~rade~ entered Middle French in the fifteenth century from an Old French *~rade~ borrowed from Middle English ~rade~ (“a ride, a sheltered anchorage”), from Old English ~rād~ (“a ride”). French ~rade~ is therefore a doublet of ~raid~ and a cousin of English ~road~.
en.radicaliser: Formed from ~radical~ with the suffix ~-iser~, which makes verbs meaning “to make” something: to radicalize is to make more radical. ~Radical~ is a learned borrowing from Late Latin ~rādīcālis~, derived from ~radix~ (“root”), and in some of its senses it was influenced by English ~radical~. The verb thus rests, etymologically, on the Latin word for “root.”
en.radier: ~Radier~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~radiāre~, a verb built on ~radius~ (“ray”) that meant to emit rays. English Wiktionary adds a cross-reference to ~rayer~, a French verb that also means to strike out. The sources do not explain how the sense of striking off or wiping clean developed from the Latin, so only the borrowing itself is settled here. The prefixed Latin verb ~irradiāre~ gave French ~irradier~.
en.radiner:
~Radiner~ is a colloquial verb meaning “to arrive, to turn up,” and its origin is obscure. French Wiktionary says so plainly and gives no chain of descent through Old French or Latin, so no source word can honestly be named here. What it records instead are rival proposals. By the first, the verb was drawn from ~radin~ in the sense of “pocket,” and built like the synonyms ~engaîner~ and ~rengaîner~ (“to arrive, to come home”) or ~enquiller~ and ~renquiller~ (“to come in”).

By the second proposal, ~radiner~ is linked to a dialect verb ~radiner~ (“to remove the crust of gratin from a pan”), itself from ~radin~ (“gratin”). A third idea, a link to ~rade~, either an old adjective meaning “fast” or a noun meaning “street, pavement,” is set aside as unsound on grounds of both meaning and chronology. Neither surviving explanation is established, so the verb's story remains an open question.
en.radiobaliser: A French formation from the noun ~radiobalise~ (a radio beacon) with the verb ending ~-er~, meaning “to provide with N.” ~Radiobaliser~ therefore means “to equip with radio beacons.” The noun is itself made of the prefix ~radio-~ and ~balise~ (“beacon, marker”). The ending ~-er~ comes from the Latin first-conjugation ending ~-are~.
en.radiodiffuser: ~Radiodiffuser~ joins the prefix ~radio-~ to the verb ~diffuser~. The prefix goes back to Latin ~radius~ (“ray, beam”) and here means “by radio waves.” The base ~diffuser~ was formed in the fifteenth century on the adjective ~diffus~, from Latin ~diffundere~ (~dis-~ + ~fundere~, “to pour out, to spread”), so the picture is of a signal poured out in every direction. The verb thus means to broadcast by radio, and it was later extended to television programmes as well.
en.radiographier: Formed from the noun ~radiographie~ (“X-ray imaging”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning “to take an X-ray picture of.” Both Wiktionaries explain the noun as a shortened form of the earlier ~radiophotographie~, a compound that named the same technique. The verb is a modern coinage of the scientific age, made on the French model by which any technical noun can be turned into a first-conjugation verb.
en.radioguider: Formed from ~guider~ and the prefix ~radio-~, meaning “by radio waves”: to steer by radio. The prefix comes from Latin ~radius~ (“ray”), the same root as in ~radioactivité~ and ~radiodiffusion~. The base ~guider~ is a reshaping, under the influence of ~guide~, of Old French ~guier~, from Old Frankish ~witan~ (“to show the way”), a Germanic verb related to German ~weisen~ and, distantly, to Latin ~vidēre~ (“to see”). The verb thus joins an ancient Germanic idea of pointing the way to a twentieth-century technology.
en.radoter:
~Radoter~ comes from Old French ~redoter~, in which the prefix ~re-~ was replaced by an expressive ~ra-~. The Old French verb was derived from a lost verb *~doter~ of Germanic origin, perhaps borrowed from Middle Dutch ~doten~ (“to be foolish”); English ~dote~ is a related word. English Wiktionary gives only a Proto-West Germanic source, so the exact route is uncertain. The participle ~radoté~ meant “mad, fallen into second childhood.”

The verb is attested from 1185 with the sense of speaking in senile, rambling, senseless terms, which fits the old participle: the original idea was the mental decline of old age. In 1833 it took the weaker modern sense of repeating the same things over and over, which is the meaning heard today in ~tu radotes~ (“you are rambling on”). The noun ~radotage~ and the agent ~radoteur~ follow the verb.
en.radouber: Formed in French from ~adouber~ with the prefix ~re-~. The base is the old verb of knighthood, which goes back to a Frankish word for striking and is a distant cousin of English ~dub~. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and here adds the idea of doing the action over, so ~radouber~ means “to refit” or “to repair.” The verb thus carries a trace of that medieval verb: to equip again what had once been fitted out.
en.radoucir: From ~re-~ + ~adoucir~. The base was built in Old French on ~douz~ (“sweet”), from Latin ~dulcis~, with the prefix ~a-~ and the ending ~-ir~, and means “to make sweet or gentler.” The prefix ~re-~ (from Latin ~re-~, “back, again”) adds the idea of a return to a gentler state, which suits the verb's usual uses: a temper, a voice or the weather that grows mild again. The result is a close cousin of ~adoucir~, with the nuance of a softening after a harsher moment.
en.raffermir: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ and ~affermir~, which is built from ~à~, the adjective ~ferme~ (“firm”) and the verb ending ~-ir~, “to make firm.” The adjective ~ferme~ comes from Latin ~firmus~. ~Raffermir~ adds a sense of renewal or reinforcement: to make firm again, to strengthen, as one firms up muscles, a voice or a resolve. The same Latin ~firmus~ underlies ~fermeté~ and ~confirmer~.
en.raffiner: Formed in French from ~affiner~ with the prefix ~re-~. The base ~affiner~ is itself built in one step from ~a-~ plus the adjective ~fin~ plus ~-er~, “to make fine or pure,” and ~fin~ goes back to Latin ~fīnis~ (“limit, end”), whose sense shifted from “utmost point” to “perfect, delicate.” The prefix ~re-~ here works as an intensifier more than as a strict “again”: ~raffiner~ means to purify or polish further, whether sugar or oil, or manners and taste.
en.raffoler: Formed from ~affoler~ with the prefix ~r-~ (English Wiktionary writes ~re-~). The base ~affoler~ is built on the old adjective ~fol~ (“mad”), the earlier form of ~fou~, with ~a-~ and ~-er~, and means to drive someone mad. The prefix does not carry the sense of “again” here, and the verb means to be wildly fond of something, as in ~raffoler de~.
en.rafistoler: Formed with the prefix ~re-~ on ~afistoler~, a verb inherited from Old French that meant “to adorn, to embellish.” English Wiktionary analyses that base as ~a-~ + ~fistuler~. The meaning then moved from adorning to the modern sense of a makeshift repair, “to patch up.”
en.rafler: Rafler is linked to the noun ~rafle~. French Wiktionary derives the verb from it and traces the noun to Middle Low German ~raffel~ (“instrument for raking the fire”), from ~raffen~ (“to seize, to clasp”). The noun is recorded in 1371 for a dice game in which one throw can sweep all the stakes, and from 1585 in the sense “loot”; the expression ~faire rafle~ (“to take everything”) appears in 1645. English Wiktionary instead derives the verb from Frankish *~raffolōn~, from Proto-Germanic *~hrapōną~ (“to scratch, snatch”), and compares German ~raffen~. Both routes lead to a Germanic word for snatching.
en.rafraîchir: Built from ~fraîchir~ (“to turn cooler”) with the prefix ~ra-~, an old variant of ~re-~. The base comes from the adjective ~frais~ (feminine ~fraîche~), a word of Germanic origin and a cousin of English ~fresh~ and German ~frisch~; the circumflex of ~fraîche~ stands in for an ~s~ of Old French spelling. In this use the prefix makes a verb from an adjective, as in ~raffermir~ and ~ralentir~, so ~rafraîchir~ means “to make cool again,” and by extension “to refresh,” whether a drink, a room or a memory.
en.ragaillardir: Formed in French from ~gaillard~ with the prefix ~ra-~, an old form of ~re-~ used to make verbs from adjectives, and the ending ~-ir~: to restore someone's vigor and good spirits. The adjective ~gaillard~ cannot come from ~gai~ plus a suffix. It comes instead from a Gaulish root *~gal-~ (“strength”), related to Irish ~gal~, so ~gaillard~ first meant “strong, vigorous.”
en.rager: Formed from the noun ~rage~ and the verb ending ~-er~, meaning to be in a rage. The noun comes from Late Latin *~rabia~, an altered form of Latin ~rabiēs~ (“rage”), with a change of declension. Spanish ~rabia~ is a cognate. The ~-bi-~ became ~-ge~ in French, as in ~singe~ from Latin ~simium~.
en.ragréer: Formed from ~agréer~ with the prefix ~re-~. The base ~agréer~ is built on the phrase ~à gré~ (“to one's liking”), from the noun ~gré~, which comes from Latin ~grātum~, the neuter of ~grātus~ (“pleasing, welcome”). The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”), though in this verb it does not simply mean repetition. The sense “to smooth” belongs to building and finishing work, and the sources give no story of how it came about.
en.raguer: Borrowed from English ~rag~, in the sense of “to ransack”. The French verb has a narrower meaning, to chafe or wear something away by rubbing. It is a borrowing, not a formation from any French base; the sense moved from plundering to damaging by friction.
en.raidir: Formed from the adjective ~raide~ (“stiff”) and the verb ending ~-ir~, which here makes a verb meaning “to make or become stiff.” ~Raide~ is a modern spelling of the older ~roide~, from Old French ~roit~, from Latin ~rigidus~. It is a doublet of the learned ~rigide~, which was borrowed from the same Latin word later.
en.railler: Inherited from Middle French ~railler~, which English Wiktionary traces to Vulgar Latin *~raglāre~, itself from *~ragulāre~. Behind these lies Late Latin ~ragō~ (“to bray”), a rare verb attested directly only once, in a 10th-century manuscript, though the word itself may date from around the 4th century. It also left Old French ~raire~ and ~réer~, both said of the cry of a deer, and Romanian ~rage~ (“to scream”). Compare Occitan ~ralhar~, Catalan ~rallar~ and Italian ~ragliare~. The sources consulted do not explain how braying came to mean mocking.
en.rainer: French Wiktionary derives ~rainer~ (“to cut a groove”) from the Old French verb ~roisnier~ and points to the related nouns ~rainure~ (“groove”) and ~rognure~ (“trimming, scrap”). English Wiktionary gives a simpler analysis: ~rainure~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. Either way, the verb belongs with ~rainure~ and means to cut a narrow channel in wood, stone or metal. The sources do not agree on which came first, the noun or the verb, so the chain is best left at that.
en.rainurer: Formed from the noun ~rainure~ (“groove”) with the ending ~-er~, “to cut a groove in.” According to English Wiktionary, ~rainure~ comes from Old French ~roisner~ plus ~-ure~, and ~roisner~ from Vulgar Latin *~rucina~, which was borrowed from Gaulish *~rucina~ and ultimately from Ancient Greek ~ῥῠκάνη~ (~rhŭkánē~, “plane, a carpenter's tool”). French Wiktionary, for its part, calls ~rainure~ an old variant of ~rognure~ and points to Old French ~roisnier~. So the groove is, etymologically, a mark left by a carpenter's tool.
en.raire: Inherited from Old French ~raire~, itself from Late Latin ~ragĕre~ (“to bellow, to low”). English Wiktionary compares Romanian ~rage~ and also the French verb ~railler~ (“to mock”), without spelling out how the words are related. In modern French ~raire~ is a rare, specialized verb for the call of the stag, so the gloss “to roar, as a stag” is the sense that survives today.
en.raisonner: Formed from the noun ~raison~ with the suffix ~-er~, in the sense “to act or speak with N”: to use reason. In Old French the verb was ~raisnier~ and meant simply “to speak”, so talking and reasoning were one activity. The noun comes from Latin ~ratio~, accusative ~rationem~ (“reckoning, calculation, reasoning”), and ~ration~ is its learned doublet, which is why ~rationner~ is a close parallel. From “to speak” the verb moved to “to argue” and then to “to think logically”.
en.rajeunir: The verb is a French formation from ~ra-~, the adjective ~jeune~ and the verb ending ~-ir~. French Wiktionary treats ~ra-~ as a single prefix, while English Wiktionary reads it as ~r-~ plus ~a-~. The adjective ~jeune~ comes from Latin ~iuvenis~ (“young”). The pattern is the deadjectival ~-ir~ meaning “to become or make A,” here “to become young again” and, with an object, “to make younger.” Old French had its own shorter verb ~jeunir~ and the prefixed ~ajovenir~, so ~rajeunir~ is a later formation.
en.rajouter:
Compound of the prefix ~re-~ and ~ajouter~ (“to add”). ~Ajouter~ comes from Old French ~ajoster~ (“to bring together, place side by side”), built on Latin ~juxta~ (“near, beside”) — the same word behind ~juxtaposer~. So to add was originally to set one thing beside another. ~Juxta~ is related to the family of ~jungere~ (“to join”), from Proto-Indo-European *~yewg-~ (“to join, yoke”), cognate with English ~yoke~ and ~join~.

Old French ~ajoster~ meant to assemble or unite; over time it narrowed to the arithmetic and everyday sense “to add, to put in addition.” Prefixing ~re-~ produced ~rajouter~, which adds again, puts back, or tops up — ~rajouter du sel~ is to add yet more salt. The two verbs coexist with a fine distinction much policed by purists: ~ajouter~ for a first addition, ~rajouter~ for a further one, though in speech ~rajouter~ has spread well beyond that rule. The buried root ~juxta~ also yields French ~juxtaposition~ and the borrowed adverb ~juxta~ in scholarly usage, while the deeper *~yewg-~ underlies ~joindre~, ~jonction~, and ~conjuguer~ — the very act of conjugation being a “yoking together” of forms.
en.rajuster: From ~ajuster~ with the prefix ~r-~, the form that ~re-~ takes before a vowel: to ~rajuster~ is to adjust again, to readjust, or to set right, as in tidying one's clothes. The base ~ajuster~ is derived from ~juste~ (“right, exact”) with ~a-~ and ~-er~. ~Juste~ goes back to Latin ~iūstus~ (“lawful, right”), from ~iūs~ (“law, right”), and English ~adjust~ reached English through the same Old French verb.
en.ralentir:
~Ralentir~ is a French construction with deep Latin roots: ~re-~ + ~alentir~ (“to slow”), itself built in the twelfth century (attested 1180–90) from ~a-~ + ~lent~ + ~-ir~. The adjective ~lent~ descends from Latin ~lentus~, whose range startles: “flexible, pliant,” “sticky, tenacious,” and only by extension “slow,” even “impassive.” Behind it stands a reconstructed *~lentos~ (“flexible”); some compare the Germanic family of German ~lind~ (“gentle”) and English ~lithe~ (“supple”), though the connection is debated. Within Romance the kinship is plain: Italian and Spanish ~lento~ — and, borrowed from Italian, the ~lento~ of musical scores. ~Ralentir~ itself is a Renaissance refit: Ronsard wrote ~rallenter~ in 1552, Montaigne ~ralentir~ in 1588, and the form in ~-ir~ prevailed, gradually pushing its own parent ~alentir~ into the attic of the language.

The buried picture deserves a pause. For a Roman, a willow switch was ~lentus~ because it bent without breaking; pitch and honey were ~lentus~ because they clung; a sluggish or unmoved person was ~lentus~ too. The senses lived side by side — pliant, sticky, slow, phlegmatic — and French ~lent~ kept only the slowness. ~Alentir~ served the Middle Ages; after the Renaissance preferred ~ralentir~, the parent verb sank into archaism, surviving as a literary rarity. The modern family runs from ~lenteur~ and ~lentement~ to two inventions of the machine age: ~ralenti~ — an engine’s idle, and cinema’s slow motion (~au ralenti~) — and ~ralentisseur~, the French speed bump. And the verb itself stands in capitals on every French road: ~RALENTIR~, an everyday imperative built, far upstream, on the suppleness of willows and the patience of honey.
en.ralinguer: Formed from the noun ~ralingue~ (the rope sewn along the edge of a sail), so it means to luff. ~Ralingue~ comes from Old Norse *~rár-lík~, a compound of ~rár~, the genitive of ~rá~ (compare Swedish ~rå~), and ~lík~ (“edge of a sail”). The verb is thus a nautical term that came into French from the Norse seafaring vocabulary.
en.raller: The sources disagree on this verb. French Wiktionary gives it both as derived from ~râler~ and as ~aller~ with the prefix ~r-~, the form that ~re-~ takes before a vowel. The sources do not choose between them. The verb ~raller~ means to roar, as a stag does. As for ~aller~, it is a famous suppletive verb: its present forms in ~v-~ come from Latin ~vādere~, its future in ~ir-~ from ~īre~, and the stem ~all-~ has a debated origin.
en.rallier: ~Rallier~ is formed from ~allier~ with the prefix ~re-~, which here carries the sense of doing again or gathering back. ~Allier~ descends from Latin ~alligāre~ (“to bind to”), a compound of ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~ligāre~ (“to bind”). To ~rallier~ is thus to bind together again, first of scattered troops called back to their banner, then of people who join a cause or opinion. English ~rally~ was borrowed from the French verb, and the same Latin ~alligāre~ lies behind both the French ~allier~ and English ~ally~.
en.rallonger: ~Rallonger~ is formed from ~allonger~ with the prefix ~re-~, here in its elided form ~r-~ before a vowel, meaning “to lengthen further.” ~Allonger~ was built in French on the adjective ~long~ with ~a-~ and ~-er~, and it replaced Old French ~alongier~. ~Long~ goes back to Latin ~longus~, which is related to English ~long~ and German ~lang~. The verb is used for adding length to a hem, a table or a deadline.
en.rallumer: Formed from ~allumer~ with the prefix ~r-~, which marks a return to an earlier state. The verb is attested as early as 1050, at first in the sense “to recover one's sight”, and took its modern sense “to light again” in the 13th century. The base ~allumer~ comes from Old French ~alumer~, from Vulgar Latin *~alluminare~, which goes back to Latin ~ad-~ and the word for light, ~lumen~.
en.ramager: ~Ramager~ is a verb formed from the noun ~ramage~, with the verb ending ~-er~, and it means to sing, said of a bird. The noun comes from Old French ~ram~ (“branch”), from Latin ~ramus~, with the suffix ~-age~, and is attested around 1160 in the sense “branchy.” The meaning “song of birds among the branches” appeared in 1549.
en.ramasser: ~Ramasser~ is built on ~amasser~ with the prefix ~r-~, a form of ~re-~ (Latin ~re-~, “back, again”). French Wiktionary calls it an intensive prefix, so the sense is “to gather up” rather than “to gather again”. The base ~amasser~ is ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “toward”) + ~masse~ (“lump, heap”) + ~-er~, “to gather into a heap.” The noun ~masse~ comes from Latin ~massa~ (“lump, dough”), which the Romans took from Greek ~mâza~ (“barley cake, kneaded lump”). To pick things up is thus, etymologically, to heap them together.
en.ramender: Formed from ~amender~ with the prefix ~ra-~, an older form of ~re-~, here with a sense of “again” or reinforcement; the verb means to mend a net. ~Amender~ comes from Old French ~amender~, from Latin ~ēmendāre~ (“to free from faults, to correct”), made of ~ex-~ (“out of”) and ~mendum~ (“a fault”). To mend a net is thus, etymologically, to take the faults out of it, and English ~mend~ is a shortened form of the same verb.
en.ramener:
A French compound built from ~re-~ (here marking a return to a starting point) and ~amener~ (“to bring, to lead toward”), which itself is ~à~ (“to”) plus ~mener~ (“to lead, to drive”). The verb ~mener~ descends from Vulgar Latin *~minare~ (“to drive animals along, to herd”), a sense derived from Classical Latin ~minārī~ (“to threaten, to brandish”) — the herdsman drove his cattle forward with shouts and threats. Spanish and Italian preserve the same image in ~menar~ and ~menare~.

The path from “threaten” to “lead” runs through the drover: to threaten an ox into motion is to make it go where you wish, and so *~minare~ slid from menacing to simply conducting. French ~mener~ kept the neutral sense “to lead,” and its prefixed forms map out directions of travel: ~amener~ (lead toward), ~emmener~ (lead away), ~promener~ (lead about, hence “to walk, stroll”). With ~re-~ added, ~ramener~ means to bring someone or something back to where it began — and figuratively to restore, to draw back, or, in slang, to ~ramener sa fraise~ (“to butt in”). The same root underlies ~menace~ and ~ménager~.
en.ramer: ~Ramer~ is a denominal verb, formed from the noun ~rame~ (“oar”) with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~rame~ comes from Latin ~rēmus~ (“oar”) by way of Old French, and Latin ~rēmus~ is also the source of Italian and Spanish ~remo~. French Wiktionary also lists a different ~rame~, from Middle Dutch or Middle High German, and another, a ream of paper, from Arabic through Catalan, but those words are unrelated to the oar. The literal sense is “to propel a boat with oars.” From the hard, repetitive effort of rowing, informal French drew the figurative sense “to toil, to struggle,” and from there, in computing, “to run slowly” of a lagging machine.
en.rameuter: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ and ~ameuter~, itself ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~, “toward”) + ~meute~ + ~-er~, “to gather into a pack.” ~Meute~ comes from Old French ~muete~, which meant a pack of hounds, a band of people and also a riot. The traditional account derives ~muete~ from a Latin *~movita~, built on ~movēre~ (“to move”), though Littré argued no such form is needed. The family includes ~émeute~ and ~mutin~. ~Rameuter~ means “to round up,” of people or a crowd.
en.ramifier:
The verb is inherited from Old French ~ramifier~, itself borrowed from Medieval Latin ~ramificāre~. That Latin verb was built from ~ramus~ (“branch”) and ~facere~ (“to do, to make”), so it literally means “to make branches.” French Wiktionary gives the same two parts, ~ramus~ and ~-fier~, the form that ~facere~ takes in verbs of this type. English ~ramify~ comes from the French verb.

Because ~ramificāre~ was a Medieval Latin formation, the verb is a learned one, not a word worn down by ordinary sound change from classical Latin. Its family shows both halves. The ~ramus~ side gives ~rameau~ (“small branch”), ~ramure~ (“the branches of a tree”) and ~ramification~. The ~-ficāre~ side gives many verbs in ~-ifier~ such as ~modifier~ and ~justifier~, and ~facere~ itself gives ~faire~. The sense of dividing like branches fits trees and anything shaped like them, such as roads, networks or families.
en.ramollir:
The sources disagree about how ~ramollir~ was made. French Wiktionary offers two accounts: it comes from Latin ~remollīre~, or it is derived from ~mollir~ with the prefix ~ra-~. English Wiktionary gives a third: ~r-~ + ~amollir~, and compares Italian ~rammollire~. In every account the core is the Latin adjective ~mollis~ (“soft”), by way of the verb ~mollir~, and the prefix is a variant of ~re-~, the one that means “again” or strengthens the verb.

The meaning has stayed close to that core: ~ramollir~ is “to make soft or softer,” and the pronominal form is “to go soft.” The other branch of the family is ~amollir~, the verb in the English account. The base ~mollir~ is a living verb, and the adjective ~mou~ and the noun ~mollesse~ descend from Latin ~mollis~ as well. The competing accounts matter little for meaning, since all three give “soften again” or “soften thoroughly,” but they differ on whether Latin supplied the finished verb or French built it.
en.ramoner:
Inherited from Old French ~ramoner~ (“to sweep”), built on ~ramon~ (“broom”) plus the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~ramon~ is generally taken to derive from Old French ~ram~ (“branch”), which comes from Latin ~rāmus~ (“branch”). A broom was thus named after the twigs it was made of. Latin ~rāmus~ also gave French ~rameau~, ~ramure~ and ~ramifier~, and it is the source of Italian and Spanish ~ramo~.

In Old French, ~ramoner~ meant simply “to sweep,” of any floor. Over time its sense narrowed, by specialization, to the one job of sweeping a chimney clean of soot, which is the only sense it keeps in modern French. The agent noun ~ramoneur~ (“chimney sweep”) and the act ~ramonage~ followed. The ordinary verb for sweeping, ~balayer~, took over the general meaning, so ~ramoner~ is a specialist word that has survived by sticking to one trade.
en.ramper:
~Ramper~ goes back to Old French ~ramper~ (“to crawl up, to climb”), which both Wiktionaries derive from a Frankish verb, *~hrampōn~ (also given as *~rampōn~). That verb was built on *~hrampa~ (“hook, claw, talon”). English Wiktionary connects the Frankish noun to Proto-Germanic *~hrimpaną~ (“to shrink up, to shrivel”). French Wiktionary adds relatives: French ~crampon~ (“clamp, hook”), Spanish ~rampa~ (“cramp”), Italian ~rampa~ (“claw”) and ~rampo~ (“hook”), and French ~ramponner~ (“to climb”).

The older meaning, “to climb,” deserves notice. It is tempting to link the claw to climbing, but the sources do not narrate the move from “climb” to “crawl along the ground,” the sense that survives in modern French. French ~rampe~ and ~rampant~ belong to the family, and English ~ramp~ and ~rampant~ were borrowed from French. In heraldry, a lion ~rampant~ rears up on its hind legs, which recalls the claw image.
en.rancarder: A spelling variant of ~rencarder~, a slang verb. The TLFi treats ~rencarder~ under the noun ~rencard~, meaning that the verb is derived from it. The main sense is to give someone secret information; the dictionary of the Académie adds a popular sense, to arrange a meeting with someone. The TLFi quotes Céline using ~rencarder~ in 1936 and records the meeting sense from Bruant in 1901. The sources consulted do not say where ~rencard~ itself comes from.
en.rancir: Derived from the adjective ~rance~ with the verb ending ~-ir~, it means to become rancid. The adjective ~rance~ was borrowed in the fourteenth century from Latin ~rancidus~, according to French Wiktionary by way of Old Occitan. The ending ~-ir~ is the second-conjugation ending, typically used to build verbs of the type “to become” plus an adjective, as in ~grandir~ from ~grand~.
en.randomiser: ~Randomiser~ is borrowed from English ~randomize~, itself built on the adjective ~random~ (“chance-based”) with the suffix ~-ize~. English ~random~ goes back to Old French ~randon~. French took the verb over by turning the English ending into its own verb-forming ~-iser~, which comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~ and ultimately from Greek verbs. The root of the word has thus made a round trip, from Old French into English and back into French.
en.randonner: Formed on the noun ~randon~ plus the suffix ~-er~; English Wiktionary describes it instead as coming from Middle French ~randonner~ and Old French ~randonner~ (“to run headlong”). The noun ~randon~ is a derivative of Old French ~randir~ (“to run”), from Old Frankish *~rand~ (“a course, running”), from Proto-Germanic *~randijō~. The headlong gallop gave English ~random~, which shares this ancestry, and French ~randonner~ eventually softened to a long, leisurely walk.
