French Wiktionary adds that modern ~randon~ may also be a re-Frenchifying of English ~random~, so the word crossed the Channel twice.
en.ranger:
~Ranger~ is derived from the noun ~rang~ (“rank, row”), from Old French ~renc~, from Old Frankish *~hring~ (“circle, ring”), a Germanic word cognate with English ~ring~ and German ~Ring~. To ~ranger~ is thus to put things into a ~rang~ — into their row or rank.

The Germanic origin hides a small surprise: the ancestor *~hring~ meant a circle, not a straight line. Warriors and assemblies once stood in a ring, and the sense of an ordered line of people — a ~rang~ — grew out of that circular formation before flattening into the modern row. From ~rang~ French built a whole household vocabulary of putting-in-order: ~ranger~ (“to tidy, arrange, put away”), ~rangée~ (“a row”), ~rangement~ (“storage, tidying”), ~rangé~ (said of a steady, orderly person), and the prefixed ~arranger~ and ~déranger~ — literally to bring into, or knock out of, the row. To ~déranger~ someone is, at root, to break the tidy ring of their arrangement. The English word ~range~ belongs to the very same family, borrowed back from this French stock.
en.ranimer: ~Ranimer~ is formed from ~animer~ with the prefix ~re-~, here in its old form ~ra-~ before a vowel, giving the sense of bringing back to life. The base ~animer~ comes from Latin ~animāre~ (“to give breath to”), from ~anima~ (“breath, soul”), which goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂enh₁-~ (“to breathe”). The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“again, back”). To ~ranimer~ is thus, etymologically, to breathe life into something once more.
en.rançonner: From Middle French ~rançonner~ and Old French ~raençonner~, formed from ~rançon~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~rançon~ comes from Latin ~redemptio~ (“buying back”), through Old French ~rençon~ and ~raençon~. It is a doublet of ~rédemption~, which French borrowed again from Latin; the religious sense was handed to ~rédemption~ from the thirteenth century on. To ~rançonner~ is to demand a ransom from someone, and by extension to extort money from them.
en.rapatrier:
French ~rapatrier~ is a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ~repatriāre~ (“to return to one's country”), built on ~re-~ (“back”) and Latin ~patria~ (“fatherland”), from ~pater~ (“father”). French replaced the Latin prefix ~re-~ with ~ra-~, giving ~rapatrier~ in place of a more regular ~repatrier~. It is a doublet of the Old French verb ~repairer~ (“to return home”), which descended from the same Latin verb by the normal sound changes, whereas ~rapatrier~ was taken in later by scholars. English ~repair~, as in “to repair to a place,” comes from that older French verb, and is thus an unexpected cousin.

The idea of returning to the ~patria~ gave the verb its modern meaning: to send prisoners, refugees or citizens back to their country of origin, and by extension to bring funds back home. The verb also carries a sense “to reconcile.” From the same family come ~patrie~, ~patriote~, ~expatrier~, ~compatriote~ and ~rapatriement~, and ~père~ is the inherited descendant of ~pater~.
en.rapatronner: Formed from the noun ~patron~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~patron~ came from Old French ~patron~ (“patron, protector”), from Latin ~patrōnus~, a derivative of ~pater~ (“father”). The verb's sense, “to join, to adjust,” is a specialized one that has no simple story from the noun.
en.raper: A recent borrowing from English ~rap~, the musical style in which words are spoken rhythmically over a beat. French has turned the English noun into a first-conjugation verb by adding its ordinary ending ~-er~, as it does with many English loans. Note that ~raper~ is a different word from ~râper~ (“to grate”), which has its own, unrelated history.
en.rapetasser:
Built on the Franco-Provençal verb ~petassar~, from ~petas~ (“patch for mending”), with the prefix ~ra-~, a form of ~re-~. The noun ~petas~ goes back to Latin ~pittacium~ (“label, small ticket”), which was borrowed in turn from Greek ~πιττάκιον~ (“writing tablet”). The word therefore passed through three languages: Greek, Latin and Franco-Provençal.

The chain shows how far a word can travel from its first meaning: a Greek writing tablet and a Latin label end up, through ~petas~, as a patch. In French, ~rapetasser~ means “to patch up.” It is a borrowing from the Franco-Provençal dialects spoken in the east of France and Switzerland, not an inherited verb.
en.rapetisser: From Old French ~rapetichier~ (“to make smaller again”), built with ~re-~ on ~apeticier~ (“to make smaller”), recorded in 1160 and derived from ~petit~. ~Apeticier~ was later spelled ~apetisser~. In 1459 ~rapetisser~ took over the sense of ~apetisser~, which became very rare and was even “eliminated” by ~rapetisser~, according to the Robert historique.
en.rapiner: A denominal verb formed from ~rapine~ (“plunder”) with the suffix ~-er~: to pilfer, to plunder, a dated word today. The noun ~rapine~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~rapīna~, from ~rapere~ (“to seize, to carry off”). French ~ravine~ is a doublet of it, and English ~rape~, in its older senses of abduction and pillage, is a cognate.
en.rapiécer: Formed from the verb ~apiécer~ with the prefix ~re-~, itself built on the noun ~pièce~ with the prefix ~a-~ and the verb ending ~-er~. English Wiktionary lays it out as ~re-~ + ~a-~ + ~pièce~ + ~-er~. The chain is thus ~pièce~ to ~piécer~ to ~apiécer~ to ~rapiécer~, each step adding one layer. The sense is to mend with a patch, a piece sewn on to make good a hole or a worn place. Here ~re-~ conveys repair, bringing something back to a sound state, rather than a simple repetition.
en.raplatir: Formed from the adjective ~plat~ (“flat”) with the prefix ~ra-~, an older form of ~re-~, and the verb ending ~-ir~, which makes verbs meaning “to make or become A.” The adjective ~plat~ comes from Old and Middle French, from Vulgar Latin *~plattus~, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~platús~ (“broad, flat”). ~Raplatir~ thus means to make something flat again or to level it.
en.rapointir: A parasynthetic formation: the old prefix ~ra-~ (“again”) and the verb ending ~-ir~ were attached together to the noun ~pointe~, giving a verb meaning “to sharpen again.” The base ~pointe~ comes from Late Latin ~puncta~, the feminine of ~punctus~, the participle of Latin ~pungō~ (“to prick”). So a point is, etymologically, what pricks, and ~rapointir~ means to give a tool its point back.
en.rappareiller: Formed from ~appareiller~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”). The TLFi treats two distinct verbs ~appareiller~, and ~rappareiller~ was built on both. The older sense, recorded around 1155 in Wace, is “to repair, to put back in order”; in 1690 it also appears as a nautical term for making the rigging ready to sail again. The sense that survives, “to rejoin something to its match,” is attested from the 12th century as “to make a number even” and, in 1690, as putting something back with its pair, as with a missing glove or chair. The Académie notes that ~rapparier~ is the more usual word.
en.rapparier: Formed from ~apparier~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”), so ~rapparier~ means “to pair up again.” The base ~apparier~ comes from Old French ~aparier~, built on ~pair~ with ~ad-~ and the verb ending ~-er~. Behind it stands Latin ~pār~ (“equal, matching”), the source of ~paire~, ~pair~, ~pareil~ and ~impair~. The doubled ~p~ of ~apparier~ echoes the Latin ~ad-~.
en.rappeler:
Built in French from the prefix ~re-~ (“again, back”) and the verb ~appeler~ (“to call”). ~Appeler~ descends from Latin ~appellāre~ (“to address, to call by name”), a frequentative-style derivative of ~appellere~, ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) + ~pellere~ (“to push, to drive”), from PIE *~pelh₂-~ (“to approach, to drive”). To call someone was, in the root image, to “drive” your voice toward them. Through Old French ~apeler~, the same Latin verb gave English ~appeal~ and ~appellation~; Romance cousins include Italian ~appellare~ and Spanish ~apelar~.

The literal sense of ~rappeler~ is “to call back”: a general ~rappelle~ his troops, a country ~rappelle~ its ambassador, and one ~rappelle~ a phone caller. From summoning a person back came summoning a thought back — ~rappeler~ now most commonly means “to remind” or, reflexively in ~se rappeler~, “to remember,” literally to call something back into one's own mind. The noun ~rappel~ covers a striking spread of these: a reminder, an encore at a concert, a booster vaccine, a back-payment of wages, and the mountaineer's ~rappel~ (abseiling, “calling oneself back down” the rope). The shared root surfaces across French ~appeler~, ~appel~, ~rappel~, ~interpeller~ (“to call out to, to question”), and the borrowed ~appellation~.
en.rapper: ~Rapper~ is a recent borrowing from English ~rap~, the musical style, with the French verb ending ~-er~ added. French thus took the English noun and gave it a first-conjugation verb, so that it conjugates like any regular verb in ~-er~: ~je rappe~, ~nous rappons~. Its meaning is simply to perform rap, that is, to deliver rhymed lyrics over a beat. Its story belongs to the English word.
en.rappliquer: Formed from ~appliquer~ with the prefix ~re-~. The base comes from Latin ~applicāre~ (“to attach to, bring into contact”), a compound of ~ad-~ and ~plicāre~ (“to fold”), and its relatives include ~plier~ and ~compliquer~. The prefix ~re-~ here carries the sense of return, which fits the modern meanings “to come back” and “to turn up.”
en.rappointir: Formed from the verb ~appointir~ with the prefix ~r-~, the form of ~re-~ (“again”) used before a vowel, so ~rappointir~ means “to sharpen again.” It is a variant of ~rapointir~, built on the same idea of the point (~pointe~) and the same sense of giving an edge back.
en.rapporter:
Attested from the twelfth century, ~rapporter~ is formed from ~apporter~ (“to bring”) with the prefix ~re-~, marking a bringing back. ~Apporter~ comes from Latin ~apportāre~ (~ad-~ “to” + ~portāre~ “to carry”), and ~portāre~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“to lead, to pass over, to carry across”). Cognate with Italian ~portare~ and Spanish ~portar~, and — through the same root — with English ~port~, ~portable~, and ~transport~.

The literal core is to carry a thing back to its place, which gives the everyday sense of retrieving or returning. From there the word branched widely: a hunting dog ~rapporte~ the game; a witness ~rapporte~ what was said, hence “to report”; a child who ~rapporte~ on a classmate is a tattletale; and money or land that ~rapporte~ “brings in” a yield — the source of ~rapport~ as “revenue” and, more abstractly, as “relation, connection.” That same carrying root *~per-~ runs through ~porter~, ~apporter~, ~emporter~, ~importer~, ~exporter~, ~port~, and ~portique~ — a whole family built on the simple act of bearing something from one place to another.
en.rapprendre: Formed within French from ~apprendre~ (“to learn”) and the prefix ~re-~ (“again”), so “to learn again” or “to learn anew.” The base ~apprendre~ goes back to Latin ~apprehendere~ (“to seize, to grasp”), made of ~ad-~ (“to”) + ~prehendere~ (“to grasp”), so learning is pictured as a mental grasping. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and is fully productive in French, which is why this verb is a transparent formation rather than an inherited one.
en.rapprocher:
A transparent compound of the prefix ~re-~ (here marking repetition and intensification, “again, anew”) and the verb ~approcher~ (“to approach, to bring near”). ~approcher~ itself descends from Late Latin ~appropiāre~ (“to draw near to”), formed from ~ad-~ (“to”) and the adverb ~prope~ (“near”), the same ~prope~ that yields French ~proche~ (“near, close”). The Old French form was ~aprochier~, attested from the twelfth century; English ~approach~ is borrowed from this same Old French verb, so the two languages share the ancestor.

Where ~approcher~ simply brings something near, ~rapprocher~ adds the idea of bringing things near once more or closer together — two people reconciled, two ideas compared, two dates moved nearer. From this comes the rich figurative life of the word: a ~rapprochement~ between former enemies, a diplomatic thaw, is one of the best-known French exports to other languages, English among them. Modern derivatives include the noun ~rapprochement~, the adjective ~rapprochable~, and the military expression ~garde rapprochée~ (“close protection”). At bottom, every use of ~rapprocher~ replays the humble Latin ~prope~: the act of making two things ~proche~ that were not so near before.
en.rapproprier: Formed from ~approprier~ and the prefix ~r-~, the form of ~re-~ that appears before a vowel: to clean, to make clean again. The base ~approprier~ comes from Latin ~appropriāre~ (“to make one's own”), built from ~ad-~ (“to”) and ~proprius~ (“one's own”). The same Latin root gave French ~propre~, which means both “own” and “clean,” and that double sense explains the verb: to make something ~propre~ once more.
en.raquer: A familiar verb meaning to pay up. French Wiktionary derives it from Old French ~rachier~ (“to spit”), noting that regional variants often replaced the ~-ch-~ sound with ~-k-~. In the south of France, the same source says the word comes instead from Occitan ~racar~ (“to vomit”). The origin is therefore stated in two versions, a northern one and a southern one, both pointing to a verb of spitting or throwing up. English Wiktionary gives a different route, through Old French ~ragier~, which does not match the French account.
en.raréfier: The two Wiktionaries frame this verb differently. French Wiktionary derives it from ~rare~ with the suffix ~-fier~, a form of the “make” suffix that goes back to Latin ~facere~. English Wiktionary treats it as borrowed from Latin ~rarefacere~, with ~rare~ + ~-fier~ only as a surface analysis. Latin ~rarefacere~ is ~rārus~ (“thin, rare”) + ~facere~ (“to make”), so the verb means “to make rare.” The adjective ~rare~ was borrowed in this form from Latin ~rārus~, while Old French had inherited ~rer~ and ~rere~.
en.raser:
French ~raser~ is inherited from Old French ~raser~, which comes from Vulgar Latin *~rāsāre~, a frequentative verb formed on ~rāsus~, the past participle of Latin ~rādō~ (“to shave, to scratch”). A frequentative verb expresses repeated or intensive action. Italian ~rasare~ is a comparable form from the same Latin source. French Wiktionary writes the Latin infinitive as ~rādere~, with the further glosses “to polish” and “to rake.” The chain is short: Latin ~rādō~, its participle ~rāsus~, a Vulgar Latin verb built on that participle, then Old French and modern French. The sources name no other language in this chain, so the word is a plain inheritance from Latin.

In modern French ~raser~ covers three senses glossed for this verb: “to shave,” “to raze,” and “to bore.” The evidence does not say how those senses developed from the Latin sense, so no order of development is claimed here. What the sources do show is the shape of the verb. The stem ~rās-~ of the Latin participle survives in ~raser~, and the ending ~-er~ is the regular French outcome of Latin ~-āre~, as in ~chanter~ from ~cantare~. Because the verb is inherited whole, it has no French base word: ~raser~ was not made by adding ~-er~ to a French noun or adjective.
en.rassasier:
French ~rassasier~ is built from the prefix ~re-~ and Old French ~assasier~ (“to satisfy, to sate”). English Wiktionary adds that ~assasier~ itself comes from ~sacier~ (compare ~saisier~), a French reshaping of Latin ~satiāre~ (“to satisfy, to fill”). That Latin verb belongs to ~satis~ (“enough”). English borrowed the same Latin verb as ~satiate~, which keeps its learned shape, while French turned it into something much further from the original.

The prefix ~re-~ does not seem to mean “again” here. The Old French base ~assasier~ already meant “to satisfy,” so ~re-~ appears only to reinforce it. The root ~satis~ lies behind several other French words, among them ~assez~, which comes from Latin ~ad satis~ (“to enough”), and ~satiété~, ~insatiable~ and ~satisfaire~. Modern French uses ~rassasier~ above all for appetite, and the adjective ~rassasié~ describes someone who has had enough.
en.rassembler:
Formed from the verb ~assembler~ (“to assemble, gather”) with the prefix ~re-~, expressing repetition or intensification. ~Assembler~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~assimulāre~ (“to bring together, make alike”), built on ~ad-~ (“to, toward”) and a stem related to ~simul~ (“together”) and ~similis~ (“like, similar”). These trace to the PIE root *~sem-~ (“one, together”). Through that root ~rassembler~ is cognate with English ~same~, ~similar~, and ~assemble~ itself, and with Greek ~homós~ (“same”); Italian keeps ~assembrare~. The buried idea is gathering many into a likeness, a oneness.

Where ~assembler~ joins parts together, the ~re-~ of ~rassembler~ adds a sense of pulling scattered things back into one — regathering a dispersed crowd, mustering troops, collecting one's thoughts. Hence its slightly more emphatic, more deliberate ring: ~rassembler ses idées~ (“to collect one's thoughts”), ~rassembler une foule~ (“to gather a crowd”). The political noun ~rassemblement~ (“rally, gathering”) grew from it. The unifying root *~sem-~ runs through a remarkable spread of French: ~sembler~, ~ensemble~, ~assemblée~, ~simple~ (“one-fold”), ~singulier~, and ~simultané~ all descend from the ancient sense of oneness and togetherness that *~sem-~ names.
en.rasseoir: ~Rasseoir~ is formed from ~asseoir~ with the prefix ~re-~, here in its older variant ~ra-~, which carries the sense of doing again: to sit back down, or to seat someone again. The base ~asseoir~ comes from Latin ~assidēre~, a compound of ~ad-~ (“toward”) and ~sedēre~ (“to sit”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~sed-~, which also gave English ~sit~. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”).
en.rassir: Formed from ~rassis~ with the verbal ending ~-ir~: to become ~rassis~, to go stale. The base is itself the old past participle of ~rasseoir~ in its earlier sense of “to harden, to set,” and the participle of ~rassir~, ~rassi~, carries the same meaning without serving as an adjective. French Wiktionary therefore treats the verb as a back-formation from an adjectival participle rather than a verb built the usual way. The ending ~-ir~ comes from the Latin infinitive ending ~-ire~ and here has the sense “become.”
en.rassurer:
Derived from ~assurer~ with the prefix ~re-~; the verb ~rasseürer~ is attested as early as 1155. The base ~assurer~ descends from Vulgar Latin *~assēcūrāre~, from ~sēcūrus~ (“safe, free from care”), which itself parses as ~sē-~ (“without”) plus ~cūra~ (“care”), the latter from Proto-Indo-European *~kʷeys-~ (“to heed, observe”). To reassure is thus, at the bottom, to set someone back into a state without care. English ~secure~ and ~sure~, and Spanish ~seguro~, are cognates from the very same Latin source.

The ~re-~ marks restoration: ~assurer~ makes someone confident, ~rassurer~ makes them confident again, calming a fear that had risen. French keeps the “care” at the heart of the family visible in ~sûr~ (sure, safe), ~assurance~ (confidence, and also insurance), ~sécurité~, and ~sécuriser~. There is a quiet etymological irony in the modern insurance industry: ~assurance~ promises freedom from care, yet rests on the careful reckoning of exactly the risks one is paying not to worry about.
en.rasséréner:
A compound formed in French from ~re-~ (here reduced to ~r-~), ~a-~, ~serein~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so that it means roughly “to make calm again.” The adjective ~serein~ comes from Latin ~serēnus~ (“clear, calm”), a word used of sky and weather. Latin ~serēnus~ also gave Italian and Spanish ~sereno~, and English ~serene~ was borrowed from the same Latin source.

The verb stacks three small pieces on one old adjective. The prefix ~re-~ adds the idea of “again,” the prefix ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad-~) points toward a state, and ~-er~ turns the whole into a first-conjugation verb. Its modern sense is figurative: to restore someone's calm or confidence, hence “to reassure.” Learned relatives of ~serein~ include ~sérénité~, from Latin ~serēnitās~, which kept the Latin vowel pattern that ~serein~ itself lost.
en.ratatiner:
The origin of ~ratatiner~ is uncertain, and the two main sources disagree. French Wiktionary analyzes it as the prefix ~ra-~ plus ~tatin~ (“small quantity”), itself probably ~tant~ plus the diminutive suffix ~-in~, and compares the formation of ~rapetisser~. English Wiktionary instead calls it onomatopoeic. The word ~tant~ is inherited from Latin ~tantum~ (“so much”).

In the first account the idea is to reduce something to a tiny amount, which fits the main senses of the verb: to shrivel, to shrink, to wrinkle up, as an apple or an old face does. In informal French the verb also means to kill or to wreck someone. Under the second account the word would be a sound-imitating coinage, and the shrinking sense would owe nothing to ~tant~. Neither theory is settled.
en.rater:
Modern French ~rater~ is a denominal verb, coined around 1715 from the noun ~rat~ (“rat”) plus the infinitive ending ~-er~. It grew not directly from the rodent but from the firearm expression ~prendre un rat~, said of a gun that failed to go off: the powder caught but no shot followed. From that misfire, ~rater~ came to mean “to fail to fire,” then simply “to fail” or “to miss.” The noun ~rat~ itself is of obscure, probably imitative Germanic origin, shared with English ~rat~, German ~Ratte~, and Italian ~ratto~.

Why a gun's misfire should be a ~rat~ is itself uncertain, and the sources do not settle it; what is documented is the path from the phrase to the verb. The sense then spread widely: one can ~rater~ a train, an exam, a photograph, or a chance, and a botched thing is ~raté~. From the same noun French also formed mulot-free coinages like ~dératiser~ (“to exterminate rats”) and the noun ~raté~ for an engine's splutter or, of a person, a failure. Few French verbs of such everyday usefulness rest on so homely and so puzzling an image.
en.ratiboiser: The origin of this slang verb is only proposed. French Wiktionary derives it from ~ratisser~ (“to rake”) combined with a dialectal Old French ~emboiser~ (“to deceive”), that is, a blend. The raking image fits the colloquial senses of the verb: to sweep someone clean of their money, to swindle them, or to crop their hair close. The sources give no date and no further detail on the blend.
en.ratifier:
From Medieval Latin ~ratificāre~, a compound of Latin ~ratus~ (“fixed, established, valid”) and the verb ~facere~ (“to make”), so literally “to make valid”. In compounds ~facere~ took the shape ~-ficāre~, which became French ~-fier~, as in ~vérifier~ and ~modifier~. The adjective ~ratus~ is the past participle of Latin ~rērī~ (“to reckon, to think”): what is ~ratus~ has been reckoned and settled. Italian ~ratificare~ and Spanish ~ratificar~ are parallel forms, and English ~ratify~ is borrowed from the same source.

The verb belongs to the language of law and diplomacy: to ~ratifier~ is to give a finished act its binding force, as when a parliament or a head of state confirms a treaty that envoys have already signed. By extension it came to mean to approve or confirm in general. The root ~rērī~ is fertile. It gave Latin ~ratiō~ (“reckoning, reason”), whence French ~raison~ and ~rationnel~, and English ~rate~, in the sense of a fixed proportion, comes from the same ~ratus~ family. A treaty is thus ratified when it has been, in the Roman sense, reckoned and fixed.
en.ratiner: Formed from the noun ~ratine~, a type of woolen cloth, with the ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~. The verb names a finishing operation on cloth, in which a nap is raised or curled on its surface. French Wiktionary gives only this derivation and does not trace ~ratine~ itself any further.
en.ratiociner: A learned borrowing from Latin ~ratiōcinārī~ (“to reckon, to calculate, to reason”). The Latin deponent verb is built on ~ratiō~ (“reckoning, reason”), itself from the verb ~rērī~ (“to reckon, to think”). The same learned loan gave English ~ratiocinate~. In modern French, ~ratiociner~ means to reason at tedious length, with overly fine distinctions, in a pedantic way. Through ~ratiō~ it belongs to a large family. The inherited branch gave ~raison~ and ~raisonner~, while the learned branch gave ~ration~, ~rationnel~, ~rationaliser~ and ~ratio~ itself, borrowed straight from Latin. ~Ratiociner~ is the rare, bookish member of that family.
en.rationaliser: Formed from ~rationnel~ and the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make”), with the ending of the base reshaped to ~rational-~. The adjective is a learned borrowing from Latin ~rationalis~ (“endowed with reason”), recorded in French from about 1120 as ~rationel~ and as ~rational~ in 1483. To ~rationaliser~ is to make something rational, whether by explaining it by reason or, in business and administration, by organizing it for efficiency.
en.rationner: Formed from ~ration~ with the verb-forming ending ~-er~. The noun ~ration~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~ratiō~ in its sense of “count, reckoning,” and it is a doublet of ~raison~, the same Latin word reaching French by the inherited route. The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, here means “to provide or deal with N,” so ~rationner~ is to measure out supplies in fixed shares. English Wiktionary compares ~raisonner~, which was coined the same way from ~raison~.
en.ratisser: ~Ratisser~ (“to rake”) is derived, according to French Wiktionary, from Old French ~raster~ or ~rater~ (“to scrape, to erase”), with the influence of ~râteau~ (“rake”). The formation is therefore a blend of a verb of scraping and the name of the garden tool, the second shaping the final form of the first. Only French Wiktionary gives an account, so details such as dates and the further ancestry of ~raster~ are left out here.
en.ratonner: Formed from ~raton~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. The base ~raton~ is built on ~rat~ with the suffix ~-on~. It names a mammal from 1753, perhaps under the influence of English raccoon, and it also served as a racist slur, a sense attested since 1937. The verb belongs to that second use and, as the gloss says, is a historical term for taking part in racist attacks. It is now dated and offensive, and it survives mainly in discussions of past violence.
en.rattacher:
Derived from ~attacher~ with the iterative prefix ~re-~. The base ~attacher~ comes from Old French ~atachier~, a variant of ~estachier~ (“to fasten, bind”), from ~estache~ (“stake, post”), from Frankish/Gothic *~stakka~ (“stake”). It is therefore a doublet of ~attaquer~ (“to attack”), the two having split from the same Germanic root, and a cognate of English ~attach~ and ~stake~. The literal image is binding something to a post.

The ~re-~ adds the sense of joining back, or joining anew: where ~attacher~ ties a thing on, ~rattacher~ re-ties it or links it to something larger. Modern French stretches this across registers — one can ~rattacher~ a loose page to a binder, a province to a state, a remark to an earlier argument, or, reflexively, a person who feels they belong (se rattacher à une tradition). The Germanic ancestor of the post left a wide family: ~tache~ in some senses, ~attache~ (a fastening, a tie of affection), ~détacher~ (to untie), and the doublet ~attaquer~, which began as a Romance variant of the same fastening verb before veering off into the language of assault.
en.rattraper:
~rattraper~ is a home-grown French formation: ~re-~ (“back, again”) plus ~attraper~ (“to catch”), itself built in the twelfth century from ~a-~ (from Latin ~ad~, “toward”) and ~trappe~ (“trap, snare”). The form ~ratraper~, “to catch again,” already appears around 1280 in Adenet le Roi. ~trappe~ came into Gallo-Romance from Old Low Frankish *~trappa~ (“snare; step”), a Germanic word recorded in medieval Latin as ~trappa~; its cousins are English ~trap~, Dutch ~trap~ (“kick; staircase”) and German ~Treppe~ (“stairs”) — the family seems to join treading and trapping, the snare being something one steps into. So to catch, in French, is etymologically to ensnare: ~rattraper~ is literally “to trap again.”

The meanings unfolded step by step: “catch again” in the Middle Ages, “catch up with” by 1636, “recover, make good” by 1690, and the reflexive ~se rattraper~ — to grab hold, or to make up for a slip — by the nineteenth century. Modern French leans on the verb for every kind of remedial catching-up: a ~rattrapage~ is a make-up exam, a salary adjustment, a recall of defective cars. The trap behind it all had its own adventures: the Germanic word that gave French ~trappe~ also gave English ~trap~, from which North America coined ~trapper~ for the fur hunters of the woods — and in 1827 French borrowed that word back as ~trappeur~. A fitting destiny for a verb of second chances: after centuries away, the language caught its own word again.
en.raturer: ~Raturer~ is formed from ~rature~ with the verb ending ~-er~, and means to cross out or correct a text. ~Rature~ appears first as ~rasture~, and two accounts of it exist. One builds it from Old French ~rater~ or ~raster~ (“to cross out, to scrape”) plus the suffix ~-ure~. The other derives it from Vulgar Latin *~rasitōria~, from ~rāsitō~, a frequentative of Latin ~rādō~ (“I scrape”). Both link it to scraping.
en.rauquer: Formed from the adjective ~rauque~ (“hoarse, harsh-voiced”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to make a hoarse sound.” In French it is the verb used of the tiger's roar. The adjective comes from Latin ~raucus~ (“hoarse”); English Wiktionary adds that it reached French through Old French ~raucus~, itself taken from Latin. The same adjective also stands behind ~enrouer~ (“to make hoarse”), which English Wiktionary suggests comparing.
en.ravager: From ~ravage~ + ~-er~, “to lay waste.” French Wiktionary treats the verb as formed on the noun ~ravage~ and points to Old French ~revagier~ (“to tear up vine plants”), but it calls that form obscure and suggests it may owe its shape to a change of prefix. The link is therefore only a possibility, and the sources trace the noun no further. What is certain is the modern pattern: a noun of devastation turned into a first-conjugation verb by the ending ~-er~.
en.ravaler: The verb is formed from ~avaler~ with the prefix ~re-~. The base is built on the adverb ~aval~ (“downward”), explained as ~à val~, from Latin ~ad~ (“to”) + ~vallis~ (“valley”). It first meant to send or go down, and later “to swallow.” The prefix ~re-~ here marks repetition, as in “to swallow again,” a sense also used figuratively. The verb's other senses, to restore a surface and to debase, are listed in the dictionary gloss without a sourced account of how they arose.
en.ravauder: From Middle French ~ravaut~ (“foolishness, nonsense”), itself said to come from ~ravaler~ (“to lower, to belittle”). The verb ~ravauder~ thus began as a word for acting or speaking foolishly, a long way from its modern sense of mending, as in mending old clothes. The sources consulted do not explain how that shift happened, so the link between the two senses is best left open. The base ~ravaler~ is itself built on ~avaler~ with the prefix ~re-~.
en.ravigoter: The origin is debated. According to the TLFi, ~ravigoter~ is an alteration of the older verb ~ravigorer~ (“to regain vigor”), which ties it to ~revigorer~ and to the word ~vigueur~. Henri Moisy proposes a different route: he holds that the prefix ~ra-~ is a frequent French and Norman alteration of older forms in ~re-~, so that ~ravigoter~ would come from a form ~revigoter~. That would not rule out a link between ~revigoter~ and ~revigorer~. Either way, the verb names the act of restoring strength, as in a drink that perks someone up.
en.raviner: Formed from the noun ~ravine~ with the verbal ending ~-er~: to furrow the ground with gullies, as running water does. The noun ~ravine~ comes from Latin ~rapīna~ (“plunder”), making it a doublet of ~rapine~. In Old French it meant impetuosity and a violent rush, then a torrent of water, and finally the hollow that a torrent cuts. English Wiktionary adds that the noun may instead come from an Old French verb ~raviner~ (“to flow with force”).
en.ravir:
From Popular Latin *~rapīre~, an alteration of Classical Latin ~rapere~ (“to seize, carry off by force”). The Latin verb descends from a PIE root usually reconstructed as *~h₁rep-~ (“to snatch, seize”). The same ~rapere~ gave the learned French doublets ~rapt~ and ~rapide~, while the popular line produced ~ravir~; English borrowed from both branches, taking ~rapid~ and ~rape~ from the Latin and ~ravish~ straight from Old French ~ravir~.

The original violence is plain: to ~ravir~ was to abduct, to plunder, to tear away by force. But French let the sense rise from the body to the soul — to be carried off in rapture, transported by delight — so that the very same verb now means both to kidnap and to enchant. The expression ~à ravir~ (“ravishingly, to perfection”) keeps only the sweetness; ~ravisseur~ (“abductor”) keeps only the menace. From the family come ~ravissement~ (“rapture”), ~ravissant~ (“delightful”), and, through ~rapere~, ~ravage~ and ~rapace~.
en.raviser: ~Raviser~ is ~aviser~ with the prefix ~re-~, here in its old spelling ~ra-~, with the sense of going back over something, which gives “to change one's mind, to reconsider.” The base ~aviser~ is explained in two ways: either from the noun ~avis~ (“opinion, advice”), or as ~a-~ + ~viser~. The second account leads to Latin ~vīsāre~ (“to look at attentively”), so the verb has to do with looking again at a decision.
en.ravitailler: Formed from the prefix ~r-~ (a form of ~re-~) and ~avitailler~, built from ~a-~, the Old French noun ~vitaille~ (“provisions”) and ~-er~, “to supply with food.” French Wiktionary traces ~vitaille~ to Late Latin ~victualia~, whose root is ~victus~ (“food”), from ~vīvere~ (“to live”). English ~victuals~, pronounced “vittles,” comes from the same source through French. ~Ravitailler~ means to resupply with food, and by extension fuel or stock, for an army, a ship or a car.
en.raviver: Formed from the prefix ~r-~ (a form of ~re-~, “again”) and ~aviver~, which is built from ~a-~, the adjective ~vif~ and the verb ending ~-er~, “to make more lively.” The adjective ~vif~ comes from Latin ~vīvus~ (“alive”), from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷih₃wós~. So ~raviver~ is “to give life again,” whether to a fire, a color or a memory: to rekindle or revive. The same Latin root underlies ~vivre~ and ~vivant~.
en.ravoir: Formed from ~avoir~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again, back”): to have again, to get back. English Wiktionary traces the verb to Middle French ~ravoir~. The base ~avoir~ comes from Latin ~habēre~ (“to have, to hold”), whose Romance siblings include Italian ~avere~ and Spanish ~haber~. In modern French ~ravoir~ is used chiefly in the infinitive, for recovering something or getting a stained item clean again.
en.rayer: Formed from the noun ~raie~ (“line, stripe”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to mark with lines,” hence “to scratch” and “to cross out.” The verb is found in Old French as ~roier~, and ~raie~ comes from Old French ~reye~, a word compared to Welsh ~rica~ and to Late Latin ~riga~. English Wiktionary adds a second possibility, that some forms such as Old French ~raier~ may instead come from Latin ~radiāre~, so the origin is not entirely settled. The most common modern sense is to cancel a word with a stroke, as in ~rayer une mention inutile~.
en.rayonner: Formed from the noun ~rayon~ (“ray”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, in allusion to rays of light or of other kinds. ~Rayon~ itself is built from Old French ~rai~ (“ray”) with the suffix ~-on~. It is a different word from the ~rayon~ meaning “honeycomb” or “shelf”, which comes from a Frankish word through Old French ~ree~, and a third ~rayon~, “furrow”, comes from ~raie~. The verb first meant to shine in rays, and it spread to cheerful faces that radiate joy, to influence that radiates from a centre, and to travelling around a place from a base.
en.razzier: ~Razzier~ is built on the noun ~razzia~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, so it means to carry out a ~razzia~, a raid. The noun comes from the Arabic ~ghazwa~ (“raid, invasion, conquest”), reaching French through North African Arabic ~ghaziya~ and Italian ~razzia~. English Wiktionary notes earlier spellings in French, ~gazia~ (1808) and ~razia~ (1830), which show the word entering French in the early nineteenth century.
en.rebaisser: ~Rebaisser~ is formed from ~baisser~ (“to lower”) with the prefix ~re-~, here simply meaning “again”: to lower something once more, or to fall back down after a rise. ~Baisser~ comes from Old French ~baissier~, from Vulgar Latin *~bassiāre~, “to make low,” a verb built on Late Latin ~bassus~ (“low, short”), the same root that gave French ~bas~.
en.rebaptiser: Formed in French from ~re-~ (“again”) and ~baptiser~, so it means “to baptize again.” The base ~baptiser~ goes back to Latin ~baptizāre~, itself from Ancient Greek ~baptízō~ (“to dip, to immerse”), related to ~báptō~ (“to dip”). The verb also took on a lighter sense: to ~rebaptiser~ a street or a company is to give it a new name, as at a christening. The Greek-built ~anabaptiste~ (“one who baptizes again”) names the sixteenth-century movement that rejected infant baptism and rebaptized adults.
en.rebattre: ~Rebattre~ is formed from the prefix ~re-~ and ~battre~ (“to beat”), and means to beat, defeat or fight again. ~Battre~ comes from Latin ~battuere~ (“to strike”), a verb generally thought to be of Gaulish origin, and it also gave Italian ~battere~ and Spanish ~batir~. The prefix ~re-~ goes back to Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and here marks repetition. The verb survives in the idiom ~rebattre les oreilles~ (“to harp on something to someone”), a repeated beating of the ears.
en.rebeller: French ~rebeller~ comes straight from Latin ~rebellāre~ (“to take up arms again, to rebel”). The Latin verb is generally analyzed as ~re-~ (“again”) + ~bellāre~ (“to wage war”), from ~bellum~ (“war”), so the idea is a fight that starts afresh. The same Latin verb gave Spanish ~rebelar~ and Italian ~ribellare~, while the related adjective and noun ~rebellis~ gave French ~rebelle~ and English ~rebel~. In modern French the verb is nearly always reflexive, ~se rebeller~, and covers any refusal to obey an authority, not only armed revolt. The root ~bellum~ is found in many French words, among them ~belliqueux~, ~belligérant~, ~rébellion~ and ~rebelle~.
en.rebiffer: ~Rebiffer~ comes from Middle French ~rebiffer~, which English Wiktionary traces to Old French ~rebiffer~ (“to rise up, to raise”), of uncertain origin. French Wiktionary presents it as a variant of ~rebuffer~ and of Old French ~rebifer~. Because the ultimate source is unknown, nothing earlier than Old French can be claimed. The older sense of rising up fits the modern one, “to rebel, to revolt,” especially in the reflexive ~se rebiffer~.
en.rebiquer: ~Rebiquer~ is derived from the noun ~bique~, here in the sense “horn,” with the verbal ending ~-er~. It began as a regional word of Franche-Comté and became ordinary French in the twentieth century. The noun ~bique~ itself has an obscure origin: it is dialectal in northern France, and a Germanic source has been suggested without being settled.
en.reboiser: Formed from ~boiser~ with the prefix ~re-~, which here means “again”: to plant trees once more on land that has lost its forest. The base ~boiser~ comes from ~bois~ (“wood”) plus the ending ~-er~, in the sense “to provide with wood.” The noun ~bois~ descends through Middle and Old French from Early Medieval Latin ~boscus~ (“grove”), borrowed from Frankish *~busk~. Its cognates include Italian ~bosco~, Spanish ~bosque~, German ~Busch~ and English ~bush~.
en.rebondir: From ~bondir~ with the prefix ~re-~. The base comes from Old French ~bundir~ (“to resound”), from Vulgar Latin *~bombitīre~, ultimately from the sound-imitating Latin ~bombus~ (“a buzz, a boom”). Like ~bondir~, ~rebondir~ first meant “to resound again,” around 1150. By the same shift from sound to sight, it later meant “to make spring back” (1393) and, intransitively, “to jut out” (1480). The sense “to bounce again” is recorded from 1530. The prefix ~re-~ carries the idea of reaction here: a bounce is a rebound.
en.reborder: Formed from ~border~ with the prefix ~re-~ in its sense of “again”: to trim an edge anew, or to tuck in a bed again. The base ~border~ is a verb made from the noun ~bord~ (“edge, side of a ship”), attested by 1170. That noun was borrowed from Frankish *~bord~ (“plank, side of a ship”), from Proto-Germanic *~burdą~, and is cognate with English ~board~ and German ~Bord~. French keeps the same maritime family in ~aborder~, ~déborder~ and ~bordure~.
en.reboucher: Formed from ~boucher~ with the prefix ~re-~ in its sense of doing again: to plug something once more, to put the stopper back. ~Boucher~ comes from Old French ~bousche~ (“bundle of straw, faggot”), from Vulgar Latin *~bosca~ (“brushwood”), so it has nothing to do with ~bouche~ (“mouth”). The same Vulgar Latin word underlies French ~bois~.
en.rebouter: French Wiktionary gives three accounts of this verb, so its history is not settled. The first reads it as ~re-~ + ~bouter~, “to push again.” The second derives it from ~rebouteux~ (“bonesetter”) with the verb ending ~-er~, which fits the sense “to set bones.” The third calls it a Frenchification of ~rebooter~. The base ~bouter~ is Old French for “to strike, to push,” from Frankish *~bautan~ or *~bōtan~. English ~beat~ is a cousin from the same Germanic family.
en.reboutonner: Formed from ~boutonner~ with the prefix ~re-~, “to do again”: to fasten buttons once more. The base is built on the noun ~bouton~, which first meant a “bud” and rests on ~bouter~ (“to push”) with the suffix ~-on~. It goes back through Vulgar Latin to Frankish *~bautō~ (“that which pushes up, a bump or knob”). A bud and a button are both small knobs, which is how one word covers both.
en.rebraguetter: Formed from ~braguette~ with the prefix ~re-~ and a verbal ending, hence “to do up one's fly again.” ~Braguette~, earlier ~brayette~, derives from ~braie~ (“breeches”) with the diminutive ~-ette~; ~braie~ comes from Gaulish ~braca~ or ~bracca~ by way of Latin ~braca~. Before it named the opening of the trousers, the ~braguette~ was a small pocket attached by the belt to the ~braies~.
en.rebroder: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ and ~broder~ (“to embroider”). The prefix ~re-~ goes back to Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and usually marks repetition, but it can also be merely intensive. The base ~broder~ is a Germanic loan hiding behind a French shape, from Old French ~brosder~, with no Latin ancestor. The verb ~rebroder~ means to embroider again, or to add fresh embellishment to something already embroidered. By extension it applies to a story or a text, since ~broder~ itself also means to elaborate a tale with invented detail.
en.rebrousser: Reached its modern shape by metathesis, a swapping of sounds, from Middle French ~rebourser~, which is a verb on the noun ~rebours~. The base ~rebours~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~rebursus~, an alteration of Late Latin ~reburrus~ (“with hair swept back, bristling”) under the influence of Latin ~reversus~ (“turned back”). The verb means “to brush against the grain,” and also “to turn back,” as in the fixed phrase ~rebrousser chemin~ (“to retrace one's steps”).
en.rebuter: ~Rebuter~ comes from Old French ~reboter~, which English Wiktionary analyses as the prefix ~re-~ plus the verb ~buter~. The sources give no further history for ~buter~, so the chain stops there. The modern senses, to reject or turn away and to disgust, are the ones the verb carries today.
en.rebâtir: Formed from ~bâtir~ (“to build”) and the prefix ~re-~ (“again”): to ~rebâtir~ is to build anew. The base comes from Old French ~bastir~, from Old Low Frankish *~bastjan~, from a Germanic word for bast, the fibrous inner bark used for binding. It is cognate with German ~Bast~, and the circumflex of ~bâtir~ marks the lost ~s~ of the older spelling. The prefix comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”).
en.recacheter: Formed from ~cacheter~ with the prefix ~re-~, meaning “again”: to seal something anew. The base ~cacheter~ is built on the noun ~cachet~ (“seal”) and the verb ending ~-er~. ~Cachet~ itself comes from ~cacher~ in the sense “to press”, a verb distinct from ~cacher~ (“to hide”), so a seal is, etymologically, a thing pressed. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”).
en.recadrer:
~recadrer~ is ~re-~ plus ~cadrer~, and ~cadrer~ answers to two masters: the noun ~cadre~ and Latin ~quadrāre~ (“to be square, to fit”). ~cadre~ was borrowed from Italian ~quadro~, from Latin ~quadrum~ (“a square”), from ~quadrus~, from ~quattuor~ (“four”), from Proto-Italic *~kʷettwōr~ and Proto-Indo-European *~kʷetwṓr~ (“four”). Italian ~quadro~ and Spanish ~cuadro~ remain the everyday words for a picture, and the same Latin stem gave English ~quadrant~ and, through a Vulgar Latin *~exquadrāre~, ~square~ itself. ~cadrer~ is attested in French from 1529 in the sense “well-proportioned,” and from 1539 as “to fit exactly” — the sense preserved in ~cela ne cadre pas~.

~cadre~ then went travelling. From “picture frame” it became, in the eighteenth century, the table of posts in a military unit; then the officers who filled those posts; then, in the twentieth century, the salaried manager — ~un cadre~ — of French corporate life. ~cadrer~ followed the concrete sense into the cinema, where it is recorded from 1921 for the framing of a shot, and ~recadrer~ began as the photographer’s word for reframing or cropping an image. It then went abstract twice over: a policy can be ~recadrée~, given a new frame, and so can a person — ~recadrer un employé~ is to call a subordinate back into line. The pleasing consequence is that in a French office one may ~recadrer~ ~un cadre~: re-square a square. The same root supplies ~carré~, ~quatre~, ~quadrilatère~, ~encadrer~ and ~cadrage~.
en.recalcifier: ~Recalcifier~ is built on ~calcifier~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”), so it means to calcify again, in practice to restore calcium to something that has lost it. ~Calcifier~ is itself a French formation: it combines ~calcium~ with the suffix ~-ifier~, a descendant of Latin ~-ficāre~ (“to make”), and means “to turn into calcium salts, to harden with calcium.” The verb is therefore a layer cake of three French pieces, a prefix, a Neo-Latin chemical name and a Latin-born verbal suffix, and it belongs to medical and scientific vocabulary.
en.recaler:
~Recaler~ is parsed as ~caler~ plus the prefix ~re-~. The base is the ~caler~ glossed “to reinforce with a wedge,” a verb built on the noun ~cale~ (“wedge, chock”). The deeper origin of that ~cale~ is uncertain; by one account it comes from German ~Keil~ (“wedge”). From wedging an object steady, ~caler~ took everyday meanings such as to chock a wheel or to prop something firm, and its relatives include ~décaler~ and the noun ~calage~.

The school sense, “to fail a candidate,” seems to have a different story. French Wiktionary says it is probably from a nautical ~caler~ meaning “to sink a boat,” so the hypothesis is that a failed candidate is figuratively sent to the bottom. A nautical ~caler~ does exist: it is attested around 1165 in the sense “to lower a sail,” and comes from Old Occitan ~calar~ (“to lower”), traced by the TLFi to Ancient Greek ~khaláō~ (“to slacken, lower the mast”). Whether the school verb belongs to that older line is only “probable” in the sources, so this origin should be read as a hypothesis, not a settled fact.
en.recarreler: Formed from ~carreler~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”): to retile. The base ~carreler~ comes from ~carrel~, an older form of ~carreau~, which descends from Old French ~quarel~ and Vulgar Latin *~quadrellus~, a diminutive of Latin ~quadrus~ (“square”). Around 1160 ~carreau~ named a small hard floor tile.
en.recaser: Formed in French from ~re-~ and ~caser~. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and here means doing the action over, so ~recaser~ is “to find a new place for.” The base ~caser~ was itself built on the noun ~case~ with the ending ~-er~, “to put in a compartment”; its sources disagree about the noun, which English Wiktionary takes from Latin ~casa~ (“hut”). The verb is used for rehousing or reassigning a person, a job or an object.
en.recauser: ~Recauser~ is formed from ~causer~ with the prefix ~re-~, “again,” and means to discuss or talk something over once more. The base ~causer~ hides two verbs that merged. One, “to cause,” comes from the noun ~cause~. The other, “to chat,” descends from Latin ~causārī~ (“to plead a case, to debate”). Both rest on Latin ~causa~ (“cause, reason, lawsuit”). The “discuss” sense of ~recauser~ fits the second verb, whose courtroom pleading softened over the centuries into ordinary conversation.
en.receler: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ (“back, again”) and ~celer~ (“to hide”). The base is inherited from Old French ~celer~, from Latin ~cēlāre~ (“to conceal”), and Italian ~celare~ comes from the same verb. ~Receler~ keeps the idea of concealment but narrows it: it means to hide, and above all to keep stolen goods knowingly, which is the offense of ~recel~ (“handling stolen goods”). More generally it can mean to contain something hidden. Its sibling ~déceler~ comes from the same base and has the opposite effect.
en.recenser:
From Latin ~recēnsēre~ (“to count again, to review, to survey”), formed from ~re-~ (“again”) and ~cēnsēre~ (“to assess, to give an opinion, to register citizens”). The verb ~cēnsēre~ is the same one that gives ~cēnsus~, the Roman registration of citizens and their property. Its deeper origin is disputed: per De Vaan it perhaps goes back to Proto-Italic *~knsēō~ and to PIE *~ḱens-~ (“to announce, to proclaim”), with a possible cognate in Sanskrit ~śáṃsati~ (“he declares”).

The Roman ~cēnsor~ counted heads and judged morals, and that double sense of “count” and “appraise” runs through the family. French ~recenser~ kept the counting side: to take a census, to make an inventory, to identify and list. From the same Latin stock come ~recensement~ (“census”), ~censeur~, ~censure~, and ~recension~ (a scholarly inventory of manuscript readings). The hedge matters: the leap from *~ḱens-~ “to announce” to “to count” is plausible but not securely proven.
en.recentrer: Formed from ~centrer~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again, back”), so it means to bring back to the centre or to refocus. The base ~centrer~ comes from ~centre~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, and ~centre~ from Latin ~centrum~, borrowed from Greek ~κέντρον~ (~kéntron~), a goad or point, and also the fixed leg of a pair of compasses. The Greek word derives from ~kentéō~ (“to prick”). The sense passed from geometry to politics and strategy: to ~recentrer~ a debate or a party is to bring it back to its essentials or to the middle ground.
en.receper: ~Receper~ is formed at once with the prefix ~re-~ and the ending ~-er~ on the noun ~cep~ (“vine stock”), so “to cut back to the stock.” ~Cep~ comes from Latin ~cippus~ (“stake, trunk, post”), which is also the source of the doublets ~cippe~, ~cèpe~ and ~sep~. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”). The verb is used in pruning, where a vine or tree is cut down to its base so that it grows again.
en.recercler: Formed from ~cercler~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”), so it means to put new hoops on something, such as a barrel. The base ~cercler~ comes from ~cercle~ (“ring, circle”), from Latin ~circulus~, a diminutive of ~circus~ (“ring”). Some accounts instead trace ~cercler~ to Late Latin ~circulāre~, which would make it a doublet of ~circuler~. Either way, ~re-~ adds only the idea of doing the work a second time.
en.recevoir:
From Old French ~recevoir~, from Latin ~recipere~ (“to take back, to receive”), a compound of the prefix ~re-~ (“back, again”) and ~capere~ (“to take, to seize”). ~capere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~keh₂p-~ (“to grasp, to seize”), through which ~recevoir~ is cognate with Ancient Greek ~káptō~ (“to gulp down”) and, on the Germanic side, with English ~have~ and ~heave~ — both, surprisingly, relatives of this Latin verb of taking. The shift from ~recipere~ to French ~recevoir~ follows the regular Latin ~-cipere~ to French ~-cevoir~ pattern.

Latin ~recipere~ meant to take back to oneself, hence to accept what is offered or returned. French kept the core sense of accepting and added social and abstract ones: to ~recevoir~ a guest (to welcome), to ~recevoir~ a blow, to ~recevoir~ a diploma. The root ~capere~ is one of the most fertile in French, surfacing in ~capable~, ~capter~, ~captif~, ~recette~ (a doublet of ~recevoir~'s noun), ~réception~, ~concevoir~, ~décevoir~, ~percevoir~, and ~apercevoir~. The verbs in ~-cevoir~ form a tidy set, all the same Latin ~capere~ taken back, taken up, taken in, or taken away by their prefixes.
en.rechampir: The TLFi dates ~rechampir~ to 1676 (Félibien) and derives it with the prefix ~re-~ from the older verb ~échampir~, “to make a figure stand out against its ground by suitable tints.” ~Échampir~ is built on ~champ~ in the sense of the ground on which something is painted, with the prefix ~é-~ and the ending ~-ir~. The verb belongs to the decorative arts: to set off the outlines, mouldings or ornaments of a piece against the background by contrasting colours. The Académie also gives the spelling ~réchampir~.
en.rechanger: Formed from ~changer~ with the prefix ~re-~, meaning “to change again.” The base ~changer~ comes from Late Latin ~cambiāre~ (“to exchange”), a word of Gaulish origin that traces back to a Celtic root meaning “bent,” and is cognate with Italian ~cambiare~ and Spanish ~cambiar~. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and attaches to almost any French verb, so ~rechanger~ is a plain repetition formation, with the Celtic word hidden in its middle.
en.rechanter: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ and ~chanter~, meaning to sing again or to sing something once more. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and here expresses plain repetition. The base ~chanter~ descends from Latin ~cantāre~ (“to sing”), a frequentative of ~canere~, which also gave Italian ~cantare~ and Spanish ~cantar~.
en.rechaper: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ (“again”), the noun ~chape~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so it means to put a new ~chape~ on a tire, that is, to retread it. ~Chape~ is inherited from Old French ~chape~, from Late Latin ~cappa~ (“cape”), and is a doublet of ~cape~. Its old sense of a covering or cloak extended to the outer layer of a tire. The verb therefore describes giving a worn tire a fresh outer covering.
en.recharger: ~Recharger~ is formed from the prefix ~re-~ (“again”) and the verb ~charger~. ~Charger~ comes from Old French ~chargier~ (“to load, to put in a cart”), attested around 1080, from Late Latin *~carricāre~ (“to load a wagon”), built on Latin ~carrus~ (“cart”), itself a Gaulish loan. So to ~recharger~ is literally to load again: to refill a weapon, to top up a cartridge, and in the modern age to charge a battery or to reload a page. The sense is plainly repetitive, with nothing fossilized in the prefix.
en.rechasser: Formed from ~chasser~ with the prefix ~re-~ in its sense of “again”: to drive away or hunt once more. The base ~chasser~ comes from Late Latin *~captiāre~, a frequentative built on ~captus~, the past participle of ~capere~ (“to take, to seize”). Its Romance cousins are Italian ~cacciare~ and Spanish ~cazar~, and English has ~chase~ and ~catch~ from the same source. ~Chasser~ covers “to hunt,” “to chase” and “to drive off,” and ~rechasser~ repeats any of these.
en.rechausser: From ~chausser~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”): to ~rechausser~ is to put shoes on again, or to fit someone with new ones. The base ~chausser~ comes from Old French ~chaucier~, inherited from Latin ~calceāre~ (“to furnish with shoes”), built on ~calceus~ (“shoe”). The same stem gives ~chaussure~, ~chaussette~ and ~chausson~, while Italian ~calzare~ and Spanish ~calzar~ come from the same Latin verb.
en.rechercher:
From Old French ~cerchier~ (later Middle French ~chercher~), the source of modern ~chercher~ (“to look for, to search”), with the iterative prefix ~re-~. The base verb descends from Late Latin ~circāre~ (“to go around, to roam in search of”), from ~circa~ (“around”), itself from ~circus~ (“ring, circle”), tied to the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)ker-~ (“to turn, to bend”). The same Latin family gave Spanish ~cercar~ and Italian ~cercare~ (“to look for”), and, through ~circulus~, English ~circle~ and ~circus~.

The path of meaning is geometric at heart: one who searches once “went around” a place, and ~chercher~ originally meant “to roam, to ransack.” In the seventeenth century it displaced the older ~querre~ (which survives as ~quérir~). Prefixed with ~re-~, ~rechercher~ both intensifies and repeats: it can mean “to search thoroughly, to seek out” and “to look for again,” the second loop around the circle. From this productive ~re-~ comes the noun ~recherche~ (“research, inquiry”), borrowed into English as ~research~, and the adjective ~recherché~ (“refined, sought-after”). The underlying *~(s)ker-~ also turns up in ~cercle~, ~cerceau~, and ~recherche~ itself — a whole vocabulary spun from the idea of going round.
en.rechigner:
From Old French ~reschignier~ (also ~rechignier~), meaning “to bare one's teeth” or “to balk, to kick out,” borrowed from Frankish *~kīnan~ (“to split open”). French Wiktionary adds that the Frankish verb meant to twist the mouth or to split and open, and that Middle Dutch ~kinen~ (“to open the earth”) is related to it. Old French also had the simpler ~eschignier~, with the sense “to bare the teeth.” The word is therefore one of the many Germanic loans that French took from the Franks.

The Old French senses of ~rechigner~ stand behind the modern meaning, to show reluctance in doing something. It is most familiar in the negative, in the phrase ~sans rechigner~ (“without complaint”). The sources trace the verb only as far as Frankish, so nothing deeper is claimed here about the root of ~kīnan~.
en.rechristianiser: Formed from ~christianiser~ with the prefix ~re-~, which here expresses a return to a former state: to give something its Christian character again. The base is a learned borrowing from Latin ~chrīstiānizō~, built on ~Chrīstiānus~ (“follower of Christ”), which rests on the Greek title ~Christós~ (“anointed”). The inherited route from the same Latin source gave ~chrétien~, while ~christianiser~ kept the full Latin shape, and ~rechristianiser~ simply adds the idea of doing it over.
en.rechuter: Formed in French from the noun ~rechute~ (“relapse”) and the verb ending ~-er~, though English Wiktionary reads it as ~re-~ + ~chuter~. The noun ~rechute~ comes from Old French ~recheoir~ (“to fall back”), itself ~cheoir~ (“to fall”) with the prefix ~re-~, which here carries the sense “back, again.” The picture is thus of someone falling back into an illness or a habit they had left. Modern French uses ~rechuter~ especially in a medical sense, of a disease that returns after improvement.
en.reclasser: Formed from ~classer~ with the prefix ~re-~: to classify or rank again, and by extension to redeploy a worker into a new post. The base ~classer~ comes from the noun ~classe~, borrowed from Latin ~classis~, the name of the groups into which the Roman census sorted citizens. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and expresses repetition here, exactly as in ~refaire~. The same family also gave ~déclasser~, “to downgrade.”
en.reclouer: Formed from ~clouer~ (“to nail”) with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”), so “to nail again.” ~Clouer~ is built on ~clou~, from Latin ~clāvus~ (“nail”), though English Wiktionary also allows that the verb comes from Late Latin ~clāvāre~. The prefix ~re-~ descends from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”).
en.recoller: ~Recoller~ is formed from ~coller~ with the prefix ~re-~, in its sense of doing again or putting back: to stick something on once more. The base ~coller~ is a verb made from the noun ~colle~ (“glue”), which comes from Vulgar Latin *~colla~, borrowed from Ancient Greek ~κόλλα~ (“glue”). The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”). The Greek word is also hidden in English ~collagen~ and in French ~collage~ and ~colloïde~.
en.recommander:
From Old French ~comander~ (“to entrust, to command”), reinforced with the prefix ~re-~, from Late Latin ~commendare~ (a variant of ~commandare~), from ~com-~ (intensive) plus ~mandare~ (“to entrust, to commit to one's charge”). ~mandare~ is itself a compound of ~manus~ (“hand”) and ~dare~ (“to give”), so its literal sense is “to place into someone's hand.” ~manus~ goes back to PIE *~man-~ (“hand”) and ~dare~ to PIE *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). Cognate with Italian ~raccomandare~ and Spanish ~recomendar~, and, through ~commendare~, with English ~recommend~ and ~commend~.

The doubled prefix is telling: to ~recommander~ was first to “entrust again” or “entrust earnestly,” and from that idea of warmly committing a person or thing to another's care grew the modern sense of speaking in someone's favor, of endorsing. The military sense of ~commander~ — to give orders — comes from the same root, the commander being the one into whose hand authority is given. The “hand-giving” core of ~mandare~ seeds a wide family in French: ~commander~, ~demander~, ~mander~, ~mandat~, and ~commande~, alongside the learned ~mandataire~. Even English ~mandate~ and ~command~ trace back to that same Latin image of a charge placed, quite literally, in the palm.
en.recommencer:
From ~re-~ (“again”) + ~commencer~ (“to begin”), inherited through Middle French ~commencer~ and Old French ~comencier~ from Vulgar Latin *~cominitiāre~, a compound of ~com-~ (“together, thoroughly”) and ~initiāre~ (“to begin, initiate”). The latter rests on ~initium~ (“a beginning”), itself from ~in-~ (“into”) plus ~īre~ (“to go”) — so a beginning was once a “going in.” Cognate with Italian ~cominciare~ and Spanish ~comenzar~, and, through the same Old French source, with English ~commence~.

Where ~commencer~ simply marks a first start, ~re-~ adds the idea of doing it once more, so ~recommencer~ is “to begin again.” The buried root ~īre~ (“to go”) runs through a wide French family: ~initial~, ~initier~, ~initiative~, and ~initiation~ all preserve the notion of stepping into something. French has long favoured ~commencer~ over its near-twin ~débuter~, and the prefixed ~recommencer~ remains the ordinary way to say that a thing — a game, a school year, a quarrel — has started over from the top.
en.recomposer: Formed from ~composer~ + the prefix ~re-~, in its sense of “again”: to compose, assemble or put together anew. ~Composer~ is the verb that descends from Latin ~componere~ (~com-~ + ~ponere~, “to put together”), remodeled in French on ~poser~ instead of following the expected ~pondre~. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and is fully productive, so ~recomposer~ can describe rewriting a piece of music or a text, reconstituting a whole from its parts, or reshuffling a political majority.
en.recompter: ~Recompter~ is ~re-~ + ~compter~, “to count again, to recount.” The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and expresses repetition here. The base ~compter~ comes from Old French ~conter~, from Latin ~computare~ (~com-~ + ~putare~, “to reckon”). In the thirteenth century a learned respelling restored the ~p~ and set ~compter~ (“to count”) apart from ~conter~ (“to tell a tale”). English ~count~ is a relative of the same Latin verb.
en.reconduire: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ and ~conduire~, with ~re-~ marking a return to the starting point: to ~reconduire~ someone is to lead them back, to see them to the door or home. ~Conduire~ comes from Latin ~conducere~, a compound of ~con-~ (“together”) and ~ducere~ (“to lead”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~dewk-~ (“to pull, to lead”), the same root as English ~tow~ and ~tug~. A second sense, “to renew,” as in ~reconduire un contrat~, takes ~re-~ in its sense of “again.”
en.reconnaître:
From Latin ~recognoscere~ (“to know again, to recall, to review”), ~re-~ (“again”) + ~cognoscere~ (“to get to know, to learn”), itself ~co(m)-~ (“thoroughly”) + ~gnoscere~ (“to know”), from PIE *~ǵneh₃-~ (“to know, to recognize”). French passed through Middle French ~recognoistre~, then ~reconnoistre~ and ~reconnoître~, before settling on ~reconnaître~ (and since the 1990 reform, optionally ~reconnaitre~). The root *~ǵneh₃-~ is one of the most fertile in Indo-European, giving English ~know~ and the ~-gnostic~ of ~agnostic~ and ~diagnosis~, Greek ~gignṓskein~, and the Romance cousins Italian ~riconoscere~ and Spanish ~reconocer~.

The Latin idea was iterative: to ~recognoscere~ was to know a second time, to identify something already encountered — which is exactly the modern ~reconnaître un visage~ (“to recognize a face”). From there the verb branched into the moral and social: to ~reconnaître~ a fault is to admit it, to ~reconnaître~ a child or a state is to acknowledge it officially, and a person who shows gratitude is ~reconnaissant~ — for to be thankful is, etymologically, to “acknowledge” a kindness received. The military scout's ~reconnaissance~ (also borrowed into English) is yet another sense: knowing the terrain in advance. The same root threads through French ~connaître~, ~connaissance~, ~reconnaissance~, ~méconnaître~ (“to fail to recognize”), and the learned ~diagnostic~.
en.reconquérir: Formed from ~conquérir~ and the prefix ~re-~, which here carries its ordinary sense of repetition: to conquer again, to win back what was lost. The base ~conquérir~ comes from Old French ~conquerre~, from Latin ~conquīrere~ (“to seek out eagerly”), itself built on ~quaerere~ (“to seek”). The Latin idea of a thorough search narrowed to winning by force, and French then widened it again to winning over a heart or a crowd. ~Reconquérir~ keeps both uses: one can retake a territory or recover someone's trust or a title.
en.reconsidérer: Built from ~considérer~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”), so “to consider again”. The base is a learned borrowing from Latin ~considerare~ (“to examine attentively”), made from ~con-~ and a stem tied, by an old explanation, to ~sidus~ (“star”), as if the word first meant to study the stars. Whatever the truth of that link, ~reconsidérer~ adds the idea of going back over a judgment or decision to weigh it afresh.
en.reconsolider: Formed from ~consolider~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”): to strengthen something afresh. The base comes from Latin ~consolidāre~ (“to make firm”), built from ~con-~, used here as an intensive, and ~solidāre~ (“to make solid”), from the adjective ~solidus~ (“solid, whole”). Italian ~solido~, Spanish ~sólido~ and French ~solide~ descend from that adjective. The repetitive ~re-~ is its ordinary sense, as in ~refaire~: a bone, an alliance or a financial position can be consolidated once and then reconsolidated.
en.reconstituer:
A transparent French formation: ~re-~ (“again”) plus ~constituer~, which French borrowed in the thirteenth century from Latin ~cōnstituere~ (“to set up, establish, fix”), from ~con-~ (“together”) plus ~statuere~ (“to set up, decree”), built on ~status~ and ultimately on ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from the great PIE root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”) — the same root that produced Italian ~stare~, Spanish ~estar~ and English ~stand~ and ~state~. ~reconstituer~ itself appeared in 1534 meaning “to establish anew,” then came into its own in 1790 in the pages of the Moniteur universel, just as revolutionary France, having dismantled its old institutions, was debating how to build new ones.

The family of *~steh₂-~ through ~statuere~ is among the densest in French: ~constitution~, ~statut~, ~statue~, ~instituer~, ~restituer~, ~destituer~, ~substituer~ — and ~état~ itself, from Old French ~estat~, from Latin ~status~. The nineteenth century then sent ~reconstituer~ in two memorable directions. Medicine produced the ~reconstituant~ (1845–1864), the restorative tonic supposed to rebuild a weakened body. Criminal procedure produced the sense “to piece together exactly how an event unfolded” (attested from the 1850s) — ancestor of the modern ~reconstitution~, in which investigators walk a suspect through the crime scene, and of the historical reenactments staged by enthusiasts in period dress. Italian ~ricostituire~, Spanish ~reconstituir~ and English ~reconstitute~ are its parallel forms — though English speakers may know the idea best from dried soup, reconstituted with hot water.
en.reconstruire:
French ~reconstruire~ is transparently ~construire~ (“to build”) plus the prefix ~re-~ (“again, anew”), thus “to build again.” ~Construire~ descends from Latin ~construere~ (“to heap together, to build”), formed from ~con-~ (“together”) and ~struere~ (“to pile up, to arrange, to build”). ~Struere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~strowō~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~strew-~ (“to strew, to spread out”). That root is shared with English ~strew~ and ~structure~, German ~streuen~ (“to scatter”), and Latin ~stratum~ (“something spread out”) — so building was first imagined as a strewing, a laying-out of layers.

The image inside ~construire~ is of piling materials together in arranged courses; ~re-~ simply runs the process again over what has fallen. The verb belongs to a tight Latin family of ~struere~ compounds that all reached French: ~instruire~ (“to instruct,” to build knowledge in), ~détruire~ (“to destroy,” to un-build), and ~obstruer~ (“to obstruct,” to pile up against). From the noun ~structure~ and the root *~strew-~ French also keeps ~construction~, ~reconstruction~, ~structure~, and ~strate~ — all heirs of an Indo-European verb for spreading things out.
en.reconvertir: ~Reconvertir~ is formed from ~convertir~ with the prefix ~re-~, which here means “again” or “back to a former state.” The base comes from Latin ~convertere~ (“to turn around, to transform”), made of ~con-~ and ~vertere~ (“to turn”). So ~reconvertir~ is “to convert again”: to turn something to a new purpose, or back to its earlier one. It is common in economic language, where a factory, a site or a worker is ~reconverti~ for another activity.
en.recopier: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ (“again”) and ~copier~, so “to copy once more,” as when one makes a clean version of a draft (~recopier au propre~) or transcribes a text by hand. The base ~copier~ comes from Medieval Latin ~copiare~, a verb drawn from Latin ~copia~ (“abundance”): to copy was to multiply the available exemplars. Here ~re-~ expresses plain repetition, and the verb is regularly formed, with nothing hidden in the prefix.
en.recorder:
Modern French has two verbs ~recorder~. The older one is inherited from Middle French and Old French ~recorder~, from Latin ~recordārī~ (“to call to mind, to remember”), itself formed from ~re-~ (“back, again”) and ~cor~ (“heart; mind”). The Latin idea is therefore of bringing something back to the heart, which in the ancient view was also the seat of memory. The same Latin verb gave Italian ~ricordare~ and Spanish and Portuguese ~recordar~, and English ~record~ came from the Old French verb.

The second ~recorder~ is a plain French formation from ~re-~ and ~corder~, and it means “to restring,” as one restrings a tennis racket. Its base ~corder~ is built on ~corde~ (“rope, string”), from Latin ~corda~, a variant of ~chorda~, from Greek ~khordḗ~ (“string of gut”). The two verbs are homonyms with unrelated stories: one is “to bring back to the heart,” the other “to put strings back on.”
en.recorriger: Formed from ~corriger~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”): to correct a second time, or to correct what was already corrected. The base is Latin ~corrigere~ (“to set straight”), a compound of ~cum~ (“together”) and ~regere~ (“to direct, rule”), and it passed into French through its learned form. Italian ~correggere~ and Spanish ~corregir~ come from the same Latin verb. The repetitive ~re-~ is the commonest use of the prefix, as in ~refaire~ or ~repenser~, and the sense here is perfectly transparent.
en.recoucher: ~Recoucher~ is formed from ~coucher~ with the prefix ~re-~, in the sense of repetition: to put to bed again, or to go back to bed. The base comes from Old French ~couchier~, from Latin ~collocare~ (“to place, lay in position”), itself made of ~con-~ (“together, thoroughly”) and ~locare~ (“to place”), from ~locus~ (“place”). French ~coucher~ narrowed that general idea of placing to the laying down of a body, which is why it came to mean “to put to bed.”
en.recoudre: ~Recoudre~ is ~coudre~ with the prefix ~re-~, meaning “to sew again, to mend by sewing.” The base ~coudre~ comes through Old French from Vulgar Latin *~cōsere~, an altered form of Latin ~cōnsuere~ (“to sew together”), itself built on ~suere~ (“to sew”). The same Latin verb gave ~couture~ and ~couturier~, and English ~sew~ is a distant cousin of ~suere~.
en.recouper: Formed from ~couper~ with the prefix ~re-~ (from Latin ~re-~, “back, again”). The base comes from Old French ~colper~, built on the noun ~colp~ (modern ~coup~, “a blow”), which reaches back through Late Latin ~colaphus~ to Greek ~kólaphos~ (“a slap on the cheek”): to cut was first to separate with a blow. The prefix adds repetition, so ~recouper~ can mean “to cut again.” Its most common modern senses are figurative: pieces of information or accounts that cross one another and thereby confirm each other are said to ~recouper~, as are lines that intersect.
en.recouponner: Formed from ~coupon~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”), so ~recouponner~ means “to reissue coupons,” here the coupons of a stock or bond. The noun ~coupon~ belongs to the family of ~couper~ (“to cut”): it is a derivative with the suffix ~-on~, and the sense is a piece cut off. The verb ending ~-er~ was added to the prefixed noun.
en.recourber: Formed from ~courber~ with the prefix ~re-~, “to bend back” or “to curl.” Here ~re-~ gives the sense of bending the other way, not of repeating. ~Courber~ comes from Latin ~curvāre~ (“to bend”), from ~curvus~ (“bent”), through Vulgar Latin *~curbare~. English ~curve~ belongs to the same family. French has the related ~courbe~ and ~courbure~.
en.recourir:
From Latin ~recurrere~ (“to run back, return”), from ~re-~ (“back, again”) + ~currere~ (“to run”). ~Currere~ descends from Proto-Italic *~korzō~ and from PIE *~ḱers-~ (“to run”), the root that, through Latin, gives French ~courir~, ~courant~, ~course~, ~courrier~, and ~secours~, and the English borrowings ~current~, ~course~, ~career~, and ~corridor~.

The verb carries two senses that the prefix ~re-~ pulls in different directions. Transparently, ~recourir~ is “to run again,” the literal repetition a runner or a racer does. But its dominant modern sense is figurative: ~recourir à~ means “to have recourse to, to fall back on” — to run back to something for help. The image is of returning at speed to a source of aid, the same metaphor frozen in the noun ~recours~ (“recourse, appeal”) and in ~secours~ (“help,” literally “running to aid”). So a single Latin verb of running back lives on in French both as the athlete's plain “run again” and as the abstract act of turning to a remedy in need.
en.recouvrer:
French ~recouvrer~ comes from Old French ~recovrer~, from Latin ~recuperare~ (also spelled ~reciperare~, “to regain, to recover”). The Latin verb is linked to ~recipio~ (“to take back, to receive”), itself ~re-~ (“back, again”) plus ~capio~ (“to take, to seize”), and thus to the Proto-Indo-European root *~kap-~ (“to grasp, to seize”). From the same Latin source comes the learned doublet ~récupérer~, borrowed later and more directly; ~recouvrer~ is the older, inherited form that passed through the mouths of speakers. English ~recover~ and ~recuperate~ are cousins through this Latin family.

The sense has always centered on getting something back — health, debts, lost property, one's rights. In careful modern French, ~recouvrer~ specializes in formal or financial recovery: one ~recouvre~ a debt, ~recouvre~ one's freedom, ~recouvre~ one's sight. It must not be confused with the homophone-rich ~recouvrir~ (“to cover again”), a different verb from ~couvrir~. The action-noun ~recouvrement~ (“collection, recovery,” as of taxes) belongs to this verb, while ~récupération~ belongs to its bookish twin — two threads spun from one Latin verb of taking back.
en.recouvrir:
~Recouvrir~ is built from ~couvrir~ with the prefix ~re-~. The base verb descends from Latin ~cooperire~ (« to cover completely, to overwhelm »), made of the intensive prefix ~co-~ and ~operire~ (« to cover, to veil »). Italian ~coprire~ and Spanish ~cubrir~ are its Romance siblings; English ~cover~ came through Old French ~covrir~. Note that ~recouvrir~ (« to cover again / completely ») must not be confused with the look-alike ~recouvrer~ (« to recover, regain »), which instead derives from Latin ~recuperare~ — same prefix, different root.

The ~re-~ in ~recouvrir~ carries two readings the French keeps lively: « again » (to cover anew what was uncovered) and « completely » (to cover all over, as paint ~recouvre~ a wall entirely). The figurative « to cover up », hiding or excusing a fault, grew naturally from the literal act of laying something over. The ~operire~ family also yielded ~ouvrir~ (« to open », from ~aperire~, its mirror-twin), ~couvercle~, ~couverture~, and ~découvrir~ (« to dis-cover », to take the lid off and so to find).
en.recracher: ~Recracher~ is formed from ~cracher~ with the prefix ~re-~, which here adds the idea of repetition or return: to spit out again, or to spit back out something just taken in. The base ~cracher~ has a debated origin. It may be pure sound-imitation, from an imitative syllable ~crac~, or a loan through Old French ~crachier~ and perhaps from a Frankish verb *~hrākijan~, which would link it to Germanic words for spitting and retching. The sources leave the question open, so ~recracher~ simply inherits that uncertainty from its base.
en.recreuser: Formed from ~creuser~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”), so “to dig again” or “to dig deeper.” The base ~creuser~ is a verb built on the noun and adjective ~creux~ (“hollow”), attested around 1121 and 1180. The origin of ~creux~ is disputed: the dictionaries propose a Late Latin *~crosus~ (“hollow”), possibly resting on a Celtic base, but the Latin form is itself unattested, and the origin is called uncertain. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”).
en.recristalliser: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ (“again”) and the verb ~cristalliser~, so it means to crystallize again. ~Cristalliser~ was built on ~cristal~ and the suffix ~-iser~; ~cristal~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~crystallus~, from Greek ~krústallos~ (“ice”), a word tied to ~krúos~ (“frost”). Rock crystal was once thought to be ice frozen hard. The ~re-~ prefix, from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”), simply repeats the process: a substance that has dissolved or melted forms crystals anew.
en.recroqueviller:
~Recroqueviller~ is an alteration of the older verb ~recoquiller~ (“to curl up”). The sources agree that the change is probably due to the influence of ~croc~ (“hook”). French Wiktionary adds a second influence, ~ville~, an old form of ~vrille~ (“tendril, gimlet”). Both are given as probable, not certain, so the origin is best described as a reshaping of ~recoquiller~ under the pull of these words.

The interest of the verb lies in this blend.
