French ~mordre~ gave ~morsure~ and ~mordant~. ~Remordre~ itself is now rare, a plain verb for biting again, kept in view by its prefix and by its famous noun.
en.remorquer: Borrowed from Italian ~rimorchiare~ (“to tow”). French Wiktionary traces the Italian verb to a Vulgar Latin *~remulculare~, an extended form of ~remulcare~, itself derived from ~remulcum~ (“towing cable”). The sources say nothing more about the path of the loan or about how the sense developed. The nouns ~remorque~ (“trailer, tow”) and ~remorqueur~ (“tug”) belong to the same family.
en.remouiller: Formed from ~mouiller~ (“to wet”) with the prefix ~re-~, in its sense of repetition: “to wet again.” The base comes from Old French ~moillier~, inherited from Vulgar Latin *~molliāre~ (“to soak”), a verb built on Latin ~mollis~ (“soft”), the same word that gives French ~mou~. Soaking was thought of as making a thing soft, hence the path from “to soften by steeping” to simply “to wet.” The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”).
en.rempailler: ~Rempailler~ is formed from ~empailler~ with the prefix ~re-~, in the sense of doing the work again: to refit a seat with fresh straw. ~Empailler~ is a parasynthetic verb, built at once with ~en-~ and ~-er~ on the noun ~paille~ (“straw”), so “to put straw in.” It is known for stuffing animals and for filling chair seats. ~Paille~ is inherited from Latin ~palea~ (“straw, chaff”). The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”). The verb is above all the craftsman's word for re-covering the seat of a straw chair.
en.rempaqueter: Formed from ~empaqueter~ (“to put in a package”) with the prefix ~r-~, the form of ~re-~ before a vowel, here meaning “again.” ~Empaqueter~ is built on ~paqueter~ with ~en-~ (“in, into”), from Latin ~in-~, and ~paqueter~ derives from the noun ~paquet~. The verb therefore means “to pack up again.”
en.rempiler: ~Rempiler~ is formed from ~empiler~ with the prefix ~re-~, which marks repetition, so literally “to pile up again.” The base ~empiler~ is built on ~pile~ (“heap”), from Latin ~pila~ (“pillar, column”), with ~en-~ and ~-er~, and is attested in the early 13th century. In French, ~rempiler~ is best known in its specialized sense of “to re-enlist,” that is, to sign up for another term of service.
en.rempiéter: Formed on ~pied~ (“foot”) with the prefix ~re-~, in the technical senses “to reknit the foot of a stocking” and “to rebuild a foundation,” in both cases to renew the foot of something. The noun ~pied~ comes from Middle French ~pied~, from Old French ~pié~, from Latin ~pedem~, the accusative of ~pēs~. It is a cousin of English ~foot~ and a doublet of it, and has relatives in Italian ~piede~ and Spanish ~pie~.
en.remplacer:
A French formation rather than an inherited Latin word: ~remplacer~ is built from the prefix ~re-~ and the verb ~emplacer~ (“to put in place”), itself ~en-~ (“in”) plus ~place~ — so the literal sense is “to put back in the place (of another).” The noun ~place~ descends from Latin ~platea~ (“broad street, open space”), borrowed from Ancient Greek ~plateîa~ (“broad way”), the feminine of ~platús~ (“broad, flat”), from a Proto-Indo-European *~pleth₂-~ (“flat, to spread”). Through the same ~platea~ come Italian ~piazza~, Spanish ~plaza~, and English ~place~.

The word thus contains a small history of substitution: to set one thing back into the space another occupied. From this came the sense of standing in for someone — a ~remplaçant~ is a substitute or stand-in — and the abstract notion of one thing superseding another. The deep root *~pleth₂-~ (“flat, broad”) underlies a surprising spread of French vocabulary: ~place~ and ~placer~, ~plat~ (“flat, a dish”), ~plaine~ (“plain”), ~plan~ (“flat surface, plan”), and ~plateau~ all carry the idea of flatness or spreading out, and English ~flat~, ~plate~, and ~plaza~ belong to the same family.
en.remplier: Formed from the prefixes ~re-~ and ~en-~, the noun ~pli~ (“fold”) and the ending ~-er~, ~remplier~ is first recorded in 1572, in Paré, with the sense “to bend a thread inward.” In 1611 Cotgrave gives “to make an inward fold in a piece of cloth to shorten it,” and in 1935 the Académie records “to fold the part brought back inside,” of the cover of a book.
en.remplir:
From the twelfth century, a compound of the prefix ~re-~ and ~emplir~ (“to fill”). ~Emplir~ comes from Latin ~implere~ (becoming ~implīre~ in Late Latin), itself ~in-~ (“into”) plus ~plere~ (“to fill”), related to ~plenus~ (“full”). All trace to the Proto-Indo-European root *~pleh₁-~ (“to fill”), which also gave English ~full~ and ~fill~, German ~voll~, Greek ~plērēs~ (“full”), and Sanskrit ~pūrṇa~.

Here ~re-~ does not really mean “again”: it intensifies, so ~remplir~ simply means “to fill completely,” and it has all but replaced the simpler ~emplir~ in everyday French. The verb spans the concrete and the abstract: one fills a glass (~remplir un verre~), fills in a form (~remplir un formulaire~), and fulfills a duty or condition (~remplir une obligation~) — the same metaphor of completion English keeps in ~fulfill~. From ~plenus~ and *~pleh₁-~ comes a broad family of French words: ~plein~, ~plénitude~, ~complet~, ~complément~, ~supplément~, ~plus~, and the borrowed ~plénier~ — a whole cluster turning on the notion of fullness and abundance.
en.remployer: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ and ~employer~, so “to use again.” The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”). The base ~employer~ comes from Old French ~emploier~, from Latin ~implicāre~ (~in-~ + ~plicāre~, “to fold in, to involve”), and is a doublet of the learned ~impliquer~, which French borrowed straight from Latin much later. ~Remployer~ means to use something a second time, as when building materials are reused in a new structure.
en.remplumer: English Wiktionary analyzes ~remplumer~ as ~re-~ plus ~en-~ plus ~plumer~ (“to refeather”), that is, ~emplumer~ with ~re-~ in front. The prefix ~en-~ is spelled ~em-~ before ~p~, and ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”). The sense “to regain weight, to put on flesh” is a figurative extension of the idea of growing feathers again.
en.rempocher: Formed from ~empocher~ with the prefix ~re-~, here meaning “back”: to put something back in one's pocket. The base ~empocher~ is ~en-~ plus ~pocher~, a verb built on ~poche~ (“pocket”), which comes from Frankish *~pokkō~ and is a cognate of English ~pouch~ and ~pocket~. ~Empocher~ also means, figuratively, to pocket money or a gain.
en.rempoissonner: Formed from ~empoissonner~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”), so the verb means to stock a pond or river with fish once more. The base goes back through Middle French to Old French ~enpuissonner~ and is built on ~poisson~ (“fish”) with ~en-~ and the verb ending ~-er~. Despite the resemblance, ~empoissonner~ has no connection with ~empoisonner~, “to poison.”
en.remporter:
From ~emporter~ (“to carry away”) with the prefix ~re-~. ~Emporter~ is itself ~porter~ (“to carry”) plus the prefix ~en-~ (Latin ~inde~, “away from there”). ~Porter~ comes from Latin ~portare~ (“to carry”), tied to ~porta~ (“gate”) and ~portus~ (“harbor, passage”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“to lead, to pass over”). Cognates from this root include Greek ~poros~ (“passage”) and English ~fare~ and ~ford~.

~Emporter~ means “to carry off, to take away with oneself”; adding ~re-~ gives both “to carry back” and the idiomatic “to carry off again,” but its liveliest modern sense is figurative: ~remporter~ une victoire, un prix, un succès — “to carry off, to win” a victory or prize, as one bears away the trophy. The construction ~l'emporter sur~ (“to prevail over”) belongs to the same image of carrying the day. From ~portare~ flows a vast family: ~porter~, ~porte~, ~port~, ~porteur~, ~portable~, ~apporter~, ~exporter~, ~importer~, ~transporter~, ~comporter~, and ~rapporter~ — all built on the simple act of carrying.
en.rempoter: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ and ~empoter~, itself ~en-~ (spelled ~em-~ before ~p~) + ~pot~ + ~-er~, “to put into a pot.” ~Re-~ adds the idea of again, so ~rempoter~ means “to repot,” moving a plant into a fresh pot. The noun ~pot~ comes from Old French ~pot~, from Vulgar Latin ~pottum~, from Frankish *~pott~, from Proto-Germanic *~puttaz~ (“pot, jar, tub”). English ~pot~ belongs to the same family.
en.remprunter: Formed from ~emprunter~ with the prefix ~re-~, here in its repetition sense: to ~remprunter~ is to borrow again. The ~r-~ is the form the prefix takes before a vowel. The base ~emprunter~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~impromutuāre~, reshaped from Latin ~promutuārī~ (“to borrow in advance”) and built on ~mutuus~ (“borrowed, reciprocal”), a word from the root behind ~mutuel~ and ~muer~.
en.remuer: Formed in French from the prefix ~re-~ and the verb ~muer~. The prefix comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”). The base ~muer~ is inherited from Latin ~mūtāre~ (“to change”), which also gave Italian ~mutare~ and Spanish ~mudar~, and, as a learned borrowing, the doublet ~muter~. Modern ~remuer~ means to move, stir or shake something, and the prefix no longer reads as simple repetition. The sources do not say how the sense “to change” narrowed to “to move”.
en.remâcher: Formed in French from ~mâcher~ (“to chew”) and the prefix ~re-~ (“again”), so literally “to chew again.” The base comes from Old French ~maschier~, inherited from Late Latin ~masticāre~, which French borrowed a second time as the learned ~mastiquer~. The verb is used for literal re-chewing and, figuratively, for turning a thought, grievance or regret over and over in the mind.
en.remédier:
French ~remédier~ is borrowed from Latin ~remediāre~ (“to heal, to cure”), as both Wiktionaries say. The Latin verb is built on the noun ~remedium~ (“cure, remedy”), a compound of ~re-~ and ~medērī~ (“to heal”). English Wiktionary points to the related French noun ~remède~, and Italian ~rimediare~ and Spanish ~remediar~ are cousins of the verb.

In modern French ~remédier~ means to find a cure for something, almost always with ~à~, as in ~remédier à un problème~ (“to fix a problem”). Its relatives come from the same Latin root ~medērī~: ~remède~ (“remedy”), ~médecin~ (“doctor”), ~médecine~ (“medicine”), ~médical~ and ~médicament~ (“drug”). English ~remedy~ and ~medicine~ belong to the same family.
en.remémorer:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~rememorārī~ (or its variant ~rememorāre~), a verb meaning “to call back to mind.” Its parts are ~re-~ (“again”) and the adjective ~memor~ (“mindful”), a standard analysis. The French verb is a doublet of ~remembrer~, the form that was inherited from the same Latin through Old French.

The two verbs thus show the learned and the popular route side by side. French Wiktionary says that ~remembrer~ was eliminated before the seventeenth century, while English Wiktionary says only that ~remémorer~ partially displaced it. The popular form was not lost to the world: English ~remember~ comes from Old French ~remembrer~. In modern French ~remémorer~ is used mostly in the pronominal form, to call something back to mind. It sits in a family with ~mémoire~, ~mémorable~, ~mémoriser~ and ~commémorer~, all from the Latin root ~memor-~.
en.renauder: ~Renauder~ is a denominal verb, formed from ~renaud~ and the ending ~-er~. The base ~renaud~ (also ~regnaud~) is a dialectal variant of ~renard~ (“fox”). English Wiktionary says the verb originally meant “to cry like a fox,” and the sense of protesting loudly or grumbling in anger developed from that.
en.renaître:
From the prefix ~re-~ (“again”) and ~naître~ (“to be born”). ~naître~ comes through Old French ~naistre~ from Vulgar Latin *~nascere~, a reshaping of Classical Latin ~nāscī~ (“to be born”), itself from earlier *~gnāscī~ and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ǵenh₁-~ (“to beget, to give birth”). That root is one of the most fertile in the family, producing Latin ~genus~ and ~gignere~, English ~kin~, ~kind~, and ~genus~, and the Romance siblings Spanish ~nacer~ and Italian ~nascere~.

~renaître~ means literally to be born a second time, and French uses it with the full weight of that image. A landscape ~renaît~ in spring; hope, courage, or a city ~renaît~ from its ashes — the verb carries an idea of return from apparent death that the plain ~naître~ lacks. It is the everyday word behind the ~Renaissance~, the “re-birth” of art and learning. Defectively, ~renaître~ famously has no past participle in standard use, so one cannot easily say “has been reborn” — a fitting grammatical gap for a verb about endless beginning again. From the same root *~ǵenh₁-~ French draws ~genre~, ~nature~, ~nation~, ~génération~, and ~gendre~ (“son-in-law”), a whole vocabulary of birth, kind, and kinship.
en.rencaisser: The verb is derived from ~encaisser~ (“to put in a crate”) with the prefix ~re-~, which here carries its sense of repetition: to pack in a crate again. ~Encaisser~ is in turn a French verb built on the noun ~caisse~ (“crate, case”), with the prefix ~en-~ marking placing inside. The sources give nothing older, so the story belongs to its base, and the verb is a transparent, two-step formation with the idea of putting something back into a ~caisse~.
en.rencarder: Formed in French from the slang noun ~rencard~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to give someone a rencard,” that is, to inform. The noun is attested with the sense “information,” and in 1898 with that of “appointment.” Its origin is uncertain. French Wiktionary lists several proposals: a link with ~racorder~ and ~recorder~ (“to instruct, to repeat”), influenced by ~renseignement~; a back-formation from ~rencarrer~ (“to go home”); a slang use of ~encarter~; or an alteration of ~rencontre~.
en.renchérir: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ and ~enchérir~, itself ~en-~ + ~chérir~ (~cher~ + ~-ir~), so “to make or become dear.” The adjective ~cher~ comes from Latin ~cārus~ (“dear, costly”). Here ~re-~ reinforces more than it repeats. The verb means “to go further, to go one better,” and the base's own sense of bidding higher at an auction shows where that figurative use comes from. Its sibling ~surenchérir~ also means to bid higher, with ~sur-~ marking the excess.
en.rencogner: ~Rencogner~ is formed from ~encogner~ with the prefix ~re-~, according to French Wiktionary. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and here is closer to an intensifier than to a repetition. ~Encogner~ is built on the French word ~coin~ (“corner”), so to ~rencogner~ is to drive someone or something into a corner.
en.rencontrer:
From Old French ~encontrer~ (“to come up against, to meet”), itself derived from ~encontre~ (“an encounter, a meeting”), from Late Latin ~incontrā~, built from ~in-~ (“in, against”) + Latin ~contrā~ (“facing, against, opposite”). The verb ~rencontrer~ adds the prefix ~re-~ to ~encontrer~ and is attested from the 14th century. The base ~contrā~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~komterād~, a feminine form meaning “the opposite one of two,” from PIE *~kom-~ (“with, together”) plus the comparative suffix *~-teros~ — making ~contrā~ a doublet of Latin ~cum~. Cognate with Italian ~incontrare~ and Spanish ~encontrar~.

The oldest French uses were martial: around 1175 ~encontrer~ meant “to clash, to do battle,” for to meet an adversary head-on is to oppose him. The softer sense “to come upon by chance” developed alongside, and once the reinforcing ~re-~ was added, ~rencontrer~ settled into its modern range — to meet a person, to come across a thing, to confront a difficulty. The reflexive ~se rencontrer~ can even mean “to coincide,” two minds meeting on the same thought. The “against” core of ~contrā~ remains visible in the noun ~rencontre~ (“an encounter,” but also “a clash”) and in the fixed phrase ~à l'encontre de~ (“contrary to”). The same root underlies a great brood of French words: ~contre~, ~contraire~, ~contredire~, ~rencontre~, and the borrowed ~contraste~.
en.rendormir: ~Rendormir~ is formed from ~endormir~ and the prefix ~re-~ (in its form ~r-~ before a vowel), which marks a return to the initial state: to put back to sleep, or, reflexively, to fall asleep again. ~Endormir~ appears in the Chanson de Roland around 1100 and continues Latin ~indormīre~, made of ~in-~ and ~dormīre~ (“to sleep”). Latin ~dormīre~ rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~drem-~ (“to sleep”). The family also gives ~dormir~, ~dormeur~ and ~dortoir~.
en.rendosser: ~Rendosser~ is formed from ~endosser~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”), so it means to put something on once more, such as a garment or a role. The base ~endosser~ was built on the noun ~dos~ (“back”), which descends from Latin ~dorsum~, and originally meant to put something on one's back. It later broadened to taking on a burden or responsibility. The prefix ~re-~ simply adds the idea of repetition to that image.
en.rendre:
From Vulgar Latin *~rendere~ (“to give back”), an altered form of Classical Latin ~reddere~ (“to give back, to return”). ~reddere~ is itself ~red-~ (“back”) plus ~dare~ (“to give”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~deh₃-~ (“to give”) — the same root that gives Latin ~dōnum~ (“gift”) and English ~donor~ and ~date~. The irregular ~-nd-~ of the popular form almost certainly arose by contamination from ~prendere~ (“to take, to seize”), so that the verb for “giving back” reshaped itself on the verb for “taking.” Cognate verbs survive as Italian ~rendere~ and Spanish ~rendir~, and the family entered English as ~render~ and ~rent~.

The core idea is restitution — to hand back what one received — and French ~rendre~ still means “to give back” or “to return” something. From there the verb fanned out remarkably: to “render” an account, to “render” a service, to “render” a verdict, and, in the construction ~rendre quelqu'un heureux~, “to make someone happy” — to give them a quality, as it were. The reflexive ~se rendre~ even means “to surrender” or “to go (somewhere),” to take oneself off. From ~reddere~ and ~red-~ come French ~rendement~ (“yield, output”), ~reddition~ (“surrender”), and the noun ~rente~ (“income, annuity”), a sum regularly “given back.”
en.reneiger: Formed from ~neiger~ (“to snow”) with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”): ~reneiger~ is “to snow again.” The base descends from Old French ~negier~ and Vulgar Latin *~nivicāre~, built on Latin ~nivem~ (“snow”), the same noun that gave Italian ~nevicare~ and the French adjective ~nival~. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”), and here it carries its plain sense of repetition.
en.renfermer: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ and ~enfermer~, itself ~en-~ (“in”) and ~fermer~ (“to close”). ~Fermer~ comes from Latin ~firmāre~ (“to make firm, secure”), from ~firmus~ (“firm”), the source of English ~firm~. The literal sense is “to lock up again,” but the prefix often adds only emphasis to ~enfermer~, which is how ~renfermer~ came to mean “to contain, to encompass”: to hold something within oneself or within a text, as in ~renfermer un secret~. The old sense of closing something in, and so of holding it, carries into ~renfermé~, said of someone withdrawn.
en.renfiler: ~Renfiler~ is formed from ~enfiler~ with the prefix ~r-~, the form of the repeating prefix ~re-~ that appears before a vowel. It means to thread again, whether a needle or beads on a cord. The base ~enfiler~ is built from ~en-~ (“in”) and ~filer~, a verb derived from ~fil~ (“thread”), which goes back to Latin ~filum~. The meaning of ~renfiler~ follows directly from its parts.
en.renflammer: The verb is formed from ~enflammer~ (“to set on fire”) with the prefix ~re-~, which here has its common sense of “again”: to reignite. ~Enflammer~ comes from Old French ~enflamer~, itself from Latin ~inflammāre~, built on ~in-~ and ~flamma~ (“flame”). The doubled ~m~ in modern spelling is a Latinizing respelling. So ~renflammer~ restores a fire, and its family reaches ~flamme~ and ~flamber~ through the Latin root.
en.renfler: ~Renfler~ is formed from ~enfler~ with the prefix ~re-~, here an intensive or repeating sense, and means to make something bulge. The base ~enfler~ is inherited from Latin ~īnflāre~ (“to blow into, to swell”), made of ~in-~ and ~flāre~ (“to blow”). The ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”), and the verb thus adds a further swelling to a swelling.
en.renflouer: The sources agree on the prefixes ~re-~ and ~en-~ but differ on the base. French Wiktionary derives the verb from ~flouée~, a Norman noun meaning “tide,” and compares ~afflouer~, ~affluer~, ~refluer~, ~flot~ and ~flotter~. English Wiktionary analyses it as ~re-~ + ~en-~ + ~flot~ + ~-er~, from the word for a wave or flood. Either way, the underlying image is of water lifting a stranded ship, which gives the sense of getting it afloat again and, by extension, rescuing a business with new funds.
en.renfoncer: Formed in French from ~enfoncer~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”): to push something in once more or further. The base is built from ~en-~ (“in”) and ~foncer~, which derives from the noun ~fond~ (“bottom”), from Latin ~fundus~ (“bottom, base”), a word cognate with English ~bottom~. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”). The literal image is of driving a nail or a stake deeper into place.
en.renforcer:
Derived from Old French ~enforcier~ (“to make strong”), formed with the prefix ~re-~ (here intensive or iterative). ~enforcier~ is itself ~en-~ plus the stem of ~force~, from Vulgar Latin ~fortia~, the neuter plural of Latin ~fortis~ (“strong, sturdy”) taken as a feminine noun. Cognate with Italian ~rinforzare~ and Spanish ~reforzar~, and — through ~fortis~ — with English ~force~ and ~fort~.

The building blocks are transparent: ~fortia~ gave French ~force~, ~en-~ turns the noun into a verb (“to put strength into”), and ~re-~ adds the idea of doing so anew or all the more — to ~renforcer~ is to strengthen what already had some strength. The same ~fortis~ underlies a broad family in French: ~fort~, ~forteresse~, ~fortifier~, ~effort~ (literally a “forcing-out” of strength), ~confort~ (originally a strengthening, a giving of courage), and ~renfort~, the noun of reinforcement. English ~comfort~ borrowed that last sense from Old French before it softened into mere coziness, so that an English ~effort~ and a French ~renfort~ are, at bottom, two ways of summoning the same Latin strength.
en.renformir: A building term, first recorded in 1690 in Furetière, meaning to repair an old rubble wall by filling in missing stones and laying a thick coat of mortar over it. The TLFi describes it as a remaking of the older verb ~renformer~, modeled on that verb's own derivative, the noun ~renformis~. It adds that the pair ~crépir~ and ~crépi~ certainly helped establish the new verb. Littré reads the word as ~re-~ plus ~en~ plus ~forme~, roughly “to put a wall back into shape.”
en.renfrogner:
From the prefix ~re-~ and Old French ~froignier~ (“to scowl”), itself from Gaulish *~frogna~ (“nose”), a word with Celtic relatives in Breton ~froen~, Welsh ~ffroen~ and Irish ~sróine~. English Wiktionary gives a slightly different path: ~renfrogner~ is a form with an inserted ~n~ from ~refrogner~, from ~frogner~, which it links to ~froncer~ (“to scowl”). Both accounts agree on a verb of frowning built with ~re-~. Other Romance languages have words that look related, such as Italian ~frignare~ (“to grimace in pain, to whine”), Occitan ~fonhar~ (“to sulk”) and Spanish ~refunfuñar~ (“to grumble”).

The verb is used mostly in the reflexive, ~se renfrogner~, to knit one's brows and put on a sullen face, and its past participle ~renfrogné~ serves as an adjective for a sulky, scowling expression. The Celtic relatives all mean “nose”, which fits an older verb ~froignier~ naming a grimace of the face. The sources thus differ on whether the base lies in ~froignier~ or in ~froncer~, and the inserted ~n~ is explained only as a later intrusion into ~refrogner~.
en.rengager: Formed from ~engager~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”), so “to engage again”: to commit, hire or enlist once more. The base ~engager~ comes from Old French ~engagier~, itself built on ~gagier~ (“to pledge”) with ~en-~ (“in”). The noun ~gage~ was borrowed from Frankish *~wadi~ (“pledge”), the same Germanic source as English ~wage~, which makes the two doublets. So a word for re-commitment rests, at its root, on the idea of putting something in pledge a second time. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”).
en.rengainer: Formed from ~engainer~ with the prefix ~re-~, in the sense of putting something back where it came from: to return a blade to its sheath. The base ~engainer~ is built on ~gaine~ (“sheath”) with ~en-~ and ~-er~, “to put into a sheath.” The noun ~gaine~ comes from Latin ~vāgīna~ (“sheath, scabbard”) by way of Old French ~guaïne~, and its initial g- reflects Germanic influence. It is a doublet of ~vagin~ and a cognate of Italian ~guaina~ and Spanish ~vaina~.
en.rengorger: ~Rengorger~ is formed from ~engorger~ with the prefix ~re-~. It is used chiefly as the reflexive ~se rengorger~, meaning “to puff oneself up with vanity,” as a bird swells its throat. The base ~engorger~ is itself built on ~gorge~ (“throat”), so the verb pictures a throat filled out again and again with self-importance.
en.rengrener: ~Rengrener~ is formed from ~engrener~ with the prefix ~re-~, in the sense of doing again. The base ~engrener~ is built from ~en-~ and ~grener~, a verb drawn from ~grain~ or ~graine~, and it goes back to Latin ~granum~ (“grain”). The sources gloss ~rengrener~ as “to mesh gear teeth again” and, in minting, “to restrike a coin or medal.” So a word of the mill and the granary ends up, in its prefixed form, in the workshop of the mechanic and the mint.
en.rengréner: ~Rengréner~ is formed from ~engrener~ with the prefix ~re-~, which here marks a repeated or further engagement. It means “to mesh into a second gear-wheel,” one toothed wheel taking up the motion of another. The base ~engrener~ is built from ~en-~ and ~grener~, a verb drawn from ~grain~ or ~graine~, and it goes back to Latin ~granum~ (“grain”). That Latin word also underlies ~grenier~, and English ~grain~ and ~garner~.
en.renier:
From Vulgar Latin *~renegāre~, built on Latin ~re-~ plus ~negāre~ (“to deny”). French Wiktionary adds that, synchronically, French speakers also read the verb as ~re-~ plus ~nier~, since ~nier~ itself descends from ~negāre~. Cognates include Italian ~rinnegare~ and Spanish ~renegar~. The two readings agree on the core idea: a denial, here of a faith, a person or a commitment.

The verb carries a strong religious and moral colour. To ~renier sa foi~ is to abandon one's faith, and ~renier ses amis~ or ~renier son fils~ is to disown them. Through the Romance cognates it also gave English two words. ~Renegade~ came by way of Spanish ~renegado~, from ~renegar~, and ~renege~ was taken from Medieval Latin ~renegare~. French itself has ~renégat~ for the person who has abandoned a faith or a cause, ~reniement~ for the act, and, from the simple verb, ~nier~ and ~dénier~.
en.renifler:
The two Wiktionaries tell the origin differently. French Wiktionary derives ~renifler~ from Old French ~nifler~, which it calls onomatopoeic, imitating the sound of a strong sniff through the nose. English Wiktionary analyzes it as ~re-~ plus ~nifler~ (“to irritate, to annoy”), and traces ~nifler~ to a Germanic root shared with Italian ~niffo~ (“snout”), Low German ~Niff~ (“nose, mouth, bill”), Dutch ~neb~ (“nose, beak”) and English ~neb~ (“nose, beak, face”). The origin is therefore debated: sound imitation by one account, a Germanic word for the nose by the other.

On either account, ~renifler~ is a verb of the nose. It means to sniff, to draw air or mucus noisily up the nose, and by extension to turn up one's nose at something or to smell it out. The prefix ~re-~ in ~renifler~ may be a simple intensifier, since the sources do not say that the sniffing is repeated. The sources also leave open whether the Old French sense of annoying and the sniffing sense are connected, so this is not asserted here.
en.renommer:
French ~renommer~ is transparently formed from the prefix ~re-~ and the verb ~nommer~ (“to name”). ~nommer~ descends from Latin ~nominare~ (“to name”), from the noun ~nomen~ (“name”), which goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₁nómn̥~ (“name”). That ancient root is one of the most widely preserved in the family: it is cognate with English ~name~, German ~Name~, Ancient Greek ~ὄνομα~, and Sanskrit ~नामन्~ (~nāman~).

The prefix ~re-~ pulls the verb in two directions. In its plainest sense ~renommer~ means to “rename,” to give a new name, or to “re-elect,” to name someone again to an office. But ~re-~ also carries an intensive force — to name “again and again,” and so with praise — which yields the older, elevated sense “to glorify, to laud.” That intensive thread is what crystallized in the nouns ~renom~ and ~renommée~ (“renown, fame”): to be much-named is to be famous, exactly as English ~renown~, borrowed from Old French ~renomer~, shows the same drift from repeated naming to celebrity.
en.renoncer:
From Old French ~renoncier~, from Latin ~renūntiāre~, formed from ~re-~ plus ~nūntiāre~ (“to announce, report”), the verb of ~nūntius~ (“messenger, message”). In classical Latin ~renūntiāre~ meant first “to report back, bring word,” and then, by a turn toward formal declaration, “to declare off, refuse, give up.” The Romance line gives Spanish ~renunciar~ and Italian ~rinunciare~, and English ~renounce~ and ~announce~ come through the same ~nūntiāre~ family.

The second Latin sense — a public, official giving-up — is the one French inherited: to ~renoncer~ is to declare formally that one relinquishes a claim, a right, a habit, or a faith. The flavour of solemn announcement still clings to it, which is why one ~renonce~ à un trône, à un héritage, à ses droits — acts of weight, not mere quitting. From the same stem French keeps ~renoncement~ (“renunciation”) and ~renonciation~, the latter especially in legal use. The hidden ~nūntius~ — the messenger bearing word — also lies behind ~annoncer~, ~énoncer~, and ~prononcer~, a small fan of verbs all about the carrying of declarations.
en.renouer: Formed from ~re-~ (“again”) and ~nouer~ (“to tie a knot”). The base ~nouer~ comes through Middle and Old French ~noer~ from Latin ~nōdāre~, built on ~nōdus~ (“knot”), which also gave French ~nœud~. ~Renouer~ first meant to tie a knot again, as in a lace that has come undone. It then moved to human ties: one ~renoue~ a friendship, a conversation or a tradition that had been broken, as if the thread had been taken up again.
en.renouveler:
Formed from Old French ~nouvel~ (“new”) with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”) and a verbal suffix, paralleled by Late Latin ~renovellāre~. Behind ~nouvel~ stands Latin ~novellus~ (“young, new”), a diminutive of ~novus~ (“new”), from Proto-Indo-European *~newos~ (“new”) — the very root of English ~new~, German ~neu~, Ancient Greek ~νέος~ (~néos~), and Sanskrit ~náva~.

The verb means literally “to make new again,” and French has spread it across many domains: one ~renouvelle~ a passport or a subscription (extending its validity), ~renouvelle~ the air in a room, ~renouvelle~ a team or a wardrobe, and even ~se renouvelle~ as an artist by reinventing oneself. The reflexive also covers natural recurrence — a phenomenon that ~se renouvelle~ happens again. Note the doubled ~l~ in conjugation (~je renouvelle~), inherited from the ~-ell-~ of ~novellus~. From the same Latin ~novus~ descend a rich crop of French words: ~nouveau~ and ~nouvelle~, ~nouveauté~, ~renouveau~ (“renewal, revival”), ~rénover~ and ~rénovation~ (a learned doublet), ~innover~ and ~innovation~, and ~novice~.
en.renquiller: Formed from ~enquiller~ with the prefix ~re-~, which here marks a return or a repetition of the action. The base ~enquiller~ was itself built on ~quille~ with the prefix ~en-~ and the verb ending, so the word is a double derivation. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and is fully productive in French.
en.renseigner:
French ~renseigner~ is ~enseigner~ (“to teach”) with the prefix ~re-~. ~Enseigner~ descends from Old French ~enseignier~, from Vulgar Latin *~īnsignāre~ (“to mark, point out”), a variant of Latin ~īnsignīre~, from ~signum~ (“sign, mark”). The deeper origin of ~signum~ is uncertain: it is referred either to Proto-Indo-European *~sek-~ (“to cut”) or to *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”), and the sources do not settle between them. Through ~signum~ the verb is cognate with English ~sign~, ~signal~, and ~ensign~, and with Italian ~insegnare~ and Spanish ~enseñar~.

The path of meaning is neat: to ~enseigner~ was to “point out by signs,” hence to instruct; ~renseigner~ adds ~re-~ and shifts from teaching a subject to “informing” a person — giving someone the precise sign or pointer they lack. From the same family come the noun ~renseignement~ (“(piece of) information,” and, in the plural, “intelligence” in the espionage sense), ~enseignement~ (“teaching”), and ~enseigne~ (“shop sign, ensign”) — all rooted in the idea of a mark that points the way.
en.rentabiliser: ~Rentabiliser~ is formed from the adjective ~rentable~ (“profitable”) with the suffix ~-iser~, “to make A.” The adjective is itself ~rente~ (“income, annuity”) + ~-able~, attested in Picard in the thirteenth century in ~terre rentable~, land that carried a charge. Before ~-iser~ the base takes the longer form ~rentabil-~, as in ~numériser~ from ~numérique~. The verb means “to make something pay,” by making an investment, a business or a piece of equipment bring in more than it costs.
en.renter: French Wiktionary lists two separate verbs ~renter~. The first, “to endow with an income,” is derived from ~rente~ (“annuity”). The second is formed from ~enter~ with the prefix ~r-~, the form that ~re-~ takes before a vowel. The base ~enter~ (“to graft”) comes from a Late Latin verb *~imputāre~, built on ~inpotus~ (“graft”), a word recorded in the Salic Law, from Ancient Greek ~ἔμφυτος~ (“implanted”). The Greek ~φ~ was rendered as ~p~. Only the first verb matches the gloss “to endow.”
en.rentoiler: Formed from ~entoiler~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”): ~rentoiler~ is “to mount on a new canvas,” as in restoring a painting. The base ~entoiler~ is itself built from ~toiler~ with the prefix ~en-~, so the verb stacks two prefixes on the word for cloth. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”), and ~en-~ from Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”).
en.rentraire: French Wiktionary analyzes ~rentraire~ as ~re-~ added to Old French ~entraire~, itself derived from Latin ~intrahere~ (“to draw in”). The Latin verb is a compound of ~in-~ (“in”) and ~trahere~ (“to draw, to pull”). In French, the verb is a term of mending, meaning to mend invisibly. The Latin ~trahere~ is the root of a large French family. Its direct descendant is ~traire~ (“to milk”), and learned or semi-learned relatives include ~extraire~, ~attraire~, ~abstraire~ and ~trait~. English shares the root in ~extract~, ~attract~ and ~tract~.
en.rentrayer: A first-conjugation variant of ~rentraire~, a textile term for mending a tear so that the join does not show. No dictionary gives ~rentrayer~ its own origin. ~Rentraire~ is attested from 1404 for joining two pieces of cloth edge to edge, and by 1694 for an invisible repair. It is built on Old French ~entraire~ (“to draw”), from Latin ~intrahere~ (“to drag, to pull”), with ~re-~. The TLFi explains the prefix by the back-and-forth motion of the needle.
en.rentrer:
From Old French ~entrer~ (“to enter, to go in”) prefixed with ~re-~, yielding the sense “to enter again, to go back in.” The base verb descends from Latin ~intrāre~ (“to enter, to go into”), itself built on ~inter~ (“among, between, within”) and ultimately on the Proto-Indo-European preposition *~h₁en~ (“in”). Cognates of the underlying family include Italian ~entrare~, Spanish ~entrar~, and — through the same root — English ~enter~ and ~interior~.

The prefix ~re-~ here is doubly productive: sometimes it means “again” (re-enter a room one has left), sometimes simply “back” or “inward,” and in many uses the iterative force has faded entirely, so that ~rentrer~ has become the ordinary verb for “to go home” (~rentrer chez soi~). It also developed transitive senses — to bring something in (~rentrer le foin~, to get the hay in before rain) and to hold something back (~rentrer ses larmes~, to hold back one's tears). From the same stem French built the noun ~rentrée~, used for the return to work or school after the summer holidays, a word with no neat English equivalent. The verb ~entrer~ and its relatives ~entrée~ and ~entremets~ all share the ancestor ~intrāre~.
en.renverser:
From earlier ~enverser~ with the prefix ~re-~; the old verb was later refashioned as ~inverser~. The base ~enverser~ derives from ~envers~ (“the reverse, the wrong side”), from Latin ~inversus~, past participle of ~invertere~ (“to turn around”), built from ~in-~ + ~versus~, from ~vertere~ (“to turn”), Proto-Indo-European *~wert-~ (“to turn”). The root is cognate with English ~verse~, ~version~, ~convert~, and ~vertigo~.

The core image is purely physical — to turn something over, onto its ~envers~ — and from it ~renverser~ fanned out into one of French's most versatile verbs: to turn upside down, knock over, spill, run over (a pedestrian), overthrow (a government), and, figuratively, to bowl someone over with astonishment. The added ~re-~ intensified the “turning back/over” rather than meaning “again.” The same *~wert-~ root pervades French: ~vers~, ~verset~, ~version~, ~convertir~, ~divertir~, ~inverser~, ~pervers~, and the noun ~revers~ (“reverse, setback”). Even ~vertige~ belongs here — the world, after all, seeming to turn.
en.renvider: Formed from ~envider~ with the prefix ~r-~, a variant of ~re-~ (“again”) used before a vowel, to give the sense “to rewind.” ~Envider~ is itself built from ~en-~ and the stem of ~dévider~, by antonymy. Where ~dévider~ unwinds thread from a reel, ~envider~ winds it on, here onto a spindle or bobbin. Its ~en-~ is the locative prefix, “in, onto,” from Latin ~in-~, set against the ~dé-~ of ~dévider~, which reverses the action. The whole family belongs to the vocabulary of spinning and weaving.
en.renvoyer:
Formed in French from ~envoyer~ (“to send”) with the iterative prefix ~r-~ (a form of ~re-~, “again, back”). ~Envoyer~ itself comes from Latin ~inviare~ (“to set on the way, to travel”), a compound of ~in-~ (“into, onto”) and ~via~ (“way, road”). The future and conditional stems of ~envoyer~ were reshaped in the 18th century under the pull of ~voir~ (“to see”), which is why French says ~enverra~. ~Via~ survives directly in English ~via~ and in Italian and Spanish ~via~ / ~vía~.

If ~envoyer~ is to put someone or something on the road, ~renvoyer~ is to put them back on it — and the prefix's two readings, “again” and “back,” fan out into a remarkable spread of senses. To ~renvoyer~ can mean to send again, to send back, to return (a ball, a favour, a letter), to refer (a reader to a footnote, a case to another court), to postpone, and — pointedly — to dismiss someone from a job or expel a pupil: putting them, so to speak, back out the door. From the same ~via~ come French ~voie~, ~voyage~, ~dévoyer~, ~convoyer~, and ~envoi~.
en.renâcler:
~Renâcler~ comes from Old French ~renaquer~, formed from ~naquer~ with the prefix ~re-~, and it appears in Middle French as ~renasquer~. English Wiktionary traces ~naquer~ further back to Old French ~naquier~ (“to sniff”) and ~nascïer~ (“to talk through the nose”). Both Wiktionaries agree that ~renifler~ influenced the form of the word.

The ancestors of the verb name sounds made through the nose, sniffing and nasal speech. The modern senses are “to snort in anger” and, figuratively, “to show reluctance.” The circumflex of ~renâcler~ stands for the ~s~ of Middle French ~renasquer~, as it does in many French words. ~Renifler~ stayed a separate verb, whose influence touched only the shape of ~renasquer~ and not its descent.
en.renégocier: Formed from ~négocier~ with the prefix ~re-~, in its sense of “again,” so “to negotiate anew.” The base is a learned borrowing from Latin ~negōtiārī~ (“to do business, to trade”), attested in French in 1484, from ~negōtium~ (“business”). That noun is analyzed as ~nec~ (“not”) + ~ōtium~ (“leisure”), business being literally “not-leisure.” The prefix ~re-~ goes back to Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and is fully productive in French, which is why a verb like this one can be coined for any deal that has to be reopened.
en.repairer:
Repairer, in its older hunting sense of an animal returning to its lair, comes from Old French ~repairier~ (“to return home”). That verb is a doublet of ~rapatrier~: both go back to the same Late Latin verb, ~repatriāre~ (“to go back to one's homeland”), built from ~re-~ and ~patria~ (“fatherland”). French ~rapatrier~ was reshaped much later by learned borrowing, while ~repairier~ followed the path of everyday speech. English took the same Old French verb as ~repair~, in the sense “to go to a place”.

The ~re-~ in this verb keeps its sense of “back”: going back to one's own place. The French noun ~repaire~ (“lair, den”) is the place an animal or a band of people returns to. This verb must not be confused with a modern homonym in French Wiktionary, a technical sense formed from ~pairer~ with ~re-~, which has no connection with Latin ~patria~. The older sense of going home is now archaic, while its noun ~repaire~ is still in everyday use.
en.reparaître: The verb is formed from ~paraître~ with the prefix ~re-~, which here carries its sense of repetition: to appear again. The base descends from Old French ~paroistre~ and Vulgar Latin *~parēscere~, an inchoative (“begin to…”) verb built on Latin ~pārēre~ (“to appear, to be visible”). ~Reparaître~ thus describes a thing coming back into view after an absence, or a title being published again.
en.reparler: Formed from ~re-~ (“again”) + ~parler~ (“to speak”). The prefix comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and here simply means repetition: to speak again, or to resume a conversation. The base ~parler~ is inherited from Old French and ultimately from Late Latin ~parabolāre~, a verb built on Latin ~parabola~ (“comparison, parable”), itself borrowed from Greek ~παραβολή~. To speak is thus, etymologically, to throw words side by side, and ~reparler~ adds nothing to that history except the second round.
en.repartir:
From ~partir~ prefixed with ~re-~ (“again, back”). ~partir~ comes from Old French ~partir~, from Latin ~partire~ / ~partiri~ (“to divide, share”), a verb on ~pars~, ~partis~ (“a part”). The modern sense “to leave” grew from “to divide”: to ~partir~ was first to part company, to separate oneself from a group — the share-out becoming a departure. Italian ~partire~ and Spanish ~partir~ keep both threads, and through ~pars~ French has ~part~, ~partie~, ~partage~, and the borrowed English ~part~.

French actually holds two close verbs here, distinguished by conjugation. ~repartir~ conjugated like ~partir~ (auxiliary ~être~) means “to set off again, to start up again, to resume.” But ~repartir~ also means “to retort, to reply sharply” — a sense that travels through the idea of “sending back” an answer, the verbal volley returned at once. Care is needed not to confuse this pair with ~répartir~ (“to distribute, apportion”), which carries the accent and stays nearer the original Latin sense of dividing into shares; that one keeps auxiliary ~avoir~. From the same family come ~départ~ (“departure”), ~répartition~, and ~repartie~ (“a quick retort”).
en.repasser: ~Repasser~ is formed from ~passer~ with the prefix ~re-~, “again, back.” The base ~passer~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~passāre~, built on Latin ~passus~ (“step, pace”), from ~pandere~ (“to spread”). The prefix gives several senses: to pass by again, to retake an exam, to go over something once more, and, by extension, to iron, since an iron is passed back and forth across the cloth. The meanings share the idea of covering the same ground a second time.
en.repaver: Formed from ~paver~ (“to pave”) with the prefix ~re-~, which here carries its ordinary sense of “again”: to lay a surface anew. The base ~paver~ is inherited from Old French and goes back to Vulgar Latin *~pavāre~ (“to beat down”), from Latin ~pavīre~ (“to beat, to tread down”). The image behind paving is a beaten surface, ground tamped flat before anything is laid on it. The same Latin family gave ~pavement~ in French, and English borrowed ~pave~ and ~pavement~ from French.
en.repayer: ~Repayer~ is a straightforward formation from the prefix ~re-~ and the verb ~payer~. The prefix, from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”), carries its usual sense of repetition, so the verb means to pay again. It is a transparent French coinage, and its meaning is fully predictable from its two parts.
en.repaître:
French ~repaître~ goes back to Old French ~repaistre~, from Latin ~repascere~ (“to feed again”), which is the verb ~pascere~ (“to graze, to feed”) with the prefix ~re-~. English Wiktionary describes it simply as ~re-~ + ~paître~, which is the same analysis seen from the French side, since ~paître~ itself descends from ~pascere~. The circumflex of ~repaître~ stands in for the s that Old French still wrote in ~repaistre~.

In current French the verb is most at home in the reflexive, ~se repaître de~, “to feast on,” often in a figurative sense. The same Latin family gave French ~repas~ (“meal”), and English ~repast~ was borrowed from Old French. From ~pascere~ itself come ~pâture~, ~pâturage~, ~pâtre~ and ~pasteur~, and English ~pasture~ and ~pastor~ belong to the same family. A pastor, in this light, is a feeder of flocks.
en.repeindre: ~Repeindre~ is formed from ~peindre~ and the prefix ~re-~, which here has its ordinary sense of doing something again. The base ~peindre~ comes from Latin ~pingere~ (“to paint, to dye, to embroider”), which goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~peyḱ-~ (“to mark, to color”). A ~repeindre~ is therefore, quite literally, a second coat of that very old act of marking a surface with color.
en.repenser: From ~penser~ (“to think”) with the prefix ~re-~ in its sense of repetition, so ~repenser~ is “to think again,” to reconsider. ~Penser~ comes from Latin ~pensāre~ (“to weigh carefully”), the frequentative of ~pendere~ (“to weigh”), so to ~repenser~ is, at root, to weigh again. The prefix goes back to Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and is fully productive in French, which is why one can rethink a plan, a system or a whole policy.
en.repentir:
~Repentir~ is inherited from Middle French ~repentir~, from Vulgar Latin *~repaenitīre~, from Late Latin ~paenitīre~, from Classical Latin ~paenitēre~. Two changes are visible along the way. The verb moved from the Latin ~-ēre~ type to the ~-īre~ type, and it took the prefix ~re-~ in Vulgar Latin. English ~repent~ is a close relative. French Wiktionary lists the noun ~repentir~ (“remorse”) as a back-formation from the verb in its reflexive form, ~se repentir~.

Latin ~paenitēre~ expressed regret and remorse, and the result in French is a verb of sorrow for one's own wrongdoing, used above all reflexively as ~se repentir~. The root of ~paenitēre~ is also found in the learned words ~pénitence~, ~pénitent~ and ~pénitencier~. The same family gave English ~penitent~ and ~penance~.
en.repercer: Formed from ~percer~ with the prefix ~re-~, in its sense of repetition: “to pierce again.” The base ~percer~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~pertusiare~, a verb derived from ~pertusum~, the supine of Latin ~pertundere~ (~per-~ “through” plus ~tundere~ “to strike”). The same source gave Old French ~pertuis~ (“a hole”). To ~repercer~ is to open a hole once more, in a plank, a wall or an ear.
en.reperdre: Formed from ~perdre~ with the prefix ~re-~, meaning “again”: to lose what one had just regained, or to lose a second time. The base ~perdre~ comes from Latin ~perdere~ (“to destroy, to lose utterly”), itself built from ~per-~ (“through, to the end”) and ~dare~ (“to give”). Italian ~perdere~ and Spanish ~perder~ descend from the same Latin verb.
en.repeupler: Formed from ~peupler~ (“to populate”) with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”), so the verb means to populate a place anew. The senses “replant” (trees) and “restock” (merchandise) extend the same idea of filling a place again. The base ~peupler~ is a native French verb built on the noun ~peuple~, which descends from Latin ~populus~ (“people, nation”). The deeper origin of ~populus~ is unsettled: it is sometimes linked to the root of ~pleō~ (“to fill”), and an Etruscan source has also been proposed.
en.repiquer: The verb is formed from ~piquer~ with the prefix ~re-~, which adds the sense of repetition: to prick again, or to replant, as when seedlings are pricked out and set anew. The base ~piquer~ has a debated origin. The TLFi favors a Vulgar Latin *~pīkkāre~ built on an expressive root, while French Wiktionary derives it from ~pic~, tied to Latin ~pīcus~ (“woodpecker”). In either case no classical Latin ancestor is attested.
en.replacer: Formed in French from ~placer~ with the prefix ~re-~, which here marks a return to a former state, “to put back in its place.” The base ~placer~ is a verb of the sixteenth century built on the noun ~place~, from Old French ~place~, from Vulgar Latin *~plattĕa~, an altered form of Latin ~platēa~ (“broad street”), itself from Ancient Greek ~plateîa~ (“broad”). Behind the Greek lies the Proto-Indo-European root *~pleth₂-~ (“flat, broad”).
en.replanter: ~Replanter~ is formed from ~planter~ with the prefix ~re-~, in its ordinary sense of doing again: to plant a second time, or to plant a place afresh. The base ~planter~ comes from Latin ~plantāre~, a verb built on ~planta~, which meant “sole of the foot” before it meant a shoot or cutting. Its relatives include Italian ~piantare~, Spanish ~plantar~ and German ~pflanzen~. In the base's own entry the link between the sole of the foot and planting is called plausible but partly conjectural.
en.repleuvoir: Formed from ~pleuvoir~ (“to rain”) with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”), so it means to rain once more. The base verb comes from Old French ~plovoir~ and Vulgar Latin *~plovēre~, a reshaping of Latin ~pluere~, which goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~plew-~ (“to flow”). The same root gave English ~flow~ and ~flood~. Like ~pleuvoir~ itself, the verb is used almost only in the impersonal.
en.replier:
Formed in French as ~re-~ plus ~plier~ (“to fold”), the prefix here meaning “again” or “back”. The form is old: Old French already had ~replier~ and ~reploier~, which line up with Latin ~replicāre~ (“to fold back”), itself ~re-~ plus ~plicāre~ (“to fold”). The Latin base comes from the Proto-Indo-European root *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, to weave”), which also gave Greek ~plékō~ (“I weave”). The sources do not settle whether the French verb is a pure French formation or in part a continuation of the Latin one; the two readings give the same result. A learned sister, ~répliquer~, was later taken from the same Latin verb, and English ~reply~ came from the Old French ~replier~.

The verb began with the plain gesture of folding something again or folding it back on itself: ~replier~ une carte, ~replier~ ses jambes. The meaning then widened in two directions. Troops that ~se replient~ fall back in order, and the noun ~repli~ names such a retreat. A person who ~se replie sur soi-même~ withdraws into themselves, folded up like the paper. The family splits in two, with ~replier~ for the physical fold and ~répliquer~ for the answer thrown back, in the same way as English ~reply~ and ~replicate~. Related modern French words include ~pli~, ~plier~, ~déplier~, ~repli~ and ~réplique~.
en.replonger: A transparent derivation from ~re-~ and ~plonger~. The base comes from Old French ~plongier~, from Vulgar Latin *~plumbicāre~, a verb built on Latin ~plumbum~ (“lead”): to plunge was first to drop like a lead weight. The prefix ~re-~ descends from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and here carries its two commonest senses, repetition and return to a former state. The verb therefore means both “to dive in once more” and, figuratively, “to sink back” into thought, gloom or a bad habit. The same ~plumbum~ gave French ~plomb~ and ~plombier~, and English ~plumb~ and ~plunge~ are related to it.
en.reployer: ~Reployer~ is formed from ~ployer~ with the prefix ~re-~, meaning to bend or fold again. ~Ployer~ is inherited from Old French ~ploier~ (attested around 1100), from Latin ~plicāre~ (“to fold”), from a Proto-Indo-European root *~pleḱ-~ (“to plait, to weave”). It is a doublet of ~plier~, which took over the everyday sense of folding, while ~ployer~ kept that of bending under pressure. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”). ~Reployer~ is a literary word, now rare next to ~replier~.
en.replâtrer: ~Replâtrer~ is formed from ~plâtrer~ and the prefix ~re-~, meaning “to plaster again,” and by extension to patch something up. The base ~plâtrer~ comes from the noun ~plâtre~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun is inherited from Old French ~plastre~ (about 1165), from Vulgar Latin *~plastrum~, from Latin ~emplastrum~, from Greek ~émplastron~ (“daub, salve”). It is a doublet of ~piastre~.
en.repolir: Formed from ~polir~ with the prefix ~re-~, in the sense of polishing again. The base was borrowed from Latin ~polīre~ (“to smooth, to polish”) through Old French ~polir~. The Latin verb also gave Italian ~pulire~ and Spanish ~pulir~, and English took ~polish~ from the Old French stem ~poliss-~. Its participle ~polītus~ (“smoothed, refined”) gave English ~polite~, as a smooth surface came to describe smooth manners.
en.reporter:
Formed from ~porter~ (“to carry”) with the prefix ~re-~ (“back, again”), so first “to carry back, to carry again.” The base ~porter~ descends from Latin ~portāre~ (“to carry, to bear”), ultimately from PIE *~per-~ (“to cross, to go through”), the same root that gave Latin ~porta~ (“gate”) and ~portus~ (“harbor”). Through that root ~portāre~ is distantly kin to English ~fare~ and ~ford~ and to German ~fahren~ — all once about passage and crossing.

The verb fanned out: to carry something back to where it was, to wear a garment again, to transfer (an emotion, a number in arithmetic), and — the sense that flowered later — to put off, to postpone. Beware a false friend within the family: the masculine noun ~reporter~ (“news reporter”) is not this verb at all but a 19th-century borrowing from English ~reporter~, itself from ~report~ + ~-er~ — so French re-borrowed a cousin that had emigrated through ~portāre~ centuries earlier. Native kin include ~report~ (“carryover, postponement”), ~reportage~, ~apporter~, ~emporter~, and ~supporter~.
en.reposer:
In the “rest” sense, from Old French ~reposer~, from Late Latin ~repausare~, from ~re-~ plus ~pausare~ (“to halt, to cease”), itself from Latin ~pausa~ (“a pause”), borrowed from Greek ~παῦσις~ (“a stopping”), from the verb ~παύειν~ (“to cease”). Cognate with Italian ~riposare~ and Spanish ~reposar~, and — through ~pausa~ — with English ~repose~ and ~pause~.

A tangle sits at the heart of this verb. Late Latin ~pausare~ (“to cease, to rest”) became so entwined with classical ~ponere~ (past participle ~positum~, “to place”) that the two fused: French ~poser~ inherits the form of ~pausare~ but much of the meaning of ~ponere~. That confusion is exactly why ~reposer~ today carries both senses at once — “to rest” (one ~se repose~) and “to put back down” (one ~repose~ a glass on the table). From ~pausare~ flow ~repos~, ~pause~, ~poser~, ~reposant~, and ~reposoir~; and the Greek ~παύειν~ behind it all surfaces in learned French through ~menopause~ and the musical ~pause~ — the silence that, etymologically, is simply a rest.
en.repositionner: Formed from ~positionner~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”), so “to position again.” ~Positionner~ is itself a recent French verb built on the noun ~position~ plus ~-er~, and ~position~ comes from Latin ~positio~ (“a placing”), from ~ponere~ (“to put, to place”). The base verb was long viewed with suspicion outside technical and military use, before it spread into everyday and commercial language. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”).
en.repousser:
~Repousser~ is formed from ~pousser~ with the prefix ~re-~. The base verb comes from Latin ~pulsare~ (« to beat, to push repeatedly »), the frequentative of ~pellere~ (« to drive, strike, thrust »), from PIE *~pelh₂-~ (« to drive, to beat »). French ~pouls~, ~pulser~, and ~pulsion~ are kin through the same ~pulsare~; English ~pulse~, ~push~, ~compel~, ~expel~, ~repel~, and ~appeal~ all trace to ~pellere~.

The ~re-~ adds the idea of « back » or « away »: to ~repousser~ is to push something back — an attacker, a temptation, a date on the calendar (one can ~repousser~ a meeting to next week). From physical shoving the senses fan out to repelling an enemy, rebuffing an offer, or turning someone away. Curiously, ~repousser~ also means « to grow back » — hair or grass that ~repousse~ — where ~pousser~ keeps its native French sense of a plant pushing upward. The ~pellere~ / ~pulsare~ root seeds a broad family: ~pousser~, ~poussée~, ~repousser~, ~propulser~, and ~impulsion~.
en.reprendre:
From Old French ~reprendre~ (attested early, “to take back, to blame”), from Latin ~reprehendere~ (“to seize again, to hold back, to reprove”), contracted in Vulgar Latin to ~reprendere~. The word is transparently ~re-~ (“back, again”) + ~prendere~, the popular form of ~prehendere~ (“to grasp, to seize”), itself ~prae-~ (“before”) + ~-hendere~ (“to grasp”). Latin ~prendere~ displaced classical ~capere~ across the Romance languages; cognate with Italian ~riprendere~ and Spanish ~reprender~.

The prefix ~re-~ carries both “again” and “back,” and ~reprendre~ exploits the whole spectrum: to take an object back, to resume an interrupted task (« reprendre le travail »), to take up a theme anew, to recover (« reprendre des forces »), and — preserving the Latin ~reprehendere~ sense of “to hold back, to check” — to reprimand someone. Commerce kept the literal grasp in ~repreneur~ (one who takes over a business) and ~reprise~ (a buy-back, a resumption, even a darned patch of cloth). The learned doublet ~répréhensible~ (“blameworthy”) descends from the same Latin verb, while ~prendre~, ~apprendre~, ~comprendre~, ~surprendre~, and ~entreprendre~ all share the grasping root.
en.repriser: Formed from the noun ~reprise~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, with the meaning “to darn.” The noun is the feminine past participle of ~reprendre~ used as a noun, attested in Old French as ~reprise~ or ~reprinse~ (“reproach, refrain”). The verb ~reprendre~ is itself ~re-~ + ~prendre~.
en.reprocher:
From Old French ~reprochier~ (attested 1132), from a Vulgar Latin *~repropiare~ (« to bring near, set before the eyes »), built on ~re-~ + a verb *~propiare~ (« to approach »), itself from Latin ~prope~ (« near »). The image is concrete: to « reproach » was first to bring a deed right up before someone's face. Romance cognates confirm the line — Spanish ~reprochar~ and, with a different prefix, Italian ~rimproverare~.

The development runs from « to set before the eyes » to « to confront with, » and so to the modern « to hold against, to blame »: one ~reproche~ a fault to a person, putting the misdeed under their nose. French syntax preserves the directional sense — « ~reprocher~ quelque chose à quelqu'un » literally moves the grievance toward the wrongdoer. The same ~prope~ underlies a wide family, including ~proche~ (« near »), ~approcher~ (« to approach »), ~prochain~ (« next, neighbor »), and ~rapprocher~ (« to bring closer »); ~reprocher~ is the one member that turned nearness into accusation.
en.reproduire:
Formed within French from ~produire~ (“to produce”) and the prefix ~re-~ (“again, anew”). ~Produire~ comes from Latin ~prōdūcere~ (“to lead forth, to bring forth”), from ~prō-~ (“forward”) and ~dūcere~ (“to lead”), from Proto-Indo-European *~dewk-~ (“to draw, to pull”). Cognate, through *~dewk-~, with English ~tow~ and ~tug~ and German ~ziehen~ (“to pull”), and with the Italian and Spanish counterparts ~riprodurre~ and ~reproducir~.

The core picture is a hand drawing something out into view: to ~produire~ is to “lead forth,” and to ~reproduire~ is to bring it forth again — hence “to copy, to depict faithfully, to breed.” The biological sense (animals that ~se reproduisent~) is a metaphor of repeated bringing-forth. From the same ~dūcere~ French inherited a long ~-duire~ family — ~conduire~, ~traduire~, ~séduire~, ~réduire~, ~induire~ — alongside ~duc~ (“duke,” a “leader”), ~conduit~, and ~aqueduc~. So a faithful ~reproduction~ is, etymologically, the same scene led out before the eyes once more.
en.reprogrammer: Formed from ~programmer~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”), so ~reprogrammer~ is “to program again” or “to reschedule.” The base ~programmer~ is built on the noun ~programme~, which French borrowed from Greek ~prógramma~ (“public written notice”), from ~prográphein~ (“to write publicly, to write beforehand”). The word moved from a notice to a printed schedule of events, and in the twentieth century to computer instructions, so ~reprogrammer~ can mean to move a screening or a meeting, or to rewrite software.
en.reprographier: ~Reprographier~ (“to photocopy”) is formed from the noun ~reprographie~ with the ending ~-er~. The noun is analyzed in French Wiktionary as a derivative of ~reprographe~ with the suffix ~-ie~, and in English Wiktionary as ~repro-~ (shortened from reproduction) + ~-graphie~. The second element ~-graphie~ comes from Greek ~graphein~ (“to write, to draw”), the same root as in ~photographie~. The word names the techniques of copying documents, and the verb applies them: to make a copy.
en.représenter:
From Latin ~repraesentare~, formed from the prefix ~re-~ and ~praesentare~ (“to make present, to present”). That verb derives from ~praesens~, the present participle of ~praesum~ — itself ~prae-~ (“before, in front of”) plus the verb of being, ~esse~ (“to be”). To “present” is thus, literally, to make something “be before” one's eyes; to ~repraesentare~ is to make it present again, to bring it back into view. The Romance descendants line up neatly: Italian ~rappresentare~, Spanish ~representar~, and French ~représenter~.

The Latin verb already carried the double charge that French keeps. In Roman usage ~repraesentare~ could mean “to pay on the spot, to deliver in person,” the sense of literal, physical presence; from there it slid toward “to depict, to portray, to stand for,” a sign standing in the place of an absent thing. Modern ~représenter~ holds both poles at once — an actor ~représente~ a character on stage, a deputy ~représente~ the voters, a painting ~représente~ a landscape. From the same family come ~présent~, ~présenter~, ~présence~, and the noun ~représentation~. To represent is to make the absent present once more.
en.repérer:
Denominal from the noun ~repère~ (“landmark, reference point”), with the verbal suffix. The noun has a tangled history. According to the TLFi, ~repère~ is the same word as ~repaire~ (“lair, den”); its ~-è-~ spelling, attested from 1676 in technical use, is a learned alteration made by associating the word with Latin ~reperire~ (“to find again, to recover”) — so the modern form was reshaped toward a Latin verb it does not actually descend from. ~Repaire~ itself comes from Old French ~repairier~ (“to return home”), traditionally referred to Late Latin ~repatriare~ (“to return to one's homeland,” from ~re-~ and ~patria~, “fatherland,” itself from ~pater~, “father”).

The development is a fine example of folk-etymological respelling. A ~repère~ began as a fixed point to which one returns and orients — a mark on a line, a survey benchmark — and ~repérer~ meant to set such marks. From there grew the modern senses: to locate, to spot, to detect. The “finding” feel of the word owes much to the very ~reperire~ that, the sources stress, shaped only its spelling and not its true descent. From the same ~patria~ family French has ~rapatrier~, ~patrie~, and ~patriote~.
en.repêcher: Formed from ~pêcher~ with the prefix ~re-~, so “to fish out again” and, more broadly, to pull something or someone back out of the water. The prefix is Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”), here with a sense of recovery. The base ~pêcher~ comes from Old French ~peschier~, inherited from Latin ~piscārī~ (“to fish”), a verb built on ~piscis~ (“fish”), which is a cousin of English ~fish~ and German ~Fisch~.
en.requalifier: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ (“again”) and the verb ~qualifier~. The base comes from Medieval Latin ~qualificare~, built on Latin ~qualis~ (“of what kind”) and ~facere~ (“to make”), so it meant “to make of a certain kind.” The prefix ~re-~ goes back to Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and here gives its usual sense of repetition. To ~requalifier~ is to give something a new qualification, whether a new designation or a different legal characterization.
en.requinquer:
The origin of ~requinquer~ is obscure. French Wiktionary reports that the word was popularized by a song from the time of Francis I, which mocked a coquettish old woman trying to dress up like a young one; its refrain ran “Requinquez-vous, vieille, requinquez-vous donc.” Some give it as Picard (compare ~quinquin~), but it was also known in Provence, and the verb exists in the speech of Touraine and Anjou and in Quebec.

A second, tentative proposal is that ~requinquer~ is a distortion of ~reclinquer~ (“to repair the planking of a clinker-built boat”), the way ~déglinguer~ would be a distortion of ~déclinquer~, its opposite. Neither account is settled, and they need not exclude each other. Today the verb means to perk someone up, to restore strength or spirits, and the reflexive ~se requinquer~ means to pick oneself up.
en.requérir:
French ~requérir~ rests on Latin ~requirere~ (“to seek, to ask after, to need”), the prefix ~re-~ (here intensive, “anew, urgently”) joined to ~quaerere~ (“to seek, to ask, to inquire”). In French the verb was actually rebuilt on the native ~quérir~ (“to fetch, to seek”), modelled on its Latin parent — which is why it keeps the awkward, archaic conjugation of ~quérir~ rather than the smoother shape of a fresh borrowing. ~Quaerere~ is traced to a Proto-Italic *~kʷaizō~ and, more deeply, to the Proto-Indo-European root *~kʷeh₂-~ (“to acquire”). Through ~requirere~, French is cousin to English ~require~ and ~request~.

The sense slid from plain seeking to formal demanding. To ~requérir~ is to call for something with authority or need: a situation ~requiert~ caution, and in court the ~procureur~ (public prosecutor) ~requiert~ a sentence — the technical heart of the word, preserved in the noun ~réquisitoire~ (“closing speech for the prosecution”). Old French ~requerre~ also carried the softer “to entreat, to court,” a shade still felt in ~requête~ (“a request, a petition”). The bare ~quaerere~ seeds a remarkable French harvest: ~quérir~, ~acquérir~ (“to acquire”), ~conquérir~ (“to conquer”), ~s'enquérir~ (“to inquire”), and the nouns ~question~, ~quête~, ~enquête~, and ~conquête~ — a whole vocabulary of seeking radiating from the same root as ~requérir~.
en.resaler: Formed from ~saler~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”): to ~resaler~ is to add more salt, or to salt a second time. The base ~saler~ comes from Latin ~sallire~ (“to salt”), built on ~sal~ (“salt”), the source of French ~sel~ and of ~salaire~ and ~salade~. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and here marks repetition.
en.resalir: ~Resalir~ is formed from ~salir~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”), and means to make dirty again. ~Salir~ comes from the adjective ~sale~ with the ending ~-ir~, and ~sale~ is of Germanic origin, from Frankish *~salu~ (“dull, dirty grey”), a relative of English ~sallow~. The prefix ~re-~ goes back to Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and marks repetition here.
en.rescinder:
Borrowed from Latin ~rescindere~, which French Wiktionary glosses as “to tear apart, to cut in two, to destroy, to annul.” The Latin verb is built from ~re-~ and ~scindere~ (“to cut, to split”). English took the same Latin verb as ~rescind~, so the two languages share both the word and its legal meaning.

In French, ~rescinder~ is a learned word of law and administration: to cancel an act, a contract or a judgment, as if cutting it away. The Latin verb ~scindere~ gave French ~scinder~ (“to split”) and ~scission~, and the noun ~rescision~ and the adjective ~rescisoire~ belong to the same family as ~rescinder~. The verb is rare outside legal prose, where it keeps the sense of annulling by cutting through what was done.
en.resemer: Formed from ~semer~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”): to sow again, to reseed. The base ~semer~ comes from Old French ~semer~, from Latin ~sēmināre~ (“to sow”), a verb drawn from ~sēmen~ (“seed”), which goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~seh₁-~ (“to sow”). Italian ~seminare~ and Spanish ~sembrar~ continue the Latin verb, and English ~sow~ and ~seed~ and German ~säen~ and ~Saat~ belong to the same root. The repetitive ~re-~ makes this a transparent formation.
en.resituer: ~Resituer~ is formed from ~situer~ and the prefix ~re-~ (“again”), with the sense “to put back in its place or context.” The base ~situer~ is a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ~situāre~ (“to place in a location”), built on the noun ~situs~ (“position”), which is the past participle of ~sinere~ (“to let, to leave in place”). English ~site~ and ~situate~ descend from the same ~situs~.
en.respectabiliser: Formed in French from the adjective ~respectable~ and the suffix ~-iser~, so the verb means “to make respectable.” The adjective is itself a derivative of the verb ~respecter~ with the suffix ~-able~, which expresses what can or deserves to be done, so the whole word stacks two suffixes on one verb. The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, from Greek, and is a productive way to coin verbs of the type “make A,” as in ~moderniser~ or ~actualiser~.
en.respecter:
From Latin ~respectāre~ (“to look back at, to keep in view, to take into account”), the frequentative of ~respicere~ (“to look back, to regard”), itself ~re-~ (“back”) + ~specere~ (“to look”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~spek̑-~ (“to observe, to watch”). The same root, through Latin ~specere~ and its noun ~speciēs~ (“appearance, sort”), gave French ~espèce~, ~spectacle~, and ~inspecter~; through Germanic it surfaces in German ~spähen~ (“to spy”) and English ~spy~.

The metaphor is one of looking: to respect something is, at root, to look back at it and hold it in view. French attests the modern verb only from 1554, in the sense « considérer comme une chose dont on doit tenir compte »; the sense « honorer », to show deference, follows by 1566, and « préserver, ne pas porter atteinte à » by 1573. The deadline sense in English — respecter un délai, « to meet a deadline » — extends the idea of scrupulously observing what is laid down. Older Old French had cousins like ~respitier~ (“to spare”), the ancestor of ~répit~ (“respite”). The same root *~spek̑-~ stands behind a sprawling French family: ~aspect~, ~suspect~, ~perspective~, ~spécial~, and the noun ~respect~ itself.
en.respirer:
Attested from the twelfth century, from Latin ~respirare~ (“to breathe back, to breathe again”), formed from ~re-~ (“again, back”) and ~spirare~ (“to breathe, to blow”). The origin of ~spirare~ is uncertain: De Vaan judges it probably onomatopoeic — an imitation of the sound of breath — while Kroonen would connect it to a PIE *~(s)peys-~ (“to blow, breathe”) and to Proto-Germanic *~fīsaną~. Through the same Latin verb, English gained ~inspire~, ~aspire~, and ~conspire~, all of them, at root, ways of breathing.

The ~re-~ in ~respirer~ suggests a breath drawn back in, the steady rhythm of inhaling once more; figuratively, to ~respirer~ is to take a breather, to feel relief. The root spirals out through French in a remarkable range of words: ~respiration~, ~soupir~ (“a sigh”), ~esprit~ (“spirit, mind” — once a “breath”), ~inspirer~, ~expirer~ (which means both to breathe out and to die), and ~aspirer~. Across this whole family runs the old intuition that breath and spirit are the same thing.
en.resplendir: ~Resplendir~ comes from Latin ~resplendēre~, a verb formed from ~splendēre~ (“to shine”) with the prefix ~re-~. The same Latin base gave French ~splendeur~ and ~splendide~, and English ~splendid~ and ~splendour~. Italian has the parallel ~risplendere~. French gave the verb its ~-ir~ ending, and it is conjugated like ~finir~, with the ~-iss-~ forms, as in ~resplendissant~ (“radiant”).
en.responsabiliser: Formed in French from the adjective ~responsable~ and the suffix ~-iser~, in the sense “to make A”: to ~responsabiliser~ someone is to make them responsible, by giving them duties and the trust that goes with them. The adjective ~responsable~ comes from Middle French and was built on ~réponse~ (“answer”) plus ~-able~, so a responsible person is one who can be called to answer. French Wiktionary traces it to Latin ~responsus~, a form of the verb for answering. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which had transcribed Greek verbs, and it is highly productive in administrative French.
en.resquiller:
~Resquiller~ is borrowed from Occitan ~resquilhar~ (“to slip, to slide”), a verb that French Wiktionary derives from Occitan ~esquilhar~. English Wiktionary gives the same chain through the noun form ~resquilha~, which it traces to ~esquilha~, and neither source goes back further than that. Occitan is the Romance language of southern France, so the word came into French as a borrowing from a regional tongue, not as an inheritance from Latin through Old French.

In modern French the verb has settled on a family of related senses: to sneak in without paying, whether onto public transport or into an event, and to jump a queue. The sources do not document how the meaning moved from the Occitan “slipping” to these uses, though the idea of getting through unnoticed fits all of them. The agent noun ~resquilleur~ names the person who does it.
en.ressaigner: Formed from ~saigner~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”): to bleed once more. The base ~saigner~ comes from Old French ~saignier~, from Latin ~sanguināre~ (“to bleed”), built on ~sanguis~ (“blood”), which also gave French ~sang~. Spanish and Portuguese ~sangrar~ and Italian ~sanguinare~ are cousins.
en.ressaisir: Formed from ~saisir~ with the prefix ~re-~, “again”: to ~ressaisir~ is to seize again, or to recover what was lost. The base ~saisir~ comes from Old French and from Medieval Latin ~sacire~ (“to take possession”), a word of Germanic origin, probably from Frankish *~sakjan~. Its first sense was legal, putting someone in possession of property. The reflexive ~se ressaisir~ has the figurative sense of pulling oneself together, regaining one's composure.
en.ressasser: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ (“again”) and ~sasser~ (“to sieve”), which is built on the noun ~sas~ (“sieve”). The noun comes from Old French ~saaz~, from Medieval Latin ~setacium~, derived from Latin ~saeta~ (“bristle, horsehair”), the stiff hair from which sieves were once made. So ~ressasser~ is literally “to sift again,” and the modern verb means to go over the same things again and again, to rehash a thought or a grievance.
en.ressauter: Formed from ~sauter~ with the prefix ~re-~, to jump again. The base ~sauter~ comes from Latin ~saltāre~ (“to dance, to leap”), the frequentative of ~salīre~ (“to jump”), literally “to keep jumping.” The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and here marks repetition. The Latin verb ~salīre~ itself survives in the more learned ~saillir~.
en.ressembler:
French ~ressembler~ is built within French itself: it is ~sembler~ (“to seem”) plus the intensive prefix ~re-~, formed in Old French. ~Sembler~ descends from Latin ~similāre~ (a variant of ~simulāre~, “to imitate, to copy”), itself from the adjective ~similis~ (“like, similar”). That adjective goes back through Proto-Italic *~semalis~ to a Proto-Indo-European root *~sem-~ (“one, together”), the same root that yields notions of sameness and unity. Cognates run wide: Ancient Greek ~homós~ (“same”) and ~homalós~ (“even”), and through Romance, Italian ~rassomigliare~ and Spanish ~semejar~. English borrowed the learned ~similar~ and ~simulate~ from the same Latin stock.

In Old French ~sembler~ meant “to seem, to appear,” and adding ~re-~ pushed it toward “to seem like one another,” hence “to resemble.” The pair drifted apart in sense: today ~sembler~ is about appearance (“Il semble fatigué,” “he seems tired”) while ~ressembler~ is about likeness, and it keeps the telltale preposition à — one resembles ~à~ someone. The root *~sem-~ is astonishingly productive in French through several channels: the native ~sembler~, ~semblable~, ~ensemble~ (“together,” literally “in one”), and ~assembler~; and the learned ~similaire~, ~similitude~, ~simuler~, and ~dissimuler~. Even ~simple~ belongs here, “one-fold.” The humble verb for looking alike thus sits at the heart of a family all about oneness and sameness.
en.ressemeler: Formed from ~semeler~ (“to sole”) with the prefix ~re-~ in its ordinary sense of “again”: to put a new sole on a shoe. The base ~semeler~ means to fit a shoe with a sole, so ~ressemeler~ is the cobbler's repair, done once the first sole has worn through. The doubled s keeps the prefix pronounced [ʁə] before the base's initial s.
en.ressemer: Formed from the prefix ~re-~, which marks repetition, and the verb ~semer~ (“to sow”), so “to sow again.” The base ~semer~ comes from Latin ~sēmināre~, a verb built on ~sēmen~ (“seed”), which is also the source of French ~semence~ (“seed”). The prefix and the base keep their separate senses here, so the verb is a transparent formation within French.
en.ressentir:
French ~ressentir~ was coined within French, around 1190, from ~sentir~ (“to feel, to sense”) plus the prefix ~re-~. ~Sentir~ descends from Latin ~sentīre~ (“to feel, to perceive, to be of an opinion”), which goes back through Proto-Italic *~sentjō~ to a Proto-Indo-European root *~sent-~ (“to feel, to go, to head for”). The root's reach is long: Old High German ~sinnan~ (“to strive, to desire”) and modern German ~Sinn~ (“sense, meaning”) are cousins, and through Old French ~sentir~ English drew ~sense~, ~scent~, and ~sentiment~. Italian ~risentire~ and Spanish ~resentir~ mirror the French compound.

The prefix ~re-~ here is intensive rather than repetitive: ~ressentir~ is to feel something deeply, inwardly, often an emotion — ~ressentir de la joie~, ~ressentir de la douleur~. That inward force gave the noun ~ressentiment~ (“resentment”), a feeling re-felt and brooded over, which French lent to English and which philosophers later adopted untranslated. The PIE root *~sent-~, with its double sense of “feeling” and “heading toward,” seeded a remarkably broad French family: ~sentir~, ~sentiment~, ~sensible~, ~sensation~, ~consentir~ (“to feel together,” to agree), ~pressentir~ (“to sense beforehand”), ~assentiment~, and the learned ~sens~ itself. To resent, in French, is simply to feel something all the way through.
en.resserrer: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ and the verb ~serrer~. The base comes from Old French ~serrer~ (“to close, lock fast”), from Late Latin ~serāre~ (“to bar”), from Latin ~sera~ (“a bolt or bar for a door”). The prefix ~re-~ (Latin “back, again”) adds the idea of doing it again, or of drawing something tighter still. So ~resserrer~ means to tighten again or further: to narrow a gap, to draw bonds closer. The same bolted door gives French ~serrure~ (“lock”).
