en.resservir: ~Resservir~ is formed from the prefix ~re-~ and ~servir~ (“to serve”), and means to serve again, whether a second helping at table or an object put back into use. ~Servir~ is inherited from Latin ~servire~ (“to serve”), a verb derived from ~servus~ (“slave, servant”), and it lives on as Italian ~servire~ and Spanish ~servir~. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and marks repetition here.
en.ressortir:
From ~re-~ + ~sortir~ (« to go out »), literally « to go out again. » The descent of ~sortir~ itself is disputed: Littré derived it from a Vulgar Latin *~surrectire~, from Latin ~surrectus~ (« raised up »), which would make it a doublet of ~sourdre~ (« to well up ») from ~surgere~; the TLFi instead ties it to ~sortiri~ (« to draw lots »), from ~sors~ (« lot, fate »). The sources do not settle the matter, so the prefixed ~ressortir~ inherits that uncertainty.

A separate, homographic ~ressortir~ — « to fall under the jurisdiction of » — comes not from ~sortir~ but from the noun ~ressort~ (« jurisdiction, spring »); the Académie française condemns conjugating that legal sense like a third-group verb. The everyday verb ranges from the literal (to step back outside, to take something out again) to the figurative « to stand out, » as a color ~ressort~ against a background. Kin of the contested base survive in ~sortie~ and, if the ~sors~ account holds, in ~sort~ (« fate ») and ~sorte~ (« kind »).
en.ressouder: Formed from ~souder~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”), so “to solder or weld back together.” The base ~souder~ comes from Old French ~solder~, inherited from Latin ~solidāre~ (“to make solid”), a verb built on the adjective ~solidus~ (“solid”). The ~l~ before the ~d~ turned into a vowel ~u~, giving ~souder~, and English ~solder~ was borrowed from the Old French verb. The prefix ~re-~, from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”), here expresses repetition: to join again what has come apart. It also serves figuratively for people or groups drawn back together.
en.ressourcer: Formed in French from the noun ~ressource~ and the suffix ~-er~, and used today above all in the reflexive ~se ressourcer~, to recover one's strength or energy. The base ~ressource~ comes from Old French ~resource~, the feminine past participle used as a noun of the old verb ~resourdre~ (“to rise again, to be restored”). English Wiktionary traces the same idea to Latin ~resurgere~ (“to rise again”), made of ~re-~ (“again”) and ~surgere~ (“to rise”). A resource was therefore first something that raises one up again. The suffix ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~.
en.ressouvenir: Formed from ~souvenir~ with the prefix ~re-~, which here adds the idea of calling something back to mind again. The base comes from Latin ~subvenīre~ (“to come up, to come to one's aid”), made of ~sub-~ (“under”) and ~venīre~ (“to come”), through Old French ~sovenir~: a memory comes up from below into the mind. The same ~venīre~ lies behind ~venir~, ~revenir~ and ~convenir~.
en.ressuer: ~Ressuer~ is formed from ~suer~ with the prefix ~re-~. The base ~suer~ is inherited from Latin ~sūdāre~ (“to sweat”), and French used it for anything that oozes, such as walls, cheese or stone. ~Ressuer~ applies the same idea to moisture escaping from a thing, with ~re-~ adding the sense of renewed or further release. Here ~re-~ is not a plain repetition marker, which is why the verb reads as its own word.
en.ressurgir:
French ~ressurgir~ is borrowed from Latin ~resurgere~ (“to rise again”), a compound of ~re-~ (“again”) and ~surgere~ (“to rise”). Wiktionary also notes that, by surface analysis, the verb can be read as ~re-~ + ~surgir~. Latin ~surgere~ is itself generally explained as a contraction of ~sub-~ and ~regere~ (“to direct, to keep straight”), so that the verb means “to lift oneself up.” Italian ~risorgere~ and Spanish ~resurgir~ are the counterparts of the French verb.

The sense stayed close to the Latin: to come up again after having disappeared, as a memory, a conflict or a tradition does. The simple verb ~surgir~ has the same source, and so do ~insurrection~ (a rising against authority) and ~résurrection~, which comes from the Latin noun built on ~resurgere~. Even the noun ~source~ belongs to the family: it is the old past participle of ~sourdre~, an inherited French form of ~surgere~, a verb that survives only as a literary term for water welling up.
en.ressusciter: Borrowed from Latin ~resuscitāre~ (“to rouse again, to revive”). By standard analysis, the Latin verb is ~re-~ (“again”) + ~suscitāre~ (“to raise up, to stir”), which is why French also has the shorter verb ~susciter~. English ~resuscitate~ comes from the same Latin verb, and Italian ~risuscitare~ and Spanish ~resucitar~ continue it. The meaning “to bring back to life” is the one French ~ressusciter~ keeps, whether said of the dead or, figuratively, of a custom or an idea.
en.ressuyer:
From Old French ~ressuiier~, formed from the prefix ~re-~ and ~essuyer~. The base ~essuyer~ comes from Latin ~exsūcāre~ (“to extract the juice”), built from ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~sūcus~ (“juice, sap”). So ~ressuyer~ originally meant something like “to wring the moisture out again,” and it has come to mean to dry, or to become dry, as a damp surface or crop does after rain.

The verb belongs to practical vocabulary. It is used of things left to dry, such as shallots or wood, and figuratively of someone recovering from a setback. It is a close relative of ~essuyer~ (“to wipe, to dry”), which is more common and keeps the transitive sense of wiping something dry. Both verbs are descendants of Latin ~exsūcāre~, and both thus keep the old idea of drawing the juice out of something.
en.restaurer:
From Latin ~restaurare~ (“to rebuild, repair, renew”), formed on ~re-~ (“again”) plus a ~-staurare~ element also seen in ~instaurare~ (“to set up, establish”). The verb passed through Old French and survives in Italian ~restaurare~ and Spanish ~restaurar~; English borrowed it twice over, as ~restore~ and ~restaurant~.

The culinary detour is the surprise. In the eighteenth century a ~restaurant~ was not a place but a thing: a ~restaurant~ was a rich, fortifying broth meant to “restore” the strength of the weak — a restorative. A Parisian bouillon-seller is traditionally said to have advertised such restoratives, and the word for the broth slid to the establishment that served it, then to any eatery, before being re-exported across the world. Meanwhile the older sense thrives: one ~restaure~ a painting, a building, a monarchy. From the same Latin source French keeps ~restauration~ (both “restoration” and “catering”), ~restaurateur~ (“restorer” and “restaurant-keeper” alike), and the doublet ~instaurer~ (“to institute, establish”), its near-twin built on the same root.
en.rester:
Attested from the twelfth century, borrowed from Latin ~restāre~ (“to stay behind, to remain, to be left over”), formed from the prefix ~re-~ and ~stāre~ (“to stand, to stand firm”). Latin ~stāre~ comes from Proto-Italic *~stāō~ and from the Proto-Indo-European root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”), one of the most fertile roots in the language family. Through ~stāre~, ~rester~ is a sibling of Italian ~restare~ and Spanish ~restar~ and ~quedar~, and, through the same PIE root, a distant cousin of English ~stand~ and ~stay~.

The word's logic is spatial: what ~restāre~ described was standing back, holding one's ground while others moved on — hence “to remain.” Old French already had the inherited ~ester~ from ~stāre~, and ~rester~ (~re-~ + ~ester~) eventually displaced it as the everyday verb of staying. A trace of the “left over” sense survives in arithmetic, where French children say ~il reste~ for a remainder. The root *~steh₂-~ stocks French with a vast family: ~stable~, ~station~, ~statue~, ~constant~, ~rester~ itself, and — surprisingly — the past participle ~été~ of ~être~, which descends not from ~esse~ but from ~status~, the participle of ~stāre~.
en.restituer:
Borrowed in the 13th century from Latin ~restituere~ (“to set up again, put back in place, restore”), from ~re-~ (“back, again”) + ~statuere~ (“to set up, establish”), itself built on ~status~, from ~stāre~ (“to stand”), PIE root *~steh₂-~. Cognate with Italian ~restituire~, Spanish ~restituir~ and English ~restitution~, which reached English through French. The verb belongs to the tidy French squad in ~-stituer~, all of them ways of making something stand: ~constituer~ (“set up together”), ~instituer~ (“set in place”), ~destituer~ (“make someone cease to stand in office”), ~substituer~ (“set one thing in another's place”).

The TLFi's record of senses reads like the program of a single idea — making what fell stand again. First the law: to give back what was wrongfully taken (13th century). Then to restore something to its earlier state (circa 1355); to reconstruct a corrupted or missing passage of text (1690); to redraw a ruined monument on paper (1835); to make the past live again in thought (1849); finally to reproduce faithfully — a recording that gives back timbre and detail (late 19th century). All these senses are still alive: philologists restitute lost readings, archaeologists restitute temples, museums debate the restitution of looted art, and sound engineers promise un son fidèlement restitué. Around the verb stand the kin of ~stāre~: ~statue~, ~statut~, ~station~ — and ~état~ itself, from Latin ~status~ via Old French ~estat~: the State, etymologically, is simply “a standing.” To restitute is the root's promise kept: what once stood will be made to stand again.
en.restreindre:
From Middle French ~restraindre~, from Latin ~restringere~ (“to bind back, draw tight”), formed from ~re-~ and ~stringere~ (“to draw tight, bind”). The Proto-Italic ~stringō~ blended two Proto-Indo-European roots: *~strengʰ-~ (“to twist, tie”) and *~streyg-~ (“to stroke, strip off”). Through Old French ~estreindre~ this verb is cognate with English ~strain~, ~strict~, and ~stringent~, and the same family connects to ~strong~.

The Latin sense was physical — to pull something tight — and French kept that grip: to ~restreindre~ is to narrow, limit, or hold in check. The doublet ~étreindre~ (“to embrace, clasp”) preserves the literal tightening, while ~restreindre~ took the figurative path toward restriction. From the same root French gathers a notable cluster: ~restriction~, ~astreindre~, ~contraindre~, and ~étreinte~ — a whole vocabulary of binding, squeezing, and compulsion grown from one idea of drawing a cord taut.
en.restructurer: Formed from ~re-~ and ~structurer~, “to structure again.” The base is a verb built in French on the noun ~structure~, from Latin ~strūctūra~ (“a building, a fitting-together”), the action noun of ~struere~ (“to pile up, to build”), a verb related to English ~strew~. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and here marks repetition: to give a company, a debt or a text a new arrangement. The family of ~struere~ also gives ~construire~, ~détruire~ and ~instruire~.
en.resurgir: ~Resurgir~ is formed from ~surgir~ and the prefix ~re-~ (“again”), so it means “to surge up again,” “to reappear.” Its base ~surgir~ goes back to Latin ~surgere~ (“to rise”), a contraction of ~surrigere~ (~sub-~ plus ~regere~), and entered French as a sailors' word in the fifteenth century. Latin already had a parallel ~resurgere~ (“to rise again”), which gave French ~ressource~ and ~résurrection~, so the modern verb recreates in French what Latin had said long before. Memories, doubts and old quarrels all ~resurgir~.
en.retailler:
~Retailler~ is the old verb ~tailler~ with the prefix ~re-~, and it was already used in Old French as ~retaillier~. The base comes from Old French ~talier~, from Late Latin ~taliare~ (“to cut, to split”), a verb derived from Latin ~talea~ (“cutting, slip, rod”), the shoot a gardener cuts off to replant. The deeper origin of ~talea~ is disputed: it is traditionally tied to a Proto-Indo-European root *~teh₂l-~ (“young shoot”), but a proposed Greek cognate is doubtful and another account links it to ~tālus~ (“ankle”). The prefix is Latin ~re-~ (“again”).

The verb began in the garden, with cutting and pruning, then spread to shaping stone, cloth, gems and cards. ~Retailler~ keeps the plain sense of cutting again: to recut a stone, to trim a garment once more. The same root gave French ~taille~, ~tailleur~, ~entaille~, ~détail~ (literally a cutting up into small pieces), ~taille-crayon~ and ~tailloir~. Italian ~tagliare~ and Spanish ~tajar~ descend from the same ~taliare~, so the verb has close cousins across the Romance languages.
en.retaper: Formed from ~taper~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”). Its senses include “to retype” (keyboard typing being one use of ~taper~) and the familiar “to revamp, to refurbish.” ~Taper~ is first attested in the 13th century and rests on an onomatopoeia imitating a short dull knock. A link to German ~tappen~, proposed by Friedrich Diez, is only a suggested connection, not an established descent.
en.retapisser: ~Retapisser~ is formed from ~tapisser~ with the prefix ~re-~, so “to cover again,” here in the sense of reupholstering a seat or re-covering a wall. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and carries its plain sense of repetition, as it does in ~refaire~ or ~repasser~. The base ~tapisser~ is itself the verb for lining a surface with tapestry or fabric, so the new verb simply says that the covering is done a second time.
en.retarder:
French ~retarder~ comes from Latin ~retardāre~ (“to delay, to hold back”), a compound of ~re-~ and ~tardāre~, itself from the adjective ~tardus~ (“slow, late”). English Wiktionary classes the French verb as inherited from Latin, so ~retardāre~ was already a Latin word and not a French formation. Italian ~ritardare~ and Spanish ~retardar~ are its cousins.

Since ~tardus~ is the base, ~retarder~ belongs to the same family as ~tard~ (“late”), ~tardif~ (“late, slow”) and ~tarder~ (“to delay”). It also gives the noun ~retard~ (“delay”) and the adjective ~retardataire~. English ~retard~ and ~retardation~ are relatives borrowed from the Latin verb. The ~re-~ here is the Latin prefix, so the verb is a fossil of Latin and not a French ~re-~ + ~tarder~ derivation, even though the two analyses give nearly the same meaning.
en.retendre: ~Retendre~ is ~tendre~ with the prefix ~re-~: to stretch or tighten again, as when one retightens a rope. ~Tendre~ comes from Latin ~tendere~ (“to stretch, to extend”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ten-~ (“to stretch”), which is also the source of English ~thin~. The prefix goes back to Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”).
en.retenir:
From Latin ~retinere~ (“to hold back, to keep”), a compound of the prefix ~re-~ (“back”) and ~tenere~ (“to hold”). Latin ~tenere~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ten-~ (“to stretch”), the notion being that to hold is to keep something stretched taut. The same root gave Latin ~tendere~ (“to stretch”), Greek ~teinein~ (“to stretch”), Sanskrit ~tanoti~ (“stretches”), and English ~thin~; the compound parallels Italian ~ritenere~ and Spanish ~retener~.

~Retenir~ fans out across many senses, all from “to hold back”: to retain or keep (~retenir une place~, “to reserve a seat”), to hold someone back (~retenir quelqu'un~), to hold back a feeling (~retenir ses larmes~, “to hold back one's tears”), in arithmetic “to carry” a digit, and — most usefully for a learner — “to remember,” to hold something in the mind. The noun ~retenue~ means both “restraint, reserve” and a school “detention.” From ~tenere~ comes a great family: ~tenir~, ~tenue~, ~contenir~, ~maintenir~, ~obtenir~, ~soutenir~, ~entretenir~, and ~appartenir~ — and, through the kindred ~tendere~, ~tendre~, ~tension~, and ~tente~.
en.retenter: French Wiktionary derives ~retenter~ from Latin ~retentāre~ (“to try again”), while English Wiktionary analyzes it simply as ~re-~ + ~tenter~. Either way the sense is plain. The prefix ~re-~ conveys repetition, “again,” and ~tenter~ is the verb “to try, attempt,” from Latin ~temptāre~ (“to try, test”). So ~retenter~ means to make another attempt at something that failed the first time.
en.retentir:
The verb is formed from the prefix ~re-~ and Old French ~tentir~ (“to give out a sound”), which was built on the participle of Latin ~tinnīre~ (“to ring, to jingle”). The form of that participle is ~tinnitus~, and French Wiktionary notes that ~tentir~ is a lexical doublet of ~tinter~, which developed from the same Latin verb. English preserves the Latin participle almost unchanged in the medical term ~tinnitus~, the ringing in the ears. The Latin verb is imitative: its sound mimics the jingle it describes.

In Old French, ~tentir~ meant to ring or resound, and ~re-~ added the idea of an echo or a sound sent back, so ~retentir~ is to resound, to ring out. Simple ~tentir~ later disappeared, leaving ~tinter~ for the bell and ~retentir~ for the louder, longer noise: a trumpet, a shot, a cry. The verb then took a figurative turn. A word, a piece of news or an event can ~retentir~ in the mind or on a situation, meaning to have repercussions, as in ~retentir sur la santé~ (“to affect one's health”). The family also gave ~retentissant~ (“resounding, far-reaching”) and ~retentissement~ (“echo, repercussion”), both used just as often of fame as of noise.
en.retercer: Formed from ~tercer~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”), meaning to do the operation once more. The base ~tercer~ is a farming verb, “to plow a field a third time,” built on ~tiers~ (“third”), from Latin ~tertius~, and ~ter~ (“three times”). ~Retercer~ also means “to remove weeds,” a sense of field work that grows out of this counting of workings of the soil.
en.retirer:
A French formation, ~re-~ (“back, again”) + ~tirer~ (“to pull, to draw”), built within Old French and gradually displacing the older ~retraire~ (from Latin ~retrahere~, “to draw back”). The base ~tirer~ has a famously disputed origin: many trace it, with Spanish ~tirar~, to a Germanic source, while others derive it from a reanalysis of Old French ~martirier~ (“to torture, to martyr”), from ~martyre~ — the present participle ~martirant~ supposedly re-cut as ~mar~ (“badly”) + a form linked to ~tirant~.

Whatever its root, ~tirer~ supplanted the Latin-derived ~traire~ (from ~trahere~, “to pull”) across much of its territory, and ~retirer~ rode that wave. The literal core is “to pull back”: one ~retire~ a hand, a sword, a candidate from a race. From there spread the senses “to remove, to take off” (clothing), “to withdraw” (money from a bank), and the reflexive ~se retirer~, “to withdraw, to retire from the world.” The same field of ~tirer~ and ~trahere~ yields ~attirer~, ~soutirer~, ~étirer~, ~tiroir~, and — from the Latin side — ~extraire~ and ~soustraire~.
en.retisser: Formed in French from ~re-~ and ~tisser~ (“to weave”), so literally “to weave again.” The prefix ~re-~ goes back to Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and here simply marks repetition, as in ~refaire~ or ~repasser~. The base ~tisser~ is a regularized form: it descends from Latin ~texō~ (“to weave”) through the Old French strong verb ~tistre~, which was reshaped as ~tissir~ and then moved into the first conjugation. The same Latin verb also lies behind ~texte~ and ~textile~.
en.retomber: Formed from ~tomber~ and the prefix ~re-~ (“back, again”), here in its senses of repetition and return to a former state or place: to fall again, to fall back down. The base verb has a lively history of its own. It comes from an expressive Vulgar Latin *~tumbāre~, which merged in Old French with ~tumer~ (“to tumble”), a verb of Frankish origin. From the fifteenth century ~tomber~ pressed in on the older ~choir~ and eventually ousted it from everyday speech, which left ~tomber~ free to build compounds such as ~retomber~ on its own.
en.retordre: Formed from ~tordre~ and the prefix ~re-~ (“again, back”), so literally “to twist again” or “to twist further.” Some accounts see in it a direct descent from Latin ~retorquēre~ (“to twist back”), built on the same ~torquēre~ that gave ~tordre~; either way the sense is the same. The verb is best known today in the phrase ~donner du fil à retordre~ (“to cause someone a lot of trouble”), literally “to give thread to twist again.”
en.retoucher: ~Retoucher~ is formed from ~toucher~ with the prefix ~re-~, “again.” The base comes from Old French ~tochier~, from Vulgar Latin *~toccāre~ (“to knock, to strike”), which is generally held to be imitative of the sound ~toc~. So ~retoucher~ first meant simply “to touch again.” It then took the specialized sense of going back over a finished work to correct it, as a painter does with a canvas, a photographer with a picture or a tailor with a garment.
en.retourner:
From Old French ~torner~, ~tourner~ (“to turn”) prefixed with ~re-~ (“again, back”). The base verb descends from Latin ~tornāre~ (“to turn on a lathe, to round off, to fashion”), from ~tornus~ (“lathe”), itself borrowed from Greek ~tórnos~ (“a lathe, a tool for drawing circles”), traced to the Proto-Indo-European root *~terh₁-~ (“to rub, to turn, to bore”). Through ~tornāre~ the family includes Italian ~tornare~, Spanish ~tornar~, and English ~turn~ and ~tourney~.

The original image is the craftsman's lathe, shaping wood or metal as it spins — so ~tourner~ began as “to turn on a wheel” and broadened to every kind of turning. With ~re-~, ~retourner~ covers both turning over (~retourner une crêpe~, to flip a pancake; ~retourner la terre~, to turn the soil) and going back (~retourner chez soi~, to return home), and reflexively ~se retourner~ is to turn around or, of a sleeper, to toss. The verb can even mean to shake someone emotionally — ~ça m'a retourné~, “it turned me upside down.” The lathe-root spread widely in French: ~tour~ (a turn, a lap, a trick — and, as a feminine noun, a tower by a different route), ~tournoi~ (a tournament, where contestants wheeled about), ~tournevis~ (screwdriver), ~contour~, ~détour~, and ~retour~ (a return) all turn on the same Greek lathe.
en.retracer:
Formed within French from the prefix ~re-~ and ~tracer~ (“to trace, to draw”), itself from Old French ~tracier~, from Vulgar Latin *~tractiāre~ (“to follow a track”), built on ~tractus~, past participle of Latin ~trahere~ (“to pull, to drag”). The deeper origin of ~trahere~ is genuinely obscure: some scholars connect it with the Germanic family of English ~drag~ and ~draw~ (Proto-Germanic *~draganą~), but the sound correspondences are irregular, and others prefer to see a loanword from some lost pre-Indo-European language — the question remains open. Cognate with Italian ~tracciare~ and Spanish ~trazar~; English ~trace~ was itself borrowed from the French verb.

The verb's own history runs from the hunt to the memoir. Around 1390, ~retracier~ meant “to follow someone's trail, to pursue”; in the sixteenth century it settled into “to draw anew”; and from the mid-seventeenth century it took on the sense that dominates today — to recount events, to call them back in words. To retrace a life is thus, etymologically, to follow its tracks a second time. The parent ~trahere~ is one of the great providers of French vocabulary: from it descend ~traire~ (“to milk” — to draw the milk), ~trait~, ~portrait~ (a likeness “drawn forth”), ~traiter~ (from the frequentative ~tractāre~, “to handle”), ~traîner~, ~train~, and the learned squad ~extraire~, ~soustraire~, ~distraire~ and ~abstraire~ — to distract someone being, literally, to drag their mind elsewhere. English worked the same vein with ~tract~, ~tractor~ and ~attract~, alongside the French loans ~trace~ and ~train~.
en.retraduire: ~Retraduire~ is formed from ~traduire~ (“to translate”) with the prefix ~re-~, in its common sense of repetition: to translate again. ~Traduire~ comes from Latin ~traducere~ (“to lead across”), from ~trans-~ (“across”) and ~ducere~ (“to lead”). The prefix goes back to Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”).
en.retraiter: ~Retraiter~ has two separate formations. In the first, French added ~-er~ to the noun ~retraite~ to make a verb meaning “to retire someone, to pension off.” In the second, it joined ~re-~ (“again”) to ~traiter~, giving “to treat again,” hence “to reprocess,” as with nuclear fuel, waste or data. The base ~traiter~ comes from Latin ~tractāre~ (“to handle, to deal with”), a frequentative of ~trahere~ (“to draw”), and is related to Italian ~trattare~ and Spanish ~tratar~. The prefix ~re-~ here keeps its plain repeating sense.
en.retrancher: Formed in French from ~re-~ and ~trancher~ (“to cut”). The prefix does not mean cutting again here; it points toward removal, so ~retrancher~ means “to cut off, to deduct, to remove.” The base ~trancher~ comes from Old French ~trenchier~, whose Latin source is uncertain: by one account a Vulgar Latin *~trinicare~ (“to cut in three”), by another an alteration of ~truncare~ (“to lop”). English ~retrench~ belongs to the same family of Old French verbs and keeps the sense of cutting back expenses.
en.retranscrire: Formed from ~transcrire~ with the prefix ~re-~, meaning “again”: to transcribe once more, or to put down afresh. The base is borrowed from Latin ~trānscrībere~, from ~trāns-~ (“across”) and ~scrībere~ (“to write”), so the root image is carrying a text across from one form to another. English ~transcribe~ is a learned borrowing of the same Latin verb. The Latin ~scrībere~ also gave French ~écrire~ and a large family, among them ~décrire~, ~inscrire~ and ~prescrire~. ~Retranscrire~ is used of redoing a recording, a score or a copy in a register.
en.retransmettre: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ and the verb ~transmettre~, which French reshaped from Latin ~transmittere~ (“to send across”), made of ~trans-~ (“across”) and ~mittere~ (“to send”). Here ~re-~ expresses repetition, so ~retransmettre~ is to transmit again: to pass a message, an order or a signal on a second time, or to relay it onward. The verb is especially common for relaying an event or a broadcast. French ~transmettre~ and English ~transmit~ share the same Latin source.
en.retravailler: Formed from ~travailler~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”): to rework a text, a piece of metal or a design, or to go back to work. The base comes from Old French ~traveillier~ (“to torment, to cause suffering”), traditionally explained from Vulgar Latin *~tripāliāre~, “to torture with the ~tripalium~,” a device of three stakes. That tidy story is disputed, and some scholars prefer a Late Latin *~trabicula~ (“little beam”) as the source. Whichever is right, the verb travelled from “to torment” to “to toil” to today's neutral “to work,” and ~retravailler~ simply repeats it.
en.retraverser: ~Retraverser~ is ~traverser~ with the prefix ~re-~: to cross again. ~Traverser~ comes from Old French ~traverser~, from Late Latin ~traversare~, a worn-down form of ~transversare~, from the adjective ~transversus~ (“lying across”), which is built on ~trans~ (“across”) and ~vertere~ (“to turn”). The prefix goes back to Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”).
en.retreindre: ~Retreindre~ (“to hammer into shape”) is a metalworking term that is the same word as ~restreindre~, altered in technical speech. By its form it ought logically to be pronounced ~rétreindre~, and that variant does exist. The underlying verb ~restreindre~ comes from Latin ~restringere~, built from ~re-~ and ~stringere~ (“to bind tight”), the verb behind ~étreindre~ and ~contraindre~ as well.
en.retremper: ~Retremper~ is formed from the prefix ~re-~ (“again”) and ~tremper~, so its basic sense is to dip or soak again. ~Tremper~ comes from Middle French, a metathesis of Old French ~temprer~, from Latin ~temperāre~ (“to mix in due proportion, to moderate”), and is a doublet of the learned ~tempérer~. Beyond the literal dipping again, the verb has a figurative sense: to brace up or reenergize.
en.retrousser: Formed in French from ~trousser~ with the prefix ~re-~. The base ~trousser~ comes from Old French ~trusser~, which goes back, with metathesis, to a Vulgar Latin *~torsāre~ built on *~torsus~, a variant of ~tortus~, the participle of Latin ~torqueō~ (“to twist”). The same Latin verb gave French ~tordre~ and English ~torque~ and ~torture~. The prefix ~re-~ (“back, again”) here points upward and backward, so ~retrousser~ means to hitch up or roll up a garment or sleeve. It belongs to a family with ~trousse~ (“kit, case”) and ~trousseau~.
en.retrouver:
From ~re-~ (“again, back”) + ~trouver~ (“to find”), the latter from Vulgar Latin *~tropāre~ (“to compose, invent a melody,” hence “to invent, devise, find”), from Late Latin ~tropus~ (“figure of speech, melody”), borrowed from Greek ~tropos~ (“turn, way, mode”), from ~trepein~ (“to turn”). Cognate with Italian ~trovare~ and Occitan ~trobar~ — the verb that gave ~troubadour~, literally “one who finds (invents) verse.”

The leap from “to compose” to “to find” runs through poetry: to ~trobar~ was to invent a song, to hit upon the right turn of phrase, and from this creative finding came the ordinary sense of coming upon anything. The prefix ~re-~ adds the nuance of recovery — to find what was lost, or to find again — so ~retrouver~ means both “to locate once more” and, of people, “to be reunited”; ~se retrouver~ is to meet up, or to find oneself in a place or a state. The same Greek ~tropos~ surfaces in learned French words far from the verb's everyday warmth — ~trope~, ~tropique~ (the “turning point” of the sun), and ~héliotrope~ (the flower that turns toward the sun) — while ~trouvère~, the northern cousin of ~troubadour~, preserves the medieval poet-finder.
en.retuber: The verb is formed from the noun ~tube~ with the prefix ~re-~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so it means to fit tubes again, or to replace the tubing of something. ~Re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and is fully productive in French. ~Tube~ is borrowed from Latin ~tubus~ (“tube, pipe”). The French sources note that ~tube~ also took a slang musical sense, a hit song, a coinage credited to Boris Vian, but that sense is not the base of this verb.
en.retâter: ~Retâter~ is formed from ~tâter~ with the prefix ~re-~, which here expresses repetition: “to feel again.” The base ~tâter~ comes from Old French ~taster~, from Vulgar Latin *~tastāre~, and the circumflex records the lost ~s~. The sources disagree on the deepest link. French Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~taxāre~ and ~tangere~ (“to touch”), while English Wiktionary sees a contraction of a frequentative of ~taxāre~ and ties that verb to ~taxus~. English ~taste~ comes from the same Old French verb.
en.retéléphoner: Formed from ~téléphoner~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”). The prefix comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and here adds the idea of repetition: to ~retéléphoner~ is to phone again, or to call back. The base is built on the noun ~téléphone~, itself made from two Greek elements, ~τῆλε~ (“afar”) and ~φωνή~ (“voice, sound”), so the word is a “far voice” that is simply being used a second time.
en.revacciner: Formed from ~vacciner~ (“to vaccinate”) with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”). The TLFi dates it to 1834, in a medical journal. It means to vaccinate someone again, giving a new dose when the earlier vaccination no longer protects. The French Academy defines it in just those terms, and a typical use is being revaccinated against tetanus.
en.revaloir: ~Revaloir~ is formed from ~valoir~ with the prefix ~re-~, here expressing an action in return, and is attested around 1165 to 1170. To ~revaloir~ is to pay back in kind, as in the phrase ~je vous le revaudrai~ (“I will repay you”), whether for a favor or for an injury. The base ~valoir~ means “to be worth,” and the prefix turns that worth into an equivalent given back.
en.revaloriser: Formed from ~valoriser~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again, back”), ~revaloriser~ means “to restore or raise the value of” something, as with a salary, a pension or a profession. The base ~valoriser~ is a twentieth-century coinage built on ~valeur~ with the suffix ~-iser~. ~Valeur~ comes from Latin ~valor~, from the verb ~valēre~ (“to be strong, to be worth”), which goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂welh₁-~ (“to be strong, to rule”). English ~wield~ and ~value~ belong to this family. Here ~re-~ expresses a return to a former level, or an increase, rather than a plain repetition.
en.revancher: ~Revancher~ comes from Old French ~revenchier~, formed from ~re-~ and ~venger~ (“to avenge”), and it is a doublet of ~revenger~. The ~-vench-~ shape is the regular outcome of Latin ~vindicāre~, just as ~pencher~ comes from *~pendicare~. Here ~re-~ gives the sense of paying back, a blow answered by a blow. ~Venger~ itself goes back to Latin ~vindicāre~, which meant first to lay legal claim and then to avenge. The related noun ~revanche~ (a return match, or an act of vengeance) was drawn from the older verb ~revenger~, and the family is also linked to ~revendiquer~.
en.revendiquer:
~Revendiquer~ is a derivative of the noun ~revendication~ and followed the same course: first ~reivendiquier~, it lost its initial ~i~ under the pull of words built with the prefix ~re-~, yielding ~revendiquier~ and then the modern ~revendiquer~. Behind it stands Latin ~vindicare~ (« to lay claim to, to avenge, to set free »), traditionally analysed as ~vim~ (« force ») + a root related to ~dicere~ (« to declare ») — the legal gesture of declaring a claim by force. From the same ~vindicare~ French also drew the doublet ~venger~ (« to avenge »).

The ~re-~ here is intensive rather than truly repetitive: to ~revendiquer~ is to claim something forcefully as one's due — a right, a territory, the authorship of an act. From the Roman courtroom, where ~vindicatio~ asserted ownership of property, the word kept its combative, assertive charge. English ~vindicate~, ~vengeance~, and ~avenge~ all descend from the same Latin verb, as do Italian ~rivendicare~ and Spanish ~reivindicar~.
en.revendre: Formed from ~re-~ (“again”) and ~vendre~, although English Wiktionary adds that it was already Latin ~revēndere~ before reaching Old French, so the prefixed form is inherited and not coined in French. The base ~vendre~ comes from Latin ~vendere~, itself a contraction of ~vēnum dare~ (“to give for sale”). ~Revendre~ means to sell again what one has bought, and so to resell. It gave ~revendeur~ (“reseller, dealer”) and ~revente~ (“resale”).
en.revenir:
Formed in Old French from the prefix ~re-~ (« back, again ») and the verb ~venir~ (« to come »), attested as early as the tenth century. ~venir~ comes from Latin ~venire~, from Proto-Italic *~gʷenjō~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʷem-~ (“to come, to step”). That root reached English through Germanic as the verb ~come~, and shows up in Ancient Greek ~baínō~ (“I go”) and Sanskrit ~gácchati~ (“he goes”).

The compound is transparent — « to come back » — and stayed close to that sense, but French let it bloom in idiom. ~revenir~ means to return in space, but also « to come to » after a faint, to « amount to » a price (~cela revient cher~), to « come down to » in argument (~cela revient au même~), and, in cooking, to brown lightly (~faire revenir des oignons~). Like its parent ~venir~, it takes the auxiliary ~être~ in compound tenses. The root *~gʷem-~ feeds a whole French clan built on ~venir~: ~devenir~, ~convenir~, ~prévenir~, ~parvenir~, the noun ~avenir~ (« what is to come »), and ~venue~.
en.reverdir: Formed from ~re-~ and ~verdir~, so “to turn green again,” of plants returning to leaf. The base is ~vert~ (“green”) with the ending ~-ir~ meaning “to become.” ~Vert~ comes from Latin ~viridis~ through Old French. English Wiktionary adds that Old French already had ~verdir~ in the twelfth century and that it may be inherited from Vulgar Latin *~vir(i)dire~, an alteration of ~viridēscere~, so the base may be older than French. Italian ~inverdire~ is a comparable verb. The prefix ~re-~ marks a return to a former state.
en.revernir: Formed from ~vernir~ (“to varnish”) with the prefix ~re-~, meaning “to varnish again.” The base verb is built on the noun ~vernis~, which appears in Old French as ~verniz~ and comes from Medieval Latin ~veronīx~, a word that also gave Italian ~vernice~. Behind that stand Byzantine Greek names for a resin or amber. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and here simply marks repetition.
en.reverser: From the prefix ~re-~ + ~verser~. The prefix ~re-~ means “again” or “back,” and ~verser~ (“to pour, to pay in”) comes from Late Latin *~versāre~, a frequentative of Latin ~vertere~ (“to turn”). To ~reverser~ is therefore to pour again, to pour back, or, in finance, to pay a sum on to someone else or into another account. A second, modern verb of the same shape exists: ~reverser~ in the sense “to reverse-engineer,” formed from English ~reverse~ + ~-er~. The two words are only homonyms.
en.revigorer: Formed from ~re-~ (“again”) and the older verb ~vigorer~ (“to give strength to”); French Wiktionary notes that the combination already existed in Old French. ~Vigorer~ belongs with ~vigueur~ (“strength”) and ~vigoureux~, words of the same Latin family as English ~vigor~. So ~revigorer~ means “to give fresh strength to”, to reinvigorate.
en.revisiter: The two sources frame it differently. English Wiktionary gives Old French ~revisiter~, from Latin ~revīsitāre~, while French Wiktionary derives it from ~visiter~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”), which is how a modern speaker hears it. ~Visiter~ comes from Latin ~visitāre~ (“to go to see, to visit often”), a frequentative of ~vidēre~ (“to see”), from Proto-Indo-European *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”), which also gave English ~wit~. The verb means to visit a place again, and figuratively to look at a familiar subject or work from a new angle.
en.revisser: Formed from ~visser~ (“to screw”) with the prefix ~re-~, which here means “again” or “back”: to screw something back on or screw it again. The base ~visser~ comes from the noun ~vis~ (“screw”), from Latin ~vītis~ (“vine, tendril”), the screw having been named for the spiral of a vine's tendril. The verb ending is ~-er~. Nothing more is hidden in ~revisser~: it is a transparent French formation that repeats an action.
en.revitaliser: ~Revitaliser~ is formed from the prefix ~re-~ and the verb ~vitaliser~, which is itself ~vital~ plus the suffix ~-iser~. French Wiktionary describes it as a single step on ~vital~ with both affixes at once, which comes to the same thing. The adjective ~vital~ comes from Old French ~vital~ and Latin ~vītālis~ (“of life, life-giving”). The suffix ~-iser~ means to make or render, and ~re-~ means again, so ~revitaliser~ is to give life back.
en.revivifier: Formed from ~re-~ and ~vivifier~, “to bring back to life.” The base is a semi-learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin ~vīvificāre~ (“to give life to the soul”), which joins ~vīvus~ (“alive”) to ~-ficāre~, a combining form of ~facere~ (“to make”). The prefix ~re-~ adds the idea of again, as in ~refaire~. The same Latin adjective gave inherited ~vif~, and its verb ~vīvere~ became ~vivre~. English ~vivify~ is a parallel borrowing.
en.revivre: From Latin ~revīvere~ (“to live again, to come back to life”), built from ~re-~ (“again”) and ~vīvere~ (“to live”). French also treats it as ~re-~ + ~vivre~, and the two analyses give the same meaning. The verb has a literal sense, “to come back to life,” and a looser one, “to feel alive again,” as when relief or good news makes someone ~revivre~. It can also be transitive, meaning “to live through again”: one ~revit~ a memory, an experience or a moment from the past.
en.revoir:
From Old French ~revoir~, ~reveoir~, from Latin ~revidere~ (“to see again, to go back to see”), compounded from the prefix ~re-~ (“again, back”) and ~videre~ (“to see”). ~Videre~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~weid-~ (“to see,” and by extension “to know”). Cognate, through ~videre~, with Italian ~rivedere~ and Spanish ~rever~, and — through the root *~weid-~ — with Greek ~eîdon~ (“I saw”), Sanskrit ~véda~ (“I know”), and English ~wit~ and ~witness~.

~Revoir~ is among the most transparent of French compounds: ~re-~ plus ~voir~, “to see again.” Its substantival use lies hidden inside the everyday farewell ~au revoir~ — literally “until the seeing-again,” a promise of reunion rather than a flat goodbye. The root *~weid-~ is one of the great Indo-European wellsprings, binding sight to knowledge: from it French draws ~voir~, ~vision~, ~évident~, ~prévoir~, ~revue~, and ~vue~, while the same root surfaces in Latin-borrowed English ~vision~ and ~evident~ and in the Germanic ~wise~, ~wisdom~, and ~idea~ (through Greek). To ~revoir~ someone is, etymologically, to let the eyes know them once more.
en.revoler: Formed from ~voler~ with the prefix ~re-~, in the senses of repetition and return: to fly again, or to fly back. The base ~voler~ comes from Latin ~volāre~ (“to fly”), attested in Old French as early as 881, and is cognate with Italian ~volare~ and Spanish ~volar~. French ~voler~ also came to mean “to steal,” a sense linked to falconry, but ~revoler~ keeps mainly the flying sense. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”). The listed sense “to squirt” is a further extension that the sources do not explain.
en.revoter: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ and the verb ~voter~, so “to vote again.” The base was borrowed in the eighteenth century from English ~vote~, which comes from Latin ~votum~ (“a vow, a solemn pledge”), from ~vovēre~ (“to vow”). A vote was thus first a solemn declaration of wish. The prefix ~re-~, from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”), carries its ordinary sense of repetition here: ~revoter~ is to hold a ballot a second time, whether on a text already put to the vote or after an election was annulled.
en.revouloir: ~Revouloir~ (“to want again, to want back”) is formed from ~vouloir~ with the prefix ~re-~, here expressing repetition. The base comes from Old French ~voloir~, from Vulgar Latin *~volēre~, a regularized remaking of the irregular Latin ~velle~ (“to want”). Italian ~volere~ and English ~will~ are relatives. The compound is transparent: ~revouloir~ is to desire a thing a second time or to ask for more of it.
en.revêtir:
From Old French ~revestir~, from ~re-~ (“again, anew”) + ~vestir~ (“to clothe”), from Latin ~vestire~ (“to dress”), a denominal of ~vestis~ (“garment”). ~Vestis~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~westis~ and to PIE *~wéstis~, from the root *~wes-~ (“to clothe, to be dressed”). The same root surfaces in Gothic ~wasti~ (“garment”), in Tocharian B ~wastsi~, and — most familiarly — in English ~wear~. Through Latin ~vestire~ and ~vestis~ it also yields the learned English borrowings ~vest~ and ~vestment~.

The ~re-~ here is not really “again”: ~revêtir~ does not mean to re-dress but to clothe fully, to robe — hence its use for donning ceremonial or official dress, and figuratively for being “clothed” with authority, dignity, or a title. From clothing a person the sense spread to clothing a thing: a wall ~revêtu~ with marble, a road surface, a coating — whence the noun ~revêtement~ (“cladding, coating, surfacing”). The plain verb ~vêtir~ and its other compound ~dévêtir~ (“to undress”) belong to the same family, as do ~vêtement~, ~veste~, and the borrowed ~investir~ and ~travesti~, all rooted in the idea of putting on a garment.
en.rewriter: ~Rewriter~ is borrowed from the English verb ~rewrite~, and it keeps its sense: to rewrite a text, especially to reword it for publication. French adapted the English verb to the first conjugation by adding the ending ~-er~, as it commonly does with English loans. The English verb itself is made of the prefix ~re-~ and ~write~.
en.rhabiller: ~Rhabiller~ is formed from ~habiller~ with the prefix ~re-~, which drops its vowel before the silent h. ~Habiller~ began as a carpentry word, from Old French ~abillier~ (“to prepare a log”), built on ~bille~ (“log”), and gained its sense “to clothe” in the 15th century under the influence of ~habit~. The prefix ~re-~ adds repetition, so ~rhabiller~ means to dress again, and by extension to mend.
en.rhumer: ~Rhumer~ is formed from the noun ~rhum~ (“rum”) and the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense “to mix or flavor with rum.” The noun is a borrowing of English ~rum~, which may be a shortened form of ~rumbullion~, attested from 1652 for this drink and of unknown origin. Another account derives it from an old Norman word ~rombollion~ (“round boil”), used for spirits distilled from cider or perry. The French verb turns the spirit into an action: to add it to a dish, a punch or a pastry.
en.ribouler: ~Ribouler~ is a variant of ~rebouler~, which French Wiktionary labels of dialectal origin, while English Wiktionary simply derives it from ~rebouler~. The only difference between the two forms is the vowel of the first syllable, ~i~ against ~e~. The verb is best known in the phrase ~ribouler des yeux~, which means to roll one's eyes. Neither source traces ~rebouler~ itself any further back.
en.ricaner: According to French Wiktionary, ~ricaner~ comes from Old French ~rechaner~ (“to bray like a donkey, to sing off-key”), formed with the prefix ~re-~ on a Frankish word *~kinni~ (“jaw, cheek”). The modern verb was influenced by ~rire~ (“to laugh”), which shaped its sense toward a mocking or scornful laugh. Only French Wiktionary gives this account; English Wiktionary supplies no etymology for the verb. The Frankish ~kinni~ is thus the hidden core of a verb that now sounds like a cousin of ~rire~.
en.ricocher: ~Ricocher~ is a denominal verb: ~ricochet~ plus ~-er~. The origin of ~ricochet~ is uncertain. It is probably derived from ~cochet~ (“young cock”) with the prefix ~ri-~, though English Wiktionary calls the sense development unclear. Its first attestation is the fable or song of the ~ricochet~, a refrain of questions and answers without end; from there the noun came to mean something that repeats, and the verb makes it an action: to rebound.
en.rider:
~Rider~ (“to wrinkle”) is probably descended from Old High German ~rīdan~, formerly ~wrīdan~ (“to turn, twist”), by way of Old French ~rider~ and Middle French ~rider~, and further back from Proto-West Germanic *~wrīþan~. German ~reiden~ (“to turn; tie up; lace”) is a cognate, and English Wiktionary points to ~writhe~ for the wider family.

A second ~rider~ also exists, a borrowing from English ~ride~, and it merely shares its spelling with the older verb. The evidence gives no meaning for it. The older verb is the one behind the French noun ~ride~ (“wrinkle”) and the verb ~dérider~ (“to smooth the wrinkles from, to cheer up”). Both Wiktionaries give “to turn, twist” for the Germanic source, but neither spells out how “twist” became “wrinkle,” so that step is left open.
en.ridiculiser: ~Ridiculiser~ is the adjective and noun ~ridicule~ + the suffix ~-iser~, “to make ridiculous.” English Wiktionary dates it to 1675 and says it displaced the older verbs ~ridiculer~ and ~ridiculariser~. The base ~ridicule~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~rīdiculus~ (“laughable”), a word related to the verb ~rīdēre~ (“to laugh”). The suffix ~-iser~ means “to render A,” so the verb literally makes someone an object of laughter.
en.rifler:
Inherited from Old French ~rifler~ (“to scrape, to scratch,” in French Wiktionary's wording “to make a scratch or groove”). English Wiktionary traces it to Proto-West Germanic *~rīfilōn~, reaching French either through Frankish *~rīffilōn~ or through Old High German ~riffilōn~ (“to tear by rubbing”). The same source calls it akin to English ~rip~ and ~ripple~.

Other Germanic languages preserve relatives: Old English ~geriflian~ (“to wrinkle”) and Old Norse ~rifa~ (“to tear, to break”). The modern French verb keeps the scraping sense, the smoothing or scraping of a surface with a tool. French Wiktionary also lists a second, separate account of a verb of the same shape, a denominal of ~rifle~ (“rifle, gun”); the two should not be confused, since their histories differ.
en.rigidifier: ~Rigidifier~ is formed from the adjective ~rigide~ with the suffix ~-ifier~, so “to make rigid.” The base ~rigide~ was borrowed from Latin ~rigidus~ (“stiff, hard, inflexible”), and it is the learned doublet of the inherited ~raide~ and ~roide~. The suffix ~-ifier~ goes back to Latin ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”). It is still productive in learned and technical French.
en.rigoler:
The origin of ~rigoler~ is explained in two competing ways. The first, given by both Wiktionaries, takes it as a blend of ~rire~ (“to laugh”) and Old French ~galer~ (“to have fun, to enjoy oneself”). ~Rire~ is inherited from Latin ~rīdēre~ (“to laugh”), and ~galer~ is of Frankish origin. On this reading the verb joins “laughing” and “making merry” into one jolly word, a pairing that suits its informal register.

The second account, found in French Wiktionary, derives the verb from ~rigole~ (“small channel, drainage trench”), with an initial sense of “to arrange the edges of a ditch or river so that the water can flow freely.” The source does not spell out how channeling water became laughing, so this is best taken as a proposal, not a settled fact. Either way, the verb is colloquial and has produced ~rigolo~ (“funny”), ~rigolade~ (“fun, a lark”) and ~rigoleur~.
en.rimailler: ~Rimailler~ is a contemptuous verb for writing bad verse, attested in 1649 in the form ~rithmailler~. French Wiktionary derives it from ~rimer~ with the pejorative suffix ~-ailler~, while English Wiktionary instead derives it from the noun ~rimaille~ plus ~-er~, so the analysis varies by source. The base ~rimer~ rests on the noun ~rime~, whose own origin is uncertain: perhaps Old High German ~rim~ (“number”), or Latin ~rhythmus~. The suffix gives the sense of doing something poorly and without conviction.
en.rimer: ~Rimer~ is formed from the noun ~rime~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, although English Wiktionary treats it simply as inherited from Old French ~rimer~. The origin of ~rime~ itself is uncertain. French Wiktionary mentions Old High German ~rim~ (“number”), modern German ~Reim~ (“rhyme”), and perhaps Latin ~rhythmus~ (“measure, cadence”). Friedrich Diez favored the German source, since ~rhythmus~ could not give Italian ~rima~. English ~rhyme~ owes its spelling to a late learned association with ~rhythm~.
en.rincer:
The origin of ~rincer~ is disputed. It is attested in Old French as ~reinser~ and ~raincer~ (thirteenth century) and as ~raïncier~ and ~recincier~, and Middle French has ~rincer~. One account goes back to Latin ~recentāre~ (“to make fresh”), from ~recēns~ (“fresh, recent”), through a Vulgar Latin *~recentiāre~, giving Old French ~recincier~ (“to rinse, to freshen, to wash”), with a later dissimilation. The rival account, which goes back to Diez, derives it from Old Norse ~hreinsa~ (“to clean”), from Proto-Germanic *~hrainisōną~ (“to purify”), cognate with Gothic ~hrains~ (“pure”) and German ~rein~. Scheler supported the Norse origin with the Picard form ~rinser~, which he said would have become ~rincher~ had it come from Latin, and rejected a third Latin candidate, ~runcāre~ (“to weed”). A further proposal, by Nisard, links it to ~rain~ (“branch”), from Latin ~ramus~, through the paddle used to beat laundry, but the objection is that the verb would then have been *~rainceler~. English ~rinse~ is a cognate.

Whatever its source, the verb is about washing clean. ~Rincer~ is to wash out a glass, a mouth or a piece of laundry in fresh water after the main wash, and the noun ~rinçage~ names the step. Slang also uses the verb for drinking: one can rincer a round of drinks, or rincer one's throat, and to be ~rincé~ is to have been cleaned out of money. In another popular phrase, rincer l'œil, a person feasts the eyes on something. The image is the same each time, a thorough flushing.
en.ringarder: ~Ringarder~ is formed from ~ringard~ and the ending ~-er~: to stir embers with a poker. The noun is in the sense of the poker traced by French Wiktionary to Walloon ~ringuéle~ (“lever”), itself borrowed from the German dialect word ~Rengel~ (“log”), with ~-ard~ replacing the ending. The other ~ringard~, for a mediocre actor and later an out-of-date person, has an uncertain origin.
en.ringardiser: Formed from ~ringard~ with the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make”), the verb means to make something seem outdated. The base ~ringard~ has an uncertain origin. French Wiktionary offers two accounts: the word first meant a mediocre actor and may come from a proper name, from slang use of an earlier word, or from a poetic coinage; or it comes from Walloon ~ringuéle~ (“lever”), borrowed from dialectal German ~Rengel~ (“log”), with ~-ard~ replacing the ending. English Wiktionary calls it unknown.
en.ripailler: ~Ripailler~ (“to feast, to revel”) is formed from the noun ~ripaille~ with the ending ~-er~. The noun is analyzed as ~riper~ (“to scrape”) + ~-aille~. A popular tradition, which French Wiktionary mentions only as oral lore, links ~ripaille~ instead to Ripaille, a castle on the shore of Lake Geneva, where Amédée VIII, Duke of Savoy, withdrew and was accused of indulging in rich food. The scraping origin is the documented one; the castle story is a charming tradition, not a proven fact.
en.riper:
The sources give two accounts of the Germanic origin of ~riper~. English Wiktionary has it inherited from Middle French ~riper~ or ~ripper~, from Old French ~riper~, of Germanic origin, ultimately from Frankish *~wrīban~ (“to rub”); compare Dutch ~wrijven~ and German ~reiben~. French Wiktionary instead calls it related to Dutch ~rippen~. Either way the verb is Germanic, not Latin.

The modern senses are scattered: “to slip,” “to scrape,” and, in the spoken language, “to go away” or “to take off.” The sources do not say how the older sense of rubbing led to them, so no path is claimed here. A separate, recent sense belongs to computing: “to rip” a disc, which comes from English ~rip~ and has its own history. France's Commission générale de terminologie et de néologie confirmed it, and the term appears on the FranceTerme site.
en.ripoliner: ~Ripoliner~ is formed from the noun ~ripolin~ with the ending ~-er~, “to paint with Ripolin,” and by extension to repaint or touch up, often with the sense of a hasty or superficial job. ~Ripolin~ was originally a brand name. According to French Wiktionary, a Dutch chemist, Carl Julius Ferdinand Riep, invented a quick-drying oil paint that he called ~Riepolin~ (1897). A French firm bought the process and gave the name a French shape, ~Ripolin~. The verb thus rests on a trade name turned into a common noun.
en.riposter: ~Riposter~ is formed from the noun ~riposte~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun was borrowed from Italian ~risposta~ (“answer”), the substantivized past participle of the verb ~rispondere~ (“to respond”). French thus took the Italian word for a reply and then turned it into a verb of its own, meaning to answer back.
en.rire:
From Middle French ~rire~, from Old French ~rire~, from Vulgar Latin *~rīdĕre~, a shift of the Classical Latin verb ~rīdēre~ (“to laugh, to smile, to mock”) from the second to the third conjugation. The change of conjugation class is what kept ~rire~ short and irregular in French. Beyond Latin the trail goes cold: ~rīdēre~ has no securely established Proto-Indo-European etymology, so cautious etymologists decline to reconstruct a deeper root. Within Romance it is cognate with Italian ~ridere~, Spanish ~reír~, and Portuguese ~rir~.

Latin ~rīdēre~ already carried the double edge the French verb keeps — open laughter on one side, derision on the other, as in ~rire de~ quelqu'un (“to laugh at someone”). The smiling sense lived in the derived ~subrīdēre~ (“to smile,” literally “to laugh a little under”), which gave French ~sourire~, where ~sous-~ + ~rire~ still means a laugh held quietly beneath the surface. The same Latin stem furnished ~ridicule~ and ~ridiculiser~ (from ~rīdiculus~, “laughable”), ~dérision~ and ~dérisoire~, and the noun ~rire~ itself. So from one uncertain ancient verb the French language draws its whole vocabulary of mirth: the belly laugh, the quiet smile, and the cutting ridicule alike.
en.risquer:
Attested from the late sixteenth century, ~risquer~ is a denominal verb formed on the noun ~risque~, borrowed from Old Italian ~risco~ (modern ~rischio~). The Italian word's ultimate origin is disputed, but the favoured account derives it from Vulgar Latin *~resecum~, literally “that which cuts,” from ~resecare~ (“to cut off”) — first a rock or reef that could gash a ship's hull, then the peril such hazards posed to seaborne cargo, and at last “risk” in the abstract. Rival proposals invoke Greek ~rhíza~ (“root, cliff”) or Arabic ~rizq~ (“fortune, what providence allots”), but neither is secure.

The maritime stamp is the memorable part: ~risque~ was a merchant's and insurer's word before it was anyone else's, naming the gamble that goods might never reach port. From the concrete cutting edge of a reef the sense broadened to any exposure to loss, and the verb ~risquer~ now ranges from “to endanger” to the everyday “to risk doing.” If the *~resecum~ etymology holds, the noun shares its root with French ~réséquer~ (“to resect, cut away”) and, through ~secare~, with ~scier~, ~section~, and ~sécateur~ — a whole family centred on the act of cutting.
en.rissoler: Formed from the noun ~rissole~ with ~-er~: to brown food, as one browns a ~rissole~. The sources give two origins for the noun. In one, Old French ~roissole~ or ~rousole~ derives from Latin ~russeolus~ (“reddish”), from ~russus~ (“red”), because of the russet colour of the preparation. In the other, it comes from Occitan ~risolo~ (“small net”), from Latin ~retiolum~, which is a different word altogether.
en.ristourner: From ~ristourne~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, which here turns a noun into a verb: to give a rebate or discount. The noun ~ristourne~ is itself a borrowing from Italian. French Wiktionary connects it to Italian ~storno~ (“cancellation of a contract”), while English Wiktionary names Italian ~ristorno~, and the noun passed through the Old French forms ~restorne~ and ~restourne~ before taking its modern shape.
en.ritualiser: Formed from ~rituel~ (“ritual”) with the verb suffix ~-iser~, so the verb means to turn something into a ritual or give it a ritual form. The noun ~rituel~ was borrowed from Latin ~ritualis~, and in its noun use from ~rituales~ (~libri~), “books dealing with rites,” itself derived from ~ritus~ (“rite”). The suffix ~-iser~ builds verbs meaning “make A” or “convert into N”, and it remains productive in learned and technical French. The learned character of the base explains the learned character of the verb.
en.rivaliser: Formed in French from the noun ~rival~ and the suffix ~-iser~, in the sense “to act as a rival”, hence “to compete”. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs. The noun ~rival~ is borrowed from Latin ~rīvālis~, which literally meant a person using the same stream as another, from ~rīvus~ (“brook”). Neighbors who shared a water source, and so quarreled over it, became the model of every competitor. The word is unrelated to ~rive~ (“bank”), despite the resemblance.
en.river: The two sources disagree. French Wiktionary treats ~river~ as formed from ~rive~ in the sense of “edge”: to rivet is to flatten and turn over the end of a nail or bolt so that it holds. ~Rive~ is inherited from Latin ~rīpa~ (“bank”), the source of ~rivage~ (“shore”). English Wiktionary instead points to a Germanic source and compares Danish ~rive~. Neither account is settled here, and the link to the edge of the nail is the one French itself gives.
en.riveter: ~Riveter~ is formed from the noun ~rivet~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~: to fasten with a rivet. The origin of ~rivet~ is not settled. One account derives it from ~river~ (“to fasten”) with the suffix ~-et~, while another links it to ~rive~ (“edge”, from Latin ~ripa~) with the same suffix, the idea being that of a border or rim. Whichever is right, ~riveter~ names the act of fixing metal parts together with rivets, and it can also be said figuratively of something fixed in place.
en.rober: Formed from ~robe~ plus ~-er~, in the narrow technical sense of wrapping a cigar in an outer sheet of tobacco. The noun ~robe~ is itself a back-formation from an Old French verb ~rober~ (“to steal”), a different verb from this one. That older verb goes back to Proto-Germanic *~raubō~ (“booty”), which also gave English ~rob~. The meaning of ~robe~ moved from war booty and spoils to a tunic and then to a dress. The old verb survives in French only in the prefixed form ~dérober~.
en.robotiser: Formed from ~robot~ plus the verbal suffix ~-iser~ (“to make, to provide with”), so “to equip with robots, to automate.” ~Robot~ was borrowed from Czech ~robota~ (“drudgery, servitude”), a word that Karel Čapek introduced in 1920 in his play Rossum's Universal Robots, first staged in 1921. Čapek is often called the inventor of the word, but he himself credited his brother Josef. Czech ~robota~ comes from Proto-Slavic *~orbota~.
en.rocher: According to French Wiktionary, ~rocher~ is a derivative of ~roche~ with the verb ending ~-er~, from an earlier form ~rochier~. The same text gives ~roche~ here the sense of “impure borax” and cites an alum called ~alun en roque~ in 1368, itself traced to medieval Latin ~alumen de roca~ in 1164. The sources do not spell out how this leads to the sense of beer foaming. ~Roche~ itself comes from Late Latin ~rocca~, of uncertain and probably pre-Latin origin. Compare Italian ~rocca~, Spanish ~roca~ and English ~rock~.
en.rocouer: A French formation from the noun ~rocou~ (annatto, a red-orange dye) with the verb ending ~-er~, so ~rocouer~ means “to dye with annatto.” The noun ~rocou~ is of American origin: French took it from Tupi ~urucú~, though another account has it reach French through Spanish ~urucú~, from Paraguayan Guarani. The ending ~-er~ comes from the Latin first-conjugation ending ~-are~.
en.roder:
French ~roder~ comes from Latin ~rōdere~ (“to gnaw, to wear away”). The Latin verb is the parent of a clear family: Italian ~rodere~ and English ~rodent~ (via ~rodens~, the present participle) show it in the same sense of “gnawer.” The same Latin root lies behind French ~éroder~ (“to erode”) and ~corroder~ (“to corrode”), and behind English ~erode~ and ~corrode~.

The Latin sense of wearing something away is the starting point for the French verb. In modern French ~roder~ means “to run in” a new engine so that its parts bed in smoothly, and by extension “to hone” or “to polish”: one can ~roder~ a method, a show or a team, meaning to try it out and smooth it through use.
en.rogner: Not a formation on a French noun. French ~rogner~ comes from Old French ~rooignier~ (with variants ~redognier~ and ~reoignier~), from a Vulgar Latin verb reconstructed as *~rotundiāre~ or *~retundiāre~, which would mean “to cut round.” It rests on Latin ~rotundus~ (“round”), the source of French ~rond~. Old Occitan ~redonhar~ is a parallel. To ~rogner~ is to trim something by cutting off its edges.
en.rognonner: The verb is linked to the Gallo-Romance stem ~ron-~, which expresses the idea of a growl or grumble. Earlier, ~rognonner~ meant to grumble between one's teeth, according to a book on words lost in dictionaries, which is the French gloss's only witness for the older sense. The same idea of low muttering appears in ~ronchonner~, a French word of similar meaning. The sources trace the verb to this sound-imitating stem rather than to any Latin source word.
en.roidir: ~Roidir~ is a variant of ~raidir~ (“to stiffen”), and French Wiktionary simply refers the reader there. It has the same meaning: to make something stiff or rigid, or to become so. The ~roi-~ spelling is the less common form and is now rare next to ~raidir~.
en.romancer: French Wiktionary treats ~romancer~ as a verb formed from ~romance~, while English Wiktionary derives it from Old French ~romancier~ (“to narrate in the vernacular”), itself from ~romanz~. The noun ~romance~ was borrowed from Spanish ~romance~, probably from Old French ~romanz~ or Old Occitan ~romans~, and meant a narrative work in the vernacular. Behind these lies Vulgar Latin *~romanĭce~ (“in a Roman manner”), from Latin ~rōmānicus~. The modern verb means to turn real events into a story, to fictionalize or romanticize them.
en.romaniser: Formed from the adjective ~romain~ with the suffix ~-iser~, which builds verbs meaning “to make or render X.” ~Romain~ comes from Latin ~Rōmānus~, through Old French, and forms a doublet with ~roman~. To ~romaniser~ is therefore to make something Roman, to bring it under Roman culture, language or religion.
en.rompre:
From Latin ~rumpere~ (“to break, burst”), which yielded Old French ~rompre~ directly. The Latin verb is a nasal-infixed present built on Proto-Indo-European *~Hrewp-~ (“to break, tear”), the same root that surfaces in Sanskrit ~lumpáti~ (“breaks, plunders”). Through Latin derivatives it is cognate with English ~rupture~ and ~disrupt~.

The core sense “to break” stayed remarkably stable, but French spun it outward into vivid idioms: ~rompre la glace~ (“to break the ice”), ~rompre le silence~, and ~à tout rompre~ (“to bursting point,” of applause). The most surprising descendant of ~rumpere~ is ~route~: a road was originally a ~via rupta~, a “broken way” cut or forced through wilderness, the past participle ~rupta~ standing alone until it became an everyday word. From the same Latin stock French also keeps ~rupture~, ~corrompre~, and ~interrompre~.
en.ronchonner: The origin is uncertain. One account derives ~ronchonner~ from Old French ~ronchier~, from Latin ~rhoncāre~, itself from Ancient Greek ~rhonkhos~ (“snoring”). English Wiktionary gives a close variant of this: a form of the dialectal verb ~roncher~, from Latin ~roncāre~. Both accounts point to the Latin family of verbs for snoring and snorting. The Latin verb has relatives in other Romance languages, and Spanish ~roncar~ (“to snore”) is one such cousin. Modern French uses ~ronchonner~ to mean “to grumble” or “to grouse”, and the adjective ~ronchon~ is related to it. Because the sources only say the descent is possible, the link from snoring to muttering is best taken as the likely explanation, not a proven one.
en.ronfler: An expressive, imitative word, inherited from Old French ~ronfler~ and from the same sound-imitating family as ~ronron~. French Wiktionary links it to Italian ~ronfare~ (“to snore”) and Provençal ~ronflar~. English Wiktionary compares Piedmontese ~romfé~, Lombard ~romfà~ and Emilian ~romfè~. Its core sense is the heavy breathing of sleep, and it extends to any deep, droning noise: a stove, an engine or a roar.
en.ronger:
French ~ronger~ comes from Old French ~rongier~, which the sources describe as a crossing of two verbs. One is Old French ~rungier~, from Latin ~rūmigāre~ (“to chew, to ruminate”). The other is a Vulgar Latin *~rodicāre~, built on Latin ~rōdō~ (“to gnaw”). English Wiktionary gives that second ingredient as a reconstructed verb, while French Wiktionary says only that the ~o~ of the nasal syllable comes from ~rōdere~, a verb close in meaning. Either way, ~ronger~ is a hybrid of two Latin verbs of chewing. Latin ~rōdere~ is also the source of English ~rodent~ and ~erode~, and of the learned French ~éroder~.

The oldest sense is physical: mice, rats and worms gnaw at whatever they find. French extended it to any slow wearing away, so that rust, damp and the sea eat at metal and rock, and illness or anxiety eat at a person. The figurative phrases are vivid: se ronger les sangs means “to worry oneself sick,” and ronger son frein means “to champ at the bit,” an image of a horse chewing on its bit. The agent noun ~rongeur~ (“rodent”) gives French its everyday word for mice and squirrels, so an old verb of chewing ended up naming a whole order of mammals.
en.ronronner: The verb is formed from the noun ~ronron~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, so it means to make a ~ronron~, the way a cat does. Both Wiktionaries describe the noun as onomatopoeic: it imitates a low, steady, vibrating sound, and the doubled syllable mimics its repetition. The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, is the default way French turns a noun into a verb, here in the sense “to produce N”.
en.ronéoter: Formed from ~ronéo~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~ronéo~ is French for a stencil duplicating machine, and it comes from the English trademark ~Roneo~, a blend of ~rotary~ and ~neo-~. The verb therefore means to make copies on such a machine, the standard way of producing leaflets and classroom handouts before photocopiers took over.
en.ronéotyper: ~Ronéotyper~ means “to duplicate with a Roneo machine.” It is best explained as the noun ~ronéotype~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~ronéo~ comes from the English trademark ~Roneo~, a portmanteau of ~rotary~ and ~neo-~. The element ~-type~ comes from Ancient Greek ~τύπος~ (~túpos~, “mark, impression”) and forms nouns for imprints and reproductions. The verb has a synonym, ~ronéoter~, built from ~ronéo~ and ~-er~ alone.
en.roquer: ~Roquer~ (“to castle” in chess) is formed from ~roc~, the old name of the rook, with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~roc~ is traced to Persian ~rokh~ (“tower, chariot”), a chess piece that European players took over from the East. English Wiktionary adds that the Persian word is possibly related to Sanskrit ~ratha~ (“chariot”). Note that a different French ~roc~ (“rock”) is a variant of ~roche~ and has nothing to do with the chess piece. The verb names the move in which the king and a rook change places.
en.roser: Formed from the noun ~rose~ with the verb ending ~-er~, meaning “to turn something pink, to give it a rosy tint.” The noun comes from Latin ~rosa~ (“rose”). English Wiktionary notes that ~rose~ was borrowed from Latin through Old French rather than inherited in the ordinary way, since an inherited word would have taken a quite different shape. The flower gave French its colour word, and the verb simply says “to colour like a rose.”
en.rosir: Formed from the noun ~rose~ plus the ending ~-ir~, in the sense of becoming rose-colored: a cheek, a sky or a face that ~rosit~ turns pink. The noun ~rose~ comes through Old and Middle French and was borrowed from Latin ~rosa~. English Wiktionary notes that a word inherited from Latin would have taken the form *~reuse~, so ~rose~ is a learned borrowing. The ending ~-ir~ forms verbs meaning “to become” the quality named by the base, as ~grandir~ does from ~grand~, though ~rosir~ builds on a noun used as a color.
en.rosser:
The origin of ~rosser~ is not settled. French Wiktionary starts from Old French ~roissier~, with the variants ~ruster~ and ~rusteier~ (“to treat roughly”), and derives it from a Vulgar Latin *~rustiāre~ (“to beat”), formed on *~rustia~ (“switch, rod”); it compares Spanish ~rustir~. English Wiktionary also starts from ~roissier~ and says it is probably from *~rustiāre~, with *~rustia~ from Late Latin ~rustum~, or less likely from a Vulgar Latin *~ruptiāre~, from Latin ~ruptus~, the participle of ~rumpō~ (“to break”).

Littré linked it instead to ~rosse~, with Provençal ~rossegar~ and ~arossar~, reading the sense as striking the way a ~rosse~ (a nag) or a horse does. If the ~ruptiāre~ route were right, ~rosser~ would be a cousin of ~rompre~ and ~rupture~, but the sources favor the ~rustiāre~ account. Modern ~rosser~ means to beat or thrash someone, and by extension to defeat an opponent soundly, in sport or in a contest.
en.roter:
~Roter~ comes from Latin ~ructāre~ (“to belch”). English Wiktionary says it probably went through a Late or Vulgar Latin *~ruptāre~; this intermediate form is a proposal, not an attested word. Seen only from within French, the verb can also be read as the noun ~rot~ plus the ending ~-er~, but that is a surface analysis, not its history.

French also has the learned verb ~éructer~, which comes from the same Latin family and is kept for formal or literary use, and for any violent emission of gas, smoke or words. English ~eructate~ comes from the same source. ~Roter~ is the everyday, familiar word, and in modern French it means simply to burp.
en.roucouler: Both Wiktionaries class ~roucouler~ as onomatopoeic, meaning its sounds imitate the call it names. French Wiktionary posits an imitative syllable ~rouc~ recalling birdsong, and the verb names the cooing of a pigeon. No older source word is recorded, so there is no Latin or Germanic ancestor to trace. The related noun ~roucoulement~ names the sound itself.
en.rouer:
Per both Wiktionaries, inherited from Latin ~rotāre~ (“to turn, to move in a circle”), a verb built on the noun ~rota~ (“wheel”). English Wiktionary also records a second analysis for the same spelling, from ~roue~ (“wheel”) + ~-er~, a verb formed within French. The Latin verb has a doublet: ~rôder~, which entered French from Provençal.

Whichever route is right, the idea is the wheel. French ~roue~ is the direct descendant of ~rota~, and ~rotation~ and ~rotatif~ are learned relatives, as is English ~rotate~. Modern ~rouer~ is used in the set phrase ~rouer de coups~ (“to beat savagely”); neither Wiktionary explains how the sense of beating arose from the wheel. The doublet ~rôder~ moved far from the wheel to mean “to prowl,” a case of one Latin verb splitting into two different French ones.
en.rougeoyer: Formed from ~rouge~ with the suffix ~-oyer~, which makes verbs of continuing action or emission: ~rougeoyer~ means to glow red. ~Rouge~ comes from Old French ~roge~, from Latin ~rubeus~ (“reddish”). The verb is attested as ~rojoier~ around 1165, then disappeared from the language and was taken up again in modern French from the nineteenth century onward.
en.rougir: Formed from the adjective ~rouge~ and the verb ending ~-ir~, with the sense “to become red,” and attested in Old French as ~rogir~. This is the usual job of the ~-ir~ conjugation with colors and qualities, as in ~blêmir~ (“to turn pale”) and ~grandir~ (“to grow”). The base ~rouge~ comes through Middle French and Old French ~roge~ from Latin ~rubeus~ (“red, reddish”). The verb covers everything from a sky or a hot metal turning red to a person blushing from shame or emotion.
en.rouiller: ~Rouiller~ is a denominal built on ~rouille~ (“rust”) with the suffix ~-er~, and it is already found in Old French. The noun ~rouille~ comes from Old French ~reoïlle~, from Late or Vulgar Latin *~robicula~, a diminutive of Latin ~rōbīgō~ (“rust”). English Wiktionary analyzes ~rōbīgō~ as ~rōbus~, a variant of ~rūfus~ (“red, reddish”), plus a suffix for diseased conditions. Rust was therefore named, at the root, for its red color. Catalan ~rovell~ and Spanish ~robín~ are cousins.
en.rouir:
From Old Frankish *~rōtjan~, which meant “to rot” and, in particular, “to ret hemp.” The same Germanic root gave Middle Dutch ~rôten~ and Middle Low German ~rôten~. English ~ret~, “to soak flax or hemp,” is a relative of English ~rot~, from the same Germanic stock. The verb names a process of flax and hemp growing: soaking the plant in water to rot away its soft tissue and free the fibres.

The process of ~rouir~ is called ~rouissage~, and the pond or vat where it was done is a ~routoir~. French ~rouir~ is a specialized verb of flax and hemp, and it is not related to the verb ~pourrir~ (“to rot”), which comes from Latin ~putrēre~. The two verbs share a sense but not a source.
en.rouler:
From Old French ~roeler~ (around 1180), a verb built on ~roele~ (“little wheel”) with the ending ~-er~. ~Roele~ comes from Late Latin ~rotella~, a diminutive of Latin ~rota~ (“wheel”), crossed along the way with ~rôle~ (from Latin ~rotulus~, “a little rolled scroll”). ~Rota~ descends from Proto-Italic *~rotā~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~Hret-~ (“to run, roll”). Cognates abound: Sanskrit ~ratha~ (“chariot”), German ~Rad~ (“wheel”), and Lithuanian ~ratas~ (“wheel”).

The verb began concretely — to turn like a wheel, to make something revolve — and then rolled outward in every direction. It came to mean to travel by wheeled vehicle (~la voiture roule~), to coil or wind, and, in vivid slang, to ~rouler quelqu'un~, “to cheat someone,” as if spinning them around. The shared root left French a wheel-shaped vocabulary: ~roue~, ~rouleau~, ~roulette~, ~roulement~, the noun ~rôle~ (originally a rolled-up list of parts), and even ~contrôle~ (from a ~contre-rôle~, a counter-roll kept for checking). English ~roll~, ~rotate~, and ~round~ trace to the same turning root, as does the ~rotary~ motion that names it.
en.roupiller: The origin is debated. French Wiktionary, citing Albert Dauzat's 1918 study of soldiers' slang, derives ~roupiller~ from Spanish ~ropilla~, itself from ~ropa~ (“clothing”): a wide infantry greatcoat that a man could sleep in. English Wiktionary instead says the verb is probably from or related to dialectal German ~ruspen~ (“to snore, groan, grumble, retch”), which would make it cognate with German ~räuspern~ (“to clear the throat”). The verb means “to sleep, to snooze.”
en.rouscailler: English Wiktionary explains ~rouscailler~ as a compound of the verb ~rousser~ and the Old French verb ~cailler~, which it glosses as “to chat.” The verb is informal and means “to grumble” or “to chat.” It belongs to familiar speech, and its sense fits the mix of complaint and talk that the two parts suggest. The sources give no date and no further history for either element, so the exact path of the formation remains undocumented.
en.rouspéter: The origin of ~rouspéter~ is probably, but not certainly, a blend of two verbs. French Wiktionary says it is no doubt from ~rousser~, modelled on ~rouscailler~, plus ~péter~; English Wiktionary agrees on ~rousser~ (as with ~rouscailler~) plus ~péter~. The verb is colloquial and means “to grumble, to protest,” often in a petty or habitual way. Neither source explains how the two components combine into that sense, so the exact path is not documented.
en.roussir: From ~roux~ (“reddish brown”) and the verb ending ~-ir~, which forms verbs meaning “to make or become” the quality in question. ~Roussir~ thus means to make or turn reddish brown, and so to scorch or singe. ~Roux~ itself comes from Latin ~russus~ (“red”).
en.roustir: ~Roustir~ has the same etymology as ~rôtir~, according to French Wiktionary, of which it is a variant form. The sources say nothing further about its descent. The verb is dated, and its senses include “to roast” and, in slang, “to rob” or “to steal.” No source explains how the slang sense developed, so none is offered here.
en.router: ~Router~ is formed from ~route~ and the verb-forming ending ~-er~: to send something along a route. The noun ~route~ comes from Old French ~rote~ and Latin ~rupta~, understood as a “broken” way, from ~rumpere~ (“to break”). French Wiktionary adds that some scholars prefer a Celtic, pre-Roman origin for the noun instead. The ending ~-er~ descends from the Latin first-conjugation ending ~-are~, and it is the default for coining new verbs in French.
en.rouvrir: Formed from ~ouvrir~ with ~r-~, the form that ~re-~ (“again”) takes before a vowel in older verbs. The base descends from Latin ~aperīre~ (“to open”) by way of Vulgar Latin *~operīre~, reshaped on its opposite ~cooperīre~ (“to cover”). French records the verb first in the reflexive, in 1160, for a heart that opens again. The transitive use appears in 1396, and the concrete sense of reopening a door or a shop, in 1560.
en.rubaner: Formed from ~ruban~ with the verb ending ~-er~, it means to put a ribbon on something. French ~ruban~ is Old French ~riban~ with the vowel rounded before the ~b~, and the word comes from Middle Dutch ~ringhband~, built from ~ring~ (“ring, collar”) and ~band~ (“band, fetter”).
