French Wiktionary compares ~hauban~ and ~raban~, which also lost a final ~d~ after passing through Dutch. A Dutch word for a collar thus became the French word for a ribbon.
en.rucher: Formed as a denominal from ~ruche~ (“beehive”), with the verb ending ~-er~. English Wiktionary gives the suffix as ~-ier~ instead. The noun ~ruche~ comes from Middle and Old French ~rusche~, from Early Medieval Latin ~rusca~ (“bark”), borrowed from Gaulish ~rūsca~, from Proto-Celtic *~rūskos~, possibly from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₃rewk-~ (“to dig up”). Catalan ~rusc~ means both “cork-oak bark” and “hive.” The verb, whose senses include stacking hay in hive-shaped mounds and gathering fabric into a frill, is built on the French noun, not on the Gaulish word.
en.rudoyer: ~Rudoyer~ is formed from ~rude~ and the suffix ~-oyer~, meaning “to treat harshly.” The adjective ~rude~ reached French through Old French ~rude~, a borrowing from Latin ~rudis~ (“unwrought, raw”). The suffix ~-oyer~ comes from Old French ~-oiier~ and expresses an action carried out on someone, as in ~tutoyer~. To rudoyer someone is thus to treat them as one would a raw, unworked thing: roughly.
en.ruer:
From Vulgar Latin *~rutāre~, an intensive verb built on ~rutum~, the supine stem of Classical Latin ~ruere~ (“to rush, to hurl, to throw down”). Both Wiktionaries give this chain, and the Vulgar Latin form is reconstructed, not attested. The plain Latin verb ~ruere~ also stands behind the noun ~ruina~ (“collapse, downfall”), which French and English both borrowed as ~ruine~ and ~ruin~. So the kick of a horse and the fall of a city share an ancestor: both start from a violent downward or forward rush.

In French, ~ruer~ first meant “to hurl, to throw with force,” which is the sense of the Latin source, and the reflexive ~se ruer~ (“to rush headlong”) keeps the Latin idea of a sudden onrush. Today the everyday meaning is that of a horse or donkey kicking out with its hind legs, and the figurative phrase ~ruer dans les brancards~ (literally “to kick against the shafts”) means to rebel. Several nouns belong to the family: ~ruade~ (“a kick”) and ~ruée~ (“a rush,” as in ~la ruée vers l'or~, the gold rush).
en.rugir: ~Rugir~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~rugīre~ (“to roar”), and it was rare before the sixteenth century. It replaced the Old French verbs ~ruir~ and ~ruire~, which had the same origin and are attested until the sixteenth century. English Wiktionary calls ~ruir~ a more gallicized variant of the Latin verb, which is to say the inherited form that borrowing eventually displaced. The noun ~rugissement~ is derived from ~rugir~.
en.ruiler: Formed from Middle French ~ruile~ (“mason's rule”) with the verb ending ~-er~, the usual way French turns a noun into a verb. The noun names a tool of the masonry trade, and the verb belongs to the same craft; its modern sense is “to put in some flashing,” a mason's task. The sources consulted give no older source for ~ruile~.
en.ruiner:
From Middle French ~ruiner~ and Old French ~ruiner~, from Latin ~ruīnāre~ (“to cause to fall down”). Synchronically, French Wiktionary also analyzes it as ~ruine~ + ~-er~, since the noun ~ruine~ comes from Latin ~ruīna~ (“collapse, downfall”), from ~ruere~ (“to rush down, to fall in a heap”). The verb has relatives across the Romance languages: Italian ~rovinare~, Occitan ~arroïnar~ and Spanish ~ruinar~ and ~arruinar~. English ~ruin~ is a loan from the French noun.

The Latin picture is physical: walls and roofs that tumble down. French kept that image and carried it over to fortunes, health and reputations, so ~ruiner~ can describe a house, a harvest or a family. The reflexive form ~se ruiner~ is the usual way to say that someone spends or loses all their money. The family includes the noun ~ruine~ and the adjective ~ruineux~, and the stem ~ruere~ also lives on in learned words such as ~irruption~.
en.ruisseler: Formed from ~ruisseau~ (“brook”) with the verb ending ~-er~, giving “to flow like a brook.” English Wiktionary shows the verb built on the stem ~ruissel-~ of the old form of the noun. ~Ruisseau~ comes from Old French ~ruissel~, from Vulgar Latin *~rivuscellus~, a diminutive of Latin ~rīvus~ (“small stream”); compare Italian ~ruscello~. Water that pours down a face or a wall is said to ~ruisseler~.
en.ruminer: Borrowed from Latin ~rūminārī~ (“to chew the cud”), a verb built on ~rūmen~, which French Wiktionary glosses as “paunch”. The same Latin family gave English ~ruminate~ and the zoological term ~rumen~. The French verb keeps both the literal sense, an animal chewing its cud again, and the figurative one, turning a thought over and over in the mind.
en.ruser: The sources disagree on the direction. French Wiktionary treats ~ruser~ as a verb made from the noun ~ruse~ (with ~-er~), and traces ~ruse~ to Old French ~reuse~, itself from Latin ~recusāre~ (“to refuse”). English Wiktionary instead derives the verb straight from ~recusāre~ by loss of the medial ~c~, and compares Provençal ~reusar~. Either way, the chain leads back to ~recusāre~. French Wiktionary adds that in Brittany the verb is also said to come from Breton ~ruzañ~, a regional account.
en.russifier: Formed from ~russe~ (“Russian”) with the verbal suffix ~-ifier~, meaning “to make Russian,” that is, to bring a people, a language or a place under Russian influence. The suffix comes from a Latin root meaning “to make”: ~-ifier~ descends from Latin ~-ficāre~, built on ~facere~ (“to do, to make”), and also gives ~purifier~, ~simplifier~ and ~personnifier~. The verb is a French coinage on the adjective and noun ~russe~, with no older Latin or Russian verb behind it.
en.rustiquer: Formed from the adjective ~rustique~ and the verb ending ~-er~, in the sense of giving a rough, rural-looking finish to masonry, which is what “roughcast” means. ~Rustique~ comes from Latin ~rūsticus~ (“rural, of the countryside”), itself a derivative of ~rūs~ (“countryside”). It is a doublet of ~rustre~ (“boor”), the same Latin word reaching French by a different route. The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, builds verbs from nouns and adjectives.
en.rutiler:
~Rutiler~ comes from Latin ~rutilāre~ (“to dye red,” and “to shine like gold”), a verb related to the adjective ~russus~ (“red”). French borrowed it as a learned word, and it keeps the double sense of the Latin: a reddish tint, then a bright, golden sparkle. The Latin verb itself belongs to a family of colour words built on the idea of redness.

The Latin adjective ~russus~ also lies behind French ~roux~, so ~rutiler~ and ~roux~ are distant relatives that share one root. English ~russet~ belongs to the same family, by way of Old French. The participle ~rutilant~ is the commoner form in modern French, used of anything that gleams with a warm, vivid light, and the verb itself is now literary.
en.rythmer: Formed in French from ~rythme~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~, in the sense of giving something a rhythm. The noun ~rythme~ is a learned word: it comes from Latin ~rhythmus~, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~rhuthmós~ (“regulated, measured movement,” hence “cadence, measure”). French spelled it ~rhythme~ until the spelling reform of 1878. The ending ~-er~ is the everyday way of coining a first-conjugation verb from a noun, here meaning “to provide with or give N.”
en.râler: The earlier form was ~raller~, which the sources trace to Middle French ~rasler~ (“to haggle, to bargain for”). Both Wiktionaries call the verb a doublet of ~racler~ (“to scrape”), meaning that the two are variant outcomes of one source. The sources do not spell out how the senses connect, so no link is claimed here. In modern French ~râler~ covers groaning, the rattling breath of the dying, and the everyday sense of grumbling or complaining.
en.râper:
From Middle French ~rasper~, from Old French ~rasper~, from Vulgar Latin *~raspāre~ (“to scrape, to rake”), a word borrowed from Frankish *~hraspōn~, a Germanic verb meaning “to rake together by scraping.” Frankish *~hraspōn~ comes from Proto-Germanic *~hraspōną~, a derivative of *~hrespaną~ (“to tear”), which English Wiktionary traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)krebʰ-~ (“to turn, to bend, to shrink”). The Romance languages share the verb: Occitan, Catalan, Spanish and Portuguese ~raspar~, and Italian ~raspare~. Cognates in the Germanic family include Old High German ~raspōn~, Dutch ~raspen~ and English ~rasp~, although English borrowed ~rasp~ from the Old French form and did not inherit it from Old English.

So ~râper~ is a Germanic word that entered French through Latin dress. Its circumflex marks a lost consonant: Old French ~rasper~ dropped its ~s~, leaving ~â~ as a scar, in the same way as ~forêt~ or ~hôpital~. The sense is the scraping of a surface against something rough. The verb serves for grating food, as cheese or carrots, and also for wearing away cloth, so that a ~vêtement râpé~ is a threadbare one. The derivatives ~râpe~ (“a grater”) and ~râpé~ keep that rasping motion.
en.râteler: Formed from ~râteau~ (“rake”) and the verb ending ~-er~. ~Râteau~ comes from Old French ~rastel~ (about 1180), from Latin ~rastellus~, the diminutive of ~raster~ or ~rastrum~ (“hoe, rake”). It was spelled ~rastiau~ in 1473, then ~rateau~ in 1534. The verb means “to rake.”
en.réabonner: Formed from ~abonner~ with the prefix ~ré-~ (“again”), so the verb means to subscribe again. The prefix, from Latin ~re-~, takes its accented form ~ré-~ before the vowel of the base, which is kept distinct. The base ~abonner~ goes back to Old French ~aboner~ (“to set boundaries”), from ~bone~ (“boundary marker, limit”). English Wiktionary instead analyses it as ~a-~ + ~borne~; the ultimate origin of that noun is unknown. The modern sense of subscribing is plausibly a development of fixing a term or sum in advance, but the sources do not document that step.
en.réabsorber: ~Réabsorber~ is formed from ~absorber~ with the prefix ~ré-~ (“again”): to absorb something once more. The spelling ~ré-~ keeps the prefix distinct before a vowel. The base ~absorber~ comes from Latin ~absorbēre~ (“to swallow up, suck in”), from ~ab-~ (“away”) and ~sorbēre~ (“to suck in, swallow”), a verb that survives in Spanish ~sorber~ and Italian ~sorbire~. French has related words in ~absorption~ and ~résorber~, and the prefix ~re-~ itself comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”).
en.réaccoutumer: ~Réaccoutumer~ is built on ~accoutumer~ with the prefix ~ré-~ (“again”), which takes this form before a vowel. The base ~accoutumer~ comes from Old French ~acostumer~, formed from ~coutume~ with the prefix ~a-~ and the ending ~-er~. ~Coutume~ goes back to Latin ~cōnsuētūdinem~ (“habit”), and it has the doublet ~costume~. To ~réaccoutumer~ someone is to get them used to something again.
en.réactiver: ~Réactiver~ is formed from ~activer~ with the prefix ~ré-~, which here expresses repetition: to activate again. ~Activer~ is built on ~actif~, from Latin ~āctīvus~ (“active, practical”), a derivative of ~agere~ (“to drive, to do”). The prefix goes back to Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and is fully productive, so ~réactiver~ is a transparent modern formation, used of a switch, an account or a dormant process.
en.réactualiser: ~Réactualiser~ is formed from ~actualiser~ with the prefix ~ré-~, meaning “again,” in the sense “to update again” or “to bring back to current relevance.” The form ~ré-~ rather than ~re-~ is the usual one in modern coinages before a vowel, where it keeps the two sounds apart. The base ~actualiser~ is a French creation from the adjective ~actuel~ and the suffix ~-iser~, and ~actuel~ was borrowed from Latin ~actuālis~ (“active, practical”), from ~āctus~ (“act, doing”). The prefix ~ré-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”). The result is a verb used of data, texts and ideas that need to be brought up to date.
en.réadapter: ~Réadapter~ is formed from ~adapter~ and the prefix ~ré-~, which means “again”: to adapt something or someone once more, for instance after a long absence or an illness. The base ~adapter~ comes from Latin ~adaptare~ (“to fit to”), made of ~ad-~ (“toward”) and ~aptare~ (“to fit”), a verb related to ~aptus~, which gave ~apte~. The prefix comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”). The reflexive ~se réadapter~ is common for people who return to a job or a way of life.
en.réadmettre: Formed from ~admettre~ with the prefix ~ré-~, in its sense of repetition: “to admit again, to let back in.” The base comes from Latin ~admittere~ (“to let in”), built from ~ad-~ (“toward”) and ~mittere~ (“to send, to let go”), and was remodeled on French ~mettre~. English borrowed the learned ~admit~ from the same Latin verb. Used of a patient, a student or a member, ~réadmettre~ describes a return through a door that had been closed.
en.réaffirmer: ~Réaffirmer~ is formed from ~affirmer~ with the prefix ~ré-~, meaning “again,” which appears in this form before a vowel in modern coinages. The base ~affirmer~ comes from Latin ~affirmāre~, built from ~ad-~ (“toward”) and ~firmāre~ (“to make firm”), from ~firmus~ (“strong, steady”). To affirm is thus to make a statement firm, and to ~réaffirmer~ it is to make it firm once more. The verb is used of principles, commitments and positions that someone restates in order to leave no doubt.
en.réagir:
Attested around 1500, ~réagir~ is a learned formation from Latin ~reagere~ (“to push back, to drive back”), built on the prefix ~re-~ (“back, in return”) and ~agere~ (“to drive, to do, to act”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive, to lead”). Its sense was later reshaped on the French verb ~agir~ (“to act”), so that ~réagir~ reads transparently as ~ré-~ + ~agir~, “to act back.” Through ~agere~ it is cognate with Italian ~reagire~, Spanish ~reaccionar~, and English ~react~, and through the PIE root with English ~act~, ~agent~, and Greek ~ágein~ (“to lead”).

The word began in the language of physics and chemistry: one substance ~réagit~ upon another, exerting a counter-force or counter-effect. From this technical “acting back” it spread into ordinary life, where to ~réagir~ is to respond — to a remark, a crisis, a provocation — with an action of one's own. The noun ~réaction~ followed the same path and even acquired a political coloring, ~réactionnaire~ naming those who wished to act back against revolutionary change. The fertile root ~agere~ seeds a vast French family: ~agir~, ~agent~, ~agile~, ~agiter~, ~action~, ~acte~, and ~rédiger~ — all turning on the idea of setting something in motion.
en.réajuster: Formed in French from ~ajuster~ with the prefix ~ré-~, whose usual sense is repetition: to ~réajuster~ is to adjust again, to bring something back into proper alignment. ~Ajuster~ is built on ~juste~ (“just, exact”) with ~a-~ and the verb ending, and ~juste~ descends from Latin ~iūstus~ (“lawful, right”). The prefix ~ré-~ goes back to Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”). English ~adjust~ was borrowed from the Old French verb, so the two languages share the base verb.
en.réaliser:
Unlike many commonly used verbs, ~réaliser~ is not a direct inheritance from Latin but a French formation of the fifteenth century, built from the adjective ~réel~ (“real”) and the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make, to render”) — literally “to make real.” ~réel~ descends from Medieval Latin ~reālis~ (“relating to a thing, actual”), from Latin ~rēs~ (“thing, matter, affair”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~reh₁-~ (“property, goods”). So at bottom ~réaliser~ means to turn an idea into a ~rēs~, a real thing. Cognates of ~réel~ survive as Italian ~reale~ and Spanish ~real~, and the verb entered English as ~realize~.

The verb's earliest French sense was the concrete one still central today: to bring a project, a dream, or a sum of money into reality — to “carry out,” to “make happen,” and in cinema to ~réaliser~ a film is to direct it. The mental sense, “to realize, to become aware of,” is a calque of English ~realize~; though long criticized by purists as an anglicism, it was defended by André Gide and has been current since the late nineteenth century. Interestingly, the English meaning echoes an old metaphor already latent in Latin ~reor~ (“to reckon, to think”), where “fixing” a thing in the mind shades into thinking it. From ~rēs~ come a large French family, including ~réel~, ~réalité~, ~réalisme~, ~réalisateur~ (“film director”), and ~république~ (~rēs pūblica~, “the public thing”).
en.réaléser: Formed from ~aléser~ with the prefix ~ré-~, which here means “again”: to ~réaléser~ is to bore or ream a hole a second time. The base goes back to Old French ~alaisier~ (“to widen”), ultimately from Latin ~lātus~ (“wide”), and in modern French it names the machining of a bore to an exact diameter. The prefix comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”). ~Ré-~ is the form used before a vowel in modern coinages, so the vowels stay distinct: ~ré-~ + ~aléser~. A reamed cylinder that has worn can thus be bored out once more.
en.réaménager: Built from the prefix ~ré-~ (“again”) and ~aménager~ (“to arrange, to fit out”), so “to arrange anew,” as when a room, a district or a timetable is laid out afresh. The base ~aménager~ is itself ~a-~ + ~ménager~ (“to manage”), from ~ménage~ (“household”), which comes from Old French ~manoir~ (“to dwell”) and Latin ~manere~ (“to remain”). The verb thus rests on the idea of a lived-in space: first a household was kept, then a space was fitted out, and ~réaménager~ does it a second time. The same Latin verb lies behind English ~remain~ and ~mansion~.
en.réanimer:
By the English Wiktionary account, ~réanimer~ is simply ~ré-~ + ~animer~. French Wiktionary is more guarded: it calls ~réanimer~ an initially incorrect form of ~ranimer~, probably shaped by confusion with French ~réanimation~ or English ~to reanimate~, while noting that it is now accepted as a synonym of ~ranimer~ in the medical sense. Either way the base is ~animer~, from Latin ~animāre~ (“to give breath to, to bring to life”), from ~anima~ (“breath, air, life, soul”), which goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂enh₁-~ (“to breathe”).

The two sources therefore agree on the pieces and differ on how they were put together. ~Ranimer~ is the older, regular verb with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”) and the base ~animer~, while ~réanimer~ is the form that won the medical field: a ~service de réanimation~ is, etymologically, a place where breath is given back. The root also gives ~animal~, ~unanime~, ~magnanime~, ~animation~ and ~inanimé~, and it is shared by Latin ~animus~ (“mind, spirit”) and Greek ~ánemos~ (“wind”).
en.réapparaître: Formed from ~ré-~ (“again”) and ~apparaître~ (“to appear”), so “to appear again”. The prefix goes back to Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and has its plain sense of repetition here. The base ~apparaître~ comes from Old French ~aparoistre~, which reshaped Latin ~appārēre~ (~ad-~ + ~pārēre~, “to be visible”) through the Late Latin inchoative ~appārēscere~, a form that stressed coming into view. The modern gloss “to respawn in a video game” is a recent extension of the same repetition, with a character appearing again after being removed.
en.réapprendre: Formed from ~apprendre~ (“to learn”) and the prefix ~ré-~, a spelling of ~re-~ (“again”) used here before a vowel, so “to learn again.” French Wiktionary also points to the variant ~rapprendre~. ~Apprendre~ itself comes from Latin ~apprehendere~ (“to seize, to grasp”), made of ~ad-~ and ~prehendere~, which Old French wore down to ~aprendre~.
en.réapprovisionner: Formed from the prefix ~ré-~ and ~approvisionner~, so “to restock.” The base verb is built on ~provisionner~, the noun ~provision~ plus ~-er~, with the prefix ~a-~ from Latin ~ad-~ (“toward”). The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin ~prōvīsiō~ (“foresight, preparation”), from ~prōvidēre~, “to see ahead.” To ~approvisionner~ is to supply or stock, and in finance to put money into an account. The prefix ~ré-~ adds the idea of repetition, “to do again”: ~réapprovisionner~ is to supply anew what has run low, a shop with goods or an account with funds.
en.réargenter: Formed from ~argenter~ with the prefix ~re-~, so “to silver again,” as when the worn coating of a mirror or plated object is renewed. The base verb comes from ~argent~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, and the noun ~argent~ from Latin ~argentum~ (“silver”), a word related to Greek ~argós~ (“white, shining”). The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and marks repetition.
en.réarmer: Formed from the prefix ~ré-~ (“again”) and the verb ~armer~, which comes from Latin ~armāre~ (“to equip with weapons”), derived from ~arma~ (“weapons”). ~Réarmer~ means to equip with weapons again, as when a country rebuilds its forces. It also has a technical sense, to reset a mechanism such as a firearm or a trap so that it is ready to fire.
en.réarranger: Formed from ~arranger~ with the prefix ~ré-~, meaning “again”: to arrange anew. The prefix goes back to Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and takes the form ~ré-~ before a vowel in modern coinages. The base ~arranger~ is attested around 1160 as Old French ~arengier~, built on ~rengier~ (modern ~ranger~), from the noun ~renc~ (“row, rank”). That noun was borrowed from Frankish *~hring~ (“ring, circle”), the same word that survives in English ~ring~. The verb began by meaning to line up fighters in formation and later softened to “put in order” and “settle”.
en.réassigner: Formed from ~assigner~ with the prefix ~ré-~, meaning “to assign again,” whether to allot something anew or to summon someone before a court a second time. ~Assigner~ goes back through Old French ~asigner~ to Latin ~assignāre~ (“to mark out, allot”), from ~ad-~ + ~signāre~, built on ~signum~ (“mark, sign”). Latin used it above all for allotting land. The sense of summoning someone to court, as in ~assigner en justice~, appeared in the fourteenth century. The form ~ré-~ is the one usually chosen before a vowel in modern coinages.
en.réassortir: ~Réassortir~ is formed from ~assortir~ with the prefix ~ré-~, which here means “again,” so the verb means “to restock, to replenish.” The base ~assortir~ is built on Old French ~sortir~ in its old sense of “to choose, to allot,” itself from Latin ~sors~ (“lot, share, fate”), the word that also gave ~sorte~ and ~sort~. To ~assortir~ is to gather things of the same sort so that they match, and to ~réassortir~ a shop is to bring its range of goods back up to a suitable assortment.
en.réassurer: Formed from ~assurer~ and the prefix ~ré-~ (“again”), the verb means to reinsure, as an insurer does by placing part of its risk with another insurer. French Wiktionary also points to ~rassurer~ for the sense “to reassure.” The base ~assurer~ comes from Old French ~asseürer~, from Late Latin ~assecūrāre~ (“to make secure”), built on ~ad-~ and Latin ~sēcūrus~ (“free from care”), itself ~sē-~ (“without”) and ~cūra~ (“care”).
en.récapituler:
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin ~recapitulāre~ (“to go over the main points again”), built from ~re-~ (“again”) and ~capitulum~, a diminutive of ~caput~ (“head”). The verb thus means, literally, to “re-head”: to run back over the headings. Latin ~caput~ goes back to a Proto-Indo-European *~kaput-~ (“head”), and English ~head~ and German ~Haupt~ are its Germanic cousins. Italian ~ricapitolare~ and Spanish ~recapitular~ come from the same Latin verb.

The diminutive ~capitulum~ named a small head, then a heading, and finally a chapter, which is how French got ~chapitre~. Christian writers favored ~recapitulāre~ for summing up a text or a body of teaching under its principal heads, and that learned sense is the one French kept: to ~récapituler~ is to go back over the essentials in order. The family is large. ~Capituler~ originally referred to negotiating terms set out in chapters, hence the sense of surrendering on agreed conditions. ~Capitulation~, ~capital~ and ~chef~ all descend from ~caput~, and ~récapitulation~, shortened in speech to ~récap~, is the noun learners meet first.
en.réceptionner: Formed from the noun ~réception~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin ~receptio~ (“the act of receiving”), from ~recipere~ (“to receive”), itself made of ~re-~ (“back”) and ~capere~ (“to take, to hold”). The verb is a relatively modern coinage of commercial and administrative French, meaning to take delivery of goods and check them on arrival. It is often criticized as a heavy substitute for the plain ~recevoir~, which comes from the same Latin ~recipere~.
en.réchampir: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ and the verb ~champir~. The French source glosses it as “to give back the field,” that is, to give a design relief by setting two different tones of paint side by side. The ~champ~ is the background field against which a motif stands out, and ~réchampir~ is the painter's and decorator's term for picking out moldings or ornaments by contrast with that ground.
en.réchapper: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ and the verb ~échapper~. Here ~re-~ does not mean “again” but reinforces the idea, so ~réchapper~ means “to come through, to survive” a danger, as in ~réchapper d'un accident~. The base ~échapper~ comes from Old French ~escaper~, from Vulgar Latin *~excappare~, built from ~ex-~ (“out of”) and Late Latin ~cappa~ (“cape”), which is “to slip out of one's cloak.” The prefix therefore adds emphasis to an escape that was narrow.
en.réchauffer: Formed in French from the prefix ~ré-~ (a form of ~re-~, Latin ~re-~, “back, again”) and the verb ~échauffer~, though English Wiktionary also traces it to Old French ~reschauffer~ and its variants. The base ~échauffer~ comes through Middle French ~eschauffer~ from Vulgar Latin *~excalfāre~, from Latin ~excalefacere~, ~ex-~ + ~calefacere~ (“to make warm”). English ~scald~ is a cognate of the related ~échauder~. ~Réchauffer~ means to warm something again, or to heat up what has cooled.
en.récidiver: ~Récidiver~ is a denominal verb formed from the noun ~récidive~ with the ending ~-er~, and means to reoffend or to relapse. ~Récidive~ comes from Latin ~recidīvus~ (“falling back, recurring”), an adjective made from ~recidere~ (“to fall back”), itself ~re-~ + ~cadere~ (“to fall”). The root image is a literal falling again: someone who has been down once and falls back into the same fault. The word is most at home in law, for a repeat offender, and in medicine, for a disease that returns after apparent recovery.
en.réciproquer: From Latin ~reciprocāre~ (“to move back and forth, to reverse”), the verb related to the adjective ~réciproque~. French Wiktionary refers the verb to that adjective, so the two share a single Latin family. In French the verb means to return a favor or feeling in kind. The Latin adjective ~reciprocus~ expressed motion in both directions, and the verb ~reciprocāre~ gave English ~reciprocate~ as well, so the English and French verbs are learned cousins from the same Latin source. In French the family is better known through ~réciproque~, ~réciprocité~ and the adverb ~réciproquement~.
en.réciter: Borrowed from Latin ~recitāre~ (“to read aloud, to recite”), a compound of ~re-~ and ~citāre~. In Latin, ~citāre~ meant “to summon, to call forth” and is the source of French ~citer~. To ~réciter~ is therefore to call something forth again, aloud and from memory or text. The sense has changed little: a poem, a lesson or a prayer is ~récité~. French Wiktionary refers readers to ~ré-~ and ~citer~ for the parts.
en.réclamer:
From Old French ~reclamer~, from Latin ~reclāmāre~ (“to cry out against, to protest loudly”), formed from the prefix ~re-~ (“back, against”) and ~clāmāre~ (“to call, to shout”), from Proto-Indo-European *~kelh₁-~ (“to call, to shout”). Cognate with Italian ~reclamare~ and Spanish ~reclamar~, and — through ~clāmāre~ — with English ~claim~ (itself borrowed from Old French) and, through the same PIE root, with English ~low~ (“to moo”) and Latin ~calāre~.

The Latin verb was originally adversarial: to ~reclāmāre~ was to shout ~re-~, “back,” at a speaker — to clamor in opposition. That confrontational sense survives in modern ~réclamer~ when it means “to protest, to object,” but the dominant modern meaning shifted from crying against something to crying for it: to ~réclamer~ is now above all to demand, to claim, to call insistently for what one is owed — ~réclamer son dû~. A child ~réclame~ its mother; a creditor ~réclame~ payment. From the same ~clāmāre~ French built a loud family: ~clamer~, ~acclamer~, ~proclamer~, ~déclamer~, ~s'exclamer~, and the noun ~clameur~ (“clamor, outcry”) — all of them, like ~réclamer~, rooted in the raised voice.
en.récoler:
From Latin ~recolere~, a verb made of ~re-~ (“again”) and ~colere~ (“to tend, to cultivate, to dwell in, to honor”). Both French and English Wiktionary give it as a direct borrowing from the Latin verb, a learned word rather than one inherited through Old French. Its Latin sense of going back over something, to revisit or review it, is the one that fits the modern verb, which means to check something against a record.

In French, ~récoler~ is a technical verb: to collate, to compare, to verify an inventory or a statement item by item. The Latin root ~colere~ lies behind French ~culture~, ~colon~ and ~culte~, so the verb belongs to a family whose basic idea is care and attention given to something, from tilling a field to honoring a god. The verb is rare today and survives mostly in legal and administrative language, where the noun ~récolement~ names the checking itself.
en.récolter:
French ~récolter~ is a denominal verb built on the noun ~récolte~ (“harvest”). That noun was borrowed in the sixteenth century from Italian ~ricolta~ (“harvest,” attested from the fourteenth century), the feminine past participle of ~ricogliere~ (“to gather, to collect”). The Italian verb descends from Latin ~recolligere~ (“to gather together again”), formed from ~re-~ plus ~colligere~ (“to collect”), itself ~com-~ (“together”) plus ~legere~ (“to gather, to pick, to read”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~leǵ-~ (“to collect, to gather”). The French verb ~cueillir~ and the noun ~collecte~ spring from the same Latin ~colligere~.

So ~récolter~ carries inside it the idea of gathering up once more what the field has produced — re-collecting the grain. From the root *~leǵ-~ the Romance languages drew a rich crop: French ~récolte~, ~collection~, ~recueil~ (“anthology,” literally a re-gathering), and ~légende~ (“legend,” from Latin “things to be read”), since the same Latin ~legere~ meant both to gather and to read. Figuratively, French ~récolter~ reaps abstractions too — one can ~récolter~ applause, information, or trouble, just as English speaks of reaping what one sows.
en.récompenser:
Attested in the fourteenth century, ~récompenser~ descends from Late Latin ~recompensāre~, formed with the prefix ~re-~ on Latin ~compensāre~ (“to balance, to weigh one thing against another”). ~compensāre~ is itself ~com-~ (“together”) plus ~pensāre~, the frequentative of ~pendere~ (“to weigh, to hang”), from a Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)pend-~ (“to stretch, to weigh”). The same ~pensāre~ underlies an astonishing range of French words and gives English ~compensate~, ~pension~, and ~pensive~.

The original image is a pair of scales: to ~compensāre~ was to set weights against each other until the balance was even. ~recompensāre~ added the sense of weighing back, of giving an equivalent in return — and from there French slid from mere balancing to rewarding. To ~récompenser~ is to give someone their due, but skewed toward the pleasant: a prize, a reward, a deserved good. The neutral metrology survives in the doublet ~compenser~ (“to compensate, to offset”), while the same ~pendere~ family scattered across French in ~peser~ (“to weigh”), ~pensée~ (“thought,” for the mind too weighs ideas), and ~dépense~ (“expenditure”).
en.réconcilier: Borrowed from Latin ~reconciliāre~ (“to restore, to bring back, to reconcile, to re-establish harmony or friendship”). The verb appears in the Roman de Troie (about 1160-1170) in the form ~reconciliier~. It is made of the prefix ~re-~ and the Latin verb ~conciliāre~, whose family also gave French ~concilier~ and ~concile~. The prefix ~re-~ here marks a return to a former state: those who were once friends are brought back together.
en.réconforter: ~Réconforter~ is formed from ~conforter~ with the prefix ~ré-~ (“back, again”). English Wiktionary segments it a little differently, as ~ré-~ plus ~confort~ plus ~-er~, which gives the same result. ~Conforter~ is inherited from Old French ~conforter~, from Late Latin ~cōnfortāre~ (“to strengthen greatly”), built from ~con-~ (“thoroughly”) and ~fortis~ (“strong”). The two French verbs divided the old range of the Old French verb: ~conforter~ kept the sense of strengthening, while ~réconforter~ came to serve for consolation.
en.récrier: From ~crier~ with the prefix ~ré-~ (“back, again”). The verb is used above all in the reflexive ~se récrier~, “to cry out, to exclaim.” The base ~crier~ comes from Old French ~crier~ (also ~crider~), from Vulgar Latin *~critare~, a reduction of Latin ~quiritare~ (“to cry out”). The origin of ~quiritare~ is disputed: one old account makes it a call upon the Roman citizens, the ~Quirites~, for help, while others link it to ~queror~ (“to complain”) or treat it as imitative of sound.
en.récriminer:
From Latin ~criminārī~ (“to accuse”), which comes from ~crīmen~ (“accusation, charge”). The two Wiktionaries frame the route differently. French Wiktionary builds the verb from ~ré-~ and Old French ~criminer~ (“to accuse”), itself from the Latin verb. English Wiktionary calls it a learned borrowing from Latin ~recrīmināre~, formed on the same noun ~crīmen~. Either way, the prefix ~ré-~ gives the idea of answering back, so ~récriminer~ is to accuse in return, to hit back with complaints. English took the verb as ~recriminate~.

The Latin noun ~crīmen~ is the root of a whole family of French words, all learned borrowings: ~crime~, ~criminel~, and ~incriminer~, which means to put someone in the position of an accused. ~Récriminer~ belongs to the same set and shares its bookish register. Today it is usually heard as a verb of protest, to complain bitterly and to answer reproaches with reproaches, most often in the plural noun ~récriminations~, a standard word for bitter grievances.
en.récrire: Formed from ~écrire~ with the prefix ~re-~, here in its ~ré-~ form before a vowel, meaning “again.” The base ~écrire~ comes from Old French ~escrivre~ and, before that, from Latin ~scribere~, a verb that originally meant “to scratch or incise,” as one cut letters into wax or stone. ~Récrire~ simply adds repetition to that old image: to write something over again, or in a new version.
en.récréer:
Borrowed from Latin ~recreāre~ (“to make anew, to restore, to refresh”), formed from ~re-~ (“again”) and ~creāre~ (“to create, to make”). Latin ~recreāre~ already had the figurative sense of restoring someone's strength or spirits, and that is the meaning French took. English ~recreate~ and ~recreation~ come from the same Latin verb, as do Italian ~ricreare~ and Spanish ~recrear~.

French ~récréer~ went from the idea of reviving someone to that of amusing them: it means to entertain, to delight, and in the reflexive ~se récréer~ to take one's pleasure. The word now sounds literary or dated. Its noun ~récréation~ is far more common, with a clipped form ~récré~ used for the school break. The verb ~récréer~ must not be confused with ~recréer~ (“to create again”), which is a separate formation on ~créer~ with a different pronunciation, though both go back to the Latin ~re-~ + ~creāre~. The root also gives ~créer~, ~création~ and ~créature~.
en.récupérer:
A learned re-borrowing (around 1495) from Latin ~recuperare~ (“to regain, to recover, to get back”), itself the prefix ~re-~ (“back, again”) on a stem related to ~capere~ (“to take, to seize”) — recovery being, etymologically, a “taking back.” The same Latin verb had already entered French much earlier by ordinary phonetic descent as ~recouvrer~ (“to recover”), so ~récupérer~ and ~recouvrer~ form a doublet: two French verbs, one inherited and worn down, the other re-cut directly from the Latin. Spanish ~recuperar~, Italian ~recuperare~, and English ~recuperate~ are parallel learned descendants.

Because it was reshaped from the Latin rather than passed down by mouth, ~récupérer~ keeps a transparent, almost technical feel, and its meanings fan out widely: to get back a lost object, to recover one's strength after effort (~récupérer~ after a hard week), to reclaim or recycle materials, and — in a distinctly modern political sense — to co-opt or appropriate a cause or a movement for one's own ends. The noun ~récupération~ covers all of these, from physical recovery to salvage to ideological appropriation. Beside it the older ~recouvrer~ survives in more formal registers, as when one ~recouvre~ a debt or ~recouvre~ one's sight.
en.récurer: Formed from ~curer~ with the prefix ~ré-~. French ~curer~ (“to clean out”) comes from Latin ~curare~ (“to take care of”), a verb built on ~cura~ (“care”). The prefix is the only addition, and the result means “to scrub, to scour” a pan or a surface. The same Latin root also gives ~cure~ and ~curatif~.
en.récuser:
From Latin ~recūsāre~ (“to refuse, to object to”), a learned borrowing built from ~re-~ (“back”) and ~causa~ (“reason, case, lawsuit”). The Latin verb meant, literally, to plead a reason against something, and it belonged both to the courtroom and to everyday refusal. The origin of ~causa~ itself is unknown. Italian ~ricusare~ and Spanish ~recusar~ continue the same Latin verb, and English borrowed it as ~recuse~ in its legal sense.

In French the verb stayed close to its legal home. ~Récuser~ means to challenge the impartiality or competence of a judge, a juror, an expert or a witness, and from there, more broadly, to reject something such as a testimony or an authority. The reflexive ~se récuser~ is what a judge does when he declares himself unfit to hear a case. The older Latin sense of plain refusal faded, while the courtroom sense survived. The same ~causa~ lies behind ~cause~, ~accuser~ (“to bring a case against”), ~excuser~ (“to take out of the case”) and even ~chose~, the popular outcome of ~causa~, whose “thing” began as a “matter in dispute.”
en.rédiger:
From Latin ~redigere~ (“to bring back, drive back, reduce”), a compound of the prefix ~re-~ (“back, again”) and ~agere~ (“to drive, do, act”). ~Agere~ derives from the PIE root *~h₂eǵ-~ (“to drive”), source also of Greek ~ágō~ (“I lead”) and, through Latin borrowings, of English ~act~, ~agent~, and ~agile~; Italian and Spanish keep the parent verb in ~agire~ and the like. The literal Latin sense is to “drive back” or “reduce” a thing to some state — to bring it down to order.

The path to “writing” runs through that idea of reduction. Medieval Latin used ~redigere in scriptis~, “to reduce into writing,” to set a matter down in fixed, orderly form — and from this phrase the “write up, compose” sense crystallized. So ~rédiger~ never meant mere scribbling: it means to compose with care, to draft a contract, an article, a report, marshalling loose material into finished prose. Its agent and act are ~rédacteur~ (“editor, writer”) and ~rédaction~ (“drafting; an editorial office; a school essay”). The driving root *~h₂eǵ-~ powers a huge French family beyond it — ~agir~, ~agent~, ~agile~, ~action~, ~rédiger~ standing among them as the one that drives words into shape.
en.rédimer:
Borrowed from Latin ~redimere~ (“to buy back, to ransom”), by way of Middle French ~redimer~. The Latin verb is made of ~re-~ (“back”) and ~emere~ (“to buy”), so the French verb says, at root, “to buy back.” English ~redeem~ answers to the same Latin verb, as do Italian ~redimere~ and Spanish ~redimir~.

In French, ~rédimer~ is a learned, literary word, used above all for ransoming or freeing someone, and for atoning for a fault. Its family is larger than it looks. ~Rédemption~ and ~rédempteur~ come from the related Latin noun, and ~rançon~ (“ransom”) is a popular, worn-down form of the same noun, so ~rédemption~ and ~rançon~ are doublets. The simple Latin verb ~emere~ also lies behind ~exempt~ and ~prompt~, both built on its compounds.
en.réduire:
From Old French ~reduire~, from Latin ~redūcere~ (“to lead back, to bring back”), which is ~re-~ (“back”) + ~dūcere~ (“to lead, to draw”). ~dūcere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~doukō~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~dewk-~ (“to pull, to lead”). That root reaches far into Germanic: it gives English ~tow~, German ~ziehen~ (“to pull”), and even the ~-zog~ of German ~Herzog~ (“duke,” literally “army-leader,” a calque of Greek ~stratēgós~). Latin built ~dux~ (“leader”) from the same root — the ancestor of ~duke~ and Italian ~duce~.

The meaning traveled a long way. ~redūcere~ first meant simply “to lead back,” and Old French ~reduire~ could mean “to bring back, to restore.” The modern sense “to make smaller” grew from the idea of bringing a thing back to a smaller, simpler, or controlled state — reducing an army, a price, a text, or a rebel “brought back” to obedience. The ~dūcere~ family is one of the richest in French: ~conduire~, ~produire~, ~traduire~, ~introduire~, ~séduire~, ~déduire~, plus the nouns ~duc~, ~conduite~, and ~aqueduc~ (“water-leader”).
en.réembaucher: From ~ré-~ + ~embaucher~, “to hire again.” The sources explain the base differently. French Wiktionary derives ~embaucher~ from ~débaucher~ by swapping the prefix ~dé-~ for ~en-~, while English Wiktionary analyzes it as ~en-~ + ~bauche~ + ~-er~. Either way, ~embaucher~ means “to take someone on.” The prefix ~ré-~, from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”), expresses repetition: ~réembaucher~ is to take on a worker once more, for instance after a layoff.
en.réemployer: Formed in French from ~employer~ with the prefix ~ré-~, meaning “to use again.” The form ~ré-~ rather than ~re-~ is the usual choice before a vowel in modern coinages, where it keeps the two vowels apart. The base ~employer~ comes from Old French ~emploier~, from Latin ~implicare~ (“to fold in, to involve”), made of ~in-~ and ~plicare~ (“to fold”). It is a doublet of the learned ~impliquer~, so to ~réemployer~ something is literally to fold it into service a second time, whether a material, a method or a worker.
en.réensemencer: Formed from ~ensemencer~ with the prefix ~ré-~, meaning “again”: to ~réensemencer~ is to sow a field or a culture a second time. The base is built from ~en-~, the noun ~semence~ (“seed”) and the ending ~-er~, in the sense of providing with seed. ~Semence~ came through Old French from Late Latin ~sementia~, derived from Latin ~sēmen~ (“seed”). The prefix ~ré-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and is spelled with an accent before the vowel ~e~, which keeps the two ~e~ sounds apart.
en.réentendre: ~Réentendre~ is built from ~entendre~ and the prefix ~ré-~, which here means “again”: to hear something a second time. The base comes from Old French ~entendre~, from Latin ~intendere~ (“to stretch toward”), made of ~in-~ and ~tendere~; its sense drifted from directing the attention, to understanding, to hearing. The prefix ~ré-~ goes back to Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and is fully productive in French, so the verb is a transparent modern formation: it simply means to hear again, whether a song, a witness or a sentence.
en.réer: The verb ~réer~ is used of a stag, whose cry it names (“to roar”). Both Wiktionaries derive it simply from Late Latin ~ragere~, and neither gives further steps, so the path through Old French is not documented here. A rare verb, it survives mainly in hunting vocabulary.
en.réescompter: ~Réescompter~ is formed from ~escompter~ with the prefix ~ré-~ (“again”), which stands before a vowel in modern coinages: to discount again. ~Escompter~ belongs to ~compter~ (“to count”), from Latin ~computāre~ (“to calculate”), and first belongs to banking, where it means to pay a bill's holder now, less a deduction for the time left to run. It later gained the everyday sense of counting on something in advance.
en.réessayer: Formed from the prefix ~ré-~ (“again”) and ~essayer~. The base is a verb built on the noun ~essai~, which comes from Late Latin ~exagium~ (“a weighing”), so ~essayer~ first meant to test, as one tests a metal. The prefix ~ré-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and appears in its ~ré-~ form before a vowel, which keeps the two vowels apart. The sense is plain repetition: to ~réessayer~ is to try again.
en.réexaminer: ~Réexaminer~ is the verb ~examiner~ with the prefix ~ré-~, “again,” so it means to examine a second time. The base ~examiner~ comes from Latin ~examināre~ (“to weigh, to test”). The prefix ~re-~ and its variants ~ré-~, ~r-~ and ~ra-~ express repetition, and the hyphenless spelling is the modern one.
en.réexporter: ~Réexporter~ is formed from ~exporter~ with the prefix ~ré-~, which here carries its ordinary sense of repetition: to export again, usually goods that were imported first. The base ~exporter~ was borrowed from Latin ~exportare~ (“to carry out”), made of ~ex-~ (“out of”) and ~portare~ (“to carry”). Its commercial sense is recorded in 1756 and may owe something to English ~to export~, though the influence is proposed rather than proven. Add the prefix and you get a verb for sending abroad what has already come in from abroad.
en.réexpédier: Formed from ~expédier~ with the prefix ~ré-~, which here marks a return to the point of departure: to send back, or to send on again. The base ~expédier~ is traced by French Wiktionary to Latin ~expedīre~, while English Wiktionary analyses it as ~expédient~ plus ~-er~, so the sources disagree. Latin ~expedīre~ is usually read as ~ex-~ and the root of ~pēs~ (“foot”), literally to free the feet. ~Réexpédier~ means to reship or forward goods or mail.
en.réfléchir:
From Latin ~reflectere~ (“to bend back, to turn back”), a compound of the prefix ~re-~ (“back, again”) and ~flectere~ (“to bend, to curve”). The ultimate root of ~flectere~ is uncertain and has no secure Indo-European cognates, though a Proto-Italic *~flektō~ is reconstructed. The verb is cognate with Italian ~flettere~ and survives, through its derivatives, in English ~reflect~, ~flexible~, and ~inflect~. French inherited a popular form ~réflechir~ alongside the learned doublet that gave the noun ~réflexion~.

The metaphor at the heart of this verb is light bending back from a surface. From the optical sense — a mirror ~reflects~ an image — French drew an inward, mental one: to “turn one's thought back” upon itself, to ponder. So ~réfléchir~ means both “to reflect (light)” and “to think hard,” and the two senses illuminate each other — the thinker turns ideas over the way a mirror turns back a beam. A reflexive verb in French is a verbe ~réfléchi~, one whose action bends back onto the subject. From the same ~flectere~ stem descend ~fléchir~ (“to bend, to yield”), ~flexible~, ~réflexe~, and ~circonflexe~ — the accent “bent around” a vowel.
en.réformer:
~réformer~ is formed from ~former~ (“to form, to shape”) with the prefix ~re-~ (“again, anew”), answering exactly to Latin ~reformāre~ (“to form again, restore, transform”). The base ~former~ comes from Latin ~forma~ (“shape, form, mould”), a word of famously uncertain origin: it has long been proposed that ~forma~ is somehow connected to Ancient Greek ~morphḗ~ (“shape, beauty”) by a metathesis of consonants, but many etymologists reject the idea — there is no evidence ~forma~ ever passed through a stage *~phorma~ — so the link is best presented as disputed rather than settled.

In its earliest French use, ~réformer~ kept the Latin sense of reshaping or restoring to a better state, and that double edge persists. To ~réformer~ a law, an institution, or a habit is to remould it for the better — the sense that gave the religious ~Réforme~ (the Reformation). But French also kept a contrary sense: to ~réformer~ a soldier or a piece of equipment is to declare it unfit and withdraw it from service. The same ~forma~ family fills French with ~forme~, ~former~, ~formation~, ~réforme~, ~conforme~, and ~déformer~ — all variations on shaping and re-shaping.
en.réfracter: A modern borrowing from English ~to refract~, which was formed on the stem of Latin ~refractus~, the past participle of ~refringere~. That Latin verb is ~re-~ plus ~frangere~ (“to break”), so refracting is literally breaking back, bending a ray of light as it passes from one medium into another. The French verb is a scientific term, used chiefly of light and waves, and it sits beside the older noun for the phenomenon.
en.réfrigérer: ~Réfrigérer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~refrigerāre~ (“to cool, to refresh”). The Latin verb is generally analyzed as ~re-~ + ~frigerāre~, from ~frigus~ (“cold”), the root of French ~frigide~ and ~réfrigérateur~, whose clipped form is ~frigo~. English ~refrigerate~ and Spanish ~refrigerar~ come from the same Latin verb.
en.réfréner:
From Latin ~refrēnāre~ (“to rein in, to hold back”), a compound of ~re-~ (“back”) and ~frēnāre~ (“to bridle”), which is built on ~frēnum~ (“bridle, bit”). The Latin verb thus literally means “to bridle back.” French borrowed it directly from Latin. English ~refrain~ (“to hold oneself back”) came from the same Latin verb through Old French ~refrener~.

The Latin noun ~frēnum~ survived in French as the inherited ~frein~ (“brake”), and the verb ~freiner~ was formed on it. ~Freiner~ is the ordinary verb of braking, while ~réfréner~ is the learned one for holding back feelings or impulses, as in ~réfréner ses envies~ (“to curb one's desires”). The adjective ~effréné~ (“unbridled, frantic”), from Latin ~effrēnātus~, is its opposite: something with no bridle left.
en.réfugier:
Built in French on the noun ~refuge~ with the infinitive ending ~-er~. ~Refuge~ comes from Latin ~refugium~ (“a place of retreat”), from the verb ~refugere~ (“to flee back, take shelter”), itself ~re-~ (“back”) + ~fugere~ (“to flee”). ~Fugere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~fugjō~ and to PIE *~bʰewg-~ (“to flee”), the root that also gives Ancient Greek ~pheugō~ (“I flee”). Through Latin ~fugere~ and its derivatives, the same root yields French ~fuir~, ~fugue~, ~fugitif~, ~refuge~, and ~subterfuge~, and the English ~fugitive~ and the suffix ~-fuge~ in ~centrifuge~.

The verb is almost always reflexive: ~se réfugier~, to take oneself off to safety. The image inside it is precise and slightly counter-intuitive — not merely to flee, but to flee ~back~, to retreat to a refuge, the ~re-~ carrying the sense of withdrawal to a place of shelter. From the physical act of seeking cover the verb extended to the figurative, one can ~se réfugier~ in silence, in work, in memory. The closely related ~réfugié~ (“refugee”) is the same formation frozen as a noun, naming the person who has fled back to safety across a border.
en.réfuter: Borrowed from Latin ~refūtāre~ (“to drive back, to repel”). Roman speakers used the verb in the courtroom and the assembly for pushing back an opponent's claim, and that figure of a blow turned aside is still the core of the French verb. French took it as a learned word, and ~réfuter~ now means to show that an argument or accusation is false. English ~refute~ comes from the same Latin verb, and so does the more formal ~confute~.
en.référencer:
A denominal verb formed in French on the noun ~référence~, which goes back through ~référer~ to Latin ~referre~ (“to carry back, report”), from ~re-~ (“back”) + ~ferre~ (“to carry, bear”). ~Ferre~ descends from Proto-Italic *~ferō~ and from PIE *~bʰer-~ (“to carry, to bear”) — one of the most widespread of all roots, source of Ancient Greek ~pherō~, Sanskrit ~bharati~, and, in the native Germanic line, English ~bear~. The same Latin verb feeds a large French family: ~référence~, ~référent~, ~conférer~, ~différer~, ~offrir~, and ~transférer~.

The oldest sense of ~référencer~ is bookish — to supply something with references or citations. The verb then drifted into commerce, where it now dominates: to ~référencer~ a product is to enter its reference number in a catalogue and so put it on the shelves; to be ~déréférencé~ is to be dropped from the listing. From that the digital age took ~référencement~ for the listing and ranking of a site, the standard French term for search-engine optimization. Other relatives include ~référenceur~ and ~référençage~, all turning on the idea of carrying something back to a fixed point of reference.
en.référer:
From Latin ~referre~ (“to carry back, report, attribute”), from ~re-~ (“back, again”) + ~ferre~ (“to carry, bear”). ~Ferre~ descends from Proto-Italic *~ferō~ and from PIE *~bʰéreti~ (“to bear, carry”), one of the most widespread Indo-European roots. Through it, ~ferre~ is cognate with English ~bear~, Ancient Greek ~φέρω~ (~phérō~), and Sanskrit ~भरति~ (~bhárati~) — all “to carry.”

The image is one of carrying a matter back to its source. To ~référer~ is to carry a question, a fact, or a name back and lay it before something else: one ~se réfère à~ a text (carries the point back to it for authority), or ~en réfère à~ a superior (carries the matter back up to them for a decision). The same ~ferre~ is astonishingly prolific in French through its prefixed compounds: ~conférer~, ~déférer~, ~différer~, ~offrir~, ~souffrir~, ~transférer~, and the nouns ~référence~, ~rapport~, and ~relation~. English drew the parallel family ~refer~, ~confer~, ~transfer~, and ~offer~ from the very same Latin verb.
en.régaler: French Wiktionary derives ~régaler~ from the noun ~régal~ (“feast, treat”) plus the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to treat someone to a feast.” ~Régal~ comes from Old French ~rigale~ (“festivity, entertainment”), which is traced to Old French ~gale~ and the verb ~galer~ (“to enjoy oneself”) with a prefix ~ri-~ borrowed from the same family as ~rigoler~. The family of ~galer~ also gave ~galant~. The sense shifted over time from a festive occasion to the meal itself, and now to anything one relishes: ~régaler~ can mean to delight, and ~se régaler~ to have a feast.
en.régater: Formed in French from the noun ~régate~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, so that ~régater~ means “to take part in a sailing race.” The noun ~régate~ is a borrowing from Venetian ~regata~ (“contest for mastery”), the name of the boat races held in Venice. The French verb is thus a late loan-plus-ending formation, built on a word that came from Italy.
en.régenter: ~Régenter~ is a denominal verb: ~régent~ plus the ending ~-er~. ~Régent~ was borrowed from Latin ~regens~, the present participle of the verb ~regere~ (“to rule”), and the same Latin verb underlies ~régir~. French Wiktionary notes that ~régenter~ was intransitive in the fourteenth century. The verb first meant to act as a regent or master, and today it means to dominate or to lay down the law, usually with disapproval.
en.régionaliser: ~Régionaliser~ is formed from the adjective ~régional~ with the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to make regional,” as when administrative power is shifted to regions. The base ~régional~ comes from Latin ~regiōnālis~, or, in English Wiktionary's analysis, was built in French from ~région~ + ~-al~. In either account the root is Latin ~regiō~ (“region”), and ~-iser~ adds the sense of converting something into that character.
en.régir:
From Latin ~regere~ (« to lead, direct, rule »), from Proto-Italic *~regō~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₃reǵ-~ (« to straighten, to direct »). The semantics run straight from the physical to the political: to make straight, hence to set a course, hence to govern. The root is one of the great Indo-European families, cognate with Sanskrit ~rā́jati~ (« he rules »), and — through the same *~h₃reǵ-~ — with English ~right~ and ~rich~ and with the ~-roy~ of ~royal~.

In French ~régir~ holds the formal, abstract sense « to govern, to rule » a state, a set of conditions, or a grammar that ~régit~ which case a verb takes. Its Latin participle ~rectus~ (« straight, right ») and the agent noun ~rector~ seeded a vast family: ~régime~, ~régisseur~ (« stage manager, steward »), ~région~, ~recteur~, ~direct~, ~correct~, and ~droit~ (« right, straight, law »), this last the popular descendant of ~rectus~. Few Latin roots so plainly preserve the metaphor that to rule is to keep things in a straight line.
en.réglementer: Formed from the noun ~règlement~ (“regulation, set of rules”) with the verbal suffix ~-er~, in the sense “to provide with” rules: to subject something to a regulation. French Wiktionary dates the verb to 1768. The base ~règlement~ belongs to the family of ~règle~, from Latin ~rēgula~ (“ruler, rule”). The verb is used for laying down official rules, while ~régler~ also covers settling a payment or adjusting a device.
en.régler:
French ~régler~ is a denominal verb, formed in the thirteenth century from the noun ~règle~ (“rule, ruler”), which comes from Latin ~rēgula~ (“straight stick, ruler, rule”). ~Rēgula~ is a derivative of ~regere~ (“to keep straight, to direct, to rule”), and that verb rests on a Proto-Indo-European root *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten, to make right”). The root is one of the great ones: Sanskrit ~rā́jati~ (“to rule, to direct”), Latin ~rēx~ (“king”), and through Germanic the English ~right~ and German ~recht~ all spring from it. Italian ~regolare~ and Spanish ~reglar~ are the Romance cousins of the verb; English borrowed ~regulate~ from the related Latin ~regulāre~.

The oldest concrete sense is wonderfully literal: to ~régler~ a sheet of paper is to rule lines on it with a straightedge — the ruler doing exactly what its name says. From “to draw straight lines” the meaning fanned out to “to set right, to adjust, to put in order”: one ~règle~ a watch, a machine, a thermostat; one ~règle~ a quarrel or a bill (~régler ses comptes~, “to settle one's accounts”). The same root underlies a sprawling French family: ~règle~, ~règlement~, ~régulier~ and ~réguler~, ~régime~ and ~régir~, ~roi~ and ~royal~ (through ~rēx~), and ~rectitude~ and ~direct~ (through ~rectus~, “straight”). To regulate is, at heart, to make crooked things straight.
en.régner:
~Régner~ is attested from the second half of the 10th century, passing through Old French ~regner~ / ~reigner~ and Middle French ~régner~. It descends from Latin ~regnare~ (« to be king, to wield absolute power »), a verb built on the noun ~regnum~ (« kingdom, royal power »). That noun belongs to ~rex~, ~regis~ (« king ») and the verb ~regere~ (« to rule, to guide straight »), from PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ (« to straighten, to direct »). Italian ~regnare~ and Spanish ~reinar~ are its Romance counterparts; English ~reign~ entered through Old French.

From designating literal monarchy, ~régner~ broadened figuratively: a fashion, a silence, or a mood can now ~régner~ — that is, prevail or hold sway over a place or an age. The synchronic French noun ~règne~ now feels like its source. The same root *~h₃reǵ-~ radiates through a remarkable family touching kingship and straightness alike — ~roi~, ~royal~, ~régir~, ~région~, ~règle~, ~direct~, and ~correct~ — a reminder that to rule, etymologically, was to keep things in a straight line.
en.régresser: ~Régresser~ is a back-formation from the noun ~régression~, a learned borrowing from Latin ~regressiō~ (“a going back”). The verb was carved out of the noun by adding the verbal ending ~-er~, on the model of ~progresser~, which in turn comes from ~progression~. The ending ~-er~ descends from the Latin first-conjugation infinitive ~-are~ and is French's default way of making a verb from another word. The result is a neat pair of opposites, ~progresser~ (“to move forward”) and ~régresser~ (“to move back”), both reached through nouns that Latin supplied first.
en.régulariser: Formed from the adjective ~régulier~ and the suffix ~-iser~, with the stem reshaped on Latin ~regulāris~ (“of a rule”), which comes from ~rēgula~ (“rule, straight rod”). ~Rēgula~ belongs to the family of ~regere~ (“to guide in a straight line, to rule”). The suffix ~-iser~ means to make or bring to a state, so ~régulariser~ is to make regular: to bring a situation, a payment or someone's papers into conformity with the rules, as in régulariser sa situation (“to sort out one's legal status”). English ~regularize~ comes from the same family.
en.réguler: Borrowed from Latin ~rēgulāre~ (“to direct, to regulate”). The verb has an unusual history in French: for centuries it fell out of use, because ~régler~ did its work, and it reappeared only in 1953. Since its return it has sometimes taken on the senses of English ~regulate~, itself a descendant of the same Latin verb, so the word has partly come back to French by way of English usage. It now belongs to the language of biology, economics and engineering, where one ~régule~ a flow, a temperature or a market.
en.régurgiter:
A learned formation, built from the prefix ~ré-~ (“back”) and the Latin noun ~gurges~ (genitive ~gurgitis~, “throat”; in Latin also “whirlpool”), with the verbal ending ~-er~. The Latin stem is the same one that stands behind French ~gorge~. The French verb thus means, literally, to send something back up through the throat, and its form shows it was assembled from Latin parts by scholars rather than handed down through everyday speech.

In modern French ~régurgiter~ is used first of the body, for bringing food back up, and it carries over figuratively to someone who repeats facts or lessons without having digested them. The prefix ~ré-~ here means “back,” the movement reversed. English ~regurgitate~ is the parallel formation. Several ordinary French words share the root through ~gorge~: ~gorger~, ~dégorger~, ~regorger~ and ~engorger~, which are inherited and belong to everyday speech, whereas ~régurgiter~ keeps the scholarly Latin stem ~gurgit-~ intact.
en.régénérer:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~regenerāre~ (“to bring forth again, to restore”), made of ~re-~ (“again”) and ~generāre~ (“to beget, to produce”). Latin ~generāre~ comes from ~genus~ (“birth, kind”), which belongs to the Proto-Indo-European root *~ǵenh₁-~ (“to give birth, to beget”). That root is very productive: Greek ~génos~ (“race, kind”) and English ~kin~ come from it, as does English ~generate~, borrowed from the Latin verb. Italian ~rigenerare~ and Spanish ~regenerar~ are parallel borrowings of the same Latin word.

In Christian Latin, ~regenerāre~ took on the spiritual sense of being born again, as in baptism, and the religious meaning lingers behind the modern one. French ~régénérer~ now covers everything that is made new: tissue, a forest, a polluted river, a political movement, or a used material put back into service. Its relatives are many. ~Générer~, ~génération~, ~genre~, ~gendre~ and ~engendrer~ all descend from the same Latin family, and ~dégénérer~ is its mirror image, to fall away from one's kind.
en.réhabiliter: ~Réhabiliter~ is formed from ~ré-~ + ~habiliter~. The prefix, from Latin ~re-~, means “back, again”, so the verb means to make someone fit or capable once more: in practice, to restore a person's standing, reputation or legal rights, or to renovate a run-down building. The base ~habiliter~ is a Latin loan, from ~habilitāre~ (“to make fit”), which rests on ~habilis~ (“easy to handle, apt”), from ~habēre~ (“to hold, to have”). The same Latin root gave French ~habile~ and English ~able~.
en.réhabituer: Formed from ~habituer~ with the prefix ~ré-~ (“again”), so it means to accustom someone to something once more. The base ~habituer~ comes from Old French ~abituer~, from Medieval Latin ~habituare~ (“to accustom”), built on Latin ~habitus~ (“condition, bearing, dress, habit”), a noun from ~habēre~ (“to have, to hold”). The deeper origin of ~habēre~ is debated.
en.réhydrater: Formed from ~hydrater~ with the prefix ~ré-~ (“again”), so “to hydrate again, to restore water to.” ~Hydrater~ is made from the noun ~hydrate~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun is a scholarly coinage built on the Greek root of ~hýdōr~ (“water”), as ~hydr-~, plus the chemical suffix ~-ate~. ~Ré-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and is fully productive in French.
en.réimperméabiliser: Formed from ~imperméabiliser~ with the prefix ~ré-~, “again,” so the verb means to make waterproof once more, as when one treats a worn raincoat or tent. The base is built on the adjective ~imperméable~ and the suffix ~-iser~. The adjective comes from Latin ~impermeabilis~ (“that cannot be crossed”), from ~in-~ (“not”) and ~permeabilis~ (“passable”). The prefix ~ré-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”).
en.réimplanter: Formed from the verb ~implanter~ with the prefix ~ré-~, which expresses repetition: to ~réimplanter~ is to implant again or to establish anew. The base ~implanter~ comes from Latin ~implantāre~, made of ~in-~ (“in, into”) and ~plantāre~ (“to plant”), from the noun ~planta~. The image is agricultural, that of setting a shoot firmly in the ground. The ~ré-~ form is used before a vowel in modern coinages, and the prefix itself goes back to Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”).
en.réimporter: From ~ré-~ + ~importer~, “to import again.” The base ~importer~ in its commercial sense (“to bring in goods”) comes from Latin ~importāre~, built from ~in-~ (“into”) and ~portāre~ (“to carry”). The prefix ~ré-~, from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”), expresses repetition here: ~réimporter~ is to bring goods or data in again, typically after they were exported or removed.
en.réimposer: Formed from ~imposer~ with the prefix ~ré-~, “to impose again.” The base ~imposer~ comes from Latin ~imponere~ (“to place upon”), from ~in-~ and ~ponere~ (“to put”), and Old French reshaped it on the model of ~poser~. Its senses run from the physical laying on of something to the figurative burden, such as a duty or a tax, and ~ré-~ adds the idea of doing it a second time.
en.réimprimer: Formed in French from ~imprimer~ with the prefix ~ré-~, which here means repetition: ~réimprimer~ is “to print again,” and especially to bring out a new printing of a book already published. The base ~imprimer~ comes from Latin ~imprimere~ (“to press into, to stamp”), a compound of ~in-~ and ~premere~ (“to press”). French applied it to the new craft of printing when movable type arrived.
en.réincarcérer: Formed from ~incarcérer~ with the prefix ~ré-~, meaning “to put back in prison” after a release. The base is a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ~incarcerare~, built from ~in-~ (“in, into”) and ~carcer~ (“prison”). English ~incarcerate~ is its exact counterpart. The prefix ~ré-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and marks the repetition. Latin ~carcer~ also reached French by the inherited route, as ~chartre~.
en.réincarner: Formed from ~incarner~ with the prefix ~ré-~. ~Incarner~ was borrowed in 1372 from Ecclesiastical Latin ~incarnāre~ (“to make flesh”), itself built from ~in-~ (“into”) and ~carō~ (“flesh”). The prefix ~ré-~ descends from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and here marks repetition: ~réincarner~ means to take on a body again, to be reborn in a new one.
en.réincorporer: Formed from the French verb ~incorporer~ with the prefix ~ré-~ (“again”), so “to incorporate again.” The base ~incorporer~ goes back to Latin ~incorporāre~, built from ~in-~ (“in”) and ~corpus~ (“body”), so that to incorporate is, literally, to put into a body. The prefix ~ré-~ is a form of ~re-~, which comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and appears as ~ré-~ before a vowel in modern coinages.
en.réinfecter: Formed from ~infecter~ with the prefix ~ré-~, to infect again. The base ~infecter~ was borrowed from Latin ~infectāre~ (“to stain, to taint”), tied to ~inficere~ (“to dip in, to dye, to taint”), which is ~in-~ plus ~facere~ (“to do, to make”). The prefix ~ré-~, the form used before a vowel in modern coinages, comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and marks repetition.
en.réinjecter: ~Réinjecter~ is formed from ~injecter~ with the prefix ~ré-~, here in its form before a vowel, and means to inject again. ~Injecter~ was borrowed from Latin ~iniectāre~, a frequentative verb built on ~iniectus~, the past participle of ~inicere~ (“to throw in”). That verb joins ~in-~ (“in”) and ~iacere~ (“to throw”), the root also behind ~jeter~. The prefix ~ré-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and marks repetition, so the verb literally means to throw something in a second time.
en.réinscrire: ~Réinscrire~ is formed from ~inscrire~ with the prefix ~ré-~ (a form of ~re-~, “again”), so it means to inscribe or enter something again, as in signing someone up once more. The TLFi dates it to 1877, citing Littré's Supplément. The base ~inscrire~ is the older verb, generally analyzed as Latin ~in-~ (“on”) + ~scrībere~ (“to write”).
en.réinstaller: ~Réinstaller~ is formed from ~installer~ with the prefix ~ré-~, meaning “again,” in the spelling used before a vowel so that the two vowels stay distinct. It means to put back in place, to set up a program or a person once more. The base ~installer~ comes from medieval Latin ~installāre~ (“to put into a stall, to establish in office”), built from ~in-~ and ~stallum~, which was borrowed from Frankish *~stall~. The earliest sense was ceremonial: to seat a canon or bishop in his choir stall. The prefix ~ré-~ descends from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”).
en.réinsérer: Formed in French from the iterative prefix ~ré-~ (“again,” from Latin ~re-~) and the verb ~insérer~, so ~réinsérer~ is “to insert again,” and, of a person, “to bring back into society or work.” The base ~insérer~ comes from Latin ~inserere~ (“to set in, to graft”), built from ~in-~ (“in”) and ~serere~ (“to join, to link”), a verb distinct from its Latin twin meaning “to sow.” That joining ~serere~ is related to ~série~ and English ~insert~. The noun ~réinsertion~ is the commonest family word today.
en.réinterpréter: Formed from ~interpréter~ and the iterative prefix ~ré-~, meaning “again”: to interpret something anew. The base comes from Latin ~interpretārī~ (“to explain, translate”), a verb built on ~interpres~ (“go-between, agent, translator”). The first element of that noun is ~inter-~ (“between”); the second is often connected to ~pretium~ (“price, value”), though it remains debated. A broker between two parties thus became, over time, someone who draws out the meaning of a text. English ~interpret~ and Italian ~interpretare~ have the same Latin source.
en.réintroduire: Formed from ~introduire~ (“to introduce”) with the prefix ~ré-~, which here expresses repetition: “to introduce again.” The form ~ré-~ rather than ~re-~ is the usual spelling before a vowel in modern coinages. The base comes from Latin ~introducere~ (“to lead in”), made of ~intro~ (“inward”) and ~ducere~ (“to lead”), so the verb means, literally, to lead something inside once more. That same Latin ~ducere~ gave French ~conduire~, ~produire~ and ~traduire~.
en.réintégrer: French Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~redintegrāre~ (“to restore, to make whole again”), which became ~reintegrāre~ in Late Latin, while English Wiktionary simply reads it as ~ré-~ plus ~intégrer~. The Latin compound was built on ~integer~ (“untouched, whole”), from ~in-~ (“not”) and the root of ~tangere~ (“to touch”). To ~réintégrer~ is therefore to make someone whole again, and so to restore them to a post, a group or a place. English ~integer~, ~entire~ and ~integrity~ share the Latin source.
en.réinventer: Formed in French from the prefix ~ré-~ and the verb ~inventer~, meaning “to invent again” or “to reshape completely”. The prefix ~ré-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“again”) and is kept apart from the vowel that follows. The base ~inventer~ comes from Latin ~invenīre~ (“to come upon, to find”), built from ~in-~ (“on”) and ~venīre~ (“to come”). Early French ~inventer~ leaned toward finding what already existed, and only later toward making something new, so ~réinventer~ is a second invention on top of a first.
en.réinvestir:
~Réinvestir~ is ~investir~ carrying the prefix ~ré-~ (“again, anew”). ~Investir~ was borrowed from Latin ~investīre~ (“to clothe in, to wrap, to cover”), a compound of ~in-~ (“in, on”) and ~vestīre~ (“to dress”), itself built on the noun ~vestis~ (“garment, clothing”), from Proto-Italic *~westis~ and PIE *~wes-~ (“to clothe”). The Latin verb spread across Europe by two different routes. A few languages inherited it directly, as Romanian ~învești~ and Catalan ~envestir~ show; most took it back later as a learned borrowing, which is how Italian ~investire~, Spanish ~investir~, German ~investieren~ and — by way of Middle French ~investir~ — English ~invest~ all arose. The underlying noun ~vestis~ is far better represented in everyday French, where it yielded ~vêtir~, ~vêtement~ and ~veste~, while the same root gives English ~vest~ and ~vestment~. Nothing in this ancestry has anything to do with money: at the outset, the entire family is about cloth.

The literal sense came first. To ~investir~ someone was to clothe him, and the ceremony that placed a bishop or a vassal in the robes of his office is still called an ~investiture~; the medieval quarrel over who had the right to perform it set popes against emperors for half a century. From wrapping a person the verb moved to wrapping a place: to ~investir~ a town is to encircle and besiege it, a military sense French keeps to this day. The financial meaning — clothing your capital in a venture — is generally traced through Italian ~investire~ and the vocabulary of banking, with English ~investment~ helping to fix it. Modern ~réinvestir~ inherits the whole spread at once: one reinvests profits, demonstrators reinvest an occupied square, and a politician is reinvested with office. From the same root come ~vêtir~ and ~revêtir~, ~vêtement~, ~travesti~ (“dressed across, disguised”), ~dévêtir~, ~investiture~ and ~investissement~.
en.réinviter: Formed from ~inviter~ with the prefix ~ré-~ (“again”), spelled with an accent before the vowel: to invite again. The base comes from Latin ~invītāre~ (“to invite, to summon”), attested in French from 1356. Its deeper origin is uncertain, so the chain beyond Latin is left open. The Latin verb passed regularly into Italian ~invitare~ and Spanish ~invitar~, and English ~invite~ came in through Middle French.
en.réitérer: ~Réitérer~ is borrowed from Latin ~reiterāre~ (“to renew, to repeat”), built on ~re-~ (“again”) and ~iterāre~ (“to do a second time”), from ~iterum~ (“again”). English Wiktionary notes that by surface analysis the French verb can also be read as ~ré-~ plus ~itérer~, a learned verb of the same meaning, but the Latin verb already contained both parts. The doubled “again” of ~re-~ and ~iterum~ is what makes ~réitérer~ emphatic: to say or do something once more, often a demand or a promise. English ~reiterate~ is the same Latin verb arrived by another road.
en.réjouir:
From the prefix ~re-~ added to the older verb ~éjouir~ (Old French ~esjoïr~), built on ~joie~ (“joy”) and the verb ~jouir~ (“to enjoy”). The chain leads back to Latin ~gaudere~ (“to rejoice, to be glad”). ~Gaudere~ likely contracts from an earlier *~gāvidēre~ and traces to Proto-Indo-European *~geh₂u-~ (“to rejoice”), the root also behind Ancient Greek ~γάνυμαι~ (“I am glad”). The intensive ~gaudia~ (“joys”) gave Old French ~joie~ directly, while ~gaudere~ itself yielded ~jouir~.

The ~re-~ here is not really “again” but an intensifier: ~réjouir~ is to gladden thoroughly, to fill with delight. Reflexively, ~se réjouir~ means to look forward to something with pleasure — a future-leaning joy the bare ~jouir~ lacks. From the same Latin source come ~joie~, ~joyeux~, ~jouir~, ~jouissance~, ~réjouissance~ (“festivity, merrymaking”), and ~réjouissant~. Through Old French ~joie~, English borrowed ~joy~, ~rejoice~, and ~enjoy~ — so the English and French families of gladness share a single Latin spring in ~gaudere~.
en.rémunérer:
French ~rémunérer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~remunerare~ (also deponent ~remunerari~, “to reward, recompense”), formed from the prefix ~re-~ and the verb ~munerare~ (“to give, to present”), itself derived from the noun ~munus~ (“gift, service, public office, duty”). ~Munus~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~moinos~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~moy-nós~, from the root *~mey-~ (“to exchange”) — the idea being a good or service rendered within a society's web of mutual obligation. The same root surfaces in Latin ~communis~ (“shared, common”) and ~immunis~ (“exempt from duty”), and, by other paths, in the Germanic family behind English ~mean~ (“held in common”).

The Latin sense already paired a service with the gift given in return for it, and ~rémunérer~ preserves that flavor: it is the elevated, soutenu word for paying someone for work or services rendered, weightier than ordinary ~payer~. From the same Latin stock French keeps a tidy cluster — ~rémunération~, ~rémunérateur~, and the adjective ~rémunératif~ (“profitable, well-paid”) — while the un-prefixed sense of ~munus~ lives on in ~commun~, ~communauté~, ~municipal~, and ~immunité~. A bonus on the same theme: the Roman ~munus~ that meant a public “duty” a magistrate owed the city included staging gladiatorial games, so a ~munus~ could literally be a show put on at one's own expense.
en.rénetter: A farriers' verb meaning to pare a hoof by cutting furrows or lines into it, formed on the tool ~rénette~, the hoof knife. Littré takes the word back to ~rainette~, which fits the Académie's cross-reference to the variant spelling ~raineter~. The formation is simply the noun plus the verb ending ~-er~. Because the noun names the blade itself, the verb means to work a hoof with that tool.
en.rénover:
An adaptation of Latin ~renovare~ (“to make new again, renew”), from ~re-~ (“again”) and ~novus~ (“new”). Latin ~novus~ descends from Proto-Italic *~nowos~ and Proto-Indo-European *~néwos~ (“new”), one of the most widely preserved of all roots: it is cognate with English ~new~, German ~neu~, Ancient Greek ~néos~ (“new”), and Sanskrit ~náva~.

Where everyday French inherited the popular descendant ~nouveau~ through centuries of sound change, ~rénover~ is a learned borrowing taken straight from the Latin verb, which is why it keeps the crisp ~nov-~ stem. Its meaning runs from renewing the spirit to renovating a building. The *~néwos~ family is vast in French: ~neuf~, ~nouveau~, ~nouvelle~, ~innover~, ~rénovation~, and even ~novice~ — someone still “new” to a calling. The doubling of ~nouveau~ and ~neuf~ shows how one ancient word for “new” kept being made new again.
en.réoccuper: Formed from the prefix ~ré-~ (“again”) and the verb ~occuper~. The base comes from Latin ~occupāre~ (“to seize, take possession of”), itself a compound of ~ob-~ and ~capere~ (“to take”). The prefix adds the idea of repetition, so ~réoccuper~ means to occupy a place or position once more, for instance to retake a territory that had been abandoned or lost.
en.réopérer: Formed from ~opérer~ with the prefix ~ré-~, which expresses repetition: to operate on someone again. The base ~opérer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~operārī~ (“to work”), from ~opus~ (“work”), and is the bookish twin of the inherited ~œuvrer~. It took on its surgical sense in French, so ~réopérer~ is what a surgeon does when a first operation must be repeated. The prefix ~ré-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”) and appears in this form before a vowel in modern coinages.
en.réorchestrer: Formed in French from ~orchestrer~ with the prefix ~re-~ (“again”), so “to orchestrate again”: to rework an arrangement for an ensemble or to reorganize a campaign. The base is built from ~orchestre~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~orchestre~ was borrowed from Ancient Greek ~ὀρχήστρα~ (~orkhḗstra~), the space between the audience and the stage where the chorus danced, and its name was later transferred to the musicians. The prefix ~re-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”).
