en.réorganiser: Formed within French from ~organiser~ and the prefix ~ré-~, which here carries its ordinary sense of “again”: to organize something anew. The TLFi dates the verb to 1791, when it turns up in the minutes of the Jacobin Club in a call to reorganize the administration and the state accounts. It thus belongs to the Revolutionary years, when many institutions were being rebuilt from scratch. The prefix is fully productive in French, and ~ré-~ rather than ~re-~ is the form that learned and modern coinages often take.
en.réorienter: Formed from ~orienter~ with the prefix ~ré-~, in the sense “to orient again.” The prefix expresses repetition, and ~ré-~ is the usual form in modern coinages. The base ~orienter~ comes from the noun ~orient~ (“the East”), from Latin ~oriens~ (“rising”), the direction of the sunrise. It first meant to turn a building toward the east, and later any act of guiding or aiming. The verb applies this to a policy, a student or a beam, giving a new direction to something already pointed.
en.répandre:
From Old French ~espandre~, from Latin ~expandere~ (“to spread out, unfold, expose to the air”), formed from the prefix ~ex-~ and ~pandere~ (“to spread, stretch, open”), from Proto-Italic *~pandō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~peth₂-~ (“to spread out”). The modern French verb is more immediately ~épandre~ (the direct heir of ~expandere~) extended by the iterative prefix ~re-~. The Latin root ~pandere~ is cognate with ~pateō~ (“to lie open”) and, through the same Indo-European root, with Ancient Greek ~πέταλον~ (“leaf, a spread-out thing”).

In Latin, ~expandere~ literally meant to unfold something so that it lay flat and open — wings, cloth, grain set out to dry. Old French ~espandre~ carried the sense of pouring out or scattering, and adding ~re-~ in ~répandre~ intensified rather than reversed it, yielding “to spread widely, to scatter, to shed.” Today the verb covers everything physical and figurative that can be diffused: ~répandre une odeur~ (“to give off a smell”), spilling a liquid, or spreading a rumor. The same root *~peth₂-~ surfaces across modern French in a botanical and spatial family of words, among them ~pétale~ (“petal,” the spread-out part of a flower), ~expansion~, and ~patent~ — all sharing the ancient image of something opening out flat.
en.réparer:
Borrowed from Latin ~reparare~ (“to restore, to make ready again”), from ~re-~ (“again”) + ~parare~ (“to prepare, to make ready”). ~Parare~ rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~perh₃-~ (“to grant, to provide”), and stands beside Latin ~pario~ (“to bring forth, to produce”). Cognate with Italian ~riparare~ and Spanish ~reparar~, and — through the same ~parare~ — with English ~repair~, ~prepare~, and ~apparatus~.

The core idea is making a thing ready once more, restoring it to its former state, so ~réparer~ covers both the workshop sense (mending a machine, fixing a roof) and the moral one: to make amends, to right a wrong — « réparer une injustice », « réparer ses torts ». A ~réparation~ can therefore be a physical repair or a reparation owed for harm, the two senses sitting comfortably together. The bare verb ~parer~ survives in French meaning both “to adorn” and “to ward off” (a blow), and the ~parare~ family is large: ~préparer~, ~séparer~ (etymologically a different parare-look-alike from ~parare~ “to make ready” — caution here), ~appareil~, ~apparat~, ~parade~, and ~rempart~ all draw on the same productive Latin stock of “making ready.”
en.répartir:
A French formation: the verb ~partir~ in its old sense “to divide, to share” plus the prefix ~ré-~ (“again, thoroughly”). That older ~partir~ descends from Latin ~partīre~ / ~partīrī~ (“to divide, to share out”), built on ~pars~ (genitive ~partis~, “a part, a share”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“to grant, to allot”). The same ~pars~ gives Italian ~parte~ and Spanish ~parte~, and through Latin a great spread of English words including ~part~, ~partition~, ~portion~, and ~partner~.

In early French ~partir~ meant “to split” — a sense now almost wholly displaced by “to leave, to depart,” which itself grew from the idea of separating oneself from a place. The compound ~répartir~ preserved the original meaning, the prefix ~ré-~ stressing a complete or renewed dividing-up: to ~répartir~ is to apportion, to distribute shares among many. (A near-twin, ~repartir~ without the accent, means “to set off again” and is conjugated differently — a reminder of how the “depart” sense overtook the “divide” sense.) From the same ~pars~ French inherited ~partie~, ~partage~, ~parti~, ~partition~, ~portion~, and ~répartition~.
en.répercuter:
Borrowed from Latin ~repercutere~ (“to strike back, to make rebound”), built from ~re-~ (“back”) and ~percutere~ (“to strike through, to beat”). That in turn is ~per-~ (“through, thoroughly”) plus ~quatere~ (“to shake, to strike”), a verb that left its mark across the Latin compounds. The same ~quatere~ lies behind ~concutere~ (“to shake violently”) and ~discutere~ (“to smash apart, to break up”). English ~repercussion~ and ~percussion~ come from the same family, and English ~concussion~ shares it too.

The Latin meaning is physical: a blow that bounces back, a ball that rebounds, a sound or a ray of light thrown back from a surface. French kept all of this, so ~répercuter~ can say that a wall echoes a sound or reflects light. The verb then took a figurative turn, in which a blow is carried from one place to another. A rise in costs is ~répercutée~ on the customer, a decision ~se répercute~ on a whole team. The sense moved from “bounce back” to “pass along a consequence.” French ~discuter~, which began by meaning to shake something apart in order to examine it, comes from the same ~quatere~ via ~discutere~, as do ~percussion~, ~concussion~ and ~répercussion~.
en.répertorier:
From French ~répertoire~ (“repertory, index, list”), with the verbal suffix ~-er~. ~Répertoire~ descends from Latin ~repertorium~ (“inventory, catalogue”), a noun built on ~reperīre~ (“to find, to discover”), itself ~re-~ plus ~parīre~ (“to bring forth, to produce, to obtain”), from Proto-Indo-European *~perh₃-~ (“to produce, to beget”). Cognate, through ~parīre~, with English ~parent~ and ~repertory~, and with Italian ~repertorio~ and Spanish ~repertorio~.

A ~repertorium~ was literally a place where things are found again — an index that lets you retrieve an item, the etymological heart of both a theatre troupe's ~répertoire~ of plays and a list one keeps. The verb ~répertorier~ is a young, practical coinage meaning “to index, to catalogue, to draw up a list of.” Its buried root is surprisingly fertile: ~parīre~, “to give birth,” also produced ~parent~ (one who begets), the medical ~parturition~, and — through the related ~parāre~, “to make ready” — a sprawling family including ~préparer~, ~séparer~, ~apparaître~, and even ~parure~. To ~répertorier~ something is, etymologically, to arrange it so it can be brought forth and found anew.
en.répliquer:
Borrowed from Latin ~replicāre~ (“to fold back, to unroll, to turn back”), formed from ~re-~ (“back”) and ~plicāre~ (“to fold”). ~Plicāre~ comes from the Proto-Indo-European root *~plek-~ (“to plait, to weave”), shared with Greek ~plékein~ (“to braid”) and German ~flechten~ (“to plait”). The same Latin verb reached French twice. The inherited route gave Old French ~replier~ (“to fold again”), whereas the learned borrowing ~répliquer~ stayed closer to the Latin shape. English ~reply~, by way of ~replier~, and English ~replicate~ descend from ~replicāre~ as well.

Latin ~replicāre~ already carried a figurative sense, and ~replicatio~ was the plaintiff's rejoinder to the defendant's answer in a lawsuit. French took up that legal and rhetorical turn: a ~réplique~ was an answer to an answer, and ~répliquer~ came to mean “to answer back,” often sharply. In the theater a ~réplique~ is a line of dialogue, and ~donner la réplique~ is to feed an actor his cue. The idea of folding survives in the rest of the family, from ~plier~ and ~pli~ to ~compliquer~, ~expliquer~ and ~multiplier~.
en.répondre:
From Old French ~respondre~ (attested 980), from Vulgar Latin *~respondĕre~, a reshaping of Classical Latin ~respondēre~ (“to answer, to reply”). The verb is ~re-~ (“back, in return”) plus ~spondēre~ (“to pledge, to promise solemnly”), from Proto-Italic *~spondejō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~spend-~ (“to make an offering, to perform a rite, to pledge”). The same root gives Greek ~spéndō~ (“to pour a libation”) and ~spondḗ~ (“libation, treaty”), and through Latin underlies English ~sponsor~ and ~spouse~ (one pledged in marriage).

The buried metaphor is legal and ceremonial: to ~respondēre~ was originally to pledge in return — to answer a sponsor's solemn promise with one's own. From this reciprocal pledging came the everyday sense “to answer, to reply,” and then the wider “to correspond to, to be answerable for.” French keeps all of these: one answers a question, and one ~répond de~ (“is answerable for”) one's acts. From ~spondēre~ and its participle ~sponsus~ French inherited ~réponse~, ~répons~, ~correspondre~, ~responsable~, ~épouser~ and ~époux~ (the betrothed), while English ~sponsor~ goes back to the same root.
en.réprimander: Formed from the noun ~réprimande~ (“reprimand”) with the verb ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary derives ~réprimande~ from ~réprimer~ (“to repress, restrain”), so a reprimand is in origin a checking of someone's conduct. The verb then means “to give such a reprimand.” ~Réprimer~ itself goes back to Latin ~reprimere~, built from ~re-~ and ~premere~ (“to press”).
en.réprimer:
French ~réprimer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~reprimere~ (“to hold back, to check, to restrain”). The Latin verb is built from ~re-~ (“back”) and ~premere~ (“to press”), so the original picture is one of pressing something back down. Italian ~reprimere~ and Spanish ~reprimir~ are its sister forms, and English ~repress~ is a close relative, formed on the Latin past participle ~repressus~. Because French took the word directly from Latin rather than inheriting it, it kept a form close to the Latin original, with the prefix intact and no popular evolution.

From the physical idea of pushing back, the verb turned figurative: one holds back a feeling, a yawn, a laugh, and above all one puts down a revolt or a disorder by force. The modern French sense is mostly political and legal, as in the noun ~répression~. The root ~premere~ is prolific in French. It gave, often through its frequentative ~pressāre~, the verbs ~presser~, ~imprimer~, ~exprimer~, ~comprimer~, ~opprimer~ and ~déprimer~, along with ~pression~. ~Réprimer~ and ~opprimer~ are close neighbors: both press down, but one suppresses an act, the other crushes a people.
en.réprouver: From Latin ~reprobāre~, an Ecclesiastical Latin verb built on Latin ~probāre~ (“to test, to approve”). The prefix ~re-~ was already attached in Latin, so the verb was not formed in French. Spanish ~reprobar~ is a cognate, and English ~reprove~ and ~reprobate~ are relatives. ~Probāre~ is the source of a large French family built on testing and approving: ~prouver~ (“to prove”), ~éprouver~ (“to put to the test, to feel”), ~approuver~, ~désapprouver~ and ~preuve~ (“proof”). The verb sits at the stern end of the family, meaning to condemn or strongly disapprove of someone's conduct. The Ecclesiastical Latin label points to a Church setting for the verb, though the sources say no more.
en.répudier: A learned borrowing from Latin ~repudiāre~ (“to reject, to cast off”). The Latin verb belongs to ~repudium~ (“rejection,” and in Roman law the casting off of a spouse). English ~repudiate~ and Spanish ~repudiar~ come from the same source. In French the verb can mean to disown a wife or a belief, or to reject a claim.
en.répugner:
~Répugner~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~repugnāre~, formed from ~re-~ (“back, against”) and ~pugnāre~ (“to fight”), so that it meant “to fight back, to resist.” ~Pugnāre~ is related to ~pugnus~ (“fist”), which French inherited as ~poing~. The same Latin verb gave Italian ~repugnare~, Spanish ~repugnar~ and English ~repugnant~, so the word is easy to recognize across the Romance languages and English.

Modern French keeps two main uses. As a verb of feeling, it says that something disgusts or repels: ~cela me répugne~. Built as ~répugner à~ with an infinitive, it expresses reluctance. The relatives of the Latin verb keep the fighting root in plain view: ~pugnace~ (“combative”), ~inexpugnable~ (“impregnable”), ~impugner~ (“to challenge”), ~pugilat~ (“fistfight”), not to mention ~répugnant~ and ~répugnance~, drawn from ~répugner~ itself.
en.réputer:
Attested in 1261, ~réputer~ was borrowed from Latin ~reputāre~ (“to count up, to reckon, to ponder”), a compound of the prefix ~re-~ (“again”) and the verb ~putāre~ (“to reckon, to think”). The same ~reputāre~ gives Spanish and Occitan ~reputar~ and Italian ~riputare~. The origin of ~putāre~ is more uncertain: it is often connected to ~putus~ (“clean”) and a physical sense “to prune, to clear,” the idea being that one who prunes a tree or a tangled account “clears it up” and so reckons it — but this prune-to-reckon path is proposed rather than proven, so it is best taken as a likely story, not a settled fact.

Whatever its deepest root, ~putāre~ already meant “to calculate” and then “to judge, to suppose” in Latin, and ~reputāre~ added the nuance of turning a matter over, weighing it again. French inherited the evaluative sense: to ~réputer~ someone is to hold or consider them as something — un homme ~réputé~ honnête, a man reputed honest. From the same family come French ~réputation~, computer’s ancestor ~computāre~, and ~dispute~, all descendants of ~putāre~, witnesses to a single Latin verb of reckoning that branched into counting, thinking, and esteeming.
en.répéter:
Attested from the twelfth century, ~répéter~ comes from Latin ~repetere~ (“to seek again, attack anew, demand back, reclaim”), formed from the iterative prefix ~re-~ (“again”) and ~petere~ (“to seek, aim at, strike, fall upon, demand”). Latin ~petere~ goes back to a Proto-Indo-European root *~peth₂-~ (“to fly, rush, fall”), the same root behind Greek ~pteron~ (“wing, feather”) and Latin ~penna~ (“feather”). Italian ~ripetere~ and Spanish ~repetir~ share the descent.

The Latin verb's “seek again” lay behind two strands of meaning that French still keeps. One is reclaiming: in law one may ~répéter~ a sum, that is, demand its repayment. The other, far more common, is doing over: to say or do something again — and, by a charming specialization, to rehearse, so that actors and musicians ~répéter~ a play or a piece, and a rehearsal is a ~répétition~. The base ~petere~, with its sense of seeking and striving toward, gave French a rich crop: ~appétit~ (a striving-toward, hunger), ~compétition~, ~pétition~, ~impétueux~, ~perpétuel~, and ~compétent~. Behind the schoolchild's tiresome repetition lies an ancient image of rushing, again and again, toward a target.
en.réquisitionner: Formed from the noun ~réquisition~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, in the sense of carrying out the noun's action: to issue a requisition, or to commandeer. The noun ~réquisition~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~requisitio~, so the verb is a French coinage built on a Latin-derived word and not an inherited Latin verb. The ending ~-er~ itself descends from the Latin first-conjugation ending ~-are~, and it remains the default way for French to turn a noun into a verb.
en.réserver:
From Latin ~reservare~ (“to keep back, hold in reserve”), a compound of the prefix ~re-~ (“back”) and the verb ~servare~ (“to keep, guard, preserve”). ~servare~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~ser-~ (“to protect, watch over”). Cognate with Italian ~riservare~ and Spanish ~reservar~, and — through the same Latin verb — with English ~reserve~ and ~conserve~.

The Latin verb already carried the idea of setting something aside for later, of holding it back from immediate use. French inherited this sense intact: to ~réserver~ a thing is to withhold it from the general flow, whether a seat, a table, or a right. The same root *~ser-~ is unusually productive: from ~servare~ French draws ~conserver~ (“to keep together, to preserve”), ~observer~ (originally “to watch over, to keep before oneself”), and ~préserver~ (“to guard beforehand”), as well as the nouns ~réserve~ and ~réservoir~, a vessel that literally keeps water back. Etymologists distinguish this family carefully from that of ~servir~ and ~serviteur~, which trace to ~servus~ (“slave”); though some link ~servus~ too to *~ser-~ in the sense of a guardian, the two strands diverged early and should not be confused.
en.résider:
From Latin ~residere~ (“to sit back, remain seated, stay behind”), a compound of the prefix ~re-~ (“back”) and ~sedere~ (“to sit”). The Latin verb ~sedere~ descends, through Proto-Italic *~sedēō~, from the well-attested PIE root *~sed-~ (“to sit”) — the same root that gives English ~sit~, ~seat~, ~settle~, and, through Latin, ~sediment~ and ~session~. Romance cognates of the compound include Spanish ~residir~ and Italian ~risedere~; English ~reside~ arrived through Old French.

The literal Latin image is of someone who stays put while others move on — who “sits back” and remains. French keeps that core in ~résider~, “to dwell, to have one's home,” and extends it figuratively: a difficulty, a power, or a quality can ~résider~ in something, that is, abide or be located there. From the same ~sedere~ French inherits ~séance~ (a “sitting”), ~résidu~ (what ~settles~ and stays), ~assidu~ (one who “sits beside” a task), and ~posséder~. The shared thread is settledness — a sitting that becomes a staying.
en.résigner: Borrowed in late Old French from Latin ~resignāre~, a compound of ~re-~ and ~signāre~ (“to mark, to seal”), itself from ~signum~ (“mark, seal”). The Latin verb meant “to unseal” and so “to cancel, to give back,” which is why ~résigner~ first meant to give up an office or a claim, a sense still alive in ~résigner ses fonctions~. The reflexive ~se résigner~, to give up resisting and accept one's lot, grew out of that idea of surrendering something. English ~resign~ is the same Latin verb arriving by the same French road.
en.résilier:
Borrowed from Latin ~resilīre~ (“to spring back, to rebound, to withdraw”), a compound of ~re-~ (“back”) and ~salīre~ (“to leap, to jump”). The Latin verb is a cousin of many familiar words. Spanish ~salir~ (“to go out”) continues ~salīre~ directly, and English ~resilient~ comes from the participle of ~resilīre~ itself, so that a resilient material is, literally, one that springs back. French has the same root in ~saillir~ (“to jut out”) and in ~sauter~, which comes from the frequentative ~saltāre~.

The Latin sense of withdrawing suits the legal use of the French verb: to ~résilier~ a contract is to step back from it, to break the commitment one had made. The modern sense (to terminate a lease, a subscription, an insurance policy) thus fits the notion of retreat from an engagement. The family is partly learned: ~résiliation~ (“termination”) and ~résilience~, which in French now covers both the toughness of materials and the psychological capacity to bounce back, the older bouncing image returning by a second door.
en.résiner: Formed from ~résine~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, to resinate, that is to treat with resin. ~Résine~ is borrowed from Latin ~resīna~. The ending ~-er~ is the usual one that turns a noun into a first-conjugation verb, as ~filtre~ gives ~filtrer~.
en.résister:
French ~résister~ continues Latin ~resistere~ (“to stand back against, take a stand, oppose”), made of the prefix ~re-~ (here “against, back”) and ~sistere~ (“to make stand, to halt, to come to a stand”). ~Sistere~ is itself a reduplicated present of the verb ~stāre~ (“to stand”): from the root ~st-~ Latin built ~si-st-ere~, “to set standing.” Both go back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”), one of the most fruitful roots in the language. ~Resistere~ gave Italian ~resistere~, Spanish ~resistir~, and English ~resist~.

The literal picture is a soldier who plants his feet and refuses to be pushed back — to ~résister~ is to stand one's ground while a force presses. From that, the meaning broadened to withstanding pressure, temptation, disease, or wear, and even to physical durability (a material that ~résiste~). History gave the word a charged second life in ~la Résistance~, the underground that stood against the Occupation. The reduplicating ~sistere~ seeded a whole rank of French verbs that all turn on standing: ~consister~, ~persister~, ~insister~, ~subsister~, and ~exister~ (“to stand forth”) — while the simpler ~stāre~ branch yields ~stable~, ~station~, and ~constant~, kin to ~résister~ through the same standing root *~steh₂-~.
en.résonner:
Borrowed from Latin ~resonāre~ (“to sound again, to echo”), a compound of ~re-~ (“back, again”) and ~sonāre~ (“to sound, to make noise”). The sense of the prefix is plain: a sound that comes back. Italian ~risonare~ and Spanish ~resonar~ are related, and English holds two descendants of the same verb. English ~resonate~ was taken straight from Latin ~resonāre~, while ~resound~ came by way of Old French ~resoner~.

The verb names what a hall, a bell or a voice does when a sound lingers and echoes, and French extended it from sound to meaning, as when a word or an event ~résonne~ in one's mind. Its family is the family of ~sonāre~: ~sonner~ (“to ring”), ~son~ (“sound”), ~sonore~, ~résonance~, ~consonne~ (a letter that “sounds with” a vowel) and ~assonance~. One caution for learners: ~résonner~ (“to echo”) sounds very close to ~raisonner~ (“to reason”), but the latter comes from ~raison~, so the two share nothing but their sound.
en.résorber:
French ~résorber~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~resorbēre~ (“to swallow again, to suck back”), made of ~re-~ (“back”) and ~sorbēre~ (“to suck up, to swallow”). Here ~re-~ was already attached in Latin, so the verb was not built from a French base. Another compound of the same Latin verb, ~absorbēre~, gave French ~absorber~, which follows the same pattern. The Latin picture is that of something drawn back in and swallowed again.

In French, a swelling, an abscess or a bruise is ~résorbé~ when the body takes its fluid back in and it disappears. One also ~résorbe~ a deficit, unemployment, a backlog or a crisis, meaning to reduce it gradually until it vanishes. The noun ~résorption~ goes with both uses. The verb thus keeps the Latin picture of a body reabsorbing what had accumulated, applied to economies and queues as well as tissues.
en.résoudre:
French ~résoudre~ descends from Latin ~resolvere~ (“to untie, to loosen, to dissolve”), formed from ~re-~ (“back, again”) plus ~solvere~ (“to loosen, to release”). ~Solvere~ is itself a compound, ~se-~ (“apart, away”) plus ~luere~ (“to release, to loosen”), and traces to a Proto-Indo-European root *~lewh₁-~ (“to cut off, to loosen”). The Latin verb left a rich Romance and learned legacy: English ~solve~, ~resolve~, and ~dissolve~ all draw on this stock, as do Italian ~risolvere~ and Spanish ~resolver~. An older, fully popular French form, ~rasoudre~ / résoudre, coexisted with the relearned shape we use today.

The literal sense was physical: ~resolvere~ meant to untie or dissolve, to take a thing apart. French preserves both threads. The concrete one survives where a fog or a tumour ~se résout~ — dissolves, breaks up. From “to take apart” grew the abstract “to settle a question by analysis,” hence ~résoudre un problème~ (“to solve a problem”), and reflexively ~se résoudre à~ (“to resolve oneself to,” to make up one's mind). The same ~solvere~ underlies a wide French family: ~résolution~, ~soluble~, ~solution~, ~dissoudre~ and ~dissolution~, ~absoudre~ (“to absolve”), and the financial ~solvable~ (“solvent,” able to pay — to “loose” one's debts). To resolve, at root, is to loosen a knot, whether of rope, of fog, or of doubt.
en.résulter:
From Latin ~resultāre~ (“to spring back, to rebound, to echo”), a frequentative formed on ~resultum~, the supine stock of ~resilīre~ (“to leap back”), itself ~re-~ (“back”) + ~salīre~ (“to leap, to jump”). The verb ~salīre~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~sel-~ (“to jump, to leap”). The same ~salīre~ underlies Italian ~salire~ and Spanish ~salir~, and through its frequentative ~saltāre~ gives the dance-word at the root of English ~saltation~ and the Spanish ~saltar~.

The literal Latin sense was physical bounce: a ball, a sound, or a beam of light ~resultāre~ — springs back from a surface. From that image of something that rebounds came the figurative idea of an effect that springs out of a cause, an outcome that leaps forth from what precedes it — so a conclusion, a profit, or a disaster may ~résulter~ from given conditions. Today the verb is almost entirely abstract, conjugated chiefly in the third person, and frequently impersonal: ~il en résulte que~ (“it follows that”). The same ~salīre~ left a lively French family, among them ~saillir~, ~sauter~, ~assaillir~, ~tressaillir~, and ~résilier~, the last sharing the very stem ~resilīre~ that produced ~résulter~.
en.résumer:
From Latin ~resūmere~ (“to take back, to take up again, to resume”), from ~re-~ (“again”) and ~sūmere~ (“to take”). ~Sūmere~ is itself ~sub-~ (“up from under”) plus ~emere~ (“to take, to buy”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁em-~ (“to take, to distribute”). Cognate, through ~resūmere~, with English ~resume~ and with Italian ~riassumere~ and Spanish ~resumir~.

The classical sense was simply “to take up again,” but in scholastic Latin ~resūmere~ acquired the narrower meaning “to take up again briefly” — to go back over an argument in short — and it is this learned sense that French inherited: to ~résumer~ is to restate the essential in few words. From the same ~sūmere~ French keeps ~assumer~, ~consumer~, and ~présumer~, while the underlying ~emere~ (“to take, to buy”) seeded a surprisingly large family — ~exemple~, ~rédempteur~, ~prompt~, ~rançon~ (a worn-down ~redemptio~), and ~péremptoire~. A ~résumé~, then, is literally what has been “taken up again” in miniature — fittingly, English borrowed the past participle whole as the name for a curriculum vitae.
en.réséquer:
~Réséquer~ was taken from Latin ~resecāre~ (“to cut, to remove”), made of ~re-~ and ~secāre~ (“to cut”). The ~re-~ here is not repetition but part of the Latin verb, which meant to cut back or cut off. Because it arrived already formed, ~réséquer~ is not the French prefix ~ré-~ added to a verb *~séquer~. English ~resect~ comes from the same Latin verb, and so does the noun ~résection~, used for the surgical removal of part of an organ.

The verb ~secāre~ is a prolific root. It gave French ~scier~ (“to saw”), and learned words such as ~section~, ~sécant~, ~secteur~, ~disséquer~ (“to cut apart”) and ~insecte~ (“cut into”, from the segmented body of the animal). In this crowd ~réséquer~ is the specialist: today it belongs mostly to medicine, where to resect is to excise a diseased portion, while its everyday cousins ~couper~ and ~scier~ cover ordinary cutting.
en.rétablir:
~rétablir~ is ~re-~ (“again, back”) added to ~établir~ (“to establish”), and the deep history lives in ~établir~. That verb comes, around 1100, from Old French ~establir~, from Latin ~stabilīre~ (“to make firm, to steady”), from ~stabilis~ (“stable, standing fast”), itself from ~stāre~ (“to stand”), from PIE *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). To establish is thus to make a thing stand firm; to ~rétablir~ is to make it stand firm again. Italian ~stabilire~ and Spanish ~establecer~ are the Romance siblings, and English borrowed the Old French form as ~establish~.

The prefix gives the verb a strong sense of return to a former good state: one can ~rétablir~ order, the truth, a connection, or one's health — ~se rétablir~ meaning “to recover.” Hence the noun ~rétablissement~ (“restoration, recovery”). The root *~steh₂-~ is one of the most prolific in the language, surfacing in ~stable~, ~stade~, ~station~, ~statue~, ~constant~, ~rester~, and ~ester~; through the same PIE source English has ~stand~, ~stay~, ~stable~, and ~stage~. Few prefixed verbs carry so plainly the picture of putting something back on its feet.
en.rétamer: Formed from ~étamer~ with the prefix ~r-~, the form that ~re-~ takes before a vowel, here with the sense “again”: to tin-plate again. The base ~étamer~ comes from ~étain~ (“tin”) plus ~-er~, “to coat with tin.” ~Étain~ comes from Old French ~estain~ and Latin ~stannum~, a word probably of Celtic origin. The verb also has a colloquial sense, “to wear out.”
en.réticuler: Taken from the French noun ~réticule~, which comes from Latin ~reticulum~, a “net with fine meshes.” The Latin word is a diminutive of ~rēte~ (“net”). The verb is thus formed in French on a Latin-derived noun, with the ending ~-er~ (from Latin ~-are~) turning the noun into an action. Related words include French ~réticulé~ (“netlike”), and English ~reticulate~ and ~reticle~, which share the Latin source ~reticulum~.
en.rétorquer:
French ~rétorquer~ is a borrowing from Latin ~retorquēre~ (“to turn back”), a compound of ~re-~ (“back”) and ~torquēre~ (“to twist, to wind, to hurl”). That same ~torquēre~ gave Italian ~torcere~ and, through the Vulgar Latin line, French ~tordre~, the inherited, everyday descendant, so the two French verbs are cousins that reached the language by different routes. English holds the learned branch twice over: ~retort~ comes from the Latin past participle ~retortus~, and ~torque~, ~torture~ and ~contort~ come from the same family.

The literal image is of twisting something back on whoever sent it, and French kept that figurative thread: ~rétorquer~ is to answer sharply, throwing someone's own words back at them. French has several other relatives of ~torquēre~, among them ~torture~, ~torsion~ and ~tortueux~ (“winding”), which show the same idea of a twist or a turn in different settings.
en.rétracter:
Borrowed from Late Latin ~retractāre~ (“to undertake again, to withdraw, to retract”), which comes from Latin ~retractus~, the past participle of ~retrahere~ (“to draw back, to pull back”). French Wiktionary gives both routes: the verb is taken from ~retractare~ (“to handle again, to take in hand again”) and is also analysed as a learned derivative of ~retractum~, the participle stem of ~retrahere~. Both lead to the same Latin family, built on ~re-~ (“back”) and ~trahere~ (“to pull”).

The two senses of the French verb follow the Latin ones. One is physical: to pull something back or make it contract, as a muscle or a tissue does. The other is mental or legal: to withdraw a statement, to take back what one has said or admitted. The root ~trahere~ also supplies ~traction~, ~attraction~, ~extraire~, ~contracter~ and ~rétraction~, and English has ~retract~ from the same Latin source, so the verb is a cousin of ~traire~, “to milk,” literally “to pull.”
en.rétreindre: Formed from ~étreindre~ with the prefix ~re-~. The prefix does not simply mean “again” here, since the verb has its own technical senses of shrinking and hammering metal thin. The base comes from Old French ~estreindre~, inherited from Latin ~stringere~ (“to tighten”), traced further to the Proto-Indo-European root *~streyg-~. French Wiktionary links ~étreindre~ to ~étrangler~. The Latin verb also gave ~restreindre~ and, in English, ~strain~, ~strict~ and ~stringent~.
en.rétribuer: Borrowed from Latin ~retribuere~ (“to give back, to repay, to recompense”), a compound of ~re-~ (“back”) and ~tribuere~ (“to allot, to assign”). The simple Latin verb ~tribuere~ is generally linked to ~tribus~ (“tribe”), as in dividing things out among the tribes. Related forms include Italian ~retribuire~, Spanish ~retribuir~ and English ~retribution~, which belong to the same Latin source. The ~tribuere~ family is large in French: ~attribuer~, ~contribuer~, ~distribuer~ and ~tribut~ all rest on it, each with a different prefix. Modern French ~rétribuer~ is therefore best understood as “to give back what is owed,” a verb about balancing an account.
en.rétroagir: ~Rétroagir~ (“to act retroactively”) is formed from the learned prefix ~rétro-~ and the verb ~agir~. The prefix is borrowed from Latin ~retrō~ (“backward, behind”), and ~agir~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~agere~ (“to drive, to do, to act”). The verb thus means “to act backward,” that is, to have an effect on what is already past. It is one of the few French verbs that are truly built on ~rétro-~ and not borrowed already formed from Latin.
en.rétrocéder:
Taken from Latin ~retrōcēdere~ (“to go back, to give back”). The Latin verb is a compound of ~retrō~ (“backward, back”) and ~cēdere~ (“to go, to yield, to withdraw”). The same pieces appear in the Romance cousins, Italian ~retrocedere~ and Spanish ~retroceder~, and in English ~retrocede~. French therefore did not build ~rétrocéder~ from ~céder~; the compound came ready-made from Latin, and ~céder~ is simply its closest relative.

In modern French ~rétrocéder~ is a formal verb of law and commerce, meaning to hand a right or a property back to the person who ceded it, or on to a third party. Its relatives share the Latin verb ~cēdere~: ~céder~, ~concéder~, ~excéder~, ~précéder~, ~procéder~ and ~succéder~, together with the nouns ~cession~ and ~rétrocession~. The first element survives in the clipped adjective ~rétro~, and in ~rétrograde~ and ~rétrospectif~.
en.rétrograder:
~Rétrograder~ was borrowed from Latin, but the two Wiktionaries name different forms. French Wiktionary gives the Latin verb ~retrogredior~ (“to go backwards”), a compound of ~retro~ (“backward”) and ~gradior~ (“to step”). English Wiktionary gives Late Latin ~retrōgradāre~. The two are close relatives, and the French verb, with its regular ending, matches the Late Latin form more naturally. English has the cognate ~retrograde~.

The Latin root is ~gradī~ (“to step”), tied to ~gradus~ (“step”). It is the source of a large French family. ~Grade~, ~degré~ and ~dégrader~ come from ~gradus~, while ~progresser~, ~régresser~, ~agresser~ and ~congrès~ come from compounds of ~gradī~. In ~rétrograder~ the “step” points backward, and the verb covers literal retreat, a drop in rank or level, and the downshift of a car. The sources consulted do not tell how these senses developed from one another.
en.rétrécir: Formed from the prefix ~re-~ and ~étrécir~, “to narrow.” That base comes from Old French ~estrecier~, from Vulgar Latin *~strictiāre~, built on Latin ~strictus~ (“narrow, drawn tight”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~streyg-~. French Wiktionary adds the intermediate forms Middle French ~extroicir~ and ~estrecir~. The same Latin adjective gave French ~étroit~, the inherited word, and ~strict~, the learned one. English ~strait~ and ~strict~ are cognates. ~Rétrécir~ means to make or become narrower, as when a wool sweater shrinks.
en.réunifier: Formed in French from ~unifier~ with the prefix ~ré-~, “again.” The base ~unifier~ comes from Old French ~unifier~, borrowed from Late Latin ~ūnificāre~, a compound of ~ūnus~ (“one”) and the verbal element ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”), so “to make one.” The prefix ~ré-~ descends from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”). ~Réunifier~ therefore means to make one again, as in the reunification of a divided country. Related words include ~un~, ~unité~, ~union~ and ~unir~, and English ~unify~.
en.réunir:
From ~unir~ (“to unite”) with the prefix ~ré-~ (“again, back”), so literally “to unite again, to bring back together.” ~unir~ descends from Latin ~unire~ (“to make one, to join”), a verb built directly on ~unus~ (“one”). ~unus~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~h₁óynos~ (“one”), the same root that gives Ancient Greek ~oîos~ (“alone”), Old Irish ~óen~, and — through Proto-Germanic — English ~one~ and ~an~. ~réunir~ is thus a close relative of Italian ~riunire~ and Spanish ~reunir~.

The semantics are transparent: to ~réunir~ people or things is to make them ~one~ once more. The prefix ~ré-~ does real work, since it presumes a prior unity broken and now restored — friends reunited, scattered papers gathered up. From the same Latin ~unus~ and its PIE root *~h₁óynos~ French drew a wide vocabulary: ~un~ (“one”), ~unique~ (from ~unicus~, “sole”), ~union~, ~unité~, ~unanime~ (“of one mind,” ~unus~ + ~animus~), and ~univers~ (from ~universus~, literally “turned into one”). The reflexive ~se réunir~ — for a committee or assembly “to meet” — preserves the image perfectly: many individuals momentarily becoming one body.
en.réussir:
From Italian ~riuscire~ (“to come out again,” hence “to succeed, to manage”), borrowed into French around 1531. The Italian verb is ~ri-~ (“again”) + ~uscire~ (“to go out, to exit”), and ~uscire~ descends from Latin ~exire~ (~ex-~, “out” + ~ire~, “to go”), the verb ~ire~ tracing to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₁ey-~ (“to go”). The word is also paralleled by Old French ~reissir~ (“to come back out, to emerge”), so the core image is consistent across both Romance lines.

The semantic leap is delightfully concrete: to ~réussir~ is, literally, to emerge — to come back out of a venture rather than getting stuck in it. Success was framed not as reaching a peak but as finding the exit. The prefix is telling: ~ri-~ adds the nuance of coming out again, a second emergence after entering the fray. From the same root *~h₁ey-~ French inherits a scattered family — among them ~issue~ (“exit, outcome”), ~initier~, ~ambition~ (etymologically a “going around” to canvass votes), and ~transitoire~ — while the everyday ~sortir~ later crowded ~réussir~ out of its spatial meaning, leaving it to specialize entirely in the sense of triumph.
en.réutiliser: Formed from ~utiliser~ with the prefix ~ré-~ (“again”): to use again. The base is a late, learned verb of the end of the eighteenth century, built from the adjective ~utile~ and the suffix ~-iser~, on the model of Italian ~utilizzare~. ~Utile~ comes from Latin ~ūtilis~ (“useful”), from the verb ~ūtī~ (“to use”). The prefix ~ré-~ descends from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”), and the accented form is the usual one before a vowel in modern coinages, since it keeps the two vowels apart.
en.réveiller:
From Middle and Old French ~esveiller~, ~réveiller~ is ~éveiller~ reinforced by the iterative prefix ~re-~. ~Éveiller~ descends from Vulgar Latin *~exvigilāre~, from Latin ~ēvigilāre~ (“to wake up, watch out”), built on ~vigilāre~ (“to keep watch, stay awake”), itself from ~vigil~ (“awake, watchful”). The deeper root is PIE *~weǵ-~ (“to be lively, strong, awake”), which also yielded English ~wake~, ~watch~, and ~vigour~.

The semantic core was always alertness rather than mere sleep: to keep a ~vigil~ is to stay awake on purpose, and Latin ~ēvigilāre~ meant to rouse oneself from that watch. French kept the ~vigilāre~ family alive twice over: directly through learned borrowings like ~vigilant~, ~vigile~, and ~vigueur~, and through the inherited popular line ~veiller~ → ~éveiller~ → ~réveiller~. The ~re-~ adds a sense of return — bringing someone back across the threshold of waking — so that ~le réveil~ (the morning alarm, and the act of waking) names exactly that crossing. A sleeper is summoned, by one account, back to the watch that vigilance once implied.
en.réveillonner: ~Réveillonner~ is built on the noun ~réveillon~ (“meal eaten on Christmas Eve or New Year's Eve”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, so it means to celebrate by such a meal. ~Réveillon~ is itself derived from ~réveil~ (“waking”), or equivalently from the stem of ~réveiller~ (“to wake up”), with the suffix ~-on~. The verb is therefore a two-step French formation, with no older source language behind it.
en.réverbérer: From Middle French ~reverberer~ (“to repeat, to reflect rays, to send back a sound, to shine”), borrowed from Latin ~reverberāre~ (“to beat back, to repel, to reflect rays”). The Latin verb is formed from ~re-~ (“back”) and ~verberāre~ (“to beat, to lash”), which comes from ~verber~, a word for a whip or lash. English ~reverberate~ is a close cousin, taken from the same Latin verb, and Italian ~riverberare~ and Spanish ~reverberar~ are its counterparts. French ~réverbérer~ means to reflect light or heat, or to send a sound back in an echo. ~Réverbération~ is the corresponding noun for the action.
en.réviser:
Old French ~reviser~ is attested around 1245, meaning “to examine”; it was borrowed from Latin ~revisere~ (“to come back to see, to revisit, to look at again”), from ~re-~ (“back, again”) and ~visere~ (“to go to see, to call on”), an old desiderative of the root that also yields ~vidēre~ (“to see”) — Proto-Indo-European *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”). The root is among the most fertile in the language family: it underlies English ~wise~ and ~wit~, Sanskrit ~Veda~ (“knowledge”) and Greek ~idéa~, whence French ~idée~. Within French, ~réviser~ is the learned twin of ~revoir~, built on the same Latin elements; Italian keeps ~rivedere~, and English ~revise~ arrived through French in the sixteenth century.

Latin ~visere~ meant not merely seeing but going to see — paying a visit; ~visiter~ descends from its frequentative ~visitare~. To ~réviser~ a text is therefore, etymologically, to pay it another visit. The senses accumulated visit by visit: examining anew with a view to amending, in Ronsard (1565); reviewing a literary work (1752); the printer's proof-revision (1835); the mechanic's overhaul (1937, when Malraux applies it to aircraft); finally the schoolchild's sense, going over one's lessons, recorded in 1946. The spelling itself got revised: ~reviser~ and ~réviser~ competed until the nineteenth century, when the accent won. From the same seeing-root: ~voir~, ~revoir~, ~vue~, ~visite~, ~viser~, ~évident~, ~providence~ — and every ~révision~, whether of a constitution, an engine or a chapter on the eve of the exam.
en.révolter: Borrowed from Italian ~rivoltare~, built on ~volta~ (“a turn, the act of turning”), so its first sense was “to turn over, to upset.” French ~révolter~ kept the idea of overturning, and it then spread to the political sense “to stir to rebellion” (and ~se révolter~, “to rise up”), and to the emotional one, “to fill with indignation, to disgust.” The latter two senses show the image of something being turned upside down inside a person or a society. The English noun and verb ~revolt~ were in turn borrowed from French.
en.révolutionner: ~Révolutionner~ is formed from the noun ~révolution~ and the verb ending ~-er~. ~Révolution~ is a learned borrowing from Late Latin ~revolūtiō~ (“a turning back, a return”), from Latin ~revolvō~ (“to roll back”). The word first described a cycle, as of a star returning to its place, and the political sense of a sudden overthrow came later. ~Révolutionner~ takes the political sense and applies it as a verb: to stir a population into revolt, and, more often today, to transform something radically, as when an invention ~révolutionne~ an industry.
en.révolvériser: ~Révolvériser~ is formed from ~révolver~ with the suffix ~-iser~, and means to shoot someone or something with a revolver. The noun ~révolver~ is a borrowing from English ~revolver~, a pistol named for its revolving cylinder. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~ and here gives the sense “to treat with” the thing named by the base. The result is a humorous coinage, one that turns a loanword for a gun into a verb.
en.révoquer:
~Révoquer~ was borrowed in Middle French from Latin ~revocāre~, a compound of ~re-~ (“back”) and ~vocāre~ (“to call”), so the verb meant “to call back.” The Latin verb is a transparent compound, and an Old French form, ~revochier~, is also recorded. Spanish ~revocar~ and Italian ~revocare~ come from the same Latin verb, and so does English ~revoke~.

Because the verb arrived already formed, ~re-~ is a fossil here rather than a prefix French speakers attach at will. In modern French the verb is used for withdrawing what was granted or decided, and for removing someone from office. The Latin ~vocāre~ stands behind a large French family, among them ~convoquer~, ~invoquer~, ~provoquer~, ~évoquer~ and ~vocation~, while the noun ~révocation~ and the adjective ~irrévocable~ stay close to the verb itself.
en.révulser: ~Révulser~ comes from Latin ~revellere~ (perfect ~revulsī~), meaning “to tear away, to overturn, to destroy.” French Wiktionary analyzes it as the intensive prefix ~re-~ plus ~vellere~ (“to pluck, to tear out, to uproot”). English ~revulsion~ comes from the same Latin verb. The Latin ~vellere~ has other relatives in French. Its compound ~convellere~, with the participle ~convulsus~, gave ~convulsion~, and ~avellere~ gave the learned ~avulsion~. The family is one of violent pulling, so ~révulser~ belongs with words of wrenching and sudden shock. Its modern senses run from the physical, as in eyes that roll back (“yeux révulsés”), to the emotional: to disgust or to outrage someone, in English to revolt or sicken.
en.révéler:
From Latin ~revēlāre~ (“to unveil, to uncover, to disclose”), compounded from ~re-~ (here reversive, “un-”) and ~vēlāre~ (“to cover, to veil”), from ~vēlum~ (“sail, curtain, covering”). ~Vēlum~ traces back through Proto-Italic *~wekslom~ to the Proto-Indo-European root *~weg-~ (“to weave”), so a veil is etymologically a woven thing. The same Latin verb gave English ~reveal~ and, more transparently, the French doublet of ~vēlum~ — ~voile~ (“veil; thin woven fabric”). Italian ~rivelare~ and Spanish ~revelar~ are siblings.

The literal sense could not be plainer: to reveal is to pull the veil off something. The word entered French heavy with religious weight — révélation is the divine unveiling of truth, God lifting the veil on His will — before broadening to any disclosure of what was hidden or secret (« révéler un secret »). A delightful technical sense survives in photography: to ~révéler~ a film is to develop it, the ~révélateur~ being the developer bath that lifts the latent image out of darkness into view — quite literally unveiling it. From ~vēlum~ French also keeps ~voile~, ~voiler~ (“to veil”), and ~dévoiler~ (“to unveil”), a near-synonym of ~révéler~.
en.révérer: Borrowed through Middle French ~reverer~ from Latin ~reverērī~ (“to stand in awe of, to respect, to honor”), which is ~re-~ plus ~vereor~ (“to fear, to respect”). Catalan ~reverir~ is comparable. The same Latin verb lies behind ~révérence~, ~révérend~ and ~irrévérencieux~, and English ~revere~ is that verb borrowed from Latin.
en.réécrire: Usually analysed as ~ré-~ + ~écrire~, with the prefix meaning “again”; the form ~ré-~ rather than ~re-~ keeps the two vowels apart. French Wiktionary adds that the verb may instead continue Latin ~rescribere~ (“to reply in writing”), the source of ~rescrit~ (“a written reply, a rescript”). The base ~écrire~ comes from Latin ~scribere~, whose oldest sense was “to scratch, to incise.” Today ~réécrire~ means to write something again or to recast a text, and it is also a technical term in computing and linguistics.
en.réédifier: Formed from ~édifier~ with the prefix ~ré-~ (“again”), so it means to build again. The base ~édifier~ comes through Old French ~edifier~ from Latin ~aedificāre~ (“to build”), a compound of ~aedēs~ (“building”) and ~-ficō~ (“to make”), which literally meant to make a building.
en.rééditer: Formed from ~éditer~ with the prefix ~ré-~ (“again”), so “to publish again”, and by extension to reissue, rerun or repeat something. The prefix descends from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”). The base ~éditer~ goes back to Latin ~ēdere~ (“to give out, to publish”), made of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~dare~ (“to give”), and appeared in French around 1784, partly rebuilt from the earlier nouns ~édition~ and ~éditeur~. So to ~rééditer~ a book is, etymologically, to give it out a second time.
en.rééduquer: Formed from ~éduquer~ with the prefix ~ré-~, which here keeps its vowel apart from the initial é of the base and means “again”. ~Éduquer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~ēducāre~ (“to rear, to train”), first attested in French in 1385, and so belongs to the family of ~dūcere~ (“to lead”). ~Ré-~ comes from Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”). The verb means to train someone anew, especially after an injury or a bad habit, as in ~rééduquer~ a muscle or a patient.
en.réélire: Formed in French from ~élire~ with the prefix ~ré-~, meaning “to elect again.” The base ~élire~ descends from Old French ~eslire~ and Latin ~ēligere~ (“to pick out”), which joined ~ex-~ (“out”) to ~legere~ (“to gather, to choose, to read”). The prefix ~ré-~ goes back to Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”), and the accented spelling is the usual one for modern coinages before a vowel. The same ~legere~ gave French ~lire~, so reading, choosing and electing again all belong to one family.
en.rééquilibrer: Formed from the prefix ~ré-~, “again,” and ~équilibrer~, “to balance.” The base verb comes from the noun ~équilibre~, borrowed from Latin ~aequilibrium~, a compound of ~aequus~ (“level, equal”) and ~libra~ (“scales”), the state in which the two pans of a balance hang even. The prefix ~ré-~ here has its ordinary sense of repetition and is kept distinct from the vowel that follows, hence the double ~é~. ~Rééquilibrer~ therefore means to restore a balance that has been lost, whether in a budget, a diet or a power relationship.
en.réévaluer: Formed from ~évaluer~ with the prefix ~ré-~, meaning “again”: to ~réévaluer~ is to assess something a second time. The base ~évaluer~ comes from Old French ~esvaluer~, which was made from ~é-~ and the noun ~value~ (“worth”), the feminine past participle of ~valoir~. That verb goes back to Latin ~valere~ (“to be strong, to be worth”). The prefix ~ré-~ is the French form of Latin ~re-~ (“back, again”), and the vowel is kept apart from the ~é~ of the base, as in many modern coinages.
en.rêvasser: ~Rêvasser~ is formed from ~rêver~ and the suffix ~-asser~, which can be depreciative, frequentative or diminutive: to dream idly, aimlessly, without any real purpose. The base ~rêver~ comes from Old French ~resver~ (“to wander, to rave”), whose origin is disputed; the likeliest account derives it from a Vulgar Latin *~exvagare~ built on ~vagus~ (“wandering”). The suffix ~-asser~ dates from the fifteenth century and is still lively in familiar speech, as in ~pleuvasser~ (“to drizzle”). ~Rêvasser~ is thus a lesser, half-hearted ~rêver~.
en.rêver:
From Old French ~resver~ (“to wander, to rave”), of disputed origin. The likeliest account derives it from an unattested Vulgar Latin *~exvagare~ or a Gallo-Romance *~esver~, ultimately from Latin ~ex-~ (“out of”) plus ~vagus~ (“wandering, roaming, vague”). On this view ~rêver~ is, at root, “to stray off, to wander” — and its Old French sibling ~desver~ meant “to go out of one's mind.” Latin ~vagus~ also gives French ~vague~ and English ~vague~ and ~vagabond~.

The semantic journey is striking. Originally ~resver~ meant “to rave, to talk wildly, to be delirious” — a wandering of the mind, not its rest. Only later did ~rêver~ glide toward the gentler sense of dreaming in one's sleep, displacing the older ~songer~ in that role, and then toward daydreaming and idle reverie. The mental-wandering sense still echoes in the noun ~rêverie~ (“reverie, musing”) and in ~délirer~ (“to be delirious”), and ~rêver~ keeps a faint edge of unreason: ~je rêve !~ means roughly “I must be dreaming — this can't be real!” The dreamer and the raver were, long ago, the same wanderer.
en.rôdailler: Formed from ~rôder~ with the suffix ~-ailler~, which gives a looser, slightly dismissive nuance: to prowl about a little, to hang around. The TLFi records it first in 1839, in Barbey d'Aurevilly, and labels it familiar. The base ~rôder~ appears from 1418 and was borrowed from Old Provençal ~rodar~ (“to wander, to turn about”), from Latin ~rotāre~ (“to move in a circle, to make turn”). English ~rotate~ comes from the same Latin verb. A verb for loitering thus has, at its root, the idea of going round and round.
en.rôder:
French ~rôder~ is borrowed from Old Occitan ~rodar~ (“to wander”), which comes from Latin ~rotāre~ (“to make turn, to whirl”), itself built on ~rota~ (“wheel”). So the verb reached French from the south rather than by direct inheritance, and the Latin source is the same as that of English ~rotate~. Spanish ~rodar~ (“to roll”) is a cognate of ~rodar~ in Occitan, both from ~rotāre~.

French therefore has two verbs from one Latin source. English Wiktionary calls ~rôder~ a doublet of ~rouer~, which is the inherited form, with a different meaning, “to break on the wheel” and, in ~rouer de coups~, “to beat soundly.” The sense of ~rôder~ moves from turning to going about aimlessly, and in modern French the verb carries the suspicion of someone loitering with bad intent. The same Latin ~rota~ gives ~roue~, ~rotation~ and ~rotatif~.
en.rôtir:
French ~rôtir~ comes from Old French ~rostir~, which English Wiktionary traces through Middle French ~roustir~ to Frankish *~rōstjan~ (“to roast”), from Proto-Germanic *~raustijaną~, and ultimately from a Proto-Indo-European root *~Hrews-~ (“to crackle, roast”). Old High German ~rōsten~ is a Germanic cognate. Among the Romance languages, Italian ~arrostire~ and Spanish ~rostir~ are comparable forms of the same Germanic loan. English ~roast~ is itself a borrowing from the Old French verb, so English and French share the word by two different routes.

The circumflex of ~rôtir~ is the trace of the lost ~s~ of Old French ~rostir~: as in ~hôpital~ or ~forêt~, the vowel kept a mark where the consonant fell silent. The verb means to cook, above all meat, by dry heat, and the root's older meaning, “to crackle,” already stands beside “to roast” in English Wiktionary's reconstruction. From the verb French drew a small family of food words: ~rôti~ (“a roast”), ~rôtisserie~, ~rôtissoire~ (“spit, rotisserie”) and ~rôtisseur~.
en.sabler: ~Sabler~ is formed from the noun ~sable~ (“sand”) and the verb ending ~-er~, meaning to sand or to sandblast. The noun comes from Old French ~sable~, from Vulgar Latin ~sablum~, a contracted form of Latin ~sabulum~ (“sand, gravel”). It is a different word from the other French ~sable~, the sable fur and heraldic color, which came from a Balto-Slavic source through Germanic. Only the sand word is behind the verb.
en.sablonner: ~Sablonner~ is formed from ~sablon~ with the ending ~-er~, and means to cover with sand or to sand. The noun ~sablon~ (“fine sand”) is inherited from Middle French and Old French ~sablon~, from Late Latin ~sablōnem~, itself from Latin ~sabulōnem~, the accusative of ~sabulo~ (“coarse sand”). ~Sablon~ is thus a close relative of ~sable~, and the verb takes the ordinary ~-er~ pattern meaning “provide with” the noun.
en.saborder: Formed in French from ~sabord~ with the verb ending ~-er~. A ~sabord~ is a square opening cut in a ship's side, and ~saborder~ means to scuttle a ship by letting water in, then, figuratively, to put an end to an enterprise on purpose. The noun ~sabord~ comes from Middle French ~sabort~, whose ultimate origin is unknown. The verb is a nautical one that moved into everyday speech with the sense of deliberately sinking a business or a project.
en.saboter:
~Saboter~ is derived from ~sabot~ (“clog”) with the verb ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary links it to Provençal ~sabotar~ (“to shake”). Its first sense was “to play with a top,” a toy also called a ~sabot~, so the verb meant literally “to make spin.” That meaning was still in use in the eighteenth century.

From there French Wiktionary lists dated senses. In 1690 it was “to make noise with one's clogs”; in 1766, “to make one's head spin” like a top; in 1808, “to botch.” In 1842 it meant “to fit a pile with a shoe,” in 1875 “to put a brake shoe on a rail,” and in 1897 “to cause failure.” The sense “to destroy covertly” appears in 1907. English Wiktionary gives the popular story that mill workers threw clogs into the machinery. The dated sequence does not need it, so treat it as a tradition. French also has ~sabotage~ and ~saboteur~.
en.sabouler: ~Sabouler~ (“to torment”) is a blend of two verbs, ~saboter~ and ~bouler~. Such a crossing merges the form and the senses of both words into a new one. The French source gives no older source language and no date, so the history of the verb stops at this blend.
en.sabrer: ~Sabrer~ is formed from ~sabre~ (“saber”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so “to strike or cut with a saber.” The noun came into French from German ~Säbel~, itself from Hungarian ~szablya~. In the popular expression “sabrer le champagne,” one explanation holds that ~sabrer~ is a corruption of ~sabler~ (“to knock back a drink in one go”), while the ritual of opening a bottle with one stroke of a blade is said to go back to the hussars of Napoleon's guard.
en.saccader: French Wiktionary derives the verb from ~saccade~ (“jerk”) and the ending ~-er~, so it means to move or shake in jerks. The noun is in turn built with the suffix ~-ade~ on ~saquer~, a verb meaning “to shake” in some dialects. English Wiktionary offers a second possibility for the noun, that it comes from ~saquer~ or from its Spanish cousin ~sacar~. Either way, the verb is a late French formation, with no Latin ancestor of its own.
en.saccager: ~Saccager~ is a borrowing from Italian ~saccheggiare~, which French Wiktionary dates to the thirteenth century in Italian. The Italian verb is derived from ~sacco~, a word meaning “sack, plunder”, and ~sacco~ comes from Latin ~saccus~ (“sack, bag”). So the French verb is not a native noun + ~-er~ formation, even though it ends in ~-er~; the ending is simply the French infinitive form given to the borrowed verb. It is a close relative of French ~sac~, and of the English word “sack” in the sense of looting a town.
en.saccharifier: Formed from the learned combining stem ~sacchar-~ and the suffix ~-ifier~, with the sense “to turn into sugar.” The stem goes back to Latin ~saccharum~, borrowed from Greek ~sákkharon~ (“sugar”). The suffix ~-ifier~ comes from Latin ~-ificāre~, itself built on ~facere~ (“to make”), and in French it coins verbs meaning “to make” or “to turn into,” above all in learned and technical vocabulary.
en.sacquer: ~Sacquer~ (also written ~saquer~) is derived from ~sac~ (“bag”). The TLFi starts from the old expression ~donner son sac~ (“to give someone his bag”), recorded in 1611 for dismissing a person. The verb itself appears as slang in 1866 with the sense “to dismiss,” then in 1878 “to reprimand under threat of losing one's job,” and by 1935 “to punish severely,” whence the modern “to mark harshly.” The sense “can't stand,” as in not being able to sacquer someone, is recorded from 1919. The TLFi reads it literally as “to put in one's bag,” on the model of ~encadrer~ and ~encaisser~.
en.sacraliser: ~Sacraliser~ (“to make sacred”) is formed from the adjective ~sacral~ and the verb-forming suffix ~-iser~, and means to treat something as holy or set it apart as untouchable. The adjective ~sacral~ is a learned coinage: French Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~sacer~ (“sacred”), and gives it as ~sacrum~ plus the suffix ~-al~. The ending ~-iser~ is the usual French suffix for coining verbs of this kind, like ~moderniser~.
en.sacrer:
From Latin ~sacrāre~ (“to consecrate, make holy, dedicate to a divinity”), from the adjective ~sacer~ (“sacred”). ~Sacer~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~sakros~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~seh₂k-~ (“to sanctify, to make binding by treaty”), the same root behind ~sānctus~ (“holy”) and the verb ~sancīre~ (“to ratify”). A famous quirk of ~sacer~ is its double edge: it could mean both “consecrated” and “accursed,” for what is set apart for the gods is untouchable in either direction.

In French, ~sacrer~ first named the sacred rite of crowning a king or ordaining a bishop — the king was ~sacré~, anointed and consecrated, at Reims. From there it broadened to “to proclaim solemnly” (~sacré champion~, crowned champion). The most colorful development belongs to Québec French, where ~sacrer~ became “to swear, to curse” — precisely by profaning the sacred, hurling church words as oaths, the ~sacres~ of Quebec. So the same verb spans crowning a monarch and blaspheming. From ~sacer~ French also keeps ~sacré~, ~sacrement~, ~consacrer~, ~sacrifice~, and ~sacerdoce~ (“priesthood”).
en.sacrifier:
~sacrifier~ appeared in French around 1155, borrowed from Latin ~sacrificāre~ (“to perform a sacred rite”), a compound of ~sacer~ (“sacred, consecrated”) and ~facere~ (“to do, to make”): to sacrifice is literally “to make sacred” — to move a thing out of human ownership and hand it over to the gods. ~sacer~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~sakros~ to the Proto-Indo-European root *~seh₂k-~, associated with the making of binding pacts; ~facere~ continues the great root *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, to do”). The Romance siblings are Italian ~sacrificare~ and Spanish ~sacrificar~; English ~sacrifice~ came through Old French.

The compound hides a famous ambivalence. Latin ~sacer~ meant not only “holy” but also “accursed”: a man declared ~sacer~ was cast out of human law, given over to the gods for destruction. Both faces survive in French. On the bright side stand ~sacré~, ~consacrer~, ~sacrement~, ~sacre~ (the anointing of kings) and ~sacerdoce~; on the darker side, ~sacré~ set before a noun voices exasperation (un sacré menteur), and in Quebec French the verb ~sacrer~ means “to swear, to curse” — the famous ~sacres~ of Quebec are oaths built from liturgical words. Meanwhile the meaning of sacrifier slid from ritual offering to any painful renunciation: one sacrifices a pawn, an evening, a career. The metaphor has worn so smooth that its literal claim is forgotten — that what you give up is not lost, but made sacred.
en.safraner: ~Safraner~ is formed from the noun ~safran~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, and means “to add saffron to,” to color or flavor with it. The noun ~safran~ is inherited from Old French ~safran~, borrowed from Medieval Latin ~safranum~, which came from Arabic ~zaʿfarān~. Beyond Arabic the origin is uncertain; English Wiktionary traces it to Aramaic. French Wiktionary links the word to the spice's color.
en.saietter: Built on the noun ~saie~, which is the Norman pronunciation of ~soie~ (“silk”). The ending ~-er~ turns the noun into a verb, so the idea is of working with something silky, in the sense given by the dictionary: to brush. The Norman form is the reason the spelling differs from standard French ~soie~.
en.saigner:
From Old French ~saignier~ (also ~seigner~), inherited from Latin ~sanguināre~ (“to bleed, to stain with blood”), a verb built on ~sanguis~ (“blood”). The noun has its own French descendant, ~sang~, from the accusative ~sanguinem~. Latin ~sanguināre~ lives on in Spanish and Portuguese ~sangrar~ and in Italian ~sanguinare~. English took the Latin family by learned borrowing instead: ~sanguine~ and ~sanguinary~ both come from ~sanguis~. The origin of ~sanguis~ itself is not settled, so no earlier root is given here.

In French, ~saigner~ is both intransitive (“to bleed”) and transitive (“to draw blood from”). The transitive use goes back to the medical practice of bloodletting, which gave ~saignée~ (“bloodletting,” and also the crook of the elbow, where the vein was opened). Butchers still ~saignent~ an animal at slaughter. Figurative uses grew from there: ~saigner à blanc~ means to bleed someone dry, as heavy taxes can bleed a population. Other words from the same family include ~saignant~ (of meat, “rare”), ~saignement~, ~ensanglanter~, ~sanguin~ and ~sanguinaire~.
en.saillir:
From Old French ~saillir~, from Latin ~salīre~ (“to leap, to jump,” and in the language of breeders “to mount, to cover a female”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~sel-~ (“to jump”). In its plainest sense ~salīre~ was crowded out early by its own frequentative ~saltāre~ (whence ~sauter~), and the palatal ~-ll-~ that marks French ~saillir~ spread from the third-person plural ~saliunt~ → ~saillent~ across the rest of the paradigm. Cognate French words include ~saut~, ~sauter~, ~assaillir~, and ~tressaillir~; through Old French ~saillie~ and ~assalir~, English borrowed ~salient~, ~sally~, and ~assault~.

Every modern meaning is a metaphor of leaping. The oldest, attested in the ~Chanson de Roland~ around 1100, is « to gush, to spring forth with force » — water or blood that leaps from a wound. From the image of a male animal that leaps upon a female came, by the 14th century, the breeding sense « to cover, to mate » and the noun ~saillie~. A stone or a beam that seems to leap out from a wall gave the architectural sense « to jut out, to project », also medieval. Modern French splits ~saillir~ across two conjugations: in the breeding sense it has gone over to the regular second group, conjugating like ~finir~ (ils ~saillissent~), whereas the project sense keeps the older, irregular pattern (il ~saille~, ils ~saillent~). From the same root come ~saillant~, ~saillie~, ~assaut~, and ~ressaut~.
en.saisir:
From Old French ~saisir~, from Medieval Latin ~sacire~ (“to take possession, to put in legal possession”), itself of Germanic origin — most likely from Frankish *~sakjan~ or, by another account, from Old High German *~sazjan~ (“to set, to place someone in possession”), related to modern German ~setzen~ (“to set, to place”) and to English ~set~. The legal Low Latin phrase ~ad proprium sacire~ (“to put into one's own”) mirrors the native ~ad proprium ponere~, betraying the Germanic verb dressed in Latin clothing.

The earliest sense was the formal, legal one — to put someone in possession of property — which survives in French law: a court is ~saisi~ of a case, and goods can be ~saisis~ (“seized”) by a bailiff. From the idea of taking legal hold the verb broadened to physical grasping (to grab, to seize), then to mental grasping (to understand, as in ~saisir une idée~), and finally to the modern act of entering data — to ~saisir~ text on a keyboard. The verb is the source of ~saisie~ (“seizure, data entry”), ~saisissant~ (“striking, gripping”), ~dessaisir~ (“to dispossess”), and ~ressaisir~, as in ~se ressaisir~ (“to pull oneself together”).
en.salarier:
A denominal verb formed from the noun ~salaire~ (“wage, pay”) plus the suffix ~-er~. ~Salaire~ comes from Latin ~salarium~, a nominalization of the adjective ~salarius~ (“pertaining to salt”), from ~sal~ (“salt”), which goes back through Proto-Italic to the Proto-Indo-European root *~seh₂l-~ (“salt”). Cognate with Italian ~salario~ and Spanish ~salario~, and, through the same Latin word, with English ~salary~; the salt-root itself is kin to English ~salt~ and ~salad~.

A famous story holds that ~salarium~ was the money paid to Roman soldiers to buy salt, or even a ration of salt itself — but this should be flagged, not narrated as fact: ancient sources give no evidence that soldiers were ever paid in salt, and modern etymologists treat the salt-pay tale as an unproven popular explanation. What is certain is the salt connection in the word's form; how exactly the sense slid from “salt-money” to “wage” remains uncertain. ~Salarier~ means to put someone on a payroll, to employ for wages, and gives ~salarié~ (“a wage-earner, an employee”) and ~salarisation~. The plain ~sel~ (“salt”) and ~saler~ (“to salt”) descend from the same ~sal~.
en.saler:
From Latin ~sallire~ (“to salt”), a verb built on ~sal~ (“salt”), but with a change of conjugation that brought it into the regular French first group. ~sal~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~seh₂l-~ (“salt”), whose exact reconstruction is still debated. Through that root ~sal~ is cognate with Greek ~háls~, Proto-Germanic *~saltą~ (whence English ~salt~ and German ~Salz~), and the Slavic word seen in Russian ~соль~ (~sol~).

The verb has kept its concrete meaning — to season or preserve with salt — almost unchanged for two millennia, a testament to how essential salt once was. That importance is fossilized in vocabulary: Latin ~sal~ gave the noun ~sel~ and, via the soldiers' allowance of salt-money, the word ~salaire~ (“salary”) and English ~salary~ itself. The same family yields French ~salade~ (originally salted greens), saler's derivatives ~salaison~ and ~dessaler~, and the figurative ~salé~ used of a price or a joke that “stings.”
en.salifier: Formed from Latin ~sāl~ (“salt”) with the French suffix ~-ifier~ (“to make”): ~salifier~ is “to turn into salt.” The Latin noun also gave French ~sel~, ~salin~ and ~saler~, and it is the root of English ~salt~ and German ~Salz~ by distant kinship. The suffix ~-ifier~ is the same one found in ~purifier~ and ~clarifier~.
en.salir: ~Salir~ is formed from the adjective ~sale~ (“dirty”) with the verb ending ~-ir~, in the sense “to make dirty.” The adjective is itself of Germanic origin: it comes from Old French ~sale~ (“dull, dirty”), from Frankish *~salu~ (“dull, dirty grey”), from Proto-Germanic *~salwaz~ (“dusky, dark, muddy”). English ~sallow~ is a cognate, as are Old High German ~salo~ and Old English ~salu~. The sources differ slightly on the deepest layers, since French Wiktionary also entertains a possible crossing with a Gaulish word, so the Frankish origin is the safest reading. The verb thus names a change of color before one of cleanliness.
en.saliver: Formed from the noun ~salive~ and the verb ending ~-er~, with the Latin verb ~salīvāre~ as a model. The noun comes from Latin ~saliva~, which meant “spittle, secretion, drool” and also “flavor, taste.” English Wiktionary notes that ~saliva~ itself may be a borrowing into Latin from an unknown source. The ending ~-er~ continues Latin ~-are~, so ~saliver~ means, simply, “to produce saliva.”
en.saloper: ~Saloper~ is a denominal verb formed from ~salope~ and the ending ~-er~, with the sense of doing something in a dirty, sloppy way. The noun ~salope~ is first attested in a text by Sigogne and is probably a compound of ~sale~ (“dirty”) and ~hoppe~, a Lorraine form of ~huppe~ (“hoopoe”), a bird with a reputation for filth because of the smell of its nest. The French saying ~sale comme une huppe~ is cited in support. Other accounts of ~salope~ exist for its separate senses, such as a coat or a fish.
en.saluer:
From Old French ~saluer~ (the form ~saludent~ is already attested around 980), from Latin ~salūtāre~ (“to greet, wish health to”), the verb of ~salūs~ (~salūtem~, “health, safety, welfare”). ~Salūs~ is a doublet of ~salvus~ (“safe, sound”), from Proto-Italic *~salūts~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~solh₂-~ (“whole, complete”). The same root of wholeness gives Greek ~ὅλος~ (~hólos~, “whole”) and, through Latin, English ~safe~, ~salvage~, and ~solid~.

The lovely logic sits right on the surface: to greet someone was to wish them health and wholeness — a spoken ~salus~. French ~saluer~ kept exactly that, narrowing over time from the wish itself to its outward gestures: the bow, the nod, the wave, the military ~salut~. The noun ~salut~ now carries both threads at once — a casual “hi” and the weighty “salvation” — while ~salutation~, ~salutaire~ (“salutary, beneficial”), and ~salubre~ (“healthful”) keep the older sense of health near the surface. Behind a daily “~salut~!” lies an ancient blessing: may you be whole.
en.sanctifier:
English Wiktionary gives the French verb as Middle French ~sanctifier~ (15th century), a re-Latinized form of Old French ~saintefier~, itself either borrowed or inherited from Latin ~sānctificāre~. French Wiktionary simply derives it from Latin ~sānctificāre~, citing the past participle ~sanctificat~. The Latin verb is ~sānctus~ (“holy”) plus ~-ficāre~, a verb ending related to ~facere~ (“to make”), so it means “to make holy”.

The two French forms show a learned correction. In the fifteenth century the Latin spelling with ~-nct-~ was restored to Old French ~saintefier~, giving ~sanctifier~, while ~saint~ descends from ~sānctus~ by the popular route. That pair is a reminder that French has two layers, popular and learned. Related words include ~saint~, ~sanctuaire~ and ~sanctification~, and English has ~sanctify~ and ~saint~.
en.sanctionner:
From the noun ~sanction~ plus the verb-forming suffix ~-er~. ~Sanction~ comes from Latin ~sanctiō~ (“the making binding of a law, a decree with its penalty”), from ~sancīre~ (“to make sacred or inviolable, to ratify”). ~Sancīre~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~sankjō~ and PIE *~seh₂k-~ (“to sanctify, to make a treaty”), the same root as Latin ~sacer~ (“sacred”) and ~sānctus~ (“holy”). Through these, English gained ~saint~, ~sacred~, ~sanctify~, ~sanction~, and ~sacrosanct~ — and French and English ~sanction~ are the same Latin word.

The noun's history hides a striking double edge. A Roman ~sanctiō~ was the clause of a law that made it ~inviolable~ by attaching a penalty — so the single word came to mean both the ~approval~ that ratifies and the ~punishment~ that enforces. French ~sanctionner~ inherits both: to ~sanctionner~ a law is to give it official approval and force, yet to ~sanctionner~ an offender is to punish — opposite-seeming senses growing from one root in inviolability. The family of *~seh₂k-~ runs deep in French: ~sacré~, ~saint~, ~sanctuaire~, ~consacrer~, ~sacrement~, and ~sacrer~ — so to ~sanctionner~ is, etymologically, to render something sacred and untouchable, whether by blessing it or by punishing its violation.
en.sanctuariser: Formed from the noun ~sanctuaire~ (“sanctuary”) with the suffix ~-iser~, which makes verbs meaning “to make or turn into N.” The noun comes from Old French ~saintuaire~, from Latin ~sanctuārium~ (“sacred place, shrine”), itself built on ~sanctus~ (“holy, sacred”). So ~sanctuariser~ means to turn a place into a sanctuary: to declare it inviolable and protect it from attack, intrusion or exploitation. The verb is modern and belongs to journalistic and political language, where one speaks of ~sanctuariser~ a territory or a budget. The ~-iser~ ending is fully productive in such registers.
en.sandwicher: ~Sandwicher~ is formed from the noun ~sandwich~ with the verb ending ~-er~, and means to eat a sandwich, or to squeeze something between two things. ~Sandwich~ is borrowed from English, where it comes from the title of John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich. He was probably not the inventor, but he was among its first great enthusiasts. According to the report, he ate them at his desk to save time.
en.sangler: Formed in French from the noun ~sangle~ (“strap, girth”) and the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense “to fasten or bind with a strap.” The noun is inherited from Old French ~cengle~, from Vulgar Latin *~cingla~, from Late Latin ~cingula~, from Latin ~cingulum~ (“belt, girdle”). That Latin word belongs to the family of ~cingere~ (“to gird”), which also gave French ~ceinture~ and ~ceindre~. The verb ~sangler~ is used of tightening a horse's girth or of cinching a garment.
en.sangloter:
From Old French ~sangloter~, inherited from Vulgar Latin *~singluttāre~, an altered form of Latin ~singultāre~ (“to sob, to gasp”) under the influence of ~gluttīre~ (“to swallow”). The Latin verb is itself derived from the noun ~singultus~ (“a sob, a hiccup”). Its relatives in other Romance languages include Italian ~singhiozzare~ and Occitan and Catalan ~sanglotar~.

In use, ~sangloter~ describes weeping with short, broken breaths. French also has the noun ~sanglot~ (“a sob”) beside the verb. The Latin noun ~singultus~ covered both a sob and a hiccup, and Italian ~singhiozzo~ still covers both, while French keeps ~sanglot~ for crying and uses ~hoquet~, an unrelated word, for the hiccup.
en.saouler: ~Saouler~ (also spelled ~soûler~) comes from Old French ~sauler~, itself from Latin ~satullāre~ (“to sate”), a verb related to ~saturer~. Latin ~satullāre~ rests on ~satur~ (“full”), the root of ~saturer~ as well. French uses the verb in the sense “to get drunk”.
en.saper: French has several homonymous verbs saper, and the sources do not trace them to one origin. For the one meaning “to dig, to undermine,” French Wiktionary gives Italian ~zappare~ (“to dig, to hoe”), and English Wiktionary agrees on a loan from Italian. A second saper, “to dress,” has an obscure origin; French Wiktionary suggests, with a maybe, a link to the first, in the sense of “cutting” a garment to clothe someone, while English Wiktionary says only that it is unknown. For a third, French Wiktionary proposes Norman ~super~ (“to suck, to draw in”), while English Wiktionary derives it from the noun ~sape~, from Latin ~sappa~, comparing Italian ~zappare~ and Romanian ~săpa~. Which of these accounts is right remains unsettled.
en.saponifier:
A learned formation from Latin ~sāpō~ (genitive ~sāpōnis~, “soap”) and the suffix ~-ifier~, which comes from Latin ~-ficāre~ (“to make”). So ~saponifier~ means, literally, to make into soap. It is a French coinage built from Latin parts, not a word inherited from Latin, and it keeps the stem ~sāpōn-~ of the Latin genitive, as scholarly words often do.

The ordinary French word for soap, ~savon~, comes from the same Latin ~sāpō~, by a long inherited route, while ~saponifier~ takes the Latin stem as it stood. The chemical sense is the one in use: to turn a fat into soap by treating it with an alkali. The family includes ~saponification~ and ~saponine~, and English has ~saponify~ from the same source.
en.saquer: ~Saquer~ is formed from ~sac~ (“sack”) with ~-er~, from the expression ~donner à quelqu'un son sac~, “to give someone his sack”, which meant to dismiss him and is attested in 1611. The sense “to put up with” works the same way: it means, literally, to put something into one's bag. The noun ~sac~ comes from Latin ~saccus~, itself from Ancient Greek ~sákkos~ (“sack, bag; sackcloth”), ultimately from a Semitic source. Old French also had the related ~saqueur~ and ~sacheur~.
en.sarcler:
~Sarcler~ is inherited from Late Latin ~sarculāre~, a verb derived from Latin ~sarculum~ (“hoe”). The noun ~sarculum~ is a tool name built on the Latin verb ~sarrire~ (“to hoe, to weed”). Italian ~sarchiare~ and Spanish ~sachar~ come from the same Late Latin verb, and both also mean to hoe or weed.

French kept the Latin sense: to clear a field of weeds with a hoe. The tool is the ~sarcloir~, the job is the ~sarclage~, and the worker is the ~sarcleur~. These nouns are built on the French verb, so a ~sarcloir~ is, etymologically, a “weeder.” The ending also shows a regular sound change: the Latin ~-āre~ of ~sarculāre~ became ~-er~, just as ~cantāre~ became ~chanter~.
en.sarmenter: Formed from the noun ~sarment~ with the verb ending ~-er~. A ~sarment~ is a woody shoot of the vine, and the verb means to gather the vine shoots cut off in pruning. The noun comes straight from Latin ~sarmentum~, and the ending ~-er~ goes back to Latin ~-are~. As the ending here means “to deal with N,” the verb names the work around the vine prunings.
en.sasser: Formed from the noun ~sas~ (“sieve”) and the verb ending ~-er~, which here makes a verb meaning “to work with N.” The noun ~sas~ comes from Old French ~saaz~ (twelfth century), from Medieval Latin ~setacium~ (“sieve”), itself derived from Latin ~saeta~ (“bristle, horsehair”), the stiff hair from which sieves were once made. An older rival idea, from Italian ~sasso~ (“stone”), has largely been set aside.
en.satelliser: Formed from ~satellite~ and the verb suffix ~-iser~, meaning to make something a satellite: to place it in orbit, or figuratively to reduce it to dependence on a stronger power. French Wiktionary traces the underlying word to Latin ~satelles~ (“attendant, companion”), whence ~satellite~. The suffix ~-iser~ is the productive French ending meaning “make into”, as in ~numériser~ or ~carboniser~. The verb thus joins an ancient Latin word for a follower to a modern technical ending.
