en.satiner: Formed from the noun ~satin~ with the verbal ending ~-er~: to give a surface the sheen of satin. ~Satin~ is borrowed from Arabic ~zaytūn~, which English Wiktionary glosses as “Zayton; olive.” French Wiktionary sees in it the Arabic transcription of the name of the Chinese city of Citong, now Quanzhou, so ~satin~ carries the name of a Chinese city.
en.satiriser: ~Satiriser~ is formed from the noun ~satire~ with the suffix ~-iser~, meaning to mock in the manner of a satire. The noun ~satire~ comes through Middle and Old French from Latin ~satira~, an earlier ~satura~. The Latin form ~satura~ is the older one, and ~satira~ is a later variant of it.
en.satisfaire:
From Latin ~satisfacere~ (“to do enough, to satisfy a claim, to give satisfaction”), a compound of ~satis~ (“enough, sufficiently”) and ~facere~ (“to do, to make”). ~satis~ comes from the Proto-Indo-European root *~seh₂-~ (“to satiate, to be full”), seen also in ~satur~ (“full, sated”) and English ~sad~ (originally “sated, weary”). ~facere~ rests on the root *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to set, to put, to do”), which gives Greek ~τίθημι~ (~títhēmi~) and English ~do~. The French form was remodelled on the native verb ~faire~. Cognate with Italian ~soddisfare~ and Spanish ~satisfacer~.

The literal sense, “to do enough,” is wonderfully plain: to satisfy is to do as much as is required and no more. In Roman law ~satisfacere~ meant to discharge an obligation, to make good on a debt — a meaning that survives in the legal and financial uses of French ~satisfaire~ (~satisfaire à ses engagements~, to meet one's commitments) alongside the everyday sense of pleasing someone. From ~satis~ French also draws ~satiété~ (“satiety”), ~rassasier~ (“to sate”), and ~saturer~; from ~facere~ comes the immense family of ~faire~ — ~défaire~, ~refaire~, ~parfaire~ — so that ~satisfaire~ sits at the meeting point of “enough” and “do.”
en.saturer:
Learned borrowing from Latin ~saturāre~ (“to fill, to sate”), from the adjective ~satur~ (“full, well fed”). That adjective belongs with Latin ~satis~ (“enough”) and the Proto-Indo-European root *~seh₂-~ (“to satisfy, to be sated”). The same root gave English its cognate ~sad~, whose oldest sense was “full, sated” before it drifted toward “sorrowful”, and German ~satt~ (“full”). French kept this Latin family close at hand: ~assez~ is built on ~satis~ (“enough”), and ~satisfaire~ means, literally, “to do enough”.

Because ~saturer~ was borrowed from learned Latin rather than inherited, it kept its Latin shape and never went through the sound changes of the spoken language. Its first sense was “to fill to the point of satiety”. The verb then entered chemistry and physics for a solution that can dissolve no more of a substance, and from there it spread to everything that can be filled past its capacity: a market, a road, a network, an inbox. In everyday speech, ~être saturé~ is to have had more than enough, which brings the word back to its Latin meaning. Its family includes ~saturation~, ~satiété~, ~satisfaction~ and ~insatiable~.
en.saucer: Formed from the noun ~sauce~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Old French ~sause~, from Vulgar Latin *~salsa~, a feminine participle of Latin ~salsus~ (“salted”) used as a noun, so a sauce was first simply “something salted.” Latin ~salsus~ belongs to ~saliō~ (“to salt”), from ~sāl~ (“salt”). To ~saucer~ is to dip into the sauce, above all to wipe a plate clean with a piece of bread.
en.saucissonner: Formed in French from ~saucisson~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so to treat something as one treats a sausage, slicing or dividing it into pieces. The noun ~saucisson~ comes from Middle French ~saulcisson~ (“large sausage”), borrowed from Italian ~salsiccione~, and it can be analyzed on the surface as ~saucisse~ plus the suffix ~-on~.
en.saumurer: Formed directly from the noun ~saumure~ (“brine”), by adding the verb ending ~-er~. Both Wiktionaries give nothing beyond this, so the verb is best seen as a simple denominal coinage: to treat something with brine, that is, to soak or preserve it in salt water. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is the ordinary way French makes a verb out of a noun, here with the sense “to put in N.”
en.sauner: The French verb ~sauner~ (“to harvest salt”) comes, according to French Wiktionary, from a Latin form *~salīnāre~, derived from ~salīnae~ (“salt works, salt pans”). That noun is built on Latin ~sāl~ (“salt”), the source of French ~sel~ and of the learned adjective ~salin~. The starred form is reconstructed rather than attested. The only evidence is the French text, and English Wiktionary has no entry to compare, so nothing more is claimed here about the dates or the history of the word.
en.saupoudrer: A compound of ~sel~ (“salt”) and ~poudrer~ (“to powder”). French Wiktionary specifies that the first element is Old French ~sal~, a rare variant of ~sel~, while English Wiktionary simply writes ~sel~. ~Sel~ comes from Latin ~sāl~ (“salt”), the same word behind English ~salt~, and ~poudrer~ is the verb of ~poudre~ (“powder”), from Latin ~pulvis~ (“dust”). The result literally describes sprinkling with salt in powder form. Today ~saupoudrer~ covers sprinkling any fine powder, such as sugar or flour, onto food.
en.saurer: ~Saurer~ is formed from ~saur~ and the verbal ending ~-er~; the spelling ~sorer~ already exists in the 14th century. ~Saur~ is a variant of ~saure~, from Old French ~sor~ and Middle French ~saur~, borrowed from Frankish *~sōri~ or *~saur~ (“dry”), from Proto-Germanic *~sauzaz~ (“dry, parched”). It is cognate with English ~sear~ and Dutch ~zoor~. The adjective survives in ~hareng saur~, a smoked herring, and the verb means to cure food by smoking it.
en.sauter:
From Latin ~saltāre~ (“to dance, to leap”), the frequentative of ~salīre~ (“to jump”) — literally “to keep jumping.” Both go back to Proto-Italic *~saljō~ and the PIE root *~sel-~ (“to spring, jump”), shared as a cognate with Ancient Greek ~hállomai~ (“I leap”). Latin ~salīre~ gave French its more learned ~saillir~ and ~assaillir~, while ~saltāre~, the dancing form, became the everyday ~sauter~.

The verb's energy spread in every direction: to jump for joy, to leap a fence, but also to blow up (~faire sauter~ un pont), to skip a step or a line (~sauter une ligne~), and, in cooking, to toss food in a hot pan — a ~sauté~ is food made to jump in butter. The same root bounds through ~saut~ (“a jump”), ~sursaut~ (“a start”), ~assaut~ (“assault”), ~sauterelle~ (“grasshopper,” the little jumper) and ~sautoir~. English borrowed from the family too, in ~salient~, ~sally~ and the ~-sault~ of ~somersault~.
en.sautiller: ~Sautiller~ is formed from the verb ~sauter~ and the suffix ~-iller~, which gives a repeated, small action, as in ~mordiller~ and ~fendiller~. The verb thus means to hop or skip: to jump again and again in little bounds. Its base ~sauter~ comes from Latin ~saltāre~ (“to dance, to leap”), the frequentative of ~salīre~ (“to jump”). The suffix is traced either to Old French ~-ille~ or to Latin ~-iculare~, and its stem drops the ending of the base: ~sauter~ becomes ~saut-~.
en.sauvegarder:
A verb built on the noun ~sauvegarde~, itself a transparent compound of ~sauve~ (the feminine of ~sauf~, “safe,” from Latin ~salvus~) and ~garde~ (“guard, protection”). The two halves come from opposite ends of Europe. ~Salvus~ is solidly Latin; but ~garde~ and its verb ~garder~ descend from a Germanic root carried into Gaul by the Franks — Frankish *~wardōn~ (“to watch over, to guard”), latinized as ~wardāre~. Through that Germanic root ~garde~ is cognate with English ~ward~, ~warden~, and ~guard~, and with German ~warten~. A “safe-guard,” then, is etymologically a “safe-watching.”

In medieval and legal French, a ~sauvegarde~ was the formal protection a lord or sovereign extended over a person or property — a safe-conduct, a guarantee of safety. The verb ~sauvegarder~ generalized this to “to protect, to preserve from harm,” and in the computer age it acquired its now-dominant sense: to ~save~ a file or back up data, keeping it safe from loss. The Germanic half lives on in ~garder~, ~gardien~, and ~regarder~ (“to look at,” originally “to watch over again”), while the Latin half survives in ~sauf~, ~sauver~, and ~salut~. To safeguard is to keep watch so that something stays whole.
en.sauver:
From Old French ~salver~, ~sauver~ (“to save, keep safe, protect”), attested as early as the ~Serments de Strasbourg~ of 842 in the form ~salvar~ — among the oldest French words on record. It descends from Late Latin ~salvāre~ (“to make safe, rescue”), a verb built on Classical Latin ~salvus~ (“safe, sound, unharmed, in good health”), from Proto-Indo-European *~solh₂wós~, from the root *~solh₂-~ (“whole, well-kept”). Cognate with Italian ~salvare~, Spanish ~salvar~, and — through Old French — with English ~save~ and ~safe~.

The sense has stayed remarkably stable: to keep something whole is to keep it safe, and the same notion of intact wholeness shows in Greek ~ὅλος~ (“whole, entire”) and Sanskrit ~sarva~ (“all, whole”), both from the same root. From ~salvus~ Latin also drew the greeting ~salvē~ (“be well, hail”), and from the family French inherited ~salut~, ~santé~, ~sauf~, ~sauveur~, ~sauvetage~, and ~sauvegarde~. English ~salvage~ and ~salvation~ are learned borrowings of the same Latin stock. A fine doublet survives in French itself: alongside the inherited ~sauver~ stands the later, scholarly form preserved in ~salvateur~ and in religious ~Sauveur~ — the Savior who makes the soul whole again.
en.savoir:
From Old French ~savoir~, earlier ~saveir~ and ~savir~ (the form recorded in the 842 ~Serments de Strasbourg~), from Vulgar Latin *~sapēre~, a remodeling of Classical Latin ~sapĕre~ (“to taste, to have flavor,” figuratively “to be wise, to understand”), from Proto-Italic *~sapiō~, from PIE *~seh₁p-~ (“to taste, to perceive”). The Latin verb already carried both senses, reinforced by the participle ~sapiēns~ (“wise”). Cognate with Italian ~sapere~ and Spanish ~saber~, both meaning “to know,” and — through the same root — with English ~savor~ and ~savvy~.

The semantic drift is striking: a verb that first meant “to taste” came to mean “to know,” the tongue's discernment standing in for the mind's. In doing so, *~sapēre~ pushed aside the classical verb for knowing, ~scīre~, which vanished from French. That lost ~scīre~ left a curious scar: from the 16th to the 18th century the verb was misspelled ~sçavoir~, a learned but false back-formation that wrongly assumed descent from ~scīre~; the Académie française restored ~savoir~ only in 1740. The same PIE root underlies a wide family of French words, among them ~sage~, ~saveur~, ~savant~, ~sapience~, and the species name ~Homo sapiens~ — the “knowing,” or rather “tasting,” human.
en.savonner: Formed from the noun ~savon~ (“soap”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, with the sense “to wash with soap” or “to lather.” ~Savon~ came through Middle and Old French from Latin ~sāpōnem~ (“soap”), which English Wiktionary traces back to Proto-Germanic *~saipǭ~ and to a Proto-Indo-European root *~seyb-~ (“to pour out, drip, trickle”). Old English ~sāpe~ is a cognate. The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, is the usual way French turns a noun into a verb meaning “provide with” or “apply” that noun.
en.savourer:
From Old French ~savorer~ and ~savourer~, derived from the noun ~savor~ or ~savour~ (“taste”), which comes from Latin ~sapor~ (“taste, flavor”). That noun belongs to Latin ~sapere~ (“to have a taste, to be wise”), the verb that also gave French ~savoir~, Italian ~sapere~ and Spanish ~saber~. The Latin ~p~ softened to ~v~ in French, which is why ~sapor~ became ~savor~. English took the same family twice: ~savor~ came in from Old French ~savour~, and ~sapient~ and ~insipid~ were borrowed from Latin.

In Old French the verb was concrete, a matter of tasting a food or a drink. Its modern sense of enjoying something slowly and fully grew out of that, and ~savourer~ now applies as readily to a victory, a silence or a sentence as to a meal. The modern noun ~saveur~ replaced ~savor~ and ~savour~, and the Old French form survives in the verb and in ~savoureux~. The same Latin source gave ~savoir~, ~sapide~ and ~insipide~. Behind it all lies a link between tasting and knowing that Latin made explicit: the scientific name ~sapiens~ means “tasting, discerning,” and is applied to the human species as “wise.”
en.scalper: Borrowed from English ~scalp~ (“the skin of the top of the head”) with the French ending ~-er~, which makes the loan a regular first-conjugation verb: ~scalper~ is to take the scalp of someone. The French verb follows the noun ~scalp~ in meaning.
en.scandaliser: ~Scandaliser~ is a learned borrowing from Late Latin ~scandalizāre~, which in turn took the verb from Ancient Greek ~skandalízō~. English Wiktionary adds that, by surface analysis, French speakers can also read it as ~scandale~ + ~-iser~, since the suffix ~-iser~ itself traces back to Greek verbs in Late Latin dress. The Greek verb is built on the noun ~skandalon~, which meant a trap or a stumbling block. The Greek image of tripping someone is the old core of the word: to scandalize is to make a person stumble, whether morally or in belief. In modern French the verb has the milder sense of provoking indignation or shocking people, and the pronominal ~se scandaliser~ means to be shocked.
en.scander:
French ~scander~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~scandere~, “to climb.” In French it means “to scan a line of verse” by marking its beats, and also “to chant or enunciate with strong stress,” as a crowd does a slogan. English ~scan~ has the same Latin origin. The sources supplied do not explain why a verb of climbing came to denote the measuring of verse.

The Latin verb is a productive root in compounds, and its prefixed forms gave French some of its most familiar verbs. ~Descendre~ comes from Latin ~dēscendere~ (~dē-~ + ~scandere~, “to climb down”), and the learned ~ascendant~ and ~transcender~ belong to the same family, as do English ~ascend~ and ~descend~. The noun ~escalade~ and the Latin ~scala~ (“ladder”) are generally linked to it as well. So ~scander~ shares a root with going down a staircase, though its modern sense has left climbing far behind.
en.scanner: A modern adaptation of English ~scan~ with the French first-group ending ~-er~. The English verb ~scan~ itself goes back to Latin ~scandere~ (“to climb”), which in late Latin was used for reading verse foot by foot, as if climbing its rhythm. English then stretched it to mean examining something closely or sweeping across it, and the arrival of electronic devices in the twentieth century made ~scan~ the word for reading a document or image into a computer. French took the verb over with an ordinary ~-er~ ending, so it conjugates like any regular verb.
en.scarifier: Inherited from Old French ~scarifier~, itself from Late Latin ~scarificāre~, from Latin ~scarifāre~ (“to scarify”), which comes from Ancient Greek ~σκαριφᾶσθαι~ (~skariphâsthai~, “to scratch an outline”), from ~σκάριφος~ (~skáriphos~, “writing, drawing, sketching”). English ~scarify~ comes from the same French and Latin line. French ~scarifier~ is used in the medical sense of making a series of small cuts or scratches in the skin, and also by gardeners and farmers who slit or scratch the surface of soil or lawn. The noun ~scarification~ names both the act and its marks, including decorative skin marks.
en.sceller:
From Old French ~seeler~ (Middle French ~sceller~), inherited from Vulgar Latin *~sigellāre~, a variant of Latin ~sigillāre~ (“to seal”), from the noun ~sigillum~ (“small figure, seal”). ~Sigillum~ is usually explained as a diminutive of ~signum~ (“mark, sign”), so a seal was originally a “little sign” pressed into wax. The same verb gave Catalan ~segellar~, Spanish ~sellar~, Portuguese ~selar~ and Italian ~suggellare~. The noun side shows two routes into English: ~seal~ came through Old French, while ~sigil~ was taken straight from Latin ~sigillum~.

The French noun ~sceau~ evolved in parallel with the verb, and the two keep the same odd ~sc-~ spelling, a learned touch grafted on the older ~seel~. The verb first meant “to close with a seal,” as a letter or a document, hence its modern sense of “to make official or binding.” From there it moved to “sealing” in the broad sense of fastening shut, as in ~sceller une porte~ or cementing something in place, and to the figurative ~sceller une amitié~ or ~sceller un pacte~, where the seal is a guarantee. The family includes ~sceau~, ~signe~, ~signer~, ~sigillographie~ (the study of seals) and ~desceller~.
en.schlinguer:
The origin of ~schlinguer~, a slang verb meaning “to stink, to reek,” is unknown. It first appeared as ~schelinguer~, meaning “to smell bad,” at first of the breath. French Wiktionary offers three guesses, two from German and one from French, and none of them is settled. Each explains the sense by a figurative detour, and each has a difficulty of its own, as the next paragraph shows.

One suggestion is German ~schlingen~ (“to swallow”), which would have given “to exhale a smell” by a deliberate reversal of sense, though that shift is hard to accept. Another is German ~schlagen~ (“to strike, to lash”), the way French slang verbs of striking such as ~cingler~, ~cogner~ and ~fouetter~ can also mean “to stink”; the change of vowel from [a] to [ɛ] is the difficulty. A third account starts from ~élingue~ (“rope, cable”), hence “to whip” and then “to stink,” with ~élinguer~ (“to sling”) as support. It needs intermediate senses that are not attested.
en.schlitter: Formed from the noun ~schlitte~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is borrowed from German ~Schlitten~ (“sledge”), so the verb means to transport something, typically wood or goods, by sledge. It is a regional word, a loan from German that kept its German spelling with ~sch-~.
en.schématiser: Formed from ~schéma~ and the suffix ~-iser~. The sources differ on the route. French Wiktionary derives it from the Ancient Greek verb ~σχηματίζω~ (“to figure, to shape”), while English Wiktionary builds it from Latin ~schēmata~ plus ~-iser~. The two accounts agree that the suffix ~-iser~ makes the verb, and both go back to the Greek word behind ~schéma~. The sense today is to reduce something to a simple diagram or outline.
en.scier:
From Middle French ~scier~, from earlier ~sier~, from Old French ~seier~, ~sier~, ~soiier~ and ~seër~, from Latin ~secāre~ (“to cut”). The silent ~c~ was added in the sixteenth century to bring the spelling closer to the Latin etymon. The line from ~secāre~ through Old French ~seier~ and ~sier~ to ~scier~ is straightforward, and ~scier~ keeps the Latin sense of cutting, narrowed to cutting with a saw.

The wider Romance family is less clear. Italian ~sciare~ and Spanish ~ciar~ are cognates with the same sense, but the further origin of the word is unknown. The theories offered, onomatopoeia or a derivation from Ancient Greek ~ἰσχίον~ (“hip-bone”), are only proposals. The Latin verb ~secāre~ is, however, firmly established as the base of other French words, such as ~section~, ~secteur~, ~sécateur~ and ~dissection~.
en.scinder: Borrowed from Latin ~scindere~ (“to cut, to split, to tear apart”). The French verb keeps the same idea, usually in an abstract sense: to ~scinder~ a party, a company or a question is to divide it into parts, as in ~se scinder en deux~. The Latin verb also stands behind related learned words such as ~scission~ (“a split”), which is the noun most often used for a breakaway within a group.
en.scintiller:
~Scintiller~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~scintillāre~ (“to sparkle, to flash”), a verb built on ~scintilla~ (“spark”). English ~scintillate~ and ~scintilla~ come from the same Latin words. English Wiktionary compares ~étinceler~ and says it may be an inherited doublet through a Vulgar Latin derivative, or else a French formation, so the link between the two verbs is uncertain.

The Latin verb described sparks and glints of light, and French uses ~scintiller~ for stars, jewels and eyes that twinkle or sparkle. Its family includes ~scintillement~ and ~scintillant~. Whether ~étinceler~ and its noun ~étincelle~ (“spark”) share the same ancestor is, as noted, an open question, so it is safest to call them neighbors in meaning.
en.scléroser: Formed from the noun ~sclérose~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is borrowed from Ancient Greek ~σκλήρωσις~ (“hardening”). The verb thus means to harden, and it is used both of tissue and, figuratively, of a system or an institution that stiffens, ossifies, or grinds to a halt.
en.scolariser: Formed from the adjective ~scolaire~ (“of school”) plus the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make, to provide with”), with the stem shortened to ~scolar-~: to send to school, to provide with schooling. The adjective comes from Late Latin ~scholāris~, built on ~schola~ (“school”), which Latin took from Greek ~σχολή~ (“leisure,” then “lecture, school”). French has a second, inherited descendant of the same Latin word, ~écolier~ (“schoolboy”), so ~scolaire~ and ~écolier~ are learned and popular doublets.
en.scorifier: ~Scorifier~ is formed from ~scorie~ (“slag, dross”) with the suffix ~-fier~, in the sense “to turn into slag.” The noun ~scorie~ is borrowed from Latin ~scoria~, which came from Greek ~skōría~, a word for the dross or “froth” of iron. The suffix ~-fier~ descends from Latin ~-ficāre~ (“to make”). The verb thus joins a Greek metallurgical term, passed on by Latin, to a Latin-born ending, and it is used chiefly in metallurgy.
en.scotcher: ~Scotcher~ is built on ~scotch~ and the verb-forming ending ~-er~. The base is ~Scotch tape~, a trademark that 3M registered in 1945 and that became, in French-speaking Europe, the ordinary word for clear adhesive tape. French Wiktionary explains the English name as ~to scotch~ (“to put a stop to”) plus ~tape~. The verb first means to stick something with this tape, and its glosses add figurative uses such as numbing or freezing.
en.scotomiser: Derived from the noun ~scotome~ (“blind spot”) with the verb suffix ~-iser~. In its figurative sense, to ~scotomiser~ is to block something out of one's awareness, as a blind spot removes part of the visual field. ~Scotome~ was borrowed from Latin ~scotoma~. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, a transcription of Greek verbal endings, and builds verbs meaning “to subject to” or “to turn into.”
en.scratcher: ~Scratcher~ is a modern borrowing from English ~scratch~ (“to scratch”), turned into a French verb of the first conjugation with the verbalizing ending ~-er~. The ending is the default one for newly coined French verbs, which is why English loans so often take it.
en.scruter:
Borrowed from Latin ~scrūtārī~ (“to search, examine, probe”), a deponent verb that French recast as a regular verb in ~-er~. ~Scrūtārī~ is usually connected with ~scrūta~ (“old clothes, junk, trash”), which would make the original idea a rummaging through rubbish. That link is traditional rather than certain. The verb has relatives across the Romance languages, such as Spanish ~escrutar~, and English took ~scrutiny~ from the Latin noun ~scrūtinium~ (“a search, an investigation”).

In Latin the word described close, methodical searching, whether of a house, a wound or a person's thoughts. French ~scruter~ kept the idea of hunting for what is hidden and extended it to the gaze, so that one scans a horizon, a face or a text with it. Today it is almost always figurative and a little literary, and it pairs naturally with objects such as intentions or the horizon. The Latin noun ~scrūtinium~ also lies behind French ~scrutin~ (“ballot, poll”), a reminder that an election was once thought of as a careful examination of votes. Other words of the family are ~scrutateur~ and ~scrutation~.
en.sculpter:
From Latin ~sculpere~ (“to carve, to engrave”), but with a twist: the ~t~ of the French verb has no justification in the Latin one. French first borrowed the Latin verb as ~sculper~, a form now obsolete, and the modern ~sculpter~ is a contamination: a blend of that older verb with ~sculpteur~, which does contain a ~t~. French Wiktionary makes the same point, noting that the ~t~ is not etymologically justified for the verb and sending the reader to ~sculpteur~ and ~sculpture~. The older verb ~sculper~ was displaced by the newcomer, so the form we conjugate today is the blended one rather than the straight descendant of the Latin.

The spelling of ~sculpter~ is therefore a small trace of its relatives, the nouns that carry a ~t~ having left their mark on the verb. Anyone who knows ~sculpteur~ and ~sculpture~ will find the spelling familiar, and that familiarity is what the contamination reflects. The meaning stayed close to the Latin: to cut a form out of stone, wood or another hard material, and by extension to give something a defined shape. Related words include ~sculpteur~, ~sculpture~, ~sculptural~ and ~sculpté~.
en.scénariser: Formed from ~scénario~ and the verbal suffix ~-iser~, which means “to make, to turn into”. The base ~scénario~ was borrowed from Italian ~scenario~ (first “stage set”, then “description of a staging”), itself built from ~scena~ (“scene”) and ~-ario~, and ~scena~ goes back through Latin ~scēna~ to Greek ~skēnē~. In French the word first meant the outline of a play; its cinema sense, the written description of a film's action, became current in 1907 (Méliès). The verb therefore means to turn material into a scenario, in practice to write it as a screenplay.
en.seconder:
The two Wiktionaries give different routes. French Wiktionary sees a borrowing from Latin ~secundāre~; English Wiktionary describes a French formation, ~second~ + ~-er~, through Old French ~segonder~. The sources therefore disagree, and the origin of ~seconder~ is not settled. Under the first account the verb was taken whole from Latin; under the second it was built in French on the word ~second~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, and the Old French form ~segonder~ is the older attested stage.

In French, ~seconder~ means to assist or support someone, to help or ease their task. The sense is that of a second, a person who stands beside another in order to help. Whichever route is right for ~seconder~, that picture is the same: to second someone is to stand with them and lend a hand.
en.secouer:
French ~secouer~ goes back to Old French ~secorre~ or ~secourre~, from Latin ~succutiō~ (infinitive ~succutere~), according to the two Wiktionaries. The Latin verb is generally analysed as ~sub-~ (“under”) + ~quatere~ (“to shake”). French Wiktionary adds that the modern form was remade in preclassical French, and it cites Rabelais, in 1532.

The root ~quatere~ lies behind several other French words, all learned formations: ~concussion~, ~percussion~, ~percuter~ and ~discuter~. English ~concussion~, ~percussion~ and ~discuss~ are related. Among them ~discuter~ is the most surprising, since it descends from a Latin compound of ~quatere~ rather than from any word for talking. Do not confuse ~secouer~ with ~secourir~ (“to help”), which has a different Latin source, ~succurrere~.
en.secourir:
~Secourir~ comes from Latin ~succurrere~, a compound of ~sub~ (“under”) and ~currere~ (“to run”), so literally “to run up from underneath,” that is, to hurry to someone's aid. Old French had the forms ~sucurre~ and ~secorre~, but the verb was later remade on the model of ~courir~, giving Middle French ~secourir~. Italian ~soccorrere~ and Spanish ~socorrer~ are cousins of the same Latin verb, and English has the related ~succor~. The French verb thus has a mixed history: the Latin shape was reworked on a common French verb.

The image behind ~secourir~ is vivid: help is given by someone who runs toward you. The remaking after ~courir~ explains why the French verb is conjugated like it (~je secours~, ~nous secourons~, ~il secourut~), unlike the Latin model. The noun ~secours~ (“help, rescue”) is the verb's close relative, found in ~premiers secours~, ~au secours!~ and ~roue de secours~. The Latin root ~currere~ also lives on in ~courir~, ~courrier~, ~cours~, ~concourir~, ~parcourir~ and ~discourir~, so a rescue, a race and a river's course are, etymologically, all runs.
en.secréter: ~Secréter~ is a technical verb of the hat trade, meaning to felt fur by treating it with mercury. French Wiktionary gives two accounts. One derives it from ~secret~, because hatters kept the process secret. The other makes it a verb formed from ~sécrétion~ with the suffix ~-er~, the noun coming from Latin ~secretio~ (“separation”). The sources do not say which account is right.
en.sectionner: The verb is formed from ~section~ and the ending ~-er~, with the sense “to divide into sections” or “to cut off.” The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin ~sectiō~ (“a cutting”), a derivative of the verb ~secāre~ (“to cut”). So the whole family rests on the idea of cutting. The same Latin verb gives French ~scier~ (“to saw”), ~insecte~ and ~secteur~, and English ~secant~.
en.sectoriser: ~Sectoriser~ is formed from ~secteur~ with the suffix ~-iser~, which makes verbs meaning to turn something into or divide it by the base, so the verb means to divide into sectors. The noun ~secteur~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~sector~ (“one who cuts”). The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and it is fully productive in administrative and technical French.
en.segmenter: ~Segmenter~ is a denominal verb formed from ~segment~ with the suffix ~-er~, and means to divide into segments. The noun ~segment~ is a borrowing from Latin ~segmentum~ (“cut, incision”), derived from the verb ~secare~ (“to cut”). The same Latin root gives French ~section~, ~secteur~ and ~scier~, along with English ~sect~ and ~insect~, the last an animal “cut into” sections. The verb is used for slicing a market, a text or an audience into parts.
en.seller: Formed in French from the noun ~selle~ (“saddle”) with the verb ending ~-er~: to ~seller~ is to put a saddle on a horse. French Wiktionary nonetheless flags the verb's origin as uncertain. The noun comes from Latin ~sella~ (“seat”), via Old French ~sele~, from Proto-Italic *~sedlā~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~sed-~ (“to sit”). Spanish ~silla~ is a cousin, and so is English ~sit~, from the same root.
en.sembler:
From Old French ~sembler~ (“to seem, resemble”), from Latin ~similāre~ / ~simulāre~ (“to make like, imitate, resemble”), from the adjective ~similis~ (“like, similar”), from Proto-Italic *~semalis~, from PIE *~sem-~ (“one, together, as one”). Cognate with Catalan ~semblar~ and Italian ~sembrare~; through ~similis~ and the same root *~sem-~, English has ~similar~, ~assemble~, ~resemble~, and ~simultaneous~.

The semantic core is likeness: to ~sembler~ is, at bottom, to present an appearance like something — hence “to seem.” The root *~sem-~ (“one”) ties this whole family to the idea of oneness and togetherness, which is why ~ensemble~ (“together,” from ~in~ + ~simul~, “at once”) is a cousin of ~sembler~. French also kept ~semblable~ (“similar; a fellow human being”), ~semblant~ (as in ~faire semblant~, “to pretend,” literally “to make a seeming”), and ~ressembler~ (“to resemble”). The borrowed doublet ~simuler~ (“to simulate, feign”) preserves the Latin form more transparently. So the gulf between merely seeming, genuinely resembling, and deliberately pretending all unfolds from a single Latin verb meaning to make one thing like another.
en.semer:
~Semer~ has hardly changed since the early twelfth century: Old French ~semer~, from Latin ~sēmināre~ (“to sow, to beget”), a verb drawn from ~sēmen~, “seed” — at root “the thing sown,” from Proto-Indo-European *~séh₁mn̥~, on the root *~seh₁-~ (“to sow”). Classical Latin’s everyday verb for sowing was ~serere~, from the same root; the Romance languages preferred the fuller derivative, whence Italian ~seminare~ and Spanish ~sembrar~ beside the French verb. The root crossed into Germanic as well, giving English ~sow~ and ~seed~ and German ~säen~ and ~Saat~: field by field, the same prehistoric formula.

From the furrow the verb scattered everywhere. Already in the twelfth century French could be ~semé de~ — “strewn with” — stars or flowers; one came to sow rumors, discord, panic. In 1867 city slang added the most modern sense: ~semer quelqu'un~, “to shake off a pursuer” — to drop them behind you like scattered grain. The family is broad: ~semence~, ~semis~, ~semailles~, ~parsemer~, ~disséminer~ (“to scatter like seed”), learned ~séminal~ — and ~séminaire~, from Latin ~sēminārium~, “seed-bed, nursery”: a seminary, and later every academic seminar, is etymologically a plot where young minds are raised like seedlings. Even ~saison~ belongs here: it continues Latin ~satiō~, “sowing,” the season of sowing par excellence, from the same root — and through Old French it produced English ~season~. When a driver sème the police in traffic, the metaphor has come a long way from the fields of Philippe de Thaon.
en.semoncer: Formed from the noun ~semonce~ with the suffix ~-er~: to ~semoncer~ is to give someone a ~semonce~, that is, to scold or reprimand them. The noun comes from Old French ~semonse~, the feminine past participle of ~semondre~ (“to exhort, to summon, to warn”) used as a noun. English ~summons~ is a cognate, from the same Old French verb. The sense thus moved from a formal summons or warning to a verbal rebuke, and the old verb ~semondre~ itself is now only a literary survivor.
en.sensibiliser:
A modern derivative of French ~sensible~ (“sensitive, perceptible”) with the suffix ~-iser~. ~sensible~ comes from Latin ~sēnsibilis~, from ~sēnsus~ (“sensation, feeling”), the past participle of ~sentīre~ (“to feel, perceive”). ~sentīre~ traces to Proto-Italic *~sentiō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~sent-~ (“to head for, go; to sense”) — a root in which finding one's way and feeling one's way are the same gesture. The Latin verb survives directly as French ~sentir~, Italian ~sentire~, and Spanish ~sentir~.

~sensibiliser~ is young and technical: it first meant “to make a photographic plate sensitive to light,” then spread to medicine (to sensitize an organism) and finally to its now-dominant social sense, “to raise awareness.” From the same ~sentīre~ root flows an enormous family: French ~sentiment~, ~sens~, ~sentinelle~, ~consentir~, ~ressentir~; English ~sense~, ~sentiment~, ~consent~, and even ~scent~ (a hound following a ~scent~ is, etymologically, feeling its way). German ~Sinn~ (“sense, mind”) belongs to the same Indo-European stock.
en.sentir:
From Latin ~sentīre~ (“to perceive, feel, be of an opinion”), which traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~sent-~ — whose oldest sense was not “to feel” but “to head for, to go.” That same root surfaces, through Germanic, in German ~Sinn~ (“sense, mind”) and the verb ~sinnen~ (“to ponder”), and in Old English ~sīþ~ (“journey, way”). Romance kin are everywhere: Italian ~sentire~, Spanish and Portuguese ~sentir~, all alive and common.

The semantic leap is the memorable part. If the root first meant “to go,” then “to find one’s way,” the step to “to perceive, to sense” looks like a mind going mentally toward something — an act of mental travel that lands on a perception. From that core, French ~sentir~ branched in two directions at once: outward, to the body’s senses (to ~sentir~ a perfume, to smell), and inward, to feeling and intuition (to ~sentir~ that something is wrong). The reflexive ~se sentir~ reports one’s own state (“to feel well”). The same ~sentīre~ and its participle ~sēnsus~ gave French a rich crop: ~sens~, ~sentiment~, ~sensible~, ~sensation~, ~consentir~ (“to feel together, agree”), ~ressentir~, ~pressentir~ (“to have a foreboding”), and the borrowed-back English ~sentiment~ and ~resent~.
en.seoir:
From Old French ~seoir~, earlier ~sedeir~, inherited from Latin ~sedēre~ (“to sit”), from Proto-Italic *~sedēō~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~sed-~ (“to sit”). The Latin verb has relatives across the family: Italian ~sedere~, and, from the same root through Germanic, English ~sit~ and German ~sitzen~. The intervocalic ~-d-~ of ~sedēre~ was lost on the way to French, which is how ~sedeir~ became ~seoir~, with the two vowels left side by side.

In Old French ~seoir~ meant “to sit” and “to be situated”, and today it also serves for “to suit, to be fitting”. Rivals took over the literal senses, ~asseoir~ and ~s'asseoir~ for the act of sitting, so ~seoir~ shrank to a defective verb found almost only in the third person: ~il sied~, ~cela vous sied~, and the participle ~séant~, as in ~bienséant~ (“seemly”). The root *~sed-~ lives on in many French words, among them ~siège~, ~séance~, ~session~, ~sédentaire~ and ~président~.
en.septupler: Littré derives ~septupler~ from the adjective ~septuple~ (“sevenfold”), with the verbal ending ~-er~. ~Septuple~ is a learned word built on Latin ~septem~ (“seven”), on the model of ~double~ and ~triple~. The verb means “to multiply by seven” (~septupler ses bénéfices~, in the Académie's example), and it is also used intransitively, of something that becomes seven times larger, as in a population that has ~septuplé~ in ten years. The Académie labels the transitive use rare.
en.serfouir:
From Old French ~cerfoir~, from Latin ~circumfodere~ (“to dig around”). The Latin verb joins ~circum~ (“around”) and ~fodere~ (“to dig”). The initial ~s-~ of the modern form is a spelling that grew out of the old ~c-~, which was pronounced like it. The word was thus a clear picture in Latin: to dig around something, such as a plant.

In French it names the gardener's job of loosening the soil around plants with a hoe, so as to clear weeds and let air and water reach the roots. The second half of the compound survives in several French words: ~fouir~ (“to dig”) comes from ~fodere~, as do ~fosse~ (“pit”) and ~fossé~ (“ditch”), from the Latin noun ~fossa~. English ~fossil~ also derives from this root, since a fossil is something “dug up.” ~Serfouir~ remains a gardening verb, little used outside that world.
en.seriner: Formed in French from ~serin~ (“canary”) and the verbal ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary says the verb “would come from” the bird, which sings intensively and with a high, slightly metallic voice. This explains the figurative sense of repeating something to someone over and over, to drum it in. The origin of the bird's name is itself disputed. French Wiktionary derives ~serin~ from Latin ~Siren~, from the Greek sirens, as the bird's song was compared to theirs. English Wiktionary instead gives Old Italian ~serino~, from Latin ~serinus~, probably from ~citrinus~ (“lemon-colored”).
en.sermonner: From Old French ~sermoner~ (also ~sermuner~), which was already formed from the noun ~sermon~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so it can be read as ~sermon~ + ~-er~ even though it was inherited rather than coined in modern French. The noun ~sermon~ comes from Old French ~sermon~, from Latin ~sermō~ (accusative ~sermōnem~), “speech, discourse.” The verb first meant to preach a sermon. It then shifted to its everyday sense: to lecture someone, to scold at tiresome length, as a parent might do. The humble Latin word for conversation thus ended up naming one of its most one-sided forms.
en.serpenter: Formed from ~serpent~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, in the sense “to behave like a snake”. The noun ~serpent~ comes through Old and Middle French from Latin ~serpēns~, the present participle of ~serpō~ (“to creep, to crawl”), so the snake is literally “the creeping one”. The verb is applied to things that follow a winding course, such as a river, a road or a line of people.
en.serrer:
From Old French ~serrer~ (“to close, lock fast”; Chrétien de Troyes, around 1180, writes of a door ~serré~), from Late Latin ~serāre~ (“to close with a bar”), from Latin ~sera~ (“a bar, bolt, or lock for a door”). The instrument-noun ~sera~ is usually tied, though with some hesitation in the sources, to the verb ~serere~ (“to join, link, plait together”). Italian ~serrare~ is the cognate Romance verb; the same ~sera~ underlies French ~serrure~ (“a lock”).

The development runs outward from the bolted door. To bar a door is to make it tight and fast, and ~serrer~ slid from “to lock” to “to hold firmly” — a raptor's talons that ~serrent~ their prey — and then to “to press close together,” so that one ~serre~ la main (squeezes a hand), ~serre~ les rangs (closes ranks), or ~serre~ les dents (clenches the teeth). The original locking sense is preserved most plainly in the noun ~serrure~ and the trade of the ~serrurier~ (“locksmith”). The verb's two prefixed kin, ~desserrer~ (“to loosen”) and ~resserrer~ (“to tighten again”), trace the same motion of bars drawn open and shut.
en.sertir: Both Wiktionaries give only one step for ~sertir~: it comes from Old French ~sartir~. The sources supply nothing further back, so no Latin source is claimed here. In modern French the verb is best known for setting a gem in its mount, and it also has the wider sense of crimping, that is, gripping something by folding metal around it.
en.servir:
From Latin ~servire~ (“to serve, to be a slave, to live in servitude”), a verb derived from ~servus~ (“slave, servant”). The deeper origin of ~servus~ is uncertain — some link it cautiously to a Proto-Indo-European root *~ser-~ (“to guard, watch over”), on the idea of the slave who keeps the household, while others suspect a pre-Latin, perhaps Etruscan, source — so the chain below the Latin level is best left open. The verb survives almost unchanged across Romance: Italian ~servire~, Spanish ~servir~, and French ~servir~, and English ~serve~ was borrowed from Old French.

The semantic spread of ~servir~ is unusually wide because it kept the full Latin range. From the bondage of the slave it climbed to honourable senses — to wait at table, to be of use, to render service — and even to the abstract “to serve a purpose.” The same root threw off a dense family in French: ~serviteur~ and ~servante~ for the people, ~service~ and ~serviette~ for the acts and objects (a ~serviette~ being literally what a servant brings), ~servile~ and ~servitude~ for the condition, and ~asservir~, ~desservir~, ~resservir~ among the compounds. Few words travel so far from slavery to a napkin.
en.sevrer:
From Old French ~sevrer~, inherited from Vulgar Latin *~sēperāre~, a variant form of Latin ~sēparāre~ (“to separate”). The Latin verb is generally analysed as ~sē-~ (“apart”) plus ~parāre~ (“to prepare, to arrange”), so “to set apart.” Modern French has both forms of the same word: ~sevrer~, which was inherited and worn down by centuries of speech, and ~séparer~, a later learned borrowing straight from Latin. Such pairs are called doublets.

The inherited verb narrowed to one very human act: separating a child from the mother's milk, hence “to wean.” That sense then widened into the figurative “to deprive of something one is used to,” as in ~sevrer quelqu'un de tabac~ or ~être sevré de liberté~. English ~sever~ is generally traced to the same Old French verb, with the general sense of cutting apart that ~sevrer~ once had alongside weaning. The family includes ~séparer~, ~séparation~, ~sevrage~ and ~parer~.
en.sextupler: Formed from the adjective ~sextuple~ with the verb suffix ~-er~: to multiply by six, or to become six times greater. The adjective is a learned formation built on the Latin numeral ~sex~ (“six”). The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is the default way to coin a verb in French.
en.sexualiser: ~Sexualiser~ is formed from the adjective ~sexuel~ with the suffix ~-iser~, and means to give a sexual character to something. ~Sexuel~ is a learned borrowing from Late Latin ~sexualis~. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs.
en.shampooiner: ~Shampooiner~ is formed from the noun ~shampooing~ with the verbal ending ~-er~; an earlier form ~shampooinguer~ is attested in 1894. The noun ~shampooing~ is a pseudo-anglicism taken from English ~shampoo~ with ~-ing~, and ~shampoo~ itself was borrowed under British colonial rule from Hindi ~champo~, the imperative of ~champana~ (“to press, to massage”). A word for massaging thus became the French name for washing hair.
en.shampouiner: ~Shampouiner~ is a denominal verb: ~shampooing~ plus the ending ~-er~, first attested in 1894 in the spelling ~shampooinguer~. The noun ~shampooing~ is a French pseudo-anglicism, built from English ~shampoo~ with the suffix ~-ing~. English ~shampoo~ itself was borrowed during British colonial rule from Hindi ~champo~, the imperative of ~champana~ (“to press, to massage”), so the word began as an instruction to massage.
en.shooter: Formed in French from the English verb ~shoot~ plus the French verb ending ~-er~, which fits borrowed English verbs into the first conjugation. English Wiktionary dates it to 1900. In French it is used in football for taking a shot at goal, and in slang for injecting a drug.
en.sidérer:
French ~sidérer~ is traced by French Wiktionary to Latin ~siderari~ (“to suffer the baleful influence of the stars”), a verb formed on Latin ~sidus~ (“star”). English Wiktionary gives a different route and treats it as a back-formation from ~sidéré~, the participial adjective meaning “stunned.” The two accounts differ in emphasis rather than clearly contradicting each other, but the sources do not say how they fit together.

The Latin sense is literally “star-struck” in a harmful way, struck by the stars' malign power. Modern French uses the verb, and especially the participle ~sidéré~, for stunning or dumbfounding someone. The noun ~sidus~ also lies behind ~sidéral~ (“of the stars”), and English ~sidereal~ comes from the same Latin family. The sources do not narrate the passage from the old astrological sense to the modern one, so it is not described here.
en.siffler:
From Old French ~sifler~, from Vulgar Latin *~sīfilāre~, which is probably a regional variant of Latin ~sībilāre~, perhaps shaped by Osco-Umbrian speech. Related forms elsewhere in the Romance world support this: Spanish ~chiflar~ and Friulian ~sivilâ~ look like the same word. Northern Old French and its dialects show other variants. A form ~sufler~ (whence Norman and Walloon forms) points to a Vulgar Latin *~sufilāre~, matched by Italian ~zufolare~, and a form ~subler~ points to *~subilāre~, matched by Italian ~sobillare~ and Romanian ~șuiera~. So the verb sits in a family of closely related variants, and the sources do not settle which one gave the standard French form.

The doubled ~f~ of modern ~siffler~ is a later spelling effect: in the sixteenth century the verb came to be written with two ~f~ by association with ~souffler~ (“to blow”). Earlier French attestations show a single ~f~ in ~sifler~, the twelfth-century phrase ~cerpent cifle~, and the variants ~chifler~ and, in the thirteenth century, ~sible~. The regional forms listed above reach further. In areas bordering Franco-Provençal dialects the form ~sibler~ is found, and Occitan ~siblar~ and ~siular~ and Catalan ~xiular~ parallel it. Taken together they show a word with many regional shapes, which is why its Latin source is stated with a hedge.
en.siffloter: Formed from ~siffler~ (“to whistle”) with the diminutive and frequentative suffix ~-oter~, so it means to whistle softly or absently, in little bursts. The base ~siffler~ comes from Old French ~sifler~, from Vulgar Latin *~sīfilāre~, probably a regional variant of Latin ~sībilāre~. The sources do not settle which of several closely related variants gave the standard French form. The doubled ~f~ appeared in the sixteenth century, by association with ~souffler~ (“to blow”).
en.signaler:
From the noun ~signal~ (attested 1572 as a verb), itself from Late Latin ~signalis~ (“serving as a sign”), an adjective derived from Latin ~signum~ (“mark, sign, military standard, signal”). ~Signum~ may go back, by one influential account, to the Proto-Indo-European root *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”) — a standard being literally that which one follows into battle — though some scholars instead connect it to a root meaning “to cut” (a mark cut into something). Cognate with Italian ~segnalare~ and Spanish ~señalar~, and with English ~signal~.

French borrowed ~signaler~ partly under the influence of Italian ~segnalare~, and its earliest sense was “to distinguish oneself, to make oneself notable” — to set oneself apart by some conspicuous mark. From this came the reflexive ~se signaler~ (“to distinguish oneself”) before the verb settled into its modern, more neutral senses of pointing out, notifying, or flagging. The root ~signum~ is extraordinarily prolific in French: ~signe~, ~signal~, ~signature~, ~désigner~, ~insigne~, ~enseigne~, and ~enseigner~ all spring from it, as do English ~ensign~, ~sign~, and ~insignia~. A ~signal~ and a teacher's lesson, etymologically, are the same gesture of marking something out for attention.
en.signaliser: Formed from ~signal~ with the suffix ~-iser~: to equip with signs or signals. The base ~signal~ is a re-Latinization of Old French ~segnal~, from Medieval Latin ~signale~, from Late Latin ~signālis~, from Latin ~signum~ (“sign, mark”). French ~signe~ descends from the same Latin ~signum~, so the verb sits in a family of marks and signals that all lead back to that one word.
en.signer:
From Latin ~signare~ (“to mark with a sign, to seal, to point out, to distinguish”), derived from ~signum~ (“sign, mark, token, military standard”). ~Signum~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~seknom~ to a Proto-Indo-European root that is genuinely disputed — either *~sek-~ (“to cut,” a sign being a notch or incision) or *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow,” a sign being something one follows); scholars have not settled which, and it is honest to leave the question open. Italian ~segnare~, Spanish ~señar~, and the borrowed English ~sign~ all share the source.

The Latin verb already covered a wide field — to mark, to seal, to signal — and French ~signer~ narrowed onto the most consequential mark of all: the signature, the personal token by which one binds oneself to a document. Religious French kept the older gesture in ~se signer~, “to make the sign of the cross.” The family is large: ~signe~, ~signal~, ~signature~, ~signataire~, ~contresigner~, ~désigner~, ~assigner~, ~résigner~, and the learned ~insigne~. Even ~enseigner~ (“to teach”) and ~enseigne~ (“sign, shop-sign”) belong here, from Latin ~insignire~, “to mark out” — for to teach was once, literally, to point out and make plain.
en.signifier:
From Latin ~significāre~ (“to make a sign, to indicate, to mean”), a compound of ~signum~ (“sign, mark, token”) and ~facere~ (“to make, to do”) — so that to signify is literally “to make a sign.” Latin ~signum~ is generally derived from the Proto-Indo-European root *~sek-~ (“to cut”), through Proto-Italic ~seknom~, the original sign being a cut or incised mark, though some link it instead to *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”). Italian ~significare~ and Spanish ~significar~ continue the verb unchanged; English ~signify~ comes through Old French ~signifier~.

The drift from the concrete to the abstract is the whole story: a ~signum~ began as a physical mark — a notch, a military standard, a seal pressed in wax — and ~significāre~ meant making such a mark visible. From “to indicate by a sign” the verb glided easily into “to mean,” which is the dominant sense of ~signifier~ today, alongside a precise legal use, “to notify formally” (signifier un congé). The root spreads through a large French family — ~signe~, ~signal~, ~signaler~, ~signature~, ~signer~, ~désigner~, ~insigne~, ~assigner~, and the learned ~signifiant~ and ~signifié~ of linguistics. The neat detail is that a word now wholly about meaning carries, deep down, the image of a blade cutting a mark into wood or stone.
en.silhouetter: Formed in French from ~silhouette~ + the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, “to outline, to render as a silhouette.” The noun comes from the surname of Étienne de Silhouette (1709–1767), France's Controller-General of Finances. Why his name stuck is only proposed: his penny-pinching policies, his brief eight-month tenure in 1759, or the outline portraits he made are all suggested. His surname is a French form of Basque ~Ziloeta~, from ~zulo~ (“hole, pit”). French Wiktionary says the common noun was recognized by the Académie in 1835.
en.siliconer: ~Siliconer~ is a denominal verb: the noun ~silicone~ plus the first-conjugation ending ~-er~, which turns a noun into a verb meaning “to provide with N.” The noun comes from German ~Silikon~, a word created by the chemist Friedrich Wöhler and built on ~silicium~ with the suffix ~-one~. The verb therefore means “to coat or fill with silicone,” and in everyday speech it is used in particular for getting silicone breast implants.
en.sillonner: Formed in French from ~sillon~ (“furrow”) and the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, so to ~sillonner~ is first to mark with furrows. The noun ~sillon~ comes from Old French ~seillon~. French Wiktionary links it to the verb ~siller~ (“to trace a line”) and to ~sillage~, the wake behind a ship, while English Wiktionary analyses ~seillon~ as ~seille~ + ~-on~. The verb then widened from ploughed lines to any lines drawn across a surface: ships ~sillonnent~ the sea, planes the sky, roads and rivers a landscape, and wrinkles a face.
en.similiser: Formed from ~simili~ and the verbal suffix ~-er~, which turns a noun into a verb. ~Simili~ comes from Latin ~similis~ (“like, resembling, the same”), the same source as ~similaire~. The verb is a technical term, glossed as giving cotton a silky sheen.
en.simplifier:
French ~simplifier~ formally derives from ~simple~ with the suffix ~-ifier~ (“to make”), modelled on Medieval Latin ~simplificāre~. ~Simple~ comes from Latin ~simplus~ / ~simplex~ (“single, plain”), and the ~-ifier~ ending continues Latin ~facere~ (“to make, do”). ~Simplex~ itself is ~sem-~ (“one, single”) plus ~-plex~ (“-fold”): the first element from Proto-Indo-European *~sem-~ (“one, together”), the second from *~pleḱ-~ (“to weave, fold”). Through those roots ~simple~ is cognate with English ~single~ and ~simple~, and ~-plex~ with English ~plait~, ~ply~, and ~fold~.

So to ~simplifier~ is, etymologically, “to make one-fold” — to reduce a thing folded over on itself to a single layer. The image of folding runs quietly through a whole family: ~double~, ~triple~, ~multiple~, ~complexe~, and ~perplexe~ all carry the same ~-plex~ / ~-pli-~ element, “fold.” Modern French keeps the abstract sense, “to make less complicated,” and built the noun ~simplification~ and intensives like ~ultrasimplifier~ — the latter a quietly ironic word, since over-simplifying rarely makes anything truly single.
en.simuler:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~simulāre~ (“to imitate, to pretend”), a verb built on the adjective ~similis~ (“like, similar”). Latin ~simulāre~ had already reached French once by the popular road, as Old French ~sembler~, so ~simuler~ and ~sembler~ are doublets: one Latin verb that entered the language twice, at different dates and in different shapes. English ~simulate~ is a borrowing of the same Latin verb and English ~similar~ of the adjective behind it, while Italian ~simulare~ and Spanish ~simular~ are its sister learned forms.

The two French descendants then divided the meaning between them. The inherited ~sembler~ drifted from “to look like” to “to seem”, and its participle gave ~semblant~, as in ~faire semblant~ (“to pretend”). The learned ~simuler~ kept the Latin sense of deliberately imitating or feigning, and later added the technical sense of reproducing a process by a model, whence ~simulation~ and ~simulateur~. In sport, especially football, it covers the player who feigns a foul to win a free kick, the “dive” of English. Its mirror image is ~dissimuler~ (“to conceal”), from Latin ~dissimulāre~: to simulate is to pretend to be what one is not, to dissimulate is to hide what one is. The family also includes ~ressembler~ (“to resemble”) and ~simulacre~.
en.singer: The verb ~singer~ has two senses with two accounts. The sense “to ape” is formed from ~singe~ (“monkey”) and the ending ~-er~, and ~singe~ is inherited from Latin ~sīmius~. French Wiktionary derives the cooking sense, to sprinkle with flour, from the same noun, explaining it by a preparation that originally used a caramel imitating the roux. The sources give no further link between the monkey and the flour.
en.singulariser: Formed from the adjective ~singulier~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-iser~, which gives the sense “to make A,” here “to make singular, to set apart.” ~Singulier~ is borrowed from Latin ~singulāris~ (“unique, special”). It is a doublet of ~sanglier~, which comes from the same Latin word through a longer, inherited route. The suffix ~-iser~ descends from Late Latin ~-izāre~, itself taken from Greek verbs.
en.siniser: ~Siniser~ is a modern coinage meaning to make Chinese in culture or character. It is formed with the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make, to convert”) either on the Latin name ~Sīnae~ (“China”) or on the combining form ~sino-~ taken from it. It is not related in sense to ~chinoiser~, which has a quite different meaning.
en.sinuer: From Latin ~sinuāre~ (“to bend, to curve”), a verb formed on ~sinus~ (“curve, fold”). French took it from Latin, and ~sinuer~ means to wind or to turn frequently, as a path or a river does. The root ~sinus~ has a sizable family in French. ~Sinueux~ (“winding”) and ~sinuosité~ describe the curves, ~sinus~ is the anatomical cavity, and ~insinuer~ comes from Latin ~insinuāre~ (“to make one's way into the curves”), whence the figurative sense of slipping an idea in. English ~sinuous~ and ~insinuate~ are cousins from the same Latin words.
en.siphonner: Formed from ~siphon~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~ (from Latin ~-are~), meaning to draw off a liquid with a siphon. The noun first meant a tube for drawing wine. It comes from Latin ~sipho~ (“pipe”), itself from Greek ~σίφων~ (“hollow tube, siphon”), a word of unknown ultimate origin.
en.siroter: Formed from ~sirop~ (“syrup”) and the verb ending ~-er~: to ~siroter~ is to sip. The noun comes from Old French ~sirop~, borrowed from Medieval Latin ~siroppus~, from Arabic ~šarāb~ (“beverage”), from ~šariba~ (“to drink”). French Wiktionary links the word with ~sorbet~, which has the same Arabic root. So a drink word became a word for drinking slowly.
en.situer:
French ~situer~ is a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ~situāre~ (“to place in a location, to establish, to assign”), a verb built from the noun ~situs~ (“position, site, location”). That noun is the past participle of the Latin verb ~sinere~ (“to let, to allow, to set down, to leave in place”) — so a ~situs~ is, etymologically, a thing that has been let stand where it is. The same ~situs~ gives English ~site~ and ~situate~, and the legal term ~situs~ survives untouched in English for the place where something legally belongs.

Unlike the battered everyday verbs of French, ~situer~ entered late and bookish, keeping the clean shape of its Latin model. Its meaning has stayed close to the source: to fix a thing in space, and figuratively to place it in a context — ~situer un événement~ (“to date or place an event”), ~se situer~ (“to be located, to position oneself”). The family that grew around it is modern and tidy: ~situation~ (“situation, location, post”), ~situé~ (“located”), ~resituer~ (“to re-place, to put back in context”), and the adjective ~situable~. From a verb of simply letting something stay put, French built its whole vocabulary of placement and circumstance.
en.siéger:
From the noun ~siège~ (“seat, see, siege”) plus the verb-forming suffix ~-er~. ~Siège~ descends through Vulgar Latin *~sedicum~ from Latin ~sēdēs~ (“seat”) and the family of ~sedēre~ (“to sit”), from Proto-Italic *~sedēō~, from PIE *~sed-~ (“to sit”). This is one of the most widespread of all Indo-European roots: it gave Latin ~sedēre~, English ~sit~, ~seat~ and ~settle~, German ~sitzen~, Sanskrit ~sī́dati~, and Greek ~hézomai~ — so a senator and a sitting hen share an ancestor.

The verb keeps the literal posture only faintly; mostly it means “to hold a seat,” hence “to sit” on a council or assembly, and by extension “to be located, to have one's seat” — a court ~siège à~ Paris, a company's headquarters ~siège~ somewhere. The noun ~siège~ carries an arresting double life: from “seat” it also became the military “siege,” an army that ~sits down~ around a city until it falls (English ~siege~ borrowed this very word and sense). The root *~sed-~ pervades learned French through Latin compounds — ~résider~, ~présider~, ~posséder~, ~sédentaire~, ~séance~, ~assidu~ (one who ~sits at~ a task), and ~obséder~ (to “sit before,” to besiege the mind) — a vast progeny of a single act: sitting down.
en.skier: ~Skier~ is formed from the noun ~ski~ with the verb ending ~-er~. French borrowed ~ski~ from Norwegian ~ski~. The word first appears in French in 1841 as ~skie~, which wavered between feminine and masculine before settling on the masculine ~ski~ in 1891, and it replaced the older ~patin à neige~. Its Old Norse source, ~skíð~, meant a billet of wood or a snow shoe, and is tied to a verb meaning “to split.” That verb is cognate with Latin ~scindere~ and Greek ~skhízein~ (both “to split”).
en.slalomer: Formed from the noun ~slalom~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, meaning to weave from side to side as a skier does between gates, and by extension any zigzagging course. The noun came into French from German ~Slalom~, which took it from Norwegian ~slalåm~, a compound of ~sla~ (“slope”) and ~låm~ (“track, trail”). French Wiktionary records its first attestation in the ski manual of Wilhelm Paulcke, translated from German by F. Achard. The ending ~-er~ turns the noun into a verb of doing: ~slalomer~ is to do a slalom.
en.slaviser: Formed from ~slave~ (“Slavic”) with the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make”): ~slaviser~ is “to make Slavic.” The adjective comes through Middle French ~Sclave~ from Medieval Latin ~Sclavus~, from Byzantine Greek ~Sklábos~, and it is a doublet of ~esclave~ (“slave”). The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, itself from Greek.
en.slicer: Borrowed from English ~slice~ (“to cut, to carve”) and given the French ending ~-er~. The English verb is the base of the French one. In French the borrowing is mostly sporting: in golf and tennis, to ~slicer~ is to strike the ball so that it spins sideways and curves. The sporting sense is what the gloss “slice the ball” records.
en.smasher: ~Smasher~ is a French verb made from the English word ~smash~, the name of the overhead tennis stroke, plus the French ending ~-er~. The noun ~smash~ was borrowed from English, and the verb followed as a calque of the English verb “to smash”. To ~smasher~ is to hit a tennis ball with that crushing overhead blow.
en.smurfer: Formed from the noun ~smurf~ (“a type of breakdance”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so “to dance the smurf.” The noun is borrowed from the English ~Smurf~, the name of the blue cartoon creatures called ~Schtroumpfs~ in French. French Wiktionary says the confusion, found only in France and Germany, would come from the soundtrack of the American film, whose song ~Let’s Do the Smurf~ was shown with popping dancers. English Wiktionary dates the word to 1983.
en.snifer: ~Snifer~ is a variant spelling of ~sniffer~, with a single f. ~Sniffer~ is borrowed from English ~sniff~ (“to sniff”), with the French ending ~-er~ added so that it fits the first conjugation. In French the verb kept the sense of drawing something in through the nose and took on the informal meaning of taking a drug that way, such as cocaine or glue. The French ~renifler~ covers much of the same ground, but ~sniffer~ is the usual choice for drugs.
en.sniffer: ~Sniffer~ is borrowed from English ~sniff~ (“to sniff”), with the French verb ending ~-er~ added to make it fit the first conjugation. In French it kept the sense of drawing something in through the nose and developed the informal meaning of taking a drug that way, such as cocaine or glue. The English word and the French ~renifler~ cover much of the same ground, but ~sniffer~ is the usual choice for drugs.
en.snober: The sources differ slightly. French Wiktionary treats ~snober~ as derived from the noun ~snob~ (borrowed from English ~snob~) plus ~-er~, so to ~snober~ is to treat someone as a ~snob~ would, with disdain. English Wiktionary instead calls it a borrowing from English ~snub~ plus the French ending ~-er~, with influence from English ~snob~. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~. Both accounts agree on the sense: to slight someone, or to ignore something deliberately, as the glosses “snub” and “disregard” put it.
en.socialiser: ~Socialiser~ is formed from the adjective ~social~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which in French makes verbs meaning “to make A” or “to convert into N.” The adjective comes from Latin ~sociālis~ (“of companionship or association”), from ~socius~ (“companion, ally”). The verb thus means, literally, to make something social, whether a person who learns to live among others or an activity or property brought into common life. French Wiktionary and English Wiktionary agree on this internal formation.
en.sodomiser: Formed from ~sodomie~ + ~-iser~, a suffix meaning “to subject to N”: ~sodomiser~ is to practice sodomy upon someone. The noun ~sodomie~ was borrowed from Late Latin ~sodomia~, and it comes from ~Sodome~, the city of the Bible associated with the prophet Lot. The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~ and is fully productive in French.
en.soigner:
Of disputed origin, ~soigner~ most likely comes from Frankish *~sunnjōn~ (“to occupy oneself with, to attend to”), borrowed into Low Latin as ~soniāre~ and related to the noun ~soin~ (“care”). The Germanic source *~sunnja~ carried the idea of “need, necessity, care.” A rival hypothesis links it instead to Latin ~somniāre~ (“to dream”), which independently gave ~songer~ (“to think, to muse”); under that view, to care for someone began as thinking attentively about them. Cognate, on the Germanic side, with forms in the older Dutch and German care-words.

Whichever root is right, the meaning settled firmly: to ~soigner~ is to take care of, to look after, to treat — a patient, a garden, a wound, or one's appearance. The reflexive ~se soigner~ means to take care of oneself or to undergo treatment. The verb belongs to a tight French family built on ~soin~: ~soin~ itself (“care”), ~soigneux~ (“careful, painstaking”), ~soigneusement~ (“carefully”), and ~soignant~ (“caregiving,” as in ~le personnel soignant~, “the nursing staff”). The lingering uncertainty between a Germanic “need” and a Latin “dreaming” is itself the memorable detail: French may have built its word for nursing either on duty or on attentive thought.
en.solder: Formed from the noun ~solde~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun has Italian roots, and its sources describe two strands that influenced each other: ~soldo~ (a soldier's pay), from Latin ~soldus~, a contracted form of ~solidus~ (“solid”) and so a doublet of ~sou~ and ~solide~, and ~saldo~ (the balance of an account), from the Italian verb ~saldare~. The verb thus has an accounting sense: to ~solder~ a bill is to settle it so that nothing remains owing.
en.solenniser: The sources differ slightly. French Wiktionary derives ~solenniser~ from the adjective ~solennel~, while English Wiktionary calls it a borrowing from Medieval Latin ~sōlemnizāre~, from Latin ~sollemnis~. The adjective ~solennel~ itself comes from Latin ~sollemnis~ (“celebrated once a year, religious, festive”), through Old French ~sollempnel~, whose ending ~-el~ was added on the pattern of words such as ~annuel~ and ~éternel~. The verb means to celebrate with solemnity, to give a ceremonial character to an event.
en.solfier:
Derived from medieval Latin ~solfa~ (“scale”), a word built in the Middle Ages from the names of two notes, ~sol~ and ~fa~, with the French suffix ~-ier~. So the verb rests on a Latin coinage that itself contains no ancient root: it is two syllables of the musical scale put side by side.

To solfier is to sing by naming the notes, ~do~, ~ré~, ~mi~ and so on, rather than the words of a piece, a training method for musicians. The same family includes ~solfège~, borrowed from Italian ~solfeggio~, and English ~sol-fa~. In all of them, a scale is named after two of its steps, as the word ~alphabet~ is named after its first two letters.
en.solidariser: Formed from the adjective ~solidaire~ with the suffix ~-iser~, so ~solidariser~ means to make people or things solidary, bound together. ~Solidaire~ is itself ~solide~ plus the suffix ~-aire~, and it is tied to the legal Latin phrase ~in solidum~ (“for the whole”), the idea of being bound jointly for the entirety. The suffix ~-iser~, from Late Latin ~-izāre~, forms verbs meaning “to make A”.
en.solidifier: ~Solidifier~ is formed from the adjective ~solide~ and the suffix ~-ifier~. ~Solide~ was borrowed from Latin ~solidus~, and it is a doublet of ~sou~, the old coin name, which descends from the same Latin word. The suffix ~-ifier~ comes from Latin ~-(i)ficāre~, which goes back to ~facere~ (“to make”), so the verb means literally “to make solid”. The suffix is still productive in learned and technical French.
en.soliloquer: Formed from the noun ~soliloque~ (“soliloquy”) with the verb ending ~-er~: to speak aloud to oneself. The noun is a learned word from Late Latin ~soliloquium~, made of ~sōlus~ (“alone”) and ~loquī~ (“to speak”), so it is literally “speaking alone.”
en.solliciter:
From Latin ~sollicitare~ (“to disturb thoroughly, stir up, agitate”), the denominal verb of the adjective ~sollicitus~ (“thoroughly moved, anxious, troubled”). That adjective is a compound of ~sollus~ (“whole, entire”) and a form related to ~ciere~ / ~citus~ (“to set in motion, rouse”). The two elements trace to PIE *~solh₂-~ (“whole”) and *~keyh₂-~ (“to set in motion”) respectively. Romance cognates include Spanish ~solicitar~ and Italian ~sollecitare~; English ~solicit~ comes from the same Latin verb.

The literal Latin picture is of something “wholly stirred up” — thoroughly shaken, hence anxious or agitated. The verb meant to disturb or rouse, and from rousing someone to act came the sense of urging, then of earnestly requesting. French keeps that progression: to ~solliciter~ is to ask for insistently (a favor, a meeting), to apply for, and, of a thing, to draw on or call upon (one's attention, a muscle). From ~sollus~ (“whole”) French also has ~solennel~ (originally a rite performed “whole,” every year), and from ~ciere~ the family of ~exciter~ and ~inciter~.
en.solubiliser: Formed from ~soluble~ + ~-iser~, a suffix meaning “to make A”: ~solubiliser~ is to make something soluble. The adjective ~soluble~ was borrowed from Late Latin ~solubilis~ (“that can be dissolved”), from the Latin verb ~solvere~ (“to loosen, dissolve”). The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, which itself transcribed Greek verbs, and it remains fully productive in technical vocabulary.
en.solutionner: ~Solutionner~ is formed from the noun ~solution~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~solution~ was inherited from Old French ~solucion~, from Latin ~solūtiō~ (“act of loosening or dissolving,” and so also “resolving a difficulty”), from the verb ~solvere~. The verb is also an example of a trend in French: irregular third-group verbs are replaced by regular first-group ones, as with ~chuter~ for ~choir~ or ~réceptionner~ for ~recevoir~.
en.somatiser: Built on the Greek word ~σῶμα~ (“body”) with the suffix ~-iser~. The verb belongs to the language of medicine and psychology, and it means to convert a psychological difficulty into physical symptoms. The same Greek word gives ~somatique~ and, in compounds, ~psychosomatique~.
en.sombrer:
The origin of ~sombrer~ (“to sink”) is disputed, and the sources give competing accounts. English Wiktionary offers one: the verb comes from Middle French ~soussombrer~, an alteration of ~soussoubrer~ with influence from the adjective ~sombre~, the first part perhaps being taken for a prefix. The word ~soussoubrer~ was probably a loan by a maritime route from Portuguese ~soçobrar~, itself likely from Spanish ~zozobrar~ (older ~sozobrar~), and that from Old Catalan ~sotsobrar~, from ~sotsobre~ (“upside down”), made of ~sots~ (“under”) and ~sobre~ (“over”). Some instead derive the Catalan from a Vulgar Latin *~subsuperāre~, from Latin ~sub~ and ~super~, but that last step is only proposed.

French Wiktionary lists the Iberian account together with two others. One treats ~sombrer~ simply as a denominal verb from ~sombre~. The other presents an Old French verb ~sombrer~ or ~somarer~ (“to plough fallow land for the first time”), from ~sombre~ and ~somart~ (“the season of the first ploughing”), which it links to German ~Sommer~ (“summer”) and to Gaulish *~samo-~ (“summer”), the first ploughing being done on the first fine days. These accounts compete, and the evidence does not settle which is right. Only the Iberian account is given by English Wiktionary. Only the modern sense is secure, that of sinking, whence one can ~sombrer~ into despair or oblivion.
en.sommeiller: ~Sommeiller~ comes from Middle French, itself from Old French ~sumeillier~, according to French Wiktionary. Synchronically it can be read as ~sommeil~ (“sleep”) + ~-er~, which is how English Wiktionary presents it. English Wiktionary also cites Vulgar Latin *~somniculāre~, “whence also” Italian ~sonnecchiare~, as a related form.
en.sommer:
A denominal verb built on the noun ~somme~ with the suffix ~-er~. The relevant ~somme~ descends from Latin ~summa~ (“the highest thing, the total, the sum”), the feminine of ~summus~ (“highest, topmost”), itself a superlative of ~superus~ (“upper”) and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~upo~ (“up, under”). Cognate nouns survive everywhere: Italian ~somma~, Spanish ~suma~, German ~Summe~, and English ~sum~, ~summary~, and ~summit~.

The two modern senses of ~sommer~ — “to sum up” and “to summon, to call upon” — both spring from ~summa~, by different routes. Roman accountants wrote the running total at the top of a column, the ~summa~ or highest line; to sum was to reach that crowning figure, which gives the arithmetic verb. The other sense passed through the medieval idea of a final, conclusive demand — the upshot of an argument pressed on someone — attested at Douai around 1250 as “to put under obligation, to enjoin,” which is why ~sommer~ today means to formally order someone to act. The same family gives French ~somme~ (“sum”), ~sommet~ (“summit”), ~sommaire~, ~consommer~, and ~suprême~, all reaching, in their way, for the top.
en.somnoler: Formed from the adjective ~somnolent~ (“drowsy”) with the verbal ending ~-er~; English Wiktionary calls it a back-formation, since the adjective came first. ~Somnolent~ comes from Latin ~somnolentus~, by way of Old French ~sompnolent~, and Latin ~somnolentus~ belongs to ~somnus~ (“sleep”). The verb means “to doze” or “to slumber”.
en.sonder:
~Sonder~ is usually explained as formed with the ending ~-er~ on ~sonde~ (“sounding line”), and it appears in Old French as ~sonder~ (“to plumb”). The noun ~sonde~ is probably of Old English origin. It comes from ~sund-~ in compounds such as ~sundġierd~ (“sounding rod”), ~sundlīne~ (“sounding line”) and ~sundrāp~ (“sounding rope”), where the first element, Old English ~sund~ (“sea, water”), came to stand for the whole tool. That word descends from Proto-Germanic *~sundą~ (“a swim, a body of water”), itself from a Proto-Indo-European root *~swem(bʰ)-~ (“to be unsteady, to swim”). Old Norse ~sund~ (“swimming, strait”) is a cognate, and English ~sound~, in the sense of a narrow arm of the sea, belongs to the same family.

French Wiktionary mentions a rival idea, that the verb comes instead from Latin ~subundāre~ (“to plunge”), but it adds that an Old French derivative is not demonstrated, so the origin of the verb is not fully settled. Either way, the meaning is clear: ~sonder~ began as the sailor's act of measuring depth by lowering a weighted line. From the sea it spread to figurative probing, as in sounding out the ground or people's feelings, and to science and medicine, where a ~sonde~ is any instrument pushed into a cavity or sent into the sky. A ~sondage~ is a poll or a survey, and ~insondable~ describes what cannot be fathomed.
en.songer:
From Latin ~somniāre~ (“to dream”), a verb formed on ~somnium~ (“a dream”), itself related to ~somnus~ (“sleep”). ~Somnus~ comes from Proto-Italic *~swepnos~ and PIE *~swépnos~ (“sleep, dream”), from the root *~swep-~ (“to sleep”) — a root with far-flung cousins: Sanskrit ~svápna~ (“sleep, dream”), Lithuanian ~sãpnas~, and, through Germanic, English ~sweven~ (an archaic word for “a dream”). Cognate Romance descendants of ~somniāre~ include Italian ~sognare~, Spanish ~soñar~, and Portuguese ~sonhar~.

The Latin verb meant literally “to dream in one's sleep,” and Old French ~songier~ kept that sense — a ~songe~ is still a dream, especially a portentous one. But French quietly shifted the everyday verb toward waking thought: to ~songer~ is now mostly “to muse, to ponder, to give thought to” (~songer à l'avenir~, “to think about the future”), the sleeping dream having drifted into reverie and reflection. Spanish ~soñar~ kept the literal “to dream,” which makes the French semantic drift the more striking. The root *~swep-~ surfaces elsewhere in French through Latin ~somnus~: ~sommeil~ (“sleep,” the inherited form), ~somnolent~, ~insomnie~, and ~somnifère~ — while ~songe~, ~songer~, and ~songerie~ trace the same root down its dreaming branch.
en.sonnailler: ~Sonnailler~ is formed from ~sonner~ (“to ring, to sound”) with the pejorative suffix ~-ailler~, and French Wiktionary dates the verb to 1748. Its main sense is informal: to ring often and to no purpose. A second sense is to make herd bells ring while tending livestock. The verb sits beside the older noun ~sonnaille~ (a bell hung on an animal), attested in 1379, and the masculine noun ~sonnailler~ names the animal that wears such a bell and leads a flock or herd.
en.sonner:
From Latin ~sonare~ (« to sound, to resound »), attested in French from the tenth century. ~sonare~ comes from Proto-Italic *~swonaō~ and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~swenh₂-~ (« to sound »). Through that root it is cognate with English ~sound~ and Sanskrit ~svanati~ (« it sounds, resounds »); Proto-Slavic *~zvoniti~ (« to ring ») belongs to the same family.

The core meaning has stayed remarkably steady — to make or give out a sound, especially of bells, clocks, and horns. Around it French grew a wealth of idiom: a clock « strikes » the hour, one « rings » at a door, a boxer's blow « ~sonne~ » its target (« stuns » him), and ~ne pas sonner mot~ means « not to say a word ». From the same root come the nouns ~son~ (« sound ») and ~sonnerie~ (« ringing, ringtone »), the borrowed ~sonnet~ (« little sound, little song »), and learned forms like ~sonore~ and ~résonner~, all still ringing with Latin ~sonare~.
en.sonoriser: The verb is formed from the adjective ~sonore~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which turns an adjective into a verb meaning “to make A.” Hence ~sonoriser~ means to make something ~sonore~, that is, to give it sound, as in voicing a film or fitting out a hall with a sound system. The adjective is borrowed from Latin ~sonōrus~ (“resounding”), a derivative of ~sonus~ (“sound”), which also lies behind ~son~ and ~sonner~.
en.sophistiquer: Often explained as a borrowing from Medieval Latin ~sophisticāre~ (“to trick, to falsify, to corrupt”), from Latin ~sophisticus~, itself from Greek ~sophistikós~, from ~sophistḗs~ (“a wise man, a clever expert”).
