Italian ~soffocare~ and Spanish ~sofocar~ come from the same Latin verb, and so does English ~suffocate~. In French, ~suffoquer~ means “to suffocate,” both of a person who cannot get air and, figuratively, of one choked by emotion, as in ~suffoquer de rage~. It lives beside the everyday verb ~étouffer~, which covers the same physical sense in plainer speech. The Latin root gave the related French words ~suffocation~ and ~suffocant~, and the learned shape of ~suffoquer~, with its ~-ff-~ kept in the spelling, still shows its Latin origin.
en.suggestionner: ~Suggestionner~ is formed from ~suggestion~ with the ending ~-er~: to influence someone by suggestion. The noun ~suggestion~ is borrowed from Latin ~suggestiō~, which covered “addition,” “advice,” “hint” and “instigation.” It belongs with the verb ~suggérer~, and the pattern is the same as in ~solutionner~, built on ~solution~.
en.suggérer:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~suggerere~ (“to carry up, supply, furnish; to prompt, advise”), formed from the prefix ~sub-~ (“under, up from below”) and the verb ~gerere~ (“to carry, bear, conduct”). ~Gerere~ comes from Proto-Italic *~gezō~; its supine stem ~gestum~ underlies a host of English words. The French verb was taken straight from Latin rather than worn down through Old French, which is why it preserves the Latin shape so cleanly.

The image inside ~suggerere~ is to “carry up” material from below — to supply or feed something to someone, and so to prompt a thought, to put an idea into another's mind without stating it outright. French ~suggérer~ keeps exactly that delicacy: one suggests rather than commands. The root ~gerere~ (“to carry, to carry on”) seeded a remarkably wide family across French and English, including ~geste~ and English ~gesture~, ~gestation~, ~digérer~ (“to digest,” to carry apart), ~registre~, ~congérer~, and the noun ~suggestion~ itself, built on the supine ~suggestum~.
en.suicider: Formed from the noun ~suicide~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, ~suicider~ is mostly met in the reflexive ~se suicider~ (“to kill oneself”). The noun ~suicide~ was built on the model of ~homicide~: French sources explain it from Latin ~sui~ (“of oneself”) and ~caedere~ (“to kill”), and English Wiktionary describes it as borrowed from New Latin ~suīcīdium~, from ~suī~ and ~-cīdium~ (“-cide”). The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, is the default way of coining a verb from a noun. The verb is therefore a late French formation, the noun having come first.
en.suiffer: Formed from ~suif~ (“tallow”) with the verb ending ~-er~: to coat or wrap in tallow. ~Suif~ comes from Old French ~seu~, from Latin ~sēbum~, which also gave Italian ~sego~ and Spanish ~sebo~; English Wiktionary traces it to Proto-Indo-European *~seyb-~ (“to pour out”). The final ~f~ of ~suif~ was added by analogy, and French Wiktionary speculates that it served to avoid a clash with similar words.
en.suinter:
The sources differ on the route. French Wiktionary derives ~suinter~ directly from Latin ~sudāre~ (“to sweat”), while English Wiktionary derives it from the noun ~suint~, which both Wiktionaries tie to ~suer~ (“to sweat”), itself from ~sudāre~. Either way the root is Latin ~sudāre~, probably from ~sūdor~ (“sweat”). The noun ~suint~ names the greasy sweat of sheep's wool, which is why the verb first suggests moisture seeping through a surface.

In French, ~suinter~ means to ooze or seep slowly, of a wall, a wound or a cheese. It is a gentler word than ~couler~ or ~suer~, and it describes liquid that appears in drops rather than in a stream. The family includes ~suer~, ~sueur~ and ~sudation~, and English ~sudorific~ comes from the same Latin root.
en.suivre:
From Old French ~sivre~, later ~suivre~ — the modern form reshaped on the third-person present ~suit~ (earlier ~siut~) — from Vulgar Latin *~sequere~, a regularized form of Classical Latin ~sequī~ (“to follow”), a deponent verb, from Proto-Italic *~sekʷor~, from PIE *~sekʷ-~ (“to follow”). Cognate with Italian ~seguire~, Spanish ~seguir~, and Occitan ~sègre~; through the same root come Greek ~hépesthai~ and Sanskrit ~sácate~, both “to follow.”

The verb's history is a tangle of irregular forms: the Latin ~q~ produced wildly different dialect outcomes, from Picard ~suire~ to Burgundian ~seugre~ and Norman ~suure~, before standard French settled on the ~-v-~ stem. The PIE root *~sekʷ-~ proved astonishingly fertile in Latin: from the participle ~secundus~ (“following,” hence “second”) French inherited ~second~, while the compounds gave ~poursuivre~, ~ensuivre~, ~exécuter~, ~persécuter~, and ~poursuite~. Even the everyday ~suite~ — a musical sequence, a hotel suite, a retinue “following” a dignitary — is the same root, as is ~conséquence~, literally a “following-together.” A single notion of one thing coming after another thus branches into law, music, logic, and hospitality.
en.sulfater: Formed from ~sulfate~ plus the verbal suffix ~-er~, meaning “to treat with a sulfate” or “to turn into one.” The noun ~sulfate~ appears in the writing of Louis-Bernard Guyton-Morveau, who built it from Latin ~sulfur~ (“sulfur”) and the chemical suffix ~-ate~. The verb is therefore a modern, technical coinage.
en.sulfurer: Formed on the noun ~sulfure~ with the verb ending ~-er~, in the sense of treating something with sulfur or combining it with sulfur. The noun ~sulfure~ is a chemical term for a compound of sulfur with another element, and it belongs to the learned vocabulary built on Latin ~sulfur~ (“sulfur”). The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is the usual way French makes verbs from nouns. English ~sulfide~ belongs to the same learned family.
en.superposer: Formed from ~poser~ and the prefix ~super-~, modeled on Latin ~superpōnere~ (“to place on top of”). The prefix is a learned borrowing from Latin ~super-~ (“over, above”), a doublet of the inherited ~sur-~, and it is rare on French verbs. The base ~poser~ has a twist of its own: it comes from Late Latin ~pausare~ (“to halt”) but took over the sense of placing that belonged to Latin ~ponere~, so the verb for putting one thing over another is built on a word that once meant stopping.
en.superviser:
French borrowed ~superviser~ from English ~supervise~, which in turn comes from Medieval Latin ~supervidere~, formed from ~super~ (“above, over”) and ~videre~ (“to see, to look at”). The Latin verb ~videre~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”), which also underlies English ~wit~ and German ~wissen~, since seeing and knowing were close neighbors. The prefix ~super~ is the Latin source of French ~sur~, so ~superviser~ is a learned cousin of ~sur~ and ~voir~ put together: to “oversee”.

The journey is a round trip of sorts. A Latin-built verb passed through English before reaching French, and it stayed close to its literal meaning: to watch over work or people from above, in order to direct or check them. The same Latin ~videre~ lies behind the French verb ~voir~ and many learned words such as ~vision~, ~vidéo~, ~évidence~ and ~prévoir~, while ~super~ gave ~superviseur~ and ~supervision~ beside the native ~sur-~.
en.supplanter: ~Supplanter~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~supplantāre~. The Latin verb is generally analyzed as ~sub-~ (“under”) plus ~planta~ (“sole of the foot”), and meant to trip someone up. In French it is used for taking someone's place. English ~supplant~ comes from the same Latin verb.
en.supplicier: Formed from the noun ~supplice~ plus the verbal suffix ~-er~, with the meaning “to put to death by torture.” The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin ~supplicium~, which French Wiktionary glosses as a forced kneeling and the blows that follow. The verb thus turns a word for punishment into the act of inflicting it, and it is used mostly of executions.
en.supplier:
From Old French ~souploier~ (also ~sosploier~), from Latin ~supplicāre~ (“to kneel down, to beg humbly”), a verb built on the adjective ~supplex~ (“kneeling, suppliant”). The modern spelling restored the Latin ~sup-~, which the Old French form had worn down. Italian ~supplicare~ and Spanish ~suplicar~ descend from the same Latin verb, and English ~supplicate~ was borrowed from it.

It is tempting to connect ~supplier~ with ~plier~ (“to fold, to bend”), since a suppliant bends the knee. French Wiktionary states clearly that the two have no etymological link, and the deeper origin of Latin ~supplex~ is itself uncertain, so it is safest to say only that the Latin word described someone kneeling in entreaty. The meaning has stayed remarkably stable, from a physical gesture to a spoken request. Related words include ~supplication~, ~suppliant~ and ~supplique~, a formal petition. More dramatically, ~supplice~ (“torture, ordeal”) comes from Latin ~supplicium~, also from ~supplex~.
en.suppléer:
~Suppléer~ goes back to Latin ~supplēre~ (“to fill up, to complete, to make good”), made of ~sub-~ and ~plēre~ (“to fill”). Latin ~plēre~ comes from the Proto-Indo-European root *~pleh₁-~ (“to fill”). The verb entered Old French as ~souploier~ or ~soupleer~, taken from Latin. The root is productive across the family: French ~plein~ (from Latin ~plēnus~) and English ~full~, a native Germanic cousin, belong to it, as do ~complete~ and ~plenty~. English also took ~supply~ from the same Old French verb, so ~suppléer~ and ~supply~ are two forms of one word that went their separate ways.

The central idea is to fill what is missing, and French uses it in two main ways. Transitively or with ~à~, ~suppléer~ means to make up for a lack (~suppléer à un manque~). Of a person, it means to stand in for someone, to take over their place. From the verb came ~suppléant~ (“substitute, deputy”) and ~suppléance~ (“temporary replacement”), while ~supplément~ was borrowed directly from Latin ~supplēmentum~. In each of them, something is added so that the whole is no longer short.
en.supplémenter: Formed from ~supplément~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, to supplement. ~Supplément~ is borrowed from Latin ~supplēmentum~ (“a filling up, a complement”), from ~supplēre~ (“to complete by adding what is missing”). The ending ~-er~ is the ordinary one that turns a noun into a first-conjugation verb, as ~filtre~ gives ~filtrer~. Latin ~supplēre~ also gave French ~suppléer~.
en.supporter:
From Latin ~supportāre~ (“to carry, to bring up, to convey”), a compound of the prefix ~sub-~ (“under, from below”) and the verb ~portāre~ (“to carry”) — literally “to carry from underneath,” the posture of one who bears a load on the back. ~Portāre~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~portāō~ and ultimately to the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“to cross, to pass through”), the same root that gave Latin ~porta~ (“gate”) and ~portus~ (“harbour”). It is cognate with the Romance family of Italian ~portare~ and Spanish ~portar~, and, through *~per-~, with English ~ford~ and ~fare~.

The Latin sense of physical bearing branched in two directions. One kept the literal idea of holding something up: a beam ~supports~ a roof. The other turned inward and moral — to “bear up under” hardship, hence “to endure, to tolerate.” Modern French keeps both: a wall ~supporte~ a weight, and one ~supporte~ a noisy neighbour, often grudgingly. A curious twist: the sporting sense “to support a team” was re-imported from English ~supporter~, itself a much older loan from French — a word that travelled the Channel and came home with new baggage. From the same root *~per-~ descend a crowd of French words, among them ~porter~, ~porte~, ~port~, ~apporter~, and ~transporter~.
en.supposer:
A French formation modelled on Latin ~supponere~ (“to put under, to substitute, to assume”), reshaped on the native verb ~poser~ (“to place”) under the influence of the prefix ~sub-~ (“under”). Strictly, ~poser~ descends from Late Latin ~pausare~ (“to pause, to set down”), which crossed paths with Latin ~ponere~ (“to put”); but the whole ~-poser~ family — ~supposer~, ~composer~, ~proposer~, ~disposer~ — was built in French to answer the Latin verbs in ~-ponere~, so ~supposer~ stands for ~supponere~, literally “to place under.” Cognate in sense with English ~suppose~ and Italian ~supporre~.

The modern abstract meaning — to assume, to conjecture, to take as a premise — grew in scholastic Latin, where ~suppositio~ rendered the logician's notion of a hypothesis, itself a calque of Greek ~ὑπόθεσις~ (~hupóthesis~, literally a “placing under,” a foundation laid beneath an argument). So both the Latin and the Greek term picture an assumption as something set underneath, a support propping up reasoning. French ~supposer~ thus spans the concrete and the mental: to place under, to substitute (~supposer un enfant~, in old law, to pass off a false heir), and to suppose, imply, or surmise. Kin in French include ~supposition~, ~présupposer~, ~suppositoire~ — literally a thing “placed underneath” — and the whole ~poser~ clan.
en.supprimer:
Borrowed from Latin ~supprimere~ (“to press down, to hold back, to stifle”), a compound of ~sub-~ (“under”) and ~premere~ (“to press”). ~Premere~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~per-~ (“to strike, to press”). It is cognate with Italian ~sopprimere~ and Spanish ~suprimir~, and — through the same Latin verb — with English ~suppress~ and ~press~ itself.

The Latin sense was physical, “to press something down so it cannot rise,” and the French verb keeps that gesture in the abstract: to suppress a revolt, to delete a line, to remove a clause is to push it out of sight. The arrival of computing gave ~supprimer~ a brisk new home as the everyday word for “to delete” a file. The root ~premere~ is one of the most fertile in French, surfacing in ~presser~ (“to press”) and its many kin — ~exprimer~ (“to express,” to press out), ~imprimer~ (“to print,” to press in), ~comprimer~ (“to compress”), ~opprimer~ (“to oppress”), and ~déprimer~ (“to depress”) — a family in which the simple act of pressing has been bent to a dozen meanings.
en.suppurer:
From Latin ~suppūrāre~ (“to form pus, to fester”), a verb built on ~sub-~ (“under”) and ~pūs~ (“pus”). French took the verb directly from Latin, and its ~-are~ ending became the usual French ~-er~. Italian ~suppurare~ and Spanish ~supurar~ come from the same Latin verb, and English ~suppurate~ is a parallel borrowing of it.

The noun at its core survives in French ~pus~, in the adjective ~purulent~ (from Latin ~purulentus~), and in English ~pus~. French also has the noun ~suppuration~ and the adjective ~suppuratif~, built on the same verb. In modern French ~suppurer~ is a medical term for a wound or abscess that discharges pus, and these related words are just as technical.
en.supputer:
Borrowed from Latin ~supputāre~ (“to count up, to reckon”), formed from ~sub-~ and ~putāre~ (“to reckon, to think”). The same Latin ~putāre~ lies behind a large family of French verbs, among them ~compter~ (by way of Latin ~computāre~), ~imputer~, ~amputer~, ~disputer~, ~députer~ and ~réputer~, each built with a different prefix. ~Supputer~ is the learned member of the family, close in sense to ~compter~.

In French, ~supputer~ is a learned word meaning to estimate or work out, often by calculation or conjecture; the related noun is ~supputation~. It sits in a more formal register than ~compter~ or ~calculer~. English has several relatives from the same Latin root through the parallel verbs: ~compute~, ~impute~, ~amputate~ and ~dispute~.
en.surabonder: Formed from ~abonder~ with the prefix ~sur-~ (“over, beyond”), so it means to abound beyond measure. The base ~abonder~ comes through Old French from Latin ~abundāre~ (“to overflow”), from ~ab-~ (“away from”) and ~undāre~ (“to rise in waves”), from ~unda~ (“wave”). English ~abound~ is a cousin from the same Latin verb.
en.surajouter: Formed from the prefix ~sur-~ and the verb ~ajouter~, so “to add on top.” The prefix comes from Old French ~sur-~, a shortened form of Latin ~super-~ (“over, above”), and here marks an extra layer or an excess. The base ~ajouter~ comes from Old French ~ajoster~, built on a Vulgar Latin *~adjuxtāre~, from ~ad-~ and ~juxtā~ (“beside”), so “to set next to.” ~Surajouter~ therefore stacks one addition upon another, and it is mostly found in literary or careful writing.
en.suralimenter: ~Suralimenter~ is formed from ~alimenter~ and the prefix ~sur-~ (“over, to excess”), so it means to overfeed. ~Alimenter~ was built, from the fourteenth century, on ~aliment~, from Latin ~alimentum~ (“nourishment”), itself from ~alere~ (“to nourish”). A mechanical sense, to supply an engine beyond its normal level, is first attested in 1932.
en.surarmer: Formed from ~armer~ with the prefix ~sur-~, which expresses excess, so the verb means to arm beyond what is needed. The prefix ~sur-~ comes from Old French ~sur-~, a shortened form of Latin ~super-~ (“over, above”). The base ~armer~ comes from Latin ~armāre~ (“to arm”), derived from ~arma~ (“weapons”), and has been attested in French since the tenth century. The word is thus a plain French formation resting on a Latin verb of equipping soldiers.
en.surbaisser: ~Surbaisser~ is ~baisser~ with the prefix ~sur-~, which here means “beyond, to excess,” so “to lower more than usual.” It is a technical word, used in particular of arches and vaults, which are said to be ~surbaissé~ when they are lower than a full semicircle. The prefix ~sur-~ comes from Old French, a shortened form of Latin ~super~ (“over”). The base ~baisser~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~bassiāre~, a verb built on Late Latin ~bassus~ (“low”).
en.surcharger: Formed from ~sur-~ and ~charger~. The prefix comes from Old French ~sur-~, a worn-down form of Latin ~super-~ (“over, above”), and here carries its common sense of excess. The base ~charger~ goes back to Late Latin *~carricāre~, built on ~carrus~, a wheeled cart borrowed from Gaulish. To ~surcharger~ is thus to load a cart, and by extension a person, a text or a system, beyond what it can bear. It also covers the commercial sense of charging too much.
en.surchauffer: ~Surchauffer~ is formed from ~chauffer~ (“to heat”) with the prefix ~sur-~, which here carries the sense of excess, “to heat too much.” The prefix comes from Old French ~sur-~, a worn-down form of Latin ~super-~ (“over, above”). The base ~chauffer~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~calefare~, a reduced form of Latin ~calefacere~ (“to make warm”), built from ~calere~ (“to be hot”) and ~facere~ (“to make”). The same Latin root gave French ~chaud~ and ~chaleur~.
en.surclasser: Formed from ~classer~ (“to class, to rank”) with the prefix ~sur-~. That prefix comes from Old French ~sur-~, a shortened form of Latin ~super-~ (“over, above”), and here it carries the sense of superiority in rank or quality: to ~surclasser~ someone is to stand a class above them, to outclass them. The base ~classer~ is built on the noun ~classe~, borrowed from Latin ~classis~, which first meant a “summons” and then the divisions into which the Roman census sorted citizens.
en.surcomprimer: Formed from ~comprimer~ with the prefix ~sur-~, “over”: to compress too much, or to raise an engine's compression ratio. ~Sur-~ comes from Old French ~sur-~, from Latin ~super-~. ~Comprimer~ is borrowed from Latin ~comprimere~ (“to press together”), from ~com-~ (“together”) and ~premere~ (“to press”), which also survives as ~presser~.
en.surcontrer: Formed from ~contrer~ with the prefix ~sur-~. The base verb is a nineteenth-century coinage from the preposition ~contre~, inherited from Latin ~contra~ (“against”). The prefix comes from Old French ~sur-~, a contracted form of Latin ~super-~ (“over, above”), and here carries the sense of a second layer on top of the first. To ~surcontrer~ is therefore to counter a counter, the card-game move of redoubling after an opponent has doubled.
en.surcouper: Formed from ~couper~ with the prefix ~sur-~ (“over”): in card games, to ~surcouper~ is to trump with a higher trump than the one already played, to overtrump. The base ~couper~ comes from Old French ~colper~, from the noun ~colp~ (modern ~coup~), from Latin ~colpus~ and Late Latin ~colaphus~, borrowed from Greek ~kólaphos~ (“a blow”). The prefix comes from Old French ~sur-~, from Latin ~super-~.
en.surenchérir: Formed from the prefix ~sur-~ and ~enchérir~, itself ~en-~ + ~chérir~ (~cher~ + ~-ir~), so “to make or become dear.” ~Sur-~ is the Old French form of Latin ~super-~ (“over, above”) and here marks excess. The adjective ~cher~ comes from Latin ~cārus~ (“dear, costly”). The base already meant to bid higher at an auction, and ~surenchérir~ adds the idea of outbidding someone, so it means “to place a higher bid.” It also has a figurative use, to go one better.
en.surentraîner: Formed in French from ~entraîner~ (“to train”) with the prefix ~sur-~ (“over, to excess”), so “to train too much.” The prefix is Old French ~sur-~, a contracted form of Latin ~super-~ (“over, above”). The base is built from ~en-~ and Old French ~traîner~ (“to drag”), which descends from Vulgar Latin *~traginare~, itself from Latin ~trahere~ (“to pull”). The athletic sense of “training” grew out of the idea of drawing someone along.
en.surestimer: Formed from ~estimer~ (“to estimate, to value”) and the prefix ~sur-~, which marks excess: to value something above its worth. The base comes from Latin ~aestimāre~ (“to appraise”), whose own origin is debated. The prefix is Old French ~sur-~, a contracted form of Latin ~super-~ (“over, above”) and a doublet of the learned prefix ~super-~. The same pattern gives ~surcharger~ and ~surchauffer~, and the opposite verb is ~sous-estimer~.
en.surexciter: ~Surexciter~ is formed from ~exciter~ and the prefix ~sur-~, which here marks excess: to ~surexciter~ is to excite beyond the normal level. The prefix comes from Old French ~sur-~, a contracted form of Latin ~super-~ (“over, above”). The base ~exciter~ comes from Latin ~excitāre~ (“to rouse, to call forth”), a frequentative of ~exciēre~ and a cousin of ~ciēre~ (“to set in motion”). The verb is used of nerves, crowds, imaginations and appetites that are stirred too far.
en.surexploiter: ~Surexploiter~ is built from ~exploiter~ with the prefix ~sur-~, which here has its commonest sense, excess: to exploit beyond a reasonable level. The prefix is the Old French form of Latin ~super-~ (“over, above”). The base ~exploiter~ goes back to a Vulgar Latin frequentative *~explicitāre~, from Latin ~explicare~ (“to unfold”), and by the sixteenth century it meant to make a farm, a mine or a resource productive. ~Surexploiter~ applies that sense to using such resources too heavily.
en.surexposer: Formed from the prefix ~sur-~ (“over, too much”) and the verb ~exposer~. The base was made in French from ~ex-~ and ~poser~ to render Latin ~exponere~ (“to set out”). In photography, ~surexposer~ means to expose film or a sensor to too much light; the figurative sense, to expose someone too much to media attention, follows from it.
en.surfacer: Formed from the noun ~surface~ with the ending ~-er~, so the verb means to work a surface, as in planing or smoothing it. The noun ~surface~ was itself built in French from ~sur-~ (“over”) and ~face~, and English Wiktionary adds that it is a calque of Latin ~superficiēs~ (“surface”). The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~.
en.surfacturer: Formed from ~facturer~ and the prefix ~sur-~ (“over, beyond”), the verb means to bill more than is due. The base ~facturer~ is built on the noun ~facture~ (“invoice”) with ~-er~. The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin ~factūra~ (“a making”), from ~facere~ (“to make, to do”), and a doublet of the Old French ~faiture~.
en.surfaire: Formed from ~faire~ (“to do, to make”) and the prefix ~sur-~ (“over, excessively”). ~Faire~ descends from Latin ~facere~. The verb is old: ~sorfeire~ is recorded in Old French in 1174-78 with the sense “to raise a price.” The related noun ~sorfait~ (“excess”) appears in Wace in 1155, and a verb ~sorfaire~ meaning “to have the advantage over” is recorded in 1160-74. The figurative sense “to make too much of, to overrate” dates from 1704.
en.surfer: A French verb formed from the English noun ~surf~ (the breaking waves, then the sport) by adding the French infinitive ending ~-er~, which comes from Latin ~-āre~ and is the default way of making a verb from a borrowed word. Both Wiktionaries agree on this simple chain. The sense “to ride waves” was later stretched to “to browse the web,” the same shift that English made with “to surf the net.” The origin of English ~surf~ itself is uncertain, so it is not traced further here.
en.surfiler: Formed from the prefix ~sur-~ (“over, on top”) and the verb ~filer~ (“to spin, to run a thread”), ~surfiler~ is first recorded in 1873 in a sewing sense, in Alphonse Daudet. In 1877 Littré's supplement adds a second sense, “to give a thread a higher degree of fineness.” A Middle French ~surfiler~ is also attested, between 1489 and 1586, in the language of the ~boursiers~ (purse-makers) and glovers, in the form ~seurfillées~.
en.surgeler: Formed from the prefix ~sur-~ and ~geler~ (“to freeze”), in the sense of freezing beyond the ordinary, that is, deep-freezing. The prefix ~sur-~ is Old French, a contracted form of Latin ~super-~ (“over, above”). The base ~geler~ is inherited from Latin ~gelāre~, built on the noun ~gelū~ (“frost”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~gel-~ (“cold; to freeze”). English ~cold~ and ~cool~ are cognates from the same root.
en.surgeonner: A derivative of ~surgeon~, with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~surgeon~ (earlier ~sorjon~, ~sourjon~) meant “spring, source” from about 1200 and, from the end of the 13th century, “shoot of a tree.” The TLFi derives it, with the suffix ~-on~, from old forms of ~sourdre~ (“to well up”), especially the present participle ~sourjant~, with later influence from Latin ~surgere~ (“to rise”). The verb therefore has two uses: dated or literary, of water, “to gush forth,” and in botany, of a tree, “to put out suckers.”
en.surgir:
~surgir~ goes back to Latin ~surgere~ (“to rise, to get up”), a contraction of ~surrigere~, from ~sub-~ (“up from below”) plus ~regere~ (“to keep straight, to direct”), from PIE *~h₃reǵ-~ (“to straighten”) — the root of English ~right~ and German ~recht~. But French already possessed the verb by inheritance: ~sourdre~, the popular descendant of ~surgere~, said of water welling up, whose old past participle gave ~source~. ~surgir~ is thus a doublet — and it arrived, surprisingly, by sea: it is first attested, as ~sourgir~, in the fifteenth century, as a sailors' term meaning “to cast anchor, to come to port,” probably taken from Catalan ~surgir~, which Mediterranean seamen had used since the thirteenth century. Italian ~sorgere~, Spanish ~surgir~ and English ~surge~ belong to the same Latin family.

So the French verb that now means “to spring up” began its career meaning, of a ship, to drop anchor and stop. Only in the nineteenth century — the figurative sense is attested in 1823 — did the modern meaning take hold, realigned on the classical Latin sense of rising; today memories, crowds and difficulties all surge up without warning. The root's French posterity is rich on both branches: from ~surgere~ come ~sourdre~, ~source~, ~ressource~ (from Old French ~resourdre~, “to rise again,” from Latin ~resurgere~), ~résurrection~ and ~insurrection~ — the insurgent and the resurrected both being, etymologically, people who rise — while ~regere~ supplied ~régir~, ~diriger~ and ~droit~ (from ~dīrēctus~, “made straight”). A word that once anchored ships now names whatever refuses to stay down.
en.surhausser: Formed from ~hausser~ (“to raise”) with the prefix ~sur-~ (“over, above”), so it means to raise higher. The TLFi records it first around 1135 in the figurative sense of exalting, in the Old French form ~sorhaucier~. The literal sense of lifting appears around 1200 but stays rare before the seventeenth century. In 1676 the participle describes an architectural vault, a ~berceau surhaussé~, and by the 1590s the verb also meant to raise taxes or prices.
en.surimposer: ~Surimposer~ is formed from the prefix ~sur-~ and the verb ~imposer~. The prefix, from Old French ~sur-~ and Latin ~super-~ (“over, above”), here adds the idea of excess, so the verb means to tax too heavily. The base ~imposer~ comes from Latin ~imponere~ (“to place upon”), made of ~in-~ and ~ponere~, and was reshaped in French on ~poser~. The fiscal noun ~impôt~ belongs to the same family, which is why the compound speaks naturally of an extra burden of tax.
en.suriner: Formed from the slang noun ~surin~ (“dagger, knife”) with the suffix ~-er~: to ~suriner~ is to stab someone, to knife them. French Wiktionary gives two possible nouns behind the spelling: one is the same word as ~chourin~, from Romani ~ćhuri~ (“knife”), and the other is a derivative of ~sur~ with the suffix ~-in~. The Romani account is the one that fits the sense of a blade. The verb belongs to the argot of the underworld, where Romani lent several words for tools of the trade.
en.surinvestir: Formed from the prefix ~sur-~ and ~investir~, in the sense of investing too much, since ~sur-~ most often marks excess. The prefix descends from Old French ~sur-~, a shortened form of Latin ~super-~ (“over, above”). The base ~investir~ comes from Latin ~investīre~ (“to clothe, surround”), from ~in-~ and ~vestīre~ (“to dress”), a verb whose financial sense, putting capital to work, is the one that ~surinvestir~ takes up and exaggerates.
en.surir: From the adjective ~sur~ in its sense of “sour,” with the infinitive ending ~-ir~, which here makes a verb meaning “to become A.” The adjective ~sur~ is a Germanic loan, a standard etymology, related to English ~sour~ and German ~sauer~. ~Surir~ means to turn sour, as milk or wine does, and it should not be confused with the preposition ~sur~ (“on”). The ending ~-ir~ goes back to Latin ~-ire~ and ~-ere~, and is used mostly on adjectives, as in ~grandir~ and ~grossir~.
en.surjaler: Formed from the nautical noun ~jas~ with the prefix ~sur-~ (“over”), and said of an anchor line that becomes fouled. The origin of ~jas~ is given in two ways: from Old French ~joal~, itself derived from ~joug~ (“yoke”), or from Occitan ~jatz~ (“bed”), from Vulgar Latin *~jacium~, which belongs to Latin ~jacēre~ (“to lie”). The sources do not settle between them.
en.surjeter: A sewing term meaning to overcast an edge, that is, to stitch over the raw edge of fabric or the join of two pieces so that it does not fray. It is formed from the prefix ~sur-~ (“over”) and the verb ~jeter~ (“to throw”), which descends from Latin ~iactāre~. The noun ~surjet~, the overcast stitch itself, was later drawn from the verb.
en.surjouer: Formed from ~jouer~ (“to play”) with the prefix ~sur-~ (“over, beyond”), in its common sense of excess: to overplay a role or a hand. ~Jouer~ comes from Old French ~joer~, from Latin ~iocāre~ (“to joke”), itself from ~iocus~ (“joke, game”), the word from which English borrowed ~joke~. In Late Latin this joking verb spread to all kinds of play and displaced ~lūdere~ in everyday speech. The prefix ~sur-~ comes from Old French ~sur-~, a worn-down form of Latin ~super-~ (“over, above”). An actor who ~surjoue~ is one who goes over the top.
en.surligner: ~Surligner~ combines the prefix ~sur-~ (“over”), the noun ~ligne~ (“line”) and the verb ending ~-er~, on the model of ~souligner~ (“to underscore”). ~Ligne~ comes from Latin ~līnea~, and ~sur-~ from Old French ~sur-~, itself from Latin ~super-~. French Wiktionary dates its first attestation to 1968, in the sense of drawing a line above a line. That is three years before the highlighter pen it now names, which it dates to 1971.
en.surmener: ~Surmener~ is built from the prefix ~sur-~ and the verb ~mener~, and means to overwork, in effect to drive someone too hard. The prefix ~sur-~ is the Old French form of Latin ~super-~ (“over, above”) and here carries its common sense of excess. The verb ~mener~ (“to lead”) comes from Old French, from Late Latin ~minare~ (“to drive animals”), which grew out of Latin ~minari~ (“to threaten”).
en.surmonter:
Formed in French from ~monter~ (“to climb, to mount”) with the prefix ~sur-~ (from Latin ~super~, “over, above”). ~Monter~ goes back to Vulgar Latin *~montāre~, derived from ~mōns~, stem ~mont-~ (“mountain”), from Proto-Italic *~monts~, from PIE *~men-~ (“to stand out, to tower”). Through that root it is cognate with English ~mountain~ and ~mount~.

The literal sense is to “mount over” — to rise above an obstacle — which gives the figurative “to overcome, to surmount, to get over” a difficulty or a fear. ~Surmonter~ can still be physical: a steeple ~surmonte~ a church, sitting atop it. The ~mōns~ family is large and visible on every map: ~mont~, ~montagne~, ~monter~, ~montée~, ~amont~, and ~promontoire~. The same PIE *~men-~ “to tower” also lies behind the borrowed ~éminent~ and ~prominent~ in their idea of jutting up.
en.surmouler: ~Surmouler~ is formed from ~mouler~ with the prefix ~sur-~, here for a second layer or a repeated operation: to mold over an existing piece. The base ~mouler~ comes from ~moule~ (“mold”), inherited from Old French ~modle~, borrowed from Latin ~modulus~ (“measure”). It is therefore a doublet of ~module~, and a different word from the ~moule~ of mussels.
en.surmédicaliser: Formed from ~médicaliser~ with the prefix ~sur-~, which marks excess: to ~surmédicaliser~ is to subject something, such as childbirth or old age, to more medical treatment and authority than it needs. The base ~médicaliser~ comes from ~médical~ and the suffix ~-iser~; ~médical~ is borrowed from Latin ~medicālis~, from ~medicus~ (“physician”), from ~medērī~ (“to heal”). The prefix comes from Old French ~sur-~, a contracted form of Latin ~super-~ (“over, above”). The verb is modern, and so is its debate over the medicalization of ordinary life.
en.surnager: ~Surnager~ is formed from ~nager~ with the prefix ~sur-~, whose senses include “over, above, on the surface.” It means to float on the surface, as oil does on water, and by extension to stay afloat in difficulty. The base ~nager~ comes from Old French ~nagier~ (“to sail, to row”), reduced from Latin ~nāvigāre~ (“to sail”), and it replaced the older verb for swimming, ~noer~. The prefix ~sur-~ goes back to Old French ~sur-~, from Latin ~super-~ (“over”). In modern French ~surnager~ is mostly figurative: a lone idea, a survivor or a minor player ~surnage~ amid a general wreck.
en.surnommer:
From ~sur-~ (“over, on top of,” from Latin ~super~) + ~nommer~ (“to name”), reinforced by the noun ~surnom~ (“nickname, surname”). ~Nommer~ descends from Latin ~nōmināre~ (“to name”), from ~nōmen~ (“name”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₃nómn̥~. The root is cognate with English ~name~, German ~Name~, Ancient Greek ~ónoma~, and Sanskrit ~nā́man~, and is often linked to the root of “knowing,” a name being how a thing is known.

The layered prefix ~sur-~ originally marked an added or supplementary name laid “over” the given one — a by-name. In medieval usage a ~surnom~ could be an honorific epithet, a descriptive tag, or the hereditary family name (the sense English ~surname~ still carries). The verb ~surnommer~ settled on the playful modern meaning “to nickname.” The same ~nōmen~ root seeded a wide French family: ~nom~, ~prénom~, ~renommée~ (“renown,” literally a re-naming), ~nominer~, ~nommément~, and the learned doublet ~pronom~. Through Latin it also gives ~nominal~ and ~dénomination~.
en.suroxyder: Formed from ~oxyder~ with the prefix ~sur-~, so “to oxidize too much.” The base verb comes from the noun ~oxyde~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary derives ~oxyde~ from Ancient Greek ~oxús~ (“sharp, acid”) plus ~-ide~, coined by Guyton de Morveau, while English Wiktionary calls it a blend of ~oxygène~ and ~acide~. The prefix ~sur-~ comes from Old French ~sur-~, from Latin ~super-~ (“over, above”), and here marks excess.
en.surpasser: Formed in French from the prefix ~sur-~ (“over, beyond”) and the verb ~passer~ (“to pass”). The prefix is the Old French shortening of Latin ~super-~ and here carries the sense of superiority: to go beyond someone or something. The base ~passer~ goes back to Vulgar Latin *~passāre~, from Latin ~passus~ (“step, pace”), so the verb pictures a runner who steps past a rival. It keeps company with ~dépasser~ and ~repasser~, and it has a reflexive use, ~se surpasser~ (“to outdo oneself”).
en.surpayer: From ~sur-~ + ~payer~, “to pay too much.” The prefix ~sur-~ comes from Old French ~sur-~ (also ~sor-~), a reduced form of Latin ~super-~ (“over, above”), and here marks excess. The base ~payer~ comes from Old French ~paiier~, from Latin ~pācāre~ (“to pacify, to appease”), built on ~pāx~ (“peace”). Paying was originally a way of appeasing a creditor, so ~surpayer~ means to give more than the debt or the work called for.
en.surpiquer: Formed in French from ~piquer~ with the prefix ~sur-~, here marking a second layer on the same support: to stitch over, adding a row of stitching on top of fabric. The prefix comes from Old French ~sur-~, a contracted form of Latin ~super-~ (“over”). The origin of ~piquer~ is debated. One account derives it from an imitative Vulgar Latin root *~pikk-~, and another from ~pic~ (“pick, woodpecker”).
en.surplomber: Formed from ~sur-~ (“over”) + ~plomb~ + ~-er~. The ~plomb~ here is the lead weight on a builder's line, the plumb line that fixes the true vertical, so ~surplomber~ describes a wall or rock that leans out beyond that line and hangs over what lies below. French Wiktionary treats the verb as formed on the noun ~surplomb~ (“overhang”), itself built on ~plomb~ with ~sur-~, while English Wiktionary derives the noun from the verb; the two accounts point the same way but disagree on which came first. From the physical overhang, the verb extended to any commanding position: to overlook a valley or a town.
en.surprendre:
A French compound of the prefix ~sur-~ (“over, upon”) and the verb ~prendre~ (“to take”), modeled on Latin ~super~ + ~prehendere~. ~Prendre~ comes from the contracted Latin ~prendere~, from ~prehendere~ (“to seize, grasp”), which breaks into ~prae-~ (“before”) and a root ~-hendere~ akin to Ancient Greek ~χανδάνω~ (~khandánō~, “to hold, contain”) and, through Proto-Indo-European *~ǵʰend-~ (“to seize”), to English ~get~. Old French had several near-variants — ~sorprendre~, ~sousprendre~ — that later merged.

The literal image is to “take from above,” to overtake. Early on ~surprendre~ meant to seize or attack someone unawares, to take a town by surprise — a military sense of catching the enemy off guard. From this grew the two modern strands: to catch out (to take someone in the act, ~surprendre un secret~) and simply to surprise, to astonish, since the unexpected catches the mind unprepared. The noun ~surprise~ (originally a “taking unawares”) followed the verb into English. Relatives in the ~prendre~ family include ~prise~, ~apprendre~, ~comprendre~, ~entreprendre~, and ~surprenant~ — a whole web spun from the idea of grasping.
en.surproduire: Formed from ~produire~ (“to produce”) with the prefix ~sur-~, in its commonest sense of excess: “to produce too much.” The base comes from Latin ~producere~ (“to lead forth”), made of ~pro-~ and ~ducere~ (“to lead”), the verb behind ~conduire~, ~réduire~ and ~traduire~. The prefix ~sur-~ is the French form of Latin ~super-~ (“over”), and it also gives the noun ~surproduction~.
en.surprotéger: Formed in French from ~protéger~ with the prefix ~sur-~, “to protect too much.” The base comes from Latin ~protegere~ (~pro-~ + ~tegere~, “to cover in front”). The prefix ~sur-~ is from Old French ~sur-~, a shortened form of Latin ~super-~ (“over, above”), and its most productive sense is excess, as in ~surcharger~ or ~surestimer~. English ~protect~ shares the Latin source.
en.sursauter: ~Sursauter~ is formed from the noun ~sursaut~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun is itself built on ~saut~ (“jump”) with the prefix ~sur-~ (“over, above”), so the verb means to give a ~sursaut~, a sudden start. English Wiktionary only cross-refers the verb and the noun, so French Wiktionary is the only source for the direction of derivation.
en.sursemer: Formed from ~semer~ (“to sow”) and the prefix ~sur-~ (“over, above”), so “to sow over,” that is, to seed again on top of what is already sown. ~Semer~ comes from Old French ~semer~ and Latin ~sēmināre~ (“to sow”), a verb built on ~sēmen~ (“seed”). The prefix ~sur-~ descends from Old French ~sur-~, a syncopated form of Latin ~super-~, and is a doublet of the learned prefix ~super-~.
en.surseoir:
~Surseoir~ comes from Latin ~supersedere~, which joins ~super-~ (“above”) and ~sedēre~ (“to sit”). French reshaped both halves in parallel: ~super-~ became ~sur-~ and ~sedēre~ became ~seoir~, the verb that also lies inside ~asseoir~. English Wiktionary reads the French word as ~sur~ (“over”) + ~seoir~ (“to be fit, proper”), and records ~superséder~ as its doublet, a learned borrowing of the same Latin verb. English ~supersede~ descends from that Latin verb too.

In modern French ~surseoir~ is a formal, chiefly legal verb meaning “to postpone, to defer,” and it takes the preposition à. A judge may ~surseoir à statuer~, that is, suspend a ruling. Its past participle gave the noun ~sursis~ (“reprieve, suspended sentence”). The Latin root ~sedēre~ is behind many other French words: ~seoir~ itself (now rare), ~asseoir~, ~séance~ (literally a “sitting”) and, as a learned borrowing, ~sédentaire~.
en.surstocker: Formed from ~stocker~ with the prefix ~sur-~, which marks excess, so the verb means to keep more in stock than is needed. The base is a French verb built on the noun ~stock~, borrowed from English ~stock~ in the commercial sense of a reserve of goods. English ~stock~ comes from Old English ~stocc~ (“tree trunk, post”), from Proto-Germanic *~stukkaz~. The prefix ~sur-~ comes from Old French ~sur-~, from Latin ~super-~ (“over, above”).
en.surtaxer: ~Surtaxer~ is a prefixed verb: ~sur-~ plus ~taxer~, though English Wiktionary also allows reading it as the noun ~surtaxe~ plus ~-er~. The prefix ~sur-~ goes back to Latin ~super-~ (“over, above”) and carries here its commonest sense, excess: to impose an extra tax. The base ~taxer~ passed through Old French from Latin ~taxāre~ (“to estimate, to rate”), and English ~tax~ is the same verb carried across the Channel.
en.surtondre: Formed from ~tondre~ (“to shear”) with the prefix ~sur-~. The base is inherited from Old French ~tondre~, from Vulgar Latin *~tondĕre~, a variant of Latin ~tondēre~, which goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~temh₂-~ (“to cut”). The prefix ~sur-~ comes from Old French, a shortened form of Latin ~super-~ (“over, above”), and often marks something done beyond or on top of the usual. Here the verb is a technical term, glossed as removing hair.
en.surveiller:
French ~surveiller~ is a French formation, ~veiller~ (“to keep watch, stay awake”) prefixed with ~sur-~ (“over, above”), attested in 1586 with the sense “to watch over.” The base ~veiller~ comes from Old French ~veillier~, from Latin ~vigilāre~ (“to be awake, keep watch”), from the adjective ~vigil~ (“awake, alert”), from Latin ~vigeō~ (“to be lively, vigorous”). The root is Proto-Indo-European *~weǵ-~ (“to be strong, lively, awake”), which also yielded English ~wake~, ~watch~, and ~vigour~.

The prefix ~sur-~ adds the idea of looking down from above, giving “to oversee, supervise.” The verb sits in a rich Latin family: ~vigilāre~ also gave learned French ~vigilant~ and ~vigile~, and through Spanish the everyday ~vigilar~. From ~surveiller~ itself descend ~surveillance~ (“surveillance”) and ~surveillant~ (“supervisor, monitor”). The English borrowing ~surveillance~ entered around the French Revolution, when the comités de surveillance gave the word its modern overtone of watchful, often suspicious, oversight — a sense already latent in the prefixed French verb.
en.survenir:
French ~survenir~ is built from ~venir~ (“to come”) with the prefix ~sur-~ (“over, upon”), literally “to come upon.” ~Venir~ descends from Old French ~venir~, from Latin ~venīre~ (“to come”), from Proto-Italic *~gʷenjō~, from Proto-Indo-European *~gʷem-~ (“to go, come”). That same root, through different sound laws, produced English ~come~, Ancient Greek ~baínō~ (“I go”), and Sanskrit ~gam~ (“to go”) — one of the clearest demonstrations of how a single PIE root scatters across the family.

The prefix ~sur-~ here conveys suddenness and superposition: something ~survient~ when it comes on top of a situation, unbidden and often unwelcome — an accident, a complication, an unexpected guest. The word thus specialises “to come” into “to occur suddenly, to crop up.” From the same Latin verb the French got an enormous family: ~venir~, ~avenir~ (“future”), ~événement~ (“event,” literally an out-coming), ~revenir~, ~devenir~, ~convenir~, and ~prévenir~ — a reminder that much of what merely “happens” in French is, etymologically, a kind of coming.
en.survirer: Formed from ~virer~ (“to turn”) with the prefix ~sur-~, which marks excess: to turn more than intended, as in oversteer. The origin of ~virer~ is debated. The favored account derives it from Late Latin *~virāre~ (“to turn, whirl”), probably an alteration of ~vibrāre~ (“to shake, brandish”), which would make it a doublet of ~vibrer~. A Celtic proposal offers Gaulish *~viru~ (“to deviate”) instead.
en.survivre:
From Old French ~survivre~, attested around 1100 in the conjugated form ~survesquiet~, from Latin ~supervīvere~, a compound of ~super~ (“over, beyond”) and ~vīvere~ (“to live”). Synchronically it reads simply as ~sur-~ + ~vivre~, “to live beyond.” Latin ~vīvere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~gʷīwō~ and the PIE root *~gʷeyh₃-~ (“to live”), one of the great roots of the family: through it ~survivre~ is a cognate of English ~quick~ (in its old sense “alive,” as in “the quick and the dead”), Ancient Greek ~bíos~ (“life”) and Sanskrit ~jīvati~ (“he lives”).

The sense has held firm: to outlive another, or to keep living past some danger or disaster. The compound carries a quiet drama — to ~survivre~ is always to live in relation to something one has outlasted. From the same ~vivre~ stem French draws ~survie~ (“survival”) and ~survivance~, and from the deeper root the whole crowd of ~vif~, ~vivace~, ~viande~, ~convive~ and ~ravitailler~.
en.survoler: The two sources differ on the chain. French Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~supervolāre~ (“to fly over”), fused from ~super~ (“over”) and ~volāre~ (“to fly”), while English Wiktionary treats it as Middle French ~survoler~, first attested around 1470, formed from ~sur-~ (“over”) + ~voler~ (“to fly”). Either way the sense is clear: to fly over. Italian ~sorvolare~ is the parallel. The figurative sense, to skim over a subject without dwelling on it, follows the same image of passing high above.
en.survolter: ~Survolter~ is formed with the prefix ~sur-~ (“over, beyond”), which here has its commonest sense of excess, and the noun ~volt~: to raise a circuit's voltage above its normal level. The prefix comes from Old French ~sur-~, a syncopated form of Latin ~super-~. The base ~volt~ is the unit of electric potential, named after the Italian physicist Alessandro Volta, and French took the word from English ~volt~. The verb also has a figurative use, “to overexcite”.
en.surélever: A compound of ~élever~ and the prefix ~sur-~ (“over, above”; from Latin ~super~): to raise something higher still, to add height to a building or a wall. ~Élever~ is Latin ~elevāre~ (~e-~ + ~levāre~, “to lift”), a verb built on ~levis~ (“light”), so that to lift is, at root, to lighten. The prefix gives the sense of going beyond the existing level.
en.suréquiper: Formed from ~équiper~ with the prefix ~sur-~ (“over, beyond”), so it means to equip beyond what is needed. The prefix is the French descendant of Latin ~super-~ and often marks excess. The base ~équiper~ comes from Old French ~esquiper~ (“to fit out a ship”), borrowed from Old Norse ~skipa~ (“to arrange, to fit out a vessel”), built on ~skip~ (“ship”). A word first used to rig a boat for a voyage is thus here pushed past the limit: the English cousins ~ship~ and ~skiff~ share its Germanic root.
en.surévaluer: Formed from ~évaluer~ with the prefix ~sur-~, the French form of Latin ~super-~ (“over”), here in its commonest sense of excess: to value something above its worth. ~Évaluer~ comes from Old French ~esvaluer~, built on the noun ~value~, a participle of ~valoir~. That verb goes back to Latin ~valere~ (“to be strong, to be worth”), whose Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂welh₁-~ is shared with English ~wield~.
en.susciter:
From Latin ~suscitāre~ (“to rouse, to stir up, to awaken, to revive”), a compound of the prefix ~sub-~ (here “up from under”) and ~citāre~ (“to set in rapid motion, to summon”). ~citāre~ is the frequentative of ~ciēre~ (“to move, to stir, to call”), which goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~kei-~ (“to set in motion”). That root also yielded Greek ~kīneîn~ (“to move”), the source of ~cinéma~ and ~kinetic~. French borrowed ~susciter~ as a learned term, so its form stayed close to the Latin.

The literal image is of stirring something up from below — rousing a sleeper, reviving the dead, calling a force into being. Old French already used it for arousing emotions or provoking events, and modern ~susciter~ keeps that abstract reach: one ~suscite~ admiration, curiosity, opposition, or a vocation, always evoking something into existence rather than handling it directly. From the same ~ciēre~ family, French gathered a striking crowd of relatives: ~citer~ (“to cite, to summon”), ~exciter~ (“to excite”), ~inciter~ (“to incite”), ~solliciter~ (“to solicit”), ~ressusciter~ (“to resurrect”), and ~récit~ and ~réciter~ (a tale being something “called back”). The same primal idea of motion even powers ~cinématographe~, so the stirred verb and the moving picture share one ancestral impulse.
en.suspecter:
Borrowed from Latin ~suspectāre~ (“to look at with mistrust, to suspect”), a frequentative of ~suspicere~. That verb joined ~sub-~ (“from below”) and ~specere~ (“to look”), so ~suspicere~ meant literally “to look up at from underneath,” and from there “to look up to” or, with a wary eye, “to mistrust.” The root of ~specere~ is the Proto-Indo-European *~spek-~ (“to observe”), shared with German ~spähen~ (“to scout”) and, by way of Frankish and Old French, with English ~spy~.

The frequentative ending ~-tāre~ marks repeated or intense action. The Latin family reached French by two roads. The popular road, through Old French, produced ~soupçon~ and ~soupçonner~. The learned road produced ~suspect~ and the verb ~suspecter~, which therefore sits beside ~soupçonner~ as a near twin in meaning. Elsewhere the same root underlies a large French family, among them ~spectacle~, ~spécimen~, ~inspecter~ and ~respecter~.
en.suspendre:
French ~suspendre~ descends from Latin ~suspendere~ (“to hang up, hang below”), a compound of the prefix ~sub-~ (“under, up from under”) and ~pendere~ (“to hang, to weigh”). ~Pendere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~pendō~ and to Proto-Indo-European *~(s)pend-~ (“to pull, to stretch, to spin”). Through ~pendere~ it is cognate with English ~pendant~, ~pension~, ~ponder~, and ~suspend~ itself, and shares its root with words of weighing and stretching.

The image is concrete — something hung from above, swinging free — and French keeps it: a lamp ~suspendue~ from the ceiling, a bridge ~suspendu~ over a gorge. From there grew the figurative “to interrupt, to leave in abeyance”: to ~suspendre~ a session, a payment, a judgement. The same hanging sense gives ~suspens~ (“abeyance,” as in en suspens) and, borrowed back through English, ~suspense~ — the held breath of a thing not yet resolved. The family also includes ~suspension~ and ~pendule~ (“pendulum, clock”), still literally swinging.
en.sustenter:
A learned calque of Latin ~sustentāre~, the frequentative of ~sustinēre~ (“to hold up, to support”). The Latin verb ~sustinēre~ is made of ~sub-~ (“under”) and ~tenēre~ (“to hold”), so it means literally “to hold from below.” Its frequentative ~sustentāre~, built from the participle stem, already covered both “to support” and “to nourish” in Latin.

French ~tenir~ comes from the same Latin ~tenēre~, and ~soutenir~ is the everyday descendant of ~sustinēre~, while ~sustenter~ is the learned doublet that kept the Latin spelling. The family also gave ~sustentation~, as well as English ~sustain~ and ~sustenance~ and Spanish ~sustentar~. In modern French the verb is rare and survives almost only in the reflexive ~se sustenter~ (“to feed oneself, to eat”), a slightly formal or jocular way to speak of a meal.
en.susurrer:
Borrowed from Latin ~susurrāre~ (“to hum, to buzz”), a verb based on the noun ~susurrus~ (“a murmur, a whisper”), a word that imitates the sound it names. French and English Wiktionary both record it as a direct borrowing from Latin. Italian ~sussurrare~, Spanish ~susurrar~ and English ~susurrus~ all come from the same Latin family.

In French, ~susurrer~ means to whisper or to speak very quietly, often with a hint of intimacy or secrecy. It also describes soft natural sounds such as the rustle of leaves or the murmur of a stream, a use that stays close to the sound-imitating character of the Latin word. French has the related noun ~susurre~ (“a soft murmur”).
en.suturer: Formed from the noun ~suture~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, which turns a noun into a verb: to close a wound with a suture. The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin ~sūtūra~ (“a seam, a stitching”), itself from ~suō~ (“to sew”). It is a learned cousin of the inherited French ~couture~. The ending ~-er~ comes from the Latin first-conjugation ending ~-are~, the default way French coins verbs from nouns.
en.suçoter: Formed from ~sucer~ (“to suck”) with the suffix ~-oter~, which gives a diminutive and repeated sense: to suck lightly and continually. The base verb comes from Vulgar Latin *~suctiare~, derived from ~suctum~, the supine of Latin ~sugere~ (“to suck”). The same Latin verb lies behind ~suçon~ and ~succion~. The suffix ~-oter~ is also found in ~tapoter~ and ~siffloter~.
en.swinguer: ~Swinguer~ is a verb built on ~swing~, a word French borrowed from English ~swing~ (“to sway”), with the ending ~-er~. It means to play, dance or move with the lilting rhythm of swing music, and by extension to be lively or fashionable. Like ~crasher~ and other recent loans, it carries no Latin heritage. The ~u~ in its spelling keeps the hard ~g~ sound before the ending, as in ~naviguer~.
en.symboliser:
~symboliser~ was built on the noun ~symbole~ with the suffix ~-iser~, on the model of medieval Latin ~symbolizāre~, attested from the ninth century in the sense “to agree, to correspond.” The noun goes back through Latin ~symbolum~ to Greek ~σύμβολον~ (~súmbolon~), from ~συμβάλλω~ (~sumbállō~, “to throw together”): ~σύν~ (“with”) plus ~βάλλω~ (“to throw”), the latter from PIE *~gʷelH-~ (“to throw”). And a ~σύμβολον~ was a literal, physical thing: a recognition token — an object such as a knucklebone or a coin snapped in two, each contracting party keeping one half. When the halves were brought together and the break matched, identity and agreement stood proven. Every modern symbol is, etymologically, half of a broken object waiting for its other half.

Strikingly, the verb's first French life followed the medieval Latin sense rather than ours: at its first attestation, around 1512, ~symboliser~ was intransitive and meant “to be in accord, to resemble.” Not until 1615 is it attested as “to represent by a symbol,” and only in 1796 as “to be the symbol of.” The Greek root ~βάλλω~ seeded French with throw-words: ~parabole~ and its astonishing doublet ~parole~ (from Latin ~parabola~ — the comparison “thrown alongside,” which in late Latin came to mean speech itself), ~hyperbole~ (a throw beyond the mark), ~problème~ (a thing thrown forward), ~emblème~ (a thing thrown in, inlaid). English ~symbol~ and ~ballistics~ belong to the same family: matching halves, flying projectiles and figures of speech, all from the art of throwing.
en.sympathiser: Formed from the noun ~sympathie~ with the suffix ~-iser~, which turns a noun or adjective into a verb meaning roughly “to act on, or toward, N”. The noun comes from Latin ~sympathia~, itself from Ancient Greek ~συμπάθεια~ (~sympátheia~). Modern French ~sympathiser~ means to hit it off with someone, to feel an easy fellow feeling for them. The suffix ~-iser~ was borrowed into Old French from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, so Greek stands behind both halves of this word.
en.synchroniser: Formed in French from the adjective ~synchrone~ with the verbal suffix ~-iser~, in the sense “to make synchronous.” The adjective comes through Latin ~synchronus~ (“contemporary”) from Ancient Greek ~sýnkhronos~, made of ~sýn~ (“with”) and ~khrónos~ (“time”), so it means literally “with the time.” The suffix ~-iser~ goes back to Greek-derived verbs in Late Latin and is still very productive for technical verbs. To ~synchroniser~ is to bring two things into the same time, such as clocks, files or dancers.
en.syncoper: ~Syncoper~ is formed from ~syncope~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so “to syncopate.” The noun came into French from Latin ~syncopa~, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~συγκοπή~ (~sunkopḗ~), which combines ~συν-~ (“together”) with ~κόπτειν~ (“to cut”) and means a “cutting short.” In music, to syncopate is to shift the stress off the expected beat.
en.syncristalliser: Formed from ~cristalliser~ with the learned prefix ~syn-~, from Ancient Greek ~σύν~ (~sún~, “with, together”), so the verb means “to crystallize together.” The base is built on ~cristal~ and the suffix ~-iser~. ~Cristal~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~crystallus~ (“ice,” then “rock crystal”), from Greek ~krústallos~ (“ice”), a derivative of ~krúos~ (“frost”). The prefix is rare and belongs to scientific vocabulary.
en.syndicaliser: Formed from ~syndical~ with the verbal suffix ~-iser~, so “to unionize.” The adjective ~syndical~ is itself built on ~syndic~ with ~-al~, and a form ~sindiqual~ is recorded around 1400 as a noun meaning “minutes, official record.” The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and is the usual way to turn an adjective into a verb of making or converting.
en.syndiquer: A French formation with the verb ending ~-er~. fr.Wiktionary derives it from ~syndic~, noting the old spelling ~syndicquer~ and a date of 1768 for the modern sense “to form a union,” while en.Wiktionary derives it from ~syndicat~ (“union”), a noun that itself comes from ~syndic~. Either way the root is ~syndic~, a learned borrowing from Late Latin ~syndicus~ (“representative of a town”), from Greek ~sundikos~ (“advocate of a defendant”), built on ~sun-~ (“together”) and ~dikē~ (“justice”). The ~syndic~ was an officer chosen to defend a community's interests, and ~syndiquer~ means to organize workers into such a collective body.
en.synthétiser:
The two Wiktionaries disagree on the route. French Wiktionary derives ~synthétiser~ from English ~synthesize~, attested in the nineteenth century, while English Wiktionary derives it from French ~synthèse~ (“synthesis”). Both go back to the Ancient Greek ~sýnthesis~ (“a putting together”), from ~syn~ (“together”) and the verb ~títhēmi~ (“to put, to place”), the latter from the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰeh₁-~ (“to put, to do”), which is also the source of English ~do~. The two accounts may not be incompatible, since English could have shaped the verb on French ~synthèse~, but the sources do not settle it.

The idea is the mirror of ~analyse~: to combine elements into a whole rather than to separate a whole into elements. The verb is used in philosophy, in chemistry, where it means to produce a compound by combining simpler ones, and in everyday speech for summarizing. In music the related ~synthétiseur~ (“synthesizer”), an instrument that builds sounds from electronic components, is a twentieth-century word. The Greek verb ~títhēmi~ also gave French ~thèse~, ~hypothèse~ and ~thème~.
en.syntoniser: French ~syntoniser~ is a borrowing from the English verb ~to syntonize~, so its deeper history belongs to English. It is a technical verb, and the French ending ~-iser~ corresponds to the English ending ~-ize~, which reached both languages from the same Late Latin source.
en.systématiser: ~Systématiser~ is formed from the adjective ~systématique~ plus the verb suffix ~-iser~ (“to make A”), so it means “to make systematic” and, by extension, “to organize.” The adjective is a learned borrowing: French took it from Latin ~systematicus~, itself from Ancient Greek ~συστηματικός~ (~sustēmatikós~, “of a system”). The noun ~système~ belongs to the same Greek family.
en.sécher:
From Latin ~siccare~ (“to make dry, to dry up”), a verb built on the adjective ~siccus~ (“dry”). The same ~siccare~ gives the Romance verbs of drying — Italian ~seccare~, Spanish ~secar~, Portuguese ~secar~ — and the French adjective ~sec~ (“dry”) descends straight from ~siccus~. French keeps a tidy cluster of derivatives around the verb: ~assécher~ (“to drain dry”), ~dessécher~ (“to desiccate”), ~séchage~ (“drying”), and ~sécheresse~ (“dryness, drought”).

From the plain physical sense, French built a vivid metaphor. A student who, faced with a question, knows nothing is said to ~sécher~ — to “dry up,” to run blank, as if the well of memory had gone empty; this is the “see-through” blankness behind the English gloss. From the late nineteenth century, school and military slang extended ~sécher~ to mean skipping a class altogether — ~sécher~ un cours — attested in student argot by the 1890s. The exact path from “to dry up” to “to play truant” is not securely documented, so we note the link without inventing a mechanism for it.
en.sécréter: ~Sécréter~ is formed from the noun ~sécrétion~, which is itself borrowed from Latin ~sēcrētiōnem~ (“separation”). English Wiktionary calls the verb a back-formation, which means the noun came first and the verb was cut out of it afterwards. French Wiktionary simply describes it as derived from ~sécrétion~. The sense “to separate off” is the one the biological term keeps: a gland sets a substance apart from the blood and releases it.
en.séculariser: Formed from ~séculaire~ with the suffix ~-iser~, the verb means to take something out of religious control, or to release a religious person from a community. ~Séculaire~ is borrowed from Latin ~saeculāris~, from ~saeculum~ (“generation, century”), and is a doublet of ~séculier~. A priest of the secular clergy lives “in the century”, that is, in the world among his fellow citizens, rather than in a monastery as a monk of the regular clergy does. That is the sense that ~séculariser~ takes up.
en.sécuriser:
A modern French formation, built from the stem of ~sécurité~ (or ~sécur-~) plus the productive verbal suffix ~-iser~. The ancestor is Latin ~sēcūrus~ (“free from care, untroubled, safe”), a transparent compound of ~sē-~ (“without, apart”) and ~cūra~ (“care, worry”): to be ~sēcūrus~ was literally to be “without a care.” Through Old French this same ~sēcūrus~ also gave the everyday adjective ~sûr~ (“sure, safe”), so that ~sûr~ and the learned ~sécurité~ are doublets, the popular and the scholarly descendants of one Latin word. English ~secure~ and ~sure~ form the very same pair.

The verb itself is strikingly recent: the adjective ~sécurisant~ appeared in the late 1950s, and the transitive ~sécuriser~ followed around 1969, first in a psychological sense — to ~sécuriser~ someone was to set their mind at ease, to free them from anxiety, true to the Latin “without care.” Only later did it broaden to the concrete senses now dominant — to ~sécuriser~ a building, a network, a payment. The same ~cūra~ underlies ~curieux~, ~cure~, ~soin~ via a different path, ~assurer~, and ~procurer~.
en.sédentariser: Formed from the adjective ~sédentaire~ and the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to make sedentary, to settle” (a nomadic people, for instance). The adjective is a learned borrowing from Latin ~sedentārius~ (“sitting”), itself derived from ~sedēre~ (“to sit”). The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and it is fully productive in modern French for verbs meaning “make A” or “convert into N.” The verb therefore means, in effect, to make a people or a person “sit down” in one place.
en.sédimenter: Formed from the noun ~sédiment~ plus the verb ending ~-er~: to ~sédimenter~ is to form a sediment, to settle out as a deposit. The noun is borrowed from Latin ~sedimentum~, from ~sedēre~ (“to sit, to settle”), so a sediment is what sits down at the bottom of a liquid. The same Latin verb gives ~seoir~ and ~asseoir~. The ending ~-er~ turns the noun into a verb of doing, and the verb is used both of particles in water and, figuratively, of knowledge or experience that gradually accumulates.
en.séduire:
From Latin ~seducere~ (“to lead aside, lead away”), a compound of the prefix ~se-~ (“apart, away”) and ~ducere~ (“to lead, draw”). The verb ~ducere~ descends from PIE *~dewk-~ (“to draw, pull, lead”), the root behind English ~tow~ and the whole ~-duce~ family — ~produce~, ~reduce~, ~conduct~. Romance cognates of the compound include Spanish ~seducir~ and Italian ~sedurre~; English ~seduce~ comes from the same Latin word.

The Latin sense was literal and often political or military: to draw someone aside, to lead troops or followers away from their allegiance. That sense of leading astray darkened in Old French into moral corruption and deception — to ~séduire~ was first to mislead or debauch. Only later did the word soften toward its dominant modern meaning, “to charm, to attract irresistibly,” while keeping an edge of the old “leading astray.” A landscape or an idea can ~séduire~ as easily as a person. From the same ~ducere~ French keeps ~conduire~, ~produire~, ~réduire~, and the noun ~séduction~.
en.ségréger:
From Latin ~segregāre~, “to separate, to set apart.” The Latin verb is built from ~sē-~ (“apart”) and ~grex~, ~gregis~ (“flock”), so its original picture is that of cutting an animal off from the flock. French took it as a learned word, with the ending adapted to the first conjugation, and kept the Latin sense nearly intact.

The Latin noun ~grex~ is the root of a sizeable French family. ~Grégaire~ describes what lives in flocks, and ~agréger~ and ~congréger~ are built on the same root with other prefixes, “to add to the flock” and “to gather into one.” English shares the family through ~segregate~, ~aggregate~ and ~congregate~. ~Ségréger~ is a fairly rare, formal verb, found mostly in social contexts where groups are kept apart, and it is much less common than the noun ~ségrégation~.
en.ségréguer:
From Latin ~segregāre~ (“to set apart”). The Latin verb is built from the prefix ~sē-~ (“apart, away”) and ~grex~ (“flock, herd”), so to segregate is, at the root, to separate from the flock. French took it as a learned verb, and in modern French it means to practise segregation, to keep a group apart from the rest. Italian ~segregare~ and Spanish ~segregar~ come from the same Latin verb, as does English ~segregate~.

The root ~grex~ underlies a whole family of French words. The noun ~ségrégation~ is the learned relative of ~ségréguer~. ~Grégaire~, from the Latin adjective ~gregārius~ (“of the flock”), describes what lives in herds, while ~agréger~ and ~congrégation~ draw flocks together, the opposite movement from ~ségréguer~, which sets apart. One image of the flock thus runs in both directions, gathering and parting.
en.séjourner:
From Old French ~sojorner~, whose first vowel became ~é~ in French by dissimilation, inherited from Vulgar Latin *~subdiurnāre~. That verb was built from Latin ~sub-~ (“under, a little over”) and Late Latin ~diurnus~ (“lasting for a day”), so the picture is of staying on for a stretch of days. Latin ~diurnus~ is the adjective of ~dies~ (“day”), and its neuter noun ~diurnum~ gave French ~jour~. English borrowed the verb from the Old French family as ~sojourn~, a literary word for a temporary stay.

The verb thus began as “to spend some days somewhere” and settled into the sense “to stay for a while,” a stay that is longer than a visit and shorter than a residence. French uses it in the language of travel and administration: ~séjourner à l'hôtel~, ~un séjour linguistique~, ~un titre de séjour~ (“a residence permit”). The noun ~séjour~ came from the same Old French verb, and the hidden ~jour~ in the middle is the reason ~séjourner~ also sits beside ~journée~, ~journal~ (originally “a daily thing”) and ~ajourner~ (“to put off to another day”).
en.sélecter:
French ~sélecter~ is taken from the English verb ~to select~. French Wiktionary traces that English verb in turn to Latin ~sēligere~ and its participle ~sēlectum~ (“to set apart”). The Latin verb combines ~sē-~ (“apart”) and ~legere~ (“to choose, to gather”), so the idea at the root is to pick something out and put it to one side. The learned French family of ~sélection~, ~sélectif~ and ~sélectionner~ comes from the same Latin source.

~Sélecter~ stands beside the far more usual ~sélectionner~, which does the same job: to choose one or several items from among others. Latin ~legere~ is the source of several French word families. It gave ~lire~ by the inherited route, and ~élire~ (“to elect”) and ~lecture~ belong to the same family. The pair ~élire~ and ~sélectionner~ shows two ways of picking out, one with the prefix ~ex-~ and one with ~sē-~, both built on the same verb.
en.sélectionner:
A nineteenth-century formation from the noun ~sélection~, from Latin ~selectio~ (“a choosing out”), the action noun of ~seligere~ (“to choose out, to single out, to cull”). ~seligere~ is a compound of ~se-~ (“apart, aside”) and ~legere~ (“to gather, to pick, to read”), so its literal sense is “to gather apart.” ~legere~ goes back to PIE *~leǵ-~ (“to collect, to gather”). Cognate, through the same Latin verb, with English ~select~ and Italian ~selezionare~.

The ~legere~ at its core is one of the most generous roots in the language: the act of “picking out” specialized in Latin into reading (picking out letters), and *~leǵ-~ underlies a striking spread of French words — ~lire~, ~élire~, ~collection~, ~légende~ (“things to be read”), and, through the Greek branch of the same root, ~lexique~ and ~dialogue~. ~sélectionner~ itself is the youngest layer: where the older ~choisir~ (a Germanic borrowing) simply picks, ~sélectionner~ carries the cooler, more deliberate flavour of choosing the best from a set — a coach who ~sélectionne~ players, a process of natural ~sélection~. The doublet ~élire~ shows the same ~legere~ worn smooth by centuries of everyday use, while ~sélectionner~ keeps the crisp Latin consonants of a learned, modern coinage.
en.séparer:
Borrowed in 1314 from Latin ~separāre~ (“to pull apart, to divide”), a learned doublet of the inherited French verb ~sevrer~ (“to wean”). The Latin verb joins ~se-~ (“apart, aside”) to ~parāre~ (“to make ready, to procure”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~perh₃-~ (“to produce, to procure”). Cognates abound: Italian ~separare~, Spanish ~separar~, English ~separate~ and its Frenchified doublet ~sever~.

The curious point is that French inherited the same Latin verb twice. The ordinary popular descendant of ~separāre~ is ~sevrer~, which narrowed to the specific sense of separating a child or young animal from the breast — to wean — while the scholarly re-borrowing ~séparer~ kept the broad Latin meaning, to set apart. Such pairs, one worn down by centuries of speech and one taken straight from books, are doublets, and ~séparer~/~sevrer~ is a textbook case. The verb branched into ~séparation~ (including the legal ~séparation de corps~, a separation short of divorce), ~séparé~, ~séparément~, ~séparateur~, and the political ~séparatisme~. The second element ~parāre~ is itself remarkably fertile, lying behind ~préparer~, ~réparer~, ~emparer~, and — through the related ~parere~ (“to give birth, to bring forth”) — the family of ~parent~.
en.séquencer: Formed from the noun ~séquence~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~, which turns a noun into a first-conjugation verb. The base ~séquence~ is borrowed from Late Latin ~sequentia~, which comes from Latin ~sequēns~, the present participle of ~sequī~ (“to follow”). The verb therefore rests on the idea of things that follow one another in order. The ending ~-er~ itself descends from Latin ~-are~, the first-conjugation infinitive ending.
en.séquestrer: ~Séquestrer~ comes from Latin ~sequestrare~, according to French Wiktionary; English Wiktionary gives no etymology. The Latin verb is a derivative of ~sequester~, a word for a neutral third party who held disputed property, and French has the noun ~séquestre~ for the legal deposit of a contested thing with such a keeper. Everyday French uses the verb for confining someone against their will, with the noun ~séquestration~.
en.sérancer: Formed from the noun ~séran~ (“flax or hemp comb”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, so it means to comb flax or hemp. The noun appears in Old French as ~cerens~, ~serang~ and ~serence~, and goes back to Gaulish *~cērā~ (“comb”). It has cognates in Old Irish ~cír~ and Manx ~kere~. The Gaulish word also gave Romansh ~tschareschar~, “to hackle.”
en.sérier: Formed from the noun ~série~ (“series”) with the verb ending ~-er~: to arrange things in a series. ~Série~ is borrowed from Latin ~seriēs~ (“chain, row, succession”), a word tied to ~serere~ (“to join, to link”), so the root image is one of things strung together in a line. The verb is learned and technical, and it describes sorting items into an ordered sequence.
en.sévir:
French ~sévir~ is a borrowing from Latin ~saevīre~ (“to rage, to be furious, to rampage”), the verb of the adjective ~saevus~ (“fierce, savage”). The Latin word described wild animals, storms, soldiers and tyrants in the grip of violence, and French took it over directly as a learned word rather than inheriting it. The same Latin family gave the noun ~saevitia~ (“cruelty”), from which French drew ~sévices~ (“physical abuse”), a legal term still in daily use.

In French, ~sévir~ kept the sense of violence but narrowed it to two main uses. The first is of a disaster or scourge that rages: a storm, an epidemic, a famine, or a drought ~sévit~. The second is of an authority that acts firmly against wrongdoing, as when a government or a school ~sévit~ against offenders, hence “to crack down.” The adjective ~sévère~, which looks like a relative, comes from a different Latin word, ~sevērus~ (“strict, serious”), so the resemblance is partly a coincidence of sound. The verb keeps the ancient Roman picture of raging violence, now applied equally to nature and to discipline.
en.tabasser: The origin of ~tabasser~ is explained in two ways. French Wiktionary derives it from Occitan ~tabassar~, of the same meaning. English Wiktionary instead analyses it as ~tabac~ plus the suffix ~-asser~, and refers to the expression ~passer à tabac~ (“to beat up”) and to ~taper~. The sources do not decide between the two, so the origin should be treated as uncertain. Either way, the verb belongs to the familiar register and means to thrash or beat someone up.
en.tabler: Formed in French from the noun ~table~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is inherited from Old French ~table~, from Latin ~tabula~ (“board, tablet”), which is also the source of the doublets ~tôle~ and ~taule~. The modern sense of ~tabler sur~, “to count on, to rely on”, is a figurative development of the noun, and the sources I used do not spell out the steps in between.
en.tabouiser: ~Tabouiser~ is built on ~tabou~ (“taboo”) with the suffix ~-iser~, and it means to consider something taboo. The TLFi treats it under the older ~tabouer~, which dates from the 1780s, when travel accounts of Oceania spoke of things declared taboo, and which was formed on ~tabou~ partly after English. In the 20th century the verb moved from Pacific customs to our own societies, as in Cocteau's journal of 1953, where the press treats a play as taboo. It remains rare.
en.tacher: The usual account makes ~tacher~ a verb built on the noun ~tache~ (“stain”), but English Wiktionary has it inherited from Old French ~tachier~ and Vulgar Latin *~tagicare~, so the direction of derivation is uncertain. The origin of the noun is itself debated. One hypothesis derives it from Gothic ~taikns~ (“sign”), a relative of German ~Zeichen~, though the leap from “sign” to “stain” is hard to follow. Another sees ~tache~ as a back-formation from the verb, with *~tagicare~ built on Latin ~tangere~ (“to touch”) and the variant Old French ~techier~ from *~tigicare~, from ~tingere~ (“to dye”). The sources do not settle the matter.
en.tacheter: Formed from ~tache~ (“spot, mark”) with ~-eter~ (~-et~ + ~-er~), a verb ending that often carries a small-scale sense: to mark with little spots. The origin of ~tache~ itself is disputed. One account derives it from Gothic ~taikns~ (“sign”) through Vulgar Latin *~tacca~, though French Wiktionary doubts that “sign” explains the many Romance senses. The other makes it a back-formation from Old French ~tachier~, linked to Vulgar Latin *~tagicare~ (from ~tangere~, “to touch”), while the variant ~techier~ would come from *~tigicare~ (from ~tingere~, “to dye”).
en.tacler: ~Tacler~ is formed from the noun ~tacle~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, which comes from Latin ~-are~ and is the default way French coins a verb from a noun. ~Tacle~ is itself a borrowing from English: French Wiktionary traces it to the English verb ~to tackle~ (“to grab, to take on an opponent, to intercept”). The French verb therefore reached French in two steps, first the noun taken from English, then a verb built on that noun.
en.taguer: ~Taguer~ is formed from ~tag~ with the ending ~-er~: to mark a surface with a tag, the stylized signature of graffiti writers. The noun ~tag~ was borrowed from English ~tag~. French thus took the word in its modern graffiti sense and gave it a regular first-conjugation verb.
en.taillader: Formed from ~taillade~ (“gash, slash”) plus the verbal ending ~-er~ (from Latin ~-are~). The noun ~taillade~ was borrowed from Italian ~tagliata~ (“cut”), and it belongs to the large French family of ~taille~ and ~tailler~, words about cutting. To ~taillader~ is therefore to make slashes in something.
en.tailler:
From Old French ~talier~ (10th century), from Late Latin ~taliare~ (“to cut, to split”), derived from Latin ~talea~ (“a cutting, slip, scion; rod, stake”) — the slip of wood a gardener slices off to replant. A Vulgar Latin ~taliatura~ (“pruning of trees”) confirms the agricultural cradle of the word. The deeper origin of ~talea~ is disputed: it is traditionally referred to PIE *~teh₂l-~ (“to grow; young shoot”), with a proposed Greek cognate ~tâlis~ (“nubile girl”) whose very existence has been questioned; an alternative ties it to ~tālus~ (“ankle”).

The verb began in horticulture — to cut and prune — then spread to every kind of shaping: cutting stone, tailoring cloth, faceting a gem, dealing cards. The same root yields a rich crop in French: ~taille~ (“cut, size, waist”), ~tailleur~ (“tailor, suit”), ~entaille~ (“notch”), ~détail~ (literally “a cutting up” into small parts), and the compounds ~taille-crayon~ (“pencil sharpener”) and ~tailloir~. Italian ~tagliare~ and Spanish ~tajar~ descend from the very same ~taliare~.
en.taire:
From Latin ~tacēre~ (“to be silent, to hold one's tongue”), from Proto-Italic *~takēō~ and PIE *~tHk-~ (“to be silent”).
