Old French had the regular form ~taisir~, which by the 12th century was reshaped into ~taire~ along the same path that turned ~plaisir~ into ~plaire~ — the noun-like infinitive yielding to the short verb. ~taisir~ itself faded out by the 15th century. Cognate with Italian ~tacere~ and Romanian ~tăcea~; the Germanic side of the same root shows in Gothic ~þahan~ and Old Norse ~þegja~. Spanish ~callar~ (“to be silent”), despite the matching sense, comes from a wholly different source.

The verb's meaning has stayed remarkably steady: to ~taire~ is to keep silent about something, and the reflexive ~se taire~ (“to fall silent, to shut up”) is one of the commonest verbs in spoken French. Where most Romance languages let the active verb survive, English kept only the adjectival branch: from the Latin participle ~tacitus~ (“silent”) come English ~tacit~ and ~taciturn~, the French ~tacite~ and ~taciturne~, and the legal ~tacitement~. So a ~tacit~ agreement is, at root, one that has kept quiet — the very thing ~taire~ asks you to do.
en.taler: Old French ~taler~ is the source, and French Wiktionary gives no further chain. English Wiktionary traces it to Frankish *~tālōn~ (“to tear away, rip off”), reaching French by way of Latin; Spanish ~talar~ is cited as a comparison. Behind the Frankish form lies Proto-Germanic *~tēlō~ (“persecution, deceit”). Cognates are Old High German ~zâlôn~ (“to root up, remove”) and Old English ~tǣl~ (“reproof, calumny, mockery”). The modern sense, damaging a fruit, is far from these, and the sources do not say how it developed.
en.taller: Formed from the noun ~talle~ (“sucker, side shoot”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to put out shoots from the base,” as cereals and grasses do. The noun ~talle~ comes from Latin ~thallus~, itself from Ancient Greek ~thallós~ (“young shoot”). The same Greek word is the source of the botanical term ~thalle~ in French. The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, forms verbs of the type “produce or grow” the noun. The verb is a technical word of agriculture and gardening.
en.talocher: Formed from ~taloche~ with the verb ending ~-er~: to clout or thump, as with a blow of the hand. The origin of the base is given two ways. French Wiktionary derives ~taloche~ from ~taler~ with a popular suffix ~-oche~, and also notes an Old French ~taloche~ (“small shield”). English Wiktionary, citing Rey, says it is first attested in 1320 as a resuffixation of Old French ~talevaz~ (1155), itself from Latin ~talapacium~, which in turn was from Gaulish. The sources thus differ, and the Gaulish route remains one account among others.
en.talonner: ~Talonner~ is formed from ~talon~ (“heel”) plus the verb ending ~-er~, according to English Wiktionary, while French Wiktionary traces it to Old French ~taluner~. The noun ~talon~ is generally traced to Vulgar Latin ~talō~, from Latin ~talus~ (“ankle”). The verb covers several senses that start from the heel: to dig the heels into a horse's flanks, to follow someone closely at their heels, and, by extension, to hound or press someone.
en.talquer: ~Talquer~ is formed from ~talc~ and the verbal ending ~-er~: to powder or coat something with talc. The noun entered the Académie's dictionary in 1694. Its origin is traced differently by the two main sources: French Wiktionary derives it from Arabic ~ṭalq~, while English Wiktionary goes through Persian ~talq~, itself from a Middle Persian word meaning “medicament.”
en.tambouriner: Formed from ~tambourin~ (“small drum”) plus the verbal ending ~-er~ (from Latin ~-are~), meaning to drum. The noun ~tambourin~ is itself built on ~tambour~ with the suffix ~-in~, so the verb adds a second French step to a noun that was already a diminutive.
en.tamiser: ~Tamiser~ is formed from ~tamis~ (“sieve”) with the ending ~-er~. The noun is usually traced through Old French ~tamis~ and Late Latin ~tamisium~ to a Frankish word, *~tamisu~, a source it shares with English ~temse~. French Wiktionary also mentions, as an alternative, an Arabic origin. The verb means “to sift,” and by extension “to filter,” so that one can ~tamiser~ flour, a sound or the light through a curtain, which is how ~lumière tamisée~ came to mean soft, diffused light.
en.tamponner: Formed from the noun ~tampon~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is a nasalized variant of ~tapon~, from Frankish *~tappō~ (“plug”), itself from Proto-Germanic *~tappô~ (“plug, tap”). Dutch ~tappe~, German ~Zapfen~ and English ~tap~ are cognates. So ~tamponner~ is a French verb whose base is a plug inherited from a Germanic word.
en.tancer:
From Old French ~tencier~, from Vulgar Latin *~tentiāre~. The sources differ on the deeper link. English Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~tentus~, the past participle of ~tendō~ (“to stretch”), while French Wiktionary connects it to ~tentāre~ (“to try, to tempt”) and, further back, to ~tendere~. Both routes lead to the same root, so the origin is best described as a Vulgar Latin verb built on the ~tend-~ family. The Occitan form ~tençar~ is a close parallel.

The root of ~tendō~ is productive in French: ~tendre~ (“to stretch”), ~tension~, ~tendance~ and ~attendre~ all belong to it, and English ~tend~ and ~tense~ come from the same Latin source. ~Tancer~ is a literary and slightly old-fashioned verb meaning “to scold, to reprimand, to rebuke,” most often found in the phrase ~tancer vertement~ (“to scold sharply”).
en.tanguer: The origin of ~tanguer~ is uncertain. One account derives it from the noun ~tangue~, a Norman word attested from the late twelfth century and taken from Old Norse ~þang~ (“seaweed”), but French Wiktionary notes that it is hard to see how “to run aground in ~tangue~” could lead to “to sway.” The other account, given by both Wiktionaries, is a probable borrowing from Old Frisian ~tüngeln~ (“to sway”), related to English ~dangle~ and Swedish ~dingla~. Today ~tanguer~ describes a ship pitching bow to stern, or anything rocking back and forth.
en.taniser: Formed from ~tan~ (bark ground for tanning hides) with the suffix ~-iser~, “to treat with, to make like.” It is first recorded in 1877, spelled ~tanniser~, in a general manual on wine. The sense is to enrich a wine in tannin, the substance that gives it its dry, astringent grip, so a word born in the tanner's workshop ended up in the winemaker's cellar.
en.tanner: ~Tanner~ is a denominal verb: the noun ~tan~ plus the ending ~-er~, meaning to treat hides with tan. The noun, the crushed bark used in tanning, came from Old French ~tan~, from Latin ~tannum~ (“oak bark”), from Gaulish *~tannos~ (“oak”), from Proto-Celtic *~tannos~ (“green oak”). French Wiktionary prefers this Gaulish origin to a link with German ~Tanne~ (“fir”), because tan is made from oak bark, not fir bark. The Occitan verb ~tanar~ has the same sense.
en.tanniser: Formed from ~tan~ with the suffix ~-iser~, a suffix from Late Latin ~-izāre~ that makes verbs meaning “to treat with.” The TLFi dates ~tanniser~ to 1877, in a general manual on wine by Robinet, and the verb means “to make richer in tannin.” It is thus a technical word of the winemaker's trade, coined to name the act of adding tannin to a wine. The sources do not trace the origin of ~tan~ itself, so the account stops there.
en.tanquer: Borrowed from Occitan ~tancar~ (“to close, to shut”), a verb that Catalan shares as ~tancar~. The meanings of the French verb, “to drive in, to get stuck, to crash,” are far from shutting, and the sources give no account of how that shift came about, so none is offered here.
en.tapager: ~Tapager~ (“to make a racket”) is formed from the noun ~tapage~ (“din, uproar”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to make a ~tapage~.” In turn, ~tapage~ is built on the verb ~taper~ (“to hit”) with the suffix ~-age~, which turns an action into a noun: the noise is that of things being banged. The verb is thus two steps removed from ~taper~, and it keeps the idea of noise made by repeated knocking.
en.taper:
First attested in the 13th century, French ~taper~ rests on an onomatopoeia ~tap~, imitating a short dull knock — the sound itself is the etymology, as the TLFi makes plain, deriving it from an onomatopoeic stem ~tapp-~ evoking a brief muffled noise. Beyond that imitative core the comparisons grow uncertain: the philologist Friedrich Diez linked it to a Germanic family — German ~tappen~ (“to grope, pad”), Dutch ~deppen~, and English ~dab~ — but this kinship is a proposed connection attributed to Diez, not an established line of descent, and is best presented as such rather than as fact.

The meaning fans out from the basic “to strike, knock”: to ~taper~ on the table, to ~taper~ someone (slap them), to ~taper~ dans le ballon (“to kick the ball”), and colloquially “to cadge” money. The most modern branch — “to type” on a keyboard — simply transfers the percussive striking of keys to the older verb of striking. French relatives and offshoots include ~tape~ (“a slap”), ~tapoter~ (“to tap lightly, to pat”), and ~tapette~. Whether any of these ultimately joins a wider Indo-European family remains, on the evidence, an open question rather than a settled one.
en.tapiner: ~Tapiner~ is a verb made from ~tapin~ with the ending ~-er~, in the sense of working the street as a prostitute, hence “to work, to labor” in slang. The noun ~tapin~ is formed from ~taper~ (“to strike”) with the suffix ~-in~. Its older sense was a soldier who beats the drum to draw a crowd, and the sense of street soliciting is said to derive from that one.
en.tapir: Inherited from Old French ~tapir~, which was borrowed from Frankish *~tappijan~ (“to close, to shut in”), from Proto-Germanic *~tappijaną~, itself related to *~tappô~ (“tap, plug”). The original sense was therefore physical, “to stop up, to shut away,” and it moved toward the modern meaning of “to hide, to crouch out of sight,” used mostly in the pronominal form ~se tapir~. The animal called ~tapir~ in both French and English is unrelated: it comes from a language of Brazil.
en.tapisser: Formed from ~tapis~ (“carpet, rug”) and the verb ending ~-er~, with the ~s~ doubled so that it stays pronounced /s/ between vowels. The noun ~tapis~ came through Middle French ~tapiz~ and ultimately from Greek: late Greek ~tapētion~ (“small cover”) is a diminutive of Greek ~tapēs~ (“carpet, rug”), itself an Eastern word of obscure origin, perhaps Iranian. ~Tapisser~ first meant to cover a wall or a floor with fabric, and so it came to mean covering any surface with a decorative layer, as in a wall ~tapissé~ with posters or ivy.
en.tapoter: From ~taper~ (“to strike”) with the frequentative and diminutive suffix ~-oter~, which makes a light action repeated in small bursts. ~Taper~ is first attested in the 13th century and rests on an onomatopoeia, ~tap~, imitating a short, dull knock. A link to Germanic words such as German ~tappen~ and English ~dab~ was proposed by Friedrich Diez, but it remains a proposal, not an established line of descent. So ~tapoter~ is “to strike a little, again and again,” as in drumming fingers on a table.
en.taquer: The origin of ~taquer~ is uncertain, and French Wiktionary offers two accounts: it is probably imitative, from the sound ~tac~, or else it comes from Latin ~tangere~ (“to touch”). For the printing term, the same source considers it probably from Old French ~tac~ (“nail, peg”). The Latin ~tangere~ also lies behind French ~tangent~ and ~contact~.
en.taquiner: ~Taquiner~ is formed from ~taquin~ with the ending ~-er~. The noun has an unexpected history. According to French Wiktionary, it comes from Old French ~taquehan~ (“illicit gathering of workers, rioter”), then ~tacain~ (“beggar, bandit”), and finally ~taquin~ (“miser”), and the Old French word comes from Middle Dutch ~takehan~, made of ~taken~ (“to take, to grasp”) and ~Han~ (“John”). Littré offered rival accounts, one from a root ~tac~ (“nail”) and one from an officer named Taquin at the court of Louis XI, but the Wiktionaries retain the Dutch origin.
en.tarabiscoter: ~Tarabiscoter~ is a denominal verb formed from ~tarabiscot~ and the ending ~-er~. The origin of ~tarabiscot~ itself is obscure; French Wiktionary refers the reader to ~tarabistouiller~ and ~tarabuster~, which belong to the same puzzling family. The verb is therefore a plain French formation on a base whose own history nobody has explained.
en.tarabuster: ~Tarabuster~ goes back to Old French ~tarrabaster~ or ~tarabustis~ (“uproar, commotion, tumult”), a word related to the verb ~tabuster~ (“to be noisy”). French Wiktionary dates the verb, in the sense of making a racket, to 1562 and points to ~tarabistouiller~ as a related word. The older meaning is all noise and disturbance, and from that disturbance the verb came to mean to pester or bother someone.
en.tarauder: The verb is formed from the noun ~taraud~ (a tap, the tool that cuts a thread) and the verbal ending ~-er~, and it means to work something with a ~taraud~, as when a nut is tapped. The noun's own origin is told two ways. French Wiktionary derives ~taraud~ from ~tarière~ (“auger”), with the suffix ~-aud~ swapped in. English Wiktionary calls it an alteration of ~tareau~ with a change of suffix. Both accounts agree that the ending was substituted, so the tool's name is a reshaped older word rather than a fresh coinage.
en.tarder:
From Latin ~tardāre~ (“to slow, to delay, to hinder”), derived from the adjective ~tardus~ (“slow, late”). The origin of ~tardus~ is debated: it is sometimes traced to Proto-Italic *~tardo-~ from PIE *~terh₂-~ (“to cross over, to pass through,” hence perhaps “drawn out, long in passing”), but De Vaan judges this uncertain for want of cognates carrying the “slow” sense, and an Etruscan origin has occasionally been proposed instead. So the deep root is genuinely unsettled, not fixed.

The meaning shifted from Latin “to slow, to impede” toward French “to be slow in coming, to be late,” and especially the impersonal turn that voices impatience: ~il me tarde de~ (“I can hardly wait to”), where lateness is felt from the waiting side. From the same family French keeps ~tard~ (“late”), ~tardif~ (“tardy, belated”), ~retard~ (“delay”) and ~retarder~ (“to delay”), ~attarder~ (“to linger”), and the musical ~retardement~. Italian ~tardare~ and Spanish ~tardar~ are its Romance siblings, and English ~tardy~ borrowed the same Latin adjective through Old French ~tardif~.
en.tarer: Formed from the noun ~tare~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun was borrowed from Italian ~tara~ (Medieval Latin ~tara~ or Italian, says English Wiktionary), from Arabic ~ṭarḥ~ (“rubbish, refuse”), itself from the verb ~ṭaraḥa~ (“to reject, to deduct”). The French verb covers the senses “to spoil, to tarnish” and “to tare”.
en.targuer:
~Targuer~ is formed from ~targe~, an old word for a small shield, and it reaches French through Old French ~targier~. French Wiktionary suggests, with a hedge, that Occitan ~targar~ may have shaped the French form. In older texts the verb was an ordinary active verb meaning “to cover, to protect”. English ~target~ is a related descendant of the same shield word.

Until the end of the sixteenth century, ~se targuer~ kept its literal sense of “to cover oneself with a ~targe~”, and by extension “to defend oneself”. Then, in the seventeenth century, the meaning moved one step further along the road of metaphor, and ~se targuer de~ came to mean “to take advantage of, to pride oneself on”. French Wiktionary also notes that the verb narrowed over time from a free verb to one that is almost only reflexive.
en.tarifer: ~Tarifer~ is a denominal verb: the noun ~tarif~ plus the ending ~-er~, with the meaning to fix the price of something. The noun is of Arabic origin, from ~taʿrīf~ (“description, information, definition”), and reached French by way of Italian ~tariffa~. English Wiktionary adds that Spanish ~tarifa~ is a possible route, and that Ottoman Turkish and Persian forms lay between the Arabic and the European languages.
en.tarir:
~Tarir~ comes from Middle and Old French ~tarir~, borrowed from Frankish *~þarʀijan~ (“to dry”), which descends from Proto-Germanic *~þarzijaną~ and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ters-~. Frankish was the Germanic language of the Franks, who gave France its name, so the verb is one of the words French took from its Germanic conquerors. Cognates include German ~dörren~ and Icelandic ~þerra~. French Wiktionary also compares English ~thirst~ and German ~Durst~, as well as Latin ~torreō~.

The modern verb says that a spring, a river or a well dries up, and by extension that a supply is exhausted or used up. It has a family of its own in ~tarissement~, ~tarissable~ and ~intarissable~ (“inexhaustible”). A spring that runs dry and a throat that thirsts are thus linked by one root, if the comparison with ~thirst~ holds. On the Latin side, ~torreō~ gave French ~torride~ and ~torréfier~.
en.tartiner: ~Tartiner~ is formed from the noun ~tartine~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, in the common sense “to apply N.” ~Tartine~, a slice of bread with something spread on it, is itself built on ~tarte~ with the suffix ~-ine~. The verb means to spread something on bread or other food.
en.tartir: By French Wiktionary, the verb comes from Italian slang ~tartire~. The source gives no further account of that word or of how it reached French, so nothing more is claimed here. In French it is a vulgar word, meaning “to defecate.”
en.tasser: ~Tasser~ is formed from the noun ~tas~ (“heap”) and the verbal ending ~-er~: to pile up, then to pack down. The origin of ~tas~ itself is uncertain. The most common account traces it to a Frankish word *~tas~ (“heap, mass”), a cousin of Dutch ~tas~ (“heap”) and of Middle English ~taas~. French Wiktionary also notes that Littré and Scheler separated two words, one meaning “heap” and one meaning “anvil, block,” and that another proposal links the heap-word to Latin ~stāre~, but the TLFi does not follow the split. The suffix ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and turns the noun into an action.
en.tatouer: A borrowing from English ~tattoo~, itself a Polynesian word that English took from the voyages of Captain James Cook, who wrote it down as “tat-tow.” Its precise source is uncertain. French Wiktionary proposes either Marquesan ~tatu~ (“marking of the skin”) or Tahitian ~ta tau~, built on ~ta~ (“to incise”). Whichever it was, the word travelled from the Pacific to English ships and then to French, which turned it into an ordinary first-conjugation verb with the ending ~-er~. Tattooing itself is far older than the word; the Pacific name simply displaced earlier terms in the European languages.
en.tauder: Formed from ~taud~ (an awning, especially a ship's) and the verbal suffix ~-er~, so the verb means “to rig an awning.” The noun ~taud~ comes from Old French ~tialz~ (“awning, tent set up on a ship”), borrowed from Old Norse ~tjald~ (“tent”), itself from Proto-Germanic *~teldą~ (“drape, tent”). A seafaring word of Norse origin, then, turned into a verb of the shipboard trade.
en.taxer:
Taken from Latin ~taxāre~ (“to estimate, to rate”, also “to censure”) through Old French ~taxer~, which replaced an older, more popular form ~tausser~. The Latin verb is often explained as a frequentative of ~tangere~ (“to touch”), but that link is only a proposal. French ~taux~ (“rate”) belongs to the same family, and English ~tax~ is the French verb passed on across the Channel.

The core idea is to fix the value or amount of something. From there ~taxer~ came to mean to set a price or duty, and then to impose a tax on goods or people. A second, figurative line developed alongside: ~taxer~ quelqu'un de lâcheté is to charge him with cowardice, that is, to put a label on him as one rates an article. In slang, ~taxer~ also means to cadge or scrounge something from someone. The family includes ~taxe~, ~taxation~, ~surtaxer~ and ~détaxer~, and also ~taxi~, which is a shortening of ~taximètre~, the meter that reckons the fare.
en.tayloriser: ~Tayloriser~ is formed from the name ~Taylor~, borrowed from English, with the suffix ~-iser~ (“to treat according to”). It means to organize work according to Taylorism, the scientific management of labor. The suffix comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, itself from Greek.
en.tchatcher: Formed from the noun ~tchatche~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. ~Tchatche~ is slang of the French settlers of Algeria (the ~pieds-noirs~), derived from Spanish ~cháchara~ (“lively but idle conversation”). The verb therefore means to talk away at length and with ease, in the spirit of its Spanish ancestor. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is the default way French turns a noun into a first-conjugation verb, which is why a word from pied-noir speech slipped so easily into everyday verb patterns.
en.tchiper: French Wiktionary derives this verb from ~tchip~, a kind of onomatopoeia, the sound made by sucking air through the teeth. The verb names the gesture itself, the sound of disapproval or contempt produced that way. The sources give no earlier source language or date, so the word is best taken as an imitation of the sound.
en.techniciser: Formed from ~technique~ with the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make”), so it means to make something more technical. The adjective ~technique~ was borrowed from Latin ~technicus~, from Ancient Greek ~τεχνικός~ (~tekhnikós~, “relating to an art or skill”), from ~τέχνη~ (~tékhnē~, “art, craft”).
en.technocratiser: ~Technocratiser~ is formed from the adjective ~technocratique~ with the suffix ~-iser~. The adjective itself comes from ~technocrate~, ~technocratie~ and the suffix ~-ique~. The suffix ~-iser~ builds verbs meaning “make or render,” so the verb means to give something a technocratic character, that is, to place it under the rule of technical experts. It is a typical coinage of journalistic and administrative vocabulary.
en.teiller: A variant spelling of ~tiller~, a verb of hemp and flax working, which French Wiktionary describes as a denominal of ~tille~. For ~tille~, French Wiktionary gives Latin ~tilia~ (“linden”) as the source, without separating the hemp and flax sense from the rest of the family. The verb thus rests on a tree name, but the sources do not narrate the path from linden to fibre, so that step is left open.
en.teindre:
From Old French ~taindre~ and ~teindre~, inherited from Latin ~tingere~ (“to dip, to dye”), itself from the Proto-Indo-European root *~teng-~ (“to soak, dip”). The Latin verb survives across the Romance languages: Italian ~tingere~ and Spanish ~teñir~ are direct descendants. English took ~tinge~ and ~tint~ from the same Latin family, so the verb has cousins in English too.

The root sense of soaking still fits the verb. French uses it for dyeing cloth and hair alike, as in ~teindre ses cheveux~, and its past participle ~teint~ also became a noun for the complexion. The same Latin verb stands behind ~teinte~ (“tint, shade”), ~teinture~ (“dye, tincture”), ~teinturier~ (“dyer, dry cleaner”) and ~déteindre~ (“to lose colour, to run”).
en.teinter: Formed from the noun ~teinte~ (“tint, hue”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to give a tint to.” ~Teinte~ is the feminine past participle of ~teindre~ (“to dye”), used as a noun. Its Latin source is ~tincta~ (“dyed”), from the verb ~tingere~ (“to dye”). Spanish ~tintar~ is a close parallel. The verb stays close to its dyeing ancestor but is gentler in meaning: one ~teinte~ something lightly, and the participle ~teinté~ often describes a mood or a style that carries a hint of another quality.
en.temporiser:
French ~temporiser~ comes from Middle French ~temporiser~, itself borrowed from Medieval Latin ~temporizāre~ (“to gain time”). French Wiktionary analyses it as a learned formation on Latin ~tempus~, genitive ~temporis~ (“time”), with the verb suffix ~-iser~. That suffix goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, which at first transcribed Greek verbs and later became a general verb-maker.

The core idea is playing for time: to put off a decision or a confrontation until circumstances improve, which is the sense of “temporize, stall.” The root ~tempus~ is the source of many French words, among them ~temps~, ~temporel~, ~temporaire~ and ~contemporain~. English ~temporize~ is the same word, and English ~temporal~ and ~tense~ (in grammar) come from the same Latin noun.
en.tempérer:
French ~tempérer~ is a learned form of an older verb. Old French had ~temprer~, and the acute accent and full ~e~ were added to bring the spelling closer to Latin ~temperāre~ (“to moderate, to soften”). The TLFi, as English Wiktionary reports, also treats ~tempérer~ as a direct learned borrowing from the Latin verb, in the sense of tempering or soothing. The two accounts are not exclusive, and the sources present both. The same Latin verb had already given the popular form ~tremper~, so French holds two descendants of one word, a doublet.

The two French verbs divided the meaning between them. ~Tremper~ kept the physical sense of soaking or drenching, while ~tempérer~ kept the sense of moderating, softening, bringing something to a measured state: one ~tempère~ an ardor, a climate, or a harsh remark. Learned relatives of the Latin family share the same idea of right measure: ~tempérament~, ~température~ and ~tempérance~. The modern adjective ~tempéré~ (“temperate”) is the most common trace of the verb in everyday French, as in a ~climat tempéré~.
en.tempêter: ~Tempêter~ is a denominal verb: ~tempête~ (“storm”) plus ~-er~. The noun reached French through Middle and Old French ~tempeste~, from Latin ~tempestās~, and English ~tempest~ comes from the same Old French word. The verb turns the storm into a figure for a person's behavior: to rant, to rave, to kick up a great fuss.
en.tenailler: Formed in French from the noun ~tenaille~ (“pincers”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, with a first attestation in 1549. The verb means “to torture with red-hot pincers,” and by extension “to torment, to rack,” as in being racked by hunger or remorse. It follows the common pattern of a verb named after the tool it uses.
en.tendre:
From Latin ~tendere~ (“to stretch, extend, strain, aim, direct oneself toward”), from Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”). Cognate with Italian ~tendere~ and Spanish ~tender~, with Greek ~τείνειν~ (“to stretch”), and — through the same root — with English ~thin~ (a thing “stretched out”) and, more distantly, ~tend~ and ~tone~.

The physical idea of pulling taut radiates into every sense of the verb: one can ~tendre~ a rope (make it tense), ~tendre~ the hand (stretch it out), or ~tendre~ toward a goal (aim oneself at it). That last, directional sense — straining toward something — is the root of ~tendance~ (“tendency, trend”) and ~tension~. Latin ~tendere~ and the kindred ~tenēre~ (“to hold”) seeded an enormous progeny in French: with prefixes come ~attendre~ (to stretch one's mind toward, hence to wait), ~entendre~ (originally to direct one's attention, hence to hear), ~prétendre~, ~étendre~, ~détendre~, and ~sous-tendre~; the participle gives ~tente~ (a “stretched” canvas) and ~tendon~. Beware the homonym: the adjective ~tendre~ (“soft, tender”) comes instead from Latin ~tener~ — a separate word that merely fell together in spelling.
en.tenir:
French ~tenir~ comes from Latin ~tenēre~ (“to hold, to keep”), which passed through a Vulgar Latin *~tenīre~ before reaching Old French ~tenir~. The Latin verb rests on Proto-Indo-European *~ten-~ (“to stretch”), the same root behind Latin ~tendere~ (“to stretch”) and ~tenuis~ (“thin”), Greek ~teínein~ (“to stretch”) and ~tónos~ (“tension, pitch”), Sanskrit ~tanoti~ (“he stretches”), and English ~thin~. The bridge from “stretch” to “hold” runs through the idea of keeping something taut — to hold a thing is to maintain it under tension.

In Romance the verb stayed central: Italian ~tenere~, Spanish ~tener~, Portuguese ~ter~ all live on as everyday words, with Spanish even pressing ~tener~ into service for “to have.” French ~tenir~ is likewise one of the busiest verbs in the language, anchoring countless idioms — ~tenir bon~ (“to hold firm”), ~tenir à~ (“to be attached to”), ~tenir de~ (“to take after”). The root *~ten-~ also yields ~tendre~ (“to stretch, to hold out”), ~tension~, ~contenir~, ~maintenir~ (literally “to hold in the hand,” from ~manu tenēre~), ~obtenir~, and ~teneur~. Even the musical ~ténor~ belongs here: the voice that originally “held” the sustained melodic line.
en.tenonner: ~Tenonner~ is a denominal verb built from ~tenon~ (the projecting end of a piece of wood cut to fit a mortise) with the verb ending ~-er~, which turns a noun into a verb meaning “to work with N” or “to provide with N.” The noun ~tenon~ is itself a French formation, from the stem of ~tenir~ (“to hold”) plus the suffix ~-on~, so a ~tenon~ is, etymologically, the part that holds. The verb therefore means “to cut a tenon on” a piece of wood, or to fit it with one.
en.tenter:
From Latin ~temptāre~ (also spelled ~tentāre~), “to feel, to handle, to test, to attempt, to attack.” The verb carries an iterative-frequentative force and rests on the Proto-Indo-European root *~ten-~ (“to stretch”); De Vaan, more cautiously, derives it from an extended base *~temp-~ (“to touch, to feel”). Cognates and descendants abound: Italian ~tentare~, Spanish ~tentar~, and — borrowed through French — English ~tempt~, ~taunt~, and ~tentative~.

The meaning travelled from the hand to the soul. To ~tenter~ originally meant to probe by touch, to test the strength of a thing — hence “to put to the test,” a sense kept in the religious ~tenter Dieu~ (“to tempt God,” i.e. to test divine patience) and in ~tenter sa chance~ (“to try one's luck”). From “to test someone” it slid easily to “to entice, to allure,” the dominant modern sense: temptation is, etymologically, a trial. If the root truly is *~ten-~, ~tenter~ belongs to one of the largest Indo-European word-families in French, alongside ~tendre~, ~tension~, ~tente~ (a stretched canvas), ~attenter~, and the borrowed ~tentative~ — all turning on the image of stretching toward something.
en.tercer:
~Tercer~ is a farming verb meaning to plow a field a third time. The French text builds it from ~ter~ (“three times”), ~tierce~ (“third”, feminine) and the ending ~-er~, and English Wiktionary traces the base to Old French ~terce~, a variant form of ~tiers~ (“third”). Both ~tiers~ and ~ter~ go back to Latin: ~tertius~ (“third”) and ~ter~ (“three times”).

The adjective ~tiers~ has a family in French. It is the everyday word for “third”, as in ~tiers~ for a third party, and it gave ~tierce~ for the third of a series. The learned adjective ~tertiaire~ comes from Latin ~tertiārius~. The other Romance languages kept the Latin root: Italian ~terzo~ and Spanish ~tercero~ both mean “third”. ~Tercer~ shows the same root in a narrow farming sense, where counting the plowings gives the verb its meaning.
en.tergiverser:
Borrowed from Latin ~tergiversārī~, a deponent verb that French Wiktionary glosses “to turn one's back” and English Wiktionary “to evade,” so the two glosses sit side by side. The Latin word is a compound of ~tergum~ (“back”) and ~versārī~ (“to turn about, to be engaged in”). English took the same word as ~tergiversate~, and French has the learned noun ~tergiversation~ alongside the verb.

In French the verb means to put off answering or deciding with excuses, and to hesitate at great length. The second half of the Latin compound, ~versāre~, is the frequentative of ~vertere~ (“to turn”), and it lives on in everyday French as ~verser~ and ~converser~. The same ~vertere~ stands behind a large family of French words, among them ~version~ and ~adversaire~, so a word for dodging a question shares its root with turning, pouring and conversing.
en.terminer:
From Latin ~terminare~ (“to set bounds to, to limit, to bring to an end”), a denominal verb built on the noun ~terminus~ (“boundary marker, limit, end”). ~terminus~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~termenos~ to a Proto-Indo-European *~térmn̥~ (“boundary”), and is cognate with Ancient Greek ~térma~ (“goal, finishing post”) and ~térmōn~ (“border”). The Romance siblings include Italian ~terminare~ and Spanish ~terminar~, both “to finish.”

The memorable detail is mythological: ~Terminus~ was also a Roman god, the deity of boundary stones, worshipped each February at the festival of the ~Terminalia~. His shrine on the Capitoline was so sacred that when the great temple of Jupiter was built around it, Terminus alone refused to be moved — a sign, the Romans said, that the bounds of their state would never recede. So at the root of “to finish” lies a stone planted in the earth to say “this far and no farther.” From the same source French has ~terme~ (“term, deadline, word”), ~terminaison~ (“ending”), ~déterminer~ (“to fix the limits of, to decide”), and ~exterminer~ (literally “to drive beyond the boundary”); English ~terminate~, ~term~, and the cinematic ~Terminator~ all share it.
en.ternir: The origin of ~ternir~ is Germanic but not fully settled. French Wiktionary says it is probably of Low Franconian origin and compares German ~tarnen~ (“to camouflage”). English Wiktionary routes it differently: Middle French ~ternir~ from Old French ~ternir~ (“to make dim, make wan”), borrowed from Old High German *~ternen~ or ~tarnen~, from Proto-West Germanic *~darnijan~ (“to cover up, conceal, hide”). Both accounts point to a Germanic verb of hiding. The Old French sense “to make dim” already lies close to the modern meaning, to dull the shine or color of something.
en.terrasser: ~Terrasser~ is formed from ~terrasse~ plus the verb-forming ending ~-er~, and is first attested in the 16th century. The noun comes from Old French ~terrace~ (“ground, daub, fuller's earth”), derived from ~terre~ (“earth”), probably with influence from Old Occitan ~terrassa~. The verb is used both for banking up with earth and, figuratively, for bringing down or defeating an opponent.
en.terreauter: Formed from the noun ~terreau~ (“compost, potting soil”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so that it means “to spread compost on” or “to enrich with loam.” The base ~terreau~ is itself derived from ~terre~ (“earth”) with the suffix ~-eau~, and appears in Old French as ~terral~. ~Terre~ goes back to Latin ~terra~. The verb is therefore an everyday gardening word with two French layers, ~terre~ then ~terreau~, then ~-er~, resting on one Latin root.
en.terrer: A denominal verb built on ~terre~ (“earth, soil”) with the verb-forming ending ~-er~, so that ~terrer~ means to spread or heap soil onto something. The noun ~terre~ is inherited from Latin ~terra~ (“earth, dry land”), which also gave Italian ~terra~ and Spanish ~tierra~. The verb is a plain French coinage with no older source of its own. The same noun lies behind ~terrain~, ~terrasse~ and ~enterrer~.
en.terrifier: ~Terrifier~ is borrowed from Latin ~terrificare~, according to French Wiktionary. English Wiktionary describes it as loaned from a Vulgar Latin *~terrificare~, built from Latin ~terrēre~ (“to frighten”) and ~facere~ (“to make”), so that it means “to make afraid.” Related French words include ~terreur~, ~terrible~ and ~terrifiant~.
en.terroriser: Formed from the noun ~terreur~ with the verb suffix ~-iser~, which turns a noun or adjective into a verb meaning “to subject to” or “to make”. So ~terroriser~ means to subject someone to terror. The noun ~terreur~ was borrowed into Old French from Latin ~terror~ (“terror, dread”), and it reached Middle French in the form ~terreur~. Both Wiktionaries give the verb as a French formation on this base.
en.terser: A variant of ~tercer~, a winegrowing term meaning to give a vineyard its third working, a third plowing. Littré derives it from Latin ~tertius~ (“third”), so the verb literally means “to third” a vine. The same Latin ordinal gave French ~tiers~ (“third”) and, as a learned word, ~tertiaire~.
en.tester:
The modern French ~tester~ (“to test, to try out”) was formed from the noun ~test~ with the suffix ~-er~, under the influence of English ~to test~. The English noun came, in the fourteenth century, from Old French ~test~ (“an earthen pot”), from Latin ~testum~ and ~testa~ (“earthenware vessel, potsherd, shell”) — the assayer's small cup in which metals were melted to prove their purity. Cognates of that Latin word include Italian ~testa~ and the French inheritance ~tête~, both “head.”

French thus has two unrelated verbs spelled ~tester~. The older, a legal term from Latin ~testārī~ (“to bear witness, to make a will”), means “to make a will” and gives ~testament~ and ~testateur~. The newer ~tester~, our verb, is the metallurgist's pot come full circle: the cup that tested gold lent its name to the noun ~test~, which English turned into a verb of trial and examination, and which French then re-imported. The most surprising relative is ~tête~: in Vulgar Latin the “little pot” ~testa~ was used jokingly for the skull, and that humorous slang ousted the classical ~caput~, so that the ordinary French word for “head” is, etymologically, a clay jug. From the same vessel come ~têt~ (a potsherd), ~tesson~, and the borrowed ~test~ and its newer kin ~tester~, ~retester~, and ~testeur~.
en.texturer: ~Texturer~ is a denominal verb, formed from the noun ~texture~ with the ending ~-er~. It means to give a texture to something, to make a surface or a substance have a particular feel or grain. The noun ~texture~ is the French form of Latin ~textūra~, itself from ~texere~ (“to weave”), so the idea of woven structure lies far behind the word. The verb is used especially in technical contexts such as food processing, cosmetics, painting and computer graphics.
en.théoriser: ~Théoriser~ is a learned derivative of ~théorie~ with the suffix ~-iser~. It is dated to 1823, when it was used without an object in the sense “to establish a theory” (Boiste). The transitive use, “to put into theory,” as in ~il a théorisé son système~, is recorded from 1902 (Barrès). The noun ~théorie~ came through Latin ~theoria~ from Ancient Greek ~θεωρία~ (“contemplation, speculation”), from ~θεωρέω~ (“to look at, to consider”), from ~θεωρός~ (“spectator”), itself from ~θέα~ (“view”) and ~ὁράω~ (“to see”).
en.thésauriser:
From Late and ecclesiastical Latin ~thesaurizāre~, which French took over as a learned borrowing. The Latin verb comes from Ancient Greek ~thēsaurízō~ (“to store, to treasure up”), from ~thēsaurós~ (“store-room, treasure, granary, strong-box”). French Wiktionary adds that the Latin verb is probably a direct Greek borrowing, or else an equivalent formation on Latin ~thesaurus~ with the suffix ~-izo~, so the exact route is uncertain, though the Greek source is not in doubt.

The Greek noun ~thēsaurós~ also passed into Latin as ~thesaurus~, from which French inherited ~trésor~ and English took both ~treasure~ and ~thesaurus~. ~Trésoriser~ is a lexical doublet of ~thésauriser~, and ~trésorier~ belongs to the same family. In modern French, ~thésauriser~ means to hoard money, to pile up wealth without spending it. The ending ~-iser~ is itself a distant descendant of the Greek ending ~-ízō~ with which the verb began.
en.théâtraliser: ~Théâtraliser~ is formed from the adjective ~théâtral~ with the suffix ~-iser~, which here means “to make A,” so “to make theatrical, to dramatize.” The base ~théâtral~ was borrowed from Latin ~theatralis~, which English Wiktionary also analyzes on the surface as ~théâtre~ + ~-al~. The suffix ~-iser~ is a French ending that goes back to Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and it is fully productive today.
en.tiercer: French Wiktionary derives ~tiercer~ from ~tierce~ or ~tiers~, or else from Latin ~tertiare~, so the sources leave a choice between a French formation and a Latin inheritance. The base ~tierce~ is the feminine of the adjective ~tiers~ (“third”), from Old French ~tierce~ and Latin ~tertia~. The verb refers to a third round of work, as in plowing a field a third time. The ending ~-er~ is the usual French verb ending.
en.tiller: ~Tiller~ is formed from the noun ~tille~ with the verb ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary lists several unrelated words spelled ~tille~. Two come from Latin ~tilia~ (“linden”), one from Old Norse ~telgja~ (“carpenter's axe, adze”), and one from Old Norse ~þilja~ (“plank, deck”), the same word as ~tillac~. The sources do not say which of them gave the verb, so its link to the scutching of flax or hemp rests on the noun alone.
en.timbrer: ~Timbrer~ is a derivative of ~timbre~ with the suffix ~-er~. The noun ~timbre~ comes from Middle French ~timbre~, itself from Old French ~tinbre~, and goes back to Greek ~τύμπανον~ (“drum”). French Wiktionary routes it through Latin ~tympanum~, whereas English Wiktionary prefers Byzantine Greek and finds a direct Latin descent less likely. Either way ~timbre~ is a doublet of ~tympan~. In French the noun first named a medieval drum, then a bell struck by a hammer, which is why a ~timbre~ can still be a bell.
en.tinter:
~Tinter~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~tinnitāre~, a frequentative of Latin ~tinniō~ (“to ring, to jingle”). A frequentative expresses repeated action, so the verb literally describes a sound that keeps sounding. The Latin noun ~tinnitus~ (“ringing”) comes from the same root and survives in medicine, in French and in English alike.

The French verb stayed close to its Latin sense. ~Tinter~ describes what a bell, a glass, a coin or a key does when it rings or jingles, and the noun ~tintement~ names the sound. It is used for a bell tolling slowly, as at a funeral, and for ears that ring after a loud noise. It is unrelated to its homophone ~teinter~ (“to tint”), which belongs to the family of ~teindre~ and goes back to a different Latin verb. The pair is a classic trap for French learners: ~tinter~ is about sound, ~teinter~ about color.
en.tintinnabuler:
From Latin ~tintinnabulum~ (“small bell, jingling bell”), itself derived from the verb ~tintinnāre~ (“to ring, to jingle”). The Latin verb imitates the sound it names, with its repeated ~tin~ syllables. French drew on the noun to make a verb, so ~tintinnabuler~ is a learned, deliberately sonorous word whose very shape rings.

The modern verb means “to tinkle, to jingle,” and it is literary, a showpiece of playful vocabulary rather than an everyday word. English borrowed from the same Latin source ~tintinnabulation~ for the ringing of bells, and ~tintinnabulate~ along with it. French also has the homely ~tinter~, which expresses the same sound with fewer syllables.
en.tiquer: ~Tiquer~ is a denominal verb, formed from ~tic~ with the ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary traces ~tic~ to an onomatopoeia ~tik~ expressing a sudden movement, and English Wiktionary notes it was first used of horses in the seventeenth century, comparing Italian ~ticchio~. The verb has two senses. In stable talk, ~tiquer~ is said of a horse that gnaws its manger with a tic, which is the gloss “crib-bite.” In everyday French, it means to wince or react with a visible twitch of disapproval, as in ~sans tiquer~ (“without batting an eyelid”).
en.tirailler: ~Tirailler~ is formed from ~tirer~ (“to pull”) with the suffix ~-ailler~, which gives verbs a repeated, petty or pejorative sense, as in ~criailler~ from ~crier~: to tug again and again. The origin of the suffix is itself disputed, either inherited from Latin ~-āculāre~ or built from ~-aille~ and ~-er~. The base ~tirer~ is also of debated origin. The leading hypothesis is Gothic *~tairan~ (“to tear”), while a rival account sees a clipping of Old French ~martirier~ (“to torture”). In either case ~tirer~ largely displaced ~traire~, from Latin ~trahere~.
en.tire-bouchonner: ~Tire-bouchonner~ is formed from the noun ~tire-bouchon~ (“corkscrew”) with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is a compound of ~tirer~ (“to pull”) and ~bouchon~ (“stopper”). The verb takes the corkscrew's spiral shape as its image: to coil, to twist, or to bunch up like a corkscrew.
en.tirebouchonner: Formed from the noun ~tire-bouchon~ (“corkscrew”) with the verbal ending ~-er~: to coil or twist like a corkscrew, or to give something that spiral shape. The noun is a compound of ~tirer~ (“to pull”) and ~bouchon~ (“cork, stopper”), literally “pull-cork,” the tool that draws a cork from a bottle. The verb is therefore a double derivation, from a compound noun, and it describes anything that curls into a spiral.
en.tirer:
The origin of ~tirer~ is debated. The leading hypothesis derives it from Gothic *~tairan~ (“to tear, to pull apart”), the same Germanic source that gave Spanish ~tirar~; this fits the kinship felt between ~tirer~, ~tirailler~, and ~déchirer~, and is paralleled by German ~zehren~ (“to consume, destroy”) and ~zerren~ (“to tug”). A rival Latin account (Wartburg) sees a clipping of Old French ~martirier~ (“to martyr, to torture”), from ~martyre~. In any case ~tirer~ largely displaced the older ~traire~, from Latin ~trahere~ (“to pull, to drag”).

The spread of meaning is wide: from the core “to pull” come ~tirer~ “to draw out” (~tirer un trait~, “to draw a line”), “to fire, to shoot” (a crossbow being drawn before release), and the printing sense (a ~tirage~ is a press-run, paper pulled off the plate). The torture connection, if true, is grimly apt — medieval racking stretched and dislocated limbs by pulling. Whatever ~tirer~'s own pedigree, the displaced ~traire~ left a productive Latin family in French: ~soustraire~, ~extraire~, ~soutirer~, ~étirer~, ~retirer~, and ~attirer~, all turning on the act of drawing.
en.tisser:
Descended from Latin ~texō~ (“to weave”), by way of Old French ~tistre~. That strong verb was reshaped by analogy into ~tissir~, which then passed into the first conjugation as ~tisser~, so the modern infinitive is a late and regularized form. Latin ~texō~ comes from Proto-Italic *~teksō~, which English Wiktionary derives from the Proto-Indo-European root *~teḱ-~ (“to beget, to produce”), by one of two competing reconstructions, so the exact PIE shape is debated. Related to it are Latin ~textus~ (“fabric, woven thing”) and its French offspring ~texte~, ~textile~ and ~contexte~. Greek ~tekhnē~ (“craft, art”) is usually placed in the same family, though the details of the root are uncertain.

The old strong verb has not entirely vanished. Some northern dialects kept it, such as Norman ~tître~, Gallo ~téstr~ and Walloon ~texhe~, and all of them preserve the older conjugation. The original past participle was ~tissu~, which gave French its word for cloth and, by extension, for living tissue and the social fabric. English ~tissue~ is borrowed from it, a “woven thing”. The verb ~tisser~ itself moved easily from the loom to metaphor: one weaves links, a plot, a web. The word ~texte~ keeps the same picture, a text being a thing woven out of sentences, which is also why ~contexte~ means what is woven together with it.
en.titiller: Taken from Latin ~titillāre~ (“to tickle”). French Wiktionary gives no other step in between. The verb originally describes light physical stimulation, the slight touch of a tickle, and French uses it today mostly in a figurative sense, to excite or tease someone’s curiosity or desire. English ~titillate~ is a close relative, from the same Latin verb.
en.titrer: Formed from the noun ~titre~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~titre~ descends from Latin ~titulus~ (“inscription, label”) and is attested from about 1225. It has two uses that explain the verb's two main senses: a heading or name, so ~titrer~ is “to give a title or headline”, and the fineness of a metal alloy, hence “to determine the strength of a solution or alloy”, the sense behind chemical titration. English Wiktionary also offers a variant account, that the verb is inherited from Old French ~titler~, itself from ~titulus~.
en.tituber:
~Tituber~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~titubāre~ (“to stagger, to totter”), which also meant, figuratively, “to waver, to hesitate.” French took the verb straight from Latin rather than inheriting it through the spoken language, and it kept the physical sense of an unsteady walk, as of someone drunk, weak or dizzy. The Latin verb has descendants in several languages, and some of them keep the idea of hesitation more vividly than French does.

Italian ~titubare~ and Spanish ~titubear~ both mean “to hesitate” or “to waver,” and keep the figurative sense more strongly than French. English has the learned cousin ~titubation~ as well. French itself has the adjective ~titubant~ (“staggering”) and the noun ~titubation~ (“staggering, unsteady gait”). The verb now suits a literary register, whether it describes a drunk leaving a bar or a fragile convalescent taking a first step.
en.titulariser: ~Titulariser~ is formed from the noun and adjective ~titulaire~ with the verb-forming suffix ~-iser~, meaning to make someone a full holder of a post. ~Titulaire~ is a borrowing from Late Latin ~titulāris~, an adjective tied to the Latin ~titulus~ (“title, inscription”). The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, itself transcribing Greek verb endings, and it is fully productive for coining verbs in administrative language. In practice, ~titulariser~ is used where a temporary employee, such as a teacher or civil servant, is given permanent status.
en.tiédir: Built on ~tiède~ (“lukewarm”) with the ending ~-ir~, which makes a verb meaning to become that adjective: to turn lukewarm. French Wiktionary notes that the transitive sense, to make something lukewarm, appears only after 1596. The adjective ~tiède~ goes back to Latin ~tepidus~, which gave Old French ~tieve~. The form ~tiède~ is first found in Middle French in the 14th century, and French Wiktionary traces it to the dialects of eastern France. The learned borrowing ~tépide~ is a doublet of ~tiède~.
en.toiletter: ~Toiletter~ is formed from ~toilette~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun ~toilette~ is itself a derivative of ~toile~ (“cloth”) with the diminutive suffix ~-ette~, so it was first a small piece of cloth, later the care of one's person. To ~toiletter~ is to give such care to an animal, grooming a dog or a cat by washing, brushing and trimming it.
en.toiser: Formed from ~toise~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to measure with a ~toise~.” ~Toise~ was an old French unit of length. It comes from Old French ~teise~ (cognate with Italian ~tesa~), from Popular Latin *~tesa~ and Latin ~tensa~ (“outstretched”), a feminine participle of ~tendere~ (“to stretch”). English Wiktionary says it was said of outstretched arms. The verb means to measure someone's height and, figuratively, to size them up with a look, from head to foot.
en.tolérer: French ~tolérer~ comes from Latin ~tolerāre~ (“to bear, to endure”), the only source given by French Wiktionary. It is a learned borrowing, like Italian ~tollerare~, Spanish ~tolerar~ and English ~tolerate~. The sense of bearing something remains the core of ~tolérer~: to put up with what one might prefer to refuse, such as a person, a behavior or a dose of a drug. The same Latin verb underlies ~tolérance~, ~tolérant~, ~intolérant~ and ~tolérable~.
en.tomber:
From an expressive Vulgar Latin *~tumbāre~ (“to fall, to tumble”), built on a root *~tumb-~ that imitates the sound and suddenness of a fall. In Old French this met and merged with ~tumer~ (“to do somersaults, to tumble”), a verb of Frankish origin from *~tūmōn~ (compare Old High German ~tūmōn~, “to turn, to reel”); through that Germanic stock the same idea survives in English ~tumble~. The two near-identical verbs blurred together, and ~tumer~ died out by the sixteenth century, leaving ~tomber~ alone.

What makes ~tomber~ remarkable is that it is an upstart. Old French already had a perfectly good verb for falling, ~choir~ (from Latin ~cadere~), but from the fifteenth century the livelier, half-onomatopoeic ~tomber~ pressed in, and by the seventeenth it had all but ousted ~choir~ from everyday speech. ~Choir~ now survives only in literary corners and in its compound ~déchoir~ (“to decline, to fall from grace”), while its participle lingers in ~échu~ and ~déchet~. ~Tomber~, meanwhile, spread into countless idioms — ~tomber amoureux~ (“to fall in love”), ~tomber malade~, ~laisser tomber~ — and spun off ~tombée~ (“nightfall”) and ~retomber~.
en.tomer: Formed in French from the noun ~tome~ (“volume of a work”) and the suffix ~-er~: to ~tomer~ is to divide a work into volumes. The noun ~tome~ was borrowed from Latin ~tomus~, a word that goes back to Greek ~tómos~ (“a cut, a slice”), the image being of a long text cut into sections. A separate word ~tome~, a variant of ~tomme~, is a cheese and has nothing to do with this one. The suffix ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~. The verb is rare and technical, used mostly by publishers and librarians.
en.tondre: Inherited from Old French ~tondre~, from Vulgar Latin *~tondĕre~, a variant of Latin ~tondēre~ (“to shear”), which English Wiktionary traces to Proto-Indo-European *~tend-~, itself from *~temh₂-~ (“to cut”). Among the learned descendants of the Latin family is ~tonsure~; French also coined ~tondeuse~ (“clippers, mower”) from the verb itself.
en.tonifier: ~Tonifier~ is derived from the adjective ~tonique~ (“tonic”) with the suffix ~-fier~, a variant of ~-ifier~ that goes back to Latin ~-ficāre~ (“to make”). The source describes this as a substitution of suffixes: the ending ~-ique~ is dropped and ~-fier~ takes its place. The base ~tonique~ comes from Ancient Greek ~tonikós~, which is related to ~ton~ and ~tonus~. The verb means to give tone to something, that is, to strengthen it.
en.tonitruer:
A learned borrowing from Late Latin ~tonitruāre~ (“to thunder”), a verb formed on Latin ~tonitrus~ (“thunder”). This noun also gave the inherited French ~tonnerre~, so ~tonitruer~ and ~tonnerre~ are cousins reached by different roads: one by oral descent, the other by the pen of scholars. Latin ~tonitrus~ belongs with the verb ~tonāre~ (“to thunder”), and the same family reaches Italian ~tuonare~, Spanish ~tronar~ and, further back, English ~thunder~ and German ~Donner~.

In French, ~tonitruer~ is a literary verb, used for a voice or a speaker that booms, or in the participle ~tonitruant~ (“thundering, booming”). It never replaced the plain ~tonner~, which comes down the popular road from ~tonāre~. The family is large: ~tonner~, ~tonnerre~, ~détoner~ and ~détonation~, and ~étonner~, which started out as a verb for being struck as if by thunder. ~Tonitruer~ keeps the fuller Latin shape that the popular forms wore down.
en.tonner:
French ~tonner~ is inherited from Old French and ultimately from Latin ~tonāre~ (“to resound loudly, to thunder”), which English Wiktionary traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)tenh₂-~ (“to thunder”). The Germanic languages hold close relatives of the same root: English ~thunder~ and German ~Donner~ are cognates. Italian ~tuonare~ is another descendant of the Latin verb.

The Latin verb already covered both the weather and the noise: the sense “to make resound like thunder” was a figure of speech built into it. French kept both. ~Tonner~ is used impersonally, as in ~il tonne~, and also of a voice or a gun that booms, or of someone who rails against something. The Latin family is large. The noun ~tonnerre~ comes from Latin ~tonitrus~, and ~détoner~ and ~détonation~ are learned formations on the same root. ~Étonner~ descends from a Vulgar Latin compound of ~ex-~ and ~tonāre~.
en.tonsurer: Formed from the noun ~tonsure~ with the verbal ending ~-er~: to give someone a tonsure, the shaved crown of a cleric or monk. The noun is inherited from Old French ~tonsure~, borrowed from Latin ~tōnsūra~ (“a clipping, a trimming”), itself from ~tondēre~ (“to shear, to clip”). So the verb keeps the plain Latin idea of shearing, narrowed to one ritual haircut.
en.tontiner: Formed from ~tontine~ with the verbal ending ~-er~: to take part in a tontine, a pooled-savings scheme. The noun comes from the name of Lorenzo Tonti, a Neapolitan banker who proposed the scheme to Cardinal Mazarin in 1653. The suffix ~-ine~ turned his name ~Tonti~ into the common noun, and the verb was then built on it.
en.toper: ~Toper~ is onomatopoeic, from ~top~, the sound of hands clapping together, with the verb ending ~-er~; compare ~taper~, which attracted it. The origin is not settled, though. Some French dictionaries derive it from Spanish ~topar~ (“to bump into”), while Le Robert derives it from ~tope~, which meant to apply with a throw. The shared picture is a handshake that seals a deal: ~toper~ means to agree and shake on it.
en.toquer:
The origin of ~toquer~ is debated. English Wiktionary derives it from Middle French ~toquer~ (also spelled ~tocquer~), most likely from an imitative root *~toc~, based on the sound of a blow. The alternative is an Old Northern French *~toquer~ (compare Old French ~tochier~), from Vulgar Latin *~tuccāre~ (“to strike; to touch”), the source of ~toucher~. French Wiktionary also names a Latin source, but writes it *~toccare~, so even the Latin form is not settled.

If the Latin account is right, ~toquer~ is closely related to ~toucher~, which comes from the same source. If the imitative account is right, ~toquer~ belongs with French words born from the sound of a knock, and its likeness to ~toucher~ would be partly accidental. In either case the modern meaning is to knock or tap. The Latin account links it to Italian ~toccare~ and Spanish ~tocar~, as well as English ~touch~, which came into English through French ~toucher~.
en.torcher: ~Torcher~ is formed from the noun ~torche~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary explains it as properly “to wipe with a ~torche~ or a cloth”, and English Wiktionary says the vulgar sense comes from wiping oneself after defecating. ~Torche~ is inherited from Old French ~torche~, from Vulgar Latin *~torca~, from ~torqua~ (“collar, garland”), a variant of ~torques~, derived from ~torquēre~ (“to twist”). Old French used ~torche~ for a twisted bundle of hay or straw and for a crude torch, which shows the noun's range.
en.torchonner: Derived from the noun ~torchon~ (“cloth, rag”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so the verb means to wipe with a cloth. ~Torchon~ comes from Old French ~torçon~ and is formed from ~torche~ plus the suffix ~-on~. The family thus begins with ~torche~, and the dishcloth is, etymologically, a small relative of it. The verb also carries the sense of doing a job carelessly, as in a piece of work that is dashed off.
en.tordre:
Inherited from Old French ~tordre~ (also spelled ~tortre~), from Vulgar Latin *~torcĕre~, itself from Classical Latin ~torquēre~ (“to twist”). The Latin verb goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~terkʷ-~ (“to twist”). Italian ~torcere~ and Spanish ~torcer~ are its sister continuations. English never inherited the verb, but borrowed a whole family from Latin ~torquēre~ and its participle ~tortus~: ~torture~, ~torment~, ~torque~, ~distort~, ~contort~ and ~retort~ all began as “twistings” of one kind or another.

In French the verb kept its physical sense: one ~tord~ a cloth to wring it out, an arm to hurt someone, a wire to bend it. The reflexive ~se tordre~ is to writhe, and ~se tordre de rire~ is to double up with laughter. The participle ~tortus~ survives in the noun ~tort~ (“wrong, harm”), literally what is twisted, as opposed to what is straight and right. Modern French words from the same root include ~tordu~ (“twisted”, and in slang “crazy”), ~torsion~, ~tortueux~ (“winding, devious”) and ~contorsion~.
en.toronner: ~Toronner~ (“to twist”) is a denominal verb: ~toron~ plus the ending ~-er~. A ~toron~ is a strand of rope, and the noun comes from Latin ~torus~, here in the sense of a small rope or a length of rope, a word that also lies behind French ~tore~. The verb therefore means to twist things into strands, in the manner of rope-making.
en.torpiller: ~Torpiller~ is formed from the noun ~torpille~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so it means to attack with a torpedo. The noun has two origins. The older one is the fish, the electric ray: ~torpille~ comes from Middle French ~torpile~ (1538), a respelling with a change of suffix of Old French ~torpin~, from Latin ~torpedo~ (genitive ~torpedinis~). The weapon sense is a calque of English ~torpedo~, itself taken from the same Latin word for the ray. French therefore used a fish's name for the explosive, and the verb followed the weapon.
en.torréfier:
~Torréfier~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~torrefacere~ (“to parch, to dry up”), a compound of ~torrēre~ (“to parch, to roast”) and ~facere~ (“to make”). The meaning is therefore to make something dry and hot, and in modern French it is used above all for roasting coffee beans, as well as cocoa, malt and other products. English has a parallel learned verb, ~torrefy~, from the same Latin source.

The Latin verb ~torrēre~ has a wide family in French. It lies behind ~torride~ (“scorching”), from Latin ~torridus~, and behind ~torrent~, from Latin ~torrēns~, the present participle of ~torrēre~. The second half, ~facere~, is the verb that gave French ~faire~ and the suffix ~-fier~ of many verbs such as ~liquéfier~ and ~putréfier~. The noun ~torréfaction~ names the process, and a ~torréfacteur~ is a coffee roaster.
en.torsader: Formed from the noun ~torsade~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~torsade~ is itself built from ~tors~ (“twisted”) and the suffix ~-ade~, and names a twisted ornament, such as a twisted cord or a cable pattern. The verb ~torsader~ means to twist something into such a shape.
en.tortiller: The origin of ~tortiller~ is not settled. English Wiktionary offers two accounts: the verb is either inherited from Vulgar Latin *~tortiliāre~, built on Latin ~tortilis~ (“twisted”), or it is a regressive derivation from ~entortiller~ (“to wrap, to twist around”), with the prefix cut off. French Wiktionary gives no etymology. Italian ~tortigliare~ and ~attortigliare~ and Spanish ~retortijar~ are cited as parallels. The Latin adjective ~tortilis~ belongs to the family of ~torquēre~ (“to twist”), which also gave French ~tordre~ and ~torsion~. Either way, the verb means to twist or twirl.
en.tortorer: Attested from 1866 in slang, where the TLFi cites Delvau's dictionary. The TLFi, following the FEW, explains it as a use of ~tortiller~ (“to twist, to wriggle”) in the sense “to eat quickly,” after the pattern of ~picorer~ (“to peck about”). The verb is informal and now dated, and means simply “to eat.”
en.torturer: A denominal verb: ~torture~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, “to inflict torture on.” The noun comes from Late Latin ~tortūra~ (“a twisting,” then “suffering”), from Latin ~tortus~, the past participle of ~torquēre~ (“to twist, to torture”). French ~torture~ first described a severe penal punishment (1459), then took its modern sense of physical suffering inflicted to extract a confession (1580), and later, by extension, moral suffering (1631). The verb carries all of these senses.
en.toréer: ~Toréer~ is borrowed from Spanish ~torear~, a verb made from ~toro~ (“bull”) with a verbal ending. It means to fight bulls in the ring, and the French verb passed along with the Spanish bullfighting tradition. French fitted the loan to its own ending in ~-er~ and added an accent to mark the vowel.
en.tosser: Borrowed from Breton ~tosañ~ (“to bump, to ram”). The verb is a maritime term meaning to bump against a quay, which fits the contact with Breton, the language of a seafaring coast. Nothing in the sources gives an earlier history for the Breton word, so the chain stops there.
en.totaliser: Formed from the adjective and noun ~total~ with the suffix ~-iser~, a suffix that builds verbs meaning “to make or turn into.” The base ~total~ was borrowed into Middle French in the fourteenth century from Medieval Latin ~tōtālis~, derived from Latin ~tōtus~ (“whole, all”). To ~totaliser~ is to add up into a total, or to reach a total. The stem is unchanged before the suffix, so the formation is a straightforward French one.
en.toucher:
From Old French ~tochier~ (“to touch, to strike, to mention”), from Vulgar Latin *~toccāre~ (“to knock, to strike, as a bell”). This *~toccāre~ is widely held to be of imitative origin, built on the sound ~toc~ — the sharp “knock” made when two hard things meet. It thus replaced the older Latin ~tangere~ (“to touch”). Romance kin include Italian ~toccare~ and Spanish ~tocar~, and through Old French it gave English ~touch~.

The semantic drift is a small marvel of physics: a blow at its very gentlest is nothing more than a touch, so “to strike” slid quietly into “to make contact with.” From bodily contact French ~toucher~ reached for figurative senses — to ~toucher~ a sum of money (to receive it), to ~toucher~ someone (to move them emotionally), and to ~toucher~ a subject (to broach it). The onomatopoeic ~toc~ left other traces: ~toquer~ (“to knock”), the alarm-bell ~tocsin~ (which once literally meant a struck signal), and the noun ~toucher~ itself, the sense of touch. The musical ~toccata~, borrowed into many languages, is from the Italian cousin ~toccare~ — a “touched” keyboard piece.
en.touer:
~Touer~ (“to tow, to haul a boat by a line”) comes, according to English Wiktionary, from Middle French ~touer~, from Old French ~touer~, itself from Frankish *~togōn~ (“to tug, to tow”). The Frankish verb belongs to a Germanic family that also includes Saterland Frisian ~toogje~ (“to tug, pull, tear”) and English ~tow~.

The sources do not fully agree on the route. English Wiktionary gives the plain inherited descent from Frankish. French Wiktionary lists two accounts. One makes ~touer~ a borrowing from English ~tow~ (“to pull, to tow”), linked to ~touline~ (a towline) and compared with Spanish ~toar~ and German ~Tau~ (“rope”). The other, introduced with “rather,” derives it from Old Frankish *~tôgon~ (“to pull”), related to German ~ziehen~ and Old Norse ~toga~. Either way the core idea is pulling, and the French verb applies it to drawing a vessel along by a rope.
en.touiller:
Inherited from Old French ~tooillier~ (attested around 1175), from Latin ~tudiculāre~ (“to grind, to crush, to mix”). The meaning in French became “to stir, to shake up, to mix,” but French Wiktionary says it was first used for “to make dirty.” The Latin verb, according to these sources, is the true ancestor, and the word has been in the language since the twelfth century.

The modern verb belongs to the familiar register and is used for stirring a mixture, such as a batter or a salad, vigorously. French Wiktionary adds a regional detail, with the hedge that it “would” be the origin of the Vendée word ~toulon~, a kind of pestle once used to churn the cream in a ~tarasson~ (a butter-making vessel) to make butter. From ~touiller~ comes also the everyday ~touillette~, a little stirrer.
en.toupiller: Formed from ~toupie~ (“spinning top”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, a woodworking verb meaning to shape with a router. The noun comes from Old French ~topoie~, probably from Frankish *~topp~ (“spinning top”), according to English Wiktionary, while French Wiktionary points to Old English ~top~. English ~top~ is a cognate in either case. The machine's rotating cutter likely explains the name, though the sources do not say so.
en.toupiner: Formed from the noun ~toupin~ with the verb ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary gives ~toupin~ as another form of ~toupie~ (“spinning top”), so ~toupiner~ is “to spin like a top.” A homonym ~toupin~, meaning “earthen pot,” is a different word: it comes from Occitan ~topin~ and ultimately from Old Frankish *~toppi~, related to German ~Topf~.
en.tourber: ~Tourber~ is formed from ~tourbe~ (“peat”) with the verb ending ~-er~: to dig peat. The noun ~tourbe~ goes back, around 1200, to Frankish *~turb~, from Proto-Germanic *~turbz~ (“turf”). It is a cognate of Old High German ~zurba~, Dutch ~turf~, German ~Torf~ and English ~turf~. French has a second, unrelated ~tourbe~ (“crowd”), which comes from Latin ~turba~ and is not the source of the verb.
en.tourbillonner: ~Tourbillonner~ is formed from the noun ~tourbillon~ (“whirlwind, whirlpool”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so it means to move like a whirl, to swirl. The noun was built with the suffix ~-on~ on Old French ~torbel~ (“melee, commotion”), which English Wiktionary spells ~torbeil~. Behind them lies Latin ~turbo~ (genitive ~turbinis~, “whirlwind”), linked to ~turba~ (“disorder, turmoil”). Spanish ~torbellino~ and Portuguese ~torvelinho~ come from the same source. Latin ~turba~ is also behind ~troubler~ and ~turbulent~.
en.tourmenter: Formed from the noun ~tourment~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun comes through Old French ~torment~ from Latin ~tormentum~, a word for an instrument of torture or a siege engine, and it is related to ~tordre~ (“to twist”), since such devices worked by twisting. To ~tourmenter~ is thus to put someone through torture, then, more loosely, to harass or to trouble the mind.
en.tournailler: ~Tournailler~ is formed from ~tourner~ with the suffix ~-ailler~, which gives verbs a repeated, petty or aimless sense, as in ~tirailler~ and ~traînailler~. So ~tournailler~ means “to wander round and round,” turning without purpose. The base ~tourner~ comes from Latin ~tornāre~ (“to turn on a lathe”), built on ~tornus~, a borrowing from Greek ~tórnos~ (“lathe”). The suffix is either inherited from Latin ~-āculāre~ or formed in French from ~-aille~ and ~-er~; the sources differ.
en.tournebouler:
From Middle French ~tournebouler~, an alteration, influenced by ~boule~ and ~bouler~, of Old French ~tourneboeler~. That verb derived from ~torneboele~ (“somersault”), a compound of ~tourner~ (“to turn”) and ~buele~ (“entrails”). The first element comes from Latin ~tornāre~ (“to turn on a lathe”), and the second belongs to the family of ~boyau~ (“gut”) and ~tord-boyau~, a name for harsh spirits.

Modern French uses ~tournebouler~ figuratively, for throwing someone into confusion or upsetting them deeply. The verb thus kept the sense of turning, while its second half drifted from the old word for entrails toward the more familiar ~boule~. Its relatives in the lexicon are ~boyau~, with its “guts” sense, and ~tord-boyau~, a name for harsh spirits.
en.tourner:
From Old French ~torner~, from Latin ~tornare~ (“to turn on a lathe, to round off”), a verb built on ~tornus~ (“a lathe, a turner's chisel”). That noun was itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~τόρνος~ (~tórnos~), a compass or lathe for tracing circles, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~terh₁-~ (“to rub, to bore by twisting”). Through the same Latin source come Italian ~tornare~, Spanish ~tornar~, and — by way of Norman and Old French — English ~turn~ and ~tour~.

The earliest sense was thoroughly mechanical: to shape wood or metal by spinning it against a fixed blade, the craft of the ~tourneur~. From this image of rotation the meaning fanned out to cover any circular movement, then a change of direction (~tourner à gauche~), then figurative reversals of fortune and mood (~tourner mal~, “to turn out badly”). The culinary sense of stirring, and the cinematic sense of shooting a film — ~tourner un film~, a memory of the hand-cranked camera — both descend from the same idea of turning. The lathe-sense survives intact in ~tour~ (“lathe”) and ~tournage~. From the Greek-Latin root spring a wide family: ~tour~, ~tournoi~, ~tournevis~, ~contour~, ~détour~, and ~retourner~.
en.tournicoter: Formed from ~tourniquer~ (“to wind”) with the suffix ~-oter~, which gives a small, repeated action: here, turning or going round and round without purpose. The base ~tourniquer~ is itself a frequentative of ~tourner~, which comes from Latin ~tornāre~ (“to turn on a lathe”), from Greek ~tórnos~ (“lathe”). The verb thus stacks two layers of repetition on a root that began with the lathe. Today it means “to flit around” or to potter about busily without getting anywhere.
en.tourniquer: The sources differ slightly on how this verb was built. French Wiktionary describes it as a form drawn from ~tourner~ with the endings ~-ique~ and ~-et~, while English Wiktionary simply calls it a frequentative of ~tourner~. Either way, it expresses repeated or aimless turning, hence “to wind around, to go round and round.” The base ~tourner~ comes from Latin ~tornāre~ (“to turn on a lathe”), itself from Greek ~tórnos~ (“lathe”).
en.tournoyer: Formed from ~tourner~ with the suffix ~-oyer~, which gives verbs of repeated or continuing action: ~tournoyer~ means “to keep turning, to whirl.” The base ~tourner~ comes from Old French ~torner~ and Latin ~tornare~ (“to turn on a lathe”), built on ~tornus~ (“lathe”), itself borrowed from Greek. The suffix ~-oyer~ descends from Old French ~-oiier~ and Late Latin ~-izāre~, which also gave the learned doublet ~-iser~. It is no longer used to coin new verbs.
en.toussailler: Formed from ~tousser~ (“to cough”) with the suffix ~-ailler~, which makes the action weak and repeated: to cough lightly and often. The TLFi gives 1821 as its first attestation. ~Tousser~ appears in the early thirteenth century and replaced the older ~toussir~, from Latin ~tussire~, derived from ~tussis~ (“cough”). Italian ~tossire~ and Portuguese ~tossir~ come from the same Latin verb.
en.tousser: ~Tousser~ comes from Old French ~tossir~ (English Wiktionary gives ~toussir~), inherited from Latin ~tussīre~ (“to cough”), a verb derived from the noun ~tussis~ (“cough”). The Romance languages preserve it widely: Italian ~tossire~, Portuguese ~tossir~ and Romanian ~tuși~ keep the old conjugation. Spanish ~toser~ and Old Occitan ~tossar~ changed conjugation class, and so did French itself, which moved from ~-ir~ to ~-er~. The noun ~toux~, which still carries the Latin noun ~tussis~ forward, belongs to the same family.
en.toussoter: Formed from ~tousser~ (“to cough”) with the suffix ~-oter~, which turns a verb into a light, repeated action: to cough a little, in small bursts. ~Tousser~ comes from Old French ~tossir~, inherited from Latin ~tussīre~, a verb built on the noun ~tussis~ (“cough”), which also lives on in French ~toux~. The same suffix appears in ~tapoter~ (from ~taper~), ~siffloter~ (from ~siffler~) and ~vivoter~ (from ~vivre~).
en.trabouler:
The origin of this Lyon regionalism is disputed. A widespread account, usually credited to the archaeologist Amable Audin, derives it from a verb *~trabulare~, a contraction of Late Latin *~transambulare~, built from ~trans-~ (“across”) and ~ambulare~ (“to walk”). But the Trésor de la langue française does not consider this idea, the Dictionnaire des régionalismes de France does not retain it and calls the origin simply obscure, and the linguist Xavier Gouvert finds it implausible on phonetic grounds.

The verb first appears only in the Lyon phrase ~allée qui traboule~, a variant of ~allée qui traverse~. Gouvert sees a slang creation crossing ~traverser~ with ~débouler~ (itself from ~bouler~, “to fall rolling”), which would give a primitive sense of “crossing while going down,” fitting the slopes of the Croix-Rousse where such passages run. The Trésor instead gives ~tra-~, an altered form of ~trans~, plus ~bouler~ in the sense of “to roll.” The first written trace dates from 1875, but it refers to an “old Lyon patois,” which suggests the verb is considerably older.
en.tracasser: Formed with the suffix ~-asser~ on ~traque~ or ~trac~, according to French Wiktionary, which leaves the exact base open. The verb first meant “to hunt animals,” and the modern sense of “to worry, to bother” is attested from 1588. The sense thus passed from pursuing animals to troubling people.
en.tracer:
Attested from the 12th century, from Vulgar Latin *~tractiare~, derived from ~tractum~, the supine of Latin ~trahere~ (“to pull, drag”). The deeper origin of ~trahere~ is genuinely unclear: the regular sound laws do not fit a clean Proto-Indo-European source, and scholars variously propose a link to the *~weǵʰ-~ family (“to carry,” as in ~vehere~), a reshaped *~dʰregʰ-~, or — per de Vaan — a non-Indo-European substrate word; the connection to English ~drag~ and German ~tragen~ remains debated rather than proven.

The semantic path is elegant: from “dragging” a stylus came “drawing a line,” then “plotting a route” and figuratively “forging ahead” — hence the colloquial ~tracer~ for “to hurry, race along.” The same Latin ~trahere~ gave French ~trait~, ~traire~, ~portrait~, ~retracer~, and the nouns ~tracé~ and ~traceur~. Whatever its murky deepest root, the idea of dragging something across a surface runs through the whole family.
en.tracter: The sources offer two accounts. The first is a back-formation from ~tracteur~ and ~traction~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, which suits the sense “to pull, to tow”. The second is a denominal verb from ~tract~, a noun borrowed from English for a short printed political or religious text, which would fit the sense of handing out leaflets. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~. The sense “to pull” matches the first account, though the second probably accounts for the other use of the verb.
en.traduire:
From Latin ~traducere~ (“to lead across, to bring over”), from ~trans-~ (“across”) + ~ducere~ (“to lead, conduct”). ~ducere~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~dewk-~ (“to draw, to pull”), cognate with English ~tow~ and ~tug~ and with German ~ziehen~ (“to pull”). The Romance siblings are Italian ~tradurre~ and Spanish ~traducir~; French had also inherited the older, properly translation-meaning verb ~translater~, from Latin ~translatare~.

The modern sense rests on a famous misreading. In classical Latin ~traducere~ meant “to lead across, to transfer, to parade” — even “to disgrace,” by leading a culprit publicly across the forum. Around 1400 the humanist Leonardo Bruni, parsing a phrase of Aulus Gellius, took ~traducere~ to mean “to render from one tongue into another,” and the brilliant error spread across Europe, ousting ~translater~ in French by the sixteenth century. A ghost of the old “lead across” sense lingers in the legal ~traduire en justice~ (“to bring before a court”). From the same ~ducere~ French drew a teeming family: ~conduire~, ~produire~, ~réduire~, ~séduire~, ~duc~, and ~aqueduc~.
en.traficoter: Formed from ~trafiquer~ (“to traffic, to deal”) and the suffix ~-oter~. ~Trafiquer~ was borrowed from Italian, from ~trafficare~ or the Venetan ~traffegare~. The suffix ~-oter~ adds a diminutive or pejorative nuance, a small, shady or fiddly version of the action, in familiar speech. The TLFi cites ~traficoter~ as a creation of the mid-twentieth century, so it is a recent colloquial coinage: to deal in a petty, murky way.
en.trafiquer: Borrowed from Italian rather than built in French. French Wiktionary says it first appears spelled ~traffiguer~ with the sense “to do business over long distances,” and takes it from Italian ~trafficare~ or from Venetan ~traffegare~. The sources do not decide between the two. Modern French ~trafiquer~ covers trading in goods and also tampering with something, as the gloss “traffic, tamper with” shows.
en.trahir:
~Trahir~ is inherited from Middle French ~trahir~, from Old French ~traïr~, from Latin ~trādere~ (“to hand over, to deliver, to betray”). The Latin verb combines ~trans-~ (“across”) with ~dare~ (“to give”), whose root is the Proto-Indo-European *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). The ~h~ of the modern spelling is a later addition that marks the two vowels as separate syllables. Italian ~tradire~, Portuguese ~trair~ and Occitan ~traïr~ come from the same Latin verb.

The Latin sense “to hand over” was neutral, and it is still visible in ~tradition~, literally “what is handed down.” The meaning “to betray” grew from handing someone over to an enemy, and the agent noun ~trāditor~ gave ~traître~ in French and ~traitor~ in English. English ~treason~ and French ~trahison~ share the same family. In French, ~trahir~ spread from persons to things: ~trahir un secret~ (“to give away”), ~trahir sa pensée~ (“to misrepresent”), and a voice that ~trahit~ emotion (“to reveal”).
