Related words are ~trahison~, ~traître~, ~tradition~, ~extradition~ and ~traditionnel~.
en.traire:
Inherited from Old French ~traire~ (also ~treire~, “to pull”), from a popular Latin *~tragere~, a reshaping of classical Latin ~trahere~ (“to pull, to drag”). English Wiktionary gives the intermediate as Early Medieval Latin ~tragō~. The classical verb is the source of Italian ~trarre~ and of a large learned family in English, including ~tract~, ~attract~ and ~extract~.

In Old French, ~traire~ meant “to pull” in the widest sense, but it was challenged by ~tirer~, a regular verb, and held on only in the narrow sense of pulling on a udder to draw out the milk. It also ousted the old French ~moudre~, which came from Latin ~mulgēre~ and is a cognate of English ~milk~; in a sense, French milks cows with the verb for pulling. The Latin ~trahere~ also gave ~trait~, ~traction~, ~extraire~, ~abstraire~, ~distraire~ and ~soustraire~, all built on the same root.
en.traiter:
From Latin ~tractāre~ (“to handle, to manage, to deal with”), the frequentative of ~trahere~ (“to draw, to pull”), whose past participle is ~tractus~. ~Trahere~ goes back to a PIE root often given as *~tregʰ-~ (“to draw, to drag”); the relationship to Germanic ~drag~ is debated, so it is left aside. Within French itself ~traiter~ is a doublet of the inherited ~traire~ (“to milk,” originally “to draw”). Cognate with Italian ~trattare~ and Spanish ~tratar~.

The frequentative force of ~tractāre~ is “to keep drawing, to handle repeatedly,” and from there “to handle” in every sense — physically, then socially, then intellectually. That spread explains the wide modern range of ~traiter~: to treat a person (well or badly), to treat a patient, to deal with a subject, to process a material or data, and, via ~traité~, to conclude a treaty. The participle ~tractus~ seeded ~trait~ (“line, feature, stroke”), and the same ~trahere~ family gives French ~tracter~, ~traction~, ~extraire~, ~abstrait~, and ~portrait~ — all built on the basic gesture of drawing something out.
en.tramer: Formed from ~trame~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~trame~ comes from Old French ~traime~, from Latin ~trāma~, the weft of a fabric. Its modern spelling was reshaped on the model of the verb ~tramer~, so the noun was altered to match the verb and not the reverse. The verb now means to weave and, by extension, to hatch or devise something.
en.tranchefiler: Formed from the noun ~tranchefile~ and the verbal suffix ~-er~. The noun is a variant of ~tranchefil~, the bookbinder's term for the headband sewn at the head and tail of a book's spine. The verb therefore means to sew that headband, a craft word with no deeper history in the sources.
en.trancher:
From Old French ~trenchier~ (around 1100), whence also the cognate Romance verbs Catalan ~trencar~ and Italian ~trinciare~. The Latin source is genuinely uncertain, and the sources offer two competing accounts. By one, it comes from a Vulgar Latin *~trinicare~ (“to cut in three”), built on ~tres~ / ~trini~ like ~duplicare~ on ~duplus~; by the other, it is an alteration of Latin ~truncare~ (“to lop, maim”), possibly crossed with a Gaulish *~trincare~. Neither is established, so the chain is best left flagged as disputed rather than forced.

Whatever the root, the meaning is “to cut cleanly through,” and from the literal blade-stroke French drew a rich figurative harvest. To ~trancher~ a question is to settle it decisively — to cut through debate — and an opinion that is ~tranché~ is sharp and unqualified, a metaphor English shares in ~trenchant~. The same Old French verb, borrowed into English, gave ~trench~ (a cut in the ground) and ~retrench~. Native French derivatives are abundant: ~tranche~ (“slice”), ~tranchant~ (“cutting edge”), ~tranchée~ (“trench”), ~trancheur~, and ~trançoir~ — a whole family turning on the clean stroke of a knife.
en.tranquilliser: Formed from the adjective ~tranquille~ plus the verb-forming suffix ~-iser~, which gives verbs meaning “to make A”: here “to make calm,” hence “to calm, to reassure.” The adjective is a learned borrowing from Latin ~tranquillus~ (“calm”) and is attested in Middle French in the 15th century. The same suffix builds ~moderniser~ and ~actualiser~.
en.transbahuter: Formed from the prefix ~trans-~ (“across”), the noun ~bahut~ and the verbal ending ~-er~: to ~transbahuter~ is, informally, to cart or lug things from one place to another. The noun ~bahut~, a chest, comes from Old French ~bahur~, and its deeper origin is unknown, since the hypotheses offered are all weak. The prefix ~trans-~ comes from Latin ~trans-~ (“across, beyond”).
en.transborder: ~Transborder~ (“to ferry”) is formed from ~border~ and the prefix ~trans-~ (“across”), so it means to carry from one side of the water to the other. The base ~border~ comes from the noun ~bord~, which was first the side of a ship, and which French borrowed from Frankish *~bord~ (“plank, side of a ship”), from Proto-Germanic *~burdą~. It is therefore cognate with English ~board~ and German ~Bord~. The learned prefix ~trans-~ is still productive in technical French, and here it turns a verb of running along an edge into one of crossing over it.
en.transcender:
Borrowed from Latin ~trānscendere~ (“to climb over, to surpass”), built from ~trāns~ (“across, beyond”) and ~scandere~ (“to climb”). French Wiktionary points to ~descendre~ and ~ascension~ as relatives, which come from the same Latin verb family with other prefixes, so ~transcender~ belongs to a small group of “climbing” words. French took it as a learned word directly from Latin, not through any inherited Old French form.

The French verb keeps the figurative picture of climbing over: to ~transcender~ is to rise above an obstacle, a condition or the ordinary range of experience. Its family in French includes ~transcendant~ and ~transcendance~, while its relatives ~ascension~ and ~descendre~ show the same Latin stem under different prefixes. Like most learned verbs of this kind, it entered French as a ready-made Latin word and was not assembled from French parts.
en.transcoder: ~Transcoder~ is formed from ~coder~ and the prefix ~trans-~, which here means “from one state to another.” To transcode is to convert something from one code to another, a sense that also reaches the computing meaning of compiling source code. The base ~coder~ is either a verb built on ~code~ or a borrowing of English ~to code~, and ~code~ goes back to Latin ~codex~, a variant of ~caudex~ (“tree trunk”). The learned prefix ~trans-~ (Latin “across, beyond”) is productive in technical French, as in ~transborder~ and ~transvaser~, so ~transcoder~ is a modern technical coinage.
en.transcrire:
Borrowed from Latin ~trānscrībere~, a compound of ~trāns-~ (“across, over”) and ~scrībere~ (“to write”). The Latin verb meant to copy out, to write over from one place or document to another. Latin ~scrībere~ goes back to a root meaning “to scratch, to cut,” which fits the earliest writing, done by scoring wax or clay with a stylus. The Romance cousins are Italian ~trascrivere~ and Spanish ~transcribir~, and English ~transcribe~ is a learned borrowing of the same Latin verb.

French ~transcrire~ keeps the picture of carrying a text across: to transcribe is to move something from one form to another while changing as little as possible. It can mean copying a document into a register, writing down speech, rendering a language in another script, or putting music in another key or for another instrument. Scientists later borrowed it for biology, where a cell transcribes a gene into RNA. The Latin verb ~scrībere~ yielded French ~écrire~ through the form ~ēscrībere~, and gave a large family: ~décrire~, ~inscrire~, ~souscrire~, ~prescrire~, ~scribe~, ~script~ and ~transcription~.
en.transfigurer: French ~transfigurer~ comes straight from Latin ~transfigurāre~ (“to change the shape of”). The Latin verb joins ~trans-~ (“across, over”) to ~figurāre~ (“to shape, to form”), a verb built on ~figūra~ (“shape, form”). Its literal sense is thus “to shape across,” that is, to change someone's form or appearance. The same Latin family gave French ~figure~, ~figurer~, ~défigurer~, ~configurer~ and the noun ~transfiguration~. French Wiktionary gives just the Latin verb.
en.transfiler: The verb is built on the noun ~fil~ (“thread”) with the prefix ~trans-~, which carries the sense of “across, through.” ~Fil~ came into French from Old French ~fil~, from Latin ~filum~ (“thread”), the same source as English ~file~ in the sense of a line of things. The verb belongs to the vocabulary of sailors and sailmakers: it describes lacing canvas together by passing thread across, and whipping the end of a rope with twine to keep it from fraying.
en.transformer:
From Latin ~transformāre~ (“to change in shape, transform”), a compound of the prefix ~trans-~ (“across, beyond”) and ~formāre~ (“to shape, form”), itself from ~forma~ (“form, shape, figure”). The verb entered French around 1295. The origin of ~forma~ is debated: it may be a borrowing from Greek ~morphḗ~ (“form, shape, beauty”) — perhaps via Etruscan — with the consonants transposed, or both words may inherit a common Proto-Indo-European source. The Latin verb also gives Italian ~trasformare~, Spanish ~transformar~, and English ~transform~.

The sense has stayed remarkably stable: to carry a thing “across” into a new form. From that core, French applies it everywhere — from caterpillar into butterfly (a metamorphosis), from raw material into product, and, in rugby, the bonus kick that ~transforme~ a try into added points. ~forma~ seeded an enormous family in French: ~former~ (“to form, train”), ~forme~, ~formule~, ~formel~, ~conforme~, ~réformer~, ~déformer~, ~informer~ (literally “to give shape to,” to put into the mind), and ~uniforme~. The disputed link to Greek ~morphḗ~ means that ~transformer~ may be a distant cousin of ~métamorphose~ — two ways of speaking about a change of shape.
en.transfuser:
~Transfuser~ was formed in French by adding the verb ending ~-er~ to ~transfus~ (“poured across”), a past participle attested in 1548. That participle belongs to a French verb ~transfundre~ (“to pass on, to transmit”), found in 1542, which was borrowed from Latin ~transfundere~ (“to pour from one vessel to another”) and, figuratively, “to pour out, to transfer onto, to spread.” The Latin verb is made of ~trans-~ (“across”) and ~fundere~ (“to pour”).

The first recorded sense, in 1668, is medical: to transfuse blood, in a report of a spaniel given the blood of a sheep. By 1701 the verb also meant to pour a liquid from one container into another, and in 1833 Balzac used it figuratively, for passing qualities or gifts on to others. In 1848 Chateaubriand wrote of a local dialect whose flavor could not be ~transfuser~ into another language. The Latin root ~fundere~ also lies behind French ~fondre~, ~fusion~, ~infuser~ and ~diffuser~.
en.transférer:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~trānsferre~ (“to carry across, to bear over, to transport”), formed from the prefix ~trāns-~ (“across, beyond”) and ~ferre~ (“to carry, to bear”), from Proto-Indo-European *~bʰer-~ (“to carry, to bear”). That root is one of the most widespread in all Indo-European: it is cognate with English ~bear~, Greek ~phérein~ (“to carry”), and Sanskrit ~bhárati~ (“he carries”). The Latin ~trānsferre~ also gave the past participle ~trānslātus~, source of the English ~translate~ — itself a “carrying across,” of meaning from one tongue to another.

French remodeled the inherited stem on the pattern of regular ~-érer~ verbs, yielding ~transférer~. Its core image is literal transport — carrying a thing from one place to another — and it still serves for moving a prisoner, an employee, a sum of money, or a body from place to place. The figurative ~transfert~ went on to a distinguished career in psychology and law. From the same ~ferre~ French inherited a great convoy of words: ~conférer~, ~déférer~, ~différer~, ~offrir~, ~souffrir~, ~préférer~, and the noun ~fertile~ (“bearing, fruitful”) — every one of them, like ~transférer~, a matter of something carried.
en.transgresser:
~Transgresser~ is built on ~transgression~ with the suffix ~-er~, and the noun in turn comes from Latin ~transgressio~, from ~transgredi~ (“to cross, to step across”), made of ~trans-~ (“across”) and ~gradi~ (“to step”). Old French had a closer relative of the Latin verb, ~transgredir~. The modern verb is thus a later French formation drawn from the noun, not a direct descendant of ~transgredi~.

The stem is a pattern shared with several other French verbs created in the same way from nouns in ~-ssion~: ~agresser~, ~digresser~, ~progresser~, ~régresser~ and ~dégresser~ all go back to a Latin compound of ~gradi~ with a different prefix. The literal image is of stepping over a line, and the figurative one is of breaking a rule, a law or a limit. Related words are ~transgression~ and ~transgresseur~. English ~transgress~ comes from the same Latin source.
en.transhumer:
French ~transhumer~ was borrowed from Spanish ~trashumar~, itself built from Latin ~trāns~ (“across, beyond”) and ~humus~ (“ground, land”). French Wiktionary gives only the two Latin parts, while English Wiktionary adds the Spanish stage. The verb thus means, literally, to cross the land, and it names the seasonal movement of livestock between lowland and mountain pastures. The noun ~transhumance~ and the Spanish ~trashumancia~ come from the same pair of parts.

Latin ~humus~ is the root of a small French family. It gave the learned ~humus~ (“soil rich in organic matter”), ~exhumer~ and ~inhumer~ (to dig up and to bury), and, by textbook etymology, ~humble~ through Latin ~humilis~, since the humble are the low, close to the ground. The Latin prefix ~trāns~ sits in ~transporter~, ~transmettre~ and ~transhumer~ alike.
en.transiger:
French took ~transiger~ as a learned borrowing from Latin ~transigere~, a compound of ~trans-~ (“through, across”) and ~agere~ (“to drive, to lead”). The literal picture is of driving a matter through to its end, and in Latin the verb meant to carry out, to complete, to settle a business. Spanish ~transigir~ is a learned cousin, and English ~transact~ is built on the same Latin verb.

In French the verb means “to compromise,” to settle a matter by giving way. Today it is heard most often in the negative, as in ~ne pas transiger sur~ (“to refuse to compromise on”). The Latin source ~agere~ is the root of a very large French family: ~agir~ (“to act”), ~agent~, ~action~, and ~transaction~, which is the noun that sits closest to ~transiger~ in both form and meaning, an agreement carried through.
en.transir:
French ~transir~ is attested in the ~Chanson de Roland~. It descends from Old French ~transir~ (“to die, to pass away”), which was still current in Middle French with the senses “to pass on, to depart.” Both sources trace it to Latin ~trānsīre~ (“to go beyond”), made of ~trāns~ (“across”) and ~īre~ (“to go”).

So the verb began with the sense of dying, of passing on. Today it has narrowed to the state of being numbed or gripped, most often by cold, and the participle ~transi~ also appears in phrases about fear or love. The sources at hand do not explain how “to die” became “to be chilled to the bone.” The same Latin verb gave French ~transit~, ~transition~ and ~transitoire~, and English ~transit~ and ~transient~.
en.transistoriser: Modeled on English ~transistorize~, itself ~transistor~ plus a verbal suffix, and formed in French from ~transistor~ with ~-iser~. It means “to equip with transistors.” French ~transistor~ was borrowed from English ~transistor~. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs.
en.transiter: Formed from ~transit~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to pass through”, as goods, travelers or data do. The noun ~transit~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~trānsitus~ (“passage”), which belongs to the verb ~trānsīre~ (“to go across”), made of ~trans-~ (“across”) and ~īre~ (“to go”). The verb is therefore a French coinage on a Latin noun, with no Latin verb behind it in this form.
en.translittérer: ~Translittérer~ is derived from the noun ~translittération~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun is a learned formation: the prefix ~trans-~ (“across”), Latin ~littera~ (“letter”) and the suffix ~-tion~. To transliterate is thus, quite literally, to carry letters across from one writing system to another, rendering the characters of one alphabet with those of another.
en.transmettre:
From Latin ~transmittere~ (“to send across, to send over”), reshaped in French on the model of ~mettre~. The Latin verb joins the prefix ~trans-~ (“across, beyond”) and ~mittere~ (“to send, to let go”), which descends from Proto-Italic *~meitō~ and a Proto-Indo-European root *~mey-~ (“to change, to exchange”). The sense traveled from “exchange” to “give, let go” to “send.” English borrowed the same compound as ~transmit~.

The image is one of carrying something across a gap — a message, a disease, an inheritance, a radio wave — and handing it on. ~Mittere~ was one of Latin's most prolific verbs, and through its French heir ~mettre~ (“to put”) and its many compounds it shaped a huge vocabulary: ~admettre~, ~commettre~, ~permettre~, ~promettre~, ~soumettre~, and ~remettre~, alongside the nouns of the ~missus~ / ~missio~ branch — ~mission~, ~message~ (literally “a thing sent”), ~messager~, ~commission~, and ~mise~. So when we ~transmettre~ knowledge from one generation to the next, we are quite literally “sending it across,” performing in the abstract the same act a Roman did when he dispatched a courier over the frontier.
en.transmigrer:
Borrowed from Latin ~trānsmigrāre~ (“to transmigrate”), the infinitive of ~trānsmigrō~, which is built from ~trāns~ (“across”) and ~migrō~ (“to move, to migrate”). English Wiktionary adds that, by surface analysis, the French verb can also be read as ~trans-~ plus ~migrer~, but the Latin verb was already formed when French took it over, so the prefix comes from Latin rather than being added in French.

The verb is learned. It means to pass from one place or state to another, and it is best known for the passage of a soul from one body to another. Its family is large. French has ~migrer~, ~émigrer~, ~immigrer~ and the noun ~transmigration~, and English has ~transmigrate~ from the same Latin verb. The shared Latin root ~migrāre~ gives all of these the idea of moving from one dwelling to another.
en.transmuer:
~Transmuer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~trānsmūtāre~ (“to change from one thing to another”), formed from ~trāns-~ (“across, over”) and ~mūtāre~ (“to change”), so the verb literally says “to change across.” It takes the conjugation of ~muer~. It is a doublet of ~transmuter~, which was remade later on the Latin source. French Wiktionary simply calls ~transmuer~ a variant of ~transmuter~.

Both verbs mean to change one thing into another. ~Muer~ comes from the same ~mūtāre~, and the learned ~muter~ and ~mutation~ share it, as do ~commuer~ (“to commute a sentence”) and ~permuter~. The pair ~transmuer~ and ~transmuter~ thus shows French going twice to one Latin verb: once fitted to the conjugation of the inherited ~muer~, once copied straight from the Latin ending.
en.transmuter:
~Transmuter~ is borrowed from Latin ~transmūtāre~ (“to change, to transform”), a verb formed from ~trans-~ (“across”) and ~mūtāre~ (“to change”). The prefix carries the idea of passing over from one state to another, so the verb literally means “to change across.” It is a doublet of ~transmuer~: the same Latin verb gave French two words, ~transmuter~ and ~transmuer~. Italian ~trasmutare~, Spanish ~transmutar~ and English ~transmute~ are its relatives.

~Transmuter~ means to change something into something of another nature, and it is at home in learned, scientific and literary writing. Its best-known setting is alchemy, with its dream of transmuting base metals into gold; the noun ~transmutation~ keeps that history. The Latin base ~mūtāre~ is the source of a large French family: the inherited ~muer~ (“to change,” as when a voice breaks or an animal moults), and learned words such as ~mutation~, ~permuter~ and ~commuer~.
en.transparaître: According to French Wiktionary, ~transparaître~ comes from an earlier ~transparêtre~, a compound of the Latin prefix ~trans-~ (“across, through, beyond”) and popular Latin ~parescere~ (“to appear”). The verb thus means “to appear through.” Its second half is the source of ~paraître~, and so it is a close relative of ~apparaître~, ~comparaître~ and ~disparaître~.
en.transpercer: ~Transpercer~ is formed from the prefix ~trans-~ and the verb ~percer~. The prefix is a learned borrowing from Latin ~trans-~ (“across, through”), and here it intensifies the idea of passing right through. The base ~percer~ goes back to Vulgar Latin *~pertusiare~, from ~pertusum~, a form of ~pertundere~ (“to bore through”). English Wiktionary adds that ~transpercer~ displaced the Old French ~trespercier~, which used the older form of the same prefix, ~tres-~.
en.transpirer:
French ~transpirer~ is a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ~trānspirāre~, built from Latin ~trāns~ (“through”) and ~spīrāre~ (“to breathe”). The French text points to the related verbs ~aspirer~ and ~expirer~, which share the same second half. The literal sense is therefore “to breathe through.” English ~transpire~ came from the same Latin source, and ~perspire~ is a close cousin.

The verb now means “to sweat” in ordinary use, and also, of news or secrets, “to leak out, to become known.” The Latin ~spīrāre~ underlies a large French family: ~respirer~, ~inspirer~, ~expirer~, ~aspirer~, ~conspirer~ and also ~esprit~, the “breath” that became “spirit.” The French sense of “sweat” and the sense of “leak” are separate branches, and the sources supplied do not say which came first.
en.transplanter: From Latin ~transplantāre~, which is built from the prefix ~trans-~ (“across”) and the verb ~plantāre~ (“to plant”), the source of French ~planter~. French Wiktionary refers readers to those two elements, ~trans-~ and ~planter~. The verb therefore means, literally, to plant across: to move a plant, and later an organ or a population, from one place to another. The only source here is French Wiktionary, and the descent is a plain Latin borrowing.
en.transporter:
From Latin ~transportāre~ (“to carry across, to convey”), composed of the prefix ~trans-~ (“across, beyond”) and ~portāre~ (“to carry”). The verb ~portāre~ goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~per-~ (“to pass through, to cross over”), the root behind Latin ~porta~ (“gate”) and ~portus~ (“harbour”), and behind English ~fare~, ~ford~, and ~ferry~ — all notions of passage and crossing. Italian ~trasportare~ and Spanish ~transportar~ are the direct Romance parallels.

The literal sense — to carry people or goods from one place to another — has stayed central since antiquity, and it powers a whole modern vocabulary of movement. But French also kept a striking figurative use: to be ~transporté~ is to be carried away by emotion, “transported” with joy, anger, or love, the soul borne off as if bodily. The noun ~transport~ likewise means both “transportation” and a “rapture” or surge of feeling (~un transport de joie~). From the shared ancestor ~portāre~ flows a vast family of French words: ~porter~ itself, ~porteur~, ~apporter~, ~emporter~, ~rapporter~, ~importer~ and ~exporter~, ~portatif~, and ~portable~ — all built on the simple idea of carrying.
en.transposer:
From Latin ~transponere~ (“to transfer, to move across”), itself built from ~trans-~ (“across”) and ~ponere~ (“to put, to place”). The French verb did not keep the Latin shape intact: English Wiktionary says it was altered based on French ~poser~, so that it now looks like ~trans-~ + ~poser~ even though the Latin verb underneath is ~ponere~.

The core sense is “to move something to another place or order,” and the verb has specialized in several directions since. In music, to ~transposer~ a melody is to move it into another key without changing its intervals. In algebra, one can ~transposer~ a term to the other side of an equation. In everyday and literary use, one can ~transposer~ a story into another period or setting, keeping its structure while changing its scenery. The noun ~transposition~ covers all these uses. The verb belongs to a family with ~poser~, ~déposer~, ~composer~ and ~proposer~, all of which share the idea of “placing,” with a different prefix each time.
en.transsuder: ~Transsuder~ is a learned formation from ~trans-~ (“through”) and Latin ~sūdāre~ (“to sweat”), so it means to ooze through a surface, as moisture does. The Latin verb is also the source of inherited French ~suer~, which lost the Latin ~d~ along the way. English ~transude~ is built in the same way from the same two parts.
en.transvaser: ~Transvaser~ is formed from the prefix ~trans-~ (“across, from one place to another”), the noun ~vase~ in its old sense of “vessel, container,” and the ending ~-er~. That ~vase~ comes from Latin ~vās~ (“vessel, pot, tableware”), and it is a different word from the ~vase~ meaning “mud.” The verb means “to pour a liquid from one container into another,” as in decanting wine, and by extension “to move” something from one place to another.
en.transvider: ~Transvider~ is formed from ~vider~ with the learned prefix ~trans-~ (“across”), so it means to move the contents of one container into another. The base ~vider~ comes from Old French ~vuidier~, from the adjective ~vuit~ / ~vuide~ (“empty”), which belongs to the family of Latin ~vacuus~ (“empty”). The prefix ~trans-~ is borrowed from Latin, and its sense of passage from one place or state to another is the same as in ~transvaser~.
en.traquer:
The origin of ~traquer~ is uncertain. French Wiktionary proposes that it is probably a verb formed from Middle French ~trac~ (“track, trace”). English Wiktionary gives a fuller chain for that noun: Middle French ~trac~ came from Old French ~trac~ (“track, beaten path, course”), from Middle Dutch ~treck~ or ~treke~ (“a drawing, a pull, a line”), from Old Dutch *~trecken~, and ultimately from Proto-Germanic *~trakjaną~ (“to drag”). If that is right, ~traquer~ shares its Germanic ancestry with English ~track~ and ~trek~, both of which are named as relatives. The hedge matters: the link from ~trac~ to ~traquer~ is a likely derivation, not a documented one.

The verb means “to track, to hunt down, to hound,” and a ~traque~ is a hunt or manhunt in which someone is followed relentlessly. A hunting origin for the sense is natural, since a track is what a hunter follows, but the sources do not spell out the stages, so the story should be taken as plausible rather than documented. In modern French the verb is used both of hunters and police and of the press, which ~traque~ its targets, and the past participle ~traqué~ describes the hunted look of someone who feels pursued. English ~trek~, which has a Dutch and Afrikaans career of its own, is a distant echo of the same Germanic idea of dragging along.
en.traumatiser: The two Wiktionaries frame ~traumatiser~ slightly differently. English Wiktionary builds it from ~traumat(isme)~ plus the verb suffix ~-iser~; French Wiktionary links it to Ancient Greek ~τραυματίζω~ (“to wound”), from ~trauma~. Greek ~trauma~ meant “wound,” and French ~traumatisme~ belongs to the same family, as does English ~trauma~.
en.travailler:
French ~travailler~ comes from Old French ~traveillier~ (“to torment, to torture, to cause suffering”), from Vulgar Latin *~tripāliāre~ (“to torture with the ~tripalium~”). The ~tripalium~ was, on the most widespread account, an instrument of restraint or torture made of three stakes — ~tri-~ (“three”) plus ~pālus~ (“stake”) — to which slaves were bound for punishment or large animals were tied to be shod. The same source gives Spanish ~trabajar~, Portuguese ~trabalhar~, and Occitan ~trabalhar~, all the ordinary words for “to work.”

The semantic journey is startling: from “to torture” the verb passed to “to suffer, to toil painfully,” then to the neutral “to labor,” and finally to today's “to work” of every kind. The older sense of anguish has not wholly vanished — the noun ~travail~ still names the pains of childbirth, and ~se travailler~ can mean “to torment oneself.” A caution is in order: this tidy ~tripalium~ story, though repeated everywhere, is disputed, and some scholars instead derive the word from a Late Latin *~trabicula~ (“little beam,” a frame for holding animals). Either way the modern ~travailleur~ (“worker”) carries, etymologically, a faint echo of the rack.
en.travailloter: Formed from ~travailler~ with the suffix ~-oter~, which gives a small, light or intermittent action: to work, but only a little and by fits and starts. The base comes from Old French ~traveillier~ (“to torment”), traditionally traced to Vulgar Latin *~tripāliāre~, from ~tripalium~, a three-stake instrument of restraint or torture, though that account is disputed. The suffix ~-oter~, familiar in register, also appears in ~tapoter~ and ~vivoter~.
en.traverser:
From Old French ~traverser~, from Late Latin ~traversare~, a worn-down form of ~transversare~, itself from the Latin adjective ~transversus~ (“lying across, turned crosswise”). ~transversus~ is the past participle of ~transvertere~, from ~trans~ (“across”) and ~vertere~ (“to turn”). ~vertere~ descends from PIE *~wert-~ (“to turn, to bend”), one of the most prolific roots in Indo-European. Cognate with Italian ~traversare~ and Spanish ~atravesar~.

The image is precise: to ~traverser~ is to move along a line “turned across” one's path, to cut from one side to the other. The same *~wert-~ root, through ~vertere~ and its participle ~versus~, fans out across French into ~tourner~, ~version~, ~vers~, ~envers~, ~divers~, and ~convertir~, and even into English ~-ward~, ~worth~, and ~versus~ — all of them carrying some ghost of turning. Closer to home, ~traverser~ has bred a small household of its own: the noun ~travers~ (“breadth, a turning aside”), the adverbial ~à travers~ and ~de travers~ (“askew”), the ~traversée~ (a sea crossing), and the ~traversin~, the long bolster that lies crosswise at the head of a French bed — a humble pillow still quietly “turned across.”
en.travestir: ~Travestir~ is borrowed from Italian ~travestire~ (“to disguise”), and French Wiktionary adds an earlier French form, ~transvestir~. The Italian verb is built on ~vestire~ (“to dress”) with the prefix ~tra-~, which French Wiktionary lists as a variant of ~trans-~ (“across, over”). Italian ~vestire~ is the Latin ~vestīre~, which French inherited as ~vêtir~ (“to clothe”). The verb means to disguise.
en.traînailler: Formed from ~traîner~ (“to drag, to dawdle”) with the suffix ~-ailler~, which gives a repeated, petty or pejorative action: to dawdle, to mooch about. The base comes from Old French ~traïner~, inherited from Vulgar Latin *~tragīnāre~, built on *~tragere~, a form of Latin ~trahere~ (“to pull”). The same *~tragere~ gave ~traire~ (“to milk”). Like ~tirailler~ from ~tirer~ and ~criailler~ from ~crier~, ~traînailler~ takes a common verb and adds a note of doing it badly or half-heartedly.
en.traînasser: ~Traînasser~ is formed from ~traîner~ (“to drag, to trail”) with the suffix ~-asser~, which gives a verb a casual, slightly pejorative or diminishing tone. Where ~traîner~ drags, ~traînasser~ dawdles: to hang around, to loiter or to mooch about without hurry or purpose.
en.traîner:
French ~traîner~ comes from Old French ~traïner~, inherited from Vulgar Latin *~tragīnāre~, a verb built on *~tragere~, itself a form of Latin ~trahere~ (“to pull”). The same *~tragere~ gave French ~traire~ (“to milk”). Wiktionary tentatively links ~trahere~ to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dʰregʰ-~, but the connection is marked uncertain. Other Romance languages hold close cousins of ~traîner~: Italian ~trascinare~, Catalan ~traginar~ and Spanish ~trajinar~ all descend from related Latin stock. English ~train~ is a loan from the French family.

The verb began as “to pull behind oneself,” as one drags a cart or a long robe. From that came the figurative sense of moving slowly, then of lingering, as in ~traîner dans les rues~ (“to hang around”) or ~ça traîne~ (“it drags on”). The modern circumflex stands where Old French had the diaeresis of ~traïner~. The family also includes ~train~, formed on ~traîner~, and, from ~trahere~, ~trait~, ~traction~, ~attraction~ and ~abstraire~. A railway ~train~ is, etymologically, a thing dragged along behind an engine.
en.treillager: Formed from the noun ~treillage~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. The TLFi treats the verb under ~treillage~, a noun built on ~treille~ with the suffix ~-age~, and records ~treillage~ from 1571, in the sense of an assembly of laths or stakes laid parallel or crossed to form arbors, palisades or espaliers. The verb means to fit something with such a framework, as one does with garden walls, or to fix a plant to one so that it grows along it.
en.treillisser: Formed from ~treillis~ (“lattice, trellis”) with the verb ending ~-er~: to fit with a lattice. The origin of ~treillis~ is explained two ways. One account derives it from ~treille~ with the suffix ~-is~, ~treille~ coming from Latin ~trichila~. The other traces it to Latin ~trilix~ (“woven of three threads”), through Late Latin ~trilicius~ and Old French ~treslis~.
en.trembler:
From Old French ~trembler~ (earlier ~trambler~), from Late Latin ~tremulāre~, a verb built on the adjective ~tremulus~ (“shaking”) and ultimately from Latin ~tremere~ (“to tremble”). That root goes back to the Proto-Indo-European *~trem-~ (“to tremble”), shared with Ancient Greek ~trémō~. The same Latin verb ~tremere~ is also one of the sources of French ~craindre~ (“to fear”), whose initial consonant shifted along the way. English Wiktionary notes that ~trembler~ has a doublet, the learned ~trémuler~, formed on the same Late Latin base. English ~tremble~ is borrowed from French.

The verb began as a physical description of shaking and then gained its emotional uses, since fear and cold make the body shake. Hence ~trembler de peur~ (“to tremble with fear”), ~trembler pour quelqu'un~ (“to fear for someone”), and the colorful ~trembler comme une feuille~ (“to shake like a leaf”). The link with ~craindre~ is a nice trace of the old connection: the Latin verb that gave one verb for shaking and another for fearing. The family includes ~tremblement~ (“tremor”), ~trembloter~ (“to quiver slightly”), ~tremblotant~, and the learned ~trémulation~, a more clinical shaking. English ~tremor~ and ~tremulous~ come from the Latin side.
en.trembloter: Formed from ~trembler~ (“to tremble”) with the suffix ~-oter~, which gives a diminutive, frequentative sense: to tremble a little, in small repeated shivers. The base descends from Old French ~trembler~, from Late Latin ~tremulāre~, built on ~tremulus~ (“shaking”), itself ultimately from Latin ~tremere~ (“to tremble”). The participle ~tremblotant~ (“quivering”) belongs to the same family.
en.tremper:
Inherited from Middle French ~tremper~, which is a metathesis of Old French ~temprer~ (the ~r~ moving forward a syllable), from Latin ~temperāre~ (“to mix in due proportion, to moderate”). It is a doublet of the learned borrowing ~tempérer~, which took the same Latin verb straight from Latin and so kept its shape. English ~temper~ and Italian ~temperare~ also descend from it, and so does Spanish ~templar~, which is a related form.

The sense progression runs from mixing to dipping. To ~temperāre~ was to blend things in the right measure, for instance wine with water, and the Old French verb kept the idea of mixing a liquid, and then of plunging something into one. In the French of the smith, ~tremper~ means to quench heated steel in water to harden it, and this gave the figurative ~la trempe~ (“quality of one's character”): a person ~de bonne trempe~ is made of strong stuff. Other senses are “to soak” and, in ~tremper dans une affaire~, “to be mixed up in an affair,” which echoes the older mixing sense. Relatives include ~trempette~, ~détremper~ and, through the learned doublet, ~tempérer~, ~tempérament~ and ~température~.
en.tressaillir: ~Tressaillir~ was already a verb in Old French. It is formed from ~saillir~ (“to leap”) and the prefix ~tres-~, the Old French form of Latin ~trans~ (“across”). The base ~saillir~ goes back to Latin ~salīre~ (“to leap, to jump”). The word means “to jump across,” which in French became “to shudder, to start” under a sudden shock.
en.tressauter: Formed from ~sauter~ with the prefix ~tres-~, the Old French form of Latin ~trans-~ (“across, beyond”), here an intensive with no clear sense of its own, as in ~tressaillir~. The base ~sauter~ comes from Latin ~saltāre~ (“to dance, to leap”), a frequentative of ~salīre~ (“to jump”). So ~tressauter~ is “to jump” with extra force, hence “to start, to jump with surprise or fear.”
en.tresser: Formed from the noun ~tresse~ (“braid”) with ~-er~: to ~tresser~ is to plait. The origin of ~tresse~ is debated. Both Wiktionaries relate it to Italian ~treccia~, and propose it may come from Vulgar Latin *~trichia~, itself from Ancient Greek ~θρίξ~ (“hair”), with Old French ~tresce~ as the intermediate form. This descent is a suggestion, not a settled fact.
en.treuiller: Formed from ~treuil~ (“winch”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, so ~treuiller~ is to hoist or haul with a winch. The noun comes from Old French ~treuil~, from Vulgar Latin *~troculum~, which is Latin ~torculum~ (“press”) in a reshaped form. A machine for pressing grapes or oil thus gave its name to a lifting device. Latin ~trochlea~ (“pulley”) is a related word.
en.trianguler: A derivation from the stem of Latin ~triangulus~ (“triangle”) with the verbal ending ~-er~. The Latin word is formed from ~tri-~ (“three”) and ~angulus~ (“corner”), so a triangle is a three-cornered figure. The TLFi records the participle ~triangulé~ in 1803 and notes an earlier Middle French ~trianguler~ (“to give the shape of a triangle”), found in 1490.
en.triballer: A denominal verb: the noun ~triballe~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary gives only that formation, and the sense of the verb, “to beat an animal skin”, is a technical one from the tanner's trade. The ending ~-er~ descends from Latin ~-are~ and here carries the sense “to work on N, to apply N”.
en.tricher:
The origin of ~tricher~ is disputed. French reaches back to Old French ~tricher~ (“to deceive, cheat”), and one account derives it from a Vulgar Latin verb *~triccāre~, from Late Latin ~tricāre~, itself from Latin ~trīcārī~ (“to look for detours, to quibble, to haggle”), a verb tied to the noun ~trīcae~. Support comes from sister languages that have the same verb: Italian ~treccare~, Old Occitan ~trichar~, and Catalan and Occitan ~trigar~.

A rival theory sees a Germanic origin instead, in Middle High German ~trechen~ (as in ~zuotrechen~, “to obtain by deceit”), with Middle Dutch ~treck~ (“ruse, stratagem”) as a relative. English Wiktionary invites a comparison with English ~trick~. It presents the Latin route first and the Germanic one as a further possibility, so neither account can be called settled. What is certain is only that the Old French verb existed; where it came from remains in dispute.
en.tricoter:
English Wiktionary traces ~tricoter~ to Old French ~tricoter~ (“to beat with sticks”), built on ~trique~ (“stick, cudgel”) and the ending ~-oter~ by surface analysis. ~Trique~ comes from earlier ~estrique~ (“stick used to knock down grain”), from a verb ~estriquer~ (“to strike”), from Frankish *~strīkan~, then Proto-Germanic *~strīkaną~ and Proto-Indo-European *~streyg-~ (“to strike”). Its Germanic cousins are Old High German ~strīhhan~ and Old English ~strīcan~ (“to stroke, to strike”), and English ~strike~ belongs to the same family.

So the knitter's verb began as a violent one. French Wiktionary derives ~tricoter~ from the noun ~tricot~, which first meant a stick, and suggests that legs, then knitting needles, were compared to sticks that one waves about. Its entry for the noun ~tricot~ runs the other way, calling it a deverbal of ~tricoter~ formed on ~trique~ with a diminutive ending, “little stick” or “knitting needle,” so the sources do not settle which came first. Either way, the stick-word is the root of ~tricoter~ (“to knit”), and ~tricot~ now means knitted fabric or a sweater.
en.trier:
The origin of French ~trier~ is disputed. It is first attested around 1175, as Old French ~trier~ (“to choose, to pick out, to sift, to cull”), and English Wiktionary labels it of uncertain origin; Occitan ~triar~ is a cognate. French Wiktionary reports two rival accounts. By one, ~trier~ is a distortion of ~tirer~ (“to draw out”). By the other, it descends from Late Latin ~trītāre~ (“to grind”), from ~trītum~, the supine of ~terere~ (“to rub, to grind”), and would originally have meant to rub the ear of wheat to separate the grain.

Neither account is settled, so the grain-threshing picture should be taken as a proposal, not a fact. What is certain is the sense of separating good from bad, which gave ~trier~ its modern uses: sorting mail, rubbish or lentils, and picking out candidates. English borrowed the verb as ~try~ by way of Anglo-Norman, where “to sift” gradually became “to test” and then “to attempt”; a ~trial~ is therefore a sorting out. The noun ~triage~, built on ~trier~, came back into English with its medical sense of sorting patients by urgency. If the ~terere~ account is right, ~trier~ would also be kin to ~triturer~ and English ~trite~, but that link remains a hypothesis.
en.trifouiller: Probably formed from ~fouiller~ (“to dig, to rummage”), under the influence of ~tripoter~ and ~tripatouiller~, two verbs of similar sound and meaning. The source states this with a hedge, and no older source language is named. The result is an expressive, informal verb for fiddling, tinkering or rummaging about in something, often with a touch of disapproval.
en.triller: Formed from the noun ~trille~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so ~triller~ means to sing or play a trill. The musical noun ~trille~ was borrowed from Italian ~trillo~ (“tremor”), a word that imitates the quick alternation of two notes. The unrelated botanical name ~trillium~ is a separate word and plays no part here. To ~triller~ is to perform that rapid shake.
en.trimarder: Formed from ~trimard~ (“road”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so the verb means to roam, to wander, to walk the earth. The sources give no older origin for ~trimard~. The sense is that of a tramp's life on the road.
en.trimbaler:
French ~trimbaler~ comes from Old French ~tribaler~ (“to shake in every direction”). English Wiktionary describes it as an alteration of that Old French verb, perhaps under the influence of ~brimbaler~ or ~trimer~, and calls ~tribaler~ itself an expressive word, probably formed on ~baller~ and ~tribo(u)ler~. It also compares Latin ~tribulō~ and ~tribulāre~. The origin is therefore probable rather than certain.

In modern French, ~trimbaler~ is a familiar word for dragging or lugging something cumbersome around, and the reflexive ~se trimbaler~ means to go about, often carrying a burden. The meaning fits well with the older idea of being jostled in all directions. Its relatives are the verbs named as its probable models, ~baller~ and ~tribouler~, and the Latin ~tribulāre~, which the sources set beside it as a comparison, not as a proven ancestor.
en.trimballer: ~Trimballer~ continues Old French ~tribaler~ (“to move about in every direction”). The modern spelling has gained an ~m~ and a doubled ~l~ compared with the Old French form. In today's French the verb means to drag or lug something cumbersome around with you.
en.trimer: The origin of ~trimer~ is uncertain, and the two sources disagree. The French text derives it from English ~trim~. English Wiktionary says only that it is uncertain, possibly an alteration of Old French ~trumer~ (“to run”), and dates the verb to the early eighteenth century. The meaning is “to slave away, to toil,” a familiar word for hard, tiring work, and the sources give no account of how either proposed origin led to that sense.
en.tringler: Formed from the noun ~tringle~ (a rod or bar) plus the verbal ending ~-er~, the usual way of coining a first-conjugation verb from a noun. The noun was ~tingle~ in Middle French, and the ~r~ is an intrusive sound added later. It comes from Middle Dutch ~tingel~, a variant of ~tengel~, which meant a wedge or wooden filler set between timbers that do not fit together properly.
en.trinquer:
From Middle French ~trinquer~ (around 1400), borrowed from Middle High German ~trinken~ (“to drink”), from Old High German ~trinkan~, from Proto-West Germanic *~drinkan~, from Proto-Germanic *~drinkaną~. French Wiktionary gives the shorter version, simply German ~trinken~. English ~drink~ is a cognate, descended from the same Germanic verb, and so is Dutch ~drinken~. French therefore took this verb from its eastern neighbors rather than inheriting it.

French already had ~boire~, from Latin ~bibere~, as its ordinary verb for drinking. By the seventeenth century ~trinquer~ had come to mean “to drink a toast,” the sense of clinking glasses that it keeps today. In 1876 it gained a figurative, informal meaning, “to take the fall,” that is, to suffer the consequences.
en.triompher:
Borrowed from Latin ~triumphāre~ (“to celebrate a triumph, to triumph”), a verb built on the noun ~triumphus~, the name of the procession that welcomed a victorious Roman general. The noun itself is generally explained as a descendant of Old Latin ~triumpus~, taken from Greek ~θρίαμβος~ (~thríambos~), a hymn to Dionysus; by one account the word reached Rome through Etruscan, but the route is not certain. The verb gave Italian ~trionfare~ and Spanish ~triunfar~, and the noun gave English ~triumph~, which entered English from the same Latin source by way of French.

In Rome, a triumph was a precisely regulated ceremony: the general rode in a chariot along the Sacred Way up to the Capitol, followed by his soldiers and his captives. French ~triompher~ means to win a victory, and more widely to succeed: to triumph over an obstacle, an enemy or one's own fear (~triompher de~), or, of a play or a performer, to be a huge hit. Related words include ~triomphe~ (“triumph”), the learned ~triomphal~, ~triomphant~ and the Parisian monument ~arc de triomphe~, which borrows the Roman image of the victor's procession.
en.tripatouiller: A blend of two verbs, ~tripoter~ and ~patouiller~, each of which contributes its first part: ~trip-~ from the first and ~-patouiller~ from the second. The result means to tamper with something, to fiddle with it in a way that alters it. It is a contamination rather than a derivation: neither ~tripoter~ nor ~patouiller~ is a prefix or a suffix, and the new verb simply combines their forms and their sense of handling roughly.
en.tripler: ~Tripler~ is formed from the adjective and noun ~triple~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~, which turns a base into a verb: to make something three times as large, or to become so. ~Triple~ comes from Latin ~triplus~ (“threefold”). It is a semi-learned form, reshaped under the influence of Latin from Old French ~treble~, the same ancestor that gave English ~treble~. French thus kept two layers of the word, the older popular one having faded.
en.tripoter: ~Tripoter~ comes from the noun ~tripot~, according to English Wiktionary, which does not say more. In modern French the verb means to fiddle or tinker with something, and also, in a familiar and slightly pejorative register, to carry on dubious dealings, as in ~tripoter des affaires~. A ~tripotage~ is a shady maneuver, and ~tripoteur~ names the person who engages in one. The noun ~tripot~ itself, a gambling den, is the base here; the verb ends in the usual ~-er~ of the first conjugation.
en.trisser:
~Trisser~ is really three words that happen to share one spelling, according to French Wiktionary. The first is the verb for the cry of the swallow. It comes from Latin ~trissāre~, itself taken from Greek ~τρίζω~ (~trízō~, “to creak”), a verb whose sound suits the thin, shrill call it names. The swallow's twittering is thus the only one of the three that comes down from Latin and Greek.

The second ~trisser~ is a coinage meaning “to repeat a third time,” made on the pattern of ~bisser~ (“to encore”) with ~tri-~ (“three”). The third is slang, “to run off,” most often as ~se trisser~, which French Wiktionary derives from German ~stritzen~. The first is therefore a borrowing from Latin and Greek, the second a formation on ~bisser~ and the third a borrowing from German, so the swallow's cry has no connection with the verb meaning “to run off.”
en.triturer:
Borrowed from Latin ~trītūrāre~, a verb built on ~trītūra~ (“a rubbing, a threshing”), from ~trītus~, the participle of ~terere~ (“to rub, to grind”). The sense is therefore of grinding something down by rubbing. English has the same Latin family twice: ~triturate~ is a loan of the verb, and ~trite~ (“worn out by use”) comes from the participle ~trītus~.

In French, ~triturer~ keeps its literal sense of pounding or grinding to a powder or paste, as in a laboratory or kitchen. It also has a figurative use, to handle something roughly or fiddle with it nervously, as in ~triturer son mouchoir~. The noun ~trituration~ belongs to the same family. The root ~terere~ is also found in ~contrit~ and ~contrition~, from Latin ~conterere~ (“to crush”).
en.tromper:
Attested from the late 12th century, ~tromper~ is a denominal verb from the noun ~trompe~ (“horn, trumpet”), and its first meaning was simply “to play the horn,” jouer de la trompe. The noun ~trompe~ is of imitative or Germanic origin, echoing the instrument's blare. How a verb for trumpeting came to mean “to deceive” is one of the small mysteries of French etymology — and the favored explanation is delightfully concrete.

The usual account runs through the reflexive expression ~se tromper de quelqu'un~, literally “to play the horn at someone” — to blare derisively in a person's face, hence “to mock, to make sport of” them. From mockery the sense slid to misleading, then to outright deceiving, and finally the plain ~tromper~ settled into its modern meaning, “to deceive, to fool, to lead astray.” The reflexive ~se tromper~ took the gentler turn “to be mistaken, to make a mistake” — to be, as it were, fooled by oneself. ~Tromper~ also acquired the specific sense of marital infidelity, “to cheat on.” From the same ~trompe~ French keeps ~tromperie~ (“deceit”), ~trompeur~ (“deceiver”), ~trompette~ (“trumpet,” a little ~trompe~), and ~se détromper~ (“to undeceive oneself”).
en.trompeter: Formed from ~trompette~ (“trumpet”) with the verbal ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary gives ~trompette~ as ~trompe~ plus the diminutive suffix ~-ette~, so the verb is built on a word that already means a little horn. Its basic sense is to play the trumpet, and it also means to proclaim something loudly or to reveal it widely. This is a typical denominal verb in ~-er~, of the type “carry out N” or “act like N.”
en.tronquer:
~Tronquer~ goes back to Latin ~truncāre~ (“to cut off, to truncate”), from ~truncus~ (“trunk”). Old French had the form ~tronchier~, and English Wiktionary describes the modern ~tronquer~ as a southern dialect form of ~troncher~, the same verb with a different treatment of its ending. English has both descendants of the Latin family: ~truncate~, a direct learned borrowing of ~truncāre~, and ~trunk~, which comes from ~truncus~ by way of Old French ~tronc~.

The noun ~tronc~ lies behind the family. French has ~tronc~, ~tronçon~ (“a cut piece”), ~tronçonner~ and ~tronçonneuse~ (“chainsaw”), all from ~truncus~. Today ~tronquer~ is mostly used for text, quotations and data cut short, as in ~citation tronquée~, which is why the participle ~tronqué~ is the form one meets most often.
en.tronçonner: Formed from ~tronçon~ (“section, chunk”) with the ending ~-er~, so “to cut into sections.” The noun ~tronçon~ comes from Old French ~trons~ and Vulgar Latin *~trunceus~, from Latin ~truncus~ (“trunk, cut-off piece”), with the suffix ~-on~ in the French account. The same Latin word gave ~tronc~ and ~tronquer~. The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, here means “to make into” the noun: to turn a log, a road or a text into pieces. The ~tronçonneuse~ (“chainsaw”) is the tool that does it.
en.tropicaliser: Formed from ~tropical~ with the suffix ~-iser~, which makes verbs meaning “to make” or “to adapt to,” so it means to adapt something to a tropical environment. The adjective ~tropical~ is itself built from ~tropique~ (the tropics) with the suffix ~-al~. The verb is thus a chain of three French steps, each adding one layer: ~tropique~, then ~tropical~, then ~tropicaliser~.
en.troquer:
From Old French ~troquer~, also written ~trochier~. Its origin is unknown, and the sources offer only guesses. English Wiktionary suggests that it may be imitative, echoing the sound of the hands of two bargainers clapping together, like ~troper~ (“to high-five”). It also allows a Germanic source that has not been identified. French Wiktionary does not choose between them and treats the verb as derived from the noun ~troque~ (“barter”).

Whatever its origin, ~troquer~ means “to exchange one thing for another.” It has relatives in other languages, though the direction of borrowing is uncertain. Middle English ~trukien~ (“to trade, to barter”) and Medieval Latin ~troco~ (“I barter”) may have been borrowed from the Old French verb. In French, the noun ~troc~ (“barter”) belongs to the same family, and ~troquer~ is still the verb for swapping, often for figurative swaps.
en.trotter:
French ~trotter~ comes from Old French ~troter~, which French Wiktionary calls an alteration of it. The two Wiktionaries give different routes. French Wiktionary derives the Old French verb from Old High German ~trotōn~ (“to press grapes,” around the year 1000), an intensive of ~tretan~ (“to walk, to tread”). English Wiktionary instead has it borrowed from Medieval Latin *~trottāre~, from Frankish *~trottōn~ (“to go, run”), from Proto-Germanic *~trudōną~ (“to go, step, tread”), and traces that to the Proto-Indo-European root *~dreh₂-~ (“to run, escape”). Which route is right is not settled by these sources, but both end in a Germanic word.

The Germanic family is still visible elsewhere. English ~trot~ and ~tread~ belong to it, and French Wiktionary adds that German ~trotten~ (“to press grapes,” now dated) and the regional ~Trotte~ (“wine press”) descend from the same Old High German verb. In French the verb came to mean “to trot,” the gait of a horse, and it has a lively family of its own, among them ~trotteur~, ~trottiner~, ~trottoir~ and ~trottinette~. A horse's gait and the treading of grapes look far apart, yet in the French account the same verb carries both.
en.trottiner: Formed in French from ~trotter~ (“to trot”) with the suffix ~-iner~, which gives the base verb a diminutive sense. To ~trottiner~ is therefore to trot in a small way, taking short, quick steps. It is used of small animals, of children and of people walking briskly with little steps. The suffix ~-iner~ works in a similar way in other French verbs that soften or shrink the action of their base.
en.troubler:
From Old French ~trobler~ (also ~trubler~), with the sounds of the “r” swapped from earlier ~torbler~, ~tourbler~ and ~turbler~, themselves from Vulgar Latin *~turbulāre~. That verb is explained in one of two ways: either as a diminutive of Latin ~turbāre~ (“to agitate, to disturb”), or as built on a noun ~turbula~, a diminutive of ~turba~ (“commotion, crowd”). Both routes lead to the same root. Occitan ~trebolar~ and Romanian ~tulbura~ are relatives of the French verb.

The swap of the ~r~ is the telling detail: ~turbler~ became ~trobler~ because the “r” moved forward in the word, and ~trobler~ then settled into modern ~troubler~. The meaning stayed close to its source, the stirring up of something calm. The Latin root also came into French a second time through learned borrowing, giving ~turbulent~, a cousin of ~troubler~ that kept the Latin vowel and the original order of the consonants.
en.trouer: ~Trouer~ is formed from the noun ~trou~ (“hole”) and the verb ending ~-er~: to make holes in. The noun's origin is debated. French Wiktionary derives it from a Vulgar Latin *~traucum~, attested as ~traugum~ in the eighth-century Ripuarian Law and as ~tro~ in Old French (1175, Chrétien de Troyes), and thinks a pre-Celtic origin most likely. English Wiktionary gives an Early Medieval Latin ~traugus~, probably Gaulish, though others have proposed a borrowing from Greek ~trûpa~ (“hole”).
en.trousser:
~Trousser~ comes from Old French ~trusser~, which is related to ~torser~. It goes back, with metathesis (the r moving to the other side of the vowel), to a Vulgar Latin *~torsāre~, built on *~torsus~, a variant of Classical Latin ~tortus~, the past participle of ~torqueō~ (“to twist”). Latin ~torqueō~ is also the source of French ~tordre~ and ~torsion~, and of English ~torque~ and ~torture~. English ~truss~ is a close cousin, borrowed from Old French.

Its senses range from folding up and hitching up a garment, as in ~trousser sa jupe~, to trussing a fowl, as in ~trousser un poulet~, and to dispatching a job quickly. The word has a sizeable family in French: ~trousse~ (“kit, case”), ~trousseau~ (“bunch of keys, set”) and ~retrousser~ (“to roll up”).
en.trouver:
From Old French ~trover~, from Vulgar Latin *~tropāre~ (“to compose a melody, then to compose verse, then to invent, to find”), derived from Latin ~tropus~ (“a figure of speech, a trope”). The Latin word was borrowed from Greek ~trópos~ (“a turn, a manner, a turn of phrase”), from ~trépein~ (“to turn”), and ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *~trep-~ (“to turn”). So at its root, to find is to “turn” a phrase.

The path of meaning is unusually beautiful. *~tropāre~ first meant to compose tropes — the sung verses added to liturgical chant — and from “to compose, to invent a song” it widened to “to invent” and then to “to come upon, to find.” The poet who composed such songs was the ~trouvère~ in the north and the ~troubadour~ in the south of medieval France, both literally “finders, inventors.” The same stem gives French ~trouvaille~ (“a lucky find”), ~retrouver~ (“to find again, to meet again”), and ~controuver~ (“to fabricate, to invent falsely”). The learned ~trope~ and ~tropical~ (a zone where the sun “turns”) preserve the original Greek sense of turning, a quiet reminder that, etymologically, every discovery is a turn of phrase.
en.truander: Formed from the noun ~truand~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning “to con, to cheat” as a ~truand~ does. The noun comes from Gaulish, from a reconstructed form *~truganto~, and is cognate with Welsh ~tru~ and Irish ~trogán~. French Wiktionary links it to a sense of “vagabond, beggar,” which Dutch carried over into ~trawant~, and also to Occitan ~truan~ (“rogue, traitor”). English ~truant~ is a relative of the same Celtic word.
en.trucider:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~trucīdāre~ (“to slice the throat, to massacre”). By the standard analysis, the Latin verb joins ~trux~ (“fierce, savage”) to a form of ~caedere~ (“to cut, to kill”), whose vowel was reduced to ~-cīd-~ inside the compound. The adjective ~trux~ also lies behind the Latin ~truculentus~, from which French ~truculent~ and English ~truculent~ come, so the verb belongs with the vocabulary of fierceness as well as that of killing.

French Wiktionary points to the suffix ~-cide~ for the second half of the story, since that element also comes from Latin ~caedere~. The verb is therefore a distant relative of ~homicide~, ~suicide~ and ~incision~, all built on the same Latin verb. The modern gloss “to kill” is broader than the Latin “to cut the throat, to massacre.”
en.truffer: ~Truffer~ is formed from the noun ~truffe~ (“truffle”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, hence “to add truffles to”; the verb also means “to cram, to stuff.” ~Truffe~ was borrowed from Old Occitan ~trufa~. French Wiktionary traces the Occitan word to Vulgar Latin ~tufera~, from ~tufer~, an Osco-Umbrian form of Classical Latin ~tuber~; English Wiktionary gives Latin ~tuber~ as the ultimate source.
en.truquer: ~Truquer~ is formed from ~truc~ and the verb-forming ending ~-er~. The noun ~truc~ comes from Middle French ~truc~ and Old French ~trut~, borrowed from Old Occitan ~truc~, a noun derived from the verb ~trucar~. That verb goes back to Vulgar Latin *~trūdicāre~, which French Wiktionary links to Latin ~trudere~ (“to push, to knock”).
en.trusquiner: Formed in French from the noun ~trusquin~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, so the verb means “to mark out with a ~trusquin~,” the marking gauge a woodworker or metalworker uses to scribe a line parallel to an edge. The noun comes from Dutch ~kruisken~ (“little cross”), itself a diminutive of the Dutch word for “cross.” The ending ~-er~ is the ordinary first-conjugation ending, from Latin ~-are~, the default way to coin a verb from a noun.
en.truster: Formed from the noun ~trust~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. ~Trust~ was borrowed from English, where it names a business combination that controls a market. To ~truster~ is therefore to monopolize, to gather up something as a ~trust~ does. The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, is the usual one for denominal verbs. The verb belongs to the same family as the loan word, so its story is the loan's story: an English commercial term turned into a French first-conjugation verb.
en.trébucher: The two sources describe it differently. English Wiktionary traces it to Old French ~trebuchier~ (“to topple”), from ~tres-~ (the older form of ~tré-~, from Latin ~trans-~) plus an unattested *~buchier~, from Old French ~buc~ (“trunk of the body”), from Frankish *~būk~ (“belly, trunk”). Old English ~būc~ and Old High German ~būh~ are cognates. French Wiktionary instead reads ~tré-~ plus ~bûcher~, the base ~bûche~ (“log”) being from Frankish *~busk~. ~Trébucher~ means to stumble, to catch one's foot.
en.tréfiler: Formed from ~filer~ with the prefix ~tré-~, the modern spelling of Old French ~tres-~, from Latin ~trans-~ (“across, through”): ~tréfiler~ is to draw metal through a die to make wire. The base ~filer~ comes from Late Latin ~filare~ (“to spin into thread”), from ~filum~ (“thread”), which also gave ~fil~ and ~profil~.
en.trémater: French Wiktionary derives this verb from ~trémat~, and proposes that the noun may come from Late Latin ~trema~ (“path”). That link is offered only as a possibility. The verb is glossed as “to overtake,” a sense that fits an image of passing along the path; the sources give no sense story, so this remains a guess. Beyond the proposed Latin source, no further history is recorded.
en.trémousser: Probably formed from ~mousse~ (“foam”), with the Old French prefix ~tres-~ (from Latin ~trāns~, “beyond, over”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, according to the TLFi, which presents the derivation as probable only. The first attestation is reflexive, ~se trémousser~ (“to bustle about, to fidget”), in Rabelais in 1532. A sense “to tremble, to quiver” is recorded from 1549, and before 1672 the reflexive verb also came to mean putting oneself to great trouble to make an undertaking succeed.
en.trémuler: A learned derivative of Latin ~tremulus~ (“trembling”), which also gave French the now outdated adjective ~trémule~. The Latin adjective comes from ~tremere~ (“to tremble”). The verb ~trémuler~ is a morphological doublet of ~trembler~, which belongs to the same Latin root family but came through the spoken language. The Latin root also gave English ~tremulous~, ~tremor~ and ~tremble~, and French ~tremblement~, ~trémulation~ and ~tremblotter~ belong to the same family.
en.trépaner: Formed from the noun ~trépan~ (a surgical drill for cutting into the skull) plus the verbal ending ~-er~, so the verb means to perform that operation. The noun comes from Medieval Latin ~trepanum~, a surgeon's instrument, which was itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~τρύπανον~ (“auger, drill”). The Greek word names an ordinary boring tool, and medicine applied it to the specialized instrument used on the skull.
en.trépasser: ~Trépasser~ comes from Old French ~trespasser~ (“to traverse, to go beyond”), formed from ~passer~ and the prefix ~tré-~ (older ~tres-~), which descends from Latin ~trans~ (“across, beyond”). The base ~passer~ goes back to Vulgar Latin *~passāre~, from Latin ~passus~ (“step”). To “go beyond” first described a crossing, then a crossing into the afterlife, hence “to pass away, to die.” The same Old French verb gave English ~trespass~, which kept the idea of crossing a boundary.
en.trépider:
Borrowed from Latin ~trepidāre~, “to be agitated, to tremble, to hurry anxiously.” The Latin verb is built on the adjective ~trepidus~ (“alarmed, agitated”). French took it as a learned word, shaping the ending to the first conjugation, and so ~trépider~ has no Old French ancestor: it is a Latin verb brought straight into modern French.

The modern verb means “to vibrate, to shudder, to throb,” and is used of machines, floors or engines that shake with repeated small tremors. It sits in a family that includes ~trépidation~, ~trépidant~ (“throbbing, hectic”) and ~intrépide~, the one who does not tremble, from Latin ~intrepidus~. English ~trepidation~ belongs to the same Latin family, and the older sense of trembling with fear is still alive in it.
en.trépigner:
From Old French ~treper~ (“to stamp, to jump”), which was borrowed from Old Low Frankish *~treppan~ (“to jump”) and then given the suffix ~-igner~ to make the modern verb. The Frankish word has Germanic relatives: Middle Dutch ~trepelen~, Dutch ~trippen~, Swedish ~trappa~ and the now old-fashioned English ~trape~ (“to run about idly”). By vowel alternation it is also linked to Latin ~trepidus~ (“agitated”), according to French Wiktionary.

The sense stayed close to the physical act: to stamp one's feet repeatedly, or to shuffle about in place. The Latin cousin ~trepidus~ places the verb, distantly, in the same family as French ~trépidation~ (“shaking, quivering”) and ~intrépide~ (“fearless”, literally “not trembling”). Those two are learned words taken from Latin, whereas this verb arrived through the Germanic speech of the Franks, one of the many Germanic words that entered Old French in the early Middle Ages.
en.trévirer: Formed from ~trévire~, a word for a kind of rope, with the verb ending ~-er~. The verb means “to hoist,” that is, to haul something up with such a rope. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~, the first-conjugation infinitive ending, and is the usual way French coins a verb from a noun. French Wiktionary gives no older source for ~trévire~ itself, so the verb is best seen as a simple French derivation on a technical rope word, of the kind found in the vocabulary of ropework.
en.trôner: ~Trôner~ is formed from the noun ~trône~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun entered Middle French as ~throne~ from Old French ~trone~, itself from Latin ~thronus~, which borrowed Ancient Greek ~thrónos~ (“seat, chair”). Italian ~trono~ is a cognate. The verb means to sit on a throne and so, figuratively, to occupy a place of honor or hold court. The ending ~-er~ comes from the Latin infinitive ending ~-are~ and is French's default way of turning a noun into a verb.
en.tuber: ~Tuber~ is a denominal verb, ~tube~ plus ~-er~, meaning to fit with a tube or to shape into one, for instance in medicine or in plumbing. The base ~tube~ is borrowed from Latin ~tubus~ (“tube, pipe”). French Wiktionary also lists a second source, ~tub~, for a different homonym, so the verb may have more than one origin. A further, musical slang sense of ~tube~ (“hit song”) was coined by Boris Vian, with an allusion to the empty words of a popular song, but it is the plain Latin ~tubus~ that is behind the verb described here.
en.tuer:
From Old French ~tuer~ (“to strike, stun, extinguish”), from Late Latin ~tūtāre~ (“to put out a fire, to smother”), an altered form of Classical Latin ~tūtāri~ (“to protect, to guard against”), the frequentative of ~tuērī~ (“to watch over, protect”), a verb of uncertain deeper origin. The startling thread here is semantic: a verb that once meant “to protect” became the ordinary French word for “to kill.”

The bridge was fire. To “protect” against a blaze meant to ~tūtāre~ it — to smother it, put it out — and from “extinguishing a flame” the sense slid to “snuffing out” more generally: stunning a blow, then dealing a fatal one. By Old French, ~tuer~ already meant “to strike down,” and it eventually crowded out the inherited ~occire~ (from Latin ~occīdere~) as the everyday verb for killing. The protective ancestor ~tuērī~ left gentler descendants in French through its participle ~tūtus~: ~tuteur~ (“guardian, tutor”) and ~tutelle~ (“guardianship”) still mean “one who watches over.” So the same Latin root for watchful protection branches into both the guardian and the killer — a vivid reminder that to “put out” can mean to shield or to slay.
en.tuméfier:
From Latin ~tumefacere~ (“to make swell, to puff up”), a compound of the verb ~tumēre~ (“to swell”) and ~facere~ (“to make, to do”). French reshaped the Latin ending into the learned verb ending ~-fier~, as it did for many verbs built on ~facere~. The verb therefore means, literally, “to make swell.”

In modern French, ~tuméfier~ belongs to the medical and literary register. It describes flesh that swells, as with a bruised, inflamed or stung face, and it is most often met in the past participle ~tuméfié~ (“swollen, puffy”). It shares its Latin root ~tumēre~ with ~tumeur~ (“tumor”), which comes from Latin ~tumor~ (“a swelling”), and with the learned adjective ~tumescent~. English has the same compound as ~tumefy~, and ~tumor~ from the same noun. Everyday French prefers ~enfler~ or ~gonfler~ for the same idea, so ~tuméfier~ keeps a clinical or slightly formal flavor.
en.turbiner:
The origin of ~turbiner~ is disputed. English Wiktionary gives it as ~turbine~ + ~-er~, but French Wiktionary calls the origin obscure and rules out a derivation from ~turbine~ for chronological reasons. The sources therefore disagree, and no firm account can be given. The verb means “to churn” and “to work hard,” and the sources do not say how those senses relate.

The noun ~turbine~ is itself borrowed from Latin ~turbo~ (accusative ~turbinem~), which meant “circular motion” and also named objects such as a spinning top, a reel, and a spindle used in magical rites. In Rabelais's Gargantua the word ~turbine~ appears with the sense of a whirlwind, a use that stayed a one-off. Whether ~turbiner~ is connected to this Latin word by some other path is not settled by the sources.
en.turlupiner: The verb comes from a proper name, ~Turlupin~, the stage name of the comic actor Henri Legrand (1587–1637). The English Wiktionary line gives only this origin, and the path from a seventeenth-century comedian's name to the modern sense of bothering or nagging someone is not documented, so it is best left unexplained. What is secure is that ~turlupiner~ is a verb built on a person's name, not on a common word.
en.tuteurer: Formed from ~tuteur~ with the ending ~-er~: to ~tuteurer~ a young plant is to give it a ~tuteur~, the stake that holds it upright. ~Tuteur~ is borrowed from Latin ~tutor~ (“guardian, protector”), derived from ~tueor~ (“to look at, to watch over”), hence “to guard, to protect.” The same noun names a legal guardian, so a staked plant and a ward share one word.
en.tutoyer: ~Tutoyer~ is formed from the pronoun ~tu~ with the suffix ~-oyer~ and an intercalary ~-t-~, and means to address someone as ~tu~. The pronoun comes from Latin ~tū~, from Proto-Indo-European *~túh₂~, and has cognates with the same informal use, such as Italian ~tu~, German ~du~ and Russian ~ты~. Parallel verbs include Icelandic ~þúa~, German ~duzen~, Portuguese and Spanish ~tutear~, Romanian ~tutui~, and English has the old ~thou~.
en.tuyauter: Derived from ~tuyau~ (“pipe, tube”) with the verb ending ~-er~. The verb began in the laundry and the dressmaker's shop: in 1822 linen was called ~tuyauté~ when it had many small cylindrical pleats, and by 1836 the verb meant to form such pleats on linen or lace with a round iron. In 1872 the word appeared of a horse that had been the object of a ~tuyau~, a tip, and by 1899 it meant “to give someone confidential information.” That is the modern everyday sense, “to give a heads-up.” The TLFi gives the intransitive use from 1872.
en.twister: Formed from the noun ~twist~ and the verbal suffix ~-er~: to dance the twist. The noun ~twist~ was borrowed from English ~twist~ (“to twist”). The dance was marked by alternating rotations of the hips and legs with bent knees, which required a twisting of the torso to keep the shoulders in line.
en.tympaniser:
From Latin ~tympanizare~, itself from Ancient Greek ~τυμπανίζω~ (~tumpanizo~, “to beat the drum”), as French Wiktionary gives it. The Greek verb is built on the noun ~τύμπανον~ (~túmpanon~, “drum”) with the verbal ending ~-ίζω~. Latin transcribed the ending as ~-izare~, and it became ~-iser~ in French, the same ending as in countless verbs from ~organiser~ to ~civiliser~. The noun was borrowed into Latin as ~tympanum~, and through it the family reached French and English.

In French the verb has the figurative sense “to disparage.” The noun side of the family is much more visible than the verb. ~Tympan~ names the eardrum, which does resemble a stretched drum skin, and the carved panel above a church doorway. The adjective ~tympanique~ and the instrument name ~tympanon~ belong to the same family. English has ~tympanum~, taken straight from the Latin form.
en.typer:
~Typer~ is a denominal verb from the noun ~type~, which French took from Latin ~typus~ (« figure, image, form »), itself a borrowing of Ancient Greek ~τύπος~ (~túpos~, « blow, imprint, mould »). That noun belongs to the verb ~τύπτω~ (~túptō~, « to strike, to beat »): a ~τύπος~ was originally the mark left by a blow, the impression a stamp or seal leaves in wax or clay. The metaphor of the die that stamps identical copies runs through the whole family.

From « imprint » the word drifted toward « model » and then « category », and the verb ~typer~ followed: to ~typer~ someone or something is to stamp them with the marks of a recognizable type, to make them typical or — pejoratively — to stereotype. The printing sense survives in ~typographie~ and ~typo~, the classifying sense in ~type~, ~typique~, and ~stéréotype~ (literally a « solid » printing plate). English ~type~, ~typical~, and ~typist~ spring from the same Greek root.
en.typographier: ~Typographier~ (“to typeset”) is formed from the noun ~typographie~ with the ending ~-er~. The noun is a borrowing of Medieval Latin ~typographia~, built, like English ~typography~, on the Greek roots for “impression, type” and “writing”. The verb means to set a text in type or to give it a typographic layout.
en.tyranniser: Formed in French from ~tyran~ (“tyrant”) and the suffix ~-iser~, “to rule or treat as a tyrant.” The noun comes from Latin ~tyrannus~, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ~τύραννος~ (~týrannos~, “master”). The Greek verb ~τυραννίζω~ meant “to be a partisan of tyranny,” so the French verb is a separate formation. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izare~, which transcribed Greek verbs.
en.tâcher:
Both French and English sources treat this verb as formed on the noun ~tâche~ (“task”), which comes from Latin ~taxāre~ (“to touch sharply, to estimate”). Latin ~taxāre~ is probably a frequentative of ~tangere~ (“to touch”), and it has two famous offspring in French: ~taxer~ (“to tax, to assess”), borrowed later in learned form, and ~tâche~, the inherited version.

The development is a good example of how a noun of labor gives a verb of effort. A ~tâche~ was a job set for someone; to ~tâcher~ was “to set oneself to a task,” then simply to try or strive. Today it is mostly found in the construction ~tâcher de~ followed by an infinitive (“to try to”), and in the demanding expression ~tâcher que~ with the subjunctive (“to make sure that”). Related words include ~tâche~, ~tâcheron~ (“a piece-work laborer,” and now “a drudge”), ~taxer~ and ~taxe~.
en.tâter:
From Old French ~taster~ (“to explore by touching”), from Vulgar Latin *~tastāre~. French Wiktionary derives this from Latin ~taxāre~, itself from ~tangere~ (“to touch”). English Wiktionary describes *~tastāre~ as a contraction of *~taxitō~, a frequentative of Late Latin ~taxāre~ (“touch repeatedly”), but traces ~taxāre~ to Latin ~taxus~, so the two sources disagree on the last step.

The circumflex of ~tâter~ marks the lost ~s~ of Old French ~taster~, a general-knowledge feature of many French words. English ~taste~ comes from the same Old French verb. Feeling with the hand survives in ~tâter le terrain~ (“to test the ground”). The derivative ~tâtonner~ (“to grope”) and the phrase ~à tâtons~ (“by feel”) belong to the same family.
en.tâtonner: Formed in French from ~tâter~ with the suffix ~-onner~, which makes verbs of repeated, softened or aimless action, as in ~chantonner~ from ~chanter~. The base ~tâter~ comes from Old French ~taster~, from Vulgar Latin *~tastāre~. The two Wiktionaries disagree on the last step: one links it to Latin ~taxāre~ and ~tangere~ (“to touch”), the other to Latin ~taxus~. The circumflex marks the lost ~s~ of ~taster~, and English ~taste~ comes from the same Old French verb. ~Tâtonner~ means to feel one's way, to grope.
en.télescoper: Formed from the noun ~télescope~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. ~Télescope~ is a learned word (~télé-~ “far” + ~-scope~ “viewer”) that goes back to Latin ~telescopium~. The verb's core image is the telescope's tubes sliding one into another: to ~télescoper~ is to crash into something so that parts drive into each other, as in a railway collision. It then extended figuratively to events or ideas that overlap and crush against one another, matching the gloss “clash with.” The ending ~-er~, from Latin ~-are~, is the usual one for denominal verbs.
en.télexer: Formed from ~télex~ with the verb ending ~-er~: to send a message by telex. ~Télex~ is borrowed from English ~telex~, which is a blend of “teleprinter exchange”. The verb simply turns the name of the machine and its network into the action.
en.télécharger:
A modern French coinage, formed from the prefix ~télé-~ (“at a distance, far off”) and the verb ~charger~ (“to load”). The prefix ~télé-~ comes through scientific Latin from Ancient Greek ~τῆλε~ (~têle~, “far, far off”); ~charger~ descends from Late Latin ~carricare~ (“to load a wagon”), from ~carrus~ (“wheeled cart”), a word the Romans borrowed from Gaulish. So the verb is a hybrid: a Greek adverb of distance bolted onto a Celtic-Latin verb of loading. Cognate with English ~charge~ and ~cargo~, both also from ~carricare~.

Unlike most verbs here, ~télécharger~ has no Roman ancestor: it was minted in French in the early 1980s, in the first age of telematics and computer networks, to name the act of “loading at a distance” — moving a file between a remote machine and a local one. French, unusually, uses the one verb for both directions, distinguishing them as ~télécharger~ for downloading versus ~téléverser~ or ~télécharger vers le serveur~ for uploading. The ~télé-~ element ties it to a whole modern cohort — ~téléphone~, ~télévision~, ~télescope~, ~télégramme~ — while ~charger~ binds it to the older ~charge~, ~chargement~, ~décharger~, and ~surcharger~, the everyday vocabulary of loads and burdens.
en.télécommander: Formed from the noun ~télécommande~ (“remote control”) with the verb ending ~-er~.
