The noun itself combines the prefix ~télé-~ (“far, at a distance,” from Greek) with ~commande~ (“control, command”). To ~télécommander~ something is therefore to command it from afar, whether a television, a drone or a machine. This is a purely French formation of the modern technical age, and it shows how the prefix ~télé-~ keeps producing verbs of distance.
en.télédiffuser: From ~diffuser~ with the prefix ~télé-~, here a clipping of ~télévision~ rather than the Greek sense of distance: to ~télédiffuser~ is to broadcast on television. The prefix goes back to Ancient Greek ~τῆλε~ (“far, at a distance”). The base ~diffuser~ was formed in French from the adjective ~diffus~, after Latin ~diffundere~ (“to pour out, to spread”), which joins ~dis-~ (“apart”) and ~fundere~ (“to pour”).
en.télégraphier: Formed from ~télégraphie~ with the verb ending, it means to send a message by telegraph. The noun ~télégraphie~ is built from ~graphie~ with the prefix ~télé-~ (“far”), so the telegraph was, etymologically, a writing at a distance. The prefix ~télé-~ comes from Greek ~tēle~ (“far”) and ~-graphie~ from Greek ~graphein~ (“to write”). The same two parts recur in ~téléphone~, ~télévision~ and ~photographie~.
en.téléguider: Formed from ~guider~ (“to guide”) with the prefix ~télé-~, from Ancient Greek ~τῆλε~ (“far, at a distance”), so the verb means to steer something from afar. By extension it means to orchestrate or manipulate from behind the scenes. The base ~guider~ is a reshaping, under the influence of the noun ~guide~, of Old French ~guier~, which goes back to Old Frankish ~witan~ (“to show the way, to watch over”). That Germanic verb is cognate with German ~weisen~ (“to show”) and, more distantly, with Latin ~vidēre~ (“to see”).
en.téléphoner: Formed from the noun ~téléphone~ with the verbal suffix ~-er~, in the sense “to use” what the noun names: to telephone. The noun was built from the prefix ~télé-~ and the element ~-phone~, both from Greek: ~τῆλε~ (“afar”) and ~φωνή~ (“voice, sound”). The word therefore means literally “a far voice”, a good description of the device. The verb followed the instrument, as French ~téléphoner~ turned the machine into an everyday action.
en.téléviser:
A modern compound formed on the model of ~télévision~, joining the prefix ~télé-~ — from Ancient Greek ~tēle~ (« far off, at a distance ») — to a base meaning « to see, » ultimately Latin ~videre~ (« to see ») through its participle ~visus~. The whole literally evokes « seeing at a distance, » the very promise the new medium advertised in the early twentieth century.

The verb is a back-formation: ~télévision~ arrived first, and ~téléviser~ was carved out of it to name the act of broadcasting images. Because it echoes ~télévision~ so closely, French keeps ~téléviser~ almost exclusively for that one medium, preferring ~diffuser~ for radio or the internet. The ~télé-~ element is enormously productive, heading a whole family that includes ~téléphone~, ~télégraphe~, ~télescope~, and the clipped ~télé~ for the set itself; the ~-viser~ side links it to ~vision~, ~visible~, ~viser~, and ~visage~, all rooted in the Latin verb of seeing.
en.témoigner:
A denominal verb from the noun ~témoin~ (“witness”), with the verb-forming suffix ~-er~. ~Témoin~ descends from Latin ~testimōnium~ (“testimony, evidence”), formed on ~testis~ (“witness”). The etymology of ~testis~ is striking: it goes back to a Proto-Indo-European compound *~tristh₂s~, “a third one standing by” — from *~tréyes~ (“three”) and the root *~steh₂-~ (“to stand”). A witness, in this ancient image, is the impartial third party who stands beside two disputants. It is cognate with Italian ~testimone~ and Spanish ~testigo~, and with English ~testimony~ and ~testify~.

So to ~témoigner~ is to act as that standing-by third party — to attest, to bear witness. From the legal courtroom the sense broadened: a gift can ~témoigner~ gratitude, and symptoms ~témoignent~ a disease, the verb meaning “to show, to be evidence of.” The path from Latin ~testimōnium~ to French ~témoin~ ran through hard wear — the loss of the medial syllable and the softening of consonants typical of inherited words. From the same ~testis~ root come French ~témoignage~, ~testament~ (a document that “bears witness” to one's will), ~attester~, and ~protester~ (literally “to witness before, to declare publicly”).
en.ténoriser: Formed from ~ténor~ with the suffix ~-iser~, in the sense of singing tenor or giving a voice a tenor quality. The base ~ténor~ was borrowed from Italian ~tenore~, from Latin ~tenorem~, and is a doublet of ~teneur~. French Wiktionary explains it as a medieval Latinization of Old French ~teneur~: in Gregorian chant it named the voice that sustains the composition, the base line. The word then came to mean a vocal range, and finally the person who sings in it. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~ and turns nouns into verbs of treating or acting as.
en.tétaniser: Formed from ~tétanos~ plus ~-iser~, a productive ending meaning “to subject to” or “to cause to become”. ~Tétanos~ is from Ancient Greek ~tétanos~ (τέτανος), “spasmodic rigidity of the body”, and French Wiktionary relates it to ~tension~ by way of Latin. To ~tétaniser~ is thus to seize with tetanic rigidity, and by extension to leave someone frozen stiff, as if petrified.
en.téter: From Old French ~tetter~, a verb formed on the noun ~tette~ (“teat”) with the verb ending ~-er~. Literally, ~téter~ is “to use the teat,” that is, to suckle. The same noun gave French ~téton~ and ~tétine~, the latter now best known as the rubber teat of a baby's bottle or a pacifier.
en.ulcérer:
~Ulcérer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~ulcerāre~ (“to make sore, to cause an ulcer”), which was built on ~ulcus~ (“sore, ulcer”). English Wiktionary adds that on the surface it can also be read as ~ulcère~ plus the ending ~-er~, but the Latin verb is the true source. Latin ~ulcus~ is generally linked to the Greek ~hélkos~ (“wound, sore”). English ~ulcer~ and Italian ~ulcerare~ come from the same Latin family, and Spanish has ~ulcerar~.

The French noun ~ulcère~ comes from ~ulcus~ too, and ~ulcérer~ stands in the same family with ~ulcération~ and ~ulcéreux~. The verb has a medical sense, to cover flesh with sores, and a figurative one that is now just as common: to ~ulcérer~ someone is to wound them deeply, to embitter them and leave them with a lasting sense of grievance, as if the hurt were an open sore. The participle ~ulcéré~ (“deeply hurt, bitter”) is the form most often seen in modern French.
en.ululer:
French ~ululer~ is borrowed from Latin ~ululāre~ (“to howl, to wail”). The Latin verb is imitative: its repeated ~u~ sounds mimic the long, hollow cry it names, whether of a wolf, a mourner or an owl, and the Latin noun ~ulula~ (“owl”) is formed the same way. The word is a learned one, taken directly from Latin rather than inherited.

French has a second, inherited descendant of the same Latin verb: ~hurler~, “to howl,” which French Wiktionary cross-references as the everyday cousin of ~ululer~. The two are a doublet, one worn down by centuries of speech and the other kept in its Latin shape. In modern use ~ululer~ is a literary or learned verb, applied above all to the hoot of an owl and, by extension, to any long mournful cry. English has taken the same Latin verb as ~ululate~.
en.unifier:
French ~unifier~ is inherited from Old French ~unifier~, which was itself borrowed from Late Latin ~ūnificāre~. English Wiktionary gives that chain, and French Wiktionary traces the verb to the same Late Latin word. The Late Latin verb is a compound of ~ūnus~ (“one”) and the verbal element ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”), so it meant “to make one”.

The verb sits in a family of French words built on ~ūnus~. ~Un~ (“one”) is its direct descendant, and ~unité~, ~union~, ~unir~ and ~uni~ come from related Latin words. The ending ~-fier~ is the same one found in ~édifier~, ~clarifier~ and ~simplifier~, each of them a verb of making. English ~unify~ and Spanish ~unificar~ are its counterparts, and the noun ~unification~ completes the set. The first element ~uni-~ also appears in learned words such as ~uniforme~ and ~unilatéral~.
en.uniformiser: ~Uniformiser~ is formed from the adjective ~uniforme~ and the suffix ~-iser~, which makes verbs meaning “to make A.” The adjective was borrowed from Latin ~ūnifōrmis~, a compound of ~ūnus~ (“one”) and ~fōrma~ (“shape”), so “of a single form.” To ~uniformiser~ is accordingly to give things one and the same form. Both Wiktionaries agree on this internal formation, and neither gives a date.
en.unir:
From Latin ~unire~ (“to unite, to make one”), from ~unus~ (“one”), from Old Latin ~oinos~, from Proto-Italic *~oinos~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₁óynos~ (“one, single”). The same root, through different branches, surfaces as English ~one~ and ~an~, German ~ein~, Greek ~oios~ (“alone”), and Old Irish ~óen~ — a rare case where the kinship is plain to the eye across the whole family.

The meaning has stayed remarkably stable: to ~unir~ is to make things one, to join them into a single whole. Latin ~unus~ poured into French as the bare numeral ~un~, and around it gathered a dense family: ~union~, ~unique~ (“being only one of its kind”), ~unité~, ~unanime~ (“of one mind,” with ~animus~), ~uniforme~ (“of one form”), and the prefixed verbs ~réunir~ (“to bring together again”) and ~désunir~ (“to un-unite”). The English borrowings ~unite~, ~union~, and ~unique~ travel the same path. From “one” as a number grew “one” as togetherness, so that ~les États-Unis~ — the United States — are, etymologically, states made into a single one.
en.universaliser: Formed from the adjective ~universel~ with the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to make universal.” ~Universel~ comes from Latin ~ūniversālis~, entering French through Old French ~universal~. The Latin word is built on ~ūniversus~ (“all together, whole”), itself from ~ūnus~ (“one”) and ~versus~ (“turned”). To ~universaliser~ is to extend something so that it applies to everyone or everywhere.
en.uploader: ~Uploader~ is a modern loan formed in French from the English noun and verb ~upload~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. The ending is the one French habitually attaches to borrowed English words to make them conjugate like ordinary first-group verbs, as in ~chatter~ or ~scanner~. The English word itself is a compound of ~up~ and ~load~, so the verb means to send a file up from one's own machine to a distant one. Its story belongs entirely to computing and the internet, and it has no deeper Latin or Germanic descent in French.
en.urbaniser: Formed from the adjective ~urbain~ (“urban”) and the verb suffix ~-iser~, which makes verbs meaning “to make, to turn into.” To ~urbaniser~ is thus to make a place urban. The adjective is a learned borrowing from Latin ~urbānus~ (“of the city”), from ~urbs~ (“city”). Latin ~urbānus~ also meant “refined, polished,” the sense that survives in English ~urbane~.
en.urger: A back-formation from the adjective ~urgent~: the French verb was drawn out of the adjective, the reverse of the usual order, and means “to be urgent.” The adjective was borrowed from Latin ~urgens~, the present participle of ~urgēre~ (“to press, to drive”), by way of Late Latin ~urgentem~. English Wiktionary compares Latin ~urgeō~ with the verb, so the Latin verb stands behind both words, although French ~urger~ did not descend from it directly. It is used almost only in the impersonal expression ~ça urge~.
en.uriner: The verb is formed from ~urine~ and the ending ~-er~, with the sense “to pass urine.” The noun comes from Latin ~urīna~ by way of Old French ~orine~, a spelling later reshaped to match the Latin. English Wiktionary adds that ~orine~ may come from a Vulgar Latin form *~aurīna~, influenced by ~aurum~ (“gold”), and compares Italian ~orina~. The hypothesis is tentative, so the safe core is simply Latin ~urīna~.
en.user:
From Vulgar Latin *~ūsāre~, a frequentative formed on ~ūsus~, the past participle of Classical Latin ~ūtī~ (“to make use of, employ, enjoy”) — a verb of uncertain, much-debated Indo-European origin, with no securely reconstructed root. Cognate with Italian ~usare~ and Spanish ~usar~, and — through the same ~ūtī~ — with English ~use~, ~utility~, and ~usual~.

The frequentative shape (“to use repeatedly”) left its mark on the meaning. Where ~utiliser~ (a later, learned coinage) simply means “to employ,” the older inherited ~user~ leans toward the consequence of repeated use: things ~usées~ by handling are worn out, and ~s'user~ is to wear away — so ~user~ de patience is to draw it down, and ~usure~ names both wear-and-tear and, by a separate route, the “using” of money for interest. Hence French keeps a telling pair: one ~utilise~ a tool but ~use~ a pair of shoes. The same Latin ~ūtī~ seeded ~usage~, ~usager~, ~usuel~, ~ustensile~, and — with ~ab-~ (“away, amiss”) — ~abuser~ and ~abus~, the “using up” turned into misuse.
en.usiner: ~Usiner~ is formed from ~usine~ (“factory”) with the suffix ~-er~, and fr.Wiktionary calls it a neologism of early industrialization. It originally meant to work something in a factory, and later to machine a part on a lathe or mill. ~Usine~ itself has a debated ancestry. English Wiktionary derives it from Latin ~officīna~ (“workshop”) through Old and Middle French, making it a doublet of ~officine~. French Wiktionary gives that route or Latin ~usus~ as the source. The word meant “workshop” in northeastern France, reached Paris in the 1700s as a mill driven by water power, and by 1830 or 1840 named the industrial plant.
en.usurper:
~Usurper~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~ūsūrpāre~, taken straight from Latin rather than handed down through the spoken language. The Latin verb is traditionally analyzed as ~ūsus~ (“use”) joined to ~rapere~ (“to seize”), though this analysis is only traditional and not certain. The same Latin verb lies behind English ~usurp~, Italian ~usurpare~ and Spanish ~usurpar~.

In Latin, ~ūsūrpāre~ could mean to make use of something or to take possession of it, and the sense of seizing without right was already there. French ~usurper~ keeps the sense of taking a power, a title or a property that belongs to someone else. The family includes ~usurpateur~ and ~usurpation~. A looser use applies the verb to reputations and qualities, as in ~une réputation usurpée~ (“an undeserved reputation”).
en.utiliser:
A late and learned formation, dating from the end of the 18th century, derived from the adjective ~utile~ (“useful”) plus the verb-forming suffix ~-iser~ (“to make, to render”). Its model was Italian ~utilizzare~. The adjective ~utile~ itself comes from Latin ~ūtilis~ (“useful”), from the verb ~ūtī~ (“to use, to make use of”), whose past participle ~ūsus~ underlies a wide family of words. Cognate in formation with Italian ~utilizzare~ and Spanish ~utilizar~, and through the Latin verb with English ~use~ and ~utility~.

Because ~utiliser~ arrived so late, older French simply said ~user de~ or ~se servir de~; the newcomer's success was so complete that purists once denounced it as a needless neologism. Its ancestor ~ūtī~ — of uncertain deeper origin, with no secure PIE root — was nonetheless prolific in Latin. From the participle ~ūsus~ French draws ~user~, ~usage~, ~usine~ (originally a place put to “use”), ~ustensile~, and ~usure~ (“wear,” and also “usury”), while ~ūtilis~ yields ~utile~, ~utilité~, ~inutile~, and ~utilitaire~. A single notion of putting things to use thus spans tools, factories, wear, and worth.
en.vacciner: Formed in French from ~vaccin~ or ~vaccine~ + ~-er~, “to inoculate.” The noun comes from the learned Latin phrase ~variola vaccina~ (“cowpox”, literally “smallpox of the cow”), where ~vaccina~ is the feminine of ~vaccinus~ (“of a cow”), from ~vacca~ (“cow”). The name records the observation that people who worked with cows, and so caught cowpox, escaped human smallpox. ~Vaccine~ took the sense “inoculation” around 1800, and the masculine ~vaccin~ is attested in 1801, with the verb built on that noun.
en.vaciller: Both Wiktionaries call ~vaciller~ a borrowing from Latin ~vacillāre~, and English Wiktionary specifies a learned borrowing. The Latin verb meant “to sway, to totter.” The same Latin source gave English ~vacillate~, and French kept both the physical sense (a drunkard, a flame or a tower can ~vaciller~) and the figurative one of wavering in a decision or a belief. Related French words include ~vacillant~ and ~vacillation~.
en.vacuoliser: Formed from ~vacuole~ with the suffix ~-iser~, which turns a noun into a verb meaning “to convert into” or “to provide with.” ~Vacuoliser~ thus means to form vacuoles in a cell. The base ~vacuole~ is a learned word built on Latin ~vacuus~ (“empty”) with the diminutive suffix ~-ole~, so it means “small cavity,” and it is a cousin of ~alvéole~.
en.vadrouiller: ~Vadrouiller~ is a denominal verb built on ~vadrouille~ (“mop”) with the verb ending ~-er~. English Wiktionary suggests the image of a mop pushed here and there in a more or less haphazard way. The noun itself dates from the 17th century and was first used in nautical speech. French Wiktionary proposes that it comes from the Lyon dialect word ~drouille~ (“old rags”) with an intensive ~va-~ from Latin ~valde~ (“very much”), while English Wiktionary only says it is possibly an extension of regional ~drouilles~, itself of unknown origin. The sense “stroll” for the noun is a backformation from the verb.
en.vagabonder: Formed from the noun and adjective ~vagabond~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, meaning “to live or move as a vagabond”, so to roam. ~Vagabond~ was borrowed from Late Latin ~vagābundus~, formed from the verb ~vagari~ (“to wander”), which also gave French ~vaguer~. The word later took on the figurative sense “perpetually changing” in the sixteenth century. The ending ~-er~ comes from the Latin ~-are~ of first-conjugation verbs.
en.vagir:
~Vagir~ comes from Latin ~vāgīre~ (“to wail, to cry,” said of a baby), a verb generally taken to imitate the sound it names. French took it over as a learned word, and it is used almost only of infants and small animals. The Latin verb is a fourth-conjugation one, which is why French has it in the ~-ir~ class, with the usual second-group endings such as ~vagissons~ and ~vagissait~.

The derived noun ~vagissement~ is much commoner than the verb, and it keeps the same restricted sense: the thin crying of a newborn. The verb is not related to ~vague~ or ~vagabond~, which come from other Latin roots, even though the spelling looks alike. Its register is literary or technical, and it appears in descriptions of newborns and in the language of naturalists.
en.vaguer:
~Vaguer~ is borrowed from Latin ~vagārī~ (“to wander, to roam”). That verb was a deponent, which means it had passive endings with an active sense. It is the source of Italian ~vagare~ and Spanish ~vagar~, and it belongs with the Latin adjective ~vagus~ (“wandering, unsettled”), the source of French ~vague~. French took the verb over by replacing the Latin infinitive ending with the regular ending ~-er~.

The Latin stem lives on in several French words. The adjective ~vague~ (“hazy, indistinct”) comes from ~vagus~, ~vagabond~ from Late Latin ~vagabundus~, and ~divaguer~ from ~dīvagārī~, with a prefix meaning “apart.” English ~vague~ and ~vagabond~ are borrowed from French. ~Vaguer~ keeps the Latin sense of wandering without a fixed aim, while ~vague~ and ~divaguer~ moved toward the mind, “indistinct” and “to ramble in speech.”
en.vaincre:
From Old French ~veintre~ (also ~vencre~, ~veincre~), from Latin ~vincere~ (“to conquer, overcome”), from Proto-Italic *~winkō~, from a nasalized PIE *~wi-n-k-~, built with a nasal infix on the root *~weyk-~ (“to overcome, fight”). The Romance siblings are transparent: Italian ~vincere~ and Spanish ~vencer~ both mean “to defeat.” Through the Indo-European root, Latin ~vincere~ stands beside Gothic ~weihan~ (“to fight”). The modern infinitive ~vaincre~ owes its shape partly to the Latin first-person ~vincō~, which kept the nasal and the ~-c-~ that several Old French variants had worn away.

In Latin ~vincere~ already meant both “to win a battle” and “to prevail” in any contest, and French inherited the full range. One conjugates ~je vaincs~, ~il vainc~ — forms whose silent consonants preserve the Latin cluster on the page. From the same root come the participial noun ~vainqueur~ (“victor”) and, via the Latin supine ~victum~, the learned family ~victoire~, ~victime~, ~convaincre~, and ~invincible~. Note that English ~win~ is a false friend here: it descends from a different PIE root, *~wenh₁-~ (“to strive, desire”), not from *~weyk-~.
en.valdinguer: A blend, or portmanteau, of ~valser~ (“to waltz”) and ~dinguer~, a colloquial verb meaning to fall or to be sent flying. The result is a familiar verb for tumbling or being thrown about in a clumsy, whirling way, as though by a dance gone wrong. Both English and French Wiktionary give this same two-part origin. It is typical of French slang to fuse two verbs into one in this manner.
en.valider:
From Latin ~validāre~ (“to make strong, to strengthen, to confirm”), built on the adjective ~validus~ (“strong, robust, effective”), which derives from the verb ~valēre~ (“to be strong, to be worth”) with the suffix ~-idus~. ~Valēre~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~walēō~ to the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂welh₁-~ (“to be strong, to rule”). Italian ~validare~ and Spanish ~validar~ share the same Latin source, and the root surfaces in English ~valid~ and ~value~, and even in the name ~Valerie~.

The earliest sense was bodily: a ~validus~ man was hale and vigorous, and to ~validāre~ was to fortify. From physical strength the meaning slid toward the strength of a thing's standing — its soundness, its force in law or logic. To ~valider~ today is to make something hold good: to confirm a ticket, ratify a decision, or certify a result as sound. The same ~valēre~ gave French the everyday ~valoir~ (“to be worth”), and the wider root spread into ~valeur~, ~valable~, ~valeureux~, ~prévaloir~, ~équivaloir~, and ~convalescence~, the last recalling the original sense of returning strength.
en.valoir:
From Latin ~valere~ (“to be strong, be well, be worth”), from Proto-Italic *~walēō~ and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂welh₁-~ (“to be strong, to rule”). The kernel of meaning is bodily strength: the Latin farewell ~vale~ was a wish of “stay strong, keep well.” Through this root ~valoir~ is cognate with English ~wield~ (to handle with power) and, by borrowing from the same Latin stem, with English ~value~ and ~valour~.

The slide from “being strong” to “being worth” is the heart of the word: what is robust and sound is what has worth, and so ~valere~ moved from health to value. French kept both edges — se porter bien lingers in ~valétudinaire~, while the worth-sense dominates ~valoir~ today, as in ~cela vaut la peine~ (“that is worth the trouble”) and ~vaille que vaille~ (“come what may”). The verb is also notably irregular, with the present ~je vaux~ and the future ~je vaudrai~ preserving old stem shifts. From the same *~h₂welh₁-~ root flow a rich French family of strength and worth: ~valeur~, ~valable~, ~valide~, ~évaluer~, ~prévaloir~, ~équivalent~, and ~polyvalent~.
en.valoriser:
A modern French coinage (around 1925), formed from ~valeur~ (“value, worth”) with the verb-forming suffix ~-iser~. ~Valeur~ comes from Latin ~valor~, the noun of the verb ~valēre~ (“to be strong, be well, be worth”), from Proto-Italic *~walēō~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂welh₁-~ (“to be strong, to rule”). That root is robust across the family: it gives English ~wield~, German ~walten~ (“to govern”), and — through Latin ~valēre~ — English ~value~, ~valiant~, and ~valid~.

The primitive idea is strength that translates into worth: to be strong is to be worth something. French ~valoriser~ is the deliberate, almost economic act of making that worth visible — to develop, enhance, or capitalise on something so its value is realised. One ~valorise~ a region's heritage, a waste product, an employee's skills. Being twentieth-century and built on a productive pattern, it spawned a tidy paradigm: ~valorisation~, ~dévaloriser~ and ~dévalorisation~, ~revaloriser~ and ~survaloriser~. Beside them stand older heirs of the same root — ~valoir~ (“to be worth”), ~valeur~, ~valable~ (“valid”), and ~vaillant~ (“valiant”) — all turning on the link between strength and worth.
en.valser: Formed from ~valse~ plus the verb ending ~-er~: “to waltz”. The noun ~valse~ was borrowed from German ~Walzer~ (“waltz”), which French Wiktionary derives from ~wälzen~ (“to turn in a circle”). The dance is thus named, in German, for its turning.
en.vamper: Formed from ~vamp~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun was borrowed from English ~vamp~ (“seductress”), itself a clipping of ~vampire~. The image is that of a woman who ruins those she hunts and charms, as a vampire would. ~Vamper~ therefore means to seduce someone in the manner of such a woman.
en.vampiriser: ~Vampiriser~ is formed from ~vampire~ with the suffix ~-iser~, which makes verbs meaning “to cause to become” or “to treat as.” ~Vampire~ was borrowed from German ~Vampir~, from Serbo-Croatian ~vampir~, reaching German by way of Hungarian ~vámpir~ according to one account. The verb means to turn into or treat as a vampire.
en.vandaliser: Formed from the noun ~vandale~ and the suffix ~-iser~, meaning “to treat as a Vandal does,” that is, to damage or destroy wantonly. The noun comes from the proper name ~Vandale~, a Germanic people who devastated several provinces of the Roman Empire, and it came to mean any destructive person. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~ and is fully productive for verbs of the “act like N” type. The verb is therefore the people's name turned into an action.
en.vanner: The oldest ~vanner~ is inherited from Vulgar Latin ~vannāre~, which came from Latin ~vannere~ (also ~vannō~), the verb for winnowing grain. It rests on the Latin noun ~vannus~, the winnowing fan, which is also the source of English ~fan~. French has more than one ~vanner~. Another verb is formed from ~vanne~ (“floodgate”) plus ~-er~. The slangy senses glossed as “to tire out” and “to kid, to crack jokes” are traced by English Wiktionary to the first verb, and later also to ~vanne~ in the sense “wisecrack” plus ~-er~.
en.vanter:
From Old French ~vanter~, descended from Late or Vulgar Latin ~vānitāre~. The sources differ on its immediate parent: French Wiktionary treats ~vānitāre~ as a verb drawn from the noun ~vānitās~ (“vanity”), while English Wiktionary says it goes back to Latin ~vānus~ (“empty”) or to ~vānitās~. Either way, the root idea is emptiness, and ~vānus~ is also the source of French ~vain~. Italian ~vantare~ is the sibling form, and English ~vaunt~ is a borrowing from the same French verb.

The reflexive ~se vanter~ means “to boast.” According to French Wiktionary, the transitive use of ~vanter~ (to praise someone or something) appears only in 1580. Today that transitive use is common in the phrase ~vanter les mérites de~ (“to extol the merits of”), and in advertising, where products are praised by those who sell them. The family includes ~vantard~ (“braggart”), ~vanterie~ (“boasting”), ~vanité~ and ~vain~, all pointing back to the Latin idea of the hollow and the empty.
en.vaporiser: Formed from Latin ~vapor~ (“steam, vapor”), the source of French ~vapeur~, with the verbal suffix ~-iser~. The suffix here has its sense “convert into”, so ~vaporiser~ is to turn something into vapor, and by extension to spray a liquid as a fine mist. The suffix ~-iser~ is fully productive in technical and administrative French, and the verb keeps the Latin form of the base rather than the French ~vapeur~.
en.vaquer:
French ~vaquer~ comes from Old French ~vaquer~, itself borrowed from Latin ~vacāre~ (“to be empty, to be idle”). The Latin verb is the source of a large learned family: ~vacant~, ~vacance~ and ~vacances~ in French, and ~vacant~, ~vacate~ and ~vacation~ in English. The step from Latin to French was a borrowing rather than a slow inheritance, which is why the verb still looks so close to its source.

The meaning took a curious U-turn. ~Vacāre~ meant to be empty or idle, and so to be at leisure, free for some pursuit. Applied to an activity, that availability flipped: to be free for something came to mean to devote oneself to it. So ~vaquer à ses occupations~ means to go about one's business, the opposite of idleness. The older sense of emptiness survives in related words such as ~vacant~ (“unoccupied”) and ~vacances~ (“holidays”, periods of being free), and in the use of ~vaquer~ for a post or office that stands empty.
en.varapper: ~Varapper~ is formed from the noun ~varappe~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun comes from a place name: ~la Grande Varappe~ and ~la Petite Varappe~ are two rocky gullies on Mount Salève in Haute-Savoie, near Geneva, where climbers practiced. Hence ~varappe~ came to mean rock climbing and ~varapper~ “to go rock climbing.” It is a rare example of a French verb that descends from the name of two particular rock faces.
en.varier:
From Latin ~variare~ (“to change, to make different, to diversify”), a verb built on the adjective ~varius~ (“varied, spotted, of different colors”). ~varius~ is perhaps related to ~varus~ (“bent, knock-kneed”), with a notion of things turned different ways; its deeper Proto-Indo-European origin is uncertain and best left unstated. Through ~variare~ the French verb is cognate with Italian ~variare~, Spanish ~variar~, and English ~vary~ and ~various~.

The core idea was diversity of appearance — ~varius~ first described things speckled or many-colored, like a dappled animal — and ~variare~ meant to make such diversity, to alter. French ~varier~ kept both the transitive “to vary, to diversify” and the intransitive “to differ, to change.” A memorable kinsman is ~varicelle~ (“chickenpox”), so named for its spots, a faint diminutive echo of the “speckled” sense; the medical ~varice~ (“varicose vein”), however, belongs to a separate Latin word. From ~varius~ French keeps ~varié~, ~variété~, ~variation~, ~variable~, and ~variante~ — a whole vocabulary of change grown from an adjective that first meant simply “of more than one color.”
en.varloper: Formed from the noun ~varlope~ (a long carpenter's plane) with the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to work with a ~varlope~,” that is, to plane. The noun ~varlope~ itself was borrowed from Dutch ~voorloper~. The verb thus shows a tool name from the Low Countries turned into a French verb by the ordinary first-group ending.
en.vaseliner: Formed from ~vaseline~ with the verbal ending ~-er~: to coat or smear with petroleum jelly. The noun is borrowed from English ~vaseline~, a trademark registered in the United States in 1872 by Robert Chesebrough, the inventor of the product. The brand name became a generic word for petroleum jelly, and French then turned it into a verb.
en.vaser: Formed on the noun ~vase~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense of raining heavily; it is an informal word of northern and eastern France. French has two nouns spelled ~vase~. The feminine one, “mud, silt,” comes through Middle French from Middle Dutch ~wase~, itself from Proto-Germanic *~wasô~ (“moisture, ground”). The masculine one, “vessel,” was borrowed from Latin ~vās~. The sources say only that ~vaser~ is a noun-based verb in ~-er~, without naming which ~vase~ it is built on, so that choice is left open.
en.vasouiller: Formed in French from the noun ~vase~ (“mud, silt”) and the familiar suffix ~-ouiller~, which gives verbs a small, loose or slightly pejorative action. The noun ~vase~ in this sense comes from Middle Dutch ~wase~ (“mud, wet ground”) and is related to Old French ~wason~, the source of ~gazon~. The Dutch word descends from Proto-Germanic *~wasô~ (“moisture, ground”). This ~vase~ is a different word from the feminine ~vase~ (“vessel”), from Latin ~vās~. The modern verb means to flounder or be muddled.
en.vaticiner:
~Vaticiner~ is borrowed from Latin ~vāticinārī~ (“to prophesy”). The Latin verb is usually analyzed as a compound of ~vātēs~ (“seer, prophet”) and a verb of singing or chanting, which suits the old idea of the oracle speaking in verse. It is a learned borrowing, so it kept its Latin shape and never went through the sound changes of inherited words.

In French the verb means to prophesy, but it now often carries a mocking edge: to speak in a solemn, obscure or pompous way, as if delivering oracles. The learned noun ~vaticination~ follows the same path. The Latin ~vātēs~ also lies behind the rare French ~vate~ (“poet-seer”). English borrowed the same Latin verb as ~vaticinate~.
en.vautrer:
The origin of ~vautrer~ is disputed. English Wiktionary derives it from Vulgar Latin *~volūtulāre~ (“to tumble over”), from Latin ~volūtum~, a form of the verb ~volvere~ (“to roll”). French Wiktionary instead derives it from the noun ~vautre~ (“hunting dog”) and points to Swedish ~vältra~ and German ~wälzen~, words for rolling. The two accounts agree on the picture of rolling about, not on the route.

If the Latin account is right, ~vautrer~ is a distant cousin of ~volume~ (originally a rolled scroll), ~révolution~ and ~évolution~, which all come from ~volvere~. The modern verb is mostly pronominal: ~se vautrer~ is to sprawl or wallow, in mud, on a sofa or, figuratively, in vice. French has no certain origin to offer here, so the story of the hunting dog and the story of the Latin roll remain two proposals.
en.veiller:
From Latin ~vigilāre~ (“to stay awake, to keep watch”), itself derived from the classical Latin adjective ~vigil~ (“awake, alert, watchful”). The root traces to Proto-Indo-European *~weǵ-~ (“to be strong, lively, awake”). From this same root spring a remarkable set of English cognates: ~wake~, ~watch~, ~vigour~, and even ~vegetable~ (originally “lively, growing”). Italian ~vegliare~ and Spanish ~velar~ are the Romance siblings of ~veiller~.

The verb has always hovered around the idea of holding off sleep. To ~veiller~ is to stay up late, but also to sit up with someone — at a bedside, or beside the dead in a ~veillée funèbre~ (“wake”) — and, more broadly, to keep watch and look after. From the notion of watchfulness comes the construction ~veiller à~ (“to see to, to take care that”) and ~veiller sur~ (“to watch over, to protect”). The same Latin family yields a rich crop of French words: ~vigile~ (“the eve of a feast,” and now a “security guard”), ~vigilant~ and ~vigilance~, ~réveiller~ (“to wake up,” literally “to watch again”), ~surveiller~ (“to supervise, to watch over”), and the noun ~veille~ (“the day before; wakefulness”).
en.veiner: Formed from the noun ~veine~ (“vein”) and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Latin ~vēna~ (“blood vessel”), which also gave Italian and Spanish ~vena~. The verb is a late arrival, recorded at the end of the 18th century (Bernardin de Saint-Pierre) and again in 1812. It means to streak a surface with marks that resemble veins, as in marble or wood.
en.velouter: ~Velouter~ is built on the adjective ~velouté~ (“velvety”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to give a velvety finish” or “to make smooth.” ~Velouté~ in turn rests on ~velours~ (“velvet”), whose family goes back to Late Latin ~villūtus~ (“hairy”), from Latin ~villus~ (“hair, tuft of hair”). The same Latin word gave French ~velu~ (“hairy”), and English ~velvet~ is a cognate. The “hairy” cloth thus became the model of smoothness.
en.vendanger: From Latin ~vindēmiāre~ (“to gather grapes”), a verb built on the noun ~vindēmia~ (“grape harvest”). The noun is a compound of ~vīnum~ (“wine”) and the root of ~dēmere~ (“to take off”), so the harvest is, literally, the taking off of the wine-bearing fruit. French ~vendange~ is the noun, and ~vendanger~ is the inherited Latin verb, which by surface analysis can also be read as ~vendange~ plus ~-er~. The family is the vocabulary of the grape harvest: ~vendange~ (“harvest, vintage”), ~vendangeur~ (“grape-picker”) and ~vendangeoir~ (“harvest basket”). Latin ~vīnum~ is also the source of French ~vin~, Italian and Spanish ~vino~, German ~Wein~ and English ~wine~.
en.vendre:
From Latin ~vendere~ (“to sell, to trade, to praise”), a contraction of ~vēnum dare~ (“to give for sale”) — that is, ~vēnum~ (“sale, that which is for sale”) plus ~dare~ (“to give”). ~Vēnum~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~wesnom~ to PIE *~wes-~ (“to buy, to sell”), the same root behind Sanskrit ~vasna~ (“price”) and Ancient Greek ~ônos~ (“price”); ~dare~ descends from PIE *~deh₃-~ (“to give”). Cognate with Italian ~vendere~ and Spanish ~vender~.

The Romans built their word for selling out of two ideas welded together: a thing offered up, ~vēnum~, and the act of handing it over, ~dare~. Latin let the phrase fuse into one verb, and French inherited it whole, so that a sale is etymologically a giving. The buyer's side of the bargain left its own trace: from the same root, through ~vēnum~, French keeps ~vénal~ (“venal, for sale”), the adjective for whatever can be bought, a conscience included. The ~dare~ half seeded a vast family too — ~donner~, ~don~, ~date~, and the learned ~dation~ — while ~vendre~ itself produced ~vente~ (“sale”) and ~vendeur~ (“seller”).
en.venger:
French ~venger~ comes from Old French ~vengier~, attested around 980, which goes back to Latin ~vindicāre~. In Latin the verb meant “to lay claim to, to demand justice,” and then “to avenge,” the legal and the personal sense running side by side. Middle French ~venger~ is the intermediate form. The Latin verb has sisters across the Romance languages, among them Italian ~vendicare~ and Spanish ~vengar~, and English holds two later descendants: ~vindicate~, taken straight from Latin, and ~avenge~, which entered through Old French.

The move from claiming a right to taking revenge is the story of the word. ~Vindicāre~ began in the law courts, where one claimed what was due, and the French verb kept only the avenging half. Related words multiplied: ~vengeance~, ~vengeur~, and ~revanche~, from the verb ~revenger~, which now serves in sport and politics for any return match. Learned vocabulary kept the legal Latin side, for example ~vindicte~, as in the phrase ~vindicte publique~ (“public prosecution”) and the adjective ~vindicatif~. French thus holds the popular verb and the learned family of one Latin word apart, each with a different shade of justice.
en.venir:
From Old French ~venir~, from Latin ~venīre~ (“to come”), from Proto-Italic *~gʷenjō~, from PIE *~gʷem-~ (“to come, to step”). Cognate with Italian ~venire~, Spanish ~venir~, and Catalan ~venir~ or ~vindre~; through the same PIE root — but down the Germanic line, where *~gʷ-~ became *~kw-~ — come English ~come~, German ~kommen~, and Dutch ~komen~. French ~venir~ and English ~come~ are thus distant cousins despite sounding nothing alike.

The Latin verb's awkward conjugation made for a famously irregular French one: the future stem buckled and shifted, ~venirát~ giving ~venrat~, then ~vendra~, then the modern ~viendra~, an intrusive ~-d-~ wedging itself between ~n~ and ~r~. The root spread widely through Latin compounds, and French inherited a great cluster of them: ~devenir~, ~revenir~, ~prévenir~, ~convenir~, ~parvenir~, ~survenir~, and ~intervenir~. Their Latinate doublets supply ~avènement~, ~convention~, ~revenu~, and ~aventure~ — literally “what is about to come,” ~adventūra~. From a single verb of motion, French built much of its vocabulary of arrival, agreement, prevention, and chance.
en.venter: Formed from ~vent~ (“wind”) and the ending ~-er~. The verb is literally “to wind” and is used impersonally of the weather, as in il vente, “it is windy.” ~Vent~ passed through Middle and Old French from Latin ~ventus~, from Proto-Italic *~wentos~ and ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂weh₁-~ (“to blow”). The same root gave English ~wind~ and German ~Wind~, and Latin ~ventus~ lives on in Italian ~vento~ and Spanish ~viento~. French words built on ~vent~ include ~venteux~ and ~éventail~.
en.ventiler:
Borrowed from Latin ~ventilāre~ (“to toss in the air, to winnow, to fan”), a verb built on ~ventus~ (“wind”). ~Ventus~ comes from the Proto-Indo-European root *~h₂weh₁-~ (“to blow”), which is also the source of English ~wind~ and German ~Wind~. Italian ~ventilare~ and Spanish ~ventilar~ are the same borrowing, and English ~ventilate~ arrived through the same Latin verb.

The first picture is farming: to ~ventilāre~ grain was to toss it in the breeze so the chaff blew away. From there Latin extended the verb to fanning, cooling and stirring up a fire, and even to scattering or divulging something. French uses the airing sense for rooms and buildings, but it also has a quite different modern meaning, to break a sum down and share it among accounts or categories. That sense is probably a figurative extension of the winnowing image of sorting and separating, though the sources do not spell out the path. Relatives include ~vent~, ~ventilateur~, ~éventer~ (“to fan, to expose to the air”) and ~éventail~ (“fan”).
en.verbaliser: ~Verbaliser~ is formed from the adjective ~verbal~ and the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make, to treat as”). ~Verbal~ is borrowed from Late Latin ~verbālis~, and can also be analysed as ~verbe~ plus ~-al~. The verb has two main uses, matching its two glosses: in police language, “to record an offence and fine the offender,” and in the general sense “to put into words.”
en.verdir: From the adjective ~vert~ (“green”) with the ending ~-ir~, which forms verbs meaning “become A.” English Wiktionary adds that Old French already had ~verdir~ in the 12th century and that it may be inherited from Vulgar Latin *~vir(i)dire~, an alteration of Classical Latin ~viridēscere~, so the French-looking formation may in fact be older than French. ~Vert~ comes from Latin ~viridis~ through Old French ~vert~, whose final ~-t~ is due to regular final devoicing. Italian ~inverdire~ and Romanian ~înverzi~ are comparable verbs.
en.verdoyer: ~Verdoyer~ is built on ~vert~ with the suffix ~-oyer~, which can mean to be like something or to give off something: to be green. The adjective ~vert~ comes from Old French ~vert~, from Latin ~viridis~ (“green, verdant; fresh, vigorous”), itself derived from the verb ~vireō~ (“to be green”). English Wiktionary gives a slightly different route, inheriting the verb from Vulgar Latin *~viridizāre~. This fits the suffix, since ~-oyer~ descends from Late Latin ~-izāre~, and ~-iser~ is its learned doublet.
en.verjuter: Formed from the noun ~verjus~ (“verjuice”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, so it means to season with verjuice, the sour juice of unripe grapes. The noun is a compound of ~vert~ (“green”) and ~jus~ (“juice”). The ~t~ before the ending is an epenthetic consonant, the same one found in ~juter~, which links the stem to the ending.
en.vermiller:
From Latin ~vermiculus~, the diminutive of ~vermis~ (“worm”), so literally “little worm.” French records the verb in 1375 in the form ~vermeiller~. The Latin noun ~vermis~ also gave French ~ver~ (“worm”), and it is a cognate of English ~worm~ and German ~Wurm~, which belong to the same Indo-European family. As a diminutive, ~vermiculus~ was a separate word from the start, and French drew several words from it over time.

The modern verb ~vermiller~ means “to dig around for worms,” a rare, specialized word. Its family is larger than it looks: ~vermisseau~ (“small worm”), ~vermifuge~ (a remedy that drives worms out), ~vermine~ and ~vermicelle~ (Italian ~vermicelli~, “little worms,” by their shape), all point to ~vermis~. ~Vermeil~ and ~vermillon~, words for a bright red, go back to the very same Latin diminutive ~vermiculus~, which is why “little worm” can end up naming a color.
en.vermillonner: Built on ~vermillon~, the bright red pigment and colour, with the verbal ending ~-er~, so that the verb means “to paint something vermilion.” French Wiktionary gives two accounts of the formation: one from ~vermillon~ and its related adjective ~vermeille~, the other from the older verb ~vermiller~. Either way, the family goes back to ~vermeil~ and, beyond it, to Latin ~vermiculus~ (“little worm”), the name of the insect that yielded a red dye.
en.vernir: A denominal verb built on the noun ~vernis~ (“varnish”), with the ending ~-ir~ rather than the usual ~-er~. The noun appears in Old French as ~verniz~, a resin-based coating, and comes from Medieval Latin ~veronīx~, which gave Italian ~vernice~ too. Behind it stands Byzantine Greek ~βερενίκη~ (“resin, amber”), from Ancient Greek ~βερενίκιον~ (“soda”). French Wiktionary ties these Greek names to the city of Berenice, now Benghazi; English Wiktionary calls that only possible and warns it may be a false etymology.
en.vernisser: Formed from the noun ~vernis~ (“varnish, glaze”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to coat with varnish,” especially to glaze pottery. The noun was attested in Old French as ~verniz~, borrowed from Medieval Latin ~veronice~ (“resin”), from Greek ~bereníkē~ (“resin, amber”). One tradition derives the Greek word from the city of Berenice, now Benghazi, which exported such products. English Wiktionary adds that this link to the city may be a false etymology, so it is best taken as a possibility. Italian ~vernice~ comes from the same Medieval Latin source.
en.verrouiller: Formed in French from ~verrou~ (“bolt”) and the verb-forming suffix ~-er~, so to ~verrouiller~ is to fasten with a bolt. The noun ~verrou~ comes from Old French ~veroil~, from a Latin form of ~veruculum~, a diminutive of ~verū~ (“spit, skewer”). The Wiktionaries differ slightly on the exact Latin shape, but both agree on the picture: a bolt is a slim rod, like a small skewer, slid across a door. The verb is used literally for locks and figuratively, for example of a political system or a negotiation that is closed off.
en.verser:
From Old French ~verser~, from Late Latin *~versāre~, a variant of ~versārī~, the frequentative of Latin ~vertere~ (“to turn”). A frequentative names a repeated or intensive action, so ~versāre~ is “to keep turning, to turn over and over.” ~Vertere~ descends from the Proto-Indo-European root *~wer-~ (“to turn, to bend”). Cognate with Italian ~versare~ and Spanish ~verter~, and — through ~vertere~ — with English ~verse~ and ~convert~.

The thread tying the modern senses together is that founding idea of turning. To pour is to tip a vessel and turn its contents out; to capsize (~se verser~, said of a cart or a boat) is to be turned right over; and the financial sense, “to pay in, to deposit,” imagines money being turned out onto the counter — which is why a French salary is ~versé~ and a payment is a ~versement~. English ~verse~ preserves the oldest picture of all: the ploughman ~turning~ at the furrow's end to start the next line, the line of poetry being a “turning.” The same root *~wer-~ feeds a wide French family — ~version~, ~vers~, ~envers~, ~renverser~, ~déverser~, ~convertir~, and ~divers~ — all of them, somewhere, a turn.
en.versifier:
French ~versifier~ is inherited from Old French ~versifier~, which was borrowed from Latin ~versificāre~ (“to put into verse”). The Latin verb is a compound of ~versus~ (“verse”) and ~faciō~ (“to make”), so to versify is literally to make verses. English ~versify~ comes from the same Latin verb, by way of French.

The two halves of the Latin verb each have a family in French. ~Versus~ is the source of ~vers~, and, in the usual account, belongs to the verb ~vertere~ (“to turn”), the verse being a line where the writer turns to begin anew. ~Faciō~ lies behind ~faire~, and the same ~-ficāre~ ending appears in many learned verbs such as ~modifier~ and ~signifier~. Related words are ~versification~ and ~versificateur~.
en.vesser: ~Vesser~ (“to fart”) is an altered form of Old French ~vessir~, which came from Vulgar Latin ~vissīre~, itself from the Classical Latin verb ~visīre~, with the same meaning. The change from the ending ~-ir~ to ~-er~ is probably due to analogy with ~péter~, the everyday verb for the same act. A second analysis is also possible: ~vesser~ may simply be built from the noun ~vesse~ plus ~-er~, that noun itself being derived from the Old French verb. The noun ~vesse~ remains in the language, notably in ~vesse-de-loup~, the name of the puffball mushroom that releases a cloud of spores when pressed.
en.vexer: ~Vexer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~vexāre~ (“to harass, to trouble”). Its older senses in French were harsh ones, to mistreat or torment, and the modern sense of hurting someone's feelings or annoying them is a weakened descendant. The noun ~vexation~ and the adjective ~vexatoire~ belong to the same family, and English ~vex~ comes from the same Latin verb.
en.viabiliser: ~Viabiliser~ is a derivative in ~-iser~, a suffix that can mean “to provide with” something. French Wiktionary derives it from the noun ~viabilité~, English Wiktionary from the adjective ~viable~, so the sources differ on the immediate base. ~Viabilité~ is itself explained in two ways: as ~viable~ + ~-ité~, or, in another sense, as a learned formation on Latin ~via~ (“road, way”) with ~-abilité~. The verb means “to provide with services.”
en.viander: Formed from ~viande~ with the verb ending ~-er~. It is a hunting term: a deer ~viande~ when it feeds or grazes. The base ~viande~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~vīvanda~, an alteration of Latin ~vīvenda~, the neuter plural of ~vīvendus~ (“to be lived”), from ~vīvere~ (“to live”), so it meant “what sustains life.” It first applied to any food and narrowed to flesh only over time, which fits the older general sense behind the verb. English ~viand~ and Italian ~vivanda~ share the same origin.
en.vibrer: Borrowed from Latin ~vibrāre~, “to shake, to brandish, to quiver.” In Latin the verb could describe a spear being brandished or hurled, a flickering flame or a trembling voice. French kept the idea of rapid back-and-forth motion, first for physical objects such as strings, then for sound and, figuratively, for emotion: to ~vibrer~ is to be stirred, to resonate with a feeling. Derived words include ~vibration~, ~vibrant~ and ~vibreur~. Italian ~vibrare~ and English ~vibrate~ are its relatives; the origin of the Latin verb itself is uncertain, so none is assigned here.
en.vibrionner: Formed from ~vibrion~ (“a very restless person”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, so that ~vibrionner~ means to fidget, to bustle about like a ~vibrion~. The noun ~vibrion~ is linked to ~vibrer~ (“to vibrate”), through the idea of constant quivering movement, and the ending ~-er~ descends from the Latin first-conjugation ending ~-are~. The word is informal and slightly humorous, used of someone who cannot keep still.
en.vicier: Borrowed from Latin ~vitiāre~ (“to make faulty, to spoil, to damage”). The Latin verb is built on ~vitium~ (“fault, defect”), which is also the source of French ~vice~ and ~vicieux~ and of English ~vice~ and ~vitiate~. The French verb covers both “to spoil” and “to invalidate”.
en.vidanger: Formed from the noun ~vidange~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so ~vidanger~ is “to carry out a ~vidange~,” that is, to drain a tank, a pit or an engine's oil. The noun ~vidange~ is attested from the twelfth century and is itself a derivative of ~vider~ (“to empty”) with the suffix ~-ange~. The verb therefore gathers two layers of French word-making on a single idea of emptying. Its commonest modern use is to change the oil of a car.
en.vider:
Derived from Old French ~vuidier~, ~voider~, from the adjective ~vuit~ / ~vuide~ (“empty”), modern French ~vide~. ~vide~ goes back through Vulgar Latin *~vocitus~ to the family of Latin ~vacuus~ (“empty”) and ~vacāre~ (“to be empty, vacant”), from Proto-Italic *~wakos~ and Proto-Indo-European *~h₁weh₂-~ (“to lack, be empty”). The modern form arose by generalizing the feminine ~vuide~ and reducing ~vui-~ to ~vi-~.

That PIE root *~h₁weh₂-~ is unexpectedly fertile. Beyond the ~vacuus~ branch — which gives French ~vide~, ~vacant~, ~vacances~, ~évacuer~, and English ~vacant~, ~vacuum~, ~void~ — the same root produced Latin ~vānus~ (“empty”), hence English ~vain~, and, through Germanic, English ~want~ and ~wane~. The verb's range in French is wide and vivid: one can ~vider~ a glass, ~vider~ a room of people, or ~vider~ a fish (gut it) — and, colloquially, be ~vidé~, “wiped out, drained.” In every case the underlying image is the ancient one: to make empty.
en.vidimer:
~Vidimer~ goes back to Latin ~vidimus~ (“we have seen”), the first-person plural perfect of ~vidēre~ (“to see”). The French verb is thus built on a ready-made conjugated Latin form, a rare case of a verb form becoming the stem of a new verb. Latin ~vidēre~ itself lives on as an everyday verb of seeing in Italian ~vedere~ and Spanish ~ver~.

~Vidimer~ is an administrative and legal verb meaning “to certify,” in particular to attest that a copy matches its original. Inherited in the ordinary way, ~vidēre~ gave French ~voir~. Learned borrowings from it include ~vision~, ~évident~, ~providence~ and ~vidéo~, which is simply Latin for “I see.” English took many of the same words, among them ~video~, ~vision~ and ~evident~.
en.vieillir: Formed in French from the adjective ~vieil~ (the form of ~vieux~ before a vowel, “old”) plus the verbal ending ~-ir~, with the sense “to become old.” The adjective comes from Old French ~viel~, itself from Latin ~vetulus~, a diminutive of ~vetus~ (“old”). The ~-ir~ ending is the second-conjugation ending, and it is the usual one for verbs meaning “to become” plus an adjective, like ~grandir~ or ~grossir~. The Romance neighbors built the same idea with a prefix: Catalan ~envellir~, Spanish ~envejecer~ and Portuguese ~envelhecer~.
en.vieller: Formed from ~vielle~ (the hurdy-gurdy or medieval fiddle) plus the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to play the ~vielle~.” The noun comes from Old French ~viele~ and is related to ~vièle~ and ~viole~ in French, to English ~fiddle~ and to German ~Fiedel~. Its ultimate source is possibly Medieval Latin ~vitula~.
en.vilipender:
~Vilipender~ is a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ~vīlipendō~ (“to disparage”), a compound of Latin ~vīlis~ (“cheap, worthless”) and ~pendō~ (“to weigh, to consider”). Literally, then, to ~vilipender~ someone is to weigh them as worthless. French took the word over in nearly its Latin shape, which is why it has the look of a Latin verb dressed in an ~-er~ ending.

In French it remains a formal, literary verb, used for publicly scorning or running down a person, a work or an idea. Its first half is the Latin ~vīlis~ that also underlies French ~vil~ (“base, contemptible”) and ~avilir~ (“to degrade”). English borrowed the same verb as ~vilipend~. Its second half belongs to a large family: the Latin derivative ~pensāre~ (“to weigh, to ponder”) gave French ~peser~ (“to weigh”) and ~penser~ (“to think”), so the idea of weighing underlies both heavy objects and thoughts.
en.villégiaturer: Derived from the noun ~villégiature~ (“a stay in the country, a holiday”) with the verb ending ~-er~, so the verb means to spend time on holiday or at a country house. The noun is a borrowing of Italian ~villeggiatura~, itself built on ~villa~ (“country house”). The verb is rare and has a slightly literary, old-fashioned ring.
en.vinaigrer: Formed from ~vinaigre~ (“vinegar”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, in the sense “provide with N”: to season, soak or preserve in vinegar. The noun is a compound of ~vin~ (“wine”) and ~aigre~ (“sour”), which French Wiktionary calls a fusion of the two words. English Wiktionary adds that ~vinaigre~ is inherited from Middle French, from Old French ~vinaigre~, and compares Catalan and Occitan ~vinagre~. Vinegar is, etymologically, sour wine.
en.viner: French has two unrelated verbs spelled ~viner~. The first is formed from ~vin~ (“wine”), which comes from Latin ~vīnum~, and means to fortify wine by adding alcohol to it. It belongs with other French words from the same Latin source, such as ~vineux~ and ~vinaigre~. The second is a recent formation from ~Vine~, the name of an online application. The two share a spelling only by coincidence.
en.vinifier: ~Vinifier~ is formed from ~vin~ (“wine”) with the suffix ~-ifier~, which comes from Latin ~-ficāre~ and ultimately from ~facere~ (“to make”): to turn grape juice into wine. The base ~vin~ descends through Old and Middle French from Latin ~vīnum~, from Proto-Italic *~wīnom~. The suffix is productive in learned and technical language, and ~vinifier~ belongs to the vocabulary of winemaking, with ~vinification~ for the process. It is a French formation on a Latin base word rather than an inherited Latin verb.
en.violacer: Formed in French from the adjective ~violacé~ (“purplish”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so the color word came first and the verb followed. ~Violacé~ belongs to the family of ~violet~ and ~violette~, the flower and the color. The verb is recorded in the nineteenth century in three steps: first as a transitive verb from 1832, in a past participle with an agent, in Balzac; then as an intransitive verb (“to turn purple”) from 1846; and finally as a pronominal verb from 1860, in Goncourt.
en.violenter: Formed from the adjective ~violent~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so “to act violently toward” someone. The adjective came into French from Latin ~violentus~, through Old French, and French Wiktionary derives the Latin from ~vis~ (“strength, force”). The verb means “to do violence to,” and in law it can refer to forcing someone against their will.
en.violer:
From Latin ~violāre~ (“to treat with force, to profane, to outrage”), in French by about 1100. The Latin verb is traditionally explained as a derivative of ~vīs~ (“force, violence”); the etymologist De Vaan prefers to reconstruct an intermediate adjective *~weyh₁-elos~ — but on either account the base is the PIE root *~weyh₁-~ (“to rush at, to pursue”), which yielded ~vīs~ itself through *~wéyh₁s~ and is cognate with Greek ~ἴς~ (“sinew, strength”) and Sanskrit ~váyas~ (“vigor”). Cognate with Italian ~violare~ and Spanish ~violar~; English ~violate~ is the same Latin verb in scholarly dress.

The French senses unfolded in a revealing order. In the Chanson de Roland, around 1100, what one violated was a sanctuary: the first attested meaning is “to break into and profane a sacred or protected place.” Around 1155 came “to transgress” — laws, oaths, treaties; only around 1170 does the language record the verb applied to the rape of a woman. All three senses flow from the single Latin idea of ~vīs~ — force applied where right forbids it — and all three remain alive: one still violates borders, tombs, secrets and ceasefires. The family stayed close and dark: ~viol~, ~violence~, ~violent~, ~violation~, ~inviolable~. Beware, though, of two innocent lookalikes: ~violette~ goes back to the Latin flower name ~viola~, and ~violon~ to the medieval fiddle ~viole~ — neither the violet nor the violin owes anything to violence.
en.violoner: The verb ~violoner~ (“to play the violin, to fiddle”) is formed from the noun ~violon~ with the verb ending ~-er~, which here means “to carry out N,” in the sense of to use an instrument. ~Violon~ is itself derived from ~viole~ with ~-on~, a diminutive suffix, so it began as a “little viol.” English Wiktionary compares Italian ~violino~, which is built in the same way. The verb is thus a French formation two steps removed from the viol.
en.virer:
The origin of ~virer~ is debated. The account both Wiktionaries lead with is that it comes from Late (Vulgar) Latin *~virāre~ (“to turn, to whirl”), probably an alteration of Latin ~vibrāre~ (“to shake, to brandish”), which would make ~virer~ a doublet of ~vibrer~. French Wiktionary adds that the alteration came under the influence of ~librāre~ (“to hurl with a whirling motion”) and ~gȳrāre~ (“to turn”). English Wiktionary mentions as a lesser possibility a form altered from the Greek-derived Latin verb for turning in circles. It also records a Celtic proposal: Gaulish *~viru~ (“to deviate, to veer off”), derived from ~viros~ (“round, crooked”). The Romance relatives are Italian ~virare~ and Spanish ~virar~.

Whatever its source, the verb was first about turning. A ship or a car ~vire~, which gave ~virage~ (“a bend”), and one speaks of ~virer de bord~ (“to tack, to change course”). From a change of direction came a change of state, so something can ~virer au rouge~ (“to turn red”) or ~virer à l'aigre~ (“to turn sour”), and a sudden reversal of opinion is a ~revirement~. The verb is also used for transferring money between accounts and, colloquially, for dismissing someone, but the sources do not say how those uses developed. If the favored account is right, ~virer~ is a distant cousin of ~vibrer~, so to turn and to tremble may share a Latin ancestor.
en.virevolter: Formed from the noun ~virevolte~ with the ending ~-er~. The noun is a calque of Italian ~giravolta~ (“a turning about”), that is, a word modelled on the Italian one rather than copied from it. The verb means to spin around or turn this way and that.
en.viriliser: Formed from the adjective ~viril~ with the verbal suffix ~-iser~, meaning to make virile or masculine. The adjective comes from Latin ~virīlis~, derived from ~vir~ (“man”), the same root that gave English ~virile~ and ~virtue~ by way of Latin. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs.
en.viroler: A verb made from the noun ~virole~ (“ferrule”), the metal ring fitted around the end of a handle, a cane or a knife blade, with the ending ~-er~. To ~viroler~ is to fit such a ring. The noun ~virole~ comes from Vulgar Latin *~viriola~ (“bracelet”), a diminutive of ~viria~, so a ferrule is etymologically a small bracelet slipped around an object.
en.viser:
From Latin ~vīsāre~, a frequentative of ~vīsere~ (“to look at attentively, to go to see”), itself an intensive of ~vidēre~ (“to see”). ~Vidēre~ descends from PIE *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”), one of the most fertile roots in the family. Through its Germanic branch the same root gave English ~wit~ and ~wise~, and through Latin ~vīsiō~ it gave ~vision~; the Greek branch yielded ~idéa~. Cognate Romance reflexes include Italian ~visare~ and Spanish ~avisar~.

The progression of sense is tidy: from simply seeing, to looking hard at one thing, to fixing one's eye and weapon upon a target — hence the modern ~viser~ (“to aim at”) and its figurative “to aim for, to have designs on.” A separate, later ~viser~, “to stamp or endorse,” was coined in the seventeenth century from the noun ~visa~ (Latin ~vīsa~, “things seen, verified”), the official's mark that a document had been examined; the travel ~visa~ is the same word. From the rich *~weyd-~ stock French also keeps ~voir~, ~vue~, ~vision~, ~évident~, and ~revoir~, every one of them a way of seeing.
en.visibiliser: Formed from the adjective ~visible~ with the verbal suffix ~-iser~, in the sense “to make visible.” The adjective is borrowed from Latin ~visibilis~ (“that can be seen”). The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and is the usual way modern French coins verbs meaning “make A” or “treat as A.” The final ~-ble~ of the base is kept intact, so the verb is simply ~visible~ + ~-iser~. It is a recent coinage of the social sciences and the press: to ~visibiliser~ a group or a problem is to bring it into public view.
en.visionner: Formed from ~vision~ plus the first-conjugation ending ~-er~, with the sense “to view, to watch closely,” especially a film, a recording or a document, often in a technical or professional setting. The noun ~vision~ is a learned borrowing, through Old and Middle French, from Latin ~vīsiō~ (“sight, appearance”), built on ~vīsus~, the past participle of ~vidēre~ (“to see”). So the verb is a recent practical word resting on one of the oldest Latin verbs of sight.
en.visiter:
From Latin ~visito~ (“to go to see, to visit often”), a frequentative of ~video~ (“to see”), the iterative form built on the participial stem ~vis-~. ~video~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”), one of the most productive roots in the family. Through that root ~visiter~ is cognate with Ancient Greek ~eîdon~ (“I saw”) and ~oîda~ (“I know”), with Sanskrit ~veda~ (“knowledge”), and with English ~wit~ and ~wise~, where the sense of seeing has shifted entirely to knowing.

The frequentative ~visito~ already implied not a single glance but repeated, attentive looking — the kind of seeing one does when inspecting, calling on, or watching over someone. That nuance survives: a doctor still ~visite~ patients, an inspector ~visite~ a site, and one ~visite~ a city by going round it thoroughly. The same root *~weyd-~ underlies a remarkable spread of French vocabulary: ~voir~ itself, ~vision~, ~visage~, ~visite~, ~visible~, ~évident~, ~revue~, and — through the knowing branch — words like ~idée~ and ~histoire~, both ultimately Greek relatives. Few roots have given French so many ways to talk about looking and learning.
en.visser: In its main sense, “to fasten with a screw,” ~visser~ is formed from the noun ~vis~ (“screw”) and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun ~vis~ comes from Latin ~vītis~ (“vine, tendril”), which French Wiktionary links to ~viēre~ (“to twist”): the screw took its name from the spiral of a vine's tendril. A second, unrelated ~visser~ is slang. It is a verlan form of ~servir~ (“to serve”), made by reversing the syllables.
en.visualiser:
Borrowed in 1887 from English ~to visualise~, itself formed on the Latin-derived adjective ~visual~, from Late Latin ~visuālis~, from Latin ~vīsus~ (“sight”), the past participle of ~vidēre~ (“to see”). ~Vidēre~ goes back through Proto-Italic *~widēō~ to Proto-Indo-European *~weyd-~ (“to see; to know”). That double meaning — seeing as knowing — runs through the cognates: English ~wit~ and ~wise~, German ~wissen~ (“to know”), Ancient Greek ~oîda~ (“I know,” literally “I have seen”) and ~idéā~, and Sanskrit ~véda~ (“knowledge”).

The word entered French as a late-19th-century import, riding the era's interest in mental imagery and, soon after, photographic and scientific display. Where older French had ~voir~ and ~vision~ for ordinary seeing, ~visualiser~ specialized in “to form a mental picture of” and later “to render visible, to display” — a screen ~visualise~ data. From the same *~weyd-~ root French holds ~voir~, ~vision~, ~visible~, ~vue~, ~aviser~, ~prévoir~, and ~évident~, while the Greek branch gave ~idée~ and ~idole~ — all, at bottom, things seen.
en.vitrer: ~Vitrer~ is formed from the noun ~vitre~ (“window pane”) and the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense “to fit with glass.” ~Vitre~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~vitrum~ (“glass”), and so a doublet of the inherited ~verre~, which took the ordinary phonetic road from the same Latin word. Spanish ~vidrio~ and Catalan ~vidre~ are related forms. Where ~verre~ names the material and the drinking vessel, ~vitre~ keeps to the glazed surface of a window, and ~vitrer~ is the act of putting that glass in place.
en.vitrifier: Formed from ~vitre~ (“windowpane”) with the suffix ~-ifier~ (“to make”, from Latin ~-ficāre~, itself from ~facere~), so it means “to turn into glass” or “to make glass-like”. ~Vitre~ was borrowed from Latin ~vitrum~ (“glass”), which makes it a doublet of ~verre~. Spanish ~vidrio~ and Catalan ~vidre~ are cousins from the same Latin word.
en.vitrioler: A denominal verb: ~vitriol~ plus the ending ~-er~, “to treat or attack with vitriol”. The noun ~vitriol~ is borrowed from Medieval Latin ~vitriolum~, derived from Latin ~vitrum~ (“glass”), so called because certain sulfates, the original vitriols, look like glass. The verb thus keeps, under its sulfuric-acid sense, a distant link to glass, and it is related to French ~verre~ only through that Latin ~vitrum~.
en.vitupérer:
~Vitupérer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~vituperāre~ (“to find fault with, to blame”), which is why it keeps the Latin shape almost untouched. The Latin verb is usually analysed as ~vitium~ (“fault, defect”) + ~parāre~ (“to prepare, to make”). Italian ~vituperare~, Spanish ~vituperar~ and English ~vituperate~ are all borrowed from the same Latin verb.

The family is easy to see in French. ~Vitium~ gave ~vice~ and ~vicieux~, and ~parāre~ lies behind ~préparer~ and ~parer~. ~Vitupérer~ itself is a formal, somewhat literary verb: it means to rail against something, to rant angrily and at length, and it is usually followed by contre, as in ~vitupérer~ contre la presse. Its nouns, ~vitupération~ and ~vitupérateur~, keep the same register. A verb that began by meaning “to find fault” now describes loud, sustained complaint.
en.vivifier:
A semi-learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin ~vīvificāre~ (“to give life to the soul”), built on ~vīvus~ (“alive, living”). The Latin verb joins ~vīvus~ to ~-ficāre~, a combining form of ~facere~ (“to make”), so it means, literally, to make alive. Italian ~vivificare~ and Spanish ~vivificar~ are its counterparts in the other Romance languages, and English ~vivify~ is another.

The Latin adjective ~vīvus~ is the root of a large family. It lives on in inherited French ~vif~ (“lively, quick”), and its related verb ~vīvere~ became ~vivre~ (“to live”). The learned adjective ~vivace~ (“long-lived, hardy”) comes from the same root. The ending ~-fier~ in ~vivifier~ is the same one found in ~purifier~, ~clarifier~ and ~fortifier~, all from Latin verbs in ~-ficāre~. Because ~vivifier~ was taken from learned Latin rather than inherited, it kept a shape close to its source. Modern French keeps “to give life to” and extends it figuratively to giving energy or freshness.
en.vivoter: Formed from the verb ~vivre~ with the suffix ~-oter~, a diminutive and frequentative ending that gives familiar verbs a sense of small, repeated or meager action, as in ~tapoter~ (“to tap lightly”) or ~siffloter~ (“to whistle softly”). Here the effect is attenuative: ~vivoter~ is to live, but only just, barely getting by on little. The base ~vivre~ comes from Latin ~vīvere~ (“to live”), which is also the source of ~vie~, ~vif~ and ~survivre~. The ending itself is built from a diminutive ~-ot~ plus the verb ending ~-er~, so the verb literally means “to live a little.”
en.vivre:
French ~vivre~ comes straight from Latin ~vīvere~ (“to live”), the present infinitive of ~vīvō~, inherited through Old French ~vivre~ with almost no change of shape. Behind the Latin lies Proto-Italic *~gʷīwō~ and, beyond it, Proto-Indo-European *~gʷíh₃weti~ (“to live, to be alive”). The cognates trace life across the whole family: Greek ~bíos~ (“life,” as in ~biology~), Sanskrit ~jīvati~ (“he lives”), Old Church Slavonic ~žiti~, and — strikingly — English ~quick~, whose old meaning was “alive,” preserved in the phrase “the quick and the dead.”

The sense has stayed remarkably stable: to be alive, and by extension to dwell, to subsist, to experience. French keeps both the bare existential sense and a worldlier one in ~savoir-vivre~ (“good manners,” literally knowing how to live). The root threw off a rich crop of French words: ~vie~ (“life”), ~vif~ (“lively, sharp”), ~vivace~ and ~vivant~, ~survivre~ (“to survive,” to out-live), ~revivre~, ~convive~ (a fellow liver, hence a dinner guest), and the borrowed cheer ~vive !~ (“long live!”). Through the Greek cousin ~bíos~ the same idea returns in ~biologie~, ~microbe~, and ~amphibie~ — so that the science of life and the act of living spring from one ancient verb.
en.vocaliser: Formed in French from the adjective ~vocal~ and the suffix ~-iser~, “to make vocal,” hence to sing or articulate sounds. ~Vocal~ comes from Latin ~vocalis~, derived from ~vox~, ~vocis~ (“voice”). It is a doublet of ~voyelle~, which took the same Latin word by the inherited route. The suffix ~-iser~ comes from Late Latin ~-izare~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and forms verbs that mean “make A” or “treat with N.”
en.vociférer: ~Vociférer~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~vōciferor~ (“to cry out, to shout”), a deponent verb. The Latin word is a compound of ~vōx~ (“voice”) and the verb ~ferre~ (“to carry, to bear”), so it literally means “to carry the voice.” It was taken into French whole, without passing through the spoken language of the Old French period, which is why it keeps its Latin shape. Italian ~vociferare~, Spanish ~vociferar~ and English ~vociferate~ are parallel learned borrowings of the same Latin verb. The family is large on both sides. From ~vōx~ come French ~voix~ (the inherited form), ~vocal~, ~vocabulaire~ and ~voyelle~. From ~ferre~ come ~offrir~, ~transférer~, ~conférer~ and ~référer~. A verb that joins them, ~vociférer~ keeps the meaning of its Latin source: to speak loudly, in a raised voice.
en.voguer:
The origin of ~voguer~ is uncertain. French Wiktionary takes it from Italian ~vogare~ (“to sail, to be rocked by the waves”) and links that to Ancient Greek ~βαυκάλη~ (~baukálē~, “cradle”). English Wiktionary is more cautious: ~voguer~ is possibly from Italian ~vogare~, itself perhaps from Latin ~vocāre~ (“to call”), possibly related to the Greek word for “cradle”. It also offers an alternative: a Germanic origin, from Proto-Germanic *~wagōną~ (“to sway, fluctuate”).

So the sources agree on a rocking, swaying motion on the water, but not on the road that led there. The verb is now mostly literary, “to sail along”. Its imperative survives in the fixed phrase ~vogue la galère~, an exclamation meaning “come what may”. English Wiktionary relates ~voguer~ to ~vogue~ (“fashion”), the noun that French sent on to English in the phrase ~en vogue~.
en.voiler:
Derived from the French noun ~voile~ (“veil”), itself from Latin ~vēlum~ (“sail, cloth, curtain”). An earlier form ~veler~ is attested in the twelfth century in the religious sense “to make someone take the veil,” the modern ~voiler~ following around 1380. The origin of Latin ~vēlum~ is debated. The favored account derives it, like its diminutive ~vexillum~ (“banner”), from a Proto-Italic *~wekslom~ and the PIE root *~weg-~ (“to weave, bind”), with which English ~wick~ is connected as a cognate; a rival proposal linking it to *~weǵʰ-~ (“to ride, convey”) is generally judged less attractive.

From the cloth itself, ~voiler~ came to mean to drape, to cover, and so to hide or dim — a sky ~voilé~ is clouded, a voice ~voilée~ is muffled. A separate technical sense, “to warp” (as a bicycle wheel goes out of true), grew from the same image of a flat surface bending like billowing fabric. The root yields ~voile~, ~voilage~, ~dévoiler~ (“to unveil, reveal”) and ~voilette~ (a small hat-veil).
en.voir:
From Old French ~veoir~, earlier ~vedeir~ and ~veder~ (c. 980), from Latin ~vidēre~ (“to see, to perceive, to witness”), the infinitive of ~videō~. The Latin verb goes back to Proto-Indo-European *~weyd-~ (“to see, to know”). Through that root ~voir~ is cognate with Italian ~vedere~ and Spanish ~ver~, and — by the same ancient stem — with English ~wit~ and ~wise~, German ~wissen~ (“to know”), and Greek ~oîda~ (“I know,” literally “I have seen”).

The pairing of seeing and knowing is no accident: across Indo-European languages, *~weyd-~ slid easily from “to perceive with the eye” to “to understand,” a metaphor French still uses when one says ~je vois~ to mean “I understand.” The intervocalic ~d~ of ~vidēre~ softened and then vanished as the word passed through Old French, leaving the smooth modern ~voir~. The root has seeded a large family in French: ~vue~ (“sight”), ~vision~, ~voyant~ (“seer, clairvoyant”), ~évident~ (“evident,” literally “seen out”), ~revoir~, ~prévoir~ (“to foresee”), and ~entrevoir~ (“to glimpse”). The learned doublet ~vidéo~, borrowed back from Latin in the twentieth century, restores the very ~d~ that ordinary speech had worn away centuries before.
en.voisiner: Formed from ~voisin~ (“neighbor”) with the ending ~-er~, which makes the noun a verb of neighborly activity: to be next door, to socialize with the neighbors. ~Voisin~ comes from Old French ~voisin~ (also ~veisin~), from Late Latin ~vēcīnus~, from Latin ~vīcīnus~ (“neighboring”), a derivative of ~vīcus~ (“quarter, village”). Spanish ~vecino~ comes from the same Latin word.
en.voiturer: Formed from ~voiture~ and the verb ending ~-er~: to ~voiturer~ is to carry or drive someone or something. The noun comes from Old French ~voiture~, from Latin ~vectūra~ (“transport”). According to French Wiktionary, the sense of a device used for transport dates from the thirteenth century, and the sense of automobile from the late nineteenth.
en.volatiliser: Formed from ~volatile~ with the suffix ~-iser~ (“to make, to turn into”). ~Volatile~ comes from Latin ~volatilia~ (“birds”); ~volatil~ and ~volaille~ (“poultry”) belong to the same family. The verb means “to turn into vapor” and, figuratively, “to make vanish”, and its colloquial sense of “to steal” is tied to ~voler~.
en.voler:
From Latin ~volāre~ (“to fly”), attested in Old French as early as 881. The deeper origin is uncertain; De Vaan connects it to a Proto-Indo-European root *~gʷelH-~ (“to throw, to reach”), the flying sense perhaps developing from “to fling (the wings).” It is cognate with Italian ~volare~, Spanish ~volar~, and Portuguese ~voar~, all keeping the plain meaning “to fly.”

French is unusual in that this same verb means both “to fly” and “to steal” — and the bridge between them is falconry. A trained falcon ~vole~, taking its quarry on the wing; the bird seizes the prey in mid-flight. The transitive sense “to seize as a bird of prey does” specialized into “to take what is not yours,” and by the seventeenth century ~voler~ in the sense “to steal” had supplanted the older ~rober~ (“to rob by force,” itself from Frankish *~raubōn~) and ~embler~ (“to steal by stealth”). So the thief and the flier share one verb, joined by the hawk. From ~volāre~ descend French ~vol~ (which means both “a flight” and “a theft”), ~voleur~ (“thief”), ~volée~, ~s'envoler~, and ~volaille~ (“poultry,” the flying farmyard).
en.voleter: Formed from ~voler~ (“to fly”) with the suffix ~-ter~, a frequentative or diminutive ending that turns one continuous action into small repeated ones. The verb is recorded from the twelfth century and means to flutter, to fly with small beats of the wings. By analogy it describes light objects that seem to float in the air, and writers have used it figuratively for fancies drifting through the mind.
en.voliger: ~Voliger~ is formed from the noun ~volige~ (“thin board, batten”) with the verbal ending ~-er~: to cover a roof or wall with battens. ~Volige~ is a dialectal variant of ~volice~, from Old French ~volisse~, the feminine of ~volis~ (“light, easily blown away”), itself built on the verb ~voler~ (“to blow away”) and the suffix ~-is~. The name thus points to the lightness of such boards.
en.volleyer: ~Volleyer~ is formed from the English ~volley~ (a stroke in tennis or football made before the ball touches the ground) with the French verb ending ~-er~. French borrowed the English noun, then made it into a regular first-conjugation verb, the usual fate of a sporting loan. ~Volleyer~ thus means “to volley,” to strike the ball on the volley.
en.volter: ~Volter~ is borrowed from Italian ~voltare~ (“to turn”). It is related to the noun ~volte~ and to the verb ~voluter~, which French took from the same Italian family. The form is a reminder that many French terms of horsemanship and movement came from Italian.
en.voltiger: Borrowed from Italian ~volteggiare~ (“to flutter, to go back and forth”), a verb related to French ~volte~ and ~volter~.
