The French verb keeps the Italian sense of light, darting movement to and fro: something that ~voltige~ flits about, here and there, without settling. The sources give no intermediate step or earlier date, so the word is best seen as a straightforward Italian loan.
en.vomir:
Inherited from Old French ~vomir~, from Vulgar Latin *~vomīre~, the popular form of Classical Latin ~vomĕre~. French Wiktionary traces the Latin verb to the Proto-Indo-European root *~wem-~ (“to vomit”). The same root is found in Ancient Greek ~ἐμέω~ (~eméō~, “to vomit”) and in Sanskrit ~vamati~, which has the same meaning. The Vulgar Latin form differs from the classical one in its long ~ī~ against the short ~ĕ~, which shows the verb passing to a different conjugation on its way into French.

The three ancient languages therefore each keep a form of one old word for the same bodily act, and the meaning of the French verb is the same as that of its Latin ancestor. The evidence records no change of sense along the way. The reconstructed root *~wem-~ is the point of connection: it is not a word anyone wrote down but the shape that Latin, Greek and Sanskrit forms together require. French ~vomir~ is thus one modern outcome of a very old verb, reaching French through Old French and spoken Latin rather than being formed in French.
en.voter:
A late arrival in French, ~voter~ was borrowed in the eighteenth century from English ~vote~. The English word goes back to Latin ~votum~ (“a vow, a solemn pledge, a prayer”), the noun from ~vovēre~ (“to vow, to promise solemnly”), from Proto-Indo-European *~h₁wegʷʰ-~ (“to promise, to praise solemnly”). Through that root it is cognate with Greek ~eúkhomai~ (“to pray, to vow”) and Sanskrit ~vāghát~ (“one who makes a vow”). English may have built its verb directly on ~votum~ or taken it from Medieval Latin ~votare~.

The path from “vow” to “ballot” runs through religion and parliament: a ~votum~ was an offering pledged to a god, and to vote was first to declare one's solemn wish — the modern ballot is, etymologically, a vow of preference. Because French acquired the word ready-made from English, it sits a little apart from its own learned cousins drawn straight from ~votum~: ~vœu~ (the inherited descendant, “a wish, a vow”), ~votif~ (“votive”), and ~dévot~ and ~dévotion~, where the original sense of solemn pledging to the divine still rings clearly.
en.vouer:
The origin of ~vouer~ is given in more than one way. One account derives it from Old French ~voer~, from Late Latin ~vōtāre~, a verb made from the noun ~vōtum~ (“a vow, a wish”). French Wiktionary instead cites the Latin verb ~voveō~ (“to vow, to promise, to wish”). A further possibility is that French simply formed it from ~vœu~ + ~-er~. In every version the root idea is a solemn promise.

In modern French the verb means “to dedicate, to devote,” as in devoting one's life to something, and a project that seems certain to fail is called ~voué~ à l'échec. Its relatives include ~vœu~, ~dévouer~, ~dévot~ and ~votif~. The verb ~voter~ is a doublet: it reached French from English ~vote~, which came from the same Latin ~vōtum~. Italian ~votare~ and Spanish and Portuguese ~votar~ are comparable verbs.
en.vouloir:
From Old French ~voloir~, from Vulgar Latin *~volēre~, a reshaping of the irregular Classical Latin ~velle~ (present ~volō~, “I want”), from Proto-Italic *~welō~, from PIE *~welh₁-~ (“to choose, to want”). Speakers smoothed the wildly irregular ~velle~ into a regular *~volēre~ built on the stem ~vol-~, already visible in the 8th-century attestation ~si voles~. Cognate with Italian ~volere~ and Romanian ~vrea~; through the same root, by the Germanic line, come English ~will~ and German ~wollen~. Spanish, tellingly, abandoned this verb for ~querer~.

The PIE root *~welh₁-~ meant “to choose” as much as “to want,” and that pairing of desire and selection runs through its descendants — to will something is to single it out. The French verb kept its irregularity to the end, with the curious imperative ~veuille~ and ~veuillez~ used in polite formulas (~veuillez agréer~). Modern French relatives include ~volonté~ (“will”), ~volontaire~ (“voluntary”), ~bienveillant~ and ~malveillant~ (“well-” and “ill-wishing”), and ~velléité~ — a faint, half-formed wish, from the Latin ~velleitās~. The same root even reaches ~voluptas~, “pleasure,” linking what one wants to what one enjoys.
en.vousoyer: Formed from the pronoun ~vous~ with the verbal ending ~-er~: “to address someone as ~vous~.” The pronoun comes from Old French ~vos~, from Latin ~vōs~. It has cognates in Italian ~voi~ and Russian ~vy~. The verb is the counterpart of ~tutoyer~, which is built the same way on ~tu~, and the pair names the two forms of address that French speakers must choose between.
en.voussoyer: Formed from the pronoun ~vous~ with the suffix ~-oyer~, the same ending as in ~tutoyer~, so “to address someone as ~vous~.” The pronoun comes from Old French ~vos~, from Latin ~vōs~ (“you,” plural), and has cognates such as Italian ~voi~. The ending ~-oyer~ goes back through Old French to Late Latin ~-izāre~. It is no longer productive for new verbs, so this verb was shaped on the older pattern.
en.vouvoyer: ~Vouvoyer~ means to address someone with ~vous~ rather than ~tu~. It is an alteration of the older ~voussoyer~, which was ~vous~ + ~-oyer~. The ending was reshaped on ~tutoyer~: just as ~tutoyer~ repeats the initial consonant of ~tu~ before ~-oyer~, ~vouvoyer~ repeats the ~v~ of ~vous~, so that the two verbs now mirror each other.
en.voyager:
Denominal from the noun ~voyage~, attested in Old French as ~voiage~, ~viage~, and ~veiage~. The noun descends from Latin ~viaticum~ (“provisions or money for a journey”), the neuter of the adjective ~viaticus~ (“of the road”), from ~via~ (“road, way”). The PIE root behind ~via~ is disputed: it is most often referred to *~weyh₁-~ (“to pursue, drive”), with Lithuanian ~vyti~ (“to chase”) as a relative, while an older account tying it to *~weǵʰ-~ (“to go, convey”) — the root of English ~way~ and German ~Weg~ — is rejected by De Vaan. English ~voyage~ is a borrowing of the same Old French word, and a doublet of the learned ~viaticum~.

The semantic drift is vivid: ~viaticum~ first named the money and supplies you packed for the road, then the journey those provisions paid for, and finally any travel at all. The Church preserved the oldest, most literal sense — ~viatique~ in French still means the Eucharist given to the dying, food for the last journey. From ~via~ also come French ~voie~, ~dévier~, ~trivial~ (from ~trivium~, “a place where three roads meet”), and ~convoyer~. To travel, in this etymology, is simply to spend what you set aside for the road.
en.voûter: Formed from the noun ~voûte~ (“vault”) with ~-er~, so it means to build a vault or to bend something into an arch, including a back. The noun comes from Old French ~vouste~ or ~volte~ and goes back to Vulgar Latin *~volvita~ (“a winding”), from Latin ~volvere~ (“to roll”). English Wiktionary also allows *~volŭta~ and compares Italian ~volta~. The spelling ~voûte~ with a circumflex appears in the 17th century.
en.vriller: Formed from the noun ~vrille~ (“gimlet, tendril”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to bore like a gimlet, to twist in a spiral.” The noun descends from Latin ~vītīcula~ (“small vine shoot, tendril”), a diminutive of ~vītis~ (“vine”), by way of Vulgar Latin and Old French ~verille~ or ~veille~. How the ~r~ got into the modern form is poorly explained; the sources suggest either an inserted sound or the semantic influence of ~virer~ (“to turn”). The verb is used of a twisting motion, of a piercing noise, or of an aircraft spiralling down.
en.vrombir: Probably onomatopoeic, formed from ~vroum~, the sound of a motor. Both French and English Wiktionary give this origin without any older source language. The ending ~-ir~ then makes the sound into a verb, “to hum, to whirr,” used of engines, insects and anything that drones at a steady pitch.
en.vulcaniser:
~Vulcaniser~ has two separate histories. The older is learned, built from the name of the Roman god ~Vulcanus~ (or the French form ~Vulcain~), the god of fire and the forge. The TLFi records it in 1706 in the sense “to cuckold,” and in 1835 as ~se vulcaniser~, “to become like Vulcan the smith,” in Balzac.

The verb in use today is a borrowing from English ~to vulcanize~, recorded in 1827 in the sense “to subject to the action of fire” and then more specifically in Thomas Hancock's patent for treating rubber. French has ~volcaniser~ in 1847 and ~caoutchouc vulcanisé~ in 1848. The technical sense is to treat rubber by mixing it with sulfur so that it becomes insoluble and less sensitive to heat and light. The god's name also lies behind ~volcan~, so rubber workers and volcanoes share an ancestor, the Roman god of fire.
en.vulgariser: Formed from ~vulgaire~ and the suffix ~-iser~, a verb-forming ending. The adjective ~vulgaire~ comes from Latin ~vulgāris~ (“of the common people”), a derivative of ~vulgus~ (“the people”). To ~vulgariser~ is to make something, such as a technical subject, accessible to the general public. English ~vulgarize~ is a parallel formation.
en.végéter: A learned borrowing from Latin ~vegetāre~; the sources give no French intermediate and no deeper chain. The same Latin word family gave French ~végétal~, ~végétation~ and ~végétarien~, and English ~vegetate~ and ~vegetable~. French ~végéter~ can describe plants growing and, figuratively, a dull, stagnant life, much as English ~vegetate~ does.
en.véhiculer: ~Véhiculer~ was formed in French from the noun ~véhicule~ and the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense “to carry, to convey.” The noun is borrowed from Latin ~vehiculum~ (“means of transport, carriage, cart”), which is built on the Latin verb ~vehere~ (“to carry”). The meaning is first literal, transporting people or goods in a vehicle. It is extended to things that travel without a body: to ~véhiculer~ an idea, an image or a rumor is to act as the vehicle that carries it from one mind to another.
en.vénérer:
French ~vénérer~ is a borrowing from Latin ~venerārī~ (“to revere, to worship”). French Wiktionary derives the Latin verb from the genitive ~Veneris~ of ~Venus~. In Latin, ~venus~ was first a common noun meaning “charm, desire, love” before it named the goddess, and it is traced to the Proto-Indo-European root *~wenh₁-~ (“to desire, to strive for”), which also yields English ~wish~ and ~win~. The original sense of ~venerārī~ was therefore to seek the favor of a deity, to court the goodwill of a god.

In Latin the verb was a religious one: one ~veneratur~ the gods with prayers and offerings. It broadened to reverence for anyone worthy of deep respect, and French kept that range: ~vénérer~ a saint, a teacher, a memory. In modern speech it is often used with a hint of exaggeration, for a devotion that is more enthusiasm than worship. Related French words include ~vénération~ and ~vénérable~ and, from the same ~Venus~, ~vénérien~ (“venereal”) and ~vendredi~, the day of ~Veneris~.
en.vérifier:
From Medieval Latin ~verificare~ (“to make true, to prove true”), a compound of ~verus~ (“true”) and ~facere~ (“to make, to do”). Latin ~verus~ descends from Proto-Italic *~wēros~ and Proto-Indo-European *~weh₁ros~ (“true, trustworthy”). The same root gave German ~wahr~ (“true”) and English ~very~ (originally “true,” as in “the very man”), while the Italian and Spanish ~verificare~/~verificar~ are direct parallels.

The word is transparent once unpacked: to verify is, etymologically, “to make-true,” to establish that a thing is ~verus~. French inherited it as a learned term, keeping the bookish ~-ifier~ ending from ~facere~ found in a long series of verbs (~modifier~, ~clarifier~, ~justifier~). From the same ~verus~ comes a substantial family: ~vrai~ (the inherited, worn-down form of ~verus~), ~vérité~, ~véritable~, ~vraisemblable~, ~véridique~, and ~vérifiable~. Curiously, the everyday adverb ~voire~ (“indeed, even”) also descends from ~verus~ — a fossil of the Latin for “truly.” So ~vérifier~ and ~vrai~ are doublets of a kind, the learned and the popular reflexes of one Latin word for truth.
en.vétiller:
The verb ~vétiller~ (“to trifle, to fuss over unimportant things”) is probably derived from Middle French ~vette~ (“ribbon, stripe”) with the verbal suffix ~-iller~. ~Vette~ comes from Old French ~vete~ (“strap, band”), which goes back to Latin ~vitta~ (“ribbon, band”). Both Wiktionaries give the derivation from ~vette~ with a hedge, so it is a probable analysis rather than a documented one.

The development of the sense is a supposition too. French Wiktionary suggests that the original meaning was probably “to busy oneself with ribbons,” that is, with futile things. The ending ~-iller~ is the one found in ~sautiller~ (“to hop about”) and ~mordiller~ (“to nibble”), where it suggests small, repeated actions, which suits the idea of petty fuss. The family also includes the noun ~vétille~ (“trifle”) and the adjective ~vétilleux~ (“finicky, pernickety”).
en.vêler:
From Middle French ~vêler~ or ~veller~, from Old French ~veler~, a verb formed from ~veel~ (“calf”) with the ending ~-er~. Old French ~veel~ is also the source of modern ~veau~. It descends from Latin ~vitellus~ (“little calf”), the diminutive of ~vitulus~. Italian ~vitello~ comes from the same Latin word, and English ~veal~ was borrowed from Old French ~veel~.

The verb means to give birth to a calf, said of a cow. The verb is built on the name of the young animal itself. A more recent sense belongs to glaciology: a glacier ~vêle~ when a mass of ice breaks off its front into the sea as icebergs. This sense is attested from 1929, and English uses ~calve~ in the same way. The noun ~vêlage~ is the matching word for the birth.
en.vêtir:
From Old French ~vestir~, inherited from Latin ~vestīre~ (“to clothe, to dress”), a verb built on the noun ~vestis~ (“garment, clothing”). Latin ~vestis~ goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *~wes-~ (“to clothe”), which also yields English ~wear~ through Germanic. The verb has close relatives across the Romance languages: Italian ~vestire~ and Spanish ~vestir~ both preserve the Latin shape. French alone shows the old ~s~ in a different way, as the circumflex of ~vêtir~. In Old French the ~s~ was still pronounced before the ~t~, then fell silent, and the accent mark was left behind as a memorial.

The idea of putting on clothes spread in two directions. One path led to prestige: ~revêtir~ meant to dress again, then to clothe someone with a dignity, which is why a document is ~revêtu~ of a signature or a seal. The Latin compound ~investīre~ (“to clothe in, to confer an office by robing”) gave ~investir~, whose financial meaning came later. Another path led to the wardrobe itself. ~Vêtement~ is the garment, ~dévêtir~ undresses, and the Latin noun ~vestis~ lives on as ~veste~, ~vestiaire~ and ~travestir~, literally “to dress across,” that is, in the clothes of another. English borrowed ~vest~, ~invest~, ~divest~ and ~travesty~ from the same source.
en.warranter: ~Warranter~ comes from ~warrant~, which French borrowed from English: in 1671 for an order of arrest, and in 1836 for a receipt proving that goods are held in storage as security. The English word is itself, according to the TLFi, taken from a dialectal form of French ~garant~, attested in 1269. So the word went to England and came back. The verb, first found in 1874 in the Journal officiel, means to equip goods with a ~warrant~ and so pledge them as security for a debt.
en.yodler: Borrowed from German ~jodeln~, the verb for the alpine singing style that leaps between chest voice and falsetto. French adapted it to its first-conjugation ending ~-er~ and spelled the initial sound with ~y~. The word came into French with the Swiss and Tyrolean tradition it names.
en.yoyoter: Formed from ~yoyo~ with the verb ending ~-er~, with a ~t~ inserted between the vowel-final noun and the ending, as in ~clouter~ and ~biseauter~. This ~-t-~ has no meaning of its own: it is an epenthetic consonant that prevents a hiatus. The noun ~yoyo~ was borrowed from English ~yo-yo~, a trademark registered in 1931 and, according to French Wiktionary, taken from a Philippine language. The verb means to play with a yo-yo.
en.yoyotter: ~Yoyotter~ is formed from ~yoyo~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, a ~t~ appearing between the final vowel of the base and the ending. It is a familiar verb meaning “to be crazy, to lose one's mind.” The base ~yoyo~ is the toy, spelled ~yo-yo~ as a trademark registered in 1931, which French Wiktionary derives from Filipino, while English Wiktionary describes the French word as a borrowing from English ~yo-yo~. The figurative verb is a French coinage on the toy's name.
en.zapper: Borrowed from English ~zap~, with the French ending ~-er~. The English word began as an imitative sound of a sudden blow or shot, then came to mean “to destroy, to hit,” and, with the arrival of the television remote control, “to switch rapidly between channels.” French took over the channel-surfing sense first, and then widened it to figurative uses: to skip over something, to drop a subject, to forget. The noun ~zapping~ belongs to the same family and was borrowed with it.
en.zieuter: A slang verb formed from ~z'yeux~, a jocular plural of ~œil~ (“eye”), with the verb ending ~-er~. The ~z~ is the liaison sound that links the plural article to ~yeux~, here treated as part of the word. ~Œil~ comes from Latin ~oculus~ through Old French ~ueil~, and the plural ~yeux~ regularly represents the Latin accusative plural ~oculos~. ~Zieuter~ means to look at, to eye or ogle.
en.zigouiller: The origin of ~zigouiller~ is uncertain, and the sources give two accounts. One traces it to the Poitevin-Saintongeais ~zigue-zigue~ (“bad knife”) combined with ~gouille~ in the sense of ~gueule~ (“mouth”). The other derives it from the onomatopoeia ~zik~, which expresses a sudden movement and also appears in ~zigzag~. English Wiktionary adds that it was first a dialect word meaning to cut something with a bad knife, ultimately onomatopoeic.
en.zigzaguer: ~Zigzaguer~ is formed from the noun ~zigzag~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, and means “to zigzag.” The noun is possibly a borrowing from a Germanic language, though that is only suggested. French spelled it ~ziczac~ until 1740, and ~zig-zag~ with a hyphen also appears in the seventeenth century. Early uses name objects as well as shapes, including an extendable wooden tool.
en.zinguer: Formed from ~zinc~ + ~-er~, the ending that turns a noun into a first-conjugation verb, here in the sense “to provide with N”: ~zinguer~ is to cover or galvanize something with zinc. The noun ~zinc~ was borrowed from German ~Zink~. (A slang ~zinc~, a clipping of ~zincou~, itself a back-slang form of ~cousin~, is a separate word.) The suffix ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~, the infinitive ending of the first conjugation.
en.zinzinuler: ~Zinzinuler~ comes from Latin ~zinzilulare~ (“to twitter,” said of certain birds), a word formed by onomatopoeia. The sound of the Latin verb imitates the high, repeated notes of small birds, and French kept the imitative character in its reshaped form. The modern verb means to warble or chirp, and it is used chiefly of birds and, by extension, of any thin, trilling sound.
en.zipper: ~Zipper~ is borrowed from English ~zip~. French Wiktionary takes ~zip~ in the sense of the compressed file format, so to ~zipper~ a file is to compress it. The English word received the French first-conjugation ending ~-er~, the default ending for new verbs, as in ~coder~, so the verb conjugates like any regular verb in ~-er~.
en.zoner: ~Zoner~ has two separate sources, according to French Wiktionary. The transitive verb is a denominal built on ~zone~ + ~-er~, while the intransitive one, “to wander around, to sleep rough”, comes from the noun ~zonard~. ~Zone~ was borrowed from Latin ~zona~ (“belt, zone”). Its sense “poor quarter” originally named the strip of land outside the Thiers fortifications of Paris, a space in theory closed to building and occupied by shantytowns in the early twentieth century. A ~zonard~ was thus someone from that ~zone~, and the verb followed the people.
en.zoomer: ~Zoomer~ is formed from the noun ~zoom~ with the verbal ending ~-er~, the usual way French adapts English loans. It means to zoom in on an image or a view. The identically spelled noun ~zoomer~ (a member of Generation Z) is a different word: it was coined by analogy with ~boomer~, with the Z of “generation Z” replacing the B.
en.zouker: Formed from the noun ~zouk~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, the usual way French turns a noun into a verb: to ~zouker~ is to dance the zouk. French Wiktionary traces ~zouk~ to a Moroccan Arabic word for “buttocks,” a reference to the hip movements of the dancer, but flags that claim as still lacking a citation, so it should be treated as unverified. The ending ~-er~ comes from the Latin infinitive ending ~-are~ and is the default for new verbs.
en.zozoter: An onomatopoeia derived from ~zézayer~ (“to lisp”). Both verbs imitate the sound of the speech defect they name, the hissing ~z~ replacing the ~s~ and ~ch~ sounds. French Wiktionary cites a contemporary printed source, the satirical weekly ~Le Triboulet~, for the word.
en.zyeuter: ~Zyeuter~ is a slang verb built from ~z'yeux~, a playful plural of ~œil~ (“eye”), with the verb ending ~-er~. The ~z~ is the liaison sound of ~les yeux~, pronounced as if ~lez-yeux~, which the slang speaker takes as part of the word. The noun ~œil~ comes from Latin ~oculus~, and its irregular plural ~yeux~ is the regular outcome of the Latin accusative plural ~oculōs~. The verb means to eye, ogle or squint at.
en.zébrer: The verb comes from the noun ~zèbre~ (“zebra”), by comparison with the animal's stripes. To ~zébrer~ a surface is to mark it with lines, as if it had been given a zebra's coat. The sources name no older source language or intermediate form, so the story is simply that of a noun used as a picture: the striped animal supplied the verb for striping.
en.zézayer: An onomatopoeic formation, made by repeating the sound [z]. The verb imitates the way a person who lisps pronounces certain consonants, and it means “to lisp, to slur.” There is no older source word behind it: the sound itself is the origin.
en.ânonner: Formed from ~ânon~ (“young donkey”) + ~-er~, the ending that turns a noun into a first-conjugation verb. The noun ~ânon~ is itself a derivative of ~âne~ (“donkey”) with the diminutive suffix ~-on~. The verb means to stumble through a text or drone on, reading or reciting haltingly and without expression.
en.ébahir:
From Old French ~esbahir~ (also ~esbaier~), which en.Wiktionary traces to a Vulgar Latin *~exbatāre~, itself from Early Medieval Latin ~batāre~. French Wiktionary gives a slightly different account: the Old French verb is built on ~béer~ with the prefix ~é-~, and its conjugation changed under the influence of the adjective ~baif~ (“astonished, stunned”). Either way, the verb belongs to the family of words that picture a mouth hanging open.

The sources agree on the shape of the story but not on every link, so the exact route from ~batāre~ to ~béer~ is better left open. What is clear is the sense: in French, ~ébahir~ means to leave someone stunned, so struck with wonder or surprise that they are speechless. It is used most often in the past participle, ~ébahi~, “dumbfounded,” as in a crowd watching a spectacle with ~ébahissement~ (“amazement”). The verb is thus a close relative of ~béer~, which survives in the fixed phrase ~bouche bée~ (“open-mouthed”).
en.ébarber: A parasynthetic verb, built at once from the prefix ~é-~, the noun ~barbe~ (“beard”) and the suffix ~-er~. The prefix ~é-~ (from Latin ~ex-~, “out of, away from”) carries the idea of removal, so ~ébarber~ means, in principle, to take off a ~barbe~, which fits its senses of shaving and trimming. ~Barbe~ is inherited from Latin ~barba~, itself from Proto-Italic *~farðā~, from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰardʰeh₂~ (“beard”).
en.ébattre: From Old French ~esbatre~, formed from the prefix ~es-~ (modern ~é-~) and ~batre~, the ancestor of ~battre~ (“to beat”). The base ~battre~ comes from Latin ~battuere~, a verb almost certainly borrowed from Gaulish. Today the verb survives mostly in the reflexive ~s'ébattre~, “to frolic.” The prefix does not simply take something away here, and the sources give no story for how the sense of striking became one of playing about, so the meaning is best taken as it stands.
en.ébaucher: ~Ébaucher~ goes back to Middle French ~esbaucher~, “to rough-hew”, said of beams. The two Wiktionaries differ on the root. French Wiktionary derives it from Old French ~bauch~ (“beam”), a Germanic borrowing (compare German ~Balken~). English Wiktionary treats ~esbaucher~ as an alteration, under the influence of ~bauche~ (“beam”), of Old French ~esbosquier~, from ~es-~ + ~bosc~ (“wood”), from Frankish *~bosk~. Either way the sense is roughing out timber, later a sketch or draft.
en.ébaudir: ~Ébaudir~ comes from Old French ~esbaudir~ (also ~esbaldir~), analyzed as the prefix ~é-~ and ~baudir~, and means to fill with joy. The base ~baudir~ is from Old French ~baudir~ or ~baldir~, from Frankish *~baldijan~, from Proto-Germanic *~balþaz~ (“bold”), and it is related to ~baud~ (“merry”). Old English ~bieldan~ (“to embolden”) is a cognate. The “bold” of the root became “cheerful” in French.
en.ébavurer: A parasynthetic formation: the noun ~bavure~ takes the prefix ~é-~, which here marks removal, and the verbal ending ~-er~, giving “to remove the ~bavure~,” that is, to deburr. The noun is itself derived from the verb ~baver~ (“to drool”) and the suffix ~-ure~. Both ~é-~ and ~-er~ are ordinary French building blocks, so the verb is a transparent coinage rather than an inherited word.
en.ébiseler: Formed from ~biseau~ with the prefix ~é-~, which Littré explains as a form of the old prefix ~es-~. To ~ébiseler~ is to cut something to a bevel, and the dictionaries also record a technical sense, giving a conical shape to a hole. The TLFi quotes a 1903 text on copper founding that describes notching a board and bevelling its edge to give the outer profile of a bell. The sources do not trace the origin of ~biseau~ itself, so the trail stops there.
en.éblouir:
French ~éblouir~ comes from Old French ~esbloir~ and ~esbleuir~ (“to dazzle”). English Wiktionary traces these to a Vulgar Latin *~exblaudō~, made of ~ex-~ and *~blaudō~ (“to overwhelm, to make weak”), a verb taken from Frankish *~blōthijan~. That Frankish verb comes from Proto-Germanic *~blauþijaną~ (“to make weak, soften”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~bʰlaw-~ (“weak, timid”). Germanic cousins include Old High German ~blōdi~ (“feeble”), Old English ~blēaþ~ (“timid, gentle”) and Danish ~blød~ (“soft”). The Latin step is attested only by reconstruction.

The path from weakness to dazzle is plausible, since a blinding light overpowers the sight, though the sources do not spell out the development. French then extended the verb from the eyes to the mind, to impress or amaze, and ~éblouissant~ now praises brilliance of any kind. German ~blöde~, from the same family as ~blōdi~, has moved in the other direction: it now means “silly” or “stupid,” a long way from soft or weak. Beyond the French family ~éblouissement~, ~éblouissant~, the verb has no close French relatives.
en.éborgner: ~Éborgner~ is formed from ~borgne~ (“one-eyed”) with the prefix ~é-~, which expresses removal, and the verb ending ~-er~. It therefore means to deprive someone of an eye, to leave them ~borgne~. The base is of uncertain origin. French Wiktionary suggests a pre-Latin ~borna~ (“hole, cavity”), perhaps tied to an Indo-European root meaning “to cut, to pierce” that also gave Latin ~forāre~, while English Wiktionary derives it from a Vulgar Latin *~bornium~. The two accounts differ, so the deeper history of ~borgne~ remains open.
en.ébouillanter: Formed from ~bouillant~ with the prefix ~é-~ and the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to treat with something boiling.” French Wiktionary explains ~bouillant~ as the present participle of ~bouillir~ (“to boil”), which comes from Latin ~bullire~ (“to bubble”). The prefix ~é-~ goes back to Latin ~ex-~ (“out of”) through Old French ~es-~, though here it shows no clear sense of removal. The verb means to scald, by pouring boiling water over something or dipping it in.
en.ébouler:
From Old French ~esboeler~ (“to disembowel, to take out the entrails”), formed on ~bouel~ (“entrail”), which comes from Latin ~botellus~ (“small sausage, gut”), a diminutive of ~botulus~ (“sausage”). The prefix is the old ~es-~ (modern ~é-~), here meaning removal: to take the guts out. So the chain runs from a Latin word for a little sausage, through the Old French word for an intestine, to a verb of butchery.

The modern sense is quite different: to crumble, collapse or fall down in a heap, as a wall, a cliff or a slope does, and the pronominal ~s'ébouler~ is the usual form. The evidence consulted does not show how “to disembowel” turned into “to collapse,” so no story is offered here. The root family is clearer. Old French ~bouel~ gave modern ~boyau~ and English ~bowel~, both from the same Latin source, and the noun ~éboulement~ (“landslide, cave-in”) is derived from the verb.
en.ébourgeonner: Formed from ~bourgeon~ (“bud”) with the prefix ~é-~, which expresses removal, and the verb ending ~-er~: to take off the superfluous buds of a plant. ~Bourgeon~ comes from Old French ~bourjon~, from Vulgar Latin *~burriō~, from Late Latin ~burra~, the source of French ~bourre~ (“fluff”). French Wiktionary says the word evoked something hairy, and adds that the sense of spots on the face appears around 1270.
en.ébouriffer: The origin of ~ébouriffer~ is obscure. The TLFi probably links it, like Provençal ~esbourrifa~ (“ruffled, scattered”), to Late Latin ~burra~, the source of French ~bourre~ (“fluff, stuffing”), but it admits that the way the word was formed remains unclear. One possible starting point is Provençal ~esbourrassa~ (“to drag by the hair, to rough up”), altered under the influence of ~rifla~. The verb is first seen in a participle in 1671, in a line of Madame de Grignan, and in 1842 it means “to rumple someone's hair.” Figurative senses followed: “agitated” in 1762, then “to astonish” before 1778, in Rousseau.
en.ébourrer: Formed from ~bourre~ with the prefix ~é-~ (removal) and the ending ~-er~: to strip the hair from a hide. ~Bourre~ was inherited from Old French ~boure~ or ~borre~, from Late Latin ~burra~ (“coarse fabric”). The prefix ~é-~ comes from Latin ~ex-~ (“out of, away from”), which gives the sense of taking something away.
en.ébouter: ~Ébouter~ is built on the noun ~bout~ (“end”), with the prefix ~é-~ and the ending ~-er~ added together. The prefix ~é-~ expresses removal, so the verb means to cut off the end of something. The noun ~bout~ is a back-formation from the older verb ~bouter~ (“to strike, push”), of Germanic origin; the idea of a push explains the sense “tip, growing end.”
en.ébrancher: ~Ébrancher~ is formed from ~branche~ with the prefix ~é-~ (“out, away”) and the ending ~-er~, and means to strip a tree of its branches. Its construction matches that of ~plumer~ (“to pluck the feathers”). ~Branche~ comes from Late Latin ~branca~ (“paw”), which in Gallo-Romance took the sense “branch,” perhaps under the influence of ~bras~ (“arm”). English Wiktionary adds that ~branca~ is possibly of Gaulish origin.
en.ébranler: Formed from the prefix ~é-~ (Old French ~es-~, from Latin ~ex-~, “out of”) and ~branler~ (“to shake”), so the verb means to set something shaking, then to shake its footing. The base is an old contraction of Old French ~brandeler~ (“to wobble”), built on ~brant~ (“sword blade”). French Wiktionary traces ~brant~ to a Germanic ~brand~ (“firebrand”), while English Wiktionary routes it through Vulgar Latin *~brandus~ and Frankish *~brand~ (“sword”). The same root gives ~brandir~ and ~brandon~. Figuratively, ~ébranler~ is used of beliefs, confidence and governments as readily as of walls.
en.ébraser: The origin is obscure, and the TLFi offers only a guess. The verb is first recorded in 1636, in Monet, for widening a window or door on all sides to admit more light, after ~embraser~ appeared in 1567. It may come from ~embraser~ with the prefix ~é-~ replacing ~em-~, either in the sense “to light up”, since an ~embrasure~ lets more light into a room, or in the sense “to set fire”, through the opening where a cannon is aimed. Littré links it to ~embrasure~, and notes that Old French ~esbraser~ meant “to set ablaze”, which does not fit. Today it is an architectural term meaning to widen the opening of a door or window obliquely inward.
en.ébrouer:
From Old French ~esbroer~, with the form ~esbrouer~ attested in 1390. The origin is not settled. The favored account is that it is probably a borrowing from Middle Dutch ~broeyen~ (“to scald”), from Proto-Germanic *~brōaną~ (“to singe; to brew”). A second possibility, mentioned by French Wiktionary, is a derivation from ~brou~ with the privative prefix ~é-~.

If the Dutch account is right, the first sense was to scald or to dip cloth in water for cleaning. French Wiktionary then proposes a second thread, “to sneeze to clear the nostrils,” probably the same word with a shift toward “to foam,” since washing involves rinsing off suds. That sense would have passed to people and animals as “to remove the froth from the mouth,” and then to animals shaking themselves dry, whence the dominant modern sense of shaking and stirring. The Dutch verb is also linked to ~brouet~ in French and to English ~brew~. Today the verb is mostly reflexive: a horse or a wet dog ~s'ébroue~.
en.ébruiter: Formed from ~bruit~ (“noise”) with the prefix ~é-~ (from Latin ~ex-~, “out”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, so “to make noise out into the world,” that is, to spread a piece of news. The noun ~bruit~ is a back-formation from the verb ~bruire~ (“to roar”), which goes back to a Latin word for bellowing altered by association with ~braire~.
en.ébrécher: Formed from the noun ~brèche~ with the prefix ~é-~ and the verb ending ~-er~ together, so ~ébrécher~ means to make a ~brèche~, a chip or notch, in something. English Wiktionary adds that it passed through Middle French ~ebrecher~ and Old French ~esbrechier~. The noun ~brèche~ comes from Frankish *~breka~ (“break, breach”), from Proto-Germanic *~brekō~, from the Indo-European root *~bʰreg-~ (“to break”). It is a cognate of English ~break~ and German ~brechen~.
en.écacher: ~Écacher~ comes from Old French ~escachier~ (“to crush”). French Wiktionary analyses it as the prefix ~é-~, from Old French ~es-~ and Latin ~ex-~ (“out”), joined to the verb ~cacher~. The modern verb keeps the idea of crushing, which gives its present sense “to flatten.” Its history is wholly French apart from the Latin prefix.
en.écailler: ~Écailler~ is formed from the noun ~écaille~ (“scale, shell”) with the verb ending ~-er~, in the sense “to deal with the N.” It covers removing the scales from a fish and, by the same logic, opening an oyster. The noun comes from Old French ~escaille~, from Old Frankish *~skalja~, from Proto-Germanic *~skaljō~ (“scale, shell, husk”), an origin shared with English ~shell~, Dutch ~schil~ and German ~Schale~. Its Proto-Indo-European root is given as *~(s)kelH-~ (“to cut, to split”). French ~écale~ (“husk”) is a doublet, and Italian ~scaglia~ is a cognate.
en.écaler: Formed from ~écale~ (“shell, husk”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, meaning to remove the shell of a nut or an egg. ~Écale~ is inherited from Old French ~escale~, from Frankish *~skala~, and is a doublet of ~écaille~ (“scale”), which shares the same ultimate source. The verb is thus a close relative of the word for a fish's scale, both going back to the same Germanic word.
en.écanguer: Formed from the noun ~écang~ with the verb ending ~-er~, so “to scutch,” that is, to beat hemp or flax to strip off the woody part of the stalk. According to the FEW, the noun ~écang~ is a borrowing from Old Low Frankish *~swank~ (“swing, movement”), whence Dutch ~zwang~ (“usage, vogue”). The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~ and is French’s default way of making a verb from a noun.
en.écarquiller: An alteration of ~équartiller~, a verb formed on ~quart~ (“fourth”) in the sense of “to cut in four”, and so related to ~écarteler~ (“to quarter”). ~Quart~ comes from Latin ~quartus~ (“fourth”) or from its neuter ~quartum~. Today ~écarquiller~ is used above all of the eyes, which one opens wide.
en.écarteler:
From Old French ~esquarterer~, formed from ~es-~ (the ancestor of ~é-~), the noun ~quarter~ and the ending ~-er~, with the sense “to cut into quarters.” The modern form shows a dissimilation: the expected *~écarterer~ would have had two ~r~ sounds in its last syllables, and the second one was replaced by ~l~, as in the ending ~-eler~. The verb is related to ~quartier~ (“quarter”) and, according to the pointers in fr.Wiktionary, to ~écarter~.

The literal meaning was to divide a body or a thing into four parts. That is why ~écarteler~ names the old punishment of drawing and quartering, in which a condemned person was torn apart, and also a term of heraldry, where it means to divide a shield into four sections. Today it also carries the figurative sense of being torn between conflicting demands. The ~quart~ at the heart of the verb comes from Latin ~quartus~ (“fourth”), so the whole family is built on the number four.
en.écarter:
The origin of ~écarter~ is debated. French Wiktionary derives the verb of separation from a Latin *~exquartāre~, built on ~quartus~ (“fourth, quarter”) — to ~écarter~ being, on this view, originally to quarter or divide; this ~quartus~ traces back through ~quattuor~ (“four”) to PIE *~kʷetwóres~. The TLFi, however, resists that account, and a distinct ~écarter~ of the card table — “to discard” — is more securely analyzed as ~é-~ + ~carte~ (“card”) + ~-er~, attested from 1611. The two senses are best kept apart rather than forced into one chain.

Whatever the precise root, the lived meaning is to push apart, to set aside, to keep at a distance — ~écarter~ les bras (to spread the arms), ~écarter~ un danger, ~écarter~ une hypothèse. The past participle ~écarté~ names something remote or out of the way. From the same field come ~écart~ (“gap, deviation”), ~écartement~ (“spacing”) and the noun ~écarté~ for the old card game played by discarding.
en.échafauder: ~Échafauder~ is formed from ~échafaud~ with the verb ending ~-er~, and means to put up scaffolding. The noun is an alteration, after ~échelle~ or ~échasse~, of Old French ~chafaud~. For that word French Wiktionary proposes a crossing of Latin ~fala~ (“wooden defensive tower”) with ~catasta~, from Greek ~katástasis~ (“platform where slaves were displayed for sale”), while English Wiktionary gives Greek ~katá-~ plus Latin ~fala~. Both reach a Late Latin form *~catafalicum~, which also gave ~catafalque~, so the two words are doublets. The noun is attested from the late 13th century as ~escaffaus~ (“platform for spectators”).
en.échalasser: The verb is a denominal of ~échalas~ (“stake, vine prop”) with the ending ~-er~, so it means to furnish with stakes. ~Échalas~ reached modern French from Old French forms such as ~eschalaz~ and ~escharat~ (1158), going back to a Vulgar Latin form *~caracium~, from Latin ~characias~ and ultimately Ancient Greek ~χάραξ~ (“reed”). The word replaced an older French term, ~paisseau~.
en.échancrer: Formed with the prefix ~é-~ on ~chancrer~, itself from ~chancre~ (“canker, ulcer”), so literally “to bite into as a canker does.” The sense is to cut a crescent-shaped notch into an edge. The noun ~chancre~ goes back to Latin ~cancer~ (“crab”), which also gave English cancer. The prefix ~é-~, from Latin ~ex-~, marks what is taken out of the edge.
en.échanger:
A French compound: the prefix ~é-~ (from Latin ~ex-~, here intensive) joined to ~changer~ (“to change”). The base ~changer~ comes from Late Latin ~cambiāre~ (“to barter, to exchange”), a verb of Gaulish origin, from Proto-Celtic *~kambos~ (“crooked, bent”) and ultimately the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)kh₂emb-~ (“to bend”). Italian ~cambiare~ and Spanish ~cambiar~ are its Romance cousins, and English borrowed the same Gaulish word through Old French as ~change~ and ~exchange~.

The Celtic root meant “bent, crooked,” and the path of meaning ran from “to turn” to “to swap one thing for another” — a fitting image, since an exchange turns goods around between two hands. ~Cambiāre~ is one of the rare everyday Romance verbs that the Romans took from the Gauls rather than from their own Latin stock. The ~é-~ prefix in ~échanger~ underscores the mutual, two-way swap. From the same root French keeps a busy family — ~changer~, ~change~, ~changement~, ~échange~, ~rechange~, ~interchanger~, and the financial ~changeur~ — all turning, in their way, on the idea of exchange.
en.échantillonner: The verb is formed from ~échantillon~ (“sample”) and the ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary traces the noun to Old French ~eschantillon~ and points to ~chantignole~ and ~échantignole~. English Wiktionary gives a fuller chain: Old French ~eschandillon~ (“standard”), from ~eschandiller~ (“to verify the measures of merchants”), a word it calls mainly Lyonnais, from Latin ~scandaculum~ (“ladder”), from ~scandere~ (“to climb”). So a verb about taking samples may go back, by this account, to a Latin word for climbing.
en.échapper:
From Old French ~escaper~, ~eschaper~ (attested around 1100), from Vulgar Latin *~excappare~, a verb built from the prefix ~ex-~ (“out of”) and Late Latin ~cappa~ (“cape, hooded cloak”). The image is vivid: to ~excappare~ was to slip out of one's cloak, leaving it in a pursuer's grasping hands. Cognate with Spanish and Portuguese ~escapar~, Catalan ~escapar~, Italian ~scappare~, and Romanian ~scăpa~, and with the English borrowing ~escape~.

The same ~cappa~ that lies behind ~échapper~ is one of Latin's most productive garments: it gave French ~chape~, ~chapeau~, ~chaperon~, and ~cape~, and through Italian even ~capot~. Old French ~escaper~ had a doublet ~eschaper~ that hardened into Modern French ~échapper~, while the un-prefixed family kept the cloak's literal sense. A curious relative survives in ~réchapper~ (“to come through, to survive”), and the noun ~échappatoire~ (“a way out, a loophole”) still carries the original gesture of wriggling free. English preserves the cloak-image twice over: ~escape~ from the French verb, and the rarer ~escapade~, a borrowing through Italian and Spanish, for a reckless break for freedom.
en.échardonner: Formed from the noun ~chardon~ (“thistle”) with the prefix ~é-~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so “to remove thistles,” as from a field. The noun comes from Late Latin ~cardō~, ~cardōnis~, an alteration of Classical Latin ~carduus~ (“thistle”), and is a doublet of ~cardon~. The prefix ~é-~ descends from Old French ~es-~, from Latin ~ex-~ (“out of, away from”), and here marks removal. The verb ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~.
en.écharner: The TLFi derives ~écharner~ from ~chair~ (“flesh,” anciently ~charn~) with the privative prefix ~é-~ and the ending ~-er~, so the verb literally means to take the flesh off. Its relatives are old: ~décharné~ (“fleshless, gaunt”) appears in the early 13th century, and an Old French ~escharner~ is found in the 14th. The sense now in use belongs to leatherwork and is dated 1680, when the verb meant to strip a hide of the flesh and fat still clinging to it.
en.écharper: Formed from the Old French verb ~charpir~ and the prefix ~é-~ (from Latin ~ex-~, “out of, away from”). The prefix gives the sense of separating or tearing apart, so ~écharper~ means to cut or tear something into pieces. The base ~charpir~ is itself Old French, and the sources say no more about its origin.
en.échauder:
From Old French ~eschauder~ or ~eschalder~, inherited from Late Latin ~excaldāre~ (“to put in hot water”), a verb built from ~ex-~ and ~caldus~ (“hot”), a contracted form of the earlier ~calidus~. The spelling ~eschalder~ keeps the ~l~ that later turned into the ~u~ of ~eschauder~, a common change in the history of French. French also has the variant ~échauler~, and ~échauder~ is a form of it.

Latin ~caldus~ lies behind French ~chaud~ (“hot”) and ~chaudière~ (“boiler”), and ~échauffer~ is a close relative. English ~scald~ descends from the same Late Latin verb, by way of Norman French. Modern ~échauder~ means “to scald” by plunging something in boiling water and, figuratively, to burn someone through a bitter experience, as in the proverb ~chat échaudé craint l'eau froide~ (“a scalded cat fears cold water”).
en.échauffer:
French ~échauffer~ comes from Middle French ~eschauffer~, from Old French ~eschaufer~ or ~eschalfer~. These go back to a Vulgar Latin verb *~excalfāre~, from Latin ~excalefacere~, built from the prefix ~ex-~ and ~calefacere~ (“to make warm”). The family has a close relative in ~échauder~ (“to scald”), and English ~scald~ is a cognate of that verb.

The core sense of ~échauffer~ is physical: to make something hot, or to warm a body. The verb also carries the figurative senses “to excite” and “to incite”: ~échauffer les esprits~ (“to stir tempers up”) and ~s'échauffer~ in a quarrel (“to grow heated”). Athletes use the reflexive form for warming up before a match, and the noun ~échauffement~ names that warm-up.
en.échelonner: Formed from the noun ~échelon~ and the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun is in turn an Old French ~eschelon~ built on ~échelle~ (“ladder”) with the suffix ~-on~, so an ~échelon~ is a “little ladder,” a rung. The verb began in military language: to ~échelonner~ troops was to arrange them in successive lines, one behind another, like the rungs of a ladder. The idea of regular steps then spread to anything set out in stages, such as payments, holidays or tasks spaced over time. English ~echelon~ is a borrowing of the French noun.
en.écheniller: ~Écheniller~ is formed from the noun ~chenille~ (“caterpillar”) with the prefix ~é-~ (“away, out”) and the ending ~-er~: to remove caterpillars from a tree or plant, and by extension to rid something of whatever harms it. The noun ~chenille~ is inherited from Latin ~canīcula~ (“little dog”), apparently because of the look of a caterpillar's head. It is a doublet of ~canicule~, the “dog days” of summer.
en.écher: ~Écher~ is a variant spelling of ~escher~, which is formed from the noun ~esche~ (“bait”) and the verb ending ~-er~: to ~escher~ a hook is to put bait on it. The noun comes from Latin ~esca~ (“food,” then “bait”). French Wiktionary adds that ~esche~ first named the small wood used to start a fire, and recovered its Latin sense of bait around the thirteenth century. The suffix ~-er~ makes a verb meaning “provide with N,” so a hook that is ~eschée~ is simply one fitted with its bait.
en.écheveler:
From Old French ~escheveler~, formed from ~chevel~ (“hair”) with the prefix ~es-~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The Old French ~chevel~ is the ancestor of modern ~cheveu~, which descends from Latin ~capillus~ (“hair”). The prefix ~es-~ comes from Latin ~ex-~ (“out of”), here giving the sense of undoing the arrangement of the hair. The verb therefore means to tousle or disarrange someone's hair.

The family is large. ~Cheveu~ and ~chevelure~ are the inherited words, while ~capillaire~ is the learned one taken straight from Latin. The past participle became an adjective, ~échevelé~ (“with tousled hair”, and by extension “wild, frenzied”). Spanish ~cabello~ and Italian ~capello~ are cousins of ~cheveu~. English also owes a word to the same Old French pattern: ~dishevel~ comes from the related Old French ~descheveler~.
en.échiner:
Formed in French from ~échine~ (“spine, back”) and the verbal ending ~-er~, perhaps under the influence of ~eschigner~ and ~rechigner~, which is how French Wiktionary hedges it. The noun ~échine~ comes from Old French ~eschine~, from Frankish *~skīna~, a word for a long thin bone such as the shinbone. Its cousins include Old High German ~scina~ and German ~Schienbein~ (“tibia”), and English ~shin~ is a relative from the same Germanic stock.

The verb means to break the back of someone or something, and the reflexive ~s'échiner~ means to wear oneself out, to toil till one's back aches. The noun also lives on in the idiom ~avoir l'échine souple~ (“to be servile”). Do not confuse it with the architectural term ~échine~ (the rounded molding under a Doric capital), which is a different word, borrowed from Latin ~echinus~ and Greek ~ekhīnos~ (“sea urchin”).
en.échoir: From Old French ~escheoir~, inherited from Vulgar Latin *~excadēre~ (“to fall out”), which combines Latin ~ex-~ (“out”) with ~cadere~ (“to fall”). French Wiktionary gives the same analysis in French terms: the prefix ~é-~ (“to take away”) added to ~choir~, the descendant of ~cadere~. The meaning moved from “to fall out” to “to fall to someone” and “to fall due,” which is how ~échoir~ is used of deadlines and payments. The noun ~échéance~ (“due date”) belongs to the family, as do ~choir~ and ~déchoir~, all from the Latin ~cadere~ that also gave Italian ~cadere~ and Spanish ~caer~.
en.échopper: ~Échopper~ is formed from the noun ~échoppe~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. An ~échoppe~ was also a pointed steel tool, a gravers' chisel, and the verb means to work with it, hence “to engrave with a chisel.” The tool name is generally traced to Old French ~eschaupre~ or ~eschalpre~, from Latin ~scalprum~ (“chisel, engraving tool”), the same source as English ~scalpel~. The identically spelled ~échoppe~ meaning “stall” is a different word, from Middle Dutch ~schoppe~, cognate with English ~shop~, and it is not the base here.
en.échouer:
The origin of ~échouer~ is famously obscure, and the sources offer no settled answer. The verb appears around 1559 of galleys run aground, takes the nautical sense “to touch bottom and stop” by 1573, and the figurative “to fail” by 1660. Several competing accounts circulate, none accepted as certain: a derivation from Latin ~cautes~ (“reef”), a variant of ~échoir~, a reshaping of Old French forms of ~escourre~ (“to shake,” from Latin ~excutere~), a development from Latin ~exaquare~ (“to drain dry”), or a shift from ~eschiver~ (“to dodge, slip sideways”). Each runs into phonetic or chronological trouble, so the TLFi leaves the question open.

Whatever its source, the meaning evolved cleanly from the concrete to the abstract: a ship that ran onto a shoal and could go no further became the model for any enterprise that ~échoue~ — that founders, fails, falls through. French keeps the maritime sense alive in ~échouage~ and ~échouement~, while ~déchouer~ means to refloat a stranded vessel.
en.écimer: Formed from ~cime~ (“top”) with the prefix ~é-~ (from Latin ~ex-~, “out, away”) and the ending ~-er~: to cut off the top of a tree or plant, to pollard. The noun ~cime~ is inherited from Old French ~cime~, from Latin ~cȳma~ (“cabbage sprout”), a borrowing from Greek ~κῦμα~ (“swelling”). It is a doublet of ~cyme~, the same Latin word borrowed again as a learned term.
en.éclabousser:
The form ~éclabousser~ is dated to 1660 in French Wiktionary, which explains it as a reshaping of Middle French ~esclabocher~ under the influence of the noun ~esclabousseure~. English Wiktionary gives a different route: Middle French ~esclabousser~ as a variant of Old French ~esclabo(u)ter~, probably built from an onomatopoeic root plus ~bouter~ (“to strike”). The two accounts differ on the exact chain, so the origin of the word is uncertain.

Whichever account is right, the sense is the same: to make liquid or mud fly in drops. The noun ~éclaboussure~ is its everyday companion. The ~bouter~ that one account proposes is an old verb for “to strike, to push”; it survives in ~débouter~ (“to dismiss a legal claim”) and in ~bouton~. Words of this expressive, sound-imitating kind often resist a tidy pedigree, which is why this entry hedges instead of naming one source.
en.éclaircir: The sources disagree. French Wiktionary derives it from ~claircir~ with the prefix ~é-~, where ~claircir~ comes from ~clair~ (“clear, bright”). English Wiktionary instead gives Late Latin *~exclāricīre~, from Latin ~clāricāre~ (“to make clear”). Either way the prefix ~é-~, from Latin ~ex-~, intensifies the sense, and the base is the idea of clearness. The verb means to make or become brighter, as when the sky clears, and then to make an idea clear, or to solve a mystery.
en.éclairer:
From Old French ~esclairier~, from Latin ~exclārāre~ (“to light up, make bright”), a compound of ~ex-~ (intensive) and the verb ~clārāre~, from the adjective ~clārus~ (“clear, bright, loud”). Latin ~clārus~ traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~kelh₁-~ (“to call, to shout”) — and the link between sound and light is the surprising heart of this word, the spreading of a cry and the spreading of brightness imagined as one. From the same root come ~clamare~ and, in English, ~claim~, ~clear~, and ~declare~.

The earliest French attestations, around the year 980, are of weather: the sky ~esclaire~ when it lightens or flashes. From “to flash, to grow bright” the verb settled into its modern senses — to give light to a room, to illuminate a path, and figuratively to enlighten the mind, to ~éclairer~ a difficult question. The noun ~éclair~ (“flash of lightning,” and hence the glazed pastry, supposedly eaten in a flash) belongs to the same family, as do ~éclaircir~ (“to clarify”), ~clair~, ~clarté~, and ~déclarer~. The verb’s whole career runs along the double track of its root: light that shines and a voice that carries.
en.éclater:
From Old French ~esclater~ (« to burst, splinter, » attested before 1150), from Frankish *~slaitan~ (« to split, tear »), from Proto-Germanic *~slītaną~ (« to tear, slit »). The Germanic line is reconstructed, the dictionaries marking those forms unattested, with the TLFi as the etymology's chief authority. Romance siblings of the Old French form survive in Spanish ~estallar~ and Catalan ~esclatar~, all turning on a core idea of bursting apart.

The semantic core is « to fly into pieces, » and French radiates it in every direction: glass ~éclate~ (« shatters »), thunder and laughter ~éclate~ (« breaks out loud »), a war or a scandal ~éclate~ (« erupts »), and colloquially « s'~éclater~ » means to have a blast. From the same base come the noun ~éclat~ (« a shard, a burst, brilliance »), ~éclatant~ (« dazzling »), and ~éclaté~ (« exploded, » as of a diagram). The journey from a Germanic verb of « tearing » to the French vocabulary of brilliance is a neat case of a violent image — bursting — softening into the language of splendor and radiance.
en.éclipser: ~Éclipser~ is formed from the noun ~éclipse~ with the verbal ending ~-er~: to cause an eclipse, and so figuratively to outshine or overshadow. The noun comes from Latin ~eclipsis~, from Ancient Greek ~ékleipsis~, which derives from ~ekleípō~ (“to abandon”), made of ~ek~ (“out of”) and ~leípō~ (“to leave”). French Wiktionary adds that the ancients believed the heavenly bodies briefly dropped out of the celestial vault during an eclipse.
en.éclisser:
Traced to ~esclicier~ (“to burst, to split”), a form attested in Old French and Middle French, which French Wiktionary derives from Old Low Frankish *~slitan~ (“to split”). The Frankish verb is also the source of English ~slit~. The French verb is thus a borrowing from the Germanic language of the Franks, and the modern ~éclisser~ continues it, with the usual change of the old spelling ~es-~ to ~é-~.

In French, the verb means “to splint,” and it goes with the noun ~éclisse~, a splint or thin sliver of wood. German ~schleißen~ (“to split, to strip”) belongs to the same Germanic family as ~slit~. French thus received this root from the Franks, while English kept its own cognate of the same ancient verb.
en.éclore:
The sources differ on how ~éclore~ was built. French Wiktionary treats it as ~clore~ with the prefix ~é-~ (“out”). English Wiktionary says it is inherited from Old French ~esclore~, from Vulgar Latin *~exclaudere~, a remodelling of Latin ~exclūdere~, and calls it a doublet of the learned borrowing ~exclure~. Either way the pieces are the same: ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~claudere~ (“to shut”), the Latin source of ~clore~. English Wiktionary adds that Piedmontese ~s-ciòde~ is comparable.

So ~éclore~ and ~exclure~ are two French outcomes of one Latin compound, and their meanings drifted far apart: ~exclure~ stayed with the idea of shutting out, while ~éclore~ came to mean emerging into the open, as an egg hatches or a flower opens. Its past participle ~éclos~ is the usual form in that use. The root ~claudere~ also gave ~clos~, ~clôture~, ~conclure~ and ~enclore~.
en.écluser: Formed from ~écluse~ (“lock”) with the verbal ending ~-er~, so that it means to pass a boat through a lock. It also has the slang sense of drinking, to knock back. ~Écluse~ comes from Old French ~escluse~, from Late Latin ~exclūsa aqua~ (“water cut off by a barrier”), a participle used as a noun, from the classical Latin verb ~exclūdere~ (“to shut out, to cut off”).
en.écobuer:
From Old French ~gobuis~ (“bare earth”), itself from ~gobe~ (“clod of earth”). French Wiktionary links ~gobe~ to a Gaulish word *~gobbo~ (“mouth”), so the chain would run from Gaulish through Old French to a verb that names the work of stripping turf from a field and burning it. The way ~gobuis~ became the modern ~écobuer~, with its initial ~é-~, is not explained in the source.

The Gaulish link rests on a hint, not a certainty, and the shift from “mouth” to “clod” is not spelled out. Still, the same Gaulish word is said to underlie several familiar French words, to which French Wiktionary points: ~gober~, ~gobet~ and ~gobelet~. The first is the verb for swallowing greedily, and the last is the small cup that English borrowed as ~goblet~. In that family, ~écobuer~ stands out for belonging to farming: it describes clearing land by lifting the roots and surface earth and burning them.
en.écoconcevoir: This verb is a back-formation in spirit: it is a verbal counterpart to the noun ~écoconception~, built on the pattern of the pair ~conception~ and ~concevoir~, in the engineers' sense of creating a new product. French Wiktionary refers readers to the prefix ~éco-~ (from “ecology”, here “environment”) and to the verb ~concevoir~. The result is a recent coinage of environmental and industrial vocabulary: to design a product with its environmental impact in mind.
en.éconduire:
From Old French ~escondire~ (“to refuse”), reshaped under the influence of ~conduire~ (“to lead”) and so spelled and conjugated as if it meant “to lead out”. ~Escondire~ itself comes from a Vulgar Latin *~excondīcere~, built on Latin ~ex-~ (“out of”) and ~condīcere~ (“to agree upon, to arrange”). The Latin verb is ~con-~ (“together”) plus ~dīcere~ (“to say”). The French verb is thus a false cousin of ~conduire~: its look comes from that verb, its sense from a Latin word of speaking.

In modern French ~éconduire~ means to turn away a caller or a suitor, politely but firmly, as in ~éconduire~ un importun. Because it was reshaped on ~conduire~, it is conjugated exactly like it, ~j'éconduis~ and ~nous éconduisons~. The Latin ~dīcere~ underlies ~dire~, ~dédire~ and ~contredire~, while ~conduire~ comes from Latin ~condūcere~. The two roots met in this one verb, which is why its spelling points to leading but its meaning, refusing, comes from speaking.
en.économiser:
~économiser~ was derived in the eighteenth century from ~économie~ with the suffix ~-iser~. The noun had entered French by 1370, as ~yconomie~, in Nicole Oresme's translation of Aristotle's Ethics, meaning the good management of a household — from Latin ~oeconomia~, from Greek ~οἰκονομία~ (~oikonomía~), built on ~οἰκονόμος~ (~oikonómos~, “household steward”): ~οἶκος~ (~oîkos~, “house”) plus ~νέμω~ (~némō~, “to deal out, to manage, to pasture”). Each half has a deep root: ~οἶκος~ goes back to PIE *~wóyḱos~ (“settlement”), cognate with Latin ~vīcus~ (“village”) — whence French ~voisin~, through ~vīcīnus~ — while ~νέμω~ goes back to *~nem-~ (“to allot, to take”), cognate with German ~nehmen~ (“to take”).

For three centuries ~économie~ meant household stewardship rather than national statistics; the sense “thrift, sparing expenditure” is attested only in 1665, in La Rochefoucauld, and it was on that sense that ~économiser~ was minted — the Académie's dictionary traces it to the eighteenth century under the spelling ~œconomiser~, “to administer with thrift.” The family fanned out meanwhile: ~économe~, ~économique~, ~économiste~. And the root ~νέμω~ hides in plain sight elsewhere in French — in the ~-nomie~ of ~astronomie~, ~autonomie~ and ~gastronomie~ (through ~νόμος~, “that which is allotted: usage, law”), and in ~nomade~ (through ~νομάς~, “roaming for pasture,” ~νέμω~ in its herdsman's sense). An economist and a nomad share a root: each, etymologically, manages how resources are dealt out — one over a ledger, the other over grazing land.
en.écoper: Formed from the noun ~écope~ (a scoop for bailing) plus ~-er~, so the core sense is to bail water out of a boat. The noun comes from Frankish *~skôpa~, a word related to Dutch ~schop~ (“spade”), German ~Schippe~ and English ~scoop~, all cognates. The informal sense, to get or take a punishment or a blow, is listed as a further meaning of the verb; the sources give no account of how it arose.
en.écorcer: ~Écorcer~ (“to strip the bark from”) is formed from ~écorce~ (“bark”) with the verb ending ~-er~, and it continues Old French ~escorcier~. The noun ~écorce~ comes from Latin ~scortea~, the feminine of ~scorteus~ (“made of skin or leather”), so bark was named as a kind of hide on the tree. Italian ~scorza~ is a cognate. The verb is distantly related to ~écorcher~ (“to skin”), another word for taking off an outer covering.
en.écorcher: Inherited from Old French ~escorchier~, itself from Late Latin ~excorticāre~, built from ~ex-~ (“off, out of”) and ~cortex~ (“bark, rind”). The Latin verb thus meant, in its parts, to strip off the bark. French also borrowed the learned form ~décortiquer~ from the same family, and Catalan ~escorxar~ is a parallel descendant. The verb ~écorcer~ is a distant relative. The Latin parts are ~ex-~ and ~cortex~.
en.écorner: Formed from ~corne~ (“horn”) with the prefix ~é-~ (“removal”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so ~écorner~ is literally “to take the horns off” and, more broadly, to chip a corner or an edge, as of a book or a piece of furniture. The base ~corne~ comes from Old French, from Vulgar Latin *~corna~, which was the Latin plural ~cornua~ of ~cornū~ taken for a feminine singular. The same ~cornū~ gave Italian ~corno~.
en.écornifler: ~Écornifler~ has no neat base-plus-suffix analysis. French Wiktionary calls it an irregular and jocular derivation from ~écorner~, itself built on ~corne~ (“horn, corner”). The same verb existed in Picard as ~écornifler~ and in Occitan as ~escorniflar~, and the sixteenth century also knew the variants ~escornicher~ and ~escornizer~. The playful ending, which does not follow any regular pattern, fits a word that came to mean cadging a meal or importuning others.
en.écosser: Formed from ~cosse~ (“pod, husk”) with the prefix ~é-~, marking removal, and the verbal ending ~-er~: to shell peas is to take them out of their pods. The origin of ~cosse~ itself is debated. The usual account derives it from Late Latin *~coccia~, from Latin ~cochlea~ (“snail, shell”), perhaps crossed with ~coccum~. Littré preferred a Germanic source, compared with Flemish ~schosse~ and German ~Schote~. One French entry even reverses the direction, deriving the verb from Old French ~escosser~ (“to shake out, to strip”), from Latin ~excutere~, and treating ~cosse~ as a back-formation.
en.écouler:
Formed from ~couler~ (“to flow, to run”) with the prefix ~é-~ (from Latin ~ex-~, “out of”), so literally “to flow out, to run off.” The base ~couler~ comes from Latin ~cōlāre~ (“to strain, to filter”), derived from ~cōlum~ (“sieve, strainer, colander”) — flowing liquid was first what a sieve let pass. (This ~cōlō~ “to strain” is distinct from the homonym ~colō~ “to cultivate.”) Italian ~colare~ and Spanish ~colar~ descend from the same straining verb.

The prefix ~ex-~ adds the idea of outward, away: water that ~écoule~ drains off, time that ~s'écoule~ slips away, money that ~s'écoule~ vanishes, a crowd that ~s'écoule~ disperses. By a vivid commercial turn the verb came to mean “to sell off, to clear stock” — goods that pour out the shop door as steadily as water through a strainer. From the same root the language keeps ~écoulement~ (“flow, drainage”), ~découler~ (“to ensue, to flow from”), and, back at the source, ~couloir~ (“corridor,” originally a strainer or channel) and colis is not akin — but ~percolateur~ and ~colature~ are.
en.écourter: On the surface the verb is ~é-~ + ~court~ + ~-er~, but English Wiktionary traces it as inherited from Old French ~escurter~, from Late Latin ~excurtāre~, from Latin ~curtāre~. The adjective ~court~ (“short”) comes from Latin ~curtus~ (“cut short, truncated”). The prefix ~é-~ comes from Old French ~es-~, from Latin ~ex-~ (“out of, away from”), which fits the idea of cutting length away. The verb means to make something shorter, whether a visit, a speech or a docked tail.
en.écouter:
From Middle and Old French ~escouter~ (also ~ascouter~), from Vulgar Latin *~escultāre~, a reshaping of Latin ~auscultāre~ (“to listen attentively, to give ear to”). The Latin verb is built on ~aus-~, the old stem of ~auris~ (“ear”), joined to a second element from the Proto-Indo-European root *~ḱlew-~ (“to hear”) — so the word is, transparently, “to ear-hear.” Cognates run across Romance: Italian ~ascoltare~, Spanish ~escuchar~, Romanian ~asculta~, and the Picard form ~acouter~, which kept the original initial vowel that standard French dropped.

The first vowel had a turbulent history: the classical ~au-~ weakened, the ~-l-~ vocalized, and ~escouter~ eventually smoothed into ~écouter~, the circumflex marking a vanished ~s~. A surprising side-branch reached English: in Old French an ~escoute~ was a person posted to listen and keep watch, and that noun, borrowed across the Channel, became English ~scout~. From the same Latin source French preserves the learned doublet ~ausculter~ — the physician's verb for listening to the chest through a stethoscope — beside the everyday ~écouter~. The root ~auris~ also surfaces in ~auriculaire~ (the little finger, small enough to fit the ear) and ~oreille~ itself, and the verb yields ~écouteur~ (earpiece, headphone) and ~écoute~ (a listening watch, or telephone tapping).
en.écouvillonner: Formed from ~écouvillon~ (a brush or swab used for cleaning) and the verb ending ~-er~, so the verb means “to clean with an ~écouvillon~.” Its earliest recorded sense, in 1611, was to clean a piece of artillery, and the Académie still gives “écouvillonner un canon” as its model example. By 1680 it was also used for cleaning an oven, and from 1930 it is recorded in surgery.
en.écrabouiller: French Wiktionary derives this expressive verb from the older form ~escarbouiller~, which is the only step the sources give. The modern verb means to squash or crush something flat, usually in a colloquial register. The earlier spelling with ~es-~ shows the usual Old French pattern, where an ~es-~ at the start of a word later became ~é-~ in modern French.
en.écraser:
Attested from around 1560 and borrowed, with the prefix ~é-~, from Middle English ~crasen~ (“to break, shatter,” source of modern ~craze~), which is itself of imitative origin — by one account from Old Norse *~krasa~ (“to shatter”). Sources mark the Scandinavian source as probable rather than certain. Through that English root, ~écraser~ is a cousin of English ~crash~, ~crush~, and ~craze~.

The word is one of the rarer cases of French borrowing a verb from English (most traffic ran the other way). Its sense is forceful and total: not merely to break but to flatten, squash, obliterate. French built a whole crushing vocabulary on it: ~écrasement~, ~écraseur~, ~écrasant~ (“crushing,” of a defeat or the heat), and the vivid ~écraser comme un ver~ (“to crush like a worm”). The colloquial ~en écraser~ even means “to sleep like a log.” From an imitative Norse-tinged English word for shattering, French forged its strongest verb for grinding a thing to nothing.
en.écrier:
The origin is debated. English Wiktionary derives it from Old French ~escrier~ (“to scream, cry out”), itself a partial blend: in part ~es-~ (“out”) + ~crier~ (“to cry, shout”), and in part Frankish *~skrīan~ (“to yell, call out”), from Proto-Germanic *~skrīhaną~ (“to cry out”), from a Proto-Indo-European root given as *~(s)kerey-~ (“to scream, caw”). French Wiktionary is more hesitant: it calls the origin uncertain, suggests the verb may be a variant of ~écriser~ or ~égriser~, and mentions the simpler analysis ~é-~ + ~crier~.

Whatever its exact descent, the verb has long had a vivid sense: to burst out in a loud cry, usually from emotion. Today it is used almost only reflexively, in ~s'écrier~, to introduce an exclamation (« s'écria-t-il »), which is why it is a staple of narrative prose. The evidence is mixed, so it is safest to say that a native prefix-plus-verb formation and a Germanic contribution have both been proposed. Related French words include ~crier~, ~cri~ and ~récrier~.
en.écrire:
From Middle French ~escrire~, from Old French ~escrivre~ (reshaped to ~escrire~ by analogy), from Latin ~scribere~ (“to write”), the infinitive of ~scribo~. ~scribere~ originally meant “to scratch, to incise,” and descends from Proto-Indo-European *~(s)kreybʰ-~ (“to scratch, to carve”), an extension of the root *~(s)ker-~ (“to cut”). Latin ~scribere~ is cognate with Ancient Greek ~skariphâsthai~ (“to scratch an outline”). Notably, it is not related to Greek ~gráphō~ (“to write”), which comes from a different root, *~gerbʰ-~, nor to English ~write~, from Proto-Germanic *~wrītaną~ — three unrelated words all born from the act of scratching marks on a surface.

The shift from scratching to writing reflects the ancient technology of the wax tablet and the stylus: to write was to scratch letters into wax or stone. That buried image survives in the modern French family, all built on the ~scrib-~ / ~script-~ stem: ~écrire~, ~écriture~, ~écrivain~, ~décrire~, ~inscrire~, ~prescrire~, ~souscrire~, ~manuscrit~, and ~scribe~. The doublet ~écrire~ (inherited, popular) beside ~scribe~ (learned, borrowed) shows the same Latin verb arriving in French by two different roads.
en.écrivailler: A French derivative of ~écrire~ (“to write”), built with the suffix ~-ailler~, which gives a verb a scornful tone. The TLFi notes that it follows the stem of ~écrivain~ (“writer”) rather than that of the verb, and Littré calls it a pejorative form of ~écrire~. It is attested from 1611, when Cotgrave recorded the participle ~escrivaillé~. The verb means to write a lot, quickly and badly, said of an author who turns out mediocre pages in haste.
en.écrivasser: Derived from ~écrire~ (“to write”) with the suffix ~-asse~ (verbal ~-asser~), which forms pejorative verbs meaning to do something badly or in quantity: ~écrivasser~ is to write a lot, and badly. The suffix is French and dates from the fifteenth century. ~Écrire~ comes from Latin ~scribere~, which originally meant “to scratch, to incise,” and is the source of the whole ~scrib-~ / ~script-~ family.
en.écrouer: Formed from the noun ~écrou~ (“prison register”) plus ~-er~, so “to enter on the jail register,” hence “to imprison.” This ~écrou~ is not the ~écrou~ of a bolt, which French Wiktionary traces separately to Latin ~scrōfa~ (“sow”). The register sense comes from Old French ~escroe~ (“strip of parchment”), borrowed from Frankish *~skrōda~ (“cut piece”), and is attested from 1499. English ~escrow~ and ~scroll~ are cognates, and English Wiktionary notes Middle French ~escrouer~ as the verb's direct source.
en.écrouir: From Walloon ~crou~ (“raw”), the Walloon counterpart of French ~cru~. The sources do not say how the sense of raw led to hardening metal, so that link is left open. The verb is used of metal worked cold so as to harden it.
en.écrouler: Formed in French from the prefix ~é-~ (from Latin ~ex-~, “out, off”) and ~crouler~ (“to give way, to sink”), as in Old French ~acroler~. The verb was first transitive, with the sense of bringing something down, in the early thirteenth century. Modern French uses it almost only in the reflexive form ~s'écrouler~, which means to collapse. The ~é-~ adds the idea of falling completely apart. It is used of walls and buildings, and of hopes, businesses and people who give way under strain.
en.écroûter: Formed from the noun ~croûte~ (“crust”) with the prefix ~é-~, which marks removal, and the verb ending ~-er~: to strip off the crust. ~Croûte~ comes from Middle French ~crouste~ and Old French ~croste~, from Latin ~crusta~ (“hard outer covering”). That in turn goes back to the Proto-Indo-European adjective *~krustós~ (“hardened”), from the root *~krews-~ (“to form a crust, begin to freeze”).
en.écrémer: Formed with the prefix ~é-~ (“out of, away from”), from Latin ~ex-~, and the noun ~crème~, plus ~-er~: “to take the cream off,” or “to skim.” French Wiktionary gives ~crémer~ as the base, and English Wiktionary gives ~crème~ + ~-er~. Either way it is the cream verb, not the other ~crémer~, a learned verb from Latin ~cremāre~ (“to burn”) that has nothing to do with it.
en.écrêter: Formed in French from ~crête~ (“crest”) with the prefix ~é-~ and the ending ~-er~, so “to take off the crest” of something, hence to clip a peak. The noun comes from Latin ~crista~ (“crest, plume”). The prefix ~é-~ descends from Old French ~es-~ and Latin ~ex-~ (“out of, away from”), here with the sense of removal. Together with ~-er~, which makes the whole a verb, it makes ~écrêter~ a verb of cutting off the top.
en.écuisser: ~Écuisser~ is built on ~cuisse~ (“thigh,” from Latin ~coxa~) with the prefix ~é-~ and the verb ending ~-er~. Its first sense was “to cut off the thighs,” found in the Roman de Renart, dated to about 1179 by the TLFi, and in a text of about 1210. Forestry later took the verb: the TLFi records it in 1571 for splitting a tree trunk, and notes a related sense “branch, fork” from about 1400.
en.écumer: ~Écumer~ is a denominal verb from ~écume~ (Old French ~escumer~). It has two opposite senses: to produce foam, and to skim foam off. French Wiktionary compares ~peupler~ and ~plumer~, which show the same split. The noun ~écume~ comes from Frankish *~skūm~ (“foam”), from Proto-Germanic *~skūmaz~, and is a cognate of English ~scum~ and German ~Schaum~. The ~c~ of ~écume~ rules out Latin ~spuma~ as its source, though English Wiktionary notes a possible influence of that word.
en.écurer: This verb is formed from ~curer~ with the prefix ~é-~, and goes back to Old French ~escurer~. English Wiktionary offers an alternative: a hypothetical Latin ~excurō~. Either way the base is ~curer~, from Latin ~cūrāre~ (“to take care of”), which comes from the noun ~cūra~ (“care”). The prefix ~é-~ conveys separation, so the verb means to clean something thoroughly by removing what soils it. The family is large: ~cure~, ~curé~, ~curieux~, ~sécurité~ and ~récurer~ (“to scour”) all come from ~cūra~.
en.écussonner: ~Écussonner~ is formed from the noun ~écusson~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. ~Écusson~ was earlier ~escusson~, from Old French ~escuchon~ and ~escusson~. French Wiktionary derives it from ~écu~ (“shield”) with the suffix ~-on~ and an added ~s~. An ~écusson~ is a small shield, and by extension a small shield-shaped piece. In grafting, ~écussonner~ is to graft a tree by inserting a bud cut with a sliver of bark, a technique called shield budding.
en.écœurer: Formed from the noun ~cœur~ with the prefix ~é-~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Middle French ~coeur~, from Old French ~cuer~, from Latin ~cor~ (genitive ~cordis~), which meant “heart” and also “stomach.” It is related to English ~heart~, German ~Herz~ and Greek ~kardía~. The prefix ~é-~ comes from Old French ~es-~, from Latin ~ex-~ (“out of, away from”). The verb therefore means to deprive of ~cœur~, and it has the sense “to nauseate, to disgust.” French still says ~avoir mal au cœur~ for feeling queasy, a reminder of the old stomach sense of ~cor~.
en.édenter: ~Édenter~ is formed from the prefix ~é-~ and ~denter~, a verb itself derived from ~dent~ (“tooth”), which comes from Latin ~dens~. The prefix ~é-~ (Old French ~es-~, from Latin ~ex-~, “out of, away from”) carries the sense of removal here, so the verb means “to take the teeth out of,” that is, to break or remove teeth.
en.édicter: ~Édicter~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~ēdictāre~, a frequentative of ~ēdīcere~ (“to proclaim, to declare”). French Wiktionary adds that it was taken over to serve as the verb of the noun ~édit~, which comes from the same Latin family. The Latin verb is built on the prefix ~ē-~ (“out”) and ~dīcere~ (“to say”), so the picture is of speaking a rule out loud, with authority. French uses ~édicter~ for a government or an authority that lays down a law, a rule or a penalty, and the sense stays firmly official. English ~edict~ is a cousin from the same Latin source, and ~dire~, ~dicter~ and ~dictature~ belong to the same ~dīcere~ family.
en.édifier:
French ~édifier~ is inherited from Middle French ~edifier~, from Old French ~edifier~, which was borrowed from Latin ~aedificāre~ (“to build, to erect, to establish”). The Latin verb is a compound of ~aedēs~ (“building”) and ~-ficō~ (“to make”), so it meant “to make a building”. English Wiktionary adds a rare cousin, Zarphatic ~eigier~, a Judeo-French language of medieval northern France.

The same compound gave the noun ~édifice~, a learned borrowing from Latin ~aedificium~, and ~édification~. English ~edify~ and ~edifice~ are relatives, borrowed through French, and the English verb ~edify~ still carries the moral sense that ~édifier~ also has. In French the verb covers both the literal act of building, now literary, and the figurative sense of improving someone morally or strengthening someone's faith. The ending ~-fier~ is the one in ~unifier~ and ~clarifier~, from Latin ~facere~ (“to make”).
en.éditer:
From Latin ~ēdere~ (supine ~ēditum~, “to give out, put forth, publish”), a compound of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~dare~ (“to give”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *~deh₃-~ (“to give”) — the same root that gives Latin ~dōnum~ (“gift”) and ~dōs~ (“dowry”), and, in French, ~donner~ and ~don~. To ~ēdere~ was literally to “give out” a thing into the world; applied to a book or text, it meant to bring it forth before the public.

French took its bookish vocabulary first from the noun side — ~édition~ (from ~ēditiō~, “a bringing forth”) and ~éditeur~ — and the verb ~éditer~ arose later, around 1784, partly built back from those nouns. The same Latin family yielded ~édit~ (a royal edict, something “given out” by authority) and ~éditorial~. A second, homonymous ~éditer~ entered French in the twentieth century as a computing term, borrowed from English ~edit~; English had clipped that verb from ~editor~, itself ultimately the same ~ēdere~. So the two French ~éditer~ verbs — publishing a book and editing a file — are long-separated descendants of one Latin root meaning “to give out.”
en.éditionner: Formed from the noun ~édition~ with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Latin ~editio~ (“publication”), derived from the verb ~edere~ (“to put out, to publish”).
