The French verb is a technical term of the book trade: to ~éditionner~ a copy is to mark it with the number of its printing.
en.édulcorer:
French borrowed ~édulcorer~ from Medieval Latin ~edulcorare~. According to French Wiktionary, that verb was itself a crossing of two others, ~dulcorare~ (“to sweeten”) and ~edulcare~ (“to make sweet”), and all three were built on Latin ~dulcis~ (“sweet”). English Wiktionary gives only the Medieval Latin source, with no crossing. Latin ~dulcis~ has well-known descendants in the Romance languages, among them Italian ~dolce~ and Spanish ~dulce~.

The literal sense, as the dictionary gloss shows, is to sweeten, especially a medicine, and the verb is also used figuratively for toning something down by removing its harshness, as when a text or a truth is made more palatable. The family of ~dulcis~ is well represented in French, in words such as ~doux~, ~douceur~, ~adoucir~, and ~doucereux~, as well as the learned ~édulcorant~ (“sweetener”).
en.éduquer:
A learned borrowing from Latin ~ēducāre~ (“to rear, to bring up, to train”), first attested in French in 1385. ~ēducāre~ belongs to the family of ~dūcere~ (“to lead”), but its exact formation is disputed: the CNRTL and the French tradition describe it as a frequentative of ~ēdūcere~ (~ex-~ + ~dūcere~, “to lead out”), while other analyses derive it instead from the noun ~dux~ (“leader”). The two accounts differ in morphology and land on the same root, the Proto-Indo-European *~dewk-~ (“to pull, to lead”), which also gives, through Germanic, English ~tow~ and German ~ziehen~. In Latin the verb was used as readily of rearing animals and raising plants as of bringing up children, a breadth the French verb never inherited. Spanish ~educar~, Italian ~educare~ and English ~educate~ take up the same Latin verb independently.

The striking thing about ~éduquer~ is how long French resisted it. The everyday verb for raising children was ~élever~, literally to raise up, and lexicographers treated the Latinate newcomer as an affectation. Voltaire mocked the fashion, remarking that people were beginning to ~éduquer~ children instead of ~élever~ them; Féraud disapproved, and as late as the nineteenth century Littré observed that the word appeared in none of the major dictionaries of his day. It climbed all the same: the Académie’s 1842 supplement admitted ~bien éduqué~ and ~mal éduqué~, and the verb is now entirely ordinary. Its Latin relatives arrived earlier and more easily — ~éducation~ and ~éducateur~ were accepted well before the verb they seem to belong to, so for a long stretch French had the nouns without a respectable verb to match. The wider ~dūcere~ family runs through a large share of the modern vocabulary: ~conduire~, ~produire~, ~réduire~, ~duc~, ~conduit~ and ~introduire~.
en.éfaufiler: A derivative of ~faufiler~ (“to baste,” to sew with long temporary stitches) with the prefix ~é-~, first recorded in 1701 in Furetière's dictionary. Where ~faufiler~ puts threads in, ~éfaufiler~ takes them out: it means to undo the weave of a fabric by pulling out its threads, as in “éfaufiler un ruban,” and the verb is also used reflexively of cloth that frays.
en.égailler:
The TLFi traces ~égailler~ (“to scatter, to disperse”) probably to a Vulgar Latin verb *~aegualiare~, an unattested form built on Latin ~aequalis~ (“equal”) and meaning “to make equal.” The sense of scattering would then come from spreading something out evenly. The earliest attestation, in 1155 in Wace's Brut, has the form ~eguaillied~ and means “levelled”: the poet says that ditches and walls were flattened.

The sense “to scatter” follows in 1474, in the accounts of King René, and the reflexive “to spread out, to disperse” appears in 1829 in Balzac's Chouans. The word belongs to the dialects of the West, particularly the Vendée, where it described the manoeuvre of the insurgents who scattered rather than fight a pitched battle. If the Latin origin holds, ~égailler~ shares its root ~aequalis~ with ~égal~, ~égaler~ and ~égalité~.
en.égaler: Formed from the adjective ~égal~ and the verb-forming ending ~-er~. The adjective was reshaped in Old French on the model of Latin ~aequālis~ (“even, level, equal”), from ~aequus~ (“level, fair”), replacing older popular forms such as ~evel~. Old Occitan ~egal~ may have been the route by which it came. The verb means to make equal, or to be equal to: one ~égale~ a record, a rival, a performance. The same Latin ~aequus~ lies behind ~équité~, ~équation~, ~adéquat~ and ~équilibre~. The ending ~-er~ makes the adjective a first-conjugation verb.
en.égaliser: Formed in French from the adjective ~égal~ and the suffix ~-iser~, in the sense “to make equal.” French Wiktionary dates the reflexive ~soi equaliser~ (“to make oneself equal to”) to the middle of the fifteenth century. ~Égal~ was recast on the model of Latin ~aequālis~, replacing popular Old French forms such as ~evel~ and ~oel~. English Wiktionary adds that Old Occitan ~egal~ may be the even likelier immediate source.
en.égarer:
The verb comes from Old French ~esgarer~ (“to lose one's way; to be troubled or worried”), through Middle French ~égarer~. English Wiktionary analyzes the Old French as the prefix ~es-~, the ancestor of modern ~é-~, joined to a verb of Frankish origin, from *~warōn~ (“to heed, to pay attention to”). French Wiktionary gives the same analysis, ~es-~ plus ~garer~. The Frankish root belongs to the Germanic family of watching and guarding: German ~wahren~ (“to preserve, to keep”) and English ~wary~ come from the same stock. Frankish, the language of the Franks who conquered Roman Gaul, left French many such words, in particular those of guarding, war and sheltering.

The story of the verb is a shift from losing one's way to losing an object. Old French ~esgarer~ described someone who wandered off course or whose mind was disturbed, and modern French keeps this in ~s'égarer~ (“to go astray”) and in ~égaré~ (“lost, bewildered”), while ~égarement~ names a lapse of judgment or a delusion. The transitive ~égarer~ then came to mean “to mislay”, as in losing one's keys. The base ~garer~ went in the opposite direction, toward safekeeping: it means “to park” a vehicle, and it is also the source of ~gare~ (“station”). So ~égarer~ and ~garer~ are, in a way, opposites built on one Frankish root.
en.égayer: ~Égayer~ is formed from ~gai~ (“merry, cheerful”) with the prefix ~é-~ (from Latin ~ex-~) and the verbal ending ~-er~, in the sense of making someone or something merry; English Wiktionary treats it as a parasynthetic of that kind. The origin of ~gai~ itself is debated. By one account, Old French ~gai~ came through Old Occitan from a Germanic word, such as Old High German ~gāhi~ (“sudden, impetuous”), related to German ~jäh~; by another, proposed by some scholars, from Latin ~vagus~ (“wandering”). Italian ~gaio~ and English ~gay~ are cognates.
en.égorger:
First attested around 1450, ~égorger~ is a French formation: the prefix ~é-~ (from Latin ~ex-~, “out”) on the noun ~gorge~ (“throat”), the compound meaning something like to bring out through the throat. ~gorge~ comes from popular Latin ~gurga~, a variant of classical ~gurges~ (“whirlpool, gulf, abyss”) — the throat was named after the gaping, swallowing hole it resembles, not the reverse. ~gurges~ is tentatively traced to the Proto-Indo-European root *~gʷerh₃-~ (“to devour”), the root behind ~vorāre~, although en.Wiktionary cautions that both the sound correspondence and the morphology are unclear. Sources compare Sanskrit ~gargara~ (“whirlpool”) and Ancient Greek ~górgura~; and Old French ~gort~ (“deep pool”), surviving dialectally as ~gour~, continues the Latin accusative directly. Italian ~gorgo~ continues the Latin noun, and English ~gorge~ and ~regurgitate~ are borrowings from the same stock.

~gorge~ meant the inside of the neck by the early twelfth century, and French built a whole vocabulary on it: ~engorger~, ~dégorger~, ~gorgée~, and the falconers’ ~gorge~, the meal of a bird of prey. ~égorger~ began, and remains, brutally literal — to cut the throat of an animal or a person — and widened to slaughtering and massacring. Its figurative turn is recorded by Furetière in 1690: to ~égorger~ a customer is to ruin him, to charge him a murderous price. That commercial cruelty echoes an older expression on the same noun, ~rendre gorge~ (1598), being forced to give back what one had swallowed. The geographical sense of ~gorge~, a narrow pass between mountains, is later (1675) and was borrowed into English as the ravine ~gorge~. Dictionaries also link the noun to an imitative ~garg-~ group of throat words, among them ~gargariser~ and ~gargouille~, though that connection is presented as a family resemblance rather than a strict line of descent.
en.égosiller: Formed in French from ~gosier~ (“throat”) with the prefix ~é-~ and the suffix ~-iller~. Old French ~esgosiller~ meant “to cut the throat,” and the modern reflexive ~s'égosiller~, “to shout oneself hoarse,” came later. The noun ~gosier~ comes from Old French ~geuse~ and ~josier~, from Late Latin ~geusiae~ (“the sides of the throat”), borrowed from Gaulish. Welsh ~gewai~ (“glutton”) is compared. The prefix ~é-~ is from Latin ~ex-~ and marks removal.
en.égoutter: Formed in French from the prefix ~é-~ and the verb ~goutter~. The prefix is from Old French ~es-~, from Latin ~ex-~ (“out of, away from”), and here marks removal, so ~égoutter~ is to take the drops off, to drain. The base ~goutter~ is formed on the noun ~goutte~ (“drop”), which comes through Old French ~gote~ from Latin ~gutta~. Do not confuse ~goutter~ with ~goûter~ (“to taste”), which comes from Latin ~gustāre~.
en.égrainer: ~Égrainer~ is a parasynthetic verb: the prefix ~é-~ (“out of, away from,” from Latin ~ex-~) and the ending ~-er~ were added together to the noun ~grain~. It means “to take the grains out of,” hence “to shell, to pod.” The noun ~grain~ comes from Latin ~granum~ (“grain”), from the Proto-Indo-European form *~ǵr̥h₂nóm~, according to English Wiktionary.
en.égrapper: Formed in French from ~grappe~ (“cluster”) with the prefix ~é-~, which expresses removal, and the ending ~-er~: to strip fruit from its stem. The noun ~grappe~ comes from Old French ~grape~ or ~crape~ (“hook”), from Frankish *~krappo~ (“hook”), a name given to the bunch for its hooked shape. Middle Dutch ~krappe~ and German ~Krapfen~ are cognates.
en.égratigner: ~Égratigner~ comes from Old French ~esgratigner~, a verb tied to ~gratter~ (“to scratch, to scrape”), which English Wiktionary gives as its base. The Old French form began with the prefix ~es-~, which became ~é-~ in modern French. The sense is to scratch lightly, enough to graze the skin without cutting deep. It is used literally for a scratch or graze, and figuratively for a barbed remark that leaves a mark on someone's reputation. A ~égratignure~ is the resulting scratch, and the same ~gratter~ gives ~grattoir~ (“scraper”) and ~gratte-ciel~ (“skyscraper”).
en.égravillonner: Built on ~gravillon~, “fine gravel,” with the privative prefix ~é-~, which marks removal, and the verb ending ~-er~. The French source cites the Petit Robert for this analysis. The verb thus means literally to take the fine gravel or earth away, and it is glossed as clearing soil from around a tree. The prefix ~é-~ comes from Old French ~es-~, from Latin ~ex-~ (“out of, away from”), and the ending ~-er~ goes back to Latin ~-are~.
en.égrener: ~Égrener~ comes from Old French ~esgrener~, built on ~grain~ with the prefix ~é-~ (from Old French ~es-~, Latin ~ex-~, “out of, away from”) and the verb ending ~-er~. The prefix expresses removal, so the verb means to take the grains off or out of something, to shell it. The noun ~grain~ comes from Latin ~grānum~, which also gave Italian ~grano~ and Spanish ~grano~.
en.égriser: This verb is borrowed from Dutch ~gruizen~ (“to crush”), with the prefix ~é-~ added in French. The sense “to grind a diamond” is a craft term. The Dutch origin is the only one the French source gives. The prefix ~é-~ expresses separation and thoroughness here, and has no further history that the sources record.
en.égruger: Formed from ~gruger~ with the prefix ~é-~. The TLFi records it in 1556, as ~esgruger~ in Saliat's translation of Herodotus, in the sense of reducing to powder. In 1617 d'Aubigné used it of hemp. Littré reads the prefix as ~es-~, the older form of ~é-~. Today the verb means to crush something, such as salt or sugar, into coarse powder in an ~égrugeoir~ (a mortar), and in textiles to comb hemp or flax so as to strip off the seeds.
en.égueuler: Formed from the noun ~gueule~ (“mouth, muzzle”) with the prefix ~é-~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The base ~gueule~ comes from Latin ~gula~ (“throat”). The verb deals with the mouth or opening of an object: to chip or deform it.
en.éjaculer:
French ~éjaculer~ is borrowed from Latin ~ēiaculārī~ (“to hurl out”), a deponent verb of Classical Latin. It was first attested only in isolated use in the sixteenth century, with the meaning “to throw.” The word reappeared in 1835, in the sixth edition of the Dictionnaire de l'Académie française, with its physiological sense. The Latin verb is generally analyzed as ~ex-~ (“out”) plus ~iaculārī~ (“to throw”).

The Latin base ~iaculārī~ comes from ~iaculum~ (“javelin, dart”), a missile that is thrown, so the verb belongs to the vocabulary of throwing and shooting. French ~éjaculer~ thus kept for a long time the general sense of throwing before narrowing to the physiological sense that the Académie recorded in 1835. The learned noun ~éjaculation~ belongs to the same family. The word is a learned medical term, not a worn-down inherited one, and it shows how a verb of throwing can narrow to a single bodily process.
en.éjecter:
French ~éjecter~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~ēiectāre~. French Wiktionary and English Wiktionary agree on the Latin source, though English Wiktionary gives it as ~ēiectō~. The Latin verb is a frequentative of ~ēicere~ (“to throw out”), built from ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~iacere~ (“to throw”), so ~éjecter~ is literally “to throw out repeatedly or forcefully.” English ~eject~ is the same borrowing.

Because ~éjecter~ was taken from written Latin, it kept the shape of its source and did not pass through Old French. The root ~iacere~ is productive in learned French, and the same stem appears, with different prefixes, in ~injecter~, ~projectile~, ~objet~ and ~sujet~, as well as in the noun ~éjection~. The everyday French verb for throwing, ~jeter~, belongs to the same family by way of a related Latin verb, but it is an inherited word and followed another path.
en.éjointer: Formed from the verb ~jointer~ with the prefix ~é-~ (from Latin ~ex-~, “out of, away from”), which often marks separation or removal. The base ~jointer~ is itself built on the noun ~joint~ (“joint”), which comes from the verb ~joindre~. The sense here is “to clip a bird's wing,” and the French source gives no further history of that sense.
en.élaborer:
Borrowed learnedly from Latin ~elaborare~ (“to work out, to take pains over, to produce by effort”), a compound of the prefix ~ex-~ (“out, thoroughly”) and the verb ~laborare~ (“to work, to toil”), from the noun ~labor~ (“work, toil, hardship”). The same ~labor~ underlies French ~labeur~ and ~labourer~ (“to plough”) — the farmer's toil — and was borrowed into English as ~labor~ / ~labour~. Romance kept the learned verb in Italian ~elaborare~ and Spanish ~elaborar~.

The force of the prefix ~ex-~ is “to the finish”: to ~elaborare~ was to work something out fully, to bring it to completion through effort. French ~élaborer~ preserves this exactly — one ~élaborer~ a plan, a theory, a strategy, or a document, building it up carefully piece by piece. Physiology borrowed it too: an organ is said to ~élaborer~ a secretion, working raw material into a finished product. The everyday English ~elaborate~ shares the ancestor but has drifted toward “add detail.” From ~labor~ the French family includes ~laboratoire~ — literally a “place for working” — along with ~collaborer~ (“to work with”) and ~laborieux~ (“laborious, painstaking”).
en.élaguer:
The origin of ~élaguer~ is not settled. French Wiktionary follows an etymology given by Grandgagnage and approved by Diez, which it calls very probable: the prefix ~é-~ plus Old High German ~lah~ (“incision in trees”), supported by regional forms such as Walloon ~liguer~, Berrichon ~alayer~ and Norman ~éliguer~. English Wiktionary agrees only that the word is probably of Germanic origin, and compares Old Norse ~laga~ (“to prepare”).

On the French account, the root is a noun for a cut made in trees. The older form ~elarguer~, used by Olivier de Serres, is either a different word or a distortion of ~élaguer~ through the influence of ~large~. Today ~élaguer~ means “to prune” trees and shrubs and, figuratively, to cut superfluous material from a text or a budget.
en.élancer: Formed in French from the prefix ~é-~ and the verb ~lancer~. Here ~é-~ carries the idea of moving out or forth, so ~élancer~ is to hurl something forward, and the reflexive ~s'élancer~ is to hurl oneself, to dash ahead. The base ~lancer~ comes from Old French ~lancier~ and Late Latin ~lanceāre~ (“to wield a lance”), from ~lancea~ (“light spear”), a word the Romans probably borrowed from a Celtic or Iberian source. The same image of a sudden thrust gave the noun ~élan~ (“momentum, surge”) and ~élancement~, a sharp, shooting pain.
en.élargir:
French ~élargir~ comes from Middle French ~eslargir~, formed from the prefix ~es-~ (from Latin ~ex-~, “out”) and the adjective ~large~ (“wide, broad”), with the inchoative ending ~-ir~. ~Large~ descends from Latin ~largus~ (“abundant, copious, generous”). The deeper origin of ~largus~ is disputed: one account links it to a root meaning “fat, grease,” which de Vaan finds problematic, doubting the long vowel is original; an alternative derives it by metathesis from *~dl̥h₁gʰós~. We give the chain only as far as ~largus~, which is secure. Through Old French ~large~ it is the source of English ~large~ and ~largesse~, alongside Italian and Spanish ~largo~.

The literal sense is “to make broad,” but ~élargir~ long carried a vivid legal meaning: “to release from prison,” to give a prisoner the wide world again. One could say the wrongly jailed man was ~élargi~ — set at liberty. Modern French keeps the spatial and figurative senses (to widen a road, to broaden a debate) and the noun ~élargissement~, used both for an enlargement and, still, for a release.
en.électrifier: ~Électrifier~ is formed from ~électrique~ plus the suffix ~-ifier~ (from Latin ~-ficāre~, “to make”), and it is probably a calque of English ~electrify~, attested from 1745. The adjective ~électrique~ comes from Latin ~electricus~, derived from ~electrum~ (“amber”), a word coined in 1600 by the English physician William Gilbert, who studied the force that rubbed amber attracts. The verb therefore means to make electric, then to equip with electricity.
en.électriser: ~Électriser~ is formed from the adjective ~électrique~ with the verb suffix ~-iser~, in the sense “to make A.” The adjective is a learned borrowing from Latin ~electricus~, derived from ~electrum~ (“amber”) with the suffix ~-icus~. The Latin form is credited to the English physician William Gilbert, who coined it in 1600. Amber was the first substance known to attract light objects once rubbed, hence the name. To ~électriser~ is therefore to charge something with electricity, and by extension to excite someone, since the verb also works figuratively.
en.électrocuter: Borrowed from English ~electrocute~, which is equivalent to a blend of ~électro-~ (“electric”) and ~exécuter~ (“to execute”). The English word was formed on the model of ~execute~, so the original idea was to put to death by electric current. French uses ~électrocuter~ for killing or seriously injuring someone with an electric shock, and the reflexive ~s'électrocuter~ for accidentally receiving one. The noun ~électrocution~ comes from the same source.
en.électrolyser: Formed from ~électrolyse~ with the verbal ending ~-er~: to subject a substance to electrolysis, that is, to decompose it with an electric current. French ~électrolyse~ was borrowed from English ~electrolysis~, itself built from the prefix ~électro-~ and the suffix ~-lyse~. The verb follows the usual pattern of French verbs coined from scientific nouns.
en.élever:
From Latin ~elevāre~ (“to lift up, to raise”), ~e-~ (a reduced form of ~ex-~, “out, up”) + ~levāre~ (“to lift, to make light”). ~Levāre~ is a verb formed on the adjective ~levis~ (“light, not heavy”), from PIE *~h₁lengʷʰ-~ (“light in weight”) — the same root, through Germanic, that gives English ~light~ (not heavy). To raise was, at root, to make something rise by relieving its weight. Through Old French ~lever~, ~levāre~ gave English ~lever~, ~levy~, and ~levee~; Italian ~elevare~ and Spanish ~elevar~ are direct cognates of ~élever~.

French split the simple verb ~lever~ (“to lift”) from the prefixed ~élever~, which specialized toward raising in degree, rank, and especially upbringing. One ~élève~ a wall or a price (raises it), one ~élève~ children (brings them up), and one ~élève~ livestock (rears it) — hence ~élevage~ (“animal husbandry”) and ~éleveur~ (“breeder”). The pupil one brings up educationally is, fittingly, an ~élève~ (“student”). The reflexive ~s'élever~ means “to rise” — a tower, a sum, or a protest. The ~levis~/~levāre~ family is enormous in French: ~lever~, ~levée~, ~élever~, ~élévation~, ~élève~, ~soulever~ (“to lift up”), ~enlever~ (“to take away, to lift off”), ~prélever~ (“to levy, to take a sample”), and ~léger~ (“light”) itself.
en.élider:
From Latin ~ēlīdere~ (“to strike out, to crush”), formed from the prefix ~ē-~ (“out”) and ~laedere~ (“to strike, to hurt”). Both Wiktionaries give the Latin verb directly as the source. In French the verb was taken over in the grammatical sense, to suppress a final vowel before the next word, which is what happens to ~le~ in ~l'ami~. English ~elide~ and Spanish ~elidir~ come from the same Latin verb.

The noun ~élision~ is the learned companion that names the act, and it is the more common of the two in everyday grammar. The root ~laedere~ is the source of ~léser~ (“to wrong, to harm”) and ~lésion~, and also of ~collision~, which comes from ~collīdere~ (“to strike together”). The same Latin root, with a different prefix, thus gives both the harm of a ~lésion~ and the cutting-off of a vowel. Modern French uses ~élider~ mostly in linguistics and in the reading of verse, where it describes how a mute ~e~ is suppressed before a vowel.
en.élimer: Formed from the prefix ~é-~ and ~lime~ (“file”), with the verbal ending ~-er~. It means to wear a fabric thin through use until the threads show, as if it had been rubbed down with a file. The prefix ~é-~ comes from Latin ~ex-~ (“out”). The past participle ~élimé~ is the form most often met, said of cloth worn to the thread.
en.éliminer:
French ~éliminer~ is a learned borrowing of Latin ~eliminare~ (“to thrust out of doors, to expel”). Its anatomy is vivid: the prefix ~ex-~ (“out of”) plus ~limen~ (“threshold, doorsill”) — literally “to put across the threshold,” to show the door. ~Limen~ is probably bound up with Latin ~limes~ (“boundary, border-path”), the word behind ~limite~, and with ~limus~ (“sideways, oblique”); its ultimate Indo-European root is not securely established. Through ~eliminare~ and ~limen~, French is cousin to English ~eliminate~ and to the modern buzzword ~liminal~ (“on the threshold”).

The original image is almost domestic — sweeping something out over the doorsill, out of the house. From that literal expulsion ~éliminer~ broadened into the abstract “to remove, to do away with”: a candidate is ~éliminé~ from a contest, a hypothesis from an argument, an unknown from an equation. Physiology kept the bodily sense — the kidneys ~éliminent~ waste. Sport made it dramatic, in the ~éliminatoires~ (“qualifying rounds”) that knock teams out. The threshold itself, ~limen~, lurks beneath a small but pointed family: ~préliminaire~ (“preliminary,” what stands before the threshold), ~liminaire~ (an opening note, “on the doorsill”), and, through its sibling ~limes~, the whole field of ~limite~ and ~limiter~.
en.élinguer: Formed from the noun ~élingue~ (“sling, lifting rope”) with the verb ending ~-er~, in the sense “to provide with N”: to secure a load with a sling. The noun comes from Old French ~eslingue~ (“sling,” then “rope”), from Frankish *~slinga~, a Germanic word related to English ~sling~ and German ~schlingen~. English Wiktionary traces the Germanic root to Proto-Germanic *~slingwaną~ (“to twist”), from a Proto-Indo-European *~slenk~ (“to turn, twist”).
en.élire:
From Old French ~eslire~, ~eslire~, from Latin ~eligere~ (“to pick out, to choose”), from ~ex-~ (“out”) + ~legere~ (“to gather, to pick, to read”). ~legere~ descends from Proto-Indo-European *~leǵ-~ (“to gather, to collect”), the same root behind Ancient Greek ~légō~ (“I gather, I say”) and the ~-logy~ of countless sciences. Romance cognates include Italian ~eleggere~ and Spanish ~elegir~.

The literal idea is to “gather out” the best from a heap — to single out by careful picking. Old French ~eslire~ covered ordinary choosing as well as formal election, and the past participle ~élu~ still means both “elected” and, in religious language, “chosen, one of the elect.” The plain sense “to choose” narrowed over time toward the political and ceremonial “to elect,” leaving everyday choosing to ~choisir~. A trace of the wider meaning lingers in the formal ~élire domicile~ (“to take up legal residence”). The fertile ~legere~ gave French a whole library of words: ~lire~, ~lecture~, ~élire~'s cousins ~sélectionner~ and ~collectionner~, plus ~légende~, ~collège~, and ~intelligent~ (“choosing between”).
en.éloigner:
From Middle French ~esloigner~, from Old French ~esloignier~ (“to move far off, to send away”), a derivative of ~loing~ (“far”) — modern ~loin~ — with the prefix ~es-~ (from Latin ~ex-~). The adverb ~loin~ descends from Latin ~longē~ (“far, at a distance”), the adverbial form of the adjective ~longus~ (“long, distant”), traced to Proto-Indo-European *~dlongʰos~ (“long”). The Italian ~lontano~ and Spanish ~lejos~ share the same Latin ancestry, while English ~long~ springs from a related branch of the same root.

The core idea is spatial: to ~éloigner~ something is to push it toward the ~loin~, the far horizon. Old French built the verb on the comparative notion of putting distance between things, and the ~es-~ prefix added the sense of separation or removal. Over time the verb gained figurative range — one can ~éloigner~ a suspicion, a danger, or a friend grown cold — so that distance became emotional and abstract as readily as physical. The reflexive ~s'éloigner~ (“to move away, to drift apart”) is now among its commonest uses. From the same Latin ~longus~ French inherited a wide family, including ~long~, ~longueur~, ~allonger~, ~prolonger~, and ~longtemps~, all turning on the measure of length or distance.
en.élonger: Derived from the adjective ~long~ with the verb ending ~-er~, with the sense of stretching something out to its full length, as when a cable is laid out along a line. ~Long~ comes from Old French ~lonc~ (attested in 1080), from Latin ~longus~ (“lasting a long time, long”). The Latin word also lies behind French ~chaise longue~, which German borrowed as ~Chaiselongue~.
en.élucider:
~Élucider~ is borrowed from Latin ~ēlūcidāre~, “to make clear, to illuminate,” formed from ~ē-~ (“out, thoroughly”) and the adjective ~lūcidus~ (“bright, clear”). English Wiktionary adds that, by surface analysis, French speakers can also read it as ~é-~ + ~lucide~ + ~-er~. Latin ~lūcidus~ comes from the verb ~lūcēre~ (“to shine”) and the noun ~lūx~ (“light”). English ~elucidate~ comes from the same Latin verb.

French now uses ~élucider~ for bringing a mystery, a murder, a text or a cause into the clear, and the noun ~élucidation~ follows it. The same Latin family is behind ~lucide~, ~luire~, ~luisant~, ~translucide~ and ~lueur~. The adjective ~lucide~ shows the two senses side by side: a ~lucide~ mind is “clear” in the way a bright room is clear.
en.élucubrer:
~Élucubrer~ is borrowed from Latin ~ēlūcubrāre~ (“to produce by dint of long vigils, to work assiduously”), which is formed on ~lūcubrum~ (“small light”). The word thus recalls work carried on through sleepless hours by a small light. French Wiktionary adds that Littré listed the verb as a neologism in 1863, in that Latin sense of producing something by long night work.

The modern sense, to produce extravagant reasoning or talk, probably comes from the change of meaning undergone by the noun ~élucubration~, rather than straight from the Latin. The same Latin root gave French the learned ~lucubration~ and English ~lucubrate~ (“to work or write laboriously, especially at night”). The verb has thus drifted from patient, lamplit labor to something closer to raving, which is also what the noun now suggests.
en.éluder:
French ~éluder~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~ēlūdere~, which French Wiktionary glosses as “to dodge, to avoid, to deceive.” The verb joins ~ē-~ (“out”) to ~lūdere~ (“to play”), a Latin verb that also covered play of every kind. English ~elude~ comes from the same Latin source, as do Spanish ~eludir~ and Italian ~eludere~.

The interest of ~éluder~ lies in its family, because ~lūdere~ and its noun ~lūdus~ (“game”) gave French a whole set of learned words: ~illusion~, ~allusion~, ~collusion~, ~prélude~, ~interlude~ and ~ludique~. They share the idea of play, with prefixes giving each its direction. French ~éluder~ itself applies to a question, a difficulty, an obligation or the law, which one avoids without facing it. The sources supplied do not say how the Latin play-sense produced “evade.”
en.éluer:
Borrowed from Latin ~ēluō~ (“to wash away”), whose infinitive is ~ēluere~. It is built from ~ē-~ (“out”) and ~luere~ (“to wash”), so the Latin verb literally means “to wash out.” In French the verb is a learned borrowing, and its main modern use is technical: to elute, that is, to wash a substance out of the material that has held it, as in chromatography.

The Latin root ~luere~ has a large French family. ~Diluer~ (“to dilute”), ~polluer~ (“to pollute”), ~alluvion~ and ~déluge~ all come from compounds of it, and each keeps some trace of washing, flooding or soiling. The learned derivatives of ~éluer~ itself, ~élution~, ~éluant~ and ~éluat~, name the act of washing out, the liquid that does it and what is washed out. English ~elute~ was borrowed from the same Latin verb.
en.élégir: Formed from the word ~lège~ with the verb ending ~-ir~. ~Lège~ was borrowed from Dutch ~leeg~ (“empty”). The verb is a woodworking term, meaning to thin down or lighten a board. Verbs in ~-ir~ built on an adjective often mean “to make or become” what the base says, and this one fits that pattern: to make a piece of wood less heavy, as though emptying it of some of its thickness.
en.émacier:
Borrowed from Latin ~emaciāre~ (“to make lean, to emaciate”), a first-conjugation verb whose ending ~-āre~ became ~-er~ (here spelled ~-ier~ after the vowel). The Latin verb is generally analyzed as ~ex-~ (“out, thoroughly”) + ~macies~ (“leanness”), from the adjective ~macer~ (“thin”). The prefix adds the sense of completeness: someone thoroughly reduced to leanness, not merely thin.

The same Latin adjective ~macer~ gave French ~maigre~ (“thin”), and from it ~maigrir~ (“to lose weight”), so ~émacier~ and ~maigre~ are cousins. English has the same pair of relatives: ~emaciate~ was borrowed from the same Latin verb as ~émacier~, and English ~meager~ comes from ~macer~ by way of Old French ~maigre~. In French the verb is rare and literary; it is met most often as the participle ~émacié~ (“emaciated”), said of a gaunt face or body, and the noun ~émaciation~ names the condition.
en.émailler: Formed from the noun ~émail~ and the verb ending ~-er~. French Wiktionary attests the Old French forms ~esmaillier~ and ~esmailler~, so the verb is old and was built within French on ~esmail~, the ancestor of ~émail~. It means “to coat with enamel,” and by extension “to decorate with bright spots,” as in a meadow enameled with flowers. The sense “to mar” belongs to this figurative family: surfaces dotted or marked with something that stands out.
en.émanciper:
~Émanciper~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~ēmancipāre~. In the standard analysis, the Latin verb combines ~ē-~ (“out of”) with ~mancipium~ (“ownership acquired by taking in hand”), itself from ~manus~ (“hand”) and ~capere~ (“to take”). French shares it with English ~emancipate~ and Italian ~emancipare~, which come from the same Latin verb. Because French borrowed it from Latin rather than inheriting it, the verb kept a learned shape and a learned feel.

In Roman law, ~ēmancipāre~ meant to release a son from his father's legal authority. The modern verb has gone far beyond law and now applies to any release from tutelage or dependence, as in ~s'émanciper~ (“to free oneself”). Its Latin parts live on elsewhere in French: ~manus~ lies behind ~main~ and ~manuel~, ~manuscrit~, and the noun ~émancipation~ is built on the verb itself. The word thus carries in its structure an old image: a hand that lets go.
en.émaner: Learned borrowing from Latin ~ēmānāre~ (“to flow out”), formed from ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~mānāre~ (“to flow”). The Latin sense was literal, of water or a spring running out. French kept the image but made it figurative: something ~émane~ from a source when it proceeds from it, as an order from an authority or a light from a lamp. English ~emanate~ comes from the same Latin verb, and the noun ~émanation~ is its French relative.
en.émarger: A parasynthetic verb: the prefix ~é-~ and the ending ~-er~ were added together to the noun ~marge~ (“margin”). The noun comes from Latin ~margō~ (accusative ~marginem~, “edge”), which English Wiktionary traces to Proto-Indo-European *~mórǵs~. To ~émarger~ was to write on the margin of a document, and the verb's senses all deal with marking or signing there: to annotate, to initial, to sign a register, and by extension to draw one's salary.
en.émasculer:
~Émasculer~ (“to castrate, to emasculate”) is a learned borrowing from Latin ~ēmasculāre~ (“to castrate”), taken over directly rather than inherited, which is why it keeps the Latin shape almost intact. The Latin verb was formed from the prefix ~ē-~ (a form of ~ex-~, “out, away”) and ~masculus~ (“male”), so it meant literally “to take the maleness out of.”

The Latin root ~masculus~, a diminutive of ~mās~ (“male”), has two lines of descent in French. The inherited line gave ~mâle~ by way of Old French ~masle~, while the learned line gave ~masculin~ and ~masculinité~. English borrowed the Latin verb as ~emasculate~. In French, as in English, ~émasculer~ is used for the physical act, but it also serves figuratively for depriving a person, a text or an institution of vigor.
en.émerger:
French ~émerger~ descends from Latin ~emergere~ (“to rise out of, to come forth”), built from the prefix ~e-~ / ~ex-~ (“out of”) and ~mergere~ (“to dip, to plunge, to immerse”). The verb ~mergere~ goes back to Proto-Italic *~mezgō~ and Proto-Indo-European *~mésgeti~, from the root *~mesg-~ (“to plunge, to dip”). Distant cognates surface in Sanskrit ~majjati~ (“dives under”) and Lithuanian ~mazgoti~ (“to wash”). So ~émerger~ is literally the undoing of immersion: to un-plunge, to break back up out of the water.

The core image is hydraulic — a swimmer or a reef rising above the surface — and from there ~émerger~ spread to anything that comes into view or prominence: a truth that emerges, a leader who emerges from the crowd. Its mirror-twin ~immerger~ (~in-~ + ~mergere~, “to plunge in”) keeps the opposite motion, and the two share the noun pair ~émersion~ and ~immersion~. The modern adjective ~émergent~ (“emerging,” as of nations or technologies) and the borrowed urgence-free term ~émergence~ all trace back to this single Latin verb of dipping and surfacing.
en.émeriser: Formed from ~émeri~ (“emery”) and the suffix ~-iser~, which here means “treat with”: to ~émeriser~ is to rub or polish something with emery. The noun ~émeri~ reached French through Old French ~esmeril~ from Italian ~smeriglio~, which goes back to Ancient Greek ~σμερίλιον~, a diminutive of ~σμερί~ (“emery”). The Greek ~σμύρις~ is a related form that also gave Latin ~smyris~. The suffix ~-iser~ itself descends from Late Latin ~-izāre~, which transcribed Greek verbs, and it is still a productive way of building technical verbs.
en.émerveiller: Formed on the noun ~merveille~, with the prefix ~é-~ and the verb ending ~-er~, in the sense of filling someone with wonder. The Old French verb is recorded as ~esmerveillier~ (and as ~esmerveler~ in English Wiktionary), so the formation is old, with ~é-~ the modern form of Old French ~es-~. The noun ~merveille~ comes from Latin ~mirabilia~ (“wondrous things”), the neuter plural of ~mirabilis~, from ~mirari~ (“to wonder at”). To ~émerveiller~ someone is to make them marvel.
en.émettre:
From Latin ~emittere~ (“to send out, let go, produce”), a compound of the prefix ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~mittere~ (“to send, let go”). The base verb ~mittere~ is of debated origin, plausibly traced to a Proto-Italic *~mitō~ and a Proto-Indo-European root meaning “to exchange” or “let go.” It is the same Latin source behind Italian ~emettere~ and Spanish ~emitir~, and behind a swarm of English borrowings in ~-mit~.

The core idea is always a sending-forth, but the object sent has multiplied delightfully. One can ~émettre~ a sound, a light, a banknote, a stamp, a radio signal, an opinion, or a vote — each a thing released into the world. The everyday French verb ~mettre~ (“to put”) descends from the very same ~mittere~, its meaning having drifted from “send” to “place.” The Latin verb is one of the most fertile in French: through it come ~mission~, ~message~, ~admettre~, ~permettre~, ~promettre~, ~soumettre~, and ~remettre~, plus the nouns ~émission~ (a radio or TV broadcast) and ~émetteur~ (“transmitter”). A television program and a postage stamp thus share an ancestor whose single task was simply to let something go.
en.émietter: ~Émietter~ is built from the prefix ~é-~ (“out, away”), the noun ~miette~ (“crumb”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so it means “to break into crumbs.” The noun ~miette~ is ~mie~ plus the diminutive ~-ette~. Once ~mie~ and ~miche~ had come to mean bread in general, French needed a small word for a tiny bit of bread, according to French Wiktionary, and ~miette~ filled the gap.
en.émigrer:
From Latin ~ēmigrāre~, a verb analyzed as ~ex-~ (“out of”) and ~migrāre~ (“to move, to depart”), so it meant to move out of a place. French took it over as a learned word. English ~emigrate~ is the same Latin verb borrowed separately, and both languages use it for leaving one's country to settle elsewhere.

The simple Latin verb ~migrāre~ gave French ~migrer~ and ~migration~, and English ~migrate~ is its cognate. The opposite movement is ~immigrer~, built on the same root with the prefix ~in-~, so the same journey is ~émigrer~ from the point of departure and ~immigrer~ from the point of arrival. The prefix ~ex-~, which became ~é-~ in many French words, is the one that opens the exit.
en.émincer: Formed in French from the prefix ~é-~ and the verb ~mincer~. The prefix ~é-~ comes from Old French ~es-~, from Latin ~ex-~ (“out of”), and here suggests cutting thin pieces off, hence “to slice thinly.” The base ~mincer~ is from Old French ~mincier~, whose origin is disputed. It is often explained as Vulgar Latin *~minūtiāre~ (from Latin ~minūtus~, “small”), but the sound changes do not fit well, since that source should have given ~menuiser~. A Frankish origin, from *~minnistō~ (“smaller”) or *~minnisōn~ (“to make smaller”), looks more likely, and it would link ~mincer~ to English ~mince~.
en.émonder:
~Émonder~ comes from Latin ~ēmundāre~ (“to clean, purify”), a verb built from the prefix ~ē-~ (“out”) and ~mundāre~ (“to clean”), itself from ~mundus~ (“clean”). French Wiktionary traces the forms: ~amonder~ in the Oxford Psalter, ~esmonder~ at the start of the thirteenth century, ~emonder~ in 1350 to 1370, and finally ~émonder~. It also points to the simple verb ~monder~ alongside the prefix.

Modern ~émonder~ means to prune trees and, in a figurative use, to proofread or tidy a text. The Latin ~mundus~ also lies behind ~immonde~ (“filthy, foul”), from Latin ~immundus~ (“unclean”), and ~immondices~ (“refuse”). The simple verb ~monder~ lives on in cookery, where it means to peel almonds or tomatoes. A verb that began as a general word for cleaning thus ended up with two quite specific trades, the gardener's and the editor's.
en.émorfiler: Formed from the noun ~morfil~ with the prefix ~é-~, so it means to remove the ~morfil~, the burr left on a blade after sharpening. The prefix ~é-~ comes from Old French ~es-~, from Latin ~ex-~ (“out of, away from”), and here it marks removal. The origin of ~morfil~ is given in two ways. By one account it is a compound of ~mort~ and ~fil~, a “dead edge.” By the other it was borrowed from Spanish ~marfil~, itself from Arabic ~azm-al-fil~ (“elephant tusk”).
en.émotionner: Formed from the noun ~émotion~ and the verb ending ~-er~, a pattern comparable to ~commotionner~. ~Émotion~ was derived from ~émouvoir~ on the model of Old and Middle French ~motion~ (“movement”), which was borrowed from Latin ~mōtio~, “act of moving, disturbance, shiver.” The verb thus carries the old idea of an inner movement: to ~émotionner~ someone is to stir them, or move them emotionally.
en.émotter: ~Émotter~ is derived from ~motter~ with the prefix ~é-~, which here has the sense of separation: to break up clods of earth. ~Motter~ comes from ~motte~, a word of Frankish origin recorded in Medieval Latin as ~motta~ in the ninth century. The Germanic word probably meant “mud, peat, turf.” The prefix ~é-~ comes from Latin ~ex-~ (“out of”).
en.émousser: Formed in French from the prefix ~é-~ (the Old French ~es-~, from Latin ~ex-~, “out of, away from”), the adjective or noun ~mousse~ and the verb ending ~-er~. The ~mousse~ in question means “blunt, without an edge,” and ~émousser~ is “to take the edge off,” hence “to dull, to blunt,” and by extension to dull a feeling or a sense. The sources offer only proposals for that ~mousse~: it is linked to a Vulgar Latin form *~muttius~ (“truncated”), of Gaulish origin by one account, or to Latin ~mutilus~, so its origin is debated. The ending ~-er~ comes from Latin ~-are~, the usual verb-forming ending.
en.émoustiller: Formed in French from the prefix ~é-~ and ~moustiller~, a verb built on ~moustille~ (“must, new wine”), itself from Old French ~moust~ (“the sparkling of wine”). The earliest recorded form, from 1534, is ~amoustiller~, with ~a-~ in place of ~é-~. The verb is thus tied to the fizz and froth of young wine, and in modern French it means “to excite, to put in high spirits.” The prefix ~é-~ here is an old intensive that adds no clear sense of removal.
en.émouvoir:
~Émouvoir~ is inherited from Middle French ~esmouvoir~ and Old French ~esmovoir~, from Vulgar Latin *~exmovēre~, a reshaping of classical Latin ~ēmovēre~ (“to move out, to remove, to stir up”). Both Latin forms join the prefix ~ex-~ (“out”) to ~movēre~ (“to move”). The Old French ~s~ is a leftover of that ~x~, and it was later dropped, the accent on ~é~ being its trace. Italian ~smuovere~ is a close parallel (“to shift, to dislodge”).

The oldest sense of ~émouvoir~ was physical or political: to set in motion, to stir up, as in stirring up a revolt. That sense lives on in ~émeute~ (“riot”), which comes from the old feminine participle of ~esmovoir~, literally something “set in motion.” The verb then turned inward, so that what is stirred is a person's feelings, and ~émotion~ is a close relative. The same Latin ~movēre~ gives ~mouvoir~, ~mobile~, ~moteur~ and ~promouvoir~. To this day, to be ~ému~ is to be, etymologically, “moved,” as in English.
en.émuler:
~Émuler~ is a learned borrowing from Latin ~aemulor~ (“to rival, to strive to equal”), a verb built on ~aemulus~ (“rival”). It never passed through the everyday speech of Old French, which is why it has the look of a scholar's word rather than a folk one. English ~emulate~ comes from the same Latin verb, so the two languages share an ancestor here.

French dictionaries that list ~émuler~ usually mark it as rare, and for a long time it was little used. It has since enjoyed what French Wiktionary calls a second youth in computing and commerce, under the influence of English ~emulate~: a program or a company can now be said to imitate or match another. The noun ~émule~ (“rival, follower who tries to equal a master”) is the verb's close relative from ~aemulus~, and is much more common in modern French than the verb itself.
en.émulsifier: Formed from ~émulsion~ with the suffix ~-ifier~, which goes back to Latin ~-ficāre~, from ~facere~ (“to make”): to turn into an emulsion. The noun ~émulsion~ is attested from 1560 and is built on the Latin supine ~ēmulsum~ of ~ēmulgēre~ (“to milk out”), the root idea being a milky liquid. French thus took a verb of milking and made a word for blending two liquids that do not mix.
en.émulsionner: ~Émulsionner~ is formed from the noun ~émulsion~ with the verbal ending ~-er~. The noun is dated to 1560 and comes from the Latin stem ~emulsum~, the supine (or participle ~emulsus~) of ~emulgeō~ (“to milk out”). An emulsion was originally a milky liquid, and to ~émulsionner~ is to turn a mixture of liquids that do not blend, such as oil and water, into a smooth, milk-like one.
en.émécher: Formed from ~mécher~ with the prefix ~é-~. The base verb comes from the noun ~mèche~ (“wick”), whose own origin is not firmly settled. The verb has two senses, to trim a candle wick and, colloquially, to make someone tipsy. The sources give no account of how the second sense arose from the first, so none is offered here.
en.énamourer: Formed from ~en-~ + ~amour~ (“love”) + the verb ending ~-er~, “to fill with love.” It is attested from the fifteenth century and is a variant spelling of ~enamourer~. The prefix ~en-~ goes back to Latin ~in-~ (“in, into”) and here has the sense of putting a person into a state; the noun ~amour~ comes from Latin ~amor~.
en.énerver:
~Énerver~ is inherited from Middle French ~enerver~, from Latin ~ēnervāre~ (“to cut the sinews of, to weaken”). The Latin verb joins ~ex-~ (“out, away”) to ~nervus~ (“sinew, tendon, strength”), so the original idea is of taking the strength out of someone. Latin ~nervus~ is usually linked to Greek ~neûron~ (“sinew, nerve”), the source of English ~neuron~. French can also read the verb as ~é-~ + ~nerf~ + ~-er~, a surface analysis that matches its form.

The modern meaning reverses the old one. For a long time ~énerver~ meant to enfeeble, to sap, and that sense is still found in literary French. Later the word ~nerf~ came to evoke the nervous system, and the verb shifted to “to irritate, to make jumpy,” as in ~ça m'énerve~. Reflexively, ~s'énerver~ is “to get worked up.” A verb that once removed the nerves now strains them. The same root appears in ~nerf~, ~nerveux~, ~nervure~ and ~innerver~ (“to supply with nerves”).
en.énoncer:
From Latin ~enuntiāre~ (“to announce, declare, set forth”), from ~ē-~ / ~ex-~ (“out”) plus ~nuntiāre~ (“to report, announce”), a verb derived from ~nuntius~ (“messenger, message”). The origin of ~nuntius~ itself is uncertain and disputed: by one account it was contracted from an obsolete formation on ~novus~ (“new”), but de Vaan rejects this as morphologically unworkable; he tentatively prefers a root *~newH-~ (“to cry, shout”), while others connect a root meaning “to nod, beckon,” and an Etruscan source has even been proposed. Cognate, through ~nuntius~, with English ~announce~, ~pronounce~, and ~denounce~.

The literal sense is “to speak out,” and French ~énoncer~ keeps that clarity: to ~énoncer~ a rule, a principle, or a verdict is to lay it out plainly in words. From the same ~nuntius~ stem French inherited ~annoncer~, ~prononcer~, ~dénoncer~, ~renoncer~, and the nouns ~énoncé~ and ~annonce~. Because the deeper origin of the messenger-word is contested, the vivid image of a herald behind ~énoncer~ is best held lightly — the family is certain, its first root is not.
en.énouer: Formed in French from the verb ~nouer~ (“to tie a knot”) and the prefix ~é-~, which here expresses removal. Where ~nouer~ makes a knot, ~énouer~ takes knots away, in the textile trade by picking the little knots and lumps out of cloth. The base ~nouer~ comes through Old French ~noer~ from Latin ~nōdāre~, built on ~nōdus~ (“knot”), the source of the noun ~nœud~. The prefix ~é-~ descends from Latin ~ex-~ (“out of, away from”), so the verb literally means “to un-knot,” and it shows the same subtractive sense as ~égoutter~ or ~étirer~.
en.énucléer: A learned borrowing from Latin ~ēnucleāre~, “to remove the kernel”, built on the prefix ~ē-~ (“out”) and ~nucleus~ (“kernel, core”). French first used it of taking the stone or kernel out of a fruit, and the word is now best known in medicine, where it means to remove an organ or a tumor whole, as one shells a nut. The same Latin ~nucleus~ gave French ~noyau~ through a different, inherited route, and the learned ~nucléaire~.
en.énumérer: A learned borrowing from Latin ~ēnumerāre~, formed from ~ē-~ (“out”) + ~numerāre~ (“to count”), itself from ~numerus~ (“number”). It means to count off the items one by one. It has a popular twin: ~dénombrer~ (“to count up”) developed by regular French sound change from ~numerāre~, with ~nombre~ as its noun, so the two verbs are cousins of nearly the same meaning. ~Énumérer~ kept the Latin shape closer to the original, as scholarly borrowings do, and French shares the root with ~numéro~ and ~numérique~.
en.épaissir: ~Épaissir~ is formed from the adjective ~épais~ (“thick”) with the verb ending ~-ir~, meaning “to make or become thick”. French Wiktionary traces ~épais~ back to Latin ~spissus~ (“thick, dense”). The verb thus belongs to the group of ~-ir~ verbs built in French on an adjective, like ~grandir~ and ~grossir~, and it can be used both transitively (to thicken a sauce) and intransitively (the fog thickens).
en.épamprer: ~Épamprer~ is a French derivative of ~pampre~ (“vine branch with its leaves”), formed with the privative prefix ~é-~ and the verb ending ~-er~, so it means to strip a vine of its leafy shoots, in order to help the grapes ripen. The TLFi dates the verb to about 1550 and attests the sense of clearing a vine in 1571. ~Pampre~ itself comes from Latin ~pampinus~.
en.épancher:
French ~épancher~ is inherited from Old French ~espancier~, from a Vulgar Latin form *~expandicāre~, itself from Latin ~expandere~ (“to spread out, to open, to unfold”). French Wiktionary analyzes ~expandere~ as ~ex-~ plus ~pandere~ (“to spread”). English ~expand~ is a separate, learned borrowing of the same Latin verb, and French has its own learned relatives in ~expansion~ and ~expansif~.

The Vulgar Latin form is an extended version of the classical verb, built with the suffix seen in ~-icāre~. Through that route, the verb that meant to spread out became one that means to pour out, whether to spurt out or to pour one's heart out. French Wiktionary refers readers to ~épandre~, the other French verb from ~expandere~, which keeps the physical sense of scattering, as in spreading manure over a field. The two verbs thus show one Latin source splitting by sense. The noun ~épanchement~ is used of a heartfelt outpouring and also in medicine, of fluid that has leaked into a body cavity.
en.épandre:
From Latin ~expandere~ (“to expose to the air, to unfold, to spread out”), borrowed into Old French as ~espandre~ and carried on in Middle French. The Latin verb is built on ~pandere~ (“to stretch out, to spread, to lay open”), with the prefix ~ex-~ (“out”) adding the idea of spreading outward. Spanish ~expandir~ and English ~expand~ come from the same Latin verb.

In modern French the verb is the farmer's word for spreading manure or slurry over a field, and it also serves, more literarily, for pouring something out. The noun ~épandage~ names the spreading of fertilizer or treated wastewater on land. The same ~pandere~ family gave French ~expansion~ and ~expansif~, which keep the Latin sense of opening out.
en.épanneler: Formed from ~épanner~ with the suffix ~-eler~, a French verb-forming suffix that, according to the TLFi, descends from Latin ~-illare~ or was built from French noun suffixes, and often marks a small or repeated action. In stonework the verb means to rough-hew a block. The sources give nothing more on the base ~épanner~, so this account stops at the formation itself.
en.épanouir:
From Old French ~espanir~ (earlier French also had ~espanouir~), whose origin is given in two ways. French Wiktionary derives it from Frankish *~spannjan~ (“to stretch”), related to Old French ~espan~ (“span, extent”), English ~span~ and German ~spannen~. English Wiktionary says it is either from Latin ~expandere~ (“to spread out”) or a Germanic loan from that same Frankish verb, itself from Proto-Germanic *~spannō~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~(s)pend-~. The origin is therefore debated between a Latin and a Frankish source, though both point to the idea of stretching or spreading.

The shift from ~espanir~ to ~espanouir~ and then ~épanouir~ is not explained phonetically. French Wiktionary notes that ~évanouir~ underwent the same change. It also relates the Frankish verb to Old French ~espan~ (“span, extent”), with English ~span~ and German ~spannen~. Whichever origin is right, the verb belongs to the idea of stretching and spreading.
en.épargner:
French ~épargner~ goes back to Old French ~esparigner~, ~espargnier~ (attested around 1100 in the Chanson de Roland) and is not Latin at all: it continues Frankish *~sparanjan~ (“to treat with indulgence, to spare”), the verb of the Germanic conquerors of Gaul, akin to Proto-Germanic *~sparōną~. Its kinship is therefore with German ~sparen~ (“to save”) and English ~spare~; Italian ~risparmiare~ was drawn from a sister Germanic form — probably Lombardic *~sparōn~. The word’s entry into Romance was caught in the act: in the eighth-century Reichenau Glosses, a scribe glossed the classical Latin ~non pepercit~ (“he did not spare”) with the new Gallo-Roman word — ~non sparniavit~. Latin’s own verb, ~parcere~, faded from the spoken language of Gaul; French keeps only the learned ~parcimonie~ from that family.

The oldest French sense, the one the Roland shows, is a warrior’s: “to leave alive, not to kill.” From mercy the verb slid toward thrift — to use with measure, then to set aside — and acquired the construction ~épargner quelque chose à quelqu'un~ (“to spare someone something”): a chore, a grief, an unwelcome detail. The development mirrors English ~spare~, which likewise runs from sparing a foe to sparing expense — the two verbs are cousins and kept pace. In modern French the family includes ~épargne~ (“saving, savings”) and ~épargnant~ (“saver”), and the old sense of mercy still surfaces whenever a storm épargne a village. A verb that began by staying the sword now mostly stays spending: the Frankish soldiers’ word hangs, peaceably, over every counter of a ~caisse d'épargne~ — a savings bank.
en.éparpiller:
The verb is attested in Old French as ~esparpeillier~, in the Oxford Psalter, an early Old French text. Its origin is disputed, and French Wiktionary lays out two proposals. One is a Vulgar Latin verb *~disparpaliāre~ (or *~disparpaleāre~), built from Latin ~dispār~ (“unequal”), ~palea~ (“chaff”) and the verb ending ~-āre~. The other starts from Latin ~dispellō~ (“to scatter”) and supposes a development through *~dispallāre~ to *~disparpallāre~, with ~dis-~ expressively altered into ~dispar-~. Neither account is settled, and the origin is best called uncertain.

On the second account, the final shape of the verb was also shaped by ~épars~ (“scattered”), which comes from Latin ~sparsus~. French Wiktionary treats ~rapailler~ (“to gather back together”) as its opposite. Modern French keeps both the literal and the figurative sense. One ~éparpille~ papers, crumbs or leaflets, and in the reflexive ~s'éparpiller~ means to spread oneself too thin, to dissipate one's energy over too many tasks. The family includes ~éparpillement~ (“scattering”) and ~éparpillé~.
en.épater: ~Épater~ is formed from the prefix ~é-~ and a verb ~patter~, itself from ~patte~, the animal's paw or foot; English Wiktionary simply gives ~é-~ + ~patte~ + ~-er~. The prefix ~é-~ goes back to Old French ~es-~ and Latin ~ex-~ (“out of, away from”), and often marks removal. The modern sense, “to amaze, to stagger,” is very far from this base, and the sources do not show how it developed.
en.épaufrer: French Wiktionary explains ~épaufrer~ as a deformation of Old French ~espautrer~, which had the same meaning. The verb means to chip stone, breaking off a small piece at an edge or corner. The sources give no earlier origin for the Old French verb, so the chain stops there.
en.épauler: Not é- + a base: the initial é- belongs to the noun, so ~épauler~ is simply ~épaule~ plus the verb ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Middle French ~espaule~ and Old French ~espalle~, from Late Latin ~spathula~, a diminutive of ~spatha~, a broad straight sword, which also gave French ~épée~. Learned French took the same Latin word again as ~spatule~. The verb first meant “to break or dislocate the shoulder,” especially of an animal (around 1200). By 1404 it had taken the technical sense “to support, to prop,” from which came “to help” and, for a rifle, “to raise it to the shoulder.”
en.épeler:
From Old French ~espeler~, earlier ~espelir~, inherited from Frankish *~spellôn~ (“to tell, to explain”), from Proto-Germanic *~spellōną~. The initial ~é-~ is not a prefix: it comes from Old French ~es-~, and there is no base without it. The verb is a Germanic word among the Romance inheritance, and the same Germanic root lies behind English ~spell~ and Dutch ~spellen~.

The Frankish verb meant “to tell” or “to explain”, whereas French ~épeler~ means to name the letters of a word one by one. The sources give the Germanic starting point but do not describe how the sense changed. English ~spell~ and Dutch ~spellen~ also refer to letters. Modern French uses ~épeler~ for dictating a name or a word letter by letter, as when a person ~épelle~ a surname over the phone. The noun ~épellation~ is the related abstract form.
en.éperonner: ~Éperonner~ comes from Old French ~esperoner~ and is formed from ~éperon~ (“spur”) and the ending ~-er~. The noun ~éperon~ descends from Old French ~esperon~, from Frankish *~sporo~ (also given as *~spurō~). It is related to German ~Sporn~, English ~spur~, Dutch ~spoor~ and Swedish ~sporre~. The verb means to prick a horse with spurs, and by extension to spur someone on or to ram a ship.
en.épeurer: Formed from the noun ~peur~ (“fear”) by parasynthetic derivation: the prefix ~é-~ and the first-conjugation verb ending ~-er~ are added together, since neither ~é-peur~ nor ~peurer~ is the intermediate step. The result means “to frighten, to scare.” The prefix ~é-~ comes from Latin ~ex-~ (“out”) and here has a privative force, as if to take someone out of calm. The noun ~peur~ comes from Latin ~pavor~, which gave French its word for fear.
en.épicer: ~Épicer~ is formed from the noun ~épice~ with the verbal ending ~-er~: to season with spices, or figuratively to add spice to something. The noun ~épice~ is inherited from Old French ~espice~, an early borrowing (12th century) from Latin ~speciēs~, which in Late Latin had come to mean “spice,” “foodstuff,” “commodity” and “drug.” It is therefore a doublet of ~espèce~, the same Latin word taken in again later in its older sense. French Wiktionary also mentions an alternative derivation from Arabic ~abzār~ and rejects it, noting that Spanish ~especia~ points to the Latin source.
en.épier:
From Old French ~espier~, which both Wiktionaries trace to Frankish *~spehōn~ (“to watch closely”), from Proto-Germanic *~spehōną~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~speḱ-~ (“to look”). English Wiktionary adds a Vulgar Latin stage, *~spiāre~, which would explain Italian ~spiare~ and Spanish ~espiar~. The Germanic relatives are German ~spähen~ (“to peer, spy”) and Middle Dutch ~spien~.

The same Old French verb gave French ~espion~ and English ~spy~, so the English word is a loan from the very verb that became ~épier~. The root *~speḱ-~ also underlies Latin ~specere~ (“to look”) and Greek ~skopeîn~ (“to examine”), which means that ~épier~ is a distant cousin of words like ~spectacle~ and ~télescope~. Do not confuse this verb with a homonym ~épier~, “to form ears of grain,” which comes from Latin ~spicāre~. In modern French, ~épier~ keeps its sense of watching someone closely, often in secret.
en.épierrer: Formed from ~pierre~ with the prefix ~é-~ (removal) and a verbal ending: to ~épierrer~ a field is to clear it of stones. The prefix comes from Old French ~es-~, from Latin ~ex-~ (“out of”). The noun ~pierre~ comes through Middle and Old French from Latin ~petra~ (“rock”), itself from Greek ~πέτρα~, which in popular Latin supplanted ~lapis~.
en.épiler: ~Épiler~ (“to remove hair”) is formed from the prefix ~é-~ and the Latin verb ~pilāre~ (“to remove hair”), according to French Wiktionary, which notes that the prefix is redundant here, since ~pilāre~ already means to strip hair. English Wiktionary presents it as Latin ~pilus~ (“hair”) with ~é-~ added. Both accounts point to the same word for hair, ~pilus~, which also gave French ~poil~. French Wiktionary links ~pilāre~ to ~peler~ (“to peel”), a close relative.
en.épiloguer: Formed from the noun ~épilogue~ plus the verb ending ~-er~; the verb means “to nitpick, to go on at length about.” The noun entered Middle French as a learned borrowing from Latin ~epilogus~, itself from Ancient Greek ~epílogos~, made of ~epí~ (“upon, in addition”) and ~lógos~ (“speech”).
en.épincer: Formed from ~pincer~ with the prefix ~é-~, which here suggests removal or working on a surface; the verb is glossed as to shear, crop or chisel. The origin of ~pincer~ is itself uncertain. English Wiktionary says only that it is inherited from Old French ~pincier~, while French Wiktionary proposes an expressive root *~pints~, perhaps from a root ~pic~ (“pointed”) by nasalization. That is a proposal, not a settled account. The prefix ~é-~ goes back to Old French ~es-~, from Latin ~ex-~ (“out of”).
en.épinceter: Formed from ~épincer~ with the suffix ~-eter~, itself ~-et~ plus ~-er~. The base ~épincer~ is ~pincer~ with the prefix ~é-~ (from Old French ~es-~, Latin ~ex-~, “out of”), which here suggests removal or work on a surface. The origin of ~pincer~ is uncertain: French Wiktionary proposes an expressive root *~pints~, perhaps from a root ~pic~ (“pointed”), but that is only a proposal. Verbs in ~-eter~ often mark a small-scale or repeated action, as in ~tacheter~.
en.épiner: ~Épiner~ is formed from ~épine~ (“thorn”) and the verb ending ~-er~, with the meaning “to protect with spikes.” The initial ~é-~ belongs to the noun and is not the removal prefix. ~Épine~ comes from Old French ~espine~, from Latin ~spīna~, itself from Proto-Italic *~speinā~ and the Proto-Indo-European root *~spey-~ (“sharp point”). The ending ~-er~ is the usual way of turning a noun into a verb of providing with it.
en.épingler: Formed from the noun ~épingle~ (“pin”) with the verb ending ~-er~. The noun comes from Old French ~espingle~, and its origin is disputed. Diez derived it from Latin ~spinula~ (“little thorn,” a diminutive of ~spina~, “thorn”) with an intrusive g; English Wiktionary describes a Vulgar Latin form *~spingula~, a cross between Late Latin ~spīnula~ and ~spīcula~. Scheler, struck by that odd g, preferred a Germanic source: ~Spange~ (“clasp”) through a diminutive.
en.épisser: A borrowing from Dutch ~splissen~ (“to splice”), a verb of the rope-worker's trade. The initial ~é-~ is not the French prefix: it is simply the vowel that French places before an initial ~sp-~, so there is no base verb ~pisser~ hiding inside. English ~splice~ comes from the same Dutch verb, which makes ~épisser~ and ~splice~ cousins by borrowing.
en.éployer:
From Middle French ~esployer~ (16th century), analyzed as ~é-~ and ~ployer~, which come respectively from Latin ~ex~ (“out”) and ~plicāre~ (“to fold”). The verb therefore means, literally, to unfold, and it is a doublet of ~expliquer~, which was learned straight from Latin ~explicāre~ (“to unfold, to unroll”). Both are children of the same Latin pair of ~ex-~ and ~plicāre~, one reached through the spoken tradition and one through the learned.

~Éployer~ is used of wings, banners and sails that open wide. The verb ~plicāre~ left a large family in French: ~plier~ and ~ployer~ (“to bend”), ~replier~, ~déployer~, ~employer~, ~impliquer~, ~compliquer~ and ~appliquer~. English borrowed several of them through French, among them ~deploy~, ~display~ and ~employ~. The sense of ~éployer~, to open out what was folded, is thus the opposite of ~plier~, and a close relative of the explanation we call ~expliquer~.
en.éplucher:
From Old French ~espeluchier~, itself derived from ~peluchier~ (“to clean tangled hairs”). That verb goes back to a Late Latin *~pilūcicāre~, an iterative of *~pilūcāre~ (“to pluck, to pull out hairs”), which is a frequentative of Latin ~pilāre~ (“to remove hair”), built on ~pilus~ (“hair”). Relatives in the other Romance languages include Italian ~piluccare~, Catalan ~pellucar~ and Occitan ~pelugar~, the latter meaning “to pluck”.

The two Wiktionaries differ slightly on the prefix. French Wiktionary derives ~espeluchier~ from ~peluchier~ inside Old French, while English Wiktionary projects a Vulgar Latin form *~expiluc(i)cāre~ already carrying the ~ex-~ prefix; it also gives Middle French ~esplucher~ as an intermediate step. The same Latin ~pilus~ is behind ~poil~, ~épiler~ and English ~depilate~.
en.épointer: ~Épointer~ is formed from ~pointe~ (“point, tip”) with the prefix ~é-~, which expresses removal, and the verb ending ~-er~. It means to blunt something by taking off its point. The noun ~pointe~ comes from Late Latin ~puncta~, the feminine of ~punctus~, a participle of Latin ~pungō~ (“to prick”). The verb thus describes the opposite of pricking: removing the very part that was meant to pierce.
en.éponger:
~Éponger~ has two accounts in the sources. French Wiktionary traces it to an older form ~spongier~, attested in 1582, from Latin ~spongiare~, and adds that, seen from the modern language, it can simply be read as ~éponge~ plus the verbal ending ~-er~. English Wiktionary gives only the second analysis. Either way the root is the Latin noun ~spongia~ (“sponge”), a loan from Greek, which also lies behind English ~sponge~ and Spanish ~esponja~.

The sense is the plain one of mopping up liquid, with a sponge or with any absorbent cloth or paper. It also serves in a figurative idiom: ~éponger une dette~ means to absorb or clear a debt. The reflexive ~s'éponger le front~ means to mop one's brow. Other French words from the same Latin noun include ~éponge~ itself and ~spongieux~ (“spongy”), which kept the Latin ~sp-~ that ~éponge~ lost to its added initial vowel.
en.épontiller: Formed from the noun ~épontille~ (a prop used in shipbuilding) with the verb ending ~-er~, so it means to shore up with such props. The TLFi explains ~épontille~ as a borrowing from Italian ~puntello~ or ~pontello~ (“prop”), a derivative of ~punta~ (“point”). It first appears as ~pontille~ in 1642 and as ~espontille~ in 1672, and the form with an initial vowel probably comes from a wrong word division of ~les pontilles~. The change of suffix was probably helped by other nautical words in ~-ille~ such as ~écoutille~ and ~quille~.
en.épouiller: Formed from ~pou~ (“louse”) with the prefix ~é-~, which here marks removal: to take the lice off. The noun comes from Old French ~pouil~, from Late Latin ~peduculus~, an altered form of Latin ~pēdīculus~, a diminutive of ~pēdis~ (“louse”). The modern singular ~pou~ was drawn back from the plural, as happened with ~genou~. The verb thus means to rid a person or an animal of lice.
en.époumoner: A parasynthetic verb: ~é-~ + ~poumon~ (“lung”) + ~-er~, literally “to take the lungs out of” someone or something. It is used almost entirely as the pronominal ~s'époumoner~, “to shout oneself out of breath,” as though one were spending one's lungs. The base ~poumon~ is attested around 1160 in Old French, as ~pulmun~ or ~poumon~, and comes from Latin ~pulmō~ (“lung”). Italian ~polmone~ and Spanish ~pulmón~ are its cognates. Here the prefix ~é-~ carries the sense of removal, with no counterpart verb *~poumonner~ behind it.
en.épouser:
~épouser~ comes from Old French ~espouser~, from Late Latin ~sponsāre~ (“to betroth, to promise in marriage”), a verb built on ~sponsus~, the participle of ~spondēre~ (“to pledge, to promise solemnly”). The PIE root is *~spend-~ (“to perform a rite, to make an offering”), and the religious flavor is no accident: the Greek cognates ~spéndō~ (“I pour a libation”) and ~spondḗ~ (“libation”) show that a solemn promise was originally sealed by an offering to the gods. From the same root English has ~spouse~, ~sponsor~, ~respond~, and ~spontaneous~.

So to marry, in this word's logic, is to be solemnly pledged — the betrothal sealed like a sacred vow. The figurative reach is wide: in French one can ~épouser~ a cause, an idea, or a shape, the verb meaning “to embrace closely, to conform to” — a dress that ~épouse~ the figure. From the family come ~épouse~ and ~époux~ (“wife, husband”), ~épousailles~ (“nuptials”), and the learned doublet ~sponsoriser~, re-borrowed from English. The metrical foot the ~spondée~ (“spondee”) preserves the Greek libation-pouring sense directly: it was the rhythm chanted over the offering. One root for the wedding vow and the poured wine alike.
en.épousseter: ~Épousseter~ is a French formation: the prefix ~é-~ (from Latin ~ex-~, which expresses removal), the stem of ~poussière~ (“dust”) and the suffix ~-eter~. To ~épousseter~ is therefore to take the dust off something. ~Poussière~ itself descends from Latin ~pulvis~ (“dust, powder”), the same source as ~poudre~, so the verb belongs to the same family as the powder that is ground fine and the dust that settles on shelves.
en.époustoufler: The origin of ~époustoufler~ is obscure. French Wiktionary suggests a possible link with ~poussif~ (“wheezy, short of breath”), and English Wiktionary adds the Old French verb ~espousser~ as another possibility. Neither is established. The verb means to amaze or stupefy.
en.époutir: Formed from Old French ~poutie~ (“waste, refuse”) with the privative prefix ~é-~, which expresses removal. To ~époutir~ cloth is therefore to clear away its waste: the specks and knots picked out of a woollen fabric. The prefix ~é-~ comes from Old French ~es-~, from Latin ~ex-~ (“out of, away from”). The base ~poutie~ has not survived in modern French, so the verb is a fossil of a vanished word.
en.épouvanter:
From Old French ~espoenter~, inherited from Vulgar Latin *~expaventāre~, a verb built on ~expavens~, the present participle of Latin ~expavēre~ (“to fear, to dread”). That Latin verb joins ~ex-~, here an intensifier, to ~pavēre~ (“to be afraid”). Its relatives in the other Romance languages all mean “to frighten”: Italian ~spaventare~, Occitan, Catalan, Spanish and Portuguese ~espantar~, and Romanian ~înspăimânta~.

The modern family is easy to see: ~épouvante~ (“terror”), ~épouvantable~ (“dreadful”) and ~épouvantail~ (“scarecrow”, literally a thing that frightens) are all built on the verb. The Latin root ~pavēre~ also produced the noun ~pavor~ (“fear”), the source of French ~peur~. The Old French spelling began with ~es-~, which became ~é-~ in modern French, as in many other words. Spanish ~espantar~ also means “to scare away” as well as “to frighten.”
en.épreindre:
From Middle French ~espraindre~, from Old French ~espreindre~, inherited from Latin ~exprimere~ (“to press out”). The Latin verb is made of ~ex-~ (“out”) and ~premere~ (“to press”). Italian ~esprimere~ comes from the same Latin verb. French thus has it twice: ~épreindre~ is the inherited form, worn down by centuries of speech, and ~exprimer~ is a later learned borrowing of the same Latin word, so the two are doublets.

The literal sense of ~épreindre~ is to squeeze something until its liquid or substance comes out, as in pressing juice from fruit or oil from seeds. Its learned twin ~exprimer~ is the verb that serves for putting a thought into words. The Latin root ~premere~ also lies behind ~presser~ and ~pression~, so ~épreindre~ sits in a large family of words about pressure.
en.éprendre: ~Éprendre~ is formed from the prefix ~é-~ and the verb ~prendre~, as both Wiktionaries say. The prefix comes from Old French ~es-~, from Latin ~ex-~ (“out of”), and here it adds no clear idea of removal. English Wiktionary points to Romanian ~aprinde~ as a comparison. ~Prendre~ comes from Latin ~prēndere~, a contracted form of ~prehendere~ (“to seize”), the verb behind ~apprendre~, ~comprendre~ and ~surprendre~. The verb is used mostly in the reflexive ~s'éprendre de~, “to fall in love with,” that is, to be taken with someone, and its participle ~épris~ (“smitten”) is the commonest form.
en.éprouver:
Derived in Old French from ~prouver~ with the prefix ~es-~ (modern ~é-~), the earliest form ~esprover~ being attested around 1080 with the meaning “to put someone to the test.” The base ~prouver~ comes from Latin ~probāre~ (“to test, to approve, to prove”), from the adjective ~probus~ (“good, upright, fit”). That adjective rests on PIE *~pro-bʰuH-~ (“being out in front, growing forward”), from *~pro-~ (“forward”) and the verbal root *~bʰuH-~ (“to be, to grow”). Cognate descendants of ~probāre~ include Spanish ~probar~, Italian ~provare~ and English ~prove~, while German ~probieren~ was borrowed from the same family.

The semantic arc is one of testing. ~Éprouver~ first meant to assay or try something — to subject it to proof — and that sense survives when one éprouve the strength of a rope or a friendship. From “to put to the trial” grew “to undergo the trial,” and from there the modern, deeply interior sense “to feel, to experience” an emotion or a sensation: one éprouve joy, doubt, or pain. French keeps the testing branch in ~épreuve~ (“trial, ordeal, proof”), ~éprouvant~ (“trying, grueling”) and ~éprouvé~ (“tried and true”).
en.épucer: ~Épucer~ is formed from ~puce~ (“flea”) with the prefix ~é-~ (“out, away”) and the verb ending ~-er~, so it means to remove fleas. The noun ~puce~ is inherited from Old French ~puce~ or ~pulce~, from Latin ~pūlicem~, the accusative of ~pūlex~, which English Wiktionary traces to the Proto-Indo-European root *~plus-~ (“flea”). The Spanish verb ~espulgar~ is a parallel formation.
en.épuiser:
From ~é-~ (Latin ~ex-~, “out, out of”) + ~puiser~ (“to draw water”). The verb ~puiser~ is itself denominal, from ~puits~ (“well”), spelled ~puis~ in Old French, from Latin ~puteus~ (“well, pit, shaft”). The deeper origin of ~puteus~ is debated — perhaps inherited, perhaps a loanword — so we leave it there. Through Germanic, the same Latin ~puteus~ was borrowed early and gave English ~pit~ and German ~Pfütze~ (“puddle”), making them distant relatives of the French well.

The image is vivid and literal: to ~épuiser~ is to draw a well dry, to bail it out bucket by bucket until nothing remains. From that came every modern sense — to ~épuiser~ a stock, a subject, a budget, or one's strength is to drain it to the bottom, and ~épuisé~ describes both a sold-out book and an exhausted person, each pumped empty. The well-drawing family endures in ~puiser~ itself, ~puits~, ~puisard~ (“soakaway, sump”), and the conjunction ~puis~ (“then”), and the “bottomless” sense crystallizes in ~inépuisable~ (“inexhaustible”) — literally a well that can never be drawn dry.
en.épurer: Formed from the prefix ~é-~, the usual French form of Latin ~ex-~ (“out, away”), and ~pur~ (“pure”), which goes back to Latin ~pūrus~. It continues Old French ~espurer~, attested by about 1220 with the senses “to purify” and “to purge.” The idea is to take something out so that what remains is clean: one ~épure~ water, a text, a style or an organization. The word has a technical side and a political one, the latter meaning to remove unwanted members from a group.
en.épépiner: Built from the prefix ~é-~, the noun ~pépin~ (“pip, seed”) and the verb ending ~-er~. The prefix ~é-~, from Latin ~ex-~, expresses removal here: to take the pips out. The noun ~pépin~ is probably an expressive formation on a root *~pep-~ that conveys smallness, according to French Wiktionary. English Wiktionary likewise calls it an expressive creation for smallness and traces it back through Old French ~pepin~.
en.équarrir:
From Old French ~escarrer~, itself from Vulgar Latin *~exquadrāre~ (“to make square”), built on ~ex-~ and Latin ~quadrāre~ (“to square”), which comes from the adjective ~quadrus~ and the noun ~quadra~ (“square”). The sources agree on this chain, though French Wiktionary glosses the Old French verb as “to dislocate.” The sense of the Latin verb is the one that survives in French: to give an object square edges.

The root also gave ~carré~, ~carrer~ and the learned ~quadrature~. English ~square~ is a relative through Old French, and Latin ~quadrus~ is tied to ~quattuor~ (“four”), the source of French ~quatre~. In modern French ~équarrir~ covers two trades: squaring off a block of stone or timber, and quartering the carcass of a slaughtered animal. The person who does the latter is an ~équarrisseur~.
en.équerrer: Formed from ~équerre~ with the verb ending ~-er~: to square off. The noun ~équerre~ is inherited from Old French ~esquarre~ (“square”), from Vulgar Latin *~exquadra~, a noun drawn from the verb *~exquadrāre~, which also gave French ~équarrir~. The root is Latin ~quadrus~ (“square”). The noun is a doublet of ~escadre~ and of English ~square~.
en.équeuter: Formed from the prefix ~é-~ (from Latin ~ex-~, “out of, away from”) and ~queuter~, itself ~queue~ + ~-er~ with a euphonic ~-t-~ between the vowel-final noun and the ending; the verb means to remove the tail, here the stem of a fruit. The noun ~queue~ comes from Old French ~coe~ or ~cue~, from Latin ~cōda~, a variant of ~cauda~ (“tail”). English ~coda~ is its learned doublet. The prefix ~é-~ gives the sense of removal, so ~équeuter~ means “to stem or hull” cherries and the like.
en.équilibrer:
~Équilibrer~ is a denominal verb formed on the noun ~équilibre~, which French took from Latin ~aequilibrium~ (« even balance »). That noun joins ~aequus~ (« equal, level ») and ~libra~ (« balance, scales; pound »): an ~aequilibrium~ is the state in which the two pans of a scale hang level. Italian ~equilibrio~ and Spanish ~equilibrio~ share the borrowing; English ~equilibrium~ and ~equilibrate~ draw on the same Latin compound.

From the very concrete image of balanced scale-pans, the verb ~équilibrer~ generalized to any act of bringing forces, accounts, or proportions into even adjustment — one can ~équilibrer~ a budget, a diet, or a composition. The ~libra~ half left a wide trail in French: ~livre~ (the unit of weight and money), ~livrer~ in its measured sense, ~équilibre~, and ~équilibriste~ (the tightrope-walker who lives by balance). From ~aequus~ come ~égal~, ~équateur~, ~équation~, and ~équité~ — the whole vocabulary of evenness and fairness.
en.équiper:
